This fragrance reminds me of a voluptuous, sexy blonde with a chignon wearing a grey Prada sheath dress and Loubutin shoes. Very pleasant to wear, it is alluring but not obtrusive.

Bendelirious is as different from Putain des Palaces as day is from night. Putain is the woman with striking feminine charms, dressed in a sexy outfit and making an impression. Bendelirious is the woman who does not seek attention. And yet, she is also pampered by luxury. Unlike my predecessor, I can perceive neither cherry, nor sweetness, nor artificiality. The scent initially reminds me of various aloe vera shampoos from the drugstore, so I would categorize it among wellness and care fragrances. I find the champagne very intriguing, and it does not make me dizzy at all; instead, it provides a pleasantly dry taste. Champagne, iris, and violet is a completely new combination for me that practically screams luxury care - very pleasant overall! However, it seems the fragrance wants to be much more. Behind all the care, a shy leather note emerges after half an hour. Hmmm, does it have to be? Admittedly, the leather fits in quite well, but for me, this facet was not necessary. Now the whole thing smells like a mix of beauty salon and leather goods store. The beauty aspect prevails, but the expensive leather handbags on the walls cannot be denied. This is a very interesting scent combination, but I don’t need to have it ;-) P.S: Cherry is present in very small amounts, and it does not smell as one might imagine, more like candied cherries or the small red cherry lollipops: This note lingers in the background, but the scent is neither sweet nor fruity. The candied cherry note becomes quite noticeable in the drydown.

“Welcome to the women's shopping center for synthetic things. Ladies, we greet you with a lab-replicated real champagne with cocktail cherry. This fabulous cherry has a color that Mother Nature could never achieve. Please take a look around our shopping paradise. How about a cherry lollipop? Very sweet, completely sugar-free. Your dentist will be pleased. And since fruit also has a natural sugar content, we have once again brought our special cherry into play. We are particularly proud of our ELDO-typical base scent in our sales rooms. Come, be amazed. You won't find such synthetic things as ours everywhere. To conclude, we would like to gift you a small pouch. It looks like leather, feels like leather, but is made of synthetic - just like everything here. To ensure your little bag smells like leather, we also offer you our fantastic “Smells-almost-like-leather spray” at the exit. You might as well buy the special offer bottle right away: Only today and just for you for €99.99. Please excuse me now, ladies. My mother just called. The sour cherries in our garden are ripe, and she has conjured up one of her delicious homemade cherry pies again.”

huiii I smell a punchy cherry and Boooouuuuum!!! I'm feeling all dizzy...huiuiui...everything is spinning...the world is pink... There are so many cherries. on a cherry hill in summer. A few girls are picking them and making cherry champagne out of it. I think that's why I feel so funny. hic! Then we roll down the flower hill together, drunk. hehehe.

In anticipation of what I call the Eldonage, namely the cold smell of cigarette ash, I am pleasantly surprised by "Bendelirious." At first, I am greeted by a rich creaminess, a violet scent. And then, for a brief moment, a flash of something sharp and piercing shoots up. I think: Oh wow, this is getting intense.

Today I tested two Bond No.9 fragrances. For Fathers and this one here. Unfortunately, this one does not convince me any more than the other. At least, in my opinion, it is not as floral as the other and is recognizable as a men's fragrance. Sweet, but still "for Him". Both NY fragrances are available in 50ml, which means you wouldn't throw as much money out the window as I did with "The Scent of Peace", but as of today, only 77 euros. So how does it smell? It smells like many new releases. Artificial and sweet. I find it very close to DKNY City Men, just three or four times as expensive. I have no idea what an energy accord smells like, but I can't pick anything out from the fragrance pyramid. In hour 5-6, a bit of amber and sandalwood comes through sweetly, but where the leather and patchouli are supposed to be, my nose cannot figure out. Well, anyone looking for something modern and sweet will find better alternatives for less money. It's better to sniff DKNY, it saves the wallet and smells at least as valuable as the "eau de luxe" here.

I love NY for Him: This is yet another one of those Bonds without individuality. It smells very familiar, like many other men's fragrances, without me being able to name a specific one. It strongly reminds me of shower gel, but at the same time is relatively sweet and a bit more floral than the average shower gel from the drugstore. If someone were to gift it to me, I would wear it during the day. I generally like the scent. But I would never buy it myself. The prices are still quite steep.

This fragrance was released in memory of the victims of the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001 Well, someone is really sticking their neck out here. Since Bond fragrances are a thing of their own, I approached this scent with a lot of skepticism. In my last Bond test (Andy Warhol Silver Factory), I gave an enthusiastic 80% (a truly convincing Bond), but here I have to revert to my standard rating for Bond fragrances. It starts off very citrusy, bittersweet with a strange middle note, possibly the aforementioned energy accord - but what on earth is THAT supposed to be???? Red Bull note? Yuck yuck This lasts for a while, but then, about an hour later, it turns into a very sweet, very ordinary note. I've smelled this a hundred times before. A truly primitive, common drugstore concoction. Not much else happens. It stays sweet for a long time, then weakens significantly and fades into a lukewarm, slightly fresh shower gel note. At least it’s not as expensive as the others. According to Bond's website, 100ml costs about € 135.00. But still quite pricey. No, I’m slowly realizing that Bond and I just won’t become friends. Mr. Silver Factory can't save this one either. In memory of the victims of the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001 - I have rarely experienced something more unworthy.

I must confess I know very little about the Sex Pistols as a band, but what intrigued me about this fragrance was the compelling combination of notes, that seems both unusual and very feasible (aldehydes, leather, lemon, pepper, plum - sounds like a party to me!). As a first impression, the opening smells more on the masculine side., but soon enough the perfume develops into something perfectly unisex, unique and very British (as I define it) - it's sharp, cold, a bit dry, provocative, witty and spicy. The black pepper, citrus and leather blend into a very refreshing piquant transparency that lasts throughout the drydown. It has a cynical, defiant air that would fit someone who's cool, detached and a tad caustic - a nonconformist, an outsider. Well targeted and marketed. Apparently, Sex Pistols have a cool personality.

Well, what associations come to mind when you think of a fragrance named 'Sex Pistols'? Probably: rebellion, defiance, tearing down all conventions, wild, chaotic appearances, infernal noise, in short: punk rock! All of this is offered by 'Sex Pistols' from 'Etat libre d’Orange' - not. Instead, the scent seems strangely familiar: a tickling pepper on a woody-amber base, combined with light citrus notes and a good portion of Iso-e-Super (Hermès, I hear you coming...). So far, so good - so boring! But then there’s something else that smells somehow strange - bitter, steely. Could that be the aldehydes ('Electric Aldehydes', as 'Luckyscent' reports), linked to the association of guitar strings? Hmm, who knows. In any case, it smells unpleasant. Yes, and plums ('Prune Jungle Essence') are also supposed to be in there, and leather, and dirty (raunchy!) patchouli, and even heliotrope! Not bad, Mr. Woodpecker - but where? In this thin little water, all sorts of things may be present, but if they are, they are so subtle and elusive that the real Sex Pistols would have swept it away with a single guitar riff. Did perfumer Mathilde Bijaoui even know the band? Only by hearsay, I suspect (and if she did, she understood nothing!). Because this fragrance conveys absolutely nothing of the revolutionary primal force of this legendary combo. Rather, it freezes in a fashionably neat posture, equipped with a pseudo-rebellious attitude - comparable to the many well-styled youngsters in H&M looks, complete with nicely draped keffiyeh and/or Che Guevara T-shirt. Have they ever heard anything about Arafat or Che? Probably just as little as Ms. Bijaoui has heard of the Sex Pistols. Meanwhile, the creators of 'Etat libre d’Orange' see themselves as troublemakers in the perfume industry, celebrating something like olfactory rebellion with rebellious, unconventional creations like 'Rien', 'Vierges et Toreros', and especially 'Sécrétions Magnifiques' (or at least trying to, which I respect). But with this fragrance, they offer pretty much the opposite of what they set out to do, namely polished, bourgeois boredom, instead of hearty punk rock. The in-house 'Rien' would be more fitting if one wanted to approach the Sex Pistols olfactorily, dirty and powerful as it is. But this lukewarm breeze - no thanks. Sid Vicious and Johnny Rotten would probably have given it the finger for that. Rightly so.

"I accidentally sprayed a bit of Eau de Cologne on your tube amplifier!" "Yes, it was still on!" "It smells a bit strange, but there was no short circuit." Fragrance development on my skin: 1. citrusy cologne note 2. floral cologne note 3. warm vacuum tubes with wood around them How do I come up with the vacuum tubes?! My mother used to have an old tape recorder. That thing had to warm up and smelled while operating just like the base of this light little water. When it comes to Sex Pistols and punk, I have no clue, but I had something different in mind here. Otherwise, it's acceptable.

I have to agree with Profumo here, there is neither punk nor rock present! But I don't find this fragrance that bad, rather a bit too tame, perhaps. The bourgeois boredom he mentions hits the nail on the head! The opening can hold its own on my skin for a brief moment against the classic aldehyde bombs, but this state doesn't last long. Whoosh, we are already moving into the heart note, which presents itself as unmotivatedly floral on my skin. After about 45 minutes, a subtly average base accord comes through and then doesn't change anymore. After a good 5 hours, only a faint memory of the Sex Pistols remains on my skin. I somehow expected that the fragrance could have an antagonism to the artificially created myth of the punk band, but not with such a random composition. As a musical style, this fragrance reminds me more of German chanson from such shallow interpreters as Peter Horton, Joana, or if it should be a bit "peppier," Reinhard Mey. Then let me give you a chill and start singing the songs of the shallow protest wave: Good night friends, it's time for me to go, what I still had to say, use jasmine & cigarette and drink one last glass while standing.

The Sex Pistols fundamentally shaped the history of punk. Simple chords, hard drums; in the beginning, for most bands, music was actually a secondary concern. Punk was meant to provoke, polarize, and differentiate. It was a youth culture, a rebellion against conservative society and conservative politics. In the milieu of the Sex Pistols was also designer Vivienne Westwood, who created punk outfits, for example, for rebellious children of wealthy parents ;). But what do I expect from a fragrance named after this band? Dirt, beer, sweat, loudness, rebellion - anything but pleasantness. Unfortunately, I am disappointed. The opening is indeed somewhat fresh, but at the same time also a bit sweet, perhaps a little synthetic-vanilla. I don't perceive any floral notes - in the later development of the fragrance, "Sex Pistols" becomes for me a kind of "Secretions Magnifique"-Light. A somewhat strange note that I associate in my fragrance memory with the holy secretions and find not very pleasant to wear. At the same time, the scent remains incredibly quiet and subtle, very soft, warm, and vanilla-like. Well... there is no real tension building up, I am not shocked, not surprised. But there is also nothing that I find really particularly beautiful. It is certainly not an ordinary fragrance - still, I miss the highs and lows. Those were indeed different times: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ymCHJ_VqZAU

Blanche is a beautiful scent, like fresh, clean laundry hanging outside on the line. The breeze dries it slowly, then I bring it inside the house to enjoy. Like clean sheets, the scent doesn’t last long. It’s very enjoyable while it’s there, but after an hour there’s nothing left on my skin.

Hello everyone, I can't hear it anymore with Bond No9... My dear ladies and gentlemen, Bleecker Street smells like freshly cut grass and that was our chart from Bond No9. NO STOP!!! Let's start over Finally, the time has come and I am on vacation in 2020 at 38 degrees Celsius and have the time and leisure to write to you. As a very new Parfumo user, it is certainly always an interesting first time to write an initial comment for a high-priced niche perfume. If you have feedback, I am always very happy to hear it. But let's get started!! That's why we're here. Appearance Beautiful box!! The design is definitely one of the most beautiful bottles ever created for me as a black and white fan and Bauhaus avant-garde. The round Pizza Hut-like cap on a star-shaped bottle with two swirling colors. Wow. I’m happy to post a few pictures to showcase the elegance but also the sophistication. This combines my America (yes, I have roots there and lived there for a long time) so wonderfully. Pizza Hut cap with star bottle and designer fragrance ;) The cap doesn’t close 100% for me. This (sorry) coolest cap ever is really a shame. The workmanship could be better for the price!! The sprayer is completely okay. Scent I have been experimenting for the last 2 days because I can see that there are only short comments on this so far, and the highly esteemed YouTuber, Monsieur Tuyau, once said he is interested in it. The scent is unisex for me. I also own some other fragrances that resemble it, but I will get to that later. I personally always differentiate by season, skin, and clothing. Soho wants to be like the district, Modern, cool, pleasant, and floral. Soho, for those who haven't seen it, is a trendy neighborhood in New York where the money from Wall Street meets art, youthfulness, freedom, individuality, and new ideas. You can eat and party very well there, but everything under a certain elegance. The owner of Bond No9 dedicates with much love and devotion each neighborhood and each beach as a summer scent, a fragrance of New York, which is certainly a great and modern idea. HOW DOES IT SMELL NOW? Yes, yes, I’m getting to the point for you now Man or woman, mix Prada L'Homme with Maison Francis Kurkdjian Baccarat Rouge 540! Done!! No, not quite, I really experimented with it and came to the following conclusion. The soapy and wonderful cleanliness of a Prada L'Homme paired with orange and blackcurrant. The scent, freshly applied to skin or polo shirt, is fruity and clean. The iris and jasmine quickly take away the femininity of the orange and especially the blackcurrant, and the scent becomes CLEAN. It is well wearable in the office, casual, but also on a date. Just a very beautifully composed perfume for her as well as for him. Sillage I usually smell it very well for 6-8 hours and quite strongly. The woody note that many value here is not perceived by me personally. Many people have approached me about this scent, in private and professional settings, and the feedback has always been very positive. Final 3 lines: Super aesthetic bottle with a clean fruit image. Prada L'Homme is a bit cleaner Baccarat Rouge 540 is minimally more intense But Together they are SOHO Simply a great neighborhood and a damn aesthetic scent.

Above The Waves is, along with You Or Someone Like You, my favorite among the Etat Libre d'Orange fragrances. Here we have this noticeable green note that runs like a red thread throughout, combined with something fresh, zesty, citrusy. I really like it! The fragrance starts off directly with this zesty, citrusy opening. For me, the bergamot combined with the tea notes comes through wonderfully. It gives you such a great, summery feeling right away. I’m into that! For me, this fragrance somehow reminds me of Green Cactus by Phil Julian. However, Green Cactus is noticeably a bit greener and less citrusy. Additionally, the fragrance has a subtly spicy character, mainly coming from the cardamom note. To be honest, I didn’t expect frankincense. I couldn’t detect frankincense while testing. However, I must say that when you read the notes and then concentrate more on the fragrance, you can sense this cardamom-frankincense mix that works wonderfully and harmonizes. The longer the fragrance sits on the skin and moves towards the end, the more you can feel the woody undertones. Otherwise, as I said, the green vibe remains. The zesty, citrusy aspect fades away more and more during the progression and is no longer present at the end. The longevity on my skin is about 6-7 hours. The sillage is moderate. It doesn’t project strongly, except for maybe the first five minutes. Otherwise, it is relatively tame and lays beautifully as a companion on the skin. Above The Waves is also wonderfully unisex wearable!

Like being winked at by a cowboy. A cowboy with a bag of parma violet sweets stuffed in the pocket of his brand new leather jacket. It’s cute, but no rodeo. It promises animalic, but comes nowhere near - it just doesn’t have the sweat and grime. But hold your horses. Maybe you’re just seeing this cowboy on his way into work, and all the roping of bulls and riding of stallions will be on the way later? Nope. The leather is too new, the violet too sweet, and it never really gets beyond those first few notes. You begin to suspect he wasn’t a real cowboy at all but an actor on his way to a Marlborough photoshoot. As the hours go by it gets sweeter still. It becomes fluffier, more friendly. This cowboy never broke a sweat in his life. Later on it hits you. You knew you’d seen that face before. This dude runs the mechanical bull at your local sports bar. Don’t get me wrong, he’s a lot of fun. But what starts out promising bucking broncos ends up all fairground ride. It’s pretty, but too tame for me. And if you’re drawn to a perfume named Rodeo, it may be too tame for you, too.

Several months ago, I picked up a discovery atomizer of Bond No. 9 Dubai - Ruby in hopes that I would finally find a Bond No. 9 scent which is worthy of purchase. I've sampled (and owned) many from this house and none have stood the test of time on my shelves. The short end of the story is that I will be purchasing a full bottle when my discovery atomizer is empty (and no, it is not worthy of the $550 full retail price.) It opens citrusy and tangy then segues almost immediately to a fruity, slightly-candied, tart and rosey scent. There is a delicate touch of animalics present as we approach the spicy-dense-warm-woody-soft-powdery (floral) and addictive dry down. Dubai Ruby is versatile in that it has a fresh component appropriate for warmer weather and it also has some significant depth in the base which many individuals seek in their perfumes in the cooler months. The fragrance is tenacious and will project easily over the course of an 8 hour shift. My rating is an overall 9.5/10

Over the years, I have realized that I am a European: my dream destinations are all here on this continent. So I don't have to fly or drive far to fulfill my travel dreams. And yet there are exceptions: Morocco fascinates me greatly; probably this is related to my cultural preference for "Al Andaluz." One cannot exist without the other here. I would also love to discover the impressive garden of Yves Saint Laurent and the museum dedicated to him. What draws me to Dubai, however, is completely inexplicable. In the late eighties, I had the opportunity to spend a very impressive week there with a "Madame" reader trip. But for the sake of peace, I gave in to my mother's constant insistence and did not book. At that time, we were not the best of friends anyway, and she would have had to look after my apartment for that one week. In hindsight, I am already annoyed; such an opportunity has never come again. So it is no wonder that I become alert and curious when I hear "Dubai" or "the Arab Emirates." "Qatar" by Roja was decanted for me (thank you, dear being!) and now I also received a decant of Bond No 9 "Dubai - Ruby." Oriental-woody: here, immediate scent images arise of an opulent, heavy fragrance that sometimes even suppresses the wearer; often even their surroundings. (How was it, Pluto: "Next to me on the train sits a perfume: It carries a woman!"?) I enjoy these heavy scent explosions, but Sweetsmells' response to my statement made it clear to me that many women find this oriental intensity not so bearable and therefore do not even get to enjoy this magic from 1,001 Nights. Now, "Dubai - Ruby" is quite a light oriental for me: it appears rather shy and remains quiet. But that does not mean that this fragrance creation lacks inner fire: the mentioned rubies shine accordingly bright. Only "Dubai - Ruby" follows its own path. Even the opening: Davana (always gladly used as a fragrance ingredient in skincare products) meets precious saffron aroma, making it somewhat unique. Saffron, always feeling a bit dull, pairs wonderfully with bergamot - neither of which exactly exudes liveliness. Thus, a scent image is created that does not immediately radiate mightily and may therefore not scare some interested parties as much. The heart, with a strong, fully blossomed and sun-kissed queen of roses, accompanied by the herbaceous rose geranium, gains an astonishing touch from the airy, slightly waxy delicacy of magnolias. As in the opening, "Dubai - Ruby" also feels a bit muted here: somewhat spicier than radiant floral is the previous scent progression: pleasantly quiet. But now the Orient makes its presence known: myrrh and cypriol bring rich woody spice. Cypriol, also known as Nargamotho, is derived from a papyrus plant and is thus distantly related to cypress trees. This explains its magnificent wood nuance. I remember reading that among various peoples it is said: "A man who smells of Nargamotho can enchant any woman." (Well, let's leave that: it's not quite that easy!) Back to the scent: spicy wood and seductive amber notes, which are enhanced here with sandalwood, form the golden-brown floating finale of this fragrance composition. For the civet cat has only slinked by once, purring, instead of cozily curling up around this fragrance phial. In my opinion, "Dubai - Ruby" lacks the grand olfactory fireworks that I always associate with the aromas of the Orient. But this makes this fragrance artwork a very wearable "everyday scent," which accompanies faithfully and pleasantly through a long day. I can easily imagine it with a business look, even during client contact. And I am known to be very particular in this regard. How it develops on hot-blooded creatures, I do not know; I can only write about my own experiences and feelings here. It was an interesting experience to get to know one of the Bond No. 9 fragrance creations. I don't quite get along with these flacons; they are a bit cumbersome for me! I love the sleek: flacons that invite you to touch and caress them again and again. So this encounter is a brief but still remarkable one: this oriental is already worth a comment to me!

Uruk Chronicles - an urban fragrance journey, where the ingredients develop closely in succession. It becomes clear that iris and cypriol leave a consistent scent impression, representing the theme of the fragrance and perhaps conveying the urban experience to the wearer? The other fragrance components, in my subjective sense of smell, fade into the background very quickly.

I envy you, well if you have the ability to detect all the notes or at least most of the ones listed here. For the first hour after application all I can make of this is a generic ho-hum-smelling violet fragrance. Okay, maybe not just violet but I'm not sure if I'm also smelling osmanthus and/or gin? A little more after an hour then an amazing woodiness kicks in, the Vetiver and suede join the violet note and turn this scent into something that is so much more than I was expecting after such an ordinary start. The vetiver, suede and violet notes are harmonious and authentic. Where is the tobacco? This one, from Byredo, projects and lasts.

Thanks to a tiny beauty supply store near me that stocks the line, I've had the chance to sample many of the perfumes in the Bond no 9 line at my leisure over the past few years. Having done so, I feel safe saying that I don't like the Bond no 9 line very much. The first perfume I tried from the line was Chinatown. I bought it, love it and wear it to this day. Exceptional perfume.  Since Chinatown, I've tried many others. Silver Factory is interesting (same perfumer, Aurélien Guichard). A portion of the line is innocuous and costs a lot. The bulk smell bad and cost a lot. New York Patchouli falls somewhere between the latter two categories.  Top notes, innocuous. A hint of butterscotch, a large dose of root beer a bit of patchouli.  Heart notes and dry down, a slender helping of Bond-ade, the house note and a heat mirage-like shimmer of cream soda. The Oriental is certainly nothing new in perfumery. The more recent gourmand/Oriental is similarly not untried.  New York Patchouli is nothing new in perfumery, but specifically is nothing innovative in a line composed mostly of gourmand/Orientals. In this case, NY Patch skips the earthy, cold, dusty aspects of patchouli and focus on its upper register, which coincides with Bond's 'house' note. Name aside, Bond-ade is the key note in New York Patchoulu. I've written about Bond-ade in previous Bond reviews. To summarize, it is a woody-amber-based lingering note somewhere between gourmand and resinous. It combines a shrillness with vertigo and is difficult to tolerate in sustained exposure. New York Patchouli has a smaller portion of this note than many others in the line.  It smells more like fruity hairspray than motion-sickness. Christ. I just read that last sentence. While writing it, in my head I was trying to say something nice about this perfume. Apparently I don’t have the wherewithal. I'll leave it at that.

Rose water, aquatic, cocaine, warmth, artificial, cosmetic-like, bright/dull at the same time, very different perceptions depending on mood/weather. For me, more of a scent than a perfume. Notes are hard to identify. Like the city of New York, bright, polished, and dirty, simultaneously penetrating. Affected superficiality, but there’s a lot behind it. Box 1A Bottle design 1A Bottle processing/spray 5 Unclean sticker, poor spray head that constantly falls apart, loose cap... this could be better! Performance is rather strong, strange sillage/projection. It definitely has vibes and aura, a very special one, but it definitely manages to spread a certain mood. Somehow both melancholic and hopeful at the same time. Not a scent that paints pictures, but one that replicates feelings/moods. Many, some quite controversial. For me personally.

Yesterday I was once again at the perfume shop "Stargazing" - because my friend is a patient companion. A royal blue bottle with curved golden writing smiled at me - Patchouli. I am a bit cautious with Patch, as this note was omnipresent in my youth. But my concerns are unfounded, as this bottle releases an extremely friendly bottle spirit - a genie that wants to serve me. He has already granted me one wish - namely that the patchouli develops bright, sweet, and light - without any oiliness or heaviness. Could it be the rose water that stretches it transparently? This blend is certainly successful. The good genie further presents me with enchanting lilac and elegant lily, but so balanced that the scent does not seem overloaded. The smoky cedar is just a hint - and the sweet brightness of the fragrance remains. The scent is as alluring and picturesque as the blue-gold star - which for me embodies the sun in the firmament. A beautiful, atmospheric interpretation of patchouli that makes the fragrance wearable for me both during the day and in the evening.

Well, one can think what they want about Bond No. 9. Here, unfortunately, the perfumes are not highly regarded. Although there are indeed some really beautiful scents, even if they may all be purely synthetic. It can also be artificial - very much in the spirit of New York City. Artificial and artistic - that describes both the city and the fragrances (including regarding the design) quite well. So: what do we have here? One thing is certain: no patchouli! Unfortunately, I will not be championing the brand with this review. At the beginning, you can clearly detect something fresh. The saleswoman also immediately mentioned that the patchouli has been freshly processed. However, there was some uncertainty about what it was processed with. I guessed grapefruit in the store. It certainly couldn't be orange or neroli. That was out of the question. Now I see: it is bergamot. Not much else happens here. Above all, it does not smell like patchouli. I wouldn't know when and where. Initially, I assumed that the fragrance should be given some time. Maybe the patchouli note would come out after a while. Unfortunately, you wait in vain. Because while the top note should have long since faded, according to the fragrance pyramid, the patchouli is supposed to follow in the heart accord. I can't smell that and therefore cannot confirm it. The base doesn't save it either. As already mentioned: not much more is happening here. If you leave the scent under the banner of fresh and floral with slightly bitter accents, it's okay. However, if you write "Patchouli" on it, where none seems to be present, that's rather disappointing. They could have certainly done better. One question still arises for me: does artificial patchouli smell like this? If so, I would like to request that only natural patchouli be used in the future. Or at least nature-identical. Because if they call it patchouli, then I want to smell patchouli. A patchouli as one knows it. Dark, heavy, mystical, perhaps with a slightly bitter cocoa note. But not like this ;-) For me, this fragrance fits into a series of various Bond perfumes that I still do not understand to this day: New York Musk, which does not smell like musk. New York Amber, which does not smell like amber. New York Oud, which does not smell like oud. And now also New York Patchouli, which does not ... well, I think everything has been said about that now. Just test it and move on! :-)

This has been polarizing for the community, but I actually kind of like it. It seems like the daytime version of Sutton place. Like its leather style bottle associates in Lafayette St (The best of them) and Sutton Place, this is not going to be a beast mode scent, but it smells great and the longevity is not half bad on my skin. If someone is close they will really like how you smell. Also like those it has a very designer feel to it... but that isn't necessarily a bad thing. It reminds me of a green take of aqua di gio, only much higher quality. I actually layered it with Sutton Place the other day at work and it worked extremely well. But like most bonds... it just isn't worth the price tag. Bond really need to understand their market segment. The prices are ridiculous for what the scents are. I firmly believe that if Bond No.9 was in the Amouage, Nishane, Mind games price range we would be talking about it as one of the better houses around. They just are way too expensive for what they offer... but the scents themselves are good.

So, got this is as my first Bond No. 9 fragrance after debating between this and Bleecker Street. Ultimately I went with Beekman Place. Here is why: This scent opens fresh, quite green with a basil note. It has that synthetic, thick Bond No.9 identity going for it which you can find in Lafayette Street or Bleecker Street. I am not saying that they smell similar, just the way the scent is built and structured clearly shows a "house signature" which I like. Beekman Place, at least to me, is not your summer high-heat freshie. To me, it's more of a casual grabber for autumn and fall, in my case even winter. It is very easy to wear, very pleasant, detectable with quite good longevity without being too loud. It smells very clean but not in the soapy, Imagination-like cleanness but rather like a clean cool morning in a herbal garden with fresh basil. It is undoubtedly green and does this with a very modern twist and not like those more classic hyper-masculine green scents like Green Irish Tweed. This one is masculine for sure, but much more modern with that thick Bond No. 9 basis. I on purpose limit myself to only 15 fragrances to make things more interesting. It forces me to not just accumulate fragrance after fragrance (way too common in this hobby) but really think, compare, benchmark, rank and then take a decision for one fragrance over another. I say this so you guys understand that Beekman Place won its spot for my winter casual scent against more than 10 competitors. Yeah, I said winter because I own 1 green fragrance in my winter collection to balance all those heavy, sweet fragrances. Bottom line: I can absolutely recommend BP if you are looking for an easy to wear, casual, green-fresh scent with an aromatic base. BUT, please do not pay retail...I paid around 280 for a full bottle versus the 400+ retail price. I hope this helps

We tested Beekmann Place in London. Everyone was thrilled by this exceptionally beautiful fragrance. An elegant fresh atmosphere is created by this scent. The bergamot, pear, and a light hint of basil were very noticeable. The tonka bean is only subtle and not dominant. A truly interesting blend in unusually beautiful air. Unfortunately, the price is also exceptionally high for this fragrance. This scent is only available in London at Selfridge.

Those who headed to Harrods on a quest for flowers but found themselves surrounded by endless belts and bags would do well to mosey on over to Saks, Bond no 9 SAKS FOR HER, to be more precise. I always knew that amongst Bond no 9's dozens of offerings there must be a BWF (big white flower) fragrance, and in SAKS FOR HER I have found it: tuberose, gardenia, and jasmine commingling amicably along with a touch of vanilla-tinged vetiver. I find the tuberose to be dominant in the opening, while gardenia and jasmine become stronger in the still slightly sweet drydown. Although SAKS FOR HER is a good Big White Floral fragrance, with the characteristically superlative sillage and lasting power of that genre, there's nothing really new here. I do like the bottle design of SAKS FOR HER quite a lot, but the contents do not beat out the best of the competition in this cup-runneth-over category. For sweet tuberose, I'll continue to turn to FRACAS and, for less sweet gardenia, to MARC JACOBS.

Skin chemistry is so different - it's just amazing. I got this as a freebie with something else and would never have sought out something that has tuberose and gardenia (both of which are problematic for me) and jasmine (which is sometimes a problem for me). It is SOOOOOO strong even in the vial. All I could think of was rancid acetone (nail polish remover). I didn't even try to put it on, but in my haste to recap the sample, I spilled a dot on myself. Some people are "big white floral" people and some are not. I put myself firmly in the NOT category. If you suspect you might not be a "big white floral" person, the abundance of big white flowers in here makes it a must to avoid. One of my worst perfume experiences. I'd be fascinated to smell it on someone who is good with white florals. (043009)

I've had a bottle of this for like, 10+ years. I smelled it in Saks and put it on my Christmas wishlist. This review is based off of that bottle, so time is a factor here (I see the reviews of this are from 2012). The sweetness has definitely come out more. The white floral is still there obviously but I just get creamy sweetness that's not childish. Nose to the bottle there is no alcoholic/acetone scent, just white floral sweetness. I like using this as a base for more citrusy fragrances, like ELDO Cologne, to give it a kick. Overall this is a great every day perfume and nice for layering. I AM a "big white floral" person. Jasmine is my favorite note.

I know a few gardenia fragrances. For example, Madison Soiree, Pure Poison, Chanel Gardenia, etc. At Saks, I encounter a suboptimal gardenia. It is a gardenia that is young, zesty, and somehow a bit sassy. In Madison Soiree, the gardenia is rather well-behaved, clean, and conservative. In Chanel, the gardenia has an irresistible charm and style. Pure Poison is a gardenia that secretly wears red lace underwear. Well, this fragrance also strongly reminds me of Love and Tears by Kilian due to the fizzy jasmine, which provides the zestiness here as well. What I don't like about this scent is the interplay of gardenia and jasmine, which meets a rancid, coconutty tuberose. This makes the fragrance suboptimal for me, as I can't imagine a suitable wearer for it, to whom I would much rather recommend one of the aforementioned gardenia fragrances. To provide a fitting image: For me, Saks smells like when you empty a very elegant designer handbag belonging to a woman with a thick bank account after a shopping spree. Then just smell the inside of the handbag. You smell something soapy, something powdery, something stuffy. And exactly this stuffiness I can only attribute to the tuberose, which does not allow the gardenia to shine in the light it deserves.

A dear Parfumo member sent me a sample of Saks Fifth Avenue a long time ago. It was just a coincidence that I didn't test it earlier, but I now think that I wouldn't have been "ready" for this scent before... I usually only comment on fragrances that excite or at least fascinate me. So I feel the fundamental need to express myself about SFA as well, albeit from a different perspective! ~ This perfume is unique! Truly unique in my sniffing career, unique and incredibly disgusting for my olfactory senses. Right after applying the "fragrance" (if I may call it that), I feel like I'm standing in the middle of Mannheim inhaling a strong peak-hour BASF note. A squeaky chemical rubber greets me, a hint of mosquito spray (without the "blue angel") and the sharpness of super glue, all wrapped in a nauseating sweetness. The scent reaches its peak in just a few minutes and then doesn't change much, except that the rubber note becomes even more unpleasant. Comparable to a cheap vanilla-scented candle from the discount store, where you forgot to remove the protective film before lighting it. At least this scent lasts exceptionally long for a Bond. However, I don't exactly welcome that, as it gives me an unprecedented nausea, something no Bond has managed to do before. So this is how natural jasmine and tuberose are supposed to smell??? I have the essential oils here and have diligently compared: NO COMPARISON! Vanilla, vetiver??? No! Gardenia? While it can occasionally produce a slightly sweet plastic smell, not in this concentration. Maybe this is how the chemical formula smells. No, sorry! If this creation contains even a single "natural" fragrance ingredient, then I will eat a broom and wash it down with 4711! ~ Conclusion: I personally can hardly believe that this scent actually sells and at such a horrendous price! At BASF, I might get a fragrance blend that evokes similar ambitions in me at a special price, but at least I could still take out a ton of mosquitoes with it. Sorry to all Bond fans, no matter how enchanting this scent may be, "on me" it is unfortunately not at all! ~ During the test, I gained the following insight: I am amazed that I didn't realize it at first sniff, because this very plastic leg note is the essence of what all Bonds have, just in a lower dose. This strange note that already bothered me in West Side, Chelsea Gardens, and especially strongly in Park Avenue. I have now also definitively come to the realization that I do not harmonize with Bond fragrances. If I was already bothered by the questionable longevity before, I now seriously doubt the qualitative justification for the price!

... besides artificial jasmine and tuberose? O.k. Aspartame or Nutrasweet maybe, but nothing more? This scent is for me like an olfactory purgatory! The place where all the sins one has committed or wanted to commit are painfully brought to mind. And Mr. Satan knows exactly how to torment the poor sinner (in this case, me).

Thanks to a lovely board beauty here, I was able to test this stunning fragrance and it has slowly snuck into my heart. At first, it is more of a warm, coconut-sweet skin caresser and I thought it was just nice, but then the wonderful tuberose explosion came, and yet the base remains soft and creamy with a subtle sweetness.

I received a sample of this incredible fragrance and was blown away; I just had to have this little treasure. Now it’s mine, and I’ve generously indulged myself with it... The tuberose is consistently very prominent for me; I don’t smell any coconut note, but my partner does. After a few hours, I can smell the vanilla, which is very soothing.

Opening with the most synthetic of synthetic apples I've come across in my fragrance journey, this is not the most pleasant of perfumes. It feels cheap from the start and lacks the depth and complexity we've grown accustomed to with these niche kinds of fragrance houses. Before the apple settles down a bit into a crispy fresh green one, it's coated with a glue like substance, or other chemical solvents and is quite aggressive and unpleasant to my nose. Luckily that doesn't last too long and stays fresh and bright for a while. Once the top notes flash off a bit, a musky peach will start to dominate the overtones of this fragrance. It's quite indolic, overripe, leaning towards fermentation. Surely past its prime as a succulent tropical snack. I also perceive hints of raisins and the crispness transfers into a musty sweet blanket covering the air. It reminds me of those raisin-filled snack box cartons we had as a kid as an alternative to candy. Deep down there are some white flowers, but it's hard to get past the heavy peach. Maybe on other skins this juice is more successful, but even on paper it can't tempt me. I will steer clear of this one and give away the remainder of my sample.

Today, I am once again anxiously pacing the carpet, as Mom has a nasty injury on her foot, and my little cousin is just getting a new hip at this very moment. How am I supposed to think around that? Then the DHL man rings the bell and asks me with concern about my red eyes. I mumble something about "allergy" and he kindly wishes me a speedy recovery, handing me a package. This contains - oh joy - the spotted star with the cheeky red bow - Park Avenue South. I had ordered the fragrance purely phenotypically, as I always get along well with this label. And Park Avenue South is characteristically friendly and approachable. Gently fruity, the apple aroma welcomes me - like the scent of our winter apples in the pantry. Cozy. The peach joins in juicy, surrounded by white jasmine, which brings brightness. Musk and amber are soft and caress me affectionately. The manageable ingredients are skillfully harmonized. Uncomplicated - but not simple. I like its quietly sweet expression, which, as always, is very long-lasting. So much can be done quietly. What a wonderful task - a life without noise.

Gramercy Park is an exclusive park in wealthy New York, accessible only to residents. It is celebrated with a wave of sparklingness and green notes, which make it a cheerful, refreshing fragrance with slightly masculine tones. I really like it and wear it with pleasure, it is elegant and casual at the same time. Average duration and wake.

.. there is nothing that doesn't exist In NYC, in this case a small park called Gramercy Park in Manhattan from the 1840s, which only residents of the immediate area have access to - if they have purchased a key annually beforehand. Now that’s what I call exclusive! This New York park fragrance is - in contrast to, for example, Central Park - rather subdued, reflecting the more grown-up surroundings with the beautiful old houses. It almost looks a bit like in Europe’s big cities. Actually, it’s not an exciting scent; it starts off fresh-creamy-green without any individual notes being recognizable, little sweetness .. along with foliage and bitter floral scents. Lily of the valley can be detected, just like the musk that serves as the base and gives the fragrance a fresh, almost cologne-like kick. Throughout, you can also perceive a delicate aquatic note, which is present in many of the New York Bond fragrances and indeed represents the city by the water well. Everything here is really understated .. Synthetics are - as with many Bond No.9s - clearly present, the longevity is good, but Gramercy Park quickly becomes a subtle skin scent and is therefore suitable for all occasions and can be worn well by anyone. The European alternative is Eau de Lierre by Diptyque .. this one, however, is more bitter and has lower longevity.

With the scents from Bond No 9, I actually associate more sweet-feminine fragrances. These are the most commonly represented in the product range and all are great in their own way. Great Jones is different. From the outset, the scent develops strongly in a mossy-green direction. The top note is skipped right away. The notes of oak moss and vetiver are very, very prominent here. Upon very careful sniffing, cardamom can also be detected. Somehow, the whole thing comes across as a bit musty-moldy, definitely not fresh. This scent could easily pass for a Guerlain; I have noticed a certain similarity to Heritage, but Great Jones is clearer and less complex. How can one evaluate it...? It is very suitable for lovers of mossy-woody fragrances. Since I received it as a gift, I couldn't test it beforehand. No, I really wouldn't have bought it. Too harsh, too green, fitting the color of the liquid. The longer I smell it, the more dreadful the scent becomes. Here, I would even appreciate a bit of variety with bergamot and orange, but both completely fail. So far, one of the most disappointing Bond scents. Suitable for the 60+ generation with a hat and cane. At least I only have the 50ml. EDIT: After a while, a musk-vetiver mix remains. Actually not bad, it goes in the direction of vetiver from Guerlain, without its citrus freshness. Still, the scent doesn't really convince me.

I agree with Sherapop about the gingery note here (is it the cardamom?). I love ginger scents, and that spicy whisper here among the wan spring florals and pale citrus just made me want to wear something more gingery. This scent is almost offensive in its dullness. But it did put me in the mood for gingery citrus, so I wound up slathering that wrist with Origins Ginger Essence lotion. OGE is not considered fine perfume - the Origins brand is more along the lines of aromatherapy. But it is so much more energetic and refreshing than New York Fling. I went to the BN9 site to see what its maker had to say about it. To my astonishment, Bond calls it a "high-energy, cork-popping scent" and sells it for $180 US for 50 ml and $250 for 100 ml. The vastly superior Ginger Essence sells at the Origins site for $57 for 100 ml and is also available in a nice array of other products (lotion, souffle, scrub, conditioner) at relatively reasonable prices. Again, Bond makes me think of the Emperor's New Clothes - all public relations, no art.

There is a glaring omission from the notes for Bond no 9 NEW YORK FLING: ginger. In fact, to my nose, this is a light gingery citrus with only very faint florality. I have no idea why this is categorized as a fragrance for women, as it is as unisex as they come: right down the line between masculine and feminine, very ambiguous, all in all. I reviewed NEW YORK FLING at another site about a year ago, based on a sample vial, and now having acquired a bottle and worn the fragrance on several occasions, I feel even more confident in my claim that this is not a floral fragrance. I wore NEW YORK FLING to a dentist appointment, where I was scheduled to have a filling replaced and was quaking in fear that it might be one of those "simple filling turns into a $3K root canal + crown"-type scenarios of which I've heard so much, but fortunately nothing of the sort transpired. What did happen was that my dentist went crazy over NEW YORK FLING. Here were her words: "You smell so good: is that perfume?" My response: "yes." To which she replied, "You smell like you just took a shower." I rest my case. QED.

Today, the ding-dong of the DHL delivery man pulled me out of my restless dreams. I stumbled sleepily to the door - and received two boxes. My Bonds? My Bonds! I release Fling from its cardboard prison and it joyfully jumps at me over its regained freedom. And what can I say - it brings life to the "place" and invigorates my weary limbs. Radio on, and I dared a few dance steps to The Story of My Life. Even my husband wakes up and becomes chatty. The intro of bergamot and clementine greets me with a sweet freshness - delicately spiced with cardamom. I think of freshly squeezed fruit juice with a crispy sugar rim on the glass. The floral aspect is cheerful - the lily of the valley chimes sweetly. Jasmine and cedar strengthen the fragrance once more as it comes to a close. Fling is a lively, cheerful companion that instantly dispels fatigue and dark thoughts. An ideal daytime fragrance for any season, with the good bonds longevity. At the same time, Fling is light and buoyant - beyond any heaviness. It is welcome to "float" in with me.

During today's extensive testing, I truly experienced all imaginable emotional facets related to this fragrance. The beginning was wonderful! A radiant diamond! When you have to get up at 5 AM, but the final awakening threatens to fail due to your inner sloth, just spray a hint of New York Fling… And… Fresh, juicy clementine with bergamot does its job perfectly! You feel instantly awake and full of energy - as if you could really take off and briefly float over the city! ………… Unfortunately, the floating lasted really "only a short while"... Not even until noon. Shortly after, you crash down. And then came the big BUT - now I was just wondering where my fragrance actually went? Did it inspire itself and fly away too? And did it take the promised bouquet of peonies, lily of the valley, and freesias that were supposed to play the role of the happiness maker at this point? Will it come back? Hmmm… I don't smell anything for a long time. The energy is slowly leaving me too… Well, what can you do… Thanks anyway for the wake-up kiss… The worst part is that afterwards, there was an even bigger BUT… The fragrance was back! Unfortunately! I suddenly felt like I had bathed in soap! And no water in sight to wash it off! The soapy feeling lasted a good hour until the fragrance finally left me… What a pity… Such a sparkling start and such a disappointing finale…

(TL;DR: Powdery, slightly fruity, very high-quality scent with extraordinary longevity, particularly suitable for autumn, winter, and cold spring days; I don't know of any other fragrance that reminds me of this one (but there are certainly some in the vast world of perfumes), the price is a crime) Plum pudding Over 11 years ago, I smelled a (for me at the time absolutely) niche perfume for the first time. It was a 2ml sample of Bond No. 9's Bleecker Street. Before that, I only knew flat "budget" perfumes and had no idea how things could actually smell, and this was where it all began. I was in love. With the scent, the quality, the longevity, the fact that there are even small samples of perfumes, the infinite expanse and the enjoyment of this hobby. It's nice that on this platform, almost everyone has probably experienced this moment as well. I still have the sample; I rarely used it and appreciated it. A few months after the first sniff, the aforementioned scent was on its way to me across the Atlantic. Back then, it was still half as expensive as it is today. The scent still lasts. Over 11 years later, same performance, same depth, same development. Back then, I wished I could stand in a perfumery and test each of the Bonds. Last week, it finally happened. I was lucky enough to not only be in the namesake store on 9 Bond St. in New York but also in the one at 399 Bleecker Street. And to have the best sales associate in front of me that I could have wished for. Alyssia wonderfully advised my partner and me and let us try the entire range at our own pace. Many would say about Bond No. 9 that they throw every fragrance direction on the market and see what works. I think that's just how Americans are; they try a lot of things, and what doesn't work gets scrapped and is a lesson learned - what is well-received is celebrated accordingly. I think that's fine and don't think the brand can be blamed for that. Especially since the quality is consistently good. I don't know of a Bond that suffers from a lack of depth or insufficient longevity. Alyssia sprayed Number One on my left inner elbow just before we left the store and Beekman Place on my right, the two new releases (end of 2024) from Bond No. 9. Number One not only lasted all day for me, but even after my shower the next morning, the heart note was still faintly perceptible. Essentially, after this shower, I decided to spend the now tear-jerkingly high price and take this scent home as a souvenir from the vacation, especially since I had wanted this for 11 years. As can already be inferred here, the manufacturer and this scent in particular have an emotional significance for me. The price for the new releases (440 USD or 460€) from Bond No. 9 is in no world justifiable; the synthetic fragrance materials, especially prevalent in the USA, are too cheap to produce. The marketing infrastructure is already established, as are the supply chains, and even though inflation has hit the USA harder than us in the EU, the price increase is proportionally too far removed from that. Perhaps the prices are demanded because the audience is specifically the New Yorkers, where the cost of living and income are particularly high. But we all are not just buying the scent but especially the emotion. Perfume is never a rational decision. Why Plum Pudding? Next to the store on Bleecker Street is a branch of the bakery chain "Magnolia Bakery," which makes a very popular "Banana Pudding." This has a hint of vanilla, contains fresh banana pieces, and a kind of soft ladyfinger, and tastes really extremely good. It's easy to eat while giving your nose a break. For me, this scent could be just like this pudding if it contained very high-quality, very ripe plums instead of the ripe bananas. I wonder why nothing about that is mentioned in the fragrance pyramid; perhaps it's just a very old bergamot that I perceive this way. The base of vanilla is consistently present and caresses the fruity note, especially in the early phase, with tonka bean and musk. The fruitiness slowly fades after several hours, leaving a soft, fresh, and high-quality scent feeling that takes on very light, spicy notes. For me, it's a calm, high-quality scent profile that reminds me of really very high-quality, very expensive sweet baked goods, macarons, high-quality plum cake/pudding, and similar things. The association with the very clean and neatly decorated store comes along with it. The manufacturer is probably hoping to have created a new flagship and classic; they likely didn't choose the name "Number One" just like that. For me, it definitely has the potential to be one.

Kenzo Amour is really lovely, beautiful in fact. I had actually imagined something stronger, more bold and heavy as Kenzo's interpretation of love, however this fragrance is flawless. Delicate and predominantly powdery, its subtlety is very likable. I am a big fan of powdery fragrances as of late, especially powdery vanilla scents. There is something very feminine and comforting about them. Kenzo Amour's softness is pleasantly unobtrusive to both the wearer and the people around you. While the vanilla and musk really do feature in this fragrance, other detectable notes, such as frangipani and Japanese cherry blossom, gives Kenzo Amour a somewhat exotic feel. The overall result can be described as creamy and alluring. I disagree that this is just baby powder, I think it has far more substance than that. I really enjoyed wearing Kenzo Amour and I thought the lasting strength was simply outstanding. Another great Kenzo offering in my opinion.

Lemon rice pudding. Or sago. With a vanillic vibe. Steaming tea. chocolate. Yes, cherries, in white chocolate. I can see that it might be kind of comforting but not something I want to smell like. Not even something I would want to eat. Lasts 8 hours.

This smells like a dream to me. It's everything I want from an everyday perfume. It's sweet and vanilla-y, and powdery in a way that is not dusty, it's powdery because of the rice. It is not gourmand though, it has a very clean smell, to the verge of being soapy. Smells like a beautiful body cream: snuggly, sexy, airy, and sweet, but in a perfume form. It has everything I like about powdery vanilla scents when executed correctly. It is pure, innocent, and clean but also sweet and very sexy. Great Longevity and decent sillage, at least on me. The only thing is, give it 5-10 seconds, because the first spay is for some reason, very sharp and synthetic. But after some seconds when all the alcohol is gone, it's DIVINE. Btw, in no way shape or form, this is similar to Hypnotic Poison. I have HP, I really like HP, and I can see someone liking both of them, but HP is way more, not obnoxious exactly, more in your face. HP is more of a night perfume and I think it's way more polarizing than this one. But if you like HP, and want a day alternative, I would say give it a shot.

I used to love this perfume few years ago. It is a powdery,sweet,spicy fragrance. The smell of rice cooking on the top is so comfy. Then comes a soapy heliotrope,and musc Wich give a nice cloudy smell. The dry down is spicy woody ,a little smoky and the sweetness of the vanilla is light here. Very nice smell, unusual at the top. Worth it if you like original spicy powdery frag. I think.again very original one when it came out.but still is... Olivier cresp is Soo good.to make elegant perfumes

I love eau de perfumes and eau de toilettes with vanilla. Usually with vanilla frags, the initial spray is not that pleasing and comes rather through after it settles into a divine, smooth, round fragrance. With Kenzo Amour however there was no waiting for a wonderful dry down, it was right up my alley right from the get go. The freshness comes through a bit later, but doesn't take away from the yummy vanilla. I do not get too much floral, but that is normal for me. When I detect it, it's usually more than I ask for. I guess my nose can only detect real flower bombs, but otherwise I recognize floral aromas just as part of the composition, not so much something I can pinpoint, unless it is overwhelming me. This is a very nice fragrance, and I am pleased I gave it a try.
The opening of Kenzo Amour starts with powdery florals and tea that hits like a truck because it is so strong.

After years of wanting of wearing it I can now try to make a review. I can see where the comparisons to Dior Hypnotic Poison are coming from. The opening to Kenzo Amour is SO almond-forward that it almost smells exactly like Hypnotic Poison in my opinion. It smells good, don't get me wrong, but as someone who already owns Hypnotic Poison, I was a little let down at first.

It smells proper rich and creamy. But it smells more like eggshell paint or a nail varnish than a perfume, like it's almost toxic. The woods are prominent and too skanky. It's mainly frangipani with the tropical nuance and cherry blossom with the creamy Vanilla vibe. Overall it's like a sickly vanilla bomb with rough woods. This isn't soft at all. Quite offensive actually.

The opening of Kenzo Amour is almost creamy vanilla and rice. Yes, like everyone's already pointed out, rice pudding! There is also a slight spiciness bringing an exotic vibe. Amour evolves smoothly. The floral notes sneak out discretly and blend so well in the vanilla. Frangipani turns a little sour on me, which also happens with some other white flowers, and I'm ok with it.

My first time with Kenzo Amour was a pure vanilla experience. I was a bit surprised that this was all. I love Kenzo, Ca Sent Beau and Flower so I was sure that this time the brand had failed. A really lovely vanilla but that seat had been taken by Dior Addict a few years earlier. So what was this? Was it just a really innovative, sculptural bottle with an uninteresting juice?

UPDATE: If Bond came out with a Dubai Amber EXTRADOSE, with the oud being even more emphasized, i would buy that, too. This fragrance is so upscale and perfect for what it sets out to be that i grow more enamored with it every time i wear it. A true shirt lifter, this is. My favorite amber. Not too sweet, not too loud... Perfect. Smells exactly how you would think amber would smell, not as a perfume but, as an odor. At least how I would conceive it. MUST try on skin. Smelling it other wise may come across too animalic or even too sweet (to some). On skin you'll find the sweetness is solely there to counter the animalic notes. Also it's persistent. So altho it's never in your face (loud) it does linger into your nostrils as you go about your day. Do NOT over spray. Doing so will only ruin the experience. Upscale. Masculine. Unique. 10/10 for me.

Sorry for putting it this way, but the first spray leaves me with the impression that I’m in a camel stable - very strong and extremely extreme. Wow, and it stays as a guest for a good hour. Then it becomes softer, milder, and tamer. As I said, this scent is really a challenge; please spray it at home first, then wait half an hour before going out among people. Definitely more of a men’s fragrance! It lasts and lasts and lasts - until the next day, and the clothing is completely coated with it - a bit too much for me! Civet and oud clearly dominate, and the saffron adds its part to it…. At some point, it becomes slightly floral and more rounded, worn by a big, confident man who isn’t afraid of being looked at strangely or questioningly. Surely, there are people on whom it smells great. The bottle is a dream - the price - in the original, horror. There are cheaper suppliers, but how fresh is the scent still? As for me, I’m out; it’s just too much in terms of ingredients - a bomb of strong individual components. But there are enthusiasts for it as well.

It's been a while since I first reviewed Kenzo FLOWER, my memory of which is best summed up as : vanilla baby powder. I fortuitously received a fresh sample in the mail recently, and as I was attempting to understand Caron ROYAL BAIN DE CHAMPAGNE, it seemed an opportune time to take up FLOWER again. The opening of FLOWER holds lots of promise for this lover of violets—whether from Parma or elsewhere! Upon initially dabbing the fragrance all over my arms and décolleté, I began to wonder whether my “vanilla baby powder” memory of FLOWER was really all wrong. Had I reviewed the perfume on a humid day, or irresponsibly allowed my blood caffeine content to dip to a dangerous low before brandishing my pen? Who knows? In those opening minutes, just enough time, coincidentally enough, to make the big sell at counters all over the world, this perfume seems like some sort of dream come true, a rich floriental with seductive appeal, clearly comprising top-notch notes which wax and wane in a lilting, lyrical way. Alas, the drydown commences shortly thereafter, during which everything flattens out and begins to smell progressively more synthetic until, at last, I recall why my memory of FLOWER as “vanilla baby powder” was right all along. Certainly not a bad perfume, but rather blunt and banal in the final analysis, when all is said and sniffed. Rather like a marriage which may endure for years in a stagnant state after an initially exciting but short-lived romance. Would poppies smell like vanilla baby powder, if they had a scent? Sure, why not? (if pigs could fly)

An aldehydic, musky floral typically has an implicit sweetness. An interesting perfume will play against type and either downplay or compensate for the sweetness. Flower learned compensation and a sort of misdirection from White Linen, which it smells like, and Tommy girl, with which it shares a conceptual similarity. White Linen’s trick is to redirect the composition’s sweetness with a peppery rose that doesn’t so much diminish the sweetness as steer it toward sweet/tart. From Tommy Girl, Flower learns the lesson of astringency. Sour, as opposed to bitter, is a hard effect to pull off in perfumery. In Flower, the sweet, powdery melon-like tone is highlighted by a slightly vinegary note just as actual melon would be by a splash of lemon juice.

Who has never seen a red wilderness of poppies overlooking the ears of wheat at the beginning of summer? Poppies are wildflowers that grow spontaneously and bloom from spring into early summer. The red petals are like rice paper, but alas, they have no scent. So why use poppy to promote a perfume like Kenzo Flower? Perhaps because its ephemeral beauty, strength, and delicacy express everything this perfume has. Noteworthy, following the trench warfare in the poppy fields of Flanders, Belgium during World War I, poppies have become a symbol of remembrance of soldiers who have died during wartime. Despite being on the market since 2000, I only discovered it these days, and I immediately fell in love with it. Alberto Morillas’ nose brought together the floral accord, which gives delicacy and sensuality, added the powdery and musky accord, which gives a feeling of intimacy and finally the vibrant accord of smoky resins that introduces an almost mystical note. Published as a masterpiece that remains very modern, not at all dated or taken for granted. When I sprayed it, it smelled of purple, softness and talc, like the dressing process of a sophisticated woman. It was exotic, completely different from the fresh perfumes that women are currently wearing. Flower shows a head full of a floral accord, similar to a slight shiver that encloses the Bulgarian rose, the Parma violet and the citrusy Sicilian lemon. While I don’t have strong tartness, what reaches my nose is an explosion of fruit along with powdery purple and sour berries. A floral opening, a subtle balance of purple and pink. Ouch, it’s so damn good and captivating. The scent is immediately light, fresh, a flowery sweet. Let the overture calm down, and immediately a lemonade magnolia blooms, rich in the accord of iris talc and the scent of synthetic hedione, a jasmine-like odour. Resinous opoponax, which is a kind of honeyed myrrh, reinforces its sweetness. Behind that lipstick vibe, there is subtle rose water, which dilutes the otherwise overly opulent blend. To keep everything clean, a musky touch exudes from the heart of this essence. But Flower is more than that. Apart from the floral and powdery facets, the base releases a smoky accord of incense, smoky but not too ecclesiastical, which merges with a whisper of dark vanilla, which makes it more intense. It is not too sweet in vanilla, and it is my opinion that it is because of the woody base and the opoponax that rounds the vanilla. It is a persistent but delicate fragrance. Beast mode as for longevity, over six hours. Nice to see and wear, to try at least once in a lifetime. Kenzo Flower is a beautiful example that shows that impressive sillage and enormous lasting potency don’t have to conflict with a nuanced and delicate overall impression. A powdery floral with an inimitable signature. There is a lot of resistance to this perfume. It is appropriate for day wear and casual events, and it is an ideal perfume for spring and summer. I love it. Did I mention that already? I based the review on a bottle I have owned since September 2021. -Elysium

Wonderful opening of violet and rose. This is a well balanced perfume from beginning to end I could pick out the notes without a problem. The middle notes occasionally smelled tangy to me! This lasts a very long time! The base notes are very vanilla on me with a touch of musk. I might buy a 1.7oz but I would not buy a whole 3.5 oz, it would go bad before I finished it!

Kenzo Flower definitely shares some of its DNA with Prince Matchabelli's Wind Song perfume. I haven't smelled that one in a very long time, but it used to be the only perfume my mother ever wore. Every day before she left for work, she would hug me goodbye, and then all day I would smell her on my clothes. Wind Song was potent and tenacious juice! And there is some component in Flower that strongly recalls these memories to my mind. I've tried comparing lists of notes, but I haven't narrowed it down yet. A couple of notes do overlap (mandarin, rose, amber, musk), but they don't stand out to me as possibilities. Mostly because the similar note feels spicy to my nose, in the way that carnation is a bit spicy. But neither perfume lists carnation! I applied two sprays to the back of my neck/hair, one to my chest, and one on each arm. That was too much. My daughter commented from the stairwell, "Wow! Someone is quite aromatic this morning!" So spray accordingly. This stuff fills a room. It has been wafting around my person all day. It smells really good, but strong. Longevity seems to be about 6-8 hours. It lasts in clothing and hair longer than on skin, but I think that is pretty well true of most perfumes. The top is a bit sharp, but it does not last long. The violet note dries down very powdery. I feel that the mimosa also renders this quite a bit more sweet-powdery than most people are willing to smell like. It's not quite a baby powder smell--it's a bit more sophisticated than that--but still, if you do not like powdery scents, best to steer clear of this one. I love powdery scents, but this one has a biting note that I can't quite place. I do like it, but it brings me to the very edge of headache territory. This is an unusual perfume. It brings to mind perfumes from a by-gone era, but also it feels modern. I first smelled it on my husband's cousin in Germany in 2001, I believe it was. It's a very memorable scent because I still remember it today, 16 years later! I feel it is in the same vein as Wind Song (as noted above), Arpege, and L'air du Temps. Bottle is tall and skinny, so if my perfume tray gets jostled, it wobbles. It seems a bit art deco for this scent. I picture more of a flacon from some time in the 1950's, but overall, it's okay. Overall, I give it a 6.5. Good, but I likely won't reach for it often. It's probably best for evening wear.

When you first smell Flower by Kenzo you will most likely recognize the scent as something that you're familiar with because you have at least known one person that wears this fragrance. This perfume is quite distinctive. It's not an overly unique or ground-breaking scent, rather it is a safe clean-smelling, powdery floral.

It has a very cosmetic mood in it, the smells of powder, lipstick, a lot of cosmetic aromas mixed together. I find it to be dissonant to a minimalistic bottle design to be honest. Apart of that it's a nice intimate cloudy composition of violet, mimosa and musk.

I find the opening a bit sharp. A lot of violet emerges out while the rose gives a soft touch. At the drydown the vanilla smoothens it into a comforting body scent. I find it indeed very powdery. And I detected some incense-like notes that tickle the nose and constantly reboost up the soft floral and vanilla, very interesting.

Why its having low 6.7 point? Somebody trolling? Its shocking ford me the see that beautys point. Thats not spicy, yuk, overly heavy, choking scent. I see the last comment from 2018/12 its not popular as it used to be. I know Flower from my past years when I was little somebody use this and it makes me feel confident, safe, relax, calm.

Divine, sweet, complicated and fresh.Flower has a sexy, sultry, seductive big sister, did you know? she comes in a red, satiny container and her name is Flower Parfum and she comes out to play after Flower has been tucked into bed and kissed to sleep.

Initially, it's almost a one for one of Giorgio for Men, but goes on to smell like Zino with cinnamon and civet in the dry down... It also has that Antaeus leather in here, too. Oddly, I REALLY like it. I know, I know, I said I was over with buying perfume. But I was looking for this thing for YEARS. I ended up giving up on it; I even took it off my want-list with stuff like Over the Musk and Pure Wood. Yeah, rare stuff. Then, while obsessively looking for items on discount sites from my want/ maybe-one-day-list (old habits die hard lol), I seen it! I almost said no. But I thought of how rare it is and how it was selling for cheap! I hit add to cart and the rest is history lol This is a SEXY scent meant for alpha males who dress sharp. Definitely falls into the proximity of the fragrances i compared them to at the top, meaning grown man stuff. I want to say mature but I don't think late 20's and up is considered mature quite yet. In any event, glad I got it. UPDATE: Since I've had this, I've been really, REALLY, liking it. To put a cherry on top, I had a random woman just follow me and come up to me saying how she "like that smell. It smells GOOD.". This with only one spray and a half, so the sillage is off the charts. The fact that she complimented the smell and not me tells me the scent is definitely niche, because she didn't say she liked the way I smelled or my cologne. Say what the want about Bond but they know how to make a mass, but expensive and niche fragrance.

I initially thought from the emanations off the top of my sample vial that Bond no 9 H.O.T. Always was going to be a rich patchouli frag. But that impression was swiftly defeated when upon application a wild beast suddenly emerged on the scene out of nowhere--or, rather, out of that forest of patchouli. This unexpected creature is similar to a centaur, well, except that it has the head of a civet cat and the torso of a bull. Hang on, you're in for quite a ride if you dare to don this powerful potion! This is dark, heavy leather, oily and dirty, so H.O.T. (heavily over the top?) Always must ALWAYS be sparingly applied. Basically, you should conduct yourself as though this were perfume, not edp--and I dare say that a bottle will last several light years! This stuff is like none of the other Bond no 9 creations that I have tried, and perhaps, unlike their genteel universal (or unisex or omnisex) frags, an overtly masculine elixir such as H.O.T. might be best suited for that rather narrow cross-section of ladies who adorn themselves with whips and chains, nail corsets and the like. Okay, so maybe that's a slight exaggeration, but as indubitable evidence of the roughness of this diamond, I offer this: upon sniffing my wrist, my cat licked his lips! As for mild-mannered little me, I'll have to tame this beast with some rose... ---------- Addendum: I need to report an update. I was sent this perfume in error (it was in the box of the one I had ordered), and I decided to give it another try. To my surprise, I have found that it is strangely addictive.

Here, they seem to want to build on the success story of Givenchy Gentleman. H.O.T. differs somewhat from GG, but to its detriment. It starts with an overdose of cinnamon and ends with a musty patchouli. I can barely detect some leather and civet later on. Where GG shows class, H.O.T. simply cannot keep up and comes off as a failure. Now this misfortune costs almost 200 euros, unbelievable. The longevity and projection are worth mentioning positively, which at least I can do without. Sammy :-)

Is it tarragon? The top notes are intensely spicy and interesting, somehow also earthy. I've smelled this somewhere before. What remains of the scent after a while unfortunately reminds me of "Le Male" by Jean Paul Gaultier. Therefore, this probably won't become my new favorite fragrance. :-) All in all, a very strange scent. Maybe I need to let it affect me a bit longer.

Kenzo Jungle L'Eléphant is such a spectacular creation that I can only regard the fact that it has been discontinued as yet more evidence that there is something seriously awry with the universe. Thank goodness I acquired a bottle, though I must admit that it was an act of faith based only on my knowledge of the perfumer's name: Dominique Ropion. This perfume is nearly entirely oriental--not very floral at all, and also not very sweet. It packs a punch of spices which, if overapplied, might well knock the wearer and those in her environs out. Not that this creation cannot be worn by men--I find it completely unisex and surmise that it would have had a longer, more successful market life had it been presented in that way. Instead, men were steered away from this fabulous composition by fears, no doubt, that it might be more along the lines of Ropion's Givenchy Amarige--also a loud perfume but very feminine, it seems to me. There are prerequisites to wearing this perfume. First, one must love cardamom, because that note perfuses the entire composition. Second, one must have a hearty appreciation for spices more generally, as they do abound. However, I hasten to add that this is very far from the "spice-cabinet" perfumes which basically dump a bunch of n'importe quoi together and hope that somehow it will work out. Instead, the perfumer has woven the spices into the woody-patchouli-amber-vanilla base, each of the elements of which is complementary to the others, and none of which dominates. As a result, one does not have the sense that this is a patchouli perfume or an amber perfume or a vanilla perfume. No, this is the sui generis creation Jungle L'Eléphant. Cumin and vanilla are two of the most obvious and readily identifiable notes to my nose, and yet here they are not independently detectable, so skillfully is this composition blended. This creation begins strong and grows massively over the course of a wear, as though the elephant decided to reproduce and gave birth to an entire herd. For this reason, modest application is highly advised. Even then, such a voluminous perfume may be best reserved for private settings. It is unclear to me that it is even possible to wear L'Eléphant discreetly, and it certainly will not work in a perfume-police monitored setting.
