It wasn't bad... back then! These days, I wouldn't buy it anymore. A little floral touch with a bit of sharpness, which probably comes from the black pepper. It doesn't sound bad... but floral sharpness? Is that really necessary? I personally don't think so anymore, as it feels somewhat boring and doesn't quite fit my style anymore. You can detect the geranium and the pepper. Maybe there's a bit of coriander hidden in there, but it's been well blended. After a while, a hint of wood makes itself known. While all of this doesn't sound bad, it's actually quite unremarkable. However, for summer, it can still be recommended for those who enjoy such scents. I just don't like it anymore. :)

Do you know what cleanliness smells like? If you do, CK Everyone Eau de Toilette smells exactly like that. When you wear the fragrance, you will feel a waterfall of coolness, cleanliness, and freshness falling on you from the sky on a very hot day. The transparent color of the bottle also confirms this impression in you. A seductive fragrance, one of the creations of the genius perfumer Alberto Morillas. Really pleasant, light, citrusy aquatic scent, perfect for personal enjoyment or light walks on hot summer mornings. The fragrance leans a little more towards being masculine than feminine, but it is definitely unisex. The performance of the fragrance is below average and somewhat acceptable, and you will accept it more if you are a fan of light CK fragrances. Note: The fragrance is very suitable for people with nasal allergies and chronic sinus congestion.

For a long time, there was only CK One. Okay, there were several flankers of it, CK Be as a bit of a black sheep as well, but it took a while for Calvin Klein to truly realize that the market and the many CK One wearers also want something new. Or at least want to try something new. So, in recent years, several interesting, always highly affordable CK fragrances have hit the market, mostly unisex and somehow already in the in-house "One" tradition, which pleasantly and surprisingly solidly expanded the repertoire. CK Two, for example, as an excellent transparent rose. Or the also very likable "CK All." Now, here comes "CK EveryOne" - and again, I marvel at how one can maintain such a clear and beautiful DNA and direction while always finding a casual new spin. CK is indeed somewhat underestimated in the designer market. And although there are hardly any new classics and milestones among them, they deserve high praise for that, and I wear/buy their "works," especially before vacations/at airports - always completely without guilt or regret. I've never regretted it. "CK Everyone" is a kind of oasis for every day, a wellness fragrance of the friendly middle class. Ginger, quite tame, not sharp but soft, warm, and fluffy. Rarely has the color orange, in my opinion, been captured so well without advertising, juice, or packaging flirting with it. "Everyone" is a smiling scent that nonchalantly spreads good vibes. At first, it may seem a bit simple and boring, but in the end, it has steadily grown on me. Especially the first third is excellent, calming, and congenial. After that, it loses its form and specialty a bit faster than one would wish, but overall, the picture holds. And the price-performance ratio is great anyway. A decent travel companion. Playful, easy to wear, a sympathetic character without pretensions. Refreshing at tables. Minimally exotic, very juicy, and neutral. With manners, without being stuffy, always galloping along. Even in the gym, it works. An all-rounder. CK stays true to itself, makes it new with a bit of hay and tea in... blue??? ;) Bottle: iconic including "fanny pack" Sillage: super, super subtle Longevity: nearly solid 4 hours, maybe even less. But as always with CK, affordable (40€/100 ml) and therefore easy to reapply Conclusion: a bit of peace, a bit of relaxation, a bit of great - "CK Everyone" is a simple but extremely effective leisure fragrance. As the name suggests: for everyone, forever. Orange ginger winner!

I am currently quite distracted. Where have my thoughts gone? I suspected I had already sent a fragrance to my friend - and where do I find it? On my dresser. I tried on a hat at the department store - and at home, I still find it on my head. Of course, I drove back and paid for the little gem properly. But by the way, I discovered CK Everyone. This fresh, clear scent did my foggy senses a world of good. Orange and ginger are invigorating - yet unexciting. The teen note wafts soothingly above it - delicately sweetened by amber. The cedar is soft - just as the entire fragrance appears mild. It gently brings me back to the present. Everyone is truly for everyone, as it provides clarity without immediately "shaking things up." Another successful CK fragrance that lands on my wish list.

With a mix of astonishment and fascination, I currently observe that the subculture of the 90s - my personal coming-of-age decade - has become hot shit again among Generation Z (those born in the late 90s and afterward), at least in part. And I remember how we listened to Dr. Alban, Haddaway, and Blümchen back then, causing traffic accidents in front of H&M posters featuring Anna Nicole Smith, and seeing a skinny Kate Moss in black and white looking sadly and hungrily into the lens of Calvin Klein ads. We, the ones born at the transition between Generation X and Millennials - we were there! In terms of perfume, the 90s brought about a paradigm shift. The boundaries of the 80s between permed, blue-eyed shadowed ladies' (Linda Evans, Morgan Fairchild) and hairy-chested, mustachioed men's scents (Tom Selleck, Jürgen Hingsen) were abolished. Aquatics and other fresh scents took over the market, and then came - bam! - CK One, one for all, unisex, crazy! That was a gamble. Uproar. New. The 90s became the decade of Klein's triumph - Obsession, Escape, Eternity, and of course Kate Moss and Marky Mark in underwear - which only culminated with Zladdi and Jürgen at the turn of the millennium. As I said - we were there! It is understandable to request a fitting olfactory soundtrack for a revival. However, many of the scents from the 90s are still available for purchase, reformulated or not, so there is little to no need for a 90s quote, especially one as bland and loveless as this. The olfactory essence of the 90s has a high recognition value, and it therefore requires a certain care and a moment of surprise to function in the present. Because why would I want to listen to a lame remix of Mr. President's legendary Coco Jamboo when I can download the original from 1996? Exactly. I confess that this test and this review only came about because someone slipped a sample of CK Everyone into my bag. I was tempted to throw it away unopened but then let my curiosity (and admittedly a certain pleasure in the expected disaster) take over. What I had in my nose was a loveless and remarkably boring 90s wannabe ginger shower gel something scent with fortunately low longevity and projection, which I won’t remember by tomorrow. I briefly thought about checking out Coco Jamboo again on YouTube. Maybe I’ll do that. Conclusion: the 90s are over. Deal with it.

After the citrus-fresh opening quickly fades away, nothing happens for hours. At night, unable to sleep, I suddenly perceive a delicate floral-creamy scent. Also, there’s… a little bit of smoke? I get the idea to sniff at my wrist and yes, that’s where the scent is coming from, it’s slightly spicy there too. Here I have - as has been the case more often lately - a fragrance that requires a bit more patience. The citrus-fresh opening is perfect for summer, while the predominantly floral-creamy rest is suitable all year round.

classically fresh, clear, clean, watery, lightly citrusy, and very lively to zesty. Not new, but the scent feels modern right away. A wonderful spring and summer fragrance. It gets better. I really don't think cK Everyone smells cheap at all.

It's actually quite a nice play on words to name the CK One flanker EveryOne. But unfortunately, that's where the creativity at Calvin Klein ends. Of course, it's legitimate to milk your cash cow with all its flankers until the last drop. EveryOne will not be the last in line, and Calvin Klein is certainly not the only brand that rides such offshoots to death.

In accordance with the spirit of the times, the original has been toned down: CK Everyone is now vegan, made from natural ingredients, and comes in recyclable packaging. Even the perfumer has been reused. The scent has always been gender-neutral, so there wasn't much to change. The fragrance is - especially in the base note - unmistakably reminiscent of the original.

"Calvin Klein" is known for casual fashion and lifestyle fragrances. There is a whole range of "Ones" in different scent directions, colors, and shapes. There’s something for everyone. While these "fragrance waters" may not shine with exclusivity, they are always good for a whiff of pleasant scents.

When the older brother appeared on the fragrance stage in 1994, I was in London and young women were standing in front of every store spraying passersby with the scent. I fell in love with this unisex freshness immediately! With Everyone, CK has conjured up an extremely pleasant freshness once again.

I'm a little contrarian by nature, so a vitriolic review is guaranteed to grab my interest rather than turn me away. Moreover, I've discovered that perfumes which appeal to a broad spectrum of people are sometimes bland and uninspiring to my rebellious nose, whereas a good "stinker" is bound to possess some distinctive quality in order to have inspired so much venom. However, in the case of Spellbound I think there is something more afoot than mere differences in taste. As Sherapop touched on in her review, Spellbound is so gluttonously rich in the resin department that it lends itself much more to judicious dabbing than spraying. In addition, there may be a variation in formula between the EDP sold in spray form and the perfume available only in non-spray flacons. The topaz-colored mini that was generously gifted to me contains a bang-on, startlingly realistic carnation note that makes me suspect that it was manufactured before the draconian IFRA regs all but did away with eugenol and iso-eugenol. While I understand that many people dislike carnation in fragrance because they find it medicinal or they associate that clove smell with a trip to the dentist, I look at it as an effective way of balancing all the gooey resins and heady white florals in Spellbound with a little piquancy. The cardomom is also a nice addition for the same reason. The top notes out of my mini are either different from the EDP formula or partially deteriorated, because all I detect is a mellow, liqueur-like peach note absent the lemon and other notes listed. All in all a fairly quiet opening, followed by the carnation blooming atop the white flowers. Most prominent among these is a creamy tuberose that is so restrained that I have to wonder how Turin could find this perfume "frightening to horses" while praising my beloved but bombastic Fracas. Aside from the aforementioned resins, the base notes feature a good sandalwood and a smidge of vanilla that would seem pathetically weak by today's sugary standards, but is enough to satisfy my underdeveloped sweet tooth. Sillage was surprisingly modest, although the longevity seems quite good. If you haven't tested Spellbound and aren't averse to a dose of clove/carnation, do make sure to seek out the perfume in the dabber flacon instead of the EDP. You might find yourself pleasantly surprised, as this fragrance is beautiful and well-behaved as long as it isn't sprayed.

Resin heaven or resin hell? That is the most pressing question posed to the perfumista mind by Estee Lauder SPELLBOUND, which abounds in opoponax and benzoin, making this elixir a perfume at any concentration! In order to stand a chance of being appreciated rather than abhorred, SPELLBOUND must be applied one drop at a time, for the line demarcating resin heaven from resin hell is a thin one indeed, very easy to cross, and it is impossible to turn back without a long hot bath. A true litmus test for resin tolerance--and appreciation!--SPELLBOUND is bound to capture your attention with its deep dark spiciness infused in thick, viscous, lusciousness! So spicy and strong that my perfume mini will suffice for the rest of my life. To my nose, the civet does not even begin to compete in this composition with the cardamom, allspice, and heavy florals...

Spellbound has managed to transcend past the boundaries of being too much. I never thought I'd see the day when I'd call something too floral or too complex, however that day has come. It's not repulsive, but it's not something that I can smell for more than a few seconds without feeling a headache coming on. Some love this fragrance for its spicy and powdery carnation note, however I much prefer Billet Doux by Fragonard for my spicy carnation fix. In a way I find this fragrance far too aggressive, particularly with the sweetness which smells like golden syrup smoothering a bunch of loud flowers. Don't get me wrong, I love big, bold scents. Classics like Must de Cartier, Arpege, Youth-Dew and Miss Dior are right up my alley. However, I get the opinion that Spellbound is trying too hard to be a big, bold floral scent, reminiscent of the florals from the 80's. I have tried for the last few hours to find something about this fragrance that I like, but I am failing miserably. Perhaps I could say that the lasting power is impressive, and the sillage quite powerful. If I had to pin-point exactly what it is that turns me off this fragrance, I'd probably blame the peach and apricot notes. It's the same nauseating, syrupy peachiness that I experienced in another powerhouse, Tresor by Lancome. Regardless of my dislike for this fragrance, I have seen many buying this fragrance over Estee Lauder counters in recent years. I don't dispute that there are lovers of Spellbound out there. I just hope that they wear this fragrance sparingly.

Ok i'm no Roger Ebert or Gene Shalit Because they Review Movies and their professionals this is a copycat Fragrance to Estee's Cinnabar and Paloma Picasso's Tentation in my opinion maybe except Tentations has more of a gardeniac syrupy cinnamon like melody but neverless copying off each other. it starts off the same a predictable Burning Cinnamon fire with a Cliche of woods and Spice leftovers. the most this will make you feel like a Jaded reviewer in the whold wide world. it has no Originalty to it. *Yawns*

Good god. I just tried this in a department store. I’d never smelled it before. It smells like the active ingredients of a chemical, medicinal balm that hasn’t yet been dosed with masking fragrance in order to be sold commercially. And, quite unfortunately for anyone nearby, linear. Sophia Grojsman?!

I am not sure I understand the high rating of Spellbound… This is one of Estee Lauder’s fragrances, that I do not agree with. The mix of Pimento and Coriander is simply too much for me. And the flowers do not help. It turns screechy/sour in my nose and on my skin.

SHE lived alone on the 3rd floor of our apartment building. SHE liked to wear high heels that were always a bit higher, skirts that were always a bit tighter and shorter, and tops that were always a bit more snug and "revealing" than what our internal "decency police," represented by the retiree M., allowed.

It was May 1992. I had just gotten my driver's license, bought my first own car (Toyota Corolla), and regained my dress size 36 (after the 3rd child), so I had to reward myself somehow. Off to a shopping trip to Dresden, the first big drive alone, in my own car. Proudly puffed chest!

....a beautiful fairy named Estee strolled through her enchanted realm behind the seven mountains among the Lauder dwarfs in her magical fragrance park. She admired her little apricot trees, her magnificent rose bushes, her fields full of lushly fragrant carnations, vanilla, and daffodils. When she arrived at the mirror lake, she performed a beloved ritual.

This classic from Estee Lauder can stir emotions - both positive and negative. A so-called "Love or Hate" fragrance. Luca Turin's wife Tania Sanchez wrote in their jointly authored, now legendary fragrance guide: "Drives away horses. Gets worse," and gave this perfume only a single ridiculous star.

Years ago...This perfume was so disappointing to me. I had hopes it would smell as heavenly as a pink mimosa tree. The scent was minimal and fleeting, not lasting even an hour with zero sillage. It was definitely not worth the price. I haven’t bought another Kenzo perfume since, either.

This is a very fine fragrance that leaves a clear, beautiful, and clean impression without appearing even the slightest bit sterile. Since I have a lot of contact with people at work, this gentle, unobtrusive scent is perfect for that. On my wrist, it lasts all day and takes me away into gentle, calm realms for a few moments whenever I take a sniff.

To be honest: I sprayed this fragrance on my wrist and... nothing! I smelled absolutely nothing. Slightly panicked, I sprayed another fragrance on my other wrist and could perceive it quite clearly. So my nose is functioning just fine. It's just that the fragrance is nonexistent for me. After about an hour, I could finally detect a slight freshness, like having just showered. Conclusion: if someone really wants to use a "fragrance water" but doesn't want to smell like anything, this is definitely a good choice.
The perfume starts off very nicely; it is fresh and sweet, nothing special but quite pleasant. However, then a not very prominent, but still clearly noticeable synthetic note comes through. baahh

A "solar oriental" - what's that? Well, Coty/Calvin Klein use this expression in their cardboard-sample text. Suppose they wanted to create a new sub-genre. Did they succeed? I can clearly smell the "solar" - component, but I'm not sure about the "oriental". Some people compare "Reveal" to Womanity, but while the latter is much stronger and salty-sweet (think of the notorious caviar-note), "Reveal" is salty, slightly flowery (iris) and woody. The iris is quite beautiful and together with the salty top note, the impression is one of a warm, enveloping floral woody gourmand. There is some cashmeran in the drydown, but it isn't overpowering. Staying-power is fine with about 5 hs on my skin. Please note that "Reveal" smells much better on skin than on paper/fabric ( a real skin-scent!). One of the better mainstream fragrances of 2014. Added bonus: "Reveal" comes in a beautifully designed bottle.

The first few minutes are very reminiscent of sea water... the salt, the minerals, the algae and the fish... but it doesn't smell BAD or "fishy"... all the things you love about the ocean smell without being too sour or weird. Just aquatic and briny. After about 30-60 minutes the brininess subsides and it becomes a powder scent, orris root and creamy sandalwood. This stage is so different from the initial stage it almost felt like a different perfume... hints of Infusion d'Iris or Cashmere Mist, that same feel. The dry down came about 8 hours after application and was hands down my favorite part. This was all ambergris and it was magic. It was like a piece of driftwood with hints of vanilla and salt. Amazing. How could they discontinue this masterpiece? It is everything you could want from an ocean scent and everything you could want from a warm powder skin scent as well. I wore it on dates because it felt like a sensual secret weapon, seductive without being obvious.

This is a salty/peppery perfume which does not remind me of Womanity since it misses the fig note. Anyway, this is a perfect summery perfume, quite unusual, long lasting with a very heavy bottle. I would say that I really like it, as most CK perfumes, this smell is very high class. I will use it more during spring and summer. Good job Ck.

Vanilla, vanilla, vanilla.All I get is a plastic chemical vanilla.Over-sweet, not salty at all.A strong chemical something that supposed to be a perfume.Shame.I wanted to like this. Sorry Reveal lovers but this perfume just don't work on me.

This is all about the "wood" and the "pepper." With those, and its slightly sweet tinge, it at first gave me the impression of something I'd never encounter in nature - like nitrous oxide at the dentist's office. It wasn't horrid but I had to talk myself into giving it a second try. (I generally give scents a second try unless I just abhor them.) Again, I found this "peppery" "wood" not entirely unpleasant but absolutely untouched by nature. Or, at least, the nature that we have here on Earth. I'm certain that this clean, impersonal scent is how corporate conference rooms smell on Mars.

Niche appealing designer for a sand/salt impression with a powdery iris twist and a traditional amber accord (vanilla-labdanum-benzoin) that helps the “cashmere” fantasy note, but it is definitely not Cashmeran alone if at all present (which is a musky velvety ingredient). Fragrantica notes are misleading at this point.

Splashes of the sea water, it is not a Northern fresh sea water, but a very warm one, hot pebbles, sun is about to go down, salty air, your skin and hair are salty as well, there is no sunscreen, it is all about a nature. Beautiful scent with great performance hidden in a divine bottle of the budget brand. Underestimated as so many other nowadays.

Salt water and milky sandalwood. A vanillic warmth from the ambergris. Kitten fur, vetiver and somewhat fruity peppercorns. Every so often I get a sparkle of something that I'm certain is bergamot. There's likely some residual perfume on the stuff around me as I'm testing this at my desk, but I swear it's coming from where I sprayed the Reveal on myself.

The opening... Is rough. It smells like wet rocks covered with algae to me , but if you give it a few minutes (like 15-20 minutes ) then it develops into a salty metallic scent( which I personally love) then the musk vetiver take over and it is cozy and nice. This is a primarily a skin scent to me and that's why I can see it being worn in the summer.

Sometimes I feel like we're sitting in our ivory tower just waiting to dismiss the next new mainstream fragrance. It's like: I knew that right away. Yes, I was also very skeptical at first when I asked the girls at my old store what was new and they sprayed me with a pink ribbon of Reveal.

Once again a stroll through the aisles of a perfumery. Here a bottle, there a bottle... Yes, quite nice... No, thanks! Then I stand in front of Kenzo! First thought: Amour is great!!! Flower stinks!!! :-) But what do I see... a small cute label with the inscription NEW! Flower LÉau Originelle! Hmmm... Alright, we can "ruin" a strip with that. Thought + done... waited a moment... moved on... sniffed - SHOCK!!! Fresh, floral, distinctive. It is typical Flower but still so different. I can hardly believe it - I like it! Very much, in fact. Somewhat confused, I leave the perfumery and return to my workplace. I skeptically place the confusing strip on the windowsill and initially pay it no more attention. End of work... I pack my things and want to go home - the strip! Sniffing again... great - spring. Outside the sun is shining and I find the scent fits perfectly in this moment. The strip flies back onto the windowsill - taste confusion! 100% taste confusion. I drive home. 06:35 AM - I unlock my office... BOOOOOM! It smells so warm, floral, somehow clean-powdery. Very pleasant, not intrusive. Where is that coming from!? THE STRIP!!!!! Unbelievable... I practically bump my nose against the windowsill and sniff again. ... I leave the office. Surprised looks from colleagues. ... I return... in my bag KENZO Flower LÉau ORIGINELLE!!!!

Wood Mystique is definitely a release that harks back to Lauder's glory days. I have a long association with this company and their fragrances (even having worked for them briefly in my youth) and imho their fragrant efforts of the last 10 years or so have been lackluster and boring. I have two bugbears about this fragrance ... the first is the damn Pink Pepper in the top (thankfully short-lived and to my nose not a necessary addition) and secondly the obtuse addition of Raspberry. Who needs the fruit? Certainly not I! Other than that, this is a very nice attempt by Lauder to use the 'note du jour' of Oud. In typical fashion, there's also a healthy dose of Patchouli here but along with the Rose, Ylang and Leather (which are the most prominent notes to my nose) Wood Mystique becomes a viable player in the 'Mid East-esque' panoply of new (ish) fragrances. Truthfully, it's very Lauder but with a fabulous twist. I like it a lot!! According to some sources, it's specifically aimed at the Middle East marketplace and as such is not available elsewhere (indeed I bought my bottle in Dubai), but very recently I noticed that it is available at the counters here in SA. I have a few friends who work for the company and have been told by them that they absolutely insisted on being able to have the chance to sell it. They do some strange things (at least to my mind) at EL ... as the new Aramis release called Perfume Calligraphy is simply Wood Mystique in a different bottle ... very weird! The saving grace is that it feels as if the Pink Pepper and Raspberry have been eliminated in PC ... a good thing!! Both frags are marketed as unisex but I guess the execs over there realized their marketing blunder because the Aramis version is available everywhere ... go figure! Wood Mystique and it's twin Perfume Calligraphy are both possessed of great sillage and longevity and I find them to be the most exiting pair of fragrances by this company in a long time. I agree that the price of them is steep, but at least it feels as if one is getting what one has paid for here ... not something that will have to be re-applied every 3 hours.

Wood Mystique is a limited EL release and EL's first unisex fragrance. Wow, makes me want to try it! How about you? If Guerlain has a guerlinade, then EL has it's own accord too - because that is exactly what I sense on first sniff - Estee Lauder. It's definitely got a EL vibe to it, and it smells A LOT like Sensuous. Yet, it also smells a lot like Givenchy Hot Couture No 1 (original) due to the persistent berry note in the drydown. The fragrance is very long-lasting - in the 12 hour range on me. It's just on the femme side of unisex. I like Wood Mystique ... alot. And I am very happy to have a small decant of it. However, since I own both Sensuous & Hot Couture -- and get plenty of wear out of them -- I'm in no rush to spend over $200 on 100ml of a "smells like" fragrance. And other reviewers are reporting that Wood Mystique "smells like" other EL fragrances too. Will it come to the States? We'll see. Maybe then every one can have a sniffy at the EL counter. Until then, know that it's good, very very good, but you're probably better off spending 200 bux on somethin' else. ;)

True, I tested Wood Mystique shortly after its launch. That means I sprayed it briefly after a tour of the Munich perfume scene. Perhaps it was the unprofessional and obviously rehearsed chatter of the saleswoman, perhaps my overloaded nose, perhaps the secret sigh of "another Oud," or perhaps the expectation of experiencing something truly mystical - whatever it was, my judgment came quickly: Weighed and found wanting. Today, I can calmly reconsider my judgment with an unburdened nose, and the result - see title. Wood Mystique opens up to me with a peppery floral note that never feels sweet or girlish for a moment. It doesn't come across as soapy like for Ergoproxy. I rather have the impression that the pepper keeps the flowers in check, while on the other hand, the floral notes soften its sharpness. As it develops, W.M. reveals a side that bothers me a bit. Now, the already distinct Oud note combines with leather, patchouli, and cedar, and for a while, that’s too much of a good thing for me. It’s almost dusty-dry and a bit scratchy. Mind you, only for a while, because Oud quickly retreats to the background and could have been completely omitted in my opinion. The base that remains is noble, a bit smoky-leathery, and now I can understand why the fragrance ends up on various wish lists. Now, true elegance emerges that is equally expressive for any gender. My conclusion: I made it too easy for myself during the first test; Wood Mystique is an interesting fragrance. But to give it full marks, I would have to make compromises. The opening is just so-so for me, the heart note is already overshadowed by the Oud, and only when that has faded away is the - however very long-lasting - base truly desirable for me. Lauder has something to offer in every fragrance era and for every taste. Fresh-floral, clean-fresh, oriental, various chypres, and refined-feminine, so it is only logical that the Oud era also gets its corresponding perfume from Lauder. Even if I don’t like the fragrance 100%. I acknowledge that Lauder has not launched a wind tunnel fragrance here, and the selective sale in selected stores contributes to making Wood Mystique something special. Wood Mystique has thus opened a new chapter in Lauder's fragrance history and has not brought out the umpteenth flanker of an existing fragrance. I find that alone remarkable, and seen in that light, I consider the launch quite successful.

On the left a tree, on the right a tree, and in the middle - you won't believe it - another tree. But let's make a fairy tale forest out of this wonderful scent. The actors are its inhabitants. And since it's a bit spooky in the woods at night, we move the action to the night. Under a full moon in a - re-emerging - primeval forest. With everything that belongs: toppled giant trees, mixed forest, ferns, blackberry thickets, wood anemones at the forest edge, a river that can still meander naturally and wildly, ponds and pools. Allow me to introduce: Bubu, the owl, who can turn his head 180°. The Badger Family: Fnuffa and Fnuffus A gang of raccoons led by Al Capone. A beaver lodge with a beaver without a tail. A stag in a leathery loincloth. Pssst, the low-flying silent barn owl. Wolf pack No. 25 with the alpha pair Lupa and Lupus. 2,583,678.3 fireflies. 2 mayflies that survived the day. Old branches creak in the wind. In the distance, a little owl calls. There’s rustling in the underbrush. The water of the pond trembles: toads on land leave their territory. Bubu watches the night with glowing eyes, feeling a bit queasy; the last mouse was too greasy. Fnuffus has now knelt in front of the badger burrow for the 6th night. He has brought a huge amount of roses. Fnuffa shouts from the burrow: “What does she have that I don’t? Broader stripes? Shorter legs? Does she smell more badger-like?” Fnuffus has even persuaded the raccoons to raid winter gardens in the nearby small town and steal mimosas, ylang-ylang, and all sorts of exotic flowers, just to appease his angry badger lady. The raccoon gang has put on their black masks, and Al Capone is planning the next heist in the city. In the clearing, the wolves howl. Barn owl Pssst flies in quietly and brakes mid-air. She has heard something. “Alarm!” calls the quiet owl. Fireflies fly in and illuminate the dark forest. A van approaches. Loaded with trash and several men. As they begin to unload the trash, Bubu circles above them, spits out the remains of the fat mouse, and adds some intestinal contents on top. The badgers forget their quarrel and shove pine needles into the guys' pant legs. The stag lowers his antlers, wraps them in his leathery loincloth, and calls: “If I catch you here again, I’ll make you a second hole in your backside!” The wolves rush in, peppery, gray, noble. Lupus promises the environmental sinners that the fairy tale of “Little Red Riding Hood and the Wolf” will come true, and Lupa wants to turn the two “Him’s” into “It’s.” The beavers loosen part of their dam and wash the idiots out of the forest. The raccoons rummage out a stolen CD player and play “The Ride of the Valkyries.”

Every year, the question about my birthday wish arises, followed by the statement: "It's really difficult to gift you a fragrance." You can hardly believe it, but this problem existed even before Parfumo, as my collection has been quite extensive for a long time. Only the expectations for new additions have somewhat increased during my time here. So that my husband doesn't show up empty-handed on my special day, we once again visited the perfumery I trust yesterday. In the running were Wood Mystique by Lauder and Tardes by Carner (the latter was preferred by my husband). As soon as I applied Wood Mystique, I was completely smitten! I had expected another typical Oud creation, like many brands currently offer, but this Lauder behaved very differently. The fragrance started on my skin with a spicy-fine soapy note, which I hadn't anticipated. However, I tried to keep my growing enthusiasm in check, as the last Lauder fragrances weren't to my taste, and behind a beautiful top note, as we all know, a lot of dreadful things can hide. It then smoothly transitioned into the heart note. Here, a very elegant floral accord was created. To my surprise, the fragrance did not become cloying or sweet here either, but retained the fine soap from the top note as a counterpoint to the flowers. However, I wasn't ready to throw my doubts overboard just yet, so I spent the entire afternoon with it on my wrist, making sure not to miss any fragrance note. The Oud note, praised by the saleswoman, was truly embedded in an elegant-spicy base note, thus clearing away any last doubts. After about three hours, my wish was clear. It had to be the Lauder, and hopefully, it will be. The longevity was, as with all fragrances from this brand, outstanding. The sillage was pleasant and emphasized the fine character of the perfumes. I was quite surprised by the price of Wood Mystique! At €160.00 for 100 ml EdP, I wouldn't have expected that from Lauder. Apparently, they want to bring the image to the same level as their in-house line Tom Ford and also penetrate the high-end segment. If I don't receive the fragrance for my birthday, I will treat myself to it! Until then, it's a waiting game. Addendum: I don't have to buy it myself; I just unpacked it. :D

It is night, the sky is pitch black, and only rarely does the moon peek out from behind a cloud, casting its silvery glow over everything. I traverse a dark, densely overgrown forest, alone. My companions have long since taken the way back because this forest was too eerie for them.

Wood Mystique is my first unisex fragrance. I became aware of it here, on Parfumo, and after reading the mostly very positive comments, I thought this might be something for me, even though I am actually a die-hard women's perfume fan. Then it arrived, and what can I say, the disillusionment was great at first.

I must confess, I am really taken aback right now. Literally glued to my wrist with my nose, I am searching for the most fitting words to do justice to this wonderfully mystical dream even halfway. I am gasping for air... and continue to sniff. Again and again. Too mysterious, too mystical, too seductive, the almost hypnotic vapors of Wood Mystique sneak into my nose.

I've been circling around this one for a long time, but somehow we always missed each other. This time, however, the timing was right, as was the price and the contents of my wallet. It starts off strong with an almost black rose, or so it seems to me. One of those incredibly dark red, velvety types that pause just before turning black.

Mystical wood… a wood that is divine or mysterious? Full of riddles perhaps? Hmm… I, the freak, have to think of video games again, where such things often occur, especially in fantasy role-playing games. But of course, this is supposed to be a fragrance that emanates a mysterious aura from its wearer (the scent is unisex). Well, why not?

I've owned CK2 for almost 7 years and have yet to review it. I always thought it wasn't the right time and kept putting it off for another time. But now, that time has come. Firstly, rarely, but it happened, CK has released perfumes of niche, disruptive, counter-current quality. To name a few, Obsession for Men Eau de Toilette and CK One Eau de Toilette . And CK2 adds to this list with its mineral, powdery, and smoky contrasts. CK2 is another genderless perfume like CK One, but they are different. CK2 has an immediate dewy, maritime character, with salty undertones, pungent green wasabi leaves, light violet, mineral pebbles and woody notes, and unlike CK One, it is a scent that recalls a clean and idealised Zen garden. CK2 opens with an aroma that is hard to describe. I try to explain it to you, but it is an ineffable feeling. It's fresh, it's watery, it's spicy, it's mineral, it's ozonic, and metallic at the same time, salty with a bit of a citrus breeze too. Something rare and unique to me that I've never smelled in any other perfume. The citrus edge of the mandarin orange is subdued and mostly obscured by the horseradish root and violet leaves. If the green, watery freshness, with a metallic touch and that smell of freshly mown grass typical of violet leaves is something I'm used to, horseradish leaves me blown away, even if the taste of wasabi is familiar to me. Wasabi is most commonly known as the spicy green paste featuring horseradish and served as a condiment to all forms of sushi, so rich in sulphur. Those who have eaten sushi know the mustard, peppery, horseradish flavour it can have. As far as I know, a few fragrances feature wasabi; you can count them on your fingers. It's hot, with no harshness and no lasting burn, with green, herbal, and pure flavour. The heart is made of stone, and I'm not kidding. This synthetic element smells like pebbles mixed with floral and powdery accords of soft rose petals and vivid iris rhizomes, creating something extraordinary together. It reminds me of the smell of wet stones drying in the sun, a tad dusty and a bit dewy. Overall mineral, I can see why some people relate it to pebbles. Underneath, I catch some nuances of watery flowers, which remind me of white jasmine and pink peony. This middle phase is filled with aquatic, floral, and a subtle powdery scents. Iris and rose to create a classic bouquet with a unique hint of wet cobblestone. The underwater and mineral notes balance out the florals, stopping them from being too strong. The dry-down is relatively quiet, with grassy and earthy vetiver notes, smoky incense and creamy sandalwood. Natural and fresh accords fuse to create a contrasted connection. A shadow of muskiness blends with a dry woodiness and a wateriness. Moreover, the distinctive pebble or mineral note lasts a bit in the base. If I smell the blotter after many hours or even days, I catch the airy, clean, and watery accords. It has a good amount of staying power, strength and spread for a watery and airy scent. It's great for summer, hot days, and casual occasions, especially with its floral and citrus notes. I'm happy to wear it in an office setting as it is not inappropriate and always puts me in a cheerful mood. With my male skin, it wears neatly. This emulates the smell of wet river pebbles, and it's incredible how the master perfumer has captured it. I'm basing my feeling on a bottle I've owned since July 2016 (BC 6081, PD 2016-03-21) -Elysium

When I first sprayed CK2 by Calvin Klein I didn't think much of it. The initial blast was very citrusy, ozonic and metallic. I stuffed the scent strip into my handbag and carried on with my day. Revisiting this fragrance again, I am amazed by how much it has developed. It's more powdery and floral on second sniff, like a subdued floral aquatic. I may be unpopular for saying this but I actually enjoy CK2 far better than CK One. The metallic accord remains throughout the entire composition, however it is by no means unpleasant. CK2 smells very clean and clinically fresh to my nose, almost like the scent of undiluted laundry detergent. CK2 would make the perfect Summer scent especially if paired with a casual t-shirt and blue jeans. At this present point in time this fragrance is leaning more towards the feminine side, especially seeing that I can smell lots of powdery violet leaf and peony emanating from my paper strip. I am however curious to see how CK2 wears on a man. I find this fragrance to have excellent staying power and moderate sillage. It's a first in a long line of CK One flankers that I actually find interesting.

Scent The scent of CK2 is too soft and light. Just a scent of a bit citrus on it and its nice scent. The middle and base notes almost none. Longevity The longevity is quite low. For non 4-seasons countries, this fragrance scent is suit for internal use especially night. The longevity scent of this fragrance is around 3-4 hours. For the 4-seasons countries, the longevity is around 5-6 hours. Performance The performance is quite low. The scent projection is only from the top notes and its for a moment. Seems like more to acqua fragrance or eau de cologne. Sillage The sillage is almost none. Uniqueness The uniqueness of this fragrance is on the bottle. Bottle Design Upside-down vaporisateur fragrance bottle is the attraction of CK2.

First of all, the bottle is a trip. It looks like a lovechild of a Magic 8-Ball and one of those fancy oil lamps that your grandma used to have. But hey, let's not judge a fragrance by its bottle. The scent is actually pretty solid. It's got a fresh, citrusy vibe with some spicy notes thrown in. It's not gonna blow your mind, but it's definitely not gonna stink up the joint either. The longevity is decent, so you can rock it all day without having to reapply.

I am one of the people that is sad this is discontinued. Yes, it smells far from something natural, but it´s so unique. Sharp wasabi and violet leaf at first whiff and then it settles more into a cold, aquatic rose. CK2 lasts very well on me, but I really recommend spraying it on clothes and hair, it will stay there for quite a while. I gave away the remainder of my bottle to my friend who needed it more than me. I don´t know if I would wear it anymore, but I´d surely give it a sniff once in a while.

A rather obnoxious, sharpish scent that smells like hairspray. It has a pleasant floral-fresh-soapy side, but it's overshadowed. I can see why they discontinued the fragrance. The longevity is legendary, it easily lasts three days after being sprayed on paper.  of my perfume reviews at The Scent Stories: thescentstories.substack.com

My dear Calvin, I never thought you would come out with something like this again! A mind-blowing surprise & a great fragrance. Yes, I dare say it: a worthy, modern, lovely successor to the classic CK1. It borders on blasphemy & I’m pinching myself every 2 minutes, but that’s how it is.

Hardly had it hit the market, and it was already in my collection. Almost untested. And although I have worn it in the meantime, strangely, I still can't say exactly how I like it. I'm waiting for real warmth or even heat, as it seems to me that it will develop best then. Apparently, everyone smells something different with this fragrance.

I really like the fresh scents from Calvin Klein. Especially the huge CK One line with all its flankers. The fresh CK fragrances may not be the best in terms of performance, but they are simply affordable, not overwhelming, and just pleasant. This CK2 was on my radar/wishlist for a long time.

I am a person who often connects scents with poems, songs, lines. The dream world has always been my daily companion, and my memory works at full speed. Something is quickly associated, diverted somewhere. When I smell something, it brings something up in me. Immediately, a thread, a line to something is sought and usually found.

It's not necessary. This fragrance is just a flanker that practically shares all the attributes of its "father" (L'Eau par Kenzo pour Homme); it is fresh, natural, and fruity, perhaps a bit more aquatic than its father. If you have this one, you don't need the father anymore, and vice versa. There have certainly been much worse flankers, and this fragrance does bring a few new aspects (yes, "this fragrance," the full name is really too long for me) to the table. As with most other Kenzo fragrances, it's a clear recommendation for those who like it fresh, natural, and unobtrusive, without the associated scent being banal or bland. Kenzo always delivers. I like Kenzo fragrances.

Estee Lauder and myself have had our ups and downs. Only recently I have become aquainted with, and fallen in love with her Sensuous range, and now I'm experiencing the same kind of feeling all over again with her exclusive Private Collection. Tuberose Gardenia is utterly breath-taking. I'm so fussy when it comes to white florals, yet this fragrance leaves me feeling content and at peace with the world. The secret lies with its beautiful floral smoothness and somewhat glamourous feel. The white floral notes compliment one another beautifully. Gardenia, tuberose, orange blossom and lily, although quite moist and green upon first application, settle so elegantly on the skin in a rather creamy fashion, that makes me feel like an ancient Goddess in all her golden splendour. There is a slight medicinal characteristic in this blend, however I don't find it particularly off-putting. I much prefer Tuberose Gardenia over the more "natural" white floral offerings from niche houses. A mild, vanillary sweetness and soft woods, combined with the white floral bouquet, evokes a strong sense of luxury. I wore Tuberose Gardenia to a romantic dinner date a few nights ago, and was flabbergasted by how attracted my man was to my perfume. He went so far to say that I smelt like an angel. I must admit, that his reaction may be due to its floral femininity and cuddly nature. It would actually make a perfect choice for a bride on her wedding day. The longevity and sillage are superb, which adds an extra star in terms of rating. I am truly enraptured by Tuberose Gardenia. It is everything I hoped it would be and more. I can't wait to get my hands on a full bottle.

The gardenia at the opening of this perfume smells remarkably like the real deal. In the topnotes, the gardenia and the tuberose circle each other at a short distance, but each remains distinct. The topnotes, though, have one of the shortest half-lives ever found in perfumery. Very soon, a blended white floral with a large tannic note becomes dominant. The white floral is smartly non-specific. It remains unidentifiable, but gives a rounded, creamy quality that harkens back to the gardenia of the topnotes. I can’t quite make out whether the tannic quality and the creamy aspect of the floral balance or oppose each other, but I suspect that this duality is what holds together the almost ghostly frame of the gardenia illusion that lasts into the drydown. What started as an olfactorealistic gardenia note in the opening becomes an abstract distillation of a few of the elements that were apparently used to compose the gardenia note. There is a creaminess that suggest texture and the feel of umami that suggest a taste. We witness that taking apart of the gardenia that we’re given at the outset. The gardenia doesn’t fall apart, it is stripped before our eyes (noses.) The perfume transitions from a rather forceful prettiness to a tight-lipped handsomeness. An amazing exercise, and a compelling scent.

The show opens with Tuberose in the blue corner. She stands first in the ring, allowing me to enjoy her true beauty. I bask in her full splendour, the heavy, creamy scent, and I am carried away to tropical places, filled with sunshine and blue skies, the air sweet with the aroma of white flowers. This glorious bliss lasts for a good 5 to 10 minutes. I have to admit, I am a fan. But then Gardenia makes her entrance, taking her spot in the red corner. She jumps into the ring with a blast; she is strong, aggressive, sharp, bitter even, demanding all the attention. And she gets all the attention, her presence commands all eyes on her, making me forget that Tuberose was the queen of the show until just a moment ago. This makes me realize that I am not a big fan of Gardenia. I like her when she is shy, subtle, remains in the background where she doesn't stand out and blends harmoniously with the group. It is at this point that I think that I don't want to be a witness to something this ugly, so I decide to leave the stage (my arm) and let those two ladies fight it out between themselves, behind closed doors (under my sleeve). Yes, I am a coward, I flee the scene. After a few hours, curiosity gets a hold of me, I want to know the results. Slowly I open the doors, afraid of the carnage I might encounter. It is quiet inside, and I am thrilled to find my lovely Tuberose still standing. She is weakened, but still there, dominating Gardenia, who probably used all her energy in her powerful entrance and ended up being trampled on all over. I was rooting for Tuberose, and she won the battle, so it's all good in the end, but I am not sure that I want to see such a violent fight again. I probably won't watch the re-broadcast.

I've learned that my nose/brain doesn't always respond well to tuberose. If it's only used as an accent, it's fine, but with something very tuberose forward, I either interpret something cinnamon, or it makes me sick (that wasn't fun to experience). Unfortunately for me, Private Collection Tuberose Gardenia made me sick my third use of my sample vial. It's a very pricey fragrance, even on the grey market, so I recommend trying it out before committing yourself to a significant volume. Since I appear to be an outlier, I am going to refrain from rating, best of luck to you!

Estee Lauder Private Collection TUBEROSE GARDENIA is a relatively simple floral perfume to my nose. Although a number of flowers are present, the most salient by far is the gardenia, which is neither very creamy (as in Marc Jacobs' presentations) nor very sharp (as in Chanel GARDENIA, among others). The gardenia in this composition strikes me instead as quite dry, which may be a result of some of the other flowers in play, especially neroli. The tuberose is much less pronounced, so if I were to name this creation, I would have called it GARDENIA TUBEROSE, rather than vice versa. In any case, although this is a perfectly fine floral composition, I do not personally feel that it is better than the less expensive gardenia-focused fragrances available for considerably less money, so I won't be actively attempting to add this one to my collection, though I'm sure that I'd wear it, if I happened to have a bottle!

Being a tuberose lover (my love for the flower came first, after I discovered the note) I would say this perfume is more about gardenia than about tuberose. That alone makes it a second choice for me but I think this is a subtle composition with Lauder's quality: good materials with good and long lasting dry down. Quite a moderate sillage in this case for my skin.

This fragrance has two faces. The opening hits you hard; it is so bombastic, piercingly green, cool, and expressive, as if a greenhouse filled with greenery has exploded and the pieces are flying around you. At this point, I must caution against unfamiliar scents, otherwise, you might end up like me, nearly in a coma...

When I look again at the adjacent section "Users who like the aforementioned fragrance also often like:", I see many of my favorites. Can I then assume that the gardenia tube fits seamlessly into this list? Let me say this upfront: Not really. The scent is not for me, period.

What, still NO review for this beauty?? One of the most beautiful tuberose scents in the WORLD for my nose at least :)! Tuberose and lilac smell balsamically intense together.. Creamy and natural here is also the gardenia (not sharp at all like in some other gardenia scents) A little orange blossom I can still sniff out with a lot of imagination, jasmine yes!
Hey you sniffers, today I'm writing "something" about "some" fragrance again. Today it's about the scent "Tuberose Gardenia" from the Private Collection by Estee Lauder.

It has taken me about, let's see, fourteen years to figure out Calvin Klein CONTRADICTION, but I do believe that I just had a breakthrough: this perfume is an aromatic pseudo-chypre! This evening I decided to pull out from the back of my armoire the long languishing cylinder hiding quietly in its sleek matte aluminum sheath, having been reminded of its existence by a soothing eucalyptus-spearmint bath courtesy of the BBW Aromatherapy line. Since I even used the eucalyptus hair conditioner, which remains fragrant long after rinsing, my compatible perfume choices were severely limited. But then it popped into my mind: Calvin Klein CONTRADICTION, the only perfume in my collection with a significant eucalyptus component. There's probably a reason why perfumers do not often reach for eucalyptus, and the mixed reception to this creation, the sole member of the classic CK collection to have been discontinued (at least to my knowledge...), may have a lot to do with it. CONTRADICTION is so unexpected and just plain weird that I strongly suspect that were it poured into a Serge Lutens bottle with a new label slapped on, say, NUAGES VERTS-GRISATRES, it would be sought out and perhaps even worshipped by countless niche-ees (no, not Nietzsche, though my understanding is that he did spend some time in Eze, along a path that I myself walked to Grasse—so who knows? Perhaps he, too, really loved perfume and his pilgrimage to the environs of Eze led to the perfume capital of the world as well? On ne sait jamais.) But I digress... While coming to terms once again with CONTRADICTION, the donning of which is always an event in itself because it is so very ODD, it dawned on my that the extreme eccentricity of this composition reminds me very much of SJP COVET. No, not the notes or even the structure of the compositions: the two are completely different. But they are united in their extreme, obstinate refusal to respect the orthodox genres of perfume, in addition to their fundamentally "challenging" demeanor. It takes some time to come to an appreciation of these perfumes. Those who are looking for instant gratification need not apply, because these creations are really quite demanding. I have no doubt that many a sniffer gave them a quick whiff and then summarily dismissed them, relegating them forever to their own private dustbin of olfactory history. In the case of CONTRADICTION, the orchid, lily, eucalyptus, and about a million other notes together produce an utterly unique creation, like nothing else I've ever smelled. Yet it's not the perfumic equivalent to a garbage pizza. No, not at all. An appealing chypre texture and strangely harmonic effect ultimately arise out of what might at first seem to be sheer cacophony. Surprise: I was delighted to discover just now (after having compared the two C's in my mind...) that the perfumer who produced this radically other perfume is none other than...drum roll...Ann Gottlieb: the creator of COVET! Brava, cara! I am truly impressed! Ordinarily, according to my own explicitly stated evaluation criteria (in my profile at Creednotes), I would only be able to give a thumbs up to a perfume in my collection which I had every intention of replenishing, but my 100ml bottle of CONTRADICTION remains one-third full after, well, fourteen years. No matter: I'm going to contradict my own evaluation scheme in honor of this splendidly original perfume.

You don't hear too much about Calvin Klein's Contradiction these days, as it is often overshadowed by newer releases like Euphoria, CK IN2U and CK One. While I don't find it to be anything overly amazing, I fear that it may be the first fragrance to be discontinued in Calvin Klein's current collection, which would be such a shame. Contradiction is a pleasant enough blend of delectable florals and powdery woods. The eucalyptus note in the heart, is possibly what causes some to refer to this fragrance as being metallic. I quite like the uniqueness of the eucalyptus note. I'm an Australian, from the country, so this particular note reminds me of home and the bush, which perhaps in turn makes me a fan. Escape for Men also gives me the same nostalgic feeling. There is a definite powderiness to this fragrance, which is a good or bad thing depending on each person's personal taste. One review of this fragrance on MakeupAlley, likened Contradiction to the scent of a warm photo-copied sheet. I quite like that description, I think it is very apt and truthful. I'm on the fence with Contradiction, while I like certain aspects of it, particularly the floral powderiness, the woodsy notes just don't work for me, neither does the lasting power which is relatively poor. After a while, Contradiction becomes tiring and somewhat generic. The eucalyptus and the odd paper smell, is what keeps this fragrance alive and different. Every now and then it shows some similarities to Armani She.

Eucalyptus… it really makes a difference. First time smelling I was intrigued by this unknown and very strange note. It made the whole scent smell like watermelon. I must say that I found it so interesting that I bought it. I have not worn it a lot of times since but this does not mean that it is a bad fragrance. It is close to your skin, and it lasts for 4-5 hours. And the scent is lovely. I think it is a great contribution to the perfume world. The top is a softly smelling bouquet of flowers. Very understated and delicate. It takes you gently into this strangely smelling eucalyptus note which is accompanied by jasmine and blackberries. We stay there for a couple of hours and finally we hit the base - lovely sandalwood and tonka bean with a whiff of musk. All in all a well composed fragrance. Beautifully done by Ann Gottlieb. The bottle is somewhat in the same spirit as a lot of other CK scents - but this has more character. I adore the minimalistic metal cylinder, which adds attitude to this - almost male impression - and the colour of the juice is so well fitted to this product. This is not a winner - it is an outsider with loads of potential. 51/365

And I do so with some statements in the previous comments. Of course, they are just as valid, because the evaluation of perfume is purely subjective; there is no objective truth. My personal perception of “Contradiction” is, however, different from that described by some other users here. Fleeting or barely noticeable? On me, “Contradiction” actually holds quite well, although that is rather rare for my skin. Eucalyptus? This note is mentioned, but in my opinion, it only gives this perfume a wintry freshness, without being clearly recognizable. “Contradiction” primarily comes across as floral-cool, rather bitter than sweet, and slightly woody to me. Perhaps even a tiny bit metallic. Horrible? No, I really cannot confirm that! I find this perfume very successful, distinctive, incomparable to any other perfume, and moreover, extremely suitable for business. For control-freak secretaries? I am neither (although I can only hope for the former. Given my frequent typos, I would be rather poorly suited for such a job anyway), but I still find the scent not inappropriate on me. Well, perception and taste are indeed highly individual... I also have the Extrait version of this scent as a mini. I cannot discern any significant differences in the fragrance composition compared to the EDT.

The name of Contradiction is absolutely fitting, and the scent is quite different from all other Calvin Klein fragrances, aside from the fact that, like many others from this brand, it is suitable for both men and women. I wasn't quite sure what to expect, but based on the fragrance pyramid, I anticipated a very floral and feminine scent. However, it is not that at all, at least not directly - which brings us back to the name, as the contradiction is indeed present here. First of all, Contradiction is surprisingly subtle. I initially tested it alongside two other perfumes and could hardly perceive it. I also thought it wouldn't last, but both assumptions were incorrect. While the scent is more of a quiet presence (only close-to-skin sillage), there is nothing to complain about in terms of longevity, and since I was approached about it multiple times - "Excuse me? THAT is Calvin Klein?!" - I can only say that this fragrance has personality and is noticed, even if it doesn't come across as blunt and obvious like some other perfumes. I find the indecisiveness between the feminine notes like lily of the valley, rose, and lilac and the more robust scent notes like eucalyptus and sandalwood very fascinating. Sometimes, Contradiction smells very businesslike (keyword: "office scent"), then again delicate and floral, and sometimes even spicy and more masculine (could there perhaps be leather in it?). Indeed, there are reasons why this fragrance has been around for so many years.

"Contradiction" is not entirely wrong, but "Confusion" might be more accurate. "Constant confusion" in my case is the best description. Because if the scent triggers something in me, it’s permanent irritation. From the first second until the moment I scrub it off with a lot of hot water and really toxic soap.

A few months ago, I received a voucher from Galeria Kaufhof and thought about what I could buy with it. As it is with an addiction, it also dominates purchasing behavior, and soon I found myself in the perfume department testing my way through the selection.

Contradiction - quickly translated - the contradiction. But it doesn't seem that contradictory to me at all. It has too few edges and corners for that. I find it rather mild and homogeneous. Not unpleasant, but not very expressive. Stylish is the word that comes to mind most.

Yes, that's right - a clean scent that isn't one - that's Contradiction. Contradiction is indeed contradictory, opposing, intriguing. Fresh and oriental, light yet seductive, clean and yet not. The fragrance has a certain dryness, similar to that of tea scents, but does not drift into an overly woody-dry direction.

This is actually a good fragrance except for the pear and eucalyptus in it. But it is precisely these notes that make Contradiction stand out and differentiate it from hundreds of other floral scents. The fragrance is floral-creamy with a woody-herbaceous undertone.

Scentrack: Taylor Dayne - Tell It To My Heart n my opinion the best from the Totem line. Pure, original, unrestrained 80's in the bottle. Absolutely energetic to the limit. Vivid explosion of synthetic kitsch. Orange, mango, apricot, tropical-flavored chewing gum. A hybrid entity between fragrance and shower gel, for urban tribe. Unreal fragrance time machine. Yes, I really like this silly perfume. Rating: 7/10

I was fascinated to discover three differently colored Totem poles on the table of my fragrance dealer today. I reached for Totem Orange. I am interested in Native American culture - and even as a child, I read Hemingway's Indian Camp and his stories about visits to Indian tribes with a dreamy expression. I liked their way of thinking and living - always in harmony with nature. It is a mockery to call them "primitive" peoples. In the Native American medicine wheel, I am a sensitive Puma, and in Western astrology, I am an equally sensitive Pisces. Both teachings complement each other perfectly. And the scent is also a combination of the elements. The light lemon blossom floats in the air - the sweet green vetiver sprouts from the ground. The warm, spicy prairie wind connects the two aromas into a whole. Well, the ingredients are manageable, but honest and easily graspable. This gives the fragrance a beautiful calmness and naturalness. Totem creates a contemplative connection between the restless human and the tranquil nature. A fragrance that I greatly appreciated today.

Yellow is chewing gum, lemon & vetiver. Blue is chewing gum, chemistry lab & rubber mat. So what does the orange totem pole offer? I would say it’s pretty much the exact mix of the other two colors. A bit darker than yellow, a bit more citrusy than blue. Cardamom chewing gum meets tonka cream, futuristic tea time & decorative orange. Nice in parts & still wearable, but definitely not a top scent for Kenzo. And that makes it clear that the entire line won’t really have a future. Nice idea, but largely a miserable execution. Yellow is worth considering, though. I’m sorry I can’t create lengthy comments with rhymes, metaphors, or vivid imagery about the scents - but honestly, some fragrances just aren’t worth discussing much! Bottle: even in orange, the opposite of beauty. Sillage: keeps a low profile. Longevity: only 6 hours is the barely longest of the trio! Conclusion: Orange has nothing to say, gave me nothing. But the direction (chewing gum + tea) of the totem line is drawn most clearly... whether that’s a good thing is questionable!

Okay, this time I couldn't come up with anything better for the title,... oh well,... Yes, these fragrances from Kenzo really entice you to test the perfume, as the totem design looks quite interesting. Unfortunately, the scent turns out to be weak and below average, leaving you a bit disappointed afterward. However, this scent doesn't start off too badly before it becomes somewhat trivial. The scent: The beginning is very citrusy, but also sweet and quite pleasant. It is supposed to smell like lemon blossom, but to me, it smells more like a delicious, slightly sweet synthetic mandarin and grapefruit. This impression lasts for a while and, as I said, smells good. The vetiver is only very subtly present and hardly detectable. Without the fragrance pyramid, one wouldn't even think of this note. However, after about 1.5 - 2 hours, the scent starts to smell even more synthetic and gives the impression that it is just a shower gel with a fruity-citrusy note. The initially pleasant magic has been lost. Additionally, there is something sweet, a bit of amber or musky, or something similar in that direction. The longevity is below average and lasts about four to five hours. The sillage is good at first, then drops to an average level. Since I haven't tested the blue totem yet, I can only say that both the longevity and the sillage are significantly better than with Totem Yellow. The bottle is interestingly designed and, as the name suggests, looks like a totem. The bottle is dark blue and features an orange T as a symbol, a circle, three stacked bars, and a triangle. The cap, which is slightly transparent, complements the design of the totem. The bottle is very handy and looks chic. Totem Orange is a nice, simple, but synthetic summer fragrance that seems to be more suitable for younger people, and is rather trivial after a good start. At around 50 euros for 50 mL, I find it a bit too expensive, considering that the scent is actually just average. A test is not necessarily required, only if one should be interested. You don't miss anything with this scent.

When I became aware of Totem Orange, the scents were just being discontinued, and I was generously given the testers (no one was fighting over them). Yellow wasn't really my thing. Blue was more to my liking. The pineapple reminded me of Les Enfants de Soleil (it has a different name now....). And when I was about to head out for a date, I grabbed Orange and doused myself in it. Then it was all over for me! I had never looked into the ingredients, and the information here is quite sparse, but what enveloped me was insane! An above-average lasting, initially tingling fresh top note, even a bit biting, followed by a soft base note with balsamic hints that accompanied me all evening. We even went to a club, and with the rising temperature, this scent just got better! And it was the first fragrance for which I received compliments from colleagues (in my business, we all know beautiful, rich, amazing scents, and just like opulent furs or the finest fabrics, no perfume in the world really blows us away anymore....). And when I truthfully answered the question about the perfume, they initially didn't believe me but then couldn't stop being amazed. Admittedly, the bottle looks cheap, and for a Kenzo scent, it's not appealing enough, but if any niche fragrance brand had released this composition, it would have become an insider tip.

Alliage is the greenest of all perfumes. In a certain way related to classics like Bandit and Cabochard, Alliage is the opposite of sweetness, the epitomy of coolness. I think it would make a fantastic male fragrance, too, it's crisp, uncompromising and - above all - the work of a genius! I hope they'll never discontinue it.

At first glance, Alliage, one of the Estée Lauder line’s inexpensive mainstays might be considered simply ‘cheap and cheerful.’ It reads, “Sport Fragrance Spray” in a functional, rather non-stylized bottle. Not exactly sexy. But cheap and cheerful implies an innocent simplicity whose grinning surface advises not digging any further. On the contrary, I’d argue that Alliage is inexpensive but sophisticated and spectacular. One of the impressive set of perfumes in the stellar-but-cheap sweepstakes. Everyone seems to talk about Alliage’s notes, and I will as well, but briefly. I don’t get the peach. I don’t get the oakmoss. I do get a heavy green (loads of galbanum accented by vetiver) brightened by citrus rind oils (bitter orange, lime?) and florals. But since the green is already firmly in place, the floral tone is a clean, airy white jasmine bolstered by musk and what smells like rosewood. I’ve heard people lament the loss of a more heavily oakmoss-laden earlier version of Alliage, but I don’t miss Miss Moss. Alliage is wonderfully balanced just the way it is. The cool white florals seem a dry counterpoint to the sweet galbanum. And galbanum’s lasting chalkiness lines up perfectly with a resinous base that gives depth and a slow-moving quality. Myrrh? Incense? It all feels very languid and heavy-lidded. I don’t need the bitter green that moss might add. Consider Alliage’s sibling Devin by Aramis for that. Alliage has a cool quality that implies poise as much as temperature. Its cool impression is similar in to the effect given by mint/basil or camphorous components, but without their harshness or muscle-balm feeling. In cooler weather, Alliage feels forest-like, a bit moist. In my dry southern California heat, Alliage keeps its cool longer and more comfortably than any other perfume I’ve tried. It doesn’t blend with the skin. It’s more like a richly colored clothing accessory, like the perfect tie. It works as an accent and draws the nose’s attention. It doesn’t blend. I think this is how Alliage remains cool through drydown. Clean and green, not so much tart as a bit sharp. This is one of the few fragrances I wear to work as an RN in a hospital. It’s cool but not quite grass-like, not quite floral. It has wonderful endurance, but after the topnotes, mild sillage. I think it just reads as quality grooming products to my patients and colleagues. Again the price dilemma. In this case a happy one. Why does this cost so little? It sells at the same department stores that flog haphazardly brewed, blaringly marketed perfumes for 3-4 times the price. Alliage is a distinctive fragrance of high quality and name-droppable pedigree (Bernard Chant) that has been typically well maintained over the years by Estée Lauder. I could wear this forever (were I not so perfume-promiscuous, that is.)

It's quite strange with fashions: today, fragrances dedicated to women often smell like roasted almonds, marshmallows, and cotton candy, bright flowers and sweet berries, or alternatively like 'fruit-chouli' or 'gourmand-chouli'. Forty years ago, however, this would have been unthinkable: fragrances like Chanel's "Cristalle" and "No 19", Dior's "Diorella" and "Dioressence", or also Lauder's "Azurée" and "Alliage" were miles away from the sweet treats of our time. It seems that since then, the entire fragrance spectrum - both women's and men's fragrances - has shifted significantly towards the sweet-feminine side, after it clearly leaned towards the masculine side in those very 70s. What was marketed as women's fragrances back then would probably today be labeled with a 'pour Homme' tag, while the men's fragrances of those years - just think of 'Yatagan' - are now considered unbearable macho scents by many. Conversely, 'Dior Homme' in 1972 would likely have been launched as a women's fragrance and 'Angel' at best as a perfume for little girls. But well, times change and so does fragrance taste. 'Alliage' is now one of those fragrances that certainly would not be launched today, except as a men's fragrance. But even as such, it would hardly see the light of day, as two of its most important characteristics endanger its existence 40 years after its creation: on one hand, its unmistakable chypre structure and on the other, its deep animalistic penetration. The latter is simply completely 'out' today, while the former has basically not existed for some time. There are many attempts to save the genre, but with so far questionable success. All the great, old chypres are today mere shadows of their former selves, sometimes, however, quite beautiful shadows. So too with 'Alliage'. The fragrance lacks a bit of the depth and aura of days gone by; it appears more one-dimensional and less complex. Still, it is unmistakably 'Alliage': a lush, green chypre scent with powdery and animalistic nuances. In contrast to its counterparts from the early 70s, 'Diorella', 'Cristalle', or the slightly older 'Y', 'Alliage' never had their delicate, slender physique. It has always been of a sturdier structure, possessing muscles and an untamed strength, almost appearing rustic. Perhaps this nature explains the subtitle 'Sport Spray' much more than the supposedly intended suggestion that one - or rather, a woman - should wear the fragrance after sports. No, rather this fragrance has done sports itself, has been in the gym, and has undergone a lot of endurance training, because with one thing 'Alliage' has nothing in common: with the sport waters of our days. 'Alliage' is not worn after sports, or to use a more contemporary term: after the workout (one shouldn't wear any fragrance anyway - all the shampoos and shower gels are perfumed enough). 'Alliage' is best worn, but not necessarily, if one is a sporty person. Then the green, the powdery, the bitter and the herbal fit wonderfully, especially since the fragrance possesses a certain natural robustness that is in direct kinship to its masculine counterpart 'Devin'. 'Devin' itself is known to carry the subtitle "Country Cologne", which mainly refers to the use of strong pine notes. These can also be found in 'Alliage', but less prominently. Rather, they are accompanied by light floral and spicy accents, which always remain within the framework of a green chypre concept. 'Devin', on the other hand, slightly breaks this concept, or better said: the fragrance expands it - starting with a fresh-citrusy opening, through a spicy-green heart, to a leathery, almost oriental conclusion. 'Alliage', however, remains, as mentioned, a thoroughly green chypre in all phases, with the already described strong physique, much dry powder, and a creaminess that completely distinguishes it from counterparts like "Cristalle" or "Diorella", which float lightly, shimmering, and elegantly, while 'Alliage' stands firmly on the ground, connected to nature. With 'Alliage', Bernard Chant, like his colleague Germaine Cellier years earlier with 'Vent Vert', created an almost archetypal green fragrance - it hardly gets greener than this. Years later, Serge Kalouguine created a fragrance for Diptyque called 'Virgilio' (unfortunately discontinued), which was just as green, just as dry, and just as animalistic, but unfortunately, far from the refinement of the 'Alliage/Devin' duo. Nevertheless, the Diptyque fragrance had something; it was even more robust and had almost shamelessly animalistic exhalations - which, however, did not make it more wearable. 'Alliage', on the other hand, remains wearable at all times, unless the slightest animalistic hint is already too much. But anyone who has no issue with a little 'skank' in their perfume - and I belong to those who consider a bit of funk in a good fragrance essential - will have no problem with 'Alliage'. Still, even in its reformulated version, a truly great fragrance!

I bought Alliage a few years ago, quite spontaneously and as a substitute for Aromatics Elixir. But something bothered me, even though this Chypre has everything I appreciate. Alliage disappeared into the closet and one day I let it go. Now I received a sample, wanted to pass it on - I know you - but again and again, whenever I was preparing packages for other perfume lovers, this sample found its way back into the cookie jar. And then I decided to test it thoroughly. After all, I love Devin, the male counterpart. Here are my notes after two test runs: Green-bitter, fresh, herbaceous, the galbanum is prominent, with a slight smoky note, earthy, unique, stubborn, and a bit scratchy. Peach, lemon? Only very subtly. A very distinctive Chypre that makes me think of dark, damp forests, simply unmistakable. With the heart note, Alliage becomes more agreeable, but not ingratiating, just softer, milder. Something for fragrance lovers who are at peace with themselves, confident, because you either like Alliage or you don’t; there’s no “oh, it’s quite okay.” Sillage and longevity are very good, a Chypre for all seasons. And this scent is also “suitable for men” - just as Devin is “suitable for women.” My ordering finger could almost twitch now, because today I have grown into Alliage, but first I will finish my sample, then it might go on the wish list and then.... Because I just gave away/sold some fragrances and I already feel much better with fewer scents. Thanks to Turandot for the sample, but the most beautiful sample is Diorling, this scent is grandiose.

In the city of my youth (medium-sized and very West German both topographically and culturally), there were only three nightclubs back then, one of which was not really an option for musical and a hundred other reasons. One of the other two - small, dingy, and beautiful - always had 'Oldie Night' on Saturdays (or Fridays? That was so long ago...) and one of the songs that would fill the dance floor in seconds (the other was Heroes del Silencio's 'Entre dos tierras', but that wasn't an oldie) was 'Am Fenster' by City, already about twenty years old at the time. 'Once know, this stays forever…' That City was an East German band and the high popularity of the song in our Rhineland West Germany was a small miracle, we didn't know back then. We loved 'Am Fenster' because it was a soulful and passionate seven minutes, and the song had so much more 'meat on the bone' in its honesty and authenticity than the thin little songs of the (then) present with its terse yet all the more poetic lyrics. In between, City wove melancholic instrumental passages inspired by Southeast European folklore, represented by a heart-wrenchingly rough fiddle. Soulful and passionate, honest and authentic, sometimes rough - and so much more 'meat on the bone' than the thin fragrances of the present is (or has) also Estée Lauder's Alliage - basically a miracle that it still exists.
