A hit of very citric lemon and oakmoss which stays throughout the life of the fragrance, coupled with a floral drydown (I'm detecting a little hedione, or jasmin-like smell). This is very "green" and sparkling, hence the name Cristalle. It smells very very mossy and lemony acidic, almost giving the impression to me of walking through a forest with the trees and flowers still wet from the spring rain. To me it doesn't exude "freshness" because of the heavy oakmoss vibe, but I can see what other people mean when they describe it that way. Who would wear this fragrance? Well, anyone who likes "green" or "hesperidic" (i.e. slightly citric) scents... or those who like a little bitterness in their fragrances. On that kind of person it will be a holy grail fragrance. For me, I enjoy it (it's also completely unisex as an EDT), but I can't fit into it so easily. Overall... is it well made? Yes. Is it a classic? Yes. For everyone? Well, for those who like this type of scent... green, bitter, mossy, damp, citric and sparkling! Like rain dew on flowers and musty, moss-covered tree logs in the forest after a downpour of heavy spring rain. You've done it again Chanel... (to me) this is slightly disturbing, yet unmistakably unique!

Word on the street is that this fragrance in vintage form is sought after. Yes well the demonic and competitive side of me always tends to seize the opportunity when I have a chance. So I went to the store, where they have a BNIB Cristalle just minding her own business, looking for a good home. I'm pretty good at giving fragrances a good home so I gave her a try.Bad Move on my part. What the what? This crap is so overly citric it's pathetic. Who wears this stuff? One sniff threw me into a coughing fit and had me wheezing (I don't have asthma). Solidly sour and equally offensive, I knew there was no way I would reconsider. We had a brief moment, lasted about 15 seconds and I knew in my heart of hearts that this Vintage Chanel would have to wait for a different taxi because there is no way I'm giving her a ride home! I told her to take a hike! null of the listed notes were present, my nose only smelled bitterness. Sour, rancid lemons or limes. Nasty, just nasty. I carefully placed her back into her cardboard coach, and gave her a final salutation. Peace out my friend, don't call me, I'll call you.

Funny how smelling a fragrance can instantly place you on a timeline where you never existed. Fragrances in the 70s took time to gain popularity, especially if they were not widely available. I imagine this was very popular by the early 80s, because that is the vibe that I got when I sprayed this in the Chanel boutique. The age of the Power Woman. Big hair, big shades, bold colors, shoulder pads and pumps. Upon the first spritz, I swear I thought I heard Jessie's Girl by Rick Springfield playing in the background. Maybe it was Cyndi Lauper or Madonna? Cristalle like many other women's fragrances from this era were composed of heady florals and woody, mossy undertones. This fragrance has a sparkling opening, delivering a burst of white flowers but heavy on the hyacinth. The conclusion is a typical, but pleasantly cool powdery dry down. Dated? Perhaps, but very refined. During the 70s and 80s, this was considered modern. We millennials and later generations often turn our noses up at classic perfumes, but ask yourself... if you were of that era and living your life as an adult in the 80s, what perfume would you be wearing? I ask myself this question often and I always come up with Chanel Antaeus and Santos de Cartier.

I was six years old when "Cristalle" was born, twenty-six when we met, and forty-six when she moved in with me. Twenty years lay between these dates, and it had to be twenty years each time. When I was a child, no one wore fragrances like "Cristalle," not in the world I lived in back then - patchouli and musk were the notes that surrounded my childhood nose, regardless of whether their wearers were male or female, had long hair or short, beards or none at all. A little sandalwood and a lot of Avon belonged to my mother's olfactory repertoire, but no Chanel, no "Cristalle," and certainly no number 5. That was not her world, and thus not mine. Twenty years later, our worlds had diverged, and I had set out to conquer mine. I met people of all genders and colors, brown and white and black - people who lived with all their senses, people who were missing one or two. By then, I had also encountered Chanel, the Great, Beautiful, Overpowering in the form of Coco, "Antaeus," and number 5. Fragrances that made me shy, small and inconspicuous according to my self-feeling and certainly not mature enough for them. "Try 'Cristalle'!" I was advised. "It's a young Chanel, a fragrance for young women - the gateway drug into the Chanel world." That sounded good; I thought I could handle it. And I took a nose accustomed to "Senso," "Moschino," and the like, one that knew warmth, softness, gentleness... ...but not the austere, green clarity, the sugar-free morning freshness that rose from my skin. Tall, slim, and blonde, "Cristalle" appeared to me very classic and very cool, much more grown-up than I was, and certainly not "young." Designer jeans and a pearl necklace, hair shoulder-length and cut precisely, eyes bright and unmade-up, skin very fine. I felt myself shrinking - that was not me, I would never be that. Chanel was simply not my world; we would never find each other. I thought. Twenty years later again: A small bottle rolls out of a letter, sent by a friend who loves fragrances as passionately as I do. It is very small, the bottle, filled with golden yellow, "Cristalle" on the label. "You must get to know her - and you will love her!" says the accompanying letter. We know each other, I think - and hesitate. Is that so? Do we really know each other, "Cristalle," you and I? You are still cool and clear and noble in a quiet, unpretentious way - grown-up, yes, and serious, but not strict, not distant, not arrogant at all. Your feet stand firmly on green ground, sinking slightly into forest-soft moss. Your back is straight, your eyes bright and clear, your skin still fine and lightly crinkled around the gaze and the delicate mouth. You wander through woods and meadows, stand confidently on parquet, love sun, wind, and rain, spring flowers, soap, dark wood. You are calm, reliable, friendly-cheerful, hold back, are quiet, but not silent. I stand next to you and can also exist here; nothing makes me small or inconspicuous or mute. Have I grown and finally also become an adult? I feel good; I am well with you.

The many subtly airy scents that Edmond Roudnitska once created for Christian Dior have held me captive for over twenty years. Therefore, it is quite clear that I have always liked 'Cristalle,' which was briefly released in 1974 under the name 'Cristal.' For many years, a small bottle of 'Eau de Toilette' has found its way into my bathroom, albeit quite rarely.

I have already dedicated a statement to Cristalle, but this special Chanel deserves a comment - like so many other fragrances, I know, but perfume and time behave reciprocally proportional to each other for me.

Here I did something that one shouldn't really do as a perfume lover. The scent is often described as challenging, and yet I took the plunge and bought it blind. I find the listed fragrance notes very interesting, there are great reviews, and I already liked the bottle of "Pour Monsieur" extraordinarily well. And now I sit here, unsure if I can wear this fragrance.

It was 1984, I was 11 years old and got my first braces. Dr. H. - a very beautiful, blonde but completely aloof and cold woman (body temperature max. 29°C) - became a fixed part of my life every 4 weeks for the next 5 years and then once a year for check-ups. Admittedly... I didn't like her and had a very, very uncomfortable kind of great respect for her.

It is a testament to eccentricity and humor to name his first fragrance King Kong. But that is Kenzo! The love for nature, animals, flowers, and tropical rainforests is quickly evident in his creations. Colorful and cheerful is his fashion, always marked with a humorous wink. In 1980, Kenzo launched his first perfume, which for me is one of the most beautiful ever, because it is so quirky and yet so wearable. With King Kong de Kenzo, he takes us into his jungle of aromas. In a rainforest where something lives that wants to get to know us. Let’s take a look at who or what it is! King Kong de Kenzo begins its journey with fresh, airy, and light aldehydes, interwoven with gentle hints of clove. Not scratchy but very delicate and spicy. Various other spices sneak in that cannot be precisely identified. This gives the perfume more depth and makes it feel richer. Then King Kong begins to transform cautiously. It takes on green and subtropical traits. The banana comes into play. But these are not sweet, yellow, and fully ripe bananas that you smell. Quite the opposite is the case. It is the scent of unripe and green bananas. It smells somewhat as if you were to break this unripe banana in the middle, and the chlorophyll of the cracked peel spreads in the air and on the skin. A bitter-green scent that lays on the spicy foundation and permeates it. This green-spicy impression is further brightened by peppermint. However, it is not artificial peppermint that resonates there, but fresh and very realistic. As if you were to pluck the leaves from the bush and crush them in your palms. Everything smells incredibly real and natural. King Kong de Kenzo lingers in this stage for a long time before it sinks into a kind of green amber. A combination of warm amber and mossy, bitter-spicy oak moss. A base that unites and binds all previous notes. Mossy and green-spicy harmonies! Conclusion King Kong de Kenzo is so refreshing and so completely different. It is wild, cheeky, warm-hearted, spicy, lovable, and charming. King Kong picks you up from the spicy-soft ground of the rainforest and sets you on his warm and broad back. From there, he swings from vine to vine through dark green-brown vegetation. He climbs with you up the largest and most resinous tree in the whole jungle to the canopy. There he sits with you shoulder to shoulder on a green-brown and soft moss bed, munching on bitter-green bananas while the sun sets on the horizon of the rainforest in warm golden and harmonious tones. King Kong is not loud and frightening. He is friendly, warm-hearted, and very protective. He is not necessarily made for the cold. He needs it warm and tropical to thrive. He is friendly to all people, whether man or woman, and accompanies them for up to six hours. Then he gets tired and retreats. King Kong de Kenzo is the essence of nature in a very unusual form. He may be a relic, but one of the most remarkable, coolest, and lovable of his time. And if you encounter a King Kong, the saying really holds true.... No fear,....he just wants to play!

Movies you don’t have to see include King Kong, Arachnophobia.......with Jaws, only the music was brilliant and created tension, I haven’t seen Jurassic Park, Jumanji was great, there were real animals involved and the unforgettable Robin Williams. But these oversized monster animal movies, no, you can chase me with that. Daktari with the cross-eyed lion Clarence - yes, Lassie - yes, and Black Beauty - yes..........I really liked those as a child. Naomi Watts, who starred in this dreadful film for me, is great. She is such a delicate person, yet also strong, this wonderful scent would suit her. Because King Kong doesn’t roar at all, the scent is strong and delicate at the same time for me. At first, I didn’t want to write anything because no one smells like rose or at least no one writes that. And then I thought I might be crazy and grabbed my Lyric, sprayed King Kong on one arm and Lyric on the other to compare. Yes, both scents have rose. In King Kong, this rose is surrounded by a banana leaf and is nestled on oak moss, that would be my short description. I love Can's description, I don’t need to add more, I just unfortunately don’t smell mint. At first, I perceive King Kong as green. Over time, it develops on the skin, becoming a bit sweeter, the clove comes through, just the right dosage for me..............and yes, I think there are other flowers too, which I can’t define, the rose also gets lost among all the flowers later and I can only perceive it faintly. I initially ended up here in the forum because my good Jungle by Kenzo was running low. And through a Google search, I suddenly found myself here. And since I was already here, after some browsing, it was clear that I had to have King Kong at some point. I was so curious about how the bananas would smell in the scent. Yes, nothing with bananas, so sweet delicious bananas, only the leaves or green bananas. My food supplier always comes on Wednesdays, and I get a box of yellow bananas and one with green ones every week. And yes, this note in the perfume smells like green bananas, I smelled it live again today when I took the bananas out of the plastic bag so they wouldn’t sweat.

"KING KONG de Kenzo" was completely unknown to me until about a year ago. As can happen to perfume enthusiasts, I stumbled upon this fragrance - 40 euros for 240ml EdT, unopened. Additionally, there was a small, old sticker on the box: "Distributed by G. Visconti di Modrone, Milano," which I know from their Acqua di Selva. So I just grabbed it, thinking it would be fine. I did a bit of research afterward: The 'first' fragrance from Kenzo is now traded at relatively high prices, with 100 euros for 60ml or even 350 USD for 120ml being common. It supposedly smells like banana! That fits King Kong. It also fits Kenzo with his stores originally called "Jungle Jap." But what am I supposed to do with this giant bottle? It's a women's fragrance; what should I do with it? I actually wanted to test it and then sell or gift it. Am I sitting on several hundred euros? If so, maybe I shouldn't open it... so I just set the box aside. Nice and dark and cool. About two weeks ago, there was a new blog post from Elena Vosnaki (Perfumshrine), a highly regarded blogger/expert in the world of perfume lovers. Title (loosely translated): "King Kong from the Jungle: A Fragrance Trail." She questions the authenticity of this fragrance - or at least the associated story as the first Kenzo scent and presents very good arguments: http://perfumeshrine.blogspot.com/2013/05/king-kong-out-of-jungle-fragrance.html This naturally piques curiosity. So the box is opened, and the stopper of the splash bottle is removed with some effort (an indication of at least somewhat higher age). Both the quality of the outer box and the bottle are high-quality and would not normally give cause for doubt. Using a pipette, I transfer 10ml into a new glass sprayer, securely close the bottle again, and set it aside. I give up on the first test after a short time and wash the scent off again. My goodness, so early in the morning and it nearly blows my mind away. Several comments online state that the scent can indeed be classified as unisex. They must be owners of completely defective olfactory bulbs. The opening is intense: Ripe, sweet, yet bitter fruity notes. Aldehydes. Ylang-Ylang, quite certainly. And probably a good dose of oakmoss. Banana? Well, maybe a very ripe one. There’s nothing fresh. Nothing Japanese and restrained. There’s a sledgehammer that rams the scent directly into your cerebellum through your nose. Yuk! Test aborted. Water and soap, march! Such a scent I need to tackle in the evening. One thing I can say already: In my opinion, it doesn't fit into the 90s, as Elena would have us believe. Intense fruity notes, or fruit-like notes, did not appear for the first time back then. This smells like the early 80s. But how does this fit with Kenzo, the Japanese, with Kenzo who loves floral patterns? Well, Kenzo Takada is also a lover of the jungle, the circus, the power of nature. Anyone who takes a close look at his fragrances will find that while he has produced, or had produced, some Asian-subtle ones - most are quite strong. A further test at a more suitable time of day was then somewhat more fruitful. Not that I am an expert in women's fragrances. I struggle to classify many ingredients that are not or hardly used in men's fragrances. I rely more on impressions than on individual notes. Moreover, King Kong seems to me to be quite a wild specimen. The opening nearly knocked me over again. Indeed: Sweet, floral, (over-)ripe fruits underpinned by a bitter, green note. Banana resonates, at least if you believe you can smell banana. I still suspect Ylang-Ylang and a mix of aldehydes. What’s interesting here is that the sweetness does not correspond to the version often encountered today. It really reminds me of ripe fruits... of slightly overripe, alcohol-producing ones. The counterpoint to this is the bitter green component. This is, at least for me, unusual but quite exciting. A slow change takes place. The fruity sweetness diminishes, and now it becomes more classic. The scent develops in a spicy-floral direction, still accompanied by a Chypre-typical oakmoss note. However, I would rather assign the spiciness to ginger and not the clove listed above, as I agree with Gaia Fishler, the non-blonde. Rose, however, is completely absent for me. Likewise peppermint. The floral component seems to lean more towards what is commonly referred to as "white flowers." Not that I know exactly what that should be... I just know how it smells. In any case, it takes several hours for the increasingly noticeable, slightly smoky-woody ambery base to break through and become dominant. What has been bothering me (and still does) is the question of the authenticity/origin of the fragrance. Kenzo Takada gave an interview in L'Express in 2008: http://www.lexpress.fr/styles/beaute/kenzo-parle-des-parfums-kenzo_473352.html He explicitly names "Kenzo de Kenzo," later renamed to "Kenzo ça sent beau," as his FIRST perfume. Does he not want to remember a flop? Or is it true that "King Kong de Kenzo" is not really by Kenzo? (To preempt critics: The corresponding comment on the Perfumshrine blog is from me) Both the scent and the (still) unclear story are interesting. ADDENDUM - 02.09.2013 Further research on my part has revealed some interesting details: "King Kong de Kenzo" was registered for trademark protection in the USA on January 7, 1980, by a law firm in Virginia on behalf of a Nodiris AG. I could not find any further information about the company, and the trademark was registered as 'abandoned' on June 30, 1984. THE SAME law firm registered the trademark "Jungle Jap" in 1982 on behalf of Kenzo's company Jungle Jap, Paris in the USA. The final registration took place in 1984. Interestingly, the trademark name "Kenzo" was only registered in the USA in 1985 and belonged jointly to the companies Jungle Jap, Paris and Kenzo SA, Paris (both owned by Kenzo Takada). Based on the available information, it can be assumed that "King Kong de Kenzo" is indeed by Kenzo. There have been and still are discussions about the year of release: Parfumo and Basenotes state 1980, while Fragrantica states 1978. I would assume that the fragrance/brand was initially only available in France, and therefore trademark protection in the USA was not the first step: 1978 seems more plausible to me personally.

My perception of this scent differs greatly from that of Gnagi in his review. Perhaps we have different versions. I auctioned a 60ml vintage bottle, the contents of which have taken on a dark orange to golden brown hue. I can't detect any top notes, but it could well be that the former top notes have already faded. Sweet-fruity or floral? Not a trace on me! To me, the scent feels resinous, spicy, unsweet, almost a bit fresh. Unisex would be completely realistic for me. I recognize the oak moss well - it gives the scent a somewhat "scratchy" quality. Well, I'm not exactly a declared fan of Chypres (although I do like some), which have that typical note. I wouldn't have thought of banana, perhaps recognizable with some imagination. The image of King Kong trampling through a lush green jungle, among giant moss- and vine-covered trees (resin, green and spicy notes!), fits the scent quite well! However, I can't detect any animalistic qualities in it. Compared to the other fragrances from the Kenzo brand, at least those I am familiar with, this perfume bears little resemblance! Overall, an interesting scent, but I still prefer the current perfumes in the resinous/spicy direction much more.

No, I can't smell banana, even though it's listed in the fragrance pyramid. There's no monkey around to grab it (Huge or not, that doesn't matter for now) But I can clearly detect a lot of other green and spicy "stuff" on my scent radar. Still, it is "completely banana" in the sense of "a bit crazy," deviating from the olfactory monotony and not found today in THIS form, not even in the most "refined niche." It's indeed a special case in the world of fragrances. But a particularly successful one! It spices things up quite nicely with the clove used for this! Cheekily, green mint pushes itself forward for a while! Fresh as the morning dew in early summer! However, fortunately without a nasty "gum note" that bites in the nose! No, completely natural and self-evident! But what’s rumbling in the background? A green thunderstorm of all sorts of leaf and conifer needle scents, which then become resinous and woody. A flash of various exotic spices cuts through. In response to the rumbling of all sorts of balsamic-dark resins. Now roses sneak in as well, initially unsure of where to go. But they then find joyful entry with clove and company. Apparently, it also becomes green and moist. Not from the rain, which refuses to fall RIGHT HERE, but from further in the background, where you can clearly make out the wet front on the horizon. And it awakens the herb-tinted oak moss on old deciduous trees to fragrant life! What a scent! Like being "stung by oats," I want to follow it further! Into the realm of a slightly "crazy" fragrance. All banana? Exactly THAT is it! ;-))

Wow, I wish I could find a way to express how this perfume smells better. It's not my normal type of scent, much more powdery and slightly more floral and herbal than I gravitate towards. However, the blend on this is impeccable. Chef's kiss, no notes, it is stunning. I'm going to try (and miserably fail) to describe how this scent smells. It smells like a dream. Like walking on a cloud just after the sun has gone down. It's cool, but not cold. Maybe late spring or early summer. The sky is light and shimmery, the stars just visible. There's a light breeze, and the world is calm. It's floral, powdery, a little earthy, and the sweetness of the plum pulls it all together into a beautiful feminine scent, somehow simultaneously very deep and very simple. I cannot get enough of this scent.

When I wake up in the morning, I occasionally remember dreams that I recall but don’t quite remember. I know it was about an important topic, but which one? I know there were others involved, friends and acquaintances, but who? I know it was all somehow complicated, but why? Only the dream atmosphere, I can name, because it is still there upon waking. I feel similarly about Sensuous Stars. Not that I can’t name the fragrance notes; they are very clear to me. The most prominent is the beautiful, dry iris, followed by plum. The lavender - well, if I read the pyramid and then search for it again, I can also smell a hint of it. But that’s not all; I also notice something very artificial, cool. I believe it’s Iso-E-Super. Perhaps there’s also a pepper scent involved. In the combination of these notes, I get the impression of a slightly sour, subtle leather. So, I can name the fragrance notes, but they seem, similar to when I wake from such a dream, somehow intangible. I smell them and I don’t smell them. I sprayed the fragrance, and after a short time, it crosses my mind whether I forgot to perfume myself today. Then I smell my wrist and realize that everything is indeed there, as expected. In the three days that I’ve worn the fragrance now, I’ve had the involuntary urge to reapply it after just two or three hours each time, because the scent felt like it was no longer there, even though it still was. It hadn’t even become weaker. How does that happen? I believe it’s the scent ingredient that I think I recognize as Iso-E-Super or another artificial component that I don’t particularly like because I perceive it as cold and lifeless, but to which I adapt very quickly. This means that, on one hand, it no longer bothers me, but unfortunately, it seems that all the other notes of the fragrance are taken along with it in a sort of collective guilt by my brain. Then it seems to me that the whole fragrance has disappeared, although when I consciously sniff, it is completely present. I find that very unfortunate. I like Sensuous Stars. I really enjoy how the plums and the iris, both distinctly present on their own, come together to form a leather note, even if they seem a bit lifeless and cool. And like with these dreams, I have the feeling that I actually want to keep Sensuous Stars, but in the end, I probably won’t keep it after all.

Outside, the sun is setting. I go into the bedroom of the little house, upstairs. I open the creaky little and wobbly wooden drawer of the nightstand. On the lilac Mille fleurs wallpaper lies a little book, somewhat dusty and yellowed. Le Petit Prince. I lie down on the freshly made bed, dressed in Laura Ashley bedding; it is cool, and I feel safe and transported back to my childhood, when everything was still slower and quieter, in the evening at my grandparents' forest cottage. I browse a bit, and it feels wonderfully unhurried, so peaceful and far away from the whole world. Outside, the first stars are now twinkling, and I feel like I’m on one of them.

Sensuous Stars contains two fragrance notes that I generally like very much: plum and lavender. The third note in the mix, iris, is often a bit too bulky and powdery for me. That the scent would also be powdery was to be expected. However, I find the perfume to be very powdery. I also mainly perceive the iris. The plum joins in, and my nose simply cannot detect the lavender. What a pity, I had imagined the combination with lavender to be really beautiful. The scent is fresh for a moment when sprayed on and then immediately becomes floral - powdery. Then I personally notice a chewing gum note. Something about the scent seemed familiar to me, as if I had smelled something similar before. And then I thought of my remaining bottle of Insolence by Guerlain. Yes, this chewing gum note is similar, and both scents are powdery. However, Insolence is significantly more potent in terms of sillage and longevity. And it also smells a bit old-fashioned. In my comparisons, I am now already detecting violets in Sensuous Stars. Of course, the two perfumes are different. I just perceive that one note in both that smells like chewing gum to me. Sensuous is modern and milder. The sillage is moderate for me, and the scent lasts about 4 - 6 hours, although it becomes quite close to the skin after 2 hours. It is pleasant to wear, even though it has a very distinctive and by no means a 08/15 DNA. That could certainly become annoying. For me, this is a perfume that can be worn well in spring and autumn and requires a certain mood. I definitely do not see it as a no-brainer, as it is too iris-heavy.

It is really exciting how differently one can perceive a fragrance. I have read many statements that made me believe I might like the scent. However, since that was not the case when testing it, I would like to share my impressions. For me, it is veeeery sweet. Someone mentioned "plum liqueur." Yes, that's true. It comes across as extremely sticky, and yes: the plum smells quite artificial. Recently, I processed a whole bucket of plums, and they definitely smelled different. The lavender is very subtly noticeable but is extremely overshadowed by the plum note. The same goes for the iris. It is not powdery for me at all. I cannot confirm that it doesn't last long. I perceived it intensely for many, many hours, to the point where it became too much for me. The dress then stayed in the laundry basket overnight, and what can I say? The scent absolutely did not fade. Anyone who enjoys extremely sweet and fruity plum fragrances with very long-lasting power will surely be satisfied. I prefer it less intense, so I’m out when it comes to this scent.

On me, the scent is not very sweet, rather delicate and mature. The lavender smells clean and, combined with the plum, is unusual, complex, and office-friendly. The iris holds everything together. Sensuous Stars seems modern and serious to me. A successful chypre fragrance that does without aldehydes. I don't like the name very much.

Lacuna is surrounded by cozy, pink velvet. White powdered sugar cascades down on her. She sticks out her tongue and the fine crystals melt like snowflakes. A light sweetness spreads. In the sky, there are soft cotton clouds. She reaches for them and pulls them towards herself. She wraps herself in the delicacy. Lacuna takes a powder box from her bag and opens the lid.

Everything in the notes say that I should absolutely love this. Fruity, floral, violet, rose, powder.. yes please! I’ve a total soft spot for feminine fragrances in spring and summer and a total soft spot for Chanel’s DNA. Splendide opens as a sweet, soft fruity floral with slightly jammy summer fruits. A little promise of tang from the raspberry that dissipates all too quickly. It dries down into a soft peachy rose on a base of slightly powdery iris, a hint of wood and musk. I thought there’d be some summer fizz from the geranium, but alas, it’s just a pretty summer scent. It doesn’t smell like a Chanel. To me, it smells more like an expensive shampoo or hair product, and that’s ok, one of my fav summer scent, Angeli Di Firenze, is a gorgeous fruity floral shampoo. Splendide is very lovely indeed and inoffensive, it aims to please, to be liked by all maybe?.. but instead it’s quite generic, forgettable and unremarkable. Very light and delicate and unfortunately it disappears after an hour an a half. It may not smell like a Chanel, but it’s price it still expensive for a scent I’d have to spray more liberally and more often than a body spray to get any sort of scent bubble. It’s not awful, it really is very nice, pretty, but it’s underwhelming and majorly disappointing for me.

I haven't really gone for Chanel fragrances in my fragrance journey since I don't think I fit their public, so when I got a free sample from SoPost I was pretty indifferent. Decided to test it out anyways to see if this would open the door to future Chanel fragrance. Let me tell you, this one has further strengthened my resolve that Chanel might not be a house for me. If I hadn't known, I would've sweared it's an Angel Nova flanker where the raspberry is more on the fresh, bright side than the sugary sweet and heavy side. There's a weird freshness that remains throughout the fragrance that's clearly synthetic. During the middle, I get some fresh rose and a subtle iris that weirdly fresh and not powdery. Freshness remains ever present. The drydown is still fresh and at the same becomes warmer and slightly woody. It's definitely a feminine fragrance and if you love Angel Nova but want a fresher take for spring and summer this could be it. For my part, I'm not an Angel Nova lover (they have already been rated and reviewed), so this one won't be making it into my collection.

I got a full size of this to sample and I’m very glad I didn’t have to pay for something so basic and watered down. This smells like cold water that has some red fruits floating around, there is some sweetness and overall freshness. The scent smells pretty fun and youthful, but this is far from being special or different or necessary in this market right now. But it would be a pretty nice gift maybe for someone graduating high school.

I was so interested by the notes, so I went to the store and sprayed it on paper. It was super powdery - fruity with hint of violet, than I sprayed on my skin: The scent completely transformed into a super condensed raspberry and violet ! It's syrupy but fades into something a little less pronounced on the raspberry and way more intense on the violet. The thing is, it reminded me A LOT of Lancôme La vie est belle - Elixir, they share that same condensed - syrup raspberry, so... The chanel DNA is not on that one, can be disappointing if you love that "Eau Chance" dna (I personally don't really, since I don't care to be honest) but surprisingly, I really enjoyed that one.

I'm usually a Chanel hater, but this is now my favorite scent in their collection. I recognized the 1-2 punch of raspberry and rose a mile away. The opening is almost the same as Angel Nova by Mugler-- very tart, fruity, and youthful. I definitely feel a distinct Chanel quality to it-- I think their florals come off too powdery and synthetic compared to other houses, and I got a big whiff of the Chanel grandma accord (I say this because my grandmother is a fiend for Chanel and the florals are always so prominent on her). The juiciness and florality make this scent feel youthful and joyous. There's no sensuality or maturity in this bottle. I you want to embody a girlish and polished scent for warmer weather, you may really enjoy this. However, I'm not a polished lady and I'm gonna wear the hell out of my Angel Nova for a similar effect.

Chanel Chance Eau Splendide is truly a joyful composition. I can’t distinguish individual notes, only a carefree sweetness—light, safe, and radiant. Longevity on fabric lasts several hours, but the sillage quickly settles close to the skin. If you want to feel carefree happiness wrapped in subtle, quiet elegance, wear this scent.

And here it is! Chanel's fourth flanker, if I counted correctly and set aside the hair perfume, its concentrations, and so on. Additionally, Chance once had an Extrait, and there are still several variations available as both EDT and EDP. What's new here is that the Eau de Parfum is released directly, and it seems they are forgoing an Eau de Toilette.

The scent is a dream for me! Raspberry is strongly noticeable at the beginning but not in a squeaky childish way, rather somehow floral-berry. The rose is very delicate, not stuffy or overwhelming, more like a soft pink rose. The violet adds a sweet floral touch, and it is very beautifully harmoniously blended.

meet for a picnic on a beautiful wide meadow adorned with many daisies... The view is stunning, one can see a crystal-clear blue lake.. The sun is shining.. There is delicious raspberry sparkling wine.. Fraiche hands Tendre a bouquet of roses.. amusingly, Tendre has brought sweet violets for Fraiche... the beautiful flowers are arranged nicely on the picnic blanket..

Eau Splendide opens with a surprisingly fresh and clear raspberry note that is not sweet but pleasantly tart and lively. This fruitiness immediately gives the fragrance an elegant lightness, almost like a cool breeze over bare skin on a bright morning. What develops next is typical Chanel - understated, finely balanced, and never intrusive.

The curtain falls. Silence. Then thunderous applause begins. Roaring. Sweat-drenched, she straightens up, friendly, welcoming hands of her colleagues surrounding her, equally exhausted but euphoric over the brilliantly successful performance, help her rise in her sumptuous yet extremely heavy costume that forces her into immobility. Before the curtain opens for the first time again, everyone must be off stage, only to gradually appear again under the sustained applause of the audience to receive it as a reward for the artistic achievement of the past hours on the boards that mean the world. As she rushes backstage with the others, a hint of clove rises to her nose, just as it had in the past hours. A peculiar scent, not liked by everyone, but loved by her precisely because of its peculiarity. Moreover, now, after all those hours of being carried, it is infused with this distinctly identifiable note of incense; a wonderful blend, harmonious, ceremonial, expressive, and yet not commonplace. Fitting for her. The curtain opens, the applause rises like waves again as the choir steps onto the stage in unison. She grants it to the choir; its performance is considerable, even if it is sometimes completely underestimated by the common masses, the discerning opera-goer knows how to appreciate its value for the overall work. Still on stage in the fourth and final act, she could only perceive the incense as an indefinable smoky note, almost earthy-sweet with balsamic undertones. Not that this scent development was unfamiliar to her; after all, she has been wearing it for as long as she can remember, it has become her chosen stage scent throughout her various engagements because it carries her, supports her, accompanies her through the performance. Now the high priest of Baal steps onto the stage to receive his well-deserved share of the applause. He is followed by the colleague who lent his voice to the Babylonian guard Abdallo as a tenor. The applause surges up and down. Similar to the scent of clove, which retrospectively also surges up and down, appearing, enveloping her in dark spiciness, then retreating again to make room for a bright floral glow in the form of a light, delicate floral scent. Thus, a constant interplay of light and dark emerges in the scent progression, reminding her of her own career, her great roles like that of the Ethiopian princess Aida, within which she felt at every performance that in the end she died a little with her role, entombed in the dark crypt beneath the temple. A demanding role that had consumed her so much that she actually had to take a longer break from touring afterward to regain her composure. A dark phase, which is reflected for her in the phases of the scent that she perceives as dark. Meanwhile, the Hebrew high priest Zaccaria, or rather the bass embodying this role, walks onto the stage to bow gratefully before the enthusiastic audience. An excellent singer from her perspective, vibrating with life and completely absorbed in his roles, very much like her. Here too, she must think of the scent that accompanied her singing career, which can also be perceived as quite lively; ever-changing, sometimes bright floral, then again dark spicy, it often seemed to her that a hint of cinnamon, just like the garden clove, was present, even if it is not always detectable and only as subtle notes in the background. Nevertheless, these scent aspects give the fragrance a shimmering garment in which she feels understood and comfortable, wonderfully scented, because it corresponds to her personality. She perceives that one after another Ismaele and the mezzo-soprano as her sister Fenena appear on stage, followed by Nabucco as the king of Babylon amidst thunderous applause. This variety of fantastic singers and magnificent voices inspires her anew each time, leaving her in awe and feeling like part of a coherent whole, even though she mostly occupied one of the lead roles and continues to do so to this day. Whether it was Freia in the Nibelungen saga, which she sang just recently, paradoxically the goddess of eternal youth portrayed by her as she has already traversed the second half of life, or whether it was the great love from Tchaikovsky's Eugene Onegin, she has always been and is one of the greats. Perhaps that is also why she chose this scent early on, a scent that knows how to present itself like a Grand Dame, even if at the beginning a magnificent aldehyde cloud envelops her. A scent that is timeless yet carries the essence of time within it, turning memories into fragrance and reviving the old. It appears aloof yet so warm-hearted, when at the beginning, together with the powdery aldehyde soapiness, a citrusy, almost slightly sweaty note, she suspects bergamot behind it, forms a duet. A scent that can never quite settle but plans its grand entrance, highlights, breaks off, and resumes. Yet it remains true to itself, as the clove, despite its diving and returning, lays the foundation for the entire scent progression from the very beginning, while allowing the various flowers scattered on the red carpet their place and sharing the final act almost ceremoniously with the incense. And she is the last to step onto the stage. The applause is overwhelming. She bows, before the audience, before Cinnabar. The curtain falls. She is still there.

…that was a saying my mother liked to use when something we kids did became too much for her, and it came to my mind again today when I unpacked the sought-after fragrance. I discovered this fragrance in the 80s and, of course, being a "know-it-all," as teenagers sometimes are, I immediately associated the name of the fragrance with this saying and told my mother. Her dry explanation: “A lot of fuss for something as unimportant as perfume!” I was momentarily speechless! I was never really silenced back then, but I had nothing to say to that. Perfume! Unimportant??? She can't be serious!? Unimportant! Pah! “Fuss” fits perfectly, the fragrance made a lot of fuss!!! Just right for a loud rebellious teenager like me! So! "Fuss" was my second name back then...I wanted it so badly, but it was too expensive for a student...grmpf... As I have mentioned here and there, it was, however, unimportant to my mother. A fragrance, only for “special occasions,” that was all she needed. Now, about Cinnabar itself: I actually liked the fragrance back then, but it always made me dizzy. It was quite strong, a real “punchy scent,” and that’s why I always got headaches from it. I couldn't afford it, and whenever there was a tester somewhere, I would always try it. Later, my beloved Obelisk made its way into my collection, another beautiful “spice scent” that I tolerated better, so Cinnabar was done for me for the time being. Clove, sandalwood, and for me the cinnamon that is no longer mentioned in the list…simply wonderful. Now that I’ve arrived here at Parfumo, I had to test it again, which I did for the first time in a long time about six months ago. On the way back from the office, I quickly stopped by a perfume store, searched for the bottle and couldn’t find it because it looks different now, but then I discovered it and boom, boom, spray…ugh…Unfortunately, I suddenly didn’t like it at all anymore. How could that be? Maybe too many other scents around me? The tester not in order? Something is not right here. I moved on, as the price is quite steep for me, so fine, let’s just forget about this fragrance. Done, that’s it. Of course, I then read a bit more closely here, yes, it’s true, the bottle looks different, so the fragrance must also be different today, only the name…sad and unfortunate…well. Since then, I have always thought that I needed to get a bottle and revisit it. My scent preferences haven’t changed that much, and surely the fragrance isn’t as different as it seemed to me during the “walk-by test,” so I went on a search in the souk. Today, the bottle finally arrived, rip it open and hissing and aaaaah….yes…fine…super….there we go!! My son comes around the corner, a nod of approval, hmmmm….it smells great here! Ha! If my son doesn’t say “stinks” or “ugh,” then that means something, so I feel like I did everything right. Yes, it does lack something compared to the old version, the sillage fades quite quickly. Yes, it’s missing something, surely the aldehydes, surely something else as well, but: It is unmistakably Cinnabar and I can tolerate it. No headaches, no dizziness…I am newly in love with the new version of Cinnabar!

How do I put this? This will probably be my first negative review.... (sorry, actually the 2nd) Normally, I like sweet, oriental, spicy fragrances. Especially when cinnamon is involved. I had been keeping an eye on this scent for a while because the ingredient list aligns with my preferences and it is rated 80% (though this is the 1978 version). The old version lists aldehydes, while the new one does not. That's a plus, as every perfume with aldehydes has failed for me so far. So I thought the reformulated Cinnabar must definitely be something for me; after all, it's a classic.... Well, this morning in the city, at the perfume department of a large department store: what jumps out at me, totally unexpectedly? The new Cinnabar. Of course, I was excited to immediately spray one (!) spritz on my wrist.... It knocked me out, but not in a positive way. I remembered a sentence from a perfumer who wrote that Cinnabar plays in the same league as Opium. That's exactly how it is. Because with Opium, I experience the same suffocating sensation (sorry to all its fans!). Do you know those crime stories where a handkerchief soaked in chloroform is pressed over the victim's mouth and nose, and then they become unconscious? You could take me down like that with Opium/Cinnabar. So, after the first sniff and the initial shock, I thought, okay, wait, give it some time. But I couldn't bear it for more than 1 hour and sought out the nearest customer restroom to scrub and scrub. I must admit, during that hour it became miniminimally better, but still headache-inducing. And after that scrubbing session, of course, it was still not completely gone. So, longevity and sillage are phenomenal; I wish that for other scents that I find beautiful. The bottle is also quite pretty and harmless, not suggesting what kind of tiger is lurking inside. As for the scent itself, I can clearly detect the sandalwood, jasmine, and clove, as well as cinnamon, even though it is not listed in the new version. Are there perhaps aldehydes in there after all? There’s something that I find so cough-inducing, biting, and headache-inducing in this type of fragrance. It happens to me with Opium, but also with Chanel No5 or Jil Sander No4..... What a pity, anyway, I've learned again that just having a suitable ingredient list and a high rating for a fragrance can still mean a misstep.

I really love this fragrance and prefer it to the original kenzo world. It’s a super sweet plum, perfect for cold days. It also lasts a long time and it is quite original to me. I don’t reckon anything quite similar. Really don’t understand the low rating. Reminds me of and evening in paris during wintertime.

I received this fragrance as a gift from my mom a few years ago. Actually, it only contains scent notes that I like, but its composition and dosage are not harmonious for me. What can I say, we just don't get along! I really don't like this scent on myself or on others! It's too strong, intrusive, intense, almost as if it triggers a headache for me. Since then, it has been sitting in the cupboard, at least the bottle is nice to look at.

You're looking at the title thinking, "Whaaa?" I'm serious though. I remember smelling this in my mother's fashion magazine back in the late 90s. I really enjoyed the quasi-feminine fruity vibe it gave off, similar to many other Estee Lauder products at the time. Needless to say, I kept the strip for years and would often go back to it when I felt I needed another fix. Fast forward to 2008, when I managed to come upon a full bottle from a legitimate vendor who made a stop at our local hospital. I immediately made the connection to my past and purchased a bottle. Although the smell wasn't exactly as I remembered, it was pretty damn good. It's very airy, sophisticated, light and fruity-fresh with a very synthetic nectarine note off the top. The spiciness comes out in the mid, but it's rather well blended and never gets cloying. Personally, I don't get any wood in the base since the entire composition just has this light, aromatic vibe, similar to what you might get from Ferrari's Light Essence Aqua. My first impression was that it smelled like freshly laundered linen, or a white cotton dress shirt. If you know Mont Blanc's Individuel, the scent is somewhat similar, just with nectarine instead of the raspberry. Pleasures also goes through a bit of a transition in the mid to become somewhat creamy, though retaining that aromatic freshness. It's ultra inoffensive and even a little generic, but I can't deny that it just smells PLEASANT. It's a fitting name, despite the poor longevity and projection.

Is it ozonic, aquatic, or what? I would like to know, so I can identify it when I am smelling. My mini-rant aside, Pleasures opens up with a pleasant burst of citrus, nectarine, and green notes, exactly as the Fragrance Notes above say. I can detect the hint of spice from the coriander, pimento and ginger, and I still get lovely woods and a hint (sadly) of oakmoss. Overall, it's still a very pleasant experience. It's fresh, green, with just a touch of spice, and would make a nice daily wear for the right person. Luca Turin kind of panned this one (3 stars), saying it was "...above average, but could have been so much better." I would have to disagree with him on this one. I love his reviews, and he has turned me on to some wonderful fragrances, but not a lot that were infinitely wearable like Pleasures for Men is. No, this isn't particularly groundbreaking, but I don't see it having to be. The ingredients are above average in this fragrance, it's well-blended and not linear at all (so it remains interesting to my nose), and, in my opinion, represents good value. Longevity is quite good with a fragrance of this type, me getting 8+ hours on my skin, sillage is moderately strong (but never offensive), and it has an adequate bottle with a great sprayer (typical of Lauder products). This is a great casual that is inoffensive, very wearable, and doesn't smell like a shampoo or body wash. I would give this a strong 7 out of 10.

No, seriously this may not have that much to do with GIT as the ambergris base is not present, but it certainly has quite some similarities to the million-bottle-selling Cool Water by Davidoff (the vintage version that is), including the aquatic notes, a hint of musk and a bit of calone. Overall it's synthetic but fresh, floral and fruity. I find it really hard to make out the different notes in this scent, but why there is no violet leaf listed in the note pyramid is beyond my understanding. Longevity is actually surprisingly good and sillage is acceptable, I find it a nice casual wear for spring or even summer.

Quote: “You don’t have to spend a fortune for good fragrances. There are excellent perfumes available for little money that are in no way inferior to the expensive products." When I read such statements, I usually react with rolling eyes and a hint of capitulation. After testing a thousand men’s fragrances and purchasing more than a hundred bottles, I have come to the conclusion that quality costs money. But let the gentlemen have their experiences, I think to myself. This reminds me of my experiences with wines or teas. One example: Dealers who sell Southern European wines often make statements like: "For a tenth of the price of a Bordeaux wine, you can get a wine here that is in no way inferior to its more expensive counterpart." Not at all! Anyone who has ever drunk a well-aged, excellent Bordeaux will know what I mean. And yet: There are exceptions. Although you have to invest a small fortune and a lot of time in research to find them, they do exist. (Back then, I discovered an excellent red wine from the southern French Pic St. Loup. It was called "Cuvee Ste. Agnes 1999." It was offered for 9.90 euros, and I bought 44 (!) bottles, each of which I enjoyed drinking or giving away.) As for men’s fragrances, I can’t name three for under 50,- euros/100ml that I would say I would pay 150,- euros for. But they do exist, these treasures. By the way, I also had to spend a small fortune on research to discover them. But the journey is at least a pleasurable part of the destination. And "Pleasures" is one of those rare gems. For me, the entire product is perfect! It starts with the bottle. It is high-quality, tasteful, fits comfortably in the hand, and is easy to use. And the scent couldn’t be more beautiful: Freshness, paired with a herbaceous, floral ozone. Incredibly well-balanced and a joy for the nose. Everything is rounded, nothing stands out. I can’t seem to describe it any more. Every ingredient is perfectly integrated. Neither the citrus notes, nor the spices, nor the woods stand out. The scent is rounded, satisfying, and high-quality. And it wears really well. Yes, there are good, affordable fragrances. Those that are not just somewhat okay (I could name dozens of those), but that completely satisfy my nose. A real pleasure! P.S. By the way, the scent has been reformulated. I used to wear it for years. But that’s not how I remember it. The Sky-Air accord has always been there. But the ozone seems new to me and fits perfectly into the scent. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Addendum in March 2022: A new bottle has arrived. With great joy, I note that the reformulation has been reversed. Perhaps the last bottle was just a batch variation. In any case, the scent is now just like it used to be: bright, clear, friendly, and fresh ... without the ozonic floral note.

Yep ... a rather suggestive title, but every time I apply Pleasures for Men, I briefly associate it with a predominantly skin-colored movie poster from the 80s, complete with 1-2 black bars ;-) And that's just because of the name, tsk tsk tsk ... "Pleasure" is actually a beautiful term, just like many others that can be interpreted in various ways - almost every second word ;) Therefore, I have preemptively marked all potential ambiguities with * to avoid any misunderstandings. Here’s the story and fragrance description: Last year, during the hottest* summer on record, I exchanged thoughts about fresh scents with a perfumer, and he recommended Pleasures for Men to me as if he were shooting from the hip*, because he knows my preferences*. I trusted him blindly*, as he has a lot of experience* … Hey, hey, both he and I are straight and we don’t even know each other personally :) … So, back to the topic and finally to the scent, which comes across as quite innocent* Pleasures is very fresh from the first spray (I’m better at rhyming ;) It is based on a fine L'Aventure Knight note (or Creed's GIT) which here is called Sky-Air Accord + green leaves. There’s a bit of citrus and a light fruity sweetness from the nectarines. A very pleasant mélange that comes across as cheerful and peaceful, almost harmless. So nothing with Pleasures* ??? Let’s wait and see … After about half an hour, a floral touch emerges, making it a bit softer and more lovable, harmoniously nestled in sandalwood. The mix is subtly interwoven with the listed spice mix, even if the individual ingredients are hardly discernible. It doesn’t have to be, because overall, Pleasures smells very balanced, a bit light green and transparent at the same time, and despite its lightness, it has a fine masculinity. A sophisticated composition that gains a refined old-school touch towards the end with ebony and moss. And how do we circle back to the asterisks * at the end? Quite simply: our dear mini-golf also comments on Pleasures very aptly, where in the scene of her first paragraph, you only need to replace the penultimate word with "Lüstling" (and she may forgive me for the fun). But back to seriousness, the real name ;-) of the culprit: Because that is our dear Turbobean, to whom I dedicate my comment. He recommended this wonderful scent to me, for which I am very grateful! Because Pleasures for Men always comes across as clean and well-groomed, is gentle yet invigorating, and seems to be almost unique (hardly any scent twins and the listed ones hardly apply). A lovely all-rounder with a fairly linear progression, best worn in spring and summer, in leisure and at work. The H&S are in the middle range, it lasts on clothing (depending on the fabric) up to 8 hours, and its sillage is always present at half an arm's length, radiating a positive aura ... Seen this way, Pleasures is indeed a fragrant giver of joy :-)

There are moments in a man's life when he doesn't quite know what to do. One of those moments is when he receives a bouquet of flowers in public, for a birthday or a company anniversary, for example. You don't know how to react or what to do with it. I felt somewhat similarly at first with this fragrance.

Pleasures, the joys, the pure delight? Hardly and yes and again no - for this is one that on the surface has little of what I appreciate in a fragrance, and beneath that almost even less. And yet I cannot hold a grudge against it, I find it difficult to use harsh words - it comes across too friendly and too puppy-like. Green leaves? Ginger? Oak moss?

Back then....1997.....my first Esteé Lauder ....freshly showered, herbaceous citrusy sharp almost metallic it comes across, somehow clean, pure, benevolent, aromatically enticing sinking into a base of fine herbal woody nuances.....it stays with you...... Today....2015....still my favorite Esteé Lauder

This brings to mind old Agatha Christie books and films. The main and supporting characters were always neat, nice, and almost polished to perfection. The ladies with lace blouses and freshly curled locks on their heads. The gentlemen often in fine suits with neatly parted hair, nickel glasses, and "styled" mustaches.

When I first sprayed Pleasures for men, I was instantly thrilled. So much carefree joy of life, such an untroubled floralness I have never experienced in any other men's fragrance! Broadly speaking, it belongs to the fragrance family of Davidoff Cool Water, Joop!

Kenzo has a great sense of humour, if you ask me. And if I translate the name of this fragrance correctly: Ça sent Beau meaning This smells good. What a great name for a perfume! But apart from being quite fun, there is a truth to it, that I shall have to comment on. Since with this astounding product I do sometimes consider the smell secondary. Perhaps that needs an explanation. Let us look at in what order this unfolds itself. It starts with the wrapping: stunning. The EdP comes in a beautiful light green box with a beautiful black (hand) writing stating Kenzo. Next to this is a red seal like decoration, a Japanese ‘hanko’. The box has structures of leaves pressed into the cardboard. Inside, the bottle is wrapped in crisp peach coloured tissue paper, almost nesting in it. Oh yes please! Now, that is what I call decent wrapping. The whole act of unwrapping makes my nervous system go bonkers. So much, that I tend to forget what it is all about - the fragrance. But then there is the bottle. I have the deodorant, the miniature EdT and the ‘real thing’ - the EdP. All are in the stunning category. The EdP, however, takes the price. It has a stopper shaped like two flowers, and the neck and bottle reminds me of the now again popular activity of stacking rocks on top of each other. Even though the top is plastic, the whole picture is a balanced, beautiful and bold design, that leaves me with a luxurious feeling. So much that I tend to forget what it is all about - the fragrance. Well, the fragrance is out of this world and should be in the Top100 - despite its high ranking, it is not in Parfumo’s Women’s Top100, which surprises me. It is creamy, floral and soapy at the same time. When it warms up it has a floral expression that makes me want it to stay like that forever. Actually, I think it is timeless. Such a shame that it is discontinued. But then again, I get to enjoy it, because it is in my collection. Year 2, 158/365

Today, I wanted to compare the Ça Sent Beau Eau de Toilette on the right and left arms with the "Ça Sent Beau / Kenzo (Eau de Parfum) | Kenzo." To my surprise, the perfume lasts only 3-4 hours on my skin with a rather weak sillage. The Eau de Toilette comes across as much more concentrated, likely due to its age - both fragrances come from collection dissolutions and are in older miniature bottles. I find the DNA of the scent not too bad but also a bit old school. It smells very floral and fruity. The top note starts fruity with peach but also floral-sweet with orange and jasmine blossoms. The heart note remains distinctly floral. I detect rose water, geraniums, tuberose, gardenias, iris, violets, and lily of the valley - what a sea of flowers! The base reminds me a bit of soap and fabric softener. Additionally, I recognize a green-earthy patchouli aroma. It also has a slightly vanillic and balsamic scent. All in all, this is a fairly successful fragrance, but I wouldn't necessarily associate it with my "dream woman," as I find it a bit outdated. EDIT 23.02.2024: Now I have tested another miniature. Here, the longevity was significantly better at around 12 hours. In the top note, I also detected bergamot and a jam-like quality. As it develops further, it also smells quite oriental, festive, and of cinnamon.

Paris-Biarritz begins with its citrus notes out in full force. According to Chanel, it is grapefruit and mandarin orange. But, I definitely pick up on a lemon note, pretty clearly. To me, it actually starts off the strongest. The citrus is juicy, refreshing, but very cold. Almost like they threw in an iced accord. The composition does have a bit of an aquatic note in there. Almost oceanic, in how it comes across. Now, it isn’t super powerful, but I get it each time I spray this perfume. Beyond all of that, the neroli not adds to the citrus, while also creating a green and spicy fresh undertone to Biarritz. Once the juiciness of the citrus has faded, this becomes drier, greener, and more floral. Neroli and lily of the valley are the floral notes here. Paris-Biarritz becomes a balanced mix of those along with some ample vetiver, musk, and patchouli. It’s a light soapy citrus with woody, green, and musky aromas exchanging places during the dry down. It’s something I’ve experienced with plenty of other scents, but the watery/sea vibe I get, does give it some distinction.

I smell it, this French flair that many women possess. Do you know that feeling when a woman walks by and I, as a woman, have to acknowledge without envy that she has class? Not super beautiful but very attractive, not necessarily chic and dressed in the latest fashion, but in a special kind of careless and unintentional yet effortless elegance, the hair a bit too wild and daring, but with every movement of her head, one is captivated. Then a scent hits me - she has already passed by, but I smell freshness, jasmine, rose, and something very oddly interesting, perhaps a hint of vanilla or what is it? Her secret! A lightly warm and cool sexiness. This is a woman you like; she could be the good friend, has nothing conceited about her but a refreshingly cheerful laugh, yet her eyes can also entice and make any man curious. I liked the scent immediately; it lasts a very long time and has that familiar statement of a Chanel fragrance. Ladies, try it and you will understand what I mean.

The small bakery is only a few hundred meters away from the holiday home. A wonderfully lukewarm breeze caresses her skin. The sun shines through scattered clouds that line the otherwise light blue sky. Her black stilettos, with a gold-embellished tip, leave a fine audible "click" on the large stone tiles, which gradually seems quieter and then increasingly unattainable to him. He spots his wife walking between the large mandarin trees; she has chosen a cream-colored satin summer dress that reveals a very generous view of her back and even just a tiny bit of her bottom. She knew he would enjoy this sight, and just before the distance becomes too great, she liked to briefly turn her head back, smiling mischievously into his deep blue eyes and leaving something unique behind. He will never forget her transparent, freshly greenish sweet, fine fruity scent; it truly describes her lightness and youthful spirit, carried by an intense elegant, powdery floral cream note of lily of the valley. Paris - Biarritz Chanel. Overall, the scent lasts 6 hours on my skin. The sillage is designed to be noticeably present for 2.5 hours at a good quarter-arm's length before it becomes intimate. I would like to express my sincere thanks to our perfume "SolisOccasum" for the decanting.

Years ago, I saw - in a castle or museum, I can't quite remember - the portrait of a lady in a dress made of airy, light silk muslin. She smiled kindly at me, her viewer, yet looked past me, into a kind of infinity behind me. In her hand, she held a lemon. I still remember that I found this very unusual at the time and therefore asked the museum lady what the mysterious lemon was all about. And she simply replied: Bitterness. In those days, when the beautiful lady had her portrait painted, it was not socially 'comme il faut' to display one's unhappiness. A countess or a lady commercial counselor - or whoever had the means and leisure to hire a portraitist - was expected to be cheerful in public. Having oneself depicted with a lemon was the only non-self-compromising way to show how unhappy she really was. This impressed me so much at the time that I remembered it. Is Chanel's Paris - Biarritz the scent for a bitter, unhappy woman..? No, of course not. Is it a perfume that invites one to pause and reflect, beyond its superficially cheerful freshness and Chanel-esque elegance? Certainly. Named after that legendary seaside resort in the far southwest of France (more so in the late 19th and early 20th centuries than today), it gives a serious echo to both - cheerfulness and worldly elegance - and that glance into a kind of infinity. If one allows it. Apart from lively, feather-light citrus cheerfulness and the established 'comme il faut' in every fiber of its fragrant being, it has a fine, bittersweet tremor - shy lily of the valley in shady ground - akin to an impatient yearning for an unreceived caress. This makes it interesting, unexpectedly elevating it above the expected - beyond hesperidic freshness and the brittle, cognac-colored undertone that is so iconic for many fragrances from the house of Chanel and from the pen of Olivier Polge. Conclusion: a superficially bright scent on its journey from Paris to the southern Atlantic coast. It is accompanied by a delicate, underlying sadness - like the painting of that beautiful, nameless lady with the lemon in her hand.

For me, a beautiful scent for summer. You definitely have to like citrus fragrances with this one. The citrus notes are really very prominent at first. After a while, however, the floral note comes through, and from there it transports me to an afternoon in the sun, a book in one hand, a lemon-(mandarin-) lemonade in the other, and a bouquet of lily of the valley on the table. Always natural, never artificial or synthetic. Unfortunately, it fades very quickly. After 2-3 hours, it is actually no longer perceivable on my skin. Paris - Biarritz decides, so you have to be prepared to spray generously and frequently. But that can also be a nice feeling.

This Chanel Vive EDT can be worn anywhere. It’s fresh with juicy grapefruit and a touch of floral. Nothing crazy here—it’s simple and youthful. I don’t believe anyone will notice you, but sometimes we want that. It’s perfect for a hot summer’s day when too heavy of a scent would cause a migraine. I like this one. Not for everyday, but definitely one to reach for when there’s no A/C.

...today I am and say: I like Chance Eau Vive. And with that, I probably out myself in the eyes of some readers as a philistine. I must admit: Chance Eau Vive is indeed not a classic Chanel fragrance. Many of my predecessors even say that it is not only not a classic, but not Chanel at all, and this criticism is absolutely justified. Anyone who knows and loves No. 5, Coco Mademoiselle, Allure, etc., wonders how on earth this citrus scent made it into the Chanel lineup. For me, he is the Jon Snow of this house: Almost everyone around him thinks he doesn't belong, even scratching the honor of the house - by his mere presence. But I like him. Because against the accusation that Chance Eau Vive smells cheap, I must defend it. And there are indeed citrus scents that, for me, show no olfactory difference from dish soap or cheap shower gel. "Light Blue," for example. With Light Blue, I believe that the quality of the fragrance experience does not match the price tag. But Chance Eau Vive has this fresh lightness that is a pure delight, especially in summer. Because even though it is not a classic Chanel, it is not without merit. It is not the Grande Dame at the opera ball, but the young girl who cools her feet in the stream during summer. At the opera ball, the barefoot girl with wet feet is, of course, out of place. The reason I still like it is not that I have anything against the Grande Dame. On the contrary, I know, own, and appreciate several Chanel classics.* But ball gown at 30°? Uff. The feet belong in the cool stream, and Chance Eau Vive on the skin. *If anyone looks at my collection now and finds none: I am new here and my collection according to Parfumo is still incomplete. Easy, easy ;-)

As for the Chance line, I must confess, I am not a big fan at all. This scent here just seals the deal for me. Is this supposed to be Chanel? My best friend placed this fragrance in the same category as all the Essence fresh "summer scents," which are significantly cheaper to acquire. And you know what? There’s actually a grain of truth to that! Chance starts off naively into the pleasure, with a freshness that seems to be making its way to the coast. Citrus notes are clearly present here, but they neither feel full nor ripe; instead, they come across as totally dull and out of place. No beautiful connections are made here, and everything feels as if it wants to succeed but just can’t. Combining elegance and lightness is truly not that easy. Yet here, it’s a loud yawn when you catch a whiff of the fragrance. Extremely shy tones come and go, where a bit of rose and jasmine dare to step up to the podium. However, both appear quite unattractive and lack any real character. After a while, a hint of spicy, lukewarm fruit wafts in, just as shy and hesitant. It feels to me as if some ingredients were stirred up by the wind and mixed together. Pale and utterly uninteresting. In the end, the fragrance presents itself with a pale woody note, where the freshness somehow resists and makes the scent even a tad more uncomfortable. The sillage is not particularly noteworthy, and the longevity for me is just about 3 hours. Well, for a lukewarm summer scent, that’s actually okay, although I must say that I do not feel comfortable with it at all and am not even remotely addressed by this fragrance. For me, Eau Vive is a boring companion. Totally insignificant, it walks through the day with its wearer, neither skillfully highlighting the light elegance of a woman nor being a handsome companion one can easily engage with. Nothing clashes here; it’s just a yawning emptiness. I’d rather reach for other things, which are also significantly cheaper.

I wanted to do Chance an injustice & assume that I could hardly remember a tested perfume as little as this one... And I haven't even written a comment about the original yet, not even about any Chance! I've smelled it often, found it nice, even seen it in women's restrooms, but never thought it was important enough to warrant a test. Chance has always seemed so inconspicuous to me. Never one of the big Chanel fragrances, not even close. But since my entire vacation felt plastered with ads for Eau Vive & Chanel apparently still holds on to its Chance, today there were 2 Chances (?) to try. I was also curious about Eau Fraiche & especially for comparing the two lighter Chances (?). Eau Vive is quite little Chanel, quite a lot of summer. And the brand doesn't have many citrusy, simple fragrances anyway, so one can somewhat understand the step. However, that doesn't mean I have to overly like the scent. Citrusy, summery, light, musk, light woods & blood orange - tempting at first impression, then quickly puts you to sleep. Nice, but no perfume should be called that anymore. Especially not by someone as fair & "nice" in their reviews as I am - because 60% from me can easily mean 30-40% for a strict commentator. You simply expect more from Chanel; such nice citrus refreshers can be found on every street corner in July - and cheaper, more refined, more special. Chanel needs to stop with so many flankers & once again take a Chance to sink a classic! Do we need an EdC, EdT, Parfum, EdP, Eau Fraiche, Eau Vive, Eau Tendre & Eau whatever from every perfume? Hell no! Bottle: slightly golden, but more than unspectacular... Sillage & Longevity: fully set for summer! (4 hours) Conclusion: no matter how I feel about Chanel - I find this flanker flood simply unnecessary, even if Eau Vive covers the simple gap in the catalog!

Since Chance has long been my companion, and I am also inclined towards Tendre, I wanted to give the "Life Water" a "Chance". However, the first impression is strangely indifferent. Neither does the subtle elegance of the original Chance embrace me, nor the tender playfulness of Tendre. Eau Vive somehow lies in between. Blood orange and grapefruit are pleasantly tart - fresh and invigorating to the nose. The jasmine is floral - green - so to speak, captured with foliage. Iris and cedar form a darker finish that seems somewhat abrupt and doesn't quite fit the fresh-green overall picture. Unfortunately, Eau Vive does not follow the promising red, pardon, green thread that introduced the fragrance at the beginning. No disturbing scent - but I miss the statement in it. It remains oddly diffuse overall and will not find its way into my shelf - unless as a gift, because it is really not bad at all.

...because I really like it a lot. I received a sample of Eau Vive during my last perfume purchase, and with the temperatures exceeding 30 degrees yesterday, it seemed like the perfect time for a test. So I sprayed myself generously, and it instantly put a smile on my face: A bitter-fresh, barely sweet, slightly sparkling citrus cloud surrounded me.

Chance is not Chanel. At no point have I perceived Chance and its flankers as part of the Chanel classics, nor do I see Coco Noir as a masterpiece of the house, but that is not up for debate here. Even the round bottle shows: I am different from my siblings and ancestors.

Right off the bat: if someone had slipped this to me as scent XY from company Z - I would have believed it. A typical Chanel signature does not reveal itself here. That’s not to say I don’t like the scent, no, I do like it, but with some small limitations that set in after the top notes fade.

....that's true. As a confessed lover of Chance in its original form, I naturally wanted to test the latest edition of the classic. At first, we were not friends at all. The soapy note bothered me completely and felt somehow uncomfortable on my skin. So I put it aside, not for me. Then I smelled Eau Vive on an acquaintance and was totally thrilled.

At the first spray, I can immediately smell the citrus note, which is actually great for me because I love everything that smells citrusy. Unfortunately, after a few seconds, a bitter note develops on my skin, probably due to the grapefruit combined with the vetiver. I think perhaps one note should have been chosen here, as both together create a bittersweet bomb.

Pine, calone and moss, its not much fresh actually. Sometimes smells chemical. Weak lasting power and sillage. In my opinion it's not worth it if you're looking for something fresh. Updated January 2014

Describing a fragrance is a difficult task. But I'll give it another try. Kenzo pour Homme smells like a salty sea breeze on a coast where citrus fruits grow. It's a beautiful image, isn't it? The color of the bottle perfectly matches the scent. If I were to describe the fragrance with a color, I would name this color. Kenzo pour Homme is fresh, fresher than fresh. Free your mind and take a whiff, you won't regret it.

Hello dears ;)! This is my forever-summer go to perfume. I love coocnut sweet perfumes for summer ( sun cream smell) but not to gourmand ( I don't want it to tempt me to eat it hahah). All in all, it's perfect sweet but not too gourmand. The only thing I disslike is that the bottle is not transparent so I cannot see how much is left. I did my full review here if you wanna see: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cP7gjmSMoQA&t=50s

I had no idea about the Bronze Goddess 2017 Eau de Parfum ... until my dear Heike sent me a sample. I mean, who can keep track of all the fragrances on the market? Moreover, I knew about Estée Lauder, but I wasn't aware that they also have fragrances. When I then went searching for this edP, I almost despaired. WHY does one have to release a new bottle every 2 years? But now to the scent: Well, I didn't expect anything when I sprayed the fragrance sample. But this citrusy, zesty start immediately captivated me. Bronze Goddess changes very quickly, though. The citrus note transforms into a very special note, a bit like skin that has been in the sun too long, hot and with a hint of sunscreen and dried sea salt. Frangipani and a delicate coconut note with beautiful jasmine sneak in and turn the fragrance into a true "summer illusion," sweet, creamy, delicate, slightly sultry. The combination of ingredients plays tricks on the senses. You really feel like you've just come from a hot day at the beach. Coconut shake and a sea of flowers, salt on the skin, and pure sunshine. Ginger, Kashmir wood, and musk make it briefly denser and more sultry. However, this doesn't last long. Vanilla and amber make it creamy, and I mean really creamy. Hence the association with sunscreen. Wow, I find this scent development very exciting. On my skin, it has quite a nice evolution. However, the longevity and sillage don't exceed a good average. Personally, I don't find that too bad. In the end (after a long search), I bought the version from 2019. I like the bottle much better than the one from the 2017 version.

Eeeeeersteeeee. This has never happened to me before. Let's see... From the title, one might think that Bronze Goddess EdP is a summer fragrance. You know...summer...the season when it gets light early and dark late. When that yellow ball in the sky is visible and even gives off warmth. Warmth. Ice. Swimming pool. Sea. The birds chirp early in the morning...well, or it's that one terror bird that starts squawking like crazy half an hour before everyone else. Preferably when you can actually sleep in. Which, of course, happens about as often as Christmas and Easter on the same day. Bronze Goddess EdP is not a true summer scent. At least I wouldn't really want to wear it in the heat, as it is quite intense and powerful. This is something it truly has over its predecessors. They lasted on my skin like a bottle of vodka in a Russian household. So, quite briefly. And I really couldn't perceive them well either. Bronze Goddess EdP is quite different. It lasts all day and has a decent projection. The first 4 hours, it is well detectable even from a distance, and it slowly but surely gets closer to you.
