The scent starts fresh and slightly fruity, then a warm, slightly alcoholic note comes in - like sweet cognac or a drink in the evening. Later, it becomes woody, vanilla-like, and a bit more sensual. I like that it stands out without being too loud.

Drunk Lovers by BORNTOSTANDOUT is a fragrance that immediately tells a story of a night full of desire and mystery. The opening bursts with energy: citrus fruits like bergamot and grapefruit dance with red berries, accompanied by a hint of juniper that gets the game started.

It surpises me that aldehydes are not mentioned in this composition (they were mentioned as being present in the scent that was in their former bottle design) because I still find this very, very aldehydic! It is a bit less 'fatty' and sharp than the former formulation was, but it still is Estée! I love this for being very fresh and 'cooling', but in a very different way than in most summer scents that are often more fresh from citrussy notes. Not everybody will find this a distinct 'summer scent' though. I do, because of it's soapy- and cool vibe. But many people may find this more suitable for other seasons. I, for instance, smell hardly any sweetness in Estée, but my sister (who's signature is First from Van Cleef & Arpels) find this very (too) sweet. So it might depend on ones chemistry. I always smell the white Dove bar in Estée (I love the white Dove bar:-)) and like to wear this on more formal occasions like job interviews or work-meetings. The Jasmine and Lily of the Valley are very beautyful balanced in this scent, I can smell the Lily of the Valley asif I just plucked the real flower. The only downside of this beautyful fragrance for me is that I suffer from olfactory adaptation with this scent: I know others smell it when I'm wearing this, telling me they love it, but I can't smell it on myself after some time. And because I wear my perfumes not just for others, but also (or mainly) to enjoy it myself, that is too bad....Other than that, beautyful fragrance! Edit: After wearing other, very different perfumes lately, I just sprayed some of this again and it is really beautyful. Now that I hadn't sprayed it for long, I keep smelling it, no olfactory fatique and sillage is stronger than rated. It is quite affordable now because it's being rebottled in their 'Legacy Collection' which is very expensive.

The time has passed when the terms Chypre and Oud meant nothing to me. I sat there, listened, made a wise face, nodded here and there, and apparently even at the right moments, and understood - nothing! First, I discovered Chypre, and later Oud fragrances for myself: What a rich world full of scent wonders has opened up to me in recent years, welcoming me kindly and patiently. I was taken by the hand and guided through a wonderland whose boundaries I am fortunately still far from reaching. Classic Chypre fragrances have impressed for generations with their radiant, opulent beauty. But modern creations, often without aldehyde rays and strong oakmoss spice, possess a special charm as well. “Chypre forever?” - It almost seems so! For even “Estée,” this graceful scent fairy with a soapy touch, is a typical Chypre fragrance, although it was only born into this world of our fragrant companions in 2015. Just by the name, this composition is genetically predisposed. Anyone who has delved a little into Estée Lauder, her life, and her care and fragrance creations knows: What bears the name of this lady cannot be loud and ostentatious; she herself was lived elegance! (And yet a clever businesswoman/entrepreneur; that should also be mentioned.) Thus, a ladylike, subtle scent profile unfolds here, once without citrus, which I find quite pleasant; it’s a nice change: no bergamot this time. (Look at that: It can be done!) Instead, an impressive floral bouquet of noble scented roses, radiant white sensual jasmine, just at the right ripeness, and a floral-spicy-earthy lily of the valley aroma surprises as the top note. The two white “little stinkers” (a warm greeting to Meggi in this context!) were arranged to pleasantly awaken the senses without becoming too dominant. All three fragrance notes are artfully bound and skillfully interwoven, allowing them time to unfold before sunny-warm ylang-ylang ribbons and powdery iris clouds join them in harmony with a refined hint of coriander. The scent of an elegant, finely spicy floral soap develops this way; however, with rich sillage and already very good longevity. The classic base note sandalwood must not be missing here, and instead of the expected oakmoss spice, we discover lush dark green moss cushions, still a bit damp (please don’t rest on that!) and partially adorned with many pinhead-sized (-small?) white flowers. There is not just one type of moss; I am continually surprised by how many varieties can be discovered when you look a little closer. This has been utilized for “Estée,” allowing for a very ladylike, classic-modern fragrance creation to emerge. As a confessed lover of richly lathering bar soap with an ample supply to avoid falling into boredom during use, I find the softly floating soapy scent note very pleasant. It caresses the skin and gently strokes the senses. “Estée” is one of those gems that could be worn daily, if it weren’t for the quite extensive competition in our fragrance box. But anyone looking for a feminine, expressive, yet not intrusive business scent as a “perennial favorite” will find themselves well accommodated with this lady. She is present like a pleasant companion, almost a good friend. So here, the name truly is the program: “Estée” fulfills it with warm, floating brilliance and rich scent fullness. This fragrance personality is already welcome simply because of its charming and cultivated nature.

Estée Lauder (1906 -2004) came from a European immigrant family with predominantly Jewish roots. She started from the simplest beginnings, mixing creams, ointments, and oils in her kitchen. She sold these at housewife parties. Her products increasingly gained popularity. Tirelessly and with great sales talent, she promoted and sold her products. She was the inventor of product samples. Thus, she surpassed the constantly feuding ladies Elizabeth Arden and Helena Rubinstein, partly because she disapproved of their kind of backbiting and believed that instead of fighting among themselves, women should use their strength to show other women a new self-confidence and to show the gentlemen who were leading in the cosmetics and perfume industry what’s what. Gradually, the idea matured to create a magnificent perfume for American women, as three-quarters of all fragrances sold in America were of French origin. Moreover, women at that time - until the 1950s - did not dare to buy their own perfume. They received fragrances as gifts from friends or men. Thus, in 1953, "Youth Dew" made its debut and began its victorious journey around the world. It remains very popular to this day. A quote from Estée: “Perfume is like love. A little is never enough.” Estée continued to work diligently and built an empire. In 1968, "Estée super," also known as "Supercologne," was released. The predecessor of today's Estée. Of course, Super Estée was more complex, characterized by an aldehydic opening and supported by what felt like 100 flowers on a typical chypre moss-cedarwood base. However, I cannot say that I am disappointed with the "new" Estée. No, the aldehydes no longer hit you in the nose. They have made way for rose and lily of the valley. Not sweet and not overly modernized. The accompanying herbal note and a powdery hint of iris prevent that. Ms. Iris is not very sweet anyway and adds a bit of fine soapiness. A beautiful, modern, moderate chypre with the typical woody-mossy base. We owe Mrs. Lauder some great chypres, such as "Private Collection," which debuted in 1972 and was originally created for herself but later marketed. Not to forget "Aliage," "Azurée," and the wonderful "Knowing." Today, the company is one of the leading manufacturers of skincare, makeup, and perfume worldwide. The Estée Lauder Group includes more than 25 brands, including Aramis, Aveda, Bobbi Brown, Clinique, Donna Karan, Darphin, Jo Malone, Kiton, La Mer, MAC, Michael Kors, Tom Ford, and Tommy Hilfiger. But Estée Lauder was also socially engaged. She donated to hospitals, museums, universities, and many more. I wrote this review retrospectively for International Women's Day to honor one of the most remarkable women in the field of cosmetics, perfume, and civil courage.

Just six years ago, I wrote: "What a disappointment! This perfume has been reformulated. How incredibly sad." By now (2022), I have gotten used to reformulations that have little in common with the original. The original Estee or "Super Perfume" was released in 1968, an extraordinary, bold scent. Radiant, sparkling. The strong aldehydes made the abstract flowers in this composition stand out fantastically. And the perfume lasted and lasted... it was strikingly different from other fragrances. It helped me concentrate, it was somehow intellectual and abstract. The revised version feels like a weak copy, a pale memory. This is probably due to the reformulation regulations that have been in place for some time now, and of course also to the fact that general tastes have changed significantly. What is sold today as "Estee" only vaguely resembles the powerhouse scent of 1968. I don't know when the reformulation took place, unfortunately. I bought my last bottle of the original scent in 1995. The "Estee" from 2015 is slightly aquatic-salty, a bit like "Acqua di Sale" by Profumum Roma. They could have taken "Estee" off the market entirely, but on the other hand, not everyone knows the original and mourns its loss. Compared to many new releases, the reformulation is probably even a rather fine scent. That I can't wear the new Estee fragrance... - that's me.

I've recently been fascinated by iris scents; most notably Iris Nobile by Acqua di Parma and Iris 39 by Le Labo. My mother had received a bunch of flowers after a performance (she's an actress), and for days the room in which she'd placed the beautifully arranged iris and lily bouquet, smelt divine. Chanel's 28 La Pausa is close to that scent, but not close enough. 28 La Pausa opens rather fresh. The prominent iris note is green and natural. I do believe that the iris note in this fragrance is the actual essential oil, rather than a synthetic take on iris. Citrus notes compliment the iris towards the heart, however when settled, 28 La Pausa transforms into a smooth, soapy scent. The soapiness, although feminine and pretty, resembles other iris-based scents on the market, most notably, Acqua di Parma's Iris Nobile EDT. The woodsy drydown only furthers my comparison to the above fragrance. I do believe vetiver may be a missing note in 28 La Pausa. It has this wonderful bitter and earthy quality that really compliments the iris. There is a great sense of simplistic subtlety to be found in this scent. It doesn't scream, "look at me!" or anything overtly sexy, however it succeeds in being soft and inoffensive. The scent lasted well on my skin, so I won't agree with the other reviewers who experienced poor lasting strength. The scent is delightfully refreshing and clean smelling. I'd most likely wear 28 La Pausa during Spring, when the weather is particularly beautiful and the world is lively.

to me this reminds me of a old grand piano dust on the ivory keys the scent of ivory wood from when the piano was played i whould enjoy it's scent it has an elegant tinge to it which i'v i fond it strange at a time and the scent of an old tin can filled with sowing needles and thread and the rust of the can at that time seemed interesting but intoxicating in a way. it is earthy but it's metalic at the same time.

Chanel 28 LA PAUSA is to my nose a veritable pause from perfume! All I detect is a light powdery cross between flour and sawdust, which does not develop and disappears from my skin shortly after application. Perhaps a bit too subtle? BEIGE would have been a perfect name for this composition, it seems to me. Clearly 28 LA PAUSA represents a pendulum swing in the opposite direction of the flamboyant, bombastic "I am perfume, hear me roar! (or, rather, "smell me stink!") creations of the 1980s--but could this be too far to the non-perfume side? I wouldn't say that this is an anti-perfume, for it is definitely not aesthetically repugnant in any way.

La Pausa's woody-floral sweetness has several facets to round out the iris, but the impression is more of an augmented soli-note than a full-on bouquet. It's neither as shocking as the brutal metallity of Iris Silver Mist, nor as affecting as the melancholic heliotrope of Après l'ondée; and, as such, it's a bit less characterful. Luca Turin gives them 5 stars and this one 4, which is about right.

28 La Pausa features an iris note that's every bit as pure as the one in Iris Silver Mist, but nowhere near as cloak-and-daggery. 28 La Pausa is like a fresh breeze off a line of linens on a summer's day. Bolstered on top by a touch of green citrus and below with a dab of creamy, peppery woods, iris is really the star of the show here. There is something to be said for just letting a fantastic raw material shine, and this is the approach Chanel has chosen here. Although the iris is sheer and ethereal, there is a slightly buttery, round tone to it that minimizes any attending severity. I love 28 La Pausa for its purity and its gentleness, but I curse it for its longevity. It lasts all of two-three hours on my skin. For this reason, and this reason alone, it is a perfume that I mentally rank alongside the great Apres L'Ondee. Art but in a format that is almost painfully ephemeral.

'Footsteps on the Snow' is a wonderful, small piano piece by Debussy, silvery shimmering, melancholically quiet, and thoughtfully still. I think of warm gray walls, the stucco radiates like meringue, fine, fluffy snowflakes fall, settling like a powder cloud on rhododendron leaves.

From the "Les Exclusifs de Chanel," "Coromandel" is my (so far) undisputed number 1 fragrance. It falls into the category of "if I like it, an immediate repurchase." "Bois des Iles" and "Sycomore" were once part of my collection as well. So, a pretty good hit rate.

La Pausa is the name of the villa in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin on the Cote d`Azur that Coco Chanel purchased as a "summer retreat." Many celebrities were her guests there, and not least Salvador Dali and his wife Gala used La Pausa as a refuge during the Spanish Civil War. Unfortunately, I do not know what connection No.28 has to this.
A popular mythical theme found in numerous cultures is that of the little water or mermaid who is in love with a human prince and must win his love to gain an immortal soul.

Thank you PontNeuf for the sample. Shortly after I applied La Pausa, I thought pfff well, Polge isn't coming up with anything new. The top note smells like green tea or better yet freshly mown grass. Pretty, nice, pleasant, but completely unexciting. I pondered what Coco Chanel would have thought about this scent, as she certainly never rode a green wave.

Why does cherry always have to be naughty? Debauched? Indecent? This cherry is upstanding. It’s clear, bright, poppy – a stock photo perfect maraschino. And clean, without feeling medicinal or hand-soapy. Every time I wear this scent a small part of me is transported back to the 90s, bubble bathing in L'Oréal Kids cherry almond shampoo (the one in the fish-shaped bottle). It’s more cherry than Lost Cherry, but lighter on the almond. And more cherry than Cherry Punk, minus the smoke and studded leather. The longest lasting of the three on my skin too, clocking 6+ hours. Mental Snapshot: Red VW beetle, with plastic eyelashes on the headlights. A heart-shaped lollipop from your kindergarten valentine. Patent leather go-go boots and prescription wayfarers. Comic book word balloons. WOW! YUM! The belle of the boardroom, a c-suite party girl. Did Andy Warhol ever silkscreen a cherry? tl;dr: pop art

I am a cherry hater. It either reminds me of cough syrup medicine or its so artificially sweet, syrupy, and headache inducing. This toes the line, I could almost fall in love with it. This starts as a juicy cherry with almond. That almond keeps it from being overwhelming, keeps it from just being candy cherry. Then it gets a little lighter and you get the rose, strawberry, and sour cherry. Its still strong and borderline artificial punch flavor candy but not. The dry down is a fluffy vanilla. My dentist also complimented while I was wearing this. She says fragrances usually give her a headache but this wasn't agitating her sensitivities. It lasted about 4 hours on my skin and the projection is good.

Indecent cherry smells like a mix between a bright red cherry lollipop and a fresh cherry shampoo. Especially the opening feels quite clean, the drydown gets sweeter. Haribo gummy cherries come to my mind. Saffron adds a slightly medicinal, warmer background hum. Rose and almond are here to emphasize the sour and sweet facets of the cherry. I like how they're subtle, but still distinguishable from the cherry. I also enjoy how this cherry really has a sour side and isn't just one-dimensionally sweet. If you only like very natural smelling fragrances, this might not be for you. There is definitely a synthetic edge to this, which I think is intentional. Imagine a cherry symbol made of neon lights, an inflatable PVC cherry or glittery cherry lipgloss from a transparent palette, and you get the vibe. It's a fun, flirty, not too serious perfume. "Indecent" is a reach. There might be a slight naughty wink to it, but nothing really lewd or dirty. I don't know why BTSO loves cringy names so much. To me, this is like the olfactory equivalent of red, heart-shaped plastic sunglasses. Almost every cherry scent kind of is, but this even more than others. Make of that what you will. Because I'm sure every cherry fragrance from the last years gets compared to Lost Cherry from time to time, I want to add quickly that I don't find these two very similar. IC is sourer, fresher, colder and less realistic. I do like both, but LC is my favorite cherry of all times, so it's hard to compete with that.

Sampling Borntostandout Indecent Cherry, a sharp and sweet, rich, somewhat spicy cherry that’s very much reminiscent of Tom Ford Lost Cherry was being a bit more cherry-centric, with a fairly prominent saffron note that plays as spicier and more herbal as opposed to Lost Cherry’s boozy, liqueur, resinous-leaning characteristics. I think the saffron is challenging, but interesting, a slight step down from the majesty that is Lost Cherry but a very welcome cherry entry that I think many will love, certainly adding diversity to a clearly robust and interesting catalogue, and it’s a pleasure to try. As with the rest of the line, it’s EDP concentration and priced at $210 for 50ml, sold in the US at boutiques like Ministry of Scent. It performs very well, consistent with the high performance of most entries in the house. 7 out of 10

Very synthetic nauseating "cherry" scent, gross. I had high hopes for this one, I love a good cherry scent, and this is NOT IT!!!!! I will leave my general impression of the brand here as well, as I have tried two of their discovery sets. All of the scents are incredibly strong and smell very artificial. A lot of them are also very sweet, and many smell the same on the dry-down. Considering the price tag, I honestly do not understand what is the point of this brand. This is strictly my opinion, if you love paying way too much for a synthetic sweet smell, you are free to do so. I will not be exploring this brand further.

My first thought: Cherry ...then ...Shampoo I'm lying in the bathtub, looking forward to a romantic :D hair wash with the cherry shampoo...a delight after a long day ... massaged into my hair...pampered with a hair massage ... The whole house smells like cherry ...

...this would be exactly my cherry scent. The opening with the tried-and-true cherry-almond combo is intensified by the saffron and is really beautifully accompanied. The cherry is supported by the zestier notes of berry and rose, making it consistently present without coming off as overly sweet or artificial.

I’ll say it like it is: I have many cherry fragrances at home, but Indecent Cherry is my undisputed favorite. The one cherry scent. Sweet, fruity, and sensual, yet really not boring at all. From the very beginning, this wild, juicy cherry hits you in the face. Not artificial or overripe - but just right.

Eh, this is really not my thing... Being indecent - and on top of that cherry! Finally, I was able to sniff through the line from Borntostandout that I approached with rather "low expectations." And I really have to say: they have something. More than I expected. I. Cherry is freshly sprayed, the dark cherry hits you right on the mark.

The Indecent Cherry by BTSO offers me a cherry combined with a strawberry upon the first spray, which makes the scent come across as somewhat sweet. In the drydown, the sweetness fades a bit and notes like amber, vanilla, and musk become more prominent, making the fragrance feel a bit more pleasant. The scent lasts quite a long time, and those nearby also notice it.

It may have been conceptually intended as a successor to Kenzo pour Homme Eau de Toilette Boisée, a fragrance that, despite its complexity, exuded a light, citrus-woody elegance. Here, the lightness has been lost. While wood and lemon are initially dominant, there is a synthetic, hygienic sharpness in the background that gradually pushes its way to the forefront.

This one took me by surprise, in a good way. My mother wore the original Beautiful growing up and I have mixed feelings about that scent as it hits differently depending on the day, but I am happy to report that this is nothing like the original Beautiful, at all. This fragrance stands on its own. It is very pretty and fresh, elegantly clean. It truly is what I want out of a magnolia perfume, where so many others have left me sad and wanting. In this, magnolia truly stands out as the star. I’ve finally got myself buying the smallest size when blind buying and this one will be a repurchase in the largest size available. I want the comfort this brings. Very reminiscent of evening walks in a sundress late spring or even comfy pajamas and a cup of tea during the fall. It does vaguely remind me of Chance Eau Tendre, a vibrant opening that settles into a soft cloud, but they are really not close enough at all for this to be a dupe. Sadly like every dang perfume I adore, my skin eats it immediately and I go nose blind in like 10 minutes. I hate that I can’t smell it on me all day when I know the people around me can. Isn’t going to stop me from wearing it and I just carry a small decant for when I need a hit. I accidentally wore this layered over L'eau d'Issey by Issey Miyake and it kicked it up a level! They complimented each other very nicely.

Such an easy and effortless scent in a good way! I don't mind it being 'not unique'; it smells good! I can sum it up as light floral. Perfect for spring and summer. It's a type of scent that you can have without giving others a headache. No risk; I bought mine with a good duty-free value. If you are not trying to limit yourself with sophisticated scents, go for it! I'm happy to find my new daily perfume.

A very fresh, aquatic and shampoo-like fragrance. Definitely has that drugstore shampoo scent. Gentle, subtle, innocent and suitable for work. I don't get any maté, but I do get the fresh roses and the lovely magnolia. Very feminine-leaning and pretty. The drydown feels a little synthetic as the sandalwood and cedarwood seem a little more watery than what I'm used to. It's a bit generic (nothing bad with it), so it could be a safe blind-buy. There's not much more to say. It's a very laid-back fragrance and linear. It's fine, but not something I'll be adding to my collection. Glad I got to try it nonetheless. A lovely fragrance for spring and summer!

This truly is a High Frequency Scent, this #22. Vibrating and resonating, my body plucked like a string pulled taut between heaven and earth. spiritual, soulful, sensual. This goes beyond scent and skin, as though I have slipped beyond my own perimeter into an boundless universe of fragrant delight.

Vintage: First let me start off my saying this is my favorite Chanel! No 22 is the envy of all ancient Chanel's! This classy beauty is by far one of thee most interesting & highly appealing fragrances I have come across! It opens up with a tremendous burst of Aldehydes in which No 5 can not compare. It then slowly progresses into a soft white rose fragrance which is later dominated by the best part of this fragrance which is the base! Incense, Vanilla & Vetiver form a highly delectable delicious aroma that is soothing to both men & women. No. 22 becomes a skin scent which is the only thing I do not like about it. I wish it could project for miles, however it is meant for close quarters & it preforms very nicely. Dare I say this is far superior than No 5 is a understatement. The vintage formula is best, altho the Les Exclusives line is not bad, I noticed they did tone down the incense in the newer version, however a remarkable structure to a underestimated fragrance IMO! Long live NO 22!

This is was a challeging fragrance to my nose. In the beginning i just did not like it and found a bit dated to my nose. After some months trying, i've realized why this is called a masterpiece by some people. This is a heavy aldehydic floral that turns to a beautiful floral and soapy scent when dries down. First notes are a bit difficult to my nose, but the powdery and woodsy drydown is just wonderful. I guess the tuberose note along with vetiver gives the fine tune to this fragrance. Very well blended, this fragrance can be used for men without problems. If you like aldehydes and florals, this is a must have. Sillage, lasting power and projection are good.

Chanel No.22 is much prettier and ten times sexier than Chanel No.5. No.5 is like sharp baby powder and old cosmetics, whereas No.22, although powdery as well, has a beautiful array of floral accords, smokey incense and bourbon vanilla. I can really smell the ylang ylang in this fragrance, along with the vanilla and the lily of the valley. These combined notes gives this scent a classically feminine appeal. It's a confident scent with a touch of youthfulness, particularly with the sweet nuances. I initially detested aldehydes when I was younger, however since reaching my 20's, powdery scents are classified by me as being sexy scents. Chanel No.22 is very white, but nowhere near being innocent. It brings to mind the feeling of being prim and proper but flirtatious at the same time. The powder in this fragrance is less alarming than some aldehydic fragrances I've tried. It has some similarities to the beautiful D&G Women (the one with the red cap), which I also adore. The sillage and lasting power is commendable, as is its ability to work well with any kind of skin chemistry. I highly recommend this classic Chanel masterpiece.

No.22 is so exquisite. I smell a gorgeous combo of white flowers and smoky incense with that signature CHANEL powdery aldehyde on top. It's simply timeless, one of the best of the Les Exclusifs line. SUMMARY: 1920's flamenco dancer having a cigarette after the show

No. 22 made me fall in love with aldehydes. Prior to our acquaintance, I only liked or appreciated aldehydes. I own a few, Chanel's No.5, Van Cleef's First, which are all glamorous beauties but left me cold. I got closer to Tauer's Noontide Petals and Guerlain's Liu but never contemplated a serious attachment until I met 22.

It seems that all les exclusifs were reformulated in 2007, so my review won’t reflect the current formula. It’s also difficult to find a review of N°22 eau de toilette, as the parfum is more common. According to the one review I could find, the top notes are aldehydes which accounts for its metallic sharpness.

This was never on my wanted list yet I have always wanted to sample it. Once again, it came to me. My white metal container is mostly full and probably came from the 1960s. Considering that the formula is 92 years old, its surprisingly youthful. I find it has the same DNA as Chanel no 5. In fact, they share a lot of note including big aldehydes and lots of neroli.

First of all: I like Chanel 22. I like aldehydes and especially the way Chanel incorporates them into a fragrance. The "22" smells aldehydic-floral and very well-groomed... I perceive the Ylang Ylang almost more distinctly than the Lily of the Valley... in the base, the vanilla clearly emerges and adds a pleasant sweetness...

My number 22, my support, my staff, my backbone. It is clean, it is perfect, it is the thread of Ariadne that leads me out of the darkness of the cave when I have once again talked myself into it. In the conference room with all the suit-wearers, I take a puff from my silk handkerchief, thank God, it is always there, my 22, don’t abandon me.

I'm really impressed with this L'eau par Kenzo flanker. Although an aquatic, L'eau 2 Kenzo for Her has a sweet juicy quality which smells really fun and invigorating on the skin. There aren't many similarities between this flanker and the original. I'm really enjoying the sweet bursts of lemon and pear, followed by some gloriously feminine florals. Freesia provides a clean base, while the rose and lotus, in turn, create an element of girlish charm. L'eau 2 Kenzo for Her is the perfect choice for Spring and Summer, and will be a sure hit with the younger segment of the population. To be completely honest, I didn't expect too much prior to testing this flanker, so I have been more than pleasantly surprised. I would most certainly wear this. Due to its flirtatious and candied sweetness, some may consider this fragrance a tooth-ache. I actually don't mind it, and that's partly because this fragrance settles in a way that is soft and discreet, rather than loud. The drydown is a subtle blend of sweetened florals, white musk and cedar. I think the composition as a whole, has been well executed. Even the sales assistants have been raving over the new L'eau 2 Kenzo for Her. In terms of longevity, I'd have to say that it really does last, a lot longer than you may expect. I assume that this could be a limited edition, or even the 2012 answer to a Summer release. Either way, snap it up now or be sorry. Originally written: July 07, 2012.

It bubbles from bright granite, sparkling, cool, wet. The top note is fresh, pure, intoxicating freshness, almost too much of a good thing. Almost. The line to pungency has not been crossed, the top note is pleasing. The further opening then reminds one of a cool mountain stream in summer. Refreshing. Natural. It bubbles along the rocks, cool, aquatic, zesty, yet not too cold; after all, a mountain stream is cool in summer, but otherwise it is warm, pleasant, a welcome refreshment. The top note that slowly transitions into the heart note recalls this mountain stream flowing down the valley. The water, light blue, clear and fresh, still sparkling and bubbling. Slowly the stream enters warmer realms. It slows down, the bubbling disappears and makes way for a slightly powdery warmth, which still hints at its original rocky nature; the cedar note allows the original freshness to still be sensed - one can see the mountain in the distance - harmonizing wonderfully with the musk, which conveys a feeling of only slightly powdery warmth, combined with the cedar, but still fresh. In particular, the slowly spreading base note surprises. After such a fresh, bubbling, overflowing opening, I did not expect to be caught in such a unique warmth that still reminds one of the clear origin not too far away. A successful journey.

Imagine a private pool with fresh water without chlorine on a hot summer day. On the green lawn, there’s a lounge chair where someone is sipping refreshing sparkling water with a hint of fruit flavor. Just relaxing. If only it weren't for the little, excessively loud, annoying brother with his sticky peach iced tea, then the chill turtle would really be in paradise here… But let's take it step by step: The opening of L’Eau 2 Kenzo freezes people who have a Marry Me! trauma à la Lanvin - at least on my skin, the two top notes are as similar as one egg (or rather peach) to another: a very dominant peach that, however, does not really come across as fruity or fresh, but rather shows the sweet, artificial presence one knows from peach yogurts or iced tea. Nice, but over time it becomes too annoying for me. Fortunately, this phase at Kenzo doesn’t last too long. Barely has the opening settled, one gets to enjoy a very special note that I haven't encountered before. Kenzo manages to make something detectable in this fragrance section that I always thought was undetectable: carbonated mineral water. You surely know this mineral water to which a small concentration of fruit juices is added. I had the impression that I was smelling not my arm, but such a drink. Not only refreshing but also, quite literally, sparkling. At first, the “fruit juice” tends more towards peach, but is later replaced by lemon. Unfortunately, this intermediate section is already over after half an hour. I don't know the original Eau fragrance from Kenzo well enough to say this for sure, but I suspect that the scent progression is now heading "back to the roots": the lemon becomes increasingly aquatic and ultimately leaves a very fine, aquatic scent that strikes me as nice but not very special. Conclusion: It's a shame that the middle part doesn't last longer, as it truly managed to excite me. I'm not quite sure if the concept with L’Eau 2 Kenzo will really work, as the opening might be too intense for lovers of subtle, aquatic-fresh scents, while the finale may be too trivial for fans of stronger fragrances. As a member of the first group, this scent will certainly not find a new spot with me.

Well, that's not entirely true, although the number of warm sunny days in a year on Capri is indeed higher than that on Norderney, that much is undisputed. But olfactorily speaking, the warmth that Estée Lauder's Bronze Goddess Capri brings on my skin fits quite well. What I expected: an orangey-citrusy scent that later drifts into a slightly sunscreen-like aroma. I probably also thought of a sour-fresh lemonade-flavored ice cream of the same name from a well-known ice cream manufacturer, which has been around since the 70s. But there was also: the chairlift ride up to Monte Solaro, when I wanted to escape the bustling, noisy tourist crowds in Capri and took a seat in the lift. It was immediately quiet, the sun was blazing, and the, well, ride wind - or better, floating wind - gently whispered around my ears and gifted me with a mild breeze around my nose. The lift traveled very close to the ground. With my feet, I could almost touch the branches of the fragrant orange and lemon trees as the chairlift glided over them. I encounter this warmth of the sun again in Bronze Goddess Capri. This lushness, this tranquility. However, I cannot find the citrus freshness of the orange grove, and that is very surprising to me, because: my skin generally absorbs a lot of sweetness, so I would have suspected, after the previous comment and the scent "cake", to find a Mediterranean citrus fragrance here. The opening is indeed citrusy, juicy, not too sour, rather with a hint of sweetness. But just like a blink of an eye, then mandarin and lemon leaf have already disappeared. Surprisingly, the fragrance takes a very sweet direction on me. I am soon overwhelmed by a large bouquet of flowers, from which I cannot explicitly pick out any individual component. Estée Lauder has created several magnificent floral scents, and here too, a large, round bouquet of various flowers is revealed, harmoniously composed and with a natural, almost American lushness and generosity. It becomes sweeter, almost dessert-like, but not "heavy". On my skin, vanilla dominates, vanilla and vanilla. Warm & sweet, sweet & warm. The transition from heart to base is very beautifully rounded and flowing. The sillage, however, is only moderate; the scent does not overwhelm (neither me nor others), neither in the floral stage nor in the vanilla stage. It does not impose itself, but is still not really close to the skin, which is quite successful. So what do I ultimately think of it? Measured by my expectations, I am disappointed, as it does not bring me enough citrus freshness. But for those who like a warm sunscreen scent, or better: a scent of sweet cream that melts on (sun)warm skin without being narcotic (even at higher outside temperatures), they will be well served here. Thanks to Jolien for kindly providing a sample!

White florals are usually too much for me — I do like them, I think they're the sexiest thing a man can wear (my boyfriend has Do Son and it always makes me howl incessantly) but most of the times they're super saturated and give me headaches...until I found Gardenia - fresh, and ethereal, like a dream... the only white floral that I can ever wear, the only one that truly suits me as a person. Soft but present. The cold beauty of early Spring in a bottle. Les Exclusifs de Chanel are truly the best thing that happened to me as an enthusiastic perfume sniffer and now I'm afraid I'll never go back: even with their ridiculous price increases. The juice is too good!!

Chanel's Gardenia is one of the original fragrances that was then rolled into the Les Exclusifs line. This is a prim, warm gardenia with a fruity note reminiscent of strawberry at the outset. As it dries down the fruitiness dissipates and a freesia like note joins the gardenia along with a bit of gentle, fatty musk and orris. The overall effect is a clean and polished, with almost gleamy 'white' feel, that also ends up being just a tiny bit reminiscent of shampoo. On it's own this stands out as as a slightly atypical offering from what the average consumer associates with Chanel, however I feel that Polge was smart to build other fragrances around this historic pillar such as Beige and 1932 which allowed for a more seamless fit within the Les Exclusifs line.

This sits heavy on my skin, overwhelmed by a bushel of gardenias and non-gardenias, though it was mostly the latter that pushed through. There is a classical floral-sweetness that is delicate and not offensive in any way. The very idea of this scent wafting through the warm air around me was incredible. However, I found it to soon become... basic? I shouldn't really call it basic. A better word could be formulaic, since Chanel has been in the game long enough to have written the formula this perfume is based off of. It fails to impress me, refresh me, or invoke a full bottle at such a price point. I am lucky enough to have enough white florals in my collection that impress me or suit my tastes. Gardenia loses her nominal charm after an hour, focusing instead on a healthy foundation of smell-good aromas.

What a beauty! The quality of Chanel fragrances is just impeccable. Gardenia is such an addictive floral bouquet, with a touch of sweetness and greenness. I cannot even tell you specifically what I smell since I always perceive this perfume as a coherent floral composition in which nothing bothers me, nothing sticks out. It is nostalgic yet not old-fashioned, it does not scream but lasts for a long time, and it smells to me like wealth, elegance, and good taste. I do not smell aldehydes and iris in this fragrance, typical notes for Chanel, but it is still very recognizable as Chanel, somehow. I think Gardenia is very likable, and it is still one of my favorites from the Exclusif collection. Sometimes that is all I want: a beautiful, good-quality fragrance that accompanies and cheers me up all day.

Gardénia opens with bright aldehydes, quickly replaced by gentle green notes and radiant white flowers. The perfume is creamy and somehow lifts your spirits when applied. As it develops, the fragrance becomes drier and a warm woody base begins to hover beneath the white flowers. Over time, Gardénia Eau de Parfum becomes increasingly sweeter... and can sometimes, unfortunately, come across as overly sweet, at times even synthetic.

Purple Stain has personally surprised me positively. Why? To be honest, I haven't been a fan of Borntostandout until now. I have always found the brand to be totally interesting, but unfortunately, every fragrance I tested didn't quite resonate with me. Here and there, there is a scent that I find okay, but really beautiful? For my personal taste, that has been quite difficult so far. With Purple Stain, it's the first time I can say: "Yep, that's nice." The fragrance starts off with a slightly fresh, fruity accent, but also with spicy facets. Saffron and nutmeg find a great harmony with ginger, mandarin, and bergamot. The listed cinnamon accord only comes to my nose a bit later, but noticeably subtle. Over time, the slightly fresh, fruity accords fade away, and it generally becomes noticeably woodier. The spiciness is still clearly present for me, but no longer so sharp. It now feels noticeably "rounder." Occasionally, I actually get vibes of a well-known fragrance. Which one could it be?... Yes, indeed, the good old Joop Homme! I have this fragrance in the EdP version, and after some thought, I realized that this is the scent where I recognize the parallels. Perhaps this arises from the combination of cinnamon, the general spiciness, and orange blossom. Furthermore, I occasionally get slight associations of red wine, but in moderation. There is also a seemingly soft and gentle leather included. The fragrance lasts on my skin for about 9-10 hours. That's really good! The sillage is also really good. Purple Stain leaves a decent scent cloud and projects very well. Is this fragrance unisex? Definitely!

Wine stains on paper?! Dear Jun Lim, the truly beautifully complex perfume: "Purple Stain" from your brand BornToStandOut has really messed up its marketing presentation. After the first sniff of this fragrance and later in its development, I wondered why this scent felt so familiar to me. The (extraordinary) development of the fragrance was noticeably easier for me to pinpoint than the (turbulent) opening of the scent. Development: Its caramel notes paired with the vanilla note made it quite simple: Werthers Original. Anyone who has lived or grown up in Germany in the last 40 - 50 years knows this scent; certainly, the association with a caramel pudding as sold in France is fitting. The Overture: of the fragrance was significantly harder to determine, but this scent also felt very familiar to me. One morning while getting up and choosing the (daily) fragrance, the chain of associations hit me like a ton of bricks. The answer is Joop Home! Compared to it, it fits of course in a modern and significantly more complex way; this scent could be found in almost every bathroom cabinet from 1989 until about 2014, and only in recent years has Homme fallen somewhat out of fashion. So I must conclude that with your fragrance Purple Stain, you have probably unconsciously bottled a part of the German DNA of the last approximately 40 years. The name: "German Childhood Memories" would describe this scent much better. Only the price is not suitable for any "Swabian skin"; at ~290 € / 50 ml, brands like Louis Vuitton and Parfums de Marly are clearly left behind. For that, you get an even more niche compliment-giver. Regards A. Ssaziel

Freshly sprayed, it feels like you've opened a can of Fanta Grape while something is burning in the next room. Even though no grape is listed, the scent strongly reminds one of it. However, this initially fresh grape note disappears very quickly, giving way to a masculine oud-saffron-patchouli dream. Even after hours, the scent remains very present and (for me) extremely pleasant. During the first test on the skin - accompanied by a walk through the city - I fell in love immediately. Just one spray on the back of my hand, and it was a constant, yet thoroughly pleasant companion.

This fragrance seems to be either a love it or hate it scent. I personally like it, which is strange because I'm rarely a fan of Estee Lauder scents. Pink Coral is refreshing and delicate. A soapy floral to say the least. I'm often bothered by Estee Lauder scents being too strong and too synthetic, but Pink Coral is quite light and although not completely natural smelling, it is bearable. This is a relatively linear fragrance, I didn't notice much of a change between the opening and the drydown. I find it to be a nice and rather pleasant blend of subdued flowers and a hint of watery freshness. The beachy and Summery aspect conveyed in the advertisement is very true to the fragrance itself. Not a particularly mind-blowing scent, but pretty none-the-less.

Pure White Linen Pink Coral immediately makes me forget everyday life and tempts me to dream of beach, sun, sea, and of course, vacation. As I am currently busy packing my suitcase, I still want to say a few words about my new favorite. This fragrance will be my vacation companion, as it comes across as so airy-light, cheerful, and buoyant. Pink Coral reminds me of fresh laundry in the summer breeze, which gets a nice, but not too intense spiciness from the light pepper note at the beginning. I can also clearly recognize the apple blossom, and fruits that have nothing artificial about them. A little later, the flowers come to the forefront, playful yet still elegant. It's great how the lightness of this perfume stands out, but you still have the impression that you are wearing a lovely scent. You won't leave a strong trail with Pink Coral, but I can notice this fragrance on myself for a nice amount of time, about 4-5 hours maximum. (with a good dose, *g*) The base then becomes warmer and woodier. What I particularly like is that there are no overly sweet or sticky additions like in many new releases that are currently flooding the market. The vanilla is just a supporting note, not prominent. If you now think, well, that sounds nice, but nothing more, I can promise you that Pink Coral has its own character, freshness paired with a gentle floral spiciness. Somehow also elegant, but nonetheless very suitable for everyday wear. Managing to combine all of this often backfires, and then you might smell more like mosquito spray. Pink Coral is a very beautiful, fruity-floral summer fragrance that is worth testing. It seems not many people know it yet, so go ahead and spray it if you see this lovely scent available.

Today I came across a fragrance that I shamefully had not known before - Pure White Linen Pink Coral. A real gap in my knowledge, as became clear with the first spray. The good old White Linen certainly has a permanent place on my shelf - but this beautiful flanker can definitely hold its own. It is like a fluffy pink cloud that you let yourself fall into, and which catches you weightlessly. You are surrounded by airy apple blossoms and berries - dusted with a hint of pink pepper. Any dullness fades away, and you feel like drifting along with the soft cloud. The wind blows fresh, floral jasmine and delicate sweet pea towards me, and the cloud bed is warmed by sunny vanilla. Swallows sail by, and you want to float south with them. A transparent fragrance, full of lightness and a touch of wanderlust, to which I gladly surrender, as it also conveys a sense of security.

For all those who feel like I do: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umw-8J-O14o As I have mentioned several times, I find temperatures below 5° to be a hardship. And in freezing temperatures, I feel the urge to report Peter for common bodily harm. I really need to wrap myself up at home on my days off with a fragrance that I usually only wear in summer. The sadly discontinued White Linen Pink Coral is a pretty good choice for that. What I like about Estee Lauder fragrances is that they always have at least a subtle vintage vibe. They are always adult and elegant scents, even the new releases. One of the few brands that doesn't launch a squeaky sweet water just to climb the Douglas Top 10. What I particularly like here is that the fragrance actually comes off very young and fresh, but at the same time also dignified and definitely not squeaky. The top note is peppery and berry-like, but the slightly soapy typical scent of aldehydes prevents it from becoming one of those typical fruity waters. Although the fragrance pyramid in the heart note suggests a lush bouquet of flowers, I mainly smell peony here. This note is usually a bit tricky for me. I often find it somewhat distant and a bit stuffy. It reminds me of a strict governess. But the berry notes create a nice contrast here. As a result, the fragrance feels beautifully light, but not too much. In the base, it becomes really soft with heliotrope and vanilla and just slightly woody. But still never sweet (I've never sniffed such an unsweet heliotrope). Throughout the entire progression, the aldehyde note hovers over the fine fragrance weave and gives it a delicate and clean elegance. My association would be a classy garden party in summer. Something like this: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nR2r__ZgO5g Unfortunately, the longevity and sillage here are really subpar. If it’s not really warm, you shouldn’t go outside with White Linen Pink Coral. Even in summer, it only lasts a few hours. Not even if you spray very generously. I really overdid it today (13 sprays four hours ago). When I sit here in front of the PC, I can still perceive the fragrance quite distinctly, but outside, it was already gone two hours ago. I recommend this fragrance to all ladies who like light but not too sweet summer scents. You can still find it on eBay. Unfortunately, you have to search a bit to find a good deal, but it’s really worth it.

Where was I when you still existed? 2009... at that time I definitely had my 2-3 standard fragrances and was satisfied in my limited little fragrance universe. Fffft... things happen... Well... if I had been already infected with perfume back then, I would have surely come across it sooner and not just now when it has been discontinued (Waaaaaaaaarum???) and is only available through eBay. This is already driving me crazy... I came to the fragrance through a very lovely perfume swap... so luckily I now have an almost full bottle at home. It was a "blind swap" for me, the best I’ve ever had. About the scent: The fragrance starts fresh and a bit fruity. I mean to sniff apples, like Granny Smith, and especially red fruits. It is subtly sweet and a bit sparkling, which I attribute to the pink pepper with my still undifferentiated nose. In the heart, I can smell the peony and I believe immediately that it is pink. It is a very soft, tame peony, which I usually find a bit herbaceous. Those who are afraid of jasmine... let it be known to them. This is not a killer jasmine, but I believe it only adds a bit more sweetness and otherwise remains transparent. Here I also think I can smell a bit of cherry... In the base, I smell vanilla and heliotrope, which makes everything beautifully soft and warm. I can still subtly perceive the fruits. The bottle: It comes across as quite valuable to me. Pink milk glass... uhaaaa at the moment pink is really appealing to me... it feels good and heavy in the hand. Longevity: The longevity for me is 5-6 hours, which I find quite okay. The sillage is rather subtle. In the first hour, it is also noticeable in the surroundings, but then it retreats more and more. The one who gets to come a bit closer will surely be delighted. I find this fragrance truly beautiful and successful, especially when I think that I can't really connect with its "mother." Due to its fruity-fresh, light nature, it fits perfectly into spring and summer for me. I immediately feel good when I wear it. I feel comfortable, refreshed, and well-groomed. It's a shame that such a great fragrance has been discontinued.

I bought two samples of Chanel 22 to give myself a good test run on it. I was surprised at how beautiful and delicate this perfume is, particularly with aldehydes. Totally noticeable on first spray, it takes a while for them to nestle down, but when that happens (barely) I smell the Lily of the valley and jasmine. It’s so beautiful! I was expecting a stronger scent, as I had owned a bottle of No. 5 years ago, but it’s nothing like that, or at least my memory of it. I don’t smell vanilla. I pick up something else, but my nose is still untrained, so I can’t tell what it is. (Apologies). I wear this fragrance day or night, but find it most pleasing when it’s warm outside. To me it’s not a winter scent. It’s about expecting a spring thunderstorm or summer rain, which in turn awakens flowers. It’s femininity and strength, luxury and self awareness. It’s something a Virgo woman wears with pride. Longevity and sillage are both higher than expected, providing a day’s worth of scent. I would splurge on a big bottle of it if I didn’t already own so many perfumes!

One of the most beautiful Chanel perfumes, perfect. Soapy, powdery, aldehydic, with hints of vanilla and vetiver. Totally unisex. This is a typical Chanel perfume with recognizable aldehydes. Very elegant. I love this fragrance so much that I bought 2 bottles. I am a big fan of retro perfumes. Performance is a fantastic, great longevity and projection.

As my name suggests, I have a favorable view of the products from the house of Chanel. It is my second favorite fragrance manufacturer. (I wouldn't turn down bags and other accessories if someone wanted to gift me something from them..) Chanel fragrances rarely take risks, or rather, you seldom have to open the same door when it comes to Chanel scents. (Well, Lion is a bit unusual, but still not outrageous or unbearable.) Recently, I acquired a partial bottle of the EdP of No. 22 at a good price, thanks to a generous perfume lover. This purchase allowed me to delve deeply into the fragrance that first appeared almost 100 years ago. So I sprayed generously. Within milliseconds, I smelled the 5. (One might interject, where are the other 17? Well, they didn't show up.) The 5 truly made itself known, immensely aldehydic, underpinned by a hint of sugared vanilla. After constant re-sniffing, I also discovered a bit of Ylang-Ylang, but it was only painstakingly detectable, hidden beneath a massive cloud of powder. And in general: Powder! Cream! If No. 5 and Nivea had a child, and this could be reduced or otherwise compressed, essentially condensed, then No. 22 would emerge. I can't identify any flowers otherwise. My nose is too powdered. And too soapy. If I previously thought White Linen, the dream of all laundresses, was the cleanest, I am now enlightened: No. 22 - the best Persil there ever was.

Once upon a time, there was No. 5. And once upon a time, there was an extremely popular, supposed nudist. The sweet, curvy Norma Jean, aka Marilyn, the crush of many men, an icon, a legend... who famously breathed that she preferred to take nothing but this No. 5 to bed with her... Well, this No. 5 never quite got to me... with its special, dark aldehydes at the beginning... Unlike No. 22, which according to Chanel is the softer successor scent and close relative of Chanel No. 5. The 22 unexpectedly snowed into my home. It was quite a surprising love at first sniff. The scent begins with soapy aldehydes. Fresh, floral-herbaceous luxury soap, which might scare some, but for me, it awakens my spirits... one can smell a hint of lily of the valley, neroli, vetiver... Gradually, the scent becomes calmer, gently creamy, as bright orange neroli blends with a fruity touch of rose and ylang ylang. Jasmine contributes a light, cheerful sweetness, and vetiver provides a beautiful, light bitterness, preventing the scent from drifting into sweetness and cuteness. At this moment, the 22 is a gentle, good-natured, androgynous scent. Never powdery. But creamy. Like the commentator Pinkdawn before me, I had to think of "the perfect woman"... but in the sense of truly perfect. Not a cold businesswoman. Rather one who is perfectly just imperfect enough that you can't help but like her. Perhaps just as beautiful as Marilyn once was. With a charming smile, humor, perfect white skin... But this one can also stand for the fact that she has something in her head. Yet, it is also quite wearable for normal women like me, who are not without their fair share of flaws. Together with Madame Perfect from the bottle, I get through the day well. For me, a fine Chanel with character and edge. If you don't overdo it, it smells wonderfully elegant-fresh-well-groomed. I believe I would love the extrait even more. This has, in addition to (not sweet) vanilla and vetiver in the base, also incense... I would find that nice here in the EdP as well. Furthermore, it probably smells a bit softer and rounder... Well, maybe I'll get that under my nose again. Until then, I am happy with this one... Thanks to Eve Mist for the sample from a year ago..

Here I sit with my shopping bags at Christian-Broda-Platz in Vienna-Mariahilf, not far from my apartment. The autumn wind blows the delicate, feathered leaves of the robinia trees that grow there down onto me. They are so bright yellow that I feel like I am in a rain of gold. I am wearing Chanel N°22 and trying to connect with this new fragrance for me, to determine whether it suits me and how I feel about it. In the Les Exclusifs de Chanel series, several exclusive and all very well-known perfumes are now united, as the name suggests. I count myself more among the Guerlain faction. Therefore, I only recently tested a fragrance from this line, namely N°22. By the way, it owes its name to its birth year, 1922. However, it has been reformulated. My comments refer to the Eau de Parfum released in 2016. N°22 has always been considered a flanker of the legendary N°5 from 1921. While this fragrance may be iconic and has its fans, I simply cannot connect with it. It just doesn’t suit me. So how do I feel about N°22? It is said to be "more feminine" than N°5, "caressing," milder, and powdery. That sounds pretty good for someone who always found N°5 too "assertive" and strong. Eagerly, I indulge in a dose of N°22. I admit that the fragrance impresses me immediately. It is floral, but not sweet; rather, it is soapy from the very beginning. Those are the aldehydes, which are not weakly represented here, I know. N°22 intensely smells of white flowers, but it is not very sweet; instead, it comes across as elegant, noble, exclusive, and ladylike. The EdP is expensive and smells that way: precious and noble. It manages the balancing act between intense and subtle. However, the subtlety creates a somewhat distant, cool aura. This aura of the unattainable reminds me of the attractive, "cool" blondes from Hitchcock films of the 1950s. N°22 is described as floral-powdery. I like powdery. I would like more of that here. However, the fragrance is rather soapy. It gives a feeling of grooming that is almost too perfect for me. I think of the well-known retro soaps from back then. They were everywhere, in every drugstore, the Lux, Camay, and whatever else they were called, these soaps with the perfume scent, but they were marketed as luxury. N°22 has something similarly vintage about it. It doesn’t change much either. In the top note, the aldehydes are very present. They give the fragrance that clean image as if fresh from the bathtub. I don’t notice much of the lily of the valley, which I love, or neroli. Rather, I notice the flowers of the heart note: jasmine, rose, tuberose, and ylang-ylang. Here, jasmine and ylang-ylang dominate. Amber and vanilla in the base note could have given the fragrance a feminine softness and sweetness. But they cannot compete with the masculine vetiver. That is probably intentional. I know the structure of N°5, which is similarly constructed. Both have a pronounced aldehyde note and finish with a ruthlessly strong vetiver. I like vetiver, but not when it is so intense that it takes away all sweetness from the floral scents and turns the fragrance into a somewhat elegant chypre. Although N°22 is described by the manufacturer Chanel as feminine, sensual, and seductive, I cannot confirm that. The fragrance has too little warmth and softness for that. It radiates for me more the soulless crystalline perfection of a lady who wants to appear almost superhumanly perfect. The fragrance has an almost frightening hardness. I can imagine it on proud queens and self-confident business ladies in elegant clothing. In my opinion, it does not suit sensitive women. I also feel "dressed up." N°22 and I are not compatible. The perfume is too perfect for me. That is not me. I do not want to be that. I think of all the wonderful flowers that have united here alongside such deliciously sweet aromas as vanilla and amber: jasmine, ylang-ylang, neroli, roses, lily of the valley, tuberose … And I wonder how one can create a fragrance with such a masculine attitude from such lovely scents. Ultimately, the soapy aldehydes and the masculine vetiver dominate here. The woman who wears N°22, I imagine to be powerful, perhaps a bit know-it-all, very mature, serious, and strict. And reserved. She always has herself and her feelings under control and knows exactly what she wants and how to achieve it. The flowers are already there, but frighteningly abstract. At least, that is how I perceive them. Passion and liveliness, emotions like tenderness, devotion, joy, playfulness, flirting, and smiling are, in my opinion, absent. No question, the fragrance not only has solid longevity, it is also good and has class. And size. I see it as a perfume for festive, perhaps even official occasions, a kind of status symbol. I like the soapy aspect, but it is too strong for me. Too much. Too much. I am probably too weak or sensitive for this classic fragrance for women who want to exude power. I am neither a queen nor a business lady, and I do not want to be. Thanks to Leons for the sample.

Recently, thanks to a dear friend, I acquired a small bottle of No22. Just visually, I could fall in love with the bottle, as it looks almost adorable next to a 200 ml bottle and feels so nice in the hand that you just want to touch it all the time (which, of course, applies to all 75 ml Les Exclusifes due to the same manufacturing shape).

Perhaps some may wonder why a young man is writing a comment about such a fragrance, but I am certainly no stranger when it comes to classic "women's fragrances." Chanel is my "home" (along with Guerlain), and I enjoy wearing Egoiste and Antaeus just as much as No 22 or Misia. Now to the scent. For me, No 22 is what one might have imagined "clean" to be in the 20s.

Chanel writes: "Caressing, very mild and powdery like an absolute of femininity." I dare to disagree: Chanel on speed, cocaine stretched with laundry detergent, crystal clear, ice cold, describes it better. Personally, I find N°5 to be significantly warmer and more approachable, while N°22 is filled with attributes that are more show than substance.

I know that there are stories about the extrait of Chanel N°5, that Ernest Beaux wanted to replicate Siberian snow and the icy cold, but I must say that I feel exactly that sensation with N°22. This fragrance has made me think so much that I even have to write a review. Of course, these are just legends, as we were not in the lab with Mr.

I love this scent because it has absolutely nothing modern or current about it - for me, it is pure nostalgia and doesn't really fit into our time. And yet (or perhaps because of that), I enjoy wearing it so much. It fits wonderfully for this transitional period, not quite summer and not really autumn yet. It radiates a very pleasant warmth, smells truly familiar and "cozy.

Reviewing women's fragrances as a man is a challenge that I am aware of. But the other way around is also not uncommon here on Parfumo, so I dare to approach L´Eau Kenzo Florale and, as I see, I am the first to comment on it. I find the scent successful. The white peony opens the fragrance softly and elegantly, and the rose bud gives it structure. The cedarwood in the base is very subtle, making the scent perfect for wearing in spring and summer. One (woman) just has to like rose fragrances. The scent progression is linear and does not change. A pleasant coolness sets in, which keeps the fragrance from being musty and constricting. The peony remains present throughout the entire scent progression. Young ladies can also wear the fragrance wonderfully. I would say the preferred age range is 20-45. A good choice for the sunny months. Thumbs up!

Sampling Borntostandout Dirty Heaven, a bright, sweet, powdery blend of jasmine, tonka, musk, neroli, vanilla, amber, and woods, overall pretty pleasant but with a bit of a peach candied quality amidst the smoother elements of flowers and sweets, definitely a bit feminine-leaning, stereotypically, but overall, fairly pleasant and likely versatile. It’s an example of a fragrance that I’d rather smell on someone else than myself, however, and I think it would likely be a turnoff for those weary of floral, powdery, or sweet fragrance, as it’s not too subtle in any of those respects. I think it’s a decent offering but not one that I particularly gravitate towards. As with the rest of the house’s collection, this is EDP concentration and priced at $210/85 for 50/15ml, not bad in the current market for niche perfume, and it performs very well on me. 6 out of 10

Imagine the whiteness of heaven. Well, now make it gloomy, enrich it with flowers at the end of flowering, with a slightly sweet and unexpectedly magnetic scent--you have dirty heaven. A combination of florals and saffron made sensual by ambroxan that makes this fragrance irresistible, alternating moderation with stronger notes, in short it's always there but every now and then it comes out even more overpoweringly. From the first time I smelled it I loved it, and immediately desired it. A temptation to which one cannot say no. "The Temptation of St. Anthony" painted by Salvador Dali.

I went through my 5ml sample in an hour. That’s how instantly obsessed I became. I sprayed it before bed and all night I kept catching these dreamy wafts like I was wrapped in some warm, hypnotic cocoon. It’s addictive, comforting, and incredibly strong for a sample. I didn’t hesitate I ordered a full bottle immediately. There’s definitely a mix of white florals here (I’m guessing tuberose and maybe hawthorn?), but they’re more like background singers. They add a soft, creamy texture without taking over. The main players are clearly saffron, vanilla, tonka, and something warm and musky probably grey amber or ambroxan. It’s smooth, radiant, and just the right amount of sweet and skin-like. Not your typical white floral bomb this one has depth and mood. I can’t stop thinking about it.

Its like when you have been eating vanilla ice cream your whole life but one day you decide to splurge on the expensive vanilla ice cream. The kind made with high quality cream and real vanilla, it has flecks of vanilla bean throughout the ice cream. This fragrance is that really good vanilla ice cream, not that artificial overly sugary vanilla stuff. This is gentle sweet with soft floral and a hint of woodiness from the saffron in the background. Its warm and complex. This is a soft aromatic, so it doesn't project off the skin without knocking people out. The scent lasted all day, over 7 hours. It is $205 for a 50ml bottle.

I have a bone to pick with BTSO, majority of fragrances retailed by this brand smell like heavy hitters from other major brands which have been selling out for a few decades, marketed under a new name with a shiny new signature packaging and promising marketing. Dirty Heaven right here smells like the Hypnotic Poison EDT, the same licorice-y, anis heavy vanilla blend, not even the muskiness has been adjusted to make it smell like anything slightly novel, Naked Laundry smells like a diluted, less aldehydic Chanel No 5 EDP, Filthy Musk is Kouros by YSL with no filth at all and the list goes on. Experimenting with this brand reminded me the importance of experiencing the classics first.
Yes, Dirty Heaven definitely smells synthetic. However, that is exactly what makes it appealing to me. Friends of pure and innocent naturalness will (probably) not be happy here. Quite the opposite!

White Linen, Knowing, Youth Dew, Beyond Paradise, Beautiful, Cinnabar, Sensuous Noir… I could go on naming Estée Lauder’s famous fragrances. Fragrances that are renowned for their remarkable and recognizable combinations. And then there is Very Estée. I was quite surprised when I sprayed it the first time because all I got was an insisting freesia. When talking about EL this was new to me. This is not the most interesting EL fragrance there is. And I do get confused when reading that EL introduced thin as “the new sexy perfume”? I do not get it at all. This is, to my nose, as far from sexy as can be. When I spray it, I see a well dressed woman ready for work at the office. So what makes it interesting? This fragrance lasts - on my skin - for up to 12 hours! The same dominant freesia all through the hours with Jasmine and rose as its companions. That is really something. I was surprised seeing that here on Parfumo the longevity is rated 6,8. Personally I would rate it 11. I feel so secure when I wear this. I know that the scent lasts all day. It is a nice and quite light fragrance perfect for work or a cafe visit. Sillage is pleasant, not more than an arm’s length, so it is a perfume that is sprayed for the wearer, not the audience. It is perfect for warm spring days and early autumn. The bottle is close to similar to Spellbound, though it is slimmer and the top is blue instead of black. I like the simplicity of both. Recommendable? Definitely. 181/365

Today, my girlfriend shooed me off the sofa, where I was lounging around - but she wanted to snag a Fahrenheit bargain at the flea market. Well - maybe I would also "accidentally" find something nice. The booth of my fragrance dealer was surrounded by a crowd, and I gave up my special right to spray. I would let my intuition speak. And it led me to a clear, almost puristically designed bottle from Estee Lauder. The name is a guarantee of quality for me - and what could possibly go wrong if this fragrance is supposed to be "very" Estee. And I am not disappointed! "Very" lives up to its name, as it is very very attractive. Very balanced, I am greeted by fruity and floral notes - with the bright freesia taking the lead. With gentle elegance, the rose joins in, and the jasmine shines white and clear. Cashmere feels soft, and the musk is shiny and smooth. However, Very is not simply smooth and straightforward; it possesses individuality and its own feminine statement. Sporty casual elegance comes to mind, intertwined with an optimistic attitude. It definitely fits a sunny day - and gives a positive reflection. In any case, it has put a smile on my formerly grumpy face - and my girlfriend is happy for me too - even though she didn't find Fahrenheit. Fate was very kind to me today.

The first time I encountered the term 'MILF' was during the 2008 U.S. presidential campaign in connection with the Alaskan vice-presidential candidate and self-proclaimed hockey mom Sarah Palin, who objected to being called such but was nonetheless proud that she knew the term. In fact, the word has been around for longer - and for a few years now, it has also become relatively established in the local youth language. In the original English, it directly refers to a woman with a certain life experience who still knows how to please, regardless of that. Very Estée - this name can only be translated into German quite clumsily. It refers to something that condenses the essence of Estée Lauder, the legendary founder of the eponymous empire, and is indeed 'very Estée.' Lauder, famous for her charm and business acumen, allowed herself to be addressed by her girlish nickname 'Esty' (she was originally an Esther, and she invented the 'Estée' herself) well into her old age and significantly changed the image of the attractive and self-confident mature woman (to whom she wanted to sell her cosmetic products) in the mid-20th century. Very Estée is both - cultivatedly expressed, the fragrance for an attractive woman who has long outgrown her girlhood, yet not without a wink, charming, light-footed, and flirtatious. In youth slang, this is the fragrance for a MILF - life-experienced, sexy, and quite aware of her charms. At its core, Very Estée is a formally arranged rose scent that is ladylike but not conservative - surrounded by initial white flowers and fruits and a kind of honey-colored undertone beneath it - like warm skin in sunlight after a day at the beach. In summary: a brief spring overture, then rose, then jasmine, then musk. Conclusion: the fragrance for a beautiful woman beyond thirty-five, perhaps forty. Unduly overlooked, but sometimes that is also a blessing. And if we set aside the ordinary in the term MILF, it is essentially nothing but a compliment. And the fact that I have deliberately withheld its literal meaning from those who may not know the term is pure intention - it is quite vulgar. And of course, there are DILFs as well.

This lady here is cool. Distant. Charming. Always appropriately dressed, no matter the time of day or night. Nothing about her seems cheap, even if not everything has to have been expensive. Her smile rarely goes unanswered. If she holds a secret, no one has unraveled it yet - or it was indeed a gentleman who enjoys it. And remains silent. The lady remembers 2012, the cool, broad-shouldered 80s, when she struggled to smell soft and elite - the perfumes of that time were so loud (and mostly terribly emotional for her). Estée Super became her signature back then. A few decades have passed, the lady has adapted to the new era. Her appearance has completely changed, yet little about her spectacular exit. The entrance, with which she descends the stairs to applause onto her stage, is strewn with freesias. And indeed with buckets of freesias (pardon, for the neighbors: buckets). So many that the brightness of this floral abundance makes one squint. The pepper awakens the senses - if anyone had dozed off during her appearance, they are now surely wide awake. Roses fly onto the stage, in all colors and variations. Now excitement sets in, but it is quickly calmed down with jasmine and nestled in woods. And suddenly, almost seamlessly, Estée stands before me, similar to how I knew her in the 80s. A little less pronounced, but suitable for the office in 2012, still very cool, still self-assured, and with a ladylike smile. Very Estée differs more than pleasantly from the current trend of "uniform-synthetic-will-please-everyone" eaux de toilettes. Just the freesia opening will surely polarize. It gently reminds one of times when fragrances radiated personality and were sold precisely for that reason. The bottle reminded me at first glance (and touch) of that of "Spellbound." Timeless, almost puristic, probably intended as a bridge between the decades. I see Very Estée as an opportunity to inspire younger ladies to embrace fragrances with personality. And those who in 2012 no longer dare to wear Estée Super to the office due to the zeitgeist can indulge in this new interpretation without guilt because of their colleagues.

On my birthday i asked my sister for a fragrance as a gift. As she lives in Machester (UK) and I in Espinho (PT), I had to wait some time before receiving my EDT. It was a little risky on my part, as I had never experienced this fragrance. As soon as my sister offered it to me, I opened the package and there it was: CK In2U for Him. But soon, all that expectation that I had initially, was lost. The aroma is super normal, nothing special. The performance is terrible, something that left me disappointed. I think the only positive aspect is the bottle. In short and concluding, don't buy anything blindly! Read about perfumes, try them in stores before you buy! I don't recommend it!

CK In2U, to me, is like a soapy version of Acqua Di Gio. It smells a lot like Imperial Leather Original Bar Soap, but with a touch of something fresh, almost leafy—especially at the opening spray. There's also a sharp, cologne-like note that reminds me of Dylan Blue. It's a clean, forward-projecting smell that isn't sweet or overly perfumed. Instead, it smells fresh, crisp, and very much "put-together," like you just stepped out of the shower and you want to continue that smell throughout the rest of the day. I’m not sure why some people don’t enjoy this fragrance—it’s actually quite nice, in my opinion. It’s fresh and clean, without being bland. Fun fact: it’s also my dad’s go-to scent. Want to guess why? Because it’s cheap. But despite the price, I think CK In2U offers more character than something like CK One, which feels a bit flat by comparison. Both have a clean vibe, but CK One doesn’t have the same depth or identity. It’s citrusy and fresh, but it doesn’t evoke much beyond that. CK In2U, on the other hand, smells more distinct—soap-like, leafy, fresh, clean. The words used in this review. That said, CK In2U could improve in a couple of areas. It could project a bit more, and its longevity could be better. But even with those flaws, it’s still a solid option for the price. You could spend 2-3 times more, and get something that doesn't perform that much better. So, who is CK In2U for? In a way, it’s perfect for most men, young or old. It’s a classic, masculine scent, and unlike some men's fragrances, it doesn’t lean toward being unisex. For the price, you could definitely do worse, but you could also do better. For some, though, this might just be the better scent. If you haven’t tried it yet, give it a shot.

It is a nice scent, easy to wear, Light , Fresh and Clean. I don't care about the negative comments and I trust my nose, It smells so good and very pleasant with reasonable price. It opens up with like fresh citrusy, slightly spicy, green and Cacao notes in the background then dry down is musky woody. The Cacao note is dominant in this perfume. This is perfect for the spring and summer. I really enjoy it and I like CK IN2U for Him by Calvin Klein. Longevity is good. Rating : 8 / 10

This was a gift, but you'll usually find the 100ml version for around $15-20. The top notes are very citric, and as they dry down a little you get more of that tomato leaf. After a minute or so on your skin I start noticing the cacao, which is very faint but does change the scent a lot. It is surprisingly smooth and very fresh. I personally wear this now everytime it's very warm (27-32c) outside. It's definitely mass appealing and won't choke anyone, which brings me to my next points, projection and longevity. It'll depend on the person, but for me this usually lasts 3-4 hours on my skin. You'll probably find yourself having to respray. It also doesn't leave a strong trail nor projects well, I find it to be too intimate as it sits pretty close to the skin. As for the bottle design, it's very nice; simple yet unique. The plastic housing and the atomizer will remind you of what it's worth though. The bottom's design is interesting, it makes the bottle a lot more unstable but also adds a lot to the design.
