It dries down to more of a sweet caramel but still with that cherry/almond extract. The Oud is pretty much gone after a few hours. Would I purchase it? Nope. Would I wear it again? Maybe once or twice. It wouldn’t be a habit.

Tropical. That's one way to describe Pleasures Exotic. Sharp, acidic and synthetic, are three others. I was not surprised when I saw grapefruit listed as a note, (I'm not a fan of it). Pleasures Exotic smells too much like a fruity beverage, very juicy and rich, yet not something I particularly want to wear. This fragrance has a very strange edge to it. The fruity opening is far too strong and sharp, and the hibiscus, peony, cassia and litchi far too prominent. I sense a shampoo/soapy aspect which doesn't blend too well with the dominant fruits. One minute it's fresh like just stepping out of the shower, the next minute I'm on a beach with tropical juice spilt all down my front. A majority of the time, Pleasures Exotic makes me nauseous. I don't know what it is, but this fragrance really isn't for me.

Pleasures Exotic is one of my Estee Lauder favorites. It is a beautiful scent for summer, fresh, light, and fruity. With Pleasures Exotic, I always feel like I'm sitting in a large fruit basket and just need to pick one of the good ripe fruits. The fruit blend is balanced and rounded. Extremely delicious! I have received many compliments when wearing Pleasures Exotic. The scent lasts a long time and feels very refreshing. In England and America, Pleasures Exotic is still available for purchase. So I had to stock up on this fine fragrance. Unfortunately, here at home, there are only remnants left.

It opens on the skin with an unexpected rush of coconut and lemon, bright yet creamy, refreshing yet indulgent. The coconut note, curiosly absent from the official opening, makes its presence known inmediately, as if it were the secret heart of the composition from the very start. Two hours later, that coconut not only remains but blooms, becoming richer and more pronounced, wrapping the wearer in a velvety sweetness that feels almost edible. This is a fragrance unapologetically crafted for those who seek and savor the pleasure of sweet, gourmand accords. As time passes and the initial vibrancy mellows, subtle hints of cardamom and patchouli begin to weave their way into the blend, adding a soft spice and an earthy depth that anchor the sweetness without overshadowing it. The cedar, though listed among its notes, stays quiet, its presence more like a distant echo than a clear voice, adding only the faintest woody shadow to the composition. The journey from bright citrus-kissed coconut to warm, spiced sweetness makes this perfume feel like a slow sunset beginning with light and brightness, and ending in the comforting glow of lingering warmth.

Subdued sweetness of the juniper berry and cozy aromatic lavender – great! A somewhat synthetic coconut note blended together with the woody backdrop – shower gel-like, but okay. Burnt rubber undertones from the Sichuan pepper – not ideal, but fleeting. It never strayed more than half an arm's length away from my skin, and about ~1,5 hours in settled on it entirely. No major changes in flavor profile – it just slowly got softer, and in another ~3,5 hours completely faded. Eh. Honestly, if it smelled just a bit more natural, I'd have no complaints. It doesn't do anything new or special, but it's clean, fresh and aromatic – as advertised; and is soft enough not to feel grating. Baby's first aftershave – not that great in the grand scheme of things, but it's always lovely to see a young man making an effort. Left me kind of bored, but also thinking that I wouldn't mind if more people on the streets smelled like this instead of whatever counterfeit Sauvage they're currently drenching themselves in. All in all, for its price – I think it's adequate both in quality and in performance. And, imo, more interesting than the original Eternity for Men Eau de Toilette .

The original Eternity for Men Eau de Toilette has nothing to do with this flanker. Instead, one could rather speak of a derivative of CH's "Bad Boy (Eau de Toilette) | Carolina Herrera," at least regarding the opening. Because Eternity for Men Aromatic Essence smells incredibly synthetic, and also very sweet. Right from the opening, a minimally spicy, slightly fresh, highly artificial sweetness rushes towards you, which most will probably love or hate. Personally, I stand somewhat perplexed before it, as sometimes it bothers me, and sometimes I find it okay. It is supposed to be a coconut, but anyone who thought that the note could hardly be made more artificial in the Le Beau series will be proven wrong here. A bit of this highly modern plastic-like Provence lavender, which has been added to every 7̶. E̶i̶ second teenage boy's fragrance ("Phantom | Rabanne," "Icon pour Homme | Dsquared²," "Guilty pour Homme (Eau de Toilette) | Gucci," "Valentino Uomo Born In Roma Intense | Valentino," etc.), can also be caught. Over time, the fragrance loses even more of its naturalness and becomes even more strangely synthetic. You really have to like that. When "Parfum Intense" is written on the front, I expect a beast - and I get it here. The sillage is intense. So intense that it is actually too much for me. Fewer sprays are more here, and the surroundings will also be happy not to be suffocated in an aroma cloud. The longevity is predictably strong. The intense projection diminishes after 3½ hours, and after 4 hours it has only become somewhat more subdued. Close to the skin, the fragrance is present after about 7½ hours. Does this thing need to exist? Another overly artificial sweet something that teenagers will douse themselves in, hoping to attract some girl? A substitute for the ubiquitous Axe body sprays of the 00s, which were still less penetrating? In my opinion, no.

Yes, I actually didn't have the brand and the perfume on my list, but I received a sample through an order. Overall, I was quite positively surprised as the scent indeed comes across as sweet and fresh as described. I may have applied a bit more spray, but the longevity and sillage are very good, and the scent is overall quite rounded. A little bit of Sculpture came to mind, but it strongly reminds me of the Le Beau line by Gaultier. However, this scent does not feel as heavy and is therefore not as intrusive and grand as those by Gaultier... Price-wise, you can't complain about the offers either, but.. Overall, it's quite interesting and perhaps a bit underrated..

... the Caribbean at a beach bar with a coconut cocktail enriched with a fresh note of lemon. A slightly peppery and woody scent wafts from the bar into my nose. On the beach, I see the breathtakingly beautiful bodies of the locals playing ball together in the sea. In the background, I see dolphins jumping through the waves. Upon applying this fragrance, you are first greeted by a citrus-peppery note. This is accompanied by a distinct accent of coconut. The perfume becomes slightly creamy fresh. It concludes with the woodiness of cedar and cardamom. There’s also a light freshness from patchouli. The longevity and sillage are good and better than some have rated here. This scent can be worn by any man (but also woman) and for any occasion. Calvin Klein has created a more long-lasting fragrance here than we usually expect from them. It is definitely worth testing this scent.

Fair warning, I am typically bored with citrus fragrances. I tend to find them all to be very similar. When I first spray this, I would actually say the citrus is so strong, its a little reminiscent of bug spray main ingredient, citronella. The rough citrus does mellow out into more of an orange and bergamot. Eventually, that becomes a more orange blossom with white floral background. The dry down is a nice jasmine and musk. One of the things that makes this scent stand out from other citrus' is that the citrus sticks around for a while, most time it is short lived. I can still pick up some orange citrus in the dry down. The other thing that makes this fragrance better than most citrus' is that fragrance has better longevity. Even 6 hours later, I can pick up the dry down on my skin. The longevity is average.

The brand name: Born to stand out (BTSO). The bottle color: Maximum contrast (red-white). The perfume name: Naked Neroli. It comes across very confidently and is usually not my style. Additionally, it’s quite unusual for an Asian (here: South Korean) brand, to tap into the cliché box. The latter characteristic (Asian brand) would have definitely made it more appealing to me if I had known about it at the time of testing. I only tried it because citrus-dominated scents - as the name promised - generally interest me. However, a healthy dose of skepticism lingered. But surprise: It’s good! In its composition, it is completely different from what the brand suggests with its slightly shrill appearance. Behind all the marketing bling-bling - although I really like the bottle shape resembling old apothecary bottles - lies a robust, neroli-dominated scent that is strongly rooted in the classic Eau de Cologne tradition. I only noticed this after wearing it a few times, as I was heavily influenced by the external impression and the - let it be known - pronounced musk base. Essentially, it is a variation of the - for me - Eau de Cologne reference scent ‘Eau de Cologne Imperiale’ (1853) by Guerlain. This almost timeless masterpiece has been modernized here with a slightly sour (aromatic chemical?) addition in the multifaceted citrus note - with dominant lemon -, a more accentuated, soapy neroli, a very clean, ethereal-fresh herbal basil note - almost reminiscent of a clean, leafy vetiver - and a musk that makes the scent appear denser. Fortunately, the latter does not come across as creamy and overpowering, but merely adds some density to the texture. The classic EdCs are indeed more permeable, complex, and nuanced, but the roots are recognizable. Comparable, for instance, to Thierry Wasser’s ‘Cologne du Parfumeur’ (his contemporary interpretation of the house classic). He uses a creamy-powdery musk base quite generously, which envelops and smoothens the scent significantly. In comparison, Wasser’s scent slightly overpowers it for my taste, while Naked Neroli remains a bit more sharply contoured. However, the scent that seems most similar to me is Tom Ford’s ‘Neroli Portofino’, which can easily be confused with this one, but for me, it doesn’t radiate as brightly as ‘Naked Neroli’, which I attribute to the use of basil. I personally prefer this, although the Tom Ford scent maintains its citrus quality until the end and remains surprisingly differentiated in that regard, which I prefer about it. The BTSO scent doesn’t quite achieve that. Overall, Daphné Bugey has created a very balanced, contemporary, and reduced Eau de Cologne in my eyes, without falling too much into the aromatic chemistry trap. And it has definitely been given significantly more endurance than is typical for traditional models. For me, therefore, one of the most successful modern colognes. So one should not be misled by the brand's presentation or be disappointed by the appearance of encountering such a scent rooted in perfume classics. For anyone for whom Neroli Portofino is too expensive, this could possibly be a more wallet-friendly, qualitatively equivalent alternative, although it is also not exactly cheap (for the same price - €165 - you currently get 50ml of the BTSO scent or 30ml of the Tom Ford scent).

The worst thing, as I once heard a wise person say, is that the worst part of getting old is the loss of friends. When those who knew us when we were different from who we are today are gone, those who can still bear witness to our lives, our failures, and our victories, we truly feel alone. When those who have always been with us are no longer there. We need this. With people as with things, including certainly perfumes. It is fun to discover new things and to see if they can fit into our lives, perhaps making them more beautiful and richer. But we also need those we have always had. For the moments when it is more about remembering than dreaming. Such as Youth-Dew. Youth-Dew is today perhaps the archetype of a women's fragrance that, with a certain lack of empathy towards its lovers, is referred to as an 'old scent.' Perfume users who grew up with La Vie est Belle and 1 Million may find it disturbing - for it tells of a time when perfumes were made in a completely different way. Youth-Dew is an opulent floral oriental that sweeps over the sweet waters of the present like a thunderstorm, heavy, powerful, passionate. It plays virtuously on the keyboard of sepia-toned old notes, which were once girlish tones seventy years ago and today are so much more woman than girl. In my comment on the Eau de Parfum, I called it 'powerhouse.' It is that and yet so much more: memory and nostalgia - and beneath the ash of its years, a hot, red, never-extinguished ember. Conclusion: soon the last ones who were young with it will be gone. And although it may seem, from a present-day perspective, a scent of long-gone days, it still exists - and it still celebrates life. It celebrates strength and power and sensuality and femininity. It made Estée Lauder - the ambitious and business-savvy daughter of Eastern European immigrants from New York City and later her company - famous and turned the kitchen where she mixed her first creams into a global corporation. Yet there are still those who can testify to its journey, who were once young like it. Let us celebrate them.

Many years ago, my colleagues gifted me a perfume bottle for my miniature collection. Since they handed it to me without a box, I had no idea what treasure I now owned. It was the Quince Blossom (Quittenblüte) bottle from Estée Lauder with a golden cap and a blue decorative tassel, containing 7 ml of perfume. As the miniatures in my collection had to look good visually, I didn’t mind at all that I was unable to open the bottle, so the heaven on earth in a bottle remained hidden from me for years. I placed it in my display case alongside the other 300 minis. These were regularly dusted, occasionally admired, and as taste changes over the years, eventually packed away in a box and forgotten in the basement. During my last move, the basement also had to be cleared out, with a friend helping me energetically. At some point, Biggi discovered the box, examined it, and after squealing with delight, she held the Youth-Dew bottle accusingly under my nose: "What is this doing in the basement???" With a lot of patience, knocking, hot water, and gentle persuasion, we finally managed to open the bottle, and I smelled it for the first time: one of the densest, spiciest, most fantastic fragrance bombs ever - aside from Opium. Due to the name, I had expected a teenage scent, and the bottle suggested a floral content. But what I sniffed was an event: intense, warm, oriental, clove, cinnamon, later vanilla, and the Peru balsam I love so much, a hint of patchouli and incense, and many other ingredients that, in perfect harmony, create a special, unique, heavenly scent. Immediately, the divas of the fifties come to mind, or the advertising slogan of a refreshing candy: if it’s too strong, you’re too weak! This scent is mature, the wearer is confident, filling the space, an event just like the fragrance itself. At the same time, RuPaul's Drag Race flashes through my mind. Who could embody a diva better than a drag queen in her stage outfit? With Youth-Dew, she has an equal fragrance. This may sound pretty silly, but I just feel this way: As much as I love it, I feel unworthy or not up to this fragrance. I wear it, if at all, at home; I leave the dog walking to others, the worthy and the unworthy :-)

How could they choose the name "Youth Dew" for this perfume? This is something other users have wondered as well, as the comments on the EDP show. Doesn’t one automatically think of a floral-fresh, bright, light, and transparent scent? But certainly not of an almost black, intensely heavy concoction bursting with spicy aromas, right? Okay, the fragrance has been around since the 1950s; it may be that there were different reasons for the naming back then that are no longer known or understandable today. The EDP version of YD strikes me as a bit "scratchy-strict," probably due to the oak moss, which I don’t particularly appreciate. I can’t clearly identify any of the other numerous listed fragrance notes, neither in the EDP nor in the Extrait. The Extrait version, which I rate slightly higher at 8.5 compared to the EDP, definitely lacks the strictness of the EDP. Despite the spicy aromas, I perceive a certain (wintery) coolness (only in the Extrait! The EDP is "warmer") - but that is, of course, my subjective impression. It is certainly not sweet in the current sense, but also not strict or bitter. If one takes the term "pitch" literally, meaning the substance - i.e., the viscous, tar-like residues from the distillation of tars and organic substances - and not in the secondary sense of "misfortune," then my comment title fits quite well... because this Extrait indeed has quite a bit in common with pitch: the very dark color, as well as an incredible density, intensity, and longevity (I want to avoid the term "sticky," as it carries too negative a connotation). And one probably associates it more with hell ("pitch and sulfur") than with heaven... What was it again? "Bad girls go everywhere!"? Although I perceive YD as a "mature" scent, I really don’t want to claim that YD is generally unsuitable for young people! Even if it would hardly meet the current mass taste of younger women... But aren’t most Parfumo members (male or female) individualists who don’t care about the zeitgeist? Therefore: test it! The Extrait is a devilish creation! But incomparable! A little experience report (rather strange): I recently wore the Extrait (moderately dosed!) to an evening business meeting. A colleague asked if I was wearing a lily scent, as she likes that sort of thing. I recommended her "Baiser vole" and "La Vierge de Fer" (I’ll show her my bottles for testing soon), but YD is probably hardly a lily perfume...

....or: The first American superdream of fragrance. Youth Dew was released in 1953. And that in the then so soap-clean, lily-of-the-valley-pure, and somewhat prudish America. Women did not choose their perfume themselves yet, but received it as a gift from husbands or fiancés. It would have been considered "presumptuous" and somewhat "offensive" to show up there and.... There were customs and traditions against it. (I had a great-aunt in the USA who had contact with my mother and passed away when I was around 20....) The resourceful Estee Lauder, already longer in the US cosmetics business, came up with something clever: A strongly perfumed bath oil that was "proper" to buy... And eventually, this evolved into Eau de Parfum, Eau de Toilette, and probably first the "Parfum," the Extrait. And I possess such a one. In a 3.5 ml little bottle, with a whimsically placed fantasy flower stopper. a simple, rectangular bottle made of frosted glass. The oily "liquid" is dark brown, and it comes from that aforementioned great-aunt... And the scent :: amazing. Much rounder and softer than the EDP, at least compared to the one from the last 5 years. Spicy, oriental, and very voluminous. The heart note, if one can even speak of such, is dominated by naturally appearing clove and cinnamon notes, which in turn are interwoven with relatively unsweet flowers and exhibit an "animalistic" touch (narcissus?) Deeper and deeper become the "tones" of the perfume. "Balsamic" moss notes from the deepest forests (perhaps in the Rocky Mountains...)? Oriental-tinged vanilla "fresh from the pod"... Noble woods, vetiver, patchouli, united with "nitromusk," This complex scent kaleidoscope radiates a shy-restrained "desire." Clever - subtle "sexiness"... Above all, however, "Youth Dew Perfume" embodies the aura of America in the 50s...

That's a wonderful take on citrus. But it has nothing to do with Allure Homme. It's just plain lemony juice from beginning to the end. Suitable for both men and woman. Below average lasting power, sillage and projection. Updated January 2014

It's super fresh, clean and elegant. It opens up with zesty lemon then dry down is musky. A refreshing balance of lively citrus notes combined with musk and a woodier base , but still retains a touch of that familiar sweetness of the tonka bean. This cologne reminds me of Dior Homme Cologne but it launched before Dior Homme Cologne! I love Chanel Allure Homme Sport Cologne. It's good for spring and summer. I'm so happy that I have it in my collection. Highly Recommended. Two Thumbs Up. Rating : 8.5/10
A hard and sharp lemon - citrus cologne with an unpleasant white musk base. Smells like the wet wipes they hand out on buses in the middle east.

One of mine designer grabs when I need to wear a refresher scent for the hottest weather in the day or a gym/workout reach. I live and I am active in the Beverly Hills area where it gets really hot in the summer and this fragrance exists to be paired in that weather. You can daily it too in most non-cold seasons at any event because it so versatile and safe with its high DNA quality known by Chanel. --- Overall, this is one of my favorite light freshie/sport scents (with Dior Cologne, Aventus Cologne, Viking Cologne, L'Eau d'Issey Pour Homme, and Allure Sport). I am not the biggest citrus fan at times, but the quality you get from Allure Homme Sport Cologne Chanel is top-notch and this fragrance handles the heat so well while not breaking the bank on the wallet too much. --- Yes, I do agree it has a citrus harsh opening, but that is what I love about this fragrance. I even get a bit of barbershop, Creed Viking vibe from it at times in the extreme heat I think because of the vanilla dry-down. The musk ratio is perfect - just enough to make it clean and masculine. --- Again, it is a quality and classy citrus-sport scent that impresses people because it is a Chanel. Plus the bottle will get you attention, I pull it out of my gym bag and people are impressed with the way it looks. Not game changing, but a good roster spot if you're playing the fragrance game in depth and want to flex a good collection. --- Pros: classy gym scent, very smooth-light vanilla dry-down, citrus blast to wake you up, price (for a Chanel it is not badly expensive), bottle (one of the best looking bottles behind the Bleu line, so slick and cool) , brand (you are wearing a Chanel), and peace of mind (freshie that will always be liked). --- However, if you need something with more depth and power but still in a sport style than you might want to look into the heavier ones in the Allure Sport line (I also love Allure Sport, Allure Sport X, and Superleggera). --- (And if you want to bump of your cologne taste even higher than you can try the Exclusifs one from Chanel but it is very expensive).

...we will not go into the name of this fragrance this time. I already commented on that in my Allure Blanche Edition review;-)! That was the last Allure I needed to test. Last week, Blanche managed to win out over the Cologne during the purchase. I really liked the Cologne in the store, though. Finally, the larger bottle arrived this weekend! You can never have enough of "these" fragrances, especially during 4 weeks of constant heat and dryness, as I need at least as much of it as mineral water;-)! The Cologne is packed with pretty much everything, but also EVERYTHING in terms of citrus and tropical fruits that botany has to offer! Just as wonderfully fresh and citrusy, lightly piercing, the Cologne starts (I don't think it's really a Cologne!?). This is quite a wake-up and refreshment... Wow! After the last 4 weeks, where we now have palm trees growing and fountain construction companies are sprouting up everywhere, I might slowly be developing a citrus allergy, and I now know where the "orange peel" actually comes from, but the beginning is really delicious. I can't recognize much of the Allure charm here anymore; the creamy-woody aspect has faded a bit, which is why Blanche was able to prevail for me. Yes, a bit of musk and a hint of cedarwood can be easily detected. Essentially, it's nothing other than Dior Homme Cologne or L'Eau Declaration by Cartier, or for that matter, Icon by Dunhill, although the latter has significantly more depth and volume. Since there’s no guarantee for the typically German summer this year, the Cologne is a perfect and reliable choice; you can't go wrong with it at all. No, it's not exciting, nor new or particularly innovative, but it perfectly fulfills its purpose... namely pure refreshment. And it lasts significantly longer than Dior Homme Cologne and L'Eau. I can easily perceive it for 6 hours, which the other two can only dream of. The sillage is quite strong at the beginning but gradually weakens... but lemon, like vanilla, is immediately well perceived everywhere. A very good all-rounder for spring and summer! Ps. It doesn't even smell remotely like the Mugler Cologne indicated on the right!!!

I believe I am now the leader in terms of quantity of comments here on Parfumo... after testing over 1300 fragrances, I've seen quite a lot pass by my nose. Who would have thought that there was still an Allure offshoot missing, which is also available at my regular perfumery? One could have approached this with very little motivation...

I generally avoid sport versions of fragrances and only test them to give my two cents here, he he he… no, but every now and then, one discovers a sport scent that is really good. This, in turn, creates a chain effect where I will likely test the entire line of a fragrance. Just like now with Chanel Allure Homme.

From Allure Sport Eau de Toilette to Cologne, it's a huge leap - instead of a "solid" floral-fresh scent, here we have a pronounced citrus note, which is, however, more elegant and noticeably softer than in the Edition Blanche.

...no, the fragrance is not just for athletes. This scent can also be worn by a man in a suit or in casual clothing. At a banquet just as much as in a restaurant or at a party. He is an all-rounder, a perfect one. Upon application, you are first greeted with a blend of pepper and lemon. But neither of them dominates the other scent.

Well, where should we start? I actually began with this fragrance as a sample. I sprayed it and thought it was good, but then it disappeared again. We were on vacation in France, and I thought: take another sample with you so I smell good. The choice fell on "Allure Homme Sport Cologne Sport | Chanel." What can I say... at 32 degrees, this scent is just perfect.

This is exactly the smell of a flowering marijuana plant. At the base of this fragrance is the photorealistic smell of the green fan leaves of a cannabis plant. The fruitiness of grapefruit and passionfruit playing the part of the flowering buds. The pine and resin accords completing the illusion that you are smelling a heavily budded THC laden plant, days before harvest. Be warned, my fiancé said it was "candy sweet" when smelling it from a few feet away, and if you think of this as more of a flower fragrance rather than a passionfruit and grapefruit fragrance that makes sense. To be clear, this is not some dank heavy smell, but green and fruity. I'm sampling from a vial, but it is impressively strong when I put it on. It also projects well for a couple of hours and has a nice dry down that's a little bit more grapefruit/passion fruit forward and last for many hours after that.

Sampling Borntostandout Mary Jane, fittingly involving cannabis, but also hemp, mint, woods, spices, and some sweets. It’s rather unique and a bit odd, a green-leaning take on cannabis that’s also fresh, tingly due to the mint, with a woody/spicy/ever-so-slightly sweet montage in the background. Despite its oddity, it’s fairly pleasant after the initial surprising burst, not overly cannabis/hemp-laden, in my opinion, one of the more restrained deployments of these notes, complemented by the green, fresh mint aspect, almost making for a bold freshie rather than something dark and edgy. I’m not sure I’d wear it myself but I applaud the creativity, and it performs well. As with the rest of the line, it’s EDP concentration, priced at $210 for 50ml, and sold at various US boutiques like Ministry of Scent. 7 out of 10

This is a juicy fruit fragrance. This is not green, woody, or spicy. There is nothing in here that makes me think of cannabis. That would be fine except the name of this fragrance is Mary Jane, this is suppose to highlight cannabis as a fragrance note. This is incredibly disappointing and honestly misleading. If you ignore the marketing fumble, this is mainly a passion fruit fragrance. There is citrus at the beginning with a tiny hint of green but it is quickly overpowered by the passion fruit. I mean overpower too, the fruitiness is borderline cloying. It'll mellow out after a couple hours but then its a sweet dry down. I think they did a really poor job with this fragrance. Its not what its marketed to be and what you do get is overwhelming your senses and fairly linear. It did last over 6 hours and the projection is strong. Its $205 for 50ml which is crazy to me but if you want a really sweet passion fruit scent, this that might be a good price range for you.

Mary Jane is a pleasantly sour fresh fragrance with a certain green undertone. It is beautifully crafted and is best suited for the warm days of the year. Right at the beginning, you can feel this beautifully zesty quality through the grapefruit, but also the passion fruit. A green vibe can also be recognized, especially through the mint. The listed hemp and cannabis note certainly contribute to this as well. The fragrance definitely comes across as pleasantly sour. On one hand, through the grapefruit and the passion fruit, but especially through the rhubarb. Rhubarb is known for its sour characteristic. Therefore, I suspect that the rhubarb is pulling the strings here. I wouldn't have recognized the sage as such, but when you read it, you can indeed identify it. The longer the fragrance sits on the skin and dries down, the more woody elements come into play. The zesty quality of the fragrance recedes a bit, but is still detectable. The sour side of the fragrance is also still recognizable. All in all, I really like the fragrance. You should definitely give it a chance and test it.

BTSO not only dares to experiment, it is actually a commercialized experimental lab, which I really like about the brand. They are eye-catching, combine new elements, and yes, it doesn’t have to appeal to everyone. With this fragrance, I found the approach truly creative and simultaneously polarizing. Long story short, let's get into it: - At the beginning, you get a special kick from a fresh-sour combination; probably the mix of mint, grapefruit, and the herbal hemp/cannabis note; very intense and at the limit, unfortunately a bit chaotic in my view, but somehow still exciting. - Then comes an intriguing contrast of sage and passion fruit, which blends with the opening; this fruitiness paired with the hemp note could deter many because it somehow doesn’t harmonize; a rather irritating break, arbitrary indeed. - In the end, the fragrance transitions into a slightly cloying-woody, sweet base. Caramel and cashmere wood create, in my opinion, an almost overloaded heaviness when combined with the rest. - The sillage and longevity are average, both, nothing that stands out, but lies in a good middle ground. Yes, an undoubtedly creative and bold fragrance, but not my cup of tea. Too unbalanced, a rollercoaster of extremes, from ultra-sour to herbal-resinous, to tropical-sweet then to caramelized-woody. The brain and the nose cannot and do not want to process this chaos.

This fragrance is a little similar to the original Pleasures, however it is a tad fruitier and not as soapy. Opening with lively fruits and citrus, Pleasures Bloom is perfect for those hot Summer days. Pretty and feminine, this fragrance is relatively strong like most Estee Lauder scents are. Despite my respect for the brand, Estee Lauder's scents have something about them that grates on my nerves. Although I find most of their fragrances pleasant enough, they smell 'plasticky' to me. Pleasures Bloom is guilty of this strange synthetic note that allows me detect an Estee Lauder scent from miles away. Disregarding my dislike of the way in which Estee Lauder's fragrances are constructed, this is a very pleasant balance of fruits and flowers. In terms of packaging, I've always liked the bottle design for the Pleasures bottles, however the strange fabric flower around the neck of the bottle is just odd and looks cheaply made. My guess is that this fragrance is intended to appeal to a younger generation as well as the established Pleasures fans. In my opinion, Pleasures Bloom caters to both. The lasting power and the sillage are both excellent, as can be expected from this brand. If you had no problems with the way Pleasures smelt, you may possibly enjoy this newer, fruitier creation.

This fragrance does not scream anything special to me.It smells like someone grabbed one of everything from a florist shop and mushed it all together. I think the peony and vanilla are different, but the heart notes remind me of Marc Jacobs Daisy. The sillage and longevity are great for a floral. The most prominent notes on me are vanilla,Peony (YUCK!), a loud grapefruit, and raspberry. I do not smell any patchouli in the base notes, just vanilla. I wanted to like it, I really did, but the grapefruit and peony combination would not let me like it, I will save up for something I like better. This does not smell like candy at all which I was expecting from the marketing.

A beautiful harmonious floral scent that envelops you like a pink powdery cloud. It warms and comforts like a fluffy soft wool blanket or the embrace of a beloved grandmother. When I'm stressed and simply long for peace and coziness, I reach for this fragrance.

Generic boring freshy-sporty male fragrance you can find at the cheapies' shelf of your local drugstore. Now it simply reincarnated into a hip-trendy-southkorean luxury minimal bottle and it costs 165 euros. It's like "Denim cologne" pretending to understand Contemporary Art with hipster acquaintances You tried :)

This fragrance is walking through a forest of juniper trees. Its just rained and the fragrant droplets fall on your face. The fresh herbs underfoot release their aroma as they are crushed underfoot. This is a great cologne without any of the harshness that you get from all the mainstream cologne departments. This is fresh and spicy, a lemony paired with balsamic juniper fragrance. An aromatic gin and tonic on your skin that feels sophisticated. I imagine a classy guy, someone with good taste, wearing this fragrance. While this fragrance is good, its not very creative. This doesn't have any longevity or projection. The lack of projection makes sense because this is more of a skin scent. It only lasted about 4 hours on my skin, its too bad that it didn't last longer on my skin. Its $205 for 50ml.

The parfum is the only version of White Linen that I can wear and enjoy, I have always found the edp a little too sharp. I have a small amount of the parfum, and it's wonderful - it may be a well-worn cliché, but I really do think it smells just like clean laundry drying in the morning sun, under the blue sky, in a garden full of flowers, in spring or early summer. Cool and warm at the same time, elegant, but still easy to wear. I think of it as mainly an aldehydic perfume supported by flowers, but the floral notes are so well blended that I cannot really pick them out separately. Rose stands out a little more than the others, and although it's not listed above, I believe I smell lilac. Same thing with the base notes, it all just melts together to a pleasant, fresh and natural sweetness. I don't wear it often, but sometimes on sunny mornings in spring, it feels like just the right choice. My teenage daughter loves it too!

I have perhaps less than a milliliter of this, found for a dollar in a thrift shop. There was another little bottle next to it, containing maybe another milliliter, and I did not buy it. From what I had heard, this was another aldehydic white floral, of the Dove-soap variety I've smelled a million times, and I figured all I would need was the one bottle to experience it for history's sake. I regret not getting the second bottle, because I really like this. It starts out with that classic aldehydic sting that feels like hot air is being blown up your nostrils. I wasn't a fan of that feeling with N°5 Parfum , and I'm not a huge fan of it here, but it doesn't last long. And yes, like I'd imagined, it's soapy. But it's soapy in a particularly lush, sparkling way, a bar of soap that foams into a rich and creamy lather instead of airy bubbles. This is the olfactory equivalent of a spa day. I love white florals, but the name of this perfume has never sounded very appealing to me, made me think of white laboratory settings and hospital beds. I have heard that the EdP is harsher than this variant, and for all I know it carries that unsettling cleanliness with it, but not this. This is white linen, but it's a warm-toned white, an ivory shade without much harshness to it at all. God, I wish I got that second bottle!

In white light The day shines Swan feathers Powdery pure shimmer Little flowers sway In fresh gentle wind The horizon fading mistily In delicate bright green From afar A softly fruity hint It almost whispers In the tender branches Shallow shadows fall gently Into the soft young moss Thoughts drift Like white clouds

...glistening bright in the midday heat, almost painful to the eyes, fall on a woman in a light linen suit. She is slim, athletic, sun-kissed, with minimal makeup, and either sun-bleached or naturally light hair. She is accustomed to high temperatures, she does not sweat - on the contrary: her outfit looks exceptionally well-kept, as if just taken off the clothesline. And this, despite the fact that she is in a southern or even tropical region. This is the image that this perfume evokes in me. Cleanliness, sunshine, vacation vibes in the south... And it explains why I never felt that "White Linen" was truly suitable for me, even though I have owned a mini for many years (which I originally thought was an EDT), which I use once a year. I am largely the opposite of the described person (okay, I do consider myself slim and well-groomed): dark-haired, perpetually pale, unathletic, preferring lace or silk over linen. High temperatures are a horror for me! I don’t go on vacation trips. I cannot identify individual notes. The perfume strikes me as a blend of white flowers, fresh, brilliantly bright, and slightly soapy, with hardly any sweetness. On me, it has an incredible presence and longevity - even for an extrait. A positive, pleasant scent, yet I feel somewhat overdressed with it, much like one would feel in a linen suit. For the right wearer, however, it is surely a timeless beautiful classic!

I had it all! The pure perfume in the beautiful little splash bottle, also once in the Frosted Shell bottle, the Eau de Parfum spray in various sizes, my treasure, the wonderful glitter-free body powder, the body cream, the body lotion, and the delicate shower gel. I was happy. I wore White Linen every day. I was Mrs. White Linen. Everyone knew that. No one ever complained. Everyone knew whether I was there or just passing by. White Linen was my signature when no one was even talking about signature scents. My White Linen collection decorated my bathroom and my room. Never, really not a single day did I not use it. It lingered in all my clothes, it was heavenly. The scent was an unprecedented total work of art. I didn't really pick out the individual notes; to me, it was white-fresh and lightly green. Perhaps it was the violet and the iris from the background that attracted me so much, I don't know. It was definitely the freshness. Only once in my life, much later, did I wear another fragrance with the same great love. It too was discontinued. Why I eventually stopped wearing White Linen, I no longer know today. Who replaced you? Why? This is the end of my love letter to this unique, wonderful, sacred scent that accompanied me for a part of my life. Thank you, White Linen! You made me happy.

I had almost forgotten about this perfume, which I received as a gift 35 years ago. Somehow, it reappeared on my radar as I was looking for various summer scents to wear. I unwrapped the precious bottle and was torn - how could I have forgotten such a light, clean, airy fragrance? It is perfect for summer clothing and a wonderful blend of sweet honey and floral notes.

L`Animal is primarily a sweet spicy gourmand. Only over time, and especially in the base, does a subtle animalic note emerge more and more. The honey combined with almond creates something that I would describe as minimally animalic-urinal. After wearing it for a few hours, it reminds me a bit of Sadonaso . However, the Borntostandout is definitely more gourmand. If you like Sadonaso, you might surely enjoy this one as well. The longevity and sillage are very good, by the way. The fragrance has an incredibly good projection in the first few hours and only becomes skin-close much later. I can't really understand the reviews here overall. Sure, the scent is not mainstream and won't appeal to everyone. It is indeed a bit unusual but definitely wearable.

The top notes intrigued me at the counter, but when I got home with a sample and tried this, it turned into a skin scent in moments. The lovely powderiness at first reminded me of Chanel's divine Misia, but it didn't live up to that fragrance in the end. Re-smelling my arm now, the powder is very subdued, the Iris is almost gone, there's only a hint of woodiness. Glad I didn't buy. Reaching for something else to put on, let's see...okay Neil Morris's Afire. I'm getting addicted to it.

opens with tanginess, softly fresh-vegetal, complete with clinging clumps of earth. a rose on the wilt whispers quietly. all this is bound in ghostly, thin threads of powdery iris. a diffusion occurs in time, blurring the whole into finely milled, pressed matte powder; everything becomes a part of the whole, an iris painted with greens, browns, purples and silvers. poised, elegant, yet somehow warm and rounded. a subtle and eloquent scent.

Iris has many elusive sides to it, and Chanel knows them so well: gloriously lipsticky in Comète, dewy and powdery in N°19 Poudre…the list goes on and on. And then there’s La Pausa, described by the brand as “a perfume of rarity" that “reveals different facets of iris: earthy, powdery, shimmering, and secretive.” That's a pretty accurate description! Iris lovers should do a field trip at their nearest Chanel counter ASAP: it's a quintessential experience since it's so well blended, that you're gonna have a fun time deciphering what's going on — and you'll have plenty of time to do so, since it emanates off the skin and clothes for much longer than expected. Actually, sniffing this one should be a fun exercise for all perfume nerds! It's tricky to decode the abstraction of La Pausa because yes, it is an iris-centered fragrance, but it's not a fantasy Iris, but it's also not super rooty/carroty. It does have quite a green profile, enveloped in a peaceful cloud of powder which aaaaalmost sinks into Nivea cream-like territory, but then there's some acid, woody elements (vetiver?) that peek in and out, adding brakes to that direction as the scent performs. La Pausa finds elegance in restraint: appropriate for the brand famous for inventing suits that did allow for more freedom way back then, but with sleeve holes cut way up high because well...let's not get too loose. A dream come true as a lover of iris/green/powdery fragrances. Makes me feel at peace when I wear it

With this beautiful quote from Friedrich Nietzsche, the description could actually end here. Good. Divine. Light. Delicate. That is LA PAUSA. However, this fragrance touches me so deeply that it is a heartfelt concern for me to pay it a bit more tribute and to share its shimmering glow with the world...... For over 35 years, I have been trying - with dutiful regularity - to explore iris fragrances..... a note that usually does not particularly appeal to me and has never led me to a purchase so far....... resulting from these countless experiences, my expectations were correspondingly low...... I tested it solely because of the "green notes," the information that vetiver is included, and the fact that it is a Chanel.... a house that I usually hold in high regard (except for the "Lion" ;-)..)..... About the Fragrance LA PAUSA is an exceedingly elegant fragrance that captivates both through pronounced noble restraint and luxurious simplicity...... it represents for me the serene lightness of being, as Mademoiselle Chanel may have experienced it while looking out over the sea at her feet from the terrace of her villa in Roquebrune...... The facets of iris that resonate in LA PAUSA lie far beyond mother earth, roots, carrots, or lipsticks...... far beyond anything too tangible..... Its sound is wonderfully natural, extraordinarily fragile, and delicately silky...... as if it were whispering a soft melody that sets the surrounding light green grasses and herbs into gentle vibration and elicits a quiet whisper from them....... if spring birdsong were a fragrance note, I would claim it is contained in LA PAUSA...... The "powdery notes" indicated in the pyramid are present, but never overwhelming or suffocating...... no comparison to fragrances like, for example, Teint de Neige...... We women know the various powder consistencies..... while the aforementioned TdN is akin to thick covering powder, LA PAUSA is a delicate hint of "translucent powder"...... it merely provides a soft, matte-shimmering finish...... In conclusion, light woods give this enchanting calm and meditative fragrance a certain substance..... just enough so that it does not break apart..... Lovers of Chanel 19 Extrait (Vintage) should give it a try..

Humorless! Herbal dusty cloud iris! Extremely polished.. I read in the descriptions here. Everything is true and yet not quite. In search of an iris that doesn’t come off quite as powdery as "N°19 Poudré", which is green-transparent, not overwhelming, and a bit more herbal (in a positive sense!), I stumbled upon this fragrance. The sample lay unnoticed in the drawer for a long time. And it wouldn’t have received any attention a few months ago. All winter long, I was wrapped in warm, sweet scents. Sweeter fragrances than I have ever worn before. But now I’ve had enough of that. The current crisis demands a lot from our household with two preschool children. The inner voice says daily, multiple times, clearly and loudly, “Stay calm..!”. I miss the uncomplicated outings into nature here in the city. Everything is currently more complicated and cumbersome. An admonishing finger is hovering over everything. No resting, reminding the children to keep their distance, etc. I craved a green-grassy scent with a hint of herbaceousness that would allow my mind clarity like the deep inhalation of sea-fresh air. Bright and cheerful like spring, yet not cuddly soft like my cottony musk excursions in the past winter months. No, I wished for a scent that is bright, radiant, and spring-fresh. And HERE IT IS! Some here complain about longevity and sillage. The longevity for me is many hours. My close ones can certainly perceive the scent, but not like a Coco Mademoiselle, which always seems to precede me a bit, but rather like a fresh, well-groomed aura. Some may find it indeed too refined and elegant. After the green-fresh opening comes this powdery note, which some describe as lipstick. But it remains fresh and bright green in its radiance. Just as one likes on days when the world spins particularly fast inside, and one still needs to keep a clear head. Conclusion: not a scent for everyone. But those who like the newer version of “N°19” might also like this one.

Many many years ago, I received samples of almost all the Chanel Exclusif fragrances available at the time and fell in love with La Pausa and Rue Cambon. Thankfully, I bought Rue Cambon as an EdT, but that's not what this is about. Years later, having missed the reformulation, I ordered La Pausa without testing it again.

I received White Linen Breeze in addition to an old bottle of Opium from the eighties. While I do like the original White Linen, I would never have thought to get this flanker. It is so completely different from its big sister. At first, I perceive a hint of water lily, but only very subtly. The rose is only detectable in a very diluted form, and jasmine can only be sensed. From the base, which is supposed to consist of musk, sandalwood, and vetiver, I notice nothing. The longevity is in the medium range, and the sillage is rather weak. The bottle will be empty in a day or two, so I'm quickly writing this comment. Aquatics can indeed be nice on hot days, but this one overall feels more like a cheap, thin facial toner.

.... should smell just like this! How lovely and pleasant it is to sink into a beautiful, clean, freshly made bed after a long day’s work and then slowly and comfortably drift off into deserved sleep!? When I saw that this amazing scent had not received any comments yet, I felt compelled not to let that stand. White Linen Breeze was my fragrance! It’s been a while, but I still remember it fondly and truly mourn its absence, as it is no longer produced. I particularly appreciate the refreshing floral and marine notes, the water lily, and the long-lasting base of moss and vetiver combined with sandalwood. I no longer associate it with musk, but perhaps it has just been too long... Unfortunately, I used up the bottle down to the last drop, marched into the perfumery, and wanted a refill. Well, back then came the shocking news..... It’s all! No longer in production!! What a pity! Really a pity, because I fear that if there ever is a re-release of this fragrance, it will, based on experience, not come close to the old one.... Goodbye White Linen Breeze *sniff*

I'm writing this review on my 'phone which is damn irritating so it won't be a long one! My bottle of Colors was on sale in a duty free I visited a few days ago during the constant traveling I am currently experiencing. There wasn't a tester, but I have enjoyed the odd Kenzo frag in the past and was willing to give this discounted bottle the benefit of the doubt. Upon applying it this morning I was immediately positive that Colors contains a huge dram of di hydro myrcenol, a la CK One ... Which I don't mind at all since I am currently working in humid, tropical weather and this is rather cooling! A fresh vibe continues all the way through to dry down ... with a herbal, powdery idea lasting on the skin for a good six hours or so. I guess it could be described as somewhat 'barber shop-ish' to some extent, but it is vaguely comforting while still maintaining its freshness. I've received about a dozen compliments on this fragrance today ... who knew it would create such a ruckus??

Somewhere in California in an upscale neighborhood. It is the early 70s. In a hall of the renowned hotel, the upper class of fashion designers, haute couture, and top cosmetics gather. The host is the owner of the American beauty company, Estee Lauder herself. She greets all participants by name with a handshake, pleasant small talk, and kindness with an important intention for her: To introduce a fragrance that is meant to send a personal greeting to the world of high fashion and beauty. In HER way, in HER style, a scent of the American fashion dream. Exclusively composed for her, it is now to be carried out into the wide world. A floral fragrance opening, lively, "clean," and radiant, is the beginning of something greater. A spiced (coriander) heart note with plenty of "feminine" ylang-ylang and orange blossoms signals "success with finesse and patience," extraordinary dresses, and elegant accessories. The "base" of the perfume, quite "classic, woody-earthy-strict, with patchouli and woods, represents a kind of endurance and longevity in olfactory form. The "private" scent of the beauty queen and her success story have been immortalized in a bottle. Whoever wears it should (in her opinion) receive a piece of it. And at the same time, maintain their private atmosphere. Estee Lauder and many of the fashion kings from that time are long gone, but the fragrance continues to remind us of them.

Being a fanatic for greens, I have been looking forward to testing Bel Respiro for a long time. After wearing it a few times now, I find it so mild and restrained in all of its aspects. I get a bit of Cristalle Eau de Parfum greens with N°5 L'Eau Eau de Toilette softness and bits of leather. The quality is there, obviously, but the character? For me a green scent should exude a "Stay away from me or I'll bite your head off" kind of attitude. That is totally missing here. On the other hand, the green-leathery drydown is magnificent and that may be Bel Respiro's best feat. As a result, Bel Respiro only works when I am feeling nice and friendly. On cold-hearted green days, I still reach out to Cristalle Eau de Parfum or N°19 Eau de Parfum

Actually, I am a child of Munich, but I have had professional dealings in Frankfurt over the decades. Just like in the last few days. I could never quite grasp the city, caught between prestigious law firms and the red-light district. Sometimes you find yourself in a luxurious restaurant - other times having a beer with colleagues at Yok Yok. Blouse, dress, or sweatpants? Anything goes, anytime. Pantha rei - everything flows. If I had to assign a scent to this city, it would be Bel Respiro Eau de Parfum . I can't grasp it. I can't evaluate it. I never know what to expect. Do I feel comfortable with this fragrance choice, or would I rather wash it off? It is greenish, so beautifully unfeminine and graceful. Are the edges sharper today or finely woven? Each time it develops differently. Sometimes the leather is very prominent, other times it accompanies me almost unnoticed throughout the day, only whispering occasionally: "I am still here." On other days, it unfolds gruffly, cranky as we Munich locals would say. Sometimes I receive a compliment from my sons about this scent, other times they say it is old-fashioned. Today, I like it very much on this cold autumn day. A little after-work walk by the Main, while the city lights come on in the urban buzz. It should actually be a spring scent, but it refuses to commit. It quickly lost its freshness today. It shows its darker side. Adapting to the evening mood. Maybe just this time. Only a few notes are listed. I could hardly identify any others. They are certainly present, but hidden just as mysteriously as this city. The other two reviews give the scent a 3 and a 9. I couldn't say it better. And even if we don't often find the same language, we will meet again. Right here at that place that strangely binds me to it.

… you are no Bel Ami! Respiro: payment deadline, grace period, deferment. It’s not always beautiful either. Is there a grace period when you pay for Respiro in installments? What is going on with Polge? What wonderful fragrances did the good Jaques create in the past! Has he lost his sense of smell? Beethoven was already deaf when he composed the Ninth, but at least something great came out of it! Perfume is supposed to stimulate the imagination, make the wearer interesting, and spark curiosity about how the scent evolves. But what do we have here? Diluted water! To somehow get a grip on this hint of nothingness, I took an elastic bandage from my medicine cabinet and wrapped it around my head and arm to somehow fix my nose to the sprayed area. However, the bandage smelled stronger than the Respiro, because of course my medicine cabinet contains everything that belongs there: water softener, glue, dog shampoo, mosquito killer, etc., and a leather eye patch (Could this be the leather note of Respiro?). My medications are in the cosmetics cabinet. I had to unwrap the bandage again (because I looked like a mummy and my dog was looking at me in fright) and went out to the balcony to sniff the pot of parsley. Finally, something green! I cannot fathom what other aromas are supposed to be in here. I would have almost preferred if Polge had whisked in a bit of Maggi, then Respiro would at least have had some polarization. Jaques Polge, I give you a grace period for a return to form!

The "Les Exclusifs de Chanel" series is a tribute to Coco Chanel. Each fragrance in the collection represents a chapter from the life of Coco Chanel (1883 - 1971): Whether it be an address (31 Rue Cambon, the location of her Haute Couture salon opened in 1918), a name (Misia, after Misia Sert, a patron of renowned artists in Paris and a close friend of Coco Chanel), a year (1932, the year Coco Chanel presented her luxurious diamond jewelry collection in her private apartment), a fabric (Jersey, which Coco Chanel frequently used and helped to bring into the fashion world, as Jersey had previously been used almost exclusively for underwear), a color (Beige, her favorite color) or even a building, Bel Respiro, the name of her spring residence in Garches, a municipality near Paris. Coco Chanel would retreat there from time to time in spring to relax and find inspiration. Now Jacques Polge has tried to capture these impressions of a picturesque landscape filled with greenery in a fragrance. Bel Respiro was first released in 2007 as an Eau de Toilette, which I was able to experience not long ago. In 2016, the fragrances from the Exclusif line were revised and reintroduced as Eau de Parfum. Some revisions did not meet full satisfaction, as I have read here and there. The EdP versions often lack that certain something. However, I do not want to dwell further on the well-known topic of revisions; it is becoming tedious, and everyone has their own opinion on the matter. I had already experienced the EdT some time ago and rated it very well. It is a fragrance that completely matches my taste. Green freshness, floral notes, and a gentle, creamy progression. The distinct green impression primarily arises from the use of galbanum, a fragrance ingredient that I particularly enjoy. Galbanum is derived from so-called umbelliferous herbs, a group of plants that often produce very aromatic spices (fennel, anise, parsley, cumin, angelica), but also very toxic plants (hemlock, giant hogweed). The distinction is often very difficult, as these plants can look very similar. Galbanum is used in some very famous and outstanding fragrances, such as Chanel N°19, Vol de Nuit, Miss Dior (from 1947 and 1992), Yatagan, to name a few. The fragrance has a balsamic, spicy quality and an unmistakable, slightly creaky green tone. However, Bel Respiro is by no means creaky. For alongside the galbanum, there are gentle notes reminiscent of fresh grass, a herbal impression emerges, and I perceive a certain floral quality. I cannot define this more closely. However, I suspect that a hint of white flowers has been used, blooms that come into their own best in spring. Later in the development, a fine trace of leather appears, but it is so soft and subtle that it is never perceived in the foreground and thus never bothers me. Because leather usually meets with great rejection from me. Here it is perfectly placed and completely unobtrusive. Bel Respiro remains cheerful and friendly at every stage of its development. A gloomy and serious mood would hardly suit a spring fragrance. Now I have the EdP, which recently came to me through a sharing. There are some differences compared to the EdT, even if they are minimal. The EdP is overall a little quieter than the EdT and feels sweeter and more floral to me in its progression, while the EdT is somewhat more robust and grassier overall. The opening is identical for both. In the EdT, the fine leather note comes out a bit more, while in the EdP it remains even more subtle or barely perceptible. In terms of longevity, both variants differ slightly as well. Since both fragrances are not loud and demanding by nature, they are also not record-breaking in longevity. I do not expect that from the quieter representatives. The EdT is perceptible to me for about 7 hours, and the EdP fades after about 6 hours. My conclusion: With Bel Respiro, a truly beautiful spring fragrance has been created, which has a consistently cheerful and pleasant effect on me. The impression of Chanel's spring residence has been well captured in this fragrance. The impressions of a beautiful green landscape surrounding the estate, some shrubs are already in full bloom, the sun sends warming rays, and being outdoors is simply enjoyable. I can very well imagine Bel Respiro as a lovely, uncomplicated everyday companion. And I also believe that the fragrance is equally suitable for both men and women. I hold this view for several other fragrances from the Exclusif line as well. I have not yet held the bottles in my hand, except for a mini. But they appear very beautifully Chanel-like in their simple and straightforward elegance. I rate both fragrances equally well, although the EdT has a slight edge due to its greater complexity. My thanks go to Mefunx for the sample of the EdT and to BeatriceA, who organized the sharing for the EdP so wonderfully. And with these hopefully delightful lines for you, I wish everyone a happy Easter.

This is a woman scorned on valentines day. She has a bouquet of jammy roses, almost fruity, that she has set on fire. The lush roses are now smoldering. It did smell a little latex or medicinal at the beginning but it quickly disappears. The jammy rose will give way to a warm spice and woody rose with smoke trailing in the background, adding depth. The projection is pretty good, it created a nice scent bubble. I expected better longevity because this lasted on my skin for 4 hours and that is fairly weak compared to other fragrances in this line. A 50ml will cost you $205.

This scent was a surprise. Influenced by its predecessor, Bronze Goddess, it initially only earned a shrug from me. However, the effect came after several sprays and "wearing it around," and I became more and more enthusiastic. In the meantime, Bronze Goddess Soleil has surpassed its predecessor. What captivates me about it is the successful balance between citrusy freshness, without being sharp, and wet fruitiness, without being musty. As it develops, it takes on something dry from a summer wildflower meadow dotted with mandarins. In the end, the woods and musk take the lead, but very softly and not at all in an "oriental sense." It remains: pure summer. I must admit that I often use this scent in the evenings after showering to help me sleep - a true cocooning scent: curl up, smell, imagine something beautiful, fall asleep, and all of this without being overwhelmed by a perfume. As for longevity: this is an Eau fraîche, so a pure body scent, lighter in the dilution class than an EdC. This should be kept in mind.

A nice scent for summer. At first refreshing citrus notes, then it becomes creamy-floral, especially orange blossom is noticeable. Overall, I find the scent very pleasant, refreshing, and yet creamy; I couldn't detect any artificial, sharp notes. It is more floral than its predecessor, but unfortunately, this delicious "sunscreen note" is missing. Very unfortunate, I think. The longevity is not exactly impressive, and the intensity of the scent leaves something to be desired. I perceive the "Eau Fraiche" as a bit too "thin" and too "light." I already use it as an all-over body spray just to notice it at all, and after 2 hours I could already reapply. Many body lotions smell longer on my skin and can still be detected after several hours. Although I think the scent is great: just average, since I have to spray a lot, and I will surely empty the 100ml bottle quickly.

I didn’t realise this was limited edition, which made it too tempting not to add it to my collection. I have no will power! When I first got my sample of this, I really didn’t like the opening which I found quite harsh. I admit I didn’t let this sit and recover from shipping and wrote it off. Coming back to the sample, I’ve changed my mind about it. This isn’t a chocolate bar scent. It’s more of a chocolate milk and coco butter to me. I think layered on top of Palmers Coco Butter lotion, this would be gorgeous. It would probably layer really well with most scents. The longevity of this is pretty poor though. It’s also quite light wearing. Definitely not worth full price, but I do enjoy it. Choco Locco is the best chocolate type of scent I’ve personally found so far. There’s nothing artificial smelling in this, although I do hope this gets stronger with time. I feel this brand in general is way overpriced for what they offer. I might still decide return my bottle before I open it. I do love this, but the cost leaves me undecided.

Ginger liqueur with cocoa liqueur opening followed by powdery cocoa which makes for a cocoa heavy opening with a boozy undertone. Scent continues to develop into something much milkier and creamier with condensed milk and cookie dough. Smells like the milk leftover from a bowl of cocoa pebbles with hints of decadent caramel. Dry down turns into a powdery chocolate marshmallow with musky notes and warm brown sugar. A fun journey through all there is to chocolate, boozy to milky to powdery. Just fun chocolate!

Realistic cocoa powder scent, rum and ginger provide a spicy twist. Still only for true chocolate lovers. I'm not really a fan of this type of gourmand, but it's significantly nicer than the full milk Chocolate Greedy. Phenomenal longevity and sillage. You smell good enough to bite. Addictive.

When I saw the fragrance in the category of new scents and read the scent pyramid, I knew immediately that I had to have it! When I ordered it from Harrods, I didn't even know it was limited edition. All the more I am happy to now own one of the 2750 pieces produced worldwide. But now let's talk about the scent itself: the scent pyramid pretty much reflects exactly what you get. A delicious chocolate, I would say about 50% cocoa content, so not too dark, not too sweet, definitely smells edible. The cocoa liqueur definitely comes through, but without being too alcoholic! I don't notice much of the ginger liqueur, but maybe it adds a certain something. It smells to me more like liquid chocolate, if that makes sense. The longevity is definitely amazing, which you can already tell when spraying it on, as the scent feels slightly sticky on the skin. Sprayed on in the afternoon, I could definitely still perceive it well on my skin the next morning. Of course, you have to love gourmand fragrances. I don't crave them every day, but on some days, such a delicious scent simply provides comfort. For those who can't get a bottle or want to spend a little less money on a delicious chocolate scent, I would recommend checking out "Choco Violette | Mancera." This one also has a strong violet note, but it is also a really delicious chocolate scent. Chocolate Greedy didn't appeal to me personally, as I don't like the combination with orange (not even in edible chocolate). Choco Loco smells the most like pure chocolate of all, without much fuss around it.

Alright, I'll be the first one to say it here, but the EDP version of 1932 smells like Chanel's take on J'adore. I have the Les Exclusifs EDP coffret and after multiple wearings it hit me. 1932 EDP is a soft multi-floral and pear perfume dressed in the usual Chanel accompaniments of aldehydes, soft waxy musks and iris. It walks that same strange set of lines that J'adore does: it's fresh but warm, and dewy or even honeyed-sweet but paradoxically almost powdered. People who don't generally appreciate aldehydes may find that this interpretation doesn't offend. The material is definitely present but used judiciously and in a manner that adds sparkle rather than the icepick-up-the-nose sensation one sometimes gets from No5 or No22. Overall 1932 EDP is easy to wear, very pretty and inoffensive. This scent is associated with Chanel's high jewelry line 1932 Bijoux de Diamants and is supposed to convey the scintillation and polish of diamonds. By that metric, I think it's a great success. For those who generally find powdery iris or muted white floral perfumes appealling I think this would be an easy reach. It would make a stellar signature scent for ladies of any age.

I had some kind of connection with this perfume before I even had it, like I used to have with almost all perfumes which I buy blindly. I don't know how it happens but first it's just a feeling that I would love the scent. After that I start to read everything possible about it and I have some kind of scent in my head, how it would smell. I close my eyes, I breathe deeply and I imagine it in my nose and in my brain. 1932 is everything which I was imagining. Beautiful crispy uplifting aldehydes with a hint of citruses in the opening. Very delicate flowers are playing hide and seek with Iris which is overpowering the other florals from time to time but between times it hides itself and you can get innocent whiffs of the paltry yet indulgent fresh flower bouquet. I can't tell those flowers apart, it's like a pastel coloured flower painting where all the pigments are faded because of a lot of water. The complex base is that style which Chanel does well - clean vibes, among others white Musk, Sandalwood and a hint of Vanilla. Roughly divided there are three kind of powdery scents for me. The one is an abstract feeling of the modern loose powder, soft, clean, delicate and fluffy. The second one is a smell of a baby powder. I have encouraged people to buy one bottle of it if they don't know how it smells. It's a small investment to know that beloved and hated style of perfumes. The third one is a smell of an old powder which was mostly scented with Iris. The powdery smell in 1932 is the last one. It's that Chanel's well known Iris smell combined with aldehydes. Glamorous, sparkling, dry, a little bit shy and bewitching. Not so dry and cold than La Pausa but dry anyway accompanied by other beautiful flowers to add light pink and even light yellow and green colour to the baby blue and violet. This perfume is utterly tender, it easily gets buried among other scents. Only to try to wear it at my home is a mistake - if my intention is to enjoy it to the fullest. After I got this scent I worn it at home and asked an opinion of it from my husband. He said that it's nothing special and it's boring. Next day I worn it at the totally empty gym. He was asking "what is this amazing scent around you". This is best when worn in an air conditioned area where it makes a pretty bubble around you. It's great outside as well but honestly it shines, it's sparkling like diamonds, in clean air indoors whether it's the gym or the office. If you have tried this in some big department store there is a huge possibility that you didn't get the right character out of it. That is not only too full of different kind of scents but too noisy as well. Believe it or not it matters as well. Thank you for reading, I hope you liked my review and it was helpful. I would appreciate if you follow me on my IG and/or YouTube (English subtitles available): @ninamariahperfumes

Ghandi is arrested in early January 1932, the Olympic Winter Games start in Lake Placid, the NSDAP gains majorities in German state elections, 6 million unemployed in Germany, Hitler obtains German citizenship, the automatic transmission is invented, CBS broadcasts the first television series, increasing turmoil between National Socialists and Communists, and the premiere of "Blonde Venus" with Marlene Dietrich and Cary Grant. 1932, Great Depression - the Union of Diamond Dealers approached Coco Chanel in Paris to promote their stones. With the borrowed diamonds, she created "Bijoux de Diamants". Coco loved not only black but everything that sparkled: a bracelet like a star made of white gold and diamonds, a necklace, a ring similar to the bracelet, a brooch in the shape of a feather........all pieces wonderfully eye-catching. The exhibition was a great success, but the jewelers were not happy. Because Coco was just a seamstress, that couldn't be. The diamonds from the collection were returned to the diamond dealers. But everyone had seen the creation and admired it. With this collection of jewelry, she rocked it and revolutionized the design of jewelry for that time and even today. The original invitation cards to the exhibition can be viewed on the Chanel website, and even today, the creations travel the world to be admired. While scents that list aldehydes as a note usually scare me off, I was pleased here. Because this scent is not an aldehyde monster for me. 1932 starts citrusy and yes, also floral, but not an overload of aldehydes, with lilac standing out particularly. Then it becomes powdery, a bit of rose flashes through. With a hint of vetiver, it rounds off. I think that with vetiver, the scent would also be wearable for a man. But of course, it is intended only for us women ;) 1932 is a classic scent that you can never overdo. Sometimes Coco is just too intense for me, or Coromandel was too much "here I am" for me. 1932 is "I am here" - all day Chanel.

So, after trying and describing the EDT of this fragrance last week, it's now time for the newer EDP, which apparently is supposed to replace (or has replaced) the EDT, as the EDT is no longer being sold. However, that doesn't really matter, as the differences, as mentioned last time, are rather minimal, and despite the few differences, no one needs to fear that a potentially beloved fragrance would now smell completely different. In my opinion, the EDP actually has the advantage of having a noticeably stronger sillage, which allows one to delight... or burden the surroundings with the scent, depending on how you take it :D The scent: The EDP of this fragrance also starts with aldehydes, neroli, slightly powdery notes from iris and bergamot. I find that the sillage is already slightly stronger at the beginning than with the EDT, and the sweet and floral notes seem to come into play more quickly here. I find the jasmine to be stronger here; with the EDT, I had the impression of smelling the lilac a bit more intensely. The cloves also seem to smell slightly more pronounced, although they, like in the EDT, quickly get overshadowed by all the other floral notes. Oh yes, despite the description on the website of this fragrance, I still don't perceive any pears at the beginning... In the heart note, the fragrance remains powdery, floral, and sweet. Aldehydes are still noticeable, which makes the scent seem a bit more mature. And you can now smell the ylang-ylang more distinctly, which makes the fragrance a bit heavier and more sultry. Strictly speaking, the fragrance from the heart note actually smells almost like the EDT, because if you don't really concentrate on the sprayed spot, the differences compared to the top note (whose differences were also only minimal) will hardly be recognizable. I would say that the jasmine still seems to be stronger than the lilac here, and as mentioned, it's the other way around with the EDT. The sillage increases significantly over time. In the base, it remains as it has been. The fragrance continues to be floral and powdery-sweet, as well as slightly sultry due to the ylang-ylang. The musk smells a bit stronger. A little later, there are resinous notes like incense and opoponax, but these notes, as with the EDT of the fragrance, would hardly have caught my attention without a fragrance pyramid, as they are simply too mixed in with all the gentle notes. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is a significantly noticeable difference from the EDT, as I find that the EDP radiates much stronger here. This radiance is therefore good this time, so that one can smell this fragrance better, and it even leaves a small scent cloud behind. The fragrance has a longevity of more than twelve hours, which I always find quite good for this duration. The bottle: The bottle is actually rectangular, but the side edges are slightly curved outward. The cap is cylindrical, black, and features the Chanel logo with the two interlocking "C" letters on the top. The label is white and square. The bottle is high-quality, quite nice in itself, but for my personal taste, a bit too simple, though that is always a matter of taste. So, with the exception of a few rather minor differences and the stronger sillage, the EDT and EDP differ only slightly from each other, so it should basically not matter which version one chooses, although the EDP is more recommended due to the better sillage. The EDT seems to have been discontinued anyway, so one doesn't really have much choice in what version to get when purchasing anew. Like the EDT, this fragrance is also a lovely, powdery scent that comes across as beautifully feminine and, due to the aldehydes, also radiates a bit more maturity and classic appeal, making it recommendable for all ladies, although it might suit very young ones less... at least that's what I think. The cuddle factor of the fragrance remains as it has been, even though fragrances that smell quite powdery might cause some to have headaches over time, I think, as I have read this about some fragrances here from time to time... I think one just has to try it out. And if one likes powdery notes but would prefer the fragrance to be less mature and classic, that is, for example, without aldehydes and ylang-ylang (without which I would have liked this fragrance even better), then one could also opt for Misia, which is also a very nice, powdery fragrance that has a high cuddle factor like a cat :)

1932 surprises me with a radiant composition of various flowers. A hint of sweetness envelops me with a floating lightness, never intrusive, not syrupy or sticky. I also appreciate that the fragrance, unlike most others from the Les Exclusifs line, does not exude the typical Chanel DNA. Definitely a candidate for purchase for next spring! My decant brings brightness and good cheer to this dreary November.

Ah, the 1980s and an afternoon at the mall led me to the Lauder bar when this was launched. I believe it was my first big purchase. It was a departure for the brand as Lauder For Men was successful. This was a very good follow up. It wasn't around very long. I have to go off of my memory on the notes. It was summer and there was no problem with heavier compositions at the time. It was actually very cool and fresh upon opening. It moved into the darker woodland notes which were pretty common for the time. It was a Powerhouse epic that lasted all day. I always wondered if Superman wore this? The bold move by Estee Lauder to launch a men's line was never repeated. The skin care line was extensive. Aramis was the official men's line, right? For one brief moment I was a "Lauder Guy". Contradictory as it seemed I was quite proud.

Metropolis opens with an aromatic blast of lavender with supporting green peppermint before transitioning to its heart.
