Rule: Only one fight at a time. 6. Rule: No shirts, no shoes. 7. Rule: The fights last exactly as long as they need to. 8. And the last rule: Anyone new to Fight Club must fight.

Wow, what a statement... ... I thought when I got to know the new rebel at the Pipipi perfumery from the house of Varvatos today. If I hadn't read the name beforehand, I would have thought I was smelling a genuine Amouage, so complex, smoky, and oriental does Dark Rebel radiate with power and elegance! And the price of a mere 44 EUR/75ml was hard to believe!

Anyone who associates this scent with a smoky biker bar has probably never been to such a pub. This leather jacket is likely worn by a nice polo-shirt-wearing business student who would rather sip still water and munch on a boiled egg sandwich from Tupperware on the train than loudly order a rum neat at the bar! This guy is not a rebel.

... we go Fallera, the forests bloom, the heights Fallera We have set out to catch the sunshine - come along and try it yourself once! This hiking song came to my mind when I sensed Rhythm Floral. I think of lively school hiking days when we took advantage of the first rays of sunshine, hummed this little song, and happily trudged through the greening nature. Bernd with his hiking guitar in front. At the roadside, the lilac was already blooming - from dark violet to light purple, and exuding its enchanting scent. The jasmine was in bud and delicately spreading its aroma. We rested in the forest, under old trees that gently exhaled a woody-spicy scent. Bernd strummed on his guitar and hummed a blues that the little birds joined in. So peaceful and natural is also the fragrance. It has quite elegant notes, but in a very relaxing, casual way. You can confidently wear comfortable outdoor clothing with it. Stylish British understatement indeed. A likable floral-natural scent that lures me outside, even now in winter.

For a few days now, I have been testing Brit Rhythm Floral and I am absolutely enchanted by the scent. It was love at first sight :-) According to Burberry, it is supposed to be rock-inspired, but I don't find that at all. The bottle is beautifully designed as always. When the sun shines on it, it sparkles beautifully ;-) The scent is not a typical Burberry fragrance. At first, the fragrance starts off very citrusy. But not as sporty as D&G Light Blue. Rather more feminine and elegant. The lilac is present from the beginning, but very subtle and elegant. After that, the citrus note recedes and what remains is a floral note. I can't pick up the woody notes on myself at all. With this scent, I associate femininity, lightness, cheerfulness, spring(-feelings) :-) The fragrance doesn't change much on me afterwards. It remains subtle in the background, yet still present. Even if you were to bathe in the scent, it would never be too much. The longevity could be a bit better, as I don't perceive it on myself after a while. But even after a few hours, a subtle hint of it remains. When I apply it in the morning (my perfume shelf is next to my bed), I can still smell it on my bed linens in the evening. If this perfume were a color, I would say it would be lilac. But not because of the lilac note, rather because of that beautiful fresh, light purple color. After watching many advertisements for fragrances and their descriptions, my advertisement for this would look like this: A young woman in her early 20s comes home from her office job to her lilac-colored bedroom with white furniture and hops around on her bed. :-) So not a girl anymore, but a self-confident young woman who still has the carefree joy of life that one had as a teenager. Or a beautiful green meadow with white and lilac flowers, sunshine, a bright blue sky, a gentle breeze,... So definitely not rock-inspired as Burberry itself advertises. According to Parfumo, many who like Burberry would also enjoy Zen, Bottega Veneta, Chloe, Love Chloe, and Flora Botanica. However, I find that all those fragrances (except for Chloe) are much stronger and do not resemble Brit Rhythm Floral at all. Chloe would be the only scent that leans towards a fresh, light direction, but I wouldn't compare it either. D&G Light Blue and Biotherm L'Eau by Lait Corporel come to mind immediately because of the citrus note, but the Burberry smells a whole lot more elegant than the two.

With the normal rhythm, I struggle - for some reason, I smell a load of patchouli and have the impression that the scent is lost in the decade. However, the bottle has always captivated me - simple, discreet, with the cut glass yet elegant, vintage, and minimalist at the same time. Just beautiful. I am all the more pleased that today Brit Floral not only caught my eye but also captivated my senses from the very first moment: Oh la la, this is sexy! And not at all stuffy or outdated. If one were to compare the scent with the fashion line, Floral would definitely be Prorsum: the younger, cooler, bolder, and at the same time more laid-back line from Christopher Bailey. The one that likes to say "Hello, here I am!" and does not shroud itself in understatement. Yet it doesn’t go overboard like, let’s say, Vivienne Westwood. Because the roots to tradition remain constantly palpable. Why this digression into fashion? Because exactly these components can be transferred to Floral. Yes, it is floral and deserves its name. At the same time, it has something classic, mature about it, in my opinion. But there is this roughness, this self-confidence that transports the classic into 2015, and at a speed that leaves one in awe. Rocking? One could gladly call it that. Let’s take it a step further and say “edgy” in modern terms. The freshness - not so citrusy, just light … rather orangey? - gives it the carefree, relaxed ease, while the wonderfully powdery-woody base keeps it close to the skin. This perfume is simply: leather jacket. With a delicate blouse underneath. All of this with a gin and tonic in hand in a dark corner, the bass makes the floor thump and first eye contacts are made. But nothing more happens that evening. Because even though Rhythm is extremely sexy - it doesn’t go all out, it remains elegant, to say the least, noble. For me, Rhythm Floral is a real surprise. It stands out pleasantly without trying hard to push itself to the forefront. I have always liked scents with a spicy, woody, powdery-creamy base that overall are not too heavy. All the more beautiful that a floral variant will soon be moving in with me. I haven’t been able to test the scent for longevity yet, but I’ll gladly provide an update in due time!

Burberry Brit Rhythm floral starts off similarly to Fresh Splash for her (Mexx). Both have a lilac-floral heart note and fruit in the top note. The Fresh Splash develops into an aquatic, watermelon direction, while the Burberry becomes creamy and a bit more complex up close. But Brit Rhythm also remains bright and lilac feather-light. It never really becomes pronounced, never dark or heavy. For a rock-inspired scent, it is too sweet for me; jasmine adds a touch of elegance - I miss the said rhythm. Nevertheless, it is a harmonious, truly noble scent pleaser. Compared to the original version, I actually like the floral variant much better. Fresh-creamy, airy, and less powdery. There is no trace of wood at all.. Addendum: I would have loved to wear Brit Rhythm Floral in the summer as well. That will probably remain a sweet dream of mine, as hot days do not suit the scent - it needs coolness to shine! In summer, it becomes too sweet, which it is not on cooler days. That’s exactly what I love about scents, how they perform when the environment changes, what brings them out the most.

When purchasing this perfume, it is already confusing that it only differs from "Brit Rhythm" by the addition of "floral," which is nowhere to be found on the bottle. Even more confusing for me was that the "floral" doesn't smell as floral as "Brit Rhythm." The saleswoman sprayed it on me saying, "this one smells like raspberry" - and it does. It clearly smells like raspberry - which only surprised me when I didn't find that in the listed fragrance notes. The scent itself is very nice, a light, pleasant raspberry scent with a hint of flowers. Unfortunately, it doesn't last long.

The Monsieur is one of a crew of wonderful masculine citrus chypres from the mid-20th century--Rochas Moustache, Chanel pour Monsieur, YSL pour Homme.) This genre smells like the middle ground between the feminine green chypre of the 1960s-1970s (Private Collection, Scherrer de Scherrer, Weil de Weil) and Eau de Cologne. Bear in mind I know the more current formulations of these citrus chypres, which according to many are ghosts of their earlier iterations. Myself, I turn to the above green chypres if I’m looking for ballsiness and volume. I like the current men’s citrus chypres for their subtlety and personal scale. I like this genre for wearing like Eau de Cologne with endurance. For this use, the Monsieur is perfect. (I have the les Mythiques formulation.) The big dog on this block is Chanel pour Monsieur. At any time since its release it’s been considered the best men’s chypre on the market. Many call it the best men’s chypre of all time. I only know a recent formulation, and while pretty, it’s so short lived, and fades to such a spectral version of itself that I have to consider it effectively discontinued. OK, obeisance and eulogy to Chanel done, on to Monsieur de Givenchy. The Monsieur is a long-lasting but light perfume that balances the simple composition, restraint and allure that leads to that rare outcome in masculine perfumery: quiet but unashamed beauty. I’ve found many who see MdG as the most damaged by reformulations of this genre. Perhaps for their purposes it is, but I find it enjoyable in the way that it accomplishes all the goals of the citrus chypre genre. It’s dry/bitter and austere. It reflects your skin. It combines an herbal citrus blend (pepper/lemon/bergamot) with a waxy musky quality that is distinctive yet easy-going. The floral notes give some depth. It starts rosy and eases into a low-key white floral tone that eventually settle into a carnation note that remains through drydown. Carnation? Or was that the pepper from the start? This little twist shows that for as unfussy as this genre is, the Monsieur wears an I’ve-got-a-secret smile from start to finish. To some, this is a faded gentleman. To me, a charmer. from scent hurdle.com

This is a review of the original formulation juice... Monsieur de Givenchy opens with a beautifully well-blended mixture of lemon verbena and mossy greens. This verbena and oak moss combo pretty much hangs around from start to finish on my skin, only being joined by a non-powdery subtle lavender in the heart notes, and slightly sweet sandalwood and light musk in the base. The entire set of notes is harmonious to the point that it is very difficult identifying individual ones. There could be a whole gob of other ingredients in here, but I stopped trying to find them and started to enjoy the end result... and what an end result it is! Longevity is average and projection is below average. Maybe I am getting a bit dated myself, but I find vintage Monsieur de Givenchy just as relevant now as it was when it was released. It is masterfully blended, extremely wearable and amazing smelling. It balances subtlety, sophistication and versatility brilliantly. Adding to the long growing list of positives, the vintage juice is quite affordable in relative terms, making this one a "must buy" for anyone into classic scents, which it most certainly is. Monsieur de Givenchy is timeless and easily earns a well-deserved 4.5+ out of 5 stars.

This is the original version of Monsieur, and - sweet though it is - it does smell old. In fact, it's so old, it reminds me of Eau de Coty (1909). Let me explain. Monsieur smelled of citrus - front and centre. But, with aromatics and powder, it had more oomph than a citrus cologne, and as it developed it got more like a powdery fougère. The brightness my mini still has makes it feel like a fat citrus cologne, the sort of thing I call Cologne de Toilette; a sub-genre that I believe was invented by that Napoleon of Perfume - François Coty - with his eponymous Eau.

My old man wore this in the 80s and 90s when I was growing up. My vintage bottle is one of my favorite collector’s items. After being discontinued for years, it was reissued in 2007 as part of Givenchy’s Les Parfums Mythiques. Today, it is back in the house’s regular lineup and is almost as good as the vintage but inevitably lacks some of the depth and complexity. Crafted in 1959 by Francis Fabron (Baghari, Quadrille, L’Air du Temps), it is, in more ways than one, halfway between Chanel Pour Monsieur (Henri Robert, 1955) and Dior Eau Sauvage (Edmond Roudnitska, 1966). Certainly the least famous of the three, it is arguably the best one — and hands down my favorite. The carnation and the verbena are the stars of the opening. The effect is invigorating and aromatic and tart in equal measures. The overall profile is refreshing but dry, without the floral flourishes of the Dior and the spiciness of the Chanel. But the real clincher is in the drydown, with the best oakmoss and the smoothest sandalwood accords you will ever come across. Just heavenly. Monsieur is discreet yet impactful, straddling the line between the citrus chypre and the traditional cologne. I’ve always found it to be the epitome of elegance, intelligence, and effortless virility. One of my all-time favorites. Not a bad introduction to perfumery, pops.

Lemon verbena. Similar to Chanel Pour Monsieur, this scent component whispers long in the top note here as well. Actually, Monsieur de Givenchy is a simple fragrance. A simple classic. Monsieur predominantly presents itself as fresh and pure, clear and bright, a perfume that lives from its top note, which remains long and distinctly present, and then transitions into a subtle heart or base note. One might describe it as a chypre note without a heart note (rose, jasmine) with hesperidic notes on moss; one might also recognize one or two other accents once the fragrance has developed on the skin for an hour or two; however, that is not the purpose of such a men's cologne. Fragrances of this kind should primarily feel fresh, refresh, and carry the gentleman lightly through or rather into the day. For this, it was necessary that the feeling of fragrant brightness and clarity remained as long as possible, which is not easy to achieve, especially with these light, hesperidic notes that can create such an impression. The lemon verbena with moss seems to be quite a good fixative, as it combines a lemony component with green, strong herbal notes that increase longevity and, together with the very subtle base of wood, spice, and moss, ensure that this cologne does not evaporate as quickly as one might fear after the first spray. Where the sandalwood should have gone has always been a mystery to me with this fragrance (however, I own a very old miniature in addition to my new bottle). In the meantime, I can isolate the component well. One should test a pure sandalwood fragrance for comparison (e.g., from Santa Maria Novella or Trumper). The other notes that may be present in the opening can also be subtly sensed. The lemon, the lemon verbena, and perhaps the lavender, which contributes to the lightness and ethereality of this fragrance, remain strongly in the foreground. I conclude that this fragrance belongs to the rare specimens where the ethereal, angelic quality has been excellently implemented as a central theme of a fragrance. With Eichendorff: And my soul spread Wide its wings, Flew through the quiet lands, As if it were flying home.

So it can go! I chatted for a long time with a nice saleswoman in the Galleries Lafayette and eventually bought Monsieur de Givenchy. However, the lighter chypre Yves Saint Laurent Pour Homme would have fit much better into my collection. And I am far from being enthusiastic about the Givenchy brand.

From the major perfume houses or designer labels, there are strikingly many men’s fragrances that bear the name “Monsieur” - especially during the period when perfumes for men were not yet so commonplace.

My impressions regarding the fragrance styles that the gentlemen of creation were to be (re)introduced to in the post-war years are slowly solidifying. Always graciously allowing the lady to take olfactory precedence, that was the decisive commandment until the 70s. At most, a pleasant and well-groomed aura was expected from the worldly man.
The opening of this fragrance is clearly citrusy, strutting around for about a minute with a slightly biting sharpness on the edge of being unpleasant.

What distinguishes Monsieur by Givenchy from similarly themed classics like Chanel's Monsieur and Dior's Eau Sauvage (which it resembles more) is its significantly warmer character. Rarely has it been so well achieved to combine spicy citrus notes with velvety fullness and aromatic woodiness.

Both the original and this later, less concentrated version of The Beat had little lasting power on my skin. Disappointed was I that they hadn't made a more intense version of The Beat. This fragrance was so light that I could barely smell it at first. A subtle citrusy opening was all that I could detect when I pressed my nose to my wrist. Eventually The Beat EDT strengthens a little allowing me to enjoy the introduction of the tea and iris notes. This fragrance is very refined and classy. However, it is a far cry from the original which possessed a boozy like quality that I really enjoyed. The original had spunk, but this lighter version is enough to make me yawn. Summing up The Beat EDT; a basic yet pleasant floral with hints of citrus and tea. Need I say more?

Today, while rushing through the Karstadt perfume department, I caught sight of the gift table with the discounted fragrances out of the corner of my eye. But I hurried up to the first floor for my hair appointment. During the relaxing head massage, my memory scanned the fleeting sight again and distinctly recalled "Burberry The Beat". I didn't know the scent, but Burberrys have always resonated with me. With my hair still half-wet, I flew back to the ground floor - and looked in disbelief at the empty gift table. A diligent saleswoman had just packed all the bottles into large boxes! But I am no stranger there, and together we heaved the boxes back up, and my trained eye spotted the desired little carton in the jumble. I thought only: I hope this effort was worth it! And I must say: Yes! Even the bitter-fruity opening of mandarin and cardamom is a delightful treat. And then comes the crowning glory in the form of bitter-noble Ceylon tea, refined with dark iris. I think of my time in London, where Big Ben at five o'clock called to tea time with its resounding Westminster chime. Very stylish and very British. The noble cedar reminds me of the wood paneling in the pubs. The special "London Beat" catches up with me again. The fragrance reflects tradition and understatement - and yet is in tune with the times, like swinging London. I believe the effort before the purchase was worth it.

Anyone who absolutely wants to wear a perfume in this heat, will inevitably end up with 4711, an eau fraiche, or with the well-known light blue... Or with this one! I would never have picked it up without friendly advice, as I don't like the other scents from Burberry (I would never wear the perfume of the same name, because of coconut and sweetness). When I tested it, I quickly fell in love and wanted to have it after two days of testing it at all times of the day. I was thrilled by the freshness, the pleasantly non-squeaky citrus note (0% refreshment wipe association), the fruitiness without becoming sweet and candy-like, and the later softness of the light wood note without the usual patchouli-musk-spice accompaniment that often comes with wood. For many, it may be too subtle and close to the body, but that's exactly what I love!

Well, the smell isn't bad in itself but it's SO balsamy and SO sugary... It very quickly became cloying and it really bothered me. The opening was promising with a very nice duo tuberose/tobacco but it all ended with ultra sweet orange blossom and very heady tuberose. The cistus is far too prominent for my taste. Very reminiscent of Quatre Absolu by Boucheron but also far more cloying in my opinion. I didn't like it.

Sweet resinous, balsamic white flower bouquet that I feel like I`ve smelt somewhere else before. I much prefer the red version, where the marriage between the ginger and jasmine-tuberose was creating a pleasing atmosphere. The cardamom in here just feels a tad weird, kind of gourmand, kind of not. I sense a peppery vanilla, even though it`s not listed in the notes. It reminds me of a waffer dessert that I had as a child, not a dessert I was crazy about, but back in those days of poverty it was the greatest thing you could get instead of that much sought-after chocolate.

I received a sample as a gift with a purchase. It's a changeable perfume on my skin (sometimes it lingers, sometimes it doesn't, sometimes it's discreet, sometimes it overwhelms me). There were times when its smell didn't put me in a good mood and for me, the most important thing in a perfume is that it gives me a good, pleasant, wonderful mood if possible... I see it being worn more by a man than a woman. It's masculine unisex, I would say. I think it's better worn in winter and autumn. It seems a bit expensive to me considering the smell it has. I won't buy it for myself unless my tastes and opinions change. Rating: 7/10

So far, Kevin-Joshua had a very clear type... She should be elegant, petite, with carefully styled hair, typically blonde, subtle make-up, lipstick: at best rosewood. She smells and looks a bit like freshly washed. She is sexy but only at the right time, click-clack, wink, wink... Just like L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum And now he was wondering how the hell he ended up on this date? L'Interdit Absolu Black leather jacket, rugged boots, blood-red lips, stormy hairstyle. A double espresso in one hand and a cigarette in the other. She is already very sexy but she interrupts him, sitting with her legs wide apart and laughing loudly. And what smells so dark and bitter here? Is she wearing a men's fragrance? She is great, thinks Kevin-Joshua...but he is also a bit scared. L'Interdit Absolu has the basic DNA of L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum but anyone expecting just intense, sexy, feminine jasmine with a little twist will probably be disappointed. For me, this is an absolutely unisex scent in the best sense with a lot of bitterness and dark spice from tobacco and a whole lot of patchouli. It lasts forever on clothing and is also beautiful the next day. I like it more with every wear. However, it is probably not everybody's darling.

The new L'Interdit Absolu, I had to have it immediately, as I am already a fan of the L'Interdit line. I can smell the neroli very well at the beginning. After that, the fragrance takes on a pleasant spiciness, which comes from the cardamom. As it develops further, the tobacco reveals itself, giving the scent that wicked, sexy side. It has a bit of a shisha vibe for me, as the fragrance becomes beautifully sweet and slightly smoky. For me personally, it's even nicer than L'Interdit Rouge, although that has always been my favorite in the line. "L'Interdit Absolu" is now my absolute favorite and will be repurchased again and again.

Once again something for the ladies: L'Interdit Absolu from Givenchy. A brand that I absolutely love and I can't really name any bad releases. The ladies' line L'Interdit I find really really beautiful and it already counts among my favorites from the women's designers.

Actually, I was on my way to the perfume store to buy a niche fragrance. However, the selection was relatively small, and despite the support of two sales associates, I couldn't find the right one for me. When it became clear that I would leave the store without a new scent, a saleswoman came around the corner with L'interdit Absolut by Givenchy.

I usually have some issues with unisex fragrances. Basically, I like sweet - sweeter - the sweetest. Vanilla is essential for me. But this Givenchy line does something to me. I've counted L'Interdit Eau de Parfum Rouge among my favorites for a long time. Now this version has also captivated me. This fragrance, paired with the right outfit, really boosts me.

The autumn sun gently brushes my face and brings with it a woolly warmth, while my feet wander through the golden, rustling leaves. A cool breeze carries the scent of warm wood and smoke through my nose - a hint of fireplace and mild autumn air. I feel cozy in my wool coat and a thick scarf - simply cozy.

The Givenchy L‘Interdit Absolu is simply an incredibly beautiful fragrance, especially when it's cold outside. The warm, slightly dark notes really come into their own and give you that cozy, elegant feeling. At the same time, it remains fresh and floral enough not to feel too heavy.

Scentrack Sheryl Crow – My Favorite Mistake John Varvatos for Men is at first sniff a generic fragrance, but beneath the simple surface are numerous dark and bright layers. All these layers are perfectly polished and harmonized to create an olfactory balance. Brighter fruity notes of plum and fig are juxtaposed to darker and plushy suede accord fortified with some woodsy notes. This main juxtapose is accompanied by the short lime note in the opening, and spicy notes of pepper and cinnamon in the heart. There is also some, to my nose, unidentified darker herbal entity. The summarized composition is masculine in a classical manner, yet so modern, clean and wearable. In my European eyes, a quintessentially American. Rating: 7/10 More on Scentimentalwords

Minty fresh aromatic and sweet gourmand accords on a woody oriental. Hold on a second! If that sounds like Shalimar with toffee and toothpaste, think again. At first whiff, this may resemble a locker room freshie but there's more going on than that. First the 'minty' accord; it isn't really mint at all but Ajowan (red thyme, caraway, cumin, fennel) and there's a sweet note of dates in the back. These are nuanced with herbaceous, powdery, woody and bitter-leathery accents, which turn a shower gel into something more interesting. It's quite a feat to make mint smell good enough to wear, and I would think about buying this if I didn't already have l'Essence de Cerruti (2009) - which smells a bit like it from a distance.

The eponymous fragrance John Varvatos gained popularity for its rich, masculine scent and sleek packaging. All John Varvatos bottles are unique works of art with emblematic bottle of sturdy glass construction and, in the case of this particular variant, a unique, leather design. It definitely stands out on a vanity or dressing table. John Varvatos was created by the perfumer Rodrigo Flores-Roux. Before becoming a perfumer, Flores-Roux studied biology and chemistry, which has given him a strong foundation in understanding how different ingredients and notes can be blended to create a harmonious fragrance. He has worked with many major fragrance houses and has created fragrances for a wide range of brands, including Calvin Klein, Jo Malone, and Dolce & Gabbana, to name a few. The top notes of John Varvatos are a blend of mediterranean herbs, which give the fragrance a fresh, aromatic start. The middle notes consist of oakmoss and jasmine, which add depth and complexity to the scent. The base notes are comprised of leather, amber, and sandalwood, which provide a woody, earthy finish that lingers on the skin. In addition to these main notes, the fragrance also contains a blend of other ingredients, such as bergamot, lemon, and black pepper, which contribute to the overall scent profile. Overall, the combination of these ingredients creates a rich, masculine fragrance that is both sophisticated and long-lasting. The mediterranean herbs and jasmine give the scent a fresh, floral edge, while the leather, amber, and sandalwood add depth and warmth. It is a complex fragrance that is sure to appeal to those who appreciate more sophisticated scents. One of the positives of John Varvatos is its versatility. It is a scent that can be worn by men of all ages, and is suitable for a variety of occasions. It is also a very sophisticated fragrance, making it perfect for those who want to make a statement or those who want to march to a different beat. Also, it is quite affordable. On the negative side, some may find the scent a bit too strong or overpowering. It is definitely not a subtle fragrance, and those who prefer more subtle scents may want to look elsewhere. Most people will find the woody, earthy scent of John Varvatos particularly well-suited for the cooler months of the fall and winter. The rich, warm notes of leather, amber, and sandalwood make it a perfect choice for those looking for a cozy, comforting scent to wear during these colder months. However, the fresh, aromatic top notes of mediterranean herbs and the floral middle notes of jasmine may make it a suitable choice for the spring and summer months as well. John Varvatos is the cousin-in-rehab to Yves Saint Laurent's La Nuit de L'homme. This fragrance also has a woody, earthy scent, with notes of cardamom, bergamot, and cedar. However, It is a bit more expensive than John Varvatos, but I personally find the price difference worthwhile as the YSL scent is much more sophisticated and indicative of higher quality ingredients. Overall, John Varvatos is a fantastic fragrance for men who are looking for a strong, masculine scent that is suitable for a variety of cold-weather occasions.
