This could be a product from Paco Rabanne. The most fitting situation I could picture would be a beach night club in the summertime. A mess of too many notes, which actually makes it too complex for me somehow. To describe it is hard, the closest I can say is a sweet, peachy, berry, fruit cocktail with watermelon, a little tobacco and floral notes. It smells very chemical and slightly oily with a touch of salty melon. I dunno.. a fruity floral with sweet freshness? - I'm talking saccharine and lots of calone. BTW, it actually somehow reminds me of Creeds Millesime Imperial without the ambergris, so if you're a fan of that, this is a much cheaper alternative.

Around 1993 and '94, the shop windows of perfumeries were decorated with advertisements for Insensé (1993). However, this had the opposite effect on me: I didn't want to get to know the scent at all. The slightly dusty aftertaste that the brand had on me back then - combined with the obnoxiously cheerful (insensé = foolish, nonsensical, sinful) gentleman in a suit (today I would call that passive-aggressive) - just didn't work for me. Bootlegs of the television commercials from that time still circulate on YouTube - equally passive-aggressive... I finally got to know Insensé many years later - and was proven wrong. Don’t judge a scent by its advert. The fragrance turned out to be a floral-balsamic composition from a time when the industry was already heavily leaning towards aquatic freshness. Insensé effortlessly combined the traditionally feminine lily of the valley note with soapiness and fir balsam - so refined that Insensé (if it were still available) would probably be passed around on a golden platter among various niche and neo-retro tastes today, receiving high praise. However: in 1993, I would not have appreciated or 'understood' this scent. Was this kind of innovation perhaps simply too much for a traditional brand like Givenchy? The following year, in 1994, Insensé Ultramarine was released - also by Christian Mathieu (1946-2020), the perfumer who had laid a deeply successful blueprint with Kenzo pour Homme (1991). 1. Insensé Ultramarine is an early representative of those flankers that stray far from the original. Over the years, Insensé Ultramarine received a total of nine (!) flankers. Matvey Yudov's article "Original vs. Flankers: Givenchy Insensé" provides a helpful overview of this. 2. Insensé Ultramarine was so strange and idiosyncratic that I wonder to what extent Givenchy's hope for an "Aquatic Hit" was fulfilled. I suspect: quite a bit, if only because the fragrance was still available for quite a while even after Givenchy was integrated into the LVMH conglomerate. Today, prices oscillate - as is often the case with recently discontinued scents - between low-budget and speculative three-digit sums. You never know... Here, a reference to external sources is worthwhile: Christos’ blog Memory of Scent - a goldmine of critical-subjective scent analyses - goes into detail about the impressively unnatural turquoise-blue color of the fragrance. His description captures the essence quite well: “It seems as if the people responsible for this (because Insensé Ultramarine was not officially signed by a perfumer, unlike the original Insensé) took a trip to the household cleaning aisle and added equal amounts of any detergent available to the original composition.” (https://memoryofscent.wordpress.com/2012/10/05/givenchy-insense-falling-through-genres/) The mixture of piercing, chlorine-like aldehydic aquatic notes, melon-like Calone streaks, and a distinctly perceivable cassis note (blackcurrant) is central to Ultramarine. This fruitiness - combined with ozonic, aromatic-herb notes and a synthetic lightness - was relatively new in this form. For instance, Jean-François Laporte relied on a similarly prominent cassis note with Route du Vétiver (1988). Matvey Yudov goes even further into detail in his analysis. He writes: “To the block of citruses, formed by several natural essential oils, they added the then already classic accord of dehydromycenol/allyl amyl glycolate - ambroxan (say hi to the aforementioned Cool Water). The fruitiness is enhanced by damascene, the floral block is mainly built on the base of hedione, hydroxycitronellal and lilial, adorned by rose odorants and plenty of other details. The aquatic accord consists of a generous dose of calone with an addition of empetal, helional and other similar substances. In the base we find a woody-musk accord on the basis of sandalwood and cedar materials.”  (https://www.fragrantica.com/news/Original-vs-Flankers-Givenchy-Insense-11455.html) I do not see similarities in the effect of dehydromycenol with the lavender-sage combination as in Cool Water; nor can I see the scent profile of Insensé Ultramarine directly connected to other early so-called aquatic perfumes. With one exception: as with the first versions of Christian Mathieu's Kenzo pour Homme, the corresponding versions of Insensé Ultramarine still clearly reveal the building blocks of the base - yes, they also show slight overlaps and provide an earthy counterbalance to the then still novel synthetic fragrance compounds. The newer version - easily identifiable by its packaging, typography, and color scheme - is overall brighter, more chlorinated, and less deep, less dense in the dry down. Surprisingly, this exactly suits the fragrance: it makes it seem even a bit more artificial and quirky than before. Good unnatural stuff.

After having the Givenchy Insense Ultramarine on my radar and wish list for a long time, I treated myself to it this year. Actually, the old releases are not really my thing. However, the fresh scents from the 90s definitely have their charm and come across as very likable. Just like CK Escape, which was released a year earlier. This Givenchy is almost 25 years old as well. Even though I don't necessarily like this old-school factor, there are some exceptions. They shouldn't be too outdated, as I am absolutely not a vintage fan. Givenchy is a brand that I appreciate. Some releases I find less exciting, but in terms of quality, they are almost all in good condition. The bottle is also very 90s, but I like it. Very simple with a nice cap and azure-blue content. The color of the fragrance is quite fitting, as it is a fresh aquatic scent. The fragrance doesn't start off to my liking. Aggressive and something piercingly annoying is present in the top note, which fortunately settles down after a few minutes. Overall, it is a scent that changes little and is hard to categorize into top-heart-base. Moreover, one shouldn't stick too closely to the pyramid. Some notes are easily perceivable, while others are not at all. Melon and blackcurrant are present, along with a very pleasant aquatic background that comes across as very maritime. Sage is also present and offers a nice freshness. Additionally, there are subtly spicy and fresh citrus notes that are not too strong. Overall, it is very balanced and has a bit of many facets. For me, it is also quite masculine. When smelled too closely, it is not as pleasant. It scores better at a certain distance and lingers nicely in the air. It has that typical 90s fresh charm. Absolutely suitable for everyday wear, for sports, and in leisure time. Moreover, despite its freshness, it is a year-round scent that also works well when it's not too warm. The performance is quite good for a fresh scent. Not spectacular, but satisfactory, especially in leisure time. The sillage is medium, not great but still noticeable beyond skin contact. You can definitely spray a bit more. Overall, a great balanced fragrance that pleasantly accompanies you in the simple situations of life.

It's terrible what Givenchy is putting us through here. Insensé Ultramarin was launched in the mid-90s as a particularly floral-fresh variant of Insensé. Ultramarin stood in the best tradition of power fragrances that were occasionally released after the success of Joop Homme at that time. It was a perfume with overwhelming floral notes sitting on a bright, soapy base. Ultramarin was the exaggerated and extreme embodiment of a bright, summery gentleman's scent. As such, it caused raised eyebrows, even for me, and that's why I never bought it. But it was great! Today I sprayed Ultramarin at Rossmann; it is still available or has returned. I should have been warned. I was already appalled by what has become of the famous Givenchy Gentleman, but Ultramarin takes the cake. Givenchy takes the liberty of offering a completely different perfume under this name, with unchanged packaging and the same bottle. I find that unfair and really annoying. I can understand that Ultramarin, which was already a controversial scent in its time, does not conform to today's trends. I begrudgingly accept when a perfume is buried for this reason or due to the unacceptability of certain ingredients. But this is simply fraud! Just recently, I referenced Insensé Ultramarin - I meant the original - as a benchmark fragrance in a comment about Yachting - sorry! Today's Ultramarin starts with a scratchy, indefinable scent chaos. After about half an hour, a soft, musky note becomes noticeable. Floral notes are hardly present anymore. A certain bitter and synthetic note remains present throughout the entire, not overly long fragrance development. Once a style-defining scent, Insensé Ultramarin today can hardly be categorized into a specific fragrance direction. It's simply nothing! Just a year or two ago, I found the original Ultramarin somewhere and tested it. The fake must have been created recently. At Givenchy, it seems that consideration for the customers is not deemed necessary. I sincerely hope that such behavior does not pay off in the long run.

Do you also remember your very first "expensive" or let's call it "real" perfume from a perfume store? For me, it happened when I was 16. The scent had just been born. My mother gifted me Givenchy's Insensé Ultramarine for my birthday, and from then on, I was a proud perfume owner, and a Givenchy was, so to speak, my olfactory companion during my first disco visits.

Now that I am finally the proud owner of the original, I had to take the opportunity to try the sporty-aquatic variant that was released under the name Ultramarine. I don't know if I had the vintage version or the reformulated one under my nose - I strongly suspect the latter and can't make any comparisons with the version from the 90s anyway.

...after a few hours, only a little marine scent remains. The opening still allows a captain to shine; for an admiral, it is far too youthful and light - it lacks experience and sea freshness. The slightly marine (aquatic) notes dissipate more and more. In the end, it is only enough for a junior sailor.

Has often accompanied me on vacation. It is fresh, aquatic, and fits well with me all day in warm weather. It occasionally wafts up to my nose and simply spreads a feeling of well-being. I think this scent has completely gone unnoticed and it doesn't deserve that. Anyone looking for a new "summer companion" should go give it a sniff.

Do not be distracted by a monk’s habit, a doctor’s white coat, a king's scepter, or a judge’s black robe. By putting on a habit, one is not instantly infused with wisdom and understanding. Why do I bring this up? Cause Artisan Black is allegedly a dark, woody interpretation of Artisan, which introduces a surprising symphony of contrasts with an initial brush of citrus evolving into a deep masculine structure of warm spices and abstracted musk with sensual woody and leathery accents. Actually, black is the color of the handcrafted rattan habit that covers the flask, ain't no the color of the scent's soul. Artisan Black is far from being the perfect misty fragrance. My first approach with John Varvatos's colognes was Artisan, which captured my senses with the fabulous bland of beachy citrus fruits, juices, peels, leaves, and blossoms and the distinctively handcrafted flask. It's without a doubt a floral scent but with fairly citrus and greenness to feel masculine and wearable. Later, I collected almost all the other JV colognes and Artisan's flankers, yet Artisan Black was a scent I craved to try for a long time but was not available at shops or online, perhaps being a limited edition. Suddenly, a few weeks ago, I was advised about an eBay seller who submitted it, I did my bid and ultimately I won. The final price tag was very advantageous for such a spur-of-the-moment blind buy, merely less than 20 bucks, no matter if it was unboxed and tested a couple of times. So, I'd be gleeful... Oh man, what a scent. On the back of my hand's skin, Artisan Black is a woody, fresh cologne suitable for warmer weather, perfect for spring and summertime. You'd probably be shocked by looking at the olfactory pyramid but the scent itself is actually not so complex at all and moderately linear. It opens up with the aroma of bright bittersweet mandarin, lemon, and plenty of blood orange, which is ruling and gives the sparkling vigorous taste of the Mediterranean isles. Blood orange is also known as Arancia Sanguinello or Rossa di Sicilia, is mainly grown in Sicily, south of Italy, and its juice is akin to fresh blood. This wonderful bitter and refreshing opening characterizes the composition even when neroli makes its entrance, and is tinged with a “water” note, but for once, I’m not at all upset by the melon-like calypsone. For a moment, I thought I was smelling Old Spice Classic, they share the same orangey spicy accord. I got some aromatic green notes, the mix of basil, mint, and thyme is fresh yet not outstanding. It is obvious that this is not going to be another citrus cologne. The heart keeps the orangey tones, spicy green ginger, and lemony coriander seeds melt gracefully with night-blooming floral jasmine, neroli, and African orange blossom, and sometimes it is closely akin to Custo Barcelona. Neroli is not the most masculine nor the most discreet note for a man’s fragrance and it takes a lot of discipline to keep it bright and calm, not allowing it to drown into sweet and dusky waters. As it warms on skin neroli blooms cheerfully capturing the essence of spring. The mixture remains light and dry and in that sense stays closer to the essence of the flower than other neroli scents that focus on the opulence of the extract and end up smelling like heavy musks instead of delicate flowers, yet the bitter orange blossoms in Artisan Black are just blooming. Then, in the blink of an eye, this spicy and citrus opening turns a bit darker and dusty thanks to the support of the woody and manly base notes such as synthetic orris root reminiscent of woody iris, modern patchouli that does not intrude on the show, white amber, sensual white musk, synthetic Givodan Kephalis, rooty vetiver and various woods finish the scent with an earthy, heady tone, Artisan Black is much stronger than original Artisan, and if you already own Artisan you could very well add Artisan Black to your collection without feeling you’ve got scent twins on the shelf. Artisan is light and bright, juicy and breezy; Artisan Black has more depth, feels a bit more “masculine” and has better sillage and lasting power, even if it is not a beast. Artisan Black is borderline sweet, but not too sweet for summer wear, and it doesn’t smell like dessert. The recurring criticism, however, is that the scent has poor projection and longevity. But, the weaker projection could actually be an unexpected bonus if you like colognes that are subtle, ones that are not meant to catch the attention of an entire room of people. In the end, this is the perfect cologne for me not similar to any other scents in my wardrobe and I am extremely content with my purchase. If you are looking for a subtle gentlemen’s cologne with spiced, citrus, and vaguely floral notes, then this is the cologne for you. -Elysium

It is a citrusy, woody fragrance that captured my attention for all of 2 hours. After the allotted time, there's hardly any drydown to remember it by. A shame, really. It could have been a perfect 10 if only it were longer lasting.

What is supposed to be black about Artisan Black is a mystery to me. It is a pure lemon scent, and as such, it is well made. It has hints of classic cologne, but is much more modern. I take the opulent fragrance pyramid with a raised eyebrow. It may all be true, but what has emerged is a very, very harmonious citrus scent. If one wishes, Artisan Black can certainly be dismissed as another representative of the current trend of citrus sports fragrances. One would not be wrong in doing so. However, for me, there is an important difference. Unlike most representatives of this genre, I feel comfortable with Artisan Black. I cannot say why. As a citrus fragrance, I see it almost on par with the characterful L'Eau d'Issey, although it does not have its green-herbaceous note. Contrary to what the extensive fragrance pyramid suggests, it is a straightforward scent without much development. There is also no time for that, as citrus notes are fleeting. After 2 hours, the entire fragrance collapses in on itself. In this case, that is not a drawback. Citrus notes that last longer are wonders of chemistry and smell like it. I find this lemon to be unexcited and casual. It is not a hectic bundle of energy, but rather suits someone who can take it easy in the summer heat, perhaps sitting in a street café and enjoying the beautiful day.

A good friend recently bought Artisan Black blind for the summer. The seemingly seductive fragrance description online was probably the deciding factor for him, along with the Greek roots of John Varvatos for patriotic reasons. The tasteful bottle with the black lacquer weave ultimately reinforced his decision to order it. He is not entirely satisfied, and after an extensive test, I now know why. Of the supposedly many different ingredients, there is only one single note that dominates - and that is lemon. However, it performs its job here so precisely and cleanly that one can speak without exaggeration of one of the best citrus fragrances ever. At times, it reminds me of Dior Homme Sport, just a bit more subtle and less sweet. The main theme is complemented by delicate, fresh-spicy nuances and a gentle, fluffy creaminess. So far, so good - but unfortunately, the scent is quite close to the skin and lasts only from now until just now. While this is not yet a refusal to perform, one can certainly expect more longevity in this price range. As far as I know, he has now taken the bottle to the office and sprays it as often as possible between clients and colleagues. And when the bottle is empty, at least he has a nice decorative piece.

Aside from Rock Vol. 1, which is almost impossible to find, I have now tested all John Varvatos fragrances, and I even own 3 of them. All are at least good, and I hold this brand with Greek roots in high regard. However, Artisan has lost popularity with me over time, as it offers a nice orange scent but is rather one-dimensional and weak. It was only when I used it recently after showering before bed that it really made an impression again. And by the next morning, it was completely gone, which has its advantages. So it was finally time for the Black version. There are significant parallels; the two Artisans are unmistakably summer brothers, having nothing in common with the syrupy Vintage and John Varvatos. Black and Artisan behave similarly to each other as Vintage does to the Original/John Varvatos. Black has a wonderful orange-clementine note, which is made serious and dark by spices like thyme or basil, extending to vetiver and a hint of leather in the base. With a few spices, the orange scent isn’t black yet, but it’s heading in that direction. This also makes the fragrance a bit more masculine and office-appropriate. I still prefer the regular Artisan for its orange juice flair a bit more. I also like it a little sweeter. Naming exotic fragrance materials like Kephalis or Serenolides is nice and good, but the scents are hardly more transparent. The Artisan bottles are handmade top class, but the sillage and especially the longevity (4 hours) are quite limited. Anyone who already has Artisan definitely doesn’t need Black. Still, it’s a solid all-rounder with a mega look!

I already had Artisan and now I had the opportunity to acquire Artisan Black, and what can I say......great, great, great. I really like these fresh scents, which might be due to my heritage, "it absolutely has to be light" and I can't deal with heavy fragrances.

I actually stumbled upon Artisan black because I liked Artisan so much. Artisan is an incredibly successful fresh citrus scent with a great drydown. Artisan black, on the other hand, comes across as a bit spicier and even fresher than its brother. The main reason for this freshness boost is probably the mint.

I would have expected a spicy "bang" after reading the fragrance pyramid, which was only partially confirmed after testing. The scent of "Artisan Black" is indeed very spicy, with hints of classic fougère, but by no means very loud. It is rather fine and subtle and serves as a loyal and pleasant companion for many occasions, especially in summer.

Olfactorily, it is especially interesting to smell in the early phase. However, the overwhelming abundance of the ingredients listed above seems a bit excessive to me; perhaps half of them are recognizable.

Who doesn't know the delicious ginger sticks that are so digestible after a heavy meal? I like them - whether with or without chocolate coating. Candied ginger - that's exactly what we encounter in Burberry Sport Ice for Men. This is by no means sharp, fresh ginger, and certainly not the indicated fantasy note of "frosted ginger." This fragrance comes across as refreshing and delicious like a ginger stick - of course, it is a sport scent, and I usually can't relate to this direction at all. However, the predecessor Burberry Sport for Men already proved with a masculine musk note a class that went far beyond the sport concept. A good reason to take a look at the newly released variant Sport Ice for Men. Burberry Sport Ice for Men is certainly not a big fragrance. After the ginger note, there isn't much left. You have it for about two hours, then it's gone. What remains are the typical characteristics of any sport fragrance, of which there are many. There's the thin but persistent citrus note, there are aquatic notes, and if you like, a cheap amber. With this residue, you then have two or three more hours to deal with - unless you reapply. Burberry Sport Ice for Men is really fun. Hardly any other fragrance smells as delicious, as unpretentious and straightforward as ginger. The citrus freshness and especially the accompanying aquatic notes ensure that the food association doesn't become too intrusive - that's how I like a gourmand fragrance! The only mediocre longevity is acceptable - Sport Ice for Men is indeed top-heavy, and the two hours it lasts are already exceptionally long for a top note. With this great note, one gladly agrees with the saying: After that, nothing more can come. Burberry Sport Ice for Men is a simple, unpretentious, but convincing summer fragrance, to be worn at temperatures above 20 degrees. In style, it resembles some of what we know from the Issey Miyake brand. This sport ice refreshes in an unusual way - well done!

Meal time! Ski flying: Jens Weissflog had to spend the night in a children's bed and was able to ski fly again for the first time since his retirement I received this one from my wife for my birthday last week. Unlike some of you, she actually thought of me! That was last Sunday in case you want to note it for next year! :-) Anyway: Our marathon nose Apicius has, as always, hit the nail pretty much on the head. However, my rather battered skin is enough to give the fragrance a fairly long-lasting quality overall. And after this slightly excessive ginger opening, B. actually manages to give the sport a slight touch of old, worn wooden tennis rackets. Toilet blocks smell far more synthetic. All in all, this is still not a successful triathlon, but it's a few real shoe sizes ahead of Nordic walking or such nonsense. Additionally, I had the joyful experience that the perfume has a headache-relieving effect after such extravagant parties, like the one last weekend. So, it's homeopathically compatible. Oh, by the way: Diving: When jumping down from 7 meters off the 10-meter board, all participants naturally got stuck at the 3-meter mark. So everyone ended up with a board in front of their heads.

... and better than the "Sport" in my opinion. First of all, I'm glad that I was able to acquire the fragrance at all; it was quite an act to organize "Sport Ice." After a bit of whining on my part, and since I represent a good customer at the Turkish store in town, the nice ladies from the shop managed to get this fragrance for me from the branch in the neighboring town. Many thanks to the friendly and lovely female staff. ;) Then there was the mistake of receiving the fragrance twice; the postal minister sent it to me as well, but I sent it back to the postal home, as the ladies had informed me by phone. :D OK, let's get to the scent. 75ml this time, a lousy size in my eyes. Either less or straight up 100ml. :D Well, whatever, to each their own. :) Sprayed on the skin, it clearly reminds me a bit of the regular Sport. But, this Sport Ice somehow has a bit more charm, I like it better. Is it fresher? Mmmhhhh..., slightly. The regular Sport is actually quite loud in the Sport Ice. However, it has a somewhat adjusted voice. My problem with the fragrance is always when I spray it... what does ginger actually smell like?? I honestly have absolutely no clue. I read about it in Apicius's post, but I can't perceive or describe it. Especially not with Sport Ice. I think I need to rummage through my mom's kitchen again and sniff some spices, but I would say 99% that I can't detect the ginger in Sport Ice. What I definitely perceive is the citrus note. It smells sporty, and that's why it deserves the typical title. That doesn't mean I'm a huge fan of this fragrance note. Sport Ice is a nice fresh scent, that’s for sure. I don’t regret ordering this fragrance blindly. I think it can be worn at any time without causing a stir. It’s not a masterpiece that Burberry has created, but solid, decent craftsmanship that one can accept. The longevity is rather average; I wouldn’t place Sporty Ice in a fragrance marathon like Antaeus... ;) :)

The original Burberry Sport is a pleasant, already quite cool fragrance for sporty occasions with a lot of grapefruit & ginger, but with a vanishingly low longevity. I like to wear it during leisure time or at the gym. However, I was not aware until a week ago that there was an even "icier" flanker. Good to know, but I wouldn't have missed much if I hadn't stumbled upon the inexpensive 10 ml decant. Sport Ice resembles the original at least 90%, much more than normal flankers, I would say. It's almost like a limited edition with a slightly altered bottle. A direct side-by-side test confirms this. However, if you really focus, I believe this icy version comes across as even a bit colder, more summery, and metallic. Logical with that name - not every advertisement or naming is a bad joke by the creators. Here it fits well, because this grapefruit spritzer is definitely to be enjoyed on the rocks. A bit more special & not quite as generic shampoo-like as its original version, but still a crowd-pleaser, a go-to fragrance & a scent that can remind one of Axe & Co. as well as Dior Homme Sport/Cologne. The Diors are much finer, while the deodorants are much bulkier. Lemon, musk, grapefruit, transparent woods, ice cubes - tada, here’s the cheap scent for the amateur bowler & the tennis student. Bottle: simple, cubic, cool Sillage & longevity: both at the lower end of acceptance - 3-4 hours. Conclusion: very similar to the normal Sport, just a bit icier. Marketing & name are not always a gag & nonsense. Both are good sporty fragrances & do not bring shame to Burberry, but one is already dispensable.

So ginger in this massive concentration has nothing to do with an appealing perfume for me. On top of that, citrus and a terribly synthetic amber-musk blend. For me, Sport Ice is the dud of 2011 so far; every Right Guard deodorant is a revelation compared to this. Fortunately, there are restrooms in the cinema later; I absolutely have to wash this off beforehand, lest my friends ... Sammy :-)

9:00 AM. It rings twice, loudly, insistently. Since she doesn’t have a “ring” doorbell - and surveillance system, she opens the door unsuspectingly and a bit naively. She is wearing a sheer organza robe and underneath only a push-up bra and a skimpy thong. Everything is tangerine-colored, and she even smells like a juicy clementine. In front of her stands a guy who looks like the spitting image of young Jack Nicholson. He grins at her widely and diabolically. The grin stretches from ear to ear. His black hair is tied back in a little braid at the nape of his neck, and he raises his eyebrows like the devil from “The Witches of Eastwick” and purrs: “Hello, I’m Daryl van Horne. I’m the postman, and I rang twice. Here I have a huge package from abroad for you!” She feels both attracted and repelled by this man who seemed neither handsome nor particularly charming. But he had a devilish allure and smelled of cinnamon. No, not the cinnamon stuff that you mix with sugar and melted butter to pour over rice pudding, but original, rusty-brown, unsweetened cinnamon sticks with an almost sharp aroma. He sets down the package. She exclaims delightedly, “Oh, this is a seedling of a jacaranda tree, it comes from South Africa and blooms in November with magnificent light blue clusters that smell like acacia flowers! I’ll plant it in my greenhouse, as it won’t tolerate the continental climate.” A few jacaranda shavings are included and emit a herb-spicy scent. He grins like Jack Torrance from The Shining and thinks: “What a little fool! Jacarandas grow over 20 meters tall and then it will blow up her conservatory.” The fool offers him a plum schnapps, and as her drunkenness progresses, her inhibitions recede, especially hers. They both giggle and philosophize about cinnamon sticks. Laughter erupts when it turns out that there are large and small cinnamon sticks, and some that are so hard you can’t even crush them. Her breath smells creamy of amber, and from the cellar, a patchouli rat sneaks in and makes a run for it when a gust of wind pushes the window open. The wind sweeps her organza robe through the room. Both think, “It doesn’t get better than this!” and soar together over the cuckoo's nest.

You do something to me something that simply mystifies me tell me, why should it be you have the pow´r to hypnotize me let me live `neath your spell do do that vodoo that you do so well ...... (Cole Porter) One of my favorite songs from this time - fits both a love and a love for fragrance! And that's exactly how I feel when I first spray this enchanting scent. S o my imaginary Ottoman princess must have smelled when she emerged from her evening milk bath and her handmaidens anointed her still warm, damp body with the most delicate fruity cinnamon oil, preparing her before she sought to please her husband. I hold the bottle in my hands - bought blindly - once again, as has happened many times since Parfumo captivated me with its wonderful comments, reviews, and scent pyramids and seduced me ;-> - Already enchanted by the outer appearance of the bottle, with its simple, straightforward elegance, I expect a lot from what these wonderfully readable components of the scent pyramid promise .... So much beautiful has already been written about this perfume - but I am currently so in love (once again - is that fickle? Could be -, probably characteristic of some Parfumos ...), that I must also contribute my two cents and want to verbally kneel here. Organza Indècence spreads at the moment of first contact with warm skin over you and the room with a distinctly fruity cinnamon woodsy aura, the mandarin is immediately perceptible. Over time, Organza becomes the confidently delicate seductress through an incredible milk cream accord of exceptional quality. The dominant cinnamon note always runs through all perceptions, but softly. This formidable composition of ingredients is wonderfully successful and turns out deliciously gourmand, without being overly sweet. A little later, when the intense opening of the fragrance softens, becomes more homogeneous and delicate, one might think of a cinnamon-enhanced crème brûlée - however without its thick brown sugar crust - served in a light, rustic wooden bowl. - Speaking of wood - the interplay: wood heart and cinnamon top makes the beautiful scent so special, catching any possible sweetness and thus providing the fascinating oriental flair. The existing plum blends in rather imperceptibly; I perceive it less. The scent veil is soft, creamy, noble, delicious, it is lovely, with a spicy-woody base, it is so beautiful you could bite into it, of particular character. Les Parfums Mythiques indeed! The sillage, or external effect, is initially intense and then pulls back a little while later. The scent may not last quite as long, about 6 hours until it becomes very close to the skin, but then it is still close to you the next morning ;) Then you could fill the sensual milk bath anew ........ ;-)

I had 2 bottles of this... The first 100 ml bottle was used up quickly. I am a "heavy sprayer" and finish a fragrance in about 5 weeks. I just couldn't get enough! Wow, I absolutely had to own this scent again. Upon the first spray: oh how lovely! No alcohol base (like in many fragrances), but instead, a feeling of comfort sets in immediately. I smell balsamic wood with cinnamon. I don't perceive any green, fresh notes at all. On the contrary: a subtle sweetness comes to my nose, along with an enchanting oriental note. I can't detect any citrus notes, but the amber is definitely present. Captivating for my olfactory organ! The patchouli stays in the background but is noticeable. Not as intrusive as one might expect from patchouli. Too much patchouli can be very impressive but also overwhelming. It doesn't smell good to every nose. In this Organza fragrance, the optimal middle ground has been found. Caressing, pleasant sillage for those around, long-lasting. I can still perceive the scent after 10 hours. It lasts even longer on clothing. It will always remain in my collection, and I will look to replenish it well in advance. It is one of my treasures!

A cinnamon roll is round. That much is certain. But this one has edges and corners. "Mythical Perfumes - Organza Indécence" is mythical without a doubt. The perfumer of this fragrance really put in the effort. He wanted to "create" something that has never existed before. Congratulations. Because: "Successful!" This powerful oriental starts off with a bang with cinnamon. The first 20 minutes are overdone and loud. The other fragrance notes don't really get a chance to speak during this time. Cinnamon knocks everything and everyone out! I wonder if I will like it, as I eagerly await the further development of the scent. Slowly, it becomes quieter and more embracing. This fairy-tale fragrance enchants me and transports me to Marrakech. This must be how it smells when walking through the narrow alleys while enjoying delicious baklava. Everything around me turns terracotta. Tonal, warm, and muted. Just like Organza Indécence. It is not a skin scent but has a good sillage, with longevity lasting several hours and is perfect for the fresh season. It has a slight sharpness that warms from within. A daring blend. Not overly sweet but spicy and gourmand. I smell 5-star Michelin chef vanilla rice pudding with delicious cinnamon sugar and secret spices.

A wonderful fragrance has reached me today, and I would like to dedicate a review to it. (A big thank you to the lovely saleswoman) Mystical is Organza Indécence indeed, its original creation takes us back to the successful, transformative 90s. I am now the owner of the version from 2007. Soft, oriental, and yet playful, it embodies the sensuality of a woman in its most beautiful form. I stand in a sun-drenched palace in the Orient, a warm breeze flows through the chambers and gently caresses the delicate, long, cream-colored sheer curtains. They are so light and fine that one can see through them. On a small golden throne sit fruits. Mandarins (peaches and pears are also present, hidden at the bottom of the bowl) create the fruity opening. Next to it is a large bowl with cinnamon sticks and other spices, the cozy-warm scent blends harmoniously with the delicate fruits. They all dance together, like fairies. Light and whispering, they float through the room and reach a large throne made of finely carved light wood. I briefly settle there. Oriental music from 1001 Nights plays softly in the background. Then she appears, a fairy, veiled. Her dark mystical eyes point to the chamber behind the curtains, she glides there. I follow her, here and there a ripe plum falls from her garment, which I pick up again. She pauses in a dark spot and I wait in anticipation. She lets her veil fall. I rush to her and want to return the lost fruits, but in that moment she has already vanished. She leaves behind, besides her magic, a hint of golden amber. Who was she? A princess? A sorceress? Or the ruler of this patchouli palace? - Horns. Voices. Somewhere a phone rings. The noise of the normal world is back - out of the dream. Organza Indécence has transported me a little to the Orient, but to the very fine one from the fairy tale world. It is wonderful when a fragrance can evoke these, but in no way indecent associations. This treasure was truly missing from my collection. - MY TREASURE - “It is a great happiness when one is able to (still) rejoice.” - George Bernard Shaw

The opening is so beautifully exciting, cinnamon-spicy, slightly green-fruity, oriental. Head says yes, how cool is that! But unfortunately, it weakens quickly, calms down fast, becomes soft, mildly fruity, slightly woody, very close to the skin. Heart says too bad! The base is a hint of amber and my beloved patchouli, also very intimate.

Very good EDT around Rose, Tonka and Ginger. To me these three notes are prominent : Ginger and Rose dominate at first, then it's a mix of Rose, Tonka and Woods. In comparison with the original Burberry Brit, this one is reinforced in fruity notes (ginger and orange). To me it's better than the original for any season. Sillage can be soft to relatively heavy depending on how much you apply. For an EDT, its longevity is really good. Its background of Rose and Tonka is charming.

Brit For Men launches the Summer Edition from Burberry with a citrusy freshness that has a somewhat bitter, sharp undertone. According to the listed notes, this is due to cardamom and ginger. The ginger is distinctly noticeable. Blind, I wouldn't have recognized it; it’s simply a bitter lemon with a slight sharpness. It has something, but only briefly, before making way for a beginning and somewhat drier phase. First, the citrusy bitterness shifts towards the resinous direction of cedar, which reminds me a bit of verbena in this composition. I am not familiar with palisander, and what one doesn't know is hardly perceived in combination. So the scent lingers for a while, fresh and woody, already with a delicate, bitter, and finely earthy note from patchouli. The scent now reminds me a little of Bleheim Bouquet, only a bit warmer and fuller due to the base notes of tonka and musk already present in the background with their slight sweetness and powderiness. I quite like this, and everything gets even better as the initial fresh aspect of the fragrance nearly disappears after half an hour, and the scent finally arrives at itself: a beautiful, warm, woody/powdery men's fragrance that can easily be worn as unisex. After about an hour, the main impression for me is the woodiness. After two hours, the scent finally reaches its base and from there on becomes only weaker and sweeter, not sticky but rather bitter-sweet. Average to good sillage, durability is okay; after about three hours, it becomes a bit weak, but overall, it is still subtly noticeable after eight hours. In the end, it becomes too agreeable for me; I don't perceive vetiver, which is actually a shame, as vetiver would be good. Instead, there is mainly a somewhat lukewarm, powdery vanilla tone with a note reminiscent of sandalwood oil in its interplay with tonka bean and very little cedar. It’s a nice scent for here and there, but overall, I find it a bit too dull. Basically, I have not yet been able to force myself to assign a specific fragrance to a season. I find that most fragrances have their different often wearable aspects depending on the mood in both summer and winter. Depending on the mood and occasion, everyone has to try it out for themselves and also take a bit of a risk that goes against traditional habits. The courage to break away leads here, as in many other areas of life, to often more exciting results... It just has to fit, and sometimes, when the pants are particularly loose and the hair is wild in the wind, the bottom button of the jacket can also be closed in a stuffy manner. In other words, sometimes even the supposedly frowned-upon socks go well with sandals in a casually falling evening dress.

Who would have thought it - a Summer Edition that completely breaks the mold! There is nothing aquatic, citrusy, or melon-green about Burberry Brit Summer Edition 2012. We are dealing here with a pure Oriental fragrance, whose cozy base of musk and tonka seems more suited to a warm fireplace during a snowstorm than to summer refreshment by the pool. And yet it works, as a gentle, creamy Nivea, Penaten, or Creme 21 accord spreads a sense of summery lightness and good cheer, especially beautifully presented in the top notes. Added to this are soft, floral notes - the tester in the store indicated a wild rose accord - which lend a certain elegance to the whole affair. In the mid-development stage, the creaminess recedes a bit, and the rosy accord gains some sharpness and a certain bite - preventing an overly soft overall impression of this men's fragrance. After three hours, the floral notes are gone, and the base, with its woody-vanilla character, may be somewhat conventional, but it is also quite harmonious. For the mid-price range, the quality is acceptable. This very gentle summer breeze is a real alternative that one could also wear in the warm season, perhaps on cooler days. What was the marketing department thinking? A fragrance labeled as a summer scent as an excuse and expression of guilt for the many hideous synthetic-sounding sport and summer fragrances that we are inundated with? Even in that area, Burberry offers better at a reasonable price than other brands. Speaking of price: those who do not want to spend a clearly three-digit amount for a gentle, rosy musk experience will gladly prefer the somewhat sturdier Burberry Brit Summer Edition 2012 over Amouage's Lyric Man.

I only tested this out of curiosity as Celine scents have been a huge disappointment, and this is no different! Yes it’s a gorgeous vanilla, but it’s a barely there skin scent. Such a huge shame! At £230 for only 100ml, it’s a total joke! It’s just not worth it if you have to hold your skin to your nose just to smell it. There are much better scents on the market for the same price or less….. Angélique Noire , Spiritueuse Double Vanille , Cozy Vanilla , Fire at Will , Lune Féline Eau de Parfum , Muse ….. I don’t find it any more different or unique to anything else I already have in my collection, and what I do own performs way better than this. It’s still a 10/10 for the smell of the scent itself, but 2/10 for performance. Currently Black Tie to me is a watered down Fire At Will / Lune Feline for double the price. Had this been MUCH stronger, it would have been a winner because it is a beautiful vanilla and would probably beat the others, if it was just more detectable. For anyone who owns this, does it get stronger over time? This also isn’t anything like Orchidee Vanilla which is a chocolate orange scent. The only thing these scents have in common is the poor performance.

It is an amber-iris vanilla wood, rounder and sweeter than Bois d’Argent but from the same father. The perfumers names of this new Celine collection have not been disclosed, but we can clearly feel the artistic direction of Mr. Hedi Slimane who creates here the sequel of his work at Dior. Black Tie is less bubbly, narrower and projects less than his big brother. Everything is very well built and will undoubtedly be one of the hit of the collection. The male - female border is murky. It looks more feminine to my nose. I tested the entire collection, and the work is sublime. Subtle enough without the desire to impress the gallery. Sober, classy, so French and perfectly in tune with the times.

I tried a lot of vanillas, and this is just right in the middle. Its very powdery, creamy vanilla, mind you, its super weak and doesnt last long. I dont know where i could wear this. Its too sweet for spring, too heavy for summer, too weak and unserious for fall, and too weak for winter! Its just...i dont know, there are like 100 other vanillas that will give you 10x more for 10x less the price. Just saying.

Since I couldn't fit the following into a 140 character statement, it will now be a review :) (I already did a review on parfumo.de, this is the english version) I like vanilla, I like iris, I like woody notes. Probably Black Tie is the perfect blend of these for me, maybe the other notes play a role here too, I can't tell. Because I can't smell out any individual notes here, I just perceive the overall result: Present, but not obtrusive. Sweet, but not sticky - a dry sweetness that is very attractive. Powdery, but not dry as dust. Just a perfect composition for me, great fragrance.

I tested Black Tie in the Celine store. At first sniff it is a glorious, sophisticated, EXPENSIVE-smelling vanilla but it did not last and what was left of the dry down felt like the normal vanilla scent. I really wanted to love this because of the reviews and branding but can't justify price for just another vanilla scent. I hope to test again and see if I'll arrive at a different conclusion.

black tie captivates me, it encompasses vanilla and supports it with iris butter and cedar. For an evening, in the middle of the day, it is of a subtlety without name. I could not separate myself from it, it is addictive, it is greedy without being synthetic. The best perfume in my taste. It has an effect on people who smell it.

For me, Black Tie smells like a luxury car interior. A car with vanille Wunderbaum air freshener :D Don't get me wrong - it's a very elegant, classy scent but I would expect more depth and volatility from that expensive fragrance. This one is too simply and can be overwhelming after longer usage.

Fragrance with an aroma of gods, the first time you try it it makes you smile from side to side and you drool like a 2-year-old boy, you go straight to look for it and buy it this the disappointment comes when at 2/3 hours you have to put your nose thoroughly in the skin to perceive it.

The scent itself is very pretty, a nice blend of vanilla and cedar, with decent longevity. It's not overly sweet, either. Unfortunately, it tends to make me feel a little bit nauseous down the line. I'm not sure why, but I think I have that issue with gourmands in general, and might well be in the minority. If I didn't, then I'd probably give this an 8 or 8.5 in terms of scent.

Light, fuzzy vanilla. Not sickly or sour (as I thought the oakmoss would make it), but just right imo. I don't really know what the oakmoss is doing in this tbh because I can't tell it's there. I'm not against it, I love Reptile from Celine, but I can't even get a hint of it in this. Would buy a FB and wear a lot, however it is expensive.

This perfume is really a pleasant breath of spring, it is really an excellent mix of freshness, sweetness and femininity. It is floral, musky and sweet, but in an elegant and never intrusive way, very easy to wear and suitable for all ages. In the dry-down it becomes more enveloping and more sensual, but maintains its lightness and sparklingness throughout the day, with a truly remarkable longevity that makes it perfect for everyday use!

Association: It is 7 PM. I come from an abstract vernissage and walk up the stairs to my beautiful modern penthouse apartment. The orange-red glowing evening sun stretches against the white walls of my light-flooded large penthouse. Slowly, I take the hairband out of my hair and finally arrive. On my way to my office, I catch sight of a large colorful and pompous bouquet of flowers. In the bouquet, there is a small note made of elegant laid paper with the inscription: "Bonsoir mon amour, take a relaxing bath and then put on an elegant black dress. We will meet at 9 PM in the bar where we first met." I prepare a bath and add a soapy foamy scented oil that my fiancée brought me from Paris last week. I lie nestled in the femininely scented bubble bath and close my eyes. The evening sun gently kisses my skin. I let the day pass by me once more. I feel a tingling, a slight excitement, euphoria. I will finally see him again. I play with my hair and think of my beloved and drift away. Daydreaming. Evening dreaming. My exciting love story. It feels mysterious and seductive. Almost a bit forbidden. I open my eyes and stand in the dressing room. In front of me hangs a black figure-hugging dress, elegant, sexy. It shows a little skin but not too much. All within the bounds of elegance. I walk to my small vanity and decisively reach for L'interdit. I spray it passionately on my warm skin. It merges with my body scent, with my skin, with my soul. I am surrounded by a seductive aura, so mysterious, so feminine, so sexy. Exactly what I need today. Exactly what he needs today. L'interdit is a beautiful soapy floral scented perfume. The combination of orange blossom, tuberose, and poppy creates a wonderful harmonious and extraordinary warmth, and the patchouli note is also very pleasant. I also perceive jasmine. Not too much, not too little, just right. The longevity is good to very good, and the scent works beautifully into the skin. Definitely love at first sniff!

L `interdit always makes me think of the beautiful Fleur d´interdit, which was my wedding fragrance at the time. But even the L interdit EDP had nothing to do with the forbidden flower - although I liked it in its own way. Would the EdT come closer to Fleur? No - not at all. It even deviates further from the EDP - and into the negative range. I am actually used to good things from Givenchy - even though Fleur is the star in the firmament for me. But the Plays and the Ange et Demons also find my approval. However, the L`interdit Edt greets me with a sweet musty opening. Could that be the poppy? The tuberose pushes through the strangely moldy curtain - but cannot displace it. No, I would rather stick with the EDP, as it has no disturbing "aftertaste." Maybe Givenchy will remember the forbidden flower and launch a fragrance twin? But the beautiful flower will probably remain forbidden.

After reading the mixed opinions and rather negative comments about the EdP that was released last year, I was curious and wanted to test and compare both. The fragrance pyramid sounds quite appealing, as I personally love tuberose and orange blossom very much, so how bad can the scent experience be? After wearing both independently as well as simultaneously - the EdT on one arm and the EdP on the other - I must say: They are not bad. The EdT is definitely more pleasant to wear; it is much milder and not overdone with just two sprays. In the opening, as well as in the EdP, the orange blossom is predominantly sweet, as if one has stumbled headfirst into a blooming little tree, but not quite as intense as in the EdP. The tuberose comes in fresh and clean, unlike some other fragrances where it smells heavy and "greasy." I can't find anything that I could compare to poppy. The scent is grounded by vetiver and a note that vaguely reminds me of cocoa butter with its powdery gourmand scent (could that be the patchouli?). And so, tuberose and orange blossom bloom throughout the day (6h+) ahead of you. In terms of longevity, the little sister is in no way inferior to the EdP; the sillage is strong but not intrusive or overwhelming. All in all, a nice fragrance with enough restraint to be wearable among people. The composition and the love-hate relationship that many have with tuberose is, of course, a matter of taste.

In the summer, I sampled JV during one of those "hurry up and smell everything that's been opened" trips to TJ Maxx. I had some unscented skin available on my left forearm, so as an afterthought I planted John Varvatos there. I must have sampled 5-6 scents that day, but I only remember one - John Varvatos. I can't tell you how JV develops, or whether JV is a chypre or not, or how long JV lasts. I can tell you that after 4 months of thinking about this fragrance -- and being unable to find an open box or tester so I could sample it again -- I finally bought it. I'm not sure if the purchase is a mark of craziness or the wait is a mark of discipline. Regardless, I think my story reflects a mark of a truly superior fragrance: JV resonated with me somehow, so I remembered it & craved it, long after trying it. The right brain reaction often trumps the left brain analysis. I am convinced that is the reason why JV is favored by so many here, regardless of the more thorough & analytic reviews that suggest JV shouldn't be held in such high esteem. -- UPDATE: I have it now. OMG, it's a gorgeous, boozy beauty according to my right & left brains! Will compete for space in my top 10. Well-blended & long-lasting too. LUV IT. PS - JV is especially luxurious and wonderful after bathing with the deep & dark Youth-Dew bath oil. I'd add that I don't usually like florals but I LOVE this. PS #2 - I now have it in parfum ($13) & body silk ($8). Neither are stellar alone, imo. However, layered with the EdP they are outstanding -- 12 hours.

I always try to guess the "official" category of fragrances which I plan to review on the basis of a sample vial (unlike FBs, which I usually wear many times before writing a review--since I have that luxury...), so upon initially spritzing JOHN VARVATOS, which I had been looking forward to with great anticipation, given the hype, my first reaction was: "Oriental Floral". A few seconds later: "Fruity floral". A couple of minutes later: "Floral Woody Musk". What I would never have guessed in a million years was the "correct" answer: "Chypre Floral"! JOHN VARVATOS is truly all over the map, as they say, but not in a pleasant way. The problem for me is summed up well by another reviewer (at another site), who also demurs from the chypre categorization of JV. There's something somehow stale or old about the fruits and the flowers. Or maybe the canned fruit cocktail cubes and spheres, in their washed-out, almost pastel oranges and yellows, have sapped the flowers of their freshness. Don't know. Don't really care. Not on my wish list. I should say that the patchouli drydown is okay, but the trajectory this fragrance follows in getting there is not a mellifluous journey--although honey is listed as a note. Rather than manna from heaven, JOHN VARVATOS is to me more like canned fruit cocktail, rather mushy and devoid of well-defined flavors. All of that said, some of my best perfume pals love JOHN VARVATOS, so it's going to vary from person to person: try before you buy.

John Varvatos for Women is an oddly captivating fragrance. I've never seen this perfume sold in Australia, however the masculine offerings from this brand are very popular in our department stores. I was lucky enough to receive a sample of John Varvatos for Women as an extra gift when I made a purchase last month. What struck me almost immediately was this fragrance's dry earthiness. The patchouli is rather dominant in John Varvatos for Women, hence the reason why some people love it, and some hate it. I can certainly see how this fragrance could be compared to the likes of Chanel's Coco Mademoiselle EDP. John Varvatos for Women opens with a tart blend of syrupy honey, juicy plum and apricot. Despite the rather fruity and sweet opening, this fragrance is far from predictable. The musky florals and patchouli in the heart keep this fragrance grounded. Although it's a fragrance intended to be worn by women, I think men could also wear John Varvatos with ease. It does fall into chypre floral territory, especially with its dominant patchouli and oakmoss drydown. I am suitably impressed by this fragrance's unique composition, and even more thrilled by the inexpensive price tag. John Varvatos for Women is a fairly versatile fragrance. However I would personally wear it during Autumn and Spring, either to the office or out to lunch. It's also inoffensive enough to be worn lightly during Summer. While the longevity is great, the sillage is fairly light, choosing to stay rather close to the skin. Layering the scent with a matching lotion might help with the projection. All in all, John Varvatos for Women is classy fragrance that all chypre lovers should sniff at least once in their lifetime. Original review written: November 2012.

Some fragrances sneak into the house through roundabout ways, and that's how it was for me with Woman. In the first weeks at Parfumo, I received several samples, which I unfortunately mixed up, and Woman was among them. The first test was pleasant, but not eye-catching. Nevertheless, I set the sample aside, along with Reve, to test both fragrances again later. During the second test, I noted: Creamy-soft, fruity cognac, a quiet scent, but not silent, it has something to say. The samples Woman and Reve set off on a journey to the next perfume lovers. Months later, strangely enough, both fragrances kept coming to mind, and I would have liked to sniff them again. Woman has now come to me through a lovely swap with Omara, while Reve is ordered and on its way to me. Woman starts off alcoholic, not crashing, but like a mild, fruity cognac. The bottle is well-chosen in color and supports this impression. Right from the start, I perceive the patchouli, not with a sledgehammer, but well-measured in the background, it can be sensed until the end of the fragrance. This luscious fruity note, especially the plum, lingers for quite a while, gradually the fruits are underlaid with floral notes, but not overshadowed. Everything arranges itself nicely and unobtrusively, yet the scent can still be perceived from a short arm's length away. Woman becomes increasingly spicier, also darker, ending in a slightly woody, sweet base. The sweetness is due to the honey, which I find pleasant here. Usually, I have a problem with honey, often finding it too sticky. Woman is a gentle, creamy year-round fragrance, at least up to 25 degrees, with medium longevity and sillage. It reminds me a bit of Laetia, which I will compare when I have the chance. I think it is more suitable for women, but who knows. And I hope it gets cooler soon so I can take this lovely lady out.

A perfumery in Darmstadt had a clearance sale (Unfortunately due to business closure). Among many other previously unknown fragrances, I encountered "John Varvatos Woman." It was early spring and cold outside. I tested the Eau de Parfum and found it quite suitable for cool temperatures. The opening of the fragrance has a warm, harvest-like plum aroma with hints of wood and earth (Patchouli?). Shortly thereafter, a pleasant powderiness joins in, which lays the ingredients on a soft carpet. Floral notes now emerge quite subtly, but they do not become dominant. I believe I can detect rose in the background of the heart note, as well as a hint of jasmine, which adds a touch of sweetness to the overall arrangement. This scent impression does not change for a long time; later, the powdery woodiness increases again and gives "John Varvatos Woman" a rugged support, along with a small pinch of moss. I would not classify the Eau de Parfum as a chypre, rather as having an oriental touch alongside a restrained chypre nuance that lends the fragrance a two-dimensionality. Nevertheless, the perfume is not "flat," but in its own way, it also has a certain depth. With its longevity of several hours and a sillage that is at least well recognizable to me, it is not a delicate splash, but a high-quality scent. I do not perceive it as a fragrance I would want to wear daily. Rather on cold, gray winter days, to give me a feeling of light brown warmth, where a hint of late summer days (plum) also benefits my nose.

Today, a mandatory appointment took place in the city amidst pouring rain. Since my husband, the little poodle, and I optimistically set out without an umbrella, no one complained when I suggested seeking refuge in the nearby luxury perfumery. We entered the "Nose's El Dorado," in the most daring sense of the word - like drenched poodles.

I am quite surprised! Yes, hard to describe: The scent is somewhat soapy, strongly spicy, with a brief glance towards the Orient. The patchouli comes through very well, the flowers are not individually definable, they sing in chorus. The perfume is just as warm as the really beautiful bottle: brown-orange. Don't be afraid of the wild honey, it's rather tame and reserved.

What could be hidden in the amphora-shaped bottle? Many of the new releases in recent years have not convinced me: similar scent pyramids and an often all-consuming synthetic fruitiness that can occasionally offer individual appealing moments, but rarely excites me in the overall concept.

So...after only knowing the scent by its notes and never having tested it, I finally got to do that thanks to Daisy. And here it is now on my skin, and I sniff and sniff... To be honest, I am surprised. Where is the familiar scent of a certain person from my family suddenly coming from? Did this person wear the perfume? Am I just imagining it? And above all: Do I like it?

No one can smell it. Don’t waste your money. You smell it once you spray it then disappears. I asked many persons and I sprayed almost 20 sprays but still even when I come near them and ask if they smell perfume and they say sorry nothing. I regret buying it and unfortunately I bought the 200 ml one. I tried to explain to the store where I bought it (Harrods, London, UK) but she just told me sorry about that.

This is such a beautiful, delicate vanilla. It is quite similar to Angelique Noir although now that I own both, I can pick out more differences: Angélique Noire is much stronger and greener. She is your femme fatale / boss lady scent. She’s the confident, fiercely independent sister and nothing stands in her way. She makes her presence known. Angelique is heavy on the Angelica root, with vanilla in the background. I have to be in the mood to wear this one, as sometimes I find it a bit in your face. Dans Paris is the scent I’d imagine a graceful ballerina wearing. She’s the elegant, reserved, put together sister everyone admires. Dans Paris has more vanilla and is definitely more balanced between all the notes. I find this one much more versatile and easier to wear. I really love both scents. They are both absolutely stunning, but I do prefer Dans Paris

Like all Celine fragrances I tried so far, Dans Paris is very powdery, fluffy and soft. It's mainly a vanilla scent, in my opinion the vanilla is similar to that in Black Tie. The musk in this is light and clean, and I think there must be some unlisted iris that is responsible for the cool, dry texture of the scent. All Celines smell kind of irisy to my nose. The standout notes that make Dans Paris different from the rest of this line are laurel (bay) blossom and coriander. They're softly spicy, slightly green and blended very thoroughly into the vanilla-musk fluff, so this could work even for people who are hesitant about spicy notes. I think the spices have a bit of an aniseed note here, too, even though that's not listed, but it's all very subtle. This is lovely, chic and perfectly balanced, but also very linear and simple. It's a strong like for me, but I prefer Black Tie, La Peau Nue and Saint-Germain-de-Pres, as they are more evocative to me. It's just personal taste though, I don't think you can really go wrong with this, provided you like vanilla and powder.

Dans Paris is a bright, soft, aromatic, airy fragrance. Powdery fluffy vanilla with light green citrus-herb sprinkles. Unlike many other vanilla scents that smell like grandma's waffles or other treats, Dans Paris has little in common. This fragrance is more elegant, refined, ethereal, and enchanting. It is not a scent that overwhelms your counterpart olfactorily, thankfully. I tested it alongside Angélique Noire , both fragrances are related yet different. Compared to Guerlain's herbaceous-green vanilla, Dans Paris is significantly brighter, less bitter, friendlier, and more straightforward. Both bottles visually reflect the characters of the fragrances very well. I can somewhat relate to the association of the top note with modeling clay, even though the scent does not smell like that to me. Anyone who has ever worked with coriander seeds in the kitchen will recognize in the top note the scent of the finely spicy, citrus-like essential oils that are released when the seeds are crushed. I also identify bay leaf, but not a dried leaf, rather a fresh, green one picked directly from the bush. null of these aromas push themselves to the forefront; it is just a fine, invigorating veil that blends with the cloud-like vanilla. In the dry down, I am caressed by the most beautiful, noblest vanilla that is in no way inferior to the legendary "Guerlain vanilla." It is subtly sweet, now a bit more musky-creamy than powdery, and still incredibly sophisticated. The entire fragrance journey makes me feel secure, which is why I particularly enjoy wearing Dans Paris at home. Sprayed in the evening, I can still perceive the scent the next morning. Not too long ago, it was a mystery to me why one would spend so much money on a bottle, but this high-quality and fine fragrance is worth every cent.

I am confused. I received a sample through a sharing, and after being absolutely fascinated by Black Tie with its incredibly well-crafted iris butter + dry, unsweetened vanilla, which moved in with me in no time, Dans Paris leaves me with a question mark. I love to quietly read the reviews and statements here before or after I test a fragrance. Usually, I understand the scent associations. Right now, I am confused :). I apparently perceive the scent quite differently than most others here. I am hit with a concentrated artificial rice pudding-vanilla sweetness. It smells very gourmand to me. Like overly sweetened, warm rice pudding. Quite tasty - I love rice pudding, but this one is way too sweet for me to want it on my skin for more than a few minutes. Mint or "green," as some perceive it, is not recognizable to me. Similarity to "Black Tie | Celine"? Not at all. Black Tie is the elegant big sister, mature, unsweetened, quiet, noble. Dans Paris comes from elementary school, throws the bag loudly into the corner, looks forward to the sweet rice pudding served for lunch, and then passionately plays with Play-Doh. After that, it’s time for the Emely strawberry dolls. (Funny, some have actually perceived it this way or similarly). Those whose heads are all intensely artificially scented. Marzipan, almond powder, vanilla crescents are the scent directions of the dolls. The little sister has significantly more endurance than the big Black Tie sister. Unfortunately, that one is very subtle, quite close to the skin, and has little staying power. Dans Paris lasts on me for hours. Don't get me wrong, I find the scent quite interesting and have been sniffing my arm for hours. However, I wouldn't want to smell like this. The sweetness overwhelms me in the long run. I think, like many gourmands, it is a scent that I find incredibly good on others as I pass by, but I wouldn't want to smell it on myself for an extended period. I remain a bit confused and eagerly follow your further impressions. I love this hobby!

Similar to Black Tie, I also find Dans Paris difficult to describe. Vanilla: Yes, definitely. Sweet: Yes, but not syrupy, rather dry, distinguished. Spicy: Yes, but not an explosion of spices, rather a subtle, very specific accompaniment to the vanilla. Especially through the combination of coriander and bay leaf, I haven't smelled anything like this before.

I was in the Celine Store in Paris yesterday and fell head over heels in love with this fragrance. So much so that I left the store with a 100ml bottle. The scent starts sweet with an explosion of coriander and vanilla, accompanied by a very pronounced bay leaf note. Everyone knows that scent that hits you when you open a bag of dried bay leaves.

After being so impressed by "Vanille Insensée | Atelier Cologne," I thought I would also try Dans Paris, since both contain vanilla and coriander. Here, it's the seeds and not the green, but since I had read many praises for "Black Tie | Celine," I thought it wouldn't hurt to test a Céline vanilla. Well, what can I say... I'm not convinced.

Well, at least from me. More than a year ago, I gave Dans Paris a statement and a score of 8.0 - I found it quite beautiful, but very (a bit too?) sweet-marzipan-creamy. I own all the Celines in travel size, and over the years, all but two have made it to me in full bottles: St. Germain de Près and, of course, Dans Paris.

Recently, I read the story of the nymph Daphne, whom the Greek god Apollo (Phoebus) fell in love with in an immortal passion. When Apollo wanted to overpower Daphne, she fled from him. Exhausted from her escape, she finally begged her father Peneios to transform her shape to escape Apollo. He granted her wish and turned her into a laurel tree.

Supposedly, the only difference in the top notes from the original is black pepper substituted for pink pepper, and the omission of nutmeg. Birch wood and mandarin orange are still listed, though once again I don't detect any woodiness, and I only get the vibe of the orange this time (slightly tangy), not actually the scent of orange. There is a spicy sweetness up top, lots of tonka bean. This scent is tonka dominant. The pepper seems to fade quickly though. One of the standout qualities of this one is an undertone of leather. This definitely comes off as much darker, sweeter, and in no way soapy and fresh like the original. The projection is not as good as the original, which is to be expected from a darker and richer version. I believe that the primary DNA of this line is spicy sweet orange up top, dying down to incense with a slightly sweet woodiness. The original just jumps out at you so much more. This one is beautifully subtle. After 10 minutes, it's already harder to detect. However, I'm really liking the addition of the leather note. It's very understated, but it adds a mysterious darkness to the scent. So far, this tonka bean-sweet, slightly smoky leather scent smells very masculine, more on the mature side, and quite alluring due to its subtle and mysterious nature. After about 30 min, I'm being reminded of another fragrance with similar notes: Armani Code Profumo. The creamy sweetness of the tonka bean, the leather undertone, and I am now getting an added sweetness from amber, which is also in ACP. Not to mention, ACP also opens with a slightly spicy mandarin orange vibe. This could be a little redundant in my collection, but I still really like it. It does have its own character. Ultimately, the scent profiles of each fragrance are only similar; not the same. It's been about an hour, and I'm loving the whiffs I'm getting of it, even from one small spray on the hand. After about 10 hours (possibly some rubbing off on my coat), I can still kind of smell it around me after 1 1/2 sprays on my neck. The scent is very pleasant. Subtle, sweet leather. Very masculine.

I think this would be the best dry down i have ever smelt, this fragrance although similar to the main gentlemen only, goes a totally different direction with the dry down. The rich smoky leather dry down is second to none, and i have no problem with the performance on my skin. I love this scent!

If it weren't for those nice €5 - or 10% - vouchers from the Turquoise, which often can only be redeemed online, I would probably order something from there only very rarely. But as a struggling perfume lover, you save where you can ;-) Well, anyway, during my last order, I chose a sample of “Gentlemen Only Intense” by Givenchy among others. Partly because I was interested in the scent and partly because it was prominently marked with “Pre-Premiere.” It's actually silly, but that kind of thing always triggers a “I-want-to-test-it reflex” in me. The opening is extremely pleasant, featuring a non-sweet, slightly tart mandarin, which is also spiced with a hint of pepper. For me, it’s more pink than black pepper, but maybe I’m mistaken. The top note is only very short-lived and is quickly overshadowed by a very, very elegant leather note. This one really packs a punch and is also extremely present, almost dominant. I interpret “dominant” in this case as a decidedly positive trait. I could perceive similar fine leather nuances, for example, in “Daimiris” by Laboratorio Olfattivo and “Cuir de Lancôme” by Lancôme. For me, this is a buttery soft suede that would gently conform to the body if worn as a jacket. It moves with every motion, fits perfectly, and smells subtly, elegantly, and distinctly expensive, like the finest suede. The color would range between champagne and sand, depending on the light, sometimes more, sometimes less beige, but definitely not pale (as beige tones often tend to be). Patchouli (rather sweet) and cedar provide supportive layers under the leather note. I am absolutely thrilled. If the scent could stay like this, it would definitely deserve a spot on my wish list. If...... However, after about 30 minutes, the leather loses its strength, overshadowed by tonka and amber. Completely and irretrievably lost. The base goes into cuddle mode. No less noble than the suede, but just not as expressive. A cultivated understatement takes over. After about 2 hours, hardly anything is perceptible anymore. It’s hard to believe that such a wonderful scent was present on the scented spots just a short while ago. I now seriously wonder what is supposed to be “intense” about “Gentlemen Only Intense”? It’s not the longevity, and definitely not the sillage. Perhaps it would have been better to launch an Eau de Parfum instead of an Eau de Toilette? I found that quite successful and fitting with Dior’s “Fahrenheit.” At Givenchy, they apparently believe that a label with “Intense” is enough. What a pity! Maybe this little gem develops better or lasts longer for others than it does for me?! Otherwise, it’s a genuine recommendation for people who want to smell good but don’t want/can’t/dare to be too noticeable at work. Nevertheless, it is a wonderful scent, but due to the described shortcomings, it will not make it into my collection.

Nowadays, a lot of nonsense is being made with the terms "Extreme," "Absolue," and "Intense" in our large, diverse, and colorful world of fragrances. And we experienced and critical perfume enthusiasts quickly realize that there isn't really much behind it. Rarely is a popular Eau de Toilette enhanced and intensified or made more long-lasting with more fragrance components. Instead, independent scents are often pushed onto the willing consumer because the original name has already sold so well. One could simply add an Intense-Extreme-Absolue to it, and people would buy that too. In the end, only the basic DNA of the fragrance remains, and the Intense has hardly anything in common with the original scent. The disappointment is often great. This is completely understandable. I don't want to go on further about marketing mistakes and the lack of ideas and courage from the designers. So I come to Gentlemen Only Intense from Givenchy. Since its release four years ago, it has settled at an average rating of 7.0, with 5 comments and 4 statements. It somehow slipped through the cracks. I suspect this is partly due to the lavishly used addition of "Intense." Nevertheless, I would like to claim that this very pleasant fragrance is worth a closer look. I came across Gentlemen Only Intense in the autumn of 2015 on the ferry from Rødby to Puttgarden. I picked up the 50 ml size in the shop on the ferry, and I still feel good with this scent. The 50 ml was quickly used up, and then a 100 ml bottle moved in. The fragrance is not particularly complex; the top, heart, and base notes are very closely related, and you can practically smell the rather sweet tonka base from the very beginning. However, it is not a sweetness that is sticky and overwhelming throughout the entire fragrance. At first, you can clearly perceive the mandarin, but it is not yet ripe and fully sweet; the sweetness clearly comes from the tonka bean-amber combination, which flashes through very early. I don't perceive pepper very distinctly, but I do notice quite a bit of green leaf. This provides a certain fresh kick with the unripe mandarin and nicely cushions the sweetness. I find that well done. Quickly, woody influences come into play, a hint of patchouli adds some depth, and I don't smell leather. Thankfully, in this case. Too much leather has already spoiled many a fragrance for me. Tonka-amber remains dominant. I also can't really smell incense distinctly. Overall, this is really not particularly exciting or innovative, but I feel exceptionally comfortable with this fragrance and think it suits me well. Intense is basically nothing here, as the fragrance neither lasts unnaturally long nor spreads an unnaturally huge scent cloud. I can definitely attest to the office suitability of GOI, as well as its everyday usability. It looks good in a suit and just as good in jeans. And for an evening at the theater or a concert, it is also not a bad choice. The cooler season seems well suited; in summer, the fragrance might seem a bit heavy. Anyone expecting something highly complex with numerous precious and rare ingredients and a longevity (Intense!) from 0:00 to midnight will naturally be disappointed; especially for the many niche-trained noses, the fragrance is nothing at all. However, if you like it warm-spicy with a certain sweetness and a hint of freshness and can cope with an average longevity of about 6 hours (significantly longer on clothing) and no room-filling sillage, feel free to go for it. I also found Gentlemen Only without Intense quite pleasant. I think GOI is somewhat overlooked and is getting a rather bad reputation here. The bottle is beautifully designed to match the fragrance, with a gradient from black to transparent, and is still very handy at 100 ml. It also seems to be gradually disappearing from stores, as new successors under the name Gentleman have appeared for some time. I have secured 2 bunker bottles just in case. You never know...
