And while I left almost all the Gentlemen aside because they could in no way excite my olfactory senses, something in Casual Chic wafted through that immediately put me in a positive mood. Wow, as gentle as a whisper of nothing, yet I could perceive a woody sweetness that was, on one hand, powdery soft, and on the other hand, ripe and needly. Somehow almost magical, like the body scent of a beautiful woman that you don’t consciously perceive, yet feel drawn to. Casual Chic is quite linear in its development, never intrusive and yet perceptible for about 5-6 hours. It starts powdery fresh, then becomes sweeter and enters into a wonderful symbiosis with the woods of birch and cedar, which give the scent something distinctive and grounded. The sweetness is a natural sweetness, not a sticky sugary concoction that gives you a headache. Overall, I consider the composition to be very successful because the ingredients come across as very natural, light, and yet high-quality. Due to the woody grounded nuances, it even reminded me, in a distant way, of Aventus. Really sexy and a fragrance that is extremely well received by women! Due to its lightness, Casual Chic is an all-rounder for spring and summer. Less for the beach, but perfect for a lovely evening for two at an Italian café by Lake Maggiore. Well done, Givenchy!

More or less shocked, I am for two reasons. On one hand, the Gentlemen line has nothing to do with the quality and elegance of the original Givenchy Gentleman. The sad low point seems to be this Casual Chic, which comes across as relatively insignificant with a decent portion of synthetics. Above all, the ginger seems too much like it's from a lab; otherwise, the individual components are hardly distinguishable. Overall, Casual Chic feels a bit fresh, somewhat aquatic with a subtle sweetness - but also relatively boring. This is in stark contrast to the Givenchy Gentleman, which is a light-footed patchouli revelation with sophistication. No wonder it is still found as a classic in the brand's portfolio and continues to have many fans. In the meantime, Casual Chic has been discontinued, which leads to - and here comes the second shock - absurd prices being asked for it on the bay. It's not forbidden, but who actually wants to pay over €300 for this mishmash of a bore? For the same money, I can get some top-quality retro old-school classics - just to throw that out there. But as is well known, everyone should know for themselves what they spend their perfume pennies on. And no one can claim they weren't warned.

You can tell that spring is here and soon summer will be at the door. Slowly but surely, there are new fragrances from well-known manufacturers, which mainly rely on already established brands in the market to offer new or different versions of them. Does that have to be bad? It can be seen either way. Personally, I don't think it's a bad thing; I mean, why not?

Peculiar. This x-th offshoot of a copy of the great 1974 "Gentleman" strikes me as such. At first, an exotic note pushes itself to the forefront, which initially seemed to me like a somewhat off-kilter laboratory tarragon, but in the end, it appears to be some sort of pseudo-birch, grounded by a strangely constructed sweet-spicy cardamom.

"Gentlemen Only Casual Chic" was a "blind purchase," based on the ingredients and various user comments. I expected more. More intense! Longer lasting! More direct! But maybe I'm already too spoiled and my sense of smell can no longer be "seduced" so easily. However, there was no trace of disappointment for me. Of course, I would buy "Gentlemen Only Casual Chic" again.

I'll put this review in this version, as I tried the version made by Inter Parfums and a more recent batch, and not the older versions by the original company or L'Oreal. I had the chance to try this some time ago, I saw the notes and I was hoping to try it before I bought it. After trying it I didn't end up buying it and probably won't, but it is nice. The opening is very citrusy but not overwhelming, and as it dries down it goes through a ton of different phases - floral, slightly green and aromatic, citrus coming and going, before eventually settling to a powdery woody musk. I found the way it changes really interesting, and it really drew me in. Having tried a few more fragrances now, in a lot of ways, it feels similar to 60s masculine powerhouses like Eau Sauvage or Habit Rouge, but with some of the cliches of masculine fragrances of the 80s. It's definitely dated, but it feels classy and gives me a nostalgic feeling somehow. It smells like something my dad used, though I don't remember ever seeing a bottle of this stuff at home. The dry-down is quite strong and it stayed on my skin for many hours through hand washing. I went to the gym on the day I tried it, and it was even stronger there. Considering you can get this for around 60 AUD for 100mL, I'd say it's pretty excellent value with that in mind. It's not for me as I would prefer something a bit more expressive of myself, but it is admittedly a very nice scent.

It's quite strange that this wonderful fragrance seems to have so few fans here. Only about 50 perfume enthusiasts claim it as their own. Perhaps that will change soon... I stumbled upon it rather by chance while watching a video about "Jaïpur Homme (Eau de Toilette) | Boucheron." Since I wasn't familiar with this brand at all, I took a little look around and came across the Pour Homme from Boucheron. Unfortunately, there wasn't much to find out, but my interest was piqued. So, once again, I took a blind leap in the Souk and just a few days later, I held this treasure in my hands. So how does it smell? Above all, wonderfully citrusy. And no, there’s no cleaner or toilet block to be found here. No worries! It has a very rounded and natural scent. Fresh, with slightly green and soapy nuances, then in the heart still citrusy, but here a bit more reminiscent of verbena. It lasts surprisingly long until the patchouli and a bit of sandalwood come through, forming the base of this EDT. The longevity can be described as really good, especially for such a fresh fragrance. 7-8 hours are definitely achievable on the skin. Who would I recommend it to? Anyone who likes Colonia Eau de Cologne or Pour Monsieur Eau de Toilette can purchase this without hesitation. I have all three fragrances here, and if I had to choose one, I would always reach for the Boucheron. The citrus notes simply last much longer than in the other two, and in terms of price/performance ratio, it also comes out on top. €40/100ml is really well spent here. So, anyone looking for a nice gentleman's fragrance for a modest price should definitely give this one a try. Thank you for reading.

First: I picked up this fragrance for 7 euros at a flea market, and the bottle was nearly full. Therefore, the price-performance ratio here is a solid 10 for me, because I got a high-quality scent for little money - regardless of whether I will like it for the rest of my life. Now, onto the rest. The bottle is a bit too flashy for my personal taste, and the plastic cap makes it feel somewhat cheap. However, it is nice and flat, making it easy to transport in a toiletry bag (or to hide in the cupboard among the other bottles). The scent itself is pleasant, especially pleasantly simple. I think I can slightly detect the listed fragrance notes. It starts off strongly citrusy, then transitions into floral-herbaceous, and bids farewell with earth and wood. However, this farewell takes its sweet time. I applied it several times in the early evening to try it out and sometimes still caught a whiff of it by the next morning. Moreover, it stays close to me; I hardly leave scent clouds in other rooms - which I personally prefer. All in all, I find this fragrance to be "high-quality, but risky." Risky, - from here on, everything should be understood as purely subjective - because I associate it with many things that don't necessarily have a place in my (perfume) world: heaviness, seriousness, conservatism, a bit of patriarchal, old-fashioned vibes. A scent that can make one appear older than they actually are and can even feel a bit "dusty." This is the kind of fragrance I would only wear for myself when I'm sitting around in the home office, or when I'm out and happen to come into contact with other people rather than intentionally. Additionally, I would never wear this fragrance in combination with a suit or any other type of formal clothing - that would be too strict. I'd rather play around with the scent now in summer and wear it with shorts, an oversized shirt, and sneakers. This creates a nice contrast between the olfactory and the visual.

There aren’t very many fragrances on the market that help induce meditation, however this particular perfume does help. I can’t explain why, but it is extremely relaxing to me. It is not overbearing or shouting out in any way. It’s totally unisex, as well. Great for any time and any place in my opinion. Jo Malone did very well on this blend!

Fresh and herbaceous from the basil, this is a sharp green scent that invigorates the senses. There is bitterness from the neroli which combines with the basil for a calming combination. I do not smell the musk notes, and unfortunately, the scent lasts around an hour on my skin. It is a pleasing scent that would work well in the summer and in casual day-to-day gatherings.

Today, oppressive humidity weighed down on the city - and the sky looked like lead. People were crawling along at a snail's pace, and I was right there among them. I dragged myself into the perfumery to rest at the Malone Bar. So many promising bottles lined up in a row. My tired eyes spelled out Neroli - and that was enough to promise relief. I only noticed the word Basil on my second reading. And so it is with the scent. The cool, refreshing Neroli is immediately present - and it tears open the looming clouds from which a relieving rain pours down. It is soft summer rain that pampers skin and hair. It also awakens the spicy green basil, and one finds oneself in a rain-soaked herb garden, from which the aromas intensely escape. Musk smooths the fragrance, keeping it soft and supple. Despite good longevity and intensity, Basil & Neroli retains a likable Cologne character that suits warm temperatures. The Malones also have a certain natural tone that appeals to me. A label that I will keep an eye on.

You know, I've been trying out a lot of Jo Malone fragrances lately. This might not come across very well here since I don't immediately write a comment on each one, but I believe that in not too long a time, I will have tested several fragrances in detail, possibly even some that have since been discontinued… and of all things, Wild Fig & Cassis I probably won't find anywhere anymore, even though this scent sounded like a lovely summer fragrance to me :((((((( But since I'm talking about summer fragrances: Well, here comes a scent that is quite new and sounds very interesting with its few notes. Basil & Neroli, so basil and well, neroli, sounds nice and also summery, plus it also reminds me a bit of the scent Néroli Doré by Hermès, which I also found quite nice. Let's see how this one is. The scent: Actually, the scent can't really be divided into top, heart, and base notes, as all the notes are present from the very beginning. Well, the musk does come in later, but still, the fragrance has a rather simple yet very beautiful progression. From the start, you can smell a herbal or somewhat bitter neroli, as it works together with the basil to give off a fragrant, summery scent. A little later, light sweet notes from the musk come in, but they all remain behind the neroli and basil. And so the scent stays this way until it unfortunately ends far too quickly. The sillage and longevity: The projection is unfortunately very moderate and won't be very strong for one to two hours. It can only be smelled nearby within an hour, and for oneself, the scent rises a little better, but overall, it remains quite weak. The same goes for longevity, where the scent is hardly detectable after just two hours. But, that's just how colognes are… unfortunately… The bottle: Here too, we have the rectangular bottle filled with a yellowish fragrance liquid. On the front, there is a rectangular label with a simple frame displaying the name and brand. The cap of the bottle is round. All in all, as always, it's quite okay, but not outstanding. So, I find the scent very successful. Although it has unfortunately turned out to be very, very weak, it still smells quite good of herbs and neroli, making it a lovely, summery fragrance. However, as mentioned, since it is weak, it can only be used as a daytime and casual scent, and one should always have a travel spray with them to reapply every two hours. Additionally, the scent reminds me quite a bit of Néroli Doré by Hermès, which is also a lovely neroli scent with herbs, only that Hermès uses saffron instead of basil. Both scents are actually equally good,… and both scents are also equally weak. I think I find this one from Jo Malone a bit better, but not so much better that both scents don't end up with a solid 7.5 points from me. And because of MrWhite's statement, I now keep thinking about the little rat Basil… well, thanks a lot… :D (tsss… and today's youth doesn't even know these classic Disney movies…)

Recently, I stumbled upon the Jo Malone counter in a Douglas. Finally. Two favorites. One order. Extensive testing upon arrival. Basil & Neroli - I thought of well-off, older ladies with very expensive leather handbags and fur collars, who do their shopping at KaDeWe. They are draped in elegant fabrics and this scent that they leave behind in the aisles of the luxury department store among cashmere sweaters, fine dark chocolates, and bottles of champagne. I envision high tea and English decadence with golden spoons and clotted cream. Now I would like to wear brocade and stroke velvet cushions, surrounded by dark woods and a fine whisky.

You can certainly wear it alone. It is beautiful. Fresh, spring-like, lively, friendly, and much more. However, I like to combine it with another Jo Malone, namely Myrrh & Tonka. Yes, that's right, you read correctly. I think these two go really well together. The scent starts for me in the first seconds with grassy notes.

Absolutely obsessed with the Givenchy L'Interdit collection, specifically the Eau De Parfum and the Rouge! I ended up ordering some decants of other flankers including the Absolu, Rouge Ultime, and the 2019 Eau de Toilette. I decided I loved the springy, floral of the 2019 Eau de Toilette, which is not being produced anymore, so I ordered it from Amazon. I know, probably a mistake. I am very new to fragrances. That being said, the 2022 Eau de Toilette arrived in its place. I was disappointed because I hadn't had the chance to try it yet and worried I wasted a new fragrance purchase on something I wouldn't wear. It is definitely not as floral as the 2019 Toilette, but I have decided it was a good purchase nonetheless. It is a mild, light version of the Eau de Parfum, perfectly suitable for the slowly rising temperatures of late winter and early spring. It's a bit more woody and citrusy than the 2019 Toilette and the Eau de Parfum. A little powdery, soft, and grassy, while maintaining the interest of the L'Interdit collection. Sad that I may not be able to obtain a larger size of the 2019 Toilette, but I did get a full refund for the wrong fragrance being sent, so a win-win! This will be a key springtime fragrance for me.

A floral sweet fragrance with slightly fruity notes. Suitable for everyday wear as well as for the evening. I was drawn to it because of the combination of my favorite notes, orange blossom and jasmine, and it convinced me right away. The tuberose is beautifully highlighted. I find the base note very well balanced. I have a lovely new fragrance in my collection that I will surely reach for often.

I find L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum too old-fashioned; it smells too earthy and nostalgic. In contrast, L'Interdit (2022) Eau de Toilette is younger and more vibrant. I simply love this version. It suits every occasion and season. What bothered me has been left out here. For everyone looking for an all-rounder or who finds L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum too old-fashioned. For me personally, it is one of the best perfumes, and you don't smell it everywhere. I always receive positive comments about it. I've had it for almost half a year and have already repurchased it.

I have heard people rave about this fragrance with almost reverent enthusiasm a few times, which is why I wanted to test it. Without this influence, it probably would never have happened, as I hadn’t considered the brand and the bottle doesn’t really appeal to me. But here we are: So the sillage is really good, the scent has punch :) And I love the opening of this fragrance: Really sweet and sticky-fruity, but in such an elegant, mature, and high-quality way that it truly impressed me! Sweet and fruity are not my favorite scent notes anymore; I used to enjoy that kind of thing 10 years ago. But L'interdit - at least how it smells in the first 30 minutes - I would still wear in my 30s. However, after that, the perfume changes significantly. The noble sweetness becomes something flatter and weaker to my nose. It somehow reminds me of desserts sweetened with artificial sweeteners or stevia. That sweetness is so different and, I think, only really comes at the very end when swallowing the bite. After 2-3 hours, there’s no trace of the fruitiness left; instead, I now smell more of the musk, patchouli, and sandalwood. So it goes from sweet-fruity to powdery-woody. For me, the fragrance makes almost a 180° turn in a direction that I unfortunately can’t really enjoy.

Today the package arrived with this blind buy. I did smell the fragrance once on my colleague, but it was a completely different scent on her :) Already when unpacking, I thought, oh dear, this is unfortunately not for me. The scent itself is not bad, I just personally don’t like it on myself. Since I applied it 2 hours ago, I’ve been suffering ;) I smell a sugary toilet spray rose here, it’s quite terrible :) As if there’s a heavy Turkish rose in the heart and base notes, but it’s not listed. I had imagined something completely different with this fragrance, so it’s definitely not a blind buy candidate, but I should have been alerted by this new feature at the top where fragrances are compared to others - I also absolutely do not like Elie Saab Le Parfum. I’m going to wash this off now, because which fragrances last the longest? The ones you don’t like ;)

It is beautiful expensive smelling creamy spicy little bit powdery sandalwood. If someone has problem sometimes with sandalwood that can be little bit piercing too much this is a choice. Very elegant and lush. I am selling decants/samples but first i need to understand how to post in Souk :)

Saying that I love Eau de Californie would be an understatement. It opens up with a dirty citrus and then settles into a mossy, slightly smoky palo santo that feels deliciously creamy and airy yet never sweet. It's my idea of effortlessly cool. A little raunchy. Messy-sexy, like stealing a few sprays from the bottle you found in the bathroom of the guy you spent the night with, maybe one of his shirts too, and slipping out bright and early while he's still peacefully asleep. Safe to say it's my #1 favorite from Celine, together with Nightclubbing. Unfortunately, it really doesn't last long - maybe 2-3 hours, before becoming a very intimate skinscent. If they ever came out with a more concentrated version, it would make me extremely happy.

This is beautiful, dry and meditative but also very classic is structure..woody bergamote and moss. I sense vanilla and orris lingering in the dry California climate. Palo Santo has a creamy, oily smell but here it is dry. It's my favorite of the Celine's I've tried. My issue with this scent lies in its lackluster performance vs the price. Yes it's classy, luxurious, refined and honestly incredible smelling, but it vanishes in an hour. For $400 bucks at least give me a little more than a skin scent version of an Eau de Cologne? It's advertised as an Eau du Parfum.

I'm obsessed with Eau de Californie. I'm not even a huge fan of this genre that straddles chypre and clean girl aesthetic, but omg this blew me away. I think it's my favorite from Celine. Definitely possesses a similar DNA to Prada Infusion d'Iris & YSL Trench, but Eau de Californie is 100x better IMO, it's just so balanced and dreamy. I can totally see this being a signature scent of mine. A must have for any Iris/Orris lover.

I only see this scent on a man, because it reminds me the most of all the Celines of a typical fresh Eau de Parfum/Toilette for men.. It feels very fresh and quite generic in the first 20-30 minutes. It could also be a regular men's fragrance from Douglas. Ouch, sorry Celine, but that's how it comes across to me in the opening. I almost gave up on the scent immediately.. Not sweet, woody, and zesty. I've smelled it a thousand times already. That's how I perceive the scent right after spraying it.. In short, uninteresting… However, in the drydown, the scent becomes significantly more interesting and almost a bit magical. A fragrance that definitely needs the warmth of the skin and time to fully develop.. But the wait is worth it… In the drydown, very soft, bright, super lovely woody notes emerge along with a very nice spiciness that becomes quite noticeable.. The scent feels significantly less zesty in the drydown and becomes almost soft/spicy and much, much more interesting.. The patchouli, considering my aversion to this note, is not overwhelming but super pleasantly earthy without being musty.. Celine is an artist when it comes to patchouli.. What could almost pass as a boring mainstream scent in the opening transforms in the drydown into a very spicy/woody yet soft and super pleasant fragrance.. It has a bit of a very bright cigar box vibe.. I see the scent on a man in a casual suit. Suitable for everyday wear but also good for the evening.. My grammar leaves much to be desired, but I am Danish and I am fighting a battle with German grammar :-/…

This is my second favourite perfume from the new lavenderland collection by jo Malone. My favourite is lavender & wisteria (probably 8.1) for smell but very close comes this silver birch & lavender (7.9). The smell is very pleasant. It has some similarities with other perfumes that yann vasnier has made for this brand. It shares fornexample the same vibe that the roasted OAK gives to the fragance in english OAK & hazelnut ir un the redcurrant one, or even the hemlock & bergamota. At the same time It has something common with other perfumes of yann vasnier like toy boy by moschino. The birch gives Also something yo the dry down which makes me think of aventus by creed (but without any fruity or sweet note) and the lavander gives to the mix some similarities with 154 also by jo Malone. In the background this perfume has some aniseed feeling very close to the vibe that you can find in the background of bronze wood and leather. Regarding to performance, this one has the BEST longevity and projection in the collection and It could be, probably, one of the fragances in the whole jo Malone collection with BEST performance. SB&L lasts for hours on skin and It is noticeable for one or two hours easyly. This is not a beast but i havent tied any JM London fragance which could be considered as a beast til the moment. Si probably if we take in count the whole fragance and not only the smell could be even better than W&L for myself. This perfume is for me totally unisex, probably even more masculine than femenino and very versatile, weareable at any time and for almost any occasion. Recommendable for lavender lovers ir the ones wwho likes the classical Green and fresh fougere scents. Scent: 8 Longevity: 8 Sillage: 6 Quality/price: 7 Versatility: 9 Originality: 6 Global: 8.5

The eyes slowly open. Light, thin, cool bed linens lie over you. Fresh and clean, as if they have just been hung up. Everything in the room is wrapped in warm white - the ceiling, the walls of light birch wood, the light. A gust of wind from the open window gently moves the curtains, allowing the clear morning air to flow into the room. With the first deep breath, various impressions blend together. Not far away, a river flows - far enough that its scent is not directly perceivable, but close enough that its moisture enriches the air with a cool, fresh note. A mix of wood, cool stone, and perhaps a hint of moss. The birch walls radiate their dry, bright wood note, which combines with a light citrus freshness, as if it were rising from the bed linens. Outside the window, an open meadow spreads out. The grass is barely noticeable, yet the lavender in front of the window adds a fine, aromatic accent to the air. Further back, birches rise at the edge of the forest, their silver trunks glowing in the morning sun. Their bark gives off an almost peppery, slightly smoky freshness that is carried over by the wind. The sun slowly rises higher. Its light shines on the wooden floor, which absorbs the warmth and gently releases it again. The air remains fresh, but with each passing minute, it becomes a little softer. A morning - clear, bright, and calm Top Note: Grapefruit - Zesty, cool, and invigorating. Like a fresh breeze in the morning that flows through the room. It does not remain dominant for long but gently transitions into the heart note. Heart Note: true lavender - Aromatic and clean. Brings a light herbal note reminiscent of bed linens. It stays in the background the whole time and feels somewhat grassy and green. Base Notes: Roasted oak adds warmth to the fragrance, but the smokiness is only faintly perceptible. White birch - Dry and finely woody, with a gentle freshness. A base that is surprisingly well noticeable despite its light nature. Conclusion: A fresh, woody-aromatic fragrance - clear, airy, and warm at the same time. Perfect for a bright morning full of calm and lightness.

... for a rather high price of the products, I find the price-performance ratio not particularly good. The fragrance pyramid is actually very promising but unfortunately does not deliver what it promises. Upon applying this scent, the first thing that hits the nose is the freshness of grapefruit, which is only present for a very short time and then shifts to lavender, which also doesn't last very long. Following that are the woods, which are simply dry. The longevity and sillage are average. This unisex fragrance can be worn year-round for any occasion. There is also no age restriction here. Anyone who enjoys a briefly fresh and then woody scent will find themselves well placed here for quite a bit of money.

Tubéreuse de Madras on my skin is mainly a milky tuberose. This once carnal flower is now devoid of camphor, butter, indole or anything animalic in Tubéreuse de Madras. It's so skimmed of fat that it kind of reminds me of soy milk at first, which is a surprising twist during the opening. However, slowly but surely, the creamy sweetness of vanilla permeates every corner of the dry down. Tubéreuse de Madras eventually becomes a generic creamy musky vanilla tuberose until the end. The fragrance mostly stays close to the skin during its 9-hour longevity. Although the soy milk opening phase is quite interesting and the fragrance itself is mostly agreeable, the vanilla white floral dry down feels rather routine and commercial, and eventually falls flat compared to the many great tuberose perfumes before it. Considering its hight price and limited availability, I'm not sure it's special enough to worth the particular effort to track it down.

Admittedly, tuberose was not exactly one of Can's favorite scents. But I bravely sacrificed myself to introduce you to the fifth Boucheron, Tubéreuse de Madras. When I first smelled Tubéreuse de Madras, a scene from my early childhood immediately came to mind. I was maybe four years old when my grandmother took me on a trip to visit her sister in Munich. We visited Aunt Lotti. Aunt Lotti had lived in London for many years and, of course, had a lot of quirky stuff at her home. Or running around, including a dog, a Pekingese she once brought from China, who answered to the name Chang-Ling. In the living room stood a huge display cabinet full of porcelain figurines. Since I was still very small, I could only see the bottom row; I didn't need to see more, because "she" was there. "She" was about twenty centimeters tall, had far too short chubby legs, wore a much too short blue dress, and had a round face with a nose that was either too small or hardly there at all. "She" stood in a pose as if she were smelling something. With her little hands clasped behind her back, her upper body slightly bent forward and her nose held up to the wind. Between you and me,... "she" was my first platonic love. Fragile, delicate, fine, and indescribably feminine. Tubéreuse de Madras would have been her scent! Tubéreuse de Madras starts with a delicate fruity accord in the form of orange blossom. Subtly citrusy and fruity. Passion fruit is also detectable, but it is hardly noticeable. A gentle sweetness slowly creeps in, slightly boozy and alcoholic. In my opinion, that's the frangipani. Tuberose soon joins in, and the whole thing takes on a slightly sweet and liqueur-like floral note. One could describe it as a floral liqueur. Tubéreuse de Madras also contains vanilla, here in the form of a dusty and dry vanilla. A slightly antique touch is added by the sandalwood. It tempers the floral aspect in a very pleasant way. Conclusion Tubéreuse de Madras is a stable yet finely delicate scent. Fragile, tender but also latently present in a very special way. Nostalgic yet modern and contemporary. For tuberose lovers, a must! Longevity: 8 to 10 hours on average. Sillage: Initially strong, but quickly settles to a good medium level. Gender: Female, absolutely!!! A beautiful neo-romantic tuberose scent. But with enough modernity in tow. Beautifully and high-quality made. To address the questions in advance. Yes! This test was difficult for me. And, no! ...my first platonic love did not shape my view of women.

I tried my sample today and instantly fell in love, but I couldn't quite put my finger on why the scent felt so familiar. Then it hit me - I have the oil versions of both the neroli and orange blossom by Ortigia, and I usually layer them because they're my dream team on very hot and humid summer days. Soleil Blanc too, now that I think about it. Un ete francais smells incredibly similar, although a little sweeter than Ortigia and more citrusy than Soleil Blanc, and much more long lasting. It opens with a bold hit of neroli, in all its bitter green glory, but as it starts to settle it becomes increasingly creamy, leaving behind a balmy, salty feeling - like the scent of your skin after a day spent sunbathing on the French Riviera. It's incredibly chic, just like the rest of the Celine offerings.

There are scenes that you immediately associate with a film - and for me, it's the scene on the skyscraper in Vanilla Sky, where Tom Cruise stands on the roof and the famous call echoes: Open your eyes. What Tom Cruise sees in that moment is a sky that couldn't be more beautiful: vanilla-colored, pastel tones, boundless, almost surreal. This sky is no coincidence, but deliberately inspired by the impressionist paintings of Claude Monet. I just can't remember which one. That's exactly the kind of sky I see when I smell Un Été Français by Celine: the most beautiful pastel yellow tones, flowing into an emerald green Mediterranean landscape - all bathed in light and full of vanilla harmony, as if Monet himself had swung the brush with buttery softness. When I smell the fragrance, however, not only does a dreamily beautiful impressionist sky unfold, but an entire daydream. Un Été Français is more than just a scent - it is a journey back to the summer memories of childhood and youth. And yes, perhaps it wasn't a vacation on the French Riviera, but afternoons at a mundane swimming pool, no Mediterranean thicket, but the smell of freshly mown grass by the poolside, no salty sea breeze, but a light scent of chlorine in the hair. And yet the feeling was surely the same: happiness, lightness, and carefreeness - something that sometimes gets lost in everyday life. It is precisely these memories that come alive through the fragrance: I perceive a subtle sunscreen note on warm skin, perhaps also a hint of coconut creaminess and a green, gentle vanilla sweetness that Celine does very well. The wheel may not be completely reinvented here, but the fragrance is truly beautiful to my nose. I would like to conclude this review with a movie quote from Sofia, alias Penélope Cruz: “Every passing minute is another chance to turn it all around.” Perhaps this fragrance will also awaken beautiful daydreams in you and remind you to stay open to the special moments that life has to offer - and the chance to make the best of it. I wish you much joy in discovering and will conclude with: “Open your eyes.”

The sample of Un Été Français reached me unexpectedly. While I always enjoy testing new releases, I wouldn't have rushed to get this one based solely on the fragrance pyramid. The combination of bergamot with petitgrain and neroli sounded too bitter/piercing/harsh to me, and I could hardly imagine how it would find a pleasant balance with gorse and vanilla. However, the manufacturer's sample was there, and it piqued my curiosity. Generally, there are few scents with neroli that I like. I usually find it piercing, rather masculine, and often old-fashioned. But here it is really well-rounded. The fragrance is equally refreshing and soft from the very beginning. I would have expected to wait longer for the vanilla base to emerge, but that is not the case. Coconut is not listed, but I perceive it along with the vanilla. In the drydown, the warm-soft notes prevail, and you smell well-groomed and moisturized. Un Été Français is a very mature summer scent, fresh, creamy, lightly woody, and unisex wearable. Typical Celine DNA - smells expensive, is not loud, and is very pleasing, but not generic. The sillage is close to the skin, which I find very fitting and pleasant. When someone wears this fragrance, it is perceived rather subtly. Very unobtrusive and stylish. I cannot assess the longevity, as I only tested one spray on my skin. Here it lasts at least a few hours, but it becomes quieter. For anyone looking for a pleasant, elegant, and unsweet summer scent, I highly recommend giving this one a try.

A fragrance like a daydream on the Riviera: Un Été Français opens like a salt-kissed breeze wafting through the open window, flooding the room with light and life. The first notes are carried by cool, zesty bergamot - they remind me of the first glass of Orangina in the shade of a pine tree while the sun dances outside. Then comes the broom, a bright yellow summer messenger that grows wild in the hills of southern France, exuding a honeyed, almost coconut-like scent with green freshness. It is soft, warm, sunny, and yet always a little wild. In France, it is deeply rooted in the landscapes of Provence and Brittany, where it shines on coastal slopes and in field edges like a living fan of sunlight. In the poetry of French literature, broom often symbolizes natural grace and resilience. No glamour, but quiet beauty. Suddenly, there is music too. Very softly, almost like a memory that doesn’t announce itself - “Di Doo Dah” by Jane Birkin. The melody hangs in the air like sunlight: playful, shy, a little offbeat. No grand gesture, but a whispered “Je suis là” - I am here. And she appears. The woman in the overalls. Not staged, but present. Her outfit, the loosely falling denim overalls, the classic Breton striped shirt, seems as if she has never worn anything else. Her sandals click softly on the warm pavement, a straw hat in her hand, a book under her arm. She is no apparition; she is part of summer. Her skin carries salt and sun, her thoughts drift like her hair. Perhaps she is thinking of nothing - or of everything that is still possible. Un Été Français is not a fragrance of grand gestures. It is a quiet film, a lived afternoon, a memory of a feeling that never quite fades.

If the color yellow had a scent, it would be this fragrance. It smells creamy from the broom and neroli, with neroli being very prominent here and making up the entire scent. It is also creamy-green rounded by petitgrain, but not sweet. The fragrance, although it resembles a sunscreen, overall feels fresh-creamy, sesame-soft, summery. After 2 hours, it settles even milder, more Nivea-creamy on the skin. Definitely a summer fragrance candidate and rather feminine for me - soft, warm, yellowish, radiating warmth. Similarity to Soleil Blanc - absolutely, but Tom Ford's creation is brighter, more present, sweeter, infused with ylang-ylang. Although I find the fragrance good for summer days, for me, its price-performance ratio is not justified. One could also smell like a sunscreen or with Nivea-Sun perfume... and perhaps even longer.

Jo Malone are extremely high quality perfumes, although they are very 'transparent', which can be displeasing to those who like denser perfumes. You can see several notes merging and evolving. Truly works of art that deserve to be known. It starts with a floral touch (lavender) that reminds us of a garden in a humid climate. Over time, it becomes sweeter with the mixture of almond milk and honey. A sweet floral, which gives us strength considering the weight of the notes. Projection is good at first, but it gets weaker and remains very light in the middle and base notes. The longevity is exceptional, it lasts for about 7 hours, but considering that it is a cologne, it is in a good average. Very different fragrance and can be used at work, as it is light and very transparent. High quality notes.

As a food and pleasure item, I find honey wonderful - from light bright acacia to velvety opaque clover to deep dark forest honey. I like to bring back local honey as souvenirs from my travels, and English honey - best on still warm, butter-soaked crumpets (these are somewhat spongy yeast cakes that are often sold pre-packaged for baking) or simply on toast - has never disappointed me. And when I first read Michael Ende's Momo as a child, the passage where she gets to eat fresh, golden-brown, crispy rolls with butter and honey from Master Hora impressed me the most. In perfumes, however, I often find honey challenging. Sometimes its sweet loveliness gives the scent an overly childlike innocence (making it a nice children's fragrance, which I find a bit silly on non-children) or it tends to become overly sweet in a Venus flytrap way, in the sense of 'Catch me' (which is no less silly). In short, honey in my subjective taste perception needs a counterbalance - something that balances the melting sweetness without overshadowing its inherent allure. Flowers or related accords are only partially suitable for this, although the attempt here is not uninteresting. Jo Malone's English Fields - Honey and Crocus is clearly more of a honey than a crocus scent. (What is a crocus scent anyway? Saffron is derived from the flower stigmas of the crocus, its aroma has a somewhat bitter and metallic quality that, as culinary evidence shows, works very well to balance sweetness.) The top note and dominant scent impression are monochromatically honey-sweet (and for me, for the aforementioned reasons, somewhat challenging). Lavender is by no means present and strong enough to serve as the required counterbalance. Only after a while does almond at least add a second facet of gourmand quality, and finally - although only very subtly and vaguely - the bitterness and fragility of the crocus with a very gently burnt accord. A bit like the roasted aromas in the crumpet or toast crumb under melting butter and golden clear flower honey - regardless of whether it's English or not. Conclusion: neither a children's nor a Venus flytrap scent. Instead, golden clear honey on butter-soaked, warm toast, very sensual and beautiful at its core. I don't need to smell like that myself.

Aaaaaah! During my last visit to the turquoise-colored fragrance store, I was shown the latest limited editions from Jo Malone without even asking. Of course, I have to say that I am somewhat known there, which brings joyful faces when I show up… at least I like to convince myself of that and hope that I am not considered the biggest nuisance there *sigh* He he, but as I said, they know that I really like both Jo Malone fragrances and fragrances in general, so I am always informed about new scents by some of them. Just like these five new, soon-to-be-released limited fragrances from Jo Malone, each of which I quite liked. The special feature of this English Fields fragrance line lies in the grain notes that the scents contain. The perfumer spent many summers in rural areas where various grains were grown. She loved the scent of these grains, especially when they were harvested. These fragrances eventually inspired her to think that grain notes could work well in a perfume. And yes, that is indeed true, as each of the five new fragrances is quite successful and worth a look or a sniff. Today, I will start with the scent Honey & Crocus, which was one of the most beautiful in the line for me. The Scent: The scent initially begins with an intense almond/almond milk note with a nutty background, briefly reminding me of treats like Ferrero Rocher and Küsschen. Next, I can smell the honey, which has a warm and quite liquid (not sticky) scent. However, the honey is somewhat weaker compared to the other fragrance notes, as the scent is sweet but leans more towards chocolate-nut-almond milk. This later makes it reminiscent of some delicious Müller milk drinks with chocolate-nut flavor :D (though the nuttiness gradually diminishes). The floral aspect of the scent is herbaceous; you can clearly tell that there is lavender in it. I'm not so sure about the crocus, as I didn't even know what crocuses were without looking it up… for your information: they are plants that include saffron, for example. Wow, I didn't know that,… hmm… but you probably did, right? :D Otherwise, there are (but more in the background) the grain notes that leave a nice impression. Nevertheless, in the base, you still smell more of the sweet scents like almond milk with chocolate-like honey, and it also seems a bit like there is tonka bean in it. The scent is generally very smooth, gentle, and creamy, and should appeal to most of you! The Sillage and Longevity: The scent has a good projection. I think it will be pleasantly detectable from a normal distance for a while, although it naturally doesn't remain strong forever and starts to fade a bit after two or three hours, well, like many fragrances do. The longevity is quite good as well, as the scent lasted on me for more than eight hours. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular and tall. It has a brownish-pink-beige color in a pastel look, making it visually very appealing (like all the other bottles in this line) and has a rocky base, resembling a rocky wallpaper, which provides a rough but great tactile experience and is of course also nice to look at. The cap is the same color as the bottle and is cylindrical, but in my opinion, it fits a bit too tightly on the bottle. All in all, a very nice-looking bottle. Ahh,… since I just described the beautiful bottle and the scent smells so great here, I am really tempted to devour the scent along with my skin and hair… uh, I meant with the bottle (in this case, including the glass and chrome) :D Seriously, this scent really smells wonderful and is a true dream fragrance for anyone who especially loves almond, almond milk, generally sweet gentle-creamy notes with a hint of honey and flowers. It is especially good for going out, although it could hold a bit longer or stronger for that purpose. On the other hand, despite some heavier fragrance notes, it is also suitable for spring, and of course, for autumn as well. I haven't said this in a long time, so please forgive me if I come back with one of my old phrases, but with this scent on your gentle skin, one would like to bite or even devour you ladies, yay! Argh,… I always wonder how such a scent smells on guys… *sigh*

Since 2015, I have been following the limited Jo Malone collections with great interest and joy. I have spent many lovely hours with these rather special fragrances. Previously, there was usually a kind of "hunt" for this or that from this family on eBay; the prices shoot up so high - it’s incredible! Thus, my expectations for the new seasonal collection "English Fields" were correspondingly high; everything sounds very nice - not to mention the photos; they tempt you to buy again. I decided on "Honey & Crocus" from this line to make a friend of mine happy and to say "thank you" for many things. Of course, I had to test this fragrance before I sent the bottle on: she knows me and has learned to live with my quirks, more or less well! The sweetness alone is something to get used to. Anyone who, like me, sees the clarity of Jo Malone creations as a great advantage must rethink here. It is indeed a clear liquid that comes from the bottle, but based on the scent, I would initially expect something creamy-white! "Honey & Crocus" immediately reminds me of a heavy body lotion, dominated by nourishing almond milk. I carry this scent veil around with me for a while: I am not entirely happy with it! Lavender and honey go very well together here, and the slightly saffron-like crocus nuance soon reveals itself. The illusion of an evening stroll along ripe, blooming fields sets in quite quickly. The longevity is like with all Jo Malone fragrances: it is rather moderate; only the almond milk endures. The bottle has the usual, almost somewhat puristic shape, but it feels as if it is not quite finished. Something about it is foreign! The familiar lightness that has always done justice to the contents is missing here. I am not quite sure whether I really like this fragrance creation. It is a strange, very strange kind of Jo Malone fragrance. My friend is also not entirely happy with it: she finds "Honey & Crocus" a bit too sweet. Although she visited the Jo Malone townhouse during her trip to London and "sniffed around" there, she cannot quite warm up to this scent. I regret that, of course. Because this fragrance should bring her joy and not unsettle her. Unfortunately, this sometimes happens with gifts: you miss the mark a bit with your own decision! Conclusion: for me, this seasonal collection from Jo Malone was unfortunately not created. On one hand, it’s a pity, on the other hand, I hardly know where to put these square bottles anymore. They don’t take up much space due to their slimness; but here, it’s the mass that counts! In this respect, it’s good that at least one more fragrance from this series doesn’t want to move in with me. Who knows what it will look like around this time next year?

I casually scattered crocus bulbs generously across various spots in my lawn - and my husband raised an eyebrow in doubt. But we both press our noses against the window when the first crocuses finally appear, forming white-lilac-yellow islands. This signifies the long-awaited departure of winter. A delicate floral scent fills the air - a hint of spring. This fragrance and the colorful sight have something comforting about them. Slowly, golden honey flows into the lavender tea - for one still needs warmth from within. Equally leisurely, almond milk spreads across my winter skin. Spring will take its time - but one knows it will come.

At the first sniff of the TZ with the sample, I thought: wow - intensely reminiscent of bitter almond or marzipan. But on the skin, the perfume turned out to be softer and creamier. Almond milk? Yes, that really fits! But a few bitter almonds have sneaked in, which is good because the sweet almond has a rather subtle aroma.

When someone who absolutely cannot stand the scent of lavender falls in love with a fragrance that contains it... The Bottle Typical for Jo Malone scents in a limited edition, all English Fields fragrances come in the classic Jo Malone design with a twist.

For me, the almond milk completely overpowers the scent. Whenever I've tried it again, I just have to think of marzipan... not my favorite scent. I can't smell honey or flowers at all here. The longevity must be quite good, as once I smell the fragrance, it unfortunately lingers in my nose for hours.

This creation by Marie Salamagne for the Givenchy La Collection Particuliere is a masterpiece. I had initially written this review based on a 10 ml mini bottle, purchased directly from Givenchy as a discovery set (3 for $99). As these perfumes are very expensive, the 10 ml bottle is more than just a sample. Recently I upgraded to a full bottle. This review has been updated accordingly. I was delighted to encounter Trouble Fête, primarily because it supports my hypothesis that fig leaf accord must be supplemented with floral notes to make it work. The opening accord in Trouble Fête is the celebrated fig leaf, but the perfumer Marie Salamagne manages to make it soft and natural. It is a fig leaf that is wafting in the wind, not something that is pungent and up your nose as in Philosykos. The green opening note is immediately complemented and enhanced by the sambac jasmine accord. Givenchy lists roasted sesame as another heart note, but it does not stand out among the fig leaf and jasmine. Trouble-Fête ends with a base note of Somalian incense essence, which I believe is a composite of frankincense, sandalwood and agar wood. My nose gets a soft, sweet woody mix, but not these distinct notes. The olfactory pyramid is very smooth and beautiful. Trouble Fête can be translated roughly as a spoilsport or party-pooper. Yet this trouble is not the raucous kind, but rather the wistful memory of a beautiful love long gone. This feeling is perhaps appropriate as Givenchy lists the intensity of Trouble Fête as moderate (2/4). It lasts 4-6 hours on my skin, but I can smell the incense even after eight hours. The sillage is appropriately subdued, but detectable a few feet away for the first few hours. This would be fantastic office perfume. I recommend Trouble Fete without any hesitation, if you can afford it. As I mentioned before, 10 ml vial is a good compromise. This is not a perfume that you appraise based on performance. But the soft elegance of Trouble Fête makes it one of the best in La Collection Particuliere, and in my personal collection.

Rarely has a name been so misleading. But I don't want to get ahead of myself. The fragrance has a wonderfully green fresh opening, for which the fig leaf is responsible according to the fragrance pyramid. Green fresh can indeed be interpreted widely, here: no grassy notes, no galbanum, no lemon-hay infusion or lawn, but simply an idea of leaf green that lingers in your mind. While many fig fragrances focus on the fruit, or at least try to, Givenchy skips this coloring and instead enriches fig leaf and woody notes with floral jasmine - and does so very skillfully! The jasmine is immediately softly buttery (but pleasant, non-indolic) present and lays down velvety on the skin in the drydown. Interestingly, even after hours, green fresh and floral notes continue to compete with each other. The fragrance remains throughout a finely tuned fig wood-jasmine composition; jasmine does not dominate the play of associations. Although at the very end, after many hours (!), jasmine naturally has the longest endurance. But since we were just talking about associations: There’s something else there. A note that I wouldn't be able to identify at all if the marketing department of Givenchy hadn't decided to willingly include it in the fragrance pyramid: sesame. Roasted sesame. Not that it is somehow prominently present. Certainly not for my nose. But I perceive a nuance that is subtly sweet and warm, which does not remind me of flowers, namely: jasmine. I imagine it helps keep the green-floral notes from galloping away, instead embracing me warmly. Unfortunately, they forgot to make the incense detectable in the same way in the fragrance, which is why I can't pick it out at all. No matter. In conclusion, regarding the placement of the fragrance in the vast universe of "figs": I don't think Trouble-Fête has much in common with other fig fragrances, especially not with those that emphasize the fruit component, drift into sandalwood, and/or emulate coconut milk. This fragrance is a very harmonious duet of fig wood and jasmine. And thus, anything but a troublemaker.

“Cologne Céleste” is a bit more than an ordinary citrus cologne. It is a vast, light blue summer sky, over which white cotton clouds float angelically. It stretches over a citrus grove radiating southern cheerfulness, beneath whose glossy green canopy a small cheerful brook murmurs. Generously, spicy angelica greens at its edges. Here, this healing plant, also known as angelica root, loves to thrive, and its pleasant, unusual aroma weaves through this light, elegant composition. Here, the delicate scent of neroli presents itself, and almost as a counterpart, the “shredded” essence of the bitter orange, also called petitgrain, appears. Once again, opposites attract magically and form a harmonious pair; greatly benefiting “Cologne Céleste” by Celine. Warm, subtly animalic musk cream, interwoven with a pleasant iris note, softens any potentially overly citrusy sharp edges. Unfortunately, most classic Eau de Colognes are too cool for me, sometimes even too “sharp-edged.” That’s why I find this stylish, refreshing, yet still pleasantly soft creation very suitable for me. Southern flair envelops and accompanies me invigoratingly and gently refreshing for several hours. A beautiful everyday scent that has nothing ordinary about it: One could simply call it an “all-rounder.” “Summer beauty” is also very fitting. “Cologne Céleste” is my first acquaintance with the fragrances of the Celine brand, and I am thrilled by its Mediterranean soft elegance. I have already tested another fragrance sample from this house and am also very taken with it. Once again, a new door to the versatile realm of scents has opened, through which I am very happy to walk: My scent explorer gene feels exceptionally at home here.

French Lime Blossom is one of the more popular scents from Jo Malone's line, and I can see why. It's very feminine and pretty. Some consider Jo Malone fragrances overrated or just plain boring, yet I personally enjoy them for all their simplicity and sophistication. A complex scent is not always a good one. French Lime Blossom is a lovely fragrance from beginning to end. This fragrance for me, captures the scent of Spring in a bottle. It's green, dewy, delicate and flowery on the skin. French Lime Blossom also has a slightly clean and crisp feel, which makes it rather inoffensive. This scent is very versatile, something that could be worn either on a lazy Sunday with jeans and a t-shirt, or used as the finishing touch when wearing formal attire. I think it's also an easy scent to fall in love with. The lasting strength isn't overly wonderful, but then again, expectations shouldn't be too high in regards to cologne concentrations. Although these fragrances are intended to be layered, I think the house of Jo Malone would have a far better reputation if they released all their scents as EDPs. Other than a dominant lime blossom accord, lily of the valley, bergamot and petit grain also tend to shine through quite strongly in this composition. The only advice I give for those of you that wish to test this fragrance; keep in mind that the composition is predominately lime blossom, which means it's a floral. There are too many reviews complaining over a lack of juicy and sweet lime accords, and I think they're being a little misled by the name, even though it says it clearly enough. Think flowery, not fruity. Original review written: September 2012.

I don't think it's just me who feels this way, but much like how orange blossoms smell nothing like oranges, so too is the disparity between the fragrance of the blossom of the lime tree and actual fruit itself. I should also note that lime blossom smells nothing like orange blossom! Just using it for an example, I guess. Though like I said, I'm pretty sure that's how most people feel, so I don't mean to offer that opinion like I'm the first person to ever come to that conclusion. Anyway! We have a small lime tree in our yard and its flowers smell heavenly, but it's a delicate scent that I find elusive of precise description. Jo Malone's version captures it somewhat, the bright charm of a spring breeze, pearlescent morning dew, and sweetly herbaceous green sap encapsulated in in a small, white flower...which if I had to compare it to another blooming thing, I might say honeysuckle. But it's got an extra element of synthetic linen freshness and a note of something that smells like how a mild tingling jolt of static electricity feels, and this gives it a bizarre bionic blossom quality. It is a little odd? Maybe. Do I love it? Also maybe.

Recently in Paris, while searching for a new fragrance, I also visited a Jo Malone store. I explained to the friendly lady what I had in mind, and she handed me "French Lime Blossom," saying I shouldn't be deterred by the initial citrus wave. So, I sprayed it on generously! Wow, very fresh indeed, not exactly lemon, but Petitgrain could definitely be in there, and luckily the bergamot softens it. I want to wrinkle my nose a bit (oh no, now I have lime on my arm!), when the olfactory picture shifts, the acidity decreases, becoming sweeter, milder, more floral, this is... wait a minute... I know this: linden blossoms! Beautiful linden blossoms are joyfully racing with subtle (!), green lily of the valley into my fragrance heart! The jasmine plays only a supporting role and, together with the tarragon (don't worry, it doesn't evoke any memories of food), ensures that it doesn't drift into a stuffy, spinsterish territory. French Lime Blossom remains lightly soapy for me for 3 - 4 hours as a beautiful, fresh-romantic scent for everyday wear, even though it becomes very close to the skin at the end. After all, it's a Cologne! I can't identify the beeswax as a standalone note. The longevity is naturally not overwhelming, and the sillage is relatively subtle, depending on the spritzing enthusiasm of the wearer (I really can't imagine this sweet scent on a man).

I breathed a linden scent! In the room stood A branch of the linden, A gift From a dear hand. How lovely was the linden scent! How lovely is the linden scent! The linden twig You broke gently! I breathe softly In the scent of the linden The gentle scent of love. text Fr. Rückert Set to music by Gustav Mahler This beautiful song by Mahler, sung by Magdalena Kozena, perfectly captures the mood that this scent puts me in. A poem of, in my opinion, lesser quality finds a strong elevation through Mahler's composition. Great calm, security, lightness, introspection, accompanied by light, a shimmer like reflections on calm waters. The soul rests and breathes, while it glides in circles like a swan. I have long wished to find a true linden scent that smells like it does in early summer when the lindens send their heavy honey scent through the streets of our city and enchant me, letting me dream. This one is very authentic, with a hint of lily of the valley, which I also love dearly, harmonizing perfectly with it. I notice how closely related these two scents are. Lime blossoms are listed, bergamot, petitgrain, they must be responsible for the lightness, but does this whole floral blend create this authentic linden scent? Wormwood, fortunately, I do not find. It remains a mystery to me how this scent and the listing of the ingredients come together. No matter, it is beautiful!

A few months ago, I had a blind buy attack (the search for the holy grail, inspired by this forum), so I ordered 4 different Malone fragrances right away, and I was totally disappointed with this one. It taught me that I can't always rely on a deliciously written fragrance pyramid. I love the scent of linden blossoms; a few streets away, we have a whole avenue of linden trees. I practically grew up with that scent. So I was quite thrilled to discover such a perfume. My expectations were correspondingly high. I opened the package, sprayed the first spritz on my wrist, and.... Mothballs! Musty, soapy, so dry and dusty that I immediately got a real coughing fit. I gave it a bit more time; it did get a little better, as the other components do soften that mustiness a bit. After 3 hours, it’s all over anyway. I experimented a bit with layering between the 4 Malones, but unfortunately, this linden blossom is beyond saving. For me, a mispurchase. At least 2 of the 4 Malones are great.

Powderiest perfume I've encountered so far. Crushed almonds, fluffy iris and musky rose below – smelled like expensive makeup upon first spray. Moderate sillage – created a small cloud around me that dissipated and settled close to my skin after ~2 hours. Withered away completely in about ~4 hours in total. It's currently being aggressively advertised by several perfume shops in my area as a shiny new choice for summer season, which I find kind of bewildering. It's super heavy, very sweet and hard to breathe in even in mellow spring weather. It's very powdery, yes, but about an hour into the experience it also develops a weird creamy undertone. Not the tasty kind, more like a sunscreen. The cheapest "pore clogger 9000" you can buy at your local convenience store. It basically made me smell like I've already spent a few hours melting outside under the scorching sun. Reminded me of the worst days of my youth where I felt too embarrassed about my teenage skin and used half a kilo of concealer even when it was +35°C outside, thus making the situation even worse. A smell of misery and defeat. I don't know, perhaps it just didn't work as intended on my skin, but the only irrésistible thing about it was my desire to get back home and take a long shower.

I was just at Marionnaud to pick a fragrance for my stepfather's birthday. Behind me, the saleswoman had just sprayed the newly arrived "Nude Velvet" on a test strip to try it out herself. The scent wafted past me and I thought, "Oh, that's powdery, amazing!" I really wanted to test it, but unfortunately, I had already sprayed too many other fragrances on my skin. The saleswoman must have sensed my dilemma and was kind enough to give me a sample to take home (THANK YOU!). I tested the fragrance a few times and I really find it very beautiful. It starts off extremely dry and powdery on me (I love powdery scents!) and becomes softer and a bit clean-floral in the drydown, I think. A very feminine, soft fragrance with decent sillage and longevity. Men like it too :)

Next up are new releases from 2025: Nude Velvet from the Irresistible line. Givenchy is already one of my favorites in the designer sector, and the women's department, especially with the L'Interdit line, is one of my favorite collections for women. Not everyone knows Irresistible, and this line hasn't received much attention. That doesn't always mean anything, as some fragrances simply haven't been in the spotlight unjustly. I find the line quite good, and with Nude Velvet, a very interesting flanker has hit the market that aims to please iris fans with its powdery overall impression. And yes, the fragrance lives up to its name, as a sensual overall picture emerges here. Whether it's irresistible or not, everyone has to determine that for themselves. Such names always do well in marketing and sell quite well in the designer sector. In my opinion, Givenchy offers very good designer quality that has an elegant touch. Nude Velvet works well in everyday life, but also in daily situations with its powdery-sensual lipstick vibes. The MSRP for these women's designers is once again steep, as niche prices are almost demanded here. However, you can occasionally find a fair price on offer. Available in 35, 50, and 80ml. The bottle is quite ordinary with the usual Irresistible appearance in feminine pink, and the box is simple. The fragrance leans very much towards a well-groomed women's scent with a very sensual appearance due to the iris, which roughly goes in the direction of lipstick. The flanker has a pleasant sweetness, floral notes, and this powdery-creamy note that runs throughout the entire progression. The top note of ambrette seeds, almond, and neroli is very successful. Ambrette seeds provide the typical clean touch that ensures a great start, together with a sweet almond note. Neroli adds an underlying freshness that doesn't quite come through against the heavier notes. At the heart of the fragrance is, of course, the heart note of floral notes. The main character is, as mentioned, the iris, which has the familiar powdery character. Alongside it are rosy notes that I find quite convincing with the powdery iris. A wonderful sensual floral mix of rose and iris develops. The rose is not too heavy, as rose water provides lighter vibes alongside the Damask rose. The base supports the iris with light musk, which appears quite fluffy and clean. A bit of cedar accompanies the gentle base. A soft and sensual overall impression that is also suitable for everyday wear. A thoroughly feminine fragrance for all women who enjoy wearing extremely feminine scents. Performance is quite good with a great projection, and longevity is in the good middle range at about 8 hours, possibly a bit more. Overall, very convincing and a great blend of clean and sensual appearance with the iris-rose combination at the center and a pleasant sweetness. Easy to wear and suitable for many occasions.

That's exactly how this fragrance smells to me. I had a pink one in the 80s. I can't remember if it was raspberry or strawberry. Back then, we grew up with scented writing instruments and erasers. I loved sharpening that pencil. Today, in Duty Free, this note hits me again as I test #Irrisistible velvet nude for the first time. Woody, in an unusually powdery way! Not that dry powder note, but as if someone had moistened doll cosmetic powder. Strangely, I smell a very subtle raspberry note. I absolutely do not like it; it has a bit of Ditas Vanitesse mixed with LVEB. Or do you know that ready-made rice pudding product for lazy people? When you open the packaging, that starch/rice note comes to the fore. This fragrance has a bit of that too.

This fragrance immediately brings back memories of my childhood, of the moments when I secretly rummaged through my mom's makeup bag. It has a soft note. It's not 100 percent my taste, but I can definitely imagine wearing it to work, with a nice blouse, a bun, and cute earrings. It definitely has something.

Boucheron has a line of perfumes, named a very unimaginative La Collection Boucheron, which highlights a specific ingredient from an exotic location. This collection was developed by Inter Parfums which currently markets Boucheron perfumes. It includes perfumes like Iris de Syracuse, Oud de Carthage, Néroli d’Ispahan and many others. Rose d’Isparta is the rose representative in this group. Unfortunately, this collection is not advertised much, perhaps lost in the complicated marketing and ownership arrangement between Inter Parfums and Boucheron. Perfume lovers are advised to seek them out and test them, because many members in this collection offer excellent value. Rose d’Isparta was created in 2020 by Sonia Constant, a perfumer affiliated with Givaudan. Moonlight Patchouli, another creation from this perfumer, is a favorite of mine. This review is based on a full bottle bought from a US discounter. The notes listed for Rose d’Isparta on the Inter Parfums website are ginger, frankincense, ambrette, cinnamon, Turkish rose, saffron, sandalwood, musk and amber. Parfumo has additional notes – freesia, hawthorn, vanilla and tonka bean – that are not perceptible to me. According to my nose, the opening notes are frankincense, ginger and ambrette, but the latter two pale before the intensity of the incense. Within a few minutes the damascene rose starts appearing, enhanced by cinnamon and saffron notes. The base notes of sandalwood, musk and amber are good, but not impactful. Both the base notes and the dry down ends up as amorphous woody notes with some rose in it. The overall vibe of Rose d’Isparta can be summarized as incense-rose-woody, which continues from beginning to the end with minor changes. This perfume smells fantastic on a paper blotter but less so on my skin. So, adequate on-skin, at-home testing is recommended. Rose d’Isparta lasts long on my skin. The intensity and projection in the opening hours are excellent, bordering on excessive. I can smell the incense and rose even after 6-8 hours, but there is a drop off after the first few hours. If you are planning to wear it at work, start early and in small quantities. I would spray at least two hours before you walk into any closed space. In summary, Rose d’Isparta is a beautiful incense and rose perfume that is moderately priced. If you over-spray it, it takes on the personality of a cheap rose incense sticks that I am familiar with from my childhood in India. I am happy to have a full bottle as I currently lack a good incense-rose perfume, but this may not a sufficient reason for others. This is a value-based recommendation from me, as it costs less than $74 at the discounters in US.

This is primarily not a rose fragrance in the strict sense. The rose is certainly perceptible, but it does not take center stage. The rose note itself closely resembles the scent of a blooming Damask rose. It is somewhat old-fashioned, but I find that appealing. The frankincense is intensely noticeable in the top notes. In my opinion, the frankincense note lasts a long time. On my skin, even for several hours. For those who are phobic about frankincense, this fragrance is probably not for them. I remember the Sunday visits to church that I could not avoid as a child. In any case, there was no skimping on the frankincense, quite the opposite. After all, I have become somewhat hardened in that regard. A liturgical ritual that often brought me dizziness in the literal sense. However, the frankincense here does not seem overly sacred; it is a very appealing soft frankincense note that even surprised me positively, and I am convinced that I would classify and evaluate the scent of this ritual quite differently today. The freesia has been subtly woven with the other components and at least partially lightens the fragrance. Rose d'Isparta is consistently sweet-spicy, but by no means a gourmand. It is not an experimental niche perfume, but rather wearable and floral-spicy-oriental. The projection is decent. The perfume brightens winter days and truly warms you up. Embracing amber and sandalwood notes blend in the base with vanilla and tonka bean. On one hand, this makes the fragrance overall quite sweet, but on the other hand, it also fits the character of this unusual rose fragrance, which can only be classified as such in a broader sense. The vanilla is at least woody. The sandalwood provides a slight dry crackle. This perfume is not extravagant, but it is convincingly crafted. Nothing scratches; it is smooth and fits any winter coat, soft cashmere sweaters and scarves, campfires, and is hardly offensive otherwise. A small scent cloud can certainly be produced with this fragrance, and it is not a sticky-sweet perfume with sparing to moderate application. I would definitely not wear it in summer. Overall, it is a beautiful scent without "syntax errors." A complete success. I almost miss the edges and corners.

Okay, my dears, I know exactly what you're wondering: is this hairspray for fixing hairstyles or is it more like a hair perfume and an alternative to the perfume bottle? That's exactly what I was wondering. Summarized disillusionment: somehow neither of the two really. The container is not pressurized, as is common with deodorants or hairsprays, so it is sprayed like perfume. When I spray it, I am indeed surrounded by a Black Tie cloud. However, this lasts more than just a short while. I really don't have the scent in my hair afterwards; I rather smell my shampoo from the day before. In short - unsuitable as a hair perfume. But is it at least good as a hairspray? Well... it doesn't make my hair "sticky" or hold it together any harder. I can still glide through my hair just as softly as if I hadn't done anything. So I haven't noticed any really better hold either. The formula is supposed to contain panthenol; maybe it will make my hair nicer and softer over time... or more well-groomed. Conclusion: Ordering was worth it because of the nice lipstick sample in the package, but not because of the product itself. It will be used up, but certainly not reordered. I'd rather indulge in the real perfume bottle.

Sensual is the perfect name for this scent, for it definitely lived up to its expectations. Very Irresistible Sensual is rather different in comparison to the original. This fragrance lacks the fruity notes and has stronger hints of peony, patchouli and rose. At first I was rather surprised by this fragrance's softness. It took a while to adjust, because I had initially expected something rather strong. The sillage is quite average here, however I don't see that as a bad thing. The sensuality comes from the deep, rich woodsy notes, the earthy patchouli and the vanilla. The peony and rose notes create a feminine, and slightly soapy clean feeling. I'd describe this fragrance as being lusciously sexy. Something that is both lusty and intriguing.

Today I was wandering around a special display in the perfume department at Karstadt. A beautiful sight to enjoy. And that’s how it should have stayed, as I had just dragged the lovely Romance to the checkout yesterday. But instinctively, the friendly saleswoman appeared out of nowhere and offered her assistance. I couldn’t refuse. A purple box from Givenchy had caught my attention: Very Irresistible Sensual. Unfortunately, there was no tester available. But dutifully, she rushed to the stockroom to look for one. Breathlessly, after a short wait, she handed me a beautifully shaped purple bottle, saying: A lovely patchouli scent. She wasn’t lying. A patchouli-rose spirit escaped from the bottle, curled around my nose - and was at my service. My resistance was gradually fading. The star anise is enticingly spicy and the vanilla is soft and warm. Truly sensual - sensuous. Delicately oriental - in short: irresistible. That was enough as a reason to buy - and my husband was understanding as well.

Sensual lacks what bothers me immensely about the regular Very Irresistible: the initial citrus jolt that has ruined quite a few delicious scents for me. The fragrance opens creamy, with an unmistakable rose cloak, nestled in the cozy, velvety murmurs of vanilla and patchouli. I can also detect the star anise, which rounds everything off in a subtly polite manner. Delicious, feminine, purring. A great scent, neither scratchy nor spicy nor zesty, a nice bottle - that is a rare occurrence among the scents I love - only the "fashion color purple!" isn't such a hit, but I can get over that. However, you really have to like roses, I agree with MsGolightly: The note is very dominant. I had a full bottle, but eventually gave it up and kept only a smaller decant - why exactly? I fear I need it back. The surveyed men in my vicinity find it very pleasing, but it doesn't achieve absolute top marks. I can imagine the scent very well for a romantic, cultured dinner.

It has been a while since I tested it. Therefore, I can't remember the scent notes very well. But I do recall what I associated with it. I believe this is definitely a fragrance for an evening for two. It is subtle and stays close to the body. The base is very sensual and rounded, but the rose stands out a bit too much. Still, a beautiful scent that I will definitely buy at some point.

Initial impressions are spicy, with the natural sweetness of flowers. The scent seems very well 'mixed', without individual discernible notes. Sort of smoothly spicy, with an overall impression of a nice, subtle and mature fragrance. It smells like I should be wearing a velvet dress, with my hair up, and sitting down at a nice restaurant for a date. After five or so minutes, the spices face away and the flowers come to the forefront. After an hour or so, it felt like the flowers intensified. Some of my favorite scents are upfront and demand attention. YSL's Opium definitely inspires one to think 'what are you wearing?' upon notice. A scent like YSL Opium or Guerlain's Mitsouko or Mugler's Alien demand to be the star of the show. Boucheron feels like a gentle background color. It enhances the scene in the front, but doesn't distract enough to draw attention to itself. At the current affordable 2023 price point, Boucheron is also a fragrance that can be worn freely without financial stress or feeling that it must be saved for a special occasion.

I first wrote my review at the page for the older version, so I deleted that one and here is my review for this (current) version: Boucheron is in my collection for quite some time now and she's one of my favourite perfumes. Batchcode of my latest bottle says it is from Juli 2022. I remember how the original smelled and don't find it too different, maybe even a bit more wearable, a bit less bold (but still strong!). I find this perfume uplifting, bright and warm at the same time and a little sexy, but in an innocent, almost unintentional way asif she just can't help herself. No use pointing out the notes here, I think. There are so many! And they can act in verious ways, depending on mood, weather and occasion, but they all are noticable when you search for them and they always compliment eachother. In summer, I get most of her eastern vibes, she seems a bit brighter and at the same time intriguing then. I also get a slight 'bubble gummy' vibe in summer. In winter she is more warm (asif the top- and middle notes perform best in warm weather and the middle- and base notes perform best in colder weather). Boucheron smells far more expensive than what you pay for it, it's almost insulting to pay so little for such good quality! I payed a little less than 40 euro's for a 100 ml bottle and a little goes a long, long way! Performance is very good! Both sillage and longevity are excellent! My boyfriend loves it when I wear this! Edit: To bad...I wore this latest bottle the other day and it is less good than my former bottles, which also were reformulations and were great and in the same bottle, but my latest bottle is different in the drydown unfortunately... Edit II Lesson learned: Don't try too many scents at a time, which is probably why I perceived Boucheron the way I did above...tried it again today and it is still lovely.

Boucheron is a scent to fall in love with! And if a woman doesn’t have a suitable partner, then she simply loves herself and throws on her self-knitted alpaca wool sweater, because Boucheron is just as soft and warming.
