I’ll rhyme a bit now: I’m disarmed (meaning divorced), so I don’t have a partner. Hum..... I don’t need one either; I enjoy Boucheron all by myself by candlelight and good wine, hum Not that you think I’ve swallowed some colorful pills. Yes, the Medusa has acquired a cuddle scent and has strayed from her rough Chypres. I have a kind of primal trust in the house of Boucheron. Woe to you if you disappoint me, then there will be trouble! Or I’ll give you a sharp look, and what happens then is very unhealthy and worse than Corona! Boucheron starts with a creamy mandarin soufflé, carried by dreamy orange blossoms. I once had little orange trees as potted plants, so I know how they smell. Ylang-Ylang provides me with a tropical, sweet scent. Everyone has probably smelled a jasmine bush at some point, unless they live in a big city and are half-dead from smog. The tuberose is finely woven, and I’m learning to love it more and more (not just in Boucheron). A nice whale has also contributed a bit of amber, which makes the drydown even creamier. Do you actually know what’s in whale vomit? It’s not really tasty. Today, amber is synthetically produced or (in rare cases) collected when it’s washed up on a beach somewhere. Well, luckily no one can keep a sperm whale. But back to the scent. I’m not a marine biologist. The “old” perfumers and -muses will now fall from grace. The Chypre crowd, which always crows when it discovers a Chypre, buys a lovely cuddle scent? I tolerate no dissent; otherwise, I’ll give you a sharp look! You know what happens then..... P.S. There’s no photo of the scent here, but the bottle looks like that of the EdT on the Boucheron website.

This perfume, unfortunately discontinued, created and still creates confusion. I will explain: When I typed the name and the brand of the perfume, i.e. Celine-Magic, I was given a list of perfumes, eaux de toilette by Celine Dion and, eventually, I found the little round bottle of the MAGIC elexir of Celine, created by Sophia Grojsman. This is the confusion related to the name . The second confusion is related to the scent. This is Magic and the other similar one is Tresor. Yet they are different although the creator is the same. Let me put it like that: If you bake a cake, you can very well use the same recipe for the pastry but use different fillings, like strawberries, vanilla, etc. Same cook, same pastry( basic material) but a different taste and aroma. I am so prosaic! Magic is distinctively beautiful, soft, letting the fruits and flowers to chant together. Well balanced base of musk, amber and sandalwood, withou the patchouli trying to shout. I want to use the term "sotto voce" to express the calm scent yet rich and satidfying. I love it. Longevity is very good and so is its sillage. I love it!

One might think that the fragrance starts off lightly fruity with the clementine and pear in the top notes. But think again, far from it;-)) One spray and bam, it’s there demanding my full attention. Really not for the faint-hearted. I also thought, phew, way too heavy. I’m too weak for this. But then, after a few minutes, lo and behold, all the harshness has vanished. A beautiful powdery softness, woody warmth envelops me. Still strong, but no longer piercing. When I smell it, an orchid comes to mind, with a sensual, dark red color, velvety large petals. The leaves are so dark green, almost black. It stands under a velvety blue canopy with golden stars on it. Come 1001 Nights, seduce me, show me what you have to offer today. Because I am here and I know exactly what I want. And everyone should know it!!!

This is a very odd fragrance that I loved at first smell. It’s photorealistic to the experience of waking up from a nap at the beach both drunk and severely dehydrated — exhausted but also comforted by the ambiance. What you get from this throughout is a boozy lime accord, and lime should 100% be more appreciated in fragrance. It opens more with the coconut water and tonka bean - that is rooted in an animalic skin-like scent. Overall this fragrance is a good experience, but like all Jo Malone fragrances, does not last long at all.

I’m not usually into fresh types of fragrances but for whatever reason, I’ve been craving them recently. This is unlike anything else I own and was a pleasant surprise. Longevity is the same with this as it is for all other Jo Malone fragrances, but this is a really gorgeous summer freshie! Beach Blossom is a perfect balance of lime, coconut and mint. From the notes I really wasn’t expecting to enjoy this, but it’s really well done and absolutely gorgeous. The coconut note also gives this a creamy quality. This would be so refreshing and relaxing on a hot summers day at the beach, or even on a humid night. This would also be gorgeous as a self care scent or after a day of being exposed to the sun, when your skin is feeling tingly and sun kissed. It’s such a shame they’ve chosen to make this a limited edition fragrance! This is one I would definitely repurchase, and I’m currently contemplating buying a bigger bottle as a back up. Im so pleased I have this in my collection!

In search of a new fragrance for spring - I stumble upon Jo Malone's "Beach Blossom" and immediately know that I really like this scent. Beach Blossom is not a complex, complicated fragrance. It presents itself quite linear, pleasing, and convincing. And sometimes, that's all you need. First things first: Jo Malone presents this limited edition fragrance in a beautiful packaging with a kind of linen texture. Simple but appropriately high-quality, harmonious. I particularly like the bottle itself. Round and substantial, even though the cap is unfortunately made of lightweight plastic. The scent itself is definitely unisex, with a slight tendency towards femininity - but I can live with that. There are some fruits that I absolutely love - and that can therefore also really appeal to me in the realm of fragrances. Mango, strawberries, apples, and of course coconut. Beach Blossom immediately presents the coconut on my skin. And it also immediately mixes in bergamot and mint noticeably. This creates a definitely crowd-pleasing cocktail that instantly puts me in a vacation mood. On Sunday, I will be walking on the beach in Brittany with my dog, and Beach Blossom enhances my anticipation for that. - And that's somehow nice, isn't it? I enjoy my niche fragrances, delight in complex structures, and have a lot of fun training and expanding my own skills in dealing with such works of art. But sometimes, it also has to be something simpler that just brings joy. Just like I don't always want to taste only fine Grand Cru red wine, but also enjoy a simple country wine on the terrace that just flows along and is enjoyable. After a few hours, by the way, the coconut recedes a bit into the background and gives way to the tonka bean. - Also very nice. The spray head is good, and the longevity and sillage are too. I often find Jo Malone fragrances to be quite weak in longevity, but Beach Blossom is rather at the upper limit. One must not forget in this context that it is not an Eau de Parfum but a Cologne. And for that, the sillage and longevity are definitely good. So, if you're looking for an easy-going spring feel-good fragrance, love coconut vibes, and don't only want to enjoy summer citrus - go for Beach Blossom! If you're not into coconut - then better not.

with Beach Blossom, I experience a journey to white sandy beaches and azure blue seas, under palm trees I drink from a coconut and limes refresh me in the heat. the tonka bean sweetens my stay. yes, I have wanderlust. S/H is moderate :) a creamy, refreshing composition. this will definitely be my top 1 summer scent for 2025.

… a terribly beautiful child, in fact. Givenchy shows no mercy to its paying customers. This year, three new creations under the "Les Jardins Particulier" label have seen the light of day. What they all have in common is the hand-picked (of course) and specially refined (sure) black tea from Sri Lanka. This indeed creates a beautifully smoky woody tea note, marketing jargon aside. Once L'Enfant Terrible is sprayed on, steaming black tea spreads around the nose. A slice of lemon floats in the glass, rock sugar and a slice of ginger join in. The scent is sweet (!), but well balanced by the bergamot; there’s no risk of a sugar shock here. On paper, I find the composition noticeably fresher, with the black tea remaining dominant for longer. On the skin, however, I am quickly greeted by a warm spiciness that my memory associates most closely with cardamom and clove (very subtle) - and here I am gently reminded of "Levitating | Floraïku." The sharpness of the ginger and the freshness of the bergamot (Hello, Imagination !) continue to accompany the unfolding scent. The musk from the base is pleasantly subdued, not particularly dominant or remarkable. I wouldn’t wear it in the height of summer due to the subtle spiciness and that slight amber warmth. However, for the rest of the year, it seems to me an interesting companion for everyday life, especially since the way I apply perfume usually doesn’t produce a strong sillage. A bolder wearer, however, would likely be noticed by their surroundings for a few (rather few) hours, should they wish to be. Lastly, a quick look at the fragrance vessel: Oh, what a chunky child! The 50ml bottle is a little block. As wide as it is tall. It might have been more elegant, but I don’t want to fat-shame here: the material is of the usual high quality, and despite its size, it sits reasonably well in the hand. In conclusion, I must say: I really like this mix of freshness (bergamot, ginger) and ambered base, even though I don’t believe this creation comes across as unconventional and unruly as one might read on the Givenchy website. L'Enfant Terrible is quite well-behaved. But that’s nice too.

... Deauville on the beach promenade in autumn, enjoying a coffee near Coco Chanel's first store while gazing at the vastness of the sea. The day is still pleasantly warm, and I relish the sea breeze with its salty accords. Just relaxing. Upon applying this fragrance, the nose first detects a citrus note combined with the spiciness of juniper. From the background, delicate floral aromas emerge. The perfume is rounded off with woody accords. The patchouli adds a fresh touch, while the vetiver gives it a dry, dusty quality, making it very masculine. The longevity and sillage are good. This is a scent that can be worn by any age group. However, it is a fragrance that loves to be worn with a suit or at least a shirt with a blazer. On warm to hot days, this perfume is very suitable for daytime wear, whether in the office, at a meeting, during a meal, or on a date. I don't see this scent on women as it is quite masculine. I imagine that women would much prefer to smell it on a gentleman. Anyone who enjoys a citrusy, woody, masculine scent with a slight old-school vibe will find this one just right.

Now it’s time to dedicate a review to the beautiful pom-pom, although, or precisely because, it was unfortunately only on the market for such a short time…… The bottle represents a pom-pom, which I find totally cute and unusual. Now during the Christmas season, one might also see it as a Christmas ornament….. The Eau de Parfum has a red plate on top of the bottle, while the Eau de Toilette has a yellow one. The scent comes immediately - typically intense for its vintage. I am instantly enveloped by the wonderful pear. Except in a few Annick Goutal fragrances, I have rarely sniffed it…… It is accompanied by a distinct powderiness, intense floral notes, and a certain sweetness, without being “sticky.” The pear remains constant; for me, the fragrance does not undergo significant change or development, which doesn’t matter at all since it is “there right away.” It arrives in its full potential, just minimally “punchy.” Very feminine, definitely not unisex. I found it very beautiful back then…… there were still “real” women’s - but also men’s fragrances. ….. It always made the agony of choice a bit easier for me - but that’s another topic. Magic works well in winter weather and Christmas spirit. It has a gently soft touch of spicy warmth from the coriander, caressingly delicious……

I'm slowly starting to love my vintage miniatures. With "Magic (Eau de Parfum) | Celine," I have yet another beautiful women's fragrance on hand. Additionally, the longevity is fantastic at around 10 hours, and the sillage is also lovely. The top note starts off beautifully fruity and sweet with a lot of pear, clementines, and a hint of green coriander. The heart note remains sweet and offers a wonderful sea of flowers consisting of jasmine blossoms, ylang-ylang, rose water, and orchids. The base has a creamy, vanilla, woody, and slightly balsamic scent of coconut, amber, and sandalwood. Over time, a lovely oriental and powdery quality emerges. Yes, as a woman, you really can't go wrong here. The fragrance is very pleasant and beautiful. This mini will stay here :-)

It is velvety, bitter, beautiful, and rich. I put a drop on my wrist and enjoy it all evening. The scent gently envelops and transports you to the land of flowers. Perfume does not want to be gelled into notes. I just want to enjoy this beauty. I have bought a full bottle and many, many miniatures to be happy for many, many years.

... go to a dance café in one of the hotels in our city. When we arrive, we are with our friends we have arranged to meet and are the youngest in the hall. Classical dance music is playing, and we start with a slow waltz and continue with a cha-cha. On the dance floor, a lady with a sexy scent crosses our path. It fits perfectly with this music. Upon applying this fragrance, the first thing that hits the nose is a fruity citrusy green sweet spicy scent. Then the sun rises, and the flowers in the beds bloom, releasing their floral accord. The perfume gains an adult sexy twist from resinous woody earthy dry dark notes. The longevity and sillage are good. Here we have a women's fragrance that makes the wearer a true lady. The lady should already be in her late twenties; I can't imagine it on younger ones. I also don't believe this perfume is suitable for men. This scent is an all-rounder for the whole year. It can be worn both during the day and in the evening for any occasion. Anyone who enjoys a fruity citrusy green sweet spicy floral resinous woody earthy dry dark scent would be well served here if it unfortunately had not been discontinued.

Incredibly bright and fresh on first spray, mouthwateringly sour, with a little bitterness of yuzu pith. Dry down is clean, herbaceous, and still zesty with some barely detectable sweetness. My repeat wear for a lifelike citrus fragrance. Compared to other Jo Malone fragrances, the longevity is on the longer side, but I'd still not call it incredibly long lasting. On me, this wears like a high-end body spray and can be safely topped off, perhaps even heavy-handedly, every several hours throughout the day. This will be a perk or a drawback depending on your needs -- the sensory experience of the top notes make it worth it for me. I wish every museum, library, and public park/pool used this scent in their soap dispenser. Great for a breezy summer vacation afternoon by the water. Reapply regularly, just like you would sunscreen and iced tea.

I'm always on the lookout for citrusy fragrances, especially with the warmer weather to come. I was excitedly waiting for it to arrive at Sephora so I could test it out. I'm trying to have different fragrances in my collection, each featuring a citrus fruit and I think I've found the one for yuzu. When I sprayed it at the store, I could feel something special which is why I immediately purchased it online and got it with a discount. Now that I've had the time to test it out at home and on me, I'm even more certain of my purchase. Yuzu Zest starts out with a zesty, almost bitter, citrusy note. It's refreshing but also light at the same time. Clary sage takes a little longer to appear, but when it does, it lends a tranquil aromatic and herb-like vibe underneath the citrusy vibrance of the fragrance. It's soothing and calming. After awhile, cedarwood comes up, but this time, it's more mild and tempered. There's also an almost creamy warmth and a resinous sweetness I can only assume comes from the fir balsam. Does Jo Malone reinvent the wheel with this one? Certainly not. But it does provide a comforting and soothing interpretation of yuzu that's sufficiently unisex. Can be worn during warm weather or anytime when you need a little pick-me up. It also has surprisingly better longevity than most of the Jo Malone I've tested which gives it a few more points in my book.

I am sure that this would be a Next purchase for my collection because It is one ofnthe BEST citrus scents that i have tried. My first association when spraying it in the store was actually the Lime Juice from my favorite Thai place around the corner. Very fresh, very citrusy with a hint of cane sugar. I’m not a big fan of sweet or gourmand fragrances; they usually don’t develop as nicely on me as they do on many others. For this reason, I was very pleased with the fresh recommendation from the lady at the Jo Malone Store. I was instantly catapulted into a summer evening by the sea, when the air cools down a bit, but that shimmer is still present. Yuzu is very strong at first, but it never gets that, excuse the somewhat unappetizing comparison, toilet bowl cleaner vibe. After about half an hour, a pleasant warmth develops beneath the freshness, which I can only compare to the cane sugar from my Lime Juice. A really great, light, and fresh fragrance that doesn’t get on your nerves and is still noticeable on my skin even after 5 hours, transporting me directly into summer and by the water. Simply wonderful.

I haven’t tried the entire L’Interdit line, but I remember L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum as rather bland, while L'Interdit Eau de Parfum Rouge , though successful (ranked 6th in women's perfume), felt too aggressive for my taste. As someone who gravitates toward niche fragrances, I rarely write about designer releases (with the exception of private collection lines). Still, L'Interdit Parfum is the work of Dominique Ropion and Anne Flipo, and that alone warrants attention from niche enthusiasts. After all, Carnal Flower Eau de Parfum - one of the most iconic white florals ever created - comes from Ropion. Like L'Interdit Eau de Parfum Rouge , this Parfum (still an EDP concentration) stands out impressively in the vast and fairly homogeneous sea of mainstream designer scents. That said, the niche world is full of floral compositions that are completely comparable to this one. This isn’t necessarily a criticism: I’ve sampled countless niche fragrances that are far less well-crafted than L’Interdit Parfum. But it does highlight two things. First, within the designer realm, this fragrance is a genuine gem and absolutely worth trying. Second, the niche landscape has expanded so rapidly in recent years that many releases no longer reflect the original meaning of “niche.” In both quality and uniqueness, niche and designer have grown closer, and the boundary between them feels increasingly fluid, more like a line drawn in water. L'Interdit Parfum is well constructed, and the notes are undeniably appealing. A fruity, lush pear note ushers in a voluptuous white floral bouquet that captures attention immediately. The tuberose is quite heady at first, but it soon settles without ever fading away. Tuberose and Jasmine are perfectly balanced with Orange Blossom being slightly more shy buried under other florals. The bright fruity nuance softens yet remains perceptible in the background. The composition leans sweet, with a creamy, rounded texture. As it dries down, the fragrance lightens and becomes airier. The base plays only a minimal role, which is where it differs most from niche scents in the same category: it lacks the depth, complexity, and challenge that niche florals often aim for. There’s nothing particularly distinctive here, yet the overall quality surpasses much of what’s found in the designer sphere. It stands among the best designer white florals currently available. For comparison, some much more complex fragrances in this genre include two of my niche favorites - Queen of Silk and Amethyst Soul - as well as Jasmin des Anges Eau de Parfum and Gold from designer private collections. In the end, L'Interdit Parfum feels like a reminder that designer fragrances can still deliver refinement and pleasure without chasing shock value or needless complexity. It may not break new ground, and "Parfum" in the name is misleading, but its polished execution, beautifully blended florals, and approachable character make it a standout in its category. For niche lovers, it won’t replace the depth or nuance found in more ambitious compositions, yet it offers an undeniably satisfying wear - proof that sometimes quality and coherence matter more than originality. If you’re exploring modern white florals, this one is well worth having on your radar. If rating among the designer scents, it’s 10. Have you tried L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum and thought to yourself "ah, if only this thing was more fruity"? Well, you're in luck. This is L'Interdit with a hefty dose of honeyed pear on top. Pear, tuberose and honey at the forefront. Jasmine – stuck in the background together with gooey resins. A miniscule amount of ginger – I can feel it, but it does nothing to offset the overall sweetness. I wish there was more of it. It's not bad, but I personally prefer the original. L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum was all about the flowers. Here – you still have that prominent white florality, but now there's also pear persistently trying to push through it and take centerstage. Feels... more like I'm watching a fight rather than listening to a well composed song. Can these notes decide between themselves who's going to be the star of the show and then call me back, please? Large initial cloud – fills the room, starts fizzling out around 4 meters away from the wearer in an enclosed space. The outer cloud is honeyed and fruity. The inner cloud is... loud. Becomes rather sharp and aggressively floral an arm's length away, give or take. Sillage slowly fizzles out over the first ~2 hours of wear. Settles on skin. Overall scent mellows out, but "Floral vs Fruity" fight from earlier never reaches a satisfying conclusion. The notes just melt into each other and become one quiet unintelligible mess. Resinous backdrop becomes more apparent – hazy, creamy, with a very clean and refined patchouli note that feels like a signature of L'Interdit to me. Takes another ~3 hours to reach drydown. Florals and pear fizzle away. A twinge of honey lingers over patchouli and vetiver. Eh..? At the end of the day, it's still L'Interdit. Even if it's not as great as whichever one I prefer – it's still relatively well made. I'm not impressed, but I know several different women who would be happy to wear it. I'll just give my tester away to one of them.

Have you ever woken up in a sweat at 3 a.m. and wondered which of your numerous perfumes you would save from the raging flames of a fire? Me neither. Well, the part about the perfumes... and yet I unexpectedly found an answer: I love my L'Interdits! I am quite sure of that. Maybe I should collect the bottles in a little pouch. I still have that pink goodie bag from Valentino - or would that be blasphemy?! The bottle comes in the familiar, rounded, slightly bulging shape and clear glass. At first glance, it looked to me like "L'Interdit Tubéreuse Noire | Givenchy," which confused me a lot. I expected a bit more creativity in the design. Upon spraying, the scent seems very loud to me. Not in a way that it tickles the nose, but rather in a room-filling manner. It initially smells like the original but more intense, somehow stronger. In the drydown, a bit of green, almost herbal scent overlays the L'Interdit DNA. Then it becomes a little quieter. On my skin, it lasts about 4 to 5 hours. I must admit that the opening impressed me a lot. However, the drydown is a bit too harsh for me. I would even go so far as to call L'Interdit Parfum unisex (aside from the fact that anyone can wear whatever they want, of course). I believe that each flanker, despite the L'Interdit typical "Bubblegum" tuberose, has its own personality. Those who have already found their favorite can consider themselves lucky and, in my opinion, can skip one or two flankers. For anyone who has been wishing for a less sweet, almost "masculine" L'Interdit or generally prefers something a bit more robust, I recommend testing this scent. Personally, I have found my favorite ( L'Interdit Eau de Parfum Rouge Ultime ) and am curious about what comes next!

Earlier there was a brief statement, now the detailed review of this flanker from the L'Interdit (2018) Eau de Parfum line. A line that is among my absolute favorites among women's designers. I love the slightly mysterious floral heart note that is the main character in every scent of this line. Mainly the extremely feminine tuberose note that runs through the entire line. My favorites are the two Rouge flankers, but so far I find all releases to be of high quality and I can recommend them all without hesitation. Especially for women who like to be very feminine and also enjoy going in this "flirty" direction: Here you get a range with elegance, sex appeal, and that slightly mysterious note that really shines in the dark or in the evening/night. As with most designer bestseller lines, the range is milked. Sometimes unnecessarily, but I like this perfume variant. If you have many from the L'Interdit line, you don't necessarily need this one, but it is a great addition that also has its own vibes. This scent is available in 35, 50, and 80ml. The RRP is, as with all women's designers, outrageously expensive, but there are already offers for this new release. Better ones will certainly come in the next 1-2 years, but for those who want it now, there are already acceptable offers. The bottle is sweetly designed and has great glass. The look is uniform and the presentation is typical for the designer sector. The packaging is just a simple cardboard box. In terms of quality, you also get a great scent with this perfume variant in my opinion. I don't agree with these mediocre ratings at all, as this scent can quickly captivate you. The changes compared to others in this line are not that significant, but there are a few special features here, of course. Cool is this wonderful fruity pear note in the top note, which is very present. Immediately fruity-floral vibes come up, paired with this great sweetness that runs through the entire line. At the start, a slight ginger spice comes through, which has a fresher vibe. Patchouli is also a note here that represents this slightly dark and mysterious note from the beginning. The main part is, of course, the floral heart around the trio of jasmine, orange blossom, and of course tuberose. The latter is, of course, the most dominant. A slightly creamy-sweet bitter almond also provides great vibes that really match well with the pear and the floral notes. Orange blossom gives a clean vibe, while tuberose and jasmine contribute to the playful feminine character with a lot of sex appeal. In the base, myrrh, benzoin, and opoponax appear. It reads very resinous-balsamic, but is rather warm and sweet. Additionally, a lot of patchouli, which lets this scent fade out beautifully. Overall, a great modern release that fits perfectly into the current time and, in my opinion, can also connect to the previous flankers. Here you also get a great evening/night scent that already catches me. Performance is not as top as some others in the L'Interdit line, but still absolutely satisfactory. Longevity is between 9-11 hours, sillage is very good at first, becoming a bit more reserved after 4-5 hours. With the dosage, you can certainly find your favorite and possibly achieve a bit more. Overall, a great flanker that I really like. I would definitely gift it, and I find it relatively easy to like due to the floral-fruity notes. Only the tuberose might overwhelm some. If you like this line: Test it :-)

By chance, I received a sample of this fragrance and was also gifted another sample. Without beating around the bush: I tried everything to like this entire line. Especially as a tuberose lover. But something bothered me about the original and its flankers. This perfume version is actually the best creation... In the opening, you immediately perceive the Nashi pear, and this moisture surprisingly lasts quite a long time. It also pairs very well with the spicy ginger. Later, this fragrance glides into the floral realm, and the mimosa shines, intertwined with jasmine and tuberose. Eventually, it becomes difficult to distinguish the flowers. Everything somehow sticks together. I don't perceive any almond at all. After a few hours, something balsamic and earthy emerges. Without really venturing into masculine territory. Longevity is up to 7 hours, on clothing 12. Sillage and projection are okay. I was definitely noticed. A patient told me it was a great fabric softener... For €80/50ml, I would like to smell a bit more distinct, not like fabric softener. Unfortunately, I am still not convinced. Underwhelming.

Quatre opens with a citrus zest. Going forward, it's a fresh aromatic citrus scent, but sweet and soapy - citrus plus fresh laundry, with a musky base. The vibe is bright, optimistic, open, accessible, and friendly, basically a gentle smile in a bottle, but with a zing. As to the downsides, you could call the the scent generic, the top might be a tad too aromatic/spicy, and the base can smell somewhat bland and powdery. The pecularity of this fragrance is an umami note, bringing egg to mind. The overall balance is good, though. At 5.6 it's very underrated.  of my perfume reviews at The Scent Stories: thescentstories.substack.com

We sat in the back garden on iron chairs - some of them slightly rusted, with cushions made of Toile de Jouy. And because there were so many of us, someone had also added a few formerly white wicker chairs. The strawberry cake and cream had been eaten, the coffee in the porcelain pot with the chipped spout, which had miraculously survived the war, was long cold. The children were sprawled on the lawn with the dogs, the grandparents were squinting in the wicker chairs in the afternoon sun. The sweet peas had crawled along the rickety fence that shielded the garden from the neighboring property throughout May, the summer breeze rustled in the old oak tree, where three generations had swung - and we wondered how much longer it would be before the first ripe gooseberries and currants could be harvested. And above all, there was the sweet scent of the climbing roses, playful and delicate and lovely - like a gift. Not always, but often, the scents from Jo Malone evoke images, memories, ideas like this - at least that’s how it seems to me. Many of their perfumes explicitly focus on British themes, but the garden that forms in my nose from English Oak & Redcurrant could just as well be located in another area - much more important than its geographical location are the inherent stillness, peace, and tranquility it embodies. A little red fruit at the start - for someone like me, who doesn’t like berry notes in perfumes, a very harmless red fruit - a moderately strong rose, a brittle-soft wood accord. That’s all it takes to outline this garden, the summer wind in the oak leaves, the dogs on the lawn, and the children’s laughter - and the porcelain coffee pot that, during the war, miraculously wasn’t lost. And that’s all a perfume needs - its purpose is merely to amuse, entertain, and accompany charmingly. Conclusion: not a great scent, nor does it need to be. Instead, it’s one for all those who long to be in that garden - if only for a few hours - under the old oak tree at the back by the fence, which is overgrown with sweet peas.

Ah, I recently told you that I finally got to test the new Jo Malone fragrances, specifically the two English Oak scents. I had been bothering the saleswomen for so long, always asking when these fragrances would finally be released… and when the scents finally arrived, they immediately handed me the samples without me even asking. …. Do you think I should take that to mean they wanted to express that I should quickly get lost? So that I should test the fragrances at home instead of continuing to annoy them? He he he… aaah, I hope not, because otherwise I would be hurt and do what every psychopath would probably do: I would go there even more often and be an even bigger nuisance, mu ha ha ha :D Isn't that a brilliant idea? Ah, I see that the old saying is indeed true: “It’s always interesting to see how close genius and madness lie next to each other!” :DD Anyway, this is the second new fragrance from Jo Malone, which I must admit I liked a bit less than the English Oak & Hazelnut,… I will explain why after the scent description. The scent: The fragrance starts off powdery sweet. You can smell fruity sweet currants that have a pleasant aroma (the powdery aspect fades quickly). Soon, there are also green notes to be detected, the acorns, which emit a slight woody scent. The woodiness becomes noticeably weaker in the heart note, allowing you to continue smelling the currants, now slightly floral thanks to the roses. At the beginning of the base, the roses become quite intense. They smell both floral and fruity-sweet together with the currants, but unfortunately overshadow the oak a bit, which had provided an interesting woody note in the English Oak & Hazelnut. Here, the oak can still be smelled in the base, but compared to the other fragrance, it has turned out quite weak, leaving the scent somewhat banal in the end. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is okay, but a bit weaker than English Oak & Hazelnut. It also smells more spring-like to me than autumnal. You will smell the fragrance nearby, but a large scent cloud probably won't linger for long. The longevity is also lower, so the scent can only be faintly detected on the skin after six hours. The bottle: The bottle is of the usual high quality and rectangular. On the front, there is a large, white-yellowish label with the name, brand, and logo. The fragrance liquid is also yellowish. The cap is round, chrome-plated, and resembles a door knob or something. A nice, but somewhat too simple bottle, whose simplicity may please many, but for me, it is too plain, especially since they all look the same (with the exception of the limited editions). So, the scent is actually quite okay, as long as you like roses, because these flowers radiate quite intensely compared to the other fragrance notes here. Moreover, I find the scent not as distinctive and refreshingly new as the better English Oak & Hazelnut. Because I miss a distinctive note here (like the wonderful hazelnuts in the other fragrance), or something that provides a (even if brief) wow effect. Instead, the fragrance is solidly made and of the usual high quality. Aside from a slightly woody note, as mentioned, you smell more floral-sweet notes that, to put it cautiously, smell like many other fragrances with a similar scent direction. Since it is so inconspicuous, it probably works best for layering with other Jo Malones, for which the fragrances are so famous. By the way, due to the roses, the scent is more feminine than unisex. It’s worth checking out, but I didn’t find it particularly special. Hmm… I suppose the scent will eventually be presented at a Jo Malone event,… should I go? After all, all the saleswomen will probably be there, so I can annoy each one of them at the same time or on the same day… sometimes, when I show up, I even hear things like “Ah, you’re here again?” from them… aaahh… nooo… I will never go back and will sit here sadly *sniff* …

Fruity, fresh, sparkling berry opening. Then the rose joins in, equally fresh-scented and lovely, also juicy. Later, the opulent queen of fragrance, very and uniquely fragrant, dominant, spicy, sweetly juicy, and very natural. A slight soapiness accompanies it, becoming woodier, drier, and more austere around the rose. I don't explicitly smell roasted oak, although I know that scent very well. But this very beautiful rose scent becomes woodier and earthier. Although the perfume is called English Oak & Redcurrant, the rose, the fullness of roses, is throughout the dominant force of the fragrance. A very beautiful fragrance experience! I thought of the fairy tale Snow White & Rose Red. The 2 sisters are out berry picking. - red currant, the bear, the enchanted prince, comes from the forest and wants to warm himself by the fire - oak wood embers, and in the end, when the spell is broken, 2 rose bushes grow from the bear's skin, in white and red for Snow White & Rose Red. The end Thank you, dear Franciska, for the sample.

My first Jo Malone fragrance. It comes across completely unpretentious, in a simple bottle without glitter and pretensions. The name "English Oak & Redcurrant" makes me think of a dreamy South English cottage set in a beautiful garden with old oak trees. The scent gives me the feeling of sitting on one of those old oak trunks, absentmindedly playing with the slightly damp, yet warm, mossy bark. I stroll over to the currant bushes. The berries there are still pale red and will need another 14 days of sunshine. Absently, I take a currant leaf and crush it between my fingers... next to it stands a lovage bush, and here too I crush a leaf, enjoying the spicy bitterness. Then I continue briskly through the oak avenue - the scent of the currant leaf combined with the scent of lovage and oak bark accompanies me on this mild early summer day. This story comes to mind with the fragrance. It is completely different from my usual preferred direction. It is green - bitter - unsweetened fruity - spicy. Rose is completely absent for me. Here, green-bitter, woody, spicy notes dominate. It is a natural scent. I perceive the currants here as unripe, more the green of the currant leaves. The sillage is present but unobtrusive. It lasts on me for 7 hours. For me, this is an early summer fragrance. And I have often wondered what kind of perfume one should wear for sports, if one were to do any... I've got it! This one! I would choose this scent for athletic activities. Conclusion: An unusual but interesting fragrance for me. The bitterness makes it almost a bit masculine. Certainly not an all-day favorite for me, but nice to have something like this in the collection.

A simple fragrance, one might think. Perhaps in its composition based on the ingredient list. But from the sniffing experience, not at all. Here, one cog turns another and "spins" the scent further, like a clockwork mechanism moving the hands. It begins on an early morning of a spring day. The air is still very fresh and forms dew on the grasses and plants, and it smells very citrusy and simultaneously green. Slowly, morning transitions into midday, the sun leisurely unfolds its strength and allows rose buds to open. The beautiful and almost spicy scent merges with the morning aroma, making it warmer. Around noon, this impression intensifies further and now absorbs the aroma of ripening currants, which seems to be strongest in the afternoon. As evening approaches, it becomes cooler again, the trees around, especially oaks, release a herbaceous and woody-scented moisture into their surroundings, which, together with the aromas of the entire day, now form a successful unity that lasts into the night. Wonderful to follow. It truly happens and in slow motion.... very long-lasting with moderate sillage.

Subdued mandarin creamy tones, somewhat floral, a bit tender and buttery soft musk in the base. Along with this, there is an almost tender cinnamon-nutmeg spice that slightly reminds me of the legendary HONOS; very subtly executed. A highly likeable and unobtrusive fragrance that reflects the lightness of the turn of the millennium: BOSS BOTTLED by the same perfumer can be recognized at least from a distance; Jil Sander SUN MEN, EAU DE CARTIER, ALLURE HOMME also hint at the direction. This is a beautiful and relaxed men's fragrance of its time that does not feel outdated at all and with which one can still excellently socialize today (and also remain!). I am referring to the rare and not listed EdT here.

Now I'm testing the next original manufacturer sample. Unfortunately, I do not like Céline pour Homme Eau de Parfum at all :-( It smells too musty-earthy for me, so I cannot rule out a "tilt." The longevity is solid at around 5 hours, and the sillage is hardly more pronounced. The top note starts with mandarins. Nutmeg and cloves bring a rather earthy and unpleasant mustiness to the scent. The heart note is floral with scents of geraniums, garden cloves, and again earthy with iris root. The base continues to smell pungently of earth and root-like with green, woody, and yet also musty hints of patchouli and vetiver.

It's one of those scents that makes you raise an eyebrow at the first spritz. Not because it’s weird, but because it’s seriously good ^_^ The opening hits warm and dense, with a slight incense vibe. Then comes the patchouli. But not that grumpy, earthy, muddy kind that hits you like a wall. This one’s clean, velvety, and elegant. After about half an hour, I start noticing a resinous softness, like there’s some myrrh or labdanum adding depth. And then that woody base, maybe a bit of sandalwood. The funny thing is, despite its bold name and strong character, it’s not a perfume that screams. Actually, it’s pretty composed. It’s a really versatile scent—probably best for evenings, cooler weather, and definitely not for teenagers.

No? He would probably leave a trail of this scent first and then once he's got you trapped...enraptured with this seductive scent...the traditional brimstone and sulfur would appear. As I sniff my wrist, I think of all those vampire legends which describe the immortals as smelling of Roses and I feel that Jo Malone's Rose Water & Vanilla has captured that haunting otherworldly aspect of the rose water. This fragrance is seductive, though not overwhelming, lasting a good 6 hours on my skin but with sillage less than 1 meter. There is a definite incense accord and is slightly sweetened by a persistent loukhoum note. There is also a touch of orange blossom, honeysuckle and finally a deep earthy natural vanilla bourbon note that reminds me of the fresh black innards of a still moist Tahitian Vanilla bean pod I bought on the shores of Moorea'a for the equivalent of 3 cents. My mind keeps flashing back to "Spencer's Gift and Gag Store" circa 1975 Americana-black lights, lava lamps and "Midnight Strawberry Orchid Incense". Not to be mistaken with todays clearly defined orchid notes or synthetic strawberries, this is very natural, not cloying. It smells very similar to my beloved "Lovely Jubblies Cream" from Lush. This is probably the most earthy, low key and yet alluring rosewater scent I have come across, given roses are not my thing and I am no expert in this area...but this Rose water and vanilla is almost like a religious experience, the wave of an ancient incense ball and incantation before some weird unspeakable psychedelic ritual which hopefully ends with soothing music and massage.

Don't ask me why, but suddenly I felt the urge to find a rose scent that could be easily worn by men. When I read the fragrance notes of "Rose Water & Vanilla," I felt somehow drawn to it, because I like vanilla, as long as it doesn't come across as too rich and especially not too artificial. I could also easily imagine the combination of rose and vanilla. Oud? I still have my issues with that... But anyway, nothing ventured, nothing gained! And I must say: My "daring" was worth it! The rose smells as if it is in full bloom, warm and very mature. It’s not a baby rose that only has a delicate and soft scent, but rather the confident rose in bloom. The vanilla harmoniously blends in (thankfully not overly sweet) and unites with the rose. Oud? Absolutely no problem here! It clearly serves to keep the sweetness of the rose and vanilla in check. I think that’s exactly what makes this scent wearable for both genders. I am absolutely thrilled, especially since the longevity is very good. I think I have found "my" rose scent! But when to wear it? In the evening, no problem. For the office, it might be a bit too "rosy" for me. Then I had the idea to layer it with "Musc Nomade by Annick Goutal." Excitement.....and.....WOW!!!! The two fragrances harmonize fantastically together. The musk takes away some intensity from the rose, making it truly suitable for everyday wear. Satisfied, I lean back and enjoy the pure rose on the left and the tamed rose on the right....it works!!

....but I like this one. Strange, I'm really not a fan of rose scents. I thought to myself, you should get to know Jo Malone, the comments sound pretty good. And then I was blown away. This rose here is so warm and dark, so beautifully layered with vanilla and oud, that I no longer know exactly why I don't like rose scents. I also didn't know how oud smells until now. A rose scent that comes across as so warm and heavy, yet can definitely be worn by men, I've never encountered such a fragrance before. It fits perfectly with the winter season. So sensually captivating, so remarkably simple, yet special. Extraordinary, but never intrusive. Oh, I'm at a loss for words! Yes, you always learn something new in this world of perfume. I find that beautiful and exciting. Exactly my thing. Thank you, Peanut, for this interesting experience!

Background: Even as a child, Malone experimented with making her own soaps using flowers from her parents' garden. Her mother was a beautician and her father an artist. Malone worked as a florist and provided facials in her kitchen in the evenings. Soon, she became one of the most sought-after skincare therapists in London. At the age of 19, she met her future husband Gary, and together they opened her first shop selling handmade fragrances and products. Jo Malone opened her first store on Walton Street in London in 1994, and more followed. In 1999, her company was acquired by Estée Lauder, with Jo Malone as Chairwoman and Creative Director. Then in 2006, she sold it to them entirely. Fragrance: The fragrance itself is reminiscent of an oriental dessert called Knaffee. This is a pastry made from wheat with a layer of chopped nuts and honey. On top, there is a thick layer of cream, all drenched in rose water. Yes, for everyone whose mouth is watering right now.... this is how Rose Water & Vanilla smells!! The opening begins with a note of rose water, very subtle and airy light. Combined with the bitter orange nuances of neroli and the sweet, floral woodiness of petitgrain, a unique scent note emerges. At the heart, the vanilla exudes its enchanting sweetness, and a slight powderiness becomes noticeable. Now I'm back at my dessert and greedily craving more! The crowning glory of this perfection are the base notes of patchouli and white musk. Overall, the fragrance gains an incredible depth and sophistication. Conclusion: I drove home intoxicated with the intention of testing its effect on the opposite sex. The gift wrap, of course sprayed with rose water, was hidden in the bedroom. Statement upon entry about 1 hour later.... “wow, it smells like a pool of sin in here.” This is absolutely a positive remark, as that evening I couldn't get my boyfriend's nose away from me.... ......Dreamy, sensual, seductive....

Sometimes the timing is perfect. Sometimes what you’ve been looking for just falls into your lap. Or is it ultimately the overdue that comes your way (I’m borrowing from Max Frisch here)? What was I looking for? As a rose fan, first and foremost, another interesting rose fragrance. Of course. But not just any rose fragrance, rather one that would satisfy me during the pre-Christmas season. One that would make it easier for me to forgo tons of butter speculoos, vanilla crescents, nut cookies, and entire truckloads of cake. I don’t belong to the few lucky ones who can inhale calories without bursting out of size 36 like a soufflé from its mold. That’s why I experience monstrous hunger every year in late autumn and winter. And I want to kill anyone who comes around the corner with vanilla-sweet, freshly baked treats. Vanilla candles and relevant fragrance lamp oil for home are nice as a trick 17 for hungry snackers, but only practical in your own four walls. On the go, you have a problem and a hatred for all bakers, pastry chefs, and munching fellow humans. A perfume to satiate is already a good idea. A satisfying rose fragrance is, for me personally, a small stroke of genius. This way, I get my dose of rose and an olfactory substitute for hip gold: for vanilla, cinnamon (yes, I can smell that too), nutty delicacies, and spicy, wintry sugar bombs. Rose fragrance: Check! Delicious and satisfying: Check! But what is this? There’s a big oriental X that I can’t assign to any culinary mess. If that’s oud / agarwood, then I find oud interesting. (But I probably couldn’t tolerate a higher dose of it.) In summary, I’m hitting even more flies with one swat than I thought: I have a delicious rose fragrance AND a satiator AND I finally know what oud smells like. ___________________________________________________________________________ Thank you, dear Flori! Your generous decant will easily carry me through the entire winter.

Rose water and vanilla, hmmm sounds good, I thought to myself. Roses are definitely my thing and I also like vanilla. Agarwood, or Oud, is a bit of a different story... Thanks to Sevda, who sent me a lovingly crafted sample with hand-painted roses - many, many thanks for that, dear Sevda - I started my test last night.

I am not a cake eater and I don't bake. And I don't like Oud. Yet the first thing I sniff is a rather unfamiliar dark spicy note, which can only be Oud! But I must immediately give a big compliment to the brand Jo Malone. For here, an unusual fragrance has been created for me. Sweet vanilla, dark red rose, and agarwood in a strange blend.

Here with us, there is a charming little shop called "Bittersweet." Alongside fresh groceries and a well-stocked selection of natural cosmetics, you will also find plenty of fragrance oils, candles, and incense. Rose Water & Vanilla awakens in me the scent memory of this very fine shop. Its fragrant aura feels meditative, almost esoteric.

Wearing this fragrance transports me back to my childhood. Grandma, a very well-read woman, who placed great value on scents, brewed rose water in the large kitchen, which was strained and bottled in small bottles. In the oven, a vanilla cake, for afternoon coffee.

Finally, it's back, it took a long time. I'm not a fan of rose scents at all, but I really like the combination with vanilla. It's soft, light, and powdery. The rose fades quickly and it remains vanilla on my skin, deliciously vanilla. Not "sticky sweet," a little bit herbal-citrusy, but powdery. For me, a really beautiful fragrance for the transition into summer.

Oranges and Spices Dominates this Perfume and i can also pick up the smell of Vanilla And a distant wisper of Incense. i love the Cleaver Gold etching of her name CELINE on the bottle i think is more for a Autumn Scent then Summer.

Beautiful, enveloping soft oriental scent. Lightly spiced (pepper) top notes, almond heart (not marzipan-like) and sensual sweet-woody base. Sillage is not outstanding; it is intended as an oriental light spring-summer perfume, just not too heavy, rather casual and suitable as a daytime option for those who, for example, love Kenzo Amour and are looking for a similar alternative, with less vanilla and outside "confection" but affordable for themselves.

I recently tested it and it was a good experience: the almond opening note is sweet, intense and soft and not at all bitter or medicinal, the peppery note and the iris give the touch of sexy feminity and the base is very warm and quite longlasting. Precious the dark "fumé" bottle. it's a night fragrance to wear when you want to feel very sexy and feminin. Another "add" in my whishlist!

Beautiful scent! I had been avoiding a blind purchase for a long time, but unfortunately, the fragrance is still nowhere to be found in my area (Mannheim). I honestly don't understand this; I thought the scent would be hyped in the big drugstores and perfumeries around Christmas time, similar to the somewhat strange Black Opium or the green Marc Jacobs handbag. This was not the case, so I had to order it online. The scent itself is truly a special composition. On one hand, it reminds me a bit of Hypnotic Poison Eau de Toilette - it might be due to the almond note. On the other hand, it is a bit more powdery, the top note is not as strong and loud as in HP. It's somewhat like HP the day after application. With Ange Noir, a smoky note becomes quite prominent after application, which strongly reminds me of the scent of a fog machine at a disco :-) So it's not a tobacco-like smoky note, but rather like steam with a good added aroma. I suspect that sesame is behind this, which sometimes also comes to the fore with closer "sniffing". As you wear the scent longer, it becomes increasingly powdery and creamy, and the smoky note fades away. It becomes downright cozy and sweet, the HP note remains and becomes more pronounced. In other forums, this has been referred to as "lipstick smell." I can relate to that well. I would describe the sillage and longevity as good; I was able to perceive it all day yesterday without needing to reapply much, and I can still smell it today. It’s not a powerhouse like Angel, but also not a wallflower like Spiriteuse Double Vanille - a good middle ground that is not intrusive but still noticeable. Ideal for me. Conclusion: Not a scent that is overly seductive and erotic, but also not a wallflower. For me, it's well wearable on weekends during shopping trips or when going out for coffee. For the office, it would be a bit too "half-hearted" for me :-) I prefer clearer scents if at all. Suitable for going out as well, but I would need to reapply more often. It's a shame that it has received many negative statements so far; I really like it.

My thoughts are swirling. The day was exhausting, the customers demanding, the recognition absent, and the bus left right in front of my nose at the end of the day. Was that enough? But no! The heavy thunderstorm on my way home soaked me to the bone despite my umbrella. Leaves and twigs, torn from the trees and bushes by the gusts of wind, stuck to my skin and clothes. My poor shoes barely made it to the front door with me before they said goodbye with their soaked soles. Still in the hallway of my apartment, I struggled to peel off my dripping wet and dirty clothes and washed all the dirt and frustration off my body in the bathroom. Outside, the storm was still raging. The rumble of thunder echoed from the dark, cloud-covered mountains surrounding our city, and the lightning transformed the usually beautiful landscape into an apocalyptic scene. Good thing I was inside. Safe in my four walls, now clean again and even able to breathe deeper and more relaxed, despite the day's adversities and thanks to a comforting cup of coffee. Later. Pitch-black night. Am I lying awake in my bed? Or am I sleeping deeply and dreaming? I don't know. Then I hear a sound in the darkness. What could that be? I don't turn on the light. Instead, I try to assign it and listen closely. It’s as if I hear the beating of large wings. The wings of a mighty bird? Or some other creature? Something seems to be circling above me. Still, I don't feel the need to turn on the light. No fear creeps over me; I am completely calm and relaxed. Somehow light and content, I try to discern the source of the wingbeats. Then I see it… A beautiful creature of the air. In the midst of the deepest night. With wings made of black feathers. It has brought me something. Despite the darkness, I recognize it as if it were broad daylight, on its wings, stardust, black diamond, magic is surely at play here, it places a bottle in my hand. The angel hovers in the room, also above me, looks at me with so much kindness, instantly bestowing comfort and love as only an angel can. With a smile, the circling ends, the angel ascends then, the wings rustle, glimmer beautifully, until I can no longer see it. The scent that then fills the room is like something from another world. Givenchy has created a work with its L’Ange Noir that deeply touches me and my senses. Deeply relaxed. Deeply impressed. A rather dark accord sets the rhythm of this work. It feels mystical, as if it does not want to reveal its secret. Indeed, for me, the scent is more of a total work of art than a series of recognizable components. Or perhaps I don’t want to break it down so clearly and distinctly? Because their interplay is the epitome of harmony for me? This black angel truly smells dark to me, but not gloomy. Rather, a pleasant darkness. A cozy and soothing darkness. Something I have never smelled before. A dense cloud in which the scent of almond, iris, and tonka mingles with amber, forming a kind of symbiosis in the air. For me, the scent is simply there. All the notes at once. No order. Not even in progression. It begins and ends for me the same. Equally dreamlike and almost unreal in its beauty. This scent allows me to find peace, to unwind and switch off. The adversities of the day have lost their terror. The world suddenly looks friendlier, and I feel safe and strengthened. Sometimes it doesn’t take much for that. A kind word. A gentle caress or a tender glance. For me, it is an encounter. The encounter with a Black Angel in the night…

I received a half-full sample as a bonus in a swap. I can't understand the negative statements, as I find it extremely pleasant. I can mainly smell almond, iris, and tonka bean. I don't necessarily need pepper and amber, and they are not noticeable to me here. All in all, very cozy, warm, soothing, and perfectly suitable for winter.

I have often smelled the bottle. It certainly catches the eye, especially during the Christmas season. However, I have never sprayed the fragrance on my skin until now. Today, while taking advantage of the many offers, I not only sniffed but also finally sprayed. Immediately, I smell the almond and the iris. The iris dominates here anyway. The scent is very sweet, not sugary, more like a very sweet laundry detergent. That remains until the base, when the erotic tonka bean rounds everything off. I don't notice amber; it blends well into the sweet laundry detergent. Sesame? Not really. This beautiful angel fits best in winter on necks, scarves, fluffy sweaters, and woolen dresses... Recommended as a Christmas gift, because as already mentioned above, the bottle is perfect for it! Anyone who likes Black Opium, Hypnotic Poison, and Loverdose will surely be well served with this.

With L'Ange Noir, I'm not having an easy time.. The blind buy turned out to be a mistake, even though the fragrance notes sounded so wonderful. I've only worn it once so far and have gone through everything from Ufff to iihh and well, it’s okay actually ;) In itself, it’s not a bad scent, but I would advise anyone considering a purchase to test it beforehand..

L'Ange noir, just the name melts on the tongue like dark chocolate and when I caught sight of the bottle, resembling a rare black orchid bloom, there was no stopping me and I ordered it blind. A heavy mistake! I sprayed myself cautiously. Ok, it smelled of sesame and almond, quite delicious if you like it, I was determined to like it....Well, others did not.

Serpent Bohème presents two timeless flowers: rose and jasmine. A simple, unpretentious fragrance that charms with its natural softness. From the first spritz, a subtle touch of anise appears, but it quickly fades, giving way to the purity of these classic flowers. Nothing extraordinary, no olfactory revolution, just a harmonious and elegant composition that remains alluring despite its simplicity. As for the bottle, it’s nothing less than a work of art. In short: a charming and elegant simplicity.

Hmmmm was my first thought when I saw and smelled the perfume for the first time. Such a beautiful box alone, I had to take a closer look. A beautiful bottle to go with it, I was almost convinced. This did not change immediately when I smelled the fragrance. For me personally, a beautiful interplay of fruity notes, as well as woody and calming components. A dream of delicate elegance that enveloped me. Unfortunately, the happiness did not last long. Neither the way the scent developed convinced me, nor its longevity. It remains a good fragrance, but not what I had hoped for. All in all, you can't go wrong with it, but my initial enthusiasm was unfortunately stifled in its infancy.

Black Vetyver Café is another star of this line although it rarely gets the praises it deserves. It has a somewhat harsh opening, reminds me of hairspray, but this lasts only for very little and is followed by a brief burst of vetiver. Very quickly the coffee notes enters the scene and this is the best coffee note I have come across in a fragrance. This is pure, plain coffee: no cappuccino, no frappuccino, no milk, no cream, no sugar added. Coffee notes very often seem to take a turn to the gourmand ending up smelling like those cheap flavoured coffee blends, a nondescript combination of coffee-chocolate-caramel-hazelnut concoction, straight out of the labs of food flavouring companies. This one however is surprisingly dry, dirty and herbal. It reminds me a lot of Greek/Turkish coffee, which is lightly roasted, preserving the herbal qualities of the bean. Coffee in this form reminds me of a light immortelle note. Throughout the development coffee is supported by the light green vetiver note and perhaps a little citrous, but it always stays the centre of attention. Many of the fans of BVC complain about its longevity. I have a different experience with this. On me it soon develops into a skin scent with incredible longevity. Just as I start forgetting I wear it I get a cloud of the rustic coffee note surrounding me again. I do not get a great deal of notes combining for this. Although Fragrantica lists vanilla in the blend I cannot detect a hint of it or of any other sweet smelling ingredient. I love BVC because it is dry, herbal and rustic and it becomes one with the skin. Sometimes it smells like I have spilled coffee on me and forgot to wash it off, which I find very charming and daring. Fortunately it has the right amount of vetiver to keep others from detecting it as such. I like the quiet storm feel, close to the skin quality, big longevity (at least on my skin) combination. I would have loved an eau de parfum version of this though. One of the best and most original of the line. Notes from my nose: hairspary, vetiver, coffee, grapefruit, woods

I kept thinking where's my coffee? It opened with Vetiver and Incense and didn't really evolve to anything else. Just vetiver and incense until it fades. I was really disappointed that I didn't get any coffee. It smells like it would be a great base to something but is un impressive on it's own. Nov 24 2013

As one who does not subscribe to the Jo Malone "the solution is dilution" aesthetic, I never approach the fragrances of this house with much hope. I really do prefer perfume to cologne and I find it absurd to pay perfume prices for a tiny bottle of weak cologne that would last me maybe a week. That said, BLACK VETYVER CAFE certainly sounds like an excellent idea to this coffee lover. What I find, however, is that this is not really very black at all--again, a result of dilution. Take a black elixir and add a ton of solvent, and it will be a pale shade of dirty gray. This fragrance does not smell dirty, but it does smell like weak coffee sweetened with sugar and seasoned with vetiver. Unfortunately, I have yet to acquire a taste for sweet vetiver (I'm also ambivalent toward Hermessence VETIVER TONKA...), so I'm afraid that BLACK VETYVER CAFE will not be the first Jo Malone to grace my collection... I would recommend this fragrance to people who think that Thierry Mugler A*MEN is way too thick and synthetic. This composition, while thin, is also natural smelling.

Krutzefix... once again such a beautiful scent that has unfortunately been discontinued. Somehow the manufacturers really have a "lucky" hand and always take the most beautiful fragrances of the brand off the market. Heaven by Chopard, the rest of the brand... rather a generous "meh", Kiton Napoli, the rest of the brand snooze.. well, Malone still has a few good scents... but maybe none so extraordinary anymore! I love this dark-spicy coffee scent, a wonderful aroma... dark, bitter, and espresso-savory! The lovely Parfuma from whom I got the decant described it just right, the coffee smells like freshly ground, but not from a packet, rather like in the still warm coffee grinder. The aroma that rises here is sooo beautiful! Less Dallmayr, but more Illy in the Galleria Milano. On top of that, there’s a rather bright and slightly sweet vetiver and a light gentle incense. Grande selezione!!! No sweet instant coffee or overly sweet chai latte like in I Love New York for all or in Intense Cafe. More bitter-sweet with mild smoke. I haven't smelled anything like this combination before. This is also the first scent that truly deserves the name coffee. A wonderfully aromatic fragrance for autumn and winter. Unfortunately, the scent fades as quickly as an espresso gets cold in the cup; after just 2 hours, only a hint can be sensed... that's a big minus and also a deal-breaker. The sillage is only strong in the first 10 minutes, after that the term "close to the skin" takes on a new dimension, even the extremely airy Musk for Men effortlessly overshadows it. Ci veddiamo... non piu.. purtroppo!

Very interesting - "Black Vetyver Café" by Jo Malone is one of those fragrances that develops very differently on paper and on the skin (at least for me). Malone presents this scent as "The aroma of roasting coffee beans. A robust, beautifully bitter coffee note is steeped in the smoky depths of vetiver and temple incense." After a slightly silvery-peppery opening note where coriander and incense from the heart and base already announce themselves, with a very slight citrus overtone, I get this dark, roasted, smoky coffee note on my skin after about a minute. This intensifies and rounds out with the support of vetiver - the less I apply, the darker and blacker the hint of smoky coffee, the more I apply, the more silvery the coriander becomes. On paper, however, there is hardly a hint of coffee from beginning to end, but a strong vetiver. In this composition, several molecules are obviously working in conjunction with the skin chemistry to bring out this defining and titular coffee note, which holds potential for quite different reactions depending on the wearer. So definitely test it multiple times on your own skin! The further development is quite linear; one could also say: not much happens anymore... Unfortunately, with the exception that later the scent always becomes slightly sour on my skin, a rather unpleasant transformation that can occasionally be observed. Incense at this point is rather weak, as is a slightly herbal, green-mossy, woody vetiver, a rather dull base beneath the still present coffee. Unfortunately, this is not wearable for me. On paper, the silvery-spicy coriander-pepper note lasts much longer into the drydown, a spicy green vetiver scent, but for me, without coffee... Therefore, definitely a recommendation, and please test on the skin!

Black Vetyver Cafe is a fragrance discovery that stands out among the many I have tested recently. Most coffee scents I know are sticky sweet, so sweet that you could easily send an average person into a sugar shock with such a coffee. This scent is by no means a pure men's fragrance, no. On a woman, it surely smells fantastic.

Black Vetyver Café doesn't get enough attention, in my opinion. How do I know this? In countless times when I've been taken to the counters of Malone, there was no fascination for the scents. I find the principle of scent layering quite good, as my nose doesn't have the same fragrance demands every day.

I was introduced to this fragrance already in the spring. My Belgian fragrance friend Jessica from the Facebook community "Eau my soul" described it so lovingly, and the photos she arranged around it - with many flowers and beautiful porcelain - sparked my desire to get to know this creation from Jo Malone. That's why I was thrilled when I received a sample of it with the last fragrance package from Heikeso. Receiving it is always a great joy! I got to know the Jo Malone brand back in spring 2015, and especially their then "Seasons Collections" captivated me. The clarity of the fragrances, the somewhat unusual combinations of fruit, flower, and wood, still fascinate me. And now the time begins when they find their enticingly fragrant place on skin and hair again. Of course, I assumed that "Sakura Cherry Blossom" would be a cherry blossom scent; so much for how much photos can influence one's imagination. But looking at the pyramid with my beloved mimosas at its heart left no room for disappointment. After testing, there is also no reason for that: this presumed "false cherry blossom" smells enchanting and holds a surprise throughout the scent progression. The freshness of awakening spring is captured in this fragrance painting by bergamot and juicy mandarin. It is this very mandarin that makes the entrance sparkling and lively, without becoming sharp or overpowering. And then they come! The little yellow beads with their scent, so sweet yet so pleasantly herbaceous: the mimosas! Most fragrance compositions that include them radiate this summery southern charm. And they do so here as well! They are cleverly blended with a rose of rich, slightly spicy aroma. Thus, both are equal partners and convey a balanced harmony. And suddenly, I also encounter the delicately fragrant cherry blossoms that give "Sakura Cherry Blossom" its name; they do exist after all, and they swirl around joyfully! The previous arrangement is also supported by a light, certainly not exotic wooden base. This makes the pleasantly fruity floral swirl a bit more grounded and dusted with a fine layer of musk. Everything here is very fine and light yet extremely fragrant. "Sakura Cherry Blossom" reminds me of Japanese painting, which is executed artfully with a very fine brush or even a feather and often adorns very thin porcelain teacups: delicate black lines depicting branches and pink petals! Or of the cherry blossoms dancing in the mild spring air, where the desire often arises to catch them like "Sterntaler" in an imagined apron before they can completely fly away. Like most Jo Malone fragrances, this one is not very long-lasting: just a breath of spring, which, when sprayed on damp hair, becomes a bit more enduring and thus brings itself back to memory in a lovely way. I love this Japanese cherry blossom festival, which, with its charming nature, still brings joy even in early summer: she is charming, the little delicate lady!

I've recently tested this fragrance and I was expecting something richer and warmer maybe influenced by the red packaging : although the pyramid seems perfect, the result is a very minimal scent, as basic as a white t-shirt. I said to myself: "This isn't in the style of the famous nose Olivier Polge!" After the fresh- watery impact, on my skin I smelled only a pale memory of a cheap aromatic water.Where are the base notes? the patchouli, the amber, the musk are only ghosts.So, not a real "perfume", but maybe a scented water .The sillage too is quite weak and the longevity isn't so good. Anyway, it could be pleasantly worn in the hot season as everyday scent, in the free time as well as at the office, because totally inoffensive!

What is the point of even pretending that Givenchy is an independent perfume house when under the management of LVMH, the perfumer is one and the same as that of Christian Dior? Everything seems to be merging in a race to the bottom to a single and solitary layer of mediocrity. DAHLIA NOIR eau de toilette is a prime example. This is another "pink" fragrance among hundreds, about as trivial as they come. And what a waste of a name! I have not tried the eau de parfum, but I can only hope that this latest launch is indeed a desecration of its namesake. I suspect that it is not. After a brief abstract fruity-floral opening with no identifiable flowers or fruits and a dilute sugar solution-type sweetness, DAHLIA NOIR steps in line with the majority of mainstream designer scents recently launched--in both the men's and the women's category--which feature a boring base of iso-E-super and ambroxan. I've smelled this so many times that by now I can only say that I'm suffering from serious pseudo woody-amber aromachemical base fatigue. This is not cedar. This is not amber. This is THAT stuff sold in vats evidently for a pittance. This may fool many consumers most of the time, but anyone who has smelled ambergris and cedar can only sigh in confronting this same old solvent over and over again. Why do I suspect that the dominant and all-too-familiar aromachemical base (iso-E-super + ambroxan) featured in DAHLIA NOIR eau de toilette is produced by a company also owned by LVMH? By the drydown, this is not even an artificial smelling fruity-floral. It's just that base.

The new "Dahlia Noir Eau de Toilette" is a completely different fragrance than the Dahlia Eau de Parfum (which I prefer). While the Eau de Parfum is a pervasive mélange of rose and patchouli with great glamour and sillage, the Eau de Toilette is light-hearted with topnotes of peach and and lemon, fading into a soft whisper of rose on a light bed of conventional woody-ambers. "Dahlia Noir EdT" is not very thrilling, but quite suitable for a polite afternoon tea party. It's a trivial perfume. If you want to give the new Givenchy releases a chance this year, go for the much better "Dahlia Noir Eau de Parfum" which combines rose, iris and mimosa for a "whammo effect" and is marketed as a "sensual powdery floral chypre" (not a bad description for a change). The Eau de Toilette is called a "radiant Fruity Floral" in the press material. Forget about the adjective "radiant" and replace it by "boring" - you'll get the idea.

At the flea market, there was a phalanx of Dahlia bottles - but without boxes. Who can read the micro-sized writing on the bottom of the bottles? My glasses were somewhere - probably thinking of me. I squinted unsuccessfully - and then had to rely on my nose. I already own the EDP and the L'Eau and didn't want to make a double purchase. This, that, and the other sprayed and quickly sorted out, as my husband was already shifting from one foot to the other. One of the scents struck me as different, despite the family resemblance - slimmer than the EdP, but fuller than the L'Eau. Moreover, it exercises an attractive restraint - yet is still well perceivable. The fruity opening is subtle, slightly sweet, and not sour. The fruits are presented appetizingly. A basket of light flowers stands right next to it, garnished with soft, non-scratchy pepper. The vanilla adds a sunny warmth and is also soft. This Dahlia version is the most romantic for me - with a touch of playfulness. Perhaps even a bit girlish. Perfect! My husband coughed in the background - and I made a turbo purchase. At home, happily reunited with my glasses, I read that I had indeed grabbed the missing EdT. As we age, eyesight is said to decline - and humor to increase. My nose seems to be just fine.

Givenchy is a name that stands for quality, for feminine, clear fashion. But also for unforgettable and unforgotten fragrances, of which the first - L'Interdit - is still my absolute favorite. So I am also inclined to test fragrances from this brand when they come my way. Fortunately, I only sprayed Dahlia Noir on a scent strip once. The fragrance is fruity floral and relatively light, but after a while, it becomes extremely sweet and develops an additional note that strikes me as synthetic sandalwood, which is clearly too much of a good thing. Dahlia Noir is undoubtedly a girl’s fragrance, light and fresh, lovely and sweet. However, this fragrance does not reach the quality of Givenchy scents from the time of Audrey Hepburn and is not a candidate for purchase for me.

I can barely smell the top notes; they blend together evenly and are very light. Most noticeable are the flowers and vanilla, and the lemon in the top note keeps everything fresh in the end. (Or is it the cedar combined with lemon?) But actually, the fragrance smells like body lotion or hand cream, which reflects in the sillage. Barely there. Pleasant, freshly applied, if it were just a bit stronger, I would buy it, because the scent itself is pleasant, powdery, wonderful! But it belongs to the type of fragrance that you can mist yourself with from head to toe without overdoing it (like with Love Chloe, CK Be, etc...)

I already have the Dahlia Divin and the Dahlia Noir Edp. Today, I have the Dahlia Noir Edt... The Dahlia Noir Edp is very strong and intense for me. Very vanilla-like and, in my opinion, more of an evening scent. The Edt, on the other hand, is more suitable for daytime :) Scent: The Dahlia Noir Edt smells more floral and citrusy to me than the Edp.

I had the chance to sniff Dahlia Noir EdT today and I am completely taken with it. It starts off a bit sweet for me, rather floral. Then it becomes more citrusy. The mandarin comes to the fore. Since I am a fan of D&G light blue and Biotherm L'Eau, I really like this scent as well. It reminds me a lot of the two fragrances.

The newest addition to my collection, Quatre Absolu de Nuit pour Homme by Boucheron, is not your run-of-the-mill fougère fragrance. It opens with a captivating blend of spicy black pepper and nutmeg tempered with lemon, lavender, and sage top notes. It dries down to a lovely, sweet mélange of vanilla with woody notes from patchouli, akigalawood, cedar, and vetiver. It is both subtle and enticing. It has good projection and longevity, pulling complements even eight hours after application.

It is a cool day as I settle into my chamber in the woods. The previous occupant laid the finest laminate and polished it splendidly with lemons. Well, quickly open the windows and let the cool forest air in. For the air is indescribably clear and invigorating, and although the thermometer indicates cold, there is a subtler and purer warmth than in summer. Under the porch, green herbs thrive, creeping through the beams. This chamber is simple, but it will suffice. I want to experience life anew, to approach real life, but without practicing any renunciation, unless it is absolutely unavoidable. Therefore, I have not brought much, just a few spices: pepper, nutmeg, and vanilla. So I stand by the window, close my eyes, and take a deep breath. Sweet grass seeps up through the cracks in the floor. Green wisps of spicy fragrance fill the chamber, overwhelming everything artificial and bringing peace to the spirit.
