Since I'm going into Summer now on my side of the globe, I'm only just getting around to sampling the 2011 Summer releases. Burberry Summer 2011 is passable, but certainly not exciting, at least not to my nose. As per usual, this Summer flanker is heavy on the citrus accords and watery fruits. Orange is the most dominant note, being rather bitter and sour at times. My skin never works too well with citrus or fruits, so seeing that Burberry Summer 2011 is all about the fruity accords, on my skin it turns acidic. The heart is nice but predictable with soapy freesia and delicate rose. The drydown isn't any more interesting with a rather bland blend of cedar and musk. The scent does become less harsh as the fragrance settles, however the underlying orange note lingers on. Not that I find orange an unpleasant note, it's just not something that easily agrees with my skin or my nose. I still prefer Burberry Summer 2009 which was much more pleasant and less generic. Unfortunately I can no longer find the 2009 release, and in the next few months the same could be said of this fragrance, which is already gracing the discount stores.

I ordered 100 ml of Burberry Summer from an online perfumery for an incredible € 24,- (blind) and it was worth it, even though winter is just around the corner. At first, I smell citrus notes, very fresh and zesty - but this fades quite quickly and the fragrance gently hugs my skin, becoming softer and reminiscent of a flower meadow. A fine scent that also reminds me of damp, freshly washed, fruity-smelling hair, barely noticeable, very delicate, light, and fresh. As the name "Summer" suggests, Burberry Summer comes across like a gentle summer breeze, a touch of freshness, a hint of good mood, not intrusive but very quiet and pleasant. (I can only agree with my predecessor, definitely not artificial and loud) Not a particularly striking scent but certainly a lovely one, perfect for spring days, summer days, or just to spray on for a boost of good mood. The longevity could be a bit better, I often have to reapply.

Ah... I am delighted. This summer fragrance is soooo beautiful! Wait a moment, let me give myself a few slaps to calm down, otherwise I can't write - SLAP. There. Now I'm back... So: Burberry Summer for Women 2011 starts citrusy, but not artificially. There isn't a heavy dose of citrus scent that takes your breath away. No. Here comes a noble freshness, very pleasant, light, and understated. In the heart, you can clearly smell the flowers. However, I am sure that there must be at least a 50 percent fruit component in the heart note, because I can still make out the fruits. A very pleasant, balanced fresh blend of flowers and fruits that lays softly on the skin. The scent feels very elegant and chic. The base notes join in without overpowering the flower-fruit duo. Absolutely wonderful - I am truly captivated. Burberry Summer for Women 2011 cannot be compared to the summer editions from Escada - which I also like very much, but in comparison seem very loud and rather artificial, at least some of them. Burberry relies on understatement without much fuss. Still, it's a strong scent. The longevity is also good. I applied the fragrance last night, and I can still clearly perceive it after more than twelve hours. Ah... The scent is simply enchanting and always wearable in spring and summer. I am constantly asked what delicious fragrance I am wearing - but I won't reveal it. Ha! ;-D

Two days ago I was at my favourite drugstore and there was a new corner with the fragrances by Jo Malone. Immediately I was attracted by a black bottle with the writing "Incense & cedrat". A unisex scent, as said me the seller. At first spray I felt a fresh sensation, given by the citrusy opening note...but then Her Majesty the incense note arrived to my nose: deep, spriritual, neither too smoky nor warm, but almost cold and liturgic . A wonderful sensation. A very long and particular sillage followed me for many hours . But I am a common woman and this one is a too expensive pleasure .... I'll reapeat my wonderful experience only at the drugstore!
In comparison to other incense fragrances like Armani Prive Ensens satin or Bois d´ensens, it is too monotonous and flat; the smoke here is less "soft" and enveloping.

The 2018 version of Eau de Givenchy is a quite straightforward eau de cologne on my skin, with a slightly more pronounced feminine touch of tender floral and cottony musk. The first 3 hours of Eau de Givenchy is dominated by the refreshingly bitter green petit grain and its more floral cousin, the verdant neroli. The orange blossom provides a suave, faintly indolic backdrop, while the various citrus fruits only briefly offer a few glimpses at the very first moment. With Eau de Givenchy focusing more on the petit grain-neroli-orange blossom trio instead of sparkling citrus fruits or Mediterranean aromatic herbs, the fragrance leans more traditionally feminine to my nose. Its focus on neroli and its cousins also reminds me of Tom Ford Neroli Portofino and Frederic Malle Cologne Indélébile. However, while they're interchangeable to a certain extent, Eau de Givenchy differs more significantly in the dry down, with its more substantial, cotton-y yet slightly metallic musk adding more heft and rendering it more opaque comparing to the sharper, leaner, soapier and somewhat more "robotic" Neroli Portofino, or the more refined and traditional Cologne Indélébile. Although I haven't yet compared them side by side, the prominently musky dry down of Eau de Givenchy is reminiscent of that of Byredo Blanche's to my nose, more than other eau de cologne-type of fragrances. The sillage of Eau de Givenchy is moderate to soft, while the longevity is at least 8 hours on me. As I haven't yet had the opportunity to smell the original Eau de Givenchy, I don't have any direct comparison to offer. But there's no doubt that this brand new version of Eau de Givenchy smells like a product conceived to fit and made in our modern era, rather than one trying to convey vintage characteristics. Without prior knowledge of the original version, I find this 2018's Eau de Givenchy an adequate eau de cologne-style fragrance, centred around green neroli and vaporous, clean white musk, and marginally more feminine than most colognes. Although arguably less polished and less nuanced than many neroli-white musk fragrances put out by well-known niche brands, the price and the accessibility of Eau de Givenchy nevertheless put it at a relative advantage. I'd recommend it as a gateway clean neroli-white musk perfume from mainstream designer brands.

For years, it has been observed that the Cologne theme is experiencing a renaissance in the world of perfume. I enjoy the immediate refreshing effect that sets in when I spray on a Cologne. Especially welcome in the heat! I am not familiar with the predecessor of this Givenchy fragrance, so I cannot provide a comparison. Upon spraying, the bergamot and oranges burst into my nose with vigor, instantly lifting my spirits. Shortly after, I smell neroli, which will come to dominate the scent. The citrus notes remain slightly perceptible; soon, this fragrance impression is anchored by a very light woody musk base. Thus, the scent lingers with me for hours, which is pleasing, especially if one cannot or does not want to reapply constantly. All in all, the Cologne theme has been modernly implemented - of course unisex - and is long-lasting in Eau de Toilette concentration.

Colognes in summer, from all sides. Slowly, I have my head full of about 100 fine cologne high-flyers. Givenchy, however, stuck with me today. Fine and delicious. It has something special. It smells high-quality. Givenchy doesn't create anything new but something very beautiful. Cologne du Parfumeur by Guerlain has always been a favorite of mine in summer. The magic here is a subtle, bright honey note in the base, just like the new Givenchy. The radiance is rather close to the body. Neroli fuels the start with green notes, mandarin, spring flowers, violet tones, musk, all creamy and round after 30 minutes of freshness. Rather feminine. Not too citrusy. Not woody. I constantly imagine lilac. Lilac flowers and again something like flower honey. One could almost call it the copied Guerlain DNA. I would have liked it to be stronger and longer green, but the great bottle already says: I am simple, clear, quiet, and noble. Humble water. Sacred. Clean. Untouched and beautiful. So be it. Delicious. Well done Guerlain... uh, Givenchy!

I love it...the water. It has a wonderfully quirky quality and brings back many memories of my childhood. The scent is not new, but it is back again. It smells like grandma's handkerchiefs from back in the day. Fresh, it clears the head and the mind, and is good for the soul...especially in this weather out there, at 38°C. It's not just green, white, or pure; it reminds one of an orange grove (sunshine and lightness, and no, not quite Kölnisch Wasser and also not Tosca...), bergamot is present like in many colognes, and our ancestors knew why. Fresh, unobtrusive, a bit old-fashioned and therefore extremely modern again. Timeless, classic, and a gentle journey for the nose. The only thing is, it doesn't last long as a scent trail, but on the skin, there's a pleasant light musk that doesn't tickle or irritate. It then changes a bit woody and eventually disappears completely. That's fine by me; it's summer.

It is very rare that my nose can really pick up almost everything listed in the fragrance pyramid of a perfume. Sometimes I think I can recognize things like chamomile or rosemary in addition to lavender after reading about them, but in blind testing: Never ever. Eau de Givenchy is probably a unique exception here: Neroli checked off, bergamot checked off, orange, yes, petitgrain and orange blossom too, musk and wood (no: not specifically cedar wood, but still wood). The only thing I wouldn't have identified additionally is mandarin. What does that tell me - aside from the rather unlikely possibility that my nose developed superpowers overnight? I suspect it is more likely that “Eau de Givenchy” is a beautifully crafted, straightforward Eau de Cologne! The opening is zesty neroli - but far from 4711, softened by bergamot and immediately underpinned with orange. Flowers, wood, and musk follow closely behind. For me, Eau de Givenchy is like a very naturally scented light version of a blend between Nerolia Bianca and Mandarin Basilic by Guerlain. A lovely light summer cologne - and for all lovers of the genre, a clear recommendation to test! By the way, my nose also recognizes something additional: lemon balm! Maybe there is something to those sniffing superpowers overnight after all!

Hello everyone who loves to spray themselves with all kinds of fragrances! Well, I’m not really any different, but I only do all this to entertain you and to impress a few ladies here! While the first part seems to be going quite well, the latter is NOT working at all… I think I really should find myself another hobby… you’re lucky I still have a few samples here, so I can write a comment or two before I storm off in a huff! :D So… one of these samples is “Bespoke - Garden Roses” by Burberry, which belongs to the slightly higher-end or more exclusive fragrances from Burberry. Well, roses then. This doesn’t necessarily increase my interest in this scent, as I’m not a big fan of roses, but maybe this is something for you ladies, even though not all of you women should like roses. Hmm… note to self: It’s best never to gift a lady a cliché rose, but to choose something else, something unusual. Well, due to my abysmally poor botanical knowledge, I can’t think of anything else one could gift a lady… maybe a prickly thistle? You have to admit that thistles look quite nice, right? :D he he Anyway, let’s take a look or rather sniff and see how the fragrance smells! The Scent: The scent starts with a wonderfully citrusy note reminiscent of creamy lemons. Alongside, there are slightly herbal and green scents that together with the lemons smell quite good and summery. In the background, it’s a bit fruity, and the scent reminds me of apples. Roses are indeed one of the main notes here, but they are less prominent than I would have expected from the name of the fragrance. The slight sweetness is somewhat indefinable, but it smells nice, unobtrusively casual, and fits well with the rest. Slightly rosy, herbaceous-green, and lightly sweet, it continues into the heart note. The creamy notes soften the herbal-scratchy scents a bit, making it feel very pleasant, so the fragrance just feels good. Later, or rather in the base, it smells of roses that now also have a slightly more robust scent. The sweet notes remain somewhat powdery, but are now also a bit stronger, as if one were smelling tuberoses or something similar. Additionally, it’s a bit herbal and also biting-herbaceous (at the beginning of the base, the herbal aspect even seems a bit biting, but this subsides as the fragrance develops). So, the scent is not a pure rose scent but is quite varied and thus quite nice. The Sillage and Longevity: The sillage is okay, neither strong nor weak. In my opinion, the scent can be detected from a moderate distance for a while. The longevity is also okay, as it lasts about six or seven hours before it becomes too weak. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular with a thick base and a clear fragrance liquid. The name of the fragrance is printed on the front. The cap is cylindrical and chrome-plated and features a pink ribbon, making the bottle at first glance reminiscent of Chloe bottles (even if these should lack the grooves in the glass). All in all, it looks quite nice. Conclusion: So… okay, even though I’m not a real fan of roses, I must say that this fragrance has turned out quite nice. It doesn’t smell exclusively of roses, which I find great, but rather of much more, so that you feel like you’re busy gardening on a sunny spring day while the cat curiously watches you and wonders what you’re trying to achieve by pulling out plants (weeds) and then replanting (e.g., roses or something else). Of course, he keeps coming over, sniffing around everything, and then wanders off again to listen to the birds chirping and, of course, to look for fluttering creatures. By the end of the day, his white fur is pitch black, so you can then sigh and get to work cleaning the scratchy creature while it naturally resists… Yes, Garden Roses is a successful fragrance for spring and summer that could be worn well during the day and in leisure time, and it can also “create” a good mood. Despite being labeled as unisex, I would still recommend the fragrance more for ladies, as it appears creamy and gentle, thus coming across as more feminine to me. Well, I would recommend a test here, although this seems to only be possible in Burberry stores, where you can also purchase the fragrance with different concentrations. And with that, I’ve come to the end and wish you all a lovely evening and good health. So then, until next time :)

Tea perfumes are some of my favorites. I drink tea as well so it is no wonder that the rare teas collection captured my imagination. Jo Malone has provided some beautiful moments with their scents over the years so I had moderate to high hopes for this collection. While the first three scents with the lighter colored juice were never going to impress me (I don't like green or white tea much), the last three did the trick. Midnight Tea is not much of a tea scent at all, and I have not seen any tea mentioned in any of the notes. This is the illusion of tea. Don't expect a big black tea scent. This is a smooth vanilla composition with honey/fruity notes. It is captivating for sure. However, the price is prohibitive despite the large bottles. If they had done a bottle half the size and charged half the price this would already be in my collection. The sillage and lasting power is better than the typical JM cologne.

With Midnight Black Tea, here comes my comment on the last Rare Teas fragrance from Jo Malone. I must say that I liked all the scents, and of course, I have a few favorites among them. And even if this one doesn't belong to my favorites, it has still turned out to be a nice fragrance. *sniff*… doesn’t it make you a bit sad when you reach the end of something? :( No? … um… me neither! :DD After all, there are still so many fragrances to test! But I’m getting tired… I’ve had enough, I’m done… (who believes that…). The scent: Ahh,… I feel like all the fragrance notes start to smell at once. There’s a light tea scent, but I can’t quite tell what kind of tea it is, as it’s being pushed aside by all the other notes (at least initially). I smell woody notes, incense like frankincense, spices, and sweet vanilla, which adds something soft to the initially “hard” spices and woods. A little later, the spices become softer and weaker, that’s surely the labdanum, although I’m not quite sure how it really smells. However, the vanilla becomes a bit stronger, making the scent generally a bit sweeter. In the end, you can really only smell a bit of tea with vanilla. The sillage and longevity: Even though the beginning shines quite well, the fragrance is medium-strong. With heavy application, it will stand out, otherwise, it might get a bit lost, especially on cold days. The longevity is unfortunately a bit short at just under four to five hours, especially for a scent that feels autumnal to me. The bottle: This bottle is also quite large, rectangular, and tall. On the front, there’s just a small, square label with the Jo Malone logo on it, which is enough, as this minimalism in information on the bottle makes it look nice. This tea scent is filled with a dark yellowish liquid and is capped with the black, oval lid known from the other bottles. A simply described, but still very nice to look at bottle. I think Jo Malone has done a great job with the entire collection of these Rare Teas fragrances, as all the scents really smell wonderful, and it really comes down to personal taste. Personally, I liked Oolong and Jade Leaf Tea the best. With Darjeeling, unfortunately, the tea scent was too weak for me; otherwise, it could have been my favorite, maybe I should test it again... But even here with Midnight Black Tea, a great scent comes, especially for black tea lovers, and one shouldn’t be put off by the initially somewhat strong spices. Because these quickly soften, allowing you to enjoy a lightly spiced and vanilla-sweetened black tea, of course, for spraying on (I certainly wouldn’t drink it, don’t say I didn’t warn you!). The scent is more suited for autumn, possibly also winter, where it might seem a bit mild or weak for very cold days. It goes as “usable for any situation.” Just at parties, disco, etc… one might want to reach for a different fragrance :D So, anyone who likes tea should check out this scent, and while you’re at it, the other Rare Teas too :)

Since no one has written anything about this edition yet, let me start with a few words about the Rare Tea Collection: Jo Malone launched tea-inspired fragrances with its Tea Fragrance Blends back in 2011. Serge Majoullier continued this idea and experimented for four years to now release six exclusive scents that stand out from the rest of the offerings due to their pricing policy (only available as 175ml bottles for around €300), elevating them to higher luxury levels. There are also interesting differences in the production: For the first time, the tea is extracted as a pure infusion, meaning it is steeped in alcohol. For Midnight Black Tea, this process supposedly takes 100 hours, as the note becomes softer over time. The perfume is consciously designed around the tea without a classic pyramid, only with complementary additions to highlight and emphasize its inherent scent. Visually, the distinction is made through the new bottles, a novelty for Jo Malone London after 25 years. Black Midnight Tea sounds so enticing that I was tempted by its exclusivity ("I probably won't get this again") to participate in my first sharing of an untested newcomer. The first attempt was disappointing: 1) I smelled, and still smell, no tea. With that, Black Midnight already misses its task, which I had blindly entrusted to it. However, I must say that despite liking the note, I am not a tea connoisseur and sometimes have difficulties recognizing it in other fragrances as well. So, an experienced nose needs to take another look to sniff out the Puerh leaves from the Chinese Yunnan province. 2) Labdanum. What I first encountered in "Sable Marocain / Morocco Sand" and which sparked a spontaneous affection in me, has now repeatedly proven to be increasingly bothersome. That the so promising labdanum dominates the heart note and detracts from my enjoyment of the midnight tea was something I did not expect at all. The second attempt, with a more cautious dosage: Much better. After the sweet, finely spicy, and somewhat scratchy beginning, the labdanum behaves more appropriately later on. Throughout the day, I perceive the amber vanilla much better, which waves its golden flag softly from a distance of my wrist. The third attempt, as a sprinkled napkin on the heater: I hoped that the tea would dare to come to the moonlight at a warmer temperature, but the Puerh spirits remain reserved. At least, it is a soft room scent, and the forbidden L-note stays shy on the cellulose. Longevity: A strong spray lasts from midnight to midnight, including a shower. For a tea scent, that is a long time, but here I allow myself the quibble that tea is, after all, not present for me ;) I like it. However, I am a bit unsure to what extent this is due to the further chances and to what extent it is because I want to justify the purchased decant. I will not buy it again, perhaps use it up, definitely trade it. Still, my desire for more fragrances from Jo Malone has been awakened.

I'm always looking for vintage fragrances so i was surfing ebay and i came across this version. It said it was for MEN but obviously it was wrong. I'm really not angry because I'm currently wearing it and i think a man can get away with it. Thia stuff is STRONG!! Top to bottom left to right front and back. This stuff rocks. Launched in 1985 and I'm not at all surprised how strong this is considering when it came out. Man the 80s were just a fantastic decade! There will never ever be another time period like it. This fragrance is spicy sweet and cinnamony throughout. It just lasts. Period! I got a good deal also so if you are interested just go on ebay or etsy or mercari and u should find it. Go easy on the application because it's quite strong and you will notice the nice peach note in the opening while the base is much more animalic. Also oakmoss, FABULOUS REAL OAKMOSS! Where have u gone my friend. I do hope that u find your way back.

Very fresh feminine fragrance, my bottle delivered what it promised, a lot of joy from a good EDP for the day. It didn't last too long, but I enjoyed wearing it very much, and it was still without a sprayer, which I prefer compared to now, where there are only sprayers. It's all about the dosage... CK probably thought the production wasn't worth it. I wouldn't have discontinued it. I don't know if there was a body lotion for it. That would surely be excellent as well. I'm not an EDP wearer of those heavy scents that you wear at night. My living space is more spread out during the day when the light is present. And this EDP or even the EDT definitely belongs there.

SCENARIO 1: The storm suddenly breaks out. Streams of rain and hail, piercing the leaves. The last few meters to the forest cabin, quickly run. Door slammed shut, relieved laughter. Soaked and dripping puddles. Leaf scraps fished from the hair. Their eyes meet. And a very awkward silence. She runs to the bathroom. He just takes a quick look around. The old cabin has stood empty for a long time. Retro furniture, flower-spice potpourri with cinnamon sticks. Ubiquitous dust. So yesterday... An open door crack. Coincidence? Intent? Droplet-drenched back. Small of the back dimples beneath the cross. Her gaze over the wet shoulder, just a step away. No more. The nose buried in the wet hair. Nape hairs bristling under fingertips. Pulse fluttering in the cradle of the collarbone. Sweet-spicy taste of the skin. Hers, his. Warmth. Cinnamon warmth. Breath warmth. Body warmth. Sensory heat. Hunt me. Catch me. Scratch me. Kiss me. Bite me. Love me. Outside, the storm rages, throwing itself against the walls with full force like a wild cat, scratching at the windows, hissing and howling along with the storm wind. Outside, AC/DC plays 'Thunderstruck'... In here, at the epicenter, it is almost silent, only wild pounding in the temples. Chris Isaac's 'Wicked Game' in the back of the mind. The rest of the world is insignificant. As long as the storm lasts... #..x&..?!?!.. What.Was.That?! That Obsession, after 20 years of determined rejection, gives me THIS head cinema... Other versions of Obsession have also been described as “sexy” and “naughty.” My feeling is somewhat hmm... strange, special - Obsession smells incredibly erotic to me, like wet (note, not freshly washed!) hair. After a storm, when green scraps are flying. Smells of wood and dust of the cabin. Of skin that is slowly warming up. And also something animalic/civet. Of warm pulsating spices, cinnamon. Of moss, of sweet resin, of “wild,” of “more!” This damp, musty, exciting scent of wet human hair I have not encountered in any other fragrance. Cookies? Christmas? I don't smell that. I don't want to either. Compared to the vintage EdP, the extrait shows no further differences apart from the dimmed volume, the finely faceted green-mossy vs. warm-spicy contrast, and a more intimate sillage. The new version (after all, one must know what to expect when vintage supplies are exhausted) can surprisingly be smelled. It almost aligns with the feeling of the old one. Emphasis on “almost.” The green leaf/herb/moss notes are replaced more quickly by the warm cinnamon base. I still wouldn't call it sweet, despite the now more present vanilla. The animalic aspect is trimmed, tamed, and with it the eroticism. To make it clearer: SCENARIO 2: The storm suddenly breaks out. Streams of rain and hail, piercing the leaves. The last few meters to the forest cabin. Door slammed shut, relieved laughter. Soaked and dripping puddles. Leaf scraps fished from the hair. Everything just like back then. Do you remember? ;) She runs to the bathroom. He should do the same please (one doesn't want to catch a cold!) He just takes a quick look around. Haven't been here in a long time, old house! The retro furniture, potpourris, cinnamon sticks. Now also vanilla candles. And dust. So far, almost everything as before. An open door crack. Definitely not a coincidence! Droplet-drenched back. Small of the back dimples beneath the cross. The nose in the wet hair, just like back then... “Sweetheart, just cuddling today, okay?” “Okay...” Outside, the storm rages, but not for long. And so the world soon sinks into the spicy warm cuddle sleep... Today's EdP is still a beautiful scent. As long as it doesn't change anymore *knockonwood*. Nothing against cuddling, but as long as vintage extrait remnants are not exhausted and available - in my mind, it's not just cuddling ;)

My subscribers (and by that, I don't mean my haters, who apparently have also subscribed to me) may have noticed that I particularly enjoy commenting on extraits. This is primarily because these higher-concentrated versions are rarer, and often there are no comments about them yet, so I like to be the pioneer here. But I do have a weakness for the precious extraits (certainly fueled by a blog from Turandot), especially when it comes to classics where the EDT or EDP version has already been reformulated once or multiple times. Since I prefer things to be more intense, complex, and expressive, I am rarely enthusiastic about the diluted new versions. It may be an illusion - but I still hope to have the original formulation in front of me with the extraits and thus go on a hunt for these treasures. Although I know that they are usually closer to the skin than EDT and EDP. But I wear perfume primarily for myself; my surroundings are quite easily overwhelmed by scents... I only have two miniatures of “Obsession Parfum” with already very dark liquid, but they seem completely intact to me. Unfortunately, I perceive a slight plastic note, which my EDP mini also has. I don't know if this is due to the age of the fragrances or if it is even intentional in the end. In my younger years (early 90s?), I once tested “Obsession,” but I found it too aggressive and piercing at the time. I had thistles as an imaginary image in my mind... No, it was nothing for me back then! Today, I can no longer relate to that, but I have much more sympathy for the “oriental” fragrance direction now. I perceive “Obsession” as warm-spicy and only slightly sweet. I can understand quite well why many have been enamored with this scent for years. However, the plastic note prevents me from giving it more than an 8.0. I am not familiar with the current version. However, I recently spoke to a colleague in the hallway who smelled wonderfully of spicy-sweet gingerbread. She was wearing “Obsession”!

Fantasque is an excellent rose oud from Givenchy, interpreted using the unique aesthetic of La Collection Particulière. Perfumes in this collection restrict themselves to a narrow range of personalities through their use of a limited palette of notes. Noctambule is another rose oud from La Collection Particulière, which maintains a younger demeanor by eschewing incense and resins. This review is based on a 10 ml travel size vial that was bought directly from Givenchy. I am unable to fully confirm that the nose behind Fantasque is Pierre-Constantin Guéros. According to my nose, Fantasque shows an inverted olfactory pyramid. Let me explain! I can smell most of the notes listed in the olfactory pyramid in the opening. I can smell oud, rose, incense and myrrh at the start. The cardamom note is weak in the opening, and you may miss it if you are not looking for it. The oud used in La Collection Particulière is listed as Malaysian oud essence. This is a westernized oud that is dry, without the sour sawdust smell associated with natural oud essence. Vanilla appears early in the heart notes, though it is listed as a base note. Vanilla is the strongest base note along with hints of the other notes. As the olfactory pyramid is a pile of bricks on the floor, I would list Fantasque as a flat oud, frankincense, myrrh, rose, oud perfume. There is some development as time passes, but it is more like waxing and waning of some notes, rather than a pyramid. The notes are too masterfully blended to worry about these nuances. The performance of Fantasque is very good, but not monstrous. After the opening blast, it settles nicely on the skin. It lasts a 6-8 hours on my skin, though in the end it is mostly an amber vanilla. The sillage is excellent in the opening hours, and for some reason, projects the oud very strongly during the first hour. Fantasque is one of the best rose-oud scents I have come across. It is a great fit for someone looking for an elegant rose oud without the pungent natural oud accord. Unfortunately, excellence alone cannot drive the decision to buy. Priced at $405 for 100 ml, this one sits at the frontier of credulity. For now, I will live off the 10 ml sample until I can swipe a full bottle below $300.

Let me start be saying that this fragrance bears no resemblance to Burberry Original for better or worse. The first 10-15 minutes of this fragrance are sheer delight. I was asking the S.A. about the various sizes and thinking- this would make a great everyday Summer scent. A chewy natural mandarin note is adorned with playful uber fresh freesia. Initially I thought, it's on the femme side, so light and clean, it could even work for the office. This screams 'Sunny Day' the same way "Ofresia" by Diptyque performs its Aria- but the comparison ends there. The middle dries to a lovely soft little rosey lily combination that is not very original but suitable for a sheer summer fragrance, thus the overall impression after about 30 minutes on my skin was still uplifted and jovial. However the JoyLuck Club Party stops right about here. Somewhere between the middle and the base this train veers off the tracks and crashes into a messy pile of extremely synthetic musky woody notes- so unnatural I can not even fathom what wood the Nose was trying to emulate, perhaps the fictitious, tawdry, frenetic and often absurd 'Deadwood'. Gone is the freesia and mandarin entirely and the last 2-3 hours here have been torture of something like Lacoste "Touch of Pink" mixed with rancid grapefruit juice layered on a haggard overworked base of synthetic woody and iso Super-E. Perhaps, I am being overly harsh but suffice it to say, give this one a thorough test before you invest, there are many other light Summer fragrances of better workmanship out there.

Burberry Summer for Woman 2013 was just on sale at my trusted drugstore, so I had to give it a try. And to make it worthwhile, I’ll write a little about it: This limited summer fragrance is a somewhat exciting little water that mixes a rather interchangeable floral-fruity drugstore note with a generous dose of aquatic note, creating a summery fresh yet synthetically sweet scent that will surely find its lovers among fans of "freshly showered" fragrances, but unfortunately gives me headaches quickly and effectively. However, there is an interesting subtext that reminds me of care fragrances: not from the shower gel, but from the cream side. Once the excess water has dried a bit, this fresh scent develops a certain well-groomed warmth. At this stage, Summer 2013 reminds me of Happy Spirit Elixir d'Amour by Chopard. The longevity is quite decent, the bottle is simple and round, and I wouldn’t mind if it were filled with a new limited Summer Edition in 2014.

The American designer John Varvatos is better known here for his (men's) perfumes than for his fashion. In the USA, however, his clothing is quite popular - the brand essence could be described as 'rockstar' style for men over 30 (with a higher income, as even plain T-shirts cost around eighty dollars) - men who appreciate the look, acoustics, and tactile feel of swing-top closures. Beer from swing-top bottles has a certain archaic charm. You can open the bottles one-handed, and it makes a nice popping sound. If, like me, you tend to be a quarterly beer drinker, the swing-top bottle delivers all the casual 'standing around a fire at sunset on the lawn' masculinity without having to resort to canned beer or opening a crown cap with your teeth. In short: swing-top = top! A characteristic of the perfumes from the Varvatos house are the distinctly masculine (and often original) designed bottles. And those of his scents that I have smelled so far are at least 'not bad at all'. And because I am drawn to bottles with swing-top closures for the aforementioned reasons, am generally curious, and didn't want to leave another John Varvatos store completely empty-handed.. It didn't start off well. The sprayer and cap of the tester were greasy and damp, and ultimately half-broken, so that I accidentally sprayed quite a bit into my own hand. It then sat there for the rest of the afternoon and a two-hour car ride (where you do move your right hand from time to time, even with an automatic transmission). Therefore, one cannot complain about its relative shortness of breath. To put it kindly, Star U.S.A. is 'nothing special'. An inconsequential fresh all-rounder like a thousand others - no matter how exciting its ingredients may sound at first glance. To put it unkindly, it is a synthetic shower gel candidate with an impertinently half-strong show-off attitude, lacking any rockstar or otherwise remarkable qualities. No 'Star U.S.A.' - not even particularly American. Conclusion: doesn't pop when opened and doesn't whine a bit afterwards.

Oh no, what a terrible, boring, unnecessary scent! And this from a brand I hold in high regard, which has a few really successful perfumes in its lineup (Original, Artisan, Vintage). But for this one, the perfumer and the brand should be ashamed, a total failure of the highest order. Please discontinue it! Why is this taking so long? Why is it still occasionally found in stores? I was in Berlin for work today and had the afternoon free to explore. I went to KaDeWe, Galerie Lafayette, and also to Herr Lehmann - I sprayed dozens of great perfumes on cards. I kept my two wrists free for something truly special; I just had to find it. If worse came to worst, I could always check the Duty Free before my flight home. Mistake! A mini-Duty Free awaited me in Tegel, which even looked small compared to my collection. Really disappointing, I knew everything in the men's section - except for Star USA in the bottom drawer. And I should have left it there! The scent reminds me of the new Lacoste Live, only even more boring, uninspired, and really weak. It doesn't stink directly, but I wouldn't call it fragrant. It's basically just an undefinable brew of light, reddish metallic synthetic fruits and a spicy component like ginger. Then the scent quickly turns woody-bitter before it disappears entirely. It also reminds me a bit of Fierce - only three classes worse. Soapy, clean, sporty would be three neutral, fitting adjectives I could pull out of my nose, but that doesn't need to happen. Some things just need to be put down! Fusion: I like the bottle opener, but it's very unwieldy. Sillage & Longevity: a joke, which suits me very well! Varvatos' worst scent by a wide margin! Keep your hands off!

I am simply crazy about what Olivier Cresp has done in here, this natural oud smelling scent combined with orange and woody notes is a major underdog in the niche world. Yes, of course .. Givenchy makes clothing, they have the designer line of scents with tons of "Gentleman" flankers .. but guys, the exclusive line from Givenchy is as niche as possible. It will last at least 12 hours on the clothes and project like nuts, and this natural smelling oud - Laotian if you ask me - is just a bit animalic, but so good and wearable. There are some other gems in the range like Garcon Manque or Oiseau Rare which are also wonderful, I will test them in the future for sure.

I tested the fragrance during a phase when I was allowed to sniff several very different "leather variants" in perfumes. Unfortunately, this one did not convince me at all - even though I have only had positive encounters with all the listed notes so far. The opening is also pleasantly fruity, the mandarin is clearly noticeable and brings a nice "understated freshness" with it. Unfortunately, this wonderful note fades quite quickly and the heart and base notes come into play, which I cannot distinguish at all. However, without spicy saffron, without a deep, rich oud. Much worse: now it really becomes unpleasant for my nose - I have rarely had such a harsh scent experience. It simply smells continuously of stale frying fat. I unfortunately could not perceive any lightness or smoothness at all. Even in a second test, I could not notice any change. I then passed Indompté on to my brother and lo and behold: it was as if it were a completely different fragrance. The mandarin was beautiful, saffron was well noticeable, and there was a quite nice leathery drydown. The whole composition suited him perfectly. A truly striking proof of the extent to which individual skin chemistry plays a role in fragrance development (and perception)! On my skin, a truly unbearable scent - on my brother, a really beautiful and stylish office companion.

Windsor Tonic really appeals to me overall. This fragrance is summery fresh with beautiful citrus elements. However, we also have a relatively prominent Neroli note here. The Neroli accord is really well balanced. Still, I find it a bit too dominant. With Neroli, my nose is always a bit cautious. Over time, this relatively prominent impression becomes milder and better integrates with the other notes, and from then on, I really like Windsor Tonic. The fragrance starts off beautifully citrusy, slightly green, and sparkling. There are subtle tea vibes coming through. I really like that! Relatively quickly, the aforementioned Neroli note joins in. Quite present and confident. In my opinion, it's a bit too much, causing the citrus elements to fall slightly out of harmony. Over time, a subtly spicy cardamom character emerges. Cardamom is lightly dosed, but just right to make the whole thing work beautifully for me. The Neroli also becomes milder and softer, which I think benefits the fragrance. Towards the end, the citrus elements diminish, the Neroli becomes softer, the cardamom is no longer perceptible, and a clean musk comes in its place. The fragrance is wonderfully unisex wearable. Longevity and sillage are decent to even really good. The longevity for me is about 8 hours, which I really didn't expect. When it comes to projection, Windsor Tonic holds back a bit. The fragrance is there, but it definitely doesn't shout and is generally more discreet in that regard.

Not a typical designer fragrance, this one has a lovely hint of incense and is deeper than most designer frags tend to be. Of course Coty still has no idea what they are doing so it can be had for under $40 even though they are trying to bring it back to the retailers at full price.

Euphoria Gold Men is a fragrance by Calvin Klein that is not very well known today. Even back then, I didn't really have it on my radar, which is really a shame. This scent is actually quite enjoyable and I like it. Euphoria Gold Men gives me the feeling of being freshly showered and shaved. It's the weekend, the weather is nice, and the mood is good. This fragrance perfectly conveys this scenario for me. Right at the beginning, it opens with fresh components. The ginger and lemon do a great job here. Additionally, I had the feeling of sniffing something herbal or slightly green. However, I wouldn't have directly expected the listed basil. A certain sweetness is also already detectable. After a while, it becomes noticeably sweeter and spicier. A wonderful honey-cinnamon blend works its way through beautifully. I can also already perceive a bit of vanilla. In fact, I thought I was smelling super delicious, but gently and pleasantly used cardamom. I was probably mistaken, but that's how it goes sometimes. Over time, it becomes increasingly sweet and the relatively fresh accords from the top note fade away more and more. The sweet impressions now completely dominate. I really like the entire composition. Of course, the fragrance does come across as somewhat synthetic, but many fragrances, especially designer ones, give that impression. However, I don't think that's necessarily a negative thing. There are many beautiful fragrances that have a synthetic quality, and Euphoria Gold Men is one of them. Overall, a great, slightly oriental fragrance with a wonderful sweetness and fresh impressions at the beginning. Generally very pleasingly designed.

...are there dentists on Parfumo? Voilà, here is the olfactory sweetness of horror for each one of them! Cap off, onto the wrist, and the scent is unexpectedly citrusy, almost fresh, spicy. One might think ginger and lemon would get lost in the sticky pond associated with cinnamon, honey, amber, and vanilla. They do. But not yet, not in the top note, where the two make their shiny appearance, and it’s not half bad! A bit synthetic but quite convincing, the 'golden' theme can be recognized, however (still) not heavy, massive gold, but more like gold leaf. More and more cinnamon comes in, which is also quite pleasant to sniff in the picture, but at the same time, it drags honey, vanilla, and amber along with it, and tadaaa, here it is, the dripping-sweet, deep-golden, sticky pond. And I really can’t write much more, lemon and ginger get stuck in there and really struggle to break free. There we have it, the ton-heavy gold nugget. The sugar crystallizes noticeably on my wrist ... Those who don’t like sweet are probably better off testing Prada Candy instead of Euphoria Gold. Because Euphoria Gold is heavily sweet, cinnamon-spicy, thoroughly edible (please don’t lick it off your wrist, it really doesn’t taste good!) and enchantingly oriental. I admit, I like it. However, in homeopathic doses. I have also surprisingly received many compliments for the scent; it seems to make an impression, not to mention the really attractive bottle, which fits quite well in a small collection like mine. I can't complain about longevity and projection either; I was told the scent trail behind me was hardly detectable even after hours. Here, in my opinion, Calvin Klein has managed to create something interesting for once, although this scent also only joins the sweet-spicy trend, and I find a version for women almost unnecessary, as the "Men" version is 100% unisex.

Givenchy Pour Homme Blue Label used to be my signature scent when it was released more than 10 years ago. I remember it was a classic woody fragrance, with a tinge of aquatic and floral notes. Originally, I was captured by the astonishing blue bottle, but when I smelled the juice inside I knew I would have liked it. It opens a little citrus-like but it is more refined, with fresh mildly sour and fruity notes coming through and a hint of spicy ones too. The spicy and sweet bergamot and the authentic bitter grapefruit hit hard in the top notes blend well with the hedione, which adds that particular floral jasmine-magnolia smell. After the opening it melds pepper and cardamon, giving it a little more depth that otherwise would not be there. Not too much floral, despite the amazing lavender presence, but the wood and pepper definitely give it a dry feel. Then when it dries down, it has a woody watery vibe going on, which reminds me of Acqua di Gio. I am not saying it is a clone of it, but they belong to the same class and have the same vibe. I do not find this to be spicy at all though, just like Chanel Allure Sport even though they are considered spicy. The resinous olibanum dominates the smoky vetiver, however, mixed with the cedar they all give a profound woody pleasure. Longevity and projection are way below average. Though, what this fragrance lacks in, it makes up for in scent and quality. Give this fragrance a try if you're into aquatics because it's a bit different than any generic summer fragrance. It is crisp, positive, light, clean, it has some depth, and it is quite uplifting. To me, the red version is good for more professional atmospheres in cooler weather, rather the blues is good for more sporty casual events in warmer weather. Recommended for the spring or summer, it’s a daytime scent perfect to wear in the office as well as on leisure or sports time. -Elysium

... I find myself at a loss in the morning about what to wear for this ordinary weekday. Now I'm standing five minutes in front of the shelf and still don't know what to choose. Then I see the blue one and think, why not. You haven't been worn in a while, you deserve it, so come on. Upon applying this perfume, the nose first encounters a citrus note. The scent then becomes slightly floral and spicy. Vetiver makes it dry, and a light incense note comes into play. The longevity and sillage are average. This fragrance is perfect for the office for men of any age. If you like it fresh and slightly smoky, this might be the one.

Price: mid-range, cheaper than most other designers and often available at a very fair price. Season: year-round, but of course perfect for the warm months Age recommendation: from 20; This fragrance is considerably younger than the Red Label variant, but also very suitable for more mature men Intensity: Not tested on skin, but very long-lasting and intense on paper Suitability: Going out, leisure, sports, office Scent: I am a big fan of Givenchy PH (red bottle) and therefore had to test the successor. Upon spraying, an ultra-synthetic fresh accord (Calone?) immediately reveals itself. The opening smells very similar to DKNY Men 2009. I don't find that bad, but it doesn't blow me away; it reminds too much of shower gel and this note has been smelled too often to still impress. What comes next I like better, Blue Label smells very similar to Red Label, the spicy notes in the middle are almost identical. The highlight is the drydown: Here, very nice woody notes emerge, which I, as a wood fan, find excellent. Red Label is somehow more balsamic and a bit sweeter due to the labdanum in the base, while Blue Label is drier and woodier. Conclusion: I like the scent very much. I still prefer the Red Label version a bit, as the synthetic and overused aquatic top note of BL speaks less to me. I find the base almost better than that of the red predecessor. Which one should you choose? Blue Label will certainly appeal to a younger audience and aqua fans, while Red Label is more for the slightly older crowd. I can recommend both. However, in my opinion, it is not worth owning both, as they are too similar. When my Red Label runs out, I will get the Blue one. Either way, I consider the scent to be highly recommendable; you get a top-notch fresh and sporty wood scent that comes in an aquatic guise but reveals entirely different qualities after the artificial top note fades. If Givenchy had released this fragrance in the 90s, it would have been far more successful, as it easily outshines most fresh scents from that time. But don't worry, GPHBL is not retro in the slightest or outdated. Like Red Label, Givenchy has created an absolutely mainstream-compatible fragrance here, which offers so much more than one initially thinks and does many things right that other designer fragrances in this genre have done wrong, resulting in boring and cheap implementations.

A powerful almond, just lightly touched by incense notes (wow), with moderate and pleasant saffron. Peach and tonka bean make it quite sweet. After about 30 minutes, patchouli kicks in while adding a slightly earthy touch. On me, just a few sprays were enough—it's very strong! Recommended for those who want to try a different kind of almond

This is very good oriental spicy/woody fragrance, i love it from the opening to the drydown, if you want a refined spiced version from Tom Ford Noir Extreme, then get yourself Liquid Gold, it's very masculine, you cannot go wrong with this scent, it's one of the best releases from Calvin Klein

Foudroyant is a beautiful spicy woody all in finesse and sophistication.for me it is completely unisex and brings a mysterious side to the one who porte.il is not too dry, just what it takes with a very nice balsamy side. Very nice one.worth a try for sure if you like this kind of perfumes. I had a sample with the perfume I bought on the souk and I m very happy with the discovery

At first glance, this woody-spicy amber fragrance seems simple, but its fresh note gives it something truly special. It is an extremely well-executed scent that radiates class and elegance, yet remains unusual. It can be worn by a man or a woman, but my husband has claimed it just for himself :))). The oud is of remarkable subtlety and delicacy. Perfect for those who fear oud, as it simply adds character to the fragrance and a captivating base note. Everything seems perfectly balanced and refined to me. It is quite possible that this could be a signature scent. I love this Givenchy collection. I always find the quality of the craftsmanship to be excellent and timelessly elegant.

This fragrance is something special. I usually wear it combined with a cherry scent (Liquor Cherry Bohoboco / Lost Cherry Tom Ford). When a woman wears this fragrance, it truly makes a statement. Mixing it with the aforementioned cherry perfumes creates a sensual smoky cherry note. For men, it’s an absolutely dominant, outstanding perfume. Not for boys.. Really for men.

At my stop in the city center, there is a large branch of the Turks. I was looking for a sweet, gourmand perfume for the last cold days. A scent that should evoke warmth and cozy feelings within me. From the fragrance pyramid, I expected exactly that from CK One Shock for her Street Edition. So after a first test on a test strip, where a fruity-warm note wafted towards me, I boldly sprayed a generous amount on my wrist. I had to slowly make my way home and got on the bus a few minutes later. I kept sniffing my wrist and was delighted. Finally, a scent where I could detect the components in exactly the order promised by the fragrance pyramid. No annoying lemon freshness, but sweet, juicy fruits, caramel, and chocolate... Wonderful! It had something of fruit cookies, thus conveying exactly the feeling I was looking for. Sitting at home on the sofa, with a steaming cup of tea and pastries in front of me, watching the snow through the window while being in the cozy warm apartment. Then, in the middle of the bus ride, an unexpected change occurred. The delicious scent began to mix with a penetrating coffee note. Coffee? Not like the drink, but like the coffee beans we use to try out more fragrances in perfumery. That this note is not listed is surprising, as it is dominant on me and pushes everything sweet-gourmand into the background. That may sound exciting to others, but I have a big problem with the smell of coffee. It makes me feel sick. Not just a little dizzy, but really nauseous. On the bus, I tried to hide my hand behind me to avoid bothering my fellow passengers. I felt like the scent was radiating in all directions. At home, my first action was to head to the bathroom to get rid of the coffee beans. Here, I can attest to the fragrance's excellent longevity, as it just wouldn't fade and mixed with the scent of my vitamin soap. With this diminished intensity, I could live quite well, but I didn't dare to bring my nose close to my wrist anymore. Nevertheless, I consider this scent to be very special and delicious. My skin is a diva, and for you, the scent might be the treat you've always been looking for. Trying it out is a must! The saleswoman mentioned that the scent is limited, and I struggled with myself about whether I should give it a new home, but ultimately, that coffee note held me back.

Another extreme one. Why always this term?! Why are there increasingly so many offshoots of originals in the mainstream? Well, Hollywood is unfortunately setting the example, and sequels that are more bad than good are becoming less and less rare. The original "Pi" I found pleasantly cozy in the winter of the late nineties, perhaps a bit endearingly sweet and balsamic, but that didn't bother me as a teenager. From today's perspective, I can hardly relate to it; even less so with the hypersynthetic techno-disco offshoot "Pi Neo," which radiates the coldness of a spaceship. "Pi Extreme" now stylistically condenses the original into darker, denser facets. At the beginning, there is noticeably too much benzoin, the first 10 minutes come off very waxy and nose-clenching. Accompanied by a mixture of milk coffee and somewhat thick, viscous cocoa butter, the new Givenchy reveals itself as a stylistic gourmand that resides in somewhat more muted realms. Less of the overly sweet, flashy sugar bomb, rather a slightly tamed excursion into the sweet zone. After an hour, "Pi Extreme" becomes quite moderate in sillage, essentially leaving the impression of a lightly bittersweet chocolate coffee. In terms of artisanal solidity, for me it is overall a bit too dull and monotonous in its composition.

Pi is an extraordinary fragrance, not only because of its bottle but also its sweet scent was groundbreaking. And although mainstream taste today points exactly in its direction & almost all new releases are sugar bombs, Pi remains distinctive enough. I have never owned it, but I have always found it great! Now, during a post-Christmas shopping spree, I had the pleasure of experiencing the Extreme version - and I like it even better in some aspects. However, it also has to endure some setbacks. But one thing at a time. Pi Extreme is a dark, mature, but still quite sweet fragrance. Extreme is a bit of a misnomer here - but I believe it has already been widely acknowledged that the new name additions in the designer sector should not be taken literally. It’s as if the almonds & tonka beans from the original have been toned down & coated with a hint of dark, somewhat synthetic leather. But you can't really identify the darkness - it could also be dark woods, amber, or shoe polish. Actually, neither synthetic nor dark sludge is positive - but here I can live with it well. One could also categorize it under chocolate - and that is never wrong in its unsweetened, cocoa-containing version. Extreme behaves towards its original similarly to how DHI does to its own. If you know it, then it is unmistakably a Pi. And certainly not a bad flanker - whether we really needed a three-day beard version after so many years is another question. Fans of LIDGE, DHI, or Diamonds Black Carat will surely be tempted. Bottle: dark, otherwise iconic as ever Sillage: thick & dark does not automatically mean more extreme & far-reaching Longevity: just shy of very good - 7 hours. Conclusion: for fans of the original who have outgrown its sweet shoes & have now turned to the dark side of the force. Not a killer, but a reasonable new release!

"Bongossi wood" or "Red Ironwood" is also referred to as ironwood in this country. It has such a high density that it does not float in water and is so hard that it cannot be drilled or nailed. According to Wikipedia, it can emit an unpleasant smell when sawed because it is a very oily wood. However, this smell is said to disappear again. In the construction of boxes in horse stables, Bongossi wood is often used when one can afford it. Because it is so hard, it is unlikely to splinter easily if a horse kicks it. Horses especially cannot gnaw on it, as they like wood and stable horses often get bored. But I cannot remember this wood having a particular smell or scent. In no way do I have any memory of the smell of Bongossi wood when testing "Pi Extreme." But not only do I have no unpleasant memory of it, I have no scent memory of Bongossi wood at all. So I cannot claim that "Pi Extreme" does not smell or even scent like it. Then there is also the scent note of leather. If I did not have an original sample of "Pi Extreme," I would have thought that the labeling of the bottle was incorrect. I do not smell a trace of leather. I am the opposite of disappointed about that. Instead, I smell one of those perfume characters that I really like. Immediately, "Pi Extreme" presents me with a wonderfully balsamic-resinous scent with rich creaminess, soft and with a bitterness that is always fascinating to me. Is the bitterness from almonds or from Calycanthus or one of the many fragrance materials that have this bitter almond-like scent? Additionally, I think I perceive the sweet resinousness of mastic. For the creaminess, I suspect a very good sandalwood. And it is possible that labdanum plays a small supporting role. I do not smell any coniferous wood. With that, I also conclude my speculations: Balsamic-resinous-woody-aromatic-bitter scent is what "Pi Extreme" is for me. Although "Pi Extreme" is a completely different perfume than "Organza," associations with it keep coming to my mind while testing. One or some of the scent materials in "Pi Extreme" are also in "Organza." Because at the same time, after a while, the scent of Organza seems to float in my olfactory memory like a playback. Perhaps it is also the base scent of Givenchy analogous to Guerlinade? I can only express it this way: Both scents have for me something soft, round, closed within themselves, and complete. However, in my opinion, "Pi Extreme" is a unisex scent, even though it is declared as a masculine fragrance.

Ah, the new Pi Extreme. After I found the regular Pi good, though not outstanding, I was curious about the Extreme version. During the first test, I found it okay, but somehow strong. In the second test, I just didn't like the top note that much. And somehow I didn't pick up much from the base, it probably wasn't my day. But now, having tested it again, I still don't like the top note, but the base has turned out quite nice. The scent: In my opinion, the scent starts off a bit sharper than the original, causing a slight tightening in the throat. It's difficult to pinpoint exactly what is in the top note (I had the same feeling with the regular Pi), but it goes in a direction like coriander, something that smells really intense at the beginning (but it's not coriander, that was just an example due to the intensity). However, after a minute or two, this impression calms down, allowing you to smell the wood and leather, quite strongly of course. You also get the impression of smelling a bit of licorice. In the heart note, this intensity calms down a bit more, but the scent itself remains strong. It still smells woody, clear..., possibly a bit resinous and slightly sweet. The scratchy, sharp feeling gradually disappears within the next hour, and the scent becomes more pleasant as it slowly transitions into the base. After about an hour, the scent reveals its true potential. It becomes softer, more balsamic, and smells sweet, indeed gourmand-like, as you all describe it here. It smells like a great tonka bean (without vanilla), with a slight smoky background and the leather accents and wood. Especially in the base, the similarities to the regular Pi are clearly noticeable, just in a much stronger form. It's funny that the fragrance description only mentions ironwood and leather... The longevity: The longevity is just like the regular Pi, possibly a bit longer. But it is definitely good and lasts at least eight hours. The sillage is noticeably stronger; the term Extreme was aptly chosen here, as the scent can still be smelled well after five to six hours before it fades. The bottle: I found that the regular Pi has one of the better and nicely designed bottles. Since the Extreme version uses exactly the same bottle, this impression remains. The bottle is a vertically stretched trapezoid with embellishments on the glass. There is still no cap, but the spray head looks elegant. The color of the perfume liquid is, aside from the name, the only difference. It is now dark brown and no longer golden. To me, the bottle still looks like an Aztec temple, which I think is great. I still wonder why this fragrance line is actually called Pi, but whatever. The most important thing is to know whether this scent smells similar to the original Pi and whether it actually represents an increase in fragrance concentration, or if it differs too much. Well, both scents are similar. But I find the top notes differ slightly from each other. Pi Extreme starts off harder, sharper, and stronger, somewhat more of an acquired taste than the regular Pi. Later, both scents are quite similar, especially in the base, but the Extreme is the stronger edition and smells a bit more leathery and significantly sweeter. The regular Pi is a bit more restrained and fades faster in sillage. But both are good autumn/winter fragrances. If you have to choose between the two, I would choose the regular Pi for the top note, but the Extreme for the sillage; both are great in the base, but the Extreme is a bit sweeter. So you need to test it for yourself, possibly several times. But one thing I can say for sure: If you already own the regular Pi, you don't necessarily need to get the Extreme as well. My rating: 75%

Vintage L'Interdit is a very special perfume. I can most definitely imagine Audrey Hepburn wearing this fragrance, and I find it a much better pairing than Marilyn Monroe with Chanel No.5. I shelled out the money to smell the original formula, and I'm so glad I did. It's a very classic scent, powdery aldehydes inclusive, yet I find it far more complex than people give it credit for. L'Interdit EDT opens with a bright, sparkling burst of aldehydes, peach and strawberry. The powdery aspect is thankfully not overpowering, although dominant. The fruits give L'Interdit a beautiful, juicy and Spring-like feel. The scent itself is rather subtle which surprised me at first, however I much prefer it this way when I come to think of it. After the fruitiness subsides, the floral accords become much more pronounced, with a rather strong focus on powdery rose and iris. The way the heart settles brings a smile to my face as I picture Audrey Hepburn decked out in her expensive Givenchy gown with an elegant string of pearls setting off her slender neck. She was a woman that stunned the world with her beauty and style, yet it came so naturally to her. L'Interdit has managed to capture the essence of her in a bottle. In some ways, this fragrance is quite refined and elegant, although its delicacy hints at something a lot more intimate and sensual. The powderiness is somewhat similar in composition to the infamous Chanel No.5, however L'Interdit caters to a variety of tastes, throwing in an array of fruits and berries, and further developing into a spicy incense drydown. Unfortunately my skin chemistry has not done justice to this fragrance, turning the peach note into something a little too fizzy and bitter. I envy those who can maintain L'Interdit's smoothness on their skin with no rude interruptions. Audrey Hepburn must have been an amazing smelling woman in her day.

I have a great admiration for Audrey Hepburn, who passed away far too young. She was of British-Dutch descent and was born on May 4, 1929, in Belgium. Her love belonged to dance, and she therefore underwent classical ballet training. Unfortunately, her career did not materialize, as her muscles could not be sufficiently developed due to the hunger years during World War II. She was then discovered by chance by the writer Sidonie-Gabrielle Colette and brought to Broadway, where she played Gigi. This was the beginning of her acting career. She achieved her breakthrough in 1953 with "Roman Holiday" alongside Gregory Peck. For "Sabrina," she traveled to Paris in 1954. Hubert Givenchy, a great fan of Katherine Hepburn, was asked if he would design the wardrobe for Miss Hepburn's next film, and he was very pleased to be able to create the wardrobe for Katherine Hepburn with her mane and classic trouser suits, so he agreed. When he first saw her, he was initially disappointed, as instead of Katherine Hepburn, a small girl with short, straight hair stood before him, but from this encounter, a lifelong close friendship blossomed. From then on, Audrey Hepburn wore almost exclusively Givenchy - he designed her wardrobe and costumes. He also created the costumes for her in the film "Funny Face." In 1957, Givenchy created a fragrance for Audrey Hepburn that was initially reserved only for her. When he later informed her that he wanted to launch the scent on the market, she reportedly exclaimed, "C'est l'interdit! C'est mon parfum!" (That's forbidden! That's my perfume!). And thus, the name for the new fragrance is said to have originated. Due to my admiration for Audrey Hepburn and my approximately one-year passion for beautiful fragrances, I recently secured a L'Interdit Vintage from 2003 EdT. It was a blind purchase; I simply wanted to know how my favorite actress smelled. It is a puristic bottle that fits well in the hand, with an equally puristic red label that simply states "L'Interdit Givenchy Paris" and a gold-colored cap. However, the scent is anything but puristic. I thought I had found "my" fragrances with Cher and So Pretty, but this one simply blew me away. I don't know how the currently available L'Interdit smells, but this one from 2003 - an EdT - is a DREAM, and I can completely understand why Audrey loved this scent and wanted to keep it for herself. L'Interdit is, for me, the most beautiful floral scent I have ever encountered and can imagine. Fine flowers, and surely a whole lot of them, are very well intertwined and optimally dosed - this is how the scent begins and how it remains for a long time. The sillage is perfect, and the scent that envelops me is so beautiful, as if it were not of this world. It is hardly sweet, rather sweetish - just like flowers are. It is soft yet well perceivable, with a fine green-bitter note. It is soft, but not creamy, rather soft like silk. Nevertheless, it lasts exceptionally well and is still easily noticeable even after 8 hours. I am very happy that I got to know Audrey Hepburn's scent and was able to acquire it. It holds a very special meaning for me. I came into the world just as Audrey Hepburn was having her breakthrough in the film industry, but her very personal fragrance is definitely one of my favorite scents.

During the Christmas holidays, I was able to test a few fragrances, L’Interdit was one of them thanks to the lovely Turandot. With the first spray, I was already fascinated, floral, strong, a bit citrusy and very cool, but not bulky, that's how L'Interdit starts. After a while, L’Interdit calms down, becomes soft-spicy and powdery, while remaining fresh, it simply becomes milder. It stays on my skin for some time until it gradually weakens and disappears. During the test, a deceased friend came to mind, this scent was not hers, but it would have suited her fantastically. For a time, she was my boss, a very demanding, sometimes slightly snobbish boss. We worked well together, but it wasn't always easy, work and private life were strictly separated. When I got married, she stood with her partner in front of the registry office waiting for us, the bride and groom. She handed us a gift, exquisite, unusual champagne glasses, which I still cherish and wash by hand today. She hugged me, wished us much happiness, and started to cry from emotion. I was happy, but slightly bewildered, as I didn't know this soft side of her at all. Only after the company was sold and we no longer worked together did we meet for dinner, which was the beginning of a good friendship that unfortunately ended much too soon due to her death from cancer. Just like she was, L’Interdit is first very cool, distant, then the ice melts and it becomes warm-hearted. L'Interdit is a fine, noble scent with medium sillage and longevity, best worn from spring to autumn.

I am now actually known for loving dark, earthy, and herbaceous-mossy scents. However, on my "I-like-list," there is also "light and cool," and in this category, L'Interdit belongs for me. I do have a romantic side, but it shies away from too much kitsch. That is exactly why I like this Givenchy fragrance. It is delicate, a bit aloof, and does not shower me with a cornucopia of flowers, but fits into the rather timid spring, where the young green prevails and the flowers are still waiting to bloom. L'Interdit impressively shows that jasmine does not always have to come across as sultry and urinous. Here, it presents itself gently, softly, and reservedly, creating for me an innocent, almost soothing atmosphere. L'Interdit is a clean scent, although nothing here smells like soap or fresh laundry. The perfume also demonstrates that it is possible to transition from the floral heart note to the powdery base so smoothly that one can only marvel. L'Interdit undergoes a development without changing its character. It plays out like a film that has a harmonious and logical progression and is not - like so many perfumes - a triptych that tells three different stories. I believe that the perfume does not do itself a favor if it is only reduced to Audrey Hepburn. She was a charming personality, but this scent is significantly more complex, as I think it would have suited Grace Kelly just as well. L'Interdit simply tells us of a time when films were still true dream cinema and perfumes were still works of art.

L'Interdit starts off wonderfully, with such a beautiful, not glaringly bright, but soft aldehyde note that I could cry. Dreamlike softness, bright, gentle, delicate, elegant, fairy-like, and unobtrusive... unfortunately, this top note fades away after just 5 minutes. If it were to last, I would need to have this fragrance IMMEDIATELY, those are my first thoughts after applying it. It transitions to an elegant, understated, warm powderiness, with the faintest spicy accents. It almost comes across as a bit dusty, but in a positive way. I would describe it as a dusty, powdery light and airy sweetness. Very noble, very understated, not a word too much speaks L'Interdit. Suddenly, I get a lump in my throat, and from this point on, I am no longer able to evaluate this fragrance objectively. It is no longer just a scent for me; it is a bittersweet memory that unexpectedly washes over me. "It's Sunday, I am 7 years old and standing next to my grandmother in church, in my hands I get to hold her beautiful delicate gloves, so I don't fidget too much." These gloves were and still are true magical things, making even the clumsiest hands (like mine) look beautifully elegant. Oh, how I loved those gloves in their elegant black! And they smelled so noble, so sublime, just like... L'Interdit. I had no idea until today that this was my grandmother's perfume, and now I sit completely moved in front of the little vial that has revealed this secret. I inherited the black gloves many years ago and cherish them, but I cannot bring myself to scent them with their original fragrance; that would be far too emotional. Therefore, L'Interdit is not a fragrance for me and will delight someone else in the future. As far as I can reach an objective conclusion, I can only say that L'Interdit is a masterpiece of restraint and nobility, without becoming too cool, with such a delicate bright glow within it that it brings tears to your eyes.

Flori, I sincerely thank you for allowing me to experience this beautiful fragrance. Florblanca has already written a lot about Audrey Hepburn, her story, and how the fragrance got its name. Please read Floris' comment. Yes, the lovely Audrey was an attractive woman, a great actress, and a style icon. I liked her and have seen all her movies.

... or rather, the lost scent. When my husband and I met, I was fond of wearing Fleur d`Interdit - and the fragrance adorned my wedding dress. For us, the forbidden flower is still a symbol of love and carefree times. These feelings are something we would love to revive! So we are still searching for a successor to "our" scent, and we tried L`Interdit.

... the first Givenchy perfume. A legend, both the fragrance and the inspiration behind it, the master’s muse Audrey Hepburn. Rarely has a woman on this earth been more memorable, sweeter, more charming. This was her scent, a fragrance that was supposed to be worthy of her. At the same time fitting, yet surprisingly edgy-rough. For many, the better, refined No. 5.

Vintage Extrait: A restrained, soft aldehydic and slightly cool opening, notes of mandarin and peach are recognizable, quickly revealing a powdery texture that accompanies the fragrance through all stages of its development.

The wonderful Audrey Hepburn was the muse of Hubert Givenchy, who created various dresses for her that she wore in her films. I read an interesting story about the fragrance "L'Interdit" by Givenchy. The legend says that the scent, which was originally created solely for Audrey Hepburn, went nameless for a long time.

bought in 2011 at the end of summer to prepare for the arrival of rainy autumn days. it's the peppery and minty scent that I like to wear on rainy days like today, even though it's July. it really brings this distinguished and refined British side, which I have only found in the tom ford oud wood. become difficult to find in France like many Burberry references, I advise you not to buy it blind, I did not find any perfume with the same scent.

So, since there hasn't been a comment here yet, I'll give it another try ;o) At the moment, this one is extremely popular with me - you can wear it in the office, as it's not too overpowering, and I think it's a pretty good all-rounder for everyday use - whether it's 28°C in the shade or on a rainy, cooler summer day - it always works! On my skin, it strangely smells like daisies - but a really lush (quickly watered before picking) bouquet of daisies. I attribute this extremely prominent scent to the gardenia - I once had a pure gardenia fragrance - it smelled similar. Just a bit stronger than what it should smell like... With this one, however, the water lily comes in at the same time, which makes it feel rounded and pleasant to me - truly an everyday all-rounder. It's also good to layer with other more citrusy scents. For my part, I'm glad I found this one - with my strange skin chemistry, it's unfortunately not always easy to find something that smells as (good!) as described by almost everyone else here... Unfortunately, the scent doesn't last too long - I can perceive it well on my skin for about 2-3 hours, but after that, it really becomes difficult to find the spray spot on my skin - so, dear perfumers: Don't forget the travel spray for when this scent should be your choice for the day ;o)

Overall, Extravagance is fresh, green, contemporary, and unusual. I wasn't expecting this -- Wow, what a delightful surprise. It leaves an impression very similar to Guepard but with a mellower marigold and without the ginger that was irritating to me. The tangerine on top is long lasting too. Thankfully, Extravagance d'Amarige is neither extravagant nor Amariage. I get a green woody scent that's not overwhelmed by all of its floral notes. The spicy notes of pink pepper and marigold are subdued. The jasmine & orange blossom really come through for me, and that's not such a good thing for my chemistry. There's a bit of soapiness that's reflective of its 1990s creation date, I think. However, it's not stuck in the 1990s. Rather, it's classic. Extravagance is wearable in any season, day or night, but probably best in Spring and on cooler summer days. Also, it's office-appropriate without being a generic "office fragrance." Long-lasting for an EdT too. One day when we look back and talk about the great mass-market perfumes of the 1990s, it would not surprise me if Extravagance is mentioned along with Cool Water, Sunflowers, Happy, Realities, and Pleasures. Sadly, Extravagance is discontinued. The reformulated version (Mythiques Extravagance) is not as strong & not as long lasting. Currently there is still plenty of old stock in the market ... but there will come a time when there's not enough and the price will rise. :( Stock up! UPDATE: I scored a part bottle of the "perfumed air." The concentration is not marked. However, it feels like an alcohol-free spray and wears wonderfully on me, better than the original. Definitely summer-appropriate. I love it!

Extravagance d`Amarige is, just like Les Parfums Mythiques Extravagance d`Amarige, the younger version from 2007, not an extravagant fragrance - the only extravagant thing here is the bottle. Although it is a child of the 90s, it is neither loud, nor sweet, nor overwhelmingly lush, nor berry-pasty or peach-mushy. Extravagance d`Amarige is green, herbal, aromatic, and a bit creamy-sweet.
