Fleur d'Interdit is - despite its large pyramid - not a Chypre and not a blockbuster (for Medusa: a bang *g*). I admit, I expected a kind of flanker to L'Interdit, but Fleur d'Interdit is not that either.

... Leopoldstraße, a very attractive lady approaches me, she walks past me, smiles, and exudes a light, wonderful floral fruity scent that accentuates her charm even more. She turns her head back to me and winks. If I weren't taken, I would be weak now. So I just smile back and continue on my way.

i was really excited about this scent from what i had seen online, but when i smelled this in store i was pretty disappointed. i sprayed this on paper only; the raspberry is definitely there, but it’s painfully artificial. a lot of the ads were involving ice cream so i expected a creamy/sweet base, but that was just not there (makes sense though because the fragrance officially doesn’t have a milk/cream/vanilla note). the scent also does not have great sillage to me, i was waving that paper around in sephora like CRAZY and i wasn’t getting anything other than a light whiff, and smelling it up close just resulted in me getting a nose full of chemicals. the bottle is cute though!

I hate to say it, but the only good thing about this fragrance was the packaging. It smelled like a very gross, artificially flavored raspberry drink that had been watered down. The raspberry note was very gross and very fake, and overall this entire fragrance was quite a miss. I'm not entirely sure why they advertised this alongside the raspberry ripple ice cream flavor when there was no resemblance of ice cream at all. Truly, it just smelled like artificial raspberry sweetener added to water.

The marketing for this, with imagery of melting ice cream, is deceptive. This is not a gourmand. It is a fruity raspberry with poor longevity. I was hoping to be impressed by this, as I've liked other JM fragrances, for the short spell they last. Raspberry Ripple reminds me of Lost in Ink by Oakcha, Lychee Rose by Nest, and Juice by Commodity (the last being my personal favorite) without their projection or depth.

This reminds me of a more mature Flowerbomb Ruby Orchid. It is missing the vanilla, but the musk has a similar effect. My main qualm? It has a medicinal quality. I think the raspberry plus the red currant is overwhelming and I’d argue that it may smell better if it were just redcurrant and musk. Ultimately, I don’t think this one is for me.

As a confessed Jo Malone fan, I was naturally thrilled when I discovered the relaunch. The scent notes appealed to me, and I hoped for a reissue of the lovely "Redcurrant & Cream | Jo Malone," which I found very pleasing with its fresh berry essence. "Raspberry Ripple" refers to a particular ice cream flavor found mainly in the UK: vanilla ice cream swirled with raspberry syrup. Sounds delicious, and so I expected a creamy vanilla note with raspberry sprinkles in this fragrance. The packaging is really quite sweet, the bottle comes in a box with a die-cut waffle pattern and the matching light brown color, and the ribbon is also designed in the colors of the ice cream (pastel yellow and pink). So the theme has been executed excellently, and as a little packaging victim, I am absolutely delighted as I free the bottle from its packaging. However, the first spray quickly brings about disillusionment, as the raspberry note is unbelievably artificial and overpowering, almost stabbing in the nose. I immediately associated it with "Smile | Akro," which also failed to convince me due to its synthetic nature. Where I had hoped for creamy vanilla ice cream, there's just a sticky sweetness stomping around in the background, and I can't perceive any scent progression at all. What I usually appreciate about Jo Malone fragrances, a certain transparency and lightness, simply British understatement, is completely missing here. It seems more like an attempt to jump on the currently prevailing gourmand trend. But good intentions don't always lead to good results, as this creation shows. The fragrance is supposed to convey cheerfulness and summer feelings, if the product images are to be believed, but for me, it only evokes annoyance due to its intensity. Fortunately, the ordeal doesn't last long, but this summer scent was a total miss for me. I would rather stick with my tried-and-true favorites from the brand and continue to mourn the "Redcurrant & Cream | Jo Malone," which managed to present berries in a way that doesn't drive one completely crazy.

Fruity scents generally appeal to me a lot. That's why I was immediately interested when my sister presented me with this new fragrance, saying, "This one is for you! I'll send you a sample!" She wasn't wrong. It actually starts off beautifully fruity. You could say it comes in with a bang.

By a nice coincidence (thanks to AngelinBlack), Summer for Men 2010 by Burberry came into my hands and I was truly surprised! I must honestly admit that I have always found quite a few fragrances from the Burberry brand (very similar to Creed) to be somewhat stuffy, dusty, or conservative; indeed, typically British in some way. However, Summer for Men makes a big exception in this case, as it has nothing to do with English drizzle or stiff royal houses; on the contrary: Summer for Men is a pleasantly light and refreshing summer scent with pronounced Mediterranean notes. Of course, it doesn't completely reinvent the wheel and therefore certainly doesn't have the highest recognition value, but it can at least be considered well done. The fragrance pyramid does seem quite adventurous, and much of it is likely a bit exaggerated, as a significant amount of synthetics is certainly at play here. Summer for Men unexpectedly opens not with citrus but with a very pleasant minty mandarin; a little later, this light and uncomplicated scent becomes a bit woodier and reveals some masculine facets. Overall, a very entertaining, understated fragrance for the interim that certainly knows how to convey a cheerful summer mood.

Firstaaaaaa ;) It's strange that no one has commented on this fragrance yet, but that's probably because only two people, including me, own this scent in this forum...!? Let's get to the actual feedback: I had the 2009 version, which I devoured (unfortunately, the Summer version was no longer available when my bottle was empty), so I eagerly awaited the 2010 version. Tested it back then at Douglas and bought it right away. Even though the fragrance notes differ significantly from the 2009 version - the new one smells quite similar. It feels zesty and spicy - I smell white pepper (but there isn't any in it), it resembles Davidoff's Champion. The biggest criticism is the longevity - it lasts about 2 hours, then it fades away... well...

This bottle made me fall in love with it since the first time smell it at the shop. The first spray has strong spices notes but once it developed The strong cedarwood notes pop up and it lasted on me till evening. The note is not too masculine to wear compared to other woody perfumes. For me this bottle suite many occasions, from working to brunch on the weekend. I tried to layer it with wood sage and sea salt. Wood sage and sea salt can help to tone down the spice top note and make the scent more subtle and casual. If you love woody perfumes. Should give this bottle a chance

I tried this scent and I have to say up front- it smells like a gin & tonic left to warm on a wooden picnic park bench next to a burnt out bonfire from the festivities of the night before. That may be good...or that may be a bad thing depending on your feelings about juniper berries, park benches and the perception of smelling like you took a "long lunch with a client" in the forest. Personally, I can't see this going well for me during the day at work and I can't say I find this seductive, soothing or even appealing enough to wear at night. This strikes me as one of the most airy, bitter masculine leaning and woody of the Jo Malone line that I have tried and I do thing it may work very well as a layering component with the, now defunct, Black Café Vetiver, 154, Dark Amber & Ginger Lily, Blue Agave & Cocoa in the Fall and Winter as well as, Lime Blossom or Grapefruit in the Summer months. The sillage is low, not more than 1-2 inches radius projection off my skin and the longevity is in keeping with the Jo Malone tradition of short lived romances. Then I smelled the large 3 wick candle and I must say- it's brisk, manly and refreshing as a room scent.

.. I thought when I read the notes. I just have to like this one! After wearing it several times, I unfortunately have to admit that this fragrance theoretically fits my preferences perfectly, but practically it is just too much. I perceive very fresh green-floral notes that are quite lovely at the beginning, but their intensity becomes overwhelming over time. The longer I have it in my nose, the more my temples throb, and I just want to get rid of it. However, for those who can’t get enough of “floral” and aren’t prone to headaches, they should definitely give it a try. The quality is definitely present, and it is beautiful too!

To begin with, I must say that I have a fondness for molecule scents, and they work very well on my skin. In my opinion, MMW is a molecule fragrance of the highest quality and absolutely melt-in-your-mouth. It does everything that Molecule 01 does, only better. More intense scent, better projection, as well as better longevity. Its scent DNA is not new - yes, it has all been smelled before - but still super individual. The synthetic-woody opening is clearly perceptible from the start and develops quietly but incredibly interestingly over time, making me not want to miss this fragrance in my collection. Unobtrusive, yet cuddly and, typical for molecule scents, simply very unique upon skin contact. Perfect for layering, perfect for events and visits where you want to smell fresh, clean, and still attractive, without overwhelming others. In my eyes, a very stylish scent that convinces with its calm nature. Woody spice, with - on my skin - good sillage and top-notch longevity.

Last weekend, I had the pleasure of getting to know MMW at Schnitzler. It was supposed to be something new and woody. New, no question, MMW was released in 2022. This fragrance definitely needs a bit of development on the skin for the beautiful cedar notes to reveal themselves alongside the spicy and balsamic notes. Vetiver is clearly noticeable, and a hint of sandalwood appears over time. What particularly benefits me as a woman are the floral and powdery notes. The longevity is outstanding. Sprayed on in the evening, went out, and smelled it again on my wrist in the morning - it’s still very present there. I find the scent to be very suitable for everyday wear and pleasing, and I also enjoy ISO E Super and Ambrox in it - well perceivable to my nose, as I like to layer. I have a bit of the impression that MMW is moody, moody (when it comes to scents) like I am. It’s a pleasure for me to smell something different every time. I cannot share the previously meager rating. MMW will certainly be good to wear in autumn, winter, and spring and will be (m-)y loyal companion.

Burberry Summer '09 is a lot fruitier and fresher than its predecessor. While this version maintains the pretty floral notes found in the original, the added notes of litchi, mandarin orange and red currant gives this fragrance so much more character. Crisp yet delicate, I find this fragrance much better suited to hot climates. I tested this fragrance on a relatively humid day in the city and I'll admit that I felt very refreshed simply by wearing this scent. Rather than being sharp or potently fruity, Burberry Summer '09 sits smoothly on the skin and never feels too sticky. It is a perfect balance of fruits, florals and woodsy notes. The cedar and sandalwood in the base notes has an almost clean, soapy quality which rounds the scent off nicely. So far this would be my choice if I had to choose a Summer scent from the Burberry line.

I smelled the fragrance for the first time in Frankfurt. I come from the countryside....everything here is calm and slowed down. Suddenly, I find myself in the hustle and bustle of the city. No one knows each other, everyone is stressed for time and has no time for others. I enter Douglas. It’s mid-June. I step onto the escalator and ride up to the second floor. There, I suddenly find this fragrance by Jo Malone. It looks interesting, so I spray it on a tester. Immediately, I am back home, everything is calm and the stress of the city disappears. For a brief moment, I lay in the bathtub and relaxed. The scent is a beautiful fresh fragrance with a lot of herbs. It reminds me of a sauna infusion in the spa. Unfortunately, like so many at Jo Malone, the scent is only an Eau de Cologne. Accordingly, it doesn’t last well. After just a few hours, it is completely gone. At first, I mainly smell lemon. After a few minutes, rosemary comes through.

When I was about eight years old, my two brothers and I had lunch in a restaurant. As is typical for children, my sense of taste was developed enough that I limited my choice of food to fries and chicken nuggets. After a filling meal, the waitress left us three packs of "Citro-refreshing wipes" to wipe our fingers, which were shining in the midday sun. We pocketed the wipes after quickly dabbing them on all the greasy spots on our skin, not without cracking a few jokes about it. Throughout the afternoon, I kept pushing the strongly artificial-smelling polyester mixture between my upper lip and nose to catch a whiff. This is what the opening, the top note of this fragrance, reminds me of-this first blind buy I ever made. It smells incredibly pungent of artificial citrus fruits when applied. As I said, it was a blind buy and, to make matters worse, a spontaneous purchase. Because the fragrance is very new, there were no reviews or independent opinions, and it couldn't be purchased anywhere in Switzerland, where I live, so I had to order it from England, which meant I paid one hundred francs for 30 ml, including shipping and customs. So I had to like the fragrance to justify the purchase (to myself). However, independent of that, I was positively surprised after an hour. The intensity and intrusiveness decreased significantly, and the fragrance gained an unimaginable depth and uniqueness. It smells like eating fresh tortellini in cream sauce on the first warm spring day after the snow has melted, while at the window, the mother is just drying the first branches from her herb garden. The fragrance is not something that stands out greatly or for which one receives a multitude of compliments, but rather something that requires you to be quiet, to surrender to it, and something that then rewards you with satisfaction and tranquility. So tranquil that you nod off, and the fragrance becomes very faint and quite quickly disappears altogether. This perfume is fantastic in the heart note and exactly what one imagines, but better. At first, however, it is a bit overzealous, which one could overlook if the longevity were better. On my skin, the fragrance lasted less than three hours, which unfortunately nullifies the strong performance of the heart note. If you go for a short spring walk or plan an Easter brunch, this fragrance is recommended for everyone, regardless of age or gender. However, if you plan to smell good all day long, you will not be perceived with this perfume after a short time.

At first this fragrance was quite strong, a sudden sharp burst of fresh apple, lemon and freesia. Taken aback by the strength of the scent when first applied, I wondered how a fragrance of this kind could not be cloying and overbearing in the Summer months. Thankfully after the initial notes subside, the scent weakens and becomes much softer and more bearable. The apple note, which is in some ways quite sour yet not overly unpleasant, blends with the rose and freesia notes making an interesting yet pretty scent. The vanilla is quite notable as it adds a certain sweetness which thankfully doesn't become too sugary or sickly. I can think of crisper and fresher Summer scents, however I like that Burberry Summer is different. In my opinion it is more of a soft floral than anything else. The lasting strength is good, as is the case with most Burberry scents I've tried on my skin. Although I can't say that this is a favourite of mine, I certainly like it enough to recommend it as a unique fragrance for Summer.

...I received this sample from one of those jovially grinning advertising ladies in a suit with a cheeky scarf matching her makeup at Kaufhof. Just as precarious as her employment situation is the perfume (by the way, there are no longer those little perfume vials (glass has become prohibitively expensive ;-)), but these aluminum pouches where the liquid immediately splashes out when you tear it open)...everything is just synthetic blend, no creative concept is recognizable, it smells like Dove men (similarly disgusting) and not like the fragrance components described above...let's spare the market from such amateurish chemical concoctions in the future. And for this, one is supposed to pay 50 euros, outrageous...if you prefer something fresh-smelling, you’d be better off with Dior Homme Sport or Habit Rouge by Guerlain.

Pi by Givenchy is for me a little vintage gem in today's perfume world. However, what Givenchy was thinking during the development of the fragrance Play Sport will forever remain a mystery to me. A fragrance that carries the words "Play" and "Sport" in its name already gives ample reason for concern, but what unfolds after spraying it on the skin is relatively easy to explain: nothing at all. It is remarkable that the sample packaging actually attempts to characterize the fragrance (vague and trivial, e.g., citrus cocktail, peppermint, ginger, etc.) - as if Play Sport had any kind of character! Play Sport does not go beyond a completely meaningless citrus-mint note. This Eau de Toilette does not develop at all. Longevity and sillage are simply weak, and the "bottle" comes in a regrettable plastic look. If one likes, they can identify a woody note, but a Rioja from Lidl for 1.99 EUR has that too. As for the ginger component mentioned in the fragrance pyramid, which often provides a charmingly spicy note in a successful perfume, you notice absolutely nothing here. What remains on the skin after a few minutes is a completely faded and shriveled lemon. A presence like a closed quarry. With a lot of goodwill, a squinted eye, and because Play Sport at least does not directly cause physical pain, I send this little water with 10% to the eternal hunting grounds.

I received a sample of this today and tried it after the sauna. Well, what can I say, a typical sport scent, with rather typical ingredients for this category. As is often the case with sport fragrances, it starts off pleasantly fresh and mildly citrusy from the top. That's nice, but nothing really mind-blowing. Unfortunately, I can't tell you about the other notes, heart and base - because after about half an hour, that's already it with Givenchy Play Sport. Pure standard fare created solely to make a little "extra money." Such a fragrance won't find long-term and convinced wearers. It simply lacks everything. It's their own fault if someone buys this stuff, uh... perfume. Many will surely regret it when they realize too late what they paid so much money for.

Now I don't wanna spoil the party... but I don't agree with the play-bashing. Play itself is primarily orange and a bit sultry for me, while Play Sport is noticeably lighter and smells on my skin like mandarin peels with a hint of mint... which I consider a coherent variant within the Play family. Nothing else happens for me in terms of scent, but it feels very natural. I love this fragrance, even though I don't have a taste for mandarins. Yet the scent feels peaceful, cheerful, invigorating, and gives me a sense of security. So far, I haven't found anything in the drugstore that brings this scent to the skin as well and costs less. I'm open to any specific tips.

What drives a brand that has launched one of my favorites (Gentleman) and other great fragrances to create such a superfluous and trivial scent? No idea, and I actually don't want to know... For me, this is a "fragrance" that should be available for a single-digit amount at a drugstore discount retailer. Really bad and not worth being described further.

It’s a hot summer day. Cherimoya is happily biting into a ripe pear. The juice is running out of her mouth. She tries to lick it up with her tongue, but it’s already running over her hands and finally dripping onto the passion flowers beneath her. Her hands are sticky from the juice, but she doesn’t care. She can’t get enough of it and licks her fingers one by one. Only when the last drop has been devoured does she sink down onto the meadow. What is this review supposed to mean? This scent smells incredibly juicy and almost a bit suggestive. This fragrance screams: “I’m irresistible.”

What Givenchy was thinking with the naming honestly escapes me. Basically, this has nothing to do with the original Pi and is actually an independent fragrance. But if anything, I would have simply named it "Pi Blue" or "Pi Lavanda". Because I associate nothing with air here. Over the years, my taste in fragrances has changed significantly. Lavender has now become one of my favorite ingredients in perfumes. And this fragrance revolves around that lavender. You get a somehow calming lavender in a powdery way with a bit of musk and woods in the background. Distantly, you can also sense tiny other floral notes. And by the way, I don’t find it any more synthetic than other fragrances in this price range. A bit of synthetics is certainly involved. In my opinion, the fragrance deserved more attention after its launch, because one thing I've always experienced when I wore it is: The scent has a very positive effect on my surroundings and I even receive occasional compliments for it. I personally find the bottle quite cool, and it has a certain weight to it, making it feel quite valuable. Its weak point is certainly the longevity, as after 5-6 hours, at least on my skin, the fun is over. For me, it’s a perfect companion for an evening on the sofa or before going to sleep because it simply puts me in a good mood and a certain satisfaction. In the office, it works well too; I don’t think any colleague will wrinkle their nose at this scent. Perhaps it’s exactly these rough edges that it lacks and could have brought it more attention in the end.

"Pi Air" takes on the heavy task of creating a lighter, fresher version of the flagship gourmand and original. It succeeds semi-well. But fundamentally, the name and bottle promise exactly the right thing. A frosted, sweetened version of the original, vented of much sweetness. A delicate gourmand that now comes across more bittersweet than sugary. As if one were to dry hay and lavender, shock-freeze it, and hang it on the balcony. Wearable, but I still need an explanation for its existence. Or is the good "Pi" still such a hit that it must be surrounded by a plethora of pointless flankers? I think not. It reminds me most of an unremarkable blend of the original and "Pour Un Homme Sport" by Caron. My world hasn't exactly cried out for this. Bottle: a frosted stunner. Sillage: airier than the original. Oh please. Longevity: 7 hours for a refresher is good. But it’s not really one at all. Conclusion: Pi rounded down to 3. Light, less sweet, more everyday. For the hardcore Pi men who cling to their magical number even on warmer days.

The hibiscus has always been a very special plant for me. A piece of southern beauty that basks in the sun and warmth with generous floral splendor, but refuses rain and wind: it loses its desire to bloom and its radiant color. An exotic guest on the balcony or by the window; delicate and finicky, when everything is not as it expects. That's why I was very surprised back then in Rhodes: this plant, which flaunts its own will with me, is planted there for hedges; whether for path or parking lot borders - they consist of hibiscus plants, which are simply shaped with a chainsaw - and still bloom abundantly. However, they do share something with my one plant: the flowers only open around 10:00 AM and close again by 6:00 PM. The "blue cocktail hour" or even nightlife remains foreign to them; their task is fulfilled! They do not negotiate! With my well-known fondness for Jo Malone fragrances, I, of course, couldn't pass up a bottle of "Yellow Hibiscus." What had they created here - again from just relatively few fragrance notes? I spray, and an almost kitschy yellow sun rises: pure summer feeling spreads! A pleasant lime freshness combines with the unique scent of hibiscus to create a surprisingly lively opening. Actually, I could already top it off with Prosecco - Salute! But of course, the two beauties, rose and jasmine, won't allow that: without them, such exuberance wouldn't exist! They join in with their lovely fragrance and immediately spread good cheer. Musk also feels the need to have its share in this fragrance cocktail. At Jo Malone, they let them have their way, combine them all, and then the shaker gets to work: it is accomplished! Light, a bit sparkling, floral, and later becoming soft and creamy all around, "Yellow Hibiscus" lounges contentedly on the skin. The impression of a fragrant place, often visited by fat bumblebees and exuberant butterflies, where noisy cicadas feel at home, intensifies with the fragrance development during the unfortunately rather short duration of wear. Just as gentle shadows lay over this fragrant picture throughout an afternoon, "Yellow Hibiscus" also disappears lightly. But its magic doesn't vanish completely: a quiet longing remains for something beautiful, bright; the image of a radiant yellow hibiscus flower in the hair of a smiling woman or as the crown of a delicious cocktail. Here I find a summer fragrance that, one might think, was created specifically after such a difficult period, promises no more than it delivers, but truly spreads joy. "Yellow Hibiscus" may stay and show me its beautiful sunny world until the bottle is empty. Jo Malone has convinced me: no more and no less!

This review is based on a 10 ml travel size bottle of Accord Particulier from Givenchy. The nose behind this perfume is Nathalie Lorson, one of my favorite perfumers who has created many great perfumes. I am not sure this is one among them. The opening note is listed as Turkish rose, but it is too mild and fleeting for me to notice. What appears as opening notes are the heart notes of vetiver and patchouli. Though these are clear and beautiful notes, they don’t really stand out as anything exceptional. The vetiver and patchouli notes also make Accord Particulier remarkably similar to the Encre Noire family of perfumes, also designed by Nathalie Lorson. However, Accord Particulier is simpler in composition and more elegant in design, characteristics associated with La Collection Particulière. The listed base note is Ambrox, a synthetic woody amber scent from Firmenich. As the original Ambrox is no longer on their perfumery ingredients catalog, I assume this must be one of the second generation Ambrox compounds. Other than an academic interest, it doesn’t really matter. I cannot pick out the woody amber in the wake of the strong vetiver and patchouli. The performance is not monstrous, but elegant and gentlemanly as expected from the profile of this perfume. It lasts about 6-8 hours on my skin, with gentle sillage for the first few hours. It would work as a good office perfume. In summary, Accord Particulier is a nice vetiver-patchouli scent that doesn’t create any commotion. The notes listed by the perfumer allude something wonderful. But when you get there, there is no there, there. I cannot recommend Accord Particulier for what it delivers for the $320 for 100 ml.

So, this will be my first longer review, which I have been working on for a while, so please bear with me, dear sniffers. We'll start with a historical narrative, followed by a more concise review that suits me better. "The Man with the Subtle Scent" He entered the room without saying a word, and yet everything seemed to stand still for a moment. Not because he was loud, not because he provoked, but because an almost invisible presence surrounded him. His suit: simple, well-tailored. The shoes: polished but unobtrusive. And yet something lingered. A fine hint that was not immediately graspable. It was the scent. No intrusive perfume, no sweet heaviness demanding attention. Something warm, clean, yes almost intimate. It was Accord Particulier . A chord of Indonesian patchouli, quietly vibrating under the skin, balsamically soft like the earth. Turkish Damask rose, not sweet but noble, almost like a cool silk cloth on warm skin. Ambrox, which one would say has more effect than scent. And of course, Haitian vetiver, dry and clear, like the suit he wore. He did not smell like someone trying to impress. He smelled like someone who already knows who he is. No pose. No noise. Just authenticity. People spoke about him later, not loudly, but softly, like one talks about a rare moment that one might have almost overlooked, yet strangely lingers. And even before one knew his name, one knew his scent. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________ About the scent: We have soft, balsamic patchouli here, which is "interrupted" by a beautiful, non-sweet rose. The Ambrox gives it a nice, modern, skin-close warmth with a hint of spice, while vetiver contributes a dry, woody freshness. The interplay does not feel overloaded; rather, the opposite is true. The composition is clear, puristic, and perfectly balanced. Occasion and wearability: It can actually do everything, whether for everyday wear, the office, or going out. It even gets along with all seasons, although it tends to shine more in the evenings during summer. Bottle: The bottle is simple and high-quality. Black glass, clear lines, elegantly understated. Fitting for the scent. Conclusion: Accord Particulier by Givenchy is a scent that is subtle yet not subtle, but always full of character. It forgoes loud effects and instead focuses on elegant depth and fine tuning.

The scent is really very good (me: male, 35, Southern European), reminiscent of Dior Fahrenheit and gives a distinctive, masculine note. Of course, the quality is right, but the price is quite heavy. At least you can use it sparingly due to its intense effect, which justifies the investment. A few sprays are enough, and the scent unfolds completely - you forget the proud price. A strong, masculine fragrance... not suitable for every type.

From the new and limited English Fields collection, this is probably my most beloved scent. A bit sweet, lightly floral, and delicate. The Bottle Typical for Jo Malone scents in a limited edition, all English Fields fragrances come in the classic Jo Malone design with a twist. This time, the glass of the bottle is painted in pastel colors and glazed in a structured and contrasting color in the lower third. This creates a texture reminiscent of stone and porcelain, as if Jo Malone had teamed up with Villeroy & Boch. It is elegant and chic and also feels great in the hand. The cap is made of plastic this time and is in the same color as the upper two-thirds of the bottle. The caps fit a bit tighter than usual, allowing the scent to be released with a satisfying "pop" sound. As beautiful as the bottles are, they do have a drawback and an advantage at the same time. On one hand, the scent is somewhat protected from light, but even when held against a light source, the fill level can only be guessed at. Additionally, the color transitions are not cleanly executed on all bottles, and some have a slight color shadow in the transition. Those who care about such details should examine the bottles closely before purchasing. The Scent Today, I kept sitting there with my nose in my primroses, sniffing at myself and the test strip repeatedly, and I truly cannot say if there is a primrose that I smell first in this fragrance. However, it is definitely floral without being stale or stuffy. This floral scent does not stay alone for long, as both the heart and base notes come in incredibly quickly. The mimosa is delicate, more of a companion than a main player like in Mimosa & Cardamom, and the grain blends incredibly well with the vanilla. It creates a creamy sweetness, and even though there is no coconut, it smells to me like freshly baked coconut macaroons. Somehow, grain scents tend to have a cookie dough quality overall. The lightly floral note constantly resonates, preventing the scent from becoming too sweet. On me, it is perceivable for 6 hours and shows hardly any development over time, only becoming softer and gradually a bit weaker. Lacking coconut macaroons, I guess I will have to eat a Raffaello first, because this scent really makes me hungry. Conclusion A wonderfully delicate, feminine scent. Like sunscreen, it pairs well with sun-warmed skin and is a lovely candidate for spring and summer.

The new scents from Jo Malone continue. As already mentioned in the first comment from this fragrance series (that is, with the scent Honey & Crocus), the idea is to create nice scents from different grains paired with flowers that match each grain. Today I am writing about Primrose & Rye, a scent that must primarily smell of primrose and rye. I probably don't need to mention that I was once again unsure about what primroses actually are, and I only realized this after Googling it and seeing pictures of the flower… :D Before I annoy you again with my lack of flower knowledge (since you should already know by now that I am absolutely hopeless when it comes to flowers… but be glad that I don't consider the term "flower" to refer to a standalone species… :D), I want to get straight to the scent, which, while not exceptionally unique, still smells quite nice and is therefore worth a look, at least for lovers of light floral fragrances looking for something pleasant for spring. The Scent: At the beginning, you can smell a lovely floral note, which must be the primrose. It smells airy and light and fortunately not stuffy like some floral fragrances. The slightly sweet note could come from the mimosa. For quite a while, the scent remains light-floral, then, upon closer inspection, you can definitely discern grain-like scent notes, although I can't say which grain you actually smell, as they are somewhat weak. Rye is listed here, but I'm not sure if you can really perceive it; moreover, the floral scents are stronger and slightly overshadow the grain (although they do come through a bit better in the base). While the top note and heart note are quite similar and only the intensity of the flowers decreases slightly over time, a light vanilla note gradually emerges in the base. Strong enough to be noticed and to enjoy its sweet-powdery scent, but weak enough to wear well in spring and summer, making it a good match for the light floral notes. And as mentioned earlier, the grain notes now seem slightly stronger, but they still come across as generally weak to me. The Sillage and Longevity: The projection is somewhat weak. It can only be perceived from a normal distance for a short time, but it is better detectable from a closer range. The longevity is about five hours, but the scent is already noticeably weaker after half that time. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular, tall, and, as usual, of high quality. This one is beige and has a brown, rocky "wallpaper" in the lower third of the bottle that feels stone-like, providing a nice tactile experience. The cap is also beige and cylindrical; I felt that it sits a bit too tightly, so you have to pull fairly hard to remove it. That said, this bottle, like all the bottles in the English Fields series, is really beautifully designed! So… yes, I must say that I quite liked this scent as well. Although I am slightly disappointed by the somewhat faint grain notes (it seemed to me that they were better represented on a test strip than on my skin…), which actually give the scent its uniqueness and help it stand out a bit from many other light floral notes, aside from that, Primrose & Rye has turned out to be a very lovely fragrance. However, it is really light and airy, so you can spray it a bit more generously or reapply it throughout the day. This makes it a daytime scent that can be worn both in leisure and at work. At least for me, it exudes the aura of spring and brings good cheer. A lovely scent if you're looking for something light in spring. In my opinion, this fragrance is definitely worth a try! Oh, and it's better not to ask the sales assistant what kind of roses primroses are, as this is just the English term for primrose… as I painfully learned when I was laughed at… :D

This perfume has a very strong rose during dry down. Wow—knocked me over. It’s nothing but ordinary overall, with the rose dying away quickly, leaving a light nice peony skin scent in its place. Sillage close, longevity average to poor. If you enjoy a skin scent, then it’s very nice. It is strong at first though.

Today, I was dazzled by a sea of pastel spring fragrances at Kstadt. I stood there enchanted, as if rooted to the spot. But my husband naturally picked out the Givenchy, as he usually likes the scents from this label. I sniffed and found the first impression to be somewhat modest. Yes, it has a pleasant floral note - but nothing special that captivates me. I practice modesty as well and put the bottle back down. My husband raises his eyebrows. However, on our further tour, a gentle rose keeps wafting up to me. Then - in the car, the sweet cocoa bean appears, wrapped in light musk. This delicate scent has a beautiful development and an even more beautiful dry-down, which I had prematurely doubted. Yes, it conveys a charming modesty - in the sense that modesty is an ornament. I regret that I didn't indulge earlier. P.S. Blossom Crush has since found a home with me - and I wear it very happily.

The second fragrance from the Rare Tea collection is "Darjeeling Tea." Like "Silver Needle Tea," it is also almost colorless, which surprised me considering that the scents are supposed to resemble brewed teas. After a brief research, my misconception that Darjeeling was a type of black tea was cleared up, as I found out that all tea varieties (green, white, Oolong, etc.) that come from the region around the Indian city of Darjeeling bear this name. You never stop learning. Immediately after spraying, "Darjeeling Tea" starts off fruity on my skin; I can distinctly smell the apricot. In this initial stage, the fragrance has a sparkling quality, reminiscent of champagne. However, this fruity note is immediately accompanied by a powdery tea note, giving it a certain finesse. I couldn't say exactly which type of tea this is, but it is definitely a juicier one. I can only agree with my predecessor that a dominant black tea is not found here, though the tea note is unmistakably present. Relatively early on, I also smell the flowers; on my skin, the jasmine comes through particularly strongly and blends beautifully with the tea. The freesia is more subtle. Both the floral notes and the tea remain present until the end, giving the fragrance an elegant, powdery aura. After the initial burst, the scent pulls back a bit over time and becomes quite close to the skin, which I do not find negative. Since the fragrance is very elegant due to the floral-tea combination, I believe it is well-suited for everyday wear and especially for work, thanks to its not overly dominant sillage. I feel that the Rare Tea fragrances develop quite differently depending on the skin, so they should definitely be tested on the skin. The longevity is above average for me, as with all Rare Teas. Sometimes I can still perceive it in my hair the next day. Like all fragrances in the collection, Darjeeling comes in a tall glass bottle with a heavy black knob as a cap, which is secured with a magnet. So far, it is only available in 175 ml, but it is said to be getting a little sibling soon. However, I do not yet know how big/small that will be. It would definitely be a good thing, as I believe that it is not the price (I find the price-performance ratio appropriate due to the good longevity and the beautiful execution of the tea theme), but rather the size that is a non-purchase criterion.

This is the second Rare Tea fragrance that I am testing from the new collection by Jo Malone. Actually, this fragrance was the first one I had tested, but since I was almost a little disappointed with this one, I initially wrote the comment for the second fragrance first, which I sprayed on after this one (which was Oolong Tea). Darjeeling was my original first choice, as I was hoping for a wonderful black tea scent. But then it turned out differently,… but: the fragrance is still not bad, not at all, especially the ladies here might like it. Just as a tea scent, it disappointed me a little. The fragrance: Well, I expected a nice black tea right from the start, and perhaps that was also the reason why the corners of my mouth turned down a little instead of forming a bigger smile. Well, well, well… However, the fragrance starts with beautiful floral notes, primarily smelling of the freesias indicated in the fragrance pyramid. I can only faintly perceive jasmine (even though it is supposed to be jasmine absolute), and the typical sweet scent of this plant is hardly present. I am also very unsure about the apricots, as they are extremely faint as well. The Darjeeling is only hinted at, and you can (with a bit of luck) only occasionally perceive it, like a breeze that comes and goes. The same applies to the occasionally appearing green notes. Even long into the base, it mostly remains floral (but the pleasantly scented floral notes, so nothing stuffy and such), a bit later it even feels a little warmer and becomes more pleasant. From the base, the tea scent thankfully becomes a little stronger, so that the fragrance smells a bit better, but it still remains weak and does not smell as intense as I would like it to. Longevity and sillage: The longevity is about six hours, but I believe it is already significantly weakened shortly before that. After six hours, you can hardly smell anything. At least on the skin. On clothing, however, it lasts longer, and I also had the feeling that the tea note smells stronger on the clothing than on the skin. The sillage is already quite weak from the beginning and even decreases further later on. Perhaps a small whiff might occasionally waft up to your nose, but I find that the fragrance is more for one’s own enjoyment. The bottle: The rectangular bottle is very large and tall, as it is only available in a 175 mL version. Nevertheless, they look great, as they appear modern despite their simplicity. There is no writing or a proper label to be seen, just a small symbol with the logo. The cap is oval and black. The fragrance liquid is light green, almost like light jade. A beautiful bottle that can seem bulky but still looks really nice. For a moment, I thought I wouldn’t be able to finish testing the fragrance because my cat had settled on my arm at home. He was not bothered by the scent (since it was already in the base and very weak), but it was distracting for me while typing. Anyway, I occasionally petted him, while the creature occasionally pushed my arm aside with his hind paw to be left alone, even though he was lying on MY arm,… are they perhaps ungrateful and silly animals :D Of course, after he was gone, he also left his rather unpleasant scent right next to the spot where the Jo Malone fragrance was *sigh* But I was lucky, as the "pheromone" of the clawed creature faded away after a while without mixing with the fragrance. So, lucky me,… However, the fragrance hadn’t changed much. Darjeeling remains a floral scent with a slightly hinted tea scent (okay, but as I said, the tea smells a bit clearer and better later on, it just takes a while, but unfortunately, it never becomes really strong..). For me, the fragrance is therefore too floral and thus not a unisex fragrance anymore, but clearly a women’s fragrance. It is suitable for warmer days. Sure, it is fresh, but not refreshing, rather more casual and (too) light, making it a good daytime fragrance. I wouldn’t recommend it for going out, as it might hardly be noticed by anyone.

No review was written yet for this beautiful fragrance? This surprises me totally. This worthy scent deserves a worthy commentary. Can I do that? I don't know, but I will do my best. As I know it from other perfumes and thus expect a classical course, this is not the case here. The bitter orange opens the panorama (more juicy ripe than fresh) and is immediately followed by flowers. The peculiarity of this perfume is that it resembles a jigsaw puzzle. The whole is a harmonious scent but every particle is individually detectable. At times, I smell amber, then it seems to be jasmine, or is it now the sandalwood? On a surface of approx. 10 cm on my skin I can pick out notes separately depending on where my nose moves. The conclusion (dry down) is slightly powdery and slightly animalic, this time the ingredients blend together into a whole. Simply fantastic, well made, and not easy to describe to give this creation justice. A tiny piece of art. The scent has a definite sillage, strong in the beginning and after a while a pleasant dose lingers on. Longevity is fair, not great. No matter, I don't mind spraying again ... just because of that pleasant sillage. Unfortunately, because of a limited edition, this perfume is hard to find but worth looking for. Neither classic, nor modern, but special in any case. An intricate painting of various notes whose little puzzle pieces I love to discover almost to the end. (Translation: Pipette)

Recently, I did a sort of inventory of my decants and noticed that many samples that have been sitting for a long time are almost empty: their contents have probably evaporated over time. (Here, "evaporated" might even fit well!) That's a shame, so I gathered all the affected ones and am now giving these accumulated fragrances the attention they deserve. This explains my relatively many statements from the last few days. I came across "Parfums de Joaillier" by Boucheron, and since I am known to be "Boucheron-affine," I had to test it thoroughly. Right from the start, this fragrance reminds me of the times when my friend came over for Advent dinner and the first thing she unpacked was the orange studded with cloves that her daughter had made for me, presented in a pretty bowl. Who among us doesn't know this classic scent of the pre-Christmas season? I wouldn't even deny that there is a hint of clove present; this nuance would indeed fit this fragrance creation well. The fruity-fresh opening, once without the bergamot that sometimes gets on my nerves, appeals to me greatly. Tangerine and bitter orange correspond well with each other; this mixture is not too sweet; rather a bit tart, but without the bitterness of grapefruit. That jasmine and orange blossom form a delightful scent alliance is no surprise at all. Both are so soft and feminine, delicate yet intensely fragrant: a treat and joy for heart and soul! They harmonize exceptionally well with the somewhat unusual freshness of the entrance. All of this rides lazily and sensually on a creamy, languid, sweet wave of vanilla: vanilla that warms, caresses, embraces, and invites you to feel good. To avoid a cozy sinking into this sensual wave, this sweet fruity heaviness has been stabilized with sandalwood. Its erotic light scratchiness is exactly what was missing. And of course, lots of spicy ambergris: what would this cuddly vanilla blanket be without golden amber scent sprinkles? I encounter a sensually warm scent blanket that I can relax into. The spirit of the pre-Christmas season seems to be hidden in it (at least for me); it smiles at me kindly before pulling me into its warm, sweet embrace! Surely, "Parfums de Joaillier" is not an extraordinary creation, not an absolute "must-have." But at the moment, it seems to be exactly what I need: a source of warmth that gently and fragrantly envelops me and leads me into a certain calm where I can linger and relax. I'm glad I found it just now. Maybe it was meant to be?

No comment on this fragrance? That’s just not possible, so I want to give it a try. It’s one of those scents that triggers a carousel of images in my mind, which means it must have something special, it’s not ordinary. In fact, at first I thought, oh yes, another one of those old chypres that quickly become overwhelming for me, but then my nose kept wandering back to my wrist, hmmm.... Warm orange blossoms and also the scent of the fruit, but not intrusive, no Neroli hammer, although one might expect that with so much citrus indicated in the pyramid, no, wonderfully integrated into a warm base, no spices that I initially expected, much more subtle, as if a delicate warm hand were gently touching me and evoking a feeling of relaxation within me. Or the light breeze of a fan, gently moved by a lady, a lady who is not stiff or elegantly conservative, no, rather a being that flitted in on light delicate feet and now radiates her charm, her grace with sparkling eyes. An image of Gustav Klimt appears in my mind, the lady with the fan, exactly this mood is spread by this fragrance, there is no gold, no ornamentation in a sultry overloaded manner, as is often the case with Klimt. Playful, yet full of elegance, shine, and yet also depth, rustling fabrics being swirled around, and yet also calm, warmth. In the background, a quartet plays softly, Mozart or Vivaldi. A cheerful, relaxed atmosphere, enveloped in warm amber and sandalwood, delicately and finely intertwined. Jasmine remains very discreet in the background, showing respect and playing second fiddle. Vanilla also does not stand out. This results in a warm, elegantly relaxed composition that I would surely wear more often if it were still available. That’s how I imagine a Sunday afternoon in a salon at the beginning of the last century. A little dreaming does one good!

A blend of latent aquatics and neo-fougère. Fresh, clean, mineral, woody, synthetic, shaving foam-spicy. A shower care product with a touch of nonchalant elegance. If you put it bluntly. Everyday-casual-elegant, dewy masculinity without machismo. If you say it nicely. Givenchy is also riding the Sauvage horse or milking the corresponding cow here, but in a charming way. With a wink and a mischievous smile. * Mint. Sage. Ambroxan. Except for the latter, used with restraint. Still, a pleasant, attractive, unobtrusive Eau de Toilette Fraîche, as it is beautifully woven. The diffusely synthetic, mineral-woody, subtly salty, rough-spicy amber imitation predominates. Somewhat softened in its vulgar-potent conquering urge by soapy-clean, slightly herbal sage. A mélange that vaguely reminds one of shaving foam. The mint freshness only plays a significant role in the wonderful "first-dip-into-the-sea" or "earlier, radiant summer morning" feeling kickoff. After that, it subtly interweaves to maintain the freshness level above sea level. Far from associations with dental care products. More of a herbal Guerlain mint. A very delicate coumarin sweetness instills a hint of classic nobility. A whisper-thin creaminess connects and rounds everything off (without softening the character). Slim like a Sander fragrance, artificially clean like Lauder's 'Pleasures for Men' and aromatic-maritime like 'Cool Water'. My current favorite almost-scent everyday sin. And the limited "Parisian Break" bottle is, for me, the most beautiful in the fragrance universe. The romantically idealized view from the left bank of the Seine onto the Île de la Cité with the (then still undamaged) Notre-Dame. One almost hears Edith Piaf and is sure that Bébel will soon appear in the picture, casually with a Gitanes in the corner of his mouth and a France-Soir under his arm. Pure Paris feeling. Cobblestones, bench, old streetlamp, Pont Sowieso. I feel like I'm there. That almost makes up for the slight misstep with Ambroxan. Non, je ne regrette rien.

Here it is, the latest fragrance from the Gentlemen Only line by Givenchy. I must say, I was very impressed with the "regular" Gentlemen Only back then. It may not be an extraordinary scent and perhaps not suitable for going out (as it is not that spectacular), but I found it simply wonderful as a daytime fragrance. I also liked all the flankers, so some of them keep making their way onto my wish list (and then eventually leave again, it always goes back and forth). I was therefore very curious about the new fragrance, as I found the Casual Chic not "fresh enough" for summer (but it is also a good scent). Let's see how Parisian Break is, at least the bottle already has a nice design and evokes a rather summery impression with its light blue sea color. The fragrance: Without revealing anything of its Gentlemen Only DNA, the scent starts off very fresh and somewhat citrusy with mint and lemon. These notes smell good, and I am quite sure they must work even better on hot days than they do now. A little later, it becomes a bit spicier as you can detect a hint of sage. But then, slowly, the amber (or Ambroxan) starts to emerge, making the scent warmer and sweeter. Now, in the heart note, you can gradually smell the typical scent of the Gentlemen Only fragrances. As always, this fragrance composition smells very nice, it is warm and gentle, sweet, yet retains its freshness from the mint and lemon (and still the sage) all the way into the base, which makes the scent more relaxed and lighter. Longevity and sillage: Parisian Break is not exactly a long-lasting fragrance, lasting about four to five hours on me, although it did emit a slightly sweet scent afterward. The same applies to the sillage; the scent becomes a bit closer to the body later on, but you can still smell it nearby. One shouldn't expect too much from the projection. The bottle: The shape of the bottle has not changed. It is rectangular with rounded corners and has a thick neck, on which the cylindrical and chrome cap sits. On the front of the bottle, there is a beautiful blue illustration of Paris and the Seine River, along with the typical Gentlemen Only label. All in all, very nice with a summery look. For many, this fragrance might land in the middle range, a scent that is somewhat too ordinary. However, I like it, as it conveys a fresh feeling while still revealing the Gentlemen Only DNA later on (albeit a bit weakly), which should please fans of this fragrance line (at least fans shouldn't immediately shout "Flanker not good!"). Since it comes across much fresher this time than the Casual Chic did back then, it is also very suitable not only for spring but also for the hot days of summer. Although not for going out, as it would seem too unspectacular and weak here, it works quite well as a daytime and leisure fragrance, as I think it smells good. I would also like to say here that one should not judge immediately just because a new flanker has appeared. I would give it a chance. There may be significantly better fragrances, but Parisian Break is not a bad scent for that reason. As I said, just give it a try.

Amber Labdanum should probably have been called "Amber Incense." It is mainly a sweetened incense accord, though for some reason I don't find it as cloying as Encens Suave Eau de Parfum , the fragrance it is being compared to the most; the sweetness is more smooth and vanilla-y than the overwhelming sugariness of Encens Suave. It also reminds me a bit of Mesmerising Oudh Accord & Gold Eau de Parfum though I think even higher quality. Really nice pleasant resinous/Oriental frag that is versatile and appealing without any of the challenging aspects that sometimes accompany scents like this.

A superb creation by the talented perfumer Yann Vansnier! We are dealing with an atypical and not at all clichéd amber! I dare to offer you, exclusively, part of the recipe used by Yann in creating this superb perfume, since I discussed it with him privately, therefore, in addition to the declared notes we have: olibanum oil and olibanol, ciste absolute, dynamone and fir balsam resin. A composition that is definitely resinous, rich, warm. The evervescent, coniferous and balsamic frankincense as we already know it feels excellent, but there is also a fantastic support from the cistus, which in addition to the balsamic/resinous and leathery facets, also comes with a fruity facet, which remains throughout the evolution of the perfume! It is not a linear perfume and will certainly surprise you, especially amber lovers. Slight similarities to Ford's Amber Absolute, but not as harsh and much more layered, slight reminiscences of Grand Soir but without the dissonant roar of Amberwoods. I give it a score of 9.5 out of 10! excellent

At first, I felt like I was in a sauna. A good pine infusion - similar to "Berserker | Marc Gebauer." The spiciness is initially in the foreground. However, it slowly but surely transforms into something smoky, which reminds me more of an oriental incense stick than a campfire. Only after a certain time - let's say 15-20 minutes - do you get the lovely finish. Alongside the strong spiciness, a light sweetness joins in, reminiscent of a frankincense-honey mix. But not too sweet. The scent lasts a long time and is very well perceived. The price could be a bit lower. Otherwise, a successful and striking fragrance.

… or also "for those who find Sorcinelli's 'Voix Humaine 8 | Filippo Sorcinelli' too sacred." Jo Malone is a keyword for me that stands for subtle and close to the skin, while amber and labdanum, in my understanding of fragrance, are not always overwhelmingly loud, but certainly have a distinct presence. So a test was necessary. In fact, this fragrance does not bring a great development or a fragrance innovation, nor is it an amber or labdanum "club." But for anyone who finds the whole woody-sacred niche nonsense too peculiar, or if one needs a resinous, semi-sacred, church-quoting, yet unobtrusive companion, or simply wants this DNA in a more worldly and friendly form, this is a very good choice. Amber Labdanum smells like I feel when I turn on the incense burner (but keep the dish high up, far from the flame), brew myself a nice hot tea with oat milk, and curl up under a fluffy blanket. Cozy, pleasant, unexcited, clean. In the base, there is a DNA that I recognize from Malone and can describe as "perfumy": slightly soapy, but without white flowers, more like a nearly forgotten hint of shaving soap that still clings to the neck in the afternoon. The scent here is not a challenging ultra-niche art; it is simply a beautiful perfume with hints of amber and the warmth of labdanum. I believe the oak leaf takes away the dark resinous depth of the whole spectacle and makes the fragrance experience lighter, adding a green-fresh sprinkle. Perhaps it also reminds me of classic shaving soap. The bitter orange is not singularly identifiable, but I think it is what creates this bright incense association. Its fresh citrus and slight bitterness help to lighten the heaviness of labdanum and the warmth of amber, framing both in a sparkling freshness that inevitably evokes thoughts of incense. Vanilla is also part of the mix, used cautiously. Just like in "Voix Humaine 8 | Filippo Sorcinelli," it brings a sweet yet bright and cozy dimension, making the Turibulum blend approachable without contributing any significant edible-like sweetness. Almost, the fragrance has a note of oat milk in black tea in the dry down. This creaminess that you feel at the back of the palate is present here as well: sweet, soft, minimally creamy, but not lactonic or greasy. I can easily imagine wearing this in everyday life when one simply wants to feel comfortable - clean, well-groomed, quietly and lightly warm with a hint of smoke.

Rare teas are well and good but when the notes don't list tea at all, I have to wonder how the accord was made. According to the official notes, hay and tobacco make this scent smell like a white tea infused with fruit. Where is the cocoa, the tonka? Eventually a delicious bergamoty note emerges that makes this perfume smell like real tea. The smoothness and finesse of the whole tea collection is definitely exquisite. I would not say this is groundbreaking but it is addictive.

I had the opportunity to test this rare tea because Franfran generously provided a traveling package and Franciska equally generously included the entire tea series from Jo Malone. Thank you very much! This particularly pleased me, as I had already extensively experienced the "Rare Teas - Midnight Black Tea" that I had in a sample, and there I completely missed the tea - the reason for the blind purchase. After testing all seven fragrances, I can now say that Jo Malone has indeed managed to capture the notes of the hot beverage, yes, even those of the Oolongs. And I say this kindly as someone who has never consciously drunk Oolong in their life ;) Furthermore, I perceive this perfume differently than my predecessors; in my heart, I even believed I unexpectedly discovered licorice! But let's go in order. Starting from the back: durability is decent (workday), sillage is poor. 15 cm away from my arm, I can no longer perceive anything after an hour, despite the two strong sample sprays that I had generously applied to the same spot to facilitate the breakdown. This may not be a big surprise with tea scents, but I still want to highlight it because I have experienced all the elements of the pyramid in much more expansive compositions. Oolong Tea starts off briefly fresh and even slightly citrusy; I quickly recognize cocoa as well. Jo Malone's other cocoa scent ("Blue Agava & Cacao") has more cocoa in comparison and is significantly sweeter, more feminine. The sweetness of the Oolong remains subtler, balanced by a fine acidity. I attribute this to the tea note, which shines pale in the first half hour. During this twenty-minute phase, it becomes too airy for me, almost glaring in comparison to the other notes despite its low intensity. However, as it progresses, it settles in as a pleasant background noise. Next, I perceive licorice. During the first test, I was almost certain; in the second test, I sprayed a few licorice scents ("Reglisse Noire," "Today Tomorrow Always for Him," "Yohji Homme") in parallel and concluded that a) the source is probably more honey tobacco and b) my Yohji sample has gone off ;) By the way: If anyone happens to know the Yogi tea Licorice (which doesn't taste like licorice at all but intensely like sweet wood) and thinks of it due to tea + licorice: Oolong Tea smells much finer and more delicate. It does not dive into such harshly spicy realms here. Nevertheless, there is a similarity in this phase that still evokes licorice thoughts in me without comparison scents. This tasty unique feature among the Rare Teas elevates the Oolong to my favorite in the series. After one to two hours, the Rare Tea remains friendly, floating with a sublime hint of smoky honey gently around the heart of tea, stirred with an inconspicuous bamboo stick. Here, I like it best, and it can be worn well by both genders. This changes in the base: four to five hours later, sweet tonka bean comes through, which I, as a man, no longer like on myself, to put it mildly, it annoys me. But even on a woman, I find the light vanilla base rather arbitrary. The fragrance would have benefited from lingering longer in the heart. Both licorice and tea are available cheaper and more perceptibly in other scents. Even disregarding the base note, I find no passion for this creation within myself despite the successful blend. However, for lovers of subtle, sweet-spicy teas, I do give this at least temporarily pleasant companion a small recommendation.

The Rare Teas collection by Jo Malone immediately made it to my wishlist when I discovered it here. Actually, just seeing the term Tea was enough, as I love tea and particularly enjoy scents with tea notes. And although I was actually looking for the fragrance Wild Fig & Cassis during my last visit to Douglas (since I also love figs), I wandered over to the tea fragrances after a saleswoman explained to me that Wild Fig had just been discontinued… (ahh, how could they dare…). But this employee (wow, she was gorgeous and sweet…) showed me these new tea fragrances and immediately pointed out the Oolong Tea here, which she personally thought was the best of all the scents. So, I tried this fragrance and saw or smelled that it definitely has the potential to join my collection someday. Just not now, as it is more of an autumn scent… The fragrance: The scent starts off quite sweet, which initially reminded me of cinnamon, but that’s not really accurate. Just a moment later, it becomes clear that this sweetness comes from honey, and the fragrance already has light cocoa notes (which become stronger later). Alongside this, there is a rather strong tobacco note at first, which actually bothers me, but starting from the heart note, it becomes very mild and recedes further into the background, so that from the heart note on, the fragrance simply remains sweet, possibly a tiny bit spicy. Of course, I should also mention that throughout, all the fragrance notes are accompanied by a wonderful, slightly creamy tea scent that somewhat resembles black tea. In the base, the tobacco, as mentioned, is very weak and only adds a slight spiciness in the background; honey and cocoa dominate, and a bit later, the honey fades further back, so that the sweet notes then come more from the chocolatey cocoa (or in other words: the cocoa becomes more noticeable). Additionally, there is a light, smoky note, like incense. Although the fragrance initially radiates strongly, it becomes milder and softer from the base onward, and the tobacco eventually disappears completely. The longevity and sillage: You can expect about eight hours of longevity, although the fragrance loses quite a bit of strength after about half that time. The sillage is initially very strong, especially due to the tobacco, and the scent remains quite noticeable for some time, even though it becomes a bit weaker later on. Nevertheless, it will surely leave a small scent trail behind. The bottle: The bottle is rectangular, tall, and… big! Yes, the bottles are very tall, as they only come in 175 mL versions, making them appear a bit bulky at first glance. However, despite all the simplicity, they are a beautiful eye-catcher, look elegant, and will surely look good on a shelf. Aside from a tiny logo, there is no writing or label on the bottle. The Oolong Tea is filled with orange or amber-colored fragrance liquid, much darker than it appears in the picture on Parfumo. So, Oolong Tea really appealed to me. I would have wished it to be stronger or more long-lasting, but its endurance is still quite sufficient and is by no means a dealbreaker. I also like that it is not just a sweet, spicy, heavy scent for the colder days, but that the tea brings a bit of variety. Well, that might just be my impression since I tried many amber fragrances in winter. The tonka bean also adds a nice (but weak) powdery note. As mentioned, the fragrance is well-suited for cold days, both as a daytime or casual scent, as well as for going out, as it simply exudes a wonderfully pleasant aura. Although it might seem a bit weaker for very cold days, it is still usable in spring. For men, it will smell quite pleasant, and the ladies will also smell quite… well, delicious! Aaah, now I have to think again about the lovely,… I mean the sweet saleswoman :D So, give the fragrance a try. I found it quite good.

No need to consult any note-breakdowns here. Lest you fall for any marketing ploy about "coffee" (??). Essentially, this tropical Kool-Aid set against balsamic basil, has got GAME ! A synthetic flirty head-turner like this isn't for everyone. But it's assertiveness, both in scent as well as performance is nevertheless appealing, owing to a structure that never seem to lose conviction even as it loses strength. A stand-out in a sea of wan puppy-dog juice aimed at a young audience. (Anne)Flippo and (Pierre)Wargnye inject just the right nuance of "mint" - to buoy this otherwise strident mix, atop the cool stratosphere of Givenchy luxury -broadening it's appeal for the more savvy, in the process. This is a step above other comparable but banal confections -like any of the cKsummer2000and-whatevs. This under-dog from the fragrance pound is my pick of the litter. The (literally) edgy bottle design seals the deal ! Lotsa fun. Longevity: 5.5/10 (in base) Projection (Spring temperatures): 8/10 (in mid) Art/Creatives: 8/10 (bottle, concept, and scent) How: wearable all seasons, night or day, casual, style-conscious, "out-going", dates, parties, flirting.

tested at the end of summer 2007 thanks to a sample, it was quickly discontinued in France, but I was able to get it in 2010 via an online store in the USA. it is a powerful, very masculine perfume, also very refreshing, therefore targeted at summer, the smell is unique, I do not remember having ever smelled this type of perfume despite the presence of a smell of lavender and freshness that I I have already looked in other perfumes. ideal for an evening by the sea with a barbecue on the coast. I nevertheless recommend it to people under 45, because it has a fairly modern effect.

More than irresistible, this is just very, very, very plastic and synthetic in the wrong meaning – smelling like something which just popped out of a futuristic complicated industrial machinery. I get some nuances that with quite some stretch and fantasy, may be connected with the notes listed (citrus, coffee, cedar), but above all I get a really loud concoction of pure plastic, with laundry-fruity-citrus nuances. Mostly due to musk and citrus, I guess, and something vaguely floral. The only notes which smell acceptably “realistic” especially after a while, are cedar and lavender. With the right name and the right marketing concept, this would be easily a best-seller among the “post-modern futuristic side” of niche perfumery. As is, it’s just more a depressing, Calvin Klein-esque mainstream fizzy burp with no interest, no depth, no taste (both meaning “no class” and literally, “no specific taste”). Surely it is a “fresh” watery version of Very Irrésistible though, as I get some connection to the original - and no, not that better - version, so at least that part of the name is realistic and won’t disappoint you. As for the rest... meh. 5/10

I still remember when the Very Irrésistible was launched to the market in 2005; at that time, I did not appreciate it. I was too attracted to aquatic, metallic, and airy accords, such as Lacoste Essential, Yves Roches Transat, YSL Kouros Eau d'Été, Bvlgari Aqua, Aramis Life, Jasper Conran II, and Joop! Homme Chill Out, to mention a few and overlooked that one. Too bad, so sad. Yet, the very same happened to all of its flankers, miserably. But it was not far ago that I came upon a relatively new tester bottle in perfume outlet, a ridiculous bargain, and I was fortunate since it is discontinued by now. Right off the bat, Very Irrésistible Fresh Attitude on my skin opens up the woody, fresh, and aromatic with the pleasant and energizing citrus-minty accord, with detectable notes of grapefruit and bergamot. Fresh spearmint adds its cooling attributes, while vivid coriander leaves balance it with its pleasingly pungent and spicy facets. Mint is striking, supported by citrus tones on one side and spicy tones on the other side. That wondrous fresh blend lasts for nearly a quarter an hour. Albeit I barely recognize the synthetic molten rubber smell that other people mentioned, yet I think this is unique and not disgusting at all. I expressly love the smell of the top notes, which are quite impressive. The combination of grapefruit, mint, and coriander is not what you would expect. It comes off more like a tart berry and not citrus fruits. When spraying it, you can appreciate these notes and perhaps think it's a little too strong to be a summer fragrance. Don't be hasty, let it develop a while, and you will see. When it comes to the heart of this fragrance, lavender blossoms and grand vert basil leaves make it up. This accord is slightly balmy, spicy with lemon tarragon like the nuance of basil. Lavender, with its clean and deep aroma, contrasts the spice, giving out an alluring scent and gives the impression of a classic perfume. As the perfume transitions to the heart, the smell is less zesty and more floral. I love the way each note can be unquestionably detected in each stage. Lastly, when it comes to the dry down, cedar plays its woody notes at the base, rendering warmth and comfort. This woody temper mixes with the dark and potent facets of coffee, here more closely akin to a fresh sugared cup of mocha, a chocolate-flavored variant of a caffè latte with sugared cocoa powder, rather than toasted and crushed coffee beans. After a couple of hours, it becomes a skin scent, and you can still feel basil and some coffee. Although it has excellent sillage, duration and projection are rather modest because the fragrance can be barely sniffed after three hours. It is a pity being a perfect summer scent and having moderate performance. I recommend it for summer and late spring daytime use with average temperatures or warm nights, as it is somewhat cumbersome and sweet once you apply it. Fresh, with a subtle unoffensive sweetness, citrusy, with a tiny pinch of mild smoke, playful and very agreeable. By the way, the tall triangular, blue-green gradient bottle is extraordinary. -Elysium

Givenchy has really tried to break records with this naming and is apparently only surpassed by the Very Irrésistible Givenchy for Men Fresh Attitude Summer Sorbet launched two years later - aside from the "Motto series" by Kilian. But was the fragrance equally creative? After all, VIGfMFA starts off absolutely fresh with the often-criticized shower gel vibe with fruity tendencies. This is neither unpleasant nor really innovative, but it was rather unusual for its time. Gradually, the mint dissolves and gives VIGfMFA an interesting development. Specifically, it heads in the direction of Ice*Men by Thierry Mugler, a short-lived creation outside the A*Men cosmos, which, although it contains completely different ingredients, radiated an absolute sensuality with its warm patchouli. The only two obvious facts that both fragrances share are the color of the bottle and the year of release. Coincidence? In any case, this phase elevates VIGfMFA with its soft coffee note, but it is not enough to make it a desirable freshie. Accordingly, this flanker is just a minor occurrence in the perfume business. Otherwise, VIGfMFA could have benefited from much more projection and longevity, which is usually quite limited in this fragrance category. Otherwise, I am still waiting for the official Ice*Men successor. Will there be anything coming?

I seem to be drawn to the ingredients bergamot and lavender. Anyone who likes Very Irrésistible should definitely give it a try and form their own opinion. It really reminds me a bit of the rather woody predecessor without coming off as a cheap remake. Unfortunately, I can't geek out enough here to say: you can really pick out the cedar and coffee in the base note. No.

I first need to rename this fragrance. Because despite the name, this "Jaipur Bracelet" and its predecessor are more like distant relatives than identical twins. How about "Jaipur Charm Bracelet"? A chic accessory for a fashion-conscious young woman who has just entered the realm of adulthood. Like the charm bracelets from Thomas Sabo, which are considered the first "real" jewelry and satisfy the playful spirit with countless combination possibilities. Outgrown the colorful bling-bling from H&M, but still far from the diamond bracelet from Cartier. The "new" Jaipur Bracelet is like an olfactory journey from little girl to grown woman. The opening smells just like the bottle looks: pink, young, innocent - like raspberry soda. A fresh, juicy mandarin is also present, ensuring that the fragrance doesn’t drift too much into the sweet and cloying territory. It is the absolute opposite of the "old" Jaipur Bracelet, which starts fresh-green-floral to herbal and initially comes off as almost unapproachable. After a short time, the pink soda is replaced by pink lychee and hyacinth. This unusual combination keeps the fragrance feeling very young, but no longer childish. Here, a similarity to the "old" Jaipur Bracelet first shows itself, although the latter remains distinctly more floral and fresh, appearing to me much more elegant and beautiful. Towards the base, the "new" undergoes another significant transformation: after a few hours, it becomes almost entirely unfruity and warm-floral thanks to iris and cashmere wood. This is, for me, the most beautiful part. The fragrance becomes calmer, rounder, and more mature. I even find it more beautiful now than its predecessor, which shares an iris note here but feels bulkier to me due to the cypress. Unfortunately, the sillage decreases significantly at this point. It was quite loud at the beginning, but is now almost skin-close. I would have preferred the opposite, as the soda note at the start does annoy me a bit. But you can't have it all - so hold your nose and push through, it's worth it ;-)

It's a light-touch, diaphanous thing, for all that it starts with a smoky leather. It's a transparent, gauzy wisp of clean woods and leather, with a hint of apricot buried within, truly reminiscent of the tea it's recalling. No harsh edges - it's smooth and well blended, and just feels classy. It's genuinely beautiful and I wish I could recommend it wholeheartedly. If the scent were a little more robust or the price cheaper, I likely could. Unfortunately, as others have said before me, the longevity and the 'presence' of the scent just isn't there. I'd love to be gifted this... but I wouldn't buy it.

Some time ago, I started testing various Jo Malone fragrances and was disheartened to find that most of the Jo Malones I was keen on had disappeared from the market (aaaah… Fig & Cassis, whhhhyyy???). Then, at some point, the rare teas were released, which were a lot of fun to test because they smelled so good. Well, I haven't tested them all yet, as other fragrances have occasionally "interfered," but now I'm continuing with one scent from this line. And why specifically with Golden Needle? Ahh, because it’s so golden…! ^_^ No, but I just fished it out from my samples,… since I have nothing better to do than (hopefully) make you happy with my comments here, so please read until the end!!! The scent: Yes, the beautiful tea scent comes through immediately. Initially quite strong, it becomes a bit weaker within just a few minutes, but it remains noticeable and recognizable as one of the main notes. Spicy notes join in, which initially smell like kitchen herbs and then are hardly identifiable. The sandalwood is also quite noticeable afterwards, providing a foundation beneath the tea scent.
