Additionally, the fragrance gives off a wonderful, creamy scent that at first even seems to smell like a cream. Later, it is more in the background, but as mentioned, it makes the scent soft and creamy and seems to soften the spicy notes. I also detect a very faint, incense-like light smoky note. Much later, the scent doesn’t change too much, but somehow I still smell a honey-like sweetness in the background. I actually smell very little leather; in any case, leather is not one of the main notes. The sillage and longevity: The scent has a rather "normal" projection, so it can be considered average, although it does become a bit weaker later on. One shouldn't expect a scent cloud and should stand closer to someone wearing this fragrance if they want to smell it. The longevity is more than average. It lasts about eight hours, but due to the weakened sillage by then, it may seem shorter to some. The bottle: The bottle, which appears simple at first glance, is nonetheless high-quality and looks good upon closer inspection, with the beautiful color of the fragrance liquid contributing to this. In any case, the bottle is quite large (175 ml), tall, and closes with a magnetic black oval cap. The front only displays the brand logo. All in all, a nice bottle. Yes, this tea scent also convinces, especially if you enjoy black tea and want it to come across as creamier. But like most of these fragrances, Golden Needle is not particularly strong, making it more of a scent for personal enjoyment (kind of like when you drink a cup of tea just for yourself, and of course WITHOUT milk, you barbarians, you have no idea…). Unfortunately, it is way too weak for going out. It is well-suited for warm days but can also work beautifully in autumn, or probably even best in autumn; I still need to try that out. However, it is too weak for winter. Since this scent is also good, the selection becomes difficult again regarding which scent from the Rare Teas one would like to have; the only solution is to test, test, and test, just like I did at the Jo Malone stand some time ago, standing there over and over again and probably annoying the girls there with my constant presence… noooo… hopefully not… :( Anyway, just give it a try.

“Enchanting and melancholic, humorous and moving - this is how ‘Breakfast at Tiffany’s’ became a classic, simultaneously a hymn to a great actress.” Yes, Holly Golightly - uh, Audrey Hepburn, delivered a fantastic star role and captured the hearts of countless fans. Holly leads a life of extremes. She parties late into the night, drinks, smokes, and is the companion of many gentlemen. Everything seems so perfect, and Paul, that is George Peppard, the writer - who lives in the same building as her - quickly falls in love with little Holly. Nevertheless, everything seems to be just a facade, and the two are like two lost souls who must find each other in the bustling chaos of New York. The film reminds me of Golden Needle Tea because it starts off so sparkling and cheeky. Leather and benzoin with spices are like an elegant outfit combined with a witty hat. Spicy, like black tea steeped lightly, exciting, invigorating, and mysterious. When you spray Golden Needle Tea, you immediately see Holly with a hat, a little costume, a cigarette on a stick, and long white leather gloves, which she - holding the cigarette in the corner of her mouth - sensually and slowly glides from her arms over her hands. And while doing so, she gives you a cheeky look! How can one not look and already feel a slight tingle and want to approach her? And then it becomes quieter. Holly sits down, elegantly ashes the cigarette, and looks around. She takes a deep breath and puts on a false smile. For others, a beautiful smile. For her, a smile so that no one sees how lonely and longing she is inside. That is then the sandalwood. Like a mist, sandalwood emerges. Starting from the feet, the ankles, all the way up to the head. Enveloped, gentle, and calm. A warm, velvety, woody, and balsamic milky scent soothes and calms. And yet, the long white glove keeps coming back, briefly waving through the air and saying --> Hello? I’m still here. Yes, the Holly! Sparkling and cheeky yet still a gentle soul.

L'interdit Nocturnal Jasmine Edition Millesime by Givenchy is a perfume that uses high quality ingredients for the main notes of the fragrance. It keeps the dna of the original edp but also has a very interesting twist that makes it more versatile. If you are interested into hearing more details about this perfume, please watch my review on Youtube.

Overload of JASMINE, a guaranteed headache for me. The name says it all; the scent reminds me of wilting cemetery bouquets in the moonlight. Longevity is very good. Once sprayed, the fragrance does not change. Spices are only faintly detectable. I can't pick up anything else because the JASMINE is so overwhelmingly opulent.

What does a jewelry house do when it has an oriental fragrance in its lineup that feels overwhelming and "too much" in the height of summer? Quite simply, it releases a soft, light, fresh summer variant. In 2006, there was also such a "casual" version of the classic Jaipur Homme, which, however, does not smell fresh or aquatic - no, it is again fruity-spicy. There are references to Jaïpur Homme Fraîcheur Épicée, but the differences are hard for the layman to recognize. Thanks to Apicius, I was able to test the 2006 flanker as well and come to a brief, somewhat sobering statement: Overall, it resembles the Fraîcheur Épicée, it has a similar fruity opening, but it feels more powdery and a bit aimless, as already mentioned by Apicius. My girlfriend and I found the opening to be more powerful than in the Fraîcheur Épicée, and the cinnamon note, which is not listed here, is also present. The longevity seems to be lower here, and I conclude that I prefer the more powerful Fraîcheur Épicée version significantly - still, I remain loyal to the original Jaipur Homme... which I have now also ordered as a 15ml Eau de Parfum ;)

Jaïpur Homme Fraîcheur Épicée was my discovery of the year. I have worn it frequently and perhaps with little regard. I feel somewhat ashamed that I have not given its little brother, Jaipur Homme Fraicheur, any attention so far. I was simply too impatient and hastily set it aside - just like I initially did with the Epicée. For perhaps even more than the Epicée, Fraicheur is a challenging fragrance that does not reveal itself immediately. To be honest, the beginning is terrible. An unstructured blend of scents without character, accompanied by a biting sharpness. But today, during a conversation with the owner of the Schwope perfumery, it was right in front of my nose the whole time, and since I still had a free wrist, I decided to give it another try, this time allowing the fragrance the time it deserves. These two limited fragrances start where others already stop. Only after half an hour did something resembling a definable scent profile begin to emerge. And after a full hour, there it was, that wonderful accord that I had also encountered in the Epicée and which fascinates me so much. In the other comment, I attempted to describe it. But the Fraicheur is different. Much more subtle. While the Epicée inevitably forms a cloud and the fragrance develops at some distance from the skin, the wonderful accord in Fraicheur stays close to the skin and has little projection. It feels so much less opulent, even though it hardly differs from the Epicée. It comes across as somewhat drier. It may be that it lacks a touch of spice. I also perceive it as powdery, which I did not notice in the Epicée. Ultimately, I must concede a certain soapiness in the Epicée, which may stem from the use of a musk. This is not noticeable in the Fraicheur. At times, I had the impression that the Fraicheur contains a minimal amount of vetiver - but really only traces, which were simultaneously light and dark in a rubber-like expression. The vetiver note from Frederick Malle's Vetiver Extraordinaire in the highest possible dilution! Am I right? Unfortunately, there is no reasonable fragrance pyramid to be found. Compared to the Epicée, which has full EdP strength despite its labeling as EdT, the longevity of the Fraicheur seems to be less. Yes, this is the subtle, office-friendly version of the Epicée, much more delicate and refined. I will likely acquire the little brother out of consideration for my colleagues, but I will not wear it only in the office. These limited fragrances are already discontinued. Those who, like me, have the opportunity to test it at the Schwope perfumery in Wolfsburg should please prepare for the necessary time it takes to develop. You will not regret it. Otherwise, I only know the Eau de Parfum version of Jaipur Homme. And that is simply a completely different fragrance. It doesn’t mess around, but is immediately present in all its glory. Fraicheur and Fraicheur Epicée do not seem to me to be “light” versions of Jaipur; rather, they are a standalone fragrance. It’s fascinating that the almost identical scent accord can be presented as both room-filling opulent and then again subtle and close to the body. I have not encountered anything like this before. I once tested Jaipur Homme EdT, the most common version, in a train station perfumery, but quickly set it aside. Now that I know that Jaipur variants require a lot of time to develop, I will take another look at the original.

It was love at first sight or rather at first sniff between Les Parfums Mythiques Extravagance d`Amarige and me - I certainly didn’t expect that with a blind purchase. Normally, I can't get excited about the flankeritis that has been rampant for a few years now, but the pyramid of this offshoot of the 90s blockbuster Amarige from 2007 simply piqued my curiosity, as it deviates significantly from the original. It starts with bittersweet mandarin and bitter marigold (Tagetes), to which the warmer and rounder notes of jasmine and orange blossom join, ultimately merging into a caressing blend with the slightly sweet amber, aromatic cedarwood, and softly creamy sandalwood - which is fortunately used very sparingly here - that hugs you like a cozy, extra-soft cardigan. A very skin-close scent that unites some contradictions within itself, as it is both gently dreamy and straight, but also floral-warm and bitter. This member of the Les Parfums Mythiques line has nothing in common with the original Amarige at all. While Amarige is bold and loud as an EDT and even when applied sparingly leaves a massive scent trail behind, Les Parfums Mythiques Extravagance d`Amarige exercises refined restraint even with lavish application. The original Extravagance d`Amarige, released nearly ten years earlier, is richer and more complex in its scent development.

The limited seasonal collections from Jo Malone are eagerly anticipated every spring: what theme will it be this time? I have consciously experienced "Rock the Ages" in 2015, "The Herb Gardens" in 2016, and this year "The Bloomsbury Set." And thus, I have also witnessed the fact that these fragrances disappear from the market very quickly, leaving someone who might want to think a bit after the first scent test standing in front of empty shelves. The paradox is: shortly thereafter, extremely overpriced bottles are offered for sale online; sometimes up to 180.00 euros for 30ml plus shipping costs. Well, that's the free market economy. But personally, that’s not for me; I resist it. Fortunately, I know the nice sales associate at the local Jo Malone counter. He allows me to sniff to my heart's content at the displayed testers; yes, even to take short notes. He knows that I write about my experiences and feelings here. Perhaps he hopes for increased sales as a result. Because there are not only the limited collections! So this spring, I had the opportunity to extensively test "Whisky & Cedarwood" from "The Bloomsbury Set." I really like this fragrance; if it comes to market at a reasonable price, it will be mine. I hinted at this in my comment about it. Recently, I accompanied my neighbor, who wanted to test the Jo Malone standard range once again, and I had the chance to refresh my acquaintance with "Tobacco & Mandarin." This was also one of the few testers from "The Bloomsbury Set" that still had more than just three drops left. We became friends while my neighbor kept complaining: "I can't smell anything! Why don't they smell today?" She was so heavily enveloped in "Jasmin Noir" by Bvlgari that we even got seats on the subway! Well, in the end, she bought a fragrance that she already has at least seven combinations of at home. The main thing is: she is happy with her purchase. Last Sunday, two auctions ended: both involved 30ml bottles of "Tobacco & Mandarin." While the one offered under "women's fragrances" exceeded my maximum price expectation (I also refuse to pay 6.95 euros for shipping within Germany), I was able to get the fragrance listed under "unisex" at a more than reasonable price. When I checked during the first major pit stop of the Formula 1 race in Spa, I was not only surprised but very pleased. Now I have a typical late summer/early autumn fragrance at home. The tobacco plant that gives its name here is very well represented. Just the fine floral scent: the white, trumpet-shaped hanging flowers of the mountain tobacco release their sweet scent in the evening hours. In contrast, the pink, upright flowers of other varieties, standing in a very loose umbel shape, are diurnal and have a somewhat shy but no less lovely fragrance. The dried, very light leaves of the tobacco exude the spicy scent of sun-drenched, very spicy hay after the typical pre-treatment for pipe tobacco (which can be read online)! (Pipe tobacco differs significantly in its processing from cigarette tobacco; this should be kept in mind.) Mixed into this sun-dried hay are sage leaves, which wonderfully add their somewhat strict, typical spiciness. This combination alone evokes in me the image of further mown meadows and fields: it’s slightly autumnal! And the cleansing, clarifying effect of the sage is pleasantly noticeable. The fresh, fruity mandarin positively enlivens this slightly herbal-spicy scent experience: it brings the golden sun into the fragrance! The circle is almost complete, but the certain non-plus-ultra is still missing: a hint of beeswax! I have always loved this scent in heavy furniture polish. After the fruity freshness of the mandarins, it rounds off this bright fragrance creation warmly and harmoniously. Thus, a sunny September day is created, whose already soft light caresses over autumnal fields and which brings the first hint of autumn with ripe mandarins and beeswax. This somewhat strange Jo Malone fragrance is also not long-lasting throughout the day. It is light and fleeting, but still lingers as a hint for a long time. "Tobacco & Mandarin" is also one of the pleasant fragrances that unfold very well in the hair. Sprayed right after washing or styling - the pleasant "hay-like" freshness surrounds me swinging - with long hair - for a day or two. Thus, Jo Malone's "Tobacco & Mandarin" is a pleasant companion for the first autumn days: it brings freshness and the spicy scent of "fresh" hay (a contradiction in itself - I know!), which evokes a certain well-being. A kind of wellness day from the well-known glass bottle: a welcome fragrance composition for frayed nerves and souls to slow down and relax.

Tobacco & Mandarin is one of the upcoming new fragrances from Jo Malone, which will be released as part of the Bloomsbury Set as limited editions. They are all inspired by the Bloomsbury Group, an artistic (and also intellectual) group that contributed to the artistic and cultural modernization of England at that time. There are a total of five fragrances set to be released in March, and all are limited, so it's best to keep an eye out if you want to test these scents. In an initial test, I found all five quite wonderful. While they don’t have a very strong projection, they are still interesting and well-crafted, beautiful fragrances that I want to test a bit more closely over time, starting today with Tobacco & Mandarin, as this scent, along with Whisky & Cedarwood, made the biggest impression on me. And you know how much I love mandarins, especially when they keep my arm-ripping cat at bay :D The Scent: Aaahh, I smell a smiling mandarin looking at me cutely, so I have to smile back :) Yes, the mandarin does smell a bit weak (although it is noticeably stronger when sprayed), but it is very pleasant and slightly sweet, making it quite delicious. Alright, I might be gushing a bit because I really like mandarins in fragrances. Even though it is weak, you can at least smell it well into the base. Shortly after, a light tobacco scent sets in, which is rather subtle, so even those who don’t particularly like tobacco might want to check it out. The combination here is well done. Aside from that, the tobacco is increasingly overshadowed by the pipe tobacco, which is also not too strong and has a slightly vanilla-sweet and powdery scent. The sweetness initially comes from the beeswax, which, although it is in the background, is clearly identifiable and gives the fragrance a lovely, sweet note without being overly feminine. The scent remains warm and sweet in the base, with the sweetness now stemming more from a vanilla scent, but possibly also combined with a residual fruity sweetness from the mandarin. The pipe tobacco scent remains, it is warm, slightly powdery, and as mentioned, you can still smell the mandarin, which together creates a very nice combination. The Sillage and Longevity: Hmm… while the scent of the mandarin makes me smile, I could almost cry over its projection. The scent is quite weak and quickly becomes close to the skin, which is a shame because it smells great. On one hand, it’s good that the tobacco notes are weaker and don’t dominate overwhelmingly, but the fragrance could have benefited from just a bit more power overall. Well, it is quite gentle and soft because of this. The longevity is longer than expected due to the vanilla pipe, but after three to four hours, it has lost much of its strength. For the remaining time, which lasts another four or five hours, it is very close to the skin. The Bottle: The bottle is small and rectangular with a brown cylindrical cap. The most striking feature is the label, which depicts a painting and thus alludes to the art group. You see rectangles that are beveled at the bottom. These motifs remind one of paintings by artists like Mark Rothko and similar artists. The name of the fragrance is on the other side of the bottle. Quite nicely done. Aaaah, the scent has turned out really beautifully. It starts, as described, with lovely mandarins and transitions after a while into the sweet and warmer pipe tobacco. Even though I am now writing that the scent feels warm, due to its not overly high intensity, it is a lovely summer companion. It is not citrusy fresh, but very pleasantly soft to wear. As I said, I would have liked it to be a bit stronger, but oh well. You can use the scent well for everyday wear, although it almost feels too precious for that, as the fragrances are only available in limited 30 mL bottles. However, we are all perfume lovers (well, some are just perfume addicts :D), and you know what that means? Of course, hardly any of us is satisfied with just two or three fragrances, so we often switch scents daily, which means a fragrance should last longer for us. By the time the bottle is emptied, hopefully a long time will have passed… I can certainly imagine getting this scent and recommend that you all at least test it once :)

I have five Boucherons in my collection. I suppose the most famous is the original Boucheron from 1988. The bottle and the beautiful fragrance are iconic. Still my own favourite is Trouble though it does not get as good a rating. Boucheron is a house that apparently produces heavy scents. Jaïpur is heavy, especially after 15 minutes. So think twice before spraying, depending on your next activity. The beginning has a very distinct fruit mix with the freesia but the fruity part disappears quickly and the scent becomes floral. A lovely but quite loud one of its kind. I keep getting whiffs of the different flowers but rose and freesia are the most explicit. The warm dry down starts after three to four hours. Compared to Boucheron Jaïpur gets the same rating when looking at the bottle. They are both unique, but I do like the bracelet shaped bottle of Jaïpur. As far as I know Jaïpur is the capital city of the Northern Indian state, Rajastahn, also known as ‘the pink city’. I suppose the perfume is named after this. 272/365

I recently discovered "Jo Malone" so i can't really compare this new scent with some of his other parfums. It smells very sweet and flowery. I have to say, that i find you smell a lot of similarities to other Jo Malone parfums, so if you are a fan of his sweet parfums, this scent is probably for you. In Addition to that, it is also not a completly unique scent, It has something of these typical women parfums you can smell when she crosses your path. But on the other hand, it kind of has something special though, underneath the sweet flowery scent lays a dark and heavy scent, which really gives me a lot of winter or fall vibes. What I really admire is, that you can wear it in winter and spring, also for going out and having a nice, calm evening, or for your daily routine. I have not smelled very often, that a parfum offers you these both sides as one scent. And i will definetly wear it often in cold reasons. So as a conclusion, I would recommend this parfum for you, if you first: like sweet flowery scents, and search something to wear in winter or cold seasons. It really smells great!

A soft veil of well balanced almost powdery fresh floral harmony. This is the opening of elegant old school perfumery at its best but it retains a very individual herbal character that almost reminds one of violet leaves, even though they are not listed on the notes. Into a few moments of wearing, a small edge of the herbal side suddenly sits up as if alarmed, nearly too sharp and a little too harsh, but it doesn't last long. The perfume sits back down, and smooths down the ruffled flowers and woods, the crisis over, relaxing gently into a soft, woodsy, jasmine, floral with a spicy edge like a carnation just to prevent any over comfortable complacency. The herbs remain just enough to keep the florals sitting in polite check. It then dries down into a gentle, herby almost powdery, musky, woodsy, spicy, floral. No one note overpowering the rest. Gentle, peaceful and very sophisticated. A tiny hint of a very playful musky note that just smoulders beneath soft amber. The well behaved side keeps this perfume in order. The rest is just hinting at what could be underneath but of course polite girls just don't go there. It might be an older dame, who still has the beauty and the elegance. Her hair immaculately coiffured. Her suit worn and comfortable but still smart. A mere hint at her racy past betrayed in the laughter lines. As the light fades, she leaves, and there is just a hint of her presence and without her there, you now notice that her room is a little dusty with the daffodils fading in the vase. This is an older bottle of edt I am testing.

Long before the days of Y, Givenchy III, and No19 there was Le De, a green muguet chypre with a sour aspect, hardened by rosewood, and paradoxically softened by powder. There’s a rosy bouquet in the back – just to show it has a heart after all, but, like those others who followed her on, this is one tough cookie. Not exactly the haughty grande dame, more of a spinsterish librarian – shushing as you whisper to your colleague, and tut tutting if you rustle a bag of mints. This was the late fifties, and long before the Swinging Sixties – so no letting your hair down; the style was -tight waist and conical skirt four foot wide- and stockings of course, blue ones probably. Basically Dior’s New Look, which was -new- ten years before this... Vintage LeDe is a bit like vintage Ma Griffe - which was meant for teenagers - and who has now matured into a grown woman. This is the total opposite of those sticky fruchouli’s you smell in the subway, and all power to it.

Givenchy was only known to me as a designer in the past. I only learned much later that he dedicated his first fragrance, L'Interdit, to Audrey Hepburn. In the meantime, I have managed to secure several bottles of this scent in vintage versions, including parfum, EdP, and EdT, because the new version cannot compare to Audrey Hepburn's L'Interdit. It's similar with Le De. Recently, I received my vintage EdT of Le De and, of course, immediately put my nose into it. Le De is for me the little sister - or in today's language, the light version - of L'interdit. Le De is finer, more delicate, and nowhere near as intense as L'Interdit. A beautiful, very fine, and absolutely everyday wearable fragrance, which primarily features white jasmine blossoms. Although not a true soliflore, jasmine is quite dominant here and reminds me a bit of Bvlgari's Voile de Jasmin, but it is by no means as sweet as that one; rather, it is more green. The woody base is hardly noticeable as such. It is more of a darkening of the jasmine scent, unsweet and very soft and fine. Absolute elegance without any intrusion. I will skip the new Le De version; I prefer to enjoy my vintage.

My dear husband doesn't like to stand with me at perfume counters for too long - but with a few select brands, he gladly takes a break. Givenchy is one of them. The Fleur d`Interdit had him genuinely excited back then! So yesterday, he held a scent strip of Le De under my nose. Oh - I caught a whiff of morning air - this could lead to a purchase. However, Le De unfortunately does not announce any "morning air" for me. The delicate spicy intro is still well captured - but the floral part seems oddly dark to me - creamy, almost oily. Jasmine and lilac do not shine; instead, they seem just before wilting. A sad mood. The dark woods do not lift the spirits. The scent has something "old" about it, but it doesn't remind me of the "good old days". My husband perceives Le De as delicately floral but full-toned, and he is taken with it. Unfortunately, we do not agree - and I couldn't bring myself to buy it with a clear heart. So I must wait until he puts on his generous pants again.

Men might know about 10 colors... Women, on the other hand, know dozens more, like undertones such as salmon, Bordeaux, or indeed mint. And Le De starts off for me absolutely green and floral - or rather mint-colored. Unfortunately, it's too green and strange for my taste. I found the more well-known L'Interdit to be significantly better, more opulent, more important, and simply more beautiful. I wouldn't exactly label both as siblings - aside from the name Givenchy and the floral direction, they are separated by small continents. I tested the current version just like with the Audrey Hepburn fragrance, unfortunately not the unreformulated original version. This is said to have smelled significantly different from what is currently sold under the name Le De. But I can't provide any insight on that. Le De feels like many Givenchy reissues: emotionless and cool. This can come off as stylish and could even be the new style & the perfume DNA of Givenchy - but it doesn't appeal to me here; it only works for jasmine lovers. Because after the minty start - green, fruity, juicy, almost like fig - the fragrance undergoes its first major, clearly defined turn. The main theme comes through more and more: a feminine, now only slightly green jasmine. The heart doesn't offer much more; it's simply too simple and not half as refined, noble, and complex as L'Interdit, the forbidden perfume. During the second turn towards bright woods, the fragrance fades increasingly until it finally disappears, making it even hard to define these summery woods more precisely. Bottle: I have nothing against the new bottles... but I do have issues with inappropriate reformulations & remakes under the same name. Sillage: even more delicate than L'Interdit, because it lacks a large part of the powdery-strong base. Longevity: after the woods have shaken off the exhausting jasmine, the fragrance is no longer worth inhaling. Short, concise name - short, concise conclusion: in the version I tested, absolutely no classic & at most worth a glance for absolute jasmine fans.

Given to me by a family member who knows my passion for perfumes and knew I didn't own this one, I was hoping for a pleasant surprise. A clean oriental scent at first, a feeling of déjà vu, like a soapy amber scent with a hint of rose. Then I felt like I was smelling a low-end perfume that could be sold in Arab bazaars for €5, and then I remembered Lord by Al Rehab, which itself resembles Sartorial by Penhaligon. The level of Givenchy's private collection has definitely fallen in comparison to the first private collection, which contained a few bangers.

After spraying, it’s not so much about “rocking” but rather about “waiting.” It takes almost half a minute for the ham-like, tarry smoky wood to reveal itself. The pepper shows its aroma close to the smoke rather than any sharpness. And then the two sit there. Like rocks. Less in terms of presence or volume (both completely moderate) but rather in their immobility. This was now - as can be easily recognized - the second “rock” explanation approach. I find it more plausible because at least the tarry note persists for hours, remaining rather static in the background, while it gradually becomes milder on top. Perhaps a hint of dark vanilla. I imagine something rubbery directly on my skin around noon. In the afternoon, the leisurely path towards gentleness and warmth continues; in close proximity to the skin, the resin note has now achieved a mellow relaxedness, appearing equally aged. Unfortunately, I don’t know what gurjun balsam smells like. I can only endorse the addition “-balsam”: A rounded resin-wood impression with a creamy musk attitude. I still sense a bit of roughness towards the end, possibly mossy, also earthy. There could be patchouli on board. The whole affair is supposed to refer to today’s London. Hmm. I think primarily of the smell of a factory area from yesterday. Sour, greasy smoke, etc. Let’s better leave the strange background thoughts about the name and theme aside; they only distract. The fragrance, as it is, is quite beautiful. Stable and straightforward, it shows us a distinctly strong character, yet due to its restraint in volume, it is universally applicable. In the opening comment, Mokka (thank you for the sample!) described that she had snagged the fragrance at the Jo Malone store in Hamburg. I had also tested it there, but did not purchase it. It’s nice that I now had the opportunity to examine the correctness of that decision more carefully. My conclusion: Very decent, but not a must-have for me. Nevertheless, I recommend a test to everyone else, especially friends of well-cultivated tar.

I ordered the Birch & Black Pepper blindly based on the description on the Jo Malone website. Black bottle? Spicy? Rebellious? Punk? Sure, that's totally me!!! Into the cart it goes... There are no samples from Jo Malone, of course. But you can easily throw the 30ml colognes into your cart blindly since they aren't too expensive and get used up quickly. So, let's get to the test... First spray: sharp, peppery, quite decent.... But it fades away in 1 minute. Then comes...... birch??? I was looking forward to something similar to the birch infusion in the sauna, but what comes is something sour-bitter-smoky, a bit of leather, little wood, no sweetness, no warm aroma like with the Lutens. And then in the dry down, there's definitely a lot of tobacco.... I feel transported to my grandpa's study with old musty wooden furniture with leather armrests, where countless cigars were smoked. The scent is definitely masculine, in my opinion not suitable for women, nor for the more rugged leather jacket-wearing types like me. It is interesting, but not a likable scent. Maybe something for layering. The longevity is (thankfully?) quite fleeting compared to the other Malones.... After an estimated 30 minutes, it's basically all over..

My rainy stroll through Hamburg led me to Jo Malone. I'll keep it brief: I took home Rock the Ages - Birch & Black Pepper - a limited edition. Here I will now attempt my first comment on it: Immediately after the first spray, black pepper greets me and I find myself in the woods. I have thought long about whether I really know how birch smells. Do you perceive the trunk, the branches, the leaves, the catkins? To be honest, I have never hugged a birch and sniffed it, but I know right away: this is birch and I am embracing it now. Not warm, dark, and soft like other woods, but a clear, bright, woody scent welcomes me. Like early in the morning, it rained a bit during the night, and somewhere nearby someone must have started a campfire. My hand touches the trunk, I feel the texture of the bark, rough and cracked. The Gurjum prevents any splinters from tearing at you. It is soft, warm, woody, and a hint of sweet* takes away the strictness of the further scent development, but not the clear line. After one to two hours, the pepper steps back, and it slowly becomes warmer. A man (and what a man!) in an old leather jacket approaches me, smiles at me, and takes my hand. With this perfume, I think it shouldn't be worn casually. I can also imagine that it will blend differently with my skin tomorrow. It doesn't flatter with compliments, isn't overly pleasing, but is incredibly interesting. Wearable by both men and women, even in spring - possibly with a tulip behind the ear, or a rose in the buttonhole. The salesperson at the Jo Malone shop had the idea of layering and tried it out himself. Somewhere I read that mandarin, patchouli, and vanilla are also listed. This forest seems quite large. Let's see what my nose whispers to me during the next test. ___ *I found the following information about Gurjum: It is a resin from trees in Southeast Asia. The botanical name is Dipterocarpus turbinatus. This oil is used not only in aromatherapy but is also said to provide relief for respiratory diseases and has anti-inflammatory properties for skin issues. Additionally, it is said to help with mental stress. Just by inhaling it, one experiences a mental boost.

Ah... Ysatis.... This is about the skyscraper shaped bottle with plastic cap, so not the original, but also not the latest version. I love Ysatis, it would've been my signature if I wouldn't have L'Air du Temps (which is a totally different scent by the way). Maybe she is in fall and winter... Ysatis is a beautyful composition of everything I love in a perfume: aldehydes, white and yellow flowers... I don't know the original, but I'm fine with this one (I just hope the latest version in the more plain bottle, is as good...) Tuberose can sometimes be too much for me, but here it is a 'bright sparkle' instead of an overly sweet or cloying note. Ysatis adjusts to whatever mood I'm in and never bores me. If you ask her to be powdery, she will; if you ask her to be bright, she will; if you ask her to be lush and sexy (but never kinky!), she will.... I love how she can change in the developing proces during the day and in different circumstances. This is what real perfume is about, they don't make them like this anymore (sadly!). To me, Ysatis feels asif she could have been made much earlier than in the eighties, I don't think 'shoulderpads' or anything like that, when wearing her.... If they would have told me she was made in early 20th century, I would have believed them. However, she is timeless. Some may find her too bold, but I think she's soft and gentle in making her statement. I now have the latest version in the plain bottle and I'm happy to be able to tell it is the same scent: Lovely, good sillage and good longevity.

I grew up in the '80s and I remember this being a popular scent. But I feel like Ysatis transcends any one era. To me, it's a timeless chypre floral and it doesn't require shoulder pads to pull off properly. I don't see this as being a boss type scent. It's quite floral and romantic without being soft. I would be more likely to wear this with a flowing ruffled skirt than with menswear. The ylang ylang is the most stand out note to me, and I like it in any season's weather. Ysatis is a classic for all the right reasons.

Gold: Not applied with a brush, but finely sprayed on the skin: What a luxury! This luxury has a name: “Ysatis,” previously known to me as Eau de Toilette and worn with enthusiasm, now as a perfume adds the crowning touch to everything familiar: It unfolds pure pleasure for the senses! Rich in exquisite fragrance notes that hint at its wedding, this scent truly flows like liquid gold. Hubert de Givenchy said: “... “Ysatis” is like a sensual woman with charm, a silhouette dressed in strict black, illuminated by precious jewelry.” Was he thinking of the “Little Black Dress” that made Audrey Hepburn so famous in the film “Breakfast at Tiffany's”? Here my contradiction arises: How does this statement reconcile with the slogan “The great perfume of the night,” with which this creation was advertised? Despite this elegant-purist thought, “Ysatis” as a perfume flows around me like a golden river, in just the right consistency: Not too airy and not too heavy, not too fast, not too slow, but wonderfully modulating, adapting to the personality and distinguishing it as special. The glow of familiar-fresh citrus notes, laced with aldehydes, resembles little flames flickering on this surface. They dance around an extraordinary blend of resinous galbanum and noble, rich rosewood nuances. Thus, this flowing stream of gold already gains depth before the multitude of so Chypre-popular floral scents is woven in. What a beautiful pattern emerges here from jasmine, rose, the noble iris, and her so fragrant beautiful companions. A spoonful of creamy-golden honey further gives the resulting fabric the comforting feeling of enveloping the senses: So rich, so luxurious! Of course, the “Ysatis” perfume also has a contemporary base, which fortunately no one has yet attempted to alter. Perhaps civet, castoreum, and also the oakmoss I love so much are no longer in vogue, but they are exactly where they belong: They give this composition that certain something, playing a bit with the already present fragrance notes before a final sensually warm blanket of rum and clove refined vanilla lays over our well-known and beloved base trio of sandalwood, patchouli, and vetiver. Above all hovers, how could it be otherwise, an aromatic cloud of noble amber smoke. “Ysatis”: A fragrance of opulence, luxury, flowing gold! A scent: No longer contemporary, perhaps even incomprehensible to many, and almost antiquated due to its rich sillage and extreme longevity? But aren’t antiques experiencing a renaissance right here in our fragrance world? Why do we rejoice over every vintage find and feel genuinely happy when we read about it, perhaps even get to be part of it? How we still long to be caressed by tender memories and fragrance richness from time to time. Not daily, but we do not want to miss these moments of sensuality. “Ysatis” as a perfume grants these precious moments that flow like liquid gold!

Ah, Givenchy. Ah, Ropion... and all the milestones in perfume history that he has gifted us... Have you ever chased someone down the street to ask them what perfume they are wearing? I have only done that twice in my life. Once in Nice... as a student... a young woman walked past me and her perfume was unbelievably beautiful. It was so good that I followed her... "Vous portez quel parfum...?" "Moi, je porte Ysatis de Givenchy". Givenchy! I didn't even know it until that moment. The next day, I immediately went to the nearest perfume store and bought Ysatis. It accompanied me for years. Today, you can no longer get the extrait... and of course, the Eau de Toilette has been reformulated. The LVMH group, which also owns Guerlain, must comply with the European regulations. Oakmoss is out, at least the real stuff, musk is a different aroma chemical today, etc. - nevertheless, even the EdT that is still available today conveys an impression of the beauty of this perfume. It has an exceptionally strong charm, something radiant, sublime, very special, particularly through the clove and tuberose. Yes, sure, some might argue that it’s just another 80's bomb or shake their heads in amusement, vintage glorification, once again. These 50+ guys who sing the praises of the scents of their youth - and I belong to that group too. People often say that everything was better in the perfume market back then... I say it too. Ysatis, for example, was a completely normal French perfume that was composed with care and love for detail. In 1984, there weren't 2000 new fragrances launched, but a very manageable number in the hundreds. Douglas didn't have a flagship store on Zeil or Kö, and Guerlain had no exclusive lines. Givenchy, Guerlain, Chanel, and Caron were luxurious enough with their perfumes that are now called mainstream. Those who bought Ysatis surrounded themselves with a noble scent and weren't looking for the next exclusive edition from Roja Dove, who was probably still an apprentice at Guerlain back then (at least that's what he always says). Today, you are simply olfactorily undereducated if you are satisfied with a "simple" mainstream scent for under 100 euros from a department store perfume counter. Let's say... a ubiquitous scent like Coco Mademoiselle. Or even No. 5. After all, there is the higher-priced segment. The glorious world of niche perfumery. Or the countless exclusive lines... from Chanel, Dior, Lalique... you name it. What started as a counter-movement to the power of the big cosmetics companies, namely the "niche sector", has been gradually taken over by the industry that was originally meant to be fought against. The jungle of new releases is almost impenetrable. Every day, countless perfumistas strive to carve out a path here, sorting, commenting, photographing... - overwhelming. Sometimes it’s overwhelming when you want to keep up with it day by day. Are we hunting the holy grail, hunter or the hunted? I am currently going through my collected notes from many years and diligently writing statements to organize the abundance of impressions and free myself, as I realize that the hunt is not doing me any good. Ultimately, it turns out that I keep returning to the vintages. So I tell myself: "Jawash, jawash". Slow down. No perfume from the last few years has touched and excited me as much as, for example, Ysatis, Mitsouko, or Parure, to name just a few. And yet I continue to test. Isn't that actually crazy? I always look forward to new perfumes, even though the old ones have already offered everything that is possible. Isn't that absolutely paradoxical? But I also keep discovering new music and enjoying it, even though I have my favorite bands and composers. However, if I had to name just one opera that I want to see again before I die, one single composer, one single feast, or one single novel - I would know what I would answer! Ultimately, it is the same with perfume. There are only a few that I would take with me to a deserted island. And if I had to choose just one? No, Ysatis would not be my "one and only perfume," but it would be among my top 10. Folks, I'm done for today!

A very nice spicy and above all very peppery oriental. The raspberry, so delicious in the edt, has completely disappeared for me here. All that remains is an amber/spices/wood trio. Personally, I prefer the edt with more raspberry but Hot Couture edp nevertheless remains a very pretty perfume for those who like orientals and spices in perfumery. For my part I don't smell any tobacco here. It won't please everyone, so try it!

Big names like Alberto Morillas and Jacques Cavalier Belletrud are responsible for this fragrance composition released in 2000: “Hot Couture” (as Eau de Parfum) from the house of Givenchy. Curiosity grows, as so much comes together here that promises pleasure. A true wave of syrupy fruity aromas of ripe, sweet raspberries, bergamots, and oranges comes towards me, interwoven and cooled by a rather generous dose of black pepper, which makes my sensitive nose itch and signals “Caution!” Magnolia with its delicate scent and familiar white-pink porcelain outfit greets me only briefly before vetiver builds a bridge from this rather sparse heart note to the base of creamy sandalwood with its usual fine animalic notes, cuddly musk, and amber. “Hot Couture” disappoints me, standing in the shadow of what once was and has only hesitantly taken the step into the 2000s. I am dissatisfied with myself because my skin is so uncooperative and simply refuses the impressions described here! Despite several tests, nothing changes; I just don’t dare to over-apply because of the pepper. But does the dose really make the fragrance in “Hot Couture,” or is it the bottling, is it too old, too weak? So Givenchy and I once again fail to live in harmony with each other. I don’t know whose fault it is, but I believe I will also give up hope for coexistence with this brand. It’s just like with the “Princess and the Pea”: They couldn’t come together! But still: What a shame, very shame!

Back to 2000. Everything was easy, the world, life, the new language. No worries, young, impulsive, wonderful. Tout était formidable. During my time in Paris, I was filled with a feeling that fluctuated between coolness and sexiness. It must be said that I snagged the most legendary jeans of all time at Mango in Paris, striking and not too stretchy with a golden M on the backside. I can only say très chic and très sexy. Who needs HAUT couture when you can get it HOT? So, on Rue de Rivoli, besides that significant Mango shop, was my favorite café, where I loved to enjoy my café au lait after a shopping spree, devouring a tiny raspberry tart and amusing myself with the tourists and their astonished eyes. From Chinese to Arabs, South Americans and North Americans, all nations were present, but many countries from all over Europe also paid their respects to the French capital. Who can blame anyone for visiting the city of love? No one. Not even me, who settled there after buying a one-way ticket from Chur to Paris and hastily quitting my job in Switzerland. After all, true love doesn’t wait for you every day, does it? Oui bébé, je t'aime à la foli et a l'infini. Hot Couture reminds me of exactly this beautiful life, the wow-life with the raspberry cherry on top, which showcases the sunny side of life in all its splendor, the sweet lightness on one hand and the opulence of heaviness on the other, with a slightly smoky and woody touch and hints of a chocolatey undertone that captivates with a spicy whisper. Edith Piaf would indeed describe it like this: Des yeux qui font baisser les miens Un rire qui se perd sur sa bouche Voilà le portrait sans retouches De l'homme auquel j'appartiens Quand il me prend dans ses bras Qu'il me parle tout bas Je vois la vie en rose Il me dit des mots d'amour....... I have smelled, tasted, touched, explored, kissed, sung, captured, learned, and enriched the moments in my heart into a sea of poetry.

I fall into the small category of lucky people with Jo Malone, my skin for some strange reason retains its scents and I can't complain about the longevity. That said, I tried Orange Mamalade as soon as it came out and I ended up buying it. Driven by an adorable campaign featuring Paddington Bear I ran to smell it. What I found is a marmalade made with bitter orange and very little sugar. I liked the linearity and simplicity of this perfume that manages to be both carefree and cheerful as well as adult and refined. When I want something more gourmand during wintertime, I layer it with the vanilla from Comptoir Sud Pacifique and the result is wonderful. Too bad it was a limited edition, I will hold on to my 30 ml.

Before I get into the scent I just gotta say, I love Paddington. I was either gonna love this fragrance or be deeply disappointed by it. I'm glad to report it ended up the former. That said, if you've never actually made marmalade from scratch, you're gonna be confused and probably a little upset at the smell here- "why is it bitter?!" is a question I've seen repeated several times on other reviews of this fragrance. It's a gourmand, for sure, and it's bright and cheerful (like the iconic little bear himself)- but it isn't the "candied orange" a lot of people were expecting from this one. It's also weirdly long-lasting for a Jo Malone fragrance so it's a bit of a 50/50 on whether you can switch to a different perfume later in the day, but I like this one enough that it isn't an issue.

Over the weekend, I had the opportunity to test Orange Marmalade at Jo Malone. It was an exciting journey. At first, the fragrance opens with a very bright orange, but not overly sweet, rather fresh with notes of refreshing citrus fruits. After a while, you sense a certain bitterness, not a rich orange, but something calmer that reminded me of grapefruit. For a long time, I couldn't figure out what the hint reminded me of; it was something very familiar. On Sunday evening at the bar, I ordered an Aperol, and it was a 100% hit. What my nose felt was very similar to what my tongue experienced. It was a cool introduction to Jo Malone; I really like this refreshingly bright orange with bitterness. A very good fragrance for everyday wear, for a democratic party. The scent has a medium sillage, like everything from Jo Malone. I invite everyone to get to know Orange Marmalade.

"Orange Peel" by Jo Malone is a feel-good fragrance like no other. And that in summer as well as during the Christmas season, when mandarins and citrus scents are also in high demand. Jo Malone represents in my mind subtle, high-quality, fruity, often rather feminine fragrance artistry. But also understatement and naturalness. And "Orange Peel" is undoubtedly one of the juiciest and most delicious perfumes of the brand. Nearly at Atelier Cologne level - and they are the kings of the citrus category. It doesn't get much better than this. Natural, invigorating, true to life, and simply delightful to bathe in. It can't cause any unpleasant reactions, and it's hard to overdo it. Not only the peel, but also a lot of the rest of the fruit. Partially green (rhubarb?), very ripe, super soft, and making your mouth water. Or the other way around. You know what I mean. This scent makes me all giddy and high. I don't want to write anymore, just want to enjoy. A citric highlight. Creamy and jammy. Bottle: unobtrusively beautiful Sillage: delicate, hissing, citrusy Longevity: 6 hours - solid. Even more than that for Jo Malone standards. Conclusion: an incredibly invigorating and delicious scent of orange peels, clean skin, and summer warmth. A carefree soul brightener and a hit in my book. It tickled so nicely in my nasal cavity.

...imagine this, you are suited and booted, going to a night club in France, but you wear a black suit, black tie, black leather boots. You are sharp as a human being can be. Mysterious personality, but there is a playful side that can easily charm, and hypnotize a lady. This is some very odd stuff, and it does smell excellent at the same time. Its like a middle eastern mystery unravelling in front of your nose. It hits you from a lot of angles. true niche stuff here in fact, this has a semi-animalic orange blossom and honey, and the incense hits you right away, next to the green angelica. This is dark, it requires a black suit and a black tie for sure, no doubt. Oud along with the amber gives you a dark, resinous base...man this just takes over you i swear. Its massive, almost gives me the feeling of when i first smelled Amouage's Interlude Man, or Chanel's Le Lion. If this was an image, imagine Tisci's rottweiler for Givenchy.

I am making a concerted effort to test, review and buy (if necessary) all the perfumes in the Givenchy La Collection Particuliére. Though not explicitly stated, this series appears to be a collaboration between Givenchy and the perfumers and products of Firmenich. La Collection Particuliére highlights many of the ingredients that are patented products from Firmenich. This review of Faux Semblant is based on a 10 ml sample I bought directly from Givenchy. The name Faux Semblant means false pretenses, though there are not many false pretenses in this perfume. Dora Baghriche has created essentially an incense smell with some ancillary notes to embellish this primary characteristic. Its intensity gets the highest rating on Givenchy’s website. The opening is a very strong duo of angelica and frankincense, obviously enhanced by Firmenich’s production techniques. The green vibe of angelica subsides quickly but a unique amber and honey accord takes its space. These opening notes persist for quite a while before an unremarkable orange blossom, listed as the heart note, comes on the scene. But this orange blossom is incapable of changing the incense personality of Faux Semblant. The base notes are a very lovely blend of sandalwood and oud, perceptible but again not strong enough to subdue the incense. Towards the end, the incense note becomes creamier because of the woody notes. Though many of the La Collection Particuliére perfumes list oud as a note, it is usually very mild and not worth mentioning. The overall sweet incense personality of Faux Semblant is a double-edged sword. The blend of angelica, honeyed-amber, incense and sandalwood also makes it veer towards the cheap incense sticks that I find in India. Because of this concern, adequate repeated testing is warranted. I wonder if I would get tired of it quickly, thus negating the need for a full bottle. As it stands, I am not planning to get a full bottle. I might even give away the 10 ml bottle. Faux Semblant is a high-performance perfume. The opening notes hang around for about 4-6 hours and the later woody notes for another four hours. The sillage is very good, particularly in the early incense phase of this perfume. I cannot recommend it as an office perfume because of its overwhelming incense note. In summary, Faux Semblant is a lovely incense perfume, demonstrating the might of Firmenich’s manufacturing processes. It is one of the costlier perfumes ($420 for 100 ml) in the La Collection Particuliére. Whether you would fork over that fortune depends on your love for incense.

I went to the neighbor's garden fence yesterday to pick a few young nettles. After all, I wanted to have a comparison to 'Nettle & Wild Achillea'. I couldn't find any yarrow in my immediate surroundings. However, I can confirm that 'Nettle & Wild Achillea' really comes close to the scent of nettle. There’s also a bit of bergamot present at the start. However, the citrus fruit doesn't stand a chance against the green notes, and then a rather intense musk note comes in as well. What slightly confuses me after about an hour is a delicate hint of lavender (not listed in the pyramid), which remains detectable for about two hours. After that, 'Nettle & Wild Achillea' is a green, softly musk-tinged spring fragrance. The scent can be worn for many occasions. The projection is rather subtle, and the longevity is a decent seven hours. I thank Mörderbiene for the sample.

Velvet pouch, you beautiful, thickly padded one, you release him with a gentle tug, the small, tiny gold blue jewel made of metal and glass………with 7.5ml of golden dream water. The mothership in large, with 15ml content, is no less jewel-like, representing an oversized ring with a blue gemstone, also made of glass and sturdy metal. Back then, value was still taken into account, both bottles are refillable. Both are exactly the right packaging for the precious drop. The fragrance pyramid is extremely diverse, only outlined here. Green, viscous opening. Asant, the thick juice of a galbanum species, is surrounded by floral nectar and very gentle, here more restrained, apricots and honey-soft broom. The pure perfume reveals itself in its full splendor as a true chypre, yet by no means too harsh. The longer it remains on warm skin, the warmer it becomes. I don’t find it sweet on me; the EdP is rather sweeter, more apricot-like. It increasingly showcases more and more rich nectars of divinely fragrant flowers, always maintaining the connection to the resin and also to a slight dose of oakmoss. The heart, as already described in my review of the EdP, is the true amber. Through it, the fragrance gains the stature that makes it special. The longevity can be measured in eternities when it comes to amber. Deep, sensual warmth. The scent can be briefly described in one word: WOW. It is a rather dark fragrance. Mystical. Enveloping, warm. A milestone of the French perfumery art of that time.

I was looking for something white-floral, summery, with piney notes for the hot spring/summer. I sniffed and smelled a lot of scents in the shop (even though I already have a good collection). null of them suited me, but I didn't want to leave without a gift for a 10th marriage Ann. And then, on the top shelf, i found it. My husband says "this one". But I spent another hour going from Versence to my beloved Hermes - all was wrong. The salesgirl helped me to decide. She said that there's a 30% discount on Givenchy. So we got this one. And what do you think?! I, who in all my 50 years had not put out even full 30 ml. bottle, because either bored or spoiled (yes, it happend), just fell in love and disappeared). Apple. Sugary but not too sweet. Fresh, but not sour, as if the red-yellow fruit was cut and sprinkled with sugar, the scent and flavour opened up from this. Very natural. There are apple lollipops next to it; if the fruit is too sour, you can snack on it. Not loud, but clear, tasty, but not confectionary. Either not persistent or I just stop hearing it. As a result, I ordered a second bottle in a few weeks, this has never happened to me, although I know Givenchy for a long time and love it. I can't find any analogues. Universal, in office and on dating, in spring/summer, not stuffy, unusual, unconventional. 10/10 scent, 6/10 longivety. Sorry for the inaccuracies, translation is automatic.

It looks enticing with its bright red shell, so crisp and yet surprisingly fruity. Just one bite: the shiny red sweet shell bursts quietly with a crackle and reveals the white innocence of the apple hidden beneath. What have angels and devils concocted here in new harmony, while strolling through the summer garden scented with jasmine and roses, leisurely sipping a cup of green tea? What secret does this fragrant candied apple hold, and what do the two have in mind? I can clearly hear them giggling: Which Eve do they want to lead astray this time? It must be something seductive they have devised; for sensual fragrance notes now permeate the scene: Patchouli and musk entice with a warmth intertwined with light eroticism, while amber adds fine beacons of light. “Ange ou Démon Le Secret” as Eau de Toilette is very light and delicate, harmoniously adapting and serving very well as a daytime fragrance that does not intrude but subtly, almost elegantly underscores the personality. Anyone looking for similarities with the original fragrance “Ange ou Démon” from 2006 will be disappointed: apart from the name, all three fragrances I tested - including the Eau de Parfum of “Le Secret” - have nothing in common. This fragrance creation and its sister deserve their own names; each a standalone creation: crafted with feeling, polite and fine, flattering and unobtrusive. Only what they have to do with angels and devils unfortunately eludes me! This original composition, so contradictory in itself, has impressed me too much for that. Therefore, my conclusion is: A charming little fragrance full of graceful lightness, but without the edges and corners that create a recognizable identity. Bon Voyage, Chérie!

Our family is characterized by a passion for collecting. For my parents and me, it’s fragrances - for my grandfather, it’s wines. Of course - he is half-French and a true hedonist. Although I never became a "wine connoisseur," I always enjoyed attending his tastings. When he savored a particularly good wine, the connoisseur in him would exclaim with a vivid description: As if a little angel is peeing on your tongue! This phrase doesn’t seem to be vulgar among wine drinkers, and it came to mind again today as I sampled Le Secret. I expected something along the lines of the original Ange ou Demon EDP, which I like for its marzipan note, but Le Secret is heavenly beautiful in a different way. The little angel approaches with a shiny candied apple, sweet yet crisp and fruity. Mmm - delicious! In addition, it offers a deep red, velvety rose - a gallant gesture. You sit under a lushly blooming jasmine bush, bite into the apple, and sniff the rose. A picture straight out of a poetry album. The caring little angel also serves a cup of bitter, steaming Earl Grey, which intriguingly blends with the other aromas. Gently, patchouli lays over it, emphasizing the mild bitterness of the tea. If a wine tastes as delicious as this fragrance smells, I can understand my grandfather's bold statement. Which also hits the nail on the head. Here too, the demon is absent, as only little angels dance around my nose. A company that I greatly enjoy.

The top note is an apple :) Not red, definitely not green, no - it’s a yellow and clearly candied apple. Fortunately, it’s not too sweet. This fragrance got me with the heart note. I smell tea, green tea, and usually that’s where it ends for me, as it often comes across as quite bitter and overwhelming. But here I find something in a direction that’s unfamiliar to me. Probably because rose and jasmine - very familiar to me - are included. The base remains subtle, just like the fragrance itself, but very delicious. I like the shape and style of the bottle. The upper part of the cap is made of plastic and feels cheap, which is a pity. Overall, however, it is coherent. It’s a fragrance that has something. It’s not the sillage, which is not outstanding. But it’s not bad either, as I can gather from the compliments I’ve received for this scent. Still, it has lured me in, even though I usually gravitate towards fragrances with a lot of sillage. The longevity is very good for an EdT. Is it due to the very warm late summer weather? Or is it the elegantly balanced dosage of the individual notes? Or perhaps the beautiful scent progression? Conclusion: I can say a lot of good things about Ange ou Demon le Secret EdT. For me, it has the familiar Givenchy quality and I’m glad to have it in my collection :) Unfortunately, I don’t know the other Ange ou Demons and therefore cannot contribute to a comparison. So, now I’m taking it with me on a late summer outing and will compare how it performs in the autumn :)

Something that always seems much more beautiful in the imagination - like on a rainy Tuesday morning in the office - is a picnic in the green. Certainly - when Mario Testino photographs the English royal family - with crystal and silver candlesticks, and in the background, dogs whose lineage can be traced back to William the Conqueror - everything looks so simple and tasteful. In reality, sitting on the ground becomes uncomfortable after no more than half an hour if you are older than eighteen, there is never a corkscrew available, but there are ants - and no dogs, only their droppings at most. Despite all that - despite paper plates and plastic forks, despite the ant invasion and cold meatballs - the picnic in the green still has something enchanted about it. When it takes place at ground level - wooden benches at highway rest stops do not count - when you lie in the grass and only the sky is above you, then it is a moment of great beauty. When you suddenly see coltsfoot up close for the first time with your face right down on the ground - and realize that four-leaf clover is indeed not easy to find. When you discover that sorrel actually tastes sour - and lemon thyme tastes like thyme and lemon. And everything else doesn't matter. It is a pity that Jo Malone's Herb Garden was only sold for a single short summer. All her herbal scents - there were five in total - tell of simple, rural green - of a green that never seemed special and precisely for that reason can bring happiness. Sorrel & Lemon Thyme and its herb-fresh greenness, reminiscent of sun-warmed grass and tickling blades, are wonderful in their calmness. There is the bitter freshness of crushed blades, dry earth bleached by the summer sun. There is a hint of clover and lemon and a diffuse earthiness. There are ants and meatballs and sheep clouds. Delightful. Conclusion, in the opening lines of Annette von Droste-Hülshoff's poem 'In the Grass': 'Sweet rest', sweet daze in the grass, surrounded by the aroma of the herb. Deep tide, deeply deeply drunken tide, when the clouds fade in the azure. When sweet laughter flutters down upon the weary, floating head. A loving voice whispers and drips like the linden blossom on a grave.'

I have to test this scent, I knew that from the very beginning. While I generally have a fondness for citrus fragrances, the scent of fresh lemon thyme is one of my absolute favorite scents in the world. So I thought, if I can smell like that too, then I can't pass it up. :D Nevertheless, this cologne from Jo Malone ultimately surprised me. The bottle is elegant, simple, and refined, as one expects from the brand. In contrast to the scents in the standard range, it is presented in a delicate green tone with a plant print that looks as if one of the herbs is actually in the bottle or reminds one of the annoying herbarium from school days. It is beautiful and perfectly underscores the theme - wonderful! But let's get to the scent. At first, it indeed starts with the note of a sweet-sour lemon drop or fresh homemade lemonade. Not artificial, but packed with power. I sniff, I sniff again, and I could become addicted to it. This is how I want to smell forever! However, as quickly as this note appears, it sadly disappears again, leaving only a very delicate citrus hint that gradually blends with the thyme. And there it is, this delicate, slightly fresh, and already somewhat warm herb garden on my skin. It is pleasant, doesn't overwhelm you, and feels smooth as if one were lingering in the garden on a not-too-warm summer morning. But then it comes, the strong midday sun, and it completely drives away the lemon. What remains is primarily the thyme, herbal, bitter, and surprisingly intense, as if one had just rubbed it between their fingers, and it stays that way until the scent ultimately fades away. I have rarely experienced such an extreme turn in a fragrance. The beginning is, in my opinion, too sweet for a men's scent, the end certainly too bitter for many women. It is therefore very special, but this seems to suit me, and so it will surely accompany me on many days in the summer and gently waft around me, with a longevity that is average for Jo Malone.

Jo Malone has very distinctive fragrance creations. So too 'Carrot Blossom & Fennel'. I am not familiar with the scent of carrot blossom, even though I grew up in the countryside and also grew a lot of vegetables myself; the carrots, or 'Goibe Ruam' as we say in our dialect, must never bloom, as the root then does not taste particularly good. 'C B & F' starts off very fresh and green. The freshness lasts barely a few minutes before it becomes more soft-green. However, I cannot claim that the green smells like fennel. After about an hour, the scent of a rose gradually emerges, bringing with it a slight sweetness. The rose is actually the dominant part of the fragrance, not too intense and quite natural. The rose is rounded off by an iris note, which gently fades the scent away. 'C B & F' is for me rather a feminine fragrance, versatile to wear in spring and autumn. The projection is relatively weak, and the longevity is just under five hours. I thank Mörderbiene for the sample.

Carrot Blossom & Fennel surprised me greatly with its revelation: on me, it is a rose in honey. I don't like honey, but this one smells so delicious, soft, gentle, and not at all bitter! It makes you want to taste it right away. The violets bring a spicy powderiness that definitely does not smell like drugstore powder! This powdery note sounds like gentle pollen from honey flowers. The mugwort is not bitter, but rather faded like the summer sun, spicy and languid, in a duet with ripe apricot flesh. Normally, I get tired of bitter scents - but this one is not like that at all! All in all, it is just a light hint of summer flowers and fruits. The remaining notes are so far just a background. The musk is also inconspicuous, shy, sometimes appearing and then modestly retreating into the background. This fragrance has truly fascinated me. It has been a long time since a scent has sparked such interest in me.

So it goes in a church song - one of those newer ones that emerged in the post-war period - about the unwavering love of dear God for his sheep. And although I am not religious (and thus not a practiced, let alone passionate church singer), I have always liked the simple and clear language of 'Lord, your love is like grass and shore' (that’s the title of this song). Even and especially for lovers of highly complex, sometimes downright challenging perfumes, it is sometimes the simple and clear (scent) language, the scent of grass and shore, that is like wind and expanse - that feels like a home for a moment. Jo Malone's Herb Garden collection employs this language, and Carrot Blossom & Fennel - namely the scent of carrot blossom and fennel - is pleasantly calm and grounded in its simplicity and green freshness. Vegetable- (or vegetable-connoted) notes like carrot blossom often seem a bit foreign in the context of perfumes. And fennel, which is essentially reminiscent of anise, is one of those polarizing ingredients that you either like or you don’t. All the more fascinating and convincing are the down-to-earth simplicity and yet the unusual and pointedness that Jo Malone hides in this herbaceous-green scent, which is neither a diva nor a show-off - and yet is steadfast in character and beautiful. Conclusion: a scent full of green-golden warmth and Protestant pinewood circle-ness. 'Nice to have you here. You are something very special.'

Hello everyone, here we have a fragrance that exaggerates, caricatures, and perverts all the innovations of the 1990s. We have: zesty bitter orange, seasoned with ginger, resulting in smoky cigarette smoke. As the fruity notes fade away, the cigarette smoke remains, and both the most kitschy orange blossom and bubblegum-popping tuberose emerge. This blend is loud, intrusive, and fits either in a smoky bar or on the Reeperbahn at half-past two in the morning. With the service providers, mind you. After what feels like hours, the scent flattens out and makes way for a mild, soft base of almond milk and vanilla. From here, L'Interdit Édition Millésime is indeed bearable, but still far from being a good fragrance. The longevity of this olfactory torture is too long at any point, the sillage screaming and intrusive. Conclusion: No recommendation from me.

Since there is no comment on this perfume yet, I'll give it a try. In contrast to CK Free, which starts with a rather strong anise and absinthe and gives a slightly medicinal impression, CK Free blue begins with a much more pleasant citrus note for me. Although mandarin is listed at the top of the pyramid, I also perceive a hint of pineapple mixed with a mint note. This freshness lasts on my skin for a maximum of 20-30 minutes, which is relatively weak. After that, the perfume develops a slightly spicy and aquatic note. Overall, the perfume gives a relatively sweet impression, and I would classify it more as a unisex sport fragrance. The longevity is honestly not that great. It fades relatively quickly, and after one or two hours, you really have to hold your nose directly to the spot where you sprayed it to smell anything. As I said, I find CK Free blue better than CK Free. However, the scent is nothing special or unique.

ah, it opens not only the nose but also the heart. A rounded fragrance, excellently composed, all scent notes come to the fore equally. I don't notice anything from the ginger I have already fallen in love with Eternity 2008 Thank you ET! In short: floral, spicy, strong, pleasant, typically CK and softly creamy underneath

In general, I like all the Eternity Summer editions. The summer variants differ from each other. While I often received compliments for earlier editions, this one has gone unnoticed by my surroundings because it doesn't stand out at all. But that doesn't matter at all, because I love the scent. I belong to those women who love delicate fragrances. For example, the scent of fabric softener on freshly washed laundry, the smell of flowers in the garden, the fragrance used in care products, etc. So, if someone is looking for a perfume that shouldn't come across as such, Eternity Summer 2008 is the perfect choice. It smells similar to classic Nivea products - as if you've just applied lotion. Even people like me who enjoy the scents of baby care products will find this fragrance satisfying. However, here, they use balm instead of chamomile - so it’s a bit more grown-up. Of the listed fragrance notes, a lot of lily of the valley, a bit of jasmine, very little ginger, and very subtle musk can be perceived. Since it is essentially a "care fragrance," it is suitable for everyone. It is age- and almost gender-independent and has good longevity.

As autumn approaches, it's time for heavier fragrances again, and this new premium Givenchy surely belongs to the select circle of new candidates. "Patchouli de Minuit" offers a decidedly confident, consistently comforting aroma potpourri, which places elements of bitter chocolate, cigar box, and a hint of earth around the central patchouli. Overall, it skillfully brushes against something gourmand, ensuring that accessibility is never in question, although the Givenchy undoubtedly possesses a lot of volume and intensity. I perceive incense and lavender only subtly, perhaps as accents for spiciness. Tonka and cashmeran envelop the earthy-chocolatey patchouli in a creamy, juicy-woody manner, fortunately rather defensively. Long-lasting, balanced, dense.

Sometimes you have the luck to stumble upon a truly special scent purely by chance. It meets all requirements, triggers all receptors, and sparks a mental movie. Occasionally, a fragrance also feels like an experience - both unknown and familiar at the same time. Let’s call it a little masterpiece of sensory impressions. Even rarer, however, is when all of this is combined with feelings. Such as well-being, melancholy, euphoria. Equally rare is a fragrance that radiates its own unique eroticism. One that you want to wear and spray at the same time. Yes, you even feel a bit sexier with it than without. So sought after and yet almost never achieved is the blend of all this. A fragrance that you perceive and that gives you everything you long for in that moment. A scent that I can manipulate - and it can manipulate me. It exudes well-being when I need it - and when it should. It gives me melancholy when I want it - and when it should. It even waits in all its splendor to radiate both at the same time. A yin and yang fragrance experience, so to speak... And especially in those moments, it shines in all colors, black. I’m glad I was able to have this last, incredibly rare fragrance experience and can continue to have it again and again from now on. For all those who prefer it factual: A lot of fantastic dark, earthy, and rough patchouli plays the leading role. Just the right unsweet lavender gives the scent a somewhat esoteric touch. Cashmeran supports the patchouli in its roughness but stays in the background. The same goes for the dirty-beautiful davana and the incense that wafts through repeatedly. However, the creamy-bitter sweet tonka bean makes the fragrance, in this composition, fully what it is. A dark, erotic, smoky-esoteric patchouli scent that, for me, clearly already plays in the personal top league of patchouli fragrances.

Like pencil shavings after finishing a large-format sketch. Like a cold sauna in an abandoned hotel in Iceland and I know where the switch is. Like a hot attic, in the beam of sunlight, just before the big find. Like twig cracking and dry needle rustling and I can already hear the sea. Like secretly hugging trees, cracked bark, amber-colored tears. Like me, a hammock, and a book. Like the piece of cedar wood that I placed between the laundry to ward off moths. Like steam rising over boiling a vanilla pod in the holiday home. Like freshly cut wood, comforting on this lonely, continuous rainy day. Like the resinous seal of a love letter that I still hold onto while sitting in the sand. Like a brown-red-yellow woven Inca blanket. Like the sunlit wooden plank steps on a hot breezy porch. Like.

The perfumer Dominique Ropion has created this limited version of L'Interdit for the LVMH group. He is known for his seductive and sensual fragrance compositions such as La Vie Est Belle, Alien, Addict, or Black Opium. L'Interdit Angélique Rouge is characterized by its floral notes (particularly angelica). It is a versatile fragrance that can be worn well in the evening or on special occasions due to its warm and sensual notes. The perfume also handles many everyday situations well, especially when one wants to emphasize elegance and modernity. Floral and spicy fragrance notes also make it a good companion for the cooler months. L'Interdit Angélique Rouge by Givenchy is not this sweet "hit-you-over-the-head" candidate that recklessly throws around sweet notes. The fragrance creation presents itself as more complex and with a good dose of sensuality. In the opening, fresh and zesty notes shape the scent. After that, floral (angelica) and spicy notes come into play. Here, the character of the fragrance emerges with a beautiful depth. In the base, warm, woody notes dominate. The scent is not made for the long haul, but it remains perceptible close to the skin for a long time. So, if you feel like sniffing at the forbidden, here is an opportunity.

I thought during today's sniffing, this reminds me of something in my house... Aah now it dawns on me, one of my favorite candles from Ava & May. Those who are occasionally on Insta surely know the candles that are supposed to smell like the country or city written on them. In this case, this little treasure here smells 1:1 like the candle "Persia". Mainly Neroli and Fig. And it will be the Fig that reminds me of it, because otherwise there aren't many notes from the candle present. There was also a corresponding perfume created by the candle brand for the mentioned candle "Persia", but I was unfortunately very disappointed by that. This one here is so special that I'm seriously considering whether I want to smell like my living room... Really nice and very special!
