Admittedly, I almost ordered this fragrance blindly because it seemed to combine two of my absolute favorite scents, Angélique Noire and "L'Interdit (Eau de Parfum Rouge) | Givenchy." But those who fly high, fall hard - and unfortunately, that was also the case with my expectations vs reality. The top note of L'Interdit Angélique Rouge strongly reminds me of the EdP. I don't know what prickly pear smells like, but to me, it smells like a very dominant pear. Very, very faintly, I get a bit of ginger, which rather amplifies the fruitiness; the spiciness of the angelica seeds is completely unnoticeable to me. How can that be, when it is the namesake of this flanker? After 10 minutes, it becomes more floral and sweeter, the tuberose hits hard. Unfortunately, it’s the kind of tuberose that does not charmingly seduce, wink, and giggle, but rather a shrill, loud screamer. I am reminded of one of the Scandal series, it could be "Scandal by Night | Jean Paul Gaultier," which I associate with a very similar dominant tuberose. As it progresses, finally some herbal, balsamic note comes in, similar to an essential oil, which clears the nose nicely and takes the loud sweetness down a notch (really just a notch). A large portion of angelica (seed or root, it doesn't matter) would have worked so well here!! But the angelica seems to only be a namesake on paper. I think the herbal note in the base is simply the vetiver-patchouli mix, which is somehow trying to capture the full force of the white florals. With moderate success, the tuberose and a somewhat prickly, synthetic note remain until the end, when the fragrance becomes very close to the skin after 4 hours. Hmm, I really had high hopes and am a bit disappointed. The similarity to L'Interdit Eau de Parfum Rouge is absolutely unclear to me; in my opinion, it is definitely closer to the classic l’interdit edp or edt. Bright and radiant, perhaps a bit shrill, and the handful of angelica doesn’t help anymore. The Rouge, on the other hand, is so much softer, richer, warmer, and has a vanilla patchouli base that is simply to die for. So as a flanker to the EdP, this one can hold its own, but you really don’t get much new. Nevertheless, it’s definitely worth a test because the l’interdits are generally well made, and noses are known to work differently!

It opens with an scent not very promising, but it improves a bit when the heart accords show up and finish with an spectacular drydown, that patchouli mixed with tonka is damn good. Still I rate just 5, I don´t think that a good drydown only qualifies for a good grade. It´s a pity this opening. This fragrance is the exact opposite of Lanvin Èclat d´Arpège pour Homme that has an amazing opening and then slip through the cracks. A mix of the good qualities of these two would be incredible.

Orange blossom and jasmine are among my favorite scents. For the office, I was looking for a light, everyday-appropriate, and unobtrusive version of that and found it in Dahlia Divin Eau de Parfum Nude. I think this is a fragrance that no one can be bothered by. The powdery scent feels very elegant.

I already own several dahlias of various kinds - and I wouldn't want to miss any of them. Should Nude be added to the bouquet? I think so, because this dahlia is sweet and smooth in a soft, enchanting way. I don't perceive this scent as "nude," as I already feel attractively dressed by it. It's like slipping into a nude-colored silk dress that barely covers the body. In a subtly erotic way, as the fragrance only hints at the allure. The apricot appears gently through a sunny veil of orange blossom. The jasmine brings the scent to light without overshadowing it - and musk adds the silky sheen. Unobtrusively feminine. My husband moves dangerously close to me and nods in approval. But since the "forbidden flowers," he has been very fond of Givenchy anyway. While Nude is not quite as seductive, it is also in a playful flirty mood. A scent for romantic summer evenings for two.

For me this is the worst from the new LAVENDERLAND line by jo Malone London, but It is still nice. I can find two different stages un this perfume... First of all the opening, for me the worst part of the perfume. It is too harsh for me, a bit weird due to the mix between the lavender and the Sage, a bit medicinal and dirty... But then It becomes much sweeter and nice, with a nice mix between lavender and tonka (like a much lighter versión of myrrh & tonka) and with the spicy and Green vibe of coriander. Probably the most classic of the three fragances, It makes me think a bit of the classical colognes like 4117 or Aqua di parma. Unisex for a daily use during the everyday activities. Better for warm weather. Fresh & spicy. Scent: 6.5 Longevity: 6.5 Sillage: 5 Quality/price: 5 Versatility: 7.5 Originality: 5 Global: 6.5

The large bouquet of lavender, tied with a loosely braided ribbon of coriander and sage, lies on the garden table. The rising sun slowly warms the cool morning air. It draws out the intense fragrance from the flowers. The herbs give the scent bundle support and character. Now and then, a hint of tonka sweetness wafts over. It briefly captures attention time and again. In the midday sun, the fresh morning scent bids farewell. A faint memory lingers until late afternoon.

A few days ago, I was standing in the subway in the morning. Next to me was a woman in her mid-fifties, dressed from head to toe in a matte, slightly grayish beige - about the color of tripe or - a bit more kindly - calf liverwurst. She had long, matte gray-blonde hair and was rummaging quite a while and desperately in her large shoulder bag. I bet you can see her in front of you - can you? Do you see her? You're mistaken - I bet you are! Because if you looked at the woman more than just fleetingly, you would see that she was wearing a wonderful long skirt made of soft cotton - gray-beige, so what? - paired with a slim top and a very fine cardigan with small mother-of-pearl buttons. She wore flat Roman sandals wrapped around her ankles, and her bag was a Bayswater from Mulberry made of beautifully patinated, soft leather. One tends - and I include myself in this - to believe that after a first - often only very fleeting glance (or sniff) one knows everything there is to know. About world events. About people. About perfumes. Lavender is one of those fragrance notes that really only allows for two associations: Provençal country life or old people. And once again, you are mistaken. And so am I. Lavender & Coriander is the last of the five herb garden scents that Jo Malone released last year that I am commenting on - and the quietest and most serious among the five. At first sniff, one might think: Lavender, got it. A soft, gray-beige brown scent. A bit austere. Liverwurst-colored. And only upon closer sniffing does one notice its fine, lyrical timbre and the underlying bitterness that coriander and sage can add to the lavender. There is also a restrained, almost matte sweetness of tonka bean that leads to a calm yet by no means boring scent - like an almost forgotten spot way back in the garden, where unexpectedly a blackbird is nesting in a tree. Conclusion: she had a serious and intelligent face - not classically beautiful, probably never was - and when I let her go ahead of me as she boarded the subway, she briefly smiled a charming, warm smile. And a very fine hint of lavender followed her. And I smiled briefly too.

I actually find the Herb Garden Collection by Jo Malone quite nicely done. There are some really pleasant scents among them, making you want to test more. This brings me to Lavender & Coriander, which makes me ponder for a long time whether I should even let it touch my skin. Those who know me can recognize the reason just from the name of the scent: coriander. One of the fragrance notes that I absolutely cannot stand, and this note only doesn’t bother me in fragrances where it comes across very weakly or is mostly covered by other scents. However, if it is strong, then *ugh ugh ugh* Well, lavender on the other hand sounds quite nice as always. Let’s see how the scent is when I face one of my enemies again… The scent: Huh? Where is the top note? Where is the coriander? Have I scared my enemy away so much (with my evil glare) that he has evaporated? Well, that suits me fine. Because the scent starts with a herbaceous lavender. You can clearly smell the sage alongside the lavender, which smells authentic, and which I find pleasant compared to coriander. A little later, you still smell the lavender, this time mixed with sweet notes. The herbaceous aspect is still there, but over time it recedes further into the background. In the end, lavender is the strongest note. The tonka bean, which emits the sweet scent, can be smelled well, but it’s not that strong. The sillage and longevity: Unfortunately, the scent is not very strong. At first, it can be perceived well, but that’s the case with most fragrances. After just 10-15 minutes, however, it loses strength and remains in the average range, meaning that you can smell the scent up close, but it doesn’t leave a scent trail behind. The longevity is a bit weak and lasts about four to five hours on the skin. The bottle: The bottle is green, slim, and tall. It has a transparent label with the name of the scent on it and is adorned with leaf motifs. The cap is also green and cylindrical. Overall, a beautiful bottle. Although Lavender & Coriander is not an extraordinary scent, I still find it pleasant and well-suited for spring and summer. It is fresh, herbaceous, and slightly sweet, making it suitable for daily wear. What I personally appreciate is that the coriander seems to be a sort of "misprint" in the scent name, as I couldn’t perceive the coriander at all, even though I can smell that dreadful note from 10 kilometers away (to make a timely escape…). What remains is a lovely lavender scent, not extraordinarily outstanding, but also not bad, which is definitely worth testing.

Temeraire is member of the La Collection Particuliere from Givenchy. I bought the 10 ml travel size with the intention of upgrading to a full bottle if the perfume is worth it. I am an ardent fan of La Collection Particuliere, as all the perfumes in this group range from very nice to great. La Collection Particuliere uses perfumers associated with Firmenich and contains many ingredients proprietary to Firmenich. Nicolas Bonneville is the perfumer behind Temeraire. Temeraire is a very nice perfume, but it is not one of the great ones from La Collection Particuliere. It is essentially an elegant tuberose on strands of spicy and woody accords running through it. The listed opening notes are cardamom and clove leaf, but these are not very perceptible to my nose. For me, Temeraire starts with a strong tuberose accord. This accord continues into the heart notes and into the bottom notes. I don’t smell the iris as a major note in the middle, though this note may be there as a subtle embellishment for the tuberose. The cedar and vetiver in the bottom notes also are too subtle for me to pick out, though they do exist as a woody memory. From top to bottom, Temeraire is a strong tuberose with very minor darkening or lightening of this accord produced by the ancillary notes. The performance is excellent. Even after twelve hours, I can smell the tuberose on my skin. Sillage is good but not monstrous, as expected for floral scents. Though Temeraire is a nice perfume, I cannot recommend it as it is too linear, simple and expensive. Should a simple monotonous tuberose cost $320? I will pass on this because I have Givenchy Desinvolte which smells similar. Anyone of the L’Interdit family members will give you better bang for the buck. Temeraire means reckless in French, which should be reserved only for someone who buys this for $320.

Somewhat sweet but at the same time warm and cozy. For me, it's a novel, modern blend of cardamom, amber, and patchouli, and it doesn't remind me of the 80s. The sea breeze and salt could be stronger, but it is a light feel-good fragrance. Also great for summer and for the whole year - unusually good!

a lonely cove found, jumped naked into the water. Over 30° in the shade made the water dry on the skin immediately. What remained: salt on the skin, salt in the hair. You lie alone in the sun, surrounded only by driftwood and beautiful rough stones and rocks. It is a scent for summer, for dreaming by wild waters, for adventures on the open sea. gentle sweet tones blend with salt and a hint of woody spice. Unfortunately, it doesn't last too long on my skin. It hugs wonderfully and doesn't impose itself.

*This review is of the vintage 1981 version. Burberrys for Men opens with fine bergamot citrus and aromatic lavender with hints of supporting mint and tarragon spice before transitioning to its heart. As the composition enters its early heart remnants of the aromatic lavender remain, now in support of an unveiled natural cedar wood note that takes the fore, with slightly sharp woody vetiver, earthy patchouli, dulled carnation and rose florals and mint-like warm marjoram spice in additional support. During the late dry-down the warm spice and aromatic woods remain, now joining moderately hard leather and slightly animalic musk from the base through the finish. Projection is slightly below average, but longevity is excellent at between 13 and 15 hours on skin. It took me a bit of time to completely warm to Burberrys for Men. Oh, I always at least "liked" it, but something about the warm spice and aromatics just didn't quite click at first. That said, the more I wear the composition the more I find myself appreciating its seemingly endless list of ingredients that near-miraculously come together to smell quite good on the whole. The composition really isn't overly innovative, but the minty marjoram spice adds a special dimension to the aromatics in particular that set Burberrys apart from its long list of competitors. If I had one wish, it would be to have the projection enhanced a bit, but that is a small "flaw" that I find easy to overlook when taking a macro view of the perfume results. The bottom line is the discontinued $150 per 50 ml bottle on the aftermarket Burberrys for Men (1981) is not the last word of what the best of 1980's perfumery has to offer, but the "very good" to "excellent" 3.5 to 4 stars out of 5 perfume is a winner that gradually makes its case for recommending a sample or even a full bottle buy.

A fougère from a time when the position of Western Male at the Top of the Heap was more or less assured (for better or for worse) and his perfume didn’t have to work too hard. Burberrys for Men was launched in 1981, the year that Indiana Jones, the ZX81 and the first IBM Personal Computers were released, and the first Stealth Plane took to the air; so you can see, it was a year that was foundational in ways that were less significant than the emergence of a new style of Men’s Cologne... But, coming back to our topic in hand. Burberrys for Men is piquant, but it isn’t like today’s generation of savages where everything is stuffed with aggressive chemicals. It uses nothing more invasive than juniper, black pepper and mint. It’s a more or less standard fougère with piquant, herbal-green, and dark woody elements, and crucially, it also uses the key anisic note of Azzaro pour Homme (1978). It -is- fair to criticise Burberrys as a peppery Azzaro clone, but I find it's quite well done (even if a bit of a Powerhouse). It’s very modern for its time and it seems to be a transition away from the late seventies fougére (which was dominated by Azzaro) and towards something more penetrating. The dark and woody-peppery style anticipates the Spiky Woods, which is still a dominant masculine trope today. In fact, I would argue this is one of the steps on the way to the Spiky Woods. But unlike many of today’s masculines, Burberrys has some of the urbane chic that the fougère always aimed for - but often failed to capture, as well as the vibrant modern feel of the Spiky Woods - but without the drawbacks.

I recently found this vintage gem on ebay for a very good price. This version was launched in 1991 and i have only positive comments to make. First off the opening is a true Chypre. They simply don't make Chypres like this currently. How sad. Anywho aftera while the heart emerges and all those little flowery woody nuances emerge. Quite pleasant i must say and then BAM! Drop that base!! Thank God the IFRA wasn't embarrassing itself with their draconian rules and restrictions back then. Leather, a blend of Civet with Amber wrapped around glorious Oakmoss. This scent goes on for hours and hours with a gentle finish that has to be sniffed to be believed. I'm telling u this is a classic, an out and out classic. Easily in my top 10.

Full of joy, I stormed the Jo Malone counter at Oberpollinger today to see if the Christmas collection was already there and tada, I was lucky. So first I sprayed it on paper (after some failed initial tests directly on my skin, where I found the scent quite dreadful and couldn't wash it off anymore ( e'L , I'm looking at you), I've learned my lesson) and found it good enough to go straight to my wrist. I am a lover of citrus notes and the mandarin at the beginning is truly wonderful. Fruity, zesty, slightly bitter (probably the peel), I am very taken with it. I wish the scent could last a bit longer, unfortunately the top note disappears after half an hour. And then the fragrance takes a direction that doesn't appeal to me. Instead of the expected honey, wood appears, which comes across as very dry. There is no trace of sticky bee nectar, and the tonka bean remains hidden from my nose. Sweetness is completely absent here, rather it is slightly spicy. The scent reminds me a bit of Saffron . Not bad at all, but once again the name does not match what is offered. I had expected a sweet Christmas scent to accompany me under the Christmas tree, but Starlit Mandarin & Honey is not that for me. I am almost annoyed that the title once again suggests something that is not delivered. The naming of some perfumes reminds me almost of politics, often big promises and nothing behind them. Since I already own a woody mandarin scent with Verveine Mandarine and Saffron is also part of my collection, I will let Starlit Mandarin & Honey pass me by and will not add it to my Christmas wish list.

No comment for my first Jo Malone bottle? Well then, I'll take over. We are in the year 2019. Back when the world was still normal. In November, I strolled from Douglas to Douglas to test fragrances. Rose & Magnolia was also on my list. Like many other Jo Malones as well. In any case, I hadn't dealt with these fragrances until then, and now that was about to change. I tested all the Jo Malones that were offered and came to the conclusion that I liked this scent the best. Compared to Red Roses, it is much more elegant, not so intrusive, which is why I even dared to layer it with 1957 by Chanel later on. That worked well too. But back to the fragrance. First of all, the bottle is beautiful. That blue and the label, wow! But the content is convincing as well. Magnolia and rose. Towards the end, a bit of patchouli. Never, however, intrusive. A very harmonious composition that is subtle and stylish at the same time. The longevity is also absolutely fine, which cannot be said for all Jo Malones. This fragrance is excellent for small but fine occasions where you dress well without overdoing it and where you don’t want to be offensive with a perfume that fills the room. Rose & Magnolia smells clean, well-groomed, and will never offend. Such fragrances are also needed.

Thanks to a dear "Parfuma," I have a small sample of the fragrance to test. When I sniff it, the first thing that strikes me is the green-spicy freshness of "Chypre Caresse." And a certain song comes to mind, whether the scent is "blue" or not: Adriano Celentano's hit, which was played often on the radio many years ago (and still is)... "Azuro." A song that simply lifts your spirits. And "Italian" it is in some way, this Eau de Toilette. A blooming spring landscape in Tuscany and "feel-good music." The jasmine that then "emerges" is quite tame and subtle. In contrast, a fresh-earthy patchouli comes through nicely. Not a gloomy "cellar chord," but an earthy, buoyant melody. A lovely scent from "Givenchy," but not one that I absolutely need to have. But it's nice to be able to sniff it from time to time.

I can definitely see how people would have different opinions about this one. However, I really like this one. This is the smell of a pink cupcake dusted in cocoa powder and covered in sugar sprinkles. You get the distinct smell of chocolate(the warm dusty cocoa powder kind) and rainbow sprinkles. I love it, it dries down to a creamy cocoa vanilla with some fruity notes. The overall impression it leaves you with is a decadently frosted birthday cake.

I guess I was searching for that scent of a birthday itself, rather than just the cake. Demeter pretty much smells like what is written on the bottle. My birthday cakes are usually vanilla with strawberry or chocolate icing. This cake is chocolate with caramel flavoured cream. The scent is not bad, perhaps a little sickeningly sweet when you first apply, but when it softens, the scent is pleasing. I actually wanted a scent of waxy candles and the scent of sugared smoke to complete my birthday wish. Unfortunately Demeter's Birthday Cake is all about chocolate cake and not much else. It can be a little coconutty at times which throws me off the chocolate track for awhile, however it doesn't last long. The scent doesn't last either, but I must point out that it is in cologne concentration anyway.

Green, sooo GREEN that I involuntarily think briefly of woodruff soda... But it is the lush green lawn, with clover, arugula, dandelions, daisies, cress (and woodruff) in between, that has just been mowed. If you, like me, have woodruff in your garden, you know that the plant itself has a slightly bitter scent - no trace of the sweetness that hits you in soda or jelly! In between, I really think I can smell the real woodruff - the one from the garden - again and again... (the initial "soda" effect was quite short-lived) But the fact that I often smell something that isn't there is nothing new... ‍️ Maybe it's also due to the review of Löwenherz in front of me, because my meadow is from our allotment garden in my childhood in the 70s - and there was also woodruff on the edge... (which is why I absolutely had to have woodruff in my garden ...) An unexcited green composition, as green (I believe) as it can almost get. I really like the scent, unfortunately too late, as it is probably discontinued, like many beautiful Malone fragrances.

Surely, each of us has it - a meadow in the memory of our childhood. A place where we frolicked with the dog, where we flew kites, where we picked wildflowers for our mother. This meadow may have been located behind the dikes of North Frisia or in the middle of Berlin, by the banks of the Isar, or in a suburb of Gelsenkirchen - or in a faraway land. null of these meadows is like the other, and yet they are all one, whole and intact and perfect in the memory of us all. Jo Malone's Nasturtium & Clover honors this meadow of our memories. It is not pretentious and dramatic - not a wild scent trying to make an impression. Nasturtium & Clover is a gentle, moist green fragrance full of kindness and cheerfulness - and then everything is back: the sound of the sea beyond the dike or the tram behind the old fire wall, the church bells in the neighboring village or the sound of the football against the garage doors. The meadow of our childhood. No more. And no less. Conclusion: 'Green, green grass of home' - this is the title of a legendary country song made famous by Tom Jones in the mid-60s.

Cuir Blanc was my first "high-priced" fragrance that I bought in Paris. I was impressed by the subtle elegance, the understated charm. Even the packaging and the bottle exude simple elegance. The ribbon wrapping on the cap is a tribute to the haute couture of the house. And then there’s the scent. The white leather is noticeable without becoming too prominent. The fragrance remains discreet at every moment, almost a bit cool. The pepper is distinctly present, while the musk gives the composition structure. After a while, this pepper asserts itself more strongly, taking the lead somewhat, which it does very well. It’s almost a kind of tenderness with which the aromas interact. A gentleman among fragrances, not a "in your face" rocker that comes charging in, testosterone-fueled and loud. One might consider it too simple, as there isn’t a dozen ingredients competing with each other. I perceive it more as a consistent minimalism that does without any frills and shows that it simply doesn’t need more. Why hasn’t this fragrance really taken off in Germany? I think there are two reasons. First, the simple unavailability. Who goes to Galeries Lafayette to buy perfume? But even more relevant seems to me the fact that the discretion of the fragrance didn’t fit the spirit of the times. It’s the Aventus and co. that were simply too loud for this concept. Now this perfume line has been discontinued for several years and has been redefined in a more contemporary way. I still enjoy this special scent.

The L'Atelier fragrances from the house of Givenchy have, unlike the premium lines of many other manufacturers, not yet established themselves in Germany. The number of their sales outlets is too low, and even here in the forum, they are hardly represented. However, at least the ones I have been able to try are wonderful, delicate scents. Cuir Blanc - the 'white leather' - is primarily that: a bright, white leather scent. There is its fine, glove-soft roughness and fragrance with faint hints of almond or apricot kernels and something gently broken, which is likely the pepper - although the word 'pepper' sounds far too wild and noisy for it and its calm nature. And there is something cool, distant, that almost seems aquatic for seconds - like a distant memory of a Nordic, perhaps Celtic winter beach. Yet beyond this coolness and roughness lies endless tenderness and softness - and a very fine, gentle, and comforting musk, which lacks any primal or animalistic associations. Cuir Blanc is a profoundly innocent scent - with a delicate and fine warmth like the breath of a child or another pure and unblemished creature. Of all the mythical beings that humans have imagined in their millennia-old cultural history, most have a rather gloomy or even malicious nature, and many are highly dangerous. The unicorn - a small horse (sometimes also a goat, in Chinese it is similar in meaning to 'Qilin') with a twisted horn on its forehead - has always been regarded as a creature of luck, innocence, and purity. The tusks of the narwhal were long traded under the name 'Ainkhürn' as its supposedly miraculous horn. The unicorn is famous for its shyness - it is said to only allow itself to be touched by children and virgins - and using violence against a unicorn was considered unlucky and sacrilegious. In contrast, the touch of its soft, white fur promised healing and comfort, its presence seen as blessing, warm, and pure. Conclusion: a scent as fine, soft, and pure as unicorn skin. And here (so far) also nearly as rare.

When you're sitting at the airport in Dubai, and you're incredibly bored, you start comparing fragrances. Tom Ford - White Suede against Givenchy - Cuir Blanc. It somehow made sense to me. A little battle. So here’s my little review: One on the left arm, one on the right. White Suede briefly described: little musk, sterile vanilla cream, soft cuddly leather, minimal floral and sweet notes, no rose, musty in the dry down, the weakest companion in the Private Blend series. Too bad. But not bad. Could it be better? Yes! It screams at me from the Givenchy counter. A fairy from the Middle East speaks of the unisex bestseller for a good €190 for 100 ml. On the other arm it goes. Uhhhhhh. A nasty first note hits me. It smells like a laundromat on a rainy day. Right after that, the leather. A good leather. Not as soft as Ford's. Rather salty and intrusive at first. The leather note is not subtly floral like Ford's. However, the leather cannot hold its own against the pepper. Are there cloves in there? The color violet comes to mind. I smell herbs and woods mixed together, yet not too overpowering. But somehow, even hours later, it’s not Cuir Blanc. It doesn’t feel bright and fresh. The musk is also better integrated in Tom Ford. Here, in my opinion, they missed the mark somewhere. In the end, what remains on my skin is a bit of warm tea, herbs, and a chemical musk note. The leather got completely lost. Too bad. Longevity is a good 5 hours on the skin. Sillage is moderate like Ford's White Suede, which ultimately has the edge in scent quality with the same longevity. In numbers: 6 out of 10 points for Cuir Blanc. 8 out of 10 for White Suede.

I have always wanted to smell like fresh apple pie without having to stand in the kitchen baking. So I set out on the internet and found Demeter's "Apple Pie". What I hoped for was a sweet, buttery, "cakey", cozy-scented explosion. However, this fragrance has very little to do with that. "Apple Pie" contains, to my nose, overripe, wormy apples that have been drowned in cinnamon sugar. That’s it... fortunately, I only purchased a sample.

Received some samples, as it was highly praised by the salesperson, as being what I looked for, an Abdul Samad Al Qurashi alternative (spolier, it is not; maybe just being more expensive) Although the first note is Rose' ish, the Longevity is really bad. Sprayed on skin, it gets to the final note in like 20 Minutes. Last note is very intimate and very feminine, and it can be smelled after 5- 6 hours, but it was worn during leisuring, so no activity/ sweating. I don't get it why it's advertised as being 'Unisex' , as to my nose, this is for a lady in her mid to late 30' s, maybe early 40' s. So, for Taif Rose, I hope there are better options, as this one being 'a limited edition ' apparently garnishes it having an obscene price - and yes, I know, real Rose perfumes are time intensive to make, thus expensive. Silage is also moderate, like 2 arms length for the first note, afterwards intimate. I don't know if the 'Cologne Intense' means it has lower concentration compared to f.e. EDP (would explain the poor performance) .

This perfume reminds me of Good Old Fashioned Loverboy by Queen. Something about the rose notes layered over what seems to be green coffee and chocolate screams Valentine’s Day, but I plan to wear this year-round. This is NOT a Soliflore; rather than just rose, it’s bringing you a bouquet of roses and a set of handmade chocolates in a heart shaped box.

- The scent: Opening is a disappointing dupe for Taif Aoud Parfum . Also reminds me of Café Rose (2023) and Rose Épicée a little bit. It's a little creamier (like a skin cream) and smokier version of the traditional rose water. Nothing new, nothing special, nothing exciting. I'd speak about the dry down but....... - Performance: No dry down since it's simply gone in a few minutes. Are they serious with this sillage and longevity? I am used to over-spraying jo malone fragrances and refreshing every hour since they can't seem to get their performance right. But this bad?! For this price point?! It's a joke. I am done with this brand.

The fragrance "Taif Rose" from one of my favorite houses, Jo Malone London, has accomplished two things - my enthusiasm for it drives me to write my first review here, and it also made me, a true rose skeptic, order two bottles of this limited edition right away. With an extraordinarily strong longevity & sillage for JML (8 hours on skin, at least 24 hours on clothing), I was immediately embraced by the enchanting combination of coffee, amber, and rose during my first test of this fragrance. A quick search explained this familiar, cozy feeling - Marie Salamagne has captured me multiple times with her creations. Above all, "Mimosa & Cardamom," one of my favorite fragrances, wraps around me like a protective sweater and has carried me through many nights working in the intensive care unit. And "Taif Rose" evokes the same feeling in me - enveloping, warm, protective, soft. Due to its high projection, this fragrance is actually rather unsuitable for my work environment, but it has accompanied me in my daily life for several weeks now, and I don't want to be without it. Perhaps I really need a third bottle... A big recommendation from me if you enjoy warm, opulent rose/coffee scents! Wishing you all the best! :)

I don't like the original Interdit, I find it bland, too sugary and a bit "clean" and that's not really my cup of tea. This one is different, with a smoked tuberose, a strong woody side and a hint of coffee. Some people don't seem to smell the coffee and yet, I assure you that it's there. The whole thing is really pleasant, sweet but not sugary, smoked, woody... I really like it.

This was my first demeter as I had just found out about them and wanted to try something, all I have to say... interesting! Smells really sweet, powdery and tobacco-ey, I personally didnt enjoy it and would never use it, but that still doesn't mean that Its not good. I gave it to my friend to try and she loved It so I let her keep It. Like all Demeter's, It does not last long (2-3 hours) but projection was okay! If you are into weird smells and scents then check it out for sure!

Star Magnolia is the new fragrance from Jo Malone that I was able to test recently. First of all, I noticed the bottle, as it had a white-milky coloration, which immediately made it clear to me: This fragrance is limited edition. Because all bottles that do not come in the standard bottles are always limited at Jo Malone, with the exception of various collections like the wonderful Rare Teas. Now, in contrast to the last new fragrances from Jo Malone (the five also limited fragrances from the Bloomsbury Set), I honestly wasn't that keen on the new fragrance this time, even though I have come to like Jo Malone's scents more and more. Because this time, magnolias are the main players in this fragrance, which sounds pretty much like, well, like a flower to me :D When I think of flowers, the first scent notes that come to mind are always dry and stuffy, although that doesn't always have to be the case, as there are also beautifully sweet-scented plants, or even watery fragrances that smell like stepping into a flower shop. Moreover, magnolias sound like a true women's fragrance, and yes, the new scent is indeed something for you ladies rather than being unisex. Hm, you know that I sometimes feel uncomfortable testing a women's fragrance "in public" (in this case, "public" means the number of all ladies in a fragrance store :D), but this time there was no "danger" for me, as I was sprayed with the new fragrance by the nice saleswomen shortly after entering the store :) So here comes my scent impression: The scent: The fragrance starts off quite citrusy. You can smell a beautiful, almost juicy lemon that comes across as quite zesty and therefore smells wonderfully refreshing. Shortly after, the ginger also releases its distinctive scent. The ginger smells nice here and fits well with the summery atmosphere. However, neither the lemon nor the ginger lasts particularly long and fades away quite quickly. The magnolias (aha, so this is what magnolias smell like…) smell, of course, floral, but not sweet. They initially have a watery scent, meaning the kind of scent you can perceive at florists. In the later base, they come across as slightly stuffy, but not as extreme as is sometimes the case with some floral fragrances. This "stuffiness" is still in a quite pleasant range. Aside from that, the flowers seem quite clean and pure. Well, basically that's it, as the notes in the base are a bit weak. You can smell the sandalwood a little in the background, but the amber is very faint, so the fragrance doesn't smell sweet, and in the base, you can really only smell floral notes. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is average, perhaps a bit weaker. The fragrance is not very close to the body, but you still have to get quite close to smell it. The longevity is about four to five hours, but it probably lasts a bit longer on clothing. The bottle: The bottle is rectangular, filled with clear fragrance liquid, and has a gradient from transparent/clear to white-milky. The label on the front is white and a bit harder to read than usual, but it looks nice with the light colors. The knob-like cap is also white this time. Additionally, the bottle has a nice floral neck ornament representing star magnolias. A beautiful bottle that visually stands out nicely from the standard bottles of Jo Malone. Yes, the new Jo Malone is quite nice. However, I must first express my main criticism: It doesn't smell incredibly spectacular. It doesn't give you a feeling of something new. It's something that you could have already sniffed many times before (as far as general floral fragrances are concerned, since the magnolias don't smell that different from many other floral fragrances). But it belongs to the well-made floral fragrances that come across nicely and should especially shine in spring and summer. Whether the fragrance really smells very much like magnolias, you'll have to find out for yourselves, as I have never "seen" magnolias in any other fragrance; besides, I don't know what magnolias look like (well, I just Googled it :D), nor how they smell. Because as I said before, I'm a guy, and guys are known to only recognize roses as flowers; everything else is simply called "flower" … or is sometimes disparagingly referred to as "vegetable," he he. If you want to test it, it's important to know that it comes across a bit differently on the skin than on a test strip. Because on paper, the citrus note unfolds weaker, and the fragrance smells generally stuffier than it actually is. And don't let my "it's stuffy" opinion unsettle you, because personally, many floral fragrances come across as so dry to me, but maybe that's also because I don't really connect with many floral fragrances. As a guy, I personally don't want to smell too intensely like "flower" :DD But I do enjoy sniffing around you ladies… um… I mean in terms of fragrance, of course… .DD As mentioned, Star Magnolia is a spring and summer fragrance that is quite nice and could especially appeal to you ladies, so testing it could be quite worthwhile, so I recommend you give the fragrance a try, even if it may not be anything new :)

Hello, fragrance lovers! Like almost every evening, I have brought a fragrance description today as well. However, today it’s about a scent that unfortunately no longer exists because it was one of those fragrances that were limited edition, and you can only get your hands on such a scent with a bit of luck. It’s about the “Rock the Ages” collection from Jo Malone, which may sound like a rock festival from the last decades, but actually represents a kind of historical tour through some eras of English history. Due to a lack of samples, I can only present this one scent for now, namely “Tudor Rose & Amber,” which is quite practical since this scent represents the Tudor era and thus (considering the collection) is the first stop in this fragrance series, which must be set between the years 1485 - 1603. I hope to be able to try the other scents and thus the other historical eras over time as well. But let’s start with the Tudors, whose ruler (Henry Tudor) from the House of Lancaster defeated Richard III from the House of York during the Wars of the Roses, then married Princess Elizabeth from the House of York, and thus became King Henry VII. WAKE UP! I know many of you get a bit bored during history class, but it goes on a little :D So, open your books to page 271, and there we learn that with what I just told you, the Wars of the Roses were ended and both houses were united, although one should not imagine that it was a war about or with roses :D No, both conflicting parties had a rose as a coat of arms or logo (the House of York had the white rose, the House of Lancaster the red rose), hence the name of the war! At least, that’s what I believe! :D After the war, as both houses were united, the roses were also combined, so that the Tudor Rose was now a white-red rose. Well, and now there’s the scent to go with it :D Hmm… I’ll say it again: Wake up, people! I hope you’re still there and that my little history lesson hasn’t bored you too much or even scared you away! The Scent: Hmm, somehow you can smell everything that is listed below right from the start. Well, okay, I don’t smell the ginger yet, but everything else is already present in varying intensities from the very beginning. true to its name, the rose is the most prominent note; it smells nice, slightly sour-floral, well, like roses do, you know! :D There’s a small portion of cloves, which are quite weak, and you can only perceive them if you really sniff closely at the sprayed spot. The amber, on the other hand, is more noticeable, and it smells quite pleasant with its light-sweet scent. Only gradually can I also smell the ginger. There are also somehow more floral notes. These feel a bit heavier and even slightly sultry, making the scent a bit more mature. However, this impression doesn’t last long. Well, the scent does give an opulent impression regarding floral notes, but it’s not sultry or overwhelming, which I appreciate. In any case, the scent also becomes a bit warmer, which many might also like. Later, it continues to smell mostly of roses with a nice amber sweetness. All other fragrance notes are then too weak to be worth mentioning. Much later, however, the amber is a bit more in the foreground, and the scent also appears slightly spicier. Overall, a lovely scent, even if it’s nothing really new in terms of rose fragrances, but still nice. The Sillage and Longevity: The sillage is good, not spectacular, but good enough to be noticeable for a while. Yes, I write “noticeable,” because despite the unisex label here, the scent is, once again..., clearly a women’s fragrance! The longevity is quite good, easily lasting eight hours. Actually even more, but at a rather late stage, the scent is very close to the skin, which is also nice to occasionally sniff on your arm or something :) The Bottle: Hmm… while I find the standard bottles from Jo Malone a bit boring, I often prefer the special editions of the limited fragrances. The Tudor scent comes in a 30 mL rectangular and slim bottle, as you already know from the 30 mL versions of the Malone bottles. Only this one has a beautiful burgundy label. A burgundy fabric or suede has been applied to the chrome-plated cap (I’m not sure, as I unfortunately didn’t have the bottle in hand), which also looks very nice. Yes, I find the bottle quite beautiful! So, I almost expected it, but I find the scent successful. Of course, it’s nothing for us men, and some women also seem not to like rose fragrances that much, but for those who don’t have a particular aversion to rose scents, they might want to check this one out. Well, that will be difficult since the scent no longer exists and was limited anyway, but just in case you should see it somewhere… And if not, it’s not really a big deal. Because honestly, the scent is good, but it also smells like many other beautiful rose fragrances (of course, every scent has its little differences, but sometimes you have to search for those with a magnifying glass, oh you know what I mean!), so you’re not missing out on too much, except maybe a beautiful bottle. This is only really unfortunate for fans of the brand who want to collect these limited fragrances; olfactorily, there are indeed quite a few similar ones. Otherwise, this scent was for me a women’s fragrance that could have been used as an all-rounder. So for any season, for many occasions. Yep, quite nice! So then, have a lovely evening and a wonderful weekend :)

I really enjoy drinking tea in winter, especially the seasonal varieties with gingerbread, cinnamon, and orange. They certainly sweeten the pre-Christmas season. This fragrance here is also a candidate that sweetens winter with its lightness, even though it comes across as a bit too light and less wintry for my taste. At first, it reminds me of a rather ordinary jasmine tea with a few splashes of orange. Winter memories don't really awaken at first, which I find a bit disappointing. However, this is rewarded after about 15 minutes, as then the gingerbread truly comes through along with a hint of cinnamon powder. Everything is very subtle, light, but very pleasant. It is sweet, but not in a gourmand way; rather, it has a restrained floral sweetness. It's a fine fragrance, no question about it, but for my taste, it could have been a bit more wintry, as the spice tends to stay in the background while the tea note is in the foreground, which actually suits warmer days more. Nevertheless, I will wear the fragrance on December 26th to gently and pleasantly conclude the Christmas festivities with all the delicious treats. So, if you enjoy tea scents and would like a hint of winter in the background, you should definitely test it when you have the chance; it's very pleasant to wear. The sillage and longevity are unfortunately not very strong for a winter fragrance, as is usually the case with tea scents, but rather subdued and fade away quite quickly.

It happened at a time when wishing was once again helpful, that a good spirit at Givenchy thought to himself: "The world needs wonders! People want to dream! Everyone longs for the beautiful days of their childhood!" And he mixed everything wildly together that came to his hands in terms of Christmas scents: Candied orange, gingerbread, cinnamon.... But - that already existed. At every Christmas market, in every gift shop, even - oh dear! - in the drugstore discount. What to do? His thoughts wandered to Grenouille, the evil genius of perfumery, who had realized that a scent only truly shines and comes into its own, ultimately being a "fragrance" (and not just a "smell"!) when it has a fitting framework. And so he refined and improved the delicious scent, adding soft jasmine notes, a bit more smoky caramel, and gave it a fresh tea note as an introduction. Then he stepped back and let it all sink in. Now the fragrance had everything it needed to gift people a little golden Christmas happiness... It began with the scent of hot, freshly brewed Lapsang Souchong, which warms the heart and spreads a cozy atmosphere. The heart note then became warm-fruity around the heart, sunny-sweet, and just a little cinnamon-spicy-refreshing. The base radiated with winter delight, gingerbread and caramel from childhood days, whose sweetness was held in check by a bit of creamy jasmine. "It is done!" thought the good spirit. "Now Christmas can come, and it will be a particularly beautiful one when the people out there use this fragrance, for it makes them happy...." Edit: Thanks to Moonlight for the sample, the fragrance is currently only available in France, Benelux, and a few other lucky countries.

You must be pretty crazy as a 45-year-old guy to even consider a perfume called "Baby Shampoo" for yourself. Crazy I am, without a doubt. But I’m also an old romantic. But let’s start from the beginning. About a month ago, I came across the Library of Fragrance line through Parfumo (as usual). At first very cautiously... Vanilla Ice Cream? OK, I’ve seen that in a perfume somewhere or can definitely imagine it. Neroli? Sure, why not? Pizza? Uh, What? Zombie? Ah yes... they must be crazy, was my thought. The folks at TLOF are definitely thinking about how to create unusual scents. Then came my first fragrance sample... "Salt Air" Kaboom. Right off the bat, a jackpot! Wow, is that fantastic. That has, of course, set a scent mark in the truest sense of the word. By now I have... no idea... 12? fragrances from them. No one has been able to match Salt Air so far. But wait. That doesn’t mean the others aren’t good too. Quite the opposite. So now it’s about "Baby Shampoo." And not that non-tearing - mostly blue - stuff that you wash babies' hair with, but actually an Eau de Cologne. That sounds so ridiculous that I HAD to try it. Well... Anyone who has kids that have outgrown the baby stage probably reminisces from time to time about how sweet and beautiful that time was. Just like I do. My son... now 18 (sniff) is hardly seen anymore, in love with the internet, GTA V Online, Dark Souls, Battlefield, and so on. This now giant guy was once a small, vulnerable baby? Yes, that’s how it really was. And of course, he also had that unmistakable baby-fresh powder-shampoo-baby-oil scent. Time flies, not only do we age. The world around us is changing rapidly (not always for the better). And of course, so is your own child. What remains are photos and memories of those days... and while I’m writing this, I old fool actually have a lump in my throat. Phew, breathe. Focus. Keep writing... "Baby Shampoo" lives up to its name 100%. It is soft, white-floral, fresh, and subtly sweet. If you have no associations with baby shampoo, this is simply a pleasant everyday scent. "Baby Shampoo" also shows no edges or corners, it only changes minimally, staying true to what it wanted to be from the very beginning. The longevity is really very good for an EdC, as is the sillage. The pillow also enjoys a spritz, it refreshes and leaves a super pleasant scent that encourages sleep. And so I wear this fragrance quite innocently, occasionally indulging in memories and thus distracting myself from some everyday worries. The initial question remains... why do I occasionally - but very gladly - wear this scent?

Whatever 'sans artifice' is supposed to mean in connection with the fragrance; - here it means unembellished, looking at Givenchy and in the vocabulary of Google it means - without craftsmanship. Craftsmanship means skill, skill in any form whether artisanal, linguistic, or artistic to create works of art. Does it mean that this fragrance was created without craftsmanship/without skill? Clumsy, uninspired, lacking creativity, lacking idea, just thrown together?! I perceive the fragrance as a work of art: straightforward, clear, light, fresh, free, unrestricted, and unpretentious. It starts with fresh, spicy ginger, wrapped in a light sharpness. Tea, white tea, and bergamot meet in a lively manner. The rose also lingers, albeit in the background. The tea seems bitter, but I do not find it too masculine. Bergamot takes some of the bitterness away and sprinkles wood shavings. In the end, a fine, pure musk base. Simple elegance and purity - unembellished - The fragrance could last longer; what a pity

It boasts a very interesting evolution. Let’s start with the opening: sandalwood and super ripe, juicy apricot — not bright or tart, but pulpy, creamy, and absolutely enjoyable because it doesn’t go full gourmand. The spices are light and hinted at, warmer rather than sharp. They add depth without breaking the harmony. After about 20–30 minutes, the sandalwood becomes much thicker. It turns round and silky, bringing with it an almost lactonic sensation (I swear I’m not crazy, I really smell it), like clean, warm skin. This is when the fragrance becomes super fluffy. As time goes by, the apricot loses its initial juiciness and turns into a soft, sweet echo… I start picking up incense-like notes, and even licorice (???)! This is a fragrance that doesn’t aim for sharp contrasts, but for continuity. Warm, creamy, spicy, with that lactonic nuance that makes it comforting and relaxing. Longevity is surprisingly medium to high, especially compared to other Jo Malone scents (clear-bottle ones). I don’t find it similar to either Sunshine Woman or Kenzo Jungle ; at most, it reminds me of Vanille Abricot , but only in its sweet/fruity soul — it has the same kind of sweetness and softness.

Top note with a surprising opening… the listed notes definitely do not correspond to the first impression of the scent. Presumably, the "Spiced" refers to the cardamom that flies around your nose at the beginning. Completely unexpected but for me as a cardamom lover, a lovely surprise. In fact, this fragrance reminds me of a less intense, less resinous but equally beautiful version of Lustre …I like! The heart note arrives after about 15-20 minutes with the promised apricot and a playful sweetness (perhaps from the vanilla). Generally, the scent now becomes (unfortunately) a bit less spiced and a bit more tame. Still beautiful but more intimate. After about 1.5 to 2 hours, the sandalwood along with the vanilla breaks through in the base note. Very creamy, very embracing, but unfortunately remaining quiet. All in all, a very beautiful fragrance with a great transformation. Those who do not like cardamom will have to hold their nose during the opening. I find it unfortunate that after the first half hour it becomes a quiet scent and stays that way, and spraying on clothing did not help in this case. Cardamom was nice to sniff, but somehow the rest of the scent development gets lost on clothing. It simply ends after the top note. I have no idea where the remaining notes have gone on the clothing. Therefore, it is more of a scent for the skin with a few more sprays than one might usually do. At the latest after 5 hours, I really perceive nothing of it anymore, but of course, it is just a cologne. Whether the price for a bottle is justified by its longevity and sillage… I am still undecided at the moment. Maybe there will be an Intense version someday?

Sandalwood & Spiced Apricot is a warm, balanced fragrance that consistently exudes a pleasant calm. Apricot, as I perceive it, is not the focal point. It does not come across as overly ripe or sticky. Gentle spices surround it very unobtrusively, along with a hint of vanilla. The vanilla adds a creamy sweetness to the whole. After this opening, which combines fruit and spice, the sandalwood becomes increasingly prominent: it smells warm, slightly smoky, and very smooth. The scent remains close to the skin, appearing very refined and well-groomed. It is not loud or intrusive, rather like an inconspicuous, warm veil. It lasts about five to six hours. That is sufficient for a cologne. An ideal companion in daily life for someone who wants to carry comfort, softness, and at the same time sophistication.

Before spraying on Encens Divin, I was a little concerned about how sharp the top notes (pepper and ginger) would be in the opening but as it turns out, I had nothing to worry about. The opening was a slightly spicey resinous vanilla that reminded me of Ambre Tigré. Rose notes along with wood and incense followed soon afterwards. After a while, amber and treacle (molasses) notes came into play. A very nice olfactory experience. Though I did enjoy Ambre Tigré, I would recommend saving your money and purchase Encens Divin instead as this is Ambre Tigré with a lot more depth. Projection is around 6ft (2m) and is still noticable after 10 hours. Can easily be worn for any occasion professional, leisure and intimate. During my first day of wearing Encens Divin, I received a few unsolicited compliments from co-workers. Full bottle and signature scent worthy for men or women. 10/10

Encens Divin was my last fragrance from Givenchy's "Atelier" line - and it is still one of my favorites. It's a shame that it is no longer available. Encens Divin is a noble, understated scent. So completely different from the current "in your face" fragrances that are in vogue today. Perhaps that is why it was doomed to disappear - even though it is such a beautiful companion. The presentation is simple and elegant. Completely in harmony with the scent itself. Again, there is a fabric wrapping on the cap, as a tribute to Givenchy's fashion tradition. The name reveals what this fragrance is about: divine incense. Almost immediately after spraying, it makes its presence known. For me, it is not smoky and rough, but velvety elegant. Soon, woody notes emerge, providing a wonderful base for this fragrance. Encens Divin was my first incense fragrance and immediately captivated me. Since then, I have tested various incense scents, but none have touched me as much as this one. The subtle hints of pepper add a delicate sharpness, which contrasts beautifully with the quickly perceptible sweet tones of rose and vanilla. The overall composition is, even in the drydown, dark, elegant, without becoming too sweet or heavy. The longevity is good. Encens Divin is not a loud fragrance. It does not project endlessly, does not fill the room, but remains with me in discreet elegance - and that is something I really appreciate about it. Anyone can be loud - but this kind of understatement is not so easy. I would recommend everyone to test this fragrance - unfortunately, it is no longer available. So why this review? Because I believe it deserves it!

For a long time, I have been waiting to leave a comment that my absolute favorite fragrance has long deserved. “Encens Divin” has been accompanying me since autumn 2018 - the “culprit” is the nice salesperson at a duty-free shop at London Heathrow Airport, who was able to accurately assess my fragrance preferences and delighted me with a spritz of the golden elixir to such an extent that I couldn't let go of my arm crease during the nearly one-and-a-half-hour flight to Hamburg. The distinguished Brit next to me deliberately ignored me until his phone disappeared under the seat during turbulence. I helped him search by using mine as a flashlight. Our eyes met upside down, and he was likely hit by a wave of “Encens Divin.” He promptly exclaimed, “Oh, it DOES smell good!” His phone was found a row behind us. But now to the scent: The peppery top note is surprisingly soft, almost with hints of honey and embedded in the already rising incense, which carries all the other notes along, enveloping, connecting, and refining them. If “Encens Divin” were a gemstone, it would be amber - a magnificent, large, highly polished amber with facets of dark orange-brown to radiant gold, in which delicate insects trapped in time dance. Its depth and long-lasting scent development are like the play of light and shadow, allowing one to discover new details within this stone that is not a stone. Like the partially millions-of-years-old tree resin, “Encens Divin” also evokes associations with prehistory and early history, a time long before our time, thanks to the incense and amber. The scent transports me to Mesopotamia to the first high cultures, to cities like Ur and Akkad. Here, a warm wind blows around the ziggurats, but not only the people, the gods are also at war and must be appeased time and again with fragrant offerings. Wise rulers like Hammurabi and Gilgamesh ensure that these rules are strictly followed, and so the incense can still be smelled in the warm stones long after the sun has fallen behind the horizon and tasted in the balmy, dusty air. That is the divine incense! The association with “Akkad” by Lubin is by no means coincidental, as these fragrances are indeed soulmates. Both evoke a depth and beauty that few fragrance compositions achieve. Both do not skimp on a wealth of ingredients from the Middle East, with the rose absolute and the balsamic cedar notes of “Encens Divin” making the scent even more beautiful and deeper for me than that of “Akkad.” Anyone who loves “Akkad” might possibly fall for “Encens Divin.” I certainly have, body and soul, and I look forward to wearing this ancient, wonderfully radiant dark-light fragrance again in the cooler months.

What can I say, I really liked it right from the first spray, and that feeling lasted for the next few hours! This perfume is very dark and mysterious, a true beauty that one rarely encounters in life. I find this fine and charismatic little potion completely deviates from previous fragrance directions. It is spicy; I almost thought I detected a fine hint of excellent espresso, but no, it’s the woods combined with the rose and the incense, really very unusual but beautiful and sensual - daring, a little dangerous. This scent requires a strong self-confidence; it is not a floral and airy-light everyday fragrance. One or two sprays are more than enough; be careful, or you’ll leave your counterpart flat - it captivates them. At some point, it becomes a bit tamer, slightly sweeter, but still with that dark undertone that quietly whispers of mysterious things that take us away. I treated myself to this somewhat pricey fragrance of almost 200 euros and enjoy this dark free spirit that presents itself quite differently. It changes from time to time, but a dark fragrance aura always remains and carries the other ingredients in the four directions of freedom. It would also suit a man; the rose absolute is very well wrapped and peeks out only timidly and cautiously. If the scent were a fairy tale, it would be for me Allerleirauh the Beautiful, wrapped in a coat made of small pieces of 1000 different furs (not real, of course, I am an animal lover), and a dark and completely beautiful being emerges that one falls for. The coat falls away, and there stands this gorgeous dark creature; you close your eyes, and the image captures the heart. The reader may excuse my fantasy journey, but the perfume has touched, fascinated, and captivated me in a wondrous way.

Burberry Sport Ice is thankfully more palatable than Burberry Sport which was a synthetic disaster to my nose. The composition is mostly citrus with an icy twist, and combines delicate musky and sandy undertones to give it that little hint of originality. Yes, it does appear to be a cold, frosty scent, and although refreshing, I think it could also suit moderately cold weather, especially a rainy day. It's not a sillage monster, but it projects rather well for a subtle citrus-based fragrance. Many are mentioning the ginger note, and while it's present, it's not particularly prominent. Burberry Sport Ice falls either into the category of being a clean citrus fragrance or an aquatic. Floral isn't the right word to describe this perfume. I'll agree that it reminds me of a chilled glass of soda water, especially since I feel that this fragrance radiates a somewhat sparkling quality. It's feminine and inoffensive, which are two things that have drawn me into liking this fragrance. However I must add that I'm disappointed in Burberry for producing way too many forgettable flankers and not coming up with new fragrances like the classics, which were the reason why I came to love Burberry in the first place. For a Summer scent, Burberry Sport Ice is right up there as being a pleasant and wearable fragrance. I find this fragrance a little similar in both style and scent to Burberry Brit Sheer, so lovers of that perfume will most likely enjoy this.

I fell for the great description of this fragrance, "ice crystals, ginger, magnolia, and musk." These are actually scent notes that I really like, described as fresh-minty. Yes, I thought it would be great for hot summer days. Well, it does smell very fresh, especially at the beginning: I perceive cool peppermint, and it is really quite pleasant, reminding me a bit of those mint drops from TicTac... for 2 minutes... after that, it just becomes artificial-synthetic like a disinfectant, strongly reminding me of Sagrotan/Kodan. I can't pick out any of the other mentioned scent notes at all, nothing of magnolia, ginger, mandarin, or warm cedar on my skin. It does resemble Burberry Sport for Women from 2010 a bit, but it’s not quite as piercing in the nose, and thankfully, that sea salt note is completely missing. Unfortunately, the longevity of this fragrance is relatively good on my skin, and I still smell like freshly disinfected hours later.

...that's why this scent ended up in my shopping cart. Actually, you really don't need more than "daisies, green notes" to describe it. You can actually smell the daisies, along with quite a bit of stems...like a flower crown. When I read the statement from BlueVelvet, it changed my perspective on this scent, as I have to admit that "any kind of fresh-scented wet wipes" also fits. So you can smell what you want to smell :D Definitely a nice, green-fresh floral scent, realistic yet somewhat one-dimensional. Longevity is rather lacking.

Wisteria a lavander is my favourite fragance from the new LAVENDERLAND collection by jo Malone. It is a floral, musky and powdery subtle fragance based on the lavander, but with a sweeter and for me nicer view of lavander than usually. At the same time It is, however, the fragance of the three with the worst performance. Longevity and projection are quite moderate which makes the fragance a perfume for daily time use during the everyday Life. For me It is also totally unisex. It makes me think of other JMLONDON perfumes like Wild bluebell. Scent: 8.5 Longevity: 6 Projection: 5 Quality/price: 6 Versatility: 9 Originality: 6 Global: 8

Wisteria and Lavender My first thought when spraying it on my skin. Oh God, Unisex, what am I supposed to do with that? - an unmistakably fresh lavender scent spreads. A bit biting, still sharp, yet unmistakable... but after a few minutes, everything becomes relative. This is not lavender as you might know it from your grandmother or a men's fragrance. No, it’s a fresh, pure, and natural scent. I am reminded of a walk on a cool early morning through the lavender fields of southern France. It is still cool. The dew moistens the wood, the flowers, you can feel the earth under your bare feet, the first rays of sunshine are warming up. Somewhere, other flowers are still blooming, trees stretch their branches, between which the wisteria presents its lavish flower clusters. Nature awakens. Birds are chirping, inside, next to coffee and croissants, the FAZ or Die Zeit are waiting to be read. I remember the film "A Good Year" with Russell Crowe, London chic, a successful stockbroker, tailored suits and jackets, an old villa, sunshine, the shine of bygone times. Cool businessman meets the sun-drenched southern France and the memories of his childhood and youth. The scent becomes more powdery, finer over time, its cool elegance wraps around you like a noble silk shawl. Wisteria and Lavender is not a scent for the beach or a boisterous girls' night out or barbecue. It is elegant, successful understatement for the executive floor, an expensive club with limited membership, a stylish tea time with champagne in an upscale London restaurant, or a visit to a fine French café with café au lait and macarons. On the skin, it lasts a good half day; I could still perceive it very well on my summer sweater the next day. A very beautiful and extraordinary scent that will keep its place in my collection.

A very fine lavender scent, more delicate than loud, aromatic with a slightly sweet lavender - no dusty note, the underlying musk makes it very feminine and clean. I liked it immediately. It is just a cologne and therefore does not last very well or long; it is more like an airy, sun-drenched scent mist that gently falls upon me when sprayed into the air. I close my eyes and find myself in a very large, beautiful lavender field in the province. The sun warms my face and this wonderful, pure smell surrounds me. A perfect companion for a wonderful summer, a gentle embrace for a woman, perhaps a bit more robust on a man? Who knows... give it a try. I wonder what wisteria smells like, I don’t know, but this cologne is refreshment par excellence. It also has something familiar for me.

...this could also be the name of this fragrance. Today, following the recommendation of the lovely Parfuma GirlofNow, I went in search of a specific scent at the upscale department store Nordstrom in the USA. Dolce Garden by D&G is supposed to smell wonderfully creamy of vanilla, coconut, and flowers, according to her description, and that sounds really good! However, they unfortunately did not have this fragrance at Nordstrom. So, following the recommendation of the friendly salesperson at the Dior counter, I tested various scents: Mon Paris by YSL, Rose Prick and Soleil Blanc by Tom Ford, and the limited Lavender line by Jo Malone. In the end, I was particularly taken with Wisteria & Lavender and Soleil Blanc, so I took home samples of both fragrances for extensive testing, and at this moment I am sitting at my desk with Wisteria & Lavender on my arm. At the start, the fragrance clearly smells of lavender, but not the kind of men’s aftershave, rather more like Provence! A beautiful, unsweetened, and slightly bitter lavender note that transports you to sunny Southern France. I only know such a lavender note from L'Occitane. After a few minutes, the fragrance settles and becomes even rounder and finer. There are definitely floral notes present, but even here they are very unsweetened, so the perfume reminds me of my beloved Chanel No. 19 in terms of its aura. I do not mean that the scents are similar, but the attitude, the aura is very similar: mature and noble. In the base, the fragrance is beautifully softened by unsweetened musk. I find this scent rounded, soft, bright, clean, and harmonious. It has something of a successful CEO, while remaining stylish and discreet. By the way, the CEO can be female or male! This fragrance requires a formal appearance as its backdrop. Jeans and a t-shirt do not suit it at all; rather, a white shirt and stylish leather shoes. It is not for very young women, but can definitely be worn from mid-20s onward (in my opinion). The sillage is moderate, and I cannot comment on the longevity yet. I find this fragrance very successful and am considering whether I should buy it. Since I am also very taken with Soleil Blanc, the decision is not so easy. I am excited to be the first to comment on this fragrance and am very curious about the opinions of you other Parfumas and Parfumos regarding this scent! A warm greeting from the USA!

One constantly tries to lose a few pounds here and there and realizes that when smelling certain fragrances, not only does one's mouth water, but the stomach also growls because it is sour and wants to be fed something sweet again after a long time. But I remain steadfast and write this drooling comment, I mean a comment about this delicious scent... argh... *drool* The scent: You smell something fruity, but you can't quite say what kind of fruits they are. In any case, it is not just plum, even though this fruit represents the strongest note. There is also the typical scent of candied fruits; you can definitely smell a lot of sugar and other sweet ingredients. The listed spices and nuts are more in the background; you can smell the nuts a little, but I don't really perceive any of the spices. If you want to imagine exactly how this scent smells, you should think of candied apples that are available at fair or Christmas markets. The longevity is normal for a Demeter scent and lasts like most fragrances from this manufacturer for two to four hours. The sillage is quite okay, as the scent of this sugary mass rises again and again, making your mouth water. The bottle is really not one of the good ones. Boring. At least you can fill it with the perfume liquid. As for the sticker, oh... you know by now what I think of boring stickers... Hmm,... this scent really smells delicious. Of course, it is not suitable for wearing at all, as it smells overly sweet, but it reminds you of many tasty treats. These could be dried or candied fruits, or these candied apples. Even though I now have a great craving for this sweet, I know that at the Dippemess, Christmas market, or similar events, I will again reach for the chocolate-covered bananas... Now I'm drifting off again. The fact is that the scent smells delicious and is well captured as part of a fragrance library, maybe just a tad too sweet.

Noctambule is an expensive spicy rose-oud perfume from Givenchy’s La Collection Particulière. Ane Ayo, a new-generation perfumer affiliated with DSM-Firmenich, is the nose behind Noctambule. La Collection Particulière uses both perfumers and ingredients from DSM-Firmenich. This review of Noctambule was initially written for a 10 ml travel size bottle. I recently purchased a full bottle. The review has been updated accordingly. Noctambule demonstrates that wonderful perfumes can be created from a few simple notes. It is a celebration of the Centifolia Rose from Grasse, enhanced by cumin and oud. Notes like papyrus and pink pepper are listed in the olfactory pyramid. Apart from a mild woodiness at the bottom, I cannot pickup papyrus and pink pepper as independent notes. Even the oud is very sophisticated exists as a woody shadow. No matter! It is a beautiful a rose darkened by cumin with some minimal contribution from the ancillary notes. Noctambule is a delicate perfume, very distinct from other heavy rose-oud perfumes such as Maison Francis Kurkdjian Oud Satin Mood or Guerlain Santal Royal. It floats and soars while the other two sink into a dense fog that can be cut with a knife. I like both light and heavy rose perfumes, each for its own occasion. Noctambule doesn’t overwhelm us with its projection, a shared characteristic of all the La Collection Particulière perfumes. It lasts more than 12 hours on my skin but the sillage is subdued as expected from a mature sophisticated Givenchy perfume. There is no concern about wearing this at work, if you can tolerate the cumin. It comes in an elegant bottle in the La Collection Particulière pattern, with a magnetic cap. Unfortunately, the only size available now is the 100 ml from Givenchy that costs $435, apart from the travel size (10 ml) which may be available on independent online shops. It is worth pondering if the full bottle is worth $435, or perhaps another simple rose oud perfume such as A Rose For (Floris) or Oud Ispahan (Dior) is a better option. It is very alarming when a member of the La Collection Privée Christian Dior is the affordable alternative to Noctambule. Update: I tested Oud Isfahan recently at Harrods in London, UK. It is very different from Noctambule and inferior to Noctambule in my opinion.

A scent that in the opening smells like "peppered pencil"..." To brighten things up, there are a few flowers" But overall "pencil, paper, unfortunately not much more..." "Not wow, but also not completely bad..." It becomes a bit nicer over time... Conclusion: A rather average and unremarkable scent... :))

Les Parfums Mythiques Le De is a subtle green-floral jasmine soliflore. The jasmine here scents without causing any side effects and does not reveal itself to be a stinker. Parfums Mythiques surrounds the wearer like a veil, enveloping her in a transparent web of jasmine and a tiny hint of soap, which flutters quietly behind her, giving her the illusion of summer and gardens filled with blooming jasmine bushes. As with Les Parfums Mythiques L'Interdit, the significantly slimmed-down and markedly altered pyramid suggests that the similarity to the original will be limited. Even though I do not know the original here, just as with Les Parfums Mythiques L'Interdit, I find Les Parfums Mythiques Le De - whether similar to the original or not - to be more successful. Undoubtedly, there are numerous fragrances that interpret the jasmine theme in a higher quality, but Les Parfums Mythiques Le De has charm and is, thanks to coriander and a hint of incense, a non-sweet jasmine scent that does not intrude on anyone and surprisingly comes across as modern.

Of course, the seasonal collection is sold out; I am also too late for my Jo Malone stash. But the testers are still there, so the way is clear to at least get to know this interesting blend. We are used to some of Jo Malone's combinations: but whisky - I don't know; I'm curious! During the usual extensive conversation with the sales assistant, the scent and my perceptions can develop. I expected "Angel's Mist": that hint that arises when the liquid evaporates from the barrels in the cellars of the distilleries. What I found was an old, full-bodied whisky that invites you to linger. To linger in a room whose polished wooden floor is only partially covered with carpets. With paneled walls, a fireplace ready to be lit. Everything is prepared for the hour between day and dream! Sitting in deep, comfortable armchairs, surrounded by large bouquets of fully blooming garden roses, which soften the scent's masculinity, the hustle and bustle of the day is bid farewell. With a glass of whisky, good conversations, and (completely out of time) a cigarette. This is a whisky that, unlike many women, is not ashamed of its age. Thus, I experience the "body" of this scent, which becomes slightly spicy in the finish. Whether it is really allspice that I perceive, I do not know for sure. The longevity is mediocre, as with all Malones. One learns to live with that. "Whisky & Cedarwood" is an extravagant fragrance creation, a bit out of time, with a slightly nostalgic touch. Or is it almost modern again? A boundary crosser: neither male nor female - a hermaphrodite! In any case, extraordinary. I am not sure whether I really like "Whisky & Cedarwood." Maybe I should treat myself to another sniff? Perhaps next time at Jo Malone. And next time, maybe instead of the usual gin and tonic, a whisky on the rocks?

Okay, unfortunately there is no rum in this fragrance, so I can't sing the pirate song properly and have replaced the rum with whisky instead. How did I come up with pirates? Hmm… oh, don’t bother me with such questions and just keep reading :D And besides, I've never really been a whisky drinker,… however, a dear friend has taken quite a liking to this alcoholic beverage and will surely be able to tell me one or two interesting details about it while she tries to force me to down some throat-burning whisky, argh… what do I know about whisky? I don’t even know if it’s called whisky or whiskey! :D She’s probably already drunk and… um… I meant of course she’s already a pro and… oh crap. I always forget that she reads most of my comments too. Now I’m lost again… But anyway, let’s get back to the fragrance. Whisky & Cedarwood belongs to the new Bloomsbury Collection by Jo Malone, which consists of limited fragrances, and you have to act quickly if you want to get them starting in March. Because when they are sold out… well, then you have to go on a treasure hunt like a pirate and try to track down the fragrance somehow :D After Tobacco & Mandarin, this is the second fragrance I’m testing a bit more closely, and I quite like it. The Fragrance: As the name suggests, the fragrance starts with a nice alcoholic note, the whisky, which, however, appears a bit floral-sweet and spring-like thanks to a lovely and very subtle rose, making it also wearable for men due to the low intensity of the rose. Overall, the fragrance quickly comes across as quite masculine, as it becomes woody with the typical, distinctive scent of cedar. By the way, I could hardly smell the allspice; perhaps it adds a slightly spicy note in the background. Be that as it may, the fragrance remains alcoholic due to the whisky and woody due to the… well… woody notes (what else? :D), with the difference that in the base the woody notes are stronger than the whisky. A simple but really great fragrance that feels warm.
