The Sillage and Longevity: I’m still not quite sure about the sillage and need to test the fragrance a few more times, as it came across quite well once and rather average another time. It doesn’t seem to be very strong, but rather above average, and should smell reasonably good up close. The fragrance lasts six to seven hours, which I find okay, although it does smell noticeably weaker after four to five hours. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular and small, as it is only available in a 30 mL version. On the front, there is a design reminiscent of abstract color field painting, which alludes to the inspiration of the fragrance, namely the Bloomsbury Group. The cap is cylindrical and light brown. A nice bottle that brings a great change from the almost always identical Jo Malone bottles. Oh, the fragrance is great, great, great. Whisky and wood convey a wonderful feeling, even though the fragrance itself is quite simply constructed. It’s somehow sexy and, despite its not overly intense projection, suitable as an evening fragrance. Moreover, I would call it an all-rounder, as I think it fits into every season. Sure, in winter it is weaker outdoors, but the fragrance unfolds particularly well on colder days, especially indoors. For example, in a nice restaurant/lounge/bar etc. with a cozy atmosphere. As mentioned, the fragrance is unfortunately limited, so testing it is definitely recommended if you find it appealing and would like to have it. Well, and what if they are sold out later? Well,… just remember that I initially thought of pirates. So, gouge out an eye, put on a patch (okay,… maybe you can skip the eye-gouging part and just put a patch over your good eye; no one will notice… :D), take a knife between your teeth, and go on a scent hunt with sword and flintlock pistol! Maybe you’ll get lucky and discover a bottle :D And now… arrrrrr, to the deck, you lazy scent rats!

Ysatis Iris is such an underrated perfume! Fresh, vibrant and so lovely! This could ealisy stand out as a classic value perfume that can be worn from a young woman who feels elegant and charming to a mature lady who enjoys her flirtious nature! The black current gives a slightly sweet opening blending so smoothly along with the violet leafs and iris. There is nothing heavy about this mix nor cheap. Is is a joyfull fruity floral blend with just a bit of a powdery touch. The sillage is great and you will definitely enjoy your self wearing Ysatis Iris if you feel feminine and playful! Don't get misled!.. nothing dated about Ysatis Iris ;)

Yesterday, I picked up this oddly shaped bottle while standing in front of an endless line of Givenchy perfumes. Oh yes, was my thought, that sounds quite elegant and looks a bit extravagant too. Just take that one! I sprayed and braced myself for a more or less citrusy top note. But what hit me was a gigantic club of something undefinably sour, piercing, and at the same time (pardon) fart-dry. My companion shot me a worried glance and sniffed a bit towards my test strip. “Oh my goodness!”, my companion exclaimed, “That smells like the Bath & Beauty that my mother used in the 80s. And that’s not a compliment!” A fashionably difficult time indeed, and one could probably say the same about the scent. I bravely stuffed the test strip into my jacket, hoping that the iris might show up at some point. Ah, that would be something! No chance! Not only did this incredibly sour note haunt me for the next hour, but it also seemed like it just wouldn’t click! and reveal the elegant floral heart. Here I read that rose and tuberose were supposed to be involved. Yes, they completely passed me by. And I know when I have a tuberose in front of me! “Can’t you throw away the test strip?”, my companion grumbled, “It smells like the 80s!!”. I would love to, I explained, but the testing phase isn’t over yet. Not until I’ve smelled iris somewhere here!!! About six hours later, my jacket pocket with the test strip finally smells like iris. But there’s also something else...OH! Vanilla! Ah! Subtly “dirty” patchouli! Beautiful base, really. Unfortunately, it suffers from the structure and middle part. What a pity, I would say the theme is missed. PS: My companion was right about Bath & Beauty. I recently got to smell a sample, and it’s 70% the same sour smell, followed by something big and floral. Crazy.

After sampling this one at the mall, I was immediately captivated by the simplicity and polished feel of this fragrance. I ended up purchasing a bottle, and I'm quite pleased with this choice. While this fragrance is marketed as a Christmas scent, I can see myself wearing this far more often, as it's shockingly versatile. This fragrance is pretty linear, but is primarily based around leafy green notes and leather. The leather note here is absolutely spectacular, and smells exactly like fresh, high-quality leather, with just a supple sweetness added to it. The leather here is not animalic or dirty, but rather quite clean and polished, like a new leather coat or bag. It's layered over a very green accord that does have the scent of pine/fir trees to it, but has a bit of a more general leafy vibe as well that keeps it from smelling exclusively like Christmas. It's a great scent overall, and definitely on the more unique side of Jo Malone releases, though it's certainly unfortunate that this was a limited time offering. Hopefully they bring it back for future holiday seasons! Overall, I'm pleased with Fir & Artemisia. It's raw, green and lightly sweet, and while it does have christmas-like undertones, I don't think I'd have any problem wearing this during other times of the year. If possible, I recommend picking up a decant/sample, or possibly even a full bottle of this fragrance, as it's a very good one to have around, especially for those who love leather notes!

I ordered the fragrance relatively quickly after its release. There were no reviews yet. So it was a complete blind buy. I was a bit nervous since I had ordered the 100ml. It arrived, and I sprayed it on immediately. First intention: I’m unwrapping my new toy, lovingly wrapped in colorful paper, under the tree. It really smells pleasant like a forest. It does lose some character towards the end, but I still smell Christmas until the very last moment. It smells as if I’m entering the living room on December 23rd. Sure, for some it might seem a bit old-fashioned, but for me, it simply smells like Christmas. It instantly evokes anticipation for Christmas Eve with family and a nice Christmas movie ;) Unfortunately, the scent doesn’t last very long, and the sillage is accordingly not great.

I feel it as a floral perfume that is also tropical. I like the way it smells. I had different expectations from it but I am neither disappointed nor impressed. It resembles some perfumes that I have worn before; I can't remember exactly which ones they are right now. I have a miniature of it. At the moment, I don't think I will need a larger quantity. I consider it feminine. It is worth testing first. Rating: 8.5/10

This review is based on a full bottle I got from Givenchy. I had previously owned 10 ml travel size. My daughter loves this so much that I bought a full bottle as a graduation gift. It is an absolute delight if you love clean white florals. Desinvolte belongs to the La Collection Particulière from Givenchy. Apparently, this collection evokes the myriad personalities that inhabited Hubert de Givenchy’s Hôtel Particulier in Paris. The hotel particulieres are private residences owned by the French aristocracy, typically for the use of guests. The eight perfumes from this collection that I own are all elegant, mature and, to a certain extent, simple in conception. The projection of these perfumes is never explosive, but the longevity is very good. Desinvolte is a trio of white floral notes - tuberose, jasmine and orange blossom - enhanced by the subtle notes of vetiver. The beauty of this perfume resides in the harmony of these three floral notes. Vetiver is so mild that it merely darkens the white floral notes without being a strong presence. I get both tuberose and jasmine as opening notes, but orange blossom is less noticeable as a separate note. The tuberose in the opening is gentle unlike that in L’Interdit. The jasmine notes move to front in the heart notes, though tuberose is still around. Before anyone complains that it is not a strong perfume, please remember that it is by design. Givenchy - or perhaps the perfumer Nathalie Larson - puts the intensity of Desinvolte at 3/4, which is in alignment with the La Collection Particulière brand. The base notes and dry down are soft and elegant with primarily white floral notes. On my skin, Desinvolte lasts comfortably for 6-8 hours, with a pleasant dry down lasting even longer. Please be aware that this is not a high intensity perfume that projects strongly for eight hours. I do not see much development, which is not shocking for what is essentially a three-note perfume. The sillage is modest befitting the personality of this perfume. Here is comparison with some other tuberose scents I know. Desinvolte is simple, elegant and linear. If you like a more dominant tuberose, Temeraire from the same collection may interest you. Givenchy L’Interdit and its flankers offer an inexpensive set of tuberose perfumes, though are too harsh for my taste. Carnal Flower (Frederic Malle) adds a green dimension with its eucalyptus, and its tuberose develops slower with no other white florals to help. Tuberoza from Nishane is more complex with tuberose and jasmine developing only in the middle notes. Tuberoza opens differently with its own unique green notes. It also ends differently with the typical woody base notes that we see commonly in Nishane scents. All these perfumes are beautiful in their own unique ways, though the Givenchy perfumes are the most expensive. It is very important to test these on your skin and track them for more than twelve hours. Paper strips produce a different version than your skin, particularly with the last two. As always, test before you buy.

Today I casually mentioned to my husband that some rose fragrances were on sale at our regular perfume shop. No significant reaction from him - as expected. But he kindly accompanied me to the scent oasis. Next to me, a customer quickly grabbed La vie est belle en Rose - and let her gaze wander over the display table. But my husband swooped down like an eagle on the 3 remaining rose fragrances - and secured them safely in his hands. I looked at him in surprise - and he coolly replied that I would have to decide if I wanted a rose fragrance - and he nodded towards the "happy" en Rose buyer. But he had captured Rosy Crush, Mon Paris florale, and Mon Guerlain Bloom of Rose for me. I tested them out of curiosity - and started with Rosy Crush, knowing that Givenchy always scores points with him. And indeed - a Bed of Roses opened up before us - soft and thornless. No soapy note, but slightly berry-like, sweet, underlined by bright patchouli. The fragrance has a certain movement to it, as if a breeze were passing through. The delicate sweet rose reminds me of a summer breeze. Despite its abundance of roses, Rosy remains light and airy. My husband nods in agreement - and I am in accord with him - if there weren't still 2 fragrances to try. More on that soon in this theater... Music: Everything is coming up roses. P.S. Rosy Crush has found its home with me - and I enjoy wearing it.

Creamy and fruity is a dream combination to me, so I was very excited to try this long-discontinued scent. I also love Jo Malone's Elderflower Cordial, which was originally issued under the name Elderflower & Gooseberry in the same collection as Redcurrant & Cream, so my hopes really were up. Well, this is not a bad scent by any means, it's just not very creamy and for sure doesn't smell like realistic cream. I only get red and black currants and raspberry on a soft musky base. It's sweet, a bit sour and kind of fizzy. The fizziness makes me think of a Lush store full of bath bombs and bubble bars. Not sure which one exactly, maybe The Comforter or just a mix of them all. This trait wears off in the drydown, but otherwise the scent doesn't change all that much. Just berries and white musk, that's it. So, this is a cute, joyful scent for the warmer months - especially if you are a fan of berry/currant scents and Lush bath products. But to me, it's not a must-have to hunt down. If it really smelled like redcurrant and cream, it might have been.

As Jo Malone fragrances go, this is a simple one. It is mostly red currant and musk. The cream is very faint in the drydown to counter the tart berry, but I am by no means disappointed. This is another refreshing favorite of mine. It was suggested to me that two good (separate) layering suggestions are with Red Roses or Nectarine Blossom and Honey to give the scent a little better longevity. I will confess that I am partial to Christine Nagel's work, and she did a decent job with the Sugar & Spice collection. edit: I will have to say that over a week later, most of the line was forgettable...which is disappointing since I did enjoy them when I tested them. I probably wouldn't recognize them if you gave me blind samples of the collection.

Jo Malone made dessert dreams come true in 2013. And I am definitely a dessert person. I love sweet things. I mean delicious and juicy berries with sweet cream. Who can say no to that? So it’s no surprise that I got all 5 fragrances from this edition. I must admit, however, that I didn’t like Redcurrant & Cream very much at first. I can’t even say what it was. Something just didn’t fit. Now I find it simply wonderful. It just took a little time. I try to eat as healthily as possible. And that’s how I discovered smoothies for myself. They are quick to make, healthy, and tasty. Among other things, I also tried a berry smoothie. With currants, blackberries, raspberries, blueberries, and strawberries. Super delicious! And this berry smoothie tastes exactly like Redcurrant & Cream smells. Fascinating. And since then, I wear it regularly. I can perceive strawberries, raspberries, and currants very well. Although the currants are a bit more prominent. The musk prevents it from becoming too sour and gives the fragrance a light and sweet creaminess. The longevity is great at just over 6 hours. The sillage is also impressive. The scent wafts around me without being intrusive. A little anecdote on the side. When I was sitting in our break room, my colleague came in and said, "It smells delicious like strawberry tea here." I could only grin. So I’ll take that as a compliment. I really like it and find it very unfortunate that it was only a limited edition. I hope it stays with me for a long time. By the way, my appetite for berry smoothies has greatly increased.

When I tested this fragrance and let others sniff it, no one but me was really convinced. Fruity, sweet, and fresh, but lacking depth, nothing special, they said. For me, the scent is a dream, fresh, sweet-sour blackcurrants that smell endlessly, authentic and not synthetic-sickly sweet like fruity fragrances often are. The blackcurrant is clear and unmistakable, definitely dominating for me, then comes a bit of raspberry, while I can't detect any strawberry at all. The "cream" in this case is not a thick layer of cream, it's a small, delicate dot that rounds off this fragrance, giving it a certain elegance and otherwise staying completely in the background. I feel like there's a tiny hint of vanilla as well, again hardly perceptible. After spraying, the berries explode, it's like fresh juice, the soft notes are not noticeable yet. The scent quickly becomes very close to the skin, it sits on the skin, is well perceivable, but does not spread in the room. After about 12 hours, the fragrance becomes creamy-soft, the berries are tamed and only faintly noticeable, but you can still sense a hint of fruity freshness. This base note is very long-lasting; if you smell directly on the skin, it lasts more than 2 days, even surviving a shower. Those looking for authentic red currants with a touch of cream are in the right place; those expecting a surprise or a mysterious scent with depth will be disappointed.

Society is, for me, a golden Burberry. Perhaps the best that has ever been created. It is an Osmanthus scent with a honey note, white flowers, and a light chypre note. The fragrance is enveloped by a fine note; if cashmere existed in fragrance notes back then, it certainly does here as well. A very long-lasting scent, a fragrance that one associates with "laughter" and "different voices." I am thankfully still in possession of 100 ml and various minis of this fragrance. It's a shame that it is no longer available.

Having discovered my great affection for chypre fragrances some time ago and always on the lookout for special treasures, I have once again found something remarkable this time. Givenchy III, which was released in 1970. And it is a pleasure for me to write a few sentences about a fragrance that has not yet been commented on. Givenchy III was unknown to me just a few weeks ago. But then a sample of the vintage EdT came to me, and I was absolutely thrilled at the first sniff. And as it always goes, you want more... So I set out to find this fragrance in a larger quantity. And in a well-known online auction house, I stumbled upon an unused Givenchy III Extrait. And it was at an incredibly low price. If that wasn't a sign... So I jumped at the chance, and a few days later, I held the treasure in my hands. Completely intact and nothing spilled, even though the perfume has certainly matured a bit and become slightly darker than what can be seen in the pictures, there is absolutely nothing to criticize about the scent. I cannot say when the Extrait I own was released. The bottle looks different from the pictures here. It is simple and straight, without any embellishments, with only the Givenchy logo featuring the four Gs on the cap. And there was also no mention of batch codes. But I don't find that so important now. If the EdT already excited me, I can say that the Extrait is a true delight and an absolute fragrance jewel! Givenchy III fits into the group of classic chypre fragrances with a citrus-green opening, a floral heart, and a mossy base, enriched with the finest animalic sequences to give the scent more spice, more body, and more depth. Givenchy III starts off herbaceous-green and a bit austere; you can notice galbanum, aldehydes buzzing around, and bergamot adds a certain zest. I cannot discern any peach. Then quickly follows this incredibly dense floral abundance; it is hard to recognize individual notes, as the elements are so artfully intertwined. However, I believe that jasmine and rose peek out a bit more boldly. This floral abundance, however, is free from any sweetness at every moment of its progression. I would rather describe the floral aspect as finely bitter, mature, and unembellished. In the base, which only reveals itself after quite a while, Givenchy III becomes even more delicious. This classic chypre base with herbaceous oakmoss (the real stuff was still used here, you can just tell), patchouli for that certain depth, and fine traces of amber and castoreum that give the fragrance its fine spiciness and corporeality. I can't help but draw a comparison with Dioressence, which was released just a year earlier and is composed of roughly the same building blocks. In between, they are very similar, but in Givenchy III, this certain corporeality in the base is less pronounced than in Dioressence. However, this corporeality cannot be missing in this type of fragrance. Givenchy III feels a bit lighter and airier to me, but it does not fall short of Dioressence in terms of class. The scent appears friendly and lovable in every phase of its progression. Spring is the perfect season; everything blooms and shines anew. Along with this beautiful fragrance, which also blooms and shines. After many hours, the scent gently and finely floral fades away; this moment is one of the most beautiful, and I can't get my nose away from the scented spot. Givenchy III was created in 1970 by Jean-François Latty, who has also created wonderful fragrances like Background for Jil Sander and Jazz for YSL, and Raymond Chaillan, who designed Anaïs Anaïs for Cacharel, Ho Hang for Balenciaga, Pour Homme for YSL, and Quartz for Molyneux, among others. So certainly very good references. The chypre theme was to remain present and popular throughout the 70s, with examples such as Rive Gauche by Yves Saint Laurent, also released in 1970, which skillfully embodies the chypre theme, No. 19 by Chanel in 1971, Diorella by Dior in 1972, Gucci N°1 by Gucci in 1974, and Parure by Guerlain in 1975. When I internalize these names and compare the fragrance compositions, I notice how unsweet and herbaceous these fragrances appear. They seem downright masculine with our today's noses, perceptions, and habits. And I would say that this type of fragrance also works excellently on men. Givenchy III has excellent longevity; after about 10 hours, the scent is still clearly perceptible. The projection is also very good for an Extrait, but it does not overwhelm, as the fragrance overall is not heavy. A scent that could still work well today if fragrance houses would once again have the courage to break out of the known patterns alongside modern and often quite adapted fragrances. It's a pity that such great fragrances have disappeared from the scene. But they live on through us fragrance lovers and vintage hunters, and we hold them in high regard. Givenchy III receives the full score from me; I have absolutely nothing to criticize about this fragrance. My thanks go to Gold, who made it possible for me to get to know the EdT and thus led me to the Extrait, which I no longer want to miss, even though it is not a large amount; 7 ml is better than nothing. And the scent is a true masterpiece!

Tangy Rhubarb, so sparkling rhubarb. However, I find the naming in this case not particularly accurate: the scent is not really sparkling at all. At least not compared to "Zara Emotions N°09 - Jo's Rhubarb | Zara" or "Eau de Rhubarbe Écarlate | Hermès." Also, Pierre Hermé - Pamplemousse-Rhubarbe fits into that category. These are much more citrusy at the start and showcase the sourness that raw rhubarb has very well. Tangy Rhubarb takes a slightly different approach, possibly because the Limited Edition it was released in is supposed to be inspired by jam? (That’s probably also why the bottles deviate quite a bit from the usual Jo Malone design, which I really don’t find very successful. But, tastes vary. At least the sprayer works perfectly, and that’s what really matters.) The scent starts off slightly fruity, but for my nose, floral notes dominate, although I can’t quite pinpoint what exactly is mixed in. The fragrance is by no means sweet, but rather green. On my skin, it develops a slightly creamy quality, but doesn’t undergo much further development; I don’t perceive the cedarwood at all, for example. The indicated sage provides a pleasant balance and prevents the somewhat present fruitiness of the rhubarb from overwhelming. The composition is quite harmonious if one doesn’t let the name mislead them. Unfortunately, the longevity is not particularly outstanding; after 4 hours, the scent is only perceptible close to the skin. It’s also not a sillage monster, but it surrounds the wearer (for me, the scent is quite clearly feminine) like a delicate veil. Not a scent for autumn and winter, as it lacks any coziness, but a nice everyday companion in spring and summer. And would I recommend it now? Definitely, if you prefer lighter, fresher scents that come without a hint of citrus and don’t have high expectations for longevity and sillage. For a special twist, it layers very well with "Elderflower Cordial / Elderflower & Gooseberry | Jo Malone," making it a bit sweeter and enhancing the creaminess.

Fresh back from vacation, and apart from a capsule tear in my left index finger and a dislocated vertebra, I feel almost brand new. I would like to present to you Burberry's summer fragrance from 2010, which accompanied me during my summer vacation in 2011. Of course, I didn't just bring one perfume with me, who do you think I am? But I had to realize that my packed Chanels and Diors didn't quite fit the atmosphere of "Dimitri's Grillbude." Summer for Women, however, fits perfectly. Not because it smells like a snack bar, but because it simply works every time it gets warmer. A beautiful composition of flowers and fruits that is light and zesty, does not push itself to the forefront, but surrounds me with a wonderful veil that is definitely present. The scent is strong. Strong enough to mask other, more unpleasant scent sources. So at the beach, it was enough to take a quick sniff at my wrist when my daughter was determined to free the world's oceans from any jellyfish and fished out everything that came her way. Anyone can pull things out of the water, so she built a jellyfish castle. Sure, other girls built beautiful sandcastles and lovingly decorated them with shells. My daughter just beautified her castle with jellyfish and musty-smelling seaweed. After many hours in the midday sun, a fishy cloud did come by, but after a quick sniff at my wrist, I hardly had to gag anymore... Back to the fragrance: The scent starts off zesty-fruity-fresh, then becomes more floral and softer, while still remaining subtly fruity and developing gently and softly on the skin. It is quite similar to the scent from 2011, although this version is a bit more zesty. I now have two summer fragrances from Burberry, and I find both of them utterly delightful. 2012 can then be bought blindly. :D PS: Of course, my daughter only fished out dead animals. She saved the living ones back into the water.

Sounds strange, but that's how it is ;) But that's exactly how you experience The Library of Fragrance's / Demeter's "Lime" To be completely honest, I didn't have high expectations for this fragrance. After "Sour Apple Lollipop" smelled clumsily like dish soap with (not so great) apple scent, I was bracing myself for something similar with "Lime". The previous reviews only reinforced this concern. So it's great that you can easily return mistakes to a very large online retailer ;) Fortunately, I was not disappointed. Of course, I am aware that such a fresh scent is more suited for warm days. But here we go. Barely sprayed on, the very first thought is: Wow, fizzy Sprite!!! You even think you can feel a carbonated touch. Unfortunately, this fresh lemon-lime scent doesn't last very long, but that's not too bad, as "Lime" - compared to many other Demeter scents - develops. A herbal lime scent makes its presence known. This smells like a mix of Almdudler and Berliner Fassbrause, lasts quite a while, and is really pleasant, albeit unexpected. The longevity is overall moderate, the sillage is initially great but fades quickly. All in all, I like the scent, which I got at a bargain price. In summer, it's guaranteed to be a great freshness kick. It surely also works great for layering. "Lime" is fun, but it doesn't overwhelm the spoiled nose.

How to describe Hot Couture No. 1? There are four flankers in Givenchys’ Hot Couture collection, all with similar boxes and with similar notes. Discerning noses can pull out the differences when wearing them. Should you want a particular Hot Couture and are shopping in a perfume store, be very specific in what you ask for from the sales associate. Some of them are not familiar with the idea that more than one Hot Couture exists and will sell you simply what is on the shelf. Look for the right packaging. Wearing this through the fall and winter has given me a lot of opportunities to decide how to review this perfume. This fragrance has so many accolades from others, I wanted to be as fair as possible in my review to make sure that I was also breathing the Hot Couture fantasy. I say this because when I first received my box and tested it, all I could get from it was a sticky, thick, syrupy, cooked raspberry jam surrounding me. It was delicious. But I longed for the smoke and sensual notes that others spoke about. It was early Fall in the States and perhaps the temperatures just weren’t right for me to be wearing this perfume. The weather was still warmer, I was still phasing out my summery perfumes and the true briskness of the Fall had not yet set in. Not all perfumes are a good match for all seasons. It just wasn’t time to pop the top of this bottle yet. Come the bitter cold of snowy winter, still the same thing happened. I needed to find the right season for Hot Couture Collection No. 1 to work its magic for me, if indeed, it would. Apparently, sub-freezing temperatures weren’t the ticket, either. Early Spring, when temperatures hover at the 30-50 degree marks and there are remnants of snow still on the ground, I tried again. And this time, I was able to discern more notes from this sophisticated gourmand. How this can be considered an oriental floral is beyond me. It’s different than your run-of-the-mill teen-age foodie gourmand. It’s rich and oppulent with raspberry, but not just any raspberry. This fruitiness is heavy and intense, as if you’re standing over the pot of jam as it’s cooking on the stove. It’s sweet, but you haven’t added sugar to the pot yet, so there’s an oppositional feel here. Blame the bergamot for a breath of Earl Grey tea or the orange for a citrus zing in the beginning, but this perfume’s run will still be under-sweetened by other notes as it progresses. There’s a woody note that weaves in and out to save the scent of the raspberries from being too linear, overpowering and childish. It’s not strong at all, but it’s there as a backdrop. A hint of smoke wisps tantalize this perfume and the addition of any type of smoke always ups the ante in a fragrance. Leather introduces itself in the drydown as a wrap-around for the ever-present cooked jam. Givenchy Hot Couture No. 1 is a gourmand that’s not commonly encountered because it strives for oppulence, seduction and sensuality in a scent that is so much a gourmand yet somehow it does work in other ways. It works because of its maturity. Its not simply a tropical fruit, its a cooked fruit, tempered with visions of smoke and leather. It’s warm and inviting. Yet, it still needs the right attitude to pull it off. It’s not a young, giggly perfume. It’s one where the wearer meets you eye-to-eye, with a formidable strength. Their actions always give you the impression of what’s to come. And that’s what Hot couture No. 1 is about. It sets the groundwork and continues on its Journey. You won’t be disappointed. The longevity is quite good, lasting for a good six hours or so. Sillage is strong and really, a gentle spritz is all that’s needed. This is a perfume that warms with your body and surrounds you. For extreme decadence one day, I decided to layer Hot Couture with two other perfumes to create a Neopolitan ice cream effect. I choose Avon’s Extraordinary for the intense chocolate note, and Taylor Swift’s Wonderstruck for the vanilla. The result was pure heaven in olfactory delight. You can mix and match your perfumes to layer them to create scents that you might enjoy. Be creative and have fun! This is a perfume that would work well in the evening, going out, for leisure or for the week-ends.

I was hooked on this at first smell. Nothing else smells like it. It starts out very sweet, but the spiciness comes out upon drydown, after which it smells sweet, spicy and animistic in almost equal measure. My hubby swears there's chocolate in this, and I agree that the sweetness makes this worthy of being called gourmand. I also agree with Awesomeness that a little goes a long way. It lasts a long time and the sillage is great too. I think this is good enough quality and unusual enough to appeal to niche fragrance fans.

I've hesitated sampling Haute Couture No 1 several times because I just didn't like how it smelled out of the bottle - it's all sweet berries on top. However, I decided to take the plunge and I'm quite surprised. No 1 is much darker & more full-bodied than I expected. Although the berries don't dry away quickly, the sweetness is tempered by the heart and base. In the heart of the fragrance, there is a lovely vetiver & pepper heart that is so nice, so different, a bit similar to EL Sensuous Noir. I also get a smokey, incense-like impression from this fragrance, although the listed notes really don't suggest this experience. In spite of the impression of the top notes, Hot Couture No. 1 is not a fragrance for the kiddies. It's got warmth & OOMPH that is unique for a contemporary fruity scent. On warm skin, this fragrance really blooms! It is a bit smokey with an almost incense quality, yet has a sweet & fruity character. I think that summarizes the scent nicely. It's warm ... no, it's HOT! :) And it's dark ... these are dark berries that may be poisonous - not the berries your grandma would serve to you in a pretty dish with whipped cream on top. Hot Couture No 1 has presence on my skin - a little goes a long way - although it does not have a lot of throw. The longevity is outstanding - in the 10+ hour range. Even the next day, after a shower, a fresh application of a different scent seems to activate the base of this one! And I still get that incense-like impression. Hot Couture comes in a number of variations, and I have the first -- Hot Couture No 1 with the lady on the bottle. The other variations are reported to be not as good. I believe Jacques Cavallier and Alberto Moraillis are credited with No 1, which is now discontinued btw. I would buy again, certainly, provided I can find a good price. BTW, Emanuel Ungaro Apparition is a smell-alike - not exactly similar but a price-friendly substitute with a berry accord that dries well into the base. EL Wood Mystique is also similar, although composed of berries & wood and terribly more expensive. Ignore the nay-sayers on this one ... try it if the thought of a smokey & sweet berry fragrance appeals to you. 21 Jan 2011

The bottle is amazing. I love the Art Deco motif seen through the bottle front. To me, it is one of Serge Mansau’s many masterpieces. Here we are talking about the designer behind Tocade and Alchimie (Rochas), Oscar, Claude Montana, Organza (Givenchy) and Dolce Vita (Dior). To mention a few - do feel free to continue. He has a unique style, which I regard as something between simplistic, sculptural and romantic. Take Kenzo Flower: a simple design with an organic vibe and a romantic flower motif added. Or the sculptural Parfum de Peau. He leaves a distinct signature in all his work. This bottle suits the name of the perfume so well. Haute couture should be something classic yet contemporary, unique and handmade. Fitted for the individual who is going to wear it. Just perfect. The juice itself is really nice. I adore the fruity/berry aspect in the beginning, but it is the heart that does it for me. The vetiver and magnolia in perfect balance. It feels so sophisticated to wear this when the two notes show up. I would love it to last longer on my skin. After four to five hours I smell mostly musk. Year 2, 188/365

Illusions, past, youth. That's what shoots through my mind in milliseconds when I smell Hot Couture. It reminds me of the late 90s. Of Jil. Not without reason, as Jil Sander released one of her best fragrances in 1997. How much I wanted to have it. But I was young and couldn't afford it. My then-boyfriend probably couldn't read between the lines either. Bad luck for me. I myself am not a fan of Givenchy perfumes (except for Ange ou Demon and Amarige), I find all that I know (and I know almost all of them) too ordinary, without reluctance. You immediately notice that No.1 is a Millennium child. It has similarities with the fragrance with the 3 letters. -Bergamot, raspberry, vetiver, amber, sandalwood- Even though there is a resemblance to Jil, H. C. smells more refined. Not so old, musty, heavy. (Fruity!? Sweet!? According to the diagram "fragrance type," this is certainly NOT!??!) It starts spicy balsamic, a bit unruly - but this is dosed just right here and thus stands out from today's (mainstream) Tütü waters. It smells of forest. Of nature. Warm and woody. The perfume develops more and more into a well-perceptible skin scent. The longevity is optimal at about 6-7 hours. 3 more sprays make it an evening fragrance and very well suited for the cooler days.

Uncommented Fragrances No. 43 In reference to Erik H. Erikson's famous work on identity and life cycle and the stage model of psychosocial development in humans, I propose a bold thesis: psychosocial development includes the development of fragrance preferences. Thin ice? I take the risk. The first stage of psychosocial development according to Erikson is based on the development of basic trust (or basic mistrust) and is generally completed by the age of 1 or 2. What role could fragrances play here? Quite obviously, a crucial one, considering studies on the infant's attachment to the mother (or father) through smell, feelings of security, scents of food, skin, etc. To avoid opening a sociological fundamental discussion about the value of psychosocial studies for fragrances, I will skip further phases and focus on the stage of childhood and early adolescence, where the desire to participate in the world of adults is a particularly important aspect of identity formation, which could lead to the "learning" of the father's aftershave (or even fragrance) and the mother's perfume, both of which have a formative influence. I, for one, smelled a vetiver fragrance for the first time here (Guerlain Vetiver). Undoubtedly, experiences in the development of intimacy, partnership, and relationships (stage 6) also lead to certain fragrances being "learned," desired, and chosen. What did the scent of the first girlfriend or boyfriend smell like? What does intimacy, skin, hair smell like? How did the desired other smell? Fragrances with strong statements and erotic promises to the opposite sex are likely to be the preferred choice. There is hardly any room for fragrances with vetiver. Only at the stage of mature adulthood are we apparently willing to engage (again) with "difficult" fragrances, using scent not (only) as an erotic stimulant. At the latest here, MY story with vetiver began, triggered by memories of my childhood (see above). Vetiver is a complex plant, and although it usually possesses a very masculine clarity, it is demanding and pretentious. Hardly any fragrance is discussed as frequently as to whether it can be worn by young people (I consciously do not say men). What astonishes me about this discussion is the fact that vetiver in perfumery has never really gone out of fashion (in the strictest sense of the word) and is rediscovered by each generation. The incredible success of the cumbersome Encre Noire can only be explained this way: vetiver is in demand, in ever new variations. While the classic earthy vetiver fragrances, some perceived as grassy-musty (Guerlain Vetiver, Carven Vetiver in both old and new formulations, Givenchy Vetyver, CdG Vettiveru, Lubin Le Vetiver, Creed Original Vetiver, Etro Vetiver, Annick Goutal Vetiver in the old formula, Vetiver de Frederic, Dominguez Vetiver Hombre, MPG Route du Vetiver and Racine, Czech & Speake Vetiver Vert, Mazzolari Vetiver, Piver Vetiver, Royall Lyme Vetyver, and Floris Vetiver) tend to have a dedicated fan club (of which I consider myself a part), they hardly attract new, younger audiences without further ado, while postmodern variations seem to succeed much better. These include the "black" and bitter vetivers like Chanel Sycomore, Lalique Encre Noire, and the vetiver from Dior's Privée line, perhaps also Grey Vetiver by Tom Ford. Not simple representatives. Even if they are somewhat successful, they are unlikely to be fragrances that inspire very young buyers to make their first fragrance purchase spontaneously. In most cases, prior experience or maturity is likely needed (see above). Thus, a bold marketing decision. I will not further consider the great success of a vetiver offshoot, which was initiated by the clever-genius Terre d'Hermès: grapefruit, patchouli, pepper, cedar, and...vetiver. This has become an endless story. Currently, I particularly enjoy the outsiders in the grand concert that interpret vetiver in a softer version (Prada Infusion de Vetiver, Diptyque Vetyverio, Lubin Le Vetiver Bluff and Itasca, 4711 Vetyver & Bergamot, Monotheme Vetiver Bourbon, TdC Sel de Vetiver, Malle Vetiver Extraordinaire, L'Artisan Timbuktu and Coeur de Vetiver Sacré, AC Vetiver Fatal, Armani Vetiver Babylone, Bois Vetiver Ambrato, Profumi di Firenze Fresco di Vetiver, L'Occitane Eau de Vetyver). This last group, which includes fascinatingly diverse representatives and many unnamed, must also include Jo Malone's Vetyver. The softer vetiver fragrances often use vetiver oil from high-quality, gently rounded Haitian vetiver or even the famous Vetiver Bourbon from Réunion. It seems to me that this oil was also processed in Malone's Vetyver, undoubtedly also vetiveryl acetate, which apparently leads to a more elegant unfolding of the woody-earthy notes. As a result, the earthiness, the mustiness is almost entirely absent; what remains, however, is the herbaceous-green component of vetiver, which gives the fragrance its unique charm. Essential for me is a citrus top note (lemon, bergamot, or neroli, etc.), which is present here. Mugwort could further emphasize the balsamic note of this fragrance. Essentially, it is a simple, charming, convincing fragrance without a long list of ingredients: plain, clear, concentrated. In conclusion, it can be stated that the aforementioned representatives, and particularly the fragrance mentioned here, essentially provide a good entry point into the world of vetiver, and that fragrances with a Vetiver Bourbon component tend to appear softer and rounder, less earthy-dark, and thus should be attractive for vetiver newcomers. Jo Malone's Vetyver could thus be a good alternative for those who find vetiver too herbaceous (top note) or too earthy (heart and base note) in all but certain phases of its fragrance development.

Another pretty, sensual, fresh rose scent with three exceptional rose qualities in it. Like they say in their website, the rose is the ultimate icon of love. What makes this rose perfume different from others, for example from Rose Kabuki Eau de Parfum , is Blackcurrant bud absolute and Basil in the opening and that vibrant, gentle green and herbal aroma is lingering with enchanting bouquet of roses. I love the airiness and feather-light texture, especially since the scent lasts and projects well and it has a glowing and addictive sillage. Patchouli and moss in the base are bright and subtle which sets this fragrance apart from the usual Rose Patchouli combo. Givenchy’s La Collection Particulière has surprised me with the versatility of course but with some uniqueness and unisex style as well. I have 5 from that collection and Cœur Fou )and Oiseau Rare ) is the most feminine of them. There is something very special in all of them and especially Noctambule , Fantasque and Enflammé are definitely unisex, more of them in the following statements/reviews. Thank you for reading, I hope you liked my review. I would appreciate if you follow me on my IG and/or YouTube (English subtitles available): @ninamariahperfumes It gives me a lot of motivation to write more

Clearly, the rose/roses are absolutely the focus. My mother has fragrant roses in her garden. One of the yellow varieties has an almost pink edge. This scent smells very similar to that for me. It has a bit more acidity for me. And then somehow with the acidity, a tiny hint of powdered sugar comes to mind. The sour currants had a bit of powdered sugar residue before they were added. Somehow, a fresh scent comes in, iris? Bright musk? Does moss smell that fresh? I don't know. A sovereign rose scent, intense and with decent sillage. However, for me, it remains just a sample. I don't need to go in search of a bottle.

A somewhat surprising scent. At first, I think it’s a somewhat light and already-seen rose fragrance. I have the impression that it is a bit watercolor-like. But the rest surprised me a little. I didn’t expect it to be so present. There is a nice acidity that accompanies it and ensures that the scent is not too sweet and very rosy. It is this slightly tangy side that keeps the fragrance fresh for a long time. Even the base note of the perfume remains a bit sparkling. By the way, that’s my favorite part. Good longevity for a fragrance of this kind. I was also complemented by people who are not necessarily familiar with perfumes. Overall, I was delighted by this rose, which may not have revolutionized the world of perfumes, but gives me a smile and good mood when I wear it. Overall, a cheerful scent.

An incredibly fresh and realistic garden rose scent. Soft, and not overpowering, and surprisingly long lasting for a cologne and for a Jo Malone perfume. If “romantic” had a smell, this would be it. I actually chose this as my wedding perfume where we got married in a garden in early spring, and it felt so fitting for the day. I just wish it wasn’t limited edition; I’m already rationing my bottle and saving it for special occasions like our wedding anniversary just to savour the juice. It really is such a beautiful fragrance.

You can collect old furniture or pictures, but only a fragrance can leap into your nose so powerfully that you are instantly whisked back 100, 50, or 30 years. L'interdit is such a fragrance. You spray it on, and you instantly transform into Jackie Kennedy in a pink suit and pillbox hat. Or into Audrey Hepburn in pointed stilettos and a flowing cocktail dress. Or into Grace Kelly in a brown raglan coat and turban hat. L'Interdit is totally retro, as if it had been frozen in 1960 and suddenly brought back like old wine. Due to the aldehydes, it may resemble Chanel No. 5 at first glance, but then it is slowed down by the jasmine that mixes in and gives it that 60s vibe. I bought the stuff because I am hopelessly nostalgic; I don't even particularly like it. But sometimes, when I crave a jasmine tea with Jackie, Audrey, and Grace, I spray myself with it.

A cloud of gentle aldehydes, delicate green notes, and an indefinable floral sweetness greets me right from the start, with the sweet floral notes condensing into a soft, slightly soapy bouquet that has a noticeable retro touch. However, everything remains light, floating, but also somehow pale and undefined. The sweet floral scent with its slightly old-fashioned nuance starts to annoy me after a while (though I am not a fan of romantic sweet floral fragrances), as there is no further development. I also looked at the comments on the original, which were almost all very taken with the creation dedicated to Audrey Hepburn. I do not know the original, but given the reduced pyramid of this harmless-innocent, somewhat boring, and very fleeting scent, I doubt that the 2007 version has much in common with the original. I also cannot imagine that Audrey Hepburn would have enjoyed the Les Parfums Mythiques version of L'Interdit. This is not a fragrance for adult women, but rather for very young women in their teenage years. I myself have always steered clear of this type of perfume since my teenage years, and so I feel with Les Parfums Mythiques L'Interdit like a sheep dressed as a lamb.

On my search for a photorealistic tea scent, I tried Demeter Black Tea. My ultimate goal is to smell the scent of the limited edition Sea Breeze tea scent (Iced Tea if I remember correctly. I live in Japan and I used that scent religiously when I was in high school, in 2019) which was a perfect mix of slight sweetness and a good tea scent, with a hint of natural freshness that some tea often has. Out of the bottle, it sure did smell like a good unsweetened tea, almost herbal like the tea leaves. However, on my skin, I found the scent becoming more and more like a generic musk—something you’d find in any masculine-leaning fragrances, sharp and clean, a bit woody but not much. In the end, I must say this one did not satisfy my craving for a good tea scent. Not particularly a bad scent, but not impressive.

I am shocked that no one has written anything about this great fragrance yet. This is a wonderfully green, unobtrusive scent that can be beautifully worn by both genders. For me, it's the best from the Rock of Ages line and the one I definitely wanted. It is so light and casual. I find it simply highlights the natural beauty of its wearer. One could almost say it is a perfume for those who do not want to smell overly perfumed. I often catch myself while wearing it thinking, >Ah, it smells so good here...

Dear readers, this perfume is like a beautiful black panther lurking around the next corner - ready to pounce and attack at any moment. Wow, it struck me immediately and brought me down. Very dark, very mysterious, and very, very sensual - erotic. But let’s allow the story to take its beginning... The Davana flower seems to me as if it has been submerged in whisky, in a very good, expensive, and smoky whisky. Patchouli and vetiver are also right there, claiming their space - what a battle of the individual high-quality ingredients. This perfume captivates you immediately like the razor-sharp teeth of the panther, and the sweet pain of surrender makes me drift away. One should directly provide the appropriate weapon permit with this scent. My dear ladies, it will paralyze every man, incapacitate him, or create an absolutely surrendering effect - I promise. It will warm up a bit after about an hour due to body heat, losing none of its presence. The lurking and dangerous essence inherent in the fragrance remains; not every man dares to approach it. For me, it is also a scent for a woman with full and conscious femininity; it leaves a truly intoxicating scent trail wherever "she" touches. The fragrance lasts easily 8-10 hours, is not cheap at 195 euros - but worth every euro. The bottle comes in a beautiful box like a precious piece of jewelry. Whoever has once embraced this scent will fall for it, a truly extraordinary blend. Dark with the mysterious promise of perhaps very unusual encounters, impactful, sensual, or even a little dangerous. Psssst, my gentlemen - Christmas is coming soon, and surely an exquisite gift for your own black panther at home or the gentle, cuddly kitten. For me, a beautiful, new, and surprisingly different perfume for a very long time.

This is genuinely what u get when u actually get a pumpkin spice latte to drink during the fall !! this scent actually has the coffee aspect of the latte that other scents usually forget !! its super strong and it lasts for a long time and you dont need to drown yourself in it to smell it,, or u could and smell strongly of coffee which is fine too because at least youll smell like a nice cafe

This is a wonderful, photorealistic pumpkin spice scent. Smells exactly like you're holding a Starbucks PSL under your nose or have freshly made pumpkin muffins in the room. Sweet, spicy, creamy, with a hint of coffee. Very comforting and cozy. Perfect for the fall and winter months. I got the perfume oil roll-on of this scent and the sillage is moderate while the longevity is about 7ish hours.

Persil fans and lovers of clean man scents, spray strength, and fabric softeners take note: the laundry detergent perfume range is expanding! Previously, The Muse and what feels like 70% of the portfolio of the US brand Clean shared the top spots in the white-fresh-synthetic league, but Jo Malone (as already mentioned in the comment, very atypically) is sending Musk Momento to challenge the big players for their territory. Both lavender and cedarwood are often placed in the wardrobe to keep moths and other textile-damaging pests at bay. Therefore, the association with fresh laundry is not far-fetched. I perceive the lavender only quite subtly as an undertone; the synthetic-woody freshness is too strong. No moth survives here! The almost obligatory musk comes on my skin neither powdery nor sweet but rather powder-dry. Some of the "dry" iris scents go in the same direction. If you like this type of fragrance (I do), you will find pleasure in Musk Momento (I do!). On the Jo Malone homepage, there is the quote "inspired by a ceramic soap dish" - that fits 100%. However, it strongly reminds me of "Pure Soap | Clean," although the Malone is drier and lacks sweetness/floral notes. This makes the Malone, in my opinion, more unisex, even though most men in my environment are not so lavish with fabric softener or scent beads (by the way: Lenor fresh cotton smells almost the same!). Meanwhile, my husband was used for the 1:1 comparison test, uh, consolidated, and he noted "a bit sweeter" for the Clean scent. For little to no difference, the price difference (Malone: RRP €74 for 30ml versus Clean 60ml for ~€40) and availability - the Malone is limited - might also be interesting. I find the bottle almost a bit too "romantic" for the harsh cleanliness of the scent; a silver instead of a matte golden cap would have been more appropriate. Otherwise, it is typically simple. Longevity is very good, by the way! After 5+ hours on the skin, still very good.

For years, I struggled with vetiver fragrances; Guerlain's Vetiver was too omnipresent, too many people around me wore it, even those who were anything but close to me, whom I often wished far, far away in vain, and who did not stop bothering me with their presence and this, their scent. I confess, I hated this fragrance, and even today I still cannot approach it somewhat unprejudiced to judge it somewhat objectively - so I’d rather leave it alone, for now. Despite all my rejection of Guerlain's Vetiver, my attitude towards vetiver fragrances in general has completely changed. Previously, I had lumped them all together and dismissed them with the verdict: I don’t like it, I can’t stand it; I must now admit: I actually like them, I can certainly appreciate them, just not that one. But who knows, time heals all wounds, and perhaps one day I will even come to like that one, I am not so far from it anymore. The vetiver fragrance that is to be discussed here is one that I liked from the very beginning, yes, one that I appreciate and admire. In 1959, the House of Givenchy launched two fragrances for men, Monsieur de Givenchy and Eau de Vétiver - the later Vetyver. Both were composed by Fabrice Fabron, who had already created L'Interdit for Givenchy two years earlier and also crafted great classics like L'Air du Temps, Le Dix, and Baghari. The Eau de Vétiver was likely created at the special request of the great designer Hubert de Givenchy, who, presumably inspired by Carven's Vetiver, which had caused a stir two years earlier - in 1957 - wanted to have his own vetiver fragrance. Two years later - in 1961 - Guerlain finally launched its Vetiver and quickly overshadowed its two predecessors. Vetyver remained in Givenchy's catalog until 1995, selling moderately, but as long as Hubert de Givenchy directed the house, it continued to be produced. He, the immensely elegant, distinguished, and good-looking man of the world and master of fashion, is said to have worn it all those years. When he finally retired in 1995, his Vetyver also disappeared from the market, much to the dismay of many perfume enthusiasts who unanimously considered it the best of all vetivers. Thirteen years later, it suddenly reappeared, launched together with many classics of the house in a series called 'Les Mythiques', and aligned with the latest IFRA regulations. According to those who still remembered the old Vetyver, the new one is just as good as ever (the other fragrances in this series are excellently reformulated!). Untested, I immediately ordered it and was instantly thrilled: a truly magnificent vetiver fragrance. A classic chypre combined with three different variations of this root that reveals a new facet in the top note, as well as in the heart and base notes - from the fresh, cooling start, through a damp, green phase, to the smoky-earthy finish, accompanied by bergamot, coriander, sandalwood, patchouli, and oakmoss. Everything is wonderfully intertwined, perfectly balanced, and exudes class, thoroughly. A scent of refined understatement, a fragrance for the well-groomed gentleman with a sense of elegant yet discreet luxury. However, it is not a fragrance for the hordes of sales representatives, office workers, or anyone else engaged in daily occupations, for the masses, that is. No, Givenchy's Vetyver is - similar to Eau d'Hermès - more of a fragrance for those who have arrived in the circle of those who let others work for them, and whose arrival and (supposed) nonchalance find a fragrant expression in this perfume. I myself certainly do not belong to the ranks of Hubert de Givenchy or Robert Dumas-Hermès, but a bit of their nonchalantly displayed calm and composure, yes, superiority is embodied in this fragrance and can also transfer to others, even if they are just small lights who have to go about their daily bread earning, just like me. Is Givenchy's Vetyver an elitist fragrance? Basically yes, and if it weren't so good, I would mark this as a flaw, but it possesses so much class, so much elegance like a tailored robe from Givenchy, that I instantly forget my elitist skepticism when the aroma of this fragrance wafts into my nose. And one truly feels better dressed when wearing this fragrance; at least, that’s how it is for me. However, since a fragrance cannot replace being well-dressed, it can at best complement it, a certain degree of dress-up is necessary: a pressed shirt and not the most worn-out pants should suffice. One more word about the longevity of the fragrance: it is rather modest by today’s standards. The scent retreats to the skin quite quickly, but remains there for a long time, surrounding the wearer with a persistently fine and subtle aroma. The projection of the fragrance is low, but an offensive or even intrusive perfume for men was not conceivable at that time - Chanel's Pour Monsieur or Dior's Eau Sauvage are similar examples of the expectations of that era regarding how 'man' should smell, namely discreetly. Back then, 'man' would still enter a restaurant before the lady to arrange everything, help her out of her coat, pull the chair back from the table for her to sit down, and above all, give her perfume the due space, namely the whole. That a man smelled as intensely of perfume as a woman was simply not desired, nor did it correspond to the typical role understanding of the time. Thus, we should not expect from this fragrance, and from others from this era as well, the qualities we know from the 'powerhouse' fragrances of the 70s and 80s - they had others, which were not necessarily worse - quite the opposite.

Givenchy has recently re-released a series of already discontinued fragrances, allowing me to test this one as well. My impression was rather negative. In the top note, the vetiver was softened by something creamy alongside the bergamot, resulting in a subtly elegant scent. However, soon the fragrance flipped to its opposite. The vetiver note became dark and scratchy, somewhat resembling Lalique's Encré Noir. Both styles have their merit, but not in the same perfume. It is rightly that Guerlain's vetiver fragrance has prevailed against this competition in the market.

This review is based on a 10 ml mini bottle, purchased directly from Givenchy as part of the discovery set (3 for $99). This bird is not all that rare. Simply put, it is a very nice white floral perfume, albeit very delicate. There are some ancillary notes to embellish the main floral notes. But that is it! Givenchy website lists pepper accord as the opening note. My unsophisticated nose gets a mild dark shadow of something before Oiseau Rare plunges into a clean white floral note. This single floral heart note comes from the pittosporum flower accord. It is a white floral somewhere in between tuberose and jasmine. Towards the end when the white floral notes disappear, you can get the soft woody vanilla base notes. It is an elegant perfume befitting the collection it comes from. But in comparison to its brothers and sisters, the Oiseau Rare is very plain. It is almost a soliflor of pittosporum. Givenchy lists the intensity of Oiseau Rare as above average (3/4). But I think it is appropriate to rate it as mild or moderate (2/4). It lasts 4-6 hours on my skin, but the soft base notes last a few hours longer. The sillage is appropriate for a mild perfume, but detectable in the wake for the first few hours. In summary, Oiseau Rare is a nice elegant perfume. But it is not worth $320 unless you have a unique fascination with pittosporum flower. Spend the money elsewhere.

This fragrance is simply indescribable. Fresh and spicy. Pleasant and intense. Anyone looking to take a risk should get this scent. I first bought it in 2022 and have only received compliments for it. The floral scent is very intense at first. After about 20 minutes, it fades away and the vanilla scent comes forward. The woody note combined with the vanilla note is a wonderful combination. Elegant and striking at the same time.

I was a bit surprised at first to find that the apple note, or what I assume is the apple note, came across to me as a bit orange juice like as well despite it having no orange notes. I had bought this along with Mulled Cider, another scent from this brand with very similar notes. And while Mulled Cider was cinnamon heavy, this one was much more fruit heavy. I'm not really sure how to feel about it. At first I was a bit disappointed, but it's certainly growing on me. It's synthetic for sure, but if you don't mind that, then I feel like this smells a lot like store bought apple cider. Overall, I can see someone enjoying this if they're okay with more synthetic smells!

What can I say about it? "Pomander" was not a term I was familiar with before this fragrance. Of course, I know the pre-Christmas tradition of studding oranges & apples with cloves to create a cozy atmosphere. Of course is also my keyword. I have rarely smelled such an authentic and 0 synthetic fragrance composition in a perfume. It even went so far that I went to my well-stocked spice rack to verify the authenticity. But let's take it step by step. I got a 5 ml test spray from Demeter / The Library of Fragrance. I will do this more often in the future to save myself from durability flops like with "Almond". That was a good investment of 5 euros. Soon, the larger bottle will follow, especially considering the upcoming cool and cold seasons. When you apply the fragrance, it feels like you are grinding your spices for Christmas red cabbage. Cinnamon, allspice, a hint of nutmeg, but ABOVE ALL, clove wafts into your nose. And not in the slightest bit restrained. "Pomander" goes all out right away and remains consistent for several hours. A hint of fruity apple also joins in. The amber note mentioned in the fragrance pyramid only becomes noticeable to me as the scent fades. The best thing about this fragrance: It is both a scent that can create a wonderful, realistic Christmas atmosphere in the home but is also quite wearable for open-minded people. I am fortunate to work in an office where my colleagues enjoy analyzing, testing, and showing interest in my fragrances. In short, they are open to new scents. Therefore, "Pomander" will definitely be tried out in the office. In my circle of friends, people are already enthusiastic about the natural charm of this EdC. Anyone who is not interested in this type of spice combination, does not like red cabbage, or generally does not want to smell like a spiced apple should steer clear of this. Everyone else should give this little unknown a chance. The sillage is fantastic; a spritz is completely sufficient. It lasts for several hours, becoming milder and warmer over time. If you don't like it as a perfume, you still have a wonderful room fragrance for the holidays. Well done, Demeter/TLOF. THIS is how an authentic scent should be.

Eau de Givenchy Rosée, comfortable as a hug. It is a lovely perfume, versatile and has a florality that I love a lot. It's not groundbreaking, but the simplicity captivates me. I appreciate Givenchy perfumes a lot, however, this is the one I like the most. The musky side is cozy and perfect for hot days.

My first Givenchy fragrance and I quite like it. In the opening, there's freshness from the tea and mandarin, then mainly rose and water hyacinth take over. The latter also immerses the rose blooms in cool water. A bit of musk adds slight longevity. A light, fresh summer scent for days above 30 degrees - off to the cool water with Eau de Givenchy Rosee!

After shoveling snow in the morning and enduring the gray, dreary weather of the day, there was a longing in the evening for more colorful, sunnier shores. Morocco is, for me, a synonym for wanderlust of a similar quality to Janosch's Panama. The travel guide for this comes from the Demeter Library of Fragrance: Morocco from the Destination Collection - The scent had been tested a few times, sporadically worn as a "sleep scent." In my memory, it was shelved somewhere between the epic Dahlia by Jesus del Pozo, the elegant version of Meharees, quotes from Feminite du bois, and Bois Marocain for Dummies, with the note "mostly harmless." And then ignorance hit me with a floral fist right in the nose. Not at all corresponding to my expected scent profile. No stroll through a painted souk with spices offered for sale in open baskets. No sweet-spicy mint tea. Not even the slightest hint of dry Saharan air. Instead, a real powerhouse of numbing, toxic tropical flowers. Overgrown and waxy, oily and shiny. I must not have paid enough attention to the travel guide, and the day trip did not lead to Djemaa el Fna, but to the 'Valley of Roses.' Only roses are present, so baroque, even brash at times, not. Accompanied by a sweet, almost shy jasmine, contrary to its usual nature, no more than a footnote. Neroli, a scribbled note at the edge. I was firmly stuck, playing Hercule Poirot, without his famous nose. The small gray cells for scent recognition seemed anesthetized. They are not lilies, too little pollen-sharp. Cloves, contrary to the first association, more in their spice form. Spices, yes. A fine powder, very lovely. No robust cinnamon, no invigorating pepper. Sweet, cardamom, anise. Or is it the triad of pimento? The perfume encyclopedia was consulted, under the keyword fragrance notes I read: Spices. Great. And in between, the little Belgian detective made his appearance on my mental stage, smoothing an imaginary, resistant hair in his brilliantine-shiny hairstyle. The evening progressed without enlightenment. Sleep, as long as I couldn't assign this scent to any botanical source, seemed unlikely, especially since Morocco - for a cologne published by Demeter - proved surprisingly long-lasting. The website of Demeter was consulted as another source, and what did I find there? Spices. "Freshly ground Moroccan spices in a 1000-year-old open-air market." Enlightening. And exactly what I had originally expected. No word about the floral component I was searching for. As further inspiration, they also mentioned a song by Crosby, Stills & Nash. Marrakesh Express. I didn't know it. With nimble fingers, I searched for the lyrics (the song itself, by the way, is not really my thing) and what did it say: "I smell the garden in your hair" Hair! Hair! Hair oil! Strongly scented hair oil! Makassar! An age-old hair cosmetic traditionally scented with ylang-ylang! Ylang-ylang! Just imagine all the exclamation marks as little light bulbs that finally lit up for me. The dear soul finally found its peace and decided the next morning to verify the scent of ylang-ylang with the existing bottle of essential oil. This clue turned out to be the solution to the puzzle. Well, my trip to Morocco didn't go as planned, but it was exciting and educational for me. Sometimes it is not so easy to get to the bottom of scents without a component list or directions. Sometimes you expect one thing and find something completely unexpected. But isn't that the exciting part of olfactory road trips? Morocco is a very floral, almost floriental scent, with a hint of fine spices. That's roughly how I imagine it was in the 1930s in Casablanca sitting at the barber's, hearing the noisy hustle and bustle of the market outside, the flowing garments of the halaq emanating a delicate scent of cardamom and pimento. And Hercule winks at you with makassar-scented hair in the speckled mirror conspiratorially.

This smells exactly like the warm milk with anise that whe drink on cold winter days.The drydown is a sweet anisy caramel scent. The heliotrope makes it a bit powdery but not to much. A nice scent for cold winterdays when you need a comforting smell

You know, I always find it quite difficult with Jo Malone fragrances. Especially this year, I've tested quite a few, but apart from the really good Rare Teas, I haven't really liked much from Jo Malone. Well, "not liked" isn't quite right; let's say I wasn't really convinced. Sure, there were some good scents among them, but with some, I felt like something was always missing. Maybe I should actually layer these fragrances together, because that's what they're known for, but with over 20 fragrances, there are almost endless possibilities. I could calculate it, but I was really bad at some mathematical topics like probability. How was it again with "drawing and replacing"? It gets even more complicated when you want to consider certain things, like that a maximum of three of the 20 fragrances can be combined (and these three fragrances cannot be replaced during layering, but can be afterwards, of course)? You can calculate it if you want... or can... :D I, on the other hand, would probably sit around for hundreds of days scribbling on paper something like: fragrance 1 combined with fragrance 2 and fragrance 3. Then, fragrance 1 with fragrance 2 and fragrance 4. Fragrance 1 with fragrance 2 and fragrance 5,… until I eventually reached fragrance 20 with fragrance 18 and fragrance 19 or something… :DD (which would then be too much and therefore wrong, because I would have already had fragrance 20 with 18 and 19 when I had fragrance 18 with 19 and 20! Waaaaaaaaaaah…..!!!!!!!!). … my head already hurts. At least it's nice that the fragrance here carries the subtitle Tea Fragrance Blends… Tea! I love tea! That makes me feel better already. Let's go! The fragrance: The fragrance starts for me sweetly milky with caramel and indeed the milk, while in the background it is briefly citrusy due to the bergamot, but this only lasts for a very short time. Then, however, the actually beautiful caramel-milk scent is totally disturbed by a note that somehow just doesn't want to fit with the rest: anise. The anise is very clearly noticeable here, and unfortunately, this is not just in the top note, where one might have hoped it would disappear afterwards, but it carries through the entire fragrance development. Later in the base, you can smell some musk and slightly powdery vanilla, which actually fit very well with the milky sweet caramel, but are too disturbed by the anise. It may also smell a little like tea with (a lot of) milk, but the tea note itself (if it even exists) is hardly detectable. Only after over an hour does the anise become noticeably weaker, so that one can start to enjoy the fragrance somewhat (this especially applies to those who don't like anise very much. Everyone who likes anise will get a great fragrance anyway). And only after several hours is the anise almost completely gone. Then, after many hours, the fragrance even smells very nice, milky caramel sweet, soft, and very pleasant. The sillage and longevity: The projection of the fragrance is low; it hardly stands out, let alone leaves a scent cloud behind. The longevity is long; it lasted over eight hours on me. The bottle: The bottle is rectangular, somewhat narrow, and has a thick glass bottom. On the front, there is a label with a frame. The label features the name, brand, and logo as usual. The cap is chrome-plated and cylindrical. It looks simple, but it's quite nice. Well. At first, I was jumping for joy when I finally got my hands on a sample of this fragrance, as I am very curious about anything that contains tea. And yet, I had to experience two disappointments with this fragrance right away. First, there is the missing tea scent. While this may be disappointing, it's not so bad in itself, as the sweet caramel notes combined with the milk and vanilla at least smell good. The second disappointment is the initial anise scent, which almost ruins the top and heart notes. Because the caramel and milk smell beautifully sweet and pleasant, but the anise is present and simply comes off as piercingly unpleasant. This impression lasts about an hour until one can start to enjoy the fragrance somewhat, as the anise thankfully loses strength. A little more patience, and the fragrance finally becomes really good. If the anise were completely absent, Sweet Milk would have become a much nicer fragrance. In any case, the fragrance smells autumnal, but it's not too heavy, so it could also be used in spring. Too weak for going out, it is therefore just an inconspicuous daytime or leisure fragrance for oneself. You can certainly test it, but you should somewhat like anise or have patience to enjoy the fragrance later with a less powerful anise scent. Perhaps it works much better with another Jo Malone fragrance? Speaking of which: Has anyone actually calculated the number of possible combinations if you want to layer 20 Jo Malones with a maximum of three fragrances? :DD As I said, I was terrible at certain math topics… :D

I was a little disappointed with the scent. Yes, I expected sweet condensed milk and did not find it again, but that is not so important. I don’t smell any tea (why the name Tea Fragrance Blends?), but I do find all the fragrance notes listed in the fragrance pyramid, except for the bergamot - and that is also the problem. Maybe you also have "no-go" fragrance notes? I wasn't aware of it until now, but I seem to not be a fan of anise ^_^ I can clearly smell the anise. No, it’s not selective perception - I didn’t know the fragrance pyramid while testing, but I immediately had the feeling that something was off regarding the anise, and the fragrance pyramid only confirmed that suspicion. The whole scent, in my opinion, takes on a completely different twist because of this. But even without the anise twist, the scent would not convince me much. The longevity is quite poor, and after just a few minutes, I only smell musk vanilla sugar porridge, which you can also get much cheaper. It personally reminds me of Vanilla & Anise, even though this one is not by Christine Nagel.

When my grandma - "Omma Änne" - was still alive, I sometimes visited her with my cousin, who is six years older than me. She owned two children's books: "Struwwelpeter" and the female counterpart, "Struwwelliese." I knew these books by heart. There was nothing else around. In the garden behind the house, the paths were lined with turned-over green glass bottles. Beans were grown there, among other things. Typical Ruhr area. It was actually always quite boring at her place. Sometimes, when Omma Änne was in a good mood, she would take something from the shelf above the door (we kids couldn't reach it) - sweetened condensed milk in tubes. Today it's sold as "Milchmädchen," but I don't know if it was called that back then. We got a tablespoon. Nothing more. I loved that taste; it was heavenly for me. And just like this sweetened condensed milk in tubes smells, Sweet Milk. Genius. I am five years old again, or six, seven, or eight (after that, Omma Änne moved to a senior apartment, and there was no shelf above the kitchen door anymore). I can't really detect much more, no bergamot, no heliotrope, maybe a bit of star anise. I can smell vanilla anyway. Sweetened condensed milk also smells a bit like vanilla. But that's enough; it's completely sufficient. Although I can actually imagine Sweet Milk layered well with various fragrances. Brit is good, I've noticed, or maybe with something spicy... But sometimes, such memories are simply beautiful.

A package has arrived again! Yes, yes, I know, I already have so many fragrances, what do I need with ANOTHER ONE ;-) But this one, I mean this one, I can't describe it, this one hit me right in the heart. YET AGAIN a fragrance that is indescribably beautiful. At first, I didn't even want it because I thought, oh dear walnut, what could that possibly be. This put me off a bit, because anyone who has ever bought walnuts with the shell knows that it can give a rather "different" scent experience. But no, you can't smell that. For me, it’s primarily honeysuckle, rose, tuberose, and cedar that come through. Although I must say, at first I thought there were also lily of the valley in it, because when the package arrived, I was a bit rushed, had to get to an appointment urgently, so I just quickly spritzed some on my décolletage, out the door and into the car and off. When I got to the appointment, I kept thinking who or what smells so wonderful like lily of the valley? It didn't even occur to me that it could be me, because I had actually sprayed Paris by Balenciaga on for this appointment, and there are no lily of the valley in that. Only now back home could I finally dedicate myself to the fragrance. It is a delight to smell this perfume; it is a noble, finely floral, full-bodied, soft, oriental, irresistible scent cloud that surrounds me, and the interplay of the woody notes (which you can only sense) with the vanilla, which peacefully lays over everything, really makes you lean back comfortably and think, nothing bad can happen, I’m wearing Organza. Although the name doesn’t quite fit, because Organza is a delicately fragrant fabric, this perfume is quite a striking fellow, but not overwhelmingly loud, rather as described above, cozy, warm, soft, and sensual. So where do I go now, so that EVERYONE can smell it? Because - I just have to say: I love it! That's it ;-)

I have once again snagged a scent that no one else has here. And I found it purely by "chance." In the large city pharmacy, there was a promotional event for Demeter products. And there were also 5 fragrances in completely unremarkable bottles. Pharmacy-medicine-like. They hardly stand out at all! At least for "non-noses." But I spotted them right away and had to test them. And the Iris scent that is now mine immediately appealed to me. And for 5 euros for 30 ml, you can't go wrong. Now I'm wearing it, and it is a true delight for the nose. If the scent has a color, then it's deep violet with a powdery-floral freshness that comes across as very natural in every respect. And although only one or two ingredients were used, it goes very deep (ultraviolet). Not just superficial and run-of-the-mill, you get exactly what it says on the label. And the images form in the mind to go along with it. April clouds and sunshine in a beautiful, humid grove with lush blooming irises by the water. And the scent of the sea of flowers.
