Slightly cool, fresh, powdery, and VIOLET!

I really like the Dahlia range - and I wondered if I also needed Initiale. But the first spray clearly says "Yes." Like its sisters, it carries a subtle elegance, but it pleasantly stands out with its citrus freshness. The right invigorating scent to start the day - the initial spark, so to speak. Its citrus notes remain soft and not sour. The rose and jasmine cushion the slightly sweet orange and form a harmonious duo. Creamy sandalwood adds a cozy closeness to Initiale. The perfect daytime fragrance with a touch of elegance - without feeling "dressed up." It has become my "favorite dahlia." The longevity is only average - but I enjoy reapplying it from time to time. Overall, a cheerful scent that also resonates with those around me.

Ange ou Demon the perfume is a mysterious, seductive scent. The Edp is for me the perfect autumn fragrance, thanks to the juicy mandarin and patchouli that exude an earthy aroma of fallen leaves. The opening is a delicious, not too bitter mandarin, blended with ethereal jasmine sambac. As the fragrance develops, these floral and citrus notes are replaced by patchouli and a hint of leather. The dry down is warm, amber-like, and opulent, accompanied by a touch of sweetness from vanilla. The Illicite accord offers more depth with a larger, pleasant dose of alcoholic patchouli and vanilla. Longevity is satisfactory and projection is rather moderate. There is no overpowering note that overwhelms everything. I detect neither strong jasmine nor too much sweetness or sharp patchouli. It is really well blended and balanced. What impresses me is the uniqueness and character of the fragrance. If Ange ou Demon were a woman, she would be sexy, mysterious, and at the same time confident, wearing lace under a leather jacket. Definitely a distinctive scent!

The Ange ou Démon EDP is one of my signature scents, especially in autumn and winter. With every new "demon child," I automatically feel the desire to possess it, although some flankers from recent years are far too "undemonic" for my taste. The EDP is simply a stunning, wonderful, deep, and dark fragrance that seduces and hides behind black lace. The Le Parfum is, in my opinion, already recognizable as a "demon child," but it has a bit more color and pulsating movement within it; it is somewhat more illuminated and playful, yet still sexy, floral, strong, and self-assured. For me as a man, the leather note comes through a bit more, paired with an elegant sweetness, which I really like. I find the sillage to be very strong and similarly long-lasting as its predecessor. Although I must say that the EDP almost has a unisex character for me, this one is significantly more feminine, more like pastel pink silk. I tried layering it once, which was absolutely sufficient because suddenly an angel with demon wings turned into an undefinable, strangely graceful forest gnome... I also think that this whole concept is more of a sales gimmick that hasn't been fully thought through, just like with J'Adore by Dior, where this playfulness also exists, because after layering, the fragrance loses everything that makes it special.

This fragrance needs no associative detours; it is exactly what is stated in the fragrance pyramid - only sugar, flour, and eggs are still missing - . Barely sprayed, it is immediately there: The blue box of the certain pastry company B. from H., which used to package its slightly more upscale products almost like confectionery. My grandma hands me a cookie (weren't they round once?), hoping to bribe me with it, as I am only three years old and we are traveling by train from Constance to Kiel! However, I didn’t like the sticky orange marmalade filling, so I devoured all the available salami sandwiches during the journey; I was probably sitting in piles of butter paper, as there were no plastic bags back then, and I played with the paper rubber bands, “flitschen.” I only remember being very impressed that at every stop, vendors with drinks came directly to the train window..., which must have put a lot of strain on my grandma..., because the “KID!” was so restless... The rest of the journey has, thank goodness, vanished into the twists of my brain, except for the smell of overripe bananas in the compartment. Opening: Besides the lovely, zesty chocolate-orange note, there is also something subtly leathery and slightly tobacco-like (more like the dried tobacco leaves for a light cigar) to sniff out, so the fragrance, along with the elegant bitter chocolate note, should also suit gentlemen who want to avoid floral notes and would still like something “sweet” and “snuggly” ;-) The development: Dark chocolate, dark chocolate, dark... with coconut! The orange takes a back seat, only maintaining a fine acidity against the sweetness of the chocolate, which is necessary because the coconut comes on strong and pure, like in macarons. After 6-7 hours, a mild noble bitter note shines on suede from the skin, with the orange only playing a dot on the “I” to prevent it from becoming sticky. The skin now seems cocoa-dusted. For me, this would be a typical autumn-winter candidate, as it is thoroughly gourmand, if it weren't for the oily coconut scent. Personally, that is too much of a good thing for me, but for coconut lovers, it is surely a pure delight! And: It doesn’t smell like Christmas, but spicy! After all: Bitter Orange & Chocolate brings no calories to the scale and is therefore perfect for “in between” :-)

This is my first comment here on Parfumo, please don't hold it against me if it's not all that perfect ;) Bitter Orange & Chocolate is one of five limited edition fragrances from the Jo Malone Sugar & Spice collection. The scents are generally very simply constructed...the name says it all. Bitter Orange & Chocolate smells exactly like that: chocolate and bitter orange. Do you know that soft cookie with orange jelly filling and half chocolate coating? Just as delicious as those cookies taste, this perfume smells. For me personally, the chocolate note dominates from the very beginning, and after a short while, the orange completely fades into the background, leaving behind a chocolate dream that makes me want to lick my wrist. I hardly perceive any coconut. So, if you enjoy the aforementioned sweets, you will love this scent. I personally love BO&C as a fragrance, but I'm still not sure if I want to wear it regularly as a perfume and smell like orange-chocolate cookies. Perhaps it will be more wearable for me in combination with another scent; I will try to find that out in the near future. In conclusion, I would like to add that this perfume -in my opinion- would also be quite wearable for the male part of the gourmand perfume fans.

I was very curious. The fragrance notes sound great, but I haven't had much luck with Jo Malone's so far. So I was a bit skeptical here, but still too curious and really wanted to test it. Now I have the sample and immediately sprayed it on my wrist. I instantly had this fabric softener association in mind. However, I find that the scent has something elegant and well-groomed about it. I only smell the plum very subtly, and the plum here is not sweet, but rather has something of an unripe plum, slightly tart. I must say, I really like the scent. For the first time, a Malone has convinced me. It fits perfectly into everyday life. The longevity is okay, not overwhelming, but that’s probably just because the scent is very light. The sillage is okay, fits perfectly in the office and everyday life. The fragrance is pleasing and, in my opinion, a recommendation for all clean scent fans.

I love clear, elegant scents. So I was skeptical when the fragrance was described to me as "a piece of freshly baked plum cake that you never want to give up." Well, I must say: This scent has NOTHING to do with plum CAKE at all. One can pleasantly sense a subtle and not at all artificial plum note that gently glides into a soft laundry detergent-fabric softener-fresh laundry closet scent pillow. The longevity of this fragrance is similarly delicate. I can very well imagine that starched collars from Windsor would smell like this on 12-year-old girls. Joking aside: It’s a very pleasant scent, and the term "perfume" would be out of place here. But splashed generously on both hands and applied to the neck and arms after showering - that has its charm. One feels as if they have been softened. By the way, it dissipates so quickly that after 1 hour, any other perfume can be applied over it without any problem.

On my skin it smells like iced green tea with flower petals and quite a few tart berries. yes I can smell fresh roses perfectly. At the base for some mysterious reason I hear sugar violet. Sprayed liberally, it lasts on my skin for up to 8 hours; there is no wake. It does not tolerate heat and air conditioning well: it disappears. The designer of the beautiful bottle of sharp silvery roses is the Argentine Pablo Reinoso. But I find nothing electric in this pleasant and calm perfume

I have almost never felt such excellent blend of blueberry and violet as at the first sniff from VERY IRRÉSISTIBLE ELECTRIC ROSE. I had almost 5 minutes, when I could not stop nosing my wrist. It is worth to sample it, to test it, to sink in the perfect balance of the notes. After a while the freshness overrun the lovely combo, and we get a lemony designer perfume, synthetic and kind of cheap ordinary mass product. I had FUEL FOR LIFE FEMME on one wrist, VERY IRRÉSISTIBLE ELECTRIC ROSE on another, and after 2 hours I could not make difference. After 3 hours I did not have to bother with differenciate, since both of them disappeared. IMO Givenchy has much better fragrances for men than for women.

Very Irresistible Electric Rose has arrived on the market a little too soon after the release of Very Irresistible L'Intense for my liking. Even the sales assistants are struggling to keep up with it all. As a result, many are unaware of this flanker's existence, which is a shame. Very Irresistible Electric Rose is quite lovely, however I wouldn't necessarily call it 'electric'. It's fresh if anything, a pleasant blend of pink roses, crisp lemon and a hint of juicy blueberries. It wears nicely during Spring and Summer, which are the seasons I assume it is intended for. The roses in Very Irresistible Electric Rose smell pink, dewy and fresh. Lemon amps up the roses, providing a zesty and bright sensation. I quite like the way this fragrance opens on the skin. The heart is a little powdery, clean almost, with lemon verbena taking over from the citrusy lemon, creating a smoother and greener blend. Despite the rather herbaceous sounding scent pyramid, this fragrance is easy to enjoy but not as unique as it may first appear to be. Like Trvevil noted, this fragrance is comfy and tender. I enjoy wearing it immensely, but it's not something that I could see myself buying. I only wish that the rose accord was slightly more dominant. The lemon is complementary, but it does tend to smother the rose from beginning to end, which bothered me. The younger consumers will most likely enjoy Very Irresistible Electric Rose. Fans of the original will also find themselves pleased with this flanker. I'm impressed, although admittedly not blown away.

~ Inspiration ~ Recently, I got to know "Very Irrésistible" by Givenchy. Now I received a sample of "Electric Rose" and was all the more curious since there are no comments about it yet. ~ Bottle ~ The narrow, square shape also reminds me of a flower vase. On the front, there are 4 blooming rose heads depicted one below the other. The name promises an electrifying scent. The colors white, silver, and pink give it a modern, slightly futuristic design. Liv Tyler fits quite well as the face of the Rock 'n Roll campaign with her black leather jacket. ~ Fragrance ~ Upon spraying, it is immediately fresh and a bit green with lemons and a hint of basil. After a few minutes, sweet-powdery roses and violets join in. Anise lingers in the background. Musk and cedarwood form a dry base. ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts about 4-5 hours (a bit longer on clothing and hair). You can comfortably apply several sprays without it feeling overwhelming; the sillage remains close to the body. ~ Occasion ~ It works well during the day in spring and autumn, also as an office scent. For evenings or in winter, it is too weak for me. ~ Conclusion ~ I had imagined a somewhat "louder" rose scent based on the name and the advertising... Anyone who likes slightly spicy, subtle, and powdery rose fragrances should give it a try.

...around in our bathroom, fidebum. Creativity is not my thing. I admit it. I couldn't come up with an even worse title, no matter how hard I tried. At least there’s a grain of truth in this. I will try to convey the exact reasons for this in the following commentary. Mr. Bubble... Hm, I don’t know him. Who is that? As a diligent perfume consumer, I of course engaged with this character before writing this text. Mr. Bubble is a very old and well-known cartoon character from the USA, promoting children's products in the care sector. There are all sorts of ancient commercials on YouTube, even in black and white. According to my research, the most popular product from this line is a children's bubble bath with a fruity sweet scent. That’s where Mr. Bubble got his name. Bubbles everywhere. Of course, I enjoyed similar bubble baths as a kid. However, I don't remember any specific scents. I do recall quirky Maya the Bee figures that came with the bubble bath. In any case, it was fun to put on a bubble mustache or a funny bubble hairstyle. American children must have had similar experiences with "Mr. Bubble". Now, finally, to the scent. I'll keep it short! Forget the fragrance pyramid. Yes, it pretends to be a fruity scent. However, since it is purely synthetic, you shouldn't hope for natural fruity scents. Unfortunately, there is a very alcoholic - almost solvent-like - smell noticeable at first. Fortunately, this is so brief that you can (almost) overlook this aspect. Now a gum-like fruity scent unfolds. It's one of those smells you also know from childhood. Indefinably fruity. Somewhere along the lines of "Bazooka Joe" (The older ones will remember). Since I am making an effort to describe the TLOF scents in detail, I would clearly label the scent as a cheap KiBa juice (which never saw a real fruit). Behind that, with a lot of goodwill, a warm-vanilla scent is recognizable. What "Mr. Bubble" does very well is not leaving an unpleasant sticky sweetness behind. The EdC remains quite fresh. If you can believe the reviews on American sites, Mr. Bubble is supposedly 100% reminiscent of the original bubble bath scent. I can't judge that unfortunately. However, I can well imagine that a children's product smells like this and is extremely well received. But how does it come across to me? Honestly, I like it. After a bath or a shower, it’s funny to wear. In everyday life, I probably wouldn’t choose it. There is virtually no sillage, but the longevity of 2-3 hours is there. That’s not the end of the world, but okay for an EdC. Would I recommend "Mr. Bubble" as a children's perfume? Well, the first unpleasant alcohol scent might be off-putting. However, the following scent will surely delight quite a few kids. The scent feels good; as an old geezer like me, you experience a little time travel back to the 80s. A time when bubblegum, bright colors, artificial flavors, and flashy outfits were normal. However, many TLOF scents carry this association; they are often thematic, trigger memories, and bring back flashbacks galore. This is yet another one of those. Anyone who is crazy enough and doesn’t mind smelling provocative can buy this without hesitation. If you have kids at home, you can also introduce them to this. People who take scents very seriously and want to perceive every ingredient should please steer clear of this. Did I regret the purchase? Not at all! I don’t have anything similar in my collection. Do I need the scent? Not really! It’s nice that it’s there, but when the 100ml bottle is empty, I won’t be mourning. Mr. Bubble is a fun scent without any serious character. Maybe that’s exactly why I like it :D Life is serious enough.

This is a flanker I didn't buy in winter and managed to grab with a great reduction now it's summer ... and doesn't it bear one of the most complicated names in Givenchy's history? "Poetry of a Winter Perfume" hits the target with this perfumed missile - provided your aim is NOT to smell like a bunch of freshly picked roses. "Poetry of a Winter Perfume" dislikes daylight and loves winter nights. It is a mix of warm spices (star anis, cinnamon, ginger) with large overlays of dark resins and a touch of a velvety rose. The fragrance is quite voluptuous and if you don't like traditional Christmas spices, you should stay away from it. I think it's a great scent for those who want to calm down when they get a bit flustered and the spicy-oriental mixture feels very comfortable. I also smell a whiff of the good old "Organza Indécence" in "Poésie d'un Parfum d'Hiver", at least it points into the same direction: warm, spicy and well-blended.

Snow-covered landscapes that sparkle and shimmer in the evening light of lanterns, the scent of fir trees in the air, crisp freshness through the winter cold. A crackling fireplace, sipping a glass of mulled wine, enjoying the winter evening. This is what one automatically thinks of when applying "Very Irrésistible Cèdre d'Hiver." While it has little in common with the original "Very Irrésistible," it is just as enchanting, accompanying you through a cold winter's day and conveying a sense of comfort and warmth. Cèdre d'Hiver begins softly and lightly fruity-woody. A delicate berry note, framed by the scent of magnolia and a touch of star anise (THE note par excellence for a winter fragrance). After a while, the rose becomes distinctly noticeable - it is a delicate, white rose, not a strong, red one; it is accompanied by light incense and cedarwood - reminiscent of the aforementioned fireplace nights in a snow-covered mountain cabin - inviting one to dream. You are surrounded by a gentle sillage that instantly lifts your spirits, even when it gets extremely crisp and cold outside ;) This fantasy of sparkling winter nights is also emphasized by the bottle design - beautiful and very original, it has a "frosted" and shimmering appearance. Cèdre d'Hiver lasts well on me, even longer than "Very Irrésistible." After 6 hours, I can still perceive the wonderful winter fragrance, which concludes with a lovely amber-cedar note. It will be my Christmas fragrance for 2012 ;)

Like all the other maisons who realized they were losing sales to the niche sector, Givenchy launched in 2014 its collection of more exclusive, sophisticated and, of course, more expensive perfumes. The focus relies on the portrait of the preciousness of materials, a haute couture approach brought to the world of perfumery in this type of collection. Basically, the brand is following the market both in concept and in olfactory tendencies and Gaiac Mystique reflects this well. Its theme is more romantic than dark and its aroma is a kind of semi gourmand and incense iris that came into fashion after the success that Dior Homme made throughout its life. The brand does not disclose which perfumer has created Gaiac Mystique , but the signature itself seems typical of Daniela Andrier, especially the work that Andrier did for the exclusive collection of another label also managed by LVMH - Bvlgari. Although the focus is on Gaiac's wood, Gaiac Mystique is more of an iris scent than Gaiac itself. Here we have the construction of a slightly powdery and creamy iris, complemented by touches of vanilla and tonka bean. The Gaiac confers its sweetish woody creaminess, but as everything is done to appear linear and homogeneous its ends up not standing out so much. What is most noticeable here is a smoky, slightly fresh incense nuance, something that seems to pass between the elemi and the frankincense and which seems to be present just to give the mystical touch promised by the name. Overall, Gaiac Mystique fulfills what is expected of an exclusive collection, but Givenchy arrived late in this field; thus it does not have much margin to stand out from what has already been done and this is reflected in the perfume itself. It is a chic and pleasant olfactory aura, but a "haute chic" with no remarkable personality.

Among Burberry women's perfumes, which are all universally "wearable and bearable," I have been searching for one for a long time. The problem lies where there is no problem at all; all Burberrys have a very typical signature within them, and that only expresses itself after hours, a secret component that bothers me, and this one is no exception, regardless of who created it. Objectively, it is a good scent that has some similarities with the Woman edP, but this one is more refined and sophisticated, more interesting.. The components are consciously and tastefully selected, it is elegant and has almost a classic tone. The pyramid is lovely, starting with peach (which reminds me of the 80s), the rose heart, and the patchouli base (a well-known pattern), polished to a shine. However, it is somewhat more special than the first, and with the unmistakable checkered signature that only reminds me of London clouds and constant rain. Good, and it doesn’t lift the mood. Ironclad smile in a pink costume.

i wanted it to smell of may - the sunlight, the blooming lilacs, the tart, juicy rhubarb dipped in sugar. it's not potent enough for the white lilac, not sweet enough for the light purple one, i guess the closest it gets to actual lilacs is the dark purple variation, with plenty of leaves and stems. it's just a tiny bit too harsh and cloying, leaning into a somber bouquet of lilacs brought into a dusty, cold room. it lacks the warmth, the dew, the refreshing aroma of spring. the longevity is not as impressive as with the other jo malone scents i have, but i sort of appreciate that in this case - i wouldn't want it to stick for too long, it would be straight up tiresome. on another note, on some days it reminds me of the smell of your hair after a swim in a lake. except the lake is blooming with cyanobacteria and has a layer of pollen foaming by the shore. but at least it's very photorealistic about it.

Although I have had this fragrance in my collection for a long time, I had always hesitated to test it - and thus wear it for an entire day. However, external circumstances applied a bit of pressure, and now I have finally gotten it over with. The intention doesn't sound too bad: Iced Berries is supposed to be a cool and crisp blend of raspberries, blueberries, and blackberries with a hint of mint. In theory, it sounds nicely fruity, but in practice, Iced Berries comes across like bright red candies of the overly sweet variety. Perhaps a little sour here and there, but it is more suited for users under 12 years old. My colleagues must have thought I had remnants of children's toothpaste on me or that I was hiding tons of gummy candies somewhere. I will probably have lost the aura of a relatively well-perfumed employee for at least an entire workday. After all, this stuff is persistent and clings to you until sunset without any transformations. At least - the illusion is perfect, and Demeter has once again managed to crank up the head and nose cinema. Nevertheless, this fragrance is more of a challenge for adults. Surely, young girls will be able to get along better with Iced Berries. Therefore, 70% because it only minimally scratches the synthetic surface and is essentially well-made - but nothing more, as it becomes annoying after just 10 seconds.

And here I am again with a Jo Malone fragrance that I will comment on. Although I had a sample of this scent and didn’t annoy the saleswomen at the Jo Malone stand. I actually couldn’t have, because since yesterday it’s known as Black Friday and I saw (yes, yes… I was once again in the fragrance shop…) how stressed the girls there were… (you can decide for yourselves whether I was just being nice by not stressing the poor girls even more with my presence or if I simply didn’t dare… :D). Well, even though I am slowly finding some Jo Malones appealing, most still seem quite ordinary to me in terms of scent. Just like this fragrance here, which starts off okay but then simply remains a spicy-herbaceous scent, like many other similar fragrances as well. The scent: The fragrance starts with lime, but then all the other notes somehow mix in. While most cannot really be distinguished from one another, you can immediately smell the gardenias, lavender, and sage, as the scent becomes slightly stuffy floral with bitter-spicy notes, although the stuffiness quickly disappears. From the top notes, there might still be a hint of pepper, but all the other notes smell like a mix of citrus scents, from which (I believe) the lime stands out a bit. Cardamom and coriander provide a strong spicy note, without having too strong a projection. I find they make the scent somehow drier and more bitter-spicy and surprisingly don’t smell as bad as I usually perceive this combination. Soon, towards the base, it also smells strongly woody, which is the cedar that gives it its name. A little later, the fragrance gains a slight sweetness from the tonka bean. Otherwise, it remains slightly citrusy at the end, but more herbaceous-bitter. The sillage and longevity: The projection is below average, so it won’t leave a large scent cloud. And the longevity is rather simple average at five to six hours. The bottle: The bottle is rectangular, clear, and filled with light yellow fragrance liquid. On the front, you can see the label, where the name and logo are displayed. The cap is chrome-plated, round, and looks like a knob. All in all, quite okay. Well,… the fragrance is, in my opinion, just nothing special, so it’s not really a shame that it has been discontinued. It’s not bad, but it’s really not good either. Which means it has become an inconsequential fragrance for me that might have some good aspects but doesn’t offer much more. Besides, there are really many fragrances that go in this direction (somewhat loosely citrusy-herbaceous for warmer days). However, I could imagine that it might smell a bit better in combination with other Jo Malone fragrances, but with so many Malones, you’ll have to find out for yourselves what mixes well with what (incredible, with Aventus there are long pages of discussion about the batch code, here there isn’t even a page with possible Malone combinations, or am I mistaken? :D That would be an idea! But I’m too lazy for that… :DD). Positively noteworthy are the scent notes themselves, which all smell natural and the fragrance shows not the slightest trace of synthetics. If you want to try the scent, it’s best used in spring and summer. As for purpose, you can take leisure time, as the sillage is not particularly high. Well,… that’s how it always is. After discovering a truly wonderful fragrance from Jo Malone with Orange Bitters, it had to happen that something inconsequential was rubbed under my nose again :D The next Malone will surely smell better for me!

This perfume starts wonderfully citrusy-fruity, with lime and pomelo dominating. It makes your mouth water, especially since it doesn’t smell artificial, but rather like a freshly prepared fruit platter. Sure, melon wouldn’t be bad either. Soon after, ylang-ylang joins in along with lavender. Jasmine and gardenia serve mainly as brighteners and are otherwise subordinate. Overall, everything is very closely knit, likely due to the sage. Amber then elongates the scent. Occasionally, I think I perceive coconut, but very discreetly. After just over an hour, the base comes in, seamlessly taking over the sour-citrusy signature. Tamarind is still new in the perfume world, which might be why it comes across as so bitter. Tonka bean is supposed to soften this a bit, but it doesn’t really work. In summary, this is a sporty/elegant citrus scent without edges or corners. The ingredients are well intertwined, nothing stands out. Those looking for "something fresh, please" might enjoy this scent. However, it’s not for me. Longevity is unfortunately also only in the lower midfield.

Most people apparently do not know this fragrance, and unfortunately, very few will have the opportunity to get to know it, which is a shame, as it seems to be discontinued. I had blind bought this scent (once again), and before I knew it, it became my favorite spring-summer fragrance. I can't remember the original Irrésistible very well, but I would say that this flanker bears almost no resemblance to the original. The title already suggests that Very Irrésistible Edition Croisière has a bit of everything and is therefore very special. It opens with a good pinch of saltwater, which immediately feels refreshing and evokes a seaside vibe. Gradually, flowers make their appearance, but in no way are they annoying (I’m not really into floral scents), rather they make the fragrance very feminine. Then, Very Irrésistible Croisière becomes delicately powdery, but not in a stuffy way; it’s airy, light, and fresh, like a fragrant veil on the skin. I also perceive a very subtle woody note, but it’s far in the background. That must be the listed driftwood. An unusual fragrance that unites many contrasts and comes across as very harmonious overall: Very Irrésistible Croisière is salty and aquatic, but not an Aquate. It contains flowers, yet it is not a floral scent. It is powdery, but not a powder scent. What one could criticize is the sillage. It does not have particularly great projection. Therefore, I always apply it generously, also spritzing it in my hair, and then Very Irrésistible Croisière can be well perceived for several hours. Conclusion: A wonderful, fresh, feminine summer fragrance that forgoes citrus, fruit, and greenery, is not too sweet, but rather fresh-powdery-salty-floral, which simply lifts the mood and is perfect for all occasions. I can't think of any summer fragrance that could be compared to this one. This makes it all the more regrettable that this beautiful and unusual scent has been discontinued. All the more I will enjoy my bottle. It is large enough that Very Irrésistible Croisière will surely accompany me next summer as well.

After spraying, it is very floral-sweet. After 5 minutes, it develops into a pleasantly fresh, but sweet-fresh scent; I think of a vacation by the sea, sea breeze, sunscreen, and Biotherm Oceane. Maybe it's because of the sea salt? Then it becomes powdery, slightly vanilla-like, but you can still sense the seawater aspect. The two types of rose blend perfectly underneath; you don't notice a distinct rose scent, but the typical Very Irresistible smell. Frangipani and driftwood, along with the marine accord that Biotherm eau Oceane also has, smell wonderful even after about 3 hours! I kept sniffing the whole time, I'm thrilled because it's something different from the typical summer scents. I wouldn't recommend it for young girls, as it might be a bit too heavy for them.

Having experienced the Demeter Vintage Naturals 2009 eau de parfum collection, I was delighted to see that some of the scents were being re-launched. They are no longer called "vintage", but they are still all natural, and the recipes look to be the same. The notes listed at the Demeter website profile for MIMOSA are: basil, ylang ylang, jasmine, mimosa, vanilla, and tonka bean This is quite close to the official list for the vintage predecessor. Geranium appears to be no longer included, and the basil appears to be toned down, as this MIMOSA really seems like a fluffy yellow soliflore and is much less green. In a side-by-side comparison, I realized that this new launch is a truer soliflore, which is good news for those who missed out on the 2009 vintage series anyway but were after an all-natural mimosa soliflore all along. I am baffled by the price of this eau de toilette. The MSRP is $29 for 1.7 ounce, which is less than half the price of the vintage naturals collection, which were already a bargain by most any measure. All natural? Nichesque? What? It is true that this is eau de toilette, and that was eau de parfum, but I don't notice the concentration difference in the performance, which is all the more striking since I'm pretty sure that the eau de parfum has undergone some evaporation as a result of the screw on atomizers used by Demeter. The good news about the Demeter bottles is that they can be re-used for cologne and what not. The bad news is that if you have them around long enough, the contents may literally evaporate away! I am very happy with this all-natural creation. One interesting difference I noted is that the liquid in these new bottles seems to have some particulate matter in them, compared to the completely transparent (albeit still colored) solutions of the vintage naturals. Maybe these were prepared by less rigorous means. Certainly they were not subjected to the same degree of filtering. Still, this is the bargain of the all-natural perfume world, so if you're in the market for a mimosa soliflore, there is no excuse for not giving this one at least a sniff. You can buy a .5 ounce splash bottle for (gasp!) $8!

"Pick-Me-Up Cologne Spray" is written on the bottle, and I can only advise you: Do it, pick this cologne up, put it in your shopping cart, and take it with you. "Each Day. Everywhere." it says, and yes: This is a so-called all-rounder, at least for me. At first, the scent surprises: Hey, this brings back memories, it smells exactly like the incense stick corner in Indian shops, the one with jasmine, melon, and floral incense sticks, not the resinous ones, but it smells unburned, fresh, and a bit artificial in my nose. That's exactly how I felt about this type of incense sticks in the past. And so the scent lingers for a few hours. After a while, however, the incense impression fades, and the slight artificiality gives way to an unexpectedly lovely, fine floral softness that is unmatched. Delicate and rather quiet, lightly sweet, but not in the way mimosa flowers are sweet, this scent envelops me with bright friendliness. And it stays - for more hours. "Simple. Subtle." as it says on the bottle. I thank LysdeKerk for this wonderful rediscovery.

Jo Malone’s Mallow on the Moors is a fragrance I hoped might smell a little haunted. Well. It does...sort of? Not really in the way I was expecting, though. More like a parody from someone who didn't realize they were writing a parody, which some might look at as a little unfortunate for their creation (no one wants to be unintentionally funny, you know?), but hey, it could also be fun, right? Imagine you’re a buttoned-up gothic novelist who’s never even taken a lover, and fate has led you straight into the arms of a rakish lothario, a real Bluebeard type. Imagine swoons, sighs, ghosts, old gothic castles, manor grounds, bodies buried in the poison gardens, dead wives in attics, and all that jazz. And then the camera pans out, and this is a Hammer horror production directed by Anna Biller starring Lana del Rey, and it’s trying real hard to be ethereal and phantasmal and misty moors and mossy castles, but somehow it is all high camp and glinting artifice, real Real Housewives of Manderley energy. As to what it smells like, imagine the luminous violet powder of broken, scattered Guerlain Meteorites and the brassy hairspray, champagne-tossed-in-your-faceness of Tom Ford Jasmine Rouge. Imagine all of that sprayed on Dita von Teese in La Perla clutching a guttering candelabra channeling Frau Blücher.

Don't let the name confuse you, there are absolutely no marshmallow notes in this fragrance. It is very fresh and green with a very slight sweetness. This is a very distinct smell but not especially unique. Like most Jo Malone fragrances, it is subtle and clean. There is very little longevity to it, but it makes for a nice, fresh, skin-scent. I belive this is a limited time release. So I don't recommend falling in love with this one. Personally I don't think I'll miss it much or even remember it.

Starts very nice with lychee and peony coming through right away. A beautiful fluid watery note comes in the heart. Floral, fresh, greenish, slightly musky. Very light and yummy. Very elegant and fresh. The only thing I didn't like is how quickly it seems to fade on me. Whiiiiiiiissh, it's gone before you know it. This is on my 'want' list for sure. Perfection for a spring or summer afternoon. This is apparently is a limited edition from for 2012 available only in duty-free shops, but I found a tiny bottle in a Givenchy set at my local drug store (along with Ange ou Démon, Eaudemoiselle, Very Irrésistible Givenchy L'Intense & Organza). I love it!

This fragrance bears a striking resemblance to its predecessor from 2012. I could hardly detect any differences; perhaps "Un Air d'Escapade 2013" is fresher. A somewhat artificially sounding rose is at the center and is rounded off with aromas reminiscent of "Juicy Fruit" gum. The bottle is not original, and the fragrance itself falls far short of the expectations that its melodious name evokes.

A rating of 6.9 is not what this fragrance deserves. Yes, it doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it is a quite pleasant citrus summer companion without any associations with cleaning products. Therefore, I feel compelled to dedicate at least a comment to it, to give it a bit of justice. Aqua Lemon was released in the summer edition of Jo Malone, inspired by the waters of Great Britain, and is supposed to evoke memories of swimming in a pool. However, it doesn't really do that-no chlorine (thankfully!), no sunscreen, no fries...nothing that I would associate with an outdoor pool, but who knows, maybe the English lidos smell different from the German ones? In this regard, it seems likely that the addition of "Aqua" is pure marketing, and they just wanted to include another citrus fragrance in the collection. Because nothing here smells aquatic. The fragrance starts off immediately citrusy (mandarin is listed, but to my nose it could also be lemon), and the mint is only faintly present in the background (I’m glad about this as I don't really care for mint, except in a mojito, and it tends to be one of the scent notes I dislike - here, however, it prevents the fragrance from drifting into mediocrity). The cedarwood also holds back elegantly but is definitely perceptible in the background upon closer sniffing. So yes, as already mentioned, no innovation, but a very likable, pleasant, and above all refreshing companion in summer. I appreciate the slight bitterness it brings without making it feel too cold...that’s an art, I think. Somehow it manages the perfect balance between cool-refreshing (like water, indeed) and a hint of sweetness. It is quite green in its scent character, yet despite the lemon in the name, it is not sour at all. And somehow, when I close my eyes, I can actually imagine swimming laps in an empty pool early in the morning when the air is still not warmed by the sun...marketing success, I would say :) Probably the perfect fragrance to dive into the novel "The Lido" by Libby Page, which, who would have thought, is about an outdoor pool in London. Anyone who enjoys heartwarming novels with likable characters and without too much drama is recommended this book as summer reading. The bottle looks great and perfectly captures the theme of water, the sprayer releases a wonderfully fine mist, and when I want to cool down in the high temperatures of the last hot days, I find myself reaching for Aqua Lemon again and again. For all Jo Malone lovers, those who enjoy citrus fragrances and don't mind the relatively short longevity (Jo Malone AND citrus fragrance, who expected anything else?

Today I rummaged through the Christmas decorations in my parents' attic and at the very bottom of the box lay this ancient little treasure. Just the refill left without the original blue container. The contents were still bright, and after so many years, I was almost a little excited when I sprayed it. And... what can I say... it is still just as brilliant as it was twenty (?) years ago when I bought it and apparently forgot to take it with me when I moved out of my parents' house. Cherry and a bit of honey at the start, and now after hours, I smell my arm and still perceive cherry and cedarwood. The memories come rushing back, the heavy, sweet yet woody scents like Dahli and the one from Princess Stephanie, what was it called again... Incredible that the fragrance hasn't gone off, I will cherish my little treasure and occasionally indulge in memories of my younger years.

A few weeks ago, I discovered Demeter and spontaneously wanted to buy half of the range. Now this is my first scent, as I found it on eBay... And unfortunately, I have to say that I am really disappointed. It doesn’t smell green to me at all, and where is the metal? Freshly sprayed, it smells "perfumy," the rose to me is a synthetic yellow one, my friend even says it smells like lemon. It doesn’t smell citrusy to me directly, but I can somehow understand the impression. It does remind me of roses, a mix of the scent when you smell it directly (so not the scent of rose water or oil, which you usually have in perfume), but it feels synthetic and reminds me a bit of hairspray. After about half a day, it smells a bit more natural to my taste, the rose is clearer to me, but still somewhat synthetic, the metallic aspect remains hidden, but I can faintly smell a few bitter leaves. Overall, it’s too sweet for my taste... All in all: What a pity, luckily I didn’t buy the scent at full price. However, I can imagine that it might appeal to someone who doesn’t expect it to smell like the description. This is definitely a completely wearable scent!

It took place around 1870. In the Old Palace somewhere in France. Inside lived the Comte De La Fosse and his wife. Old nobility, mind you. And impoverished long ago due to the revolution. The only things they had left were the palace and two loyal servants. The old Adele was already part of the family, as was the chamberlain Serge. When the two passed away shortly after one another, the Countess was deeply grieved by her sudden loneliness. She had long lost her "position" in society. What remained for her was her passion, or hobby as one would say today, her interest in composing fragrances. She had conceived so many scents: from lavender-rose fragrances to musk-incense scents to cheerful floral bouquets. Now she sought a formula for a fragrance that reflected her mood. A "dark" scent full of melancholy but also full of hope for a candid life. She searched for rare ingredients, for incense and balms, to create "her" scent. She found much of this at the markets of the nearest larger towns, where some merchants from the East also offered their goods. The myrrh, the comforting element of the fragrance, the ginger and the incense as a balm for the soul, to soften the darkness of patchouli, she found rose oils, and the memories were to be carried by woods and tonka. She devoted herself wholeheartedly to the composition of the ingredients, pouring all her knowledge and "heart and soul" into it, and found the right measure for each component. A wonderfully mystical-melancholic-dark and finely reminiscent fragrance was created. The one we now call Eaudemoiselle Essence des Palais. The fragrance formula was rediscovered long after the Comtes de La Fosse in the old walls. The palace was restored to honor its former inhabitants and now serves as an "antique" workshop for perfumers who create wonderful dark-melancholic-mystical fragrances...

Ten years ago, I was in love with Eaudemoiselle. So noble and elegant. Curious about this offshoot, I ordered it blindly. Well, Bravo, the Eaudemoiselle of the past only makes a brief appearance as a hint with the first spray. Then it becomes mystical, dark, bitter, and smoky. I always think of poison.... this could smell like a very old poison mixture. All wild imagination. Basically, I enter an old wooden church, decorated with red roses and wild incense being waved around. I am not good at being able to list all the individual notes. I experience moods and images through a scent. And sometimes it is quite appropriate to think about poison mixtures in an old wooden church. That does not mean this Eaudemoiselle smells unpleasant. It smells very special. If you want to appear very mysterious, you are well served with it. I miss something soft, delicate among all that harsh stuff.

To wrap up Friday, here’s another quick Demeter review. Today I’m testing Hot Toddy. For those who don’t know what that is: Hot Toddy is an alcoholic drink that is mixed with water and sugar and served hot. Spices like nutmeg may also be added. Hot Toddy doesn’t quite suit my taste, as I don’t like warm or even hot alcohol at all, but I must admit that it doesn’t smell bad. The scent: It starts with an alcoholic note, ha ha! Of course, it has to start with alcohol since it contains rum (though it’s hard to distinguish whether it might actually be whiskey). So it really smells like the alcoholic drink and not just an alcoholic undertone. Then, for a brief moment, you can smell tea, but that is quickly overshadowed by nutmeg and cinnamon, along with sugar that makes the scent even sweeter. If you sniff closely, you can even catch a whiff of a slice of lemon that was added to the drink. All in all, it’s not a bad scent at all. Towards the end, however, the lemon becomes stronger, the alcohol content weaker, and it smells more like tea with strong lemon. The longevity is normal, lasting about three to four hours. The sillage is okay; it is noticeable, but I don’t think it’s strong enough to make you smell like you just walked out of a pub after spraying it on. The perfume liquid is contained in a vessel that is supposed to represent a simple bottle, without any frills. The label is, as always, boring and unremarkable, well, at least it has the name of the scent on a light brown bar. Hot Toddy has a good scent that is pleasant. At least if you don’t have an aversion to various alcoholic fragrances. It also includes some spices and a lemon, which make the scent milder. In the end, it resembles tea with lemon, but also a bit of mulled wine. The scent is not wearable, but it’s okay if you want to sniff it occasionally. Just don’t drink it!

Flowers have always been one of my weaknesses when it comes to scents, as I can barely distinguish a handful of them, if at all. Geraniums? Heard of them often, even seen them, but never remembered the scent. I had imagined something pleasantly floral, and instead received something that I absolutely did not like. The scent: Uuurgh,… so this is what geraniums smell like? Really that terrible? I smell an extremely stuffy scent, not pleasant at all and quite unpleasant. But it has the typical stuffy-soapy character of some flowers, so I suppose this must be geraniums. Fortunately, the somewhat piercing-stuffy scent fades a bit into the background later, and the soapy character comes to the forefront, yet I just cannot bring myself to like the scent. The longevity is not very long, so the scent is completely gone after 2-3 hours. The sillage is also rather low, but it keeps wafting up to my nose. Unfortunately... The bottle is rectangular, tapering pyramidally at the neck and topped with a tall, cylindrical cap. It’s not beautiful, but it’s perfectly adequate. The label is still poorly made and even looks similar in color to some other Demeter scents, as if they were running out of colors. How about a picture instead?? No, I did not like geranium. Sure, not all flowers or plants smell good, but well, this scent is something Demeter could have done without. I found it stuffy, slightly piercing, and therefore disturbing, and I was glad when the scent finally faded away. What do we learn from this? That not all flowers smell good, which is indeed the case.

How I would have loved to dedicate a more extensive review to this fragrance, the only problem is... it disappears so quickly and is generally so weak that the spell is already over before I could gather a clear thought. But even that is worth mentioning, as I have never experienced something quite like this before. The Jo Malone fragrances are often criticized for their longevity and sillage, but since those things are not that important to me, I can usually overlook them. But here? The name and theme suggest that this is a scent one might apply in the evening before going to sleep, to wind down and relax. It actually works quite well, as the herbal chamomile used here, combined with the clean musk, does indeed have a relaxing effect. It reminds me a bit of the scent that clings to your skin after you’ve stepped out of a bubble bath as a child; the intensity is also the same (so basically non-existent, just a very gentle whisper...). The problem is that the fragrance disappears so quickly that you would have to fall asleep within 5 minutes to even catch a whiff of it. And not everyone is blessed to glide into dreamland in such a short time. To be honest, for those 5 minutes of evening relaxation, I find the fragrance simply too expensive; one would be better off picking up an aromatherapy spray at the nearest drugstore for the same effect. So unfortunately, Jo Malone does not convince me with this fragrance, even though I am otherwise a big fan of this house. For those looking for a chamomile scent, I recommend Mémoire d'une Odeur at this point, which manages to impress with a beautifully dreamy bottle and definitely a bit more substance.

An opulent scent of leather, resinous labdanum and oud that seems to take me back in time to an ancient market with a leather tannery and an incense shop nearby that is sells oud. A weird experience. Oud Flamboyant is really comforting to wear. As with most Western fragrances, the oud is synthetic but it was definitely satisfying. Projection was about 6ft (2 meters) for about 6 hours then it backed up to about an arms length for the other 6 hours. Can be worn for any occasion, day or night and can be worn year-round as well. Highly Recommended 9.5/10

Dear Very, thank you for the generous sample. Admittedly, I was a bit biased before I tested LBu.WL with the pyramid of apple (grrr) and incense, and I thought (wrongly) that apple in perfume would result in fruit salad, and I can't deal with incense either, so what is this going to be? No! Okay, the fruity salad opening bothers me for a moment, but then I was immediately catapulted to a beautiful lake where water lilies bloom and in the mud, water lilies that smell yellow and sweet. Bring on the hammock, throw myself in, let my soul dangle. In the sun, dragonflies hover over the water, their colorful wings sparkling and reflecting in the water. When the sun sets in a fiery red, you can see water spirits dancing over the lily pads. A beautiful summer scent, with a very light sweetness, but even more freshness, that actually smells like sun rays and interestingly fades warm and woody, giving it a certain kick. Yes, LBu.WL really makes you forget this ugly summer.

I received a very generous sample of this today. Thanks to the lovely sample giver! Today was really a terrible day. I was angry, had already pulled the blanket over my head. I do nothing without fragrance. So I took this little bottle with the firm intention of hating the scent. I have to vent my anger on someone. But it doesn’t work. Jo Malone's Lotus Blossom & Water Lily is absolutely fascinating! At first, it smells somewhat medicinal, fresh, citrusy-herbaceous. Something scratches in the throat like with Si Lolita. But soon the fragrance develops into spicy flowers with a very fine aquatic note. For me, this is a wellness scent! I have a feeling of walking by the sea and the water gently washes around my feet. A piece of wood drifts to the shore. Yes, it’s becoming woody now with a hint of amber. Overall, the scent is always a bit scratchy, but not unpleasant. I had never encountered anything like LB&WL before. I expected something much more floral and aquatic. I am pleasantly surprised. I wouldn’t buy the fragrance, but I will use this sample all by myself while meditating.

Had this scent now almost 20 years ago. It still seems like just yesterday. Funny how anyone who is younger wants to act more mature, and now that I am older I am asking myself, What was my rush? Why did I act so offended at the perfume that my husband suggested back then? He actually liked Candies, and honestly, that would have just fitted me perfectly at the time. I was in my early 20s. But, no that 20 year old had expensive French perfume tastes, let me tell you!!! So of course, after trying many different ones at the posh department store, I chose Amarige D’Amore. I guess it was befitting and I recall the scent being very beautiful but also it can be easily worn today. Not vintage in feeling at all. Compared to the original Amarige, it had very little similarity. It is a bright sparkling white floral. Very pretty, light and romantic. I don’t have it anymore but I still recall it. Definitely behind the times in terms of the name and the message. Makes me feel melancholy at the passage of time.

Kir royal is a delicious aperitif that is particularly enjoyed in Swabian teachers' lounges on special occasions, such as appointments, leaves of absence, or retirements. It is popular because it caters to the famous Swabian thriftiness, is easy to mix without much effort, and still looks impressive. Kir royal became popular through the eponymous television series by Dietl from the 1980s, in which the scandal reporter Baby Schimmerlos introduced us to the lifestyle of the Munich "bussi-bussi" society with much "süffisanz". Mixing a kir royal is no witchcraft and can be quickly explained: Take 9cl of champagne (for the Swabian, a dry sparkling wine from Aldi will do) and 1cl of cassis (blackcurrant liqueur). And there you have a refreshing, fruity-bitter drinking pleasure! The eternal question of what should go in first, champagne or cassis, is for each bartender to decide for themselves - both are correct! While testing Amarige d'Amour, the kir royal immediately came to my mind: The top note: Sparkling like champagne, the scent opens fruity-bitter, beautifully rounded with cinnamon from the cassia. The heart note: Very floral, dominated by lily of the valley with fresh rose, the piercing lily of the valley is elegantly softened by a sweet mimosa and remains pleasantly light. The base note: The floral overall impression remains intact and only darkens slightly over time due to the amber and sandalwood. Sillage and longevity do not really convince me. Average, despite the impressive opening, the scent remains rather close to the skin and fades after about 4-6 hours. I like Amarige d'Amour! It gives me a French chic! Next spring, I will wear it while shopping in the first spring sun and sip a kir royal at a street café. In this sense: à votre santé!

On my skin this is a beautiful sweetly floral waterlily fortified by crisp green notes (hints of freshly cut grass among others) and dancing in a cloud of white musk. Ylang Ylang is subtly present, providing it's slightly sour fruity note deep in the background. As the fragrance dries down, warm vanilla creeps through as if playing peek-a-boo. A new favorite!

This somewhat atypical Jo Malone fragrance seemed to want to come to me. Recently, I came across a bottle of "The Bloomsbury Set - Whisky & Cedarwood" on eBay. I had tested this fragrance several times and commented on it based on the experiences I had; the prices were just too outrageous for me. But this time it was meant to be, and the seller, still a novice in this sales arena, asked if I might also be interested in a leftover "Garden Lilies" from this seasonal series. I was, and she packed this bottle for me. I would like to express my gratitude here: that is very, very kind! "Garden Lilies" reminds me of the evening scent of white lilies, whose petals bend back when fully ripe, showcasing the thick yellow stamens. According to the listed fragrance notes, this floral sensation seems to be more attributed to the white musk and a generous portion of warming vanilla. I have never consciously encountered fragrant water lilies, so I must tread on unfamiliar ground here. A green note, on the other hand, does not develop for me at all; perhaps I am simply too fish-bloody for it to dare to come out. Be that as it may: this Jo Malone fragrance is very full and rounded right from the first acquaintance. Ylang-ylang ultimately makes it shine; this makes it even a bit more extraordinary. This year's limited fragrance collection "The Bloomsbury Set" by Jo Malone differs not only in the artistic design of the bottle from its classic predecessors. Of the three of the four scents from the set that I now know well, "Tobacco & Mandarin", "Whisky & Cedarwood", and now "Garden Lilies", the last two actually have a slightly longer longevity. They lack the fragrant lightness of the other fragrance variants, to which I also count "Tobacco & Mandarin". This makes frequent reapplication unnecessary. "Garden Lilies" is a very warm, feminine fragrance that evokes memories of one of the first cozy summer evenings on the terrace or in the Hollywood swing, while the frogs croak in the dark garden.

When one cannot deny the family resemblance. Right upon spraying the fragrance, I felt vaguely reminded of something. Again and again, I inhaled the scent until I realized - it was another Jo Malone fragrance. Garden Lillies is unmistakably related to Mimosa & Cardamom by Jo Malone. It is like the little sister, a bit younger and fresher, but it carries a similarly lovely undertone. Bottle: The Bloomsbury Collection deviates somewhat from the usual Jo Malone design with its bottle. While the classic shape has been retained, the cap is colored and satin-finished, matching the overall color scheme. Unfortunately, this makes the cap somewhat prone to scratches and small dents. The bottle is adorned with a colored background in a geometric style, meant to remind of the inspiration for the collection - the Bloomsbury Group. In the case of Garden Lillies, this color scheme is in shades of blue. Scent: Garden Lillies is a fragrance that shows little development and maintains its delicate and lovely note for several hours. Thus, the naming with just one fragrance note is truly fitting. While in Mimosa & Cardamom the tonka bean is very dominant, in Garden Lillies the vanilla holds back a bit. It does not overpower the scent but accompanies it throughout with its creamy sweetness. Meanwhile, ylang-ylang and the water lily provide a freshness that does not become too aquatic and has a very delicate floral quality. The musk stays quite subdued, presumably it is what keeps the vanilla in check. In today's time, where fragrances often seem heavy, artificially fruity, or extremely sweet, I have rarely experienced a scent that radiates spring as much as this one. Longevity and Sillage: The sillage of Garden Lillies is very close to the skin, like many of the Jo Malone fragrances. Nevertheless, it lasted exceptionally long on me. Even after 5 hours, I could still perceive it. Conclusion: For those who find Mimosa & Cardamom a companion in the cooler seasons, they will discover a wonderful fragrance for spring or even summer here.

Tested at printemps boulevard haussman paris in 2019. Another great fragrance of collection privée givenchy. My favorite with cuir blanc.fresh and woody perfect fo spring and the beginning of fall.more masculine. I never smelled another perfum which can be similar.unfortunately because givenchy stops this collection. A masterpiece if you can buy it don t hesitate

Bois Martial is part of the Atelier line from Givenchy, which unfortunately no longer exists in this form. The simple bottle rests in high-quality packaging. 100% coherent and successful. Bois Martial opens with an elegant sweetness, from which the first wood notes slowly emerge from its depths. Initial notes of light cedar wood become perceptible and take hold. At the same time, a certain light sweetness remains, which makes the wood warm and gentle. And so this fragrance continues to develop. Gradually, the cedar aspect recedes a bit into the background, but the overall feeling remains softly woody. The whole thing is wonderfully elegant - and almost discreet - simply excellent! Bois Martial, like the other fragrances I know from this line, unfortunately no longer corresponds to the spirit of the times. There is nothing loud, nothing is “in your face” - because this fragrance simply doesn’t need that. Today, it is a bit like a perfect gentleman in the middle of a football stadium. He doesn’t quite fit in, but one has to somehow pay him respect. Since I bought it many years ago in Paris, it has never disappointed me, and it is still one of my absolute favorites today.

For about ten years now, it seems to have become the norm for many perfume-producing houses to add a second, exclusive premium line to their (often established and quite successful) retail fragrances. The esteemed Tom Ford was one of the first with his Private Blends, followed by houses like Dior, Chanel, and Dolce & Gabbana - Guerlain has always masterfully navigated the duality between mainstream and niche. One can certainly debate whether these - always high-priced and artificially scarce - premium fragrances are worth their asking price, but there are gems among them that I wouldn't want to miss. The house of Givenchy was one of the last to join the ranks of 'small, fine, expensive, hard to get' with their L'Atelier line - yet these fragrances (beautifully presented and reminiscent in their understated (scent) language and aesthetics of spools of thread) are worth every nose they encounter. Bois Martial - the gray one among the L'Ateliers - is a light-footed and extremely supple wood scent that, in its delicacy and precision, manages to evoke a quality from the eponymous woods that is new yet not scandalous. It oscillates equally between the bright, warm hint of an old, bleached softwood table and the almost metallic echo of a dance floor or a fencing piste, today mostly made of copper or aluminum. Bois Martial is a lively, charming wood scent full of lightness and mischief - unusual, yet not foreign. Conclusion: In the early 50s, Stewart Granger slipped into the role of 'Scaramouche, the Gallant Marquis' as a jester and engaged in a nearly ten-minute sword duel with Mel Ferrer in a theater, which is legendary within the cloak-and-sword genre and is still considered the best fencing scene in film history. Powerful, yet elegant and extremely precise - just like Bois Martial, Givenchy's light gray warrior wood.

These mint leaves leave nothing to the imagination. If you want a subtle fresh mint note added to any of your current or future fragrance layering projects...this will get 'er done. It's not a strong mint, it's more like a piece of mint gum after the first hour of chewing. A warm, rounded mint with a moist hot texture. That may not sound appealing, but this fragrance does layer very well with the Jo Malone Sweet Milk, "Earl Grey", "Nutmeg & Ginger" and "Verbena's of Provence" scents. I can't personally imagine wearing this all on its own. It seemed flat and certainly, I can find something and Bath and Body Works or Demeter that is just as good for a 1/4 of the price, but as a layering agent with other Jo Malone's, I believe this has a real purpose and is a decent representation of fresh spritely mint leaves.

Thanks to the lovely Fantajuice, I had the opportunity to test this beautiful tea fragrance. My impression is that the name perfectly reflects the scent: I smell tea, I smell grapefruit, and I smell nothing else. I don't need to, the fragrance is lovely just as it is; puristic, fresh, clean, and completely free of any sour or piercing undertone, instead featuring a slight creaminess that likely comes from the musk. The only downside is the longevity and sillage -- at least on my skin -- which is very poor. I have to press my nose against my arm to perceive the lovely notes, and after about half an hour, I feel like I can't smell anything anymore.

On their way to New York, Audrey Hepburn and her then-husband Mel Ferrer made a brief stop in Paris, where they met with Audrey's dear friend Hubert de Givenchy for a festive dinner. On this occasion at the end of December 1956, Hubert presented her with a small box wrapped in a satin ribbon. "A gift? A gift for me?" Audrey surely asked. "A perfume?" she asked in confusion after unwrapping the box. Yes, it was a perfume; an exclusive perfume: dedicated to her, his muse. It smelled floral and powdery, of roses, jasmine, violets, and something indefinable - woody? A perfume that had no name yet: it was meant to be Audrey Hepburn's own scent for a whole year. After this time, they planned to start selling it. Audrey and Givenchy thought about a fitting name and then said: "L'Interdit" - the forbidden one! Because it was forbidden for all other women for an entire year! You really can't give a more personal gift to your muse. Audrey Hepburn was not only the muse of this fashion designer, but she also remained his closest friend until her early death. They trusted each other, and later, Hubert's life partner Philippe joined the group; he was also welcomed into the circle of friends. Their first meeting actually came about due to a mix-up. For the film "Sabrina," the film studios in the USA expected an appropriate wardrobe and asked Ms. Hepburn to choose a couturier who would also accompany her through other films as a costume designer. Audrey had liked the style of the young Frenchman her age from the very beginning, so she requested a meeting and flew to Paris the very next day, overjoyed. She was led into his office; he stood behind his desk and froze slightly: Had they only informed him that Ms. Hepburn wanted an appointment, and he thought of Katherine Hepburn! Instead of that lady, a young woman stood before him, who had just taken a stroll through the city and was dressed very casually. How embarrassing it was for both of them, and yet it was the beginning of a wonderful friendship! Her request for him to design the complete wardrobe for "Sabrina" interested and flattered him, but he had to decline: it was July, and in August all of France would be on vacation; filming was set to begin at the end of September 1953. How could that work? For the disappointed Audrey, Hubert de Givenchy couldn't quickly tailor a new outfit. But as a "quasi-friend" - they had gone out to eat together that same day - he found a solution. He also had a chamber with "forgotten dresses." He took her there: beautiful and tailored, they hung there, the most diverse garments, on meter-long rolling racks. Even fitting for Audrey's delicacy; as if they had been waiting for her. Within two hours, both had joyfully assembled the collection for "Sabrina"; any necessary changes were made, and by the time filming began, everything was securely packed and flown across the Atlantic on time. "Sabrina" was dressed appropriately! And now, three years later, a fragrance of her own: "L'Interdit," a scent that would belong to her alone for an entire year and for which she would later become the advertising icon - the "face." (By the way, she did not receive any commission from the sales he made through her and her name; she mostly bought her perfume and wardrobe herself. That was completely natural for her: Hubert de Givenchy was a friend! When her then-husband Mel Ferrer came up with the glorious idea of demanding a share of the profits behind her back and setting up an account in Paris, he fell out of favor. During her next visit there, she withdrew the entire amount and handed it to Hubert in an envelope. She was so embarrassed!) The Eau de Toilette, which resided in a rather crusty glass vial, left very intense scent impressions. In contrast to the perfume, it is not floral-powdery; instead, it has a bit more floral freshness; but it is very much a child of its time: opulent, mysteriously feminine, and enchanting. Of course, the sparkling, lively, fluttering aldehydes were not to be missed. The fruit basket that adorns the entrance is as uncomplicated in content as the rest of the fragrance composition, and yet the combination of bergamot, mandarin, peach, and fresh strawberries appears elegant and tasteful. It seems a little peppery (with the strawberries?) to me, and perhaps the peaches were even speckled with some cloves for aromatic enrichment. The selection of the following floral scent sequence is not particularly exotic either. No, it seems as if Hubert strolled through a summer garden with a flower basket and scissors, searching for the most beautiful treasures for the planned heart note: Here some roses, there a few branches of jasmine, the proud, slightly powdery iris also joins in. Some daffodils with friendly yellow faces, of course, lily of the valley, and some vines of ylang-ylang fall victim to the scissors. This basket ultimately contains a large floral bouquet fresh from the summer garden, full of intensely sensual scents. It is placed next to the already filled fruit basket. Now a base is still needed to create a fragrance worthy of a woman whose elegance is so obvious. Here too, they stick to the obvious: a dose of tonka bean, to replace the vanilla, is the only exotic in the fragrance weave. Classically, earthbound, and sensually, it continues: vetiver, cistus/labdanum? and benzoin resin stand for that; sandalwood oil must also not be missing. Musk promises a bit of passion, and ambergris guarantees the overall perfection of this fragrance woman! If a perfume is to feel like a forbidden fruit, then "L'Interdit" has fully succeeded in that. Those who approach this forbidden fruit (and aren't the forbidden ones the sweetest?) discover a woman who radiates both romance and perfection and charm. This is how Hubert de Givenchy saw his everlasting muse in wardrobe and fragrance: the doe-eyed, delicate (always too thin due to the aftermath of war and her high cigarette consumption) Audrey Hepburn. In the meantime, I've sniffed around the glass vial so often that, of course, my fingers are all sticky. The original crusts are dissolving, and by tomorrow morning at the latest, I can say how clingy this charming being will be. But it doesn't seem too fleeting to me. So we will first spend the night together. I just see that a new edition has also been released here. So there is still the possibility to smell like Audrey Hepburn, just not so exclusively anymore. However, we no longer have to fear committing a taboo with it! We spray a little, buy a paper cup of coffee and something sweet from the bag, and then we go window shopping! Come on, Holly! It's Breakfast-Time at Tiffany's!

First yellow, light, floral-light, then increasingly spicy, woody, cool, and bitter, vetiver becomes more prominent. The girlishness recedes a bit within the first half hour, without losing its feminine-soft charm. The colors become somewhat darker, cooler, blue-green, violet, but rather the colors of a watercolor than oil or acrylic. Light remains abundant, more like an impressionist play of light. Sometimes the iris appears, over time more iris root? (as it becomes more bitter, not powdery) sometimes the geranium, which also brings in a slightly bitter note (at least that’s how those on mother’s balcony smelled), well balanced by the bitter freshness of the vetiver. Not an exciting fragrance, yet cheerful like a Saturday afternoon in the garden during iris blooming. Due to its spiciness, it might also appeal to some men.

I am not a specialist in iris fragrances, but here the iris is as dominant as it is enchanting. Alongside the vetiver, which becomes clearly prominent later on, the geranium plays the second lead role. For me, geranium appears generally here; I do not know the specific variety "Lady Moore." This all sounds very straightforward at first, but this does not come at the expense of the brilliance of the scent, which is capable of surprising the wearer at all times. When trying to describe it, the following words always come to mind: straightforward, but not unwelcoming floral, but not overly ornate transparent, yet powerful subtly elegant, yet uncomplicated woody, yet comforting mature, in no way old-fashioned and very subtly powdery and subtly romantic Hardly any scent can be better translated into color (a little quirk of mine: which colors match which scent, this is then the perfect coordination of clothing and perfume). Here, cool colors immediately come to mind - the floral colors of the beautiful bottle suggest it - blue, purple, violet, and cool pink, also green, definitely not warm colors. The longevity is excellent; when sprayed multiple times in the morning, you can enjoy this beautiful scent all day long. Overapplication is certainly possible with this Jo Malone. Unfortunately, it is a limited fragrance that was released as part of the 3-piece series "London Blooms"; now only remaining stocks should be available for purchase.

The great thing about L'Atelier is its exclusivity. Givenchy is already known for something special. With the Atelier fragrances, you can be sure that you won't smell them on every corner. In Berlin, the creations are available at Lafayette and KaDeWe - and of course in the Givenchy boutiques. I particularly like iris because of its sensually alluring and aphrodisiac effect. So I decided to try the harmony... The pretty girl (maybe in her mid-20s) from the Givenchy department sprays the fragrance into the air and wafts the Givenchy card through the vapor spray mist - very elegant. I always do it differently: 10 cm away and straight onto my wrist. Why do I mention this here? I'll come back to that later. Top Note: Wow, what a bold iris this is! The scent caresses my nose so much that it settles in my brain. One perceives floral notes that have a bold carrier. Ylang and neroli are almost restrained in their floral quality by the warm and woody immortelle. The top note is so beautiful that I would have to give it 15 points... Heart Note: The top note quickly transitions into the heart note. Neroli fades away, and slightly spicier nuances emerge. Yes, it becomes a bit bolder, but this does not detract from the fragrance's harmony, as the top note was not a pure floral sea due to the straw flower (immortelle) anyway. The heart note is very subtle and sensual. Like a small shy and vulnerable kitten, it lays on the skin. Unfortunately, really such a pity: The scent becomes increasingly subtle, so that after about 3 hours, you only perceive it up close. I can't explain why that is. It should have the strong oud in the base... Heart Note: 8 points Base Note: Well, the base. Where is the oud now? The scent remains warm, woody, and earthy, while subtly fixing the lovely iris. The guaiac wood is probably responsible for that. But where the hell is the oud? I can live with it if oud is not wasted, as it is quite expensive. But I hardly perceive the oud here - maybe a pinch. That's not a big deal, since the fragrance is not called Oud Harmonique but Iris Harmonique. And those who know oud know that it can be quite a heavy hitter. However, perhaps a second pinch of oud would have given the fragrance in the base a bit more strength and longevity - it certainly wouldn't have hurt, as Iris Harmonique offers hardly any olfactory perception in the base. That's such a shame. You would have to reapply it every three hours if you want a corresponding sillage. After four hours, the scent is only barely detectable, like a subtle quickly absorbing cream. The skin smells pleasantly sweet, spicy, and earthy. This means: With a trained nose, one can still perceive the wonderfully transformed iris. Maybe you just need to apply a bit more (e.g., also on hair, shirt/blouse), but at a price of €200.00, that’s a tough sell. Perhaps it’s better to pre-treat the corresponding body areas (neck, décolletage, nape, wrists) with oil or cream... 7.5 points Conclusion: Because the top note is so exceptionally good, it still gets a total of 10 points. Longevity: Unfortunately, rather below average, but maybe it’s (hopefully) due to my skin's pH value, hence - 7 points. Sillage: Well, I hardly perceive any. I don’t think my surroundings do either. This fits with the restraint and the extremely subtle appearance of this harmony. 6 points Bottle: The bottle is excessively elegant. The thread on the cap of the L'Artelier series is supposed to indicate that the L'Atelier perfumes were inspired by certain fashion collections. 10 points Who: everyone - ladies, gentlemen, young, older When: always and forever - spring, summer, autumn, winter I just bought the last bottle at Galeries Lafayette - the fragrance is supposedly being discontinued... ;-( P.S.: What SabriNoir experienced three years ago can't be true somehow. At least I can't comprehend that.

This is a classic fougere that is complete 1980s powerhouse! Boys, step aside, this is men only! A little background to Xeryus is erroneously controversial. It was originally to be called Kereus. YSL cried Kouros came first! In Greek X is pronounced K. Hence the swapped letter. Both have common elements, yet Xeryus is very dark. Oakmoss is used liberally, from start to finish. The projection is a good 3 feet in all directions! The composition is dense, some florals and complex woods, developing for several hours. Smoky tobacco is somewhat obvious. The powerful Fougere accord can last all night. It is a walk in a deep dark rich forest under a full moon. Bela Lugosi would have worn this in Dracula (sic).

A beautiful scent that lives up to its name. The green notes, which I can clearly perceive shortly after application, unfortunately fade quite quickly. What remains is a delicate floral fragrance that is quite pleasant, not too sweet with a slight freshness. I think of a young woman walking through a wildflower meadow in a long white summer dress, letting her hands brush over the tall grass and small, colorful flowers. But just as fleeting as the sight of this young woman, who quickly disappears from my field of vision in the vastness of this summer meadow, is the scent. After just two hours, I can hardly perceive it anymore and need to reapply.

A watery, fresh floral with a citrus opening, quickly dries down to a soft rose scent. After about an hour this is a skin scent on me. Lingers, though it is barely detectable. Very pleasant and perfect if you are in an environment where perfume might be bothersome to others. However, there is nothing exciting about this and I won't be purchasing a full bottle once I'm done with my mini.

Demeter Nutmeg Ice Cream is subtle and stays close to the skin. At first I thought it had faded immediately and entirely, but the sweet cream and a hint of spices are there. I’ve gotten better results with Demeter’s atomizers, and I wonder if the problem here is that it’s a roller ball. It was also a freebie though so I can’t complain.

I was sent a sample of this and I have to say, I really enjoyed wearing it! I was craving something comforting and Autumn-like and I figured that this would be perfect and as it turns out, it worked in my favour. Really lovely concoction!
