This is a clean and marine tuberose, not as heavy as in Poison or Fracas, but still powerful with its creamy, coconutty, fatty, almost bready aspects.

4/5 of my Discovery Set: I am extremely biased towards white florals. Perhaps part of my body will always long for my parent's provincial birth place that celebrated and doused itself in jasmine flowers. This scent was like a jolt of love for me: sweet and heavy.

This is a fresh, modern take on a classic white floral. Jasmine and orange blossom dominate, especially at first, but the tuberose is there. I generally tend to avoid tuberose, but since it is not screeching its presence here, I can tolerate it--actually, I enjoy the way it enhances the jasmine. (Please note: I love jasmine, especially the richer, velvety, damp-tropical kinds.

Some people may think this is not tuberose but jasmine. This tuberose has a tropical feel to it. I also recommend it to those who like gardenia. Gardenia perfumes almost always contain coconut or vanilla for some reason, which makes it feel like "using oil paintings with the scent of watercolors" (does that make sense?), but this one doesn't, so it's very transparent.

For more than two years, she has been preparing for this day. She has not spared herself during this time to improve her performance over and over again. She wanted the victory, only once, and despite all the oddities, but first of all for herself. She wanted to know, wanted to prove to herself that she could do it if she just worked hard enough. Then it was her turn and she showed her best performance, better than in all training sessions and better than in any other competition that she completed - as a kind of training unit - within the last year. When she finished she knew she had made it! Even if a few other candidates came after her, they were all too far back to the preliminaries. Full of happiness, she went into the resting room, pulled the rubber from her long, blond hair and shook it right. She opened her bag and took out her little bottle. Semicircle, like a handcuffer and heavy as a stone. She turned the ground plug slightly and dabbed a drop of her favorite perfume behind each ear: Amarige! It is her very personal scent and now also her winner's perfume. But she always bought the extrait, because this did not have the sharpness and scratchiness of EdT or EdP. It starts with slightly sour fruits, which she does not like so much, but luckily it flies very fast and then appear all the flowers, which she loves so much. She feels Amarige as a cool scent, with a cornucopia of all "cool" flowers, like lily of the valley, violet, jasmine, honeysuckle and the like. A bright yellow rose is also included. The scent is luminous, even radiant and fits to her, like no other. Amarige also lasts very long and is also very good noticeable in her surrounding. When she wears it, she feels safe and strong. She knows she can achieve anything she wants. At the Victory, she takes the golden cup and the beautiful bouquet of flowers, which, without a doubt, tries to smell her perfume. After a long and so successful day, she comes home, peels off the shoes and puts the bouquet into the vase. Then she pours herself a splendid tea and cuddles herself into her sofa, now accompanied by the quiet, gentle side of her perfume. Although the flowers are still present, but now accompanied by powdery and woody notes.

Tempo is foremost a patchouli fragrance on my skin, albeit an exceptionally gentle one at that. Upon spraying, the spicy, medicinal and woody aspects of patchouli are there, but they feel so soft and tender that I start to imagine a baby patchouli if there ever was one. The creamy and gently powdered cacao nuance also makes an appearance, which further stretches the innocent feeling of this patchouli. Although I love patchouli in general, I very often gravitate towards those more earthy, darker, bitter chocolate type of interpretations of this fantastically complex note. And when the patchouli is stripped clean and appears bright in mood, I tend to find them too sweet for my taste. Thanks to the overall gentleness of Tempo, I didn't find its sweetness unbearable to me, but not far though. Thankfully, the sage and maté soon come to rescue, subduing the fruity sweetness of pink pepper with their herbal and slightly bitter aroma. Tempo then remains this occasionally medicinal and woody-cacao, but mostly herbal patchouli skin scent until the end. Although the fragrance is not dense, it projects moderately. The longevity is around 8 hours on me. I personally don't care much about Tempo because of my own preferences regarding patchouli in perfumery. However, being one of the most mild patchouli fragrances that I smelt, Tempo might be a quite friendly start point to further explore patchouli, or an unobtrusive patchouli for daily routine thanks to it retaining the quiet elegance of modern Diptyque fragrances.

Tempo conjures an atmosphere of dolorous elegance, patchouli’s murky woods and dusky loam, with a wraithlike metallic chill and an herbal shiver of something green and strange simmering underneath. It carries a disquieting heaviness, the shape of a feeling impossible to give voice to; like having to climb into bed with someone and tell them they’re dead. It also reminds me of this passage from Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House, "No live organism can continue for long to exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality; even larks and katydids are supposed, by some, to dream. Hill House, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within… and whatever walked there, walked alone." This is a patchouli that has walked the long shadows of Hill House, has become lost in the thick, unspoken secrets of its notorious halls, and suffered its mad face in the growing darkness. This is a twisted, haunted patchouli that has seen some shit, but all the edges of that unnerving terror have been blurred by the creeping of moss, the settling of dust, and the softness of time and memory, of unreality and dream.

I have come to recognise the house of Diptyque has its own style and level of quality, and their patchouli pillar fits in just perfectly. Thank you for watching as always and I hope you enjoy the review.

What would time smell like? Of course, it is a non-sensical question, but it might be different depending on what aspect of time you are thinking of. Tempo means time in Italian, and to me and others, it specifically refers to the speed at which a musical piece is played at. In an orchestra, the tempo of piece can completely shatter your expectations for it. One of my favorite examples is the beginning/first half of Dvorak's 9th symphony, movement II, an incredibly popular piece for good reason. In most recordings I have heard, the tempo is 'largo' meaning slow. In Sergiu Celibidache's recording (of particular interest that he abhorred recordings), the tempo is indubitably 'molto largo'. This slowing down of the piece makes you appreciate things you otherwise may not notice. I am particularly thinking right now of a passage for the double bass, where the star is the oboe, but in Celibidache's recording, it's the double bass. If you know the piece, you know what I am talking about. If not, please do yourself a favor and go listen to it. Tempo, now by Diptyque, has struck me in a similar manner. Others have written about how it is 'superfluous', and how others have done patchouli in better ways. Can anything truly original be created? Perhaps you wish to debate that. To me, patchouli is the symphony. It was written by nature and recorded by the many thousands of perfumers who have put their talents out there. Tempo, if the allegory wasn't obvious yet, is the tempo. There is something about this composition that makes you appreciate this symphony in a different light. It's not damp, but it's earthy. It's not sophisticated, but it is refined. It's a delicious envelopment of patchouli in an honest light, with minor herbal and spices' support Projection is strong 2-3 hours, muted after. Sillage is good. Definitely leans masculine, perhaps someone who works in an office but has fingernail dirt from the garden. Tempo is a green jacket and a brown waistcoat. Someone who can listen to the same thing everyone else can and hear something else.

“Tempo” is the Italian word for time. I didn’t know why Diptyque chose to give this name to one of its creations, but after three weeks with it I might see why. I wanted to buy a Diptyque fragrance for months because I am a sucker for their style and their candles: even though I tried many because their offer is massive, I ended up with Tempo. I wanted something versatile (so not Oud Palao) and a little bit different from what the creamy woodyness I am already used to (Santal Austral by Matiere Premiere has basically been my signature this year and I also have Egoïste by Chanel, so Tam Dao and 34 Bvd. St Germain were off) without breaking the bank (so no Eau Rihla, even though it might be the most beautiful fragrance I’ve smelled from them. Maybe in the future…). Considering that I love drinking mate I was eyeing Tempo since I became interested in niche perfumery, and when it was time to choose I basically went for the fragrance that thicked as many boxes as possible even though it wasn’t what captured me the most at the time (Eau Rihla) or the one I felt better suited for my personality (34 Bvd St. Germain EDP). However, I was pretty confident that a green-earthy fragrance would have enriched my collection and was happy overall with the purchase. When I smelled the fragrance more closely, I felt two things. The first was how well blended were all the elements from the citrusy, spicy opening to the earthy but gentle drydown; the second, was that the mate was not the focal point but rather a great enforcer to the patchouli. I wasn’t a big on this ingredient since recently, but I think that Tempo really made me a fan in this iteration: I feel like it’s damp but warm at the same time, and I think that the violet leaves help smoothen it in the drydown. However, something really unexpected happened like the third day I wore it: something seemed unpleasant once I sprayed it in the morning before going to work, and once I got home I tried to spray it again on my wrist and on a mouillette. I smelled nothing but Martini Extra Dry, and it was a nightmare for me because I have a negative memory associated to it (when I was younger I bought a bottle of it during a summer when I was alone at my parents’ home, but soon I threw it away because its smell became repulsive to me). I think that it might have done with the aromatic profile of the fragrance, but at the time I was upset because it was the most expensive fragrance I’ve ever bought: I even thought about selling it to recover some money and keep buying ambery woody or spicy woody fragrances for the rest of my life. Luckily, I chose to wait a couple of days, wear my beloved woody fragrances and then try Tempo again on the next week. It worked perfectly, since I don’t smell Martini Extra Dry anymore and I seem to like it every day more. Tempo, as its name suggests, might have taken some time to truly convince me. But now that it made it, I think that it’s going to be smelled many times on me in the next few years.

I will NEVER get rid of this fragrance. I'm crazy of mate and patchouli combination. They work together perfectly. Lime and herbs add a little bit of freshness to this earthy composition. Tempo has a great sillage, I feel it on myself with every move and people feel it too! Every perfume lover should try this.

Admittedly, I'm not a patchouli fan, so I also don't have a ton of experience with patchouli-forward fragrances. I get the earthy appeal, especially as a base note in other fragrances, but as a hero note... I need to be convinced. Tempo, for me, feels like a patchouli solinote.

Tempo smells pleasantly bitter and medicinal like herbal tonics or Angostura bitters. If you like eating bitter melon, chances are you’ll enjoy this. As Tempo is a patchouli fragrance, longevity and sillage are great. The maté note really shines through and makes me think of yerba maté.

I absolutely adore how this smells and I wear it purely for myself as I find it's sillage is not very strong. As soon as I smell this I relax. I love how earthy it is, and the maté note tickles my brain in the most wonderful way. I can spray this on in the morning and still smell it late into the evening, so great value for money

I am a huge fan of Diptyque and love all their creations. I got Tempo as a birthday gift from my hubby today. I wore it to work and oh boy. I love it!! Just 2 sprays and that was enough. The dry down is very delicious. The fragrance lasts and lasts. I love the patchouli and mate notes. Very, very earthy and chocolatey.

This body spray is perfect for sleeping or for at home. It is floral, creamy, almost milky-sweet with a pleasantly dosed musk base. It also works well for layering. The concentration is lower than that of an EDT, which is just right for my taste when you simply want to smell fresh after showering and moisturizing for longer. Very subtle and intimate.

While I typically don’t enjoy rose scents, and I never fuck with berry fragrances, Diptyque L’Ombre dans L’Eau is one of the exceptions. Perhaps because the rose only just shyly peeps out of the lush, leafy greenery and aromatic botanicals. The berries are bittersweet and biting, rather than overripe and cloying, and pair marvelously with lemony, herbaceous geranium. It feels practical and beautiful, like an artful object that actually serves a useful function, as opposed to a remaining a dusty shelf-turd. This is the sort of perfume that makes me think of how someone said that self-care is doing the things that maybe you don’t feel like doing now, so that you can set future-you up for success. Like making some sort of wellness appointment. I would wear this to visit the chiropractor and think the whole time, “good job you! You are doing your best!”

This must have been a groundbreaking fragrance when it came out in 1983. I can sense traces of L'Ombre dans L'Eau in so many newer scents, from classics like Jo Malone Blackberry & Bay or YSL In Love Again to more recent niche offerings like LM Kingkydise, Victoria Minya Cassis or Linari Capelli D'Oro. The scent profile still feels fresh and modern after all these years, unlike most other releases from the 80s. In the opening the fact that this is an older fragrance is the most apparent. It has a grassy-green floral note that definitely reads as "vintagey" to me, which is honestly not my favorite thing in fragrances. But this part is gone soon, and then we're left with dewy roses, tart, juicy blackcurrant, a creamy, musky base and a soft hint of greenery. This kind of scent always conjures the colors pink and dark green in my mind. In this case, it's a darker, richer pink that borders on burgundy, while most of the similar fragrances I mentioned above feel more hot pink to me. Why is L'Ombre dans L'Eau darker? Well, even though nothing like that is listed, it has a slightly smokey undertone, like a curl of incense in the fruity floral scent. And maybe the absence of other fruits besides the blackcurrant also plays a role in this. It's a refreshing scent that has just enough sweetness to keep it from going unpleasantly sour, but still feels a little mouth-puckering, like an unsweetened currant would. There are some other, more playful fragrances in this genre that fit my style a little better, but I still really enjoyed testing this and respect the art behind it. I also noticed it shines on warm skin. Perfect for a hot, humid summer day right before it finally starts to rain. If you like rose/cassis combos, you should really try it, even if it's only to get to know the original that started it all.

L'Ombre dans l'Eau (Shadow in the Water) had been spinning around my head for some time, along with Philosykos Eau de Toilette , and I finally tried it. I had read some reviews before ordering a test sample, most notably the description on Diptyque's official website. The more I read, the more this sour and sour rose tempted me, and I tried to figure the scent out in my mind. Well, I can confirm the perfume left me speechless when I first smelled it. It is not the rose I am used to, which I often encounter in the scents I own or know. I reviewed the Delina Exclusif jammy rose a few days ago, and it is definitely not it. It is something I have never experienced before, a sort of unknown greenness that pleasantly surprised me. Ironically, I can't tell if the perfume was premature when it was created or if they meant it for the future. And I say this because despite being released in the early eighties, the perfume is very modern and avant-garde, so much so that it can be mistaken for a new niche creation. Nothing here stresses the powerhouse of that period in which the opulent Paris Eau de Toilette , Opium (1977) Parfum , Diva Eau de Parfum , or K de Krizia (1980) Eau de Toilette , to name a few, reigned. I immediately start by saying that the declared keynotes are the floral ones of the dew-soaked rose, which contrast with the fruity ones of the blackcurrant buds and the greener and fresher ones of the petitgrain, all supported by the acidulous nuances of the blackcurrant leaves. Everything else? These few notes create a fresh, summery, and rosy accord that closely resembles the green sap flowing through plants. L'Ombre dans l'Eau evokes the scent of a green garden near the water, and I feel all life pulsating within this essence. Somehow, L'Ombre dans L'Eau captures something of the fresh pleasure of a deep breath of natural outside air better than anything I've smelled so far. Until now, when I approached a green family scent, I felt the notes of foliage, branches, shrubs, and reeds, for example, those of bamboo, figs, tomatoes, galbanum, or ivy, but I had smelled nothing of so close to the lifeblood. L’Ombre dans l’Eau has an incisive and pungent opening, vivid, full of tartness, and even a little astringent. I dare say, polarising and unwelcome to a large audience. For a few seconds, an accord develops on my skin that reminds me of the green intensity that the peel of the slightly unripe pomegranate gives off when it is cut to extract the precious ruby juicy grains. There is a watery side, but not like cucumber slices, and an earthy side, but not quite like vetiver roots. Instead, a smell that recalls the soaked soil after a storm. All this green freshness comes from the leaves of the black currant, from the smell of the brushed and broken leaves, with a note of bitter citrus given by the citrus leaves, the petitgrain. In some ways, this pungent aspect also reminds me of the unmistakable smell of tomato leaves, but that of unripe pomegranate seeds is more likely for my sense of smell. In the heart, the flowery aspects of the rose stand out, slowly emerging without dominating or overwhelming the other notes. It does not claim to be a soliflores rose, but it is as if the leaves and fruits of the black currant were in my hands while the wild rose bushes were much further away from me and their scent reached me carried by a light breeze. These aren't just the fragrant petals that make up the central part. The aqueous shades of the freesia buds and the slightly bitter ones of the narcissus are clear to me, although only Bulgarian rose and black currant berries are listed. Besides the watery and dewy aspects, the blackcurrant leaves' herbaceousness, the fruity, sour accents, and the floral intensity of the rose, on the other, pop up clearly. The berries aren't too fruity, but they lean on the wet, green scent of the leaves. If I put my nose on my skin, I also feel a lemony and pungent tinge that recalls the smell of coriander leaves or its seeds crushed between my fingers, a spicy flavour I love to meet in Indian cuisine. These notes and chords brought up so far lie against a musky background of ambergris and musk, which makes for an attractive scent as the rose continues to dominate, and some subtle hints of warm amber sweetness manifest. Ambergris and musk provide a touch of salty, sweet and warm, at first, a pleasant contrast to the fresh outdoor smells of the rest of the ingredients. Moss does not take over and is not animalic but softens and strengthens the dewy rose. There is a hint of coumarin, but it only gives a powdery sense without making the fragrance too sweet, spicy, or gourmand. You won't detect even the tiniest trace of dust in this perfume if you don't like powdery undertones in perfumes. Hence, the fragrance is undoubtedly perfect for wearing on hot days; spring and summer months seem appropriate. As it is not aggressive, I think it is safe for the office and a lazy weekend at home or out of town. Not a noble beast from a longevity standpoint, but it projects well in the early hours with a good sillage, and that's okay with me. Did L’Ombre dans l’Eau disappoint me? Not, indeed. I base my opinion and review on a decant I have owned since October 2022. -Elysium

Diptyque L'OMBRE DANS L'EAU opens with a ferny feeling and then suddenly a rosebush pops up out of nowhere. After a couple of minutes, though, the “fern” note, which I believe is angelica, given its behavior—takes over the composition completely, shrouding the rose in relative obscurity. I've learned through a few niche testings that angelica is really not a note that works well for me. Perhaps I am extra-sensitive to the point of finding even a modest dose excessive. Whatever the case may be, L'OMBRE DANS L'EAU ends up being yet another (quasi-)angelica-focused niche offering that I really cannot see myself wearing much. I own the solid compact of this perfume, which unfortunately offers an even stronger presentation of the fernish angelica (or reasonable facsimile) note and while it does not make me ill, neither is it a perfume that I would reach for before, say, 200+ others. This was a bad blind buy on my part, a gamble based on the entirely arbitrary fact that Diptyque has chosen to offer only a few of its perfumes in solid form, all of which I decided to acquire as a part of my quest to expand my understanding of that much-neglected medium. Maybe if I wear L'OMBRE DANS L'EAU enough I'll develop a tolerance to this hyper-super-ueber-fernishness. On ne sait jamais. Hope springs eternal, and sundry other hackneyed clichés, not to mention pleonasms and, yes, redundancies!!!!!

This is simply delightful. Jammy tart blackcurrant and rose bushes. A slight lemony citrus from petitgrain. It's sweeter than I was expecting. Some people here are reporting sharp and bitter notes. I get none of that save for in the first two minutes of spraying where there is a strong waft of herbaceous greenery. Not at all unpleasant. It has surprisingly good sillage, the kind that you get gentle wafts of but doesn't overpower. I can see myself wearing this often. Many will disagree, but to me this comes off like the classier and more naturalistic version of La Fille De Berlin. Except that this has a fruitiness from blackcurrant that creates the jammy quality, and no metallic edge to speak of. It's certainly a quieter, less "bright" scent than La Fille. Still jammy, and has that dark rose vibe. They don't share the same notes, so this could be controversial but I do see them as being almost unruly little sister and sophisticated big sister. I really can't believe this was first marketed in 1983, it really strikes me as ahead of it's time. And worn by the goddess herself, Lauren Bacall.

2/5 of my Discovery Set: I am floored with this scent. To me, it smells like honey being poured over a garden. It's distinct and so very sweet. I feel that it can be overwhelmingly strong if used in excess, but this is a lovely green that I did not expect.

Messy, acrid cheap synthetic cassis, synthetic rose and synthetic blackcurrant all the way. It may have been better some years ago, now it’s this – and nothing else. It smells halfway a drugstore green-rose cologne from the 1980’s and a contemporary fruity-musky scent right out of a suburban Chinese emporium.

This was one of my first niche fragrance purchases and an almost instant regret. If you're into very vivid, naturalistic garden settings, the opening is fantastic (and what initially lured me into putting my money down for it). It is like walking through a lush, wet tomato patch, snapping the leaves as you go. The blackcurrant leaf note is particularly mouth-watering.

I love this scent so much.. it's pretty linear but it lasts FOREVER! I like to spray it on my pajamas sometimes and I can smell it for multiple nights. My skin also doesn't turn this into a soapy smell like it does the EdP. Smell-wise it's a very dark green tomato vine mixed with a heavy dose of cassis/blackcurrant.

If you expect a floral fruity fragrance, let me stop you right there. It's green, through and through. It's fresh, and slightly bitter, it has an aquatic quality to it. Picture this: A very dense, heavy and wild blackcurrent foliage, whose leaves are brushing the surface of a small stream, almost fully hidden by the tall, wet grass.

I'm glad to see oud becoming more and more popular in mainstream fragrances. It's a bold move I must admit, but an interesting one. As a consumer, I was more than intrigued, especially when Givenchy decided to experiment with this largely oriental and tricky note. Eaudemoiselle de Givenchy Bois de Oud, may not be oud in all its glory, but the note certainly does feature. It has a slight resinous and woodsy feel, however this is counteracted by a smooth, clean orange blossom heart. I see this fragrance as oud for beginners. To the average consumer it won't strike them as being too strong, masculine or offensive. It also has some lovely floral undertones and a warm, ambery base. This flanker doesn't have much in common with its fresh, floral predecessor at all, so I applaud Givenchy for delving into a brand new fragrance genre. As a result, Eaudemoiselle de Givenchy Bois de Oud has a darker, more mysterious vibe. It's unique, and I could definitely fall in love with it for that reason alone. Unfortunately Eaudemoiselle de Givenchy Bois de Oud hasn't sold particularly well in Australia where I live, so I know that its existence will be relatively short-lived. This is a real shame seeing that it is such a pleasant and interesting scent. I can't say that the longevity is all that great, even though it does last a few hours on the skin. I just wish that it was more well known. I'd love to read some more reviews on this flanker. Original review written: November 2012.

And again, I'm reporting on one of my blind purchases. Since I unfortunately couldn't find much information about this fragrance, I had to buy it and try it out. :D I must admit, at first we weren't friends. But over time, it adapted more to my skin. And you have to give it time because this fragrance is wonderful. Now let me start from the beginning. For some reason, I wanted to get an oud fragrance. Well, I tested the Alien Oud Majestueux, but I didn't buy it back then. The price put me off a bit, as did the size, because I just can't use up such large quantities. And if the great Alien were to go off, I simply couldn't handle it. So, a little later, I looked around at the ouds and spontaneously bid on this fragrance at a very low price. Yes, it's a full 100 ml, but at that price, I just jumped at it without thinking too much. With the scent of Alien Oud Majestueux still in my mind, I sprayed my new perfume on my wrist. What hit my nose at first was off-putting. Spicy notes, piercing and sharp - immediately reminded me of pickle juice, no tangerine in sight! Fortunately, these notes disappeared quickly. Not entirely, but they became softer and more pleasant, a creamy orange blossom joined in, and the fragrance became gentler, yet still spicy in nature. Over time, the base notes joined in. The vanilla is the most prominent - it envelops the woody base in a soft and powdery cloud. Overall, I find the fragrance to be very spicy, woody, and warm. I can imagine it very well on a lady; I believe the scent is a bit too heavy for young girls. It fits well in the workplace, as it - in my opinion - doesn't leave a huge scent cloud behind and can't be described as unpleasant. P.S.: I did end up buying the Alien Oud Majestueux later :D

Bought it 50% off. 110€ original price. A more round version of the original. Better ingredients Givenchy says. I do like it over the original. It is well crafted. Classy. UNISEX! Slightly comparable to Acqua di parma - mandorlo di sicilia. Well, Pi leather Edition is more balmy, darker, heavier and I get more intense Almond. Beware. If you like leather scents, there is no leather inside. There is only a tiny leatherband on the Bottle. Sillage is "OKAY".Longevity a joke. It is a EDT! Not EDP! Not the BIG HIT it could have been but a classy Scent with better shapes in a Sexy Bottle. Expensive for 60 ml EDT that wont stay to long.

My '34' story is relatively convoluted. I first sampled it from a friend who had a bottle given to her by her husband. Following this I received a sample from a Diptyque boutique whilst trotting around London and finally, was sent a 10ml decant by a very generous swap buddy :) ... so I still don't have a full bottle, and I really should because I like it a lot!! The observations of my learned fellow parfumistas below are spot on! I find 34 Boulevard Saint Germain to be an extremely mutable fragrance, in that it really doesn't follow the rules of fragrance progression at all. An initial blast of florals is quickly followed by green, resiny notes ... quickly taken over by florals again although this time they exhibit a slightly woody character. A faint citrus/fruity pop is periodically evident ... it really is quite bizarre ... in a lovely, wearable way! In fact, I would probably describe 34 Boulevard Saint Germain as such ... 'imminently wearable'. On my skin this fragrance would do poorly in the cold, as it comes in EDT concentration. Would that it were a big strong EDP ... in that case it would probably be gracing my collection already!! I find the sillage and longevity here a little less than average ... but as my skin really eats perfume this shouldn't dissuade anyone from trying it. With this beautiful combination of notes I really wouldn't mind it being one of the few I own that I had to reapply two or three times a day! For people with more sensitive noses than I this probably sounds mad LOL ... but there it is :). Imho ... 34 Boulevard Saint Germain is a lovely, invigoratingly floral fragrance for a hot summer weather. I need to remedy the fact that I don't own it yet very, very soon.

I have vacillated back and forth as to whether to attempt describing individual notes for the usual objective portion of the review, but in the end I don't think I could possibly do 34 Boulevard Saint Germain proper justice as there are a ton of ingredients and they are all so well-blended that it just is near impossible to capture them all so I'm not even going to try... Instead, I think I will just give some general impressions of what I smell and my thoughts about the end result... For reference, projection is excellent and longevity exceptional at about 15 hours on skin. White florals and dulled rose mix with a slightly sweet clove and eucalyptus infused smooth woody incense primary heart accord over candle wax-like iris. The end result is highly complex and quite unique, but completely versatile and easy to wear. I have read elsewhere that Diptyque was going for an approximation of the smell of entering their flagship store with the scent of candles, incense sticks and fragrances wafting in the air. While I have never been there myself, I can definitely visualize the picture well from what I am sniffing for sure. There pretty much is a bit of everything in the composition and it would be all too easy to completely overdo it, yet 34 Boulevard Saint Germain just plain works. The bottom line is despite its enormous list of ingredients and great complexity the $120 per 100ml bottle 34 Boulevard Saint Germain by Dyptique is an amazingly easy to wear success that earns a strong 4 star out of 5 rating and is highly recommended to all.

Diptyque 34 BOULEVARD SAINT GERMAIN is a complex woody oriental perfume which manages to roll together a surprising number of relatively intense scents into a coherent whole. Different notes are salient at different times and this is not according to any consistent progression or development. Perhaps this is a post-modern perfume? At moments, 34 seems more oriental, then suddenly more aromatic, then very woody with an incense-like edge. Overall, I'd have to say that this is an interesting and unpredictable composition. Despite being somewhat chaotic, 34 never seems incoherent and is pleasant to smell at every stage. A chameleon could wear this perfume well.

I have nothing but praise for 34 Blvd St Germain. A plethora of notes blended in harmony to yield a long lasting, massively projecting fragrance. It renders a 3D sensation to me. no single note dominates the perfume. It's a harmony of notes collectively working to produce a medley of goodness. I have designated this as my travel perfume. If constrained when traveling and i can only take one perfume , this is it. I smell new accords in every wearing. For the first 10 wearings i smelled different accords and different notes more prominently. A magical and captivating perfume.

This is supposed to represent the olfactory journey through the flagship Diptyque store in Paris (hence the address of the name). Woods (cedar and sandalwood), florals, fig-leaf, hints of earth. Very well blended. To me it reminds me of walking through the latin quarter in Paris on a cold winter's days, wearing sunglasses to shade out the light. Tobacco, spices, clove, incense, berries, geranium, patchouli. Very much going on in this fragrance. Even if it may not be totally unique, it's still a great exotic balsamic amber oriental layered with fig. Full bodied without being too heavy. Keeping the notes in checque in the yin/yang of this one is quite an accomplishment. Truly unisex. A caleidoscope of notes and overall it's surprisingly easy to wear.

This was my first "real" perfume I bought for myself. I was introduced to Diptyque in Berlin in their magical store on Ku'Damm. I bought it with my first check from an internship during college and I didn't look back since. It is my go-to and signature scent for any serious or business occasion.
God, how I love the camphoric, balsamic quality of this scent.

I think this might be the most complex perfume I've ever put on, which is a statement that doesn't hold much value (as I haven't put on many perfumes), but nevertheless shows how much of a symphony this is. When I tried it on, it was like stepping into a pine forest, or walking along the eucalyptus trees. It also reminds me of incense, and mint...

this is a transportive fragrance. so, let's immerse ourselves. a dark dining hall. stone-walled dormitories. a wooden panelled library, with high arched windows; the smell of old books, leather-bound, slightly musty. there are students, and teachers sat in small reading nooks, or at one of the rows of desks and worn wooden tables.
One that probably gets overlooked a little from this house. It was inspired by the house's 50th anniversary and the Paris flagship store. I hope you find my review useful.

I wasn’t familiar with Olivier Pescheux’s work before this, but after experiencing this fragrance, I’m convinced it’s one of his most masterful creations. It’s not just a perfume—it’s a vivid, living portrait of a bitter orange tree in full bloom, nestled in a sun-drenched garden. Absolutely inspired. Citrus in perfumery is a double-edged sword. It’s been explored so thoroughly that it’s hard to find a new angle, and its fleeting nature often relegates it to a mere top note. But here, Pescheux doesn’t just use citrus—he elevates it. Rather than chasing novelty, he leans into the essence of the orange tree and builds an entire world around it. The result is a fragrance that captures not just the fruit, but the entire tree: the bitter green leaves, the delicate white blossoms, the juicy tang of the fruit, the soft wood of the trunk, and even the damp earth beneath it. The composition is deceptively simple but brilliantly layered. Neroli and orange blossom bring a floral brightness, while bitter orange adds a juicy, slightly tart edge. Juniper berries cut through with a peppery freshness, angelica lends a sweet, green floral nuance, and patchouli grounds everything with its earthy, woody warmth. Together, they create a scent that’s both radiant and contemplative—like standing under an orange tree at golden hour, breathing in every part of it. If you love citrus fragrances but crave something with more soul—something that goes beyond the usual sparkle and dives into something richer, greener, and more textured—this is a must-try. I usually wear it on its own, but it also layers beautifully. Just yesterday, I paired it with Tam Dao, and the result was nothing short of glorious. And for a citrus-forward scent, the performance is outstanding. It projects confidently and lasts for hours, which only adds to its charm. This isn’t just another citrus perfume—it’s a sensory journey, and one I can’t recommend highly enough. 9/10

An ode to the orange tree? Again? That lucky orange tree is getting all the praise in the world. How about an ode to the olive tree for a change? Or the magnolia with its beautiful fragrant flowers? Anyway, Eau des Sens. In the opening, I get a lot of bitter-aromatic citrus. Orange blossom with a bite so zesty, it is close to being harsh. But as soon as this is properly settled on skin, the character gets 'nice and easy'. A mellow blossom with barely detectable woody notes as support. Eau des Sens is an easy to wear summer refreshment and exudes a joyful vibe. It is pretty by itself, but in the orange grove it is just another orange tree.

This is a lovely, kind and mild orange blossom scent, the scent of a distant orange blossom, brought to you by a summer's breeze. I don't find it very citrus-forward, just realistic orange blossom. Usually orange blossom goes (too) wild on my skin, so if I was to choose an orange blossom scent, this would be it. I don't know how Diptyque does that, but - as in many of their scents - there is this soapy accord that will only come to you in sudden wafts, like the smell of linnen, drying in the sun. I saw it being compared to Echt Kölnisch Wasser Eau de Cologne , but no way! I don't get any barbershop or cologne vibes either; this is so gentle and soft (leaning feminine to my nose) and has much more depth than a simple cologne. Sillage and longevity are moderate as far as I can tell now. Not quite sure yet if I would want a full bottle, there still are some scents I want to test first. But I do find it nice.

If Philosykos celebrates the fig tree and Tam Dao is a poem to wood, Eau des Sens is the house of Diptyque's bottled tribute to the orange tree, from the leaves to the fruit and everything in between. The juice is blended with just a handful of elements: aromatic orange blossom, bitter orange zest, sweet patchouli, green juniper berries and herbal angelica, combining to create a simple but effective floral fragrance: a sort of modern, smoother version of Geo F. Trumper's classic Eau de Portugal cologne. Another success story by Diptyque.

What a nice surprise to find out that in Qatar Airways amenity kit you can enjoy Eau des Sens... it must have been the testing altitude, or the fact that it was middle of the night, but I must admit this was my first test up in the sky. This fragrance is on the light spectrum with a clear orange note that is spiced up by juniper berries. I could personally not feel the patchouli that much.

An unexpected treasure that I have recently discovered. I had a distinct feeling upon smelling this darling that I remembered it from somewhere. There is something so comforting and genuine about this fragrance. The opening is full of feathery sunlight, curling vines on walls, and unripe oranges from the wild west.

Ok, I'm not well-versed in this family of smells, but I love this one so much I bought a 20mL decant. Very crisp opening. It remains crisp throughout. There are bitter notes at the beginning. My only complaint is one that others have made...it's got weak longevity. Although we're moving in to fall where I live, I bought it as a summer time scent. I really love it.

This is the signature scent of one of my favorite hotels, The Lafayette in San Diego. As such, it's got a real memory imprint for me, and I think adds very nicely to the overall vibe of the place: refined but not stuffy. It's present, but not overwhelming, linear and pleasant but not boring.

This is one of the best offers from the house and a must have if you are into clean fragrances. The first 3 minutes might put off because the smell of orange flower and tree is way too realistic but trust me, wait for it. It quickly settles into a very very clean soap bar with neroli, and it has that typical diptyque core which smells like white clean wood flakes.

Eau des Sens places the orange tree in a delicate and sentimental frame. The first spray is pure orange blossom, with bitter orange, juniper and patchouli pushing through not long after, providing a welcome botanical balance to this white floral. The sharpness of the bitter orange acts as an anchor for the blossom, keeping it from fading into a generic whisper.

I bought Eau Capitale last year and I've already emptied a bottle, although I shared it with my wife. It's not only wearable but also outstanding in every way, originality and performance. I'm considering it to be the best work of Diptyque and going to put it back in my collection in soon. Now let's compare this with L'Ombre Dans L'Eau, which is very well known rose perfume, among Diptyque's existing works. L'Ombre Dans L'Eau is a complete representation of the scent of a wet red rose, so to speak. That contains all the green fresh scents of leaves and a stem, in addition to the colorful and seductive scents of a rose and a bud. By comparison, this one, Eau Capitale is the scent of thousands of roses what are blooming in a moist greenhouse. As soon as you open the greenhouse, you can feel the scent of many flowers with strong vitality. They are young buds just about to bloom, firmly rooted in the oily soil, and in pretty ceramic pots. That is my impression of Eau Capitale. Eau capitale is a type of perfume that not only satisfies myself but also pleases others. We can divide the compliments that we hear when wearing some perfume into several levels. Words just like "You smell good" or "What perfume are you wearing?" can be mere ceremonial greetings. But if someone sniffs constantly and repeat "Somewhere smells incredibly good!", so it means your smell is really good. I heard a lot of compliments at that level when I wore the Eau Capitale, and I could see cultured and sophisticated people walking around me and repeating compliments like that. Of course it's because of the scent of Eau Capitale itself that anyone can easily enjoy, but it's also because there are still very few people who wear it. I've been wearing this steadily for the past year, so I'll also be able to comment on the weather and season. Eau Capitale works well at any time, except on cold days when temperatures drop below zero Celsius. However, even in winter, there's no problem if you wear it indoors. What I would like to say in particular is that this is more affected by humidity than temperature. Eau Capitale, like L'Ombre Dans L'Eau, gives off a much more vivid scent in wet weather: the scent of REAL roses. I think it's the best weather to wear Eau Capitale on a drizzling day, a dark cloud day, and a thick fog day. Eau Capitale can be worn regardless of gender and age, but it has a very fancy and showy scent, so it may not be appropriate for casual attire or frugal gatherings. But surely that's not to say at all it's too formal perfume. And, blind buy? If you like the scent of rose or have already tried L'Ombre Dans L'Eau and like it, you won't fail. But only if you like the glamorous flower scent and the scent of nature with the strong projection. What if you already have another rose perfumes? Eau Capitale is very original perfume with no alternative, at least so far now in 2021, so you'll never feel bored. Despite my poor English writing, I hope this review will help someone.

A Subversive Parisian Chypre. I find myself once again seduced by a genre I ordinarily avoid. I, who wage a quiet battle against chypres, have been hopelessly entranced by Diptyque’s first chypre—an olfactory ode to the Ville Lumière. But this is no ordinary chypre; it is rebellion, revolution bottled. It departs from the ancestral formula to embrace a diaphanous modernity: less oppressive, free of the suffocating opulence that defines its forebears. Here, moss is not a tyrant imposing its will upon the other accords, but a diplomat, generously ceding ground to floral notes and verdant ingredients. A vintage soul breathing contemporary air. On first spray, Diptyque’s unmistakable DNA materialises like a fragrant ghost—an invisible yet indelible signature instantly recognised by anyone familiar with L'Ombre dans L'Eau Eau de Toilette . The initial rose–patchouli accord proves prophetic. What invades the senses first are the balsamic, camphorous, mentholated—and faintly sweaty—nuances of cumin seed, accompanied by a flourish of pink pepper dancing upon the olfactory stage, and the bitter tang of citrus zest. The pepper marks the first deviation from a classic chypre. Ubiquitous bergamot appears green, unripe, and tart. A sour sweetness emerges, but the cool spice of pink pepper and cumin rules this opening scene. Beneath the surface, a whispering rose gently caresses the nose, its slightly metallic facets evoking geranium. Those wary of cumin can rest assured: its presence is fleeting, a brief actor making a swift exit. The first impression, then, is of a sweaty, earthy rose essence with spicy, fruity accents—never crude, yet unmistakably present. After a few moments of patient waiting, the scented rose of deep garnet hue takes centre stage. It is a masterful fusion of Turkish and Bulgarian qualities: silky, perfectly integrated with the peppery opening and looming moss. This sanguine rose emerges green, waxy, mossy, and dewy, with an almost virile undertone—earthy but neither gelatinous nor decaying. It possesses considerable depth without ever feeling oppressive. I picture not a bud atop a thorny stem poised to bloom—its scent forcing you to lean in to perceive it—but rather petals of a spent bloom falling upon a carpet of muddy, withered leaves, dirtied by damp earth and soaked in morning dew, the surrounding air suffused with a mossy aroma detectable even at a distance. At its heart, foliage collides with florals. A trained nose discerns a faint warm spice courtesy of clove and cinnamon bark. I also detect a honeyed aroma, surprisingly imparted by yellow ylang-ylang butter and a whisper of white jasmine absolute. I adore floral compositions crafted thus—drifting towards a genderless, modern, and energetic direction. Woods, leaves, and amber form the final phase. true to form, the moss remains restrained—evernyl replaces oakmoss—yet it carries the salty, smoky, woody character of the Ambrofix molecule. As it dries down, amber facets deepen. Patchouli, present from the outset, becomes distinctly herbaceous and more prominent, lending the depth that contrasts with the florals, occasionally revealing the woody, rooty tones of vetiver. What ultimately clings close to the skin, leaving a seductive trail, is a patch of crisp, piquant ambered woodiness familiar from many modern niche and indie creations. As for longevity and sillage, Eau Capitale does not disappoint. It is rather potent and surprisingly long-lasting. Given the facets I perceived on a dull February day, I deem it ideal for the shoulder seasons, though it may yield pleasant surprises on humid summer evenings. What begins with feminine traits evolves towards more masculine aspects, forging an olfactory bridge between genders. It is, without doubt, a marvellous creation. One aspect perhaps worthy of further exploration is how this fragrance interacts with different environments: how it behaves indoors versus in open air, how it transforms with body heat across various climates, and how it engages with personal memories and the cultural associations Paris evokes. There is also the intriguing manner in which Olivier Pescheux has reinterpreted the chypre concept—rendering it contemporary while maintaining ties to the French perfumery tradition. This review is based on a bottle I have owned since January 2025, an olfactory companion through numerous experiences and moments of reflection. — Elysium

I'm glad I sprayed this again before reviewing as I think I needed some time to sit with this one. I currently have POAL on one wrist and Eau Capitale on the other. Eau Capitale is a very powdery, soapy pink rose with patchouli, pepper, bergamot and a hint of cinammon/woodiness and ylang ylang. It's quite girly and feminine in my opinion, and a bit sweet, aldehydey. POAL on the other hand is deep and rich, with a warm woodiness, subtle dark berry accord, and dominant frankincense note that I don't find in this perfume — it's less powdery sweet and more incensey and complex. If they are at all comparable, and I would venture to say they're distant relatives, Eau Capitale is the chic and bubbly Parisian girl in white (fresh and bright), and POAL is the gothic and mysterious seductress in crimson (dark and brooding). I think Eau Capitale could be suitable for daily wear, unlike POAL. I am not entirely convinced that I love it, I guess I wasn't expecting it to be so powdery and sweet. It borders on parma violets/candy for me. The citrus is too prominent for my taste. But as it dries down it gets smoother and I enjoy it slightly more. I can't help but feel that it's not quite as naturalistic as I would like.

What a lovely fragrance! I’m a bit wary with sweet-spicy leaning woody notes like patchouli and sandalwood, as they easily turn overly sweet or masculine on my skin. However, based on other Diptyque fragrances I like (Do Son EdT, Eau Rose EdT/EdP, L’Eau Papier…), the salesperson suggested I took a whiff of Eau Capitale. On the tester strip, it’s what it says on the tin. There aren’t many notes, and they are all there (pink peppercorn only faintly), in a good way. Upon spraying it on my skin, I was immediately disappointed: there it was, the pungent, spicy sweet kick that I feared. But by its side, an elegant and bright ode to rose in bloom, accompanied by a fresh but rounded bergamot. To my relief, the sharp opening evaporated very quickly (within minutes), leaving me with a straightforward, sophisticated chypre. Apart from the sharpness, the dry-down remained surprisingly true to the opening. The bergamot tagged along with surprising persistence; the rose stayed fresh for hours and eventually wilted into a velvety afterscent rather than dusty powderiness; I even made peace with the patchouli, which settled into a sensual earthiness with just a touch of sweetness. Longevity is good on my skin; I forgot to note how long it lasted, exactly, but at least a good 6 hours, probably another 1–2h. Eau Capitale is now firmly on my wishlist! It probably won't find its way in my shopping bag until fall, as I want to indulge citrusy fresh and aquatic scents over summer.

Composed of just a few notes, this is simple but stunning. The shining star is of course rose, and is the scent of a room full of them in full bloom. The opening of this fragrance fills my flat when I spray it. It subsides into something gently peppery and citrusy that as you get whiffs of it throughout the day, recaptures your interest every time. I dislike pepper intensely most of the time, and gregarious citrus often bores me. This is combined so masterfully though that I may need to reconsider this opinion, lest I miss out some other masterpieces. I put this one away except for fall and winter, such is its strength. It makes me a bit sick in the heat. But saved for the right season, this is as another reviewer so aptly said: cool, elegant, and flirty.

I like this perfume, but I have to say, very sadly because people write so many beautiful reviews about this one, but it didnt enchant me. For me, this is all about violets, not rose, which for my personal tastes.... It is good because violets are my fav flowers in perfumery but this perfume, at least on my skin, it is very plain and dull and... A little boring.

Eau Capitale is a fragrance created to embody, according to Diptyque, none other than Paris. Paris, a city with immense culture and history, represented by a modern chypre-esque fragrance, seems quite fitting to me.

Full blooming rose and effervescent peppercorn, like Baie Rose 26 but more overtly floral. It is definitely elegant and feminine. Initially I almost hoped for more complication, something in the base to draw me in further, but the more I wear it I'm appreciating the simplicity. The brand's comparison to a vintage Paris isn't off track, it's romantic like that.

Patchouli starts head strong but soon it is overtaken by the soapy scent of rose. Reminds me of bathgoods or a pillowcase at a nice hotel. The issue lies exactly in that association; somehow there is a sterile accord beneath the flourishing flowers that does not sit well with me. Maybe it’s the chypre?

I must take a moment to champion this fragrance, which hardly receives any attention or comments on its page. One reason might be that Very Irrésistible Summer has almost completely disappeared from the market, and only a few people will have the chance to discover its profound scent and enjoy its warmth, freshness, and beauty. Secondly, it could also be due to the high price that is asked for this rarity. At the well-known auction, one must shell out well over €100 for this piece. For enthusiasts like me, who associate certain nostalgic memories with it (of a woman), it is absolutely affordable. For those who do not have such a strong emotional connection to it, perhaps not. However, I believe it should not be missing from any collection. The bottle is tall, square, and poison green. A real eye-catcher. The scent reveals its full potential immediately after spraying. The grapefruit competes from the start with the mint and fights for dominance, but they quickly blend together so well, creating a harmonious symbiosis of sweet citrus freshness. The rivalry between the two loosens up the sesame a bit as it subtly emerges, giving the fragrance a slight saltiness. The walnut acts like a stalker in the background, occasionally throwing in a green note, which makes for an outstanding combination. Very Irrésistible Summer does not have a dramatically changing development. It remains true to its line from the beginning and changes little, perhaps becoming a bit powdery. The only downside is the poor longevity and sillage. Unfortunately, the scent is only perceptible up close. There is no significant projection for the outside world. This is really a shame; back then, I believe the fragrance cost about €30 and could be unapologetically sprayed. Today? I cherish it like a treasure and wear it only on very special occasions. I hope you seize the opportunity and grab a decant or even a bottle if you have the chance. And perhaps you will even share my enthusiasm.

EAU ROSE by Diptyque Breathtakingly beautiful Rose. Opens with a rush of bittersweet bergamot and juicy tart vine-ripe black currants followed immediately with a saturating flood of soft, tropical, delicately sweet litchi fruit. A pristinely fresh and glorious rose makes her entrance among the sparkling lemony threads of dewy-green geranium, which provides a zesty citric strength and additional support to the principal rose scent itself. A subdued non-indolic jasmine woven throughout provides an extra touch of sweetly refined floral complexity without intruding on the precedence of the roses. A warm, clean cedar houses the entire creation beautifully, while a cozy white musk adds a delicate hint of tender sensuality. A fascinatingly delectable drop of honey infuses just a trace of voluptuously natural silken sweetness with complexity and depth. The Rose here is poised gracefully between the refreshing cool vivid clarity of the Black Currant/Geranium, and the sumptuously smooth warm sweetness of the Litchi/Jasmine. The perfect balance achieved here between the pull of these four exceptionally contrasting elements, both of which are supportive of the Rose, yet diametrically opposed to each other, is what makes this composition a unique masterpiece. It is both simple and extremely refined. The myriad of subtle, elegant nuances woven within and throughout the strands of this scent tapestry succeed brilliantly. This is exquisitely beautiful. Perhaps the most beautiful rose I have ever smelled on my skin. Sublime beauty personified in scent. I love this one completely and utterly.

This is such a beautiful and green rose that dries down to a clean, soapy scent. The opening is so bright and beautiful, it completely drew me in and made me keep smelling my wrist to get deeper and deeper into the scent. Unfortunately, the full bouquet of rose only lasts about 30 minutes before fading to a soft soapy smell. Don't get me wrong; it's a very nice clean scent on the dry down but it just doesn't compare to the opening. It's probably my own fault considering Eau Rose= Rose Water, but please!! Give me more rose and less water!!

Eau Rose EDT smells like small, pink roses freshly picked and strewn over a bowl of water - it's very fresh, sweet (without being jammy or saccharine), and unlikely to offend anyone. What I appreciate about it in particular is that it maintains its perky, full-figured character all the way through and never turns sour. I hate sourness in a rose , or excessive greenness. The litchi and blackcurrant add a juicy fruitiness that tickles the tongue, and the geranium a hint of cool minty leafiness that plays nicely against the sweet, pink rosiness. In the dry down, there's a quiet (white) honey and musk combo forming a cushion under the fruity rose, and it all feels quite natural and solid. Although ultimately a little too simple for my tastes, Eau Rose would be an excellent starter rose for anyone (well, honestly probably just those of the female persuasion) who wants a true rose without any greenery, woods, oud, or heavy gourmand notes to sully its purity. I suspect that it would also be brilliant for layering.

Whoever loves perfumes knows that rose is a polarizing note: some will say it’s an old lady perfume, some love it. I’m a rose lover, always have been, since I was I kid, I loved the rose water tonic we all had in our bathroom; rose to me is a comforting note that makes me feel pretty, or sexy depending how the perfume is declined, makes me smile. Eau Rose eau de toilette is the prettiest of them all: bright, flirty, light, it’s a fairy of the roses kinda of scent in which the rose mixes with a touch of berries and a zest. I love the fact that it’s not invasive, doesn’t last all day long, if I want to reapply, I just do that. Addictive, a signature scent.

5/5 of My Discovery Set: If someone were to ask me about what a rose would ideally smell like then it would be Eau Rose. From the initial scent from the bottle, it embodies the rich, luxurious smell of a rose. It is a mature scent that I feel would suit everyday wear, perhaps my nose is not sophisticated enough, but I was surprised to see lychee as a note. true, there is a sweetness that lingers, but to me, this is a pure rose scent.

Excellent "clean girl" spa rose, with just enough depth to keep it from being too much of a freshie. Watery but not thin. A pink rose, one of those big cabbage-head types with too many petals. There's no sharpness or sourness here. I don't typically like fruitiness in a rose scent, and I feel like lychee and black currant are done to death, but here they are quite restrained.

This isn't your grandmother’s powdery rose, nothing heavy or old-fashioned. Eau Rose by Diptyque is fresh, juicy, and modern, like walking through a blooming rose garden while sipping berry tea. It reminds me of a Rose Petal Confit from France, very light, a little sweet, cool, fresh, and playful.

Diptyque Rose Very watery, fresh rose at first sligthly as body mist, i was also thinking this could be girl fragrance as for a teenager when starting to be interested in fragrances. but after circa hour it starts to smell more as parfum and adult woman fragrance but still very soft, light and floral and clean smell.

Diptyque's Eau Rose is, in my eyes, a truly unique, wonderfully rounded, and above all, genuinely "ideal" rose fragrance in its fine complexity. For me, it corresponds to the (imaginary) crossing of a light pink, airy-fine Rosa Centifolia (e.g., the original or Maiden's Blush) with a carmine red, elegantly fruity Rose de Resht (a rose almost without thorns, how fitting!

“And walk out into the garden to the rose bush, there I will wait for you according to old custom…” The poem “Secret Invitation” by John Henry Mackay is admittedly quite sentimental overall and would likely be forgotten today without the music composed by Richard Strauss (delightfully sung by Fritz Wunderlich), perhaps not entirely without reason.

Unfortunately or luckily, there is no huge difference between this limited edition from 2006 and the original Organza, which I adore and treasure in my collection. To my nose, it is as floral, sweet and oriental as the Organza I have known since 1996. I am possibly a bit disappointed, since I bought this to smell the difference. But apparently, my nose is not that sensitive or trained - I do not think that one is better than the other. They are both great. I do, however, miss the Walnut note in this 2006 edition. It is part of the earthy/dry part of the original that I find - well, original. Scentwise, the overall expression is the same. It takes a really great nose to notice the difference and value it. But the longevity on this… wauw! It goes on and on. I am amazed by how long this can perform. Way better than the 1996 edition. This bottle has a nice decoration on the back. But I prefer the original bottle. Simpler and more elegant. Year 2, 197/365

Can you believe I used to hate tuberose? It’s actually insane because I’m a huge tuberose fan now and LOVE to see it incorporated into many fragrances. While I love tuberose in many different interpretations and compositions, I particularly have a soft spot for the photorealistic tuberose scents. Ones that are strictly floral and natural, and that exactly what Do Son EDP is. Do Son is a simple and easy with just four notes: tuberose, orange leaf, pink pepper, and musk. You get all four notes, but with tuberose obviously being at the center of attention. It’s slightly green and spicy, and dries down to a more musky tuberose scent. It’s not overly indolic, but tuberose is one of those white florals that always smells ever so slightly indolic to my nose. Even so, this fragrance feels so clean and easy to wear. I wore it out to my friends graduation brunch over the weekend and after reapplying it on myself, my sister and friend complimented me on how good it smelled. It has this alluring sexiness to it, but done in a very effortless way. It’s chic and smells expensive, but done in such a humble way. It has this beautiful duality to it while being such a simply composed scent. I just love it. I have the EDP and *had* the EDT and I think the EDP is better by a long shot. The EDT is still nice, but definitely is not as tuberose-straight forward because of the other floral notes in the composition. The EDT gives more of an orange blossom-iris-tuberose vibe with benzoin, while the EDP is just mainly tuberose. As with most Diptyques, the sillage is intimate to moderate but the longevity is very good. Another plus for Do Son (and honestly all the Diptyques) is the beautiful artistry of the bottles. They’re just so stunning to me and feel so classy to hold and wear. I promise you it’s all part of the experience. If you ever get a chance to try Do Son EDP, definitely don’t hesitate to give it a sniff and wear. This will be a permanent fixture in my collection for the spring and summer months.

Do Son EdP is best observed from a distance. The trail it leaves in the air is magnificent. Consistently present, close to being a tuberose-'soliflor' and yet it is feather-light and inobtrusive. When studied from up close, Do Son appears as a plain white floral blend. No frills, no drama. Similar to the EdT, the scent develops from jasmin-tuberose to orange blossom-tuberose. While the EdP feels less stingy and way smoother than the EdT, it is also kind of straightforward. The EdT has a salty sea breeze note, which provides personality and makes it more fun to wear if you ask me.

I have Do Son EDT and EDP, each on a separate wrist. The orange leaf really shines and makes this fragrance. It’s all the glory and all the things you love about a white floral (there’s jasmine and orange blossom in there as well, not just tuberose), but in the shaded and dappled light of branches and foliage overhead. It’s greener and a little more neroli-like. For me, it’s my preference between the two. Tuberose always gets this slutty reputation, “indolic” this, “seductive” that. Sensual, voluptuous, etc. But here in Do Son EDP, the tuberose is a little more reserved and subtle. More nuanced, I guess. In some ways, it kind of reminds me of a more mature and greener version of Tocca Florence which is a lovely gardenia, but a bit too young and girly for my tastes.

When I first tested both the Do Son EDT and EDP on paper strips, back in my early fragrance days, the EDT was the clear winner. I was looking for a photorealistic white floral that captured the scent of jasmine in my grandmother’s garden in the Middle East. But on skin? The EDP won. Hands down. On skin, the EDP delivers beautifully on that photorealistic white floral experience, with a touch of orange blossom in the background that keeps it fresh and clean. The EDT, on the other hand, fell flat for me. And unlike many tuberose-heavy fragrances, neither version of Do Son gives off that indolic, almost fecal note that some jasmine or tuberose fragrances have (I’m looking at you, Olène!). The Do Son EDP is the perfect white floral fragrance for anyone craving the scent of real, living jasmine—fresh, clean, and true to life. No rotten or fecal undertones in sight. It smells like you’re standing right next to a blooming jasmine bush, basking in that fresh and creamy, natural scent. That said, this isn’t a safe blind buy. What Do Son delivers, it delivers unapologetically—you have to love what it’s going for to truly enjoy it: a pure, living jasmine bush in a summer garden. If you don’t have a soft spot for jasmine or aren’t already a little obsessed with tuberose, it might come across as too intense. And if you typically lean toward more conventional fragrances or blended florals, this one might feel a bit too raw or singular. But in my opinion, it’s absolutely worth trying. Especially on skin.

If you like florals WITHOUT the aldehydes (think Chanel No.5) , you will probably like this. It's sweet in bright-sweet, floral way. Diptyque does not produce scents for the mass market the same way other designers do, and they're very unapologetic about their notes. If you like gourmands, there's not even a hint of vanilla here and you should pass. This is a very fresh, vibrant floral like you were walking through a botanical garden but instead of just a whiff of passing jasmine, tuberose, etc. you picked a bunch and held it up to your nose for a few hours. One thing I like about Diptyque fragrances is that they pack a punch, and a spray on each wrist is almost too much. This is not a safe blind buy if you're only familiar with Diptyque's most popular scents. Definitely not a safe blind buy for gourmand lovers.

Do son was my introduction to the beauty of white florals, and it literally stole my heart. If the edt is very airy and aquatic (the description on the official website is spot on - tuberose borne on the sea breeze), the edp is much fuller, creamier and just intoxicatingly beautiful. Like sticking your nose in a jasmine bush on a late spring night. So romantic. So pure.

It’s one of the best scents I’ve smelled in the last years! It’s a photorealistic jasmine bush in the evening, when the sun has released all those gorgeous oils from the flower during the day and it’s still vibrating from the heat. It smells like a holiday in Tuscany.

On paper- a very basic clean elegant white floral- light honey jasmine, almost untraceable orange, adds splash of citrusiness nOn skin- smells exactly of Breathe of Angels by PK perfume- which is apricot and white tuberose. Very fruity and candy floss like nNot for me, too floral powdery sweet. Reminds me of a powder blush, new makeup

One should face their fears... so I’m diving straight in after the multifaceted hate masterpiece Carnal Flower with Do Son by Diptyque, as EdP. The week of truth, the week of clarity, the week of tuberoses. Here lie a few of the most famous & best tuberose fragrances in the world on the table - and yet none have converted me so far.

This fragrance take me back to when i was Young and Got a hold of my dads fragrance Drakkar Noir and respect to Guy who made that. Huge compliment. I did not like it back then but now when i am like 35 years older i love it. nnBut hornestly, Diptyque just made a clone / dupe of that great 80’s fragrance. nnDrakkar Noir I a bit stronger and hits some other notes in the dry-down but otherwise it is the same scent for it longevity. nnIn my opinion you get more bang for your Bucks if you by Drakkar Noir. nnTo Diptyque: if sombody from Diptyque reads this, sorry but why did you have to make a dupe. This smells identical to Irish Spring soap. It took me a few hours to figure out what minty-fresh scent of my memories this was evoking, but now I think I've cracked the code. Perhaps it leans a little closer to those soft peppermint candies. It maybe has a creamy smoothness that differentiates it from Irish Spring proper. After about 20min, it starts to trend toward Lush's Dirty. It is lovely and nostalgic, but the price point for essentially an Irish Spring dupe is crazy.

I really wanted to love this one, but to me it smells like a drug store cologne from 40 years ago. It's what I always imagined what Stetson or Halston must have smelled like, especially for the first couple minutes. Once the dry down starts, it does smell better, but it still has that old-man cologne backdrop that I just can't get past. The mint barely peaks his head out. Sadly, this is a no for me. Off to try Orpheon next

Sorry because I can't write a proper review though to I only have tried it on a sample paper at a Diptyque boutique (I havent more free skin to try lol), but I have to say that as someone that doesnt like fougeres and that I doesnt like the geranium note, I really like the opening on this one! Most of diptyque fragrances need time to develope but this one has one of the best openings from the whole boutique!

Contrary to popular opinion, I think Diptyque Eau de Minthe is good. Really good. Off the top, you get just a bit of minty freshness that makes this an absolute awesome warmer weather fragrance. It then goes into such a classy and timeless barbershop fougere that is appropriate for literally any occasion. It can be dressed up or down and will still right at home. To me this is not a grandpa fragrance, it’s a mature, well put together, masculine gentleman’s fragrance. I do get the comparisons to Drakkar Noir. They are both fougeres after all. But Drakkar tends to wear A LOT heavier and can be a bit much for hot weather. It’s also much screechier and loud. Eau de Minthe is present but polite and a lot smoother of a formulation. You can tell the ingredients used are not bargain bin quality like you get with a lot of the reformulated and neutered 80’s powerhouse fougeres. With current masculine fragrance trends over the past 10 or so years, it’s no wonder that Eau de Minthe was not that well received. Most masculine marketed fragrances have gone the way of sugary sweet with heavy vanilla and tonka bean bases. But for those of us that want to smell like a fresh straight razor shave and bald fade, this one hits the spot hard.

I love Diptyque and mint, but this one really isn't for me. I have a strong association with something teenage boys used in the late 90s. It could be aftershave or some kind of deodorant. This was clearly gendered to my nose, based on my associations.

Eau de Minthé is at its best during its sparkling and airy mint opening; it's not too sweet or reminiscent of toothpaste, but gives the sensation of fresh spearmint, ready to be muddled with sugar and soda water in a cocktail tumbler.

Sometimes, you should just leave memories where they belong—in the past. It's nice to think back on the old times, but that doesn't mean you have to revive them. My memories of Drakkar Noir are linked to many moments in my youth. That woody, mossy scent with a strong lavender note was just incredibly good. It accompanied me to many parties.

Much of what is written here about Eau de Minthé resonates with me. But I draw somewhat different conclusions from it. Yes, a Fougère through and through. Yes, Fougère, but not old-fashioned in the process. Yes, it is fresh and spicy. Yes, the mint plays a significantly lesser role than the name might suggest. So far, so good.

In my opinion, the name Eau de Minthé is quite misleading, as the mint is only noticeably present in the top notes for a relatively short time. What truly defines the fragrance is a rather modern, but by no means groundbreaking, Fougère accord.

Very interesting and seductive scent. I really like this one and find it intriguing. A very seductive scent which has a combination of all my favourite notes. Iris, honey, tobacco. All work together wonderfully in this. This reminds me a little of Chergui by Serge Lutens. I think it has a very similar vibe and I find it intriguing. The iris note is great and I always appreciate iris in a perfume. It does smell like tobacco smoke, or at least a sweet incense. I find this would suit winter and autumn the best in my opinion, especially in the Eau de Parfum. I think if you like amber, incense or tobacco themes in fragrances, this is one to check out. Unisex and very noir, this is a great mysterious fragrance which would smell great on a well-dressed elegant person with style. Intriguing, seductive, and quite special.

Diptyque has so many good spicy scents, and so many good woody scents, that Volutes gets overlooked very often. In my shop, people are usually dazzled by the sparkling Orpheon, the popular leather note in Eau Rihla or the incense in Eau Duelle (which is another one of my favourites, don't get me wrong). But Volutes is a cosy gem of its own, and one that I wish more people would notice. The combination of cinnamon and honey is like no other that Diptyque makes, and since cinnamon is a sweeter type of spice, it blends with the honey very smoothly, and almost makes you feel all cocooned and wrapped up in an olfactory hug. Additionally, the honey note isn't too common in Diptyque perfumes and it really makes this scent special for it. And then you have the resinous opopanax grounding the whole composition, so it never comes across as too sweet or heady. I find that Diptyque does resinous notes really well across the board, and Volutes is no exception. The iris isn't perceptible to my nose, but it probably helps keep the scent well-rounded, brightening it where the opopanax darkens it. Volutes projects just enough to be noticeable, yet not too much so it never gets overwhelming. It has a pretty satisfying longevity too! All in all, a really well-done warm spicy fragrance that works just as well as a daily winter scent as it does as a bedtime olfactory blanket.

The EdP opens with more creamy-powdery iris and less dried fruit/tobacco/immortelle than the EdT. The fragrance is again smooth and creamy, but has a better balance between sweet/powdery/herbal notes. The woodsy-herbal base does not dominate the orris note, but enhances its vegetal-rooty nature. The EdP is less warm and sweet than the EdT and it vaguely reminds me of Chanel's 28 La Pausa. They share the same peppery woodsiness in their bases, but otherwise they are totally different. Volutes is a lot denser and opaque than the 28 La Pausa. Just like the EdT, Volutes EdP quickly dries down into a generic woodsy-herbal blend ( with an unpleasant acidic facet) and then into nothingness.
