Ultimately, it is a very synthetic scent, which is certainly wearable in the cold season, but does not delight me at all like the old "Aromatics Elixir." However, "Black Cherry" smells somewhat better to me than the predecessor flanker "In Black," which I do not like at all. Among the Aromatics flankers so far, "In White" has pleased me the most. "Aromatics Black Cherry" is interesting for all those who want to try a good dose of cardamom mixed with an artificial floral-fruity-and-wood arrangement. "Black Cherry" is not an alternative to the old "Aromatics." By the way, definitely "unisex"! Update August 2017: The longevity is outstanding. Having owned this scent for 10 months now, I have to rate it even lower than originally. I can hardly wear it; it is overwhelming and far too pseudo-oudh-like. Unfortunately, it is indeed a misstep. By the way, the scent is now also available online at Notino. Well. There it costs only 55 euros and not 89 pounds as in London at Harrods.

I can never get enough of this one. Discovered it from a sample, and I can't live without it. It smells first like soap, a really nice soapy smell. I have a lot of trouble deciding what else I smell. That's why I'm here though.
It smells like freshly cut cedar wood but with a soapy freshness added to it. It's only average in sillage and longevity but to me, that's great, because it makes it so versatile.
Excellent somehow fresh somehow calming fragrance, with tons of ingredients so it's hard to describe with other words than excellent.

When fragrances inspire enthusiasm, one should also talk about it and share the excitement with others. If the details about the perfume house etc. are absolutely uninteresting, feel free to skip to the fifth paragraph! Actually, I wanted to say a few words about a completely different fragrance, and that is already finished, but first of all, things always turn out differently than expected. Now, I came across a very extensive bag filled with a wide range of selected samples, and there were also several from Diptyque. I admit that the name has been familiar to me for quite a while, and I have encountered one or another beautiful fragrance from this house among acquaintances, but I have never owned a Diptyque fragrance myself. The house of Diptyque, located on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, was founded in 1961 and initially sold fabrics, furniture, and English fragrances. In 1963, specially designed scented candles were added to the range. From 1968 onwards, their own fragrance creations were offered, which turned out to be quite successful. Over the years, room fragrances and soaps were eventually added to the assortment. Now I have been looking into the series that bears the house number of the headquarters in Paris (34 Boulevard Saint-Germain EdT and EdP, both of which I like very much, the EdP even a little more) and now the wonderful L´Eau du Trente-Quatre has also come into play, so once again the 34. Designed by Olivier Pescheux, who has been quite active for various fragrance houses. And I find that I also like several fragrances created by him or that are even in my possession/used to be. Among others, he is responsible for the very well-known and polarizing One Million (yes, that one!) along with various flankers, the fragrances sold at H&M, such as the wonderful Makassar Patchouli, or several fragrances for Yves Rocher. He has also created fragrances for Azzaro, Jil Sander, and Davidoff. However, some of his works fly a bit under the radar, in my opinion, and deserve closer examination. Therefore, I am a bit surprised that besides a few statements, nothing else has been written about this beautiful fragrance. Let’s change that. L´Eau du Trente-Quatre is an extraordinary fragrance that skillfully combines bittersweet citrus aspects, herbal influences, woody notes, and spices into a very coherent and harmonious whole. Right from the start, bitter oranges and grapefruit make their presence known, already spiced with nutmeg. Herbal-green impressions come into play, accompanied by a bit of lavender, while verbena adds a certain light strictness. A hint of floral notes emerges after a while; tuberose seems to have been used only in the smallest doses, as it doesn’t stand out much. The geranium comes forward a bit more but doesn’t push itself too much into the foreground. The fragrance remains spicy and green. When the citrus notes have receded a bit, a warm woody note develops, beautifully balanced. Patchouli and a hint of incense round it off and provide a certain depth. L´Eau du Trente-Quatre feels warm, friendly, attractive, and quite complex to me, with a very nice progression. The fragrance is not loud; it strikes a rather calm tone, which fits perfectly here. A certain classic touch cannot be denied, but I am far from calling the fragrance old-fashioned. It is certainly not that. In my opinion, this fragrance belongs to the class of timeless scents that work just as well today as they will in 10 years. And I cannot deny a distant resemblance to Passion for Men by Elizabeth Taylor. I do not want to claim that they are fragrance twins, but I can observe a certain fundamental kinship. Although the Diptyque is more subtle and multifaceted. Both share this warm woody spiciness, and the nutmeg note runs through the entire fragrance progression. I find the longevity to be quite decent, around 6-7 hours, and it becomes quite close to the skin quickly, making it very suitable as an office fragrance. The areas of application are actually unlimited, whether as a casual scent, an office fragrance, in a suit, or as a nature guy. With L´Eau du Trente-Quatre, you definitely make a good impression. I personally perceive the fragrance as somewhat more masculine, but that should not be a limitation on recommendations. If the overall package fits, then the fragrance fits as well, regardless of which gender is reaching for it. And the number 34 definitely seems to be a very good number. L´Eau du Trente-Quatre is for me a truly wonderful fragrance, to which I can definitely assign a green hue, but here and there some yellow and orange specks flash and give the fragrance light and warmth. And it has the potential to be a candidate for purchase for me. Even though I am currently adhering to my recently self-imposed acceptance stop. But eventually, there will be Christmas, a birthday, or some other nice occasion. I sincerely thank Ergoproxy for this truly beautiful fragrance experience.

Raising a tuberose is not exactly easy due to its character, and so it is not surprising that many perfumers, despite their best intentions, fail at it. To avoid serious mistakes, the house of Diptyque has set up a guide to raising tuberoses, which, through a practical example, should be of great help to many colleagues in nurturing their tuberoses. Especially with tuberoses, which tend to become somewhat dominant without a guiding hand, early socialization is essential. Therefore, it is important to embed them in a diverse environment that should gradually change over time in accordance with the evolving needs of the tuberose. In the early years, it is ideal to seek contact with hesperidic notes, preferably rather bitter-sour representatives. However, to avoid making the environment too one-sided, which also poses dangers, the tuberose should be introduced to herbs and spices in moderation; here, gently bitter representatives have proven effective. Soon, the tuberose will enter a new phase of life, bringing with it a certain shift in interests. At this point, the tuberose should be given the opportunity to meet similar flowers, preferably rather reserved characters of the opposite sex. These should be carefully selected, as they are tasked with guiding the tuberose as calmly as possible through this otherwise turbulent time. With the entry into the third and final phase of life, it is important to ensure very versatile, profound acquaintances that can tell the tuberose many stories, so that it is essentially kept busy with listening and learning. Smoky-earthy characters are a good choice here, as well as woody fellows. With such an upbringing, you will have very few problems; your tuberose will undergo an extraordinary development and make many friendships along the way, and you will continue to be envied by many for your wonderfully successful, civilized and reserved tuberose. The correct upbringing of tuberoses is not rocket science; Diptyque demonstrates this with L'Eau du Trente-Quatre. A fragrance that kept me guessing for a while before it revealed itself to me. A scent of extraordinary complexity and exceptional composition, which smells so novel on one hand, yet fits so perfectly on the other, as if it has existed forever. With the tuberose, it is a bold fragrance for men, which, due to its perfect embedding, will never clash. With the tuberose, it is an elegant and special fragrance for women, for whom smooth, floral scent blends are too characterless. Essentially, it is a test recommendation for all perfume lovers out there who are already excited about the Diptyque brand or want to be without current knowledge. And for everyone else too.

Now the restless summer has finally decided to put aside its bad mood and is trying to appease us with a few beautiful days. And it is succeeding quite well. A bit surprised by the friendly gesture, I reach for the cheerful and light-footed summer fragrances in my collection during these last days of September.

Greenergy is a soft, easy to wear green and fruity chypre. It opens brightly with lemon but also sweetly with notes of orange and mandarin to which a faint (and brief) aromatic note of basil is added. The mint and cardamom could be more pronounced here, I think, to counter-balance the sweetness. A light vetiver then appears, mixed with an array of floral notes, in the same vein as what is done in Insensé. I also get melon every time, although I have never seen it listed in the notes. The two keywords here are, again, soft and sweet. Greenergy stays pretty much linear after that. While it's pleasant, to my nose its name was not aptly chosen. From "Greenergy" I was expecting an explosion of sharp green notes. And while it is green — because of the vetiver and a light moss-like note that develops in the final stages — it's also very flowery and has a sweet, soft, fruity side that I do not find "energetic". All in all, this is not what I expected but nevertheless an inoffensive light fragrance for spring and summer. Longevity and sillage are on the weak side.

Then he or she can bring back truly enchanting souvenirs. And how delighted I was to embrace Mrs. Nur again after her long stay in the USA. Thank you very much for this. For surely good reason - as one will learn from Givenchy - the house did not create this fragrance for the European market, and so it is not surprising that I am writing the first fragrance comment on Greenergy here at Parfumo, my very personal third creation from Givenchy. Impatiently, I open the bottle and apply the first spray to my wrist. In the air now materializes what was just a name on a bottle: A lot of energy that my spirit draws from the green freshness. I perceive a light and pleasantly soft chypre scent - bright green like a peridot (gemstone) and slightly cypric *g*. Greenergy opens brightly with lemon, but also sweetly thanks to notes of orange and mandarin, to which a faint and fleeting aromatic note of basil has been added. Mint and cardamom, on the other hand, remain shyly in the background at first. I must confess, upon seeing the bottle, I imagined a resemblance to Givenchy's Insensé brothers (yellow and blue). However, I found no truly conclusive connections that were not pulled from fairy-green hair. What stands out, however, is the skillful linking of fresh notes with floral accords, which was also beautifully unconventional in Insensé. After the wonderfully summery freshness of the flower meadow, spices now come to the fore. A bright vetiver shines as if a bouquet of flowers had been woven onto a wreath of vetiver. In the base, Greenergy remains quite linear, soft, and slightly spicy. A pleasant third Givenchy in the Insensé bottle. However, I find the name not well chosen. It does not manage to perform a true energy transition. From "Greenergy," I would have expected a more sparkling and explosive olfactory experience. Nevertheless, this harmonious fragrance with its beautiful vetiver note - which I find particularly pleasant here - and a hint of moss, which it culminates in during the final phase, is very pleasant to wear. This Givenchy also has something private, which I would gladly label as a Sunday fragrance. Longevity and aura are perfectly fine. I would like to give it the name "Insensé Peridot": The green aura enclosed in a drop of storax.

I love how this scent smells. This scent has the gourmand notes without the gourmand weight. The vanilla and chocolate notes are present throughout the scent's development, though the other notes make the profile more sweet, powdery feel. The other notes some together really beautifully but the end product is so light and whisper soft that you have to overspray just to get the full picture. As a result, I've gone through half of my 0.5ml travel bottle in 5 days. It also has poor sillage and turns into a skin scent in less than an hour. If this fragrance performed better and was available at a higher concentration, I would absolutely repurchase this, but I cant justify using 0.1ml per use on a perfume that costs more than $1/ml The scent is cozy and appropriate for all ages. I do think this scent would be good for a tween whose getting into fragrance. It's mostly inoffensive, doesn't leave a scent trail, and lends itself well to oversprayers.

Clinique My Happy’s Cocoa & Cashmere was regifted to me by my grandmother. I presume she did not like it, and I can understand why. “Cocoa and cashmere” as a description prepares me for a fragrance that is warm, sweet, and soft. I don’t believe it achieves this well. I’m really not a fan of the peppery note, and I think it smells too bright and synthetic and almost too… sour/tart, to live up to the name overall. The cocoa scent isn’t very strong either. It is more airy floral and vanilla than cocoa. The muskiness is gentle and the sweetness isn’t too sweet. There are far better gourmand fragrances out there in my opinion. If you do enjoy lighter clean/fresh fragrances, you might enjoy it more than me. That being said, I don’t think it’s a terrible fragrance, but I wouldn’t buy it for myself. Youthful but not immature. A cashmere sweater fresh out of the laundry, sure, but the powdery flower-scented detergent lingers, overpowering your cup of hot cocoa— and you spilled pepper in it somewhere along the way... Hey, I wanted to like it, and the price is fantastic, but I just can’t love it. Cocoa & Cashmere would function best as a daytime winter/early spring fragrance, suitable for work, leisure, or sports.

Starts out smelling exactly like an oatmeal raisin cookie, then quickly moves into the bulk of the fragrance: a super soft, true-to-life homemade cocoa powder. Not the screechy, store-bought packets - but a true unsweetened cocoa powder, blended with a touch of vanilla and sweetness; but quiet and more velvety. In dry-down, it's oddly-similar to a scratch-and-sniff sticker version of chocolate - synthetic, not actually an accurate depiction of chocolate and more just... generic, artificial sweetness. Strange turn, given how velvety and smooth the middle was. This was a very muted fragrance and overall, didn't wow me. If you're looking for a better chocolate-y fragrance, I'd recommend Chocolate Greedy or "Hot Cocoa & Cream | Bath & Body Works" instead.

Diptyque makes high-quality, elegant fragrances. Regrettably, most of the house's offerings leave a lot to be desired in terms of sillage, projection, and longevity. So, if you're deliberating between the eau de parfum and eau de toilette versions of a given Diptyque fragrance, a good rule of thumb is to opt for the EDP. The only exception to this rule, in my view, lies in the case of Vetyverio. While Vetyverio EDT is fresh, bright, and tantalizing, its EDP sibling is dirty, musty, and borderline repulsive; it's the only Diptyque I've ever scrubbed off my skin. Perhaps this response owes to some olfactory idiosyncrasy of mine—your nose may very well relish the smell of putrid soil. But do yourself a favour and buy a decant of this perfume before splurging on a full bottle :) Or check out the EDT!

I was so excited to try this out I beelined it for the Diptyque stand in the Nordstrom. Both on the paper and my skin, this just smelt like an anti mosquito candle with citronella. It punched me back to my time in college when I cared for a Pelargonium citrosum plant, or citronella geranium, a gorgeous plant with a faint scent of lemon, whose essential oil alongside others of the lemongrass family is used to fight mosquitoes in candles or sprays. This was unexpected, as I felt both repulsed and addicted to the smell on my wrist. I could not stop smelling and going to those summer nights with the candles on and watching the stars. I was disappointed by the lack of vetiver and the emergence of the rose (which to me smells like Geranium, or perhaps the combination of rose and grapefruit which gives the illusion of geranium) in the heart of the fragrance, until at the very end, did vetiver appear in the dry down. Now, the dry down is gorgeous. The vetiver with a hint of florals is great, but the opening and the first hour or two are a little off putting, although I could see myself loving this after a few more tests. Performance wise, lasts from before lunch to midnight, is powerful, but not incredibly overpowering. I think its a pretty safe scent, but not a safe blind buy if you expect vetiver.

At first, you get a strong wasabi scent. It's like the stinging feeling you get when you put wasabi in your mouth, and it makes you tear up. It also smells a bit like cypress. This is best when it's on paper. If you were to hand out a paper introducing this scent, most people would frown. It smells like burnt fallen leaves, and some people find the notes unpleasant. It's difficult to smell vetiver essential oil unless you have a good impression of it. I can understand why cockroaches run away. But I love the combination of sweet scents and vetiver. Adding a little bitterness from vetiver makes the fruit or flower suddenly "three-dimensional" and more realistic. It wasn't until I was a lot older that I realized that adding wasabi to sushi tasted good, but I feel that there is something similar to that. It complements the bitterness of the grapefruit pulp and skin to make it more realistic. This is the same. The reproduction of the bitterness of biting into the grapefruit skin in the back is wonderful. (No fruit juice) The EDT is a more precise version of ZARA's Bench Bar Pamplemousse, using good fragrances and allowing you to clearly see the contours of the ingredients. (ZARA's is a more conceptual grapefruit) The EDP is for those who want to taste more vetiver. There is no heavy musk or amber, so it is very light. It is also good for those who like not only vetiver but also the scent of shaved wood. Whether you think this scent is beautiful or not depends a lot on your fragrance experience and preferences, so I recommend trying the sample first. It made me want to eat sushi. It may seem strange, but it reminded me of the smell of vinegared rice and a sushi restaurant. It has a great effect on nausea and stomach upset. I think people who find wasabi delicious will like it. Probably

This is a salient point in case of how it’s better to apply fragrance to get a rounded experience of it. From the atomizer is good, from a blotter’s good, but those aspects only allow you to experience a facet of a fragrance. So, i say that to say: when i first purchased this (2018) i did so only after having worn it via a sample from Diptyque. I couldn’t get enough of the stuff. However, after having purchased it, i seldomly reached for it. Big reason being: i decide my sotd by sniffing the atomizer. Hence, my point. Whenever i do wear this, i almost always kick myself for not using it more because it SMELLS SO GOOD on skin. Via atomizer it smells slightly dirty and kinda weird. This is indeed unique. Done in a way only Diptyque can construct. The smell like section, in typical fashion—at least of the ones I’ve smelled—is straight cap. The only tie between them being a prominent vetiver note. Anyways: unisex-male, any age above 20, casual, daytime, transitional weather and office appropriate… Good stuff. NOTE: I’m going to stand on there being iris in this. Most notably in the drydown. Does anyone else get that??

And then it struck eight from the cathedral, the last customers paid, the others tore themselves away from the shelves and strolled towards the exit. Gradually, the store emptied. Finally, the salespeople left as well, the glass door was locked, and the grille was lowered. Slowly, the voices and sounds of the day faded into the distance, and suddenly the perfumery lay deserted and still in the twilight. But it didn’t take long before life stirred in the rooms and it began to whisper and murmur and crackle. “It wouldn’t have taken much, and the blonde would have taken me with her...,” said a soft voice. It came right from the Diptyque shelf and belonged to the proud Madame Eau Duelle. “Well, tomorrow she’ll buy me, I’m sure of it,” she continued - and that was quite well-spoken, even if it might have been true. “Oh, I don’t even know if I want to go to such a home… perhaps to the bathroom, where primitive, insensitive deodorant folks have the say…” remarked a somewhat too quiet, almost cowardly-sounding gentleman named Philosykos. Then everyone fell silent for a moment, as a soft, suppressed sob was heard. “What’s wrong with you? Wanderlust again?” asked the cheeky dandy Habit Rouge from the shelf across. Of course, everyone knew who was sobbing - it was, of course, the little Vetyverio again. “Oh woe, no one will buy me anymore! I’ll never end up in a perfume home, will never be revered and taken out for outings, never loved and admired…” “Oh, you little fool! You have the best qualities,” replied the neighbor of Habit Rouge, the sturdy, cheerful, and also noble Vetiver from Guerlain. “You’re almost related to me, just a bit more softened…” Suddenly, the mop, which stood right next to its cleaning bucket, joined the conversation. He had quite a bit to say, as he had been around a lot and was a down-to-earth guy whom everyone appreciated. “My dear Vetyverio, let me tell you something. You are a special character, you know that! You have the magic of the vetiver root just like that of the rose within you, you’re a little maverick with a rugged scrubber charm and also a velvety, soft flatterer. That’s not something you find often! Enjoy your life and your uniqueness!” “But I want to be sprayed! A lot! And… “Those are just your immature grapefruit whims! Enjoy what you have, here among your kind, as long as you still can…” “Listen to these normals, what a simple folk, without any elegance and healthy pride, how ordinary, n’est ce pas?…” That came from the back of the Tom Ford Private Blend altar, it was probably the somewhat conceited Oud Wood, which loved to moss. However, it only knew real moss by hearsay. And then the big day came. A young man in a midnight blue duffle coat grabbed our Vetyverio and quickly went with him to the checkout. He must have known it already - and Vetyverio was at least as happy about the fine, surely very wealthy young man, whose dark coat matched so well with the black Vetyverio Eau de Parfum outfit. He was stuffed into a dark bag and in a terribly bumpy up and down, he was off, away from his long-familiar brothers and sisters. But then it became very bright, and he was unpacked and placed on a table. The young man came very close, lifted him, and sprayed himself several times on his neck and the snow-white shirt collar. “Aaah…” he said, “hmmm…” and also “wonderful…”. Vetyverio wanted to almost fade away from joy. Then the young man wrote something in a notebook, murmuring to himself, but perfumes hear everything and Vetyverio clearly heard: …an astonishing étude in green… the bright green of the above-ground vetiver is here more countered by the smoky-dark earthy root tones of the deep vetiver, much more clearly than in the EdT. However, before unpleasant associations like rubber or dirt can arise, a leaf-green floral delicacy first joins in, bright and sunny, then finally the whole accompanying rose. Soft and flattering, almost a bit sweet, it certainly appears elegant. And it also fits quite well with the second melody, which quietly resonates in the background of the scent development - that of a fine fruity citrus, also rather green, almost unripe. It oscillates around the bright green, grassy vetiver notes and naturally forms another appealing contrast to the smoky vetiver aspects… Now the pen was laid aside. Then the young man’s hand reached for Vetyverio again and he was delighted - he was to be sprayed again. Wasn’t that quite extraordinary? But instead, he was carried a piece through the room and then placed in a cupboard, the door creaked, it went bang, then it was closed and Vetyverio stood in the dark. Slowly, his molecules got used to the sparse remaining light, and he realized that he was not alone. “Welcome to the cemetery of scent creatures,” said a bulky gentleman dressed entirely in black, who introduced himself as Encre Noir. “Oh, you old Iso-E-Super slinger, don’t scare the newcomer right away…” The one who said that was also dressed in black from head to toe, but was slimmer and called himself Antaeus. “But Uncle Noir, is this really your serious tone?” Vetyverio asked timidly. “Oh, don’t mind him, he likes to smell himself and isn’t as grim as he pretends…” said Antaeus. “But one thing is true, many of us don’t get out of here for months… you get used to it!” “Oh dear…” said Vetyverio. “Oh come on, there are almost 40 of us here! Or rather, women!” The good-looking, adventurously optimistic smiling Devin moved closer to Vetyverio. Or was it just his imagination? “We’re quite a fun group here, you’ll see…” Devin added boldly. “Yes, yes, especially you K.R.s, you’re a kind of your own, but a lovable one, I think,” said Madame Diorissimo. “What does K.R. mean?” asked Vetyverio. “Well, those are the barely reformulated, a caste of their own, but luckily all very sweet. The Bernard-Chant kids, for example. Unfortunately, I don’t belong to that group…” A sigh of regret escaped from Diorissimo’s spray head. “But you get used to it!” called Mr. Fahrenheit from the back. “By the way, this evening the Hèrmes scents invite you to listen to the Faubourg St.Honorè tales…” “You have to be there too, you creamy newcomer!” shouted the lively Lalique White, “you don’t have anything planned, do you?” “Uh, no, not directly…” “Good, good, I would be happy if you… or may I say ‘you’…?” Vetyverio was a little startled. But he was nice, that White. Or was it the White? Well, did it matter? In any case, there was at least a bit of action in here. He would have to make the best of it. Was this perhaps the “art of living” that Jaipur had always talked about? Back in the store? How beautiful it had been there, bright and friendly, full of life and curious people. How long ago that seemed. But his rugged vetiver vein and his sovereign rosiness would surely help him cope with the situation. And maybe, who knows, his owner would someday get the idea to take him out again. That was what Vetyverio would dream of from now on.

When the world spins too quickly around you, Vetyverio invites you to pause. It is a green shield against the hustle and bustle and soothes you immediately upon spraying. Earth. Overgrown with greenery. A squirrel is currently burying a nut somewhere. The campfire has long since gone out. Sweet sandalwood and lovely rose shine brightly through the withered underbrush.

A full-bodied peppery grapefruit greets AugustA's nose. Soon, a velvety green note joins in. Full, pulsating vetiver, fresh, woody, grassy, and earth and sky in one. So green and blue - in the best sense. The rose adds a floral, almost fruity moment; it is deep dark red, but does not stand out decoratively or dominantly, certainly not soapy.

"Olfactory illusions" do not (yet) exist. Optical ones, however, are abundant! But with this wonderful fragrance, there are likely to be acoustic elements as well, because I can almost "hear" the scent. The wind brushing over grass that rustles softly, and the clouds drifting across the sky. Gray misty clouds, interspersed with azure blue.

Bottled Monet. A lily pond lullaby. The nectar that buds out of a fresh-cut stem. Its elements – cardamom, violet, vanilla – somehow meld into a impressionist’s garden. I don’t think “vegetal” when I hear any of those scents, so Lilyphea must have some clever perfumer’s sorcery behind it. If I strain, I can imagine their roles in the painting. The airiness of violet turns aquatic, the sweetness of vanilla a sappy green, and the buzz of cardamom something earthen and herbal. It’s an elegant, fey skin scent, which feels somewhat maternal. Like a more organic Jardin Sur de Nil meets a powder-free L’Eau d’Hiver. If this scent were a movie, it'd be Pride and Prejudice (2005). Unfortunately, as with Rose Roche, I like Lily P. far more on fabric, as she ages rather tallowy on my skin. I’m impressed, but not bewitched. Mental Snapshot: A modern fairy godmother, a Central Park naiad. She looks like a John Williams Waterhouse nymph. Works as a florist, a Tai Chi instructor, a concierge dermatologist. Amongst countless other talents. She’ll be a plein air pastellist next week, a calligrapher tomorrow. She's a lifetime member of every museum in the city. tl;dr: frog mom

Truly an unusual vanilla! Out of the five Essences, this was immediately the most memorable to me because it wasn't what I expected at all. It's first and foremost, a fresh green scent. Not an ounce of gourmand vanilla at all. I expected something almost tea-like with the addition of ginger and cardamom. The second I sprayed it on my skin, it instantly reminded me of biting into a green guava. The kind with the white flesh, not the pink kind that's more nectary and tropical. It's fresh, leafy, wet, and such an optimistic scent. I had a guava tree in the backyard of my mom's house, and I remember my grandma slicing them up for me as a kid, reminding me to not eat too many of the seeds (according to Vietnamese people, it can cause indigestion). It's such a specific scent that I was surprised to see it replicated so realistically here. Looking back at these adjectives (fresh, leafy, wet) they make perfect sense for a fragrance inspired by water lilies. The staying power isn't great, but gosh, maybe it's worth it for something so unique and evocative.

i am a diptyque lover- almost everything i've tried from them i really enjoyed. but this is the one for me; my true love, my sweet pea, my good time girl. aquatic and green, crisp and fresh, sharp and almost bitter. not sweet. very cooling, lovely to wear in the warm weather. and yes i think if there was a fairy who lives in a magical pond, with the lily pads and flowers, this is what she would smell like.

Of the newest line of Diptyque fragrances, this one and Lunamaris were my absolute favs. Funny enough, violets and violet leaves are some of the most challenging plant notes in perfumery for me. They often come off too sharp, cold, and uninviting for me. But Lilyphéa may just be the perfect one for me. The name of this one is brilliant because it tricked me into thinking this would be a lily or water lily focused scent. Come to find out no such florals exist in this, but actually, no florals exist at all here. It’s just a big, plush, violet leaf in all its ozonic and dewy glory. There is a *sparkle* to this scent, reminiscent of sun reflecting off the water of a pond. I take it the ginger + cardamom give that effect without the scent ever going too spicy. And then there’s the vanilla that likes to reveal itself and then hide again. It gives the fragrance some sweetness without overpowering its green, aquatic nature. As if it exists on a green screen that keeps glitching. The whole composition definitely gives an atmospheric vibe (as often ozonic scents do) and I just adore the association of ‘naiad’ that others have brought up. Think of the cutest toad at a local pond, jumping from lily pad to pad (hence, Lilypheá!) on a hot sunny day. Now this line wasn’t built to project and shout like some of the EDPs from Diptyque, but I will say the staying power is fairly good and I do think these scents were meant to be sprayed with a bit of a heavier hand. This one lasted well on clothes and I think it’s going to be a summer stunner. Grabbing a full bottle as soon as I can get my hands on a slightly discounted one (these are pricey!!!)

This is light, slightly powdery, but also wet and floral. I wouldn't call it green at all, but there is something plant-like, perhaps a lilypad. This is my favorite of this line from Diptyque and it leads with a wide margin. It sits closer to the skin on me and lasts ~4 hours without reapplication which is totally fine. Beast mode perfumes are a hype moment. :)

I like some of Diptyque´s perfumes, but most of the perfumes have a feel of some kind of unexplained old fashion heaviness, but this is like a fresh breeze in their collection. It has this unexpected freshness that I have not smelled anywhere before... fresh, aquatic, feel of cool early morning air in the park.

This fragrance has become my obsession. I have to forcefully make myself wear something else, because this has dug it's claws into me. It feels like a drop of water when I'm parched. It's like a shred of light during a storm. It is the feeling of a loved one next to you when you wake from a dream.

Why Lilyphea is not held up and shouted about by the Diptyque fans more, I don't understand. I am not the biggest fan of the house despite trying most of their scents and even Lilyphea was a pass on a few tries. I am trying to say, do not pass this off after trying in a perfume-heavy environment. Do as I did, unknowingly in my case - spray on your arm and head out.

Open green and fresh, dries down into a soft, watery floral with the barest whisper of vanilla. The aquatic element is like morning on a quiet pond. Perfect for spring and I think it would be lovely in the summer heat. It's a shame the longevity is so poor; I can't justify the price of a full bottle as it's so fleeting.

Lilyphéa opens with a crisp, green freshness, evoking water lilies floating on the surface of a tranquil pond. A pure and soothing sensation. Then, the vanilla emerges gently, as light as a white veil resting on the water. Not too sweet, not too heavy, just enough to soften the initial freshness and add a hint of warmth.

I’ve had a bottle of this since its release almost 20 years ago. Every few years, I’ll pull it out and use it, usually in spring or summer. It’s definitely sweet but not cloying. I don’t see this specifically called out in the notes, but I detect some pear in there. The lily and other white florals are also present. It has pretty decent longevity. If I spray it on skin and clothes, I’ll still smell it at the end of the day. This is not a controversial fragrance. I feel comfortable wearing a couple sprays to the office. Once it’s gone, I won’t feel a big gap in my perfume collection. That being said, I have enjoyed it.

My friend isn't laughing much at the moment - so I feel the urge to do something nice for her. Small gifts keep friendship alive - but what can cheer her up? A discount voucher from Karstadt flutters into my thoughts. Only today and only valid for perfume items. So - question answered. I rush to the fragrance department - but alas, Karstadt is not allowed to set up testers. I am an intuitive Pisces and wander around the shelves with my antennas extended. A single bottle catches my eye - and I read Happy in Bloom. Well - what a coincidence! I made a blind purchase and sprayed it at home out of curiosity. Wow! What a spectacular start! Fruits roll towards me, still with foliage where the soft plum dominates. The freesia makes its presence known, accompanied by fresh lily of the valley and delicately tart mimosa. Amber appears subtly sweet, and the wood note adds a casual elegance. A cheerful, lively scent that is not shy - yet doesn't impose itself. It has momentum and energy - but still feels mature and serious. Happy in Bloom is a likable go-to - for one should always open the door and the gate to joy when it arrives.

I swapped this fragrance blindly and what can I say, I am HAPPY! It is the ultimate spring scent and yes, it really does make you happy. It starts fruity (thankfully without berries), citrusy, and even though it's not listed, just slightly aquatic. This top note actually lasts throughout most of the fragrance's development. The yellow plums are also wonderfully detectable. Then, as is typical in spring, the flowers start to emerge from the ground. However, they are totally sweet and not overwhelming (as can often be the case with lily of the valley). It truly smells unique (good) and for a spring fragrance in this price range, it lasts really long. This is not a scent for the office or for the evening... this fragrance would rather suit a cozy day strolling through the city, a trip to the ice cream parlor, or a day in the park with family. It is a romantic scent, playful, sweet, nice, puts you in a positive mood and lifts your spirits, simply makes you happy. And don't worry, it is by no means too girly. More for the age of 25 and up.

Happy In Bloom smells like a meadow full of flowers. I had the predecessor already. It smelled just the same, only the flowers on the bottle were different. A lovely scent for spring. Very intense and long-lasting. But please don't use it after nights of partying. I always get a headache from that, anyway.

At the beginning of the year, I accompanied a friend while shopping - the bitterly self-imposed resolution was to really start the Capri pants and bikini season super fit this year. So, running shoes and tops and pants were bought, a nice yoga mat with a matching water bottle - and then a second water bottle because the one that came with the yoga mat didn't quite match the other items. They also wanted to schedule a training session at the gym - very soon, for sure. The afternoon reminded me a bit of our university days, when after literature research, copying, stapling, punching holes, and filing (I studied very analog), no one could really expect to read all that stuff, right? Recently, I saw the items - still with tags on - lying in the trunk of her car. If only I had known Clinique's Chemistry that day! It would have made everything perfect with its clean, straight fitness studio vibe, subtly infused with the rubber scent of yoga mats and running shoes - unused ones, at least. It has the straightforwardness of a Pilates session, the freshness of a morning run by the riverbank, and the toned arms of Michelle Obama. All of this is so stylized, almost artificially like all the (recent) fragrances from Clinique: unexciting, unobtrusive, unpretentious. Chemistry is the muted, unisex-made version of the 90s men's shower gel sport scent archetype: ozonically fresh, sometimes almost metallic, soft and effortless in the finish - and thus actually suitable for workouts, if one (or woman) absolutely wants to wear a perfume while doing so. If I had put that in the bag(s) that January day - where could the BMI be now? Conclusion: a lot of what I don't want in a perfume - I, who prefers not to wear any perfume while exercising. For those who like to smell of something fresh and artificial that goes well with yoga mats and running shoes - here we go!

Ah Volutes..... I haven't been that excited about a scent in a long long time. Volutes is absolutely mind blowing. I could run a bath tub full of this beauty, bath in it and consider myself in heaven. I have tried the EDT and the EDP version and both have more in common than there are differences. That said, there are differences though. The EDT version opens with a slightly sweet and powdery note. After a few minutes the light tobacco note joins the opening, together and a nice (noticable) leathery note. Volutes EDT feels dry, slightly sweet, spicey and soft. The EDP opens with a somewhat stronger sweet and powdery note. After that I feel that the EDP is rounder, thicker, warmer and slightly sweeter. Also it has a more prominent tobacco note (cherry pipe tobacco to be exact). The leather note is less prominent here. I love both the EDT and the EDP and I had a really hard time to figure out which one I preferred. I prefer the opening of the EDT because it is somewhat fresher. If a man had to choose I'd recommend the EDT, because overal it is slightly more masculin. For me, I prefer the EDP, because of it's fullness and I love the warm cherry tobacco note in it. The EDP feels more feminine. As for longevity I think they are both equally good. Both about 4 to 6 hours on me, maybe the EDP is slightly more longlasting. As for the sillage I think the EDT outshines the EDP. Projection power in the EDT is heavy and in the EDP moderate. I love both versions from start to dry down, which is in both cases sweet vanilla-like benzoin/ opoponax (somewhat sweeter and more resinous in the EDP concentration and somewhat dryer in the EDT concentration) and I consider them both masterpiece material. I would be happy owning both and personally only slightly preferring the EDP version.

Diptyque Volutes does smell very natural. Almost too natural in our world of sweet gourmands and synthetics. It's a surprise scent that I did not expect. And It's not for everyone's discerning nose, but it's an interesting perfume. My first impression of the first phase was of peppered hay in a barn. (As if there is such a commodity.) And then pipe tobacco quickly came into the mix. Volutes met me head-on, looked me in the eye and didn't back down. It continued with a pleasing composition of vanilla and woods. But that doesn't completely describe its complexity. Immortelle and honey further complicate this fragrance all together with what I've mentioned immediately vying for attention. I've been wearing it through two seasons now to try and pin it down, but Volutes just seems to be difficult. Just when I think it's clean and sweet, a barrage of notes swirl around me making me think it's mysterious. I truly can't compare this to another. Add in it's earthiness with hints of saffron spice and heavy on its resin influence with its four, yes, count 'em, four base notes of benzoin, styrax, myrhh, and opoponax and this is a powerful fragrance. So where does Volutes take me when I'm wearing it? To a bazaar filled with wonderful, wondrous smells from heavy spices that are sold in open barrels under tents in the hot summer sun, where you can smell the aromas of Mediterranean food cooking nearby. Or I'm in a barn, laying in the hay. It transports me away from home, that's for certain. And that's its allure. It doesn't change me, it just takes me someplace else for a few hours. Simple bottle with a plain white label. Dry down is a softer, spicier version of the main attack. Better suited for spring and summer wear when the weather is warmer. What a fascinating unisex perfume!

Opens with iris, honey, dried fruit and a sheer tobacco/hay/immortelle note. The fragrance is smooth and creamy with a pleasant subtle sweetness. Alas, the iris top note is not very strong, which is why I'd say the EdT is more aromatic-gourmand than iris-centric. As the notes bloom on my skin the fragrance becomes woodsier with a pinch of incense, honey and iris to liven things up. Volutes EdT dries down quickly into a generic woodsy-herbal blend and then nothingness.

With a wardrobe stuffed with challenging, amazing, difficult, tempestuous perfumes, Volutes stands out not because it 'stands out' but rather because it doesn't. It's the battered leather jacket in your wardrobe that you just can't bear to part with, and reach for over your fancier coats even though it's falling to pieces. Love isn't rational. It may not even be love - it may be simply a reflex. I smell a cool, starchy iris, warm honey, blond tobacco, a hint of rubbery leather from the saffron (only at the start), and some nebulous resins in the base. These notes all smell quite blurred and perfumey to me, in the same way that baby powder smells like rose, chamomile, and heliotrope all swirled together but never distinctly of themselves. Volutes sits on the skin like a creamy balm at first, but as time goes on, dries to a texture like fine, powdered sugar. This is not a sweet scent, however. The iris exerts its influence here from top to bottom, reflected in that cold, vegetal starchiness. The tobacco, although not smoky, adds body to the iris and makes it slightly more 'of this earth' than irises tend to be. It is not exotic, but it is even-tempered. When I still had it - I finished the last of my two bottles a few years ago - I would wear buckets of it, carelessly sprayed around my person until it dripped, like honey, from the tips of my fingers. I let it run in rivers down to my belly button. No matter how much I sprayed, Volutes remains this utterly pleasant, low key piece of background music to my day. It's a fragrance on cruise control. Can anyone tell me if the EDP retains the magic of the EDT?

Volutes, in German 'Voluten', are snail-shaped rolled forms, a decorative element that has been used in Western architectural and art history for millennia, although not equally loved in every stylistic period. Volutes first appeared in ancient Greece, in Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite capitals, and remained an exceedingly popular decoration of the column order until the decline of Western Rome. In the medieval language of forms, there was no use for volutes, until they regained popularity in the Renaissance, ultimately reaching the peak of their popularity in Baroque and Rococo. Even in Art Nouveau and its variations, volute-like ornaments can be found. The use of volutes is - simply put - a sign that more material is present than is needed. They thus express a lavish attitude oriented towards decorative ornamentation. Inherent to them is a drive, a sensuality, a richness that in turn expresses the aspiration to please - a general, a king, (a) god(dess). Volutes grow from the capitals of columns and pilasters, entwine over the facades of churches and palaces, and nestle into gables and tympani, the decorative areas above portals. Art historians may undoubtedly criticize this representation as overly simplified, yet we might find 'common ground' with the statement: Volutes are very beautiful. Drive, sensuality, richness - can even more be said about Volutes, Diptyque's homage to beauty and the fine arts? This is a fragrance of restrained sweetness and great depth - overflowing, indulgent, devoted to beauty in every moment of its being, yet never loud. It is a pleasure-driven scent, yet nothing lewd is contained within - it is a fragrance like fresh bread, like cake, fruits, and a few flowers. Honey and beeswax give its sweetness maturity and something very enduring - and an almost provocative slowness that culminates in a resinous dryness, devoid of any disturbing or even biting elements. A fragrance like dark, warm sugar, full of oriental ingredients - dates, figs, saffron, a hint of incense - and yet not an oriental. Pure pleasure and delight. Conclusion: a fragrance of sensuality and abundance. The American actress Mae West, star of the 30s and 40s, aptly remarked: 'Too much of a good thing can be wonderful.'

If I have researched the translation of Volutes correctly, it means spiral-shaped or rolled. I don't really understand what the name has to do with the scent, but whatever. In the first few minutes, Volutes reminds me a bit of Shalimar, as there is a citrusy powdery accord that takes center stage. With the heart note, the lemon fades away, but the powdery aspect remains.

This week, I received a sample of Volutes from a very charming woman..from a brand that had completely passed me by except for "Eau Duelle." Perhaps it was also due to the rather inconspicuous bottles that the brand hadn't really caught my attention in the perfumery. The fragrance notes sound great..

I have long waited for someone to have mercy on my troubled soul and offer a sharing for Volutes. The dear Thadl has heard my prayers, which happens far too rarely in real life. Volutes, a worthy name for a very beautiful fragrance. I couldn't care less what Volutes means in translation. I find the word Volutes itself simply beautiful.

I don't think I've had the chance to test a Diptyque fragrance until now, so I was all the more delighted to finally receive a sample. And in the case of Volutes, it was certainly not an inappropriate choice, as sweet iris scents have been among my favorites since Dior Homme or Lanvin's Arpege Pour Homme. It could have turned out much worse than Volutes.

I couldn't stand this scent. It had a piercing pear note. The floral notes were overshadowed by this note, and then there was the cocoa-sandalwood note that smelled quite strange. Not very pleasant. The fragrance had some sillage and didn't last very long on the skin... I write this because it is no longer available. I wonder why? ^^ Best, Kitty17

This fragrance is all about that beetroot accord. The rose makes it a cohesive perfume and the frankincense serves to complement the rose (as it often does in perfumery) as well as to complement the smokey quality of the vetiver with it's own smokiness. Lastly, the vetiver is here to legitimize the beetroot accord by lending it's earthy/ grassy facets to the overall composition. Heads up: I smell suede. The jury is still out on whether I like this or not. Something tells me this shines in the air vs sniffing it on a forearm or wrist. Not to say it smells bad doing that but sometimes you need to back up from the trees to see the beauty of the forest. If that made sense. The quality is typical Diptyque, which is high along with their signature "je ne sais quo" smell that transfers over to all their offerings. I can't speak on longevity, yet. Overall, it seems like a solid offering and above that: it's UNIQUE! At least I've never smelled anything like this. I'm curious to know what you guys think..

Beetroot is a tuber that could give sensory problems to the sense of smell, very emotional issues that depend significantly on experience. Once removed from the soil and washed, the tuber still has an organic-type odour similar to the ground but more concentrated or enhanced. Besides its unique appearance, the root vegetable has a sweet and earthy taste due to a compound called geosmin produced by the plant. This substance gives off the earthy smell we all know. You know, after a storm, we smell this earthy smell coming from the ground? It is caused by a substance in the soil, in this case. So it gives this not-too-sweet vegetable a touch of sourness. Everyone doesn't like or appreciate beetroot, which can be a polarizing tuber. Given that I like it, it has never happened to me before to come across a fragrance with this note among its ingredients. This bizarre element led me to make a blind purchase, which was a wise decision. First, Kyoto is a fragrance with balanced incense, rose and vetiver scents. It belongs to the rosy, earthy, rooty, musky, smoky, and unconventional categories. However, as soon as I smelled Kyoto, I couldn't help but imagine something earthly, the smell of damp autumn foliage. Call it what you prefer: Frondescence, leafage, or foliage — but that's what I feel. Kyoto gives off a very intense herbaceous scent, dizzying, reminiscent of freshly picked field vegetables. There is a decadent rosy scent that overlaps the earthy, a bit sweet, a tad tart, and a hint of a floral smell. The Turkish rose emerges undaunted, slow but astonishing, bittersweet and slightly peppery. I don't remember any other perfume with this fantastic opening, an earthy rose raised to the umpteenth degree. Not outdated, not the ordinary rose, but spicy and green, a genuinely revolutionary rose. As well as being earthy, the opening also has a slightly metallic undertone. This could be due to the rose petals and beetroot tubers immediately coming to mind. A dry incense, austere, very faint, with lemony hints, fills the heart of Kyoto. While I find the slightly clerical incense appealing, it appears airy and sober as a feather. It mixes with the rose and takes on musky tones. Bursts of incense flutter throughout Kyoto's development. But the real magic is the sweet earthiness of the beetroot; it changes everything. If you are fond of incense, this might not be what you're looking for. In this movie, it is not one of the principal actors but an extra who serves to fill the scene without dominating it. It blends seamlessly with the rose and gives the vetiver a smokier undertone. The dry-down reveals a smooth, vegetal, grassy, and slightly astringent vetiver, only a touch. The same vetiver that we also find in the homonymous Guerlain, very fickle, is sometimes sweeter and earthy and other times more herbaceous and peppery. Towards the end, the incense floats above everything. On my skin, it begins earthier and then floral but then becomes musky and animalic, with fresh vetiver balancing the rose from becoming too overpowering. Including a tinge of white musk in the concoction would not be unreasonable. Floral, earthy, loamy, and smoky, Kyoto is a fragrance that is very sensitive to temperature and humidity. There are a lot of changes in the scent throughout the day, which I appreciate in a perfume. This scent has a moderate projection and lasts for a long time on the skin and even more on clothing. It screams cold weather, fall, and a great day and evening scent. If it were embroidery, the beetroot would be the thread covering the warp from all the other notes. I base the review on a bottle I have owned since October 2022. -Elysium

My taste in perfume tends to lean towards oriental bombshells, old school, heavy, almost overwhelming scents. But I also really like complex, difficult and challenging perfumes. However, I'm a bit promiscuous when it comes to perfumes, and this one, which is totally different, won me over. I've never smelled beetroot in a fragrance, I've tried other vegetables in perfumery, but nothing like this one. It automatically took me back to the heyday of my European ancestors, where this vegetable comes from. I immediately thought of my grandmother preparing lunch for my mother and uncles, which is curious, as none of them like beets. The perfume gives me a delicious melancholy, even meditative. It is an introspective perfume, without anything sweet, complemented with a dry and airy incense. And with pink, lots of pink. Its longevity is pretty cool, around 7 hours, and the projection is medium, but very noticeable. It's that aroma that you can feel again with just one movement, even after forgetting you were wearing it.

Got an almost full bottle secondhand from a guy that works in a department store. That last part is relevant, since it appears that most of the bottles you can find of this online appear to not be genuine. I had years prior bought a decant and they smell the same. Earthy, wet, floral. There is a compost vibe to it that I really enjoy (call me a hippie!). The closest diptyque has vibe-vise would be Eau Capital, but they do not actually smell that similar. I do also own musc amarante, and I suppose you could mix those two at home to try and capture the vibe of kyoto

Crime scene: Oberpollinger a grinning sweetsmell with bright eyes ... "Look what I discovered, it's great, isn't it?" ... and that was until I held my sprayed sweetie arm under the noses of everyone at the perfume meeting in Munich ... most found Kyoto nice too ;) I probably wouldn't have tested it otherwise ... beetroot ... yuck! ... I don't like to eat it ... can't smell good at all ;) But it turned out differently ... test me whispered the red bottle ... I am limited so don't waste time! 3 G ... (sprayed - marveled - bought!) :) Kyoto starts berry-like and absolutely not veggie (so no fear of the beetroot!) The scent is earthy with green-woody nuances from the vetiver. Over time, it becomes rosy and a fine veil of incense runs through the fragrance. Yes, it is a fine rose that reveals itself to me ... but on my skin, red berries, earth, dust & green dominate! The test strip smelled significantly rosier ;) I perceive Kyoto as a dull-dry scent ... green but also berry-red! The base becomes woody and suddenly there is musk ... a delicate fluff ... that holds everything together! Soft tones ... full of harmony ... but with a staying power of nearly 8 hours! I can imagine wearing Kyoto all year round. Unisex ... yes indeed :) The berry-red bottle is a real eye-catcher, wrapped in a cloth :) Let yourself fall into daydreams with Kyoto ... it can really sweeten a stressful workday/routine! Conclusion: *World, stand still for a moment ...* Harmony of rose-incense-vetiver & beetroot :) Green-berry-earthy-woody dry dust ... *Daydreaming*

I love Limited. Until there’s a favorite from a series that is no longer available. This is where it gets dangerous, as I have lost my favorites from Diptyque in the past too many times. I particularly miss the rosy Eau Dominotee. Excitedly, I spray myself with “Kyoto” and look forward to the aura it brings. The bottle comes in a chic cloth.

You really have to like beetroot and greens! I feel like I have my hands full of earth and I can taste the beetroot. It smells green, like freshly cut grass, and earthy with a few very fine, beautiful, and slightly sweet roses nearby, and the vetiver here is a dream!

An absolutely unique fragrance and certainly not something we will see again anytime soon! Besides the beetroot, earthy tones play an important role - and you have to like them. When I first tried the scent at the Diptyque store, I found it to be very special, but I wasn't sure if it completely suited my taste.

"The beet is the most intense of all vegetables. Admittedly, the radish is more exciting, but the fire of the radish is a cold fire of discontent, not one of passion. Tomatoes are at least vibrantly fresh, but tomatoes are tinged with a hint of frivolity. Beets are dead serious." after "pan aroma" by Tom Robbins.

Green opens this fragrance in the top note. The beetroot is initially present and remains so. I find it particularly rounded and, in a certain way, different. The rose reveals itself after a shorter time and makes the whole thing a bit softer.

I love cute, colorful animal figurines. Anyone who knows my perfume photos is aware of this. For some, this may be kitsch - for me, it is art. I also adore the Koons Poodle, and I wear it in a highly miniature form on my necklace. A valuable porcelain deer head, adorned with LED lights, decorates the wall - and it polarizes opinions. A green, cute little snail also watches over the front door, smiling a welcome to guests. But this funny little guy had to endure an attack on his person yesterday. Upon returning home, he was covered in shards, as an art-ignorant individual had smashed a beer bottle on him. He had withstood the brutal assault, but such reckless behavior makes me sad. Can't one accept another's taste? Or at least respect their belongings? The friendly figurine does no harm to anyone. And so is the scent. Fresh and friendly - and in a pleasant way, harmless. It smiles at me and wants to be loved. That comes easily to me. The delicious rhubarb cupcake is adorned with rose petals and rounded off with tonka. The mandarin, with its aquatic notes, ensures that the fragrance doesn’t feel sticky, and the hyacinth doesn’t sting but also feels rounded. Patchouli gives a delicate oriental touch that invites you to look into the distance. An unpretentious Givenchy that warmly welcomes you - just like my little green doorman in the front yard.

Autumn is a time of ripeness, the completion of the yearly cycle of growth and maturity, and so, to the weary farmer - with fields are full of waving grain - it’s a time of plenitude and celebration. But there's another side to autumn, the decline of summer into barren winter, a shift from growth to decay, from life springing forth to its return back to the earth. And it’s this poignant, melancholy side to autumn that Eau Lente captures, its brown resiny scent is full, over ripe, almost putrid. It's said that the formula derives from an ancient scent known to Alexander the Great, and it wouldn’t surprise me to learn that it was used to embalm his body, such is the sweet spicy ripeness of it all. With Eau Lente I was looking for an autumn perfume, but instead of a harvest festival I found something more like a funeral.

Eau Lente is to opoponax what Shalimar is to golden, ambery ‘oriental’ perfumes, except with its barbershoppy vibe, it’s more Daddy than Mommy. From its vigorous loins sprang Imperial Opoponax (Les Nereides), Ligea la Sirena (Carthusia), Bengale Rouge (Papillon Perfumery) and Empire des Indes (Oriza L. Legrand). I love that opoponax is a resin that can’t decide whether it wants to be a spice or a herb, which is why Eau Lente’s searing topnote lurches wildly between the metallic, sweaty sting of clove and the aromatic camphor of bay leaf. The base reveals a rich toffee-like resinousness, with a boozy, almond butter tonality and a touch of Johnson and Johnson’s Baby Powder. It is this disjointed transition between the astringent spicy-herbal top and the almond taffy base that make it an interesting perfume to wear. A chunk of amber dunked into a cup of Old Spice. You get the honey of a resin and the soapiness of a barbershop fougère. What’s not to love?

Got a sample for this one and well...Eau Lente definitely shows her age at first but then becomes warmly comfortable, just like when Grandma used to take her false teeth out right at the dinner table then say “you’re my favorite grandson” some minutes after. Not ideal for people who don't like spicy or vintage profiles.

The first time I applied Diptyque EAU LENTE I discovered that it is as strong as its golden amber color would suggest—more of a perfume concentration than an edt, it seems to me. Eventually, the composition dries down to a smooth and luscious amber. Unfortunately, to get there one must suffer through a spice-cabinet opening, which is so clove-heavy that it somewhat ruins the journey for me. I tried a second time, applying the edt quite a bit more lightly but still found the opening unpleasant. To my nose, this perfume is simply unbalanced, and it's not worth the wait to get to the fine drydown since there are plenty of amber perfumes around town which are a joy to wear from start to finish. Désolée.

I have a 2ml decant from another purchase. It smells like a dessert that in spanish is called "Arroz con leche" (rice with milk) that I love to eat with a lot of cinamon. It is the strongest eau de toillete I have ever smelled although it only lasts on me like the 4h of rigour. Very strong and warm cinamon perfume, somehow it feels vintage and decadent, it has something very nostalgic and a little dirty. It is too plain and linear for my tastes but I can enjoy it for the days I want something spicy and cosy

Recently, while sitting with a friend in Cologne for a beer, we unintentionally encountered a bachelorette party, let’s just call them Sandy, Mandy, Candy, and Wendy - all in tight, black-and-yellow striped tops with little bee wings on their backs.

Yes, yes, yes; everything has already been said below, but: Eau Lente is by far the best cinnamon scent I have ever had in my fine pastry nose. And I have tried them all. Not the pastry chefs, the fragrances. Bond's Chinatown, Diesel's Zero Plus Masculine, Aramis's Devin, Calvin's Obsession (Why are THOSE not in the user-friendly fragrance favorites sidebar?
Unlike Bronze by Nanadebary, it starts with cinnamon, but not just that.

This scent is CINNAMON CINNAMON CINNAMON!!! It starts with cinnamon, then transitions to cinnamon, unfolds very cinnamon-like, and completely blossoms into cinnamon. The cinnamon base is full of cinnamon, and after a few hours, cinnamon remains.

This was yet another spice oriental that really tempted me. Cinnamon and a whole lot of clove. It starts off well. I also like to use cinnamon and clove in the kitchen - alongside really a lot of other spices; my arsenal of spices and blends would surely astonish the average innkeeper. I enjoy Arabic, Indian, Chinese, South African, Indonesian, Persian cuisine.

There is something about this scent that I really don’t like. I think it’s the cooked apple scent in there, it does remind me of by the fireplace by Replica because it has that same smoky caramel quality that I did not enjoy in either. It smells like fall decor, not so much cookies or kisses. I think if you want a more toned down By the Fireplace this would be a good option for you

The name here is misleading - it's not gourmand like a real cookie or apple pie. No apple notes detected, as some claim. Also many compared it to "Replica - By the Fireplace | Maison Margiela" , which isn't close in my mind (that one is so smokey, I couldn't stand it). This is soft vanilla gourmand + ambery-musk + cedar chest + "forest". I saw someone say it was like tossing baked goods into a pile of leaves and that is absolutely spot-on - but they're freshly-fallen autumn leaves that are still wet from a cold rain, and there's a fire inside a cedar cabin nearby that you're about to go enjoy. This definitely is more masculine-leaning, but it's still slightly sweet - like a sexy patchouli bomb, with some spicy warmth. I'm a "gourmand girl" but would 100% wear this on a cold, rainy autumn day with a chunky sweater, or out to a hay maze.

I hate that every leather with any kind of fruity note is compared to Tuscan Leather Eau de Parfum . So many times, like in the case of Eau Rihla, I have entirely ignored a perfume because I look at the reviews and think "oh, this is just this brand's version of Tuscan Leather." Yes, some have obvious similarities like Godolphin or Black Saffron Eau de Parfum but Eau Rihla is very different. It has the same leather-raspberry spine, but that only makes it similar in the vein that Hacivat is "similar" to Aventus since they both have oakmoss and pineapple or Kalan is "similar" to Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum since it has the same ambroxan/ethyl maltol combo. After the first blast of raspberry that settles into the famous sharp leather of the Tom Ford fragrance, they go in wildly different directions. The iris here is almost gourmand. I get a chocolatey vibe that is similar to Bojnokopff . Another user mentioned a "carrot"-y scent which I can also see. It is dark and sweet, but retains the "sharpness" of the leather and fruity components as well, as opposed to something like Ombré Leather Parfum or "Bacio Immortale (Eau de Parfum) | Argos" for example where it gets sort of smoothed out. There is also a certain smokiness that pervades throughout, making the scent even more mysterious. It stands out in Diptyque's collection not just because of the beautiful gold bottle, but because of its darkness and intensity which is missing from a lot of their line. Even the woody masculine leaning scents are light and playful like Tam Dao Eau de Toilette . Ultimately, this is an amazing fragrance, and I'm annoyed that I missed out for so long on trying it because it's "just another Tuscan Leather." If you like leather, and combining it with dark, almost smoky, gourmand components sounds appealing, definitely give Eau Rihla a sniff.

What It Is: Daddy's Bentley after his mistress drove it home from the bank. Posh leather seats, fruity perfume, and fresh crisp beautiful paper money. The raspberry note is pronounced and for the first 20-30min, you'll think "oh this is nice" and then the sharp saffron & leather kick in and don't let up for the next 8+ hours. An absolute powerhouse from Fabrice Pellegrin and a stunning departure for Diptyque's usual Parisian restraint. Who It's For: You wanted a leather fragrance, right? Right??!! You're 30+, confident, chic, and not afraid to "go there" when it comes to taking fragrance risks. Your nose is made of steel. ProTip: spray once and walk through it or, better yet, buy the hair mist for 1/4 the cost... the water-based formula is lighter, brighter, and mercifully wears off in 2-3hrs. Alternatives: TF Tuscan Leather, though it gets a bit tannery-like, and TF Ombre Leather which captures the new car smell sans the fruit. Even if it's too strong, I find Eau Rihla more pleasing than both. For me, I *adored* this fragrance at first sniff and couldn't get it out of my head for weeks after testing it. But the full EDP was too strong, especially for an office environment, so I gave it away.

This isn't a 10 but a 15. As a leather lover, I’ve found the ultimate weapon. Sure, people say it’s reminiscent of Tuscan Leather or Ombre Leather… and they’re not wrong. But while Tom Ford may have pioneered the modern leather genre, Diptyque came in and perfected it. This version is more refined, deeper, and adapts to its surroundings. Where Tuscan/Ombre Leather can feel heavy or overwhelming, this one keeps the same sensuality, eroticism and elegance, but adds an unexpected freshness. Something I never thought a leather scent could pull off. Wearing it brings back memories of a fancy shoe store I used to visit in Barcelona. That blend of clean wood, high-end leather, and flowers. Though it leans fall-winter, it's surprisingly versatile. On warm nights, it smells like opening a leather shoebox in a Mediterranean garden near the sea. On colder evenings, it becomes smoky, mysterious, like sitting on a leather couch in a chic lounge or talking to strangers in a smoky Berlin club. I'm completely in love with this scent, my number one in the collection. And honestly, I hope it stays underrated. It only adds to its charm.

I picked this up when i was in london at Liberty and i must say that this is the most interesting fragrance ever. I loved it immediately. Theres something about the raspeberry leather combo that makes it so unique. However this is not mass appealing and its definetely and acquired taste, ive had people say its very heavy and suffocating so only do one spray as its one the strongest perfumes i have ever owned. Its quite hard to wear but when the weather is cold i reach out for this warm scent. My friend and my barber both thought i had bought tom ford ombre leather which i have never tried in my life but im taking there word for it. This is definetly a gatekeep fragrance that i hope doesnt go mainstream and you will definitely be remembered by this scent as its atomic and fills up a room.

I was so looking forward to this as I had heard it was a very realistic leather scent and it is, just not the leather I was thinking of! I'm old enough that growing up I'd ride around in vintage or oldtimer cars that people still used as their everyday car. There's a particular leather scent of old car that's been sitting in the sun for 30+ years, a sharpness to it and that's what this scent smells like on my skin. Not the luxurious experience I was hoping for! It does have strong longevity as I could not scrub it off my skin and it lasted for a good 6+ hours.

When one goes on a journey, they have much to tell.... Rihla - Arabic for journey, gently takes us on a trip through the Orient. Until now, I was unfamiliar with Diptyque, and so I made my way to a branch in Berlin. To my surprise, we were guided through the collection by a French woman who entertained us with many anecdotes about the house and the fragrances.

For me, Eau Rihla was a lucky find. I was testing my way through the Diptyque range and then saw this beautiful bottle. I had to realize that this scent doesn’t smell like the other Diptyques at all, but is much heavier and leatherier. It immediately reminded me of Ombre Leather and Widian. I got a tester and fell in love with this scent.

Eau Rihla is not just a composition - it is a whisper from another time. The fragrance envelops the skin like warm desert sand, interwoven with rough leather, secret spices, and a hint of foreign nights. It speaks of hidden paths, of longing and silence. I do not wear it - it carries me away.

Eau Rihla stands out to me distinctly from all other leather fragrances I have smelled, as I perceive the scent to be fresher and more transparent than most leather scents. Not as sweet as Ombre Leather or Widian London and not as dry as Tuscan Leather. Although the raspberry is noticeable, it does not come across as a raspberry syrup, like in Widian London.

So it does start out a bit synthetic - but I'm not sure why this gets so much hate, because to me it's a lovely beachy, coconutty, yellow-flower blend. You MUST love coconut to like this, yes. But the frangipani is there, and so is the creamy lily. It feels like your favorite sunscreen, with a hint of hairspray (the lily). This is a 100% beachy, poolside fragrance. Safe choice for summer.

This is not very citrusy, despite the notes listed. It's mostly lily - a "softened white" hairspray fragrance. Fairly inoffensive, but the way it was done in Baby Bouquet specifically reminded me of being at funerals and the floral arrangements that are usually there. So as far as floral fragrances go, this is one I'd definitely test first instead of blind-buy.

This is a greener and more grown-up version of Cucumber Melon Eau de Toilette : - Melon-forward - Distinct notes of violet leaf and orris root (feels more grounded and earthy, because of these notes) Has the potential to feel refreshing, especially for summer. Not a melon fan, so this wasn't for me.

Well, I used to enjoy drinking Martini a lot some time ago, but this scent only vaguely reminds me of that. Rather, I was surprised that the perfume is generally veeeery appealing. Little sweetness and great vermouth notes create a wonderful effect with the gin. If only the longevity were better :/

...or: the elusive hare Let me calculate according to hare type: Grapefruit + Lavender = White Pepper! And hares are caught by sprinkling pepper on their little tails, at least according to fable. But first, you have to have the hare! ;) In any case, Lucky Charms starts with a fresh grapefruit that squints into the daylight so sourly for a few seconds that lavender quickly comes to soothe and caress it. They then retreat under a blanket of White Pepper and have not been seen since! In fact, this White Pepper note is so strong that I had to sneeze quite loudly! And then nothing else happens. At least not for me. I have experienced this quite often, that with perfumes containing pepper in the fragrance pyramid, only and very strongly the pepper shows itself - Lily & Spice by Penhaligon's comes to mind, as does Etra by Etro. There, too, only White Pepper revealed itself to me - Black Pepper I perceive as somewhat sharper and more aggressive in scent, while White Pepper is finer, brighter, "nicer" - covering everything else. I can discern nothing else here but pepper, underlaid after some time by a mild sweetness that I would attribute to vanilla. Whether the White Pepper is hidden in the "spicy notes" mentioned here, or if sneezewort has been smuggled among the flowers, I cannot say; in any case, the ground powder of the underground plant parts of sneezewort - also known as Christ- or snow rose - triggers a sneezing sensation. It worked for me, but with this pepper, you won't catch me; you can spray or sprinkle as much as you want! http://tinyurl.com/ompv2mq

Having commented on some really good scents from "The Library of Fragrance/Demeter," I must mention upfront that this is my first not-so-great EdC from a manufacturer known for such crazy fragrances as pizza, dust, dirt, rain, and the like. This time, I don't want to go into detail about the cookie "Graham Cracker," which is so popular in America. What I unfortunately notice right after applying it is the immediate reminder of the Cinnamon Challenge, which enjoyed great popularity on YouTube and elsewhere some time ago. Why is that? What's wrong with it? Cinnamon is great... some might think. Yes, that's true. I love cinnamon and of course I also own the TLOF scent Cinnamon Bun. Unfortunately, here the cinnamon is so extremely strong after application that it takes your breath away and even triggers a coughing fit. Hence the comparison with the aforementioned challenge. At this point, you actually lose the desire to continue with the rest of the EdC. And that is confirmed for me as well. With the fading cinnamon intensity, I could have made my peace, but what follows is not really refreshing either. Now a bitter-sweet maple syrup scent emerges, which comes off slightly smoky and almost leans towards pipe tobacco. It's just too dry, rough, and ordinary for me. The fact that the longevity is not particularly good can be overlooked given the scent. The sillage is indeed breathtaking at first, in the truest sense of the word. Now, what do I want to complain about a scent of an American cookie that I don't even know? Maybe this scent is incredibly well done, and anyone who knows the Graham Cracker can find a lot to love in it. Unfortunately, I cannot; the opening is simply not pleasant, and the rest doesn't really pamper my little nose with its quirky sweetness either. Since many Americans can hardly exist without their maple syrup, my German-Italian nose may just not be made for this aroma. Therefore, I try to keep my review fair. Connoisseurs and lovers of the Graham Cracker should definitely give it a try, as should perfume lovers who feel drawn to the described scent composition. Personally, I like it less; the combination is not "My Cup of Tea." But at least... I still have countless other (muuch better) TLOFs that I will comment on here gradually :) That's a warning ;)

This smells just like the blue, semi-opaque Elmer's glue sticks that "dry clear": kind of sweet, kind of aquatic, a little bit... mineral? Plastic? Somehow, Demeter makes it work though - smells like glue, but also smells like an aquatic unisex scent you could actually wear. If you were a kid who ate glue (and even if you didn't), you might find this one kind of quirky and fun.

...to acquire such scents A: to obtain them through over 10 corners B: to own them C: to find them good D: and then to wear them in public ??? First and foremost, it should be mentioned that my collecting frenzy has taken over, especially with Demeter fragrances. No matter how absurd, terrible, or borderline genius the scents may be, I must have them. "Glue" clearly falls into the absurd category. I mean, "Clean Windows" and "Earthworm" are already ridiculous just by the thought of using them as perfume, but maybe that’s precisely the appeal. I am well aware that hardly anyone out there is interested in these scents. Especially not here in Germany. This is not only due to the very limited availability but also because you can hardly test them in advance. I am sure that some people would be interested in trying one or another Demeter scent.
