Well, let’s focus on the scent of good old glue. What can I say? First off, longevity and sillage are really not great. After less than 60 minutes, the big magic is already over. But what exactly happens in those 60 minutes when it makes its presence known? Even though it’s hard to imagine, this thing really smells like glue, however...before anyone wrinkles their nose, it actually smells REALLY good. This is mainly due to the almost gum-like apple note. Phew, it’s incredibly hard to describe that "Glue" still smells like what it says on the label despite the notes mentioned above, but it does. A slightly solvent-like and nail polish-like scent can be detected, and the association with glue is 100% there. I read in a previous comment, "Who would want to wear something like this?"...and here I (unfortunately) come into play. I actually find this stuff very wearable. Especially now in summer, this apple glue note (oh God, did I really say that?) is really fun. It smells fresh and fruity, a bit sharp at the start, and you definitely haven’t smelled a similar perfume anywhere else. "Glue" doesn’t go through a development; only the solvent note fades quickly, leaving behind a fruity fresh, clear summer scent that doesn’t hurt anyone. It’s probably silly to say that "Glue" bears a certain resemblance to "Clean Windows," as hardly anyone knows that scent either ;) However, I actually find Glue to be somewhat more balanced and even less chemical. If it made sense, I would say: Go out and test the scent, you will be surprised. But since this is hardly possible, it remains just a recommendation to a tiny target group. Have a lovely day :)

Smells somewhat like the solvent in nail polish or like nail polish remover. There are also some types of glue that remind me of this scent. The execution is very successful by Demeter .. but who wants to wear something like this?

Champagne Brut doesn't quite hit the mark, only grape comes through with a slightly sparkling note as if you were smelling a carbonated drink. And that's damn cool. Grape soda perfume, what more could you want? As a top note, a strong alcohol scent appears in the first few minutes, but this fades quite quickly and the aforementioned sparkle in the nose sets in along with a strong fruity Muscat bleu aroma.

A hint of champagne is present.... But it's so transparent at the forefront.. My skin reacts very poorly to Demeter perfumes. People, sorry for such comments, but I have to write this... It smells like a horse......... I've never smelled anything so animalistic...... Horse... pure!
Well, it can't be a good champagne. The scent is way too floral-fruity for me. The alcoholic note fades very quickly, leaving something that (at least for me) doesn't really remind me of champagne.

For the first time, Clinique has labeled some of their Clinique "summer" flankers as unisex. This is the one that I fell in love with. The prices aren't great when you look at it from a $/mL standpoint, but the size makes it a great price for a fragrance that is all but guaranteed to lift your spirits! See my full thoughts in the video review.

So far, I have found all Demeter fragrances extremely fitting to their names. This one is supposedly supposed to smell like salad. The good question is, what does salad even smell like? You can detect a typical plant juice note, which could lean towards salad. But somehow I also catch a perfumey base note here that doesn’t fit with the salad. I wouldn't wear this scent. ;)

Play by Givenchy was citrusy and sharp, perfect for Spring and Summer. Play Intense on the otherhand was dark and woodsy, preferable for Winter and Fall. This fragrance, Play Summer Vibrations while refreshing, does tend to dry down to something quite woodsy and aromatic, so I'm tempted to say that this new flanker is a combination of the two previously mentioned fragrances. Play Summer Vibrations is all about the watery citrus and pepper at first. It was energetic, lively and sporty to boot. There was a hint of it becoming quite aquatic towards the heart, however the coriander and pepper notes prevented it from doing so. The drydown was the most interesting aspect, with a delicate woodsiness, a touch of creamy sweetness and a dash of herbs. It took on an almost clean approach, less zesty and fruity than the opening. The clean, soapy and soft drydown is what brings me to suggest this fragrance for the colder seasons and not just Summer. Another thing, Play Summer Vibrations is versatile enough to be worn by women too. I certainly believe I could get away with wearing it, and I'm very feminine in how I dress and act. Play Summer Vibrations is certainly not linear, but I can understand those who find it a little boring and mediocre. Personally I quite like it, but like Vertigo on Fragrantica, I think it's a little overpriced for what you get. The lasting power is average.

Ange Ou Demon Jasmin Sambac 2008, has little variation to the original Ange Ou Demon, but I can assure you that they are different. I perhaps prefer this fragrance in many ways. Ange Ou Demon Jasmin Sambac 2008 opens a little less dark and presents more jasmine and lily notes. The overall blend is quite lush and vanillary. At times I can detect a vanilla ice-cream accord, which is in one word, delicious. The powderiness tends to be absent, and is replaced by an interesting and rich creaminess. It is perhaps more angellic than the original, however it has lost a lot of that gothic aura which made the original so enticing. Ange Ou Demon Jasmin Sambac 2008 feels a little gourmand at times, particularly when the tonka bean creates a nutty texture in the heart and base. I guess I find this fragrance a touch more feminine and sweet, hence the reason why I'm more inclined to wear this version of Ange Ou Demon. The sillage is pleasantly soft and intimate, it gives me the sense of floating on top of the clouds. The longevity is good, but in all honesty it could be better. I'm actually intrigued to see whether the 2010 Harvest version varies all that much. From what I've heard it's a fruitier take.

Like the previous reviewers on other sites have stated, this isn't terribly impressive, however it is pleasant nonetheless. Opening with a sparkling cranberry note, there are similarities to the original Very Irresistible. It is a very Summery version of a fruity-rose scent. The sorbet idea hasn't been conveyed well in my opinion. I can't find anything smooth or cold about it. A typical fruity floral really. Nothing vastly different from anything else on the market these days.

And whether! All four: The EdP 1957 - discussed here - the EdT 1957, the Extrait de Parfum 1957 and the EdT 2002. What's that supposed to mean? One scent is enough! No, my dear fragrance friends, one of these four is simply not enough, because the differences between these four fragrance variants are extremely clear, sometimes even serious. So now to the Eau de Parfum from 1957. At that time, the ozone layer or the CFCs that destroy this layer were not yet an issue. And so this bottle is the only one under pressure, so to speak. Luckily this doesn't affect the scent. The gold-colored cap matches the gold-colored label of the EdP, but sits very loosely on the bottle. Like most bottles of the time, this is not refillable; the cap is pressed on by machine. The advantage of this method, however, is that it largely avoids counterfeiting of the content. The EdP 1957 has a very, very green start, dominated by aldehydes and it takes quite a while for the L'Interdit to emerge. But even then it is still quite different from the EdT and Extrait de Parfum of the same year. In contrast to these two, the EdP remains green, with clear features of a classic chypre. I can't perceive anything fruity, but that doesn't mean it isn't there. After this bitter-green start and a little patience, a beautiful, softer but green heart emerges. Like the freshly sprouting nature in late spring, before the flowers can take over. Green and smooth, fine with a soft woody background and a very slight animalic note that I would attribute to musk. The similarity of the three scent variants is most clear in the base. Here it is soft, smells a bit vanilla - which is probably what the tonka does in combination with amber. The EdP is a chypre and, for my taste, the only scent of the three that I would also use for sports. This is also supported by the lowest durability of the 1957 variants. It's a really nice scent, but I have to admit that if I had bought the EdP first, the other variants would probably never have been available to me. Chypre was never my first choice. As it is, the EdP can complement my group of four with its beautiful “greenness”.

From a first sniff, this is a smooth, warm, citrusy fragrance. This is what a worn in, sweaty, orange head scarf would smell like if worn by a classy Babushka. It hits like a lot of medicinal fragrances do, right at the top of the throat. It’s that same runny and prickly feeling you get when drinking cough medicine, just dried down with orange notes. The orange notes themselves are very dry, it reminds me more of orange peel than, say, orange marmalade. It doesn’t have that sticky, syrupy quality to it. Primarily formulated for the cold winters, this scent warms you from the inside the way a shot of vodka or cough medicine would. The longevity was greatly disappointing. Such an in-your-face fragrance should at least be able to stick. Furry and prickly, Elvira’s Sexy Witch is indeed a fragrance for a sexy witch! Cuddly and intimate, with the right stir of spice. As most Demeter fragrances, although it is a great scent and sits amazing on the skin, the longevity is what kills this for me. And as most Demeter fragrances, it’s another small, fun concept worth your money. Such a nostalgic fragrance for me. I used to wear this for my utterly miserable night class I had last Autumn, and this smell goes hand in hand with an itchy orange sweater and Here’s Where The Story Ends by The Sundays through a pair of half broken earbuds.

Mild, non-offensive, light, refined and gentle, yet masculine. A real summer gentleman. It seems that the creators deliberately made it so that it does not give off too much of an aura around it. It simply stays close to the body and does not scream to announce its presence and draw attention. Its drawback is its low durability. It happens that after half an hour after applying it I don't feel it on me at all.

Somewhere between Petit Matin and "Orange Blossom | The 7 Virtues" lies this one. It's a pretty straightforward, linear, simple, yet lovely scent. I'm still debating whether I'd want this scent on my skin or as a room fragrance / candle. There's absolutely nothing wrong with it, but it misses that sparkle, that something that makes it a skin fragrance. You've got bright, fresh bergamot with soft spoken, light and pure white florals. Beeswax offers a lovely warmth and an undertone of resinous wax (which might be the reason why I'm contemplating it as a candle). It's refreshing, easily oversprayable without much consequences, but has abyssmal performance. It becomes a skin scent not long after having first sprayed it (about an hour). I'm not sure I'm willing to pay such a price for something that is so subtle. What I did enjoy about this fragrance is that it stays on the floral, fresh side of things, never going soapy or powdery which is different from other neroli / orange flower fragrances I've smelled up until now. If you're looking for a subtle, clean fragrance that doesn't last too long, this might be it, but for me, I think I'll be passing on it.

L'Eau de Neroli by Diptyque is a fairly simplistic fragrance, both citrusy and sweet when applied to the skin. It's the kind of fragrance that I would reach for on those really hot, almost unbearable Summer days. I adore the smell of neroli and orange blossoms during Summer, so it makes perfect sense that this fragrance should appeal to me. L'eau de Neroli is light, zesty and fresh. Really lovely when used to lighten your mood or to refresh yourself after a long, tiresome day. I had some initial fears, particularly in regards to the opening, that the citruses would overwhelm me with their presence, but fortunately they do not. This fragrance is the perfect blend of citrus and florals. It's also a fantastic unisex fragrance, a great balance of masculine and feminine accords. It is important to note that L'eau de Neroli only comes in the cologne concentration, meaning that it will be neither too strong nor too lasting. I'm not going to lie, this fragrance is fleeting on the skin, so it's up to the individual to decide whether or not this niche fragrance is worth the high price tag. I doubt that I would ever buy a full bottle of L'eau de Neroli, but I would definitely consider buying the 20ml rollerball. It's easy to carry on the go, and to re-apply throughout the day. They are also the cheaper option. Original review written: September 2012.

Smooth, effervescent and classy neroli fragrance, which is definitely worth the more than average price point. Unlike many other colognes centered around neroli this never enters astringent territory and I get insane longevity on my skin (over 6 hours). I also adore the artwork: this makes me want to lie naked in a hammock under a canopy of orange trees in blossom, all the while pensively peering at a romantic ruin in the distance, too!

I love it. Especially in summer. For neroli lovers, it's unnecessary to feel anything other than neroli. If Guerlain's Nerolia Vetiver is the neroli that French aristocrats had their court painters paint, this is a realistic depiction of neroli that an unknown town artist painstakingly painted. It is the result of staring intently at neroli and trying to faithfully reproduce it, and does not focus on anything else. As a result, it may be said to have a common scent, but it is not. It has a very high level of precision. It is almost a single note, so it is fine for people who tend to get headaches from perfume. The musk and honey are merely "elements that supplement the floral scent," and what I wanted to express is the scent of neroli flowers and the refreshing scent of orange peel. It feels like an elaborate sketch of a neroli flower has been turned into liquid. I think it is a wonderful work of art. I can feel the intention of "I want to create this kind of scent" in each stroke. It is a scent that goes beyond essential oils. However, there is one drawback... it has a really short lifespan. It is good if it lasts for 2 hours, but in summer it may last about an hour and a half. I think I'll hold off on buying a full bottle as long as I still feel it's too expensive. (Prices aren't going to stop going up But I really want it. I'll probably finish it in a year.

A bit of 4711 is swinging in, well, that might have been expected, but Diptyque quickly takes a turn towards the generally orangey. Verbena can be detected, not biting, but cool-fresh. Very nice! A wonderfully fresh start that can hold its own against the best in its class. Within minutes, a hint of that soda powder note appears, which is one of several ways to extend freshness in citrus fragrances. I have finally gotten to the bottom of this note. My thanks go to Centifolia, and I quote from their response to my comment on ‘Ray of Light’: “...for example, you can achieve an extremely long-lasting citrus note with lemongrass oil, Litsea Cubeba, or verbena (or any oils that predominantly consist of citral). Some (bitter) orange oils or bergamot are also quite durable, it depends on the variety.” This fits perfectly with the information here. Diptyque, of course, does not rely solely on citrus, even if it is camouflage. The verbena is allowed to play its own role, and tarragon is also plausible; at least something from the kitchen spice corner is faintly floating in. The first test of endurance announces itself after just five minutes. L'Eau de Neroli approaches the cleaning product-like. Oh dear. But it holds up bravely, only letting through a clean impression and otherwise remaining citrusy, just no longer as expansive as at the beginning. A proximity to 4711 cannot be denied as it progresses, but Diptyque is airier. Nevertheless, as the freshness recedes throughout the morning, it turns a bit too much towards white floral. The cedarwood is already present, but it cannot “dismiss” my slightly plush associations. In my mind's eye, I see the 4711 jug in my late grandmother's bathroom, honorably draped on a small, brocade-look doily. L'Eau de Neroli can’t be blamed for this image, but it doesn’t help me any further. Unfortunately, not much happens in the afternoon. The scent character remains fundamentally preserved, while it gradually shifts in appearance from “perfume” towards “body cream, latently soapy” - a contribution from the white musk. I notice nothing of wax, however. In the eighth or ninth hour, it’s over - that’s decent, especially since remnants last into the evening. Conclusion: For me, it’s one from the long line of half-hour deliciously fresh bombs. After that, I like it less and less. I recommend it to friends (and friends) of orangey-floral-creamy scents. I thank Yatagan for the sample.

My first Diptyque. The very first whiff reminds me of the good old Echt Kölnisch Wasser Eau de Cologne . Probably (?) due to the neroli. Then follows a lovely, refreshing scent. Citrusy-fresh, the Cologne vibes (again, it's the first time I'm using the word "vibes") fade away. Unfortunately, I can hardly detect the beeswax, it's only very subtly present.

I didn't know what to expect after reading the note pyramid, because it reads as definitely unique, so I purchased a sample and well, all I can smell is a mix of fennel and sesame, I don't detect any other notes, not the marine ones or the coffee. And I don't wanna smell like fennel sesame salad. I tried spraying on clothes too, but it's pretty consistent, or maybe this is all my nose can detect. Not blind buy purchas imo.

'...I will fade away, disperse - ah, everything happens only once, but once everything must happen...' Thus bids farewell the bodiless Uyulála, who consists of nothing but her voice, in the Southern Oracle of Atréju - not without first revealing to him the secret of how the Childlike Empress - and with her the entire realm of Fantastica - can be saved. Two generations of children (and adults) have been immersed in Michael Ende's legendary The Neverending Story since 1979 and have lost themselves within it - following the journey of Bastian Balthasar Bux from the attic of a schoolhouse to the waters of life. 'Over mountains and valleys, over fields and meadows' also guides us with Florabellio, Diptyque's latest fragrance. Sea spray and sea fennel - a succulent umbellifer that sailors have long used against scurvy due to its high vitamin C content - are mentioned as characteristics of its top note - and few things make me more suspicious than aquatic top notes - especially when an abstract scent accord like 'sea spray' is invoked. However, it succeeds wonderfully here: it begins with a sharply salty freshness, only subtly hinted at - like stones in the upper part of the surf, hastily drying in the midday sun before the next long wave wets them again. Following the initial freshness is a delicate, almost dainty floral sweetness - apple blossom and osmanthus are noted - which overlays the saltiness just as quickly dissipates or is driven away. One almost believes they can see dandelion seeds drifting away, tumbling over green hills in the summer wind, and then quickly disappearing from our view. There is something playful, something cheerful in Florabellio, which slowly sinks in its base to something warm, bright, like the sun-drenched ground of a heath - with lemon butterflies dancing in the breeze over dry, creeping underbrush. One almost wants to sit down and watch their play and courtship - for an hour or two, while Florabellio slowly disperses in the wind. Conclusion: it is not infinite like Michael Ende's story, but rather of a more fleeting pleasure, which does not detract from its beauty. A scent like warm summer wind in hair crowned with daisies - gentle and friendly and full of cheerfulness and character.

With Florabellio, I am testing a Diptyque fragrance again after a long time. This brand holds a special status for me because they released Philosykos, which I believe is one of the best or most beautiful fig scents. I am therefore always curious about fragrances from this brand that I do not know yet. The description of this scent intrigued me because it reminded me of a summery sea/vacation fragrance. And even though the scent does indeed evoke the sea, it somehow becomes too much of a good thing, as the very high "salt content" almost gives the feeling of drowning in the sea... The scent: So, the scent begins... well, I have no idea, slightly peculiar. After an initial and very brief freshness, I catch a whiff of fennel (which I do not particularly like), before the fragrance almost overwhelms me with a load of sea salt. The salt is so strong that I can almost taste it in my mouth, and it feels as if I were swimming in the sea. But not in a pleasant way; rather, it is associated with the negative experiences of getting larger amounts of seawater in your mouth and even swallowing some, which leaves your throat burning from the salt (not to mention the slight nausea). The fruitiness of the scent seems very minimal to me, as the salt covers everything, even the apple blossoms are hardly discernible and disappear very quickly (or they get drowned in the salt). Only after more than an hour does the salt become somewhat milder, but that does not mean it is no longer present. It remains the main actor, but it does not overwhelm me as much anymore. I could not perceive any coffee at all. Longevity and sillage: The longevity is very good; the scent lasts more than 10 hours on me. The sillage is above average, and the fragrance can be perceived by someone nearby. Since the salt comes across very strong to me, I think the scent will also leave a small fragrance cloud in places where the wearer appears. The bottle: The bottle is, like most of Diptyque's, round-oval and closes with a large, black, cylindrical cap. The label of this brand always features a beautiful black-and-white illustration. Here, you can see a person standing in front of a sea, and there is also an apple tree visible. Actually, salty scents can be quite nice when they are done subtly. Because then such fragrances really represent beautiful vacation scents. An example would be Seathalasso by Douglas (which I discovered through my dearest friend), which is also salty but comes across much better and does not overwhelm you right away or provoke that unpleasant tickling in the throat that you get when you swallow too much seawater, as mentioned at the beginning. Uuuhhh... The scent fits well with the warm season, but since the salty notes are too intense for too long, I do not really like the fragrance. For those who do like it, I would recommend using it on vacation or as an alternative by the lake, but as I said, there are some salty fragrances that are significantly better. Therefore, I do not really recommend testing it and definitely not a blind purchase, even though tastes are known to vary. If the scent still seems very interesting to you, then it is better to test it first.

At first, one can perceive a strong sweetish, very subtly spicy note that I couldn't identify at all, and I would never have guessed it was sea fennel. At the same time, this note is enveloped by an aquatic, intensely salty note, where I would have rather guessed at seawater instead of spray. One could imagine that the sea fennel is planted on a cliff with gray stones and is occasionally washed over by the salty sea wave - "that's roughly how I would describe the top note." A little later, a fine, very very subtle floral note of apple blossom joins these two notes, which carries a delicate hint of green apple in my nose, and I don't find it appealing at all. "I hate apples, even as a child I successfully resisted having to eat those things - But you can't do anything about that!" :-) Why do I hate apples, you ask? - I always had the same result, namely bleeding gums, and who wants that, please?!" :-) The apple blossom is underscored by a rather curious scent note for me. In the sillage, it smells slightly floral and subtly woody, where I also guessed lotus, but the closer I get with my nose to the pulse, it becomes slightly spicier, almost a bit animalistic one might say, which isn't quite right; rather, I feel that this note highlights and emphasizes the skin's own texture and should smell somewhat different on each wearer - Here too, I didn't come up with osmanthus. In the last 3 hours, unfortunately, I don't perceive any roasted coffee or roasted sesame, but only Iso - E Super in its pure form, and Florabellio fades away pleasantly transparent and softly woody. Overall, the scent lasts 7 hours on my skin. The sillage is designed from the beginning to be perceived well at half an arm's length, and this is maintained for 3 hours before it gradually reduces until the scent fades away. I would like to express my sincere thanks to our Parfumo "Honk1510" for the sample.

Immediately, a feeling of the sea arises, accompanied by what seems to be sweet wood (fennel). Moments later, the coffee from the base comes through, and it becomes sweet as well. Both soon disappear again, leaving the sensation of the sea. Aquatic is probably the right term. This is well supported by the apple blossom, as it also carries this synthetic-aquatic quality. Whether the slight sweetness that I can still detect on my wrist comes from the osmanthus or from the roasted sesame... I cannot judge. On the second test day, I even detected the coffee first in my nose, and I believe I can also recognize sesame. Only behind that can I then "see" the sea. As the scent develops, the top notes dominate; apple blossom and osmanthus remain rather supportive and are only sniffed directly at my wrist. In the sillage, there is a light, aquatic-synthetic, and slightly salty note that is clearly intended for a hot summer day to simulate freshness. The base of roasted coffee and roasted sesame makes its appearance for me within the first few minutes and then does not return. I find the coffee somewhat bothersome at the beginning; I am not quite sure what it is doing in this composition. So, I am not convinced by "Florabellio," but it is not really bad either. Perhaps it should be fairly tried again in the summer.

I wanted a new perfume - it had to be from Diptyque, as I already love their candles so much. The saleswoman sprayed one after another on test strips - until she reached Florabellio. At first, I was totally thrilled, I smelled the apple component, in the dry down the coffee, and I could see the apple trees in front of me. I had never smelled anything so special!

I recently bought Florabellio online, blind and used, and I really have to say that I expected something different. The combination of apple and the marine notes smells slightly like garlic on my skin. Of course, it could also be due to my skin, but no other fragrance has developed this way on me so far.

A deciduous forest, where the cedars ooze vanilla bourbon and tempered chocolate leaves alight upon coffee ground soil. It’s an artful dessert. Like something enjoyed over fika or featured in a Le Creuset advertisement. Not a nuclear Starbucks meltdown (a la Kerosene’s Followed) or a craft-store candle. I’m obsessed with these rare “bittersweet” gourmands. It’s Soie Malaquais, but subtract the rose and add malty tonka. If I didn’t already own (and spend a similar fortune on) Soie, Bois would be an auto-buy. Head-to-head, I found Soie had greater endurance and intensity than Bois, however Bois dried into the most alluring cocoa powder-y scent for its final hours. I guess you could say I’m a soie-boi. Mental Snapshot: The perfect afternoon in your hygge hideaway, tucked snug in a childhood treehouse. You nurse a ramekin of homemade sticky toffee pudding whilst rereading Redwall. Or some Robert Frost. You are most definitely wearing something cable-knit. And something corduroy. tl;dr: tiramisu yule log

This one's grown on me. Bois Corse seems to be the darling fan-fave of the five Essences. People have such an appetite for gourmands these days, and with Diptyque carrying none at all, I think this really scratched that itch. Touted as coffee-centric, I mainly get this chocolate candy-ish, Tootsie Roll-like accord which I suppose is the tonka. In theory, I love tonka. it sounds so cozy and vanilla-adjacent. But in practice, I always get this plasticky, rubber-like smell which I'm told is coumarin. (Apparently coumarin is also used in industrial manufacture of plastics and paints to neutralize unpleasant odors. I wonder if this is why I have that mental connection.) With that said, I find Bois Corse much more appealing than other tonka’s on the market since it doesn’t have that plasticky quality. It’s not my favorite note, but I’ve come to appreciate it more than I used to, especially on chillier days with overcast weather.

I’m still a bit confused on Diptyque’s Les Essences de Diptyques line. For a brand that has decent prestige, and is know for having some quite stellar creations, their ‘exclusive’ fragrance line is not feeling very exclusive, but rather a bit bland. Bois Corsé is not an exception to this, and I still found it an odd, and not entirely pleasant fragrance. The opening is very astringent, with a dry and powdery side as well. There is a very prominent woody note with a turpentine feel to it that seems to dominate the opening. To add, there’s also an underlying sweetness from the tonka , which is making the entire thing clash. This opening actually lasts for a fair amount of time, but the dry down is a somewhat better experience. The dry down consists mainly of powdery tonka, and the same woods from the opening, but they’re now toned down and easier on the nose. Despite it being more enjoyable I still found it to be awfully bland. It never really goes anywhere deeper than just vague sweetness, which is disappointing. I am truly having a hard time imagining this fragrance being the ‘essence’ of anything other than perhaps a furniture polish of sorts, or maybe some kind of unpleasant cocktail with lots of bitters? I can’t fault Diptyque for much here though. From what I’m gathering this line as a whole seems to be aimed more at an abstract concept where they are attempting to capture the scents of things that don’t really have a scent. This is especially the case with Corail Oscuro, and the newly released Lauzulio, both of which seem like they wouldn’t strike as much of a nerve. Looking at it from a more artistic point of view, I can definitely appreciate the work, but at this price point I can think of better options that are more enjoyable and exciting to wear.

Generally a good scent with sweet woodsy overtones with a bit of an overly sweetened coffee (think of Starbucks macchiato that has so much other stuff in it for those who don't like the taste of coffee) I used up the whole tester since it is a nice manly leaning Gourmonty wood scent but what makes it one I will never buy is the combination of the non-existing longevity (after 1-2 hours skin only and after 4 undetectable) in combination with the exorbitant price not worth it there are so much better and cheaper scents out there. Good, but expected more from Diptique, especially because the price is higher than their usual Perfumes and is not as unique as most of their other scents.

Smells like something Imaginary Authors or Rania J would make, and I mean that in a positive way. The opening can be challenging due to an unapologetic combination of "wet" tree bark and sweet coffee. Very earthy, woody, slightly chocolaty yet dry. Almost inspiring and therapeutic in some way due to the woody earthiness from the tree bark accord. But it's the drydown that is worth waiting for: Some of the milkiest most delicious sandalwood accords I have smelled. Slightly smoky too. Smells like a sacred ritual. It's so good. If you ever test this, give it at least an hour, because that's when the real magic happens.

Delicious cocoa notes, crackling wood, warm woolen socks, soft indulgence, caramelized coffee, velvety cream liqueur - This perfume smells like a visit to the Christmas market, like a romantic evening for two, like a firm hug from my grandpa at Christmas.

WHAT IT IS Ancient Babylonian shaving oil with a bouquet of fresh immortelle nearby. Eau Nabati opens with some bergamot and herbaceous pettigrain, giving a spicy fougere-like vibe, then settles into a *superb* green, honey-sweet immortelle. The opening and mid last 4+ hours with noticeable sillage, then dry down into a beautiful amber-woody scent which leans slightly vanilla on my skin by the 8-9hr mark. Even without marketing language about desert gardens, the effect is one of mixing typically "green" notes (bergamot, immortelle) and "blue" notes (palm tree, Peru balsam) to create a deep teal composition... refreshing yet rich, not unlike a blooming oasis in hot desert air. WHO IT'S FOR You like Oriental fragrances, but don't want to stray too far into heavy resinous accords or gas the people around you. You want something you can feel good about wearing to work in the morning and still be subtly there at happy hour in the evening. You're likely a guy, but this is absolutely unisex - especially if you love immortelle. ALTERNATIVES Dior Dune captures a similar melange of green notes with vanilla accords, though it's sharper and more synthetic. Eight & Bob's The Original is a creamy green fougere anchored by amber; there's no immortelle, but the overall effect is similar. Pellegrin's own Eau de Minthe is a minty-geranium barbershop fougere, but sits at the opposite end of the spectrum from Nabati... icy, bracing, and short-lived (though beautiful). FINAL THOUGHTS If Eau Rihla's nuclear powered sillage put me off to Diptyque's Middle Eastern fragrances, Nabati brought me back. Some reviews have criticized that Nabati isn't "original enough" for a niche house like Diptyque, but I strongly believe this is one of Pellegrin's most wearable fragrances to date, seamlessly transitioning from day to night, warm to cool, casual to elegant, and striking the right balance of intimate vs loud - I'll take that any day over a piece of art I can't wear!

On a blotter it opens sharp and cool the way it's supposed to be, but on me it's a little weird, like warmed-up lime which isn't very nice. The dry-down is actually really beautiful, though. I smell the bergamot and petitgrain a lot, keeping it fresh, but the Peru balsam note grounds it all and helps the other notes last and shine. While it never turns into a full-on woody scent, it's great because it is deep and almost full-bodied, yet still fresh and bright. And of course, as people often mention online, it smells fancy, expensive, luxurious. And yet it's not your typical rich-person-smell (do I even know what I mean by this? I don't know), it doesn't feel like the perfume is trying to show off its opulence. It has an ancient energy to it, I can almost see Odysseus wearing this in an oil form brought for him to Ithaca. Really beautiful, wearable and long-lasting, and still it makes a statement.

Eau Nabati became my signature fragrance and got me into the world of perfume. I had gotten a sample at Diptyque when purchasing the discovery set and I’m so glad the SA picked it. It’s smokey and mysterious upon application with sharp wood and green notes. It would almost be offensive but the bergamot comes in and smooths it out. It wears more like a traditional designer fragrance than most niche perfumes. The magical thing is, as the day goes on it transforms into a friendly sweet green scent and finally trails off into a warm amber scent by the end of the day. It’s borderline too much for a daily office wear. But if I have morning meetings I love the grown up facade the top notes give. By the end of the day when it’s time to go home and relax I have a comforting sweet sticky amber scent left. It is by far my most complimented perfume but it also has a strong personality that may not be fitting on some. My favorite compliment was from a little kid running by saying “you smell good!” lol. The sweet amber notes also stick! I have shirts that still smell faintly out of the wash, I can get a whiff of it in my car every once in a while. I would definitely sample this first and experience its shifting moods before determining if it’s right for you.

So, so gorgeous. I have always thought Eau Nabati was the best of this three fragrance collection including Eau Rihla Eau de Parfum and Benjoin Bohème . I honestly delayed trying it on myself for YEARS because I found the price unattractive. I had always imagined this as a "winter fragrance" and had categorised it as heavy compared to my other fragrances. I got my bottle in the Summer and I wanted to try it immediately, of course! I had a shower before bed and then slept in it. The next day was a hot day and this fragrance was wafting up from my skin all day long. It was incredible and I was still enjoying it 18 hours later. It's a total summer fragrance! It blossoms in the heat. Who knew? If it had a color, it would be deep orange. The scent reminds me of the desert plants warming and drying out in the sun (immortelle). It's amber-y and golden, smooth and almost sweet, just almost. What is Peru Balsam? Is this the smooth almost sweet note? I have the kind of skin that turns perfume sweet, so this was wonderful for me, like an "almost gourmand" since I can't usually wear gourmands. I did not get as much green in the opening from my bottle as I did with the sample, so perhaps it has matured a bit from the previous owner. The dry down is exactly the same. I hope Diptyque will offer refills on this eventually, but I'm now convinced it is worth the price because it has much better longevity than other Diptyque fragrances. I have to say, I'm a huge fan of Fabrice Pellegrin. He has created another stunner here. *edited for typos

It is a charming affair to wear a fragrance that captures a scene so completely and yet so subtly, as the new Eau Nabati from Diptyque does. Under the skilled hand of renowned perfumer Fabrice Pellegrin, it is a delightful journey through the sensual landscape of olfactory perception towards... the Mediterranean National Park of Samaria Gorge in Crete. Pellegrin, a nose admired for his ability to dare the unexpected and extract the unusual from the ordinary, can be experienced in top form once again with Eau Nabati. In his last success, "L'Eau Papier | Diptyque," he took us into a papyrus landscape that was surprisingly multifaceted in its simplicity. With Eau Nabati, however, Pellegrin steps onto a completely different stage and plays a symphony that feels like a glimpse into a mirror with many facets. With the first spray, I am greeted by an outburst of bergamot and green notes, a saluting welcome that is as unusual as it is refreshing. It feels as if one is on a dusty road and suddenly discovers a vibrant oasis, full of palm trees and juicy citrus fruits. The citrus green of the fragrance makes us believe that we are strolling through the shady parts of the national park in Crete, a region known for its lush lemon groves. The initial sharpness soon dissipates, and we dive into the warm, waxy heart of the fragrance, where the prominence of immortelle becomes noticeable. The whole thing, with woody and balsamic notes, reflects well the wildness of the gorge and the surrounding mountainous landscape. What also makes Eau Nabati so interesting is the dialogue between amber and Peru balsam. This combination creates a resinous bed that is both creamy-soft and subtly warm. Yet, Eau Nabati remains surprisingly uncomplicated and creates a discreet, pleasant atmosphere. As for longevity, Eau Nabati understands itself as a quiet but steadfast companion. It remains present for a few hours before it hugs the skin closely. Some may see this as a disadvantage, but let us champion the principle of modesty. Not all fragrances need to enter a room before we do. Sometimes, it is enough for a fragrance to accompany us quietly and discreetly. Although the price may be set too high, it cannot be denied that the fragrance manages to transport me to a place and time that is both fascinating and nostalgic. A decidedly masculine scent that is, however, unisex enough to be worn by any gender. Unmistakably a Diptyque fragrance, yet it has a distinctiveness that sets it apart from the previous offerings of the house. A quite remarkable achievement.

Who would have thought that this fragrance would be the first one I write about here. Why is that surprising? I usually prefer bold scents, Diptyque is subtle, I’m more of a cowgirl than understated. And yet, this fragrance has taken me away. What I (occasionally) seek is an abandoned desert and the sun on my skin.

Eau Nabati is a very special fragrance that you won't smell on every corner, and it's somehow difficult to describe in just a few words. Yes, it's a bit elusive - but truly beautiful! I would place it on the spectrum from unisex to masculine. Thanks to its freshness, I think it suits the warm months and everyday wear best.

I love this fragrance! I can't believe I got multiple samples of it on my last visit to the Diptyque counter several months ago and have never tried it until today. I was busy trying to convince myself that somewhere within Diptyque's Volutes, L'eau Tarocco and L'eau de Lente, lay my new Summer signature scent. I love the low-moderate sillage as well as the transparent quality of Diptyque creations and I also love the dichotomy of surprisingly good longevity with this line, at least on my skin. L'eau de L'eau starts off very citrusy and fresh on the top notes with a sunny lemon note with a pinch of dry cinnamon powder. I don't really smell any grapefruit or petitgrain, but perhaps I am blocking these out since they are not my favorite notes. For the first five minutes my reaction was "Meh, that is just o.k." and then suddenly it was as if someone wearing a beautiful orange blossom, lavender and geranium scent walked in, lit a clove cigarette and ordered a chilled candied ginger martini with mandarin zest peel curled over the side. Then I realized it was, in fact, L'eau de L'eau. This scent definitely changes and expands over time. The top was fresh, almost professional, brisk and urban. The middle is clove-a-licious, dark and spicy almost Goth and the base is a mello, soft and calming Tonka and Benzoin. I don't detect the patchouli here, but that is a good thing, IMO. It all mélanges together culminating in a Your-skin-but-spicy-scent. This is masterfully blended and would make an ideal signature scent for a man or woman. I would wear this primarily for daytime- it's very close to the skin after the first hour, but seems to be lasting a good 6 hours. I'm almost sorry I got into this sample because now definitely need a full bottle ASAP!

L’Eau de L’Eau… so if I understand correctly, the scent is now water from water or water out of water or something like that? How does one come up with such a name? This could have been thought up directly by Aquaman himself… and I, being a nerd, am already mentioning a comic book character again… oh no, oh dear! … and to top it off, a rather unpopular character (I quote Raj from The Big Bang Theory: “Shitty Aquaman!”). Be that as it may, since Philosykos I have been testing Diptyque fragrances from time to time, but I have hardly found a scent that I liked as much as the mentioned fig scent. I even found some quite dreadful (e.g., Olène), but as they say, one does not give up (unless you don’t want to read any more comments from me, then I’ll quickly and sadly disappear from here *sniffle*). Well then, let’s get to the scent… The scent: At the beginning, you can definitely smell a grapefruit, which also smells nice, but for a scent that one might think is fresh because of the name, it is quite spicy. Because right after application, you can perceive a very intense cinnamon and clove note, with the clove being so strong that it can almost overwhelm you if overapplied. A little later, the scent has a slightly classic touch in the background, which might be due to the notes of lemon and lavender. The cinnamon fades a bit, and the clove also becomes calmer. Along with the roses, slightly floral notes come in, lightening up the scent a little. The fruity notes from the base remind more of oranges and fit well with the other scents. A bit later, you can detect a slightly soapy-synthetic component, which you have to smell for specifically, and the impression is almost lost through the somewhat sharp clove, which is still well detectable in the base, while the slightly sweet cinnamon remains in the background. The sillage and longevity: The projection is strong, the scent will definitely be noticed by others, and that for a somewhat longer period of time. If sprayed on generously, a scent cloud will surely remain! The longevity is quite good at about eight hours! The bottle: The bottle is tall and more rectangular than the somewhat rounder bottles usually known from Diptyque. It is clear and has a transparent label with a frame on the front. Besides the name, there is a drawing of a rocky stream and trees. The cap is black and cylindrical. Everything is nicely done, although it might have looked better if the label had a white background. Okay, I am glad to be able to write here that L’Eau de L’Eau has turned out to be quite a nice scent (and not yet another Diptyque flop for me). The scent gives off a rather autumnal atmosphere for me, as it comes across warm and is not as fresh as the name L’Eau might suggest. As a daytime scent for the somewhat not-so-warm summer days or early autumn as well as in spring, it is quite usable. Additionally, it is more of a daytime or casual scent than one meant for going out. I wonder how Aquaman sprays himself with a scent underwater? No,… I’ll stop with the comics, you probably don’t want to know anything about that anyway (whyyyy...??). Yes, the scent is finally a Diptyque fragrance worth checking out, as long as you don’t have an aversion to a strong clove scent!

This scent is strangely good! You definitely have to like the combination of cinnamon, fruit, and clove. I really enjoy what I'm smelling. My first impression after spraying: mulled wine in a fresh-fruity summer version. Although the cinnamon and clove are noticeable from the very beginning, this fragrance is not heavy at all. Even with the heart note, the scent remains pleasant and does not drift into a wintry territory. The ginger gives the heart a nice light spiciness. It then transitions into the base with a spicy-fresh character. This becomes a bit sweeter, while the cinnamon note fades. Patchouli and tonka bean are well balanced. Despite the oriental note, it lacks the typical heaviness often found in orientals. As a fan of oriental perfumes, I say in this case: thumbs up for L´Eau de L´Eau!

Whoopie! Cinnamon is in charge here. All phobics, hands off, please. What’s amazing is that even in the top note, a strong cinnamon note stands out. It seems to detach itself from the back of the hand and waft around in the air. You can’t ignore it at all. Occasionally, a few fresh, slightly prickly tones peek out cautiously from under the spice cloud, but they don’t really dare to come out. This scent is for spice lovers. After the spectacular cinnamon appearance, the clove slowly joins in, running protectively in front of the ginger. This doesn’t weaken the intense onslaught (somehow the blend reminds me of rice pudding with sugar and cinnamon, warm, cinnamon freshly sprinkled), but it does become calmer now. Where can you wear this scent? Naturally, everywhere. I would be a bit cautious with it in the office.

Yesss, bought at Duty Free before the Corfu vacation, this scent will always be instant vacation for me. That's why it literally screams sunny and herbal at me to have fun. This fragrance is citrusy due to the prominent and lasting lime, herbal because of the honeysuckle, and spicy because of ginger. I don't really get the cherry. It's not a very sweet scent. I could imagine that some might find it a bit medicinal since the honeysuckle is very prominent. This spicy, invigorating sun greeting is unusual and makes me want to pack my bags again. Ah, cypress trees, blue sea, sunburn, and my first and last attempt to look cool on a scooter. - By the way, it didn't work out; those things are incredibly wobbly - and it's raining here. Okay, I'm off.

Most of the older Diptyques smell like ancient medicinal salves made out of crushing various barks, spices, and unguents down into a fiery yellow paste and applied to an open wound (Eau Lente, L’ Eau). L’ Eau Trois flips the trope a little, taking it outside to the sunburnt hillsides of Greece or Southern France where the healer combs up tufts of wild rosemary, pine needles, and mastic from the maquis, and uses his cocaine fingernail to dig out sticky yellow globules of myrrh and pine sap from ancient, shrubby trees bent over with age and wind, before singeing it all over a fire so that greenery takes on a burnt, bitter flavor, and mashing it all down to a paste in a pestle and mortar. Smoky, wild, and herbaceous, L’Eau Trois this is myrrh at its most confrontational. It smells of incense, yes, but also of bitter greenery that will either kill you or cure you if ingested. Less like a perfume than something born of the bowels of the earth.

L'Eau Trois is a typical unisex wood and spice representative. L'Eau Trois (Third Water) was launched in 1975 and is unique to this day - its full face. Personally, I think it's Diptyque's best work. Top notes are rosemary and myrtle; middle notes are spices, myrrh and caraway; base notes are kyara incense (olibanum), pine tree and myrrh. Greenery, conifers, lots of spices and once again green with incense. Very good durability and just in time for forest idols, fairies and lost in forest, smoky spacetime. I recommend

Three images: The first is a peaceful hammam or steam bath, where a camphorus oil is mixed with the water vapour, mixing the warm and the fresh in a delicious, calming, yet invigorating sensation. The second is a still, quiet pine forest after the rain. The third is a small empty chapel where myrrh and olibanum have just been burnt without smoke, leaving the visitor with a ghost presence. * On skin and blotter, the opening is very aromatic, herbal and forest-y even, with a hint of pine and a camphorous facet that strongly associates with eucalyptus, and not rosemary (rosemary oil contains high levels of 1-8 cineole, also known as eucalyptol.... so that could explain it). Here we are, where the hammam meets the forest for a grounding effect that makes you want to breathe deeply and stay in the moment. Past the first few minutes, the caraway hits hard on skin. On blotter and fabric, the first notes persist and the caraway just makes a peek that complements the olibanum and the myrrh that then start to come out. The perfume then turns to a skin smell barely an hour after application on any kind of surface, staying close to the wearer, so intimate one could barely smell it on themselves unless they have applied a healthy dose of sprays, or resprayed. Past the first few hours, the camphorous notes are gone, leaving us with a pure, calming, churchy vibe of olibanum and myrrh. This incense finale can linger in for many hours, albeit very discreetly: tried on my pillowcase at night, I could still smell it in the morning. A naturalistic, timeless delight. Smells like the colors: dark green, brown.

As the title says, this is my association for this scent, I never smelled something like this in a perfume. A mix out of resin, pine and incense. As a fan of churchy scents, this is one of my favorites and the most unique so far, but not for anyone and not a blind buy. One or two sprays are enough to fill a room and a spray on your clothes last a wash at least (and it can stain a bit so be carefull with white clothing)

After the cumin high of the second, and the spice potpourri of the first, here comes the shrub, herb, and wood orgy of the third 'Eau'. The small, at that time quite unconventional company Diptyque stirred up the oh-so-distinguished perfume scene of Paris in the early 70s with creations that fell completely outside the norm. But what remains of the departure to new shores, of daring and rebellion? Unfortunately, almost nothing. Today, others are going against the grain (think of Etat Libre d’Orange), and Diptyque has long ceased to take entrepreneurial risks with daring, rather offbeat works - they have become well-behaved, conformist, in a certain way 'grown-up'. Let others struggle in youthful exuberance and try to distinguish themselves - Diptyque has arrived in the niche mainstream (yes, I believe this exists now: almost every company dabbling in the 'niche' has, sooner or later, their amber scent, their gourmand, vetiver, rose, incense, iris scent, etc.). But in order to carry out the image change as thoroughly as possible, Diptyque has not only changed its own direction and strategy but has also distanced itself from its rebellious heritage - 'L’Autre' and 'L’Eau Trois' disappeared, as did the not-so-old but extremely indolent and today’s nose quite offensive 'Virgilio'. Thus, the company's catalog today presents itself in a form cleansed of quirky creations - no potential customer should be excessively frightened here, questioning whether something like this is even wearable (and 'L’Autre' was indeed a challenge - and what a challenge!). Sadly, the great 'L’Eau Trois' has also entered the Hades of perfume history. Will there be an Orpheus who tries to bring it back? We will see. In the meantime, the memory of an extreme scent remains. Herbaceous, smoky, and woody is hardly imaginable. A whole 'bouquet garni' is contained in this fragrance: bay leaf, thyme, rosemary, and oregano, but also a decent quantum of aromatic, fragrant Mediterranean shrubs and woods, such as myrtle and pine, a lot of incense, and above all, a great deal of resins - a lot of labdanum and even more myrrh. It is the myrrh that gives the otherwise extremely herbaceous-aromatic brew a slight balsamic undertone, thus returning a touch of softness and pliability to the otherwise parched aromatics under the summer heat. Ultimately, it is what prevents the scent from being perceived solely as scratchy and woody, yes, bone-dry, because any flowers, sweet fruits, or palate-pleasing spices are sought in vain here. 'L’Eau Trois' is said to be the scent of the rugged, jagged coastline of northern Greece - so, or at least something like that, was the description from Diptyque. I have never been there and cannot judge whether that is true. But I can imagine that it doesn’t smell much different than in the mountains of Corsica or on the hills of Provence. And just as Annick Goutal's scent 'Sables' brings to mind the ubiquitous maquis along the coasts, 'L’Eau Trois' indeed always made me think of the harsh spice and creaky dryness of Mediterranean mountain slopes. 'L’Eau Trois' also reminded me of another scent - Caron’s 'Yatagan'. Here too, many resins from wild, sun-scorched scrub and little that pleases the senses with blooming. But unlike 'Yatagan', 'L’Eau Trois' lacked the animalistic penetration - there is nothing, absolutely nothing of animal origin here. However, this did not make the scent more wearable; quite the opposite. For ultimately, it lacked a bit of sensual strength and erotic radiance (which 'Yatagan' possesses almost in excess). Thus, it always had something stiff and old-fashioned for me: a scent made for a domineering admiral on a large, ancient sailing ship. Strict, aloof, and woody, radiating authority, yet without any emotional movement - such was the scent. Still somehow magnificent. So different!

The names have partly slipped my mind, but there are 2-3 very similarly structured fragrances, including "Sables" by Goutal, to which this surprisingly old Diptyque must have obviously been the forerunner. You find yourself in Southern Europe on a hiking tour, shimmering heat, dry vegetation all around you.

I have asked myself this question very often throughout my perfume addict career. Starting with the purchase of Chanel No. 5 at sweet almost-19, through Lady Million at a time when I regularly used to bathe in patchouli, to hopelessly dusty and dismissed as grandma scents classics, and quite a few strange niche fragrances I found here on Parfumo.

Top: dark green, spicy herbs without a real focus Heart: silvery-gray incense mist Base: modern "the good old days" soap Soapy is really not my thing, but this one came close. A fine, noble scent with a tendency towards minimalism and a lot of clarity. Far removed from the powerhouse sins of the 70s.

I finally got a chance to go into Diptyque today and sniff their new line of fragrances. Of all the ones I smelled, this one happened to be my favorite surprise. Based on the notes, I wasn’t expecting something so soft. From first spray, you get a strong blast of pink pepper, and that remains the prominent note for the first 10-15 minutes. As the scent dries down, the pepper fades to the back and reveals an incense-like scent that’s very resinous but somehow clean? With the combo of labdanum + frankincense, I wasn’t expecting this to give me “your skin but better vibes” when I first checked the notes, but I guess it makes sense cause most molecular type scents are amber-based. It’s linear, but actually very pretty and kind of sensual. It also doesn’t feel as synthetic has other ambroxan/iso E super based fragrances feel. It has a natural vibe. Now as for longevity, they can be hit or miss. But in my experience, even if they aren’t major projectors, they know how to stick around for sometime, especially on your clothes. You can easily get 6-7+ hours with this, with a soft to moderate sillage depending on how much you apply. Pleasantly shocked with this one and may consider getting a full bottle in the future.

A gossamer amber. The amber is dry, smoky, almost mineral. In between the veils of incense smoke there’s flashes of pink pepper. All this would have been dreamy but, as with Lilypheá, she went straight to soap on my skin. And not even a bougie Diptyque soap – I got chalky Dove bar, bitter and fatty. At least this was the most low-volume scent of the Les Essences lot. I feel like Lunamaris is the wallflower of the Les Essences party. If you take the time to chat, do so away from her more gregarious siblings. And definitely test with skin chemistry! The folks that won her favour seem to report that pearly amber I briefly caught on paper. Mental Snapshot: A siren ceremony, hidden amidst the craggy tidepools. Raw ambergris smoulders in abalone shell braziers. When you try to join the revel the creatures startle, hissing into seafoam, its miasma sour against the ocean air. tl;dr: fickle pearl

This perfume strikes me as the kindest, most light and well-behaved incense perfume I've ever smelled. On my skin, it starts off very peppery, and quickly surrounds itself with a cloud of soft and polite labdanum. It stops right there, and doesn't have much evolution from that moment on. You get hints of it as the first one, maybe two hours go by. After that, it kind of mutes itself into an elegant and soft scent that lingers close to the skin. It almost has a molecular, clean & fresh out of the shower feeling to it. I like it on days where I need to feel sterile and concise. A very contemplative fragrance.

I fell in love with this on first spray on paper and that only got firmer after a 2ml tester was tried and loved. It only comes in 100ml and is not cheap, which is the only downside in my view. A month or so with my bottle and here are my thoughts: The first spray brings spiciness from the pink pepper and it very quickly settles into incense (which carries it all the way through), labdanum and a hint of rose which is not in the notes but I get it anyway. Does anyone else? It's not too layered beyond that, typical to most Diptyque, and the scent just stays more muted after the 2 hour mark. I can get whiffs of it through the day so it's a skin scent+ on me. I find it quite addictive and LOVE smelling of this wonderful fragrance. I don't get any of the pearly iridescence, Lunamaris is more sparkle after gentle rain or a lukewarm shower on a spring day. Very inoffensive and wearable in all weathers. It's also perfectly unisex.

In another review, @byrehoe mentioned this was the most low-volume of the five Essences, and I completely agree. In the store, I could barely smell it. But trying it at home, it's more pleasant than I had initially assumed. That pink pepper in the beginning immediately reminded me of Glossier You, but it doesn't linger for too long before revealing the dark and woody labdanum. I don't have the sample anymore, but it reminded me of a Etat Libre d'Orange scent, Attaquer le Soleil, which is said to be solely labdanum. That one was far more heavy, incensy, and dark. Keeping with Diptyque's .... less polarizing style, the labdanum here never gets too crazy or unapproachable. I'd love to smell this on a guy in the winter, I think it could be really lovely in an Aesop sort of way. Lunamaris, despite the beautiful name, also doesn't really evoke that iridescent quality of mother-of-pearl, which it's said to be inspired by, so that's a bit of a miss. On it's own, it's alright. But I think it was marketed more beautifully than the scent deserves.

As an avid lover of Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum , I kind of had mixed feelings about this EDT release because I wasn’t sure how they were going to take such a unique floral-musk and not only tone it down, but give it its own novelty. I tested the EDT out in the store recently and from first spray, I was met with that beautiful and familiar, iris-musk-ambrette of the original. It was when I left the store with the blotter card that made me go, “oh wow, they are different!” After about 5-10 minutes of settling, "Fleur de Peau (Eau de Toilette) | Diptyque" blossoms with a prominent magnolia flower that I don’t believe exists at all in the original. You also get a burst of citrus that again, is not found in the original. I often associate the EDP with coldness and melancholy, but I get quite the opposite from the EDT. It’s brighter, more floral dominant, and feels more joyous. It also feels more “fresh” as it’s missing the earthiness that the original has. I didn’t think my love for Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum could grow even deeper, but that’s exactly what "Fleur de Peau (Eau de Toilette) | Diptyque" has done. Is it necessary to have both in your collection? Probably not. But if you couldn’t get with the carrot and aldehydes in the original, it’s worth it to give the EDT a shot. I’m still deciding on whether or not I need to add it to my collection, but I’m glad I tried it and I’m happy that I like it. Would be interested to see if they release a similar flanker for Orphéon Eau de Parfum next!

Opens with a sharp hit of lipstick that quickly develops into freeze dried irises with a bit of sweetness from the magnolia that mellows it out (the magnolia in this smells like a white floral with a hint of that pink blush that some magnolia petals have. I'm not sure if magnolia can be extracted as an aroma chemical, but they captured it very well as a background component here. Very silky and lightly sweet). It's icy florals with a white musk base that supports the whole as a sort of creamy anchor. I can't pinpoint the mandarin in this but I assume it might just be expressed in a sort of acidity/juiciness. Fun textural experience here that stands out even more so than just the florals which by themselves might not have been very exciting. A wonderful everyday perfume even on colder days despite the pyramid suggesting something more spring like.

This is my first sample ever. I haven't tried any other fragrances before it so I'm not really familiar with a lot of the notes I was smelling. My first day impression of the fragrance was that there were some flower smells, something of a self-care product and an overall projection of my skin's natural odor. After reviewing some descriptions, I could pin-point these notes as the iris note, musk, and powder. Iris isn't really like other flowers I know. It's refreshing like grape koolaid?? I asked how it smelled to my friends and they said it smells motherly and something you'd smell on a put-together woman. In colder weather, the fragrance pushes more waxy citrus-like notes. This was probably the magnolia I heard others talk about! I personally get more nose-blind when it gets colder but it still has the same projection to my friends. edit 1: I found it smells best for me if I spray it 6 inches or more from the skin. The bottle atomizer has enough pressure that it can spray that far. At any closer distance, more of the alcohol smell is present, giving a sharp unpleasant body. The projection is quite good! With a spray on both wrists and one on the neck, people within 6 feet behind you can definitely smell it. edit 2: It's mid-December and it's harder to enjoy the scent. The Iris has mainly turned dusty. The other notes are still doing their thing smelling good though. edit 3: In late December, the iris has turned really dusty. I'ts not pleasant but I hope it turns beautiful again in the summer. I've been keeping my bottle in a cool dark place so I really feel like this is an effect of the season.

Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum was my first expensive fragrance. The first one that made me forget my “I would never spend so much money on PERFUME!” completely. Unfortunately, my family does not share this love. “What smells like mothballs here?” and “Mom, you kind of smell” have led me to wear Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum only when I am alone - a true, real love that doesn’t just have to move out. When I found out that there would be an Eau de Toilette version, it was clear: I have to have it! Today, "Fleur de Peau (Eau de Toilette) | Diptyque" arrived, and full of expectations, I treated myself to two sprays on my arm. Oh no. Please not. What is this? It’s scratchy and somehow musty. My God, I think I'm getting a headache. Well, wonderful. Is this supposed to be the scent I’ve been looking forward to? No, that’s not it yet. The scratchy mustiness disappears quickly. The headache isn’t coming after all. Does it lack the depth of Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum ? Yep. And is the iris not as present? Yep. Is that bad? Not at all! You get a very nice, light skin scent here that is still not boring. A dreamy fairy scent, delicate, clean, without sweetness. I think I just love them both! And no one has told me today that I smell.

“Fleur de Peau” is a masterpiece of subtle elegance for me. The scent is powdery, clean, and close to the skin. Iris and musk blend into a feeling of cozy warmth, almost like freshly dried laundry on the skin. It is intimate, soothing, and feels incredibly natural - like the scent of your own skin, only more beautiful. Simply perfectly balanced: gentle, modern, and yet with depth. A perfume that doesn’t need to speak loudly to be remembered for a long time.

I want this to stand as my warning to anyone else who was sold on the exotic promise of the copy – zukoh powder, incense, benzoin, osmanthus, the art of kōdō, etc. I was emotionally invested in this perfume, sight unseen, for about six months before I was even financially invested in it. I fantasized daily about it – apricots, leather, incense, sandalwood, oh my! I just knew that this scent was going to be my personal osmanthus GOAT. I even adored Diptyque’s clever portmanteau of osmanthe and kimono, which emphasized the connection between osmanthus and Japanese rituals and dress. Kimonanthe proved to be excruciatingly difficult to get a hold of. I kept trying to buy directly from Diptyque in Paris, but their dropdown menus were continuously bedeviled at the suggestion that Ireland was part of Europe (perhaps the French are generally bemused at the thought that they share geopolitical space with clodhoppers like us). Anyway, when I finally got Collette to ship it to me – right before they closed their doors for good – I thought all my ducks had come home to roost. Good Lord. Listen, I am familiar with Japanese incense. I understand that clove, benzoin, camphor, and aloeswood (agarwood) are the main recurring ‘flavor’ motifs in these delicate, coreless sticks. I also own a bit of zukoh powder. I do understand, therefore, the general aroma-scape of Kimonanthe. But the unfortunate thing that Diptyque failed to consider is that, when you put camphor, syrupy apricots (osmanthus) and benzoin together, it is almost impossible to not end up with cherry-flavored antibiotic syrup, the type you give to small children who can't swallow pills yet. Each time I pick up my bottle of Kimonanthe, I hope that my nose has gotten more sophisticated in the meantime and that I will now be able to smell the tart osmanthus leather, incense, and sandalwood power as intended. And each time, I run into that thick wall of cherry antibiotic syrup. Kimonanthe is undeniably a striking osmanthus perfume. It is strong, rich, and with that camphor-cherry syrup opening, unique. I admire it, study it, contemplate it – but do not like it. Not even one little bit. I keep wishing that I did because I spent upwards of €175 to get it. I wish I understood better what the perfumer had been going for, so that I might unlock its appeal. I know enough about the behavior of raw materials to be able to pick out benzoin, camphor, clove. But I cannot understand why someone would put them together in this way to produce an olfactory effect that is so jarring. Yes, the drydown is better, but hardly more special than any other incensey sandalwood thing you might already own, like Samsara (Guerlain).

Green, fresh, and slightly floral, 'Kimonanthe' begins. However, after just a few minutes, a smoky note overtakes the pleasant start, and I don't really like the scent at this point. After half an hour, some leather joins the smoke, and I find that it doesn't quite fit. Only after the scent mingles with ripe cherry can I warm up to 'Kimonanthe'. And the longer I smell it, the more I like the fragrance. For the next few hours, smoke, leather, and cherry alternate in prominence. At some point, the smoke runs out of steam, and only the scent of leather and sweet cherry can be detected. 'Kimonanthe' is always good to wear except in hot temperatures and is versatile. The projection is moderate, and the longevity is a solid eight hours. I thank Mörderbiene for the sample.

...the second time it happened. I travel to Paris frequently to visit my sister and my delightful godchild, and when time allows, I always embark on a "fragrance safari," often to Boulevard Saint Germain, especially to number 34. During my penultimate trip in July, I stocked up on L' Autre and L'Eau Trois and, of course, tested various fragrances. Among them was Kimonanthe. The first impression of this little water was not the best; it smelled to me like a sticky-sweet cough syrup that I had to take as a child. The disappointment after this first contact was great, as I had quite high expectations for this scent due to its ingredients. However, the charming saleswoman made sure to give me a generous sample with my purchase. This included a test vial of Kimonanthe. Back home in Cologne, I dared to try it again, initially encountering that unbearable cough syrup attic again, but after about half an hour, what I had hoped for from this blend began to emerge. A spicy-exotic mélange typical of Diptyque, which transforms from minute to minute. Osmanthus dominates the top and heart notes, while camphor is likely responsible for the cough syrup-like odor in the top notes. However, as mentioned, this subsides after a good half hour. In the base, a very harmonious fusion of leather and incense reveals itself. The latter is a gentler representative, like in Kyoto by C.d.G. The leathery note gives the fragrance a certain wickedness without being too prominent. The spices, cloves, and sandalwood are also more perceptible in the base and slightly soften the harsh leather note. I was back in Paris last week and again at Boulevard Saint Germain, No. 34.... Kimonanthe then got to accompany me back to Cologne and will surely be worn more often in the cooler season :-) In short, an extraordinary fragrance that absolutely fits into the Diptyque cosmos, not for every day, but certainly a wearable little water for both genders. Certainly not a milestone for Maison Diptyque, but still something special; I highly recommend a test. The fragrance belongs to the 34 Collection and is available only in Diptyque boutiques, like Opôné, Eau Mage, and Benjoin Bohème. The longevity for me is about 8 hours, the sillage is present but not overwhelming; my only criticism is the bottle. I like the crackled glass itself, but that dreadful orange plastic stopper.... No :-)

This fragrance would be an absolute masterpiece, masculine, fresh, spicy, elegant, and above all, completely unobtrusive and pleasant to the nose even after multiple uses. The weakness, however, as the title suggests, is an absolutely miserable longevity and sillage. I may have come across a counterfeit here, or the gentlemen and ladies at Givenchy clearly missed the mark when selecting their oils.. It's really a shame for a great all-rounder that only fails due to its longevity.

A very distinct scent - one that I'm still not sure about and is leaning towards my "incredible, impressive, but not quite for me" pile. There's something very alluring about Opsis. It's a refined, classy musk and I very almost love it. One thing I know for certain is that it's one that I enjoy more in retrospect than I do in the moment of wearing it; I was enchanted the first time I tried it, though the second time I was very much oversprayed by the lady at the desk and this may have tainted it for me - so, top tip, this only requires a wee spritz! As a gentle accent and in the drydown, it's really something. Opsis is marketed as "a scent that captures the electrifying atmosphere of an evening at the theatre in 1920s London" which it wholeheartedly succeeds at. It's slightly bougey, old fashioned, but confident and alluring. Very evocative, very classy. The iris is light but the smoky incense note is what really makes it stand out. It's moreish - a scent that really tugs at your curiosity. I love a unisex, lightly femme fragrance but I do think this one leans more femme than some of Diptyque's other releases. I may yet change my mind, but right now I think the heavy and powdery aspect is a tad too strong, and I would have liked just a touch of something fresh, but this is one that others will surely love :)

I must admin I was a bit worried buying Opsis just basing on the description and my feeling towards the brand. I was unboxing the package slowly and with great tenderness, cherishing my eyes with the bottle design. And right after the first splash I felt so over the moon! The mixture od bergamot, iris and discrete incense didnt transport me to the old theatre. It was about gentle feeling of relaxation, aticipation, peace and comfort. I didnt miss anything in coming momenta, that was- and still is- a pleasure to indulge in Opsis experience. Cant find better words to describe it than: just try it yourself and dont try to compare it to anything you know. Worth every penny.

Yesterday was one of those days when I felt both happy and annoyed at the same time. The new Harrods-exclusive Opsis from Diptyque arrived and completely turned my feathered little head. An iris like I have never smelled before, so refined. After a citrusy bergamot opening, which initially gives off a tiny bit of the A-Milano aura (so many are doing that now), it quickly transitions into floral notes. In the background, there’s a light, very delicate incense that might even appeal to those who don’t necessarily prefer incense. Lady Iris clearly presents herself as the protagonist to me. Unlike Susan, who lent me this little treasure for testing, I definitely detect a pronounced iris note here. The fragrance exudes an aura of blooming gardens for me. A bit spring-like and summery at the same time. Delicate like a veil. A subtle sillage, never too much, yet the scent holds up quite well overall. I was already floating on musk-iris clouds and was contemplating how I could procure it from London. I had daydreams about upcoming London trips, which my husband enthusiastically agreed to, and I even contacted a dear customer to gently inquire if a souvenir from the British metropolis might still be possible this year. Well, today everything is different. Because today I am wearing Opsis for the first time properly and realize that it doesn’t really suit me after all. This homage to the theater is, overall, not overly made-up and dry, as I initially feared, but fluffy and wonderfully soft. However, the scent is still too floral for me overall. I imagine I can smell roses. It’s truly beautiful, but it’s just not really me what I perceive. And now I don’t know whether I should be happy that I can ultimately save myself the trouble of procuring this Harrods item, or should I be sad because I would have loved to have the little one? The Swabian grins and says, “Hehe, saved money.” And what about my Polly heart? It’s bleeding just a little. But what am I saying? Who doesn’t know that? Therefore, I can only keep repeating: fragrances must be worn. Before that, a purchasing decision is usually pointless, because a scent always shows different facets when worn than when tested on tissues, wrists, backs of hands, inner elbows, or elsewhere. Opsis has once again made that very clear to me. Still, I stick with a 9, because objectively it is one of the most beautiful new releases I have had under my nose in a long time. And despite all the Harrods exclusivity, it’s not as overpriced as many other fragrances that are currently being thrown onto the market almost by the ton. Anyone who loves delicate blossoms and prefers fragrances to be intricate and refined must definitely test this one. It’s beautiful. A big thank you to Susan for the opportunity to test.

I've been nursing a sample of Lazulio for a while now, wearing it daily to get a good grasp on how it makes me feel. First and foremost, the atomizer on the sampler is a bit dainty. I think the full bottle gives a more healthy dose per spray. With that being said, when I spray this fragrance onto my heat points and usual places (inner elbow, wrist, behind the ear, nape of the neck, chest) I either get anosmic or it fades very fast. I do think it could be the former. It ebbs and flows for about 4 hours, before permanently reducing into a soft skin scent for the rest of its 8+ hour life. It never really goes away like some colognes tend to. It starts with sweet and tangy rhubarb. Thank goodness. No cute soda-like rhubarb facets like Infusion de Rhubarbe placed upon a clean musk. Lazulio is almost rhubarb-custard like; the benzoin pulls up like a brown sugar creme brulee base to a tart rhubarb compote. The vetiver is something I personally can't smell.
