I thought it would be an unpleasant feeling to sense this cold. But contrary to my expectations, I step outside and find nature in the most beautiful green and colorful, rainy leaves.
I don't particularly like green tea (for drinking), I have no connections to the Bulgari brand, and the bottle and the name of the fragrance wouldn't have necessarily prompted me to test it.

This is truly a delightful scent, but I perceive it a bit differently and would describe it differently than most here. I got a miniature because I am looking for a new signature scent and actually want something fresh, distinctive with flowers and a statement, but still feminine.

do you feel the same way? as soon as the weather is nice outside, a blind activism takes over and you try to pack everything into this beautiful summer day that brings fun and joy of life. on weekdays, I can spend hours digging in the garden and planting, wandering through the woods and fields with the dogs, or hopping from one ice cream parlor to another in the city.

La Nuit Trésor has some flankers that can stand on their own feet, and some that are only minimally different from the original. I generally think it's easy to burn out and get confused by too many very similar flankers, so I'm more drawn to those that keep a little of the original DNA, but also bring something new to the table. LNT Le Parfum is only mimimally different from the original. I haven't compared them directly, but this scent feels really familiar. It has it all: A warm, sweet vanilla base, Lancôme's signature rose, berry notes, patchouli, and the intriguing smokiness that is so typical for this line. I'm a fan of that, so I can't hate this, and I can hardly imagine anyone who loves La Nuit Trésor will. The main difference is a prominent blackcurrant note that especially stands out in the opening. It has a bit of a scratchy, green facet, as if some leaves were still attached to the fruit, but later it turns rich and juicy. I don't really get the listed cocoa note here, honestly I would never have guessed it if I didn't read the list. So, in my opinion this is a very nice scent that works perfectly well for evening wear or cold winter days, but I prefer the original LNT - and the wonderful, discontinued À La Folie version, the cherry-infused Intense, even the rosier (but otherwise quite similar) Dentelle de Roses. Le Parfum doesn't add anything I was missing to the collection.

The latest flanker in the la nuit line is a dark powdery cocoa patchouli take on the original. And it’s very similar to the original which in comparison I find it to me a tad muskier. Overall I prefer the original edp but this one may suits the ose looking. For a darker earthy take. If you want to hear more about this perfume and most of the latest releases please watch my YouTube video here below where I share my thoughts on them.

The La Nuit Trésor line is SO good. They all smell like something from the past, but not outdated. You recognize the scent and yet it's not off-putting. Le Parfum smells, compared to its sisters, powdery and rich. I almost miss a bit of the cheekiness and fruitiness. And yet, almost everything is right here. The fragrance lasts forever, leaves a mile-long trail, and is for me one of the most seductive ones I know.

At the start, I can perceive all the listed notes (there aren't many) right away. A deep, dark rose, a bit of cocoa powder, and also a sour currant. Shortly after, the rose and the currant take center stage. It is definitely not a fresh-floral rose. It is a mysterious, dark rose. The currant flashes up now and then, scattering a bit of acidity. After a while, the currant bids farewell, leaving behind the rose, which has been sprinkled with some bitter cocoa powder. The scent becomes more powdery, settling on the skin: like a black velvet dress. For me, it is definitely not a daily scent. It can be wonderfully worn on a date, or generally when going out. In everyday life or for the office, it would be too much. The sillage is really good in the first 2-3 hours. It can quickly become over-applied, as the scent is so powdery. After that, it becomes a bit softer, but is still well perceived by others. It lasts a good 8 hours on me, but fortunately, it is not constantly so overpowering. The first few minutes after spraying, it is almost too much for me, even though I like it. I think it is not necessarily something for very young ladies. At least I know that I personally would not have liked it at 20, as it has something quite mature about it. But of course, tastes vary, and if you are into dark, bitter, and slightly sour rose scents, you should definitely give it a try!

Winter is here at last, and Annick Goutal's Myrrhe Ardente can be regarded as a winter fragrance - but with a special twist. In the colder season, people develop a longing for cosiness, for smoky fireplaces and warming ambry or oriental notes. However, Myrrhe Ardente lacks some of the typical ingredients of fragrant cosiness such as ambergris or Christmas gingerbread spiciness. This strange perfume is very straightforward with not much development. It is all about one single contrast: oriental broadness and volume as represented by the myrrh and some vanillic tonka bean is one side. The other side is smoky woodiness as it may come along with the Guaiac wood. A resinous, gum-like note, presumably benzoin (?), sticks them together. And that's about it – Myrrhe Ardente is simple but good! The overall character is considerably dry and smoky which makes this fragrance something particular different to the usual ambry, spicy and oriental fireplace fragrances. Myrrhe Ardente is rather red-hot than warm, and yes, I do get pictures of ardent myrrh or bright glowing wooden logs. You can almost hear the crackling and sizzling from the fireplace. There is only little development: Myrrhe Ardente might become slightly dryer and dustier as the fire burns down. Insofar, Myrrhe Ardente refers directly to glow and blaze, and not in a way as to use these imaginations to underline the idea of cosiness. I would say, the fire in it is a bit too dangerous to perfectly fit into such a concept. With its red-hot approach it could almost put you into a state of alert as real fire and smoke would do – if not the calming notes of myrrh and tonka soothed this impression. Yet, Myrrhe Ardente is disturbing enough to be taken seriously – it is nothing that can be worn easily and without consideration. And Myrrhe Ardente is a strange fragrance: although it is without any too exotic notes, the scent impression is anything but common or banal. There is more to it than just a combination of notes, the perfumer obviously achieved one of those magic moments of alchemy where everything is transferred into something new and unique. Myrrhe Ardente comes in Annick Goutal's square bottle and must be considered unisex. I think it can be a special treat for ladies who are looking for an unsweet fragrance. It should fit well to brown and beige colour tones and to suede leather outfits.

I spent most of my childhood wondering what root beer or sarsparilla would taste like. Without it being a reference base I can appreciate the beauty of Myrrhe Ardente for what it is. Hickory stick for one. English toffee is another. Fifty five years ago My Father eagerly awaited his Xmas parcels from London. We, the kids, got British smarties (essentially M&Ms) and he got a burnt toffee from post war Britian. Closer to home there's Kauri gum, or beach amber which has this delicate resin smell. I collect beach amber on my walks and Myrrhe Ardente is like wearing a whiff of it. The gum is, after all, the resin from giant trees burnt down 2,500 years ago, Agathis Australis. It's gorgeous, unisex, wondrous and addictive, as someone else pointed out. Discontinued, so I will probably buy a small back up Here's a school song my Mother used to sing School days, school days, dear old golden rules days Reading, and writing and arithmetic, Taught to the tune of a Hickory stick You were my queen in calico, I was your barefoot bashful beau You wrote on my slate, I love you Joe, When we were a couple of kids

What people find difficult to like, I usually enjoy, and vice-versa. Myrrhe Ardente, and the whole Les Orientalistes series in general, are extremely well-constructed, beautiful fragrances. I love rich, bold, resinous and smoky scents, so this fragrance is 'right up my alley'. Exotic is indeed what this fragrance is. If you love fragrances like Oud 27 by Le Labo, Chanel Coromandel, Tauer's perfumes and anything woodsy and masculine, Myrrhe Ardente could possibly suit you. Opening rather strongly, Myrrhe Ardente is a combination of dark woods, spicy incense and syrupy honey. I also get the reference being made in a few reviews to that slight booziness, a rum-like note that appears briefly in the heart. Due to this fragrance's subtle sweetness, I find myself desiring this fragrance quite often. It would make a perfect scent for a couple to share, depending upon the fact that his taste is similar to your own. While this fragrance is rough and foreign, it is incredibly sexy and alluring at the same time. Once the drydown has developed, I am often left in a peaceful state, shrouded in a smoky and sweet aroma, a little chocolatey and vanillary in certain moments. The price is a little disheartening, seeing that it is nearly twice the price of other Annick Goutal fragrances. However, for this particular beauty I would shell out every, single penny to own even a drop of its exquisite juice.

I'm so sad that Myrrhe Ardente is discontinued. This one is my favorite Annick Goutal perfume and it's my favorite smoky perfume. I own the extrait as well as the edp and although I love both, my favorite is the extrait. It's smoky, sweet, balmy and soft. I could wear this exclusively for a whole week without being bored.

AG Myrrhe Ardente (Burning Myrrh) is a sweet, smoky fragrance that is easy to wear and stays close to the skin. It wears linear on me and for about 5 hours. Myrrhe Ardente is unique, enjoyable & unisex. More smoky than myrrh, imo - that aspect reminds me of that campfire fragrance from Tauer (Lonestar?), although the AG is harsh compared to the Tauer. My EdP is marked 88% alcohol by volume, which really puts it in the EdT territory imo. Like all AG's that I've owned or tried, I don't think the price & longevity justify a full bottle purchase. I picked up Myrrhe Ardente (and the rest of the Les Orientales series) in 15ml bottles for about $10 each, plus shipping, on ebay. At that price, I say go ahead if this strikes your fancy. However, I wouldn't recommend a FB blind-buy without sampling.

At first, it is decidedly medicinal… like an antique herbal expectorant one might procure at the local apothecary run by an unlicensed homeopathic elf. It might cure you, it might kill you. It soon becomes whispery smoke and mysterious veils and soft, powdery incense made from mystical tree resins.

A balmy, sweet type of Myrrh perfume which I can detect Amber and Benzoin as the main notes. Tonka Bean and Guaiac Wood add to the composition, along with a slight hint of Vetiver. The note which really makes this enjoyable, and which brings the "sweetness" to this fragrance, is the Beeswax. It gives a syrupy, honey like quality and I like it very much.

Myrrhe Ardente is multifaceted, and that in several ways. Herb-sweet, toffee-like, liqueur-like, and smoky all at once are the first impressions. Tonka-vanilla. Wax. Myrrh. Dark, serious, bitter. A Goutal that comes with a furrowed brow for a change?

Even Grandma and Confucius said, every dish that has sugar also needs a pinch of salt and vice versa; the wisdom of the complementary question. This is probably also true for the creaky myrrh and the sweet dusty dry tonka. The two play a confusing love game of contrasts with themselves and my nose.

Myrrhe Ardente was a scent I had wanted to test for a long time. It seems to me that there are simply too few fragrances where myrrh is truly dominant, so I was naturally excited when I received a sample of this. I was initially skeptical when I dabbed this liquid on, as I don't actually like vanilla.

This is a wonderful unisex-musk from Annick Goutal. Very wearable, very pleasant, quite nice in winter, because it wrapps the wearer into a soft, warm cloud of well-being. Tender musc notes are mingled with lactonic chords leading to a sweet dessert-like dry-down. Not cloying or annoying, one of the best musks around.

I always wonder about this one. It’s made with a large serving of muscone, a musk with high molecular weight. Apparently the musks to which people are anosmic are these large ones. What does this smell like to them? To me it’s lovely. My take on MN is that it has the softness and rounded fruity sweetness of the non-threatening wing of musk fragrances, “white musks, “ but also the complexity over time that the beastier musks have. This is more baby skin than rank armpit. There is a little of the waxy quality common to some musks, but the note that really fixes itself to the sweetness is the booziness. Booze and baby-skin. If that’s not enough complexity, consider therapy. Once into the basenotes, MN wears close to the skin but also loses some sweetness, becoming a bit woody. MN’s drydown has a long trajectory and traces of woody berry sweetness drift up to your nose 12 hours after applying it. I love that this has the happy-happy angles of the clean musks, but the complexity-without-skank of the heavier musks. I keep wedging MN between the two ends of the musk spectrum that I’m positing, and I shouldn’t. If anything, the center area that MN seems to occupy shows that moderation can be a smart and definitive choice and not just a compromise. A great scent for SoCal dry summer nights.

Musk is a note that I am unfortunately anosmic to. Every now and then I capture wafts of it, but as soon as it appears, it's gone again. Musc Nomade, from what I have managed to smell, is a nice blend of musky woods and milk. It's more soothing than anything else. I would probably wear Musc Nomade as a bed-time scent, as it is something that would keep me feeling snuggly and warm. This fragrance isn't as spicy or as oriental as I expected it to be. Musc Nomade is the tamest of the four in the Les Orientalistes series, yet no less superior. Clean and pretty, there's a sense of sensuous silkiness that pleases me greatly. For those that hold Narciso Rodriguez in such high esteem, should experience musk at its very best as it is represented in this fragrance. I want to say animalic musk, however I refrain from doing so, because while it is sexy, it doesn't seem like the perfect remedy to rouse up the beast inside of us. For that fact alone, Musc Nomade is categorised by me as being a clean, white musk with a touch of woods. However you perceive this fragrance, you are sure to agree that this is a wonderful interpretation of musk, having a wonderful versatility to be worn by both men and women alike.

Musc Nomade is another interpretation of „Withe Musk“ which is a collective term for the kinds of musk, that take soft, creamy and clean (but not necessaryly and rather undesirably soapy) effect on the bright side of musk. For starters it opens however with a quite sharp and brusque musk of the animalistic kind, consanguineous to my favorite musk „Kiehl´s Original Musk Blend“. As irritating as this clear, but very clearly anti-creamy musk is in the beginning, it lasts for only short time and soon takes big steps on the way to the creamy and soft musk-territory. The name „Musc Nomade“ is well chosen: Ideas of a wide and open country with dry shrubs, sand and stone under a burning sun and in the same time cold wind are answered by a certain naturalness, a kind of brittleness and a somehow straw-like note. Not hay (too grassy), but actually straw; I cannot name the note or accord responsible. Even the nature of human nomadism is sort of sniffable in MN: Unsettled and moving, but not in the slightest way jittery or fussed is this musk-note. It does not rest too long, but develops and changes constantly, without harsh character alternation or uneasy bustle. There is lots of creamyness, the typical musk-clearness, a pale and dusty soft-rosa and a super-tiny whiff of something fruity. With the base even more creamyness and a spot of sweetness of tonka bean and a dry and warm woodyness lay under the calming and finally down-settling musk. The sillage is not very strong, in the same time the longevity is good. You should spray LOTS of it, but then you will rejoice in a high-grade musk fragrance. Decidedly unisex, suitable through the whole year and all sorts of weather, this fluffy soft musk opens a clear and tidy, far wide, cloudless sky where a bracing wind is coming up.

Boiing! The mightly gong of Rank Organisation reverberates, the movie begins. Musc Nomade is a huge brass gong going off "This is why I wear perfume" …oh, and to read jtd's review that cannot be bettered, so I won't try

Fell for it. Once again. By now, I should have known better: Thinking in stereotypes based solely on external appearances can only lead to disappointment. I encountered this olfactory surprise today from "Musc Nomade".

Ripieno, you are right! I also smell something fruity. And I like it extraordinarily well! While I usually have a bit of fear of overtly musky scents, because musk sometimes smells so animalistic, musty, soapy, prickly, or makeup-like to me. But Musc Nomade is different. There’s something going on! This musk is delicate and warm and soft and round, like skin.
Fragrances from the house of Annick Goutal are sure to capture my attention: We have liked each other for many years!
I love musk fragrances that don't overwhelm - and Musc Nomade scored big with me! I was super skeptical whether a musk EDP might be too much of a good thing, but I was quickly proven wrong.....

Bvlgari Man when released was advertised for the middle-aged gentlemen. Brilliant white and piano laquer black were the colours, with plain polished metal applications and a grey-haired guy in a casual outfit. The message seems clear – Bvlgari Man claims to be straightforward, with a simple look and feel, but nevertheless noble and stylish and without any chi-chi. We must not expect anything too opulent or oriental. This is about a certain style, a cultural identity is to be sold along with the perfume. Presumably these simple messages work out – at least I felt attracted by the simple elegance of it. Nevertheless, I hope that this presentation does not affect my evaluation too much, because it is positive. For a few years now, and especially for the colder seasons, a certain kind of gent's perfumes have been released which I would like to call puristic: Wonderwood, Bang, Michalski and others. Bvlgari Man follows this path as well – no citruses, few notes, and not a lot of development. Bvlgari Man is all about tart and bitter woodiness. There is something lean and spicy-herbal like fennel, juniper or gentian in the top, but then comes the very bitter woodiness. Woodiness and herbal or spicy aspects interchange a little. During drydown, you might realise that there is something more to it as well. I guess it is a basically musky blend of something that adds some warmth to the bitter woods, as well as volume. This is what makes Bvlgari Man an after all balanced fragrance, despite the focus on bitter and dry woods. It makes this fragrance attractive and a little sexy. I dare say it saves this fragrance from being just boring. Although it is marketed as Eau de Toilette, Bvlgari Man has a considerable longevity of 12 hours and more. The longer you wear it, the more attractive it gets as the warmer aspects of it come into view. Bvlgari is not really my favourite brand. One can blame them of some of the sins that are so widespread in mainstream perfumery. Having tested most of their line-up I would value Bvlgari Man as their currently best gent's cologne. Bvlgari Man is availabe in different sizes, even 30 ml. This will do if you are just looking for one reference of this rather new, puristic style in gent's perfumery. Otherwise, Bvlgari Man is recommendable as an every day or office wear which keeps modestly in the background, but adds a little bit of attraction to the wearer.

My dad had accidentally bought this for himself when i recommended him Bvlgari black. He wasn’t disappointed, and neither was i when i smelled this. It doesn’t try to make you smell more like a man, it more or less assists the smell you’re already naturally born with. This scent will smell different on every person that wears it, guaranteed. I believe that’s what Bvlgari was going to with this fragrance. Clear and sheer, Bvlgari man is definitely one of the better, more original releases from any designer house as of late. It begins very clean with a soft accord of lotus blossom and violet leaves. Violet leaves are a gamble for me, sometimes they smell very dirty and now that i think of it, liken to patchouli in some ways and other times they can assist in a proper “crispness” without the addition of “calone”. The lotus blossom is very “white floral-y” if you catch my drift (powdery dewy), but something that this flower has over other white flowers is that it sniffs out sort of velvety, smooth and a hint green. In the heart of the scent i smell a VERY strong vetiver. Not the same vetiver you’ll find in a Guerlain with the same name. This vetiver is very earthy and soft accented by sandalwoods which only further the notion of “earth”. Finally in the base of this wonderful perfume we find honey, white musks, cashmere woods, amber and benzoin crystals. When i first saw the base of this scent i just KNEW i had to have it and by GOD is it good. The white musks work together with honey to sort of assist in the sillage and aromatic properties of the base. Smooth cashmere woods paired with amber and benzoin crystals finish up the fragrance with a clap/eyebrows up, as yo suggest “Well, that’s it. What do you think?”

this a sort of very watered and superlight terre d'hermes ,spicy and musky i don't detect any honey or lotus ,this should b a perfect office perfume ,in my humble opinion projection and longevity below average 5/10

Bvlgari Man is pleasantly light and airy, a slightly more conservative and clean release from the house of Bvlgari. This fragrance is suitable for pretty much everyone. Because of its simplicity however, I can see many people getting bored by it. It doesn't tend to develop much past a clean and musky woods scent, and in some ways it smells like many other fragrances on the market today. I find Bvlgari Man quite watery at times and a tad too simple, however it's one fragrance I can safely say won't offend anyone with its presence. For my own personal wear I don't find it all too feminine and in some ways it can be too discreet. On a rather warm day, I do believe this fragrance could be quite refreshing, yet I think it could work well in any season. When I tested this fragrance out on a male friend of mine I was quite surprised by how clean and natural this fragrance was on him, which was a relief seeing that his skin often turns a fragrance bitter and strong. Overall a likable fragrance, while although playing it safe, is worthy of a purchase for those that aren't into anything too bold.

One of the unique fragrances mixed with very high craftsmanship in which the ingredients interact to produce a wonderful scent that you will never get tired of no matter how you use it. One of the creations of the famous perfumer Alberto Morillas...a fragrance that will attract compliments from others and you will feel very happy when wearing it. A very classy, clean, safe and aristocratic fragrance, suitable for the summer and spring seasons, and suitable for distinguished men only. One of the best fragrances I have ever used in my life. Note: The favorite fragrance of my close friend who passed away suddenly in 2019 and this fragrance reminds me a lot of him.

That was the conclusion after a blind product test conducted by college students of a Marketing 101 course. Both were considered for mature men, howver, the Bulgari was regarded as less formal than the Chanel.

As a big fan of Bvlgari fragrances, this one has naturally been in my collection for a long time. In my large collection, it was slightly hidden, and I dug it out for a cooler autumn day. Even though most Bvlgari fragrances don’t really get good reviews here, I wouldn’t want to miss them in my collection. Especially the Aqva line and this one as well.

I would love to get this fragrance. I adore it and it ranks right after Wonderwood on my wish list. But the bottle is designed in such a way that it can only be handled by men's fists. With just one index finger, I simply don't have enough strength to press the spray button, especially since it is set in a completely unnecessary metal ring.

Let's start with the After Shave Balm. From there, it can only get better. Not that I've recently developed an interest in such niche products that the cosmetics folks want to squeeze the market with, but the sample sachet contained not only 1.5 ml of EdT but also 10 ml of gooey lotion for alleviating freezer burn... or something like that.

This review will be - for my standards - disproportionately short: Bulgari Man simply has nothing that ignites my writing enthusiasm. It’s not annoying enough for a grandiose takedown; it would be completely inappropriate to sing its praises given its inconspicuous mediocrity. The kindest word that slips from my keyboard is “Nice”!

LA NUIT TRESOR FLEUR DE NUIT by Lancôme is a flanker of the very famous line. The name and the pyramid may suggest you what this is going to smell like but imagination would not dare to go that far. To me this is closer to another famous perfume rather to its OG LNT. Please test it before buying it as even if you may love the original, you may despise this one. I believe a licorice note is not reported in the pyramid. If you are interested in a video review please take a look at the YouTube video linked here below.

I love the La Nuit Trésor line. There hasn't been a flanker I disliked so far, but of course, they're not all some marvelous must-haves for me. Fleur de Nuit isn't. But it still smells good. The caffè macchiato note is the biggest difference to the original. It's very milky and mild, you can smell the coffee, but it's definitely a macchiato with loats of foam and not a strong black coffee. The coffee part of this macchiato reminds me a little of YSL Black Opium, which gives me ambivalent feelings. On the one hand I love Black Opium, but on the other hand I think it's a bit lame to mix the DNA of one extremely popular 10 year old fragrance into another. The rest of the fragrance has a lot of elements from the original La Nuit Trésor: Rose, patchouli, sweet, fruity and balsamic notes all stirred into one intoxicating blend. I don't think I will get tired of it anytime soon, no matter how many similar flankers they make, it's just such a good scent profile. Some more small differences in Fleur de Nuit are that it isn't smokey and doesn't have a pronounced fruit note (like the lychee of the original). It feels a little softer and cozier due to the milkiness and a tad less complex all in all. Both are evening scents to me, but if I had to chose one of them for daytime, it would be this one.

I believe I don't need to mention how much I love La Nuit Tresor and also the flankers that have been released in recent years :) Normally, many are fed up after the third flanker... I, however, am not; with the Tresor La Nuit line, every year when a new one is released, it is filled with great joy and curiosity! :) So it was with Fleur de Nuit :) Normally, the Lancome fragrances are quickly available in Swiss perfumeries starting from January, but this year, for some reason, there was a delay with this new treasure. Regardless, what matters is that I can test it, and that's all that counts for me. Unfortunately, I couldn't test it with my grandfather, even though he also celebrates the La Nuit Tresor line; to make a long story short, he is currently on vacation, so I had to test it alone this time :) On Thursday, I went to my favorite perfumery hoping that Fleur de Nuit was finally there, and lo and behold, it was right in front of the entrance... FINALLY! I marveled first with great joy at the beautiful bottle and knew I would like it as always :D I sprayed it on my wrist after a long admiration and let it work on me. It smells simply unbelievably GOOD! Too good! I had it filled for me before I bought it and went home happily :D I kept smelling my wrist and was captivated by this scent *.* Now I won't keep you in suspense any longer and will start with the scent description :) The scent: Starts with a sensual hint of smoky berries on my skin, the rose doesn't take long to appear and unfolds from its erotic side.... What more could you want? The rose in Fleur de Nuit reminds me a lot of the one from La Nuit Tresor a la Folié because it is sweet, velvety, and also a bit wicked. The tuberose is addictive with its sweet-creamy note that I keep perceiving, jasmine is also present but this time very noble and warm with a subtle fresh note in the background. Caffé macchiato adds an irresistible creamy note to the whole, making it a dream come true for my nose :D Although this fragrance brings so many sweet notes, I can say that it is neither sticky sweet nor that penetrating sweetness; it is simply a good mix of sweet and fresh. If some of you are worried that it smells like Black Opium, I can reassure you that not even the coffee note in Fleur de Nuit has anything to do with the good Black Opium, at least not on my skin. (My mother also agreed since she finds Black Opium rather overwhelming, and she liked Fleur de Nuit right away, so it's a green light.) For my nose, it is a successful blend of the original La Nuit Tresor and a la Folié. H+S is a 10/10 for me, just like every La Nuit so far, or better said, like every Lancome perfume :) I am happy with the new Tresor La Nuit and can only recommend it as always for every sweet nose ;) Ps: For the upcoming Valentine's Day, Fleur de Nuit is certainly a great seduction for your partner ;)

... I would like to sing, because today - early April - the weather is showing its harsh side once again. The cold ruined our planned flea market visit - my husband prefers to take a hot bath. And I also don't feel like facing the icy wind. So I prefer to rummage through my samples. Oh - Fleur de Nuit comes into my hands, and I realize that I don't know it at all. A gap in my knowledge, as it turns out, because this fragrance shows itself at its best. I still like the original Tresor, but Fleur can hold its own. From the floral notes, the tuberose stands out, fresh and enchanting. It is accompanied by jasmine and roses - very soft and smooth. The scent wraps around you, subtle and trustworthy. Patchouli adds depth and a romantic mood. One feels like lighting candles and snuggling up with a good book under a blanket. Winter can stay outside - because Fleur de Nuit provides warmth.

La Nuit Trésor Fleur de Nuit is a new flanker from the La Nuit Trésor line. The dark bottle in the style of a diamond perfectly reflects the scent. At first, I smell floral notes that "capture" me. Shortly after, a delicious coffee and cappuccino scent wafts into my nose, underscored by a chocolaty soft vanilla note. La Nuit Trésor Fleur de Nuit is enchanting. It is a mix of Black Opium Eau de Parfum , Naomi Campbell and Good Girl Eau de Parfum . The fragrance radiates calm, erotic energy, and serenity. A "relaxing" mix of sweetness, flowers, and gourmand notes. I bought the fragrance because I got discounts, making it somewhat affordable. The scent is perfect to wear with a loved one during a nice meal; it might happen that you become the dessert :). I do not regret purchasing this fragrance.

I was super excited about this fragrance because I simply love the composition of the scent notes. I took the first spray and thought to myself "Wow," I love it.....do I know you from somewhere? What can I say, it strongly reminds me of Poison Girl Unexpected in the drydown. Dior, on the other hand, has the strong fresh opening with orange and ginger.

What a baffling composition. I am told that twenty-three notes are present. Of course, we all know that notes are mere metaphors, but in the extremely bizarre case of BVLGARI POUR HOMME, the metaphors clash head-on with my experience. Aldehydes? Certainly not. Bergamot, well, okay, yes, I suppose, since it is present in 33% of all perfumes. Maybe I can conceive of this as a tea scent. But the rest? They may as well say that this perfume contains unicorns and elves, since I smell them just about as well! null of this is to say that there is anything essentially wrong with BVLGARI POUR HOMME. It's nice. It's light. It's polite. It's clean and keen. It's the perfect scent for the twenty-first-century open-cubicle office. Indeed: it smells to me rather like just pressed and starched long-sleeved cotton Oxford shirts complete with linked cuffs and button-down collars!

Bias warning: I was completely blown away by this scent. I expected something decent, but received something outstanding. I promise not to spill too much drool on your keyboard nor to be overly fanboi, but prepare yourself for the happy adjectives! Bvlgari Pour Home goes on a smoky and a little bit resiny. Within minutes, it smells even better -- the smokiness amps; the psuedo-resins turn sweet; and the smell of new clothes appears. All of this is definitely masculine. Maybe there's a touch of cumin in here; there's a slight warmth. If you want to smell like a gentleman, this is it. Moderate silage -- two feet at best. By five hours, it is down to little more than a skin scent, but it still smells great -- smoky, musky, slightly sweet in a resiny way. At nine it is absolutely seductive in a sense of power and refinement. This is the scent that a CEO would wear relaxing in his office with a view over the bay at the end of the day -- masculine power, poise, refinement, and strength -- all without using stereotypical notes or being crude or carnal. The only negative is its lack of silage, which I am forgiving just this once. Every guy should at least sample this.

There are some scents you get, experience and can't wait to review, to gush words of praise and tell the world from the rooftops. When I first encountered BPH, it was almost a decade after its release (2006) and I bought it scent unsniffed, from an online retailer after reading the reviews of parfumisti far wiser and experienced than myself. It was an obviously well-made woody floral musk fragrance: clean and fresh without the tsunami of calone most newer men's scents of that era contained. Flowers musk and woods are deftly entwined, without too much sweetness or spice, and only enough citrus to tease out the freshness of the prevailing tea accord. A slightly above average cologne with decent longevity and respectable projection, this found itself filed in the BVLGARI row of the designer shelf of my armoire after a few wearings and though it was solid...it failed to wow me. Had I reviewed this in my earlier reviews, I daresay I would have "sold it short"; mostly because I have an entirely new outlook on this scent, perfumer and house. A prelude of freshness results from a cacophony of notes Jacques Cavallier-Belletrud has soothed to an harmonious choir of soft whispers, wafting as fresh as a breeze. Aldehydes add an airiness (as opposed to an expanding sparkle) while orange and bergamot add the needed citricity (and not a drop more) to attenuate the tea and petit grain; as they perfectly dissolve into leaf-tinged powdery floral notes of lavender and neroli closing a veritable perfect circle of clean, sans any of the usual soapy associations. BPH's aura of pristine masculinity makes it an utterly versatile scent choice suitable for the office, school, casual gatherings or a first date. The floral choir in the heart (cyclamen, geranium and carnation led by iris) continues the floral theme of the opening lavender and develops it, making it deeper (not louder) and at the same time smoother with rosewood and guaiac. Cardamom (warm green sharp) pepper (piquant and sharp) and coriander (cool & leafy but bitter) are, like most notes in Msr. Cavallier-Belletrud's works especially for this House, imperceptible as individuals yet their additions are what makes this a flawless silk and velvet tapestry, as opposed to a flashy silk screen on simple material. The weaving of the aromatic threads and olfactive colors "just so" truly makes BPH more than the sum of the parts. In the far drydown, the core of musk and cedar glows as it serves as a balancing point for the sweetness of amber (translucent amber is listed on Bvlgari's site) and *one single small?* tonka bean, against the dynamic duo of vetiver and oak moss while they hint at a hidden wildness underneath it all. BPH is a rather charming and very polite rascal beneath those starched collars and pressed trousers. Despite the fact this may seem cool or even aloof should not give you pause. Everyone needs a nice pressed neutral button-down shirt, that you can use with any outfit or situation. This is "that" shirt in a bottle-complete with mother-of-pearl buttons and hand sewn silk thread seams. Bravo!! Sillage: moderate to very good Longevity: above average (7-12 hours) Overall: 4.25/5 Now BVLGARI's perfume catalog numbers upwards of seventy fragrances; but, when BVLGARI POUR HOMME hit the market, in 1996, there were only two! (EAU PARFUMEE AU THE VERTE '92 and BVLGARI POUR FEMME '94) Later that year another *new* favorite of mine was released: EAU PARFUMEE AU THE VERT EXTREME-nosed by Jean-Claude Ellena. Currently BPH is still available at several online retailers (some for as little as .50/ml!) and remains a fixture worldwide at high-end fragrance counters and flagship stores. BVLGARI POUR HOMME seems to "play well with others" while offering year-round versatility, excellent quality-to-price ratio (or QPR) and sheer stunningness. I, therefore, dub BVLGARI POUR HOMME a Modern Masterpiece. Not only for how it has stayed the course over the last two decades, defining and setting the bar for men's elegance and style; but also for its uniqueness, considering its time and contemporaries, and subtle balance of softspoken luxury with graceful sensibility.

Bvlgari has a knack for making beautiful, refreshing, casual yet classy fragrances that are always sure crowd pleasers. There is so much to love when it comes to Bvlgari Pour Homme. It's not the most amazing thing you'll ever smell, yet it is undeniably charming. Quiet yet bold enough to make a statement, Bvlgari Pour Homme is a nicely balanced blend of light citrus, musky florals and aromatic herbs. Not a spectacular scent by any means, but one that is clean and soothing. I think a lot of men tend to go overboard with fragrances because there is so much media these days telling them that they have to smell great for the ladies. Many over-apply, wear something they don't even like or just spritz it on for the hell of it. Something like Bvlgari Pour Homme is sometimes all you need to get female attention. Smell fresh and masculine and the rest is history. Unfortunately the projection of this fragrance is not great. It is incredibly weak and even worse on the skin. The subtlety although admirable, could do with a boost in the sillage department so both the wearer and the people around him can enjoy this fragrance through all its stages. I'm surprised to like something so subtle, however after many partners with strong fragrances, I've been craving a man that wears lighter scents. Bvlgari Pour Homme is what I'm after.

Bvlgari pour homme was my signature scent in late 90s when I was a teenager. A girl I used to date loved this fragrance. The scent is a well mixed sophisticated flowery tea. Of the many listed notes, with enough sniffing I can detect (or imagine?) certain delicate citrus, flowers and cedar/musk that surrounds you close to skin. I could never smell the aldehyde before but now that my bottle has gone bad, the top notes are almost gone except the aldehyde. Interestingly the heart and base notes appear to be the same from what I recall in my memory. Later when I smelled a tester I confirmed my suspicion, but a side-by-side comparison may reveal more differences. Back to the scent: I had two issues with him. First, he is not very masculine. He is versatile in warm weather and certainly not offensive, but lacked enough character. Second, and major issue was that the scent is TOO delicate. Body lotion or hair products with any scents will easily overpower this guy. Worst case for me as a smoker was that the combined smell of this perfume with cigarettes was not pleasant. Obviously cigarette smell (not tobacco but the ash-like aura of smell from smoking) is not very pleasant but this combo was something else. While I have many fond memories, I no longer use him and there is no plan to re-purchase him. He is officially retired and hanging out in my retired display collection for occasional trip down the memory lane.

Invisible. It is the perfect adjective for this perfume. Very thin, too thin to be called a good scent, and yet the basics were there, reading the pyramid looks like anything else perfume. A woody frescolino that is not worth buying.

The floral notes come through immediately, producing a soft, happy tone to this scent. There is an overall powdery sense to Bvlgari pour Homme, a feel which I find alluring and attractive, though not especially masculine. This is not a macho macho product. The heavy, strong base notes are not overplayed, show themselves well in drydown.

Cool, spicy, woody, dry, clear, unobtrusive. A synonym for masculine understatement in fragrance form. It has the aura of a non-perfume. Like a whisper on the skin that could easily be mistaken for the wearer's natural scent. An outdoor fragrance. With elegant attitude. The skin after a stay in the cool, fresh air. The body in a suit. Nothing here is irritating.

It's astonishing how Jacques Cavallier could use so many unrelated ingredients to end up with a scent that one has to search for like a bloodhound. Bulgari Pour Homme is largely odorless, which somewhat reminds me of the anemia of Kenzo Power or Lacoste's Challenge.

Along with a few others, it ended up being tested on my wrist in the perfumery and, at first impression, it completely failed. My primary impression was that of ironing fine from the spray bottle. Not for me. I want to smell sporty or masculine and not like a spring freshling. Preferably something uncomplicated.

Compared to Mandragore (which I enjoy) Mandragore Pourpre is richer and warmer, making it ideal for colder weather. The first minute is an intense blast of pepper and mint, with bergamot gradually increasing but less intense than in Mandragore. Next up is a very pleasant but fleeting rosemary note, soon joined then replaced by warm ginger and star anise – these two notes, as in the original Mandragore, are the most prominent on my skin. The anise is particularly lovely. We're then off to a patchouli/incense base with more caracter than Mandragore's (which is just lightly woody). Really good and unusual, and a thumbs up from me. Very good longevity, moderate but noticeable sillage.

I got a sample vial of this one when I ordered at AlzD. The description sounded very promising to me. Actually I have no clue what Mandragore is and how it usually smells like. This one is a true unisex scent, maybe leaning a bit to the masculine side. It smells very natural. Maybe too natural. To my taste some of the Goutals lack abstraction. Sometimes I feel as if I was in a herb garden. In the beginning I get a lot of anise, which I like. The scent is very herbal, and there is a beautiful incense note. The drydown gets interesing and is better balanced. The herbal feel fades slightly but I still smell a slight herbal bitterness. Can't say much about the longevity because I haven't had a full day trial yet. I got the impression that it stays close to the body, a still water. But close to the skin it has presence. A beautiful scent, but not a clear buy. But I'll try again. Update december 2011: I tried again and liked it. I noticed a slight rubber note. But somehow it doesn't get me. When I had put it on my sisted asked me to stay away for her (well, don't take it too seriously, she hasn't got taste *lol*). She said that I smelled of cloves. Strange, it is not listed. Don't know if there was some Equipage lingering on my collar.

I own the original Mandragore and to be completely honest, some days I like it, some days I don't. The sharp citrus notes are often too much for me, however with the release of Mandragore Pourpre, I've come to enjoy the composition minus the stinging citrus. As Flannelman has mentioned, "Mandragore Pourpre is richer and warmer than the original". I find it a touch more masculine and mystical as well. Opening with delectable mint and licoricey anise, with a touch of pepper, Mandragore Pourpre has me impressed. The composition tends to be a lot darker and ultimately richer. The blend of geranium, incense and patchouli is wonderfully unique and tastefully done. In some instances I feel as if this could be the Winter version of Mandragore, however upon further thought, in my opinion this is just an improved and more complex version. The lasting strength and sillage is good, yet not overpowering or particularly strong. As some have already mentioned, the longevity is much improved, yet it is still relatively weak. I get a thick, syrupy espresso note for some reason, noticeably in the drydown, which eludes me. Perhaps it is just me that smells this, however I do believe it is what makes me like this fragrance so much.

Mandragore Pourpre, compared to the original Mandragore, opens much darker, earthier and spicier. The bergamot and the mint are still present throughout the development. But it's no longer as green and crisp as Mandragore. The anise and the pepper turn the whole composition into another deeper colour. In the drydown, Mandragore Pourpre has a sweeter facet than the original edition. The amber and the myrhh give an oriental vibe. If sniffed closely, the heliotrope and the incense are also distinguishable. Although Mandragore Pourpre has quite a different character from the orginal Mandragore, their connection is evident: the same elements they share are embodied in the same way. Interestingly, Mandragore Pourpre has the same ethereal texture as the origianl edition even it's significantly spicer, which makes it inoffensive while keeping it stand out. The fact that it's spicer and darker, also helps to keep its strength and its vivacity, contrary to the original Mandragore which tends to fall bland in the drydown. The sillage is relatively close even sprayed liberally. The longevity is around 6 hours, which is ok for an EDT. I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. An interesting olfactory experience it shall be.

Fragrances like this one should be more common. If it were up to me, only this. Annick Goutal knows how to create something that is sorely needed in the perfume market, namely scents with a completely unartificial quality and the concentrated sprouting power of plants. There are so many eaux and whatever else, but which of them truly makes the buds explode and allows you to hear the cracking of the umbels? Perfumery is something that started with natural materials, but for my taste, it has drifted a bit into the overly cultivated. Human luxury, human exclusivity, personal attractiveness - all of that is actually quite outdated and irrelevant in the face of wild plants that grow freely like crazy and release the most wonderful fragrance materials that can make you genuinely happy in an unadulterated way. Mandragore Pourpre is a very honest, straightforward scent. It has a truly lively herbal fraction that wonderfully clears the air and gives the fragrance its immense aromatic clarity. Especially the anise and mint have real bite and deserve individual praise. :) From the ethereal base note, a very special floral note emerges over time, determined by the mandrake. It is dignifiedly feminine and enriches the herbal power with a very subtle sweetness. This strangely beautiful mixture flows more and more beautifully into one another over time and ultimately becomes a single, inseparable good fragrance that gently and lightly reaches perfect tranquility, especially due to the very velvety amber base. On one hand, this scent is a prime example of wild radiance; on the other hand, it is simply a great composition with very understandable fragrance phases that blend together very finely. I would recommend all of you to give it a sniff!

Why one-handed comment? I’m writing the comment with my free right hand because I have my nose pressed closely to my left wrist to track the scent development, and I’ve been doing this for quite some time. I hope I don’t get a cramp.

The noteworthy comment from Stanze about the fragrance sister "Mandragore" reminded me of two things: my bottle of "Mandragore Pourpre" and my old mandrake. I quickly found the bottle among all my samples; the mandrake was harder to locate.
I like to walk disheveled my head on my shoulders like a lamp and I enjoy brightening your autumn without feathers.

Certainly, criticism of the overly thin essence Mandragore has not been absent. Perhaps this is the reason why Annick Goutal presents a significantly stronger variant on the same theme with Mandragore Pourpre. Once again, we encounter the beautiful fruity-floral-citrus note that I have already compared in my comment on Mandragore to hibiscus or rose hip tea.

After I got to know Mandragore and liked it very much, but couldn't wear it because it's already "occupied" by a dear friend, I took another look at Mandragore Pourpre. The first time, it failed miserably. Too much mint, too much anise, and too little green freshness. This was probably also because I judged it in direct comparison to Mandragore.

Since I already own the original and love it very, very much and don't want to do without it anymore, I also dared to try Caresse. When I sprayed it on my wrist, the first thing I smelled was bergamot and lychee, which then dissipate very quickly. After 2 minutes, a creamy freshness emerges that has a slightly sweet scent, making the whole thing even more interesting and better because you can smell a certain almond note with a hint of light vanilla. You can tell that it has a certain similarity to the original, but it is much lighter, nicer, and more suitable for everyday wear. I also perceived jasmine lightly; it wasn't very present, much more in the background. In this perfume, I find that the tonka bean, lychee, and vanilla are much more prominent. Sometimes I caught a whiff of a certain but slightly sweet raspberry note, which makes the whole thing very feminine and playful ;). Overall, this perfume is very successful; those who can't stand the original will likely warm up to this one since it is much lighter and should be significantly more bearable for most who don't like the real Tresor. I still stick with my favorite, but I also really like this one :)

I love the Trésors. They are, for me, the gem among designer fragrances. Always pleasant, loving, high-quality, and unbeatable in price. This scent completely flew under my radar. You can't find it in any of the big department stores, so I thought it was just a failed experiment by Lancôme. But by chance, I came across the fragrance, and since lychee and raspberry are two of my favorite notes for summer, I took the plunge and bought it blind. And now I wonder … how on earth is this fragrance not sold at the counters?? The top note was the most delicious, loving experience I have smelled in a long time. So fruity, perfectly balanced, and simply feminine. Over time, the scent becomes a bit darker, but it still retains its playful quality. The base is heavenly and a true pleasure. One could say it is La Nuit Trésor L'Eau de Parfum in a softer, slightly more youthful and romantic version. This fragrance is definitely my summer scent for 2021 and for the coming years as well. I also assume it will be discontinued, so I need to get a backup bottle before that happens. If you like the Trésors, I would definitely recommend you give it a try.

I love Trésor la nuit. I really wanted this one just because of the name Caresse: Who says no to promised caresses? There is a similarity, but for me, it is still an independent fragrance. It starts off really fresh with a subtle sweetness; the freshness likely comes from the pink pepper, and it is fruity as well, especially the raspberries which smell delicious. As it develops, Caresse becomes softer and warmer. However, compared to the original, it is overall lighter and thus more suitable for everyday wear. I couldn't perceive any patchouli, so the smoky aspect that I appreciate in La Nuit is missing. I still like it; finally, a successful blind buy again. The bottle is almost the same as the original, beautiful and elegant, but unfortunately, I was expecting a light pink like in the photo here. Only the floral ribbon is pink. Also important to know: You can smell the rose, but it is more of a wild rose, which is very pleasant and quite nice even for rose fragrance haters (like me).

After I really liked La Nuit Trésor, I bought a bottle of Caresse today since it was 50 percent off. It definitely smells similar to La Nuit, but it is lighter and therefore more suitable for everyday wear and warmer temperatures. I agree with the comment below; while La Nuit is dark and sexy, Caresse is more playful and romantic, making it a good fit for a date. In the opening, you can clearly identify juicy lychee, and then, after a few minutes, the scent becomes more floral. Jasmine, almond blossom, and rose are said to be responsible for this. The whole thing is supported by a cozy base of tonka bean, musk, and vanilla. I don't smell patchouli. This fragrance is beautiful, no question about it, but I prefer La Nuit a bit more because of the delicious praline and incense. Caresse is brighter, more delicate. A fine fruity tonka bean-vanilla scent veil surrounds you. Delicious! A very fine little fragrance, lovely for evenings and going out. This scent pairs even better with "A Little Bit of Your Heart" by Ariana Grande than with La Nuit. "A little bit of your heart is all I want." Sigh.

Through an engaging conversation with the lovely GirlofNow about our favorite La nuits (hers the classic, mine a la folie), I took a closer look at Caresse. I was familiar with it, but I hadn’t really considered it. I was very confused by the color of the bottle online. It is advertised as light pink, but in reality, the liquid is creamy and slightly honey-yellow-powdery. Is this definitely the "Caresse"? I wondered. But after various comparisons and googling, I was sure. Since it has already been discontinued, my hunting instinct was awakened, and I managed to snag a new bottle at a good price. When it arrived, I was delighted with the pretty bottle, which fits wonderfully with "Nude" and "a la folie." It has the rose ribbon around the neck again, while the other two have the loop. Upon the first spray (I always do this with my blind buys, but thankfully none have gone really wrong yet), I immediately thought of "Armani Diamonds" and grimaced. Exactly the same association, as both contain lychee and raspberry. Loud, present lychee and raspberry in each of them, I wouldn’t have expected that from Lancome. I must say, I have somehow outgrown "Diamonds." Suddenly, it feels too shrill to me, the raspberries seem modernly muted, it is piercing and synthetic, although not off-putting. Perhaps my nose and fragrance preferences have simply evolved. But since the bottle is pretty and it accompanied me during my rehab from my major hip surgery, I can’t seem to part with it. Sentimental value and all that. But I digress. Thank goodness we are dealing with a perfume from Lancome, which always promises me noble and high-quality scents. That’s why "Caresse" also has a nice development, and despite the initial insane similarity to "Diamonds," you can smell that it is a perfume from Lancome and the "La Nuit Tresor" line. The well-known Damask rose unites in the heart note with almond blossom, which I find extraordinarily pleasing. I also think I smell a hint of honey, although it is not listed. The longevity is, as always for me, very good, and even the next morning I can still smell it close to the skin. However, I had to test "Caresse" several times to decide whether it should stay or move on. The heart and base notes have, however, put me in a mild mood, especially the beautiful almond blossom, which reminds me a bit of the Kneipp body oil that I always add to the bathwater on baby bath days. It can be worn both in the evening and during the day, but please dose sparingly, as it can also be a little headache-inducing. On cooler to cold days, it wafts around you like a creamy, yellow-gold veil. I almost have to force myself to spray it on, and then stubbornly ignore the penetrating top note; it really borders on love-hate. Although the love grows stronger each time. The beautiful Tahitian vanilla and musk engage in a battle with lychee and raspberry until the end. Sometimes one team wins, sometimes the other, but thankfully Team Fruit has had its big and intrusive appearance behind it. Who knows, maybe I’ll give "Diamonds" another chance soon and compare both directly with each other. But I already know that "Diamonds" is clearer, sharper, more piercing, and much less round-creamy than "Caresse." Same same but different indeed.
Powdery, soft and delicately sweet but with a delightful freshness. It conjures up clean babies and young skin. It's also such good value and the bottle is very cute too.

Cayennes, Land Rovers, and a few X6s are parked here in the second row. Inside sits a Managing or Executive Director, around fifty, in Tod's Gommini and a Woolrich parka, secretly glancing at his Blackberry - after all, it's Saturday! Next to him on the sidewalk stands a - mostly significantly younger - blonde (rarely brunette, but that happens too) in Size Zero jeans and Barbour or also in Woolrich, casually draping a Neverfull in Monogram or Damier over her shoulder - after all, it's Saturday! In between - in front of the open back door, in small Barbour or very similar jackets and Ralph Lauren sweaters - stand little boys and little girls. I have often wondered, whenever I had the chance to take a whiff of Bvlgari's Petits et Mamans, if it is these mommies - definitely not the daddies - who spray their little boys and little girls with perfume in the open Cayenne door - perhaps so they don't smell too much like polo horse in the car? I don't know any children who are keen on such a perfume. The boys generally want nothing at all, and the girls - there is nothing pink about the little bottle, and it doesn't smell like raspberry and vanilla and fairy dust! This scent really can't be for these children. And then - amidst the well-to-do family idyll - you sometimes see couples strolling - very similar in appearance to the ones described above - who are still out and about without a child, still 'in good hope'. They are in the process of setting up a lovely nursery - in French country style - and today they are stopping by Petit Bateau to check out a onesie or picking up the silver family baptismal bowl from Wempe after restoration. And then - among other pretty little things they still need to acquire - the expectant mommy, tempted by the pretty bottle (which would look so nice on the Biedermeier changing table), takes a sniff of Bvlgari's little, light fragrance. She briefly closes her eyes, dreaming herself into the yet-to-be-furnished nursery, lovingly cradles her belly, and then the arm of the soon-to-be daddy next to her. And then she looks forward to powder and anti-cradle cap cream. And simply takes Petits et Mamans with her. Conclusion: a small fragrance that, in a not unpleasant way, smells like almost nothing. Soft and lovely. One that you spray into the air and then sniff with a dreamy smile. A pretty accessory, nothing more. For mommies, not for children.

Finally, I have my little ones in bed. They are no longer as fragrant, warm, and cuddly as they once were. Today, I am dealing more with little fire- and sulfur-snorting dragons. Exhausted, Maman lets herself fall onto the sofa. Stretching her heavy limbs. Calming her tense nerves. Sometimes I feel so burnt out. In the past, there was always chamomile tea when I was exhausted, tense, or unwell. My mother would brew it and bring it to me. She would stroke my head with her hand, which always smelled a bit like Nivea. Along with the steam of the chamomile tea. "Take a little nap," she whispered to me. "Then everything will be alright again." Oh, how I sometimes wished on my sofa that it would be like it was back then. In such moments, I slip into the bedroom to my cabinet where I keep my perfumes. There stands a bottle of Petits et Mamas. I bought it used a few weeks ago because the fragrance can no longer be found in drugstores. I spray it on my wrist. As soon as its alcoholic opening dissipates, it feels like my mother's hand, warm and soft. First, the soothing chamomile. Underneath, delicately, refreshing citrus, just strong enough for me to notice it. Distinct enough to give me the assurance that after a break, everything will be alright again. But not too strong and underlaid with a hint of vanilla, so that I won't feel awake or hyper. (Just Google "wake-up lemon." You will be amazed.) Finally, a hint of fresh flowers. Like back then, I feel comforted and relaxed. This fragrance was not made for children! It is for the child in me! And the child in every woman who urgently needs a whiff of relaxation after work.

Petits et Mamans was a blind buy for me. I am quite adventurous in this regard; I rely on my instincts, which rarely let me down. Here too, I made a lucky find. Petits et Mamans is said to be made for babies, but I believe that hardly anyone perfumes their infant, why would they? Anyone who has kissed a newborn on the head knows that babies exude an irresistible scent that practically compels you to "love" them. I have often wondered where this scent comes from. Do babies have special scent glands that then regress? Nature certainly had a thought behind it. In any case, this scent does not directly remind me of the scent of a baby’s head. Rather, it strongly reminds me of Nivea Baby cream, a light blue jar with little dots. I don’t even know if this cream still exists. In any case, it smells wonderful. If Nivea EdT is the scent of Nivea cream, then Petit et Mamans is the scent of Nivea Baby. I have an opened alcohol-free splash bottle here. From the aforementioned fragrance pyramid, I perceive delicate chamomile flowers right at the beginning, but a nice fresh one, not dusty, reminiscent of tea. After that, a lot of iris unfolds; I would even describe Petits et Mamans as a delicate iris scent. Somehow, I perceive something like very subtle white musk in the base note, although it is not mentioned in the fragrance pyramid. Or maybe I am just imagining it, and it is simply the result of the scent interacting with my skin chemistry. The longevity is in the medium range for me, as is the sillage. The bottle is very nicely designed with its "baby blanket pattern" and yet not too kitschy. I don’t find it that innocent; it is definitely made for adult women, and I can even imagine it on men. For me, it is a well-groomed, clean, and yet not innocent scent that iris lovers might enjoy. I still have a backup bottle, but I think I need to stock up on another bottle because I don’t want to miss out on this beautiful scent!

You dear little diaper poopers: Come all to Aunt Peanut. Aunt Peanut doesn’t go “Eww” or “Yuck,” but willingly changes your bottoms. Because Aunt Peanut loves to sniff talcum powder. Penaten, Johnson’s Baby, Bübchen -- everything! But since Aunt Peanut is afraid of pulmonary fibrosis, she prefers to buy “Petits et Mamans” by Bvlgari. Because this little perfume is a dream of perfect baby powder, gentleness, purity, softness, tenderness. Clearly: It doesn’t get any drier. After all, it’s powder, just for spraying. But all the more beautiful for it. The innocence of chamomile, the gentleness of sunflower, the cool dryness of iris. A combination to dream of, which I had the pleasure of discovering thanks to Lobelia and had to own in a mega bottle within hours! By the way, quite an intense combination. As shy as it appears further down, it doesn’t seem that way to me. Maybe it’s due to the dryness, but more than three spritzes and you’re knocked out!

I associate the scent with a warm bubble bath from the brand Bübchen, only much gentler, powdery, fluffier. A fragrance for big girls who like it powdery and pastel-colored, who want to give their appearance an innocent and soft frame, or who simply need to escape from everyday life in a dense, nude-colored cotton cloud....

Oh no, another Monday morning? The sky is full of rain clouds, I'm a bit tired, and I have no desire to conquer the world today. Classic case of PWS: Post-Weekend-Syndrome. My emergency plan: hot coffee, hot shower, hot coffee - and then I squeeze the last three drops of "Petits et Mamans" from the test tube.

Autumn... It's storming and raining... Wet and cold... I run a bath .... hot... soft foam .... candles.... I'm listening to Lana Del Rey I apply lotion and slip into my warm loungewear. I reach for Petits et Mamans.... With hand-knitted wool socks and a thick sofa blanket, I snuggle into my favorite armchair. I drink hot tea and listen to Gregory Porter...

Up in Cloud Cuckoo Land, there lives a little child. In the high cloud mountains, with the grumpy, nasty dwarfs, it has made a home for itself, and left its life behind. The dwarfs don't like little humans, no matter how pure they may be. They would prefer to be rid of it again, but the little child is fabulous. It loves lightness, joy, and happiness.

I was really looking forward to the fruity peach twist. Well, I won't be too harsh; even a splash of mandarin would have satisfied me. To my nose, this is a simple iris-vanilla scent. Very powdery, so those looking for baby powder rather than baby cream will be happy with this.

Sweet candy lemon, honeysuckle, jasmine, and daffodil. Every note listed comes through brilliantly. The honeysuckle and jasmine here are bright and greenish rather than overpoweringly sweet, and the daffodil note is stunning. The lemon starts off sweet but eventually becomes a little sharp. I am very picky when it comes to florals, and I might not have sampled any purely floral fragrance on my own, but I received Le Chevrefeuille in a Goutal sample set, and I'm glad I did. This fragrance is so bright and joyful, a celebration of rebirth after a long cold winter.

Le Chevrefeuille is an extremely green scent, almost bitter but lovely all the same. For those who aren't usually wearers of green fragrances, this may take a while to get acquainted with. Le Chevrefeuille is actually quite delicate and fresh. The honeysuckle, jasmine and narcissus gives this scent an unusual femininity while the petit grain creates an interesting grassy and herbaceous finish. The lemon is quite dominant alongside the honeysuckle, however this isn't sour citruses, it's more fresh and energizing, with a definite 'zing'. Oddly enough this fragrance is not sweet. It's rich and quite brash. I disagree with those reviewers that call this a simplistic scent, I think there's a lot going on which makes it very complex for me. All in all this is a very luscious and happy fragrance which would wear wonderfully in Spring and Summer. The lasting strength is so-so in my opinion, not terrible but certainly not as lasting as other Annick Goutal's that I've tried. If it's possible to get Le Chevrefeuille in eau de parfum concentration then disregard the price tag because that would be your best option.

In my search for the ultimate Honeysuckle fragrance, I've come across Le Chevrefeuille's sample. I’m unhappy to report that my first few tries have ended in bitter disappointment. This is a very light fragrance predictably centered around the Honeysuckle note. It begins with nondescript citrus which then leads to a green Honeysuckle drydown. The fragrance lasted about an hour on my skin before it completely faded away. It had no sillage (I had to shove my nose into my arm to get a whiff right after first application) and the lasting power left much to be desired. To ensure that my chemistry wasn't playing tricks on me, I tried this in different seasonal temperatures, several times, and on paper as well. I keep getting the same result. Now I may raise a few eye brows when I say this but... If you are looking for an affordable, simple, and yet realistic Honeysuckle fragrance, look into Victoria Secret’s Sexy Little Things / Heartbreaker. That composition is just as simple as this one – it actually follows a similar note pyramid – however, it’s light enough for warm temperatures with better staying power, balance, and a much more realistic rendition of the Honeysuckle note.

Spring in a bottle! This perfumer is very skilled in recreating the fragrance of a single flower. The only other perfume I know that can reach this level is Synactif from Shiseido, which recreates roses in all their freshness. I would like to challenge Isabelle Doyen to create the same wonder for freesias, my favorite flower that unfortunately smells very artificial in perfumery. Le Chevrefeuille is wonderful and fresh and unfortunately much too expensive for how little it lasts... But! I'm so in love that I've already finished my third bottle, and it will always be part of my wardrobe. Usually after I buy a bottle, I let it macerate for about a year or so and only after that I use it. What I noticed with Le Chevrefeuille, and the same with other Goutal perfumes, is that they become more concentrated in this way, and then they also have a little more projection and longevity. If you apply them to your hair or clothes, then they last even longer. This perfume is mana for my soul and will always be part of my collection. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Primavara intr-o sticluta! Acest parfumier este foarte priceput in a recrea parfumul unei singure flori. Singurul alt parfum care il cunosc si care poate atinge nivelul acesta este Synactif de la Shiseido, care recreaza trandafiri in toata prospetimea lor. As dori sa o provoc pe doamna Doyen sa creeze aceeasi minune pentru frezii, floarea mea preferata care din pacate miroase foarte artificial in parfumerie. Le Chevrefeuille este minunat si proaspat si din pacate mult prea scump la cat de putin tine... Dar! Sint atat de enamorata ca am terminat deja a treia sticluta si intotdeauna va fi parte din garderoba mea. De obicei dupa ce cumpar o sticla, o las sa stea in dulap cam vreun an si ceva si doar dupa aceea o folosesc. Ce am observat cu Le Chevrefeuille si la fel si cu Quel Amour! este ca ele devin mai concentrate in felul asta, si atunci au si un pic mai multa proiectie si siaj. Daca indraznesti sa le aplici pe par sau haine, atunci tin si mai mult. Acest parfum este mana pentru sufletul meu, atat de mult il iubesc.

Le chevrefeuille opens very green an citrus-y, with a sharpness that is unpleasant to me. It's definitely honeysuckle, but it is the whole plant, including a lot of vines and only a small proportion of flowers. There is some petitgrain and jasmine in the background. I blame the petitgrain for the sharp sourness. It reminds me of the smell when cutting our honeysuckle plant in shape. I guess I'd smell like that if I subsequently took all the cut vines and bathed in them - occasional crushed insect included. A bit too vine-like for me. I expected sweet honeysuckle flowers. This one is not that. Still deserves a good rating for how photorealistic the honeysuckle scent is.

This is a very beautiful, fresh, green creation which should serve as a model for other honeysuckle fragrances. I loved "Chevrefeuille" by Yves Rocher as a child, but don't like the current reformulated version as much as the vintage.

My first encounter with this flower was somewhat romantic: by chance, in the gardens near the cathedral that overlooks the sea. The tiny flower I had picked had a pleasant smell that was somewhat creamy and sweet as flowers can be. This perfume, sadly, is not a still image of that moment.

Annick Goutal nearly always produces perfumes which I'd be happy to wear again and again. The compositions are sometimes simple, but the quality is dependable, and the soliflores usually offer a slight twist on the named flower. LE CHEVREFEUILLE is a perfect example.

This fragrance starts with a very pleasant yet extremely brief fresh green blast. One minute or two later, it started to become progressively soapier and soapier. Nice soap mind you. A huge bar of french honeysuckle milled soap. It has faint lemon undertones. Projection is at half an arm but could increase to an arm with lavish application.

The most astonishing thing upfront: In the first few minutes after application, the scent has a rather musty quality by Goutal standards, which surprises me greatly. Otherwise, Le Chèvrefeuille is, despite its name, less a honeysuckle scent and primarily a jasmine fragrance, and I can only agree with my predecessor on that.

I can still remember very well two years ago seeing Lancome la vie e belle (the original version) advertised everywhere, no matter which TV channel or advertising wallpaper in the city, it was simply everywhere. You could smell it on every corner; it was, so to speak, the star among women's fragrances, and yet it repelled me more than it attracted me back then. Well, tastes change, as we all know, and that was the case for me too. I decided to give this scent a try, so I went into a perfume shop, and I could smell it very strongly as soon as I entered the store, which, to be honest, didn’t surprise me at all. I first tested the original and have to admit that I didn’t like it because it was simply too strong and too floral for me. The saleswoman said that the floral version is very popular among young people because it is softer and sweeter in its scent progression. So, I trusted the saleswoman and tested it, and I must say that this one is not floral at all; rather, it is gourmand (at least that’s how I perceived it on my skin). And yes, as you could read in the title, it was my first real perfume, and yes, I liked it very much; this scent has accompanied me to this day. Anyone who feels put off by the original should give this one a try, as it is simply softer and still, in a certain way, special and attractive.

I had initially eyed La vie est belle with suspicion, but then on a whim bought the Intense, and I do not regret it. Therefore, today I approached the Floral with confidence, sprayed it, and did my obligatory test run through the city. Surprisingly, it starts off just as intensely sweet and powdery as the Intense - but I found the similarity to be striking. I was searching for the floral note. No, I don't need it - I already have it, was my apparently hasty conclusion, because on the way home, from the sweet powderiness emerged a noble abundance of blossoms, led by exclusive Osmanthus. Bright jasmine and white roses go hand in hand, elegantly accompanied by delicately herbaceous violet. The heavy lily is full and elegant, supported by amber wood. The longevity is also enormous here - without being cloying. Floral takes its time to bloom, but then thoroughly and sustainably. Once again, it holds true - good things take time. Quickly called the perfumery and reserved a bottle. This beautiful life has a floral happy ending.

So far, all LVEB creations have been too mainstream for me. Although I am a big fan of gourmand scents, most of the new perfume releases from the 2010s are too sugary and not subtle enough. But now, this floral flanker of LVEB has made its way into my perfume collection. It actually differs only slightly from the original, mainly because the sticky sweet praline note is missing. The floral EDT exudes a lighter sweetness, likely stemming from the mix of fruity notes (blackcurrant bud) with orange blossom, violet, amberwood, and patchouli. In the background, the sweet notes are tamed by a noble iris that runs through the entire scent progression and gives the perfume a luxurious touch. Love it!

Absolute disaster. I smell rotten oranges. The worst opening I've ever had the chance to experience. It is that bad. It gets better as it dries down. Anyway, do not blind buy. Terre d'Hermès is always going to be held as a classic. This one though is going to be forgotten very soon. It lacks effort and genius.

Man… this one is awesome I can “understand” where the TDH comparisons may be coming from, but it does NOT “smell like” TDH… at all… there’s a “familiar feeling” that wafts in the sillage trail, a masculine, earthy tone that someone can say “feels ALMOST like” TDH, but the same? No. When I read these reviews and comparisons, I was expecting it to be the citrus feeling that was the root of the similarity, but it isn’t. I was expecting it to be a citrus bomb by the way it is portrayed and described, but I wouldn’t say that’s the case. It leaves a very proud, very masculine sillage trail. If I close my eyes and try to describe the vibe, i would say it reminds me of a very red sky at sunset, on a very dry, red sanded desert. Egyptian artwork appears in my mind as I try and give a closed eye description. Dusk, dry, hot, and red-orange colors. The citrus IS there, it’s just not very loud or sharp… it’s almost as if you’re spraying a vibe/feeling than a fragrance. A very confident, respected man would wear this. I see it working in all seasons. Performance is medium. While the sillage resonates nicely, the projection radius is medium-small, and the longevity backs off to a skin mode rather quickly (maybe 2-3 hours). It remains present for a solid 8+ hours, it’s just close to the skin. I’m enjoying this a lot. It is an experience, to say the least. I can understand the TDH comparison, and if that is WHY you’re skeptical, give it a test spray, as it’s not what the reviews paint in your head. I really reminds me more of Aqva Amara more than TDH, but not because of the citrus. It’s what’s in the air as it resonates… hard to put into words… how the last 4 hours of Amara smells on a very hot day, but amplified… that’s how I feel it.

Alberto Morillas, a old smart e experienced man, reuse his old creation, added more citrus fruits to the top and rounded the perfume into a more wearable version of the gucci guilty absolute. Money....Money..... but a beautiful recreation, a improvement of the OG .Still a challenging fragance..... made for the Fragcomm

Pretty much a more wearable version of Guilty Absolute pour Homme . Added citruses and just feels a little bit lighter. Almost like a cross between the grapefruit/vetiver of Terre d'Hermès Eau de Toilette and the woody leather of Guilty Absolute pour Homme .
