The twist at the end: ginkgo, very unusual and definitely quite green, teak wood with a chic gray patina, that's shabby chic, and tobacco blossom, guaranteed spicy and politically correct nicotine-free. You think so, but you're mistaken. Five sprays on the arm, took a sniff: there's something there, no question, but what? A little spicy, a little fresh, but what? Not unpleasant, but rather for the reason that there's almost nothing there, hence nothing can disturb. It stays like this for an hour or two, then there's really nothing left. It's a cheeky move to lure with beautiful scent notes. Well, serves you right, the hint about the bluff was actually obvious: gray teak wood! This is not a particularly noble new breed from the venerable hardwood supplier, but wood that has been intentionally made to look antique, artificially bleached like garden furniture in the grandparents' house, which has been standing outside in wind and weather for two decades without being oiled. Really charming. Conclusion: A perfume fitting for the emperor's new clothes. And why does Nefertiti have it? She had Blv when it came out, and she liked it. It must have been good once, as DirkDS also raves about it, reminiscing about how it was years ago and rates it 8.0. When the bottle was empty, Nefertiti was really sad. And now, struck by a renewed passion for fragrance, she ordered it out of sheer nostalgia, without reading the reviews. A mistake, tsss.

There are brands that you can hardly relate to. For me, alongside Burberry, Bvlgari is one of them. But each of these brands has - as I have found out - its little treasures to offer. In the case of Bvlgari, one of them is Blv pour Homme. Blv pour Homme is described quite quickly. It is a light version of Prada's Infusion d'Homme.

Quite nice. I can't really write much about this scent because it comes off as relatively unspectacular, yet it does smell quite nice. Clean, fresh, friendly. I find the tobacco blossom quite interesting, however, the whole thing fails qualitatively due to the incredibly weak and shallow sillage.

A good, soapy-fresh, but by no means outstanding or surprising scent from Bulgari... stylish packaging, very understated content that makes you smell pleasantly fresh, but it lacks both sillage and that special kick... it could and should have gone much more in the direction of the sea, given such an elegant, sea-inspired packaging and name.

Bulgari is not a good brand for perfumes. So far, I haven't liked anything. Everything fits the label "designer scent" - unattractive creations made from rather inexpensive materials, sometimes in scent directions that seem strange to my taste. The pyramid of Blv features quite rare, but attractively sounding fragrance notes.

I bought this fragrance years ago. It was something quite extraordinary for me back then. I found the top note with the refreshing strong ginger note delightful! A very beautiful scent that reminded me of "freshness and cleanliness" even during the first test back then.

I associate the mint with penny royal, crushed underfoot on a walk, releasing its fragrance momentarily. I was unprepared for the creamy Jaffa likeness to Elixir des Merveilles, or following on by association to Terre D'Hermes (JCE describes Eau de Merveilles as the sister scent to TDH) Now push those comments aside. The amber and Iris heart of Nuit Etoilee is what remains. If this is what camping under the stars is then I can only suggest that it's 'glamping' and the lackeys doing all the work don't smell at all like this! It's not overpowering even as an EDP. I want more of it. I want to apply in in the morning and keep it going all day. It's beautiful.....and different, and soft but refined. I don't find as much smoke in this as exists in Eau du Sud, which I am also fond of. A winner for sure.

From its very unusual notes, I wouldn't have expected Nuit Etoilée, starry night, to captivate me, but it has. The unusual doesn't always work, as we know, and for me, Iris is iffy indeed. One false step and I detest it in a fragrance. Not this time. Sniff, close my eyes and I am outside on a Balkan night, mint and citrus growing nearby, pine and fir. As I let a delicious piece of savory herb infused caramel (Immortelle's scent) melt in my mouth, I hold a single iris to my nose and look up at the stars. What a magical, strong and, in my experience, original perfume!

Nuit Etoilee Eau de Parfum opens with a refreshing cloud of spicy sweet peppermint. Its sparkling, stimulating, and uplifting. Pine bolsters the mint, steering your mind to images of a forest. As the initial burst of fresh mint begins to quickly fade, a fluffy warm bed of immortelle and soft woodsy notes reveal themselves. This dry, sweetened, aromatic immortelle steers the mind from forest to sun-warmed wildflower pastures in late summer or autumn. The contrast of cooling and warming notes creates an interesting tension, but I'm not fully convinced of a "Starry Night". The warm immortelle lacks the crisp transparency I desire from the name. Despite some disappointments, I wear this fragrance for its calming and transportive effects. Its not something I would consider mass-appealing or stylish and yet I still find it compelling enough to keep.

Upon application, Nuit Étoilée EDP has a deeper ambiance and the mint and the citrus are less prominent than in EDT. But overall they're very similar and it's really difficult for me to tell them apart. The sillage is moderate and the longevity is just excellent, 12h+. Since the EDT already has a pretty good longevity on me, I'm going to stick with my EDT and save myself some extra bucks. But for those who have difficulties with perfume longevity in general, EDP is a good option to experience this wonderful fragrance and it worths the price totally.

...a winter's tale. I have already told you about my winter love for "Nuit Etoilée EDT." After enjoying this fragrance so much, I simply couldn't resist trying the EDP as well. However, although the two perfumes are quite similar at first, the EDP is not a winter scent for me. Both fragrances start off minty fresh, but the lemon skillfully prevents it from drifting into a gum-like territory and perfectly rounds off the peaks that mint can sometimes display. Fir and pine add spice and depth, creating a naturalness reminiscent of an evening walk in the woods. While the EDT retains this nuance and only becomes a bit warmer in its aura through angelica and strawflower, the EDP takes a different direction. Where the EDT shines with clarity, amber and iris turn the tide for the EDP, laying a powdery veil over everything. This makes the EDP feel a bit more..., how should I say..., like perfume. It sacrifices a touch of its naturalness but appears somewhat finer and more elegant. This fragrance wants to be taken into the city, perhaps to a nice little café under the starry sky of Paris on a not-too-cool late summer night, while its cousin would surely love to accompany me on my nocturnal strolls through nature in icy cold. Thus, the EDP and the EDT remind me a little bit of a book from my childhood: "The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse." Both mice were fundamentally very similar, yet so different. A very charming tale!

A starry night. Sounds beautiful, right? This might come off as a cliché question from some movies, but when was the last time you saw a star-filled sky? In big cities, probably not very often, right?
Anyone who saw Damien Chazelle's enchanted little wonder called La La Land last winter will have the images immediately in their mind.

The clear, cool freshness of the Eau de Toilette from "Nuit Etoilée" deeply touches me time and again. I feel the quiet vibration of the wintry night’s silence and even expect to see the green shimmering Northern Lights: "Aurora borealis" - how beautiful that sounds!

What a pity, what a pity, I wanted a scent that smells of resin and pine needles: fresh, a little bitter and spicy and...affordable. Since I appreciate the natural fragrances from Goutal and they develop nicely on my skin, I made a blind purchase and am surprised.

A winter thunderstorm begins. Lightning flashes, dark gray clouds, darkness. Hail beats wildly against the windows. Thunderstorms are rather unusual in winter. And yet they are occurring more and more often, just like today, right now. When warm and cold air masses meet, it rattles.

A friend of mine owns this fragrance, and absolutely detests it. BLV has always made me curious, yet it wasn't until yesterday that I made it my mission to test it. BLV is very unique, at least in my opinion. My friend tends to like fresh, citrusy scents like D&G Light Blue and Moschino I Love, Love, which this fragrance is not. BLV is fresh and clean in some ways, however the soapy and citrusy bergamot qualities are balanced and smooth. The ginger comes across rather strongly at first, however the more the scent settles, the softer the scent becomes. Particularly in the heart, the wisteria and flax notes smelt a little powdery. The drydown tends to veer away from the powdery aspect and becomes much sharper and more woodsy. Just before it fades away, the last impression it gives is that of a lotion-type smell. The complexity of this fragrance is pleasing. Bvlgari has a way of constructing interesting, inoffensive and delicate Summer scents that really stand out from the other rival brands. The longevity is commendable, however the scent stays rather close to the skin. This is probably best seeing that powdery ginger and florals don't usually work too well in large, loud doses. I do like this fragrance, however I preferred it much more in the heart where it was powdery, smooth and creamy. The drydown was a little mediocre for me.

Bulgari BLV is a unique, subtle floral fragrance somewhat surprisingly anchored in aromatics, not musk or sandalwood, as one might have expected, at least from looking at the notes. The opening is unabashedly aromatic, with strong ginger and bergamot inducing a veritable wake-up effect. The dominant florals, wisteria and flax--chosen apparently for their blue color!--are so subtle as to never really compete with the opening aromatics. They do become stronger in the drydown, but never does BLV lose its essentially aromatic quality, and the wood and the musk, like the flowers, adorn the aromatics, not the other way around. I would call BLV an aromatic floral, if I were the Great Conferrer of Categories, and I would market this to men as well as women, since it is a truly unisex scent with great appeal to those who appreciate florals but prefer them to remain light accessories rather than the centerpiece of a scent. The longevity of BLV is excellent, and I would recommend this especially for hot summer days, when the cooling aromatics would be most welcome and a light floral touch is appropriate.

B.L.V has a boozy Elegance without making you lush Picturing a swank lounge Spacious and ultra modern Blue and ultravioet lights pulsating in Unisen with the throbing beat of Electronica Whiff of smoke lingers as vodkas and martinis being served reveals Evervesent clearness of it's Elegant drink, B.V.L Captures The artistry in a bottle, The Opening Starts with dry ginger but it's also a thinly disguised note of Tabacco which I dectect at the very begining Lemmon slices comes steeping in semi-sweetened with a bit of suger Westeria waters the sour edges to smooth the scent pallets Vanilla turns B.V.L Warm and sweet almost like silk a tinge of sandalwood adds a powdery subtle nuance, B.V.L Reflects the Modernity of perfumery and fashion That Big is Out and Less is More.

Wisteria is one of perfumery’s lost boys; pendant racemes of flowers with an aromatic odour, they're not in favour due to a chilly edge when you get up close. Here they are weaved together with ginger to form an angular foil to the other half of Blu; the powdery smell of baby in a (maybe not so) clean nappy. Clearly meant to appeal to nursing mums, Blu gets a mild positive for the unusual combination, even if it's derivative of Eau parfumée au thé vert and Johnson's Baby Powder.
I had this around 7 years before and I loved this scent. The only problem that I felt is its sillage and longevity was so poor.

I've recently had the pleasure of using BLV by Bvlgari, and it's quickly become one of my go-to fragrances. The scent is a captivating blend of fresh, spicy, and woody notes, creating a bold and elegant aroma that stands out. One of the standout features of BLV is its versatility.

Let's see if I can somewhat relativize the criticism of Asphaltblume. My favorite among the BLV fragrances is Notte, but now that I have the opportunity to wear BLV for a while again, I want to try to do it justice. The peculiar note that bothers Asphaltblume, I can smell, but for me, it is not unpleasant.

I really can't understand why this perfume is described as so disgusting here!! It definitely does not smell like Maggi! Blv is a fresh-light citrus floral scent. The perfume is very nice and versatile, suitable for different occasions. However, I personally think it fits better for spring and summer!

I was pleasantly surprised by BLV. A long time ago, I briefly tested it and found it to be bad. Now I received a sample and can test it more extensively. Actually, the Notte is supposed to correspond more to the Nivea scent, but this one also bears a strong resemblance to it. Although it starts fresh and citrusy, it is immediately surrounded by a fine creamy fragrance aura.

To put it straight: I cannot understand the harsh criticism of this fragrance. Sure, it is not particularly elegant; its aura is more reminiscent of a picnic or a bike ride than a glamorous ball night. But for a small summer rendezvous in the park, it is quite suitable, as well as for conferences with somewhat proper attire in the heat.

Aroma Fit is not really a perfume. Lancome labels it an "eau de forme/healthy body treatment fragrance" and, as such, it isn't meant to last long. I bought it in my quest to own all coffee fragrances, but I don't smell any coffee here. Rather, it is a light, perky mandarin orange with an anchoring note of rooty carrot. Both the color orange and the scent of oranges are so perky. This is a perfect thing to spritz on before working out or when you feel blah and can't decide what perfume to wear. Because of its low longevity, you'll be free to put on another scent in a couple of hours.

...here a short comment. Very fresh and fruity due to mandarin and orange, but not sweet because of coffee and carrot, rather a bit spicy. An ideal summer fragrance, but not very long-lasting on the skin, which was also not to be expected. It may be that Aroma Fit is still being produced, but unfortunately, I haven't come across it on the shelves for a while. Anyone who finds it should definitely give it a try!

This is a deep, dark, mysterious, sultry tuberose scent. It's resinous, woodsy, creamy, balsamic, chocolaty, boozy, and floral with a touch of flirty fruitiness. The tuberose feels thick and in lush full bloom almost on the verge of decline. The opening of the sweet black current is offset by the bitter and woodsy davana, opening the door to that big, bold, bodacious tuberose soon followed by a luscious, subtly spicy, chocolaty vanilla. No doubt the spicy myrrh combined with the vanilla and benzoin is creating that accord to my nose. This is a rich, voluptuous fragrance whose presence will be known. I am getting the full effect of what I think Sophie Labbe intended, which is a deep, dark and mysterious bittersweet fragrance, and I am really enjoying it.

I get a lot of myrrh under a sweet bubble gummy tuberose. I don’t have anything else that smells like this in my 100+ piece collection and I really enjoy it for when I want something different. I purchased it really wanting a fragrance with myrrh and this does not disappoint. The tuberose is very voluminous and feels like it has a dash of jasmine. High projection the first hour and then settles to a gentle moderate scent bubble. 6 hours longevity unless you go out into any type of heat. Seems to sizzle away very quickly and all I am left with is an almost berry vanilla type of skin scent.

I like tuberose scents - as long as they are not too intense. Often it’s more of a "tuba" rose - that blows me away directly - like the full-toned instrument. That’s why I sprayed Tubereuse Mystique carefully, as I didn’t want to overwhelm either myself or my husband. Caution is better than regret. But precautions are not necessary with Mystique. Instead of the full tuba, a bright flute plays here. The tuberose surrounds me lightly and airy - enchanting but not oppressive. Vanilla softly joins in - topped with delicately spicy myrrh. An attractively feminine scent - enveloped in a quiet secret. Despite its elegant statement, it is a good daytime fragrance - as it remains close to the skin and transparent. The mystical tuberose would make a welcome Christmas gift.

I have mixed feelings about this rather un-mysterious tuberose. It is not very animalic here and somehow comes off almost powdery, leaving more of a buttery tuberose whisper. Mixed with vanilla. The vanilla note overpowers the tuberose. At least that's how my nose perceives it. I definitely miss a green trace here. Something wild, something that suggests a tension. The fruity note has slipped past me. It is most akin to a "cuddle scent". The tuberose seems almost snuggly. A concept that finds favor. Testing the perfume has brought me joy, but I am still not entirely convinced, as the vanilla is very prominent here. For winter, this scent is certainly a good choice, one that keeps the wearer on the safe side. My sense of discovery is limited, as the notes do not coalesce into a mood that stimulates me. It is a perfume that initially feels heavy, but then it wraps you in a rather soothing way, appearing pleasant and bright, charming.

Wow, I didn't expect that. The old Jasmin Noir is one of my favorites, Omnia Crystalline is quite decent, you can wear it anytime, but the Bvlgari fragrances just don't have great longevity. Especially the Splendida line... I was super disappointed with the predecessor Magnolia Sensuel. Nothing that blew me away and the poor longevity again... And that's why I didn't expect much from Tubereuse Mystique either. But this bottle..... Oh my God, I just had to test it despite that... Just like the reviews, they sounded so promising :) It took a long time until I finally found a tester. But a few days ago, it happened. I sprayed it on the test strip and was initially puzzled... What? This isn't a Bvlgari???? I was both confused and delighted. So I continued to stroll and couldn't stop smelling the test strip. So I went back and applied it to my skin. Incredible!!! I haven't smelled anything like this in a long time. I can't describe it properly, but it starts off simply BEAUTIFULLY. Somehow lightly herbal-sweet. But so pleasant and, well, maybe not necessarily unique, but everything fits together, despite this herbal note that I usually don't like. It really stands out from the rest of what is currently being released. The tuberose is there, yes, but (still) not gum-like. The blend makes it, you could say. The scent is mysterious, velvety, and due to the myrrh, it has an oriental-balsamic quality that I don't know from Bvlgari's. My enchantment lasts about two hours. H&S are, as already mentioned, quite decent for the brand. Only then does Tubereuse Mystique become sweeter, of course also due to the vanilla, but we come back to the dear tuberose that ruins everything for me. Because here it comes. The gum :( Towards the end, I feel like I'm wearing l'interdit... I wish the tuberose wouldn't take center stage at the end, but it loves to do that. Because then I don't know if it will be enough for a purchase... Let's wait until November 29, 2019 ;)

First of all, it must be said that either you like tuberose or you don’t like it at all, that’s how it has always been for me. I like it because it represents something very feminine for me and can be quite seductive. Here we have a truly velvety, cozy, and perfectly staged fragrance - created for the discerning noses.

I am currently sitting in the car, and a hailstorm is sweeping over me. The pattering is so loud that I can't even hear the radio anymore. It's flashing, thundering, and of course, I don't have an umbrella with me. I observe the hazy weather and notice that the lighting conditions are quite mysterious.

This was a limited edition when Diptyque was releasing perfume oil versions of a few of their scents. When I bought it, I was impressed with the quality of the scent. It was a softer version of Philosykos with more fig than green, compared to the EDT. This bottle managed to last me so many years, as I only used it for travel. I think it has been 5 years now... Unfortunately, the scent degrades after about a year and by now only smells like oil which has gone bad and a hint of philosykos. I do not recommend buying the oils used if they have been opened and if you own this, don't wait to long to use it.

Absolue - 6AM Rose by Lancôme is a fragrance that lives up to its name. It offers a fresh, natural rose, one you can easily picture in the early morning, still covered in dew in your garden. It’s beautiful, delicate, and incredibly realistic; a dream for rose lovers. But at €165 for 50ml, I sadly won’t be buying it.

Quite long lasting on me too. I got through about 25% of the eau de toilette before it fixed in my head as pot pourri, then I started layering it with Sa majeste in order to enjoy it more. Yes it's fizzy, like sherbet is fizzy. Do kids suck sherbet through a liquorice stick anymore? These days that sounds like a gateway drug. Quel Amour could well be a portal to a POAL type fragrance. For a period of ten years we took holidays in a peony growing district though I was so taken with the mass planted profusion of flowers that I didn't analyse the perfumed varieties for scent. At Goutal they try to weave a story around their fragrances and the romance of Camille's floral strewn path back to her apartment after an absence from her fiancee is the back story to this one. Compared to others of this genre, say Parisienne by YSL, Quel Amour wins hands down but I can't recommend it whole heartedly. You can buy 'Floralisme' by Gres at a fraction of the cost and get a similar experience. As Chapeauclack has observed, firmly backed up by Luca Turin and Tania Sanchez, if you must have this floral fruity thing at least Quel Amour is nicely made. A bit of snob value? Quite likely.

This is a sparkling, fruity-flowery creation which redefines this genre by using a "dynamic" rose and fruit structure. "Quel Amour" seems to be composed of natural ingredients, this is why it does not have the typical artificial smell of all the fruity mainstream-scents on the market. The floral-fruity aspect is amplified through the inclusion of tiny woody facets and the softness of musk to be felt in the drydown. I think it is a beautiful alternative to all the average and artificial fruit-salad fragrances on the market.

Extremely chemical out of the vial, this little frou-frou floral was not an easy test ride for me. It took me a whole week of cautiously unscrewing, sniffing and hastily putting away until I finally decided I had to give it a skin test. On my very warm, olive skin Quel Amour! performs the usual fresh fruity floral routine, oscillating between sweet, vaguely sour, slightly powdery and clean musky. Within three hours it's completely gone from my wrists and what remains in the crease of the elbow is a verdant, slightly sour musk with detectable hints of ammonia. I do suspect the initial vinegary impression, as well as this, is due to certain facets of Peony and Berry accords rather than some vile chemical soup. One thing that makes Quel Amour! stand out is the high quality rose done with the signature Goutal twist of liquid, viscous green. Sadly, the "unbearable lightness" of this fragrance prevents the regal rose from truly shining for me, endowing it with all the typical anti gravity properties of the modern fruity floral. I do suspect that a drier, paler and cooler skin would do Quel Amour! more justice, as would someone with a disposition towards lighter, more cheerful scents than I prefer. I also think this is a good choice for a very young girl in need of some careful steering in the right direction, lest she picks a bieber as her entry-level fragrance and ends up with consequently bad choices later on.

I see red! Wear QUEL AMOUR! and you will too: wild roses, rose geranium, red currants, pomegranates, and cherries. Yes, there's an awful lot of red going on in this rich fruity-floral perfume, and all of it is good! The fruits and florals are well-balanced, each carrying their weight and not being drowned out as is often the case in fragrances of this kind. The other primary virtue of this creation to someone like me, with whom fruit notes are notoriously uncooperative, is that these juicy red fruits really are fresh. They are not plastic or artificially sweetened or rotting or sour or vaguely (or profoundly...) emetic. Not at all. It goes perhaps without saying that I am not really, in my throbbing red heart of hearts, the fruity-floral type, but QUEL AMOUR! has made a believer out of me (along with Ineke BRIAR ROSE, which is even better...). Yes, it is at least *possible* to create a wearable, enjoyable, fruity-floral perfume for adults. For years, I believed that the sheer possibility might be precluded by some arcane law of perfume logic, but this sort of composition, albeit rare, roundly refutes that hypothesis. Although QUEL AMOUR! is relatively simple, it's quite nice for what it is and certainly leaps and bounds better than the vast majority of fruity-floral BHT nightmares on the market today, most of which are pointless and some of which I find even painful to wear. The red here is saturated, making this perfume rather assertive. The longevity is also good, like a deep red wine stain on a white linen tablecloth.

I was so relieved when I read here that Quel Amour had a note of mint. I spent many hours trying to determine whether or not my nose had become incredibly confused. Strangely enough, I sensed the mint when I first applied Quel Amour to my skin. It was almost like a breath of toothpaste wafting up to my nose. Although to many that description may be unpleasant, to me it was different and somewhat appealing. The scent began with its minty freshness, before developing into a rich, romantic and classic floral. Peony and rose are very prominent notes in this fragrance. The scent reminded me of beautiful, old-fashioned trinket shops where the smell of pure rose oil used to fill the store. Like most Annick Goutal fragrances, Quel Amour has such a charming presence. In my opinion however, you won't like this fragrance if you don't like her previous scents. Quel Amour is more of an old-fashioned, classic, early 1900's inspired fragrance rather than being a modern scent. The fruity notes in Quel Amour aren't all that strong, although they are present. The peach is hidden in there somewhere however it has been overshadowed by the peony and rose. Quel Amour is your quintessential, rose scented Spring/Fall scent. Thinking of possible similarities, Stella by Stella McCartney comes to mind, however Quel Amour is much lighter and not as modern. This fragrance contains all natural oils and ingredients so you are guaranteed no artificial surprises. The scent is actually really long-lasting on my skin, and that is just for the EDT.

I really miss this little gem! It's a scent full of the innocence and optimism of youth. A syrup of red currant and pomegranates with rose water. Not at all sweet or fruity cloying, this was effervescent and contagious, a truly unique blend in this scent profile.

The combination of rose, peony, & peach sounds really appealing. But I've tried two different carded samples of this, and all I get is medium-grade rose oil and not even a particularly long-lasting one.I know that there are many musks that someone people smell strongly and others can't detect, but have no idea how my nose is missing the peach and peony here.
"Quel Amour," my great love and practically the beginning of a somewhat expensive addiction. About 2 years ago, something changed in my olfactory perception.

When I was a child, my grandmother always sent us to the fields in autumn to collect rose hips. There were miles of wild rose bushes. I didn't really enjoy this task with my grandmother because the wild roses have massive thorns, and we often came back scratched and pricked.

(...) because I can only explain this fragrance experience with the evil, bitterly evil skin chemistry! Oh, dearest Flori. I have tested it so many times (greedy like a predator). But the only thing I smell is highly concentrated Kappus soap in the rose scent. In the bar, lathered up, as soap flakes, in the bathwater, no matter how. But always just Kappus soap.

With the multitude of components listed in the pyramid, one might be inclined to think that the fragrance offers a true explosion of aromas, but that is far from the case. On the contrary, Eau Particulière is quite monotonous and essentially focuses on a fresh-green blend of mint, citrus, and rose with a subtle woody base. The scent starts fresh-fruity with various citrus fruits competing for dominance in the top note alongside the very prominent mint. The citrus components soon give way to the mint and retreat before the rose. This rose emits a particular note, not heavy and voluminous, no, rather a soft-soapy hint of rose that seems somewhat pale against the still prevailing mint note. My grandparents used to have various ancient rose bushes in their garden, among them one with light blue-violet giant blooms. This variety was my grandfather's pride and was called "Mainzer Fastnacht," and the rose note in Eau Particulière reminds me exactly of the scent of this rose. Lavender and rose geranium quietly join in later on but remain in the background, leaving mint and rose to continue leading the charge. The base fades very softly into woody-resinous notes, with cedar and benzoin being the most recognizable to me. In short, a very subtle fresh-green-powdery summer water that evaporates very quickly. If you want to wear the scent, you really have to use the atomizer generously to get anything from it. Nevertheless, the fragrance is well done and offers a good alternative to purely citrus-heavy summer scents. The longevity of the scent for me is a maximum of 3 hours, and the sillage is very close to the body; one has to get quite close to catch a whiff of it. Since the fragrance is only offered in a 240ml bottle with an atomizer, there is enough potential to refresh it a bit in between. On Diptyque's homepage, the fragrance is no longer listed; under the category "Multi-Use Eaux," only Eau Plurielle and Vinaigre de Toilette can be found, and even the recently released Eau Dominotée is no longer listed there. During my last visit to Paris in December 2016, Eau Particulière was also no longer available at the flagship store at Boulevard Saint-Germain 34....

Tested at the Spring store in Lyon, I had already tried most of this collection, which is one of my wife's favorites. Today's test concerned 1001 Rose, already available in the previous collection, one of the few survivors with an oud bouquet. From the outset, the rose takes center stage, elegant, distinguished, but also fresh. It reminds me of Penhaligon's Coveted Duchess Rose, but the closest resemblance is to Armani's Rose Milano. Even in the Lancôme fragrance, the citrus note is more fleeting. Two hours after applying it to my skin, I recognize a resemblance to Montale's Rose Musc. It lasts very well on clothing for about three days and on the skin for a solid 12 hours, with a good sillage. There is nothing new about this fragrance, which remains elegant but fairly basic despite a well-crafted rose note.

I love both Vanille Charnelle and Vanille Exquise by Annick Goutal. While the latter is lighter and more almondy, Charnelle is more on the caramel/spice side. The fluffy vanilla notes wear off pretty quickly and the scent becomes rich and deep. At first I was wondering why this house would make two similar vanillas, or why I would buy both of them, but now I see why. Charnelle is much denser and chewier while Exquise is light as air. Is Charnelle really carnal? I don't think so. It would have to be woodier and more peppery for that. But an admirable effort nonetheless. The projection could use some work but the quality is there: it is expensive for what you get but it is fairly worth it if you love vanilla and spice.

A gorgeous vanilla pod type of vanilla with just the right touch of incense and a tiny bit of oud. It is sweet but not gourmand. Very much of a sexy grown up vanilla fragrance. It is an absolute concentration. It feels very luxurious!

That I am happy with the scents from the house of Goutal is no secret anymore. I always appreciate the pronounced femininity of these compositions. There are not too many that I have tested and not liked. After years of abstinence, I have now developed a taste for vanilla; not only in the kitchen but surprisingly also as a fragrance. So, of course, I couldn't pass by this "Vanille Charnelle" - and I was not disappointed. It fits the season a little: the delicate yet rich vanilla that is present from the very first moment reminds me of Vanillekipferl; fine, crumbly pastries that never last long with me, no matter how often I put a tray of them in the oven! There are probably "kipferl thieves" lurking somewhere in my home: but who knows! This, not Viennese but Parisian delicacy gets its sweetness from the tonka bean: the two complement each other excellently - here they make a lovely pair! Sometimes they dance like fine snowflakes! However, in my feeling, this whole airy fragrance dream would just be a little froth if it weren't for the generous dose of pepper added. This "spices up" this sweet vanilla dream waltz in the truest sense of the word: it gains body and a slightly erotic aura. Now, most women's fragrances by Camille Goutal and Isabel Doyen are not creations that make a loud statement: they are feminine and for me, very corporeal and sensual! Since this "Vanille Charnelle" also has the shimmering glow of golden ylang-ylang at the end - practically like a sugar topping, to stick with the kipferl theme - this vanilla scent becomes simply enchanting. The sillage of this fragrance being resembles the corporeality of a petite woman who is truly not thin. The longevity is comparable to many of Goutal's fragrances; this spell of vanilla and spices lasts a few hours on me. It feels as if I am dressed in a light cashmere jacket that provides warmth without suffocating. And of course, it invites cuddling! For me, another very successful fragrance from the house of Annick Goutal: a little sweet, created for tender dreaming - and guaranteed calorie-free! Thus, perfectly suitable for this festive season!

It is the one vanilla scent that completely stands out. Regardless of what has already been written about this fragrance, it must be clearly stated: It is an absolute loner that cannot be compared to anything else. The closest comparison might be "Métallique," if you disregard the floral and hairspray notes (are those the famous aldehydes?) at Tom Ford. Because Vanille Charnelle starts with an intensely non-vanilla aroma. My novice nose primarily thinks of metal, but it must be the pepper, as Ylang-Ylang and tonka bean only reveal themselves hours later. The pepper note, as I call it, takes away any sweetness from the vanilla that follows and instead gives it something metallic-woody, nothing reminiscent of spices. I would guess black pepper, which behaves completely differently, much harder than white or mixed pepper in my spice rack and has little spice character, meaning little multiperspective depth - I can't express it any other way. Vanille Charnelle remains unsweet and dry despite the vanilla, yet it is very elegant and very, very individual. The scent is so extraordinary that I feel immediately secure when I wear it; the reason is the unique recognizability that marks the fragrance as "mine" right away. So I practically meet myself and feel at home - not every fragrance can do that. Vanille Charnelle is incredibly comforting and stabilizing for this reason. If one has lost their inner balance for a moment, this fragrance can help to find it again, as it strengthens one's self, the identity through the feeling of familiarity. The exclusivity of the fragrance having such an effect may be a form of self-deception from a psychological perspective. But the fragrance simply feels incredibly good. I can recognize many scents and could do so even as a teenager, though they were not niche fragrances. But Vanille Charnelle is a scent that I cannot compare to any other, which is why I find it so extraordinary, even if it may not be in terms of its fragrance quality. I stand by it: After 19 scent tests, it is one of my favorites. And I recommend it to anyone looking for a non-sweet vanilla. By the way, the bottle is very pretty, as is the packaging. I particularly love the sprayer, as it mists very, very finely. I still need to catch up on two comments, from yesterday and today. This evening after the Christmas shopping, I will check in with "Vanille de la Réunion"!

Nice of Goutal to name a fragrance after me to catch my attention. I will conveniently overlook the small typo. After I didn't warm up to Vanille Exquise, this "Absolu" is my next Goutal vanilla attempt. By now, I can hardly stand my early vanilla faves, far too sweet and pudding-like. But a fragrance can be gourmand, and tonka is a welcome ingredient for me, whether in perfume or crème brûlée. All in all, many plus points for Vanille Charnelle on paper. Then I saw the price. "Okay," I thought, "It's an Absolu and a Goutal of the prestige class. Let's see if it delivers." Mmnjein, I would say after a few hours with it. Pro: No vanilla pudding, does not smell synthetic or mainstream-billivanilli. Con: The namesake ingredient is actually a bit lacking. Pro: A nice smoky, nutty base note. Con: Nutty can be done better by some other fragrances. Pro: Not too strong sillage; some vanilla gourmands can be quite annoying to the environment. Con: For an "Absolu" and at this price, the longevity is not okay. Nevertheless, I can recommend Vanille Charnelle, as it bridges the gap between "delicious" gourmand and adult, slightly woody nut scent. Perfect for fans of skinniness.

After a relaxing weekend by the lake, despite the campsite, sleeping in a wooden barrel, and family attachments with four children under 5, I now sit on my sofa in the muggy big city on a Sunday afternoon. The rain has brought the hoped-for cooling after this Sahara heat week, and it is now cool enough for a perfume test. I sneak into the bedroom.

The fragrance starts with a hazelnut underpinned by vanilla, which is strangely listed as pepper in the fragrance pyramid. I immediately like the vanilla in the background. The nut macaron that jumps into my nose is less appealing to me. Other noses might interpret pastries as sensual, but as meaty? A nut simply smells like a nut.

For the mind to work properly, the heart must feel at ease. This could easily be from a self-help guide... but it happens to me quite often. It's so disruptive when intrusive thoughts catch up with me just when I can't afford them at all.

The scent absolutely does not suit me at all (30, more belonging to the crust punk scene, not girly at all). Old-fashioned, dusty - and an absolute feel-good fragrance. I think of an alternative old 68-year-old grandma, whose apartment hasn't seen a dust cloth in a while, it smells of incense sticks, tarot cards are lying around, and cat hair is everywhere.

It opens a bit sharp and zesty, the ginger is quite loud for the first few minutes. then come the tea accords, which I find the most pleasing and long lasting out of the tea fragrances I had the luck of smelling and trying on myself so far! I would describe it as a lemony/gingery tea with some bitterness to it, but not as much bitterness as in Wulong Cha which is quite photorealistic, but unfortunately the tea in that doesnt last long. the tea accords in Bulgari pour Homme EDP last way longer, I can still get wiffs of the tea after 3-4 hours. The Musk and Guaic Wood become stronger as it dries down. I would describe it as damp woods with an animalistic touch to it, but in a good way! Overall to me the scent profile is just soo soo soothing whilst maintaining a masculinity that I miss in many male perfumes these days. (almost no sweetness/fruitiness) Its very well balanced IMO. And for a freshie it lasts long. The only "negative" is the price, since its almost nowhere to be found in discounters, and if it is, its still around 100.-, despite it apparently not selling very well (Ive got my bottle from a store which had it on sale) and the Bach is from 2023, so probably one of the earliest ones, since its only out for a short time. So i dont really get why its not marked down more. Apparently Bulgari is trying to do something similar to Chanel where they only want their frags to be sold in High-End Stores and not at Discounters. This to me is a real Masterpiece and also kinda unique smelling! 10/10 for the scent - this will be my new signature for the warmer months for sure!

With the success of Imagination in the perfume community, it is now established that many men also enjoy tea scents. The Bvlgari pour Homme Eau de Parfum is my absolute favorite fragrance in this category. I had previously tested Wūlóng Chá Extrait de Parfum , which is also quite popular, but I did not like it at all as I found it too piercing. I also tested Imagination , which is a wonderful tea scent with a bright but very distinctive aura. Nevertheless, I must say that I prefer the Bvlgari pour Homme Eau de Parfum . The Imagination has more bitterness. Imagine a black tea that has steeped for one minute too long. It is known that brewing tea well is an art. I must say, given the price difference, that I find the Bvlgari pour Homme Eau de Parfum more beautiful and softer. To be clear: The LV is very good for me, but the Bvlgari is perfect! Because it is softer and more rounded. A lovely black tea scent that is bright, with the ginger bringing a gentle spritz and in the drydown, the musk adds a warm, soft, and slightly sweet note that wraps the fragrance composition like a light, cozy cotton blanket. Voilà: The perfect artwork that shines through simplicity is ready. I find the bottle wonderfully designed. With the heavy glass, the also high-quality looking cap, and the beautiful green of the liquid, the bottle is quite impressive. The bright sillage radiates nicely from my neck, but since the scent is so bright, light, and pleasant for everyone, I let it shine. Overall, a very calming aura surrounds me when I wear the fragrance. Perhaps a study should be done to see if such scents make one more relaxed and composed. It almost seems that way to me. ;-) The longevity, which is a problem for me, is remarkable. This belongs to the fragrances that I perceive very clearly for about 8 hours. I find the scent linear, which does not bother me at all. The fragrance is best suited for spring. In very warm temperatures, I think it becomes slightly too sweet. In spring, however, the sweetness is in perfect balance. Conclusion: With the Bvlgari pour Homme Eau de Parfum , a perfect everyday fragrance has been created in my view, which should not displease anyone. Sometimes the challenge lies in getting something (seemingly) simple just right. I like fragrances that have a certain modesty. I also appreciate the absence of nonsense, embellishments, and excessive self-absorption in people. The saying "to drink an honest beer" captures quite well what I am trying to express. This fragrance embodies the aesthetic of honest beer. P.s.: For me, the fragrance is perfect. Still, I wonder how it would be if one could add a splash of mint without it becoming too green or piercing. That would be worth a flanker in my opinion. A kind of summery version.

In contrast to the Eau de Toilette, which has been on the market for many years, the Eau de Parfum manifests itself as less sporty, less fresh, but somewhat darker and more complex. Upon spraying, the top note is immediately noticeable, high-quality black tea, slightly bitter, with ginger, slightly sour. The first seconds cleanse the nose, much like ginger neutralizes the taste between sushi bites. However, this only lasts a short while, and then the Eau de Parfum becomes distinctly sweeter and softer, with musk becoming prominent, and the woody notes quickly revealing themselves. Despite the sweetness and the slightly dark heaviness, the scent remains fresh, but not in the sense of citrus fragrances. It is rather a silvery freshness, bright, crystal-clear, and somehow warm and embedded. Thus, this creation has its own character, setting it apart from personal creations like my dearly loved Eau Parfumée au Thé Blanc as well as from popular tea scents from other houses like Imagination. This scent here is more complex and has a more varied development. After 1-2 hours of sweet-bitter tea note with wood and contrasting harmonization through the musk, the fragrance undergoes another small transformation, with the fine woody aspects receding more into the background, though they do not completely disappear, and a slightly fruity, perhaps even subtly animalistic-erotic note pushes a bit more to the forefront. The ambrette seeds, this scent chameleon from hibiscus plants, make their appearance and blend perfectly into the fragrance, which is still clearly dominated by black tea. In this form, the scent then gradually fades away. As with other fragrances from Bulgari, no sillage monster is to be expected here. The projection is stronger than that of the less concentrated Eau de Toilette, but the Eau de Parfum is - fortunately - a personal and individual scent and not a room filler. The longevity is decent. Well, and here I must briefly comment on the bottle: in this puristic clarity, it’s a stunner. All in all, a very beautiful scent for the transitional seasons and for a morning awakening in white sheets, despite "pour homme" with unisex potential, perfectly suitable even after breakfast, for example, for work and restaurants, and thanks to the ambrette seeds, perhaps even for a particularly pleasurable arousal in the face of sunrise and glistening morning dew.

… I get up and go to the kitchen, I want a cup of black tea today. In the cupboard, there are exactly two bags left and, as fate would have it, two different ones. Oh well, both into the big cup, turn on the kettle and cut a piece of ginger and toss it in the cup. The water boils, wait a moment until it stops bubbling and pour it over. The aromas released already invigorate me. Take the bags out of the cup. Add a bit of honey and it’s not bad at all with two different tea varieties. In any case, I’m awake now. When applying this fragrance, the first thing that hits the nose is a tea note, underscored by the sharpness and freshness of ginger. Another tea accord blends in with woods. Juicy floral and very slightly fruity accents then mix in. The musk makes this perfume dry, masculine, and mature with a delicate powdery twist. There’s also a bit of green herbal added, but not too strong. The longevity and sillage are good. Here, the house of Bulgari has launched a fine gentleman's tea fragrance, created by Jacques Cavallier-Belletrud, on the international market. Since this perfume is quite mature and not a loud scent, I see it suited for those from mid-twenties to early thirties and beyond. If any lady enjoys a tea scent that is fresh, green, herbal, dry, she is exactly right here. This successful fragrance works just as well in a suit as it does in jeans with a white shirt. Its elegance is showcased in the evening at the opera or theater just as much as at dinner or in a bar. I can’t really imagine it in a club or disco due to its unobtrusive nature, as it would get lost among the loud, aggressive scents. Anyone who enjoys a sharp, fresh, woody, floral, fruity, green, herbal, dry tea scent should take a look at this underrated gem from Bulgari.

...namely Bvlgari Pour Homme EdT. God, how I love this stuff. This is still one of those dinosaurs from the mid-nineties, a time that produced so many cult fragrances (Aqua di Gio, Fahrenheit, L'Eau d'Issey, Le Male, Hugo, Opium, just to name a few). And of course Bvlgari Pour Homme EdT. Unfortunately, after decades, I can only perceive it for about 30 minutes after spraying. So, I thought, let's try the successor/flanker, whatever the new EdP is supposed to be. The DNA has remained. But the new EdP is sharper, a bit rougher, and therefore likely comes across as somewhat more characterful, perhaps even more masculine, than the EdT. Just like black tea is often stronger, more robust, and darker than green tea. Both are tea, but still different. Still: No sweetness. No powder. Thank God Bvlgari has not followed the current trend of powdery-sweet elixirs with the new EdP, but has positively evolved the old DNA. I still love it! H/S for a freshie is very good, better than the EdT. The spray head has been improved, and the cap feels heavier and more valuable than with the EdT.

When the Bvlgari pour homme EdP was announced, I was immediately very curious. The fragrance pyramid had already lured me in back then, and yet I was torn about whether this scent would be good. Now I can say, yes, I really like this fragrance. The Pour Homme EdT is characterized by its beautifully summery freshness without being too fresh or citrusy.

Transparent, airy, brightly glowing. Aromatic bitter tea, smoky guaiac wood, refreshing ginger. The blend reminds me of typical creations by the perfumer (Jacques Cavallier-Belletrud) that he has also crafted for Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.

This fragrance was already a disappointment for me. Based on the notes and reviews, I was expecting a strong tea scent with a spiciness of ginger, not that I expected too much, in terms of imagination or anything like that... no... but I did wish for something in that direction. It's not bad.

Hello everyone, I recently acquired the Bvlgari Homme EDP and have had several opportunities to wear it - here’s my experience report! It’s great. In my opinion, there are some fragrances that fall into the "For-Me Fragrance" category, which I understand to mean comforting scents that never become annoying and can be worn in any situation. This is one of those.

I received a sample of this fragrance and I am pleasantly surprised by the DNA, H/S. Green, fresh, and slightly woody. The top notes unfold right at the beginning shortly after spraying. After about 1 hour, Pour Homme becomes a bit softer and woodier. It fits perfectly into spring. The longevity is quite okay for a fresh designer fragrance.

A delightful, fresh, underrated green scent! Don't let the "aqua" in its name fool you, this is definitely not a marine or watery fragrance. It is however very tonic and uplifting. During the first seconds, a very classic citrus note is present but the star here is a burst of bitter but delicious orange. A great way to start the day! Aquatonic then turns into a medium sweet, but also spicy green scent with grass, vetiver and fern notes being the most obvious. There is at times a very faint foody aspect to the fragrance, perhaps because of the rhubarb note. Some have noted vegetables notes such as green pepper and celery, and although I can understand the (subconscious?) reasoning behind this, I can't say I have ever experienced it when I used to wear Aquatonic on a regular basis. Which is just as well (-sigh of relief-): nobody wants to smell like a market stall. And you won't, trust me... The drydown is still green (vétiver) and woody (rosewood mostly, I find). But when it kicks off, the far end of Aquatonic's longevity has already been reached. So, to me, Aquatonic is green, leafy and fresh all the way during the middle notes with a round and bright aspect, à la Guerlain Vétiver. There are also definite similarities with Mugler Cologne in the way the fragrance is built and orchestrated. And there are worst things to be compared to than these two fragrances... If you haven't tried Miracle Aquatonic yet, I recommend it.

I received this fragrance as a gift from my mother for Easter about 7 or 8 years ago. She knew about my search for a fresh, masculine scent that was in no way aquatic for the upcoming summer. While the name of the perfume suggests the use of aquatic notes, this is not the case at all. Upon the first spray, memories of 4711, my grandmother's favorite scent, immediately came flooding back. To be clear: I did a disservice to the fragrance. It was the citrusy opening that reminded me of 4711 back then. I felt instantly too young for this scent; it came across as too old-fashioned. I didn't even bother to check the fragrance again after some time. My mother, who had sparked my interest in perfumes when I was just 12 or 13, unfortunately never gifted me anything from the fragrance world again over the years. :o( Three years ago - by then I was using Acqua di Parma's Colonia, Thierry Mugler’s Cologne, and my aversion to 4711 had faded - I rediscovered the fragrance and remembered my superficial approach from years before. I sprayed it on and gave it a sincere chance for the first time. Since then, I have finished one bottle and have two more waiting in the cabinet for their turn. Today, I wore it for the first time this year. At the beginning, the citrus notes hit hard, and after about 5 minutes, something green-spicy joins in - I suspect it's the fern. I can definitely smell coriander on my skin. The citrus notes gradually recede into the background. After about 15 minutes, a woody note appears, and over time the fragrance becomes spicy-woody. It stays this way for about an hour, then the coriander slowly retreats until it eventually disappears completely. Now the citrus notes make a comeback, and I can also smell rose. The woodiness is noticeably reduced in intensity. After about 2.5 hours, I perceive vetiver, and the rose is still faintly present along with the citrus, but not as bright and lemony as right after spraying. The fragrance is now neither greener. It stays this way for several hours, and as the intensity diminishes, the rose becomes more prominent again. I just took another sniff: Rose and wood are what remains on my skin after 13 hours. I usually wear this fragrance in spring, my favorite season. However, it is also absolutely wearable in summer. While I prefer the scent on beautiful, sunny days in spring, I occasionally spray it on warm but not really hot days in summer. Bottle: Nothing extraordinary, but quite attractively designed and fits well in the hand. Sillage: Only noticeably perceptible in the first 60-90 minutes, after which it quickly becomes very close to the skin. Longevity: I am extremely positively surprised! I had sprayed Mugler’s Cologne on the other arm for comparison, but this one is - at least on my skin - a bit weaker than L’Aquatonic. However, after about 7 hours, the magic of L’Aquatonic is pretty much over, and except for the wearer, no one else perceives the fragrance anymore.

I was a little dubious about Rose Splendide at first. I was wondering how Annick Goutal was going to manage another rose scent when it was already competing with Ce Soir Ou Jamais, Rose Absolue and Quel Amour! Rose Splendide has proven itself a different composition altogether, and one that I am happy to own a sample of. Rose Splendide is in two words, fresh and green. The scent opens very garden-like, rather like the scent of a rose bush rather than the flower. There's even a slight hint of the soil, creating a strangely addictive naturalness. This seems to be a new trend with Annick Goutal, since their other 2010 release, Ninfeo Mio has a similar garden-like feel. This fragrance is original and very unique. I have honestly never smelt a rose fragrance quite like this one. It takes a lot of getting used to, but after some time, Rose Splendide begins to grow on you. Towards the heart, the pear is clearly noticeable, however it is more tart than sweet and fruity. It's like pureed pears and crushed red rose petals. As the scent settles, there's a subtle hint of sweet musk and powder. This is obviously a fragrance that defies the stereotypical rose perfume. It aims to be breath-takingly beautiful and natural, like something you'd find in the wilderness, not bottled up with added synthetics and alcohol. I am amazed that Annick Goutal has gone in this direction, leaving behind its signature, old-fashioned vibe. Rose Splendide's delicate, Spring-like vivaciousness is rather adorable as it sets itself apart from the fruitier rose in Quel Amour! The lasting power is rather good, however I am reviewing the EDP. This new release is worthy of a sniff from all rose lovers alike.

I was a bit surprised to find that Annick Goutal ROSE SPLENDIDE is just as much about magnolia and pear as it is about rose. The opening does smell mostly of rose, but as the fragrance ("eau parfumée" is the concentration indicated on the manufacturer's produced sample"--not sure, actually what that means...) develops, the magnolia and the pear become much stronger. I'd say that the magnolia is on an equal footing with the rose for quite a while, but by the drydown, this ends up being a fairly fruity experience. Not overly sweet, but fruity enough to mention, since some people in the market for a "splendid rose" are bound to be disappointed by what they will regard as the adulterant pear in this composition. ROSE SPLENDIDE is a fine, albeit simple fruity-floral fragrance. It smells very natural, and I would recommend this as a gift to younger perfume users, to help wean them off celebrity scents. It does not really hold a candle to some of the truly splendid truly and mostly rose perfumes readily available, but it is certainly pleasant to wear.

Well, sorry, but if something is called Rose Splendide, or magnificent rose, it should at least smell a bit like rose. Right upon spraying, a wonderful, rich ... pear scent spreads. I love pears, that's not the issue. When I was a child, we had a very large pear tree at home that bore sugar pears. They looked like Williams pears in shape, were grass green on the outside but honey yellow, sweet, and juicy on the inside. This scent reminds me of those pears. A little green comes in as well, and also a flower. But if this is supposed to be a magnificent rose, then I am the goddess Diana. It is a flower, simply a beautifully scented flower, without me being able to identify it. I really like it, I enjoy this pear-grass scent and it suits me. But the name is simply wrongly chosen, Mme. Goutal. But the pear and the lovely green grass note are still there. The longevity for me is no more than 2 hours. That is, with all due respect, simply outrageous for a 100 Euro fragrance. I can tolerate that with Red by A. Basi, but not with a scent from Goutal. Therefore, it only gets 70% from me. I really like Annick Goutal fragrances, but I would only buy a few. This one definitely does not belong to that category, even though I like it.

and had a large cold room where I could collect and preserve all the delicious scents that are often taken off the market far too quickly. Like Rose Splendide. This is a very extraordinary creation that excites me more with each application. At first, I must admit, the scent rather irritated me, which may be due to the fact that one expects a distinct rose scent with that name. As described multiple times below, it turns out differently than one thinks. Right from the first spray, the pear takes center stage and forms a magical connection with the rather shy rose. In addition, I can still perceive a zesty-citrusy note that, as expected, quickly evaporates. Furthermore, I always have the impression of detecting a strong pinch of white pepper alongside the rosy pear, which tickles my nose. This rose-pear-pepper trio remains unchanged until the end, and I can smell the fragrance all day long when sprayed on clothing. On my skin, it lasts about 5 hours, which I don't find too bad. The combination of the fragrance components is special here, but very successful. Rose Splendide expresses pure joy of life for me, and I particularly love the scent in spring when the air is clean and fresh, and this ripe, juicy pear alongside the fine and noble rose fuels the anticipation of summer with its abundance and warmth. It's a pity that it is no longer produced.

How many beautiful fragrance experiences would I have missed without knowledgeable sales staff. I would have quickly passed by this little gem just by glancing at the notes. "Rose Splendide": How many radiant, sublime ones should this be now? The ladies from Goutal have already missed the mark a few times with naming, so let's keep looking - Pear: Thanks, I still have enough "sweet and mushy" from Petite Chérie. Magnolia? Maybe again when I've somewhat overcome my Yves Rocher Magnolia trauma from the 80s. But what I have on my skin now is not exalted at all. It is delicate, fresh, small, and still very green behind the leaves. For me, this is not a gold medal-winning diva that has been fed with three types of pesticides even before budding. I have a robust little vinegar rose on my skin, along with its healthy leaf green in equal measure. This strong impression of chlorophyll makes this perfume my absolute favorite rose scent. No magnolia, no pear, no. I breathe in in in in. I inhale until the CO2 partial pressure drops below the critical mark. No magnolia, no pear, sorry. Edit: We call the little beauty vinegar rose, in the north I believe they say apothecary rose. It is related to the Sylt rose, but as far as I know, not quite as prolific.

Rose Splendide starts immediately after spraying with a citrus-sweet opening. A slightly floral pear quickly comes to the forefront for me, but it graciously yields to the rose and retreats discreetly into the background. After that, the scent doesn’t change much on my skin. So... this doesn’t sound bad so far.

there's a pear tree, blooming blue! I sit underneath it, sniffing Rose Splendide and juggling with pears, the juiciest of which I will soon devour. Luckily, I brought enough napkins, because these pears are sun-kissed and fully ripe, not the brick substitutes from the supermarkets. I smell, as one might have guessed, mainly pears in "Rose Splendide.
A wonderful scent! I smell the sweet rose, but also the sharp aroma of freshly cut grass and what others have described as "pear," which also reminds me of good honey. Definitely a "keeper" for me.

I wanted to own this fragrance even before I had smelled it. I could easily imagine the scent composition, especially for spring and summer. A rose fragrance with slightly fruity-green notes? Mmmmmhhmm.... and I must honestly admit: I also found the bottle super beautiful (but they all are at AG :-)).

......especially because of the fine bottle. But for me, it was just too much pear; it wasn't the fruity aspect that bothered me, but the developing fruit basket that didn't necessarily hide behind the description. Pear, soften for me, I enjoy it occasionally in a fruit brandy, but I don't want it in a perfume, especially when it carries the name Rose ;-)

One would think with a name like the Roman Night and an elegant black bottle that this would be a dark and mysterious fragrance. But other than the name and the bottle, there is nothing dark here. It is just a simple fruity floral fragrance. I have tried three fragrances from the Goldea line and find not one stands out. Though simply pretty, they are also somewhat generic, which is a surprise considering the great Albertos Morillas created them. I have a travel sprayer of this particular scent and while I think this is the nicest out of this line, I don't like it enough to invest in a full bottle. Mulberry, which I am not a big fan of as it has a very syrupy sweet profile, is the most prominent note, with a mixture of barely there floral notes. The black pepper does nothing to offset the sweetness of the mulberry. It just adds a light aromatic quality. Though patchouli is listed, I am not getting that at all, nor anything earthy, which might have been an improvement. I was hoping that the night blooming jasmine and tuberose would be a little more prominent, but they are not. I do enjoy the musky dry down but can only smell it when I sniff my wrist. Longevity is pretty poor too. I only got about two hours of silage before it became a skin scent. When I think of a night perfume, I think of something dramatic, maybe even a little animalic. If they had increased the jasmine and tuberose and toned down the mulberry, this might have fallen into that class. As it is, this is just a day wear type scent, which might work well for someone needing to wear something low key, like at work or someplace where you'll be in close quarters. I highly doubt it will offend anyone because I don't think many people will be able to smell it unless they get very close to you. Overall, while this is okay for a daytime scent, if you are looking for something sexy and mysterious, look elsewhere as this is not it. I suggest you try this before you buy.

If you look at the black and precious bottle you imagine to smell strong and intense night scent....but it isn't so! The fragrance is pleasant, but very light and wearable by day and I don't smell at all the tuberose and night Jasmine notes (at least on my skin). it's a quite good and feminin fragrance , but very evanescent and for this reason I think that the price is too hight in comparison with the product.It's only a precious object to show on the toilette shelf.

This perfume smells strong at first, but within five minutes it evaporates. I smell no tuberose at all, which is beyond strange to me since tuberose is a favorite of mine. I only smell patchouli, which isn’t a favorite. I’m putting this up until we have a cooler day to try it again, but for now I’m not impressed by this perfume at all. Stay tuned for future edits. Sillage after one hour: 0 Longevity: 25 minutes Bottle: misbranded with black Price: $$$$

Good evening, you fragrant bunch. Hm,… let’s rather say you sniffing bunch. When I say “fragrant,” it almost sounds like I’m implying that you smell bad. And since you are all perfume lovers, I don’t assume that you smell bad,… as long as you’re not using bizarre scents like Ylang-Ylang or coriander :D So… now comes Goldea The Roman Night from the Goldea series, of which I only know the Rose Goldea Blossom Delight, which is a nice scent, but not necessarily an outstanding one. Anyway, The Roman Night contains the note “mulberry leaf,” which always reminds me of a specific scene from Bud Spencer and Terence Hill movies, namely how the two are trained to be police officers and then experience their first autopsy of a corpse. Of course, both are tough and watch without flinching, while Bud Spencer offers his buddy chewing gum. When asked what flavor the gum is, Bud Spencer replies “mulberry leaf,” to which Terence Hill responds, “I hate mulberry leaf!” Hence my title for this fragrance, because I always think of this scene when I hear the term mulberry leaf. This may not seem funny to many, but I remember how I used to search for chewing gums with mulberry leaf flavor, especially as a teenager, not to mention that I had no idea what mulberries even were :DD But enough of my rambling for now, I don’t want to bore you, so let’s see how this scent is. The Scent: At the beginning, I smell a rose-like note, which is also quite powdery, but smells all the more beautiful. There’s a fruity-sweet note that I can’t identify. It has a scent that somewhat resembles blackberries, which might be due to the similarity of mulberries to blackberries. However, I would also venture to say that the fruity notes remind me a bit of currants. Additionally, I smell intense floral-sweet notes, namely tuberoses (but also jasmine) as well as earthy patchouli, which starts off weak but seems to become more intense. A little later, another sweetness joins the sweet notes with the musk. The fruity notes gradually fade, but the powdery sweetness remains, as do the floral notes. It actually stays like this until the end and just smells quite nice. The Sillage and Longevity: The projection is quite strong at the beginning and leaves a decent scent cloud. However, it loses strength significantly in the next 30 minutes, but still leaves a small scent cloud, so you’ll be noticed for a while. Nevertheless, I found the longevity to be generally not that high. While you can smell it for over eight hours, for half of that time it seemed a bit weak to me. The Bottle: The bottle is round and shiny black. On the front, you can see the name of the fragrance and the brand in golden letters. The neck is adorned with embedded black stones that resemble the shell of a turtle. The cap is disc-shaped and transparent. Overall, it’s a beautiful bottle that also comes across as elegant. The Conclusion: So, this Bvlgari has turned out to be a very nice fragrance that smells beautifully floral and sweet. While the sweet notes come across as fruity at the beginning, the sweetness becomes “darker” as the fragrance develops and smells of musk, making the scent not only pleasant but also more elegant. Therefore, I would say that this fragrance could be great for going out. Or for the evening in general. But I wish it were a little stronger for that, but well, that’s just how it is. Still, it’s definitely worth a try! So don’t let my title confuse you, because the scent of mulberry leaf here (or the berry scent in general at the beginning of the fragrance) is very nice, and I’m sure that mulberry leaf or mulberries don’t taste bad at all :D (It could also be that I’ve devoured those things thinking they were blackberries, who knows, anything is possible! :D). So… what else? Oh yes,… you can scratch another line in your calendars because this was one of my rare comments on a women’s fragrance where I unusually didn’t complain or grumble about women (or did both) :DD Which, of course, means that next time I’ll have to complain even more!! Well then, I wish you all a lovely evening and see you next time :D

Well Goldea, here we are. We need to talk, you said. Hmm… We’ve been together for exactly a year now. I saw you the winter before, on vacation at the airport. Your bottle was so sexy, black, elegant, and curvy. And your name was so promising: The Roman Night! Okay, I’ve never been to Rome, but I imagine the nights there to be hot and romantic, a bit wicked and mysterious. Yes, my fault, I admit it. A few months later, you made me an offer I couldn’t refuse, 20% off in the sale! I already knew a few relatives from your honorable family, and so you moved in with me. On our first date, we went to a Spanish restaurant, which you shouldn’t do with a proud Roman woman. After an hour, you disappeared, and I was left sitting alone. The second time, I took you to a public viewing, thinking every Italian woman loves football! Yes, I know Italy wasn’t even in the World Cup, but Germany wasn’t either at that point! You left me again soon after. I tried one more time with you, a romantic dinner at an Italian restaurant, I have no idea what you didn’t like, but you were gone faster than a street thief! Oh, that evening it was just too hot for you, sure. You know what, Goldea? I don’t think you’re a going-out fragrance at all. What, you never claimed that? And your name? Well, you can’t help that, you’re right. It comes from the jasmine that blooms at night and from peony and musk that are sometimes black, but to me, they don’t smell very different from the lighter version. The very sweet opening probably comes from the mulberry, and I thought you were just buttering me up with honey. Maybe we just don’t match. Aha, you think so too? Because I once said you smell so much better on my blouse than on me? Not so sweet and a bit cloying but much more delicate, floral creamy, really beautiful, sigh. Do you think we should try again together? Maybe during the day on clothes, when it’s not so warm? Okay, and then we’ll talk about it again!

I love and cherish all the Goldeas - and Roman Night fits perfectly into that collection. It truly reminds me of Roman nights - sitting on the terrace, overlooking the dome of St. Peter's Basilica. The air is mild and soft - time passes more slowly.

Profound and dark, alluring, clean and innocent, with woody accords. Neither a whore nor a saint. A lady of the heart. It was love at first sight. For a long time, I believed I absolutely needed a creation from Bvlgari in my flank collection.

Warm summer night, crickets chirping deafeningly in the nearby park, lights on black cobblestones, cool white wine in a fogged glass, exhaust fumes, a cacophony of voices, heated stones radiate city scent, too elegant for me - doesn’t match with flat shoes. It was nice to meet.

Balafre Brun is a masculine chypre like no other. It can summarily be compared, at least in terms of similarity and olfactory genre, to other classics such as Monsieur by Givenchy and Pour Monsieur by Chanel but compared to these it is denser, more robust, deeper and much more structured. In fact Balafre Brun is characterized by an earthy and bitter, woody and sometimes leathery tone that the other two chypres do not have. In any case, whether you like it or not, it's a perfume that expresses a quality of ingredients that is certainly no longer common today. Even the citrus notes at the opening have an extremely natural and sparkling scent (I have bottles from almost 50 years ago...!), the oakmoss, cedar, tobacco and vetiver with skin arrive immediately afterwards and remain strong and stable for the entire duration on the skin. An aromatic, woody and dry scent tending towards bitter will remain. It smells like a man, adult, mature and self-confident. It has a discreet projection, it can be felt well at a distance of one meter for the first 2 hours or so and it lasts for at least 6 hours on the skin. If you are thinking that having this perfume could perhaps be redundant in a collection where pieces such as Givenchy, Chanel, YSL or Dior are already present, you are mistaken because this Lancome has a very very different structure and base which gives it an aromatic very different and peculiar compared to the other category mates. A great perfume, today unfortunately (or fortunately, given the IFRA restrictions) discontinued and very very difficult to find but, if you like classic perfumes like the ones our dads and grandparents used and you should happen upon a bottle for sale ... I strongly advise you to take it.

The scents of the 80s of the last century have captivated me. Yes, I am a child of the 80s. That doesn't mean I was born in the 80s, but rather that my teenage and young adult years fell in that decade. During this time, my taste, preferences, and aversions were profoundly shaped. This seems to be especially true for fragrances. But the 80s and the scents of the 80s also have a history. Here on Parfumo, I discovered that it is indeed possible to experience fragrances from the past. It is inherent to the nature of things that these experiences are becoming increasingly rare. But they are still possible. I consider myself fortunate to own a bottle of Balafre Brun. This is a rare occurrence and a treasure. Anyone who smells Balafre Brun for the first time quickly realizes that some fragrances from the 80s could have their origins here. At the same time, the roots are clearly visible. Balafre Brun is spicy and earthy, herbal and green. A densely woven carpet of powerful colors. A tall forest with ferns in the underbrush as far as the eye can see. For me, this is a fougère. The first half of the fragrance development is a clear, masculine statement. The question of unisex doesn't even arise. The scent has radiance at the beginning, without being sharp or medicinal. Only in the further development does it become a bit softer, but it retains its strength. After about two or three hours, the herbal notes gradually fade, and it becomes distinctly woody: the cedar emerges. It is so pronounced, especially in rainy weather, that one almost believes they can smell pure cedar oil. It remains woody and green, but with its journey, one is now long out of the valley and into higher fields. It also becomes colder. The scent draws ever closer to the wearer. It stays woody-green for a while, near the skin. Eventually, the fragrance completely disappears. If the scent weren't so precious, I would love to reapply more often. I cannot assess what role the fragrance played in the pricing structure forty years ago. Today, it seems precious to me. I handle it with care. It's incredibly sad that such fragrances are threatened with extinction. I tried to find a current scent for comparison on short notice, so that others could get a more concrete idea, but unfortunately, no luck. I know the new Fougère Royal by Houbigant. It smells much fresher, almost lemony. But I imagine that the original version from 1882, which I of course do not know, is very close to Balafre Brun. All the young people who populate the streets with smartphones and iLive will never experience this quality of scent. Never. What a shame.

Very elegant amber. Lavender really elevates in the opening. Interesting effect here: from afar, this appears a classic, albeit linear vanilla-heavy amber. But upon closer inspection, there's a distinct almost ebony wood accord a bit splintery thanks to smoky styrax. Someone below mentioned "gun powder" and damned if I don't get that, too. I get the sense that Sauvage is more a warm-weather amber due to its general "lightness" attributable to those aromatic accords. Perfectly unisex, as I think all ambers are. Also, pretty unlike Ambre Fetiche, which is much more dense, boozy, and leathery to my nose. That one is the dark, this the light.

A magnificent scent of amber loaded with vanilla and gunpowder. Light the wick of Ambre Sauvage and detonate a firework full of spices and medicinal herbs. This fragrance moves with beautiful grace like a big jungle cat and purrs for a long time on the skin. Like it very much.

There I stood in front of a Goutal shelf. On the top level were the three bottles from the "Les Absolus" line. I had neither seen nor heard of them before. I found the bottle design and decor very appealing. Silently, I contemplated the ensemble. The consultant (we have known each other for some time) said softly: "The one on the right." pfffft.......................... then a deep breath. Top note?... more like a bang, a hammer strike that calls for order. Heart note?... of enormous intensity and warmth. (Pure presence) Base note?... a vibrating oscillation. It starts off extremely concentrated (warm wood, spicy-smoky resins, and pepper full of liveliness). Everything is already present at the beginning, only the "volumes" change over time. First, the warm wood note becomes quieter. The spicy-resinous, almost incense-like tones come to the forefront. This phase lasted for me 4-5 hours. The pepper note is perfectly integrated.
