With this premise in mind: At first spray on my skin, it's sharp, green crushed leaves. It feels almost metallic and mustardy. Thankfully this first stage goes away quickly. It turns into something that smells soapy clean (vintage style) and grass like, fresh. The clean aspect reminds me of freshly washed hands and the grass facet reminds me of the times I used to rip off grass stems in the garden. At this point it has some flowery sweetness to it. Rather than smelling like perfume, I feel this smells rather natural. It changes becoming faint and delicate. It smells like taking a stroll in the sunny countryside, of tiny white flowers and what feels like small amounts of green powder from milled dried grass. Kind of a dry herbal feel in the nose. Can you recall the sweetness dried herbs can have? I feel it's like that. Compared to more recent releases, the sweetness in this has nothing to do with the new generation of perfumes, but it's not bitter either. My mom, who supposedly loves the smell of cut grass, doesn't like this perfume! I've asked others, and they tell me it just smells like countryside flowers to them. It stays very close to the skin, meaning I can smell it only if I get my nose on it. Near the end, It has something that reminds me of the smokiness in Palais Jamais. How weird. It's still herbal and I find it intriguing. After all, it's a fresh, more on the dry side, herbal perfume that I think shows it's age. It doesn't last long and it stays close to one's skin. It's very faint, but I think that's the beauty of this perfume. It's very unique and special that I am not sure if I was able to describe it fully. I don't think it's a crowd-pleaser, but I have to agree with the other reviewer that the feelings this perfume conveys are of past days of innocence and purity. So lovely... With all this being said... I wish it was a little sweeter and juicy, I wish the grass aspect of it was stronger and that it smelled of fresh green throughout. I like it and appreciate its peculiarity- but I don't love it as I expected. Perhaps it has to do with the fact that I was born during the times when the concept of a perfume was about sweetness that is not necessarily gourmand but not as unsweet like women's perfume from the 80's. I prefer Fathom V for a grassy perfume but they are nothing alike, not even on the conceptual side. I disagree with who compares it to Eau de Lierre. To me, they smell nothing alike (supposedly they share a note). EdL smells more like Finisterre by Maria Candida Gentile, which unfortunately I do not like at all since to me it smells like sulfuric sea waters (a little eggy). Eau de Camille is nothing like that, fortunately! If you also happen to be asking yourself if Eau de Camille smells like Hedera by l'erbolario, the answer is: absolutely not. They only share the Ivy imagery. If you have read my thoughts up until now on this rare little gem, thank you- and if you'd like, let me and others know what you think of Eau de Camille!

Annick Goutal fragrances are like heaven to me. There is something so distinguishably old-fashioned and classic about them, particularly the more feminine creations from this line. Eau de Camille is a beautiful, delicate floral with green undertones. The greeness in this fragrance is neither harsh nor bitter. It's more of a subtle grassy-ness more than anything else. A very crisp and Summery scent. The jasmine and honeysuckle are really pretty. After an hour or so, the floral blend becomes quite clean and soapy, making it an excellent choice for those that enjoy their florals soft and refreshing. Eau de Camille has been created with love. The perfect gift from a mother to her daughter. There is such a strong sense of purity and child-like innocence conveyed through the composition. I was amazed at how well this fragrance lasted on the skin, especially for that of an EDT. I usually prefer the EDPs for longevity, however in this particular case the EDT suited me fine. Honestly I prefer Annick Goutal's louder scents, however I have come to appreciate all her fragrances, and if I had the money, I would most definitely buy them all. Like some have already mentioned, if strong honeysuckle is what you're after I'd tend to lean more on Le Chevrefeuille for my honeysuckle fix, however for something lighter and prettier, Eau de Camille is perfection.

S Efai blooms only after seven years - we learned that back in elementary school. Of course, that's nonsense, as it suggests that ivy is a hapaxanthic plant. In retrospect, I'm not sure if our teacher simply misspoke - according to my current understanding, ivy actually blooms for the first time after about seven years, but then annually - or if this was one of those cloaked life lessons she liked to throw around. Eau de Camille was created by Annick Goutal for her then seven-year-old daughter, who liked the smell of ivy. And if the ivy was as old as she was, it must have just bloomed for the first time back then. Well aware that ivy does not necessarily smell pleasant when in bloom, I still imagine an ivy-covered wall in full bloom - not with the actual, inconspicuous flowers of ivy, but more splendid, matching the lovely floral scent of this perfume. I think of golden-green garden happiness, wrapped in the late summer September sun. Idyllic, with dancing bees around late flowers and the wild ivy by the west wall. In ancient times, ivy was consistently regarded as a symbol of the joyfully celebrating gods and their feasts, which were often crowned with ivy as much as with vine leaves. And Eau de Camille is a cheerful, light-hearted fragrance, playful and telling of freedom, defying all late summer melancholy. Somehow fitting the image of the seven-year-old girl dancing with the bees, while the adults comment benevolently on the flowerbeds with wine glasses and beer bottles, or discuss the last game of the first local handball team over the grill. A light summer scent that can be worn by both young and young-at-heart - and by those who become more beautiful with age. Eau de Camille is the fragrance that makes the sun sing of summer on this snowy February morning.

I’m not exactly someone who cries easily. I hardly ever weep. The only reading that has ever made me sob was "Kabale und Liebe", the only film ending was the final sequence of "Pay It Forward", and the only song was "Tears in Heaven". And the only perfume that makes tears spring to my eyes spontaneously is "Eau de Camille" by Annick Goutal (thank you, dear Respira, for this experience!). What I expected was tortured tea-bag chamomile (i.e., common cultivated chamomile), which you drink by the liter when you have a cold or repurpose for a facial sauna. But what I got was the floral-spicy, authentic scent of WILD CHAMOMILE. A chamomile that grew everywhere in my area, which I used by the pound as a child: I adorned dogs with it, mixed it into the chickens' feed, cooked "lunch" for my dolls from it, and garnished ice creations made of dirt and sand with it. This wild chamomile has been pressed into her fragrance by Madame Goutal (albeit with the help of entirely different plants). And that’s why I have to cry about it. Especially the wonderfully intense top note (if we can even speak of a top note here) presses on my tear ducts. The heart comes in much softer, and the scent of delicate meadow flowers mixes with the wild chamomile. Beautiful, sunny, delicate, and touching. And then, unfortunately, the magic is over far too soon. Just like childhood. P.S. *crying my eyes out*

I searched for you, under the stones, but I did not find you, in the cold morning and in the night I searched for you, until I went crazy. But you came into my life like a light, healing the wounds of my heart, you made me feel alive again!" (Te busque, Juannes) It doesn't happen often that I can perceive such a wonderful fragrance and at the same time call it my own. Only my beloved rose scents - at least some of them - create a similar effect. Today Camille arrived with me and of course, I tried her immediately. This fragrance is the most beautiful floral scent I have encountered so far, and that's despite the fact that there is no rose in it. I feel like I have been searching for this scent for a long time. It is a magical fragrance; from the very first moment, I am enchanted. I can't stop sniffing my arm constantly. I am greeted with a pleasant, green freshness that also contains a certain spiciness - this is very surprising, as I somehow expected something different. Perhaps it was the name that made me think of chamomile. But here, there is nothing sweet or pleasing, but something completely different. In this greenness, the flowers blend in. They are of such beauty that I almost forget to breathe, so as not to miss anything. Like made by fairies or elves, the scent lies on my skin and spreads throughout the room. Nothing sweet - neither honey, nor vanilla, nor patchouli or anything similar - disturbs this fragrance. It is as if I were on a green island, it is spring, and the island is dotted with natural flowers of all kinds. Wildflowers that draw their strength and scent from the sun, wind, dark earth, and water. It could be green Ireland, so beautifully green is the foundation of Camille. Although I cannot perceive the listed flowers individually, the way the flowers are woven with the green notes is absolutely unique. Although the scent lasts only a few hours - about 4 - 5 hours - I give it 100%, because this beauty, which is hardly describable in words, deserves it. I am very, very happy that I did not say no to this offer from Eternity. Thank you, Eternity, I will cherish it. Such a fragrance always has its place with me.

Honeysuckle (Chèvrefeuille), also known as "Jelängerjelieber," plays a significant role in this perfume that Annick Goutal dedicated to her daughter Camille (for the other daughter, A. G. created Eau de Charlotte).

This is the very first Goutal that I get to test. I have always been curious about these pretty bottles, but I thought that the contents would be too "special" for me based on the descriptions. Camille opens with a whiskey note, in my opinion, and immediately shifts to a very gentle, green direction. I instantly associate it with Penaten baby care products.

We lay on the meadow… And we chewed grass…. Whoever knows these opening lines of the song will be able to follow me or understand me. Veronika Fischer sang it successfully back then, more or less. The Sunday in her song was all too telling and also fitting for me at that time, be that as it may. One has learned to walk again. Upright.

With many fragrances, I am unsure which category to place them in - is it floral-sweet or oriental, is it fresh or chypre, is it floral or rather fruity? With Eau de Camille, however, I am certain, this is a grass-green scent. The fragrance direction "Green" is characterized by notes that remind one of freshly cut grass, fresh herbs, and crushed green leaves, or even moss.

Oh yes, this is something very fine! Finally, a truly floral perfume. The first impression: Like a late spring walk through a park in full bloom. Enchanting floral scents are all that hits the nose. The lilac may be at the center, as a powerful, flowering bush. Perhaps a bit of grass, perhaps some scruffy underbrush, but fortunately only a little creamy musk.

A very resinous, herbal vanilla. The dark green of the packaging matches the scent perfectly. Veridia has a spa or sauna vibe to me: Calming, relaxing and a bit mentholated. On the other hand it also feels witchy, like some mysterious potion brewed from ingredients picked in the woods. While the vanilla in this is light and creamy, the rest of the scent is pretty dark. I smell a lot of dark, earthy patchouli, dry sage, cooling angelica and black pepper. To me this is not much of a dark chocolate scent, I think if you expect this to be a gourmand you might be disappointed. Any chocolatey notes here are thoroughly intervowen with patchouli. Galbanum is not a favorite of mine, I often find it musty and too bitter, but it works in this context. The vanilla tames it. The overall texture is ambery like dried tree sap, which works nicely with the coniferous note of cypress. So, everything feels very foresty with a subtle sweetness that makes it wearable as a perfume. Veridia is not among my most favorite green vanillas ever, it might be a tad too resinous for my personal taste and I also wouldn't pay the steep price even before this got discontinued. But I do like it, it's a very well-done scent if you're looking for an extra-foresty take on vanilla.

You are so wonderful natural modest - simply enchanting my heart warms beats for you because you are so precious and different... -Hans-Christoph Neuert- With the first sniff, I am enchanted ... I immediately had hearts in my eyes :) About the scent: Veridia starts with a truckload of galbanum and woodruff doesn't take long to appear. Wood and powder blend into the green-herbaceous woodruff feeling. And then comes the vanilla ... it is green and refined with incense, patchouli, and resins. This vanilla is absolutely unique and enchanting for me! With the green-resinous-woody-powdery impression, Veridia is sweet but not cloyingly sweet. For me, it is definitely a scent for autumn/winter! The longevity is a good 8 hours plus ... I would rate the sillage as moderate. A beautiful vanilla veil wraps me tenderly and comfortably! Brave men are welcome to try it :) The bottle ... well ... personally too much plastic for me. Yesterday in the ticker, a user said it looks like an urn .... he is right. However, the cap is really beautiful, although it is also made of plastic. Conclusion: Bezaubernste Vanille Green-resinous-woody-powdery it comes! Hearts-in-my-eyes Such a beautiful vanilla dream! Thank you, Morillas :) Despite the high price of this exclusive Bvlgari line, I recommend testing it for anyone still looking for a green magic vanilla ;)

This is always true for fragrances, but with Veridia, this Aristotelian saying immediately came to mind as the top note slowly melted away. Three flashes of thought are now competing with each other: 1. I know this scent, even though I have never tested it. 2. No, I don’t know it like this, but at times it bears a striking resemblance to Estee Lauder's brilliant vintage "Private Collection". 3. It’s so good, why is no one commenting on it here? Veridia had been sitting unnoticed in a box with other luxury Bvlgaris for almost 2 years. I still remember when I received it as a beautifully packaged luxury sample: in the Düsseldorf palatial Bvlgari boutique on Königsallee, where even the doorman could claim the title of "Sexiest Man alive," his suit certainly could. I stepped into the temple, where occasionally (Königsallee doesn’t cost anything, the square meter, right?) there were little display cases, each containing ONE piece of jewelry, unpriced, waiting for the millionaire's wife or the oil sheikh who doesn’t have to ask about the price. Surprisingly/nicely, I was treated like one of the mentioned, even though I was dressed, in my opinion, completely in H&M or worse. I purchased a different fragrance from the quite exclusive La Gemme line for an acquaintance and was added to the customer database. (I’m still waiting for the entry goodie in the form of a cute little diamond or something like that!) In conclusion, I received a few of those stylish samples from the same series. I was able to take a look at Veridia and its siblings at the Kö flagship, but despite the breathtaking beauty of the bottles and the entire presentation, I didn’t give a thought to a blind purchase due to the price and made the mistake at home of putting aside and forgetting the two samples I kept (Veridia and Rubinia). Recently, they fell back into my hands. Veridia is a little wonder: The scent has so many facets that you don’t just think you’re wearing one fragrance. The top note, green and herbal, yet velvety and flattering, morphs into a kind of Double Vanilla with soft wood and fresh woodruff, while the scent develops similarly to the aforementioned Lauder classic, without being identical in a single note of the pyramid (on paper..., but that is patient). Gradually, the scent moves in the caramel-woody direction of Baiser de Russie, has considerable presence, and dances around the aromatic herb field in the garden. If summer were to come back today, I would indulge in a hefty dose of Veridia and head into the woods; then I would be appropriately perfumed, I think. No, seriously: overall a hit. Green-golden the dream bottle, green-golden the scent.

Do you all know this green jelly stuff called woodruff jelly? It is usually served with vanilla sauce - all from Dr. Öddga. I always thought the smell was great as a child. But eating it, no, I never ate it, terrible consistency. Who wants to chew a pudding? My grandma used to make the finest red fruit jelly with sago - you could slurp that. If there was Dr. Öddga pudding, she would whip egg whites and fold them in, which made the pudding fluffier. So I never had to chew pudding. In Spain, I have never seen woodruff pudding. Alberto certainly hasn't either. Sure, you can buy gelatin with fruit flavor, but woodruff seems to only exist in our jelly pudding. Alberto Morillas was so fascinated as a teenager by an interview with Jean-Paul Guerlain in the fashion magazine "Vogue" that he decided to become a perfumer himself. He then joined the fragrance manufacturer Firmenich. This company develops fragrances for cosmetics and food. "There is no perfection in perfumery, and often it is an imperfection that gives a perfume its signature" - what a cool guy Alberto is, and he is right: There is no perfect scent! But now to the fragrance. I spray it on and think the whole time yes, it smells like woodruff, smoky vanilla, but it also has something green. It lingers in the brain for a long time, of course, it has something of Vent Vert. I think it’s due to the galbanum, but as a layperson, I’m just going to claim that. The woodruff note becomes weaker and yes, in the end, it feels like someone added good vanilla to Vent Vert. I have already celebrated Mr. Morillas for Play Intense EDT Man. Although there is no woodruff in it, tonka is not too dissimilar. The truth is, Veridia is close to perfection - at least for me, dear Mr. Morillas. And if you ever find yourself near Munich, I would be happy to cook you woodruff jelly with vanilla sauce, and I have a little sample of Vent Vert, which you can just spray on for dessert.

I have so far tested far too little from Bvlgari's noble “Le Gemme” collection. Somehow, it always seems so fine and luxurious in the few stores where it reigns that I usually thought of jewelry and investments rather than perfume, often tending toward other lines out of false reverence. Now, I finally dared to try Morillas' “Veridia” and pulled out the nose magnifier... “Veridia” is a balsamic-sweet forest witch. Slightly smoky, very soft, super mysterious and special. I don't know any other fragrance that smells like this. Even if slight “Cuir Beluga” vibes can't be dismissed. Still quite unique. Imperial vanilla. Anything but the same in green. Emerald-soft. Anaconda in cuddle paradise. Moss in the damp lap. Milky Way of the old hippies. Dessert of the forest trolls. Modeling clay that empties bank accounts. Artificiality with a brilliant touch. Morillas' mastery once again boldly laid on the table. Creamy Contessa. Druid church. Mildest marzipan. Sympathy sorbet. Highlander. Somewhat leaning feminine. Delicious! Bottle: high glass art Sillage: calm strength Longevity: 8 hours - depends on the nervousness of the spray finger Conclusion: a deep green vanilla patch between muse, fairy, witch, and alieness - simply built differently!

Veridia starts juicy-fruity. Only after the second spray do I pick up on fig. Surprisingly, I find that acceptable. From the very beginning, it is underlined by a gentle creamy vanilla. Over time, the juicy-fruity note fades, and the vanilla takes on slight resinous hints, which then slowly transform into a nutty note.

A fragrance that exhibits contrasts! It has both a bright and a dark side. The bright side is bursting with green notes of galbanum. Like the old desk lamps of yesteryear, casting their cool light over files on bulky desks. The "darker side" consists of resins and patchouli. Smoky, balsamic, and fluffy warm vanilla notes neutralize the strict green as the fragrance develops.

Actually, I wanted to write a statement about this fragrance. However, I couldn't manage to fit my olfactory experience into the given framework, as my imagery tends to become a bit more flowery and elaborate than planned. And Veridia is one of those perfumes that creates a landscape before my inner eye: an atmospheric scent that invites you to dream.

Personally, I find Rose on the Moon to be a very beautiful and elegant fragrance. I don’t see it as challenging or overpowering. On the contrary, it feels rather soft and enveloping, with its creamy sandalwood and delicately vanilla-kissed rose. But since sandalwood and rose are two notes I particularly love in perfumery, your experience might differ…

tested at the spring store in Lyon Bellecour, I was very excited by this collection which contained many olfactory gems, so I hoped to discover new ones thanks to this renewal of the private collection. Rose on the Moon is a really tough perfume, straight away I perceive a sandalwood rose for 30 minutes then the rose takes over and attenuates this combo even making the result pleasant, making me think of coveted duchess probably because of the rose vanilla combo at the end. then the sandalwood only remains after 2h30 making the perfume on the skin very banal, reminiscent of sandalwood 33 and boss private energetic fougère. on the other hand, no evolution on the havit we remain on the rather rare and new notes of the top notes. a fragrance clearly for winter because it is powerful, even heady. The sillage is strong. the staying power on the skin is good for between 5 and 7 hours. on the garment 4 days. my rating of this perfume on skin 4/10 on the outfit 8/10 but too feminine for me

Well, Divinity has arrived in the building. Everything else, previously called divine, is looking a bit faint and dusty. Being not too much in the habit of idolising flowers in a perfume, let alone idolise a 'flowers-only' scent (I'm an overall 'woody oriental' (Lutens!!) worshipper), I am confused by the fact that this perfume compels me to "throw heaps of praise upon it".. So I question myself: Would I want to smell like a goddess? Would I want to own the stature of an empress? Would I want heads to bow in awe and recognition? Hm. Do I bow for Heure Exquise? Yes.

Annick Goutal HEURE EXQUISE is such a complex and compelling creation, constructed of such high-quality components, that it could easily have come out of the house of Guerlain in the early twentieth century, back in the good old days, long before the devastating coup staged by industrial chemists and venture capitalists. Wow, I'm impressed. Unbelievably, HEURE EXQUISE actually lives up to its name. This exquisite chypre-like floral approaches the stratum occupied by the likes of MITSOUKO and ARPEGE. You won't find any sour, synthetic sandalwood here. Du vrai parfum, this is just stunning! Rose and iris mingle with a variety of unlisted chypre notes to produce an intoxicating composition with excellent longevity and big, beautiful sillage.

The use of galbanum in Heure Exquise is outstanding. She's managed to compose a perfume that's absolutely sultry. The soft floral accord pierced and ravished by the galbanum. Rendering a perfume that would've aptly been named Carnal Orchard. Galbanum , in my experience , is mostly used detached whatever accord the perfumer has going in that perfume. Imagine a floral accord and the galbanum note in tandem but on different tangents. But in Heure Exquise the galbanum intertwines, harasses if you will, those shy spoken florals. I recently picked up a bottle of the EdP and have been mesmerized by the craftsmanship deployed in utilizing the galbanum to compose such an animalic scent.

An iris fragrance in my mind, and based upon what I've experienced, is often counteracted with a distinguishable soapiness, heavy powder or an array of other floral notes. Heure Exquise is very different from what I'm used to. This is no Iris Nobile, Le Labo Iris 39 or Chanel 28 La Pausa. I was actually surprised to see iris listed as a note here. When I first smelt this fragrance the dominant iris did not occur to me. I was too fascinated with the overall composition rather than determining particular notes. Upon further reflection, Heure Exquise does have a lovely iris accord. This fragrance is stunningly simple. Somewhat dry, spiced powder with smokey undertones. To me this fragrance is almost animalistic. It has many sensual qualities and it exudes confidence and an element of class. When the iris blends with the turkish rose, sandalwood and subtle spices, the result is almost ethereal. Heure Exquise almost surpasses my undying love for Passion, also by Annick Goutal. Combined with great lasting power and an iris that shines above and beyond many iris scents on the market today, Heure Exquise is a sure winner in my eyes. I cannot wait to get my hands on a bottle. The wait is almost too hard to bare.

Heure Exquise opens with aldehydes, which I did not expect at all. Then, galbanum, and lots of it, accompanied by rose. There's some iris here too, but the galbanum dominates on me, even into the drydown, which is a sweet sandalwood, simultaneously powdery and rounded. Lovely, really.

I fought tooth and nail to get my hands on a vintage-ish bottle of Annick Goutal’s Heure Exquise, and each time I wear it, I am less and less convinced that the juice was worth the squeeze. Yes, the sandalwood in the drydown is gloriously real, yes, the rose is a powdery delight, and yes, the iris is the starchiest, whitest Irish linen tablecloth you ever did touch.

Hi, this scent reminds me of some hundreds ago times of classical Lady having wisdom at Heart connected to mind. Peacefull and comforting nature. Not femme fatale at all or club queen. But this scent is a scent of royal court, large gardens with people enjoying each others company, labyrinth plays on summer day. Old fashioned scent and so stylish.

I cannot add much more to what other reviewers have said about this fragrance already. Heure Exquise is quite simply a drop dead gorgeous fragrance, and if I did not know better, I would be convinced that it is a legendary Guerlain creation.

I have always been a huge fan of Annick Goutal ever since I've started on my scent journey years ago. Her scents have always struck me as very successful reinterpretations of classic combinations of notes from an unusual, delicate and feminine perspective.

First of all, I would like to doubt that Heure Exquise consists only of the components mentioned above. The perfume is far too expressive for that. In the opening, I perceive green but powdery notes, and here I can follow the association with No.19. However, the Chanel scent remains distinctly cooler. The fragrance also reminds me of the floral chypres of bygone times.

... but a beautiful one. In the opening, there is a subtle fresh fruitiness, later accompanied by pleasantly warm, spicy-woody notes, while always maintaining a delicate, unsweetened, and (thankfully) not at all soapy rose. Very harmonious and rounded. The longevity is also impressive; I still detected the scent very lightly on my clothes after two days. If rose had a color, it would probably be cream, apricot, perhaps light red. Not a girlish, kitschy pink or fuchsia, not a cool white, not a bright, eye-catching yellow. Also not a strong red that draws all the attention. This rose does not stand in the spotlight, yet radiates in elegant, unobtrusive, adult beauty. I am surprised, as I have found pure rose scents to be rather boring until now. But perhaps it is like so often in life: You just have to find the right one... ;-)

I can't say no to rose scents, so I gladly accepted the Rose Rose sample. Even in my garden, I am already enchanted by some early but magnificent rose blooms. Just yesterday, I sniffed a palm-sized, apricot-red bloom of my Augusta Louise and was captivated by its full, softly powdery scent. Rose Rose emulates this aroma, only the impression is more rose to nude-colored. These petals are also softly powdered. A green note is added. Could it be the mulberry? I perceive something berry-like - but it doesn’t seem fruity. The mandarin is flowing and aquatic - dew drops on the petals enhance the rose scent even more. Slightly woody notes symbolize the rose stem - and musk bathes the entire plant in sunlight. Moreover, Rose Rose is not soapy. This one spray inspires me to rush to the garden center and acquire two rose bushes - a white Polar Star for dear mother-in-law and a pink Leonardo da Vinci for dear mom. And for myself, a rose nude-colored Carla. I love to let roses speak.

When thoughts float on clouds, your notes give me images, when your veils adorn the air, then I can only lose my heart. To you, I write the ode, to one, like there can be only one, one in which I get entangled, perhaps even for a lifetime. You do what many cannot, allow me amber moments, make me pause in it, unfolding colors, feelings, and soul. You bloom with passion flower muse-kiss, that I simply have to write this. Count the blossoms and check the lines, you like to linger for many hours. You place your hands firmly around my face, but still, I do not see you. I feel your sweetness even more, for you come with great power. You breathe vanilla breath into me, then let me dream and just be, your fingertips with vetiver, no place I would rather be! Long story short: A thoroughbred romantic. A thick syrup with jasmine and passion flowers, flowing over vanilla balls and amber pieces. With wooden sticks, you stir in some vetiver. Ready is a scent for autumn/winter to spring, which envelops densely, softly, nobly, and magically fragrant for many hours. Not overly sweet, but very gourmand, not exhausting but "mood lifting." But above all, not mainstream. Those who are already attracted to Hypnôse or find it too lacking in substance can find a profound and "fuller" variant for cooler temperatures here. And I would bet one of my nose hairs that I sniff jasmine sambac or even an absolute, as it appears in Arden Untold Absolu, or at least a rich and dark jasmine note like in Mauboussin (the pyramid bottle) resonates.

The bottle has the same shape as the Lancome Magie from the year 1950 and is reminiscent of the perfume Eau Legere Hypnose Hypnose. In the top notes, there is orange or orange blossom. The heart of the fragrance is the scent of Hypnose and the base is much nobler and silkier. In comparison to the regular Hypnose: this one does not have the strength and assertiveness, even though it is an Elixir de Parfum. It is much softer and closer to the skin, more subtle, and refined. Extremely long-lasting and definitely not a penetrating intruder. Perfect oriental-woody scent.

Very feminine, the mix of passion flower (and not fruit, thankfully it doesn’t smell fruity at all), woods, and vanilla. The name "Hypnôse Parfum Intense" would have suited the scent well. The fragrance is very harmonious, not a bomb, rather an enticing feel-good scent. Very feminine, but not overpowering. It has the soft sensuality of Kashmir, a velvety touch, and the creaminess of vanilla. It is also Eau de Parfum, like the original, but it is better rounded. I find it to be more velvety. They must have used a different vanilla to achieve that velvety aroma. This edition truly surpasses the original by miles.

So, now that the long-awaited treasure from England has finally arrived, here’s my report. Lancôme isn’t really revealing what’s in the “substance.” Judging by the development of the scent, it definitely includes passion fruit, vanilla, and vetiver. Which flowers and woods meet for the rendezvous, I cannot say. The fact is: The scent profile is very similar to the “normal” Hypnôse, but it is significantly longer-lasting and more intense. What I like about it is the clearly noticeable vetiver note, which blends perfectly with the passion fruit and vanilla, while the vanilla remains subtly in the background. Since I already really like the “normal” Hypnôse, it’s only natural that I also like this variant. The Elixir is a limited edition. I will stash away another little bottle :@)

Foreword: How long have I waited to get my hands on you. Yesterday, I could hardly believe my eyes: The wonderful Sternenklar has fulfilled this dream for me. Thank you once again. If anyone has missed my fragrance stories, you have her alone to thank for that. Therefore, this is naturally dedicated to her. Story: Did you know that there was a time when humans and fairies were best friends? In the past, every child received not only a guardian angel at birth but also a good fairy by their side. And so it happened that Gari also got to know her ward. Gari loved to fly over lavender fields. Every time she carried her delicate wings over the purple sea, she brought her human child a few blossoms. The human child grew, and the bond between them became stronger and stronger. But there was turmoil in the heavenly realm. Humans became greedier, their wishes more selfish. The angels knew they had to act if they wanted to save the Earth. And so they flew over the blue planet, sprinkling their fine angel dust everywhere. The whole world was wrapped in a romantic white. The Ice Age had begun. The fairies were horrified by the decision, but most bowed to the great council and stopped helping humans. Gari was a very gentle being, and she could not abandon her ward. She provided warmth, nourishment, and conjured up a few lavender blossoms whenever her powers allowed. The high council caught wind of this and clipped her magical wings. Gari was utterly unhappy; she had lost not only the lavender but also her beloved ability to fly. One day, the angel of sweet dreams appeared. Ashlemah knew that Gari's dearest wish was to soar into the skies again. She spread her wings and enveloped Gari in the finest angel dust, which surrounded her with a gentle iris scent, and as if by magic, powdery wings formed, lifting Gari back into the air.

During the eagerly anticipated testing as part of a traveling package, this sample (just like the wonderfully beautiful bottle) immediately appealed to me visually because of the purple "gemstone" - and the same goes for the scent. It is a multifaceted, balanced iris fragrance that will surely please many who enjoy such scents with its many facets. In the top notes, both an ethereal, slightly herbal lavender and a zesty fruit juice note, caramel, powdery iris, and already the warm musk note emerge. It sounds like a lot at once, and it is, but it harmonizes beautifully. I have somewhat simplified the harmony between lavender and gourmand notes (in this case tonka bean) in "Twilight" by Lush. I used to think that lavender was rather difficult to incorporate into a fragrance because of its distinct (though wonderful on its own) note... I only found a few fresh-spicy men's fragrances where this worked. Here, however, one can tell that the different lavender notes (herbal, ethereal, caramel, warm, floral) have a "common denominator" with the notes of this fragrance (iris, gourmand notes, musk) and are further developed through them. This iris fragrance does have a somewhat "snobbish," noble, doll-like facet, but due to the pleasant and warm musk notes, it becomes inviting overall. On the other hand, the powdery note evokes associations with delicate baby powder; I would describe the colors of the fragrance as white to satin purple. An iris-powder-tonka-gourmand gemstone that I will probably acquire in the summer in Nice at Galeries Lafayette, should I not manage to get a decant by then! ...the traveling package has thus found a victim :D

One face is the first 15 minutes, during which lavender and dusty-dry iris have their fun. This does indeed remind me of Prada Infusion d'Iris, somewhat softened, or I would agree with Hannah (who has described the scent so perfectly) that the scent progression somewhat resembles Jersey by Chanel. This first face will be quickly missed by one part of fragrance enthusiasts, while the other part, who prefers it more subtle, creamier, softer, and skinnier, like me, would rather skip those first 10 minutes. For that, I love the second face all the more. The fragrance becomes one of the most beautiful cream scents with slight powdery nuances that I have ever smelled. This is likely due to violets, heliotrope, and musk. You can recognize the master of their craft who developed this fragrance, or rather, the masteress. While the Nivea scent itself, or Blue by Wolkenseifen, or even Kind of Blue can become quite annoying at some point, this one remains beautifully skinnier, restrained, with ever so slightly fresh hints of lavender, but so minimal that it doesn't disturb; just like with Jersey in style, but distinctly different in scent. A truly excellent fragrance that once again sparks a desire to purchase. I just don’t wear the first 15 minutes on me.

So Bulgari now has an exclusive series as well. Bottles resembling black amphorae, adorned with gold rims and gemstones - striking, radiant, not exactly subtle, rather dramatic. Ashlemah means "sweet dreams" and is inspired by the amethyst, the symbol of perfect balance. Only four ingredients are listed in the fragrance created by Daniela Andrier: lavender, iris, violet, heliotrope. Upon spraying, the herbal lavender note stands out distinctly and alone for a brief moment. It is aromatic and clear, but is already enveloped in the next moment by a dry, powdery, and somewhat earthy iris root. This is a combination that feels almost a bit aloof, similar to what I first perceived in Jersey. The interplay of lavender and iris appears elegantly restrained and slightly veiled. However, the two delicate gray to light purple, broken nuances do not remain alone for long, and a strong violet rushes forward, momentarily mixing in a bit too dominantly into this discreet interplay and takes the lead role with elbow arguments. By no means is it "the violet in the moss, modest, demure, and fine," but rather a spicy one, with leaves, stem, and stalk, delicately bitter, leathery, and with a slight licorice accord. For a good while, it makes quite a fuss until a balancing veil of musk gently reins in the forward little plant, puts it in its place, and appeals to its team spirit. Now Ashlemah becomes calm, unexcited, grounded. The somewhat combative opening is just a short episode of about 15 minutes. Under the supervision of musk and heliotrope, Ashlemah becomes significantly milder and softer, and the violet performers no longer want to be soloists but harmonize as a team. Heliotrope is used subtly. It adds little sweetness but relaxes the initially quite strong fragrance, balances it out, and leads it back into a calm, gray-matt-blue-light-purple course. Now it is a wonderful scent just to my liking, and this relaxed mood lasts until its gentle fading after many hours. I perceive - if one disregards the relatively intense violet phase - a similarity to the iris-powdery lavender note in Jersey, even though the latter develops as a whole still more delicately vanilla-like than Ashlemah. I would classify the fragrance as feminine to unisex, the longevity is decent, and the sillage is rather close to the body. Suitable for adults. Even though I would have preferred the violet note to be more subdued and the lavender to be a bit less fleeting: Ashlemah is a beautiful fragrance with a delightfully soft-powdery base that is definitely worth testing. It is neither fashionable nor mainstream and avoids the overly common characteristics of fruity, sweet, gourmand, oudy, or oriental. For that alone, Bulgari deserves respect.

As soon as the first alcoholic note fades away, the scent reminds one of something that could be made in a bathhouse from essential oils and flowers. It is delicately floral and slightly musky. On me, it is a lovely aldehydic floral fragrance, primarily rose in the top note. Iris follows as it dries. It is elegant, soft, and soothing at the same time. Nothing extraordinary but beautiful. The bottle is the same. For Peut-Être, I would love to live in an old building, it fits well there. According to my research, the 2008 fragrance is a reissue of the same name from 1937. I have never tested the vintage version, but I would claim that in this version, one can recognize that the scent is not contemporary. Not old-fashioned either, but from another era.

Well, I have to say that this one surprised me. I thought this would be a very easy to wear with no Oud in here but, surprisingly, this has a little bit of that skanky Oud in the background, which is quite good, to be honest. When you spray this you'll be able to smell the rose with some bergamot and a shy tea note. Love this unisex fresh opening! 10min later the tea will dominate the fragrance and the leather accord appears. There's a good accord here. Like the one you'll find in Black from the same brand or even Midnight in Paris but without the rubber note. Excellent! The Oud is there basically since the tea starts to shine. Is giving a skanky yet sexy vibe and later on, the fragrance turns a little bit yummy. It's complex and has the three stages very well achieved! The Oud isn't potent (which for those who don't like it is good and for lovers it's pleasant too) but isn't that synthetic so I really appreciate it. Bravo Mr. Jacques Cavallier! Heavenly! The performance is not beastly. It's suave but I love it that way. I get 7+ hours although with low projection. It's comforting and I love to wear it on a breezy spring/summer nights. The price is very adequate and you can find a 75ml bottle for less than 50€. The quality is great too! I recommend it to everyone that likes Rose-Oud combos with a twist. It's different enough thanks to that Tea note.

Oud and the black tea immediately create a wave of smoky black tea, like Lapsang Souchong, for example. Then the rose oil slowly mixes in. For the brief moment when these three are roughly in balance, it is a smoky tea-rose scent. The black tea then retreats first, leaving behind an oud-rose fragrance, slightly smoky and woody. From here on, the scent quickly pulls back to the skin. It oscillates between oud and rose. Interestingly, it fades out softly smoky and creamy. However, I can't explain the cream. I see the longevity in the medium range at about six hours. The sillage, aside from the first moments, is rather weak. This Bulgari doesn't excite me, but I think it's an oud-rose fragrance that can be worn without being overwhelming.

Here I am, sniffing my hand for some time now. At first, I couldn't quite place the Thé Noir, good - not good ... it was balanced. But now my skin has decided and is giving off a very soft yet strong pleasant scent for me. Not a room fragrance, but I can't express it any other way. The rose is well embedded in a soft wood. I assume it's oud. I have no other experience with oud and have so far avoided all the oud fragrances. Bergamot did not come through for me, which I think is good, as it doesn't quite fit my taste in this blend. Patchouli integrates wonderfully. It actually suits a winter evening, sitting snuggled up on the couch with a great book. The sillage is quite good. The longevity for me is about 5 - 6 hours, which I find surprising for an Eau de Cologne. My conclusion: highly recommendable but rather for winter, and I like it a lot, even though it's currently 24 degrees warm for me.

Even though black tea is the focus in the title, I know other perfumes where the tea note is much more pronounced. On my skin, this scent primarily presents itself as a rose-oud combination. While I have a few perfumes (as a bottle or decant) that contain oud at least in name, some probably also as a scent note - I am really anything but an expert on the topic of oud. Therefore, I will only share my personal experiences with this scent note, which can apparently present itself in quite a few facets. In a few oud perfumes, I perceive a distinct manure note. The most extreme case for me was "Oud Assam" (Rania) - but apparently this perception is very individually shaped. Some perfumers actually appreciate this animalistic-dirty expression of oud, but for me, it’s not appealing at all. It seems to be similar in everyday life. "Spicy country air" can be seen as a somewhat ironic designation for the emissions of freshly fertilized fields in rural areas, but some people actually do not find this smell unpleasant. Ammonia itself is a pungent but not rotten-smelling gas (keyword smelling salts!), which in low concentrations can indeed come across as a bit fresh. The more or less pronounced rotten aspect comes from the hydrogen sulfide that also escapes from manure, which we also know from rotten eggs. In this perfume, I also perceive a very slight manure note. But it is so weak that it doesn’t really bother me; rather, it adds a certain something to this perfume. The following image probably describes best how I perceive this perfume: I am sitting on the terrace of a beautiful, well-kept country hotel with a cup of black tea, surrounded by lush blooming rose bushes. However, in the surrounding fields, a farmer has recently fertilized. A very faint breeze sometimes wafts over to me... But it is so weak that I actually perceive it more as fresh-spicy than truly unpleasant - because the roses are closer and stronger!

Vacation flashback, Day 6 on Norderney: First, I need to rest after a restless night. I couldn't fall asleep well and wonder if it was due to the island's silence. Our usual street concert from the big city is absent. That's good; it brings relaxation. Theoretically… because it always takes a little while for the body to adjust to this new situation, even if it is healing for the soul. Today, I simply stay lying down and read the entertaining little book "The Café on the Edge of the World" in one go. I try to enjoy the silence, which is currently interrupted by loud birdsong. Why do we do this so rarely at home? Time for a long-overdue test: Bulgari - Eau Parfumée au Thé Noir is up next. My first impression: smoky, oppressive oud, with black tea very subtly in the background. Hopefully, it will develop a bit more! So let's see how the scent evolves. In the meantime, I tidy up our holiday apartment and wonder where we get the ability to completely devastate our temporary habitat in such a short time. Even the birds observe a moment of silence in accusation, or was it because a large seagull crossed its flight? A second sniff reveals to me that the scent is still musty. Too bad, I'm just not an oud fan. Only this perfume from Clean Reserve, Sueded Oud, has managed to win my heart. But back to Bulgari: black tea is subtly present, but if I hadn't known that this is a tea scent, I probably wouldn't have been able to identify that note, not to mention the stated rose essence. A bit depressed, I now have to admit that I still find the scent musty after an hour and am a little glad about the low longevity of this Eau Parfumée. Yes, oud, a good idea overall. But in terms of smell, mostly yuck.

Unusual, odd, strange, unique, bizarre, yes, it's true what the other reviewers have said: Bvlgari BLV NOTTE is all of the above--and more! This composition really is one of a kind, yes, in the way that SJP COVET is. BLV NOTTE, too, defies categorization and combines chocolate with an unexpected array of aromatic notes. If I were forced to select a category, I'd have to call this an aromatic oriental fougère, but even that would be misleading. BLV NOTTE is downright eccentric. Do I like it? Well, yes, I guess I do. I find it not exactly beautiful but totally fascinating. BLV NOTTE is both masculine and feminine without being either. It combines aromatic, gourmand and oriental components with green and floral notes. There is so much sheer complexity here that I find myself studying this composition as I wear it, trying to wrap my nose around it, but never quite catching up, as the individual notes come and go and wax and wane in utterly unpredictable ways. Near the end, a strong KENZO-oid baby powder/clean diaper base emerges, but it is much more appealing here, thanks to the admixture of incense. I wonder whether Morillas got in trouble for using a FLOWER building block for a Bvlgari commission... seems a bit like submitting a big chunk of text in term papers for two different classes. (-: Or maybe that's a bad analogy here, since the note in question is basically a Demeter-like facsimile of clean diapers, and diapers long pre-dated Morillas' involvement in perfumery. Anyway, I bought this blind, and I have no idea why, but I am glad that I did because this composition is totally unique. I cannot truly say that I love BLV NOTTE, but I respect its deviant nature and will continue to explore its undulating twists and turns.

This scent contains three notes I am not so familiar with: galagal, tobacco flower and vodka. I suppose that is why I find this scent very interesting. I have had it on my shelf for many years. Usually I wear a lot of other scents but sometimes I use this for a whole week. As soon as I spray it, my nose starts to work and I find myself sniffing my wrist several times every hour. It starts out fruity but with a really intriguing note blended in. This opening lasts for half an hour, and then slowly the flowers declare their entrance. Lovely Iris in a really alluring mix with the acacia and vodka - so strange and exotic. I bet it is the Tobacco flower that leaves this really sweet impression. Finally I land in a base of ginger, a huge favourite of mine. With the amber and chocolate it becomes even more vivid than in a lot of other fragrances. The longevity is really something. Many hours’ journey with this interesting companion. Sadly, this is discontinued. I can heartily recommend everyone to seek this out and buy it whenever possible. This is not necessarily your next favourite fragrance, but it is a different fragrance compared to a lot of the block busters. 39/365

Just the term "Nivea scent" is not enough to describe BLV Notte; it is simply too multifaceted, too elegant, seductive, and sensual. But there is something of the good old mother of all-purpose creams somewhere deep within it, a little note that reminds me... - the color, of course, is also wonderful blue, it matches my rose. BLV Notte EDP is an oriental, but a spicy one. I would initially describe the opening of BLV Notte as fresh and herbaceous - lightly lemony. Bergamot and already the first hint of ginger quickly push you into the base. Suddenly, the scent turns and becomes powdery. Unmistakably there is the iris and the wonderful acacia, which I find in so few fragrances, except in my beloved Sensi, which unfortunately is no longer on the market. The often criticized vodka note completely goes unnoticed for me. With its chocolate note in the base, BLV Notte is not a heavy and burdensome chocolate gourmet scent. The chocolate note is rather bitter - one can expect at least 80% chocolate, and it is completely unsweetened. I find the combination with ginger refined; it brings real sharpness and spice to the base and really heats up the chocolate, and I find this mixture extremely successful. Ginger is quite dominant in this fragrance. Anyone who has ever had this spice in a wok knows what I am talking about. I have had this scent for quite a while and have never gotten tired of it. It existed before the big chocolate scent wave, and by the way, I also find the counterpart for HIM very successful. My little point of criticism: Typical Bvlgari, the longevity; I would wish for more persistence. Despite the slight weakness in longevity, I am now going to stick my neck out and call BLV Notte my personal blue fragrance tip!

Wow, once again a beautiful scent.. People who prefer oriental or animalistic powerhouses might feel out of place here. For me, it always fluctuates; on one hand, I love expressive fragrances with strong sillage and a decent "punch"! But on the other hand, I also adore fine, powdery scents, and they can be delicately floral as well. I especially love it when the entire fragrance transitions into a woody/powdery profile, or like here, slightly leans towards gourmand. This is how you can always get me to soften up, even if the scent doesn't have the strong intensity that is the case here. I don't perceive Blv Notte as creamy, as has been mentioned here before. Initially, in the top notes, I can detect a slightly creamy/soapy note, but after a very short time, Blv Notte becomes sweeter and powdery. The acacia blossom (as I remember it) smells very sweet and slightly bitter; I believe this gives the entire fragrance a bit of freshness, but the scent remains slightly sweet and somehow reminds me of a flower cocktail, where the iris sets the tone. Vodka is indicated in the heart notes; maybe that's why Blv Notte reminds me a bit of something tipsy with flowers? I find this fragrance to be very soft and feminine. In the base, the alcoholic touch disappears, and the sweetness somehow becomes lighter. With this scent, I have the feeling that the different components merge together, resulting in a super fine fragrance concept.

I haven't had a Bvlgari fragrance on my nose for a long time. Somehow, this brand has never really been a favorite of mine,… it's funny, I can't even say why. Yet every time I look at the fragrance shelves again, I seem to skip Blvgari over and over. If I didn't have a sample of Blv Notte, this fragrance would probably pass me by as well. But it's not that bad… The scent: The top note is somewhat spicy, but mainly woody-sweet. I can't immediately tell where the sweetness comes from; the spicy-woody aspect should come from the galangal. A hint of mandarin and bergamot adds a slightly citrusy note, but that quickly fades away. And yes, a light, alcoholic vodka note can also be perceived, but one shouldn't just down the fragrance because of that (I know how you all are, you drinkers! :D), yet it gives the scent a somewhat special touch. A bit later, the fragrance becomes slightly powdery due to the iris, and you can smell an even lighter tobacco note, which quickly fades away, and the scent becomes mainly woody-sweet again. And even in the base, the fragrance remains so, but with dark chocolate, it gains another delicious note, while in the background, there seems to be a light, bitter scent as well. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is quite okay and will be good to smell. However, it does weaken a bit too quickly for my taste, but well, one has to live with that. Yet, especially for a woody-spicy fragrance, I had imagined a stronger sillage. The longevity is very good. I could still smell the fragrance on my skin after more than ten hours. The bottle: The blue bottle is rectangular and tapers upwards. The name of the fragrance is on the front. The neck and cap are chrome-plated, and the brand is embossed on the top side of the cap. It's quite okay. To be honest, I expected a fresh and aquatic fragrance from Blv. At least from the color of the bottle and without looking at the notes beforehand (and of course from the name "blu"). What came out was anything but fresh. Although the scent is not heavy, somehow it can be seen as an all-rounder. In any case, the fragrance is woody and spicy. Together with the powdery and sweet notes, it smells very good, but especially at the beginning (and still in the middle part), it seems more masculine. Blv Notte is a good going-out fragrance, as it has an oriental vibe with its scent direction, and the sweet and slightly powdery notes make it pleasant. And the alcoholic note, which unfortunately only has a slight presence, makes the fragrance smell even better. I think I should be a bit more open to Blvgari in the future and test more from this brand,… of course also men's fragrances, after all, I want to wear a fragrance now and then and not always rave about how lovely women can smell… and speaking of lovely. Yes, the fragrance is nice here, it must smell good on you ladies *sigh* So, feel free to test it. Even if the beginning seems rather masculine…

Finally, it's mine;-) Thanks to Delica's help;-) I came across this scent through a sample, and from that moment on, it didn't leave my mind or my nose. So I first checked locally to see if there were any remaining stocks, but unfortunately, I couldn't find anything.

...I had actually decided differently, but then Blv Notte arrived by post. And with Stylessence, I don't think it fits that well. Great scent and somehow different from everything else I own. Even though it is described as oriental. There's not much to add to the comments below. Creamy, powdery, spicy, not sweet.

I find Kalix's comment so lovely and I actually don't want to disagree. I had a little Bulgari intermezzo today due to the Nivea theme. It's true, at the beginning there is a delightful Aha-cream experience. It's not really Nivea, but definitely a nice cream scent. Later, however, the cream turns into powder, and not just a little.

Blv Notte definitely does not smell like Nivea cream in my opinion. It smells very powdery, and that’s apparent from the first spray, and it doesn’t develop on my skin at all. When I think about it, it does smell like a cream, and quite specifically like a certain diaper rash cream for babies, namely Penaten. I don’t want to smell like that. Next please!

My partner and I agree on a lot of things. Even perfume. But there is a certain category of fragrances that we disagree on: vintage versions of 70s’ and 80s’ successes. I love to spray these opulent and loud fragrances - and he comments on it whenever I do. The code is: “Hon, what perfume are you wearing today?” I have come to know that it means: “ please never wear this again!” His explanation is that it makes me smell like old women in the supermarket. I think I know what he means - but I disagree. It happened again last time I sprayed Ô de Lancôme Intense… this beautiful, complex and surprising fragrance, that I just recently got my hands on. It starts soapy and fruity, a mix of the two that is so well done I have not met it in a fragrance made after 2000. I suppose that is the ‘old woman’ note. This then really explodes into a lot of flowers - warming up and then - POW! It makes me think of me standing with a huge bouquet of flowers and smelling from different angles, swiftly changing. And then, finally, the base appears with its amber/musk/cedar. The whole journey reminds me of Estée Lauder’s Beautiful EdP. But ÔdLI is a bit naughtier… a bit more sexy. Even though we do not agree, my partner and I, this one gets to stay in my collection. Year 2, 24/365

Powdery spicy floral scent, very intense. Galbanum peeks out cheekily, unable to be tamed. But the apricot is slowly catching up. Yet the hyacinth overtakes them all. On the way to the fragrance Eldorado, shrouded in legend, hard to reach. But Lancôme has managed to lead its aromas there. A huge crowd of flowers trails behind the "leaders," initially a bit sluggish, but in the face of the "greens," "powder beings," and fruits rolling ahead like nimble balls, they now hurry to catch up. Among them, brightly ringing lily of the valley, roses in festive Sunday attire, shyly presenting jasmine, royally striding carnations, and many more. But they must cross a valley where woodland companions reside, who are to accompany them on their journey. Moss joins in, wobbling in as a dark green cushion, flanked and supported by large cedars and amberwood trees, which in turn house small musk creatures. Now almost everyone is together, continuing to wander side by side, eager for the grand moment of their arrival in the "Land of Gold." But only late do the "migratory birds" realize: "We have been here for a long time... Together, we awaken the legendary spectacle in the 'El Dorado' of fragrances. We are IT, and we are right in the middle of it..

I like that Bvlgari has transformed this fragrance into a jewel and created a scent for young girls from the modern world. Its delicate and intense aroma is capable of awakening every sense and showcasing the beauty of the dreamy and extravagant woman; leaving stiffness and seriousness far away from this fragrance. Omnia Pink Sapphire is presented as a bubbly scent for young women. Its aroma features citrus fruits and refreshing accents like grapefruit as the characteristic notes of the fragrance. In terms of projection, the sillage of this Bvlgari starts quite moderately but quickly transforms into a lighter or airy perfume. It has a fresh, almost ethereal quality and it will not be a powerhouse EDT. Longevity is not great. It is a lighter fragrance, so it’s not a marathon performer. Pink Sapphire is all about spring/summer. It can definitely be worn with casual daywear, both for work and school/university, as it can appeal to a younger set. Do I like Omnia Pink Sapphire overall? It’s okay..., it smells good but doesn’t stand out. It’s pretty enough, but not a sexy kind of perfume. I would enjoy smelling it, but I probably wouldn’t be fascinated by Pink Sapphire. The performance could be much better, but it’s not terrible. As mentioned, it takes a familiar citrus-floral formula and adds some less commonly used notes. It would be a solid option for those looking for a more tropical version of this type of fragrance for summer.

After all the statements, I really have to write a comment. The bottle is well-known, like the other Omnia fragrances. I find the application a bit tricky, as it's hard to aim. The scent is said to be insignificant, boring, a drugstore fragrance. That may be true. However, I don't think so. Tastes differ. The fragrance is fresh but not blue, aquatic. It is fruity, but not an Escada fruit bomb. Here I smell pink grapefruit, immediately followed by something slightly rosy, like peonies. Yet the scent remains fruity, somewhat sweet and light - which I find lovely. Overall, it’s a light fragrance, pleasant, not overpowering. But even a fresh, simple scent can be attractive. You don’t always have to make a statement or burst in the door. Clean, fresh, fruity, subtle can also be appealing. For me, it is currently the case that I really like subtle and clean fragrances. And this one has a wonderful fruity note. Nice for driving away the gray days in winter and getting in the mood for spring. Tomorrow it’s supposed to be 16 degrees with sunshine for me, on February 21st! A perfect day for Omnia Pink Sapphire, garden, sun, relaxing on Sunday. In my statement, I already mentioned that I think the fragrance is great. The longevity is very good for me, by the way. I often have problems with fragrances dissipating quickly. Not here. I can still smell the fragrance on my clothes in the evening. Very good for a light, subtle scent.

With Pink Sapphire, here comes another fragrance from the Omnia line by Bvlgari, which are all nice scents in themselves, but none really stand out, at least in my opinion. I haven't (yet) tried all the fragrances, but of the ones I already know, I have liked Amethyste the best so far. Anyway, Pink Sapphire sounds really good too. Because first of all, I just read that the top note consists of grapefruit, which I always find great as a citrus note. And secondly, Pink Sapphire sounds like Star Sapphire, which, as you might expect, makes me think of comics again. Because the Star Sapphires (there are different ones among them, but all consist of women) are a corps (similar to the Green Lantern Corps, which aim to protect the entire universe from evil) that want to spread and protect love throughout the universe, if necessary with violence... well... :DD But anyway, back to the fragrance! The Fragrance: The fragrance starts with the grapefruit, which smells nice but doesn't come across as sparkling as I thought it would. Nevertheless, it gives off a pleasant scent, and together with the sweet notes that also appear, it almost feels like you’ve sprinkled some sugar on this (previously peeled) fruit to soften the bitter taste :D Since this sweetness comes off a bit spicy, I would say it's from the pink pepper. After that, the fragrance remains sweet, which is likely due to the sweet flowers, but I can't really say which of the listed flowers can actually be detected. I'm not really familiar with frangipani or tiaré :D In the base, I still smell a light grapefruit, while the floral notes have become a bit more inconspicuous, but it still smells sweet. This could also be due to the musk, which, although not particularly strong, is still somewhat detectable. And at some point, the fragrance seems to suddenly weaken and fades slowly, which is also because the vanilla somehow doesn't come into play at all, even though it is listed in the base. Yes, the fragrance is simple, but quite nice overall. The Sillage and Longevity: Unfortunately, the sillage is below average. Initially, it might be detectable from two or three meters away, but soon you'll only be able to smell it up close. And if the weather is a bit cooler, it will probably dissipate even faster than one would like. The longevity is around six hours, which is average. But that's okay in summer. The Bottle: The bottles from this fragrance line haven't changed in years. You still see two round, thick discs that look like they are stacked together. The slightly transparent edge of the bottle is now a fitting pink. The sides are made of metal plaques, each displaying the brand name. The upper part is pressed down lightly to spray, so there is no cap. A beautiful bottle! So, I find this fragrance successful. Of course, it is a bit inconspicuous, especially because of the not-so-strong sillage, but it smells quite nice, even if it could strictly speaking, like so many others, smell like a typical scent for most people. But it belongs to the well-made typical scents where you can't really go wrong, especially if you're looking for a slightly citrus-sweet fragrance for summer and don't mind using simpler or mainstream fragrances; I mean, it doesn't always have to be some niche fragrance :D However, among the casual, summery mainstream scents, I would rather recommend the Aqua Allegorias by Guerlain in summer. Anyway, this fragrance is quite nice as an occasional refresher on hot days. It's too weak for going out. It fits perfectly for daytime. So, would the Star Sapphires perfume themselves with this fragrance? Well, probably yes, after all, it is a nice women's scent, plus the bottle is pink and resembles the violet color of the Star Sapphire Corps, which consists only of women! … Sooo,… you’ve learned something about comics again, he he he, I will turn you all into true comic nerds :DD

I like to call the colorful Omnias "Saturn rings," and I enjoy their original design, and the scents appeal to me as well. Nice, light everyday fragrances that fit perfectly into daily life. Drugstore scents? I'm fine with that. I also like wearing the Aguileras. I don't always need to smell "special." Often, I'm in the mood for mainstream scents. But Pink Sapphire pleasantly dances out of line. The grapefruit is natural and full - very invigorating. The pink pepper blends softly underneath, and frangipani appears delightfully exotic. The vanilla sweetly rounds off the rings. A harmonious round Saturn ring - from the outer Space.

We stood before an old gate, tightly entwined with green foliage. The evening breeze played within it, making the leaves dance, while the last rays of sunshine broke through the vines in golden splendor. I placed my hand on the warm wooden gate and slowly pushed it open. Before us lay a garden - a sea of blooming roses. But my gaze was caught by a single flower: the Centifolia, which shone in deep purple. People called it the Forbidden Rose. But a legend surrounded it: above it reigned a mighty fig tree, deeply rooted in the earth. He loved this rose so much that night after night he leaned his crown towards her, as if wanting to touch her velvety cheeks. But his roots held him fast. He could never reach her. And so he wept in the dark golden tears of love, nourished from his innermost being, sweet as fig jam. The rose, however, opened up and received the tears in her chalice. She transformed and gifted him a scent, as lovely as an invisible kiss that touched his wooden heart. Perhaps this sounds like too much of a fairy tale. Probably, the fig tree himself would have just rolled his eyes. But this is precisely where I find the magic of Forbidden Rose. This fragrance has conjured an entire legend before my inner eye, and not every scent can achieve that. The fragrance notes sound very tempting to me as a lover of sweet perfumes: juicy fig, sweet jam, lush rose, and a warm musk bed. The opening, however, initially seems a bit confusing, as the fig wavers between bitter freshness and fruity sweetness. But it quickly decides on the sweet path. I would have done the same. From that point on, it seems to ripen before my eyes. From unripe fruits, plump, juicy beauties emerge, which eventually burst and pour their jammy sweetness into the blossoms. The rose radiates powerfully, surrounded by an aura that shifts from fresh green to deep dark red. In the end, it loses its velvety petals, which softly fall onto a warm musk bed. Sensual, seductive, almost like a reflection of the forbidden fruit in the Garden of Eden. No coincidence that Adam and Eve reached for fig leaves. Forbidden Rose is officially a unisex fragrance. However, I suspect that Adam would have been rather reserved with all that sweetness. Yet, had he smelled it on Eve, he surely would not have been able to resist her.

I wish I still had my decant of Le Gemme - Onekh to compare this one to side-by-side. They seem very similar from first spray but I believe Falkar goes in a more leathery direction while Onekh stays more in the oudy-resinous realm. Very very dark leather. No sweetness at all. This is a fragrance for a heavy-metal dude in a biker gang. Almost gasoline-like leather with a splash of medicinal oud, and a dose of musk to keep it going.

I secreted this perfume through a sample. I heard a lot of good things about this collection, so my expectations were high. besides, i already have ambero and tygar who are excellent. what a disappointment, one of the most classic ouds, aggressive animal, it reminds me of mysterious wood from guerlain and rosewood oud from dior. to flee, I recommend that you do not buy it blind 380€ for that?it s a joke

Discovered Falkar in Athens at the airport. I was totally thrilled! However, the price was too high for me back then. I had the scent lingering on the strap of my messenger bag for days. Now it was on sale at Douglas. Ordered it quickly. But the disappointment is huge. Much is different. The fragrance seems to have been heavily reformulated. Longevity is really poor. I can spray as much as I want, it disappears in no time. Sprayed the whole polo shirt with it. The next day, there's nothing left to smell.

I was surprised that Le Gemme - Falkar has no reviews at all; in general, apart from "Le Gemme - Tygar | Bvlgari," the rest of the Le Gemme line seems to receive little attention. After testing Le Gemme - Onekh - which I found a bit too synthetic and piercing (see review) - I now continue with "Le Gemme - Falkar | Bvlgari." Another dark oud fragrance from the Le Gemme collection, but it aims to embody the idea of the Brazilian forest rather than capturing the Orient. In this respect, the gemstone is designed with a green shimmer. What is the scent like? - Unlike "Le Gemme - Onekh | Bvlgari," Falkar does not start off smoky dark but instead begins with a sweet freshness, likely coming from the saffron note added to the oud; opulent and strong! - Then a leathery accord joins in, which, together with the oud and yes, dark musk, prevents the scent from drifting into a dark leathery oud fragrance. Instead, the scent maintains a light, fresh oud-leather-musk base. This base smells quite unique, and you find few fragrances that smell similar - even if it's not entirely my thing; but that's exactly what makes the scent almost more wearable and versatile than "Le Gemme - Onekh | Bvlgari." - This contrasting musk makes the scent not only more interesting but somehow less appealing to me in the drydown; the longer the fragrance lingers on the skin, the more this "bright" oud-musk combination emerges, and from my perspective, it then smells synthetic and unpleasant, somewhat inappropriate. Not bad, but for me, it’s somewhat annoying; the bright musk note with the oud and leather is creative, yes, but at times it smells slightly "stale" for a long time, until it then slightly retreats in the final phase of the drydown, allowing the oud-leather combo to regain dominance. - The sillage and longevity are also top-notch with this fragrance, just like with Le Gemme - Onekh ; the scent lasts and projects really well and is definitely in the upper third. Overall, a solid fragrance that has character but simply does not match my preferences and unfortunately also appears slightly synthetic.

Too creamy on the dry down and not much longevity. If you want something jasminy but not strong or multi-faceted, you could still find something better than this. No discernible jasmine left on clothing or skin, after 4-5 hours. And it goes creamy/powdery, super fast. I only recommend this if a light powder scent (maybe for sleeping in?) is your goal. Personally, I think they would do well to change the name to "S.

I purchased this as it’s been described as a sultry gardenia sandalwood, despite it being called Jasmine Noir. Gardenia and sandalwood are a couple of my favorite notes and I am in love with the Patchouli Tentation and strong like with Tubereuse Mystique from the same line. This did not disappoint. Gothic gardenia all the way. The sandalwood blended with tonka bean and cashmere makes a beautiful, soft creamy bed for the gardenia with a hint of jasmine. I get a little patchouli but it’s the powdery soft kind like in Patchouli Tentation. On paper it pulls play doughy, but thankfully not on skin. This really is a beautiful fragrance. It is the weakest and shortest lived of the three that I own from the Splendida line, which is kind of a bummer since I think I like it the most, but I’ve only had my bottle for a short time. Edit to add: Rereading the notes I now realize it is almond, not sandalwood. Typically almond comes off very play-doh on my skin and thankfully this does not! I now know it’s almond adding to the creaminess but it still feels like a smooth sandalwood to me.

When we found something particularly special or outstanding as students, we called it "splendid". Our parents would surely have exclaimed: Fabulous! That's why I was curious about Splendida. Additionally, I also have Mon Jasmin Noir and want to see if Splendida can match its "fragrance" water. I do believe that both scents have their place and do not interfere with each other. The much lighter Mon is suitable for the day, while Splendida is for the evening, when one has dressed up for a night out. However, it is not too heavy or cloying, but exudes velvety elegance. The opening reaches me softly with a plant juice - delicate green and creamy. Jasmine and gardenia are gently muted by milky almond - without the marzipan aroma. A hint of woodiness surrounds the fragrance, and patchouli adds evening depth. Rounded and complete, Splendida is enhanced by tonka. I wouldn't want to exclaim a resounding Fabulous! or Splendid!, as Splendida impresses more with quiet, understated elegance - which I prefer. The right fragrance for a contemplative theater evening, as it indulges the senses and stays close to the skin. For me, a candidate for purchase.

I am surprised that there are relatively few reviews and statements about this fragrance. I don't know if it's because many still have the previous Jasmin Noir in their collection or if the new perfume in the old guise doesn't have the noses on its side. Anyway, I feel a bit sorry for this beautiful scent, which, in direct comparison to its predecessor, is not as bad as I think. And the differences are, at least for me, not really earth-shattering, even though the sweet root is clearly missing. But let's start from the beginning: Splendia Jasmin Noir begins for me with a distinctly noticeable plant sap, not my absolute favorite start, I must admit, but the gardenia quickly softens the beginning and the scent becomes more lovely, yet remains, in my opinion, green. Jasmine is clearly present in the next step, but is gently toned down by the almond. The transition to the woods is fluid, patchouli grounding for me, and the tonka adds a bit of sweetness on top. Splendia Jasmin Noir is not a loud fragrance; it impresses more with quiet but distinct elegance. And it is very attractive with an erotic aura. This develops quietly, sneaks up on you, and then bam, you are lost. Or you find your nose glued to your arm. I actually experience this development with the previous Jasmin Noir as well. The longer the fragrance is on my skin, the more I love it. As for longevity, it is quite good for me, but I find the Splendia version overall a bit quieter, which could lead to the impression that the scent fades quickly. Interestingly, I found the tester in the perfumery to be more intense, and I actually went back to the store a few days later to check if it was really the Splendia and not the old tester. For me, it is a scent for the evening and night, suitable for visiting the opera as well as for the smoky corner pub. It does not shout, it does not need to convince, it does not throw itself at you - it is there and works on its own. But, in my opinion, it is best in the cold winter.

What does a perfume-addicted shopping freak do when all the stores (except for groceries) are closed? The determined perfume tester can only go to Müller... So, let's dive into the fun! To avoid going overboard right away, I decided to try the Splendida series. The first candidate was Patchouli Tentation, and now it's Jasmin Noir's turn. The first impression after spraying it on the skin is green, yet sweet. Cut tulips with vanilla sugar. This striking note quickly fades away, revealing a floral scent, which is the jasmine. It doesn't stay in the foreground for long, as the cashmere wood scent takes over. This lasts until it completely fades away. The scent now reminds me of Casmir by Chopard, but much more subtle. The longevity on the skin is moderate at about 5 hours. On textiles, it lasts longer. If you use 2 to 3 sprays, it's a universally wearable fragrance that wouldn't disturb anyone... very delicate and warm.

Originally, I wanted to get the EdT, even though it is not that popular/well-known. Since the EdT is hardly available, I decided on the EdP Splendida in the souk :) This one is more mystical, darker, more oriental - Noir indeed. I suspect I miss a bit of the licorice from the EdT, which made the scent a bit softer, creamier, milder & sweeter.

Bvlgari EAU PARFUMEE AU THE VERT EXTREME sounds oxymoronic to me.
