And then I wake up. 'Temps des rêves' means 'the time of dreams'. The perfumers at Goutal surely did not have such disturbing school dreams in mind when naming this fragrance (which still haunt me from time to time, even though school is a long, long time ago....please don't tell any psychologists). No, with this scent, one can dream of wandering in herb gardens. Orange blossom, neroli, and myrtle create a lovely hint of spring, a notion. The musk and sandalwood do not lose the lightness. One wants to lie in the grass, listen to the birds, and let the freckles sprout. The short scent progression is linear, and brief; it really lasts a maximum of 3 hours, and that is its biggest flaw. A beautiful scent that took away my fear of herbs, but I will probably dream of others.

This new fresh scent from the house of Annick Goutal feels a bit foreign to me. Beautiful and lovely in its appeal, but foreign. My senses are divided: on one hand, I want to fully surrender to this dream of a fragrance, but on the other hand, I want to find out what makes me feel a bit estranged. The internet and the newsletter from Goutal that just arrived yesterday, introducing fresh summer scents and featuring this one at the top, provide quick answers. It wasn't Camille Goutal and Isabelle Doyen, in their proven partnership, who worked on this fragrance: they have strayed from the house of Annick Goutal! So my little nose wasn't mistaken after all! For "Le Temps des Rêves," Camille Goutal collaborated with two perfumer friends from Grasse, the city to which this fragrance is dedicated. Annick's daughter has thus "dreamt elsewhere" while simultaneously creating a tribute to her mother, who began to live her fragrant dream in Grasse. Annick Goutal experienced her "fragrance apprenticeship" here. Mother and daughter are still deeply connected through scent. Thus, the "lively ode to Grasse and the orange blossom" (quote: AG) has come to be. Now that this irritation of my sensory perception has been resolved, I can finally fully and leisurely immerse myself in this new fragrance composition and discover and "sniff" it. For it is lived summer under the sun of Provence that settles on my skin: delicate yet grounded, balanced and at peace, with natural sensuality and a smile. Yes, "Le Temps des Rêves" is once again a smiling fragrance! Neroli shines from the very beginning and brings comfort. One of the most beautiful and important characteristics of this flower oil; it has a balancing effect; like the gentle movements of a loving hand that smooths away all burdens: how good this tenderness in fragrance form feels. Bergamot arrives lightly and with a fresh spritz, accompanied by the spicy myrtle. Immediately, these three beauties of the south begin to chat and laugh; you can tell they feel very comfortable with each other. They want to go to the orange groves, where orange blossoms will add their fragile yet warm and strong heart to this fragrant gem. These cheerful children of the sun now finally settle with me and even brought company. The already touching warmth of this fragrance dream is deepened and extended by smooth sandalwood. (And yet, here too, the only mediocre longevity remains the weakness of Annick Goutal fragrances!) A caressing musk nuance rounds off a very beautiful, summery-light yet deeply touching fragrance watercolor in soft colors. "Le Temps des Rêves" is a fragrant walk through Grasse; this time not over the vast flower fields outside the city, but a stroll through narrow alleys (with bad paving), where people and houses still know the most beautiful stories and are willing to share them. You sit at a small table, with the first pastis of the day in front of you, and dream yourself into a fragrant impression during a lightly flowing conversation. Here too, the house of Annick Goutal has conveyed its most loving quality and told stories through a charming summer fragrance. A beautiful summer story in a (no longer quite so beautiful) bottle, spreading comfort through references to aromatherapy and making summer and its dreams come alive in scent. As already mentioned, one cannot expect too long a longevity from "Le Temps des Rêves." But this is not uncommon for this brand. But aren’t dreams also just temporary guests? "Le Temps des Rêves" allows these fleeting visitors, who often leave deep impressions, to come alive again at the push of a button. So here it is "after the dream before the dream"!

Le Temps des Rêves, what should I do with you? On the first day, I was already slightly enchanted, intrigued, wanting more, burying my nose deeper into my skin to grasp you, yet you were as unreachable as the horizon. Soft and bright and floating, you refused to be pinned down. White and pastel-colored bed linens flutter on a clothesline in a small garden in a gentle breeze. But is it spring, is it summer? Where am I? You don’t want to reveal it, remaining indefinable like a dream. Are you aloof? No. Not in the sense of being cool. Yet you have something distant, you are not entirely present. That’s why I want to return to you again and again. On the second day, I encountered you once more. And now I felt completely seduced, almost hypnotized. You are creamy-refreshing, smelling clean like the finest soap, hesitantly floral and so delicate - infinitely fine and subtle in every respect. But you are perceptible, a transparent quiet presence. A whisper, a hushed, hidden promise and at the same time the memory of the lightness of carefree days gone by. Perhaps you carry me - and not the other way around - and I float a little.

This is very fresh with an opening of Lemon and earthy Patchouli, A creamy heart of Peach with a sweet undertone of Jasmine. Very light, bright and airy. Also quite Acidic. But the White Florals help to mellow and soften it from getting overly sharp or Citric. Overall a well balanced, silky smooth formulation.

Maravilla is the Spanish word for "wonder." And in a way, it really borders on a wonder - no, actually two wonders: 1. I accidentally found my peach scent that I have been searching for so long. 2. I like it despite the patchouli. I had actually given up my search for a perfume that smells really fine, fruity like peach, after Peau de Pêche was also just a disappointment for me. After all, this one is considered THE peach scent - unfortunately not for me. Well, some time ago I fell in love with "Calaluna," also from the Le Gemme line, and somehow "Maravilla" drew me in magically. I wanted to get to know this citrine-inspired scent. I wanted the summer scent as a counterpart to the winter scent ("Calaluna" is clearly a fragrance for the cool season for me). So, I made my way to Zurich to test "Maravilla," because it is described as citrusy, joy-giving, and summery. However, patchouli in the base made me uncertain, and this is probably also the reason why I waited so long to test it. Patchouli or earthy notes and I are usually at odds. I was quite fidgety at the Bvlgari counter and sprayed away. Lemon, of course, and zesty as I had expected from the description. And then after a while came the joyful surprise! A wonderfully fruity peach joined in and took the lead. Peach clearly plays "first fiddle" here, always nicely accompanied by a light hint of lemon. Patchouli ensures that the scent does not drift into shower gel freshness but remains warm and sunny. My skin smells pure, warm, and somehow innocent like peach, slightly sweet and just, just a bit citrusy. Oh yes, and I almost forgot - very shy in the background is also the orange blossom, which adds a touch of floralness. Longevity is in the middle range (a few hours, somewhat disappointing for a fragrance in this price segment). The same goes for me regarding the sillage, but perhaps that is exactly the intention of Daniela Andrier: luxurious understatement and not loud, ostentatious, and screaming. For me, it is a women's fragrance, but everyone should decide for themselves. Fortunately, we are all still free regarding which scent we want to wear and do not have to adhere to conventions or follow rules. That is almost a "Maravilla" in today's world.

splendia and maravilla - both fragrances from the le gemme series by bulgari, are related to each other. both exude delicious elegance and lightness. what is clear and cool in splendia, is sensual and familiar in maravilla. a scent that perfectly reflects the mysterious glow of citrine: jasmine and peach in a luminous, warm balance fresh and profound at the same time. a masterpiece. now I must unfortunately add: sprayed enthusiastically on a friend, it caused a 10-hour allergic reaction. so, caution!

The fragrances caught my attention, truly jumped out at me, when they were displayed very royally at Jelmoli, each on a pedestal, in the shop window. Very special bottles that personally appealed to me a lot. In particular, the choice of colors suited me very well. Here’s some background information: "The latest line from Bulgari is titled Le Gemme - Italian for gemstones - and includes six top-quality perfumes in dark bottles shaped like Greco-Roman amphorae, representing various semi-precious stones." Today, I finally started the scent test with two of the fragrances. One of them is Maravilla. I actually wanted to test Calaluna, but the saleswoman first handed me a black, elegant piece of paper, and it smelled of sun, summer, sunshine, and cheerfulness. It simply smelled of happiness, refreshing, I instantly liked the scent immensely, as rarely a fragrance in this direction can do. The top note is very citrusy, but not typically citrusy, like a thousand others I’ve smelled before; it’s a very harmonious, deep yellow, cheerful, summery aroma. The scent truly delights, it brings a smile to the face, this harmonious composition achieves that. The peach initially remains subtly in the background, but caresses with a very soft jasmine (and often I really, really don’t like jasmine), it complements the citrus, refines it. It is an exceedingly successful, yellow composition that I would have immediately added to my collection - if it weren't for the price. It’s not as special and unique as Calaluna, where I haven’t smelled anything comparable, but it has a harmonious, summery cheerfulness that I instantly liked immensely. In the base, then, when the citrus has completely evaporated, a gentle patchouli, still embraced by a soft, light jasmine. The sillage is not very pronounced, but the scent itself is finely tuned, harmoniously and cheerfully designed. Again, a must-try candidate :)

Today, I enjoyed the most unusual vetiver that has probably ever been created. Annick Goutal's approach to vetiver is completely different from any other, and it is truly outstanding. What makes it so special is the fact that it is – an aquatic! It has a dark and smoky appeal which comes not only from the vetiver, but from the smoky tobacco base note that shows up right from the beginning. It resembles a little the style of Myrrhe Ardente. However, it is the aquatic note in it that provides a disturbing contrast. Don't be afraid: none of the well known synthetic freshness notes that spoil so many mid-priced aquatics is contained here. Annick Goutal describes this note as "hint of iodine". This iodine does not meet the usual expectations. It is more salty than fresh. And together with the smokiness and greenness of the tobacco and vetiver, it is far away from any idea of mediterrean summer holidays. This Vétiver is an aquatic of the north – it has the grey shades of of Iceland's vulcanic landscapes, the grandness of the Norwegian fjords, and of course, the scantiness of the coasts of Scotland. The iodine flavor gives you the idea of spindrift - froth and rocks on a stormy day. It's music would be the Peer Gynt Suite and Mendelssohn-Bartholdy's Ouverture “The Hebrids”. If you enjoy this vetiver, sit down and have a tumbler of the smokiest Islay malt whiskey you can get while listening and smelling! Only one thing will remind you that this perfume does not come from any of those northern countries – it's true elegance stands for the very best of French perfumery. I had first met Annick Goutal's Vétiver many years ago, long before my passion for perfume started. Somehow I found this was a ladies' fragrance (which it is not) – probably because of the perfect composition. And despite its rough and smoky aspects it is nevertheless classy and elegant. I still think it would be a great choice for a lady who wants an unsweet, tart fragrance that nevertheless provides the grandness and respectability of the great classy florals – only by completely different means. Annick Goutal's Vétiver is partly discontinued. It had to give way to the soft and harmless fig leaf fragrance Ninfeo. You will not find Vétiver in the shops, but it still is available directly at Annick Goutale*s online store. I am not sure if this is planned for long, or if they are just selling off their stock – let's hope for the best. Annick Goutal recommends their perfumes for layering with each other. To give it a more oriental touch, I think, Myrrhe Ardente would surely be a good partner. Annick Goutal's most unusual Vétiver would be a big loss for our perfume culture if it really was completely discontinued. Nobody should have to die before receiving a sample of it!

This Vetiver is such an odd mix of the elements. It’s the surf-and-turf perfume. I hear the words marine, aquatic and salty used often to describe fragrances and I always wonder what they mean. I understand marine when talking about Secretions Magnifiques. In that case it’s the scent of drying and decaying beach debris. I understand aquatic to be a marketing term to describe calone and related aromachemicals. Salty? You got me. Annick Goutal’s Vetiver gives you that blast of iodine at the outset that actually does suggest the scent of crashing surf thrown into the air. It’s very specific. It’s a scent that reminds you of the sea and not of iodine tincture or povidone-iodine. After the sea-air feel fades, though, Vetiver becomes an earthy scent. There is a tonka-coumarin note that combines with the less rootlike aspects of the vetiver to give a nice moist-hay, grassy scent. It smells a bit like a peaty Scotch. All of these elemental notes must sound a bit grim, but there is something that keeps Vetiver buoyant. It doesn’t actually smell floral, but in the heart something emerges that gives an impression that a soft white floral heart would also give. I’m not sure how it’s done, but it’s a great effect.

Annick Goutal VETIVER is a very complex and unusual vetiver perfume. What to my nose is a seriously sinus-clearing component (is that iodine?) combines with a smokiness evocative of Lapsang Souchong tea to pull the vetiver in opposite directions simultaneously. This is not a clean vetiver, but nor is it dirty. And yet, paradoxically, it seems at the same time to be both! Upon donning this perfume, a sample of which was kindly sent to me by MissK, Australia's national treasure and reigning scent maven, I was immediately taken aback. This is Annick Goutal? I thought to myself. Most of the Goutal perfumes I have tried are quite feminine, and the unisex fragrances such as MANDRAGORE and EAU D'HADRIEN display a simplicity of purpose and design. VETIVER, in contrast, is all about contrasts and complexity. Aquatic fragrances do not generally agree with me, but maybe I just have not encountered any good ones? If Annick Goutal VETIVER is classified as an aquatic perfume, then it appears that I have finally met my match: an aquatic perfume which I can and would actually choose to wear. No seasickness, no malaise, none of the telltale signs of aquatics run amuck to induce physiological shock arose during my experience of this perfume. Aesthetically, this composition seems to me to be in some ways similar to Lalique ENCRE NOIRE. However, the iodine used in VETIVER to produce a sort of salty seaspray effect is far more appealing to me than is the je ne sais quoi "ink" of ENCRE NOIRE which makes that fragrance seem somewhat otherworldly--in the sense of alien. The smokiness also makes VETIVER more complex, and while the Lalique is something of an iso-E-super cheat, this perfume is not. I like it a lot.

The first time you spray this you may start looking around, wondering, "what on earth is burning?" Once you realise it's your own skin rather than the house burning down with you inside it, you can appreciate a beautiful, smoky vetiver in all its glory. This vetiver is the dirty kind. It's earthy and concentrated, more true to the real scent of vetiver than any other scent before it. It's bold, brash and sometimes shocking. It really encompasses the scent of nature. Vetiver, rich in saltiness conjures up the image of a hidden beach, complete with seaweed and wet sand. It has a slightly 'inky' smell, particularly towards the heart I found. Annick Goutal's Vetiver has pointed out to me how strange and weird the scent of true vetiver is. Prior to testing this fragrance, I knew vetiver when it was smothered with citrus, green accords or sweetness. In fact vetiver doesn't get much more masculine than this. As a woman I struggle to wear Annick Goutal's Vetiver and do it justice. I would find it far more intriguing on a man's skin I'm sure. I'm just so taken aback by how obscure this fragrance is, and I love it even more for its quirkiness. It's a rather refreshing day-time scent for me, recommended to those that love the smell and feel of natural scents. Vetiver lasted a good six or more hours on my skin and projected relatively well. I recommend.

I found a brand new vintage bottle of this recently and couldn’t be happier (the original, square bottle). It’s truly special. One of the best vetivers I’ve ever put my nose to, it feels like stepping into a coastal reverie. Imagine driftwood washed ashore, sea spray in the air, and the earthy scent of vetiver roots mingling with the ocean breeze. A marine fragrance before marine fragrances dreamed of existing, it pairs the vetiver centerpiece with a briny iodine note that is wholly unique and unexpected. No Calone, no Iso E Super, no Timbersilk in sight here, mercifully. Just a salty, earthy, silky breeze by the seaside, with tasteful sandalwood, subtle tonka, and the suggestion of tobacco leaves blending delicately with a raw, natural vetiver. There’s a smoky undertone reminiscent of Lapsang Souchong tea, adding depth and complexity. Mesmerizing.

Several years ago, when Annick Goutal's original Vétiver was still available, I had a sample of this fragrance. I couldn't remember my impressions from back then at all, but for some reason, the idea of a particularly beautiful Vétiver had lodged itself in my mind.
Goutal's Vetiver marks one of the turning points for vetiver in the 80s - before and after, the category was different: Paris, 6th Arrondissement, Place Saint-Sulpice.

For some time now, a quiet suspicion has been creeping up on me. Now that I have visited the Goutal Boutique in Strasbourg and spoken with customer service in Paris, that suspicion has turned into certainty. The house of Goutal has decided not to continue the Vetiver.

A large, old, earthenware jug in a cool corner of an otherwise sunny terrace, filled to the brim with countless thick, yellow dandelion flowers, along with a handful of other wildflowers and herbs, infused with vetiver, which slowly releases the essential oils over several days while also capturing the scent of the nearby sea and salt marshes.

After I was very taken with the new Les Colognes Series by Annick Goutal recently, it was both coincidence and joy that I also had a sample of the discontinued Original Vetivers in my possession. Unfortunately, this is the exception that confirms the rule for me: here, the original is not the version that is better.

This formulation is drier than Irina. Reminds me of those lovely triple milled Italian Rose soaps. It is Vegetal in texture. It is very musk heavy and smooth. But It lacks any sparkle or shine. Still very clean and organic smelling like a nice soap. Just a little too flattened by the musks. I prefer Prada Rose.

I usually hate leather in any form in perfume; a leather note can chase me away, but in this scent, the leather is so soft and so well integrated that it simply makes the fragrance unique and very innovative, and the best part is that I can't smell any leather. So beautiful and so interesting, I haven't found a fragrance from this brand like this until now. I'm only now reading the pyramid because I tested the scent yesterday and was curious about which dreamy notes might be hiding in the fragrance.. Now I can't stop being amazed. Leather! The scent starts with a very spicy, slightly resinous dark rose. Pink pepper gives the fragrance a light pepper note for the first 30 minutes. The dark rose is sprinkled with a lot of dark cocoa powder, so much that you can only guess the rose, and over this powdery cocoa rose, clouds of balsamic myrrh float.. I can smell cocoa powder and myrrh most distinctly, along with a powdery, velvety dark rose. The fragrance is slightly oriental/powdery/smoky.. I must admit that I didn't smell any leather yesterday and still can only vaguely sense a very soft suede note with good imagination.. I'm not a fan of the brand, but this fragrance might just earn a small spot on my shelf someday. We'll see.. I would almost push the fragrance into the slightly oriental corner. A surprise..

My new signature.I absolutely adore this!Heavenly scent.Feminine,classy,elegant.I love it :) I also adore Tresor classique.This is a more deep floral but sweeter version of Tresor Classique.D.Ropion's version is warmer and adds a stronger tone of rose and vanilla.This version is absolutely desirable.You may wonder what this nose is capable to do.Yes, he can take Sophia Grosjman's inspiration and add his .Two wonderful noses in one.The result?Magnificent!A treasure of desire.:)

You're about to take a trip without leaving the farm. It begins at the farm where Grandpa is burning a pile of hoary leaves that didn't make the compost. They're comfrey and borage, sorrel and thistle, and the herbal smoke assaults your nose followed by the taste of bitter lettuce swirling in your palette. It blends strangely with your perfume, First by Van Cleef and Arpels. A worse combination would be hard to find. At this stage it's, quite frankly, unpleasant. The floral joss sticks mentioned by other reviews are there in abundance, wafting the attar of the funeral pyre. Whoosh! It's gone, you've dropped into the sultry air of the tropics, transported by a Matrix. Now you're engulfed by climbers, Mandevillea and Port St John creeper, the air treacle thick in the tropic of Capricorn. They exert their pressure on the jasmine as vines do on trellis work, insidiously twining. Passion is a boa constrictor. The dry down is beautiful, and it needed to be after the previous two hours. Is it worth the struggle? You must decide. Forewarned is forearmed.

The emotion passion has come to be confused with the expression of passion. Focussing on quixotic symbolic gesture, passion has come to mean any attention seeking act. With a vocabulary borrowed from the romantic comedy, it’s a very long short-hand. Set this in a culture where an action’s value varies directly with the number of people who witness it and passion loses its meaning as an internal state. Annick Goutal’s Passion fits an older definition that describes an emotional state on the spectrum from enthusiasm to compulsion. Yes, there are objects of passion, but passion is what you yourself feel. Passion, the perfume, is gorgeous. It’s a blended floral, a prospect that by itself is hit-or-miss, but it’s also a combination of tropical and seasonal white florals. A failure with this mix of genres could be a disaster, but Passion is exquisite. It is identifiable and has excellent form along with an ambiguity that lends itself to mystery rather than indecision. Mixed florals such as Patou’s Joy and de Nicolai’s Number One show that the ‘prettier’ aspects of a flower, the sweetness and light, are important, but the expertise lies in the perfumer's use of the rawer, less obviously fetching side of the flower. Passion draws on this underbelly of the flower to paint a mixed floral, but because it used both classical and tropical flowers, it has a larger palette to draw on. I don’t find Passion overwhelming or oversized. It is buttery and textured and relaxed. Passion lets its hair down. As for us men, Passion leaves its shirt-tails untucked suggesting not so much informality as the desire for an easy range of motion. Again, passion isn’t about the reading. it’s about the inspired state.

When I first smelt this, I melted. Passion is so unbelievably unique, warm, enticing and sexy. Whilst wearing this scent for only a few minutes, and walking down a crowded street, heads were turning and men were stopping me and asking me what I was wearing. With only one simple spray of this potion on my wrist, I felt confident, beautiful and glamorous. The first initial spray is indeed rather heady and strong, but the scent itself is unlike anything else. The warm vanilla, jasmine and tuberose blend is to die for. The scent reminds me of old fashioned stores filled with lace, rose scented oils and antiques. Passion is such a comforting scent with a slight incense touch in the base which settles beautifully on the skin. Because this fragrance is niche you won't find many women wearing this, hence the reason why I love this fragrance so dearly. The lasting power is fantastic and the warmth in the drydown is unlike anything I've ever tried before.

I find this beautifull scent to reminding me of true nature of passion and longing. Its not the goal to action. But its that feel... when You are missing, longing and feeling inside of You our passionate feels. Its that distance what is existing between You and your loved one. If You can see carefully and deep of the true nature of passion, there is beauty in that space between lovers, in your longing feel. Not in action, not in this scent. This scent reminds me of spiritual passion, longing. Love from Finland.

Passion - gave this one away. Boring white floral. White floral perfumes don't excite me - ylang ylang is a yuk yuk cheap and nasty hippy oil, patchouli and I are not friends and I love the tuberose my mother grows but it rarely translates into a lovely perfume - it has to be done well for me to appreciate it. A strange aspect of this perfume was that it had little smell on me until my body was warmed up - by the sun or through exertion. Then just a boring white floral, stronger as my body got hotter. I think my girlfriend likes it. I do however love AG Ce Soir Au Jamais - a luscious dewy dripping red rose. PS my girlfriend gave it back. she didn't like it that much. Now gone to a new home.

On me, Passion smells like a warm vanilla rose scent- somehow brings to mind Coty Vanilla Woods, a real blast from the past. Passion has far more potency/longevity than do most of the AGs, for which it gets a few extra credit points

It took me a little while to embrace this fragrance. At first, it reminded me of my mother, and I didn't know why. It might be due to the "too much" tick. For a Goutal, this scent is unusually present and intense. Now I am firmly convinced that this is a very sensual and noble-erotic fragrance. It comes across as very velvety and powdery.

This beautiful fragrance was the inspiration for the classic Poison by Dior, and Passion and Dior can be fragrance siblings! It would also fit well: Passionate Poison! Passionately, the top note blows a full force of tuberose mixed with jasmine into my nose. Fascinating and moving, one can also sense ylang-ylang and a hint of vanilla that does not smell overly sweet.

At the beginning of my fragrance commentary, I must preface that the scent seems familiar to me from somewhere, even though I am testing Passion for the first time today. Only, the perfume that I can’t recall at the moment took a while to smell like THIS. It had top, heart, and base notes. This one has everything almost at the same time all at once.

That's a 10 /10 for me. This is what Terre D'Hermes I imagined to be. The "eggy" vibe comes from the real ginger extract mixed with some mineral "Ambergris" notes and Orange peel. Just make your hands wet and then remove the orange peel and eat it, then cut a fresh ginger and chopp it .. that's the "eggy vibe" Which is not a bad thing for me. I just love it ( Sandalwood, Ginger, Orange peel + some extra "dust from the Moon" (in my mind only)

Pyrite is a stone whose name derives from the Greek Pyr, meaning fire. A stone which, if chipped, produces sparks and which represents a very important step for civilization: the invention of fire. This fragrance initially appears cold, reminding us of a stone, but the notes of sandalwood and labdanum mean that it gradually warms up and reveals its "warm" heart. Worth trying, not my type but certainly pleasant.

...will love this scent!!! I had it on for almost an hour, then I couldn't take it anymore and washed it off - as best as I could. I couldn't get through the pyramid, I'm just a softie;) To explain the whole thing: I love black pepper. I can live with white pepper (unless it's already packaged and ground, then I could run away because I think it tastes and smells like asleep feet). I enjoy eating green pepper (oh dear, I'm getting hungry). Aaaand: I have absolutely no affinity for PINK PEPPER. Don't ask me why, it just is. If I get the wrong pepper mix for the pepper mill (it's happened to me twice), and there's even a minimal amount of PINK PEPPER in it, it starts to make me gag. The PEPPER contained here is definitely PINK!!! However, I'm certainly not a benchmark for others who might really enjoy this little fragrance. I also love ginger! No matter if it's drunk, eaten, smelled, just in any form. But it doesn't stand a chance against PINK PEPPER on my skin:(, even jasmine and magnolia completely fade away for me. Lastly, I didn't even catch a hint of the base due to my softie nature;) Summary: NOT FOR ME, but that doesn't mean someone among you won't love it. It's definitely long-lasting; the PINK PEPPER was still noticeable after washing, and it speaks for the fragrance that the nose behind it managed to convey an ingredient so authentically. ;)

Blacamán the Good relates how he came to know and work for Blacamán the Bad, an itinerant confidence man who, dressed in extravagant and preposterous garb, would sell all manner of things to the unsuspecting villagers in the north Colombian province of La Guajira. Hypnose Cologne, or Hypnosis in English, is kind of like Blacamán the Good, Vendor of Miracles. It is the second scent I own from Lancome house, and the other one is Miracle Homme L'Aquatonic. Both are crisp, and allegedly flankers of Hypnose and Miracle pour Homme, respectively, yet they have a different smell and vibe to one another. The appearance of Hypnose struck me because it was eccentric. The bottle is uniquely twisted, and so with the cover, the juice is mint green. The scent starts with an outburst of fresh, zesty aroma, mainly due to the presence of citrus bergamot, lemon, and orange fruits altogether. I appreciated the whole blend. When you sniff it first, it might remind you of other husky citrusy scents around the world. But as it lightens up, the presence of aromatic lavender and pungent coriander gave the whole fragrance a sharpened intensity that warms the citrusy glow. A little kiss of petitgrain makes the heart so soothing, uplifting, and shining at the same time. It is what makes the scent mysterious or hypnotic because you would never anticipate the warmth of lavender by looking at the lightness of the juice. As the scent finishes with the woody accord of sandalwood and cedar, yet lavender still lingering in the background, it further interprets the fragrance to have beaming masculinity that is so prominent and sexy. The whole redolence is unique, as best manifested in its appearance. Unfortunately, by that time, it hardly projects at all. But it is an EDC, so it has to be expected, I guess. Conclusively, this is a lovely late spring and full summer fragrance for day and evening, but you need to reapply during the day. The longevity is not any worse, yet it is below the average, the projection is weak, and the sillage is close to your skin. It can be worn safely at work, and the weak performance won't bother your co-workers. I wish it could fly higher, the overall scent is excellent in my opinion, but performance let you down a bit. -Elysium

A very fresh citrus scent. When applying, there's an explosion of citrus fruits (orange, bergamot and lemon) with a hint of lavender. After a couple of hours the background of sandalwood (and I'm guessing cedar) pushes through a bit more and the citrus takes a step back. So it becomes more of a lavender-woody scent, with some citrus thrown in. Unfortunately by that time, it hardly projects at all ... But it's an EdC, so it's to be expected I guess. All in all, this is a very nice summery cologne smell, but you definitely need a decant for reapplication on the road ;)

Hypnose by Lancome still appeals to me today, but I have always wondered why an EdC was released as well. 1. I have never seen this lighter version in stores, and 2. the original was rather on the quiet side in terms of concentration and strength, making an even lighter version seem pointless to me. And now I also see that there is an Eau Fraiche available. Big question marks over my head. When I finally saw the EdC in the store today, I didn't wait long to test it. And I remain skeptical and extremely critical. The Cologne version does not convince me at all. On the positive side, it swims against the tide and does not release an Intense or Sport version. On the negative side, a diluted good date perfume is no longer a good perfume. You can understand EdCs like Joop Homme, One Million, or Fleur de Male - but not here! What does this watered-down Hypnose smell like? A lot of lavender, some citrus, a bit aquatic. If you know the original, you know it all. This is like a cut film - hands off. At least I don't smell the fig that many detected in the original. Luckily, because I hate that (e.g., in Marc Jacobs). The bottle remains elegant and is a top reason to buy. Sillage and longevity can be completely forgotten here. Even for an EdC, summer, or light - this is a weak number, a laughingstock. Hypnose is and remains for me an intimate, little gem. But please in the original version!

There are so few notes but I feel much more than that. No fruit in the pyramid but I smell a slight smell of fruit (apricot peach and mango smoothie). The benzoin brings a little creaminess. The color of the bottle reflects its content very well, it is bright, a bit honeyed (even if there is no honey). The cinnamon does not bother me here it will season just a bit but without being too present. In drying it becomes creamy and always luminous. I'm not a fan of orientals but here everything is in the subtlety, distinguishes. He is so sensual

The Cinnamon and Sandalwood gel well to create a nice creamy, woody warmth. The Ylang-Ylang and Jasmine soften the wood medley with the Ylang-Ylang being most prominent. The Benzion adds a sweet resinous edge to the formulation. It's fairly Vanilla like. But never goes into full Gourmand territory. As the balsamic Benzion and Woody Sandalwood give the composition an earthy edge and powdery texture.

As already mentioned in the comment on "Noorah," Bvlgari's olfactory journey around the world (and through the world of colorful gemstones) began with 6 fragrances. However, these were not meant to stand alone, as the journey continued the following year into the realm of the Arabian Peninsula. This resulted in three new fragrances that bear the family name "Le Gemme Orientali" and are accordingly infused with oriental notes. The bottle shape, which is meant to resemble an amphora (these were used in ancient Rome for transporting precious materials), has been retained. Since the black part of the bottle is opaque, it protects the fragrance from excessive light exposure. The cap is designed in the color and shape of a gemstone with a cabochon cut. Additionally, a golden mosaic has been added, inspired by the Intarsio Bvlgari jewelry collection. According to the information brochure for the Orientali fragrances, "the name 'Zahira' comes from Arabic and means shining and radiant, an ode to the golden glow of the Imperial Topaz, which rivals the sun." This yellow gemstone is also the one symbolized by the cap. Not many fragrance components are specified, but they still describe the scent quite well. Sprayed on the skin, "Zahira" starts off directly radiant and lush. The creamy Ylang-Ylang is dominant, yet it has a somehow fruity undertone. I can't say exactly which fruits they are, perhaps apricot or, as CarlMacau writes, mango and passion fruit. However, I don't really smell pineapple. Maybe this fruity note also comes from the Ylang-Ylang itself. In any case, the whole fragrance somehow radiates yellow. The floral note becomes increasingly intense over time. Gradually, spices sneak in quietly, yet the scent remains primarily floral-creamy. There isn't much more happening here. The benzoin resin, which according to the brochure is even added in "OrPur" quality, I don't really smell, which could also be because it is beautifully intertwined with the floral notes, and I don't know benzoin in its pure form, so I can't say how it should smell. The fragrance remains predominantly Ylang-dominated, but without being unpleasant or overpowering. The sillage is moderate, making it suitable for daytime wear. I find it appropriate for all seasons, except perhaps the height of summer. However, since it is quite one-dimensional, it wouldn't be something I would wear for long periods. This is more due to my desire for variety and not because the fragrance is somehow annoying. From the Orientali collection (or actually from the entire Le Gemme collection), "Zahira" is my clear favorite. The longevity is very good, fitting for the Bvlgari exclusive collection.

I’ve sprayed myself nicely. It’s once again from Dubai Airport to Hong Kong. Bvlgari has brewed wonderful fragrances with Zahira, Selima, and Lazulia for a juicy €180. Zahira clearly wins in the new trio. I’ve known it since September 2015. The opening is fresh and exotic. That means I smell pineapple, mango, and passion fruit. You could say it’s a multivitamin in a refined form. It seems like there’s a white, light musk in the background. It develops into a sweet and warm Ylang Ylang-amber blend. Spices? Yes, but not really spicy. More subtly Arabic and honey-gold resinous. Medium sillage at arm's length, but quite good longevity of now more than 6 hours. That’s it. A great all-rounder that can be worn anytime. It leans more towards the feminine side for those over 30. I envision a lively woman in a nice apricot dress on the beach in Bali. Pure sex on the beach. Anyone who finds it and loves tropical scents should definitely test it. The bottle is beautiful but tips over quickly due to the heavy cap and small base. A real eye-catcher. So. My flight continues. See you soon, Dubai. Hello, Hong Kong.

For the longest time I was looking for a perfume that smelled like black locust flowers(Robinia pseudoacacia) with little success. Then a couple of years ago I tested this at a duty free store with no expectations and was immediately surprised by how closely it resembled black locust. Once it's settled on my skin it shifts towards the citrus flower/leaf dimension, but that black locust flower nuance doesn't go away. It's beautiful and unpretentious and definitely a love for me.

I chose this scent to break away from my gourmand concept. To get into a late summer mood, I wear the fragrance in the morning, at noon, and in the evening. Lightly sweet and powdery, it settles on the skin. Barely noticeable yet present. However, as soon as I start to sweat, it comes out just as I want it: Fresh, green, and clean. It lasts the longest on clothing. I also have fairly light skin. I don't know if skin type plays a significant role. Lemon blossom is there; I don't know what the scent of sweet pea is like. Due to its volatility, there is hardly any noticeable scent development. Almost as if it is hiding. I would rename it to "playing hide and seek." Nevertheless, a great, almost powdery scent. Throwing myself into the grass and making a grass angel out of sheer joy. I love it!

When the child was a child, it walked with hanging arms, wanted the brook to be a river, the river to be a stream, and this puddle the sea. When the child was a child, it did not know that it was a child, everything was alive to it, and all souls were one. When the child was a child, it had no opinion about anything, had no habits, often sat cross-legged, ran from a standstill, had a swirl in its hair and made no face when being photographed. When the child was a child, it was the time of the following questions: Why am I me and why not you? Why am I here and why not there? When did time begin and where does space end? Is life under the sun not just a dream? Is what I see and hear and smell not just the appearance of a world before the world? [...] When the child was a child, it played with enthusiasm [...] When the child was a child, berries fell into its hand like mere berries and still now, [...] it reached for cherries in the treetop in a high feeling just as it does today, [...] it waited for the first snow, and still waits for it. When the child was a child, it threw a stick like a lance against the tree, and it still trembles there today. ("Song of Being a Child", Peter Handke) When the child was a child, it played with enthusiasm tag on a wild meadow, then smelled fresh flowers and bitter green, got stains on its pants and did not care. When the child was a child, it soon ran further, crushed lemon blossoms with its small hands, sniffed at them and did not know that this lemon scent resembles that of British men’s fragrances, bitter-soapy, it just kept sniffing and did not care about the note. When the child was a child, it could still perceive the finest scents, needed little of it, did not want to wrap itself in clouds and noticed two hours later the delicate transformation of the lemon blossom into feather-light floral musk. When the child was a child, it did not want to sit still for long, finally broke free after three hours in search of something new. When the child was a child, it asked itself: How can it be that I, who I am, before I became, was not, and that once I, who I am, will no longer be who I am? When it finally was no longer a child, it knew that it could be again, anytime it wanted, the one it was, even if only for a while. (With thanks to Stanze for the great scent mail)

Chat Perché is a pleasant fragrance with a slightly playful charm, just like the character of its target audience is meant to be. "For big and small children from 3 years old," says Goutal. Well, you don’t have to be a child to wear this scent, nor do you have to be a child at heart. It is also perfectly suitable for full-fledged adults to wear this fragrance. It starts with a pleasing freshness and a juicy green, reminiscent of the scent of a meadow after the spring rain. The smell is very pleasant and also suitable for midsummer weather. I inevitably associate it with nature, spring, and sunshine. At first, the last raindrops still fall from the sky. After the shower has passed and the sun's rays slowly dry the blades of grass, the meadow flowers release a subtly sweet scent that fits perfectly into the progression of the fragrance. Cozy and soft like the contact of warm cat fur with the skin, the scent guides the wearer into a tranquil spring idyll. Pause, reflect, let the chirping of birds and the buzzing of insects wash over you, spread out a blanket, take a drink from the cooler, grab a book or doze in the sun. Whatever pleases you at the moment. Chat Perché may be relatively inconspicuous and reserved, but even shy fragrances know how to please and find their admirers.

A piece of paper is small place to sprout a linden tree – it still happened in the shop, where I first smelled LES COLOGNES – NEROLI. After donning – everything depends on body chemistry. On my Sister it is linden, acacia and flowers. Beautiful and fresh. My skin answers neroli, fresh citrus scent. Beneath you can find a kind creamy sweetness, to which you have to breath extremely deep, as you wanted to see behind a sparkling neon shopwindow – into the secret reserves of the fragrance. LES COLOGNES – NEROLI is a refined, herbal perfume, rather unisex-masculine than feminine, developing to a choky cloud with a fortunate metallic overtone. Sooo realistic, that I can not love it. Kindness is banned to come up to the surface. Endurance is maximum 5 hours even with generous dosage.

Of course, I can't overlook "Les Colognes" by Annick Goutal. I love many of the fragrances that both ladies create with such taste, and "Néroli" from this line also appeals to me. In aromatherapy, Neroli, one of the most beautiful floral oils, derived from the newly opened blossoms of the bitter orange tree, is known for its special gift. It is a balm for the soul and is therefore often used for anxiety, depression, tension, discouragement, and vulnerability. Even in our "world of fragrances," compositions containing Neroli are increasingly a caress, a support, a comfort = a source of joy. So too is "Les Colognes - Néroli." Both ladies at Goutal are well aware of the gray veil over life, and that is why this charming creation is a particular blessing. As a cologne, "Néroli" comes across lightly: this spicy, slightly bitter-scented floral being is combined here with the heartwarming sweetness of orange blossom. Again, entirely according to the principles of aromatherapy: heart and soul must be particularly cared for. (To be honest: How often do we take the time for that?) Petitgrain, to fully utilize the gifts of the bitter orange tree, transforms this fine duo into a trio that refreshingly feels simply good; it floats a little, it dances a little! The vanilla-laden dark violet flowers of heliotrope (not without reason called "vanilla flower") add warmth and a slightly erotic touch to the light citrus fragrance; this is something that "real" vanilla cannot do alone. Here too, the senses are tenderly touched. This impression is further deepened by a musk note dosed with a great deal of feminine experience. "Les Colognes - Néroli" thus gains a much warming depth than what a "normal" Eau de Cologne usually possesses. It ennobles this genre of fragrances, which are as fleeting as they are pleasant. This light scent does not accompany me for too long; I do not expect it to. "Les Colognes - Néroli" is a fine, graceful being that can chase away light clouds from the mood sky. It is a ray of sunshine in bright gray; however, it is not strong enough to alleviate sorrow or dry tears. For that, other "calibers" from this family must step in. This Neroli creation is like a light coat that protects against a cool breeze but does not provide lasting warmth. That is certainly not its purpose. It is a fragrance that pleasantly envelops from hair to feet; a loving, friendly being. That is one more reason to spray generously! For one thing is certain: this cologne bothers no one and is very, very friendly!

Neroli has been released as a slightly altered reissue in this Cologne series, just like Vetiver and Eau d'Hadrien. But while Vetiver and the unforgettable Eau d'Hadrien are still available in their original versions, at least with a bit of luck, Neroli fans are almost forced to opt for the remake. Is it worth it? A safe bet for summer? Or should you just go for the 3-pack with the other 2 summer favorites (usually available at the airport)? Neroli is simple, easily understood - and that’s what this transparent refreshment aims for. It could just as well have been called Orange Blossom. The scent somewhat reminds me of Jardin d'Amalfi and almost gives Creed's creation a "Run for The Money." The fact that Creed immediately comes to mind is probably due to the Petitgrain coming across very Creed-like here. Even though I prefer its two brothers, I would feel pleasantly accompanied every day in summer if I wore it. You would just need to reapply 1-2 times throughout the day. Unfortunately, you never really experience the sweetness of the base on its own; it only contributes to the pleasant citrus-floral-sweet overall mood of the fragrance. It is also noteworthy that the scent does not become boring due to its consistently high-quality composition. Bottle: simple, with an effective giant sprayer. Sillage: does no harm even to sweaty summer flies. Longevity: fades quickly, quickly reapplied - 3-4 hours on my skin. Conclusion: a brief refreshment, not much to complain about, fleeting, fun, summery sparkling - with the 3-pack from Annick Goutal around Vetiver (my favorite), Eau d'Hadrien (classic) & Neroli (solid refreshment), you are always covered in summer, practically set for life. In this trio, AG really shows its strengths, even if the original versions back then were probably a bit more substantial.

The warm, or rather, the unbearably hot summer days are on their way to us and will drive some of our fellow humans away. To make it a bit more bearable, one can confidently reach for Les Colognes - Néroli, as this will provide a true cooling effect. I would like to express my sincere thanks to our dear Parfuma "Turandot" for allowing me to test this fragrance. Les Colognes - Néroli begins with a wonderfully bitter neroli note that reminds one of chilled tonic water. The orange blossom supports the neroli with a lovely floral touch. Les Colognes - Néroli is the most bitter fragrance that has come under my nose so far, and I like it very much. The top note is perceptible on my skin for about 15 minutes before the petitgrain, with its slightly orangey nuances, settles on my skin, not taking away the bitterness of the fragrance but rather dimming it and making it a bit sweeter. This constellation lasts about 4 hours on my skin before it fades with heliotrope, which has a slightly cherry-like quality, and white clean musk. Overall, the fragrance can be detected for a remarkable 6.5 hours on my skin, which is truly impressive for an Eau de Cologne. The sillage is well-defined in the first 15 minutes and provides the aforementioned cooling effect in summer, but then it doesn't stay too close to the skin, rather just above it, so that with a light breeze, one occasionally catches a pleasant whiff.

Annick Goutal fragrances usually appeal to me because they offer good quality (meaning good ingredients) and a certain recognizability. So I was curious about the "Les Colognes" series (consisting of the three Eau de Colognes "Eau d'Hadrien," "Vétiver," and "Néroli"), with Néroli particularly intriguing me due to its citrus notes paired with white musk. I expected a summer/vacation scent that doesn't require a fragrance license even on warmer days and doesn't overwhelm people and their noses in its environment. Yes, so far so good. My thoughts seemed to be confirmed, as Néroli gives an overall citrus-fresh and lively impression. The namesake along with orange blossom and petitgrain is clearly recognizable and comes across as very green. I perceive a freshness that is almost clean and pure. I also fancy that I can detect a hint of fig, which is not listed in the fragrance pyramid. The "fig" is not yet in bloom, rather green and sour. Now the whole thing is becoming almost too fresh for me. OK, at 30 degrees it might be a blessing, but since we rarely have that, the fragrance should start revealing its base notes (heliotrope and white musk) to make the whole affair a bit warmer and rounder. And just as I am pondering which direction it will take with the base, it’s over...the end...finished...finito! The fragrance is simply "gone." After not even an hour on my skin! I still catch a whiff of the remaining scent, but it only reminds me of the initial freshness. Is this possible? Are there fragrances without a base? Although I know that the biggest drawback of Goutal fragrances is their lack of longevity, I find this particular example to be an affront to us customers! OK, you do get 200ml of Cologne for around €130, but that runs out quickly when you have to reapply every hour. For me, this fragrance is therefore a disappointment and goes down as "the unfinished" in my personal fragrance archive. I hope that it only has this flaw with me and that it hopefully works for others!

~ Inspiration ~ I haven't heard or seen anything about this Lancome perfume until now... ~ Bottle ~ What stands out is the exceptionally curved shape. The gradient from a warm orange to a cool blue evokes summery associations. The name "Calypso" reminds me of a popsicle (Calippo), further enhancing the summer feeling. ~ Scent ~ Sour bergamot flashes briefly upon spraying, but then gives way to ripe, sweet pears, plums, and a bit of pepper that tingles lightly in the nose. After a short time, floral accords in the form of roses, lily of the valley, jasmine, and slightly more robust freesias join in, preventing the scent from becoming too sweet. Delicious raspberries and vanilla form the base note with a hint of patchouli. ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts about 4-5 hours (a bit longer on hair and clothing). ~ Occasion ~ A pleasant spring and summer perfume for the warmer days of the year. ~ Conclusion ~ I wouldn't have thought this perfume was from Lancome. It's very fruity (pears) and floral (roses), which I don't typically associate with this brand - but I like it :)

It’s possible! After recently having constant involuntary encounters with pears while testing fragrances from Marc Jacobs, I was on the lookout for a Williams Christ pear scent that I would finally like. And voila - here it is. Calypso has slipped by me unnoticed until now; apparently, it is no longer available in stores, so it was a great coincidence that I came across a sample of it. (What the name Lollipop is all about, however, escapes me, especially since I thought the divine Miss Carey had claimed that name for herself...) Calypso starts with a fresh-fruity (who would have thought?) note, with pepper adding the necessary kick. The heart note is fantastically deliciously pear-like, and not too sweet. Also not too artificial. More freesia-pear-like. But still primarily pear. I unfortunately don’t know where the plum and all the supposed flowers are hanging out, but I don’t really care. The base is quite nice and wearable with a hint of patchouli and barely noticeable vanilla, even if it doesn’t quite fit the pear impression overall, like with Liberté by Cacharel, where the base also doesn’t fit, otherwise I would like it better. Overall, a lovely summer scent, not too far from Escadas, but more refined and less sweet.

Calypso is a rather unremarkable fruity, fresh perfume. I bought it a few years ago but could never really warm up to it. It was very peach/pear heavy. The other notes remained subtle in the background. I ultimately sold it again.

The fragrance starts off very intense for me and envelops the room as you walk through it. On me, the scent lasted incredibly long; applied at 7:00 AM, 10 hours in the office, then a shower, and the next morning, my girlfriend and I could still perceive it. The scent feels very dark and spicy; I really like the saffron, but it's not to everyone's taste.

Le Gemme - Azaran was, according to my reviews, the absolute last in the series, and maybe that has to do with personal preferences, but I am actually open to any fragrances and try to evaluate neutrally as much as possible. But with "Le Gemme - Azaran | Bvlgari," it even left me a bit speechless.... Now to my impression: - The Le Gemme - Azaran starts off slightly fresh with bergamot, it smells like fresh, green saffron at the beginning. This phase is indeed special, and actually still the bearable side of the fragrance. - Then the cedar comes into play, very green and somehow in combination with the saffron, it creates the feeling of a leather accord. If one did not know the ingredients, one would quickly guess leather and green accords. In the drydown, the fragrance loses me a bit; yes, it is special at the beginning, but somewhat bearable, in the drydown this green leather note simply becomes unharmonious for me. - The longevity and sillage of this Le Gemme, like the others, is very good, the fragrance lasts a long time and projects very strongly. In summary, the Le Gemme - Azaran unfortunately ranks last in my previous reviews of the Le Gemme collection; the fragrance has good aspects in the opening, but overall, for me personally, it leaves an inconsistent overall impression of green leather, which simply does not resonate with me.

I was reading Luca Turin and Tania Sanchez's opinions regarding Gardenia Passion before I went into reviewing this fragrance. They mentioned that Annick Goutal was not fond of gardenias, hence the reason as to why this fragrance is more tuberose than anything else. I'll sum up Gardenia Passion as being a rather loud, yet beautiful white floral. I remember the moment when I first tried this fragrance some years ago. I was so very repulsed by it all. I found it much too strong, and in some ways bitter. I also felt the same way about Fracas then. Currently I'm an avid lover of white florals, especially when they've been constructed well and come minus the synthetic components. Gardenia Passion smells natural and real to me. Almost perfection in a way. While Fracas is too buttery for my tastes, Gardenia Passion is like traipsing through a florist's shop and inhaling various floral aromas. Gardenia Passion is rich and powdery once settled. Believe it or not, this fragrance smells absolutely divine on smokers. Despite the belief that white florals smell like 'old ladies', Gardenia Passion does not fuel this idea and instead comes across as being very seductive and elegant on the skin. I absolutely love Passion by Annick Goutal, and in some ways Gardenia Passion is a more floral and less earthy and/or incensey version. Despite its tendency to be rather strong, Gardenia Passion is never cloying. It has that real classic appeal, something that screams sophistication and femininity. I might also add that the lasting strength is impressive, especially for that of an EDT.

It's so funny that Annick Goutal GARDENIA PASSION features tuberose only garnished with gardenia, while Estée Lauder Private Collection TUBEROSE GARDENIA is much more about gardenia than it is about tuberose! Both are obviously big white flower perfumes, so the names are a warning sign to those with issues with this genre. The tuberose in GARDENIA PASSION is the thick, wilted kind. It smells rather dark and damp to me, as though the flowers are being held in captivity in a huge greenhouse amidst lots of other plant growth, not all of it tuberose, but not very much of it gardenia. The first time I tried this perfume, I entertained the possibility that there had been some sort of decanting error, but now that I have a bottle, it is undeniable that this is essentially a tuberose soliflore. This of course raises all of the usual comparison questions: how does it stack up against FRACAS, BLONDE, CARNAL FLOWER, and the slew of other tuberose perfumes which continue to appear on the market, including the Histoires de Parfums trilogy? To my nose, GARDENIA PASSION is not as good as those creations. The thick, somewhat muddled quality of the tuberose note here makes this composition seem more primitive. It actually reminds me a bit of Honore des Pres VAMP A NY, which I did not review very favorably. I won't say that GARDENIA PASSION is crude, but it is less refined.

"Light-Weakness" is a perfectly fitting neologism. Compliments to Lav! For me, however, the emphasis lies more on weakness, as the methylanthranilate, which is presumably the main contributor to the trombone choir of tuberose and orange blossom amplified by a bass tuba, pushes itself quite prominently to the forefront with its heaviness and sweetness. The trumpets of Jericho could hardly have been louder. I would wish for the theme "Gardenia" to be distinctly greener and fresher and indeed lighter. Gardenia Concrète has a sweet undertone reminiscent of tuberose, but the green of fresh leaves is strongly accentuated. It is noticeable that Goutal has worked with synthetic flowers, and it seems to hold true that a successful gardenia imitation is rarer to find than convincing violet or lily of the valley imitations. At least the task has been solved with a wide margin better than with Tom Ford's Velvet Gardenia, whose fecal note I find disgusting. And despite all the criticism, it should be noted that Goutal has succeeded here in creating an original and exotic union of two fragrance families, namely the green-floral and the sweet-floral, that the result has quality and the scent rightly finds its admirers. Addendum Tania Sanchez takes her critique a step further: Gardénia Passion is not even a gardenia at all. In reality, we have a tuberose here trying to hide behind a thin veil of green foliage - like an uninvited guest in red satin sneaking in for dinner, believing it can hide behind a fern plant. I fear I must join her.

It took me a long time to dare to try a fragrance from Annick Goutal again, as Eau du Sud was quite a bitter disappointment for me. But I was indeed curious, and there were also these two samples. So yesterday I chose candidate No. 2 and tested it again today to make sure that my first impression of Gardénia Passion wasn't misleading. It starts off very floral, but it doesn't go in the sweet direction, which I didn't expect at all. These flowers are lush and heavy, a bit intoxicating, but this is tempered by a green, fresh accord. Well... not so bad at all, this might be something for the summer. However - if only the scent note would stay like this, but of course it doesn't. In the heart note, I perceive something that vaguely reminds me of a cream, even though orange blossom and tuberose don't suggest that. I ponder back and forth about what this scent reminds me of, and suddenly I have the revelation - but it's so far-fetched that I preferred to test Gardénia Passion again today. But the result is the same as yesterday: The heart of this fragrance smells like butter! Yes, you read that right. I could hardly believe it myself, but at least for my nose, this gardenia perfume develops into a butter-flower scent. I don't want that on my skin, even though the base brings another change. There's not much left of the butter scent, now it just smells somewhat green-fresh to me. Without any recognizability. The longevity is okay, it lasts half a day. But since I won't be purchasing this perfume anyway, I don't need to tie a knot in my handkerchief to remind me to reapply.

Lav, thank you so much for allowing me to experience this wonderful treasure. In short: I was so overwhelmed with delight that I couldn't contain myself. I find Gardenia Passion to be lushly floral, but in a very pleasant way. It does have a certain similarity to Intense Tiaré by Montale, but where Montale comes on strong, Annick gently sways with a delicate veil. The opening is lushly floral and then the gardenia develops into a floral-vanilla veil that is simply delicious. The scent is very long-lasting, and even after hours, the tuberose, which is likely responsible for the delicate hint of vanilla, can still be detected. For me, the scent of gardenia always has a protective quality; it envelops me softly and gives me a cozy feeling. I think that Gardenia Passion fits perfectly into the warm season. A beautiful fragrance that surely has many fans and will find even more. Try it, ladies!

Gardenias and I, somehow that just doesn't work. They simply suffocate me. However, this one is the gentlest I have encountered so far. Anyone who knows and likes the scent of fresh gardenias, and who enjoys gardenia fragrances, will love this one. Nothing about this scent is sharp or intrusive, cloying or inappropriate in any way.

I love heavy fragrances and expected a breathtaking scent from this blend of gardenia, jasmine, and tuberose....but not at all! Gardenia Passion is exactly how you would imagine it with this fragrance mix, just a light version, and I don’t mean the longevity, as that is good. But even though it is "only" a light fainting version, I find the scent beautiful!

I tested this perfume and was immediately thrilled. It is truly unique. The scent has a delicate lightness that is unobtrusive. I quickly got myself a 100ml bottle. The fragrance is like a flower garden after the rain - very refreshing!

This is the perfect example of a rose scent. As every Gemme line fragrance from Bvlgari, the quality and blend of the scent is mastered and well done. In the first moments, the characteristic oud (not animalic or dirty) of this line emerges, giving way to a rose that is the undisputed star. If you don't like roses, this perfume isn't for you. Here, a bouquet of fresh roses is perfectly bottled, with exceptional longevity that fills any room you're in. Its a pretty, elegant scent.

When my mother gifted me Ur Tresor years ago, I initially struggled to warm up to it. But as it often goes with "love at second sight," it tends to be all the more lasting. I have since become a fan of the full fragrance and eagerly collect its flankers. L`eau was a must-have in my collection. It has an engaging powdery sweetness, like its original mother, but the fruitiness reaches me in a more subtle way. The juicy peach drips sweetly and deliciously on my skin, but is then guided into a soft floral direction by the rose and jasmine. The heliotrope adds a shimmering elegance that lacks any stiffness. The milky note wraps itself smoothly around, accompanied by warm vanilla and rounded tonka. A pinch of nutmeg adds a very distinctive touch. A heartfelt, closeness-seeking fragrance that unabashedly expresses its femininity. It will not overshadow my Ur Tresor - but it can certainly stand alongside it very well. Today, I already received compliments for my "feminine - erotic" aura - because despite its gentleness, L`eau is not demure. A pleasant completion of my Tresor family.

Rose scent can be, at least for me, a bothersome affair. When the rose comes at me so sharp, harsh, and scratchy, I'm usually out. But rose in fresh form like Rosissismo or in spicy seductive form like Rose Kashmirie, I'm all in. And since we perfumistas are constantly on the hunt for THE ONE FRAGRANCE, I want this in the form of an irresistible rose. Let’s not kid ourselves, if I have this scent, the search will of course continue for the... we shall see. Rose Pompon fulfills an important criterion for me, the rose has no thorns, it is also not a soloist. This fragrance starts liqueur-like and sweet, the tipsy raspberry is garnished with tart currant and a bit of citrus, which is a clever counterpart and tickles the olfactory nerves. It's somewhat like a good pinch of sugar that softens the acidity of tomato soup and gives it the final touch. Then the rose makes its appearance, luscious, resinous, with a slightly powdery vanilla. Fruit and rose dance harmoniously together here, spicy and sensual. Longevity and sillage are very good, please dose with care. And even though I believe everyone should wear what they like… I think most guys prefer this rose on the ladies. The scent will not be intrusive. I have learned this over the years. In the long run, Madame Pompon would be too sweet and cute for me, by the way, it slightly reminds me of Si. And Mr. Pluto was not exactly thrilled with Madame. But for those who love a lovely and sweet rose, this offers a harmonious fragrance. Goutal knows how to do it. One more thing, Rosa Purpurea is worth testing for rose lovers. Initially cool and a bit scratchy... but then this rose blooms... L’Erbolario knows how to do it too. And at an affordable price. Oh, actually I have already found the rose scent.

I sit on the porch and enjoy one of the last beautiful evenings of late summer. On the table next to me, there is a bowl with a few citrus fruits. From afar, I catch a hint of fresh hay, the last time this year. Right beside me is a stack of dry wood, exuding its delicate scent, waiting to be used in the soon-to-be-cooler nights. This is roughly how I perceive this fragrance, although the citrus fruits quickly fade away. Everything is very delicate, almost skin-close yet noticeable, more of a mood than a scent explosion. I am very happy that I was able to test this exclusive and rare fragrance thanks to a very dear parfuma.

Lilaia is the second Le Gemme fragrance that I am testing, having been sprayed with it by a nice employee from Turquoise. As I mentioned with Calaluna, I was not familiar with this luxury series from Bvlgari at all, which is partly because I hadn’t really engaged with the Bvlgari brand, but that will change over time. In any case, each of the six different Le Gemme fragrances is inspired by a rare or precious gemstone. It’s no wonder, as Bvlgari has been one of the largest jewelry manufacturers for a century and is always on the lookout for gemstones. And this fragrance, Lilaia, represents the Peridot, a rare green gemstone. And green are also the main fragrance notes, which makes the scent come across as fresh and, of course, it smells good. The fragrance: The scent starts off greenish for me. And although it is not specified, you get the feeling of smelling a bit of vetiver. Well, a lot of galbanum has been indicated here. I still don’t quite know what galbanum is and especially how it smells, but it should be responsible for the greener notes, as according to the description, galbanum is said to smell somewhat woody/coniferous and balsamic. In any case, the fragrance is also fresh and has a hint of peppermint and citrus notes at the beginning. After that, you can also smell a distinct resin scent, namely mastic, which I find quite pleasant and fits very well with the green notes. Additionally, there is musk, which has only been lightly touched upon and is hardly noticeable, making the fragrance hardly sweet. Overall, I would describe the scent as lightly green-floral. The sillage and longevity: I think Lilaia is one of the weaker fragrances from the Le Gemme Collection, as its projection is quite weak and shortly after spraying, it doesn’t have a good sillage. The longevity isn’t particularly long either, as it lasted about five to six hours on me. The bottle: The bottle looks like a modernized version of an ancient amphora, which was used in the past to transport gemstones among other things. The main part of the bottle body is black with golden decorative stripes. The cap is gem-like green, thus resembling the color of a peridot. All in all, the bottle has turned out very beautifully. Aside from the weak sillage for me, I find the fragrance very pleasant. It smells wonderfully green with woody notes, a hint of fresh peppermint, and a later, slightly floral-sweet note. It fits very well into summer and can be worn for many occasions, but unfortunately, as mentioned, it has become too weak for going out. And although the fragrance is a women’s scent, I think it could possibly also pass as unisex, well, with a slightly feminine touch :D Outstanding it is, however, despite the pleasant scent, not really, which raises the question of whether it is worth the nearly 250 - 300 euros, especially since there are many other fragrances that smell beautifully green and woody. Unless you are a packaging victim, as the bottles look so great :D

I was recently back in my favorite perfume shop looking for a fresh-citrusy, possibly fresh-fruity scent. I tried various ones, some known, some unknown, some heading in the right direction, others not. At some point, my gaze also fell on the Annick Goutal range, and I remembered that I had really liked the description of one of their citrus scents. I wasn't sure if it was the Eau du Sud or the Eau d'Hadrien. So I tried both. The du Sud was a bit too dry-bitter for me, but when I then caught a whiff of the d'Hadrien, I was done for. I liked the scent immediately, without any little annoyance here and there. It was so pleasant that I didn't even have to think for a second about whether I liked it or how much. It went straight to the brain (or wherever scent impressions are analyzed), without detours, and it was clear that no other scent could compare. It hit the scent nerve perfectly :) I was a bit surprised, though, as I thought I had tested the Eau d'Hadrien before and couldn't remember it having impressed me so much at that time. When I asked if the scent was available for purchase (since there was no packaged bottle present), the saleswoman checked the stock and returned with a rounded bottle. I then mentioned that I didn't like it as much as the square one, to which she replied that there was the Eau de Toilette (rounded), the Cologne (square), and the Parfum (also rounded). That clarified a lot for me! I then tested the Eau de Toilette and noticed that it differed significantly from the Cologne (so in my opinion, it is not a scent twin). I didn't like it nearly as much, as it was much more bitter and the citrus note was noticeably muted. When I wanted to order it, I had to find out that it was no longer available for order, as its production had been discontinued :( Scent Development: There is basically none. It is immediately clear citrus, really pure, with a very slight personal comfort nuance that sets it apart from all the pure citrus scents I have tested so far. For example, I really like the citrus scents from Guerlain, like "Eau Imperiale" or "Eau de Guerlain," and I marvel at their delicacy and naturalness. But they don't hit the nerve like this one does. It is certainly not as refined, but rather seems simple and one-dimensional, yet it just suits me. This one-dimensionality is, for me, its strength, as it keeps the first scent impression I love so much simple. Its citrus quality is very clear, almost zesty, but only almost. It is incredibly fresh with a very slight soft undertone, which is not soapy. Its citrus note reminds me a bit of the note in Allure Homme Sport Cologne, Mugler Cologne, or Dior Homme Cologne, but without coming off as artificial. For an Annick Goutal scent, it does seem somewhat unusual, more modern, possibly slightly artificial, but in no way does it smell like glass cleaner, as mentioned in a response to the comment below. I find it a lovely mix of a purely natural and slightly artificial citrus note. Longevity and Sillage: I find it quite durable for a Cologne, surely influenced by the cypress oil. The sillage is noticeable in the first 15 minutes and then fades quite quickly. However, I can still perceive the scent on me after hours, without having to concentrate hard on it. With movements, I also catch a slight waft of the scent now and then. Bottle: As unpretentious as the scent. I really like it in its simplicity and clarity. Conclusion: My current feel-good scent and absolute mood lifter! It fully meets my taste, even though I never thought a purely citrus scent, without any other nuance, could ever achieve this. An absolute summer scent, perfect for hot days. I can't yet assess how it will come across when it gets cooler. Suitable for both genders equally. For me at the moment, it feels like a second skin under my skin.

The Hadrien Cologne opens with fruity, not overly sour lemon, surely the bitter orange acts as a moderating influence. Underneath, basil gives a certain snap effect. I am on vacation in Italy. The blend of citrus fruits is overall more rounded than sharp. It describes not a glaring Mediterranean light, but a waking morning. The air is pleasantly mild, the heat of a summer day still far away. I am on vacation in Italy, I opened the balcony door early in the morning. Within a few minutes, the citrus fruit recedes in favor of a watery-(*first suspicion arises…*)-fruity veil. Underneath, a spicy-woody note forms. I immediately think of cypress. I am on vacation in Italy, I opened the balcony door early in the morning and breathe in the Mediterranean-spicy, morning air deeply. Through bright, persistently unchanging musky notes, a lasting impression of cleanliness is already created within the first half hour. I am on vacation in Italy, I opened the balcony door early in the morning and breathe in the Mediterranean-spicy, morning air deeply, after I had just stepped out of the shower, where I had smeared myself with some chemical stuff typically found in hotel bathrooms. Perhaps the year of release for the Hadrien Cologne is a kind of Goutal fate year. For me, it definitely is, and since this test - in both senses. Initially, Goutal and I got to know each other in mid-July 2013. The kids were at their grandparents for two weeks, my wife and I enjoyed the unusual freedom while strolling. Then the thought occurred to us that we could sniff something again after a long time… Well, and that’s how things took their course: Shortly after, I signed up here. And now I have the salad, but that’s another story. The mentioned perfumery had a wide selection of Annick Goutal fragrances. Over the last nearly three years, many have been tested and a round dozen bottles found their way to us, more than from any other provider. They did not all turn out to be lasting hits, but some my wife, my daughter, and/or I cannot do without anymore: Eau d'Hadrien, Petite Chérie, Ninfeo Mio, Nuit Étoilée, and the Vetiver Cologne. These five mentioned span 32 years of Goutal, from the very beginning (Eau d’Hadrien) to 2013 (Vetiver Cologne). And it seems that a profound decision was made then, which first became apparent to me with the tests of the Hedion bombs Vent de Folie (released in 2014) and L'Île au Thé (2015): The ladies fully embraced chemistry. And with the present candidate, it shows that this apparently began in 2013 - at least I do not know an older Goutal from the pro-synthetic category. Thus, I reaffirm the appeal I made during the review of Vent de Folie: “Personally, I hope that the alleged start of a new chapter for the house of Goutal (as the advertising text states) does not mark the beginning of a synthetic pseudo-event perfumery series that reverses, if not betrays, the previous style of the house. Dear Goutals: Rather endure the lamenting and repetitive durability complaints!” In any case, I will not follow the new path. Perhaps I should test the three absolutes from 2015 before I definitively conclude that 2013 is not only the year when Goutal and I made contact, but also the year when we lost it.

The tester bottle of Jasmin Noir L'Elixir looked so stunning on the shelves of my local department store that I just had to try it. Unfortunately, as attractive as the puff atomiser is, it's not very functional. I spent nearly fifteen minutes with the sales assistants trying to get the damn thing to spray, but to no avail. The testers in other stores also malfunctioned, so I almost gave up on ever being able to test Jasmin Noir L'Elixir. Thankfully while browsing JR Duty Free I found a tester that worked. If you were to buy yourself a bottle of this flanker, I would decant half of it into another bottle just in case. It looks like the atomiser and its on/off function can easily break.
