In regards to scent, Jasmin Noir L'Elixir is slightly better than the original EDP. The scent pyramid worked from the base notes to the top notes when I tested this fragrance. Essentially everything was back to front. Jasmin Noir L'Elixir opened with a thick, balmy accord, not unlike a heady blend of patchouli, resins and white woods. It smelt kind of sexy and mysterious; very 'noir'. Unfortunately this fragrance becomes fresher and more citrusy as the scent develops. The jasmine note is clean and feminine, with a juicy, almost candied orange accord. This blend is not unpleasant, just a tad disappointing, especially since the opening was so promising. The drydown smelt almost identical to the original EDP's drydown. A very musky jasmine scent with pink pepper and earthy patchouli. The only thing I can say in favour of Jasmin Noir L'Elixir is that it had slightly better lasting power. I think Bvlgari should lay these Jasmin Noir flankers to rest and release something new and exciting. Original review written: March 2013.

As I stand in front of my fragrance shelf, my scent samples come into my hands. Since my separation from my signature scent, nothing has been the same. Nothing can excite me, nothing can sway me, nothing can blow me away - or can it? And before I change my mind, I engage in this fragrance flirt and spray...... Anyone hoping for the queen of scents - Miss Jasmine - in this fragrance must be disappointed. For despite the name, she only makes a radiant appearance in the opening of this composition to introduce this masterpiece. She refreshes and provides support, and as quickly as she came, she disappears just as fast. But what happens now? The scent captivates me. Could this perhaps be the start of a new fragrance love? Have I ever encountered a more feminine, cleaner scent? Is it the tuberose that clouds my senses and releases my happiness hormones? NOOOOO! NOOOOO! It is the ALMOND - oh my God - I am lost. Lost in this divine fragrance! My nose constantly wanders to my arm. It’s like an addiction. And for the first time since my separation from Hypnose Senses, I feel like I have been FOUND. For the first time since my great fragrance love, this is a scent that could be a worthy successor. And with its unexpected eroticism and uniqueness, the fragrance hits me in the face and transports me back to the past. I stand there as a young scent punk, wearing only what I like and loving only those who touch my heart. There are no compromises. There is only yes or no. Black or white. Love or forget. I have always loved with all my heart. All my loves. Even my platonic ones. And what has happened? One becomes a little gray with the diplomacy of the world. And in the midst of all the daily tasks, one forgets the facets and the voice of one’s own heart? PLEASE NOT! And what was that about Nemesis, you might have wondered at the beginning? In Greek mythology, she is the goddess of revenge. Today we know Nemesis as modern Justitia, yet one of her swords has been replaced by a scale, and she now stands as a goddess for righteous wrath. But in Greek mythology, she stands above all as THE AVENGER FOR ALL THOSE WHO DO NOT LOVE WITH THEIR HEARTS! Why does this fragrance lead me back to this wisdom of my heart? Why does it become such a part of me that my mind shuts off and I simply become myself again? And I realize, Nemesis rightly punishes those who do not love from the heart. Thank you, L'Elixir. It is time to become myself again and to be true to my old motto of freedom and ONLY true love. So: if you are looking for a new fragrance flirt, believe in it - in true fragrance love and no matter whom or what you love - love with all your heart. I believe that only this love comes back and stays.

For quite some time, I have ordered the Elixir from the Jasmin Noir line, and today it has finally arrived. I originally tested the EdP, but there is some note in it that I just can't quite like. I once again blame the gardenia, which I tolerate well when it takes a back seat, but in higher concentrations, it causes discomfort in my head and stomach. A closer look at the fragrance compositions of the Jasmin Noir series made the Elixir very appealing to me, as it is omitted here, and the composition of L'Essence doesn't read quite as "syrupy". Once the decorative and elegantly designed spray nozzle finally sets aside its initial diva-like stubbornness, we can begin. The opening is like the others in the line, featuring the typical jasmine touch. Together with bergamot and orange, it is an olfactory revelation. This trio immediately captivates my nose and senses, allowing me to breathe a dreamy sigh of relief. While the top notes in the others come through a bit fresher, here they are much sweeter, richer, and softer. I feel a slight tingling from the pepper, but it's more in the background. The almond accord is also very prominent, just like the opening trio, and it fits in absolutely harmoniously with them. Together, they form a fluffy, gourmand unit, very heavy, sophisticated, and rich. Instantly, I am reminded of the Italian restaurant in town where we often enjoyed good meals and drank a glass of Chianti. When setting down the glass, the wine didn't flow smoothly like other wines back down the rim to the bottom of the glass. Here, it "crept" back almost syrupy. Its taste was sweetly rich and very full-bodied, almost sublime. This is how I would compare L'Elixir to the EdP. L'Elixir opens strongly, but its perfected visage only reveals itself after a while, when the initial notes have settled a bit. And it gains intensity. However, this does not overwhelm; instead, it blends into balsamic-smoky notes and musk. The dark green of the fir can still be sensed at the end. Whether one could guess it blindly without the fragrance pyramid remains open. What matters is the perfect interplay of all factors into a sensual and delicious fragrance experience that is unique. The longevity here is above average; I can confidently say this already, as after over 5 hours, I still smell as if I just freshly sprayed it. The sillage is also enormous, and I would again say "less is more." Unfortunately, my skin absorbs L'Elixir immediately, while on fabric, it blooms and blooms, and just when you think it can't go on, another intense wave comes, as if it keeps recharging itself. With its energy and strength, I envision it as a "confident feel-good fragrance." It carries you, taking on the role of an aura. You will definitely stand out with it and must be aware of that. Its seasons will likely be autumn and winter, as the warmth it radiates will come across well on cold days. It will also surely be suitable in spring as the cool days fade. However, warm temperatures and its weight could overwhelm it. All in all, a very feminine, elegant scent, perfect for snuggling and warming up. Finest cashmere wardrobe to spray on ;-). Postscript: Even after lingering on fabric at the end of the day, it is still distinctly perceptible.

At the beginning, it's still manageable - slightly fresh and subtly woody-sweet. But then… an unparalleled escalation, a combination of freshly sharpened pencil with an undefined sweetness. This scent weighs heavily on my chest, breathing becomes a bit more laborious, and I can only cautiously approach it in small doses. I was excited to try this fragrance, as I often enjoy Annick Goutal's creations, but this one is a disappointment. The cloying sweetness comes off as stuffy and heavy, trying to assert itself, while the wood smells stale and dull. The myrrh, on the other hand, is sharp and piercing, and I can't detect any possibly soothing rose. I can't comment on the longevity because I don't want to have this scent around me for too long. Once again, a failed attempt to get closer to Oud finds its end here.

Annick Goutal almost always works for me, which I can't say for any other brand. Consequently, I was a bit anxious about this test. Afraid that 1001 Ouds might not appeal to me. I find the name original. It's quite possible that 1001 Ouds is the thousand and first Oud to be launched on the European market. The question arises whether it can hold its own. I hope so! Once the alcohol has evaporated, the scent unfolds on my skin as if it belongs there. Spontaneously, it reminds me of Oud Assam by Rania J. Of the phase where the cow shed evaporates and makes way for a pretty old wooden cabinet that unfortunately bids farewell far too quickly. Here, nothing bids farewell too quickly. My skin smells of dry old wood for hours. In the background, I perceive chocolate. It adds a touch of sweetness to the scent without making it sweet. No trace of cow shed. I have the impression that great care has been taken here. The end product is so absolutely harmonious that it almost borders on boredom. In fact, I have no desire to make grand speeches about this scent. I much prefer to enjoy - and remain silent.

What a bottle. An incredibly beautiful decorative piece, one simply must own it visually. Turned it around, saw the price, quickly put it back down. Such a decorative object over 300 € is just not feasible right now. The content must be just as good as the exterior, right? For the start, I would have immediately given it ten points. An incredibly soft mandarin on subtle pepper notes. Feminine, soft, cuddly, and lightly refreshing. This is what luxury smells like! Yes! Osmanthus? Yes, maybe, I wouldn't have thought of that at all. A bit weak in the middle. Amouage and Aqua di Parma can do this better or rather more authentically. But one shouldn't compare. Somehow, there's too little in the middle for me. There's something pink and something gray. There's something close to the skin like a super body lotion. Creamy and slightly summery (amber). At the same time, there's something earthy, musty, musky. I imagine there must be something very expensive in there. But others have that too, Tom Ford for example. A wood note, very mild, white-gray. Suppressed a bit animalistic and resinous. But overall, it's too unspectacular for me. After 2 hours, it's just a standard musky cuddle scent. Somehow a shame and yet true! Allegedly only 50 bottles in all of Germany. Here we are again with the bottle! I want to have it; the content is not that important to me. Still available with luck at Hamburger Hof.

Elbphilharmonie? A trifle. Berlin Airport? A joke. All mere sandbox games compared to the renovation project currently unfolding within my daughter. These sudden, extreme mood swings and unfathomable tantrums (worse than before!) can only be explained by the term "prepubescent" - at least I hope so, because that would mean it’s a time-limited phenomenon. I don’t want to think about the alternative. So it should almost fit marketing-wise with what Mrs. Doyen & Co. have come up with this time, more on that shortly. The fragrance itself strikes me as simply spectacular for Goutal standards, given the bold use of Hedion. They must have poured that stuff in by the barrel. Right at the start, the scent comes across as almost metallic; on the paper strip, it’s even more intense than on the skin. I was quite surprised by that. But even in body wear, this note takes center stage for me; a small blackcurrant at the beginning is immediately overshadowed. I can only speculate about the concept behind it. Such a thing from a house that usually values naturalness, which occasionally seems so simple and thus so skillfully executed. In the translation of the accompanying eulogies, online translators (I don’t speak French) come up with bizarre suggestions, indicating that some sort of young country pomeranian has been swept away by the spirit of the big city. The English version, as well as the sparse English blurb for the sample, convey something similar to me: that a free-spirited and reckless young woman embraces her life in a whirlwind of madness. Alternatively, it’s a radiant and sensual whirlwind. Aha. Perhaps instead of madness, youthful folly is meant. Francophiles, step forward! You might also explain to us what "pois de senteur" is all about. I somehow suspect it’s not just the ingredient scent pea, but also a play on words with an idiomatic expression from the adolescent corner or something. Whirlwind. I directly pick up on that keyword: Yes, I know it. A nice understatement for describing my daughter's behavior when something displeases her. What I really don’t need right now is a fragrance that might encourage these crazinesses. But it probably won’t come to that. I find the scent - aside from the comparatively drastic, because unexpected chemistry spectacle - rather straightforward, low in variation, and composed. Aside from the lab, it seems to me that the rose geranium is at the center in the first hours. I like that, as it sets itself apart from some other Goutals that seem primarily aimed at an even younger target audience with their winking, sweet, or floral notes and that exclusively delight me on a meta-level - in other words: I find them cute on my daughter. It’s a pity that the nuances of the other ingredients, be it blackcurrant, or even later musk and cedar, are so ruthlessly smothered with Hedion. I can’t fight against that either and throw in the towel or rather all fours. Only after about seven hours does the stuff give a bit of peace, allowing the others to at least peek out. I can well imagine that the fragrance is suitable for layering with other AG perfumes. Goutal itself encourages such experimentation with its in-house products, although my brochure on this is a few days old and therefore doesn’t contain a recommendation for this new release. Just try it out. Personally, I hope that the alleged start of a new chapter for the house of Goutal (as the advertising text states) does not mark the beginning of a synthetic pseudo-event perfumery series that reverses, if not betrays, the previous style of the house. Dear Goutals: Please endure the lamenting, repetitive shelf-life whining! No madness, with or without wind!

The scent is herbaceous-green and sweetly-floral. Not exactly the classic floral bouquet of rose, jasmine, etc., but unknown flowers, or at least kept unrecognizable, abstract and natural at the same time. This is somewhat irritating, which is why the scent might not score particularly well here. AugustA likes this foil, though. In the end, there’s a slightly austere dry cedar, possibly, or something of the sort, and the naughty floral scent is complete.

I confess, I was a bit afraid of vent de folie. It has been rated so poorly here. I have already tested several Goutals and know the little stinkers that capture life with all its aromas (including sweat or mildew). Nevertheless, I decided to give it a try, and I am very happy that I dared to do so. It develops on my skin exceptionally beautifully - exciting, almost thrilling, while being a little innocent, a mix of loud and quiet feel-good and Ooops! moments. It should be noted that my skin sometimes devours a perfume, like Prada Candy (which was confirmed by the ladies in the perfumery who also smell nothing on my arm); I could lay myself in the caramel scent spread across the kitchen floor. For that, cedar usually explodes on my skin, leaving a lingering, penetrating hardware store feeling for hours. But now to vent de folie. It has a wonderfully spicy-fresh note with a slight citrus touch right upon spraying. Then, within seconds, the metallic scent follows, which, however, softens in the next minutes, allowing the flowers to take the lead. It becomes increasingly rosy, while the metallic scent does not disappear but subtly retreats to the background. Unfortunately, I do not detect the candies described by previous reviewers at all. For a fraction of a second, the scent of Ahoi Brausen raspberry hops around on my skin, but it also quietly retreats to the background when the rose comes out, just like the powdery aspect in the fragrance. If I had to estimate the mixing ratio, I would say that for a 1-liter bottle of rosy-floral, there is a shot glass of powdery-sweet, with both mixed in a freshly brushed metal cup and sitting on an older, no longer strongly scented cedar wood table. I do not perceive the scent as mainstream, although I do not have to sniff every new flanker in perfumeries but rather go through my watchlist or the manufacturers I know and like. If I had to compare, I would find it similar to Armani's Diamonds. But only very minimally, as Diamonds is really pleasing and calm, containing only flowers, raspberries, and a light powder as components. I would like to emphasize that similar does not mean fragrance twin, but merely the direction of the perfume. The Armani is much smoother and more pleasing, almost boring compared to the Goutal.

Annick Goutal fragrances are among the first scents I got to test since I became a Parfumo user exactly four years ago today. Some of them even made it into my collection, especially the two rose fragrances. Fortunately, these four years have been much more diverse and full of divine (shout out to Louce) scents, aside from the few duds. So today I survived test number two of Vent de Folie to ultimately be able to evaluate and describe it. I had to Google what Hedione is. It is said to smell jasmine-like and slightly metallic. The latter is true, but jasmine... In the late 60s, there were mini dresses that sometimes looked very futuristic and reminded one more of space travel than fashion. Shift dresses without or with short sleeves, straight or slightly A-line, and of course ultra-short. Some of these dresses were made of metal plates, and I think of those when I smell Vent de Folie. As if you dipped these metal plate dresses into a concoction of iris roots and then into a brew of currants, raspberries, and rose geraniums. Candy scent on a metallic base, very mainstream. At times, Vent de Folie shows a slight resemblance to Rose Splendide - but it in no way reaches its beauty. My appeal to the perfumers of Annick Goutal: better to have lower longevity and spray more often than to get lost in the sea of mainstream.

A novice perfume lover found herself in a small, ambitious perfumery, eager to acquire something exquisite for the first time. On one side, there were Serge Lutens with his creations Nuit de Celophane and Daim blond. On the other side, something from Annick Goutal. Yes, with the latter, I must admit, it was the beautifully romantic bottle that captivated me. The eye does play, one must concede, not infrequently. And in the selection, there must surely be something worthwhile. Until that point, I had no knowledge of eau de charlotte or anything hadrien; I only knew that Annick Goutal was supposed to be Parisian good. Then the saleswoman came and raved about the recently released "vent de folie." Yes, it is really great, it unfolds brilliantly and is overall very unique, like all of Goutal's creations, definitely worth trying. So I did, on the back of my hand and all. It was indeed somewhat nice. Hard to categorize: fresh and herbaceous, maybe a tiny bit sweet. Completely lulled into believing it was something very special, I bought it, wore it, and was quickly disappointed. Disappointed by the longevity, which, I am being generous, is under an hour. A "very special" Goutal, then. In the end, I repurposed Vent de folie as a hair perfume, but even here: every shampoo smells longer, and I must now say, also more exciting... and all this at the expense of the good Serge... oh dear. Conclusion: A valuable lesson in the early stages of my passion for perfume. And quite a fall for Annick Goutal. Come on, connoisseurs of the house, and tell me what here is truly worthy of the brand's rank and name.

I am still new here and this is my first comment so please forgive me if it’s not very professional ;) I recently received my first fragrance from Annick Goutal as a gift and I have to say I am torn. There is something in Vent de Folie that bites my nose, probably the blood orange. Furthermore, it is unfortunately way too synthetic for me, maybe the Hedione?

It comes along briskly, the being in the pink-white domino: in wide soft folds, this garment flows around the slender figure; the hood has been pulled over the head of the mysterious beauty in such a way that only the elegantly made-up face with the black mask over the eyes is visible. Radiant, laughing eyes they are! Starry eyes!

At least on me it is very subtle for a noir fragrance, but quite nice, round and pleasing. I think I will be wearing it more as a daytime fragrance than an evening fragrance, unless I want to wear something in the evening with less oompf than usual. If that frag were just a little bit more potent, I would be in heaven. It is however still a real beauty and a worthy addition to my collection.

If I were to buy a Jasmine Noir, it would definitely be this one. It smells almost identical to the EdP, but is much sweeter and more gourmand. More substantial. Bvlgari fragrances are known for their elegance. The l' Essence is a true tonka bean-almond-licorice-jasmine bomb with a woody undertone. Pink pepper? I don't smell it. Bergamot is at most very subtle, vanilla is not present, but maybe it is after all. All in all, for me, it is an intense, gourmand, yet still noble, elegant fragrance. I have to have it :-)

This i an ultimate lily-of -the-valley scent.Fresh and sweet floral green. Feminine lasting and elegant.The berries add a bit of tartness in it. A feel of smelling fresh valley wild flowers in a sunny spring day.Bright and luminous. I have nothing more to say than this is a nice floral suitable for all occasions and wearable of all the ages.

Le Muguet by Annick Goutal is one of those fragrances that I feel so-so about. Occasionally I catch a waft of it and enjoy its freshness, however most of the time I find it a little too strong. I usually enjoy lily of the valley and its Spring-like properties. Le Muguet is most definitely fresh and bright on the skin, yet I find its greeness and touch of sugaryness annoying. In fact, I'll agree with the other reviewers, perhaps it is the benzoin accord that makes this fragrance's opening so harsh and chemical. The heart turns the lily of the valley note, sweet, soapy and clean. It actually smells quite lovely on the skin, like you've just stepped out of the shower. I wouldn't call the sillage intimate at this stage, but it certainly isn't as loud as the top notes. I can't say that I'm a big fan of Annick Goutal's so-called soliflores. The only one I've enjoyed so far is La Violette. I expected a lot from this particular scent, however Diorissimo still reigns supreme as the best interpretation of lily of the valley. I must admit that the bottle is really beautiful, with a striking aqua-marine ribbon. It caught my eye the moment I entered the store. I think this whole range has been re-released, hence the reason why this once discontinued fragrance has recently reappeared. The drydown is the best bit in my humble opinion. The lily of the valley is much smoother, with a light and delicate woodsiness cancelling out that somewhat sharp greeness. I may have enjoyed this fragrance more if the top notes were as good as the base notes. On a more positive note, this EDT lasts extremely well, which is rare for a Annick Goutal. I tentatively recommend Le Muguet for both Spring and Summer, and urge people to muster up the courage to experience the drydown even if the top notes encourage you to scrub.

As almost everyone wrote on their review on this perfume, even cross website, I will also say that the first seconds of Le Muguet are strong and challenging. The opening is very strong green juice, somewhat fizzy. To my interpretation it also has a synthetic, fruity facet. Is it like pear granita? Thankfully, this stage is brief, and the perfume turns into white, little LoTV bells. It feels cold. Certainly, there is a starch-like feeling which together with the flowers this perfume represents it still makes me think of the colour white. It smells of soaps, clean clothes fresh out of the laundry or freshly washed hands in cold water. It feels refreshing, or like the crisp air of an icy morning. I could say it's a little sweet if I don't sniff anything else for a long time. But after wearing this for a day and spraying something else at night like Petite Cherie on my other wrist, I feel like it's really not. Even comparing it with Penhaligon's LoTV, Annick Goutal's is not as sweet. But what I can say is that it's not bitter or certainly not salty. Continuing with the realm of the sense of taste, Le Muguet has a certain tartness to it although not strongly noticeable unless you stick your nose on your wrist or spray yourself in a lot of it. As time goes it becomes less arrogant, and it calms down to a soft, pretty LoTV scent which smells of innocence. I like the scent, I think its cold trait fits well with the Winter season too. It could remind us younger perfume enthusiasts of their grandma. But, in my opinion, it has freshness and feels clean, two traits I also associate with youth. I am happy to have this bottle. Although, something inside tells me that it's my collector's side that's talking and that I would have actually preferred to own Penhaligon's interpretation of the LoTV first rather than Annick Goutal's.

Boiled cabbage to begin with. George Michaels sings "You gotta have faith, the faith, the faith" in my ear. But I struggle with faith every which way, not in my DNA The minutes tick by "Oh no, Vegetal, stultifying" in the way that Jean Claude Ellena was dumped on for Apres La Mousson; this is considerably more intense, I'm a fan of APLM, I don't mind it a bit brackish, I can wait for the dry down, but seven minutes plus goes by and I still don't feel it, and then, miraculously, it clears. Isabelle Doyene does this with more than one AG, torture before it steers into calm waters. Yes, theres Convallaria majalis, the lily of the valley, a rhizomatous perennial that will not grow in my Zone 9 garden, although I grew it successfully at 45 degrees South (we're talking Southern Hemisphere now) I couldn't find the rose the first time I wore it, shock maybe; it appeared the following wearing along with a powdery fixative smell that I associate with a cornstarch talcum worn by very elderly people. There's Narcissus at play here, I think, scent brain says indoles. At the dry down it's lovely and it becomes ultra fresh, which is amazing considering the beginning but will you buy it? Fleur de Cristal by Lalique is a beautiful alternative, albeit a little synthetic, and nothing has knocked Diorrissimo off its perch. Is AG's LOTV sweet, as some have commented? I don't find Le Muguet at all sweet, better on skin than on clothes, so maybe don't spray garments. Spring approaches here. I find Cristalle EDP to be my perfect spring fragrance and this won't make me change

1. "It's a kind of magic..." - because even though there is no natural "bio" or "organic" lily of the valley perfume, many think that the scent wafting from a bottle of "Lily of the Valley" or "Muguet" is not synthetic. Unfortunately, that's not true. There simply is no natural lily of the valley oil that would be suitable for making a perfume. Here’s an example of a simple synthetic base... oh no, too long, 19 chemical compounds alone in the simple basic formula according to Louis Appell. It contains, among other things, Hydroxycitronellal, Hedione, Linalool, Alpha-Terpineol, Geraniol, Heliotropin, Benzylsalicylate... etc. etc. What makes Isabelle Doyen's "Le Muguet" is not stated on the packaging or on the internet, but my nose tells me that she has used a lot of Hedione and Heliotropin, because the scent is not typically "lily of the valley" at all. 2. Lily of the Valley - a song by Queen from 1975: "Wars will never cease, is there time enough for peace, but the lily of the valley doesn't know... Freddy M. - what a performer, what a voice. And what a talent! Would a lily of the valley scent have suited him? Maybe, since he named a great song after it. 3. On May 1, 1561, a sprig of lily of the valley was presented to the French King Charles IX. According to legend, this marked the beginning of the flower's triumph as a symbol of spring. Yes, the king, a real man (but who knows that for sure - and when is a man a man, folks?) loved the scent. 4. "Labor Day" coincides with "Lily of the Valley Day" in France. Goodness, the French again. Work and love always united. 5. By the way, lily of the valley is toxic. Do not eat! Wash your hands after you have tied or served a bouquet. 6. We call them lily of the valley, the English call them "Lily of the Valley," the French "Muguet." You cannot translate "Le Lys dans la Vallée" as "The Lily of the Valley," but only as "The Lily in the Valley." This is also the title of a novel by Honoré de Balzac from 1835, which is said to have autobiographical traits. "The Lily in the Valley" tells the story of the high school student Felix de Vandernese, whose passionate love for the 20 years older and married Henriette de Mortsauf violated the conventions of the time (both then and now?). A lily of the valley does not explicitly appear in the novel, but I just wanted to mention it... - so the thing about the different names in different languages. (The topic "ageism" = the discrimination or unfair treatment based on a person's age - of course not...). - 7. Kate Middleton's bridal bouquet consisted of lily of the valley back in April 2011. Did she wear gloves? I didn't watch live. 8. Can another lily of the valley scent dethrone "Diorissimo"? No. Period. ("Muguet de Bonheur" by Caron is too soapy, "Lily of the Valley" by Yardley is too fleeting, Molton Brown's "Dewy Lily of the Valley & Star Anise" ... well, unfortunately, there is anise in it, Penhaligon's "Lily of the Valley" from 1976 has been - yuck! - reformulated (and the store belongs to Puig, who also produces fragrances for Zara, which is basically great, but the savvy shopper should know this), "Spring!" from the company Esscentials, marketed by Amazon, claims their scent is "spring in a bottle," which I cannot verify, but the bottle can be used as a vase for lily of the valley, "Lily of the Valley" by Woods of Windsor is nice, low budget (also available at Douglas), Yves Rocher also has a Muguet, plus there is a good lily of the valley scent from Russia by Novaya Sarya.) And the "Le Muguet" by Goutal, which is the focus here? It cannot compete with Diorissimo at all, as it is much duller, becomes rather powdery in the drydown, and does not feel nearly as spring-fresh as the brilliant Roudnitska. 9. Why think about lily of the valley in the middle of winter? Luca Turin says: "I have a thing for Diorissimo when it snows." Sometimes he just has cool sayings. I found that inspiring. In my opinion, the Goutal lily of the valley can be worn year-round. By anyone, everyone, all who love this floral, special note. Charles, the King showed us how. Choosing is, by the way, important to me not only when it comes to lily of the valley perfumes. Therefore, I am currently reducing my number of bottles. Call it downsizing, does it still spark joy... You know how it is. 10. "The state of indecision about what we love - as caused by an excess of choices, the difficulty of determining one's own feelings through self-examination, and the ideal of autonomy - prevents passionate attachments and ultimately obscures for us who we are in ourselves and to the world." (From the wise book by Eva Illouz: "Why Love Hurts.") Why do I like this quote so much? Make a guess. But what I still want to say in conclusion... takes less time than a cigarette: Everyone should be allowed to wear lily of the valley. Whether Freddy, Charles, Luca, or Kate.

What a fragrance. Today, the package with this unusual scent finally arrived at my place. Full of anticipation and curiosity, I opened the package and there lay this, in my opinion, beautiful and noble bottle. My hands were almost trembling; I absolutely wanted to spray it.

The scent of lily of the valley, just like that of violets, belongs to the somewhat old-fashioned fragrances. The memory of a prim "old maid" with gloves and a little hat or a knitting grandmother sitting on a bench in the sun in front of the house comes to mind. Annick Goutal's "Soliflores" line quickly dispels this impression.

I appreciate the perfumes of the Annick Goutal brand. null of the fragrances I know from the company have disappointed me so far. I also value the extraordinary talent of Isabelle Doyen as the creator of the olfactory creations she now realizes together with Camille Goutal.

...of lily of the valley. For me, after a long search, this is the first fragrance that instantly transports me to the lily of the valley paradise... fresh green spring forest in the morning, the air still so wonderfully unspoiled, birds chirping and no one else around... for a few moments, no worries and problems, just simply enjoying existence...

I have been searching for a replacement for this fragrance for at least 15 years. It was mine. By now, I only have a memory of it, but I won't give up the search. The regular Miracle is not a true substitute.

I bought this perfume in 2009 for the summer because it seemed exceptionally balanced during my first testing. However, for a summer fragrance with the explicit claim of "Fraiche," it is clearly too sweet, so I left it disappointed in the closet on warm days. A perfume that I will hardly repurchase. Although it leaves an overall pleasant impression, it lacks everything that would set it apart from the crowd and, above all: It fails with its overly heavy sweetness to meet its own claim of being a summer scent. Then the classic Hypnose is to be preferred, because it is authentic!

Because I happened to be wearing Eau du Ciel today, I decided to check out its Parfumo page. I was shocked to see the low ratings for sillage and longevity. Since I know a lot of the members here and respect their noses, I can't help but suspect a reformulation. My bottle is about ten years old, and I'm trying to conserve it because it was my wedding perfume and I'm goofy and sentimental that way. To compare my bottle's sillage and lasting power to something that is familiar to most perfume enthusiasts, I would say it is similar to the original EL White Linen. In any event, my old, possibly pre-reformulation EdC fit the whole "blushing bride" cliche in that it has an innocent, young vibe that seems to be a thread running through some of the early Goutals, such as Petite Cherie and Eau de Charlotte. You absolutely have to be a fan of linden blossom in order to warm up to this perfume, as that is the most prominent note in the composition. There's also neroli, which lends a soft, soapy touch and a whisper of iris and violet. It's not a complex fragrance, but it is a bit unusual, as are quite a few of the Goutals. If I ever (God forbid!) get married again, I'll be sporting a tuberose bomb like Carnal Flower or the like, but I nevertheless look back on my Eau du Ciel days with fond memories and happiness. Hopefully I'm dead wrong about the reformulation and what I'm seeing is just a disagreement among noses, but I will try to find a new bottle to compare to my old one and report back. Update: Yes, Ciel has been reformulated. :( Not only watered down, but the big linden note that made it so special has been scaled back and the rosewood trimmed, as well. Some people actually might prefer the reformulation as it is no doubt more of a blended floral now, but I find it a bit vapid compared to the quirky, off-center beauty of the original, however unbalanced it might have been. So, my precious old bottle that used to sit on my dresser next to my husband's wedding boutonnière is now wrapped up in tissue and stowed away from the light of day. :: sniff ::

Eau du Ciel is old fashioned and rather stately; imagine ... the swishy green stockings of Y on the shapely legs of Diorissimo. And like many of the best ideas, it's very simple, basically a marriage of oil and alcohol: hydroxycitronellol - the fresh muguet-like floral, and the oily-dry varnish of rosewood. But, why is a woody-green lime-flower named sky water? It smells nothing like rain... [The old one]

Ciel means sky in Spanish (and also in French), and I keep puzzling over why this fragrance is named that way. It has nothing heavenly about it and doesn’t smell like the sky either. How does the sky even smell... Let’s leave that aside. Ciel opens fresh-green and simultaneously sweet-floral, so far so good. But as soon as the first cloud settles, a very harsh herbal note emerges that I really don’t like. However, it doesn’t last long. Then comes violet, a beautiful, just-bloomed lilac violet. Everything else has crumbled away, leaving the violet completely alone. It makes a valiant effort to maintain the scent, and for 2 - 3 hours it succeeds, later with the help of woods. The orange blossom has no desire to show up and has already said goodbye before its appearance. So it remains with the violet and the woods, at least to last the full 3 hours before also giving up the ghost. A lovely Goutal fragrance, as the violet doesn’t overwhelm you here, but very very poor longevity, although - at least longer than Mandragore! For me, it’s not a must-have, despite my enthusiasm for Goutal!

For me, it is very difficult to comment on this fragrance. It is light, green, fresh powdery, somewhat woody and floral. The whole time I wonder which other scent Eau du Ciel reminds me of. I can't figure it out and only dare to make a cursory comparison with a mix of 2 Serge Lutens fragrances Fleur de Citronnier + Sa majesté La Rose. Yes, it reminds me of Sergio, but this Goutal doesn't reach the intensities of those fragrances. It is like a whisper even though it contains such powerful scent components. It wouldn't fit into my usual preferences, but I like the fragrance. It's one of those that you wouldn't buy for yourself, but would gladly accept as a gift. On the official Goutal website, the fragrance is compared to the flutter of an angel's wings, and it is said to be a scent for all those who have not yet lost the child within. Hmmmm, until now I always thought heaven must smell different. Neroli and woods have not been part of my imaginary heaven until now. Perhaps it makes sense to compare this fragrance to a summer garden that has just been hit by rain. As soon as the rain subsides, the strong and delicate scents of trees, earth, flowers, leaves, grasses, etc. blend together. This hint of a mix of delicate and strong is what defines this fragrance. It is rounded and quite interesting because everything is just brushed on - it is a very delicate scent that probably disappears far too quickly. Perhaps it would be more lasting as an EdP. I still give it a high rating because it smells so elegant and, despite the woods, is still quite feminine - that is not always a given.

Two summers ago, I was browsing through a sales portal once again, and what did I see among the offers? "Eau du Ciel" by Annick Goutal! No sample, no decant: no, a nearly full bottle! Well, I had to grab it right away! Because I do like some Goutal fragrances very much. The contact with the seller was made quickly, everything was settled in no time, and the fragrance embarked on its rather long journey to me. In this case, this spring scent came from Greece! Of course, I had to spray it immediately - but what was that? I hesitated, thought about it, and then came the realization: It was the heavy scent of linden blossoms that greeted me first - yes, it almost jumped at me! Linden blossoms, releasing their sweet heaviness into the air after a sunny, warm day at dusk. After my initial enthusiasm, I discovered other soul-soothing floral scents: Iris, neroli, and finally, indeed, the delicate orange blossom - incredible! Each fragrant component is a "soul caresser" that makes the sun shine! This is certainly not for every nose; but I liked it immediately! This is how spring smells - my spring! I felt so light, as if I were floating on a pleasant scent cloud towards the sky. Therefore, "Eau du Ciel" - the "Water of the Sky," I thought spontaneously! "Fly me to the Moon, let me Play among the Stars, let me see what spring is like on Jupiter and Mars ..." Contrary to my other experiences with Annick Goutal fragrances, I was pleasantly surprised by the relatively long-lasting scent. The linden blossoms unfold immediately: "Hello! Hello! Here I am!" they call out; the other flowers approach more slowly, almost shyly. Their scent, however, is all the more enduring. "Eau du Ciel" accompanies me for several hours, to my delight, even on warm days. It is certainly a somewhat unusual companion that you don't encounter on every corner. The seller wrote to me that my bottle of "Eau du Ciel" is still one from the original creation of 1985. There is supposedly a reissue available: but who knows - these are not necessarily better than the originals! I am certainly very happy with my "Eau du Ciel," a very successful blind purchase!

Yes, Mrs. Goutal was once here and has relatively young followed her water of the heavens, having died young at 54, I believe. I'm sorry about that. No one should leave us so young, and age-wise, I have now outlived her. But yes, Mrs. Goutal, let’s believe you live again or still. The idea behind your fragrances was mostly genius.

Yes, of course, Anto and ET, you are right. We are in a garden, somewhere on the outskirts of Cologne, the 4711 factory no more than five kilometers away with a headwind. Let’s toast with a cocktail of limes, lemons, and grapefruit pieces decorated with a violet leaf.

The perfect balance between the creamy, sweet and animalic Jasmine and the sharp, soapy and silky Magnolia. Combine to create a gorgeous, jammy sweet, fresh floral bouquet. All wrapped up in a cotton soft musk. Very unique, sparkly and oppulent. My favourite of the Imperiali line. And the one that stands out the most.

irina is a twin; a person with two faces. a fragrance with two, actually mutually exclusive components. irina is a cheerful, carefree, light-footed young woman who wants to be a lady. yes, of course, her idea of ladylike is intoxicating: magnolia in creamy perfection. but her nature: the bright, pearly, fresh jasmine, slightly bitter,... her nature rubs against her desire. thus the scent: the nose cannot decide between fresh and elegant. perhaps it doesn't have to. but she would like to.

The black sheep of the 'Absolue les parfums' line in terms of bottle design does not wrap itself in cheerful candy colors like its siblings; no, smoky gray already spoils the surprise that we are likely not dealing with a fresh and cheerful rose scent here. 'From the dark' - how fitting, as I am currently sitting in my completely darkened room against the heat. Temperature-wise, perhaps not the most optimal conditions, but let's see.. With Buffy and her demons, this is no little rose! This is the seller in the restaurant with two arms full of "Wolluuu kaufe' Rose?"! Rose! Lots of rose! Dark, thick, opulent rose! Piled high on the dark wooden table. In the background, an incense stick is smoldering somewhere. Aromatically dense, warm and spicy. Come get me, Lucifer, there's no frankincense or anything like that in here? Well, at least not listed, which means nothing... Compared to the relatively recently released "Taif Rose | Jo Malone," the Lancome is completely (!) unsweetened, but has the same rose opulence. And the Lancome roses are prettier/more realistic. I am usually not a huge fan of heavy or oriental-leaning rose fragrances and would therefore wear this rose only for going out/evenings or in the darker season. The scent also works in warmth/in summer - but please not in combination with high humidity, rather in dry heat! And perhaps more after sunset, nomen est omen! Tremor-finger sprayers need to be careful; less is more. Here, just one spray was enough for complete room fragrance, more and it threatens to become a sweet death 'in the name of the rose' in enclosed spaces. The child of the night lasts at least from Dusk till Dawn, although after 2 hours, almost only woody amber remains (or I can no longer smell the roses, which I do not want to rule out).

Very fresh, sweet and floral, with a hint of citrus on my skin, I love the dry down of this perfume, feels very old fashioned and beautiful. This one is a first, and blind purchase from Annick Goutal, and I must say I have to try more. they are definetly unique, and dont have that "modern" sharp soapy smell drying down. For me Un Matin d'Orage is a very floral perfume, although the top notes are definetly green and somewhat citrusy. When I first smelled it, I wasn't sure it's my cup of tea, I really wanted a white floral scent, but wasn't expecting it to be so strong. But, after a few uses I grew to love this one, escpesially in cold winter for some reason, the sweetness is much more pleasant, just like with ice cream... On me it dries down floraly sweet, almost into a candy like scent, with secondary citrucy notes in the air, and after a few uses i couldn't get enough of it. That being said it's definetly a cold weather scent for me, in summer it can be overwhelming. I would recommend it for sweet perfume lovers, who really enjoy floral smells. The sillage is moderate, on myself I can feel its scent throughout the day, and after a night of sleep it can still linger, but people around you won't smell it strongly if at all after a few hours. Overall I was pleasantly pleased with this brand, and with my blind purchase, and will definitely explore more of it. Great floral scent.

I was able to compare both the EDT and the latest EDP of Un Matin d'Orage side by side. These two concentrations are pretty similar in the opening: creamy dewy gardenia. The EDP feels a bit more intense and sweeter, but only slightly. The major difference is in the drydown. The gardenia in the EDT gradually mellows into a soapy green ambiance, while in the EDP, it insteand becomes more luscious. The gardenia note in the EDP is still pretty similar to that in the EDT, but the tuberose nuance is also more detectable. Although I can't really discern amber, myrrh and vanilla, but they certainly add more heft to the gardenia. I would say the EDP is one step closer to those big florals from the same house, such as Songes and Passion, than the EDT. On me, the gardenia in EDT gets lost in the green elements after about 4 to 5 hours, but in EDP it's more present even after 7 hours and the total longevity is almost 12 hours. The sillage of EDP is also moderate to heavy, espacially during the first 2 hours. Personally, I still find the EDT suits best 'a stormy morning' with its brilliant dewy green elements accompanying the creamy gardenia, but its performance and the elusive gardenia do leave me desiring something more. If you happen to have similar feeling towards the EDT, you may want to try the lastest EDP version of Un Matin d'Orage.

With great enthusiasm, I discovered the Eau de Toilette (!) yesterday in a perfume shop. What a subtle, gentle scent. I can only echo the comments about the EdT: the mood and scents after a thunderstorm in the morning have probably never been captured olfactorily so successfully. Everything is there, the freshness, the slightly musty-moldy note, the feeling of relief and new beginnings, of cleansing and brief moments of pause, of sprouting leaves and blossoms, steaming asphalt. The scent lies like a light cloud on the skin. As if one is both rain and air at the same time. Unfortunately, only the Eau de Parfum was available in a smaller size. And I foolishly purchased it without testing (the tester was missing...). At home, I sprayed it on with great expectation, ready again for this thunderstorm wonder. Hmm, it was immediately clear that the EDP is quite different. Louder, more floral, somewhat synthetic at first, by no means as pastel-like, although the base tone of the scent is clearly the same. All of this would actually be quite nice... if it weren't for... yes, if it weren't for the vanilla... I just don't like vanilla in perfumes! And here it doesn't take long before it becomes omnipresent until the end (for me about 6 to 8 hours later). Even though it is a very spicy, unsweetened, elegant vanilla, it quickly became clear that I unfortunately, unfortunately have to part with it again... The EdP is undoubtedly very high quality and interesting. A must for all vanilla lovers, nicer, for example, than Vanille Galante. My recommendation is to test both the EdT and EdP thoroughly before considering a purchase.

At first blast this is an absolute pungent powerhouse of rich ingredients. The Pink Pepper is prominent with the leathery Saffron and Cedar. The gorgeous Bulgarian Rose anchors everything and is quite jammy sweet. As it settles and dries that's when everything melds so smoothly together. And the deep, sticky and almost vanillic Date note shines through with the Rose and heavy musks. Making it predominately hazy , creamy and floral with subtle woods, leather and spice. High amounts of naturals for sure

This noble fragrance starts off with a generous portion of smoke, reminiscent of many Serge Lutens scents... a mysterious tonka bean smoke. In the background, I notice a sweetness, likely from dates... Among the spices, I particularly detect clove... the spices are rather dry, dark, and perhaps a bit stale - but they fit the scent very well. Candied rose petals are added, creating a very heavy, "ripe," and dark red rose. Some Jo Malone Intense Colognes resemble this Bvlgari scent. When I think of occasions to wear this fragrance, a lacquer-and-leather ball comes to mind (dress code lacquer and leather, location an old castle...) or an elegant evening or celebration, award ceremony, or gala... here, rather suited for a mature lady. A mystical-noble-smoky-spicy oriental, which has the only drawback for me that it doesn't last very long.

Songes pursues a roughly similar track to Manoumalia in that the jutting sharpness of ylang, jasmine, tiaré, and frangipani has been softened by, and partially subsumed into, a creamy sandalwood. However, while the flowers in Manoumalia have been melted down entirely into a fine floral silt, only partially identified by hints of identifying rubber or fuel (ylang) or fruity cream cheese (tiaré), in Songes, the individual flowers still smell brightly and recognizably of themselves. The shiny-dirty-plasticky jasmine is the main player in the EDT, which has a woody but still quite bright, translucent texture, while a banana-ish ylang dominates in the EDP, with tons of creamy, animalic musks fleshing out the landing. Both versions are supremely graceful and classically beautiful; but only the EDP smells as cuminy as a woman’s inner thigh. Well, ok, listen. Both versions have cumin. But the addition of billowing, cumulus-sized white musks to the sandalwood and vanilla of the EDP has the effect of blowing hotly on the cumin, amplifying it to a point that makes me blush. The EDT is bright, clear, and sensual – the EDP is dense, creamy, and frankly suggestive. I own both, because I love Songes in every way, shape, or form, and also because sometimes I like to choose between single and double cream.

This was really good. At first it smells like indole. People who like flowery scents with indole will like it. It's jasmine sambac, so it's probably the indole of ylang-ylang. It doesn't smell cosmetic. It has a slightly peppery flavor, but it's more like the bitterness of fresh flowers, and it doesn't go as far as being spicy. Have you ever smelled the center of an orchid? It has a pungent indole smell. Goutal is a brand that focuses on natural fragrances. That's why the scent is very light. I think there are fewer brands these days that offer scents that don't give you a headache even when you put your nose close to your skin, so I think this is very valuable. This is amazing. In other words, they don't extend the scent time with synthesis. It's very aristocratic, contrary to the tropical mood of note. I feel that women who use this probably only go to very comfortable spaces. It may take about five pushes to make it smell good enough for others to notice. So, it's consumed in large quantities, so the price may seem high. But still, this is a nice scent. Frangipani and ylang-ylang waft from afar. It's a very European scent, but at the same time, it has a tropical mood. It has the atmosphere of a tropical country as seen by European aristocrats. Do you like gardenia? It smells very gardenia-like. This feels like a more European arrangement of Diptyque's Do Son. It's an abstract expression, but Do Son feels fresh, Asian, beautiful, but somehow decadent. Songju is bright. When I was a child, there was a video tape of a Disney animation that showed a moment of someone's wedding in Hawaii, and (for some reason) I feel that kind of happiness. It's like a blurry, distant, beautiful memory, and there's a euphoric feeling like a home video. But it was not filmed by local people, but by Europeans. In other words, the director is European, and the location is a resort outside of Europe. I was surprised at the background to the birth of this fragrance. In other words, it's full of soul. It's wonderful. From my perspective, it's too expensive for the cost-effectiveness, so I don't buy a bottle, but if I got it for free, I'd be happy all day.Women who wear this are high-income women who live a careful life and go to places like the Maldives on vacation. They are not the kind of people who accidentally leave the refrigerator open and let their important ingredients rot (a felony for meat.People who waste food have no right to wear expensive perfume.) or who are too lazy to take out the trash on trash day and let it pile up at home. That's me. Please meet more wonderful people.

Songes caresses the wearer with a temperamental, warm, and sweet, floral, and ripe scent. Tiare, a South Sea gardenia, clings on, and a spicy vanilla cloud whets the appetite. Despite its expansive aura, the perfume does not come across as artificial or kitschy, a feat with these ingredients. The spices and ylang-ylang add more depth to the fragrance. Beautifully floral and, in my opinion, much better than "Terracotta" by Guerlain. There is no dust here; the scent feels juicy, very feminine, and seductive to me. Frangipani and jasmine further brighten the mood, and one imagines walking along the beach with flowers in their hair, forgetting the asphalt beneath their feet, painting pictures in their mind. Songes, a calm yellow-and-white floral scent, has a slightly lactonic quality and is rich. Some may find it offers too few facets, but Songes consistently shows its best side. I have never liked a tiare perfume as much as this one.

Having smelled this in store, I originally passed it over. The other omnia option there for test stood out to me a bit more, and I didn't get much from this off a strip of paper after I'd already smelled 7 or 8 other things. But with the little sprayer sample I've received in a variety pack, I have found myself pleasantly surprised. The jasmine is of a greener variety, invoking leaves and stems and crisp white flowers over anything indolic, sweet or creamy. It blends nicely with the more aquatic lotus note and very lightly herbal tea. The pear and mandarin meld together in an inoffensive but difficult to distinguish fruity note that fades quickly to reveal the bitter, herbal tea note in the middle. When setting out to write this review, I didn't think I'd have so much to say! Now I feel like I'm convincing myself not to buy a bottle. My real opinion is: it's fine! I just love fresh florals so much. It's nothing to write home about. Looking at the notes, I think I'd really love to smell the original version - I read that Bvlgari customer support responded to a user saying the scent didn't change with the bottle, but that seems dubious to me. I'm glad I have a sample, I think at most I'd want like a 10ml of this. I would so wear this to a waterpark just to smell like nothing after 2 minutes in the wave pool.

Unfortunately bought in a moment of excitement after a short test... it is simply piercing and pinches the nose. Lotus lotus lotus. I didn't smell anything else. I had perceived it in the store as much creamier, wonderfully soft, but at home I was ruthlessly overwhelmed by great disappointment. It stings and scratches and almost hurts, it is so rough. A brute. What did I perceive in the store? I only tried this fragrance. I don't know. I'm wearing it now, but it's just hard to endure when you are constantly pinched and bitten. It is also so artificially sour... When I close my eyes, I see a pickled cucumber wrapped in a spiky fur, trying to wildly jump up and down and bore into my nose... That was pure waste of money. I'm super angry at myself. I was blinded by the beautiful color of the bottle!

The harmless-sounding name of the fragrance has a lot more to it than meets the eye, I agree with Zora. Joyeux Eté delighted the ladies in the same year as Miss Dior and Le Dix, and this type of perfume continues through the following years, as L`Air du Temps, Diorama, or Jolie Madame radiate that elegance which conceals a considerable portion of sophistication behind femininity. The top note is still somewhat restrained chypre-like, but Calendula, the marigold, sounds interesting in this context, though I wouldn't know what role it should play here. Calendula is related to our harmless daisy and has just as much or as little scent as the marigold. It was indeed used as a medicinal plant in the Middle Ages, but certainly not for its aphrodisiac properties; there were surely more erotically scented flowers even back then. Rather, Calendula is still a proven extract today for improving wound healing and alleviating inflammation of any kind. Back then, before the time of penicillin & Co., it was a plant that was essential in every monastery garden. I cannot understand why it has sneaked into this perfume. However, Galbanum clearly presents itself with its rather green, balsamic note, and this opening first sets the mood for the further development. While the floral aromas of the heart note sound rather opulent, Joyeux Eté develops in a refined, understated manner for my nose and makes one crave more. And you do get more, as an animalistic and decidedly less tame base already makes itself known through the flowers. In this fragrance, the heart note is actually the prelude to the theme. The perfume becomes heavier without feeling sweeter or even oriental to me, and it shows excellent longevity on the skin. It becomes skinnier in the best sense of the word. Now I can no longer categorize the scent into our known categories. It is far too complex for that. If I want to classify it as powdery and at the same time as a floral chypre, that may be true for my nose, but I think any reasonably experienced Parfumo user would shake their head in doubt. It is neither bitter nor sweet, certainly not fresh, and the other parts of our cake don't really fit either. It cannot be pigeonholed and certainly cannot be broken down into its components. Simply refined - my father used to rave in such moments: Raffizinös *smile* or to put it in the words of Mary Poppins: supercalifragilisticexpialidocious;) As harmless as the opening is, Joyeux Eté leads us into the world of feminine and refined perfumes of past times with great sophistication. I will refrain from further pondering on this now.

No one can deny that scents carry both positive and negative memories. Over 30 years ago, when I was still a young woman working in an office and joyfully exploring perfume shops with my best colleagues, we had a rather unpleasant coworker in the office. Miss Don’t Touch Me. So natural, that even plucking her eyebrows was akin to a disgrace. She was a nice mix of Heidi and Miss Rottenmeyer. Oriental or even animalic scents, what cruelty in her eyes, a conspiracy against humanity. When we emerged from the perfume shop, richly equipped with our oriental fragrances, she looked at us disdainfully as if we were nothing but brainless sluts. No, not our colleague, of course. Only one scent found grace in her eyes and was worn by her every day. A well-known scent from Lancome. A scent of lemon trees. Soaps smelled of lemons, cleaning products smelled of lemons, and our dear colleague did too. Day in, day out, all year round. That was pretty much the time when my aversion grew not only against this scent, although it was actually beautiful, but against the whole brand and stubbornly persisted to this day. But at some point, I have to process this scent trauma and have decided to at least give the brand a new chance. A good offer, a large bottle of 240ml of a well-preserved vintage scent and packaging with sweet delicate roses, I could no longer resist. Since I didn’t know the pyramid yet, I imagined a delicate, elegant, and rosy scent fitting my idea of that time. But, not at all. After a very brief bitter and fresh opening, a seductively slightly sweet note takes the lead. I think it must be the marigold, which was considered a healing plant and also a love charm in the Middle Ages, and which was said to have aphrodisiac effects. Well, the magic continues into the heart note and then mixes mainly with the iris root and the daffodil. The other beautiful flowers underscore the whole, but never really come fully to the fore. It becomes powdery yet remains elegantly floral. Already there, I have the feeling that the scent is not as innocent as I initially assumed. However, at the latest in the base, my quiet suspicion is confirmed. Apparently, times were not as prim back then as I thought, and the cheerful summer was more likely a lascivious summer night, where hands were not only under the bedcovers. It becomes quite animalic and still heavily sweet, like sweaty bodies after a hot summer night. For me, the cheerful summer has now lasted all day, and I think it will survive the night as well. What would Miss Don’t Touch Me have said about that?

At the moment, life is treating me harshly - and I have a lot to cope with. Every day I reach for the fine, yet expressive L `elixir to ease my worries. Beautiful, as an intro, is the light sweetness of candied fruits, garnished with a delicate orange blossom. The jasmine is distinctly floral - white and radiant. That brightens even dark days. The musk shines, and the nougat melts softly and appetizingly in the nose. A delicacy that I gladly indulge in. Only today did I discover with shock that my bottle is almost empty. Oh - what a pity. But as fate would have it, I found a single box of L `elixir in the department store earlier - and it was nicely discounted! I blink up at the sky with a smile - and whisper: Thank you, Mom!

“Mon Jasmin Noir L'Elixir” landed on my wish list because I find this Bvlgari line intriguing, but somehow it doesn't quite suit me. During a swap, I received a sample to test. Kristen Dunst perfectly embodies this advertising campaign as a cool, blonde beauty! ~ Bottle ~ The nostalgic spray balloon is an absolute eye-catcher! The glass, slightly curved bottle is adorned with a transparent-black ribbon around the neck and contains a delicately shimmering liquid. However, the name addition "Noir" (French for "black") does not fit the citrus fragrance. ~ Scent ~ Upon spraying, it is immediately very refreshing with zesty bergamot and oranges (I can't detect that they are supposed to be candied). White jasmine blossoms appear in the form of intense sambac absolute, but they are somewhat subdued by the predominantly citrus accords. In the base, it finishes lightly creamy with dry woods, musk, and amber (honey and nougat remain hidden from me). ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts about 5 hours (not much longer on clothes and hair). I find 2-3 sprays sufficient; otherwise, it becomes too scratchy and bitter for me. ~ Occasion ~ It fits well into the warmer days of spring and (late) summer. It can also be worn to the office, as it is quite unobtrusive yet elegant when dosed discreetly. ~ Conclusion ~ I quite like this variant as well, but it is too citrusy-bitter for me. I can't detect a significant difference from "Mon Jasmin Noir L'Eau Exquise." Those who find other summer perfumes too sweet and who enjoy citrus fruits with jasmine should definitely give this a try!

After several quite "subtle" hints, I received this perfume from my friend for my birthday. The joy was, of course, immense. While I also really like the regular MJN, L'Elixir has simply triggered a greater desire to have it in me, just with the beautiful bottle featuring a balloon sprayer ;-) The entire packaging is also very elegant and lovingly done. The "shell" of the fragrance definitely appears very high-quality and beautiful. After initial problems with the sprayer (it's my first one in the balloon variant), the first spray... Sigh, it’s beautiful! Delicate, fine, elegant, and somehow special. Time and again, my nose moves almost on its own to my wrist to truly absorb all the impressions of the scent. Right off the bat, I have to admit that I didn’t manage to do that :-P At least for me as a "beginner perfumista," it’s hard to pick out all the details. After a few minutes, I sniff again and... bang! Suddenly, I feel like I'm dealing with Alien by TM. For those who are not fond of Alien, don’t worry... this impression doesn’t last too long, as the jasmine gradually retreats to make way for something much softer and gently caressing. I always somehow associate this scent with a cream-colored satin blanket that hugs my body, making me feel very comfortable and elegant as I am beautifully enveloped by it. In terms of scent progression, it starts off floral with something fruity (which is only very light and in the background), in the middle it’s really jasmine-heavy but beautiful, and towards the end, it becomes softer and gentler. I unfortunately have to mention one flaw; the sillage and longevity are too weak for a fragrance of this price range and presentation. After 4 hours, the scent is hardly perceptible on me. Overall, a beautiful and very feminine fragrance. Perhaps also something for those among us who do not like Alien due to its heaviness. Here is a very elegant and still not too common alternative for jasmine lovers. Personally, I wouldn’t wear this scent every day; it’s too precious for that... but for special occasions, it will likely be my first-choice companion in the near future, always giving me the feeling of being something special.

The beginning of this is really delicious. The most beautiful neroli, just the way I like it and mixed with the freshness of the sharp bergamot. The beginning, unfortunately, does not last more than fifteen to thirty minutes and the rest of the journey is not worth mentioning - very subtle and discreet. A summer scent if you want to wear it 237/365

I like the impression of this scent, and the opening is fantastic. Dries down to a jasmine-musk on my skin, so I find Cyclades pleasant but unremarkable ... and not a good reference to Greek isles. I'm not a fan of jasmine, so I am not a fan of this. So glad that I sniffed before purchase. Cyclades is part of the Lancome Voyages collection. There are three fragrances currently in the collection, and I find Benghal & Tropiques much more unique and enjoyable than Cyclades.

Annick Goutal's Eau du Fier is one of the more sharply polarizing perfumes I know. In fact, my own feelings about it have swung from one pole to the other. When I first received a sample of it some years ago, it had spilled a bit in the package. For weeks afterward, I kept sniffing my living room (where I had opened it) to make sure nothing was smoldering. Very intense stuff. I hated it. But over time it worked its salty birchtar charms on me, and I grew to love it. Unfortunately, it was discontinued 5 or more years ago and is now nearly impossible to find. I was never able to talk myself into splurging on it because I'm afraid to wear it in public, not wanting to make anyone else call the fire department! There are some other lovely scents out there that capture saltiness (my favorites being Miller Harris Fleur de Sel and The Different Company's Sel de Vetiver). But this captures a level of saltiness I never thought a perfume could. If I were writing a video to go with this, it would be an "adult" version of Katy Perry's "Last Friday Night": a swank party in the Hollywood Hills, lots of people in leather, a campfire, too much whiskey, some rough sex, and waking up in the morning to drink a gigantic glass of water with a large and slightly rueful smile. Note: This is the first time I've worn it for 12 hours without showering. At 12 hours, it's a lovely, refined osmanthus. And, on second thought, I just found an inexpensive used bottle on eBay - it didn't seem right to let this pass into "just a memory" yet.

Not having had any exposure to the Annick Goutal range of fragrances I was pleased to find this one included in an envelope of mystery samples :). I had absolutely no idea what to expect so I went into this test totally blind ... and was utterly flabbergasted! Now when I say 'flabbergasted' I don't necessarily mean it in a positive way, but neither is this fragrance a negative for me. It's just completely surprising and catches one totally off guard. Eau du Fier (or Proud Water) is über masculine ... very much in the same way that the really hot guy who services your car is masculine ... all grease stained and muscle armed ... with piercing blue eyes gazing quirkily at you while explaining the problems with your manifold! But I digress ... An almost overwhelming note of petrol dominates this Goutal offering. Now for some, this can be a complete winner. Indeed, I am one of those who sticks my head out of the window at the gas station to catch a whiff or three of petrol fumes ... but as something to perfume my body with? That would be about as silly as The Rock wearing a Tutu to the Oscars :) ... there is not enough testosterone flowing around in me to pull this one off! I'd love to smell this on the aforementioned blue-eyed mechanic tho' ... especially all spruced up and waiting on my doorstep to take me to dinner. There is also a delicious saltiness to the dry down ... clean sweat on clean skin? *Shudder*!! The sillage here is not massive (so one would have to get in close *nudge, nudge - wink, wink*) and the longevity quite decent at about 5 hours on my perfume munching skin. As can be gauged by my above reaction, suffice it to say that on the right guy Eau du Fier would be incredibly sexy .... INCREDIBLY!!

In-house Annick Goutal nose Isabelle Doyen has a resumé of perfumed creations that reads like a shopping list of the rich and rare. Having studied as Goutal's apprentice prior to her passing, Doyen inherited her master's keen intuitiveness and passion, which translate into a portfolio of fine fragrances that are resolutely French in their approach. In 2000, Goutal launched the polarising masculine Eau du Fier to a mixed reception. A scent that focuses chiefly on the marriage of organic birch tar and black tea, Eau du Fier is quite possibly the blackest, sootiest perfume one might ever encounter. Coming right off the back of a decade of sanitised androgyny in perfume, Eau du Fier proved the absolute antithesis of perfume models that were popular at the time. By 2005, it had been already been retired. In the years since the early 2000's, appreciation for niche, rare and artisanal perfumery has grown exponentially, thanks in part, to flourishing fragrance communities both online and offline. How peculiar that the scent which was globally rebuked in 2003, is now generally regarded by perfume aficionados in 2012 as a triumph, and arguably Doyen's magnum opus. Olfactory notes aside, this fragrance launches from the flacon like a flame-thrower - an impenetrable wall of fire and embers, fed by combustable accelerants. On skin, Eau du Fier is equally as uncompromising... I am automatically transported to mechanic's workshop... I smell of a man who has worked under a car for a whole day; hands blackened with grease lying on a floor littered with oily rags. Open jerrycans in one corner reek of evaporating gasoline, whilst in the other, a fire is burning in a barrel that has been lit with small combustable firestarters. This daydream plays out for 6-8 hours, until a final lingering huff of smoke eventually vaporises from my skin. Black tea and tarry birch are the key components upon which this perfume is built, but one has to turn away from the vivid film playing out in their mind's eye to become cognisant of the individual accords. Doyen's masterful hand has interwoven subtle floral nuances of osmanthus and herbaceous/citrusy facets into this scent, which can only be picked when one knows where to look. Every note is treated like a fine brushstroke, forming a small but integral part of the whole. Eau du Fier will unquestionably evoke a response in the wearer. Some will fan the air around them and cough and wheeze, and others will sit, silent, and wait for the visions to begin. If only more perfumes could be as accomplished and profound.

Opens with only a second's worth of a just barely perceptible fresh mint before turning into a smokey burnt rubber accord with a mild tea undertone. The rubbery birch bark is by far the dominant note and it overpowers everything else on my skin. Projection is minimal, but longevity is excellent. I wish I could say this one appealed to me, but the birch bark is just too much. Eau du Fier just does not have enough going on to keep my interest long. It, like Cuir from Mona di Orio makes the error of just being *too* smokey, instead of using the smoke to complement other notes. I don't hate Eau du Fier, but I definitely don't enjoy wearing it and can't recommend it. This one is not good, earning 2 stars out of 5.

Profumo, first of all, congratulations on writing such a detailed comment about this MASTERPIECE of a perfume. My experiences with this scent were very similar to yours. However, I had no opportunity to try the fragrance. I had read about it in a trade magazine (which I believe no longer exists). Hmm, I thought. Smoky, leathery, slightly woody (that’s how the scent was described); I must have it as a fan of Lapsang Souchong. So, off to my regular perfumery in Cologne (Goldkopf) and I ordered it "blind." When the fragrance arrived a few days later, specially ordered from France, I was informed. When I went to pick up the item, the saleswoman had a strange reaction: Mr. Ö., we ordered the perfume just for you from France. You will understand that we cannot accept returns in this case. She had a smirking face and glanced at the tester that was included. Then she continued: we really can’t sell such a scent. I agreed and was about to pay when she asked if I wanted to try the tester. She probably wanted to see the horror in my eyes with a hint of schadenfreude. I thought to myself: that’s enough. I didn’t grant her the schadenfreude and shot back: "No need. I know what the scent is like. It should remind one of a campfire with smoldering charcoal, where you feel the coolness of the night and the warmth of the coals at the same time. And you sip a good Chinese Souchong." She was astonished at how differently people perceive scents. Now, onto the fragrance. Once home, my wife was just so thrilled with the scent that she had an urgent desire to run out onto the balcony for some fresh air. No wonder; she had sprayed the scent for testing just like she does with her fresh fruity or aquatic everyday scents like Laura or Cool Water Woman, so very generously. My first experiences were quite different. I applied the scent discreetly on my forearm; on the hairy side, not on the wrist. I don’t need pulsating spots if I keep sticking my nose there to follow the scent development. I was astonished at how consistent and gradual the development was. The scent reveals its true nature right from the start: unusual, extreme, with a woody-smoky focus and leathery accents. One must say about the scent progression that a top note is almost completely missing, only minimally present. But that is neither necessary nor sensible; after all, what should one use to set the mood for a campfire with charcoal: citrus fruits (yuck), or even fresh fruits (ugh). No, but herbs like lavender, sage, or clary sage would work. But only a little of that. Especially lavender and clary sage have a wonderful property in perfume compositions: they can give scents body and a shell even in small doses, without standing out themselves. In this fragrance, they probably added a nuance of bergamot to guarantee a tiny, airy freshness at the start. And then about Ho leaves (or Linaloe, rosewood), to ensure a bridge later between the woody overall picture and the base of the tar-like leathery something (probably a base based on juniper and birch) with a hint of amber. But this fragrance has much more to offer, as indicated above in the fragrance note composition by bitter orange, osmanthus, and clove. Namely, this spicy delicate-floral facet without appearing fruity. Certainly achieved through a second combination strand of bitter orange (including leaves, neroli, and absolute), which also creates a connection to the other strand via bergamot. Furthermore, in this strand osmanthus serves as a floral-delicate transition to the actually perceivable, almost drinkable black tea (yummy). Clove (spice as well as carnation absolute) at the end then creates the second bridge (alongside lavender, clary sage, etc.) to the amber note. This time, however, via the spicy-floral route. Amber appears in the fragrance description above, just like bergamot, lavender, and co, but I am convinced that it is this linalool-linalyl acetate combo that, in a very subtle interplay with amber, gives the whole fragrance a kind of transparent dress. A transparent, yet inexplicably alluring, all-encompassing shell. And thus, the fragrance receives a well-rounded overall picture from me and the highest possible score, even though I find Annick Goutal fragrances, like most Serge Lutens fragrances, simply not great. For me, they only represent partially lavishly built bases. Exceptions might be Sables (Goutal) and Louve or Douce Amere (Lutens). My personal experiences with Eau Du Fier, as far as other people are concerned, were also consistently positive, apart from the first ones described above. Anecdote: When I attended a Turkish celebration, I wore Eau Du Fier because I wanted to maintain the typical distance of discretion for myself. Perhaps this perfume struck the Turkish scent nerve just like it did for me. I could hardly resist the "attention." Otherwise, I could say about this scent that it is better suited for cooler seasons and for use from late afternoon onwards. Ideal for salespeople who shy away from customer contact, but not for career-minded employees (at least not in the workplace). Very nice for going out in the evening, provided the companion can tolerate this note, which unfortunately is not the case with my wife :-(. But ultimately, this fragrance might be the best choice when sitting with dear friends around a campfire, the cool wind blowing around your ears, and you sip a nice cup of hot black tea. It doesn’t even have to be Lapsang Souchong. Eau Du Fier already provides the smoky tea feeling.
