Yesterday, on my birthday, Mercedes actually managed to bring me my new car. A toast to Benz's service! No - not a big limousine, but the baby, the Smart for Four. My husband said that we should actually sprinkle it a bit with champagne so it doesn't squeak. But since our last break-in, all the champagne bottles are gone - the thieves must have been thirsty. No matter - I don't care much for that drink - I care about perfume. So I suggested we rather spray a few puffs from a bottle - for the new little car. The right scent seemed to be The Scent, as it comes across friendly and a bit playful like the Töff Töff - which could also come from Duckburg. The fragrance is transparent due to the aquatic mandarin, floral from the freesia, and deliciously sweet from the cocoa. Completely uncomplicated and unpretentious - like my little "heat ball." I spray a few puffs on the seats and say: Always a good ride. Festive champagne wouldn't have suited better.

Romantic rosebud jam. But still plush and petally, like wearing a velvet robe. While the name hearkens to the nurses of WWI, fortunately no battlefield or hospital to this beauty. It has an ageless feel, like I could waft it on a Downton Abbey duchess or at a Euphoria house party and not find it incongruous. While linear, it hits that single, burgundy-toned note impeccably well. Not too sweet, not too spicy, not too earthy, not too fresh. My closest comparison is Régime des Fleur’s Little Flower, if you subtracted the pomelo and added crushed raspberries. It is beautiful and wears well (at least 5h on my skin), but didn't feel personal (aka: weird) enough for me to need a bottle. Mental Snapshot: A postcard-perfect rose garden, next to the Bonne Maman factory. The Goldilocks answer to those who found Young Rose too kiki or Rose Noir too bouba. tl;dr: rosebud jam

I don't like rose scents unless it's the smell of Bulgarian rose jam which I tried only once in my life when I was 5 years old. This fragrance here is a garden full of blossoming roses, which, though maintaining their natural roseness, have the appearance of epoxy resin. Their shape is even and round, occasionally round-spiky, the colour is light-peachy. Oh, they start multiplying disproportionally, and I find myself yet to drown ("Hey, we are roses, and we will eat you," they say). I then open my eyes and see a pond full of synthetic roses, just as if it were a children's ball pit. I am not drowning, I am having fun, and I do enjoy my laughs in this place.

This scent opens up with fresh roses, but soon after it settles in with the musk and papyrus blending in. That's what makes this such a beautiful, comforting scent to me. It makes perfect sense why this is an ode to the nurses of WWI, since their job was to heal and comfort. It reminds me of Diptyque Orpheon, but more feminine-leaning with the florals. I love this, but I'll have to think long and hard about purchasing a full bottle due to the price.

A very lovely fresh rose. It does not last that long at all but it gets better longevity after spraying it on freshly showered, moisturised skin and/or clothes. Worth the extra effort for sure. People around me seem to love it, one of the most complimented fragrances in my collection, I've had multiple colleagues, strangers, etc. ask me what I was wearing.

When I first tested this on paper, it came across as a boozy, rose liquor type of scent which intrigued me since I love a bit of twist in fragrances and I adore rose by itself, later on when I tested it on my skin it became this smoky and ambery rose, lost all it's booze, became smoky and a bit candle wax-y, the candle wax thing happened with Bibliotheque as well, and I ended up being disappointed, nonetheless, It's still a good fragrance and has a unique scent profile if you're interested. Side note: my skin amplifies florals and sweetens up the scents

....the scent feels almost destructive to me. I can understand every single comment about Rose of No Man's Land. I find the background information about Byredo and its creator highly interesting. I like Scandinavian design (jewelry even more than furniture) and was excited when I first had a sample to test. My result back then for the scent rating was a solid 9.

The first days after my registration on Parfumo passed in a daze. I read comments - when I had enough time - from dawn until sunset. Soon, I had the fixed idea of building a small, manageable collection that only includes the "Best of the Best." I didn't strictly follow classical concepts.

No man's land: The land between the front lines of a war. In common parlance, it stands for inhospitable territory. Ownerless, uncultured, uninhabited, unkempt, or farmed by anyone. I imagine it to be desolate and barren in every respect. Hardly any vegetation except for a few thorny plants that wrest their sustenance from the harsh nature.

The opening rose quickly becomes surprisingly tarry after a gentle start, but soon regains its balance and navigates its contrasting forms into a charming tension field of delicate fragrance on one hand and bitterness on the other. It’s lovely to experience how both can coexist. Raspberry as an announcement fits perfectly, but is unnecessary in content.

… or maybe not? Fleeting start: the rose flies by, followed by the raspberry. What remains are the peppercorns, tingling on the skin, dry but pleasant. And...? Is that all there is..? Not at all! The rose comes back and stays. It is pink and delicate, but not girlish, dry and cool, yet not a diva. Soon the raspberry joins in, slightly sweet, more citrusy.

Excellent pepper perfume, very long lasting with a genius bottle. I could wear this all year round even if it is very hot cause this perfume is growing on me and at some point it gets sweet and very sexy. I want to try the etd as well. I love it and recommend this to all pepper lovers. Finally is very modern and not heady at all. Super hit for this summer !!!!!!!!

What has happened so far: Our Ma Dame is a cheeky little fruit who loves to provoke. She makes a big splash and enjoys life to the fullest. But: what happened next? Our rebel has grown up. She has found the man of her life, settled down. She has started a family that she lovingly cares for. She no longer needs to stand out and dance out of line at all costs. She doesn't need that anymore. She has found her style. She knows how to present herself elegantly. She knows how to charm men without strutting around in a crop top. She understands that make-up is not to be used like a paint box. She has found herself and is satisfied with her life. She appreciates waking up next to her husband in the morning - and not next to a stranger from whose apartment she then has to sneak out. She is no longer in her twenties. She gets a hangover after drinking. She can no longer turn nights into days. She carries responsibility - and she enjoys it. But: Sometimes, she pulls her high heels out of the closet, throws on a top with a killer neckline, gets herself ready, and hits the dance floor. On other days, she cranks up her sound system and dances on the table. Because she still has the heart of a revolutionary. She still doesn’t want to please everyone. After a night of dancing, she comes home tired. She has a headache and her feet hurt. And as she watches her aspirin dissolve in water, she smiles. It was a beautiful time back then. But she doesn’t long for it. Now is better. Every now and then, she reclaims that time. For one night. Adult? Yes. Boring? No! Thank you very much for your attention to our documentary series: Ma Dame - Paths of a Rebel. Goodbye.

It is rounder, softer, and smoother than the EdT, more pleasing and feminine; overall similar, but distinctly different. But what really annoys me is this widespread, increasingly pervasive, probably dictated by marketing strategists mania for diversification: For a well-performing fragrance, three flankers (Chérie, Belle, and Amour) first appear, then a winter, summer, uh, summer, autumn, and Christmas edition, and also, under every conceivable pretext, a limited series, often one for each of the twelve zodiac signs.

With my 50th comment, I actually wanted to delight/burden you with a comment journey through the 3 Alien summer editions (depending on how you feel about them), but apparently deliveries (I’m expecting the first of the triplets) from the German Post to Switzerland are still being transported by horse-drawn carriage. However, since I did the "Ma Dame" original vs. Eau de Parfum test last night before going to sleep & a lightbulb moment struck me, I dedicate the 50th to the "Ma Dame Eau de Parfum" As I’ve mentioned elsewhere, "Ma Dame" is quite a cheeky thing, and in direct comparison with the perfume variant, a very specific woman came to mind during a very specific dialogue. I’m talking about Pippa Lee from the film "The Private Lives of Pippa Lee." The (very good) film tells the life story of Pippa Lee, who - psychologically scarred by a drug-addicted mother - spends her life searching for true affection but finds drugs & a much older husband, and now at 40, she is questioning her life for the first time. First the dialogue, then the explanation of why I’m bringing this up: (Pippa is sitting in a café with her friend and discussing love & men) Pippa: Pick any man over 50 in this room. Either one of us could be married to him. Friend: OK. What about that one? Pippa: He just needs his routines, that’s all. I bet if you anticipate his needs before he knows he has them, he’ll be docile as a lamb. Friend: And that one? Pippa: He needs a lot of praise, but as long as you stick your finger up his ass while he’s coming, he won’t give you any trouble at all. ...Shocked that she actually said that, she dismisses her comment as a joke and bursts into loud laughter with her friend. The scene is descriptive for me because the "Ma Dame Eau de Parfum" has a similar character to the adult Pippa: occasionally, her true self shines through, which then - like in the dialogue - manifests in a concentrated burst, but otherwise, all the cheeky and willful traits that characterize this perfume are covered up with spices and warm notes. She has pepper in her ass, but fundamentally doesn’t dare to be herself anymore. Personally, I would recommend the original Eau de Toilette, because if you want to get a spicy going-out scent, there are better perfumes in my opinion (Midnight Poison or Elle Intense). Let "Ma Dame" be cheeky, zesty, and youthful; anything else feels inauthentic to me with this perfume.

One of my two blind buys (the first JPG fragrances I have ever tried) was the Ma Dame EdP. I wanted to be surprised and today I spontaneously decided to wear Ma Dame… When I first sprayed the perfume, I had a scratchy feeling in my throat…. And then I sensed this plastic-like note… but shortly after: “oh la la! who do we have here??? what a firework... not bad, Ma Dame… with a zesty sharp character then…” Even though this artificial rose made of vinyl seemed strange to me. I can't say that I didn't like the perfume; I was much more confused and surprised by this composition. It's an incredible mix of fresh citrus notes, cooled by patchouli, a pop art rose, and sharp pepper…. More interesting than I thought. After the sharpness mellowed, the true beauty of the perfume emerged. This perfume is ambiguous, meant for an urban woman who is multifaceted, self-confident, and at the same time very feminine, who has no qualms about showing her emotions and continually surprising herself and others. Defiant, cheeky, even a bit sassy at first, Ma Dame later appears quite tamed and somewhat cool. All these phases, how the perfume unfolds and changes over time, are exciting and interesting! You just have to give it some time. The perfume wears like a little black dress, which has flair and spice but still remains somewhat classic and timeless. Monsieur Kurkdjian has once again created a remarkable fragrance here!

Thanks to Murcielago for the sample. My experience with Monsieur Gaultier is almost virgin. I was therefore very curious about this fragrance, which is being advertised very beautifully. The rose here, a yellow or delicate pink tea rose, does not come across as forcefully as its Bulgarian or Turkish relatives, and is already carried by the musk in the top note.

I am pleasantly surprised that the scent is very fresh and not overpowering. It really lasts all day for me. Since I work in a laundry, many fragrances are practically washed away by the strong steam, but not my Ma Dame; I could still smell it at noon when the workday is over. Therefore, thumbs up from me. :-)

No, kiddos! This is the ultimate no-go. Help, I always thought pomace stinks, but Pulp tops even that. Whoever detects something fruity here must have a disturbed sense of smell. SORRY, no offense, don't take it personal. This here is simply a mashed fruitbasket, left to rot for four days. The flies are buzzing around. To make things worse a bitter note comes through, not being able to get rid of the allover rotten smell. And it has a staying power that devils brew. I really had problems to clean the back of my hand of the smell without rubbing the skin of. No, thank you, not for me. And thank you, Antoine, for the tester.

I'm testing this stuff right at the moment. My opinion could change by tomorrow. I'm in the middle of testing quite a few of the Byredo line, Pulp definitely stands out in terms of sillage. The other scents to test just could not compete. This leads me to think that it is very difficult to be ambivalent to this fragrance. I'm not sure about fig, I find it a very difficult note, in that I cannot decide if I like of hate it. The opening of Pulp is bombastic and demands of the attention. A combination of Bergamot and the the Fig assaulting the senses. It was a close call whether I washed the stuff off, but I persevered. Currently I'm experiencing something sweet and green, not unpleasant. I think I'll try this one again.

Not a nice title I know. I grew up in Spain and we used to have lots of citrus fruit trees, all of the fruit that had fallen off the trees was piled up at the bottom of the garden. This smells like this pile of fruit. I guess this is why I love it. It reminds me of happy places and that's what fragrance is all about. Its really the opening that's hard to digest but it settles down nicely. This is in my 2021 summer fragrance wardrobe and great to wear on a summers evening. Go easy on the trigger and it's lovely. Lasts for a long time too.

Before trying this, I didn't know what to expect. I heard things like "rotten fruit" and I wondered if this would be worth even trying at all. I was pleasantly surprised! What I get from this actually, is almost the smell of (like the name) pulp. Fruit pulp. For me it's Mango pulp, and it's a smell I actually really like. I do also get apple and citrus in there, and some grape etc. This is one I would recommend to people who like fruit and freshness. I do feel that it is a very cleverly made perfume and one which is composed intelligently. I would recommend it and would advise to try out first in good weather. I think this would be suitable for year round and would say that it is unisex. This is the smell of very ripe fruit up close. But it also has a balance which can only come from a well made perfume. One to try for sure. I thoroughly enjoy it.
Here is my video review of Pulp from the Swedish niche house, Byredo. As far as fruity powerhouses go, this one certainly fits into that category, I hope you find the review useful.

What I get from Pulp is a loud opening of blackcurrant that manages to give off an overly ripened profile outcoming from the combination of fig, apple and tiaré which I am not sure people are familiar with and its uneasy facet.

When I first gave Pulp a sniff from the sample vial, I thought, “raw fruit, a little boring”. But after wearing awhile, I see there’s more to it than that. The more I smell Pulp, the more I smell something vegetal, rather than fruity.

Pulp is a journey that starts at the final destination –the proverbial six feet under– with the last stages of decay and decomposition not happening underground but on our skin and under our nose. Straight out of the sprayer the figs, apples and berries are already way past their prime and beginning to soak in their own morbid, pungent syrupy juice.

This is an intriguing scent which I found likeable, but the list of where best to wear it outside of one's home would be a rather short one, I'm afraid- it smells a bit like over-ripe fruit which is starting to ferment-

Pulp is giving a bunch of crushed fruit, left in scorching sun, on the verge of being too ripe and going bad. It starts intense, is kept intense, and only slows down at the end, when it turns into a nearly sickening sweetness. Yet it is still very interesting, and I would say a one of a kind fruity fragrance. Anyone thinking of buying it blindly, or as a gift- don't.

Smells soo good! Fresh, sweet and flowery but masculine in my opinion. It’s on the weak side though considering it’s a perfume. I need to overspray and it projects within an arms lenght. Lasts around 5-6 hours on my skin and sillage is good I think. I walked past my son and he said I smelled good. I use this when I don’t want to smell coconutty from JPGPG.

A strongly different composition compared to the whole Le Beau line, but at the same time I find it relatively interesting - especially for warm days. The perfume is very linear, only the opening stands out with a lot of sweetness and flowers, then the fragrance becomes very simple. I smell a light sweetness here, flowers and a slightly biting ozone note in the background - as if you were standing by a heavily salted sea or taking a bath in brine. I really like this smell. It’s clean, it’s fresh and I think that’s best one from Le Beau collection.

Number 4 of the Le Beau series - and already from the indication of the fragrance notes, one that will go in a completely different direction. How does one combine this typically tropical aspect of the series with flowers? - The answer is: not at all. - The Le Beau Flower Edition is, for me, an independent fragrance that has little to no connection to its relatives. What it is, however: a good perfume and after Paradise Garden, the number 2 of the series. The opening is the most similar to the rest. It starts very fresh and delicious - no coconut this time, but a broader citrus note that really refreshes. A bit of pineapple, and it almost has something aquatic about it. Pretty quickly, a floral sweetness comes through. No resemblance to the typical Le Beau coconut sweetness - really a different direction. But it smells super pleasant: floral, sweet - very light. This one is best suited for 25 degrees and above. The scent development is very straightforward. The Flower Edition lives up to its name: sweet floral notes, fresh, absolutely unisex - but never powdery or too overwhelming. I clearly find: this is not a heavy fragrance and the most summery of the four. The drydown remains very light - no woods or any heavy components. When you hold the four side by side, this one is clearly different in scent profile - absolutely not a blind-buy candidate if you like the series. On its own, I really like it as a summer fragrance - if you enjoy many flowers and blossoms mixed with a synthetic, but well-made sweetness. The fresh lemon in the opening could last longer - that would be my critique. Sillage and longevity: around 7 points - quite decent for such a fresh scent.

This scent wasn't instant love, but it grew on me. Now, several years after I purchased it, and having sampled other perfumes (both niche and designer, hyped and sleepers), I can honestly say that VC is one of the best truly masculine scent (if you believe in there being such a thing in perfumery), a signature-worthy perfume. It is green and mossy, almost linear with perhaps only one noticeable change within the first hour (as the initial citrusy accord dies out giving room to the mossy and patchouli-based background). It's not a compliment magnet, it's neither playful nor romantic, not something you'd choose for a night out in a club or a bar-type situation. In other words, it's not universally likable, unlike the Elysiums, Bleu de Chanels, Laytons of this world (all of which I beautiful, by the way, and I really enjoy wearing all of them), but it IS an all-year-round, universally applicable scent, and could be a signature-scent worthy addition to your collection. The thing that distinguishes this perfume from a bunch of others for me is that it has a backbone, its own voice, character, a footprint, if you will. To my nose, it's similar to Brutus by Orto Parisi but smoother and is actually wearable, unlike Orto's eccentric olfactory experiment. It is blended very well, and what you get a couple of hours into spraying is just a deep green, a bit rough and heavy, but uncompromisingly straightforward razor-focused scent of inner calm, experienced-backed self-awareness, willpower and perseverance (sounds corny and mawkish, but it is these associations that come to mind when I wear it). There are other perfumes that have a similar feel to my nose (not similar in scent, but in their overall olfactory message): FM Vetiver Extraordinaire, Roja's Apex, Chanel's Sycamore, among others. If you're looking for a "no-chuckles" green and earthy scent that's a bit rough but uncompromisingly "masculine," do try this one (sample first before buying), you may find it strangely appealing, if not to others than at least to yourself.

Vigorous Cologne is a fragrance by Hugo Boss that belongs to the higher-priced collection. It is the first scent I could test from this collection. Is Vigorous Cologne worth the higher price? Honestly, my opinion is no. For me, you get a rather nice, but ordinary cologne here. The price is around 200€. Vigorous Cologne has that typical cologne-like freshness for me. The fresh notes are somewhat bitter and especially greenish. Bergamot, rosemary, and the moss listed in the base come through well for me. However, I also had the impression of smelling some ginger, which is not listed. Nevertheless, the scent has a strange synthetic quality for me. The smell that occasionally wafts into my nose is not entirely pleasant. Sometimes I associate it with cleaning products. My girlfriend said for the first time: "Ugh, what’s in the air? Did you put on hair removal cream?" I said it was a scent for testing. Today I tested the fragrance again without her knowing, and suddenly she said again: "Did you spray that hair removal perfume again? It smells so disgusting here." So you can see, opinions differ, and this cologne doesn’t seem to please everyone. Still, I don’t find it nearly as bad as my partner does. A positive note is the longevity for a cologne. The scent lasts a good seven to eight hours on me. The projection in the first hour is also remarkable, then it weakens, but that’s perfectly fine.

I stumbled upon this fragrance from Hugo Boss quite by chance. It's not really well-known, judging by the current 6 reviews, at least not in this lovely community yet. Perhaps I can help drum up some publicity for Vigorous Cologne with my contribution. 'Vigorous' was a term I wasn't familiar with until now. According to the internet (which I personally believe won't catch on), 'vigorous' means something like 'strong' and 'energetic'. One thing upfront: The scent is by no means a head note blender! In some statements, people mention that the fragrance has too much synthetic quality. I had that impression during my first testing as well. The first 20 minutes had a slightly unpleasant sour, stinging component. This reminded me of Bohemian Lime, which I also find rather exhausting in the initial phase. However, once the opening was over, this Boss revealed its full potential. The orange blossom, rosemary, and I believe there's also a lemon in there, create exactly the composition I wish for in a distinctive cologne. Herb, fresh, with a slight edge and minimal heaviness. Simply dreamy! Already on the second try, the head note seemed much more pleasant and less synthetic to me. With the current temperatures around 30°C, though, the good scent is only perceptible for a few hours. Since I currently only have a 5 ml sample, I have to be a bit frugal. At moderate temperatures, the longevity will certainly increase a bit. But one must also not forget that it is, after all, a cologne. In the few hours when it radiates really well, it is definitely invigorating, fresh, herbaceous, and zesty, making it a very good choice for the hot summer. Whether it can establish itself permanently with me, I can't say at the moment, as it competes with many other summery scents that are already in my collection. But: It was a pleasure to get to know Vigorous Cologne! Thank you for reading.

Yet another hipster amber-patchouli-vanillic scent with an faint leathery heart and a spicy floral whiff, most of all with that distinctive “niche texture” we’ve been so used to these years – thin, transparent, dusty, kind of cheaply synthetic, terribly reminding of so many other “artistic perfumes” (...) of recent times. Think of any amber and/or leather niche scent – this will easily be identical to them, and viceversa. Leather is again that synthetic suede note, amber is again basically ambroxan, and so on... juniper berries, ok, that's maybe less common. I don't get any iris out of this. Not tragic but tragically uninspired and without the slightest hint of something justifying its price. 4,5-5/10

I confess that i always had a peeve with the fragrance house Byredo. Not that its creations were bad, but the didn't seemed consistent with the position that their price put them I felt that there was lacking a clear nexus bettwen the very personal inspirations and the fragrances, that could been part of any other brand. Because of this i got surprised with 1996, born from the parternship bewteern the brand and photrographers duo Inez Van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin. The idea was born initially as a gift limited edition to the friends of the photrographers duo, one which was inspired in their favorite notes and the 'Kirsten, 1996', photography. I imagine that the reaction was quite positive and both the brand and photrographers saw that they had in their hands a product which could be commercial success. As they describe, 1996 is really cozy, warm and doesn't seem exactly ultra modern neither old fashioned. If i was going to sum up, i would say that it's an iris creation in a good ambar and patchouli background. The iris here seems for me delicate, devoid of its violet nuances or its cold aroma. It's an iris accord that reminds me a lot of the carrot aroma, that texture of a carrot which is slightly sweet, earthy and, somehow, orange on its smell. It's an organic aroma delicious for me, which goes along with good mixture of patchouli and ambar - an ambar which gives more emphasiss on the vanilla part and that with patchouli ends producing a sensation of semisweet chocolate on skin. I like how the spices are used in this creation, giving a fresh spicy touch which is secondary and it's used to soften the base notes intensity. If you are looking for a good oriental iris, 1996 is a great choice.

Niche genre: smudged eyeliner musks. 1996 is crystals shop patchouli splashed with Chanel vanilla. Add a leather moto jacket, last night’s rouge, a spilt cocktail on a fur coat, and a single midnight cigarette and you’ve got 1996. It’s the scent of a rowdy, self-indulgent night out. Like you got dolled up to your ritziest and then closed out a basement rave. 1996 has the same dustiness and brandied woods as Bibliotheque and the same leather and smoke of Black Saffron, but feels more authentically “lived-in” than either. Heard someone on the internet say this smells like indie sleaze and it’s all I can see now. Longevity is uncharacteristically un-Byredolike. Mental Snapshot: Skater skirt, hooflike heels. A sweaty dancefloor, glitter tears. Polaroids of modern muses. A self-mythologizing Lana lyric. The NYC skyline, hazed into a dapple of bokeh lights in the night. tl;dr: my 2014 Tumblr feed

I tried it in Berlin and it is a really nice but not that special composition from Byredo. It is hard to get and mostly it is sold out in Berlin. Created by Byredo as a gift for friends they decided to sell the Scent limited to the ordinary crowd. Sillage was average and it ended up in the Base notes with something like a vanilla/Iris Sirup. The Drydown is deep, dark vanilla. A bit to much for me. Starting with pepper/juniper top notes I was so amazed and curious about this Limited 50 ml Version from Stockholm... I waited for stunning Middle Notes that would blast me away but no. Violet and Iris hidden behind the vanilla cloud. Not much leather to find here for my nose too. I see Byredos Creation on a lady over 30. Mens could try it too but will be afraid of the creamy Vanilla ending. That sweet ending lasts for days on fabric and 24 hous on skin. Still I think it is so well rounded I give 80%. Around 120€ for 50ml You need to spend in Germany. 100ml is not available.

Love love love this fragrance. I disagree with the two reviews below. The air is cold and the leaves are falling and it's time to bring out this underrated GEM from ByeByeRedo. 1996 is in the vien of something like Tempo (earthy patchouli) but wears drier, more ambery and much longer lasting. There is juniper up top giving it a little piney dry fruit but it only sticks around for the opening. It has also has this intriguing glossy magazine paper smell. I find a lot of the fragrances from this house have a plastic quality. Back to 1996...This is an art space patchouli bomb, but with dusty iris/orris and a subtle worn leather accord that is more fitting for an antique book shop or vintage furniture store. I have some ambers and patch scents but this one is super unique. *Not a blind buy scent unless you really love a big patchouli/amber! I also heard it's been discontinued.

1996 is a syrupy, medicinal, labdanum rich amber that begins with a sharp and tangy juniper note in the opening. It's a piercing, clarifying note that serves to liven up what is otherwise an almost leaden feeling composition. There is not much development beyond the point that the juniper disappears in the heart.

Byredo has often (and so far predominantly) fragrances in their portfolio that don't really entice me. Until now, after testing around 6-7 scents from Sweden, only "Baudelaire" has convinced me, and even that one is quite mood-dependent, although undoubtedly a good and slightly mythical scent.

But first, it has to start: The opening from 1996 is less sharp or spicy than I expected given the paper form. On the contrary, I find it pleasantly piquant, so to speak. The leather makes a brief appearance, but otherwise, the first hour is characterized by a licorice-violet throat lozenge accord. I like that. Nicely sweet-woody-not sweet.

You can think what you want about the Beckhams, but you can't deny Victoria's style and taste. And when she highlights a fragrance, you can be curious. Additionally, it was particularly emphasized today in the perfumery from the Byredo line and it also appealed to me on paper. That's how easily I secured a testing spot on my wrist.
In my opinion, this fragrance is a masterpiece not only from Byredo, but in general in recent times. I have already ordered a 50 ml bottle in Prague.

The La Belle Flower Edition is the best of the two recently launched Flower Edition fragrances. In the world of JPG women's perfumes, the La Belle EDP profile wins me over. I find La Belle Le Parfum too heavy, and Divine doesn't quite charm me. Therefore, I had high hopes for this new release. It's seductive, replacing the pear of the original La Belle with fresh apricot. Vanilla and patchouli form the woody base, while a white floral, osmanthus, adds a sophisticated touch. The result is an enveloping fragrance with a fresh top note and a velvety body. Classified as fruity, amber, and floral, it's perfect for transitional seasons, with notes that adapt to both cooler days and cooler nights. It has good longevity and moderate projection, ideal for special occasions, leaving a noticeable but not overwhelming impression.

La Belle Flower Edition is a fragrance that primarily smells of apricot. A sweet, jam-like apricot. But to me, there’s an underlying scent that feels off. The apricot seems overripe, past its prime - almost spoiled. There’s a hint of dampness, something reminiscent of an old, musty cellar, which spoils what could have been a lovely fruity jam. I can only assume this comes from the patchouli. It’s not entirely bad, but this undertone keeps me from fully enjoying it. For a beautiful apricot or osmanthus fragrance, I would rather go for Osmanthus .

The latest iteration of la belle is a departure from the former ones and it is also one of the most original perfume releases of recent times. Hopefully won’t really be a limited edition. This is a sophisticated and easy to wear perfume that gives a carefree allure. It starts with the impression of being surrounded by apricot trees in the orchard, there are the smells of nature around you and sweet flowers are blooming. It’s morning and it’s a bit humid, some slight marine breeze through your hair brings to your nose your vanilla flavored hair oil. For more details pls watch my YT video linked here below.

strong la belle fruity icing DNA as expected, with a beautiful white floral bouquet note and a slight powedery almond twist. there's a gorgeous vanilla icing base that provides extra sweetness with the fruit and slices through those white florals. it caused a strong surface allergic reaction in my coworker so there's definitely coconut in there

I am trying my hand at my first review today, please don't be too harsh on me. When I saw that the new La Belle Flower Edition Limited Edition was out, and I saw the fragrance notes, I knew immediately that I had to have it. Unfortunately, I am not a fan of the La Belle OG or its flankers, so I was extremely curious whether this one would live up to my expectations. Since Quentin Bisch is one of my favorite perfumers, I was optimistic. The opening starts fruity with the apricot, but not a sticky sweet apricot, rather a beautiful airy apricot that is incredibly suitable for spring and summer. As it develops, the floral notes of jasmine absolute, magnolia, and osmanthus join in, making the scent fruity-floral-fresh. My fear that the patchouli would make the scent too green or earthy in the drydown did not come true, and combined with vanilla, it creates a beautifully rounded fragrance. So see if you can find it and give it a sniff. I immediately secured a second bottle because I liked the scent so much.

The limoncello note is absolutely delicious. Mixed with incense, patchouli, oud and papyrus is pushing the somewhat sweet opening into a very woody experience. Love at first sight. Anytime, any season. Powerful start, lasts long on skin and projects well. One of my most complimented perfumes. Reminds me of Morning Chess.

Starts very woody and sorta hay like, with prominent incensy cardamom which later turns into smoky papyrus with very light oud nuances and mossy tobacco lurking somewhere underneath! Nice fragrance that suits my skin very well during the spring time! One of the most wearable oud fragrances I ever tried..although not sure if the term oud should be used here because it's barely recognizable. It asted around 4 hours on my skin with nice moderate sillage.

This fragrance opens with a bright flower note to which an accord of dried grass adds an interesting nuance of smoke and hay. As this pleasant accord blooms on my skin, I am able to see the tobacco and the papyrus leaves that compose it. The floral top note is quickly engulfed by the tobacco-papyrus melange and from this moment onwards frames the composition. To me this scent is more about hay, dried flowers, mown meadows in August than about humidors, pipe smoke and the smoking rooms of a gentlemen's club. However, as the fragrance progresses there is a shift from the outside (countryside) to the inside (gentlemen's club), because it gradually morphs into the clean, purposely old-fashioned scent of expensive handmade soap. I cannot say which combination of notes is responsible for that, but the result is very nice, but ultimately rather common. I would compare this Byredo offering to Etro's Gomma, although this time I frankly prefer the Byredo.

Adlerwood Meets Ikea We all know Ikea. Surely, each of us has assembled a shelf or a table with one of those cute names at some point. And while doing so, wished we had studied architecture just to understand the seemingly straightforward assembly instructions halfway.

"Not dying. No one would hate anyone anymore. No one would envy anyone anymore. People would love each other. One could start anew infinitely, and now and then something would come to fruition. Once in a hundred, once in a thousand times there would be a success. According to probability theory. We know that we don't have time to endlessly chase happiness.

It somehow took a while for me to get into Byredo and the Flui. At first, I thought, what are all these overpriced, strange scents in such beautiful sterile bottles? I have always found the sterile bottles super cool, almost reminiscent of Chanel. Then came my first test: Black Saffron. I didn't understand the scent progression and didn't know what to make of it.

Byredo has yet to impress me with the 5 Swedish scents I have tested so far, aside from the positively unique "Baudelaire," which is truly well-crafted and very distinctive. The others strike me as somewhat too medicinal, unbalanced, or banal. "Oud Immortel" now combines aromas that I find very heterogeneous - well, it's no surprise that most comments score between 6.

It starts, as I have read so many times before, with just a quick peek. Really quick. It doesn't take long at all. And it's on the way. In this case, it was Beck in Munich, as Andi136 made me curious about whether there might still be something decent on the bargain table inviting a spontaneous purchase.

But it isn’t the worst either. For me, it feels like Invictus got a few shots of testosterone kicked into it. It’s got a similar “bubble gummy” vibe, but it’s a hair more masculine, and a tad more mature. You can definitely feel the similarities, but it’s a bit quieter on how it resonates. While the projection isn’t what you normally expect from a “Le Male” scent, it’s nowhere near as bad as the word on the street makes it sound. It’s definitely THERE, it’s just not quite as flamboyant as the other members of its family. Maybe a 1-2ft bubble radius. The same factors apply to the sillage trail; it resonates there, just not as loud as one would expect for something that’s similar to Invictus in aromatics. Longevity is also bludgeoned in online reviews, but it gets you 7-8 hours of life. People notice it on you when you stop smelling it. It’s probably the ambroxan fatigue kicking in. As it dries down, the bubblegum notes back off and leave a lighter, very blue, masculine base. You can tell it’s an attempt to replicate Invictus, but it isn’t a horrible grab, especially now. I grabbed 125ml for $50; at this price it delivers “enough”. If you have an Invictus scent in your collection, you won’t need it, but if you want something more masculine and less loud, this one is something you might want to try.

As a Gaultier perfume enthusiast and "Le Mâle" die-hard fan, I couldn't help but get my hands on this edition as quickly as possible. Just on principle. :) Because I am genuinely excited about their original work, as well as some flankers. Most of all, I love "Le Mâle eau de Toilette," "Le Mâle Eau Fraîche Popeye Edition," "Fleur du Mâle," "Ultra Mâle," and "Le Mâle Terrible." The scent, I find, doesn't really smell like the Le Mâle DNA for the first time. Well, it doesn't have to, as long as it's good... but what does it smell like then? Honestly, it's hard to say, as it is just SO weak. I'm not exaggerating... even with 20 sprays, you can only smell a very faint veil that soon disappears. Or is the nose just getting tired of it so quickly? Or both? Hm. In any case, it smells somewhat fresh, salty, sweet. When I bury my nose in the spot on my T-shirt where I intentionally applied it for the "clothing test," it briefly reminds me of Coach for Men. But the best description is this: It smells extremely similar to Dunhill Icon Racing, just a bit less sweet, fresher, and noticeably weaker. Since Icon Racing also draws parallels to Invictus, some who don't know Icon Racing might recognize this in it. But Icon Racing really hits the nail on the head... although I find the scent of Navy better and more pleasant, but without the performance, that unfortunately doesn't help much. During further testing, it also gave me brief "La Nuit de L'Homme Eau Electrique" moments. I would say 70% Icon Racing + 30% Eau Electrique = In the Navy. If I had to try to understand Gaultier, I could explain it like this: When you watch the commercials for "Le Mâle," where muscular guys spray themselves with 1000 sprays after sports... one would think Gaultier wants their fragrances to be applied generously. Why? -> Maybe because they think their rather maritime scents work better when applied during sports or in the summer heat, if applied in low concentration but generously and massively? Then you don't offend anyone, but the distribution of the scent aura on the body is more even / better. -> Or, because they would like people to absorb the "spray effect," the experience *pff pff pff*, more into their consciousness and see it as part of their daily routine? Don't laugh at me!! The sound of a car door closing is meticulously crafted by scientists... for the premium car experience! ;) -> Or is it simply because they believe they will sell more if people have to bathe in it to feel it? Hmm... I can already guess how most of you will see this.. ;P Feel free to tell us in the replies! I just hope this isn't a sign that PUIG is now completely sinking the Gaultier brand... -.- I found the original Le Mâle so great because it made a statement. It was a bit edgy and provocative, almost intrusive with its spice blend, probably due to the tarragon, lavender, etc.; but it still had something attractive and appealed to most because the sweetness and freshness provided a veil over it all that softened it. This contrasting interplay was also so strong in intensity, even with 1-2 sprays of the vintage version, that it added even more to the whole and made it even more distinctive. (And exhausting if someone overdid it excessively...) And I would really find it a shame if the brand no longer tried to uphold this spirit in a worthy manner. I mean, is it so hard to dare a little more and step out of the comfort zone? I know there is quite a bit of affordable competition now, and it probably doesn't come from nowhere that Gaultier has sold out / been bought or something. Where Le Mâle Terrible was a step in the right direction for me, although also already weaker in concentration but still good and daring, this is now a bit of an indictment. Not very independent anymore, and also weaker than usual. The Eau Fraîche Popeye Edition is very successful though! Was that before PUIG? Never has the label "For Fans" fit so well... because anyone who is not an idealist and lover of the brand, or has a screw loose like me, or both, is really well advised to get Dunhill Icon Racing for a fraction of the price, and thus already celebrate the intense version of "In the Navy," which will only be available in Austria in March. (: EDIT: We're reporting live from the testing ground! I just applied a massive dose again, 2x underarms, 4x under the shirt, 2x on the neck, and 3x on the arms... In this dose, the salty scent comes across almost citrusy. And yes, now it's really good. Let's see how long haha ^^

LE MALE by Jean Paul Gaultier .... This bottle and its scent have been with me since the mid-90s. I have already noticed in everyday life and of course here in the forum that this name associated with the fragrance divides opinions and tastes. For my part, I still remember very well how I had to have this scent with a bottle packaged as a male torso in a tin can (how crazy! ;-) ) with my apprentice salary - no matter how it actually smells or how it smells on me. In the meantime, there are several LE MALE fragrance versions that I mostly have in my collection. Today, or rather in 2018, there was an announcement for LE MALE - IN THE NAVY. Unfortunately, this fragrance was not available at any of my usual places - and it also seemed difficult to get it online. At least in the online stores I know here. By chance, I was able to win this edition as a "buy it now bargain". Here on the perfume site, I was able to get a first impression - of what this time awaits me as a fragrance variation. The scent actually arrived unopened and after unpacking, the first spray went directly under the shirt on my skin. The first impression was rather unpleasant. I found the scent to be light & very chemical & salty. For me, there was no trace of mint ... This smell reminds me a lot of my time in the Bundeswehr. I mean, some items back then smelled like that too. Not really sexy. For me, one spray was absolutely enough. That the scent should be very weak was not something I could relate to. However, it actually doesn't take long for the salty smell to fade and only a light hint of vanilla can be sensed. As much as I like the fragrances of Jean Paul Gaultier - this one is really not for me. There was surely a vision from the creators of this fragrance. I am glad that I was able to get it for myself - I certainly won't sell it. But 2019 is just around the corner and I suspect that there will be a new vision for LE MALE then. Until then, I will enjoy the other fragrances in my collection. ;-)

Honestly, Le Male is my "heavyweight" motorcycle scent that I wear very often and usually only alternate with Kouros or Issey Miyake. I bought the NAVY solely because of the brilliant can - and without trying it beforehand - just like the AVIATOR, which is a must for me as a passionate air breather. Both are visual can statements; the Navy guy smells - to me - pleasant; he is not as "unnoticeable" as has been complained about here before. I've been smelling him for some time, of course: (also) my(!) nose gets used to these relatively quickly - for those around me, however, he remains recognizable (= if I can't smell anything anymore, I turn around while walking and can still surprisingly perceive quite a lot in the slipstream). And I am definitely not the re-sprayer par excellence - I never do that. An unfortunate (are there others?) Austrian politician once coined the much-ridiculed term "situationally elastic," which I've adapted for the NAVY: it is, for me, the situation-independent scent, when you need to step out quickly and can't really sample much, you can't go wrong with it in case of doubt. I find him likable, yep!

One of the worst fragrances of all time, of course the one from Le Mâle Eau de Toilette lasts quite briefly as an eau de toilette, I don't like all of them. This one feels too short, you only perceive it for a moment. I tested it again yesterday, just before work I sprayed a bit more than enough. You don't really get approached about it. I even asked if they could smell me today, unfortunately no. I like its freshness, the mint stands out a lot, the rest doesn't really come to the fore.

Arrived at my Le Male journey at In the Navy - and quickly realized: This one has no significant online following, so expectations were immediately tempered. But curiosity remained. Contrary to my fears, this one hits - for me. Because it is simple and knows exactly what it wants to be.

After a longer break, I want to speak up again. As can be seen from the missing umlauts, I am currently abroad, specifically in Vancouver, Canada. Of course, I had to explore the perfume shops here and was more than just positively surprised: while there are also the usual suspects (Armani, Boss, Joop, etc.), right next to them are brands like Tom Ford, Creed, Il Profvmo, or bottles from the Editions de Parfums Frédéric Malle line. I am certainly not used to this from my small-town drugstores and even perfume shops, so I felt like a kid in a candy store here. :-) As a former resident of the city of Metzingen, where the headquarters of Hugo Boss is located, I am naturally more or less... well, rather "more" familiar with this brand - and almost everyone knows its fragrances. However, the five samples from the new collection were not available even there. It’s just not outlet goods - or at least it shouldn't give that impression. "Cashmere Patchouli" was one of my first trial candidates, and wow, I haven't been blown away like this in a long time. However, in a somewhat unexpected way, as I initially didn't notice much patchouli. Perhaps it's due to my imagination or the fact that my nose hasn't come into contact with many different fragrances lately, but a bell started ringing for me immediately: Iris! And this apparently in the most pleasant variant I have ever encountered. It was complemented by a light vetiver note, which I believe makes the fragrance perfect for the cold season. Only towards the base did the patchouli become more prominent, but it was never really dominant. "Too bad" regarding my expectations - I really like patchouli - but all the better regarding what I ultimately got. And to illustrate how much I like this scent: on the other wrist, I treated myself to a spray of Dior Homme that evening - from a bottle with a SILVER tube, meaning: the pre-2011 version! Not that bitter brew that you get today. Nevertheless: if I had to choose between the two fragrances, my choice would probably have fallen on the somewhat "boringly" designed (but high-quality) bottle from Hugo Boss. Unfortunately, a purchase isn't feasible at the moment due to tight travel budgets, but the Canadians somehow don't mind if you freshen up at the sample table for a Saturday night. :-) Let's see what treasures I can acquire tomorrow. Until then, I will remain in the "Cashmere Iris/Vetiver/Patchouli" delirium. P.S.: The longevity is absolutely phenomenal! Although, for those who often want to switch their fragrance, perhaps a bit TOO good. After over 24 hours, there is still a distinctly noticeable, now somewhat patchouli-heavy base present. The same goes for Dior Homme, although there it’s more about a slightly powdery cocoa note. But that's just by the way. :-)

tested yesterday. one of the purest patchouli scents I have ever smelled... There are hardly any other fragrance notes present. For patchouli lovers, this scent is therefore a must. Especially because it completely avoids any gender-specific embellishments, it can be wonderfully worn by both men and women alike. All in all, a very elegantly appearing collection that Boss has launched here. The bottles are made of real crystal glass. Each of the fragrances is truly worth a test. Cashmere Patchouli particularly stood out in my opinion. Facit: patchouli in its purest form.

No, the Boss Luxury Collection will not convince me with the third fragrance tested, "Cashmere Patchouli." What I find most annoying is the somehow hastily thrown-together composition, which I repeatedly recognize in Boss Premium. Fragrance development is a foreign word; the scents are somehow stiff. Additionally, the fragrance is quite simply constructed: At its core is a very earthy patchouli that smells very much like damp, slightly clayey forest floor. Air accord? Is that a joke again? As far as I'm concerned, the fragrance has a slightly floating note in the form of soft, balsamic touches. A mix of fresh and vegetable, green elements. For me, it's neither fish nor fowl. It lacks the spirit, the truly creative moment, the essence of a composition. Boss absolutely fails at this.

It was probably in mid-2011 when HUGO BOSS decided to launch an even more exclusive special series of fragrances within its already exclusive "HUGO BOSS SELECTION" series: "The Collection" Essentially, bespoke fragrances that are meant to reflect the experience of high-quality materials. These include: Cotton+Verbena Silk+Jasmine Velvet+Amber Wool+Musk and Cashmere+Patchouli And now we will focus on the latter: First, one must ask, what do I get for the hefty 110€/50ml?! A lot, I think!! Packaging: Even the packaging celebrates the fragrance. Each of these scents comes in a box approximately 30x20cm in size, with the front adorned by the material referenced in the fragrance - in this case, cashmere. When you open the sleeve, a small pouch with a cord reveals the real crystal bottle - simply wonderful! The Fragrance: One could say, the Patchoulifaust in the "Cashmere Glove" strikes! Patchouli in its purest form. First Impression: In contrast to Wool+Musk, which carries several fragrance accords, Cashmere+Patchouli really smells almost exclusively of patchouli - so certainly not everyone’s scent - and thus exclusive. Longevity: The fragrance is as described, the Patchoulifaust in the "Cashmere Glove". After 5 minutes on the skin, it explodes - so use it sparingly, or else the office will clear out. Although... Application: Speaking of the office. I wouldn't want to wear this fragrance there. a) too many philistines without an understanding of fragrance... b) the scent hits a bit too mercilessly at first impression... Better to use it intentionally in the cold season and generally in the evening! Conclusion: Here too, HUGO BOSS has created a true exotic with charm and style with its COLLECTION (in contrast to the usual waters). Bravo!

How does this fictional character from Thomas Mann's family saga come to this, moreover unsolicited perfume recommendation? Quite simply: By the fact that he came to my mind and I possess the audacity for everything that follows. I explain the appropriateness as follows: The fragrance opens with a proper cloud of perfume, of which one could suspect (like colleague "Hibernation") not only patchouli but also musk. This seems quite fitting for the status of a respected and wealthy merchant who has acquired his riches in grain trading. It lends a certain aura. However, soon patchouli takes on an even more prominent role in an increasingly scratchy and beige-colored olfactory impression, which eventually reaches a point where one would have to deny its beauty due to the overwhelming scratchiness. But only almost. Thus, one becomes aware of the fields where Buddenbrooks' harvested bales of wheat lie scattered. Or one thinks of the linen sacks full of grain loaded onto ships, specifically regarding the texture and beige color of these sacks. In the base, the fragrance becomes softer and loses some of the masculinity present in the heart. In any case, I associate this olfactory progression with food and its consumption in a social setting. Perhaps it would be worth a try to counter unwanted loss of appetite by sniffing this perfume. Ladies can also wear the fragrance, especially if they are traditional (not to be confused with pregnant) operators of country inns, to which city dwellers gladly seek refuge for some stylish celebration. With all these summery associations, I would see Cashmere Patchouli's use more in colder temperatures, even if cashmere plays a role mainly in the top note. For more cashmere, one should probably test Encre Noir, if I remember correctly. May this fragrance not meet the same fate as the Buddenbrook family, namely to disappear back into obscurity.

Sometimes, when I was a kid, having a cold felt kind of cozy. Sure, having a runny nose and a cough sucks, but it had its perks. Not having to go to school and having your mom pamper you, maybe watching more TV than usually and getting some magazines... It wasn't all bad, but it's not something I'm really nostalgic for either. As an adult with responsibilities, being sick is even worse. Why do I tell you all this? Because Mixed Emotions kind of smells like being sick! Not in the gross "sickly human sweat" way, but like things you might have next to you when you have a cold: Blackcurrant flavored throat lozenges, vaporub and a nice cup of hot black tea. I don't know where it's coming from, but something in here really makes me think of eukalyptus, which I'm not a fan of. Besides the medical notes, the violet is quite strong and adds a bit of a magical forest vibe. All in all this fragrance is sweet and lush, and does a nice job replicating the texture of tea, but it's too camphorous for me to really enjoy. Interesting in a way, but not what I'd ever want to smell like.

Not sure about this one. I have official sample now and it's wonky. Opening is more raspberries than blackcurrant to me. Tea is there and a lot. Also some dark tar vibe. Like hot asphalt almost. Very odd release. Yet here we are, I still I want to sniff it a bit more. Very unexpected and name fits the bill perfectly.

Cat piss or masterpiece - that’s what I’ve heard and read about this Byredo’s creation. I wouldn’t dive deep into the brand as everyone on this sub should know it. I will just say that to me it’s a somewhat “commercialized” niche (like PDM or Roja) that focuses more on sales and less on the art component compared to an average (not in terms of quality) niche brand. But that’s fine, I really don’t mind it, they shouldn’t be there to please me or anything. This one might evoke some mixed emotions in some people as I repeatedly heard people labeling it as cat’s piss. That’s the good old blackcurrant performing :) To me, there’s nothing urin-y in the scent. It opens up with a sharp and sweet blackcurrant note, then gradually transforms into a black tea infused with birch tree smoke. The sweetness doesn’t fade away entirely, just gets more quiet. This is the only scent from Byredo that I’ve truly enjoyed and wanted to own. Interesting and quite unusual combo of notes, well-crafted too. Reminds me of spring and early summer in the place I grew up :)

I was looking for a transition scent for winter to spring as The Noir 29 is my go-to for fall and winter. The London Byredo store clerk was amazing as I came in and said, I like Biblitheque but find it too sweet. Mixed Emotions was the first suggestion and it was spot on what I was looking for. The top note is sweet but not cloying and the mate pulls it down so well. Really wearable on my skin as well as scarves and cardigans. The other two scents recommended, Eleventh Hour and Mumbai Noise, were close in different ways to what I was looking for (Eleventh Hour was too smokey, Mumbai Noise was too spicy) but I think the fruity quality of Mixed Emotions made it an immediate purchase.

A blackcurrant-flavoured Vicks throat lozenge, complete with that wintergreen edge that probably doesn’t even have a therapeutic effect but never fails to remind you that you’re under the weather and ingesting this out of necessity, not choice. Underneath the clear, hard candy gloss of this topnote lurks a cat piss note so sharp and winey you are right back in those abandoned lots at the corners of your estate where the weeds and stray cats have colonized every inch of the floor space. Later, much later, and some might say, too late, a pleasant Ombre Leather-like suede accord comes in – no tea, mind, just the plainest of all glove box suede and new mid-range car upholstery.  The catpissy blackcurrant note lingers like a feeling of malaise, developing an unpleasantly BO-ish nuance that only adds to my distress.  Though unhappy to have ceded so much skin space to this horrid perfume during a lunch break, I am happy to have smelled it, as it had been occupying quite a large part of my imagination for some time.

It is a sweet currant scent on my skin. I've smelled a few perfumes with black currant note, and this is a well-done currant. However, I was hoping for a woody scent, but all I get is currant. Maybe a hint of violet leaf. Cute but not worth the price for me. Not to be a hater but I tried a lot of Byredo perfumes, and I am not impressed...

I received a sample of this with an order. I had never heard of this perfume and had zero idea what to expect. STRAIGHT CAMPFIRE SMOKE in literally the worst way possible. I had to immediately jump online to find reviews because I could not believe what I was smelling, ain’t no way this was suppose to smell like grilling fruit in the summer and sitting around a campfire.

With the name Mixed Emotions, I definitely get a bad feeling, as that was the name of a Euro-disco pop duo initiated and produced by Drafi Deutscher in the mid-80s, which produced a few minor hits. The music was definitely not my thing, and I can hardly remember the titles, but the name has had a negative connotation for me ever since.

Tea fragrances are always a bit of a thing. Often I find them grand and special, imagining how I would wear them to relax, read, and unwind on the couch. But once they are in the collection, they gather dust faster than I can say “Bvlgari.

This is the case when the name perfectly matches the scent. The beginning is intense: it smells like sour lemonade and burnt rubber. Only after about 30 minutes does the beauty begin - green, currants, iced tea, good vibes. After that comes the sweet woody base that lingers on the skin for a long time. There are such extremes in this fragrance.

With the blood orange and orange blossoms in the top and heart notes, Classique comes across as very fresh and citrusy. The fragrance is the perfect partner and motivator for sports. It also has a subtle woody note that lingers lightly. However, it usually doesn't last after sports, as a few new spritzes of fragrance after the shower carry the positive energy and citrus freshness with them. In the 2024 edition, the bottle is designed in the Pop Art style of Keith Haring.

Hugo Boss, Boss Bottled Oud Aromatic was first released in 2019 but is still seemingly difficult to find. It has a relatively simple note breakdown of orange blossom, myrrh, and oud, which feels pretty spot-on. It’s fresh and resinous and even slightly sweet with something in the oud that vaguely hints at a dirty, animalic side, but mostly a clean oud ala Oud Wood. It feels fairly well rounded among its varying contrasting points, but just feels a tad incomplete to me, full of plenty but missing something While I cannot find it in stock anywhere, it is for sale via FragranceBuy.CA for $90 for 100ml. It’s a decent fragrance but a bit overpriced for what it is; that is, it’s neither especially imaginative and artistic nor wholly well-rounded enough for everyday wear. Still, I expect that a lot of people will like this since it feels right at the intersection of a few different genres. 7 out of 10

This is such a beautiful and special fragrance. From the opening, it smells like bright, happy, sweet, perfectly ripe citrus fruit. As it dries, you start to notice the marshmallowy, cotton candy sweetness in the base notes. I was glad to see Oriana as one of the "similar fragrances" because fragrance is exactly what I thought of as well. However, I will say this one smells more elevated than Oriana. If you read my review from Oriana, I compared it to a cheap walmart cotton candy fragrance that I used to wear in middle school. This one, is similar to Oriana but much less juvenile. This is a more grown up, luxurious version but still with that same kind of fun, playful energy. This fragrance makes me smile just from smelling it. It's like the feeling of sunshine on your cheeks on a perfect summer day.

Byredo is one of those houses that I haven’t been super interested in trying because of how expensive it all is and how bad the performance is across the board. I have not heard of one person say that these fragrances are TOO strong or TOO long-lasting, and personally, I like my perfumes on the stronger side (especially if they’re going to cost THIS MUCH). Anyways, I kept that in mind when I got a decant of Sundazed. As a Neroli fiend, I really do enjoy this fragrance a lot. It’s your traditional white floral-citrus combo, but with a big dose of sweetness from the cotton candy in the base. I would say the cotton candy and musk have an equal dosing here, at least for me because this becomes very musky on my skin on the dry down. It’s a really beautiful fragrance actually, and works best in the heat of summer. It’s unisex, with moderate sillage and longevity. It’s bright, fun, and flirty. It reminds me a lot of Jo Malone Rose Water & Vanilla, without the rosey accords. I see that people have compared it to PDM Oriana and I don’t see it at all, considering how sugary sweet Oriana is and how noticeably floral Sundazed is. This perfume is good for summer fanatics, citrus lovers, and those who don’t mind a mildly sweet fragrances. While neroli is my love forever and always, I think I can do without this one. I have other neroli scents in my collection that I’d rather wear besides this.

A summery, synthetic carnival of a fragrance. It’s rainbow sherbet made scent. There’s a sprightly citrus lean – I can clock the candied lemon and mandarin – but it’s more Starburst than fresh-squeezed. There’s also an overarching plasticky feel to the scent, which I hope is intentional, as it makes me think of jelly sandals and beach balls. It’s juvenile, but in a nostalgic way. Grade school birthday parties, complete with cotton candy machine. The jewelry rack in the back of Claire’s, the air fizzing with a spectrum of body mists. I have a soft spot for these gummy-fruity-nerolis, but I think Regime des Fleurs’s Nitesurf Neroli has a more interesting execution with its seasalt and amber. Mental Snapshot: It’s the last week of junior high and you’re on a sugar high. You’re on a field trip to the boardwalk. Or a waterpark. Heart-shaped sunglasses, hibiscus-print tankini, holographic plastic fanny pack. You spend all your change on Dance Dance Revolution rounds at the arcade. Or on Dippin Dots. You don't even feel the sunburn. tl;dr: rainbow sherbet aerosol ️

Orange blossom, emphasis on the orange. It’s sweet and refreshing like an orange Jarritos. As it dries down I start to get more of the jasmine which is a note I am usually either hot or cold on and I’m happy to say I like it here. This isn’t the most complex fragrance but it’s very pleasant and I see why so many people like it for everyday use. As always, citrus fades to the background far too quickly and it’s a sort of beachy jasmine orange fragrance that’s quite mild. Not a buy for me but I get the hype.

The name is carefully chosen, it has exactly that relaxed feel that you have after a day in the sun. I had not read about it before I tried it, and when read the notes description it is EXACTLY the ones I got. Citrus/mandarin, Neroli, Jasmine, some light musk and a sweet, sugery candy note, perfectly split and getting 1/6 of the attention each. It is very summery, light and pleasant. After a few hours the citrus accords dries down a bit in favour of the musk and cotton candy. The musk is light and easy, not the dirty heavy type. It is well made, but not in any way revolutionary, even if the cotton candy gives it a slight difference compared to other similar scents. It reminds me quite a bit of Atelier Cologne's Bergamote Soleil, but the slightly bitter tone tone in Bergamote Soleil is swapped out for sweet candy, and the musk is more airy and light in Byredos offering. I like Byredo better. It's nice and pleaseant, great for summer and has reasonably good longevity for a summer citrus, but if you are financially interested you can find similar offerings at much better prices. Maybe without the cotton candy, but for the money you save you can buy some real cotton candy instead perhaps.

“Your perfume smells like cotton candy!” said my sister the day I wore my sample. I don’t know why I expected this to smell like any kind of real citrus fruit. It smells like cotton candy. Any orange or lemon notes are the artificial flavorings used in candy. No florals detected. This is ridiculously tooth achingly sweet. Orange syrup continuously poured into warm spun sugar.

Sundazed is my signature scent. I get that Parfumo bases notes off the "official" notes from the brand, but this is a beautiful cotton candy and citrus fragrance. It is sweet, airy, and gorgeous, plus longevity on clothes is amazing. Skin, too, but clothes always amazes me here.

Pure orange juice and cotton candy. Sweet, linear (if this has ever evolved on my skin I haven't noticed), summery in a way that feels youthful and energetic and a little whimsical. It's an uncomplicated feel-good scent for me.

I wore Sundazed for a movie night at a friend's house, and the first thing she said when she hugged me was "you smell like a blueberry muffin". lol I used to really like this perfume at the start of my fragrance journey (it was my very first big-girl purchase) but my taste has changed significantly since then, and now I find it a little too sweet.

Very sweet and citrusy. It opens up quite floral, almost like yellow florals to my nose, before drying down into sugary, candied citrus. I definitely see the cotton candy comparison. In my mind, this scent embodies the color yellow - Lemons, candies, sunshine. The sillage is pretty quiet, and I wish it lasted longer.

WHAT IT IS A man's suede jacket after he lets his girlfriend wear it on a cool spring evening. The citrus upfront is lightweight before opening into a *beautiful* gray suede layered on top of spiced & sugared pipe tobacco. The first thing that came to mind was a suede bomber jacket that's been worn over a sweet Azzaro men's fragrance and an ethereal Chanel-like women's floral. This is among the cleanest, most mercifully restrained (4-5hrs max) leather fragrances out there and a home run for cool weather. WHO IT'S FOR You don't like leather fragrances, but wish you did. Almost masculine up close, but feminine in the sillage... as though a woman wearing Coco Mademoiselle has just hugged you. Skews youthful, not young. ALTERNATIVES Hawthorne's Play Wild and Botanic is the more masculine version of Animalique; suede and moss in a cool forest without any of the florals. Tom Ford's Ombre Leather and Diptyque's Eau Rihla are both similarly clean leathers, but are fruity instead of floral (and less wearable due to their strength). Tom Ford's White Suede comes closest, but the sharpness from the saffron is missing here. FINAL THOUGHTS Whether it's "for me" is less important than the fact that Jerome Epinette has created a fragrance that evokes a very specific and (I think) pretty common situation: at some point, many of us have smelled Coco Mademoiselle's sweet mimosa *and* the scent of leather from a jacket, handbag, or car in the same breath. For me, this is every art gallery opening, birthday happy hour, and night out with some new clothes - and somehow, now it's in a bottle. Beautiful work.

I went to the Byredo counter to try out some that I thought I’d like with the hope of buying one but nothing set in stone. Animalique was quite far down on my list and truthfully I didn’t think I would like it. First thoughts were mixed with love and apprehension as I felt it was too “clean” and synthetic. Once it dried down it became more and more appealing and the deciding factor was my partner saying how good it smelled and you could tell he meant it in his eyes! I bought the bigger size instantly and haven’t looked back.nn This in my opinion is A perfect everyday scent and can easily become a signature. It’s not overly powerful but I think that’s perfect for this, it helps add to the intimacy of the scent and I think it creates a nice cosy bubble around the individual. It’s a perfect unisex fragrance and I’d say it’s one that definitely compliments the individual wearing it, like it adds a certain attraction and desire if that makes sense. Would highly recommend this to anyone and would suggest this over Byredo’s more popular fragrances

DHP was a huge disappointment. I was hyped on it after enjoying the other iris-y Homme flankers, namely Dior Homme Original (2011) Eau de Toilette and Dior Homme Intense (2011) and thought that it was going to be a leathery version of the same DNA. It ended up having a weird cheap cleaning solution/"fresh" smell that I wasn't expecting, and not much leather at all. But here in Byredo Animalique of all places, the woody powdery iris and leather come together at last. It does take the DNA in a more feminine direction. There are more floral aspects and a light soft musky undertone that makes it seem more femme, but I think it is perfectly unisex and the right guy can absolutely pull this one off. I still prefer the scent of Dior Homme Original (2011) Eau de Toilette as a superior woody-iris scent (unfortunately the performance is subpar), but Animalique is a close second. Really nice well-balanced soft unisex scent.

A fleecy musk, clean and plushy. A domesticated animalic, bottle-fed from birth and snug in a handknit jumper. On second thought, I wouldn’t even call it animalic in the slightest. It’s a distant, fond memory of animals. If this scent were an item, it’d be a suede and shearling jacket. Or a very expensive teddy bear. The suede is already soft, but further gentled by classic Byredo violet, cool and powdery. The whole fragrance is very Byredo. (You can take that as either a complement or warning). Longevity is well above average, though. Lasted me a whole ten-hour coach flight and had me dreaming I was cozied up in first. Mental Snapshot: The Ikea monkey. This scent makes me feel like I’m the Ikea monkey. Cosseted, pampered, aloofly Scandinavian. Lonesome, yet stylish. tl;dr: Ikea monkey

First, don't except it to project, it can easilly smell like your own clothes. It's a warm and cosy suede, with hints of vanilla tonka, but very smooth. A beautiful combination of suede, coton and ambroxan It's not a perfume for those who want to be smelled by other, no one will notice it but you. I personnaly wear it at home when i need to cheer up, 3 spray under my blanket and i feel like in a warm, soft leathery and cosy nest/cocoon. It last 3hr on skin and 5hr on clothes (depend of what you wear) I don't smell lemon or bergamot at opening. It reminds me of Babycat but a lot smoother and discret

Soft, comforting, safe. I can definitely sense the similarities with White Suede by Tom Ford, with that soft and bitter leather note. But I also smell something that reminds me of the hazelnut and orris of Oh La La by Teo Cabanel (altough a little sweeter and creamier here)!!

400 euros. That’s how much my brother and I made on a blisteringly hot summer day at our flea market stand, where we sold old junk all day long. The day was long, the sun relentless, and when we finally packed up in the evening, we laughed tears over my completely absurd sunburn.

Right off the bat: this perfume is my favorite discovery and best achievement of 2024! I participated in a sharing. Violet, mimosa, sandalwood, and white suede… some of my favorite notes were calling my name! “Either this will be a hit or really disgusting.” Actually, Byredo usually manages to beautifully blend the notes; but with this one, I was somehow unsure.

In my restless dream, I see this city. You promised to bring me back there one day. But you never did. Now, I am alone there, at our 'special place'. I am waiting for you. In the late afternoon, a storm began, first just a restless rustling between the roofs, eventually a trembling at the windows.

PROLOG: Animalique, what does this name stand for? Is it about "anima," Latin for soul, or does the perfume smell animalistic? Curious about what lies behind it, I read a quote from Ben Gorham, the founder and Creative Director at Byredo: "I wanted to explore what all humans have in common: our primal nature and our primal instincts.

This fragrance opens with spicy, pungent woods and a sweet, vibrant red berry note. This combinations is rather unusual, but the mix of fruit and resin, sparkly sugar and rich woods is very interesting. As the notes bloom on my skin I detect a third note, saffron. The spice is lush and fatty and therefore the ideal base for the accord. As the scent develops, the fruit aroma soars into the air, whereas the woods sink to the base. In this stage I see all three notes very distinctly, they are separate, layered on top of each other. Once the berry notes have burned out, saffron engulfs everything that remains, peppery woods frame the smooth spice note, giving it a welcome edge. This is the heart accord of the scent which remains the same until the fragrance disappears with a final whisper of the main notes.

WRoth described the top and middle well. The sweet top notes do not prepare you for the leathery dry down. This scent last a long time despite me washing my hand. The leather and patchouli stick around for a long time. The sillage is in the middle.

This perfume is disappointment in a bottle, at least for me. I usually don't care much about projection or longevity when reviewing, but here it's worth mentioning because this fragrance lacks both and no, I'm not nose blind. The opening greets you with blackberry, which is easily the most detectable note. Alongside it, there’s a hint of alcohol presumably rum, but it’s so mild it barely registers. What I surprisingly picked up quite quickly was the clary sage. Now, the oud… it feels watered down, too clean, almost synthetic. It gives off the vibe of “hey, this is oud, but don’t worry, it’s special and inoffensive,” like it’s been sterilized for people who don’t actually like oud in the first place. The leather here is overly clean as well it reminds me more of brand new shoes or an "expensive leathery bag" that is on sale with a heavy plastic coating. It’s there, but only if you really search for it. I’ve seen some people mention a slightly animalic note, but honestly, I get none. If there is any animalic quality here, it’s the smell of an animal that’s been killed, thoroughly cleaned, and prepped for taxidermy. If I had to describe it, it’s closer to the sterile scent of a stuffed animal than anything animalic. I’d like to call this perfume minimalistic, but even that feels like an overstatement. In the end, it’s just a mild, underwhelming fragrance with a synthetic edge and nothing particularly memorable about it.

When it comes to copy & paste, one can notoriously make a huge mistake. This applies not only to highborn wannabe-doctors, but a similar error has occurred at Byredo: The in-house poet had called up the old file of Oud Immortel to write the new sermon directly in the correct text format. It had to be done quickly, considering there were five new releases in 2010. While creating the title line, he simply copied the term “Leather Accord” from the pyramid as the name for the stuff, even correctly omitting the “Immortel,” but then accidentally deleted the “Leather” instead of the “Oud.” Silly. Now the stuff is called Accord Oud instead of Leather Accord, and Byredo just pretends that the two fragrances somehow belong together. And everyone else is sent on a wild goose chase looking for the agarwood. It must have been like that, because: “Where is Oud?” I feel like the esteemed water lily. I recognize no Oud.
