All of this is contained in this colorful little bottle. Anyone looking for an uncomplicated, pleasing skin caresser that can be splashed on generously should grab this right away. The Classique summer edition starts fruity fresh, but not sweet. As the fragrance develops, the scent character of the original Classique Eau de Toilette is quite noticeable, but it is significantly lighter and doesn't hit you over the head. Nevertheless, the fragrance has enough power to remain perceptible on the skin for a few hours. Gaultier hasn't reinvented the wheel here, but with a hint of sunscreen on warm skin, you can definitely win me over. So, it's basically vacation in a bottle. But I wouldn't drink this little concoction.

It was probably in mid-2011 when HUGO BOSS decided to launch an even more exclusive special series of fragrances within its already exclusive "HUGO BOSS SELECTION" series: "The Collection" Essentially tailored fragrances that are meant to reflect the experience of high-quality materials. These are: Cotton+Verbena Silk+Jasmine Velvet+Amber Cashmere+Patchouli and Wool+Musk Now, let's talk about the latter: First, one must ask, what do I get for a hefty 110€/50ml!? A lot, I think!! Packaging: Even the packaging celebrates the fragrance. Each of these scents comes in a box approximately 30x20cm in size, with the front adorned by the material referenced in the fragrance - in this case, wool. When you open the sleeve, a small pouch with a cord reveals the real crystal bottle - simply wonderful! The fragrance: One could say, "what you see, is what you get..." First impression: Primarily, Wool+Musk really smells like musk and wool. The scent is not "loud," but rather elegant, which I believe is also due to a hint of cinnamon and sandalwood. Delightful! The only comparable fragrance that comes to mind is White Linen, although this classic a) is for women and b) is sweeter and lacks the woody accord. Longevity: The "wool" lasts well on the skin for 4-5 hours... Occasion: Since I find the fragrance very noble, the occasion should be chosen accordingly. For "Daily Office," in my opinion, it is too precious. Conclusion: Whoever appreciates the extraordinary, seeks a truly noble and well-composed fragrance that you don't smell on every corner. This fragrance and this series cannot be overlooked!!

Don't let the marketing graphics fool you. This isn't some bleak end of the world outdoorsy fragrance. It is a sweet soft woody fig with a ton of cashmeran. It's more along the lines of Gyspy Water or Velvet Haze than say Super Cedar. The fig in it isn't the green fig you get in something like Philosykos - its sweet and ripe like a fig candy. Usually Byredo is on point with their marketing but I think they missed the mark this time. If they had've gone for a youthful, fun and delicate campaign, it would have fit better. Overall its quite nice, but not challenging or exceptional. Regardless, the people who love to post monochromatic shelfies on instagram will lap this up.

Sichuan pepper always smells ashen, like the face of a lifetime smoker (see Journey Man for reference), but in Eleventh Hour it gains a Vicks Vapor Rub dimension that gives it a jaunty flourish of something minty-fresh. Cigarettes and mouthwash, feathered out at the edges by the musky, vegetal warmth of carrot seeds. There is not much - to my nose, at least - of the advertized 'mulled wine' effect and it doesn't smell like Christmas at all, unless Christmas smells like cheap men's cologne, wood pulp, and the silver foil inside an empty pack of mentholated cigarettes.

I added this to my sample list because I've been watching "The Home Edit" on Netflix and I noticed this on Danielle Brooks perfume shelf. I loved her in "Orange is the New Black" and I just think she's so gorgeous, talented and humble. She also seems to have great taste, so I thought "what could go wrong?" Well I'm sure this fragrance must smell amazing on Miss Taystee herself, but it's not my cup of tea. Honestly, I am shocked to see so many notes listed on this fragrance because all I smell is a BIG blast of cloves. It is a very linear aroma from beginning to end. Cloves, cloves, and more cloves! It's not a bad smell per se. In fact clove is one of my favorite spice smells, especially around the holidays. I like to stick cloves into an orange to make a homemade potpourri around the holidays. Maybe this perfume could benefit from a hint of orange. Or maybe you could layer it with something orangey? Either way, it smells like an ingredient for Christmas potpourri. It also smells medicinal or like an all natural cleaning product like "Thieves" oil from Young Living. Not a bad smell, just not interesting to me.

I was on a hunt for a spicy but cool and clarifying perfume. I bought this as a blind buy and thought the description of the notes were what I was looking for. It is definitely something else what I was looking for or what I had read from most of the reviews. It has this burned plastic vibe at first and then turns really minty. I don’t get anything that reminds me of christmas it’s just minty for me. No one seems to like it either, the comments are mainly just polite or no comments at all. I’ve been trying to use this all winter this and last year but is hardly a dent on my bottle. This bottle which I’m not too fond of seems to last forever.

One of my recurring nightmares, not too often, but now and then, involves images of giant tidal waves racing towards the shore and burying us without a chance. "Eleventh Hour" taps into similar myths, (primal) fears, and premonitions; or at least its name is oriented in that direction. That it is almost too late and that we have been violently destroying our unique planet for decades should be known even to the biggest dimwit (Trump excluded for now), and that it might already be too late to change anything is also clear. However, this still quite fresh Byredo is anything but a pessimistic apocalypse scent that screams "after me the flood." It is a very green, spicy fig-rum cocktail that does not suit me at all. It solidly captures the hopelessness and fear, the alcohol consumption, and the escape to higher green mountain ranges. One should stick to that thought. But there are definitely more fun and pleasant associations that a fragrance can evoke and should... On a purely olfactory level, this Byredo also appeals to me less. As always, it is made with high quality, a fine "blend" so to speak, but I still do not like figs in my perfume. In "Eleventh Hour," a triumvirate of pepper, fig, and rum sets the tone. And it does not hold back... Cinnamon associations also spread among me, though rather green and spring-fresh tinted. A very textured, enticing paradise scent, surely a hit for many, but in ME it only creates a migraine paradise that I can hardly wear. And fragrance reviews are, after all, highly subjective and personal. Those who like tangible figs must test it. And even face the apocalypse... ;-) Bottle: nordic by nature Sillage: breathtaking at first, then quickly subdued Longevity: 7 hours but very comfortably Conclusion: if the world ends, then one can get drunk on rum and smell like figs. Or something like that. But even if the sky falls to the earth, I will not become a friend of "cowardly" scents anymore... sorry.

The marketing department of Byredo has not done Eleventh Hour Eau de Parfum any favors. "Hey, fragrance enthusiasts, here’s a lovely scent for you that smells like late summer. Yummy, yummy! We hope you like fig and rum...

As Annarosa already noted, the central theme of Eleventh Hour is the last hour or the final moment on Earth. Almost as the end of all things, when the oceans rise and the highest areas become the final refuges.

This review is about the probably most difficult scent in my collection. My mother comments on it with "interesting," my husband with "it's okay." I can understand every single comment about "Eleventh Hour," including all the critics. Still, I have it, still, I like it. Theoretically, the scent should have something to do with the apocalypse.
The scent is something unique. Pepper opening - the strength varies by bottle .. In the tester, it was super strong, which I liked, but in my large bottle, it is somewhat toned down.

Interestingly, this perfume is supposed to reflect the perfumer's vision of what the last hour of humanity would look like after a global flood. Well, apparently the last surviving humans are happily eating apricot jam on a high mountain peak :) At first, it smells sweet-sour fruity-apricot. I don't particularly appreciate apricot jam and its scent.

Recently started testing the classics of men's fragrances, I had the chance to smell Le Mâle on my skin for the first time in a long time - now I have also tried its offshoots Le Mâle Terrible and Le Mâle Summer 2015 for comparison. First of all: I do not agree at all with the descriptions of the fragrance pyramid. Now that I read lavender and cardamom, I think I can detect them, and sure - to some extent, the vanilla base of its father is present in Summer 2015 just like in Le Mâle Terrible, but grass and green leaves in the heart? Pas du tout. The first thing I smell is coconut, honey, milk. This fits perfectly with the theme, as it immediately transports you to a sunny beach. These sweet tones are countered by a masculine note that becomes more pronounced over time - that is the sandalwood in the base. Thanks to the vanilla as a counterbalance, the fragrance remains very sweet overall and surprisingly gourmand for a scent that is actually aimed at the mass market, especially due to the ever-present coconut and milk. After several hours, this vanilla takes over and lets the fragrance end classically Mâle. Just like Le Mâle Terrible, Summer 2015 plays with this classic Mâle base, expands it, interprets it, and gives it completely new, unique facets. As I will also write about Terrible, I have a problem with this: The vanilla base of classic Le Mâle is perfect because it is so simple and clear. Its offshoots often feel overloaded due to the variety of scents and lose the grace, the simple elegance that has made Le Mâle a timeless classic. Overall, Summer 2015 is not bad. It definitely achieves its goal of evoking a summer mood, conjuring images of a beach bar with a thatched roof, where a Latino bartender with a bare torso in swim shorts mixes you an ice-cold piña colada, with which you can lie down on the mat after an extensive volleyball game in the sand and let the sun shine on your belly. It gets just over three stars because it certainly has more to offer than the other short-lived summer fragrances that Joop, CK, and their ilk throw onto the market every year. Fairly, it must be said that it is not an art when you simply reinterpret a long-proven concept for summer. However, if you don't view the fragrance in the shadow of its father, it deserves a good rating. For me, it is nothing - too sweet, too fruity, too little aquatic. I am looking for a zesty, masculine summer scent, and Summer 2015 is not clear enough for that. But if I had it on the shelf, I would definitely reach for it from time to time - and I would recommend every man who is more adventurous in this regard than I am to test Le Mâle Summer 2015 - because many guys out there might perfectly sign their summer with this fragrance. The bottle fits the scent, but like many summer editions, it is a bit gaudy due to the bright colors. The longevity is decent, but the Mâles last forever for me anyway. The sillage is weak because the fragrance is generally designed to be rather soft.

A successful perfume as a total work of art that resonates with the spirit and soul is not only about the fragrance itself but almost equally about its accidentals: its color, the shape and material of its bottle, and its packaging. It is no different from a good meal, which, to provide the perfect enjoyment, should not only have the right flavor composition but also appealing form and color, and should be presented on a beautiful plate. The name of the fragrance is also part of these accidentals. It awakens expectations, fuels our imagination, and directs our olfactory perceptions in a certain direction. In the case of Byredo's "Baudelaire," this was, as the comments and statements show, exemplarily the case. The life of the French poet, critic, and translator Charles Baudelaire was a hellish ride of physical and mental illnesses, alcohol and drug abuse, experiences of failure in work and love, and ultimately poverty, misery, and death. In his work, Baudelaire grapples with these experiences; it can be read partly as a rebellion against the forces of darkness and destruction, as an attempt at self-therapy, but also as a flirtatious game at the edge, as an affirmative or at least resignative celebration of a corrupted beauty. The titles of two major works by the namesake of this fragrance speak for themselves: "Les fleurs du mal" ("The Flowers of Evil") and "Les paradis artificiels" ("The Artificial Paradises" - On Drug Experiences). His poem "Spleen" is a quintessential literary depiction of severe clinical depression. The overwhelming majority of the reviews here refer to this and attest to "Baudelaire" predominantly extremely disturbing, abyssal, dark, and almost self- and other-murderous qualities. With their own unique emphases, one can (just exemplarily) refer to the linguistically and descriptively analytical literary miniatures by Cravache, Ergreifend, and Turandot, which rightly carry the predicate "first-class." However, a significant difference becomes apparent: the first two appreciate the horror: Cravache perceives decaying corpses, Ergreifend feels how their soul is being drained, and both honor this with top ratings. Turandot, on the other hand, recoils from the abyss, rates the fragrance low, but apologizes to us for her supposed nervous weakness. I consider this approach to "Baudelaire" legitimate and fruitful, but not obligatory. I advocate for opening an alternative access to this fragrant work of art, which may require us to boldly sever the ties that bind us to its name and first forget everything we have ever heard about the sad Charles. This could lead us - as is the case for me, and in quite rare olfactory harmony also for the nose beside me - to perceive this fragrance as immensely beautiful, and while excitingly special, contrasting, and rich in tension, not as disturbing, neither in terms of the perception of individual foul-smelling notes nor in terms of dissonances in the composition. I perceive an initial phase of about half an hour or a bit more, which I understood during the first "full test" rather as a dry, strong, distinctly unsweet spiciness, to then experience on the next attempt the following day a still unsweet, somewhat bitter, and surprisingly fruity tone. The main phase lasting several hours, during which I believe no single note dominates, impresses me as serious, contrasting, and dynamic, yes, a bit cool and perhaps even dark, but certainly also powerful and energetic. When the fragrance pyramid indicates hyacinth, leather, and incense here, I take that at face value and believe that the juniper berry from the top note and the spicy-fresh amber and probably also papyrus (without knowing exactly how that smells) already play into this overall impression, as the head and heart notes here congenially transition into one another. However, this is somewhat less the case with the transition from the heart note to the stable, still gently perceptible at medium dosage after 14 hours, strongly patchouli-influenced base. I find this very pleasant, but in comparison to the previous dynamic events, it falls off a bit too strongly. That is very nice and very serene, but no longer exciting, which takes away the chance for a top rating for this fragrance. Three fragrances that I really like and consider "related" to this scent - however, rather freely associating in terms of a distant spiritual kinship and certainly not in the sense of "fragrance twins" - are "Dior Homme" (minus its deep, rich softness; instead harder, cooler, and more open), "Ambre 114" by "Histoire des Parfums" (minus its overwhelming opulence, but stricter, more reduced, and concentrated), and "Heritage" by Guerlain (minus its sparkling-playful citrus freshness in the top note, but much more frontal) - overall, I find "Baudelaire" quite guerlinesque. The elimination of all associations connected to the life and work of the poet could then further lead to this beautiful, powerfully driving, and serious fragrance evoking entirely different images and values than hell and demons. This severing of the umbilical cord to the name "Baudelaire" could result in us not thinking at all about vampires, corpses, decay, and misery when experiencing this fragrance. I did not have to. During testing, very bright and humanistic impulses came to me, such as the brave pursuit of hidden beauty and humanity and the calm and steady struggle against suffering and malice. And, just on the side, we are allowed to do this! We are not morally obliged to search for any traces of decadence and illness in this fragrance. We do not even have to necessarily read Baudelaire's works (although their beauty and value should not be denied)! We are even allowed to do this without feeling like we have to sneak away, being softies, shadow parkers, and warm showerers. Because even those who are ready to face human misery in all its seriousness and irreducible greatness do not have to be a friend of its literary or olfactory poetization. But did I not say at the beginning that the name is inseparably linked to the fragrance? Well, let us imagine that Byredo wanted to lay an ironic false trail with the naming "Baudelaire." Or that it is not even Charles Baudelaire who is meant, but the (so far completely unknown) brave firefighter Jean-Pierre Baudelaire from the Parisian suburbs, shining through everyday heroic deeds.

Anyone reading Baudelaire on a bottle expects a fragrance that harbors an immense, tearing tension between light and dark. Here, the ugly, dark, tragic, and morbid dominate, ultimately triumphing over the light, beautiful, and lively. Although this is repeatedly interrupted by brief moments of brightness and radiance, which the person drowning in the raging storm believes to perceive from the nearby lighthouse or some blue patches in the sky. Charles Baudelaire was a failed, unloved, unhappy, and depressed person in life. Throughout his life, he was tormented by feelings of inferiority, financial problems, and venereal diseases. His most famous work, Les Fleurs du Mal, is marked by deep pessimism, overwhelming darkness, great disillusionment, fragile structure, and omnipresent ugliness. The world around 1840 to 1860 appears to him entirely gloomy, paralyzingly melancholic, hopelessly morbid, and broken. People live-or rather vegetate-torn between the good, the light, and the often prevailing evil, the dark. They often tragically fail at life. The top note of Baudelaire paints a picture of impending doom with bold strokes. An imminent catastrophic storm. A flood in which immense, all-consuming forces of nature unleash their tremendous fury. After spraying Baudelaire, aromatic notes dominate. Mild spicy caraway, black pepper, and herbal, smoky to leathery juniper. And then, as ominously announced, the sky opens, and hell, indistinguishable from one another, reveals its dark, hissing maw. The calamity crashes down with tremendous force upon the defenseless land. In the form of dark hyacinth, leafy notes, dark leather, and smoky, dry incense that darkens to the base. Even though the ominous wall of clouds could collapse at any moment and obliterate all living things forever, the oppressive threat of the fearsome wall of the darkest and most powerful clouds remains always stronger and more menacing than the raging storm itself. Now and then, flashes of light from a solitary flickering lighthouse can be discerned on the distant mainland. One imagines catching a glimpse of a timid piece of sky, which is immediately swallowed again by monstrous black clouds. true hope sprouts in the storm. Time and again, it is crushed in the roar of the overpowering tempest. A hovering between life and death, where death repeatedly claims its prey to devour it. The immense wall of clouds slowly pulls back a bit. The darkest clouds gradually give way to dark gray ones. A note can be discerned that resembles broken, sour reeds lying gray and miserable on the foggy and earthy ground after an autumn storm. From now on, patchouli determines the course of the fragrance. Moist, woody, earthy, sweet. Some souls have been swept away by the storm and the icy waves. Their corpses slowly rot on the wet, earthy shore. Together with some shattered wooden planks. Earth and reeds gradually overgrow their bodies, erasing the memory of the deceased. Referring to Charles Baudelaire's "Les Fleurs du Mal," the fragrance journey should end here. However, at Byredo, the scent story continues. After a few hours, amber emerges, still dark as night, but hopeful, woody, dry, sweet, and somewhat tobacco-like. Some people have been swept away by the floods of the storm. But not in paralyzing resignation, rather in a deadly serious, yet not hopeless struggle between the dark and the light. The dark could not sweep away everything human. Even if the bright, silver sparkling on the horizon is not yet visible, the calamity recedes. It does not become bright, but night falls. A calm, dry, warm night that does not let the hope of experiencing the next day die.

Baudelaire should really only be worn by someone who is in a good mood, because in rather melancholic times, the scent, at least for me, is prone to slip from melancholy into depression. Perhaps I simply tested the perfume at the wrong time. Therefore, my comment may say much less about the scent than about me. Please do not see my description as a harsh criticism, as it is certainly not. The pyramid sounds enticing to me at first, as juniper, incense, patchouli, these are the ingredients from which dreams are sometimes made for me, but with this perfume, it is just too much of everything. Perhaps it is simply too complicated and serious for my taste. And when Immel brings Alban Berg, Stravinsky, and Hindemith into play, I agree with him, because I cannot make anything of these composers either; this music has not yet revealed itself to me. However, I have nothing against scents that do not come across as cheerful and friendly. It can certainly be olfactorily contemplative, and a bit of drama can sometimes benefit a fragrance. But to stick with music, in such a situation, I would still prefer Beethoven. That Baudelaire is a dark scent that does not change in character even down to the base must be assumed based on the pyramid. Those who can engage with it may still, like me, regret that the heart note has hardly any chance to truly shine against the all-dominating base. Perhaps a splash of strong dark rose would have done well here. As it stands, it remains delicately floral for a moment before the hyacinth is once again overshadowed. The incense could also have been more pronounced and cooler for me, and the leather is not soft enough. All these beautiful accords, in themselves, are covered by dusty dry papyrus and a scratchy musty patchouli base. Patchouli has many manifestations, from soft and caressing to earthy and moist, to scratchy and herbaceous like in Baudelaire. This base endures even washing and 8 hours of sleep and does not convey the joy of a new day upon waking, but rather a sense of smallness. Dead serious, just like Louce, I perceive the scent, but beauty and death are not related for me in this fragrance; one cannot die beautifully here, but rather in resignation. I would have wished for a bit of a wink, a small glimmer of light, a spark of hope for this perfume. And yet, I am not angry with the scent, because while I only knew "The Flowers of Evil" by hearsay until now, my interest is now piqued, and I will read Baudelaire soon, if not wear it as a fragrance. Perhaps I would associate the mood of the poetry with a completely different scent.

It's a shame that someone from the family has already written about Memoir Man. I came to that conclusion on my own. And I certainly don't mean the explicit reference to Baudelaire in both. One might overlook that with a marketing-saturated shrug. Rather, there is a surprising similarity in the scent, although they take some time to develop and relativize in direct comparison. First, there is the impression of wormwood, even absinthe (though I must assume the latter due to a lack of corresponding liquid experience) in the later initial phase. Memoir Man wraps this in a slightly smokier and woodier manner, while Baudelaire carries a spicy, almost fruity note. I wonder if this might be attributed to juniper, whose "raw" berries I unfortunately have not yet smelled. Fruity is basically the wrong term; I just can't think of a better one. The scent is at best vaguely fruity or floral. It is a kind of spice that is not yet dried like a spice from a packet. It is fresher, oily, yet free from any ethereal sharpness. Sigh. I give up. Try it out. It’s a test tip here anyway (yes, despite the following paragraph...), so I might as well mention that upfront. In another respect, the beginnings each offer very clear differences. Two are nose-visible, and the first is downright brutal. The opening mix of Baudelaire with its peculiar musty cumin reminds me - I can't put it any other way - of the smell of a shoe when, for example, you haven't paid attention to where you're stepping on the unpaved path in front of our house. Unpaved walkways are known to be particularly suitable for driving away any decency (I won't even talk about rights) among light-shy dog-walking riffraff. Perhaps (certainly!) Mr. Baudelaire occasionally woke up in the gutter, and we are meant to remember that. Enough of that; it is quickly overcome and forgiven. Let’s turn to more pleasant deviations: The sweet licorice throat lozenge note, for instance (reminds me of the one from the same manufacturer in 1996), which lasts about four hours, is limited to the Byredo, as is the leather, which mainly makes its appearance in the second and third hours. Subsequently, the Byredo gradually threads itself into the territory where Memoir has already arrived: into a mahogany wood note, gently surrounded by smoke and a remnant of herb, while Baudelaire is slightly roughened by a patchouli addition. As different as the pyramid notes of the two dark fragrances may be, the character similarity is now greater than the paper form suggests. Or? Somehow not again. Baudelaire is sweeter, airier, and above all more restrained. The wood note develops from the sweet licorice impression, remaining more amber-like and particularly (patchouli)-dusty. After the comparison day with Memoir Man, I, of course, followed up with another individual test day for safety, as the Amouage is indeed significantly louder and more enduring. Its wood note accompanies me well into the evening, while this one in Baudelaire has long yielded to the patchouli hours earlier, which in turn has already taken on the status of a lingering hint by the evening. And now? Do I want to have it, since I already own Memoir Man? Years ago, I overheard a kind of self-talk at a well-known discount store. A…uh…strange guy (at least he apparently could read, which was not self-evident from his facial expression) held a pack of two microfiber cloths in his hand and said to no one in particular: "Wow, that's cool - you can put them in the washing machine and they’re good as new!" He said that and tossed three packs with two cloths each into the shopping cart. Aha. Or like in that East Frisian joke with the three wishes. After the first granted a beer glass that fills itself on command, the other two were: Two more of those! Do I have to feel just as silly if I get this one now? After all, Byredo is slightly more expensive than a bag of microfiber cloths at A…. I do like it quite a lot. And it is somehow quite different... Hey, you’re different, do you hear? Hello? Doesn’t listen. It's gone. Hm.

It is always something positive when a perfume does not jump at me with citrus notes. So Baudelaire. Instead, the aromatic juniper berry strides into my nose, while the pepper provides a certain depth and adds some spice and grace to the top note. The pepper then dominates this image for a while. Some woody notes also blend in, and leathery nuances subtly appear in the picture. From the very beginning, Baudelaire shows an impenetrable depth and density. The scent resembles a dense cloud that continuously devours itself while simultaneously radiating animalistic power, sensual poetry, and aesthetics, almost lightness. Baudelaire also appears threatening. At this point, it somehow seems a bit too pompous, a little inauthentic as the scent lies in wait and then takes its time to reveal itself. Now, the gate of threat slowly opens, and behind it, the moods become heavy. Although we can expect a bit of floral notes, they almost remain absent. It is too overshadowed by the patchouli. Here, great effort has been made to conjure up a feeling in the scent of dark fire and the dull smoldering of old thoughts. One is meant to contemplate transience from that point onward. I do think one must approach the scent with a bit of irony. Otherwise, it comes off as overly serious. Despite its dark character, it is a wonderfully beautiful fragrance, masterfully crafted. Baudelaire always reminds me of Stravinsky's "The Rite of Spring" in its mystical character or Hindemith in his spiritualization. Perhaps also Mozart's or Zimmermann's Requiem. At least, it is deeply expressive music. Thus, I am also an absolute lover of Baudelaire. This scent is a captivating homage to "The Flowers of Evil" and its author (who, by the way, was the first to describe the effects of hashish, both scientifically and poetically). Gradually, the heart note becomes increasingly leathery, and a spicy aftertaste mixes in. The scent appears less deep but broader. At times, it radiates brightly. Occasionally, hints of fruity-sour yet dry notes emerge, possibly from the papyrus. I could also imagine smelling some musk here. Ben Gorham creates a tension field here, a fragrance that always hovers between bitter fruitiness and amber warmth. A difficult undertaking, but very successful. The development now steadily moves towards earthy warm and animalistic accords. The scent becomes more sublime and calmer. The power that was present at the beginning is no longer discernible. It becomes increasingly earthy and warm, and ultimately our leathery poet fades into profound twilight, dense woody earth accords.

and devouring you! Byredo is a powerful work of the dark soul, which seems heartless. A perfume that does not distract you from depression on gloomy days, but rather pushes you deep into it! Although Baudelaire is a sad, dark perfume, it will surely resonate with those who immensely enjoy approaching such dense incense and spice bombs.

As I hungrily bite into my sandwich, I watch the dust dance in the dull light of the midday sun over the wooden floor. Outside, it is bright, and I hear swallows as they chase mosquitoes and flies high above us - free and limitless! In my thoughts, I am with them, soaring through the air. Where could these little acrobats have been in winter?

"Because there are scents, fresh as children's cheeks, Sweet as oboes, green as young leaves, Corrupted scents, lush, full of splendor, Like incense, amber, which bring to us in the dust The breath of the limitless And sing the highest joys of our souls.

well, here we go again with bad mood regarding THIS designer nonsense, maybe I should slowly change my username to Statler and Waldorf, since I apparently just want to grumble about almost all newer fragrance releases ...

My first comment goes to this fragrance. My first encounter with Baudelaire was this summer. It was part of a small sample order, and I was incredibly excited about it in advance, as the pyramid reads just as well as the reviews on all the websites. I was not disappointed - on the contrary.

I really wished it would differ more from last year's version, as I find the bottle sooo beautiful, so that there would be a good reason to buy it as well. Unfortunately, I couldn't smell any extreme differences, although I didn't test them side by side. I think the new one is a bit more biting, fresher than last year's version, which seems a bit creamier and more pleasing.

Tobacco Mandarin opens with a very sweet tobacco scent. Too sweet for me. Missing is any hint of mandarin or any citrus. As it dries down, got a distinct appearance of some sort of flowery note. Outside of being too sweet, Tobacco Mandarin is ruined with that floral note. Leans feminine to me. Did not get any strong cumin or body odor note. Longevity is very good. Was at about 9 hours and still going strong when I showered to get ready for the evening. Projection and sillage is more average. Overall, not my style. The price this is going for is ridiculous for what it is.

For me, it's a resounding no. I had high expectations, but after trying it, I found it quite unpleasant. It's a strong blend of spices and citrus, and when I say strong, I'm referring more to the aroma than the perfomance (which is quite good, by the way). It's definitely not a blind purchase. Maybe it's because I'm used to sweet tobacco perfumes and it's my fault.

Summer, sun, vacation time ... the Parfumo wanders through the Free and Hanseatic City, and so that the author's wife does not have to wait in the blazing sun at Jungfernstieg like a package unclaimed, she follows him with almost Hanseatic restrained enthusiasm into the Altsterhaus to the air-conditioned perfume department. She displays a cultivated indifference until she catches sight of the Byredo counter and the illuminated bottle captures her attention. Instead of the usual subtly yellow liquid, the intense red of Night Veils - Tobacco Mandarin immediately stands out. Yes, it looks beautiful, I really like it. Otherwise, Byredo does not indulge in any particular experiments with this fragrance. The typical simple but very high-quality white box has merely been adorned with a playful Night Veils inscription. The wonderful cylindrical bottle with the magnetic cap, where the overall impression and proportions are reduced to the essentials and create a harmonious consistency, is made to shine from within by the red liquid. This is how a bottle should be! Period. The fragrance grabs all attention with the first sniff, as it gets straight to the point. An accord of leather, wood, and smoky tobacco is immediately present and shows little intention of disappearing quickly. If you let Tobacco Mandarin settle a bit, a few citrus and homeopathically more spicy notes come into play, but always very subtly, keeping a few steps back and only vaguely identifiable. Over time, the bright leather recedes and makes way for what will dominate the fragrance and make it whole: resinous smoke and an oud that is neither too dark, too musty, nor fecal. A somewhat soft, composed oriental base tone that is not too foggy or gloomy. And where is the mandarin now? It does not appear in this fragrance in my nose. Quite the opposite of other mandarin fragrances that bear the word mandarin in their names. Perhaps the mandarin in Tobacco Mandarin refers to the Chinese standard language and is meant to hint at Chinese tobacco. However, since I am not a smoker, I cannot draw any enlightening comparisons. I do not want to hide a certain disappointment due to the absence of the mandarin. Nevertheless, Night Veils - Tobacco Mandarin is a beautiful fragrance, not particularly exciting, but extremely pleasant. It is immediately present. Not too loud, but still noticeable, without being annoying or overwhelming. If Night Veils - Tobacco Mandarin had a perceivable mandarin fruit note for me, the fragrance would also have a feminine side. As it stands, it remains rather masculine in its projection for me. A nice going-out fragrance, I would say, rather not for the office. Even though it lasts long, carries you through the day, and accompanies you into the evening. After a quick shower in the evening, there is still a pleasant remnant to fall asleep with, and the next morning, a respectable hint remains to remind you of the previous day. Night Veils - Tobacco Mandarin did not excite her. However, the illuminated counter did. It is questionable whether she would like the fragrance - in connection with such an illuminated perfume shelf - on me as well. Perhaps, if there were some mandarin to be recognized in it.

This is my first review. And it lands on Tobacco Mandarin. Did I choose this fragrance? Of all brands, Byredo for a first review? Did this fragrance choose me? Well, something drew me to this little differently colored bottle. Among all the Byredo bottles, it was more present to me than the others. Its dark color made it seem to me like a waiting, dark event inviting me to have a new experience. My black swan. An olfactory journey into worlds of the ingredient universe that couldn't be more different for me. The other Byredo bottles just stood there. Tobacco Mandarin, however, spoke to me. Even now. With my mind. “How does that fit together? Tobacco-Mandarin?” I spray once on my pulse point on my wrist. I breathe in. “I hate you,” said the mandarin. “I can't live without you. I can't let you go,” replied the tobacco. It determines the everlasting olfactory dialogue between the two. Thanks to its friends? Leather, sandalwood… At first, the citrus freshness breaks into the heaviness of the main accords, like a sunbeam that has dared to break all the laws of nature to shine into the dark night. Strangely, this contrast (for me) remains a molecular unity. Always. Even after hours. Is the quarrel settled? Things seem to fall into place. I smell harmony where there shouldn't be any. I think of Franz Kafka. After more hours, still this darkness of the woods, of the tobacco. Like a recurring dark mantra. A warning: “Stay alert, I am still here. And waiting. Just as I once waited for you.” The fragrance now appears to me, after hours, like an olfactory, mystical rune from ancient times. Unfathomable. A hermeneutic labyrinth, woven into a strangely harmonious whole. This strangeness. It has its place in this fragrance. It belongs there. This indefinable element, which I think of, that rises from this woody depth, and that might be as certain as element 115 in the UFOs of Area 51, is it responsible for this almost atomic performance? (In my case). A fragrance, like light and darkness. I smell again on my wrist and look into the night sky, I sense that darkness is winning here. Yet hope is budding within me. I know you are somewhere down there in the darkness, beneath the woods, the tobacco. “Don't give up,” I hear myself say. For I think of the mandarin. I know it will come. As surely as the first sunbeam ends the night I am currently looking at. I smile. For I know I am now ready for a wonderful journey.

I only want to smell this fragrance on someone else, and I'm not even sure if this scent suits a real person. I first smelled it in Munich at Oberpollinger, under the slightly irritated gaze of the person behind the counter, who immediately wanted to recommend something else to me. I took the strip anyway and naively held it to my nose at home, dreamy-eyed.

How does one imagine a perfume solely based on the listed notes on one of the most well-known and certainly most popular pages of a fashion designer? Well, I had envisioned it somewhat differently… saffron, jasmine, sandalwood… ambered chypre… expressive and seductive was my thought. However, what my nose perceives right from the start is a pure confusion of my expectations. Perhaps my personal scent does not align with the top note: an inexplicable jumble of essences that remind more of a shelf soaked with oriental soaps... Far Eastern potpourri… hard to bear for unaccustomed noses! But what the heart note reveals is somewhat more interesting: a strong dominance of patchouli and saffron alternating with a light honey-jasmine wrapping, which finally brings it closer to "expressive." Unfortunately, though, I still miss the seduction. The benzoin becomes increasingly apparent to me over time, which is not necessarily a good thing. I am curious to see which scent combination will make me exclaim "this is indescribably good," but at the moment, a "what a pity" is unfortunately all I can say!

Such a fizzy and sparkling rose, it almost feels carbonated! If soda was less sweet and came in rose flavor, it would surely smell like this. Szechuan pepper in food has a tingly, tongue-numbing quality instead of just being spicy like regular pepper. That's obviously difficult to translate into scent, so I think Byredo went for a sparkling, slightly peppery note to get a similar feeling. There is also a lot of refreshing citrus in this, so it creates a similar sensation to opening a can of sprite, just with less sugar and added rose. I think the name Young Rose is quite fitting, not because I find this only suitable for a young people (age-grouping fragrances is my pet peeves), but because the rose itself feels young, fresh and dewy, like it just started to bloom. This is a very clean and cool scent, so I find it most fitting for warm days. I really enjoy fresh, bubbly scents like this and it's a nice idea to have this texture in a rose scent. But if I had to chose a summer scent by Byredo, would rather buy Bal d'Afrique or Sundazed, they just feel even more exciting and special to me.

A spring-in-your-step rose. A sweet-n-sour candy rose. The dozens of reviewers before me said it best: this is pink lemonade. Surprised how well the pepper plays like a seltzer-y citrus, as I caught lemon long before I could even appreciate any rose. I love the tiniest bite it has. But they’re gentle thorns, like kitten claws or puppy teeth. Filed under: “a great rose for people who don’t like rose.” (If you want a true, youthful pepper-rose, Raving Rose by Dries Van Noten may be a better bet). She doesn’t last very long on my skin (~2h) and fades out as a classic Byredo just-showered musk, but still one of my favourite roses. Mental Snapshot: Peach-cheeked lovebirds. Friendship bracelets. Scented stationery. A beach cruiser, built for two. A week of unseasonably sunny weather, of picnics in the park. A pair of jelly sandals, already broken in. Springtime, personified. tl;dr: pink lemonade

I have been considering myself a perfume hater before I tried Young rose from Byredo. It felt like a fresh air on a mountain where flowers soak in the morning rain. And I sit there to have a picnic with my first love who brought a homemade lemon jam. After 2 years standing on my shelf, it started to be much stronger, therefore I believe its best time autumn or spring being a perfect choice for a raining day, or on a frost early morning in winter.

I tried all the popular Byredo fragrances (yes in absolu forms too) before landing on Young Rose and it’s still my only full bottle from the house, in my modest collection. To me, this fragrance is less a scent and more an image. A lush field of beautiful pink roses, their leaves are fresh, green and dewy; the thorns are soft yet present. The scent captures a single stalk from this field - flower, stalk, stem, leaves, thorns and all. I don’t get any citrus or pepper in particular but just the rose and I’m not complaining. The longevity is decent for Byredo, ~4 hours on skin before settling into an intimate scent, almost 8 hours on clothes.

This is what the Copenhagen it-girls smell like in my head - fun, colorful, modern!! As the name suggests, this is a young, happy rose that is a little musky and green. Almost dewy. I think it wears best at the start of spring, when the sun is finally out but the weather is still a little chilly... I feel like it would bring out the zesty freshness of the sichuan pepper and leave such a nice suble trail. I enjoy it, it makes me feel pretty :)

Rose scents are totally my thing. Unbeatable for me are Eau Rose and Eau Dominotee by Diptyque. I like my rose fragrances green, light, and with a slightly woody finish. What Byredo of Stockholm offers me here is a rose for the molecular fragrance age. A very spring-like composition.

These keywords capture the scent for me perfectly. It caught my attention from the very first second. The rose in this fragrance reminds me a bit of the Delina rose. However, this scent has less depth than Delina and is simply a bit more sparkling & fresh. The classic Byredo price and bottle are also present with this fragrance.

After some experiments as a teenager, I didn't wear any perfume for years, and since most designer fragrances (and still do) overwhelm me, I thought: perfume is just not for me. However, thanks to a fragrance-obsessed friend, I gave it another try. She introduced me to Byredo scents, which I found much more pleasant and refined than what the designer sector has to offer.

I have been searching for a rose scent for a while. It should be doable, the selection is not exactly small. But nothing appealed to me: too sharp, too heavy, old-fashioned, help headaches, etc. Okay, I guess I just don’t like rose.... I wanted to give it one last try with Young Rose . I didn't expect much. And then, bam, simply wonderful!

The scent is one of my favorites from Byredo. It is super zesty and absolutely perfect for summer. I can smell citrus notes, but I can't explain where they come from. The scent reminds me a bit of Ahoi Brause, in a very pleasant way. My 100ml bottle is already more than half empty and this fragrance is definitely a candidate for repurchase.

I'm reviewing Classique Summer 2010 without a comparison seeing that I've never tested the original Classique, however I do intend to in the near future. Summer flankers tend to smell the same every year, however in this case, I'd certainly consider wearing this due to its somewhat original and refreshing composition. Classique Summer 2010 opens with a mild, citrusy soap scent. The fragrance is polite and natural in a way that makes it very suitable for Summer. The heart tends to give way to a more floral approach, with delicately feminine jasmine, iris, ylang ylang and lily of the valley coming to the fore. I should perhaps add that this fragrance is supposedly alcohol-free. Despite my perfume knowledge I'm not exactly certain of how much that differs from a fragrance with alcohol, however it could suggest that this fragrance may be less irritable on sensitive skin types. There is a beautiful lightness about this fragrance that makes it so enjoyable. It's a mixture of powdery florals, a touch of soapy citrus and sugary vanilla. Classique Summer 2010 has quite impressive lasting strength, so I can guarantee that it will leave you feeling refreshed all day long during the warmer weather.

To my nose, Byredo ROSE NOIR packs a powerful punch of patchouli. It's really unmistakeable, and I am confused by the omission of this note from the official list offered above and at the house's website. If this isn't patchouli, then I must not know what patchouli is! Do cistus and moss combine to form a patchouli-like scent? Well, it doesn't really matter. What matters is that this "patchouli"-rose perfume smells beautiful. I'd rank it right up there with Heeley HIPPIE ROSE, although the rose is far less dominant here. That just makes this composition more unisex and probably wearable also by men. I'd have to do a side-by-side test in order to be able to decide between all of the high-quality, natural-smelling, niche patchouli rose perfumes currently available, including Frédéric Malle PORTRAIT OF A LADY and Juliette Has a Gun VENGEANCE EXTREME, but this one is definitely in the running. I myself do not find this perfume very dirty, as it has been marketed. To me this composition presents a clean darkness. ROSE NOIR does not smell animalic to me in the least. Maybe a bit like the soil clinging to the roots of a patchouli plant, but not a touch of skank is present here, according to my nose. ROSE NOIR is earthy in the way that L'Artisan Parfumeur VOLEUR DE ROSES is earthy, and I do think that this would make a fine choice for guys as well as gals. ROSE NOIR is my favorite of the creations of the house of Byredo which I've tested so far... Excellent longevity, too, and it actually becomes stronger over the course of the day. I'd call this one parfum/extrait strength, given its projection and heft.

Baroque, night-purple rose with curls of patchouli and ripe-to-bursting berries. It opens like a Concord grape jelly, but spends most of its lifespan as a mossy musk. The patchouli is decidedly menthol-y, which I think provides a beautiful contrast, and lifts the scent off the forest floor. The rose heart is rich, but thorn-free. I feel this whole scent is thick with petrichor. It’s like running Rose of No Man’s Land through the blue-tinged Twilight filter. The musk lingers the whole day without being overbearing. A pleasant surprise in my book. Mental Snapshot: A gothic romance novel cover. Dew-lacquered rosettes, moonlit pine boughs. Amy Lee of Evanescence cloaked in crimson velvet. Silver-foil calligraphy. Forbidden romance, between Little Red and a werewolf, or Maleficent and Beauty. tl;dr: *weeping rose emoji*

A small sample of the fragrance Rose Noir from the company Byredo, which I had not known until then, now prompts me to write a comment about this Eau de Parfum. The fragrance pyramid piqued my curiosity to get my own "nasal" impression of it. Although the initial scent hints at a certain floral-citrus freshness, "dark clouds" can be sensed on the horizon from the very beginning, which then become more and more dense as the fragrance develops. The darkness is not meant negatively, but rather as a mysterious aspect of an idea of an ancient forest where legends and fairy tales unfold. A rose that exudes a very harsh, yet distinctly characteristic scent of rose. Along with it, a hint of inky, somewhat bitter oak moss or tree moss. The rock rose, with its well-recognizable dark scent, gives the whole thing a touch that makes one feel as if they are amidst the stark, yet comforting spaces of a monastery. The matte glass windows of the room let in the shifting light of the nearby forest. A notion that seems somewhat strange upon "logical" consideration. But strange is often the BEST part of an idea, and individual scent impressions are rarely "logical." Fragrances appeal to one of the oldest parts of the brain and also evoke unconscious experiences and impressions. This type of perfume speaks to me deeply and invites me to travel in spirit to mysterious places.

The name suggested a dark, heavy rose scent to me. I like that. However, one is quite misled here. In reality, Rose Noir is a sprightly, feather-light summer fragrance. The rose is indeed present, but always remains transparent and is accompanied by a slightly tart blackcurrant note. In the top notes, I also smell grapefruit, which makes the fragrance appear extraordinarily fresh, but this fades quite quickly during the scent development. The tartness is certainly invigorating, but with the base, patchouli and moss come in the background, which makes the fragrance somehow feel dull. Or rather, it simply doesn’t feel quite rounded. Tart freshness on one hand, elegant rose on the other, and then this dull-earthy base. It may also be that I expected something completely different because of the name, but I’m not entirely satisfied here. The overall impression feels quite inconsistent to me. The quality of this Byredo fragrance is evident in its good longevity. A few sprays are sufficient for the whole day, and the sillage is subtle but consistently noticeable. Please make sure to test it before buying.

I received the Byredo sample this week during my shopping at HL. I eagerly sprayed the fragrance on after showering. This scent is beautiful, but not really black. More ambiguous, or dark. I find the top note balanced. You can already sense the heart and base notes, but both are initially well restrained by the bright, fruity-floral accord. The rose is very lovely, and the earthy nuances give it a certain masculinity. The romance that rose fragrances often embody is also present here. However, it is composed in a beautiful, dark Gothic variant. In the drydown, the rose holds on well before the earthy base takes over. The musk is rather subtly used and lends the fragrance a distant eroticism. Although the longevity could be better, Rose Noir is a poem.

The grammatical error in the name - it should actually be rose noire - did irritate me a bit at first. Can the people at Byredo not speak French?! But then I thought: Wait, maybe it’s intentional, maybe it’s not supposed to mean "black rose" (which doesn’t really fit, as noted by others), but rather "Rose ... Black".

"Rose Noir" is rosy but not dark. At least not by my definition of dark, black, dreary. Because here, Byredo has delivered a soapy, watery, and almost transparent rose scent that I can't imagine on either a goth, Sam Spade, or Veronica Lake...

In search of an exciting rose fragrance, I came across a sample of Rose Noir. Exciting is a good description, as right after the first spray, I was struck by the association of a piano with several keys pressed at once - energetic, straightforward, loud, and dark. Citrusy, yet sharp, peppery, and somehow gloomy.

the poor...green rose…white rose…lonely rose, yet thriving in the shade, near the underbrush. Small, rather inconspicuous... but with plenty of thorns. It’s a light fragrance, very fresh and unsweetened, slightly mossy right from the start. No rose in sight at all. It’s surely hiding, I think, waiting and waiting.

At first, you are very fresh, personally much too citrusy for me. But I want to get to know you better and watch you closely. It seems this doesn’t please you, as you become very cool and play hard to get. This makes you even more interesting. I believe I discover a warm side to you, realizing that there is so much more behind the facade.

The aftershave version of Le Mâle Eau de Toilette pleases me a lot and resembles the Eau de Toilette very much in scent. Unfortunately, there is again a classic case: it does not last as long or as intensely. Accordingly, longevity and sillage are negligible. The top note is floral, citrusy, and herbal. I recognize lavender, cardamom, mint, and bergamot. The heart note is sweet-floral with neroli and lovely cinnamon. In the base, I detect tonka beans, bourbon vanilla, a bit of rum, and marzipan, but also a certain woodiness with cedarwood as well as balsamic sandalwood notes.

A very cheerful, light watercolor. Peony, tea rose, fresh flowers, a bit of water plants (clean, without the rot effect that many people complain about who don't like water plants). Simply composed, but recognizable. I haven't liked anything else from Boss so far, but this fragrance pleased me and lifted my spirits. Thank you, Hugo. You cannot agree that it is "simple." It is simply light and the niche is a different one. It's like comparing a nail file with a hammer: the things are incomparable and each is good in its place. Personally, I find it more pleasant to hear it on others than another tired Ganymed.

Still, I rarely reach for you. The scent is floral, fresh, and well-groomed. Not intrusive, definitely suitable for work. It could be a nice business fragrance. It has something serious without being stuffy. Surely many will like it, actually a go-to for everyday life. But somehow also unremarkable. It has no recognizability for me. I don't always need to draw all eyes to me with my perfume, but I also don't want to smell "like everyone else." Even a light, unobtrusive scent should be recognized, should be special. Ma vie smells like a fresh flower meadow. Which flowers are growing there? Not to be defined more precisely, many floral notes blend together, harmoniously, but I miss the recognizable scent DNA.

It’s not that I like EVERY fragrance that starts with B and ends with Yredo. For example, I find Mojave Ghost rather terrible, and Seven Veils is just okay. But generally, it is quite alarming that I almost always find what they come up with in terms of fragrances absolutely delightful. And it gets even more alarming, as my nose companion feels the same way - and unfortunately, we usually have divergent fragrance preferences otherwise. During my last perfume purchase, which involved a longer consultation with the saleswoman, she apparently got it into her head that modern citrus fragrances were the right choice for me (despite my slight resistance) and purposefully included a sample of "Carthusia Uomo" and "Byredo Sunday Cologne" (The Eau de Parfum formerly known as Fantastic Man Eau de Toilette, not to be confused with Byredo Sunday Cologne - The Cologne!) with my purchase. In the store, she also recommended Orto Parisi's "Bergamask." All three are quite similar fragrances in a way; initially a classic citrus summer cologne, but then modern and somewhat unconventional, refined with ingredients that don’t immediately seem orthodox; Carthusia presents itself with a "classic-conservative" image, while the other two lean more towards experimental. By the way, none of the three enjoys top ratings here on Parfumo. While I found the scent of Carthusia agreeable, significantly better than its average rating here, it didn’t sweep me off my feet. I already liked Bergamask very much, although I perceived the supposed sweat note, which many reviewers found borderline stinky, more as clean salty-mineral than musty. Byredo, on the other hand, really makes an impression on me once again. And how could it be otherwise, it does so with my constant companion as well. Her exclamation during the blind test on my skin: "Buy this and throw away all your other fragrances, well, almost all of them!". As Hibou correctly noted in his initial review, this is yet another fragrance that does not develop in clearly distinguishable phases chronologically, like a classical symphony with several movements, but rather flows in and out like a modern sound installation. Thus, the division into top, heart, and base notes seems more like a playful exercise here. And in general, the individual notes, here it seems to me even less than with other fragrances, are daunting to dissect too analytically; the harmonious yet tension-filled overall impression is what counts here. If I were to attempt to describe the whole thing in words (instead of just telling a story or painting pictures of the scent), it is undoubtedly a quite dominant citrus, more dominant than the fragrance pyramid might suggest. This does not turn out to be a quickly dissipating top note explosion but runs through the entire scent progression; in fact, I occasionally feel it gets even stronger over time. Sometimes, it seems more like blood orange than bergamot to me, incredibly juicy and fleshy, sometimes bitter-herb, sometimes sweetly accented; perhaps these could be the influences of patchouli and geranium, but that’s just a guess. This (fruit-)fleshy-citrus-bitter-sweet scent tapestry constantly flows into a second one, which I would describe (as the descriptions of "Bergamask" actually promise) as somewhat animalistic-dirty, leathery, sweaty, and coarse-bitter, but still safe, just two handbreadths this side of the border to stinkiness. When I look at the fragrance pyramid and consider the notes vetiver, oakmoss, incense (which always works for me, perhaps contributing to why I like the scent so much), geranium, star anise, and patchouli, that could be about right. I am aware that I have counted geranium and patchouli twice, but I’m saying, everything flows together here. And around the interplay of these two scent tapestries, there is a constant sparkling sharpness that sometimes aligns with the animalistic side as "dangerously and abyssally sharp" and sometimes with the citrus side as "refreshingly sharp," which might come from cardamom (which I actually almost always like). Visually and tactilely, it is a very bright, but not glaringly radiant, rather pasty-syrupy scent, creamy matte orange, earthy light brown colors, occasionally dark and colorful. Liquids that flow into each other and separate again, sometimes irritating pearls, enchanting plays of color and form. For me, a great work of fragrance art, just barely missing a ten. Yesterday we went out, she wore Sminta by Harry Lehmann, I wore this Byredo: I felt we had never smelled so good together as a couple. The only downside: As correctly noted by others, the fragrance has weak longevity (for me, despite good dosing, about 4-5 hours), rather oriented towards the fragrance name "Sunday COLOGNE" than the concentration indication "EDP." And after about 1-2 hours, the scent becomes very skinny, which, since the fragrance is so captivating, leads to the constant wrist-to-nose pressing syndrome, the fragrance lover's counterpart to the borderline idiotic staring at a smartphone while walking through the city. With a rather high-priced fragrance, this is somewhat annoying, and the recommendation to "constantly reapply" might seem a bit decadent. Thus, it may not be a suitable "work fragrance" for constant wear. On the other hand: Those who own 30, 50, or even 100 or more fragrances like many Parfumos and use them regularly in rotation can easily get by with a 50-ml bottle, even with generous dosing, for many years.

A Sunday morning: Well-rested, showered, and with the scent of coffee already in my nose, I eagerly apply Sunday Cologne for a free and relaxing day. It conveys freshness, is elegant, well-groomed, somewhat serious, modern, and at the same time rooted in classic Eau de Colognes. I became aware of it through the lovely comment from FvSpee. Scent development: Sunday Cologne opens with a distinctive, sharply sour-citrusy-herbaceous note, which I primarily attribute to the bergamot, which here comes across as quite aromatic-chemical. Furthermore, geranium and incense play a significant role in the background. Star anise supports the herb-fresh orientation with a slightly bitter, somewhat licorice-like note. To protect the fragrance from being overly strict, there is a very subtle, underlying sweetness. From the base, vetiver can be discerned very discreetly. Overall, the scent tends slightly towards the artificial, but in a positive sense (high-quality synthetics), and especially at the beginning, almost to the point of exaggeration. This gives the fragrance a clear modern character that reminds me of today's aromatic-chemical-bergamot-centered scents. In my experience, these are characterized by an intense sourness while being dense and rather muted in expression. Due to its linearity, you experience the same scent impression from beginning to end. Longevity and sillage: On my skin, the scent lasts about 3-4 hours, well perceptible, after which it quickly diminishes and is present close to the skin for about the same length of time. For an EdP, this is already a rather limited longevity. The sillage is very discreet. In my view, an overdose is not possible. Usability: Due to the scent characteristics described above, the fragrance comes across as rather elegant and is suitable for more formal occasions. Because of its muted citrus-sour freshness, it is a good choice on very warm days, as well as due to its distinctive herbaceousness on cooler days. Conclusion: With Sunday Cologne, Byredo has created a very modern interpretation of a classic Eau de Cologne that combines freshness with seriousness. It tends slightly towards exaggeration, but is thus distinctive and has character.

It was clear to me that Byredo's Minimalsimus aligns well with classic Eau de Colognes or summer fragrances, and I was rather surprised why the brand doesn't offer many more scents in this citrus-chilled direction. On the other hand, I haven't tested Blanche, Palermo, and to this day, Sunday Cologne either. Sunday Cologne, formerly known as Fantastic Man, starts explosively citrusy, dynamic, bright, and ice-cold. The perfume knows no feelings, but offers plenty of refreshment. The anise particularly gives these ultra-high notes a nice boost and liqueur flavor. A minimal cardamom sweetness quickly follows, transitioning into a green, truly wonderful incense-oak moss. The scent may not refresh as strongly after that, but it is beautifully spring-green and classically bitter, not to say masculine. However, this might scare off female wearers, for whom this bitter style shouldn't necessarily be a thorn in the nose. Everything is very high-quality and beautiful, but for me, it doesn't completely justify the price, and an upcoming EdC version seems a bit pointless, as this version here is already quite weak on the chest. Bottle: have I mentioned that I really like the magnetic caps? Sillage: biting citrusy, but somehow toothless. Longevity: a major sticking point, after 5 hours max. it's over for me. An ultra-modern summer fragrance, whether EdC or EdP. However, it also has its weaknesses and is not for collections that already feature many citrus summer fragrances.

Tuesday: When Flui recently looked out the window in the evening and was thoroughly dissatisfied with the weather, he thought a decisive *Hrmpf* and stomped over to his DVD shelf. In went the Skyfall disc, as it’s also raining in London at the beginning. All that was missing was a suitable fragrance for the evening's DVD watching. And since everything looked like a rainy Sunday in November (no people on the street in Muc Downtown, even though it was Tuesday), Sunday Cologne was allowed to keep Flui company while watching the DVD. Thursday: Same here. Had university from 10 in the morning until 7 in the evening non-stop. What is Flui longing for here? Right, for the weekend. For a nice scent to mentally unwind in the evening: Sunday Cologne. And so Flui lay on his bed with the laptop on his stomach (really comfortable right now, honestly) and began to work on a comment. (2nd test run) Hibou's comment is great, and the scent progression is also described superbly. As Hibou says, the scent fits into a modernly furnished city apartment. Except for the rooftop terrace, Flui also lives in a purely black and white, minimalist, aseptic apartment (Zen-like). A black and white Byredo bottle fits in well here, as a Byredo already adorns my fragrance shelf. Byredo is a modern brand. Skyfall is a Bond that has arrived in the 21st century and paints a picture of the modern world. I find some characteristics (how objectively am I writing right now, well whatever) fit wonderfully with SC. First and foremost, and obviously: SC is subtle and restrained, well, Flui isn’t winning a Nobel Prize for epistemology just yet. But it’s important to situate the scent in the 21st century. So to put it all positively: SC relies on understatement. Being grossly noticeable is just as out as a loud ringtone on the subway and is not appropriate. This leads me to another point. In Skyfall, the London Underground network is the expression of how operations are conducted in our world. Everything operates smartly in the data chaos and remains in the shadows. Compared to the past, there are fewer concrete and tradition-laden boundaries; everything has become more ambiguous. National belonging? Is secondary, the individual is independent. Borders on maps? Don’t matter. Contours and boundaries, which are maintained more or less only for tradition's sake, are dissolved. In place of obvious clarity comes something nebulous, elusive, ambiguous. (Wow, what a Flui-esque social analysis ;) So, and now comes perhaps Flui's favorite character in Skyfall: Patrice. An ambivalent symbol. Just the name, one doesn’t really know if it’s a man or a woman. He is described as a ghost, as he has no country of origin and no official residence. He works worldwide, regardless of who commissions him, whether a capitalist, a communist, a terrorist, or a freedom fighter. These antiquated labels/categories can no longer be distinctly differentiated in the 21st century. And even with the villain Silva, what an ambivalent name, both are possible, he is bisexual. So again, all the traditional categorizations that one used to swear by are blurred. Oh, yes, Sunday Cologne. SC is also ambivalent. This fundamentally includes that it is a unisex scent, thus a subtle unisex scent. Maybe like this: The freshness questions itself, due to the spiciness integrated into the freshness. Yes, that might be the twist of the composition, and that’s why I like SC. It is very soft and at the same time fresh and spicy. Yet it is so “tidy” spicy. The spiciness remains very subtly in the background and sends the “empty” freshness ahead. What has a clear face stays in the background; the nebulous, elusive is showcased. The freshness is citrusy and just so vaguely defined; it is simply kept very vague, as I have never smelled in a fresh scent, perhaps it is the spiciness that makes this freshness so elusive, yes, unavailable somehow. So much development doesn’t really show itself to me, just that the spiciness flickers a little and provides a bit of variety. One could describe the scent as a theme with variation (Flui has to let the musicologist out here ;) . The spiciness takes away a possible clarity from the freshness and thus keeps the entire scent in suspension. Fresh-spicy-soft is what comes out for Flui in the end with this wonderful scent. Lemon and spice obscure the freshness. Unfortunately, the longevity is discreet, as is typical for the 21st century, but I find it too discreet. So it’s supposed to be an EdP, but real EdP longevity is different. (Damn 21st century in that regard). All Byredo bottles are black/white, who is that for? Man or woman. Many Byredo scents change their notes as abruptly as a chameleon changes color. In M/Mink, many different arts melt into a total work of art. And last but not least, Sunday Cologne used to be called something else, namely Fantastic Man. So, and now my phase of analytically, head-heavy approaching scents is thankfully over again. Ultimately, it can be said that there are no distinct, tradition-laden boundaries anymore, which is also reflected in the world of fragrances.

Well, what is it now? An Eau de Cologne, an Eau de Toilette, or even an Eau de Parfum, as stated on the label?? The manufacturer doesn't help with certainty when I hear that the predecessor (with the same composition) was an EdT.... Undoubtedly a great summer scent for men, but the longevity of the fragrance, or rather its expiration time, oh man.....I sprayed it on in the evening, but by the next morning you can't smell anything anymore....with an EdP, I have different expectations than with an EdT or EdC.... My "autumn/winter perfume" is Invigorating by Boadicea and I wanted to switch to summer, but that's not so easy.... I got the scent right, but - as I said - the duration of the fragrance..... Maybe it lasts longer for other people.

Yesterday, I had to make a detour to Rossi, as my husband needs special dental care products. Of course, I also rang the fragrance bell, as my eyes discovered Femme L`eau fraiche. My husband loves the original Femme on me, finds it "indescribably feminine," and always faithfully ensures I have a supply. I agree with his assessment and also think that this feminine scent suits me well. L´eau fraiche cannot deny its family resemblance - but it is more like the distant cousin of Femme. Moreover, she wears two sizes smaller, is a few years younger - and less experienced. She belongs to the delicate, ethereal types - which certainly have their charm. She is attractive through the fruity notes, which subtly draw attention to themselves. Stephanotis is bright and exclusive, and Amber skillfully rounds off the scent. The young lady has taste - and will mature into the perfect lady. But it will take some time - and most likely a few more sizes, until she is on par with her more mature cousin. I let my dear husband sniff it, and his brief response was: "Too thin." Well, I wasn't surprised by the answer, as it is an open secret that men prefer it "more voluptuous." Even slender top models only elicit head shakes in my male acquaintances. I believe these little figures are only liked by women.

Femme L'Eau Fraiche by Boss piqued my curiosity because it is said to have a lot of Stephanotis, a type of jasmine, and since I wanted to experience the jasmine-like scent in commercial perfumery, I chose this fragrance as my test subject. I don't know the old woman from Boss, so I can't make comparisons, but his fresh woman - I mean Boss Femme L'Eau Fraiche, has a very fruity opening. Sour mandarin and a few other super fruity fruits are clearly discernible. So far, so "not me". Then the scent of the homewrecker starts to appeal to me. It must be the bridal bouquet jasmine. So that's how it is, the new one not only snagged the boss, she wants to get hitched right away. That's why the little fruits in the top note, that's her ulterior motive. Stephanotis is an amazing thing when you smell it, slightly erotic, yet superficially innocent-white. Here it fits like a glove, because someone who is street-smart knows how to use their charms skillfully to achieve their goals, right, future Mrs. Boss? The base of the fragrance is no longer so sweet-nice and floral-fresh, but warm and almost animalistic. And that's how it will end with the boss and his new one - the hot battle for filthy lucre, and both will turn into beasts.

Femme L’Eau Fraiche is the lighter version of Femme. Although the fragrance pyramid of the Light version is somewhat less known, I estimate that it contains the same notes as its big sister. I can clearly detect the blackcurrant, even though it is not listed. Following that is the scent of the wreath vine, lat. Stephanothis floribunda, which is popularly known as Madagascar jasmine. It is often sold as a houseplant and exudes a captivating fragrance that characterizes Femme L’Eau Fraiche, while being wonderfully balanced. The rose plays its little game with the jasmine mimic, partially accompanied in the background by fruity accords, which thankfully are not dominant. Femme is by no means a fruit bomb; the floral notes are the main actors. The EdT has the advantage of being much more subtle than the original. This was also the reason why I chose it. I had considered Femme as a potential purchase some time ago, but Jil Sander Sensations won the race back then because both smelled similarly intense (but not alike), and one fragrance of that strength was enough for me. However, I have to pay for the wonderful floral scent, which with its lightness is absolutely not a headache candidate, with lower longevity, which is easy to overlook given its delicate elegance. You might need to reapply after two to three hours. Femme L’Eau Fraiche is well-suited for daytime wear and is universally applicable. A feel-good fragrance that I can’t get enough of. Addendum: Femme is often classified as feminine. This limitation does not apply to L'Eau Fraiche at all. I believe it suits all age groups equally well.

WHAT IT IS The spiced carrot side dish you throw together in a rush for your friend's Thanksgiving party which becomes an unexpected star next to dry turkey, craggy stuffing, and salty green beans. This is a savory-ish gourmand which opens with peppery cinnamon notes, then quickly settles into buttery braised carrots and fresh grated ginger. It's strong for a Byredo with an easy 3-4hrs of noticeable sillage and a lightweight patchouli dry down which can stretch to the 6hr mark. Gets a little loud in warm weather, utter knockout in fall & winter. WHO IT'S FOR You just want a little something special for sweater season, but don't want to smell like cotton candy, a speakeasy, or a humidor. You want something unique, a little classy, a little odd. ALTERNATIVES Goldfield & Banks' Ingenious Ginger runs parallel in a citrusy fresh direction more suitable for warm weather - if you love ginger, a bottle of each could easily be your only fragrances. On the men's side, Roja Enigma and YSL l'Homme both feature prominent ginger notes, but it's quickly subsumed by the other spices in the blend and neither has the green sweetness of Epinette's carrot. FINAL THOUGHTS Most Byredos have a sheer, gossamer-like quality which I find beautiful, but fleeting... and while I'm not usually hung up on projection or longevity, they're expensive for a 1-2hr flash in the pan. Eyes Closed was a shock, an off-chance spritz on a warm June day because ginger and carrot sounded delicious. Two hours later I wandered back to the shop and bought a (small) bottle which has now become my staple for fall. Great stuff *if* you like ginger and carrots.

Eyes Closed dresses up a dove-grey iris suede (very much like Dior Homme) in a fine coating of baking spices, mostly cinnamon and cardamom. This accord is distinguished in the opening by a remarkable carrot seed material that gives it an earthy, musky ‘cloudiness’ – like someone coming in and smudging all the lines on a charcoal drawing. It smells rather like the dry ingredients of a carrot cake or a Christmas cake before all the booze, melted butter, and sozzled dried fruit get poured in. I like this fragrance because it is arid and unsweet, the richness of its spice mélange untethered to any gooey basenotes, cutting it free to float on the air. I find it to be pleasingly masculine. But it is too intense – almost unpleasant – to smell straight from the skin, and so powerful that the scent gets a bit monotonous after a few hours. That’s why the way you wear this one counts. Like Chergui and Patchouli 24, a discreet dab on the end of your scarf or on one knuckle is enough to scent your entire ecosystem.

Eyes Closed starts out very dry and powdery. The orris and carrot give it a rooty, earthy scent, but also a hint of waxy lipstick. Iris/orris notes can sometimes smell like carrots, too, so I'm not sure where one note ends and the other begins between these two. The cinnamon is also noticeable right from the start. It's warm and spicy as it should be, and I definitely understand why this is a Christmas scent for some, even though I think there is more to it. The ginger is more subtle, but adds to the spiciness. It smells a little candied to me, not like freshly grated ginger. In the heart of the scent, something darkly fruity unfolds and adds to the festive atmosphere. It smells a bit like a spiced plum compote at this stage, even if nothing in the listed notes indicates it. Later the scent turns drier again and the patchouli finally shows up, tamed by a dusting of cinnamon and powder. This has an interesting mix of hot and cold, dry and jammy, sweet and sharp notes. I can't think of a similar fragrance. At times it's a little too cool and bracing for me, but then I find it really cozy again. The cinnamon really makes the scent. I like this a lot, especially for autumn.

Imagine standing in your kitchen on a cold rainy day, the beep of your oven timer going off in your ears. Opening the oven door your body is washed over in warmth, the smell of cinnamon and cardamom overtaking your being. That's what Eyes Closed by Byredo is like on first spray.
