Cardamom and cinnamon overtake your senses and radiate off your body. It is comforting and cozy - naming it blanket would have pronably been more appropriate. As time goes on it begins to soften into a powdery and slightly woody orris, the carrot coming through with traces of cinnamon almost giving it carrot cake vibes. Thankfully I don't much, if any, of the patchouli in the dry down just the smokiness of the papyrus. On me I get about 7 hours of wear time, it projects off of the skin creating its own little bubble and does leave a nice little sillage trail. I was a little worried given the performance of Vanille Antique but I'm glad I tool the plunge.

I find most Byredos to be pretty linear; what I get within two minutes in is usually what lingers for the rest of its lifespan, however Eyes Closed gave me more evolution. I got crisp baby carrot out the gate, but within a minute it had transformed into raw, green cinnamon – think curls of true cinnamon bark, sliced off the trunk. I liked it best at this turning point; there was a spot there in which the cinnamon, cardamon, and backing herbals formed a chewy, rich, "vanished wood" sort of aroma. Had it arrested here, I would have been a huge fan. However, by thirty minutes the spices had dulled into a sanitary, artificial cinnamon – slightly medicinal, with a ghost of menthol. Essentially cinnamon gum, without any candied gourmand to it. Longevity: It's a Byredo. With four spritzes I got four hours tops. It's not a secret, but also not a scream. You'll get enough emanation for yourself and a close partner to enjoy, but not the whole Thanksgiving party. Mental Snapshot: All I felt like was that I'd been closely embraced by the Old Spice Man. tl;dr: a clean, savoury, unisex spice. Think cinnamint.

I feel like i’m being pranked with the current reviews. This does not smell like some spicy carrot cake at ALL. When I sprayed on paper, the top notes reminded me of that glittery lip smackers berry flavor + the chocolate lip smackers had a love child. Balmy, creamy, sweet but not cloying. I was instantly a fan.
This doesn’t smell like carrot cake to me, nor do I detect any booziness. I get a lovely blend of baking spices without the usual accompanying vanilla/lactonic accords.

this smells like a carrot cake but no cream cheese and very little sugar lol. maybe more like a loaf of slightly sweet & spiced carrot bread? this opens with a warm and dry blend of cinnamon and cardamom, it’s autumnal, powdery and spiced. Then you quickly get a vegetal carrot paired with an earthy sweetness, and a powdery and slightly bready orris root.

Musty dress in a forgotten corner of a antique store still redolent of over-sprayed vintage perfume....I had to scrub it off; although it is surprisingly tenacious for a Byredo and, unfortunately for me, I can still smell a bit of it even though I only used two sprays.

This fragrance is an orris bomb with a spicy twist from cinnamon. While the cinnamon becomes less prominent in the drydown, it still leaves a warm iris scent. As someone who isn't the biggest fan of iris fragrances, I find this to be a good option for those who enjoy that note.

And another comment, because there isn't one for this stuff yet. The green round Boss, yet another completely useless creation. I don't understand why so many people are after these fragrances. The green color reminds me of a toilet cleaning gel that you could spray under the rim of the toilet bowl. Although the cleaning gel has at least some utility. :D The green Boss is rather less useful. :D Well then, there's not much more to say about this stuff, except that it's just laaaaaaaaaaaame again.

Mumbai noise is mainly a coffe-tonka scent on a sweet oudy base. This is not a laid-back or watery scent like many other byredos. You feel the presence of the scent for many hours. Not unique in composition, i had many similar scents in the past few years. But the sweet oud base made me buy this scent. You get that intense oud blending with somewhat nutty coffee vibe, and it becomes heady and daring. Definitely a winter scent, it is very rich for hot weather. Has a dominant ethnic quality, really suits the rich indian scents. Not listed in notes, but i suspect a dash of incense is there in the midnotes. I will have this in my collection for many years if it doesnt get spoiled by reformulations. The sweet oud base may be challenging for many people, be sure to try before you buy.

No, really, please, don't do more than 1, maybe 2. And why would you? This thing is strong. It's been 10 hours and I still hear it on my skin pretty well. And goddamn it's good. Eastern, sweet, lush. Davana note gives it a unique religious tone, although I wouldn't call the scent itself unique. I've tried some similar ones, but I just kept coming back to this at the store, driven by some magical force (which is my love for spicy scent to be honest) Definitely recommend it to oud lovers, to people who are not afraid of a powerful scent. Also, I recommend buying only a miniature. It's rather expensive, and really requires one, maybe two sprays a day to shine. You won't need a big one if this is not your favourite scent of all time.

Sampling Mumbai Noise by Byredo, a 2021 release, a blend of oud, coffee, labdanum, sandalwood, davana, and tonka. It has almost a “chocolate with spice” vibe, something perhaps that I’m imagining from the coffee, and has a good bit of coziness mixed with provocation, an ever-so-slightly funkiness of oud and spiciness of davana mixed in with otherwise familiar and centered, yet robust, coffee/sandalwood/labdanum trio. It feels like an evocation of a coffee house or log cabin, with touches of smoke and fire, but overall, a semi-gourmand experience that’s dense and quite fitting Its concentration is EDP and retail pricing is $330/235 for 100/50ml, in line with most of the house’s catalogue, though it’s also available via discounters. Currently the only Byredo bottle that I have is Eleventh Hour (though I once owned Sunday Cologne), and Mumbai Noise is pleasant and striking enough that I might look into it. 8 out of 10

In the past, "Mumbai" was called "Bombay". The name comes from Portuguese and means something like: Beautiful Bay. Because back then, Bombay/Mumbai belonged to the Portuguese colonies. This can still be recognized today in architecture and language habits that have flowed into everyday life, among other things. Mumbai is a huge, bustling, and noisy metropolis. Others have told me that as soon as the plane begins to land, one can distinctly perceive the unpleasant smell of a not particularly clean metropolis with the typical scent of garbage and smog. I cannot confirm this, as I have never been there. On one hand, I expected from the name of the perfume "Mumbai Noise," which is listed for the Oud, that I would have an animalistic, loud, and possibly disturbing olfactory experience in line with the common reporting and perception of Mumbai. On the other hand, I couldn't quite imagine that for Byredo. Perhaps the historical Bombay with its fine villa neighborhoods in Portuguese style could have been sketched in "Mumbai Noise." And so it is. "Mumbai Noise" opens with labdanum. Woody, coffee-scented Oud takes on the creamy-bitter scent/taste of a fine 90% cocoa chocolate with vanilla and citrus zest, combined with tonka and creamy sandalwood. It results in a refined fragrance with medium sillage. The woody Oud with coffee note smells very unique and is new to me and very pleasant. Together with the other ingredients, a rich gourmand could emerge. However, that does not happen with "Mumbai Noise." It remains an exquisitely unusual yet sweetly lovable, understated perfume. A typically noble, subtle Byredo that exudes what is promised in the pyramid. Just as I have perceived some Byredos so far. Although the sillage is not so intense, "Mumbai Noise" has good longevity. "Mumbai Noise" is unreservedly a unisex fragrance. I will remember this scent.

India. Mumbai. It unites opposites like people living on the brink of existence from the lower castes and the luxury of a wealthy financial metropolis, temple complexes built centuries ago, and the loudly colorful Bollywood industry. One inevitably imagines streets dominated by traffic chaos, spice markets and street kitchens, beggars, tourists - a kaleidoscope of various impressions. However, Mumbai Noise is a very quiet, understated fragrance that, for me, fits more into the ambiance of a luxury resort or an Ayurvedic wellness oasis. It begins balsamic and resinous, then a dark note joins in, which for me is neither distinctly coffee nor bittersweet chocolate, along with a slightly muted scent of sandalwood. I cannot detect any oud. Everything is very pleasant, warm, and enveloping, which is probably why I associate it with a wellness temple. There is not a significant change in the fragrance progression on my skin, and I do not constantly have it in my nose; rather, I have to get close to the sprayed area. Occasionally, I think I have lost it, but for example, when transitioning from indoors to outdoors, I catch a whiff of it again. Very subtle and without the headache potential like with the Afghan. For its weak projection, it lasts quite long, which is probably due to the resins. No noise, but a fine, enticing whisper. Beautiful, but expensive, and definitely reserved for the upper caste ;-)

A glamorous, summery shapeshifter. Hour 1: sugared citrus. Hours 2-4: “Baccarat d’Afrique.” Hours 5-12+: Bal d’Afrique. Not the near-identical twin I found with the Mojave Ghost Absolu, but definitely a sibling. The citrus, which was invisible to me in the OG, plays a far more dominant role here. The praline interlude is a new addition and conjures up wartime Baccarat Rouge flashbacks. Far more sugary and brassy than the boho-clean marigold shampoo of the original. Feels like the summertime foil to the wintry rose-cocoa of my beloved Soie Malaquais, in that near-gourmand vein. The longevity and sillage defy every Byredo stereotype (two sprays to a tester card was enough to make my car a BdA bubble for 3 days, so much that I could even smell it percolating from the trunk when loading groceries). I was easily clocking 12+h on skin. Would have sprung for a bottle if I didn’t get the amber syrup intercession, as the drydown is divine, but if you like your fragrances sweet and showy this would be a winner. Mental Snapshot: Southern California. Summer night first date. Five-star tapas bar. Aperol Spritzes al fresco. Tango lessons in the park. Cruising down the coastline at sunset, “Soak Up the Sun” thumping from your sunburst-coloured Boxster. tl;dr: summer nights, not-from-concentrate

Bal d'Afrique Absolu opens with a sharp juicy blackcurrant and lemon combination smoothed out by musk and violet. The woody ambery notes in the base provide body and support to make for a linear yet beautiful creation. Smooth, well-blended, without one note dominating or synthetics becoming overwhelming. Mass-appealing, unisex, and versatile. On the fence about this being full bottle worthy—I think the price is too high at the moment; might jump in if I can find a 50ml for under $200. Haven't gotten a chance to compare this directly to its predecessor Bal d'Afrique Eau de Parfum but I currently have Bal d'Afrique Absolu and Contralto on opposite wrists and I have to say the Absolu is so much better. Contralto is giving lemon cleaner, while BdAA is so much smoother and more natural. Not sure what possessed folks to compare this to Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum , there is not really any overlap other than ambroxan which is in literally every fragrance, and much less maltol sweetness. null of BR540's signature sharp mossiness (evernyl) is present.

I sprayed this on at my local Skins and my first reaction was - hell no. This is not the Bal d'Afrique I absolutely fell in love with. This is sugar and citrus on steroids ... or something. I decided against it right then and there. Nope, I'd do with my lovely Bal d'Afrique, spray it a little more, and then buy a new bottle. Right? RIGHT? So when I walked back to my car with another lovely fragrance, I thought - dang, that Kurky that I sprayed on my skin to test it out smells gosh darn lovely. Shall I go back to get it too? Wait. That was my other wrist. Then what is it that I am smelling? Yep. The absolu. Between spraying, then deciding against it, getting another perfume and walking back to my car it had morphed into Bal d'Afrique again. And one that projected and filled the car, and still lingers lovely on my skin now, six hours later. I am so on the fence. Can I forgive the sugary opening? It's gosh darn pricey, but I know I love love love the dry down and it absolutely lasts longer than the original one. Gah! Haha!

My closing coverage for 2025 is still on-going with 62 fragrances now being rated. A weak year overall means some products have an easier opportunity at making the top of the charts and one of Swedish niche brand Byredo's latest, that being the flanker to hero franchise Bal d'Afrique Eau de Parfum , appears set for a top 10 finish on the year with potential for a top 5. I first wore the EDP a month ago (September 2025) and for this review, I am wearing the two versions side-by-side to offer the strongest overview. One thing has surprised me when I first wore Bal d'Afrique Eau de Parfum is that very few people were describing it the way I was: the scent's main DNA is of a citrusy sugared amber and it's to the point where it could easily be viewed as being adjacent to the profile of Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum , i.e. the sweetness stems from a derivative play on saffron. The EDP version's dry-down quality is less impressive with the florals coming in and the musks reminding me of that glossy newspaper smell that you see in fragrances like Le Labo's AnOther 13 Eau de Parfum and Byredo's own Super Cedar as well as De Los Santos . With Bal d'Afrique Absolu de Parfum , I feel like the DNA leans even more heavily into the sugared amber smell. The primary accords of the EDP version, i.e. fresh-sweet-citrusy-fruity, are all still there, but the Absolu version (to my nose) has stripped out most of the florals and built the fragrances around the blackcurrant, lemon, musk and amber. That is to say there is less development with the scent and I'd say that actually places Bal d'Afrique Absolu de Parfum in the same genre of fragrances as Clive Christian's Town & Country and Fragrance du Bois' Lucius , i.e. citrusy BR540 alternatives. However, unlike these two comps, Bal d'Afrique Absolu de Parfum leans into the fruitiness (which the 2 comps don't even have). The profile offered by the EDP has garnered such success that calling it the female market equivalent of Bvlgari's hero franchise "Le Gemme - Tygar | Bvlgari" feels accurate. I'd argue Bal d'Afrique Absolu de Parfum takes the better parts of the EDP and structures the scent around them, worthy of a 1 point improvement over the EDP. The result is a longevity improvement of at least 3-4 hours (longevity +3 points; 7/10) and a sillage where people will actually be able to smell you when you're nearby (sillage +4 points; 6/10). Given the retail of €290/100ml, I am placing the value at 6/10 with some upside potential. For years, the problems of Bal d'Afrique Eau de Parfum allowed competitors like Initio's Musk Therapy Extrait de Parfum and Boadicea's Hanuman to carve into their market. From my experience with all of the products, I would argue the Initio and the Boadicea are more-so competing against one-another than Bal d'Afrique Eau de Parfum as they made relevant improvements to the DNA. With Bal d'Afrique Absolu de Parfum , Byredo has a direct competitor to those fragrances and while I believe Hanuman is still the top product in the genre, Absolu has tightened the gap to the point where spending that extra money may no longer be worth it.

I first tried this in Skins and took a sample home. At the counter, I smelled a sweet, rich, almost gourmand fragrance after a quick citrus opening. Later, when I checked the listed notes and reviews for Bal d’Afrique, I was very surprised; everyone seemed to describe something fresh, clean, lemony, juicy. That was the opposite of what I was smelling. Turns out Byredo released this Absolu version of Bal d’Afrique in 2025, so this must be what I had smelled and got a sample of instead if the OG version - they just hadn't written in on the label of the sample. Apparently this newer take leans much deeper, sweeter and more gourmand than the original. It introduces praline, which adds warmth and chocolatey richness. The typical Byredo “DNA” I often pick up (something powdery, creamy, earthy, almost orris-like) is definitely present here as well. For me, this isn’t an everyday scent, nor something I’d wear in an office or enclosed space. It’s quite rich and sweet and on the wrong day it could easily tip into being cloying and headache-inducing. But worn in the right setting (outdoors, evenings, or special occasions) it has a cosy, comforting quality that’s hard to resist.

I received this fragrance as a gift. I have loved Bal d’Afrique for a long time and wear it very often, so I was naturally thrilled. But to be honest: This version has exceeded my expectations. It is familiar yet more intense, deeper, and somehow rounder. You immediately recognize the typical Bal d’Afrique character, but everything feels warmer and more mature.

The original Bal d’Afrique has accompanied me for years and is still one of the most beautiful fragrances in my collection. Whether during the day or in the evening, summer or winter: to me, it always smells luxurious and well-groomed, without ever being intrusive. I love it, but the longevity is simply not good.

In this review, I will try to summarize the most important points without poetry, to describe as best as possible what I missed when Googling. First of all: EDP vs. Absolu - you can forget about that. If I were to make a clear statement about Mojave Ghost or Blanche, that is absolutely not the case here.

I bought this fragrance here as a sample in the souk and I was pleasantly surprised. Bal d’Afrique is overall a very beautiful scent. It feels warm, fresh, and pleasantly addictive without being too heavy. A fragrance that is immediately appealing and very harmoniously composed. The fragrance notes are rather soft and well-balanced.

Whisky. And wood. And whisky. And wood. An oak barrel with whisky, but not the boozy, fruity kind. The dryer, maltier one. The naming of the scent is confusing: if there’s oud in it, it sure doesn’t show itself up front. There is no classic oudy cheesy barnyard smell whatsoever (and I do appreciate the dirtiness of the “raw” oud like in Amouages King Blue!) and the woody part is more of an old branch your dog picks up from the ditch and adopts. Though it has a sourness to it that might come from the oud, I feel like it’s more in line with a raw (not pipe!) tobacco note? Nevertheless I quite like it - it’s far from anything else in my collection and for the odd occasion when I want to smell like a newly cracked cask of Speyside single malt, it’s perfect. Powerfull sillage for the first two/three hours, slowly settling to a long lasting skin scent that matches the fall vibe well. Worth noting I blind bought this (in search of Daring Saffiano also from The Collection) for close to 100€. I would not pay full retail for it. Highly recommend sampling if you want a bit of an outlier in the woody category, but definitely not a crowd pleaser. Oh, and the bottle is…a bit bland and “cheap”. Good weight but no magnetic cap and the label just looks a bit low budget. Doesn’t match the price level in my opinion.

… I go for a walk in the Bavarian Forest. I arrive with my dog at a fish pond where fish have been caught. Near the pond stands a house and also a smoking chamber that is in operation, spreading its smoky aromas. I ask the fisherman what that smell is, which is not really familiar to me, and he explains that he uses wood along with bran for smoking. Shortly thereafter, he pulls out the trout and I buy one from him. My little one and I enjoy it immediately, as hot as it is. Delicious. Upon applying this fragrance, the first thing that hits the nose is a smoky, spicy, dry scent. Underneath, the oud blends in a gentle but distinctly noticeable way and is dust-dry. This perfume matures and takes on a pronounced masculine twist. The longevity and sillage are very good. Here we have a fragrance from Hugo Boss's luxury line. Dear people at Boss, a higher price for the line is acceptable, but the price you quote on your site is ridiculously exaggerated. Nevertheless, it is a great scent and I don't understand why it is rated so poorly in some cases. Is it again because it is from a designer and there are people who think that such a house shouldn't release such a fragrance? In any case, it is also wearable by women. Since it is quite mature, I would say that 25 years is a good starting age and there is no upper limit. But younger guys can certainly try it out to see if they like it. Since it is not sweet, it is an all-rounder that can be worn all year round. During the day, it works well with a suit, in jeans, leather clothes, but also casually, just as well as in the evening at the opera, in a theater, in a pub, in a bar, in a club, at a meal in a fine dining restaurant, and of course also for certain hours. Anyone who enjoys a smoky, spicy, dust-dry, adult masculine oud scent should take a close look at this one. It is also significantly cheaper than at Hugo Boss. It is not a discreet perfume; you will be clearly noticed, but it is not overwhelming like its sweet brothers from other brands. There are other ways to smell like this, simply masculine.

Ah yes, Dominique Ropion.. a love-hate relationship that will probably always remain so. On one hand, he creates masterpieces like Frederic Malle The Night/Cologne Indelebile or Papilefiko by Nishane, on the other hand, there are works that I just don’t quite.. understand, or to put it bluntly, I don’t particularly like, foremost among them is Paco Rabanne Phantom. Enough rambling, now to the scent. This fragrance is, like most of this line, quite linear and dry. Upon the initial spray, a strong, smoky, alcoholic scent immediately hits the nose, reminiscent of a bottle of whiskey - not some perfume interpretation of whiskey, but the actual smell when you open a new bottle. For some, including myself, this directly evokes a few flashbacks from the first parties at 18, which didn’t quite end as wonderfully as they began. Smoky, alcoholic, absolutely not sweet, and very woody, that’s how I would describe the entire progression of this scent. It strongly reminds me of Oud Wood Intense, which has since been discontinued, but this one is more alcoholic and woodier, while Oud Wood Intense is leatherier. Confident Oud evokes dark wooden barrels full of aging alcohol, it reminds of evenings when things may have gone a bit off the rails, of old, smoky bars where you mostly encounter regulars aged 50+, of people who couldn’t care less about other opinions and do what they want, of absolute darkness, of a mafia boss casually smoking his cigar before commissioning a new murder, of bad life choices and an unhealthy lifestyle, of dirty alleyways that hardly anyone dares to enter. This fragrance absolutely lives up to its name "Confident Oud" and is definitely a scent that should be tested beforehand. It is edgy, it is absolutely not mass-appeal, and should be worn with a healthy dose of self-confidence. An absolute statement among boss fragrances.

Casablanca Lily reminds me of Neroli & Orchid by L'Occitane en Provence, even though they hardly overlap in notes. In a way, they are similar, yes, but Casablanca Lily is definitely better. The scent is soft, feminine, and floral without being too sweet or too fresh. Simply elegant. At first sniff, it may not seem like a major innovation, yet it lingers pleasantly in the memory, and you find yourself wanting to sniff it again and again. The fragrance initially feels familiar and known, but that is a bit misleading. It is indeed something special, a beautiful blend of elegance and lightness. By the way, the fragrance is officially a unisex; for me personally, it feels more feminine, which certainly doesn't make it a women's fragrance. Casablanca Lily is definitely going on my wishlist!

Yes, the scent is not an innovation. Nevertheless, the individual notes are wonderfully harmoniously intertwined. At the top, there is a very delicate, fruity floral note. In the heart, a tuberose that comes across as incredibly beautiful. It's rare that this note doesn't evoke bubblegum associations in me. In the base, the scent feels warm and enveloping. Throughout, a moderate sweetness resonates. I would almost classify the scent as mainstream. I can imagine it on the shelves of the relevant perfumeries.

The scent starts off very feminine. Very noble, almost powdery floral but also not particularly innovative.. Category "quite nice".. The tuberose dominates with a hint of honey and comes across to me as a bit old-fashioned and unspectacular. The plum is only perceptible for a very short time in the first minutes before it fades away and makes room for the tuberose. The scent is actually very beautiful, but it has something almost boring and almost shy about it. If the scent were to remain like this, it would be a light noble but not very exciting summer fragrance for me. However, the scent quickly shifts into sleep mode.. The heart notes do not stay on my skin for long.. A short hour, if at all, before any very airy and almost transparent notes take over. These notes are supposed to be rosewood and honey, but I can't smell them.. I only detect something almost bitter, almost transparent.. H+ S a disaster.. Price/performance or let's say clearly that the quality for the price is a slap in the face..

I admit I initially had my doubts about whether this small exclusive line from Byredo was worth it. Nevertheless, this fragrance had to be thoroughly tested; I was too curious. And what can I say, this is probably one of the most complex creations from the house. I am not a big lover of tuberose and usually try to avoid it, but here it is so finely balanced that it is not only bearable but absolutely beautiful and complementary! It's amazing that I find myself praising the use of tuberose again. The entire creation is simply rounded, and it seems to me that this composition was not created in haste. The scent constantly oscillates between classic and modern, compelling one to sniff at their own wrist continuously. The plum is, in my opinion, clearly noticeable throughout the entire top and heart note. During the heart note, a play unfolds between jasmine, lily, and rose, which together smell like a €1000 flower bouquet. I don't really pick out the clove, but rather a steady, very gentle woody undertone that becomes more pronounced over the hours. One thing that always excites me is the progression of sweetness. The fragrance has a certain base sweetness, not too bold, rather well-measured. The first sweetness you perceive is a plum sweetness, and at some point, this sweetness subtly transforms into a honey sweetness that is quite atypical for honey. In the last hours, I perceive a kind of rosewood along with the aforementioned honey note. I see this fragrance for evening occasions, extraordinary events, and special moments. Too special to wear it just like that. The price alone makes this perfume hardly suitable as an everyday scent. A commendable creation from Byredo!

Even though the more noble, expensive Boss collection (every brand seems to need such a line by now) was launched shortly before I really got into perfumes (early 2012), it is certainly not just because I knew nothing about this small & probably not so fine line until recently. This is likely also due to the fact that apart from the packaging & presentation, the contents cannot quite keep up. At least that's what people say... and I don't really want to contradict that with my new addition Cotton Verbena. But what doesn’t one buy when it’s extremely discounted? If I had paid the full retail price, I would certainly be (even more) disappointed and the rating would be lower as well. So I am currently still lenient, but I can't promise that the rating won't slip to a truly mediocre level. Let's just wait and see what warmer times bring & reveal. The entire collection is not really being advertised, commented on, discussed, or even hyped - and Cotton Verbena is certainly the most inconspicuous little plant from this wallflower collection... Like all perfumes from "The Collection," Cotton Verbena, as the name suggests, is based on a fabric. Here it’s the good old cotton. But anyone expecting something cozy here is mistaken & should rather go sniff the musk scent from the same collection. Cotton Verbena is a citrus-woody summer scent that couldn't be more transparent and office-appropriate. However, since I am not the only one who doesn’t always wear the most inconspicuous perfumes in the office, this hardly makes it any more positive. In fact, CV consists only of lemon, moss, light woods - and it’s all elegantly diluted. So diluted and marginalized that the scent reminds one of cheaper fragrances and even deodorants. It is pleasant and not synthetic, but somehow it lacks not just a certain something, it lacks much more. So much more that I can easily imagine (not just because of the clearance sale) that this could be the first candidate for discontinuation from the collection after just a few years. I would have wished for more sweetness and more cotton feeling, even if that wouldn’t have saved it from the mud. Moreover, a significant similarity to D&G Masculine cannot be denied. Bottle: what a brilliant, high-quality presentation... it can even compete with the very, very big names in the perfume business & deserved a separate section. I think it couldn’t be more valuable. Sillage & Longevity: not worth mentioning, it does nothing for any office fly for 3-5 hours. Conclusion: a safe choice for the office in summer... but I simply have to remain silent about many things, because that’s what one should do when one has nothing good to say ;) I hope for improvement with its brothers, but I don’t believe in it... you hardly ever see them to test :(

Can I be honest + vulnerable for a moment? I still have no idea what saffron smells like. I've considered buying a bottle of the spice at Trader Joe's for the sole purpose of ID-ing this note/ingredient, but have yet to commit to the endeavor of it all. That said, I instead drew an immediate comparison to Maison Crivelli's Lys Solaberg which also has dark plummy notes. Both have an evening, autumnal feel with sweet, dark fruits. If I had to distinguish the two... LS is more purple-colored in my mind, whereas RC seems more burgundy. Am I being swayed by the color of said juice? Maybe so. But it still has a fruitier, red berry kind of feel which I think is in part to the cassis and the sweetness of praline. Do note the juice is colored and doesn't go clear when you spray it. I have the blotter that's stained pink from the liquid.

This fragrance is undoubtedly well-blended; within the chaos suggested by its name, there is a distinct sense of harmony and originality. It is clearly the result of meticulous craftsmanship. At first, the initial spray bursts with fruity notes, filling me with high expectations. However, soon after, saffron emerges - a note that, I must admit, I personally do not enjoy. Though it does not overpower the composition, its presence remains persistent. That said, I cannot deny the originality, the artistry, and the sheer quality of this fragrance. It has a clear purpose, an undeniable character, even if its price is quite prohibitive.

The "Night Veils" collection by Byredo features dark fragrances with a high concentration of scent, inspired by the duality of night. After "Vanille Antique," there is finally a new fragrance from this collection. Rouge Chaotique is the first gourmand scent in the "Night Veils" collection, attempting to pair heavy "chaotic" notes with sweet fruity notes. The beauty of the fragrance thus emerges from chaos, so to speak :D Now, finally, to the scent! The perfume opens with a wonderful saffron note, which smells as clean and cool as in "Crystal Saffron." Juicy dark fruits immediately join the saffron, accompanied by a hint of fresh bergamot and a very subtle leather accord. The opening is very unique and I totally love it! In the heart of the fragrance, it becomes truly seductive! A sweet and delicious praline note, accompanied by delicate plum, creates an incredible spectacle. It's rare to encounter something so seductively delicious that still smells sophisticated and unique. In the dry-down, the initially barely noticeable oud note becomes a bit stronger, but definitely not to the point of being inappropriate. It’s a super interesting addition to the scent profile and mega intriguing! Finally, papyrus and patchouli notes come in, rounding off the fragrance into a rather earthy dry-down. For me, this scent is truly something completely new that I haven't smelled in this composition anywhere else. Beautifully executed, and the quality and longevity, as usual from the Night Veils collection, leave nothing to be desired. The fragrance is also very unisex and wearable by everyone! I would recommend wearing it more in the evenings or during the colder months, as it is quite heavy and strong. For me, it's definitely a scent that you MUST really try! Thank you for your time, feel free to let me know how you perceive the fragrance and enjoy the experience! See you soon, Your Luis :)

The new perfume is a unique combination of contradictions and beauty. The sacrament of gourmet aroma with notes of oud from the Byredo Night Veils collection. Rouge Chaotique, the first gourmet flavor with oud notes, is a unique symphony. It is inspired by the belief that embracing chaos in the creative process can lead to unique forms of self-expression. At the heart of the fragrance, shades of spicy leather and precious saffron blend with juicy notes of blackcurrant and fresh bergamot. The syrupy character of the plum and the sweetness of the praline create an irresistible delight. Every drop of this extract is distilled as pure essence. The perfume is applied to the skin, where it spreads its unique scent and envelops you in warmth and magic for many hours. "Rouge Chaotique is the new permanent fragrance of Extrait de Parfum for the refined line of Night Veils. It is created for those who believe in the power of chaos and want to experience the beauty that arises from it." Notes: saffron, blackcurrant, lemon, bergamot, praline, plum, patchouli, oud, papyrus... Yes, that's great, everything is fine, but a few hours pass and I hear Ganymede!?..... Really??? And whether there was a plum with pralines, there was no trace of them until the end .... I will deal with this beast again .

"Rouge Chaotique" is not just a fragrance, but an emotion, like a interplay of chaos and passion. It is for those who seek the unusual and provocative while still appreciating elegance and sophistication. This scent leaves a lasting impression and is perfect for special occasions when a touch of mystery and seduction is required. The opening is a fiery spectacle of saffron, blackcurrant, and an unexpected leather note, with bergamot and lemon bringing freshness to this bold blend. The allure comes from the juicy plum, paired with sweet praline. Oud and papyrus create a dry smokiness, giving it an "edgy" quality. Here, all elements of warmth, freshness, sweetness, and sensuality come together. Great projection, great longevity, and a truly beautiful gourmand oud fragrance.

The latest fragrance from the Night Veils collection captivates me, firstly, with its extremely successful opening. A slightly sour-citrusy background of bergamot and lemon allows the dominant black currant to shine brightly. Dark and still sweet, the fragrance develops further thanks to saffron and a fruitily delicious plum.

A beautiful scent. I tested the fragrance as a 2 ml sample. Considering that it is an extrait and somewhat heavier, the scent did not cause me any headaches. More suitable for special occasions and seductive. A very good alternative to Baccarat Rouge, which I personally can no longer stand. I would describe the fragrance as sweet, feminine, and bitter at the same time.

I looked at and tried the scent in the Boss Store. The strip had such a great scent for 3 days, which I needed. Ideal for summer evenings, not too hot office days, or simply as a daily scent in winter. Thanks to the leather, you can wear it (as long as it’s not over 25 degrees) almost all the time, and unlike other fresh scents like Dylan Blue, Legend Spirit, or Acqua di Gio, it has something deep and somewhat noble due to the leather note. I then bought it for €185 in the Flaconi discount. Price-wise it's okay, €185 for 100 ml is expensive, but you get a beautifully crafted bottle and a scent that lasts forever. Sillage is quite good for a fresh scent without synthetics. On clothes, the drydown lasts a few days.

Flowerhead blends together beautifully as it settles on your skin - authentic rather than synthetic, a beautiful bouquet of white florals, fresh greens and sweet complementary berries & fruit. If you dig white florals, do yourself a favor and check this one out. If you find white florals offputting - well, go on... get outta here! =P

This fragrance should come with a warning label that it could be obnoxious if heavily sprayed. It really packs a punch. I could not imagine owning a bottle of this as one spray is all that is needed to perfume yourself and whatever building you are in. It is a huge, very dewy white floral, primarily tuberose and jasmine which appears intensely right out the gate. Has lots of green notes and an aquatic, cold aspect to it too, so descriptions I've read elsewhere of a florist refrigerator are pretty apt. There is iso and ambroxan mixed with the slightly animalic base of suede and ambergris. Fortunately, not enough synthetics to totally ruin the scent, but it shouldn't be here in the first place, especially at the prices being asked for a bottle. While this starts out with enormous projection, it does seem to lighten up as it goes along. I am using "seem to" as opposed to "does" as I am not sure if it is actually lightening up, or if my body's defenses are making me nose blind so I don't incapacitate myself. I'll have to test this around people and see. Overall, while I do think it is pretty, I seriously have no idea where I could ever wear this scent as it is just too overwhelmingly strong. I also do not understand the unisex designation as this is extremely feminine. More than likely Byredo is just trying to increase sales labeling it that way. But of course, one can wear whatever one likes.

Flowerhead from Byredo is what a rainbow smells like, or rather the dizzying polychromatic shimmer from the faceted crystalline prism that hangs in front of your window when it bends the light of a morning sunbeam. It’s an incandescent, kaleidoscopic, hallucinatory jasmine-tuberose-lemon explosion that is not particularly complex and is certainly not subtle. It’s a heady, obnoxious white floral fizzing citrus, and, perversely...I think I adore it.

Flowerhead starts with an extreme blast of flowers (jasmine, tuberose) and cranberries. After that, I mostly get heavy bubblegum tuberose heavy white florals and musk for a while, with a very impressive sillage. About an hour in, the tuberose is joined and slowly becomes overpowered by a strong ambergris smell (a sweet , earthy, and marine musk). It also reminds me a bit of rice powder. While interesting, I find this one quite cloying - first by the sickly sweet tuberose and then by the very strong musk. It stays a long while. Comparison to some other tuberose perfumes I prefer: - Dyptique Do son: less bubblegum, less sweet, more green, less musk, lighter, less longevity - Frederic Malle Carnal flower: much more green, much better blending, far less bubblegum, even better longevity and projection - L'Artisan Parfumeur La chasse aux papillons: also a lot of bubblegum tuberose/jasmine, but much lighter (less musky), less longevity - Dior pure poison: more orange blossom, more flower-centric, less powdery, similar projection and longevity

It's almost identical to acacia-scented mint chewing gum but better. Tuberose dominates the whole scent, but it's not offensive. Flower Head is not as flowery and heady as the name suggests, so even I, who is not fond of floral fragrance, could enjoy it. As someone mentioned before, it has outdoor wedding vibes, too, due to its vibrant and realistic white flower, beautifully combined with green notes. Flower Head has very clean, fresh, and minty vibes, so it'll be great in spring to early summer. It has a sweet, minty sensation that evokes a chewing gum vibe, so I suggest sampling it first. It's not for everyone. It doesn't match my vibe, so I won't personally buy it, but I'd love it on others.

Admittedly, a Byredo new release is for Flui like Christmas, birthday, Easter, university diploma, New Year's Eve, and whatever else comes together. So it is with Flowerhead. And there stood the bottle among the others, no special place for the new release.

Well, my title may not be very creative for a perfume name like "Flowerhead," but I couldn't think of anything better at the moment. After more than 1300 comments, I'm starting to get tired... I'm really fed up... I don't feel like writing comments anymore... baaaah! I know you are NOT shocked... since you don't believe me anyway.

My first Byredo! It pushed its way in front of my previous wish candidates... I've actually been eyeing the southern French wildflower bouquet Inflorescence by Byredo for a long time, but then I was introduced to "the new one," and it captivated me immediately, it left me pleasantly dazed with its floral charm.

...that's literally what this fragrance is called. I treated myself to it a few weeks ago at the traditional department store in Berlin. Why? When testing, it smelled really good of jasmine and tuberose, and I let myself be lulled into it during my hunt.

When Ben Gorham, the founder of the Scandinavian niche label Byredo, invites us to the premiere of a new launch, fragrance lovers around the world are eager to be front and center. His latest creation bears the promising name Flowerhead and is meant to be a tribute to the colorful and extravagant weddings of India.

Eau des Baux goes on with a spicy pink pepper and cardamom tandem before slowly transitioning to its early heart. After the spicy open the spice recedes but remains now in support, ceding ground to a somewhat woody coniferous cypress with hints of smooth incense peeping through. As the fragrance progresses in the heart the incense deepens and intensifies to take the fore, moderately sweetened by tonka bean from the base which gives the overall accord a relatively sweet pipe tobacco like vibe with the cypress and cardamom dirtying the overall accord somewhat. During the late dry-down the initial spice all but completely dissipates, leaving the tonka bean, incense and remaining supporting cypress to give a relatively sweet sendoff. Projection is good to very good and longevity is average at about 8 hours on skin. Eau des Baux was quite a surprise when I finally got around to trying it. Tobacco is not listed in the notes and indeed it most likely contains none but it does have a very deep pipe tobacco vibe that permeates the heart of the fragrance and it smells incredible. The cypress utilized throughout the composition is key to making everything work, as it adds a woody slightly coniferous underlying facet that counters the sweetness of the tonka bean laden incense to balance the composition. Eau des Baux is frequently compared to Tobacco Vanille by Tom Ford and I can definitely see why folks may make the comparison, but Eau des Baux is the more complete and interesting composition of the two that sells for a heck of a lot less money at its $52 a 100 ml bottle price tag. The bottom line is after sampling this one at my local mall, I left L'Occitane, got to my car and then turned around and bought a bottle as it completely impressed me (relatively low cost aside). Values like this 4 star out of 5 "excellent" rated fragrance are relatively scarce, so I recommend seeking Eau des Baux out for trial and possible purchase.

Contrary to what I expected after my first experience, this has really grown on me. I never was a big fan of vanilla, but this is a very nice take on that theme. The opening is very 'in your face', especially when sprayed on the neck or somewhere close to the nose. But it soon turns into a warm and smooth scent. The cypress becomes very apparent and the incense gives it a full bodied smokiness without becoming too overpowering. Most incense perfumes give me the image of a dark and smoky church, but this one makes me feel as if I'm in a small chapel somewhere in the Provence, where the hot sun warms the stone of the church and the wind blows in the air over the cypresstrees. Very beautiful! And to think I wasn't sure about this one at first. It also layers well with Encre Noire, creates an interesting scent. Especially when it's fully dried down, you get a very warm and almost creamy like vanilla, very full bodied. But I prefer Eau des Baux without the dark and dirty vetiver of Encre Noire.

I am so pleasantly surprised by this one. Eau des Baux strikes me as a fragrance which is worth a lot more than it's price tag. Extremely well made, to a level beyond what is expected from a house such as L'Occitane. It is a sweet, herbal woody scent which is reminiscent of other woody orientals (notably Tobacco Vanille). There is little not to like here, as it is warm, soft and never too loud. I find it strikes just the right balance of each note and works beautifully throughout the day. I get the cypress, a wonderfully green and also dry herbal note, mixed with tonka bean and incense. The dryness comes from the woods, incense and cypress, with a hint of herbal background, and the sweetness, which is almost honey-like, comes from the vanilla and tonka bean. I really think that, as a masculine fragrance, you cannot go wrong. It could even work on a daring lady. Eau des Baux really is phenomenal when you consider the price it costs. I think that people who like the honey, tobacco like fragrances, or woody orientals in general, will like this. Otherwise I would recommend trying this first. Another aspect which I like about L'Occitance is that they offer matching products to this, and I tried out the shower gel before trying this, which in itself has a fantastic aroma and feel. Overall, I cannot recommend this highly enough, for lovers of dry, herbal, woody orientals etc. Really nice. Lovely!
Please see my video review for one of my favourite vanilla, incense based fragrances. I cannot think of another fragrance in my collection where you get the same quality, dollar per millilitre.

Scentrack Incognito - Autumn Song A beautiful and inexpensive offering from L'Occitane. Gorgeous mix of cypress, incense, tobacco, sweet tonka and vanilla. This vanilla is one of the best I have ever tried. It really reminds me of old book smell in the library. Not similar to Tom Ford's Tobacco Vanille, but share the similar vibe. It has some ancient, natural smell. Perfect for autumn chilling with your favorite book. One can say it's niche. Great fragrance for a great price. A true gem. Rating: 7.5/10 More on Scentimentalwords

Number One: This stuff is not for men only, I will snatch it away and use it liberally. Number Two: This reminds me of a room spray, like Febreeze. There is something chalky next to very fresh notes which remind me of a white linen shirt, freshly ironed. Soft powdery notes continue to a "dry" dry down.

This is the perfume of my soul. Natural and spiritual fragrance, i feel the not too sweet vanilla and frankincense dancing together... when i was a kid my cousin from France offered me a wood box full of new pencils and rubbers. This perfume reminds me the experience of open that box and smell those woods mixed with the natural vanilla.

Eau des Baux--what a glorious and natural creation. It's woody, smoky vanilla incense with a bit of citrus to keep it fresh. The incense is exotic, not austere. If this were created by any other house, you would be paying through your nose for a scent of this quality and complexity.
Well, I simply loved this perfume. It is a woody water of smoked cypress, with a sweet background of vanilla and tonka, very warm and cozy.

In the opening it's the cardamom that is most apparent to me. There's no vanilla at all yet. After several minutes I start smelling incense with still a hint of the cardamom. On top of that, the vanilla starts to slowly show itself, until it dominates. All in all, I find it a very lovely, warm scent. Ideal for the colder months. To me it also seems a bit ... creamy.

Sometimes you come across fragrances like "the virgin to the child." This one is from the neighbor...! He was "clearing out" and was tired of some fragrances. Just at the "right time," I ran into him in the hallway. A basket with "old glass" in one hand. On top, I spotted 2 fragrance bottles - WITH CONTENT! Of course, I immediately asked him if they were also going to "the bin." And the answer: "I probably won't wear this (Boss) anymore. And this one, 'Horizon | Davidoff,' I don't like anymore either. Do you want them? I don't know if they're still good!" Well, both are still "good," and especially the "vintage Boss"! The nose along with its receptors and "hairy insides" stands tall.. Although it's an "after-shave," I don't care. It outperforms current Eau de Toilette versions by a long shot. In endurance, presence, and quality. What I get to sniff is a well-tempered, powerful Fougére gem. It starts off very spicy-fruity and gradually reveals the "heart note." Aromas from the highest league are at play here. Herbal lavender, delicate rose, fine subtle bitter honey, powdery iris, and beautiful spices. What’s the "classiest" part: The oak moss awakens early with its fairy-tale forest-like depths. Accompanied by all the "predecessor aromas" and later patchouli, smoke, noble woods, and dark "leather" (birch tar) along with vetiver-like grassy notes. Full throttle indeed! Wonderful - "old-fashioned"... And so vintage! Thank you - Mr. O. Adieu - old glass bin.. MINE!!!

Reine de Nuit, Night Queen. Such a fitting name for beautifully mysterious rose. This is the type of fragrance that paints an image. I immediately envision a woman of breathtaking allure. The kind of woman that makes you stutter and trip over your words when she makes eye contact. When she looks at you, the rest of the world is black & white while time stands still. Reine de Nuit is an erotic and intoxicating rose. She evolves elegantly, but remains soft and intimate. Musk Mallow, being a nutty, tobacco-like aroma gives the composition an exotic facet. Black currant offers the right kind of sweetness to compliment the rose. You can't have the "Nuit" without incense and patchouli. I am quite taken with this sexy ensemble of notes. She is who she is; gorgeous and unapologetic.

While Beth is getting her legs waxed, good Dean is at the car dealership, sitting at his desk and having fun with the secretary. Meanwhile, Beth is informed that her credit card is not being accepted. Beth is great, around 40, attractive, confident. She has style, is educated, and a full-blooded mother..........and apparently they are broke and her husband is cheating on her. How can she change this now? First, she and her sister, along with another friend, rob a supermarket. It seems as if Beth has never done anything else. She knows it’s wrong. But she enjoys it. Will this one heist be enough to get back on her feet financially? No, of course not! The journey continues. Beth is business-savvy and starts money laundering for the drug lord in town. She even starts something with this hot guy........... before she kicks the secretary out and takes over the car dealership. The lives of these three women are exciting, funny, and truly entertaining. A series that I binge-watched. Beth naturally wears Reine de Nuit when she goes out in the evening. Together with Portrait of a Lady, one of the most beautiful rose fragrances for me. Here, the saffron gives a slightly smoky note. And while I perceive more raspberry in POAL, here it’s the blackcurrant. Reine de Nuit is softer, cuddly, almost cozy, not as harsh as the Lady. The patchouli-amber combo makes the scent perfect.

I’ll start with a confession: I hate patchouli. Therefore, perfumes that contain even a hint of patchouli notes in the fragrance pyramid are immediately out. Now, by coincidence, I receive a sample of "Reine de nuit" with a perfume order. I dutifully research what to expect: Rose (jackpot!), patchouli (oh no!). I cautiously sniff the sample. I like the scent. So I boldly spray it on. The saffron tickles pleasantly in my nose until the rose, paired with the incense, makes its entrance. What can I say? The scent is amazing! No grandma - floral blanket, no garishly colorful teenage fantasy. Just an elegant, dark, beautiful rose. Anxiously, I wait for the patchouli in the base that will ruin this lovely fragrance experience. It takes its time, and I indulge a bit longer in the rose garden. Until the mood changes. The patchouli is here. I smell it quite clearly and... it doesn’t bother me in the slightest! On the contrary. I find it very fitting at this point! Before my brain has taken control of my relief, "Reine de nuit" is on my wish list. That was yesterday at 6:00 PM. This morning I wake up and the scent is still there, on my pillow, on my skin. The patchouli has also spent the night there, and I still don’t feel the urge to wash it off. My perfume - prey pattern has probably expanded.

Something new has emerged from Byredo. A Night Veils line has been launched, setting all parameters to extreme. First, we are dealing with an Extrait, then there are only 30 ml instead of the previous 50 or 100, and finally, the bottle is black and no longer glass, with a slight change in design. The most shocking aspect is probably the price; if you look at ALzD, for example, the eyes pop out of your head at 350 euros for 30 ml and 35 euros for a sample. Has the entire style shift and especially the new pricing been worth it? Let's sniff and check: Personally, I prefer the regular bottles; if dark, then like Oliver Peoples, but this one does seem visually a bit unbalanced when I look at the spray button. Otherwise, a black Byredo bottle is a nice contrast and a welcome change. Now let's move from the visual to the olfactory. Upon spraying, one is even briefly dazzled, as one finally gets something substantial and not something so flimsy as has been the case with Byredo recently, when recalling Flowerhead or Mojave Ghost. However, one quickly realizes that this interesting opening has been experienced several times before. You are thrown into the thick of things, and just as quickly, you notice that this coup, with its fruitiness paired with rose, has taken some cues from Agonist's Dark Saphir; the rose is so prominent that RdN can also be interpreted as a homage to Montale's Black Aoud. As quickly as a highlight disappears, so does this temperamental and promising opening in no time. What remains is minimal, and I am almost running out of words to continue the commentary, as the scent diminishes and fades away, with so little hiding behind the impressive and voluminous opening. A faint reference to Seven Veils can be discerned, but only in very light, shadowy outlines. Here we are at the "Extrait." Well, for an Extrait, this is indeed a very meager affair; longevity and even less sillage are unfortunately indicated. It is understandable that with an Extrait, the projection has been dialed back a bit, but that it barely qualifies as a skin scent and is almost not even close to the body is rather disappointing to my nose. I probably don't need to say any more about the price.

Yes, I admit: For me, the "Queen of the Night" is first and foremost a cactus flower. And what a flower it is! Its blooming period lasts only a few hours, which gives it a magical quality, and our Botanical Garden even announces this event in the newsletter and opens this greenhouse for a few hours for lovers of this nocturnal floral splendor! But luckily, this term is not patented or otherwise protected: I also think of the "Queen of the Night" from Mozart's "The Magic Flute"; I particularly love her aria "Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen," especially when sung by Diana Damrau. (By the way, Ms. Damrau mentioned in a conversation that singing this aria is akin to physical hard labor. This also explains why the actress playing this queen on stage is usually younger than Pamina, her daughter!) But back to the luxurious, profound rose scent that bears this name. I really don't belong to the "fan base" of the Byredo brand; however, I was drawn in by the name and the deep golden-brown liquid in the small vial that was sent to me. What might it reveal, what will bloom fragrantly on my rather special, always somewhat cool skin? Let's take a look: Having passed the tart fruitiness of the hedges of blackcurrant bushes and snacked on a few of the dark berries along the way, we find ourselves in a small pavilion behind dark, dense veils of incense and amber, rooting in golden-brown, rich patchouli earth and blooming into full, saffron-spiced beauty: A deep red, intensely fragrant ripe rose that exudes its rich floral aroma in velvety waves, reminiscent of mysterious warm nights in the fairy-tale Orient. This veiled "Queen of the Night" is a dark, aromatic spiced rose-patchouli beauty that I can also very well imagine as soap or even fragrant body powder. (That would be a pleasure!) Byredo's "Night Veils - Reine de Nuit" is not a "must-have," but it is a pleasant, rich rose scent experience that shows me that this brand and I do harmonize from time to time. Here it works, and I will place the vial beside my bed this evening so that I don't forget to apply it: Perhaps this "Reine de Nuit" will tell me tales from 1,001 Nights while smoke veils scented with noble roses (from Aladdin's magic lamp?) accompany me into sleep. It's worth a try!

Why do we like something and why do we not like something... I don't like floral scents, I've known that since I became interested in perfumery. Rose, jasmine, geranium, white flowers, yellow flowers - no thanks, tuberose is a downright horror word. I like some oriental rose fragrances with a mild oud note on other skins, but not on my own.

I had already written a longer text in which I explain how I first bought Oud Wood by Tom Ford, discovered this fragrance three days later, and have worn nothing else since that day. I'll spare you that. In short: I simply don't know of any other fragrance that comes close to the alluring, almost erotic effect of this Extrait.

In 2019, I had the opportunity to test the fragrance "Reine de Nuit" by Byredo and would like to reflect on my feelings and perceptions. In the first few minutes, the "Extrait de Parfum" pricks at my nose and it tingles quite a bit. It is of course possible that I was too close to my freshly sprayed skin... I can be a bit impatient sometimes!

I smelled this in the L’Occitane boutique – actually two different boutiques – before pulling the trigger. I was ready for a deep, woodsy, masculine scent, but before I opened up the box I knew I was in for something else. I smelled something light and floral - lavender. My wife had just bought lavender scent packets that help us sleep, so it wasn’t that kind of concentrated, herbal lavender, but a lighter take on it. The first outing led to a scrubbing party. I wore it on my wrists and my skin amps lavender (for trade: one slightly used set of skin; amps lavender and pepper). I was walking around in a cloud feeling like a metrosexual Frenchman. Not my thing. The second time I sprayed it on the back of my wrists and it smelled like lavender for a good fifteen minutes before the licorice showed up. The two played off each other for six to seven hours and then the scent became more soapy in its orientation and a touch more woodsy. The lavender returned to lay over the woods, for up to fourteen hours, and only after that did the accursed lavender finally exit, leaving behind faintly aromatic woods. Eau de L'Occitan pour Homme is longlasting, well-blended, and well-balanced, but just not my thing. If anyone wants a bottle, hit me up.

A rich, herbal lavender bomb given a healthy sprinkling of earthy black pepper and other spices, sitting atop a cedar base. The lavender has a sort of lemony fresh polish to it, likely the elemi in the official fragrance pyramid, well balanced by the warmth of the spices. Moderately soft projection for 2-3hr, longevity 8-10hr. Really highlights the beautiful and soothing nature of lavender, with minimal interference, in a way that few other perfumes do.

This fragrance was a blind buy for me and probably the best blind buy ever. I fell in love after the first spray as i was hit with a burst of lavender and after a while i started to get a lot of black pepper and some woody notes and maybe a bit of burnt wood or smoke. this is what i have been looking for all this time while wearing mostly generic designer fragrances. this fragrance really started my journey down the rabbit hole and will always have a special place in my heart and collection.

When reaching for a lavender scent I want a lavender fragrance, and this is that. Simplicity and linear at its best when I want to be comfortable in my own self. So many other fragrances with complex notes, in my opinion, cause a ruckus when you want lavender to be the focus of the olfactory experience. Lavender is so nuanced with many different facets; herbal, woody, floral so it needs attention. In the top, the lavender is mixed with the black pepper just so it becomes more than a room spray. The mix between the two gives the fresh spicy top some interest. In the heart, the lavender is still there along with the introduction of nutmeg and cedar. Picture some cedar wood overlaid with lavender sprigs topped with pinches of nutmeg. This is that "burnt" wood accord. If it's smokey, then that smoke is a fantasy accord conjured up by associations in the mind. The cedar rubbed here together with the lavender and nutmeg loses pepperiness in the top. Finally, after two or three hours, in the tails of the fragrance, much of the lavender has dissipated along with the woods and nutmeg. What's left is a very clean and very fuzzy musk that is interwoven with tonka bean. Overall, this is a very approachable scent. Because of the fresh spicy opening and the musky dry down this scent is very clean and appealing. One of my favorites for any time.

I tried this on a paper strip, and it smelled EXACTLY like Prada Luna Rossa! Then later on I tried it on my skin, and I got confused because the scent was a lot warmer than it was on the paper strip. It ressembled Eau des Baux (also by L'Occitane En Provence) more now. And then once it dried down, it basically became a mix of both to me. So take Eau des Baux, remove the vanilla and incense to replace it with lavender, and that's pretty much what it smells like to me. The tonka bean and woodsy notes are still discernable.

Wood, pepper and nutmeg - that what i smell. This is a comforting and relaxing scent, that smells very good and has a great price. Good projection, lasting power and sillage. Definetely worth a bottle! Updated January 2014

I just looooove this fragrance! I get a lot of lavender and the burnt wood accord (and it's glorious) with some pepper and a little musk. This is my first l'Occitane and it certainly is a great scent. It's manly, clean, and woody with a twist that keeps it apart from most lavender based fragrances however, there's a downside and it's the performance.

This is a fragrance which has been a hit for L'Occitane. It shows that they can compete with the designer brands. This is a lavender based fragrance with herbs and a hint of a spicy, woody backdrop. The cinnamon, nutmeg and black pepper really supply the spicy background, along with the woods and tonka bean. It's hard not to like this one.

First spray, instantly reminded me of another scent - then I remembered : this is a total clone of Prada Luna Rossa (and this one seemingly came out seven years earlier?), fortunately without the hideous pepper blast that is included in the Extreme version of LR.

I love this one. That's the summary. I love lavender scents. Call me weak or boring oldschool. Natural Lavender is a fragrance on its own. Unisex but leaning masculine. It's got its own top notes, base notes and dry down. In this fragrance the pepper and musky woods are there to enhance the lavender only. Very masculine take. And it succeeded.

This fragrance has such an elegant vibe, with the leather and sandalwood coming together perfectly, and just a touch of tobacco adding a smooth, slightly sweet richness. It’s balanced, sophisticated. I like to think that it has that confident, successful feel to it—I wear it for in days where I need an extra confidence boost in the office. The only downside is that it’s a little on the pricey side.

A very organic, cosmetic-like, pleasant, oily composition (at least on my skin). I do not get any dry, harsh, smokey notes, only a slightly green, earl grey tea with a drop of milk and sugar. Although not listed, there must be some sort of sandal wood in the base as it is very prominent. A creamy, almost buttery like, pleasant sandalwood seasond with some tea and a couple green leaves. Simple but very tasty. I saw someone mentioning the smell of old furniture, I get it but the sweet and woody accord is very pleasant, round and does not attack the nose as the spiky, dark, old wood and dust smell. I cannot get enough of this scent and since I got a decant, I've been using it daily. Perfect for fall, very cosy and appealing to the wearer. It's a love from the first sniff for me. The composition I would rate a 10/10 but the price is way too high. I was lucky enough to buy it for half the price but otherwise I would not get a bottle.

For me this fragrance is a 10/10 Straight up when you spray this you get reminded of santal33, but its better.. I get this beautiful leather accord that suits just perfectly with the sandalwood, A slight sweatness from the tabacco makes this a beautifull wellrounded fragrance. High quality, and altough it leans to santal33 i still find this to be very unique. Maybe it doesn't sound very sexy (it is sexy), but it reminds me of a leather briefcase. It smells manly, smart, integer, succesfull, sophisticated, very good looking, and just minding his own business. A man going its own way. casual chic. Maybe the briefcase would be from a business man sitting in the backseat of a maybach. Anyway, this fragrance is a perfect everyday signature scent. For the casual chic man who doesn't want to grab too much attention, but does stand out of the crowd by his aura.

Yes, there is leather, but it's a backgound to the sweet tobacco that the fragrance revolves around. The black tea and woods are nowhere to be found, when they are very much needed to cut through the rich sweetness. Longevity is abysmal, it lastes all of 2 hours before becoming a whisper on my skin. Given that, the price is unjustifiable. Not a bad fragrance, but entirely too sweet for me to appreciate. There are better tobacco leathers out there for much better prices.

The review is based on the previous release with the black cap. Cuir Sellier is a peak autumnal fragrance for me. It opens with a potent whiff of cashmeran and strong black tea, and settles into smooth brown leather and tobacco accord. The oakmoss in the base adds diffusion and slight salty sharpness to the overall composition, and birch notes act like a nice underpinning that holds it all together. Of all the Night Veils, this one is probably my favorite. I can detect and understand each note, but the whole composition is seamlessly blended together. It feels very cozy and warm, and develops beautifully in colder autumn and winter days. Longevity is fantastic.

Thanks to a sample, I was able to test the fragrance "Sellier". This perfume belongs to the more intense scents from Byredo, which are presented as "Extrait de Parfum", with a fairly strong fragrance concentration (approximately 15 - 30% solution of a fragrance composition dissolved in about 96% alcohol). The scent starts on my skin smoky and fresh-leathery.

Expensive, but it also smells expensive. Sellier is talked about far too rarely. Most Byredo fragrances are already great scents, but often somehow "empty"? Sellier, on the other hand, smells luxurious, memorable, and mysterious. Naturally leathery, slightly bitter, dry, and then there’s something lightly fruity.

After reading the relevant reviews, I was a bit uncertain and tried to detect the cucumber in my sample: for all concerned parties, I did not find it. Instead, I discovered a fragrance that invites with a (though unnamed) sandalwood note, lasting a long time and finding a good balance between sweet and spicy.

L'Occitane Ambre is a resinous, thick, syrupy EdT that should be labeled an EdP. I happened upon a new storefront over 60 miles from my home and with delight sampled Ambre. The entire drive home I kept smiffing my wrists and inner elbows, thankfully on the dark roads home, else truck drivers would wonder what this woman was doing. So many images were coming to mind and I could not immediately ledger them. A neighbor greeted me when I arrived home, and as we were talking, she interrupted me with, "You wear perfume like a woman should. That's how I want to smell. How do you do it?" This was well over three hours after I had sprayed myself in the store. I had already known Ambre would be a purchase, but her telling me this cinched the deal in my thoughts. One of the images this fragrance brought to mind was a very old memory of when I would open my violin case, pull out the chunk of rosin to coat my bow, and inhale deep scents encompassed in the case. No matter how small the rosin cubes would get, I'd still keep then in the corner pocket of the violin case, because there was something about the mellowness and odor of aged rosins. Ambre brings to mind old libraries to me, structures built centuries ago, the interiors of old panels of deep, dark wood. Twenty-foot high tall ceilings that are dimly lit, with stacks of books that are endless. Clean, dry, leathery smells that I would enjoy as I browsed the volumes. An airyness amongst the deep richness that I could inhale and not feel overwhelmed. Vanilla plays into Ambre salaciously, almost lasciviously. Not sweet, not cloying, but mysterious, vampy and almost boozy. An adult vanilla that mixes with the notes beautifully to create a fragrance so warm and coy it can turn heads on the right person. Some tea influences with the bergamot mix well with the leathery notes of the labdanum, while the amber creates a delightfully creamy and warm vanilla-amber. Ambre lasted well over six hours for me, and that included a hand-washing. The bottle looks vintage, quaint and I find it rather appealing. I have found out that L'Occitane has discontinued Ambre. I went back to the store and purchased a bottle (or two) for my stock. Why oh why must such delightful fragrances be discontinued? The SA remembered me and remarked that she had compared the Vanilla/Narcisse to the Ambre and noticed the Ambre had such a delicious dry down of mature vanilla also. It's still available in the catalog tho.

Here there is no horizon. Here is a small cloud. It casts its scent particles into the vast field of feelings. Fragrances from the distance of dreams. With veil-like smoke from small southern fires, with storax from the amber tree or also from amber resins from southern regions. Scents from a world full of secrets. From Provence. Ambre de L'Occitane. Brought forth from a memory, amber caresses us. Soft and warm. Powdery and flattering. Sweet and dry. Bright like brown-glimmering gold. A pinch of cinnamon, secretly hidden juniper, fine extract of tonka bean, and essence of vanilla give the ambre a velvety background. In delicate company from the floral notes of freesia, from sparks of the green world of bergamot, from caramelized cedar and smoky resins of cistus, we are on the trail to personal happiness. The scent lingers long, very softly, in sunbeams up into the darkening firmament. Or it gets lost on the cuffs of a carefully ironed shirt. In the folds of the hands. We are captivated. And let ourselves be carried by a gondola in the clouds, by a carpet from a thousand and one nights, towards the horizon of transience. Out into the distance of dreams. To Occitania with L'Ambre de L'Occitane. ** Ambre No. 6 The original "Ambre by L'Occitane" is no longer available. "Les Classiques de L'Occitane - Ambre (2016)" is the successor. With the same pyramid and almost the same, lovely message.

There are these fragrance samples that are treated with neglect. I can't explain why, but they slip down in the drawer, hide for months in your handbag, or fall behind your bathroom laundry basket. Such is the case with Ambre. Probably included as a sample by a dear perfumer, I hadn't laid eyes on this little scent for a long time. It was only when I desperately searched for a fragrance (staying overnight at a friend's, forgot my perfume, felt "naked" in the morning) that I found the small sample again. Behind the laundry basket, of course. Unaware, I boldly spray it on (on some days, any perfume is better than none) and am completely blown away. OOOOOOOMMMPHHHH What wafts under my nose is by far the most wonderful, golden, sweetest, spiciest, and most sensual amber scent in the whole wide world. Yes, I want to say it that way. Amber is dense and delicate at the same time, holding the perfect balance between delicious and "but you can't eat me." Vanilla and labdanum give the fragrance a woody depth without becoming dry and add such a narcotic touch to the composition that I could fall into a coma from happiness. I have rarely experienced such feelings of bliss with a fragrance. It's a dream that it lasts forever and brings joy to those around me through its sillage just as it does to me. However, less dreamy is the fact that it has been discontinued. Upon realizing this, my jaw dropped to the floor and my heart sank into the aforementioned fluffy socks. Talk about a blow! After extensive research (which in this case took 10 minutes), I found out that L'Occitane has re-released this fragrance. As a limited edition, listed as a "classic." My heart can rise again! And I can only conclude: those looking for the most beautiful amber scent will find a very strong candidate in Ambre. It has captured my heart in a storm, because the unexpected often happens!

I have read so much exciting information about the amber scent from L’Occitane here that it immediately made its way onto my wish list. It is said to be hard to find now, so I set out to search for it, knowing that a large drugstore in Hamburg has a L’Occitane shop. Since I had some business nearby, I kept an eye out for it. And lo and behold: there was exactly one available bottle smiling at me, and to my great joy, it even came with a balloon spray! And then for only 25 euros! I had remembered the bottle differently, but that didn’t matter. Completely happy, I carried it home and unfortunately only put on my glasses there. And what did I have to read? It was a ROOM FRAGRANCE!! How mean!! I didn’t want a room fragrance. I was incredibly annoyed with myself that my greed had driven me to snatch up that one remaining bottle without looking closely. The price should have raised my suspicions. Those who can read are clearly at an advantage. What does this teach us? Glasses and eyes open when buying perfume! However, thanks to a dear perfumer, I have now had the pleasure of trying a sample of this little water and was able to let it work on me in peace. As I look outside at how the leaves change color every day, how they swirl through the air, there is hardly a scent that fits this season better than Ambre L’Occitane. It is golden, spicy, and soft. Despite its softness, it is also powerful and radiates great warmth. Its sweetness is perfectly balanced: not too much and not too little. And its longevity leaves nothing to be desired; it stays with you for many hours. A clear autumn day, a walk through rustling leaves, and Ambre L’Occitane - it couldn’t be more perfect. I think it suits a man just as well. By the way, the room fragrance smelled almost exactly like the perfume. But 25 euros for a room fragrance was too much for me, plus I was stubborn. Fortunately, I was able to return it without any issues. I have not yet encountered the “real” Ambre. Addendum April 20, 2015 Yes, and here it is: MY PERFECT AMBER SCENT! A few weeks ago, I purchased an almost full bottle of it and was curious if I would still feel the same way about it as I did back then. The answer is: YES! In every respect! This scent fulfills everything I had wished for: It is warm, spicy, sweet, but not too much, it doesn’t overwhelm, it warms and caresses me, it is drinkable, vanillic, and melting, and it lasts very well! Therefore, the rating is now quickly going up to 100! I could scream, cry, and tear my hair out that they discontinued this beautiful scent. Alone, it won’t help. So, I’ve organized another full bunker bottle. That should last me a while, and I will enjoy every single drop!

A minimalist beautiful scent is A. While other amber fragrances may receive more recognition, A is an introspective scent, just as I like amber. I do not enjoy overly extroverted amber fragrances but rather those that present their oriental sweetness contemplatively with a subdued impact, just like here: A. No nonsense amber or amber that serves merely to showcase itself. A is almost ashamed of itself at the beginning because it has so many reserves that, if unleashed, would result in a self-promoting amber fragrance. Yet it restrains itself before the wearer and exchanges its potential penetrance for pure beauty. Here, I have found the most beautiful amber scent for myself with Alambar from LO. A is similar to Alambar, but it is not as voluminous; instead, it is slimmer. Almost leaner and somehow freed from all bombast, excess, and empty opulence that some amber fragrances have to offer. A possesses an inner purity known only to Alambar and a modesty that even Alambar does not know. The longevity may be very good, but the sillage is restrained, for what would be too much need not be. A is an endless loop within itself. It upholds the amber and repeats it, meditates on it, preaches it to itself. Caught in its own sinfulness, this amber prays for its righteous life. Without looking up, solely directed towards the wearer, it circles around amber and vanilla. There is not much more that would tempt amber and vanilla.
