It is pure unpretentious beauty, a righteous amber that walks in sweet light. It is entirely impeccable, standing back from the amber fragrances that rely on competition and the favor of the wearer. A converts the amber fragrances that indulge in vanity. It almost seems to punish conceited amber fragrances. The amber scent that worships the just God is A. L'Occitane has created a knowledgeable amber scent here, not a conceited one. A seems born rich; the first seconds after spraying reveal immense pressure that immediately gives way to the right path. A does not say much in its course; on the contrary, it refrains from moving forward. It is pure amber with vanilla in poverty, yet of its own beauty: The uselessness of wealth is justly punished for its lie here. While other amber fragrances may stand better due to their greed, hedonism, and pursuit of transience, A walks the path of reverent amber. The scent of numerous amber fragrances is conditional. What is the opposite of a conditional amber fragrance? Ambre/Amber. A is concerned with beauty and aesthetics, not with the ingratiation or lustfulness inherent in some ambers. What is the opposite of ingratiation? Ambre/Amber!

It is late May and actually the time for spring fragrances: Lily of the valley, lilacs, and other beauties up to the peonies should now accompany us with their enticing aromas through the sunny days, uplifting and cheerful. But what do we have (at least in the north)?

I actually encountered a guy who looked like George Clooney or Brad Pitt, I can't remember exactly, I couldn't focus on his face. He walked past me without even giving me a glance and sat down three benches away, facing away from me; I knew right away, he wanted something from me. I'm familiar with body language.

In the last 2 years, I have visited L'Occitane shops several times and always wondered how natural, sweet, and beautiful it smelled there. The store has always been more appealing to me than Lush, Body Shop, and the like...

This morning I was at Kieser Training, so I initially didn't apply any fragrance. But before we left, I came across the sample of Ambre / Amber that I wanted to test yesterday. I couldn't resist and sprayed just a little on my wrist.

Please follow me into the study, which we simply call "the library." Here you will see the most beautiful inlaid wooden table you can possibly imagine. Please do not touch it, as you cannot afford it anyway.

"You know what? Let's not name this one at all! Hear me out, you will love it. What we're gonna do is we add a sheet of letter stickers. So the customers can put whatever name on the label themselves. Customization, man, customization! That's the magic word. They will love it. Plus it will save us the branding efforts. Isn't it brilliant?" So, the marketing department is run by interns. Hopefully more professionalism went into the fragrance itself. Well, let's say it is not a complete failure. What I got is a violet powder carried by a fresh musk. Bits of iris enhance the violet's powderiness. Tiny green accents appear sometimes and in the end a little woodiness. Other than that, nothing really stands out. It is a quiet scent, easy-going but also unexciting. I guess they extended the "blank page" idea into the fragrance itself. Only they did not add any DIY components to spice up the scent. Now THAT would have been a concept, Byredo! Bottom line, the effort that went into this fragrance - if any - did not pay off and the whole thing lacks creativity. If the brand does not take its concepts seriously, why should we?

Unnamed was a surprise for me. I blind bought it at a nice discount. Started as a sweet summer cocktail, boozy but plush. Alcoholic vibe is very well balanced. You get a nice accord of florals staying behind. Good performance for 2 hours and mellows nicely. I liked the transition of notes. The drydown is reminiscent of top notes, there is that ambery byredo dna and some fruity accord. A funny fragrance not really competing to be anything at all. Good for a daily and simple use. I liked that casual attitude.

The scent doesn't tempt one to judge it by its name. Or does it? After all, I was just considering how I would use the attached letters to give it a worthy frame. So unfinished, that's just not acceptable. However, I realize that this isn't entirely wrong, because Unnamed really doesn't tell a story. Unnamed is reserved, clean, herbaceous, cool, and reminds me of an autumn walk in the fog. It's not the golden October that is the theme here, but rather fog that muffles sounds and gives even banal suburbs a mysterious aura. Yet, as fleeting as impressions during a foggy walk appear and disappear, so subtle and transparent Unnamed also shows itself on my skin. A relatively short, sprightly opening leads into a gentle and calm heart note. I really liked this during the test, and since I also have the Rose from No Man's Land on my wish list from Byredo, I wanted to compare. However, Unnamed scores significantly lower in that regard. Even though the base aligns with my preferences for cool and rather herbaceous notes. All in all, the scent just lacks expression for me. It conveys a feeling of gray everyday life. Nothing bad happens, nothing great happens, everything fits, but it doesn't stick in the memory. The scent fades quietly, and the longevity is satisfactory for an "everyday scent." I wouldn't push Unnamed out of my collection and might wear it from time to time, but I'm not sure if the perfume wouldn't simply fade into oblivion. The scent without a name doesn't need one. For me, Unnamed becomes "No Name," and "Rose of No Man's Land" remains on the wish list.

I spend significantly more time on field tests than on writing comments. I would have completely refrained from this one if "unnamed" did not appear in a completely false light for me here. And this already starts with the typical side effects of color psychology. Fragrances that are not colored generally perform poorly in terms of performance assessment. And this one is crystal clear like a triple-distilled gin, but it does not smell like such or juniper. My not insignificant, niche gin collection would not contradict me here. The concept of tacking cyclamen aldehyde and other floral notes onto needles is far from new. This was already done in the early 90s, for example, with "Adidas Adventure." The second major hit of the sports brand before it sank in the ocean of meaningless shower gel topics. Just in the context of the time. Fresh-focused, with all sorts of kitchen herbs. If Jérôme Epinette excels at anything from my perspective, it is juggling his standard accords, paying attention to balance, and conjuring up slim, cool, and simultaneously highly modern compositions. A bit heretically, I had "Unnamed" face off against "Oud Satin Mood" a few days ago. "Unnamed" was still noticeably present on the skin after 15 hours [!] compared to its competitor. It had significantly more projection in the first hour at temperatures around 0 degrees. The same phenomenon with "Mojave Ghost." It is also significantly underestimated here due to its performance. The actual art of dealing with this fragrance is to test and wear it in the right season to tame what is sold here as violet. Unnamed clearly prefers it cold. This not only significantly affects longevity. Such an approach also keeps the persistent violet and the indirectly associated sweetness in check and allows it to appear from the outside for hours in a balanced floral-aromatic balsamic, softly tannic green, without touching or attempting a grass and stem theme. A nice side effect is that by changing wearing habits, it is able to conjure a little light into the dreary season while everyone else seeks solace in vanilla-spice baths. I completely understand if the ladies are not thrilled with "Unnamed"; I also see at home that it does not work on women. This "unisex curse," which is spreading in the niche, constantly creates expectations from all genders that hardly any fragrance can meet. I see this one as a continuation of the woody-floral-aromatics that were highly regarded in the 90s and were transcribed into the 21st century without taking any prisoners. But clearly in the men's department. The once clearly accompanying spice has given way to a very subtle powderiness. One does not smell a listed iris note prominently, but it at least knows how to dust a little, like some geraniums I have had under my nose. This means that healthy self-confidence is not a disadvantage for us men here. A fragrance for the business everyday in fine attire. Not for a date, nor would "unnamed" want to watch a football match in the stadium. The fragrance rewards this with an innovative aromatic profile and, through the "limited edition" marketing, with just barely affordable exclusivity, provided one manages to snag one without seriously risking crossing the identical scent trail of a third party. The actual criticism of this fragrance from my perspective is that it is quite ungrateful to comment on. I would have liked to conduct a few layer experiments with "Black Citrus," but unfortunately, I ran out of the test material of the latter. A hint of birch tar would probably position the fragrance more clearly. So it remains a completely nameless one for most.

Just a few examples of names that could have been chosen for this fragrance - instead of leaving it nameless. The 'suggestions' are of course not entirely randomly selected - they are the names of the nine Valkyries from Richard Wagner's introductory opera of the same name in his legendary Ring of the Nibelung. Essentially, Wagner is to blame. It is thanks to him and his portrayal of the Valkyries through singers who simply require a certain resonance body to deliver the demanded singing appropriately, that the term 'Valkyrie' today mostly evokes the image of a thunderous war woman of imposing stature, wearing a horned helmet and an iron breastplate. The use of the 'Ride of the Valkyries' in the film 'Apocalypse Now' - the piece accompanies the attack on a Vietnamese village by US Army helicopters - did the rest. In fact, the Valkyrie in her tradition from Norse mythology is not like that. Valkyries were the beautiful, female spirit beings who selected the honorably fallen - the so-called 'Einherjar' - on the battlefield and guided them to Valhalla, Odin's legendary hall of fame located in Asgard, which has five hundred and forty gates - each wide enough for eight hundred warriors to pass through side by side. The northern lights were interpreted as the reflection of moonlight on the armors and shields of those Einherjar who were led home by the Valkyries to Odin's hall. Their names are also different from Wagner's; the thirteen preserved in the Old Icelandic Edda are: Geirölul, Göll, Herfjötur, Hildr, Hlökk, Hrist, Mist, Radgrídr, Randgrídr, Reginleifr, Skeggjöld, Skögull, and Thrúdr - Byredo could have chosen any of these names. Unnamed captures the essence of those Nordic mythical Valkyries - exalted, shimmering, translucent shieldmaidens with winged helmets who carry the honorably fallen from the battlefield homeward - ethereal, cool, and aloof on one hand - and protective, warm, and nurturing on the other. With gin (therefore: juniper berry) and violet (or its root), Jérôme Epinette selects two of the most reliable accords for coolness and distance, achieving a coldly glowing powderiness reminiscent of northern lights on jagged armors. Yet beyond that, Unnamed's burst of green herbaceousness speaks of comfort and healing and of homecoming - so delicate, fine, and quiet - and is so much more the gentle smile of the Valkyrie who gathers the fallen from the battlefield than that impressive vocal power that Wagner gives to his nine armored thunder women. Conclusion: a calm fragrance with a fascinating journey from cool to moderately warm. Very restrained and quiet - and therefore probably not one that will be remembered.

Hmmmm. This scent makes me doubt my "sniffing skills." Pink pepper in the opening - Yes. 100%. Typical Byredo. But I smell little violet?! And I love violet! All I smell after about 30 minutes is a beautiful, adult sweetness with pepper. It smells to me like fruit tea. Berry fruit tea with violet. Where does this sweetness come from?! Very nice (!

I received Byredo Unnamed as a bonus with a purchase at the Souk. Unnamed was one of those fragrances that I never really took a closer look at. The Byredo brand has never had anything truly interesting for me; there was always something missing to ultimately persuade me to make a purchase. Unfortunately, Unnamed continues this tradition.

Be like the violet in the moss, modestly humble and pure….. the violet stands in the forest among magnificent large old trees, nestled on soft moss, pine needles that the north wind sometimes blows over give off their fragrant aroma. A very beautiful and calming scent, a bit harmonious-mental.

bought blindly I wanted to see what this collection had in store, too little known and too little publicized. my test today concerns courageous rose, only 2 ingredients which suggest a simplicity and banality in the world of perfumery but the real perception of this perfume will be quite different. the first seconds and the opening remind me a lot of Arabian Rose from Armani Privé, then quickly a sparkling side reminiscent of champagne is added to this smell and subsequently a sweet side reminiscent of cola and slightly tonka cola from Mancera. this sweet side softens the rose and subsequently the smell of oud, always reminiscent of this combo on Arabian rose. the trail is good, the perfume has passed through my sleeve to perfume my forearm. the hold is good, a good 8 hours despite washing my forearm 3 times with water during my day. Rose perfumes are omnipresent on the perfume market, but this perfume clearly stands out for its originality, the sparkling side gives it elegance, a luxury champagne side. an ideal perfume in the evening or otherwise for winter and autumn congratulations to boss for this work even if I have the impression that there are other ingredients not indicated in this perfume which creates this surprise.

I'm a huge fan of the TV series, The L Word, so when I saw one of my favourite characters, Shane, pull a bottle of this out of her bathroom cabinet, I just knew I had to try it. L'Occitane's Verveine is the essential Summer scent for a country girl like myself. I love the scent of nature, particularly that of a citrus orchard. This fragrance comes very close to re-creating that smell. This is a sparkling and refreshing interpretation of a lemon tree, complete with the leaves and fruit. It is olfactory heaven to my nose. I wish all lemon inspired fragrances smelt like this. Far too many of them resemble the scent of detergent rather than the scent of the natural, raw citrus. It's a really easy scent to wear due to its simplistic composition. Both men and women could wear this, or even share a bottle between them and fully enjoy its versatility. I can't believe I've left it this late to try it. L'Occitane Verveine should have come into my life sooner. At times, it's so fresh, lively and sweet that it reminds me of a chilled glass of lemonade. Seeing that I'm going into Summer now, there's nothing else I'd rather smell. It's so perfect, and this is coming from a girl that usually hates citrus scents. The sillage may be soft, but the longevity is superb. It clings even better to fabric. To increase the projection, I would recommend layering Verveine with the matching lotion, shower gel and soap. I'm so glad this is one of L'Occitane's best sellers. Original review written: November 2012.
crushed lemon leaves, sweet and a little bit bitter, zesty, uplifting, fresh, perfect for hot summer days. Much sweeter than their green tea. Good trail and lasts about 4 hours on me.

Quite simply put, this is the most natural smelling, non-synthetic, invigorating and green leafy verbena in a bottle. As I smell this I am reminded of the green leafy tips of lemon, oranges, and citrus zests, all slightly shaken by the swift breeze, on a spring morning in a lush, green garden. It has a tart, sour grapefruit like wince inducing opening reminiscent of lemon sorbets that morphs beautifully and seamlessly into a sweet, creamy and fruity textured verbena. Its longevity has much to be expected from and for a citrus heavy fragrance is too standard,(relatively better than the original 4711 Eau De Cologne), on my skin I don't get much beyond 4 hours mark, which is the only major letdown especially given that is not as affordable as 4711. However if longevity is not your concern you are left with one of the most beautiful and natural renditions of verbena, that is at once verdant, lush, leafy and momentarily potent. Add a little zesty zing to your stride when you wake up in the spring morning to go out for a walk in the lush green fields. Verveine is a very easy fragrance to fall in love with, and as the opening dissipates you are still left with a sweet, creamy and blissfully fruity version of the Provencal fields with a little spiciness of geranium. Overall Rating: 8 /10

A very strong lemon scent that stays just on the right side of kitchen cleaner. I wouldn't wear it on its own, personally, but it's great for layering with woodsy, aromatic, or other citrusy scents. I particularly enjoy layering it with Maison Louis Marie Bousval; the two blend to create a very fresh spring scent, citrusy but with additional woodsy and aromatic notes that are absent from Verveine on its own. If you really, really like lemon, you'll probably like this one more than I do. Regardless, it's a good layering fragrance for fans of citrus.

Heat. Bright, shimmering heat. The scorching breath of the Sahara wafts through the streets, coalescing in the dried brick walls, flowing thickly in the sparse shade of the trees. No escape. From the white-hot sky, a merciless sun burns down. This heat is suffocating, making breathing a torment. The air you gasp for tastes of exhaust fumes and is nothing but a thick, viscous mush. To breathe ... oh, if only one could breathe ... If there were just a little wind, a little cooling. If only one could change the sweat-soaked shirt ... right now ... Water. Cool water, fresh and pure, that makes you forget the heat, that would let us breathe easy ... You want to jump in and feel how it envelops us, embraces us, saves us. From the scorching embrace of the midsummer day. That exhausts us, drains us, dries us out like the faded brick walls of the city that enclose us, close in on us, want to suffocate us. We need freshness, coolness, we need water, we need peace. Immediately. The salvation lies in a rather unremarkable bottle. Two, three, or even five sprays, and we finally manage to breathe again, to exhale. Bitter grapefruit alongside light, spicy cedar, finely embedded in green, extremely fresh, and very natural lemons, cools and calms, dispelling the oppression. It’s as if you have finally reached the shade of great, old trees, under which a crystal-clear stream provides coolness. This scent is green, initially even forest green and almost dark, but then bright and citrusy, without being sweet. Like a surge of ice-cold water, pure, clear ... distinctly perceptible, without ever pushing itself to the forefront. Reserved, yet very self-assured, it stands up to the summer heat. It needs the heat, the white-hot sun, to unfold. To show its bright, simple beauty, its strict linearity, its grand, refreshing effect. It’s as if you are building around yourself a subtly fragrant, long-lasting, and extremely stylish shield.

L'Occitane has been one of my favorite companions in the shower as well as in skin and hand care for many years. Additionally, the wonderfully packaged products in various combinations are always a great gift idea. But now, let's talk about this fragrance. The Verveine fragrance line is one of the best mood lifters for summer for me.

Whenever I find myself in a L'Occitane store, I like to shop there - the products may not be cheap, but they look beautiful, all smell good, and are also perfect for gifting... So what prompted me to buy a set of "Verveine," including shower gel, fragrance sachet, hand cream, and a 100ml bottle on a cold, dreary winter day before Christmas?

Without the lovely Punx13, I would have never or probably never tested this. I'm not a fan of lemons. I just grimace and Brrr. Every cleaning product advertises with "citrus freshness" Even the glasses cleaning cloths in my parents' bathroom. And who wants to smell like a freshly washed plate or a cleaned toilet?

Unfortunately, I don't have a trained nose for distinguishing fragrance notes. Therefore, I mainly notice the lemon and the grapefruit. I can also sense a hint of cedar. However, the geranium is hiding from me. But that's okay. The composition of the other fragrance notes is so delicious that one is tempted to drink the stuff.

A rare squeaky-clean amber. An aldebrox? An ambrohyde? Fresh laundry, coconut water, and a fuzzy, dulcet musk. The coconut is raw, freshly cracked. Nothing reminiscent of sunscreen or body butter, and unfortunately only lasts the opening hour. However, its sparkly, spun-sugar heart hit 6+ hours on skin. Recommend testing on different substrates, as I found it a bit of a personality splitter between skin (hella ambroxy), paper (hella aldehydey), and fabric (just right). Overall, smells remarkably akin to the Bal d’Afrique Absolu, in that same sweet-n'-clean family. A great option for those who might have found Blanche too sterile or Baccarat too sticky. Mental Snapshot: A celestial laundromat. Dirty clothes go in the machine, white cashmere and golden chiffon comes out. One of the spin cycles is called “candyfloss.” You are pleased to find the iridescent bubbles drifting from your wash are made of helium and glass candy. tl;dr: Laundromat Rouge 540

I'm so surprised by some of the reviews on this one. Firstly, the performance is outstanding for me--easily 10 hours with a gorgeous sillage that's still subtle. Secondly, I don't know how people are getting laundry, pineapple, or whatever else. This is, to me, a linear and gorgeous fresh coconut--not sunscreeny or sickly-sweet, but airy and softly sweet. If I put my nose to my skin, the scent is very aldehydic and perfumes--the magic is in the scent bubble, which remains beautifully sot and sweet and airy all day long. I have trouble detecting any individual notes besides the coconut water, though it does have that sparkling character many aldehydic scents have. I would be thrilled if this one remains just popular enough to not be discontinued, but not as popular as Byredo's big names. It feels tailor-made for me, and I've been wearing it almost every day for the last two months. If it became omnipresent I would be a tiny bit annoyed (but I wouldn't stop wearing it!)

This is a very interesting fragrance from Byredo and also amazing. First whiffs smells like a milky sophisticated pina colada that is sweet with a hint of pineapple, even though it’s not in the fragrance notes. It’s creamy and sweet with the coconut water, I usually detest coconut perfumes because they give this sunscreen scent but not this one. Has to be the first coconut perfume that I enjoy. I feel like this is what Blanche Bette should have been and how I imagined it would smell like. I love this, great for warmer months, but would be interested in wearing it in cooler temperatures too as it’s so cosy. Give it time to develop and test it, it’s truly lovely!

-You're stuck in Orlando for a week with your mom and little sister. That’s what summer vacation looks like when you're from the Midwest. The hotel lobby greets you with a fountain straight out of the movie Splash. You say it outloud. No one laughs. Upstairs, the room is a humid time capsule. Tropical leaf bedspreads, pink wallpaper peeling like sunburnt skin. A flickering nightstand lamp struggles to stay alive. It smells like coconut air freshener and mildew. The AC groans in the corner, condensation dripping onto the carpet, blooming dark stains like bruises. Your mom’s on the phone with the front desk, asking for a cot. Your sister whines from the bed. Outside the window, pale kids from other Midwestern towns cannonball into the pool below. “Get ready,” Mom says. “Dinner’s a big surprise!” You groan. All you want is to stay in the room, let the AC freeze your soul, and watch some half-funny sitcom reruns. Instead, you climb into the sticky rental car, thighs fusing to the seat. The surprise reveals itself in the form of a fake volcano, a waterfall trying its best, and a neon plastic frog glaring down like it knows you hate fun. Rainforest Café. Your mom claps. Your sister gasps. The frog keeps staring. You briefly wonder if the volcano is hot enough to jump into.-

I was able to get a sample of this (thanks, Michael at Nordstroms!) and actually tried it for the days I'd be visiting family in hospital as I wanted something that would kind of match and override some of the more astringent smells there. It worked! As for an everyday fragrance for me, there was just too much coconut for my liking. However, if you are looking for something very bright and breezy, sweet and sultry, this is your fragrance. It has a very similar base to other Byredo fragrances, kind of a warm comforting scent.

To my nose, it smells like a watered down, western styled, Purpose 50 or within that ballpark. The opening is much better than the dry down. The opening is a pearl clutcher. Ultimately, i like it. If you smell hard you can discern the coconut, but it’s really well done. They paired it well with the base notes and aldehydes.

I find the opening of this to be really challenging for me. It reminded me of hot milk by hilde soliani but less sweet and a little less weird. But definitely still a bit weird. Like sweet milky peppery wood with a hint of something fresh and tropical. It’s a blend that feels unnatural to me.
This is one of those scents that changes dramatically on my skin. Initially, I get a bubbly bright fruity sweet scent - it's almost more something I'd expect in a body spray than from Byredo.

Cute, nice scent, but not 200+ dollars cute. I think it has an interesting mix of notes and it's nicely executed, but Im not convinced by it. Alto Astral smells like a milky coconut with very light and faint sweet resinous touches. It also has a bit of a synthetic and molecular woody aspect to it that I think makes it interesting (dont forget the poor Byredo performance).

Could it be? Have I finally found the perfect unisex gourmand? I was told that the scent feels like a summer dream - captured in a bottle. Cooling, milky coconut water meets the transparency and clarity of aldehydes. Ambroxan, cashmere wood, and sandalwood provide this warm creaminess, so enveloping and almost skin-like.

I must sincerely apologize for the above monstrosity of a word, but I cannot describe the scent that flows from the delicately ornate bottle any other way. The Provençal creation is indeed like a mobile with cherries made of semi-transparent silk paper, floating against the backdrop of a perfectly baby blue sky. Why so convoluted? Why not just say, "Smells like delicate cherry blossoms"? Well, because I am primarily writing for those who (like me) have not stored anything noteworthy under "cherry blossoms" in their scent memory. Sure, most of us have seen cherry blossoms live and in color somewhere at some point, but a scent memory? Hence the silk paper cherry mobile association. A wonderful scent. Somewhat like cherries, but less fruity. Somewhat like flowers, but not floral. Delicate, transparent, fragile, yet not inconspicuous. Despite all its delicacy, strangely sensual. Mysterious. Only seemingly innocent. Slightly dry, but not powdery-dry. Paper-dry. Rice-dry. Unsweet? Hard to say. Sour? Hard to say. Just when you think, "Oh how pleasant, but nothing more," you’ve already lied to yourself. One tends to underestimate this cherry blossom too easily. At least that was the case for me. I got myself a rather large bottle: mainly because of the (well?) bottle. Strangely enough, I ended up reaching for this scent so often that the cute little bottle was empty within a few weeks. Such a thing has happened to me very rarely with a perfume. Not at all since Parfumo.

Think of that one spark. In your darkest hour. Think of the last straw you clung to. When you thought you had lost everything. Think of your loneliest hour. When right then the spring of friendship touched your soul. Full of bloom. Full of banalities. Full of mercy. You know, it’s not just the cherry tree in spring that stands for the awakening of life. For the rebirth of goodness in this incomprehensible uncertain world. For the tear of happiness that is born like a dewdrop from your sadness. For that deep trust that only the freshness of unconditional friendship and the miracle of spring reward in summer with its fruits. Sometimes that spark fades too quickly. Sometimes too fleeting. But sometimes, yes sometimes it is real. ------------ Addendum to the fragrance: A statement for this fragrance beauty would have been too little to do justice to the depth of this unbearable lightness of being. Of course, the reformulations have become so weak in longevity that one would almost skip the test. However, I have repeatedly brought this fragrance up to someone and must admit that sometimes you can indeed smell beauty. Fresh through and through. I think it’s the lily of the valley that, when sniffed, turns on the light with its loud brightness (a bit like Reflection Man by Amouage, which also brightens every room, although the fragrance is definitely wearable for everyone). The freesia should provide the cleanliness. Although there is a newer flanker of this fragrance that is even a bit cleaner. All in all, though, a fragrance that makes you happy in every way when worn! Epilogue “Be proud. You survived the days you thought you would not.” - Power of Thoughts -

Pharmacies are probably the only places where you don’t have to worry about how you look when you want to test fragrances :-) Sanis' comment below made me very curious about this scent. So today, in my Cindy from Marzahn outfit along with a thick scarf and a stubborn cold in tow, I waddled into the nearest pharmacy where L'Occitane fragrances are often sold. Cherry Blossom is indeed a very beautiful scent with a few caveats. Anyone who likes this fragrance direction will not be disappointed. Why doesn’t it hit my taste perfectly? Well, floral-fruity scents are a broad field. Since the cherry blossom is clearly supposed to dominate here, it is indeed a summery, fruity fragrance. However, the cherry blossom comes across as a bit overpowering to me. It smells like a very noble cherry soda mixed with rose aromas. The scent feels fine and cute. But for this cuteness, I already feel too old. In other words: it is a girlish fragrance, and somehow the wearer should fit that description. I imagine her to be girlish but feminine, not very tall or strong, and perhaps a bit cheeky, somewhere between 10-30 years old. Ideally, I picture a Japanese schoolgirl. This scent would fit her 100%. But not me, as I am quite tall and dark and already come across as much too grown-up and not so innocent-flirty as this fragrance. It doesn’t smell exactly like fresh cherries, because for that the scent would need to be darker (I come from a well-known cherry-growing region and have practically consumed cherries with my mother’s milk). The cherry here is very fresh and light. That can only come from the combination with floral notes like rose. However, I find the dry down of the fragrance much more beautiful, as the soda-like quality fades a bit, and then it smells a little creamy with cherry flavor. So anyone who loves cherry scents will have a lot of joy with this one. Unfortunately, I am not a fan of fruity scents, and therefore, regarding the rating, I am completely undecided somewhere between 70-80%. The intensity and longevity are unfortunately not as overwhelming as, for example, with Eaux de Baux, but I think that wouldn’t be the intention behind this cute fragrance.

If you don't like cherries, you can stop reading now. Everyone else should definitely take this truly great fragrance with an incredible price-performance ratio to heart. L’Occitane uses only top-quality natural ingredients, and the 100ml costs less than €45. But enough with the mundane economics. When you eat cherries for the first time in summer - real cherries, not frozen or from a jar - they smell like the first fifteen minutes of this Eau de Toilette. A juicy, fruity cherry scent that brings happiness - and would be somewhat boring like all the fruit perfumes if it lasted the whole time. But it doesn't. A hint of it may linger, but this is about cherry blossoms, not the fruit. It is a spring fragrance, not a summer scent. The cherry blooms when it's still cold, in March/April, and gives a hint of sunshine and blue skies. Fleurs de Cerisier becomes floral now, but without powderiness, without creamy opulence. It smells clean and almost innocent of cherry, of blossoms, of cool clear air ... ... and wood. Rosewood, the notes say, but that should be decided by finer noses than mine. An ambery warmth and a not-so-innocent musk accent blend into the fragrance. The perfume now stays close to the skin. But whoever comes so close to you will love it.

At my grandparents' house, there is a large cherry tree in the back garden by the ditch. Under the tree, there is a bench from which you can look out over a horse pasture and a large biotope area. Fleur de Cerisier evokes beautiful memories for me, of the time when my grandma and I would sit under that cherry tree playing Mau Mau or simply watching the horses grazing on the other side of the ditch. It was such a wonderful and carefree time! This scent smells exactly like the pink cherry blossoms that grow there. There is nothing artificial or synthetic about it. Just a sea of blossoms and lightness. A little later, a delicate breeze carries the scent of the branches over, giving it a light woody base. But it does not come across as dry at all, rather like the fresh, juicy branches that are still very young. A fine, delicate spring fragrance that awakens memories in me is not quite my usual preference, but I gladly let myself be transported back to old times.

As poetic as Burberry London is for autumn, Cherry Blossom is perfect for spring. I have had it since last February and have enjoyed wearing it on typical spring days or on days when I long for spring. Imagine a warm spring day: the trees are getting their first buds, the early bloomers have fought their way through the ground, which is still quite muddy from the melted snow.

Yesterday I bought 10 ml of cherry blossom because the box looked so delicate and bright and simply so inviting :-). So no testing beforehand or anything. Well. I applied it right away and indeed, in the opening, I got the promised delicate floral freshness. Wow! That never happens to me. But unfortunately, that was also the best part of the whole fragrance.

As a native Frenchwoman, I have been surrounded by L'Occitane products for what feels like my entire childhood. Various sets, creams, oils, and more are a staple for almost every French woman and are passed down extensively from grandmother to mother, to aunt, to cousin, to daughter, and then to the next generation.

Naaaa, who let themselves be seduced by the beautiful description and the great bottle and of course ordered the large bottle blindly? ? I live in a very rural area and have the scent of cherry blossoms firmly in my mind. And I believe that can sometimes be a problem for me. My expectations are too set, and I can be a bit disappointed when the scent doesn’t match exactly.

Ah yes, L'Occitane and my blind buys. It has always been worth it for me. Because especially with this one (and in times when I didn't care about H/S), I find myself immediately in the middle of spring as soon as I spray it on. That's why I like to spray it even in February when I'm finally wishing the cold away and bringing in the sun.

Rating: 9/10 Suddenly on my wish list, I’m hopelessly in love with Lil Fleur. The sample I received is almost gone. At first I thought it had the strangest scent, like a plastic, but after dry-down I was smitten. At first it has an almost synthetic odor with vanilla and leather prominent, but it disappears and leaves a truly unusual rose scent. My husband said I smell delicious, which is always a great thing! Top notes: cassis, tangerine Heart: Damask rose leather Base: woody, vanilla Sillage: 4 feet Longevity: 7 hours

...but LIL FLEUR has impressed me. I can't understand the less favorable reviews. This perfume is completely different from the well-known and even lesser-known scents. I would call this work an "interesting combination" of tasteful notes. Unfortunately, it comes across as a bit artificial, which is why it gets "only" 7 points. But precisely because this scent doesn't appeal to everyone, it makes it even more interesting to me. Black currant, saffron, and mandarin merge into a clashing triad, loud and somewhat biting. I think the fragrance needs to harmonize with the skin, and it does for me! :-) A thought that came to me immediately upon the first sniff: what does this smell like... I find it hard to categorize, as the notes - as mentioned - blend together. What synonyms fit? Well... clashing, metallic but still soft and gentle, citrusy, confident, and simply different. Everything about this scent is right! I'm excited about my new perfume.

Why does the scent score so poorly here? Pungent? No. Smelling like plastic? Not at all. Artificial, sweet rose? Definitely! But that has worked for many with Delina as well. And here, the saffron and leather save you from the typical Delina nausea. I enter a candy store and am enveloped by a bubble of pink Hubba Bubba. On the floor, a sea of red rose petals. Saffron threads hang like tinsel from the ceiling. In front of me appears a candy dish filled with red currant gummy candies. I reach for it. Sweetness and acidity in perfect harmony. I close my eyes and begin to float. Wrapped in a pleasant sweetness that carries me. The bubble bursts, but I don't fall far… As I land on soft, pink cotton candy, I am brought back to reality: I am 33 and feel too old for this scent. It’s just too playful. And in the end, they are indeed there: Minimal plastic vibes.
First spray on my skin: plastic! - in its raw form... petroleum... sharp, biting, bituminous.... Alright, let's wait... Nothing happens, except that the plastic becomes slightly sweeter...

…for my nose or on my skin. I sprayed this scent on a strip and thought: “mmmm fruity…” and then immediately sprayed two spritzes on my forearm… Then I ran a few errands and time and again, I was hit by an extremely biting, piercing, and slightly animalistic smell. “Weird, it was interesting on the strip…” It became somewhat uncomfortable for me when I walked closely past people who might smell me…. I almost wanted to apologize for this stinking, penetrating cloud that I was dragging behind me… The worst scenario one can imagine with a fragrance! And on top of that, the scent - unlike others from Byredo - has EXTREMELY good longevity! When I got home, I naturally wanted to wash it off right away - think again! No chance… it stayed on my skin until the next morning! Sounds harsh: but for me, it’s a mystery how anyone can like this “scent”…:( sorry…

Why do the fragrances that I don't particularly like always last so damn well? Lil Fleur sounded like a perfect match for me according to the fragrance notes. When I tested it, I was quite taken with it. Unfortunately, I made the mistake of only spraying it on a test strip and not on my skin.

Full-on synthetic. So far, I have tested 5 fragrances from Byredo and none of them really appealed to me. Lil Fleur came as a free gift with a perfume order. I sprayed it on and I could almost run away from what I smell in the air. On my skin, it doesn't smell any better. It smells like a chemical bomb to me; I can't perceive anything that smells natural at all.

A few years have passed, but this autumn I decided to resume my encyclopedic journey regarding those fragrances that have tea notes more or less perceptible in their spectrum. Not a few of those I have acquired over the years I have not yet been able to test in detail, so I'm diving back in now :-) A fragrance that supposedly belongs to this category of "once known/cult/legendary tea scents" (the most well-known representative: "Gucci Pour Homme II") is the limited and long-gone "Edition IV" from "Boss in Motion". I admit: I bought this fragrance not only because of its cult status but mainly because of what I think is a pretty cool bottle in shimmering chrome with dark steel blue accents ;-) However, since the "Ur-Boss" (now called "Number One"), none of the Boss fragrances have really convinced me, and unfortunately, this one fits seamlessly into that list. The basic architecture, with an initial build of dark citrus-orange notes, contrasted by dark spicy shimmering cardamom and deepened by a spreading black tea note in between and around it, is a very appealing constellation. This is well-balanced and interestingly conceived, but unfortunately implemented in a brand-typical manner in its synthetic weak watery-citrusy overall appearance. In my perception, the fragrance retreats very quickly; alongside citrus hints and a touch of tea, soon only a sadly rather indefinable arbitrary, yet in its distinctly orange packaging still beautiful and appealing sandy-cedar note with underlying patchouli tones remains. For fans of the "Boss In Motion" line, it is certainly interesting, but as a powerful tea fragrance or even cult, it is certainly not suitable.

"Boss in Motion Edition IV" comes to my nose like the classic "Boss in Motion" with a touch of "HUGO". Very pleasant, not too heavy, fits every outfit and every situation. It was a "bycatch" during a bargain purchase. A scent I no longer want to miss. If you don't like "In Motion" and "Hugo": DO NOT READ FURTHER :-) I find both "In Motion" for its sportiness and "HUGO" for its casual "suit compatibility" great. Therefore, "Boss in Motion Edition IV" forms a great symbiosis for me.

An oven. The world must have turned into an oven, one with convection and the grill switched on. No idea what the Holy Spirit was thinking - it was too hot for me to understand the connection, my brain was working slower than the rest of my sluggish body. Had it ever been this hot at Pentecost? I didn’t know, my memory had switched off, ultimately it didn’t matter - it was hot, very hot, way too hot, even for midsummer it would have been remarkably hot, even more so for this year’s Pentecost. I was no longer dreaming of days by the pool, I was dreaming of a cozy freezer, where I could stay until Peter or whoever had baked enough. Eventually, this heat had to pass, this scorching, burning, life-energy-sucking Sahara heat that had scorched the yesterday bright green lawn and finished off the last snail-protected pea seedlings. Eventually, eventually - please... There isn’t much that helps me function on days like these. Coffee, strong and sweet and hot with spoonfuls of crema. Strawberries straight from the field, scalp massages from my loved one, and scents that are no longer just scents, but lifesavers. Their freshness hisses when it touches the skin, clear and pure like mountain lakes, like glaciers, cool and sun-soaked like plump yellow fruit bombs, smooth and firm in my hand, anticipating the sharp cut. Scents like this. Bitter and herbaceous yet delicately sweet, gathering water in my mouth, tickling, expanding the nose, the lungs, green and yellow and cool and gentle. Nothing stings, nothing bites, no bath and no kitchen - peels and zests, leaf and wood, eyes closed, their image on the retina, plastic, authentic, within reach. For a moment, for a breath - which fades away far too quickly.

Hmm… I have often written here that my cat doesn't really like citrus fruits. He always makes a face, and the interesting thing is that he can even remember what doesn't smell pleasant to him. Well, after a while, he forgets it again, but some things stay in his cuddly little head for a few days. These include mandarins, disinfectant spray, Duplo foil (it's good that he doesn't like that, since cats shouldn't eat chocolate anyway, not at all!) or lemons. The mandarins are usually a victim of my cat, as the poor round citrus fruits like to be rolled around. Well, let's say they used to be, since the fruits are now in a larger and deeper bowl and he can't get them out anymore,… and using his claw to help is not an option, because apparently, you only make the mistake of injuring a mandarin with your claw and then having the citrus juice seep out of the fruit once! :D The lemons, on the other hand, the main component of this fragrance here, are fortunately in the kitchen, where he can't reach them, even though the kitchen is one of his favorite places since it's full of food :D Anyway, despite the freezing cold, I am testing a summer fragrance today in the warm apartment, as the colder days will surely come to an end eventually! And this fragrance is one to remember! Especially if, like me, you find citrus perfumes very refreshing on hot days. The scent: The scent starts off citrusy and slightly sweet. I smell lemons that have a very natural scent and then gradually transition into lemon verbena. Then there’s the grapefruit, another fruit that my cat doesn't like at all :D The grapefruit also smells citrusy sour, but with a slight sweet touch, like when you dip this fruit in sugar if it seems a bit too bitter while eating. In any case, all the citrus notes smell very good and are very refreshing. A little later, the scent remains citrusy-fresh but also slightly warm sweet with woody notes. It doesn't change much more than that, but it doesn't need to, as this simplicity comes across as both refreshing and very pleasant. The sillage and longevity: The projection is citrusy low and will hardly be noticeable to anyone standing far away. The longevity is as short as a summer breeze. Well, maybe not quite that short, but after two or three hours, you might want to reapply if you want to continue enjoying the full scent experience! *The bottle: The bottle is rectangular and tall. The upper part is rounded like a dome. On one side of the glass, there is an engraving of a lemon verbena leaf and on the other side, a lemon fruit, which looks great. On the sides of the bottle, you can see (also engraved into the glass) the name of the fragrance or the brand. The cap is a simple, cylindrical, and transparent plastic cap that just covers the spray head. A very beautiful bottle. Ah, Verveine Agrumes is a wonderful fragrance. It is perfect for refreshing (and of course smelling good) on really hot days. Even more so for those who prefer simpler scents with a straightforward scent progression, meaning fragrances that don't consist of 1000 notes and have a complex and diverse scent journey. Since the scent is not too strong and long-lasting, it is only suitable for short-term use, whether during the day or in the evening on warm days, it doesn't matter; you just have to be prepared to possibly reapply it. It costs just under 50 euros (for 100 mL), which makes it worth considering getting the fragrance. If it were cheaper, I would even recommend it without reservation. Anyway: Anyone who still doesn't know what they could wear in summer should definitely check this one out! There may be many citrus fragrances that refresh well, but this one also belongs to the scents that should smell very nice and pleasant for most… Well, probably not for the cat, who is only concerned about whether he should have a little snack before dinner or rather afterwards… and we all know that the little cuddly fat sack probably has a snack both before and after dinner… *sigh* I should have named the little creature Garfield! :D

Is it green? Of course it is green! That’s already thanks to the verbena. Oh my love! Do you remember the 5th Element and Chris Tucker’s character? “Was I green? No? It must just be... green...!” Everyone was at his feet, and he almost overshadowed Bruce Willis, who was just there to get it on with the 5th Element. Well, you won’t save the world with citruses, and you don’t have to grow your hair like Chris Tucker or squeeze yourself into a green catsuit. It doesn’t suit most of us anyway. The fragrance does! Alright, Verveine is not a perfume for a grand entrance, for an extravagant gown, or for the opera. But who even goes there nowadays? If so, there are perfumes from Caron or the good ones from Dior... Also quite a few niche brands. But with those, you might want to stick a price tag around your neck next to the jewelry. Back to green, nature, and the mentioned fragrance. Somehow casual, citrusy, clean! You feel transported to places with forests and meadows. Where the moon is pushed up at night and when darkness falls, the sidewalks are rolled up. Well-scrubbed people with a thirst for adventure. Morning 5:00 AM! After the shower, it’s time to go. Wrapped in a clean scent that has no sweetness whipped into it. Polo with lemons, grapefruits under the cedar grove. Well, either I’m flying to Fhloston Paradise tomorrow or I’m going to vote, and then I’m definitely for the Mondoshawan.

Besides the obligatory morning coffee, this little potion works wonders to start the day awake and in a good mood. The very authentic zesty-sharp lemon note (in my opinion like freshly grated lemon peel) is invigorating and remains present and natural throughout the entire scent development. I don't really pick out grapefruit strongly, but it seems to harmoniously blend into the fragrance experience. What I particularly like is that these citrus aromas smell natural, not overly softened or sweetened like in some other fragrances, but simply authentic. After about a quarter of an hour, a slightly herbal note emerges on the skin, which does not stand out but integrates pleasantly. After an hour, a lovely aromatic cedar note comes into play. The citrus aromas are still present, not as strong anymore, but they round off the cedar base. Overall, a wonderfully natural unsweetened citrus scent with a woody base, which subjectively has similar wake-up properties as a fresh morning coffee!

A big thank you to Palonera, from whom I received the sample, should be mentioned at the beginning. This much too unknown fragrance has truly refreshed me, and I want to reveal why: The opening sizzles and cools, just as one would expect from a scent of this kind. The listed lemon and grapefruit may be somewhat misleading, as the acidity is really kept in check. The freshness is unusually pretty and rounded, and is less of the overpowering, intensely bitter variety. Thus, every additional spray is not too much. Its rather delicate, soft character is already shaped by what lies beneath, the lemon shrub, which is simply the same as lemon verbena, which in turn belongs to the verbena family, but that’s enough of the botanical lessons for now. The aroma of this beautiful shrub has, in addition to its delicate lemony quality, a wonderfully fine-leaved, light green facet. This is so beautifully executed here that one occasionally feels reminded of the moment when one rubs a part of the plant between their fingertips. This lovely mild leaf green I have only known so far from Heeley's "Menthe Fraiche." Furthermore, verbena always has an underlying appetizing component for me, which makes me think of warm bundt cake fresh from the oven. All of this makes this fragrance very appealing to me. It has a supple lightness that still brings the full freshness package and becomes uncomplicatedly warm with the skin. And because the beautiful shrubby accord also culminates in a slender, cedar-dominated finish, it all comes together nicely and is truly worth recommending. :) My next purchase is set.

First of all - I don’t detect a heart or base note in Verveine Agrumes; it consists solely of the top note, at least to my nose, but what a note it is: juiciest, not sweet, slightly tart lemon, nothing more and nothing less, but plenty of it. And that’s a good thing.

I first smelled this fragrance in Rome; my sister discovered it and bought it right away. It was August and it was scorching hot, so we constantly treated ourselves to a spritz of it, and it was a wonderful refreshment. The days were very nice despite the heat, and the scent always reminds me of that. My sister loves the fragrance; she feels something is missing without it.
great fresh, soft scent. I like to wear it in the summer.

... and another dull, synthetic, vaguely “fizzy” incense with the usual base nuances of “pencil sharpener” cedar wood, here contrasted by spices and a sort of citrus-candied note (elemi). A bit ambery and vanillic, with a pleasant undertone of musky-soapy notes which provide a decent sort of “dusty” mood, a bit moldy too (ambroxan, I guess), enhanced by the slightly “rotten” sweetishness of some nuances of elemi. Then pepper, ginger, nutmeg. Basically, think of some (neo)classic woody-spicy scents like Cacharel pour l’Homme or Envy Men, rewritten with a prominent synthetic incense note to fit the current requirements of fashion (back then). In my opinion: uncreative, plastic, overpriced, still decently pleasant albeit in the least interesting meaning ever. 5,5-6/10

I like the mix of citrus and sweet spice in this fragrance and since I'm partial to elemi, to say nothing of labdanum, this works for me. It's a fresher, more accessible incense than most I own and for me leans toward the feminine side, if with sophistication. Very pleasant and very wearable for a variety of occasions.

Lately, I've found myself roused by Byredo Parfums, but Encens Chembur smells to me like a sheer, zesty impression of Armani Bois d'Encens. For all of the obvious reasons. Incense confined by citrus notes and a faint smoke of burning resins. Perhaps I'm not partial to citrus, but this line has much more to offer.

I am currently exploring the fragrance world of Byredo. Sweden has not really been known to me as a stronghold of perfumery, but most of the creations appeal to me quite positively; I would certainly recognize quality, skill, and dedication at first glance. I am particularly fascinated and enchanted by "Chembur." Unbelievable, I can't get enough of it :-) Everything has already been said about the notes and structure of the fragrance: a strong, rounded, radiant incense note, very much the churchly-familiar variant like in Comme des Garcons' "Avignon" (which I love dearly), but on top of that, a delicate brilliance from softly citrusy notes of bergamot and lemon, underneath a solid, richly resting strong and wonderfully aromatic base with nutmeg and ginger as well as amber and resins. I have never experienced this combination before and I am amazed at how wonderfully it works (at least for me)! This overall composition is making me almost addicted - however, I doubt that this clerically radiant cloud of vapor is a scent I want to smell IN PUBLIC; rather, it is one that I want to smell, sniff, enjoy, and absorb, and that is more of a very private experience :-) As already mentioned in previous comments: Those who are not repelled by incense can experience something very interesting here!

Chembur radiates for me a very interesting blend of contemplative calm and pure joy of life: I am deeply anchored within myself and from this feeling, I am free in my actions… The fragrance starts off very fresh, citrus-spicy with lemon, ginger, perhaps also a hint of nutmeg. Quickly, the bright, lemony smokiness of Elemi joins in with a slight resinous note. I really enjoy using Elemi at home for incense, especially when I have a lot on my plate professionally; the scent evokes such a relaxed, light yet grounded feeling. After a few minutes, the fragrance becomes a touch warmer, more amber-like and resinous, giving depth to the light, green, and subtly spicy notes. The incense that now mingles in is anything but church-like heavy, a very fine lemon incense. From the heart to the base, the fragrance becomes a bit warmer, simultaneously sweeter, delicious but not gourmand (on my skin, however, I often perceive many scents as a bit sweeter than others do). This lemony-resinous-warm blend hardly changes now, accompanying me for hours with a fine aura. The scent progression is quite straightforward and simple, but very beautiful. However, the fragrance really comes alive on my skin; on paper, I find it rather flat, the deeper, warmer notes hardly develop there. It stays quite close to my body, the intensity is not too strong (well, a matter of dosage), but the longevity on the skin is very good. For me, a pronounced feel-good fragrance, very balanced and refined, fresh yet warm and a little sweet, with the Elemi and incense notes making it somewhat more unusual. It fits every season, even now in summer it is lovely and definitely unisex wearable. The feeling I associate with the fragrance can best be described as creative and simultaneously grounded, free, independent, yet positively approaching the world.

As with many fragrances with strange names, I try to uncover the origin or meaning. In my research on Chembur, a district 22 km northwest of the city of Mumbai (formerly Bombay) emerged as the namesake online. Well, I have a somewhat different olfactory impression of India, and when I think of a big city, this kind of scent is not what comes to mind.

Anyone who thinks they have tried everything there is to offer in incense perfumes should take a surprised look at this citrusy Happy-Incense. There is nothing ecclesiastical about it, even less so cold, dark, or peppery. Usually, one can draw parallels to other scents, but here it is really difficult.

EC greets right from the beginning from its end. The opening is maintained until the very end. There are no significant cuts or strong shades discernible throughout the entire scent progression. Viewed this way, EC is rather an atypical Byredo, as the otherwise always experimental scent progression has indeed receded quite into the background.

Byredo, a brand previously unknown to me, is based in beautiful Stockholm. Sweden in the perfume sector? I had never encountered that before. You can definitely tell that "Encens Chembur," the Indian frankincense, comes from a cooler country. As Leimbacher already notes, the main theme of the perfume, the frankincense, has turned out to be comparatively bright.

Very beautifully presented is the incense here, with this fresh lemony top note making it quite suitable for summer, perhaps not on a hot day but definitely very fitting for a mild summer night in the city.

The first thought upon first detecting it: Wow!, where did the soy sauce from the Chinese takeout end up here?! The second thought: Finally, a plant-based vanilla. Absolutely elegant. Zero sweetness, zero gourmand. The synthetic aspect is a serious idea, considering that it is supposed to compare to a soft bomber jacket. Since almost every piece of fabric nowadays contains polyester anyway, I can totally understand that. However, there is a differentiable situation behind it. The smoke that burns in the eyes, the finely oiled wood on the floor, and the vanilla scraped from the pod. A room where stories are created, thoughts expressed, and people interact. A warm room, shielded from the damp cold winter outside the window. A room that has experienced a lot. Just recently, someone was smoking. The floor, prepared for the dance evening, has already absorbed much sweat and energy. The ladies had taken their furs and coats yesterday, leaving a hint of their perfume in the air. The room between yesterday and today. Where time stands still, between what was and what will come again. It reminds me a bit of confident oud, which I really like. Only what is the dry wood from the sawmill there, is revealed here in the oiled herringbone floor. Over time, a spicy (naturally sweet) vanilla remains under clouds of smoke. Thus, we are far away from the bomber jacket and any notion of modern mainstream. Exhilarating?!....sure, but different. I am glad to have finally found a vanilla for myself. Try it if you want to smell vanilla from a different perspective.

So far, L'Occitane has been a brand that I have enjoyed testing repeatedly...also because the shops always seem so inviting. Unfortunately, none of the scents have really "grabbed" me, not even the beautiful Eau des Baux. I was very curious to see if Eau de Cade would change that. The previous comments have sounded promising. Eau de Cade is wonderfully fresh at the beginning...green-citrusy and slightly bitter. There’s also a good dose of pepper. In principle, all the notes are immediately present, including the beautifully spicy cedarwood. So, I can't really say that there’s a classic development according to the fragrance pyramid. Essentially, the scent strongly reminds me of D600 by Carner Barcelona at the start, without possessing its elegance. However, the powderiness of D600 is present. After about an hour, the scent "tips" into the classically masculine...unfortunately...I don't like the soapy shaving foam note. If it has to be, it should smell like Prada's lilac Beau. Not much more happens...Eau de Cade increasingly moves towards woodiness and then weakens more and more. Good scent, fundamentally solid and also pleasing...but it evokes as much emotion and desire as a Golf in city traffic. From great likability, it quickly turned into boredom. If I'm looking for an affordable wood scent, I think I’d be better off with Dsquared. But I must say one last thing, I understand that everyone has a different nose and perception, but the idea that Eau de Cade is supposed to smell similar to Aventus (see right side) can only bring tears of laughter to my eyes...that’s ridiculous...a glance at the respective fragrance pyramids is enough...but well...I’ve also read here that APOM and Green Irish Tweed are supposed to be twins...Helau:-)!

I can hardly speak highly enough of L'Occitane. Starting from their natural approach, simply beautiful scents to unbeatable prices - there’s hardly anything to complain about. The best fragrance remains Eau de Baux, even after Eau de Cade, but the Cade EdT is a long-awaited treat for wood fans and followers of the successful aftershave. I had also received samples of the Cade After Shave Balm with a previous purchase and was thrilled, but I still use scent-neutral aftershave to avoid disturbing my daily perfumes. And at the moment, I’m growing a beard anyway, but I digress^^... In short: I had long wished for a perfume to accompany this Cade, and now that dream has successfully become a reality. I was very surprised that it happened so quickly and looked happily like a fool when the saleswoman introduced the new addition to me a few weeks ago here in Cologne. I didn’t buy it right away, but now in Munich, I couldn’t resist any longer. So this isn’t my first comment on this fragrance, but it is a very complimentary one! All fragrances from L'Occitane are natural, light, and not easy to hate, but Eau de Cade creates a light petitgrain wood feeling underlined by a minimal berry note that even Creed would be jealous of. The refreshingly woody and masculine feeling of the aftershave has been slightly altered but perfectly woven into a fragrance. Whether the scent reminds some of Fahrenheit and others of Aventus - it is unique enough, and the mentioned ones are certainly not the worst role models. The scent evokes in me the image of a crystal-clear and pure stream, flowing not through an earthy stone riverbed but through a woody cedar bed, thus gaining a woodiness to its cool freshness. In this cold water, the Cade berries occasionally float, without breaking or leaking. A very versatile fragrance that you can never go brutally wrong with. Bottle: I like it, or at least I don’t find it unpleasant. Sillage: very close to the skin and not intruding on anyone. Longevity: a good 6-7 hours speaks against poor quality. A fresh and exceptionally fruity wood all-rounder, for which some companies would shamelessly charge triple the price. Don’t underestimate it and give it a try! I think it will hold up, as the Cade fans alone will boost sales and surely won’t be disappointed!

If we set aside Eau de Baux, I found the fragrances released by L'Occitane in the last few years to be rather interchangeable. Well, that's of course a matter of taste, but many of the really good scents have been replaced by nice little waters, which has somewhat alienated me as a former loyal customer. If my husband didn't occasionally buy body care products for his mother, I would hardly ever step into one of the Hamburg stores anymore. So it happened by chance that while waiting for the Mother's Day gift to be wrapped, I spotted Eau de Cade on the shelf and spritzed it on with enthusiasm. I was familiar with the scent from the care line (especially the shower gel) and was curious to see how the Eau would smell. The sourly fresh opening combined with bitter green nuances is really delicious and pleasantly unique, in my opinion. The woody character can also be discerned right from the first spray. As the top note fades, Eau de Cade changes very little. A beautiful, herbaceous juniper-wood accord defines the scent until the very end. The longevity on my skin is good at over 12 hours, but the intensity is only close to the skin, which fits well with the rather monothematic scent. At the same time, I tested the new fragrance from CdG, Serpentine, that day, which faded significantly in comparison to Eau de Cade. Speaking of CdG, I think Eau de Cade would fit well into the Monocle series thematically. I am curious to see how long Eau de Cade will remain in L'Occitane's range, as I don't find the scent particularly mass-compatible. It requires a pronounced preference for wood and nature, in my opinion. For me, as a self-proclaimed woodworm, it's clear that Eau de Cade will soon be a part of my collection. I recommend a test to all other woodworms out there.

For a long time, I have been circling around various fragrances from L'Occitane. The supposed naturalness, the regional image, and the calmness of the brand appeal to me. By chance, I discovered that there is a small L'Occitane shop in Cologne. I already knew from tests in the duty-free area at the airport that I liked the scents "Eau de Cade" and "L'Eau de L'Occitane." I just couldn't get into "Eau des Baux," which was too harsh-smoky for me, a bit too overpowering. So it has become "Eau de Cade," which comes across as a bit earthier and woodier than its almost identical brother "L'Eau de L'Occitane." It should be noted that juniper plays a crucial role here, specifically the so-called prickly or cedar juniper, as the ingredient list on the packaging reveals. In the fragrance pyramid, one should definitely replace cedar with juniper! Now to the scent itself. "Eau de Cade" starts for me with one of the best top notes I know: fresh-balsamic-herbaceous, simply delightful. Nothing artificial penetrates my nose, and a subtle soapy touch joins in, promising purity. Gradually, the woodiness takes center stage, and it plays virtuously: no sawdust, no ash, just beautifully scented wood, paired with the spice of juniper. But even after two hours, the scent remains fresh-peppery in its basic orientation. Chapeau! With "Eau de Cade," I have certainly found one of those fragrances I may have been searching for years. Neither grandpa image nor hipster nonsense, and completely free of any disturbing element. Somehow soft yet still distinctive. And (very importantly): no comparison to anything that has come my way, so absolutely unique, in my opinion. One can even feel cool with it when someone asks again, "What's that?" :-) Because here, image is nothing and scent is everything! However, after a while, I now have to deduct points in the B-grade. Due to my initial enthusiasm, I initially gave this fragrance a full score, but I must now admit that this EDT, while smelling exceptionally good, does not come across as sensual or seductive at all. As I already mentioned about its brother L'Eau de L'Occitane, Eau de Cade is, after some testing and reflection, more of a smell than a scent for me, even if it is a very, very good one!

Under this title, Agatha Christie published a classic 'whodunnit' - originally set on Burgh Island off the English south coast, but later adapted to a private island in the Mediterranean in its film version. Under the scorching sun, the aging diva Arlena Marshall is strangled in a secluded cove, and unsurprisingly, each of the island visitors has an unshakeable alibi at the time of the crime. But if Hercule Poirot were not Hercule Poirot, he would not effortlessly reconstruct the sequence of events, wandering between turquoise bays, gardens lying still in the midday heat, and groves of fragrant macchia. L'Occitane's Eau de Cade captures the atmosphere of these walks and this nameless little island - primarily filmed in Mallorca - and offers a new, surprisingly calm interpretation of the often-played theme of 'Mediterranean.' It lacks almost any freshness - the bergamot noted at the top barely lasts seconds. Instead, it weaves a framework of balsamic softness and a heaviness that is too dense to be blown away by the summer wind - yet remains too light to be considered leaden. The absence of the turquoise component often used in Mediterranean fragrances also distances it from the usual connotations of palm-lined promenades and the harbor of Saint-Tropez. Instead, it (un)leads to a bright pine forest - perhaps in the hinterland of Juan-les-Pins or that very island mentioned at the beginning. This is a summer scent for a late afternoon in the south - when the day is winding down, but the evening has not yet awakened. One for the moment when sunbathers wonder if it is time to slowly start heading back. Conclusion: a warm and characterful scent of ultimately surprising quality. Not highly complex - yet an interesting alternative for a hot, sunless summer day. By the way, there is nothing evil about it.

Although there are already several speakers here, I also want to leave a few lines due to the - in every respect - still fresh impressions. Since I had the pleasure of receiving a sample (Thank you, Globomanni!) and had to test it right away because this scent is somehow and at some point appealing to me, I seize the opportunity.

Hello, hello everyone. Welcome to another comment from me. I'm glad that you apparently still haven't had enough of me and continue to read my fragrance reports,… for whatever reason :D Today it's about Eau de Cade from L'Occitane en Provence, which translates to Eau de Juniper, and that already gives you an idea of what kind of scent this could be.

L'Occitane is one of those brands that I enjoy being surprised by. I like the strong connections to nature and especially the saleswoman in the store just around the corner, who once gifted me some of the lavender that was actually meant for decoration. It dries gracefully, adorns the room, and I was once told that it supposedly keeps evil spirits away...

Curious from the positive comments here, I ventured into the local L'Occitane store some time ago. I don't know exactly why, but for some inexplicable reason, L'Occitane has always been outside my perception. So far, so good. I bravely moved on and, after a brief orientation phase, immediately discovered the bottle of the 'New' one, Cade.

My second L'Occitan and just as beautiful an experience, albeit different from Eau des Baux. I was already familiar with Cade from the men's care products and a test run in a boutique a couple of weeks ago. Yesterday, I brought it home as I passed by a L'Occitan store and couldn't resist the Father's Day set (55€ for EdT + Aftershave Balm + Shower Gel + Soap).

A very special and unique spiced-up vanilla. The red pepper and carrot notes give it a naughty piquant feel with an oddly attractive touch of vegetal pungency. Like the seductive Salome, who served as inspiration for this perfume, Seven Veils conveys a certain self-confident playfulness which is loaded with sex-appeal. It's not your typical sweet creamy vanilla. It's peppery, it's mischievous and quite lively. In fact to my nose there's more orchid in there than plain vanilla - it's more floral than dessert. Seven Veils wears nicely in all seasons but the super hot summer days and it's a fabulous companion for everyday wear. It will perk you up and make your eyes sparkle. Longevity is great - 12h+ on me - with pleasant, noticeable sillage all throughout.

Do you know that too? My Grandmother kept all her supplies for baking and cooking in one huge drawer.This drawer had a distinctive scent: There you could find vanilla beans, cinnamon, cloves, safron, allspice, flour and so on. In wintertimes this drawer was frequented quite often – we´d use cloves for making red cabbage, bay leaves for the sauerkraut and for baking a whole lot of spices and baking supplies – mostly the drawer was left open and the whole kitchen smelled spicy and kind of dusty thanks to the flour. In my olfactorial memory this distinctive drawer-scent is closely linked to christmas time with my family. Now, why do I tell you all this? That´s because the perfume “Seven Veils” - the seven veils of seduction, epitome of oriental eroticism, symbol of sexuality smells like the drawer my grandmother kept her baking supplies in. It smells of comfort, of overindulgence but mostly it smells of cloves, star aniseeds and floury dust. Some time later, after the spices have vanished partially, I can smell lush flowers – roses and orchids I recognize. Also there´s a warm and woody note behind these flowers and deep in the back of my nose I can taste the scent of carrotseeds. This typical soft, sweet-flowery scent like marzipan – if ever you smelled it you will always recognize it, even in small contents. The headnotes of Byredos Seven Veils are too much for me - too much spices. Furthermore it reminds me of Coeur de Noisette which, in my opinion, is softer and more wearable.

Seven Veils is emotive and captivating. The faction of notes creates a warm and momentous presence. An intimate hug of vanilla with a dash of herbs and spices. Ironically, this fragrance is inspired by "The Dance of The Seven Veils." Every note dances on the senses, leaving you euphoric, charmed and enthralled. There is an allure about Seven Veils that evokes romance, passion and sensuality.

Byredo SEVEN VEILS offers a unique take on the oriental gourmand. In this case the composition opens very culinarily but rather than sweet, it is savory. I have no idea what causes the effect, but it looks to be the combination of the carrot and the pimento. The vanilla is very, very, low key--if detectable at all. I smell either clove or allspice in this mix, but it is not the usual sweet christmas cake presentation. Closer to the use of nutmeg to season spinach, it seems to me. I do believe that SEVEN VEILS is original, but it smells like something that a creative vegan chef might whip up in her kitchen. Perhaps a carrot-tofu loaf? Bon appetit! I don't know, but this one is not for me. It's just too foody to wear as a perfume. Some good news for those who like this creation: the longevity is excellent. This stuff is strong! In the far drydown, SEVEN VEILS evokes vague memories of Calvin Klein ETERNITY, so I'm guessing that it, too, packs a mighty punch of eugenol.

"Seven Veils", what memories do I have of that and thus expectations. When I think about it, this fragrance is like how the imagined veil dance probably originated: as an acrobatic dance play with fabric strips that were by no means delicate and translucent. When I read the name to choose a fragrance for testing, I immediately thought of back then, about 30 years ago. When we were still unaware of everything that was to come, starting with the disappearance of the "Iron Curtain". When we were still innocent regarding the oriental cultures and full of curiosity. One summer evening, I was invited to a women's party: "Arabian Dance" in the neighboring town: A skirt or loose pants with an elastic waistband and a large scarf were to be brought. An Egyptian woman was the host, Mariam. I went there out of curiosity; until then, I knew nothing about it, except for a few short film sequences on television, which I found fascinating. And then I danced along. There were solo and group performances, sketches that were hilariously funny, even if still a bit incomprehensible to me. Mariam danced the veil dance, she danced the stick dance, she danced the candle dance. Amazing! And again and again, she and her group encouraged us guests to dance; we just had to "copy" them. It was essential to wear the skirts, the waistband pulled down a bit, and the scarf tightly wrapped around the hips. "Tight, otherwise you won't feel your hips!" commanded Mariam. When the catchy Egyptian dance music played for the last time and I eagerly joined in, Mariam pointed at me and said: "You there, you are gifted and flexible like a ball joint in your belly, you are tall and slim, you can immediately join my private group if you want; we practice every Wednesday for 2 hours. At least once in my life, I was "discovered" after all. Training was done in simple skirts, large scarves wrapped around the hips, without any frills; when several people dance with them, it gets really annoying in smaller rooms. And only barefoot or with ballet slippers. It was strict: "What are you doing, pull the skirt higher, that looks obscene, don't wiggle your breasts so much, that's vulgar! What are those big convulsive movements, what are you doing with the men when you dance like that? Where do you hold your hands, what does that mean?... From time to time, workshops were organized on weekends. Men always came as teachers, Arab ballet dancers from European stages. And so there were also intensive courses in veil dancing. The first time we looked a bit bewildered. A man, maybe around 50, tall, a well-groomed nice belly, nothing like a washboard, otherwise slim, gray hair, and a "knee baldness". And then he came out of the gym's dressing room in a brown gym suit, barefoot, with a large semi-transparent veil changing from brown to sunny yellow, adorned with softly jingling thin coins. Mariam looked at us sternly so that we wouldn't giggle; the man understood no fun, even if the instructions were always kindly given: "Habibi" here and "Habibi" there. The dance veils must be individually adjusted for each body size, arm span length plus about 30 cm, and the height reaching to the waist. Of course, made of fine fabric that doesn't move too easily but resonates. This was all determined beforehand with Mariam. It's quite a large piece of fabric when you whirl around with it, and if you're clumsy, you step on it and - uh - come a bit awkwardly off balance. If you don't get nailed to the spot because the veil pulls you back when you stand on it with your heel. Or when it tangles around your head and arms, and you have to free yourself from it looking like a plucked chicken. So, the whole weekend went up and down the large gymnasium with big leg swings.
