Taking up so much space that you could turn around with outstretched arms without touching the others. And always practicing how to make this fabric strip float and whirl around you acrobatically to the music and the appropriate body movements and the prescribed steps. How to let it elegantly float to the side at the right moment so that you can continue dancing without interruption. How to approach the audience at the beginning, promisingly elegant, wrapped in the veil, dancing, and then always unfolding the veil while in motion. But this man and dancer first demonstrated the dance with the veil to us. We no longer noticed the gym suit, the little belly, or the gray hair once he started dancing. He danced so perfectly, moving the veil so inimitably elegantly and powerfully around him that I can't even describe it here. As soon as he and the music started, you wanted to dance along like magically. But first, he drove us to complete exhaustion. So, I lost at least a kilo over such a weekend. Unforgettable for me, and I feel sad when I sometimes see photos in newspapers of these wannabe belly dancers, how they awkwardly and incorrectly hold the veil in their hands, "indecently" exposing themselves publicly; then I think of Mariam, the workshops, the intoxication one feels during "Shimmy" (very quick fine shaking of individual body regions) and also during veil dancing. And now "Seven Veils" as a fragrance: A dry, strong, and spicy scent, woody. And fruity; it must be the sultanas in the tajine, in which a dish is currently cooking. Veil dance completely burlesque with a colorful, striped coarse cloth. And I imagine how we would have invented a little choreography with tajine together with Mariam. We, with tajine, to the sensual movements of the dance with fiery music, would pantomime the cooking utensil as a teaching piece, for example, how to cook with it. The audience would have had fun with it, and so would we. Seriously, "Seven Veils" is a strong fragrance; now, after several hours, sandalwood and vanilla have fought their way through, the scent becomes softer, a hint of sweetness. In the meantime, I also smelled it slightly metallic. I couldn't perceive any flowers like wisteria, whose scent I know exactly, unfortunately. I don't know what oleander smells like. "Seven Veils" also reminded me at intervals of certain "Demeter Fragrance Library" scents, like "Humidor". However, it has been a year since I tested the latter. What I find beautiful about "Seven Veils" is that, as clumsy as it may be, it has brought back vivid memories for me.

Applied early in the morning during foggy, dreary weather to curb my morning grumpiness. Just looking at the bright reddish color of the fragrance lifts my spirits. The first impression: bitter, dark chocolate. Pimento and a strong dose of clove enhance this impression. Then it turns sweet, and I would love to take a sip of this wintry spiced punch.

"Seven Veils" was given to me as a sample after a brief sniffing excursion. What started promisingly on the test strip unfortunately ended up being yet another gourmand disappointment on my skin. The fragrance starts for me with an almost piercing whiskey note with the typical smoky undertone.

* This tingling in the little nose that you never forget like when you eat too many fizzy sticks this tingling in the little nose you miss that too just bubbling over with happiness... Yes, so another great Byredo for me! I thought PULP was the ultimate for me - but think again. Seven Veils looks like syrup with its orange liquid. Is that visible on the clothes?

I had almost suspected it, it has shot straight into my fragrance heart!!!! It doesn't really come off as spicy for me; I find it smells like sniffing a freshly bloomed vanilla flower plus a little powder and a bit more cream. It smells just like I had hoped Kiss me Tender would, which unfortunately got on my nerves quite quickly.

I am always a bit hesitant when vanilla is prominently mentioned in the fragrance notes, but since I really like combinations with carrot, I dared to test it. Upon the first spray, I can also perceive the carrot well, I even recognize the allspice, a very floral wisteria joins in, everything very nice, blooming fresh, sweet, pleasing, until...

...comes this wonderful warm-spicy fragrance. The company L'Occitane has launched its first gourmet fragrance with this. I like both: warm soft scents and Provence. Obviously, Guerlain and L'Occitane had the same idea here: they wanted to capture the warmth of Provence in a perfume bottle. Perhaps they discussed it over a bottle of wine under the fig tree and devised a concept: lavender must be included, and a bit of good honey, almonds belong in Provence - yes, and maybe a bit of fig too? Or perhaps better iris? You can hear the crickets chirping in the acacia trees, and the scent from the lavender field gently wafts over. I prefer the result from L'Occitane: the fragrance is spicy and rounded from the very beginning with the ambrette seeds and lavender. The lavender is well noticeable and lasts longer than in Mon Guerlain. Lavender seems to be trendy at the moment anyway. The annoying and piercing notes of Mon Guerlain are completely absent. The base with almond, musk, tonka, and acacia is very harmonious and warm but not too sweet. Overall, Terre de Lumiere is a sunny, sensual, and feminine feel-good fragrance that beautifully conveys the spice and warmth of Provence and brings a piece of vacation into everyday life.

When Terre de Lumiere was released, I was still regularly in France and it was really heavily promoted there. In the Galerie Lafayette, you stumbled over a promotional stand every few meters. I don't know that at all from L'Occitane. The whole presentation wasn't really my thing. It looked very suspiciously like one of those "don't offend anyone" scents. And then there was this overwhelming presence in the perfumeries. That kind of thing tends to put me off. And on the test strip, the scent actually seemed very disjointed. With so much excessive advertising, I couldn't seek cover in time during a sample attack (no, that's not true, I always take samples because you can test anything once), but the same was deeply buried in the sample box and only taken out at some point. Today I'm wearing it for the second time and I can once again scold myself for not always going by how a fragrance is presented. Terre de Lumiere does not smell at all like the advertising suggests. Overall, it reminds me a bit of a mix between Mon Guerlain and La Vie est Belle. I don't get along too well with either. But L'Occitane seems to have picked the usable parts from both fragrances and crafted something pretty out of it: Definitely test it on your skin! On the test strip, it just smells like chaos. And dose carefully! Terre de Lumiere starts off with a very sweet tonka bean. The lavender also has a somewhat sticky consistency. (It does say lavenderHONEY). Pepper adds a rather sharp note. You have to be careful with that. When dosed sparingly, it's SICKLY SWEET but not cloying or chemical, so I quite like it. When the pepper fades, the ambrette seeds add a subtle spiciness. (That's exactly what I miss in LVEB... sickly sweet fragrances always need a little balance). Lavender and tonka bean remain equally present throughout the entire scent development. After a few hours, the characteristic clean scent of white musk joins in, along with bitter almond, which then creates a little friction point with the very sweet fragrance. I really like that a lot. This is how a very sweet fragrance should be for me. Primarily as sweet as possible, but always with a little spicy, sharp, or bitter balance in the background. Regarding the Mon Guerlain comparisons: What makes it so sweet is the vanilla. This gave me a terrible migraine when I tested it. Terre de Lumiere is overall sweeter than Mon Guerlain, but that all-encompassing vanilla was left out. And I am spared the headaches. Therefore, a complete victory for Terre de Lumiere! So here’s a clear recommendation for everyone who likes it sweet (really SWEET). The spring freshness that the advertising tries to suggest is definitely not offered by this fragrance. I would rather recommend it in the deepest winter. And dosed discreetly. You definitely don't need to reapply. Terre de Lumiere isn't quite as sillage-bombastic as La Vie est Belle, but you should definitely dose carefully.

Often it is an unfulfilled longing that leads us on journeys of discovery and scent. The flying carpet of imagination is set in motion by opening a bottle, the first spray. Are you ready for Take-off? That is why the scent journey offered to me by "Terre de Lumière" is very welcome. One spray and I float through a kind of fragrant tunnel into the sunlit Provence: "Bonjour!" A late afternoon in summer, golden, slightly drowsy light, the air is sluggish and heavy with scent; the cicadas greet me with a very special concert. A gently rolling meadow is my landing spot; I land on a fragrant cushion of grasses, flowers, and herbs. I even find purple-blooming thistles here (do they really have to be here?). Only the usually so cozy bumblebees, which are foraging and already have quite plump "pants," seem a bit disturbed; they buzz quite angrily. On the edge of this meadow, in the shade of some old, lushly blooming acacias, sits a young smiling woman and greets me warmly. She beams from ear to ear. She invites me to take a seat on her blanket and first offers a snack: "Après le Voyage!" she announces with a radiant smile. She comes from a nearby farm, has finished her work for the day, and treats herself to a break in this idyllic spot: peace before it’s time for evening milking of the goats. And indeed: A herd of small brown-and-white goats grazes a little way off from this beautifully blooming, fragrant meadow. They bleat to themselves: A fine fence prevents them from entering this splendor. This growth is too valuable to be trampled by small hooves and end up in the bellies of the friendly animals. Their own area is large and just as green and fragrant (the milk will tell about it later): But as we all know, the grass on the other side of the fence is always particularly green and tasty! A small jug of house wine has been cooling in the stream that gurgles behind the shade-giving acacia trees. I am offered a cup full: How refreshing! The dark crusty bread is from the morning, freshly baked, and the goat cheese comes from the farm’s own dairy. The small loaves are sold on market day in the next village. She hospitably offers me some. She also shares pickled olives and fresh summer vegetables from the garden with me. Everything tastes wonderfully fresh and natural; and when does one ever get to personally meet the suppliers of such delicacies - even if they bleat and stretch their long necks to look over the fence. But the goats seem more interested in the long blades of grass than in me. The crowning glory of this wonderful meal is the honey: lavender honey from her own bees and the flowers of the fields that border the farm. Dipping the fresh crusty bread into the large jar of golden honey: truly delicious! "Terre de Lumière" by L'Occitane en Provence immediately transports me to this paradise of aromas and scent dreams. Indeed, among other things, a fresh hint of noble bergamot is in the air, pink pepper adds to the whole. But everything is dominated by honey: honey, golden, viscous, sluggish, and precious, dripping from the spoon. Honey that carries more than just lavender blossoms and golden sunbeams; my feeling senses many beautiful summer flowers spreading out here. It would be a shame if they were missing. Acacias, which I like very much like their related mimosa, perfume the air with a sweet floral scent yet slightly herbaceous; a bit of their leaf green seems to mix in. I will certainly never become a big fan of tonka bean; its scent is simply too special for me and often just annoying. But here, as with the last fragrances I tested, it wonderfully expands the scent spectrum; just like the white musk, which I also don’t particularly care for. Both of these rich scent notes ride very harmoniously on the gentle waves of honey and acacia. A combination that seems a bit daring at first, but surprisingly close to an idyllic, pastoral creation. "Terre de Lumière" is very successful and communicative. It tells of fragrant meadows, old trees, leisurely flying and softly buzzing bumblebees and bees, and lets the little bells that the goats wear around their necks ring softly. A scent that breathes relaxed silence, and I wouldn’t be surprised if Pan peeked out grinning from behind a bush or tree. "Mr. Spiderweb," "Miss Pea Blossom," and all their companions from Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream" are already here anyway. You can hear them quietly chatting and laughing in this scent seduction. For "Terre de Lumière" is not just light and earth: It is so much more! So much that anyone can feel and wish for: This scent fulfills wishes and it fulfills dreams!

Hey there, how are you all doing? Are you ready to eagerly devour a new comment from me? :D Well, don't get too excited too soon, because the fragrance I'm about to introduce is quite nice in itself, but somehow it feels a bit weak, as if it’s missing some bite. It’s Terre de Lumière by L’Occitane en Provence. The scent is a honey fragrance that surely makes your mouths... um, let's say, makes your mouths water just at the mention of honey, right? It's almost cliché for you women, but it seems there isn’t a single woman who doesn’t like honey! :D But okay, I have to admit, I really like honey too. It doesn’t necessarily have to be the scent for me, but the taste is absolutely fantastic. The sweet gold that feels wonderful in the mouth, but is terribly, TERRIBLY annoying when it drips off the bread. Even worse is when you’re too clumsy and drop the bread on the floor while eating... because you know exactly which side the bread lands on and then everything gets extremely sticky... oh how I hate that!! :D The scent: The fragrance starts with amber and lightly spicy pepper. In the background, you briefly smell bergamot and general citrus notes, but these are weak and quickly fade away. For a brief moment, you also get the feeling that the scent has a sunscreen-like note. Shortly after, you can smell slightly herbal notes that must come from the lavender, or rather from the lavender honey, even though I shouldn’t perceive any honey-like sweetness yet, as that takes a few more minutes. This is also because the scent has a somewhat low sillage, meaning you have to sniff closer to the sprayed area to catch some of the listed notes. Well, anyway, you can still smell the honey later on, but it’s faint. Other notes like tonka bean come into play, while I can perceive almonds less. A little later, the honey seems to become a bit stronger. And with the musk, another sweet note is added. The sillage and longevity: The projection is very weak for a fragrance that is supposed to contain honey, which is a shame. At least to me, the scent seemed quite weak, so it will be perceived more closely. The longevity, on the other hand, is okay at eight to nine hours. The bottle: The bottle is a round, bulbous container with a yellowish fragrance liquid inside. The cap is shaped like cut stones and provides a nice contrast to the yellow liquid with its red color. All in all, despite its simplicity, it’s quite nice. So! The scent has turned out to be quite nice. It has a light, gentle sweetness, in which honey can also be detected. There’s also a slight spiciness coming from the lavender. Unfortunately, it’s the case (or at least I found it so) that the scent is a bit too weak. Moreover, I also have the feeling that despite its beautiful notes, the fragrance just doesn’t want to really take off. That’s a shame, but this can still have its advantages. Because it could, for example, be used as a honey scent during the day, possibly even in the office, without projecting the spicy note that many other honey fragrances have, which often comes across as quite intense (like with the Angel fragrances, for example) and can be overwhelming for some. Of course, it could also be that my nose is a bit deceiving me, as I’ve been trying stronger fragrances lately and therefore perceive this one as weaker than it actually is. Well, the best way to find out is to try the scent yourself! But as I said, it smells quite nice and could appeal to some of you ladies! I would mainly use it in autumn; otherwise, spring and winter work well too. So... I'm done again. And somehow I'm feeling a bit hungry. The big question now is: Should I put honey on the slice of bread... or rather Nutella? Aaargh, I bet you can't decide either, right? I think I’ll spread BOTH on it, mu ha ha ha :D

Terre de Lumiere is a sun fragrance. That's what we're led to believe. Not only does all the advertising and presentation revolve around the theme of the sun, but the bottle also has distinct features reminiscent of warm sun rays. But how much sun is actually in this bottle? I had certain expectations of how a sun fragrance should smell and, above all, how it should unfold on my skin. Land of Light. A beautiful name, thoughtfully chosen, although I would find something else more fitting. Because it’s not that radiant. Rather, it has more to do with honey-drenched Winnie the Pooh than with any lights. The fragrance starts off very warm, sweet. Honey is immediately the main theme here. It becomes quite sweet, and it remains so throughout the development and until the end. A hint of spice and lavender only play a minor role. Almond, very creamy, is blended in, and over time, tonka bean drips into the scent like in slow motion. It feels very tailored, almost endearing. One might think it is very sweet, but the sweetness actually stays quite restrained over time and is almost subdued. So it definitely lacks a punch. It is beautiful, no question, but nothing special. Those who enjoy warm, sweet honey fragrances with a touch of spice and lavender will find this appealing. However, it is not the sun in a bottle; I will have to look elsewhere for that. Rather, it is a lovely counterpart for Winnie the Pooh. Longevity and sillage are average. I like the bottle; it looks elegant and beautiful. Perhaps the name simply fits the bottle and not the content.

I can confidently call Provence my second home. I have always spent my summers at a Verdon reservoir, on the yellow rocks by the water surrounded by wild thyme, savory, lavender, pines, oaks, and many other fragrant plants, all in the unique light of the Provençal sun. The air is spicy and warm, with an almost earthy base. Wonderful - and the scent of my dreams.

Some time ago, while browsing on Parfumo, I stumbled upon this wonderful fragrance. I can't quite remember how it happened, but I do recall being fascinated by the statements from the very beginning. So, during my next stroll, I paid a visit to the L’Occitane shop in my city and sprayed the fragrance on myself there.

I tested this perfume without reading a description or review beforehand, so as not to be influenced. First of all: L'Occitane is stepping away from its well-known line of herbal, fresh, clear, floral scents towards concentrated sweetness. Right from the shop, the innovative packaging and the atypical look of the bottle stand out.

A sunny, optimistic fragrance that radiates depth and sunny warmth. A lavender bush in the afternoon sun, Provence, longing and fulfillment, a deep gaze over the expanse of the landscape, a spicy opening and a sensual, tender finish. A harmonious embrace. I only wish for a more intense longevity.

Facing the sun, lying on a summer meadow amidst buzzing and chirping, warm sun rays dripping on my skin like honey, not sticky or unpleasant, but promising and comforting, with a blade of grass in the corner of my mouth, and the gentle summer breeze carries the delicate scent of lavender over to me. That’s exactly how it feels when I apply Terre de Lumière.

bought blindly to discover new olfactory gems, I was apprehensive due to the presence of geranium which until then had only led to disappointments in my fragrant discoveries. at the opening, deliciousness, pep, which reminds me very briefly of Arabian Tonka, then which quickly dissipates, for a fruity and spicy freshness which reminds me a lot of the first version of the one milion edt, which has become impossible to find. a perfume of seduction, ideal for mid-season, even winter and night. the trail is quite discreet unlike the effective hold for well 9 hours despite 2 washes with water on the perfumed area. a great discovery which ends up in my top 10 of this year, the best boss the collection so far in my humble opinion

I knew I had to buy a full bottle the first time I sniffed it in the small 7,5ml miniature. A classic floral scent, but not too overwhelming. Fruity, but not too sweet. Fresh, but not too citrusy. It resembles spring, when it's no longer getting dark quickly and you could see some flowers and some colors. Places get more lively and you start dreaming of vacation somewhere in France, thinking of wearing your favourite summer dress. Such a lovely, dreamy, feminine, elegant scent. I just hope it lasts longer. With the miniature, it lasts around 1,5 - 2 hours on me, as the miniature doesn't include a spray and I had to dab it on my wrist. With the full bottle, of course with a spray, it lasts a little bit longer, but around 3,5 hours at best. I was obsessed to find a dupe of it or an EdP version that lasts longer, but until now, no hope.

A really beautiful fresh - floral scent that I wore for the first time at work today! I was able to perceive it the whole time and felt truly comfortable, fresh, and floral wrapped up! This is exactly what I was looking for! Not too intrusive yet not too weak! Unfortunately, some fragrances do not have the longevity one wishes for. But my new L'occitane did not let me down and kept me cheerful and uplifted every time a pleasant whiff from my wrist wafted into my nose. And that despite wearing a mask! What I must mention: I had been at work for no more than five minutes when I received the first compliment and had to immediately share which wonderful scent I was wearing today! I can only praise the longevity and sillage! I also really like the bottle! A great fragrance that I can only recommend if you prefer floral fresh scents.

Not far from one of my workplaces, I suddenly discovered a shop with the sign L'Occitane en Provence during my lunchtime strolls... In my mind's eye, the radiant Provençal lavender fields and the silhouette of the city of Grasse, the capital of fragrances, come to life. Of course, I thoroughly explore the selection there, enjoying the beautiful southern French atmosphere in the tastefully decorated shop, and I don't leave without a perfume. I chose a miniature set that includes this scent. It captivates with a very light fruity opening, not juicy-sweet, but harmoniously soft, accompanied by a delicate refreshing neroli note. Then the fragrance settles onto a fluffy floral bed, it smells softly floral and cozy, slightly playful with a subtle sweetness in the background, a warm depth that allows you to happily wear the scent on a cool autumn morning or even on a cozy winter evening. In any case, it is a lovely companion for everyday life in spring or cool summer days, rather not for hot days. A fragrance without edges and corners, unobtrusively gentle and simply beautiful.

A dry, blushy woodspice. A Scandi-Western. Bone-white driftwood and rose gold sand. Quintessential Byredo DNA with the airy, unisex quality. It’s got the De Los Santos backbone, but with cedar CRISPR’d in place of the sage. And instead of your typical Byredoy powdery violet, it uses starchy papyrus. There’s something about it that smells like virgin carpet, that elusive “new house smell.” Or maybe even a box of fresh coloured pencils and crayons. All this is fabulous, except for the fact that I can barely eek more than an hour out of it. Its lifespan is nil on my skin and makes Mojave Ghost feel like a heavyweight on fabric. My favourite fragrance to date is De Los Santos, so I was afraid I’d soon be $200+ poorer, but I can’t rationalize the price with the performance. A pity, as it is a beautiful blend. Mental Snapshot: An adobe villa ripples on the horizon. Wind-polished stucco, lofty rafters of raw timber. There’s lots of sleek midcentury furniture. Probably Danish. And animal skulls. Probably bison. There’s not a soul inside. Just a pair of palomino mustangs capering in the half-light outside. You blink and the whole vision dissolves into the dunes. (It's a millennial allegory for home-ownership). tl;dr: sepia-tone mirage

Sampled this at Neiman Marcus. Soft projecting, very Scandinavian. Immediately hit with smooth creamy sandalwood and cedar. I didn’t get much rose or cardamom. I only tested this on paper but it didn’t smell like anything new. Just a very pleasant sandalwood. With the name of dessert dawn I was expecting something more evocative of a sunrise coloring the painted dessert not a cedar sauna.

Desert Dawn,is an amazing musky/woody genre fragrance,that yes maybe it's been done before(santal 33) many times,but it still manages to be so so different. When you first spray it you get a strong dose of lemony cardamom,then sandalwood takes the stage with its milky facets and along with the cedar they create something that reminds me of freshly parqueted wooden floor. It gets muskier and a little bit more masculine as time goes by,but it never loses it's first impression.It is lemony,woody and clean musk,it's dryness feels like you've just licked a piece of wood,like you can feel it in your mouth.Signature worthy for sure and a true unisex.

I’ve been testing a number of new fumes lately (not that I need more) and this was a standout because it smells exactly like its ingredients. Cardamom and Rose. Sandalwood and cedar. Papyrus and musk. For freshness subtle carrot, vetiver, All distinctly there but blended into the creamy loveliness they imply. How so? They are authentic to my finicky nose. No undertones of the gas station, no hints of kerosene. Even the Maison Francis Kurkdjian I sampled on my right wrist now, more than an hour later, reeks of gasoline, Not so Desert Dawn on my left wrist. It still invites hungry sniffing of its dry deliciousness as the sun rises.

This is reminiscent of Santal 33 but far superior in my opinion. I've never understood the hype with Santal 33 as I really don't get anything other than the dry sandalwood; here, the florals and musk come through better making it a more well rounded and somewhat prettier (though still unisex) scent. It's one I could see being my signature scent as it's subtle enough for every day wear and just about any setting. I think you can get a similar affect with a number of other scents however - You Doux is the one that comes to mind for me as a far cheaper option - they don't share any listed notes, but the effect is the same on me - a slightly sweet, woody skin scent.

I have to express my feelings about this new release! I organized a sharing with this fragrance. Since the scent wasn’t on the market at that time, it was quite bold. You could also say naive... But I’ll stick with bold! :D All the notes appealed to me a lot! Well, sharing done, bottle in hand.

My first review - have mercy :D I already had Super Cedar by Byredo, which I always enjoyed wearing. This scent is similar to Super Cedar (of course because of the cedarwood), but I find it much more exciting! At first - as some have already described - you get a brief whiff of dill, but then it really becomes pleasantly warm and woody, also a bit creamy.

As is almost always the case with the brand, the scent is very, very weak and subtle when it comes to H+S. 30 minutes after spraying, I can only smell the fragrance very faintly if I sniff directly at the spray point. The sillage is virtually non-existent..

Bullion goes on with a burst of moderately sweet fruity floral osmanthus enhanced plum supported by black pepper before gradually transitioning to its heart. As the composition enters its early heart the plum fades into the background with the osmanthus remaining to leave traces of the fruit still detectable in subtle support to the black pepper that takes on a co-starring role, adding a waxy sheen to natural smelling dark woods rising from the base. During the late dry-down the composition gradually sheds its black peppery facet as it turns somewhat musky sans all but just the hint of any animalic heaviness, with remnants of the dark woods remaining, now in support. Projection is good and longevity excellent at well over 12 hours on skin. Bullion is a perfume that on its surface is pretty simplistic with its peppery, almost incense-like woody focus. The osmanthus floral element is quite intriguing though, as in the heart section of the perfume's development it allows the plum from the open to remain to a degree, even though now it really is the floral primarily driving its detection. The woods used are quite pleasant and natural smelling but difficult for this writer to make any real distinction as the which ones are used. There is a waxy, almost iris aspect added to the peppery woods in the heart that to a modest degree reminds me of Declaration by Cartier, without the cumin. The late dry-down is a rather mundane, safe affair with the perfume never really taking major risks with its sanitized musky woody finish. There is no doubt Bullion is well put-together, but I never quite feel it distinguishes itself from a relatively crowded space of perfumes with similar fragrance profiles. The bottom line is the apparently discontinued $175 per 100ml EdP bottle at liquidators Bullion implies wealth and opulence, but delivers the more commonplace earning it a "good" 3 stars out of 5 rating but a neutral recommendation to most except peppery woods collection completionists.

When my "Chambre Noir" runs out, I might switch to "Bullion"... that was my first thought during my test of this earthy Byredo plum. A clear gourmand, but with such a high animalistic edge that it could deter many potential fans. A sledgehammer for more serious, slightly naughty, and definitely trained noses. You have to like it - and I really do! Since "Sausage Party," it’s known that even fruit needs sex... "Bullion" is the best proof of that. Dirty, erotic, slimy - jammy! It’s almost clearer in its structures, more refined in its extraction of the fragrance notes than "the Dark Room" from Olfactive Studio. Leather + plum, intensified and penetrating. But there are also supporting characters that make things even more exciting. Pepper adds spice and sharpness, swirl and a sexy bite. Sharp is hot - not just when it comes to food. The soft, dark brown plum stands in excellent contrast, and the leather ultimately makes the scent the perfect symbiosis of bad boy and cuddly bear. A fragrance that you can almost only love or hate. Even the often rebellious Osmanthus here only adds texture and even more love aroma. In short: Horniness. It’s a sexy scent. You can say that again, right? Bottle: Scandinavian understatement doesn’t get much better. In contrast to the dark, mysterious fetish fragrance experience. Sillage: seems stronger and grumpier at first than it actually is. Still lasts 9 hours. Conclusion: doesn’t do things by halves - a S&M mushy plum! A strong piece - from every angle, in every position, in every flavor direction. Head cinema on.

Yes, the name causes either confusion or laughter in German-speaking countries. Lieschen Müller and Otto Normalverbraucher simply associate the name with the world-famous brew from France. This is, as one can find out on the WWW, however spelled with o u. Bullion, on the other hand, means something entirely different, namely an investment coin. The Krugerrand would be an example of a bullion coin. Anyone who wants to learn more about the topic can gladly do so on the WWW. I will now turn to the scent. For the first time, I was able to test Bullion at Douglas in Düsseldorf KÖ. I had just picked up the bottle when suddenly an extremely effeminate and overly excited salesperson jumped at me from the side and loudly fluted with a French accent: "Ahhh. Buuulllioooong, a wonderful scent. It's only available in Mailonde, in New Yorke, and at uuhhns." He said this and then flitted away to attend to a no less excitable customer. My husband and I looked at each other questioningly before bursting into loud laughter and hastily leaving the perfume shop. Once outside, my husband then asked if that was really true, to which I replied with an "Oh, come on!" "The scent is also available in Hamburg and at ALzD." During my last visit to Lubi, I then received a sample of Bullion and was able to try the scent in peace. Bullion is definitely characterized by a truly successful fruity note (I smell more peach than plum), which never drifts into the kitschy or artificial. In the opening, this fruity note is pleasantly peppery, and from the heart note on, I can hardly make out any significant change. Bullion then remains very soft, noble, pleasantly leathery with a really well-balanced sweetness, and the base notes support the heart accord until the scent completely fades away, without pushing itself into the foreground. The longevity is great, as Bullion lasts on me for a solid 24 hours. The sillage is, for such a noble scent, pleasantly restrained. More would be rather counterproductive here. For the warm season, I find Bullion only conditionally suitable and it is, if at all, only wearable on a mild summer night. In cooler temperatures, it can also be worn during the day. Bullion is, unsurprisingly, climbing right to the top of my wish list. And I have long stopped wondering why I can't afford investment coins.

The journey through the "Swedish Steppe" continues. Today, the particularly rare Bullion was on the agenda, and there must be a reason why it is so hard to find or is being hidden;-)! I find the brand extremely likeable, although it is very difficult to find. Unfortunately, there hasn't been a real standout among them so far. Mister Marvelous and Bal d' Afrique have only managed to score points with me so far. Bullion starts off super fresh and zesty with a slightly sweet touch, a spicy-sweet overall impression. The top notes do not reflect this... but for me, it is clearly bergamot in a very green form. A peppery sharpness comes into play. This top note gets full points from me... it almost has a medicinal sharpness like in Mister Marvelous. Unfortunately, it doesn't continue as nicely for me. The rather spicy-sweet suede... gradually turns into a dull and slightly musty mix, and the leather buries all other facets of the fragrance beneath it. I can only partially understand the often-cited parallels to Chambre Noire. There, it is an irresistible mix of plum, cinnamon, and a hint of leather that is perfectly balanced. Here, the result is full of edges and corners, neither romantic nor easily accessible. Fairly, I must say that leather in a fragrance can chase me away, CN is the big exception. My nose simply cannot get used to Bullion, also because it is too harsh and too scratchy. Leather fans will definitely get their money's worth here. For me, Bullion has no charm and no beautiful aura, rather dark and depressive. The woods in the base try to save what can be saved, but they don't quite succeed. Also, because there is already enough spice from the pepper and osmanthus, the already very spicy sandalwood didn’t need to be added. For me, it’s an unrefined oriental perfume. If I were to rate it based on my own scent preferences, it would come out at a maximum of 50%, but for leather fans, it will be a highlight, as it is surely well-made, but completely ignores my fragrance preferences. The longevity is at a good level of 6-7 hours, similar to Chambre Noire, the sillage is strong, but I could also be mistaken because I pay too much attention to the disliked note, and everything one rejects sticks like tar.

...and once again a Byredo fragrance with esprit. Here is a stylistic device that can be recognized here and there in certain scents. To me, BB smells quite different from a distance than when you perceive it directly on yourself. But step by step, first things first. The beginning strongly reminds me of Cuir Velours by Naomi Goodsir and Daim blond. The leather is immediately present and spreads out nicely. The pivot here is the leather, which holds everything together. For me, the leather is even there before the pepper. There are some peppery highlights in the development, so it has been used rather sparingly. The leather is the unpredictable constant here. It doesn't fade away and presents itself like a nimble rascal. It has the character of a chameleon. It is sweet but also dry and spicy. Just as the pepper in the top note is indicated, but becomes pleasantly cheeky from time to time, the plum is by no means evaporating prematurely. The scent carpet here consists of the plum and the leather. I find that the fragrance smells sweeter from a distance than up close. Up close, the spiciness dominates more, and the sweetness is less detectable. The fragrance doesn't really have a top note in the classical sense; it's more of an A - B form. The A part is characterized by the shimmering leather and the plum, while the B part consists of shimmering wood, partly balsamic, partly dark, a bit clouded. The floral component, in my opinion, has not quite faded away yet. The flowers are also more like dry flowers, so they almost remind me of pressed flowers. As a child, I used to do this occasionally, collecting a few flowers and placing them in a book overnight, then stacking about 20 other books (preferably Brockhaus) on top. Typical Byredo, despite all its versatility, is very tasteful and harmonious. I prefer Daim blond over Bullion and Cuir Velours Bullion. Bullion may have more power, while Cuir Velours is fluffier. What I find beautiful is that Byredo is truly omnipresent and versatile; just as flexible as the fragrance is in its appearance, so flexible is it as an olfactory accessory for the wearer.

Inspired by Showdown's review, I ordered a sample, as I greatly appreciate Chambre Noire and have it on my wishlist for autumn. And indeed, I can largely agree with Showdown. What I really like about Chambre Noire, the concept with plum and leather, is here more subtly developed, more finely balanced.

I am a fan of L'Occitane so I was initially excited about this scent when I found out they had an amber in their line. I hope you find the review useful, thanks for watching.............................................

I must confess that when I saw this new version of the glorious amber by L'Occitane en Provence I said to myself: "Another wrong remake". It wasn't so. At the first spray I recognized a warm, round acchord composed by the tonka bean made smoother by floery accents. The, I smelled the wonderful and longlasting base notes: Amber, sweet and not medicinal, vanilla, warm and not sweetish but well balanced. A warm oriental cloud involved me and made me dream of middle eastern landscapes . The longevity and the sillage remain good , although the clear coluor of the reformulated scent seem suggest a lighter perfume. Only a remark for the bottle: maybe I'm too old fashioned, but I prefer the old version, so "art déco" and multifaceted. Anyway, a new bottle simple and minimal, but refined and maybe more ergonomic. The price is high for a 75ml one size, but the result is amazing. I love it.

Golden autumn. An afternoon on one of the last days of September. The still warming light of the day filters through the rustling crowns of the apple trees, and sunny patches of light flit across the orchard among the orange and brown speckled leaves and overripe apples. The heavy sweet scent of the rosy-cheeked fruits hangs in the evening air. Bronze. Fullness. Sweet wafting. A light breeze carries blossoms onto the heavy wooden garden table. The bitter earthy and dry smell of the wood tanned by sun, rain, wind, and time is wonderfully intertwined with the fragrant atmosphere of the golden shimmering afternoon and the overripe fruits fallen from the trees. Evening descends and gently pours a last quickly fading light over the garden, the trees, over the fields. Many baskets of apples stand on the porch and in the kitchen. A magnificent scent of vanilla and gentle sweet melancholy wafts through the house. Little happiness. The windows are closed. It is getting quickly cooler outside now. The oven hums softly its evening song. The first time this year.

The main role in HAMLET is Hamlet, in FAUST it is Faust, and in L'Occitane-Ambre from the Classiques Collection, it is sweet-spicy amber. From the very beginning, it sets the tone and does not relinquish the lead role throughout the entire piece. The citrus and floral notes mentioned in the fragrance pyramid play only supporting roles, and they won't be winning any Oscars for their appearances. Even the oriental additions of tonka bean, vanilla, and cedar pay homage to the king. "Ambre" is undoubtedly a perfume whose name does not mislead - as can sometimes be the case with fragrances named after their notes. In the beautiful drydown, it even takes on a slightly tobacco-like quality and lets subtle roasted coffee notes shine through. On my skin, the scent lasts an impressive 18 hours (almost too long). The sillage is of very decent but also pleasantly unobtrusive presence. There is actually nothing wrong with this fragrance. Perhaps it comes off a bit too sweet and a bit too one-dimensional. Fans of great fragrance developments may not find what they are looking for here. But it achieves something that I fundamentally consider a beautiful characteristic of a (ultimately synthetically produced) fragrance: it smells in the long-lasting base not like a perfume, but simply like "warm skin" - if you understand what I mean? It forms such a connection with the skin that it seems to emanate warmth and comfort. An "aura fragrance" in the best sense. And that is already lovely. Period.

The uniquely beautiful colors of Provence: the radiant yellow of sunflowers, the bright purple of blooming lavender fields, the velvety green of summer plane tree leaves, the warm golden-brown of deliciously ripe chestnuts. AND: of "Amber". ... in the nose a fine scent of thyme, rosemary, rockrose, and many other wild herbs that defy even the most barren soil, a lot of sun, and then the cold Mistral wind ... along with the taste of small seductive treats like Nougat de Montélimar or the equally almond-infused Callisons d'Aix on the tongue, perhaps accompanied by a glass of perfectly chilled rosé or - depending on my mood - a deep dark red wine. This (life) feeling is exactly what this incredibly beautiful fragrance from L'Occitane embodies for me. Admittedly, I love France anyway, and especially this southern part of the country, which comes pretty close to my idea of paradise. I first caught a whiff of it there at a friend's place, and it actually took very little effort to immediately capture my fragrance-loving heart. Sure, there are more complex, more exciting, eccentric scents than this one. But often, beauty doesn’t need grand embellishments and speeches. Even after years, it manages to make my soul resonate, and on days that may appear more soft gray than sunny yellow at first glance, it sends bright rays of sunshine directly to me. Sometimes, when I mentally write lists of what I am grateful for in life, this fragrance ranks relatively high. Not because of its material value; not just because it is warm, soft, and harmoniously rounded; but especially because of what lies behind the scenes.

The cosmetics brand L'Occitane has surprised and fascinated me several times, thinking of "Eau des Baux," which evoked some emotions in me! Since I was looking for a warm and spicy-balsamic amber scent, I thought to myself, "You have to test this 'perfume candidate'," and I got a sample from a nice user here on Parfumo.

Difficult to do justice to this scent. In the past few weeks, I have come across several amber fragrances and was amazed by the range. If I only knew this one, the assessment would be easy. It is beautiful, no question: sweet, but not too sweet, warm, a bit woody, not overwhelming - I like it.

Amber scents have captivated me; I love the heaviness, the presence, this blend of sweetness and spice. This inevitably led me to this representative here, whom I actually didn’t expect much from without testing.

Most people surely know L'Occitane en Provence from the bright yellow boutiques found in the city centers of many medium-sized towns across the country. They always struck me as quite generic - neither particularly disturbing nor exceptionally inviting.

This scent simply reminds me of vanilla in a different way. The formulation makes this fragrance truly unique - amber/vanilla is a great combination. I always receive compliments when I wear this scent. Unfortunately, it has been discontinued. If I were to describe this fragrance in my own way, it would be like this: a little warm, a bit sweet, and you’re already in love.

A very fresh summer scent. It really does embody the name incredibly well. It a breath of fresh air, lung opening and uplifting in the mid and opening. It is marvellously well blended, I find it difficult to pull out the distinct notes, and they all marry very very well with one another. It projects remarkably well for a scent of this genre I find, and it's longevity is shocking! I found it lasting up to 7/8 hours on me, after 12 hours the vetiver was still detectable against my skin and softly on my clothes as a grassy soft hayzy scent. I was very surprised by this fragrance as I am not that hot on Byredo. Slightly more masculine leaning but can be paired with a more feminine floral scent to give a more feminine edge, or can be used with gourmands to add some air to it. I wore it alone as it was almost 30 degrees here and it was just what I needed.

I'm always down for putting my nose on cannabis scents, and this one really brings it. I think it's a great one for layering, as it has a pretty loud personality, but not much to bring it down to earth, per se. I know it's called "Open Sky" but it's a little too open for me. it can definitely be quite harsh at first, and as it dries down, again it lacks some depth,... I think it could be really quite nice if the cannabis smell was a bit more earthy or deep as well. it smelled like a fruity sativa, maybe a chocolate-y indica would be great to balance it out.

Byredo's "Open Sky" is an interesting and surprisingly complex fragrance that accurately represents its name by invoking images of vast, open landscapes and the fresh feeling one gets from clean air. Released a couple of years ago, as a limited edition, it managed to capture a sense of wanderlust, and freedom in a bottle. The first spray offers a bright, nearly biting citrus opening. This is not a juicy-sweet citrus, but a more tart, slightly green pomelo, instantly cutting through with a bright freshness. This opening is soon accompanied by the unmistakable and somewhat peppery scent of black pepper, adding a warm, stimulating and slightly spicy note to the citrus opening to make it more than just one-dimensional. As the perfume dries, the interesting and somewhat surprising scent of hemp leaves comes up in the heart stage of the perfume. This is certainly not a bad, overly earthy or also overly cannabis smelling scent, rather it offers a green aroma and slightly herbaceous note added to the beautiful freshness making it an interesting depth or dimension, with a little unconventionality thrown in. It integrates with the original spice, and has an almost carbonated-feel as it is quite airy. The dry-down is where Open Sky feels particularly grounded, with the woody, warm, slightly sweet, and resinous aspect of palo santo sitting on the base, and vetiver. Palo santo has the purifying/spiritual quality, and the vetiver has earthy, smoky, and a bit of green notes which add an elegant lasting finish. The two fragrances combined remind one of the smell of sun warmed earth and dry wood, which lastly completes the sense of the great outdoors and boundless sky. Open Sky is a great daytime wear fragrance especially during the warmer months, or any time you want to feel clear-headed and a sense of openness.

First of all, I would like to thank Narcoperfume for the sample; it was once again a cool experience. The opening is quite sharp and piercing at first, not necessarily pleasant, it smells a bit like window cleaner to me, but that subsides after about 2 minutes. The slight fresh sharpness remains, though, which could very well be due to the pomelo, which I can smell for quite a long time here. The pomelo particularly makes the fragrance interesting; you definitely don't smell this every day. After about 20 minutes, the sharpness fades, and what remains is the pomelo with vetiver, pepper, and possibly hemp, which is very faint on my skin, and you have to imagine it more than actually smell it. From here on, the fragrance is very linear, fresh, green, herbal, and a bit citrusy, quite pleasant, but not really special, which one would somewhat expect given the brand and the price point, which is not exactly low. Of course, not every fragrance has to break the mold and distinguish itself from all other works, but then you also shouldn't have to pay over 100 euros to experience such a scent direction and quality. This brings me to the point about the H/S: on me, it is very comparable to Coolwater; it is relatively long-lasting for a fresh scent, but at no point is it really perceivable to others. Even after spraying, you can only smell me from half a meter away, so don't expect any crazy performance here. The advantage of this fragrance: it is wearable for everyone; I would even claim it is unisex, nothing here really feels super masculine. The scent is light and relatively modern, although I would argue that it has a slight vintage touch, especially in the late drydown, where you can smell a herbal freshness that reminds me of aftershave. Conclusion: A solid fresh herbal spring and summer scent with mediocre performance; whether the price is justified for one is something everyone must decide for themselves.

A modern, slightly offbeat fragrance. Pomelo and cannabis that together veer into sharp and green-bitter territory. Fresh, but not clean. To me, Open Sky smells like summer in Amsterdam. Smoke in the street and a vacation vibe. The pomelo quickly tips into the sweaty, but in a good way. Not unkempt, but physical. Like sweaty skin after a hot summer evening. In the drydown, it becomes woodier with vetiver and something resinous, still slightly smoky, but calmer. Open Sky is not a crowd-pleaser; rather, it's a scent for those who enjoy freshness but with a bit of dirtiness. That's exactly what makes it exciting.

This is a really nice fragrance. The notes are probably scaring people away and also the fact that this is exclusive to Galeries Lafayette. Very sexy, warm spicy red rose+pink pepper wrapped around leather with vanilla and amber in the base. Performance is solid too, not beastmode but strong. Sexy!!

A delightful fruity green. Even though it's not listed in the notes, this smells so much of rhubarb. The blackberry is also noticeable, but rhubarb even more so. Both are fresh and tart and only slightly sweetened. The fruitiness feels sparkling and almost thirst-quenching. Imagine drinking a homemade berry lemonade on a meadow in the woods and you're close to Herbae. Despite the name, the greenness in this doesn't feel too herbal, it's rather leafy and a little grassy. I'm not sure what nettles really smell like, I'm afraid to sniff them, so I can't say if that note is really there... But I can say that this is a beautiful summer scent with a slight hint of creamy sweetness in the base. If you want to compare it to other popular fruity scents, this is not as ethereal and sophisticated as a Hermes, but not as sugary as an Escada. It's just uplifting and summery. Strong like, maybe bordering on a love.

Very light and with nonexistent projection, it immediately presents its green notes ,the a certain kind of sourness and acidity that is definitely fresh, almost citrusy, perhaps given by the nettle (almost similar to a lime). My throat certainly felt like I swallowed a slice of lime. Towards the end it warms up and ironically lets out some ambrette (presumably in the top, I did have to wait twenty minutes or so to perceive it). Sweet fruit undetectable by my nose.

Grandpa was always my childhood hero. We visited my grandparents very often, and he had a beautiful large garden. In the summer, the flowers bloomed, the lawn smelled fresh after mowing, and the herbs released a wonderful scent. I often stayed in the garden for hours until the sun went down. Years passed, and unfortunately, Grandma became seriously ill and had to be placed in a nursing home. Grandpa was still fit, so I went shopping with him to distract him. We browsed at L'Occitane, and I sprayed Herbae. Grandpa looked at me: It smells like our garden! You have to buy this scent! Said and done. I bought this wonderful fragrance. Every time I visited Grandpa, I wore it, and he always got a spritz of it too. The scent is simply wonderful to me, smelling of herbs, sunshine, and flowers. It smells like Provence on a spring day. The sweet grass comes through beautifully, and the fruits are a must. I even think I perceive raspberries every time. Time went by, and Grandpa also became a nursing case. During my visits to the nursing home, I sprayed the fragrance, and we reminisced about old times. Grandpa reached a beautiful age and passed away. I often think back to our wonderful time together. Recently, I visited my dear grandparents again at the cemetery. A warm summer breeze blew through my dress-there it was again, Grandpa's garden. Grandpa is just somewhere else, still present for me. He will always remain in my heart. How I wish I could be carefree in the garden again, enjoying the summer. But no one can take my memories away from me, nor the scent. This fragrance touches me deeply, even though it is actually not my usual scent profile. If you're looking for a beautiful summer fragrance, you are in the right place here. Anyone dreaming of summer in Provence, perhaps in a convertible :-) will not be disappointed. It's great that it is still available to buy at L'Occitane.

With a name like Herbae, I think of something herbal, very green without much else. All of this is not "Herbae | L'Occitane en Provence." The opening is very fruity; I can already perceive the blackberry alongside the listed bergamot. But not just the fruits, rather the whole bush including the leaves. This makes the scent not sweet, but rather lightly green - fitting for the color of the bottle. I can also sniff out the sage, which complements the slightly green character very well. The wild rose takes a back seat. Sweet grass also joins in, while the musk fluff can only be detected if you sniff very closely. The scent remains soft, light, and pleasant; it will never be off-putting. It doesn't stand out significantly either (especially since the sillage is quite restrained), but sometimes you don't want that at all, rather just a scent for feeling good. And that is absolutely "Herbae | L'Occitane en Provence" for me. A lovely everyday companion for the office or leisure time; for a big evening appearance, something more substantial would be in order.

Smells to me like riding a bike, freshly showered, with my hair down. Sun on my skin, a breeze of fresh wind, and orange lemonade. Buds are blooming, birds are chirping, and in the air, there’s a sense of a new beginning. I don’t know how L‘Occitane managed to bottle this scent… I wish the world would smell like this in spring.

Since I prefer perfumes accompanied by an aftershave, it was clear to me that this aftershave had to come along with the purchased Eau de Toilette. A truly surprisingly intense aftershave that certainly has a bit longer lasting power. I was surprised by the spray head, which significantly improves the dosing here.

M/mink gives you two choices.  Read the story and believe the myth, or smell the perfume.   I'd recommend smelling perfume.  It's wonderful. The story goes that, in lieu of a traditional brief, the perfumer was asked to translate a block of solid ink into a perfume. I’m cynical enough to believe that this sort of premise is intended more for its ex post facto story value than for any actual artistic impetus. The block of ink might have been a motivating factor in the conceptualization of mink, but it is a fallacy to believe that the perfume continues to be 'about' ink. For the wearer, the ink bit is just a back-story.  After the fact, such stories actually make a perfume appear contrived or a producer pretentious, and to get hooked into this sort of narrative even before you’ve smelled the perfume is limiting for the wearer. Please don't get me wrong. I'm a fan of M/mink. I simply disagree with everything I've ever read about it starting with the PR from Byredo. I don't find it linear. I don't think it's an assault on the senses. I don't find it anything like Sécrétions Magnifiques. It does share a cool, object-like quality with Comme des Garçon 2 Woman. While it does have a matte sweetness to it that suggests an inky quality, this is just one of its many abstract attributes. Like Bvlgari Black by Annick Menardo, M/mink is a successful creation of a new, beautiful scent that neither imitates a botanical scent, nor attempts to to offer you a recognizeable fragrance. from scenthurdle.com

M/Mink is the most original and strange perfume that has passed through my hands, it is rare, but within that rarity, there is an exotic beauty, almost hypnotic, that is difficult to explain. I compare it to the Chihuahua dog breed, the uglier they are, the more we like them, because they seem funnier, because this perfume is the same, despite its eccentricity, not ugliness, it has something that I love and could not say It is, but I like it. It has an almost linear aroma, from the beginning it smells the same, a mixture of natural ink and the fresh sap of a freshly cut plant, a warm and sticky sap, with a lovely resinous tone. I do not know how to explain it, it is complex to describe, it could be one of the most difficult perfumes to explain that I have found. This scent of the beginning, remains almost all the life of the perfume, except that, in the output is very intense and as it develops, it is wrapped by a warm tone, which makes it more warm and enveloping, and very cozy. Sometimes I get the image of a mortar full of plants crushed with a pestle, and that green smell, fresh and undefined, is what floods my nostrils. Others, I smell the ink of my printer, with that metallic touch, I suppose, for the aldehydes, and although the description of the odoriferous sensation is not very cozy, the aroma has something that hooks, it is a subliminal beauty that whispers to you Heard a spell, so that you fall before it. The performance of this perfume is very good, I put it this morning around 9:00, right now it is 6:45 pm and I still perceive it clearly, and wake is not bad at all, being very diffusive from the beginning. It is a nocturnal perfume and cold and temperate climates, winter and autumn could be your best allies, although, on a cold morning, like today, you can enjoy it, perfectly, this goes, according to the tastes of the consumer. A risky perfume and not suitable for everyone, but if you have the opportunity to try it, do not let it pass, because you could find a lost treasure.

The title (the contents of the quotation marks, that is) is a direct copy & paste of the ¯odour descriptor¯ of ~aldoxal~ fræ the data sheet of same of the website of the ~Good Scents Company~. Somehow, I think the notes-list given herein is a little ^incomplete^, to say the least! I'm sure this stuff ^must^ have civet, or something like that, in it. Or oil of cypriol - why didn't I think of that in the first place. Yes, it's a very °oil-of-cypriol-y° 'fume, this one! even if it's not actually that that does it. I was also surprised at how camphoraceous the aroma of this stuff is. I normally ^do not want^ my 'fume to smell camphoraceous; but in this case I'll make an exception: it has so much other °goodies° in it, I'm willing to abide a little ¯camphoraceosity¯! This is pretty-much what I expected (unlike ~Sécretions Magnifique~, by which I am just baffled). It's a thunderously skanky, almost ~industrial~ brew: I think ~industrial skank~ might even be the best figure for it - it is the best I can think of so far; & I unequivocally (apart fræ the camphoraceosity) love it. It ^does indeed^ thoroughly requite its ~controversial~ label.

My taste is the opposite of edgy. I once bought a set of that Ephemera Sound perfumes - you know, the ones that smell like burned-out electrical sockets and plastic sheeting - and sold it on as quickly as was decent. I don't ever want to smell Secretions Magnifiques, not out of intellectual curiosity, not even as an exercise to expand my olfactory knowledge, and definitely not by accident. But I like M/Mink. I had smelled it once before, in Rome in 2013, just when I was beginning to get into fragrances and I really liked it. Two years on, reacquainting myself with it in Senteurs d'Aillheurs in Belgium, I found it extraordinary - a salt-encrusted, honey-lacquered door in an abandoned building in a post-industrial city. If perfume has a color, this is a sort of matte buff-nude-tan thing. There's a fair amount of anchovy paste in this, too - a metallic saltiness that is really quite objectionable, but very arresting. Reviews for M/Mink tend to paint it as either genius or the most disgusting smell in the world (up there with Secretions Magnifiques), but this is a perfume that depends on the specific set of olfactory memories we all carry around in our heads. So where many people pick up on a horrendous stench of fruity bleach in the topnotes, I smell only the clean, fishy stink of calligraphy ink and toner fluid from the school supplies closet. The high-toned, metallic bleach/ink note is followed by a denatured patchouli, by which I mean patchouli that has been leached of its damp, earthy nuances and made into a dry, unsweet dust, casting a glum, matte brown, stale-cocoa powder like shade over the whole thing. Incense too, but this is not the ecclesiastical smoke that cleanses the soul during mass. This is the cold, dead air creeping among the vestments and flagstones in the sacristy. Rather like Messe de Minuit, another perfume that smells like dead, inert air in a sacristy, it reminds me of my Catholic childhood. Not of high mass, but of the ordinary, day-to-day dealings I would have had in the church, which was located across from my school and played a huge role in our lives. This part of M/Mink reminds me being in and out of the sacristy before doing a reading for Sunday mass, or helping the priest fold away his amice. It smells like creeping mold, dust, inert air. The likeable stench of centuries-old church things. What creates this mold effect? It must be the combination of metallic incense with that dry, matte-brown patchouli dust, and unsweet honey and beeswax. I don't know though. It's a mysterious alchemy, how all of these alive, moving elements combine to produce a smell that is so stale, so centuries-dead.

Being in the full wave of experimentalism, and since this kind of attitude is hardly backed by the chance of sample-smelling, this was a blind buy (as was the case with Secretions Magnifique by ELDO). To be clear: I’m not one of those inexhaustibly worshipping Byredo fans. So, back to us, this frag «is not for the uninitiated». On paper and on my skin is two different stories. On paper, it opens strongly uric, pretty repulsive, to quickly turn into salty and floral notes (which then stay till the end). On my skin, it’s pure ink (I used to work in publishing facilities, and M/MINK reminds me of the mixed smell of ink and solvents from the printing film developing machines). There’s a floral touch from time to time, but it’s subtle and powdery. I can’t say it’s unwearable, but you need to exactly know when and why.

We all know Uncle Darwin and his slogan "Survival of the fittest." So, the organisms that adapt best to their environment survive, while those poorly adapted have little chance of survival. School psychology likes to slap the label "schizophrenic" on highly creative people from time to time. What is classified as a disease in our culture is celebrated in other cultures.

My first encounter with M/Mink was in January, and my reaction at the time when testing it in the perfumery was rather - how can one describe it? - dismissive. Somehow, I found the scent fascinating on the strip, yet simultaneously repulsive. What the fragrance definitely achieves is being completely different from what scents in perfumeries should be.

A visit to the Breuninger department store in Nuremberg. Unbeknownst to me, I greet my acquaintance at the BB Counter and chat about this and that. We get onto the topic of niche fragrances, and I excitedly share my passion for perfume. So far, so good. "I have a fragrance for you that you absolutely must try!

M/Mink is the 3rd Byredo fragrance that I got to know and - thanks, but no thanks. By now, I am familiar with plenty of polarizing scents, most of which are somewhat wearable with some reservations, but a few (e.g. Secretions Magnifiques by Etat libre d'Orange) are absolutely and completely not, "no-go", totally repulsive and nauseating. M/Mink comes close to that.

When I sprayed M/Mink earlier, I closed my eyes and immediately thought of the Roman steam bath in the Bartholomäustherme. Now I know what the bath attendants use to scent the steam. M/Mink! I perceive fresh pine wood with all sorts of fir needles and juniper berries as the opening scent.

Some fragrances from L'Occitane I really like, but this one hits me rather negatively. The fragrance pyramid reads, for me as an oriental junkie, almost perfectly. But what my nose detected was no art. Alcoholic opening, total, synthetic sandalwood bombardment, plastic amber and... That’s it. Eventually, the alcohol faded away and then it was just pure sandalwood. But not the fine, balsamic-warm-wonderful kind, no, still this synthetic bombardment. I am olfactorily very resistant, but here I almost got a headache. On me, it smells rather terrible, but on a friend, it smells as the pyramid might suggest. Therefore, there’s still a healthy middle ground in the rating.

At first, a strong burst of spicy sweet vanilla with floral notes. After about half an hour, a green-floral note joins in with a leathery-sweet undertone. The aforementioned notes gradually fade, revealing a dark woody base tone that can counterbalance the overly eager vanilla and create a good equilibrium. A skin-close sillage with really good longevity: For fans of spicy woody vanilla fragrances! For me personally, it's too vanilla-heavy, sandalwood notes are rather found in the background, hence for me 50%.

With a delicate spray from the simple yet beautiful bottle, I am transported back 8 years to Denmark with my parents. It is autumn, almost winter, and we have been wandering along the beach all afternoon. Now we sit by the warm fire in the cozy living room of our landlady, who has known my parents for a long time. She hands us a glass filled with collected amber, and I marvel: How beautifully warm and golden it looks, like autumn sunshine captured in a glass. I feel cozy, tired, secure, and snuggle up to my mother. How good she smells! - It is sandalwood oil and a hint of something else warm and sweet-spicy. Time jump, 2013... Our little family, my husband, our daughter, and I are at the Baltic Sea, it is kite festival. The wind blows icy cold and strong, and after a day full of fun and movement, we sit inside by the fireplace, the fire crackling and glowing golden. We cuddle up in warm, soft blankets. My daughter snuggles against me and sleepily murmurs: “Mama, you smell so nice!” It is Ambre & Santal by L'Occitane. I usually don't have strong color associations with a fragrance, but here it was immediately clear: honey-amber-gold! Warm, soft, gentle, golden.... Right after spraying, I get the warm “golden shower,” soft, slightly sweet, but also spicy resin and gentle woods. I seem to be a bit blind to the top notes, as I only catch a fleeting whiff of bergamot and rosemary. The rose is also very, very subtle in the background, which doesn't bother me, as I love this “golden shower.” It envelops me distinctly, but gently like a soft blanket. It is warm and soft, spicy and slightly sweet, but never cloying. The scent is balanced, immediately “there,” and stays that way. It has a very subtle sillage, but please don’t spray too much, as the scent is very present up close! After about 4 hours, I notice the sandalwood more distinctly, and a hint of vanilla pleasantly sneaks into my nose. Mmmm, lovely! The longevity is decent; after over 12 hours, it still smells fine, sandalwood-spicy-light-vanilla. Ambre & Santal is definitely unisex, and it will be my (our!) autumn and winter cuddle scent!

So this is what it smells like to me it's synthetic but pleasant? it's aldehydic but it doesn't send your nose hair flying it's clean but it's not sterile it's soapy and powdery but it doesn't choke you up it's quite musky and creamy in a laudry detergent way but not screechy at all there's no edge no sharpness here just laundry hanging on a line soaking up the sun, there's a gentle warmth to it. It is so polite and inoffensive one might even say it's boring but I want to paint you a picture, it is the sort of scent that conjure this feeling of waking in the morning after a good night sleep on your day off knowing you could indulge in your freshly washed bedsheet and blanket just a little bit more, the ad campaign byredo did for blanche absolu convey the scent and the sort of feeling you get from the perfume very well. Lazy saturday morning perhaps? it's better because you know you have another day off tomorrow.

Laundrette Deluxe. Luxury laundromat. Baccarat Rouge with fresh fabric softener vibes. This is exactly what I expected after reading the statements here. And I was not disappointed! (Thank goodness, at that price...) Blanche and Baccarat Rouge come together in this fragrance to create a truly beautiful laundry masterpiece. Clearly recognizable to me are the beloved floral-soft and creamy peony-violet notes known from the Blanche EDP, along with the crisp-fresh aldehydes, although these take a bit of a backseat for a touch more Ambroxan and Cashmeran. Yes, you can definitely recognize (especially a few hours later) the modern DNA of the woody-floating-synthetic character of Ambroxan and Cashmeran. You have to like it; I find it elegant in any case. The longevity is really very good, and I have already received compliments for it. This is Blanche Absolu just as it was advertised - a luxury version of the iconic laundry scent with more sexiness. Still clean, but significantly more skin is shown.

This is a bright spring/summer wonder! A very white floral heavy fragrance. In the opening the citrus shows up until very quickly the tuberose takes the show and dominates. After a few more minuts the rest of the white florals with orange blossom gives it this bubblegummy effect and in the drydown the milk note gives it this beautiful warmth and together with the sandalwood and musk you get this dreamy cozy scent. Don't overspray or the tuberose might give you headaches! Another banger from this house, uplifting beautiful fragrance, feminine but a guy can wear it too.

Rose 4 Reines (i prefer Eau des 4 Reines, though) is marketed as a rose soliflore that features 4 different roses (french, bulgarian, turkish and moroccan, which are actually 2 types, one centifollia and 3 damascenas, so i better say 4 origin denominations) so one would expect a very intense rose experience. Thats what i expected and, well, Rose 4 Reines is indeed a very rose centered fragance but i wouldn´t remark the intensity or the beauty of the rose here, to be completely honest. Basically i don´t enjoy the approach to this ingredient. Not every rose soliflore is my personal taste, like Diptyque´s Eau Rose or Goutal´s Ce Soir Ou Jamais (compared to some beloved roses like Frederic Malle´s or Perfumer Workshop´s roses) but they are well done and the rose is beautifully portayed and enhanced. Not the case of this 4 slumbering (perhaps drunk?) queens. Rose is there, all the time, but smells kind of dimmed under a thick layer of powder and a slightly skunky musk. Truly a very conventionally femenine, boudouir type of fragance. A touch of violet pastilles, slightly cosmetic (ylang?) and definitely a very warm, almost ambery approach to the rose note that makes it not very suitable for the warmer seasons. Therefore, not a very fresh rose, and not a trace of the promised green opening (i have experienced this with other L´Occitane fragances, the opening notes are really thin and fleeting) and definitely lacking the depth, intensity and multiple facets that this rose compilation promises. Is it regal? i guess you can say that, if for you regal means boring. On its favour, very good longevity and diffusion.

I quite like this little rose interpretation by L'Occitane. Although the rose note is dominant, it's not a soliflore. Other interesting notes that make up this fragrance's composition are, powdery violets, smooth heliotrope and musty cedarwood. I've come to love this fragrance due to its rather subtle nature. Some rose scents tend to be overpowering, but this fragrance keeps it soft and simple. It smells feminine and fresh on the skin, with a slight Spring-like aura, which makes it suitable for those beautiful, sunny days. Some reviewers have noted a fruity accord which tends to compliment the rose throughout. I'm not so certain that it's fruits or citruses that I smell, but more likely the crisp roses creating a somewhat tarty finish on the skin. The heart and drydown are both clean but one-dimensional, with soft roses and slightly powdery violets on a rich cedar base. You won't be blown away by Eau de 4 Reines, but you should be pleased. The scent is certainly pleasant and refreshing. I do enjoy wearing Eau de 4 Reines for the most part, although I must admit that occasionally I desire something a little more complex. For days when I struggle to choose what to wear, Eau de 4 Reines is a good and safe choice. The sillage and longevity are average, but definitely not disappointing. I'm happy that I've tried this one.

I appreciate this rose perfume is fresh and woody and not too sweet. Violet and heliotrope are faint and soft. I'm not too fond of rose soliflor perfumes but I like this one in spring mornings. Clean, formal and austere without being dated or too cold. Longevity is around six hours and sillage is soft to moderate

I have had this fragrance for over two years and I love it very much. It is my favorite rose scent from L'Occitane and is definitely one of my top rose favorites. Just like Rose 4 Reines, it smells like real, white roses. Very delicate, green, with only minimal sweetness and a fairy-like aura. Simply wonderful. The sillage is fine, but good enough to provide a nice projection. Wrapped in this fragrance, every day somehow looks rosier, as it lasts very well. An absolute pleasure fragrance and a MUST for rose lovers!

Roses 4 Reines by L'OCCITANE was introduced to me by an old perfume seller who recommended rose fragrances to me back then. I was looking for Rose von Montfort Vienna, a scent from the sixties/seventies that apparently no one knows. He knew it... and was surprised where I had such an ancient perfume (I had the bottle with me). This nice old gentleman had a charming little perfumery with dark wooden floors and a lovely atmosphere. The old-fashioned wooden floors reminded me of the first half of the last century. At least five or six years ago, he closed his shop and retired. It's such a shame that this perfumery no longer exists! The seller must be around seventy by now. He gave me a test strip of this fragrance, which I kept for a long time in a perfume lexicon. I only bought the fragrance a few years ago, unfortunately not in his lovely shop. If I had been as perfume-obsessed back then as I am today, I would have loved to chat with the nice gentleman more often. Rose 4 Reines is a light and fresh scent that revolves entirely around the rose, as the name suggests. It is dedicated to the scent essences of four types of roses: the French Grasse rose, the Bulgarian rose, the Turkish rose, and the Moroccan rose. Unfortunately, I don't know as much about the different types of roses from a botanical perspective as others here. But I do know one thing: I like roses in various forms. So the scent smells of fresh, delicate roses, yet it is strong enough to perceive the roses clearly. I also detect a bit of violet leaf, without the fragrance going in a powdery direction. It remains fresh and not musty at all. A hint of cedar adds a touch of spice, just a little. Heliotrope sweetens it ever so slightly. All in all, the scent remains very natural with a light fragrance character. I find it fits well in autumn and spring, as that is when, at least for me, the roses can unfold best. With too much or too little warmth (I need to test that again), it develops a slightly bitter note (tea?), which I personally don't like much. It could last a bit longer on the skin. On clothing, it lasts at least a day. On myself, maybe three to four hours. In the meantime, the EdT has been discontinued, but it has been re-released as EdP "4 Reines". I am glad that I got to know this beautiful rose fragrance.

For a long time, I have been searching for the perfect rose scent. The rose is my favorite flower, which is mainly due to its majestic appearance and its fragrance. However, I fear that I will never find the absolutely perfectly crafted rose scent. They all smell somewhat synthetic. The scent of fruits, on the other hand, often comes very close to the originals.

About 5 years ago, my mom (she's a bit of a L'Occitane junkie) made one of her obligatory orders again, and I decided to try the Rose 4 Reines - shampoo, which was also on sale at the time. It arrived - and I found the rose scent to be quite overpowering right from the start - but of course, I tried it anyway.

The scent of the rose casts a sweet spell on you, gently caressing you softly, like a melody, touching you with a sense of full beauty. Hermann Hesse This dark red rose blooms and scents itself in competition with its sisters. It smells floral, fresh, these roses are slightly sweet.

A beautiful, fresh rose fragrance that lacks the heaviness often found in rose scents, as it leans more towards a fresh-green-light direction: The rose note is present but does not overwhelm, and sweet, heavy additional notes like musk or vanilla are absent. Even in the drydown, there are no balsamic-sweet notes sneaking in, only the slightly bitter woodiness of cedar.
