Green is a compillation of green (duh) (Well it is not my fault they didn´t bleed to death thinking for a name) floral clean notes that somehow have a very warm, enveloping effect instead of being chilly and invigorating as i expected. Think more of new tendrils rather than dark forests. Green smells very clean and there is nothing wrong with it. I mean, the ingredients don´t feel "chemical" at all, nevertheless i support the opinion that Green reminds of a very nice smelling home-care/body-care product. I quite enjoy shampoo-like perfumes if they are well done, so it is not an issue for me. The fragance starts very grassy and sparkling and then it gets more delicate and sweeter. With the petitgrain i smell something like linden. It is green, but it oozes nectar too. The slight metallic buzz of violet leaves is mainly the responsible for Green´s green-ness, being softened by delicious honeysuckle, but also a light rose, closer to rosewater than to rose oil. As the fragance evolves, mild touches of bitterness from green almonds arise and along the calming tonka define a very confortable drydown, and never looses completely its leafy, spring-like nature. Maybe because it smells so clean and foamy it is perfectly suitable both for women, men and i am thinking, it could be a great choice for children, because it has this innocent vibe (and in Spain at least we soak children in cologne) and absolutely not a shadow. Just loving tendrils, wild flowering vines and soap bubbles.

I love the bright and crisp petit grain opening of Byredo GREEN. After a few minutes, the scent smells closer to an organic green cleaning product, but somehow it does not become a scrubber. Am I being slowly indoctrinated into the "clean" perfumery movement? I have to wonder, because I do not really think that this smells like anything more than the scent added to such cleaning products. I would like to use this to clean my bathroom, but I also do not mind it on my skin. I guess that I am ultimately conflicted about Byredo GREEN. I should not like it, but I sort of do... Would I pay $200+ to smell like this? In a word: No.

I am at the swimming pool. (imagine February gone!) The sun is blazing. I'm sitting soaking wet on my straw mat and craving a Perlipop. (ok, I haven't been to the swimming pool in a while) Mom had said at home: 'Make sure to apply sunscreen well after swimming!' Yes, I do that too, and with delial SPF fifteen, the yellow bottle! That exact sunscreen note accompanies me in Green for about two hours. Only after that, when the silly associations of the super slide, where you always had to adjust your swimsuit into position, and Kai Tobolewski finally stops constantly dunking you, are gone, does the scent transform into a true, still green delight... but with vanilla, with almonds and the many colorful little balls from the Perlipop! :) ______________ edit Aug. 2011: A very clear hay note like in L'Été en Douce by L'Artisan.

Green, green, green, is some of what I have Why do I like some things that are green, because the color somehow suits me well. O. k., that doesn't really rhyme, but I don't really care, because it fits this Byredo quite well. This Byredo simply smells really good on me. There's nothing to complain about. The top note is pleasantly distinctive and has a clear green fragrance statement. I particularly like that a certain freshness has been created here, without citrus notes. With the heart note, the green hue diminishes a bit. Here, the honeysuckle and rose pleasantly define the scent. The jasmine and violet remain subtly in the background. However, the fragrance still retains a green tint, which is now slowly becoming a bit more pastel and creamy. With the base, a subtle sweetness emerges; I wouldn't necessarily call the note sweet. A delicate almond note resonates here at the beginning and reminds me of the taste of green April almonds. The musk adds a fine soapy note and somewhat tempers the tonka bean. Since most have torn apart the scent here, I would like to praise it over the green clover. Green is, for me, a very successful composition that, despite a harmonious fragrance progression, still exhibits a pleasant awkwardness and presents the color theme green in various shades. The longevity is superb, and the intensity is extremely pleasant. I am noticed, but without claiming the entire room for myself. This one is definitely going on my Christmas wish list.

Today is already the third green fragrance that I have had the pleasure of testing thanks to Lila. Green fragrances can be incredibly different. I could not have imagined such a wealth of facets. Green by Byredo initially smells exactly like herbal Nivea cream, as my predecessors have similarly noted. I really like the creaminess and am initially quite taken with the Nivea note. Unfortunately, I don't know what happens next, as the fragrance develops a bitterness and smokiness on my skin that sadly destroys the beautiful Nivea note. It smells a bit like herbs during a drying process in the oven when they have been left in for too long. I can only attribute this to the sage. Anyone who has ever sucked on unsweetened sage candies, which taste more bitter than good, will find that flavor here in the fragrance.. Unfortunately, I no longer like the fragrance because of this. It still smells interesting and unusual, but there are better fragrances in the green category.

In summary, one could say that Byredo Green smells like a mix of Cologne and Nivea cream: At the start, there is an overwhelming dose of Petitgrain, which, in my opinion, comes across as anything but green. Petitgrain smells very similar to Neroli (orange blossom), so it is more floral than green (even though it is extracted from leaves and stems).

The comment below me fits. Cologne and Nivea. But even more fitting for me is perfumed cream soap. And so intensely that you smell like you've just bathed in aftershave and slathered with Nivea from miles away, and that's just from one test spray. It's a strange scent, and I can't say whether I like it or not.

In my search for my summer fragrance, I stumbled upon Byredo Green. For me, after the first sniff, it was very, very green. After that, it develops on my skin into a creamy and milky scent, and I found it to be very intense. After 15 minutes, I felt like the scent was overwhelming me, and if I sniffed my wrist again, I would get a headache.

After my last comment was written an eternity ago, I want to try to express my thoughts on various fragrances more regularly... here we go. Green starts off very pleasantly fresh with an artificial citrus note for me. My first association is crumb tea (that instant tea drink with lemon flavor).

Green: A green, fresh start, I can very finely detect a hint of sage. It stays relatively long like this until the other ingredients blend into a creamy base that I have never sniffed in this form before. Those who enjoy delicious, creamy scents should definitely try Green. I tell you: This stuff is addictive. Hypnose Senses also develops a cream note, but Green is different.

To be honest i was so suprised that i read that this one is a kind of citrusy scent. I really don’t smell any citrus fruit. I just smell kind af a peper and thats the good point because im not i to citrus perfumes. Anyway this is sooo les lasting ( like many byredo perfumes) its almost gone in 1 hour so if you are i to long lasting/ great silage perfumes. Skip this one. And what about the scent. Hmmm i just smell peper and only pepper

Well, Palermo doesn't really make loud or even noisy scents. It's a rather gentle fragrance from a stylish brand. Somehow the name doesn't quite fit... because before one thinks of the beautiful island and its southern fruits, one rather thinks of well-organized "big families" that have a lot to do with pride, honor, and respect. But maybe that hasn't reached Sweden yet... or perhaps the spread was halted when they found out that Abba, Roxette, Ikea, and Ace of Base also come from Sweden... I don't know. Now I do know that the top note of Mister Marvelous and Bullion is no coincidence. Rather, it seems to be the Guerlainade of Sweden. This seems to slowly become a trademark... at least for the fresh scents of the brand. Palermo is zesty-citrusy in the first minutes, slightly bitter from bitter orange/grapefruit and a big scoop of bergamot. The citrus kings of Atelier Colognes can't do much better than this. It's mega refreshing, slightly spicy, and unripe-green. The counterpart that comes to the forefront after a few minutes is a totally delicious musk. There's nothing new in this combination, nor is it particularly exciting or innovative... but it can still please time and again. Where the roses or even the rose absolute are supposed to be, I can't say for the life of me! Maybe I've gotten used to a completely different dose of rose by now, and the scent stimulation is too little for my nose. But even on Swedish shelves, parts are sometimes missing or there's too much in it... let's take it easy! Speaking of relaxation, Palermo is excellent for meditation... because not much more happens with the scent... meaning you don't have to worry about a possible development... you can close your eyes and wonderfully switch off your mind. But as a complete fragrance, Palermolino doesn't excite me or even inspire me to make a purchase. Even though I'll never find out, they surely have something like this at the Body Shop... for a fifth of the price. The longevity is not bad at all with 3-4 hours, as the scent notes would suggest, but even in summer, it's too little for me. The sillage barely deserves the category "close to the skin"... which isn't really surprising. Better to buy Mister Marvelous and layer it with Musk Man from the Body Shop... then you have both.

The topic of lemon in perfume is, in my opinion, quite a challenging one! As with any fragrance direction, individual tastes vary greatly here. What delights some can be horrendous to others, and vice versa. For my fragrance taste, Palermo is unfortunately just horrendous, boring, and it lasts exactly from here to our bathroom door (about 5 m). It consists, so to speak, only of a top note. Barely sprayed, a piercingly sour synthetic lemon scent spreads with the charm of dish soap. Once this has faded, the sour misery comes to an end altogether. My kitchen soap, used to remove unpleasant food odors, lasts five times longer and the lemon scent is far more refined than the smell of Palermo. I won’t go on about which lemon perfumes I prefer and why. Every fool likes his cap..... In the case of Palermo, sour does not make me laugh at all, and now I know why Mr. Riebmann lives between the walls. He wanted to escape the sour smell.

I am already a bit of a fan of Byredo, both of individual outstanding and often polarizing creations like Pulp or Bal d'Afrique, as well as the cool and super modern style. However, Palermo definitely takes this minimalism too far, consisting basically of a top note, albeit a beautiful one, and is therefore not even remotely worth the demanded price. The top note is, as mentioned, beautiful, saves the perfume, and refreshes very successfully after physical activity. Zesty vetiver, pomelo, a summery lightness from petitgrain and musk, as even Creed cannot achieve. A radiant yellow-green-white with recognizability due to quality that is beyond reproach. Now I will describe the heart and base: Bottle: Palermo on a white background - appeals to me as a half-Italian... Sillage: I can’t stop laughing... but within the first 20 minutes, you have the chance to receive compliments with greeting kisses... Of course, that’s not enough for me! Longevity: with 2 hours, a record low is set in this price range! One of the most disappointing creations of the brand, because fortunately the own standards are now very high (both from Byredo and from me) and also because all the powder is shot within the 30-head minutes!
Light, summery, and predominantly a citrus-musk blend for my nose. However, it does say so :) It strongly reminds me of H. Lehmann's New York. Pleasant.

(After a long time, finally taking the time again) Kinsale is a small harbor town in the south of the Irish Republic. For me, as a history enthusiast, Kinsale is always worth a visit. In 1601, the Battle of Kinsale resulted in a defeat for the Irish-Spanish alliance against the English, but even afterwards, Kinsale remained a gateway for European powers because Ireland, due to its location, always invited attempts to conquer the neighboring island. Over time, two forts were built in Kinsale to stop the expansionist ambitions of the Spanish and French. The most famous fort is Charles Fort, an imposing structure and supposedly one of the "Most Haunted Buildings" (which I unfortunately experienced myself), opposite lies James Fort, commissioned by King James due to the battle in 1602, which, according to description, blew up in 1645 because one of the soldiers lit a pipe in the powder magazine during his watch. How does this bring me to Eau de Cédrat? Quite simply. Anyone who wants to visit James Fort must walk through Kinsale along the harbor and the bay. When they are almost at the beach, they turn left over a bridge, then go left again towards the fort, passing a hill covered with gorse. Gorse, which can be found everywhere in Ireland, has yellow flowers when it blooms. It can be seen from afar, the hill shines yellow. This is exactly what I am reminded of when I spray Eau de Cédrat. Bergamot and lemon form the beginning, and even if it is said to smell artificial, I must admit that I do not have that impression. After a short time, I smell nutmeg, until cedar and cashmere wood give the fragrance a spicy warmth (sounds silly, right?). Normally a scent for summer, I actually bought it for that purpose last year, but I must confess that I wear it practically all year round. In fact, besides Eau de Cédrat, Eau de Cologne (which I have wanted to write about for a long time) and Eau de Baux are my current favorites. I like this simplicity, well-crafted fragrances, simply constructed and, as I find, produced with natural scent materials and not these sweet synthetic bombs that can now be found in abundance and that essentially only differ by name. Added to this are the simple and plain bottles. One is reminded of old pharmacies or barbershops, where the barber would ask the customer which scent he preferred after shaving and then reach for a shelf with these simple brown bottles, pouring the liquid generously into his hand and gently massaging the customer's face. Maybe I am becoming senile with age, or developing into a green sectarian, I don't know, but I like this simplicity, especially since I work in IT, where everything has to be fast and the surroundings become more colorful and ostentatious. There is the Slow Food movement, maybe it's time for Slow Smell...

I can't really understand the classification of the scent as citrus-fresh. Cedrat starts off quite lushly synthetic citrus, similar to the citron used for baking, but for me, it is by no means fresh. Alongside the citron, there is already something dull, almost cloyingly sweet, which does not come across as fresh at all, but rather has gourmand qualities, making it feel cozy to me. The scent progression, if one can even speak of that here, is quite linear. The initially lush citron note dissipates quite quickly, revealing the pronounced dull sweet-woody base, which weakens over the course of 4-5 hours and fades close to the skin. Linking the citron with almost gourmand notes is something one has to appreciate. Overall, it feels somehow unusual, quite idiosyncratic, and unsuitable for summer. But perhaps it is precisely this idiosyncrasy that is the allure of the scent. For me, Cedrat is a "transitional scent" between the cold and warm seasons. As a nice gimmick, L'Occitane has given the bottle the look/texture of the cedrat.

What is an authentic citrus scent? What does that even mean? Do you even want that? Is it achievable? How do fresh lemons smell? Do you smell the juice, the flesh, the peel? All together? What is the best citrus scent? Does a citrus scent have to be complex, or the opposite? Am I spending more than 100€ for a light lemon bomb? Is the market flooded with summer fragrances? Am I saturated? Are there still surprises? Does everyone see a different perfect citrus fruit? Is Eau de Cedrat a good scent? Does L'Occitane maintain its high reputation with me? All these were questions that crossed my mind while testing the new L'Occitane perfume for summer 2015. Undoubtedly one of the refreshing highlights of the year, for the price you can't go wrong with the bottle reminiscent of CK One summer flankers & at the same time a lemon. However, the new nonplusultra is unfortunately not the scent in terms of lemon refreshment for me - I found the new Atelier Cologne Pomelo Paradis much more impressive & special, even more natural. But that's all a matter of taste or subjective perception - my predecessor rightly found his summer scent 2015 with Eau de Cedrat & made a great blind purchase, for me it just didn't completely click, there was no urge to buy, which could very well have happened at that price. Eau de Cedrat is a modern summer scent, full of lemon & sparkling refreshment, for summer, office & after showering. However, the lemon didn't seem so natural to me, more like lemon-lime & incredibly fizzy at the beginning - that's by far my favorite part of the scent, because it doesn't always have to be authentic & boring. How it sparkles in the nose, it's insane! The scent consists of fizz, high-quality lemon shampoo &... sweet woods in the noticeably thick base. A successful blend of Bergamot 22 & Eau de Fleurs de Cedrat by Guerlain - just with the naturalness, the light, but this time cool eco- & FairTrade flair of L'Occitane. Very fluffy, soft, not aggressive & surely always pleasant to wear. Unfortunately, nothing after the top note excites me as much as this, and I can't really make connections to 24 Gold or even M7. Although to M7 Fresh, I can relate a little again. Bottle: a mix of typical L'Occitane & a lemon - sour makes funny?! Sillage: Longevity: better, a fleshy, quite heavy base (for a summer scent) contributes to at least 6-7 hours. Conclusion: L'Occitane once again shows how to combine quality, individuality (and that in such a worn-out genre!) & a fair price. Let the rating be a rating & believe me: it's worth testing!

I didn't expect too much this time. Not after all the criticism from certain noses whose judgment I greatly respect. Noses that expressed their disappointment over mainstream mediocrity, over boredom and lack of edge, over a Byredo that didn't smell like Byredo. That didn't sound good, it didn't sound like Ben Gorham, the man who gave "Gypsy Water" and "Baudelaire" that soul that fascinates me again and again. Ben Gorham and I got along well, at least until now. Should that really change this time? The content of my sample is concentrated, much of the alcohol has evaporated. What remains is almost just the pure oil. So I was cautious in the test, careful with the dosage, one spray was enough, distributed on wrists, skin, and hair. It didn't take more to encounter Ben Gorham in this scent, which probably didn't become a bestseller, which is nowhere in the collection, that I only found in one shop - and yet it is certainly not a cash model, not an olfactory nose bicycle, which I would never wear voluntarily. Bitter dark fruit opens day after day on my skin, enveloped, underlaid with wood and smoke - "Pulp" comes to mind, immediately and again, the fermented-bitter fruit that places certain demands on the wearer. I would also guess black currant this time, authentically sour-bitter with fruit and green and brown, but that is not listed and juniper - well, the bitter woodiness fits. Unlike in "Pulp," however, nothing is fermented here, the fruits are embedded in dark, hard wood with smoke and leather, which again directs the thought to "Tuscan Leather." That is a bit irritating, I admit, because it doesn't fit into the pyramid, doesn't match the texts that can be read, and perhaps only happens on my skin. "Oliver Peoples" comes across as very mature, yet not strict or dark - unlike in "Tuscan Leather," the smoke here is transparent, it doesn't dominate the fruit but rather enhances it. At some point, sometimes half an hour earlier, sometimes later, a hint of barbershop joins in - shaving foam, freshly fluffed, almost carried by, never present. Nothing at all is pushy in "Oliver Peoples," nothing is loud, noisy, or intrusive - you perceive the scent, it turns the noses to the wind, it brings the man by my side closer, but it doesn't flood a room, doesn't surround me like a cloud, doesn't carry banners and fanfares before me. That makes it very pleasant for me, I would wear it well beyond this test - if I could get it... Ben Gorham or Jérôme Epinette hasn't reinvented the wheel, neither the olfactory nor the one on my nose. He has quoted himself and at the same time Tom Ford, which many before him did and will continue to do. That's a bit of a shame, as it comes at the expense of his independence, but he hasn't presented a truly bad scent with "Oliver Peoples," and "boring" would certainly not be an adjective I would use in this case. And I'm sure that it's not just due to the concentrate. PS: Puck1 - thank you!

Byredo's collaboration with eyewear manufacturer Oliver Peoples starts off fruity sweet. It then transitions into a warm, powdery, fruity sweetness. On top of that lies what is commercially referred to as a warm sand accord. Quite interesting, actually, but forced, and not well integrated into the very small whole. A modern fragrance that aims to please everyone and doesn’t want to go wrong. No complicated scent development that confuses unnecessarily. Flacon design matching the fragrance? Who cares! The main thing is that everyone finds the right color for their glasses frame. Masculine? Feminine? Unisex, of course! This broadens the target audience. Indifferent and banal. So always and everywhere wearable. Meaningless and boring. Perfect for the office.

Here it is, this extremely rare Limited Edition, consisting of 75 ml of AS and EdT at a very fair price. I personally can't remember ever crossing paths with this colleague in the 80s/90s. Thanks to this community (Nasenmann and Hordak), I have now been able to fill this gap. Release year probably before 1993? Quite certain, as it was distributed by Eurocos, noted here with a four-digit postal code, and just in 1993, postal codes in Germany became five digits. So we are most likely dealing with a variant of the first Boss men's fragrance (before it was renamed Boss Number One), thus with the original formulation. And here comes the big surprise. The term "Concentrated" is initially misleading. One would spontaneously expect a "puffed-up," even louder version, but that's far from the case: "Concentrated" should be taken literally here. What is offered is a kind of essence, in which the bright and loud notes of the original fragrance have been toned down, creating a much more harmonious scent progression due to the absence of the peaks. Also, longevity and sillage are nowhere near as frightening as with the 1985 version. For those who find the original too honey- and patchouli-heavy (which I can totally understand), I recommend giving this fragrance a sniff, which emphasizes the spicy and woody-leathery notes without denying or distorting the DNA of the "standard version." Unfortunately, "Limited" here also means exactly what it implies, as Boss Concentrated is now almost impossible to find.

Even though the word "vanille" is right there in the name, this one is sooooo smooth and balanced that I suspect it might appeal to even the vanilla-aversed among us, both male and female, because this vanilla is so down-to-earth and non-girly. No cupcakes, cookies or vanilla extract here. Tonka bean and vanilla provide a natural smelling base for subtle amounts of bergamot, black current and floral notes to intermingle and complement one another in such a way that, had I not seen the list of notes, I would not have been able to guess them except for the vanilla, tonka and bergamot. Even though it's designated as unisex, I feel it leans enough toward the masculine that it could easily have been marketed exclusively to men, due in part, I'm guessing, to the bergamot, which always seems to impart a touch of cool freshness, and is so commonly found in men's fragrances. With only a couple dabs to my wrists, I detect the subtle smoothness of this scent all day long, so it does indeed behave like an EDP. I am enjoying my sample very much, but I would prefer to smell this on a man rather than on myself. It seems timeless, as though it would feel right on anyone from a trendy 20-something to my dad, if he were still around. Classy, is what I guess I'm trying to say. I like it a lot. Edit: several years later, rediscovering my sample vial in a bathroom drawer. Now it reminds me of Shalimar. And, alas, it has been discontinued.

It's a good thing the Occitane lady told me this is discontinued: as soon as I found out about that, I had to have one. At first, I liked the perfume but was not blown away. On second try, the vanilla became much more prominent and a little smoky. It comes our right at the beginning and the narcissus opens up in the heart. I love the way the vanilla and narcissus play up one another. The scent is smooth, flowery but not overwhelming.

La Collection de Grasse included 4 new fragances which are rather nice, but quite forgettable too, with the exception of Vanille & Narcisse, which is the only one i would consider purchasing. This is unusual for me, since i am not a huge admirer of vanilla-centered fragances, specially if they are too sweet or fluffy. In the case of Vanille & Narcisse, the vanilla note is probably closer to the "fermented orchid" than to the dessert ingredient and it is not overpowering at all. So this perfect balance between the vanilla and the narcissus where both boost each other instead or being one the supporter of the other, fulfills the aspirations of L´Occitane when they say they pursued a fusion of exotic and autocthonous ingredients, being the narcissus the french one. Narcissus, a note that in my opinion was not used as much as it deserves (because i love it) has been the focus of several recent launches, starting with the TF Jonquille de Nuit, and then the (stunning) Eau de Narcisse Bleu of Hermes, Nest´s limited White Narcissus, a Diptyque candle and now this. It is a sensual, cheeky fragance from the beginning. Narcissus is handsomely featured and smells natural. This flower that stands on the crossroad of the green and the animalic, veers to the warmth of the white flower. Vanilla is the one to blame,and a touch of creamy carnality of gardenia that is really hard to catch by itself, since is so semlessly integrated in the narcissus... but the fragance is not heavy at all, but quite light and wearable. I noticed some spice, but i should smell it again, maybe nutmeg. Definitely a floriental. After a 2/3 hours, when the narcissus is not more than a whisper, the tonkilla stay for longer. The drydown is not overly sweet, slightly resinous, a tad of smoke. Sexy stuff. The price is higher than the other L´Occitane perfumes. The Lady of L´Occitane told me they are indeed eaux de parfums, but they labeled as eaux de toilette because they were going to be launched in summer and didnt´t want the people to perceive them as "heavy". I guess marketing brains think of this things, but why such a positive feature, as high concentration is, would be concealed and reduced to a (suspicious) customer-Lady of L´Occitane secret confession? I dont know what to think. Not so much not so little. It lasts much longer than other eaux de toilettes of the brand, but it´s not incredibly intense (intensity is not a L´Occitane forté) which makes it a good choice for summer too despite the vanilla/tonka based perfumes seem more appropriate for cold weather. Nice one, L´Occitane. UPDATE: the cassis and the gardenia are somehow more noticeable on the bath line. The fragance after a shower really stays on the skin, although is a bit pricey.

The opening of Vanille & Narcisse does have some black currants. It then soon evolves into a combination of vanilla, tonka beans and some yellow flowers, which strangely smells a little sour to me. Actually I'm not sure if I smell narcissus. The floral part slightly reminds of Lancôme Poême. Towards the end, with yellow flowers fading, the powdery vanilla and tonka beans combo also has some caramel-like aspect. The longevity is around 7 hours on me. The sillage is moderate and manages to keep the intensity during the wearing. It's quite sweet and intense. Overdoing it will be tiring.

I was able to snag a bottle of this off eBay for a good price and I’m so happy I did! This is a beautiful combination of narcissus (aka daffodil) and vanilla. It’s perfectly sweet and vanillic, but has this deep, floral presence to it and it’s just stunning. I really love the composition of this as well. Vanilla & Narcisse starts of a little syrupy + citrusy, with a heavy dose of vanilla and tonka. It’s sweet, surprisingly powdery, and very rich smelling. Then the narcissus with the supporting gardenia come in and add the heavy florals and the narcissus is a little green and pollen-y as well? It’s just delicious without being nauseating. This is the perfect example of a floranilla (aka floral-vanilla). It doesn’t lean too much one what or the other, and is perfectly balanced. You get all the notes in a well-blended harmony. V&N is definitely a cooler weather scent, but I think you could get away with wearing this in the springtime. The performance isn’t anything outstanding, but this collection from L’Occitane wasn’t meant to be a lineup of beast mode frags. Projection and longevity are average, but it’s worth it for how amazing this scent is. My juice in my bottle has a deep, brown coloring to it, so you know it’s had time to sit and age beautiful to be more potent. I’m going to be sparing as I use through it because I really do enjoy this scent and would love it if I can find another bottle. I hate when companies discontinue such great fragrances.

My last purchasing experiences with L'Occitane go back almost a decade. I was once very keen on their products. At some point, however, I started to look into ingredients and moved away from them. The fragrances were a bit too specific for me ten years ago. I even sold a rose scent from back then because I absolutely disliked a harsh undertone.

My title makes it clear - I am very uncertain about this fragrance. It is not poorly made and I even like it in parts, but... Vanilla & Narcisse starts with a sweet, intense, and typically "powdery" tonka note. I can somewhat perceive a lightly dry citrus scent afterwards, but I wouldn't call it bergamot and certainly not black currant.

Casually bought the Time Capsule discovery set, and didn't pay much mind to Tero. Was really excited to try Papilefiko since it is the one that gets the most hype out of the 4 in this collection. Surprisingly, did not care much for it. Kredo was a big like, and Tero was an instant love. My god, the first time I have sampled something and 30 mins later found a bought a full 100 ml BNIB bottle. That instantaneous of a love. Is it gourmand? Maybe Is it spicy? Oh yes Is it sexy? To my nose, absolutely I love caramel, and I love the smell of freshly crushed black pepper. If those two things sound appealing to you, give this one a try. I can understand this not being a love for everyone, the pepperiness is hyper realistic, to an extent that surprised beyond my expectations. That kick remains faintly in the background during the drydown while mixing with sticky sweet and salty caramel. Deep into the drydown you get some dry patchouli hints with light ambers, but the caramel is always front and center. This is a dream "gourmand" for me. Balanced to perfection, blended incredibly well, longevity is insane, 14+ hours on my skin, leaves a trail that never fails to get positive attention. Price wise on discounters, $150 for this insanely good scent? Incredible value. If you feel that most sweet scents are cloying, this one will not disappoint. Horrible scent, 2/10 (gatekeep this one please)

When you first spray it on, you get a heavy waft of sweetness - this clearly opens as a gourmand scent. If you didn't look at the notes, you'd most likely expect some combination of caramel/toffee/burnt sugar, but there's a bitter edge to it at first and that's the other core component of this scent - the patchouli. This scent, in its entirety, is caramel-patchouli. There are other elements in the blend, but they won't be anywhere near as easy to separate - for example, you'll get some spices within the first 15-30 minutes which dissipate over time. The patchouli is not too earthy and the caramel overpowers it in the blend. What I appreciate the most about scents like Tero is the uniqueness which is an interesting pun in this context, because the only scent in the niche market that smells anything like Tero, to me, is "Crush on Me" by Unique'e Luxury. Regarding comparables: on the other site, I saw people referring to Black Phantom. I have a bottle of Black Phantom and think it's a slight reach - BP in its entirety is a gourmand while this has certain alternative tones to it. As for the Crush on Me comparison, what you get with Crush on Me is 85-15 patchouli-caramel, giving that scent a clear masculine edge. Here I'd say we are around 45-55 patchouli-caramel, making it straight-down-the-middle unisex. Performance is somewhere in the 90th percentile - there aren't that many niche gourmands pulling 10-12h nowadays. The scent is very airy, at least for 3 hours - optimal as a fall-winter fragrance and for open-air events. Pricing is in-line with what well-recognized gourmand brands (like Kilian) ask. Almost instantly after this review was written, the 100ml became available for €315. I subsequently added a bottle on the 19th of October.

The beginning felt a bit muddled as if the notes were trying to settle down, but didn't yet know their place. When they settled down, though, it started smelling incredible. Warm, drizzled, salted caramel with a subtle undertone of peppery spiciness. Very realistic and just so beautiful! After awhile, the warmth starts receding and a dark, grounded, earthy patchouli rises up, still accompanied by the salted caramel note. It's giving gourmand, but subtle, fit for those who don't enjoy very sweet gourmands (think vanilla, crème brulée, chocolate and the likes). Drydown becomes woodier as the salted caramel gives up its center place and vetiver starts giving a more masculine-leaning spiciness allied with the cinnamon that is still going strong from the middle notes. I really didn't have any expectations with this fragrance as Nishane hasn't been a brand that has wowed me yet (different strokes, for different folks), but this one was very nice.

Its a bold, mesmerising fragrance that exudes elegance and strength. With its rich blend of warm spices, amber, and smoky undertones, it creates a unique and unforgettable scent. Perfect for those who love deep , complex perfumes that leave a lasting impression. Tero is both sophisticated and daring, making it ideal for evening wear or special occasions.

It was a quiet morning in Istanbul, the city still half asleep, when I first sprayed Tero on my skin. The air was cool, the Bosporus shimmered gray and salty, and this very feeling was carried by the fragrance. The first flash of salty caramel reminded me of a piece of sea foam, sweet yet mineral, while the pepper danced like tiny sparks.

Warm, delicious, special. That's the first thing that comes to mind when I think of Tero. The salty caramel, which particularly stands out on my skin, lasts all day long. I can still smell it in my hair and on my clothes the next day. Longevity 10/10! In the dry down, a slightly spicy cinnamon note slowly and subtly joins in, which ultimately crowns the whole fragrance.

My first Nishane and I have no regrets! The opening of Tero is like the first bite of a salted caramel dessert. The salty sweetness of the caramel dances on the tongue, while the pepper adds a spicy note. The heart note of Tero is like a mysterious forest in autumn. Patchouli exudes an earthy warmth, while the cinnamon breaks through the canopy like a sunbeam.

It's true that it starts off very caramel-like, but then it shifts into a professional and mature scent at full speed. For me, it's an incredibly well-balanced mix of amber, leather, and earthy vetiver/oak notes. I would compare the drydown to the MFK Grand Soir. However, it's important to note that the Nishane puts the Grand Soir to shame in every aspect.

I don't know why this perfume is rated so low, it's quite delicious. The immediate spray gives off a sweet apple scent like a Pink Lady or a Honeycrisp, then slowly fades into more of a lighter, woody Fuji apple. Originally I was worried about the "sugared woods" note being too strong, but the balance in this fragrance is perfect in my opinion. Genuinely such a perfect scent for fall, and I hope more people give it a try.

... but I like the old formulation (tall bottle) much better. I discovered Arlésienne at Kaufhof. Sprayed it and thought... yes, it has something... but I couldn't quite pinpoint what... I couldn't find a particularly prominent note, somehow nice but not convincing. And I didn't want to buy a huge bottle of something that didn't really hook me. I sniffed around on L'Occitane's website and found a mini set (including shower gel and cream) for a mere 12.00 euros and bought it. Yes... pleasant and not painful... so okay for everyday use. Then I read Brigida's statement and became aware of the old formulation... Curious as I am, I went in search of the tall bottle and found it. Since yesterday, I now own the old Arlésienne and what can I say... it is soooooooooo much better, smells so much nicer than the new blend. I'm blown away. How wonderful this scent is. Much more vibrant and fresh and not as dull and fleeting as the new one. Still (for me) not definable but just good!! Not intrusive, not cloyingly sweet, not old, not bitter, not headache-inducing floral... Classy! I will definitely continue searching for remaining stocks, this EDT is really, really great.

So: today is the day: My new acquisition for summer 2015 makes its debut as an office scent. The fruitiness and the spice burst forth explosively at first - and they remain that way for about 1 hour. But then: The rose steps onto the stage, joins the saffron, and then does it switch over to the lily of the valley? A refined interplay of the flowers with the saffron is perceived by my nose. Nothing is sweet, nothing is heavy. After 4 hours, I wonder where the rose might be? Ah, there!! It seems to have just made way for the lily of the valley, so that it can also have a dalliance with the saffron. And suddenly: There it is again! The Rose! Powdery, light, with a woody base. Due to the delicate woodiness of the fragrance, which lingers in the base for a long time, I made my purchasing decision. However, the addictive factor is probably due to the tonka bean. Overall, Arlesienne seems to be very close to the skin, as there have been (still) no reactions from my surroundings………………..

When I read here that Arlésienne should smell similar to Chloé Love, I was curious and went to L'Occitane to possibly add it to my perfume collection. - Expectation - I thought it would be buttery soft, a bit sharp from the saffron, and would smell wonderful like roses. - Fragrance - It turned out to be quite different from what I expected and surprised me with its mandarin and saffron note, which is very prominent at first. An extremely piercing and sharp scent shot up my nose, and I was momentarily shocked. But then something very strange happened. Suddenly, the remaining components emerged and conjured a beautifully unique perfume. The prominent roses are gently enveloped by the lily of the valley and violets. The woods and tonka bean give the Eau de Cologne a certain depth. The saffron adds a clever twist that sweetly retreats to the background. An addictive scent that definitely bears no resemblance to Chloé. - Conclusion - I still can't decide whether I need the fragrance or not. Somehow I like it, but the saffron note prevents me from making a final decision. Yes, it doesn't become boring because of that, but it is very sharp. Maybe it will be love at second sight?

The women of Arles are referred to as the most beautiful women in France. Whether that is true, I cannot judge, as I only know Paris and the cities of Normandy in France. I have never been to Arles and have not met any of the "charming" women there. Alphonse Daudet has immortalized the city with his tragedy "Lettres de mon Moulin," and his play L'Arlésienne was masterfully adapted into a musical stage piece by Bizet in 1872. -By the way, my favorite opera by Bizet. L'Occitane must have had the city in mind when they drew inspiration for their perfume and chose Arlésienne for their product. The result is a very pleasant fragrance, where the rose clearly dominates and the other components remain politely in the background. However, the perfume is not designed in such a way that the rose prevails from beginning to end, giving the impression that one is standing in a rose garden. The other components, while remaining politely in the background, are detectable and give the perfume a truly pleasant note. I bought Arlésienne for my wife because she loved the packaging, so I went to L'Occitane to smell the fragrance, and I was so impressed that I did what one normally wouldn’t do and bought the gift box blind -Never change a winning system-. However, I knew that she would like the perfume and that the scent would flatter her, and I was right in my assessment. She is thrilled, and I must admit that it smells even more pleasant on her and unfolds its warm components on her skin. Although it is not listed, I perceive a scent of honey, which gives it this warm and gentle component. It’s possible that it’s due to the ingredients, but I’m not sure. She feels like a "lady," and indeed, Arlésienne can be sprayed on with a costume or jeans and a blouse; it always fits and contrasts with her other perfumes "Magic Noir" by Lancôme and Acqua di Gioia by Armani. It lacks the lightness of Aqua and the aura of Magic, but I find this scent very seductive on her. A truly beautiful fragrance for autumn or winter, inviting dreams of girls from Arles strolling through the streets. Whether they are pretty, I do not know, but my wife is beautiful even without perfume; it enhances her natural beauty many times over.

After the initial spicy opening, Mana has a sweet blast of oud and jammy rose. Smells quite girlie. After a short while, the sweetness pulls back but the rose has a very jammy or fruity smell. Overall, I'd say it's a unisex fragrance. Oud and rose last for a considerable time. Towards the end, all that remains is a sorta creamy/woody scent. Performance is very good. Long lasting with good sillage and projection for a few hours at least. Overall, Mana is not my style.

I was surprised not to see civet or some other strongly animalic note in this perfume. There is something about it that reminds me of animal urine. Perhaps it's the musk? The leather and suede are also very strong. Cardamom and tobacco give it an overwhelming pungent spiciness. The dry-down does improve slightly, as the rose note appears and brings about a pleasant, albeit "vintage," soapiness. This is a primal and very manly "stink" to me. I'm sure this is for someone, but it's definitely not for me. I truly cannot stand this fragrance.

Hello everyone, today I would like to TALK about a fragrance that, in my personal perception, deserves much more attention. So today it's about Mana ! I'll start directly with the question that most of you are surely interested in. Do the comparisons to Ombre Nomade hold true? My personal opinion (!!!) is rather no, BUT I can understand anyone who sees it that way. Why? Nishane is a house that sometimes LIKES to look left and right, observes the market, and draws inspiration from things, and this also happened here with Ombre Nomade ! (Inspiration is not cloning, as that is not the case here!) The Mana is rounder, nobler, and of higher quality - yes, LV lovers might tear me apart for this, but let me explain why I like the Ombre Nomade less. It is good and noble - no question about it, and the price factor compared to Mana is hefty, I completely agree with that, but I have the problem that the Ombre Nomade is too aggressive for ME; it screams all the time, HERE, HEY HERE, I AM HERE! and that is too exhausting and annoying for me (even as a wearer). I only know the batches up to 2022, if anything has changed to be "softer," please let me know! In my perception, the Ombre Nomade only plays with oud, incense, and occasionally the raspberry says HELLO, and only after x to xx hours does the benzoin actively join in). With the "Mana | Nishane," it is a interplay of oud, rose, saffron (and some other spices), and in the background, there are immediately more woods, musk, and a bit of labdanum, but the fragrance lingers for a very long time and develops slowly - please note! For me, there is more to discover here, and it often shows me new facets / develops differently and is not a loudmouth like the "Ombre Nomade | Louis Vuitton." Test both against each other and you may also see / notice / sniff it. Performance: Anyone who gives the Mana less than a 9 or 10 in the H/S category, I cannot understand, sorry. Whether you like it is another matter, that is clear, but when it comes to performance, it is a true monster in terms of 12h, 14h, 16h and only after (!) does it become calm and gentle, but certainly not before! For whom and when is it recommended: This is always very, very difficult to say with such special fragrances; some would say work, some would say when going out to eat - I would say YES YES, but it is a matter of dosage, as it is strong. Primarily, for me, it is a STATEMENT FRAGRANCE, it is one as it should be, it is very CONSISTENT! And when? From October to March, it works really well in my opinion! Is it worth the money? This can only be evaluated subjectively and relatively. If I say yes and you say no, or I say no and you say yes, it really brings it down to relativity in my opinion. I like to evaluate a fragrance based on what it can do, what it offers, how it is made, and so on. And with this fragrance, you can really feel the quality, and that is no lie! Nishane always delivers in terms of quality, and you often see what is possible and feasible, and I would say it like this, you should definitely test it! So far, 99% of everyone has liked / loved the fragrance, but only with a subtle dosage of 2 - 3 sprays; otherwise, it becomes modest here :P! Recommendation: If I really weren't convinced, I wouldn't recommend it to you! (At least for a test, and if you like this direction, then I wish you heartfelt congratulations on your new Mana ) And now have a nice day / evening or whenever you read this review, best regards, Benny _______ (Now the same as almost always - because it applies!) Now to the topic of luxury: As you can see in part in my profile, I have really smelled many fragrances, and there are fragrances where you can smell a certain (sometimes strong) synthetics, and you quickly realize that some fragrance houses tend to go for quantity over quality, and there are some where you can tell, "Oh come on, let's just put in more + better," and you can smell that at the end of the day. A brief note on the topic of packaging, bottle, sprayer: I'll keep it short: I give a 10 out of 10 in every category, and I know very well that tastes are very different. So if someone honestly rates this with an 8 or less... - PHEW. Beautiful and very high-quality cap, nice timeless bottle design, leather case, etc.... so I find it very hard to rate it differently, and I don't say this because I like or dislike a brand! Now a short note on my opinion: I am not sponsored, influenced by anyone, receiving money or anything else. I approach the topic of perfume as I am, being honest; everything else is not my style. My true personal opinion is very VALUABLE to me, and I hope perhaps ;) that this is noticeable. If I don't like something, like packaging, bottle, sprayer, or H/S, I will communicate that too!

I have wanted to test Mana for a long time because I really like the bottles from the Prestige Collection. Of course, in the end, the scent is more important than the bottle, but the bottle was somehow the trigger for me to get a sample of Mana. My expectations are naturally higher for Mana, as the retail price here is already above that of a 50 ml bottle of Roja and also above a 50 ml bottle of Spirit of Dubai Gen 1. Now to the scent itself: Mana is an absolutely solid fragrance, that could be my short description for Mana if I had to compress my review into one sentence. Now I want to explain why I only find Mana solid. Mana is a rose oud fragrance with a soft leather note and a light saffron note. Unfortunately, this exact combination already exists very often, almost identically or comparably. Examples include Oud Pashmina and Ombre Nomade or also Tuscan Leather Eau de Parfum (without oud but otherwise similar). I can hardly recognize the notes of the base; only a bit of patchouli and labdanum. Unfortunately, Mana is far too one-dimensional for me; nothing new comes after spraying, the scent remains mostly identical from the top note to the base note. That’s why I am also disappointed with Mana, because with other brands I simply get much more for my money. I just miss something that makes Mana unique or memorable. Mana simply hasn’t stuck in my memory at all. In 2-3 months, I would probably have forgotten about Mana and would have to look at my notes on it. However, the longevity is, as typical for Nishane, impressive. Mana lasted over 14 hours on me, and the sillage was also in a very good range, perceptible for almost 10 hours at arm's length, and only becomes close to the skin after 12-13 hours.

Mana completely convinced me at first sniff. Qualitatively in the absolute top class, this is truly a dark, direct, and confident rose-oud combination, perfectly balanced in my eyes. Elegant leather, incense, and spicy notes with subtle animalic nuances blend in. Despite the animalic aspect, it's wearable for me every day and I've only received positive compliments so far.

After being completely thrilled by Nefs , it was only natural to test the next powerhouse, Mana . Sprayed on, first impression: WOW! A rich, dark rose-oud fragrance that strongly connects to the successful formula of Ombre Nomade !

At night, there is a bustling activity in the cities, the streets brightly lit by oriental shops, kebab stands, shisha bars. On the corner, three young men stand, looking gloomy, smoking. A dry, warm, musty wind from the subway blows into my face. Foreign yet melodious sounds resonate from elegant sports cars. The bright Mercury dazzles in the reflection of the waxed leather.

Longevity is insane Today I want to talk about Mana by Nishane. First of all, the price: it really is something. 550 euros for 50ml is quite a hefty sum. However, I believe it is truly worth every cent. The reason is the unbelievable strength and longevity of this fragrance. 1-2 sprays are enough for the whole day, and others can smell you from a distance.

Strong scent, animalistic, leathery, spicy. The animalistic notes are immediately present after the first spray and are very powerful, obvious, probably also of excellent quality given the high price. Strong and spicy leather notes contribute to giving this fragrance even more structure and masculinity.

I really do like this one! It's a beautiful combination of green smells from the French countryside. You have hay, thyme, bitter orange (a very refreshing note!), with a combination of a set of other "green" and refreshing notes (mate - a green herbal tea from south america... and Chinese pure green tea). I absolutely recommend this one for summer and hot weather! Once again L'Occitane proves that they can make outstanding fragrances whilst being natural and with quality. Give this one a try in summer and you'll see what I mean!

The third fragrance from the Collection de Grasse is my absolute favorite. It seems that tea scents are something L'Occitane does particularly well, as there are already several tea fragrances in the L'Occitane fragrance collection and they are very popular. Now there is also one in La Collection de Grasse. Thé Vert & Bigarade (Bigarade = Bitter Orange or Sevilla Orange) lives up to its name perfectly. The opening features a big burst of orange, so juicy, sweet, and appetizing that it makes me crave a ripe orange right away. Then the tea comes in, and it is impressive. A very high-quality premium green tea, enhanced with equally fresh jasmine blossoms, without sweetness. I really enjoy drinking tea, especially green tea - though I tend to prefer it in the winter months. In the summer, I usually switch to more coffee or iced tea, with citrus juice and a bit of sweetness. Therefore, this tea as a fragrance is a wonderful way to enjoy green tea sufficiently even in summer. Every now and then, the musk flashes through, but not very strongly and certainly not unpleasantly. For over 6 hours, I enjoy this fresh, floral-fruity tea note that envelops me in a pleasantly fresh cloud. The fragrance is so beautiful that I want to declare it my summer scent for 2013.

Hey guys, I'm back and today I'm coming to a fragrance from the brand L’Occitane, which has really confused me lately. A while ago, I was out sniffing with a nice perfumer (yes, there are really nice ones among you! :DD). It was still summer and she was wearing a lovely black dress. Her beautiful legs were shining in the sun and… ahh wait… I think I'm getting sidetracked… :DD Anyway, we went to a L’Occitane store in Frankfurt. She was looking for a fragrance, and when we couldn't find it, I asked one of the salespeople if they had the scent (though I can't remember which fragrance it was!). In response, I heard something like, "Sorry, we are not that L’Occitane." And that, even though the brand name, logo, font, and lettering were exactly the same. I just said, "Okaaay…" and slowly walked away because it felt a bit strange to me. The perfumer I was with, as far as I know, also didn't know what to make of it, did she? (I know you're reading this,… he he he). Well, I still need to find that out, but I might also be mistaken and confusing everything with another brand… anyway, let's get to "Thé Vert & Bigarade," which sounds extremely great for tea lovers like me! The fragrance: Ooooh!! The scent really starts with an excellent tea note. By that, I mean that you can smell green tea, which has a very authentic aroma. Then another type of tea comes in, which (at least in this fragrance) resembles the scent of green tea a bit, as it also comes across as somewhat green and bitter, but in my opinion, it has a slightly softer aroma, namely the also wonderful yerba mate tea. However, both tea notes blend together too quickly, so that soon I can no longer really distinguish between the two teas. Just a little later, you can also smell the thyme. An herb that may taste a bit stronger or more bitter than other herbs, but has just as wonderful and herbaceous a scent. In my opinion, such herbal fragrances can unfold beautifully, especially in summery scents, as I find that the so-called "kitchen herbs" fit excellently into summer fragrances, especially citrus scents or with notes like tea, etc. So, despite the fresh and casual aura, the fragrance is also a bit dry in the background. This is surely due to the many bitter notes, but it doesn't bother me, as this dry feeling doesn't come across as stuffy like it does with many floral fragrances. Besides, the green tea scents are significantly stronger, which are, of course, also somewhat bitter scents :D And that's it, as you don't smell much more. Basically, it's just tea and a bit of herb. But the little that you can sniff is all the more beautiful and, above all, quite authentic! A lovely, refreshing fragrance! The sillage and longevity: I bet you already guessed that I'm going to write here that the fragrance isn't particularly strong. Sadly, it actually turned out to be quite weak, so that others probably wouldn't even smell it from close by. Therefore, this is a fragrance for personal enjoyment, which you could reapply in the summer. This makes the scent feel quite short, even though it should last about three or four hours on the sprayed area. The bottle: The fragrance comes in a rectangular bottle made of fairly thick glass. The "&" symbol is prominently embedded in the glass on the front. The fragrance liquid is greenish and looks delicious. The black cap is cylindrical, with a threaded shape at the bottom. A somewhat inconspicuous but still nice bottle. Aaah, I really liked this tea scent as well. There are now really beautiful and many (green) tea fragrances, making it quite difficult to decide which one to get. Because this might sound a bit critical, but it is indeed the case that most of these green tea fragrances are quite similar, so it probably isn't worth getting too many different ones, at least if the scent only smells like green tea (it's different with the Elizabeth Arden Green Teas, which have various "types" that actually smell quite different!). However, this fragrance is definitely worth trying, and I found it very good, so it will be added to my "Good Tea Fragrances" list :) Because it is especially refreshing in summer, particularly on really hot days, so it might help you get through heatwaves a bit better, at least if you can muster the energy to spray on a fragrance. Because usually, on such hot days, you stick somewhere in a corner hoping for some cooling, only to ultimately despair when you read in the weather report that the heatwave will last for over a week… ugh… just 5-7 more months, and we'll have heatwaves again *sigh* Anyway, the fragrance is certainly recommendable, but unfortunately only for oneself, as others surely won't smell it on you due to the weak sillage. Well, that's it, thank you for reading and have a nice evening :)

After the blind test #9 from this afternoon, I am eager to test another fragrance, this time as First Impressions: I pull L’Occitane - Thé Vert & Bigarade, a green tea-bitter orange, from my testing box. My references for green tea scents are, on one hand, the wonderfully refreshing "Green Tea (Eau Parfumée) | Elizabeth Arden," which has practically saved my life on many hot summer days, and the almost almond-macha-like "Un Matin au Jardin - Thé Vert | Yves Rocher," I seem to like Francis' signature.... I haven't had much experience with bitter orange; Happy Chopard - Bigaradia felt too stuffy to me, so I am very curious how this rather fresh bitter orange will behave on my skin. It starts fresh, subtly citrusy, the bitter orange comes across more fruity than bitter. The bitterness that shines through afterward, I attribute to the herbs. The green tea feels soft, the overall scent impression is rather airy. A slight soapiness joins in. The fragrance presents itself as rather cold and herbal. The thyme feels almost like a foreign body, a wrong note that bites my nose; perhaps the mate tea also contributes to this and adds a second bite. The harshness reminds me of "Eau Parfumée au Thé Vert Extrême | Bvlgari." I wouldn't want to compare it to my favorite green tea fragrances, as this one lags far behind. After a while, however, it warms up a bit, loses some soapiness, becomes rounder, more aromatic, and now I find the delicate interplay between green tea and bitter orange quite charming, with the tea clearly dominating here. I can’t do much with the herbs, though; I still perceive them as a somewhat more peaceful wrong note. However, it could appeal to those who have nothing against herbs and are not put off by initial soapiness. It will not be joining my collection. When it comes to green tea, I prefer to stick with my tried-and-true treasures.

The scent seemed, from the description, to be made for me: orange, green tea, thyme, cedar, and hay - just green-fresh. However, citrusy-fresh describes it better. The orange and tea aromas right after spraying are great. Until about 15 minutes later, when a rather biting smell sets in that seems to overshadow everything else?! I was asked in the kitchen while baking why it smelled so much like vinegar! So we were already two who couldn't handle the unbalanced, let's call it, citrus note. After about an hour, tea, fresh thyme, and musk are wonderfully unsweet and perceivable side by side - a true (delayed) pleasure. Too late for me. I really don't want to wait that long.

another absolute banger from vs. i think this is very similar to autumn shore with its dry smoky notes, but with the added bare vanilla dna. like autumn shore, it's definitely a unisex scent to me and i wouldn't say it's blind buy safe if you're looking for a more mass-appealing vanilla, but please do give it a sniff if you're in stores. if you're looking for a gourmand, super sweet vanilla, this isn't it, but it is an amazing scent. perfect for a cold night. on clothes, i mostly get the smoky notes, but the vanilla and orchid become very distinct on my skin and make it lean slightly more feminine. it's honestly such a confidence booster for me, it makes me feel so sultry and sexy. plus, the smoky/woody notes give it great longevity!

I didn't like the opening. It was strong in orange at first. Citrus, sweet, this is not what I expected for a green tea scent. The drydown is much better. The tea and the jasmin is calming and comforting. Unfortunately citrus notes still linger somewhere around. I wish it could be bitterer like White Tea by l'Occitane. It's still a lovely fragrance, green and fresh, inoffensive and suitable for many occasions, unisex as well. But it just doesn't fit the image of green tea for me. It's some sort of fruit tea IMHO. I also have White Tea by l'Occitane and I prefer the scent of White Tea. But Green Tea lasts longer and its sillage is better. Originally written in 2013

This time of year I start to crave spring, and that usually manifests itself by me craving, purchasing and wearing cool, fresh, sunny and yummy breezy perfumes, and turning my back more and more on the Oriental bombs and the smokey silage beasts. "The Vert L'Occitane en Provence" is just my cup of tea for the last days of January and it will be a favorite far into the spring and summer months! Cool green freshness, citric zest, floral feminine beauty and herbal depth without that it is too much of one thing. It's a very elegant and yummy scent with an herbal dry-down, reminiscent of standing in the middle of an herbal garden in the Provence looking for just the right herbs to go with your dinner that is cooking on your Aga. Whilst you can smell the freshly pressed orange & lemon juice still on your fingers. On the way to the herbal garden you stopped and picked a jasmine or two out of the big terra-cotta flowerpots. Lost in thought you inhale deeply...and you can feel your lungs fill with a clean spring-air that already holds a promise of a summer that will be reminiscent of holidays with family & friends and lots of laughter. (Darn! This potion makes me lyrical!! lol ; ) A beautiful mood-lifter that is suitable for all occasions and moods since it's not the type of Green Tea scent that smells like you're wearing your morning tea. It's too well blended for that. Tea notes swirling around juicy citric vibes that have a strong jasmines note and a very well adjusted mate vibe. It's herbal without being 'medicinal', tea & orangey-like without being 'food-like' and has a wonderful balance of mate and jasmine. It's addictive, I am wearing it often: (at home, work, leisure-time and on casual dates) and I must get another bottle to have it on stand-by for when the first spring-like days arrive! Silage is: Yummy and pretty aromatherapy for body & mind -- Longevity is: depending on chemistry and amount of sprays. On me three sprays on skin and one on clothes make it last 5+ hours. Good luck and enjoy! : )

Citrusy green tea with soft jasmine, and a deep woodsy base. It's fresh and delicious.. It feels crisp & cool, making it the perfect scent for summer. A clean, inoffensive scent, and has almost a medicinal or sterile quality. In a good way.

The Vert is possibly my favourite green tea scent from those that I've smelt so far. It definitely tops Green Tea by Elizabeth Arden and Bvlgari Eau Parfumee au The Vert. It smells natural, herbaceous, citrusy and fresh. The trouble with most green tea fragrances on the market today, is the tendency to make the scent unnaturally sweet. Thankfully L'Occitane has refrained from altering the composition, leaving the green tea note in its most natural form. The Vert smells like actual tea leaves, rather than a watered down cup of tea. An added touch of bitter orange in the top notes, and jasmine in the heart, provide a sparkling and fresh quality. This fragrance is definitely unisex. Both men and women will enjoy sharing this one during the Summer months. The cedar, thyme and nutmeg drydown, strikes me as being more musky and green than anything else. It was a pleasant end to such a fresh and revitalising scent. I know that L'Occitane prices can be a little off-putting for some, especially considering how simplistic some of their fragrances can be. However, I think The Vert is worth it, especially seeing that it lasts almost the entire day on the skin. I would definitely recommend this fragrance as being one of the better scents from the house of L'Occitane. It was well worth discovering. Original review written: February 2013.

Since this is my sister's current everyday scent, testing it was easy. Straight into the bathroom, sprayed on, and back out. Fluis' impression: The green tea here is actually an organic green tea with jasmine. The opening is very citrusy, fresh. As it develops, this freshness recedes a bit to make way for the natural tea. It doesn't take long to make its presence known and spreads out nicely. Naturalness is emphasized here. However, this tea is not a "I'm sick" tea; it's more of a "Hello world!! *waves*" tea for after getting up. Full of energy, it allows for a cheerful start to the day. The weak point might be that the green tea has to stand on its own. There are no companions (coffee or similar) by its side; the entire scent progression is green tea. In the end, it fades away, and there is no counterpoint or any other facet to spice up the progression a bit. Now, I don't know how to put this into words, but the scent is not flat; it "foams," so to speak. Perhaps it is this naturalness captured in the fragrance that makes it feel fluffy and light. Or another quirky formulation: the "density" of the scent is not very high. My association with this is the good old bath foam, thin, graceful, yet robust in a natural way, but by no means massive. So, as a casual scent, I would say it's really not to be underestimated. And another positive aspect, in my opinion, is that this is not a sticky scent (like Britney Spears, Rihanna, or similar), but rather a convincingly natural, albeit not spectacularly crafted, all-rounder.

Yes, there are days when, besides the more dramatic ones that call for an oriental fragrance, I feel like wearing a subtle, wearable perfume. For that, Thé Vert seems quite suitable. Fresh, green, subtle with a slightly bitter note and well-composed, but not too seductive or opulent. Just perfect for everyday wear.

Green Tea is, in my opinion, fresh, fresh, and green, and I think I can sniff out the indicated jasmine. But there’s no trace of fragrance development for my nose. It was an impulse of "must-have" without really testing it extensively.

Fruity-sweet fragrances are a bit of a tougher pill to swallow for me. I guess Hawas for Him is to blame, my first ever fragrance, which is just a complete mess of fruity sweetness, along with an uncalled-for cinnamon note. I remember I used to enjoy it back when I first got it, but now, as I've matured, I have realized it's a piece of crap. nulltheless, it would be a madness to compare a fragrance such as Hawas for Him with one such as Zenne . And while the latter also sits in the realm of fruity-sweet, it's a whole different take, one that doesn't make me nauseous. Upon spraying, the blackcurrant's dark fruitiness and tart scent is the first to strike, having that wild berries vibe which I find quite pleasing. The rhubarb, a component I haven't met too often before, adds a zingy, tart, refreshing fruity-sweetness which just blends in perfectly with the blackcurrant. Admittedly, they blend well enough to be kind of hard to tell each apart, although my lack of experience with the scent of rhubarb could just as well be to blame. Surely enough, the grapefruit and its lively citrus touch tries its best to shine through, but it submissively fades in the background. With the blackcurrant and rhubarb combo still going strong, the heart and base notes take slightly longer to push through. Eventually, a delicate honeyed floral scent appears in a faint manner, but it's not nearly faint enough to be unrecognizable - the iconic rose. Turkish rose, to specify. The Gardenia alongside pushes the floral odor as hard as it can as well, adding a slight creaminess similar to Jasmine. Smooth, but overpowered by the dark fruitiness from the opening, and things start balancing out (the fruitiness being toned down) somewhere around half an hour to an hour after spraying. Not to forget about the sandalwood, listed as a heart note here, apparently. Woodiness in the traditional sense, I hardly get any, but a faint touch of comforting, buttery warmth I do get hidden in the backstage. Reached the base, the musk becomes the quickest to debut. Still overpowered by the fruitiness, the warm, subtle, clean, slightly powdery typical muskiness, along with the ambergris which is also near-impossible to pinpoint on its own, take their place in the background. The vanilla sweetness becomes properly noticeable somewhere like an hour or two after the initial spray (at least on my skin). As a whole, this could easily sit in designer territory. It doesn't really do anything special, nor does it present excellent blending/development. In the context of performance, there's some good news and some not so good news. Longevity, quite good; got a solid 8-9 hours, at that mark an extremely faint, dark fruitiness with vanilla being detectable. But for projection, not impressed. On my skin, the first half an hour to about two hours, I got one foot of projection, one and a half at the very best, but most of the time it felt like it sat closer to the skin. However, it does leave a fairly noticeable scent trail, and it's consistent at it too. So not all that bad, overall - I'd go with about 5 sprays. Moving on to the occasions best suited for Zenne , I would comfortably wear it in a variety of situations across most of the year (except for summer). Dressed-up events, parties, clubbing, work... maybe even as a daily too, although personally, I prefer 'lighter' scents for daily/leisure wear. Zenne leans too fruity-sweet in a dark way to just wear casually, in my opinion, but in the context of a wedding, this would suit a woman quite nicely. And yes, by that I also mean it might lean slightly more feminine. But still, I don't love it. Zenne just lacks some development and a stronger base, which is also an issue I found with Tuberóza Extrait de Parfum . The intense, dark fruity sweetness right from the start makes up for about 70-80% of all that I smell for the first few hours, with the rest being a smooth and subtle floral sweetness. And while it doesn't smell bad as a whole, it still sits in the fruity-sweet category that I tend to avoid. It's one of the better interpretations of that combination that I've smelt, and if you particularly enjoy such blends, with a darker twist, then it's worth checking out Zenne . But otherwise, I don't find it worthwhile, especially at the $200-$250 price. Overall Rating: 6.2/10

As everyone is giving attention to Ani, I decided to write a review about this perfume that stays in the shadows, which is almost the source of its inspiration (shadow puppetry). I hope I give the perfume the description it deserves and to you all a good picture of it. The Brand: Nishane has become one of my favorite brands. Their perfumes smell quality, they have a great performance and I blame them for raising my standards in perfumes. After I bought their perfumes, I see one of another brand of the same price and I m like “I would better buy a Nishane in this price”. Why? Because they are quality perfumes they smell amazing. The story behind the perfume: I love it when a perfume is inspired by something and I get that something from smelling it. Nishane has released 3 perfumes inspired by traditional shadow puppetry characters: Karagoz, Hacivat and Zenne. First two are male characters so the perfumes are masculine (Karagoz could be unisex) and third character is female so the perfume is a feminine perfume. Zenne in the puppetry, is a woman who is a symbol of beauty, confidence, she achieves what she wants at any cost and she is desired by every man. And this is exactly the feeling of this perfume. The smell: Dreamy, seductive, sexy, feminine, OMG it’s a masterpiece! It’s a fruity floral vanilla scent that doesn’t change with time. You get what you smell from the first spray, it just becomes more smooth with time. You get that sour smell of a grapefruit, with the intensity of the gardenia and the rose on a soft bed of sweet vanilla and musk. The performance: The performance is unique! On skin, it smells for hours and on clothes it smells for days. Season/ Occasion I have bought this fragrance on November and I am wearing it since then with cold weather and it responds amazing, but I believe that it is a fragrance for spring summer and early autumn. I personally don’t enjoy wearing it with a sweater because it gives me different vibes, more fresh, more delicate, more elegant. I could wear it on winter for an occasion with a silk dress and high heels. So, about the occasion, on spring and summer you can wear it at any occasion and on autumn and winter only on occasion when you are dressed more formal. It smells femininity. Conclusion: It is an amazing perfume for a woman. Its totally worth buying it. It totally stays in my collection for looooong!!! Thank you for your time.

“ZENNE is a tribute to beauty, self-confidence, and flirtation.” Female leaning “Inspired by the female character in the traditional shadow puppetry, ZENNE will teleport you to the enigmas of the paradise gardens full of joy and romance with a deliberate mix of the fruity and floral accords along with vanilla, ambergris and musk at the base.” This interesting and delicious scent opens up with fruity notes of Grapefruit, Rhubarb and Black Currant and that mix luckily remains longer than top notes usually do. That is because Nishane uses synthetic molecules which make the notes not only last longer but make a sillage more potent as well. The floral heart of Turkish Rose and Gardenia joins and mingles with the fruits but in overall the blend continues being mouthwatering and juicy yet elegant and sensual. Sandalwood makes the blend soft, a little bit milky (not creamy)and even if it’s rich there is even aromatic nuances in the blend. The base of Vanilla, Ambergris and Musk brings a warm and slightly powdery very pleasant touch without being too sweet. This is so alluring and voluptuous perfume with enormous projection and longevity. I feel youthful, lively and inviting while wearing this. This is really mellow and potent juice. Zenne is suitable to wear year around because of how it has been built, there is a depth and warm enough for colder days even if it’s floral fruity. I think that this is quite underrated and it has stayed literally in the shadow of another scent from the Shadow Play Collection, very popular Hacivat. Thank you for reading, I hope you liked my review and it was helpful. I would appreciate if you follow me on my IG and/or YouTube (English subtitles available): @ninamariahperfumes

This is so stunning! Thick, jammy red fruits, vanilla and a mysterious darkness in the background. This is not as tart and fresh as the rhubarb, black currant and grapefruit might suggest, it's a heavy, substantial perfume. All the fruits are noticeable, especially the black currant, but they smell like they were cooked down into a sweet jam together with plush red rose petals. It smells like berries, too, not only currants, even though I can't say which berries exactly. There is a lot of vanilla in the base, so this is warm and inviting. But there is also a bitterness in the background that I can't quite put my finger on, and something lush and balsamic that really elevates the scent. Not sure where all this is coming from, maybe the ambergris, maybe something not in the notes list. This is my favorite by Nishane so far. Ani and Hundred Silent Ways were nice, but Zenne is unique and fits my taste perfectly. If you like the darker side of sweet and fruity scents, you need to try it and see for yourself. In my opinion it's ultra feminine and voluptuous, like red lipstick as a scent. No, I don't mean that this smells like lipstick, it doesn't, but it has the same effect. Of course anyone can wear whatever they want regardless of gender, but this is definitely not your typical unisex scent.

Overall, it's a beautiful fragrance, but it has a designer quality to it and at the price point it's at, I'm convinced something better and cheaper exists out there. It's also missing that spark and that oomph that makes me want to go for a full bottle. The start is very sour and tart from the blackcurrant, grapefruit and rhubarb combo. I haven't tried much rhubarb scent, but I did enjoy this one. Fruity and sweet, it gives a little boost of uplifting energy. It does start to get more feminine when the rose enters the chat. It's giving freshness, but also a fruity, sweet facet that pairs well with the fruits at the top. The transition is smooth. I didn't get gardeni or sandalwood though. Drydown remains tart and floral, but also morphs slowly into a sweet vanilla backed by skin warmth. It's slightly powdery, but still enjoyable overall. The fragrance teeters on the edge of chic, sophisticated, but also effortless and leisurely-like. A lovely scent for many occasions, I enjoyed it more than I thought I would. It's still missing that spark I'm looking for (overall Nishane might not be the house for me), but this is one of the better Nishane I've tried.

my calm harbor, far away from the wild storm. Beautiful, delicate, and intimate, you lay upon my head. You shower me with gentle kisses, caressing me with rich spices. Creaky vanilla sinks into honey. Blackcurrant juice, heavily diluted, with a splash of lemon juice. Delicious, refreshing. Fruity. The tongue glides over blood-red lips. The heart pulses, the blood rushes.
