But maybe this will drive some of you to Harrods now - they also have great juices and sandwiches that don't strain the wallet as much as Favonius. Maybe you'll see me on the sixth floor at Xerjoff or Favonius. But definitely at Nishane on the ground floor.

Hello everyone, Actually, this review was planned as my 100th (!) but it turned into a different fragrance, and I wanted to get to know and LOVE the Favonius even more than I did about two months ago (or so). Quietly and unassumingly, it has become one of my favorite fragrances, and I’ll tell you why! Some would say it’s just one of x - hundred Rose - Oud fragrances, but to all those who only say that, I must say..., please move along! Because those who only see + think that simply do not know the fragrance! Yes, in terms of pure craftsmanship, it is that, and anyone who knows Oud Satin Mood Eau de Parfum knows about 40% which direction it goes, but it is certainly not an expensive "KNOCKOFF" of Oud Satin Mood Eau de Parfum .... How does it differ? It offers such perfect facets, for example, the frankincense, and NO we are not talking about churchly "sacred" frankincense - not at all. There are also noticeably other spices present that are really detectable, like pepper and, for example, mugwort - those create a wonderful picture in the background (they paint the picture for me). However, the fragrance gets a special and yes "unique" touch from the patchouli. I don’t know of any fragrance on the market that does it as well as Favonius . Some will also think now, oh no I don’t want to smell like (damp) earth and that with frankincense..., ok I am done! I am honest (as always), my way of thinking was not that different ;) , but I was so surprised! Also, it is not at all "damp earthy", but rather cooling, and that in combination with the non-sacred frankincense + rose with beautiful oud + 1 or 2 spices makes the "fragrance" a true work of art! I see it more for men, but NOT strongly/clearly. Yes, it has a certain tendency, but it can also be worn by women! Now to the performance: I must say that I only have a 2021 batch, which is quite interesting because it was not as brutal back then as it is today! I find the performance today to be almost "absurd" in a Nishane typical way, in the sense of 20h+ with 6 sprays, and the sillage is CRAZY and still comfortably in the 2m+ range after 8h, which is not insignificant in my opinion! Is it worth the money? This can only be assessed subjectively and relatively. If I say yes and you say no, or I say no and you say yes, it really doesn’t bring much in my opinion. I like to evaluate a fragrance based on what it can do, what it offers, how it is made, and so on. And with this fragrance, you can really notice the quality, and that’s no lie! Nishane consistently delivers quality, and you often see what is possible and achievable, and I’ll put it this way, you should definitely test it! So far, 99% of people have liked/loved the fragrance, but only with a dosage of 7+ sprays does it become mediocre :P ! Recommendation: If I really weren’t convinced, I wouldn’t recommend it to you! (At least for one test for sure, and if you like this direction, then congratulations on your new Favonius ) And now have a nice day/evening or whenever you read this review, best regards, Benny _______ (Now the same as almost always - because it applies!) Now to the topic of luxury: As you can see in part in my profile, I have really smelled many fragrances, and there are fragrances where you can smell a certain (partly) strong synthetic note, and you quickly realize that some fragrance houses focus more on quantity than quality, and there are some where you notice "oh come on, let’s add more + better ingredients" and you can smell that at the end of the day. A quick note on the packaging, bottle, sprayer: I’ll keep it short, I give a 9 - 10 out of 10 in every category, and I know very well that tastes are very different, I like everything very much. So, if someone honestly rates this with an 8 or less... - PHEW. Beautiful and very high-quality cap, beautiful timeless bottle design, etc. .... so I find it very hard to rate it differently, and I’m not saying this because I like or dislike a brand! Now a brief note on my opinion: I am not sponsored, influenced by anyone, receiving money or anything else. I approach the topic of perfume as I am, being honest, everything else is not for me. My true personal opinion is very VALUABLE to me, and I hope maybe ;) that this is noticeable. If I don’t like something, like packaging, bottle, sprayer, or H/S, I will communicate that too!

Favonius is a fragrance that fits Nishane's romantic narrative. It is inspired by an ancient mythological love story surrounding Flora, the Roman goddess of flowers. It is therefore no surprise that Favonius has a distinctly floral composition, defined by a persistently elemental rose and conveying the beauty associated with the flower.

To be honest, Favonius pleasantly surprised me, and I found the scent to be very beautiful, lovely, and quite unisex. The longevity on my skin was around 10 hours. I would describe the sillage as rather mediocre; at least I wasn't approached about the scent. The top note starts off quite sweet and exceptionally fruity for me.

The regular exclusive fragrances that Harrods has in its range for a while, and which eventually all make their way to the "general" market, make things exciting. A hefty price tag adds to the intrigue. So here in a very simple green bottle, the Favonius, the story behind the name is worth reading and fits well.

I tested Favonius at the Lubner perfumery and fell in love immediately! It was wrapped up shortly after. Upon spraying, I perceive its initially very fruity character. I sense a wild berry mix. Then, relatively quickly, the rosy character comes to the fore; combined with pink pepper and incense, it becomes slightly spicier, but without losing its rosy lightness.

This was my absolute favorite scent for work on the plane. I like that the fragrance comes across as elegant but minimal. Often, I find scents to be too overpowering and aggressive in the direction of 'fresh.' This scent felt very warm to me with a hint of sweetness, just enough that it doesn't make you feel nauseous. I have always imagined this fragrance as being worn by those people you can smell pleasantly when standing next to them, wondering what they are wearing that exudes such quiet confidence. I don't know if the perfume differs significantly, but for me, the body mist is a favorite and a great companion for situations where you want to smell like you are seeking affirmation.

The creators of Vain & Naïve must've really been inspired when they were naming the fragrance, because it's a spot-on description of what you can expect from it. If the same amount of inspiration was used in creating the scent itself, I believe we would've gotten a different story. Now, frankly, fruity-floral sweet fragrances sit in a category that has never appealed to my tastes. So I guess I might be biased because of that. But I still can appreciate a good, well-crafted fragrance, even if it doesn't exactly suit me. And although Vain & Naïve is far above Lattafa-level fruity fumes that can pass as "Terrible & Disastrous", it is still nowhere near to the level of perfumery I'd expect given its price tag. The opening brings a very short-lived burst of citruses, soon overpowered by an unexciting blend of florals and fruits. The jasmine, in particular, sticks out the most with its intensely floral-sweet aroma and slight muskiness. The rose is harder to pinpoint on its own, but it surely aids to the overall floral fruitiness of the composition, maybe even adding sort of a 'tea' vibe underneath. The raspberry is not overly strong with its fresh, sweet, tart, and vibrant fruitiness, while the plum is yet again, harder to spot, due to it having a combination of soft, fruity, sweet, and floral characters which just makes it nearly impossible to stick out in a composition with other notes that bring similar accords. Things don't get any more interesting at the base. Actually, things get even more boring. A clean, slightly powdery musk arises, with a faint ambery warmth and sweetness, which dominate the other base notes, whilst they themselves being dominated by the floral fruitiness of the heart notes. The benzoin and tonka bean notes would supposedly sweeten things more with a vanillic-like scent, but I don't get any. At best, I get a balsamic undertone from the benzoin. As for the patchouli, it brings no earthiness or woodiness typical to it, but rather an understated, yet deep musky sweetness. And regarding the sandalwood/cedarwood, you sort of can tell that there is something going on behind curtains, like a mild spicy sweetness tied to sandalwood, but woodiness on itself stands rather hidden in the overall blend. Once the fragrance has properly developed and all the notes are through, I'm left with a fruity, feminine-leaning, floral soap-like scent, which translates to lack of originality. The quality won't impress anyone either, and the development of the scent on-skin is lackluster. If I were to put the last two paragraphs in a single word, then that would be: unimpressive. Performance disappointed me further, with about 3-4 hours of longevity, becoming a skin scent somewhere around the one hour mark. The projection wasn't something to bloat about either, although for that first half an hour to maybe an hour, the fragrance did have pretty decent sillage. But as for projection on its own, 1 foot and a half at best. So I'd say it's safe to add a few extra sprays. However, keep in mind that my skin chemistry lacks... chemistry with many fragrances, and looking at other's votes around here, it seems I sit in the minority getting such poor performance from it. One good thing that comes out of all of this is the versatility of Vain & Naïve . It's not about finding the right occasions for it, it's about finding occasions where it wouldn't fit. It can work as a daily, for work, for school, dressed-up events, dates... The list goes on. But as I mentioned already, this leans feminine, so it might not be the best choice for a man, even though I still think it can pass as unisex just fine. "Soft & Generic", "Boring & Bland, "Unexciting & Unimpressive"... pick your choice. Any of these would fit as a substitute for Vain & Naïve . From the couple of Nishanes I've tried so far, this one is the least inspiring one yet. It doesn't smell bad per se; it just doesn't do anything that makes it stand out. And when talking about niche perfumery, "Different & Unique" are the keywords I'm looking for, ESPECIALLY if I'm paying $200. So even if you were to love this scent for whichever of its not-so-bright attributes, I still would hardly see myself recommending it, simply because you can find many other similar scents for less money, or even better overall fumes for less money. So truly, this does seem like a fragrance made in vain. Overall Rating: 4.8/10

This is a sweet rose with dusty pineapple scent. I know, I know, there's no pineapple in the pyramid of notes, but this is how it reads on my skin. Probably that combination of fruit with jasmine has created this olfactory illusion for me. I wasn't drawn to it at first, but it grew on me the more I wore it, until I found myself craving to give it one more sniff, and one more sniff. There's a kind of dusty-sweet aspect here, almost like you're blowing away the sugar on dried pineapple slices. I think the name, Vain & Naive, is perfect for it: this is one of the cuter, younger roses out there, and she's almost a little silly, but still likeable.

So the start is a bit muddled and all over the place. I get a fleeting, but very citric start with the citrus fruits, almost mouth-puckering. After that, it's a salad fruit fight where plum ends up coming out on top after a few dozen minutes. Plum on my skin is usually a hit or miss. This time it's a miss: it has a weird fresh synthetic vibe to it, but also teeters close to the plum jam territory and is very dark, moody-like. It's almost like it doesn't know if it has to stay fresh, or become a dark, sultry, sweet plum. I get a synthetic, fresh rose that ends up coming along for the ride and, overall, the partnership doesn't fare well to my nose. The drydown is an absolute mess of different notes clashing together: dirty and earthy patchouli, weird warm musk, powdery tonka bean and a resinous benzoin mixed in with the previous plum and rose. Just overall not my kind of fragrance, nor my vibe. At this price-point, it also ain't it. Not a blind-buy for sure.

Dear little prince, you have been traveling through the galaxy for a long time, and I miss you so much. The fox and I are at the Tonka festival. Oranges, lemons, plums, and raspberries are competing with each other here. You know, I am a delicate little rose - not as strong as the desert roses in neighboring Tauerville. And just watching costs me a lot of strength. Jasmine is here too; she sends her regards. This year, the tonka beans are hosting this spectacular festival. The fox thinks they have gone overboard, tonka bean here - tonka bean there. I tell you, I prefer the Guerlinade - much more peaceful, and it wasn’t so loud there. And the girls in the black dresses had such delicious nectar. They even traveled from the star Cassiopeia; I like the golden hats of the ladies in white on the stands. It’s sooo hot here at the Bosporus, the fox keeps handing me water. We are having fun, but we miss you very much. And we are worried about you. I know the snake will eventually bring you to us. But until then, enjoy your life. Feel embraced, my dear Your rose

I don't know why I ordered this sample, because if I had studied the notes, I would have known right away that the scent would be a big no for me. And that's exactly how it is.. I am absolutely not a fan of too much fruit in a perfume, so much for that, but somehow I hoped that rose and jasmine would be the main players in the drydown.. That is definitely not the case at all.. The scent starts off extremely fruity. In the first 30 minutes, I only smell freshly squeezed orange juice with a few splashes of bergamot.. Quite sour and absolutely not my thing.. In the drydown, unfortunately, I don't smell any floral notes except for a hint of a very unripe pink rose that almost smells green. However, I clearly smell an overripe plum, which makes the whole fruit cocktail even worse and almost overwhelming for me.. I unfortunately don't smell tonka or sandalwood at all. The scent remains very fruity and zesty and tends more towards the masculine side for me. For my nose, something soft, elegant, and feminine is missing.. I also have no idea who could wear this scent.. I see no images in my mind except for a weird mix of fruit juice and mixed canned fruits.. (Childhood trauma)…

Nishane is usually reliable, for me this Turkish niche brand is right at the top of my list when it comes to the overall package and value for money. Of course, one should always look in shops with a lot of discounts, and then you can get fantastic fragrances with great longevity and quality.

Vain & Naïve reminds me of Bitter Peach by Tom Ford. Although it doesn’t list a peach note, I perceive this characteristic iced tea peach note. I find it a bit brighter and more beautifully balanced. Cheerful, bright iced tea with flowers and cream in the background. Very underrated and comes across beautifully, especially in summer.

L'Artisan Parfumeur VANILIA has apparently been discontinued, but I reviewed it a while back and happened upon the remaining milliliter in my sample vial while looking for something else. Apparently some people regard this perfume as a masterpiece (ahem). It smells to me most like vanilla wafers, which I happen to love, although I cannot say that I've ever considered dusting my body with their scent. I suppose that I could pulverize them and see how that works... Another reviewer has reported that VANILIA calls to her mind banana pudding. I'm wondering whether she may be confusing the smell of vanilla wafers--used to line the pie shell of a banana pie--with the banana cream proper. All good Americans have tasted this dessert, a veritable institution of middle class suburban culture, and particularly prevalent in parts south of the Mason-Dixon line. It's basically a layer of vanilla wafers on top of which sliced bananas are placed before being covered with what is usually vanilla pudding. Yes, that is what VANILIA is to my nose: a comfort food, not a great perfume! (-;

This fragrance starts with an accord made of vanilla and ylang ylang. Reminiscent of Vanilla Galante, this fragrance is sweeter and heavier than the Hermessence. The two notes, spice and floral, are well-blended and harmonise perfectly. Underneath the two note I detect a trace of amber which gives the fragrance depth and a slight saltiness which boosts by contrast the vanilla note. As the fragrance progresses, it sheds most of the vanilla note and all there remains is ylang ylang framed by amber and a touch of vanilla. Now a true floral, the fragrance is soft and feminine, perfect to wear on a spring or early autumn evening. As the fragrance dries down, it gets fuller and softer, the floral note slowly fades and amber and sandalwood characterise this last stage. Lasts for hours on my skin.

What did I write in my "preferences"?: I don't like explicit vanilla scents! I hate the overpowering, almost aggressive smell of vanilla in cheap scented candles and bath oils, room fragrances during Christmas time, etc. Vanilla often comes with a kitschy candy sweetness. Terrible! Even the vanilla gourmands from Comptoir Sud are too one-dimensional for me, lacking in refinement. So, a tricky terrain for me. When I became interested in your opinions on L'Artisan Parfumeur, I noticed the almost hymnic reviews for "Vanille Absolument," and intrigued by that, I dared to take a sniff test. I did have "Vanilia" under my nose, but by the time I realized that there were actually two vanilla scents in the line, I was already vanilla-seduced and on a sniffing trip, so to speak, hooked. Kankuro has described the process well: the first accords are indeed almost green and fresh, but then it quickly becomes softer and rounder, until the vanilla opens up wide and velvety. I can understand the association with sweet, sexy banana, but I smell a much stronger burnt caramel, which gives the vanilla a soft brown depth and calmness. The amber note keeps it from being prickly and jarring, from greedily pushing forward. That's how I like vanilla, and the "hmm" factor is quite high. I am now very happy to have been seduced by you Parfumos to vanilla. I can hardly believe it. What else might be coming my way?

Thanks to the lovely medicine who left me a leftover bottle of this delicious fragrance. I am completely enchanted, I have always loved vanilla perfumes, but this one is truly something special. Namely for adult women. Not a cheap vanilla that smells like scented candles, but a very gentle, noble scent, and the sandalwood and ylang-ylang give it that special touch. This morning, after spraying it on, the scent surrounded me all day, light, not overpowering, and every time the fragrance wafted into my nose, I was genuinely delighted to realize that it was me who smelled so wonderful..... Ah, I am completely in love. Finally, a vanilla scent without that annoying rubber note that I have experienced in many fragrances of this kind.
Ylang Ylang and vanilla describes it quite accurately but much spicier than the Ylang Vanille from Guerlain Aqua Allegoria.

It was an experiment, a present for my gf, and at the beginning was out of my taste (the fragrance, of course!). By the moment I smelled praline wrapped into woods and some citrus blasts. Never met a fragrance like that before. Not obvious - which is a lot these days. Worth tasting, however the price is high.

Lovely creamy saffron (slightly metallic) at the top that ends up sharing the spotlight with plenty of powdery-like florals. The powderiness of this fragrance is what overall turned me off from this fragrance. The praline note is sweet, but not overpowering: adds dimension to the fragrance. Notes seem a bit muddled to my nose. Drydown is woody with a sweet vanilla: gives warmth and comfort. Overall it's a fragrance that leans more feminine, but I think anyone could pull it off. It has that lovely, effortless vibe to it and a certain level of comfort and cozyness. I can understand why people love it, but I find it a bit pricey for the overall scent I'm getting. Won't be making it into my collection, but I'm glad I got to try it!

To level set, I have a decant, so my opinion might not be accurate to the actual bottle with a way better atomizer. I smelled straight-up sweet candy and gummies. It could be the fruits mixed with saffron but I honestly did not get anything else. One day when I have access to a bottle, I will try again but for now it is too sweet for me!

No review for this fragrance yet? I'm surprised. Even this rather mediocre rating for a niche fragrance is disappointing, especially when considering the previously hyped scents from this brand. Overall, this brand seems to have faded away in terms of hype, and the more recent releases have flopped. I haven't tested the newer releases, but fortunately, I did test this one, as I find it damn good. A sample was included with an order, and it was love at first sniff. Not for me, but for a lady. Even though it is labeled as unisex and can also be worn by confident men: This scent reminds me too much of Libre Eau de Parfum Intense from YSL. I find it difficult when a man smells like a women's bestseller. Although there are some masculine elements present here. Nishane and Anne Flipo? Quite an unusual combo. Anne Flipo's creations are rather mainstream, and the entire Libre line is from her. Nishane's releases have been more elegant, classic, and less mainstream. With this Tempfluo, you get a very mainstream DNA, but in a very high-quality execution. The suggested retail prices are therefore quite inflated. 100ml regularly costs over €300. However, you can get the 50ml for around €120 and the 100ml for about €170, which is relatively fair. Since this is labeled as unisex, I pondered for a long time whether it would suit me. However, I have come to the conclusion that I prefer it on women. With saffron and cedarwood, there are some unisex notes present, but this Libre-like DNA remains, especially prominent in the first hours. The praline and jasmine also give off a slight Good Girl vibe. The spicy saffron makes it somewhat more unisex, but I have decided to leave this one for the ladies. The best part of this fragrance, in my opinion, is the wonderful top note: sweet praline surrounded by soft, sensual flowers. Orange blossom and jasmine are clearly detectable here, and anyone who likes these notes should definitely test this fragrance. Especially if you enjoy these mainstream DNAs. Here, you also get a lovely saffron spice that doesn't overpower, like in BR540 or Oud for Greatness. The floral sweetness is at the forefront in the first half of the fragrance. In the second part, the scent relaxes and leans more towards a woody sweetness. Pleasant cashmere wood with great cedarwood, along with a not-too-sticky sweetness. Sensual, soft, and somewhat reserved compared to the top note. But overall, a fragrance that impresses and convinces me. The performance is quite good, as expected for this type of fragrance. Longevity is in the double digits, but with good sillage in the first 3-4 hours. After that, it is still somewhat perceptible close to the skin. Sufficient and never too much. Overall, for me, a great fragrance for women and also for confident men. Those who like the Libre DNA should definitely give this one a try.

As a fan of "Libre (Eau de Parfum Intense) | Yves Saint Laurent," I had to try this fragrance here, as both scents are often compared in their DNA. The opening is a saffron explosion that I have never experienced in a fragrance before. Strangely, the opening doesn't remind me of saffron but rather of the typical bitter almond aroma (the one used in baking). Very herbaceous, very bitter, and, in my opinion, even quite almond-like, almost reminiscent of marzipan (even though almond is not listed). However, this explosion dissipates within a few short minutes, leaving behind a sensual, sweet, warm, yet fresh oriental scent. The soft orange blossom and vanilla come through, paired with a freshness that I can't quite place. For me personally, there is even a hint of mint detectable in the background (although, again, not listed). I can somewhat understand the comparison to "Libre (Eau de Parfum Intense) | Yves Saint Laurent." Nevertheless, I find this fragrance to be very unique and "standing on its own." The heart notes, in a very distant way, remind me of the typical Libre intense DNA, but they have their own personal character. The scent is warm and sweet. However, because there is always a certain freshness present in the background, it is not a headache-inducing scent that overwhelms you. In my opinion, it leans more towards the masculine side. A light note of men's shower gel or aftershave, which is still pleasant for a woman, is noticeable. The fragrance is warm and inviting. It definitely tends towards a southern aesthetic (dark hair, dark eyes, and sun-kissed skin). Over time, the praline note comes out more, and it even starts to smell somewhat edible. The image and scent of raw cookie dough come to mind. In the drydown, it develops woody and soft at the same time, even with a hint of creaminess. Anyone who knows the scent of cashmere candles will find a bit of it here as well. Sweet, woody, and soft at the same time. Overall, I find the fragrance very pleasant, inviting, warm, and incredibly sensual. I just put it on and can't stop sniffing my arm. It definitely has a certain addictive quality.

For a long time, I searched for a fragrance for spring. It should be fruity-gourmand and multi-layered, preferably with orange or mandarin, and if necessary, with lemon. However, I wanted to avoid any cleaning product vibes, like with "Arancia di Capri | Acqua di Parma.

I first heard of Jatamansi when I pulled the sample from the magnificent travel letter by JilMare. The more interested I became, as Jatamansi, in English "Indian Spikenard," has a rich history in its use. Mentioned as a healing oil in the Old Testament, and applied in Ayurveda, it is still used today, among other things, for its calming effect. The start is quite fruity; everyone knows the smell of the mess caused by peeling grapefruit. Then comes the sage in full force. This musty mintiness is louder than I have ever perceived it before. In no perfume. It transforms into something curry-like, but authentic curry, which is not necessarily spicy but smells of a variety of spices, not this watered-down fast-food curry. I don't know the scent of Indian Spikenard and unfortunately can't place it; it may be that what I perceive as curry is the spikenard. Additionally, I perceive something like "skin care," which fortunately stays more in the background. That should be the rose. Soon it dips away again, and this curry-like scent plays a one-two with the sage. When I think of sage here, I think of the moist, pleasant feeling of sauna infusions. Here, Jatamansi occasionally makes brief forays into spicy "tea-scented realms." I must say that this perfume truly fascinates me. The transformability of the individual notes, which alternately come to the forefront and create strong images, I find really rare. I had long planned a trip to India or Sri Lanka, and this scent grabs me right at this longing and brings my travel urge to the surface. In the base, everything settles a bit; this "back and forth" I perceive loses itself in the consistency of the smell of a small shop where you can traditionally purchase Asian groceries, as well as small figurines, teas, oils, and incense. For me, it's not a scent I want to wear, even though I really like this perfume in its composition and the scent appeals to me; I would rather see it on women of any age. Unfortunately, this scent is no longer available, which is a shame because it is truly something special. It seems to remain the quirky aspect of the fragrance world that numerous dupes and copies coexist while unique scents fall by the wayside and get discontinued. Hopefully, this round bottle flacon remains, in which it appeared alongside the beautiful slender 50 ml bottles (which are unfortunately no longer available). Thank you very much for reading my comment.

I have something that I call 'places of longing.' Places of longing are places I have not yet been, which exert an irresistible attraction on me, without my being able to rationally justify it. I have already been to some of my previous places of longing - mostly it was quite different than I had expected - yet always wonderful. One of the current (and already old) places of longing is the Windamere Hotel in Darjeeling. Darjeeling is a town located in the far northeast of India, nestled between Nepal and Bhutan on the slopes of the Himalayas, surrounded by tea gardens, the product of which bears the same name as the town at its center. Once a significant caravan station, Darjeeling became a popular refuge for British colonial officials and officers in the 19th century, who fled to the cool mountains during the heat of summer. The Windamere Hotel dates back to this time; initially founded as a simple lodging establishment on Observatory Hill in the middle of the town, it has gradually been expanded to become quite comfortable over the years. Today, it is a rather luxurious hotel, albeit architecturally largely unchanged - nostalgically British and Indian-colonial at the same time. From its terraces, one can see Kangchenjunga, the third highest mountain on Earth at 8,586 meters. The place of longing Windamere Hotel envisions that I stay there for at least a month and am treated like an old friend. I would take long walks through the tea gardens early in the morning, and a weather-beaten planter would instruct me in the details of cultivation. I would spend the afternoons with Lord Byron or the letters of unhappy lovers in a deck chair on the terrace or in one of the salons - if it gets too cool there, with a blanket over my knees. In the evenings, guests are served Indian dishes and tea by the fireplace, and after dinner, I would engage in long, meaningful conversations with the other solo travelers staying at the hotel whom I meet there. Wild Jatamansi will grow around the hotel, a plant related to our valerian in its effects and uses, also known as 'Indian spikenard.' The old tea planter will crush its leaves between his hands and then let me smell its aroma - healing, cool, serious, and full of tranquility. He will silently instruct me to close my eyes and do the same, and I will follow how its delicate scent gently lingers - flowers and fruits at most quite shyly involved. Towards the end, there are slightly balsamic notes, hardly more than a hint of incense and an accord like clean paper - and then it is over. Conclusion: the scent of the Windamere Hotel in Darjeeling - a scent full of seriousness and precise, quiet coolness. One that calms the spirit and gives things a center - and requires time and contemplation.

Indian spikenard (Valeriana jatamansi), a useful and medicinal plant from the valerian genus, is native to the Himalayas and is now threatened with extinction due to wild harvesting. Known and valued since ancient times, the most famous mention of spikenard oil can be found in the New Testament, when Jesus has his feet anointed in Bethany. In Indian Ayurveda, spikenard is used as a calming agent, while also strengthening the mind, stabilizing, and balancing. The scent is described as heavy, sweet-woody, and reminiscent of valerian. L'Artisan had a time when fragrances with 100% natural ingredients from controlled organic cultivation were produced. This one belongs to that category, as does the Côte d'Amour launched in 2009. L'Eau de Jatamansi places spikenard at the center of the fragrance, as the listing of the notes shows. Slightly floral, with a pleasant sweetness, but without the indicated citrus fruits, a balsamic tone quickly emerges. Ergoproxy's pharmacy association is understandable. A hint of iodine and brown adhesive tape also wafts into my nose, but this is just a fleeting moment and soon dissipates. From this point on, there is little progression. The spikenard takes a woody path, becoming a bit drier and, after a good longevity of at least six hours, settles into its earthy bed, slightly reminiscent of patchouli. I really like the scent. Balsamic, but in a delicate way, close to the body and warming, this could become a welcome companion for the upcoming dreary weather. Unfortunately, L'Eau de Jatamansi has already been discontinued, and L'Artisan is now moving in other directions.

Do you know that strange smell that greets you when you enter a pharmacy? I perceive the scent as a mixture of disinfectant, cardboard, and chamomile tea. The opening of L´Eau de Jatamansi smells somewhat like this. This olfactory impression is more fascinating than beautiful, and I don’t necessarily need to have it as a perfume. After the pharmacy whiff, the perfume completely fades into the background, meaning you only perceive it on the skin. The heart note then develops into a floral-spicy scent with a bitter taste in the finish. With the arrival of the base, only a subtle, spicy afterglow of the fragrance remains, and after two hours, it’s all over. If you overlook the little pharmacy smell at the beginning, this L´Artisan is a calm, pleasant scent that you forget just as quickly as it dissolves into pleasantness.

The opening is a sharp, sparkly amber. Then it settles in a soft marshmallow, a bit creamy and vanilla, with an underlying scent I can't quite pinpoint, spicy and a bit smokey. It's a perfect mist for a cold fall evening, it's cosy and slightly sultry at the same time, it has this warmth you're looking for in an autumn fragrance. Some people may find it cloying and heavy tho. Its lasting power is quite good and it projects fairly well for a body mist. Layered with By the fireplace, it's a photorealistic smore's treat enjoyed by a bonfire.

Obscuratio, it’s ylang, but not the sunny, enveloping kind. Here, the flower becomes harsh, almost biting, with a sharp greenness that grips the throat. A raw intensity, almost aggressive, far from the caressing exoticism one might expect. Maybe the patchouli has something to do with it. Vanilla tries to make an appearance, but it stays in the background, far too shy next to this dominating ylang. No roundness, no comfort, just a lingering tension, a shadow without softness. A fragrance that doesn’t leave you indifferent, but, for me, it’s sorely lacking in balance.

A gift from my parents after a trip to Paris. They asked the sales person for a sweet perfume with vanilla and this is what they recommended. I don’t know if I’d describe it as such though. To me, this is a perfect fall perfume, but it’s Patchouli with a capital P. Now, I personally do love patchouli, and it’s very well done here, but it’s not for everyone. I find this so unique because it’s patchouli, which is usually sweet, dark and earthy, with vanilla and ylang ylang. I’d never think to combine those notes. The ylang gives it a brightness that makes it unlike any patchouli scents I’ve tried. It smells like a happier sister to Lush’s Lord of Misrule. It’s very beautiful and my go-to around Halloween Time. Sillage 6/10, Longevity 8/10

This one's a highlight from the La Botanique collection for me. Banana candy from the ylang ylang + smooth and dark vanilla + ...and a patchouli that rounds out the whole thing with depth and maturity. The patchouli (or maybe another unlisted note) is lightly camphorous, too—a bit like Vicks VapoRub, but only gently. It's a really solid trio that makes sense olfactorily. As a color, it's butter yellow and amber brown. As a personality, it's sensitively masculine.

obscuratio, lat. - 1. Darkening, obscuration 2. the unnoticed _________________________________________ I didn't expect this anymore. But the trap closed, and now I'm inhaling this blood-orange flower dust. Like an intoxicating, hot surge of tiger lilies, it takes my breath away, only to breathe it back in. My eyelids fall as the paradisiacal perversion of this nectar dusts my synapses and exhales in a warm cloud of ochre, vanilla, and pollen. In the red aura of a timeless afternoon under a shady canopy, I bask like a blissful snake in the triad of noble exoticism, earthy breath, and velvety spice, patiently sniffing and waiting for Adam's new desire... _________________________________________ The perfect acoustic accompaniment to this fragrance for me is the song "Duality" by DIE FORM. OBSCURATIO represents for me the duality of danger and seduction, sin and sensuality, elegance and assault. A floral trap that falls shut. Heavy, yet in a state of suspension. _________________________________________ I already mentioned in my statement the similarity to BLACK ORCHID, which I found interesting but also disturbing, and with which I had more or less put the explicitly floral direction to rest. I saw it as my last hope in this regard. However, OBSCURATIO possesses all the good aspects of BLACK ORCHID while lacking the bad ones. No rot, no black mold, or organic waste here, because this dark flower stands not only in aromatic, rain-fresh earth but also in full sap, pulsing in its thick, fleshy petals, revitalizing, aphrodisiac! Sillage and longevity seem to fluctuate; I would generally place them in the good average. The matte glowing orange of the flower on the bottle and packaging in contrast to the dark background is extremely well chosen, just like the fragrance itself. The price initially put me off; I find it too high. In its defense, it must be said that the scent gives a truly very natural and high-quality impression. Since I also had space in my collection for a predominantly floral fragrance, I decided to let it slide a bit (well, a little more). Thanks again to FrauKirsche for the random sample! I probably wouldn’t have tested anything in this direction after my Black Orchid trauma. You really never know what else is lurking in obscurity out there, waiting to go unnoticed. ;)

I remember finding this scent for myself in a small perfumery. This fragrance hits me really hard. So hard that I feel like I'm back in my school days when I smell it. It smells great, the bottle looks beautiful, but this scent. I've experienced this scent before. Specifically, back when I was in school. Those little brown cola candies that you could buy at the bakery back then. That's exactly what it smells like to me. It's not bad, you just have to like it. I had my fun with it, but I wouldn't get this scent a second time due to the price. Thanks for reading. Best regards

If you've always wanted to smell like a real, freshly carved pumpkin, then this is the perfect fragrance. And I mean that in no way derogatory. Because it is a realistic pumpkin scent. It smells exactly like when you cut open a pumpkin. Nothing more, nothing less. Without spices or caramel, which are usually found in such fragrances. I love this scent precisely for that reason.

This is probably in my Top 5 OF all time. It's smoother than the OG. I wore it today and was stopped twice to ask what I was wearing. Very surprising since it's not a mass appealing scent. Yes, fresh but more complex than most freshies. The price is a lighter steep right now but I think next year it will be on discounters.

I'll keep for myself the memories this one evokes, but I consider it to be the best of Nishane. Yes, the best of them all. That creamy peach in the opening, that unsweetened vanilla mixed with leather in the drydown... this is pure class, and a wonderful creation. A total must. I don't know why Ani or Hacivat get so much praise and this one is criminally overseen.

I really enjoyed HSW-X; the blend of youthful white florals with vanilla and darker and more mature leathery undertones is truly sublime. It has got a solid performance as well. It may be fem leaning for some but any man can pull it off in my opinion. It is very safe to be worn in the office or public places as well as night outs and events.

This scent doesn't really appeal to me and I feel its a little disjointed but I actually got complimented by a co-worker today. I like the start of the scent but the middle notes were non-existent and the dry down smelled a little synthetic to me. It starts with powdery sharp citrus that isn't bitter. It transforms into a sweet citrus, but not overwhelming. That fades into almost undetectable white floral notes. I thought the scent had disappeared. But then comes the vanilla sweetness comes back with a smoky leather scent that is a little synthetic, almost like the smell of a band aide. So it starts soft and citrus, disappears, then comes back as sweet smoky synthetic. I don't feel a natural progression with this fragrance. It must project very well because my co-worker immediately noticed it when I clocked in, I did smell it on my skin for at least 5 hours.

This is where elegance meets danger. This fragrance makes me feel like a film noir queen. It's sensual and fierce. It screams confidence. Really love that the vanilla isn't sweet and how the leather notes stays strong on me. This is complex and powerful. Some say it's more on the "feminine" side but I think it would suit anybody confident enough. One of my top fragrances!

Champ de Baies is a rather straightforward red berries solinote fragrance on me. When sprayed on skin, the fruity sweetness of blackberry and raspberry immediately takes charge. Unfortunately, none of the earthy green tartness of rhubarb or any other vegetal elements come through. Maybe it's because of the eau de cologne concentration, or the lack of a prominent caramel note, the fruity sweetness of red berries thankfully doesn't feel too saccharine. However, Champ de Baies is still pretty monotonous throughout its wear. A clean patchouli pops up here and there with time, but it's mainly a meek cedar-white musk raft that the red berries latch on in the dry down. Champ de Baies now essentially smells like the dry down of the 2006 Nina by Nina Ricci on my skin, albeit slightly more refined and less sweet. The longevity of Champ de Baies is around 6-7 hours on me, and it stays rather close to skin for the most time. While the first two instalments of L'Artisan's Cologne series seemingly aim at reinventing eau de cologne, Champ de Baies no longer adheres to the structure, but is more like a diluted version of a conventional sweet red berries-clean musk fragrance. It's surely a pretty perfume, but not necessarily remarkable among the crowded fruity floral genre. I'd recommend it to those who enjoy the dry down of Nina Ricci Nina, but find the first few hours too sweet and have more budget.

As a die-hard L'artisan lover, I purchased this fragrance last week and am truly surprised by its addictive effect on me. Normally, I don't like fruity scents, but this one has really captivated me. I perceive it as fruity, zesty, and slightly tangy at first before it transitions into a lightly floral note, followed by warm woody notes that last about 4 to 5 hours on me. I am currently using it every day and am grateful for your reviews. It’s only because of them that I even became aware of this fragrance.

This is my only fragrance that contains real oud. The oud in here is barnyardy but not overly fecal. Slightly animalic but much less than Africa Olifant. The oud doesn't come out as leathery at all. It is sweetened up in this formulation. Very easy to wear if you chose the right time and place for it. The word Musiqa might refer to how harmonious these woody notes blend together. The grapefruit in the opening is there just to make the fragrance more palatable and not to scare you away. The dry down is a beautiful woods blend with soft spices. You can make a statement wearing Musiqa Oud. This is my longest lasting Nishane with around 24 hours on the skin. Projection is a above avarage to great, 10 hours.

It is with great pleasure that I discover more perfumes from the Nishane brand originating in Istanbul. Recently, I've been wearing "Musiqa Oud" and I must admit that it is a real olfactory music for my ears. Thick, intense, step by step majestically revealing its chords. It stands out from many other European oudish perfumes. The realism of the aroma makes it shifting towards the Middle East aesthetics. The smell opens up like a dented resin-fruit chord, a bit tanninous, a bit towards a strong, dense bourbon, which gradually transforms into the central oud theme as the minutes pass. This chord - in a manner which is characteristic to very concentrated perfumes ("Musiqa Oud" is an "extract de parfum" - concentration is higher than that of eau de parfum) - is blooming on skin gradually with each quadrant. It is acquiring power and clarity. In its woody, sweet-resinous heart it smells like Dior's "Oud Leather", but it is less obtrusive and much more acceptable to me. Less animalic and persevering, more resinous and sweet. The heart lasts here for a few hours (yes!) to finally give the way to the dry-wood base - the one I like the most. It is dominated by guaiac and sandalwood, both strengthened by cypriol which seems to be almost irreplaceable in such compositions. Still, an echo of the animal's heart can be smelled in the base. "Musiqa Oud" smells rather close to the skin (as it is usually with extrait de parfume). It let's me enjoying its extraordinary beauty without overwhelming people around me. The base lasts on the skin more than 24 hours. The smell of the fragrance is perfectly highlighted by the dark brown color of the liquid, which is so saturated that it almost looks dense. To sum it up: fantastic perfume with a connoisseur's charm. Especially for the fans of oud - it is necessary to test. I personally love it.

o be fair i have yo say that the quality of this perfume, as most nishane's, which is turning one of my favourite brands, is very high. Good raw materiales, Well blended, good performance, nice smell... But the last times i have a problem with ouds. Nowadays wverybody has an oud un his collection and It begining to get me bored a little bit. This one, of course, is different, as most are, this one has the medicinal toich of the oud, mixed with the tipical Green & creamy background that most nishane have and, qlthought It is not listed, for me the mix give a very chocolated smell... According to the feelings that It produces on me i would call It chocolate oud ???? so, if you are looking for an oud fragance, medicinal but not very dirty, intense and sweet this could be a very good opción but for me this is too similar to other fragances that i already have. Smell: 7.5 Longevity: 8 Sillage: 8 Originality: 6 Versatility: 6 Quality/price: 5 Global: 8

One of the cleanest, most refreshing oud-forward fragrances that I've had the pleasure to get my nose on. Opens animalic, but quickly dries to to an eminently pleasing, sweet, medicinal oud accord. Longevity is shorter-lived than I had hoped. Musiqa Oud is so good. It's a cross between Tiziana Terenzi Laudono Nero and Nasomatto Black Afgano. If I can find a bottle at a discount, I may have to make it a regular in the rotation.

Well, I am really tough when it comes to dirty and animalic scents. I like this kind of fragrance. However, if I hadn't been able to roughly gauge what to expect here - especially in the top notes - based on the previous comments and statements, it probably would have blown my mind. Virgin and even sensitive noses might be completely overwhelmed and possibly even repulsed by this. Those who do not like animalic scents will find no pleasure in this fragrance. Furthermore, those who find dirty animalics unpleasant or even disgusting will likely have found a true nemesis here. The opening is, without exaggerating for illustration, a genuine animalic club. Of the dirtiest kind. Anyone familiar with the base notes of Hyrax and Peau de Bête can expect similarly harsh stuff with Mūsīqá Oud. However, it also offers a completely different olfactory experience. There is, however, a not insignificant difference from the aforementioned animalic flagships, namely the restraining and caressing other notes that spread throughout the scent development. While I cannot perceive any flowers or floral nuances on my skin throughout the entire scent journey, I do get some of the most characteristic, best, and richest Oud I have ever smelled. And resins. And smoke. And wood. And leather. And very, very faintly at the back, thick and sluggish wild honey. The scent eventually settles down and becomes a bit cozier and sweeter - even though, in my perception, it remains light-years away from being a cozy scent. Nevertheless, all the nuances create a fragrance picture that is as skillful and harmonious as it can be. While we're at it, I really must mention the striking similarity of the animalic base note to Hyrax. Where Hyrax simply overwhelms me (overwhelms, not repulses), Mūsīqá Oud manages to completely engage and carry me along. The fecal note, which recedes somewhat over time, remains ever-present on my skin, but is so skillfully embedded and intertwined that I would almost call it beautiful (which sounds somewhat strange in relation to the word fecal). By the way, now that the word has come up about 20 times: is there a less negatively connoted word for "fecal"?? I usually use the term out of lack of a better word... Fantastic animalic Oud fragrance that scores on composition, longevity (the longevity described as 'enormous' is still an understatement) and character. I have completely fallen for this scent, which, given the price, has not only brought me happiness hormones. It is actually not that low... But it became clear to me (which rarely happens) after just a few seconds that this candidate belongs in my collection. And because it fits so well in multiple ways (and I am already celebrating myself a little for the resulting headline), I conclude by saying: beautiful shit!

From the Nishane samples, I, always greedy for oud, immediately reached for the fragrance named "Musiqá Oud." From an oriental perfume with oud, I expect an overwhelming oud, one way or another, depending on the day. After applying the oily "Musiqá Oud," I first smelled a slightly unpleasant oud accord. But I'm familiar with that. "It will get better," I thought.

Thanks to @Florian0886, I got a sample of this fragrance. After reading the comments, I was expecting an animalic bomb. However, it is far from that in my opinion. "Mūsīqá Oud" starts off fruity-floral. This top note fades quite quickly. After that, a rather strong and, in my view, at most moderately animalic oud sets in, accompanied by a pleasant saffron note.
Musiqa Oud and I did not have a good start (excluding the impressive packaging). Sprayed on and immediately detected the cow stall - grassy, earthy, and dirty - right in your face.

Some may surely think that this will be another negative review from me, but Mūsīqá Oud has really disappointed me. Perhaps I am just too spoiled by brands like Roja, Xerjoff Attars, Ensar Oud, or "The Night | Editions de Parfums Frédéric Malle" and "The Moon | Editions de Parfums Frédéric Malle.

.. wait a moment. Grapefruit dipped in Oud! Mūsīqá Oud is really very peculiar. It’s turning my head! Oud is very present, while the grapefruit is not at all. Although that’s not entirely true. I do sense a fruity, graceful component in the opening, but that could be anything.

My first 'niche' fragrance back in 2014 and one of the few scents in my collection that blew me away instantly. After reading all I could find about it and decided for another blind buy, I couldn't believe at first wearing it is a fragrance created in the 80's !...it has so many notes I usualy appreciate in a man's fragrance: bitter roasted coffee, spices, leather, dry florals, incense, tobacco - everything packed harmoniously and delivering a stunning and intriguing oriental-spicy scent. When I wear this, I imagine myself on a chill morning in a torn leather jacket on the upper deck of an old sail, drinking coffee from a tin can and enjoying the smell of Eastern spices coming from under the deck. In this regard, for me, L'Eau du Navigateur is more than a fragrance...it's a marvelous adventure of senses. It really stood the test of time, still high-ranking in my book. My humble rank 9.5/10 ☣☣☣☣☣. Highly recommended, specially for bitter-coffee fans.

I read that Luca Turin called l'Eau du Navigateur (1982) dated. He'd know better than I. I never smelled before 2013. Still, there is a distinction between dated, meaning era-specific, and tired, even if 'dated' has a negative connotation. Navigateur might be dated today, 32 years after its release, but it's held up well. To be innovative in 1982 and still smell good in 2013? Sounds successful. As a point of comparison Pink Sugar is both era-specific and tired, and was hardly innovative at the time of its release. There are worse things than dated. Does this make Navigateur the male equivalent of old lady perfume? I can live with that. I understand the classifications of the era: loud, spicy, woody as in Antaeus/Quorum/Krizia Uomo; basso fougere like Drakkar Noir and Azzaro pour Homme. I don't see Navigateur as just a crude precursor of more refined hybrids from the more discriminating 1990s. Rather, it's a re-imagined oriental with coffee in lieu of vanilla. Coffee bridges culinary spice to resin via woodiness, just as vanilla does. And while Navigateur might also have heralded the gourmand era, its focus is the roasted coffee bean. No cotton candy, no frappuccino. We twist ourselves into knots to imagine that without oakmoss and coumarin the chypre and the fougere are still alive; witness the original Miss Dior Cherie, already redacted by Dior, and Penhaligon's Sartorial. If we want to view perfumery historically, I vote for acknowledging and embracing the extant, significant perfumes such as Navigateur. Learn from it and enjoy it while it's here. Who knows when the IFRA will limit coffee use?

L'Eau de Navigateur is completely crazy. A vivid olfactory image. A great 1979 offering by Jean Laporte. Ahead of the time then, and now somehow stuck in space-time continuum. Synthetic at the moments, transparent and dense at the same time. It's hard to describe. A lot's going on here... spices, coffee, leather, tobacco, a bouquet of flowers, resins, incense... The notes hard to imagine together are successfully combined. The work of a genius. I can easily imagine it on a man in a white suit on some Caribbean island, drinking his first morning coffee and smoking cigarillos while reading the newspapers about last night's coup. It perfectly describes the small, but important rituals of life. L'Artisan please bring this beauty back.

The description of the notes sounded so beautiful, just like the picture that emerged with the story behind this fragrance. Maybe I let myself be influenced too much by my experiences with the smell of a CSP that bears a similar name; Eau du Gouverneur. However, L'Eau de L'Artisan Parfumeur navigator does not work for me. Where the CSP released in almost the same year can hold itself great against modern day scents, I think L'Eau du navigator has something old-fashioned and almost dated, I'd say. Something in there reminds me strongly of New West Him by Aramis and of the final stage of Amouage Interlude Man. Typical how smells can differ when compared to your expectations after studying the notes and reviews. /edit; So I gave this another chance. The first time I spilled a little of the fragrance all over the back of my hand, so this was rather overpowering and heavy. However, after applying just a little, it is a lot brighter and more detailed than I initially thought. I need to give this a full wear to give a more detailed insight into this fragrance. Guess I'll decant a little into a small spray vial. To be continued..

This fragrance opens with the familiar aroma of coffee, however, it is enhanced by smoky vetiver. A floral or citrus note lightens the impact of the two top notes, creating an interesting juxtaposition of smoke and floral, light and dark, earth and air. The scent is similar to Eau des Iles, but it is fresher and a tad sweeter. I ask myself if there is jasmine in this composition, because there is a faint indolic facet in the accord. It is a very pleasant fragrance, but not as rugged as Eau des Iles, the Artisan seaman is much more groomed.A well-crafted blend of coffee, vetiver, tobacco and flowers leads the scent into the dry down.

I will never understand. Not in this life and in none of my next ones. Not why my bread always falls on the buttered side. Not why the washing machine always eats just one sock. Not why a water pipe inevitably breaks on a Sunday, on Easter or Father's Day. And why a person like Donald Trump... But well, that doesn't belong here.

Artisans often reinvent the aromatic fougère theme, using different notes than the classics, while still achieving similar scent experiences. This was the case with Timbuktu, with Navegar - and very clearly also with L’Eau du Navigateur.

... because with a navigator that smells like this, I wouldn't know what to do. No, this is not my thing. At first, there is way too much lovage, which creates that strange Maggi smell that keeps coming through intensely. I'm not a soup chicken!! There is also a small amount of tobacco present, but this combination doesn't improve the overall impression.

..because I already had Maggi recently in the L'Artisan instant soup test series. Or maybe I mixed something up? Could be. Right now, I am also a bit overworked because no one thinks it's necessary to give me a break, uh, to keep my back free.

I was debating between Musc K and Meant to Be Seen, and something about Meant to Be Seen just captivated me a bit more (though I’m still thinking about getting Musc K as well!). This fragrance is a gorgeous, clean, quietly magnetic scent that feels both effortless and intentional. It opens soft, airy, and subtly sweet — like fresh skin after a shower, touched with a whisper of floral musk. As it settles, it becomes this cocooning, intimate aura that’s incredibly comforting yet still elegant. A perfect choice for any occasion and/or season.

Meant to be Seen is the epitome of a feminine fragrance. Initially, it has clean vibes from Musc K Ella K. Over time, it becomes increasingly floral. Sandalwood is also beautifully incorporated into this scent! A truly lovely fragrance that, to be honest, I see more on women. I've always been a fan of clean scents. And when something floral is added, jackpot :-D

After testing it twice, I simply couldn't resist last Saturday. "Meant to be Seen | Nishane," the new one from Nishane, had to join my collection. From the very first spray, I knew: This is no ordinary fragrance. The opening is a true highlight for me. A strong, crystal-clear iris immediately dominates the scene and gives the fragrance its very special, niche character. I love that moment when the iris leaves this dry, slightly powdery, almost paper-like impression. Like the smell of a freshly printed newspaper or a sharpened pencil. Beautiful, unique, and instantly captivating for me. However, this special top note unfortunately doesn't last too long. After a short while, the citrus and floral notes of bergamot and violet become more pronounced, before ambrettolid comes into play, a well-known molecule found in fragrances like Fleur de Peau Eau de Parfum or "Moscow Mule | Juliette Has A Gun." I'm not usually a big fan of this note, but here it works surprisingly well. Perhaps it's due to the fine balance between the delicate, sweet softness of the violet, the fresh bergamot, and the slightly animalic civet note. Together, they create a fascinating, intimate skin note that is not intrusive but perfect for everyday wear. The association with Tilia also becomes noticeable at this stage. This clean purity through musk and flowers makes one think of Tilia, without being as loud and radiant. After about an hour, the fragrance begins to unfold its warmth. The ambrettolid steps back, and Meant to be Seen develops into a creamier, woodier direction. The sesame note emerges, adding a slight nuttiness, while violet and freshness continue to resonate. At this stage, the scent actually reminds me a bit of "Bal d'Afrique (Eau de Parfum) | Byredo." It becomes creamier, sweeter, cheerier, yes somehow sunny and carefree. The base lasts surprisingly long, remaining close to the skin but consistently present. I can still smell it on my clothes the next day. What makes Meant to be Seen special for me is its complexity and beautiful evolution. It starts elevated, niche, clear, and dry. Then it becomes molecular, close to the skin, animalistically attractive, and warm. And finally ends creamy, woody, nutty, and sweetly cheerful. A fragrance that transforms yet is wearable in every phase. A fragrance doesn't have to be loud to be noticed. I absolutely cannot understand why this fragrance is labeled as mainstream. For me, it is a scent with personality, a quiet statement... special, elegant, yet approachable and suitable for everyday wear.

The cool morning light filters through the shutters, bathing the room in the Beverly Carlton Hotel in silvery blue. From the clock radio, "I Wanna Be Loved by You" plays. Marilyn sits in bed wearing her white silk shirt, her pouting lips shining perfectly. She sharpens a pencil and blows the fine shavings over the soft sheets. With a steady hand, she writes a sentence in her notebook: "I don’t want to make money. I Just want to be wonderful." Meant to be Seen is meant to be a tribute to Marilyn Monroe. A fragrance that aims to capture her multifaceted personality. When I first sprayed "Meant to be Seen | Nishane," it immediately reminded me of adr_ett or "You (Eau de Parfum) | Glossier." I compared the three on test strips and could only detect minimal differences. So, anyone who loves these delicate, powdery, musky pencil scents will also enjoy this one. The fragrance starts cool, crystal clear, almost fragile, reminiscent of a mix of pencil shavings and creamy lipstick. Meant to be Seen might be a bit sweeter, which could be due to the sesame. The civet cat is just a little baby cat quietly tiptoeing over Marilyn's bed. The development of the fragrance reflects the image we have of this woman. After the fragile, cool start, it becomes warmer and creamier. Enveloping like a cozy blanket. It then feels like a loving embrace, holding Marilyn to comfort her. And perhaps it elicits a liberating "I Am wonderful" from her. In conclusion, I would say it is a truly beautiful fragrance. However, since I already own adr_ett and "You (Eau de Parfum) | Glossier," I wouldn’t buy it at the moment, even though the longevity is longer. Although... The bottle really does look lovely.

Marketing ad absurdum - this fragrance from a fairly well-known label is available worldwide in only one single store: at Ludwig Beck in Munich. You can only achieve more exclusivity for the sake of exclusivity if you simply do not offer a fragrance after an elaborate launch. Rumors about its wonderful aroma would circulate, and fragrance aficionados around the world would be eager to hold it in their hands, even just once. At the same time, only a few chosen ones would be granted this honor, and behold: a new legend would be born - a new ‘Iris Gris’, a new ‘Chypre’, a new ‘Nombre Noir’, fragrances that everyone interested knows, but that have yet to be experienced by anyone... Well, Munich it is then - it’s not that far away, at least if you live in southern Germany. And the fact that a fragrance from a renowned French perfumer is not exclusively available at Boutique X on Boulevard Y, but at ‘Ludwig Beck am Rathauseck’ (as an earlier advertising slogan once stated) - that has its charm, doesn’t it? But to the fragrance: ‘Mon Numero 3’ is a vetiver study à la Duchaufour. Typical for this extraordinary perfumer (who presented similarly surprising works on the theme of tuberose, or aoud - ‘Nuit de Tubéreuse’ and ‘Al Oudh’) and at the same time atypical, when comparing the many interpretations of recent years. When you spray ‘Mon Numero 3’, the well-known vetiver cloud in shades of light green to dark green does not develop. No, Bertrand Duchaufour masterfully tames his material, taking away the loudness and penetrating quality, even if it would tend to dominate the scene like in the case of vetiver (or tuberose, or aoud). ‘Mon Numero 3’ is thoroughly a vetiver fragrance, with a linear vetiver structure from the top (Vetiveryl Acetate) through the heart (Vetiverol) down to the base (Vetiver de Java) - three vetiver building blocks with highly diverse facets: initially fresh-sour, then green-grassy, finally smoky-woody. At first, Duchaufour combines the central top note, the vetiveryl, with an alcoholic accent, enriched with fresh lime-like nuances, which immediately remind me of the scent of a margarita with a salted rim or a gin and tonic - a beautiful opening that whets the appetite for more. And there is more, much more. Nuances of lavender and herb-spicy cardamom briefly remind me of Duchaufour’s ‘Sartorial’ for Penhaligons, while the fragrance becomes increasingly colorful, floral, but also greener as it approaches the heart: a bouquet of rose, iris, orange blossom, and magnolia finally joins the anchor note vetiver, whose now distinctly greener facet is thanks to the vetiverol. Towards the base, the fragrance becomes darker. Warm amber tones and balsamic resins intertwine with the deep, smoky base notes of vetiver de Java. All of this sounds quite lush and voluminous, but it is not. Despite the richness of nuances, the fragrance does not develop heaviness and opulence. It is also not a lightweight that evaporates into the realms of nothingness. No, rather it possesses a subtle presence, while simultaneously shifting between transparency and density. Here, Duchaufour is at his very best: a man who unleashes a whole orchestra with great virtuosity without allowing the sound to swell excessively, who perfectly calibrates the individual voices, half suspended, half grounded, and who manages to let a fine, shimmering, yet resonant sound bloom. That the various phases are perfectly blended and glide seamlessly into each other goes without saying, as does the fact that the fragrance is wonderfully long-lasting and has a pleasant, rather moderate projection. It is a quiet companion, one that convinces with refinement, not with loudness. But beware! One must appreciate Duchaufour and his penchant for exceedingly complex, sometimes even complicated fragrances. Those who lament the supposedly missing aoud in ‘Al Oudh’ or point out the lack of tuberose in ‘Nuit de Tubéreuse’, who feel overwhelmed by ‘Sienne l’Hiver’ and cannot make sense of the unfamiliar charms of ‘Timbuktu’, will also struggle with this fragrance. It is simply not the vetiver scent one expects; especially not if one knows one or another and knows from experience that they all somehow smell quite similar (even if, for example, there are worlds between Guerlain’s ‘Vetiver’ and Etro’s version). Bertrand Duchaufour has created a highly idiosyncratic interpretation here, which, after initial irritation, convinced me quite quickly. In stark contrast to Karine Vinchon-Spehner’s equally idiosyncratic work ‘Coeur de Vétiver Sacré’ created for L’Artisan: this no less idiosyncratic fragrance initially convinced me, only to later greatly irritate me due to an unbalanced balance and lack of presence. ‘Mon Numero 3’ is by far the more interesting and original vetiver fragrance compared to that second vetiver scent from the house, and unlike ‘Coeur de Vétiver Sacré’, one does not feel as if unsolicited advertising pages are popping up, unfortunately reminding one that this fragrance is a hodgepodge of familiar pieces. A truly independent work, that is ‘Mon Numero 3’, which of course does not mean that the fragrance is without quotes (I have already mentioned ‘Sartorial’, and strangely I always have a bit of a ‘Mitsouko’ feeling at the very end of the fragrance development...), but one can indeed tell that a creative mind was striving to create something extraordinary, yet also something typical, something typical for him. He has succeeded.

I think men are so sick of the blue/shower gel style of fragrance that any similarity to Bleu de Chanel Eau de Toilette or Fierce Cologne is immediately dismissed as bland, unoriginal, played out, etc. I'm not going to say that Deziro is revolutionizing the scent game, but it's not a bad twist on the genre, and it's not as unoriginal as many reviewers are making it seem. To be honest, I think a few reviews are just based on smelling on a strip, since the scent opens up nicely on skin. There's a couple of differences I find between Deziro and other, more generic blue fragrances: firstly, in the opening/mid, the carrot and marine notes combine to give off a bit of a sunscreen/beachy vibe, which is what the marketing for this fragrance seems to focus on, even though it is not a summertime fragrance per se. Second, it has a really nice vetiver drydown that makes it seem more gentlemanly and refined than other blue fragrances. It almost goes the direction of a full on fougere, giving me the Platinum Égoïste Eau de Toilette kind of vibes. Except the oakmoss is replaced with vetiver in the base. Not a bad fragrance, maybe a bit boring compared to other Nishane fragrances, but a really nice dumb reach that can work in any situation.

I was originally drawn to Deziro because I'm a sucker for marine fragrances. I live in the tropics so marine fragrances are versatile and work for most of the year and on top of that it was created bu master perfumer Alberto Morillas so, it's safe to blind buy right? I started watching/reading reviews raising some concerns so I waited for a good deal to make sure I didn't spend as much. There are good and bad aspects to Deziro. The good: is very nice and clean, as mass appealing as they come so if you're a casual fragrance user it's a safe bet. You'll smell good and you might even get compliments. The bad: if you're a fragrance enthusiast this just won't cut it, it's far too generic. I can bump into someone wearing it and you'll probably won't recognize it because it can be any of the run of a mill blue fragrances out there. Deziro's performance is good but I'm not sure I wanna smell like it all day, after a while I just want it to stop so I can wear something more exciting.

Deziro is a surpisingly dull release from the brand. While not every fragrance needs to be highly complex, this one is excessively boring, even within its category. It's strange that Nishane chose to realease somthing so uninspiring. The simplicity of this scent doesn't justify its price, and i would choose any other Nishane fragrance over this one. Unnecessery release..

Deziro ! At the beginning, a zesty citrus accord where the mandarin pairs exceptionally well with the maritime notes. This gives the whole fragrance an excellent fresh start. As it develops, the geranium, mint, and cypriol become more prominent. The scent evolves into a slightly creamy direction with a lighter sharpness, imparted by the sandalwood and vetiver. The amber adds a sensual aura and contributes to the slightly creamy note. Hidden among all these notes is a little coconut; even though it is not listed, it is present. And that's a good thing! The freshness and the aquatic note remain consistently present. In the dry down, a calming and sensual hint of vetiver, aquatic notes, and sandalwood lingers. Deziro is, in my opinion, an excellent fragrance. Exotic yet elegant. The perfect companion at the beach and for a sophisticated dinner. A brilliant, summery scent for warm temperatures.

Nishane Deziro, received as a sample a month ago: Is it something special/new? “No, definitely not.” Are there more interesting fragrances? “Yes, of course.” Should it get a rating above 7? “No.” Nevertheless, it’s good to have such a fragrance in your collection! In everyday life, between work, family, daycare, hobbies, etc., there simply isn't the time and sometimes the desire to think every morning about which fragrance fits best today. Deziro is made for such days - category: “uncomplicated all-rounder,” similar to Percival or Bleu de Chanel. Its fresh orientation makes it especially wearable for me in spring and summer. However, it can also be worn year-round without any issues. And although there are undoubtedly cheaper alternatives, I personally like Deziro the most at the moment. Perhaps also because it is worn less frequently compared to Chanel or Parfums de Marly. In summary, one can say that it is not a must-have for fragrance lovers, or if you already have fragrances like Percival or Bleu de Chanel in your collection. Since my Percival has now run out, I will choose Deziro. Such a fragrance should not be missing in my collection at least.

The opening of this fragrance is not good to me (it smells green, almost soapy at first), but wait for about 10 minutes and there it is: delicate, elegant rose backed by a juicy, decadent plum, like sniffing a rose bush someone planted next to a plum orchard. This scent is soft, uber feminine yet isn't very sweet: people who dislike cloying fragrances may enjoy this one. This fragrance is best for women who like to smell feminine yet dislike super sweet scents. When I'm in a girly mood, this and Bombshell Passion are what I reach for. While not a skin scent, hardcore rose is more of the intimate side which is exactly what I want for a fragrance such as this: present yet not overbearing or screechy. I get about 4-5 hours on my skin. I took points off for the bottle because I dislike opaque bottles, but the scent itself is solid.

MA reads as freshly cleaned beetroots in liquid form! I can picture the kitchen towel used to wipe off the soil from the beets, and the veggies are in a bowl ready to be pickled or sliced. This is a faithful interpretation of beetroots. I’ve seen some reviews highlight an earth note, but my nose doesn’t detect it. I don’t get petrichor or the smell of fluffy, dark soil. In my humble gardening experience, beets (even when cleaned) have an earthy quality that’s complicated by an unexpected sweetness, similar to a carrot. Smelling this makes me feel closer to a homestead or garden. MA is definitely a photorealistic beetroot. Because of that, MA is not a mass-appealing scent. Few people are going to want to smell like the least loved root vegetable, and I can’t blame folks for that. I think MA could quiet a craving for gardeners and cooks, but I don’t think this will ever debut at Sephora, Ulta or Boots.

I feel this one preceded the vegetal trend we'll continue to see through 2024. It's a tender and humble fragrance with unquestionable beetroot note. I love beetroot and in this iteration, it's a little softer and tidier. It's... beetroots washed and prepped in a the kitchen, rather than beetroots yanked out of the ground with dirt flying around. I think the musk and pink pepper adds a quiet, sentimental quality about it that's more refined and less photo-realistic and earthy. But with beetroot being inherently an earthy note, I think this would be really nice (and an unexpected choice) for a younger, 20-something guy. The sort of guy who likes Aesop and Malin + Goetz, but isn't necessarily a hypebeast. If I think about it, this scent is almost like the younger, more timid brother to CDG's Rouge which is a much heavier beetroot/incense scent.

The American writer Tom Robbins begins his novel "Pan Aroma" with the following words: "The beet is the most intense of all vegetables. Admittedly, the radish is more exciting, but the fire of the radish is a cold fire, the fire of dissatisfaction, not that of passion. Tomatoes are at least lively fresh, but tomatoes are tinged with a hint of frivolity. Beets are dead serious." The beet, also known as red beet, beetroot, or simply beet, is a serious vegetable? Absolutely. It is earthy and often unremarkable, something that people ate in winter because there was hardly anything else available, a peasant vegetable. Beets may be intense, but they do not stand out. The same applies to Musc Amarante. The scent is individual, something that not everyone wears, but it does not overwhelm anyone. I must confess that I mainly know beets pickled from a jar and therefore do not really know how the actual beet smells (note to self: discreetly sniff at the supermarket without making people think I'm silly), but I will just assume for a moment that what I perceive as pleasantly earthy and down-to-earth, with a slight unobtrusive sweetness, is the beet. This remains present throughout, but towards the end, it is increasingly caressed by a gentle, also unobtrusive sweetness. The perfume is an understatement, but a successful one! It smells of groundedness, elegant modesty, in short, of someone who is at peace with themselves and the world. Someone who is content without having to shout it out to the world. In the aforementioned novel "Pan Aroma," the search for the recipe of a divine perfume is central, and the beet plays a crucial role as a component. And perhaps it is precisely in this "serious groundedness" of the beet that the divinity lies, for I think the world would indeed be a better place if we all were a little more like Musc Amarante.

MUSC AMARANTE is another fragrance from the new "Le Potager" series, which is dedicated to individual vegetables…… Here, it is the Beetroot. The scent starts citrusy-fruity and slightly peppery……after just a few seconds, the Beetroot joins in with a distinctly pleasant earthy and subtly sweet note…… This earth does not remind one of a grave, nor of musty decay….. Rather, this earth exudes the rich-aromatic scent of dark potting soil that has just been freshly raked…… Fine Ambrette and silky Musk "air out" and "lift" the darker earthy tones…… According to the manufacturer's specifications, Vetiver and Ambergris are also included as additional fragrance components in MUSC AMARANTE….. I can perceive the Vetiver quite well at the base in the form of a lasting freshness…..though it does not stand out prominently……. Ambergris, on the other hand, I cannot perceive in isolation…….it may reveal itself in the gentle, soft, and rather dark character of the fragrance…… Despite its earthy character, MUSC AMARANTE remains consistently delicate and airy…… Like IRIS DE GRIS from the "Le Potager" series, this fragrance also becomes intimately and almost completely "transparent" within a maximum of 2 hours…… What remains is merely a delicate diffuse veil that only faintly recalls the fulminant opening……

Here I go again, ranting about the state of niche perfumery. I'm not even entirely sure where I'm going to take this review right now, so lets start with Oudous Lux Solis itself. I, for one, feel fortunate that I managed to source a 2ml of this and Reception , but that fortune only goes as far as the opportunity, not the content itself.
