If it had gone away for good, I could have rated this perfume higher. Alas, like a bad penny, it just kept coming back. Such a shame.

While my collection keeps evolving, this one is a constant, my signature that I can't wait to bring out once the leaves start changing and falling. It's a woody, smoky scent that doesn't usually lean too dark, and in the rare cases it does I brighten it up with M by Mariah Carey. I think the spices and woods in Santal Blush layer well with the frankincense in M, and M's marshmallow adds the sweetness to perk this up for day time. This fragrance is perpetually classy and stands out in the best way. I wear this when we go somewhere special, and always feel a bit more confident and classy when I do.

First intake of this perfume is definitely cedar. To me it smells of a faint campfire (smoky). Then I can sense a little floral I believe it's the ylang ylang and not so much rose. Someone referenced spiced wood chips and saw dust and that's exactly the feeling I get from this delightful scent. The dry down is better as I tend to gravitate towards the powdery. Staying power not so great but if there was a lotion or creme it might have more staying power once layered together.
I smelled australian sandalwood essential oil earlier today and it smelled like curdled cedar. Incidentally, it also smelled a lot like Santal Blush. I’d blush, too. from scent hurdle.com

To celebrate my "Club 10" milestone—a decade of writing about fragrance—let me share one that exemplifies what I've learned: that the most sophisticated scents often whisper. This is Santal Blush. Among the many sandalwood-based fragrances, Santal Blush chooses softness over volume, combining spicy sensuality with floral refinement.

This fragrance reveals the nature of sandalwood and all its facets. Santal Blush starts with a sharp oud, smoothly intertwining with cedar, which gives me a feeling of a cold fougere backbone (quite similar to Venetian Bergamot) and somewhere in the background a hint of pickles.

Spicy, creamy, soft sandlewood combined with light floral, musky woods. I adore this perfume. This smells like being in a carpenters workshop with musky flowers sat in a vase in the window in the distance! The creamy sandlewood takes centre stage throughout and is beautiful. This is one of my top 5 scents and is unisex in my opinion.

There's something about Santal Blush that makes me blush. It's the sort of blush that comes from when you've been standing next to a bonfire and drinking spiced hot wine. It's not a smooth sandalwood, rather it's like logs on a fire and there is a choppiness to the wood notes here. Everything about this scent screams fall.

This is my favorite fragrance in my collection, and for good reason. Woody, Creamy, Spicy, a hint of floral notes, and what feels like a slight smoke accord, this fragrance just smells incredible on skin to me. It gives me a kind of reserved, yet adventurous feel to wear this, like someone who goes to work and comes home only to go climb a mountain or something.

tested in May 2023 at the Printemps store on Boulevard Haussmann in Paris. it is an ideal feminine fragrance for spring because it is floral. However, after testing several women's perfumes from this brand, this one stood out. it differs from the majority of floral perfumes which are too common and similar to each other. this perfume smells of the refinement and elegance of British royalty in women, a great discovery and an experience that I encourage you to do if you have to choose a penhaligon perfume. a perfume that will suit these young ladies as well as the most mature ladies. it will most certainly be part of my lady's collection for next spring. a safe bet Hope this review was helpful to you

This is a very green floral with a sort of metallic musk to it. This is dry, powdery, and vintage with a soft woody touch. There’s a bit of an underlying alluring smokiness here too that’s hard to pinpoint. It has that locked away in an attic and forgotten about hazy nostalgic charm to it, it’s almost witchy, old ladyish but in a good way. I don’t think I love the scent but it’s a weird one I found myself going back to smell over and over again.

Lady Blanche is Like walking at dawn and breathing in the smell of dew on the flowers. Typical British landscape. humid, sometimes earthy, green and clean. A realistic orris, not at all dusty. Imagine Mr Darcy walk around Derbyshire. A typical balance of English perfumery: do not overload the fragrance. It’s not my favorite of Portraits but the effect is not old style but bright and sophisticated. I’ve a decant and sometimes I love go the bed with her!

Opens with the fresh floral and green spiciness of spring flowers; fresh cut daffodils in a vase and a distant aroma of a hyacinth breezing in as its warms in the spring sun on a kitchen windowsill somewhere, the daffodil sap still sticky on your fingers. The sandalwood in the base and green, earthy, herbaceous Angelica pull the subtle flowers together into a beautiful, calming, aromatic, slightly spicy effervescent floral accord. This continues on into the dry down with a little bit of creamy orris butter, some sweet violet, powdery iris, green damp angelica.. it’s refreshing, cool and clean yet gentle and very much at one with nature, like I’ve just sprayed a pure botanical on my skin, with crushed petals distilling in the bottle. This is an understated, elegant and unique shear perfume of fresh, green, cool, dewy muted powdery florals. I actually think it’s quite unisex and yet I feel confidently feminine wearing it. I can imagine Lady Blanche sitting on a blanket at the side of a large pond on her estate, a white lace parasol blocks the sun from her face as she gazes onto to a beautiful scene, reminiscent of Monet’s The Waterlily Pond. She is poised in ladylike elegance yet a little curl on the corner of her smile indicates that she just might be full of mischief. Whilst the other ladies walked, she rode, defiantly astride her horse definitely not sidesaddle, on her way here. I found this perfume a beautiful and divine skin scent. I could have happily breathed it in all day long. Alas, unlike a Monet painting, its long lasting oil medium that has lived on for over a century later for all to enjoy, this beautiful yet light fragrance disappears all too quickly. Frustratingly so. Lady Blanche has got her revenge, she’s rode off to frolic with the stable hand and left me olfactorily bereft!

Lady Blanche sounds just as amazing as Yasmine - a spicy, floral and woody scent. Perfect in Autumn! But oh how different the two are! Lady Blanche is a powdery and light fragrance, whereas Yasmine was spicy, deep and smokey. I'm sorry Penhaligon's, but in what world is Lady Blanche a spicy fragrance? This reminds me so much of Infusion d'Iris by Prada. Both are elegant, powdery, feminine and floral. Lady Blanche has in comparison to Infusion d'Iris a notable note of hyacinth. The one who wrote the pamphlet in the set needs to revise it Lady Blanche is definitely for spring and maybe summer, but not my cup of tea for autumn. On skin, the hyacinth is very much noticeable. When spraying myself with Lady Blanche, I made a note to myself that she and Infusion d'Iris are identical, but when smelling my wrist, I distinguish the hyacinth as being the sole noticeable note. It is so strong that I find Lady Blanche to be a purely hyacinth fragrance. The similarity to Infusion d'Iris is still there, but between those two scent experiences is another one too. A terrible one. Something really synthetic and plastic like. It might just be my dislike of anything floral, especially hyacinth. This is the type of fragrance that I struggle to write a review of from a full day's wear. I think I've gotten the jist of it - a green scent of a predominantly hyacinth note, floral of course, powdery and moderately sweet. That's it, you won't get more out of me. Maybe just a last remark that I tried to wash it off and it ain't budging, to my dismay.

The Penhaligon website states that this fragrance is elegant yet understated, reminiscent of a spring floral garden after it has rained. They describe this as a fresh yet spicy, floral and woody fragrance. I would agree that this is an understated floral fragrance, but its too understated. Its forgettable and weak.

Airy greenness – freshly trimmed flower stalks being submerged into a vase full of clean water. Gentle florality – very mellow, off-white, out of focus. Doesn't necessarily strike me as narcissus in particular, but then again – I don't often get to smell real narcissus.

"I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o’er vales and hills,/ When all at once I saw a crowd,/ A host, of golden daffodils;/ Beside the lake, beneath the trees,/ Fluttering and dancing in the breeze". I always think of this poem by William Wordsworth when I use Lady Blanche - for me, a second perfect harbinger of spring.

Lord George awoke with an unfamiliar sense of unease. He felt nauseous, had stomach pains, and could barely move. Seemingly with his last bit of strength, he dragged himself into the spacious bathroom to wash his face with cold water, hoping for a refreshment and a slight improvement in his condition.

I haven't commented on a fragrance for quite some time. I'm pretty lazy in this regard. Shame on me! The Revenge of Lady Blache is the first fragrance I bought simply because of the bottle cap. That amazing leopard head!!! I just had to have it. But it's not just the bottle that impresses; the contents are equally delightful.

The new rose based perfume by Tom Ford is like the rest of the private blend's perfumes: It has an awesome smell but a weak performance. The scent makes me think of fragances like lyric by amouage but more simple, more creamy and with worse projection. Although It shares some notes with other TF like noir noir is totally different. I find It unisex and better for a dayly use more than a perfume to go into special events. For me It is more like wearing a roses body milk than a proper perfume. Scent: 9 Longevity: 6.5 Sillage: 5.5 Quality/price: 4 (more expensive than other private blend's only for marketing) Versatility: 9 Originality: 7 Global: 7.5

Tom Ford may name his fragrances like they're one-note wonders, but they're frequently complex and often divisive. Except for Tobacco Vanille, you old charmer, you. Anyway, Rose Prick is so aptly named, I hope whoever thought of that got a raise. If you're worried about being deluged in a downpour of petals like Mena Suvari in that one scene in American Beauty, fear not. Rose Prick is exactly that; it pricks your nose with opening notes of rose, then quickly moves on to its peppery-tart compliment, a blend that doesn't hit you immediately, but keeps bringing you back around to sniff it again. That's what happened when my friend brought samples back from her trip through a duty-free shop. We kept coming back to Rose Prick, at first not giving it much for props, but eventually admitting we couldn't stop sniffing it. Though (like many Tom Ford fragrances) it doesn't project like a beast, I'd keep this one out of the office. It's a *declarative* scent, and unless you're gonna yass qween your way to the top of the pecking order, maybe keep it reserved for when you want to make a statement. A sly, winking, knowing statement. You don't worry if their head didn't turn; you know they'll be back, noses pricked for whatever that intriguing fragrance is.

I do not know what’s going on with my skin? The perfume smells super cheap and loud, I mean it’s shouting I’m here!…The scent was not what I expected. It felt like a bottle from the dollar store. If this is what great fashion and sensual means, man oh man….do I have the wrong picture…..This a loud, loud, loud scent. Cheap smell. You can obtain the same smell by combining 2-3 bottles from the dollar store and pouring it over your head. Maybe the dollar store perfume won’t last as long as this one……Maybe it’s my skin but this is not what I expected from rose scent.

This was a big surprise for me. I usually steer clear of rose/patchouli fragrances because they have become so ubiquitous over the past several years that I thought the last thing needed is another one added to the market. So, I had zero interest in even trying it until I received a sample with a recent purchase and immediately fell in love. This is beautiful. A jammy rose, slightly spicy from the Sichuan pepper, with an herby patchouli and delicious tonka dry down. I usually hate sweet notes blended with patchouli, but here the spice notes blend with the patchouli creating a warm earthiness that balances out the sweetness of the rose and tonka. And unlike other rose scents in the spicy rose genre, it isn't Middle Eastern, or syrupy sweet, but just sweet enough that it should satisfy those with gourmand tastes and green, spicy, and earthy enough for those who enjoy rose chypres too. Since I enjoy both, this is a delight for me. I think because of that, it should have wide appeal to both young and old alike. I had purchased a travel sprayer which should last quite a while since this lasts and projects very well on me, though a fb is not out of the question in the future.

I own amazing rose scents in my collection like: Portrait of a Lady Eau de Parfum , Nahema Parfum , "Nombre Noir / ノンブル ノワール (Parfum) | Shiseido / 資生堂" One would think that I would actually despise Rose Prick Eau de Parfum . But yhis one is one of my guilty pleasure. It is a jammy rose, with the right amount of spice to give it some bits but not too much in order to keep it cuddly enough. The rose patchouli combination reminds me of POAL but less sumptuous and majestic. I feel this one gets a lot of hype because its flashy double entendre name. But please try to get past this, and try it. For me it is leaning a bit feminine but I do know a few men who love wearing this scent. Longevity is fairly good. It is an amazing wear during colder months.

Got it in a mystery box and was pleasantly surprised. I hadn't heard about it before, but this scent is stunning! It's a perfect mix of sweet roses with earthy patchouli and hot sichuan pepper. I like feminine, sweet and floral fragrances with an edge of a spicy note. The notes in this perfume balance each other perfectly.

Some call him the greatest fashion god of our time, others a provocateur, and others a pervert. Tom Ford polarizes like hardly any other designer with exorbitantly high prices and some of the most suggestive marketing strategies in the fashion world. Tom Ford is sex, Tom Ford is erotic, Tom Ford is not for everyone. This is exactly what Rose Prick stands for.

Rose Prick is a representative example of my current relationship with Tom Ford. This must be what the cliché of the dreaded seventh year feels like. Once the great love at first sight, suddenly we have drifted apart and wonder where our beloved has gone. I wake up in the morning longing for the shine of the early hours.

The title may sound confusing - and yet it makes sense. I discovered Rose Prick thanks to my partner, who treated herself to a 30 ml bottle of this fragrance. I found it incredibly sexy on her, wildly alluring, and extremely captivating. The combination of three authentic roses (not sweet!

I don't know what you all have against it. The scent is fine! Admittedly, Tom Ford has, in the eyes (noses) of many, transitioned from "successful" to "forced," almost like Kilian. But I won't let anyone badmouth this little rose on the heath! Interesting top note: Turkish rose jelly. I've always liked the smell, less so the taste. But it disappears quickly, that's clear.

Big citrusy shaving cream opening — the notes promise mandarin but it’s all lemon-lime for me. After about 20 minutes, a little mild cardamom and white florals emerge and then quickly recede. That shaving cream vibe never really leaves though, and combined with the mildly musky amber base, my wrists smell like freshly shaved skin for the next 6-7 hours. Projection is fairly quiet, and it’s definitely a traditionally masculine coded fragrance. In the end, although this is a pleasant enough for its genre, it suffers from the same fate as most of Penhaligon’s fragrances: it’s simply not special enough to warrant that eye watering price tag.

Anyone who wants to sell fragrances to a family man in peace must keep his entourage happy. In a well-known, non-turquoise perfumery here (that is, in HH), the little ones also received a treat from time to time. This way, my son has already acquired a respectable number of samples of Quercus at elementary school age, and then Dad got to test it. Quercus is a freshling. Not one that later becomes a wild boar rubbing against the very oak whose scientific name the fragrance bears. No, a fresh-ling is meant. A cologne-like clean scent. At first, the bergamot pairs somewhat awkwardly with the emerging floral notes, especially the lily of the valley. However, fortunately, this settles down within one or two hours, and a floral-fresh jasmine-polished lily of the valley cleanliness forms on a herb-strong oak moss base, with the latter, of course, holding back elegantly and only showing its strength directly on the skin. There, the two notes mix in a charming and characterful way, keeping me well-groomed and classic throughout the day. In terms of projection, Quercus is surprisingly present. While others here in the office are at best (if at all!) wandering around with flabby aquatics, I still stand out less with Quercus than usual. However, no one ever says anything anyway except for my favorite colleague, and she is sick. My supplementary remedy for not standing out enough: I first brewed a Lapsang Souchong tea on the test morning. As soon as its smoky scent wafted in, the fragrance in my room became sufficiently amusing. Regarding the much-criticized plagiarizing Abcologning of CK One, I can't contribute anything since I don't know the original, but aside from possibly too close a relationship, Quercus certainly doesn't have to hide in terms of content. Reliable and almost unchangeable, the scent lasts a good eight hours; by the ninth, it almost only smells of Lapsang Souchong in my office. Moreover, even I, as someone without a classical perfume career, definitely know plenty of painfully fresh stuff that comes across as more annoying. The price-performance ratio is another question. For such an un-special scent, I wouldn't want to spend a lot of money in a niche perfumery, even if I were a fan of this direction. Perhaps there's a reason my son happened to receive several samples of it. Funny, by the way, how he pronounces the name: roughly like Quir-l-Kiss, just without the "L." What a sweetie!

As a follower of the ancestors of the venerable London perfumer Penhaligon's, I have lamented its development in recent years at length. With the exception of Sartorial and Bayolea, I follow the effort for innovation with little enthusiasm - as it seems to latch onto trends that do not quite fit the essence of the house for me - and not even particularly well. I love its traditional scents, which are so wonderfully old-fashioned English - those that made Penhaligon's what it is: English Fern, Blenheim Bouquet, Bluebell, Lily of the Valley - all beautifully crafted. Amidst it all, in the nowhere between the venerable eaux de toilette of a romanticized British past, which was probably far from as idyllic as Penhaligon's scents suggest, and the soulless commercial products of the present, one seems a bit out of place, almost lost: Quercus, one of the few new creations from the 90s and not particularly popular here. Quercus - it should be admitted right away, and there is nothing inherently wrong with it - succumbs to the olfactory zeitgeist of its decade, and the 90s (aka 'Rhythm is a dancer') can indeed be considered somewhat challenging. Quercus is the Latin name for the oak family, and if Penhaligon's eponymous scent is anything, it is certainly not a woody, let alone forest-like fragrance; however, 'Quercus' also playfully engages with the English adjective 'quirky', meaning: 'eccentric', 'peculiar', or 'odd'. In this sense, the oak-referencing name can be understood as a winking 'false friend', because apart from oak moss (a lichen that merely likes to grow on oaks), there is nothing 'oak-like' in this scent, which could just as well describe someone as 'peculiar', which is certainly not a dishonorable thing on the British Isles. Quercus is not of the caliber of a Douro, a Hamam Bouquet, or any of the aforementioned. It is a cheerful cologne with hints of a friendly meadow bordered by hedges under low-hanging summer clouds. A bit floral, a bit soapy, a bit Chypre - almost playful, like a freckled boy in knickerbockers who has just broken the milk jug and is now whistling while pushing a tire ahead of him on his way home. It is 'modern' not in the sense of 'contemporary', but rather in the sense of 'enlightened' and 'post-traditional' - and it does not deserve the bitter scorn. Conclusion: even its detractors should give the little oddity a benevolent second chance. It deserves it.

Once again. After "LP No.9" already being a 90% copy of "Opium homme", "Quercus" also represents a rather simply plagiarized scent. What’s the point? Does a 144-year-old English heritage brand need this? Bad enough. Which customer is going to be attracted to this when they can get the original for significantly less? 50 ml "Quercus" = 70 euros. For that, you can get almost 300 ml(!) of Calvin Klein's unisex scent. Ridiculous. "Quercus" starts citrusy-mandarin, slightly musky and soapy-clean. Exactly like... of course. In the middle, it becomes a bit more floral - instead of Klein's slightly harsh violet, there's a fresh, herbaceous lily of the valley here, but similarly arranged. A light spicy note of somewhat shell-like, peppery cardamom comes into play in both scents, but the clean laundry tone of the musk hovers over it persistently. Otherwise, not much else happens; the scent lingers with a lukewarm sillage and very average longevity. The world doesn’t need this; it already has "CK One".

"As English as can be" - with this recommendation, almost ten years ago, a very English friend and advanced dandy pointed to the bottle in his tiny, appropriately British shabby bathroom of his one-room apartment in Hampstead, where I had once again found a place to stay on the futon for a few days. It was Opus 1870, which I then reverently sprayed on to make the most of a beautiful spring day between Brompton Oratory and the V&A. Penhaligon's - it took me a while to remember this name! In the meantime, I have had my experiences with this venerable house as well. I used Endymion for a while and emptied a bottle of it - and that was enough. I bought Opus next - and I couldn't really warm up to it either. I initially got Quercus as a shower gel for my wife - she liked it, and then she wanted the fragrance. However, it flopped for her - I took over, from the outset without particularly loving it, used it for several summers .. and it just won't run out! So it ultimately came about through Quercus that I could bring my relationship with fragrances to a fundamental clarification! After a phase of almost complete abstinence, I finally embarked on a more systematic search for fragrances that suited me better - and in essence, it was Quercus that drove me into the arms of Parfumo.. But what is there to say against or perhaps for Quercus? Positive: it doesn't smell "bad," I have even been approached positively about it a couple of times. Neutral: it doesn't last long, especially in summer, sometimes hardly from morning to noon. Negative: I simply can't think of much else. Unfortunately, I find it rather uninspiring. "Oak" is written on it, but it smells like little flowers. However, not sweetly, but somehow soapy, slightly spicy, and initially quite alcoholic. More rural than urban, more for mornings than for evenings, something like a morning walk through a still damp, now sunlit, orderly landscape in early summer, with a little bit of residual alcohol in the blood and after a good shower.. What all this has to do with CK One, I cannot say from my own experience; however, it seems plausible to me that there is a huge similarity to something very popular, as I seem to encounter Quercus on the street much more often than one would actually expect. I probably need to give Blenheim Bouquet or English Fern a chance someday, which I have always found too contrived, too nostalgic, too Downton.. Until then, I will likely have a bit of Quercus left as a decent office scent for a long time, which, however, completely lacks anything solemn, mystical, alluring, or elevating the everyday. A scent to wake up to, not to stay awake with. A scent for further searching.

In fresh, citrus fragrances, the brand Penhaligons shines with the excellent Blenheim Bouquet from 1902. Perhaps it didn't earn enough money with that - in any case, 1996 was the time ripe for a more modern, less dusty counterpart. Quercus is also, like Blenheim Bouquet, a kind of sport scent of its time, but of course more modern.

Last Saturday, in what felt like 40 degrees Celsius, I made my way to Bruchtal...sorry, Bruchsal, the home of ALZD. I was on the hunt for a new fragrance or something similar to Dsquared's Rocky Mountains. Immediately, I was led through a narrow corridor (please walk sideways if you are size 38 or above) into the holy hall where the most diverse fragrances were gathered.

I received a sample of Quercus from Florin, and I really like it. Thank you for that! Quercus is quite a fresh everyday scent, and really a beautiful unisex perfume for both genders without age restrictions. I find that it bears a strong resemblance to CK one from 1995, as it smelled quite similar back then, in my opinion.

Today I activated the Parfumo perfume advisor and included scents from my decants as well. One of the recommendations was Quercus by Penhaligon, of which I still had a few drops in a sample vial. Since I thought this would be a good moment to test it and my sample wouldn’t get any better, it should be on this mixed spring day.

After wearing the fragrance last Saturday and not quite knowing what to write about it, I applied it again today. But I still can't quite put it into words (or in this case, fingers). The scent starts off very fresh with a certain bitterness in the undertone. Lemon, lime, and a bit of basil can be perceived, but honestly, nothing more than that.

The whole raunchy campaign that surrounds this fragrance's release, had me somewhat excited to see what made this fragrance so sexual. Tom Ford for Men is sexy, at least in my opinion, however not to the extent that its advertisement suggests. I won't be posing naked with a bottle of this anytime soon, that's for sure. The scent is an interesting concoction of smooth woods, spicy sweetness and rich, earthy tobacco and patchouli. Surprisingly, Tom Ford for Men is rather soft on the skin, I expected a much louder fragrance. Not nearly as citrusy in the opening as one would expect, Tom Ford for Men, is smooth and classy. I am somewhat addicted to smelling this fragrance every few seconds, even though it's not what I'd call particularly outstanding or unique. There's definitely something very appealing about this fragrance, and there's no way I'd be offended by any man wearing this. In fact I'd be elated if they did. Tom Ford for Men has a somewhat oily quality that makes me feel as if this fragrance is more concentrated than it is. Every now and then the scent becomes dark and musky, however the honey-like sweetness tends to brighten this fragrance, bringing it up out of its dullness. While the sillage is fairly intimate, I do rave about the lasting power which is amazing, lasting well into the next day. In some ways, Tom Ford for Men reminds me of BLV pour Homme, especially with the presence of the ginger note. I must say that if you love BLV for Summer, you'd most likely love this fragrance for Winter.

I’ve never been much of a fan of Tom Ford’s masculine offerings, as I find them either nice but overpriced, or fairly dull (Noir, for example). For some reasons I always never cared for this one, maybe unconsciously thinking, given the name, that it was a sort of epitome of all of that, and... bingo, this is instead the first one which works for me. Mostly because it’s finally something solid, with a fair price (well, sort of). Maybe a bit boring, surely too discreet for the needs of the average “bros” building pools to bath in their Private Blends, and however miles away from being ground-breaking: just solid and mature, unpretentious and versatile, with a remarkably decent quality and overall, extremely pleasant to wear. The composition smells simple and clear, and notes seem all built with really decent materials: the spiced, gingerish orange-citrus notes are sparkling, tangy and juicy; the floral-infused musky-ambery base smells compellingly warm, slightly creamy and slightly salty too, the whole woody-herbal accord is a bit aseptic and nondescript (I only get some faint, weakly mossy vetiver), but working fine within the composition, providing an office-safe “boisé” feel which will get some more credit on the drydown, and the suede-ish tobacco smells, well, like most other tobacco notes on the market - which means “nothing like real tobacco” for me, but nice anyway; smooth, sweet, “brownish” and affably, youthfully distinguished. Like for some other reviewers, two fragrances came to my mind while wearing this the first time: Hugo Boss Baldessarini and to a much lesser extent, yet worthy a mention, a sort of spicier and watered-down version of L’Instant pour Homme by Guerlain. Maybe Carolina Herrera for Men too, just for the tobacco accord (an “orange-amber” flanker of that would be close to this Ford’s, I guess), and Kenzo pour Homme Boisée just for a similar citrus-scented light woody accord. Above all I’d mention Baldessarini though, and I would say Tom Ford for Men smells quite a bit better than that – more crisp, more appealing, definitely more quality too. So, anyway: a zesty, classy, politely self-confident fragrance with just the right hint of musky tackiness and a pleasant spicy-woody drydown with a warm whiff of amber. Surely a mild, maybe pedantic, kind of “generic” office-safe fragrance based on a really conventional and mainstream concept of “tart-spicy Oriental cologne” with pretty much the sole scope of making you smell nice in the most mannered, discreet and crowd-pleasing meaning possible... but hell, it does it impeccably good (sadly with a short persistence, but it does). 7-7,5/10

When i think about Tom Ford three letters S.E.X spanked across the bottle, Mr Ford known for Kinky and Luschious Ads brings shock and bad taste T.F channels Larry Flynt the king of smut and pubisher of Adult Entertainment Hustler to the bone and leaves no puches. Tom Ford for Men gives an air of elite and arrogant tenure only a select few can share Exculsive and V.I.P it may be shallow but one's gulity pleasure starts creeping in and want to know about the rich and the elitist, The opening which i was a bit disappointed and expected to be more deeper and more Resinous with incense woods leather and Myrrah, Instend it was more aromatic and in a fougere class because of it's sharp citric opening but still it was nice, then dries sort of boozy like a tinge of vodka swiming around the Lemon almost like a cocktail drink. Violet leaf opens the middle drydown and bring a sweet and crisp wet texture to the fragrance underpinning of pepper lays below the violet and counteracts well and basil adding to the spiciness to the middle base,The sweet and smoky Tobacco closes the Heart, The Finishing is suble and not as loud like the top opening and middle Grounded Patchouli gives a Earthy feel to the scent dry vetiver which i can dectect nomally i can't dectect vetiver in T.F it's visible warm amber is a bit diluted but noticible and Ceder finishes it.

Scentrack: Sting - Englishman in New York Tom Ford for Men is full of soft citruses, spiced with fiery ginger and just a touch of herbal basil. I really like the gentle orange flower and masculine tobacco slowly burning on the skin. Clean, but in the same time dirty enough to be masculine. Unfortunately it's so introverted. I wish it was just a little bit louder. Another great Yves Cassar's work. A pleasant and mellow daytime/ evening scent for walks in the park in autumn. Rating: 7.5/10

Im sorry to say but there's nothing actually unique here. Opens with a good citrus notes with ginger, but dries down to a sweet ambery tobacco base that smells a bit generic. Weak lasting power, timid sillage and projection. Try before you buy. It does even get close to some of TF Private Blend line. Revised January 2014

Great freshness from the ginger, almost like a daytime version of D&Gs The One due to the tobacco being a little stronger than the amber note. Excellent blending of notes and a great versatile scent for e.g. office work in autumn and winter. It’s woody, spicy and sweet with tobacco and hints of patchouli.

Warm, Yellow, powerful: this Tom Ford's masterpiece is the energy of a sunny day made perfume. First of all, why the name "For men"? this powerful and opulent scent is genderless in my opinion and it has all the "atouts" for being a wonderful feminine Eighties style, rich and vibrant.

I guess the title would tell you what I think about this one, Really men’s perfume but i guess 50+ old guys It starts some kind of a synthetic scent after it changes to little spicy and citrus hits in like old designs aftershave that my grandpa smelled when i was a kid. So i don’t know what to say.

The opening offers not just the promised ('citrus notes') home cooking, it is indeed that, which is not a bad thing. A slight hint of hesperidic freshness, toned down after a few minutes. Over the course of the first hour, a timid-watery wash-me-but-don't-get-me-wet mandarin emerges. A slightly riper, almost completely unsour one.

I could of course write something really mean to thoroughly trample and dissect the fragrance.... But malice is not in my nature, and discontent can also be expressed kindly. And unfortunately, I cannot avoid that with this scent. This Tom Ford for Men has been in my collection for quite some time, purchased more or less on a whim. However, I use it very rarely.

I had a hard time believing that raspberry + sandalwood would = raspberry cheesecake before trying this (like I saw some other reviews say)... but that's exactly what this smells like! Although it doesn't list the following notes, this is what my nose picks up: - black raspberry - brown sugar crust - creamy vanilla rum This is a delicious and surprising fragrance. Not too sweet, despite being all "bakery" notes - the raspberry is darker, the brown sugar crust is muted, and the vanilla rum rounds it out/brings a bit of depth, booze, and musk. On dry down the raspberry softens and the brown sugar + rum notes remain.

~ Inspiration ~ With a sample of "Pure Daydream," I also received one of these from the lovely Jeli (I have since taken over both bottles from her). ~ Bottle ~ Here too, it transitions from pink to rose - the typical Victoria's Secret colors. Above the name sits a small bow. The name "Midnight Dare" means something like "Midnight Challenge" and doesn't really fit the playful scent. ~ Scent ~ Very sweet, fruity raspberries meet warm, sensual sandalwood. To my nose, there’s a hint of vanilla-caramel-coconut. ~ Longevity ~ Unfortunately, it only lasts 3-4 hours on my skin (a bit longer on clothing and hair). 2-3 sprays are enough, as it can become quite artificial and cloying. ~ Occasion ~ A delicious scent for the colder days and evenings in autumn and winter (not necessarily for the office). ~ Conclusion ~ A squeaky-pink Barbie scent that has a bit of the vanilla tree air fresheners for cars (with a raspberry flair).

This is simply the best Halfeti. The one to rule them all. Cedar was too boozy, the OG is too generic. This one just has a certain 'je ne sais quoi', I don’t know what, that makes it wearable and cool. Spray it on and immediately you’ll smell that familiar Halfeti syrup. Sweet, boozy. After half an hour this transitions into a subtle incense fest. Subtle, so not full on catholic mass. It’s contained beautifully by some flower and spicy notes. Then the dry down where leather and patchouli come into play. Again, it’s subtle. It’s a Penhaligon’s after all so don’t expect to be blown your socks off. It’s just having a good time, picking up those notes late in the game. And I like it for what it is. It’s not a powerhouse, it won’t push boundaries on levels of stank or projection. I’d love to have a FB of this if it just wasn’t so bloody expensive.

On my latest trip to Sacks I stopped by Penhaligon's stand and sampled some of their offerings. The first one I tried was The Omniscient Mister Thompson - it was pleasant nice iris based smell, inoffensive and great for the office. The second was Halfeti which I liked but I have too many oud & rose fragrances therefore I passed. The third was Sartorial which did not make a lasting impression, I should have probably sprayed it on skin to get a better impression but unfortunately I did not. Last was Halfeti Leather which was a love of first sniff. When I smelled Halfeti Leather initially I got a blast of red fruit, oud and citruses, as it was on a strip it quickly went into drydown which was dominated by Cedar/Sandalwood and incense. I sprayed it on my skin and the fragrance actually exhibited deeper notes - initially besides the red fruit, oud and citruses I could detect cardamon and whiffs of cinnamon. As the scent developed and moved to drydown I could detect the leather woven through the cedarwood and incense. This is my first Penhaligon's and will be the only one for a while as my collection is pretty big and I will probably add as I dispose of what I have. However, I am definitely going to order a discovery set as I am really impressed by what I tried out in Sacks.

This is my first Penhaligon. Was expecting a lot but am not impressed. Don't get me wrong, it's a nice scent in a generic way, but nothing special. Really no leather in the opening and for about an hour or so. After the initial opening, it's sorta creamy, slightly floral, with the plum and almost a little boozy. After about an hour, the leather starts to appear, very mild at first then amps up a bit. Towards the end, the leather was almost gone and it was mostly cedar. Until near the end, it's unisex and then leans masculine. Performance moderate all the way around. Got about 6 hours until it was gone from my skin. Modest sillage but a little better projection. Don't know if it's been reformulated or if the sample is tainted (sample from a decanter). All in all, not impressed.

Halfeti Leather is the third Penhaligon's perfume after the classic Halfeti and Cairo and for the third time I wonder why they are classified as unisex fragrances. I don't see any of them on the woman. Especially Halfeti Leather sounds very masculine. Contrary to the author of the previous review, I do not think that this flanker is better than the classic Halfeti, on the contrary, Leather is less complex, bulkier and heavier. The skin itself that I feel here is not special and rather lacking in character. The leathery chord in this composition is very fruity. The main violin is played by plum and it is the plum leather that dominates, it is dry and slightly alcoholic. Incense and oud, if any, are firmly hidden beneath this plum-leather coat. I don't catch the rest of the notes. The ingredients are of rather good quality, the parameters are also good, but Halfeti is more interesting, I also like Cairo more, although that is another story.

I actually wanted to get Halfeti first. Since it was no longer in stock at my trusted perfumery, I tried the Leather briefly on my arm………… and reached for the box. If you can call it a box. Just the packaging alone is a dream and made of coated resin plastic. Beautifully kept in black with a nice sticker. And adorned with a Trade Routes stamp. The scent itself is a wonderful homage to the traditional Halfeti. Rounded off with the finest leather. However, I wouldn't label the scent as a leather fragrance. The leather is not the main focus; it is a wonderfully complementary addition. It makes the scent less sweet than the original. I find both wonderfully wearable in autumn and winter. The H/S is, as always, very good with the Trade Routes. I give it 8-10 hours. I think anyone who owns Halfeti will find this a very good alternative and can grab it without hesitation. Those who own neither... well, that's their loss. ;-)

On Friday, our Radcliff finally arrived from the winter sale in the UK, and at an amazing price. And there were samples included; I really wanted to test Halfeti Leather. I love the original Halfeti very much; I don't wear it often, as it's not an everyday scent that works all the time - I find it quite special. So, Halfeti Leather.

It may be because my first encounter with Penhaligon's Halfeti Leather took place amidst the hustle and bustle of the Advent season - this EdT strongly reminds me of a Christmas treat! But let's start from the beginning: I was actually searching for a completely different fragrance, a tobacco scent.
I would say it's a must for every Halfeti lover and for those who enjoy the scent of leather on their clothing for days. I would describe Halfeti Leather as the bittersweet counterpart to Halfeti.

... call for an anecdote. Admittedly, I don't have a suitable one yet, as I still need to experience my fragrance adventure with this perfume. However, I am happy to share my first impressions. I am very glad that I tested this scent simply at the perfumery supplier of my choice BEFORE I looked at the fragrance pyramid.

After years of trying out "conventional" perfumes, I finally dared to enter a slightly more exclusive perfumery. I have always been fascinated by scents and discovered classic fragrances that smelled good (to me) in my early youth. That hasn't changed to this day. About a month ago, I was testing fragrances in a perfumery and eventually stumbled upon this scent here.

I don't know where to start, such this fragrance is... Sublime. With this Vert d'Encens, it's almost Christmas before its time. One of my favorites from the prestigious Private Blend collection. This fragrance is close to unique in many ways. Green, woody, resinous, mystic, smoky, fascinating, addictive... Probably one of my favorite scents if not my favorite for fall/winter. All the notes are perfectly mixed and are at no time disgusting. An enchanting opening, such a warm, resinous pine. An hour later settles a sweetness and smoke of disturbing precision. To finish with a beautiful incense on a background of green fir... Fascinating. A long drying ensues which lasts, which lasts... Longevity for at least 8 hours on me, with a moderate or even powerful sillage, and this is enough because more would have been unsightly for my taste. An almost magical scent, not for novices, which some sensitive noses might put off. There is almost a mystic side to this fragrance. This juice reminds me of a glass of Absinthe, like the one tasted by Inspector Abberline (Johnny Depp) in From Hell (2001), or even the red embers of a gentle fire slowly being consumed... The best of the 3 Vert for me. We are no longer here in the presence of a simple perfume, but rather a beautiful elixir. It transports you from one place to another, as if you were traveling with a closed eyes... Vert d'Encens? A contemplative treasure. A fragrance that will make you feel good, near a fireplace, warm, relaxed, savoring your glass of Hennessy. One regret however... Mr Ford, why did you discontinued this gem??? We do not give up the Holy Grail. My rating: 10/10

Incense spectacular, green, balsamic, and even an earthy tint, original without doubt, had not smelled such a green and natural incense until now, simply amazing. The exit is green green, where you can see the fir and pine with an amazing naturalness, it is like when you place the Christmas tree and after having been touching the branches and needles, you smell your hands, and that green and natural smell that gets impregnated, it's what it smells like to me. This beginning lasts a sigh, and at the moment the incense and resins appear, sweetening the green notes, which do not disappear after this beginning, recreating a green, very natural aroma, with a precious resinous sweetness, in which they begin to distinguish the first blows of a spectacular incense. Gradually the green notes begin to decay and the incense takes possession of the aroma, which, together with the resins and a very delicate floral reflection, speak of the East and its stories, offering us a sweetly resinous and fragile floral fragrance with a veil beautiful background woody. In its final phase the wood feels more, feeling a resinous incense on a woody background, almost dusty, fine, elegant and full of mystery. Very good performance, in skin it is maintained for more than 8 or 9 hours with few sprays, its wake is moderate high at the beginning and then it goes to moderate, and although it is not exaggerated, it marks presence very dignified. As for its use, I see it more appropriate for cold and temperate seasons and for the night, although it would also not fall apart on a cool winter or autumn morning. It has been a perfume that I loved, with a magnificent quality, but with an important tare, its price, although, if you can afford it, the perfume is highly recommended, but, if not, you better not smell it, because You'll want to have it and it really hurts your pocket hehehe.

Vert d'Encens is an amusing incense, that presents serious face of smoke mixed with jovial floral notes. The core still carries floral and newly cut woody tone, uplifted with a comfortable catholic coniferous incense. The only thing I obsess is this perfume verges to ambiance odor rather to be a personal fine fragrance, which is a common feature in all members of Les Extraits Vert. 3/5

Vert D'Encens is very similar to what I remember Imaginary Authors' Cape Heartache smells like, except you replace the strawberry with whatever the sweet note in Vert D'Encens is (heliotrope?). I found the strawberry note in Cape Heartache far too synthetic and I get a tiny bit of that with Vert D'Ecens, but I am really digging this juice nonetheless and will likely buy a full bottle when I can get my hands on it. Vert D'Encens starts off far more green to my nose than Vert Des Bois. After a short period the green notes mellow out and you are left with a incense, woods, and the sweet note. A really delicious scent. Not as heavy on the incense and green notes as you would expect given the name. This might disappoint some people, but I think this makes Vert D'Encens wearable year round.

... that's how I felt spaying this on my wrist. The camphoric beast hit my nose in the opening ... so powdery (dusty) and sweet it made my nostrils burn and my stomach churn. Also this TF has huge projection and silage and one small spray won't give you a break for quite some time. In other words, although I rarely really dislike a perfume, I am sorry to write that Vert d' Encens is a scrubber for me. It does settle to a sweet dusty liturgical green (still camphor to my nose) but it is so overly perfumy that it screams. Thanks, but no thanks.

Under this title - fully: 'Under Trees - The Germans and the Forest' - the German Historical Museum in Berlin showcased an exhibition five years ago that analyzed, explained, and beautifully illustrated the special significance of the forest for Germans and their culture.

On one of my running routes, there is a small chapel that is situated almost exactly between my hometown and the neighboring city. Many years ago, this corner of Baden-Württemberg was still well populated. Now, there are only meadows and forests and a lonely farm. The chapel is small and yet so beautiful.

Yes, I can understand the voices that say they can't relate to Tom Ford's style, that they feel overwhelmed and crushed by the opulence. I feel the same way with one or two scents, like Tobacco Vanille and Tuscan Leather. This eccentricity that some attribute to him (the fragrances) is something you have to like.

Green incense, Ford knows how to name his fragrances, it fits, because at this fir high stand, one is all too happy to take a break. Ford himself doesn't fit into a dense forest, he prefers to buy a whole piece of his massive salary.

As much as I like bold perfumes - the first 2-3 hours are too dense, too thick, and too exhausting for me. Like a test of strength, green and smoky scent clouds face off against each other, with overweight, heavy-breathing heliotrope in between, not quite knowing what it's doing here.

I'm sorry, but I'm laughing because this has no "body" to it whatsoever Pretty? Yes. It's a light, musky, airy, whispery type of fresh affair. A heart of shy, indistinct florals and an aquatic accord combine to create a fresh, shampoo-y tone that lasts the entire wear length before becoming a clean skin scent. It's ok. Nothing about this is remarkable, or even memorable. I finished editing this review because I smelled this yesterday...and already the scent has faded from my mind.

Sohan is a very nice Laos Oud and Rose type of smell, in the same category with Santal Royal from Guerlain or Oud Ispahan from DIOR. My impression about the presentation, sprayer and the box is very good .. nothing less than a Penhaligon´s luxurious product. It is lacking in uniqueness on a market saturated with Rose Ouds, almost every house makes one nowadays. The official price is the biggest enemy of this perfume, in my opinion .. for 150€ or your equivalent in local currency one can consider this on a short list, if the smell is appealing, but for 235€ full price I think it is madly overpriced. You can get two Santal Royals 125ml from Guerlain with this money as of today Feb 2022. The scent is nice and pleasant, the rose is not the sweet grandma powder like in The Portrait of a lady Frederic Malle so it can be worn very well by men and also women. The oud is pleasant and has no animalic notes into it, typical for Laotian Oud. I would pick any day L´Autre Oud Lancome or Oud Ispahan instead of this, but this is not to say Sohan is bad .. it just has a ton of competition and it must work to get a sale, I would say. If you find a good deal somewhere or your favorite perfumery has a discount for Valentine´s or Black Friday and you can get it with 140-150€ then I would consider it.

Sohan, ambitious businessman. With talent and cunning has managed to build a noteworthy reputation. Compromises? Not allowed: here is the shameless and fearless soul of this fragrance. A rose full of spiene paired with a very resinous oud present themselves at once, with character, to let you know that you are not messing around here. Saffron, with almost leathery hints, adds more and more oriental undertones with a strong impact. A scent that looks at everyone from the other side, proud of itself, continuing on its path with no middle ground; just like the eagle depicted in the cap.

I initially purchased this because I am collecting Penhaligon's portraits and I heard this is being discontinued. I have not owned any oud fragrances prior to this and boy this is STRONG. I don't know how this compares to other fragrances with similar profile but this is one where people will definitely notice if you are wearing this. I got this when it started to turn cold here and it grew on me. Still not wearing this to work but I enjoying wearing this at home in cooler weather. The dry down on this is quite pleasant, with the woody base and faint rose scent. It is one of the better ones in terms of longevity in the Portrait collection. And what's not to love about the majestic eagle bottle. You can probably get a better value rose oud fragrance from other houses but I do enjoy having this in my collection

To me this one smells like some kind of an Egyptian souk I can describe this one as a spicy oud and rose scent Which is very good and later it gets more animalic and rose, not bad at all if you Like rose and oud perfumes you will like this. To me this o e smells like Tobacco mandarin and Oud Ispahan. I olso understand the falcon head i guess the The coat of arms of Egypt, is a golden eagle looking towards the left.

Stunning oud and saffron with vetiver, sandalwood, and spices. Rose is listed in the notes, but I certainly can't smell it very much. This is rugged, muscular, sophisticated and manly af. It has this leatheriness to it with that cumin flow and oud that is just divine. Of all the Potraits Collection, this and Monsieur Beauregard are my favorites. This would be glorious on a cold night. 8.5/10

I like it. Ok projection Horrible longevity (strength) - people voted this as the longest lasting from the house- ykes Reminds me of FM The moon in the opening, but quickly transitions to Marly Herod- the sour sweetness Blend is quality, no abrupt transitioning between the notes. However, if bought at MSRP, it's overpriced.

I first came across this fragrance in the summer of 2018, when I popped into a Penhaligon’s boutique to replace my bottle of Halfeti. I was with my sister and my friend, and was drawn to The Uncompromising Sohan mainly by the Indian-Iranian name and the appetising colour of its juice. I was hooked at first spray.

Uncommented Fragrances No. 105 The beauty of Penhaligon's is that they sometimes go over the top. Unlike Geo F. Trumper and D.R. Harris, two English brands that I greatly admire, some of Penhaligon's are loud and vulgar, yet still as British as Monty Python.

Uncompromising is Penhaligon's creation from 2017 in that it relies on the popular combination of oud, rose, and saffron, despite countless similarly structured fragrances. One could certainly argue that this is a blend of tried-and-true elements. I can easily imagine fans of the genre nodding along and finding The Uncompromising Sohan to be solid.

What is a fixed biological law for us humans, namely that twins have the same parents, is rather a rarity in the world of perfumes. However, it almost happened at Penhaligon's. From a distance, Sohan seems to be a twin brother of Halfeti. The first clue that they are not lies in their names: "Halfeti" is rooted in Turkey, while "Sohan" is based in India.

Has a generally classy, and appropriate for the name, charcoal like feel overall but specifically opens with bergamot and Sichuan pepper then some vaguely familiar elements of the noir edt with the spices, ginger and cedar, although I really wouldn't say it's very similar to the others in the TF Noir line. Feels like the dark wood and sandalwood just slightly tempers the assertiveness of the fragrance overall, but just enough to be well rounded. It is also very linear with the exception of the fleeting bergamot and ginger in the beginning, but I'm glad because I really enjoy what remains. If I had to describe it only by a few notes, I would say its mainly Sichuan pepper, cedar, and spices. Not sweet at all, and definitely more of a mature masculine fragrance than the other TF Noirs, which I personally found to be very sweet and borderline unisex. Performs fairly well and has decent longevity, I had a spray on my arm from the tester at the store and kept getting wafts from it hours later. Enjoyed it so much, I ended up going back in the evening and buying a bottle.

Very surprising scent that this Noir Anthracite... Somewhat confusing at first for the uninitiated, i thought this perfume would fall into my ranking of the most horrible scents... In top notes, i seemed to breathe cold cigarette ashes in an ashtray... Sichuan pepper has a lot to do with it, it's full-bodied, it comes to your nose like a strong mustard. Then the spices make their appearances, and that's where it gets interesting. The fragrance arises, is released, becomes a little "softer", to finally release all its olfactory potential, to finish with woody notes, leather and patchouli... A true delight. So don't be fooled by this spicy start, because the rest is worth the effort. It is not a perfume for young beginners, but for men of at least 30 years old, or more... My advice, test it before buying it blindly. After reflection and several tests, this perfume has the art of disturbing, with its spicy, incisive, original, seductive, elaborate and very original side, to have its place in my top 10. Very good and long lasting on the skin, with an above average wake without going overboard. Bottle is very chic, sober with petroleum reflections, and evokes the mystery of its contents. Conclusion: To perfume yourself with this Noir Anthracite fragrance means to embark on troubled waters... Gentlemen, you have therefore been warned. My rating: 9/10

I am not a huge fan of Tom Ford. Surely, they have some good fragrances but I get the feeling that all the interesting and “experimental” perfumes that they’ve created will be inevitably discontinued if they aren’t already. The same fate befell Noir Anthracite and I genuinely don’t know why. It is the best and the least sweet and boring perfume in the noir line. Instead of developing anthracite TF decided to stick to the “safer” options to sell more bottles I guess. Sadly, their other noir perfumes are not to my liking. Anthracite is a beast in a suit. Why in a suit? Because I believe the best occasion for this beauty is a formal meeting where you’re not scared to “offend” people a little bit and show your strength at the same time. It opens with a sharp note of pencil shavings and coal? At least that’s what I smell here: the coal is not burnt yet. Later on, I sense some pepper grounded on top of that mix. That’s all I sense until the end of its performance but that’s all I need from it to be honest. It’s quite straightforward and doesn’t evolve much as I said or maybe I am just noseblind. I don’t smell a lot of notes listed on Fragrantica, to me it’s all well-blended in one strong and dark composition. I hope TF will re-think about the discontinuation and will bring it back to life.

The title is really just a retrodiction of that of my previous review; and whereas in that case it was meant in full earnest, in this it is a tad (and some) hyperbolick! However, when I first picked up the sample-bottle of this & squirted from it, my thoughts went something like "anthracite? ... yeah right! ... how is a perfume going to smell of ... oh my dark angels! it does too!". How it is rendered I do not know, but this is a stunning piece of perfumery innovation. I think these TF ~Noir~-themed 'fumes are very much a trade-off between performance & originality, with the see-saw falling very much on the side of originality. Having tried this one ^and^ ~Extreme~ really quite thoroughly, I unfortunately cannot but agree with those reviewers who scathe these 'fumes for having rather weak performance; but in exchange uw ^do^ get originality, & that in generous measure. Both are ^extremely^ °interessante°, and a delight to wear going out. That sweet powdery coaly note is just a total salvager of any other deficiency it can reasonably be said to have - and I think sheer weight-of-metal-brought-to-the-field is indeed the ^only^ index whereat it is weak, forthat in every other respect, like ~Extreme~, maugre its innovativity, it is a perfectly plausible reasonable & °proper° perfume. A little aside if I may in connection with this: when I was a youngster in the seventies, occasionally as one was a-walking down the street, a tar-truck would go past on the way to road-works, with smoke billowing out of the back. I would always intraspire deeply on such occasions, loving the aroma loving it. In fact, I find the smell of petrochemickals in general pleasant. It seems to me that persons might be divided into two distinct categories of those who like such aromata & those who don't (& I ^extremely^ heartily deplore the modern fashion for suffusing petrochemickally produce with cheapo aromachemicals, the result being that it just smells ^stupid^!). I think quite likely this 'fume will be liked or disliked according as the putative °liker° is in one category or the other, the way-round being self-evident. I am willing to be wrong about this; but I am very curious apropos the matter. ... a day or so later ... I'm reconsidering what I said about heft & durance in this case. Wearing it another day (coz I ran out if time for selecting a new one) I found it really quite stupborn, in that it just wasn't going away °any-time-soon°; although it did dry down to something that, quite frankly, smelt even more of coal-type stuff (in fact, much like the aforementioned espirations of the tar-truck) than it does in the opening. And this was fine by me - I love that sort of thing. ^Not^ a safe acquisition for anyone who is not into °maverick° 'fumes! What's this ~macassar wood~; has that got something tæ do with it? I've just remembered: another 'fume that smells kind of similar in the dry down, but ^much^ more unexoectedly, is Kilian's (no! I'm ^not^ saying 'By Kilian''s!) ~Incense Oud~: but I say 'kind of' because that's more evocative of smouldering wood than of smouldering petroleum-type produce.

From the very begining, pepper hits you hard, spicy, dense, almost solid. It is stubborn and expansive, and in little time, it goes in a cold direction, without much to say about the citrus and ginger declared. It is supported soon by green, resinous notes that my nose can't differentiate properly, that go on to a woody, dry base. The perfume suits the colour of the flacon, reminding me strongly of the smell of a road after rain, that crosses a forestal setting. It is mature, demands attention and, if we go by traditional standards, it would fit perfectly a stern, well dressed in a dark suit. This fragrance starts strong and can be perceived up to 8-10 hours after application. It could be a daily driver for some, it is definitely interesting but I think you need a certain assertiveness to pull this fragrance off. If you don't, it's one of those that can wear you instead.

This fragrance isn't for everyone. Right off the bat the sichuan pepper slaps u in the face and leaves a welt for a while. After that it lessens a bit to a more tolerable leathery scent. It does have very good longevity which is a Tom Ford staple. I gef a good 8hrs or more and i got super lucky. A guy on ebay was selling an almost brand new full bottle for $40!!

By far this is my favourite TF in my collection aside from Oud Wood. The very first note I get is Sichuan Pepper, and it is so loaded that it almost overwhelms me for a minute before lessening to a much more tolerable scent. But I love to wear this when I want to smell like the future/the inside of a very modern spaceship. There's really no other way I can describe it.

The new flanker of the Tom Ford bestseller "Noir" is called Anthracite, and it behaves accordingly - a film noir scent as it should be. It would have suited a certain Mr. Marlowe well. Gray, silver, anthracite. It has hardly anything in common with the original Noir, but on its own, it is excellent. And the name certainly has its pull now...

The 70s and 80s were characterized by rich, mossy, heavy, room-filling, testosterone-laden distinctive fragrances like “Azzaro pour homme,” “Antaeus,” “Patou pour homme,” “Quorum,” to name just a few. A bit later, “Boss No. 1” and “Zino” were added. Unisex fragrances weren't really a thing yet.

So… wow… come on… what is… nah… wow… amazing!!! This was my inner monologue the first time I sniffed Tom Ford's Noir Anthracite. I immediately envisioned Harvey Specter from the series "Suits." For those who don't know him: An extremely successful, highly intelligent, arrogant, self-absorbed lawyer and senior partner at a New York law firm.
