Thus, Inspector Snuffsmith ultimately had an easy time, managed to arrest the gang, and return the lords their diamonds, cereals, the castle ghost, and even the mice, along with their babies.

Cornubia is an ancient Latin name for Cornwall. The peninsula was called that from 700 AD until the Middle Ages. If Cornwall smells like Cornubia, I would love to visit. At first, I wasn't sure what to make of this fragrance. Is it floral, sweet, woody, oriental, or??? And to be honest, I'm still not quite sure.

I'm glad I didn't write a comment on "Cornubia" after the first tests, looking at my handwritten notes. Today, after applying it again, the fog lifted and I smelled the true heart of "Cornubia." This is probably how one should translate the name. From "nubia" = cloud and "cor" = heart. For "Cornubia" is a sweet, lush fragrance. And yet it is herbaceous like a Chypre.

Although only 20 years old, I count this fragrance among the "old-fashioned" types in a very positive sense. Similar to some of Caron’s or Dezprez's "Bal a Versaille," or some scents from Mona di Orio, which impress with timeless, understated luxury.

Cornubia, with its wonderfully warm aura, is a fragrance for cold days or nights, perfectly suited for a ride in a horse-drawn sleigh through the white winter forest. Surrounded by this protective, warming cocoon, the biting cold cannot harm me.

Cornubia is a perfume that has recognizability, I think! I like it very much and can only recommend trying it! It has become a classic for a reason ;) I immediately notice this powdery sweetness, briefly mandarin, but then in the next moment I am overwhelmed by a powdery-sweet floral wave, especially white freesia, jasmine, neroli oil, and orange blossom are very present!

AMETHYST by Lalique Opens with a succulently overwhelming wine-dark flood of juicy vine-ripened black currant, blueberries, blackberries, mulberries, and strawberries. The delectable sweet-tart mouthwatering fragrance remains true to the natural plant essence and is unsullied by any added artificial sugary cloying sweetness. A subdued dusting of spicy pepper enhances the intensity of the rich fruity juice aromas, rather like an encounter in a wild meadow when the berry bushes are surrounded by a number of other zesty flowering plants and herbs. This blends seamlessly into an elegant shower of crisp peony and freshly blooming rose petals woven through just a trace of tenderly dreamy ylang-ylang. Everything smoothly comes to rest on a delicately sensual base of clean musky light cedar woods and just a drop of warm, silky vanilla. The berries remain jubilantly dominant on my skin to the end of the dry down with the subtly sensual spice hovering over them, and the subdued florals meander elegantly through the tantalizingly complex layers of fruits. This melds exquisitely with my skin and brings to mind the elegance of ancient vineyards and old castles, and enjoying a magnificently dark aged wine with hints of ripe berries on a warm summer evening, surrounded by blooming rose bushes and peonies in a mysterious little romantic garden. Richly evocative of the warm summer nights with delicious seasonal fruit and flora to be savored and enjoyed with loved ones. Magnificent. I adore this completely and without reservation.

Before this came today, I thought I wasn't much of a fan of fruity florals. Amethyst made me do a 180 on first whiff! Talk about gorgeous! The non-syrupy-sweet top note smells so good I didn't think berries right away. I thought, wait, what's this flower I've never smelled? Of course when most of us think Lalique, we think crystal. They're the house that designed the bottle for L'Air du Temps, the one with two doves, and many others. When the granddaughter, Marie-Claude, decided to start a perfume line in 1992, Lalique de Lalique was the first result and every year they make a stunning limited edition flacon of it. The bottle for my Amethyst EdP is pretty darned cool, too, a dark purple squarish affair, etched with a design of berries on the vine. Alluringly it implies its contents are special and they are. The floral heart is perfection, as is the vanilla-woody-musky base. Amethyst is the kind of richly fragrant perfume I search for, to fall and stay headlong in love. I snagged it for under $30, an utter bargain.

This fragrance opens with a ripe berry accord that is sweet and juicy. A touch of spices adds depth to the composition which otherwise would have been too girlish. After a while the fragrance gradually transitions from fruity to floral, allowing the gorgeous rose note to shine. The reign of the queen of flowers does not last the entire heart accord, for towards the end lily and ylang-ylang share this duty with her. The final stage of this fragrance is characterised by vanilla with a dash of musk. Young and sophisticated this fragrance just screams spring to me.

Lalique Amethyst opens like a basket full of black currants, blueberries and blackberries. And dare I say, the real berries! Not cloying sweet berry-flavour, but juicy, green, fresh, with a hint of acedity. The transition to the floral heart is smooth. Without noticing, peony, rose and ylang-ylang are already there. The pepper adds some sharpness to the soft scent, like spikes on the stem of a rose. The delicious fruits are still present and smell sweeter than in the opening. But the sweetness is fortunately still in a subtle way, as if the berries have ripened during the development of the fragrance. The sillage is soft and the longevity is 7h+. It's not a conventional girly floral-fruity fragrance. To me, it's an ode to the nature, the summer in forests. And I agree with tommy_girl that it focuses more on mind than body. I'd recommend it if someone's looking for a fragrance that smells like real berries. However, I suggest testing prior to buying as it's rather sharp during the first hours of development. Originally written in 2013

Lalique as a fragrance house, continues to amaze me. Their scents are both affordable and elegant, often put together by some very talented noses. Recently I've found myself enjoying scents with black currant as the main note, so I made it my duty to test the popular Lalique Amethyst. When you first spray Lalique Amethyst, you could be forgiven for thinking that it's just another rich berry scent, along the same lines as Britney Spears Midnight Fantasy and Anna Sui's Forbidden Affair. Although this fragrance does open with juicy, candied berries, the heart and drydown establishes Amethyst as a serious and complex fragrance. I absolutely adore the pepper in this composition. When blended with the black currant, blueberries and blackberries, the pepper softens the juicy aspect, even adding a masculine touch. On that note, Lalique Amethyst would make an excellent unisex fragrance. It's one kick-ass fruity floral. Who knew that blackcurrant, peony, rose and pepper could work so well together? I'm so glad that Amethyst is not your typical 'girly', sweet scent. It has quite a commanding presence. The drydown is a touch dry, woodsy and smooth. The more I wear it, the more I'm convinced that a man could definitely pull it off. I'd even suggest Amethyst to those that usually don't like fruity florals. Lalique Amethyst is quite a dark, fruity fragrance, so I'd more than likely choose to wear it during the cooler months, however it could work on a warm Summer's night too. All in all, Lalique Amethyst is a quality scent that has average longevity. Original review written: February 2013.

Just like the genuine, rough, amethysts given to an expert jeweler to cut and polish to perfection. And it comes out sparking with violet fires. From looking at the elements composing this perfume, a good number of them are dark purple, dark pink, dark red, and thus the Amethyste is deliciously dark, deep and beautiful.

When I wear this, people around me think I wear very expensive and rare perfume. I enjoy their reaction. I think Amethyst is a thing that's dry berries and some dark wine on a manly peppery woody base. It's less sweet and doesn't feel too young or too thin. Roses (which are in fact close to geraniums) also work like a hint of classic men's colognes.

Scentrack: Ultravox - Vienna n my opinion one of the most beautiful female perfumes. The explosion of all kind of berry fruits on the strong woody (Iso E Super) background and peppery musky notes. Very contemporary and almost unisex due to potent woody notes. The smell of fruit rhapsody during summer afternoon in the forest. Perfect Art Nouveau bottle.

I fell in love with Meliora, but I couldn't justify buying it, so seeing that Amethyst is similar I had to try it. And yes, I love it as well. It's smooth, berries are juicy and not too sweet, great for summer. Do I still need Meliora? Unfortunately yes I do. Berries are similar in both, but in Meliora's berries sit on this gorgeous background of fresh roses.

Opens really bright and fresh. Sweet, jammy sun-ripened berries and rose. There’s juicy, wet blackberries and blackcurrants with hints of strawberry and pineapple and a slight touch of sensuality from the mulberry.

My disdain of Tom Ford is well documented ... this is a house owned by the Lauder group and as such, I don't really see these fragrances as being in any way 'special' or even worth the money that they are sold at. This is simply big business trading off a niche concept ... which is how 'niche' became mainstream. There is nothing wrong with this fragrance per sé ... except that this concept has been done to death by pretty much every fragrance house out there ... and lately ad nauseum by the Lauder group. Oud has had its moment in the spotlight ... it's time to move on!! Sahara Noir is just another floral, amber-centric and 'incensy' fragrance, which imho has been done much better by the likes of Montale, Nejma and by Killian. In fact, Sahara Noir bears a remarkable resemblance to Amber Oud made by Calice Becker for byKillian ... who has also worked for Lauder and Ford. The mind boggles at thoughts of formulae being altered infinitesimally to create yet another 'new' and 'exciting' launch. Perhaps my nose is just not sophisticated enough to smell the differences. There is LOTS of Labdanum here, which makes this fragrance smell more like high Mass on a Sunday morning than hot wind driving over the desolate expanses of the Saharan wastes. Perhaps the main tent of a wealthy bedouin smells like this when the incense braziers are lit for the night. At the end of the day, Sahara Noir is overpriced for what it is ... a chemical Amber/ Floral/Oud that reminds of too many others. Don't even stop here ... just move on by!

Oriental? In every sense. Floral? Hardly. The Egyptian jasmine carries more life than the Moroccan rose, but initially present to contribute balance. For the first few seconds Sahara Noir is calm, like the eye of a storm. Then there is a whirlwind of notes wafting aggressively. Through smoke and sand, sweet cedar and oud emerge. How appropriate for the classic Tom Ford flacon to be made gold, as it represents the remarkable royal resins used in eastern luxury. Like most of Tom Ford's fragrances, Sahara Noir is acquired taste.

Can I begin by saying that I've just got this today and I'm in love with it. I'm generally an amber and incense fan so it came as no surprise that it was love at first sniff. I used to have this lovely little fragrance called Gucci Pour Homme, Sahara Noir reminds me of this so much that it is uncanny. The difference being that Sahara Noir is more unrelenting in it's insistence to be noticed, Gucci Pour Homme was a bit more layered. For what it is Sahara Noir is extraordinarily hyped and overpriced. I still bought it and like it though.

Tom Ford's Sahara Noir is a scent in my cupboard I've long been ignoring and I couldn't tell you why. It's intensely evocative in an incredibly specific way, so first my nerd review and then a translation for those who don't have a tolerance for silliness. Sahara Noir is the blazing binary sunset seen from the still, dry heat of sand dune on the desert planet Tatooine; a midnight canyon campfire crackling with the spicy resin of the Japor tree, the aromatic blossoms of the molo shrub, and acrid ribbons of poonten grass incense while the ground rumbles with the snores and snuffles of a slumbering bantha herd nearby. Which is to say this is the driest frankincense, lemony woodsy pinon sawdust, a circle of fragrant burning woods, and brittle, smoky papyrus ash. Whatever your preferred fandom or even if you stick solely to reality, Sahara Noir is utterly divine.

Who knows what was running in Tom Ford's head while labeling it 'for women ' and Noir de Noir for both 'Women and Men', anyway the fragrance is very good despite the overwhelming top notes of Incense and Ambre making it an 'in your face' type of scent for those not into the similar sort of fragrances. As I am already in love with woody / Incensy fragrances like GPH and Amouage offerings , I really like it a lot especially the dry down which is tried to be made to serve the purpose of the label with some floral notes but its overall a very masculine rather macho fragrance especially in first one or two hours. The dry down is calming and soothing rather very well rounded.

These days I write perfume reviews based on the incensed accord. It is a somewhat peculiar note, and not everyone likes it. I have always loved the scent of incense, and thanks to these fragrances, I am discovering all its facets and shades.

If you're an incense lover, you must try Sahara Noir. Don't be fooled by the fact that it's classified as a women's fragrance; it's not feminine at all, in my opinion, but totally unisex. Dark and mysterious, with exquisite longevity and sillage, I always wear it during Easter time, I think it's the perfect occasion. If you have the chance to buy a bottle, don't miss it!
As inexplicably discontinued as its sibling, Amber Absolute, Sahara Noir is for many the standout of the frankincense field.

No Tom Ford release dares to hold a candle to Sahara Noir, not even the very best of their private blend. It's like when lab scientists in horror movies come up with a "Frankenstein" molecule, and then it grows and evolves into a monster. This is what might have happened at Tom Ford beauty.

First of all, it must be clarified: I was, to put it mildly, not a particularly diligent student. With corresponding and completely deserved results. Studying in Kiel means: beach, Kieler Woche, etc. Consequently, no one with their five senses intact would have even remotely thought of the term doctorate in connection with my academic achievements.

At first you get this very citrusy feeling to it where the blood orange comes and gives it a little sour touch. The peach is there in the background but its very subtle so to not make sure this becomes too sweet of a fragrance. The rose is not the dominant factor here but it still makes its little appearance with hints of nature-like freshness. The smell has after a few minutes evolved into something you could smell on a shampoo or when you wash your hands. As time goes on, sweetness in forms of sugar starts to seep through and swallow the rose making a love child bearing the fruits of both. A interesting fragrance that takes you on a little journey.

I think I have some kind of noseblindness with this one or something, because I feel this is supposed to be a strong sofisticated perfume, but for me is just some creamy soft peaches with some touches of dark green that make it fresher and reminds more a soapy chypre. Very clean and soapy. But yeah, the main player here is peach, milky peaches I will try in different weathers because Penhaligon's to me change in my skin depending of how hot it is

Empressa opens with a sharp, strong citrus burst. So bold it initially feels like a classic men’s cologne. There’s a moment of surprise, almost dissonance, as it leans unexpectedly masculine. But give it time: the sharpness smooths into a clean, crisp elegance that closely echoes Chanel Chance, though Empressa is subtler, softer, and more refined. It’s not a floral-forward scent. If there are flowers here, my nose is not persiving them. Or maybe i need to wait longer for them to come out. Anyway, to me, the focus remains on that fresh, polished citrus - smooth, non-bitter, and pleasantly unisex. This is a classical, inoffensive fragrance that plays it safe in the best way. I picture myself wearing it during daytime in an office setting. Projection is soft, and longevity is modest. On paper, it fades close to the skin within 20–30 minutes, even though it starts very strong. You might find yourself reaching for a re-spray sooner than expected.

The initial cloud is full of bitter citrus with spicy and almost earthy undertones. Feels like someone sprayed their citrus freshie at an antiques shop. As the cloud settles, fruitiness starts sprouting from below. Mostly peach, a little bit of currant. A variety of peppers. A very fitting hint of dusty geranium. The kind of scent that can be picked apart if you concentrate on it, but if you relax and let its soft sillage envelop you – it just feels like one subdued and reasonable fruity whole. It's... perfumey, but in a non-derogatory way. Feels like I found this decant at the back of a cabinet drawer in an abandoned 19th century mansion. Citrus fizzles out after the first ~20 minutes and leaves just spices and fruits in the spotlight. But unlike with most other perfumes I've tried, rather than being "spicy fruits", this composition smells more like "fruity spices", if that makes any sense. It's not overly sweet, and something about this spice blend reminds me of how my bottle of 50% French absinthe tastes when diluted with sugar water. It's lovable! A low 5 of sillage for the first ~2 hours. There is a cloud around me, but it's pretty faint. I do notice a trail when I move my arms around in an enclosed space, but it doesn't leave my immediate vicinity. It wouldn't choke me out an open space office, and I probably wouldn't even notice it on a busy street. After the first ~2 hours it gets softer and the fruits fizzle away. What's left is a delightful spicy patchouli. A skin scent. Somewhat earthy, lovable. Another hour and patchouli also mostly withers away. The drydown is a bit sweeter – musk, frankincense. A tasteful hint of vanilla. And a mellow herbal aftertaste. Slightly bitter. Barely there. I adore it while it lasts, but for some reason come next morning I barely remember it. Good thing I take extensive notes, or otherwise I'd have nothing to say except "eh, I guess it was okay". It's like whatever spark I've felt between us withered away from my body together with absinthe, and now that I see it in the light of day – I'm completely uninterested and just want to get this encounter over with. A shame.

Empressa is a slightly nondescript fruity-floral musk with a tinge of that clean, syrupy patchouli that passes for the nu-chypre base these days, i.e., a fruitchouli in the mold of Coco Mademoiselle. It is pretty, pleasantly tart and arresting in the topnotes, but a bit too brisk in its progression to the sweet, sugary florals in the heart to be to my taste.

The comparisons to Mademoiselle are spot on. This is extremely similar. Citrusy, light and creamy. Probably one of the most inoffensive perfumes I've ever smelled. A good spring, clean fragrance. Reminds me of Nivea deodorant, Perfect for the office or any other skin scent appropriate environment. It's well crafted, but It's not for me.
What, pray tell, has become of Penhaligon's? One of the most English of fragrance houses, which has given us sweeties like the - even created by the same perfumer - LP No. 9, formerly Love Potion No.

Oops, I seem to have put on a women's perfume. In the men's section of my perfume store, I once again followed the Trade Routes. I hadn't even considered the Empressa. So on it goes………..! I am reviewing this perfume from a man's perspective. The opening is very fresh and floral. At that point, the warning lights should have gone off for me. But no such luck.

The Empressa is a superficially fruity fragrance. Along with the strong fruity component, there are also pleasant freshness and floral impressions. You get a consistently solid scent here. Feminine? Tendentially yes, but still definitely wearable as Unisex!! The fragrance starts off directly with this "fruit explosion." Fruity impressions par excellence shoot into the nose.

I have a karmic relationship with this perfume. I love it so much! I like everything! Its scent, the bottle .... A wonderful vanilla that becomes one with my body. Tonka complements it. Perfume for every day, that you never get bored. Fortunately for me that is still on the market, and at a very good price. A YEAR OF LOVE❣️

In my entire life, I have never taken so many blind fragrance purchases as during the Corona period. Buying a perfume without smelling it first? Impossible for me before. Powdery? Floral? Yes, all good and well, but that still doesn’t tell me how it smells. Puhhh... Whatever... Ordered. When Satin arrived, I first stumbled upon its elegant bottle. Wow, very well done... Then the first spray, and yes, I was really excited! The spray mist is already an experience! No joke! Totally fine and high-quality. Now to the scent. A sense of relief spreads. First thought: wow, does this smell goooooood!!!! Nothing, absolutely nothing, jumps out at me negatively. Everything smells rounded, feminine, elegant, with a hint of nostalgia (No, not old-fashioned!!) floral and simply elegant. Normally, I can easily recognize and describe individual notes in a fragrance. Here, it is really, really difficult for me. Everything is very well intertwined and connected. A scent that truly works anytime. It smells well-groomed, feminine, and simply likeable. For the office? Yes. For everyday life? Yes. For going out to eat? Yep. For visiting the in-laws? Of course. If I had to explain to someone who has never smelled a perfume in their life how a perfume generally smells, I would probably spray Satine by Lalique on their wrist.

Satine... yes, the name fits this beautiful fragrance. The first time I read about Satine here, I found it in a small perfumery so I could test it out first. I personally find it always difficult to evaluate a scent among many other fragrance impressions, and so I couldn't take it home at first because I didn't smell anything except for a bit of powder. Once home, however, my nose couldn't get away from my wrist. I was thrilled and went back the next day to bring Satine home. Now to the scent: Satine starts off with a powerful dose of powder that comes across quite spicy. I don't smell any flowers here. But that doesn't bother me. Too floral is always too much for me anyway. So, spicy powder... not bad. Over time, Satine becomes warmer and softer. It hugs the skin so wonderfully. It's not loud but also not really quiet... somewhere in between. Tonka bean and vanilla give it sweetness, while woods and patchouli prevent the scent from drifting into overly sweet territory. I don't pick up suede. Satine is truly an extraordinary sweet-spicy-woody powder scent. It flatters and warms. With Satine, I feel seductive and very feminine! The longevity is fantastic. I can smell the fragrance on me for a good 8 hours. Satine is also noticeable to others in the first hours before it becomes more intimate. I can imagine Satine for any season, but in the height of summer, it would be more suitable for the evenings. The bottle is beautiful, delicate, and elegant. Conclusion: Satine is a seductive magic powder scent for me!

I believe each of us knows this. So much happens in our lives and in this world. Despite everything, we always try to stay positive and make the best of everything. But there are also days when this is particularly difficult for us, and we feel vulnerable and helpless. Today is one of those days for me. Then I seek comfort, security, and protection in a fragrance, and I always find it in Satine. At first, warm tonka bean embraces me, and heliotrope softly says hello. Gardenia brings lightness like a fresh morning, and jasmine whispers...Hey...I’ll sweeten your day a little. But not too sweet...whispers the pink pepper...because I bring a little looseness with me. Soft sandalwood and gentle vanilla join in, and I already feel much better. Just a bit of fine patchouli as a balm for the soul and vetiver for grounding. Satine has done it again. I feel comforted, secure, protected, gently embraced, and grounded once more. With a small smile on my face, everything feels much lighter. I hope each of you has a soul warmer like this for yourselves. Take good care of yourselves!!!

Today my eyes were caught by the noble Satine bottle - and my nose followed my eyes. I haven't experienced such a fine powderiness in a long time. However, the powder does not dull the fragrance; instead, it allows the soft satin to shine. Delicate sweetness skillfully pairs with mild bitterness - yet the scent remains gentle and embracing. Heliotrope shimmers like silk and is illuminated further by the jasmine. Pepper and vanilla appear mildly sweet - but the cedar adds a smoky touch. The patchouli is deep and sandalwood slightly spicy. A balanced fragrance that conveys style and nobility. I think of Moody Blues: Nights in White Satin - although to me, Satine seems more nude-colored than white. But "Nights" float to my mind rather than "Days," as Satine lets delicate eroticism rustle softly like silk lingerie. A feminine fragrance that celebrates femininity.

Perhaps it is only parents who are fortunate enough to witness the final, highest peaks of cuteness. One or another scene burns itself deep into memory (a camera would have ruined everything!) and evokes blissful smiles and a "Do you remember?" even years later.

Parfumo, what are you doing to me? Here I have another classic case of: Hooked and bought. I now like Lalique so much that I want to call the brand my favorite perfume brand. Blind purchases are a tricky thing; after two successful and one unsuccessful blind buy from the brand, I dared to try this bottle.

Stevie Nicks whispered to Don Henley in 1981. Leather and Lace is, in my opinion, a very honest duet. I think of this song when I wear Satine, because this fragrance combines the aromas of suede, patchouli, and pink peppercorns with tonka and vanilla. The pyramid reads somewhat like a latent niche hit - which this fragrance is not, yet it quickly captured my heart.

I absolutely have to tell you about my latest acquisition. Satine by Lalique is simply a powdery dream fragrance of a special kind, creamy, soft, and cuddly. I tend to be a bit of a coward when it comes to blind purchases, but here you really couldn't go wrong. I can say that now.

I'll keep it short, because first of all, I'm not qualified to detect fragrance notes, and besides, they have already been described expertly here - so I'll pass at this point. What I can say about the scent: Although I really like it very, very sweet, even sticky sweet, and a strong sillage doesn't scare me off, Satine is not for me.

Tom Ford has by no means been wowing over the last couple of years, and while Bois Pacifique may not be the most inventive fragrance of theirs, it's far better than many of their other recent releases. At it's simplest, Bois Pacifique is basically a woodier version of Myrrhe Mystere, which is honestly a good thing. It shares a lot of Myrrhe Mystere's resinous DNA, especially in the dry down, but the added woody notes help balance the sweetness/thickness that the resin notes can have at times. There is a bit of a sharp zing to this in the opening, which I didn't get the first couple of times wearing this, but became more prominent the more I got to know this fragrance. I think that this fragrance is a much easier wear than Myrrhe Mystere as well, as this is not as heavy or cloying, though it does not perform as well as the former, which is certainly a caveat. While inventiveness is not exactly in the cards for Bois Pacifique, it is certainly a great fragrance that is far more enjoyable, and far better priced as well, than many of the other current Tom Ford offerings. It's a very solid resinous-woody fragrance that is easy to pick up and get to know, while still having enough character to set itself out from others.

I got this as a free sample on Facebook. I really liked the fragrance. I have always said that one of my favorite smells is the scent of dry pine needles, wood, and sand that we get during the summer in my home country of Spain. Since I moved to the USA (Illinois) for work, I have missed this smell. The first spray of this fragrance transports me there, to that smell, although it is not quite accurate. It is slightly too spicy and not dry enough for that. Perhaps, this is what the pine forests of the Pacific coast smell like. I can't quite decide whether the incense is too strong or not strong enough - it strangely seems to vary for me. However, as others have said, it lasts too short. I spray this on in the morning, and after lunch it is barely noticeable. I wouldn't buy a full bottle at retail price, as I don't find it super versatile.

Its nice but too ephemeral! Its so thin on the skin and disappears quickly! Also, this has nothing to do with almighty Gucci Pour Homme 1. Wich is very different. Gucci is much smokyer, like real cedar and olibanum, with dark/gothic nuances, with a much warmer, waxy balsamic and heavy profile! This is a decent Iso E + new wave of Akigalawood usage in modern parfumery.

Tested it now for 2 days and I love the smell. The opening is nice but the mid and dry down are divine. Unfortunately the performance is not good enough for me and also I get a bit of an headache if I over spray. So I probably won't buy a full bottle although I love the scent :( I hope the perfume version will fix these issues.

For me it opens with a lot of fresher spicier notes and some woods. As it dried down the spices became softer, mostly leaving behind cardamom, and other notes appear. It became very resinous and woody to me with a prominent sandalwood in the dry down. Overall: woody and spicy. Can’t exactly pinpoint which occasions this would suit the best but I guess as sort of an allrounder at the slightly colder months. Perhaps quite suitable for slightly more formal occasions. Not a head turner but something that could be used to be taken more seriously. I appreciate the scent but personally think it’s kind of meh, and I find the price quite high. So wouldn’t buy it myself. Still a pretty solid scent though.

Here is a new one from Tom Ford - in that ribbed cylindrical bottle, which is now used for the Signature Blends instead of the old flat one, priced a bit more accessibly than the Private Blends - and which somewhat breaks with the established Ford DNA or rather evolves it in a direction that might be unexpected.

…something big. At least from my perspective - and for my taste. Sometimes you hear an old song and feel transported to another time. When I happen to hear Lenny Kravitz's "Fly Away" or Cher's "Believe" today, I feel for a moment like the child in the passenger seat of my mother’s car, the radio on, the sun shining, and life is easy.

... on the Baja California at the beach. We guys are sitting, each with a Dos Equis, on the sand and looking at the Pacific. A slightly salty, spicy breeze from the sea wafts into our noses. In the distance, we see dolphins surfacing from the water again and again. It's just a beautiful, relaxed day by the water with friends.

Bois Pacifique by TF is one of those fragrances for me where you read the scent pyramid and think - yes, this is exactly my fragrance, I'm sure I'll like it. And that's how it was. I received a sample, wore it for a day, and ordered it right away without much thought. If only it were always that easy :) For me, there are two main notes here: dry wood and incense.

How does the perfume smell... I would say it smells like a forest landscape, interspersed with sunbeams. A vibrant blend of cardamom, turmeric, and wood. Frankincense unfolds in the middle, and the iris, cedarwood, oak, and sandalwood add a beautiful elegance and depth. Amber and vanilla wonderfully round off the experience with warmth.

I really like Blazing Mr Sam, it’s a great fragrance and it made me confident enough to purchase another fragrance from the house (for the right price, of course) so I found The Inimitable William at a discounter and found the notes interesting enough to go for it. My first impression was: what the hell, did someone mess up and bottled Mr Sam in a William bottle!? well it seems that despite the difference in the notes they are pretty much the same but with William besides the same scent you get whiffs of citrus and vetiver every once in a while (which I thought was what this fragrance’s focus would’ve been based on the note breakdown) so, I don’t know what this fragrance wants to be a Sam look alike or a Green, Citrus, Vetiver scent but it doesn’t achieve any of both. Does it smell bad? no, does it smell good? sorta! it smells confused and not only do I not enjoy it but it made my enjoyment for Mr Sam less. If you’re a casual fragrance user save your money and by something cheaper that will smell just as good or even better, if you’re a fragrance enthusiast save you money as this doesn’t go one way nor the other.

I'm very sorry. There was a time I was extremely hyped, since I treated myself with the Portaits Collection Discovery Set, and I eventually got to TIWP. I apologize, because I can't really remember what it was that I felt one year ago. But it looks like something bewitched me and it didn’t take me too long to purchase it. Later on, during the time I got around 80 perfumes and ended up selling 50 of them, I spent most of my perfume journey sampling, so I didn't really spray perfumes in my collection much. However, from time to time I enjoyed taking this marvelous and luxurious cap off and get a reminiscence of why I loved the perfume. Two/three days ago, I had near +260 sampled perfumes on my back, respectively, from the beginning of my journey. So this time I took the cap off for the good dose. For the spray. And then... I wasn't in love with William anymore. In fact, my frustration and anger escalated pretty quickly before the "inimitable" question rose in me: What in the world brought me to purchase that scent? I feel a velvety synthetic and astringent floral-citrus supported by a very synthetic woody backbone. I'm very sorry, but it's not anything else to me. As 95% of Penhaligon's, projection is mediocre and sillage is weak. And that is, giving so much way to imagination. It doesn't even smell like wood: you gotta force yourself into believing it. Frankincense? Oh boy, not a tiny trace. And then there's the below-average citrus and floral notes. I don't like to denigrate professional work, but it really doesn't feel any good quality-wise. Heck, where's Myslf when we need it. "Class doesn't need to be loud." Well, I don't mean to be radical, but there's no middle term regarding TIWP's performance. It is bad. Also, there are Portraits' perfumes that aren't as classy and also perform ridiculously: "Portraits - The World According To Arthur | Penhaligon's" ; "Portraits - The Blazing Mister Sam | Penhaligon's" . I think I'm over Master Morillas' creation. I'm over the pretty and ostentuous bottles. I truly believe we only get better and wiser based on mistakes. I personally confirm to all of you that this is one I will remember. I'm not sorry, Mr. William Penhaligon. Thank y'all for your time. Bodomic

For those who don't know, inimitable means that something is so good or so unusual, it is impossible to copy. I think it says something when the brand decided to put their name specifically onto this bottle, it is one of the star fragrances from this collection. As to whether it is so good it cannot be copied, that remains to be seen. This fragrance is the epitome of unisex fragrance. It starts with citrus and floral, little tart and a little sweet. The spice and woodiness slowly creeps in over time and it becomes a gentle incense woody fragrance that is just interesting enough but not offensive. It seems like a perfect day to day fragrance with just enough personality to be interesting to a very wide audience. This fragrance created a nice scent bubble that trailed behind you, it just noticeable enough. It also lasted all day, about 8 hours on my skin. Like other fragrances from this line, it is expensive sitting at $315 for 75ml. I would say this is one of the few that might be worth $200, but I am not entirely sure its worth over $300.

Carrying the name of the house, William Penhaligon has something to prove. I hope that we'll finish off with a bang! Vetiver and warm, earthy notes. Oh I do hope William is nice. He promises a fresh opening with bergamot, potentially from cedarwood too, but the frankincense, vetiver and sandalwood invite something creamy and divine. On paper, William Penhaligon is just that. Wow. I'm at a loss for words. He is elegantly creamy. An ever so slight note of fresh bergamot at top, but so faint. Just like Mr Sam, I cannot stop smelling it. They are very different. Mr Sam was spicy and warm, whereas William Penhaligon is smooth and creamy. I am honestly wanting them both in my collection! What a wonderful way to finish off the portraits set.

William Penhaligon was born under the sign of Aries. According to stories, the sharp wit attributed to this zodiac sign is what allowed the former master barber from picturesque Cornwall to possess the rare gift of being able to smell even the finest stubble of his blond, highborn clients before they even entered his bathhouse. This truly made him unique in his trade, and soon he was able to personally attend to the scent and beard of Queen Victoria by royal decree. I just (almost) made all of that up. Which aspects of this are true and which spring from my imagination ... is actually completely irrelevant. I myself am a Cancer - imaginative beings, just like the animal counterparts in the wild! Sideways walking, being the favorite food of all seabirds, having delicious leg meat ... great! Oh, let's leave that. I have absolutely no idea about astrology. In any case, this introduction fits perfectly with the marketing of the Portraits series from the British fragrance house Penhaligon’s, which has been practiced since 2016. A deeply intertwined story about an English noble family, in which each fragrance in the series tells and contributes its part to this tale. Let’s call it kitsch. Let’s call it pastiche. Let’s call it British humor. Let’s call it incredibly effective marketing - and let’s also call it much ado about nothing. I openly admit: I am a sucker for it - as the French say - although so far only one of the Portraits fragrances, Lord George, has truly knocked my socks off. But it did so with great intensity, as I find it to be one of the most beautiful and stylish men’s fragrances on the market. Now, the founder of this fragrance house, William Penhaligon, is being honored with his own scent in this series - at least that much from the opening paragraph is true. It must be a fragrance with flagship qualities - anything less would surely be a bitter disappointment. That would be like a traditional German car brand naming a small city car after its founder instead of its luxury model - unthinkable! Oh, oops - that has already happened long ago. So it seems to be possible after all. In this sense, it sets a healthy expectation for me regarding this fragrance. By a wonderful coincidence, I was able to test this new release before the arrival of my official sharing post, allowing me to spend the last two days enveloped in the scent of Penhaligon’s founder fragrance. The nose elixir comes in a dark green hue, bottled in a heavy flacon that is, typical of the Portraits series, simply beautiful ... for my taste. But we already covered that topic above - Newspeak: I love it. In the official announcement of the fragrance by the brand itself, the focus was clearly placed on the expected vetiver. Green liquid, vetiver - got it, I know what’s coming. That’s what I initially thought, inevitably. And in the initial minutes, the fragrance partially fulfills this preconceived image. A soft, slightly herbal, very polished vetiver, which surprisingly does not seem to correspond to my synaptically anchored definition of a “green” fragrance - which I could never effectively put into words - thus presenting me with a first paradox regarding expectations. Rather, it is a vanillic, almost gourmand impression that dominates the first minutes. To make a comparison: despite the fundamental difference between the two fragrances, I can’t help but think of the later development of Hermès Vetiver Tonka during this phase. Accompanied by a somewhat subtly dripping ... rosemary?! Soon, the nominal main actor nearly completely withdraws and makes way for the impressive performance of what I perceive to be the true star of this composition - the sandalwood. If a firm, ingredient-centered classification of the fragrance were needed, my nose would undoubtedly place it in the sandalwood corner. To cautiously draw a comparison here: creamy sandalwood à la Jacques Fath's Pour l'Homme, or the red aftershave from Proraso - both of which are certainly all-time favorites in the Nordique household. At this stage, the fragrance ultimately lingers for several hours, remaining understated - perhaps even a bit too much so. A stylish pleasant scent, a slightly sweet, sandalwood, modern barbershop fragrance, devoid of any fresh elements. Classifications that bring it spiritually close to its incense-bearing counterpart from the same house, Lord George, without exhibiting too many similarities in the scent development. Cedarwood? Unfortunately no. Frankincense? Yes, with a good dose of imagination ... not really. The often maligned Ambroxan in widely scent-affine circles? God forbid, devil's stuff - it seems the latter has once again taken it with him to the purgatory. For my part, I am quite taken with this new addition to the exclusive Penhaligon’s series. Nevertheless, the wonderful ram's head flacon does not contain a brew that attempts to reinvent the olfactory wheel in the slightest. So be it. I have enjoyed wearing it over the last two days - and I am already looking forward to the next time. In the meantime, I will simply enjoy the pure sight of the latest addition to the Portraits series - and wait for Penhaligon’s to perhaps bring my zodiac sign into the series in the form of a crab cap. Maybe as “Crappy Cedric” ... or “The Cringy Cupbearer Colin.” That would be something! Thank you for your time! PS: I just HAD to bring up the ram joke from the title first! I’m sorry.

...in the truest sense of the word! :D I have tested almost all the perfumes from the "Portraits" line and also own a few. But not this one: Good old "William Penhaligon" has for me a sandalwood-dominated, almost cloyingly sweet DNA base, which it shares a little with "Blazing Mr. Sam," but quite a lot with "Monsieur Beauregard.

My highlight for spring and summer. I’m already looking forward to next year to rock this scent again. The fragrance combines fresh citrus notes with woody and slightly smoky accents, making it versatile and suitable for any situation for me. Light enough for a shopping trip in the city yet deep enough for an evening out with friends.

A super elegant, unique, and pleasant fragrance. The very pleasant jasmine opening and the beautiful cedar and amber notes make you happy to spray it on. It is not very intense, both in sillage and longevity, but that is nothing new for the Portrait line from Penhaligon’s. On my skin, it lasts about 7 hours, of which it is "loud" for 2-3 hours.

Well, you definitely can't complain about the caps of Penhaligon's. Unique, high-quality, they fit snugly and look TOP. The bottles themselves are the same. They also feel nice in the hand. The spray head is great too. An appropriate amount of fragrance mist escapes from the nozzle. The scent of Portraits - The Inimitable William starts with a pleasant fresh opening.

LOVE Lalique Pour Homme!!! My first imported perfume! I bought it at a time when I knew nothing about perfumes, or even their fragrances. I was younger, time from my first job. I went into an imported perfume store (something chic), saw that bottle of perfume, and bought the perfume because of the magnificence of its bottle, that face of a rustic lion, and when I tasted that fragrance it won me over at first. Since the first time I felt it in the store, or so many other times I've used it, it reminds me of a fougere, powdery, classy perfume, which also has a BARBERSHOP vibe, which reminds me of cleanliness, a feeling that you just showered, and used LUXURY soap, in a 5 STAR hotel. NOTE: Don't be a reductionist, and don't just sum it up there is something vintage, or even dated! This is stupid! Be smart, try to understand the perfume! Don't be part of this NUTELA generation, which is used to this sweet vibe that is already a pain in today's perfumes! - Fixation on my skin for at least 8 hours (always quite remarkable). - Average projection of 1 hour and a half, whoever comes close to me always praises.

Yes, you hear it right, i think this is the perfect multidimensional fougere in this genre! Lalique, what a house, with more than 130 years of history. Lalique its also visible, without question, within their perfumes. This is an absolutely uncompromising creation, the great perfumer Maurice Roucel, who makes perfumest since the 70s, managed to bring an ode, to the classic male perfumes from the 80s, achieving a masterpiece, in 1997! The theme is excellently chosen, the bottle is pur Lalique, their own creation, the embossed lion makes this bottle one of the most beautiful perfume bottles created. The perfume begins with green, evervescent and sharp notes, the lavender is as French as possible, the herbal elements through rosemary and citrus begin excellently, followed strongly from behind by a healthy dose of oak moss, at least in the vintage bottle I have , from 2003, absolutely yellow-brown in color, the dose of oak moss is generous and gives the perfume depth and sharpness. An iris, perfectly centered by Roucel, as creamy as possible but dusty at the same time, all placed on a creamy base of real ambragris (in the old versions) and a vanilla with a sandalwood, flawless! The perfume has a backbone, it has everything it needs to design and accompany you all day! Superlative performance and I think it is the best fougere in this area! Congratulations to Lalique and the perfumer for this creation! 10/10

To me, this is one of the greatest designer scents ever created. The subtle genius of Roucel's handiwork is readily apparent in the blend of lavender and vanilla - similar to Kurkdjian's Le Male at times - but with the added dapper elements of crisp cedarwood and a touch of florals for a regal and professional edge. The opening is a superb blend of herbal lavender, rosemary and tart grapefruit. Immediately, the florals feel "full" as if warmed up by a creamy sandalwood and vanilla right from the start. For me, it was love at first sniff. But just wait...within about 5 minutes, the composition opens up with a fantasticly enveloping cedar note that is seldom found in the designer realm these days. Although it does remind me of Bois du Portugal, I prefer Lalique's iteration by a landslide. It's far less harsh IMO, and with just the right amount of spice, melding perfectly with the velvety lavender and vanilla to create one of the most comforting woody barbershop scents I've ever smelled. 30 minutes in, the rosemary has all but disappeared, and replaced with a synthetic green oakmoss. It's certainly not overdone, but adds a slight sour and musty edge to balance the sweet vanilla, warm lavender and woods. It's such a comforting aroma, that the calming effect on the mind and spirit cannot be understated. Personally, I don't get much iris, jasmine or ambergris, but I'm not complaining. To experience this kind of quality at such a low price is just staggering. Truth be told, I was on the fence about purchasing this one for a very long time over concerns that it would smell too dated, old-fashioned or like grampa's underpants. Well.....I don't know about grampa's underpants but I can certainly vouch for it having a vintage aftershave feel on account of the lavender and oakmoss. Fortunately, the GENEROUS amount of vanilla in the base comes straight from the 90s and is in NO WAY out of place in today's professional aesthetic. If you imagine JPG's Le Male to be a young, loud, flirty, rebellious and irresponsible teenager, Lalique Pour Homme is his gentle, level-headed and business-minded aristocratic father - always well shaved, well dressed, informed and respectful of his roots - a true scholar, but also the dreamer as it were, a visionary and optimist. Incidentally, there are times when I am reminded of elements from Versace's The Dreamer, perhaps on account of the green notes combining with the warm and watery sweetness? Either way, the effect is wonderfully nostalgic. The bulk of the fragrance is dominated by cedar, oakmoss, lavender and vanilla well into the drydown, until it disappears as a soothing and powdery woody vanilla about 7 hours in. Overall performance is about average on my skin, with very modest projection (being an edp), but I suppose that's why it comes in a 125 mL bottle! So glad I finally gave this scent the benefit of the doubt. I've yet to try the edt version, but I'm sure the effect is similar, albeit a tad brighter on account of the added citrus. Nevertheless, this is easily the best blind-buy I ever made - timeless, regal, professional and grounded. Wouldn't necessarily recommend it to most people under the ages of 20 or 25, but if dapper is your style, definitely go for it. Might as well scoop up a second bottle. I know I am.

Now THIS is what a man's fragrance is. Class, style and grace going back to 1997 which was at the tail end of Greatest Era of Perfumerie. From top to bottom and on both sides this Bois du Portugal clone is just a powdery fantastic gem. At a much cheaper price to boot. This very grown up Eau de Parfum behaves and acts just like the sign says. Lalique is an underrated fragrance house with many masculines to choose from and me myself I own at least 6 different bottles from this house. It just goes to show that you don't have to take out a 2nd mortgage to enjoy the finer things. Every time I put this on I Immediately feel like a better man. YES! SOMETIMES A FRAGRANCE WILL HAVE THAT KIND OF EFFECT ON ME. I grew up in the 1970s when men's fragrances had balls and character and not the sickly sweet garbage being fluttered around nowadays. But that aside, this Fragrance has been around for a few and I'm so glad I've had the opportunity to own 2 of Pour Homme's and I'm working on a 3rd. That's how highly I think of this classic masculine creation. Longevity is an all day beast. No decants necessary BTW. The many different notes take it to the limit and the drydown is the climactic event that'll still be on your chest the following day. There aren't too many fragrances priced under $40 that can do that. So go buy it, wear it and you'll understand

Although released in 1997, Lion looks back to the great masculine fougeres of the 80's. Awesome aromatic and woody scent. However, Lion is smoother than or not as biting as many from that period. It's also more reserved in that there is no strong animalic component. I'd say more of a classy and formal fragrance. Projection and sillage are more modest. You definitely won't be fumigating a room with Lion, even if you over spray. Longevity is pretty good - I get about 9 hours at which point it's still a pretty strong skin scent. Bottle is beautiful with the lion figure being an actual intaglio in the glass, not a sticker or label - a real artwork worthy of the Lalique name.

Preface: My experience with this scent is largely the same as Harrock's review below. I'm newer to fragrances and expanding my palette. This is my first review! TL;DR - Lalique Pour Homme (Lion EDP) was challenging to start, but became something wonderful. Vintage, clean, bright, and relaxing.

This is a lovely lavender and vanilla combination, with citrus and fresh herbs at the top and dry woods at the bottom. It's gentle, not sweet at all. There's a fougere accent that keeps it sharp and interesting. I get a faint soap vibe as well, a bit old-school yes, which may explain why people call it 'barbershop'.

The first thing that strikes me is the quality Lalique keeps having for all their scents, regardless of the price range they are in. When you open the box, you will see a bottle of classy and sturdy design that immediately looks and feels nice.

My signature perfume! I love him and ... if he had a bigger sillage he would have been perfect. He is warm ... woody ... and he gives you a good mood.Of course, there are many perfumes that I like ... in fact ... all !!! :) but this one is from my family. That's how I feel. I will always buy him as long as I live.

It's a true classic, Never gets old, Green, Floral, Woody and Complex. It opens up with like citrusy, spicy, green and floral notes in the background then dry down is vanilla woody. This is perfect for the spring and fall. The art of bottle design is very beautiful. I like Lalique Pour Homme EDP. Longevity is good. Thumbs Up. Rating : 8 / 10

Tom Ford CAFE ROSE opens as a rather peppery rose, reminding me quite a bit of Etat Libre d'Orange ROSSY DE PALMA. The rose is palpably red, and the pepper accentuates its redness. Shortly thereafter, a patchouli complex vaguely reminiscent of BLACK ORCHID arrives on the scene. It's somewhat chewy and sweet, but not overly so, and I cannot help thinking that this creation was crafted specifically with Tom Ford fragrance devotees in mind. I should say, however, that the coffee does mingle with the other notes in a most enticing way, giving this particular presentation of patchouli its own distinct personality, despite its overlap with BLACK ORCHID (and perhaps WHITE PATCHOULI as well...). By the drydown, CAFE ROSE seems much closer to BLACK ORCHID than to ROSSY DE PALMA--or any other spicy rose--so I'd say that what we have here are really two completely distinct fragrances: first there's rose, and then there's the cafe. I imagine that the opening burst of rose is going to make a lot of sales at the counter: it's vibrant and enticing and beautiful. But the BLACK ORCHID lovers will be pleased, too, if they have the patience to wait for the drydown of this perfume. Is this a coherent two-stage creation? To me, it seems like a split personality. I do not think that they are completely incompatible, but the two stages really are very different from one another. Still, since I like both stages, I cannot dislike their conjunction!

Café Rose is one of four new introductions for Fall 2012 from Tom Ford's Private Blend Collection. The film noir inspired name itself suggests that this fragrance has a dark and disturbing past, but Café Rose is as familiar and comfortable as a warm fur coat. When I first saw the name, I couldn't help but think of some of my other all time favorites from Tom Ford Private Blend, issues like Tobacco Vanille and Amber Absolute. I was hoping that Café Rose would be as interesting and memorable. While Café Rose is interesting, it is by no means memorable. Café Rose opens with sweet rose, then sharp and spicy black pepper. The top notes contain a sheer, cozy saffron that further intrigues you by coupling with a dark, semisweet chocolate, drizzled with a luscious bit of rich coffee. This combination is quite alluring but very short-lived. There is no lack of rose in Café Rose with May, Bulgarian and Turkish varieties being the primary scent of top and heart notes. The base of Café Rose is an old fashioned combination of patchouli and sandalwood, with a slap of amber for good measure. It also has a puff of frankincense to make it mysterious. There are no big surprises here from Tom Ford. Café Rose alludes to a gourmand fragrance but this fragrance ultimately boils down to a sweet innocent garden rose enjoying a morning coffee. I must admit that I was mildly impressed with Café Rose upon first sniff. All the allure of coffee and chocolate disappeared very quickly making the fragrance extremely one note. I feel that Café Rose is one of the most interesting of the four new introductions by Tom Ford. The primary issue with Café Rose is the lack of complexity in the fragrance in the dry-down stage. I find Café Rose to be a little bland and uninteresting, and quickly turns into a subtle and lovely rose skin scent, but not much more. The gourmand coffee and chocolate notes made this fragrance intriguing. Unfortunately, those elements just evaporate leaving your skin smelling of a lovely rose garden.

This is the Rose of the twisted Garden? Antoine Lie, l’enfant terrible, was the perfumer? Maybe I’ve gotten high on the fumes the smoldering rose chypres of the 70s-80s, but twisted or noir this ain’t. Woody roses are easy in concept. There is a logical fit and a mutual enhancement. Because rose provides its own top, middle and base, the pairing with woods is logical. Patchouli, incense, sandlewood: Cafe Rose has them all. Amber, another expected match with rose, rounds out the mix. Antoine Lie has visited this idea with colleague Antoine Maisondieu in Rossy de Palma Eau de Protection for Etat Libre d’Orange. Rossy plays with a dark rose and woods, also, but uses spice and chocolate as well as tones of metal, dust and blood. Unfortunately, Cafe Rose is best captured in what it is not. Not outstanding, not inspiring, not polarizing (not a good sign) and to my mind, given the competition in the niche market, not worth the price. Cafe Rose isn’t a particularly ambitious perfume. The only sense of noir it conveys is, ‘Hey. It’s dark in here. Where’s the light switch?’ The concept isn’t new and the execution is uneventful. It conveys a feeling of the satisfaction of connecting the dots. The components are in place, the bits all connect; therefore the perfume is good. To its credit, the perfume doesn’t fall apart or become unbalanced. If you like the opening, you’ll likely enjoy the rest of the perfume. But the bar just seems to be set low, and the risk-averse Cafe Rose favors balance over richness, competence over inspiration. from scent hurdle.com

The lavender comes out strong direct after spraying where as you can not smell anything else at the start. On my body it was colder, more airy and herbal. On my partner's warmer skin – more resinous and almost smoky, like sitting a bit too close to a fireplace. Not too sweet, not too sour. Spicy, but mellow. A clear vision with a relatively elegant execution. Well made. Lovable. It took around ~3,5 hours to dry down to a soft balsamic base and another ~1,5 to wither away, leaving just a faint aftertaste of frankincense. A memorable scent doing its own thing. Confident, yet subdued and reasonable. I can see the appeal in it! That said, it's not for me. Despite a very moderate initial sillage (that faded away and became a skin scent in an hour), despite delicate sweetness of the suede – the composition still felt too coarse for my comfort. Like a stiff collar on a borrowed suit that doesn't fit me quite right. It smells good! But it has a very particular vibe to it. A strong individual character is what we typically experience with gent's perfumes by Lalique. Hommage à L'Homme is on the market for a while now and also part of my collection, yet, I find it difficult to evaluate. Not only due to its outer appearance, Hommage à L'Homme is breaking up with the Lalique tradition. This perfume is background only, nothing in there is distinctive or unwieldy, and one has to look for good to find a certain statement. Even though this note is not listed: Hommage à L'Homme for me classifies into the group of modern, dry amber perfumes, like Prada Amber pour Homme Intense or Eau de Iceberg 74. A very discreet, dry and greyish smoke stands in the main focus – nothing else. This smells somehow transparent, with a minimal rubber appeal and the idea of burnt amber at last. More friendly and brighter notes - such as violet or bergamot – may be in but are not very discernible. It is a downright anti-perfume! Hommage a L'Homme projects a dry smoke into the aura of its wearer. I don't see a development that is worth mentioning. This fragrance is as discreet as convenient to wear. There is nothing distracting in there, nothing to provoke objection – one cannot go wrong with it. Wearing Hommage à L'Homme is just as thrilling as choosing silver metallic as the colour of your new car. Okay, this fragrance is really well done and refined: silver metallic with pearl effect! When should one wear this, and why? I think Hommage à L'Homme should be granted a spot on your bath room shelf, always within reach. You can grab this bottle quickly when you are late in the morning and have no time for musing about your perfume of the day. Hommage à L'Homme will enfold a pleasant carpet before you which with its transparent mist will protect you from the worst demands of the beginning working day. On your way to your job you will notice that you have caught something nice. And the car you are driving (silver metallic, of course!) will slide throught the morning traffic just a little bit more relaxed and elegant . Such a lot of understatement, but what a bulky flacon! That doesn't fit for me – but maybe for Lalique's marketing people. The massive appearance pretends what is missing in there. Does Lalique have success with it? I have already seen bargains. Presumably, most buyers would prefer something more gaudy, and so shop assistants will have to work a little for this perfume. When you finally own a bottle of it, you will have to grow into it first before Hommage à L'Homme finally will become your grey working day companion.

Every time I wear this scent it never fails to impress. From the first spray, just imagine cracking open a brand new bag of organic dried figs and giving it a good sniff. Bam. Like fresh prunes or raisins with that dusty crystalline sweetness quality - that's what the violet, labdanum, oud and saffron does in this. Very ethereal, high frequency, but with a touch of that grunge from the woody pepper. It's funny, the first time I ever smelled it on a test strip, it was an immediate love. Dusty and understated sweet man-spice. Big smile. Morever, I couldn't help but get bits of nearly every association that other people have made - Fahrenheit (yup), Gucci Pour Homme II (yup), grape? (more of a raisin or wine), cherries (yup), L'homme Libre (yup) and get this....after sitting for about 8 hours on a test strip...I kid you not - the drydown of Guerlain's L'homme Ideal Cologne. As crazy as that sounds, it took me a while before I figured it out, but yeah. Mostly on paper though. On skin, the black pepper, saffron and cistus combine to give the high frequency sweetness and ethereal violet a slightly earthy, burned match quality up close that combines with a bare dusting of wood to give it just the right amount of groundedness. It's amazing. Many people have compared the smell in the drydown to dry tobacco leaves and I can see why. But to me, it's really more of a mashup of dry, resinous fruit that sometimes approaches wine territory in the sillage. Like two scoops of raisins decided to waltz around a bowl of freshly poured cherry juice laying on a bed of smouldering leaves or paper. Oud? Not even a hint. At least, not the middle-eastern kind. And the longevity and projection is just about perfect for a scent of this class. Nothing really juvenille about it, despite the sweetness giving it a playful wink. Overall, if the idea was to create a product reminiscent of the fine glass work that Lalique is known for with just a touch of grounded masculinity and intrigue, Hommage a L'homme is nothing short of a homerun. Even in its current bottle it exudes precision and refinement, all the way up to the logo at the very tip of the reflective cap. Superb attention to detail, and at an incredible price to boot. If I were to sum it up in one word, "lovely" would certainly be it. Not a surprise that Lalique remains my favourite designer fragrance brand right next to Guerlain. Affordable elegance without compromise. THAT, I can count on.

As the name suggests, Hommage à l’Homme is exactly that — a tribute to the man. But this isn’t just another generic masculine scent. This is a nuanced, layered fragrance that pulls classic elements from iconic men’s perfumery and reassembles them into something unexpectedly modern, elegant, and just a bit mysterious. This was a blind buy for me — and frankly, I had no idea violet and agarwood could make such an addictive duo. Oud is typically married to rose in those well-known oriental formulas, but here it dances with violet leaf, and the result is something truly original. The contrast is sharp yet refined. It keeps your attention. And it works. If you're a fan of Fahrenheit Eau de Toilette , you’ll instantly recognize that signature accord — woody, petrol-inflected violet leaf — that unmistakable profile that manages to be fresh, warm, and polished all at once. But let me be clear: beyond the violet, Hommage à l’Homme is not a Fahrenheit clone. They share some DNA, sure, but they walk very different paths. The opening is a surprise — more sour than you'd expect. It starts off with crisp citrus and herbal-green violet leaf, with a faint powdery undertone humming in the background. There's also this very specific vibe of that old-school Italian grape soda — violet-sweet, a bit fizzy — wrapped in leathery saffron. That floral note sticks around, softened yet distinct, resting on the shadowy warmth of oud. As it develops, the fragrance leans more into that violet and oud duet. The oud here isn’t loud or animalic — it's a smooth, synthetic kind of oud, like you’d find in Ferrari Oud. Safe and balanced, creamy more than dirty, lending a subtle dark warmth rather than overwhelming the composition. It becomes this tug-of-war between hot, resinous oud and cool, airy violet — pulsing, unsettled, and totally compelling. Eventually, the two begin to blur into a sleek, lacquered woodiness that feels both vintage and futuristic. Fast forward an hour or two, and Hommage shifts again. The violet softens, melting into a clean, slightly soapy stage. Not full-on barbershop, but clean in a subtle, nostalgic way. At this point, notes of hay and pepper start to whisper through, adding dryness and depth. This phase lingers the longest, mellow and grounded. And just when you think it’s done evolving — around hour five or six — the oud resurfaces, joined by a gentle powdery musk. It’s delicate but persistent. By the ten-hour mark, it's still quietly present on my skin. I sprayed this in the early afternoon, and the next morning I could still detect it on the shirt I wore underneath. That soft oud trail? Absolutely phenomenal. In terms of wearability, Hommage à l’Homme is a modern gentleman’s scent. Casual yet refined, reserved but confident. Projection is subtle — arm’s length, if that — but longevity is excellent. It’s creamy yet light, slightly sweet, gently bitter in the drydown. I even get whiffs of something resembling tobacco — more like the scent of an empty cigarette pack, which oddly enough adds to the charm. If you're chasing a beast-mode oud bomb, this won’t satisfy you. There’s more oud in the marketing than in the actual formula. But if you’re looking for a quiet, well-constructed, violet-oud fusion with an understated charm — this one delivers. I’ve had this bottle since January 2017, and every time I wear it, I’m reminded why I fell for it in the first place. Lalique Hommage à l’Homme is a rare find — a smooth, modern classic that whispers instead of shouts. And that’s exactly its power. — Elysium

Scentrack Drago Diklic – Moja Draga A truly dedicated to men. Lalique’s man is gentle, but masculine. Quiet, well behaved and optimistic. A proper 21st century gentleman. This fragrance has a retro old school vibe paired with contemporary oud/Tonka tendencies. Duo Nagel – Bijaoui did a tremendous job – a perfectly tweaked masculine composition with multiple layers. Beautiful neoclassic violet rides together with its green leaf and some black pepper. The opening is masculine, somehow boozy, and green like a freshly cut grass, reminding of Dior’s Fahrenheit. The powdery floral notes of violet and saffron are prominent. The saffron note in my opinion gives that needed Oriental twist to otherwise complete Western composition, and successfully balance the oud note. This synthetic oud is dim, yet dark. It gives slightly skunky, dirty undertones. Tonka bean from the base is responsible for that sweet contemporary touch, while cistus for resinous tone. I enjoy discovering these layers over and over again. Hommage is a special everyday scent. Unreal hybrid of modern and classic. For men who open a door for their ladies and carry a linen handkerchief. An olfactory echoes of a better past. Rating; 8/10 More on Scentimentalwords

The notes just don't come across as harmonious or seem to "jive", to me. Violet is okay but does not do well with oud/agarwood to my nose.

Something NEW! Hey Hey! I really like this scent. In the beginning I only get flowers. Violet and Rose are playing together. Pepper is frsh and loud too. After 30 minutes the musk/ woody warm feeling begins. Could there really be Oud inside? I am not sure. Smells different from the OUD Scents I know. I really like what Lalique crafted here.

That's fine by me because I love the smell. This is along the lines of Soleil Blanc which I also like but surprisingly this performs rather well. It's close to the body not a massive projector but has lasted for about 8 hours on me today. It doesn't break any barriers but it is nice. Over priced? 100%. But all of the Private Blends are and its to be expected.

First wearing of the latest release from the Tom Ford Private Blend collection, Soleil Brulant, which follows Soleil Blanc, Eau de Soleil Blanc, and Soleil Neige as another offering using the “sun” name. While Soleil Blanc conjured a beachy, sun tan lotion vibe and Soleil Neige was inspired by fresh, sparkling snow, Soleil Brulant seems to loosely translate “burning sun,” and there’s certainly something bolder about it that Blanc or Neige before it. Upon initial spray, it smells of resins and sunflowers, a sort of semi-sweet, semi-floral, fairly dense concoction, and seeing the note breakdown, it sort of makes sense: orange flower, honey, pepper, and other resins. It’s vivacious and slightly spicy while not being fresh per se, but the mix of spicy, sweet, and resinous elements, all while not being too heavy, is very interesting. It’s priced in the higher echelon of the Tom Ford Private Blend, currently $350 for 50ml, and is available directly from the Tom Ford website as well as department stores like Neiman Marcus, Nordstrom, and Macy’s. Overall it seems to perform well but I’m not so amazed but it that I feel the inclination to buy a bottle, but perhaps just a larger decant to enjoy sometimes. Still, I could this being a major hit with many, as it sorts of works at the intersection of an amber and a fresh spicy men’s fragrance, all while coming off pretty unisex, semi-sweet, and versatile. 7 out of 10

Tom Ford, the brand that launches perfumes faster than we have time to chronicle them... A real collection !!!! A brand that, historically, release perfumes like a baker takes breads out of the oven. Okay, let's get straight into the heart of the matter as usual. I had already been somewhat disappointed by the latest creations of the sumptuous, wonderful, iconic and cult Private Blend collection. Bitter Peach and its super sweet scents of peach candy... Tubéreuse Nue and its Ylang Ylang/Monoï imprint undeniably reminding me of a shower gel from Yves Rocher... And now, here we go again with this Soleil Brûlant. Finally... Soleil Brûlant only "burning" in the name. This new 2021 scent gave me the impression of sniffing spicy vegetable soup... Rather interesting on paper, the olfactory pyramid is described as containing pink pepper, bergamot, tangerine, honey, resin, amber, vetiver, leather, etc etc... My first impression was quite... Spicy. Pink pepper in the lead, maybe a little too much... As for the bergamot, tangerine, honey and amber, i only detect a tiny ounce of tangerine in the background, and when i say in the background, it's really well stashed. For the rest, it's pretty boring... It stays spicy for a while. To once again give you a realistic idea of Soleil Brûlant, imagine a mix of cloves, turmeric and celery. Yea Yea !! Strange you say to me for a fragrance containing as only spice, pink pepper... To give you even more the olfactory idea of ​​the fragrance, think of this soup on a winter evening and these vegetables that you have previously cut and that you are about to lock up in your pressure cooker to make it boil it all. Add a big and nice pinch of ground clove, a cup of turmeric, 20 stalks of celery at least, a light, i mean light drop of tangerine essential oil, sprinkle the whole thing with a little leather coupled with vetiver, and you will get more or less the recipe of that Soleil Brûlant. The positive point is all the same a beautiful drying, more suited to summer than winter, because it must be remembered, in my humble opinion, Soleil Brûlant is NOT a summer scent. (Or else only outdoors) Unless you like to smell the spices by 104°... In terms of longevity and sillage, it's... Average to moderate. So i ask myself the following question: Of TOM FORD's latest creations, this one is unfinished, incomplete, disappointing for a collection like Private Blend and its legendary fragrances. The bottle, as shiny as a gold bar, would be worth its exorbitant price on its own. As for the content, that will be up to you. On the other hand, lovers of called "solar" perfumes will be delighted. Soleil Brûlant remains a scent that is difficult to describe, but from the first sniffs, it will be enough for you to form an opinion. I know almost all of the Private Blend in its entirety, and apart from a few fragrances like TF London (the only one that really makes me sick because it's too spicy and smelling of cat piss), Vanille Fatale (one more too sickening and heady) ), Soleil Brûlant and its "vegetable soup" side, the entire Private Blend is class embodied in all its splendor. So, Soleil Brûlant is therefore not a fragrance that will proudly stand in my collection. Very sincerely, i think that TF is moving away little by little, and more and more, from its original creations which made its success. The sumptuous and iconic creations of Noir de Noir, Oud Minérale, Oud Wood, Tobacco Vanille, Plum Japonais, Shanghai Lily, Vert d'Encens to name just a few of them, in comparison with this Soleil Brûlant, we are at light years... It remains to be seen whether the next creations will be in the continuity of those of 2020/2021... Too sweet, too much this, too much that, i think it will be a good future debate. So please, Uncle Tom, a return to the origins will be necessary. Conclusion: It's up to you, but for almost $300, that's expensive for a bunch of vegetables... For the skeptics, NO, Soleil Brûlant has NOTHING to do with Soleil Blanc, even less with Eau de Soleil Blanc, and nothing at all with Soleil Neige. For fans fanatics of TF fragrances of which i am a part, and more particularly of the Private Blend, try it. For me, it's a No. For those in need of vitamins, will you take a bowl of soup? My rating: 6/10

Note to myself: double-check the notes on Parfumo before assuming I've picked an innocent scent to try on. So... I'm now trying the three Tom Ford travel size set I picked up at Winners Homesense a few months ago. Thought I had stored them in alphabetical order so when I picked this one up, I thought I had Soleil Blanc Eau de Parfum in hand. A mistake was made here. Strong and overwhelming pink pepper assaulted my nose immediately. Pink pepper that smelled like spicy pencil shavings. Definitely not my thing. Like FAR from it. Then, there's the animalic leather that also came up. Within the first few seconds, I knew it was a no-go to me. I'm just not someone who loves spicy and leathery fragrances and the opening was an in-your-face kind of moment that definitely did not change my mind about my taste in leather fragrances. The beginning was also way too masculine-leaning. After about 30 minutes, the strong peppery smell subsides a little bit, giving way to the powdery orange blossom accompanied by a subtle, faint, dark and sweet note (probably from the black honey). Smells almost like charred leather with a hint of spices and florals. Still not my kind of vibe. The drydown is a bit less "screaming" and a little more palatable. It smells like the sun-warmed leather interior of a brand new luxury car where a man's spicy cologne and a woman's floral perfume still linger in the air. Moves towards a warm, leathery, woody and resinous accord. Settles into a masculine fragrance. In the heart of the afternoon, when the smell was less pungent, I could smell a warm, ambery, almost vanillic accord with leather in the background, quite reminiscent of "Vanilla Royale Sugar Patchouli | Kayali". This is LOUD. The beginning is... something. The ride is both horrifying and intriguing. All in all, it's definitely not something I want in my collection (got rid of the travel size after the first few minutes of trying the perfume). This fragrance hasn't changed my mind about scents that feature heavy doses of leather, woods and spices. This trio will always lean masculine to me. As for this perfume specifically, I would never want a bottle in my collection. Not for the faint of heart.

«Love is a burning thing And it makes a fiery ring Bound by wild desire I fell into a ring of fire» Benzoin: thank you for existing. for me you are a guarantee, and here you make yourself heard and make this tuberose different, warm, fiery. I bought it in the middle of July, as a blind buy because all the fragrances that have the sun in their name deserve to be in my collection. I was reckless because it's not a perfume that everyone can like but it worked for me. It is a tuberose that dares, which goes beyond the nocturnal tuberose, beyond the carnal tuberose, beyond the green tuberose. This is fiery and crackles on you thanks to the amber and benzoin. extremely feminine and alluring. the sandal gives a perfect sillage that stays on for hours and hours. high performance

Some from my generation or even from previous ones may still remember that iconic scene in Loriot's first feature film Ödipussi, in which Paul Winkelmann, owner of a decoration and interior design store, and Dr.

No, sorry, the part about the foot comes later. It may be due to the brand, the name of the fragrance, the scent itself, or a combination of all (who is free from associative marketing manipulations): Soleil Brûlant immediately presents itself to me as a sun fragrance and catapults me to Saint Tropez.

I am surprised by the previous partly miserable reviews, especially in the statements? - that do not do this fragrance justice.
