It seems to depend extremely on skin chemistry and does not unfold well for many? (I don't smell anything medicinal, synthetic, or burnt old tires, for example) It probably polarizes mainly due to high expectations because of the high price.

I received my sample of Soleil Brûlant yesterday. I was really looking forward to this new Tom Ford, as all the other new Private Blend perfumes were too floral, too feminine, or smelled like iced tea (Bitter Peach). Soleil Brûlant is certainly better than the other new Tom Fords, but unfortunately, it is also not really special or unique.

Well, what can I say, I like Tom Ford fragrances. Unfortunately. Because the pricing and longevity often leave much to be desired. That's why I only own Lost Cherry and Black Orchid as full bottles and a few others that I rotate as samples or decants. Soleil Brûlant then.

Alright, so late last year I rode over a speed bump near my house just a tad too fast thus causing my water pump to shift and leak. Gratefully my car was still under warranty and was able to get it replaced for free (hurray!!). Fast forward to today I spray 4 spritz’s of Halfeti Cedar on and leave out the door to my car. I had been careful over the past few months to be cautious of the speed bump near my house since the incident, but today I got distracted and once more went over the same speed bump a tad too fast. Surly I thought “yep, I’ve done it again.” But preceded to my destination anyway. On my way I was getting wafts of a sweet aroma that resembled maple syrup or a candied like treat; at this point I was sure I shifted the water pump yet again. I get to my destination and the person that greets me says “Wow, you smell like antifreeze.” I quickly sniffed the crease of my arm only to realize on the whole drive I was smelling Halfeti Cedar. The good news is my car wasn’t leaking antifreeze. #trueStory

Wow , I did not expect this punch from the opening . When I first sprayed on my hand , its like Boom , like all listed notes were fighting each other to win the TOP , Great great opening . Mainly , Its a cedar based Fragrance but Its sweet , lt's little fruity and load of spices . Excellent projection & longevity , just 01 spray filled up the room . Its really a superb release from this Brand . Just one problem and its lack of versatility . Its strictly for winter and spring ( Under 20 degree temperature ) .

Halfeti Cedar is one of the best mass-appealing boozy-woody scents in my opinion. It opens with a sharp rum note, and the strong woody cedar is apparent immediately as well. Smooth peach sweetness rounds the scent out and the spicy cardamom, saffron, and cinnamon provide lift. The basic spine is that of a fougere, but modified drastically by all the gourmand and oriental notes. Masculine yet sweet, super classy. The "Halfeti" accord comes in after the opening, but does not dominate such as in Cedar Malaki . The drydown gets more and more woody and syrupy with the fruity and boozy aspects slowly dying off, and lasts forever on skin. Works in casual or formal situations in colder weather, this one might choke someone out if it's too warm outside.

I’m in search of that perfect smell of pencil shavings. In my understanding that would be Cedarwood. How could I go wrong with this fragrance, I thought by myself. Well it might have quite a woody scent, it’s incredibly sweet and boozy. If you’ve ever smelled a glass of finished strong beer that’s been on the counter for a while, that’s what you’ll find in this bottle. It’s nice, don’t get me wrong. But please don’t wear it to the office or at school because people will think you’re an alcoholic.

I ordered decants of the entire line. I had smelled Halfeti before but wanted more wears before I committed. With the decant order, I added H. Cedar to try as it was free shipping with the add on. Love Halfeti but Cedar blew me away. Off the cap, it’s nothing special and Halfeti is superior here. But, on my skin it sings…10-12hr longevity and well over 8hrs projection. I was complimented the first day I tried this. Without prompting a lady said “Someone smells like a cedar chest, but not dry. It’s really good. Is that you?” I confessed and told her the name and she wrote it down for a Christmas gift idea. This is Christmas with the sweet notes mixed with spicy and a very creamy cedar. I think it’s more versatile than what’s listed in other reviews. I would say office safe BUT be conservative with the sprays…2 and definitely no more than 3. Think classic gentlemanly scent turned up a notch with sweat creamy cedar. Absolutely classic! Perfect for Christmas get togethers and fall-Spring day/night. Works as a date night scent as well.

Yesterday, my path led me once again to a small shop I discovered a few weeks ago, where you can find a variety of niche fragrances. My goal was actually to test Gunymede, but unfortunately, it wasn't available in the store. So, I took the opportunity to test other perfumes. One bottle particularly caught my eye: Halfeti Cedar by Penhaligon's.
This Penhaligon's has truly impressed me, as it features a fascinating combination of woody aspects and dry fruits, along with a hint of rum that sets it apart from many other woody scents.

While I find the "regular" Halfeti simply wonderful, the Halfeti Cedar unfortunately has nothing in common with the scent. In the end, I am not really impressed. The performance is also lacking. The longevity on my skin is about 8 hours with a moderate sillage - I expect a bit more in this category.

That Penhaligon's can also create good flankers was impressively proven with Halfeti Leather. I never thought it would be possible to top such a great fragrance as Halfeti, but with this leathery woody successor, they have more than succeeded. Well, I thought to myself...that’s it, the topic of Halfeti has been exhausted and settled.

The English lord enjoys it oriental. The classic Halfeti - spicy, with a sweet elegance. Almost sacred. Today we’re going out hunting. But first, the bullet briefly falls into the whisky glass before being shot into the resinous cedar at the edge of the property. Just like a peripheral phenomenon: longevity and sillage.

I can’t get enough. It’s become my go-to spring/summer scent. Bright, MUCH sweeter than I’d usually go for, but I love it. Candy-like cherry, but also a bit of cherry blossom? And a zing of ginger. There is definitely a soapy element but that’s why I love it for the summer heat! I don’t really get the pepper and the sandalwood is very much in the background. It’s not the most complex, but it is a beautiful and unique fresh cherry in a world of cherry/almond/vanilla (which I also love, don’t get me wrong). Layers beautifully with Tobacco Vanille for a similar feel to Lost Cherry in the fall. Currently layering with Une Pistache for the summer, which accentuates that soapy/nutty undertone. Would love to try layering with a clean citrus. Reminds me of falling in love, it’s heady yet youthful. Doesn’t last all day, however.

I don’t smell any cherry in this at all. I was curious to try this after seeing some people state this was better than Lost Cherry, which I love. Well this has nothing on Lost Cherry whatsoever. My partner instantly said this smelt like washing up liquid, and I have to agree! It absolutely does. It’s soapy as hell. Just awful! It smells like it should be a Maison Margiela scent named “At The Car Wash” because that is this scent.

I'm into cherry right now, and while I've found a lost cherry dupe that I love, I wanted to see what the buzz was about around Electric Cherry and so I purchased a sample. I was not expecting such an expensive fragrance to basically smell like fake cherry on top of soapy dishwater. When a previous commenter says it smells like washing up liquid, they're not kidding; this is so evocative of dish soap. It doesn't smell expensive, it smells like something I might have purchased in a sampler set at TJMaxx for $7.99 -- it's like there needed to be something else to round out the cherry. It feels unfinished, rushed. The soapiness lessened into the drydown, when the scent just became cherry, but I have to be honest, this was weak. I'm not even sure layering can save it due to the soapiness, maybe with a sweet floral to tone down the dishwater scent.

This is the name of a relatively popular reality TV show that has been produced by MTV since the late 2010s, serving as a successor to the legendary Jersey Shore at the time. While you could observe Italian-American individuals with a refreshingly simple mindset during their mating rituals there - the New Yorker commented back then, 'one could hardly resist the feeling of being an anthropologist, secretly observing a new indigenous tribe through a gap in the trees' - the spin-off moves the action to the US Gulf Coast, shortening the artful combination of the states Florida and Alabama to 'Floribama'. The concept is identical. The very different broad Southern accent, compared to the Mid Atlantic idiom, adds a new component to the theme, yet the actions and rituals remain the same as those in the coastal strip known in the USA as the 'Redneck Riviera'. Plenty of alcohol meets zigzagging chicken crap meets large-scale, not always expertly executed tattoos - and there you have it. And even if the principle 'the self-perceived non-underclass observes the underclass and shouts: Hey, look - the trash!' can still withstand many repetitions, one gets the feeling here: 'Seen it before. Boring.' Seen it before. Boring. While I secretly acknowledged Tom Ford for his chutzpah with Lost Cherry, confidently placing a perfume with rather 'ordinary' attributes in the Private Blend league - because he can! - I do notice here: even the concept cannot be repeated indefinitely. Once was funny, once was cool. The second and third time, a cheap fragrance is simply just a cheap fragrance. And when, in the early 2010s, one was still reasonably entertained by the confidently displayed lack of refinement in the first Jersey Shore, the little sidekick "Southern Accent" is no longer enough ten years later. Lost Cherry, which somehow balances between 'classy' and 'trashy', was no longer a risk as a fragrance. At the latest since Guerlain's La Petite Robe Noire and its offshoots, the cherry accord, including all its more or less subtle connotations, has become indispensable in the perfume mainstream. Lost Cherry was thus already a freeloader, albeit a charming one, one that could be allowed for the Tom Ford brand. Another one is simply too much of a new emperor's dress, even for a die-hard disciple of his oeuvre like me, who fundamentally doesn't care about the so-called price-performance ratio in perfumes. However, Electric Cherry as a fragrance is not even outrageously bad. Those who like light, frivolous girl scents might find it appealing: cherry and sugar and jasmine - sexy and cheeky, all clear? What is outrageous is that here - and one cannot really blame the merchant Tom Ford for this, as it worked with the blue summer scents - a second-rate idea is reproduced in a second-rate manner, which already required a considerable amount of goodwill to pass as somewhat 'classy' the first time around. Electric Cherry does not oscillate between trash and class. Electric Cherry simply smells - sorry - thin and cheap. Conclusion: my first critique of a Tom Ford Private Blend. I'm really sorry, Tom. And I hope you are too.

* I want to emphasize once again, there will be some people who will love this immensely, and that's fine, but it's absolutely not for me... * Hello everyone, I've mentioned it here and there, years ago, 10 or 15 years ago, I was a real big supporter of the brand because of the fragrances. They were different, new directions, very creative, and had edges and certain character... and today? Even humbler bottles (completely), dizzying prices, and modest scents that perform little to not at all and smell cheap... if it weren't for the utopian price tag, one could still forgive the scent for smelling like a cheap synthetic drugstore fragrance, but like this... What do we have here: Something synthetic, kitschy, cherry-like, with a bit of jasmine and not really much more. Performance: One would assume that if one primarily works on a synthetic basis, certain performance would be achieved, like with "DUA", but it almost seems as if that part was forgotten... Not even with Molecule 01 does one achieve a truly noticeable INCREASE. When I read the name, I have certain expectations..., but when I see everything that came after Lost Cherry Eau de Parfum ... And here it’s the same...! My "sincere, friendly, and pleading" advice to you, save your money and DO NOT buy this fragrance, it’s wasted money, unfortunately... And now have a nice day/evening or whenever you read this review, best regards, Benny _______

I really think this scent is fantastic! It smells deliciously of cherries and is not as heavy and dark as Lost Cherry, but rather refreshing. I would wear it in any season! Unfortunately, it’s not cheap. But that’s something you expect from Tom Ford :) So anyone who likes fresh/fruity fragrances will enjoy it.. regardless of gender.

And once again it shows - tastes are very different. The vast majority finds Lost Cherry good or even better, and I can't confirm that at all. Something about Lost Cherry bothers me, but that's not what we're talking about. As many have already written: yes, the price-performance ratio is honestly not in proportion, neither in terms of longevity nor sillage - okay.

As excited as I was about the predecessor "Lost Cherry," I am just as disappointed with Electric Cherry. The longevity is very weak, and the scent itself is nothing special. It smells good, but very generic. It brings back memories of various Escada fragrances. For me, the price of this perfume is not justified by the scent and longevity.

Following the great success of Lost Cherry from 2018, two more fragrance creations focusing on cherry joined Tom Ford's portfolio in 2023. Electric Cherry presents itself as fruity-sweet with slight spicy nuances. The sour cherry is at the center. Beautifully soft and harmoniously composed with a pleasant hint of jasmine.

I really love the scent a lot. Lost Cherry is too cough syrup-like for me and Cherry Smoke is nice but also heavy. This one, on the other hand, is light, fruity, and clean, and so wonderfully uncomplicated. I would love to bathe in it. I can understand that some might find it too basic, especially considering the price.

To me, this is one of Penhaligon's very best offerings. A delightfully spicy opening, with distinctive cinnamon and cardamom notes. The eucalyptus is surprising here, but it works to lighten the spices in a very interesting manner. The incense appears quite early. You won't have to wait until the base for this note. It insinuates itself into the spices from the very start. The heart is a rose and jasmine accord, still spiked with incense. The woody drydown is deliciously complex, with the incense still holding the compostion together.

I love hot, spicy fragrances, particularly those along the lines of Givenchy's Xeryus Rouge with its fiery chilli notes and its raw sexuality. Elixir opens a little similar to Xeryus Rouge with a fiery burst of spices, however it soon settles, like a fire that's beginning to burn out. It had the potential to be a smoking hot fragrance, yet it has left me slightly underwhelmed, which is a massive shame. It's too light and polite on the skin for my tastes. During the opening notes, I can smell the cinnamon, cardamom and what appears to be hot peppers. The scent rapidly cools down into a pleasant, subtly spiced floral with a slightly soapy quality. The fragrance chops and changes, one minute it's spicy the next it's soft and flowery. The drydown shows some signs of the scent heating up again, but it never seems to reach boiling point. Rich woods and resins tend to dominate in the drydown, with the incense and vanilla being barely detectable to my nose. I guess I'm still on the hunt for something similar to Xeryus Rouge for women. For those not expecting a hot fragrance for passionate wear, Elixir would most likely pass as an interesting, soft and wearable spicy oriental, yet for me this just couldn't make the mark.

Expectation is a really weird thing. I thougth that the lid of ELIXIR should be covered with bandage because a serious danger was locked up in the bottle. I was wrong. If Penhaligon's would have a fragrance, only one with the same name as the perfume house has, ELIXIR would deserve the name. It is so typical from them! My first impression is a season: autumn, or even winter. Chestnut forest, woods, balms, warm yellow-red-brown leaves on the ground. It took more than one hour till I torn myself away from the picture of roasted chestnuts and arrived to the heaven of nutmeg. The whole composition is ruled by nutmeg seed, a very pleasant and comforting scent. My soul is satisfied and preparing for winter. Longevity - at first I also had problem with it, but I have got only a sample vial without sprayer(and longing for a full bottle).

First of all, a heartfelt hello. After a long period of silent participation, I have decided to end this in favor of a somewhat less silent one. One reason is the urgent desire to try my hand at commenting. Another is to strengthen the Swabian Parfumo faction :) I have consciously chosen to dedicate my first comment to Penhaligon's Elixir. The reason why should become clear in the following lines. I am by no means a professional when it comes to sniffing out individual ingredients, and I am quite glad that there are already extremely informative comments on this fragrance. I would like to start with a brief definition of terms. The study of aesthetics (from ancient Greek aisthesis "perception") deals scientifically with everything that can be perceived through the human senses. Optics, acoustics, gustatory, haptic, and of course olfactory. The evaluation plays no role here, contrary to colloquial usage; aesthetics does not decide between "beautiful" and "ugly." This evaluation is the concern of a subfield of aesthetics. Kallistik (from ancient Greek kallista "very beautiful") deals with beauty in the field of aesthetics, which is characterized by laws and harmony according to the theory. But is proportion, symmetry, and harmony really equivalent to beauty? Every day, we unconsciously perceive so many things that we do not consciously notice because they are so normal and ordinary, almost boring. Only when something stands out do we become aware of it. Initially, we are disturbed by it, analyze it roughly at first, but through this, we gain the time to engage with it. Elixir unites the cool incense and the warm rose, two unequal partners that enter into a fascinating symbiosis together. The contrast runs through the entire scent progression. The fresh but subtle eucalyptus and cardamom transition to the incense through the heart, while the orange blossom soon introduces the rose (dark purple), which later fades out slightly vanillic. This slowly pulsating dance of hot and cold in the sillage takes place on a stage of subtle, dark wood and lasts throughout the entire day. It is precisely the unusual that exudes an incredible fascination; the otherness defines the uniqueness. How beautiful can a small scar be on perfect female skin, how captivating two differently colored eyes can be. How interesting can the traces of decades of use on an old herringbone parquet be, how successful an orchestral interpretation of drinking songs (cf. Orff's Carmina Burana), how refreshing the combination of sharp mustard and sweet figs. And yes, how enchanting can a fragrance of incense and roses be. The disharmonious can also be so beautiful because it stays much more in memory, as associations are created and memories are linked. On our floor, unlikely childlike primal forces have shattered Lego bricks, leaving deep grooves and dents, yet it would never occur to me to have them sanded down. And - well, this little scar, I love it anew every time. This fragrance was a gift from a good friend who said it would fit me perfectly, as I too have two sides. Outwardly always a bit cool, distant, politely formal, but also romantic and passionate. This may be a Swabian trait to be somewhat reserved outwardly, but I have absolutely discovered Elixir for myself, and it has become my - possibly somewhat unusual - signature scent. Even though I would spontaneously place the fragrance in the colder and darker seasons, that does not prevent me from enjoying it in summer as well. Moreover, I see Elixir as authentic for almost any occasion. The bottle is, apart from the label, known from other Penhaligon's fragrances, but to be honest, I don't care at all. Penhaligon's could deliver Elixir in a cognac barrel or a milk bucket (then I would have more of it), and it would not detract from the quality of the fragrance. Experience teaches that beauty is hidden everywhere, sometimes more, sometimes less; sometimes more obvious, sometimes less obvious. Therefore, paradoxically, contrary to scientific opinion, aesthetics in its entirety actually deals with the "beautiful" and thus renders Kallistik, which so misdefines the concept of beauty, superfluous. Best regards, your Murderbee

Whoever declares the interpretation in the nave to be finished may have sniffed the actual point of this macabre creation. For Elixir hardly stylizes the guilt-ridden attendance of Sunday mass, but rather a kind of church visit that even non-believers are converted to murmuring the Our Father. Roses on rosewood, enveloped by heavy incense in an environment of damp earth - one cannot lead the common burial ritual to the olfactory organs more aptly. During the dissection of this fragrance, I honestly let out several sighs. At the top, a sharp eucalyptus also skims over the festive darkness, as if one had consulted the embalmer a bit too late. I wouldn't actually want to punish such courage for the morbid with depressing percentage deductions, but as the owner of this cryptic masterpiece, one must indeed lead a life that constantly drowns out the church bells.

The modestly chaste world of the 80s was thrown a little out of balance when a certain Maggie Cleary fell in love with the priest Ralph de Bricassart - during prime time and thus in front of everyone!

Elixir - is already a telling name. What could be in it, one wonders? What is it against or for, this elixir? An elixir is actually an extract of preserved medicinal plants. But medically, this creation from Penhaligon's does not smell like that. Here, abysses open up for me that I never thought possible.

I was browsing at TK-Maxx again and found a true gem. To be precise, one of the beautiful Penhaligon's fragrances in the lovely "medicine bottle" with a ball stopper. "Elixir". I had previously researched some Penhaligon's on Parfumo and made a note of them. And when I saw the ONLY box available there, it reminded me, and I bought the perfume "blind".

At Elixier, we are finally talking about truly beautiful Catholic incense. So here’s an incense scent that deserves the name. As if incense alone wouldn’t already be a bit overwhelming, it also gets an extra boost of eucalyptus in the top notes, making the whole thing piercingly ethereal.

Lalique’s take on spicy-woody is quite successful, I must say. It gets well-deserved high ratings across the boards. Equus opens extremely bright and crisp with juniper and zesty citrus. It is instantly recognizable and immediately sets a comfortable mood. Classy, timeless - some might say 'mature' - and still informal. The spicy-woody character is there from the start. The woods here are super dry. Some refer to a horse stall, but I don’t get that. There's nothing funky or barnyard here. This is crisp and clean to me. Dry wood fibers. About the spice.. It doesn't come across 'culinary', although there's loads of nutmeg and mace. It scores seriously high on the scoville scale. The scent does not develop much. The opening notes fade a bit and then it stays comfortably in this dry spicy-woody area with a subtle resin in the background. At all times, the sillage is moderate. Longevity just so-so. All in all a lovely creative composition. Great value for money.

This mesmerizer caused me to follow a strange man onto an elevator and stand in the doors, asking what he was wearing. Understanding me fully, he answered quite seriously but all I heard was "Lalique Pour Homme" before I stepped back and let him get on his way. Bad manners, yes, but there are worse things—like never finding out what this was! I panicked when I discovered that Lalique Pour Homme comes in versions: Lion, Horse (Equus), Deer (Le Faune), also Cristal which includes Panther, Bouddha and Athletes. Off I went to the nearest Lalique counter, to no avail except narrowing it down to this and the one above (Lion) because they weren't in stock. I ordered them both from an online discounter and, voila! The elevator man was wearing the intoxicant, Equus. It has Juniper, mainly. Also cardamom and citrus zest in the top. Violet leaf, Mace (mace? oh, the seasoning) and Sequoia wood in the heart. When I put the test strip to my nose, I didn't want to interrupt smelling to take it down and do a skin test. On paper, my nose loved it as much as faves of this group: Pour Monsieur and Heritage. Okay, skin test. Yum to the max. I love this fresh, appealingly bracing scent. My nose does twitch a tiny tad, eventually, so there may be an aromachemical in there, but not enough to close a nose like so many new ones do.

A very original Juniper+Nutmeg combination. But I feel like the smell of Malaysian halal food restaurants. Just only some hints are shared with Spicebomb and Bvlgari MIB. The three are actually quite different. Equus is essentially a type of chef fragrance. Anyway I have both EDP and EDT. Performance doesn't seem to make much difference. EDP pours more nutmeg and mace, and EDT seamlessly connects from citrus to vetiver-woody notes. But really not a big difference. Both are great value for about $ 25. It's best for a day off at home. Equus is a domestic and caring husband, and a father holding his two years old child in his arms and cooking in the kitchen. It's not useful at all for outdoor or official events. Unless you're a novice, it's not good for business also. Wear it only on weekends to fool your wife that you did some houseworks. * The engraved bottle is really artistic.

Scentrack: Jakatta – The Other World In my opinion Lalique is one of the most underappreciated fragrance houses. Lalique always delivers well-composed imaginative creations for a good price. Just to mention Encre Noire, Hommage a l’Homme, Hommage a l’Homme Voyageur, Perles, Amethyst, Ombre Noire... Yes, performance is sometimes subpar, but no one could deny their timeless beauty and sophistication. Equus is the typical story of Lalique fragrance. Launched too early, nicely polished, reminiscent of a classic era and completely under the radar. It opens with a certain Asian citrus touch that almost immediately transforms in spice cabinet nutmeg and cardamom. This introduction is rounded by juniper with gin qualities and just a hint of green violet leaf. Then gradually morphs in woody phase characterized by the guitar rosewood, subtle vetiver and musk. In the base there is also a touch of gentle powder. The most impressive is the connection between the name and the composition. From the first smell Equus transported me way back in the past, directly in the circus. Although it is clean, polite and well groomed, underneath the surface is a funky animal hidden note, probably by the usage of some woods. Equus is very natural smelling composition. Relaxing as a walk through a peaceful forest on a sunny day. The sun is muted by ancient trees, but still bright enough to enjoy the walk. A composition that came out too early. Later this theme will be relaunched in a denser way inside Spicebomb and Bvlgari Man in Black. It has some qualities of radiant Perles, but still, it is not its male counterpart. A beautiful woodsy fougere that confirms my theory that 2000s were the most creative years for perfumes.

I am totally in love with and impressed by this fragrance. A gentleman's scent. With extreme longevity. I'm surprised it has a longevity rating of 7.1 when really this easily lasts at least 14 hours I received this as a gift and didn't expect much but boy was I wrong. I will definitely be buying another bottle for myself soon.

Very nice, rather fresh spicy-woody aromatic. Very versatile and unoffending. Good longevity but unfortunately sillage is way below average - it becomes a skin scent very quickly. Certainly not something I would expect from Lalique. Because of a poor projection it has rather no chance to impress other people, but scent-wise it deffinitly has the potential.

I ordered this fragrance because the reviews and scent pyramid were exceptionally good. When I first sprayed the fragrance, feelings of peace, sweetness, beauty, and simplicity arose. The scent is truly very pleasant. The bottle is beautiful, an absolute feast for the eyes, wonderfully reflecting the feelings that come up with the fragrance.

Equus pour Homme was a blind buy for me, so to speak, the filler to save on shipping costs. Like almost all Lalique fragrances, it can be found online at a very reasonable price, while in many perfumeries, Lalique is not even on the shelves. I was curious as a cat about the first - and let me say upfront, last test, due to the very good rating of currently 8.5.

"Here it feels cool and 'Nordic'!".. I thought to myself during the first sniff. Green, fresh, needly, coniferous. Swedish? Canadian? Siberian? Partly! But there is also something that seems to rise from the cool depths and "powders" with spice. Finely milled and slightly "sharp" at first smell, warm and gentle as it develops. Wonderful transformable contrasts with flair!

Never smelled it and yet vague memories. Dried hay in the shed? The sun-warmed wooden bench under an old tree? I’m not exactly sure what this scent wants to remind me of so melancholically. However, I can tell you how I perceive it or what image it paints for me: In front of me stands a small, rather unremarkable wooden cabinet. I open the door.

tested this year at the Printemps Boulevard Haussmann store in Paris. I had heard a lot about this perfume which was one of the last releases of the brand, the bottle being very pretty, my expectations were quite high, I was really hoping to find a nugget. after having smelled it, I can clearly tell you that it is a thick and totally unisex gourmet perfume. quite happy because it reminds me of lolita lempicka in the masculine, a perfume which was discontinued and which had been successful when I was in high school, so we really have the liquorice notes which stand out a lot. and on the other side a little disappointed because it is more expensive than the lolita lempicka even if the bottle is prettier. it also bears a lot of resemblance to bdk gris carnel which I believe contains licorice too. perfect for winter and for a mixed audience between 16 and 40 years old. in my humble opinion. Hope this review was helpful to you

I expected this to be sweeter based on other reviews here and elsewhere online. On my (female) skin, it's quite dry and spicy with only a hint of sweet balsams. Immediately remided me of vintage Opium. Mostly an aromatic and smoky incense bomb. Love the addition of kitchen herbs -- anise, fennel, even a black tea. Lends a bright and bitter vegetal aspect to this thick cloud of burning incense. Very definitely myrrh here--slightly medicinal and ashy. One word: exotic. I can see Petra in my minds' eye (which I first learned about from Indiana Jones; some world traveler I am!) and I am suddenly stung a little by blowing desert sands. This is Penhaligon's, after all, so there is this constant restraint (as always with the English house) and Petra never goes (or even tries to go) fully wild or primal. A semi-sterile exoticism, if you will. Will happily wear this as a woman, though likely not to work. It calls for warm, outside air.

I absolutely love this. Legacy is an absolute treasure for serious lovers of licorice and myrrh. Legacy of Petra smells like tea leaves, syrupy dates, fennel and bitter sweet licorice root. Benzoin and myrrh swirl together, producing the scents of incense smoke and sun baked desert stone. The dry down is delicately sweet and herbal, underscored with the powdery mineral smell of desert caves. This lovely mystical journey lasts for about 4-5 hours, only leaving my skin after 6 with a soft, sweetly scented sigh.

Once there was a man who loved to crack his whip He preferred to do this in exotic places, especially in front of many people He always made people scream, and everyone wanted to reach for him He was dressed in leather, but surely didn’t smell like cedar ... Alright, the rhyme may not be the best, but you naughty ones are probably thinking of something indecent, aren’t you? Of course, I’m talking about leather, whips, and screaming… But this is about… Indiana Jones!!! Ha! You didn’t see that coming, did you? But how did I get to him? Come on, you know I’m into things like Star Wars, Batman, and Indiana Jones! What else should I think of when the term “Petra” appears in the fragrance name? And the scent is from a collection called “Trade Route Collection”? Petra here is not a woman’s name, but this ancient rock city in Jordan, where according to the film, the 700-year-old knight awaits you with the Holy Grail :D You don’t believe it? Recently, a tomb was actually discovered in Petra, where they even unearthed a chalice that looks extremely similar to the one from the film! Well? WELL? If that’s not a reason to watch “Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade” right now, he he :D Anyway, the Trade Route Collection, from which I’m currently describing the scent Legacy of Petra, was inspired by the goods from the Silk Road that were primarily traded in the London docks. According to the manufacturer’s description, the rock city Petra is about rocks and mountains warmed by the rising sun. Oh, and sadly, Indiana Jones is not mentioned even once… *sigh* :DD But let’s get to the scent! The Scent: The scent starts sweetly spicy with a gentle and soft background. You can distinctly smell fennel, dark sweet licorice, and myrrh. In the background, I detect rosy-floral notes; could that be rockrose? Honestly, I don’t even know what rockroses are or how they smell :D A little later, the scent remains spicy and sweet, softened by the resins. Additionally, I get a tea-like scent, specifically tea spiced with fennel, like some acquaintances of mine here do with black tea. This scent is quite faint, but you can smell it when you’re very close to the skin. The sweet notes smell like amber; perhaps that’s this “Belambre,” if it has anything to do with amber. The licorice gradually becomes weaker and is replaced by resinous and sweeter notes. In the end, the scent mainly smells sweetly of resinous notes, but especially of vanilla. That’s okay, but I find the finish a bit less spectacular, as it smells nice but like many other vanilla fragrances. The Sillage and Longevity: The projection is good, but not as strong as one might think. Nevertheless, you will be noticed easily. The longevity is easily 10 hours, but for a large part of that time, you mainly smell myrrh and vanilla. The Bottle: The bottle is cylindrical and filled with an amber-colored fragrance liquid. On the front, there’s a beautiful label that shows a pattern in the style of a mosaic. As always, you can see the brand name and fragrance name on the label. The cap consists of a cylinder at the bottom and a sphere at the top. Unlike most Penhaligon’s fragrances, this time the cap doesn’t have a ribbon; instead, a cord is wrapped around it, ending in a tassel. That’s nice too, but personally, I prefer the ribbons. Still, all in all, a beautiful bottle. Conclusion: Hmm, okay, so I’m not exactly sure whether this collection was inspired more by the ancient places or by the goods from those places, but with Petra as the inspiration, I expected some rocky or at least mineral notes. Well, even if those scent notes are not present, the fragrance is by no means a disappointment, as it smells quite nice with its spicy-resinous and sweet notes, provided you like this scent direction. Seasonally, the scent clearly belongs to autumn and winter. It may not start heavy, but the end could feel overwhelming on warmer days, especially with excessive application. Otherwise, I think it could be used both during the day and for going out, even though it’s certainly not a party scent. The scent is not a must-have for me… although… the name includes “Petra,” and that always makes me think of Indiana Jones… oh no… I’d rather get the golden idol from the first film and maybe the Sankara stones from the second film, he he… phew… what one spends money on, besides you probably have no idea what I’m talking about, right?… :DD Well, that’s it for today. I wish you all a lovely evening, see you later :)

So there we were. The big day had come. My girlfriend and I boarded the train to Brussels. After a night and some astonishment that Brussels isn’t as beautiful as others claim, we took the Eurostar to the island. I was determined to buy a niche fragrance that would remind me of this vacation forever, so after checking in at the hotel, we headed straight to Harrods. Countless amazing scents and brands caught my eye (and nose), but nothing really stood out yet. A few days later - by now we were engaged - we went to a small department store and suddenly I discovered Penhaligon's. The advertisement for Legacy of Petra was plastered on large posters in the windows. So we went inside and first enjoyed the atmosphere a bit. Small shop and few customers. The salesperson was very nice, and when I asked which scents are typically English, he showed us a handful of fragrances. null of them really convinced me. Then I looked again at the posters and cardboard displays and hmm, what is that scent? Tested and instantly in love. My arm was adorned with the fragrance, and we went back to the hotel. The next day we wanted to go back to the shop, and then the shock... it was his day off.. I had already given up hope because we were leaving London the next day and heading to Brighton. I thought if I don’t buy the fragrance on the island, I definitely won’t buy it back home. Luckily, there was also a small Penhaligon's shop in Brighton. So we went back into the store and tested it again... Yes, this is it. Every time I smell this fragrance with that delicious licorice, my thoughts immediately travel back to that wonderful vacation. The longevity is really great for me. My girlfriend can still smell it on me the next day. I think it lasts over 10 hours. Price-wise, it’s definitely not cheap, but that way I don’t smell it on every second person I pass in the city.

I couldn't help but grin right from the first spray; it smells niche, surprisingly very niche in the initial burst even for Penhaligon's, which tends to be relatively conservative and balanced in their compositions. But bam, there's a direct hit of licorice and fennel right from the start.

There are some fragrances where you just know they are perfect for you. Legacy of Petra is such a fragrance for me. Tested in London, at Penhaligon's, Covent Garden, found to be good - only to discover that it was sold out. Often, the object of desire then falls into oblivion. Not so here.

Shanghai Lily... This is exactly we expect from a TF fragrance. A devastating beauty, an absolute masterpiece, an olfactory jewel, no more, no less. How happy im to own a full bottle of this wonderful nectar !! After sniffing the juice for the first time, i literally fell on my knees... I was left speechless !! I couldn't help but sniff the back of my hand over and over... That's the old TF that we love, one of those unfortunately discontinued fragrances that gave all the charm to the fabulous Private Blend Collection. Amber, spicy, floral, sweet, addictive, warm, powdery, chic, sexy, mysterious, smoky, suave, languorous, hot... Words fail me... It's as if Noir de Noir and Plum Japonais had merged. A kind of a thousand old and sweet spices, bouquets of flowers that have reached perfect maturity, coupled with a mystical incense, all forming a magical threesome !! You almost feel even more beautiful, more confident when you wearing this perfume. Rather strong in the opening, and with a moderate/powerful sillage, almost eternal longevity and absolutely divine drying, it will therefore be completely useless to spray yourself with it excessively. From my personal opinion, this perfume represents the perfect balance between seductive mystery and pure innocence. A real olfactory cocktail, i also really appreciate this vintage, mature, almost old-fashioned side in the good sense of the word. For me, both masculine and feminine, it will be perfect for the cold months, but not really recommended in summer. One and only regret however, his discontinuity :( Conclusion: Shanghai Lily, to be reserved only for REAL perfume lovers. So only wear this gem on rare occasions. My note: No need to mention it, it's a 2x5 out of 10 So even for 10 000 bucks, you won't get my bottle of Shanghai Lily :)

Shanghai Lily is amazingly well blended, so well blended in fact that its almost hard to pick out individual notes. On my skin it opened woody and spicy and then quickly developed into a muddled, thick, rich, floralized spiced incense. The scent is interesting and distinctive, full bodied but not actually lush since the spicy elements balance and dry the floral elements. Many in the community have said it smells like YSL's Opium. I can see where they are coming from. I can't say that I think it actually smells like Opium myself, but it does remind me of it a bit. Though SL is complex, spicy and incensey, it is much more subdued. Opium relies heavily on spice and incense where this is more balanced between spice, floral, wood and incense. The underlying creamy florals change the timbre of the fragrance from Opium's throaty purr to something just as pleasant but a bit higher on the register. I can see SL's potential as a unique but accessible signature scent for a particularly fashionable and polished person.

Study abroad semester. USA. The first time I visited the States and the first time I lived in such a multicultural haven as my dorm, where there were so many different nationalities that no one cared where you came from and everyone was just human. No one asked where you were from, what kind of accent that was, but rather, “what are your dreams?”, “which places on this planet have you traveled to?”, “what do you want to achieve and accomplish in life?”. An ambitious and at the same time totally human atmosphere. And that was Lily. Lily, the exchange student from Shanghai. Right on the first day, she caught my eye and sparked my interest. Her skin was so pure, smooth, like porcelain with a slight tan. Her eyes, large and dark, her long, straight, deep black hair flowed over her shoulders as if it were silk. The hosts, the students who lived there and helped us exchange students settle in during our semester, organized a first shopping trip to the nearest Walmart on the first evening. There we gathered our supplies, and I kept trying to get closer to Lily. She didn’t make it easy for me, as she was wandering around in the unmistakable women’s sections while I struggled to pretend there was something I needed. Again and again, I caught a pleasant and unique scent from her, so I quickly found her again when I walked down the neighboring aisles to gather my things. But soon I also noticed the numerous rivals who had the same intentions as I did. One of them clearly had her attention, Alejo, a spirited Ecuadorian who stood out from the group because he carried his guitar everywhere to strum on it. On the way back, she sat next to him on the bus, and a mix of jealousy, disappointment, and despair left me simmering with a lump in my throat throughout the ride. During the trip, I tried to cheer myself up; there were still so many other pretty girls sitting with us on the bus. The Irish and British girls were dressed quite revealingly and made it clear how they wanted to spend their study abroad semester. It would have been so easy, but my head wouldn’t allow it. They were sexy and pretty, but too easy to get, and besides, they smelled like crap - compared to Lily. The first week passed, there was a lot of partying, kisses were exchanged here and there with the easy girls, my roommate was a square, went to bed at exactly 10 PM, and wouldn’t let me bring any girls to our room. So I spent more time in the girls’ section of our dorm than with the guys. Lily was still present in my mind, and every time I saw her with Alejo, a bit of jealousy boiled up, but that feeling gradually subsided. I avoided getting too close to her because I knew it would only bring me down. But then in the second week, it became unavoidable. We were out partying again, and on the way back from the club to the dorm, I got into the same shuttle as Lily and Alejo, along with a few others from our group. Alejo sat at the front, directing the shuttle driver, and Lily took a seat next to me. Slightly tipsy, she laid her legs across my lap and leaned back against the door. The heat rose to my head, my hands rested on her legs, and I didn’t know what better to do with them than to stroke her. Alejo kept looking back, concerned, asking Lily if she was okay. Slightly annoyed, she let him know that everything was fine. At some point, she leaned forward and whispered in my ear “Schrein.” I asked her what she meant by that. “Pig” was the answer. “Aaah, you mean Schwein…”, I replied. Yes, that was the word she meant, and she nibbled on my earlobe. Goosebumps spread all over me, and I probably sounded like a complete idiot as I started to chuckle nervously. When I finally managed to stop the ridiculous chuckling and began to ignore Alejo’s disapproving look, I turned my head to Lily. The moment I wanted to ask her what she was doing, she kissed me. Explosion. In my head, in my chest, in my pants. Alejo no longer existed at that moment, and everyone else seemed not to care about what was happening. With our arrival at the dorm, my senses returned; until then, it had been a whirlwind of passion in which I was trapped, like a dream that lasted forever. Alejo flung the door open, offered Lily his hand, and escorted her out. To this day, I don’t know how much he saw; it felt to me as if he hadn’t seen the kiss at all, but realistically, that borders on impossibility. Again, only a hint of Shanghai Lily remained in my nose. She always wore it; it was her signature scent, her identifying mark, her personal fragrance brand. The next day, I ran into her in the communal kitchen. I asked her if she remembered yesterday. Her smile, the lowered gaze, and silence revealed to me that what had happened was real and not a drunken accident. Her cheeks turned slightly red, and I knew that if I didn’t show her what that moment meant to me, I would never play a bigger role than a brief, passionate moment in her life. I stroked her cheeks with both thumbs, tilted her head up, and kissed her like I had never kissed a woman before. She tasted good, she smelled good, like an aphrodisiac that released powers; I grabbed her by the waist and lifted her onto the table. If there hadn’t been others in the room, I don’t know if I would have known any boundaries. My semester became turbulent because of that. I wanted to spend every free minute with Lily; unfortunately, that wasn’t 100% mutual. She still spent time with Alejo. Alejo and I had become something like friends. We actually liked each other; I found his style cool and it impressed me. Likewise, he liked my easygoing and open-minded nature. We accepted that Lily was a free spirit and didn’t want to settle down. We also had flings with other girls when she left us hanging. When I look back on that time today, I miss it like nothing else. It was the best time of my life. Lily is now married and has a child. Her husband looks a lot like me… me and not Alejo. Sometimes, no, actually quite often, I think that I should have just tried and asked her if she wanted to be my girlfriend. I’m sure I would have married her one day. All that remains for me now is this scent from Tom Ford. Now I’ve told a long story, but the information about how I actually learned about Shanghai Lily is still missing. At first, I didn’t know that Lily wore a perfume and thought it was her own body scent that simply smelled fantastic. Because she tasted good too, I attributed it to her body chemistry.

The Tom Ford fragrances from the 'Atelier d'Orient' series, which arrived two weeks ago, were eagerly waiting at the House of Beauty, not far from Steffel, for their chance to touch my skin and be explored nasally. I already knew them from a quick test on a strip, which is why my primary interest was initially in Plum Japonais and Rive d'Ambre. Hm...yes. Plum reminds me of Noir de Noir, a bit of TV, but mostly of Powidl:-) Rive comes across very friendly, a bit sweet like mandarin, but not for long, then Amber arrives, that gray amber which already shows me in the scent Versilia Vintage-Ambra Aurea where my limit is:) I'm an amber softie, the one that's too sweet, the gray one is too strict. And that’s why I want to emphasize again, such a test only on paper usually leads to error. Shanghai Lily, the name appealed to me, it has a cheeky quality :-) I was curious, wondering what would come my way, how the courtesan (if that’s what it is) would present herself to me. Is she as charismatic, mysterious, dramatic, and seductive as Marlene in Sternberg's film? She comes across spicy, sprinkled with cloves, fruity and well-peppered, loud and very very interesting her top note shows itself to me. Orange/clove, there is no significant transition into the heart note, it quickly moves forward, bright floral. Honey-sweet jasmine (nothing indolic far and wide), tuberose (you have to like it too;) and of course rose, which I don’t find so blonde, it is a dark, velvety/heavy, bloomed, dew-drenched and sugar-dipped, a wicked representative of its kind. Fruity sweetness gives our heroine a certain youthful/happy cheerfulness, lightening the heaviness a bit, and the rising incense prevents a slide into too floral. The flowers are well embedded in this oriental floral. A little smoky, somewhat melancholic, styrax does its calming duty, benzoin, milky - soft and heavy with vanilla sweetness is the base. A hint of castoreum may be in the base, but it doesn’t affect me at all. Kashmir wood/Cashmeran works particularly well with lush-sweet flowers and cedar, I love this full soft musky note:-) In the drydown, a light vetiver note joins cedar/incense and gives this caressing, sweet, very feminine scent a dry - bitter touch, something crackly. So the lily remains sexy, enticing, lascivious for a good 6 hours now, a hint of played tristesse paired with elegance lingers in the air and yet also something light, casually cheerful. I found the sillage very filling in the first stretch, not just me ;D A tendency towards kitsch, to loud 80s orientals like Opium is certainly not a mistake but rather a prerequisite. A similarity to Nu 2001 cannot be denied:) I also have the feeling, when I take my nose off my wrist, that I catch a whiff of Teint de Neige... A very close, full, multi-layered Tom Ford, and yet I find the series considerably lighter to wear (also younger) than other scents from the Blend Collection. The four have a certain relaxed charm, don’t take themselves too seriously and despite the apparent theatricality, there’s a wink. An absolutely feminine scent, clearly intended only for us women;) I’m still unsure whether I see Lily dancing under a disco ball to Falco's young Romans rather than in the thirties.... http://tinyurl.com/o3g6nrl http://tinyurl.com/psvv2q9 ….. still considering:-) Kitsch as Kitsch can! And a little about Cashmeran: http://tinyurl.com/og69ak3

Sometimes you encounter astonishing beauty in unexpected, truly completely unexpected places. The reasons for this are convoluted and of little interest to the uninvolved reader, but just recently I found myself on a website featuring collector Barbies that were explicitly intended for adults, not children. That there are Barbies of Scarlett O'Hara and Holly Golightly hardly surprised me - I found the Chancellor (our) much more surprising - especially since her face and body are those of a completely normal Barbie. She just has shorter hair and a (surprise!) pantsuit, but if she weren't standing next to a black-red-gold flag at a podium, hardly anyone would recognize her. However, I found the relatively new 'Haunted Beauty' edition truly magnificent - dark, eerie dolls with serious, sometimes sinister faces. My undisputed favorite in the collection is the Zombie Bride Barbie. Her complexion and hair are pale gray, she has demonic blue eyes and cracked, blood-red yet empty lips, and she wears a yellowed lace wedding dress that is soiled and torn at the hem from all the wandering - and dirty white shoes. In her hair, she has three gray roses and in her hand, a pale pink bridal bouquet - as if she is still wandering in search of her lost groom. She is the coolest Barbie I have ever seen - and beautiful. I lead in so circuitously because the metaphor 'Zombie Bride' may seem unflattering at first glance for a fragrance - and 'bloodless', 'undead', and 'apocalyptic' are hardly attributes a perfumer desires. Yet it fits remarkably well with Tom Ford's Shanghai Lily, which is highly dramatic and dark - and in its over-processed density and opulence, simultaneously beautiful. It has a darkly flickering floral quality that is both alluring and untouchable (jasmine and tuberose, both squadrons among floral aromas) and profoundly flickering. These are the bittersweet clove and burnt resins that do not constrict its playful floral nature but give it a resonating body and a kind of silent echo. There is nothing undead, let alone apocalyptic about Shanghai Lily (and in my nose, nothing Chinese either), yet its aloofness and surreal beauty remind one of the pallid bride in the soiled white dress, as she stumbles through a nocturnal park landscape with empty eyes. The Ford-immanent endurance and strength of its floral character are fascinating and relentless, bordering on obsession. If you love it, it is like a staggering moth before a pale moon, whose gaze follows until the night devours it. However, if you feel alienated by the accord of heavy flowers and burnt resin, it is like a gray doll bride with dull eyes, who steelily constricts the throat until breath is stifled. Conclusion: just another manic Tom Ford Private Blend.

Basically: My 1st, 2nd, and 3rd impression of Ford's "Shanghai Lily" are positive. The fragrance stands out stylistically from many others - even in the niche sector - in a pleasantly distinctive way and has a very unique DNA.

While Kilian, Byredo, and all the others still have to prove themselves to me and I haven't quite fallen for their marketing and hype, no one can tell me that in Tom Ford's now vast selection of perfumes there aren't a few absolute masterpieces that hopefully stand the test of time.

So, first comment, please be lenient, and here we go: Shanghai Lily was a blind buy. I dared to try it despite all my concerns, as I do like quite a few TF fragrances. I generally appreciate the character of the house and its scents. As soon as the fragrance was there and I tore it out of the packaging, the first spray... and immediately a bit of disappointment.

Unfortunately, you have been banished from the Private Blend by Tom Ford, even though I believe this is one of the best Tom Fords. Let's start with the longevity and sillage: In terms of sillage, TF SL shows good performance; it’s not a sillage monster, but the scent does make its presence known in a subtle way.

With Shanghai, I associate a truly massive, breathtaking metropolis. A place of contrasts between maglev trains and ancient traditions, between soothing gardens and exciting buildings, between small, quaint markets and gigantic shopping temples. Nowhere else can one spend money quite like in Shanghai. Whether it's snacks to eat or clothes for going out...

My first impression of Encre Noire Pour Elle: To my nose this perfume consists of approximately 40% rose, 30% musk, 20% vetiver and 10% other things. It has a 'serious' rose, but not a funeral rose, that is smoothed by pleasant musky notes. The smoothness reminds me of the smooth base in Jour d'Hermès and Voyage. The musky notes make it more feminine, but a guy can wear this fragrance. Perhaps the best reason to read these reviews is to find out more about the vetiver. It is not like Guerlain's or Tom Ford's. But I smell the vetiver from Encre Noire Pour Homme, a relatively warm vetiver. Encre Noire Pour Elle has this vetiver in moderate-to-small amounts. In the heart, a fruity osmanthus peeks out a little, making the composition more interesting. Summarized: Take, for example, one of the musky rose scents from Narciso Rodriguez. Well, Encre Noire Pour Elle is the more interesting, prettier sister of the Rodriguez perfume. Looking for a rose? Try this one.

If I were to give Encre Noire pour Elle a Sanchez/Turin-style two-word fly-by, it would be boozy detergent. Despite the apt but snipey sounding description, there are aspects of ENpE that I appreciate and like. Categorically it’s a musky, woody floral---an enormous field. In spite of the common pedigree, though, it’s clever. The various floral elements (rose, osmanthus, freesia) come together to strike one metallic note. The wood is cedar, and I suppose is a nod to the cedar-like vetiver of the original Encre Noire, but I don’t in fact smell vetiver. The musk sews it up. This is not a luscious, round, fruity or animalic musk. Not soft, not cuddly. It is glaringly bright, a bit harsh and utterly desiccates the florals. The dewy, fruity aspects of rose and osmanthus, and the delicate sweetness of freesia are obliterated by the musk. When magnified by the musk, the flowers become a floral eau de vie, giving that double-distilled, blanched feel. A few points. 1) Unlike the original, ENpE does smell like ink. 2) Noire? This is so bright I see spots. 3) To make the first in a line a masculine but without a gender descriptor in the title is fine. Then to use the name of the original, adding “pour Elle” the same way one would add “light,” “fraiche,” or “sport" makes it a flanker. My issue, though, is that by extension, a woman is presented as a flanker to the universal-since-unnamed man. This boy/girl thing is only interesting if there is a twist---imagine the Rochas flanker Femme pour Lui.

This is an absolute chiaroscuro masterpiece of scent. It brings to mind the whole of Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, or Rembrandt’s1667 painting “The Jewish Bride,” or Gerrit van Honthorst’s 1625 painting “The Matchmaker,” as it blooms on my skin. On my skin, it is a magnificently balanced, opulent renaissance symphony in rose. The brilliant liquid gold citrus lights of bergamot, ambrette, and freesia swirl smoothly onto a lavish heart of an incredibly beautiful rose. A touch of spicy osmanthus, kephalis, and heliotrope continue to smoothly shade this deeply rich colored composition, blending the contrasting light and shadow into a seamless masterpiece, finally descending into a mysterious, tenderly subtle darkness of cedar, vetiver, and musk. It’s fascinating to note that the top of the chiaro effect is perfectly illustrated by the elegantly fanciful gold decorative script used to label the bottle as contrasted with the base scuro effect of the simple, spare blackness of the bottle. Many have been obsessed and commenting on the blackness of the glass bottle, criticizing that the juice inside as being not dark enough. Well I say it’s dark enough. Frankly it’s an example of shadowy dark perfection in a bottle. Not too dark. Not wallowing blindly in a vulgar miasma of overdone patchouli, excessive spices, woods, or animalic substances. On my skin this translates as inky black, velvet shadows with a few slender threads of golden light swirling throughout. Ultrafeminine, deeply rosey, woody, and rich with an elegant shot of musk. No overdone sickening sweetness. No overdone masculinity in the woodiness. Just a perfectly balanced contrast between darkness and light. Beautifully balanced for me. I have to admit, my skin picks up base notes, amplifies them, and tends to overwhelm with them. The base notes that give this scent it’s “shadow” are very prominent with my chemistry. I feel lucky…. And I love this one. If your skin is like mine, and cannot stand overly ripe tuberose, tropical tanning oil like gardenia, indolic jasmine, too much patchouli, too dark a musk, heavy handed civet or castoreum, or too much gourmand sweetness, this may work wonderfully for you. This is a deeply subtle and luxuriously complex scent. She never screams, there is no need. She smiles gently, caresses, then speaks softly, staying close to the skin. Although it is a dangerous smile...sometimes. It brings to mind the sober, iron hand of a bejeweled, voluptuous Medici queen swathed in a crimson velvet glove. Truly, a masterpiece. Gloria in excelsis Christine Nagel. Bravo Lalique.

Although I do not believe that Lalique ENCRE NOIRE POUR ELLE is a bad fragrance, I also do not find it all that memorable. Part of the disappointment may derive from what I regard as the house's mistake of naming this creation as a flanker to the male version, ENCRE NOIRE, which does have a unique personality and develops through very distinct stages (whether one happens to like them or not...). In contrast, POUR ELLE seems a bit vague and linear, yet another somewhat thin, lightly woody floriental among hundreds. I find this composition wearable but inoffensive to the point of being forgettable. While the original ENCRE NOIRE prominently features Iso Super E, the female version is said to contain Kephalis, a synthetic molecule whose acquaintance I have not made elsewhere (at least to my knowledge...). I wish that this composition contained more ambrette, which I do not detect at all. Instead, this seems to me like a somewhat generic, ever-so-slightly soapy (in the drydown) lightly woody rose. Even the formerly beautiful bottle of the original ENCRE NOIRE has been marred by the over-the-top wedding invitation script used on this flanker. Kind of a sad metaphor on Adam's rib: an afterthought.

Encre Noire Pour Elle is not Black Ink. Instead, it's a boozy vetiver rose. ENPE opens quite soapy to my nose but doesn't stay there, but the soap comes back well into the wear. In the heart, ENPE reveals a rose in the heart which strikes a balance between classic and modern. The base is woody with a touch of musk. Although I like this fragrance ALOT, there is something synthetic that I just can't shake off. I've been doing side-by-side tests lately, and ENPE is failing against other fragrances which seem smoother and more natural. As I pare down my collection, ENPE is not going to make the cut, I'm sad to say. The bottle -- reminiscent of an ink well -- is unusual, chunky, & substantial. It's perfect for storing and maintaining a fragrance, although I'm not sure of why this references ink, other than it's an Encre Noire flanker, as Shera suggests. I purchased a manufacturer's tester ... it was perfect, included the top, but came in a generic box. For the price I paid, it's worth seeking these out on evilbay. Overall, Encre Noire is a well-balanced, close-wearing, soft feminine fragrance. It smells like a high-quality fragrance as well. I highly recommend this one for sampling by rose lovers, if not blind buying. Those who like SJP Lovely and Narciso Rodriguez for Her will likely like ENPE as well.

This a nice old fashioned rose scent. The rose oil kind, it's a little bit sour in the beginning, but not for too long. Very natural rose oil note, a warm wraparound. Beware, rose oil and rose flower are different. This is the first. The base is musky and cedar, powdery. The fragrance is old-fashioned in a good way, lady like.

No, this is definitely not NOIRE, this is BLANC, WEISS, WHITE, BIANCO, BLANCO, BLEEK, BRANCO, BAI. And beautiful. Attention, all fans of clean/fresh laundry/just showered scents, please come here immediately. Encre Noire pour Elle is a clean scent at a very high level. Very bright and clear, clean and pure, soft and warm, carefree and stylish, uncomplicated and attractive.

Vetiver is one of the most interestingly scented ingredients that a perfume can offer. I know and appreciate the dark and pure vetiver scent Encre Noire, intended for men, also as a woman very much, because it is free of any decorative frills, and I enjoy wearing it in autumn and winter.

Basically, I can agree with all the positive comments. I see Fiona’s girl becoming a lady, I recognize the elegance, the beauty of this perfume, but I have thought for quite a while about what bothers me nonetheless, or rather, what I lack to want Encre Noire.

In 2009: "Hello, marketing department here! Encre Noire is doing well, let's make one for women!" "What? Ideas are running low..." "Oh, never mind, anything with roses always works!" When I first asked about "Encre Noire" what feels like an eternity ago (OK, about 5 years), I was sold this one despite my repeated assurances that I really wanted to test the men's version.

Even the word. Dandy. It evokes an image of this well-dressed man who wears a suit every day. Even on his days off. Even when taking a hike in the woods. With his leather shoes and his blazer. Does this perfume fit that man? I’m not sure because I’m the exact opposite and I love how fresh and fruity The Dandy is. There’s a note of whiskey listed. I don’t know much about spirits but doing some research I’d say that it’s more of a brandy. Brandy is more fruit-forward and that’s exactly what The Dandy is. But The Dandy containing brandy.. that sounds weird right? Anyway! The Dandy is a beautiful soury fruity cocktail that dries down ever so slightly into the beautiful woody base. Does it project? Not really. Doesn’t last not too long either. Say a couple of hours max, turns into a skinscent after that and stays that way right through the day.

Spray this on! Go on! All the pulse points, and a few extra areas too, let the aroma infuse the air around you. Go on! Spray yourself with Penhaligon’s The Dandy, transport yourself to the Jazz Age. Good gravy this could be a great scent, I would recommend it to the type of person who wants to give off an air of sophistication. With a dash of ennui The brief for this scent must of been, a fancifully dressed aesthete, replete in a beautiful suit dazzling shirt adorned with carefully selected accessories. And it hit the brief to the note. I can just imagine plump raspberries floating in a deep amber pool of rum? Whiskey? Whatever is all held inside an old barrel characteristically battered, beaten and old, but still robust. I can almost hear the big band striking up, the feet moving to the dance floor and champagne corks popping…. Almost, almost, almost…all of that imagery, all of those notes. Gone by the time you’ve read this, that impression a fleeing moment in time, almost fantastically insultingly fleeting Like a pixie fart.

'A dandy...' so wrote Baudelaire in his diaries '...must direct all his striving towards being sublime without cease.' The legendary George 'Beau' Brummell, who is still regarded as the archetype of the dandy, broke with the norms of his time in an unprecedented manner. He did this by refusing the usual style borrowed from the French court ceremonial on one hand, while simultaneously leading personal vanities and fashionable quirks into narcissistic excesses that have been passed down to this day, such as having the fingers and thumbs of his gloves made by different tailors. Many dandies, like Beau Brummell, were British and mingled - as he did - in the highest aristocratic circles. So who could be more suitable to create a perfume named Dandy than the house of Penhaligon's? Perhaps it is expectation management. Perhaps this is where the mistake begins. Perhaps it is my fault. How do I envision a scent called The Dandy? Stately in nature, yet tumultuous. Classic, but a bit provocative. Distinctively masculine and yet androgynous. Gardenia - the quintessential attribute of the dandy - with leather, for example. If necessary - if the accord weren't so far off - rose with oud. Hyacinth with peat, violet on a fougère foundation - all possible and all splendid! Instead - and the disappointment drips between the lines as I write this - Penhaligon's opted for the seemingly easiest, most zeitgeisty, and thus not timeless answer at all. The fragrance they named Dandy is the essence of the early 2020s - top-heavy, synthetic, and interchangeable. Not provocatively foul-smelling - not even that! - but a shapeless fashion scent that will be forgotten in a few years. Conclusion: citrusy sweetness meets man cave meets synthetics. A crowd-pleasing scent that is fundamentally unexciting. And precisely for that reason, so disappointing.

The fragrance starts fresh and citrusy, with a strong raspberry that makes it fruity at the same time. 30 minutes later, the freshness has faded and the woody and slightly sweet notes take over (oak, patchouli, and whisky are dominant). Not a substitute for Kilian's Angels Share!!! But it is a very delicious scent in its own right. Addendum: The fragrance is not modern and has a classic and simply elegant character, as the bottle suggests.

... has led me to The Dandy . First of all, I really like Penhaligon's as a house. Some fragrances are already in my collection, and others have the potential to join. How about The Dandy ?! The opening, phew... The Dandy starts very earthy, dusty, almost musty. I can only perceive a hint of whiskey in combination with wood. The Dandy resembles the smell of a stage (Swabian for attic ;)) from my parents' house. So to put it briefly, a very strict, mature, and unmodern start. The boozy note is omnipresent, but rather in the background. As it develops, a light/subtle sweetness of raspberry breaks through, making the overall impression significantly more pleasant and rounded. I don't perceive too much of the synthetic notes, but they generally don't bother me in other fragrances either. In summary, one can say that The Dandy is a good release in the realm of boozy scents. Personally, I find it extremely difficult with the overly sweet, often extremely hyped boozy fragrances of modern times. This is not the case with The Dandy , but I also miss that certain something, which is why it won't become a candidate for my collection. The search for THE new boozy scent continues.

The Dandy initially has a pleasant lemon aroma, a splash of raspberry, and the well-known refreshing bergamot. However, the woods are already pushing forward from behind, so the citrus notes are directly supported by the woodiness, and you can definitely notice that in the nose.

London, Covent Garden. For the first time, I can try fragrances from Penhaligon's. And in an ambiance that couldn't be more fitting. After a few attempts, I am offered "The Dandy" - and I hesitate, because I am personally not a "Dandy" at all. But what the heck - it's just a name. I really like the presentation.

Right after spraying, it’s super exciting and interesting. The wood is very well rounded at the beginning by the sweet raspberry and a bit of citrus. After 2-3 hours, only the wood notes are actually dominant. I associate this scent with whiskey barrels or older gentlemen smoking a cigar in a cozy pub. For me, it's definitely more for the sophisticated gentlemen among you.

Do you remember controversial and provocative ad for YSL M7 featuring nude guy? I'm sure this is the fragrance that guy would wear. Masculinity bottled, refined, smooth, and unfortunately fleeting. You have best 2-3 hours of your life, but after that, it will become only memory. For me this is very linear fragrance, which is good because it is great from the start.

One of the top offerings, if not the best from Tom Ford line including private blends, don't be misguided by testing it on blotter paper or on your wrist for an hour or two, give it a full day wearing , feel the quality and count the compliments. Its a classy woody, a lil sweet(fruity) / spicy fragrance with an earthy feel which is very nicely done and the blending is awesome.

For me it smells like a men's version of Black Orchid - or Black Orchid for men. Not very unique and not extreme also. Longevity is average, around 6 hours in my skin. Projection and sillage are medium. It's a good fragrance, but if you expect something heavy and dark you'll get disappointed. I smell a nice plum note in the middle of its development. The drydown is great and there is the moment that remembers me of Black Orchid. Updated January 2014

The first time I smelled this fragrance,i fell in love !! The fragrance of TF EXTREME comes from an artistic vision and a modernist thinking that eventually captures the courage of the heart of every lover of the fragrance... A stylish and luxurious fragrance like a groom wearing Tom Ford's tailor-made suit And he knows well that all looks are towards him!

For the ridiculous amount of ingredients, TF Extreme is an incredibly rich and well blended frag that somehow pulls it all together. This one easily lasts 8-10 hours as well. I’m not a fan of iris or violet, but this one has just the right amount of powder in the heart to compliment the sweetness from the fig and richness from the truffle. I can dig it. Unfortunately discontinued, Extreme for Men is a really brilliant composition of a masculine fragrance that covers all the bases - rich, dark, smooth, boozy sweetness, and leather. 4.5 stars

I discovered this perfume in 2017 at Sephora Lyon. it's a good perfume for autumn and for nightfall.masculine.it's a rather atypical spicy fresh scent that can surprise and please as much as the opposite, so I advise you to test it before buying. its hold is incredible, it stayed on my suit for 3 days and on my skin for 30 hours despite a shower.

Tom Ford for men Extreme checks all the boxes for perfume lovers male signature scent - unique, undeniably masculine, exudes authority without aggression, mass appealing, non-intrusive. Projection gets intimate after 2-3h but then lasts for at least 8 more hours. I imagine a man who knows what he's doing with his life.

Well, so this is the much-praised ‘Tom Ford Extreme’... I must say, it leaves me somewhat perplexed. Not that it smells bad, no: It smells good. A whole kaleidoscope of various woody, spicy, fruity, and leathery notes unfolds on my skin. Somehow, though, I have the feeling that I have smelled all of this before.

Oh yes, this is something good. I clearly prefer the Extreme version to the very average fragrance Tom Ford for Men. What I smell first is an interesting gin-like note that immediately takes on the quality of old, moldy paper. You have to sniff it right away; it could even have a certain addictive potential.

Bonnie Tyler sang hoarsely at the beginning of the 80s - in a dress and hairstyle reminiscent of Krystle Carrington and with a music video that spared no expense and truly left nothing out that was considered grand and beautiful in the visual language of that time.

It's not a particularly original scent, on the lavender theme I really like Chanel's Jersey, but this one has that caramel twist that makes it worth staying in the collection. As the name itself says, "brilliantly British", the brand faithfully tried to convey a typically British everyday scene through lavender, which is an important and one of the oldest ingredients of British perfumery, and toffee, which should evoke the British tradition of drinking tea with scones. I can't say that I have British associations with this scent, but because of that unexpected twist with caramel, it occupies a special place among lavender-themed scents.

A crystal-clear lavender. I wish it had more labdanum and musk. There are these beautiful hints of sweet notes, just barely there, that make it a total knockout. BUT, like with all good things, there’s a catch—and this one’s gonna make me cry my heart out: the poor longevity. It feels weak on my skin... I’m afraid it won’t last long. If anyone’s got it, shout out 'cause I want to know if I should get it or not... IT’S REALLY BEAUTIFUL—WIIIIIIIIISH LIST!

Uncommented Fragrances No. 161 One could take the easy route with this fragrance and refer to the strong parallels with the legendary Pour Un Homme de Caron (my signature scent). In both cases, lavender dominates, especially in the opening, but also throughout the fragrance development; both scents have a moderately powdery musk note, and in the base, since neither fragrance really has a heart, there is a sweet note that is indicated here as salted caramel. One could also say fudge. And there we have the typically British scent: (1.) Lavender: In the UK, there are large lavender farms in some regions that cultivate the herb. And there is (2.) Fudge: everywhere. While the parallels to fabulously French Caron are striking, the salted caramel note still ensures that the new Penhaligon's differs in the drydown. I still prefer my Caron because I find the vanilla note with a hint of amber in the base more refined, as that’s how the French are, always a bit more elegant than the rest of the world. However, I must say that Penhaligon's Brilliantly British was worth 9 points to me. How close fabulously French and brilliantly British are to each other, and whether the small difference might be worth a double purchase, is best decided after an intense comparison test. And one should like fudge.

You can smell it from afar - the aromatic scent of lavender. You take a deep breath, open your eyes, and let your gaze wander over the endless purple sea. Bees buzz busily around you, and as you walk through the field, the warm, pleasant wind carries even more of this soothing scent to your nose. Cheerfully, you continue, your hands brushing against the occasional flower, along the small path through the field. The path now leads you to a small bakery with its own beekeeping, whose facade is completely made of wood and gives a cozy, inviting impression. You take a seat outside on a wooden bench, and the scent of blooming lavender in the midday sun blends with the sweet baking aroma from inside. The owner warmly welcomes you and tells you that the honey she uses for baking and sweetening drinks comes from the bees that are so diligently working on the lavender. This is noticeably responsible for the aroma of this special honey. In some selected baked goods, the purple flowers are also directly incorporated. You indulge in a thorough consultation and then decide on hot milk with the aforementioned honey and a piece of buttery salt caramel lavender cake. You enjoy your break and realize that the spicy-aromatic lavender pairs excellently with sweetness. You take another deep breath and then relaxedly make your way back through the purple sea, with the taste of salted caramel in your mouth.
