However, what follows is all the more beautiful and very long-lasting; after 12 hours, I can still perceive Lavandula softly. I can't pick out the top notes and base notes, but they are surely responsible for the "lavender progression." Lavandula is going on my decant wish list for next summer, but it doesn't trigger a compelling "must-have" feeling for me.

The namesake lavender appears not only in the heart note but shines from beginning to end. An authentic lavender scent, highly recommended for fans of the plant. The composition is green, herbal, fresh, clear, and strong. It is not a dusty-dry, powdery version of the theme, but rather a very juicy one. Even tonka bean and vanilla in the base do not manage to turn this into a typical fougère. Worth mentioning is the light, but for me clearly perceptible lily of the valley note, which fits harmoniously. Men should not be deterred by this. A very successful little water, which I would not have expected from the traditional company Penhaligon's in such a "de-dusted" form. Speaking of little water, the longevity and sillage of this Eau de Parfum are excellent and have far exceeded my expectations. Still, it was probably a mistake to only purchase the 50 ml bottle, as the addictive factor is very high. Lavandula is a refreshing-herbal alternative to the classic citrus Eau de Cologne, especially in high summer temperatures. The lavender-containing Estivalia by Puig used to fulfill exactly this function for me. A true delight!

The year of creation of the fragrance from the house of Penhaligon's is well hidden behind the apothecary bottles that have been used for 130 years and the nostalgically designed labels, often featuring a curved silhouette and antique-looking color and typography. Despite this classic exterior charm, Lavandula has only been on the market for eight years. So, one does not have to labor through the gallery of royal wearers of this fragrance, as often seems to be a requirement with Penhaligon's. However, with an English fragrance named Lavandula, one might think less of royal children strolling in grand parklands and more of an older Miss Marple carrying an aromatic garden shrub into her slightly musty-smelling brick building, where it is to be processed into scent pillows. Both images and thus all lavender prejudices can be confidently set aside. This fragrance is neither romantic nor old-fashioned. Rather, Lavandula is a large, wild mixture of herbs, spices, and musk that provides great wearing pleasure, especially in spring and summer months. Lavandula starts with a surprisingly strong, almost biting green note of lavender, enriched with soft white cinnamon and a large portion of green basil with a hint of black pepper. A few moments later, the invigorating opening transforms into a warm, earthy note, carried by the gentle side of lavender, which is underscored by lily of the valley. Sage provides a successful counterbalance with its aromatic nature. In the base, warm tones of well-perceptible musk, vanilla, amber, and tonka bean come together. With Lavandula, Penhaligon's has created a multifaceted fragrance and a modern, herbaceous "oriental" interpretation of traditional perfume ingredients. In English-speaking forums, one encounters many overwhelmingly positive reviews, often accompanied by the note that the reviewer generally does not like lavender scents but is nonetheless enthusiastic about this one. I would be pleased if a few perfume lovers feel encouraged to discover this fragrance. At least those who have found pleasure in Guerlain's Aqua Allegoria Herba-Fresca should not be disappointed here. Unfortunately, the availability in Germany is not good, even though it must be quite popular in England, as the availability at almost every street corner suggests. The fact that it is an Eau de Parfum is reflected in both the price and the longevity.

And I should only show off after XD, but it would be hard to hide such a treasure. I have always wanted to see how the niche of this brand smells, but the prices have always been outrageous. Since perfumes are my passion, I am fascinated by tobacco. I made a top list on parfumo.com and was out with Cola. I even had the opportunity to test pdm Herod, which is not so popular. On my shelf stands the Cuban Aramis Tobacco Reserve, which I love, but I think it will have to make room today, because there can only be one winner. Or Intemporel 1888 Lalique is truly a fragrance worth every cent and is currently available as a tester in 4 stores for a quarter of the price. How can this beautiful bottle smell? Try rolling a cigar for at least a thousand zloty to understand how tobacco smells, which is not just a stinky cigarette. I sense juicy cherries, dry pencil cedar, and cellar patchouli. And all of this without sugar or honey. It is served half sweet, half dry based on the beautiful tolu balsam, which reminds of smoky vanilla without too much sweetness. Trust me and take the chance, Insurrection II Wild Reyane Tradition, Al Hamarain Amber Oud Tobacco Edition, Thierry Mugler Pure Havane, Burberry London, or even Tom Ford Tobacco Vanille will be set aside. Lalique has proven once again with the creation of Encre Noire that it knows what it is doing. Today's fragrance is my 600th review, so this bottle fits as an Oscar statuette.

You don't know what a steppe runner is? Well then, Google it. You don't know how a violet smells? Buy this fragrance. Previous commentators clearly do NOT know how violets smell, otherwise they would have certainly mentioned it somewhere, BUT I CAN'T FIND ANYTHING ABOUT VIOLETS FOR THE LIFE OF ME! And that, EVEN THOUGH IT'S WRITTEN RIGHT THERE IN THE FRAGRANCE PYRAMID!!! HEY! WHAT'S WRONG WITH YOU!? You usually copy everything! VIOLET. Diminutive form. Just right. Romanticized, flowery, silly violet, you. From front to back. It rolls and rolls and rolls through the perfume, so that no development is recognizable at all. THIS is EXACTLY the nonsense violet that Kormann has already "refined" with his "Steampunk," THAT is what you smell here, and it undermines all the surely well-meaning attempts of the perfumer to construct a tobacco-smoke-pepper-patchouli scent, which is such a shame because THAT is exactly what the user expects and hopes for, AND IS SURELY SUPER SOUR IF. HE. DOESN'T. GET. IT!!! Lalique, you can do better with fruits, so stick to that.

Hey,… I didn't even know that Lalique has more exclusive fragrances… well, here on Parfumo you learn something new every day… well,… provided you have a sample of a fragrance that you then search for in the database, I mean how else would you know that there are one or another fragrance if you don't know anything about it? Sure, you could go through each fragrance brand by brand, but try doing that with 80,000 fragrances! Wow, even the biggest fragrance freak (no,… I'm not talking about myself for once…!) wouldn't want to do that! But now comes the description of Noir Premier - Or Intemporel, which is quite nice but has a somewhat tobacco-heavy character (although the tobacco itself is not very intense, it is noticeable for quite a while), which is of course not bad. But anyone who likes tobacco will find even more pleasure in this fragrance. The Fragrance: I immediately smell the notes from the heart note… mainly tobacco, which surprisingly doesn't smell that bad (sometimes I actually don't like intense tobacco, but it could also be that I occasionally like the note quite well in a fragrance, like here…), as well as coffee, which quickly evaporates at first. Shortly after, you can then smell the black pepper. Additionally, a light fruity note came to me, but it wasn't bergamot… it briefly reminded me of apples,… strange. The tobacco continues to be the main note a little later and mixes well with nutmeg and the pepper, which is not overpoweringly strong but rather subtle. A little later, you can smell a noticeably earthy note with the patchouli, which fits quite well with the tobacco-based fragrance. So the fragrance lingers for a while, until after a few hours the tobacco noticeably weakens, but still remains the main note in the base. To be honest, all the other fragrance notes are hardly discernible at this point, apart from the vanilla. So in the base, alongside the tobacco, you smell a hint of sweet notes, and combined with the tobacco, this then reminds one of vanilla pipes. And in the later hours, I again had the feeling that there was an inconspicuous fruity note in the background. The Sillage and Longevity: Even though the fragrance starts off quite well, it unfortunately becomes too weak for my taste too quickly. I find that especially tobacco and vanilla often radiate a bit more intensity than is the case here. However, the fragrance lasts for fifteen, sixteen hours, which is pretty good. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular and gold-plated. What might come across as a wooden decoration in the photo is actually the patterned glass behind which you can see the fragrance liquid. In the middle, there is a simple black label with the name of the fragrance. The cap is a half-sphere, glossy black, and also has a glass pattern on the top (I think…). A very beautiful and elegant bottle. I found Or Intemporel actually quite okay, but still a bit disappointing. Disappointing only because I was hoping for a stronger and especially longer-lasting coffee, as I quite like the smell of coffee (as I said before: yes, I like coffee and not just tea. Now you just have to guess which drink… I mean beverage I prefer with milk :D). But apart from that, I found the fragrance really good, especially since it smells very pleasant in the later hours in the base. Otherwise, the fragrance has become a gentle tobacco scent, which later reminds me of pipes with vanilla tobacco flavor (at least for me). It would actually fit quite well for going out, not necessarily for partying, but for a nice dinner or sitting in a bar, etc… it could work well in any season, maybe just not on very hot summer days, but it is certainly not overwhelming, so it could also be tried in summer. Well, that's it again. Even if at first you might feel that the fragrance is not a must-have, I believe it gets better over time, making it truly worth a test.

As someone who absolutely loves myrrh based fragrances, it's not often that ones as good as Myrrhe Mystere come around. Myrrhe Mystere is an extremely dense, rich and luxurious myrrh based fragrance that is extremely well blended. While this is certainly not a mainstream fragrance profile, it's one that I think most people would find pleasant due to the sheer amount of warmth present here. This fragrance is fairly linear, relying primarily on the myrrh as a driving factor, with a bit of vanilla and woody notes in the background that give the fragrance some sweetness and spice respectively. This is a perfect example of a fragrance where a natural and synthetic ingredients are used in perfect combination to the advantage of the scent, as this relies on both elements in unison to create the accords here. I do also get some warm-spicy notes as it dries, namely some cinnamon and something that smells sort of like clove as well. It's blended extremely well with the rest of the fragrance, and it truly works for the benefit of the scent profile here. In terms of Tom Ford, I certainly think this is one of their best fragrances overall, and certainly one of my favorite myrrh based fragrances period. It's extremely well blended with fantastic performance and a very charming, warm feeling to it. If this was cheaper, it would likely becoming one of my signature scents, but for now I will save it for special occasions.

Myrrhe Mystere from Tom Ford is a scent that I really, desperately wanted to love, and in theory, with its notes of myrrh resins, sandalwood, and vanilla I feel like I should love it, I feel like it should sort of be the platonic ideal of a gothic romance novel cover art fragrance…and it is that for a few mysteriously fleeting moments. But then there arises something inexplicably off-putting about it. It is the scented equivalent of bringing to class a very special item, something incredibly dear to you, to share for the weekly round of show and tell. As you tell the story of your precious thing’s origins you become too aware of how it looks through other people’s eyes, a little weird, a bit unsettling, maybe it exudes an underlying strange and vaguely unpleasant smell of cumin’s unwashed gym clothes’ B.O. pungency that has been masked with an herbaceous bouquet of anisette and mothballs from crinkled cough drop wrappers at the bottom of your handbag. You realize that maybe people aren’t as excited about your collection of teeth and bones and taxidermy as you’d initially hoped. You go back to your earlier comparison or metaphor or whatever and realize your gothic romance heroine is written with more human flaws and foibles than you prefer and in fact she reminds you an awful lot of yourself, with equal parts hideous conceit and treacherously low self-esteem, that befuddling balance of the you you’re trying to put out into the world, charming, elegant, enigmatic, and the you that you try to keep locked in a secret attic, the one who hates to wash her hair and snorts like a truffle pig when they laugh and inevitably has food stuck in their teeth or a stain on their shirt. I wanted a Myrrhe Mystere representative of the gorgeous, doomed figures in those marvelously illustrated midnight tales of passion and madness–so that I could feel a bit of that beautiful gloom myself– and what I got was a mirror reflecting the glum reality of all of the ways I am none of that at all.

I would hate to be the perfumer having to release a new Tom Ford Private Blend right now. People cannot stop comparing it to 'the Tom Ford that used to be', in reality comparing it to a nostalgia colored memory of falling in love with Tom Ford's perfumery in general. How could anything new live up to all that? That being said, back to the perfume: This is a wonderful original release. A fairly linear but nonetheless powerful accord of high quality myrrh, sandalwood en just enough vanilla. A skilled combination of synthetic and natural ingredients. It is warm, inviting and indeed mysterious. I recently added it to my collection and I have been wearing it pretty much daily. I think many have been overlooking this perfume, it has a high concentration of sandalwood which needs some time to settle. Don't be too quick to write this one off as an unoriginal and people pleasing flanker of Ébène Fumé. You will be missing out. 9/10

Tested at printemps shop last week,i was worry to discover it cause i disliked myrrhe imperial of armani private. But i have a lot of fragrances tom ford and i need discover it. In fact this totally different,it s, warming ,oriental with a scent of aa sweet bakkhour ,it reminds me mitzah dior private and black afghano . Its a good fragrance for winter little more feminine ,but already smelled with alternative less expensive. So i will not buy this one

I really, really wished I liked this. It's a warm, deep, dark resinous scent that settles thickly in the air. There's light spice throughout its lifespan—not an airy, fresh spice but a heavy spice that isn’t as prominent. It's the faintest bit sweet, enough to stop it from feeling dry and chalky, and overall pretty good. Trying it on tester paper gave this effect but trying it on skin really amped it up. Objectively good fragrance, and when I had this fragrance on one arm and Noir Extreme Parfum on the other, I favored Myrrhe Mystère. The only problem I have is that, on my skin, it's too bitter. It’s by far the most bitter myrrh I’ve smelled. It definitely faded as it dried down, but that bitter, sort of metallic tanginess completely ruined everything else for me. It wasn't even necessarily strong, just very off-putting. Myrrh is just a very finicky note to my nose, no matter how much I wish otherwise. However, disregarding skin chemistry, this is a very well-made fragrance, and I’d recommend it to any myrrh enjoyer.

The end of the story was that I was doubled over with laughter over a fancy glass display case, thinking it was about to collapse. The saleswomen apparently thought so too; they had gathered around me and silently disapproved of my performance. I didn’t even know one could disapprove so silently.

I sometimes miss the first generations of Tom Ford Private Blends. I miss how they were conceived and crafted - and who they were, and the stories they had to tell - which the recent products from the Tom Ford label no longer do.

Whether the scent is mysterious is debatable, but it is seductive, as myrrh plays the main role. And it is known that myrrh can stimulate the production of pheromones, our body's natural sexual attractants that shape our allure. The fragrance combines two powerful myrrh essences with a peppery opening and a hint of vanilla in the background, creating seductive eroticism.

This was my first very smoky fragrance. I find this to be a very masculine perfume and would not wear it as a woman, but tastes are fortunately different and everyone should wear what they like. The myrrh in this scent is very strong, which is definitely not for every nose. The longevity of this Tom Ford fragrance is relatively good compared to the others.

This is how Myrrhe Mystère feels. Or rather, it evokes exactly this reaction in me as well as in the people around me. Anyone who has ever been in an old church and knows how incense and myrrh smell will understand this fragrance for the most part.

The Impudent Cousin Matthew has similar characteristics to Castile, another great fragrance from Penhaligon’s. To me, Cousin Matthew is a more refined version of Castile. If Castile were a signature scent worn day to day, Cousin Matthew would be its equivalent for formal situations. It’s less soapy and a little more citrusy than Castile, though not sharp or abrasive whatsoever. Both are linear, clean fragrances that are quite appealing and pleasant. For the price, one can do better in my opinion, especially if looking for a fragrance that’s unique and “stands out”. The current price for 75ml of Cousin Matthew is $310 USD, up $15 from several months ago, while the price for 100ml of Castile has jumped $5 USD to $170 USD. If you can find them for roughly 50% off, then they’re worth it. Otherwise, keep looking.

A Cologne. Smooth. Aromatic. Flattering. High-quality. Fresh. But not spritz! Reminds me of Guerlain's Cologne du Parfumeur, Givenchy's Gentlemen Givenchy Cologne, and Acqua di Parma's Colonia. Perhaps a blend of these. Both in terms of fragrance characteristics and modernity. And with charm. Compared to the mentioned ones, however, it leans more towards the somewhat reserved, English style. The individual components are so closely intertwined that I can’t identify any clearly. There is a muted, soft citrus note (mandarin is much clearer in many fragrances), embedded in an aromatic-creamy, slightly powdery spiciness with nuances of barbershop and soap. This note strongly reminds me of Colonia, but feels a bit more modern. A very slight edge is given by a subtly green-bitter touch that really only works on a subconscious level. There is probably also something like rosemary (which would speak for the slight soapiness) included. A small dose of lavender is also conceivable. Patchouli is not recognizable to me; the tone is too little earthy and woody for that. If anything, it is a smoothed-out and very soft variant. I would rather place it towards a non-sweet, slightly powdery tonka bean. Perhaps with a splash of vetiver and probably a creamy-mossy base that blends everything together (without having a musky tone in the nose). It is possible that the slightly green-bitter, soft aromatic-creamy-soapy spiciness arises completely from the indicated petitgrain. Overall, the scent feels very rounded, soft, well-groomed, and pleasant. The high-quality ingredients do not develop even a hint of unpleasant aroma chemistry on the test strip over weeks. The fragrance remains consistently dense and compact. The longevity on the skin is unusually high for a cologne, with about 8 hours of good perceptibility. Wearable in any situation and absolutely unisex. Cologne lovers will find here a non-spritz, soft aromatic edition that moderately modernizes its classic structure. An absolute recommendation for testing. Addendum from 14.04.: The "Remix Cologne Anniversary Edition" by 4711 (tested today) is also a good reference scent. The Cologne is a bit more neroli and thus feels a touch more classic. It has a slightly floral component that is missing in Penhaligon's and feels a bit more orange-fruity. Additionally, the 4711 is quite spritz in the fruity note. Otherwise, they are very similar, although the English one lasts significantly longer and appears a bit more high-quality.

"I immediately noticed, this is a pressure pain when you press it." (Lothar Matthäus) There are truths in life that hardly lack a certain logic. This is often similar with seemingly simply constructed fragrances, like those from the Portraits series: You get what it says on the label, and you can clearly identify the individual components. "I always liked simple songs," I quoted John Lennon for "Radcliff" from the same series. This also partially applies to "Matthew," but when it comes to the logic and recognizability in the composition of the components, and especially its endurance, it somehow fails to truly convince me. It doesn't really touch me. "The problem with Matthew seems to be just a problem of place and time [...]," begins the official characterization at Penhaligon's. I would reduce the sentence to: "The problem with Matthew is time." The opening is furious. The duet of mandarin and petitgrain is delightful; here, the leaves, twigs, and unripe fruits of the bitter orange seem to be dominant, while the mandarin adds at best a hint of lemon pulp, and the whole thing feels creamy. It's British and noble and indeed a bit youthful nonchalant. Within the first hour, this initially strong citrus impression in terms of sillage turns more into a vetiver-like green. The leaves and twigs seem to take command. Far off, I believe I am hallucinating a slightly leathery hint; I attribute this to a certain similarity to "Agua Fresca Vetiver" in this phase. And then, after about two to three more hours, the boy with the duck head runs out of steam. That is truly cheeky. Wasn't there something with patch as a base? Unfortunately, not at all for me. But even if it was only used as a fixative here, it hasn't done a sustainably good job. That would all be fine and good, but not for the price. This then triggers a pressure pain every time you press the spray head.

Cousin Matthew is quite a character - but what a delightful tropical bird he is?! What a not-so-dull duck?! Okay, essentially this summery-creamy Penhaligon's is just an extended neroli accord and for many, it might seem a bit too simple for the price. But this Petitgrain parade stick came in very handy for me, as it shows that you can conjure a lot from the rather minimal and straightforward neroli/citrus direction. "Matthew" has hints of fluffy lemon cake, very gentle and pleasant. The adjective assigned to him should definitely be enjoyed with a wink. Because at its core, he is a kind of everybody's darling. That can be annoying too. But it feels completely unforced or contrived here, strikingly honest, authentic, and of high quality without limits. 4711 in elegant tweed. Cool. Easily accessible. Always within reach. Patch spreads smooth hugs, mandarin colors yellow-orange from the start. A bit overpriced. Very much so. But that doesn’t detract from the fragrance note. Bottle: incredibly beautiful, elegant duck Sillage: neroli & cream in comfort Longevity: 6-7 hours, rather less if you’re strict Conclusion: a neroli treat that is always welcome at family gatherings - no matter how outrageous it may be!

Almost everyone has him in their family: that one cousin whose exact origins are a bit of a mystery - or at least one you want to question his supposed background. Matthew is definitely a light fragrance. Clean, fresh, and perhaps a bit floral with a splash of citrus - that must be the mandarin. It reminds me of classic colognes that Dad used to apply after shaving in the early 2000s. I’m not a big fan of Matthew, not to say that it’s inherently a bad fragrance. It just doesn’t suit my taste - certainly also because I don’t understand the scent notes and can’t specifically match them to the descriptions in the fragrance pyramid. He’s just sitting at the table during a big family gathering; the relatives tell you where he’s from, but the story isn’t really convincing.

Many Lalique scents share a positive feature: they smell creative. Maybe not entirely compelling, but really unusual, quite “niche” despite the really low price and the wide availability. L’Homme Equus isn’t an exception: it is in fact a really peculiar sort of herbal-woody fragrance standing quite on its own among herbal-woody fragrances. The woody notes smell vibrant and exotic, with that sort of aromatic “African” mood of scents like Idole de Lubin or Trussardi Inside Man (and similar fragrances featuring slightly less common woody notes such as mahogany or rosewood). Bracing and really realistic, powerful “woody” in the best and most natural meaning. There’s vetiver too, but just more as a nuance of the main woody accord, which smells quite complex and colorful. I never smelled a sequoia so I don’t know about that sequoia note, but it smells really good. Then, something leathery (the only flaw here; the exact same sweet-mellow dull leather note as in CH Men by Herrera) provides some “mainstream feature” to the exotic woody base, giving it a shade of weight and “masculinity” (and dullness as I said). Now imagine this, topped with a sort of Mediterranean herbal-spicy-citrus bouquet a bit similar to Rochas Aquaman, or Lanvin Oxygene. Grassy, kind of pungent, really aromatic and again, quite exotic (juniper stands quite above the rest). Some slight resinous-fruity nuances give some warmth and sweetness. And that’s it, there is no significant evolution to my nose except a general drift towards woody-ambery tones. A woody-herbal scent with a colourful sweet vibe and a unique, decidedly “exotic” feel. Refined, totally versatile and really enjoyable. Sadly it smells also a bit thin and quite short-lasting, but it’s a fascinating piece of mainstream perfumery surely worthy a try. 7/10

Amazing fragrance! Elegant, Classy and Sophisticated. The scent is spicy- woody but is not heavy. This perfume has a well-balanced composition . The Sequoia note is dominant in this scent. It opens up with like warm spicy then dry down is musky woody. It smells so good and reminds me of walking through the forest of the Giant Sequoia trees. The art of bottle design is very wonderful. Lalique Equus is suitable for the spring ,fall and winter. I really enjoy it and I love Lalique Pour Homme EQUUS EDT. I'm so glad that I have it in my collection. TWO THUMBS UP. Rating : 9 / 10

Lalique fascinates me time and again. For an outrageously low price online, I am thrilled by almost all of their fragrances; White and Encre Noir even belong to my permanent collection. And I won't even start raving about the skillfully crafted glass bottles. Unfortunately, not everyone thinks this way; I have even read occasionally that they should stick to beautiful bottles from other brands and leave the contents to others. I really can't understand this thesis, as I consider even the often-criticized Hommage to be outstandingly beautiful, so I am also curious about its flankers. Therefore, I didn't have to think long when it came to blind-testing Equus Pour Homme. I own and tested the EdT version; unfortunately, I can't compare it to the EdP. But perhaps a fan of the fragrance can briefly comment on the differences in the responses. So where does this ride take me across the glassy landscapes of the Lalique kingdom? First, a little anecdote about the longevity or rather the surprise effect of this seemingly innocent little horse. After the fragrance started beautifully fresh, spicy, slightly sweet, and exceptionally bright-woody, it bid farewell after a few hours; my nose was blind to the entire heart note, which seems more likely than blaming the fragrance for failing at this stage. Only hours later, when I was already tinkering with new tests, I smelled a fine-sweet woodiness on my wrist. I hadn't sprayed anything new there; it had to be Equus. Sometimes it goes like this; those who are declared dead live longer. I just want to highlight again about the fragrance itself: it is just as smooth and stylish and a unity as its bottle - all the fragrance notes create a pleasant everyday buffet from which the modern man likes to choose. Few edges and corners, but also no boredom. Bottle: a heavy glass artwork Sillage: not even a slow trot. Longevity: due to the described issue, mega difficult - 3-10 hours :D A fragrance with more facets and surprises than a superficial examination reveals. I'm glad I bought it and now have time to explore. And I can do this due to its enormous versatility all year round 24/7, especially in the office. But cardamom, a whisper of leather, vetiver, and juniper berries form the foundation, that much is clear!

It took me a long time to engage with the men’s fragrances from LALIQUE. In fact, I was quite familiar with some of the wonderful women’s scents and logically fell in love early on with the beautiful bottles and the glass/quartz art of Lalique. One day, my search for a leathery scent led me to the perfumery I trust. I have some issues with leather fragrances, as they often cause me headaches and sometimes nausea. Not infrequently, especially with BULGARI Black pour Homme, these scents remind me of the smell of an empty car after long exposure to sunlight, which I don’t find very pleasant. “Are you familiar with LALIQUE?” asked the owner of the perfumery, and at that moment I could already perceive the first slightly peppery fresh note of this fantastic fragrance. I did something I never do and immediately held my wrist out for spraying, sniffing this scent for a good half hour. God, was I happy to have found this fragrance, especially since I was already quite satisfied with Dior-Homme. The scent is, like all Lalique fragrances, very clean and natural, which also applies to the ethyl alcohol used. The top note is very subtle, fresh, and somehow English. Perhaps it smells like this at the Royal Ascot Derby; English lawn, leather saddle, and Earl Grey. The spicy notes of the heart are also very pure and long-lasting. The pepper-like note probably comes from the cardamom, which, in my opinion, has been very pleasantly combined with the leather. The leather in the base is for me very soft, clean, light brown, and pleasantly warm. When enough is applied, one can smell a slightly woody-sweet scent the next day, almost a hint of caramel alongside the still-present leather. For me, the most exquisite leather scent I know (and I know a few). By the way, the fragrance is housed in a glass work of art. However, the plastic cap leaves something to be desired; I would have preferred something heavier, like with Fougere royale (Houbigand). The scent is particularly elegant and has a moderate sillage at lower doses, being fully perceived only at close range. In larger doses and with a bit more warmth, it spreads quickly and can definitely be noticed in an entire room. I love the scent.

Actually, I have my issues with some of the Lalique fragrances. Without much nose grumbling, I personally can't easily pass them. Also, the topic of horses is not so familiar to me as a city person - which doesn't mean that one hasn't had some touchpoints there or possibly out in the countryside. Nevertheless, my eye is pleased by the finely crafted horse head on the back of the glass bottle - and my nose is delighted by the pleasant contents. From the very beginning, Equus gallops in a fresh to slightly sweet direction, where the bergamot groves can only be sensed from afar, while the spicy cardamom along with juniper berries seem much more tangible. Especially the juniper somewhat transforms into distilled gin and occasionally gives the impression that one is getting a few splashes of pear schnapps around the nostrils. At least that's how it plays out on my skin; on paper, the citrus notes come across more intensely. After the long ride, it intensifies into a light, rather bright and soft wood. Gradually, citrus wafts shimmer through the air again, and I think that the citrus plant Amarys comes into play here, as a slightly bright resinous note cannot be denied. Vetiver also makes its presence known. This combination, especially in the drydown, is really different from the usual soft base note banter with amber, vanilla, and tonka bean. However, those who speculated on leather, which is indicated and would have fit thematically, unfortunately come away empty-handed. At least I didn't perceive any of that. Nevertheless, Equus is a loyal companion, a jack-of-all-trades that can impress with both elegance and robust long-distance qualities while also showcasing original features. Thus, I am somewhat reconciled with Lalique and the theme of horses!

It is the year 1674, the Thirty Years' War is nearing its end, and it will be a few more years until Charles Perrault publishes "Le petit chaperon rouge." Yet the legend has been part of the population for many generations. In these harsh times, warnings about what lurks in the deep dark forest are more prevalent than ever.
Since I was asked to be more concise, I will try a short version. It's all very nice, very subtle, very rounded, very pleasant and very boring.

Somehow, I don't particularly like the men's fragrances from Lalique. Encre Noir is somewhat acceptable, but the rest is just too dull for me personally. Equus unfortunately makes no exception. What I had suspected to be a spirited stallion turns out to be a lame nag on my skin.

The horse really has a tough time next to the lion. Equus is quite leathery and herbaceous, and I also suspect there's a drop of oud in the mix. This perfume holds its own against the lion, although the lion still has the edge for me. Longevity and projection are spot on with the Eau de Parfum. A powerful yet sensitive horse with a healthy appearance. Sammy :-)
Compared to Lalique Lion, one of my favorite fragrances, this one is fresher and less long-lasting. For me, it is slightly above average among fresh-herbal scents.

Full disclosure: I tested 4 Tom Fords last week within 2 hours. This was the first applied and I was wild for it at the beginning! Springlike magnolia breeze and just a tiny wisp of buttery gardenia, with a gentleness and never overwhelming Earl Grey note. I sensed a dull steady woody backbone, wearing a spicy ginger suit. My initial reaction was "Ummm...creamy, yet fresh...definitely Unisex, easily a 3-season signature scent...sold!" Then as I contemplated the infamous Tom Ford price tags, and let the scent open up on my arm, that cashmere and sandalwood base became louder and more insistent "Hey Girl, Can I have your number?", it began to shout. I felt that sudden sense of annoyance I have experienced with Illuminum's "Bergamot Blossom" and Lubin's "Nuit de Longchamp". null of these are bombastic, cheaply acquired, all are substantial and display masterful work...but as inexplicably as a heartfelt ballad by Michael Bolton, these three scents just get on my nerves, literally. What was happening to my 'Precious' was it a malvolent Sauron in disguise? I wondered on to test TF's "Shanghai Lily" on paper and then gave "Champaca Absolute" a second testing on my other arm. Meanwhile chatting away about fragrance with the SR and how "Neroli Portofino" is my go-to summer fragrance but I can't bare it when it is cold and grey and I am filled with bitter tears...30 minutes flew by like 10. Back to the Venetian Bergamot, now fully warm and fully developed on my arm, I went from Love to definitely not happening in the span of an hour. But you can't knock a guy for trying. The good news is that if you are looking for an effervescent splash of ginger, not unlike Origins "Ginger Essence", to chaperon a dry woody bergamot-centric main event with notes of light fresh magnolia dancing about, this will provide adequate sillage of 6-8 hours, fairly close to the skin and without compromising on quality ingredients. It's perfectly fine really, just not perfect enough for me.

This is a very well done lemon-y fragrance that plays well in cooler weather. The primary note I get is a bright citrus with some white floral notes and a nice creamy vanilla base. It reminds me of a lemon cheesecake in the best way. I don’t get a lot of development in the scent profile, but that’s just fine by me. I know others may disagree with me, but this feels like a warmer weather fragrance that can work in slightly cooler weather thanks to the creamy base. I don’t get many woody notes off it. The performance is quite good; I get a full workday out of it and projection is decent without being overbearing. Due to the price, this isn’t the easiest to recommend for blind buy, but it feels like a hidden gem compared to the rest of the Private Blend!

Its name initially evokes associations of a rich and opulent fragrance - lush and full of ripe, perhaps overripe fruits - akin to the feast at the table of a prince who is both unrestrained and immoral. Instead, however, it reminds one of another, a dark and nocturnal Venice. When you find yourself lost among the canals, when every light appears very close yet remains out of reach, when foreign voices seem to whisper an enticing song in the gurgling of the water, when the nighttime houses and the shadows between them possess a strange and surreal beauty. And then a child in a red raincoat fleetingly appears between the bridge pillars - and when you try to look, there is nothing but darkness and deceptive emptiness. 'When the Gondolas Wear Mourning' is the title of one of the most famous horror films in cinematic history from 1973, which profoundly changed its viewers' relationship with Venice (and with children in red raincoats). The city in the lagoon appears in the film as shady and abyssal, and as is not uncommon in this genre, there is something threatening in every scene, no comfort, no protection, and no safety. Tom Ford's Venetian Bergamot plays with all these associations and the same dark images. A shimmering transparent citrus blossom reveals a pale glowing gardenia between ylang-ylang and fleeting white feathery flowers, and an ambivalent, dark accord follows in its wake - patchouli seems to be present, and upon closer sniffing, it also seems to be absent. And then - equally incredulous as it is unexpected, the hint of recognition between strangely familiar woods and a velvety alluring sweetness - as if a dark, eerie voice whispered very softly from the depths: 'Beware!' Conclusion: those who appreciate dark, challenging, and abyssal fragrances should take Venetian Bergamot to heart. It is dark and pale and hauntingly beautiful.

No, I know, I usually can't rely on Tom Ford. I've had that realization for a while now. So much is inflated, so overly American, lacking the nonchalance of French or Italian fragrances, even though Mr. Ford often names his scents after regions of these countries. Here, however, I thought it might end up being something cheerful and Mediterranean. But one must probably understand the "Venetian" in the sense of Mann's "Death in Venice" or - as Löwenherz mentioned below - the "mourning gondolas." Yes, the namesake bergamot is a bad joke. Exactly - I looked at the clock - 17 seconds after spraying, a joyful citrus delight lasts, inviting, Mediterranean, summery. And then - bang!!! It's over. A unfortunately painfully intrusive floral composition of gardenia, ylang-ylang, and magnolia steps so affected and narcissistically into the foreground that it hurts. I don't mean that the scent is loud - compared to other shouty "Hi! Everything fine, guys!!!" Fords, this one is quite refined, at best a bit louder than a sunscreen. And this brings me back to my title. A sunscreen composed of these intrusive-smelling flowers, which are more suited for mourning attire than wedding arrangements, cool, somewhat dull, underlined by (unfortunately) somewhat persistent Pepperwood (TM!), weaving a milky synthetic veil underneath. No, I can't make anything of it - perhaps the ladies have a slightly different perspective on this - but I don't perceive it as unisex, rather distinctly feminine. Unfortunately, no photo of me. Really not.

The pepper-spiced opening immediately appeals to AugustA. It briefly becomes ultra-dry, then the juicy bergamot comes in, drawing the pepperiness to itself and gaining a slightly floral touch. Ylang Ylang pushes its way up from below into the top note. And gardenia. Through the Venetian mask, mysterious glances flash. The sillage occupies space like a velvet cloak thrown around the shoulders with flair. The gardenia presents itself as seriously seductive, and in combination with the radiant, zesty bergamot, it cannot become overwhelming; the overall impression remains somewhat flirtatious at first. But gradually, the scent takes on a hint of melancholy. This is definitely something for the evening or when the citrus scent can be a bit heavier. I briefly look around to see if we suddenly have heavy brocade wallpaper on the walls. Phew, no. Then the heaviness recedes, it becomes fresh and bright again, but no less expressive; one catches a hint of powder behind the mask. Soon the scent becomes calm, but it retains an underlying charm. Above the delicate woody base, a velvety floral scent lingers, and until the end, a hint of bergamot remains. A semi-dramatic composition that unfortunately becomes a bit quiet too quickly at the end; perhaps that’s for the best, as I like it this way. Especially the shimmer.

The Venetian special agent was on a secret mission for his house. He was one of the best in his field, and not just because of his code name. In professional circles, he was known as "Venetian Bergamot," which was deliberately a clever deception. While bergamot was certainly perceptible in him, it never took the lead.

at night, in summer by the stream. the wind carries warm, spicy veils over, the water bubbles and exudes a clear, cool breath from the dark grass, flower heads shine. magnolia and gardenia in duet, delicate, without heaviness. everything is calm. a deep secret lies over the scene.

So, if he were as weak in my bed, he would fly *lol* Yes, maybe that's a bit exaggerated, but sorry Tom..., he was nothing. It starts off so beautifully zesty, tangy, that you instantly feel good. Unfortunately, this only lasts 1-3 minutes. And then, with a bang, Ylang-Ylang and Magnolia come in.

I walked into my then-boss's office one day, and she was just spraying on Venetian Bergamot. I thought the scent was simply amazing! I told her she smelled good. She looked at me, handed me the bottle, and said: here, this suits you better than me anyway. And so I went home with my new signature scent. I loved the fragrance!

Tom Ford's Venetian Bergamot is an impressive fragrance that combines freshness and depth. When you wear this scent, you will experience a blend of style and energy that is ideal for various occasions. The fragrance opens with a lively and zesty hint of Italian bergamot that instantly revitalizes the senses.

This is my Penhaligon’s Belgravia Chypre Review on YouTube. Penhaligon’s Belgravia Chypre was launched along with Marylebone Wood and Kensington Amber as part of a trio of fragrances inspired by journeys on foot in London’s neighborhoods. After sampling in a store I immediately loved Belgravia Chypre and wanted to review it. But when I was researching the three fragrances Marylebone Wood seemed like the fragrance I would love over three and Belgravia Chypre was my least favorite. This means always sample your fragrances prior to blind buys. But Belgravia Chypre is a fruity, rose chypre. It's fresh but not a wimp, it's spicy but not overwhelming and it's also slightly green. I like this one and it hints at one of my favorite rose fragrances although this is fruitier and really enjoy it as an alternative to the other fragrance. If you're curious to find out more about Belgravia Chypre please watch my review on YouTube. Thank you.

...lies Belgravia, one of the three London districts to which the traditional house Penhaligon's has dedicated its latest collection, all elegant and highly coveted neighborhoods. The one named here is - after Kensington - only my second favorite among the three, but Belgravia Chypre, the fragrance being commented on here - it is the most beautiful among them. Belgravia is a residential area with stately cream-colored and white townhouses behind shiny black railings. The Eaton Square, famous from the television series named after it (in the series: 'Eaton Place'), is located here, along with many embassies, expensive galleries, and restaurants. Sloane Street has long been considered the territory of the young, party-loving high aristocracy. Belgravia Chypre pays tribute to the formal elegance of the district through its understated and distinguished character. 'Vibrant-floral' could be a fitting description, with its arrangement being modest and very refined. 'Chypre,' on the other hand, leads the overly naive perfume lover down a somewhat misleading path, because despite a classic Chypre architecture of hesperidic top notes, floral or rose heart, and oakmoss base - everything is there! - nothing about it comes across as one that could be classically called 'Chypre.' Instead, here is a restrained, subtle rose scent, lively at the outset, pale and colorful beyond the middle - cultivated-urban and far beyond English country house delight. The raspberry - like all red fruits, one of my most dreaded fragrance notes - fits wonderfully into its bright freshness, accentuated by little more than a hint of pepper, followed by a delicate pink climbing rose that sways quietly in the London June wind. Conclusion: Belgravia is a district for walking, for strolling. There is certainly more to do and experience in other neighborhoods - in Mayfair or Kensington, for example. Belgravia is a district for a cheerful afternoon under trees. Along shiny black railings. Roses. Belgravia Chypre is indeed the fragrance for that.

Rarely has a new release from Penhaligon's in recent years elicited such a unanimously positive response as Belgravia Chypre. One might even say that the great, old brand has succeeded, just eight years after the masterfully crafted Sartorial, in introducing another neo-classic of the highest quality - not a bad track record, which makes the numerous failures and zeitgeist-driven quick shots of past years seem forgivable. On the occasion of the transaction in the souk, I asked the saleswoman (one of the most well-known and knowledgeable ladies on Parfumo) about the reason for the sale. The answer was charmingly declined, my judgment should not be influenced. Understandable. All the more curious I was about what could possibly provoke such a strong reaction to this alleged super scent that a deserving perfume would be led to say "No, thank you" after 0.5 of the available 10 milliliters. After weeks of testing, I have a suspicion. However, first I must join the chorus of praise: Belgravia Chypre is remarkable. A thoroughly modern, fruity chypre that, in its top and heart notes, breathes such unmistakably old-world charm that it is a joy. And it is precisely the currently trendy raspberry note that serves as the pivot around which the fragrance effortlessly swings between the 19th and 21st centuries. Combined with the relaxed, never waxy or stuffy chypre framework (vibrantly floral, slightly woody, tartly fresh), it creates a peculiarly utopian-cheerful, well-mannered dollhouse retro-vintage constellation that strongly stimulates my imagination. The good user Loewenherz already mentioned in his review the London district of Belgravia and the way this fragrance embodies its "genius loci." I would only add that it paints a pastel-colored, almost steampunk alternative version of this district. One could enter "Belgravia house fronts" into Google Image Search and imagine a low-flying, brass-clad airship from which a friendly gentleman of indeterminate age waves casually with a twirled mustache. So far, everything sounds like at least 9.5 points, right? Indeed, and my 8.5 points are, although it sounds strange, to be understood as disappointed praise. For towards the end, or rather downward, the fragrance loses some of its magic and substance. Like so many contemporary compositions, here too, from about the midpoint of the scent's progression, a slightly sharp, synthetic smelling everyday woodiness increasingly pushes its way into the picture, which does not devalue what came before but makes its construction seem questionable and strangely hollow: Were the house walls just a facade? Were the suits and Sunday dresses from Zalando? Is the airship even hanging by nylon threads? It sounds more esoteric than it is: In retrospect, Belgravia Chypre indeed gives me the impression that everything was designed on a base intended to create a certain effect all the way into the top note. This impression noticeably unsettles me and makes me wish to commission Fabrice Pellegrin for a reformulation without budget constraints; a sort of "Belgravia Chypre - Premium Edition," so to speak. Despite all the limitations, Penhaligon's deserves praise for the courage to launch such a peculiar, yet timeless and out-of-time fragrance. And if the new series by the "Downton Abbey" creators called "Belgravia" had not just started this year: Based on the trailers, it could certainly have served as inspiration for this scent.

In great "sorrow" and silent remembrance, I had almost said goodbye to the hope for a future for true Chypres. Because so much revolves around restrictions on many ingredients in the fragrance world, even bans on those considered "particularly harmful and even toxic." This includes, not least, oakmoss and patchouli. That’s why I was all the more delighted when I uncovered this fragrance, classified as vintage, as NEW. It doesn’t come from a felt 1918 but from an actual 2018. It’s written in black and white! Now I am thoroughly sniffing, comparing, and capturing the "progress" of the fragrance on my wrist. The only thing I can ascertain is that it is damn CLASSY. And this "only" consists of diverse fragrance elements. First, there’s the so-called top note, which impresses with a triad of bergamot, a bit of pepper, and berry fruit. This combination is quite rare but fits together wonderfully. Slowly, the "heart" of the fragrance takes over this introduction without completely overshadowing it. A fresh, crisp, and almost "green" impression arises from the rose and mate, while patchouli has been lurking the whole time. It becomes increasingly present and teams up with wonderfully "inky" oakmoss. MAGNIFICENT!! CLASSY!! WONDERFUL!! is my reaction. And then, when a balsamic hint of myrrh and labdanum joins in.... I am smitten. THIS happens quite rarely with a "modern creation" when I have it right under my nose. Every now and then, "respectable" or "really very successful" come into play. But such enthusiasm for Belgravia Chypre is indeed a rarity. Thank you, dear perfumers, for bringing this back and hopefully for a long time to come!!

Hello, you sniffers. Welcome to my new comment, where today we’re talking about a Penhaligon's fragrance, an English fragrance brand that offers quite beautiful scents. Those who know me will of course expect that I would first recommend the scent "Lothair" from Penhaligon's. It's no wonder, as Lothair is not only a lovely, spicy autumn scent, but it also features great tea notes. And those who know me know how much I love tea and tea fragrances, right? Today, however, I’m coming to a fragrance without tea in it, even though you might not expect that from an English scent :D But maybe that makes it all the more interesting for those of you here who don’t like tea fragrances or even tea at all… unbelievable… how can anyone not like that? I would understand if people didn’t like bizarre things like coriander, capers, eggplants, Brussels sprouts, and so on, but tea??? :DD Well, whatever, because if I think about it longer, I’ll surely start calling you all crazy again, and I assume you don’t want that, he he :D So, let’s get to Belgravia Chypre, which is dedicated to the Belgravia district in West London, which is now considered one of the wealthiest neighborhoods in London. The Scent: The scent begins with sweet pink pepper and raspberries, although I can’t say which one is more prominent, as pink pepper often has a berry-like quality, after all, pink pepper is actually a berry and not real pepper, so it doesn’t have the distinctive pepper scent like black pepper. A slight spicy note is still present in the background, which also appears a bit woody. Additionally, the scent has a creamy touch. Later, the scent remains as described but becomes a bit creamier, which might also be due to the mate that can now be faintly detected. Even much later, the scent remains berry-fruity but is now also sweeter, with the sweetness reminding me of amber, among other things. Could it be labdanum? Argh, labdanum is one of those notes where I’m never quite sure how it really smells… Otherwise, there is a lot of patchouli in the base, although it comes across as less intense than in many other fragrances. Even the oakmoss is quite weak, so the scent might even appeal to those who don’t like oakmoss… who knows? :) Be that as it may, the scent is nice and comes across as somewhat simple, yet it still radiates elegance. Sillage and Longevity: The sillage is rather mediocre for me; it doesn’t project as strongly as I had assumed from the average reviews here. But it’s not that weak either. The longevity is better; I could smell the scent on me for about seven to eight hours. The Bottle: The bottle is cylindrical and clear, featuring a large label on the front with a black-and-white illustration of the London district. The cap is cylindrical at the bottom (and seems to be gilded this time) and round on top. As usual, it has a silk ribbon around the cylindrical part, which is green this time. A beautifully designed bottle, as usual. Conclusion: Okay, so I think you need a bit of patience with this scent. It starts off quite nicely but also somewhat weak or rather simple, as you mostly smell fruity sweetness. While that doesn’t really change later, the base notes give the scent a better projection, making it appear more elegant and a bit more mature. It works well as an all-rounder, suitable for any occasion and season, at least in my opinion, as it is neither heavy nor light. Well, maybe it’s not a scent for going out or partying, but it could still be worn in the evening, for example, when going out to dinner or something like that. I must say, though, that the scent comes across as quite feminine to me. Therefore, I don’t find it unisex at all. I think it’s worth a look or rather a sniff. Why this scent is supposed to reflect the Belgravia district in London, I’m not quite sure. Perhaps its elegant aura represents the genteel society there, who knows? What does it smell like in your area? :D Uuuuh, sometimes it stinks to high heaven around here, especially when the sewage system is full, and you can somewhat guess how often the neighbors are doing their business in the bathroom… while in winter, thankfully, it’s only occasionally noticeable, in summer, especially during heatwaves, it’s really bad… baaaaaah!!!! :D Anyway, it’s winter now, and that problem isn’t often encountered. Well then, that’s it from me. Wishing you all a lovely evening and see you next time :)

I remembered the first time: The sales associate at the perfume shop looked at me. "I have something for you," he said. And: "But it needs a lot of time to develop.

Can one still create a Chypre perfume today? That was the question I asked myself when I purchased this wonderful and original scent from Penhaligon's. Of course, the answer cannot be direct and immediate.

Hommage à l’Homme Voyageur is a spicy-woody scent with a quite “glueish”, rubbery texture, inky polished notes of vetiver and cedar with a slight sort of “petrol” aftertaste, softened by floral notes (I get something like violet although I don’t see it listed, however something talc-powdery), sandalwood on the base, all refreshed by a conventional citrus-bergamot accord. As I said the vetiver (and all the scent actually) is quite on the Encre Noire genre, salty and “waxy”: together with cypriol, patchouli and oak moss notes, all the three basically smelling like nuances of plastic, it creates and smell halfway ink and brand new leather (freshly-cleaned with shoe polish). Good persistence. Besides Encre Noire it also reminds me slightly of Jil Sander Man from 2007, although less smoky, less soft, less elegant. Overall a bit uninspired and surely not “realistic” at all as regards of the woody notes (so definitely fans of earthy & raw vetiver may want to skip this); but in its chemical, “urban”, polished and office-safe contemporariness, it’s not bad. An easy-going scent, decently nice for all situations. It should just cost a couple of dozens of euros less. 6,5/10

I do believe in Lalique. Their most generous fragrances have quality and class. This one is a nice touch of spicy fresh notes and papyrus. Cardamom potentially is a dandy note. It's rounded and biting at the same time. Hommage Voyageur is a juxtaposition of spicy and icy citrus opening, plus ambery vetiver surprise coming much earlier than expected. The core of the fragrance is on frosted dry vetiver and light patchouli infused in vanilla oriented amber. The result is so instant and dandy, green, foggy, earthy and spicy. Nice item to get rid of stress. 7/10

Cardamom is accompanied by masculine notes of patchouli and vetiver – the main players throughout the life of this fragrance. This dark and inky vetiver is similar to the famous Encre Noir, but easier to wear. Construction of Voyageur is somehow similar to Gucci Pour Homme and Rochas Lui. Voyageur does not have the same smell, but still possesses some woody fragments of these late giants. Maybe the note of papyrus, cypriol oil or Iso E Super cedar are responsible for this effect, but I cannot vouch for that. Interesting is a subtle note of leather, like a pair of new Italian shoes which is stronger manifested in late Canali Style. Through the evolution Voyageur becomes a little bit sweeter from vanilla (vanilla cigarillos) and ambery notes. The drydown is not strong and recognizable, but warms the heart of Voyageur. Rating: 8/10 More on Scentimentalwords

Great freakin' scent and a great bang for your buck! The fresh bergamot opening with cardamom is actually moving at great haste and within 15-20 minutes you're transported right to the heart of vetiver and patchouli. I actually keep getting hints of saffron with this one, reminding me of a slightly tuned down Versace Man mixed with Dunhill Icon - but it's not listed, so it could be due to the blending of other notes. It's woody, floral, spicy and rubbery but in a very smooth way even if there is a hint of similarity to fresh shoe polish sometimes. It may come off as slightly synthetic, but the composition itself is really blended with masterfull skill. The heart is musky sweet woody patchouli, featuring vetiver, vanilla and amber. I'm not really sure how papyrus smells but if this is it, I'll def be rocking more scents with that note. Others mention this being a suit-and-tie fragrance, but I rather see it as fitting both formal and informal situations alike - very versatile. Fits perfectly on a spring day, but could be used most of the year as well. Projection is modest to be honest, but longevity is very decent. If you find Encre Noire too dark and earthy, this could be a lighter alternative for you. Why this hasn't been hyped like crazy is beyond me - but hey, the more for me.

The 3D bottle is blue as the tint of deep Ocean, blue like the waves of the Atlantic at night, blue like the Riband won by the Normandie, the ole French passenger liner to have broken the speed record for a transatlantic crossing. But that is all about the blue in this scent. Hommage Voyageur is not just another aquatic scent in the world, and it is a story that is utterly different from the original Hommage à l'Homme. It has way more in common DNA wise with Encre Noire than being a flanker of L'Hommage à L'Homme. It is a wonderfully crafted take on ashen spices, that feels utterly smart and luxurious; it is a dark, productive, and smooth uncompromisingly woodlike fragrance. A scent that powerfully revolves around three manly notes, with the woody, earthy and animalistic elements in the foreground: patchouli, vetiver, and papyrus. Albeit they are part of its heart yet dominate the scene since the very beginning. The perfume hugs your skin with a fragrant and medicinal aroma of green cardamom and just a tiny hint of bright and powdery bergamot, together they create a delicate balance of citrus, spice, and sweet resinous blend. The opening here is superb. Following this dynamic opening, things gently become carefully subdued and muted. Vetiver's woody, arid quality dominates, accented by papyrus earthy dryness. Nuances of patchouli and it's dark edge pierce through but never distracting from the overall composition. I pretty much get a dirty, dry, and sort of dusty patchouli, rounded out by smoky and leathery notes, with a cedar wood accord as well that adds its unmistakeable pencil sharpener and inky gleaming timbre almost present in Lalique trademark works. Noteworthy, there is indeed something else that just hit me. I swear it saffron, like how it smells when you pick up the dried strands of that precious spice and inhale deeply! So captivating, this leaves me wondering whether saffron has been inadvertently omitted from the notes listed. Otherwise, the perfumers did an astounding job recreating that accord with all the other notes! I know for sure that Nathalie Lorson, for instance, recreated the vanillic tone in Zara Deep Vanilla using additional notes, but vanilla. In the base, warm ambergris offers a touch of sensuality, and a sincere sweetness mirrored well with an albeit subtle and velvety vanilla note. It never becomes sweet, slightly the amber and vanilla expertly round out the edges, adding to its depth and smooth feel. Oakmoss further embellishes the musky and rich earthy tonalities of the fragrance, pairing well with the vetiver mentioned above. This mix-up of vanilla, papyrus, and moss is subtle, spicy, and divine. To me, this new extension to the Lalique line stands apart from its predecessor Hommage a l'Homme. They smell nothing alike, in my opinion, which is a good thing. Same name, same bottle, yet each stands alone as a separate fragrance, neither leaning on nor referencing the other. Hommage Voyageur is a strange journey into the Orient. Generative, emotional, and open to discovery. Lastly, to conclude, Hommage Voyageur is relatively linear, and where this would perhaps be a criticism in most cases, it isn't here as the fragrance smells so darn lovely that one doesn't want it to change much at all. Longevity is okay, I sprayed it on generously, and after a few hours, I can still smell it. If, however, you are looking for a projection/sillage monster, then this is not for you. This one is subtle and classy, intimate, like a whisper. Just perfect for work, I recommend this for cold seasons, spring and fall are ideal if you are looking for a non-floral, non-citrus, non-sweet cologne. -Elysium

It smells good, a bit dark but rather unique among the common day sugar juices. I like it better than Hommage a l’homme and even more than the Encre Noire trio. It has that nice patchouli, vetiver papyrus combo that gives a certain class. A gentleman’s smell, doesn’t screm for attention and although quite polite in projection the longevity is 6h+.

Voyageur's scent is another LALIQUE fragrance after ENCRE NOIRE, ENCRE NOIRE SPORT, ENCRE NOIRE L'EXTREME, which I really like and which, taking into account the fragrance composition, the duration of the fragrance, the sensations and the price, I consider a CLOSE FACE MUST HAVE.

Wow this is a stunner. I found a 50ml of this on sale for $40 and had to pick it up since I know it's been discontinued for some time. The first spray really wow'd me, especially because I'm familiar with the original Hommage. This smells nothing like it, not at all.

I love Lalique's "Hommage a L'Homme." For me, one of the most underrated men's fragrances of recent years. However, I haven't quite figured out its only flanker, with the snazzy title "Voyageur" (something different from Light, Extreme, or Night). I've tested it several times - never really able to grasp it.

Yes, I also clearly see the parallel to Oud Wood. However, I have only been able to test it in passing and under pressure from the responsible employee at KaDeWe. But the top note of both is almost identical. I think it mainly comes down to the cardamom-bergamot combination; I also find hints of it in D.STRICT by Strellson and in Tabac Man.

Well, without looking at the notes, i expected Rive d'Ambre to be, due to the amber on its name, thick, sweet, more oriental overall. But maybe Tom Ford was wanting to allude to the ambient where you collect the ambergris? I don't know, but this is fresh, citrusy, sparkling, not thick or very oriental at all. It opens with for me with what seems to be lemons, oranges, tangerines, their leaves mixed with neroli flowers and something sweet citrusy juice. It calms quickly after the mouthwatering opening, which can be a little bit disappointing, because you want the first pleasant impression to last much more. I like it, but i question myself how does this fit in a private collection of fragrances, since it has such a pleasant and easy to like aura that it would seems more right to put into mainstream instead.

Of all the substances whose pleasant scents have fascinated humans and which we have consequently sought to grasp in our long cultural history, the animal-derived ones are perhaps the most astonishing in terms of their discovery. It is quite natural to attempt to capture and preserve the scent of a rose. However, trying to smell small deer, cats, or rodents 'down below' to see if any fragrant substances can be extracted from their glands requires a greater sense of adventure. Not to mention the inconspicuous waxy-gray lumps that drift on the surface of oceans. For centuries, the origin of ambergris has been a subject of speculation and debate. Most of the (very rare) lumps, as mentioned, were found floating on the ocean's surface; very rarely did one of these pieces wash ashore - and even there, it had to be discovered. That the lumps come from the digestive tract of sperm whales - and whether from all of them or only those with a metabolic disorder - remained a mystery for a long time, as the fresh substance smells repulsive - it is only through decades of contact with saltwater and oxygen that the pleasant scent for which ambergris is known emerges. Recent ambergris is almost exclusively of synthetic origin. Contrary to its wet origins, its aroma can be described as dry and woody, with balsamic, sometimes musky undertones. Typically, ambergris is arranged into sensually serious base notes and is traditionally used more in women's fragrances, although I can find nothing distinctly feminine in its nature. Tom Ford takes a new and surprising approach in Rive d'Ambre, embedding the namesake substance in fleeting citrus and mild herbal spices, thus creating a surprising, bright fragrance from it. Rive d'Ambre is not at all what one might expect from an amber fragrance - especially not from the house of Tom Ford. Weightless scents are not really Tom's specialty, and 'weightless' might even be a bit of an exaggeration. Nevertheless, this is a perfume of feather-lightness and dryness, and yet: freshness that is radiant and golden like a desert wind. It is not a joker or a player - the woody notes give it enough character and substance beyond the initial citrus note, lending it elegance and maturity, and something warm, almost blinding, as if one were looking into white sunlight. Conclusion: an elegantly ambered non-amber fragrance. Not a typical Tom Ford Private Blend. Yet, or precisely because of that, it is worth a sniff.

...than an Amber River...but that's just fine with me, because amber is not my great love; I don't like 9 out of 10 amber fragrances, and Ambre Nuit only on a woman! Many voices and opinions about the scent say that Rive d'Ambre is one of the more ordinary Tom Ford fragrances and the one that deserves the purchase price the least. In one respect, I have to agree; yes, it is one of the more ordinary scents in Ford's fragrance offerings, but in the segment of citrusy spring and summer fragrances, it occupies a rather above-average position. The concentrated citrus top note, which offers everything that a tropical fruit heart desires, seems somewhat ordinary at first sniff, even a bit arbitrary...as one knows from many fragrances. But especially when compared to the citrus scents of designers, it has a completely different level-authentic, no synthetics, and a rich volume. The top note could easily be from Atelier Cologne. What further supports my quality assumption is that Ambre Ford does not draw from the turquoise in-house series; for example, Mandarino di Amalfi smells quite different despite similar scent notes...the mandarin stands out clearly...but presents an independent fragrance. Because after just 4-5 minutes, a slightly warm, balsamic, and subtle note emerges in the background, giving the fragrance a very special touch...here I definitely suspect cardamom. Nevertheless, RdA remains a somewhat calm fellow, refined and gentlemanly, noble, perhaps a bit too polished, but incredibly flattering. The development is already completed after about 1 hour, which is always very quick with citrus scents...the fragrance reaches its peak only in the base, a dreamy creamy, balsamic amber mix, so incredibly fine, warm, and mild...simply wonderful. Unfortunately, the whole experience takes place just slightly above skin level. Despite this warm facet, the fragrance is easy to wear in summer, as its citrus freshness, interwoven with various nuances, remains intact until the end. Unfortunately, I can't detect any cognac, but there is a hint of wood...without it being too prominent. Conclusion: A more than successful fragrance that is mainly used in spring and summer but can certainly be worn year-round; in winter, it might be too subtle outdoors. The longevity is quite okay at 5, sometimes 6 hours, but the sillage is a bit subtle, aside from the first 30 minutes. To be honest...it wouldn't have been worth €200 to me, but for €130, I simply indulged in this luxury. It stands out pleasantly from the other blockbusters in the series, which I have come to like very much! The turquoise series may be more consistent, going even more uncompromisingly towards freshness and refreshment, but also a bit more one-dimensional...Rive d'Ambre connects both worlds very well!

Yesterday, while clearing out my briefcase, a forgotten sample of this lovely fragrance rolled out at me. I've had RdA on my wishlist for quite a while, but I wasn't aware that I had already received a sample of it. My surprise and joy were immense! Even though I was wearing a completely different scent behind my ears yesterday, I immediately sprayed Rive d'Ambre generously on my wrist, as my joy was not only great, but my impatience was even a bit greater. At first, I was reminded a bit of Mandarino di Amalfi, although in the top note of RdA, the mandarin/lemon has been rather replaced by a ripe orange. Later, the composition becomes significantly darker and loses more and more of its citrus notes in my nose, transitioning into a dark, sweet realm. I find this absolutely delightful. If "Cognac" weren't mentioned in the fragrance description, I probably wouldn't identify it as such. But once you know what to look for, it is clearly perceptible and makes the dark citrus/sweet overall masterpiece even more special. Even though the good Rive d'Ambre will probably never find its way into my collection due to its glaringly high retail price, as I don't find it valuable enough for ownership (essentially, the price makes it a niche fragrance), it is truly a special yet well-rounded scent, very pleasing and somehow drinkable. The sillage is socially acceptable and the longevity is okay. However, testing on the wrist is not necessarily conducive to longevity, as the shirt sleeve or resting the wrist while typing on keyboards certainly wears the scent down more than spraying behind the ears. For me, this would be the first citrus fragrance that one could perfectly wear in a stormy autumn, during an Antarctic crossing, or on a January mudflat hike. In heat, it would be just a tad too heavy for me personally. My motto "shut up and take my money!" does not apply here, however. A sniff test is definitely worth it, and maybe one can snag a "bargain" somewhere. Thanks for reading and have a lovely rest of the weekend.

Rive d'Ambre was a summer discovery. It is light and sparkling, shimmering like the sun on the waves. A bit citrusy, as if the scent of a peeled tangerine still lingers on the hands. A touch of salt on the skin, a woody finish like the dashboard of a boat, for example. Gold-orange shimmer on tanned skin. Voilá, a summer amber full of carefree spirit. For those who want to remember such things even in winter. Doesn't always have to be a boat.

Through its ostentatious presentation, reminiscent of an altar, TF draws attention to its Private Blend line in some perfumeries. Well-read and spurred on by the comments and reviews here in the forum, I took a closer look at some classics from this line. Alongside TL and TV, the previously unremarkable Rive d’ambre caught my eye.

What only 70% for this new Tom Ford? I wouldn't have thought that myself a few days ago before testing it. Unfortunately, it has fallen from a very good 90% to a good 70%... If it were only half as expensive, it might still be a candidate for purchase, but as it stands, I have to say: nice scent, but totally overpriced and much too ordinary for that.

Your youthful beauty is enchanting. Initially shy yet full of self-assurance, you stand by your opinion and with just a wink, you can seduce me. But you have a delicate nature and wish to be protected; your playful demeanor can captivate me. Your graceful curves beguile my senses and the scent of your skin dispels all clarity.

I am not a fan of typical amber scents, but Rive d'Ambre is not one of them. Normally, I don't even smell or test amber fragrances, but my mother had the scent sprayed on a test strip and was so enthusiastic that I had to smell it too. And I was very positively surprised. I had to test it on my skin. The opening is very fresh and citrusy.

I always get confused by the names of these Penhaligon’s bottles. It’s a horses head, what the heck was its name again? At least Zoologist has got their animal names straight. Aaaaaanyway we’re not here to talk about the name of a freaking perfume are we? We want to know what it smells like. And you wouldn’t believe it but it smells pretty darn nice. First time I saw this bottle in the store it was brand new. Sprayed it on a paper strip and left it in the car. It smelled so nice, definitely flowers but none of that rose, jasmine or lavender you’ve smelled 1000 times before. Definitely unique and not per se feminine, as a matter of fact I find it leaning masculine. In my car this smell was pretty straightforward, but now I’ve tested it on skin a couple of times and it’s a different story. The flowery bit stays for a good part of the starting phase. But it retreats a bit after that and what stays is a very creamy woody base that’s not bad either. I don’t know if you know the smell of this cod liver oil ointment, but it reminds me a bit of it. And it gives me this feeling of being nurtured. I’ve gotten quite a good performance out of it. I could smell it myself pretty good even after 8 to 10 hours. As such I’d say it’s a great perfume for relaxing, lazy weekends, but it would definitely work in the office as well.

This latest addition to the Penhaligon's Portraits line was a Fortnum & Mason exclusive for only a week, but was thankfully released officially by Penhaligon's on April 1st, 2025. From the moment I tried it on paper for the first time, I was pleasantly surprised by its fresh, green notes of matcha and cardamom and the subtle pistachio, balanced by calm earthiness from the black pepper. During the drydown I noticed the saltiness from the pistachio coming out more, almost like a marine oceanic note, and the subtle suede leather note becoming stronger. The gourmand note from the pistachio could also be interpreted as ice cream or coconut. When I tried this on skin the same note progression as above resulted. Overall though, since the leather is not dominant, this perfume can appeal to both genders. Never trust anyone who says that a Penhaligon's scent is "masculine" as most scents that this brand releases are intended as unisex scents. Considering the overwhelming amount of sticky sweet, overtly gourmand cake pistachios that have been released in 2024 (looking at you, Theodoros Kalotinis Pistachio Latte), this perfume is fairly unique as a fresh, balanced gourmand. Others have noted with concern that the projection or longevity is not great. For me personally, I get at least 4-5 hours on skin with a moderate sillage. The overall impression is nothing you would get from Finley the stable boy. Nothing at all that is dusty, oudy or animalic. Luckily for me, I did not have to hold onto my 5 ml decant for long. I found a bargain on a new bottle on Vinted and added it to my collection!

Fortuitous Finley is a fragrance that I really liked! To be honest, I didn't expect that at all beforehand. Moments like these are all the more delightful. For me, the interplay of matcha, pistachio, and the spicy facets fits perfectly here. The scent starts for me directly with the matcha accord from the heart note. I absolutely did not expect that, but it made me all the more happy, as I personally really love matcha. The matcha accord blends with pleasantly spicy cardamom facets and the slightly nutty pistachio. In my opinion, many people don't really get pistachio accords right. There are now many fragrances with pistachio. Some are just okay or only manage to highlight the pistachio briefly. Here at Penhaligon's, this note is not meant to play the main role, but it still manages to come across better than in some other fragrances. The aforementioned notes almost merge together, and shortly thereafter, a very soft pepper note joins in. This is really subtle! Furthermore, I now get certain hints of a wonderfully beautiful, but discontinued fragrance! From the house of Guerlain, there used to be L'Homme Idéal Cool.
