For me, this is an incredibly beautiful scent for the warmer days of the year and always brings me certain "woodruff" vibes. The matcha tea accord in Fortuitous Finley goes in a similar direction, and yes, I just really like that. Over time, a bit of this sweet, floral, woody aspect from the orris root comes through. In combination with the violet note, this is also very thoughtfully chosen. Violets and orris, or also orris root, simply harmonize perfectly with each other. The longevity on my skin is about seven hours. Sillage is completely solid and fine. The scent is also super unisex wearable.

Penhaligon’s once again does what the house does best - it creates a fragrance with history, character, and British charm. Fortuitous Finley sounds noble and understated, like a true gentleman in a pristine suit. For me, it is clearly a masculine scent. It speaks of inner strength without any aggression: cleanly composed woody and spicy accents, a slightly bitter freshness, a hint of leather, and velvety depth. The composition is strict, controlled, but not without a certain irony - as if the fragrance is smiling at you with a wink under an English hat. On my skin, it unfolds dry, almost crispy, without any excessive sweetness. It is not a universal scent - it demands a certain style, a mood, a personality. But therein lies its character. For lovers of distinctly masculine notes and perfumery intelligence: definitely worth trying.

This fragrance flies so under the radar that it hits you unexpectedly. I don't know why so few people talk about this scent; Lalique already makes very fine, balanced fragrances, but this one, from the presentation to the scent, is top-notch. I have rarely smelled strawflower, and this one unlocks a new facet for me!! Rum + cinnamon + cardamom are like the three musketeers; they always work and fit in anywhere, but flanked by pink pepper and patchouli, it’s a sensory enlightenment... every time I wear it through the nights, it feels like a knight in evening attire, and everyone in the room knows how to appreciate the aura. This fragrance has sealed many evenings!!!

It opens explosively spicy with zesty, almost fruity pepper. Hello, what a beautiful start, really great! The rum disappears quickly, the scent is not boozy. Lucky me. The straw flower expresses itself as a dry warmth, not as curry powder, which is good, and connects in a slightly bitter way with something else. That is very good. Then it becomes somewhat balsamic-resinous but not sweet. No complaints there. Unfortunately, the cinnamon then holds the entire beautiful perfume hostage for a while. That’s not good anymore (for me). But still OK. The perfume frees itself, which is optimistic. Finally, Lorenox takes the stage. At least I assume so, as I have no idea how this substance smells on its own. However, it seems to be an amber wood from the piercing and long-lasting pseudo-cedar faction. That really gets on my nerves. To comfort myself (quite successfully), it gets gently powdered. There’s something for everyone. Thus, the scent lingers for what feels like five and a half weeks, and does absolutely nothing anymore, not even being nice. And goodbye. PS: Lorenox (TM) is an aroma chemical from the company Mane. It allegedly has woody, amber-like, and leathery facets. It is a proprietary substance, and only Mane perfumers are allowed to use it. (Source: The Scented Salamander, May 2010) This is confirmed by a sample of about a dozen perfumes containing this ingredient on Parfumo.

"Noir Premier - Fleur Universelle 1900" lives up to its name. This spicy-dark fragrance conglomerate is suitable for both autumn and winter, and despite its rather universal seasonal applicability in my eyes - summer and spring evenings work too - it feels like a premiere with every wear. It is a premiere because throughout the scent journey, several components, whether alone or combined, celebrate their very own debut - whether lavish, dominant, or particularly attention-grabbing is yet to be determined. The rum and pepper, as a duo, take the stage first, but they hardly get the chance to introduce themselves separately to the audience. With a quick follow-up appearance, the straw flower emerges, whose scent character resembles that of curry, without evoking associations with Indian cuisine - which is a relief. Gourmand aspects are not catered to here. At times overshadowing everything else, one of my favorite spice notes joins in. Some of you might know which one it is. It is cinnamon, whose appearance is exactly what I always wish for from it. It is not sweet and syrupy, not sticky, not reminiscent of rice pudding and other diabetes-inducing treats, but rather airy-spicy and adorned with its very own, typical aroma that everyone should be familiar with. In the first half hour, it steals a bit of the show from its stage companions, pushing the subtly "curry-like" straw flower aside and allowing the rum to peek through the curtain only occasionally, which I appreciate. After all, I am a lover of cinnamon, and it can certainly be loud and dominant. I also enjoy the olfactory character of rum, but not in an exaggerated, alcohol-excess-evoking manner. Here, everything fits perfectly, so the audience is presented with a cinnamon spice with a little kick in front of their ... uh ... noses. Some time later, the tonka bean, preparing for the finale, finds its way onto the stage. Its slightly vanillic face shines through, but it knows how to hold back and fulfill its role. This role must harmonize perfectly with its other stage companions to ensure that no one is scared away. The straw flower does not want to be overshadowed again after it has fought its way back into the action, which could happen with a sticky-sweet tonka bean. Likewise, the cinnamon does not want to end up as Müller rice pudding either. Even though the tonka bean does not want to completely hide its sweetness from everyone, one can kindly note that it plays its role very well. The bit of sweetness is just right, actually even perfect, and the focus is on the powderiness that its appearance brings. In the end, everyone knows how to appreciate all its companions on stage; no performance is diminished in its value, importance, or relevance. The cinnamon had to hold back a bit for this, but the broad audience certainly honors that in the end. The audience benefits from the smooth interplay, which is characterized by so much warmth and harmony, so that by the end of the evening, everyone, both men and women, wants to catch a brief signature from the one who played with the audience's senses on that stage.

It's about time. And indeed for a comment. And specifically about this fragrance, which is still completely uncommented and yet so magnificent. But, and here comes the first big problem, how to comment?! After all, this is the first detailed scent description of this perfume, and the reader wants to receive information. At first, I thought of something lyrical, perhaps in the style of Ringelnatz, The high-proof start Of rum with lots of spins In a slightly tipsy manner, To literal circumventions Of dry objectivity, To present to the reader, But I am not immune To -hic- all these complaints, That it might not be objective enough or even incomprehensible, since it is ultimately a scent description and we are not in a poetry or literature forum here. The complaint is therefore upheld, so the rum must just rumble along, which it does quite well at the beginning, that the wearer might even risk being subjected to an alcohol test during a police check. The next comment idea brought to my mind the East Westphalian couple in their unmistakable dialect; it fit so wonderfully with the high-proof start and the simultaneously very spicy-woody-resinous beginning... “Mutta, did you have a little schnapps? No, what are you talking about, that's rum!” “Heeerbert! That's the new perfume from Doris at her perfumery! It has to be like this!” “But you smell like a whole fir forest with resin in it! I mean, in the forest it's fine, but as a perfume..?!” “Heeerbeeert, don’t talk about things you know nothing about!” “Oh mother, then give me a little shot with a schnapps, then you'll smell something better right away!” But since dialect dialogues are already quite represented here and one doesn’t want to be guilty of plagiarism (politicians already have a patent on that), since there is only one dialect... oh wait, there are really many, just in Germany alone ... and also on Parfumo: I've already read Püttsprache, the Berlin Jeheimrat is already a cornerstone here ... But whatever, then I will just report on the simultaneously very spicy-resinous-woody scent that reminds one of freshly felled coniferous forests and the associated resin. And something almost fruity plays along as well; if you smell it close to the skin, you might even briefly mistake it for something hesperidic, which reveals itself in projection as pink pepper, but without that tickling sharpness in the nose. This opening is a blast, truly! You simply have to smell it!!! And already a small press report from Mr. Olf Aktorisch unfolds as the next comment possibility about a small village on the edge of the Teutoburg Forest, which, to the general horror of the village community, is about to be deforested, as the smell of freshly felled coniferous wood spreads throughout the village and persists, leading to the first petitions against the unnecessary slaughter of the Teutons, as the forest is lovingly called by the indigenous people, being drafted over a spiced tea with cinnamon and spice (hence the name 'spiced tea') cloves. However, to avoid coming across as too contrived and attention-seeking with this comment variant - dear goodness, one certainly does not want that! - I prefer to describe the further development of the scent with vivid words: still spicy-resinous, the impression of coniferous wood remains, clove is clearly detectable despite its absence in the pyramid, and a fine cinnamon note in the background. Okay, I admit, this is a bit boring and linguistically rather uninspired. Then I should perhaps present the rest of the description in a factual yet eloquent, informative yet still elaborate, technical yet simultaneously verbally vivid manner. But please - for heaven's sake - don’t recite the pyramid! That would have been the last straw; after all, we can all read that ourselves! Well then, nothing easier than that... Into the pine resinousness plays a balsamic sweetness, probably due to myrrh; however, patchouli could also be held responsible, as a sweet earthiness can indeed be perceived. The immortelle, which is noted in the pyramid, is also said to have a certain sweetness, but since the earthy, resinous-balsamic impression is strongly in the foreground, it does not seem to be the cause, and if it is, then only acting in the background, namely contributing a certain sweetness. This scent impression indeed lasts for hours, even though after about 3 to 4 hours a certain skin proximity can be attested (at least on my skin). The overall projection or sillage is present but not overwhelming, which is advantageous given the scent direction if this fragrance is to be worn, for example, in the office. The longevity, based on my experience, is a good 8 to 10 hours on the skin, a test of longevity on clothing has not yet been conducted. Finally, when only a hint is still detectable, a very light woodruff scent can be discerned, which mixes into the balsamic-resinous-spicy. Better? To be honest: No idea! But what is more than an idea, for me even certainty is: This scent is special, very special indeed, not artificial at all and completely unisex. One of my absolute autumn favorites! And I really don’t care if my comment conforms to a - if they even exist - comment norm, because what was most important to me was primarily to promote this scent! And now I am done ;-))

Lovely scent. Beautifully balanced rose and Oudh combo with a nice slightly spicy floral touch to it. I’ve read plenty with regards to performance issues and Tom Ford blends but this is great on my skin in that respect. This is interesting without being too challenging. Sweet without being cloying. Rich enough without being too dense such that it would become overly heavy. Great scent

I'm no rose expert nor do I find it to be my favorite note amongst men's scents but this Oud Fleur fragrance has a nice kind of rose. The oud is soft while the rose is not the usual dry red rose kind. Have you ever walked around a rose garden and noticed the difference between various rose bushes? Have you ever smelled a rose, a darker rose where the aroma is fuller, juicier and seems more complex? That's what Ford seems to have here in this scent, a little incense-like and, yes, like the name implies-floral. Projects very well and lasts a good amount of time.

One of the smoothest perfumes I've experienced so far. Very soft oud, just a soupçon, to use a French turn of phrase, in a floral blend that may bring to mind a dark rose or a similarly dark pansy, plus the sandalwood somewhere in the background. Very elegant and distinguished! Something to wear to a formal occasion, to the opera perhaps, if and when that becomes a possibility again.

This scents makes you take a journey from a harsh animalic realistic oud smell where rose is barely smellable to a completely unisex fragrance where rose and sandalwood play the main role. I love how complicated and mature it is. It’s a fact that it may not be liked by some because of its dirty opening but despite that fact it’s still in my opinion one of the best scents released by Tom Ford

Lana Del Rey states more than she asks - not horrified, not shocked, she just wants to know. Oud Fleur, one of Tom's two new dark gray fragrances. Opulent and blooming, it is deep and - in a very American way - rich and very relaxed, calm. Magnificent flowers, broken white, porcelain pink waxy, pulsating scarlet, take center stage. Soft oud and gray woods provide a framework, playfully elegant and beautiful. Patchouli underlines the blooming heart with dragging creaminess and vibrating weight, intimate and sometimes almost a bit vulgar. Oud Fleur, a scent of idleness - and vice and decay. Something tragic surrounds it, something wounded behind all that glamour. The woman in sunglasses, the Birkin on her lap in the car in the parking lot, she is not wearing any panties under her dress. The handsome man, a bundle of cash crackling in the pocket of his jacket, but what has he done for it, just recently? The blonde lady with the little dog, carefully covering her bruises with makeup, is now at Boucheron looking at diamonds. Not an easy fragrance, not one for every day. One for the fallen, who walk upright with their scars - full of profound, thoughtful splendor, full of sex and life wisdom - and a little regret. Conclusion: one for the bad girls - and those who like them.

Oud Fleur is absolutely not what one typically imagines when thinking of a rose-oud. I wouldn't have even thought of rose without knowing the pyramid. More likely jasmine or tuberose, but not necessarily rose. Oud Fleur starts off intensely animalistic. Indolic animalic flowers and almost piercing oud. Sultry, sweaty, animalistic.

Admittedly, the title promises nothing positive, especially with the word Maybe carrying a relatively negative connotation. Years ago, there was an article about Generation Z, titled "Generation Maybe," which discussed how this generation has gotten lost in the Either-Or, unable to make decisions, having no answers to any questions, and not wanting to commit.

Anyone expecting Oud Fleur to be just another "Rose/Oud" candidate (something that the majority of comments and statements here seem to suggest) is mistaken. Oud Fleur takes a completely different approach to this already overused theme. On my skin, the fragrance starts with a hefty dose of Oud.

I was skeptical - but it was love at first sniff. What lies behind this fragrance is the mysterious. It is not a deep secret that this scent carries - but it is the mysterious, it is the contemplative, it represents for me the multifaceted and yet complicated person. Whoever wears this fragrance does not necessarily want to please - and yet they do.

This beautiful fragrance truly deserves a first comment, as it should not go unremarked. First and foremost, I am greeted by sandalwood in large quantities, followed by a sweetness. The rose tickles me gently, and the oud gives it all a lightness. The patchouli, which I usually dislike, actually rounds it off harmoniously.

Again a creature of Bertrand Duchaufour... Again a list of notes, that does not help you to translate the impression to ingredients. Unfortunately I had no possibility to test this fragrance normally, blown, only donning, and I suspect that the result is different. Top and heart are almost inseparable: fresh, electrifying, tingly, a surprising and pleasurable experience. It reminds me to pine needles, but behind this dark green freshness I felt a gentle caress, the peaceful base unfolds under the fresh leaves as a mist in a valley. If AMARANTHINE would be music, it should be polyphonic. Later on clove is in limelight, the slightly creamy and metallic scents surround clove as musical accompaniment. AMARANTHINE was not durable on my skin, and it is also a bit shy, but I really like it. It is totally unisex in my opinion. I encourage the future AMARANTHINE owner, that sample it and test it minimum twice in different circumstances before buying a full bottle.

In 2009, when this fume came out, Penhaligon's tarted up the release with the idea that Amaranthine smelled like the inside of a woman's thigh...I believe Duchaufour was quoted to that effect. That was a tease to create a frisson of excitement, but it's not entirely baseless. The lactonic notes of the composition could be construed to connote female secretions, although the jasmine is a bit too clean to suggest a woman's crack. (More indoles please!) Not a bad perfume, although not a great one. For jasmine, i much prefer Samsara or VCA's Mumure.

Like Ostara, Amaranthine seems to have fallen victim to a cull of ‘old wood’ when Puig bought Penhaligon’s and L’Artisan Parfumeur from Fox Paine & Company. Perfumes by ‘star’ perfumers like Bertrand Duchaufour, who composed both Ostara and Amaranthine, were promptly kyboshed from the Penhaligon’s line up. A heartbreaking decision that probably only a CPA would understand. Anyway, what a pity, because Amaranthine is my true North of two specific genres – the steamy tropical genre and the milk-custard genre. Though it opens on a green, almost fruity musk note (Galaxolide?), it quickly settles into its defining accord of what I would define as plant milk, frothed in a steamer, and lightly spiced with cardamom, ginger, and cumin, and cooled until it sets into a nutty vegan custard. It’s the ylang brings the custard, of course, its banana-ish intensity ratcheted up a few notches by the way of an exotic banana leaf note, a condensed milk accord, and a feverish Casablanca lily impression. But overall, I think that the real sleight of hand here is in how the cooler-toned, crisp green tea notes have been feathered in to keep the creaminess from weighing the whole thing down. The use of cumin here is also very well thought out. There is just enough to give Amaranthine warmth and intimacy – the slightly moist skin under your collar bone on a humid day – but not enough for it to smell scarily sexual. On the cumin scale of things, therefore, Amaranthine tends more towards Songes (Annick Goutal) than towards Jubilation 25 (Amouage), Femme (Rochas), Rubj eau de parfum (Vero Profumo) or even Al Oudh (L’Artisan Parfumeur). But still, the (female) sensuality factor is clearly present. Ylang custard, yes, but nothing near as innocent or as pure as Tasneem or Ylang de Mayotte.

This is once again a truly unique perfume that is timeless and has recognizability! With Amaranthine, it is similar to the Etro perfumes! It has a scent that suggests natural ingredients, which is why I think it is so precious! After spraying, it smells very strongly of green tea, the precious cardamom absolute that brings a bit of sharpness and spice, and coriander oil that is sweet-sour and spicy. I can hardly perceive the freesia in this scent, almost not at all! In the heart note, green notes remain with clove aromas, the also very precious jasmine absolute, roses that seem to have a slightly harsher aroma, and ylang-ylang which has a banana-like and somewhat sweet character. In the end, these ingredients unite with a hint of bitter musk, sandalwood, and the balsamic-sweet scent of tonka bean absolute and vanilla. The longevity is already to be rated as very good. I can still perceive the scent in the afternoon when I apply it in the morning! Definitely worth a test!

Antoine, noble dispenser, may you forgive me, but this fragrance completely misses the mark for me. My fault, I really wanted to get to know this aristocratic little water. Well, lindworms really do exist! In England! They've been lounging around in moats for 1000 years. This one is female, named Amaranthine, and resides in the caves of Lady and Lord Stinkwater's castle. Amaranthine devours a commoner once every 100 years, who smells of tea and some oily fruits and spices. Then there’s another hundred years of peace. To keep her in check, people sacrifice flowers, spices, and woods to her. But today she has emerged from the moat and has devoured Medusa, as well as Lady and Lord Stinkwater (who were just sharing a pack of "After Eight" for dinner) and then burped terribly. What happened next in the digestive tract, I’d rather spare you from.

Here my thanks to ParfumFan for the sample of this lush fragrance. Few scents from Penhaligons do I find distinctly feminine. This one, however, is an absolute women's fragrance and of the unusually floral kind. The top note starts rather harmlessly and almost modestly with a somewhat green floral note.

After a long time, I pulled out the little bottle again, which had really been in a deep sleep. Undeserved?! At least not as long as Sleeping Beauty. And I am not the prince. A peculiar scent. I wouldn’t even water any lindworms with it. A dull leafiness, I really imagine more velvety leaves than a smooth banana leaf, which I can see here in the greenhouse.

When I read this, it became clear to me what Amanranthine reminded me of: carnations. Garden carnations but also clove mixed with honey and dissolved in green tea. The opening was almost a bit too intense for me, green and very spice-heavy. Cardamom slightly overdosed, white freesia absent, but I can faintly perceive cloves.

Bertrand Duchaufour has a distinctive style, which he excellently documents here with a work for the English traditional house Penhaligon's. "Amaranthine" (2009) is a fruity oriental, but not an extreme powerhouse fragrance that overwhelms everything.

...it makes my weak heart race.*gg* Wow...what a fragrance. I don't really know where all the notes are placed, but I don't need to. It's enough that Amaranthine is so beautifully floral that it causes heart palpitations for lovers of such scents.

Absolutely lovely, bright and sunny, slightly floral citrus blended to perfection! Stays quite linear with the main focus on bittersweet citruses surrounded by naturally soft and sweet flowers gradually yielding to a smoothly green and mossy base; It perfoms well on me, the way the spring/summer fragrance has to perform. So beautiful! 9/10

The opening is a paradigmatic citric summer blast: bergamot (Calabrian per the company blurb), oranges, mandarin and a lemon - the latter determines the overall lack of sweetness and that touch of a tangy undertone I get. Very lovely and refreshing, but only lasting for the first couple of hours or so. Then floral notes emerge, with an orange blossom being dominant on me; although a muguet with touches of a very light ylang-ylang, a touch of pallid shiso leaves, and a faint jasmine in the background. Towards the end a bit a wood-free neroli and a bland set of white musks make brief appearances. I get moderate sillage, good projection, and five hours of longevity on my skin. This summer scent lives by the first part, the citrus blast. The rest is rather mediocre, except for the orange blossom. 3.25/5

How many are left now? After I tried (in vain) Ford's "Portofino Forte" last year, which doesn't stand out among dozens of previously released summer Mediterranos (and unfortunately comes off as somewhat artificial due to a slightly clean-washed cleanliness), it's time to test an "American Italian" again. The price hits the wallet in a typically arrogant (and ultimately completely exaggerated) Ford manner (100 ml - 298 Euro). People who love surprises and felt the greatest excitement as a child when opening a Kinder Egg should steer clear of the Positano sun. Because there is really nothing new this year either. Compared to last year's "Forte," I actually prefer the new one a bit more. The opening is predominantly summer lively, dominated by mandarin, lemon, and bergamot. This is quite uplifting, especially considering the rather mixed German summer so far. Orange blossom also comes into play after about a quarter of an hour, accompanied by noticeably measured jasmine, which gives the fragrance a slightly feminine touch. Overall, it is creamy, soft, very rounded - and yet I am slightly bothered - as noted last year with "Forte" - by a very slightly laundry-clean hyper-clean (Iso-E-Super?) accord that contributes to the longevity, but at the same time (once again) weaves in this somewhat flat cleanliness note. Fortunately, it is more subtle than with "Forte," but still noticeable. Overall, it's nicely (and reliably boring) made, ultimately no mistake in summer for people who can playfully handle their money.

The small town of Positano - located about fifty kilometers south of Naples above the Tyrrhenian Sea and probably the most famous place on the Amalfi Coast - inspired Tom Ford for his latest summer fragrance. Many of these summer perfumes - most in beautiful blue bottles - revolve around the similarly named and comparably legendary Portofino, which is located much further north in Liguria. The older ones thematize the fleeting lightness of neroli, while the newer ones are oriented towards an elegant floral sunscreen accord: Soleil Blanc, for example, or Orchid Soleil and Fleur de Portofino. Sole di Positano - it tells of steep alleys in dazzling sunlight over an azure bay and beautiful signore and signori making 'bella figura' on the piazza - joins this group. And it is precisely here that Tom Ford disappoints with this fundamentally beautiful and expressive scent - which does not more than join in, recite, and regurgitate - and which strives to create nothing new, not even attempting to do so. There are many themes, certainly also summery ones, that are still completely missing from Mr. Ford's portfolio from Texas - one with tuberose, for example, or a moist green aquatic plant scent. Instead, Sole di Positano relies entirely on Ford's successful recipe from recent years and varies it only as slightly as the shading of the bottle. The result is elegant summer freshness in delicate lagoon blue - and yet, as if Casa Ford had served pasta with tomato sauce and pasta with seafood, now simply pasta with seafood in tomato sauce. Not bad. But for Casa Ford, it's actually not enough. Conclusion: in economics, there is the term 'Fordism' - named after Henry Ford and not Tom. Strongly simplified, Fordism refers to an extremely high standardization of the product and its manufacturing method: machine, mass, mainstream. And thus, it is actually not at all what Tom, the younger Mr. Ford of the two (the older - Henry - lived and worked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, but they are both Americans), seeks to convey in his perfumes. Sole di Positano seems almost as if one simply mixed equal parts of Fleur de Portofino, Orchid Soleil, and Soleil Blanc and added a splash of Mandarino di Amalfi and Neroli Portofino. It was quick and required little effort, and it still smells quite good. Nevertheless: it could be better.

What a simple, great summer scent this is?! Elegant, consistent, high-quality down to the tips of the hair. Monotonous, bitter, but overall extraordinarily versatile and simply wearable for me. Of course, a bit outrageously priced, but as a fragrance itself, it's already a big deal. Old-school luxury, casual and relaxed, masculine and self-assured. Oak moss refined with citrus splashes, aldehydes meet chest hair, jasmine goes to the gym. Typical Tom Ford. It's all been done before, but not in such a polished and refined way, defined and trained, laid-back and powerful. This is artificial naturalness to the max. It smells of adventurers and thick wallets, of the Mediterranean and beach villas, of coupes and salty breezes. A poem and grand advertisement for Positano. Sunny, sensual, contemplative. Perfect with olives, a fine wine, and a relaxed snack. A secret member of the upper echelons. Without bragging or showing off. The opposite of the Geissens. Even if some themes and accents of other blue-turquoise Tom Fords are just repeated. Bottle: Tom Ford has created something iconic here... Sillage: delicate and summery. Longevity: super nice, but disappears too quickly - 3-5 hours in the sun. But that's what it should be made for. Conclusion: an almost perfect holiday scent. If one is a millionaire. Or just looking for the one. Masculine, summery, light, green and blue and southern in every molecule. A classic men's fragrance, sexy and fresh. You have to manage a lot of jasmine first. And actually super simple. Here just flawlessly and luxuriously prepared and updated.

Every morning I look out from my office - well, except for my weekends - and soberly note the following fact. Summer is gone. Dead. Irrevocably. For a long time. The sky is gray and crying. It's dark early. There’s no talk of snow and Christmas spirit yet. Even Last Christmas cannot conjure up the wonderful moments and joyful hours that the pre-Christmas season brings.

Do you remember her? Ariel, the Little Mermaid. I can very well imagine that if they existed, mermaids would smell exactly like this. Although citrus-green fragrances are not found above my Cobb-Douglas utility function or my indifference curve, Sole di Positano manages to displace some of my Oud preferences.

As already mentioned in the comment on Mandarino di Amalfi Acqua, one can also have mixed feelings about Tom Ford's new product policy with Sole di Positano. Here, too, nothing revolutionary is being newly created, but rather existing fragrance families are being reinterpreted and further developed, yet the result is still impressive!

Casual, light, lively, and profound. For many, Gunter Sachs may have seemed like just another playboy stumbling around this world, but he was certainly not that. On a rather boring Sunday evening, I once watched a documentary about this fascinating man. My initial attitude towards him was extremely critical.

I am really a big Tom Ford fan (see picture) I think he set a benchmark with his first drop (Oud Wood, Tobacco Vanille) that continues to inspire the niche world to this day. Filled with joy, I am currently exploring the cologne-like Private Blend fragrances. Sole di Positano is one of them.

First things first, this perfume preceded Dior by Dune by a year or two. I have often wondered if the Behometh that is Dior took a little known British fragrance, tweaked it, gave it a completely new marketing persona and took on the world with it, and won. LP NO 9 was taken from the market in 2006 and reintroduced a couple of years later. It is Dune meets Middle Earth, the fougere is apparent in the opening which is chocked full of spicy, herbal nuances; there's quite a silage cloud to this ravishing perfume. Being ravished by it, though, is a little bit exhausting and I'm grateful for the dry down. It has wonderful tenacity, enough to slay the Habit Rouge dragon when my husband wears that particular powerhouse, so it's definitely a good toy to have in your munitions cabinet. The bottle and silly cap are not to my liking though. If you like Annick Goutal's Passion you will probably like this, just imagine Dune in EDP form, less mineral, more floral with herbs and lavender at the beginning. That's a good thing, right?

But for me it smelled strongly of kerosene with an urinal undercurrent, and then some herbs and flowers desperately trying to cover this mess up. I feel really bad for the flowers. I feel even worse for myself - blind buying it on account of a cutesy name and bottle.

Contrary to the belief that Sauce Bearnaise originates from Bern - no, it comes from Bearn, a region in France. I learned classical French cuisine. My mentor always had Escoffier at hand. This is the Guide Culinaire, standard literature for chefs - it contains everything you need to know about cooking. August Escoffier wrote this masterpiece - as a little boy, he always watched his grandmother cook, then learned to be a chef, was drafted as a soldier .......... and eventually became the head chef at the Ritz Carlton. Ho Chi Minh is said to have even been a kitchen assistant under his leadership. Sauce Bearnaise, simply put, is Hollandaise sauce with tarragon, often served with meat and fish. Personally, I think it goes particularly well with lukewarm roast beef or Chateaubriand. You make a reduction, let it cool, and then whisk it with egg yolks over a water bath; just before completion, you add the melted butter. Finally, the finely sliced tarragon is added - done. I love tarragon in food, the feeling when you pull the leaves from the stem and your fingers smell of it. But I also love it in perfume. LP starts right away with this wonderful note, combined with the harsh rose geranium and citrus, a challenge for the nose. I also perceive a slight metallic note, which fades over time. In the heart, I smell rose, clove, and jasmine. I notice cinnamon less, vanilla a bit more. The cedar also gives the fragrance a slight anise note in the base, which is similar to tarragon, and I think the amber adds sweetness to the scent. For me, there are two great tarragon fragrances. This one and Memoir Man by Amouage - I particularly like the tarragon in that one. And one more thing I want to say about Auguste Escoffier, the master chef. He revolutionized haute cuisine, divided chefs into positions like saucier, poissonier, patissier ............. simplified recipes, tried to make cooking easier, and wrote about it. He founded a committee to better support the families of chefs who were drafted into the war financially. For me, he was one of the greats.

I first smelled this perfume about a year ago at my aunt's, who had made a blind purchase of "Love Potion No.9" and "Lily & Spice" from Penhaligon's, which she expressed disappointment about. "They're totally awful," she told me, explaining that one smelled like a man (Love Potion), the other like a cemetery (Lily & Spice), and then suddenly sprayed her bathroom wall without any warning. A bit confused by this unusual way of testing a fragrance, I first stuck my nose to the wall and had to agree with her, while also feeling somewhat perplexed by the very pink, feminine packaging and the name, which stood in stark contrast to what I was smelling on the bathroom tiles. When I visited her again today, I wanted to give it another try and dared to spray it on my wrist. I once again detected that piercing, bitter scent, which conjured up the image of a bearded man after his second bottle of Jack Daniels, trying to mask his odor with the excessive application of a cheap deodorant. "Phew," I thought, disgusted, and I still get a slight shiver when I think back to it. However, as the evening went on and I continued to sniff myself, the fragrance underwent an almost incredible transformation. The unpleasant sharpness had disappeared, the bitterness was still present but had receded far into the background. Instead, the scent somehow reminded me of a mix between Arpege and Miss Dior (Original), and I now perceived it as floral, elegant, and distinctly feminine. "That's not so bad as I thought," I announced and let my aunt smell it on me. She had to agree and even said I could have it, as she wouldn't use it. On top of that, she also gave me the similarly rejected Lily & Spice. While Love Potion No. 9 probably won't become my favorite, I'm still glad to now own such a surprising and multifaceted fragrance. Oh yes, spontaneous gifts are really great!

With this razor-sharp scent, I couldn't resist myself. However, only if I were a man wearing this fragrance. Then, as a woman, I would be inclined to chase after myself. But I would have to be the woman. Or a man? Uhhhm -- I'm getting confused now. Anyway: What I mean to say is that this is an extremely seductive scent, but clearly mislabelled. "For Ladies"? This concoction is not a Boxershorts-Dropper, but a Palmers-Top-Panty-Dropper, for heaven's sake! At least I would much rather smell it on a man than on myself. So: The labelling is already wrong in my opinion. The fragrance pyramid is correct to some extent, except that the floral and cozy accords hide behind the strong shoulder of the rugged accords. From the very beginning, masculine, core patchouli crowns the entire composition. In the top note, slightly scratchy rosewood overpowers the mandarin and bergamot. In the heart note, I mainly smell darkly singed ylang-ylang. And in the base, testosterone patchouli ultimately triumphs, albeit slightly tamed by vanilla, amber, and musk. No question: For me, it's far too rugged. I can even smell something like "AXE Alaska"! But let's see how this stuff performs on my male guinea pig. I need to spray it on him: I'm curious to see how fast he can run away from me! (First, I should probably peel the label off the sample: Otherwise, I'll have to run!). Thanks, Peet!

A fragrance that leaves me feeling somewhat divided. The opening is a bit too harsh and scratchy for my taste, reminding me of masculine scents. But there is also a hint of elegance. Love Potion No.9 seems particularly suitable for ladies like Marlene Dietrich. Sporty, elegant, and in a pantsuit or a slightly stricter costume.

Love Potion No.9 for Ladies is a rather ladylike yet elegantly appealing perfume that both young and older ladies can wear, I think! This perfume reminds me a lot of Dune by Dior; it has something of that scent, I think it might be broom, as it is also included in Dune! The typical sweet scent of hay-like broom is quite noticeable here.

I’ve fallen in love! I’ve just gone crazy for Love Potion No.9! Sprayed, smelled = in love! WOW, what an amazing scent! Exactly WHAT I’ve always been looking for! An excellently balanced creation! A composition of fragrance notes that I love so much! Rosewood, jasmine... beautiful jasmine, a hint of mandarin, perfectly balanced with musk, patchouli, and vanilla!

In my opinion, this scent is not for women. Too intrusive, too herbal, too strong, and razor-sharp. And, dear owners and enthusiasts present, please forgive me, it smells unpleasant in places. Whether it's an excess of jasmine-rose-ylang-ylang, the carroty iris root combined with a "dirty" patchouli... I don't know! I just thought at times, "No way, right?".

You have a promising name. I fell in love with you immediately and wear you in every season, but not every day. Delightfully dark, herbaceous, bittersweet. You are not to everyone's taste because you are difficult to handle. I love you for ever

Neroli Portofino opens with a blast of exotic smelling floral notes and a sharp-yet-suave citrus over a delicate base of thick, creamy musk (the type that smells very nice but could easily grow cloying in high heat). The first 5-10 minutes of this perfume are entirely transportive, and easily evoke a sense of the ocean, or at least of the "Italian Riviera" described in the advertising campaign for this fragrance. I can't fathom why people don't like this. That being said, the performance is horrible. 20 minutes after applying it all but completely fades into the background. Not kidding, this scent has all the longevity of an essential oil based room spray. Usually I tend not to think performance is a huge issue as I'm of the mindset that perfume should be used in moderation, and that you can always reapply--but considering the price of Neroli Portofino Acqua I would say that longevity is a bigger issue here, and even more so if you plan on wearing this every day. That being said, if you have infinite money to waste, then hey--throw a bottle in your gym bag and reapply every half hour. I would go so far as to say if the performance was improved and the price was lowered, this would be an almost flawless scent.

Up to a certain point, I actually don't care much about the price-performance ratio of perfumes; if a scent smells unique and is artfully composed, it stands alone and can cost whatever it wants as far as I'm concerned. If I can't afford it or don't want to: Well, that's just how it is. However, when I recently came into possession of a sample of Tom Ford's current "Acqua" flanker to "Neroli Portofino" through a nice giveaway win, I really thought I was going crazy during the test: It smelled so damn identical to "4711 - Echt Kölnisch Wasser" that I decided to verify this impression in an A-B comparison. Here are my notes; preceded by the results of an online price search: 4711 - Echt Kölnisch Wasser: Currently between €12 and €16 for 100ml. Neroli P.A.: Currently between €140 and €150 for 100ml. Impression: 4711: A bit greener and more herbaceous, more leaf than fruit. More refreshing. The familiar "metallic" bitterness. Initially even more intense than the Tom Ford. Creamy towards the end. Neroli P.A.: Very similar, but a bit fleshier, more mandarin-like. A little less metal, but soon the softest hint of amber appears, which you only notice because it's the only component that doesn't smell like Kölnisch Wasser. Quieter, but somewhat linear in the scent progression. Becoming aquatic towards the end, which doesn't play a major role due to the skin proximity that has occurred by then. I admit, those who don't like the classic metallic note in 4711 might be better off with Neroli Portofino (Acqua). Or even with ten, twenty other good - no: better, more specific - colognes that are available for comparatively inexpensive money. "Farina Gegenüber," for example, wipes the floor with Neroli P.A. The significantly longer longevity of the Ford compared to 4711 is advantageous: two hours instead of just under one. But please: Anyone who mounts the 800ml Molanus bottle of 4711 (around €60) with a few cable ties behind the driver's seat only needs a hose and an industrial mayo pump (maybe ask at the local fry shop) to give themselves a proper shower before work in the summer. You'll smell fantastic for the rest of the day and still save money. For these reasons, I cannot evaluate the scent to the best of my ability. And it doesn't have to be.

Tom Ford, always good for an outrage, that rascal. With the new Acqua from the Neroli Portofino line, he once again delightfully shows all the critics the finger - and not the ring finger! Was the original just an overpriced 4711 copy? Not worth the price at all? Like a urinal cake in a golden toilet? It was quickly gone back then & too light? Then here for you is the lighter EdT version of the Neroli luxury fragrance - even lighter, very similar to the original, but a good deal cheaper. Nobody really cried out for this, and innovation looks different; TF quality & creativity probably too. In the following comment, I will try to teach you why I still jumped at the Düsseldorf airport and treated myself to this refresher in 100 ml for vacation. It will be tough, but I’ll give it a shot. First of all, I like the original, as well as the 4711. Not love, but like, respect. Both. I even fancy that I can smell the more luxurious undertone in the TF and can distinguish both quite clearly when blind. Not that this justifies the 20-fold price in any way; you are always paying for the name. But it explains why I liked the Acqua version immediately on the test strip. Add to that the hot new release label & the knowledge that hardly anyone knows it yet, plus the reasonable price for a TF product, at €148 for 100 ml. Almost a steal ;). So one can definitely go for it, especially if you already have a fondness for the brand & expect salty-masculine differences from the original & undertones. Enough explained, let’s get to the scent. NP Acqua is 80% the original - a Neroli blast, combined with clean flowers, clean musk & a bit of lemon. The cleanliness in scent form, so to speak. It’s very hard to distinguish the two in the top note, almost harder than with the real Kölnisch Wasser. Acqua unfortunately doesn’t really offer salty, Caribbean characteristics, which I tried to imagine in the duty-free area. Here at the beach, however, it takes on an elegant character with 30 degrees, saltwater & sand, so I can hardly be upset with it. Even in the evening at dinner, only a few here smell so good, I must admit with a bit of pride :). It creates something strange, namely, despite more potent flowers, it seems sharper, even more sparkling & cutting. It has hardly anything to do with a natural lemon, more with a high-end product from the chemistry lab. But I still like it. Due to the sparkling aggression of the neroli, the whole thing even comes across as a bit more masculine than the original, which I certainly welcome, without my girlfriend having to keep her hands completely off it. It withstands the heat & humidity here, cutting through powerfully, then quickly fades. Too quickly, what I almost thought, not hoped for. Reapplying is a must, which makes it expensive again. Now I would just love to smell the also new Forte. Bottle: high-quality, beautiful, handy - top class with minimalist style. Sillage: so fresh & so clean - but only you really perceive it. Longevity: if the original was already too short-lived for you, you will be tearing your hair out here - 2-3 hours. Conclusion: those who hate the original will smell the devil himself here & see Tom Ford. Those who want to whirl stylishly fresh, pure white & with a sharp neroli bombardment will get a price tip here - of course in TF dimensions ;) The rest can, to put it bluntly, almost reach for 4711.

When driving to Italy in the summer, there are two moments on this journey that are particularly special - moments of great beauty that draw their essence from their rarity and transience, as so many beautiful moments do. The first is after crossing the Alps, when one - whether via Gotthard or Brenner, whether tunnel or pass - suddenly notices that the light has changed. As the Etsch Valley widens, and the first villages suddenly look a bit Italian, and saffron-colored light floods down the mountainsides, one searches for an Italian-speaking radio station and hopes - actually always in vain - for Adriano Celentano. However, the second moment is even more magical, even greater. This is the moment when one - often between two tunnels, sometimes lucky enough to be lined with palm trees, sometimes just next to industrial ports and cranes - it doesn't matter! - can see the sea for the first time. It lies there, infinitely blue and sparkling under the blazing sun - and then comes darkness again (the next tunnel) or the next rundown industrial building in some gray-faced suburb of Genoa. And yet everything is different after this moment - one wants to roll down the window and hopes - again in vain, which is why I have it specifically for this moment - for Al Bano and Romina Power's 'Felicità'. From Genoa, it is not far to Portofino, that famous azure-blue village by the sea, which Tom Ford chose as the namesake for his Neroli series. He imbues the idea of 'finally arriving in Italy' into all these fragrances, which are blue and fresh and - yes indeed! - not unrelated to Eau de Cologne. Contrary to the original Neroli Portofino, which is quite enduring given that the flower oil of the bitter orange is a highly volatile one, the Acqua variant has something even more delicate and even more attached to the beauty of the moment. However, anyone who has the 'normal' Neroli Portofino has everything they need for their journey along Italy's blue coast - and does not need the Acqua. Conclusion: when the Alps widen, and I drive towards the southern sunlight - and the towns are no longer called Brixen, but Rovereto - I want to take Neroli Portofino (Acqua) from the glove compartment and take a deep breath of the scent of the south. And when I see the Mediterranean for the first time through Genoa's cranes, once again - while I softly say: 'Ciao carino...'

Neroli Portofino is one of the Tom Ford fragrances that I really liked back then, and I only had complaints about the sillage and longevity (*sigh* when do I ever not complain?). It's been a while since I had the scent under my nose, so I can't directly compare it to the Acqua here, well, what can you do :D Nevertheless, it seems like the right opportunity has finally come to test such fragrances, now that the weather is getting better. The sun is shining right now and it's noticeably warmer… but I know for sure that as soon as I pack away the heavy jackets, the icy weather will come back, argh! :D Hmm… Bergamot, Neroli, Lemon, Mandarin… all citrus scents that suggest the fragrance could provide a really nice freshness kick! But I probably don't need to mention that my cat's fur is already standing on end and he has long since made a run for it at the sight of the sample :D The Scent: The scent starts off quite fresh, it's citrusy and a bit zesty. The first thing that comes to mind is vacation. Vacation by the sea, vacation in generally Mediterranean places, where you get roasted under the blazing sun and a scent like this one feels really good because it refreshes! I can smell all the citrus notes that are listed, some more clearly than others. I think the bergamot and lemon stand out the most, Neroli is detectable but weak for a note that gives the fragrance its name, and the mandarins are only faintly present. And flowers? Yes, maybe a little, but too weak to really pick up well, so they fade further into the background later on. Over time, the scent also develops a light, pleasant sweetness, probably from amber. Initially, the sweetness is still a bit weak, but later in the base, it's about as pronounced as the remaining citrus notes. And so the scent remains until it gradually becomes weaker and eventually fades away, although I still felt that the Neroli lingered the longest among the citrus notes in the base. The Sillage and Longevity: The projection is sufficient at first for a freshness effect, but it dissipates quickly, as the scent is really not that strong. I'm sure it will be a bit more noticeable on very hot days, but I wouldn't expect much projection here. The longevity is okay for a summer fragrance, it lasts about four to five hours, more or less… The Bottle: The bottle is basically the same as most Tom Ford bottles. It has the shape of ancient columns, at least in my opinion. The rectangular bottle could represent the column shaft while the cap forms the capital,… possibly Tuscan, I would say, in terms of the order of columns. Anyway, the fragrances with fresh scent contents are light blue (which in turn beautifully reminds of the sea) and have a frosted glass-like material. I really like the bottles anyway. Hmm yes, the scent smells quite nice. But,… perhaps the following is due to the fact that I have tested so many fragrances, the scent doesn't seem particularly special to me now. As always, this shouldn't be misunderstood, because the scent composition is done well here, it smells good, refreshes, and is quite suitable for vacation or summer in general, but it also doesn't stand out from many other similar fragrances, and since the price is also higher, I don't find the price-performance ratio to be super. Nevertheless, it’s worth checking out. Be that as it may, it belongs (now independent of price and longevity) to the good summer fragrances that smell nice, as long as you like citrus scents. Everyone who enjoys that can definitely take a "look" here. The same goes for me for the regular Portofino, which I also find nice, but also for other summer fragrances from Tom Ford like Mandarino di Amalfi, which I would even recommend more, as it is even more refreshing and zesty.

The first time I smelled this fragrance in a perfumery in Munich, I thought to myself: Wow ... this scent reminds me of something I know. I asked the consultant if she had a comparable fragrance (since it was quite expensive for the small amount), but after several attempts by the lady, I realized there was nothing comparable. So I decided to go for this fragrance.

This scent does not make it easy for you. Great fresh-citrusy fragrance. One can hardly imagine a more suitable scent for summer, sun, Italy. Those who like Neroli will definitely be happy with this. BUT: The fragrance is not particularly innovative, and I can understand anyone who belittles this scent as "4711 in expensive.

This scent is truly a beautiful fresh-citrus fragrance. I smell it and am reminded of Italy, how I traveled to Tuscany with my family as a child. We stayed in a lovely Tuscan villa with many lemon trees, a huge pool, and a breathtaking view. This fragrance takes me back to my childhood and makes me crave Italy right away.

To get straight to the point: I like it. Really. But unfortunately, most people don't know what to make of it. It could be the grandma with the gold earrings at the bus stop, it could be the room fragrance of the next rest area toilet, but it could also be the well-dressed gentleman on the southern Italian promenade. I use it for the latter. A summer fragrance.

Citrusy-aquatic fresh summer scent. Very pleasant to wear. However, it is hard on the edge of bathroom stone. Longevity is unfortunately not convincing, which is a shame for the price. Price-performance is therefore rather below average. I still like it very much and associate it with holidays in Italy and good mood.

tested today after acoir made a blind purchase and saw a positive rating on parfumo. the bottle is really beautiful and out of the ordinary. Regarding the smell, I find it similar to one milion by paco Rabanne but the generic or the new smell has changed since its release in 2008. otherwise there is a resemblance I find with stronger with u leather by armani. It is a sweet, unisex fragrance preferred for fall and winter. hoping that this vius review was helpful

The Preparation Berlin, March 14, 1927. Today was her fiftieth birthday. As always, she was alone. Her husband had left her long ago. She had also long since gotten used to the solitude, but she made the best of it. Every year on her birthday, she went to one of the most beautiful and elegant dance halls in Berlin. She never had much money, but she saved all year for this one evening. She put on her simple black silk dress. She draped her deceased mother's pearl necklace around her neck. She touched up her lips with red lipstick and stood in front of the mirror. She was still a very beautiful woman. You couldn't tell that she had already passed her prime. She nodded confidently at her reflection and thought...-Less is more!-. And left the room. The Venue For the last few years, she had always sat at the same table at the edge of the dance floor. She ordered a bottle of champagne and observed the lively antics of the guests. The most beautiful gigolos from all over Berlin frequented this place as well. But no! She would not pay someone to dance with her. She was too proud for that and didn't have the money like the other wealthy ladies in the dance palace. One of the most famous gigolos was Caruso. You inevitably heard his name because all the ladies called for him and constantly vied for his favor and attention. He was apparently the oldest among the gigolos. He had black-gray streaked hair. A stately figure, and in his tuxedo, he looked like a beautiful prince. What made him so special were his lavender-blue eyes. They seemed to glow in the dim light of the venue. The Scent There it was again...this scent! Whenever dancing took place, she could perceive it. The scent was like a cool breeze carrying a spicy-warm zephyr. A fine and powdery-spicy lavender with earthy-bitter nuances from vetiver and a delicate resinous amber note wafted across the dance floor. It was like every year again when she sat at this table. This scent was so sovereign, elegant, mature, and in a subtle way, very seductive. Impossible to tell where it came from. This scent accompanied her every year on her birthday when she was here, and secretly she was already looking forward to encountering this scent again. Even if it was only once a year and she never knew who wore it. She could never have afforded such a beautiful fragrance. But she enjoyed it with every breath when it brushed past her. The Early Morning It was four o'clock in the morning. She loved this time in the dance palace. The staff began to slowly tidy up, and the venue had significantly emptied. But what she loved most was the sound of the band, which at this time played calm and gentle songs. It was time for her to go. She took the last sip of champagne and was just about to leave when he stood before her. It was Caruso. He stood before her, gently smiling, and said in a calm voice: -Madame...would you grant me a dance?-. She was startled and shy in equal measure and was just about to decline when he gently and tenderly placed his index finger on her lips and said: - It would be my pleasure...Madame. And don't worry...I'm off duty!-. Tenderly, he led her to the dance floor, and she rested her face on his shoulder as they danced while the band played their very last songs. And there it was again, accompanying her. The beautiful scent. The scent of the beautiful gigolo! The End

Vetiver, airy, graceful and full of restraint. A light buttery note, fresh and fruity intertwined. Broken, fragrant earth and strawy lavender blossoms, carefully garnished with fine pepper sprinkles. A enchanting, sensual promise.

Hello folks, I'm back. By now, you know what that means: Either I'm complaining about you ladies or describing a new fragrance. However, it's more likely that I'll be doing a bit of both :D But let's wait and see, I've just started. So today, we're talking about the fragrance "Noir Premier - Terres Aromatiques 1905" by Lalique. The year 1905 doesn't refer to the year this fragrance was first created, but is rather a homage to the year when perfumers Francois Coty and René Lalique first met and collaborated on perfumes, with a brilliant idea: At that time, fragrances were either sold in quite simple phials or in very expensive individual bottles, which naturally drove the price of a fragrance up. However, the two perfumers (yes, there were already perfumers in 1905! :D) then developed bottles with closures that could be produced cheaply in large quantities, fulfilling Coty's wish: namely, individual, beautiful, but also affordable flacons for each of his fragrances. This surely also increased the visual recognition of the scents. Now that we know this and all this talk hasn't really said anything about the scent itself, I think it's time to describe the fragrance, unless you enjoy listening to me ramble on endlessly here :D The Scent: The scent begins with lavender and lemon and has a slightly classic touch (but without classic fragrance notes like oakmoss), which makes the fragrance seem slightly more mature. Soon, the cardamom comes into play, giving the fragrance a spicy note. Whether the beautiful sweetness also comes from the cardamom or if it's already the tonka bean that is now becoming noticeable, I can't say for sure yet, but I suspect it's the tonka bean, as the fragrance also begins to smell softly powdery, and tonka bean often comes across as very powdery. In the background, I can now also smell some thyme, making the scent, together with the lavender, quite herbal and bitter, but still not sharp or anything, as there is also a strong, powdery-sweet fragrance note radiating alongside. A little later, you can best smell the spicy-sweet and bitter notes from a distance, but when sniffed closely on the skin, you can still detect the citrus notes. Over time, a further sweet note comes in with the amber, which becomes the stronger sweet note towards the base. Here in the fragrance listing, Orcanox is mentioned for this, and I assume it refers to an amber-like note, after all, Orcanox sounds like the term for an orca (killer whale), and amber is derived from (sperm) whales (even though most amber today is probably produced synthetically). The base is sweet due to the mix of tonka and amber, but the bitter notes are still quite noticeable, which together creates a nice mix, preventing the fragrance from appearing "just overly sweet." By the way, vetiver smells more earthy here than "grassy." The Sillage and Longevity: The sillage is good; in my opinion, the fragrance should be well perceived by others for a while, and not just up close. I found the longevity to be quite good at over eight hours. The Bottle: The bottle is tall and black, with glass sides where you can see the fragrance inside. If you look closely, the black parts of the bottle form the Roman numeral one, which is a homage to the first black bottle by Lalique, the "Quatre Aigles," which was also tall and black and featured a female figure at each corner (you can also see the bottle in a transparent version in image searches). On the front, you can see the first part of the fragrance name, while the other part is on the side. It is topped with a hemispherical cap that displays the brand's logo on top. A very beautiful bottle! Conclusion: So, I think Terres Aromatiques is a beautiful fragrance. It comes across as quite elegant, so it's probably not for you fire-breathing, devilish beasts with pitchforks in hand… :D Well, of course, you perfumers can use the fragrance if you like; at least you'll smell quite elegant while doing something totally beastly! :DD Why are you always so beastly, anyway? *sigh* Can't you be as cute as my cat figurines? :D (like the ones from my children's books "Skilled Cats,"... it was clear that I would do something with cats… :DDD). But nooo,… He he, yes, it's a fragrance that is especially good for the evening or going out. Not for partying, but for all other occasions. Due to its slightly heavy aura, I would categorize the fragrance for autumn and winter. Yes, I would recommend testing the fragrance; as I said, it's not just sweet, but in the end, it is especially a bit earthier, making it suitable for everyone, not just for younger people who only like sweet scents. The only downside is that the fragrance is not exactly cheap, and one should look closely, as prices can vary between 120 - 250 euros. And that's it for today. Have a nice evening and see you next time :)

These beautiful flacons, designed by the house of Lalique for its fragrance series, are simply eye-catchers. And even with the knowledge that samples arrive in simple vials, this beauty plays a significant role for me when selecting fragrances in the departure folders of dear fragrance friends from whom I get to "raid." Here, there is no scrutinizing glance at the fragrance pyramid; it’s simply: I must test this!! So it was, of course, with "Terres Aromatiques 1905" from this "black" Lalique series. The sample arrived; I had to spray it almost immediately, and my nose exclaimed: "Hey! Don’t I know you?" And the fragrance recognition truly works. Just a few days ago, I commented on "Cologne Pour le Matin" by MFK; this rugged, herbal freshie that I liked very much. Now both fragrance companions generously contain lavender and thyme; the original scent of the Mediterranean earth unites them, making them relatives from the same region. So I am visiting a kind of sibling reunion in "Aromatien"! Although comparisons are not really my thing. "Cologne Pour le Matin" is the more rustic brother of the two; more natural, fresher, and spicier. "Terres Aromatiques 1905," on the other hand, has dressed itself up a bit more; it seems more vain and is fruitier and sweeter. Lavender and thyme, along with herbs, leaves, and blossoms, also form the robustly spicy aromatic framework of this creation. They are immediately present and never fade away - clearly symbolizing the power of the southern earth, the well-known maquis. The delicate, fleeting lemon freshness that appears a bit later is accompanied by a pleasant, not biting or overly sweet pineapple scent. Cardamom spices things up and simultaneously beckons the delicate freesia: "Come on over! You are welcome!" Freesia scent is for me both fragile and powerful. I am always fascinated by how these little trumpet flowers can smell both sweet and herbaceous. They seem to possess a special scent secret. Before the base note rushes in, the previous fragrance notes still have a bit of time to develop and reveal their earthy intensity. "Terres Aromatiques 1905" is now the reflection of a landscape that blooms and greens, awakening all the senses. Vetiver embodies strong earthy moisture and fertile sensuality. Cupid with his bow now flits through the underbrush and herbs, enhancing the previous aromas. Here, (thankfully) the sweetness of the tonka bean is not fully exploited; it rather smooths the edges of the herbaceous power leading the fragrance. A somewhat overly synthetic amber glow forms the highlight of this fragrance composition: well, yes ... Although I actually quite like these golden additions, the result does somewhat perplex me. It seems to me here that this fragrance youngling has dipped a bit too deep into the pot of pomade: it shines. (Sorry, Lalique! Perhaps it would be different if I didn’t have "Cologne Pour le Matin" so freshly showered in my memory.) "Terres Aromatiques 1905" lives up to its name: a pleasantly woody-spicy fragrance that has set out to seduce at the same time. Against this backdrop, it enchants for several hours. Its spiciness lasts long, softening over time, becoming more balsamic. I know that this sample will travel on to Gelis. "Cologne Pour le Matin" stays with me, and I think she will evaluate this already very noble fragrance without regard to the "brother" and hopefully enjoy it as well. So it’s not as easy to objectively judge two similar fragrance masterpieces as I actually thought! Conclusion: Those who prefer something less rustic will find the right address with this tasteful, deeply rooted nobleman in aromatic soil. "Terres Aromatiques 1905" is flattering and refined. I wish it "Bon Voyage" and am already curious whether and how it can enchant Gelis.

When I took the first sniff of Terres Aromatiques 1905, I immediately knew that I would like to wear it, as it has the potential to win my heart. Until now, the Laliques haven't really captivated me, neither in a positive nor a negative sense, but this one has succeeded. Since I tested Creed Aventus and this one, I also know that I really like pineapple scents.

I have been searching for a lavender scent for several years that is similar to the set Lavande velours from the Aqua Allegoria series. Not too dense, not overly sweet, not heavily impregnated with other notes, fine and fluffy like a summer breeze. Here it is: Terre aromatique is a lavender field just like I experienced it when I was 15 years old in France.

This fragrance is worth discovering. The packaging is already quite elaborate, and the bottle is no less impressive, but the scent is a perfectly balanced dance on a tightrope. The pineapple combined with cardamom creates a harmonious blend, while the lemon subtly supports this and is simply brilliantly done.

I am in a small, cozy kitchen room. Sitting at the kitchen table with a corner bench, I am a child with my best friend, doing homework while her mother prepares a very finely crafted spice cake. Every now and then, a light breeze from the lavender bush on the windowsill wafts over. I am so looking forward to having a piece of this masterpiece later.

In the decade since its acquisition by Puig, Penhaligon's has undergone a significant transformation. The storied British perfumer, once renowned for creating iconic scents such as Endymion, Sartorial, Bayolea, and Juniper Sling, has pivoted to cater to a markedly different consumer base. This evolution brings both advantages and challenges. On the positive side, Penhaligon's has become remarkably agile in responding to market trends. More impressively, the brand has demonstrated a knack for creating hybrid fragrances that deftly combine multiple contemporary olfactory themes. Their latest offering, Al Ula, exemplifies this approach. This oriental fragrance seeks to transcend the global oudy-oriental phenomenon by ingeniously blending several current trends: sweet, boozy masculine scents; fizzy, creamy frankincense notes; and crisp vanilla accords with spicy undertones. From a 2024 perspective, Al Ula represents not only a faithful interpretation of recent fragrance trends but also a harbinger of future directions in perfumery. However, this shift in strategy is not without its drawbacks. Penhaligon's, once a bastion of British olfactory tradition, now risks being perceived as just another designer brand chasing the latest fads. The similarity between Al Ula and mainstream offerings like Boss Bottled Elixir or YSL Black Opium Over Red is hard to ignore. While not exact replicas, these fragrances share a common trajectory, seemingly driven by the same market forces. This transformation raises questions about brand identity and the balance between innovation and heritage in the ever-evolving world of luxury perfumery. Moreover, Al Ula's similarities to other Puig-era Penhaligon's fragrances - such as Halfeti, Cairo, and Legacy of Petra - raise concerns about brand cohesion and product differentiation. While Al Ula may represent an evolution of these scents, it inevitably competes with its predecessors. This proliferation of similar offerings could lead to a paradox of choice for consumers, potentially relegating some purchases to mere collectibles, occupying valuable space but rarely used. This approach stands in stark contrast to Penhaligon's traditional ethos. The classic Penhaligon's catered to a conservative clientele who valued timelessness over trendiness. These fragrances were crafted to be versatile, suitable for any season or occasion, designed to become lifelong companions rather than fleeting indulgences. A prime example is Endymion, a scent that, despite its lack of avant-garde characteristics, has remained a personal favorite for over 15 years. Its enduring appeal lies not in its ability to capture the zeitgeist, but in its power to evoke nostalgia - transporting the wearer to an era before the ubiquity of digital distractions like TikTok or Netflix. The longevity of fragrances like Endymion speaks to a deeper truth about perfumery: the most impactful scents are those that become intertwined with our personal narratives. They cease to be mere products and transform into olfactory bookmarks of our lives, marking chapters and evoking memories with each application. This shift in Penhaligon's strategy prompts reflection on the nature of luxury in the fragrance industry. Is true luxury found in chasing the latest trends, or in creating timeless classics that stand the test of time? As Penhaligon's navigates its new identity under Puig's ownership, it faces the challenge of balancing innovation with the heritage that has made it a beloved name in British perfumery for over 150 years. In its current incarnation, Penhaligon's has positioned itself at the apex of the luxury fragrance market, catering to avid collectors who often acquire scents beyond practical need. Al Ula epitomizes this shift, representing both the zenith of the brand's new direction and the potential pitfalls of such a strategy. While undeniably sophisticated, it raises questions about its long-term relevance in an already saturated personal collection. This fragrance, despite its undeniable quality, may struggle to establish itself as a staple in the way its predecessors did. It's conceivable that Al Ula might become a relic of a particular moment in olfactory trends rather than a timeless classic. The rapid pace of new releases in the industry, coupled with Penhaligon's own evolving portfolio, makes it difficult to envision Al Ula maintaining its prominence over a 15-year span. Indeed, it seems almost inevitable that Penhaligon's will introduce even more captivating creations in the near future, potentially overshadowing today's novelties. However, when viewed through the lens of present enjoyment rather than future legacy, Al Ula's merits become clear. It stands as a testament to Penhaligon's current prowess in fragrance creation - a clever, intellectually stimulating scent that offers significant pleasure to its wearer. This dichotomy between immediate gratification and lasting value encapsulates the challenges faced by luxury perfume houses in an era of fast fashion and rapidly changing consumer preferences.

As soon as you spray it you smell the plum and its a really fruity sweet one. Combined with the black peppar it gives some spice to it. Its a really pleasant suprise to say the least because the plum is not overly sweet but still sweet enough to make you feel like you just had bought it fresh from a market. After some time the vanilla and saffron starts to appear with the cardamom. The sweetness from the plum has dissapeared and turned to a more spicy vanilla. This is rather dissapointing because the plum was a really pleasant smell that should stay throughout the wear. The scent has now become rather unpleasant to say the least. Finally the tobacco comes in and saves this from being an absolutely mess. It gives this more rich feeling to it which I rather enjoy. Overall this is a rollercoaster type of scent for me where as you get this very sweet fruity scent to then becoming spicy. If it were not for the cardamom ruining this fragrance in the middle then i would have instantly bought a bottle of it.

I have just tried this new Penhaligon’s fragrance and I have been surprised by the modern twist given to classic Arabic scents. The softness of plum smooths the incense notes and the vanilla is the unexpected companion and binds everything together. I have just been disappointed by the longevity which I would describe as a bit disappointing.

Superficially, this name might initially please ornithologists, as "Alula" refers to the feathers on a bird's wing thumb. However, this joy is likely to be short-lived... upon closer inspection, Penhaligon's named their new creation after "Al-Ula"... an oasis in Saudi Arabia, which is home to the UNESCO World Heritage site Hegra, among other things. Once an important trading post on the historical spice route (specifically known for the incense trade), it is naturally a place that fits into the Trade Routes Collection, like Ernie to Bert... To begin with: Like my favorites from this "Collection" "Trade Routes Collection - Halfeti | Penhaligon's" and "Trade Routes Collection - Babylon | Penhaligon's," "Trade Routes - AlUla | Penhaligon's" is also in the top league. When I heard someone refer to this scent as "Herod-Light," I was, of course, immediately fired up; because Herod is my "signature scent"... What can I say: It's true! Generally, "AlUlA" may not have the indescribable depth of the PDM hit, but the DNA is certainly heading strongly in that direction and is extremely complex. With Herod, the heaviness prevents some people from wearing the scent during the day or in warmer temperatures (I use it year-round... but dose it accordingly differently). AlUla is therefore significantly more suitable for daytime wear. Right from the opening, sweet spices, paired with shisha tobacco and a fruity note, waft into my nose. Contrary to what the name might suggest, the amount of incense is quite low. Personally, I don't find that problematic, as the richness of the perceptions exceeds most of what other fragrances in this price range have to offer. After about an hour, the spiciness subsides a bit, and the scent takes on a balsamic/honey-like vibe. The plum also becomes more prominent now. What I find fantastic is that AL manages to never come across as heavy despite all its complexity. Gourmand nuances similar to Althaïr are subtly present, as are the fruitiness of some cherry scents like "Lost Cherry (Eau de Parfum) | Tom Ford." The pleasure lasts 7-8 hours; at least for me. After that, AlUla is still perceptible on the skin, but not as present in the environment. Conclusion: Once again, a great hit from the Londoners with the potential to become a classic. Niche specialists will again complain that it is too tame/pleasing and that they would have preferred a charred, oriental incense bomb; but I think it is just right... just as it is. P.S.: I wore this scent twice in the last few days and I receive compliments non-stop... even in the supermarket and at the snack stand.

AlUla is a fragrance that I liked quite a bit from the very beginning. However, I occasionally struggled a bit with the top note. By now, I actually enjoy this phase as well, and I have come to love the progression even more piece by piece. The scent starts with a recognizable plum. There are noticeable oriental spices present, but they are pleasant. In my opinion, the spiciness is by no means overdone. I find that the saffron seeps through a bit here, and even the patchouli hints at itself. Furthermore, the tobacco is already somewhat detectable, along with a super subtle smoky veil. Over time, AlUla develops a certain kind of sweetness and creaminess. The saffron becomes more intense, but it has two companions in vanilla and cardamom that make it come across gently and sweetly. I like this kind of saffron. As more time passes, even fruity impressions emerge. I can't quite explain where they come from, but they are definitely there. In my opinion, this smells really good and fits the overall impression of the fragrance. This fruitiness even gave me "partially" bubble gum vibes. Quite crazy! Additionally, the tobacco becomes a bit more intense, but remains very pleasant. The composition of all the notes fits well together, and the various accords and impressions harmonize nicely with each other. I can also rate the performance as very positive. I cannot confirm the rating of 7.3 regarding longevity. For me, it easily lasts through a workday. It is even still recognizable on the skin afterwards. I perceive the sillage as weaker, but it is not bad. All in all, a great fragrance that I have come to like more and more over time. AlUla is definitely worth a test.

And after 10 minutes, I found myself wondering what smells so good? The fragrance is oriental and heavy, but I find it becomes lighter over time. Unfortunately, it doesn't last very well on my skin.

REACTION! So, I recently received my bottle of Tom Ford Oud Wood Parfum. I generously spritzed myself and I can say - this is fantastic perfume!
