In the next change of direction, the bergamot flashes again behind the rose, and then 1898 completely shifts to vanilla, grounded with patchouli, preventing an exaggerated sweetness. Cedar adds slightly woody nuances. Thus, this flight continues, with brief flashes of rose. The whole experience is cool-warm, juicy-dry, sensual-daredevil, full of complementary opposites, and never really graspable, which keeps 1898 from becoming boring. The bottle is another piece of Lalique glass art that is unparalleled. The price has now dropped to under 200 euros on offer, making the fragrance even more attractive. I give it a clear recommendation for testing.

And once again, a fragrance gives me a beautiful memory. Of a place I have told you about before. Of that small Greek island in the northern Aegean Sea. Samothraki. There is a small town there. Therma. Near Therma, there are many springs and countless small waterfalls, interspersed with little streams and natural pools. A place of enchantment. On the way to the springs, there are huge and ancient fig trees. Their fruits can be picked sweet and ripe directly from the tree. The green of the fig trees lingers delicately in the air, and I sit by this little stream. Right next to me, one of the countless springs emerges. So fresh and pure. I drink from it, and the water tastes indescribably gentle. Softly and meditatively, the stream gurgles. The large stones on the shore are warmed by the sun, which powerfully casts its rays through the green canopy. Thick, soft, lush moss protects the old tree trunks and gives a wonderfully gentle feeling. Whispering, the leaves of the trees rustle a story from ancient times. Warmly caressed by the constant wind of the island. In the air, there is a magical scent of jasmine and wild roses. Accompanied by fine resinous notes of rockrose. Delicately green and spicy, shifting.....magically soft and gently ending. And while I sit by this little stream, I notice the lively activity. Countless dragonflies dance over the water. Some rest on the warm stones, their delicate wings shimmering in the sunlight. Their bodies shine and shimmer in beautiful colors. A peaceful togetherness. In the distance, I hear the bells of passing sheep. Caught in the illusion?....No, for me, this was a very special moment in reality. Illusion Captive 1898

Exit. The exit. The goal. The end. The glorious farewell to all that once was. The Exit fragrance is the scent that unites everything you love. It is the destination of a long journey through the universes of perfumes. A fragrance that completely replaces and fills everything that was with its presence. You miss nothing anymore because you have everything you always sought and hoped to find in a perfume. The Exit fragrance is more than just a signature scent because it wants you, and you want it until the end of your days. A fragrance that brands you with its beauty and grace and absolves you from all other perfumes that ever existed by your side. The last door you walk through to finally find peace, because you know you have arrived at your destination. This perfume - The Dragonfly Woman - Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 by Lalique could be such a scent for me! The Fragrance Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 is like the life cycle of a dragonfly. It begins in the form of a cocoon. A cocoon made of lush green fig leaves slowly begins to open. It exudes a herbaceous-sweet scent as it gradually reveals its shell. The scent of heavy and alluring rose nectar finds its way to the surface and breaks through the cocoon with a sinful, rich sweetness. It is the scent of a rose like I have rarely smelled. In the form of cinnamon, a body timidly emerges. Still transparent, but you can recognize a warm-spicy throbbing heart within. The heart of cinnamon begins to beat louder in the warmest and softest tones of deepest security. Then it breaks open and once again changes its form and structure. Delicate tendrils of powdery-spicy vanilla seek freedom and light and are the vanguard for what follows. An elegant body of resinous, glossy labdanum (cistus) comes to light. Adorned with ornaments of spicy-green myrrh. Slightly smoky, shifting in color. Filigree wings interwoven with cedar unfold with the scent of the finest and purest patchouli and rise to flight with an animalistic hum of tonka and jasmine in pursuit of the skies. Conclusion Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 is a flight on the back of a shimmering dragonfly that shows you its kingdom. A wild and elegant flight through the flora and fauna of sensual impressions. A gentle gliding through sweet-resinous and earthy air currents. A lingering on nectar-soaked flowers and leaves on a misty morning. Or a delicate-animalistic chase through the night that knows no dawn. Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 is as multifaceted as the eye of a dragonfly and just as elusive as it is. A fragrance that elegantly changes direction in flight or hovers almost motionless before you. Majestic, graceful, and iridescently beautiful. Longevity/Lifespan: An 8 to 12 hour flight through the Garden of Eden. Sillage/Hunting Radius: Initially very large. However, it becomes very anticyclical and fluctuates between strong, medium, and light. Gender: Hard to assess, but in my opinion, unisex. Type: A spicy-sweet chypre. Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 or the - Captured Illusions - is a perfume that astonished and left me speechless from the very first moment because it is so beautiful, unique, and magical to me that I don't want to wear any other perfume. Noir Premier - Illusion Captive 1898 could be my personal Exit fragrance. The goal of all dreams and the end of the journey. And from that moment on, it has already been elevated to my new signature scent, at least by me. And I wouldn't know what could ever dethrone it!

This is a very natural smelling fragrance. To me it really feels like a walk in nature. I get a green, dark and mossy scent, with hints of crisp freshness along the way. I think it's balanced really well actually. I get the lime and bergamot, as well as the lemon and pepper and lavender. There's also petitgrain, cedar and cloves. I really like it. I think it could be interpreted as old fashioned but I think it's a great fragrance for spring and summer. Like a crisp, spring morning this fills me with energy and hope. Definitely one to try if you like a green, slightly bitter and very traditional eau de cologne structure. If you are a fan of this style, then it will definitely appeal to you. Again, I am yet to find a badly made fragrance by this house. Really great work.

Penhaligon EAU DE VERVEINE opens with a somewhat odd smell to my nose--it might be the coriander and clary sage which together impart a slightly offputting dirtiness. Shortly thereafter, however, the composition smooths out as the lavender, vanilla, and cedarwood all reveal themselves in a delightful unfurling and swirling of notes, which includes just a touch of clove. The drydown of EAU DE VERVEINE is rather rich and complex, certainly much more so than I would have predicted from a fragrance with this name. EAU DE VERVEINE also has good staying power, thanks probably to the musk. All things considered, this is a well-crafted aromatic woody fragrance which I can recommend to gals and guys alike for warm-weather wear.

Eau de Verveine initially gives the impression of a zesty cologne, before various greens and herbs push through the rather fleeting citrus notes. Later, Eau de Verveine transforms into a musky, creamy, spicy lavender scent that almost possesses a certain warmth. I can't specifically identify the clove here, but I readily believe in the presence of this note - I assume that the warm-spicy impression couldn't arise without it. I also can't pinpoint a real base. However, since the scent lasts unusually long, it likely serves only a supportive function. The namesake verbena is probably not included as a fragrance ingredient, yet it seems justified as a name through the refined interplay of citrus and herbal notes. I prefer to wear Eau de Verveine in early and late summer, when the evenings are cool. Then, the initial freshness of the fragrance carries me through the hot hours, and the comforting warmth of the herbal heart becomes even more pronounced in the coolness of the evening. I greatly appreciate the concept here of a citrus scent that warms from within, starting fresh. I think I recognize something similar in the Eau de Patou from the Heritage Collection (btw: I love retro series...), whose even more pronounced autumnal warmth also arises from a spiced lavender. However, in my opinion, it's not clove responsible for that, but rather caraway. In conclusion - since this commentary has been quite sober so far - I want to point out that Eau de Verveine is one of the best fragrances not only from the Anthology Collection, not only from Penhaligon’s, but overall. Those who don't know it have missed out. And should catch up.

Eau de Verveine. Verbena as well, presumably lemon verbena. An essential oil or a scent that usually works quite well in summer, as it is fresh and light, but of course also smells good. A good example here with a wonderful verbena scent or vervain is Ninfeo Mio by Annick Goutal, which has stayed in my memory because I slowly got in touch with niche fragrances through a really dear friend, fragrances that were not Hugo Boss, CK, Chanel, Dior, etc… She showed me various Annick Goutal scents, especially Ninfeo Mio, as she was totally enthusiastic about the fragrance (rightly so, because it smells so wonderful!). That was quite a while ago… hard to believe that I knew much less about fragrances back then :D But enough about Annick Goutal for now. Because now comes a verbena scent from Penhaligon’s and as you know, I am currently testing more Penhaligon’s fragrances, as I have really started to like the brand since Lothair. And no, don’t look up the scent, you can probably guess that I liked Lothair because of its wonderful tea note… yes, yes, I’m a tea fragrance freak, you already know that! But honestly, Lothair has become a damn great scent and I would recommend you to test it. But now, let’s finally get to Eau de Verveine. Unfortunately, the time to wear this fragrance is probably already over, as summer is gone, but maybe it’s a scent to keep in mind for next summer?! And by the way,… while I’m testing this scent and writing down my impression, I’m also drinking black tea again! Ha! :D The Scent: Yes, the scent starts as expected with the fragrance of vervain and lemony notes that, while not sparkling, smell nice, pleasant, and fresh. There’s also a classic, more mature note along with slightly green and spicy herbal scents, primarily sage. I can only perceive coriander very faintly. And I think that’s a good thing, because whether as a scent note or real coriander, the smell is just dreadful, brrrr…. but so low and finely dosed, it can be overlooked :D A few minutes later, there’s a herbaceous note with clove and lavender (which both smell equally intense, by the way). I also smell something sweet that I can’t quite identify yet. However, this sweetness is not of floral origin. It’s probably the vanilla that can already be detected, but it’s still not clearly recognizable. In the middle or towards the end of the heart note, the scent is mainly characterized by lavender and clove, and slowly the sweet notes become stronger, although never really strong. However, the sweet notes can now also be better categorized, as the scent begins to smell of musk, as well as a little vanilla. Lemon, vervain, and all the other scent notes from the beginning have now almost completely disappeared. The later base smells a bit spicy-herbaceous with the mentioned scent notes of lavender and clove. Besides the musk and vanilla, cedar can also be well perceived at the end. The Sillage and Longevity: Unfortunately, the sillage is only moderate, and the scent will only be detectable for a short time up close before it becomes faint for oneself later on. The longevity is about five to six hours, which is above average. The Bottle: The bottle is clear, cylindrical, and has a large label on the front. As always, the name and logo are visible, as well as a drawing of a… a… what a mess, what kind of plant is that?? Somehow it’s not lemon verbena, nor the flower of limes, lemons, or cloves…? Yes, it must be something simple, but you know I’m not familiar with this, so don’t keep me in suspense any longer. Laugh at me for a moment, but then tell me what flower is depicted on the label :DD The cap, by the way, is clear, round, and has a yellow ribbon with black stripes at the bottom. A beautiful bottle! This Penhaligon’s scent is nice, but I find that the fresh or citrus notes last far too briefly and the scent smells more herbaceous and then sweeter than one would expect from the name of the fragrance. That doesn’t mean that the scent isn’t suitable for summer, but I had thought that lemon and vervain would simply last a bit longer. So, you can check out the scent for warmer days, as long as you don’t mind the scent of spicy clove, which is particularly noticeable from the heart note onwards (just like the herbaceous lavender). You should also like scents that smell a bit more mature or classic (just look at when the scent was first released, no wonder it has this classic touch, right?). Well, I’m at the end now, and my tea is finished (… darn! :D), so I’ll come to a conclusion. Eau de Verveine pleased me. Not so much that I feel I need to have it, but it’s nicely done and by the way, smells more masculine than unisex. Usable, of course, in spring and summer as a nice daytime scent. But honestly, I liked the initially mentioned Ninfeo Mio by Goutal better.

Fresh, citrusy, and herbaceous-green is the start of 'Eau de Verveine'. It feels truly refreshing and invigorating. However, the citrus freshness lasts barely a few minutes, as lavender quickly takes center stage. The green note of the verbena becomes a bit more robust and blends very pleasantly with the floral lavender. After about an hour, some wood and especially musk join in, but verbena and lavender remain dominant for the rest of the development. 'Eau de Verveine' is now a soft and really beautifully rounded fragrance. From the fifth hour, a hint of vanillic sweetness also appears, but unfortunately, this is already the final phase of the development. 'Eau de Verveine' is a pleasant scent that can especially delight lavender lovers. The best times to wear it are likely spring and autumn. It simply lacks the fresh note for summer. The projection is rather subtle, and the longevity is not overwhelming at about six hours. I thank Mörderbiene for the sample.

Black Orchid EDP has been titled "cucumber chocolate" by renown perfume critic Luca Turin, and it is so match. Not very far from the original version which is a nighty fragrance, the EDT flanker stays nigh with less chocolate of form sweetness that makes it capable for daytime. This sweet creamy air comes from the note he once used in For Man Extreme; tuber; to get the same fungal effect, and, honestly, the result is much better than EDP version. Nevertheless, Ford could not or would not get rid of that cucumber layer that blatantly dances in the opening till the heart layer. The EDP version is used by men as much as by women, that, to be straight, for me it is like men with 6.2ft height and 12 shoe size wearing pantyhose!! Black Orchid, both EDP and EDT, have strong level of carnality, nevertheless, at the same time both have kind of immaturity. A kind of oxymoron feature behind punchy insisting sexiness and incognito presence of character. Never mind, who cares! What is good is good and it sells so. 6.5/10
This review is on the edt version of the original Black Orchid. Normally marketed to women, this has gained some popularity with men as well. How unisex is this version? Please watch for more.

After a long drive to Neiman Marcus for Creed-related purposes, I nearly walked right past this beauty, sitting in a sad, dark, lonely corner. I'm glad I caught it out of the corner of my eye and ran over, "Ohh! The Eau de Toilette!" I became school-girl giddy at the opportunity to try this one, but sadly I had dozens of Creeds all up and down my forearms.. So, I only got to smell it on the card. First, so you know where my perspective is coming from - Black Orchid EDP is probably my absolute favorite. Though, admittedly, it's a once in a while, special occasion kind of fragrance. (It's more of a secret weapon!) Black Orchid gives you that just-fallen-hard-in-love stomach ache that sends your head swirling in a way you feel like you can't control. But wait a sec, I'm here to comment on the Eau de Toilette! The EDT smells, to me, almost exactly like the Parfum, just without that swirly, weak-in-the-knees witchcraft element. Oh, it's still plenty sly, seductive, and likewise gives you that tingly sensation after smelling it, but overall it's much more concise, approachable, and makes less of a fuss about itself. If you like Black Orchid, but don't feel up to making the statement it requires, EDT would be the perfect fit. It's a bit softer, with a little less smoke and a little more fruit, and altogether less polarizing. It's also more of a feminine take on Black Orchid, whereas the EDP seems rather unisex to me. All in all, if you dig the EDP, you'll almost certainly dig the EDT. They're both otherworldly lovely and unique.

Black Orchid Eau de Toilette is Tom Ford's third opus to the glory of the orchid. After Velvet Orchid and Black Orchid, two fragrances available in eau de parfum of rare intensity, Tom Ford softens his interpretation of the orchid with this new fragrance in an eau de toilette version. This Black Orchid is nonetheless original with its magical and mystical notes of black truffles and ylang-ylang accompanied by fresh bergamot and succulent blackcurrant. But this fragrance blossoms on a powerful festival of irresistible and bewitching black orchid notes. The base notes with consonances of chocolate and vanilla bring the gourmet and voluptuous sweetness of Tom Ford perfumes. As an absolute fan of the brand, i really appreciate the powerful side, the bitter smokiness of the dark chocolate and the somewhat "musty" tone. This eau de toilette is always dark and daring, without being heady. It's quite sexy, exotic, creamy, sensual, voluptuous, a bit provocative... A very enveloping fragrance, quite similar to the eau de parfum, although somewhat different, with some attenuated notes. Perfect fragrance for a chic restaurant outing. The composition is worthy of a voluptuous cocktail !! Top notes are black truffle, ylang-ylang, bergamot, blackcurrant. The heart notes of black orchid, tuberose and fruity notes follow. To finish in base note with Lotus, patchouli, vetiver, sandalwood, vanilla, chocolate and incense. This mix is not disgusting and does not give that feeling of being "suffocated". For me it's a mixed scent. To give you an idea, this fragrance reminds me of fresh truffles, and a bit as if flower petals were melted in dark chocolate... A real treat. It is a rather easy perfume to wear, but certainly not a perfume for young beginners. However, do not have the hand too heavy when spraying... The bottle is beautiful, thin, matte black with pretty curves. Surrounded by a small black TF "collar" enhanced with inverted golden writing on a black plate. Everything remains in the image of its elixir, the aptly named Black Orchid. The longevity is exceptional, the sillage is powerful, even enormous, and this for many hours... Conclusion: A classy fragrance, a safe bet in all circumstances. Wear it with caution, but always with pride. Thanks Mr Tom Ford. My rating: 9/10

Crazy strong, how is this an edt? Comes across as an edp or concentree, one spray and that was well enough. I get that awesome, sophisticated, deep earthy aroma of truffle. Lasts forever, radiates dang far and the drydown is more masculine. If you spray more than once and wear in tight quarters or work space then I wouldn't blame others for asking you to take the day off. This is definitely for cooler weather and more formal events, certainly not for going to a pub and watching a match.

I love the vintage vibe of this fragrance. A smoky Oriental floral gourmand scent which was released for women, but also myriads of men wear this scent.The combination of notes is lovely except the note of fruits for me.

Dear perfume friends, dear readers, Do you know my younger sister? Certainly not, and that is why I am asking for a bit more attention for the little one with this open letter. Our scent is loved by many ladies and gentlemen, often with enthusiasm and uncompromising passion.

"Let yourself go!" commands Vincent Cassel mischievously - he is more her nemesis than "just" her ballet master - Natalie Portman in her role as the fragile-frigid Nina Sayers in Darren Aronofsky's critically acclaimed 'Black Swan.' "Forget control - I want to see passion! Surrender yourself!

Bam! One thing the scent is not: boring. I personally have never smelled anything like this. I really appreciate that. Without a fragrance pyramid, I wouldn't have been able to say what is in it. But: It doesn't start off nicely. I don't find it terrible, but I don't like it either.

Seductive, dark, heavy. Images flash through your mind, but wow. It was a bit too much for me. Another heavy fragrance without this seductive touch is Montale Golden Aoud. For fans of heavy scents, undefined floral.

What does the remarkable success of Mr. Harrod smell like? I want to get to the bottom of this question today. The occasion? A fragrance from the house of Penhaligon’s, available exclusively at the legendary department store Harrods. But enough of the preamble - It opens with an intense plum note, accompanied by a slight raspberry nuance. Right from the start, oud and tobacco are also clearly perceptible. However, this is not a particularly heavy, oriental oud. Rather, subtle woody notes ensure that the scent does not feel overwhelming. It reflects the style of a British businessman even more. As the woods gradually recede, bright flowers - led by jasmine - and spicy accents take the stage. But two main characters remain until the end: the sweet, sensual plum and the smoky-warm tobacco, reminiscent of fine pipe tobacco. The longevity on my skin is about six hours, with the scent remaining quite close to the skin - which one would hardly expect given the intense notes. However, this makes it wonderfully wearable. Although the fragrance is officially classified as masculine, I find it absolutely unisex.

My trip to London had many reasons, but one of them was of course the search for an exclusive fragrance. The Remarkable Success of Mr Harrod intrigued me right from the start with its notes. Upon arriving at the department store, I immediately set out to find Penhaligon's. When I got there, I saw several bottles of The Remarkable Success of Mr Harrod and started testing them right away. The fragrance starts off very sweet but not overly so. Plum, raspberry, and cinnamon already promise that this is a very sweet scent. What I really like here is that the fragrance does not smell synthetic or sticky at all. As it develops, the sweetness remains and the tobacco becomes noticeable. The notes harmonize very well together. Unfortunately, I can hardly smell any oud, but the fragrance is still very successful. I wouldn't have guessed Mr Harrods would be so sweet in real life :) The fragrance convinced me and has made its way straight into my collection. Anyone who wants to have this fragrance should definitely test it first. It is by no means a blind buy candidate and stands out from the classic fruit/tobacco/oud scents.

Since 2017, Penhaligons has dedicated a character fragrance exclusively to Harrod in the Portrait series. Alongside many members and friends of Lord George's family, the supplier to the high nobility finds his way into the story of a very interesting and very English family setup. Undoubtedly, the fragrance is dedicated to the department store founder Charles Henry Harrod, who indeed became a court supplier and built one of the most successful and well-known luxury department stores in the world. How does this remarkably successful merchant, who amassed a considerable fortune, fit into the story of Lord George and his family? The imagination knows no bounds here. Mr. Harrod is depicted on the beautifully designed perfume box as an elegantly dressed, mustachioed man of a certain age with his avatar, a large brown bear. Due to his reliability as a supplier of the finest goods, as well as being a wealthy bourgeois with the finest manners and almost aristocratic features, he must have become a welcome guest in the Lord's house. Especially the ladies of the house, particularly Lady Blanche, enjoy the company of this successful charismatic man, who, after all, also supplies the royal household with all the goods that such a house requires. In the background, the main house, built in the eclectic style after a fire of the predecessor building around 1900, is beautifully depicted in the upscale London neighborhood of Knightsbridge. Alongside tropical plants in the elegantly furnished salon, one finds exotic fruits, fresh local fruits, a barrel of the finest tobacco, bags and leather goods, noble chandeliers, and selected silverware. The salon is refreshed everywhere by flowers, especially white blooms and colorful butterflies. This is meant to represent a part of the goods that Mr. Harrod so successfully delivers to the high nobility and bourgeoisie. But why the bear? This cannot be explained by the character attributed to him in fables, where he appears nice, friendly, good-natured, a bit naive, and simple-minded. Not exactly what one imagines a successful merchant to be. Nor can it be the bear's role on the stock market, as the bear attacks from above downwards and describes a declining trend, which certainly was not compatible with Mr. Harrod's success. It is likely the courage, strength, and persistence that Mr. Harrod brought to this avatar. And so we approach the fragrance. I must admit that, given the avatar, the brown bear, I would have expected a completely different scent. What does success and wealth smell like? Conversely, I honestly do not want to know what a bear smells like. To my surprise, the fragrance is distinctly fruity-floral. The scent captures the fruits displayed in his salon, plums, raspberries. I could also swear that I smell hints of pineapple and perhaps peach. The fruits and a light note of cinnamon, which pairs well with the plums, set the stage. Does it perhaps smell like this in the food halls on the ground floor of Harrods, where exquisite foods are offered? Without the fruits noticeably retreating, noble warm woods and white blooms join in. And I do not only smell jasmine; there is at least a hint of lily of the valley or another early bloomer. The fragrance becomes sweeter and is harmoniously rounded off. Oud and tobacco are used very sparingly and do not stand out prominently. I would have liked to have these more pronounced. A little cocoa, coffee, or even tea could have refined the selection, perhaps even a noble leather note. But here the perfume remains true to its time in the 19th century, when men confidently wore flowers in their buttonholes and the cloth around their necks or the pocket square was sprayed with flower extracts. Elegant and stylish, this is all the same. It turns the heads of the ladies of the house and flatters the nose. For me, the fragrance is also unisex. It is just as well perceived on an elegantly dressed gentleman as on a lady who is not afraid of bears. The fragrance has outstanding performance and should be applied sparingly. The bottle, like the entire Portrait series, is very elegant with the golden animal head, somewhat playful, but very detailed, making it a must-have in the collection for me. Unfortunately, it is only available exclusively at Harrods, which is why it has remained somewhat unknown.

Soleil de Feu's opening is kind of weird. There's an indistinct warm spiciness I can't quite identify along the lines of allspice berries or maybe even something like clove + bay leaf. There is also a very clear celery seed note here that's present in the opening for about 5 minutes, however that dissipates quickly. The heart is a tuberose tinged coconut cream supported by tonka and benzoin. It's thick and rich and delicious but not overwhelming, there's a subtle powdery suede like note that keeps it from smelling entirely edible. The sandalwood really comes out in the base of Soleil de Feu and reminds of that powdered sandalwood incense; it's delicate, slightly peppery, and supports the coconut cream accord and suede note well. Really gorgeous stuff!

Love how the initial spicy opening followed by the creamy notes. Sandalwood gives it a smooth, woody tone which I love. Quite a unique cozy creamy fragrance, perfect for fall. Personally I do not get too much floral notes from this but if you like a good creamy scent, you definitely should try this!

Soleil de Feu is a surprising blend of Christmas spices and coconut water, a fragrance that straddles the fine line between winter and summer. On one side, you have warm, comforting spices, and on the other, the fresh, exotic scent of coconut. It’s a rather unique composition, but for me, it’s a bit too peculiar. I’m not a fan, though I can understand why some people might enjoy it (after all, you could almost imagine it as a coconut chai, a surprising fusion of traditions). But for me, it just doesn’t click. Too offbeat, too hybrid.

From the first application, Soleil de Feu embraces you with a warm, ambery cinnamon, like a freshy baked cake straight out of the oven. The sandalwood and benzoin are also present, almost from the beginning, but as it evolves, they start to dominate. It's almost like you're walking on the beach and you come across a bonfire that has just been put out. Reminds me a little of Estee Lauder's Bronze Goddess but without the artificial coconut and sweeter and milkier, probably thanks to the tuberose. Pretty linear, kind of pleasant, much too pricey. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Dupa primul puff, te invaluieste o scortisoara calda, ambrata, ca o prajitura proaspat scoasa din cuptor. Lemnul de santal si rasina sint si ele prezente de la inceput, dar pe parcurs devin mai predominante si e ca si cum te plimbi pe o plaja unde un foc de tabara tocmai a fost stins. Imi aduce aminte un pic de Bronze Goddess de la Estee Lauder, dar fara nuca de cocos artificiala si dulce, si mult mai intim si laptos, probabil datorita tuberozei. Nu evolueaza prin multe stagii, este destul de linear, si desi imi place foarte mult, totusi, la pretul acela nu m-as incumeta.

Tom Ford's Soleil de Feu initially smells extremely elegant to me. In the second impression, it is creamy, bright, almost white. The white is like that of the sun, sometimes golden and sometimes beige, when it hits us on the sand. The fragrance has a beauty that I can only summarize in the following image: A woman lies on a bed.

Once I wondered - as a Tom Ford fan from the very beginning - why he so extensively avoided the white floral accord for so long. For someone who never shied away from iconic accords and the trends that accompany them, I found this surprising - especially since the Ford label has always been about making money.

Since I have become a big Tom Ford fan, I had to check out the new Soleil de Feu as well. As has already been mentioned here, I also find that many Tom Ford fragrances lean more towards the masculine than the feminine. This one, however, is exactly the opposite!

Soleil de Feu has been available for a few weeks now and is the fourth addition to the Soleil line from Tom Ford. After testing it several times over the past weeks, I can describe it a bit better, which is why I am writing this review.

In one sentence: A feminine version of Tom Ford's spicy wood fragrances. The scent starts off spicy fresh with smoky notes. Very quickly, a floral sweet scent (tuberose) joins in. In addition to the listed notes (benzoin, tuberose, sandalwood, amber), I can also smell pepper, coconut, cinnamon, and a bit of a dry chemical scent (similar to chlorine).

Élégance Animale 1989 is complex and deep. Sweet, smoky, leathery rose opening. Leather intensifies in the drydown, while that warm jammy rose clings and gives the scent more character and mystery. It's a luxurious-smelling fragrance that is hard to pull off and not for everyone. Unisex though slightly masculine-leaning. I like this and how unique it feels. I'll save this sample for *really* special formal occasions.

So, that was quite a nice shock this afternoon! You walk into your local perfume shop unsuspectingly and ask about the Noir Premier series from Lalique, knowing full well that it’s not on the shelf and therefore can’t be there at all. But what does my now somewhat eerie favorite saleswoman do? She opens a secret drawer and says with an almost diabolical grin... -They are kept under lock and key!-. There they were! Also, the object of my desire. Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989. It wasn't my first encounter with Lalique. Many years ago, I had a signature scent from Lalique called Lalique pour Homme Le Faune, which I loved very much. I have a great appreciation for Lalique; they create beautiful fragrances similar to Hermès, but you don’t often come across them. Not to mention the beautiful collectible bottles that are hardly affordable. About the fragrance As the name suggests, we are dealing with a "biting variant" from the house. A scent that doesn’t fit the crystalline image of the house at all, but that makes it so exciting. A saffron-dusted peach with a few splashes of rose geranium opens the scene. A spicy-fruity top note with a peach that doesn’t come from a can but is already more than ripe and sweet. Now, waiting for the use of rose and jasmine would be a waste of time because they are hardly perceptible or have been exchanged. For what? I would say for a small, fine dose of oud and civet. Or should one perhaps attribute that to gurjun balsam? I have been told that such an animalistic impression can also be achieved with it. Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989 is also balsamic-animalistic. But not in a way that makes you feel like you’ve been spat on. The fragrance has elegance and cultivated shamelessness. Everything happens under the guise of leather, which is also kept very soft and supple. And sandalwood, which adds a creamy discretion to it. The scent fits an intrigue or a little, dirty "slip-up." Lalique has gotten its hands dirty here. Exceptionally, not with crystal dust! If Lalique ever comes up with the idea of making a figurine bottle in crystal for this fragrance, it would probably be more than obscene and daring. I would even take out a loan or save for it. For sure! Conclusion Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989 is, as feared, very much to my taste. The name is program. This fragrance is elegant, spirited, frivolous, intriguing, shameless, gallant, extroverted, biting, wild, and..... unfortunately expensive! But I have my birthday coming up soon, and I can already hear myself saying: -Sweetheart, I’ve found something for my birthday!-. She won’t like it, I know that already. But she will have to get used to it! Durability: 8 hours of cozy purring. Sillage: Initially a bit biting. Everyone in the vicinity gets a scratch. Later, collateral damage is taken care of, and we become a bit kinder and calmer. Gender: Can be used by both without hesitation. Just like all the stated attributes! Bottle: Flawless like a gold bar. It feels that way in the hand too. Have I mentioned that the fragrance is really sharp?!

Cats, including big cats, are extremely fascinating beings: just the grace of their movements, their attentiveness, and the devotion with which they are occupied with themselves. Also the "dance" when they turn around themselves, as if trying to catch themselves - I could watch these cats, big and small, for hours. Yes, I am a "cat woman"! Rainer Maria Rilke felt the same way; not without reason did he write in his poem "The Panther": "The soft gait of powerful steps, that turns in the smallest circle, is like a dance of strength from a center, in which a great will stands numbed." This feline elegance, this primal animality has likely inspired the house of Lalique to compose "Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989". Thus, a woody-spicy oriental was created, which is both powerful and sensual. Fruits, flowers, and leather form the basis for an extraordinary fragrance creation. Sweet juicy peach, ripe and plump in its velvety skin, meets noble saffron; both are immediately drawn to each other in an intimate embrace. They seek a comfortable resting place, surrounded by fragrant flowers and leaves of geranium, fully bloomed roses with heavy dark blossoms, and thick branches with rich jasmine clusters, which shine as intensely from the foliage as they smell! What an exclusive fragrance society has gathered here! The finale of strongly fragrant leather and smooth sandalwood (these two also harmonize excellently) is introduced with a balsamic touch. For without a "balsamic fragrance bridge," a break in the scent progression would occur, which Gurjun balsam smoothly closes. "Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989" is not a clean, bright, and innocent fragrance. In its powerful sensuality lies something wicked, lived - an experience of a life enjoyed! Not an easy fragrance companion! But who would have expected that from a sample I received from Can777! Remarkably appealing is the already mentioned blend of yellow fruit, red spice, white and red flowers, and black leather. A fragrance painting of clear and vibrant colors that drive each other towards their completion. A true work of art that Lalique has created here. And of course, it also includes a bottle inspired by Art Deco in black and gold, which draws attention! This fragrance reminds one of a charismatic black cat with golden eyes: It is cuddly and at the same time willful, hissing and purring! "Noir Premier - Élégance Animale 1989" - black magic turned into fragrance!

Lalique describes Elégance Animale as a glossy panther silently stalking its prey.... An image that immediately finds its way into my mind's eye. In my mind's eye, which I admit is a bit whimsical, this panther belongs to a French castle lord and wears a negligee. Yes, just sigh, what can I do about it? What concerns me much more is the question of whether I can still trust my nose. Just recently, I dealt with Copaiba in my Malabrigo comment, which was uncharted olfactory territory for me - and now I believe I smell Copaiba again, even though it is not listed in the fragrance pyramid. Have the (fragrance) drawers in my brain gotten mixed up, or is it simply the case that from now on, due to unauthorized cost-cutting measures, only the next best one is drawn? Mr. Google knows, as often, what to do. No, my nose is not playing tricks on me; the Gurjumbalsam that I believe is abundantly present in Elégance Animale is described as very similar to Copaiba. It is also used in medicine for the same purposes as Copaiba, and additionally, it is used to produce varnish and lacquer. It is obtained from species of the winged fruit tree, which are primarily found in Malaysia, Sumatra, and Burma. The yield is even more abundant than that of South American Copaiba; a single tree produces not just 50, but 135 to 180 liters of resin. For production, a hollow is carved into the trunk, in which a fire is maintained. After this ordeal, the tree is given four to five years to recover. So far, so good. Whether one likes the somewhat bitter, woody-animalic scent of Copaiba or Gurjumbalsam is a matter of taste. I like it, very much. But - opened with a sickly sweet peach and covered from beginning to the unfortunately! completely non-bitter end with a thick layer of powder, my desire for joy fades. Fruits and flowers do not connect with the animalic in this fragrance, let alone cradle it; they provide it with a cockfight where the winner is predetermined. I find that boring and unfair. I would almost be tempted to say: Here, French chic is celebrated, at the expense of animals. That I read in the advertising that René, Marie-Claude, and Marc Lalique were great animal lovers, and that animals represented a periodically recurring element in their work, does not cheer me up either. In the only clever comment I find online (The Candy Perfume Boy), it is noted that what would surprise most about Elégance Animale is the fact that it is not particularly animalic at all. On the contrary, it distinguishes itself in a refreshing way from the pretentious nonsense that most animalic fragrances on the market produce. Among other things, through doughy wood and the fact that the animal here feels like plush. If you ask me, that hits the nail on the head. I am sure this fragrance will find its followers. As for me, I have no desire to smell like doughy wood. And certainly not like a stuffed animal, no matter how elegantly it may come in a black glass coffin and at such a high price.

At first glance harmless, sweet, a little kitten. I turn my back to the kitten. Then it leaps at me, powerful, claws in, is a b r e a t h t a k i n g! It has me in its grip, the sweetness is gone. Intense wood burns a bit, unmistakably. What does this remind me of, 1989? The turning point? The burning barricades? Was that what Lalique meant? Over time, the cat becomes elegant, but has clearly left its scent mark and reminds me that it could leap again at any moment!

Leather, dry, a splash of fruit, saffron a resinous combination that reminds of old times The Art Deco style is excellently embodied Very well-balanced, no animalic notes Job well done The varnish, the bottle I find is a 9.

An Eau de Cologne is always a welcome sight – provided that you do not suffer from 4711-phobia! Common thread of this type of fragrance is the typical, often dominant neroli note which more or less stands out from other citric notes. Such perfumes are available as true Eau de Colognes – which means that they exclusively consist of top notes – but also as regular Eau de Toilettes. Penhaligon's is competing with itself: next to the Eau de Cologne, we have the slightly floral Castile, with emphasis on the neroli note, voluminous and with comparatively long longevity. On the other side, there is the citric-green classic called Blenheim Bouquet. And in between, we have the Eau de Cologne. Here, the neroli note is quite dominant as well, but it is put together with a lemony note that is quite strong at the beginning. Not bad: on one side, we have the more robust style provided by a strong lemony note, on the other side neroli brings in a fine elegance. This is best of both worlds! The citric note in the top soon looses some of its strength, the neroli stays much longer. Maybe, also lavender is part of the game, because this Eau de Cologne “hovers” a bit. Penhaligon‘s Eau de Cologne is well done, fresh and rather citrusy. With these attributes, it gets near Guerlain's classic Eau de Cologne Imperiale which perfect airiness it might not quite achieve. This is not necessarily a con, it is just a shade different. It is sufficient to own just one of these simple, but very beautiful fragrances – there are no big differences. A good Eau de Cologne is a superb, short refreshment in midsummer, on a hot day. It is not supposed to last very long, because then it would become annoying. Penhaligon‘s Eau de Cologne meets all those requirements and can be recommended without any reservation.

Now after the first Spanish one, here’s also a first English cologne in this series, and although "Penhaligon's Eau de Cologne" has been chosen rather randomly (many thanks to Mörderbiene for the sample!), the transition could not be better. For this fragrance, created in 1927 (I rely here on the previous comment), is hardly English and very pan-European. I think it did not aim to be particularly original or very British indeed, but simply to pick up the German-French tradition of light colognes and take root on the island. Thus, the British gentleman, who during his educational travels, or possibly as an officer during the "Great War," had come to love the classic 4711 in Cologne or Guerlain's Eau de Cologne du Coq in Paris, could reproduce the fragrance experience at home in his at least equally beloved "Penhaligon's" shop and did not have to rely on imported goods; especially since during the interwar period, customs barriers were lowered everywhere. The cologne-appropriate very fleeting scent features the complete classic 4711 accord of lemon, bergamot, neroli, and rosemary, but comes across (which is not very difficult) somewhat softer, rounder, and more lemony compared to the original (and in this respect reminds one of Maravilla's "Feines Kölnisch Wasser"). The indicated orange content may also contribute to this. I am quite sure I can also hear a slight lavender undertone here, albeit much more delicate than in the last colognes tested in this series, and possibly also traces of other green herbs besides rosemary. Not directly unmistakable, but still a tiny bit special, this cologne has a darker, woody, or perhaps even leathery note that becomes noticeable after a few minutes, which vaguely reminds me of the diffuse animalistic element in "Coq" or even more distantly of the bubbling undercurrent of Habit Rouge, but these are really just the faintest hints. Thus, I find myself completely in line with the two esteemed previous commentators, who classify this scent as a solid, successful, and therefore also recommendable cologne that neither represents a peak of its kind nor adds any significant new nuances. That Penhaligon's has now discontinued this scent for the second time does represent another farewell of England from the continent, but it is less epochal and easier to bear than the withdrawal of the Roman legions in 440 AD (due to stress at home and the annoying incursions of the Angles and Saxons), the break of the English church from Rome in 1531 (due to Henry's marital problems), and the exit from the European Union in 2020 (because... yes, why actually...).

Aquae Mirabilis, later Eaux de Cologne, dominated the perfume market until the late 19th century and became the leading men's fragrance in Great Britain, partly thanks to Beau Brummell. These Eaux de Cologne were often sold by pharmacists and barbers, resulting in a multitude of different formulations. Walter Penhaligon, son of the company founder who ran a barber shop in London, created his own formulation for such cologne in 1927, which was reissued in 2010 as part of the Anthology Collection. Whether the original recipe was used unchanged or reformulated remains uncertain. The fact is that this Eau de Cologne is very close to its oldest brother, the original from Farina, certainly much closer than to 4711, the middle brother. The herb-fresh dynamics of lemon, bergamot, and neroli are boldly mixed with waves of sweet orange and spicy herbs, gradually drifting the fragrance into soapy realms, while the initial freshness remains almost unchanged. A - like most colognes - very invigorating water, also praised by Voltaire as "the spirit-reviving." Especially on hot summer days, a splash after getting up and after work works wonders. That the fun is soon over is inherent to the fragrance genre and does not detract from the wearing pleasure. To echo the wonderful words of my predecessor: Penhaligon’s Eau de Cologne meets all expectations and can be recommended without reservation.

I’ve sprayed this on three times now. The initial spray takes all the bitterness and sharp lemon, mint and lime and it awakens the senses in such a great way! I love how it then dries down to a slightly more complicated, almost muted fruity, woody fragrance. It’s simply wonderful! I adore it. Would I own it? Not a chance….. The longevity is as bad as I’ve known a fragrance to be. There isn’t even a remnant of this left on my skin inside three hours of application. Absolutely gutting, and for the price, unforgivable. You’d have to spent your whole time walking round with the bottle or a decant just to get you through the day! UPDATE: Still love the fragrance, had to try and persevere with it. Tried it with some moisturiser and ISO E Super….. Game changing! Stayed on my skin for 10 hours! Bottle purchased!

If you think of Azure Lime as an Eau de Cologne, it makes sense. By concentration, it is an eau de parfum, but by taxonomy it is an edc. Whether an edc should cost this much will be a function of your budget. Lime is such a tight note. It is so specific and so concise. Citrus notes tend to be sharp, reading as fresh and bracing, but lime is narrower than other citrus notes. There is no lead-in and no denouement. Azure Lime takes advantage of this sharpness. The topnotes are a blast of lime and turpentine, like a face-scrunching reduction of gin and lime. The lime note (wonderfully!) doesn’t grow softer. Despite the flowers, musk and spice notes that eventually join it, the lime itself never submits. In a classic edc, floral and spice notes broaden the chief citrus note (typically lemon or bergamot) and musks soften it. In what feels like a reversal, the lime bends the other notes to its will. The floral note (jasmine?) dries as soon as it appears and the musk note gives the lime more backbone than padding, lending a woody feel to the composition. Azure Lime stays dry and cool from top to bottom, ending on a quiet, dusty note. A woody/spicy, cardamom/cedar scent stays attached to the lime so that even into the basenotes, the fragrance has a juniper/gin sting. Azure Lime wears like and eau de cologne and should be splashed with abandon for full effect. It captures a very specific notion of luxury, one that I have to say I find appealing: the $10 dose of cologne. It is the anti-bling of perfumery. Forget the rare, the exotic, the over-the-top. This is the luxe of the simple done well. from scent hurdle.com

Much is said about the Private Blend line. Although there are many great perfumes from this line, Azure Lime disappointed me. That is not a bad fragrance, but I think it lacks character. It's missing something else that justifies its price, as with many Creeds. Its opening is wonderful, with some floral and citrus notes. However, its drydown is disappointing and mediocre because it leads to a common place of summer fragrances. The drydown is basically composed of woody notes, remaining with some floral tones, something totally harmless and boring. It has good lasting power and projection.

Azure Lime is sometimes treated somewhat like a stepchild among the established heavyweights of the Tom Ford Private Blends. Yet he cannot and does not want to compete with Tuscan Leather, Noir de Noir, Oud Wood, and the others. How could he? He is the little brother in a sailor suit, breathlessly trailing behind, perhaps shyer than the others, yet of a friendly disposition, and very entertaining once you get to know him. He is gentle and cheerful, opulent but not cloying, refreshing without being fresh. He tells a small, joyful story in which southern sunshine shines, and he tells it - if you listen closely - in the unmistakable language of his stronger brothers and more capricious sisters. He is a gust of wind in a stack of light blue sheets on a dazzling white terrace, he is glistening banana leaves after a brief rain, and he is a misted glass of sweet iced tea. And he is the gentle wave lapping in a bay marked by prosperity and good living, and the memory of warm afternoon sun on a white sheet. I wear Azure Lime in spring and summer - alternating with other perfumes. You can recognize the related disposition, the roundness, the very opulence here as well. It is just an octave higher than with the others. He bends perhaps one or two times less within the eight to twelve hours during which a fragrance changes on the skin, lingers longer in between, and may even arrive a bit earlier. But he entertains with his usual confidence, never becoming arbitrary, never thin. Conclusion: perhaps the most underrated of all Tom Ford Private Blends. One that deserves a second nose.

Pff… I'm just sitting here (well, while I'm typing this, which has probably long happened by the time you read this :D) and wondering when my internet will be back up. There’s been an outage with Vodafone for two days now, but there’s no explanation anywhere. No wonder that the people affected are throwing around some pretty unkind words to vent their frustration,… and yes… it's slowly getting on my nerves too *sigh* Especially when I see the red LEDs of my router blinking ominously… (and yes, I'm publishing this comment from my phone, at least that still works,…). I'm glad I still have a few samples to at least pass the time while I reach into the sample box and pull out a scent. And when I pull out a Tom Ford and am reminded of fragrances like Black Orchid, I think that the day can't get any worse… :DD But let's see, Azure Lime sounds quite nice just from the name. Lime does sound citrusy-summery, so fresh and presumably fragrant! Hmpf… I just see that this sample was also sealed with tape on the cap,… now I have to get this thing open… so much for the day not getting worse :D The scent: The scent starts off with a slightly classic aroma (like a barbershop, as it’s sometimes referred to here). It smells of lemon or lime and is quite aquatic. The mint is refreshingly nice and smells good, complemented by basil, which pairs well with the citrusy and fresh notes. A little later, the scent becomes slightly sweeter, but really only a little, as it mainly remains aquatically fresh. This sweetness could come from the violets. There’s also a hint of neroli, but otherwise I can hardly make out the rest of the heart notes (that is, the fragrance notes in the fragrance pyramid). In the background, I somehow perceive light, green notes. In the base, oak moss is listed, and now I understand why the scent seemed to me like a classic men's fragrance; it was the well-known combination of bergamot/lemon with oak moss (especially since the moss is already fragrant at the beginning). The sweetness becomes a bit stronger, and you can now also smell tonka bean, but it doesn’t last even an hour, so the scent in the later base hardly smells sweet, but rather just aquatic and citrusy. Overall, it’s quite okay, but not really great. The sillage and longevity: The projection is enough to refresh oneself and perceive the scent somewhat, but others need to come a bit closer over time. The longevity is about five to six hours, after which the scent is almost gone. The bottle: The scent comes in the well-known rectangular bottles that somewhat resemble columns. However, considering that the scent is translated as Sky Blue Lime, the bottle could also have been blue or turquoise like most of the fresh Tom Ford fragrances instead of being black. It still looks good, as I personally like the design of the bottles. Azure Lime is nicely made, but it also doesn't smell like anything special and is furthermore not particularly strong (which is the case with all citrus scents). If someone wants a little refreshment, this scent can certainly do well, but there are many citrus fragrances that smell much better and are significantly cheaper. To be honest, Azure Lime is not bad, but I find fragrances (by Tom Ford) like Neroli Portofino or especially Mandarino di Amalfi to be much better crafted, so I would recommend those scents over this one. The strength of this scent is merely that it sometimes smells like classic men's fragrances, if that’s what you’re into. The other two mentioned fragrances do not have this classic approach with oak moss. Oh, and the scent also lasts a bit better. Soo… the day is almost over, my internet still isn’t working, and the fragrances I tested today weren’t exactly stellar… a rather disappointing day overall *sigh* … the rain that has made everything nice and wet fits perfectly with that. All that’s missing is for my cat to get diarrhea, argh… :D I wish everyone a nice weekend… however, there will be new comments from me tomorrow as usual… because I’ve probably become a nuisance here *waaaaaaah* :DD

If you know the Private Blend line, you know that the name is the game. But he would be a poor salesperson if he hadn't also introduced me to a few. Rose and coffee weren't my thing. I had some from the Private Line.

I have to agree with Kankuro. This scent simply smells like a thin citrus water that absolutely does not last long on the skin. Even the good old AXE DEO would be better *laughs* Unfortunately, it can't be compared at all with the others from the line. Thumbs Down

A very unusual fruit scent, which starts with sparkling and juicy opening, thinking Prima Vera Prosecco with raspberries and apple slices mixed with the drink. Playful, fun and slightly ticklish on the those (must be the bubbles). Moves on to the nectarines and green plums, sweet and fresh, with a hint of apricot glistening on occasion. The fruits are many and for such a complex concoction they are amazingly well balanced and matched together. Each is distinct, but none overpower the other, the synchrony is most pleasant and elegant. Florals and spices are more ghostly than anything else, and, to me, most likely used to keep the fruits from running wild. Projection is very good, noticeable without being too attention-grabbing or suffocating. The sparkling, crystal notes permeate throughout the perfume's metamorphosis. The dry down is soft and classy, like the final accords of a great piano concerto. Unwinding and relaxing the composition into the skin. Feeling light and still colourful, as if you are hold a feather of a bird of paradise in your hand after it took off. Great perfume to wear in the fall or spring-summer, safe and distinct.

I always enjoy it when a comment on a fragrance contains clear statements, as I can learn a lot depending on the writer, or at least make some sense of it! Here, this would be the first comment, and I suspect that the previous restraint might align with my impression - I am quite ambivalent about it. Of course, I was aware that there is a better time to test than a late summer day with 28°C in the shade, but first of all, I don't have that in the room, and secondly, I would argue that an autumn-winter fragrance should at least be bearable in summer. I find the fragrance notes interesting, fruity notes darkened with dried plum, along with the spicy-sounding base...hmmm. This could actually be something for the good Holly! Well, after the first spray, there was an irritation because I think I smell tea, so certain that I quickly glanced at the pyramid again - nope, nothing there. The tea holds its ground, though. The plum note is not as dark and strong as I expected, and the jasmine note is at least not unpleasant. So, various impressions are swirling around my nose: Tea - shifts to fruity notes - then, oh my, caramel? - then I perceive jasmine blossom. This jasmine combo could be tricking me into thinking of the (jasmine) tea that I like to smell but don't enjoy drinking. (Flower water) In my opinion, this fragrance is indeed a gourmand, but I don't get the impression of smelling something particularly delicious; the other notes ensure that. This wonderfully tasty hint of caramel seems to be teasing me and slips away very quickly. Probably a dried plum/Cashmeran coupling or something like that - no, wait - when I press my nose to my arm, it remains caramel-like. Now I know what it is: this fragrance doesn't seem to be exquisitely balanced; it smells a bit "bumpy," the notes are simply not woven together tightly. It sounds harsh, but I have to say: it triggers a "neither here nor there" feeling in me. On the bay, it is currently relatively inexpensive. I bought a decant and will definitely test it again in autumn...who knows. In any case, the damage is low for me, as the "running alongside," "torn" notes, while not entirely harmonious enough to form a unit, are not unpleasant or disturbing at all. Conclusion: For fruit or gourmand fans, a possible test candidate, but not a compelling recommendation to test.

A fine example of truth in advertising, Penhaligon EXTRACT OF LIMES features, you guessed it: extract of limes! This bright citrus composition is very fresh and natural and perfect for the summertime. There is a touch of neroli here, but not much, and I find that the lime--both juice and rind--is much stronger than the lemon. The longevity is typical for this sort of composition, which is suitable for anyone who likes citrus scents. I recommend this high-quality composition for hot weather as a cologne or splash.

There were a few heroes in my very young years. Most of them - like Grisu, the little dragon who wanted to be a firefighter - quickly faded away as I grew older. But then came an English gentleman with the wonderful name Phileas Fogg, who wagered half his fortune in his London club that he could travel around the world in 80 days. Together with his servant Passepartout, he set off on the journey (which today could be done effortlessly in significantly less than 80 hours) and won the bet after an adventurous ride in literally the last second. What I particularly admired about Phileas Fogg back then was that unflustered gallantry that is commonly attributed to English gentlemen. I have since seen several English gentlemen who were not exclusively unflustered and gallant (e.g., in the context of beer and football matches), but Phileas Fogg - he was always in control, impeccably dressed, and hardly ever had even a speck of dust on his impeccable tailored suits. The Irish actor Pierce Brosnan played him wonderfully - in the late 80s, when he was still known as Remington Steele and not as James Bond 007. A gentleman like Phileas Fogg, I imagine, does not smell perfumed, never. He has a scent - only when one comes close - at most of some fresh citrus with just a hint of soapiness. And this fine, very British touch of citrus freshness is what the venerable house of Penhaligon's infused into its delicate Extract of Limes. After long flights (or car rides), one sometimes feels as if they haven't washed for days. A spritz of a pleasant fragrance like this (and perhaps a toothbrush) is often enough - and everything is just as it should be again. Conclusion: about Camilla Mountbatten-Windsor, the Duchess of Cornwall - at a time when she was still known as Parker-Bowles and rather uncharmingly referred to as 'the Rottweiler' (I liked her even back then) - it was once said that she would sometimes wipe herself down with a damp towel behind the open door of the Land Rover after a sweaty hunt instead of taking a time-consuming bath, and then immediately slip into her evening gown. Provided she took a drop of Extract of Limes from the pocket of her worn Barbour jacket beforehand, one might almost say - so what?

Lemons and limes are different types of citrus fruits, but they have similar properties and can therefore be used interchangeably, for example in the kitchen. However, compared to lemon, lime has a slightly milder acidity along with characteristic aromatic-spicy notes that I personally appreciate very much. I prefer to drink a Whiskey Sour with a mix of lemon and lime juice, sometimes even just with the latter. Penhaligon’s must have taken the opening sentence literally, as Extract of Limes is essentially just a lime twist on the classic Eau de Cologne, which olfactorily embodies the mentioned aromas. Neroli and Petitgrain seem to support the extremely naturalistic representation of lime. This fragrance concept is very simply constructed, but it works brilliantly. All in all, a somewhat different, but at least just as refreshing Cologne with typical longevity, which I greatly appreciate in the summer. And, as a side tip: In these crazy times, mood enhancers like this fine, invigorating water can work wonders - good vibes in a bottle! And the short longevity leads to frequent mood boosts - you just have to reach for the bottle often and a lot :D Another pleasant side effect is that due to the alcohol solution, Extract of Limes also has a disinfecting effect. Just like any other perfume, by the way. So I wish you a few particularly fragrant weeks, stay healthy!

Recently, I received a 15 ml bottle of "Extract of Limes" as a souvenir from a trip to London. Joy! And the joy continued even after testing it. I could hardly pull my nose away from my pulse point. And promptly, the mood-lifting effect attributed to citrus scents kicked in! I never thought that such a "simple" fragrance with so few ingredients could excite me so much! No surprises, but also nothing that could distract from the pure beauty of lime in combination with lemon. Petitgrain and neroli perfectly round off the scent without stealing the show from the citrus fruits. What is remarkable here is that this is the first citrus fragrance where I actually perceive the sourness, but without aggression, rather beautifully, refreshingly, and aromatically. "Extract of Limes" is a somewhat different citrus fragrance, pure, but by no means boring, almost extreme in its restraint, as it has no frills or unnecessary embellishments. It is also not an average cologne, neither in character nor in longevity, as it is surprisingly long-lasting despite lacking a base note. I love gifts like this!

I have now purchased this wonderful perfume from Penhaligon's, and it feels especially refreshing to me at the beginning, somewhat relaxing, yet invigorating. Extract of Limes is so intense that even the unopened cap smells of this wonderful perfume! Right after applying, this wonderful scent wafts into my nose. It is a blend of precious lime oil, fresh lemon with peel, and petitgrain, which is moderately to strongly present here. This mixture of notes is not sweet, but rather has a dry scent! One might think it also includes the peel of these fruits, as this water becomes somewhat dry in the further scent development! Extract of Limes has no other base note, except for the very subtle, sweetly fragrant neroli that comes in the heart base note. I can detect the scent of neroli here as rather light to moderate. In this beautiful water, the chypre notes clearly play the main role! For perfume lovers who enjoy refreshing, classic citrus perfumes, Extract of Limes is a true treasure worth trying! I highly recommend this beautiful classic scent; it has nothing artificial about it and is a truly good companion for summer, even on hot days! The scent is always worth a test!

Due to a misunderstanding, I ordered a sample of Penhaligon's Extract of Limes. I actually wanted to test the similarly named water from the company Geo F. Trumpers, which had been recommended to me by a friend. I thought, not so bad, it's also a traditional English perfume house.

Coarse opening of green vinegary notes immediately reminds macho verdant works of 70's and their brutal greenness but some powdery and woody air tones down this sour spicy aura. Vert des Bois is so similar to iconic greens like Halston and some others and less Tom Ford'ian. Gives me a sense of worry just the way classic greens do, but if you're a man for classics seize it cause no one dares to produce such greens these days. 3/5

'…our heads full of crazy ideas. Then he just said for fun: come, let’s go on a journey! But the smoke tasted bitter, yet Conny told me what he saw: a sea of light and colors - we had no idea what would happen next.' Thus began the very young Juliane Werding (guitar! On a bar stool!) in the early 70s her German cover version of Joan Baez's famous 'The night they drove old Dixie down' (which - and few know this - was itself already a cover). 'On the day Conny Kramer died' became her first hit. 'He often promised: I’ll stop! That gave me new courage. And I convinced myself - with love, everything will be fine. But from the joints came trips - there was no stopping on the slippery slope. People started to talk, but no one offered Conny help!' A bit naive, the lyrics sound after now more than forty years. The song is a wonderfully surreal time travel into a long-lost decade, told through guitar sounds on green meadows, from joints, bitter smoke and swirling colors, from illusions and dreams, it is wistful and sad. 'The last time he said: now I can see heaven! I shouted at him: oh, come back! He could no longer understand. I didn’t even have tears left, I had lost everything I had. Life just goes on - all I have left are the flowers on his grave.' Vert des Bois, this is a swirl of color in fresh vibrant green and bitter smoke, a bit wistful and sad - just like so many fragrances by Tom Ford. Its essence revolves around a kind of tuning note from bitter leaf juices - whether poplar, olive, or another tree. This central fragrant bottled green is complemented by resinous-smoky and sweetish accords - the plum is surprisingly and remarkably arranged as 'non-alcoholic' compared to the other two Private Blends - Japon Noir and Plum Japonais - in which Tom Ford has used plum. Vert des Bois develops a strangely vibrating warmth over the hours yet remains oddly cold. It is harsh yet sensual - harmonious and yet underlyingly damaged - and full of veiled nostalgia and foreign beauty. From jasmine, it has only a distant hint - just like the flowers on Conny's grave. Conclusion, in Juliane Werding's lamenting words: 'On the day Conny Kramer died - and all the bells rang on the day Conny Kramer died - and all the friends wept for him. That was a heavy day, because a world broke within me.'

Vert des Bois belongs to the Les Extraits Verts collection, along with Vert d'Encens, Vert de Fleur, and Vert Bohème, which was launched in the German market in September 2016. It is available in sizes of 50ml and 250ml. Appropriately, but somewhat lagging behind, TF presented his new autumn-winter fashion collection on 09.09.2016, which was heavily influenced by the ideas of the 70s. In fact, the 70s trend, if we look at it very closely, is already over. But one must consider: TF has always incorporated ideas from the 50s, 60s, 70s, and 80s into his designs since his Gucci days. Nothing can go wrong there; you just have to keep rewarming and repackaging the old stuff. TF is a master at this. Therefore, in my eyes, Tom Ford is a good GJ, a Garment Jockey. And because the clothing is so damn expensive and thus almost unattainable for me, I settle for the tears of the collection, which are the wonderful fragrances. So, fitting to the 70s look, here is the olfactory green late seventies flashback named Vert des Bois from the TF brand. For those who don't want to read further and want to know quickly how it smells, I provide the following information: It smells somewhat like the original Bogner Men, just a bit softer and more refined, so that women can wear it too. Very roughly speaking. Upon closer analysis, the elixir is indeed a bit trickier than the green 70s-80s scent bombs. It behaves similarly to the comparison (which has been made by many) of Neroli Portofino with 4711. This is, of course, very inaccurate and wrong. The scent: VdB has, of course, much more to offer on the mundane side, starting with a harmonious blend of mastic resin, poplar, a slightly salty note of olive tree leaves, and a pinch of ouzo. The pulsating green is underpinned with fruity plum, wild pistachio, and jasmine star dust. In the basement, we find a warm pepperwood note and highly concentrated oak wood absolute. Once mixed, the individual components are hard to separate. As is fitting for a good fragrance, something new has emerged, and it smells extremely green and warm. The longevity is enormous. On the non-mundane, or inexplicable side, it smells like the extremely twisted idea of a neo-structural greenhouse in the wildest fantasies of an LSD trip with many strangely beautiful plants... well, I should probably stop here. It smells fantastically woody green. The bottle: The shape of the 50ml bottle somewhat resembles a small square pepper mill. Overall, the product appears very valuable and elegant due to the heavy glass and the golden remaining parts (labels, spray head). Occasion: In my opinion, the fragrance is wearable for any occasion and at any time. Personally, I wear it in my leisure time. What do others say about it: Green, unusual, fresh, creative, cool, sexy. What I like best about it: As a child of the 80s, I already loved Bogner Men, and this is not unlike that. I love the unusual aspect of this fragrance and promise myself individuality. My available duel on the wrist: Bogner Men is much more casual and rough, but not entirely dissimilar. Italian Cypress is much woodier and resinous, hardly green. Eau de Gentiane Blanche by Hermès is much drier, rougher, and more one-dimensional. Pricing: Don't think about it and pay quickly with a card. By the way, a liter of good 100 octane gasoline costs only one five-hundredth of that. Conclusion: I like the fragrance, which for me is not so 70s at all. The positive earthy-green energy that the fragrance radiates was my main buying argument.

It seems more and more common of late that newly released fragrances smell 'just the same as' something that was released only a few years ago. I would've thought that a house as revered as Lalique would not stoop to these levels but I have just been proved wrong. It may be that my schnozz is malfunctioning or that I have become anosmic from the testfest I have been on since yesterday (doubt it tho'... the old honker is quite robust!!) but I swear that Nilang is almost an exact copy of Coco Mademoiselle. For the first 10 minutes at least and then it drifts in an 'Angel-esque' direction and even reminds me somewhat of Hilfiger's true Star ( did I ever think that was good??? ... can't remember!). I think the thing to do when I have some free skin space is to wear all three side by side and then make an informed decision ... in all fairness. It's really not a bad fragrance ... very sparkly and champagne like. It just gnaws at me that it's so much 'the same as' ... HATE THAT!! Where is the creativity? Expended on the (imho) lovely bottle spoiled by the floral arrangement stopper? More than likely. I'll investigate and then update :).

Oh, those miracles, that the human bravery and intuition creates! Sometimes they are wonderful and can save your day, sometimes they are anough interesting to keep you sniffing your wrist while wondering, what on earth is going on down there, in the deepest bundles of your body chemistry. First breath is definitely fruity, melon contaminated with a foot odor. The melon hides a bomb of powder, and I like it. Together with food odor. At times I am so unprotected against surprising fragrances... I can accept almost everything, if it is enough astounding. NILANG is. Second stage: Odor of toothpick after long usage. With a certain dose of kindliness I could call that „woody note”, but I definitely miss the necessary level of tact. Afterwards the fruits come back, a fresh blueberry is my tip from the list, but the end altogether is so animalic, that I would not wonder, if the perfume grew fur. Of course, if hair could break through the present heavy wax/resins. NILANG is one of the most interesting frangraces that I had the pleasure to meet. I wish it smelled better at the base, and I would gladly wear it, but the resinous end keeps me away. I usually prefer leaner scents. So sad, that I can not feel Coco Mademoiselle here, as mentioned by Coutureguru, Gold and Sherapop.

…“bravely!” The fragrance has nothing to do with the drinking from Mozart's canon; I just wanted to point out the lance-breaking. I don’t find it as bad as it is sometimes portrayed here. Certainly, it doesn’t stand out, at least not among the elevated mediocre ones among the women’s fragrances I have tested so far. It is probably not for the very few individual cases among our perfumes, whose collections or lists are already overflowing. But for those looking for a very affordable, distinctly feminine fragrance that is likely not overly widespread, it’s worth occasionally swimming through the bay, where it can be found for quite manageable amounts (in the lower double-digit range). The price called by Lalique on its own website is definitely not something one needs to pay - this is not an isolated case with this provider. To me, Nilang presents itself as subtly floral and certainly with a certain something (see below). Regarding the mentioned fruit basket (which could aptly be described as a fruit fanfare, borrowing this term from Angelliese), I’m fine with it; who is to dissect all that? I can imagine blueberry in the forefront. The prick mentioned in other comments does not stand out to me (unpleasantly); on the contrary, I appreciate the soon noticeable, slightly clove-like note, as it enhances the cornucopia of fruit. For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that my wife has also been bothered by a prickly note. Nevertheless, she wears Nilang quite often. For the daffodil - carefully used here! - it equally applies that it provides a botanical balance, especially in the middle hours, during which a gentle soapy note also emerges. Even the base is not nearly as cloying as the paper form might suggest. To be precise, one hardly notices it. The fragrance retains its floral-fruity basic charm until the end, when it withdraws to the skin after a solid eight hours, yet still remains present for a long time. Conclusion: Undoubtedly not a great hit, somewhat synthetic in my opinion, but overall decent, well wearable, and with a respectable price-performance ratio. I just wanted to have a little lance-breaking. I choose to rate it as middle-of-the-road.

Unpopular Scents No. 2 In my teenage years, the little cream pots from the baby brand "Bübchen" were very popular. When our teachers entered the classroom, they must have been overwhelmed by a cloud of peach-raspberry-apple fruit dwarf, because - and this was very important - it had to be reapplied during every five-minute break. Even today, I really like the scent of these Bübchen creams; it is simple, yet beautiful and not overly childish. Plus, I enjoy reminiscing about that time. If there were a blueberry Bübchen, it would smell like Nilang: The artificial blueberry note is very distinct, but not unpleasant. Real blueberries have, in my opinion, a minty-earthy scent that I have not found in any other perfume. Nilang is also sweet, delicate, and only slightly floral. It is close to the skin, has hardly any scent development, and a low longevity (about 4 hours). Nevertheless, I quite like it, simple as it is.

"Nilang" was the first fragrance from Lalique that I had the pleasure of testing, and it says nothing that it had to give way to others in the comments: this is not a value judgment! Like all the others, this fragrance also does justice to the name Lalique: it is as clear as glass, very lively, cool, and pure like spring water!
