With the exception of the men's fragrance "Encre Noire" (whose comment from me found surprising resonance here - thank you for that!), I am continually enchanted by all the "normal" Lalique women's fragrances - excluding the distinctly luxurious "Noir Premier" collection, which belongs to a different category. They are straightforward and composed without frills, neither creamy nor powdery - simply elegant and feminine, subtle yet very present! "Nilang" is no exception. The mini-spray is a bit leaky, so I was greeted by the fully developed fragrance as soon as I opened the envelope with the samples. Enthusiastically, I went on a quest for the cause and found "Nilang". Fresh summer fruits, with the exception of the always somewhat critically regarded mandarin, greet you warmly right away. Melon and peach come together for a refreshing sorbet; the mandarin is not much of a bother here. The still somewhat exotic lotus, whose floating leaves and flowers are so well-known from Egyptian art, fits perfectly with this fragrance opening. Freesias, like the daffodils, surely in white or very light yellow, enrich the already slightly fruit-laden creation with their delicate yet intense scent. Water jasmine, for me always a synonym for a young beautiful nymph, joins in fragrant harmony before the somewhat robust blueberry with its dark fruity nuance takes the stage. The always somewhat prickly clove once again provides a surprise here: the delicate, airy scent gains more body! The water nymph named "Nilang" was allowed to become a woman here! A fragile woman adorned richly with flowers and fruits, whose smile is so enchanting that one simply has to turn around after her! Will she meet her prince, who redeems her and ultimately makes her happy? Happy ever after? Who knows? The praline announced in the fragrance pyramid does not appear even after frequent testing - I do not miss it. Instead, all the delights of the erotic, sensual category unfold, which the initial clarity of this fragrance, which sometimes seems almost virginal, does not lead one to expect at all. Sandalwood - always a little on the edge of unpleasantness, appears with patchouli and amber as a tempting trio. For a moment, the impression arises: everything is perfect, nothing is missing! Perfect! But after musk and the creamy-warm, highly appealing vanilla join in, it becomes clear: the previous impression was simply wrong! It gets even better, even fuller, even richer: "Nilang" has lost its innocence; it now caresses the soul! And simply makes one happy! Summer-light yet expressive, "Nilang" fits almost all situations of daily life. Only in the gym and during athletic runs (even if it’s not exactly a marathon), it feels a bit out of place! The woman who embraces "Nilang" and surrounds herself with it will certainly not be disappointed. She is granted a few hours of this clear yet mysterious freshness before she has to reapply. In areas where it is better not to stand out, "Nilang", like the other Lalique fragrances I mentioned, plays an important role. The feeling of fragrant cleanliness, like a light protective cape, is a faithful companion. Even this light, unobtrusive scent reminds of its wearer; long after she has left a room, she is still present through "Nilang"! What more could one want? Having now had the chance to get to know these crystal-clear fragrance artworks better, I like them all! I find it hard to decide which one is my favorite! Fortunately, I have well-stocked samples of all of them - thank you for that! So I can think a little longer about which of the fine fragrance companions will move in with me. Unfortunately, it is not possible to host them all here: but for a while, we will enjoy ourselves together! This harmony is exactly what is needed on some days: a little protection, a little warmth - the name Lalique stands for that for me.

In the last few days, I had the chance to test some mainstream fragrances. Among them was this Lalique. I was already fascinated by the bottle of the predecessor, and the new bottle is at least just as beautiful. Less beautiful is the price of this little masterpiece: 1200€!

... no, not still wet from sweating, the scent is not that bad at all, in my opinion, it has been exaggerated a bit. Rather still wet because the sports clothes have just been hung up after washing. It sounds very natural, floral, and fresh, but unfortunately, the perfume is not that beautiful. Nilang sounds Asian, but hardly exudes any Asian flair.

This scent was sprayed on me in a tiny side street perfumery, and I liked it so much that I ended up winning a significantly cheaper bottle on eBay. If I hadn't gotten it much cheaper than in the store, I probably wouldn't have bought the fragrance. However, I have grown quite fond of it.

Today I am wearing Nilang by Lalique... In the pyramid, watermelon is listed among other notes, but to me, the scent smells like a juicy, overripe honey melon. The opening is loud and striking, and the similarity to Angel by Mugler is, at least for me, only minimal. It lasts a long time on clothing, and these sunny accents warm and uplift the mood. I really like it!

My brother is a shipbuilding engineer and recently switched employers out of frustration. A few years at a well-known technical service company in a prominent northern German Hanseatic city were enough for him. A huge place where every few months a new management philosophy pig was driven through the halls, until even the last employee lost track of where the journey was supposed to go. But perhaps the undoubtedly well-paid management along with the equally generously compensated consultants knew what they were doing. One expects nothing less from big companies. Penhaligon’s may not be that big, yet some of their (product) decisions leave me puzzled. Why did you remove this fragrance from the lineup? A comparatively warm and mild, certainly not arbitrary chypre, which in my humble opinion definitely had a right to exist. Beyond typical top note behavior, mugwort contributes a decent portion of a certain something. Nevertheless, a jasmine-soapy clean impression quickly emerges, which I find well-groomed and also suitable for the (gentle)man. I wouldn't have come to chamomile on my own so quickly, but it is surprisingly clear when pointed out. I had already wondered what that mossy-herbaceous prickling was - it was a composite flower note. Amber, moss, jasmine, and a splash of bergamot are finely balanced. Although this is not at all to my taste - my rating should be understood particularly in this context! - I surprisingly enjoy smelling it in this case and take pleasure in the pleasantly rounded composition. In the afternoon, the subtle jasmine soapiness and moss complement each other. Not scratchy. Creamy. Herbaceous. Tending to be perhaps a bit more feminine now. From the seventh or eighth hour, the fragrance gradually weakens, but it remains perceptible for several more hours. Admittedly: The progression, aside from the mugwort surprise, is not exactly bursting with originality; yet Ormulu never, really never loses control over the moss and remains balanced until the end. Nice. I don't like it when stuff gets too scratchy. Ormulu is well-suited for those who, for example, do not want to subject their colleagues to a chypre bomb. Or for beginners in the world of more herbaceous women’s fragrances. Is? Would be. We’ve already covered that. Perhaps this subtlety, which may be interpreted as a lack of courage or even as a weakness, has become its downfall. Alternatively, a new pig may have shoved it aside. I thank Ergoproxy for the sample.

I was never a big Tom Ford fan. Never liked Black Orchid but it grown on me heavily. Matter of fact Ive been obsessed with it for quite a while now. Personally this fragrance could be worn all year long and to any occasion. Intoxicating, elegant, sexy. Absolutely unisex The plum heavy opening is amazing with the various spices and chocolaty patchouli later dominating the scent. Lasts all day long and projects very well. But obviously not everyone will like it, like me back in the day. It’s an absolutely stunning and unique fragrance that’s worth the hype and i believe it’s a must try. It’s a modern classic at this point even tho it got reformulated.

I love vampiric, dark, sweet but earthy scents. That's why I also loved Black Orchid edp, however I wasn't always in the mood for the very earthy and damp truffle. Sometimes I want to feel like I'm in an abandoned, haunted castle prancing around in a silken dress with a glass of red wine, enchanted by Count Orlok's lingering spirit, and not a tomb. With the edp the truffle was sometimes all I got, overpowering the sweetness entirely. Like spilled wine in decaying moss as I'm fleeing the castle of an awakened Nosferatu.

I expected much better from a Tom Ford scent, especially considering how many people gave it a 10/10... Where is the clove? Where is the plum? Both notes are barely there! (I only tried this scent BECAUSE of the cloves and plum!) Patchouli is also absent, not even a faint memory of it. What's dominating is, what I guess, supposed to be the "orchid" smell (supported by tuberose). I admit, I haven't smelled many perfumes with the orchid note but this smells like a generic fresh and nearly aquatic floral scent! Which is the opposite of what the notes promise! Zero spices, it's so underwhelming... The longevity is also average, but I guess it's an EdT, so I shouldn't expect much (although Dior Poison EdT lasts me all day, but Poison is special). I do get the chocolate-y smell from it that other people report, that's true. Although, I couldn't give less of a damn about chocolate, when cloves and plum were promised and not delivered! This smells like a rich person who tries to substitute the lack of personality with money. I'm out.

I had the rare opportunity to test a version of the classic by Tom Ford over the last three days: Black Orchid (2023) Eau de Toilette , Black Orchid Eau de Parfum , and Black Orchid Parfum . I will try to outline which version might be the best for you in the following reviews. Even though one might easily assume that only the concentration of the fragrance oil differs and that the scents do not distinguish themselves otherwise, both the ingredient list and the real test show that each version presents the orchid in a different light. Black Orchid (2023) Eau de Toilette is, in my opinion, the most expressive and loudest scent of all the versions. The opening creates an enormous sweetness that almost leans towards a chewing gum direction but fades relatively quickly and then transitions into the fruity-floral heart of the fragrance. As it develops, the orchid scent becomes creamier until it completely bids farewell. I feel that this version of the fragrance might appeal more to younger women because it is floral/fruity/sweet, almost playful compared to the darker EdP or gourmand parfum. The fact is, and this is well-known about Black Orchid, although it is a declared women's fragrance, men also enjoy using it very much. In numbers: Of the 61 users on Parfumo, 52 percent are female and a solid 48 percent are male. That is a huge share for a women's fragrance and underscores its unisex suitability, although I would describe this version as the "most feminine" of all. The performance is also commendable for an EdT, lasting longer than four hours with four sprays. The EdP and parfum perform even better, but still, hats off. The bottle is beautiful and has its own style, as it belongs to the Signature line. I find it questionable why they decided to keep the bottle entirely black without adding any color accents, as the scent is the most colorful and playful of all versions and certainly not that dark. Price-wise, there’s nothing to complain about, as I have already found 100 ml online for about 100 euros. For a Tom Ford fragrance, that’s almost a bargain. In fact, I would give my highest recommendation for the EdT variant, as the scent is relatively affordable, extremely expressive in its individual phases, and performs really well.

Background: Parfumos sends me samples, I test the perfumes sent without any prior knowledge and describe my reaction - that of an untrained dilettante. Moldy and musty, I emerge from my stalactite cave and conquer the nose that tries to suck me in with dark floral notes. Actually, it’s not a truly floral note, rather the obviously chemical imitation in a dark, heavy variant. When I then draw attention to myself with my penetrance, I can see how tense the interaction with me seems to be. Wrinkles on the face, half-closed eyes, and the futile attempt to decipher me. Something sweet-resinous softens the first encounter, even though I maintain: it’s complicated with me, even if my woodiness remains supple rather than rigid. If I could manifest in human form, I would be over 60, female, and take pleasure in making life difficult for others. A black widow, so to speak. If I am now smelled by a 5-year-old, I encounter not much fondness. There are cries of derision that, due to the censorship of this forum, are better left unpublished. Otherwise, I’ll end up back in the crypt!

Here, not everything that can be had from roses comes rushing into the nose in a massive wave. And yet, the noble blooms dominate. Not only these, but also their stems, leaves, and thorns. It presents itself with a slight green touch. At first. Only to then turn dark violet. Still green, but underneath. Not quite there yet: Woods! They are still developing. From completely unsweet, fuzzy-skinned, not fully ripe peaches and apricots. Not "lovely" or "cute," but very interesting. It’s somehow like being part of the harvest. In a plantation, surrounded by rose petals on one side and a forest on the other. In late summer/early autumn, when the days are still warm, but the nights and early mornings are already noticeably cool. Dew lays over everything and gently sets all the scents in motion. Before, in the afternoons and evenings, the scent of roses weakens again and wood and fruits take over the "regiment." Only to unite with her again at night and in the morning, resonating fully. Including "powdery" osmanthus, which drapes everything like a fine veil.

Scentrack Nicola Conte – Bossa Per Due Apparently,for parfumer Olivier Gillotin the role model for this fragrance was legendary Guerlain Habit Rouge. It has all the qualities of Habit Rouge, only little bit updated – easier to wear and cleaner. It opens with a yellow lemon kick and a touch of bergamot, while strong mint gives a huge green aspect. Gentle Pink pepper is present in the opening as well. Very soon flowery bouquet of fresh, but subdued roses and slightly powdery iris opens. This fresh, flowery, pollen-like, but still not feminine heart is gorgeous. In the drydown vanilla becomes a more pronounced, with just a touch of patchouli. In the background something woody, and almost animalic is present. This note is not strong, but still giving needed masculine edge. Noir EdT is smart, easy to wear masculine fragrance. It has some retro vibe, but still perfectly contemporary. It possesses a Mediterranean charm and refined relaxed attitude. Rating 8/10 More on Scentimentalwords

I spontaneously bought the black EdP version of Noir last year in-store right after its release because I liked it so much. Then I wrote one of my longest comments here, and since then it has been sitting almost unused in my perfume cabinet. A shame, because I still really like this powdery vanilla-civet combo / Shalimar homage. I only have a sparse explanation for not wearing it, probably because it's too intense for everyday use, I don't go out partying as often anymore, and when I do, the competition of scents in my closet is also not small. Now I was all the more curious about the lighter, more citrusy EdT version, from which I was lucky enough to snag a sample at the Parfumo meeting. It is definitely a Tom Ford, definitely a Noir. Because the difference to the black version is not very big; fortunately, it is simply called EdT and the bottle is lightened up. An L'eau or something similar would be too much to ask for. Noir EdT opens citrusy-powdery, but already here quite oriental. Civet and vanilla are also present, but everything is lighter, airier. From a going-out scent, it has become an opulent all-rounder. I probably would have significantly more wearing opportunities for the EdT than for the EdP. But you certainly don't need both. I particularly like the mint at the beginning, which immediately indicates the bright direction, although it doesn't stay for long. I found it amusing that the EdT somehow appeared not only more powdery but also more chocolatey on me, reminiscent of Hanae Mori's HM and other citrus-chocolate representatives at times. Overall, a nice product that in this version lives more from its references to masterpieces of the fragrance world than from its own ideas. But you have to be able to do that too, just look at Tarantino in cinema. I like the bottle in light almost better than in dark, although it naturally doesn't match the name as well anymore. The scent lasted no shorter than the original, which is commendable. The sillage was a bit lighter and less intrusive than with the EdP. Conclusion: I almost want to recommend the EdT more than the black bottle. It is definitely more versatile, but only deviates minimally from the established path.

I’ll admit it straight away - even though I appreciate the black monolith "Noir" in certain aspects - its playfulness with old fragrance concepts, its partially visible homage to "Shalimar" or "Habit Rouge" - for me personally, it is simply too "over-composed": Too dense, too heavy, too much pepper, too much sillage brashness. A "relieving" EdT variant can only be welcomed, right? Stylistically unmistakable, the brighter, more accessible, and more refined Eau de Toilette carries the "Noir" signature. A bit citrusy at the start, livelier and fresher due to a noticeably expanded sourness, moving even more towards my beloved "Habit Rouge". The animalic background, strongly reminiscent of "Shalimar", reveals itself after a few minutes - a powerful, powdered puma cage, as some critics who dislike civet might maliciously call it. Personally, I really enjoy this contrast of a clean citrus start and slightly sultry animal notes, and Tom Ford has clearly refined, reworked, and polished his too raw, angular, and also cloying EdP variant here. The long dry down of the fragrance convinces with a style that continues to dwell in the powdery, slightly woody, gently peppery, and still animalic nuances, where a few floral aspects may also be hiding. Thank you for this improvement of a well-intentioned but half-heartedly executed fragrance idea, Mr. Ford!

Tom Ford and the olfactory creations attributed to him are to be taken seriously. I don't know why I haven't paid more attention to them until now, because everything I have tested so far has been better - than expected, than the mainstream, and above all different! Different from what one might expect from the name, the stylish appearance, and the price, that is my opinion. Tom Ford Noir EdT is a powdery, metrosexual oriental. For me, it comes close to the scale of the sexiest fragrances, ranking just below Gucci Rush, which is equally cool and addictive. Nevertheless, I also smell a resemblance to Dior Homme, insofar as Noir subtly holds dark chocolate wood notes that take some of the sweetness away from the powder, coming across much more subtly and skillfully than, for example, in Kokorico. I wanted to explore Noir as a men's fragrance on myself after I had been chasing a former colleague for months, whose scent was the best until I found out what he was using. After that, the colleague naturally had his peace from me, but I no longer want to miss Noir. I think it suits the suit-wearing Suit Supply customer around 27 just as much as the casual mid-50s guy with horn-rimmed glasses and a title.

So - without the '(n't)' - is the title of a famous song by the British band Pulp from 1998. In the accompanying (truly, truly great!) video, lead singer Jarvis Cocker pulls all the Glamrock and Old Hollywood strings there are - he is alternately loud and quiet, androgynously sexy, glamorous and highly dramatic, almost painfully retro kitsch, overprocessed and self-ironic - including undulating showgirls with feather fans - and the clip is beautifully fascinating in its otherworldly way. Everything I wrote about the video for 'This is hardcore' can essentially be said for the fragrance creations of the house of Tom Ford: loud and quiet, androgynous and sexy, glamorous and highly dramatic, retro kitsch, overprocessed and self-ironic - yes! You either love or hate his fragrances for always being a bit over the top, a little 'over the top' - small divas and salon lions all wanting a stage and becoming whiny when they don't get one. Noir (Eau de Toilette) is not like that at all. The eponymous Eau de Parfum and its Extreme variant are, as is the similarly named Noir de Noir, hardly anyone more than that. Noir (Eau de Toilette), on the other hand, is quite normal - without assigning any value to the adjective 'normal' here. It lacks the Fordian attitude, the penchant for drama, and that fragrance-turned-diadem grip (the back of the hand theatrically to the forehead, eyes to the heavens, and a quietly suffering sigh). On the other hand, it does quite well without it. It is close to what one might call a classic men's fragrance, albeit quite modern. There is a misty, pale citrus, cool and sovereign, in front of a diffuse, sometimes only hinted background that could almost stem from a men's fragrance of the 80s, gently brought into the present. It is a bit spicy and a bit animalistic - and this 'a bit' is actually not very Tom Ford at all. Only Grey Vetiver (both Eau de Parfum and Eau de Toilette) and For Men are a bit like that. Nevertheless - anyone looking for another drama king will probably first search the Private Blends and not the Signature Blends. For everyone else (or those who are simply curious): try him! Conclusion: one of the few down-to-earth fragrances in Mr. Ford's oeuvre. It is not black or even just dark.

Wow! This is how I imagine a somewhat older, mature man, wearing a suit and bearing responsibility, charming towards his employees, self-assured, smoothing the waves with a smile, romantic and open-minded. Not every man can wear a powdery note. He can. Character to spray on.

Back then my 1st Ford, because it was affordable. It's a shame that it's no longer available, even though it could have been a bit stronger. Powdery fresh, simply pleasant. I always liked to reapply and searched for a replacement for ages. I have more or less found it in the layering of 2 Guerlain classics (with the help of Parfumos).

Lalique Azalee is a neo-chypre with patchouli, so basically a fruitchouli. The peach is very prominent here — it’s a good peach, slightly cool, not syrupy. Think realistic peach slices and peach skin. The bottle caught my eye first, and with my love for peach-based fragrances, I couldn't resist. At just $25, it was too tempting to pass up. But let’s be real: it’s not groundbreaking. It’s simple, linear, and doesn’t evolve much after it settles in. The base notes bring in a smooth patchouli, amber, and a dash of woodiness, which anchors the fragrance without making it too heavy. It’s a basic, easy-to-wear scent. If you’re looking for complexity, this might not be the one... The florals are pretty muted here, blending together in a way that makes it hard to pick out any specific notes. It’s just a generic, soft mix of florals that doesn’t stand out much. They’re there to add a touch of freshness, but they don’t take center stage. The fragrance reminds me of the peach scents that were all the rage in the '90s. Think Gucci Rush, but with an elegant, refined twist. Whereas Gucci Rush was bold and wild — definitely a "mistress" vibe — Azalee feels like a more grounded, stable version: the stay-at-home wife and mom. It’s a sophisticated take on a fruity chypre.

The inspiration for this beautiful new Lalique fragrance came from the "lys motif" René Lalique used for a flacon in 1924. The motif of the "lys noir" was based on Egyptian frescoes and reinvented by René Lalique, whose entire œuvre is teeming with floral symbols. So it isn't suprising that the company behind the Lalique fragrances ("Arts&fragrances") opted for a new floral scent in 2014. The azalée itself is a flower that is supposed to symbolize love, but azalée doesn't boast of a particular scent. Therefore the perfumers used roses to express this concept. I can smell radiant roses admidst a sunny garden, where peaches grow and lemons sparkle. The scent was announced as a "fruity chypre" and its base is indeed marked by patchouli, a fact I enjoy. By the way, the inclusion of bergamot and peach in the top notes rings a bell, and first I was reminded of "Mitsouko", but the rosy, flowery heart speaks a different language. There is no oakmoss in "Azalée", it is clearly a contemporary take on the chypre genre with the fruity-ambery aspect of the scent pointing into the direction of the popular "fruitchouli". "Azalée" is no bold, subversive fragrance, but a pretty mainstream flower in a beautiful bottle. Not too loud, not too brash, not dramatic. Very much in line with the company's classic style.

I love azaleas - on one hand because they announce spring as early bloomers in the garden, and on the other hand because I enjoy receiving them as a February child. On some birthdays, several gift pots compete with each other in color - and exude their fine, sweet-green scent. Although the azalea does not appear in the fragrance pyramid, I can still perceive it. When I opened the fragrance sample, I certainly felt that special birthday feeling. Freesia and peach also seem to gently come through this transparent scent. Rose and jasmine make it charmingly old-fashioned, harmonizing with the Art Deco style of the bottle. In fact, just the bottle alone could tempt me to buy it. Patchouli and sandalwood give the fragrance blend a creamy softness. Today, I experienced azalea as a promise of spring, and I look forward to when my garden azaleas curiously stretch their little heads out of the earth.

Every day the same old story: arrive at work, boot up servers and PCs, get to work. Daily I deal with What you see is what you get - it comes from computer jargon (wysiwyg = what you see is what you get) and refers to the screen representation as you see it here as normal users + its exact transfer as, for example, a printout on paper - just a brief explanation on the side. Today I have to install a new operating system on all PCs. It's called Azalée 1.0. Supposed to be quite user-friendly. Not groundbreaking, but okay. So I booted up the PC, inserted the disc, and started the installation. Already during the setup, I get a message "Warning, fruity! Do you want to save this information? [Yes] [No] [remind me later]" I click "Yes". "Warning! Are you really sure you want to save this scent experience? [Yes] [No]." For heaven's sake, annoying system. "YES"! Of course. Now I've got myself into a mess again. Nice backup of other existing software vendors, nothing new, better, just as cumbersome; but if that's what the average users prefer?! Although, I have to retrain these "dummies" even with this simple system. And then I have the name "somebody" plastered on my forehead. "Somebody has to help me", "somebody will sort it out"; well, that's how it is, because "Somebody" has to help these poor souls - sigh. So, finally, the software is installed and now floral textures are added. Oh, how lovely! Another email from the office... As if I didn't have enough work already... Wait... This is a virus. Damn. Roses everywhere on the screen. Oh God.. Ctrl-Alt-Del... Ctrl-Alt-Del... Ctrl-Alt-Del... Ctrl-Alt-Del... These stupid macro viruses. Just wait until I get my hands on the colleague who thought this was funny! *grumble* Ctrl-Alt-Del... This just doesn't end, with these roses. And how they look already... Ctrl-Alt-Del... So, pink, they really catch the eye; I can almost smell them! Yuck, I really don't like kitsch at all... Ctrl-Alt-Del... And then this sound accompaniment: squeaky, piercing... No, I've never experienced anything like this, it's unbearable. So, before I put myself through this all day... Ctrl-Alt-Del... Ctrl-Alt-Del... That's enough! No trace of wysiwyg; stupid software! "Shut down" "Are you really sure you want to shut down? [Yes] [No] [Okay, I'll work a little longer]" "Yes" I'm going home and treating myself to a hot bath, let the others deal with the annoying, biting, scratchy rose mess; but WITHOUT me!!

I just received a decant of this fragrance last year and my initial thoughts are that it beautiful, but it reminds me a few other fragrances. Out of the TF rose trio, I am most intrigued to smell Rose de Chine, which I’ll be leaving a review for as soon as I get it. Rose D’Amalfi reminds me of three different frags, the first and most prominent being Maison Lancôme’s Parfait de Roses. It’s got the same rose + vanilla + powdery vibe that Parfait has and tbh if I smelled this on someone outside, I would have sworn they were wearing PdR. I don’t get the comments that say they don’t smell alike because they very much do. Although, PdR has a noticeable boozy-ness to it that this doesn’t. Also, this to me smells nothing like any of the Delina’s, which many have compared Rose D’Amalfi to. null of them are as powdery as this perfume is. The rose is also more sharp in all the Delina’s and here, it’s been sugar-coated and mixed in with a bunch of almond-y heliotrope. TF was smart to create a scent that emulates the legendary PdR and I think they did it in a beautiful way. The second fragrance I’m reminded of when I smell this is MFK Oud Satin Mood, which is another powdery rose-vanilla scent. Both fragrances are extremely well blended and use the highest quality ingredients, and I think that’s why they remind me so much of each other. Even though OSM has that big, fat oud note, the vibes are similar. The third fragrance I’m reminded of when I smell Rd’A is MFK A La Rose. The combo of the rose and bergamot is giving the similar bright citrusy punch + rose. The only difference is A La Rose is more citrusy + woody, while Rd’A is sweet, fluffy, and powdery. This fragrance has a good projection, and while I can’t speak to longevity just yet, you can tell it’s a good quality fragrance that’ll linger on your skin for a long time (and it better for the damn price). It’s appropriate to wear in any season, but will be best in spring. I’m unsure of if I’ll add it to my collection, but I’m happy to have smelled it and have this decant of it. Very beautiful and feminine, and can appeal to those who don’t like rose scents.

Although swans are generally popular on public waters and in the adjacent gardens and parks, they hold a unique significance in Hamburg that is unmatched in any other city. For over four hundred years, they have been lovingly cared for here - injuring or even insulting them is prohibited under penalty - for legend has it that the city of Hamburg will lose its status as a Free City should the swans ever leave the Alster. And that can and must never happen. To make the swans comfortable, the Hamburg district office employs the so-called Swan Father. He looks after and monitors the well-being of the animals and - this is indeed a kind of event in Hamburg - catches them in late autumn and brings them to the so-called winter quarters at the specially kept ice-free Eppendorfer Mühlenteich. In March or April, he then guides them back - in Hamburg, the day of the return of the Alster swans is traditionally seen as the official end of winter - for it embodies a sense of departure. Lyricism. Youth. Departure, lyricism, and youth may also have been the impulses that inspired Tom Ford's palest rose-colored fragrance among his three rose scents - even more so than the namesake rose and the coast south of Naples itself. It has hints of baby powder and the delicate echo of a gourmand - sweet cream or very light toast - beyond awakening, tender blossoms - a harbinger of spring, almost childlike in its curiosity and innocence. It is tender like a mother's embrace - asexual and completely unfrivolous, if such a word exists. And amidst this youthful softness and sweetness lies awakening, a gentle urging - briefly hesperidic and cheeky, not mandarin or bergamot or perhaps? - like the white swans that, after the long winter months, swarm back from a pond to the fleetes and canals, towards the free Alster, towards the light. Rose d'Amalfi is a fragrance for spring, composed in weightless girl colors - sweet and powdery like a sketch in pastel - one for the days of reawakening warmth, for a new beginning, carefree and young. Conclusion: anyone who has ever seen the swans pushed back from their winter quarters to the Alster has recognized what spring is. For everyone else, there is this light and youthful fragrance.

Rose d’Amalfi was the first one I tested from the new Tom Ford line and is - Spoiler Alert - also the one I like the most. Rose d’Amalfi starts off fresh, but I can't specifically smell bergamot or mandarin. It could be the mandarin, but then it's the slightly sweet juice, not the peel or anything bitter. Since a delicate rose note is already present from the beginning, this fresh start is not citrusy. The rose becomes increasingly dominant over time, but not overpowering. If I had to describe the whole thing with a color, it would be very light pink roses. I don't know if that's strange, but I have associated colors with some fragrances for a long time (even before I started delving into specific scent notes and getting deeper into the perfume hobby). Perhaps it’s also the light pink liquid of the perfume that enhances this impression. Although only "Rose" is listed in the pyramid, I wonder if there is just one type of rose in it, as I perceive various rose notes. The impression evolves throughout the scent from a delicately bloomed light pink rose or even just individual rose petals to a scent that could also be more concentrated rose oil, but still not overwhelmingly strong. Sweet is the term that describes the scent well. Rose d’Amalfi remains subtly in the background, making it a lovely scent for everyday wear. It doesn’t disturb, but it’s also not particularly niche. I will elaborate on that shortly. From the heart note, a lovely (baby) powdery note joins the rose. It could be the combination of heliotrope and almond, although I don't distinctly smell either, which I welcome in this case because the notes blend nicely into this powdery base for the delicate rose. The scent doesn’t have much evolution; it stays with this sweet, powdery rose. However, it is pleasant to smell throughout, and the sillage is nice, but average compared to other TF powerhouses like Tobacco Vanille. But that also fits well with the scent, especially considering that warmer days are coming again, to which this fragrance is suited. The conclusion about the scent, simply as a fragrance: It is beautiful, really beautiful. A sweet, powdery rose scent that almost has a romantic quality. But it is a Tom Ford and thus comes with its price. Should we apply a different standard here? Can we really expect niche brands to reinvent the wheel? And is that even what we want, or do the scents then become “unwearable artworks”? This raises the next question: is Tom Ford even niche or more... well, what? Designer? Not really. For me, those are the mainstream fragrances from Armani, Gucci & Co. Well, some scent equivalent to haute couture. After many years here on parfumo and the accompanying journey through my own scent preferences (from “I discover the diversity,” to “I find myself in the niche and hype everything new with oud because it’s so special,” to “oud has entered the mainstream and somehow isn’t really my thing anymore,” to “I have arrived at the point where I can clearly say what I like to smell and what I don’t, regardless of how hyped it is”), it ultimately comes down to the fact that the fragrance must smell good and be pleasing. Rose d’Amalfi does that. Whether one wants to spend the money for it is something everyone must decide for themselves.

The Janus-faced metaphor of the 'face in the crowd' I have used before for another fragrance, namely Jil Sanders Strictly - in that case, because I found it uninteresting and not memorable - simply a perfume that I couldn't recall just minutes after smelling it. And yet, I sometimes find a certain charm in being 'just a face in the crowd'. On some days, I don't want to stand out, I don't need to shine - without feeling uncomfortable or wanting to hide. Sometimes I am just fine and completely content with low visibility. For such days, there are hardly any perfumes. When I follow the marketing campaigns for any fragrance - or the blogs and comments here, I always read demands for 'distinctive', 'characterful', 'unmistakable', 'long-lasting', and 'sillage'. I think that's great, and I often want that too. However, I certainly don't want that all the time. What is largely missing are beautiful, high-quality, and special fragrances that are like a white cotton shirt or good, well-worn shoes and do not immediately triumphantly scream 'classic!' as soon as you smell them - and which are not cozy scents but can confidently take a step back. In my comment on Penhaligon's Savoy Steam in the Eau de Parfum variant, I have already tried to express my enthusiasm. Finally, there is one that brings history to rock - finally, Penhaligon's is cool again! Here is now the Eau de Cologne, which - at least I have perceived it this way in several British Penhaligon's stores - is presented more as masculine than unisex. And even in the Eau de Cologne variant, Savoy Steam is wonderful - it is related to the Eau de Parfum - of course! - and yet different. Here is a fine gray-blue breeze for all those days when I want to be 'just' a face in the crowd. When the same melody, the same song is played once by a full orchestra - and once only with the piano - or sung a capella - you will certainly recognize the song again - and yet it will sound completely different, the mood it conveys will be different. Savoy Steam Eau de Cologne has less Jermyn Street grandeur (what a wonderful paradox - now that I write it), less rose and less fougère - both are there! - but it has more bath towel, more fine soapiness - and more poetry. For all the many days when it shouldn't be a grand appearance - and yet it is a truly fabulous fragrance. Conclusion: Penhaligon's has got it again. I never really doubted that.

This is a gossamer mist of pale loveliness from initial spray dusting the skin to total dry down, which on me is approximately 6 hours. This opens with top notes of crisp breezy bergamot and a very elegant blooming of cool-clear floral aldehyde of lily. The pink peppercorns then come rolling in, making a delicately spicy counterpoint in the midst of the luminous floral glow. (It’s not jasminum grandiflorum or jasminum sambac, it’s lily. There is no animalic taint or indolic fecality to pollute the limpid transparency of this gem. It’s not even synthetic jasmine. The scent is distinctly colder than jasmine. You can even look on the bottom of the Lalique box and the chemical ingredient list states that one of the components is LILIAL. Chemical name is butylphenyl methylpropional. This is a lily aldehyde.) Well bravo to the synthetics. This makes for a balanced and moderately fresh floral. The central notes soon progress into a 1st distillation type of ylang-ylang note and a very understated carnation which is bolstered by the already present peppercorns. Then comes the star of this creation; a ravishingly creamy, buttery, and silky smooth stephanotis. I adore stephanotis. Stephanotis is more sultry, deep, and rich than jasmine, more sensual than lily or lily of the valley, but much less heady than tuberose. It is also devoid of any mentholated, overly-ripe astringency or animalic fecal smelling indoles. I would bathe in stephanotis if I could. Lily of the Valley is the supporting cast member to the Stephanotis star here. The delicate lily of the valley gently whispers and swirls around the velvety Stephanotis like embroidered strands of pure white silk; a scintillating shimmer of freshness. There are tantalizingly subtle nuances of woody violet, a hint of cloves, and even the barest trace of melons woven through this delightful brocade of scent as it unfurls completely from top to bottom. All of this eventually comes to resolve into a gracefully sensual, refined base of pale musk, elegant blond woods, and a just a touch of rich-warm amber; it remains close to the skin. This is an exquisitely feminine floral fragrance that strikes me as being relaxed, casual, unpretentious, tender, intimate, and refined.

Lalique FLEUR DE CRISTAL is a seriously potent white floral perfume, rivaling some of the old school 1980s creations in its projection and tenacity. To me, this is a virtue. I am very disenchanted with the flood of weak juices being fobbed of as eaux de parfum. This eau de parfum is much closer to an extrait or parfum. So if white flowers are your thing, specifically lily of the valley and jasmine, both of which are in abundance here, then FLEUR DE CRISTAL may satisfy the urge to dive into a big pile of white petals which wells up in all of us from time to time. The composition is clear and sharp and bright, precisely as the name implies. In fact, the first thing I noted upon applying FLEUR DE CRISTAL is that this is an extraordinarily well-named perfume! It is so sharp and pointed, however, that it holds within it serious headache potential for those sensitive to strong floral compositions, so a caveat emptor is definitely in order for anyone considering a blind buy. One thing is for sure: if I acquire a bottle, it will be the smallest one available, because this is the sort of perfume of which I could not use 100ml of even in multiple lifetimes. I do like it, but only sparingly applied. The whiteness is almost blinding, if overapplied, rather like staring at the sun. Thank you Guusje for introducing me to this perfume! ------------------- update: I acquired a bottle of this creation and have decided that the fleeting opening is beautiful LOTV, but the cashmeran drydown swiftly overwhelms and becomes tedious after a short while. The headache potential is not due to the white floral but the aromachemical component, which is quite persistent. The bottle is somewhat amusing, with little plastic LOTV bulbs encased in lucite atop a hefty glass bottle. Not Lalique's best effort, imnsho

I am always pleased to see a new lily of the valley fragrance introduced into today's market. Muguet fragrances successfully straddle youth and classic for me, so I was very keen to try this. An opening burst of slighty soapy bergamot qickly turns into a lovely soft veil of lily of the valley and jasmine, that floats around you. The dry down is a softly wooded musk, I don't get any amber from this. Very elegant.

Would it be an outrage to say that I find Fleur de Cristal a better representation of lily of the valley than Dior's Diorissimo? It probably would be scandalous, but heaven help me, I think it is. Fleur de Cristal is the essential Spring-like floral. I can say this now as I attempt to wear this in freezing temperatures, and although nice, this fragrance only blossoms when I stand next to the heater. Lily of the valley of course shines all the way through this composition, with jasmine and stephanotis creating a soft, soapy and white bouquet. Fleur de Cristal could actually work as a fragrance for a bride on her wedding day. There's a beautiful tenderness to this fragrance that is both inviting and romantic. It's not a strong fragrance, but in this particular case the softness works in its favour. Fleur de Cristal has the ability to make me feel calm and clean. White florals have that undeniable charm that speaks femininity and purity. Fleur de Cristal is sensual too in a very strange way. It's not a come-hither scent, but it's intriguing to a male nose, like a symbol of innocence that a man can not wait to corrupt. All in all, Fleur de Cristal is a love that I find difficult to describe, but something that I know I need to wear every now and then.

Fleur de Cristal is one of the "easy and comfortable" perfumes in my scent wardrobe. I would not call it casual, it most certainly is not, but it is elegant and timeless, suiting almost any occasion and purpose. It opens with the (shock - horror LOL!) lily-of-the-valley (LOTV), instead of old-fashioned lemongrass or citruses. Jasmine catches up pretty fast, without becoming cloying, and not overpowering the delicate LOTV blooms. Bergamot is evoked as "sun bunnies", playfully hopping between the two flowers, while they achieve their synchrony. Then it takes a step back and provides a fresh, golden-green background without any acidity or overt citrus signature. I find this a most unusual and, probably, my most favourite execution of bergamot in a floral composition. Even though my favourite - the carnation - is listed as part of the bouquet, - I struggle find it, for the life of me. It think it is a white spray variety, the one which is very faint and ultra-delicate, supporting the soft zest of bergamot. Ylang-ylang adds to the golden-green background, allowing the duet of LOTV and jasmine hold the centre stage. Unlike most other LOTV fragrances, here the impressionism and realistic portryal of the florals are evenly balanced. Jasmine shifts the composition towards the sensual and indulgent facet, while LOTV and bergamot keep the impression of the real forest flower very well projected, without getting lost. I wear this perfume throughout the year as it sounds amazing in different temperatures and settings. It is perfect for an al fresco lunch/dinner as well as a boardroom or when visiting another country (although I would highly recommend to use it as an evening only scent in South East Asia, due to their cultural preferences). Whether you wear only a sliver of Fleur de Cristal or decide to wrap yourself in it head to toe, it will still remain elegant and unobtrusive. Its projection is strong but moderated by the well-thought and balanced formula and sillage matches it perfectly. A few good hours will pass before you get to its dry down, which for me, can be described in one word - " sunny". Sandalwood and amber project their gold and luxurious notes without being sharp or loud. I think it's musk and cashmeran (which also has a musky facet) that temper the other two, as well as the remaining bergamot, that completes the final, and nevertheless most uplifting, note. Fleur de Cristal is a perfect companion for a day in the sun (whether summer or fall), when you need a "pick me up" and/or a reassuring friendly embrace. Even during the grey, rainy days - a few sprays will transport you to the world of sun and meadow flowers, with butterflies fluttering in the air and a ripening pears hanging above your head. It does not need a special occasion to make its wearer become special and joyful. And there lies its soft but undeniable power.

Yesterday was a clear summer day, just the way I love it. A bright blue sky without a cloud in sight, the sun smiled gently and didn’t burn - and no muggy heat on my forehead, as a gentle breeze was blowing. Le soleil brille. It matched perfectly with the elegantly shaped crystal-clear Lalique flacon, with the embedded white flowers in the glass cap.

I find the scent to be like crystals, but just like the famous S...ski crystals, which sparkle like diamonds, yet are merely cut glass, albeit well-crafted. In the past, such things were dismissed as trinkets, but today every ballpoint pen becomes exponentially more expensive when it has a little artificial gem glittering on it.

For all fans of very floral fragrances. Fleur de Cristal starts off clear, delicately spicy, and heavily jasmine-oriented. The jasmine is lovely and slightly sparkling due to the bergamot. I find that it resembles Bvlgari Voile de Jasmin, only Fleur de Cristal has a much stronger scent aura and, like many Lalique fragrances, is very long-lasting.

Dear God, Lalique has created beautiful glass bottles for decades. And now these lily of the valley encased in acrylic glass. No trace of crystals. What were the designers and fragrance developers thinking? Is there even Stephanotis (wedding flower) and Jasmine in there? It feels very cheap and like a plagiarism mix. A light-sun-flower scent.

~ Inspiration ~ I also received a sample of this in a package. I am now familiar with the brand "Lalique," as I have several fragrances at home for testing. ~ Bottle ~ The special feature of the round glass bottle is the incorporated lily of the valley (branches). "Fleur de Cristal" means "Crystal Flower" and skillfully reflects the clear bottle with its floral accords.

I have this in my top 20 summer fragrances. I have most of Tom Ford’s summer private blends and this is the best for me. It is a sexy and long lasting unisex fragrance. I will always have it every year and love to wear it. It has everything the original lacks. So good.

Neroli Portofino Forte! This stuff is pure gold! The additions of leather and blood orange really do change this fragrance in a good way! It gives it a more zesty, spicy smell along with a clean soapy smell keeping the original DNA of NP and amping it up with some masculinity. You need both in your collection. 10/10

A fresh and green fragrance with neroli, orange blossom. To me this is taking a walk through a blossoming citrus orchard in the Mediterranean next to the sea. It's all of these things: fresh, warm, perfectly sophisticated. For a citrus, this has impossible performance, this is the single longest lasting citrus fragrance I have come across. The silage is incredible, the projection is incredible and I can smell this all day. If George Clooney doesn't smell like this when he's at his home on Lake Como -- he's doing it wrong.

Could it be that this is the most overpriced summer fragrance ever? 295 euros/100 ml are often demanded, and I wonder what - apart from the generally self-staged Tom Ford hype - justifies this approach. Much more interesting, however, seems to me the question of what necessity justifies the appearance of the 4th Portofino Ford and what artistic new insights the fragrance still holds. I would say: little to nothing. Once you've sniffed through the numerous summer Mediterranean scents, you would have to conclude with this "Forte" that it all has almost 100% already been done before. I think of Chanel's "Eau de Cologne," Dior's "Escale à Portofino," Hermès' "Eau d'Orange Verte," or even Creed's "Original Vetiver," all of which more or less delineate the territory that Ford is here - very exclusively priced - encroaching upon. A lot of powdery soft bergamot, juicy orange slices, which to me personally - and that may contribute to the "Forte" in the name - seem a bit too dense and too juicy. I don't know if it's again due to synthetic components that iron out a certain closed coherence in the fragrance; the fruitiness and juiciness feel somewhat flat and at the same time densely filling, satiating in my nose. Could it perhaps be the (labor-created) Italian coastal woods that evoke or solidify this impression? I certainly believe that all the fragrances I listed above achieve the summer package of orange/bergamot in a more delicate, natural, and also complex way (with the exception of Creed). I really expected more, especially given the 7.9 average.

True story: recently I followed a woman across half the city (by subway) because she smelled so great. Well, to be honest, we were on the same route anyway. When we reached the final stop, I approached her, and she told me the fragrance: Tom Ford's Neroli Portofino. Wow, it smelled amazing on her, so fresh, so Mediterranean, so incredibly friendly and likable! So I immediately googled it and saw the shocking price. 290 bucks for 50 ml? No way. On my last shopping trip, I sprayed it on as a test, but it didn't quite live up to its promise, mainly because it didn't last. Mugler's Cologne, as a relative approximation, is now my interim solution since it's significantly cheaper. I wore Mugler today on this lovely spring day when I went to KaDeWe. Coincidentally (haha!), my path led me to the Fords, and I thought, why not try something new. I reached for Neroli Portofino forte, which I already like just because its name sounds like a medication. So what do you get for your money? From my perspective, the same as the original NP, just a bit stronger and longer - forte, after all. So delightful, juicy citrus notes at the start, which then darken a bit over time, but remain cheerful throughout. Hints of sunscreen and beach breeze, friendliness and carefreeness. Towards the end, it develops a somewhat - can you say grainy? A bit like the scent of plant seeds, not unpleasant. Only the leather, which is supposed to unfold here according to the TF website, doesn't show itself to me at all. NPF remains quite linear. So if you like NP, you'll also enjoy this flanker. The longevity is acceptable, in my opinion better than NP. This afternoon, I sprayed a little on my wrist, and I can still perceive the scent now, after seven hours, but only if my nose is pressed against my wrist. The sillage is very moderate. Do I need to have it? No, not for the price. But it's not bad.

I own a wonderful CD by the Italian singer Claudio Villa. He and his playful, melting, almost operatic melodious tenor celebrated their greatest successes in the 50s and 60s of the last century, and when one tries to imagine 'old-fashioned Italian hits', one automatically thinks of someone like Claudio Villa, who sang throughout his life in the dialect of his Roman homeland.

Do you know that feeling: you breathe slowly and powerfully, almost meditatively, drawing the air deep into your lungs until the last alveolus is fully filled........ then a brief pause in breathing. Close your eyes. Forget the world around you. A warm wave turns into a bursting swell and spreads from the belly throughout the entire body.

Lord… you know (Warning, something is coming that you might laugh at me for, hmm…), as a child, I always wanted to be a lord. I don’t know why, but this English noble title just sounded so wonderful to my ears. I must admit, though, that I was also very influenced by … Star Wars. Well, can you guess? No? How is Darth Vader often referred to? Of course, LORD Vader! I always found that so cool, especially because Lord Vader was one of my favorite characters from Star Wars and in general, until Hayden Christensen nearly ruined this character when he played the annoying Anakin Skywalker… Anyway, even today, the title Lord just sounds cool to me. Of course, I come from Turkey and will never be able to become an English lord, but one can dream and fantasize a little… Oh, and this fragrance here is called Lords because it was originally composed for Lord Percy Croft (no, not Lara Croft…) from the Croft Port Dynasty, and that was a long time ago, back in 1911… so you can expect a pretty classic scent. The scent: The scent starts citrusy and, as expected, classic, well, just like a classic men’s fragrance, but that’s clear, because first of all, lemons are present, secondly, you can already smell a bit of the oak moss from the base, and thirdly, as mentioned, the scent is also a bit older… and I won’t even start on the lavender. All “ingredients” for classic fragrances (which some might derogatorily refer to as grandpa scents…). Besides the lemons, you can also smell the Petitgrains reminiscent of oranges very well. In addition, there’s a wonderful, herbal-spicy note with the basil, which I think always goes well with summer fragrances. While you can smell the lavender in the heart note, I’m not so sure about the lily of the valley. However, you can slightly perceive the rose geraniums in the base, and the scent becomes sweeter, albeit only slightly. The aforementioned sweetness, however, diminishes over the course of the fragrance, so that the classic elements (i.e., lavender, oak moss, and the remaining citrus notes) become more pronounced again. Towards the base, it also becomes earthier, as you can smell patchouli, and somehow there’s a light, spicy, or rather, bitter note in the background that I couldn’t quite identify. The sillage and longevity: The projection is quite okay; you can smell the fragrance well for some time. Initially, there might even be a small scent cloud left behind. The longevity, on the other hand, is average and lasts six to seven hours. The bottle: The bottle is cylindrical with a thick glass bottom and is slightly dome-shaped at the top. The label on the front has, fitting to the name of the fragrance, the shape of a blue coat of arms. The cap has been wrapped at the bottom with a ribbon in the national colors of England (actually more like Great Britain). All in all, quite okay. Yes, Lords has become a very classic men’s fragrance that starts off citrusy, almost barbershop-like, but later becomes somewhat more bitter. And by bitter, I mean almost darker, gloomier, more mysterious… and my thoughts wander back to Lord Vader… (the Imperial march is already booming in my head,… oh, I’m such a freak…). In any case, the fragrance is good for spring and summer, but it also makes a good impression on slightly cooler days (well, but not necessarily in winter). As for occasions, it’s more of an all-rounder; it might be good for … dinner… well, or just for general social occasions and meetings. Thus, it suits men over 30 better than younger ones. Oh, by the way, the fragrance was only made available to the public in the 1980s. Until then, it had apparently been exclusively produced for Lord Croft. And in 2009, the fragrance was renamed Douro Eau de Portugal, although I don’t know if this scent smells the same or slightly different. But you can definitely give it a try if you’re into bitter and classic fragrances with a soapy touch.

Yes, I like to "poach"! Of course not in the woods, but with "men's perfumes". You wouldn't suspect it at first glance if you met me. I am of medium height, with a delicate build, and I have a distinctly feminine clothing style: one-piece dresses, almost never pants, figure-hugging or sometimes flowing wide, preferably made of silk, lace, chiffon, often with floral patterns, sometimes colorful in a hippie style or deep black. Complemented by matching jewelry and pumps. But never, really never will you see me in jeans, a polo shirt, and sneakers! That would simply not be me! So why occasionally men's perfumes? Since I've been part of Parfumo, my fragrance taste has broadened immensely! While I used to prefer floral and fruity perfumes to match my clothing style, I have now also discovered my love for spicy and resinous scents. And there are some great candidates in the "men's section"! Anything with the label "Sport" I leave aside, but otherwise nothing is safe from my curious nose! Many of the spicy men's fragrances I wear just for myself in my free time, but some I also enjoy wearing at work to consciously create a contrast to my feminine outfit. After this long introduction, let's talk about "Lords": A dear Parfumo friend lent me this bottle, along with some other bottles from his collection. Yes, it is certainly more of a masculine than a unisex perfume. After the citrus notes in the opening, lavender dominates on me; I can hardly recognize the lily of the valley. The base, which I perceive as more spicy than resinous, gives the perfume a rather warm aura, despite the cool freshness of the lavender. I have categorized Lords as a spring fragrance for myself, but it would fit just as well in late summer or the first days of autumn. The perfumes from Penhaligon's are almost all a little quirky, and this one is too. In that respect, it fits wonderfully with my character!

This autumn, I spent a few days privately in London for the first time in years - completely without time pressure and appointments. When I'm out and about, my thoughts sometimes drift towards perfume, but usually, that's not the focus (even spontaneous airport purchases are not really my thing). However, this time was a bit different. Lords has been weighing on my mind for a long time! I am a bottle buyer and - in moderation, but then almost obsessively - also a collector. I could buy a bottle of Douro, which is exactly the same scent (that I greatly appreciate) that Penhaligon's just renamed a few years ago - one day I might do that. But Lords, the real one - a 50 ml bottle of Cologne (just that, not 100 ml and certainly not the After Shave) - I would love to have. The little ribbon with the Union Jack pattern and the crest-shaped label - simply wonderful! On St. John’s Wood Road in London, there is the Lord's Cricket Ground, the home stadium of the Marylebone Cricket Club - and the most famous cricket stadium in the world. I knew little about cricket, this most British of sports - except that it resembles baseball from the perspective of an outsider and can last for days under unfavorable conditions. Lord's is an institution in Great Britain, and I had the vague idea - since Penhaligon's also created a perfume specifically for the London tailor Turnbull & Asser - that this scent might have been or still is dedicated to the institution of Lord's - and they might know something about it there (or even still have it!). The club is a bit off the beaten path, and the opening hours on the website turned out to be more of a suggestion. Outside of the season, hardly anyone seems to wander here, but after a dreary half-hour wait in English drizzle (hey, it was about perfume!), they finally took pity on me. It quickly became clear that Lords and Lord's (without apostrophe vs. with apostrophe) probably have nothing to do with each other, but - and that's why I'm telling this story - they really went out of their way for me. After I presented my little request, the woman in the shop called someone in specifically - all my assurances that it wasn't that important went unheard - who seemed to be something like the curator of the club's memorabilia and an intimate connoisseur of its history - whether he had heard of a perfume called Lords? He had not, but because he knew someone who knew someone, he insisted on calling that person as well. I was almost a bit embarrassed to have caused so much commotion on that gray Tuesday morning, but everyone was so terribly nice and offered me cookies. Long story short - Lords has nothing to do with Lord's. But I met wonderful people and had wonderful conversations - about cricket, about London, and about perfume - just like a gift. Conclusion: regarding possible future connections to Lords, it seems that only the English nobility and the American adult film actress Traci Lords remain - let's see who I call first. More about the scent itself (it's wonderful, did I mention that?) I will write in the meantime under Douro - it’s still available under that name.

Uncommented Fragrances No. 48 Lord Wisebottom, a distinguished gentleman of the old school, preferred English attire (Harris Tweed, handcrafted horse leather shoes, corduroy), English cars (for years, only Bristol was an option for him; he ignored the fact that the brand had to file for bankruptcy as long as he could still get spare parts for his Bristol 603) and... surprisingly, mostly mundane fragrances from the continent. In his bathroom, alongside an abandoned bottle of Woods of Windsor (see comment there), the only British fragrance in his small collection, stood a bottle of Grey Flannel (see comment there) and a bottle of Robert Piguet Cravache (see comment there). However, when he realized the extent of this scandal, he banished the American and French fragrances to the back corner of his dressing room and set out to finally stock up on sufficient English goods. We do not know which fragrances he currently has in his bathroom; however, from his reliable housekeeper Rose, who remained loyal to him even after his social decline, the details of which we shall remain silent about, I heard that a bottle of Lords by Penhaligon's (now available in almost the same formulation under the name Douro) made its way into his collection. Now, there would be nothing more to report if the connoisseur of English fragrances did not know that this scent (especially in the older version noted here under the name "Lords") is one that can turn even the most distinguished lord into a colorful peacock. Alongside a bright, citrusy opening (it contains the bergamot oil beloved by Lord Wisebottom not only in his Earl Grey tea, as well as lemon and petitgrain, and a hint of lavender, of course, as it must never be missing in English fragrances), this scent features a combination with explosive potential, namely lily of the valley, patchouli, and labdanum, probably also sandalwood. I suspect at least that this combination is responsible for the devastating effect of this fragrance. In any case, the scent unfolds a power and potential that is truly delightful. Anyone who risks even a single spray too much will not only notice irritated glances but will also experience that one or another lady with a sensitive nose will keep their distance. Lord Wisebottom has already had to endure disrespectful comments about this upper-class fragrance called "Lords". I will attempt to describe this extremely volatile fragrance mixture in more detail. There is this almost penetrating sweetness, which never runs out of citrus overtones (similar to an orange, which can be almost animalistically juicy, sweet, and sour at the same time), a almost intoxicating floral note (which can only come from the lily of the valley, a plant often generously used in English fragrances), and a resinous-heavy base, which - of course - is likely derived from labdanum (and sandalwood). Interwoven into these components, patchouli seems to change its character significantly. It lacks, unsurprisingly, its characteristic hippie touch; instead, it acquires an accent that reminds me a bit of the corridors of English castles: a mix of candle wax (beeswax), heavy, dusty, long velvet curtains, and the smell of oil (the typical smell of oil paint) wafting over from various paintings of the indispensable ancestral gallery. Somehow, these English mansions are also a bit eerie and crypt-like - and I do not mean this negatively. Lord Wisebottom tended to wear the fragrance with dignity but overly dosed. Most ladies of the English upper class were not thrilled, rather irritated, and decided not to invite him anymore. However, this suited Rose, his housekeeper. She had long had her eye on her lord and secretly rejoiced at the lack of female competition. Poor Lord. If only he had dosed the fragrance more discreetly. Or listened to me: I recommended layering it with a fresh, citrusy scent that enhances the bright overtones. I particularly recommend Eau d'Hadrien by Annick Goutal. But Lord Wisebottom remained stubborn.

Top notes impressions: Cinnamon-spiced storms, warm-brown glowing, sweep across vast areas, gently raining down on cardamom pods. Upon hitting cinnamon-covered grounds, they burst open, like a marvel, and roll in spicy-soft pirouettes around peppercorns, perhaps shimmering pink or rather black-glossy in all its intensely enveloping sharpness. I wander over endlessly fragrant plains of sheltered coziness, under a balsamic-spicy starry sky, while the cinnamon dust envelops my hair, my body like a second, golden-glowing skin. The scent of wintery Christmas warmth from the past surrounds me, rocks me, holds me. Heart notes impressions: Woodruff. Clearly. And sweetness. A rather comprehensive sweetness. That’s what I smell not only up close after 2-3 hours but also in the very distinct projection of the fragrance. The cinnamon remains faithfully present, though more as a background note than as the lead, if I may explain it with musical imagery. Front and center is clearly the tonka sweetness, from which this woodruff impression might also stem. Cardamom, pepper? Blown away. Bergamot, lavender have not been present from the start. At least these fragrance components could not significantly assert themselves against the cinnamon-cardamom storm, as far as my olfactory impressions are concerned. The tonka bean remains. Persistent. Intense. Unchanging. And long. Very long … Base despair: Yes, yes! Tonka. Still. And loud. Goodness, is it loud. And so sweet! And yes, the fragrance resembles the l’occitan EdB, but even there I eventually felt overwhelmed by this sweetness a bit. Be it spicy sweetness. But here … here the tonka sweetness knocks me down. And not just a little! Completely! What would I give for a bit of patchouli, a scent that I can only tolerate in minimal amounts, or a proper portion of incense. But no! Nothing with patchouli or incense! Tonka! Really now?! Really now: Tonka! Yes, I know, I’m repeating myself, damn it! But the fragrance does too - on a loop, so what?!?! And I’ll say it again: Tonka! Tonka! TONKA!!! And sweet, sweeter, sweetest! And the superlative makes it really hard for me towards the end of the fragrance (when is the end anyway? 10 hours and an attempt to wash it off later, there’s absolutely no sign of an end or, better said, a scent of it!) to remember this wonderful beginning. Damn the great beginning, the sweet glue should stop lulling me in its now unyielding sweetness! Good heavens, this has to go! Sorry, but I have to stop; the fragrance must finally come off my skin! Off!!! Goodness …

How should I begin? I've never found it so hard to find a starting point. Let's start from the back. This special collection from Lalique simply blows me away with the flacons. The wonderful clear-milky glass. They clearly know what they are doing. The truly noble box around it - wonderful. As for the name, I really can't make sense of it. Zinc??? I don't understand. The scent: Yes, you can catch a whiff of lavender, but for my nose, it takes a lot of imagination. I don't perceive fig either. It starts with cardamom, but then it directly transforms into a tonka bean rolled in cinnamon. Accompanied by a light vanilla, which you then smell paired with the bean for many hours. Always or the whole time with a milky undertone. Not a bad scent, God knows, but for me, it's too sweet. Wearing it for an entire day gives me headaches and makes me feel nauseous. Of course, it’s a completely different scent, but for the first few seconds, I had a small reminder of “Tonka Imperiale,” but that one plays in the top league, while this one here only kicks in the amateur league for me. The combination of cardamom, tonka, vanilla, and cinnamon is just too coarse for me, too fluffy, too candy house-like. BUT, tastes differ.

Lalique's Oriental Zinc was my first niche perfume and I was truly enchanted from the very first moment. With notes of patchouli and incense, several fragrances were presented to me. Among them was this masterpiece, which convinced me from the start. The oriental and powdery note is excellently crafted. The spiciness completes the picture perfectly. I really enjoy wearing this scent often (autumn/winter). The longevity and sillage are incredibly good, at least that's my impression and the feedback from the people around me. The fragrance simply radiates power and is at the same time very gentle, wrapping around you like a cashmere cloth. You can tell I'm unable to stop raving about it. For me, it's simply one of my absolute favorite scents forever.

A few days ago, I had the opportunity to purchase a bottle of Oriental Zinc at a very reasonable price. The fragrance pyramid sounded very promising. Just the way I usually like it. However, some rather negative reviews initially made me hesitate to take the plunge with this scent. Although it actually fits my preferences perfectly... In the end, I managed to convince myself to buy Oriental Zinc on a whim and was very curious to see how I would like it. After extensive testing, spraying, and sniffing, I must now say: I absolutely CANNOT understand the negative reviews! Right upon spraying, I perceive a very cool, almost metallic freshness, from which I can distinctly smell lavender. The other fragrance notes are rather indistinguishable to me. I must admit, if the scent were to remain like this, it would not be my cup of tea, as I generally do not like fresh, cool perfumes, but rather sweet, warm gourmands. However, it only takes a few minutes, and then the freshness begins to transform into spiciness; cardamom and cinnamon start to give the oriental zinc significantly more warmth and depth, and from that point on, it becomes really interesting for me! With "Zinc" in the name, I couldn't really make sense of it beforehand, but with "Oriental," I usually expect a spicy, sweet, and preferably heavy scent. I cannot understand why these aspects seem to be grounds for criticism of this perfume, as the scent develops after a while exactly in the direction one would expect from an oriental fragrance. At the latest, after half an hour, tonka, patchouli, and incense come through more strongly, giving the fragrance a wonderful sweetness, almost gourmand-like, and still very spicy note. Yes, definitely oriental, but admittedly in a rather subtle rendition. Those who know real oriental perfumes know that this one is more "oriental for western noses." Over time, the tonka note becomes more pronounced, and I smell a very beautifully soft, warm, sweet-spicy fragrance for hours, which is still suitable for everyday wear and not too intrusive, yet lasts quite a long time. For the cooler and cold months, this is definitely a great perfume that I can wonderfully imagine on both women and men! It should definitely be mentioned that the beautifully designed and heavy bottle comes in a very decorative and elegant box. As is typical with Lalique, the bottle is an absolute eye-catcher. Just for that reason alone, my blind purchase was worth it. Fortunately, I also really like the content!

... a gentleman enters an upscale bar in his well-tailored suit. The ladies watch him, and he is fully aware of it. He smiles into the room and fills it with his charisma. He walks to the bar and orders a whisky. Upon applying this fragrance, the first thing that hits the nose is a green sweet fig note, underscored by lavender and bergamot. Cardamom, pepper, and cinnamon add spiciness to this scent, while a slight leather aroma emerges from the frankincense. The fig scent remains present throughout. The longevity is very good, and the sillage is decent. The perfume can be worn well in the office or even in a bar. This scent is unisex. Those who like figs have a good chance of finding something they enjoy here. So give it a try.

I only have a few ml of this animalic leather masterpiece left. It's such a shame. Although I do like the newer versions, this in its original state is one of the best leather fragrances created. Its a leather that smells of real leather unlike so many leather fragrance wannabees. I know I will have to say goodbye very soon to this amazing perfume because I have so little left. But if you can still find it. You will never be disappointed.

Tom Ford’s Ombre Leather is a fragrance I both weirdly like and I don’t like and I can’t make up my mind. The new car leather scent is front and center, like you literally just slid into the seat of some posh, luxury vehicle to take it for a test drive. The smarmy salesperson slithered into the passenger seat next to you and they are wearing that screechy-sweet jasmine scent from Tom Ford that you really despise and at first you want to roll down the windows but you can’t figure out how they work so you just give up. But somehow the syrupy musk of the jasmine alongside the smooth, slightly bright, slightly animalic leather is a striking combination. But the two notes never really meld, they sit separately for the duration of the scent’s journey, and much like that trip twice around the car lot with the stranger that you’re not going to buy the car from anyway, it’s ultimately an awkward ride.

The opening is coarse leather, displaying both akin to Tuscan Leather's darkness, and its own leathery characteristics. A simple touch of violet and cardamom in the beginning gives it a grease-smeared olfactory statement that tones down in a half way suede half way leather side, with warm earthy floral aspect, and a promise of fruity notes that never materialize. Never materialize, yet the whole performance goes to a curvy femininity in dry down, using masculine ingredients. If it's compared to TL, it is rigid, spicy, fruitless and bitter version of TL. Kind of uncertain on luxury and ordinary. It also lurks between two genders without tending to both or either. 2/5

This is American Haute Luxe at its finest, a rich but dry leather with a smooth ombré effect not unlike the brown-on-brown tones of the set of his movie, A Single Man, where the tonal shifts between mahogany and chocolate and sepia are barely perceptible to the naked eye but still manage to convey the happy meeting of taste and wealth. The fragrance is also, like the movie, ever so slightly soulless. The leather note is similar to that of Tuscan Leather but here is given a darker, drier treatment  there is no raspberry sweetness and the musky, sueded finish of Tuscan Leather has been swapped out for a very streamlined, almost buttery texture. It slides as seamlessly onto the skin as a handmade shoe slides onto a foot. Opening on a potent blast of leather, it momentarily skates close to chemical/tanning pungency but thankfully banks back in time. It develops into a rich, sturdy leather that speaks of fantastic wealth, like the interior of a Jaguar or the mingling aromas in a bespoke leather shop on Saville Row. For this reason, I find Ombre Leather 16 to be far more refined and more formal than Tuscan Leather, which seems outdoorsy and rugged in comparison. Ombre Leather 16 also seems to deftly sidestep all the common faults people pick with leather scents - there is no powder, no excessive floralcy, and crucially for a lot of men out there, it does not in any way resemble the lipsticky, dusty insides of a lady's handbag. But neither is this a big, butch leather a la Peau d'Espagne or Rien. It is a masculine, stern, be-suited thing, to be sure, but this is a leather that stays firmly in the boardroom and well away from both fuel-soaked garage and prairie. All the other listed notes (patchouli, violet leaf, jasmine, white moss, cardamom) are there to pull together towards creating that sumptuous but dry leather accord, and are not incredibly distinct in and of themselves. Towards the start, I can pick out a slightly fresh, watery herbal accent, which I assume is the violet leaf, but the effect is more of a dark, smooth leather that's been rubbed with something green to put a high shine on it than a note that sings strongly on its own. Certainly, I can smell a clean, saline moss in the far dry down and shadowy patchouli, but they blend so completely with the leather accord that I see them for what they really are: overlapping building blocks used to create that ombré effect .
