I thought I picked up on an ambery resin there in the background, which might account for the slight uptick in sweetness in the base of an otherwise dry (unsweet) fragrance, but none is listed. Longevity is phenomenal - easily 12-18 hours, and projection is pretty good too. It's a little quieter overall than Tuscan Leather, which makes sense as the character of Ombre Leather 16 is dark, dry, and refined as opposed to the more outgoing and cheerful Tuscan Leather.

I unfortunately do not know why Tom Ford has launched a scent that is very similar to Tuscan Leather, why he named it the only fragrance after a collection, and why this scent is supposed to be discontinued by the end of this year (according to the Tom Ford counter lady). I only know that Ombre Leather has its justification for existence. Perhaps I am making it a bit too easy for myself by claiming that those who found Tuscan Leather often too intense, too overwhelming, and too exhausting for everyday wear might find a more everyday version here. So far, this is how I feel while wearing it! Not that we misunderstand each other, there have been days when I loved Tuscan Leather - mostly in autumn and winter - I always felt extremely elegant "dressed" in it, a bit of nobility, slightly cool distance, with charming arrogance. Then there were days and weeks when I didn't even want to come close to TL; it was too massive, too dense, too penetrating and consuming was the intoxicating aroma. Tom has quite a few of that sort in his collection. But if one is ready for such a scent, such an aroma complex, it can be quite delightful, both for oneself and for others. Ombre Leather is indeed the everyday version for me, more the daytime version, even though it is also great to wear in the evening. Raspberry has been thrown out (after 5 comparable scents, I must say "finally"), violet has been included. More Fahrenheit than Steampunk. It has received a minimal floral touch, really just a hint, as well as a mini woody touch. It could very well be a 2:1 mix of Tuscan Leather and AdP Colonia Leather, with the latter still having a slight edge for me when it comes to leather scents. Everything feels a bit airier and slimmer with Ombre Leather compared to Tuscan Leather, yet I still find it strong and dense enough. Diluted would probably be the wrong term here; the violet simply makes the nose feel less occupied than with the monster raspberry;-)! The leather here is still of the best and softest quality, thickest Walk Nappa without grain, spicy, soft, velvety... wonderful. It definitely appeals to me more, yet I understand the Tuscan fans. Here, the longevity is really great, easily 7 hours, sillage probably just above office-appropriate... but autumn will ultimately show!

Cultural question: which film starts like this? Schloss Possenhofen on Lake Starnberg in the morning sun, on a boat dock a mustachioed, stately man in traditional attire, fishing. Yodeling loggers pass by, politely wishing 'Good morning, Your Royal Highness!' He heartily replies: 'Grüß euch Gott!', jovially waving.

Friday evenings, a small pub in the Ruhr area: expectantly and attention-seeking, the four blondes stood at the bar. Sweat was already beading down on them, as they had long noticed that they were being watched and four gentlemen were heading straight for them and.... downed their four pilsners in one go.

What I particularly appreciate about Tom Ford fragrances is that certain darkness that every scent of his possesses. Even the seemingly bright summer fragrances like Soleil Blanc. They all have something tragic, melancholic about them, yet still smell incredibly high-quality. Decadence in its purest form.
First of all: I am a big fan of Tuscan Leather even though I wear it rarely (it will be cooler soon *g*). From time to time, I smell the bottle because I really like the scent in a crazy way.

Leather. There are many things one can imagine when it comes to leather. Leather seats in cars for car enthusiasts, leather and latex games for those with, well... dirty thoughts (so all of you here :D) or Indiana Jones' jacket, hat, and whip for the Indy freaks :D (and you can guess who that is again… *sigh* …).

Chypchen Posy translates to something like little bouquet. And for this fragrance, there could be no better name, as Victorian Posy embodies the olfactory diminutive. I think of a little house with flowers in the garden and a little tree beside it, a house with a garden on a little cliff by a little sea under a radiant little sun. At Penhaligon’s Victorian Posy, clear parallels emerge with the two-year-older Ormolu from the same house. Both are unmistakable representatives of the Chypre genre, and even Ormolu is not one of the usual bombastic fragrances. Victorian Posy is even sweeter and milder. While the combination of jasmine and rose with chamomile on the typical moss base is common to both, Victorian Posy expresses the theme in a more subtle, elegant, and lively manner. The wonderful obligatory hesperidic-citrus opening certainly plays a role, but so does the overall more discreet, elegant presence and the underlying green tone. Ormolu represents its roots as a Chypre from the late seventies more vehemently, making no secret of it. Victorian Posy, on the other hand, is also quite bitter, almost austere, but remains overall more reserved and does not seem quite so obviously out of time today. Ladies and Gents, I present to you Victorian Posy aka Chypchen, little sister of Ormolu. Unfortunately, like its older sister, it is already in early retirement.

That plants thrive in South England just like in Cyprus, due to the very mild climate, is probably known to some. And that Chypre fragrances par excellence are composed (were composed) in England is known only to a few. I too have been enlightened to this fact. Penhaligon's has masterfully demonstrated this with their "Victorian Posy". However, it was anything but masterful to remove this wonderful fragrance from the lineup, or rather from production. Thanks to a dear perfumista, I now have the privilege of owning a mini and delighting in its bouquet. At first, galbanum together with hyacinth manages to produce an astonishingly green-intense violet-like scent, which is only accompanied by a slightly fresh citrus. As it wears, a triad emerges between roses, the gentle bloom of jasmine, and the aforementioned violet intro, which is not just an entry into the fragrance, Carried by its leisurely-pleasant herbal sweetness, sandalwood makes its way to my nose and thus immediately to the "reptilian brain". "Ancient 70s hippie sandalwood," along with the same kind of patchouli. Beneath lies a "darker" layer of scent that reaches into great depths. "Inky" slightly bittersweet oakmoss in duet with herbaceous-earthy vetiver. And on top, the "full blast" from the green-floral perfume layers above. A densely woven "carpet" of aromas. Everything smells so wonderfully "old-fashioned" that it already seems "modern" to me. Some niche brands are literally struggling to create a fragrance that appears "old-fashioned". Some succeed as well. But now a big, pleading request to the house of Penhaligon's: Please dig up the old original formula of "Victorian Posy" again, start production, and don’t stop it again. Friends and fans of an "Old English Chypre" will thank you.

When I first shared my thoughts on this fragrance, I only had a previously opened auction bottle in my possession, and I wasn't quite sure if the scent was still completely intact. The perfume struck me as somewhat quirky... Since I am a fan of Penhaligon perfumes, especially the older, often very decorative bottles, I also jumped at an offer for a like-new bottle (along with the pretty box), which is what my comment refers to now. Right from the first spray, "Victorian Posy" makes it clear that it belongs to the Chypre family. The oakmoss is unmistakable and adds a slightly bitter note. Those who know my comments are aware that I am not a big fan of Chypres. In my childhood in the 70s, this fragrance direction was apparently much more widespread than today; many of the perfumes from that time I found to be piercing or headache-inducing. Today, I am more open to Chypres, some I quite like, but they rarely receive high ratings from me. The floral classification certainly applies as well, but anyone expecting a lush or sweet floral bouquet - the perfume's name suggests something like that - might be disappointed. The flowers tend to stay more in the background. I can hardly perceive any sweetness. For my taste, it's a rather austere perfume. I have revised my initial classification of "creamy" (referring to the opened bottle I purchased) and instead clicked on "woody." Either there are different formulations, or the opened fragrance has indeed changed somewhat. VP feels a bit "out of time" to me. However, anyone who enjoys the Chypres of the 70s should definitely give it a try! About the bottle: I apparently have two examples of an older version with a fir green ribbon and a larger label, on which the bouquet takes up more space. In my opinion, it's prettier than the more minimalist version shown here. Photo to follow!

It's always interesting how different perceptions can be. I was very much looking forward to this Lalique and was surprised during the testing of the sample that it developed quite differently than expected. During the first test, it somehow got lost on my arm. I guess we tested too many fragrances at once... So today, a bold and not timid spray for the next test: The top note starts off engagingly green and woody, completely without citrus, and suggests a few aldehydes instead. Then it smells like shoe polish, the old kind with beeswax, which gives a real shine when polished. This is also the case with this fragrance. Suddenly, I find myself sitting in an old trunk, where rubber tires and a jar of honey are also stored, and I look out in surprise. Not a bad perspective, but where is the chypre? An hour later, when Mediterranean herbs waft into my nose, it could point in the right direction, but it gets a bit stuffy in the trunk. Maybe it's just too warm outside. I find a pack of Swiss herbal sugar and suck on one for refreshment. They taste a bit powdery. Perhaps I'll try it again in winter.

My last comment was a long time ago, too much work, few fragrances that excited me, and not least, little desire. When you’ve been here for more than 7 years, a lot repeats itself and the enthusiasm noticeably wanes. But now there’s a fragrance that only allows for a 10 in my rating, so I have to say a few words about it, because Chypre Silver truly deserves a comment. I’ve been circling around this Lalique for a while. The latest statements from some perfumistas made me pay more attention, and when I saw that a perfumista (who often serves as a benchmark since we have similar tastes) rated the fragrance a 9, I took the plunge and ordered it blind; given the price, it was a risk, but I love taking risks. Bullseye!!! At the beginning, I actually perceive violet, soft, supple leather is also immediately present in my mind. This truly makes my heart race, and I shine as brightly as the fragrance. Bergamot provides the citrus freshness, and then a rose blossoms, fresh and adorned with dewdrops. All together it has a light powdery quality, is herbaceous, hardly sweet. Patchouli flanks the rose, benzoin adds a bit of spice and resin, and the leather remains all the way to the base. For me, the fragrance is perfect, enchanting from beginning to end. Elegant, fresh, and noticeable, but not loud would be my tags. However, I would advise against blind buying; a colleague was delighted by the fragrance, and I sprayed a little on her. The next colleague walked in, scrutinized us with a critical look over her mask, and asked: Did you cream yourselves with rheumatism ointment? Yes, that can happen, but she belongs to the LVeB faction, so she finds it too herbaceous. Sillage and longevity are good to strong, and the bottle? It’s a Lalique, nothing more to say.

Many fragrances at TOM FORD have unfortunately been discontinued... Costa Azzurra, Fougère Platine, White Patchouli, Oud Fleur, Plum Japonais (what a shame), Vert d'Encens (same), Tobacco Oud, Tuscan Leather Intense... To name just a few of them. It is therefore of course necessary to find replacements for them. Tubéreuse Nue is one of them. It is a very strong fragrance at the opening, a little "cold" in the Soleil Neige genre, very gripping on the nose, but also very floral, almost a whole bouquet of white flowers. Jasmin is omnipresent for the first 10/15 minutes. Sichuan pepper almost non-existent in my nose. Just like Tonka, and later, the Oud. About 45mins later you have the perfect clone of Soleil Blanc and its scents of Ylang Ylang, monoï and coconut... A true paradise in a bottle. Once drying, the fragrance becomes softer, powdery, with this little touch of vanilla. Always present also this discreet background of Ylang Ylang... Needless to say, the sillage and longevity are powerful. Conclusion: A very strong and powerful fragrance, very (too) floral, which may temporarily make you hate white flowers, but not islands and their scents of monoï... Do NOT buy blind. My rating: 8/10

Tubéreuse Nue is an opulent and dramatic fragrance; it's as sweet as candy and as boisterous as that mother of all tuberose scents, Fracas Eau de Parfum . It's classically proportioned but also chic and modern, and doesn't take itself too seriously. But while it may seem carefree and youthful, Tubéreuse Nue demands a certain level of poise to truly carry it off. Tuberose can be a difficuly note to wear, and here is dialled up to the maximum, with little to offer those who don't love the scent. Nue, indeed. The first impression is of rich tuberose with a hint of jamsine. The tuberose here is done right; it is creamy, sweet, and camphorous, with plenty of bubblegum. It's tropical, too, but much too strident to be breezy or beachy, thanks in part to the gentle suede accord. I don't detect much pepper or akigalawood, but perhaps their presence is bolstering the tuberose's camphorous aspects, with the latter aiding diffusion. Sillage and longevity are excellent. It's a strange fragrance in that I don't dislike it, and in fact admire it, but I'm struggling to think of an occasion where I'd actually wear it.

To begin with, for the context of this review: Tuberose is one of those accords that I personally can hardly tolerate. Many discover their olfactory nemesis during their journey into the world of beautiful fragrances - for some, it’s aquatics, for others, it’s oud; for me, it’s white florals and red (berry) fruits. In hell, it smells like tuberose and cassis. Moreover (and I have praised this elsewhere!), the fragrances from the house of Ford - with one or two exceptions - always go 'all in'. Where leather is labeled, there is (a lot of) leather inside, and even fleeting beings like neroli are given (sometimes artificial) presence and longevity. Accordingly, there is a lot of tuberose here, many white flowers. Tubéreuse Nue is a striking, dense, opulent, and - if you don’t love tuberose very much - suffocatingly appealing scent, which adds a musk accord to the white flowers that is somewhere between highly artificial and animalistic, a numbing sweaty note with hints of warm animal furs and burnt car tires - not uninteresting, but definitely not my thing. For a long time, a perfume centered around tuberose was missing from Ford's oeuvre - and that one like this would (if not must) exist is hardly surprising. Tubéreuse Nue is promise (the flood of sweet white flowers), sex (the skin or sweat accord), and regret (the scorched rubber note), it is entirely Private Blend and as such academically consistent. Those who love tuberose and Ford's 'too much of everything' will find here a fleet of sensuality and voluptuousness and passion, and within it a hint - and this is again very Tom Ford - of subtle injury and damage. And a perfume like (or for) an anatomically complete adult doll that has been lying too close to an open fire. Conclusion: white flowers, numbing sweetness, as far as the nose can reach. Inside, sex and guilt and sin, and for me (and everything else) way too much.

I tried this fragrance over the weekend in an exclusive perfumery in Luxembourg. When I saw the TF commercial for it, I had a feeling that would later be confirmed. So I went into the perfumery hoping they would have it. I mentioned it and was immediately hyped. Then the lovely lady applied the fragrance on me... and I felt confirmed: A scent that, in its floral creaminess, resembles Soleil Blanc, Soleil Neige, Eau de Soleil Blanc, eau de bla bla bla. In the first few sniffs, I only recognized minimal deviations in the fragrance DNA... Ultimately, it remains just another TF. Justified (even though I like SOLEIL BLANC) the price is still not. On one hand, it is positioned like F *ing Fabulous, Rose Prick, Lavender Extreme, Bitter Peach,... in the EVEN higher-priced selection, on the other hand, the initially mentioned ones don't even cost as much as the regular TFPBs. Conclusion: Quite okay, but not justified in price. And please, stop packaging this DNA into fragrances 100 times (in memory of Dior Privée, where there are four pieces with the same DNA: Santal Noir-Oud Ispahan-Purple Oud-Oud Rosewood).

After Tom Ford has already tried out several trends and lines, such as the Oud line at the end of the 2000s, the "strange names" line in the late 2010s, and the fruit line with Lost Cherry and Bitter Peach in the early 2020s, it seems that it was now time to go in a new direction - clean, bright, musky, and floral, and Tubereuse Nue seems to be an absolute hit in this regard. I have been able to test it several times now and had the feeling right from the first spray that it evokes a certain emotion and memory in me, but as so often, I couldn't quite pinpoint what those emotions and memories were, which is why I had to test it multiple times. After a few attempts, however, it became clear: It reminds me of my childhood, of the old apartment we used to have, of freshly washed laundry on Sunday mornings, which my mother takes out of the washing machine and hangs up while I stand next to her handing her the clothes, of a carefree and beautiful time when the biggest worry was that the sandcastle built the day before at the playground was now destroyed, of joy and of the sun that wakes you through the window on weekends and signals: "It's time to get up and enjoy the day!" Tubereuse Nue does not have a classic fragrance pyramid; rather, it is a rounded overall package. When sprayed, as the name suggests, it starts relatively quickly with the tuberose, which is accompanied by jasmine and musk. I personally hardly perceive the pepper at all. The scent is initially quiet for a short time, but then suddenly transforms into a gigantic cumulus cloud, which can overwhelm you if you are not expecting it or did not know better beforehand. The scent then fades a bit, and something leather-like comes through, although this leather is extremely delicate and light - hardly comparable to typical leather scents both in the Tom Ford lineup and from other brands. The scent performs quite well, which actually surprised me due to the light, white bottle, as I had expected a very soft and short-lasting fragrance, which is certainly not uncommon for Tom Ford. Instead, I got quite a performance beast, which ultimately caused headaches after about 10 hours of persistent tuberose in the evening. Ultimately, this fragrance is another one of those "clean" types that strongly remind of the already available Soleils from the Private Blend Collection, which makes it somewhat redundant. Nevertheless, I have developed a certain love for it and even added it to my wish list. The bottle is, as always with Tom Ford, very beautiful, but that is certainly a matter of taste. The price is ultimately what significantly downgrades this fragrance, as it is set at an exorbitantly high level without any reason. It is hard to say who I would ultimately recommend this fragrance to, as it is actually far too expensive and far too... boring to really recommend it. It seems as if the marketing was aimed at unsuspecting customers entering the store, stumbling over the fragrance, finding it beautiful, swallowing hard, and then paying the absurd price. You can do it that way, but you might have to discontinue it again in 2023. ... oh.

I honestly don't understand how some people can describe this scent as insignificant or a tuberose fragrance that has been smelled a thousand times with a meaningless typical tuberose DNA. Luckily, tastes are different, because I like this scent and I find it anything but insignificant and pleasing..

Hm, sometimes one might think that Penhaligon’s uses quite exotic names for its fragrances. Especially if you don’t know the background or can’t make sense of the name in general. Nevertheless, I find these names much better than if the fragrance name were simply a reference to a scent note or just called “for him” or “for her.” With Ninevah, the Assyrian/Mesopotamian city is meant, which was located in the vicinity of today’s city of Mosul in Iraq. One might assume that the scent could therefore smell oriental. However, cotton candy and candied apples seem to suggest quite the opposite, but who knows, maybe the Assyrians were already making cotton candy around 600 BC and enjoying it, only to curse later because the cotton candy had stuck to their beards, assuming the gentlemen wore long beards back then, though… with the exception of the Romans and Egyptians, almost all gentlemen in the world at that time seemed to have been bearded, if I’m not mistaken… And currently, long beards are totally in style again, so watch out when eating cotton candy or pizza :D *sigh* Why can’t I grow a “cooler” beard… darn! Anyway, I’m excited to test another Penhaligon’s fragrance, even though most of the tested scents can’t compare to the wonderful Lothair (at least in my opinion!). The Scent: Hm, the scent smells a bit strange for a moment. It’s hard to describe; it’s as if spices like coriander or cardamom are present. It’s certainly not very pleasant. Only gradually (especially in the rising scent cloud, not at the sprayed spot) do the sugary notes emerge. Here, you can mainly smell the candied apples, which smell just like at a fair or Christmas market. I find that great and delicious. Raspberries and cinnamon can be detected, but they are quite weak and really best smelled only when sniffing at the sprayed spot. The sweet notes fade a bit into the background, as the scent also has a rather peculiar, coriander-like aroma in the base, which will only please lovers of these spices/herbs. Personally, I didn’t like the scent that much. The Projection and Longevity: The projection is good and radiates quite well. You can smell the fragrance from a bit further away, even though it shouldn’t be overpowering. The longevity is also good, as the scent lasts for more than ten hours. The Bottle: The bottle is clear and cylindrical. On the front, there is a label with a nice frame, which somehow seems less oriental than one might expect for a fragrance with an Assyrian name. The cap is rounded at the top and features a bow at the bottom, which this time is not made of fabric but seems to be metallic and has a golden color. It’s nice to look at, as always. Hm… I don’t know why the fragrance is named after an ancient Assyrian city. Perhaps it’s due to the spicy-herbaceous notes, which smell to me like coriander and cardamom, that are quite intense throughout and, in my opinion, don’t really match the sweet notes, especially when these sweet notes aren’t jasmine or amber or something, but cotton candy and candied apples, thus coming off more candy-like. I have the feeling that the scent notes don’t harmonize very well together. Sure, this makes the fragrance distinctive and unique, but also strange and quite special, which I personally didn’t like that much. But maybe you’ll like the scent better, especially if you’re into scent notes like coriander, etc.? In any case, it’s a fragrance for autumn and could work well in leisure time, as it might be too intense for some at work and should be applied in smaller amounts. As I mentioned in the introduction, I enjoy testing Penhaligon’s fragrances, and I know that not all can be as wonderful as the great Lothair, which, to be honest, smells amazing not just because of the tea :D But this one didn’t convince me at all. Sure, scent perception is always subjective, and this is just my opinion, but I expected something better and am therefore slightly disappointed… Other quite good Penhaligon’s fragrances besides Lothair, which I would actually recommend more than Ninevah, include Eau Sans Pareil, Elizabethan Rose, Gardenia, Luna, or Malabah. Don’t forget, these are all just my opinions :)

In 2015, the house of Penhaligon's launched six new fragrances at once, and it was not a good year for all those who love its scents for their slightly old-fashioned, sometimes mischievous restraint - or simply because of their slightly quirky 'Englishness'. After the new releases of the previous years - from Sartorial to Tralala - honored or at least maintained the legacy of over 140 years of company history, the 2015 Penhaligon's (at least the ones I have encountered) took entirely new paths - and it can be doubted whether the lovers of the aforementioned restraint and Englishness will appreciate these paths. Hardly any fragrance family has grown in the last decade as much as that of gourmands: what once started with simple vanilla scents has exponentially expanded to include cakes, cookies, warm bread, and candied fruits, as well as heliotrope, tonka, and ambroxan. I have often wondered if in twenty years people will say: 'Oh yes, the 00s and the 10s - we all wanted to smell like oud and dessert...' Penhaligon's now follows this trend with Ninevah - rather late, one might think - and following a trend very late may be economically understandable, but it rarely benefits artistic ambition (and thus reputation). And as if to catch up with what the gourmands of the 00s have on years ahead, Ninevah has been packed with enough for two perfumes, at least! Loud and raucous like a washed-up diva, it indulges in garish carnival sweetness - not cheap - at least not that - but at least ordinary in a plomb-pulling paradise apple sweetness that would make any dentist wince. And what might work in a bath additive or a scented candle appears here overprocessed and overdone, leaving every mischievous restraint painfully missed. Only hints of Brighton Pier and deep-fried Mars bars (and the quirkiness of creating a store exclusive for an outlet) at least quote (contemporary) Englishness, at least that. Conclusion: 'get rich or die tryin'' - loosely translated: 'get rich or die trying' - is the title of the semi-biographical (and exceedingly self-absorbed) film in which rapper 50 Cent tells the story of the rise of a young hip-hop star, as well as his eponymous debut album. Ninevah is everything that the film and album are: loud and ordinary, shrill and terribly bling-bling. And none of that is Penhaligon's.

There are thousands of perfumes named after gold, platinum, and silver, and surely a few that bear the names of less noble metals like copper and iron. Alloys like brass and bronze are likely represented as well. However, I would bet that this fragrance here is the only one in the past, present, and future that proudly carries the name of the industrial metal alloy Zamak, consisting of zinc, aluminum, magnesium, and copper in its title. That already earns it an originality award; worthy of a company that has developed a perfume not only named after black ink but also meant to smell like it (besides Breath of God by Lush, Encre Noir was one of my two horror experiences during scent testing). But I digress, Zamak then. Why, one does not know, and perhaps one does not need to know. The fragrance certainly does not smell metallic, but One Million doesn't smell like gold either. Zamak is a technical alloy used for die casting, from which model trains and zippers are made, among other things. It may be that there is something of "toys for men" implied here - I actually find the scent quite masculine, more on that shortly. Perhaps one could think of the naming as indicative of an innovative development, an alloy indeed - here a tinkerer had the idea to mix things together that no one had dared to mix before. And there is indeed something to that, as I find this scent exceptionally original. Its central note is orange blossom, a white flower, and in my little perfume universe, orange blossom scents always go in one of two directions. Either (floral or musky underlay) into the clean-white-soft-floral-blossomy-creamy-sweet-fluffy like "APOM" or "Jil Sander Sun" (yes, stone me for the comparison, you APOM fans). Or, what I usually prefer, citrusy enhanced into the radiant-happy-sparkling-sunny-colognish like (to take another example from the upper and lower ends of the price scale) "Yves Rocher Fleurs d'Oranger/Petitgrain/Lavande" or "Le Labo Fleurs d'Oranger 27". Here, they have done both, with vanilla in the base and all sorts of (peppered) citrus on top. Above all, and this is now (as it seems to me) really new, they have amalgamated the orange blossom with a razor-watery-barbershop-like, warm-spicy-nutty men's scent. Wood, leather, nutmeg (to me it also smells quite a bit like crunchy clove), this is almost rugged, evoking thoughts of "Old Spice" and the like. I find this really (at least in the top and heart notes) as exciting as it is successful. The late phase is, in my opinion, the least convincing part of the fragrance; it is too sweet and one-dimensional for me, at times almost sticky, but that sounds harsher than intended. Our Zamak has juice and power; with a moderate dosage, it holds up well for seven hours and then still lingers on skinny after that. Just narrowly missed the wishlist, but all in all, a lovely scent, and above all, almost as original as the name.

Sole di Positano Acqua is a fresh, floral, and aquatic EdT. I got it along with Tom Ford Costa Azzurra Acqua and must say that Costa Azzurra comes across as more masculine and spicier. Sole di Positano Acqua is very fresh but also floral. I smell, although not mentioned, jasmine and other flowers. The freshness comes from the sandalwood and citrus notes, especially in the opening. The scent is fleeting, light, and well-suited for summer, for sports, on summer evenings, during vacations, or as an everyday fragrance. Although labeled as unisex, I find it more feminine than masculine; still, I enjoy wearing it from time to time. Simply because it has this carefree quality and is not too sweet or overpowering. Those who prefer something a bit spicier yet still summery should reach for Costa Azzurra Acqua. Price is better than the EdP, as it is EdT and diluted.

I have surely financed one or two Botox injections for Mr. Ford by now. Despite the sometimes crazy prices, some of his fragrances have extreme addictive potential and then need to be reordered as 250ml. With Sole di Positano Acqua, I was tempted to make an exception and buy it blind; I have been testing it repeatedly for several months and now come to my conclusion, which I believe sums up everything worth knowing about the scent: Meh. A bit more detailed? "Citrusy-fresh" fits quite well, the name says it all. Sillage and longevity are at the lower end, even for citrus, rather disappointing. What is completely missing, however, is that certain something that many of Ford's fragrances usually have. There’s no punch, no impact, and nothing remarkable at all. As a complete package, this thing simply sinks without a trace, or my olfactory senses are immune to the certain nuances that other testers have picked up. But even though I am generally very fond of both citrus and fresh scents, Positano Acqua does not bring any joy - what a pity. You can wear it, it smells okay in the short term. But with this house (and at this price!), I simply had different expectations. Sorry, Tom Ford - you can't get everything right. So on my next trip to Italy, I will prefer to pack the tried and tested Acqua di Parma Colonia Essenza: It lasts significantly longer, offers a comparatively outstanding sillage, is fresh and cheerful, citrusy and fresh - and: It gives the Dolce Vita feeling that I had so hoped for from Positano Acqua.

We all know such offers, you can choose three different items from a pool and only have to pay for the most expensive one, while the other two are free. I thought of such promotions while testing Sole di Positano Acqua. At first, however, I thought I was only getting one scent, namely a 4711. In the opening and throughout the first hour, Sole di Positano Acqua strongly resembles the admittedly natural, transparent, and refreshingly uncomplicated 4711 Acqua Colonia scents: In my nose, gentle orange blossom and petitgrain, without petitgrain being too dominant. Somewhat outraged that a Tom Ford would dare to smell like a fragrance from the lowest price range, I had already placed the vial in the sample box for the extras. If I want to smell like this, which I do sometimes, I’ll buy a 4711 for €18.00 and not a Tom Ford for €108.00. And then I tidied up, emptied the mailbox.... Suddenly, a strange smell wafted into my nose. What was that? It smelled just like all those fragrances with water lily or lotus, which seem so oddly musty and swampy that I always recoil when I read about them in pyramids. Could this be the Tom Ford? Indeed. From my 4711 impression, only a hint of citrus freshness remained, and over that lay a whole swamp of stagnant, decaying freshwater tainted with a bit of plastic. Hmm, the Tom Ford obviously has more to offer than a classic 4711 cologne, but unfortunately exactly the wrong thing for me. On one hand, this realization made me feel reconciled (not a rip-off), but on the other hand, I was now disappointed for the second time. Now was actually the time to wash off the scent, but I still had a few things to do and one thing led to another... What was that? Something wonderfully floral was in the air. Could this be the Tom Ford? Indeed. Now the puddle had regained its ecological balance: An interesting, oddly crisp freshness of freshwater and green plants mingled with wonderful, slightly sweet, enchanting flowers. Fresh, but warm like on a mild spring evening, gentle, friendly, and unusual. What flowers are these? Without knowing the pyramid, I would almost guess lily of the valley. I love the true scent of lily of the valley. I suspect that the shiso leaf is my water lily, and together with the remnants of the citrus notes, the moss, and the Mohéli ylang-ylang, it creates for me a lily of the valley meadow by the lake on a mild spring evening. Pay for one and you get three: Firstly, a 4711. Secondly, a light women's fragrance with dominant water lily. Thirdly, a mild, warm dream of lily of the valley by the freshwater. I really like two out of the three. Since the spring evening by the lake lasts almost the entire night and eventually somehow returns to 4711, I can easily endure the half hour of stagnant puddle with plastic. I fished the sample out of the box again. I will wear Sole di Positano Acqua again. At the latest in spring.

There are already several fragrances that roughly go in this direction: Berry-Floral-Woody. Jeanne Lanvin Couture , bright, pastel, berry-sweet. Or Sung Homme Eau de Toilette , herb-berry-floral-woody, mystical. And Amethyst , the "normal" one - also very beautiful. This "Amethyst Exquise" is right in the middle. Berry? Very! - Sweet? A little! - Floral? - Light! - Herb? A bit! - Mystical? Could very well be! ---- "Fragrance twin"? No! Not at all!! So what is it then? For me, an "affinity"! Through the fragrance direction and reference to "models". And a development of the "normal" "Amethyst"! Here, what was envisioned in the former has been completed. And yet, the "Exquise" is only somewhat similar to the "Just-Amethyst" like cousins. No direct siblings. Even less twins. But all have their right to exist, if only because there are different "berry lovers" :-))

I had to have it, the bottle alone is wonderfully Art Nouveau. Purple glass with vines and beautiful berries that seem to come to life and glow magically when the light shines through the bottle. And since all fragrances were on sale shortly after Christmas, I quickly bought it. Hehehe ..Good thing. On my skin. One spray is completely sufficient, and I am enveloped by the darkest and strongest fruits. Only slightly sweet, rather delicate in the background. Fresh creamy blackberry, which I can smell, and after 1 hour the tart but velvety blackcurrant. And then after 4 hours, the scent becomes a super dream. It reduces its strong dark presence here and remains only perceptible on the skin, but with the finest raspberry. Sweet, pleasant, tempting, no longer as heavy and dark as at the beginning, but light and lively. I could probably wear it in any season, but in summer only on cooler evenings, as the scent opening is really heavy. Longevity is truly enormous. After 12 hours still delicately tart on the skin. The sillage is also very good, and after 4 hours it can only be sniffed from a short distance. Conclusion: I transform into a berry fairy and roam the garden at full moon with my gang of dark blackcurrant and the delicate, somewhat shy but sweet raspberry. We are initially quite grown-up, but then we let loose, spread our wings, and paint the garden plants in dark violet, purple, and soft pastel lilac. DeliciousBerryDreamSweetFruityDarkLovelyFine even the night owls are drawn to it, like moths to a flame.

that pear has recently been called blackcurrant. For me, Amethyst Exquise starts with a fruity pear aroma that is both warm and fresh - actually a paradox. (Is the orchid behind it?) My biggest fear was that this blind purchase could go wrong because the fragrance notes sound quite sticky-sweet. However, the reality is very pleasant. The scent is fruity-powdery-creamy, in that order. I have noticed that fragrances can be powdery in different ways: scratchy-powdery, makeup-powdery, fluffy-powdery, sawdust-powdery, etc. I would describe Exquise at times as chalky-powdery, but unfortunately also at times as grape sugar-powdery. Slowly, the pear transforms into the promised berries, and I wonder if there might be a tiny hint of oud in the fragrance - not perceivable on its own, but perhaps as a playful enhancer? In the dry down, the perfume becomes distinctly raspberry-creamy and I like it very much. However, I need to think carefully about whether the bottle will have a permanent place in my collection. The original Amethyst far surpasses this one. By the way, I couldn't identify any woody notes, and the longevity and sillage are decent. Rumpelstiltskin ends.

For me this is the opening of Tuscan Leather and it stays that way. While the normal tuscan leather evolves, the intense stays till the end as the “opening”. Clearly marketing strategy, but a nice scent. Closed doors of a church, a cowboy who has’nt showered in a week. Nice scent but a bit overpriced.

Before I begin, it’s worth mentioning the original Tuscan Leather, as one can still pose the Gretchen question regarding taste, but not regarding the reference. Everyone must acknowledge that Tom Ford has created a fragrance with TL that has inspired numerous works, similar scents, and even very identical creations. Some are very successful, some are quite botched. I also enjoy the original precisely because it is so wild in saffron and yet so smooth and rough at the same time. Is it my favorite leather perfume? No. But it doesn’t have to be. Other leather fragrances from Tom Ford, like Ombre Leather or Ombre Leather 16, have absolutely not convinced me; they are too sweet for my taste. So, Intense. What is intense - at least in terms of focus - is the saffron. While it appears wild and unruly in the original, here it is captured and perceived as more concentrated. The raspberry also seems greener and more unripe to me. There is no raspberry included, supposedly Davana, which I have only known to be intensely exotic-fruity and rather unpleasant because it reminds me of mango, which I do not appreciate. I wouldn’t have recognized it as such. In any case, the Davana is also smoky and, in combination with the woods, probably provides the saffron-replacement feeling, as saffron is supposedly not included. This leads to a bitter aroma at the beginning, but not overwhelmingly saffron-heavy, logically somewhere, yet still rather dark and rough-leathery. Relatively quickly, the scent becomes monothematic. One wonders why TL has been put on a leash; it only became clear to me when studying the ingredients. The leather smells intense, but not refined, rather coarse but not too coarse. The woods, indefinable to me, enhance this impression but do not improve the fragrance. I know, saffron is a matter of taste, but it is bold and expressive. Unfortunately, that is lacking here. The bitter note is nice but becomes progressively smoother. It continues like this; I also miss development. Is it more mature or perhaps just more boring? Honestly? Intense is not more mature than the original, it is not finer, not more complex; it is simply different and feels to me like a copy of the original. Too forced, too constructed despite bold bitterness. Sure, fundamentally a pleasant scent. However, I miss the wild creativity, the somewhat lacking balance. Therefore, no, this was not necessary.

Tuscan Leather, Tuscan Leather Intense, and Ombré Leather - These are the leather fragrances from Tom Ford that are commonly known to me and currently available in regular retail and specialty stores. Now, the average consumer might wonder which of the three fragrances they should acquire, as all of them offer the same program: high-performance, long-lasting, and incredibly projecting leather scents. As a big fan of Tom Ford and leather fragrances, I took the time to test all three scents, analyze them, and ultimately provide a recommendation. Let’s start with TUSCAN LEATHER, the original and patriarch of all leather fragrances: The scent is leathery-smoky, just like the other two fragrances. In the opening, I primarily perceive a strong portion of heavy raspberry paired with the finest smooth leather. Imagine a brand-new black AMG with the most luxurious interior - do you see the dark smooth leather seats? Just like the seats, this fragrance radiates an aura of luxury and superiority, while at the same time conveying a feeling of endless security and comfort. Just like an AMG...: dynamic, powerful, luxurious, safe, and comfortable. Throughout the scent's development, the heavy raspberry and dark smooth leather dominate. At one moment or another, you might catch a whiff of warm woods and perhaps a slightly smoky aura - like driving your AMG through short forest stretches and small villages with many chimneys in winter. Even when these scent notes occasionally emerge, they never take over; they always leave the scepter to raspberry and leather. Scent: 8/10 - A very good fragrance, but not entirely suitable for everyday wear. The occasion must be right. I envision a romantic candlelight dinner, a club night, or an official event where one needs to make an impression. In the workplace, whether in the office or at meetings, I see this scent as only somewhat appropriate, as its strong sillage and extremely distinctive notes could indeed clash. Longevity: 9/10 - Tom Ford has once again surpassed himself in longevity. Sillage: 9/10 - strong, very, very strong. Bottle: 10/10 - Tom Ford Private Blend, indeed. Now to TUSCAN LEATHER INTENSE, the son of the patriarch, who wants to inherit sooner rather than later: This leathery-woody scent is the perfect offspring of such a powerful patriarch. It seems he has passed on only the best of his genes and DNA. Raspberry? Even heavier! Leather? Yes, rougher, more tempestuous, more angular, and only for connoisseurs. Woody? Yes, the forest sections are longer. Smokier? Yes, the villages with the chimneys are larger, and the chimneys are running at full capacity. If it smoked like that in my neighborhood, I would probably move away. Intense is truly serious here. The fragrance operates at its fullest capacity, even more intense, stronger, and more dynamic than the original. However, this scent is also significantly "brutal," much more angular and edgy. Where one could still speak of dark smooth leather in the brand-new AMG, we are now talking about a leather workshop in South American Argentina. And believe me: I have been there! It smells of pure leather, the sweat of the workers, rough hands, the smoke, the diesel, and the oil from the machines... It is hot, sweaty, and dirty. And these piercing odors accompany me long after I have left that factory. For a very, very long time - one shower will not be enough. That’s Tuscan Leather Intense. Scent: 7/10 - For me, a true work of art. But as it is with art - some like it, others do not. And with this fragrance, I clash. It is so loud, so strong, and so angular that it truly divides opinions. It is biting, but for me in a beautiful way. Negative comments and compliments guaranteed. Longevity: 20/10 - Still very noticeable even after showering. Use with caution! INTENSE is truly serious here. Sillage: 10/10 - Two sprays and 10 minutes of airing out, and the apartment still smells of it. Bottle: 10/10 - Tom Ford Private Blend, indeed; I love the inscription on the silver. Lastly, my beloved OMBRÉ LEATHER, my absolute favorite: This scent is leathery-spicy, and even though it is not a direct descendant of the Tuscan patriarchs, it simply cannot deny its family ties. In this fragrance, leather also predominates. However, not in such an intense form as in the two previously mentioned scents. The raspberry is suddenly gone, replaced by the finest, exquisite spices and unobtrusive jasmine. Woody? Yes, still, but much more subtle and elegant through the use of patchouli and vetiver, which in this scent comes across as deeply woody, not green at all. Smoky? No. But wicked, yes. I attribute the wickedness not to any single note, but to the composition as a whole: The dominant leather is continually underscored by spicy cardamom and subtly used saffron. Jasmine also plays only a subordinate, yet passionate supporting role and is used in just the right amount and dosage. The leather here is smooth, still dark, but so comfortable and cozy. The Tuscan patriarchs scream, and the shaded leather is not known for its discretion - it is also strongly present and omnipresent. However, it is loud in a completely different way: It is simply there. Where the Tuscan relatives scream for attention, no, roar, Ombré Leather is just there. Like a guy in a black, tailored designer suit entering a packed ballroom, causing the music to suddenly stop and all eyes to turn to him. Loud in a beautifully charming way. Loud without having to say a word. Sexy, playful, and wicked in one moment, and serious, comfortable, and strong in the next. The rock in the surf. And for me, an incredible compliment-getter. Scent: 10/10 - Tom Ford has outdone himself with this leather fragrance. I wear it almost on every occasion: in the office, on business trips, at meetings, in the club, on dates - simply everywhere; and everywhere I receive compliments for it. The only catch: Definitely only conditionally wearable in summer, more of an autumn/winter scent. In summer, perhaps in the evenings at a well-air-conditioned bar. Longevity: 10/10 - It lasts and lasts and lasts, truly competing with Tuscan Leather Intense. On clothing, it lasts until the next wash and is extremely present every time I walk past the laundry basket. On skin, it lasts until the next shower and is still partially noticeable even after that. Sillage: 8/10 - Strong, but not a monster. I could describe it as a pleasant room filler. Bottle: 6/10 - As a big fan of the Private Blend line, I can't find much to appreciate in the design of this bottle, but: Only the content matters. RECOMMENDATION: For lovers of great and high-quality leather fragrances: All three! For those looking for a good all-rounder: Ombré Leather!

Sometimes I wonder why all designers are after modified reissues of their classics. Intense, Extreme, Absolut, Aqua, what else is there... And in my personal opinion, at least two-thirds of all these reissues could be left out. But there are exceptions. I find Oud Wood Intense, for example, worlds better and more interesting than the original. Ombre Leather 16 and Ombre Leather are also such a case, at least for me. With Tuscan Leather, I was more skeptical, as I really, really like the original. To get one thing straight, Tuscan Leather and its Intense brother are much more similar in scent than Oud Wood and Oud Wood Intense, which don’t really have anything in common. It is a leather fragrance where the leather is always at the forefront. The most significant difference here may (now it gets a bit tricky to grasp) even be the underlying accentuation of the leather. It comes across much rougher here than with the little brother. Where Tuscan Leather wraps around you in a balsamic-sweet way, the Intense version hisses much more. If one would describe Tuscan Leather as wicked, elegant, and snug, one would use the words wild, animalistic, and ready to pair here... The leather is also present here in a purer form, which may partly be due to the fact that the ingredients have been drastically reduced. Davana and woods aromatize and harmonize in the background, but are more like companions that present the leather aroma rather than envelop it. Any sweetness and a direct coating of the leather aroma are absent here. Nevertheless, the scent is full and captivating but colder and scratchier - in a very pleasant way. This rawness does the scent a lot of good. I really like it and it makes for me the essential difference between the two fragrances. It's a bit like deciding in the morning which leather jacket I want to wear today. Tuscan Leather Intense makes no secret of where its lineage lies. But it interprets it in a much more masculine way, perhaps even in a more macho manner. Tuscan Leather can certainly be called a classic, while the Intense version scores (for me) mainly with its roughness and rawness, which ultimately is really a matter of personal taste. Both have their justification, although I would spontaneously say that I like the Intense version just a bit better. The only problem might be the name Intense, as it raises false expectations. The scent is neither more intense nor an intense edition of Tuscan Leather. It is a variation that some may prefer and others may consider unnecessary. Perhaps Tuscan Leather Raw would have been the better choice. Oh, and just to throw in a little (not at all meant to be malicious) jab that I can’t resist: Before speculation arises again, I got the scent from Selfridges. ;-)

then I will think of the scent you wore. The sadness seems to vanish when I smell your cloak. This gentle rum note, soaked in honey, enveloped in smoke. So lovely, yet so sensual. So rich and seductive. So incredibly profound, yet so sweet. Yes, if we happen to meet again.. in this dreary city, then stop at the cobblestone, for I can hear your heartbeat even without a step. And do not cover your face with your hands, I have it deeply anchored in my memory anyway. Hold your head high, love is our key word to happiness. And do not ask me in that situation, why the night once enveloped us. Let the sadness drift away from you, give your tears free rein. For I will hold you, as long as I still live. Yes, if we happen to meet again.. in this dreary city, then reach me your arms, for only then is happiness achieved. And we know that it is not over and never was. Do not cover your face with your hands, I know it inside and out. Give me your hands, hold them to my heart. Yes, if we happen to meet again.. then we will never let go. Velvet Orchid Lumière is a scent of romance. A scent of sensuality. Of desire and also of elegance. Wonderful rum note that spreads right from the start. Light hints of resin, rich smoke. Everything in beautiful blue/purple tones - no deep black. Gently it lays in honey, covered by the night. Rose, lightly illuminated by the moon, lets its scent deeply relax into the darkness. One can only sip it enjoyably in thought, sinking into sleep tipsy. So lovely and sweet - so sensual and seductive. The sweetness feels rich, but does not overwhelm. It is a wonderful balance to feel in the scent, indeed a good atmosphere that Velvet Orchid Lumière spreads. Towards the end, it becomes a bit sharper, the sweetness slightly pulled into the background. A gentle, bright wood note joins in. All this unfolds for a long time - for the sillage and longevity are remarkable. So I praise it to myself - I could wrap myself in my bathrobe for hours, for I have almost "drenched" myself generously with the scent. The big sister has not much to do with this scent. I may claim that they are a different pair, but you can tell that there is a common line, even if it does not lead to the same destination. I am raving and am surprised that I let myself be guided by this scent - for as far as the black orchid is concerned, I have to completely pass. But here I feel comfortable and born.

When Tom needed the cash, he got a bit closer to being lifted by me ;-) What I mean is: I recently became the owner of his latest creation, which I can't find anything negative about. Tom Ford can't either. Although I don't know him personally (haha), I hold him in high regard as a creative mind and visionary. A man who seems to be able to do it all. Making films included - touché. But now to the exciting part, the one that is relevant for us perfume lovers: The scent. Velvet Orchid Lumière cannot deny its lineage from Velvet Orchid; they undoubtedly share the same DNA. However, while Velvet Orchid still hints at minimal notes of decaying flowers, furniture polish, and "feminine charm," Lumière is more straightforward. And by that, I certainly don't mean blandly polished-boring. Its floral quality is much more of a summery tingle than dusty; the scent feels shimmering and sparkling, strongly reminiscent of flower pollen tickling the nose when you stick it too deep into a bouquet. Honey as another element seems only logical and consistent here. It provides minimal sweetness, underlined by citrusy aromas - did the bees nibble on the mandarin blossom? I find the rum to be less alcoholic than in the previous version. It is milder, with vanilla and caramelized notes, just the way I like it. The overall picture is a bit creamier; one should not be misled by the sparkling top and partly heart notes. For me, this new interpretation is an absolute hit! Lively, cheerful, light (without becoming shallow or trivial!), and above all, incredibly stimulating. It really makes me crave warm summer nights, shimmering heat, and joyful evenings with my girlfriends. It feels young without being girly, sensual without wanting to seduce, and cheerful without appearing forced. Wonderful!

Distinct Black Orchid DNA, with fruity mandarins dipped in sweet honey and then soaked in rum at the top. In the heart, black orchid and jasmine, which makes the perfume dark and heavy. The base of vanilla, myrrh, sandalwood, and labdanum holds everything together and gives the scent a warm and oriental creamy quality. Lasts long, especially on clothing, and the sillage is also great. A wonderful perfume for the evening, even in summer, as Velvet Orchid Lumière is somewhat lighter than, for example, Black Orchid. The Tom Ford bottles are also very elegant and I like them extraordinarily well.

This scent is something special for me. It's the rum note that does it. I find it somewhat disturbing in one way, but also invigorating in another. Somehow, it feels cheerful to me. I wore the fragrance at a Detroit Techno party; it's actually too elegant for that, but it just fit. The colorful yet minimalist visuals in the club, the dark music, and a crackle in the air. That evening, I found the person I want to grow old with. I'm not really familiar with the scent of orchids. I've taken care of a few of them and find them quite beautiful as plants, but olfactorily, I haven't been able to make the right connection yet. What I like best is the deep dark rose, the heavy sweetness, and the oriental framework that casually holds all the components together. Labdanum fits so well into the concept. Myrrh and vanilla round off the perfume. I personally don't perceive sandalwood. Conclusion: Festive.

I have both versions in my collection - Velvet Orchid and Velvet Orchid Lumière. I tested them in parallel, and in my opinion, the two fragrances are almost identical. Lumière feels a bit softer and more floral, but not so much that it would be worth seeking out specifically, as long as the regular version is readily available.

I bought a decant of this and at first I thought that I got a bad sample that wasn’t stored properly and turned, because I barely could smell anything. Do you know the feeling when you perceive something dense in your nostrils and you understand that it must be a smell, but you cannot “read” it, no matter how you try? That’s was my first experience with Amethyst Eclat. Although when I asked my husband to sniff my wrist he said that is smelt like candy, so it must be me “glitching”, not the sample. A few days later, upon second application, I do feel something sweet and faintly fruity, but I still don’t “read” it clearly. I think I do get the pear, light blackcurrant, and musk notes. What I do manage to catch reminds me of Jeanne Arthes Boum Candy Land, which also comes in a purple bottle, so maybe it’s not a coincidence. I must say, the original Amethyst feels very gentle and transparent to me, a kind of “barely there” fragrance, so maybe it was to be expected that I wouldn’t be able to smell the “lighter version” of it. I think there is something with the Lalique formula that makes me “nose blind” to it. When I tried “Perles de Lalique” I couldn’t distinguish flower notes there, only patchouli and pepper - and it was an official tester, not a decant. Anyway, sorry for a not very informative review, but hopefully, it will help anyone experiencing similar anosmia with these frags to not feel alone. I wanted to try Lalique Amethyst series very much, because the notes sounded lovely in each of the three, but so far I drew a blank after a blank. Maybe Amethyst Exquise (supposedly a “darker, more intense” version) will be it for me? I do love blackberries and purple fragrances so much!

I had high hopes for this fragrance, as the notes sound quite enchanting and the original Amethyst seems to have many fans. Additionally, I am currently testing the "red gourmands" (small hint: Outrageously Vibrant by Diana Vreeland is fantastic! Definitely worth trying!), but I am very disappointed with this one because it is simply too weak and remains a very short pleasure. I do like the scent itself quite a bit: It starts with a fresh, berry note that I wouldn't have necessarily identified if it weren't listed here as blackcurrant and raspberry. The special, sour-deep scent that cassis usually exudes is, for my personal taste, too delicately intertwined with the raspberry, leaving a slightly diluted olfactory impression. In general, I find it hard to pick out the individual notes; the fragrance impresses as a delicate lilac-floral veil, slightly powdery and more cool than warm. As an everyday scent, it would be quite suitable, as it is nice, but on one hand, it has hardly any recognizability, and on the other hand, it is simply so delicate and quickly fades away... I was particularly curious about the blackberry base, but that’s already gone. I find that very unfortunate, as the idea that I think I can recognize behind it would have fit quite well into my current preferences.

I really like the original Amethyst, at least the opening, that freshness, berry-like. Unfortunately, I don't like the further development, so I occasionally spray it on in the perfume store, but I wouldn't buy it. Amethyst Eclat is exactly how I would like the original Amethyst to be. It starts just as fresh, just as berry-like. However, the freshness remains here; the Eclat doesn’t get too sweet, not as heavy as the original. I perceive the scent as cool, which is why I think it fits perfectly for spring and summer. The longevity is, despite the fresh scent profile, still very good; I can perceive the scent for a long time. It is definitely on my wish list for the upcoming spring!

Starts with a bitter and green opening then becomes a skin scent in about 3 hours. I like the scent after the bitterness has gone but it's performance, especially in warm weather is very poor. Boheme would suggest mystery and flamboyance but this unfortunately has neither in my opinion.

Green are hope, spring, and this fragrance. For me, this treasure is like a walk (mountain biking trip) in spring. Green in all its facets, with flowers and blossoms appearing again and again. The scent always remains dominantly green, but new sweet, floral aspects seem to emerge constantly. It is remarkable that the fragrance never really becomes sweet. An olfactory masterpiece! I do not understand why Vert bohème is classified as a women's fragrance. For me, the scent is perfectly unisex and suitable for everyone due to its constantly changing facets. The longevity is top-notch, the fragrance lasts almost 8 hours and comes with a good sillage. Thank you for reading, may we always smell good. Lars

A fascinating and recurring motif in the literary memory of many countries is that of the beautiful and vain woman who, for the selfish preservation of her youth and beauty, resorts to - mostly evil - magical powers. A recent example is Rapunzel's 'foster mother' Gothel in Walt Disney's entertaining animated film, who kept the girl trapped in a tower because combing her golden hair secured her eternal youth, and Snow White's evil queen Ravenna - played by an icy-demonic Charlize Theron - who drained the life from girls to remain forever young and beautiful herself. For the sake of completeness (and gender fairness), one should also mention Oscar Wilde's Dorian Gray, in whose place a painting of himself aged and morally as well as physically decayed. These 'Forever young' stories never end well. Something very beautiful, something very vain, something not young, and something ominous - these are the essential attributes of Tom Ford's Vert Bohème. The 'Vert', the Green, leads one down a false trail, for in reality, it is a darkly dramatic floral scent, not unlike Oud Fleur in its essence. It too has something superficially magnificent and opulent with a hint of something damaged within, and their top notes are similar, bright, blooming, overripe. Following this very Ford-typical intro, Vert Bohème presents a bitter and serious forest note, devoid of any sweetness or charm. Rather, it reminds one of an enchanted, dark forest - like Tolkien's Fangorn or the garden Oglais in The NeverEnding Story, that forest of carnivorous orchids, in the midst of which the evil sorceress Xayíde resides. Conclusion: 'Bohème' - often misinterpreted as 'just' a party-loving artistic crowd - actually refers to an intellectually and aesthetically elevated subculture with a deeply anti-bourgeois self-understanding, and thus the name of this fragrance is explained. Hard to ignore. Difficult and beautiful.

The exclusive scent of an exclusive men's outfitter - surely intended for the elegant gentleman, dressed in fine fabric... And yesterday, by me, a somewhat quirky woman who doesn't care about conventions, misappropriated! For a hike with friends in the Franconian Switzerland. For my - atypical for me, but suitable for the occasion - rather sporty outfit with hiking boots, I didn't want a floral perfume and certainly nothing sweet that would attract even more insects. For the summer warmth yesterday, however, I was happy to have something citrusy that could also be a bit bitter. Chypres are usually not my thing; they often come across as very harsh or almost bitter on me, but in this case, my choice fit exceptionally well! The citrus notes were well pronounced, but unfortunately, I could only recognize the lavender with a lot of imagination. The harsh base notes, especially the moss, became milder over time and matched well with the scent impressions during a hike through the summer forest. "Turnbull & Asser" stayed close to me the whole time, which also meant that critical comments from my absolutely non-fragrance-affine friends were absent. At the same time, T&A showed an unusually high longevity for my skin. I could still perceive it on my wrist even after 8 hours. Presumably, the warmth and the physical exertion that was unusual for me contributed to this. I find T&A to be a perfume that is worth a try for women who prefer citrusy-bitter scents.

With Turnbull & Asser comes a fragrance from Penhaligon’s that was created exclusively for this menswear retailer and is therefore only sold there (according to the information here). Exclusive fragrances always make it difficult to obtain a sample or a bottle, and that's why I find it particularly exciting to see how these scents actually smell. The fragrance: Lemon, lavender, and oakmoss. The three main components that create a typical, classically scented fragrance. Thus, the beginning is characterized and offers almost nothing new, smelling solidly familiar, suitable for a gentleman who likely dresses in Turnbull & Asser (well, of course, this scent also suits all other gentlemen!). Anyway, at the start, you can also smell the pepper, which has a strong scent for a short time but then disappears immediately. The cardamom provides a light, spicy note in the background. After that, you can smell hints of orange blossom, but there isn't much else to discern in the heart note. In the base, it continues to smell of the chypre combination of lemon-oakmoss-lavender, now of course a bit weaker. Earthy patchouli notes come in, and you can also smell vetiver, which gradually gains strength and later becomes the main note of the base. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is somewhat weak and therefore will not leave a scent trail. You have to get closer if you want to smell the fragrance on a gentleman. The longevity is also rather below average, lasting about four hours. The bottle: The bottle is cylindrical and seems almost imperceptibly trapezoidal as it rises. On the front, there is a nicely crafted label, which also features the emblem of Prince Charles, as he is a regular customer of Turnbull & Asser. The cap consists of a cylindrical lower part wrapped with a ribbon and a round upper section. All in all, a nicely made bottle. The fragrance smells, as one might expect from a scent for a menswear retailer, quite classic and good, without reinventing the wheel. I would prefer to say that the fragrance is quite solid, but the sillage could have been better for that. Otherwise, the fragrance is fresh and therefore well-suited for spring and summer. Normally, such scents can also be used for elegant outings (by that, I don’t necessarily mean going out partying :D), but this one is more suitable as a daytime and casual scent. Whether Prince Charles uses this fragrance, I do not know, but it is said that he at least uses Blenheim Bouquet from Penhaligon’s. Even though the fragrance is now exclusive, I don't think it's anything special, and therefore, one shouldn't be sad if they never get to this scent. As mentioned, it smells nice, but just like many other fragrances, and it also has a weaker sillage.

in German 'Bespoke' means 'custom-made according to personal measurement and consultation' and is essentially the holiest of British tailoring arts, highly sought after now more than ever. The center of this tradition lies in the heart of London, on Savile Row in Mayfair and Jermyn Street at Piccadilly. Here, Turnbull & Asser also operates a store - the flagship in Jermyn Street and a new flagship store in Mayfair's Davies Street for a few years now. Off-the-rack shirts start here at £175 (around €250, made-to-measure shirts are significantly more expensive) - everything is made exclusively in England. A certain Charles Mountbatten-Windsor is among Turnbull & Asser's regular clientele, which allows the company to adorn its logo with his coat of arms - three ostrich feathers above a crown. Shopping (even off-the-rack, which is not 'bespoke') at Turnbull & Asser is not like a normal shopping experience. Here, almost exclusively older gentlemen work - I've never seen a woman at Turnbull & Asser, I just notice - can women even go in there? - who know how to convince their clientele of the correctness of their advice with authoritative expertise and sometimes lenient Santa Claus strictness. This happens completely beyond the passive-aggressive arrogance one sometimes encounters in local shops, but is always friendly and patient: 'Yes, sir. Of course, sir. Very good, sir. May I perhaps, sir..?' You still feel like a four-year-old who just spilled ice cream on himself. Even for one of London's most venerable gentlemen's outfitters and royal suppliers, it was a kind of knighthood when the house of Penhaligon's created a fragrance specifically for its anniversary, which is sold here - and nowhere else, not even at Penhaligon's itself. And it would have been a great surprise - indeed an outrage - if this fragrance had turned out to be anything other than a classic English cologne, timeless and unique at the same time. Penhaligon's took no risks and created, drawing on its entire tradition, an Eau de Cologne that could hardly be more traditional (citrus, leather, moss as a base) and yet has that certain 'twist' - something special, unique. In the top note, this is the cardamom, which adds an interesting, unexpected momentum to the initial citrus, while pepper and jasmine take on the role of this 'charming disruptor' as it develops. This is an Eau de Cologne - breath and endurance are therefore of limited duration - and yet it is details like these that distinguish 'Bespoke' from off-the-rack goods and allow this fragrance to carve out its own place amidst the splendors of Turnbull & Asser's stores. Conclusion: unfortunately, I do not source my basic wardrobe from Turnbull & Asser, so it remains a small purchase here and there. I like the anachronistic high wooden shelves and the small windows, I like the venerable 'Gandalf/Dumbledore' salesmen with their stern looks. And I like the Eau de Cologne that Penhaligon's created for this London institution.

I haven't intensively tested any new Tom Ford releases for quite some time. Too often I was disappointed with what you got in terms of performance for a sometimes mid-three-digit amount. But there it was, catching my eye during my stroll: the Oud Voyager . In typical Tom Ford fashion. With the usual, not really high-quality but still appealing bottle in subtle purple. And so it happened that I tested it after all. And that a Tom Ford convinced me again after a long time (actually since Tuscan Leather and Tobacco Vanille). Oud Voyager starts off rosy and stays that way. Initially quite feminine and floral, but also fresh, lightly woody, and surprisingly very wearable for me as a man. Very elegant, very noble. The oud is never animalistic; rather subtle and pleasant. Saffron, cardamom, and musk give the fragrance a nice, deep spiciness that manages to keep the rose prominent but never intrusive. Oud Voyager changes little; but that's not a problem, as the notes create a wonderful, balanced composition from the start. Now, a brief point that has rightly been heavily criticized in recent times regarding Tom Ford fragrances; the longevity. Here it is really very good. The radiance of Oud Voyager diminishes a bit over time and becomes close to the skin after about 4 hours. However, the longevity on my skin is a very solid 7 - 8 hours. Definitely worth a test.

With Oud Voyager, Tom Ford has indeed brought a fragrance to the market that I find really strong! I really like it, and the performance, which has significantly declined in parts at Tom Ford, is once again on point here! The scent may start off a bit "demanding" for some. Personally, I get the Oud right from the beginning, and it is not totally "agreeable." It definitely has noticeable edges and facets, but I like that! The Cypriol is also making its rounds, as well as the rose accord. After a little while, a wonderful, slightly sweetened saffron note emerges. It even feels a bit fresh. The Oud becomes smoother, and I also really like the rose in this fragrance. Towards the end, it becomes a bit "drier" and more austere, as well as woodier. Otherwise, not much else happens. I really have to say: Great job, Tom Ford! It's been a long time since a release has truly convinced me. The scent lasts about 9 hours on my skin, by the way! The sillage is really strong at first, but over time it doesn't project as dominantly. It becomes "normal," I would say. In other words, the performance is really good! Is the fragrance to be classified as unisex? Ultimately, that's something everyone has to decide for themselves. Everyone should wear what they feel like. Tendentially, I actually see this fragrance a bit more on the masculine side.

For a long time, Tom Ford's hype had faded. One bad perfume after another. But Tom Ford's latest fragrance, Oud Voyager, has shown me that it's wrong to give up on Tom Ford. I have always believed in Tom Ford and was not disappointed! In my opinion, this is one of the best Tom Fords and can share the crown with Tobacco Vanille or Oud Wood. A truly beautiful scent with satisfactory longevity this time. There are already enough Rose Oud fragrances, and there have been plenty in the past. But anyone who thinks Tom Ford's Rose Oud fragrance doesn't fit in 2025 really has no idea. It is not an ordinary Rose Oud fragrance; it is different, it sets itself apart. This one is distinctly fresher. A fresh, slightly citrusy rose dominates the scent here. I was initially shocked; it was too floral for me, almost a bit too feminine, but I learned to love it. The oud here does not come across as animalistic, but rather slightly earthy and gentle, it really only plays a background role. So, anyone expecting something oud-heavy or a strong oud scent will be disappointed, but that's what the other Rose Oud fragrances are for =) Conclusion: A very beautiful scent with a dominating fresh rose and a hint of earthy oud in the background. Absolutely unisex, though I would rather see it on a woman. It can definitely be purchased blind, as it is very mass-appealing, unless you are a lumberjack who bathes in gasoline and the most feminine thing about you is your sleep…

Oh no, it’s not that bad at all, don’t worry. Not even a little bad, quite the opposite. Nevertheless - what a strange fragrance Oud Voyager is - and what a peculiar time it comes at. I must (and want to) explain right away why I find it so strange, so odd - and why it has something dramatic and driving about it - 'haunting' is what one would say in English - of which I somewhat theatrically claim in the title that it may bring one to tears. Rose and Oud - hasn’t that been over for a good decade? And now here comes Tom Ford (who launched something quite similar with Oud Fleur about ten years ago) and lets the great Dominique Ropion create a fragrance that seems to be out of time in the mid-2020s. Has it simply been forgotten back then with Oud Fleur, Oud Minérale, Tobacco Oud, and all the others that were supposed to make the cash registers ring in the shadow of Oud Wood? I could now ramble on about how Oud Voyager is indeed contemporary. But it is not; it could just as well be from 2010 or even earlier. And it doesn’t matter here, because it presents the well-trodden fashion accord of rose and oud so finely and delicately, so approachable, so intimate, and so fragile - possibly the timeless hand of the timeless Monsieur Ropion? - that it works just as well as a reminiscence of past Private Blends as it does as a creation of the present. Oud Voyager, whose name speaks of longing and distance, has that minor rhythm - like beautiful cursive on parchment or a sad waltz danced in half-shadow - driving and pressing, yet executed with precision. Rose with a hint of regret like a never-given bouquet and dry, almost paper-like wood like letters full of devotion and love that no one ever read. A fragrance full of vulnerability, full of hurt - and yet complete and intact. Conclusion: a strange wanderer between the olfactory yesterday and today. Very Tom Ford in its own way and yet also très Ropion. And - who would have thought? - it works.

Today my package from notino arrived, and this fragrance was included. The flacon and the packaging promised a lot. In the end, I was not disappointed, but I immediately knew that this is the new interpretation of Allure Homme Sport Extreme, only this is more of the "niche" version. Much rounder and softer, but also somewhat greener. Unfortunately, the longevity of both fragrances is absolutely terrible; after 4-5 hours, there's nothing left to smell. That's a real shame because it's a lovely scent, but it's not worth the retail price of €200. Thank goodness I paid less than a third of that, so it was okay. Definitely a nice summer fragrance, somehow reminds me of the vineyards of Italy. Edit: After testing it multiple times, I notice a very metallic note in the drydown that is quite unusual. It smells like cold, fresh metal.
