In almost every point, I can only agree with my predecessor. This is also my first comment, and then on this fragrance. It’s hard to believe that there are only one or two entries about Emperial Green. I have enjoyed around 150 different fragrances, always on the lookout for a fresh creation without a synthetic aftertaste or undertone, as is unfortunately often the case. And I have found it. After acquiring many warm, wintry scents, herbal fragrances that also fit into spring and autumn, or incredible all-rounders like Layton from PdM, after sweet-oriental classics like Egypt Dreams from Tabac and artistic ones like J'Ose from Eisenberg, I have encountered a sweet-fresh masterpiece. The first whiff after spraying carries me nostalgically away to a summer evening almost a decade ago. Without a doubt, the fragrance opens with mandarin and lavender, even though I rarely detect these in combination with other oils. The tonka bean is subtly and slightly bitter, always present from the beginning until (almost) the end, 9 hours later. The mandarin shifts within the first hour into a slightly warmer orange blossom, just as the pyramid suggests. A certain powderiness seems to linger in my nose, even though I have yet to find any agreement on this. And time passes, until after many hours only a bitter-warm-tempting ambrox remains, at least I recognize it in reference to synthetic (or real, who knows) amber notes that have already established themselves as a base note in other fragrances. For lovers of amber, I recommend Theta from the Svea fragrances, which hardly gain any reputation online, perhaps because they are very new, lack a known platform, or because their marketing is strange. Emperial Green is labeled as a unisex fragrance, and I can fully agree with that. I am a big fan of fragrances that are typically feminine, but I don’t dare to wear them myself; this is a wonderful scent for men too! I look forward to spring and summer, when this fragrance will finally come into its own. All in all: My search for a fresh-sweet perfume has come to an end. But as most here can surely empathize: For now, just one.

My first comment and also the first on this fragrance.....well then, let's get to work and I apologize in advance for the newbie comment. The beautiful, high-quality bottle and the pyramid intrigued me, so I immediately ordered a sample. As a "freshy," I have been on the lookout for clean, fresh scents that are still not run-of-the-mill. Imperial Green starts off soapy-fresh and slightly fruity with mandarin and lavender. I even think I can perceive the orange blossom, as a floral nuance emerges. It brings to mind a clearing in spring, illuminated by the sun. The initial brightness of the fragrance fades very quickly, and the scent becomes a bit more austere. Here, the first clouds begin to gather over the clearing. Tonka and vanilla soon make their presence known, and the fragrance remains overall pleasantly soft....velvety. As the journey continues, the clouds gather more and more, becoming darker. It becomes sultry, oppressive, and tension hangs in the air over the initially so peaceful clearing. For now, vetiver and cedar are battling against patchouli and vanilla for their lives.....with no hope of success. Any effort to maintain a fresh impression is smothered by the velvety patchouli and vanilla. Due to the velvety sweetness, I would classify the fragrance at least in the unisex category. An interesting development, but unfortunately not my thing. The search will continue.

Arabian? This smells Arabian in the manner of a Penhaligon's fragrance, that is to say, British. First and foremost, can we dispense with “Arabian” unless we’re referring to horses or history? I assume Tom Ford uses the word because it’s Fashion Fantastical. Ariabian, you know, like A Thousand and One Nights. It’s the orientalism of early 20th century perfumery all over again. Stale, offensive exoticism. Also, the imagery and allusion is just cheesy. Makes the line seem like a spin on The House of Creed. Replace the tassels and epaulets with glossy pseudo-mod and you still have the same thing: hot air and cuff links. The perfume is nice, though. I can't say that I smell lavender per se, but I do smell the soapy, herb-on-hay sweetness of a fougere. At the same time there is a dry bitter green angle, like a tight-assed chypre. Maybe galbanum dressed up as lavender and took its place in the fougere. This tinderbox-dry woodiness balances the moist feel of the fougere, but in the end the fougere wins, and a fairly dark, minor chord similar to that of Rive Gauche pour Homme's basenotes lasts until you wash it off. Arabian Wood is a fine old-school barbershop fougere. Simplicity is a virtue in the classic aromatic fougere. Messing around too much with the basic formula diminishes the stride of the old boy. Ford have added enough to make it stand on its own, but haven’t muddied the waters. The name is a bit of misdirection, but the perfume is straightforward and handsome in a classic, soapy, manly fashion. Women, give it a try. from scenthurdle.com

Arabian Wood stood out to me, so i decided i'd smell it This is BEAUTIFUL!. ABSOLUTLEY BEAUTIFUL!. Like a MONSTER. I have been to the UAE and it is one of the most incredibly luxurious and personified places to visit in the world. Arabian wood is a testament to the beauty of the culture it has interpreted. Tom Ford himself should be congratulated for such a fantastic and complex scent and all with woods. The Chypre is definetly evident to me but it is sort of like the ribbon around the present, its pretty much what ties the woody notes all together and whilst i usually dislike an overload of woods, this works beautifully. I can pick up the luscious Gardenia in this fragrance, its prominent and strong, it gives the fragrance a very feminine sort of elegance but there might also be rosewood in this scent to, giving it a feminine touch, but its very muted, the oud is extremely dominant and well so it should be- its beautiful. Im not to sure if i get a spiciness from Arabian Wood but i definetly get a sense of warmth and that could be from notes of spices but to my nose its not as present as it might be for other reviewers. I think when you're purchasing a Tom Ford product and intend on wearing this, then you should be packed with confidence because i think it would take some guts to wear Arabian Wood- not that its overpowering or awful but the strength and the character of this fragrance is not going to sit right with everyone, which is a shame because i love exotic scents like this- its sexy and unashamed of how luxurious it is. In my opinion this is definetly a unisex scent. I ended up buying the 50ml bottle, which is incredibly expensive but worth every single penny

Arabian Wood by Tom Ford is quite an unpredictable fragrance. I approached this scent expecting thick, spicy and slightly smoky wood notes, however Arabian Wood is mossy, complex and utterly fascinating. This is a mossy chypre for both sexes, as it has both masculine and feminine tendencies. It's really one of those Tom Ford fragrances that shouldn't be missed. However you might have to wear it a few times to fully grasp and understand its beauty. The opening is really masculine and in some ways, harsh. It's quite a dense blend of damp woods, orris root and bergamot. I had a friend with me the first time I smelt Arabian Wood. I think she might have been questioning why I would ever want to smell something along these lines. It makes a much louder statement than she's probably used to smelling in mainstream perfume. Arabian Wood is quick to settle on the skin. The most interesting aspect of this fragrance's development is how it blossoms under varied temperatures. I came to test Arabian Wood three times in one week because I struggled to find the words to describe it. In cool weather, the heart smells spicy-sweet with a hint of flowers. This is obviously due to the honey, lavender, rose and jasmine. Surprisingly, on a hot Summer's day, Arabian Wood shows its mossy and earthy side. There is also a hint of masculine soapiness, lending an almost powdery feel. When I say that this fragrance is unpredictable, I mean what I say. Arabian Wood is not really a woods based fragrance. It tends to encompass the smell of a musty, earthy forest, complete with the forest floor. I won't lie, it's an acquired taste. However it is something that I'm sure perfumistas will enjoy smelling, especially if chypres are their cup of tea. The longevity is superb, but then again I wouldn't expect anything less from an overly expensive Tom Ford fragrance. It's worth checking out. Original review written: January 2013.

Arabian Wood feels like siting cross-legged on a woven rug in a grand courtyard in an ancient city in the Middle East. The air is hot and there's a bright sun but you're under the shade of a fragrant cypress tree. The fragrance has a mediative vibe. Wearing it makes me feel like the most well-groomed super clean man in the city. As the name suggests, the fragrance is woody, aromatic but also a lot of green and a tiny bit incense. At some point the fragrance gradually starts smelling like an aftershave.

I discovered this perfume in 2017 through a sample. it is a very strong heady perfume, intoxicating, outdated, outdated, old fashioned. this smell. it looks like a perfume designed by mistake, an accident. the price of 300€ also seems like an accident to make us feel the way he keeps it. one of the worst in the collection.

Opens with a blend of unidentifiable flowers, green notes, cumin and dry woods. It may seem like an odd composition, but it manages to work just fine. It is rough yet polished - dark yet crystalline, all at the same time. The fragrance becomes warmer and denser as the notes bloom on my skin.

Arabian Wood - with this name, everything seems to be clear again. In fact, I had to check other reports to make sure that my sample wasn’t perhaps mislabeled and that I wasn’t wearing something completely different on my skin. However, we seem to have a case here where a perfume completely disappoints all the expectations that its name evokes.

The name hits completely the wrong note. I had the same experience with Tom Ford's "Tobacco Vanille," where I only smell unpleasantly sugary clove tea, neither vanilla nor tobacco. In my opinion, Arabian wood hardly appears here at all.

There is usually a lot of fuss surrounding Tom Ford fragrances. There is general excitement when a new scent is announced, money tends to flow quite freely, and many fragrances enjoy great popularity. I took a look, and the average rating of all Tom Ford fragrances listed here is 7.9, which is really a very respectable score. Until a few years ago, the ratings for fragrances were given in percentages here at Parfumo. I thought that was very good too. I probably don’t need to say anything more about Tom Ford himself. It also probably doesn’t need to be mentioned that he doesn’t stand at the lab table himself, diligently handling test tubes. Not all fragrances enjoy widespread recognition. Some are quite polarizing. Vert de Fleur is one of the less common fragrances. But it is one of the scents that I find particularly appealing, so much so that I absolutely had to have it. Anyone who knows me a little better knows by now that I am very fond of fragrances with floral notes. I also really like green notes in fragrances, and when Chypre notes appear, I am usually over the moon. Vert de Fleur embodies all of this. Created in 2016 by the French perfumer Yann Vasnier, who works for the Swiss flavor and fragrance manufacturer Givaudan and has created various scents for brands like Comme des Garçons, Jo Malone, Divine, and of course Tom Ford. Currently, 26 people own it, including 10 female and 16 male noses. Here, classic ingredients have been mixed in a modern way, with some differences from the "great old Chypre fragrances." The opening is already very floral and green, a big splash of galbanum brings this rich, gnarly-green note that persists throughout the entire fragrance. Galbanum can often come across as a bit unwieldy, but I have grown very fond of this note over time. A distinct hyacinth makes itself known very quickly and remains present throughout the entire fragrance journey. I have noticed that I really like hyacinth in fragrances; it is also very noticeable in Cristalle EdP. As a houseplant, I don’t like to have hyacinth around, as its penetrating scent often gives me headaches. However, in fragrances with various accompanying notes, it is a lovely note. And hyacinth is inherently rather unsweet, which I also appreciate. It always brings a certain sharpness that clearly runs through this fragrance. The hyacinth has several floral companions, none of which really step into the foreground, but together they show a certain fleshiness that suggests a hint of animalic quality. However, a true animalic component, as often found in classic Chypre fragrances, is absent here. Towards the base, it becomes a bit darker and earthier. I also notice that the fragrance has a generally cooler aura. With the vaguely defined green notes and the moss, the fragrance has a certain underlying "swampiness." Such notes sometimes bother me because they can remind me of old, musty floral water. Here, it fits perfectly and ensures that the fragrance doesn’t slip into the overly floral and generic. Counterpoints are important in fragrances; otherwise, they quickly become boring. And I don’t find this fragrance boring at all. It also exudes a large portion of self-confidence, which fits the image of the Tom Ford brand excellently. Vert de Fleur has good longevity; the fragrance can be perceived for 8-9 hours and radiates quite well for the first 2 hours before it then pulls back. I see it in spring and in the not-too-warm summer; at temperatures above 25 degrees, the fragrance could be too dense and might feel too cool in the cold season. That there is a certain synthetic quality hovering over everything cannot be denied. But so much synthetic material is now used, even in the high-priced segment, and if it is well integrated, I can handle it well. The fragrance is labeled as unisex here. I believe that floral fragrances can work well on men. And the slightly higher proportion of male owners apparently confirms this. However, I do have to nitpick a bit. Specifically regarding the craftsmanship of the bottle. Certain details are not attended to very closely. As valuable and appealing as the design appears at first glance, I cannot overlook a few flaws. For example, the label is a bit crooked, and the cap sits quite loosely. You have to be careful when taking the bottle out of the outer box. I find this a bit annoying, as the exclusive series is not exactly one of the budget fragrance lines. While the content is what counts, the packaging is also part of the purchase, and this one is a bit sloppy. Vert de Fleur came to me some time ago in a sample package from Kovex and sparked such enthusiasm that I had to quickly add it to my wish list. Now the fragrance is quite hard to find, and I had no choice but to look in a well-known online auction house. After some searching and a bit of patience, the fragrance then arrived from Great Britain. And at a more than acceptable price. I thank Kovex for allowing me to get to know this fragrance, and I am very pleased with it. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ Just a small note: I did not fall for a fake; the bottle and fragrance are real. I have noticed several times that there are occasional lapses in the craftsmanship of the bottles. My Mandarino di Amalfi Acqua (purchased at Karstadt) has similar small flaws.

I am a big fan of the green collection, but I can't find anything appealing about this scent, try as I might (although I would have liked it for the collection). No images or associations come to mind for me. What I miss the most are the flowers. Everything is green and remains green. Just green. And while green is very beautiful, without any additional splashes of color, it becomes rather boring to look at over time.

I do enjoy wearing so-called women's fragrances from time to time. 'So-called' because these are perfumes that the manufacturer has categorized as women's scents at some point - what the individual makes of it is entirely a matter of personal preference. I don't even register this in individual cases (anymore) when I do - let alone that it would be a conscious decision - much less intended as a deliberate provocation. Particularly the highly esteemed Mr. Ford operates with many of his perfumes in the border area between supposed women's and men's fragrances. And Vert de Fleur - the last of the four new 'Les Extraits Verts' collection that I tested - masterfully plays with this very ambivalence. Quite sincerely - more than with Vert des Bois and Vert Bohème, similar yet entirely different from Vert d'Encens - I am thrilled. Vert de Fleur begins with the grandiose quote of a women's chypre reminiscent of the 80s - dramatic and full of grandeur. There is a hint of Alexis Colby in the air - enough to draw attention - but not so much as to be tacky or outdated. And then - only from the heart note, which is as remarkable as it is fascinating - it develops a radiance that seems to grow stronger and brighter the longer it lasts. This is unusual - most fragrances tend to darken during their development. Its name should not mislead: Vert de Fleur is not a floral scent, not in the sense of the delicate waters that usually call themselves 'floral.' And it can only be limitedly described as green in the sense of herbal (and even less so as fresh). It is confident and - like so many of its brothers - clearly situated in an urban context for me - a fragrance for men who appreciate quotes from feminine scents on themselves - and for women who enjoy powerful and expressive fragrances with an androgynous, perhaps even masculine allure. Conclusion: 'Everything is illuminated' was the debut novel of the great New York writer Jonathan Safran Foer, who made it famous almost overnight fifteen years ago, and I had to think of its title while wearing Vert de Fleur. Because here too, everything shines.

Lalique TENDRE KISS reminds me a bit of Lancôme MIRACLE. Both feature pepper, flowers, and lychee, but TENDRE KISS offers a somewhat more subtle presentation of these notes to my nose. In addition, TENDRE KISS has a less musky base. The labdanum here imparts a smooth texture and viscosity apparent from the opening. It may also account for the good longevity of this low sillage edp. I would call TENDRE KISS an oriental floral, since the spices are just as important as the rose. If I were in the market for a lychee pepper floral perfume, I'd choose TENDRE KISS over MIRACLE since the pepper is more measured in this composition and does not overwhelm the florals. But anyone who likes the Lancôme will surely like the Lalique as well.

Lalique fragrances were once characterized by particularly beautiful bottles, which is why I had always been enamored with this scent. In the meantime, Lalique has changed the bottle; it now has the rectangular shape of the classics and no longer excites me, but just in time, I managed to snag one in the prettier design: The name and the romantic bottle suggest innocence. But even the first whiff speaks a different language: endless pink pepper. Are we at Maredo? Lychee, berries: no. The development is just as surprising: sweet, gourmand notes blend in my nose into a rosy fruit puree with a hint of spiciness. A summer gourmand with a twist? However, it is not light; it doesn't kiss but rather thumps. Still, the sillage is wonderfully fresh-rosy-spicy. And it lasts and lasts. I hope that the scent hasn’t been altered in the rectangular bottle, as is often done these days, because this one in the kitschy bottle is a great, sharp, modern rose scent for anyone who wants to make a statement.

Tendre Kiss was recently a bargain and “blind purchase” for me. On one hand, the reviews here were so good and on the other hand, I like some of the Laliques. The opening is fresh and slightly fruity, quickly followed by spicy pepper, accompanied by a bouquet of roses. The pepper gives the fragrance a nice, slightly bitter note; Tendre Kiss is not a soft, pleasing scent. I find it a bit cumbersome, which I actually like a lot. Towards the end, it becomes woody and warm; I can't smell the vanilla, and I have no idea what labdanum smells like. According to classification, many perfume enthusiasts (after all, 12%) perceive it as sweet, but my nose does not. However, if I've learned anything here, it's that the degree of sweetness is a topic for excellent debate. Tendre Kiss lasts surprisingly well on me, the sillage is rather subtle. In autumn and spring, it feels most comfortable; my bottle is rectangular, rosy, and the color matches the scent beautifully. The purchase was truly worth it; unfortunately, I don't have the aforementioned bottle, but you can't have everything; it's the content that matters, and that has class.

..fragrance gem, in my opinion. It is spicy, peppery, rosy, and somewhat leathery. It is not a smooth scent like Lalique Le Parfum, but it has edges and facets that make it a special and interesting little fragrance... If you like spices in perfumes and also enjoy rose, then you will find pleasure in this scent. I, for one, think it’s good :)

I am - as you can probably tell - a true Lalique fan. My partner is also well-equipped with the fragrances from this perfume manufacturer. Tendre Kiss was a "blind buy." The listed fragrance pyramid and the two positive comments about the scent inspired me. I am already looking forward to summer when the fragrance can fully justify its existence. Right now in winter, it doesn't quite dare to show itself with its "tenderness." But as I said, I ordered it very, very cheaply without trying it first -> had some doubts about whether it would be good at such a great price -> fragrance arrived, unpacked, sprayed -> all doubts vanished, fragrance remained!! On my skin, it starts very softly with the berry aroma, then briefly makes way for the pink pepper. It lingers with the rose and labdanum for quite a while. Sandalwood and vanilla are a bit shy and don't quite want to come forward on my skin with this scent. Perhaps they will lose their shyness in summer. Conclusion: Longevity is very soft... it is indeed "Tendre" Kiss, with the pink pepper pleasantly boosting the rose in its dominance. A worthwhile purchase! Bottle: The predecessor does more justice to the fragrance, beautifully romantic and playful. The new one is okay. Lalique can indeed create beautiful glass art and wonderful perfumes. And: They can finely combine the two.
This fragrance strongly reminds me of Eau de Cartier, the unisex scent from Cartier. It is light and not overpowering, perfect for spring.

Japon Noir I walked through the garden today, a cloudy cold rainy day...wearing Japon Noir makes me feel sad in a way, aside from its warmth, it comes off very hostile..almost abrupt..the leather squeezes hold of my neck, the patchouli runs its way down my lips leaving a dirty earthy after taste and the jasmine looks me in the eye...all the beauty in the world slowly tormented and destroied by the powerful leather. I kept walking through the garden..fallen petals kissing my toes, grass caressing my ankles..my finger tips brushing against the flowers. I cant help but feel somewhat dangerous with Japon Noir on my skin, almost as if this were the scent of an assasinator. Dark, violent and so beautiful..so perfect. I think the sense of fear i get from this is that the leather note doesnt quit, it literally enevelopes my body as if i were in a bondage dungeon with an audience of beautiful angelic people, looking at me..looking at my destruction. I dont think this represents the beauty and the heritage of Japanese culture, but it for me..represents the underground..the people beneath the streets and the sakura trees...filled with darkness..waiting hungrily to release themselves out onto the night. I love the spiciness of Japon Noir, its as if im sitting in an old Japanese tea house with steam bursting from the small tea pots and beautiful geishas fanning themselves in anticipation for what is to come. But once this settles and calms down..i find myself floating in water..confused but at peace with this fragrance and all its strange beauty

Overall, Japon Noir is a wonderfully smokey and sweet fragrance. It opens just a bit spicy & oriental on me, but quickly peels back to reveal it's smokey character which is maintained throughout the wear. As it dries, it becomes a bit sweet. The smokiness tames but still is present. JN has that tell-tale Tom Ford signature accord that's also in his Noir de Noir and Tobacco Vanille. The fragrance is a bit low on sillage and doesn't have the greatest longevity considering the price point. Many people regard JN as the most masculine of the TF Private Blend line, and I usually don't care for masculines on my skin. However, JN strikes me as solidly unisex. Japon Noir is quite unique, very wearable, and sadly discontinued. Highly recommend for sampling.

In the summer of 1989, I strolled through blooming Kyoto, the residence of the Japanese Emperor, the Tenno, for over 1000 years. I could hardly believe that I was here, washed ashore in distant Japan by chance and fate, with the time and leisure to explore the city and its surroundings for almost two months. Besides the Imperial Palace and the beautiful gardens, it was primarily the Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines (the term for a temple of the Japanese national religion) that stayed in my memory. While the shrines were often light and bright, dominated by the colors orange and white, the temples were generally dark, a bit gloomy, and occasionally mysterious, saturated with incense. Japon Noir: Just the name triggered various associations in me, memories of my time in Japan came flooding back. I have now owned a sample for a few days, giving me the chance to test this rare fragrance. What stands out to me initially is that the warm spicy note, which forms the opening, overshadows the patchouli note all the way to the base note. This is rather rare. Patchouli often has a strong presence and is, in my personal experience, too intrusive in many fragrances. I actually like it best when it remains subtly in the background and only casts its shadows, like a dark, softly burning candle. This is exactly how it appears in Japon Noir and provides a warm, soft foundation. As noted multiple times in the instructive comments of my predecessors, the port wine note in the fragrance is clearly perceptible. Less in the sense of an alcoholic accent, more as if the port wine had been used as a fond for a roast dish and had left its scent lingering in the kitchen while cooking. This scent note is also known from spice cakes that have been refined with a splash of red wine. And yet, the combination of spices and wine in this fragrance is not intrusive and strong, as one might know from the penetrating aroma of mulled wine. Here it is subtle, almost sweet, as if the fragrance always wanted to remain a little in the shadows, reserved and considerate, like a Japanese geisha. The fragrance components listed in the base note are, in my opinion, also well recognizable. The sour sharpness of the vetiver gently resonates for a while, a floral note (perhaps jasmine) remains perceptibly underlying, and after a longer time, one might even speak of a leather note. Does this fragrance now match my experience with Japan? The parallel to plum wine, Umeshu, has been drawn several times and is certainly not to be dismissed. Perhaps that was also what Tom Ford wanted to remind us of with this fragrance. Personally, the thought of the dark, mysterious Japanese temples does not leave me, even though it smelled quite different there: of incense and dark wood, masterfully captured, for example, in Comme des Garcons Kyoto. What I actually mean, however, is the impression of shadows, of cozy darkness, of the feeling of security that occasionally enveloped one in these temples, before a Japanese garden full of white flowers in the light. All these impressions and memories also arise with Japon Noir, so strongly that I have to apply the fragrance again and again to keep this beautiful feeling from leaving me. A fragrance that gently embraces the wearer. Thus, for me, the name stands less for something concrete, but rather for an impression of shadows and candlelight in the darkness, of exoticism and foreign lands, which has been well captured here, and whose great harmony, while simultaneously having a dark allure, certainly suggested the name Japon Noir.

After my praise for a fragrance from Japan, I found it exciting to engage with Japon Noir by Tom Ford. However, as soon as I applied the fragrance, one thing became clear to me: this scent does not want to align with my (probably completely idealized) fragrant image of Japan. I think Japon Noir presents a similar picture of the Land of the Rising Sun as the German village in Disneyland represents Germany, or in other words, the theme has been exaggerated to the point where Japon Noir skims dangerously close to being a caricature. The top note indeed has something alcoholic, but it doesn't really smell like Asian plum wine to me. I find it smells like what it contains, port wine, because alongside the alcohol, Japon Noir has a distinctly woody character right from the start. The spices that are supposed to be in the top note only come through for me with the heart note and add to the woody port wine. At the same time, Japon Noir also becomes sweeter and more opulent. Only after hours can I recognize a shift towards the base. Here, Japon Noir becomes distinctly balsamic sweet, and the spiciness takes a back seat. The projection is very pronounced, and the longevity can easily compete with any 80s perfume. Japon Noir is a great fragrance, and if it were still available, I would have eagerly purchased it. However, regarding the thematic implementation, the name Kabuki Theater gives one the impression of something grand, while the fragrance offers something akin to Miss Saigon à la Las Vegas (the source material for the musical, like Puccini's opera, is a French novella called Madame Chrysanthème by Pierre Loti). Conclusion: Here, the theme has been wonderfully missed for a change!

it is famously said about Greek wine. I am not an outright connoisseur or lover of Greek winemaking, but the analogy seems fitting for this extraordinary fragrance. More than most fragrances I know, even among the other not-so-lightweight TFs, Japon Noir is a grand, profound, and exceedingly serious scent. One that I never wear casually, where I must be sure whether I can endure it until the end of the day or night. Japon Noir does not necessarily appear Eastern. It is black wood, it is great emptiness, and it is solemn silence. That may seem Eastern, may seem Japanese. But it is also dark ink, it is heavy sacramental wine, it is bitter smoke and cold ash and heavy cloth. It is profoundly erotic and sensual and not at all provocative, not sexy. It is of great wisdom and composure, like a gaze from infinite distance into infinite depth. It is like a consecrated fire, a fragrance to be worn in enclosed spaces, in late autumn or winter. It is aloof, invites nothing, seduces to nothing. The alcoholic plum gives it a hovering, almost warning sweetness - like a premonition of danger. At first, it is leaden in weight, yet after four or five hours it rises hesitantly and staggering like a gigantic black bird and takes its wearer along. Conclusion: a very special fragrance. I will use my remaining amount with caution.

First of all, thanks to Reckoner for the sample! I had a rough start with Tom Ford regarding Oud Wood. Now, this is my second attempt with Japon Noir. I can't say why "Japon," but one thing is for sure: this fragrance is quite unusual. It starts right away with an insane, rounded depth of fruity alcohol, which is probably the port wine.

I stumbled upon the fragrance while shopping. I don’t want to miss it now; in my eyes, it’s one of the best, if not the best, fragrance on the market. At first, it smells very strongly of that warm plum schnapps you always get after eating at a restaurant, which I personally find very pleasant.

Many thanks to WitweBolte for lending me Japon Noir, one of his absolute favorite bottles. This bottle is really hard to come by these days, and unfortunately, there are no plans for a revival anytime soon, nor am I aware of a similar scent, as TF often does himself.

Yes, European. Perhaps somewhat Oriental. I find it a bit difficult to name the fragrance, especially considering the ingredients listed above, because I can only olfactorily connect to Japan in the early stages. This happens to me often with Tom Ford.

No, I consciously do not say Grandpa scent... because it is not one. ;) This perfume belongs to the gentlemen of creation, dear ladies, and there is no arguing about it, we just have to accept it. Cool Water, Dhofar, Acqua Di Parma, Vetiver Guerlain; these are the first candidates that come to mind.

I enjoy the impression of TF Black Violet, and I appreciate its uniqueness. It's a darkish floral with just a hint of grumbling underneath. BV dries to a woody floral, medium longevity and short throw. I don't find it as oakmossy or as powdery as others have reported, so I hesitate to mention those qualities. Overall, I think BV is best described as a masculine floral. Unfortunately, TF Black Violet just doesn't seem agreeable on my skin. It's got an artificial synthetic quality to it, plasticity ... not a Barbie doll head, but more like dated plastic army men that have got a bit dusty and a bit warmed, perhaps. BV wafts in and out of magnificence, and it's in those moments of brilliance that I debate a purchase. However, it turns again, and I get that plastic army man again. I know, it's an impression. But at this price point, a mediocre scent on my skin, only occasionally punctuated with brilliance, is not a fragrance that I'll own ... or tolerant. I see this as just on the femme side of unisex, but a violet that a man could easily pull off without any problem. I have difficulty wearing masculines, so perhaps that's why I have difficulty with TF Black Violet. Personally, I have fallen for Violet Blonde, of which I have a full bottle. In the TF Private Blend line-up, it's Noir de Noir that tops my list. But this one ... Let's just say that I'm glad to only have a small rollerball of TF Black Violet.

Black Violet Tom Ford Nothing is ordinary about this heady scent Everything is naturally extraordinary. Extraordinary or even extravagant, manufactured for a hedonistic lifestyle of sustainable beauty and eccentric elegance. How wonderful! Black Violet is Overt hedonistic sexiness .... TOM FORD at his apex of cool designing for GUCCI! back in the 90's A Humid Hothouse of Florals exuding strong scent of SEX! Beautiful Men lost in boredom of a lush ORCHID filled room or is it Sensual Torpor...wearing GUCCI Black Shirts...and little to nothing else.... Extravagant Rubelli textiles.....VENETIAN opulence..... a purple laser cut velvet floral dress languid and luxe... Charlotte Rampling as imagined by HELMUT NEWTON at the NEGRESCO Hotel in Nice MAD and BAD and Dangerous to know... this fragrance promises danger....loudly its not a Shrinking Violet at all... more like a poisonous flower saturated scent which arouses strong sensations in its pure essence, it dominates the space after seducing you ....it retreats into the shadows of of those luxurious velvets. ..sweet fruity notes linger ... as they deliver us to reality we....luxuriate in spreading confiture de myrtilles sauvages, wild berry jam over our warm Blinis realizing that the BELUGA caviar has long been finished.... ahhhhh how decadent .

Tom Ford fragrances mean for me endurance, power, opulent and massive perfumes, and BLACK VIOLET is a perfect example for experiencing all of these preconceptions/observations. The scent is: - lewd - powdery - strong - sweet (soo sweet, that I would invoke coconut here) Violet belongs to the most elegant and refined part of the flowers’ realm, a calm-cold beauty – but the violet in BLACK VIOLET is coughing from the powder. It depends certainly on body chemistry, on others it shows more citrus and is definitely more tartish. The base tends to ooze the same notes on different skins - I smelled wallet of an old lady once, and it had almost the same fragrance. The very end is near to LOVE POTION no. 9 by Penhaligon’s (for Ladies of course).

I don't mean the one sung by Pink Floyd or the one from Darth Vader. I mean the dark side that slumbers in each of us. It doesn't have to be criminal, but rather disreputable, dirty, perhaps vulgar... They say still waters run deep. Sometimes we don't want to be angels, but rather a temptress. We want to be looked at greedily, so that the thoughts of the eager are loud and clear: I want you! With skin and hair - NOW! Black Violet awakens the desire to dress provocatively and go to a bar. To be flirted with. To feel desired. To see that longing in the eyes of others, to be wanted. That sexual tension that is almost unbearable... Black Violet is dark, mystical, sexy. Only slightly sparkling at the beginning, then the soft scent of violets envelops my skin in a velvety way. PS: My husband is once again in the bathtub. Let's see... ;-)

I found myself at the Tom Ford counter once again today. I assume the saleswoman has slowly memorized my face, which is why it’s becoming increasingly embarrassing for me to keep testing Black Violet and not buying it. “I want to see how it develops on my skin” doesn’t cut it anymore, and “I want to ask for it as a Christmas gift and just wanted to sniff it again” is probably not very believable on December 28th. I got lucky and she had to leave her little stand in the corner. I weaved through the shelves. Spritz spritz (neck left and right). When I saw her coming back, I had already disappeared into the handbag section. For inexplicable reasons - there’s little Morticia Adams in me - Black Violet and I really go very well together. Last week, I asked the saleswoman: Which one do you like better on me? She smelled Black Violet (dark scent) and Champaca Absolute (light scent) on my forearms. Her decision was quick and clear: Black Violet. Black Violet reminds me of Cigarillos, specifically the “Sweets” (flavored with vanilla) from Dannemann. And what Cigarillos do to women, Black Violet does to them too. When lighting/applying it, one’s posture automatically improves, the previously hunched back suddenly becomes very noticeable. One suddenly feels much more self-confident and with the wrong discussion partner, perhaps even a bit fierce. Black Violet is dark, full, round, and velvety, but it also has something strict and straightforward about it. On my skin, it feels very feminine. There are few citrus notes and no fruits at all, but plenty of violets and - it seems - delicate woods. I find Black Violet more pleasant and not as loud as Tobacco Vanille or Noir de Noir. These two are too loud for my taste; on me, they feel intrusive and inappropriate. Black Violet is more muted, softer, the perfect dose of darkness and mystique for me as a light type. That’s why the memory of the Sweets emerged only here - for me, an absolute moment of enjoyment - and not while testing Tobacco Vanille. This violet is truly black and it smokes Cigarillos.

I had the day off today, the sun was shining, and I felt like doing a bit of perfume shopping. One of my first stops was a perfumery that carries the scents from the "Tom Ford Private Collection," and since I've been discovering violets for myself lately, I first tried a spritz of "Black Violet.

He never made it into Tom Ford's very first line. Too little drama, too little 'oomph' it seems at first glance. And his name, the black violet, leads one down the wrong path - this is not the scent of the stepmother, not the scent of the wicked fairy. Black Violet is playfully soft and deeply intoxicating and promising.

Do you like the Tom Ford ads where trendy people are depicted in aggressive, dominant sexual scenarios? As if there’s nothing else between man and woman than seeing each other as sexual objects and as if life only ever happens after the party.

Today, for the first time in my life, I tested a fragrance from the Tom Ford Private Blend line. I should do this more often. I had already been eyeing Tobacco Vanille for quite a while due to its name and content. But first up is Black Violet, a rich Eau de Parfum that makes it clear within the first few seconds that the craftsmanship is top-notch.

So why is this violet black? In my case, the matter is crystal clear, it wasn't allowed to smell and then got annoyed black! BV is once again one of those scents where the name conjures up an image that the fragrance does not fulfill. I had expected something floral-sweet with plenty of opulence. Okay.

Once again too much text for a statement. I always try so hard to keep my thoughts brief, because all I want to say is: Between fresh soap and resin on the hands. Between ground and footwear, the fallen leaves, the damp earth, dead rock. In a suit through the quiet forest in the middle of the night. Incense, tobacco, tranquility. It’s not cold enough to freeze, but cool enough to think clearly. For a moment you smell Terre d'Hermès, in the next Cacharel pour l'Homme. Then everything is different again. Incense wherever you smell. Cedarwood and tobacco make the scent very masculine. Fougère Platine is not sweet, not pleasing, not always understandable to outsiders. Related to Fougère d'Argent, but not so easily charming. At least not at first glance. Fougère Platine is more direct, woodier, smokier than its brother. Fougère d'Argent never takes off its suit. Fougère Platine sometimes looks better in it. Instead of lavender, there is wood and incense. I like both.

“Fougere Platine” is a creamy fougere, steel gray and not very natural. Bayer meets Cyprus, Wall Street meets ebony, forest on concrete. But most of the time, I like it. Until it eventually gets on my nerves. But that takes a while. A gray panther. An old boy, a silent scream. A delicately marbled cedar cream meets green moss spots. Definitely an upscale perfume for me. Subtly smoky, dignified, artificial modesty. Maybe even dementia. Who knows. In any case, Tom Ford has more better scents than worse ones in his portfolio than this one. However, fougeres do have a magnetic pull on me, which is why I had to test it, even giving it precedence over illustrious names like “Lost Cherry” or “F*cking Fabulous.” But unfortunately, this synthetic fougere doesn’t play in that weight class. Not even close. Delicate, gray, green, classic, creamy. Cedar, moss, minimal incense. There’s not much more to it. Well stirred and mixed. Fine blend. But still quite plain, boring, and after a certain period, even slightly bitter, piercing, and dull. Not a good last third. Everything before that is simple and solid. “Platinum Egoiste” meets something like “Lavender Palm,” just with cedar and other light woods. Could also be a Comme des Garçons. Just without their edge and creativity. Here it feels smoother, greener, and more sophisticated. Calculated and the opposite of wild and passionate. Cool warmth. Almost a bit robotic. The suit scent of an A.I.? Bottle: the epitome of modern, cool elegance. Tom Ford could hardly have done it better. Perhaps THE bottles that have defined this century so far. Despite their price and often perceived aloofness. Sillage: office-appropriate and, as is often the case with TF, not totally quiet. The man is not one for the sidelines. And neither are his perfumes. This one is clearly “discreet” for him. Longevity: 7-9 hours was enough for me - although I generally really like this silver cedar eminence. Conclusion: a fougere with gray hair and a lot of experience. Chemistry lab meets business class, creamy meets artificial and (quickly) bitter. Forced cool.

You have to love strong floral perfumes to appreciate this beauty. It is like being in the florist shop. The air is heavy with a floral mist from so many different flowers. As you move from one floral arrangement to another, different flowers become stronger in the bouquet. They entice you with their intoxicating aroma and lovely colors and shapes. Flora Bella is just like that - as the scent develops, you got to experience various floral arrangements masterfully put together. The scent is very romantic, elegant and alluring. I can imagine it as a wedding scent for an outdoor summer wedding. After zesty opening of bergamot and mandarin, Flora Bella sets into a strong, cold and fresh bouquet of freesia, lilacs and orchids. It is a bit overpowering but nevertheless quite elegant in its icy, regal beauty. The scent gradually becomes warmer and spicier in the heart notes with frangipani, tiare, mimosa, tuberose and a touch of pepper. This warm, tropical flowers phase is softer but still quite powerful. The base notes are delicate amber and vanilla layered on light floral notes. The sillage is strong, so I suggest using this perfume lightly. It could be allergy-inducing in large quantities. The longevity is good. Do you love being surrounded by flowers? If your answer is yes, then Flora Bella will be a nice addition to your collection.

I rarely wear Lalique FLORA BELLA, but every time I do, I wonder why I don't. It's an odd, eccentric floral creation, unlike most of the others available today. I thought of FLORA BELLA because I was reminded of it by Rancé 1795 JOSEPHINE. Hmmm... does that mean that this strangely opaque combination of mystery ingredients actually existed two centuries ago? Well, they are not exactly alike, and I prefer FLORA BELLA, truth be told. I see only today that "in the doghouse" Bertrand Duchafour was the perfumer. I have not read up on the case which bloggers have been venting about all over the internet, but I doubt that I'll be boycotting Duchafour's creations, although if it turns out that he boils people alive, I'll probably start thinking of him along the lines of Jean-Baptiste Grenouille. Somehow I doubt that that's the case... Anyway, why is this so weird? It has a fluffy whiteness but is not a big fat white floral fragrance. The texture is completely different: grainy and creamy at the very same time, as contradictory as that may seem. Back when I first tested this perfume from a sample vial (a couple of years ago), I felt that it had a tropical vibe, which I no longer detect at all now that I own a bottle. Fortunately, despite what appear to be either batch problems or a radical shift in my own olfactory capacities, I like this creation, too. There is a slight similarity in style to Donna Karan GOLD, and the same texture is also found, according to my nose, in Boucheron MISS BOUCHERON. I hasten to add, however, that the notes in all of these cases are very different. The greatest similarity between the three perfumes is that they are all eminently overdosable. Some perfumes can be spritzed on with reckless abandon and a consistent result can be expected nonetheless. Not so with perfumes boasting whatever it is that makes this smell so different from all of the other floral perfumes. One spritz too much and suffocation will ensue. But lightly applied, these are all quite nice. I think that FLORA BELLA is the best of the bunch. It shares the quirkiness of everything else launched by this house. Although the Lalique perfumes are all very different, they exhibit an undeniable quality and flair, in addition to being unique. Maybe that's because Lalique consistently enlists excellent perfumers for its launches. In the end, although I find it difficult to articulate exactly why, I like FLORA BELLA not in spite but because of its weirdness!

I both like it and can't stand Flora Bella. The drydown of a light dose of FB is a metallic, Forbidden Planet flower---from the tropics of Altair. Enticingly alien in a 1950s, sci-fi modernist sort of way. More metal and form than flower. On the downside, every moment until the drydown is tinged with cheap pina colada mix and an air-freshener style caricature of a pan-tropical floral note. Smother that in fabric softener and you have an overview of Flora Bella.

At the moment, I am focusing on my decants that have accumulated over time. Recently, I haven't paid much attention to this part of my new additions, and now, instead of being out and about forever, I have spent more time testing some of them. Flora Bella is a lovely scent, one could say. ;-) It starts with a decent portion of violet with roses. However, the violets are not powdery enough to give me a headache. A delicate green note is present here, overall very pleasant. After the violet-rose opening, I can distinctly identify lilac along with a subtle, unsweet vanilla. Shortly thereafter, frangipani joins in, along with a little mimosa, freesia, and daphne. The whole thing results in a beautiful blend that is well-balanced. I still smell something green-woody, but I am at a loss as to what it exactly is. Vanilla and clean white musk form the base; I don't detect any spices or amber. What pleases my nose is that I don't particularly like either of those scents on myself. On others, however, I do, just not on me. For me, Flora Bella is a beautiful, well-balanced scent that brings just the right amount of everything. It is not sweet at all on me. The longevity is about 6 hours, and it neither triggers asthma nor headaches for me.

Spring feelings awaken...Summer vibes too...probably one could attract plenty of bees and butterflies with Flora Bella...I was looking for a frangipani perfume and have (somewhat) found it. Although it is not a pure frangipani perfume, this beautiful note comes through very well. Sweet, but it doesn't overwhelm. I can also perceive vanilla. A great scent for anyone who loves to daydream...My first 100 ml bottle, as this fragrance is affordable for an Eau de Parfum...Finally spritzing without guilt...I notice a certain similarity to Alien, but I am not an Alien expert...(still on my wishlist...) Flora Bella is probably more for someone who doesn't want to stand out too much from the 0815 perfume junkies.

Rose Exposed by Tom Ford is this time not a mass-appeal fragrance, it is a niche scent. If I were to describe this fragrance, I can really only think of these two terms: rose and leather. I don't smell much more than that. But it's not your typical rose; it's an old rose, a fragile rose, and old leather, like from grandma. Probably the incense, cypress, and pepper ensure that the rose and leather smell like "grandma." The leather truly smells like that of a handbag that is 30 years old and has seen it all. The rose and leather even lean slightly towards a musty direction. The scent may smell old, but it is very unique. It draws attention, both in a positive and negative sense. It is more of a fragrance for men and not worth a blind buy! You need to test it beforehand.

His (re-)test came completely unexpectedly - at an airport and with not really comfortable transfer time - and therefore was not very meticulous and thus not really fair. However, I dare to say that I have acquired sufficient fragrance experience over the years to recognize and somewhat describe the essence of a scent even under such unfavorable conditions, and - as has already been suspected - I am quite sure: this is the discontinued Rose de Russie from two years ago or a very closely related bastard of it. Not very meticulous and not fair for two reasons: first - obviously - because sprinting from one gate to another with a paper strip in hand (I consider myself considerate enough not to spray something on my skin just before a flight) is hardly the ideal setting to test a perfume without prejudice. And secondly, I did not have the comparison - Rose de Russie - with me, of course. Comparing a several hours old test strip from my coat pocket with a fresh scent from the bottle - I think you understand me... Excursus: how did I come to Rose de Russie? I already liked it back then (as you can tell from my review), but I never saw it as one that would really improve my collection and therefore never seriously considered acquiring it. Then it was - for the well-known reasons that I do not wish to comment on or evaluate in this apolitical place (and I appreciate it as such and ask to keep it that way) - taken out of the program and suddenly became as rare as the lost Amber Room, as the owners of the Tom Ford perfume brand had decided not to sell it anymore, anywhere. However, when Galeries Lafayette in Berlin closed its doors forever last year, they may have thought: who cares - and simply put the last three flacons they still secretly had back on the shelf, unreduced until the last day, by the way. One of them then ended up with me - now or never! - as silly as such a desire-to-have buying impulse may be. And before the other collectors immediately ask me: no, I’m keeping it. Tom Ford's Rose Exposed is - if not exactly the same scent as Rose de Russie - at least one that undoubtedly draws on its scent DNA: suede meets rose. Dusty pink meets burnt umbra. Androgyny meets bittersweetness. Temptation takes a backseat to aloofness. Pale light and tenderness-less warmth like a stranger's breath on cold fur. A rose scent serious and mature and grown-up and beyond playful flirtation. A leather scent like rough gloves in an abandoned park in winter - melancholic and deserted. Conclusion: let’s simply forget that it ever existed. Rose Exposed deserves to be seen, experienced, and discovered today and here and for itself - in the name 'Russian' or 'exposed/uncovered', one adjective fits as poorly as the other. And yet this scent - although a relaunch from not too distant days - is special and beautiful.

Rose de Russie is not the rose of someone who defers to others, or adapts. It evokes quiet confidence. It is moody, yet soft in projection…not a pink rose, perhaps an orange one. It is a tarry and leathery and peppery rose, yet it is not overwhelming. There is some smoky, tarry almost black tea note, yet it is a soft facet of this mood. This is quite nice and I could see adding this to my collection.

It literally smells like pungent incense to me. I remember being so excited to try a Tom Ford fragrance and then being immediately put off by the smell of ashes. I do detect a nice rose underneath that burnt smokiness but man.... this just reminds me of the temple in all the bad ways. Maybe someone who likes darker fragrances would like this, but not me.

is the current Olympic champion in women's figure skating. Although she competed as the reigning world champion, she was almost a bit of an underdog among the three favored Russian skaters in February in Beijing - overshadowed by the athletic jumping wonder Alexandra Trussova and the fifteen-year-old prodigy Kamila Valieva, all of whom came from the controversial school of Eteri Tutberidze. Trussova did indeed land five quadruple jumps in her free skate, but she skated sloppily and stumbled one too many times, and Valieva was caught doping just before the competition, yet still competed and could not withstand the pressure in the individual event; her fall was the scandal of these Winter Games. Shcherbakova finished second in both the short program and the free skate with flawless performances - and because the respective first-place skaters in the other segment (Valieva and Trussova once each) made mistakes, it was enough for her to take the gold in the end. Anna Shcherbakova embodies the appearance and style of the archetype of the delicate yet steely figure skater, positioned somewhere between Haunted Beauty and a hunted doe, trained by the iron hand of Tutberidze, who drives even eight-year-olds with blood on their skates to jump higher and further - and if there were complaints, there were plenty of other girls ready to take their place within minutes if one truly did not want it. Details of figure skating bored here, but in the combination of the highest technical demands (albeit 'only' two quadruple jumps in the free skate and without the still mythical triple axel among women) and her musicality, choreographic precision, and a remarkable skating maturity for someone who was then seventeen, she rightfully won Olympic gold (which weighs many times more than a world or even European championship title). All the described characteristics - the serious, the highly disciplined and controlled, the dramatic, and the grace and elegance - can also be found in Rose de Russie, the tragic one among the three rose fragrances that Tom Ford launched in early 2022 - and which was hastily and quietly withdrawn from the market in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, as the Russian in its name suddenly made it unsellable. One might find this exaggerated or silly, yet it is also consistent and right as a signal - especially when considering how indifferent a perfume is, more or less, in light of the circumstances. The only chance to smell it since then is as part of a little-noticed miniature set of all three rose fragrances, which is still available in a few places. (I smelled it in the USA.) Rumours say it might be re-released under another name. Yet Rose de Russie is a special and very beautiful fragrance - performing like the delicate Anna Shcherbakova, as she skated first in dramatic black and then in pale purple on the ice of Beijing to win the gold medal. The playful and teasing nature of the rose recedes immediately after the top note behind something unattainable, dark, which is presumably meant to be 'Russian,' making Rose de Russie even more androgynous, serious, and very special than Rose de Chine and Rose d'Amalfi, the other two from the rose collection - and one that you remember, even if you believe you have smelled the 'dark rose' accord a hundred times before. Nothing here is sweet, let alone sugary - instead, it lays something bitter and pale, something vulnerably graceful beneath the rose timbre, making it an intimate winter fragrance - perhaps damaged, but not broken - and one that is missed. Conclusion: we probably won't see them again: Tom Ford's serious rose fragrance and the beautiful Anna Shcherbakova. The former, because it received the wrong name at the wrong time. And the latter, because Russian female skaters are excluded from all international competitions for the foreseeable future for the same reason (which one might find unfair as well as consistent and right). And because, for a figure skater - shaped in the style of Tutberidze, who seeks girl bodies and not women's bodies - she has simply become too old at eighteen. Both can be lamented.

At the very beginning (the first 5 minutes), it smells completely innocent like a beautiful rose from the garden, similar to Rose Privée L'Artisan, aaaaber with the pepper and woodiness that doesn't continue in a very feminine way, and after about 10 minutes, it's absolutely no longer feminine and definitely not innocent ))) To me, it smells somewhat similar to fresh hemp even ))) (I don't smoke, but I prefer this direction of fragrances )) so there must be something similar in it ))) I would say the longevity on my skin is about 6 hours, which is very good; after that, it's quite close to the skin. Strangely, it smells much more intense on my clothes and still has the rose compared to my skin... And after 7 hours on my clothes, I no longer smell rose, more like wood + leather and something similar to oregano or so... (on my skin, the scent is very subtle, almost nothing left) The sillage is nice but not too much, which is sometimes great; it always stays with me and only with me ))) I suspect it will definitely be renamed soon, so I had to be quick ) So I must have it :)

And finally, the fragrance dedicated to Russia, more specifically "Russian Black Leather"! This is a high-quality, specially tanned cowhide (also known as Yuft), produced in Russia. The notes of this leather are present in the taste. The seductive charm of the night is the foundation of Rose de Russie. This luxurious and fascinating dark rose merges with the brightness of the sharp oil of white pepper and wood, and the passionately sexy and supple black leather demands a touch. A fragrance for men and women, sensual and dramatic, underscored by a bouquet of woody, citrus, and fresh notes as well as milder fruity, dry, and spicy tones. It begins with spicy top notes of pepper that meet a rose in the heart, and deep base notes are revealed through leather and wood. Lasting power all day, on clothing for two days. I plan to have all three perfumes from this Ford line; they are incomparable ️

Its name is definitely a program. It actually smells distinctly Russian. In my mind's eye, I see those overpriced, black real fur coats, even though I don't know how they would smell. At least this association remains with me. I find it interesting how this combination of black leather and rose works here.

Victoria's Secret body sprays - hated at home, especially by my mother, but universally loved by my friends. Admittedly, after I got rid of Bare Vanilla at the beginning of my fragrance journey due to the synthetic Victoria's Secret DNA, I never thought I could love a scent from this brand so much. However, when I was in Venice looking for a souvenir for my little sister, I had to realize in the Victoria's Secret store: this scent is somehow special. On the "bottle," I smelled, alongside peach and mango, a distinct note of sun-melted vanilla ice cream. When sprayed, this note initially takes a back seat, and you are enveloped by a very fresh, aquatic peach-hibiscus iced tea. This creates incredibly good vibes, especially in summer. In the drydown, the scent becomes sweeter - but never too sweet - and regains that light, transparent vanilla ice cream note. I also perceive sweetened amber and a slight floral aspect, which are not listed in the notes, but since there are several other ingredients listed, I think some notes have been omitted. The scent is somewhat reminiscent of Sparkling Lychee by KAYALI with a hint of Vanilla Candy Rock Sugar, but in a much more natural, less sweet, and indeed transparent way, like an iced tea. Sillage and longevity are, as expected from a body spray, not outstanding. You can still perceive it, and it lasts several hours on clothes. At this price, I find that acceptable. Especially since, in terms of scent character, it can definitely compete with designers in this direction and, in my opinion, even surpasses them in authenticity. In the end, I am very glad I didn't give this scent to my sister (she got a basic vanilla scent from the same edition:)) and by now, many memories are attached to it. Also, I have to share it with my friends, who love it just as much as I do. I guard it like my prized possession due to its limited edition and personal value. I will probably get a backup as long as it's still available…

Tom Ford OMBRE DE HYACINTH is a fine greyish-green chypre which reminds me a lot of a couple of the Annick Goutal perfumes: HEURE EXQUISE and GRAND AMOUR. The chypre quality leans more toward the former, and the declarative hyacinth toward the latter. There is also a touch of nuttiness, which reminds me of Creed IRISIA. Needless to say, given all of these comparisons, this is not at all a sweet perfume, and the drydown is even rather soapy. Nor does OMBRE DE HYACINTH remind me of much that I've tried before in the Tom Ford line. Most notably, there is no patchouli anywhere here to be sniffed. And no truffles, either! I quite like OMBRE DE HYACINTH, but I like classic chypres. I see that galbanum is listed as both a top and a base note, but to me this perfume is more gray than green, and I'd have guessed the presence of oakmoss, though it is not indicated either in the hierarchy or on the manufacturer's card. I also believe that I detect something akin to lily of the valley in this composition. OMBRE DE HYACINTH is unquestionably a well-made and pleasing soapy chypre perfume, but I believe that I can achieve the same effect by mixing a spritz of GRAND AMOUR with a spritz of HEURE EXQUISE. Yes, I'll have to give that a try!

Ombre de Hyacinth is the scent that got me into fragrances. I randomly applied it on myself, visiting a beautiful perfume shop in Rome, and from then on I felt enveloped in a dark, purple cloud of beauty and joy. I use this fragrance now only very very rarely because firstly it has been discontinued and I'm fearing the moment that bottles get rarer and rarer and secondly this fragrance has an almost hypnotizing effect on me. I can't trust myself in traffic wearing this. :) I haven't come across anything like it since. Utter love.

Green fragrances often touch me a little more than purely floral, citrus, oriental, or even gourmand ones. They are often serious and a bit aloof, melancholic and reserved, especially the darker, sometimes harsh representatives - with plenty of galbanum, moss, and forest accents - are rarely shallow and cheerful. The somewhat milder, lighter ones - grassy and green-leaved - are more lively and airy, they are the cheerful, spring-fresh scents. Ombre de Hyacinth is one of the melancholics, yet it is touchingly porcelain-like fragile. One hardly dares to expose it to the hostile world; a breath of wind could carry it away, fatally injuring it. It is as if one has stripped away ten masks, especially those of heaviness and bitterness that galbanum can radiate, leaving only the very bottom one, the one that separates the soul as thinly as parchment from the body. Ombre de Hyacinth thus presents itself as contemplatively introspective as it is weightlessly fragile. It oscillates between delicate violet, powdery flowers and dark green, ethereal depth, like a pale cool morning under densely packed tree shadows. We humans are also fragile. Some more, others less. Our hearts sometimes appear stronger than they will ever be, ultimately they are just like a thousand layers of leaves, and each individual leaf is highly vulnerable, quickly crushed by a raindrop, torn by a gust of wind. “Every magic has an end” is the title of a piece of music by Bersarin Quartett. And here it is very fitting, because Ombre de Hyacinth is no longer available. And in its fleetingness, its last slow breaths remind one of all the good that passes, fades away, and perhaps falls silent forever. (I thank KatharinaG and Achilles)

Ombre de Hyacinth from the Jardin Noir Private Blends line makes a spectacular, promising start for me, namely green-floral with a beautiful, very natural hyacinth note, which - energetically supported by the harsh violet leaves and bitter galbanum - deepens into a dark, herbaceous floral scent. I am already mentally justifying the very high price to myself - but before I convince myself to invest nearly 200 euros in 50 ml, Ombre de Hyacinth loses its strength. The scent noticeably weakens and no longer holds what the grandiose opening promises. It noticeably declines, becomes flatter, and develops in a more masculine, aftershave-like direction. In the top and heart notes, it seduces and enchants with its harsh, dark-floral sensuality, but in the base, it disappoints immensely and is simply boring aftershave.

So goes the title of the third of seven stories in Hans Christian Andersen's epochal fairy tale of the Snow Queen, equally rich in pages as in metaphors. Metaphors that I, as a little boy, of course did not understand when I first heard about little Kay, who fell under the spell of the demonic queen - and Gerda, his companion, who set out to find him - a long, arduous journey, always northward, all alone, facing uncertainty and snow, with nothing in her heart but her confidence and hope. I remember that the story both frightened and fascinated me at that time, already in the aforementioned third story, at the beginning of the great search: 'What did the hyacinths say? 'There were three beautiful sisters, transparent and fine. One wore a red dress, the other a blue dress, the third a white dress; hand in hand they danced by the quiet lake in the bright moonlight. They were not elves, they were human children. There it smelled so sweet, and the girls disappeared into the forest. The scent grew stronger; three coffins, in which lay the beautiful girls, glided from the thicket of the forest across the lake; the fireflies flew glowing all around, like little floating lights. Are the dancing girls sleeping or are they dead? - The flower scent says they are corpses; the evening bell tolls the funeral song!' 'You make me very sad,' said little Gerda. 'You smell so strong; I must think of the dead girls! Oh, is little Kay really dead? The roses have been down in the earth and say: No!' 'Ding, dong!' chimed the hyacinth bells. 'We do not ring for little Kay, we do not know him; we only sing our song, the only one we know.' Ombre de Hyacinth, one of four from Tom's dark garden, the labels here pale mauve. null of them in my very first row - they all remain a step behind their brothers in the brown bottles. And yet here, the hyacinth manages to extract a new, an exciting note. Not dark, yet fascinatingly dark-surreal - moonlit - a bit like the dead girls in Andersen's wonderful story. Nothing here of the sweet cheerfulness and bright friendliness of the hyacinth, as we know it, for example, from Penhaligon's Bluebell. Here it is heavy and dragging, accompanied by a diffuse earthiness and the shadowiness of long-standing water - and fleeting, unexpectedly fleeting for a Private Blend. Conclusion: faithful Gerda will find him in the end, her Kay. He was not in the realm of the dark hyacinths.

A scent that can captivate. And yet it is unexcited and still goes very deep. Here I have the impression that it is tactile and "transparent" at the same time. With a kaleidoscopic play of colors, in all conceivable shades of brown and blue. Starting with the warm-spicy impressions of an oriental night through saffron, cinnamon, and vanilla, over the dark-resinous "heart" with its labdanum and the "grounding" patchouli, all the way to the very noble-looking woods that seem almost contemplative. Attention is directed into quiet depths, which can be very calming and comforting. I can also clearly recognize blue and green moments. The somewhat rooty-grassy papyrus aroma blends with "blue" elements, almost "ozonic," whose origin I cannot identify in the above ingredient list. However, I suspect it is the interplay of the ingredients, especially with the sandalwood and the papyrus. This impression remains until the end, as the subtle background notes gradually push themselves forward. A scent for "coming down," for concentrating on the essentials :-))

Very noble and fine fragrance. Even if the bottle says something different. The scent color doesn't quite match the color on the bottle. I would have kept the bottle in nut brown. Like a noble walnut wood table. Refined and darkened with fine oils. At the table sits a middle-aged man. The cashmere wool collar sweater subtly rolled up. Looking into the distance, he sips from a nosing glass with a noble 20-year-old Isle of Arran Single Malt Whisky. No worries, no fears, just enjoyment. That's how I imagine the intimate moment with this fragrance. It vaguely reminds me of Babylon by Penhaligons. Just less sweet and much drier. A wonderful fragrance for autumn/winter. The H/S could be better. But otherwise top and worth buying.

Everyone knows it, chic, noble, and elegant. DNA 1:1 like Bentley, but in the drydown more subtle, less impulsive. I smell leather. This would also suit a noble lady wearing fine black gloves and a Chanel clutch, who just glides into an upscale boutique in Paris and then disappears in a black limousine.

Tom Ford knows Asia better than I do, but I can't help but see his new ‘Atelier‘ collection as reflecting a white guy asian fascination. I can't imagine a Tom Ford product release without a fairytale marketing strategy, and Fleur de Chine and the others in this collection (Plum Japonais, Rive d’Ambre, and Shangai Lily) don’t disappoint.  The fairy tale is an unexamined take on the ‘mysterious orient / dragon lady / inscrutable east’. It relies on well-know imagery. It is based on irrational fear and defensiveness. It is rich with generations of bigotry. Effectively, it’s precision-built for the fashion industry. The trigger is in the name of the perfume. Say Shanghai Lily 3 times in a row while looking into a mirror and it just comes to life. A wonderful thing about stereotypes is that they are timeless.  Ford's oriental bit is straight out of 1920s European Orientalism.  Not updating a stereotype to contemporary standards is a way of distancing one's self from the prejudice originally associated with the stereotypes and innoculating one's self against accusations of xenophobia and racial predjudice. That is, referring to old stereotypes is unlike actively engaging in stereotyping. It is historical. Literary. Post-modern. Post-colonial. If only wishing could make it so. Take-away # 1 is never look to fashion for a history lesson. Take-away # 2 should be apparent even to the fashion-minded. Smugly using anachronistic Asian references from the late-colonial sensibilility (the Ford line is called the "Atelier d'Orient" collection) doesn't do a thing toward defusing the racism of such language. It simply relies on exotic side of racism. The mystery, the exoticism.  Oooohh... The fetish. It would be more offensive if it weren't so tired. The perfume: Interesting for the fact that it starts like insecticide, and then grows creamy. A fascinating technical trick, I’m sure, but ‘creamy’ in this case is synonymous with ‘vague’. This olfactory pairing is much more clearly expressed in Calvin Klein Truth, a discontinued perfume available cheap online. from scenthurdle.com

a delicious, sparkling bouquet of flowers and fruits. bright, light, spicy, enchanting..... you haven't even finished sniffing out the individual components and unfortunately, unfortunately... after just 5 minutes, the precious scent comet has vanished, leaving behind a hint of sweetness and a flat scent trail how sad!!!! ....and rather untypical for fragrances by tom ford. even with the 2nd sample from another source, the same result: a scent dream that quickly disappears.... and could be a fragrance jewel if only it had better longevity!!!

This is the title of a novel by American Nobel Prize-winning author Pearl S. Buck, in which she tells the story of the life and rise of the Chinese Empress Dowager Ci Xi - starting with her entry into the imperial harem up to the suppression of the Boxer Rebellion. Buck describes Ci Xi in her development, equally her career from a simple concubine to an imperial consort and finally to the influential Empress Mother and Empress Dowager as a power-hungry, morally corrupt, and unscrupulous woman - based on sources that are now considered at least questionable. Undeniably, Ci Xi is one of the most ambivalent and colorful personalities of the Qing Dynasty and the waning Chinese Empire, which was to end in 1912 with the proclamation of the Republic. On one hand, she was regarded as power-hungry, lustful, and cruel - and at the same time, she had the New Summer Palace rebuilt and surrounded by magnificent gardens, which are still considered highlights of Chinese garden art and landscape architecture today. She was also known as a talented calligrapher and painter - her portraits of cranes and peonies are famous. Tom Ford's Fleur de Chine is by far too powerful and too little cheerfully arranged to be considered a shy, delicately fragrant floral bouquet, as its name might suggest. This can hardly be surprising if you know his fragrances, although there are even darker and more dramatic candidates among them. The multitude of flowers that shape its character initially appear innocent and almost 'sweet' (in the sense of 'cute') - much like Ci Xi may have been when she became an imperial concubine at the age of sixteen. However, as it develops, more expressive, almost commanding blooms push into its center - peony and lilac can be discerned among them - imparting something increasingly lustful, even sexualized. It becomes louder and more complex, developing a magnificent, extraordinarily expressive note - like the nameless triumph in Ci Xi's heart and eyes when she gave birth to the emperor's first son and heir. Plum and a diffuse, only occasionally perceptible accord of tea subtly (more or less) remind (one could argue about this) of its Chinese theme and its name. Resins, vetiver, and woods provide the base note with a dignified, aristocratic accompaniment, carrying the weight of heavy, vividly painted silk and - after all, it is a Tom Ford - an exceedingly enduring fade. Conclusion: perhaps the most authentically Asian among the four Atelier d'Orient Private Blends. Deliciously sweet and voluptuously radiant at the same time. Commanding in nature yet delicately Chinese: Ci Xi, Empress Dowager of China.

What went wrong with Fleur de Chine: Tom Ford's inspiration for this fragrance, namely "scandalous femininity," as exemplified by Ruan Lingyu in the Shanghai films of the 1930s, radiating with dark red lipstick and in a silk cheongsam (those ankle-length dresses with a side slit and high collar). It is neither dramatic nor bold nor glowing or seductive, as it is advertised. What succeeded with Fleur de Chine: Creating a fragrance that is lovely and innocent, yet not boring. And I haven't experienced that often, as I quickly get bored with scents that do not engage me in conversation but merely smile vacantly while lifting their skirts to please. But I notice that this one wants to tell me something, so I open my senses, listen, and wait. Say something. But it only raises a finger to its lips and indicates silence. I cautiously glance down: the skirt is modestly over the knees, good. It takes my hand, and we stand under a mandarin tree in the midst of a Chinese garden. Exotic Asian flowers bloom everywhere, fragile and enchanting. In the center of the garden is a pond where colorful koi carp swim lazily in circles. A bamboo bridge leads to an island in the pond, on which a pavilion in traditional Chinese architectural style stands. We settle down on soft cushions, and Fleur de Chine pours me a flower tea. A wind chime tinkers meditatively in the breeze... Fleur de Chine has a wellness character. There are many ingredients, but they harmonize so well that it remains light and uncomplicated. An Asian bouquet of flowers and tea. Very natural. I can most clearly identify clementine, peony, magnolia, plum, wisteria, and of course, tea, lots of tea. I read about hinoki as an ingredient for the first time here; it is a type of cypress whose wood smells of lemon. By the way, hinoki pollen is the most common allergen for hay fever in Japan. Fleur de Chine still hasn't spoken to me, but it feels good to just keep quiet for a while. And I don't have to sneeze either. I am relaxed and fall asleep. I do find it a little boring after a while. When I wake up two hours later, the garden, tea, and pavilion have vanished. I sniff the fragrance again and unfortunately encounter a slightly woody-musty note. I think the cheongsam wasn't silk after all, but polyester.
