Still: In the category of floral, feminine, nice, I haven't smelled much better! I'm surprised that this young fragrance has received so little attention so far, especially since we Parfumos are usually quite keen on fresh fl...acons. Therefore: Absolutely a must-try!

Very pleasant, fruity citric opening. The dry down is a pretty prominent woody lavender. This is very similar to Montblanc Legend, maybe less sweet, and more aromatic and woodier instead, I do find it better blended. Easy to like and nothing groundbreaking. Decent freshie with average performance and not bad for its price. 7/10

When I saw the bottle here on Parfumo, I had to rub my eyes a bit. The Lalique label has actually been known for fine glass art since the late 19th century, which includes exquisite perfume bottles made of crystal glass. About 100 years later, they came up with the idea of making money with perfumes, which in itself is not reprehensible. So far, the Lalique fragrances have also been relatively well made, even if they have been more or less adapted to the spirit of the times here and there. But with L´Insoumis Ma Force, the powerful rebellious one, they take a heavy step towards snooze-worthy insignificance, which I never thought possible for Lalique. The bottle is already practically the first warning shot, even though one shouldn't judge inner qualities by outward appearances. However, it looks so carelessly designed and reminds me with its matte satin finish not only by name of Baldessarini "Cool Force." That one is already a relatively clumsy attempt to appeal to Armani's Acqua di Giò, but Ma Force seems to undercut that. I would ignore the pyramid here, because everything that comes out of the sprayer is not a sparkling freshness, but a synthetic audacity that I have rarely experienced. The top note is more piercing than fruity and so inferior that one wonders who is supposed to buy this, as the likely target audience will definitely find something more exciting in the supermarket aisle. It doesn't get any better later, as a persistently dull synthetic note remains on the sprayed areas, which wants to lean towards woods and spices but immediately tips into the cheapest cheap. And the base? Come on, let's just forget it in the truest sense of the word, because anyone who still considers purchasing this despite this warning has still not understood the matter of beautiful and quality fragrances. Thus, Ma Force is practically a copy of a copy. So please do not support it, otherwise, those at Lalique might think they can get away with this junk, even if the margin is tempting. This can seriously ruin a brand's reputation. L´Insoumis Ma Force - simply disgustingly weak!

Tested at printemps shop. It was from new collection with electric cherry ,cherry smoke. Really creamy and gourmand fragrance ,it reminds me kilian love don t be shy ,burberry for her elixir . Very discreet and a hold weak a few 2 hours .perfect if u like change your fragrance many time each day. More for spring and summer.more feminine but i adopt it,i buy it

Rose de Chine by Tom Ford - Rose de Chine is one of three rose fragrances that were released in 2022 in "The Private Rose Garden Collection." The scents are inspired by roses from various countries that are native to Tom Ford's garden. In the opening, I perceive a slightly metallic note in the background, which quickly takes a backseat to the dominance of the rose and the Chinese peony. At first, the fragrance strikes me as very feminine due to the floral presence. Gradually, the spicier notes begin to emerge. Labdanum and myrrh give the fragrance a contrasting twist. The scent gains sensuality for me through the very successful balsamic-smoky development. A very light and pleasant unisex rose fragrance that is suitable for any season and occasion. The longevity is average.

sang the twenty-five-year-old and hardly bearably beautiful Klaus Hoffmann in 1976 in 'Adieu Emile', his German version of Jacques Brel's 'Le moribond', in English 'The Dying One'. In its original lines, it had already said ten years earlier: 'C'est dur de mourir au printemps tu sais...' - for what could feel more wrong than to close your eyes forever just when everything is blooming outside in spring? Although by no means its earliest messenger, the peony is one of those flowers whose scent we associate like hardly any other with the blossoming spring in May and June - when the year has already progressed to a point where we can hardly remember that just a few weeks ago, winter was still pale. Together with the rose, it welcomes summer, serving as an ambassador of youth, exuberance, and the joy of being alive. The rockrose, on the other hand - despite its name, it is almost even further from the rose than the peony, which botanically is also not a rose - smells less through its - albeit pretty - flowers than through the oily, camphor-like resin in its woody stems, which we incense and call labdanum. Myrrh belongs to the same fragrance family - both are serious accords that sometimes appear almost ceremonial and are closely related to liturgies and rites. Who made a perfume out of just these two? Tom Ford does. And he succeeds. It is the apparent contradiction of blooming and fading, of celebrating youth and accepting transience, that gives Rose de Chine its unusual yet completely unexotic nature. In fact, it is not remotely East Asian in character - like his other fragrances that carry Asian attributes in their names. It plays with the dualism of floral volatility - and 'volatility' here means neither short-livedness nor a lack of presence, but merely a limitation of the time given to the floral accord - and a resinous base note, dry like cracked wood in the cold December wind. And it is its architecture of delicate spring flowers and serious cold resins, as if under pale winter sun - uncompromising and powerful both - that makes this scent a little challenging and special. Nevertheless, Tom Ford's Rose de Chine is surprisingly wearable - neither sweetly girlish nor darkly sacred - yet one that wants to be chosen and worn with a certain seriousness and respect. Then it is beautiful. Conclusion, in Klaus Hoffmann's almost defiantly thrown words: 'I want song, want play and dance - want people to have fun like crazy! I want song, want play and dance - when they plow me under the grass!'

This is a beautiful floral in the most gorgeous bottle. Better suited for cooler weather, in my opinion, due to the pepperish, ambery, and musky undertones. On my skin, this is a blast of violets and roses. For those of you who are looking for a pure violet perfume might be disappointed, as on my skin other flowers such as gardenia & jasmine are present and rose is equally as strong as the violet. I bought this while I was in search of a great violet perfume, lead by the reviews that it is a violet perfume. However, this is a well-balanced floral that has a pronounced violet note. But it is in no way a soliflore. Don’t get me wrong, I still love this fragrance. It is elegant and wonderfully refined. It also has great projection and staying power. However, for those for you who are looking for a real “violet” perfume (soliflore) are better off looking elsewhere.

Lalique LE BAISER edt is a surprisingly intense little floral perfume! The florals--primarily rose, violet, and jasmine, to my nose--seem quite concentrated and somewhat sweet. There is also a slight fruitiness, as though the petals were scented with black currant. I am curious whether my edt is stronger because it has condensed somewhat, although the volume of my 50ml bottle does not give any indication of that sort of thing. Hmmm... maybe this is just one of the more potent Lalique offerings. In my experience, Lalique perfumes are sometimes quite strong. PERLES and FLORA BELLA can easily overwhelm if overapplied, and the same is probably true for LE BAISER, which holds real floral headache potential. Lightly applied, however, this really smells rich and perfumey. There is a something of a vintage quality to this creation, and I also perceive a waxiness which reminds me a bit of Caron PARFUM SACRE. I am happy to have acquired this very floral perfume in a quaintly exquisite bottle!

I am a huge fan of House Lalique. Their bottles are small masterpieces and their fragrances are often quite good. My favourite is Amethyst but I am sure there are yet some gems to dig out, since I only know four from their collection well. This goes into the sweet category in my collection. I like the way it stays sweet all through the journey. I get a strong berry note and the flowers accompany it so well. The way it changes on my skin is perfect, from sweet to sweeter due to the Jasmine in the heart. The base is like a comfortable cream white sweater on a winter’s day. I must say I adore Lalique’s bottles, but Le Baiser is indisputably one of the best - perhaps the best. I love the see through/opaque pattern and how it lets the colour of the perfume through. It is almost impossible to take bad photos of this gem. It goes so well with the perfume; the smell, the colour and the bottle. Marvelously done. 144/365

This is really the first fragrance that makes me a little scared. First tested on the paper strip - ugh - what is that? An unearthly synthetic, indefinable artificial floral scent stabs at my nose. To be honest, I didn't dare to test it on my skin at first, but then I gave Le Baiser another chance. I've often found that some fragrances smell very artificial on the paper strip but then perform much better on the skin. So I sprayed it on my forearm....waited a moment...sniffed...nooooo!!! Even after half an hour, I still perceived that artificial note. I must honestly say I felt a little nauseous when I smelled my arm. On me, it smells artificially floral, like a bunch of flowers thrown into a pot, all nicely mashed up and then left to sit for a few days in extreme humidity, then opening the pot and adding a nice splash of artificially produced rose water (but the extremely unpleasant-squeaky-artificial kind!). Fortunately, after 2 hours, the worst was over, and I only detected a faint hint of nothing. It's really a matter of taste, but I honestly don't understand how anyone can feel comfortable with this. Well, tastes are just different, I guess^^ I give Le Baiser 10%, but only because I find the bottle cute!

Le Baiser is a floral romantic fragrance similar to the scent of Tresor by Lancome. The fragrance unfolds a floral sweetness, which becomes slightly darker and spicier due to cedar and sandalwood in the base. Overall, this is a bright scent with a very romantic aura, seeking its special wearers. Friends of rational, cool, and straightforward fragrances (like those from Tommy Hilfiger, for example) will not appreciate this perfume. It also does not fit into today's sugary gourmand trend. It is no surprise that Le Baiser has not survived in today's increasingly one-dimensional perfume market. Therefore, I particularly cherish and enjoy the contents of the miniature I own of Le Baiser, using it only sparingly.

It’s not hard to separate the Ford sales pitch from the perfumes. The pitch is so bare, so hungry. ‘Tom Ford has everything that could be desired. Don’t you wish you were Tom?!’ I won’t go further into the reading of the marketing, since I believe I just captured it in its entirety. But one bit of marketing that catches me with Jonquille de Nuit is the mix-and-match bit. Whether in the press or in person, the perfumes are sold as spectacular on their own, but also amazing in combination. I think the pairing the Bloomingdales sales associate was telling me about today was Neroli Portofino and Arabian Wood. Interesting as a cultural notion, I suppose, but really? Really?? I thought the assemble-your-own esthetic was considered fairly dime-store and ran out of steam at about the sophistication level of the Jo Malone line. But then I tried Jonquille de Nuit. Jonquille de Nuit isn’t a narcissus solifor, but it does seem to paint a the notion of a particular spring floral tone, albeit a very jasmine-like one to my nose. I’ve read others who’ve have called it indolic, dirty. Tom calls it “de Nuit” and in the TF world that means dinner jackets and gowns, or oiled bodies---nothing in between. But to me it’s springtime sunshine. It has that bursting at the cell wall acceleration of Spring flowers that suggests water, oiliness, flow, viscosity, rigid stems, crisp flower and dirt all at once. The topnotes are not terribly complex, but Jonquille de Nuit is balanced and buoyant. As the topnotes fade, though, it gets plucked petal by petal and lands on ‘he loves me not’ with a recognizably floral note, but one that is thinner, flatter and sweeter than the opening Spring still-life. Here, I suppose, is the flower of the mix and match premise. If these perfumes are to be combined willy-nilly to form ‘personalized’ fragrances, they must be fairly simplistic in construction or the outcome would be a pile-up. So although Jonquille de Nuit appears to aim for a deliberate simplicity that might lend itself to the indiscriminate combining of perfumes, I don’t really buy it. from scenthurdle.com

"What are ice flowers??" I could now ask mockingly in the group. In the absence of a "winter," at least until now, the existence of the aforementioned may have been "forgotten" by many. I was able to admire them as a child at my grandma's window in the unheated bedroom. Delicate icy formations, like transparent paintings, each one different and beautiful. And cold down to the little toe. "The touching of the figures" soon brought them to melt, only to form new and different patterns again. These ice flowers did not have a scent, but if they did, it would smell quite similar to "Jonquille de Nuit" by the imaginative Tom Ford. The "color" of it is just as pastel (cool blue and turquoise tones) as those wonderfully cold formations. An "icy iris," powdery like powdered snow, waiting outside to be shoveled, but which cannot be properly "stored" because it slips away again... A violet that defies the cold March winds and endures beneath the snow. Daffodils at the icy beginning of April with night frosts down to minus 5 degrees... And somehow this cold fascinates me. Both in nature (ice days, frost, with a brilliantly blue sky) and in fragrances. And the unfortunately discontinued "Jonquille de Nuit" is one of the coldest I have ever smelled.

There are plants that develop shoots for the next spring before winter and then overwinter in this preliminary stage. These shoots are called 'Hibernaculum' or 'winter bud', in which - if you cut them open - tiny leaf and partially flower structures are already recognizable, protected by outer leaves like an embryo. From these shoots, growth can proceed very quickly after the frosts - when the spring sun finally has enough strength and endurance - sometimes almost overnight. Jonquille de Nuit, Tom's nocturnal daffodil, makes me think of such a winter bud - and this is rather unusual for a Tom Ford Private Blend (even one from the Jardin Noir group). The delicate, quiet word is actually not Mr. Ford's language at all - on the contrary, he likes to approach it powerfully and expressively, so my impression of Jonquille de Nuit and its unexpected winter bud association surprises me all the more. Especially in the top note, this is a rather shy scent - the daffodil (or perhaps something resembling an iris?) is already noticeably there, yet strangely muted and overlaid or enveloped by a green accord - just like the tiny bud inside the Hibernaculum is embedded in its layers of leaves. To avoid misunderstandings: the floral aspect is present here from the very beginning. It is the very unusual development of this fragrance that stands out - and that one remembers. The oddly indifferent, damp green is followed by an awakening - just as spring sometimes explodes in April within two weeks after a long winter. And from here on, this is a 'real Tom', as it is powerfully enchanting and intoxicating, an ocean of flowers - the pale March is forgotten, even April passes quickly, and now - in May - life vibrates everywhere. Conclusion: an unusual fragrance. It begins - and this is a quote and not from me - 'like a pale morning in spring, still infused with winter's chill' and only later grows into its full splendor. Dark or nocturnal is only its wintry beginning; its heart and base are bright and playfully beautiful.

Black Orchid Voile de Fleur edt wears like pure perfume: very strong, very insistent, with big sillage and a seriously commanding presence. This composition seems extremely feminine to me, and the huge bouquet of white flowers--especially gardenia, but also tuberose--would be enough to knock some people out, I am sure. I, however, love this intoxicating potion, which exudes quality and richness. It's difficult to convey the distinction between a perfume such as this and those evidently sourced from the vast vats of low-brow juice factories, but it's absolutely palpable. The composition is itself excellent, but there is another factor which makes this perfume what it is. The house of Tom Ford appears to use much better basic ingredients, and as a result it feels and wears very differently from most designer perfumes. Although Black Orchid Voile de Fleur is indisputably a big white floral fragrance, it is much more than that, and achieves its oriental quality from the patchouli and spices, in addition to the mysterious "noir" accord. The abundant white flowers have been thus dusted with darkness, but it is only a screen: the white flowers are still there in all of their splendor, and they really do dominate this perfume.

Black Orchid Voile de Fleur is a strange, yet interesting fragrance that at first sniff was very sharp & floral.. I recently wore this to my brothers wedding & let me tell you... THIS STUFF LAST FOR AGES!!!!! I put this on & my mother claims that she could smell this before I came down stairs... IT WAS THAT STRONG! However, the scent is rather a creative masterpiece from Mr. Tom Ford! I really dont like it for the first 30-45 minutes, but I tolerate it, then the worst note of this frag appears.. That awful rotten mushroom smell which I just find simply dreadful... Thank goodness it does not last long & the best part kicks in which is the base! SIMPLY MARVELOUS! When I took my rental tux back the next day, the lady who opened the bag to make sure everything was there she said MY U WORE SOMETHING THAT SMELLS JUST GREAT! WHAT IS IT???? Mind you I did not spray any on the tux. I grinned & said Black Orchid! She smiled back & said I'll have to give that a go!

Originally reviewed on April 19, 2012: Plums are very seductive fruits and they do not get any more sensuous than they do here in BOVdF. They are dark, opulent, and slyly sinister here. I am over the moon in love with Tom Ford’s misunderstood boozy villain. This villain in velvets also brings gardenias to woo its prey in the cloak of darkness. Its drydown is consistently dark and dense, with heady fruits and berries, spicy sandalwood, and loads of amber and patchouli. Compared to its older sibling, Black Orchid, this is a lighter, effervescent version but it’s still heavy hitter with a secret double life. This is a dense cloak of a fragrance with sillage that announces, “The wearer has left the building.” It is certainly a fragrance with a bullhorn! Very much like anyone with a bullhorn, this fragrance is unconcerned with offending others, though it has the potential to do so. I know I’ll be wearing this the next time I go bar-hopping in Downtown L.A. BOVdF was made for upscale nightlife and devil-may-care urban adventures. Updated (but not really) on September 26, 2023: I sounded like such a blowhard in this review. This was my first Tom Ford fragrance so I thought I was on the cutting edge of fragrance. Still, I agree with 2012 Me's assessment, more or less. My best friend talked me out of my bottle when he got married—he said it was the perfect goth wedding scent. I could not argue with that. This is the perfect goth wedding scent: larger-than-life funereal white gardenia, blackened fruits, and other witch's cauldron ingredients. Giving him the bottle was the right thing to do but it didn't stop me from missing it terribly. I spent seven years hawking auction sites and Facebook for a reasonably priced bottle and vigilantly watching for viable swaps. (One such swap interaction: "No, I won't send you my "Parure | Guerlain" for your 1 oz. half bottle of Black Orchid Voile de Fleur .) I finally got my precious Black Orchid Voile de Fleur . No one is talking me out of my bottle a second time.

I really didn't like the original Black Orchid with its somewhat putrid smelling fruit accords and loud chocolate notes. Black Orchid Voile de Fleur is much softer and more wearable on my skin, provided that you don't apply too much. The strange fruity accords found in the original are also present in this fragrance, which is kind of off-putting. They actually smell sharp and metallic when blended with my chemistry. In the opening I sense a subtle hint of milk and cinnamon alongside the rich and dark plum accords which is very pleasant to my nose, however the heart washes out this softness bringing forth those fruity notes that I so detest. Thankfully the heart is relatively short-lived, which makes way for a soft, delicate and sugary blend of gardenia, milk, cinnamon, lily and plum. I like Black Orchid Voile de Fleur's softer side, but I'm not so keen on its sharp and peppery fruitiness. I enthusiastically applaud this fragrance's unique approach, but I can't seem to mourn its disappearance from our shelves. Occasionally this fragrance makes me nauseous, particularly if I'm not feeling the best to start with. I sometimes wonder whether I would enjoy this fragrance more if all of the fruit notes were removed. But I came to the conclusion that Black Orchid Voile de Fleur would lose a lot of its boldness and complexity. While it's not my cup of tea, I will certainly be passing on my sample to someone who I'm sure will appreciate it.

Ladies and gentlemen, I warmly welcome you to the Tom Ford Arena, which is sold out to the last seat. All spectators have very high expectations of the two contenders who have just entered the arena under the bright lights of the spotlights. In the left corner, Black Orchid, very self-assured and completely confident in its effect. In the right corner, its younger brother Black Orchid Voile de Fleur, entering the scene with youthful nonchalance. The gong sounds - Ring free for the first round. And Black Orchid does not take long to make its move, immediately saturating the arena with its signature fruit-herb blend. Black Orchid Voile de Fleur reacts just a second too late, trying to counter its older brother with a cornucopia of flowers, but to no avail. The flowers drown in BO's fruit-herb mixture. The first round clearly goes to Black Orchid, making it 1 : 0. That was a promising start, ladies and gentlemen, we can look forward to what awaits us next. Here comes the gong for the second round. And now both contenders gather their courage and throw all their strengths into the ring. A long struggle for the title begins. Black Orchid shines with its incredible softness and light sweetness, into which the fruitiness and gentle floral aromas blend. BO Voile de Fleur throws all its flowers into the race, offering not sweetness but floral power, especially the gardenia, lily, and honeysuckle set the tone, supported by pepper, plum, and tuberose, which add additional strength. This is the most exciting competition I have ever witnessed, ladies and gentlemen, head to head both contenders fight for the title until the gong releases them. It's a tie! The score is 2 : 1 for Black Orchid. The hall is boiling, the audience is enthusiastically engaged, and then the gong sounds for the third and final round. I must admit, ladies and gentlemen, this round is the most thrilling for me. Both contenders unleash their gourmand strength. Black Orchid with a wonderfully soft, woody, slightly sweet note. BO Voile de Fleur with all the power of youth. It uses the flowers to set a very beautiful, rounded base. Its sweetness is very well measured, clearly relying on the strength of the flowers and soft spices to showcase its base. Several hours have already passed, but both contenders still appear very fresh and lively. The gong sounds and it’s another tie. The final score: 3 : 2 for Black Orchid, which was able to overcome its younger brother once again with its soft sweetness. What a fight, ladies and gentlemen, it couldn't have been more exciting. I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did and will honor us again soon when it’s time for another comparison of two contenders: Ring free!

A profound cassis-cherry fruit and very ripe, dark oranges with a beautiful ylang-ylang sweetness make for a quite impressive start. Cloves, dark plum jam, and a well-measured peppery component in the heart note give Black Orchid Voile de Fleur by Tom Ford a lot of refinement and a distinctive profile. Very intense and aromatic-spicy, this is what reveals itself here.

from now on we will go our separate ways. For three years you have patiently waited in my collection for my affection, but it was not meant to be for us. Your direction is too unclear to me, as you move in several at once.

Black Orchid Voile de Fleur. What a long name for a perfume. As soon as it cooled down today, I chose a lush women's fragrance as my test subject once again. When I read through the list of ingredients, I was surprised that I didn't have a headache yet. The top note starts on my skin with a nicely sweet floral accord. The little bit of bergamot is hardly worth mentioning.

After I never really got along with Black Orchid EdP, this version in front of me didn’t stand a chance either. Not even a huge detour. Black Orchid VdF fluttered into my house a few weeks ago. Quite unexpectedly. Or perhaps intentionally?

Celtic mythology and folklore - and the popular (trivial) literature built upon it - know the motif of the so-called Summer King. In spring, a young man is chosen - depending on the tale, either voluntarily or without question. For one summer, he is presented with the finest foods, dressed in the most precious garments, and the most beautiful, untouched girls are brought to him, again, voluntarily or not. After this summer of idleness, abundance, and indulgence, the young man is submerged in the bog for the favor of the gods, where voluntariness no longer plays a significant role. The following spring, a new young man is chosen, and the game begins anew. The product cycle of light summer fragrances resembles this a bit: usually in late winter, the new fresh scents are introduced - sometimes pushing the old favorites to the lower shelves. Sun-kissed models pose with them against southern backdrops, and we know that without a new blue fragrance, summer cannot truly be summer. In autumn, after a financial review, it is decided whether the candidate should remain hot stuff for another year - or be sunk in the (business) bog. Tom Ford's Neroli Portofino has - resisting countless Cassandra calls - survived many summers. Whether his perfume can be prophesied a similar multitude of summers remains to be seen. Neroli Portofino perfume promises something like the completion of its azure DNA: endless neroli and eternal blue. What to make of the promise of hesperidic immortality has been discussed controversially - my views on this have been described in my comment on Hermès' Eau de Pamplemousse Rose, among others. The essence of such fragrances is their transience - robbing them of this always risks making them lifeless and stiff, taking away their lightness and ease. And yet, one like Neroli Portofino perfume can work - with tempered excess and well-measured infinity. Like the Celtic Summer King, he has too much of everything - but only for one summer. Here, Neroli Portofino is 'with the volume turned up', which is exhausting but pleasing and intentional. Here is Neroli Portofino for all those who want to enjoy the illusion of hesperidic eternity without believing in it. Here is radiant summer blue and a southern cologne-like glow that celebrates excess and abundance without regret. There is something absurd about it, just as the Summer King - crowned with fruits and flowers - feels absurd, as everything here is too much of everything and too much of now. And yet, there is magic in this celebration of the moment, and Tom Ford's concentrated neroli works, as paradoxical and not-quite-right as it may seem. For one summer or two. Conclusion: the whole magic of 'too much of everything' and 'too much now'.

Uncommented Fragrances No. 183 "The German word Zeitgeist has been adopted into numerous other languages as a loanword through English. The English adjective zeitgeisty is also derived from it." (Wikipedia: Zeitgeist). Indeed, I immediately thought of this word because the American fashion designer Tom Ford has always had a nose for trends in fragrance and was one of the first to launch classic Cologne waters anew in his exclusive line, after decades of everything related to so-called Cologne (in the strict sense - so not Cologne) being handled with kid gloves. Not a few fragrance lovers passionately collect the azure blue bottles from TF, yet wrinkle their noses at "Real Cologne Water (Eau de Cologne) | 4711," even though both belong to the same fragrance family and are accordingly related. The reorientation with aggressive advertising was certainly a clever move by TF, and I also have Neroli Portofino Eau de Parfum alongside the aforementioned 4711 in my collection. By the way, I like both equally well. Anyone wanting to learn more about the entire market of classic Cologne waters (broadly defined: hesperidic, neroli, herbs - otherwise usually nothing or little) can find almost all the common ones in my following collection: https://www.parfumo.de/Benutzer/Yatagan/Sammlung/1921 If you prefer something darker and warmer without wanting to give up the Cologne water tone, you might be happy with my following collection of "black colognes": https://www.parfumo.de/Benutzer/Yatagan/Sammlung/1919 Back to the zeitgeist and the current variant of Neroli Portofino, the perfume of the neo-classic: In light of the never-ending, in my opinion, nonsensical discussions about insufficient longevity and sillage in niche fragrances, TF has now decided to release a more intense version of the extremely ethereal Eau de Parfum of Neroli Portofino: Neroli Portofino Parfum . I predict that a good portion of the community will appreciate this and celebrate the fragrance, which seems entirely legitimate to me given the quality, but the question of whether it is the better Neroli Portofino can indeed be answered differently depending on perspective. If I want more longevity and sillage (which are both nearly completely indifferent to me personally), then I probably need this newer version. However, I also have to live with the fact that the fragrance develops a synthetic base rather quickly after a pretty but predictable opening with hesperidic notes and neroli, and fades into a somewhat mushy and musky drydown, while the original remains bright and fresh, but also disappears just as quickly - spiritedly - altogether. I personally stick with the original "Neroli Portofino (Eau de Parfum) | Tom Ford," because a Cologne water should not cling, should not cloud the environment, but rather appear pure and clear, discreet and refreshing, and can happily be ephemeral, as there is nothing worse than a clingy perfume on a hot summer day in Italy. I choose tradition over zeitgeist, even if both variants are beautiful and charming. I can live with it if you feel the opposite.

Lalique NILANG is definitely unique: an oriental floral perfume with an aquatic facet. This is odd enough that it could have been put out by a niche house, but instead it was Lalique. The fact that it's still around 16 years after its launch despite the complete absence of marketing--I for one have never seen any!--places NILANG in a special category of perfumes: the few, the proud, the survivors! I like NILANG with its lotus, water lily and blueberry mingling with sandalwood, vanilla, and caramel, and I do not find it overly sweet--certainly not when compared to the sugar sprays available everywhere today. NILANG is rather strange but likeable and worth a sniff to anyone who appreciates oriental perfumes, and also those who do not, as this creation has a playfulness and levity which may appeal to them as well.

- "The majority of people shed their childhood like an old hat. They forget it like a phone number that is no longer valid. They were children once, then they became adults, but what are they now? Only those who grow up and remain a child are truly human." Erich Kästner - I have often thought of these words by Erich Kästner lately in connection with "Nilang". I have noticed that many people have a problem categorizing this fragrance. I felt the same way until a few years ago. Then I thought to myself: "Does this fragrance want to be categorized by me? Or does it simply want to challenge me like a woman who does not want to be placed in a caste and just wants to be understood as 'human'?" But before this turns into philosophy, I would like to share my thoughts and the fragrance with the following story. It is about that 'woman' who just wants to be 'human'. Sara is a young woman. Actually still a girl. She lives somewhere in a country, in an area between the Orient and the Occident. She is 19 years old. The year is 2000. At the beginning of April, she is preparing for the entrance exams for a university place. She talks with her former schoolmates about preparing for the exams. She dreams of being able to secure a spot at a music academy. She has a very beautiful voice and loves to sing. All her attention is focused on preparing for the tests and her family. Her brother, who is five years younger, is going through his rebellious phase, which often causes problems in the family. Sara always tries to smooth things over between her parents and her brother. This takes up all her time and energy alongside the stress of the exams. She does not have a boyfriend and cannot think of a relationship for now. What she does not know is that life sometimes brings surprises for which one is not at all prepared. Like on that afternoon. On April 4th, the neighbor comes to visit in the afternoon. Two of her brothers, one of whom is single, accompany her. Sara quickly puts on her fragrance "Caldion for Women". At first sight, the younger brother of the neighbor, let’s call him John, is fascinated by Sara's natural beauty. Although he is very shy, he thinks to himself that he will not have many opportunities to talk to Sara. After all, he comes from a country thousands of kilometers away. He gathers all his courage and follows Sara into the kitchen during a brief opportunity. He perceives her fragrance, a cheerful, fruity floral scent. Still fresh and lovely, like Sara's delicate facial skin. He introduces himself again and tells her that he would like to get to know her better. Sara openly says that she does not want to think about a relationship at all. She presents her arguments; her connection to her family, her desire for a university place, and her fears about life in a faraway country. But then she realizes how prejudiced that sounds. She does not know this man at all. How often does a girl have the chance to find her Prince Charming? What if this man is indeed her Prince Charming, even if he does not look like a frog? Therefore, she agrees to meet the next day to at least get to know him a little. The next day, John explains that a person always separates from their parental home in the case of marriage. Whether one lives in the house across the street or moves to another country does not matter much. He also points out that a person can learn in other countries as well. After all, music exists everywhere. Regarding the fear of life in a foreign country, a person always has a certain fear of life, no matter where they are. What matters is the partner by one’s side with whom one must endure these fears. When Sara smiles hopefully in response, John notices how the fruity notes from the previous day give way to promising blooming flowers like jasmine and lotus. Above all, daffodils, Sara's favorite flower, as John will learn later. In the following days, Sara and John become so emotionally close that a week after their first encounter, on April 11th, they make an important decision; they get engaged. Just three months later, the most important day of their lives together would follow. At the beginning of July 2000, John must hurriedly fly back to the distant country between the Orient and the Occident. Sara and her parents could only arrange a very specific date for the wedding at the local registry offices. On July 11th, Sara and John officially marry. Yes, Sara really dares to take a chance. Now also in terms of relationships. However, she remains in her parental home for now until the official wedding celebration, which for organizational reasons will take place later, in three more months. At this wedding celebration, John makes another olfactory discovery about Sara. He can see the most beautiful flowers on her delicate face. They have fully bloomed and shine in all their splendor. Only her smile holds a beautiful memory of the fruity and lovely scents of her youth and childhood. But in her eyes, in her deep and joyful gaze, he already suspects the heavier scents. The scents of amber, musk, and sandalwood that make her appear more mature. But also notes of vanilla and chocolate that always remind her of her lively past. While John looks into Sara's eyes, he dreams of a perfume. It should tell the story of this beautiful woman’s life, from childhood to maturity. It should remind her of melons, peaches, and berries from her childhood; of aquatic flowers like lotus and water lily that she cherished in her youth; of jasmine, roses, and daffodils, her flower of adulthood. Furthermore, this perfume must, in its dry-down, remind them of the life that lies ahead and which they want to spend together from now on. A little musk would suffice for eternity. John could not explain why, but his inner voice told him: "Nilang". It would accompany Sara for a lifetime. And so it happened. He gifted her this perfume. Sara was fascinated by the scent from the very beginning. After all, this scent told her life. Even after years, nothing would change about that. In a few days, it will be an anniversary. The anniversary of their marriage is approaching. On July 11th, it will be time. Then she will have spent 14 years by John's side. Will she apply "Nilang" again that day and reflect on her life? - Dedicated to the most beautiful and loving woman in the world: Mrs. DuftJunkie ;-)

Nilang by Lalique is a somewhat crazy, unappealing fragrance. The extraordinary mixture is so contrasting that it actually smells highly interesting. When I first tested NILANG in 1995, I was truly shocked. I immediately smelled a wild blend of Angel and L'Eau d'Issey in a 50:50 ratio. Many on Parfumo write down their fantasies that come to mind as soon as they smell a fragrance. I don't do that. Although I have a romantic disposition, I only smell the fragrance and know whether I like it or not. If I were to squeeze a fantasy about Nilang from my head, I would claim that a fashionable woman smelling of Angel is mopping her bathroom floor with a cleaning product that reminds one of the aquatic L'Eau d'Issey. But hey, that's really not a thrilling image. Nilang (the vintage version) is very special. So special that I bought it back then and tried to wear it because it smelled so unique. But there was no friendship between us. How could there be? The combination of "aquatic oriental perfume" is not really what I want to smell like. And I neither love Angel nor L'Eau d'Issey. But sometimes one is unreasonable and gets carried away, spraying something very fashionable and hoping that love will ignite. If I stretch it a bit, this wild mixture reminds me somewhat of Krazy by Krizia. At first, you think you smell an oriental fragrance that somewhat resembles the warm-spicy Obsession, only to find in the base note a similarity to Escape that overshadows everything oriental. For me, that just doesn't fit together. Something in me directly rebels against it, even though I like contrasts. Also, the comment below me from LButterfly mentions Angel and ends with Ming Shu in the base note. From that, I can tell that I'm not mistaken. If I were mean, I would say that the perfumer Gérard Anthony simply mixed two fragrances together just before quitting time and was curious about what would come out.

a vast field, dry hot sand, hot vibrating desert air, veiled figures on the horizon and as a counterpart, a river. It winds through the hot sandy ground, cool, refreshing, and so invigorating. Above all this is the endless sky. This space merges with the two opposites… and what emerges?? Nilang? … no sorry Angel!! I don’t understand how this scent can smell like Angel to me. I can only explain it by the pralines and the vanilla in the base (they hit me pretty hard right on the head) a kind of sweet sultriness emerges. The base is prominent at first, after a short time I smell the flowers, especially jasmine. But after 5 to 10 minutes, the show is already over, now something softer comes (berry-like, floral, somewhat aquatic) but the head still feels the sultriness. In the end, it also reminds me a bit of Ming Shu by Yves Rocher, but softer, even cozier. This comment should not be a criticism, but there is definitely a disappointment. I imagined it differently! More interesting and somehow more spiritual. It’s tough when the expectations are so high, especially when I envisioned such a magical landscape as described above. But what did I expect? An aquatic oriental? When I think about it :) Longevity: after 3-4 hours I have to get relatively close to my wrist to smell something, but the light aftertaste lingers for half the day. But Nilang is definitely individual. Why has there been no comment here until now? Who does the scent actually suit and for what occasion? I can imagine it on a cold rainy autumn day. I can picture the scent on a young mother. The smell that a child perceives, the gentle scent that imprints itself and reminds of a soft, familiar embrace. A scent that makes the world seem smaller and friendlier.

The name Lys Fume is only half correct. The lily is there, the smoke is not.  No complaint, though. This is a handsome and well composed floriental. Lily is the centerpiece but other elements that fly in and out of this perfume include other flowers, fruit, plastic, spices, India ink and resins. A soliflor this ain’t. It’s been compared to Donna Karen's Gold, and the comparison is appropriate. Gold is a lily floral amber that alternatingly purrs and growls. The smoky, ambery base notes start to rumble up through the topnotes almost immediately after you spray it on.  Lys Fume is less overtly louche than Gold, but is sweeter in both scent and personality. In Gold, Amber is the accompanying score to the flower, but it can feel like a Phantom of the Opera theater organ taking  over the room.  This is how Gold plays with contrasts (growl) as well as the common threads (purr) between the lily and the amber. Lys Fume has amber, but it doesn’t ride it like a parade float as Gold does. Amber serves the end goal of the composition, it doesn’t take over. It joins the other elements to give a rich, plastic-smelling feel that holds the balance of the sweetness and the spiciness just so. The base is spiced but not spicy. Lys Fume unfolds at a leisurely pace, and the extended heart notes are similar in character to the plastic floral notes of Vierges et Toreros. The plastic sheen in Vierges suggests shrink-wrapping. Lys Fume’s plastic smells like India ink and seems to be a fortunate side effect of the wonderfully 'off' note that form the scent of ylang ylang. The composition is balanced, and notes like plastic and ink don't stand out anymore than do spices and florals.  Is this plastic note a Maisondieu family secret?  Antoine employed it to striking effect in Vierges et Toreros. Here, perfumer Shyamala Maisondieu integrates the plastic note in such a way that it could be the base note for a whole new generation of floral Oriental perfumes.  Delicate, but not at all sheer. Strong, but effortless. Often in perfumery, 'distinctive' is code for odd and undesirable.  Lys Fume is distinctive in that it is striking and memorable. It has just the sort of beauty that I look for in a perfume. It draws you in not merely because it's pretty, but because it has some thought to it and is equally interesting and beautiful.  The inky plastic keeps the Lily note aloft. Sillage is low, endurance is good. But Lys Fume gets its highest marks  for integrity and coherence of overall shape from top to bottom. from scent hurdle.com

Some niche perfumes are weak, seemingly dilute, with poor longevity and laughable claims to eau de parfum strength. Not so with the house of Tom Ford! There is some real dependability when it comes to the strength of the perfumes of this house. (Do you want a neroli perfume to last forever or until your next bath? Tom Ford is your man: NEROLI PORTOFINO). Another virtue of this house's private collection is the truth in naming everywhere on display. LYS FUME offers a veritable bomb of lily up front and center. Incredibly potent with huge sillage and a funereal concentration of the dark billowy flower, this creation is going to distinguish the lily lovers from those who are mere friends. Lily foes need not apply, obviously... The lily in LYS FUME is anchored in a rich styrax-labdanum base which eventually, in the far drydown, smells really beautiful. By then, the lily bomb has been defused and only the lingering smokiness of the extinguished wick remains behind as a floral tinge. The opening is a bit hard to take, I do hereby aver. I was literally waiting for a bit of air to break through the hundred thousand lily petals. I won't say that it's a scrubber, but this perfume needs to be very sparingly applied to avoid suffocation of self and others. Lily is a distinctive floral scent and obviously not as popular as rose, iris, violet, narcissus, tuberose, geranium, the list goes on and on. There are not that many big lily perfumes, which probably means that it is an acquired taste, and it is true that other lily perfumes have sometimes seemed overwhelming to me. Donna Karan GOLD is another example which must be very sparingly applied. The search is over for those looking for a concentrated lily olfactory experience. The search for such a perfume ends here: LYS FUME.

The camphorous ylang steals the show here. So yummy, with a cooling almost icy element (similar to the one I get from Psychedelic Love). The lily is actually my least favorite part, it opens with kind of an anemic sweetness thats somehow melancholy? It slowly fades until it's just a subtle sweetness in the background, enhancing the overall "chill". Lovely, at least sample it while you still can, especially if you love ylang.

is the title of Lucia di Lammermoor's disturbing aria in Donizetti's opera of the same name, also known as the 'Mad Scene', one of the most dramatic moments in operatic literature. Betrayed by her own, married to one she does not love, and trapped in love for another, Lucia stabs her fiancé on their wedding night. The white dress completely stained with blood and the knife still in her hand, she staggers into the assembled wedding guests and sings there - in the most famous section in a duet with a glass harmonica or a flute - dramatically losing her mind for twenty minutes. Lys Fume, Tom Ford's smoky lily, embodies all of this; it is highly dramatic, it is immense and - when over-applied - undoubtedly disturbing. The lily alone, intoxicatingly fragrant, stands at the center here and silences everything else. Nutmeg, pepper, labdanum, styrax are little more than bystanders, standing in the half-light at the balustrade, only able to watch as Lucia descends into madness in their midst. The commanding presence, this 'silencing everything else', bears a distant resemblance to the dark rose in Noir de Noir. Lys Fume is also one that seeks a stage, that needs a stage, that can become whiny and unbearable if it does not get one. Its sillage is breathtaking, and its longevity lasts for hours. And because the lily - at least in my perception - is even more intoxicating and expansive than the rose, one might caution to choose it with care and consideration! Conclusion: the fragrance is beautiful. However, I can hardly imagine where one would want to wear it. After all, one rarely intends to wander around disturbed and bloodstained - and if one does, I imagine one has other concerns than choosing an appropriate perfume.

Last Friday, it was (once again) time: Professionally quite stressed, I needed a "balance." And what does a proper perfume enthusiast prescribe? Of course, a new fragrance (depending on the situation, often more than one). The "Akkad" by Lubin was already a given, so I needed a second scent. I quickly jotted down a few supposed highlights from my wish list and off I went to Düsseldorf. I quickly picked up the Akkad, and first headed to the Prada store to test some of the Prada exclusive fragrances (which they didn't even carry). Great, this was starting off well! So off to "Edel-Douglas" on Königsallee, where I kept an eye out. One of the fragrances on my wish list was "Lys Fume" by Tom Ford. And I was lucky, they had it there too. I took a quick sniff of the test strip and found what hit my nose quite pleasant. So I applied it to my skin. What started off well on the test strip (mandarin, a hint of nutmeg, and pepper) took a completely different turn on my skin. Barely sprayed, the lily immediately delivered a nose punch. And what a punch! I had no idea that Ford's lilies had undergone boxing training. For my taste, definitely too much of the noble plant! All I could do was hope for a quick change, but the fragrance was not inclined to grant me that favor. With every hand movement, the super intense lily was back. Only after hours did the base in the form of a very successful vanilla-styrax mix emerge, and the lily lost some of its sharpness. As always with Tom Ford fragrances, this one is also very consistent and stays true to its theme. This will certainly be a lesson for my future tests! Lys Fume is certainly in the top league in terms of quality; even though I don't like the lily scent so highly concentrated, it doesn't smell cheap or synthetic at all. The longevity is gigantic, and the sillage is also not to be underestimated. A few too many sprays and one could easily become a nuisance to their surroundings. From my perspective, it's a crystal-clear autumn/winter/women's fragrance. But luckily, that is in the eye of the beholder. I would rather continue to enjoy the beauty of the lilies than the scent. Oh yes, despite everything, I did find a second fragrance... the stunningly beautiful "D600" by Carner Barcelona. What a contrast to Lys Fume! And so, this Friday ended up being more than a happy one ;-)

it is sometimes the curse of great beauty that the observer's eye sticks to the surface, as if blinded. thrown back on possessiveness or envious comparison, deeper, more nuanced, idiosyncratic, and frictional aspects escape him. but a dazzling beauty of fragrance, as seen by tom ford, need never fear this superficiality: it aims for her heart. and it reveals it.

Let's take a look at VS Tease Heartbreaker. I liked it from the first spray. I'm not usually a fan of fruity scents, but this one has something. Definitely something for summer, it starts with a strawberry note, definitely not a synthetic strawberry. Do you know Coach Love? That's like a chemistry set in comparison. I find this perfume to be pure delicious refreshment. The vanilla is also very nice. If you're looking for a fragrance that has a fruity opening and then becomes powdery, this is a great choice. This freshness at the beginning probably also comes from the starfruit.

So with this creation Tom Ford meant to evoke California (and specifically L.A.) in bottle. As someone who hasn't been to California, I'll have to take his word for it here. The smell... To me this is a wonderfully authentic Lavender which is surrounded by herbs and fresh citrus. There are actually two types of Lavender being used here by the perfumer, Yann Vasnier (Lavanillin & Lavender Absolute), which are supported by clary sage, bergamot, oakmoss, and both lemon and lemon blossom. At the bottom of this herbal base is vetiver and olibanum... and the overall feel is that of a dry, salty, yet fresh, herbal lavender. Personally I am someone who loves the smell of lavender, and although lavender is sometimes seen as a masculine note, I think this could work on male or female. The composition is fresh in the beginning, turning to dry and herbal in the base. It's almost like a "salty" lavender... as if the lavender bushes are growing by the sea coast, with the salt in the air and the dry herbal aroma coming from the bush being baked in the sun. It's a wonderful feeling, but the problem is (as with most Tom Ford Private Blends), is that the price can be a little high. Lavender Palm is a wonderful, authentic lavender fragrance, but it's just as good as any other really good lavenders I have smelled, if you have the money for this (and want to smell like California luxury), go for it. But you can also check out a classic like Caron's Pour Un Homme which will also give an authentic lavender. But for a herbal, dry, citrus lavender, this is probably one of the best out there (if you have the money for it).

I love black coffee, but I’d rather not drink coffee at all than to drink it with sugar. My preference has led me to have my own category of coffee, which is defined by a lack of sweetener. Lavender Palm is the sweetened coffee of lavender to my nose. It’s a creamy, sweet lavender, nothing like the resinous, woody, incense lavender of my favorite lavender, Parfums de Nicolai pour Homme. But as with coffee, who the fuck cares what I think? Lavender Palm is distinct, coherent and inventive. The shape of the perfume holds green herbal facets, sweet creaminess, and the nutty-woody notes without becoming unbalanced or falling to pieces. The composition holds the lavender in the center, but keeps it from overpowering the other notes, something a sharp lavender often does. If you can get past paying hundreds of dollars for a lavender fragrance, Lavender Palm is one of the better options. from scenthurdle.com

Now sadly discontinued, Lavender Palm encapsulates the warmth, wealth, and whiffs of Los Angeles in a bottle. The heat of LA, its summery flora, and even the wafts of buttery suntan lotion carried in the air are all here in this eau de parfum, which builds to an almost gourmand crescendo towards the end of its cycle in a manner not unlike Caron's Pour Un Homme. This very transporting and tenacious scent has been much maligned and misunderstood during its commercial life. It will doubtless gradually gain in popularity now that it's off the shelves.

Thanks to Ephitelium, we now know, that Lavender Palm is supposed to be made without artificial or chemical fragrances. Thus, Tom Ford has apparently succeeded in assembling the most natural and noble ingredients in LP in such a way that they smell not even remotely natural on my skin, but rather, on the contrary, extremely ARTIFICIAL. Sounds strange, but it is so! For me, LP primarily smells like the spray one would use to keep mosquitoes or other biting and sucking pests at bay. Unfortunately, I cannot explain how this impression comes about. Is it the aldehydes in this fragrance cocktail? I have, for example, had the impression a few times that aldehydes in combination with neroli can smell like hairspray. Could it be due to the combination of aldehydes with bergamot? And aren't aldehydes chemical compounds that are produced outside of nature in laboratories? With this penetrating insect spray note of LP, one risks giving one's nasal hairs an involuntary permanent wave, if one has neglected to trim them for aesthetic reasons. Here, lavender, lemon & co. stand no chance. They are about as effective in the case of LP as lilac room spray in a windowless bathroom. The mosquito-death note diminishes the precious, naturally sourced ingredients obtained through new methods (if they indeed have been used in the claimed extent and corresponding quality in this EdP) to the level of a tree air freshener. Fortunately, the scent quickly becomes weaker and more pleasant, but it remains far from suddenly transforming into a delight for the nose during the dry-down. Now, according to the advertisement, this fragrance is supposed to evoke the free-spirited mindset and chic elegance of California. Aha! Since in California, NATURAL beauty is rather declining due to the world-record density of silicone breasts, implantable doormats in washboard stomach design, Botox faces, anabolic muscles and inflated lips, one might be tempted to consider the advertising promise of Lavender Palm as fully fulfilled.

It hasn't been easy for Lavender Palm and me - despite all my passion for Tom Ford and his fragrances. On one hand, lavender - although I know some truly beautiful lavender scents - is not one of those fragrance components that storm in and capture my curiosity. I find the name combination with the palm a bit silly. And ultimately: Los Angeles, to which this Private Blend's flagship store is dedicated, will never be one of my favorite cities - it's a bit like the Ruhr area with better weather and, of course, with palms. In the opening of Lavender Palm, the lavender - not surprisingly - is dominant. It presents itself classically, dusty gray, with the mothball association also present, while the accompanying sage and bergamot contribute to the mix. But then it slowly gains volume, Tom's lavender Angeleño spreads and unfolds its aromatic foliage - cedar, bay leaf, and surely the namesake palm, although its supposed scent remains somewhat puzzling to me. Gradually, Lavender Palm picks up pace, accelerates, and spins faster. A lively sweetness is added, and there is something soft, exceedingly rich in body in this sweetness, which becomes all the more intoxicating the longer it lasts. In the end, it almost overdoes it a little. Valse triste, the 'sad waltz', probably the most famous piece by the most renowned Finnish composer Jean (actually 'Johan' or 'Janne') Sibelius, follows exactly the same pattern. For three minutes - that's just under half its duration - it is hesitant and very restrained, hardly identifiable as a waltz. Then, however, the volume and tempo increase, its circles begin to turn, developing a sort of sluggish lament, one imagines seeing widows in gray dresses silently dancing in the light of pale gas lamps. It is a small piece of great beauty, Sibelius' Valse triste - urgent and full of lament, yet with all the passion of a waltz within it, equally a last desperate grasp at life. Conclusion: a fragrance that takes its time and deserves that time - its serious opening leads to a magnificent, very spirited ending. By the way, I cannot find any understandable borrowings from the second largest city in the USA.
According to KADEWE sales staff, this fragrance is free of artificial or chemical scents! Well done...Great Tom!

HAHAHA I could laugh heartily about our different perceptions of scents.. you noses!! :) By now, I have tested enough fragrances to have enough self-confidence to positively evaluate this scent that has been criticized here. Lavender Palm is definitely the most extraordinary lavender scent I have ever smelled. And that alone makes it interesting enough.

I actually wanted to start with a revered line like Tom Ford's Private Line with a bestseller like Tobacco Vanille or Tuscan Leather. But then I got my hands on Lavender Palm, and since I'm currently a bit obsessed with lavender thanks to Caron's Pour Un Homme, I didn't hesitate long to test it.

I do like lavender itself, but this combination is not my cup of tea. In my opinion, a fragrance for mature men has been composed here. The top and heart notes on my skin almost resemble aftershave with a strange lavender note. Only in the base does the harshness ease up a bit, but not enough to excite me. Unfortunately, this Ford has not made the cut for me.

Moss Breches is definitely a nod to the beautiful masculine classic Pour Monsieur created by Pierre Cardin. Smelling this instantly took me back to my childhood. I remember smelling Pour Monsieur lingering in the atmosphere of the department stores while shopping with my parents. I’m glad to own an 8ml decant of Moss Breches, however this is not full bottle worthy. Especially with the aftermarket prices they are fetching. It definitely brought back great memories.

Moss Breches, I have not run for anyone else. It was in the very first series of the Private Blends, and one of the first to disappear, along with Purple Patchouli and Bois Rouge. And because I wanted both, the Moss and the Breches, and was hooked by its wonderful brothers, I embarked on the Great Search, long in vain, as it was too short-lived, especially in Europe. And then, Nordstrom, Seattle, a lost decanter was found. And an infinitely friendly and kind salesperson - who couldn't sell me anything more, as the fragrance was first taken off the program, and the decanter was secondly opened - filled two of those wonderful little bottles with the black screw cap for me and gifted them to me. Well, I did buy something from him afterwards, but: 'Sir, you really don't have to!' Moss Breches is dark gold-green, a sunlit summer forest, the ground drenched with dry needles and leaves of liquid gold. Herbs come into play - tarragon bothers me a bit, and I believe I perceive woodruff - and honey and resin. And beeswax, an animal note in it, like hair from the fur of a bear that it lost while raiding for honey - and I believe it is the bear's fur and the beeswax and the duration of their presence that leave some distance between Moss Breches and me. I am not saddened by this, for how much more terrible it would have been had I fallen in love - with less than 10 ml from the hands of the kind salesperson? Conclusion: I would not want to miss having gotten to know it. 60% is for the fragrance and 10% is for the Great Search. I still have a full bottle. I will cherish it.

Today, quite coincidentally, a Tom Ford fragrance bar was on my way. After a long back and forth with various test strips, I decided to leave Moss Breches (how is that pronounced and what does it mean?) on my wrist. Moss Breches begins with a mossy, green top note in the style of Fougère, very much leaning towards a classic English men's fragrance. But right from the start, it mixes with a broad, creamy note. Beeswax and perhaps the benzoin resin could be responsible for this from the listed components. While the "moss and fern" section signals a masculine freshness of the old school, the creaminess forces the fragrance into a very opulent breadth. This natural guy not only has a slight overweight, he is heavily obese! After about 2 hours, all the green-herbaceous notes bid farewell, and the core of the matter emerges: Moss Breches now presents itself as a classic oriental, with a lot of dirty vanilla. The similarity to the classic Jicky by Guerlain is obvious. I find it a positive surprise that a new fragrance dares to venture into this territory, but Moss Breches is clearly niche. So how should one feel about this? Moss Breches is spectacular; after all, it has made its way onto my hand past all the other Tom Fords. The combination of green herbaceousness and classic oriental vanilla in the base is very bold. Nevertheless: Fougère accords in an oriental - isn't that somewhat like herring matjes on vanilla ice cream? I don't think these two worlds fit well together. The civet note in Jicky is so much better than all the greenery here! And as for the vanilla drydown - Moss Breches has to measure up to Jicky there too and, of course, falls short. If one is going to imitate, one must be better than the original; being equally good is not enough. Measured against the opulent start, the fragrance departs far too early. After four hours, it’s over, leaving only vanilla remnants. I find that completely insufficient for a perfume in this price range. Since it starts off so strong, one cannot spray heavily. Thus, one would be compelled to carry the fragrance in a travel atomizer for reapplication. I am always suspicious when suddenly a fragrance bar is set up with as many as twenty high-priced scents. It can't all be good. In such cases, I suspect more appearance than reality. This somewhat spectacular approach, which leads perfumers from Tom Ford, Serge Lutens, and others to present strange fragrance combinations, does not appeal to me. It has something of fine dining: always interesting, yet rarely truly tasty. If Fougère accords were to fit well with orientals, someone would have successfully marketed that in the past 100 years of perfume history long ago. One wouldn't have had to wait for Tom Ford.

Thank you very much, Apicius! Now I can understand why I can't get along with this fragrance. Until now, it has simply been impossible for me to put my irritation into words. The components that are apparently combined in this scent are each not bad on their own, and therefore I initially mistrusted my nose's verdict (thumbs down in the fragrance arena!). Some scent fragments - besides the herbs, I think I smell honey and a tiny hint of cinnamon, which I wouldn't mind separately. But unfortunately, the components neither come together harmoniously, nor do they create an interesting twist. This also inspired my headline in the style of the newspaper with the big letters. Therefore, as a rather uncultured person with my cultivated ignorance, I would prefer not to add too much to Apicius's remarks about this fragrance. Except that for me, this "chubby fellow" has a slightly sharp-sour undertone in the top note that I can't stomach... the smell of (and I sincerely apologize to all sensitive users!)... baby vomit! With all my unbridled enthusiasm for expensive niche fragrances from noble designers, I get the feeling that the multitude of scents in a line like Private Blend by Tom Ford leads to a bad purchase. And if the rumor is true that one should also combine several of these fragrances at will, the olfactory disaster is pre-programmed. That would then be like putting a cocktail cherry on top of matjes herring with vanilla ice cream!

Generally, I love Tom's fragrances and the longevity is enormous; as is the sillage. The bottles always remind me of pharmacy bottles. I love these glasses. Now, let's talk about "Moss Breches." I pronounce it as it is written and it sounds terrible. What kind of scent would one expect from that??? When I sniff Moss Breches, it immediately reminds me of the 80s/90s. There was a similar scent back then. Unfortunately, I can't recall it at the moment. It is described as an oriental - seriously? To me, it has more of a vibe of rumpled bed linen, a polished Tom Hardy from LEGEND *swoon* and a sauna session with 3 rounds. It smells somehow juicy dirty and somehow innocent like a lamb. Powdery and wet at the same time. Sage and labdanum, as well as patchouli and moss definitely give it that dirty aspect. And beeswax holds it all together a bit, so nothing leaks or runs away. Unfortunately, I can't smell rosemary, although that would certainly be a special kick, as rosemary with its essential oils is supposed to stimulate thinking - at least for me - that didn't really work here ;-) There aren't many spices present, and I can't really say which ones they might be, but they give Moss Breches a cozy, familiar feeling. And fresh wood, yes, more towards the end, when the bed is freshly made. I like it; it envelops you as if you are being hugged, without distance, but pressed firmly to the chest. However, I would see it more as a woman magnet. On a man, it must be divine. Okay, it also depends a bit on the situation *laughs*

Tom Ford created Fougère d'Argent in 2018, which for me is a top 3 candidate in the entire Private Blend line. The Moss Breches from 2007 was previously unknown to me, like so many old fragrances from the house.

My favorite of all time, I love it. The way it’s so powdery, clean, fresh, smooth, slightly florally is sooo tuff. If you ever catch me without a bottle of Prada lhomme in my collection put me down. Don’t get me started on versatility, you can wear this anywhere anytime anyplace. Huzz, bruzz, gruzz, muzz all love this. The performance is perfect not too bad not too beast mode. Oh… how I love you Prada L’homme

Ever been worried that the kids at school don't like your fragrance choices? Unsure if your coworkers can stand the same scent over an entire workday? Going in for a job interview and can't risk a bad impression? The potential scenarios are endless, and the answer is always the same- Prada L'Homme. To me, far and away the safest and most mass appealing scent you can get, even more than Imagination. Not to mention, at a much better price point. Realistically everyone should have a bottle, but it's good that everyone doesn't, otherwise it would become very boring. Of course its not a mind blowing scent, but it will never offend and always make you feel clean and confident. Jack of all trades.

This fragrance is a pleasant surprise. It manages to be both safe and interesting, avoiding the pitfalls of generic or overly simplistic scents. Described as a smooth, creamy, and subtly spicy floral, it masterfully balances a lovely floral heart without becoming too feminine or cloying. The pepper and cedar notes provide a masculine edge. While not groundbreaking, the opening is incredible, leading into a gorgeous drydown. It has a cosmetic feel, but maintains a warm and inviting character, unlike the soapy and overwhelming Ambroxan of some popular fragrances. This scent offers a more refined and dimensional take on a floral-based fragrance, making it potentially one of the best in its category, even for those who typically shy away from florals. Word on the street is that women love it. Recommended, especially if found at a discounted price, but definitely sample before committing. It's an odd yet captivating fragrance – simple, classy, complex, cosmetic, warm, interesting, flowery, and yet somehow light and charming. Simply put, it's lovely and worth exploring.

This one is an icon. If you're looking for a fresh, clean scent for the office that everyone will love, go for Prada L'Homme. It's long-lasting, but won't be too strong for your colleagues. Works well with a suit or a white T-shirt. It's one of the best versatile everyday fragrances I know. Used to wear Icon from Dunhill but for me the real office Icon is Prada L'Homme.

I originally got this fragrance on my birthday back in 2021. I was so happy with what I received that I immediately took it for testing and reviewed it not even an hour later. In all fairness, my review back then was rushed and may not provide an accurate representation of how I could possibly feel about this fragrance over time. I always enjoy looking back at older reviews that I've done to see if my opinion has improved or changed as my fragrance taste has changed. At the end, I'll show you my original ratings compared to my ratings now to see if Prada L'Homme is my designer signature scent and has remained in that spot for the past 3 years. The Smell: If you're a fan of Dior Homme or DHI, chances are you're a fan of the iris. Dior nails that note and just makes it upscale. Prada's L'Homme utilizes iris as its main player but adds neroli to really bring out the floral aspect with that amber to help smooth the fragrance out and give it some added density. It's honestly refreshing. I have about 20 mL left in my bottle if that tells you about my usage on this stuff. I'm a fan. Rating: 9/10 Projection: The projection is ok. Not crazy strong but the beauty about this fragrance is, it doesn't have to be. Prada balanced the scent profile while still making it project just enough to where you know it's there and sticks around for a while as well. It projects for about 2-3 hours and begins softening on my skin and hangs close until it eventually dissipates from my skin. Usually, I'm hard on a fragrance for not performing versus its price point and that will continue here. It's a designer so I'm not expecting mind blowing performance but I'm still expecting it to be noticeable. I stated early that it does that but not for as long as I would have liked. Just a little more "oomph" and I think my rating on this category would have been much higher. Rating: 5/10 Price: Depending on where you search, you can find this anywhere from $57 USD (Amazon) or $130 (Prada's website). If you can get it cheaper, more power to ya. I will say it's worth every cent that I paid for it when I snagged my bottle from Dillard's. It was a buy on first sniff and I didn't even care about the price. If you can find a fragrance to cause you to make foolish financial decisions, you've found a winner. Rating: 8/10 Versatility: My ultimate "anytime, anywhere" fragrance. This is my "Swiss army knife" of the designer world and the proof is in the pudding. I have used up almost the entire bottle in 3 years and I own a little over 80 fragrances in total so that speaks volumes. I reach for this stuff for work, dates, casual wear, you name it. It's perfect and that's why it gets perfect marks here. Rating: 10/10 Final Verdict: 8/10 by the numbers. My original review on Fragrantica had this at an 8.3. I will say that my subjective rating has changed. I rated it as an 8 back then. It's been bumped up to a 9/10 for me now. A very solid 9 at that, with me nearly giving this a 10. If it's projection were slightly better, I'd be giving it a 10. I have owned two Prada scents and both of them saw lots of use from me, though I'd argue at the time, Prada Amber Intense was my favorite. Prada L'Homme has now taken that top spot for me. It's been my designer signature scent for 3 years and unless something mind-blowing comes out, that's not changing anytime soon. Bonus section: Ratings then versus Now Smell: 9. It remained the same. Nothing changed here and I actually expected this. Projection: 6 (then) vs 5 (now). This is why I say don't review stuff only an hour after testing. I was not far off though because my rating only changed by a single point. Price: Didn't rate this back then Versatility: 10. This category didn't change, as expected. Final Rating: 8.3/8 (then) versus 8/9 (now). My objective rating decreased slightly but my subjective rating went up a full point. This surprised me because not only did this fragrance grow on me, it's become my safety net. When I don't know what to wear, this is a sure bet.

Fresh and clean enough to wear to work. Sexy enough to wear for a date night. Everybody should at least try this fragrance. It’s perfect for any occasion any time of the year. All the notes work together so well. Timeless scent imo Wearing this at work right now (hospital setting) and 5 hours later walking by somebody she said “you smell sexy!

Prada L'homme smells very clean and inoffensive. Very versatile and safe. You can also wear it all year round. It is very fresh and soapy type of fragrance. The longevity and silage is average. Price with regards to cost and value is reasonable. Blind buy worthy if you are in to fresh, clean, and all year rounder scent.

THE office scent they said in reviews everywhere all over the internet, and I have to say maybe. This scent really intrigues me with its powdery sweet iris and creamy sandalwood. To me it's not really the epitome of office scents, but rather a calm spring date scent.

Prada L'Homme stands out as an exceptional fragrance in my extensive perfume collection, which predominantly consists of niche scents. If I were to curate a selection of only five fragrances, this masterpiece would undoubtedly secure a spot. Its aroma is truly captivating, making it my go-to choice for the workplace, where its clean and incredible scent truly shines.

A very nice iris-dominant fragrance that lasts surprisingly long given its scent profile. This smells like a room of freshly pressed newly washed cotton shirts with some spices and powder filling the air. Too powdery for summer, but well-suited for the rest of the seasons. May be the best office scent around due to its pleasant, non-offensive and professional nature.

I was very curious to test the interesting fragrance notes and the sample. What does lip gloss actually smell like? While I have an idea for lipstick, as I really enjoy the cosmetic powder note of classic lipsticks in fragrances, I am rather clueless when it comes to lip gloss. I remember the glittery lip glosses that smell like sugary fruits and can be compared to the taste of a lollipop. Is that what is meant? I still don’t know, because the scent smells like watermelon or cucumber to me, similar to Sorbetto Rosso . Should this represent the lip gloss? I did like it, but it is too similar to the already existing Sorbetto Rosso.

Hello my dear sniffers fans :D Hmm… if you are already my fans, why is there never any fan screaming from you ladies, shouting loudly and throwing bras and panties at me?? :DD Tsss… Well, anyway. Today there’s a comment on Lalique’s “Mon Premier Cristal - Lumière,” which was released about two years ago. It belongs to the fragrance line of “Mon Premier” - scents of which I don’t know any others so far. I’m not quite sure if I’ve ever seen these fragrances in stores, but even if I did, they belong to the scents that I could hardly ever spray on myself. Some of you may remember that I used to have big problems spraying a women’s fragrance in public. Although that has improved significantly today, when a scent comes in SUCH a bottle like this one and looks like a classic women’s fragrance from days long gone, I’d rather continue to seek the exit than take the thing in my hand and spray myself, especially with this PUMPBALL, which is almost only found in women’s fragrances, aaaaargh!!! :DD Anyway, luckily I had a sample of it and can test the scent here in the dark all alone for myself with a wicked smile, which just sounded a bit psycho, didn’t it? Oh… whatever, who knows what you all think about me anyway, waaah!!!! *sigh* The scent: Hmm, the scent begins quite diversely with spicy saffron, sweet jasmine, this distinctive licorice scent (which admittedly might not be everyone’s cup of tea) and especially the bitter bitter almond scent. All together, it creates a distinctive, not immediately everyday scent that smells nice but also comes across quite intense. Just a little later, the rather intense notes like bitter almond and licorice become a bit softer, making the whole thing even more pleasant, as everything now appears much better blended together. Later on, the scent becomes again softer and now also powdery, thanks mainly to musk and cashmere wood.
