It’s a very realistic, fresh green fig scent. It opens milky and vegetal, almost lactonic, but not sweet at all. There is nothing dirty, skanky, or truly “erotic” happening here, unless your idea of erotica is sitting on the grass in a fig orchard, enjoying fresh air. As it dries down, it turns creamier, and the fruity, berry-like undertones start to peek out quietly. What I really like is the muted creaminess and the realism. This smells like an actual fig, not coconutty, not jammy, not overripe, and not too grassy either. Just a clean, green fig, captured very accurately. On my skin, it became especially nice and creamy, with slightly sweet-tart fruity notes coming out later. On the blotter, it stayed true to the opening the whole time: fresh, green, almost cucumber-like fig. So I think this is skin-chemistry dependent, since it smelled so different on skin versus blotter. It reminds me of Womanity Eau de Parfum , but imagine someone carefully removed the ocean and marine notes and left you alone with just the fig. I like it, I really do, but let’s talk about the price. The largest bottle is around $1,400 and… absolutely not. This is a very simple, very one-note fig fragrance. In short, it’s a stunningly realistic fig, but not complex enough to justify that price tag.

was said in my youth, and I’ll just claim that it’s still true. And (too) much talk unfortunately still comes from Tom Ford, which I find regrettable for several reasons. After - both in English and in its translation - linguistically questionable original finds like Lost Cherry, Rose Prick, and Vanilla Sex, I actually thought that the Ford house would finally be done with risqué double entendres (especially since something quite acceptable like Black Lacquer or more recently Oud Voyager was being offered at the same time). Wrongly thought. That now, of all things, the fig accord, which I personally don’t find very easy, has been given a particularly lamentably clumsy name does not help either. I look for and appreciate, in addition to the scent itself, the underlying concept of perfumes - hopefully it has one. So not just how it is crafted, but also how it is academically thought out and implemented. And 'Figue Érotique' has the depth and maturity of a group of drunken teenage boys who are lewdly licking a halved fig. And then - muhaha! - sticking their fingers in. The subtlety of a truck driver magazine from the 90s, whose title reveals: 'Secret Sex Tips from Uninhibited Hairdressers!'. A scent concept that reminds me more of Bruno Banani (sorry, Bruno - I don’t know any of your fragrances, I’m sure they are great!) than of one that can stand alongside truly sensual classics like Santal Blush or Noir de Noir. Tom Ford's fig is made quite 'okay-ish' - if you like sweet, fruity, and fig. I almost hoped to hate it more, but instead I have almost forgotten the scent itself. This may partly be due to its en passant test at an airport, but it also shows how little it sticks with me. From the idea of 'erotic fig', one could have boldly done something with the quote of skin and sweat and bodily juices - instead of just being a bit bitter and a bit green and then very sweet for a long time - even if Muscovado sugar sounds a bit fancier. But that would probably have been too much sex for the prudish average American, who should ideally buy Figue Érotique before New Year’s Eve. Conclusion: just talk less about it, Tom. Do more!

It should be clear to everyone that Tom Ford does not have the absolute best quality. But that's often not the point; fragrances like Tobacco Vanille Eau de Parfum or Fucking Fabulous Eau de Parfum are simply so iconic and special that people are willing to pay this price. However, in recent years, it has become increasingly common for Tom Ford to release fragrances just to make money, rather than to create something unique, which is extremely unfortunate. With a rating of 8.9, you expect a lot, especially when the scent notes resemble those of "Gris Charnel (Eau de Parfum) | bdk Parfums," but well, what can you do. The scent itself doesn't smell bad; it even smells good, but not Tom Ford good. The fig is by no means as good as the one from Gris Charnel Eau de Parfum and smells much more synthetic to me. Overall, the entire fragrance has a somewhat synthetic smell and lacks real depth for me. It is very flat and fades away after not too long. The whole concept is a nice idea, but it feels executed without love or passion, which is something you can smell here. But well, if you have money to throw around, go for it. If not, I would first get a sample; everyone perceives fragrances differently, but for me, in this price segment, it's a clear no! :)

Both the name and color of "Figue Érotique" have their charm, especially considering how Mr. Ford, or the current brand owner, knows how to market and entice with his creations. In French, it all sounds much more seductive and poetic than "Erotic Fig" The fig already has the reputation of universal sensuality, but can it meet the high expectations here? First of all, this fragrance is one of the few where fig is officially listed, without straying into coconut territory. It is rather fresh, fruity, green, rich, and very sweet. In addition, I detect a good dose of floral notes; at times, I would even have guessed rose, although ylang-ylang is definitely present and recognizable. Overall, it comes across as absolutely pleasant, but for my taste, it leans more towards the feminine side. Moreover, there is the question of value for money. The same creation from a mainstream designer in a chic package as a women's fragrance would surely be very well received. With Tom Ford, there is always a slight feeling of being charged a premium. But one must give credit: of all the fig fragrances I have encountered so far, "Figue Érotique" indeed has the most seductive aura.

It reminds me of summer nights spent in my grandma's garden. She loved the Queen of the night and she would plant it everywhere. The air was thick richly filled with this flowers because they would bloom at night. It is a sweet fragrance, delicate soft and fleeting. I only get like 3 hours before it disappears on me. The bottle and the scent are still gorgeous though.

First of all: I cannot understand the reviews here and on other sites regarding low longevity and sillage! Even after 24 hours, the powdery amber base remains on my skin (which is otherwise a sponge par excellence), still with a slight projection after 12 hours. This is by far the strongest fragrance I have ever tested! Although I can imagine that I simply don't become nose-blind like with many others. About the scent itself: It starts in a fruity sea of blossoms: mandarin, pear, velvety sugared orange blossom (probably magnolia). It becomes increasingly floral, yet you never feel like you're walking through a blooming garden, as the distinct powderiness of heliotrope, ambrette, and musk keeps everything far from "green" plant notes. Once the fruity notes have faded, the oak moss comes to the forefront. In the heart, there is the impression of an ancient forest where delicate petals dance in the wind. However, everything, really everything, in this forest is under a thick, crunchy layer of sugar. If you don't like sweet scents, you won't be happy here. I can definitely understand the Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum comparisons, although unfortunately, I only know the twins, not the OG. The drydown is dominated by oak moss, which leaves a brittle, fragile impression, further intensified by the crystal-clear sugar. Only when everything else has faded does warm, powdery amber appear in its pure form, giving a pleasant, skin-like warmth from start to finish. The fragrance is meant to mimic the passage of a sunset, which I find successful: I think the transition from fruity - floral - mossy - amber is very beautiful. Bottle absolute 10000/10. P/L top.

Maybe it’s the pendant with the moon and the little sun or the color scheme of the bottle or its shape, which reminds me of a big bow - I had to think of Sailor Moon right away when I saw the first pictures of the bottle! Especially the Eternal Outfit with its yellow-pink skirt (not the elegant white Queen Serenity!) Okay, enough of the 90s TV memories... Lalique itself describes the fragrance as "[...] a free-spirited child of the sun, moved by the rhythm of the sun and moon [...] - and asserts itself as the mistress of its own destiny." - hey, that’s Sailor Moon... Soleil Lunar starts extremely fruity with super ripe, sweet mandarins/oranges. Alongside, there’s lovely magnolia, I’m still looking for pepper and I’m already tempted to pull out the disappointment from the drawer, because this is threatening to become another sugary soda thing, but let’s wait and see... On the product page, the fragrance is beautifully described as "a hug of the sun, seamlessly transitioning into the realm of night as the moon takes its place in the sky," and this characterizes the further development of the fragrance excellently. The warm, fruity, borderline sweet start dims down like a sunset. The fruit salad is done for the day, a few mandarins are still rolling around in the background but can’t quite let go. The transition to the already mentioned night should not be interpreted as "cool/dark" but rather as "resting/relaxed." On my skin, a very nice musk spectacle begins in the best Narciso manner. Add a decent scoop of amber, cozy warmth guaranteed. As the willing reader of some of my other reviews may have noticed, I’m not a big fan of vanilla. It’s all the more surprising that my vanilla-phobic nose doesn’t react to either heliotrope (aka vanilla plant) or queen of the night (you guessed it: vanilla!) and raise alarms. I feel more reminded of "Izia | Sisley," even though the pyramids are completely different... NOW it could still become something between us, dear Soleil Lunar! The longer I have it on my skin, the more I like it. Soleil Lunar leaves me a bit confused. Is this now a fruity summer scent (opening) or rather a candidate for autumn/winter (cuddle musk)? Does it want to be young-girly (opening) or feminine-adult (drydown)? To me, it comes across as contradictory - but maybe that’s just a subjective thing and there are plenty of wearers for whom this is not a problem. Due to the - in my opinion - too sweet opening, it just falls short of a solid 7. I find the sillage quite socially acceptable, depending on the dosage, it’s definitely noticeable - especially at the beginning! Longevity is also completely within the normal range, not a fleeting scent but also not one that requires amputating body parts to get rid of it. And the bottle, well, it’s a little kitschy dream ;) Moonstone, fly and conquer!

This fragrance resembles the original, with some minor differences. This fragrance seems to have added some sparkling ginger in the opening and has dialed back on the overall powdery aroma. I have seen some say that this fragrance doesn't lave the same longevity as the original, however from my journey with this fragrance I would have to disagree. I love this flanker, I love the original L'Homme, however I actually prefer the ginger and less projected powdery aroma. When i purchased this fragrance I was looking for something to replace Dior Homme Eau, I still feel neither this or the original did that, but I still added 2 great fragrances to my collection.

A really good scent, fresh, clean and soapy, suitable for daytime use. I feel a lot of iris, which makes it a bit sweet, but it is well balanced by the neroli which instead gives it that aura of cleanliness. Overall it is not an ultra masculine perfume, on the contrary, it is definitely unisex and versatile, it adapts well to any context as long as it is daytime, as its simplicity and linearity does not make it sexy and inviting enough for an evening / night use. Certainly a safe purchase for everyday use and with a really high quality / price ratio.

Love at first sniff! This is a masterpiece of a fragrance. Classy and clean all the way through. Comes off as being suitable for spring and summer but I think one can pull it off in the fall too. This would be a stable in my collection for years to come.

Notes: Amber, Iris, Ginger, Neroli, Sandalwood and Cedarwood Perfumer: Danjela Andrier L'Homme L'Eau opens fresh and zesty but not bright. Iris combined with Neroli creates a gorgeous white floral blend with a touch of aquatic. Overall a really good scent, prefect for casual wear, fresh, Soapy and clean.

First of all let me say I'm in love with the whole Prada L'Homme line so do not expect this to be negative review. To put everything into context, I have to mention the whole line one by one. My journey with this line started with the original L'Homme and it was a love at first sniff. It's all you hear about it and then some. Clean, unique, professional, unforgettable. Great for spring / summer day use. Very likable and inoffensive. Nobody will complain about the way you semll. I couldn't resist and shortly after the purchase of L'Homme I went to a store to smell also L'Homme Intense and L'Homme L'Eau. From the two I immediatelly decided to purchase Intense version as a counterpart to the OG. It is more aggresive, sharper version suitable for cold weather and night occasions. Performance is almost unbeliveable: 12+ hours with 3-4 hours of great projection and sillage. Just wonderful! On the other hand I did not enjoy L'Eau that much at first. Sure, it is a fresher version of the original, but that goes only for the opening. Once it hits the mid and later a drydown, it loses part of the magic the original has. At the time I felt it is not necessary as for the office use original L'Homme has it all and I always felt this line is targeted for professional environment / dressed up occasions where you more often spend time in air conditioned rooms. If you are looking for a summer freshie, you can do much better then L'Eau imho. But wait: isn't that what everybody says about L'Homme Absolu? Excessive, unnecessary release? In my opinion? ABSOLUtely NOT!!! Instead of thinking why not to like it I immediately discovered what hole it is supposed to fill in the line. Imagine you spend your work day wearing L'Homme during the spring / summer and then decide to hit the downtown with your colleagues for some evening dinner / drink. (I know, during this Covid situation it sounds like a sci-fi). Here the Intense version would be too much and that's when it's the right time for Absolu. You don't even need to worry about getting rid of the L'Homme version and you can just layer it with Absolu and be ready to go! Later in the year when the weather starts to get colder, original L'homme might not be strong enough to cut through the cold air even during the day and Absolu becomes great substitute for your daily office driver. I find the performance to be on the level of Intense version, but it is a bit less loud and better suited for daily use in professional environment. Combine it with Intense and you are covered for nights out/ business dinners / drinks. I noticed some people are complaining about the performance of Absolu...maybe I'm just lucky, but it performs the same as the Intense on my skin. Yesterday at 1pm I sprayed my forearm once and I could still smell it when I woke up today at 8am. Not projecting, but it still was easilly recognizable skin scent. And did I mention I took a shower before I went to bad? It's a monster! After falling in love with L'Homme / Absolu / Intense I decided to give L'Eau another chance and you can probably guess how it all went :) Yes, I went with a full bottle of that one as well as Water Splash. Honestly if there is any redundancy in this line, it's between these two flankers. They are very similar and if you do not need to own the whole line, you can easily skip one of these two. My recommandation would be to buy L'Eeu. In my opinion the whole Prada L'Homme line is a masterpiece and every professional should have in their arsenal.

I needed time to like this perfume. At first, the opening felt too feminine and it surprised me. But then, it changed! This is the best floral perfume for men. You need to be a confident man to wear this, someone who is always clean, well-groomed, and looks great and you'll get complimented. The drydown is absolutely wonderful and the best part of the scent.

I think it's a well-rounded perfume. Aside from the notes, it has a clean, neat, fresh, luminous fragrance, etc. It's ideal for almost any occasion (perhaps not so suitable for winter evenings, but only because there are better options). For everything else, it's perfect. No one will ever say you smell bad, quite the contrary.

This has become, in my wardrobe, a Springtime staple. Neroli & Orange Blossom are not only my 2 favourite white florals, but florals in general. And L'homme L'eau uses Neroli incredibly well in this creation. It's bright & zesty but not fresh (to my nose) if that makes sense. The combination of Neroli & Ginger off the top has become one of my favourite openings in a perfume.

The opening of L’Homme L’eau is really quite fresh and features iris, neroli, and the wood notes also peak through at the start. To my nose, it doesn’t have as much iris as the original L’Homme, but it is fairly strong towards the beginning of the wear and is present throughout. I get more wood in this one than its predecessor, with less amber, and some added ginger.

Definitely for warmer weather but not a clear 'summer scent'. If I had to choose between this and Dior's Homme Eau I'd pick Dior. This Prada has the signature powdery aspect. If you choose this as an office scent or a more formal summer party then this would do well, not a monster that arrives before you.

A classy gem I neglected for too long, I used to own Infusion d’Homme some years ago and got rid of it since it smelled too light and a bit dull for me - and I thought this was just its feminine counterpart (therefore even lighter and – not to sound sexist – probably duller). I was so wrong! This is so better than that – and ironically, way more suitable for men. Easily however this is one of the nicest iris-based scents on the market for me, especially of the fresher/gentler sub-family. And even more easily, the best offering by Prada so far, but it didn’t take much for that. Infusion d’iris is a tremendously radiant, bright and bracing blend centered on a minimalistic structure of iris petals (no buttery/waxy/lipstick orris root), bergamot, something slightly and elegantly candied-fruity, soft incense and a silky, really discreet base accord of musk and bright vetiver. The notes seem common, their smell isn’t at all: the quality is clearly high and unique, particularly more than usual, and you can definitely feel it. All smells clean and light, but decidedly more intense and substantial than one may expect. The evolution is also really catchy and irresistibly pleasant, moving from a zesty pastel opening of fresh bergamot and bright iris petals through a soapy, stronger central phase centered on iris (blossoming in its earthier-leafier side) and musk, ending on a beautiful vetiver drydown still infused with a powdery touch of iris. Like a really consistent three-movement piece of intimate piano music, with iris being the recurrent theme. And aside from its brilliant evolution, it just smells great - period. And persistent, too: very few perfumes manage to smell this crisp, weightless and luminous keeping some intensity and persistence, and also ending up in being exceedingly perfect for men and women. Probably only the best Ellena’s for Hermès managed to do that – and Infusion d’Iris could easily stand among them in fact. Together with Rush for Men, probably one of the best works by Roche-Andrier, showing that exact same feel of discreet, bright, extremely clean sense of quality, refinement and sophistication (now let’s all wait until Prada discontinues it to realize that!). 8,5-9/10

Picturing A Librian/Chic College Student A Gray Cloudy Morning in fall. will be the perfect fragrance for these Occasions and Lifestyle. it's not a flashy bold in your face fragrance it's refined A Bit Melancholic an austere perfume A perfume for a conservative Woman. for a time of introspective Moments or a quiet space to study for exams. I Love the blending of Irises with incenses it gives it an Refined character and with a touch woods gives it a bit of an impression. A Great Perfume for New England's High Society

Worthy piece from brand. I think that scent start the idea of= '' Powdery scents are mass appealing and compliment getters. '' in Prada brand. It has citrusy feeling but that lasts short time. (according to fragrantica =neroli but here listed as orange blossom) also from the opening galbanum, pistachio leaf gives green feeling. The heart notes are skeleton of scent(iris, vetiver, cedar). İris makes Infusion D'iris powdery and baby oily baby shampoo type with vetiver and cedarwood. Prada did good job. Profile of smell is certainly unisex. Then they released new ones with different names but %80 similar type. (Infusion d'homme, Infusion d'iris absolute...)

Prada Infusion d'Iris is the definition of elegance and class. For those of you that want lots of flowers, sweetness and strength, this fragrance probably isn't for you. Infusion d'Iris is a clean, inoffensive floral. Slightly musky and woodsy. In truth, I hated this fragrance at first. It opened with a harshness that was both soapy and herbaceous. All I wanted was a delicate floral note, yet what I first experienced was odd and unpleasant to my nose. Thankfully the heart was much nicer with the iris and orange blossom notes peeking through and eventually taking over. Well Infusion d'Iris is certainly a Prada fragrance in its sophistication and simplicity. I do appreciate those aspects in Infusion d'Iris, I think that more simplistic, classic scents are needed on the market these days. There are too many overly sweetened and overly fruity scents that people seem to prefer wearing. This fragrance is not something I'd personally buy for myself and to be completely honest, I do prefer Acqua di Parma's Iris Nobile for my iris fix. However, this fragrance is beautiful in a soapy, clean sense. It is perfect for those days at the office or when you want to feel fresh and feminine all day long.

I didn't expect to like this. I'm not generally fond of iris, which tends to make perfumes too powdery for my taste, and because Infusion de Fleur d'Oranger dryed down to pretty much powder and not much else on me. This is powdery for sure, but it is much more than that. Now that I look at the notes, I can see why I like it. It has some of my absolute favorites: orange blossom, neroli and cedar. And in this case, unlike Fleur d'Oranger, these notes are detectable throughout. Made a convert out of a powder hater like me

My bottle of Infusion d'Iris plays a very useful part in my fragrance wardrobe. Specifically, I use it after a cold shower on a hot day, when its chilly, citrusy scent provides a most welcome cooling sensation on my skin. Infusion d'Iris opens with tart citrus and thin, almost austere woods, reminding me more of a cup of chilled green tea than a true iris fragrance.
The hit! I could only smell the testing paper strip (my arms were overdosed on other scents) but this is so much my taste. Smoky flowers with a little wood. Marvelous.

This scent starts citric and fresh, but without the lemon and bergamot. I smell a freshly peeled orange. The galbanum makes it tart and spicy. "Infusion d'Iris" Eau de Parfum radiates an incredible warmth as if it were the "Nice Weather God" himself. The image of a holiday in Tuscany comes to mind. As expected, the Iris now takes the floor.

If I hadn't found my perfect iris in Iris de Syracuse , I most likely would have sprung for a full bottle of this gorgeousness. They are very similar, in fact: they both have that diaphanous pencil shavings aroma that makes me dream of a rainbow in all shades of purple.

I had tested INFUSION D'IRIS several times - always inside in air-conditioned environment - and every time it gave off an aura of an impeccably dressed, elegant, unapproachable woman. There was a cold, slightly powdery vibe. When I came upon a good deal for a big bottle, I could not resist though I remained a bit skeptical.

What is an urban musk? And, importantly for fashionistas, who prioritize urban above all else, what would a rural musk or a suburban musk smell like. Accordingly, cow shit and hell? Urban musk smells to me like Kiehl's Musk Number One that has been watered down both in fact and in concept. It smells like a bland, slightly berry-like musk that has been accented with a drop of an animalic musk then diluted by a non-descript sweet floral.. When the Ford Privée line offers a deliberately simple product, such as Azure Lime, or a new take on a familiar piece, such as Lavender Palm’s take on lavender, I'll cut them some slack. When their product is a shoddy take on a simple product available at 1/10 the cost, I say fuck 'em. Don't buy it. from scent hurdle.com

Yeap, this is exactly what Urban Musk is... The perfume itself is the most interesting of the White Musk collection. It opens with a strange note that oscillates between wood and halitosis. Now the idea of smelling like bad breath and liking it is something that has most of you frowning in disgust already, but it is not just me. Kevin of Now Smell This has reviewed all four from the White Musk collection and he also reports the “bad breath” note and agrees with me that Urban Musk is the most interesting of the quartet. I cannot quite explain how this note can be attractive in a perfume. All I can imagine is that it feels warm and alive. I smell the same note in the opening of Le Labo Oud 27. In the opening of Urban Musk it is more restrained and has a woody quality. How can this relate to filmstrip projectors? Film strips contain lignin which is a form of cellulose, the sugar that gives rigidity to plants. Pyrolysis (a heat mediated reaction) of lignin yields guaiacol, and yes, this is the connection between the smell of my projector and perfume. The heat of the projector lamp slowly turns film lignin to an aromatic derivative usually isolated from guaiac wood and palo santo tree. I do not know how all this connects to halitosis but the fact is that both Urban Musk and Oud 27 have been accused of this association. The opening of Urban Musk feels grey and woolly. This doesn’t last long. Ylang-ylang and musk add familiarity, sweetness and warmth. The musk is slightly dirty and animalic but in an elegant way. Honey and benzoin added in moderation increase the balmy sensation but they never impose on the composition. The overall effect remains airy and velvety. The drydown is powdery. Although iris is not listed in the semi-official lists of Fragrantica and parfyym.pri.ee there is a striking similarity with L’Homme de Coeur, a stellar iris perfume.

Out of the corner of my eye, I glance over at Schatzi. He’s just adjusting his glasses on his nose and shifting his weight nervously from his right foot to his left and back again. Then he looks out the shop window onto the street. Oh-oh, my time window is closing. Half an hour, at least. I quickly sprint over to the Tom Ford fragrances for a final sniff. This has to be quick. I pop the caps off the bottles and hold my nose to the spray buttons. Black Orchid, Sahara Noir, Neroli Portofino - too heavy, too strange, too expected... My skin is still clean, I’ve only tested on cosmetic tissues so far - and haven’t found anything, especially since I’ve just smashed my piggy bank for this shopping spree! Am I really supposed to go home WITH money? Wait, what’s that on the bottom shelf? I’ve never seen these bottles before...! How much time do I have left? Schatzi is looking around, but since I’m crouched down, he scans over me. Phew. That was close. Desperate circumstances call for bold measures: I roll up my sleeves and spray a spritz on each forearm. Then I rush back up, put on a grateful, encouraging look, hurry to Schatzi, and link my arm with his. “We can go.” Schatzi beams. The saleswoman does not. Outside, I first smell to the left, Jasmine Musk: floral, clean, pleasant. You like it right away. But a bit too accommodating. Then I sniff to the right, Urban Musk: Whoa! Definitely NOT accommodating, it smells like camel. What a shame, damn! We stroll along Zurich's Bahnhofstrasse. While Schatzi stops in front of an art gallery, I ponder why a fragrance called Urban Musk smells like camel. I sniff again. It has become smaller. A baby camel. Freshly bathed, with fluffy, curly fur and a creamed snout, it lies in a bed of hay, happily munching on a banana with honey glaze. Am I crazy? A baby camel, as only a mother camel could love, and yet it somehow touches my heart and nose, must be the hormones at the end of my 30s. I would have guessed saffron, which I’ve known as a camel note, but it’s a very animalistic musk that makes Urban Musk a fragrance one could wonderfully argue about. Definitely not for beginner noses and not a compliment catcher. Still, it’s not so quirky or imitating a known scent that it would be a concept fragrance. It does want to please, but it also rubs you the wrong way. You either love it or hate it. My skin and the camel get along very well, I’m falling in love. I can’t detect jasmine or plum at all, and I don’t know cumin as a fragrance note. Frankincense and pepper create a combination that could also be compared to a light, gentle patchouli. The animalistic aspect remains in the foreground, but behaves tamed and becomes cozy, increasingly creamy, warm, and cuddly through honey, the chocolate-vanilla-like benzoin, and ambrette. Ambrette is a very precious musk seed oil with a warm, deep, sweet musk scent that is said to be strongly erotic. Is that it? The idea of the musky animalistic in the big city? The loud roar for a partner, to be heard in urban anonymity? For me, it remains my little cuddly camel, I don’t need to roar anymore, I have Schatzi, and he loves me even if I smell like camel. I extend my arm to him: “Here, what do you think of this?” - “I don’t know.” - “Well, is it good or bad or what?” - “I haven’t smelled anything after five minutes in the perfume shop.” Oh. - “Can we please turn around again? I want to get it.” - “Okay.” Back in the perfume shop, I grab Urban Musk and head to the register. I look at the price and gulp: I will be going home without money today. The saleswoman beams. Schatzi is waiting outside and is cleaning his nose. I’ve had Urban Musk for a few weeks now and wear it with unbroken enthusiasm. It requires a bit of courage and individuality, but it’s suitable for every season, except maybe in high summer. It’s also quite suitable for men. I just wish for a longer longevity for the high price.

David Bowie has gone to the stars, it was read this morning. I was never a true fan of his music and art - I’m probably just too young for that - but I always perceived and respected him in everything he did. And he will be missed - perhaps the last great universal performance artist of the 20th century, who seems all the greater next to Justin Bieber and the others whose names I can’t remember. David Bowie was pop and punk and porn, was loud and shrill and thoughtful and quiet, was devilish and moral - simultaneously and seemingly effortlessly. One of his most famous songs is 'Ziggy Stardust', in which he sings about the rise and fall of a drug and sex god, and thus barely veils his own story. Pop and punk and porn is also Urban Musk, perhaps the craziest among the four white Private Blends that Tom Ford released after already leaving a deep footprint with Tobacco Vanille, Tuscan Leather, and Noir de Noir. Alongside the sultry Jasmine Musk and the damply lustful Musk Pure (there was also White Suede, the only one without musk, and the only one of the four that still exists - irony of fate?), Urban Musk is the disco musk among the white Private Blends. Confident and androgynous, it arranges its central accord genderlessly and seemingly weightlessly between pounding sweet bitter resins and a tipsy plum, adding incense and sharp spices - it is loud and sexy yet smooth and cultivated. Perhaps that is what makes it 'urban.' Like David Bowie, sexy and simultaneously lost in himself and highly controlled, metallic and Mephistophelian, alluring and cursing at the same time as he sang of Ziggy Stardust - that damned pop messiah that he himself was. Conclusion: farewell, David Bowie! Greet the stars for us.

and overpriced. From above, we all know that musk likes to play crazy little games from time to time, from skin to skin. Here the game begins with the words 'Rien ne va plus'. HEY! Yuck! Kankuro says urine. Let's agree on damp hay. Jasmine can be so terribly musty, oddly animalistic. Lady-like? Nothing is beautiful, noble, or elegant about this scent. At least not in the first hour. The honey is well incorporated, as I don't smell it. Also no revelation of the plum, the incense, or the pepper. But in the end, Urban Musk develops, as it should for a proper musk fragrance, into an average amber perfume. Mr. Ford, what have we done wrong now?

Thanks to Kankuro for the sample. I simply love testing Tom Ford's Private Blend line; you always experience something new. Strangely enough, right after spraying it, I immediately had the memory of my Andy Warhol: Success is a Job in New York in my mind as I sniffed the scent.

I didn't have a Male test subject handy for this so I am using a complex, top secret algorythm and my best intuition to acertain my reaction on this clearly "Pour Homme" scent I recieved with a recent fragrance purchase. The first impression is "Energy!" with a capital E. There is much life force and stregth in this scent, young Grasshopper.I get that brisk vigorous green and awakening minty note along with a robust clary sage. This is definitely a daytime fully alert and on the job kind of vibe. There is something that catches my personal Libido in this formulation- Ambrette- love this note on Men & Women- it smells great on humans, in general and soothes. The Lavender here is a whisper, I would not even notice it if it wasn't pointed out to me.I can imagine that this heats up on the body to a warm day to night signature scent...o.k., I am just going to say it, it's become like an elephant in the room...underneath the zippy clary sage and moden spearmint is something almost Polo-like. All too familiar and still alluring since 1985! This scent fades on my skin fairly quickly- into a clean soapy background- which is a good thing, IMHO. I could stand to be in a room, trapped in an elevator or on a desserted island with someone who smelled like this indefinitely...and I am pretty picky in this facet. I would call this a lightweight sillage, moderate projection green woodsy fresh scent that reminds me a little bit of D&G's "Le Fou". It is definitely work-able. Have your people call my people.
Very fresh smell, mint in this reminds of Lush Dirty. Here though it's not so harsh. After the lavander takes. The strange thing is that this is more Sport than the actual Sport version. Go figure!

Well, i did expect much of this, but what i've got is a weak release, very similar to Infusion D'Homme althought lighter. Opens with lavander and oranges, then there comes a bit of mint and vetiver. Actually only okay, not outstanding neither bad. Sillage, projection and lasting power are weak. Updated January 2014

Prior to testing Luna Rossa, I glanced at the scent pyramid and prepared myself for yet another predictable citrus masculine. Now that I have actually tested it, I can fully admit that I was wrong to prejudge this fragrance. Luna Rossa is a quality scent. The opening is a fresh and summery burst of bitter orange, which in this case, smells much nicer than straight-up lemon. When the bitter orange softens, the herbaceous nature of this fragrance becomes more apparent. Lavender, mint and clary sage come together nicely in the heart. The drydown can be either a love it or a hate it. Iso E Super as a note can get on some people's nerves. It is after all a synthetic ingredient, commonly known as an aromachemical. However I personally think it works well in this composition, providing a smooth, woody touch when paired with the ambrette accord. I would quite happily buy this fragrance for a man. It's one of the few citrus masculines that I actually like. I am after all a fan of lavender on men, so perhaps that is the reason why I rate this fragrance so highly. I found Luna Rossa's sillage to be average, however I must say that the longevity is excellent. I can trust Prada to deliver. The only thing I didn't like about Luna Rossa was the odd packaging. It's quite unattractive in real-life. Original review written: February 2013.

From Tom Ford's first generation of Private Blends - it's been a good ten years since then - some fragrances - Tobacco Vanille, Oud Wood, or Neroli Portofino, for example - quickly became hits that you can smell on almost every corner. Others, however - this one: Purple Patchouli, as well as Moss Breches or Bois Rouge - turned out to be too difficult and unsuitable for the masses. And because Mr. Ford - at least on the side - is also a businessman, they quickly disappeared from his portfolio. Today, aside from mostly shockingly clumsy fakes on the internet, it is practically impossible to smell them anymore. After the flop Purple Patchouli - and one must at least label it as such commercially - Tom Ford has experimented with the theme of patchouli several more times: White Patchouli has at least endured to this day, although not in the very forefront - and what will become of Patchouli Absolu remains to be seen. I also believe I perceive patchouli in Fucking Fabulous, even though it is not listed among its ingredients. Nevertheless: Patchouli seems to be no easy terrain for the fragrance portfolio of the Ford house, although he is otherwise not shy about difficult and dramatic scents. In Latin America - especially in Mexico - there is the figure of La Llorona, which translates to: the Weeping Woman. The composer Andres Henestrosa dedicated a wonderfully lamenting song to her in the mid-20th century, which has become a kind of folk tune in Mexico. According to legend - which varies a bit from country to country - La Llorona is the wandering spirit of a beautiful young woman who, in anger over her husband's infidelity, drowned her children in the river and now cannot enter the kingdom of heaven until she has found them again. It is said that La Llorona drowns people in the river to claim them as her children. Purple Patchouli is told and composed in the language of the story of La Llorona. There is the damp leaf green of aquatic plants, the hint of gray water that has been stagnant for far too long. There are intoxicating, sometimes almost fermented, sultry flowers, a dull earthiness, and a strangely floral resinous quality that is too much patchouli for those who do not like patchouli - and not nearly enough for those who love it. Purple Patchouli is an almost surreal scent - as if one were seeing La Llorona wandering through the riverside thicket in wet clothes with a lost gaze, searching for her lost children. Conclusion: the blue Mauritius among Tom Ford Private Blends. Far too serious, unwieldy, and unyielding to have captivated the masses, yet highly interesting as a fragrance concept.

During a pre-Christmas turbo shopping spree, I wanted to treat myself to something "nice" and bought - blindly and only because of the promising name - a bottle the size of a rum pot. Following the motto: a quick shot under time pressure doesn't have to be wrong ;-) Due to its oversized nature, the precious liquid couldn't go on the plane and I had to check my hand luggage. So I had plenty of time from London to home to imagine what Purple Patchouli might smell like... Then the big moment: I sniff and smell ...the color purple!! ... and indeed in the form of violets! For me, the promised patchouli on the label is completely overshadowed, in a scent I haven't smelled like this since childhood. Namely the scent of Viola dragées, a piece for 1 pfennig. Available at the corner shop across from the school. The violet bomb is also slightly herbaceous for reasons of pleasantness, but I can't sniff out any other scent components: my big nose simply gets stuck like the needle of a record player on a scratched vinyl at the violet odor. For someone who likes violets....okay! For patchouli fetishists, in my opinion, this scent is absolutely nothing.

Today I had the pleasure of testing this fragrance. I like it, but it wasn't love at first sniff. It may be that I'm unjustly labeling it as "not my scent" today, and perhaps we will become a couple someday, but it's not there yet.. Too much floral that takes away the uniqueness of the patchouli. There's also a bit of sourness in there. Not unpleasant, but somehow out of place. There's just too much going on in this fragrance. But it might also just be that I'm addicted to patchouli and find every note that changes it disturbing. When the fragrance notes appear one after the other, that's fine, but such a mix... no. Let's see if I will lose my heart to Purple Patchouli on the second, third, or fourth testing..

I should have finished a comment on this fragrance a long time ago. But I just find it hard to describe this scent. When thinking of Purple Patchouli, one usually imagines a dark fragrance, something along the lines of Gothic or similar. At least, that's how I envisioned it. But it's not. Uncle Tom has pulled another surprise out of the hat. Purple Patchouli is an surprisingly floral and light fragrance that only hints at patchouli. In any case, the scent develops surprisingly easily on my skin and is definitely wearable for everyday use. Compared to White Patchouli, which has a somewhat cold, metallic quality, Purple Patchouli is more of a bright, floral scent with slight woody undertones, which are more derived from vetiver. So, anyone expecting a patchouli bomb will be rather disappointed here. I initially didn't find it that great either, but maybe we will become really good friends. I hope, Lav, that this description is sufficient for you.

This is the scent of a significant other who treats you with kindness. His hugs smell like safety and and secure masculinity - and when you borrow his sweatshirt, you realize you're catching whiffs of Luna Rossa Sport . Secure masculinity, why? Because this is lavender-vanilla forward. Some men might not want to smell like anything sweet, which is valid in its own right - but in my opinion, there's an appeal to a lavender-vanilla blend like this one. The lavender-vanilla is more prominent in the opening - and even with the vanilla, the lavender itself is still herbal rather than gourmand. The juniper berry adds just enough of a masculine, cooling, and woodsy touch to keep the sweetness in check - and the subtle ginger brings an aura of freshness, like the clarity of a soft ginger tea. The heliotrope is well-balanced with the tonka bean and musk. Not too powdery to veer into cosmetic territory - but just enough to contribute towards the feeling of a slightly-creamy bar of soap. In dry-down, it does become more powdery (with a "cool"/metallic undertone, and a bit of a synthetic quality). The projection isn't "beast mode" - but that enhances the intimacy. Despite this, it does have an inviting scent trail/sillage. Overall it's somehow calming, comforting, & sexy all at once. P.S. While I'd love to smell this on someone else, I did spray myself with the tester bottle - and have been enjoying it thoroughly. It feels similar to the concept of Boyfriend Eau de Parfum (Kate Walsh created the fragrance after missing the smell of her boyfriend on her skin/clothes). So if I had a significant other who owned Luna Rossa Sport , I might steal his bottle from time to time - or possibly just get my own!

If you're reading reviews because you're looking for a fragrance for hot weather or for physical activity then you might keep looking. This is good for not-so-hot temps. Maybe for evenings or casual events? Definitely can be worn by the ladies. Easily projects and has longevity.

…that people were comparing this to Le Male/Reflection. I would see it in the store and see the word “sport” on the bottle, and continue walking on my way. Then more recently, I saw that this was being discontinued, and read all of the reviews comparing it to JPG. As a big Le Male fan, I grabbed it while I could still find it. I am GLAD I did. While it isn’t as VERBATIM as some suggest, I definitely DO get the comparison, and I enjoy it very much. It’s actually different enough to the point where a JPG fan walking by might think it’s a flanker of some sort. (Kind of how the Carbon is compared to Sauvage, you can kind of see WHY people do, but it in no way is it the SAME scent). It’s got decent performance, projecting 2-3ft for about 2 hours, with an OK sillage trail for that duration, before fading into a skin scent that lasts an additional 4-6 hours or so, depending on how much you spray. Not too shabby at all. I grabbed it asap, as I have a feeling that this is going to be another one that people start to remember as being greater than it was, and long for it when it is no more. It’s fun to have and wear the frags that aren’t available, and to read the reviews, seeing the timeline switch; and how the opinions switch from yin to yang. If you see it, and you like that Le Male feeling, grab it. More like Le Male then Reflection Man or Darley, FYI, but worthy if you like the “barbershop vanilla mint” scents.

This fragrance and I go a long way back, and it is a fragrance that is dear to my heart, even though I acquired a full bottle for the first time just a couple of months ago. A scent that is easy to love, smells great in the air, and most people around you will equally enjoy this beautiful perfume when you decide to wear it. This "magic" is the reason why I finally decided to get this flanker of Luna Rossa, and that’s why it’s my favourite release from the house for over 10 years now. TOP NOTES The unusual combination of juniper berries, matched with a zesty rush of ginger, is the reason why Prada calls this an “explosive-opening”, which matches my experience. There are also citric elements in the first couple of minutes, but that feeling comes from the ginger. Overall, that initial burst is bold and invigorating, setting an active tone for the fragrance. HEART NOTES After the fireworks of the opening fade, Luna Rossa settles into a clean lavender heart. Thankfully, the lavender is not the cheap detergent-smelling variety, but a realistic representation of this herb. Truth be told, this lavender is not on the level of the one found in Caron Pour Un Homme de Caron, but this comparison wouldn’t be far. Not a single fragrance on this planet possesses the quality of lavender oils that Caron does. BASE NOTES Eventually, the fragrance dries down to a dusty, semi-sweet, and warm base. On the web, base notes vary significantly, but what I get is vanilla and tonka beans. The vanilla is smooth, comforting, and slightly powdery, while the tonka (coumarin) adds a sweet almond-hay aroma. This base feels cosy and gourmand, like a warm dessert accord, but thanks to Prada’s ingenuity, it does not venture into whole gourmand territory, and remains barbershop-like. OVERALL In conclusion, Sport is a great, well-rounded aromatic oriental fougère by Prada. A scent that is probably a little bit overpriced, but also a memory-making perfume that, once you decide to buy it, I hardly doubt that you will regret it. 100% recommended! This is the name of the probably most famous aria of the Baroque, from the opera Xerxes by Georg Friedrich Handel. 'Ombra mai fù...' translates to German roughly as: 'Never was the shadow...', and it continues: '...of a plant more lovely and pleasant, sweet.' ('...di vegetabile cara ed amabile soave più.') The object of the aria is the plane tree, which was considered sacred to the people in Xerxes' homeland of Persia - its shadow is so lovely, sweet, and pleasant. Ombra mai fù is playful and melting - and yet from a contemporary perspective (even for advanced opera aficionados) not easy to listen to. For it is sung by a male soprano - in Handel's time actually by castrati, today by countertenors - and anyone who has attended a song recital with male singers performing the upper voice knows how unusual that can be, despite all technical mastery. That 'never a shadow more lovely and pleasant, sweet' would have existed than that of these red woods (of which surprisingly few are listed in its ingredients) would be an exaggeration. Nevertheless, Tom Ford's Bois Rouge - perhaps the least known among the now so numerous Private Blends - is fundamentally akin to Handel's famous aria: playful and melting yet challenging and foreign even for trained noses. Bois Rouge is strangely not a wood scent. And yet it is one. It blends a lovely and sweet, very feminine floral note - lily of the valley and jasmine - with a serious, masculine woodiness, bitter and brittle like tanned leather - expansive and voluminous. As if a large, muscular man in Persian battle armor were passionately singing with a playful soprano about the grace and beauty of the shadow of the plane tree. Conclusion: in my comment on Purple Patchouli, I referred to it as the Blue Mauritius among Tom Ford Private Blends. Here is the Red one.

Just another synthetic mess of vague spiciness, vague woodiness, and vague ambers. By "amber" I don't mean the traditional amber accord of vanilla, labdanum, and benzoin, but rather synthetic amber aromachemicals like amberwood, amber xtreme, ambroxan, etc which in theory try to replicate the scent of ambergris but in reality can't be further. Even though there is sweetness, I don't get any vanilla from Luna Rossa "Ocean." Possibly a bit of vanillin that provides a bit of powderiness way at the end, but it seems like the sweetness is provided by ethyl maltol, which is more akin to cotton candy when there's a lot of it like in BR540, but here it's mixed in with the woody aromachemicals and doesn't stand out on its own. Any grapefruit/citrus note is so fleeting it is hardly worth mentioning. And if you smell frankincense from this fragrance, I'm convinced you've never actually smelled frankincense before. Not sure what they were thinking with this note pyramid. All in all, this is just another collection of aromachemicals that sat on some perfumer's shelf called "generic male scent #18" until they shipped it off to Prada to make it the umpteenth (actually, let's call it what it is, it is even more embarrassing: ELEVENTH) uninspiring flanker of an old, tired, boring line.

I wore this scent through my freshman year of highschool. It remained a sort of holy grail for me all these years later. I bought two bottles, entirely used one, and drained the second down to a few sprays before realizing it was discontinued. Since then, my tastes have shifted, and Midnight Ivy itself is no longer my love. It's the idea. Midnight Ivy is, as all Victoria's Secret body sprays, wrapped in an overly sweet, pink, "perfume"-y patchouli scent. It is soft and reserved in this youthful fragrance. I would describe Midnight Ivy as a blonde scent. It is a synthetic yet comforting blend of vanilla, raisins, rum, and woods. Vanilla dominates, yet blends with the spicier undertones to form a light, silky, feminine fragrance. If this fragrance was reformulated and the Victoria's Secret DNA removed, it would be the perfect gourmand.

Looking for an 'eau de cologne' like fragrance that doesn't smell like 4711 becomes quite a search. It's the Neroli that often takes it over the top ... and while I really love this note when it is treated with respect, it can also become the horror that is Ford's Neroli Portofino. Infusion d'Homme has quickly become my daytime signature in the hot and humid weather I currently find myself working in. The best way to describe Infusion d'Homme is 'fresh and powdery', but these words don't seem to do it very much justice as there is a certain mystery involved here too. I own Infusion de Vetivér also and I must admit to preferring Infusion d'Homme ... a rather strange state of affairs, simply because I have sampled this one often in the last few years and dismissed it as dull and uninteresting. What could possibly have made such a turnaround in my sense of smell? Firstly, I have had some ear problems of late, causing the need for a grommet in my left eardrum. While this has taken care of the medical issue, the amazing thing is that it has also sharpened up my sense of smell. Medical professionals will more than likely sneer at this ... but as far as I know nose, ears and throat all rely on each other to perform the way they should. Now that my left eustachian tube is clear of obstruction and has sufficient drainage again ... my sense of smell is definitely sharper and more refined ... but back to the fragrance! I admit to being a bit of a compliment whore, and love it when those around me compliment my fragrance. I don't think a day has gone by in the past month when someone hasn't turned around and said 'oooh ... you smell wonderful' ... and when I wear Infusion d'Homme I really do. A cloud of clean freshness floats around me, unobtrusive but present ... and outstandingly pleasant!! It's the combination here that is quite magical ... subtle Neroli, smooth Iris, slightly prickly Vetiver ... all grounded by a dash of Frankincence. Yes, it's soapy to an extent ... but it is so much more than that. This is a fragrance that likes heat ... it simply grows and grows and then coasts along for hours. The longevity here was quite unexpected ... but I'm not sure if it will be the same in cooler climes. Time will tell. I haven't had a signature for quite some time ... I'm relatively blown away that it came to me in the unassuming form of Prada's Infusion d'Homme!!

Finally, spring is in the air, and so I dug down deeply in my collection and pulled out Prada's Infusion d'Homme. Infusion d'Homme has the image of being a modern version of a classic orris root fragrance. Indeed, it does not have too much in common with a classic orris gent's cologne such as Mouchoir de Monsieur. Its freshness also discriminates Infusion d'Homme from the contemporaries such as Dior Homme or Divine' L'Homme de Coeur. Orris root is expensive – and Prada may very well have used something else that is providing an iris resemblance. I.e., for their flanker Infusion de Vetiver they dropped the orris note in the pyramid, yet the typical iris smell is still there. Be that as it may, the orris in Infusion d'Homme is not quite as powdery as one would expect. There is no “carrot smell” either that the less well done iris perfumes can have. What strikes me as orris-like has a certain resemblance to the violet candy note in Prada's Amber pour Homme, and so Prada keeps a certain style. Violet and orris may not be too far away from each other for our olfactory sense. The orris-maybe-violet accord in Infusion d'Homme is topped with a nice citrus, but then more or less determines the whole fragrance. It is combined with a very comfortable soapiness and freshness the style of washed and ironed cotton shirts, and a specific green twist apparently denominated as vetiver. Personally, I would not take the known scent pyramid too literally. Possibly, the unique Infusion d'Homme accord does not consist of lots of different notes at all as there is not much development. Infusion d'Homme is quite a unique fragrance. It was popular when it was launched in 2008, and with full right. However, it is not everybody's darling. Some men want something more than freshness and cleanliness in a perfume, and the very slight powder and violet candy note may be irritating. Despite its name Infusion d'Homme will not infuse masculinity where it is missing. I like Infusion d'Homme, and looking at my statistics I have to ask myself why I haven't worn it more often. It is comfortable to wear, on a sunny spring morning where it would reflect the freshness and energy of the new season. As it transports the image of “cleanliness” and optimism, it would work as an office scent - although the less “sunny” flanker Infusion de Vetiver would fit even better there. Infusion d'Homme is not strongly advertised any longer, but I think it is about to become a classic. Other than its predecessor Prada Amber pour Homme there is no scratchy or rough cheap amber note spoiling it, and so the quality is very good. I suppose it is still easily available and so you should not find it too difficult to test it if you don't know it already.

If Heaven had a smell I can say that it could be like this. Flowery, citrusy, extremely clean but a very soft kind of cleanliness. Like the Prada L'homme relative, it's somehow leaning a bit powdery, a bit feminine and however you want to call it. I simply love this one. It is just gorgeous ! L'homme by Prada checks a bit more professionalism as a scent, a bit sharper that may scratch some noses a bit, whereas this one is a lot more casual and a lot more versatile IMO. This is a fragrance for a true collector. Will not impress that many people but it's simply very easy to pull off. It doesn't smell mature or too young either. It's very well balanced. Nowadays it's pretty hard to find it and when you do, the price may be pretty high and maybe it's not the best offer to take in consideration. When you wear this, you are letting the others know that you are enjoying life. It smells like pure happiness. Very bright, very happy, very friendly. Imagine a field full of blooming flowers, the sun is shining and you also feel the freshness of the trees passing you by. A ray of light comes in your way and the air is perfectly well balanced, not too hot not too cold. This fragrance puts me instantly in a better mood. I don't know how but it simply works. Versatility ? Spring & Summer for sure but I cheat and wear it for myself much more, no matter the season. It's the kind of fragrance that cannot offend anyone and can't do any harm. I can say that the age is not a problem. Any age, anytime. Price ? As I said, pretty high now but maybe you can catch a good offer that you won't refuse lol. If you are a fan of this kind of smell, very clean, citrusy and you don't mind a bit of flowery/creamy nuance, you'll definitely enjoy it. If you are smelling more deeply you'll also feel a bit of a luxury aspect here and there in it. Performance ? I have a batch from 2012 and I can't complain. 6-8 hours range with a decent sillage in the first hours. If I apply it after a good shower at night, the next day I can still feel it on myself, after 7-8 hours. Maybe outside it will lack a bit of performance, where the temperature may change more often, also the sun can dry the skin faster but even with 5-6 hours I still can't complain. You know yourself better than anyone, if you are a fan of these kind of smells/fragrances, clean, citrusy, flowery, powdery, I am friendly advising you to try this ! You may end up loving it just like me. Overall : 8.25/10 #clean #luxurious #powdery #friendly #citrusy #soft
