Both Pradas discussed here are decidedly artificial and, in this sense, urban representatives: they do not strive for a nature-close narrative of their ingredients, but rather present their literally refined essence in a very modern context, which may be a bit too stylish for some. One does not have to like it, but one can at least admire it - or outright reject the androgynous result in its almost monothematic powderiness. I like it very much - as well as the straightforward, only slightly curved glass bottle, which fits perfectly into any urban apartment. The longevity is - similar to 'Infusion d’Homme' - neither embarrassing nor outstanding on my skin, while the sillage in both cases is quite elegant: a little more oomph would not be unpleasant for me. Conclusion: My curiosity about the unisex successor in 2015 is definitely piqued, even if I only see one necessity for this reboot - the undeserved discontinuation of 'Infusion de Vetiver'.

I sprayed this fragrance multiple times at the Duty Free during my vacation. Alongside other Pradas, especially Infusion d'Iris and Infusion d'Homme. I always found the top note nice, but compared to the latter two, it seemed a bit weak.

When Prada launched Infusion d’Homme in 2008, it was, in my opinion, the fragrance event of the year - a fresh modern iris scent for men of very good quality, easily available at a moderate price. Now Prada follows up. Recently, Infusion de Vetiver has been released. Since the two fragrances differ only in nuances, I have compared them.

A few weeks ago, I bought Infusion D'Homme blind and I am quite enthusiastic about the simple yet brilliant soap scent, so of course I looked into the similar relatives of the Infusions by Prada. I haven't tested D'Iris extensively yet, but since I like Iris, it could be something for me or at least for my girlfriend. However, the main focus was on Infusion de Vetiver - 1.
What a wonderfully fresh scent! Currently one of my two favorite office fragrances (along with Terre d'Hermes - to which I don't see many parallels; but I don't want to digress).

Infusion de Vetiver presents itself as a departure from the Andriessen soap and powder doctrine, but at the same time takes Prada's "purity law" to the extreme. What touches the skin here is of such clinically clean freshness that you can almost hear dying microbes scream.

Victoria’s Secret, a huge American brand that sells female lingerie, swimwear, clothes and beauty products. Founded in 1977 by Roy Raymond. In Europe, where I live, the first store was opened in 2011 at Schiphol Airport in Amsterdam and a year later in London, UK. I suppose that is why, VS’s products have never been a huge part of my life. But I can see that it is a hit among teenagers, when I pass by the shop at Copenhagen Airport. Maybe I am not that familiar with star fruit either. To me, Such a Flirt! smells like pineapple. Star fruit is not that overwhelmingly sweet, whereas pineapple knocks me out every time. I am mildly allergic to it. When eating anything with pineapple my face, and in particular my lips, start to itch. I do like the smell, though. It reminds me of an ice pop I used to like, when I was a child. A red and yellow mix with a face on the side. Really delicious. Such a Flirt smells exactly like this ice pop tasted. I am not sure that this fragrance is ‘flirty’. I get a very young vibe here, since the fragrance is really linear and not much happens. Gourmand/fruity, yes. A flirt, no. I can recommend if you are a huge pineapple fan. Year 2, 129/365

this is a "Love Don't Be Shy"-flavored LaCroix... if you know what I mean. It's nice, but it's soooooo wispy and musky that I find myself craving more scent. I can think of 4 people in my life who would love this as a signature scent, and if you're a collector of Prada or the Candy line, I think this is an awesome addition. I'll be gifting my mini dabber to my cousin, who'll probably make this her summer scent (she's a LDBS fanatic in the cooler weather).

imagine you've just had a baby. you're nearing your late 30's. and every little bone in your aging, not-active-enough body is wondering why you did this to yourself again after all these years. but you finally get to sneak away for an anxiety-ridden shower, hop out and give yourself a couple of sprays of Prada Candy Kiss, and retire to the couch with your French Bulldogs for the night, appreciating the little bit of even somewhat-quiet time you've got. this fragrance is actual magic and including it in your nighttime routine becomes a necessity. not too fresh, not too sweet, not too powdery, it gives GOLDILOCKS in that it's *just right* i had purchased this years ago due to it's supposed similarity to the scent of MoroccanOil products. when i opened it, i was in heaven because yes, it did smell like that. i don't love musk, but in here...it's ethereal. it's floating. like falling asleep up in the stars; this musk is a cushion of the softest, billowing cashmere cloud keeping you from falling. the vanilla is just sweet enough to remind you that you're a girl and that girls deserve sweet things! and the delicate orange blossom gives it an upscale-dryer-sheet touch to complete the whole thing. she doesn't smell like Tide, Gain, Snuggle--it's probably something fancy, she probably has 'people' who do her laundry for her. it's actually wild to read the simple list of notes and, at least for me, not necessarily be able to smell any one of them separately, though they're all very obviously there. they're mixed into this gorgeous, entirely new smell. which, i guess...is...the...point. lol! in the land of "the opening smells like...," "in the mid you've got...," and "but in the dry down, you're left with..." course of evolution, it's nice to have a nice, safe, predicable, linear scent. but i personally get tired of chasing one phase of a fragrance anyway. AN ABSOLUTE SHAME it's discontinued; no matter how many backups i have, it's just not fair. oh, not to mention, WORLDS BETTER than the MoroccanOil perfume. how you gonna let Prada out-do you on your own product's signature scent lol

The fourth kiss. No, I meant the fourth candy. Candy kiss. Candy Kiss… oh, I’m tired. Of course, I’m tired, because it was yet another little adventure testing this fragrance. Prada Candy belongs to the scents that come in cute, pretty bottles and look colorful and beautiful on the shelves. And as a guy, I have to brave those shelves! So I dressed in all black like a special unit to approach the women’s fragrances (in my head, “something” kept humming the Mission Impossible melody). Suddenly, I realized that I had made a fateful mistake. The aisles are flooded with light, most of the women’s bottles have bright and colorful shades, everything somehow shines. And me in black stands out even more!!! Well, my small stature is still a slight advantage for me. Crouching slightly, I scurry from shelf to shelf and am glad that the candies are in the farthest corner where no one can see me. I approach, look around, have almost reached the Kiss, and suddenly a lady turns into my aisle. Nooo! Never mind, I have to wait. The lady, a bit too heavily made up, comes closer and stops right at the candies. “No, not the candies!” I think to myself, but she reaches for the Angel, which is right above the candies. Almost as expected, she sprays herself for three minutes, all over… I almost want to shout after her: “Lady, you forgot your hair!”. Suddenly, as if she read my thoughts, she stops, I gulp in shock, but then notice that she is just checking the price of the Angel. Yes, yes, the fragrances aren’t cheap, right? And then she grabs the bottle again and gives herself a few more sprays… Never mind, when she finally leaves, I look around one more time, grab the Candy, and spray my arm full. Since I’ve learned from past mistakes and don’t just vanish with a small spray, I spray my whole arm FULL before I make my escape. I occasionally have to hide my dripping wet arm from enemy contact (= women), but I still manage to get a good impression of the scent, which I will now describe: The scent: The scent starts with musk. It is heavy or dark sweet, which also applies to the neroli. Combined, they create a dark, sweet fragrance that smells very pleasant. The Prada Candy DNA is only slightly present and is noticeable mainly through the musk, but Candy Kiss smells quite different from the other Candys. The typical Prada “soapy” note is also only slightly present here (yes, yes, the soap haters can breathe a sigh of relief!). As I said, the Kiss smells darker, not as cotton candy sweet as the regular Candy. And it’s not floral fresh like the Candy Florale either. Maybe Kiss leans a little towards Candy L’Eau, as you can also smell the musk well in L’Eau, but L’Eau is not as dark, rather fresher. A little later, vanilla mixes in, making the Kiss a bit heavier, but like all Candys, it smells excellent. At the very end, the fragrance does acquire a sugary note in the background, but the musk continues to dominate with the vanilla. The sillage and longevity: Despite the dark sweetness, I found the sillage of the Kiss to be rather subtle. The scent will be noticed by you girls, but it won’t leave a large fragrance cloud behind. The longevity didn’t seem very long to me either. It lasts a maximum of five to six hours, but unfortunately not more. The bottle: The bottle is still the same bottle, just in a different color. This time, the color scheme is very successful and looks beautiful in its pink and white tones. The upper band with the golden Prada lettering is white and has gilded edges. The umbrella-like cap or spray head is also white with a golden lower part. All in all, as always, very well done. Like all Candys, you can’t go wrong with the Kiss itself, but you shouldn’t expect a scent that smells like caramel or cotton candy or sugar, as it is more musk-sweet, thus a bit darker, but also more seductive. I wrote that the scent is heavily sweet, but it’s not really heavy, so it can be worn in all seasons, even in (not too hot) summer, and is suitable either as a casual scent or for going out. For partying, I would still recommend the regular Candy, as it smells a bit stronger and significantly sweeter and yummier (and lasts a little longer). The Kiss, on the other hand, is more suitable for seduction, for a date, and such occasions. Well, at least in my opinion. As for me, I think all Candys are absolutely great. All women must smell wonderful with these fragrances. Therefore, I think you should definitely test this scent, as well as the other Candys! Phew, mission accomplished. All Candys have been tested and commented on :D Come on, what are you still reading for? Go test. And give me a kiss if you liked my comment :)

Today, my loyal perfume saleswoman called me to share some offers. Ah - how nice and attentive! From my hasty, scribbled notes, Candy Kiss caught my eye. Oh, it would be worth the rainy trip for that. I really like the Candy, with its fluffy, light caramel sweetness. How sweet would a kiss taste? Arriving drenched in the store, I was immediately hopeful and sprayed. Oh dear - the start is unexpected. A strangely bitter soap mixture approaches my nose, gradually but relentlessly taking possession of it. Could this be the musk? It has always had a smooth, shiny presence for me - but here it seems oddly fragile. Some warmth is conveyed by the orange blossom, but only faintly in the background. Softly but dryly, vanilla joins in - and the scent remains unyielding. No, I don’t want to be kissed like this. As I enter the house, my husband calls out from offstage: It smells like bad soap in here! So the "Do Not Buy" was indeed worth it.

Two things are not really well received on Parfumo: new releases and flankers. What does today's perfume youth have to offer that an Opium or a Shalimar couldn't also satisfy?! Clearly, Candy Kiss has a tough time here. Unjustly. I even think Candy Kiss is a very successful Prada release. With typical Prada DNA. If you take away the caramel from the original Candy, what remains is a fluffy body lotion musk. Many might find that too little. I’m into that:-) I even go so far as to say that right now there are numerous successful new perfumes (Narciso Poudrée, Olympea Aqua) and Candy Kiss is one of them. Even the name, although it is really silly, I find fitting. Candy Kiss is not a loud scent; it is fluffy, soft, skin-like, and as intimate as a tender kiss. I can only smell the orange blossom at the beginning, then the musk takes over. In my opinion, there are no similarities with For Her. Anyone who enjoys clean, intimate, slightly sweet musk scents should give Candy Kiss a chance. Despite the silly name and flanker rage.

Actually, I am neither a fan of sweet scents, nor do I like it when one flanker after another is thrown out by perfume brands, and since I found Candy far too sweet, too sugary, too girly, I paid no attention to the flankers at all. A quick sniff of Candy when it was released made me think that everything that followed could only be a copy of caramel and cream candy.

When I first tested "Candy Kiss" by Prada, I was - in a word - uncertain. Something didn’t sit right with me, yet I found the perfume quite alluring. I was simply torn. So I tested the perfume again in winter; the first trial took place during the summer months.

...in this case! For a long time, I have almost exclusively used perfumes from Armani or Viktor and Rolf as my "signature scents." I would never have considered Prada Candy Kiss due to my usual preferences in perfumes. As a woman, I particularly noticed the hair color of the model in the advertisement for Prada Candy Kiss.

After I was thrilled with "Candy Florale," I couldn't resist trying the Kiss variant - um, yes... I bought it as well... The "Candy Kiss" has nothing to do with the original. While the scent is quite sweet, you will search in vain for caramel.

Thanks to the sharing of a perfume, I managed to get a sample of Candy Kiss. It was a blind buy, as the scent was not available in the small-town turquoise, and I couldn't test it beforehand. However, based on the descriptions here, I took the plunge and was not disappointed. I don't know the classic Candy, so I can't make a comparison to it.

I tried Prada Candy a few times; try as I might, I couldn't smell a thing. So I scoffed at the idea of a l'eau version; how much lighter can a no scent perfume get? Well, I was proven wrong. This fragrance is much stronger, a nice fruity caramel on my skin. I can smell coconut too, but it must be something else in the composition causing such an effect. Longevity isn't all that great, maybe a couple of hours, 3 at most. But this is a light, noncloying fruity floral gourmand and smells of quality compared to other fragrances in the same genre.

I must admit, I fell to the bias of a name and never gave this a try either Prada Candy or Prada Candy L'Eau seems like it was going to be too sweet for me. Well surprise, surprise! This is a smooth powdery opening with a creamy, slightly soapy middle, akin to Dolce & Gabana's defunct "Sicily" but with out that same sickly sweet dry down that ruins the whole Sicily experience for me, personally. Prada Candy L'Eau remains ladylike, glimmering with young exuberance and yet supple, creamy smooth and a little spicy at times. A gorgeous Winter floral scent for every day into night wear that will be both memorable and yet, not overwhelming in its projection. It's been on my arm for about 6 hours and is still very noticeable, yet not too strong. This is not at all cloying as I might have imagined, nor is it childlike or heavy. The dry down is more floral than sweet and more clean musk than sticky brown caramel on me. By now it has melted into my skin and the sillage is about 3-5 inches (7.62 cm) radius off my skin. Pleasant, but not suffocating. Perfect for a night out on the town or an intimate dinner by candlelight. I am going to work through my sample before deciding whether I need this in a larger size, but I must say as someone who frequently finds mainstream fragrances to be overwhelming, I was totally delighted with this soft, feminine powdery creamy fresh scent- it was like opening a box of live butterflies and watching them fly into a clear blue sunny sky- utterly delightful and simply uplifting!

I can't stand this. For me this is, basically, the "fruitchouli" version of Prada Candy. Gone is the animalic benzoin creamy vanillic musky goodness of the original, and in the place of the original's understated sophistication and beauty is this generic patchouli/praline crap that's the basis of so many modern scents today, though I might add that I believe this trend to be, thankfully, coming to an end! Flowerbomb, La vie est Belle, So Elixir, Coco Mademoiselle, Etc, I.E you get the idea. (This genre is not my niche nor my forte.) The best of the Prada Candy range, in my personal opinion, are the original and the "Kiss" variation - which ups the muskiness of the original to dizzying heights, with more nuanced floral notes and a removal of the citrus. Adore.

I bought a decant of this perfume because I love sweet scents, but I wanted something that was a bit lighter to wear while I'm visiting my relatives over the holidays. Unfortunately, this is not at all what I was expecting. The most prominent notes in this fragrance to me are amber and sweet pea, with something vaguely sweet in the background. The longer you wear it, it does become a bit sweeter, but it doesn't smell at all like caramel. It is a nice scent and has grown on me a bit, I do not think it is at all the way it has been described or advertised.

Another scent from Prada's candy line. This time it's L’Eau, which at least by name suggests something lighter or more diluted. And this scent could also divide the ladies into two camps. On one side are the soap haters (what do you actually do when you're in the shower?? Probably bathe with a clothespin on your nose ha ha ha...), and on the other side are those who can distinguish that there are differences between well-crafted scents that are a bit soapy, but therefore also smell clean, and those scents that actually just smell like (cheap) shower gel. Anyway, I would, as so often, recommend both camps to test this scent here, as it smells sweet as always and... is simply a great fragrance. The scent: The fragrance starts off citrus-fresh due to the citrus fruits, but then you immediately smell the very sweet caramel that you know all too well from all the candy scents. The caramel is intense, but seems to be a bit "brighter," by which I mean that the sweet notes appear a bit lighter than, for example, in the regular Candy. In addition, you can smell the well-known Prada DNA in the background, which means something clean and slightly soapy. A few minutes later, you can also smell the musk, and I find that the musk (but also the soapy DNA) in this scent is even a bit more noticeable than in the other Candys, which may be due to the fact that the caramel here feels a bit lighter. Longevity and sillage: The longevity is four to five hours, after which it becomes weaker so that you can only smell it if you go with your nose to the spot. But let's stick with four to five hours. The sillage is not very strong, despite the main sweet notes. But as mentioned in the scent description, L’Eau radiates these sweet notes more softly and loosely, so it doesn't come across as strongly. Perhaps still detectable up close, but by no means strong enough to leave even a scent cloud. The bottle: The bottle is the same as all the Candys, so it's cylindrical with a thick glass bottom. The fragrance liquid is beige (or skin-colored). Just before the umbrella-like spray head, there is again the familiar strip in a darker beige color, where the Prada logo is written in golden letters. The aforementioned umbrella-like spray head has, as always, a golden edge and is black. I find the bottle, as always, very nice, but I prefer the colors of the other Candys. So, as with almost every Candy scent, you can hardly go wrong with this one either, unless you just don't like occasionally occurring, clean-smelling soapy notes. I must admit that I sometimes don't like soapy scents either, it just depends on how they are made, and Prada does it very well, so I have become a big Prada fan (*sigh* the women always have a larger selection of different scents) and therefore really like their fragrances. This Candy is best used as a daytime scent, as it doesn't come across as extremely sweet like the others, so it can also be worn on hot days. However, this makes it the least suitable for going out, as the sillage and longevity are even worse than they already are with the Candys (unfortunately). But, you can always spray yourself several times throughout the day, which I would also recommend, because it really smells wonderfully delicious and cute and sweet and whatever else :D So, go test it! Right now! Or even right away,… just make sure you go test it :D And? Are you going to test it? So, now we just need the Candy Kiss, the brand new one. Oh dear,… I have to go to the shelf where the Candys are, which means that this shelf will be full of pink-sweet-cute colored bottles,… oh no!

How I hate it: You test a perfume, get excited, and then at home comes the disillusionment when you want to write your comment here on Parfumo. Which perfume was it again, or rather which version? It was heavily advertised at Müller, but was it Prada Candy or Candy L'eau?

Candy has good three and a half minutes of film material. Prada (the first Prada fragrance I'm writing about, I just realized, well never mind) has come up with a whole story for this scent, a bit of a crazy affair, but funny. It's subtly reminiscent of "Jules et Jim".

„He’s a sweet-talking sugar-coated candyman!“ Christina Aguilera - Candyman (2009) Who? This candy here? No, he’s more like a box of macarons, contents: 3 pieces. On top lemon (like that icing made by mixing powdered sugar with lemon juice), something like caramel, and finally caramel. But let’s start from the beginning. Where was I? Oh yes, exactly!

I am still completely enchanted by my test fragrance, which I sprayed on during my lunch break at Müller today. It is now half past nine in the evening, and I can still smell it very well, so the longevity is perfectly fine. I actually liked Prada Candy quite a bit, although it was sometimes a little too sweet. However, Candy L'Eau is absolutely delicious!

I really have to say a few high-praising words about this little potion. I don't know the original, not even briefly held it to my nose until now. But Candy L'eau has been accompanying me on every warm summer day this year, and I love it. So stylish, subtle, and at the same time synthetically sweet. This sweetness is delicate and very fleeting.

I am not a fan of Prada Candy, too powdery on my skin. Candy L'eau is better, I don't love it but I do like it. It's lighter and fresher than its predecessor, it's a shame that it was discontinued. Prada Candy Gloss is a solid love for me. It's a complete deviation from the other two that I mentioned. It was a blind-buy so I was understandably nervous but after the first spray hit my body and I got a good whiff of it, I breathed a sigh of relief. I recognized the cherry right away, that's the note that stands out to me in the beginning. It settles on the skin quickly and I can smell the almond and vanilla mingling with the cherry and I have to say, I really do get a "cherry lip gloss" feel from this fragrance and I truly enjoy it. If I didn't know what this was and someone told me that it was a unisex niche fragrance, I would believe them. I can't pick out the rest of the notes because they're so well blended but the overall effect is so pleasing. Not the same by any means but certainly in the same vein as Maison Margiela's Lipstick On (which I also have) but true to its name, it's more glossy and less lipsticky. I find this fragrance different, unique and interesting. No one will be able to guess what you're wearing with this one. Staying power on my skin is good. Three sprays in the morning easily lasts me all day. The Fall-like weather we've been getting in Ontario has been perfect for this scent to really shine. I don't think that it's a safe-blind buy for most people so be sure to try before you buy.

In here= Turkey we have cherry candies and I like eating them. It smells like cherry candy. (Not relate with original. I used to have it in highschool it is more caramel.) On clothes performance is good but I bet on my skin not good. Sometimes it smells unfortunately synthetic, artificial to me. + I like it overall and younger girls must like. Pink is suitable color. If SYRUPY/SYNTHETİC smell no longer in here I would like more. But it is still in my want list :)
Yes, it smells like lip gloss. And it smells like girls that wear lip gloss. I leave you with that thought.

I wanted to love this. The concept of a higher end cherry lipgloss perfume really speaks to me, and I enjoy the original Candy and the musky flanker Candy Kiss. But Candy Gloss doesn't smell like a cherry lipgloss to me, in fact, I don't think of anything glossy when I smell it. I find it rather soapy instead, and I would never put a soapy smelling product on my lips. The sour cherry note is tart, fresh and juicy with just a light sweetness, which I like. A hint of blackcurrant emphasizes the tartness. It's always interesting to try cherry fragrances that were issued before Lost Cherry and all the hype around it, they often do cherry differently from the average cherry perfume of today. Cherry is definitely the most important note in Candy Gloss. Next come orange blossom and musk, adding a clean base for the cherry. I can sense the peach and benzoin, too, but very faintly. I wished they were amped up a bit and made the scent a little warmer. Or as another option, I prefer like it if the musk was a little creamier, like it is in Candy Kiss. The way it is, this is an okay, even likeable scent, but nothing I would really want to smell like and a bit disappointing based on the name and idea behind it.

I blind bought Candy Gloss and was hesitant to spray before bedtime. I sprayed it into the air and walked into the mist to be sure it wasn’t too potent on my wrists. What a lovely scent! The first whiff of cherries made me immediately fall in love. It’s not too sweet. It’s a bit powdery though, and very feminine. I’m always seeking a new cherry perfume that isn’t cloying or migraine inducing. This perfume is absolutely lovely!

Some noses may initially pick up the rose way more than the cherry. Especially if you have ever smelled Bvlgari Rose Essentielle, you'll be able to identify serious similarities between the rose and the berry wine-ness of rose essentielle with what many people perceive in candy gloss as the cherry note!

Candy! Aaaaah, Candy! I love candy fragrances. Well, not to wear them myself, but on you ladies. In any case, I assume that most ladies would look great in them. If I were a perpetual single, I would recommend Candy to my girlfriend. No, I would spray her with every Candy scent from head to toe, that is, from the tips of her hair to the toes of her feet...

I have a new obsession. Cherry Coke. Recently, the sugar-free version has also become available in Germany, and now there's always a case in my pantry. Ice cold from the fridge, in the appropriate Coke glass, maybe with a little ice cube... Wow! I would say that's probably my vice.

With the Prada Candy fragrances, I have developed a love-hate relationship. Sometimes I like them all, and other times I just can't stand them. They often feel too suffocatingly sweet to me. Candy Gloss, however, is not quite as sweet and cloying; instead, it is very beautifully fruity. Candy Gloss starts off very fresh and fruity right away.

Well, perfume or not, this is certainly not one. It is a simple 2-phase body splash that you can spray on your body in generous amounts for a refreshment in between or after a bath. It smells strongly of artificial raspberry and strawberry aroma, and the scent disappears after about 10 minutes. There is no scent development, as expected with 2 "ingredients." It has nothing to do with EdT or perfume at all. I took it out of curiosity once, and now it is languishing in the bathroom cabinet until it eventually gets thrown away. Victoria's Secret hasn't come up with anything special here; maybe they should focus more on designing beautiful lingerie instead. Wishing everyone a nice Monday evening :)

I love this creamy sweet oriental leather. It begins a bit medicinal with the oud and incense then it sparkles on a shiny amber and ends with the sweet creamy leather and a grown up vanilla. It is subtle but long lasting. Pretty serious for a sweet drydown perfume. Pleasurable and chic. I'm really enjoying it, it is very versatile as well. It has a stronger character than Day for Night which is also beautiful but more of an almost transparent chocolated leathery amber perfume. Don't let the notes mislead you, this perfume can perfectly be used in spring and summer as it is extremely polite.

I admit I am a lover of nostalgic spa resorts. I enjoy the charmingly old-fashioned yet well-kept atmosphere, letting myself be transported to times long past, and I indulge the old ladies by allowing them to take their furs, received many decades ago, for a stroll in the spa park once again in winter. Where else would they go with them...? Whether it’s Marienbad, Bad Pyrmont, Baden-Baden, or even the small, somewhat shy Bad Wörishofen just around the corner. The elegance of such places is a bit dusty, and the splendor of past grand festivities is now just a memory. How we young girls enjoyed being invited by our boss to the casino in Baden-Baden after an annual conference, and with a few tokens as play money, we were allowed to test our luck. There were no one-armed bandits back then, and we fascinatedly observed the dexterity of the croupiers, admiring how they kept an eye on the happenings at the tables at all times. We were astonished to learn that the residents of Baden-Baden were not allowed entry to the gambling establishment, so they wouldn’t ruin themselves. Thus, a bit of the mysterious, perhaps even forbidden, charm was part of the nostalgia back then, thanks in no small part to one or two shadows of the course. I am amazed at how well Prada has captured the atmosphere of such places and especially that time with "Marienbad." The scent lays infinitely soft, powdery, and flattering on the skin, pampering the wearer with harmony, silkiness, understated elegance, and a nobility that fits the images I have in mind when I perceive the perfume. As substantial as the pyramid appears, the ingredients seem enveloping and golden after Daniela Andrier has woven them into a precious perfume. The leather is as soft as fine fabric, the incense casts only a dull veil over the whole, amber envelops with warmth and tenderness, and the vanilla holds back with refined restraint. How often these notes are used in a blatant manner, but here it shows how one can handle, for example, oud and amber without the front Orient taking away one’s breath. Simply wonderful. Marienbad does not need to hide behind more famous scents, e.g., from Guerlain. However, a drop of melancholy falls into my cup when I look at the bottle. Yes, it is modern, unadorned, clear, and also beautiful - but it could have adapted a bit to the romance of old spa resorts, even if the heyday of the bathing temples belongs to the past in times of health insurance, rehabilitation, co-payments, and budget cuts. But one is allowed to dream, after all. It’s a pity that the scents from that time are not also protected like the drinking halls and villas of the spa resorts. "Marienbad" at least brings a bit of that magic into the present.

When I saw the announcement of the new Prada fragrance series "Olfactories" here on Parfumo last year, it was clear that some of the 10 fragrances in the series had to land on my watchlist. I really like and appreciate several Prada fragrances (Amber pour Homme Intense, some of the Infusions, and Prada L’Eau Ambrée I now consider almost classics), so I was of course very curious about the new series. * * The Prada website states the following about the fragrances: Prada Olfactories - intense fragrances that transport you like silent harbingers of the unexpected into the surreal world of dreams. As tangible syntheses of the unreal, they convey the essence of mysterious contrasts: the feminine meets the masculine, reality merges with the imaginary, and the mundane becomes precious. The ten different fragrances gently tease the subconscious. These sensory fragments unite contradictions against all tradition and outsmart the mind to bring the fantastic to life.” About Marienbad: A hotel, hovering between the Occident and the Orient. A forgotten memento of an empire that gracefully crumbled: leather-bound volumes await to be devoured along with delicious cakes, black coffee, and a view of the Danube. Marienbad is the scent of a baroque refuge, charming and rich in its uniqueness. (Quote from: www.prada.com/de/fragrance/collections/olfactories) * * Phew, someone really put in a lot of effort to wrap the series and the fragrance in beautiful and intriguing words. Understatement is different, but can the beautiful words do justice to the fragrance? To find that out, there was no way around Prada, or rather, I went directly there. The complete series is presented unmistakably and extensively. The first thing that catches the eye are the large black-and-white boxes. When you remove the white lid, the fragrance "sits" upright in the characteristic black ribbed thick-walled box typical of Prada. It makes quite an impression and gives a more than valuable impression. The bottle itself is made of heavy glass, and the fragrance seems to float in the bottle. The cap is a magnetic closure, like that of Dior, which closes perfectly. The spray head works flawlessly and sprays moderate amounts of fragrance to the desired spots. So far so good, but what good is all the exterior if the fragrance is not well made? And so it came to the first encounter between Marienbad and me. I should mention that I had several Olfactories on my watchlist, all of which were initially sprayed on the corresponding cards (each fragrance has its own test card). Marienbad was the only one that was immediately present and went straight not only to my nose but almost directly to my heart. I can't really discern a proper fragrance progression; all the notes are more or less immediately present, with each note introducing itself visually until ultimately a vanilla-amber-leather-oud-incense mélange forms on the skin. Dark vanilla with bright sprinkles and amber-colored spicy amber merge with the finest glove-soft leather, which has been carefully drizzled with spicy warm oud. The incense brings a bit of dark balance, but it lacks any sacredness. I could swear that there is always a hint of iris in the fragrance air, contributing a certain (very moderate) powderiness. The fact is that Marienbad appears incredibly soft (in the best sense), warm, and noble. Marienbad knows no corners or edges, but appears just as rounded as its cap. Oud and incense lovers who prefer it dark, profound, and a bit "dirty" will explicitly NOT find their satisfaction here. I cannot agree with the description that Marienbad is a sweet oriental. Okay, maybe the oriental part (though it would then be an oriental adjusted for European noses), but an excessive sweetness? No, perhaps sweetish, but leather, incense, and oud ensure that the sweetness does not become overwhelming. I also cannot relate to the listed reference fragrances "Silver Musk" (Marienbad lacks the powdery musk), "Cuir Beluga" (the leather note in Marienbad is different, patchouli is not found), and "Gris Montaigne" (the wonderful rose note is not present in Marienbad). And to return to my initial question: No, the beautiful words of the copywriters could not do justice to the fragrance, as they describe everything except the fragrance itself. But I don't care, because the fragrance convinces me more than all the words. Marienbad is, for me, a dreamlike fragrance that conveys well-being and exclusivity, lasts a very long time (10 - 12 hours), and whose opulence has been so skillfully toned down that one never stands out unpleasantly. On the contrary. I have received such a large number of positive feedbacks on very few fragrances from my collection in such a short time as I have on Marienbad. I could not escape the magic of this fragrance. Marienbad caught me off guard and completely overwhelmed me, but did not leave me disturbed; rather, it embraced and enveloped me, almost merging with me. I cannot expect more from a fragrance, no matter how hard I try. So, anyone who likes/seeks a rounded, warm, soft, and very flattering oriental is strongly recommended to test it. (Small warning: Where there is light, there is also shadow... As exclusive as the fragrance is, the price is unfortunately just as exclusive, as one must lay down a proud 250€ for 100ml EdP on the Prada table.)

Marienbad is a spa town in Bohemia, where sick people sought healing at the healing springs since the Middle Ages, and which has been expanded over the centuries. Due to the unpleasant sulfur smell of the carbonated Marien spring, where a bathhouse was built in the early 19th century, it was also called the Stink Spring. The place became popular when Johann Wolfgang von Goethe regularly took the waters in Marienbad and met his last great love, Ulrike von Levetzow, who rejected his later marriage proposal (he was almost 72 years old, she was just 19 years old), inspiring him to write the so-called "Marienbad Elegy," a melancholic love poem. But many other historical celebrities also visited for treatment. Among them were Frédérique Chopin, Thomas Alva Edison, Sigmund Freud, Maxim Gorki, Henrik Ibsen, Franz Kafka, Friedrich Nietzsche, Tsar Nicholas II, and many more. Today, Marienbad is a quaint little town with just over 10,000 inhabitants, over 40 different healing springs, and many sights, including several Neoclassical baths and thermal spas with cloisters and parks. One wonders what Prada was thinking and how their house perfumer Daniela Andrier implemented the theme for the Olfactories series. The first question probably remains unanswered for now. For the second, I would personally respond with quite pleasant. The result is a fragrance that begins primarily with softly caressing sweet-powdery vanilla, giving the wearer almost the feeling of having landed in a wellness oasis, which likely aligns with the wellness concept of Marienbad. Amber also contributes to a fluffy, cozy atmosphere. However, beneath the cotton-soft powderiness lies a slightly bitter counterpoint with incense, oud, and a hint of birch-tar-like leather. It almost has a slightly medicinal bitterness, but it harmoniously integrates into the overall composition. After all, spa treatments are not just about feeling good around the clock, but also about throwing certain habits overboard with a bit of discipline in the form of workouts, dietary changes, or medical measures to recover or heal. Thus, the concept works, and Marienbad lives up to the name of this perfume as a high-quality substance for well-being and expression of positive energies. Many thanks to my favorite perfumer for the loan :-)

so listless my little soul wings… so powerless sometimes my heart… entangled in the thicket what am I really is everything an illusion where is support You show me a vanilla light wrap me in a protective cloak of incense power strengthen me with styrax at my back lay iris powder at my feet place civet powers beside me For the first time, I am testing a fragrance here where vanilla is prominently listed, and I am even rating it positively. This is a small sensation for me, as vanilla scents usually run the risk of becoming overly sweet and/or musty. Neither is the case here! The notes listed here and on the Prada homepage (Vanilla - Styrax - Incense - Amber) might suggest a rather simple amber scent, but that would be completely wrong. This one is very complex and beautifully crafted, surprising me time and again. Other sources also list additional ingredients that confirm my olfactory impression - I had begun to doubt myself and thought I was imagining them all. This very uncertainty, a certain aimless floating and yet being carried seems to be the theme of this fragrance: a vanilla glow in uncertainty and aimlessness. ----- It begins for me with an amber vanilla that already has a kind of glow at the start and also something very delicate and buoyant citrus-fresh. (I initially thought I was mistaken, but some sources also list bergamot.) Then, as it develops, it becomes denser and deeper, resinous-powdery-sweet. The brightness of the beginning acquires some shadows. I perceive a delicate but very dark leather note, and I also suspect amber with its slight animalic quality, which typically contributes to the theme of darkness/light - as I know it especially from the fragrances of Annette Neuffer. And I would guess that some oud is also involved. Sometimes it reveals itself shortly after spraying, but not always. The slight animalic quality is enhanced by a bit of civet, I am quite sure of that. Here, the fragrance gains vintage qualities with its - yes, should I call it opulence? It is a successful modern and somewhat lighter interpretation of vintage opulence. The incense is present but remains part of this light-dark interplay and does not stand out as a separate note. And I can imagine that the powderiness also involves some iris. So: “Marienbad” is a very complex, very well-made fragrance. The components create a vibrant whole, like different layers that intertwine and continually reveal each other and something new. (I have never engaged with the works of Daniela Andrier - I am only now seeing how many major houses she has worked for. I must look into that at some point.) ----- This fragrance thus has three thematic facets for me: On the one hand, what could be described as baroque or opulent, reminding me of vintage fragrances. On the Prada homepage, it is described as “baroque” and “decadent,” which doesn’t quite capture it for me - rather, it is the aforementioned vintage echoes in a modern interpretation. If one wishes, parallels can be drawn to the bath architecture of the 19th and early 20th centuries, which has been preserved in Marienbad/Czech Republic with the splendor of classicist and Art Nouveau buildings. Secondly, I perceive the theme of the fragrance as the difficulty of objectifying impressions of reality. This is evoked by the bright, floating, misty quality of the beginning, as well as by the interaction of the ingredients, which unfolds anew each time. Here, connections can be made to the film “Last Year at Marienbad” (1961), which addresses the question of what makes my memories of past loves and wounds “accurate.” It is about love, soul depths, confusions, and the questions of what is real and what I truly want. These questions remain unresolved in the film, and the ambiguity persists. Thirdly, it is the light-dark theme that is beautifully realized here. The fragrance begins bright and light, and then the dynamics between light and shadow, between illusion and clarity unfold. Many thanks to @FrauKirsche for the sample and to both of you, dear @FrauKirsche and @Can777, for your beautiful presentations of the fragrance, without which I would not have tried it; that would have been a shame. Now it is on my wish list.

So with this fragrance, I only hear déjà vus... also because I tested Boy by Chanel a bit more intensely yesterday and because in the last 2 weeks, Amber PH from our own house has come into focus due to positive comments. I really liked Amber PH two years ago; I was riding high on a Prada wave, Infusion D'Homme, Vetiver, Luna Rossa, etc.

Thank you, ParfumAholic, for your wonderful words about this fragrance today. Rarely has a comment so precisely captured my feelings for a scent. I'm jumping on the bandwagon and joining in. Marienbad is one of two smashers I’ve experienced in the last few weeks. I’ve already lingered around Prada four times and was kindly introduced to the scent each time.
Ah yes, Prada. Even though I currently only own one Prada fragrance, I am a true Prada fan. I find most of the scents from this brand wonderful, whether for men or women.

First: The title of my review should not create any false impressions. I do not mean to suggest that this is a "grandma scent" or smells like an "older lady." For months, the perfume "Olfactories - Marienbad | Prada" has been calling me to test it.

Today I randomly found a sample of Marienbad and tried it immediately. In the first few seconds, it smelled like being at the doctor's for a flu shot. Oh dear! Oh no! That must be the oud! But after a few seconds, that biting smell faded away, and warm leather began to spread on my skin - a shot of amber added and seasoned with vanilla...

When I tried Infusion de Tubéreuse shortly after it's release the year before last I thought 'Meh ... why bother?'. You see, I have come to the realization that my nose was a bit immature back then ... not attuned to picking out the subtle nuances of well crafted fragrances such as this one. Back then, Tuberose was all about Fracas and Carnal Flower! I wanted them bold and elephantine (and I still do!), so this little gem didn't stand a chance. Happily, the education of my nose has continued to the point where my recent purchase of Infusion de Tubéreuse has come as a bit of a revelation. The phrase 'less is more' is bouncing around in my head as I write this ... I don't think I really understood that until now. Infusion de Tubéreuse is all about this most precious of all flowers in youthful bud. The flowers are still slightly green and only just opening, hinting at the immense power that is to come. I also love Petitgrain ... and this fragrance is full of it. To get all 'head-spacey' for a second, some of the main constituents of petitgrain oil are geraniol, linalool, linalyl acetate, and terpineol ... the first two of which are found in pretty much every bottle of fragrance out there! I have, of late, also become acutely aware of the odor of terpenes (for those of you who have ever painted anything just recall the smell of turpentine) and this is relatively present here too. Chemistry lesson almost over ... I do find it strange (and a little facetious) that Dynamone is listed as a main ingredient. A little bit of research leads me to believe that this is simply an 'attention-getting' way of describing Labdanum (the resin from Rockrose or Cistus Ladaniferus) which is also present in a big chunk of perfumes today. It is apparently a wonderful fixative, which simply means that it holds faster evaporating molecules together longer, thereby enhancing their longevity on the skin, vis-à-vis the Petitgrain in this fragrance ... which is generally a fast evaporating top note. As soft as the Tuberose in this creation is, it's definitely present ... but there is also a delightful soapiness here, as there is in all of the other Prada Infusions I have tried. If you've tried Infusion d'Iris just imagine it with a very slight 'white floral' shadow ... and you'll have Infusion de Tubéreuse. Yes, it's similar ... but it's also quite unique. Longevity here quite substantial at about 5 hours and the sillage adequate, but not immense. Infusion de Tubéreuse sticks beautifully to clothing, providing gorgeous little wafts when one is in motion. As a die hard fan of the heaviest Tuberose fragrances, I'm happy to report that I find a great deal of joy in wearing this Daniela Andrier creation. This is a Tuberose fragrance for those who find the white floral bombs intimidating. Highly recommended!

It opens really bright and sparkling with the Blood Orange and Petitgrain. Very much like Fleur D'Oranger with it's Neroli and Orange Flower which I love. Then it has a brief spell of sticky sweet Labdanum in the centre of the transformation which quickly subsides to the dry down which I'm not so keen on. It's fresh and aldehydic. But a bit Hairspray /Shampoo esq must be the watered down tubereuse.

Wonderful light citrus tuberose, very subtle and elegant. It is a joy to wear it on warm days specially if you layer it with the body lotion. I really like it very much, it is contained , reserved, fresh and I love the light labdanum note. I tend to like Daniela Andrier compositions, I find them usually at least interesting and not repetitive. The only inconvenient of this one is it works as a edc on my skin so I need to apply substantially and I keep myself from using it too much as it was discontinued... Please Prada, bring this one back, it was one of your best ones.

I quite like this fragrance, however I must admit it took awhile to grow on me. Prada Infusion de Tubereuse is a lot fresher than I expected it to be. Most tuberose scents tend to be creamy and heavy, whereas this particular fragrance focuses on being light and crisp. It certainly wears well in hot, dry weather where this fragrance really has its chance to shine. The tuberose is subtle and fresh, further complimented by a rich blood orange note which adds a citrusy touch. The opening is mostly watery and inoffensive. The scent also stays relatively close to the skin, which is nice. It doesn't smell like a typical white floral, in fact, it tends to be much cleaner than flowery. I quite like the way it develops on the skin although it's a tad linear. The heart is a beautiful tuberose in all its glory with only the slightest hint of natural sweetness. Unfortunately the longevity is not all that great. I'm rather disappointed that it didn't last more than two hours on my pulse points. The drydown is so faint that I could barely detect the white woods base which was a little disappointing to say the least. I enjoy Infusion de Tubereuse but I save it for days when I feel like it. I wore it to my Grandmother's funeral recently and I felt that its subtlety and simplicity suited the occasion well.

This was a nice surprise! I didn't expect to like it, but as it turns out I love wearing Infusion de Tubereuse. It's definitely dominated by tuberose, but nicely blended with oranges and petit grain. This makes it a light (but not overly light) and easy to wear scent for spring, summer and fall. I'm usually not very fond of tuberose and I'm normally not a light scent lover, but I absolutely dig this one. Another plus is that it's so different from the other scents in my collection. Sillage is average and lastingpower is also average. About 3 hours.

I like tuberose scents IF they are not so "tuberosy" that they bore me and/or give me a headache. I also like powdery and orangey; but again: not too much please! Infusion de Tubereuse is not a 'TuberoseBomb'. It's also not a citric scent. Instead it's much, much better. It's a perfect mix of all the above!

Prada INFUSION DE TUBEREUSE may be the tuberose perfume for people who hate tuberose. It's really a very odd fragrance in that it offers an airy, transparent interpretation of tuberose which is completely at odds with most other tuberose perfumes. Basically this is the antithesis of FRACAS or BLONDE.

I'm an anti-white-flower gal. Orange blossom and tuberose almost always smell terrible to me when I'm wearing them, and jasmine usually does. They have a high-pitched screechiness to them that I find about as comfortable as chewing on aluminum foil. But sometimes there are surprises.

And once again, I am in the process of testing a Prada fragrance that I received from a lovely perfumer here (thanks again for that!). Well, this brings me a step closer to my goal of testing all the Infusion scents, and I don’t have to be sad afterward, as another fragrance has even been announced for this year (Infusion de Mimosa), which I am also very curious about.

I love Infusion d'Iris - why haven’t I gotten it yet - and I really tried to like Infusion de Tuberéuse. Unfortunately, it doesn’t like me, and so we haven’t become friends. Many thanks to Igraine for allowing me this experience.

After I received a miniature of Nue au Soleil, which was included in a swap package by a dear perfumer (Violett, if you’re reading this, you made me incredibly happy with that), I became aware of the Olfactories series by Prada. Nue au Soleil bears a strong resemblance to Infusion d' Orange, and in the reviews of Purple Rain, I read that this fragrance is similarly related to Infusion d' Iris. Purple Rain indeed has a great similarity to Infusion d' Iris. However, the scents are different. Purple Rain starts off warm, soft, rounded, and flattering, whereas Infusion d' Iris begins much more austere, citrusy, and somewhat herbal. Perhaps this is due to the galbanum present in the top note of Infusion d' Iris. In the heart note, the two fragrances become more similar; Infusion d' Iris becomes softer, less scratchy, yet it still smells greener and more herbal compared to Purple Rain. Purple Rain is much gentler, more flattering, and remains so until the dry down, with a very linear progression. Unfortunately, the sillage is really not outstanding, and the price is quite high. Considering the similarity to Infusion d' Iris, many will likely opt for the more affordable fragrance. Nevertheless - I have fallen in love with this scent, and it is definitely going on my wish list! Delicate, silky cuddling with an addictive factor... who wouldn’t want that? ;-)

Purple Rain and Infusion d'Iris smell alike, many say. Exciting... Since I love Infusion d'Iris, I had to test both fragrances, of course :-) Together! On the left, two sprays of Purple Rain and on the right, two sprays of Infusion d'Iris. Lo and behold, they are indeed closely related yet different. No big surprise for me, BUT: Purple Rain: Starts creamy-buttery and remains creamy-buttery throughout. The scent is less citrusy and less spicy. Purple Rain is denser and softer. It feels refined, stylish, and elegant. With its straightforward progression, it has something mature about it. I wouldn't want to call the scent conservative, as that sounds negative at this point, but it has a timeless quality. This is exactly how I envision my elegant-fresh iris scent. For me, one of the best iris interpretations from Prada. Infusion d'Iris: A lovely everyday scent, a go-to, feels sportier and uncomplicated. Starts citrusy and remains more citrusy and spicy throughout. Jeans on, T-shirt over it, and out. At one point, I caught the two relatives meeting in their similarities, only to go their separate ways again. Although I have loved Infusion d'Iris for a long time and rated it a full 10 points, if I had to choose, I would take Olfactories - Purple Rain. But I will stick with both ;-)

no powder cloud that suffocates you, nothing metallic, fortunately I don't smell any neroli, and the vetiver stays very much in the background. Much more likely, there could be a few violets subtly participating. Beautifully creamy and soft. The scent slightly reminds me of Lilac Love. Enchanting and delicate iris, just how it should be.

I believe this line from Prada doesn’t get enough love from the perfume community. The hype goes to the beast mode fragrances, and so something as chic and elegant as this line gets ignored (well, sort of, as I think this is quite the popular line). I love it, it’s like bathing in vanilla water, it’s a perfume that whispers and doesn’t scream, and the vanilla that comes out of it it’s a true vanilla pod, almost dirty (reminds me of ylang-ylang) and I absolutely adore how they were able to create such a delicate scent while maintaining that DNA that usually is quite strong. I believe this is a perfume (a line) perfect for the book lovers, for the quiet people, those who enter a room without announcing they’re there and after a while their comforting aura is there. Beautifully executed, I love to wear it after a warm shower.

Smells like Vanilla Sex with a nice helping of Coty Airspun powder at the end. If you're a movie fan, VS is the scene from Pearl with the scarecrow and this is the scene from X with the homeowners. I got it from a Sephora sampler set and I think it's the angelica seed that's giving it that screechy powdery old lady smell. In fact I find the vanilla is barely detectable underneath that after just a few minutes. Definitely will not be redeeming the voucher on a full size version of this. Will probably be scrubbing this off of my wrists in the next few minutes.

All the Infusions by Prada are so clean, understated and elegant. I thought Infusion d'Amande was the sweetest, most playful one out of the bunch, but that was before I tried Infusion de Vanille. It's such a cute scent, it feels much less serious and also less soapy than the other Infusions. Don't get me wrong, it still has a powdery texture and feels clean, and it's definitely not a super-warm and gourmand kind of vanilla. It even has a cooling aspect and a green, anisic opening due to the angelica. But it also kind of smells like a vanilla scented plastic doll from the 90s. In the best possible way, I love dollskin-like scents! And this one is not too overly sweet, maybe because there are no fruity or foody notes to compete with the vanilla. So, this feels very feminine to me, in a soft, fluffy, pastel-colored way. The brown coloring of the bottle feels very off, literally anything from baby blue to yellow to soft pink or mint would have felt more fitting. I guess because Prada aready used these colors for other Infusions, there was nothing better than brown left for their vanilla. Even though my description might make this sound very girly, I actually think it's a versatile scent that can easily be worn for work or whatever occasion. Not only because I think we should not hide our feminine side, but also because it still carries enough of the Infusions-DNA to come off as clean and understated. Just with a little sweet twist.

I recently had the chance to test Infusion de Vanille by Prada. I applied it with joy, without noticing at first glance that it was vanilla. The bottles are familiar from, for example, the Iris, etc. What immediately hits the nose is the pleasant vanilla; it is sweet, creamy, slightly powdery, and distinctly noticeable. Paired with a light acidity from the citrus fruits, it creates a wonderful combination, especially for spring. In summer, it might be a bit overwhelming. As time goes on, the scent hardly changes; the vanilla remains clearly detectable. A hint of musk joins in. I find the longevity to be good personally. However, the sillage seems a bit disappointing. I can perceive the scent distinctly for several hours, but my companions (who always notice everything) hardly smelled it at all. All in all, a great everyday scent if you like sweet vanilla.

I like almost all of VS. But Romantic Wish has something that puts the others in the shade; unfortunately, it's very hard to get. Here in Germany, it's hardly available, and in the USA, the price has risen quite a bit for this rather rare specimen. But the perfume itself smells amazing... it leans towards sweet and fruity at the same time... I can only recommend it to anyone who insists on something unique.....!

It's a little sharp and green in the opening with the Mandarin, Neroli and Galbanum but also fresh. Then it dries and mellows into a beautiful creamy , powdery and pungent Rosie soap with a little peppery edge. Very feminine and soft

Another wonderful infusion by Prada: I was expecting the classic rose , instead I smelled a wonderful and very classy bouquet with citrusy and powdery accents . Very refined, modern and pleasant. Soft and elegant as a silk shirt .Recommended for classy women of all ages. The price is very high, but the quality too.

Infusion de Rose is a beautiful, subtle tribute to the rose in its purest form. It’s fresh, light, and natural, without the heavy sweetness often associated with floral scents. The fragrance evokes the image of roses in a quiet garden, their delicate scent gently filling the air. This isn't a perfume that leans toward edible or overly perfumed roses. Instead, it’s serene and refined, perfectly matching its name. As someone who’s always adored the rose, it’s hard not to be enchanted by its simplicity and elegance.

… but I exceed the character limit. Starts off a bit too much like potpourri but after 30 minutes the dry down is divine. I was expecting some of the powdery iris which I love from l’Homme & iris cedre, but it doesn’t have either to my nose. Quite feminine. I think I could still pull it off as a man, but I wouldn’t feel like wearing it often enough to justify a purchase. Can’t stop sniffing my arm though.

What a wonderful, clean, and fresh scent, my clean girl heart skips a beat. No trace of stuffiness, heaviness, or being outdated. Not a complicated or complex fragrance. I like simple scents; long lists of numerous fragrance notes rather scare me off. And yes, it does have a soapy quality, but nothing sharp. Soft, clean, freshly showered and moisturized. Nothing pokes or clashes. Longevity is fantastic on me; I can still smell it after 12 hours. Sillage is hard to say; I find it quite "non-perfumey," as it simply smells super clean and freshly washed. It works anytime, day or night, in any season. Listed as unisex, but I can hardly imagine it on a man, especially since the bottle with its gentle pink is rather typically feminine. But of course, everyone should wear what they like.

In my mid-20s, I wasn't as obsessed with fragrances as I am today. Free samples were enough for me for the whole year. And no scent ever really caught my interest; there was never an “wow” or “oh no,” even though I often tested several perfumes in the perfumery. A signature scent, a few samples, and that was it.

Another member of the Prada Infusion line. There was already an Infusion de Rose in 2011, this one is a reinterpretation from 2017. A clean, fresh rose. Not a sweet, heavy rose; the mandarin directs it. Soft and fresh, galbanum also contributes to the freshness, which can smell woody and balsamic, but that is not the case here.

The sky is blue, except for a few fluffy white clouds, and the sun gently streams through the window of my bathroom. I notice with satisfaction how my body care products harmonize in their shades of pink. Well, that is certainly because they all share a common scent note: pink roses; those young, fresh, juicy ones. With spring, my desire for this note has awakened.

I absolutely love this line of Infusions from Prada and almost all of them smell a bit like the signature Iris scent but I did not detect any of the signature iris here. All I get is a strong and dry, duty , sour fig with no sweetness to balance it out. Maybe it's my chemistry or maybe this is a dud. I have other fig scents that work much better on me. Although in all fairness I am not a huge fan of fig, my favourite is the Rosabotanica by Balenciaga.

Infusion de Figue captures the essence of a fresh fig, soft but not sweet, velvety yet never heavy. Far from jammy or dried fruit accords, it retains the green crispness of its leaves, carried by an aromatic breeze drifting through the fig trees. Everything feels airy, luminous, and effortlessly elegant. A sensory journey that paints the fig with grace and sophistication.

Ah Prada, you and I took a little while to warm up to each other. I actually didn’t want to buy blindly anymore... And I was probably only so patient because I love your sister Infusion d'Amande so much and your bottles look so wonderful together. So I gave you time. And now: Je ne regrette rien Yes, it’s true, Infusion de Figue is such a different fig than one might know from other fragrances. But that’s what makes it special for me. I understand that it may not resonate with everyone. I had my difficulties with the Prada fig at first. During the first testing, the spark just didn’t seem to ignite. Even when I first wore it, I was still uncertain. But somehow, the scent quietly crept into my heart. Since then, I reach for it incredibly often. So often that I have to force myself to use another fragrance from my collection. The scent starts off zesty, fruity, with a wonderful mandarin. The mandarin quickly becomes sticky and resinous, and then the fig makes its appearance. The fig also wallows in the same resin, a wonderful symbiosis of the specified mastic resin and galbanum. Prada manages to be spring-fresh through the combination of mandarin and fig while still providing a warmth that is incredibly special. When it’s still bitterly cold in the early morning, the scent warms me. When the sun shines and the thermometer climbs to a spring-like 18 degrees, it refreshes me. Infusion de Figue is not a green fig. It is fruity, resinous, and becomes wonderfully creamy in the dry down. It doesn’t disturb anyone, as the notes harmonize beautifully together. This creamy Infusion DNA is clearly recognizable. Nevertheless, it is a standalone scent with many unique features. Longevity and sillage are not particularly remarkable. Those who read my reviews know that I have skin on which everything holds well. However, I do actually spray this one again in the afternoon. Maybe just because I want to smell it in full force again. Fig lovers should definitely try this one, but it’s best to erase all their expectations beforehand and fully immerse themselves in this beauty.

Prada's Infusion de figue is the new fragrance from the Infusion series. I have been wearing Infusion d'Iris for years and love fig scents. For me, these are perfect for late summer / September. The heat has eased, and you no longer need the maritime freshness, Portofino, and mandarins; fresh scents are still suitable, but in a milder and creamier way. This fragrance smells very similar to Diptyque's Philosykos. Leather fig, but not heavy saddle leather, rather fine Röckl gloves. Fresh, soapy, green stems. Yet a bit fruitier than Diptyque, which leans towards a bitter green direction. In the drydown, more fig and less fruit. Galbanum with balsamic notes clears the way. In any case, here too, a green, unripe fig. The nose behind it: Daniela Roche Andrier. Other good fig fragrances: Mancera Fig Extasy or Bdk Gris Charnel. Unisex; if I absolutely had to decide, this fragrance would be masculine, but only for a young city boy. Perfect for the office. In the end, the scent becomes velvety and elegant, elevated; it would be worn by a well-groomed woman over 50 who wants to smell refined but not outdated. Projection is good, longevity is medium.

The first spray opens powdery and soapy. Normally, I perceive soapy as clean and well-groomed, but in this case, it smells unpleasant and makes me think of "old lady." The fig is only faintly sensed if you know the fragrance pyramid. For the first 15 minutes, I find the scent unpleasant and outdated. So, apparently, this fragrance is super divisive and there are three, equally numerous groups of people: 1 – OMG, this is heaven in a bottle, can’t get enough of it! 2 – Fruity, pleasant, nothing special... 3 – Please ban the use of this god-awful thing in public, it burns my sinuses and physically chokes me. And I kinda see all of this. I feel the passionfruit the most, and a bit of pear and peach. I agree with the “fruity” and “tropical,” and it should be delightful, but I cannot say that I 100% enjoy it. Something about this one does sit at the back of my throat and deep in my sinuses like hairspray I carelessly inhaled while fixing my do. It’s like no matter how much I use, it’s always too much. It even tingles my tongue like when you eat too much pineapple. This sensation subsides within 4 hours, then it’s indeed soft and pleasant. Despite seemingly inoffensive notes, it’s bold and commands attention – sometimes compliments, sometimes dirty looks. Two things are certain – you won’t confuse this with anything, and it’s a super unsafe blind-buy. Something about the mix of the notes in this makes a portion of the population physically uncomfortable – borderline allergic. By the way, learned about this fragrance from a colleague who suffers every winter, when Kirke becomes popular where I live. She has a violent gaging reaction, and not only to the original Kirke, but to all sorts of imitations and dupes. This drives me to a conclusion that the cause is exactly the combination of notes, not specific ingredients that the Tiziana Terenzi house uses. Anyway, sample this before purchase!

TLDR - if you’ve seen comparisons to Erba Pura convincing you they’re extremely close to one another as I had, and avoid one or the other, sample them both and let your nose be thy guide. My nose tells me that while they share a loosely similar dna, they are VERY different and unique from the other. Close and sharing a similar dna in the first few minutes, and the more time passes the further apart they become such that several hours in and with both still quite noticeable I’m almost willing to say I don’t even pick up on a similar dna any longer. Both winners in my book with Kirkè seeming far more tropical, shimmering and summery and with powdery nuances in the deep dry down, where Erba Pura feels like a warmer silkier base with much less dominance by fruity notes and the amber and vanilla driving this one with fruity notes being distant supporting notes after 30 or 45 minutes. Where Kirkè strikes me as tropical, Erba strikes me as more apt for spring with extremely different textural qualities. I don’t necessarily reserve certain frags for certain seasons, and if I had them both, where now I do wish I would have picked up Erba Pura when I had the chance to do so at a price so low it would feel criminal… I likely would generally tier them out as Erba for spring and Kirkè for summer. Sure, similar in the opening for a few minutes, but the similarities for my nose just about end there. A couple times a year on hot summer days I reach for Kirkè and I’ve always enjoyed it. Tiziana Terenzi fragrances were some of the first I hit my head on when I tripped and fell into the niche rabbit hole and I must admit I’ve been a fan of the brand / Paolo Terenzi as a nose / perfumer ever since. I’ve often seen people refer to him as essentially a clone fragrance maker but my nose has just never seen it that way. Instead, my nose has seen it much in the same way my ears can hear a song witten in the same key with the same chord progression, but a different beat and lyrics reveal an entirely new song. Sure there perhaps may have been some level of inspiration, or perhaps not, but the end products are vastly different. This morning I realized I had a sample of Xerjoff’s Erba Pura perfumed by nose Chris Maurice, but had never done a side by side. I felt inspired to do so, to answer that similarity question or whether Kirkè seemed like a clone to my nose as I’ve seen alluded to or outright claimed on many occasions. For the first few moments I pick up on strong similarities, but within 5-10 minutes they become vastly different fragrances to my nose. They both open quite fruity, but Kirkè, after those first few moments hits my nose as a much more tropically inspired creation. I tend not to categorize fragrances by seasons, but where many do, I can see Erba Pura as a spring whereas Kirkè is more apropos for summer. Rather than seeing them as quite different and thus no “cloning” of a fragrance, I can concur with the notion they share a similar DNA while being quite distinctively different. While I often do associate bergamot, lemon, and Orange with fresher / more apt for summer fragrances, the opening in Kirkè with peach, pear, passion fruit, black currant, and raspberry create a much more “summery” feel to me. I can see how some may associate it with a more “feminine leaning” vibe, however, with male audience targeted fragrances over the last several years becoming more and more sweet and fruity, and my nose just having become accustomed to things I likely wouldn’t wear 10 or 20 years ago, this to me is unisex right down the line. Perhaps the very most noticeable differes my nose picks up on is textural in nature. It seems to my nose, while both fragrances list musk and vanilla as notes, I believe the mix of vanilla and amber makes Erba Pura feel “warmer” which is why it strikes my nose as one, should people be deadset on fragrances based upon seasonality / temperatures, Erba would strike me as more of a spring than summer, for the warmth it exudes comparative to Kirkè. Several hours into my wearing of one on the back of each hand with very frequent sniff checks, Kirkè has retained a very tropical feel where the passion fruit, Lily, clean musk, and sandalwood have become the dominant players, with the zing of passion fruit and I’ll call it a sparkle from the raspberry really setting the tone. At this juncture Erba has become more ambery and vanillic with the “fruit basket from the Mediterranean” mid and very minor lingering of citrus sort of dancing off in the distant background. My nose doesn’t pick up on the “warm sand” accord, or much in the way of vanilla and patchouli, as these seem to minor supporting players that I'm sure if removed would alter the end product fragrance but I’m just not picking them up. The further into the dry down, the more prevalent the heliotrope becomes, through it comes through as making the tropical vibe have a powdery quality. All in all, while I don’t own a bottle of Erba Pura, and on a couple occasions when I was adding to my collection, almost did that very thing, I do wish to someday add it. It’s quite pleasant and to my nose is a standalone fragrance with minimum comparison to Kirkè. That being said, I love Paolo’s works as much as ever, feel reassured once again that he does his own thing with the end products being quite unique comparative to those his works get compared to, and Kirkè is a tropical summery gem in my collection. I have been trying to be more diligent with making sure I frequently rotate my fragrances such that they all receive wearings and love and as such I was going to go mow the lawn, and then spray something entirely different than either of these on for the rest of the day after I shower… particularly since Kirkè made the rotation not all that long ago, but I’m enjoying the passion fruit dominant tropical feel so much, Kirkè is going to get a full wearing for all of today as I head out a little later on.

Hello dear community, after my last test/comparison between Algemar... and Aoud BlueNotes was so much fun, I have now started a new project. As with Aoud.. I wanted to check for myself whether the two fragrances are really as similar as described by some previous speakers. To clarify, I am not a perfume expert, but I deal with scents and vapors in my profession. Fragrances are a hobby for me, NOT a profession. I finally got both fragrances. I conducted two tests, one on longevity and one on the fragrance itself. The starting conditions were as follows: Start of the test at 7 AM. Weather: Windy, cloudy, humidity 66%, 12 degrees Celsius outside, 22 degrees Celsius inside. Tester: me, male Helpers: 3 voluntary, 2 involuntary Div.: Neighbor's dog named Balduin Comparison 1. The name: Aventus Creed: nice name, rolls off the tongue easily, somewhat edgy and assertive. Orion Tiziana Terenzi: sounds like the beginning of an Italian poem. With 3 voluntary testers, vacation feelings immediately arose. The wagging of the dog's tail was always the same when the names were mentioned. Comparison 2. Bottle: Aventus: beautiful shape, great logo with a rider, appeals to me as a man. 2 voluntary testers agree. Orion: not a particularly striking bottle shape, nice cap with moon phases, initially a bit boring for me as a man. Could also pass as a cream jar for women. 2 voluntary testers share the same opinion. Ps: the dog didn’t care. Comparison 3. Sillage: Almost equal. On my skin, a slight edge for Orion. 3 voluntary testers and 1 involuntary tester (neighbor) also found this. The dog apparently didn’t care. Comparison 4. Longevity: Aventus: hardly perceptible after 6 hours, completely gone after about 8 hours. Orion: after 8 hours, only a shadow of its former self, but still perceptible the next day. Comparison 5. Fragrance: Spray and go. Very different starts. Aventus: fresh, light pineapple, citrusy. Reminds me of pineapple on lemon ice. Orion: slightly citrusy, strong sweet pineapple, light apple note. Reminds more of pineapple-sour apple compote. ..after 15 min Aventus: becomes fresher, clearer, cooler. Orion: very fruity, slightly sweet but softer, rounder, gentler than Aventus. 3 voluntary testers agree. The dog reacted to Aventus with tail wagging and brought his ball for Orion..!? ...after 30 min to 1.5 hours Aventus: slightly piercing, somewhat woody and mossy, probably from the oak moss ^^ Orion: now the birch comes into play, gently balsamic ^^ Two completely different fragrances! 3 voluntary testers and 1 involuntary tester (postman) also found this :D The dog is sleeping.... ...after 1.5 to 3 hours Both become weaker. Strangely, now both smell very similar, no extreme distinctions to be detected. 3 voluntary testers and 1 involuntary tester (neighbor) also noticed this. The dog doesn’t come anymore when you call his name... :D ...after 3 to 5 hours Now there is some movement again. Of course, both are now a bit weaker, Aventus more than Orion. Aventus: now you can also detect some vanilla. Orion: a nice harmonious oud-incense "scent" in the background. 1 voluntary tester also found this. The rest of the testers just say "smells good," so no longer evaluable. The dog is gone. Somehow he looked happy when his owner picked him up. ?!? ...everything after 5 hours Now nothing changes anymore. Individual scent components are gradually fading. Aventus: retains its freshness until the end. Orion: retains its fruitiness until the end. Well, a comparison is difficult. I could compare it to football players. Carlos vs. Messi Aventus = Roberto Carlos. Small, powerful, but known and notorious for his rough style and extremely hard shot. Orion = Lionel Messi. Also small and powerful, but much more sensitive with the ball and has better overview. Or comparison, Hulk vs Thor Aventus = Hulk. Superhero, strong, hits everything, breaks everything. Orion = Thor. Also a superhero and strong, hits hard and breaks things, but with more overview and only what is necessary. Much more elegant. I hope I was able to convey my comparison well to both men and women. I had a lot of fun again and it was very interesting, also for all testers and the dog. See you... Thank you for your time.
