First of all - I can definitely understand all the negative comments. The scent is relatively synthetic, not particularly creative, especially since there are similar counterparts like Foconero, Fierce, and Percival, and it is probably overpriced as well.

It is a bit sad for me to say, but unfortunately this fragrance is a flop. To get straight to the point, it is completely unbalanced and lacks any real harmony. The alcoholic note has a somewhat medicinal-salty quality that does not suit this scent at all. It is a jumble of aquatic and herbal notes that are not balanced enough to be pleasant to wear.

I tested the fragrance for the first time a few months ago while on vacation. I was actually very positively impressed. I liked both the opening and the drydown. Now I have procured a decant. I was really looking forward to smelling the fragrance again. A few days later it arrived. Unpacked with great anticipation and sprayed on….. Disillusionment.

As a confessed Terenzi lover, I must also bring out the negative side here... So far, I have liked all the fragrances I have tested from this brand. I haven't gone through all the scents yet, especially not at these prices, but a certain fondness for this brand is hard to deny. However, I cannot quite understand what this fragrance is supposed to do, and I solidarize with a number of rather negative reviews. It is not uncommon to find that Terenzi does not feature all the fragrance components listed in the pyramid, and this becomes particularly evident here, in an unpleasant way. Tyrenum, whose name is inspired by the city of Apulia, which is now called Trani (formerly Tyrenum). The city of Trani is known by the saying "the beauty that looks out to the sea". The reason for this is the orientation of all monumental works, which are consistently directed towards the sea and occasionally reflect in it. The beautiful image cannot be captured or preserved by the fragrance in any way. The feeling of a coastal scent, which one presumably wanted to achieve with the limestone, does not materialize. I do not perceive any real minerality. Instead, one receives an overly sweet, artificially appearing, poorly balanced, and hardly discernible freshness that is supposed to resemble an ocean, more like a puddle. In a statement, it says that bergamot beats caramel; I would express it similarly, just the other way around. Caramel beats bergamot. And not a fine, gourmand caramel, no. Rather a sweet slush that splatters an almost indefinable, synthetic, and uncharming sweetness. I rarely make comparisons, but this cloud of scent could also be found on the lower shelves of a drugstore. As it develops, a bit of salt joins in, quiet maritime notes. Bringing that into harmony with the sweetness is not so easy. Longevity and sillage are in the moderate middle range. However, there was not much interest in letting it linger on me longer. Terenzi? You can do much better!

Tyrenum or today Trani, a beautiful city by the Mediterranean. This fragrance owes its name to it, and rightly so. Dolce Vita, summer evening, sweet scents wafting from the patisserie on the corner, it smells of caramel and orange mixed with the cool aroma of the limestone houses. From the harbor, a pleasant sea breeze sweeps over the bustling terraces of the cafes. Before night falls, a tea with mint. Tyrenum, not to everyone's taste but worth a try.

Sirrah opens for me with a wonderfully fruity freshness that also carries a hint of soap. One would want to indulge in a whole bath of it right away. Despite the elegant cleanliness, the fragrance also has a sensual quality that makes it absolutely wearable for men. Especially on hot summer days, Sirrah showcases its strengths: The fruity floral, slightly sweet note remains present for a long time without ever being overwhelming. The sillage is distinctly noticeable without becoming too loud, and the performance is, as is often the case with Tiziana Terenzi, more than solid. On my skin, it lasts significantly above average, so that even in the evening, one can still perceive the pleasant, clean fruitiness. A fragrance that truly blossoms in the warm season and instantly lifts your spirits.

I like fragrances from Tiziana Terenzi. They are usually very high quality, intense, have character, and great performance. Not so with "Sirrah"... At first, I thought "Wow, what a great scent! A must-have." It started off very nicely: finely green. If those are fruits, then they are not ripe and juicy, but still green-fresh. Over time, very subtle leather notes join in - this makes the fragrance incredibly appealing. A lovely musk (a lot of it) comes in and turns the whole thing into a very fine, green-milky, noble skin scent. I say skin scent because at this stage (1st hour) the fragrance does not project properly yet. In the 2nd hour, a distinct birch tar note comes in (at least that's how I perceive it). It makes the fragrance significantly more masculine, but also more interesting. (By the way, I don't perceive any floral notes at all). A nasty transformation happens unexpectedly in the 3rd hour: gone is the ethereal-fine green-resinous scent. Long live the exhaust fumes! Or the chlorine cleaners! I can't describe this extremely unpleasantly synthetic, toxic-smelling note any other way. (Similar note to the JNxNJ-John Varvatos x Nick Jonas (crimson) in the red bottle, which ruined any enjoyment I had of that fragrance) I still don't know what exactly it is that smells so much like chlorine to me. But this note or accord projects quite strongly, it's very hard to wash away, and it's annoying!!!! But the fragrance remains so chlorine-rich all day long. For me, definitely a big flop. What a shame, it could have been so beautiful between us.

To be completely honest, I must admit that until now the formula Tiziana Terenzi fragrances + me = not compatible has applied. No, it is certainly not because the fragrances are poorly made. On the contrary, I always find them to be of very high quality and in many ways also unique. They all last a very long time and usually have a noticeable projection. Actually, these are all characteristics that I like. I have just often experienced them as willful, dominant, and sometimes scratchy (bristly), so the desire to have a TT fragrance in my collection has rarely arisen. However, my perspective has changed somewhat through the new fragrances of the Luna Collection and through “Porpora” (a constant inner struggle about whether I want it or not). “Sirrah” (a star in the constellation Andromeda) entered my personal test orbit: Immediately after spraying, I have the impression of standing ankle-deep in tart, sour fruits (quince / passion fruit). I am not a big fan of fruity scents, especially when they appear sticky-sweet. However, I appreciate the tart fruits because they seem particularly vital and lively to me, often providing a pleasant freshness kick. At this point, I am already taken with what Paolo and Tiziana Terenzi have created here. The label “they can do fruits” is certainly justified in my view. Gradually and slowly, the fruits “ripen,” gaining in fruitiness and restrained sweetness. Very fine saffron threads and sparkling pepper weave through the fruits, providing a very special twist. All the fragrance components seem to be very agile, tumbling wildly together and adhering to no order. But that is exactly what makes this fragrance so lively. Rose and amber throw their advantages into the ring, creating a finely floral-ambered atmosphere. Not too much and not too little, but perfectly balanced. That takes skill, and the Terenzis seem to have it. Aromas from light woods and fluffy soft musk underpin the lively activity. Still, there is no real order in sight; all participants dance around and yet manage to create a uniformity and synchrony that greatly benefits the fragrance. And then there is a special note that is present throughout the entire (very long) fragrance journey. At first, I thought it was light oud. However, in my research, I came across the idea that it must be this special oxygen molecule that is responsible for this particularly bright and slightly cutting scent impression. How does that work? No idea. But it doesn’t matter, as it does a pretty good job. “Sirrah” is far from a classic fruity fragrance for me. I perceive it as rather herb-fresh-tart for a longer time. This changes in the course of the fragrance as the other fragrance protagonists join in, bringing restrained sweetness, floral notes, and spiciness. “Sirrah” doesn’t become really sweet for me, but rather milder, finer, and equipped with a feel-good base. Personally, I like “Sirrah” best when it’s a bit warmer and the fragrance can fully showcase its refreshing side. This is also supported by the sillage, which is clearly noticeable but not exaggerated. Based on my personal testing experiences, I would classify it as unisex, as the tart-fruity aspect stands out for me. But that can, of course, be different for everyone. As is customary with the Terenzis, “Sirrah” is also an Extrait de Parfum, which has an ambitious price of €365 for 100ml. Whether the truly high-quality ingredients and the beautiful bottle are worth it is something everyone must decide for themselves. However, I will gladly change my initially mentioned formula… ********** Here is a quote from “AusLiebezumDuft” that I find very beautiful and fitting for the Luna Collection: “The project of Tiziana Terenzi deals with the ‘future of memories.’ According to a legend, matters of the heart, everything incomplete and lonely, end up on the moon. Here, thoughts, feelings, dreams, and tears, missed opportunities and unfinished actions are preserved in precious glass vials. Tiziana Terenzi has drawn inspiration from these images for her collection of exquisite Extraits de Parfum. By perceiving them through the sense of smell, we regain possession of what we believed was lost. By wearing them on our skin, we experience once again a feeling of happiness and wonderful wonder. This collection is dedicated to ‘rediscovery,’ to what we seem to have forgotten and to what we could not forget. Tiziana Terenzi goes back to the places with their warm summer nights under a radiant moon and sparkling stars. Viewed through the eyes of a child, they appear full of magic and wonder. The memory itself makes them seem even more enchanting.”

You all know Vincent van Gogh right? He went a bit mad and cut off his ear after drinking too much absinth. Well back in the days there was load of absinth balm in the booze, probably provoking dilutions. Nowadays it’s just a strong liquor based mostly on anise. Which is a very nice smell indeed. I do, however, associate it with childhood. Not being able to sleep my mom always made me a cup of milk with some anise. Worked like a charm. This fragrance has an incredible smell, the drydown is a bit woody, really nice. Kilian knows its woods. It takes forever to get to that drydown though. First 6 - 8 hours is really spicy anise with moderate projection in the first hour or two. On my first wear I immediately put this on my wishlist but I’m not sure if I want to smell like anise all day. Probably scared to doze off, or that I want to cut off organs.

Very good sillage and quite potent, particularly on the anise front. I would say lasting-power is about 4-5 hours on me. I wish this could have been better, but alas. Initally, I picked this one up primarily for it's Absinthe note, for I've always been very fond of Absinthe and it's scent. And I'm very pleased to inform you that it indeed smells of a true Absinthe! From what I've read from others - the anise, violet and liquorice root mellows down and settles into a smooth, cool and woodsy scent after a few hours. This doesn't seem to be the case for me. I get to keep the notes - as they are on first spray - throughout my wear. Albeit a bit warmer. I presume it depends on your skin chemistry. Overall, this is a wonderful scent for those who love fresh, cool and unisex fragrances. The bottle is lovely to look at too, though the cap could have been made of glass rather than plastic.

This opens with ANISE. Anise and absinthe are at the front, with a green patchouli. There is a strong bitter green woody note, it smells like the inside of a still-green twig.There is a subtle smokiness as well... As it dries the bitterness settles a bit and it gets a sweeter and smoother. A bit like herbs steeped in sugar syrup. It is not inviting, but there is something very powerful about it. A poisoned dagger of a scent.

So I was scared of this frag for the longest time until I wore it out by accident. It's bloody beautiful and surprisingly great, even in humid and hot weather. It's a spicy, forest green scent, not cloying or headache-inducing at all whatsoever and develops beautifully on my skin. There's an authoritative, androgynous air about it with the anise and absinthe, like some kind of dark fae forest commander. Lasts you the whole evening but don't overspray on this one. Definitely very bitter and not everyone's cup of tea, kind of recalls Mississipi Medicine a little but much smoother, more well-balanced and sophisticated. I like it! Absolutely wearable but requires confidence to pull off. Still, really expensive. I got a 10ML of this for free at a Kilian PR event but I would hesitate to pull the trigger for a full bottle. Grade: A-

So! Bam! There it is! Long sought, finally found! Just as intense as I was looking for the roasted almond with cotton candy scent of the Christmas market or the fair, I was on the hunt for a perfume that captures the scent of the candy stands. Those stands with the light yellow anise candies that you can smell from afar. Last week, I smelled the liquors from Kilian at Breuninger. I was actually only interested in Angels Share because I had heard a lot about it (thanks to the hype ;)) and I knew it would fall into my taste profile. Of course, I also wanted to get to know the other two. Apple Brandy didn't quite convince me, and then completely unexpectedly, the fanfares went off in my head. Or the flourish. Or the violins, or everything at once. When I smelled "L'Heure Verte | Kilian," my heart truly opened! There it is, the anise stand to spray on. I was about to take the bottle with me right away, but reason prevailed. Because usually, I test a perfume several times first to see if I like it on myself and want to wear it. Now I sit here with my sample and keep sniffing at my wrist. The anise stand top note could have stayed beautifully linear for me. But the development is still very appealing. After the sweet - licorice anise candy opening follows the violet-licorice liqueur. Everything becomes a bit darker, more serious, sharper. While in the afternoon you bought the anise candies at the Christmas market and enjoyed the scent, the evening follows in a dark, cozy bar, sitting on nostalgic, solid wooden chairs, the scent of absinthe hangs in the somewhat dusty air, and in the glass, which naturally looks like the bottle, is this noble drop of licorice liqueur. The scent has something incredibly alluring about it. The sweetness and sharpness in the fragrance are not contradictory; they complement each other very well. You stay in the bar for a long time and can't find the end because the atmosphere is so captivating and pleasant that you simply don't want to leave. Late at night, the last drops of liqueur still linger in the glass, exuding this warm, soft, licorice-sweet scent. In this atmosphere, surely one or the other didn't go home alone ;). For me, this perfume is absolutely underrated.

Alandia, the enchanting fairy with the dark soul, once again felt a deep longing within her to be completely herself and to sink into the depths of her imagination. So she sprayed her darkest green fairy dress at exactly 5:00 PM and immediately immersed herself in a wonderful aura of anise, wormwood, and alcohol.
This fragrance is like a place in a warmer forest with a refreshing waterfall. Very boozy, elegant, and luxurious.

New Year - New Paths - New Fragrance My first fragrance from Kilian L 'Heure Verte. A home run for me, as it reminded me of my childhood. As a small child, I always loved drinking fennel-anise-caraway tea with lots of grape sugar; at the pediatrician's office, the tea was always in the waiting area. Everyone could help themselves and have a glass of tea.

I am a big fan of licorice, ouzo, absinthe, or even fennel-anise-caraway tea and have always been looking for a fragrance that goes exactly in this direction, while not being too disturbing for my surroundings. With "Opus XIV - Royal Tobacco | Amouage," I actually thought I had found exactly this scent, but it turned out to be too smoky and strong for everyday wear.

I tested L'Heure Verte yesterday after the sample had been sitting with me for a few days, as Apple Brandy on the Rocks had simply piqued my interest more. I find absinthe has a very interesting scent, so I was even more curious about what L'Heure Verte has to offer. I wouldn't really describe L'Heure Verte as an absinthe fragrance.

Hello dear community, I have only sampled Tiziana Terenzi sporadically and haven't quite warmed up to the house yet. However, when purchasing a sample collection, this fragrance was included among others, and what can I say, it impressed me so positively that I ordered the bottle at a good price right away. The fragrance starts off spicy, sweet floral but also somewhat fresh and fruity, and has a pleasant lightness. For me, the impression of the top note lasts relatively long (>1h), with increasingly more balsamic woods and an elegant light rose joining in, making the scent progressively drier. The very bright Oud never comes across as animalic to my nose. As the Oud unfolds, there is also the impression of a light leather note, which, if you focus on it, always smells like wood to me. In the drydown, the fragrance remains sweet and dry, dominated by very light woods. The longevity of the fragrance is above average for me. You can still perceive it on the skin the next day. What I liked about the fragrance is the certain lightness and carefree feeling it conveys. The scent feels a bit crazy, works with certain (slightly) contrasting impressions, and radiates joy of life for me. It simply puts me in a good mood and reminds me not to take everything, and perhaps especially myself, too seriously. Additionally, I really like the unusually bright wood notes. For me, the fragrance is exactly 50:50 unisex. Edit: Regarding my price evaluation. You can find the fragrance in some shops for less than half of the MSRP. At ~2€/ml, I find the fragrance very good.

It may be that I am peculiar, but this fragrance has caused one thing for me: shaking my head and wondering what some perfumes are slowly supposed to represent.. Maybe Tiziana Terenzi is an artist, that may be true, but the scent is simply unbearable for me and has absolutely nothing to do with a body scent or perfume, in my humble opinion.. I am used to many things from my scent journeys in the Emirates when it comes to animalistic and extreme fragrances, but this "scent" here is the pinnacle.. Does it smell good? No, absolutely not, but it is special.. I smell a mixture of very animalistic, different oud notes that lean very much towards a leopard cage in the zoo and a type of herbal mixture that I know from the little voodoo shops in Louisiana, which is supposed to drive away evil spirits and surely does.. A wondrous blend of animalistic herbal notes that drives every spirit away.. I am slowly wondering if some fragrances are like haute couture fashion.. Creations that are supposed to represent works of art but are not made for wearing. Works of art to marvel at but not to wear.. For me, this scent is exactly like that. It may be a work of art, but only for wonder and amazement, absolutely not for wearing.

Morillas' first innovative formula, used in Gucci Guilty Absolute, revitalized with a dreamy jasmine and warm spices. From my point of view, Gucci Guilty Absolute was an experiment for Morillas, and an extremely successful one! As the master is extremely perfectionist in his ideas, I consider Dark Lord to be the perfection for the basic idea started from GGA. Morillas reached the absolute in perfumery with this creation! It remains one of my signatures! An absolute masterpiece!

Looking at the notes I was really surprised to see rum in there. A By Kilian isn’t finished until some form of booze is added I guess. Well I don’t get any of that. What I do get is this animalic leathery scent in the first couple of hours. It’s quite heavy, anyone who’s ever smelled Gucci Guilty Absolute knows the horse-stable smell I’m talking about. It’s nicely combined with peppery spices, taking the edge off a little bit. After an hour or two it slowly starts to reveal woody notes. Images of pencil shavings come to mind and I absolutely love that. And things evolve even further, getting a bit more airy, lighter, the vetiver takes control. The animalic nature of the fragrance makes it hard to pull off in formal occasions. But it’s an absolute pleasure for the nose.

This is truly niche in the sense that this is hard to pull off...or rather requires a specific vibe to pull off correctly. You must embrace the aggressive & polarizing nature of this perfume and not care what people think you smell like. Those around you will be challenged or sometimes offended if they catch a whiff and the wearer must take glee in this. It is not bad, especially in the opening/mid it is a nice Jasmine, spicey, leather blend. It takes the wearer to a dark place of indifference, nihilism, but holds a unique power of individuality. Bitter dark leather is the dry-down. The wearer stands alone.

If you check the fragrances Guilty Absolute pour Homme and Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux , you'll see a VERY large amount of votes in the "similar fragrances" section. People love to compare these two, and I totally understand why: - both fragrances are made by the same perfume, Alberto Morillas - Guilty Absolute pour Homme came out one year before Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux and Kilian as a brand does have a tendency of getting "inspired" - both have a very similar leathery vibe (?) As an absolute (haha) lover of Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux , I am aware that it's expensive - and that's why I rarely wear it. I've been on the hunt for a leather fragrances that captures that unique feeling that I get from Kilian's fragrance... and all paths seem to lead me to Guilty Absolute pour Homme . But are they the same? And is Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux just a "scam"? After owning both fragrances and testing them back to back, here's my verdict: Nope, they're not the same BUT they have SOME similarities. Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux is like a black dark leather jacket: it's still a new polished jacket, smells a bit like gasoline but there's a subtle floral touch to it that really gives it some elegance and mystery - it's so intriguing! Guilty Absolute pour Homme has a leathery vibe that is SUPER close to No Limit$ - they probably use similar leather ingredients because here I really smell a similarity. That leathery vibe is different in Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux - it's more cold. The leather accord of Guilty Absolute pour Homme is warmer! It's much more woody and is rather linear in it's performance: it does one thing well, leather AND woods! Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux starts more classy masculine: bergamot in the opening, jasmine-esque florals bring some life to the composition and that leather binds everything together! But here's the kicker: as Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux dries down, it gets closer and closer to Guilty Absolute pour Homme ! Let's finish this off by mentioning that I enjoy both fragrances! Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux has a special place in my heart, as it was my first big niche fragrance that I fell in love with, so at the end of the day, nothing can really compare to that ;) But Guilty Absolute pour Homme is essentially a "warmer drydown of Dark Lord - Ex Tenebris Lux ", that's what it feels like. Definitely more woody and warmer, it's more cozy in it's take on leather in perfumery - which I find awesome, as a lot of leather perfumes tend to go in that "new polished black leather jacket" vein. And of course, that price difference is immense. Whether it's worth it to you or not, noone can really say. You have to try them for yourself. My preference is clear, I have a favorite. But if I want to get a similar feeling AND I want it woodier on a particular day, I'd go with Guilty Absolute pour Homme instead.

Dark Lord opens up with a fairly dense and intense aroma. Bergamot gives it a bit of bright citrus up top, but this is offset by peppery and smoky rum, and a rather dirty-ish leather that permeates through the entire wear. The booziness of the rum is there, but it isn’t a completely soaked feeling during the wear. Jasmine, however, may be the strongest player in the opening stage of Dark Lord. It sits right in the middle flanked by the other notes, giving Dark Lord an early floral scent. For me, the spiciness, is really only in the opening act. From there, it takes on an earthier and woodier quality for the rest of the wear. Kilian says that the pepper is one of the key notes, but on my skin at least, that’s not the case. In fact, I get a lot more vetiver, cedar, and other general woods than I ever do the pepper. As we move forward, the jasmine will start to lose its position within the composition. The leather and vetiver become pretty strong here and I’m still getting the smokiness sans the spice. Dark, earthy, and has an herbal or medicinal sort of finish to it. The latter stage is leather, cypress, vetiver and the faded remnants of cedar and jasmine. Cypress really climbs the ladder and contributes towards the tail end. It really doesn’t do all that much for me early in the wear, then, it’s basically the same weighting as the leather.

Looking for the Vetiver in that by Kilian Dark Lord on the brisk outdoors stroll, pretty much hidden starts to mount up 45 mins in. Crazy good smoke simulation like canvas, perfect aboundant ballance, excellent dark scent, robust, got the warmth, got the humble, nonloud oversprayable, like the behaved Voice of the Snake, with the high degree of refinement to it.

This is how it was ... Quite an ordinary day at the perfumery. Me - Good afternoon, I'd like to try something from Kilian. For example ... do you have a Dark Lord? Saleswoman - Let me think. Hold on. Nobody has asked us for that perfume so far. Here it is. We have. Want to try it directly on the skin? Me - Yes I want And then, after the first spray, darkness fell on my eyes.

Dark Lord the name is intriguing and has something special to it. If Harry Potter and Voldemort would be in a fight in the middle of a car dealer place and the miss some shots and hit some cars and the doors fly away it might actually smell like Dark Lord. It smells like burned rubber and leather. Strang enough it’s quite nice. But not to wear I think.

(this is a copy from a review I left on fragrantica before deleting my account,and that reflects in some aspects of it-the sigma male comment for example lmao) As a person who loves gothic themes,this one is gorgeous.I tried it first in summertime and found it overwhelming,but could picture myself wearing it with a long black coat or a leather jacket in the winter.

With Dark Lord, Kilian offers a kind of counterpart to the rather tame sensual-gourmand Black Phantom, in the best Fifty Shades of Grey manner. And this counterpart is not only dark and dominant in name, but olfactorily swings the nine-tailed cat quite vigorously, making one see black from all the leather and latex. That's quite a bold statement!

When you, like me, research lily of the valley perfumes, you eventually come across this arguably most controversial lily of the valley scent of all. From praises declaring it art to denigrations calling it slurry, cow barn, and the little pile on the flower meadow, everything is included. "Hahaha," thinks Aspasia with a devilish grin, "this one has to go in the lily of the valley package!" Said and done, but of course, I want to test it myself too, where's the fun otherwise? Fearlessly (?) I spray Tempel on my wrist. On the other wrist went "Replica - Lazy Sunday Morning (Eau de Toilette) | Maison Margiela," basically a harmless lily of the valley for comparison. And in the first seconds, the two actually smell quite similar. A fresh lily of the valley, indeed. But then, from one second to the next, the oud kicks in with Tempel, at least I think that's what it is; I don't have much experience with this controversial trend ingredient. And that's the moment when the fragrance descriptions here at Parfumo start to get funny, because what hits your nose is indeed special. To me, it smelled, now please don't laugh, like soft cheese, not aged for long, but fresh out of the package. And what’s even crazier than the cheese on the flower meadow is the fact that I didn’t find it that bad at all. I was irritated but also fascinated. This ambivalence between sweet lily of the valley and fine camembert occupied my mind continuously, and it kept drawing my nose back to my wrist to understand what I was smelling. I didn’t find it disgusting at all, just simply unusual. After about 20 minutes, the "cheese fun" was over. The oud now smelled significantly resinous, with an undertone that I would describe as a skin accord. Still not a scent that those who care about such things would call a crowd-pleaser, but at least something very individual. I definitely had a lot of fun testing it and am already curious to see how the scent will be received in the Wp. A quick note on the sillage: This is more of an estimate. I found it quite close to the skin, but I only sprayed once briefly to use little, as it is still supposed to travel. With a proper spray, the sillage may therefore be more pronounced.

Tempel has received a phenomenally bad review here. Therefore, I wanted to take this fragrance as an opportunity to delve deeper into it and explore its mystery, if it possesses one at all... Right off the bat: In my view, Terenzi belongs to one of the best Oud fragrances; it is an unusual, wonderful floral-oud combination. And yes, even though I am quite aware of the numerous negative associations regarding "stable scent" and "cheesy note": I believe that Oud smells like this in a perfume when it is used subtly. Tempel is therefore, in my opinion, a fascinating scent that is by no means ordinary. How to describe the fragrance? It is pleasantly sweet and unites two opposites. On one side, the two specified types of Oud, Cambodian and Indian Oud. In addition, there is a lot of lily of the valley with an intensely floral and sweet character, as well as amber. Due to the skillful composition, the fragrance comes across as controversial, yet also unique; and, surprisingly for me, Tempel smells inexplicably fruity in my nose. Is it really due to the magnolia or the daffodil? So intertwined, it is oudy-floral-fruity-sweet - a delight! It is suitable for women because of the floral components, for men because of the Oud varieties; however, it is more for a middle-aged or older audience. It is definitely a powerhouse, meaning the longevity, projection, and sillage are enormous. Of course, you can also wear Tempel in the office if applied discreetly - but I would find it hard to recommend it as a business scent. I would also not recommend it for sports; but for any social event where you want to stand out and impress with an unusual scent DNA, it is perfect. No matter how one feels about Tempel, whether one likes it or rejects it: This perfume from the house of Terenzi is, for me, a prime example of what a niche fragrance can "be." Tempel certainly hints at artisanal craftsmanship, the ingredients seem to be of high quality and also unusually "orchestrated" together; and through the composition, a fragrance has been created that is worth discussing with others. And this is certainly something that most fragrance lovers hope for and desire.

I have found so beautiful perfumes with citrusy touch lately. That note isn’t easy for me but when it’s blended seamlessly with other notes it’s absolutely charming. I’m totally in love with Woman in Gold. Creamy composition with a captivating combination of vanilla and bergamot, refined rose and deepening Tonka and patchouli create a special and unique scent. It feels like a fragrance from decades past updated for the modern era. It has a glowing glamour, a stylish, sensual and seductive character, and yet it is extremely versatile. The scent is powdery, fluffy, a bit hazy, but still bright. The patchouli doesn’t make it dark in any way. This is not a rose perfume in the way that you can smell clearly it’s petals. The most prominent notes are Bergamot and Vanilla. I’m totally hooked on this. Woman in Gold is great for parties with an evening dress, but I can’t resist wearing it after a shower in the evening. It brings a touch of luxury to an ordinary day. Longevity is excellent and it leaves a seductive scent trail behind you. The scent is office safe and it’s suitable to wear year around. Thank you for reading, I hope you liked my review. I would appreciate if you follow me on my IG and/or YouTube (English subtitles available): @ninamariahperfumes It gives me a lot of motivation to write more

I just received a new perfume: Kilian Woman in Gold. I opened the box, sprayed once on my wrist… and I was done. A prisoner. I can’t stop smelling it. Woman in Gold is that perfume — the one I didn’t know I was missing until now. And suddenly, here we are. We’ve met. She is luminous, bright, easygoing, kind. She smiles as early sun rays warm her skin. Flirtatious, confident, elegant — a true girl’s girl. She leans in and says, “You’re worth it.” And I believe her. I am. I feel soft and feminine — guarded, but brave. The gourmand base wraps me in warmth. Tonka and vanilla take my hand and spin me into a slow dance. Rose petals glow in the sunlight, gently finding their rhythm. And then it clicks. I finally feel it. I am luminous. I am bright. I am easygoing and kind. I am that woman. Woman in Gold.

I was so unprepared. What a beautiful vanilla. Incredible. Along with bergamot and rose. It immediately transports me to another setting. Chandeliers, evening, gala, expensive clothing, expensive guests, you know. When the air smells of luxury and is so good that you don’t want to leave. Then calm sets in, who walks in? It must be this woman in gold. Golden earrings, long white dress, subtle makeup. She smells of vanilla, bergamot, rose. Oh how elegant. She just stands there and captivates everyone around her. How does she do it? When I smell this fragrance, I have to think of moments I haven’t experienced but would love to. I already liked Kilian before. But now I’m sitting here and can’t stop smelling my arm. How soft can vanilla be? How pleasant the composition? I am completely enchanted.

It is a wonderful scent that I didn't understand right away. At first, I thought it was too mature, but after further testing, I now find it age-neutral. I associate the vanilla note in many fragrances with simplicity. I cannot describe this scent as typical and simple, even though I can't find anything incredibly special about it. Just a harmonious, full, and feminine composition. The perfume smells expensive, and with it, you really feel like a woman in gold. I smell burnt caramel, unobtrusive and warm. It is not monotonous, and the light floral notes are really very pleasant. Longevity and sillage are very good.

… and that sums it up perfectly. I was afraid of the described patchouli. I smell wonderful things but little patch. The fragrance starts with a very delicate, powdery rose. Very slightly vanillic, a bit caramel-like, elegant, light. What I particularly appreciate: Without the alcohol punch at the beginning that many fragrances bring with them. The scent settles pleasantly on the skin and stays there for the next 5 hours. Rosy Powdery Vanillic Creamy Unfortunately, the rated longevity does not seem to set in for me. I have to reapply after 5 hours. But still, it is heavenly and excellently wearable, always and at any time of day. Whether in the office or going out. Always appropriate. Never too loud. I like the bottle, which for me - expresses elegance - femininity - neatness . The price is horrendous (without a doubt far too high). With percentage promotions, it becomes a bit more bearable. It’s worth waiting.

I am very picky when it comes to perfume, and out of about 100 samples, maybe 5 make it to a second testing phase.. Woman in Gold was initially a home run. Such a beautiful, soft, and super elegant scent. You probably know the feeling: you test a fragrance for the first time and you almost freak out with excitement.. I was just too quick with my enthusiasm.

I was very curious about the scent, as it sounded really beautiful and I believe it will appeal to many; unfortunately, I am not one of them. It starts off very nicely with a sweet freshness like lime cream sprinkled with sugar, but not gourmand-edible. There’s something about the opening that I find ordinary, but not bad.

The scent is so creamy feminine as if one were entering a ballroom adorned in gold. Quite Luxury, as one would say today. Mega pleasant, and as soon as it gets warm, the creamy scent - the tonka bean in the base - always rises again. The sillage of this fragrance is subtle but noticeable, not loud but perfectly blends with one's own body scent, and that is unbeatable.

Very beautiful scent, so relaxing and cozy. On skin this projects for a long time. You can't fail to catch the wifts of this throughout the day. Kilian did a good job on this, best in the line. This one is backup worth for me. Never want to be without.

Woman in Gold starts off with a citrusy and fresh note from the bergamot. It becomes a bit creamier over time, but the fresh citrus note remains. The fragrance has a truly noble effect on me. The rose beautifully integrates into the scent's progression. Like a very lovely body lotion that you’ve applied. I believe Woman in Gold can be worn in any season.

This could be a part of the Hermés un Jardin line. If you're into summer freshies like e.g. Mugler Cologne but would like to soften up the soapiness with some white tea and fig plus added spices, this is made for you. Not sure if I can pick up the bamboo though ? A little linear, but at the same time it seems sophisticated and unpretentious to me, reminiscent of a high class spa product. Green, clean and quite long lasting for this kind of scent.

I love tea scents, I really do, but as much as I hate to say this, Bvlgari and Elizabeth Arden have already done this scent to death. I was hoping for something more bamboo-like, but supposedly this fragrance is meant to emulate the scent of white tea being drunk from a bamboo cup or leaf... or something along those lines. I expected to smell a luscious, green jungle, but instead Bamboo Harmony greeted me with crisp tea notes and aromatic spices. It's not bad in terms of composition, although I do admittedly find it a little bland and boring at times. It wears splendidly on the skin. The unisex qualities are quite apparent, with refreshingly green and spicy notes combining to create a smooth, non-gender specific scent. I actually quite like it for its versatility and easy-going approach. So far I am beginning to realise that this Asian Tales series is intended for Summer. On my side of the world, I am in the midst of a freezing, cold Winter, so it's probably not the best time to test these scents. Either way, I will be looking forward to giving Bamboo Harmony a whirl in forty degree celsius weather. The drydown smelt quite earthy on my skin, which was certainly pleasing. The longevity for me wasn't as disappointing as it was for others. I got at least a good five or so hours from Bamboo Harmony, and what I'd call moderate sillage. It may not be the most innovative Summer scent, but I will agree that it does smell nice and has the ability to grow on you over time. I found the simplicity the only bothering factor.

I am a huge By Kilian fan. However, I had never tried this older scent, so I was eager to receive a tiny sample in the mail. I’m not overly impressed by it, as it is a little too common for me. It has strong citrus notes, which are fine, but again common. Oakmoss isn’t my friend here. I don’t know what maté smells like. There’s not much longevity or sillage with this particular perfume. It was a little disappointing all-in-all. I would not buy this, as for me it’s not worth the price tag, and I hesitate to say that about anything By Kilian, as I love his perfumes. I’m going to give it another chance when the weather warms up to see if perhaps my body temperature has anything to do with the reaction. I will update this post at that point.
For me this opens with a burst of white tea and bergamot.Then you can smell the spices, cant smell the mimosa though. Its a nice tea scent but not for my taste. I find it a bit blend

Better well copied than poorly made... A well-known saying that holds some truth. But I think By Kilian is exaggerating a bit in this regard. Changing or refining bestseller concepts minimally and selling them as great masterpieces happens here far too often, which annoys me a bit. Anyone wanting to know more about the fragrance doppelgängers should just click through the Kilian collection and look to the right; with seemingly every second perfume, there are super similar classics that have been shamelessly copied. And when this occurs so frequently, it is done knowingly, not by accident. Everyone draws inspiration, I also read the pre-comments before my comments and watch YouTube videos about the fragrance if available, but this is a whole different level of shamelessness and obviousness. Anyway, I can't change anything about it, it seems to sell anyway, and occasionally, really great perfumes come out of it. Still, this should never go unmentioned when talking about Kilian. And who was copied this time, you ask? Clearly, the white and especially green tea scent from Bulgari. Once again, a well-known, successful formula has been spruced up a bit and made more luxurious for the customer segment that doesn't care about money. That’s not enough for me, and such a copy really has an extremely hard time receiving a similar rating as the original - even if the actual perfume might seem a bit better. The scent is light, more like a room fragrance, green, citrusy, light-woody, and all underpinned by an unmistakable tea note. I'm not a tea lover, so I would have to guess if I were to associate the smell with green and white tea. The perfume definitely has an Asian touch and could find many admirers in those regions, as it is known that they prefer scents that are light and airy-fruity. Bottle: the best in its class. Sillage: more of a room fragrance than a perfume, although stronger than the Bulgari counterpart. Longevity: a quarter of a day. Little bamboo, few original ideas. Lots of tea, lots of stealing. And yet the end product is enjoyable, sometimes even more than that.

your comments made me curious, but also cautious: and the scent convinced me. yes, it's true, it can only be smelled very close to the skin. but it has good longevity on my skin. and it speaks in soft tones: yet these are so harmonious, so balanced and fresh-calm, that I gladly forgive it its delicacy. a hint of spice and clarity.

I don't want to offend anyone, but does every brand really need to have a fragrance in the shallow tea segment in their lineup? As long as there's a foot in every door, nobody will notice! Right from the application, the scent felt strangely familiar to me. A fresh, interchangeable breeze surrounds me and leaves no doubt about where the fragrance journey will lead.

Facts: Green, Yellow, Beige, healthy, tea-like; mate-jasmine-tea-like, warm, first grassy then hay-like, very hay-like; natural. Leathery, outdoors, sunset, sweaty, dirty but not filthy; confident, tough, slightly sour, not bitter, androgynous, unisex; dull but not dull-witted; maybe a bit old-fashioned. Kelly Calèche.

Definitely a summer refresher. Green, green, green, are all my associations, plus a bit of Asia feeling, a splash of lemon, and something soft, fluffy... overall a more sensible investment than Water Calligraphy, even if it feels very familiar. However, I would have attributed it to a regular green Bvlgari tea rather than Kelly Caleche.

I have already had the opportunity to extensively test several Kilian fragrances, and there are indeed some good scents among them for me. From the Louvre Noir Collection, A taste of Heaven, Strait to Heaven, and Sweet Redemption are the ones I still like.

The rose in By Kilian ROSE OUD is very pronounced, which makes this perfume feel rather feminine to me. There is also a strong saffron presence, so the first time I donned this composition I thought immediately of Bond no 9 NY OUD. However, when I re-tried the Bond earlier today, I discovered that the saffron was far more dominant than the rose in that composition. What I am not detecting a lot of in these rose-saffron-oud perfumes is the third member of the triad: oud. It may be that I am more sensitive to saffron than to oud, and so the oud note ends up being overwhelmed by the saffon. In any case, what's in a name? ROSE OUD is a beautiful perfume which blooms as a rose and dries down as a saffron rose. The rose abides through and through. I highly recommend this creation for testing by rose lovers. It may not give the oud-ies the fix they're looking for. To my nose, this is a floriental, not an oriental woody perfume. I suspect that ROSE OUD may be too feminine for some gents. I, on the other hand, would love to have a bottle.

One of the easiest rose-oud fragrances to wear, as well as the most serenely beautiful. It has none of the exciting harshness of the oud accord used in most other Western oud fragrances, and is all the better for it. Think of the most beautiful supermodel you've ever laid eyes on - but one who nonetheless fails to either move you or turn you on - and that's Rose Oud by Kilian. The secret to the success of Rose Oud is this: all the major elements (the rose, the oud, the gaiac wood, and the saffron) do not possess a strong character of their own but instead melt together to form a small black velvet pocket into which you find your hand fits perfectly. So the green, slightly sour wet rose at the start gains a dulcet depth from the subtle oud, growing sweeter, jammier, and fuller as time goes on. The oud provides the dark backdrop without muscling its way into the composition in that bullying way oud tends to have. The saffron casts only a fine patina of sweet gold dust rather than its usual iodine-y leather scream. It's a very subtle, smooth fragrance - almost ephemeral. When I think the show has ended, eight hours on, I am surprised to find that golden, almost pudding-like saffron emerge on my skin, and a pleasantly sour tinge of oud. The oud, by the way, is synthetic but has the virtue of not smelling like it, so carefully woven into the fabric of the fragrance has it been. Rose Oud is a beautiful, delicate piece of work whose subtleties could easily go unnoticed if you weren't paying attention. It is by far one of my favorite rose-oud fragrances, and despite the cost, I have a feeling that I will own a (refill) bottle of this someday, even if I have to sell off some of my (many) other oud fragrances to afford it. I have finally reached the stage where I am content to do away with five or six inferior bottles of perfume to get my hands on just one bottle of something that satisfies and pleases from every angle. Rose Oud may not be the most exciting or unusual rose oud on the market - many think it is pretty but mundane - but I think it's one of the best-smelling rose-ouds around, alongside Tom Ford's wonderful Noir de Noir or Guerlain's Rose Nacree du Desert.

I’m not really a big fan of by Kilian. Too many of the fragrances seemed to me more about appearance than substance, not worth the money, uninspired. Now, Rose Oud doesn’t exactly reinvent the wheel, but it is simply beautifully crafted. You can’t smell Oud here at all. No Oud accord, no real Oud. The name seems to me like pure fantasy. Rather, Rose Oud reminds me of fragrances like Calligraphy Rose by Aramis, Un Rose de Kandahar by Tauer, or 13 Brûlure de Rose by PG. Rosengourmands. Fragrances that don’t emphasize the lush, dark rose but rather incorporate it into a delicious context. However, these comparison fragrances have a small weakness: they are incredibly lush, and both the Aramis and the Tauer have an amber note that I find a bit dusty-dirty. That wouldn’t be appropriate for by Kilian. By Kilian plays it safe. That’s how I know them, and that’s why I haven’t liked their fragrances so far. But here... here it’s simply wonderful. The rose in the opening is more reminiscent of rose jam, accompanied by a light, transparent beeswax. It’s not about the consistency of wax. The scent feels quite airy for a rather sweet and oriental fragrance, which is wonderfully done. It’s just a delicate, soft smell that reminds one of beeswax. The development is quite linear and unspectacular, yet the fragrance never becomes boring. I wore Rose Oud today at work, and a colleague, who can sometimes be a bit snappy, was surprisingly lovely and often came quite close to me, as if she wanted to sniff me. Apparently, Rose Oud is well-received, and I liked it too, even though I doubted for a moment whether it was too feminine for me. Rose Oud goes through phases where the rose smells a bit more narcotic and less jam-like. It never loses its elegance, never becomes cloying, too thick, or exhausting. In those moments, it simply feels less sweet and, in an interesting way, particularly sexy. At other moments, the delicate jammy or sweet honey-wax aspects come to the fore. Of course, you can always smell all of this, but there isn’t a proper development; rather, it’s more of a slow shifting of the scent-defining poles. In the end, a velvety, delicate, silky veil remains on the skin, which reminded me most of this beeswax note. Mind you, some special, transparent, silky luxury beeswax. Imagine silk that smells a bit like beeswax. Now, my sentence about the comparison fragrances from Tauer & Co. may have sounded as if I valued them less. No, not necessarily. I actually find the Tauer to be the most unisex-friendly, because nothing about it is as delicate and cleanly polished. The Kilian is, I believe, more for women. But it is beautiful. And I say that as someone who is not the biggest fan of this brand.

Rose and Oud. Aha. Upon reading the title, I already had no desire to test this fragrance - this combination has simply come my way far too often lately. Whether Montale, Micallef, Armani, or Fréderic Malle, they all have at least one Rose-Oud fragrance in their lineup. The brand by Kilian is not exactly known for innovative, daring scent experiments, so I expected nothing more than the familiar from Rose Oud. Wrong! Calice Becker has approached this often-explored theme in a completely different way. So much in advance, you don't have to like either Oud or Rose to be captivated by this fragrance. Both main players take a back seat in Rose Oud; the Oud is subdued to the point that I can't identify it as a standalone note at all. There is a subtle woodiness present deep in the base - however, I search in vain for the distinctive, characteristic Oud. But the Rose is also given no more space due to its restraint. At the beginning, it is clearly recognizable, a delicate, light pink Rose with green nuances, but soon Rose Oud takes a different path. And the fragrance strongly leans into the gourmand genre. Rose Oud smells VERY edible. It doesn't go in the dark, chocolatey direction, like in Noir de Noir, but rather in the fruity-creamy one. Cinnamon and cardamom contribute a fine, equally delicate spiciness and further enhance the edible character. Incredibly delicious and sensual. I also distinctly smell honey, which inevitably reminds me of Micallef's Oud creations. Amidst all these treats, the Rose is not really tangible for me in Rose Oud; the familiar scent of rose petals or rose oil does not characterize Rose Oud. If the title didn't already suggest the Rose, I probably wouldn't even think of it as a note! Because for hours, I am solely seduced by this original, softly gourmand, and truly non-floral main accord. Rose Oud feels tidy, clear, and remains stationary in its development for hours; despite its high intensity, it maintains a consistently transparent, floating character. The creation bears a great resemblance to the works of Kurkdjian, as it is so effortlessly, lightly, and perfectly blended. For me, it is the most beautiful Kilian fragrance - I have now tested them all. Calice Becker is said to have created Rose Oud in just a few weeks. And in contrast to the two namesakes, I perceive this technical finesse, this skillful naturalness very distinctly.

I'll keep it brief for once. I received this fragrance as a sample a year ago, and it hasn't left my mind since. So, after months, I treated myself to it. At this price, one must do so. This creation needs to be applied very sparingly; otherwise, it overwhelms not only the surroundings but also oneself. My first impression was a rose in full bloom, vibrantly supported by luxurious oud. The sillage is strong, and if you make the mistake (as I did at first) of applying a full spray, you will be overwhelmed at first. The scent is very, very intense, and I wear it to the theater or for a night out. But VERY sparingly. :) I was told at the beginning that I smelled like a "brothel madam." Outrageous, but understandable, because with excessive application, you only perceive the development of this creation after hours - if you haven't fainted by then. ;) Haters gonna hate! I love bold fragrances, and Kilian is a master at creating something special. Conclusion: The scent may not please everyone, but a refined nose will be delighted! Roses and oud are exactly my thing. I have certainly never encountered such a creation in such perfection. Thumbs up and give it a try? ;)

Rose and Oud - these are the classic ingredients of precious Arabian perfume oils. It was essentially Pierre Montale who opened up this beautiful combination for the Western perfume market. Since the success of the Montale Ouds, dimmed copies have been appearing from time to time: Arabian Diamond by Micallef and Dark Rose by Czech & Speake come to mind.

Enate is a winery in the northwest of Catalonia. The red wines produced there are among the best in Spain and are still somewhat of a hidden gem. There are single-varietal wines, such as Merlot or Tempranillo, but also wonderful, excellent blends of Merlot-Cabernet-Tempranillo, for example, the Enate Classico.

I am so excited to be able to test Maharanih Rose Oud. Thank you, generous sweetheart. As a Kankuro fan, I was particularly curious about how this fragrance is, which the master praises as so unique and special. I am glad that I did not fall in love with the scent for the sake of my wallet.

I received a sample of this fragrance, many thanks to MonCherie! With great anticipation, I immediately used the sample to test the scent. The top note consists solely of rose for me. I have never smelled such a beautiful rose in a perfume, oh not just one, many rose bushes are present in this small sample. I have never encountered such a beautifully natural rose scent.

At the outset, the fragrance surprises with a truly intense yet very harmonious and pleasantly captivating rose note. This fine opening accord remains, blended with a very light but subtle smoky note, for about 4 hours. This Killian is like rose water enveloped in the finest smoke. Thus, it appears both invigorating and elegant, as well as enchanting.

With Kristina, I have found the next great Terenzi that can once again be categorized in the direction of Rosso Pompei . Not too long ago, I reviewed Sunsation , my first number 10, and tried to point out the differences to Rosso. While Sunsation represents a slightly spicier, more pronounced, and masculine version, Kristina tends towards a softer, somewhat citrusy and green direction. The magenta bottle is certainly eye-catching, but it hardly provides any clues about the scent. For neither does it lean too feminine, nor can I draw any other parallels. The iris plays no role for me, at least not with its well-known powdery note. The scent remains consistently fresh-fruity with a touch of sweetness and green accents underpinning it. Grapefruit and mandarin create an exceptionally good balance between citrus and fruity freshness, truly excellent! The black currant complements this mixture perfectly in my view, so that the green tea only accounts for nuances and accents. Sandalwood and musk are probably among the best base notes to envelop a certain calmness, something soft and harmonious. So it is here as well. Little of the "Terenzi-synthetic" that characterizes some fragrances is noticeable here. A very significant difference to Rosso Pompei is also the longevity and sillage. While the red one comes across as extremely strong, Kristina feels quite restrained. After a maximum of 6 hours, it’s over on my skin; sillage and projection are present, but in a moderate middle ground.

What made me buy the most expensive perfume in my collection (not including discounts)? Well, I'm a girl, and girls love pink. The bottle is visually a dream. The color Zylam or Magenta is obviously the favorite color of the artist to whom this pink treasure is dedicated. Along with the gold-colored design details, it really stands out. Before I write about the scent, I want to mention the showcase in which the bottle rests. Weighing more than 1.5 kg, an LED lights up the golden bottle cap, making it sparkle beautifully. The bottle itself weighs 366g, suggesting that you get a lot for your money. A pink bottle raises the expectation of a really sweet, girly scent cloud. However, that is not the case with Kristina. Kristina is a zesty-fruity unisex fragrance with only a subtle sweetness. Kristina offers a pink grapefruit upon spraying, zesty, never sharp. The cascade of top notes is interesting. The grapefruit takes a step back, a green mandarin comes in, followed by bergamot. The whole thing is soft and fresh, with green tea and iris rounding it out and making it exceptionally pleasant. This is a quality scent, but on me, it is quiet, becoming more intimate over time. This is probably due to my skin, but I have niche fragrances that project significantly more. I don't mind that. I like the scent and its later development into a soft sandalwood-musk blanket. The fruity notes, especially the grapefruit, smell not synthetic at all but rather natural. For me, it's not a winter scent; it will likely be suitable for men year-round. Kristina is pure luxury that one doesn't necessarily need. I have nothing comparable in my collection and will gladly wear the scent.

The fragrance begins with a sparkling accord of Italian citrus fruits, reflecting the notes of Calabrian bergamot, grapefruit, and green mandarin, in harmony with the recognizable suede tone of Florentine iris, which has a charmingly delicate sound. Later, a green tea accord with a hint of blackcurrant comes into play. In the base, iris is accompanied by woody notes of patchouli, Australian sandalwood, and musk.

Time after time, Kilian reminds you of just how piss-poor they are at making anything mildly interesting for the spring-summer seasons - it feels like everything has become a blatant cash-grab. The most recent blue bottle release Kologne Shield of Protection falls into this category all the same, and the blue bottle Kilians that have received praise in the past all lack something, whether it be performance, uniqueness, quality etc. Initial spray impressions: absolutely abysmal - a lot of synthetic sludge. Definitely getting ambroxan/fresh shower gel vibes that we've seen before with scents like Vodka on the Rocks . As it dries, the calone and the lemon become a little more blatant, but the main accords here remain fresh-synthetic-ozonic and not citrusy. When I first tried to smell it up-close, I could barely smell it because the air surrounding me is all synthetics which is definitely the Kilian DNA on fresher fragrances. The fact that this scent is inspired by blue lagoon (the beachside party drink from the 90s) aligns pretty well with the scent profile, because this is the equivalent of a cheap designer fragrance from ~30 years ago. This being a 50ml for €210 retail niche fragrance is just another deuce on top of the s*t sundae that niche perfumery has become.

D and G light blue, eau intense for men, mixed with window cleaner-windex. This is absolutely nothing to write home about. Embarrassing. This is my first Kilian, and absolutely last. I hear the others of the alcohol line are amazing. Should of spent money elsewhere. Absolutely disappointing. Very little to ZERO ginger, poor performance overall (for 200$ 50ml, piss poor) and very similar to D and G light blue intense, if I had to name a close comparison. Not saying "hey they are 90% alike note wise..." just saying buy that instead. This is A RIP OFF.

The best thing about this is the design: a nice gradient bottle that invokes the blue moon theme well. The smell is alright, nothing groundbreaking, minor similarities to Chrome. It's about average in performance, but the value is abysmal. If you're dropping two bills on a fragrance, get one that stands out. I had one of my non-fragrance-enthusiast friends smell it and he said it was generic, to which I agree. It smells like a ginger ale, with alcohol in it (I have never seen, let alone smelt the cocktail the fragrance is based on, so this is my closest description). I enjoy it, but I would not repurchase. 6/10.

Days by the sea Under a warm sun Water in the nose Salt in the air Vodka in the hand Break at the beach bar Freshly mixed Shaken, not stirred Lemons squeezed Vodka in copious amounts Salt rim on the glass Ginger garnish Topped up with soda Memories of beaches Memories of relaxation Wanderlust Happy feelings A drink with Kilian ** Blue Moon Ginger Dash is another Kilian that will divide opinions. Some will find it too simple, others will love it just the way it is. On point, I would say. Intensely priced, of course, but perfectly balanced between the fresh, citrusy sharpness and the pleasant, airy, salty aquaticness of the Calone. Fresh and fruity-sour lemon juice meets peppery ginger and great aquatics. Saltiness, seawater, fresh breezes and light green seaweed aromas are brought together to create a beach scent in a class of its own. The alcoholic vodka note gives it the typical Kilian touch. Simple, very wearable and well made. Sidonie Lancesseur's Kilians rarely disappoint.

While ginger is a common note in designer fragrances, it's rarely used as a dominant note. This fragrance offers a slightly improved version of the typical designer fragrance, with a modernized and higher quality ginger note. The ginger is blended with other notes such as lemon and ambroxan, creating a unique scent that's not photorealistic. However, given the price point of a Kilian fragrance, I'm not sure if it's worth paying for a slightly better version of a designer scent. Personally, I'd be happy with a decant, but wouldn't invest in a full bottle. Additionally, the performance could be better.

I blind bought this scent. Full bottle. Despite people on the internet telling me this is not one for the blind buys. Apparently many people are not a fan. But something told me this scent would be right up my alley. And it was! I had to get used to it a bit.

Ah, how I have been waiting for a great, promising new summer fragrance. I also have a strong affinity for boozy notes. Then, in the new releases, this blue Kilian bottle actually caught my eye. In short: It came just in time. The story behind it sounded great too: Did they really create a spirit fragrance that comes across as absolutely fresh and summery?

The first reviews of this fragrance show that the new Kilian will likely bring quite a bit of discussion potential. First of all, it is worth considering what expectations I have for a fragrance that, a) is in this price range b) is presumably meant to represent a fresh, citrusy summer scent. From this alone, I believe discrepancies can be drawn.

... or the blue side of the moon? Whatever it is, the scent is great. There are extremely cold spots, especially at the beginning. It indulges in lemon and "Calone," a somewhat mysterious fragrance ingredient that is supposed to evoke "sea air." Slightly salty, very cool, along with spicy notes reminiscent of "Norwegian fjords" .. "Stella Polaris" - and blue Moon.

Have you ever wondered what it smells like when you get accidentally drenched with a 25-euro gin and tonic by a model in a luxury club on Mykonos? Just like this. The opening is so incredibly fresh and citrusy that you briefly forget you’re actually sitting in a stuffy subway and not on the deck of a super yacht.

I tested this fragrance in a perfume store, directly on the skin, and also received a sample. Right from the first spray, a dominant oud cloud greets you. Very animalistic and powerful, yet not overwhelming. It feels very balanced, and there’s a kind of freshness, almost menthol-like smokiness that complements it very well. The rose is very much in the background, but is perceptible from the very beginning. For me, this is by far the best oud fragrance so far. The only downside is the unfortunately very high price.

After being able to test the scent on my skin once again today, I now feel ready to write a full comment about it. The scent is exceptional in a certain way. With many oud fragrances, the oud is hardly noticeable in the opening until it eventually bursts forth, making it difficult to perceive anything else. Here, it's exactly the opposite. The opening is pure oud, almost a bit stinky. Hour by hour, more fruity-citrus notes become present. In addition to the oud, which continues to play the main role but is no longer stinky. And Kankuro is right in his statement. The fruity-citrus notes are not light but rather intensely liqueur-like. This fits well with the also extremely intense oud! The longevity and sillage are out of this world, corresponding to 10/10. There’s no other word for it than "room-filling." Conclusion: An extremely intense oud fragrance, where the oud is not undressed but dressed. That's something different. I recommend buying it, as long as money is no object! Cheers!

I love sweets, but there are times I would trade one of those stylized, mouthwatering desserts made from the kitchen full of component parts for a perfect croissant. Plug-in whatever other $300+ perfume for the dessert, Amber Oud is the croissant. Forget that it costs the price of a ticket to Paris to get said ideal croissant, Amber Oud is the perfect combination, the ideal calibration of amber and oud (big amber, little oud) that makes me want to sniff myself all day. A croissant is the product of superb quality simple ingredients, understanding of the role of the ingredients and skill. All the bad croissants in the world tell you that simple doesn't mean easy. Ditto for AO. The problem is the price and my lust for more perfume. If I could afford Amber Oud I first have to make the Odyssey across the following dessert courses: Histoires de Parfum: 1804, Petroleum and Noir Patchouli Parfumerie Generale: Cuir d’Iris, Felania and Tubereuse Couture Andy Tauer: Loretta, Carillon pour un Ange and l’Air du Désert Marocain The entire line of les Nereides null of these choices is slumming it. It's not as though I'd be taking a loaf of Wonder Bread instead of the croissant. Set against this competition AO wouldn't stand a chance.

I was truly surprised by Amber Oud, because I actually expected oud. But instead, I got a very pretty amber, comprised of vanilla and benzoin with a dash of spice. This amber is nicely balanced, and it smells like the base of a classic, well-crafted oriental. Perhaps that is the intention of this fragrance: you get the name "oud" on the bottle, so you're trendy without actually having to like oud. But if you're expecting a deep, beautiful oud, as I was, look elsewhere.

Today a sample of amber oud came with te mail. A small present from Kilian. When I spray it on I smell the dry scent from the oud, but only briefly. The amber and vanilla are very prominent. This is a sweet woody scent, but oud? no.

So far the perfume of By kilian that I liked the most. Amber Oud is a resinous, woody, sweet and warm perfume, with a green touch at the beginning, which differentiates it from the rest and makes it extremely interesting. From the beginning you feel amber and benzoin with a vaporous halo of vanilla, amazing, but at the beginning they are cushioned by a green and fresh sensation. I did not know the note of malagueta, but it has to be she who brings this freshness. This does not last more than 5 minutes and soon, a few nuances of precious amber and benzoin, wrapped in an almost dusty vanilla that oozes an extraordinary elegance, emerge in all its splendor. It is not a gourmand vanilla of current style, it is more, a semi-vanilla, sober and fine vanilla. The aroma gradually loses that dusty sensation and begins to appear woody nuances in the background, which are becoming sharp while the aroma is dying. The end is a very tame oud, nothing wild, westernized to the fullest, resinous, spicy, warm and velvety, with a benzoin and amber, dim, but notorious, of exceptional quality. The duration has been about 8 hours or so, and its wake is rather moderate from the beginning, a tad more intense at the beginning, but not somewhat exaggerated. It is a warm and resinous perfume of cold or temperate climates and preferably nocturnal, but, for a cold winter morning it is also perfect. I loved the perfume, but its price is an earthenware that obscures everything else, it is excessive and prohibitive, we go armed robbery. If you are interested, better go for the recharge that is much cheaper, but if you can afford it, go ahead, it is beautiful, to everyone else, better not to try it, because as you like, you are lost lol.

By Kilian Amber Oud is a refined take on a Western-style amber – leathery, woody, and ever-so-slightly-characterless. There’s a whiff of campfire smoke at the edges, but its unique selling point is really its politeness. An amber that merely hints at the spice and roughness of other ambers, and an oud that is non-existent. I am always surprised at this scent’s popularity until I remember that it is the perfect solution for people who dislike both amber and oud.

I have had my sample for a long while & have used it on/off for sometime. So now that I am wearing it to bed, I decided to write a review. Kilian tires to create a nice Amber/Oud concoction since it seems as if the rest of the fragrance world is going into that direction. I find that Amber Oud is made with good ingredients, & the presentation is nice as well.
Since I finally visited BeautyAffair in Düsseldorf, I wanted to try out the Kilian fragrances alongside the Frederic Malle collection - they looked so elegantly expensive.

Last night, I happened to come across the fragrance "Amber Oud" by by Kilian again. The nice lady from Beauty Affair in Düsseldorf had given it to me with the note that it is an Oud scent that is not "bitey". My previous experiences with Oud mostly fall into the category of "you can wear it, but you don't have to".

Well, I like amber and I like oud, but the latter only when it's processed correctly. I actually like this scent as well, but the top note is horrendous. I really struggle to put into words the almost foul smell of the top note. AO starts off very sweet, and the oud note is already distinctly present.

Which scent is worthy of being my first after a long abstinence, I thought to myself... This one! I am not a fan of oud scents, I am old school. But Fumerie Turque by Serge Lutens is still buzzing around on my "faves" list and there has been nothing comparable... until now! Amber Oud! The top note didn't take my breath away, just my breath.

By Kilian CRUEL INTENTIONS is an oddly beautiful perfume. It takes a few wearings to wrap one's nose around it, but once one gets over the fact that this creation is completely intergeneric, not falling squarely into any of the standard categories, then one can begin to appreciate the composition. The opening of CRUEL INTENTIONS, to my nose, is quite green, but there is also a strong incense presence. As the fragrance dries down, the wood becomes more prominent, and I begin to detect an ebony-like facet, which appears to be produced as a result of the oud conjoined with some of the other components. By the drydown, I find the quasi-ebony note so marked that I am reminded of Tokyo Milk DEAD SEXY or Love & Toast POMME POIVRE, both of which I would recommend for testing by anyone who likes CRUEL INTENTIONS. I should say that the two Margot Elena creations are not at all the same--devoid as they are of the green-tinged incense opening of the By Kilian--but they are oddly appealing in the same way. The texture of all three seems somehow chewy to me. I find CRUEL INTENTIONS rather addictive and would love to have a bottle. It's neither feminine or nor masculine. Not overly oriental but also not exactly green or woody. Eccentric and unique is what I'd call it! Of the perfumes of this line which I've tested, this is by far one of the best.

Cruel Intentions reminds me something ... can't put my finger on it. I get a bit of Encre Noir (Femme) with the rose & vetiver, but it's the styrax, I think ... or maybe gaiac or agarwood. Puzzles me and causes me to take even more deep breathes of this fine fragrance. I love this. Very well-balanced fragrance with just a hint of florals. I've had some difficulty wearing the sweet or boozy Kilian fragrances. However, I find Cruel Intentions unusual and right up my alley. Unisex for sure, maybe just on the femme side, if that. I've sampled most everything in the sampler pack, and for me Cruel Intentions & Back to Black are full bottle worthy. Highly recommend giving this one a try.

Not one of By Kilian's better efforts. I find Cruel Intentions very cloying with a synthetic smelling rose/orange combination that just does not work. The scent is pretty linear and has very good staying power. In this case, both of those are *not* good things. Not worth the selling price, and not a recommended buy at any price, IMO. I think By Kilian must have had "Cruel Intentions" indeed when they unleashed this 2 star out of 5 composition on prospective buyers.

I love dark fragrances, but only when they truly come across as bitter, smoky, and cool. Cruel Intentions starts off beautifully for me. Up until the heart note, I really like the scent and I was already ready to pull the trigger to add it to my wish list. Oud is - very pleasantly for me - only very subtly present, and I can understand Egoproxy's comparison to M7 well. The Kilian scent is even more elegant. However, as the fragrance develops, Cruel Intentions takes on a creamy, almost greasy animalistic note that ruins the mood for me again. It somehow doesn’t fit together. The character of the fragrance changes so much for my nose that I no longer want it. I also don’t really know what Castoreum truly smells like. Perhaps, unlike musk and especially civet, I am overly sensitive here, but this note is extremely unpleasant for me. For a creamy fragrance, Cruel Intentions is too dark and too bitter, and for a dark bitter fragrance, the animalistic note is too soft and sticky. There’s also nothing that softens the transition, giving the fragrance a framework. I find Cruel Intentions unharmonious, and that’s very unfortunate because I had high expectations for it.

Of course, the name of this fragrance first made me think of the film of the same name with Ryan Philippe and Sarah Michelle Gellar, as I belong to the generation that watched it giggling far below the age rating with a handful of friends during late-night movie nights in Dad's hobby cellar. My enthusiasm for the film only lasted a short time, but I still think the soundtrack is great. Who doesn't know the heartbreakingly beautiful song by The Verve from the dramatic closing scene of Cruel Intentions? I find the fragrance bittersweet as well, and it is undoubtedly dramatic. Here, in contrast to the song, the "bitter" is emphasized, not the sweetness. Those who can't handle this scent mood should better stay away from it altogether, because the opening alone is medicinal, herbal, and yes... in my nose, even a bit metallic. A heavy, dark rose only greets me after about five minutes of pharmacy feeling. The scent exudes a classic Gothic aura for me, or, if you prefer, it gets quite noir. Mysterious and dramatic, it sneaks up on you without immediately making a loud olfactory statement. (Unlike "A taste of heaven". For Cruel Intentions, you definitely need more time to form a clear judgment. It is dark but not warm. It becomes increasingly sweetish but not sweet. This is more of a human, as they say, animalistic sweetness that becomes heavier over time. Behind the rosy romance, it slumbers resinous and bitter. The combination of rose and oud certainly has seductive qualities, as found in "Loukhoum parfum du soir". But this is a different caliber altogether. Cruel Intentions does not arrive on velvet paws, and delicious is something else. This fragrance is not for flirting and batting eyelashes. It bites you in the neck after the first twenty minutes. Not everyone appreciates that. What I definitely want to express is the question of wearability. Of course, there are more intense, aggressive scents in this direction. Still, I seriously wonder whom I would really buy this fragrance from. I have a classic, seductive villain in mind. And yes, here we come to the "evil intentions" for which Ryan Philippe is clearly too boyish and well-behaved. With Cruel Intentions, you certainly won't get a prude virgin into bed, that much is certain. Moreover, this perfume remains, despite its darkness, quietly and subtly in the broadest sense. I don't even think you would stand out or make an impression with it at first sniff. You would definitely have to get closer, as the sillage is quite polite by Kilian standards. But the truly nasty villains, as we know, don't just barge in; they sneak up slowly. Can I identify with it? No. Therefore, this fragrance remains for me a kind of superhero dream to which I can occasionally escape. That's why the sample will also be saved for special occasions.

Well, what 'cruel intentions' might Madame Lancesseur have had in mind when she created this fragrance? Were they wicked intentions of an 'ice-cold angel', or mean plans of 'dangerous liaisons'..... Or did her 'cruel intentions' simply amount to an attempt to place a copy?

Price: Abnormally high 30ml travel spray for €90; 50ml bottle for €175; however, the refills are significantly cheaper.
