THE TURNING POINT: I held my arm as far from my nose as possible, afraid I would have to smell it again. I thought, “you can’t possibly give this fragrance away. You can’t be responsible for that.” It had something of drain cleaner, toilet bowl cleaner, and air freshener. After half an hour, suddenly, cedar and ambrette mix in... and the scent becomes WONDERFUL. All of a sudden, the peach smells so velvety and powdery that you almost want to cry for it and wish you had more. Light Clouds becomes warmer, less sterile, and gets a very, very sweet plastic note. Plastic note? Yes, I mean it seriously. I love this note and wish I could say exactly how it comes about and what fragrance ingredient it is. Then I would only buy fragrances with such a pyramid. Maybe it’s the cedarwood? I’ll try to describe it. It’s very warm (not sensual-sexy but peaceful-cozy-baby warm) and smells slightly sweet (maybe vanilla-like). Do you remember those dolls from back in the day? Cabbage Patch Kids? EXACTLY like their skin, THAT’S how the base of this perfume smells. In summary, it smells in the drydown like doll skin with a hint of peach, anything but cheap. And just when it becomes so wonderful, Light Clouds fades away again. Just like clouds do... The most beautiful moments are unfortunately also the most fleeting. Well. The scent experience lasts a mere 2 hours on my skin, and if you subtract the first terrible 30 minutes, you’re left with only 90 minutes. The name says it all. These clouds are so LIGHT, it’s a shame that there’s only the EDT; I would pay more for an EdP. So terribly beautiful, this fragrance definitely deserves a comment and should be sniffed, especially by peach fans, musk fans, lotus fans, clean and baby care fans. Whether terribly beautiful or quite terrible, anything in between is really possible! I’m curious to see how you perceive it.

Light Clouds bounces and frolics right at the beginning, full of energy and good mood, at my feet. (o; Pleasantly unsweet, fresh and clean, a bit like foamy laundry detergent, and thus also captivating, bubbling and "Hello - here I am." A fresh, floral-woody musk scent that lifts the spirits and embodies lightness. Moschino has captured the character of the fragrance not only with the name but also visually very aptly with the motif of this radiant blue sky plus white clouds. However, I find that the little cloud could be driven by a bit more of a brisk wind. Light Clouds has dynamism for me, but less depth than other musk fragrances. Still, I find it good just the way it is, as it occupies its corner very independently, and maybe it is meant to be exactly that? The longevity is, for me, like with almost all Moschino fragrances, not so great. A tip: definitely wear it in high heat! That's when it develops the most beautifully.

Attention, good vibes come from this bottle! When people say "Baaah, who drinks that?", I usually raise my finger. Of course, I also drink plenty of healthy water and spritzers and so on, but I confess: I have a thing for bizarre drinks. Dr. Pepper, Cherry Coke, Cream Soda, Vanilla Snapple - bring it on! The more artificial and extravagant, the better. And if Light Clouds were a drink, it would fit perfectly into this category. This musk smells so strangely artificial, so oddly synthetic - and so incredibly delicious. This interplay of jasmine and rose with peach and lotus (I get along quite well with lotus) is so sparklingly composed, one immediately thinks of fizzing bubbles dancing at the top of a glass of fizzy lemonade. A light, bright woodiness captures the scent a bit, without losing its lightness. But the musk is the main theme, and this is not a cuddly musk, but rather one of the clean kind. However, it does not become sharply soapy, but instead becomes fluffy-fresh and quite delicately citrus-sweet through the floral and fruity notes. Moschino Cheap and Chic Light Clouds is a cheerful, fun, sparkling, bubbly, bright, and carefree musk scent, like I believe there is no second one. Tivellon is right: it occupies its corner very independently. One more word about the bottle: Yes, yes, they are funny, the originally Popeye's Olive-inspired comic-like figurative perfume containers from Moschino Cheap and Chic. And not at all to my taste. And that white "collar" is dangerous: if the sprayer is not positioned exactly over the indentation of the heart-shaped plastic part, the lovely scent gets stuck halfway in the collar while spraying and shoots right back onto the spraying fingers. Category: impractical bottles. But once you get the hang of it (in the truest sense of the word), nothing can dampen the good mood that comes from this bottle.

I have loved Light Clouds since it was first released and have repurchased it several times! Not because the scent smells like blue skies, white clouds, or a spring morning, as one might expect, but because it is a unique blend of many different notes that I equally enjoy.

So, red top, black skirt, hair up, misted with Light Clouds. Today I'm trying to see how Olivia Oyl feels while cleaning. I can definitely say that I'm more motivated than usual. Who really enjoys cleaning? The lovely violet surrounds me. It feels cool, which is nice since it’s 23 degrees today. Very refreshing. Jasmine, rose, peach, they are all there.

...like on clouds when I wear this fragrance. Right now in spring, this scent absolutely lifts my spirits. I predominantly perceive the violet, jasmine, and peach. Not overpowering - just refreshing (as if made for this season). In the end, a hint of musk sneaks into my nose - also very pleasant.

Joséphine de Beauharnais was the first wife of Napoleon Bonaparte. The marriage lasted from 1796 to 1810. She was divorced because the 16 years older Josephine could not bear children for the Emperor. During her marriage, Josephine was essentially the pop icon of her time. She was devoted to all beautiful things and brought the fashion and hairstyles of the Empire (in the style of ancient Roman women) into vogue. As she was also a fragrance enthusiast, she had perfumes created for her. These were primarily musky. When Josephine had to move out after her divorce from Napoleon, the musk scent could not be removed from her chambers. Everything had to be thoroughly renovated. That is exactly the crux of the matter for me. I have nothing against musk in fragrances. It gives them depth, warmth, and something unfathomable. But here, the spirit of Josephine is chasing after me, and she has been dead since 1814. Whenever a little cloud rises, I feel like the Ghostbusters, who see the apparition in the library in the first movie. The slightly sharp ginger opening note quickly evaporates, and the ghost from the library puts a finger to its lips, only to immediately rush at me, stuffing me with a Christmas spice mix. Then the floating lady opens her mouth and spits musk at me. I wish for a ghost trap! But since there is no perfume ghost trap, this scent poltergeist haunts me for hours. If anyone wants it, here you go. I have packed it with pointed fingers into my decants.

With a bare (red) carpet, today's rose is not satisfied - here it is tarred. Specifically: that twist on some scents with rose and labdanum, which, despite certain sweetness and floral notes, leans towards the oily-tarry. Yet, although characteristically quite strong, the application is careful and measured. The second layer of the designated let’s-call-it-carpet consists of unclean musk, while the third layer is creamy-waxy from the borderline resin corner. Perhaps the base has become a bit slippery after applying the second and third layers, as the actual appearance of the rose is relatively cautious, and more candy-like fruity than floral-heavy. More young woman than lady, one could say pointedly. All the more striking is the interplay with the musk, which opts for hints rather than boldness. The not particularly queenly queen of flowers indeed gradually allows the musk to take the lead, which in turn is enhanced by waxy sweetness at the threshold of vanilla and mild creamy resin. Nothing becomes "animalistic" in the stricter sense, although the scent is pleasantly far from the typical clean musk. Still, I find it more cozy than animalistic. A hint of light wood adds a pleasant airiness in context. Around noon, I can finally detect a hint of a medicinal oud note in the mixture, and this at the latest underscores the firmly established impression that we are dealing with a tastefully balanced mixture of very characterful, yet subtly used ingredients that truly deserves the attribute "exquisite." And since "exquisite" and "biscuit" sound quite similar, I only wonder with a half raised eyebrow about a note reminiscent of gently caramelized shortcrust pastry with a dollop of cream filling in the afternoon. Conceptually, it may dampen the matter a bit - but I enjoy it. In any case, it can be considered an intermezzo, as 'Exquisite Musk' had already found its final line hours earlier. Conclusion: Successful. I thank Ergoproxy for the sample.

Liminality describes a threshold state. The term comes from ritual theory. It precisely describes the transitional state of an individual who is about to shift from one condition or status to another. A prime example is the knighting ceremony, just at the moment when one, so to speak - (to put it quite bluntly) - "receives" the new status, one glides into it, and it is precisely there that the liminal phase exists, between the so-called "before" and "after" states. Sounds complicated and cumbersome? Yes, that's correct. EM has that special something that only appears in a wonderfully magical moment. The most magnificent and moving feature of the fragrance is its balance. The proportions are so harmonious and aesthetically pleasing, yet so tasteful. Everything is rounded and coordinated, simply cultivated. The blend of strength and elegance is also perfectly balanced. EM is a lush and quite powerful fragrance, impressive and substantial. The notes are naturally delicate, but the emphasis with which the fragrance is composed is paradisiacal. The balance begins right at the opening, when the rose is interwoven and surrounded by spice, unveiling the exquisite musk. The aesthetic brilliance was already evident in this way with Musc by Mona di Orio. I find that both fragrances are somewhat similar in this regard. The distinctly feminine charisma of the fragrance is not merely complemented by animalistic notes but enriched. The balancing act between strength and beauty is superbly achieved. Flowers and strong animalistic nuances simultaneously centralize and complement each other. Wonderful soft musk with velvety gentle labdanum form a symbiosis of worlds. The notes are so artistically composed that one would think they are actually smelling them for the first time. My nose detects a gasoline note, which it has already sniffed out in Trance by Schwarzlose Berlin, Caldo Orientale by Officina delle Essenze, and Bois de Gayac by Antonio Visconti. However, this gasoline note is not the crux of the fragrance, although it is a contributing factor. EM is more feminine than masculine, even though this discussion is somewhat tedious and I do not advocate for any differentiation between men's and women's fragrances. It just seems to me that the ladies will probably enjoy this fragrance more than we male noses. And aside from that, this categorization does not change the fact that the "Collection Orientale" has been enriched with a true work of art.

I'm quite an admirer of Moschino, particularly their fruity florals. I do however enjoy their stronger, more 'golden', sophisticated scents like Couture, Moschino and of course Glamour. I did not take my nose from my wrist for many an hour when I first sprayed Glamour. I was initially intrigued by its smooth elegance and distinguishable Italian style. To me it smells cozy yet extravagant. It has a really pretty exotic richness, mostly brought about by the salt and frangipani notes. I can tell it's a different kind of fragrance straight away, and that's what I love about Moschino, they take risks. I liken this fragrance to the scent of an exclusive bar in a five star restaurant. It's slightly boozy, but it also smells of flowers and a mixture of women's expensive perfumes wafting through the air. The scent is balanced, even a touch smokey at times, but all in all, quite fresh and feminine. The drydown is smooth, naturally sweet and woodsy, a delicious blend of amber and cedar. I'm really enjoying this fragrance throughout every part of its development. I'm a little shocked to see that there are some people that dislike Glamour. I think it deserves more praise than it is given.

Usually flankers are launched subsequent to a wildly popular iconic perfume in order to capitalize on the successful marketing campaign already underway by quickly creating some other juice and putting it in more or less the same bottle and giving it a similar name. All of this creates the impression that the new release is going to be just as exciting as its namesake. More often than not, in my experience, the flanker is a disappointment relative to the original, often, I believe, because less effort and financial investment is put into the composition of flanker formulas. They seem usually to be slightly tweaked versions which may or may not work as well as the original perfume did. In the case of Moschino GLAMOUR, I find that basically the opposite happened. Perhaps it is because I wore Moschino TOUJOURS GLAMOUR (the flanker) several times before trying its namesake, but the truth is that I feel that the flanker is a vastly improved version. true, I love violets, and they are prominent in the flanker and absent in GLAMOUR. In a side-by-side comparison, I definitely prefer TOUJOURS GLAMOUR to GLAMOUR, but I also think that GLAMOUR, judged on its own terms, is a pretty basic and generic light floriental fragrance which does not stand out from the crowd. Despite the exciting list of notes, GLAMOUR ends up smelling to me like just another inoffensive floriental among hundreds. It's definitely wearable, and does not turn stale or rank, but the sillage is low and longevity poor, and although I'll wear what I have, I probably will not purchase it again. If you like violets and are trying to decide between GLAMOUR and TOUJOURS GLAMOUR, I'd definitely recommend the latter. On the other hand, if you are a violet-phobe, you might prefer GLAMOUR!

Glamour is an upbeat and modern scent. When I bought this perfume I was somewhat influenced by the name thinking that this will be a glamorous evening scent but after wearing it a few times I can picture it more on a young model in a funky designer outfit walking on the runway to an upbeat song. This scent definitely has a modern vibe and could be worn on a casual night out with friends or to work. The opening of this fragrance is sweet and fresh at the same time. There is also almost an herbal note from the artemisia. The scent develops into a floral bouquet, mostly hibiscus, coated in a large doze of sweetness. The composition remains linear in this sweet hibiscus state for quite some time. The sillage is quite nice on my skin. It is not overpowering but not too light. After 4 hours I end up with a skin scent of a light musk. It is definitely a nice, modern scent to try but I recommend testing before buying. At times I absolutely love it and other times it just does not work for me. Perhaps this is due to its rather unique composition that mixes the warm, sweet floral notes with slightly cool, herbal and salty accord. I find that it works better for me in the fall and winter time and when it works, it smells chic and sophisticated.

With about 500 women's fragrances on our shelves (I stopped counting at 370), there are always some that are overlooked for inexplicable reasons. By customers and by us as well. Glamour is one of them, and I only stumbled upon it again because we wonderfully received samples of it. I sprayed the fragrance in the store and shrugged it back onto the shelf. Today, however, at home in a neutral environment, I am giving Glamour another chance, trying to commit it to my fragrance memory. Glamour contains mugwort in the top note. That doesn’t sound particularly glamorous. They could have at least mentioned the Latin name Artemisia. That sounds quite different. Mugwort is part of the medicinal herbs, and even in old goose roast recipes, it is recommended to include the herb in the stuffing. We all know mugwort as a weed by the roadside, but hardly anyone knows that today. So here, the fine spicy, almost bitter note in the opening of the perfume is triggered by it. Unfortunately, only in the top note; I wish the aroma would accompany the fragrance further. I can't detect salt, but I do perceive the fruity floral aroma of hibiscus alongside the other floral notes. This heart note also appears radiant, becoming more lovely, and here the glamour does indeed shine through. But I would wish for it to be louder and more extraordinary. The shine feels somewhat muted, and I also miss a note that could give the fragrance more recognizability. The well-known base gives the flowers adhesion and warmth, and surprisingly, the Artemisia theme becomes more noticeable again, and the longevity is quite satisfactory. I now also know what bothers me about this fragrance, what triggers the shrug. It’s not the scent experience, but the name. It evokes certain expectations that the perfume cannot fulfill. If the fragrance were called "Private Moschino," "Moschino Fleur," or "My Moschino," Glamour would surely get more chances to be considered. But when a customer is looking for an evening fragrance, I think of everything possible, just not Moschino Glamour. And a customer searching for a daytime fragrance wouldn’t even reach for the tester because of the name. So once again, the target group is missed. Well, let’s see if the samples distributed bring any feedback, and I’m also curious if Moschino Glamour will come to mind in the future when someone is looking for a pleasant floral-fruity scent with an adult presence.

~ Inspiration ~ In my last swap, I received a sample of "Glamour" from the lovely CrazyCat. ~ Bottle ~ The shape reminds me of an apple - similar to the "Poison" series by Dior. The bottle is adorned in various shiny gold shades, decorated with a kind of stole and a striking red cap. ~ Scent ~ Upon spraying, it is still a bit green and slightly piercing due to the mugwort, a breeze of salt, and tangerine blossoms. After a few minutes, a floral heart unfolds with hibiscus, lotus, and orchids. It dries down warm and slightly woody with amber, white musk, and cedar. ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts around 7 hours (a bit longer on clothes and hair). 2 sprays are enough; otherwise, it becomes too piercing for me at first. ~ Occasion ~ It fits well in spring and autumn (also for the office). You can wear it both during the day and in the evening, as it is neither too light nor too heavy. ~ Conclusion ~ I really like the scent. By the way, I find it has a slight resemblance to "Amor Amor" by Cacharel.

I admit, with this perfume I unfortunately let myself be too much swayed by the appearance when making the purchase. A small apple-shaped bottle, with a red cap, a golden top scarf, and champagne-colored liquid. All in all, it came across very royal, fit excellently in the hand, and matched the name "Glamour." Unfortunately, I do not find the scent particularly glamorous.

I received the fragrance as a Christmas gift in 2008. My mom took me to Müller, and I was allowed to choose a perfume. I remember that I grabbed a bottle from the shelf more or less aimlessly, as I had no idea back then. However, I was particularly drawn to the aesthetically questionable bottles ("Just look at that kitschy bottle!

Today, my sample bottles from Essenza Nobile arrived. Among them was this delicious scent. I roughly sniffed all 6 bottles. You're not really supposed to judge a fragrance this way, but the scent already smelled amazing on the tester. I had to spray it on myself immediately and was completely thrilled. The scent feels very familiar to me.

Dior Addict. Chanel Allure. Lalique Amethyst. I love fragrances with vanilla… but those with Bourbon Vanilla wins. Somehow my nose tunes in and tells my brain that my knees should start shaking, my lips should tremble and then drip and my heart should go crazy. The fullness, the sweetness, the spicy element in this note - it is to die for. If I would ever be so privileged to design my own personal perfume, bourbon vanilla will be in the base. In huge amounts. Together with almond. The two get along well. I could dive into it - swim in it - and scrub my skin with it. It is a note, that calms and makes you smile. In Cinéma it is too little. The scent is nice but it never assures me that it is worth wearing. The vanilla, however, is a good reason why one would try and wear this. Not the best of the wonderful YSL’s. 322/365

I remember very well when this scent came out but I never tested before, I don't know why it didn't attract me in the past. Today, while I was coming home, I went in a drugstore for testing some scents and I found this fragrance too , so I decided to try it, finally. it was a very nice surprise. Immediately the bright and fizzy clementine note came to my nose with its energizing and renvigorating effect (I was so tired!) , then I smelled the flowery bouquet, soft and well harmonized , extremely feminin. So, I thought: "Now I understand the reason of the name...maybe because it's a fragrance as bright as a movie star !" At last, the vanilla base note arrived: round, sweet but not sweetish, perfectly balanced and cocooning, giving that special warmth to this "limelight-scent". The longevity and the sillage are quite good although it isn't a heavy and so longlasting fragrance. it could be perfect for an event in crowded places because it's a pleasant and intoxicating scent , but quite discrete at the same time. Last but not least, the particular and refined squared bottle with the golden cap and the writings . Ysl scent are usually quite expensive and this one too isn't cheap, but I think it could be considered one of the contemporary classics of the perfumery.Let's play to the movie stars!
This is a review for a fragrance I rarely wear myself but i do enjoy it as something on to smell on others. Yves Saint Laurent's Cinema (edt version). Hope you enjoy the review.

I love autumn, especially for its smells. Cinema's warm vanilla-balsamic scent reminds me so much of October evenings when the air feels crisp and clear and the maple leaves give off a slight sweetness as they curl up and turn brown on the lawn and crunch underfoot. I wore it a lot (during my air-conditioned evenings) to get me through the hottest parts of last summer (in the 90s F/33+C) and remind me that the soothing coolness is coming. It enchants me much less when the weather is actually cool, at which time it seems a little bit too high-pitched.

The first Moschino fragrance (and the best, frankly) was launched in 1990 and discontinued somewhere in the 00's. This is an example of a good fragrance that came pretty later in the party. At 1990, we already had the big wave of brutal macho leather-animalic scents that became popular among every guy. Kouros, Antaeus, Jules, etc... and the classics Cuir de Russie, Knize ten, etc... we're a bit dated too. At that time, freshness was the key and the "soup de jour". Cool Water (1988), New West (1988) or even Fahrenheit (1988) with its fresh violet leaf were great successes and Moschino wanted to enter in the perfume world. They could chose a fresh scent or citrusy one, or even a classic fougère but they opted to make something more bold and, perhaps, dated. Allegedly created by Françoise Caron, this is basically a leather chypre scent with some spicy woods and creamy balsamics. Opens very bitter, fresh and green but with a woody sweetness underneath. As it dries down, the labdanum and styrax help intensify the leather creaminess and the scent became more rounded, a bit sweet and still, somehow, bitter. The leather here is not like a new car leather (Tuscan Leather, Ombré Leather, Etc...) neither a classical floral one (Knize Ten, for example). It's more something between the creamy greeness of BelAmi (1986) and the rich bitter leather accord of Antaeus (1981). Very rich and multilayered, this masculine combines every bit of leather chypre compositions in the past and make it, somehow, italian. Rounded, sexy, fresh and relaxed. But it came out later in the game and no one cared. It would had been a real classic if it came out 10 years earlier. The longevity is not beast mode, rather average but it works. It gives this relaxed Italian vibe which I think it's brilliant. 6-8h with moderate projection. If you overspray it, it would last a bit more. I think this is one of those that needs more sprays to fully enjoy it. The good news here is that you can find pretty good deals on this one. Because it not a very well known fragrance, the prices are quite decent actually. I recommend it as a piece of history, a relaxed version of BelAmi or just for the bottle that looks awesome, by the way. I have the Vice-versa version from 1990 (pre barcode) with Spray and Splash mechanism and it looks great! Moschino hasn't many masculine fragrances and, apart from this, I really like Uomo? Eau de Toilette but the rest is very average, including the more recent Toy Boy . So, do yourself a favor and, if you like leathers and chypres, try to find a bottle of this gem and enjoy it. 4/5

Moschino pour Homme goes on with aromatic lavender with a faint slightly animalic castoreum laden leathery undertone. Moving to the early heart a strong green oakmoss emerges as co-star with the castoreum, labdanum and styrax derived animalic leather, with the aromatic lavender remaining as diminished support, joined by significant carnation and slightly powdery rose florals. During the late dry-down the composition eschews its florals and most of the oakmoss, leaving dry leather sans its animalic facet as sole star through the finish. Projection is very good and longevity excellent at around 12 hours on skin. Moschino pour Homme may technically be a 90's composition, but stylistically it takes me back to my favorite decade of perfumery, the 80s. The composition starts off with a tremendous hit of aromatic lavender, but even from the start the animalic leather peeps into the open, asserting itself early. By the time the composition moves to its middle, the animalic leather takes command, though with a very strong oakmoss co-star. The combination of the leather and oakmoss tandem with the supporting carnation and rose florals is absolutely superb smelling. By the time the composition moves to its late dry-down the leather sheds its animalic castoreum infusion, utilizing the remnants of the styrax and labdanum to create its dry leather finish with maybe just a touch of tonka bean derived sweetness, but not much. The leather dry-down is fabulous, completing the wonderful experience provided top-to-bottom. I have heard Moschino pour Homme compared to Puredistance M and vintage Bel Ami by some, but I really don't see much similarity between them (aside from them all being superb smelling leather compositions). A bit closer to my nose, though still quite different is Leonard pour Homme, a composition composed a decade earlier and one of the best leathers ever created. When a composition is compared to so many leather greats, you know the perfumer has done something right, and Moschino pour Homme can rightfully take its place alongside those great leathers of past and present with pride. The bottom line is the under $100 per 100ml bottle on the aftermarket discontinued Moschino pour Homme is an excellent example of how to do a leather composition right, representing one of the best offerings of the 90s and earning an "Excellent" to "Outstanding" 4 to 4.5 stars out of 5 and an extremely strong recommendation.

I found a well preserved bottle of this rugged Italian marvel. I remember sampling Moschino in a magazine in the early 90s. It has all of the strength of other 80s Italian powerhouses like Fendi or Versace. Its larger than life with the leather and rose. You just don't find this in anymore in the men's market. The box is golden with clever logos-hearts, spades and yin-yangs. The bottle is stunning. Its hefty and resembles a whisky bottle. One spray on the skin has a warming and intoxicating effect. Everything about it is perfect. The opening is refreshing, the leather is soft yet rugged and the rose floral notes flirt openly. Then, like a big pair of arms hugs you in its warmth of amber, benzoin and laudanum. I really feel there was a new class evolving for men. It was the "leather floriental" that began in Italy and has been lost. Ironically, it was popular for about 20 years and has vanished from todays market. This was easily worn at raves until dawn. Its a dragonfly in amber and worth having in any serious collection

Françoise Caron. Françoise Caron, who worked at Roure Bertrand Dupont in 1990, is at least mentioned in the recently published book 'The Handbook of Great Italian Perfumery: Fifty Years of Exceptional Scents' (2021) by Italian author and perfume blogger Marika Vecchiattini. When I think of Françoise Caron, I first think of the eponymous house, whose Poivre and Le 3e Homme de Caron left formative impressions during my youthful encounters with perfume. Whether Françoise is related to Caron is unclear, but her name appears repeatedly as a co-author of Le 3e Homme. I also associate Françoise Caron with Eau d'Orange Verte (1979) and Cuiron pour Homme (2002). The identities of perfumers only came back into discussion in the 70s and 80s, aside from cases like Guerlain, where it was clear: family business, the perfumers could just as well be the Guerlains - Jean François Laporte's projects like Artisan and later Maitre Parfumeur are well-known examples of author perfumery from that time. Frédéric Malle's concept starting in 2000, to bring perfumers back into the spotlight as authors, quickly gained traction; nowadays, it is rather unusual for the perfumer not to be mentioned by name, at least in fine fragrances. For over 32 years, I had no idea who was behind Moschino Pour Homme. Like many Italian releases from the nebulous time of the late 80s and early 90s. A brief moment that represents a peak time for Italian men's fragrances for me. All of them herbal-medical and already slightly experimental, industrial, even kitschy, the l'air du temps of the late 80s. Post-Italodisco zeitgeist, craft-solid, a bit modern. But it didn't really matter who invented or designed it; we are talking about designer fragrances: Versace (Versus Uomo), Trussardi (Action Uomo), or Moschino - the brand was in the spotlight. As I said, I did not learn about Françoise Caron's attribution to Moschino Pour Homme through a database entry; Vecchiattini's book contains an entry (1 page, two columns) on Moschino Pour Homme. Italian (men's) perfumes from the late 80s fascinate me; they often stand out clearly from releases from other countries, happily combining herbal-heavy, slightly conservative elements with playful touches, which might have been considered pure heresy elsewhere. The mentioned Versus and also Action Uomo belong to this category, as do the Krizia trilogy Uomo, Moods, and Spazio. However, until now, I have been able to find little about the raison d'être of these differences, especially since, in the case of Moschino Pour Homme or Romeo Gigli's Uomo, non-Italian perfumers were involved. In short, with a 'Handbook of Great Italian Perfumery,' I hoped to gain some background information. I first heard about the book through a review by the enterprising Miguel Matos. Matos, whose work has not yet reached me - too retro-realistic, similar to bands that want to sound like Joy Division but better - nevertheless represented a potential guarantee due to his certainly meticulously executed vintage studies and confessions to Italian classics like Action Uomo. Unfortunately, I was far off; anyone hoping for insights into 70s, 80s, and early 90s perfumery in Italy will be disappointed here. The book covers a history of the Renaissance, Medici Italo-French connections, monastic influences, and early 20th century - thus providing the essential foundations for the base - but as it approaches the 'now,' it becomes thinner and often gets stuck in the common sense of marketing language. Besides the relevant information about Moschino Pour Homme, the best part is an index of Italian perfumes from 1970 to 2020, which also has questionable gaps; an iconic brand like Santa Maria Novella is only addressed with a few entries, while others, far more commercial, are considered with all flankers and Christmas editions. A good index is a Sisyphean task; a handbook for such a vast field is an even more complex one - the given production time of just 2 or 3 years may simply have been too short. Back to Moschino. This perfume is far from experimental approaches, and therein lies its difference. Franco Moschino was at times the Italian counterpart of the enfants terribles, as it was often said for Gaultier. From today's perspective, perhaps for what Vetements or Balenciaga are trying with sampling. The sublabel of Moschino was called 'Cheap & Chic'; there were peace signs, copyright symbols, acid house smileys, slogans like CONDOME, in short, it united even sworn enemies, Armani hardcore minimalists and Versace baroque enthusiasts, in a common fine image. Moschino Pour Homme was, however, an exceptionally classic Eau de Toilette, a kind of leather-chypre, which is often compared to Bel Ami - for me, that has never worked; it's like weighing an Hermès silk tie or horse blanket from the 80s (Bel Ami cocktail times) against a Moschino suit from 1990. Does not compute. Sure, there are overlapping contents, but processing, production, effect, and message are fundamentally different. In this regard, Moschino Pour Homme is not cheap at all, perhaps not even tres chic: it is leathery-floral, consistently spicier than, say, Bel Ami, slightly chypre, and equipped with a shimmering aldehydic opening and a balsamic drydown. The bottle and packaging were much closer to Moschino's principles: stamped gold paper, yin & yang, playing card motifs, spray, shake, as well as a 'vice-versa' version that was supposed to combine spray and shake mechanisms for the first time. Lastly, I had to think of Je suis un homme or Eau de Gloire - albeit with distinctly noticeable differences, this Moschino. Sometimes I still see the fragrance in pharmacies, where they still have aftershaves and eaux on some bottom shelf, dusty but surprisingly well preserved: Françoise Caron's wonderful Moschino Pour Homme.

... and indeed in classic perfumeries in Italy, and at a price that is charged here for mainstream fluff. One of the treasures I was able to acquire last month in Bolzano. A classically heavy winter fragrance. Naturally, warming, powerful. I initially notice a certain olfactory resemblance to the vintage of "Bel Ami," while the scent develops in a different direction as it progresses. It could be the coconut that adds a gourmand touch to it, alongside the chocolate and cocoa notes. Definitely not unsweet, but the sweetness is so beautifully integrated, and the scent overall is so elegantly composed that an old-schooler like me feels their heart swell once again. And once again, I stand somewhat moved, lost in memories of the good old days, in front of my perfume cabinet in my perfume room. Well, I am well-prepared for winter.

Proud as can be, I won one of the rare miniatures on eBay, full of anticipation for this fragrance that I last smelled 20 years ago. Disillusionment. The peppery top note that I greatly appreciated, which made this scent unique in my memory, dissipates within the first few minutes.
I had IT IN THE EARLY 90s, it was something extraordinary back then, but it’s no longer available, not even in Italy WHAT A SHAME))))))

For many years, I considered Opium (1977) as one of mom's scents: an oriental powerhouse that she overused and that I hated. But the older I've gotten, the more fragrances have descended into blend sameness, and the more Opium has seemed bold, original and gorgeous by comparison to the dreary rabble. Recently, I found a bottle of this concentration, Secret de Parfum, and love it is. The astringency of the mandarin and spices in the original softens here; the floracy amps up. The creaminess is off the charts. Highly recommended, if you can find it.

I definitely get the "cinnabar" vibe here. It's sweet, very balmy. Resinous. Incredibly intriguing to smell and wear. A lovely fragrance. Perfect on anyone "grown-up". Plus it's Yves Saint-Laurent, and a well worthy variation on the "Opium" name. Definitely recommended. Classy, mature and elegant.

I am the lucky owner of a 50ml bottle of The Gorgeous Juice from Heaven - aka Opium Secret de Parfum. I love the original Opium - a spicy and delicate classic from one of my favourite houses. So why bother making flankers, if the original is close to perfect? The answer is obvious: Opium SdP is the female version of the original, which in my world is a unisex. SdP has less notes than Opium (11 compared to 30 registered on Parfumo), so of course it is a different experience. It starts soapy/creamy and very soft. This feeling continues for a long time - more than three to four hours. Then it turns slightly more spicy and the base notes show their faces. It has an amazing longevity and sillage is 'enters the room a minute before the person and stays in the room for a week'-ish. It has an overall feminie expression, perhaps even seductive in a passive way. The bottle is lovely. If there was room for it in my top20, this would be an option. 234/365

It wasn't long ago that I would have vehemently excluded wearing, perhaps even testing, certain fragrances. Then, when I was absolutely sure: That's not me, not a part of me, not one of my many facets - this scent is not made for me. Fragrances like "Trésor," like "Poison" - although already worn - the old "Fahrenheit" and of course "Opium." Those oversized blockbusters that took your breath away and captivated the senses in a time long before this one. When no one thought of lightweight scents called "CK One," various Giò Acquas, and "Light Blue." They seemed slender, pale, and a bit undernourished like Kate Moss and all the boys and girls who wore them, aware of their otherness, which in itself is not a bad thing - as long as one survives it. Too weak for the blockbusters, not flat-chested enough for the model types, I sought my fortune in olfactory realms that were called "Senso" and "Moschino," "Azzaro 9," and whatever else they were called, the more-or-less signatures of that time. With them, I felt well-dressed in jeans, in a suit, or even in nothing; they were never too much and never too little. "You smell so good!" I was often told, rarely "We can smell you in the stairwell." Two sprays, at most three, that was all it needed. It couldn't be more, otherwise the scent would go to my head, prick my nose, punch my stomach, and it would no longer be pleasant. That this might be the reason for my problem with "Opium," "Fahrenheit," and co. only occurred to me later, many years later. In a time when hardly anyone wears these scents, when the air is saturated with sugary sweet life, "Hypnotic Poison," and black Opium. And of all that, usually far too much. Perhaps I had to grow and mature first, to learn to understand the stories that a life writes, and with it the scents we wear then and there. I had to become more awake and calmer until the door opened and from some source that can no longer be found, "Opium" found its way into my cave - not that new Opium, not that black one that is everywhere in stores today. A little vial of "Secret de Parfum" found its way to me - a spray-me-not, a dab-me-up with a long, narrow stick. That worked well, allowing me to feel my way forward in dosage like in a test that lasted long, many days, and yet hardly made the vial's contents noticeably dwindle. It was a "Hello again!" on the first breath - whoever has experienced "Opium" will always find it familiar. A "Hello again" with the early nineties, with excited, long nights, with too much cigarette smoke and far too little sleep. Black-red-dark-golden glow, deep and bitter and spicy-cool. Serious and dense and let-me-go. "A Chypre!" comes to my mind - a Chypre without fresh green, far from Paris and the island, a Chypre somewhere in Bangladesh. Dark earth, dense green, a deep splinter of wood, hovering above it dry-dusty cinnamon. Very heavy, very black, yet not gloomy - a heart of old, heavy gold. Dense, dark velvet on white skin, brocade-embroidered - the gaze charred, the mouth deep red. And yet brittle, keep your distance, distant. Lived time and its traces, here a scar, there a mark. A little bitterness, a hint of melancholy. Picasso's daughter would have loved it. We have not become one over time, not "Opium" and I. I do not find myself in the scent, do not find "Opium" in my mirror. But that doesn't have to be - it is not necessary to like, understand, and now also respect the scent. All those days it was just a whisper that connected us, that made me listen, see, feel the stories that are in this vial, waiting to be heard, told. By women, by men, by me, and soon by you.

this is what a drop of this fragrance does to me ... I was still young and not very experienced with scents when I was riding home on the S-Bahn in the evening. A lady, in her mid-thirties I assume, if I remember correctly, got on, elegantly dressed, she obviously had just come from a concert, I thought, and immediately the space was filled with a heavy, opulent, seductive scent. She sat down across from me and I could hardly take my eyes off her as I inhaled this intense, never overpowering fragrance that slowly clouded my senses. Back then, the scent was not so well-known yet. And I loved or rather had already loved such heavy oriental fragrances, which smelled strong but not intrusive on this lady, only accentuating her elegant and very attractive appearance. I was enchanted and felt like I was in a tale from One Thousand and One Nights. In any case, after two stops, I gathered all my courage and asked her what enchanting fragrance she was wearing... Opium by YSL was her answer, with a wonderful smile. I believe I was sitting there bright red in my seat and didn't know what to say anymore... When she got off shortly after, that wonderful cloud of fragrance lingered in the compartment. Later, I smelled this fragrance again and again, but it never touched me or transported me to the oriental fairy tale world quite like that. After receiving a sample from a dear perfumer, that image and olfactory experience immediately resurfaced in my mind, and I see myself again as the shy young man opposite that pretty lady. I close my eyes and I'm gone. I wonder what became of that pretty lady ... The fragrance makes her appear before me again. A drop is enough... A magical scent from the distant Orient, I am intoxicated, that's how I imagine an opium high .... I could hardly describe the scent, as soon as I smell it, I see myself in Marrakech at the spice market, bustling activity around me, foreign voices, the world from the film "The Thief of Bagdad" rises before my mind's eye.

... is this beautiful, dreamy vintage scent. I must say I never had much to do with Opium and have already experienced several vintage women's fragrances. But this scent clearly stands out from everything I have smelled so far as well as from the rest of the Opium line. Unfortunately, one can only dream of such scents today.

Opium Secret was once a perfume of my mother, which was worn far too rarely. With this scent, I have the following associations. With Opium Secret, the olfactory senses dive into the abysses of the human soul and touch on the deep psychological approach. It revolves around a figure that mingles in the best circles of New York society and wears Opium Secret.
just got it a month a go its citrusy minty cooling fresh scent i really like it and i recommend it for anyone who wants a versatile summer scent

When I saw the fragrance pyramid of Moschino Forever Sailing, I thought I had finally found the fresh aquatic scent to my taste, as I really liked all the components individually. Bought it blind, tried it out, and was absolutely surprised. But not in a good way! The top note unfortunately turned out to be very piercing and, despite an excess of mint, significantly less fresh than I had hoped. As the fragrance develops, it takes on a character that gives me headaches. This is a scent that I would not want to perceive on myself or on anyone else. I noticed the sillage more strongly than it seems here, but that is probably because I do not like the scent. Fortunately, it actually dissipates faster on me than the rating here suggests. I actually really like the design. I find the pairing of the typically kitschy Moschino logo as a cap with a simple yet elegantly designed bottle quite cool. I think the fragrance is not poorly crafted; I would be doing it a disservice. However, since I really feel unwell after a while when I smell it, it unfortunately has to sail on without me.

This fragrance has been on my radar for a while. The reason: I love aquatic scents. I really enjoy wearing them on warmer days and in my leisure time. Additionally, this one is very affordable. I like budget-friendly fragrances because you can grab them without a guilty conscience. Moschino is marketed by EuroItalia like the Versace scents. At least the performance of both brands is top-notch; when it comes to the fragrances, it's a matter of taste. I really like both brands. I purchased a small 30ml bottle. It was available for about 15 euros. A fair price for this fragrance. The bottle looks typically Moschino. Striking with a large trashy Moschino inscription. The same bottle as the original Forever, just with blue liquid. I find bottles from Moschino like Fresh Couture to be very original and fun. This one, on the other hand, is rather boring. Freshly sprayed, a sharp penetrating note hits you. It's not really disgusting, but slightly unpleasantly penetrating. A lot of mint, that's probably the reason. Lemon and grapefruit add a burst of freshness. After a short time, the fragrance becomes softer. A bit of lavender and aquatic notes join in. The Blue-Sky Accord will be a fantasy note, but it fits well. A great freshness that would be perfect for a blue sky. Towards the end, it becomes even more pleasant. Then musk and really very pleasant fresh woods come into play. A truly great final phase. In my first test, I quickly wrote it off because the top note isn't the nicest. But as with many fragrances: You have to give them time. In the second test, I was surprised at how much it had changed. The performance is really great as well. It lasts about 10 hours, although the last hours are only faintly perceptible. But for a fragrance in this price range, that's commendable. The sillage is also really good for many hours. If you like Nautica "Voyage," you might find a great alternative here. It's not a big compliment-getter, but it's absolutely suitable for a great aquatic everyday freshness. It can also be used for sports activities. Not a complex fragrance.

I can't help it, I have no connection to the fashion of Moschino at all. Yet every time I pass by a Moschino tester bottle, I have to spray it. I find the fragrances, with one exception, not particularly noteworthy or worth buying. And, oh, there's another bottle that I don't know yet. A deep blue box with eye-catching lettering certainly grabs attention, but it's not really a showstopper. The bottle can be confused with the classic "Forever," with only the light blue liquid and the addition of "Sailing" providing a distinguishing feature. Still, I am repeatedly fascinated by the "stopper" made of silver "Moschino" letters. Such ostentation is otherwise hard to find for miles. Well, yes, a feast for the eyes is ultimately something different. The scent opens fresh, aquatic, and spicy, in line with the term "Sailing." A little bit Mediterranean. You can clearly recognize the citrus fruits, and the mint together with the lavender does make an impression. There’s something synthetic that comes through, which I can't quite name, but it doesn't bother me much; rather, it enhances the aquatic undertone. Nevertheless, I’m not particularly fond of the term "Blue-Sky Accord." In the base, there’s subtle musk, stronger woods, and a restrained patchouli. I really like the transition from fresh to spicy, slightly oriental notes; the progression is harmonious and well-composed. Probably because the freshness subtly breaks through in the base, the fragrance doesn't lose its character. For my part, I can easily detect and appreciate the "Sailing" character - and that's truly not common with many other contemporary fragrances! In this formulation, it's a solid, masculine scent that may not withstand every somewhat stiff breeze, but it certainly has adequate projection for home use. I also find the longevity quite successful for a fresh scent, lasting just under eight hours. I find it refreshing that "Sailing" rides the wave of fresh summer fragrances while still managing to stand out. Certainly, Moschino hasn't created a milestone here, and against the team from "Luna Rossa," it won't score many stage victories, but this fragrance is definitely worth a test.

I know some people are bored with the recent abundance of "fruitchoulis," but not me. Particularly in cool weather, I enjoy the way that fruit and patchouli play off against each other. I was particularly interested in this one because raspberries and lychee play such a nice part in several scents I own. But have you ever played with the balance adjustment on a car or home stereo? Turned to one side or another, it can turn your favorite song into a high-pitched screech or a thumping, unintelligible bass. When I tried YSL's Elle, I got all of the treble (pink berries, lychee, sweetness). When I tried Elle Intense, I got all of the bass (patchouli, a hint of spice, patchouli, and more patchouli). For the pleasure of my nose, I would set the balance knob at the fruit/patchouli level of YSL's own Belle d'Opium and forget about the unbalanced Elle and Elle Intense.

Elle EdP Intense came to me a few years ago as a partially used bottle from a blind purchase. I only realized it was the Intense version when the bottle arrived, but that didn’t bother me since I liked the scent immediately - a successful blind buy that I do not regret. Since then, I have worn it often and with pleasure, and the 50 ml bottle, which is by the way an elegant piece of jewelry, is slowly coming to an end. Elle Intense starts with a strong burst of raspberries that are neither too sweet nor artificial. I don’t perceive lychee; the raspberries seem too dominant for that. This is followed by lush jasmine blossoms that join the berries. Patchouli and amber provide additional warmth and depth, yet the scent simultaneously radiates a slightly metallic coolness. I believe that comes from the benzoin. In the meantime, I also own the regular Elle. However, I haven’t used it much yet and have not been able to notice many differences compared to the Intense, but perhaps I will provide an update on that later. The scent is beautiful, in any case. Unfortunately, it seems to be somewhat absorbed by my skin. Although it has a very good sillage, one spray on my colleague seems stronger than three sprays on me... it’s probably a matter of skin chemistry. She has a darker skin type than I do with my snow-white complexion. Elle Intense radiates the elegance of a dark-haired, cultured lady with long wavy hair in a luxurious long purple evening gown and black high heels. She knows what she wants and exudes a certain eroticism without ever appearing cheap. It would certainly suit Catherine Zeta-Jones well and especially Monica Bellucci. Elle Intense is a scent with class. Maybe I will get another bottle, otherwise I still have the "normal" Elle.

Yes, this stuff is really BOMBIG, I have to agree with Blanche, who also provided me with a sample that I was really excited about. First of all: THIS is how a high-quality fragrance should smell. Elle Intense smells totally high-end and "expensive." It is intense without being overpowering and delicious without being gourmand. Awesome, really. This perfume smells extremely berry-like, floral, feminine, and powerful. I would generally describe the scent as rather oriental. It-is-simply-a-well-made-perfume! And that, even though the composition seems quite simple. Very interesting. I think the scent adapts well too. I would wear it during the day, in the office, or who knows where. I just wouldn't overdo it. That gets annoying. Not just for the people around but also for oneself. Addendum: Now I know what Elle Intense reminds me of: Midnight Poison, in the broadest sense. But I don't know why. Basically, Elle Intense doesn't really smell like Midnight Poison. Or does it?

That's how I wished it. Everything fits perfectly together because finally everything is right and it captivates my heart. And while I was humming along to this song by Ich + Ich - of course, I know the lyrics by heart and can carry a tune - in the evening traffic jam, the wonderful scent of Elle Intense wafted up to my nose again and I thought, yes, everything fits perfectly together here too, and the stylish guy in the Audi TT next to me probably found it interesting that women also perfume themselves in traffic jams. He couldn't know how wonderful I smelled, but he would have liked to. ;-) The structure of the fragrance is so refreshingly simple. It's such a delicate fruity raspberry, no rough grains to disturb me, more the fine delicate juice, and I find it really brilliant that this raspberry stays, yes it stays, do you hear Lolle, this raspberry stays (at least on my skin)!!! It harmonizes with the iris, the divine jasmine, it rolls over the wood, and even the tough guys from the base like this little berry, it simply wraps everyone up. Patchouli has been made really velvety soft, no comparison to the original Elle variant. Eternity, you absolutely must try Elle Intense, you will be surprised. I ignored the recommendation "elegant version for the evening," but I do pay attention to the dosage, because this fragrance has an excellent long-lasting skin-close hold, is sensual - but not intrusive or too opulent, but definitely an extraordinary creation. The berry note gives Intense a bit of lightness, which suits this fragrance very well and makes it wearable not just for the evening. But if it should be the evening in the little black dress - dose higher! With that, Intense and the environment can handle it, I mean, adjust the dosage to the occasion, with this fragrance it works, I have already tested it. I don't know who created this variant of the fragrance from Yves Saint Laurent, but compliments! For me, a real discovery this year, which fits perfectly into my taste.

After about 2 years of abstinence, "Elle Intense" has found its way back into my collection. And not without reason, because this fragrance is truly very special. The scent starts for me with a rich raspberry; later it becomes slightly spicy and woody, but always remains sweet. In contrast to the regular Elle EdP, this one becomes a bit softer and richer at the end. The sillage is remarkable and the longevity is enormous. Applied in the morning, I can still smell it in the evening. I was often approached by both men and women about this fragrance back then. All packaged in an elegant and simple bottle - Thank you Yves Saint Laurent :)

It’s time for a tribute to this fragrance, as it is truly exceptional! Elle Intense has an oriental character, very sensual and powerful. As an extension of the original, the fragrance lives up to its name, namely intensity (both in scent and longevity on the skin).

I only became aware of this fragrance and curious about it through the forum. Said and done... I was at my trusted perfumery today and tested the scent. What I noticed two hours later is that the fragrance doesn't change much anymore... which I personally find pleasant... instead, it becomes more lovely and settles like a veil on the skin.

I am a classic type. Now that I spend a lot of time with the dogs, I am more of a sporty-classic type. That's how I've always been and will probably remain. And yet there are days when I step out of the mold. On those days, I wear Pink Bouquet by Moschino. Not only does the pink heart bottle with a pink satin bow on top in the pink box with a glitter heart stand out in my collection; no, the scent is different too. On one of my "pink days," I tested Pink Bouquet and immediately liked the scent. I can't relate to comparisons with toilet cleaner, air fresheners, or Klostein, as mentioned in previous comments. Pink Bouquet by Moschino is a fruity-sweet-fresh fragrance - and I like it. The beginning is lovely. The pink heart greets me with fresh pineapple and ripe raspberries. After a while, flowers join in. I can clearly recognize the peony and jasmine, but the lily of the valley and violet are unfortunately hiding from me. After a while, the scent becomes sweeter and creamier. I can distinctly smell the ripe peach. Very delicious and very fine! The longevity could be better. After five or six hours, the delicate peach cream scent disappears. Pink Bouquet by Moschino is certainly not a fragrance that moves the world or makes hearts race. But it definitely deserves a test. It is a scent that brings joy, makes the world seem pink, and carefree. On some days, it’s just nice to "hang up" marine, white, and beige and see the world through rose-colored glasses.

The pink bottle and the scent note "gingerbread" immediately caught my attention. When I discovered the little bottle in an airport store, I sprayed it on my wrist without a second thought. I figured with the gentle pink design, the contents couldn't be that bad - HOW WRONG I WAS! For the entire flight (a solid 3 hours!), I had Toilet Stone scent in my nose! I was so embarrassed that the other people on the plane could smell it. The overpowering pineapple scent didn't help either. It actually made me feel sick. I have no idea if it's due to my skin chemistry, as the scent notes don't sound bad at all. Still, never again! 10% for the cute bottle design... and the gingerbread *irony* -.-

So. I was early for an appointment, so I passed the time in a small, well-stocked perfume shop. Then this bright pink, glittering bottle in a hinted heart shape caught my eye. It came with matching test strips (small hearts with the Moschino logo), so I sprayed it right away. "Hmm, you know this scent," I thought to myself. Then it hit me: DKNY Pink Macaroon smells exactly the same as this one!!! Although the two have completely different components, I can't distinguish the top note. Pink Bouquet starts with a pleasant fruity sweetness, where I imagine I can smell something marzipan-like. It's definitely not just fruit; something slightly creamy and spicy mixes in (maybe the premature gingerbread?). I was lucky, and the nice saleswoman gave me a sample. Yes, I've learned from my mistakes! So I went to my meeting with my light, sweet pink scent cloud. There I sat, and after a while, I thought: "Oh man, is there a bathroom next door?" The room seemed to fill with a mix of citrus bathroom cleaner and, as Igli rightly said, toilet duck. Absolutely disgusting: the smell of pseudo-freshness and pure chemistry. And at 32°C, no one can really concentrate. At some point, I asked my colleagues in frustration if we could open the windows to get rid of the smell. I was met with confused looks, and then work continued. That's when I realized: the stench was coming from my arm! Oh my God!!!! Attempts to wash it off with soap failed, and so I had to endure it until the end. Unfortunately, it only got worse, until all that was left was a sharp, chemical citrus smell with a disgusting sweetness. Along with bathroom cleaner and toilet duck, there was also spirit and peach-scented fabric softener. Brrrrrrrr.... It's really nauseating! I have to say, Igli is right: I was embarrassed. I smelled like a janitor or a cleaning lady. Nothing against cleaning ladies, please don't get me wrong: I just don't want to smell like one all day. Yes, what a shame! It had started so beautifully. Kitschily beautiful bottle, great top note, but then? The absolute worst-case scenario. I had been looking forward to the promised gingerbread/musk mix! But forget it, I can't honestly say I can recognize either of those in the scent development. I can really only advise anyone who likes the top note to quickly go to Douglas. Try testing the DKNY Sweet Delicious Pink Macaroon; it really smells exactly the same at first. But: it becomes creamier and warmer over time, smells great like marzipan, and not as disgusting as this Scent Tree Bouquet! Besides, it's also cheaper. So, I'm going to stand under the shower for an hour now and try to get the toilet duck off my skin!

anyone who knows the pink toilet duck can imagine what this "scent" smells like! I wouldn't feel comfortable with it, I'd even be embarrassed! who would voluntarily stand in the toilet duck cloud after spraying it in the bathroom? I'm really sorry, but I have nothing more to add!

~ Inspiration ~ After I enjoyed "Glamour," "Pink Bouquet" also made it onto my wishlist, and I received a sample from the lovely Inger. ~ Bottle ~ This kitschy-bling-pink bottle with embellishments is great! :D The name suggests a sweet floral scent. ~ Fragrance ~ It starts fruity-sweet with pineapple, raspberries, and a hint of citrusy bergamot. Pink flowers in the form of lily of the valley, peonies, and violets create the floral bouquet. With musk and a touch of peach, it fades softly. Unfortunately, the gingerbread note remains completely hidden from me :( ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts about 3-4 hours (not much longer on clothes and hair). 2-3 sprays are enough; otherwise, it becomes too artificial and synthetic for me. ~ Occasion ~ A nice everyday scent for the mild and warmer days in spring and summer. ~ Conclusion ~ It's not bad... just unfortunately nothing special, but rather a 0815-floral-fruity medley... I was curious about the (non-existent) gingerbread note :(

This stuff costs $185 retail. You know what else costs around that price? And I'm talking retail here. A bottle of Mancera, or Montale, or Frapin, or Orto Parisi. We're getting close to private line territory too. Armani's private line, i.e. Armani Privé - Thé Yulong costs $195 for 100ml. Heck, 50mls of Dior's private line, which is top of the line perfumery, only costs $30 more than this. And this fragrance is not going to get much cheaper at discounters; the old Y Le Parfum (2021) is still going for over $100 at discounters — you can get a Nishane at that price. So let's throw all notion of "oh it's a department store designer, it's supposed to be low-quality and synthetic" out the window. If they want to give it premium pricing, I'll review it as a premium fragrance. And as a premium fragrance, this is absolutely god-awful. It's like paying $30 for a gourmet hamburger and then finding out the chef just went to Mcds and bought one for you. Because at the end of the day, this is drugstore swill. It smells like one of those peel-and-sniff fragrance samples they used to have in magazines, where the weird plasticky scent of the page and glue would get mixed in with the fragrance. The citrus in the opening is unbelievably synthetic. There's also a strange sweet fruity note that I can't really describe further, because it doesn't smell like a specific fruit, or realistic in any way. The "patchouli" and "pine" in here are just chemicals that don't really resemble those natural plants. Some spicy geraniol wraps things up, a hollow shell of the geranium flower, stripped of all character. It's like if they made a Gatorade flavor into a scent. What does "Glacier Freeze" taste like? A bunch of chemicals, just like how this fragrance smells. And on top of the synthetic and low-quality nature of this fragrance, it even manages to be not just unoriginal, but unfashionable. This scent wouldn't have been out of place 10 or 15 years ago. I wouldn't recommend this fragrance to anyone under 30, and if you're above 30, it's going to smell like you haven't updated your fragrance since you were in high school. It sits in that hole where it is not vintage and cool like a fougere or chypre, and not cutting edge and modern like Sauvage Elixir or Pacific Chill . And wouldn't you expect a chemical concoction like this to at least have good performance? Nope. Sits close to the skin after about an hour. The one purpose this could have been used for would be as a loud, brash clubbing fragrance (albeit for an aging Millennial), but it can't even do that. What an absolute disappointment, not that expectations were very high in the first place. I think the high point of this line was Y Eau Fraîche and it's been all downhill from there. We're not even halfway through 2025 but this might be a good candidate for worst 2025 release. Edit: this one stayed on my skin for like 10 hours as a skin scent (just a musk note), so I'll update my longevity rating. Still stand by what I said about the performance. Projection is very poor.

You know, you'd be inclined to expect that a fragrance such as Y Le Parfum (2025) from a house as big and as well-established as YSL to be a proper, mass-appealing, commercial hit. Not doing anything crazy like a niche house, nor asking for niche fragrance prices. It should be just your regular, everyday, pleasing and boring designer. And while I believe that most people will see Y Le Parfum (2025) just like that, if you really care a little about fragrances and if you've got just a bit of experience with them, then you'd know to stay away from this one. Omnipotato's review below prompted me into getting a sample of Y Le Parfum (2025) , as I just had to see with my own nose if it really is that bad. And from a level of perfumery and marketing, yes, this is possibly the worst designer release of the year, and that wouldn't be pushing it. Now, I love a piney scent. Such fragrances that might evoke the feeling of walking through a pine forest just make me nostalgic, as I have grown in the middle of the mountains, surrounded by the endless forest. But let me tell you, if the smell that I got every time I went outside was anything close to Y Le Parfum (2025) , I would've brunt the place to the ground. There's nothing 'natural'-smelling about this fragrance, nor anything that reminds me of being in nature, surrounded by pine trees. All I get is an incredibly screechy, synthetic opening, at best reminding of an overdose of citruses. There is some slight sweetness in the background, as well as some crisp freshness, the latter being the only positive thing I find here. The "woodiness" and "resinous" accords you should get from the pine and fir balsam are nothing but a mishmash of cloying chemicals. Nothing TRULY resinous or woody here. The geranium is lost somewhere in this chaotic soup, adding a minty/aromatic touch, which again, are anything but natural. And the patchouli just unbalances things further with its muskiness, even medicinal-like undertone which I get here. There's no development, no smoothness, no balance... Frankly, this smells like a lab experiment gone bad. Longevity is about what I'd expect. I got 6 hours of this synthetic, aromatic mess on me. And yes, it keeps its synthetic/chemical tone throughout most of the wearing, even if not as pronounced. As for projection, I think this might be one of the only times that I'm glad projection is subpar (on my skin, at least). I got like around a foot bubble around me for the first hour or less, then settling close to my skin, but not turning into a skin scent; that happens around the 3 hour mark. I do believe that in the air it doesn't smell as bad as it does if you shove your nose on your wrist. That doesn't cut it any slack, though. Now, if I'd be inclined to be generous, for whatever reason, I'll admit that versatility is a pro here, especially since in the air it doesn't smell as synthetic (but still hardly natural). You probably won't be offending anyone but yourself with Y Le Parfum (2025) . As a daily or leisure/sports wear, I actually believe it's not terrible. But you've got significantly better choices out there. That leads us to the worst part of it all: the price. It seems to vary from country to country, but generally, it revolves around the $100-$150 mark. Given the level of perfumery that you receive here, it could've costed $40, and I still wouldn't have recommended it. It's just seriously unbalanced and synthetic, without even mentioning its unoriginality and lack of proper marketing. The biggest issue, however, is that people will still buy it. Whether because of the brand's name or because of their lack of understanding what makes a fragrance good, I think that YSL will still get solid numbers from Y Le Parfum (2025) 's sales. And that's just unfortunate - normalizing this level of laziness and poor perfumery, even for a designer. Either way, if you want your money to be well-spent, I urge you to look elsewhere, even in the Y lineup. Overall Rating: 4.3/10

First thoughts, it starts off similar to the original Y EDP/ Y EDP Intense. Y Le Parfum 2025 is a mature and less sweeter version of the original Y EDP. It's completely different compared to the original Y Le parfum but leans more towards the original Y DNA with the citrus fresh aromatic scent. I sprayed a total of 5 times. Twice behind each ear, twice on the front of neck, and once in front of my chest. The longevity is great, it lasts approximately 8-9 hours on my skin. This fragrance projects average too, with about a 6 ft radius for the 30 minutes, and a skin scent after about 2 hours. (Depends on skin types) Overall Rating (8/10) It's not a crazy new fragrance nor it's a bad reformulation. It's just the same Y EDP DNA recycled to make it much more mature and less juvenile. I'd suggest you to try it first before you commit a full bottle.

This is perhaps the biggest disappointment from YSL of all time. I can't fathom the brain process that went through the top brass into deciding that Y le Parfum needed a whole new formula. If you were hoping this had any resemblance to the original, then I'm sorry to say there isn't a hint of similarity between the two. YSL decided to butcher the original dna of this frag and created something stupidly generic, kinda reminded me of one of the dior sauvages. The scent itself is just basic woody, doesn't have much character to it. You can say it's 100% a safe scent, but for the price when you can get one of the other more popular woody scents? This isn't worth it. I just can't believe they scraped one of their most popular scents and just butchered it with this goofy reformulation. Didn't bother keeping at least a few of the original notes, this is just an entirely different scent. The atomizer sucks too, not surprising I guess, probably because they now have the refillable option for this scent so you can pop off the atomizer to refill.

Of course this fragrance is going to get so much negative attention right out of the gate due to it being a replacement. People are so ignorant sometimes in the way they will judge a fragrance.. Well straight out of the gate I will say this to me is a better fragrance overall than the 2021 Le Parfum was. I won’t go into too many details on the 2021 version but I will say it was overly rich/sweet with a bunch of mashed together notes and the performance was not very good. This new Le Parfum actually has some nice depth and character about it as well as the performance being great! This takes the Y scent profile to a much more suitable gentleman level. An extremely easy reach suited for any season or time for when you’re not sure just what to wear. Very appealing and not overbearing in any sense. People can keep being mad at this release but in actual reality this is a very well done fragrance.

If you have a garden with conifers, you can have fun rubbing a branch between your hands and smelling it. This is a simplified way to describe the scent. Green citrus dominates here both in the opening and in the drydown, with minimal sweetness only appearing in the base note (by then it's already a skin scent).

On the map of pine and cypress scents, there is a glaring emptiness in the designer sector, which I have always lamented. Aside from Polo Intense, Bottega Veneta, I can think of perhaps Varvatos Vintage off the top of my head, and that's it. I was all the more surprised when I found a promising candidate in YSL Y Le Parfum, which convinced me after several tests.

Elegant, masculine, and long-lasting, perfect for both evening and everyday wear. A modern classic with noble, seductive depth. It smells like what you would imagine a 20-year-old in a leading position in a business would smell like. Perfect for any season and always a standout among all-rounder fragrances.

OPENING: powdery, candied rose - very pretty, fresh, feminine, clean MIDDLE: very strong jasmine (not listed, but it smelled so distinctive!) mixed with lily of the valley DRY-DOWN: indistinct white-floral hairspray, with hint of rose The opening lasted only a few moments, middle felt too "screechy" (this part of the fragrance ruined it for me), and dry-down was pleasant but forgettable. Worth a sample, but not full-bottle worthy for me personally.

I bought this one almost exclusively for the bottle, and the 5mL mini at that, so I didn't care that much about the smell. And I think I got what I paid for: I struggle to imagine wearing this. It's actually not terrible, but it's not very me. It's synthetic through and through, but the opening is especially harsh. It's better as it dries down, but surviving the opening is a bit of an ask. When it settles, it's a very pink-synthetic floral with a slight tart-sweet edge (maybe the pomegranate?). I guess I could layer with it (using a very, very light hand lol) but I'm okay with it just being decor in my collection.

Five minutes of sour, pickled grapefruit (???) leading into a clean, if a bit bland and flat, rose. The smooth, musky cedar base is trying to make the overall profile more mature, but the rest of the scent feels out of place beside it, like a preschooler trying on her mom's heels and lipstick. Pink Fresh Couture is a safe, pink floral, not at all what I expected from a design house known for its ironic humor and edge. This could be a dollar store dupe of a Victoria's Secret flanker, tbh, and not a good one. It leans feminine, weak staying power, almost nonexistent sillage. You have to really stick your nose to your skin to get anything from it, and what you DO get isn't worth the trouble. It's not a young, fresh and fashionable girly, but rather juvenile instead. Linear. Boring. I can't imagine gifting this to anyone older than fourteen, though I can easily picture someone whose chemistry can make these notes sing even if mine can't. It is BAD on me, y'all. This is disappointing not just as a fragrance, but especially as a flanker contrasted next to Fresh Couture. I tested them with a spray of each on each wrist, so I could compare directly. The OG has a lot more depth and the notes are more intricately balanced, even as the overall fragrance retains a sparkling, friendly simplicity. Kind of a bummer that Pink Fresh Couture is so dull beside it. I wanted to like this, as I ADORE almost all the notes here, but my skin chemistry just refuses to play nice with it. -- This review previously appeared on another site under the name "PrincessPrickleson." That's me! I'm moving my collection to Parfumo.

I may have my quirks - but the cleaning obsession is unfortunately not one of them. Dust does give some furniture that antique charm, doesn’t it? My husband sees it a bit differently and grabs the cloth with more enthusiasm. He is particularly fond of the windows - a blessing, because I have a fear of heights and get shaky knees even on a little stool. Thanks to his height, my husband always has the ladder at hand. So, the window cleaning is his responsibility, for which he has even ordered a mysterious tincture online. The other day, I entered the room where the sunlight streamed in through the spotless windows. In the midst of the shine was my satisfied husband. But I also liked the scent of the room. What is that? Carlo Carlotti - was his serious answer - the new fragrance, straight from Milano. I pondered. Never heard of it. Then he waved his secret bottle in front of my nose with a smirk and hid it importantly in the cupboard. Indeed, today I found a resemblance between this magical cleaning agent and Moschino Pink Fresh Couture. A fruity - clean scent blend - that plays into the pink. Somehow nice and neat. Rose and hyacinth spring from the original bottle, which I particularly like. The pomegranate is sweet and juicy - but everything feels overall synthetic. Still, I don’t reject the scent, as it has a comic-like, unserious quality. Even the quirky bottle is a collector's item - but I prefer the scent in the room rather than on my skin. Even without the elaborate window cleaning.

Cleaning and tidying up is always a bit of a challenge. There are many methods one can use to make cleaning easier. One probably frowned-upon, yet still widely used method is cleaning with the motto "Don't clean where you can't see!" (Is that why "sweeping dirt under the rug" has become so established? :D). Another effective method, especially for playfully removing light dust and dirt from floors like laminate, is the cat method. You simply grab the fat tomcat (or cat) lying lazily on the floor and push it back and forth. The little creature looks a bit confused at first, but then purrs contentedly because it thinks you are playing with it (or bites if it’s in its little brat phase), and you simultaneously clean the floor with the animal's fluffy fur! Unfortunately, when it comes to windows, you still have to reach for the cleaning cloth. Then comes the choice of the right cleaner, which sometimes sadly overwhelms us guys a bit (Glass cleaner? Window cleaner? What the hell is the difference? Or maybe the all-purpose cleaner?)... best to do what you always do... ask Mom :DD Of course, you could also ask your girlfriend, or if you don’t have one, one or two good friends, but the downside is that they all laugh at such questions for days on end! Well,... and if you then also mistakenly grab the fragrance bottle and spray the windows with this scent instead of a cleaning product, the chaos is probably perfect and all the windows "smell" like perfume... The scent: It smells briefly citrusy sweet, the grapefruit comes across like a mix of grapefruit and tangerine. The sweet notes come from both floral notes and fruity ones like blackcurrants. I couldn't really detect hyacinths and pomegranates. The fruity notes fade quickly, leaving the scent more floral sweet. Later, in the base, the sweetness becomes a bit warmer when musk joins in.
