I am not an athlete - but I enjoy moving, especially to music. So I always found riding and ice skating to beautiful melodies particularly fulfilling. And of course, dancing as well. Aoud ever takes me to a shimmering dance floor, where I sway and twirl with my dance partner to Shostakovich's waltz. Life - it is a floating - that's all that goes through my mind. That's good - because sometimes you just have to "take off." Ever conveys this lively lightness that makes you forget all heaviness. The dance floor breathes woodiness, and the citrus notes add a lively touch. Amber and sandalwood create intimacy - and I trustingly lean against my dance partner. A hint of eroticism mingles with fine leather. Come dance with me - sings Demis Roussos - and I gladly surrender to this invitation. For those whom the angels love - they let dance.

I recently acquired this fragrance because I was particularly drawn to the very long-lasting citrus top note of bergamot and citron combined with Aoud. I have never experienced such a citrus-fresh top note that lasts so long... the Aoud and amber, as well as sandalwood oil and patchouli, are already quite noticeable, while the top note shows no signs of fading. This completely fascinated me. I cannot detect any similarity to Black Afgano, as that one comes off much woodier from the start and is simply much better. The longevity of Aoud EVER is not as enduring as one would expect from Montale perfumes, despite having the longest citrus top note in the history of perfumery. However, the perfume is already pleasant early on without smelling chemical, as is the case with Montale Black Aoud... you can only cautiously sniff after 10 minutes without burning your nose. In any case, Aoud EVER has encouraged me that there are also some quieter fragrance masterpieces at Montale.

Aoud Ever is presented here as a fragrance twin of Black Afgano, and since I liked the latter so much, I ordered a sample of the Montale scent blindly. After the first test, I also chose the black Afghan as a fragrance twin, but I am now retracting this assessment after another test with both scents on my wrist at the same time - Aoud Ever differs too much. From the bottle and right after application, a medicinal note hits my nose, which fortunately dissipates almost immediately, giving way to a powerful bergamot. Together with the other citrus ingredients, which I cannot identify individually, it gives the fragrance a wonderful freshness, but this is already underpinned by the dark, smoky Aoud. The scent then slowly becomes a bit warmer, somewhat woody, with patchouli joining in pleasantly subtly and taking away some of the freshness from the still present citrus note, without completely covering it. Only after more than an hour, when the soft notes of the base come in, can the kinship with Black Afgano no longer be denied. However, the two are not brothers, but rather distant cousins. Aoud Ever lacks the heavy, cloying sweetness, but has an interesting scent development and a consistently noticeable citrus freshness that is completely absent in the Afghan. Longevity and sillage are, as with all the Montales tested so far, at the very top.

Tuscan Soul sounds quite kitschy at first. It’s a region where I love to be... the term Vendemmia (which means harvest, vintage) always comes to mind. But there, it’s more in 0.75l bottles and the content is deep red! You don’t exactly come across this brand in every store (the regular series, yes)... so I was all the more delighted to have received this sample in a tiny perfumery in Ulm. The "harvest/vintage" is very successful... but I wouldn’t recommend storing these "bottles" lying down in the cellar and waiting a few years... that could turn into Aceto. For those born after 1990, this scent is probably new. For the 70s and 80s generation, this fragrance is practically known. Back then, Salvatore Ferragamo Pour Homme was an absolutely extraordinary scent and has since become a classic. Especially since figs are rarely found in men's fragrances. That was almost revolutionary at the time. Vendemmia is the premium version of SF PH. Everything is finer without being particularly niche. The fig has been toned down to a tolerable level, which initially drove me a bit crazy with its addictive bursts. Here it is much warmer-spicier, more masculine... especially due to the spicy woods and a slight cognac/whisky note in the background, which (unfortunately) only has more presence in the base. Vendemmia has become a wonderful scent that you can only feel good in. Many who had the original will love this fragrance!! Conclusion: A very sensual, almost romantic scent, which fits very well with Tuscany. Longevity is somewhat lower than the original, but at 6 hours it’s just okay, considering that the bottle costs around €140... rather below average. Sillage is quite decent in the first 30 minutes... afterwards, it’s more average. I can very well imagine getting this pretty bottle next autumn/winter.

Starts punchy and extremely fruity, with the leather coming out more and more as the perfume ages on skin. A little does go a long way; the perfume projected far more than I was expecting from my body heat. The fruitiness definitely brings out the sweetness of the leather; I'd say that for the first hour, it seemed much more like a plum fragrance than a leather one. Because of that, the fragrance definitely leans feminine for me.

Well, it really isn't that beastly. Rather, it's a skillful combination of soft, delicate powdery/creamy notes paired with a hearty leather accord. Beastlove starts pleasantly soft with sweet pear, tough plum, and bergamot; after a few moments/minutes, the masculine leather joins in, creating a nice twist between the fruity/sweet and the strong dominant notes. Rose, cedar, and vetiver are slightly noticeable but remain in the background, blending in. In the end, the powdery musk, vanilla, amber, and tonka bean allow the fragrance to fade softly, while the leather still shows some presence. Typical for Montale, it has an almost linear progression. Some synthetic notes, but still good performance and longevity.

My friend Coriolon surprised me wonderfully and successfully with his gift - a full 250-300 ml bottle of "Eau Libre." He had already hinted at it when he wrote his blog post on June 13, 2013, about his trip to Bolzano. The contents of the bottle seem to be completely free of signs of aging due to unintentional excellent storage. I am absolutely thrilled. Therefore, I gladly had to correct a few sentences from my comment starting from the following paragraph dated May 11, 2012, as the overall impression of the fragrance has changed a bit for the better. Anyone reading my profile name might imagine that I am a big admirer of Yves Saint Laurent's work. Of course, I knew that "Eau Libre" existed, and that it had been a huge flop despite a large advertising budget, but for some reason, it had never really interested me. And although I hold the old fragrances from this house very dear. Information online is scarce, and no one seems to know it, but miniatures do occasionally pop up on eBay. Since Skylab generously left me his miniature (and now thanks to Coriolon, I hold a full bottle in my hands), I can now report on it. I will cherish it. "Eau Libre" clearly starts in 1975. The top note begins herbaceous, green, citrusy, and with a hint of civet. Young people might turn away in irritation now because this small animalistic hint seems unappealing and above all old to them. Surprisingly, the civet note diminishes in the further development of the fragrance to a barely perceptible remnant in the background. The entire fragrance progression is, as the name of this unisex fragrance "Eau Libre" already implies, not quite so complex and powerful, but still has good presence and longevity, as was typical for a fragrance of this time. "Eau Libre" quickly follows the classic structure of top, heart, and base notes. In the dominant heart note, which is already present in the top note, dark green herbal notes immediately follow. It is likely to be ethereal herbal rosemary and thyme, a bit angular and herbaceous galbanum, as well as coniferous pine notes. Skillfully intertwined, it seems that a few cool citrus fruits have also found their way into the formula. A strongly green soapiness is created, accompanied by a slightly ethereal freshness. A few minutes later, the base mixes into the permanently present cool green soapy and herbal heart note with a portion of earthy dark patchouli, herbaceous woody vetiver, and a decent dose of bitter oak moss. Unfortunately, this clearly comes at the expense of freshness, but the soapy note remains undeterred. The combination of soapy freshness plus "musty" patchouli is already very familiar to me from YSL's "Pour Homme," and strong chypre undertones can no longer be denied. From the entirety of the ingredients, there also emerges a vaguely identifiable metallic accord, which briefly reminds me of "Paco Rabanne Pour Homme" in combination with the green notes. After all, "Eau Libre" feels very natural and evokes thoughts of forest, moss, earth, and nature. As a lover of old fresh green chypres, all of this could actually excite me a lot, but the base with its darker mood due to patchouli, vetiver, and civet feels too little cheerful and radiant for an "Eau." There is also a certain elegance that is associated with the YSL brand, although YSL's life partner Pierre Bergé always resists the word "elegant" when discussing YSL's fashion. He prefers the statement that YSL's fashion implies a certain attitude. "Eau Libre" quotes some fragrances from the 1970s as a typical witness of its generation, which may have contributed to its inability to succeed. Launched as an "Eau," it surely aimed at the already established competition of light fragrances of that time, when I think of Eau de Guerlain, Eau de Rochas, Ô de Lancôme, Eau Sauvage, or even L'Eau Neuve by Lubin. In contrast to these fragrances, "Eau Libre" simply comes too late... a bit sluggish, a touch too dark and not very radiant, metallic, herbal, and somehow a bit unfriendly... one would wish for more lightheartedness and cheerfulness from an "Eau." The complete absence of any floral notes likely made the "normal" ladies of that time wrinkle their noses in doubt. To this was added the idea of a unisex fragrance with an advertising campaign that rather seems like a gay man is out and about in thought with his best friend... I know what I'm talking about ;-) When I think of the men of that time like Jean Gabin, Burt Reynolds, or Anthony Quinn, men still wanted to be men and not soft boys. As far as I know, at least Anthony Quinn always charmed the ladies with Guerlain's "Habit Rouge." And the strong, independent Yves Saint Laurent power woman in a tuxedo would go straight for the "Pour Homme" from the same house rather than settle for something in between. That would only be half the fun; shocking with "Eau Libre" was not. Although there was even a complete bath line for the fragrance, it apparently flopped completely. The packaging was stolen from the in-house "Rive Gauche." "The same in green," even the containers of the bath line were identical to "Rive Gauche." Production was probably discontinued around 1980/82.

The 1970s were turbulent and wild times. Be it politically, musically, technically, or fashion-wise! Still - despite all the pioneering spirit and freedoms of opinion - provocations like homosexuality, nudism, or lasciviousness in public were frowned upon, hated, and not well received. The great Monsieur Yves Saint Laurent was known for provocation and the associated scandals! Leading the way were the YSL fragrance stories: Be it his naked presence in the campaign for Pour Homme, his first men's fragrance, or the "scandalous" Opium. Twenty years before the androgynous CK One by Calvin Klein, Laurent already launched a (first commercial) unisex fragrance. With the French saying "Tout ce quit est à toi est à moi," which means "Everything that is yours is also mine," they advertised for "Eau Libre." The campaign was again revolutionary - a colored man sits back to back with a dark-haired woman, dressed in brown (of course YSL). A brown scarf around their necks connects them and embodies gender neutrality. The bottle - a simple glass look in the shape of a modern, slender drop. The cap is green and round. A silver sticker with the fragrance title and the brand name adorns the top of the bottle like a seal. The packaging reflects the look of the Rive Gauche launched four years earlier and presents itself in beige, white, and green. In addition, there was a wide range of fragrance and care products. And how does a "unisex" fragrance from 1975 smell, which presents itself to me as Eau De Cologne emotionally! Eau Libre starts with a dry, even rough citrus note. This comes across as bitter, rather than refreshingly zesty! After a very short time, a green woody nuance joins in, which feels quite oily. It smells of leather, and I believe I can recognize vetiver. In general, it is a very linear scent progression that offers no further leap. It reminds one of Guerlain's Vetiver and Eau Savage by Dior. The finish presents itself after just 1 hour, making the EDC assumption plausible. Contrary to the differentiation of "women's fragrance" and "men's fragrance" - the women of that time did indeed wear men's perfumes - the theme of "unisex fragrance" was ahead of its time and received little attention. Eau Libre disappeared from the scene after a short time, leaving behind miniatures at quite affordable prices. C'est la vie.

I smelled it on my friend, and I was like wtf is that! it smells amazing, fresh and inviting. earthy and green. its smells incredible, I see hugo by hugo boss down in the suggestions which happens to be one of my favorites. so If you like hugo, by hugo boss. we have a similar nose. this is right here will be worth a blind buy

By chance, I was offered Montale fougeres marine as a bargain. Apparently, my acquaintance didn't like it. After a first test, my clear classification is rather masculine, as it is marketed as a fragrance for men. But then a friend said, why shouldn't a woman wear this scent! After all, women have also embraced marine fragrances today. And so, for very little cash, I acquired an almost full bottle of FM from Montale. My first impression, I've been wearing it for two days now, good longevity, 7 hours on me, a maritime freshness kick, a feel-good scent for a cool head, I smell mint, the distance it creates clarifies my emotional state, bringing me to calm. It reminds me in scent expression of a mix between Allure Sport Homme and Davidoff Cool Water women. FM is very civilized for Montale, not overpowering, but rather pleasing in expression. It is well-suited for the masculine side in us women, namely to go through the day calmly, coolly, and distantly.

I had a bit of a hard time trying to describe this Montale fragrance, as I could hardly identify any note without knowing the details in the pyramid. My first impression was: Hm, is this Montale? Surely, there must be something similar that is cheaper and not niche (although one could debate whether Montale really falls under "niche"). The second thought: This is not unisex; it is clearly for men. The third: It smells somewhat synthetic, although I couldn't quite say why. It’s not an aquatic Calone that jumps out at you, nor is it the penetrating substance sometimes listed as ozone, but it is certainly not the true rough sea. Despite the slightly synthetic impression, this is, after all, the most pleasant and accurate interpretation of "sea water" that I have encountered so far. Admittedly, I don't really know much in this direction, which I will change when I get the chance. An impressive freshness spreads from the very beginning. I don't perceive it as indefinably synthetic; it feels menthol-like, like very sharp mint, with a hint of squeaky sour lemon juice. This cool, bitter freshness is extremely pleasant and compensates for the somewhat chemical-seeming sea water. It actually reminds me of a brisk breeze on a very cool day during a walk on the beach, clearing your head. The coastal vegetation definitely provides a lot of oak moss, because to my nose, there is far more "fern" than "marine" present here. I don't smell lavender at all, at least nothing I would recognize as such. Patchouli is at most perceptible as a very subtle hint if you look for it. I can easily find the geranium and musk on the paper strip (where the scent becomes much rounder), while on my skin, a mixture of sea water and moss dominates. I used up 2 samples of this marine fougère with some enthusiasm when it was around 40 degrees in the shade during the summer. If the climate catastrophe should lead to such sweltering heat occurring more frequently, I will definitely get myself a whole bottle of refreshing sea water. Otherwise, I would clearly leave this scent to men and wouldn't mind if I came across it on one or another specimen.

First, thanks to Awin for the sample! Fougères Marine. I was curious how Montale would interpret the blend of herb-green and aquatic. I usually find aquatic notes boring or they remind me of the scent of men's deodorant. When first sprayed, I was a bit disappointed. The scent smelled strange. But then the top note developed into a spicy freshness. Only very faintly could one perceive a subtle sweetness. Are all the ingredients listed here? I predominantly smell a fresh herbiness. I do not detect lemon. I wonder where the seawater is supposed to be? Was that the strange scent opening? The heart note then develops a bit sweeter, but the summer character of the fragrance remains well preserved. The intensity is okay. The lavender wanders around in the heart undefined. The base clearly has a fougère accord. Only the musk could have been toned down a bit, as there is a slight hairspray note in the dry down. Conclusion: well done, but still not to my taste.

With an order from Montale, I was able to add a 20ml travel spray with a fragrance of my choice. I chose the Fougeres Marines. With its marine touch, I would say it’s not a typical Fougere scent. It’s an easy-to-wear, non-intrusive everyday fragrance. It wafts a fine fresh breeze around the nose.

... sitting on the beach with my feet in the sea on Sylt. A floral scent and something green comes from the island. From the sea, there’s a salty fresh aquatic note. Just tilt your head back and enjoy. When the fragrance is applied, you get aquatic seawater and lavender, complemented by the green of moss and the freshness of patchouli. It is rounded off at the end by musk.

I feel similarly to Igraine that FM gives a synthetic impression - this happens to me with almost all Montale fragrances. After spraying, a citrus freshness becomes noticeable, which within a minute lets the mint come to the forefront. Shortly thereafter, it develops into a sharp freshness, which, however, is overly overshadowed by a sweetness accompanied by menthol.

For me, one of the most joyful surprises this spring. More woody-fresh than woody-green, but of course still green, the vetiver makes it possible. I experience the scent as rather linear, which does not diminish its quality at all. A bit like freshly cut underbrush, slightly creamy, unsweet, with a minimal bitter note from a mineral corner. Therefore, it tends to be rather masculine, even though it is still fully unisex. In my view, it suits really any occasion and season, something that not everyone can achieve. That sounds quite technical at first, but it is only meant for clarification. A friendly, bright scent. Fresh, without being synthetically overdone. Woody, without coming across as overly serious. A fruity layer could have been conceivable as well, but it might have brought in too much randomness. Thus, it remains a scent with edges and character, which can probably unfold particularly well in the warm season. The rating on Parfumo is incomprehensible to me; on textiles, it lasts about 8-10 hours for me, but it does not have a particularly lavish sillage, rather staying at about an arm's length projection. Overall, it has a very similar DNA to K by Dolce & Gabbana, although it is significantly more floral and refined. I can only recommend it!

Foreste Di Seta translates to Silk Forest. In the Silk Forest, there are mainly mulberry trees, predominantly white mulberry trees, as their leaves are the primary food for the silkworm. These trees originate from Asia and were planted in Europe during the Middle Ages to establish a local silk production. The silkworm thrived best in the Mediterranean region. That’s why there is also a great tradition of silk production in Italy. Now, let’s talk about the perfume released by a well-known Italian designer brand. Foreste Di Seta features the scent of silk in its heart note. Fortunately, that is also the only connection the perfume has to the mulberry tree. The bottle is beautifully printed, just like the entire silk collection from Salvatore Ferragamo. I really like that. Upon spraying, you briefly get a fresh breeze of forest and sea. The clary sage often gives me marine vibes. Then, after about 5 minutes, the scent transitions into the heart note. The spiciness of the sage remains, and silk and walnut provide a creamy veil that envelops the clary sage. On the test strip, the scent stays slightly fresh. But on the skin, it becomes creamy and smells, after about half an hour, as if it had rained in the forest. Misty steam rises, the air is clean and still very warm. To me, this designer fragrance smells slightly niche. I generally need to get used to scents that smell of rain or fog. The fragrance is well-balanced and rounded. The creaminess makes me feel well-groomed. The longevity for me is good at 5-6 hours. The sillage is only perceptible close to the body. I will continue to test the perfume for a while and will definitely give it a chance to stay in my collection.

update 7 months later ... really liking this. the more i smell it, the more unisex it is. im taken by the lemony, rosey oud. this is a 'heavy' dense scent. its eveningy elegance ranks among naxos & dubai gold. 7.5 > 8.5 rating avoid overspraying this. 3 neck sprays is headache-inducing. ---------------------------------------------- 5/11/22 rose takes the stage on initial spray for 4 mins (leaning 90% feminine), until oud surfaces to equally share the spotlight. 3 mins later, the leather appears to smooth everything out. then it gets a lil minty, as the oud falls back. im a note novice, but it could be the rose's reaction to another note freshening it up. 'mint' then sweetens to be a bit lemony, but remains 'fresh' & classy at around 65% fem, as rose enjoys a well-rounded dominance. i didnt get a hit of the other notes, but again, i have not yet well trained myself to. more suitable name would be 'fresh rose' this is better suited for cooler weather, & would suggest on a 25+ female. outside of layering, aoud night appeals to me not. * my current montale fav is chocolate greedy. oud tabacco disgusted me & i scrubbed it off after 15 mins. will give it another shot, another time ty for reading. smell well

Today I ventured into Aoud Night - first with a spray. No, that wasn't a spray, but a spray blast! My support leg lost some stability as Night sharply and spicy rained down on me. It felt like when I fired my first shot from a rifle, and the recoil of the weapon nearly knocked me over. Well, I am a dwarf - and of course, I only shot at a target. But the fragrance hit me just as unprepared. A whole load of Aoud in a leather pouch. This prominent combination also lasts for a while - and I’m glad I sprayed sparingly. Up to this point - definitely a men's fragrance. But then the rose sneaks in, calming the scent and also me. The woody notes are pleasantly forest-like - but also rather jungle-like. The patch is deep - profoundly deep. Definitely suitable for daring gentlemen and ladies - but I do not belong to that species. I prefer to turn to Aoud Ambre.

I like this Montale better! "Intense Café" and "Black Aoud" were quite disappointing for me, but this one actually looks a bit different. Not so clumsy, so loud, so oppressive, but rather showing more artisanal perfumer skill. The aforementioned triad determines the events on my skin. Although I must also say about "Aoud Night" that it seems a bit "over-perfumed" (that seems to be a typical Montale DNA), the ingredients are well balanced and create a pleasantly composed oriental atmosphere. I don't recognize any phases; basically, it starts with a lightly fruity, subtly bitter rose that has indeed turned out a bit smoky. This is rather rare and likely due to the slightly smoky leather that provides a nice contrast. The whole thing is enveloped by oud, which is noble, somewhat resinous, and also a bit sweet. Atmospherically, one already feels quite fittingly on a marketplace in Egypt or Morocco. After 30 minutes, the slightly affected sillage hits the brakes a bit; from then on, one can speak of appropriate harmony. Longevity is otherwise very good; it should be sufficient for the entirety of a club visit on the weekend.

The thicket of Montale fragrances is hard to penetrate. Desperately, I often search for corresponding perfume reviews. With this one, I took the plunge and made a blind purchase due to the excellently sounding fragrance pyramid and the good ratings. And I was very lucky. Now it’s my turn to add a comment. Finally, I have found a leathery oud fragrance that I like. This is due to its perfect balance and its richness of facets. The scent progression is somewhat linear, so no tension is to be expected here. However, the three pillars of the fragrance that harmonize wonderfully make it great for me. (By the way, I do not like the animalistic leather-oud blockbuster “Cuir d'Arabie” and its weaker brother “Aoud Leather.” The former is too dirty for me, while the latter is nicer but too sweet.) The dominant pillar is a rose-oud scent. That’s nice, but it’s something one knows well enough. My favorite in this direction is “Aoud Flowers,” which is even rosier than the more famous “Black Aoud.” The rose in “Aoud Night” is very restrained and much weaker than the oud used. The oud is dry, smoky, morbid, and at the same time noble. The second pillar is an ambered leather. Wonderful, because here too, the settings have been made virtuously. Leather is a difficult yet so beautiful topic. I like leathery fragrances, but dominant leather is usually too piercing and coarse for me. For example, I do not like “Bel Ami.” Leather must always play second or third fiddle, I think. And that’s exactly how it is here. The leather ranks third after oud and rose. For the uninitiated, it is probably hardly noticeable. This level of intensity allows the leather to spread its masculine aura and give the fragrance substance and impact, yet it does not impose itself. I usually do not like amber because it often becomes too stuffy, cloying, and sweaty for me. However, ambered leather can be a highly erotic affair. Thus, the set “Boss Spirit” (a green-leathery chypre) is my second favorite fragrance. In “Aoud Night,” the amber does not bother me at all; rather, it leads to a similarly crackling undertone. The third pillar consists of “patched” woods. Patchouli as well as sandalwood and guaiac wood provide a soft, harmonious, oriental woody background. All three of these ingredients are also difficult for my taste (patch often too slimy or herbaceous, sandalwood often too sweetly-lovely, guaiac mostly too fatty-papery-sweet). But in “Aoud Night,” they are perfectly dosed. Isolated, I can hardly perceive them; to me, they seem equally present and thus very intertwined. Sweetness is hardly present in “Aoud Night,” which I find excellent. The longevity is just okay for Montale standards. The fragrance retreats to the skin after a few hours. However, this is essential for wearability, as one could not endure the initial intensity for hours. Especially the weakening rose allows the other components to come into their own sufficiently. No matter, I like to spray again. I see the application area for “Aoud Night” as going out from autumn to spring. Since the fragrance is never breathtaking, a summer night would also work, but then very cautiously dosed. Leisure and other evening activities are, of course, also suitable. Whether the fragrance survives sports (or whether the leather then becomes sour and piercing as it often does) remains to be tested, but I am optimistic. Overall, I consider “Aoud Night” a valuable addition to the fragrance landscape. Unlike many Montale fragrances, it is not superfluous or redundant. The theme of a leathery and woody oud fragrance has been perfectly implemented for me. If I could get to the fragrance regulators, I would change nothing - what would I change anyway? In this respect, that’s 100% for me, even if the theme certainly does not appeal to everyone. I am happy to have filled the gap in my collection with a beautiful leathery oud fragrance. Phew, done. --- Addendum (from 01.04.2015): In the meantime, I have subjected the fragrance to its stress test, using it during sports. And it passed with flying colors!

When asked what she would be doing on New Year's Eve, Catherine Deneuve once replied: "What I always do, toasting the new year with good friends and a glass of champagne." This not only perfectly captures my idea of a successful New Year's Eve, but she was also one of the few people who received a personal New Year's card from Yves Saint Laurent himself as a regular customer and muse. YSL apparently began printing self-designed drawings and collages, all titled "LOVE," in small quantities as New Year's cards in 1970. These were sent out every New Year "with love" to friends, muses, and possibly good business clients until his death. These collages became so popular that a small book was published in two different editions, and the collages were offered as prints for sale in Paris at the "Fondation Pierre Bergé-Yves Saint Laurent." The collage from 1982 now hangs above my sofa next to a lithograph by the painter Bernard Buffet, whom Pierre Bergé once left for YSL. We remember, Kouros was launched in 1981. Spending the summer - especially the nights - in the Cyclades, especially on the trendy island of Mykonos, was just as fashionable as the nights at New York's Studio 54. The Greek islands, with their untouched nature, island hopping from Paros, Naxos to Santorini, the dry scent of grasses burned in the heat, and the cooling refreshment of the Aegean were made for the hippest of this world. One of them was YSL. His love for this country and the rich history of the "cradle of Europe" culminated in the idea for the scent Kouros and the collage for the following year, 1982. This collage was used as an idea for the summer version of Kouros in 2005. Not the only one, as excerpts from other collages were used for the old versions of "In Love again." And I think that's fantastic. For me, this Kouros packaging is one of the most beautiful ever created by YSL. Discovering the rich past of this artist in a scent in 2005 is wonderful. Unfortunately, it was limited and not sold in Germany. And what does a fragrance smell like that was released in 2005 without much attention... that no one really needed... and that added nothing new to the history of fragrance, unlike the original? It smells excellent, but there is not a big difference from Kouros Cologne Sport. Both are lightly wearable, contemporary scents for everyday use that can be freely sprayed in summer, at the beach, and in the office, differing only in nuances in perception. I do not recommend them for the colder seasons. While the KCS starts off a bit more floral with a hint of jasmine and violet, the Été begins with the scents of Mediterranean countries: rosemary, grapefruit, lemon, and mint. This feels very natural. Both fragrances are characterized by a light note of essential oil, which in the KCS is achieved through menthol, creating a hot-cold effect. In the Été, this is achieved through rosemary and mint, but the hot-cold effect is absent. I would describe the Été as more classic (a bit closer to Kouros), powerful, and less floral. In contrast, the KCS is more modern and woody (cedar), minimalist, matte, and factual. In the base, both are very close together and are made lasting by a skin-like musk and amber accord, although this does not seem as present in the Été. For me, it is the best summer version that was released alongside KSC. I can recommend the vintages 2002, 2005, and 2006, which are all very similar. Less good vintages *Cheers* are 2007 and 2008. 2010 and 2011 are unfortunately incredibly long-lasting, but strangely synthetic, harsh, and unpleasant. Although Kouros has withstood the reformulation quite well, it now comes without silver edges and the care line has been completely discontinued, which unfortunately diminishes its value that it had for the company for decades, which is a shame.

Honestly, it smells good. It's a bubblegum pear scent. It's very popular, probably a crowd favorite. The bottle is cute, so no complaints. But, I don't think I want it, and I wouldn't shell out the money for it. I'd be happy to receive it as a gift. It's a floral designer perfume with a sherbet flavor. It's perfect for enhancing a feminine mood, but not for me. Unfortunately, the white musk at the end reminds me of "the designer perfume" and makes me feel like "gum that has lost its flavor." Well, it's a designer perfume so it's to be expected, but it's not very pretty.

Here I am again, surrounded by women's fragrances. And as if that weren't bad enough, I'm here among the Turquoises on a Saturday, when the store is really crowded (and statistically speaking, there are more women around, especially in this warm weather). To top it off, I'm out with my mother, as she's going on vacation soon and is looking for a new scent. Nothing complicated, nothing overly expensive, just something fresh and/or sweet. Okay, I say,… let's take a look… and that should be the last thing I said before I ultimately regretted the whole thing… Anyway, first a few words about this fragrance here (which she actually picked up among others). Pushed onto us by a saleswoman with a test strip (who, to be fair, also looked really hot…), we tested the scent. Unfortunately, the saleswoman spotted us quite late, so my mother had no free spot left to spray. You can probably guess what happened next… well, you'll find out shortly after the scent description…! Oh, by the way, I don't know the other Signorinas (um… not yet??). Therefore, unfortunately, there's no comparison to see what's new or different from the other flankers in this line. The scent: The beginning is fruity sweet. I smell pears, which have a nice and fruity-summery scent. Cherry blossoms or cherries and sweet floral notes from jasmine come in as well. The pears are long-lasting and smell nice and light with the jasmine. The scent has a very summery aura, even though it isn't particularly extraordinary when strictly considered. In the background, I perceive slightly stuffy floral notes, but they are too weak to be bothersome (besides, the slight stuffiness is extremely short-lived, so you don't notice it later on). In the base, the scent continues to smell fruity and delicious. The sweetness is no longer purely floral but also comes a bit from the musk, although the musk isn't particularly strong. An overall nice scent. The sillage and longevity: The projection is okay, could have been a bit stronger. It's good to smell up close, but generally, despite the sweet notes, it's a bit too light. The longevity is acceptable, as it lasts five to seven hours. The bottle: The bottle is rectangular and filled with pink fragrance liquid. There are a few bows around the neck that are also pink and make the whole bottle look somewhat cute (by the way, my mother was quite enchanted by the bottle :D). It is topped with a gold, round cap, which is a bit harder to remove than expected. All in all, though, it's a nicely made bottle. So… *sigh* Yes,… I'm sighing again… Because, as I said, I was out with my mother. And you can't imagine how exhausting that can sometimes be. We tested various fragrances (not to mention other purchases… because when my father isn't around, I have to take care of everything, especially since her German isn't that great… what I have to endure… :D), but most of the scents she liked a lot were heavy sweet fragrances, which are rather unsuitable for summer. But then she discovered a few other scents and, of course, wanted to hear my opinion about them. Naturally, I eventually got bored and wanted to start whining like a little kid to finally leave. But at least I could distract myself a bit. But not with fragrances…. Not even with my smartphone… but with… legs. Well, what can I say? You know I'm single. No, I'm an extreme perpetual single. … so I tend to look at attractive women more often and for longer than perhaps others do! And when I get bored, I start focusing only on the ladies in short skirts to make time pass faster and, above all, more pleasantly, and okay… because it's always such a nice sight (and because I'm such a pig *sigh*). It doesn't matter whether the girls are between 20 and 40 or so or even hot…. um… *clears throat*… MILFs… (oh, you know what I mean! :DD) and regardless of whether they are light or dark, all that doesn't matter, because everyone looks hot in summer, so hot that you want to reach into your pants and… aaargh, I meant so hot that your eyes pop out!! *phew, I managed to steer back on track* :D Oh man, I might be terrible…. My summer motto is always "Legs are fine because I'm a swine!"…. *sigh* This is made worse by the fact that shorts and skirts get shorter every year (okay, I still like it aaaaah!). Anyway, while I was busy observing, my mother suddenly dragged me to another fragrance she had discovered (or rather, a saleswoman had shown her). And this fragrance here. Unfortunately, she had no free space left to test. Who had to step in? Me, of course. While I initially resisted, I simultaneously noticed the pretty saleswoman (who, of course, was also wearing a short skirt, argh :D), who was observing the whole situation. I smiled at her because I thought she was cute, and she even smiled back! But,… she was more laughing because the situation was funny and she noticed that my mother was just using me as a test strip *sigh* … and not because I smiled at her *sigh again* … honestly, I would rather test women's fragrances in public, sweaty and full of fear, than go shopping with my mother, brrr… it took a long time before we left the store, and I actually like hanging out in fragrance shops… As for this fragrance here, I was pleasantly surprised. I thought it would be TOO generic, but I think anyone looking for a nice, sweet summer scent that should also be affordable can go for it without hesitation! Sure, it's nothing really special, but it's still nice. Optimal, for example, for a short vacation trip or as a daytime scent on warm days. …*sigh*… now everyone will surely show up at the next Parfumo meeting in long pants… :D

I always enjoy reaching for the Signorinas, as they all have an overwhelmingly positive attitude - plus style and flair. Today, I was the only lady in a group of men - so to speak, the hen in the basket. Nevertheless, I found myself somewhat overshadowed in the heated political discussions - as the looming ban on diesel vehicles was the focus. This topic doesn't leave me cold either, but I fiddled with my In Fiore box during the conversation and, by the way, applied a spray. Oops - the heads of my gentlemen turned to me in unison. A general pause and deep inhalation. Fragrance against diesel. And the winner was: in fiore. Synchronized, unusual interest from the gentlemen in the "little scent." "Delicious!" my friend on the left exclaimed, and from the right came the remark: "spring-like feminine!" Short and to the point - but well said. The pear-pomegranate combination is truly delightful - yet in a transparent way, so that no gourmand impression is created. The cherry blossoms drift down lightly and spring-like - illuminated by white jasmine. Creamy sandalwood lays over it, and musk adds a delicate elegance. A pleasant, relaxing pause sets in - somehow soothing after the debate. In Fiore caused a stir - and the fine dust has given way to the pollen.

No question, Idole is a very beautiful fragrance, but it can have a bit of a nerve potential when overapplied. Gentle pear, fruity pomegranate, no synthetics. Floral, powdery, creamy, slightly woody. I walk in a pastel-colored dress, sun-kissed through the streets of Italy, treat myself to a pear sorbet, drink pomegranate juice, and catch a hint of cherry blossoms (Sakura!) The longevity and sillage are exactly as they should be for a spring/summer fragrance. Noticeable but not overwhelming. Scents like this are what I love alongside Givenchy Irresistible le Parfum and Kogai.

Amber & Spices opens with an alcohol blast that left my nasal passages completely clear and sterilized. Once the alcohol opening settles, Amber & Spices moves into a very dry and saturated woody oud note. The oud has just a sprinkle of nutmeg and finally, a very soft rose layer. This transition is pleasing but nothing remarkable. The rose note in this fragrance is pretty and mild and is a nice companion to the oud. The rose slowly and methodically pushes it way into the heart of the fragrance a bit more boldly like an uninvited guest. You will also detect a bit of cumin spicing up the rose just a tad, but as far as the overall progression of this fragrance, it is quite linear. Just as you were getting used to the rose's more robust appearance, you find sandalwood knocking on the door. I found the introduction of sandalwood in the base to be the most interesting part of Amber & Spices. There is something quite foreign about this scent combination and very intriguing. Even though the word amber is the first word in the title, I find a vague reference to it in Amber & Spices' base, not so much amber and not so much spice. If this were titled Oud & Rose, that would be somewhat more believable. Amber & Spices didn't impress me much. It is as memorable as a nicely scented hand lotion or closet freshener. This fragrance has average longevity and doesn't really develop much after the end of the heart note stage. Everything in the base notes either rushes in or is so vague that you hardly notice its presence. Considering the large number of fragrances Montale produces, they seem more interested in quantity over quality these days. Forget Amber & Spices being stiff competition for any of the more well-known veterans of this category.

It goes on and on!!! It won't quit! This fragrance is very linear and over it's life I sense only a slight evolution... I smell sweaty man! This is the dirtiest amber I have ever smelled! All of my family thought it was sweaty man body on my arm. Despite the BO smell it is still distinctly amber in the end. Not for me!

Opens a little dirty and woody, then calms down to a woody-sweety smell. Lots of cumin, nutmeg and ebony wood. In the late drydown it does smells like Aoud Lime. I actually dont smell any amber. Sillage, lasting power and projection are high. Updated January 2014

Yes, I know - the saying goes differently and is borrowed from our favorite quote acrobat Lothar Mätthäus. But just as clumsy as the headline is Amber & Spices in its progression. This Montale starts off quite ambitiously, yet without amber. The opening actually promises more of a classic Oud scent, meaning heavy woody-resinous with good brightening spicy and minimal rosy undertones without becoming barn-like. Simply elegant, but for many already too ordinary and established, if not even boring. However, after a few minutes, one wonders what has happened to the namesake amber. It simply does not show up or sniff around. Instead, after some time, cumin takes the reins. Unfortunately, in an increasingly dry, if not even dusty variant. As it progresses, it resembles more of rubber that has been slightly scorched with cumin - a smell I have occasionally encountered on the streets or alleys of India. There are definitely worse things one can accidentally pick up olfactorily, yet this cumin in this form is definitely out of place. In the later closing phase, a bit of Oud appears again along with woody notes, but still without amber. A conciliatory ending, which nonetheless leaves one wondering what the inclusion of cumin was all about. What would the scent have been without its questionable appearance? And would more amber and less eagle wood have improved the whole thing? Oud & Cumin would definitely have been a more honest name for it all.

For a long time, I hesitated to comment on Amber & Spices. This is primarily because it is very difficult to describe. But now I want to try to say what simply needs to be said. The opening indeed has notes of hairspray, and even hints of nitro thinner, but that lasts only about 5 minutes, nothing more. A fragrance should be given that much time to unfold. Once these initial nuances have faded, it does not smell synthetic to me at all; I believe there are a lot of good ingredients in it, that’s my impression. And if something is synthetic, then it is damn well done. I find this endless debate about whether something is synthetic or not absolutely unnecessary; it’s primarily about whether it smells good or not. And the coin always has two sides. On one hand, many want a fragrance made from natural essences, while on the other hand, hardly anyone wants nature to be exploited for it. Just a side note. This fragrance is a true work of art, one of those that really blows you away. It cannot be classified as a typical oriental, not at all. Resin and wood clearly dominate here. And if you love that, like I do, then you are absolutely right here. I actually don’t smell any Oud in this. Cumin, I just went to the spice cabinet to check, can be perceived minimally, but only to give a slight directional correction to the more prominent ingredients in the base. Amber dominates here. I have worked a lot with ebony and even burned pieces of it, so I can perceive that, while the sandalwood is less noticeable. But enough analysis; in any case, Amber & Spices is a really rich resin bomb in the first hour that then increasingly takes on a beautiful fine wood note, the resin is still present but becomes noticeably quieter. Even though there are more female wearers, I find it distinctly masculine, not like Blue Amber, which is sweeter and vanillic. But of course, I don’t want to put the ladies off; I’m well aware that one wouldn’t just leave such a fragrance sitting on the shelf. So let’s say it is quite wearable for men.

This is not a simple scent. First of all, it clearly belongs to the Oud line, and it certainly contains more of it than some of the fragrances that carry Oud in the name at Montale. I can't make much sense of the name "Amber and Spices." In any case, this Oud perfume, which develops very linearly, has for me a punch of the technical-industrial.

What is it with me: Am I a closet SadoMasoFan, have I been married too long to a man who spends a significant part of his free time tinkering with his two- or four- - but at least not three-wheeled vehicles?? Is the former a possible or even necessary consequence of the latter?

"Amber & Spices" is something atypical from Montale... there is no Oud in the name! However, I perceive it right after spraying for a moment. From a distance, "Amber & Spices" smells like a mix of Kellog's Smacks combined with a Michelin tire. Rubber and honey sweetness? It smells surprisingly good! After 6 minutes, the scent changes.

This scent has absolutely nothing fresh about it. For a brief moment, the top note right after application reminds me of perm solution. It brought back memories! But relatively quickly, the fragrance starts to intensify with spiciness, and it does so quite abundantly. After about 15 minutes, a certain sweetness sets in, softening the sharpness of the spicy top note.

Another scent from Montale..... In general, I have to say that Montale fragrances smell totally synthetic and generally have a medicinal note, which I don't know how it comes about, and that I actually don't like! Both are actually negative traits, yet something captivates me about the Montales.

"Amo Ferragamo Flowerful" (can a perfume with such a filling name really be successful?!) is a naive-hip fruit cocktail. Blood orange, blood young, blood inexperienced, not yet in its bloom. Charming, caressing. A bit trashy and not too high-quality. But it comes with a few beach balls and ideas that have been washed and a certain lack of quality, ambition, and nobility... "Flowerful" is quite a sugary gem for in-between. (Not) a real little fruit! Synthetics, watery notes, and sugar play major roles. But I like this carefree attitude. Always laughing, always in a good mood, always open-hearted and sexy. Real advertising for Campari, which is much more bitter and sharper in reality. Sparkling, pink. Cheeky - but never too much. Visually, it’s a bit as if Sabrina Carpenter (one of the few current pop ladies whose appearance I know!) were a perfume. Bottle: girly and glittery Sillage: playful and lovely Longevity: 3-5 hours, rather on the lower end Conclusion: a light and uncomplicated "daytime" party scent between cocktails and cocktail dresses. Just no cocktail tomatoes.

Starts off fresh and then immediately transitions to a softly neutral floral. The blackcurrant is only present for a very brief moment. An indefinable floral amalgam emerges, also calm... While waiting for woods, musk, and vanilla, the perfume quietly fades away.... It leaves no memory...

After the Amo EDP really blew me away, the mother-of-pearl bottle of flowerful also caught my interest. It shimmered in all pastel colors and encouraged me to make a blind purchase. However, this flanker reminds me not of the EDP, but rather, with its Campari start, of Nina l `elixir, which joyfully clinks glasses with Caipirinha as a greeting. But then flowerful lives up to its name and heads in the direction of light blooms. An afternoon in the garden with a slightly bitter glass of Campari mix, a good book - in the shade of the jasmine bushes. The aroma of the currant bushes wafts over aromatically. The sun's rays are softened by light foliage, and there is a mix of vanilla and smoky notes in the air. Flowerful radiates calm and tranquility - a Sunday afternoon in the garden - when time seems to pass more slowly. It is no longer hot - but the autumn sun still warms gently. Its light shimmers over the lawn - and from the house sounds: Wish you were here - by Pink Floyd. One might wish for company - but is content with the company of flowerful.

lounging chair on mediterranean beach under an umbrella - new leather sandals laying on the sand, hot from the sun - sparkling earl grey iced tea - white cliffs towering over warm waters - salt crusted hair - gasoline leaking at the marina - driving a cabriolet on a winding coastal cliffside road - moscow mules

I received a sample of this wonderful perfume through a sharing here in the Souk. A big thank you to Fabian for the professional handling. I had never smelled a fresh oud fragrance before, but the combination of fresh, citrus notes and the spicy oud is something I really like! I could hardly imagine it that way. It does have, as others have described, a certain similarity to Bleu de Chanel or Versace Dylan Blue, but I also detect something like Noir de Noir by Tom Ford. If you like these fragrances and are looking for something with its own twist, you are certainly in the right place. The projection of Oudessey is quite good, although it is not a beast like some other Montale fragrances. However, it is very versatile and can be worn in summer as well as winter for almost any occasion. You probably won't run into any trouble wearing it at work either. A truly successful fragrance with, in my opinion, a distinctly unique DNA.

The first seconds after spraying: Barbershop / Aftershave + deodorant in a very high quality. After that, woody, fresh, masculine, slightly sweet & slightly powdery For me, we have a classic designer compliment getter DNA here, but in something more high-quality and not so synthetic. So nothing new! Longevity on my skin is very poor for the price...after 6 hours it was over. Tom Ford Oud Wood has more to do with oud than this fragrance here...really a shame! I think people who like YSL Y EDP, Armani Code Parfum, Acqua di Gio EDT/EDP will enjoy this scent. Due to the longevity, I would rather reach for the other fragrances, as they last longer on me.

That I had something like a Kouros Day & Festival today, I have already written in the somewhat longer Kouros Cologne Sport comment, as well as the quiet suspicion that perhaps something in my sample labeling might be mixed up. Here now is my impression of the perfume that was on my right wrist, where the sample is labeled Kouros Tattoo 2007 & where I hope it is indeed the aforementioned summer flanker from the year 2007. I have hardly any direct memories of the summer of 2007, a year before my high school graduation... this was not only because there was no major football event nor a personal milestone, and also not because I was just partying and drinking too much... but maybe it has to do with such shapeless, generic summer perfumes like this one here? ;) Kouros Tattoo 2007 is, for me, closer to any designer quick-shot summer mass product than to the original, even quite far from the simultaneously tested Cologne Sport. A lot of mandarin, a few salty sparkling notes (still the best!), very faint Kouros magic, synthetic & diluted turned up, statistics shortened, character softened - and there you have a mediocre summer remix that has been more or less thrown onto the market every year since then. Bottle: beautiful Greek summer vibe... if I ever find myself in a duty-free shop before a Greece vacation... I will almost certainly buy a Kouros bottle & bathe in it on Crete & Co. ;) Sillage & longevity: exceptionally quiet & unfortunately gone after 4-5 hours over all the Greek mountains. Conclusion: unfortunately, I can hardly relate to the Kouros summer versions at all & would rather wish for the old Sport version back... but YSL prefers to bring out half-baked flankers annually and thousands of unnecessary L'Hommes :(

Today I received my next limited summer fragrance from Yves Saint Laurent's Kouros. This time I snagged it at a large online auction house. It is the summer flanker from the year 2007: Kouros Tattoo Edition Its advertising poster featured the muscular torso of a Greek athlete against the blue sky of Greece. In the sky floats the bottle, and the athlete's upper arm is adorned with a black tattoo of the classic Greek symbol that decorates the packaging and the bottles. The bottle is turquoise blue, the color of the Mediterranean as it caresses the Greek islands. The center of the bottle is adorned with the well-known Greek symbol, which this time has been elaborated into a tattoo with delicate lines added in the middle. The fragrance starts with the spicy-animalic top note typical of the classic, just a bit more subdued. After about 15 minutes, I detect the added mandarin lightly fruity in the background, but it quickly disappears again. The more the fragrance transitions into the heart note, the weaker it becomes. After half an hour, the spicy-animalic aspect from the top note has also receded significantly. Finally, the cool cedarwood note comes in, with the spicy incense lingering in the background, but also only very subtly. Overall, this flanker starts off with a lot of the original, but the heart and base notes are a diluted variation in intensity. A Kouros fan will surely appreciate it, as the original is easily recognizable and not too much has been added; only the intensity is noticeably weaker, and it feels more refreshing and cooler. A perfect companion for very hot summer days or indeed a vacation in Greece.

Ferragamo F Free Time is another flanker, but unlike F and F Black, FFFT is a sporty EdT. The DNA of the other two is, if at all, only subtly perceivable. The fragrance stands on its own: it is fresh, citrusy, and slightly aquatic. Only the pepper is common among the 3 Fs. In FFFT, the lemon is the most prominent, with pepper and maritime notes also present. The woody notes come into play at the end of the fragrance development, although this is anything but complex. Unlike F and F Black, the longevity here, typical for a fresh, citrus-aquatic scent, is significantly lower. It is perceptible close to the skin for 3 to a maximum of 4 hours, and the sillage is not particularly strong even shortly after spraying. Its weaknesses are also its strengths in my opinion: I use this light, carefree scent either before or after training, in the height of summer, or right after showering. Always when I don't want to wear something heavy or complex, or when I need to be quick. I paid €25 for 100ml, it doesn't get much better than that. If you can still find it, even up to €40/100ml, then you should grab it. Absolutely a candidate for a blind buy, you can't go wrong with it!

Honestly - I was looking for a perfume that reminded me of the scent of a freshly cut flower meadow. In the Duty Free, I stood there with a huge selection of perfumes in front of me. I just wanted something that smelled green. In Love Again came to me with its freshness, this light green breeze, just right. On the first spray, it is bitter-herb, and this note remains. It becomes a bit softer and more floral when you give the scent some time. However, In Love Again remains, to my regret, somewhat scratchy and not very complex in my nose. Perhaps it’s the star anise… Anne-Cage has already described this; this version of In Love Again indeed does not come across as very sweet or rounded. It is rather sporty-elegant, cool. Today, I would only wear it in spring, and if so, then very sparingly.

Since In Love Again is one of my absolute favorite fragrances, I am more than disappointed with this extended edition. I ordered it online and hoped for a light floral/sweet summer scent.... Unfortunately, the fragrance is very heavy, starting off with a strong scent of teak wood.... It is very woody and overloaded with flowers, not at all my taste; I really don't like using it.

Boisé Vanillé is one of the rare fragrances that nobody should die before having smelled it. It is very much off the beaten track with its surprisingly different handling of vanilla. Whenever this note is being found in the pyramid, we are quick to call the fragrance an oriental. However, despite vanilla, Boisé Vanillé is very much the style of a a dark chypre! The fragrance has a fruity opening which salutes us with a rather strange contrast to the vanilla note. It is a little bit the kind of dried fruits style although with lemon and bergamot, the known scent notes do not reveal much. Fruitiness is top notes only in here, and it dies away quickly into a solid but very, very dark kind of vanilla and patchouli accord without lots of further development. This vanilla is far from being broad or sweetish. No custard! It has has herbal aspects, and a wonderful deep and dark transparency or iridescence which is the core of its very unique style. Besides that, it might have some reminiscence to certain ambery perfumes. Enough said, Boisé Vanillé is one of those where the list of scent notes does not reveal the essential. It is listed as a ladies fragrance on Parfumo, but if so, then it is one of the very few that I wear. I think it can also be worn by men and some women: no girlies, no blondes – rather for self confident ladies with a darker complexion who are proud of their live experience. It is definitely old-fashioned, and if you want to make use of a clichée, you may very well link it to the concept of the femme fatale. While being not the best choice for everybody, it should have a gorgeous effect on those who fit to it. The brand Montale is best known for their ouds, and to be honest, many of their other perfumes are not that interesting. Boisé Vanillé, however, is one of the few exceptions. It is a true gem and highly recommendable. Test it if you can find it!

Sharp, biting opening, a medicine-like smell, slightly reminiscent of some juniper-tar based ointment prescribed against rheumatism. I can't agree with Apicus on this one: hate it! Can neither detect any vanilla-warmth or pleasant woody ingredients in Boisé Vanillé which - like many scents I don't fancy - lasts for hours. A total bummer for me. This is a fragrance which would really put me off, if someone wore it in my presence. But I'm lucky, I've never smelled it on anybody before, just sampled it today. Sniffing my way around samples is always a fascinating experience - and I conclude that Montale is a house behind which I have to put a very big question mark. One more perfume from their range which I cannot stand. Good to know.

Blind tests are sometimes so exciting, and I enjoy doing them again and again, even though I often miss the mark when it comes to the results. This was also the case with Montale Boisé Vanille. A fragrance I would have never considered testing. Montale is simply not my brand. I tried a few and was mostly put off by the loud chemical punch and the hours-long longevity and sillage reaching all the way to Düsseldorf. And that’s quite a distance from the beautiful Albtrauf here in Baden-Württemberg. Boisé Vanille, one of the older Montales, certainly has such a sillage. However, it smells very nice here. And since I only applied a drop for testing, that works for me. I wouldn’t spray this fragrance if I wanted to wear it properly, but rather not. This is one to dab. For the pulse points. It is a sensual scent with a beautiful balsamic quality. To me, it initially smells like a classic vintage perfume from the fifties or sixties. It could even be older. This spicy top note briefly reminds me of classics like Opium or Must de Cartier. But quickly the fragrance reveals its heart. A full, rich amber introduces the heart note. The perfume becomes sweeter, more sensual, but never drifts into a gourmand direction. This classic quality inherent in the fragrance remains throughout. Later in the base, it becomes spicier with patchouli. I also perceive labdanum and a hint of animalic notes, probably musk. I wouldn’t rule out civet, very subtly. Well, with my first assumption of having a vintage classic under my nose, I was completely off. I would have guessed many things. A Lagerfeld, an Armani, or perhaps something older from Nicolaï, Maître Parfumeur et Gantier, or maybe even Villoresi. It does have some traits of Amre Tibet from MPeG in its amber phase. But Montale? No, I would have never guessed this brand here. The surprise is all the more delightful. And it’s proof that we should never completely dismiss a brand when the first test fragrances don’t appeal to us. After all, there are quite a few candidates in the portfolios of my favorite houses that wouldn’t receive particularly good ratings from me. This Montale does it, even though it’s not at all my type of fragrance. Those who love classics and amber and enjoy a bit more sillage will definitely find this one appealing. Many thanks to Ergoproxy for the testing opportunity.

This scent is driving me almost out of my mind. I read the name, I read the notes, I read the comments. And I am more confused than ever after the first sniff. Somehow, nothing here adds up. Woody? Yes. Yes. And yes. Vanilla? No. Not even dry, transparent, ethereal vanilla. Fruity opening? Maybe. For me, it’s more Montale-like medicinal. Fizzy? Yes, somewhat. You could almost call it scratchy. Aoud? No. Definitely not. I, the Aoud pig, found none. Patchouli? But yes. However, and this is quite rare: this time with really little earth, mold, and crypt. Still not cuddly chocolatey, as patchouli often becomes when it doesn’t smell cool and damp. Galbanum? It’s not listed here, but there must be something galbanum-like, as the perfume becomes very bitter-sharp-moldy-gray-green on me after a while. Pepper? Maybe. Boisé Vanillé is more spicy than sharp in this regard. Perhaps lemon pepper, as there is a sour-spicy touch. Geranium? No. Maybe a bit of the soapy note that Lila mentioned. Feminine? No. Masculine? Yes, I also confess to being part of the faction that considers Boisé Vanillé to be a rather masculine-rough fragrance. Let’s say it’s an interesting creation, to which I find absolutely no access. While it is anything but a difficult bomb, I still perceive Boisé Vanillé as unbalanced. Bitter woods dominate for me, paired with a scratchy sour spice, and since the vanilla doesn’t show up on me, unfortunately no fine (not even dry) sweetness can soothe and unite the biting scent notes. I obviously do not have the right hydro-lipid coat for this perfume.

Today I had the pleasure of testing Boise Vanille by Montale, and I was quite surprised by what I perceived after spraying it ... The scent felt very familiar and instantly transported me back in time ... After all, I used the fragrance twin almost daily for quite a while and still like it today. It's strange that no one has noticed it so far, but in my eyes, or rather my nose, Boise Vanille is almost a 100% copy of the legendary Lagerfeld Classic - comparing both fragrance pyramids, you can already see many similarities - on the nose, both are nearly identical, except for a slight variance in the top note ... Boise Vanille is soft, warm, slightly bitter, and at the same time sweet - it is clearly dominated by patchouli, vanilla, and tonka bean, underpinned by a pleasantly woody cedar that keeps the scent in balance - the beginning seems rather angular and slightly scratchy to me, but this impression fades very quickly - sillage is moderate, longevity - at least on my skin - is noticeably weaker than the mentioned counterpart - I like it, although I find the "original" much better - in my opinion, despite its softness, it is more of a scent for the distinguished over 30 gentleman - therefore, I find it remarkable that Boise Vanille is listed here as a women's perfume & that far more perfumistas own it than parfumos ... Considering the rather high prices - compared to the fragrance twin - I certainly wouldn't buy this scent ...

My first Montale, a steal, so heavily discounted. I couldn't help it, I had to take it home blind. BV is more of a women's fragrance, which I don't mean to imply is not wearable for men, that's nonsense. Everyone can wear what suits them in terms of scents. But the character is rather feminine.

I happened to read the description and the included fragrance notes - Whoa, all great scent components that I love dearly, this had to be MY fragrance. I had to get a sample: Unfortunately, the Boise Vanilla is not for me :-( The scent is very vanilla, no question about it, but a very bitter, dry vanilla with a distinct pepper note.

Inspired by the enthusiasm and intrigued by the fragrance notes, I had to test it as well, but it’s probably not made for me. I mainly smell the piercing musk, which has already spoiled several other Montale fragrances for me. In addition, a good amount of pepper develops on a sweet vanilla powder base. This combination is definitely too strange for me.

A scent that I have NEVER smelled like this before! To my nose! And to the beards of all prophets! A floral-fine flicker hangs in the air! As a visual counterpart, I think of a mirage (as if a path or road were wet at a certain distance). It usually occurs when the sun is shining brightly, but the air is still and very cool. As if radio waves were "visible over the ether"...

A lot has already been written about this scent. I would now like to express my praise for this little treasure in my own words. Boisé Vanille has an interesting structure. The smoky opening makes one fear that it is an Aoud bomb. However, there is no Aoud listed in the ingredients.

When I first sprayed this on, my face must have transformed into something quite ugly when I detected that dreaded pineapple, my arch-nemesis, the one note that I cannot seem to be friends with no matter how hard I try. Even tropical passionfruit and my beloved bergamot couldn't hide that all too familiar sour note wafting up towards my nose and giving me such an intense headache. I was cross most of the day, but just to be fair I would keep sniffing my wrist hoping that the pineapple note would disappear or at the very least soften. Thankfully it did and I was then greeted by an array of beautiful florals blended with peach. Quite a refreshing and bright scent, that smells very clean, like Sunsilk shampoo. Okay so it's not a scent for me, but I absolutely adore, no, actually I'm enchanted by the cute, rainbow printed bottle. It's something you'd imagine a fairytale princess displaying on her dresser and quite possibly wearing. Seeing that this scent has managed to bring out the inner child in me, I would definitely recommend this to young girls or even the young at heart. Either way this fresh, pretty and sweet scent is sure to capture your heart, that is if you enjoy pineapple.

Incanto Shine smells floral-fruity-fresh with a subtle sweetness. Actually not bad at first, but I am bothered by a hated note that emerges after about half an hour, becoming more and more present, which I refer to as the "shaving lotion note." I recognize this synthetic-sounding note from countless deodorants and men's fragrances (mainly with descriptors like "Sport," "Fresh," or "Men"), but also from cleaning products ("Fresh," "Forest Fresh," or "Ocean") and from corresponding room sprays that are primarily intended for use in bathrooms and toilets. I can completely understand Lakritzengel's association. I have long wondered which ingredient is responsible for this note, and I have now concluded that it must be due to cedarwood. Or more likely, a synthetic ingredient that is meant to simulate cedarwood or intensify natural cedarwood oil. I am familiar with natural cedarwood oil and enjoy its scent without perceiving this hated note.
it smells strongly of toilet air fresheners.

This is a perfume I did not think I would really enjoy, but man was I wrong! It is an absolutely beautiful scent, full of roses and vanilla, mixed with some musk. There’s a tiny bit of raspberry there, but only enough to make it super interesting. It doesn’t smell of berries, but a delightful mixture. The sillage and longevity are both great! I’m shocked at how much I love this one, as it’s a new style for me.

For vanilla amber lovers, this is a cool change and definitely worth testing. The raspberry note is very strong and, in my opinion, comes out beautifully; the musk and sandalwood give the fragrance a wonderful dry down combined with the vanilla and amber. Definitely a very strong sillage and projection-heavy scent that one must like; I smelled it on a friend and fell in love.

A lot of heckling and a wave of criticism covered up such an interesting fragrance, causing curiosity about it to quickly fall away. People chose to regard it as a bathroom air freshener instead of actually considering its scent.... This highly aromatic perfume is a brilliant solution for hot days, and basil provides us with just that. Very fresh and well diffused in the hands, it gives the whole fragrance a sensational character. Just plucked from the garden, grown in ideal conditions, it conveys its nature unpretentiously. This beautiful herb is given an original twist by kumquat and pear. In an original way, they provide a hint of that sweetness gradually turning into a citrus garden thing. A few moments later, tuberose provides an organic scent, giving the fragrance that 'green' vibe. The very soft and smooth layer of the plant makes the perfume even more appetising. And the slight note of plumeria really puts us in a mesmerising state. The whole fragrance is very gently spiced with Indian black pepper and tonka bean, which are not as noticeable as the rest, but definetely give us that needed spice. For a citrus-fresh fragrance, it lingers on the skin for quite a long time, just like the rest of the montale perfumes. Its price is affordable and satisfactory. Overall, it is a really noteworthy fragrance, found on the shelf of a fresh spring or hot summer.

I admit, I have hardly paid attention to Montale fragrances until now. Yes, the brand exists, I've heard of it, but it never really interested me. *cough* Maybe also because the bottles are so ugly. But a fragrance that has basil in its name was impossible for me to resist; it had to be tested, as I love basil as a scent note. Not just like, love! And what a wonderful interpretation of basil was presented to me here. I had already tested "Thé Basilic | Molinard," and while I found it very nice, it was rather monotonous. Just basil, nothing else. Montale, on the other hand, has really built a composition around the basil. The fragrance begins with a lovely mix of pear and kumquat, which, to my delight, comes across very naturally here and not so synthetic-fruity like with many designer fruit fragrances. The pepper is also noticeable, but very subtle in the background. After this naturally fruity opening, the star takes the stage: the basil. However, it does not overshadow the pear and kumquat; instead, it dances around them, and at that moment, it smells to me like a mega delicious Italian dessert. Basil ice cream with fruits or something, heavenly, I want to sink into this scent. After this first act, the basil then takes a solo for a while until the white flowers and base notes come in and gently lead it to the dry down, even though they continue to leave the spotlight to it as the star. In the end, our star herb bows elegantly and leaves the stage hand in hand with the vetiver in a sweet-bitter-herb cloud, and I in the audience have long since jumped up from my seat, shouting and applauding, wildly waving a "Fantastic Basil - I love you!!!!!!!" sign back and forth, as if I were trying to guide a jumbo jet to the runway.

I have to admit I have some issues with Montales. So far, none of them have found a place in my collection because none have fit 100%. Sometimes too sweet, sometimes too synthetic, sometimes too harsh, always too loud. Therefore, I didn’t expect much when I participated in the sharing from the lovely @Diana870411. Basil was not unfamiliar to me… as a side note, so to speak… as a secondary scent, but not as the main actor. After 3 days of testing, I must say: it has potential to settle in. I do not perceive this Montale as synthetic at all. Neither in the top note nor in the heart note. With the first spray, a beautiful fresh basil comes through, paired with kumquat. I can barely smell pear and frangipani. After about half an hour, the scent loses some of its freshness and becomes a bit more bitter. Gradually, a little tuberose and tonka join in. Not sweet, as one often knows tuberose and tonka, but still a bit fresh and bitter. Now for the longevity and sillage: again, not a typical Montale: Longevity for me: max. 4-5 hours (depending on temperature), sillage hardly noticeable. Both are not necessarily positive at first, but for summer, it’s just right for me. The scent is not loud, exciting, and striking but rather quiet and a dreamy summer fragrance… because it is not like the others. In any case: IT WILL… it will be the first one to settle in with me (even though I really don’t like the can design) because I don’t have anything like this in my collection.

Ferragamo can also do Private Blend a la Tom Ford. Long-lasting. Good sillage. Smells of luxury and quality. Black bottles with mahogany caps. Consistent and elegant. So how do the 3 new oriental creations from the Italian house Ferragamo smell now? The Tuscan Scent Collection is truly well done! One targets leather/incense customers, the second one is for honey lovers, and the third? Mimosa, vanilla, oud. Those are the keywords! I bought White Mimosa because it fits perfectly with the cold, upcoming winter. Oriental warm gourmand. For connoisseurs of Tom Ford, it smells as if Tuscan Leather and Tobacco Vanille were mixed together, with tobacco removed and mimosa added. Almost done. Unfortunately, no one currently does mimosa as well as Diptyque with 34 Essences Insensées... but Ferragamo comes very, very close! The mimosa never feels too much or even bothersome. No headaches. No wrinkling of the nose. Real class! White Mimosa starts chocolatey, woody, slightly smoky, and ambrette. This opening is one of the best! So incredibly deep and seductive. Unfortunately, it lasts only about 15 minutes. The mimosa is not white and light for me, but deep golden-yellow and heavy. It is somewhat suppressed by a kind of oud accord. Chemical oud, but soft and good. Slightly sweet and leathery. Not stinky and oily at all. Not musty, marked, or off-putting. Creamy and gourmand is the centerpiece of this super beautiful creation. Heavy and a bit feminine. For women aged 35 and up. Men can wear it too, but the scent leans more towards the feminine side of well-known fragrances. I don't mind. The base: Chypre notes and golden vanilla are the core of the matter after 4 hours of dry down. Not quite as sweet as Tobacco Vanille by Tom Ford or Collection Extraordinaire - Orchidée Vanille by V. C&A. Iris is a bit lacking... which isn’t so bad. More mimosa in the base would have been great. 200€ for 75 ml. Hamburger Hof, for example, offers it. Otherwise, only selected Ferragamo stores. What can I say.... Recommendation to buy for the winter... if you have the money.

Aoud Queen Roses opens with an assertive oud, more rubbery and leathery than musty, animalic or acridly smoky. The oud stays at the front for about 30 minutes, waiting for a ruby rose unfolding its velvety petals before retreating to the sideline. I was a bit worried at first, that Aoud Queen Roses might subsequently choose the gourmand jammy raspberry-oud-rose path. But fortunately, the fragrance doesn't hesitate to shed most of its spotlight on the vegetal, more natural aspects of the rose: slightly honeyed, but mostly wine-y and tart, with deep red hue of prune and herbal geranium nuances. A medicinal, earthy patchouli is her faithful companion, enhancing the vegetal and wine-like facets of rose without taking away its soliflore status. When the rose finally grows tired of this dance and fades away after about 7 hours, the patchouli continues to hold on the skin with ambrette, leaving a musky floral trail with a medicinal zing. The sillage is moderate throughout, and the longevity can reach 10 hours. The development of Aoud Queen Roses is arguably not too complexe, with rose as the center and oud, patchouli and ambrette adding an extra-flavour, all three trustworthy pairings with rose and the execution is well handled. The result is a very effective woody rose, slightly darker than a rose soliflore, but still very recognisably the queenly rose. Personally speaking, Aoud Queen Roses is not my favourite rose-oud-patchouli fragrance because of its simplicity, as this genre has become quite crowded in recent years and I'd prefer something with a twist or two.
