It is nice that he created a fragrance for the summer that can be wonderful in Moscow, even if it doesn’t last long. In my opinion, this fragrance has nothing to do with clichés like Matryoshka, Balalaika, Red Square, and Kalinka. The modern city of Moscow has long been such a multinational and multi-religious "Babylon," where everything in the world has mixed, where the West and the East have long and firmly grown into each other. I really liked the fragrance; the composition is very harmonious. The top notes feature very light citrus fruits, then the flowers open up, pleasant, not suffocating, feminine. The base is sweet, delicate, and lasts a very long time. "А я иду шагаю по Москве, И я ещё пройти смогу, Солёный Тихий океан И тундру, и тайгу. Над лодкой белый парус распущу Пока не знаю с кем А если я по дому загрущу Под снегом я фиалку отыщу И вспомню о Москве!" With love, Olga

Now Montale Embruns d' Essaouria seems to have not been extensively tested here yet, or it is not worth writing a comment about. This is now my second fragrance from Montale that I have had the chance to experience, and I would like to share my impressions regarding it. D' Essaouria is a port city on the Moroccan Atlantic coast, and its old town was recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. Embruns d’ Essaouria means "The Scent of Essaouria" and is most likely a tribute to this city. Pierre Montale must have developed an affinity for this small coastal town through his love for the Arab and oriental world, in order to express his appreciation for this World Heritage Site with "Montale Embruns d’ Essaouria". He probably wanted to convey the lightness and beauty of his fragrance to us, allowing us to partake in it. The opening conveys a light breeze of seawater, evoking feelings of air, sun, the marketplace with its many spices, and the vastness of the blue ocean. Very maritime with a slight spiciness, without the salty note of seawater that is often present in many other fragrances. It is like a spring day, a blue sky with light white clouds, flowers blooming, leaving a floral and sweet-scented air throughout the city that develops into an aromatic and slightly fruity fragrance with the gentle sea breeze. The scent of woods dried by coastal air and warm sunny days leaves behind a beautiful soft, slightly warm scent profile that harmonizes beautifully with the floral-maritime nuances, giving the fragrance a more mature appearance. Montale’s Embruns d’ Essaouria is completed with a soft, almost mild creaminess or powderiness that does not complicate this fragrance but makes it appear very rounded and balanced. It is a light spring/summer fragrance that Pierre Montale also wants to convey to bring us closer to the carefree nature of this small port city, where tranquility and relaxation are lived and communicated. The fragrance is meant to transport us to this place to enjoy its beauty with all its facets and to understand it to some extent. A light fragrance that, due to its unobtrusiveness, is well-suited for both genders and does not overwhelm its wearer. Unobtrusive, light, and summery but also nothing special. I could hardly perceive the fragrance after an hour, and the sillage is almost non-existent. It is not disturbing but also not inspiring.

With the overwhelming number of Montale releases, no one should be surprised if a fragrance completely gets lost here and there. Especially those scents that do not have Aoud in the name - although it is precisely these that could show how much more the brand has to offer. Embruns d'Essaouria, however, did not really seize this opportunity today, even though I was very curious about it. Sea water often divides me like Moses did with it - sometimes I really enjoy that salty tingling, other times everything just smells too strongly of it, too fishy & algal. But this question did not really arise with EdE, as the scent is much more of a misguided all-rounder than an Aquatic. Embruns d'Essaouria - I have no idea what that is supposed to mean, but it promised a lot: exoticism, variety, something different, no Oud, humidity, wood, Africa. Unfortunately, what I got was a lukewarm impression of it. The scent starts floral-woody with a hint of gentle spice. An inconspicuous mix of Fleurs de Sel and Jungle Pour Homme. Sea salt is at most a figment on the sidelines, only projected into the environment with extremely good circulation. Cardamom, musk & a dry wood mix play a larger role. Exotic for the open-plan office, but rather boring for everything else. Furthermore, the scent seemed to fall apart over time; I felt it lost form & also a bit of my interest. It did fit on a stormy, gloomy spring day like today - as if the North Sea were in Tunisia. At times, the scent really reminded me of fog banks on the beach in Tunisia. Bottle: do I need to say anything about that? Sillage: above average. Longevity: likewise - 8 hours. Conclusion: a scent that you often have to test... only to then realize with disappointment that you hardly know it. Quite simply, because it is unfathomable - not unfathomably great, but just unfathomable, indecisive, erratic, trivial - sometimes sea, sometimes flowers, sometimes woody. Unfortunately nothing quite.

The Montale fragrances either elicit a joyful Oh la la - or an irritated Oh well. However, when reading the ingredient list, I was in a positive mood, as lavender always suits me, and oud, when it’s not too spicy. But the first spray leaves me taken aback. I have never smelled such a harsh lavender before. The oud stands its ground against it - and I envision two strong little rams measuring strength, heads pressed together, unwilling to give an inch. And that’s how the main players, lavender and oud, behave as well. Both vehemently shout " Here! " and do so with an unpleasant sharpness. The other listed ingredients are not recognizable behind the " fighting rams." A brittle scent - without commitment. The pyramid sounded so interesting. Perhaps a fragrance for gentlemen who like dominant scents? I prefer the more pleasing Montales.

Montale is a brand where the hurried & overwhelming quantity of fragrances not only often suffers in terms of quality & originality, but as a consumer, you hardly feel inclined to engage with it more closely. You are simply overwhelmed, confused & much of it not only sounds similar, it also smells that way - I’m just saying Rose + (A)Oud. Sometimes, however, you have to jump over your shadow & so it happened that I had a Montale in front of my nose once again today. Once again Aoud, only this time with lavender - an unusual combination that piques curiosity. Another disappointment & quick shot? Or a little masterpiece in the mud, like "Chocolate Greedy" or "Intense Cafe"? Aoud Lavender starts promisingly aggressive, with a somewhat synthetic lavender steam hammer that, while sharp, cutting & hardcore, does have something to it. The usually smooth-soothing flower is here at the beginning ruffled & overshadows everything. Unfortunately, this top note is already the highlight - and if you can excellently argue about the highlight, that doesn’t bode well for the perfume. For now, the aggressiveness of the lavender subsides, it becomes creamier, oudier & quieter, and it reveals what a synthetically-boring mush has actually been squished together here. Not only does oud & lavender struggle to get along, the lavender used is simply outrageously cheap & artificial, at drugstore level. The oud is the usual Montale oud, which is fine. But the rest is weak. No, I don’t want to smell like this, the initially overpowering lavender that then ruins everything clearly goes the wrong way here. Not a good scent, not a game changer for Montale. Bottle: I like the Montales in purple-black the best! Sillage: close to a monster, especially exuberant at the beginning. Then it retreats like a turtle on the fast lane. Longevity: proves staying power - 9 hours. Not a pleasant time. Conclusion: between boring & unbearable - Aoud Lavender is a combination that appeals to me extremely little & should rather be avoided. Only the sharp beginning is good, the rest is a dull Montale mix that once again underscores that quantity is increasingly prioritized over quality :(

Before I actually took a sniff of this latest offshoot of the far-reaching Montale-Aoud dynasty, I thought the combination of the rather harsh and strict eaglewood in Montale's interpretation with lavender was a pretty wild idea. I couldn't imagine for the life of me that THIS could smell good. But it does, and quite well, in fact. An extremely powerful, aromatic wave of a fully blooming lavender field washes over my nose. Not a delicate, fine, silvery-bright lavender hint, like the one I love so much in Gris Clair, but rather, as expected from Montale, a solid slap with the lavender bush right in the face. If bergamots, lemons, and saffron were included in the top note, I’ll take that as a given; after the lavender onslaught, I can no longer distinguish them. A somewhat clearly defined heart note doesn’t reach me either, as the oud immediately joins the rather boisterous lavender. You can't really call its appearance quiet, yet I find this scent note relatively restrained compared to some other Montale-Aouds, subordinating itself to the lavender, only to then harmoniously merge with it into a spicy-balsamic whole. As the scent progresses, lavender and oud remain the primarily perceivable components, but the lavender gradually loses its clear freshness, becoming warmer and silkier. The same goes for the oud, which is stripped of its sharpness by a very subtle sweetness and a few scattered petals, without turning directly into a cuddly scent. The initially strong scent trail, which does not reach beyond closed doors, quickly settles into an environmentally friendly measure without becoming too intimate. In terms of longevity, Montale typically leaves no wishes unfulfilled. Friends of refined, fine scent compositions and surprising twists in the scent journey will likely turn away with a shudder. However, those who are tired of the inflationary market of oud-rose-with-something-else combinations, whether from Montale or other manufacturers, who enjoy strong fragrances and have no issues with lavender and Montale oud, should definitely give it a sniff. I generally quite like Montale fragrances - including this one. What’s written on the bottle is what I get: lavender and oud, both straightforward, powerful, enduring, and without much fuss around it.

Montale gets raves for quality and deservedly so: Chypré Fruité is no exception. This fragrance is full-bodied with presence and persistence. It's just lovely. Or perhaps I should say, it could have been lovely on me. As a fruity chypre kind of gal, Chypré Fruité should be right up my alley, right? Well, should be, but it ain't. For me and on me, Chypré Fruité is just too much sweet patchouli. Not just too much patchouli, too much _sweet_ patchouli. I'm pretty agnostic about patchouli, and I can usually carry it just fine, but this particular accord that's being used in Chypré Fruité is far too much for me. I suspect it is far too much for many others as well. Overall, Chypré Fruité has a character similar to Badgley Mischka. However, the Chypré Fruité is less boozy, less fruity, and more patchouli. The Montale certainly feels like a better fragrance to me, and I sense some pineapple in here. However, it is missing the fleshy fruits I'm accustomed to - like pear & peaches. So I enjoy the Badgley Mischka much more.

I enjoy wearing Pretty Fruity by Montale, so I eagerly reached for Chypre Fruite. However, the two fragrances are very dissimilar. While Fruity bursts with cheerfulness, Fruite speaks of elegance and distinction - without appearing forced. The scent is mature and playful, but not stiff. The Chypre note is soft, non-scratchy, and not soapy - rather silky. Very cuddly and pleasant. The tropical fruits hold back gently - with a touch of bitterness, nestled in velvety rose petals. The oak moss also provides only a subtle support, brightened by the jasmine. Patchouli lightly wafts above it. Despite its elegance, Fruite flatters and does not constrict. You don't have to rummage through your finest attire to be compatible with the scent. Chypre Fruite is definitely suitable for everyday wear - yet still imparts an exclusive wearing experience. The longevity is excellent, the sillage noticeable but not overwhelming. On "adult" days, I enjoy wearing Fruite very much - in "big kid moments," Pretty Fruity comes into play. Everything in its time.

Forgive me my admittedly far-fetched association: I don't know if any of you girls enjoy sewing. I had no choice but to learn, because try finding something in size 34 that doesn't look girly. The most important thing is a well-fitting basic cut. Once you have that, it's not so difficult to alter the piece again and again. That's what I think of when I spray on Chyprè-Fruitè. The basic cut, the theme of Chypre fits perfectly. Fresh and delicately floral in the top note, then it becomes a bit fruity, thankfully not red-berry, but rather yellow (pineapple, mango?) juicy, and the familiar spicy Chypre base rounds off the fragrance. In this case, relatively light, patchouli and oakmoss hold back. To stick with my initial comparison, a precious fabric has also been chosen, but the model is a bit too plain for me. I always expect something extraordinary to happen, a break, a flare-up of an unusual note, but no, I have to provide the accessories myself. 70% means again: Yes, I would wear it, but it doesn't have to be on my wish list.

So.... actually, I don't like fruity scents. Despite the name C.F., this isn't one either. A perfect combination of earthy chypre fragrance mixed with a softening component. For me, the discovery of the week... month? The so-called tropical fruits provide the balance of this scent and carry it into a new era. Here, they fit perfectly. Absolutely modern, confident with fruit. A reinterpretation of chypre variants. Simply classy. But I do like this fragrance direction anyway. You can still sniff me out for minutes after I’ve disappeared. That's how it should be :)

Today was somehow Chypre weather, so the only question was, which one should it be? The choice fell on Chypré Fruité, which I remembered as rather light, and it did not deceive me. Overall, the theme is well executed, coherent and harmonious, elegant and bright. The opening is floral and fresh, in the heart note the rather yellow fruits, and at the end the familiar base, here however light, fluffy, and quite unobtrusive. Alone, I miss the "raucous" aspect that I am used to from other representatives of this genre, and that bothers me here, because when I'm in the mood for Chypre, it should really pack a punch. Chypré Fruité is suitable for the office, in spring and summer, and it doesn't really offend anyone. The longevity is average. The sillage is in the medium range.

I'm generally not an oud fan, but a kind swapper threw this in as an extra. I liked it more than I thought I would - in other words, I didn't despise it. Steam Aoud is medicinal, but in a somewhat pleasant way. Surprisingly, it reminds me of Parfum d'Empire's Eau Suave, which contains no oud. It seems like the rose-oud here is reminding me of ES's rose-saffron, perhaps because saffron and oud are so often used together that I'm associating them with each other. If you would like to smell like a home remedy involving mysterious, dank herbs and rose petals, this might be for you.

My husband dropped me off at my favorite perfume shop because he had a doctor's appointment to attend. I love this place of tranquility and contemplation. So much better than being barked at and coughed on in the doctor's waiting room. I indulge in the sight of the many bottles and test the special offers. My hand wanders to Steam Aoud - and I am surprised by the energy with which the scent hits me. There is definitely steam on the kettle. The oud note is not rough - but very full-bodied. The rose bends under the stiff oud wind - and so do I, as I was not prepared for such an energy boost. One wants to clap their hands and exclaim: Where is the piano?! But not to play it, rather to carry it energetically up to the third floor. The cumin is kept in check - and amber has a slightly sweet quality. An impressive scent - but too daring for me. I am not the type of "Hans Dampf in allen Gassen". However, ladies and gentlemen with a more impulsive character might indeed enjoy this stormy fragrance. I am more of a friend of calm contemplation - Steam is too turbulent for me.

Thanks to Muenchner for the sample (which has made the rounds) Well, let's continue with the legendary Aoud series. Today I focused on the model Steam. And as we've heard, it can be quite aggressive. However, only in the initial acquaintance phase. Because right away, I would almost say immediately after it has had the decency to dry on the skin, it's pretty much over. At first, you get the impression that you have a - don’t hit me - Black Aoud light! Aoud and Rose are battling each other, but this time not so resinous. And also not particularly long-lasting. And what can I say, the Oud loses! :-( Yep, not good. The Rose takes the upper hand, inviting the old buddies Amber and Caraway into the mix (I still get Caraway, but I've only read about Amber) and all together they become quite scarce. This means that the scent loses immense intensity on my skin. Sprayed at 7:00, around 10-10:30 the transformation took place, by 13:00 I had to sniff closely to see if there was anything left to catch. Such a pity, such a pity, such a pity. The scent is pleasant, but it's not as Oud as Black Aoud. Less intrusive, less aggressive. But certainly more suitable for everyday wear. It has the Montale spice but is quite subdued. This Rose didn’t have a tattoo; it was more like the RTL Bachelor Rose. You can also apply Steam when shaved or with a slight smile... A good mainstream Oud!

This is my preferred oud. I will refrain from my own description and align myself with the impression of another reviewer: It reminds me of a dry Finnish sauna, of infusions, the steam, and the aromatic spruce wood. Contains relatively little rose, a lot of oud, and a completely unknown Cambodian herb.

Finally, I got a sample of a Montale fragrance. When purchasing the "LiboCedro" from Acca Kappa, I specified: "Please Oud perfumes". So, I am somewhat torn. When I saw the first comment below from Apicius, my heart soared. Since I work at a swimming pool, celebrate infusions every day, and regularly let my soul dangle in sauna cabins, I was really looking forward to the scent. However, I don't completely like it yet. The hairspray thing is beside the point; I don't use such stuff. But it does have a bit of a hair salon style, at least in the first few moments when it’s just on the skin. What I do clearly smell is a sweetness. And that comes from the amber. Very faintly in the background, I can also detect the rose. Actually, that sounds quite tempting; I am always up for amber if it’s a good scent that can showcase it. But I just find it hard to say: "Hey, what an amazing scent, I need to have it". Strangely enough, I don’t smell any Oud at all. Nothing woody in any way. Or maybe I just need to try other Oud scents to be able to make a comparison. I also somehow expected quite a punch, but "Steam Aoud" is rather subdued. Therefore, I would say that I would also consider it as an everyday Oud scent. Conclusion: Good first Oud experience with a rather positive outcome.

Oudh oil can smell very different; this depends not only on the origin but also on the age: Similar to great Bordeaux wines, it takes a few years for the optimal quality to develop. Oudh has a leathery scent, and in principle, I like it.

The idea here is clear. A light rose scent, yet still herbaceous and masculine. An apparently difficult implementation, but successful. As Black Aoud shows. The idea of creating a lighter, spicier Black Aoud appealed to me. However, this idea has drifted far from Steam Aoud. The scent is superb, and it corresponds to the Montale line.

Thanks to Kankuro for the sample. When I read the name, I was very curious about how Oud would smell in steam. Right after spraying, I took a strong whiff, which was a clear mistake because the scent is not light as one might expect from the word steam, but bit me hard in the nose.

A Chinese legend tells of a capricious empress with magical powers who one winter morning ordered all the flowers in the imperial garden to bloom. Afraid of the young empress's wrath, all the flowers pleased her. All except one: the Peony. The irate empress ordered that all the peonies be moved to a cold and distant region, but the plant resisted the weather and blossomed. The resigned empress had no choice but to crown the peony queen of all flowers. A floral fragrance with character, which I, not too fond of the genre, find wonderful, airy and spring-like. Peony, peach and jasmine intertwine to create a most pleasant, mostly feminine creation. Spring in a bottle, with one of my favorite flowers as the star: the peony. "Peony" painted by Manet.

Unicorns. They seem to be the only animals, or rather mythical creatures, that make you women seemingly crazier than when you see cute cats or even horses and already freak out. But seriously, why are women so crazy about horses? You don't even need to ask guys here, because as soon as you ask a guy what he thinks about horses, he would only respond that he finds horses cool solely because of the size of their "thingy" and that he wishes his "thingy" were at least as big :D … This is even a cliché topic in movies or series (Leonard from The Big Bang Theory, for example, wishes in one scene that he would like to have a "manly strength" like that of a horse, to which Sheldon admonishes him to behave properly… :D). But seriously, what is it about that? So this love for horses, ponies, and unicorns and so on? But I can already guess that the answer is hard to fathom, since we could all be asked the same question about cats. Why do we love these creatures so much? On the other hand, cats just look so cute! So the answer here would be rather simpler… And horses? Um… I’d rather not say anything about that before I get all the women here against me! :DD So how did I even get onto horses? Quite simply: Because I’m TOO STUPID to read!!! This fragrance here is called Sweet Peony,… so it has something to do with peonies! But I, the fool, keep reading it as Sweet PONY!!! Well,… and somehow I had to think, since this is a women’s fragrance, about how much some women really like horses and ponies! And that you freak out even more at unicorns (as certain Ritter Sport chocolate with unicorn motifs clearly proved a few years ago!) :DD The fragrance: The fragrance begins with rose scents, while almost simultaneously the coffee comes into play. And by "comes into play," I mean that it starts to smell like coffee, not that you either wake up or feel the need to take care of a certain business after enjoying coffee :D Coconut is the next note that can be quite well detected, which always smells nice and gives it an exotic touch. A little later, the coffee weakens again, and the coconut is not as strong anymore. The fragrance generally becomes more floral, but I find that the roses can still be best detected among the flowers, as the scent has this slightly sour (but also somewhat sweet) aroma of roses. The floral and sweet scent remains almost unchanged for quite a while, although at some point a slight woody note can be perceived. This should be sandalwood, even if it cannot be precisely identified. Many might find it bothersome that the fragrance also has a distinctly noticeable synthetic note, which in my opinion is not really disturbing. Moreover, it is most intense for a while in the heart note and significantly decreases towards the base. In the base, the fragrance remains mainly floral (where roses can still be best smelled) and is slightly sweet-woody. The sillage and longevity: The sillage is average and thus best detectable from a normal to lesser distance. I found the longevity quite good, as the fragrance lasted more than ten hours. The bottle: Hmm, I have never been able to warm up to Montale bottles. They just seem to me like fancier deodorant cans made of shiny aluminum. This one has a pink color with a yellow gradient. The neck of the bottle looks like a screw cap, which is at least interesting; there is no lid. To prevent accidentally pressing the sprayer, there is, as always, a clamp attached, to which the metallic Montale logo is also attached. Well, it’s just okay. Hmm, the fragrance is quite nice in itself. It starts off unusually with the combination of rose-coffee-coconut, but then settles into the more floral area with sweet notes. Aside from the beginning, most of the fragrance is almost like an average floral scent like many others, only here you still have a somewhat synthetic note for a little while, which one might not necessarily like, although this synthetic aspect noticeably weakens later. Usable in spring and summer as a casual daytime fragrance. Overall, the fragrance turned out to be mediocre for me, well, maybe slightly better than that, so a test might be worth it, but it’s not something you necessarily need to know. Unless, of course, you find the pink bottle somehow cute :D And since we’re talking about cute: I still think cats are the coolest animals ever, not only because they are so beautifully soft and naturally cute, but also because they sometimes have the most confused and silly looks when they don’t know what to do. Horses, on the other hand, I find… somehow… I really shouldn’t mention this, as I said,… just like this fragrance here: Nice, but slightly boring! *running away* :DD

"Sweet Peony" contains everything a young woman dreams of in spring: pink-white floral foam, very youthful and still quite innocent, meets mature coffee and sandalwood notes. These fully bloomed peonies, splendor and adornment in every garden, in every vase, generously exude their enchanting scent. How often did I have to place the large bouquets I received for my birthday on the balcony at night: their almost intoxicating fragrance made it hard for me to sleep. However, the beauty of these originally somewhat rustic flowers completely makes up for it. Spending a night on the balcony in June is not too much of a hassle when the numerous June beetles come to visit. The peonies in "Sweet Peony" surround themselves with equally fragrant companions: together with the large-flowered white jasmine and the proud rose, they unite, richly perfumed with the aroma of sun-ripened peaches, into a fluffy foam creation. Coconut and the always slightly scratchy clove dance eagerly in this circle. They bring, along with a lot of warm, erotic vanilla scent, a bit of "the fragrance of the great wide world" into the originally somewhat rustic garden. So far, "Sweet Peony" is very young and carefree; aromatic strong coffee and the ever-popular sandalwood make this fragrance mature - it is growing up! As a loyal companion for many hours, it retains its floral lightness without major changes in the scent progression. "Sweet Peony" remains true to itself until the very end! For me, "Sweet Peony" embodies the ideal wedding fragrance. A bride, radiant with love, happiness, and full of expectations despite all modernity, dressed entirely in pink and white, could wear this scent wonderfully. The bridal bouquet, elegantly tied as a floral cascade of all these blooms in bloom and perhaps a few sweet peas, completes this romantic fragrance picture. We don’t even need the obligatory crown of apple blossoms here to paint a delightful picture. A "May bride" who smells of "Sweet Peony" surely brings all the prerequisites for "the great romantic cinema." But all other women who fall in love with this fragrance will have a wonderful time. They have already found the right companion with this Montale fragrance being. Good luck!

If you love sweet, rosy-scented, and full peonies, you are exactly in the right place. The fragrance is not distorted by inappropriate or unpleasant companions. Everything fits together and transports you to a cloud of sweet rose petals, a rose scent I have been searching for a long time. In the base, delicate rose petals meet velvety vanilla with a hint of sandalwood.

I am currently testing this fragrance :) So far, it tells me a nice story .. I’m out with the girls and we feel like having a latte macchiato .. Since we don’t necessarily want to sit on a terrace, we grab a latte to go from our favorite coffee shop. While we wait for our order, a wonderful floral scent wafts into our noses. It’s a lovely combination with the coffee smell :) ... With the coffee in hand, we leave the café and right around the corner is a flower shop. Peonies! Mhhh! That was the floral scent from earlier.. "Could you please make me a nice mixed bouquet?! Mainly peonies." ... We sip our coffees and sniff the bouquet .. A wonderful sweetness emerges.. my brain associates the sweetness with a children's song and hits play: "Where is the coconut, where is the coconut.. who stole the coconut.." :) ... The coffee is long gone and the scent has faded .. the flowers and the sweetness remain the main stars .. occasionally a woody note makes itself known.. ... Arriving home, after hours of walking, I place the flowers in a vase and continue to enjoy this sweet floral splendor. Floral/sweet/slightly woody.. .. a bit artificial - Montale after all ..

which is beautifully framed by its companions. The only thing that slightly irritates me is the clove. It might be because I didn't expect it like this. However, I like the coffee as an undertone even more, just like the peach, which I generally enjoy in fragrances. If you like peonies and roses, this perfume serves you very well.

Montale was one of the first houses that brought Arabian style perfumery to the boulevards of Paris, the streets of London, and to New York's avenues. Their numerous oud perfumes focus quite much on the classic rose and oud combo. One could line up these perfumes on a scale ranging from the deeply intense Black Aoud to the most powdery variants of that theme – like White Aoud and others. I have tested quite a few of their ouds, and besides that scale of black (or masculine) to white (or feminine), there are some Montale ouds that follow other concepts. Another group of Montale ouds are actually crossovers between the rose-oud combo and a certain style of Western perfumery. I'd count in Aoud Forest which leans very much towards the so called „Sport“ fragrance wave, as well as Wild Aoud with its mainstream musk and amber notes. For quite a long time, I had no idea how Sliver Aoud would fit in there – it just seemed something completely different. By now, I know that it is indeed quite traditional – however, in a different way than those with a focus on rose and oud. Sliver Aoud is – a mukhallat! Mukhallat simply means blend, and those perfumes are just that: only a sliver of oud combined with fruity-floral, citric and herbal notes. The result is very often a friendlier appeal that may make such a perfume more accessible to the Western nose. I once bought tiny decants of a cheap mukhallat for my colleagues at work, and for some of them I had to return to my local Arab shop for a refill. It seems, everybody loves a nice mukhallat! Montale's Sliver Aoud is of very decent quality – much better, more elegant and congenial than those mukhallats I can get from my local Islam shop. Montale quality means for me: their oud notes have nothing to do with real oud oil. The oud hype that was initiated mainly by Montale does not copy the many woody facets of real oud oil at all. Instead, they went for the very cheap chemical replacements that Arab brands had invented for their mass marked “oud” perfumes. While those cheap “ouds” can be really horrible, Montale has always presented us high quality and refined copies of that. However, the main scent impression of artificial oud is musty, not woody. And that mustiness fits perfectly into the Western clichée of sultry oriental harems with opulent and mysterious fragrances evaporating from Aladin's wonder lamp. It is all a big lie, but one that people want to hear and smell! Back to Sliver Aoud, it indeed contains just a tiny sliver of that false opulence. That fruity, herbal and citric melange has always made me think about classic Italian perfumery with its acque full of bergamot, orange and Mediterranean herbs. And this combination works! I have to admit, Sliver Aoud is the most wearable of all Montale ouds for me. It contains all the warmth of a Mediterranean summer's day. There are so many more respectable and highly praised Montales: Black Aoud, Steam Aoud, Aoud Flowers – but none of them is as easy-going as Sliver Aoud. If Black Aoud was an oak aged Bordeaux wine from a famous Chateau, then Sliver Aoud would be a light and pleasing Grenache that people would love to drink at any occasion. I highly recommend testing Sliver Aoud with an open mind. It is something special, and as far as I can see, no other Western brand has yet succeeded in catching the vibes of a good Arab mukhallat fragrance.

Montale offers the ever popular combination of citrus and herbs to create Aoud Sliver. This fragrances starts with the delivery of an intense lemon and rosemary one-two punch. The opening notes might remind you more of a nice marinade for a piece of chicken or fish. Lavender makes its presence known just at the end of the top notes, adding a minty element to the herbal mixture. The lavender increases in intensity during the heart note, and subsequently, making a memorable statement. Geranium and the slight suggestion of oud follow next. There is very little oud in Aoud Sliver, considering Montale's Arabian roots. This fragrance seems to be dominated by an herbal theme with base notes of vetiver and cedar. Is Aoud Sliver reminiscent of the ever-popular scents of the 80's that used lavender as a primary element? Perhaps so. The tonka bean adds sweetness and the cedar seems thrown in for warmth and good measure. It seems that Montale should consider creating some classically-inspired Arabian scent, and put much less emphasis on trying to market them for Western tastes. The modernization is somewhat boring, and unfortunately, I've smelled this one too many times.

Very sharp amalfi lemon opening. Later it softens and gives room to lavender, tonka bean and oud. "laundry detergent" and "nailpolish note" are unfortunately match with my experiences. Not my cup of tea for sure, but that is fine, because Montale has a nice selection of fragrances. They are not afraid to come out with something new. It might be a really great scent on somebody else's skin. No blind purchase recommended! ........ You can find me on Fragrantica under the same username!

Sorry, I'm the new guy when it comes to Oud. I don't know why this mushroom-infected agarwood is so trendy, as it hasn't introduced itself to me apart from M7. And the monumental chaos of M7 cannot be compared at all to Sliver. Maybe I should smell pure Oud to get a better idea of it. Sliver Aoud seems to be just an entry-level drug, as I discovered hardly anything strange here in the highly classic fougère structure with nicely bitter citrus notes that vigorously carve their way to the woody, slightly bitter vetiver-cedar base alongside their well-known allies rosemary and lavender. At the latest five minutes after spraying, I realized that the scent is not a bad one, and the positive impression stayed with me for quite a while, without ruining its appeal with any unpleasant surprises. Ah, how nice it is to get by without any cream cakes, chocolate, or pudding. thx@Apicius

I can only confirm Kankuro here. It somehow reminds me of lacquer or glue. On my skin (I might be imagining it), I even perceive a certain sting; the first time ever with a perfume. Gradually, citrus notes come through. The oud has hidden itself very well and only appears very slightly. I think there are more beautiful oud fragrances, especially from Montale. ____Update____ So I need to correct myself again. I perceive the scent quite differently today. Much better than before! I smell more oud, it feels completely different. It gets 80%.

This Is a strange scent. Frankincense Is dominating for at least 1/2 hours then for all the rest (maybe 10 ...also the day after so 20 hours) i was able to smell just a lot of roses. Montale Is a great brand, by the way, but from this bottle i expected more...Just tried in a shop but i wont buy, the scent Is intense and longevity is crazy. Maybe i would suggest this one for ladies due to the floral part, but also of you are looking for a good combination incense/roses...still strange because i think is only perfect for the church.

Warm blend of roses and oud, but rather average if compared to other releases of the same house. Well, i can say its just an ordinary roses+oud combo. In the late drydown it becomes a little dusty - dusty roses. Sillage is okay, projection medium and lasting power weak for a Montale. Updated October 2014

Unfortunately, this headline fits all too well with the current situation in Syria. It is an incomprehensible tragedy! I wish everything could be as wonderful and heavenly there as this fragrance! However, I primarily mean the sillage, the intensity, and the longevity of Aoud Damascus. A true fragrance aura is conjured around and on your body. The Orient calls! Here, at least in terms of the fragrance development that AD takes on me, the rose clearly plays the absolute leading role - a bright rose, an intense rose, a wonderfully natural rose. Although I have no other experiences with rose fragrances, this is exactly how I imagine a rose perfume par excellence. The incense, which I would have liked a bit more of, I only perceive very subtly when sniffing intensely on myself, and regarding the eagle wood, I also lack the expanded horizon of experience. As the rock classic by the band Poison goes: "Every rose has its thorn ..." - The thorn that particularly pricks me with this rose, with this fragrance, is the one that likely defines the limited suitability of Aoud Damascus for men. If we were in the Orient, I wouldn't hesitate for a second to wear this perfume from time to time, but in our latitudes, that might be rather difficult or at least more than bold. Let's see what I make of it ... I really like the smell of roses, but as I have already admitted, I have little experience with corresponding perfumes. Perhaps the experts among you can send me a few tips regarding rose fragrances suitable for men. But it could also be that a gentleman can indeed smell "rosy" ... Unfortunately, I don't know. In summary, I say: Aoud Damascus is divine! Ladies in love with roses must definitely test it (and grab it)! Bold gentlemen - go for it! But definitely dose it with a lot of sensitivity!

The weather has been cold and wet for months. Combined with the long days of Covid confinement at home it can get depressing or melancholic the least. So when a few rays of sunlight appeared last week, I decided that it's time to prepare for summer and find myself a new summer scent. Or two, or three, or maybe let's not limit myself so soon :) I remember last year I had a sample of Gucci's 'Mémoire d'une Odeur'. Not my favorite in any way, but I did remember the chamomile touch and I enjoyed that a lot. It felt bright like summer. So why not explore chamomile a bit further, right? Thanks to Parfumo's directory I can easily find a few candidates. And although I only know Montale from its endless collection of Aoud variations, this 'Sunset Flowers' seemed different and thus interesting. The name itself is promising already. So I got myself a 2ml sample. And it turned out just lovely. Summertime all over. Dry flowers form the heart of this scent. Dehydrated grass and flowers due to intense heat and sunshine. Around this you will find apple juice in the opening and chamomille in the drydown. The overall quality didn't really impress and endurance is average -that may change when temperature goes up- but I still got lots of positive vibes from this. So for sure I'm glad I gave it a try. Not going to make it a full bottle, but it definitely did inspire me to learn more herbals and florals. On the downside, I'm only longing for summer even more now. Sigh.

I wanted a herbal, chamomile scent and that's what I've got with Sunset flowers and although obviously not a popular one with reviewers I love it. I find it a calming, dried flowers, chamomile based Spring flowered fragrance that I enjoy wearing after a bath before bed. I feel it's unisex, it starts with a burst of lemon which fades quickly to a medicinal chamomile which I'm loving, try before buying but if you love chamomile you can't go wrong with this one.

Montale SUNSET FLOWERS seems well-named to me, as the composition features dried flowers and dried grass, parched perhaps by a long day in the sun. At the very opening, I do detect a bit of violet, but mainly this creation is not very sweet, despite the green apple note listed in the official pyramid. Could chamomile be creating the grass effect? I suppose. Often I find chamomile to be rather bitter (as in Clinique AROMATICS ELIXIR), but here it smells more like dried grass. SUNSET FLOWERS is a pleasant perfume, provided that one enjoys the scent of mixed dried flowers and grass. To me it has something of a vintage vibe, and I do find the scent to smell natural. Parched petals and sun-dried, brittle brown blades of grass are what I perceive. Rather like the scent of foliage after a brutally hot summer with no rain for weeks.

Now I will attempt a comment on Sunset Flowers... I ordered this fragrance as a sample along with two other Montale scents from ALzD. Unfortunately, I can report little positive here as well. It's a shame, as I was really looking forward to the Montales. To get straight to the point, I stopped the test after about 2 hours, as by that time it was already clear to me that I would not be purchasing this perfume, and the scent increasingly bothered me, leading me to ultimately wash it off. Therefore, I cannot assess the longevity conclusively. Sunset Flowers starts for me with a very bitter, unsweet lemon. After a short time, I also detected a rather sour and equally bitter, I would say, green unripe apple. From the berries described in the fragrance pyramid, I could perceive nothing on my skin. I also could not detect the chamomile and honeysuckle (which is supposed to be rather sweet and reminiscent of jasmine - at least that's what I read online), I think it simply got lost in the fruity bitter scent. What I did smell, at least according to my personal perception, is a distinct grass or at least grass-like note beneath this sour fruit scent. I would almost say that this bitter smell combined with the grass note created a subtly compost-like image for me. A musty grassy compost note. The scent faintly reminded me of another fragrance I know, and it took me some time to pinpoint it. It is this subtly compost-like note that also resonates in Un Jardin sur le Toit by Hérmes. Only there, it simply appears much more complex and interesting, as in Un Jardin sur le Toit the fruit and floral notes contribute delicately to the overall picture, softening or balancing it out. This is unfortunately not the case with Sunset Flowers on my skin, which is why the scent did not convince me at all. Within the 2 hours, I also did not notice any significant scent development. However, with a fragrance that I like from the start and that convinces me in the top notes, I don't necessarily need a significant development. If a scent starts off very well, it can just stay that way... (but this is just a side note) I don't want to speak poorly of Sunset Flowers; this is simply my subjective opinion based on the scent experience on my skin. Perhaps it develops wonderfully for others?

Addictive. Not harsh neither medicinal oud if compared to Aoud Lime or White Aoud first notes. Oud here is soft and rose is sweet and comforting. I can clearly detect the geranium note and a light woody note. It reminds a lot of Aseel by Al-Rehab for sure - Aseel is slightly less sweet and more earthy roses. Aoud Rose Petals is unisex and has a great lasting power and sillage. I prefer this to Aoud Queen Roses and to Aoud Damascus. Updated January 2014

The trend of aoud fragrances is here. Why not to try and see if you like aoud or not. And , as I learned from my dear reviewers, it highly depends of the quality of the aoud. Montale named his perfume Aoud( first thing first) and Roses Petales(last). It was ment for me, the novice, to understand that what I have to evaluate is the aoud. And I did. I did not like it. Heavy like a huge door that does not let you open it, or, maybe, I was the one who could not find the way to do it. While standing in front of this door you can smell roses, petals of roses, but I imagine that not too many novices opened the door becase the rose petals are dried up. Eventually I drew a parralel with Crown- Rose Bouquet- with its smell of dried roses. I am still learning. That's all .

Montale AOUD ROSE PETALS opens as a strong greenish rose bush perfume, by which I mean complete with stems, leaves and thorns-—and a few petals, too. This stage lasts sufficiently long to remind me of TEA ROSE and lead me to ask why I would buy another rosebush-in-a-blender perfume for 50x (or more…) the price of the queen of green rose, readily available for single-digit dollars. After several minutes, however, the regality of AOUD ROSE PETALS finally begins to shine through, at this point reminding more of Amouage UBAR than TEA ROSE. But I hasten to add that I still do not think that the oud (or aoud or oudh) note ever asserts itself enough to warrant classifying this as an oud perfume. This is a beautiful floral composition, but it is, in the end, a floral, not an oriental perfume. The drydown of ROSE PETALS OUD manifests the same vintage quality shared by UBAR and L’OMBRE ROSE, so for now (for the same crassly economic reason) I’ll stick with the latter. All in all, while I like ROSE PETALS OUD, its various stages are so similar to other, far less expensive perfumes that it seems best to save the big Montale bucks for something else from their vast collection, which I am only beginning to explore. ----- After acquiring some manufacturer's carded samples from this house, I decided to try AOUD ROSES PETALS again and found that it is much more oriental than it seemed from my initial testing from a decanted vial. Hmmm.... I do not think that it is heavily oudified, but there is definitely a lot more going on than just roses.

...and that for the little rose! I can't with Montale! I have already tried several of his fragrances, and the result was always the same: I don't like them. This one doesn't change anything about that. It reminds me of Rosewater Eau Fresh by Crabtree & Evelyn, from which all sweetness has been removed and a homeopathic portion of Oud has been added. The scent starts off slightly rosy-woody and doesn't change over time on my skin. It is also dry, faintly rosy, soapy, and woody. There is no mood for me in which I would wear such a fragrance. I find it cold and masculine, harsh, and I mourn the rose petals... I guess this will be my last Montale attempt.

As already mentioned with Aoud Flowers, there are Montale Oud fragrances that differ only minimally from one another. And Aoud Rose Petal - thanks to CocoLeFay for the sample - is one of them. I immediately compared it with Aoud Flowers. In the first few minutes, there is absolutely no noticeable difference! I almost believed someone had made a mistake during the bottling. The description "Perfect harmony of rose and oud" fits here as well as there. Only gradually does a minimal difference become perceptible. The pyramid of Aoud Rose Petals additionally features saffron and cedarwood, while Aoud Flowers lists geranium, bergamot, and musk. First of all: The difference does not lie in the rose, which is identical in both perfumes. A slightly citrusy bergamot also seems to be present in both cases in the top notes, perhaps a tad more in Aoud Flowers, or better said, bergamot is differently present in various scent phases. It is saffron and cedarwood that make the small difference in Aoud Rose Petals. How to describe it? One could say the rose bush in Aoud Flowers grows on a dark background. The bush of Aoud Rose Petals, however, grows on sandy soil! Saffron and cedarwood add something else, and that makes me think of sand. At the same time, the scent spreads a bit more, I wouldn't call it opulent. Due to the cedarwood, Aoud Rose Petals feels slightly drier and more bitter, while Aoud Rose Petals feels slightly fruitier and more medicinal. Should one now say Aoud Flowers is better because it is more purist? Or should one prefer Aoud Rose Petals because it might be a bit more interesting? If I were faced with the choice, I would probably choose Aoud Flowers. Strangely, one always encounters Aoud Rose Petals in perfumeries, never Aoud Flowers, for whatever reason.

...actually, I don't like rose scents, as they tend to smell like soap on me! But this Montale, I find it super. It smells quite rosy but mild and very elegant. While you perceive this noble rose note at the beginning, it changes on my skin later and smells completely different. Not at all like roses. I can't really define what it smells like.

This is my first review, so please be lenient with me ;) My first text and then about this fragrance of all things?! I remember it was a gift for my girlfriend from another friend for her birthday; at first, she liked it, but then she desperately tried to sell it, and no one showed any mercy, except for me - who actually has enough fragrances. For me, it was love at the second/third sniff because no one wanted to admit to Pink Ecstasy! At least I knew that no one would buy this fragrance for me! Admittedly, it starts off powerfully orangey-raspberry and slightly peppery, somehow also artificial, like when you open a bag of dragon tongue candies. It stays that way, but the raspberry gradually breaks through and makes it creamier, at least that's how I perceive it. I can also smell jasmine and rose; the other ingredients are rather subdued. And the scent lasts a good 4-6 hours! After an 11-hour shift as a waiter, I was repeatedly asked in the evening by others what smelled so wonderfully creamy, wonderfully soft, fluffy, and how it would always lightly waft through the air with me while walking - that must have been Pink Ecstasy - very versatile! Maybe that's why it's named that?! At first, boom, a bit too much, and then nice, and finally softly fading away - who knows what the nose behind it was thinking. I was approached about this fragrance more than any other; for some, it wasn't even an on/off relationship, but for me, it developed into a long-term relationship! Especially in summer, it is incredibly wonderful, lifts the mood, and has just a magical transformation! Gummy Dragon Tongue Love ️ Thanks for reading!

This is my first comment, so please be forgiving, there is certainly still room for improvement... Not too long ago, I ordered a few samples from ALzD. Among them was Pink Extasy by Montale. According to ALzD, Pink Extasy is a "playful, feminine fragrance that seduces with fruity notes from Cuba." The individual fragrance notes are already listed above. Now I have tested PE extensively and must say that I was very surprised (I expected something quite different based on the name). Right after spraying, I perceive a very strong herbaceous sour fruit note. On my skin, I almost exclusively smell the orange and mandarin. However, I do not find the two fruity, sweet, or juicy, but rather very herbaceous and sour. Like unripe and still almost entirely green fruits, I miss any sweetness. Only very subtly does the raspberry listed in the base note flash through. It makes the fragrance more interesting and pleasant for me, but unfortunately, it only has a short guest appearance in the top and heart notes, as it stands no chance against the orange/mandarin. Then the heart note comes through with a subtle hint of rose. I do not perceive any other flowers. The heart note is very, very similar to the top note, meaning that up to this point, there is no significant fragrance progression for me. The entire fragrance is, until suddenly and almost abruptly reaching the base, very fruity herbaceous in my perception. Up to this point, I do not find the fragrance very feminine or playful. It is simply too sour and herbaceous for me. After about 1.5 hours - this herbaceous fruitiness remains almost unchanged for me - I stopped sniffing my arm for about 15 - 20 minutes, as I honestly did not expect any significant change. When I then smelled it again directly, I thought for a moment that I had confused arms. I had to search for the fragrance. From this sour herbaceous fruit, there was suddenly almost nothing left to smell. The fragrance had, in my perception, almost completely transformed. Instead of playful, one could rather say it is a play of contrasts. Now I must absolutely agree with my predecessor, what remains in the base is a quite pleasant subtle creamy and soft scent with a very light fruity note, which, however, would not be discernible without the preceding fragrance progression. Perhaps one can sense the raspberry again... I also think I can make out the vanilla. I perceive the base as a very beautiful and pleasant fragrance. However, at least for me, it is so subtle that it is likely not perceived by others at all. The fragrance is then already very close to the skin. Overall, I perceive it for about 6 hours. The base reminds me a little of the base of Balkis by Perfumes de Nicolai (thank you again for the sample of this from Lapislazuli). Probably because of the raspberry. But as I said, it only slightly reminds me of it; the fragrance itself is not comparable. My conclusion from the test is that I find the fragrance of the base note very beautiful, but unfortunately, it is too subtle for me. The top and heart notes did not convince me. (Perhaps I will test it again in the height of summer and then the acidity might appeal to me). Thus, it is definitely not a candidate for purchase for me at this time. However, it was the one I liked best among the three Montale fragrances I ordered for testing. The other two (Soleil de Capri and Sunset Flower) are unfortunately also not for me.

like wool detergent, fruity, fresh and fine, then powdery, creamy, could be nivea creme intense. later a warm cream scent lingers, with a bit of raspberry and peach like lip balm or lipstick with this note. longevity is 7 hours for me, but the sillage is not very strong.

There is no orient in Orient Extreme. It's an oakmoss chypre in a classic style. By today's standards, it can easily be worn by a guy, but it also could be a fragrance of the 1970s or earlier - you know, the era when chypres were chypres. Unfortunately, chypres aren't for me as I am one of those people who is sensitive to oakmoss. If you are looking for the real stuff, you have found it. Oakmoss. Just not for me.

Montale ORIENT EXTREME is a bizarre creation. It lacks most of the qualities we currently associate with oriental perfumes, above all, any source of sweetness or culinary spices. Instead, it packs a punch of dry, dry, dry wood, which smells like firewood after the fire has gone out and is no longer even smoldering. Very stern, like a plank of wood used to punish an errant child. No, this is not a warm cuddly oriental perfume. Far from it, in fact. Still, I think that ORIENT EXTREME has its virtues. For one thing, it is very unique. The only perfumes I remember being this dry and woody are incense perfumes, but this does not smell at all like incense. It's rather like an incense perfume with charred wood instead of incense. It called to my mind one of the Chanel special edition (exclusifs) perfumes--was it SYCOMORE?--I'll have to go check. Whichever one it was, it reminded me of a campfire. Not a seductive elixir at all, but truly thought-provoking. That's about how I feel about ORIENT EXTREME. This is a thought-provoking composition, not very inviting in the usual way, and not at all cuddly but fascinating nonetheless. It reminds me a bit of some of the Serge Lutens creations, as a matter of fact--not in terms of the composition itself but in terms of the challenge it poses to the nose and also to one's mind. This is a challenging perfume which requires some patience to appreciate.

Orient Extréme - this name seems to be the program. This perfume smells like the proverbial "all the scents of the Orient," although in this case, the Oud is clearly missing. Here, rose and honey blend together, perhaps with other floral or fruity notes with an oriental background, creating a truly beautiful cuddly scent! This is perfect for the fireside when it's raining and storming outside, and the logs crackle comfortably inside. The oriental opulence feels warm and soothing. That's nice, but Orient Extréme is not a truly great fragrance. I search in vain for edges and corners - for something that would contradict this "I've-known-it-forever" impression. Thus, I count Orient Extréme among the less significant releases of a brand that occupies a lot of shelf space with an almost overwhelming number of perfumes. By the way, I view the only mediocre longevity positively - this always suits opulent fragrances well, as it means you don't get tired of this perfume quite so quickly.

Even though it’s hard to believe, this scent is an almost identical clone of Ulrich Lang's Anvers 2. A bit rounder, less complex, but still extremely similar. I don’t know what this has to do with the Orient. The fragrance smells really pleasant, but under an oriental scent that also calls itself "Extreme," I imagine something more along the lines of musk-dried fruits-amber. You can clearly smell the rose here, along with the soft sandalwood. Very nice. I really like it.

A good to very good fragrance... but only for perfume connoisseurs or extroverted people. It starts very opulently with a rose that comes across as very dark and sweet. Together with honey and a slight super gasoline note, it offers a very strong and, at the beginning, almost intrusive olfactory experience. After about 15-20 minutes, the oak moss and a strongly herbal facade emerge, reminiscent of the top note of Antaeus. After about an hour, it becomes more monotonous, chypre-like, and herbal. The sweetness from the opening completely disappears, leaving a very masculine oak moss-rose chypre scent. Herbs, saffron, and oak moss then form the base of this still not too dry oriental. An oriental that is more chypre than oriental. Anyone looking for an extraordinary, socially acceptable fragrance that comes in the style of the 80s should give it a try. It feels more mature than Black Aoud, yet less playful than, for example, Oudmazing. Those seeking something herbal, rather elegant, and entirely without fruit will find it here. For me personally, one of the best from the house of Montale.

I find the scent smells like Arabie by Serge Lutens, which I also own. Everything is just a bit lighter, more buoyant, not as dark as with Uncle Serge. Not worse but also not better. I now have 2 samples from Montale, but whether I will buy any of them, I don't know yet; the fragrances are very, very different, and they certainly should be.

I ordered this scent as a sample to test more oud fragrances and because I wanted to get to know more perfumes from the brand Montale. At the first spray, I was immediately surprised, as a strong animalistic dirty oud dominates, overshadowing all other notes. The scent takes a long time before I catch a hint of rose, and then it becomes totally gourmand, probably due to the amber. There’s no trace of flowers in the base anymore, and the oud almost completely dilutes. The other fragrance notes remain completely hidden from me. Personally, I don't like this strong animalistic oud, and I find the notes are not intertwined. They seem to stumble in one after the other and slam the door while leaving. Somehow too little elegant and subtle for me. On the other hand, the longevity is good and the sillage is moderate. I find it unisex and would rather place it for evenings out and in winter, as it is quite assertive. Additionally, I would not recommend it for a blind buy. However, those who enjoy assertive scents with strong oud might find this just right.

Ah - I can hardly remember how many Oud fragrances have crossed my path in recent years. However, that doesn’t make me an expert by any means. On the contrary. Perhaps one eventually becomes saturated and overstimulated by the inflationary flood of Oud. Unfortunately, Aoud Legend doesn’t stand out as much as the first fragrances of this kind did back then. Well, the combination of Oud with Rose is anything but innovative. Certainly, the agarwood is dominant. It’s beautifully soft and without any barn-like off-notes. The leather is subtly noticeable, while the rose is a bit more intrusive. I would have preferred it the other way around. As it is, the fragrance overall feels a bit too tame and too feminine. Not even the pleasantly gender-neutral saffron can save it. The other ingredients also fail to make an impact. Oud and rose dictate the pace and direction - and so it relentlessly heads towards "experienced a thousand times." Of course - for those who like Oud and Rose, are looking for something cultivated for cooler days, and don’t want to spray themselves constantly from morning till night, Aoud Legend is an optimal choice. Everyone else can continue their search for the legendary fragrance or the Oud grail.

Musk to Musk Eau De Parfum by Montale at The Perfume Shoppe. With Musk to Musk, Montale presents us with the musk that is spicy and resinous not clean and white nor dark and animalic. The warmly aromatic nutmeg and the dry, leathery aoud bring an exotic quality to the composition; the rich balsamic woods and the amber embellish the silky musk note like exquisite eastern ornaments. Austere and soft, dense and transparent, Musk to Musk smells wonderfully unique, like no other musk perfume we have ever encountered and it can be mixed with another perfumes in one time .

I love the brand Montale. I’ve loved every perfume I’ve bought from them up until now. Velvet Flowers is not one I can honestly say I like whatsoever and I’m sad I blind bought it based on the other scents I’ve loved. For me it’s way too strong. It’s extremely fruity and nauseating to the point where after a couple hours of nearly vomiting I had to scrub it off. Unfortunately for me, it continues to linger for another few hours. This is a fruit perfume 100%. Perhaps a touch of jasmine, but not enough to detract from the fruit cocktail. It’s just gross. It’s definitely feminine, too. Don’t blind buy it. Get a sample first. I’m curious to know other users thoughts on this one.

It took me a couple of tries to love this, and I'm glad I gave it another shot. The first time I tried velvet flowers, I was rather unimpressed. Perhaps it was the weather that suppressed the notes? Maybe I just wasn't receptive enough? For whatever reason, I brushed it off. Luckily, I was going through my samples box and decided to try this on again. It opens as a watery fruit basket before it starts to settle a bit and becomes more heavy. It's sweet and very fruity (straight up peaches), almost sharp (perhaps from the tiniest bit of saffron that is detectable), but not intrusive. Right from the start, I also pick up a lot of musk playing around in the background, but it's a light girly musk, not a very mature one, if that makes sense. A sniff closer to the skin reveals the rosy notes that never really take flight. This is the only part of the entire fragrance that lives up to its name, "Velvet Flowers". It is definitely the smoothest part of the entire fragrance, and is so incredibly feminine and mildly intoxicating - so well rounded and addictive, with beautiful musky wood notes backing it. It's a shame it sits so close to the skin, but I suppose one could see that as an added dimension. As the fragrance develops, it gains an almost syrupy texture and a bitterness that I find rather confusing. The first thing that comes to mind is jasmine, but I have not known jasmine to be bitter on my skin. It's not unpleasant though; if anything, it simply contributes another facet. It ends with airy musk and a faint fruity floral sweetness, with a hint of spice and wood. This stage is very much a skin scent on me. Is this fragrance exquisitely different or unique? Perhaps not, but for the fruity floral enthusiast, this is worth trying. Projection was noticeable throughout, and total wear on me was about 5.5-6 hours.

Montale always smells different from "non-Montale." Usually very long-lasting. It’s not one of those scents where you wonder at noon: "Where did the euros go that it cost?" You can smell it yourself and others notice it too. Very balanced, dominated by Gurjum. A blend of flowers and fruit. Subdued yet present. I don’t find it sweet either. This scent is one of the few that I wear year-round, although not for days in a row. I can’t say it’s metallic-musty for my olfactory perception.

I think musk is great. Unfortunately, musk is a bit problematic for me. Musk has to be somewhat sweet for me, at least fluffy-delicious-clean. Otherwise, musk smells sharp, bitter, and scratchy on me. Then it doesn’t smell like it should, fluffy-white, but rather moldy-yellow-gray. The musk in Montale Velvet Flowers unfortunately ruins the scent for me. It’s the same musk as in Les Nereides Fleur Poudrée de Musc. Bad-breath musk, yikes. Otherwise, the fragrance has really beautiful notes. The golden bottle with the deep violet splash at the bottom visually points in the right direction. First, there are bright fruity notes. Not a fruit salad, but a noble-perfumed fruitiness. A little later, rich flowers join in. Jasmine, rose, and peach blossom. All fresh-sweet-sensual. Unfortunately, the metallic-musty musk is there right from the start. Therefore, it immediately disturbs the otherwise very beautiful composition for me. On another skin, it probably comes across wonderfully. Unfortunately, not on me. The name sounds so beautiful. Many thanks to Elchen for the sample! I’m glad to have gotten to know the scent.

My stepmother always wished for Montale fragrances during celebrations. From her perspective, it was understandable, as she was an awe-inspiring figure - tall, always elegant, self-assured, professionally successful, and endowed with a portion of natural authority. She was politically active and the founder of the Suffragette Club in Dortmund. Although she had her heart in the right place, her confidence and activities intimidated me a bit. But the straightforward, expressive fragrance suited her very well. In heated political debates, I was always surrounded by her impressive serious aura. Not a scent for the faint-hearted - but for individuals with convictions. The amber adds a certain wildness - I would almost say a nonconformity - which is deepened by the oud. However, the rose creates a sense of commitment and is pleasantly emotional. Still, it’s not a fragrance to bring along for a relaxed café chat - the scent demands something more essential. For me, it was too strict at the time - too demanding - but now that I have a few more years under my belt, I am slowly approaching Aoud Ambre. Of course, my stepmother's shoes are still quite large - but now and then, I slip into them as if I wanted to "play grown-up". And for a few moments, I feel comfortable in them - because I greatly admired my life-experienced stepmother. Yet the fragrance feels somehow oversized for me - and I look forward to being a child again - with dreams, fantasies, utopias - which my realistic stepmother probably appreciated in me as well. I am sure of it - even though it was never spoken. I miss her - my impressive stepmother.

Rumor has it that an amber fan places great value on this fine, animalistic sweetness, which I am missing today, not necessarily mentally due to the weather and my mood, but physically in this fragrance. One doesn’t have to be a genius to assume that a perfume with the little word amber in the title contains this ingredient. So let’s establish that this is not the case. Instead, a rather attractive rose blooms on a field of labdanum, which is then dumped with several wheelbarrows full of oud by a “let’s get to work” television crew before the garden door even opens. Aoud Ambre is very, very similar to Montale's White Aoud and leaves, the more I experience it, a more positive impression, which can be attributed to its immense intensity, longevity, and distinctiveness.

In my excitement while reading the fragrance notes, I was tempted to order the scent blindly. But reason prevailed, as it was too expensive in case it turned out to be a flop. So I ordered a sample and could hardly wait for it to arrive. So, I sprayed it on and immediately another fragrance came to mind that smells just like this one and that I also own: Aromatics Elixir. The second test yielded the same result; my nose remains consistent. Both have almost nothing in common, but the similarity is quite astonishing.

I tried the Golden Aoud a day after sampling Montale Black Oud. The roses in Golden Aoud are much different from the dark, sinister ones of Black Aoud. Golden Aoud's roses are lighter, less overwhelming, and mixed with another very fresh floral note I can't identify. (The notes listed above say geranium, and that makes sense.) And of course the oud. I did not experience the middle note of leather shown above, but I did catch a waft of patchouli. The base notes arrived a few hours later. The base is oud, of course, and cedar tinged with saffron.

Golden Aoud is another oud-based scent as many of Montale. But in this case the roses are very shy. The geranium, a bit of pepper and leather takes its place. This fragrance is far from being any sweet, but a dry oud with a touch of leather from beginning to the end. Sillage, projection and lasting power are medium-high.

The dark-haired lady in the black leather corset lounges indulgently on her exquisite teak bed, which a smitten admirer has lavishly covered with rose petals. No, not the cheap ones; it had to be the expensive dark roses for which he sacrificed a small fortune. Is she worth it? Yes, she is, for he is eagerly anticipating the things that may happen over the course of the evening. Everything is possible, sweetness or whip... What starts so innocently with a breathtaking opulence of rose gradually reveals its spicy, woody claws.

Montale probably has a dozen of these in their lineup, so just a quick and painless comment on this one: Hefty, spicy, very rose-heavy, expansive, lush, far-reaching, hairspray-thundering. For my nose, this is a - as usual - exaggerated aroma bomb that sticks to the headache threshold. Rose, patchouli, oud exaggerate in their triad a lot, too much spice, too much rose concentrate, too much waving of the Oriental flag. Unnecessary given the uninspired brand portfolio.

Black Orchid, Tom Ford, without a floral component. If that's too much, you can try the heavy Golden Aoud. You have to give it a try. Either you love it or you hate it. In the evening, the scent is bearable, but in the morning ...not a sunny wake-up call. Rose or something similar cannot be clearly identified here. The fragrance is soft, sweet, distinctive without burning or stinging. In line at the cinema, some already stepped back.

I find the scent quite okay, it has a lot of fresh-floral notes rather than warm woody ones. It also doesn’t smell strongly of rose, so it’s good for those who don’t like it too floral. Unfortunately, the scent doesn’t last very long on the skin/clothing. The good thing is that the fragrances are not too expensive online.

"The New Rose" is really not my thing. Apparently, my scent receptors were completely confused during testing when I bought the tester (admittedly half-full, for little money) at a flea market in a small perfumery. The fragrance is paper-sweet and largely fruity, I can only interpret the rose here. It starts off very sweet and penetrating (and a bit synthetic too) with blackcurrant jam, lingering for a long time and annoying me until it finally transitions into the sweet-woody base. This base is anything but original, but still enjoyable. The downsides also include low longevity and sillage. All in all, for me this purchase is a disappointment.

A unique, twisted and niche WORK. For me, it is less incense (I rather don't associate it with classic incense, but rather with some smoke ... something burnt, but it is difficult for me to find any associations). Once upon a time, someone ... I think when describing Dark Aoud (Montale) wrote about railway sleepers, lubricants, a workshop - and for me this is the smell. Wooden (of various types of wood) railway sleepers, a wooden workshop smelling of grease, wooden blocks under the wheels and chassis, a slightly smoky and veeery dry smell (very well describing the word 'dry' as Zanzibar37 wrote). To sum up - if you like such fragrances, including Dark Aoud (Montale), Kabul (Montale), Black Tourmaline (Olivier Durbano) - it's worth trying, and whether to have ... it's a personal matter, because it's not a fancy guy. If I had to compare it to something that is closest in smell, in my opinion: Dark Aoud and Kabul. A niche with a capital N.

Montale refers to one of its new 2018 fragrance creations as raw and wild. And that captures it, unfortunately especially at the beginning, completely from my perspective. Because I really don’t know how to describe this top note. While I was left somewhat perplexed, my daughters commented something along the lines of, "Wow, you smell terrible" or "Eww, that’s really disgusting." Well, I am still searching for the right words, as the opening is so sharp (in the literal sense) that it takes your breath away. Domestos? It has a certain resemblance. Vinegar cleaner? No, much more aggressive, somehow caustic. Mentally back in chemistry class 30 years ago... Nitric acid??? Whatever, the scent was on my skin, so there was no changing it anyway. Mentally checked off. Even after 15-20 minutes, that piercing, unpleasant sensation remains. And then, after about an hour, the surprise. The scent becomes almost mild compared to the opening. The heart note reveals resins and woods; I would even go so far as to suspect oriental oils - and not even as roughly as I would have expected after the beginning. And when the whole story arrives at the base note after another hour, we have here a strongly oriental, spicy-smoky-woody representative of its kind. But in a remarkably fine manner that has surprised me incredibly positively. Sillage: Thank goodness, after half an hour it decreases significantly, while the longevity is relatively good. The bottle is okay, fitting for the scent, in my opinion. Conclusion: I advise against a blind purchase. Maybe there are people who find the opening somehow attractive; I am not one of them. I have never tested a perfume that comes across as so ambivalent. While I am completely convinced by the base note, the top note almost knocked me out. And that’s exactly why Bakhoor will not find a place in my collection. 0 points for the top note, 6 for the heart note, and 9 for the base note. That makes, according to Adam Riese and Eva Klein, 5. It’s a pity really; without that sting at the beginning, something really good could have come out of it. But as they say, tastes differ - give it a try - I’m curious about further comments.

Montale AOUD BLOSSOM is first and foremost a big fat floral fragrance. I was having difficulty figuring out which precise flowers were represented, and small wonder since all of them are! Well, that may be a slight exaggeration. The named flowers here include jasmine, rose, tuberose, violet, and ylang. What about the other "floral notes" note listed at another site? Your guess is as good as mine, but I suspect that narcissus is present. Taken together, the whole bouquet is quite strong, and some may find it overwhelming, especially since the petals are coated with a very potent resin, gurjum, which, in addition to having its own distinctive and penetrating scent, seems to make the flowers last forever--or until a bath. Is there oud in this composition? I've no doubt that there is--this is Montale, after all!--but it is hidden behind all of the flowers and gurjum to the point where I feel that this perfume has been misnamed. It should really be called GURJUM BLOSSOM. To my nose, this is a very feminine floral perfume with a classical feeling. The ylang seems to be the strongest of the many strong florals vying for attention in this creation. This is a heady mix, no matter how lightly it is applied! The florals do subside eventually, leaving behind a persistent (or is it durable????) gurjum layer.

At first, it smells fresh, quite citrusy, sweet, and somewhat piercing. I can clearly perceive the mandarin peel, the chocolate only slightly lingers in the background, and the pear is nowhere to be found. Soon, a barely identifiable floral note emerges. I think I can smell the rose, but not much else. I don't find Diamond Greedy gourmand, not even in the top notes. However, it definitely smells synthetic. I received a sample of the fragrance as a freebie at a souk, so I approached it without any expectations. Without really knowing what I was smelling or what price range it belonged to, my first thought was: Smells like at DM in the fragrance department (translation = boring and cheap). Even after longer contemplation and a look at the fragrance notes, I can't shake this impression: Diamond Greedy indeed feels like one of the 100 drugstore fragrances that generally fall into this fresh-floral category. Of course, it can't be completely compared to those. The longevity is too good for that: I could still smell Diamond Greedy after 6-7 hours. Even after a shower, it was still faintly detectable. But is that worth the price? From my perspective, no. I am not convinced.

Aoud Amber Rose is my first introduction to the house of Montale. Perhaps I should have gone for another, more famous Montale offering, however the name of this one intrigued me, so much that I felt it was right. Initially it reminds me of Tauer's Incense Rose, but as the fragrance develops I find this scent much woodsier, leathery and in some ways, metallic. The rose note is beautiful, earthy and rich, just the way I like my roses, especially during the Winter months. I knew Montale produced heavy-hitting fragrances, and for that I'm very glad. It has a slight medicinal feel, and although a little sharp, it leaves me curious. The oud note is as promised, strong and bold, however the amber is fairly light on. The more I wear this fragrance, the more I come to adore it. It's a little bit sexy, in a slightly masculine and powerful way. My man might disagree, but then again, I haven't tried it on him yet. I'll have to agree that this fragrance has the potential to be unisex. Stating the obvious, this fragrance not only lasts but has fantastic sillage.
