It's a great rose-based fragrance for those, like myself, that enjoy deep, earthy and somewhat dirty florals intermixed with oud, spices or patchouli. It gets the thumbs up from me.

Montale SANDAL SLIVER--at least my sample of it--is a floral bomb. I do believe that the correct notes are listed above: Bergamot, *Jasmine*, *Neroli*, *Orange blossom*, Sandalwood, Vanilla, Citruses Lots of jasmine, neroli, and orange blossom are blended with a touch of sandalwood and citrus. The composition is not really sweet, and I do not detect much in the way of vanilla. To my nose this is a big floral perfume in the 1980s style, which would probably appeal to femmes d'un certain âge who wear the Elizabeth Taylor DIAMONDS series. The quality here is obviously much better, but the spirit is the same. I would never call this a unisex perfume, to be honest, and I cannot think of any gents off the top of my head who would want to wear SANDAL SLIVER. I imagine that the low ratings derive from dashed expectations. Is this a sandalwood perfume? No, not at all. Flowers, not sandalwood, are the focus. I have smelled a few other recent perfumes in this style: DAVID YURMAN and some of the La Praire Life Threads series members inhabit the same general olfactory neighborhood. Lots of over-the-top richness combined with abundant and potent flowers! This is not really my style, but it is extremely strong, more like a parfum than an eau de parfum, so for those who like huge floral compositions, a small bottle would suffice for a lifetime. The color of the liquid in my sample vial is dark burnt orange, so it even looks like a parfum!

Unobtrusive scents are not typically associated with Montale. The oriental oud bombs always take center stage - much else is simply overlooked. Only a sliver ("Sliver") in the eye of the beholder is meant to represent this sandalwood - rarely does Montale present itself so modestly. Sandal Sliver is an unobtrusive - but pleasant - fragrance. It features a rather delicate than robust sandalwood note, which the scent development leads to over several hours. The top and heart notes form a rather vague framework that only slightly recalls the oriental opulence of many other Montale fragrances. This is not bad, but also nothing that one must necessarily buy. When it comes to simple sandalwood scents, I think of the beautiful sandalwood by Harry Lehmann. It feels fresher, cheerier, and lighter with its introduction through the rose-like geranium than the somewhat sluggish way Montale approaches sandalwood here. Additionally, it comes at an unbeatable price. I think Sandal Sliver will appeal more to women due to its floriental introduction. As an uncomplicated scent for everyday wear, it is certainly useful - however, Sandal Sliver does not particularly appeal to me.

I can't understand why something as noble as sandalwood has to be overwhelmed with half a ton of sticky vanilla syrup. I don't smell any citrus fruits at all; however, they probably wouldn't have toned down the vanilla bomb anyway. After a few minutes, the sweetness becomes bearable, and Sandal Sliver actually turns a bit woody. However, I need quite a bit of imagination to recognize sandalwood. The scent becomes very soapy on me - I would have guessed musk, even though it's not mentioned. Expensive soap with something floral, which I wouldn't have identified as neroli. Everything is very intense, as is typical with Montale fragrances, and still dominated by indestructible sweet vanilla. For me, this is not appealing, but the fragrance will surely find some lovers in the vanilla-musk faction. I would quietly doubt the unisex aspect. Personally, I can't imagine a man wanting to smell like this. On my male test subject, Sandal Sliver smelled even more soapy-floral than on my skin.

The scent initially smells a bit soapy, with Christmas spices, then it only smells of Christmas spices, and later beautifully of sandalwood with vanilla and a hint of lemon. Since it wasn't really my thing at first, I didn't pay much attention to it until I thought, what smells so good here - Sandalsliver!

My first Montale! I eagerly awaited my fragrance mail. Since I had informed the dear donor that I would like to test something from Montale, but I don't quite get along with the oriental bombshells, she suggested the Crystal Aoud based on some fruity scents in my collection. Aoud and fruits, how might that smell together... Now I know: The scent is quite interesting, and I feel similarly to Ergoproxy - I am captivated and pulled in. For me, however, this does not refer to the rooms, but to the time of day. This morning, leaning more towards "not so great," this afternoon, reapplied, "hmm, there is something to it." I also perceive that the fruit aroma has a somewhat artificial touch. I can detect it even in the base note. Before my eyes, the image of an abandoned campfire in a clearing emerges. All participants have dutifully taken their things back with them during the night, except for one. A basket of fruit still stands there, lonely and forgotten. The sun has made its way to the clearing, and its rays have reached the fruit basket. Since it is midsummer and also midday, the fruits are just about to ferment, a smell that is not unpleasant but almost overshadows the scent of the smoky fire pit. I find this scent quite interesting, and it has indeed conjured up the described scene before my mind's eye. Anyone who likes fruity scents but wants to step away from the generally typical line of this fragrance family should really give the Crystal Aoud a try.

With this scent, I am fascinated and torn! Depending on the room in our apartment, I either love Chrystal Oud or I hate it! I'm not sure what causes this. I suspect it has to do with the artificial fruitiness, paired with oud, woods, and a good dash of vanilla. In the kitchen, I find the scent interesting; in the living room, I want to wash it off immediately. I can't decide! I wonder what about this scent is supposed to evoke a crystal association? It strikes me as neither clear nor fragile! I smell spicy sweetness with an artificial fruit aroma. But somehow, that has its own charm! Although the fruits are listed in the top notes, they persist almost all the way to the base! This results in the scent progression being hardly noticeable. Here, a certain boredom sets in. Only when the scent has long settled into the base does this fruitiness fade, and the fragrance takes on a soft, bittersweet note. Should I ever decide whether I like CA or not, I will add a note to my comment. Turandot, thank you for the olfactory confusion!

I do like oud fragrances and I am also a confessed blind buyer. With Original Aouds (as it says on the bottle and box), it was the same again; I stumbled upon the comment and was curious. I already like Montale fragrances, so I went for it. The little witch is as happy as a child with a package of scents, so I naturally unpacked the fragrance right away and sprayed it on. The comment says that Original Aouds have no medicinal note, which piqued my curiosity. Not at all! It practically screams out loud, just as you would expect from Montale, if not even sharper! So, this blind purchase was a bit of a flop! But the little witch doesn’t give up that easily! Patience is key; it has often paid off. So, alright, said and done... Almost an hour passes, and I consider whether I should scrub off the fragrance. No, I have to get through this! The notes sound interesting and must show up eventually. Giving up is still not an option! After about another half hour of struggle, the sharp note finally gives in and makes way for woods and sweet tobacco, paired with earthy oud. All three then take turns peacefully dominating, so the fragrance is not one-dimensional. The little witch is satisfied; this blind purchase was once again successful. If you have a lot of patience, the raging wolf turns into a friendly (shepherd) dog. I'm not really into cats, sorry! ;-)

Original Aoud absolutely lives up to its name. And I have been waiting for this for a long time. An authentic Aoud from Montale, without any medicinal note! It is the earthy-sweet scent of the Oud that matters, and it is fully present here. This fragrance bears an uncanny resemblance to Mukhallat Dehn al Oudh Moattaq by Ajmal, one of my favorite Ouds. And I must say that I prefer the Ajmal version, as it is much more layered and complex. There is a very interesting development, which is not present in Original Aoud by Montale.

Sampling Montale – Rendez-Vous Chez Harrods, a release exclusive the UK’s Harrods department store, a great example of a multifaceted blend from the house that works very well and has gravitas while not being specifically heavy in rose or oud. Its character is accented mostly by saffron, pink pepper, and caramel, a sharp, heady, spicy, sweet mix. It’s enjoyable, has a familiar Montale/Mancera DNA, and performs well. While not remarkably different from various entries in the line, it does not smell particularly like any other that I’ve smelled before, though I’m sure some could correct me and find some similar entries. It has standard Montale concentration of EDP and pricing of $170 for 100ml, though unlike most entries in the line, it cannot be found on grey market sites in the US. I think I need to give it some further wearing but overall quite like it. 7 out of 10

I am a big fan of Pierre Montale. Whether you choose Mancera or Montale you can find some great fragrances with great performance and longevity at an affordable price. I adore leather fragrances and when I stumbled upon this at Harrods I had to give it a try. I do find it funny that whenever a perfumer creates a fragrance for London or Harrods they predominantly design leather fragrances. Perfumers must think that Londoner's are all into leather fetish or perhaps they picture us sitting in a leather Churchill armchair, supping malt whisky while smoking a big fat Churchill Cuban cigar at our club in Pall Mall lol. Perhaps both are true but for me London smells of damp, musky cardboard with a hint of grass (not the medicinal kind). At the time Rendez-vous Chez Harrods was selling for £127 for 100ml which is a good price, but that all depends on the performance and the scent in my opinion. I tried this on skin because you can't get a good idea of a fragrance on paper. Sprayed around 4 sprays and walked around the shop for an hour. This was ample time for me to get a good idea of how this fragrance developed, or didn't in this case. I'm not one for comparing fragrances but this reminded me of many. Ombre Leather, C: Woody Leather to name a couple. But in no way as projecting or enveloping as those two. Chez Harrods smells of sweet, smooth leather with a very slight hint of floral. The rose is almost non existent. It's not overly sweet which is nice. You get a slight woody nuance but the rose I can't detect at all. Perhaps it was my nose playing up but it is very much a skin scent, which is not normal for a Montale fragrance. My girlfriend could smell it being up close but all she could smell was a faint sweet leather. The fruity notes we couldn't smell either. I know that it can be difficult to smell a perfume in a perfume department due to all the other fragrances bombarding your nose at once. Hence that's why we walked around the shop. We went back for another spritz before having lunch but it still remained the same. Unfortunately, this will not be added to my collection.

Elegant, beautiful scent. I see it more on a man during the top notes and very unisex in the drydown. I don't find the DNA striking - I would have wished for that certain extra. With Arabians Tonka, it shares the smoky-sweet character (as it develops), otherwise absolutely nothing. I perceive Oud, pepper, tonka, musk, amber, and sandalwood as the most present. Leather-sweet spicy with wood and spices describes it well. Nice but no WOW.

Wow... no review and just a few statements. No exceptionally good ratings...?! What a pity, but I can only rave about it. Iris, rose, jasmine, amber, sandalwood, and vanilla are actually popular fragrance notes, and they make this perfume an irresistible everyday companion for me personally. It was my first niche fragrance because it convinced me right away. It radiates, typical of Montale, with a slightly synthetic note and smells, as the name suggests, floral. In my opinion, it has a slightly molecular aura, and I am regularly approached about it. The bottle is very light and may not seem very high-quality because of that. Personally, I really like the bling-bling and gold.

… because So Flowers smells of flowers, flowers, and nothing but flowers. And not in a sweetly romantic feminine way, but intensely, tough, and consistently, in a somewhat floral-aggressive manner. So Flowers offers floral scent as far as the nose can reach, from the top note to the drydown, without bergamot, without herbs, without fruits(!), without spices, without woods, and hardly sweet. Only towards the end does a faint sandalwood note seem to emerge, but perhaps that is also "just" the ylang-ylang. Individual floral notes are not identifiable to me; So Flowers smells like a floral-unsweet floral cocktail, like "nose-deep-in-the-noble-flower-bouquet." No meadow flowers and no wild roses, but top-notch goods from the expensive florist. Sometimes a hint of rose, hyacinth, or jasmine wafts out, but only very briefly, similar to how one might catch a glimpse of individual faces or figures on a rapidly spinning carousel, which then quickly disappear back into the whirl. If I were to imagine a dose of aldehydes along with the many flowers, we would be looking at a typical 60s scent in the direction of Rive Gauche (before reformulation) or Madame Rochas. However, as it is - aldehyde-free - So Flowers is a consistent and interesting reinterpretation of the floral scent theme. SF doesn't make it easy for you, though - you have to like this floral scent excess; this is not a fragrance of the type "it-always-works-when-I-don't-really-know-what-I-feel-like-today." I am not really a big fan of pure floral scents, but I find So Flowers beautiful and interesting in its consistent, unsweet florality. Because So Flowers is fruit-free and unsweet, I can also easily imagine it on men; provided, of course, that the man has the courage to embrace flowers. Men and distinctly floral scents are, at least according to prevailing prejudices, a combination that doesn't exactly scream for attention, but with So Flowers, that could work.

A brief comment: I spray it on and there’s a bit of freshness: pear I wait 30 minutes and what’s there: pear I wait 2 hours and what’s there - besides a few flowers under the tree -: pear Even though the flowers bloom a bit more later, the tree has so many ripe pears on it, I just smell very, very ripe pears, which I know very well from my childhood; we had a giant pear tree in the yard. It’s neither soapy nor powdery for me, it’s simply juicy, ripe pear. And that’s how it stays, so I can’t say much more about it. Thank you EP for the sample, an interesting story this So Flowers.

Whenever a fragrance has flowers in its name, I become particularly cautious! The right combination of floral essences can easily give me a headache. Nervously and cautiously, I sprayed the scent on my arm and strategically positioned myself near the sink. What enveloped me at first was a floral bouquet that had been plunged into a large vat of fine soap. Soapiness is, unlike for many perfume lovers, not a drawback for me. In the right mood and in the right dose, I even find soapy notes very pleasant. However, in the top note, it is a bit too intense for So Flowers. In the heart note, jasmine and hyacinth predominantly take over. You have to like this combination, though. Unconsciously, I moved away from the sink as no headache was looming. This bouquet truly becomes beautiful only in the base. Here, all the flowers harmonize with each other and linger for a long time to diffuse. Ultimately, So Flowers is still a tad too floral and feminine. C, thank you very much for the flowers!

So Flowers is a loud floral fragrance. For me, it is not refined enough. At first, one might think it is a floral hairspray, and the scent reminds one of the 80s, when all the aunts were sporting killer hairspray manes à la Dynasty. That's how many women smelled in my childhood. Therefore, I find the scent quite feminine, but I wouldn't turn my head or ask what she was using, because I find nothing special about the fragrance. It actually smells like the sum of its notes. Refinement is lacking. Conclusion: a gift, yes, but a purchase, no.

A beautiful floral scent that has nothing to criticize, but I find it a bit too simple for this house and this price. An everyday fragrance without edges and corners, but also without anything extraordinary. Also, Montale - So Flowers, I had tested that one before and described it as a floral scent without edges and corners. It is that, but somehow a beautiful waft keeps blowing around my nose, making me constantly sniff my arm again, somewhat like freshly lotioned with a very floral lotion. I think it might just go on the wish list... it works very well in the warmth.

This is quite an intense floral scent. Although I like all the components of the pyramid except for rose, I don't like this fragrance. It is cloying, annoying, and somehow also dusty. The base feels a bit soapy and artificial.

I need to start saying that I absolutely disagree with the current Scent rating (6.8) is by far a superior perfume. First of all, is refreshing, in the opening a zesty orange with an oud support (of course we know that it is not oud, Montale uses two "oud" the dark animal one, and the heavy wood support, in this case we have this second case), it will add in some minutes to a strong saffron, and a little bit mild and a little bit earthy patchouli. So we have and oudrangish smell in all layers, plus saffron in the heart and patchouli in the base, this one is in the range of quality of the good Montales, superb sillage and longevity, not beast mode, but quite high. People will like it, it's perfect for almost every occasion and for every season except hot summers.

It took me a while to have to have a certain view on Montal spicy Aoud. In short it is a more well done version of Versace oud Noir. It has a softer smell and it doesn't have that sharp pepperiness and certainly has better and more high quality material used in it the performance on this is fantastic it projects and lasts a long time. A rich dense musky faux Oud with some spices sprinkled in the background.

I got a sample here (thanks, Fraglove!) and tested it this morning. I was unsure about the orange in the scent and wanted to test it first. Unfortunately, my fears were confirmed: the orange makes the top note of Spicy Aoud smell like a grandma scent. Whether my grandma smelled like this, I can't say anymore, but this slightly powdery-creamy sweetness of the orange at the beginning reminds me of the cleaning foam my great-grandfather always used. After five minutes, the orange took a break, and a wonderfully spicy, almost peppery scent remained. Hooray! It's something for me! Unfortunately no, because the orange, now nicely underlaid with saffron, returns and pulls the Spicy Aoud back into the grandma corner. I deliberately say grandma and not grandpa, because I perceive the scent as feminine. However, I can imagine that it might smell completely different on male skin. It's a shame, I really like the spicy base, but this orange sweetness in the foreground ruins the scent for me. I don't perceive hairspray, but rather something slightly soapy. Too bad, Spicy Aoud! I will find you a worthy wearer who suits you better. Edit: Even though I'm risking a shitstorm - I let my son (almost 4) test the scent today, and I'm blown away. On him, Spicy Aoud smells wonderfully masculine and dark, just like a real pirate. ;) Maybe the scent is simply better suited for men. Of course, my son is still a few years away from being a man, but still, the scent clings to him, while it would rather run away from me. A clear recommendation for men!

Aoud Musk is one of my favorite scents, alongside Bois Vanille, but this musk fragrance overwhelms me. It is very intense and practically fills the room with its strange smell. It reminds me of my childhood when I occasionally had to go to the hairdresser with my grandmother. As was customary back then, she regularly went for a wash and set. After an extensive hair wash, a generous amount of setting lotion was applied to her hair, and that’s exactly how Dew Musk smells on my skin. Musk-soapy and somehow a bit off with a hint of alcohol and sweet old maid flowers in the dry down, that’s how I would describe this Montale scent on my skin. This fragrance does not evolve at all and simply does not lose its intensity. I have now endured three hours in the hair studio of horror and will wash this stuff off now, if it can indeed be washed off.

When I first sprayed this fragrance, I thought: Oh dear, it’s gone off. Sharp, sour, unusual. But a look at the bottling date of 3/11 enlightened me. And with attentive reapplication, I also recognized the pomegranate scent, very naturalistic, fruity, but only for a brief moment, as the top note is hardly worth mentioning, then the fragrance truly blossoms. Dew Must should definitely be tested and worn on the skin, as it merges with the natural scent, indeed almost fuses into something very individual. The floral notes provide elegance and glamour without being too loud, and patchouli grounds the perfume. Strangely enough, after a while, the pomegranate, which supposedly played a fateful role in Adam and Eve, makes another appearance. This time, however, as a fragrant aroma and not as fruity acidity. Until then, it is a very pleasant fragrance, but I miss a more expressive base. I wish for woods, a rounding off, a conclusion. As it stands, Dew Musk simply becomes weaker. This leaves me somewhat perplexed. As a scent for an independent, high-quality body care line, I can well imagine Dew Musk, but as a perfume, it feels too flat to me, despite the forbidden fruit.

What a surprise: Santa Maria Novella MELOGRANO is a glorious green chypre! The green is so intense as to be almost galbanum-like. The oakmoss is also quite detectable. Despite the name, what is not readily evident is the pomegranate. I've spent some time with my nose to my wrist attempting to find the pomegranate, but my commitment to truth in reviewing obliges me to confess that I cannot tease out any pomegranate from the intense chypre elements of this perfume. Maybe I could imagine pomegranate as detectable here, if I really, really tried, but I would never, ever, have guessed that it was present in a mystery scent vial trial. No, this is unequivocally a green chypre! It may as well be called grapefruit or banana or cherry or melon--all would be every bit as appropriate as pomegranate, it seems. But enough about the name. This smells great! I definitely recommend MELOGRANO for testing by anyone who loves classic chypres. People who are looking for an intensely red-pomegranate-stained perfume may, on the other hand, be disappointed.

Melograno (Pomegranate) is by far and away the bestselling fragrance in the Santa Maria Novella line-up, a fact that surprises me every time I smell it. It's not so much that it's an odd fragrance (although it is) but that it's extremely hard to pin down. If you read the reviews for Melograno, you will see that it seems to be a different fragrance from one wearer to the next - to some, it is a green chypre along the lines of Givenchy III, to others it is the edgier twin of the grandest aldehydic monster ever created, Chanel No. 22, and to yet others, it is nothing more than detergent soap made into a fragrance. The one thing that everybody agrees upon is that it doesn't smell like pomegranates. Perhaps Melograno is successful because it is so dependent on the individual skin chemistry and scent memories of each wearer, and is therefore the olfactory equivalent of a mood ring. For what it's worth, to me it smells like a mixture of aldehydes, green flowers, luxury soap, and church incense, with a faint but stirring note of urinal puck running through the base. Why this odd mish mash of elements should work is beyond me, but without doubt, the end result is resolutely appealing. What it will smell on you, and whether you'll like it, is anyone's guess.

So, I guess I'm the odd one here, because I DO smell pomegranate seeds along with a late summer sunshine and fallen leaves. I bought Melograno Eau de Cologne without really knowing what "melograno" meant, because it reminded me of ordering nar suyu, or freshly squeezed pomegranate juice from the stall next to my little hotel in Istanbul. It certainly has a lot more than the acerbic, sour-sweet little rubies of a freshly peeled pomegranate, but they're unmistakenly present in there, along with a spicy rose. And yes, there's also the aroma of those old European soap bars, the ones that used to be hidden like precious gems in Eastern European homes during the dark years of the Iron Curtain. It has so much nostalgia, I simply couldn't pass it by. This and Pot Pourri are the two Santa Maria Novella colognes that have incredible performance in terms of silage and longevity.

This is a duplicate of my blog review on this fragrance :) Today, I randomly picked Melograno, a cologne made by the Italian house Santa Maria Novella. Summer 2022. It is blazing hot outside. I’ve decided to google fragrance stores near me and found out that I’ve actually never visited one small store hidden almost in the city center. Excited I went there as their website promised a clearance sale. Upon my arrival there were just couple items left. I found out they’re closing the store and moving it to another country (If only I knew it earlier, they had like 60% off on Clive Christian and Amouage). So there were just couple fragrances left, mostly from the Santa Maria. I smelled this one and instantly bought it: amazing eau de cologne that stays quite long on your skin. Despite it being called Melograno (or Pomegranate in English), it smells nothing like pomegranate but rather like an old but well-crafted bar of soap. Old-school vibes, so this one is definitely not for everyone. Earthy-musky notes dominate here. The notes listed on fragrantica are not the ones you actually feel. It feels exactly like if you went to your grandma’s summer house and took a bath with an old, hand-crafted bar of soap. Felt amazing in the summer as you instantly imagine going out of the shower refreshed, ready to face the heat of the day. You can say that Melograno is an old but elegant gradfather of another soapy fragrance - Artisan Pure by John Varvatos. It doesn't smell anything like any kind of pomegranate I've consumed; whether that be fresh fruit, pomegranate molasses, pomegranate juice, or fruit leather. The opening is very aldehydic, harkening back to bad memories of the time I spilt my aunt's bottle of Chanel No 5 on the carpet. However, Melograno settles down much more warmly than No 5, and has a comforting woody note. Almost toffee-like at its heart, but not sweet enough to be overwhelming. Unfortunately, once we get to the base notes it starts smelling like nappy-rash cream. When I was wearing it I thought I'd left a jar of zinc oxide open because I could not stop smelling medicinal ointment.

I bought this fragrance in Italy, certainly under the assumption that I was not bringing home a highlight of my collection, but simply a nice herbal-fresh souvenir. Now, souvenirs can be a tricky thing.

Most fragrances from Santa Maria Novella are not to my taste. Some I found solid, a few beautiful, and some simply harsh. Not just cool, which I usually like, but strict and unwelcoming. However, I really like two, Acqua di Sicilia and Melograno, the latter was love at first sniff. Melograno... pomegranate, oh, oh.

After Ginestra, Melograno is the second fragrance from the house of Santa Maria Novella to join my collection. And like Ginestra, Melograno is for me more of a typical scent for the warmer seasons. If I had to assign a color to it, Melograno would be the warm, golden yellow of a late summer sunset, with a hint of orange.

With a description of the ingredients and the scent progression, the aura of this Eau de Cologne cannot be explained. Melograno by Santa Maria Novella embodies for me absolute purity. Never before have I smelled a perfume that radiates such venerability and clarity. I associate it with the Middle Ages.

Many thanks to Sören for the sample of Melograno Eau de Cologne :-) This is a really great Chypre that definitely needs to find a place in my collection! The "Melograno" (translated: pomegranate), however, is not something I can really perceive olfactorily. The longevity is impressive at 8 to 10 hours, and the sillage is quite decent.

I really like Taif Roses by Montale. It is a very intense and soapy rose. At first, it is very strong, but over time it becomes very pleasant. Taif Roses is my favorite rose perfume. I don't wear Taif Roses when I'm with my girlfriend because she doesn't like it at all. But otherwise, when I wear it, I often get approached with positive comments. The longevity and sillage are great.

I could smell the rose aroma right when I unpacked it! It's so strong! There are an enormous number of roses in here.....nothing sweet and soft, but rather chypre-like and a bit animalistic (right at the beginning, very background, very faint and very brief). I must emphasize that the animalistic note is very slight and only lasts for about a minute, then it completely fades away..... so there's no reason to worry if you don't like it. Taif Roses is proud and sovereign! I find it a very interesting combination. It reminds me of Louban, the green rose. Taif Roses starts off with a bang! When this scent enters the room.....everything must stand at attention. It feels mobilizing, awakening...and instills respect. I would most likely wear it all day in the summer. Yellow roses to the max with slightly bitter mossy chypre notes. It is very similar to the Tea Rose from Perfumer's Workshop.... To be precise, I perceive it as Tea Rose but much stronger, richer, and more opulent. So strong that my husband feels nauseous from it.....unfortunately. That's why I couldn't keep the perfume. Is Taif Roses plump and intense? Yes, it is! Once you've survived the opening punch.... you are left with an enormous amount of wonderful roses that smell aromatic on a mossy, slightly bitter base all day long! The projection and longevity are excellent in this case! For the mature, established women with an independent character..... and for the men who like rose chypres.... Taif Roses is an exciting, noble, distinctive rose scent.... A rose scent......like no other. Until recently, this perfume was not available in Germany, only now can you find it at i.parfümerie. Since fragrance experiences are very individual, I definitely recommend a scent test before purchasing. Addendum on 5.9.15: Yesterday I received the new edition "Taif Rose" in a pink bottle. The scent is also somewhat different from what I remember. Has my perception changed or has the perfume itself? In any case, the new pink edition is significantly less bitter, just very subtle now. I also no longer find any resemblance to "Louban" or "Tea Rose". The scent has become rounder, more opulent, and lovely. The oud note (in the background) now resembles "Moon Aoud", a bit like hot glue (not cow dung or goat cheese). That’s exactly what makes "Taif Rose" a hot perfume now, as I stated. Hot roses for cold days!

Subdued tobacco scent that's reminds me of the highest quality pipe tobacco along with soft sweet vanilla and fresh green accords. The overall impression is that of a extremely high quality sweet tobacco yet surprisingly fresh EDC. Wonderful, definately one of my favourites from S. Maria Novella. Highly recommend giving this one a try!

I have the SMN discovery set of 8 fragrances, and this was a completely unexpected standout for me. My only previous experience with a tobacco fragrance was with Maison Margiela Replica Jazz Club, which was a massive failure on me (two words: wet ashtray!). So I was quite nervous about Tabacco Toscano and sampled it thinking it would be another case of instant dislike. …and happily, I was so wrong. This is light, spicy, and woody, with a touch of smoke and sweetness. Like the scent left on your clothes after standing around a bonfire, but lighter and a tad sweeter. If you’re like me and generally hesitant about tobacco fragrances, please try this one! I promise you will not smell like a chain smoker or a barbecue grill. It has an intimate sillage, so the scent sticks close to you, and it’s just soooo cozy and evocative of fall to me. Also, I do see a lot of men reviewing this and loving it, but I am a woman and I feel like I can wear this too. It’s truly unisex. It’s in the same general vein as soft, spicy, woodsy, vanillic scents like Diptyque Eau Duelle and MM Replica Whispers in the Library (sadly discontinued), which is what makes it so wearable in my opinion and why it appears to be such a crowd-pleaser. (I’m NOT saying it’s a dupe of those, FYI - Tabacco Toscano is less sweet and more spicy/smoky. But the general vibes are similar to me.) Contemplating a full bottle of this one, and god knows I don’t need any more full bottles right now!

Opens with the smell of rich, sweet tobacco. If there’s bergamot here it’s completely overwhelmed by spiced, vanillic leaves. That heady opening is mellowed a little by the addition of soft leather and hints of wood in the dry down, but this is an unapologetically tobacco forward scent. It doesn’t read as smoky to me at all — this is the scent of someone packing a pipe, not smoking it. I’m not really a believer in perfume seasonality, but this definitely has a warm, spiced autumnal vibe. Projection is intimate, and longevity is solid (8+ hours). Although tobacco is often gendered as a masculine note, this is totally unisex.

Tabacco Toscano is primarily a labdanum-vanilla amber accord with a secondary accord of smoky tobacco which resembles lapsang souchong tea. It is very warm, smooth, and cosy; and for some reason, reminds me strongly of sitting by the fireplace in winter. I think the smoke note really resembles burning logs in a wood fire. It’s a beautiful scent, which would be really comforting in winter (it’s the wrong season for it in my country atm). Despite the listed leather note, I don’t smell anything resembling leather. A lot of reviewers seem to think there is a “freshness” to this that makes it wearable in warmer weather, but I don’t get that, and it feels unsuitable for summer. I love ambers, and I love this scent, but unfortunately, I think it is far too expensive for the performance. Of course, this is a cologne, so it’s expected to be quite weak, however if I can still barely smell something after several sprays I’m not inclined to dish out over 200AUD for a full bottle, no matter how beautiful the smell. I also have another (MUCH cheaper) fragrance with a very similar amber accord, which I prefer over this one due to its seasonal versatility, so I probably won’t bother buying a bottle of Tabacco Toscano once my sample runs out. It’s a pity, because I really do like the amber+tobacco combination.

The beginning is quite dry, sharp… skin, beautiful tobacco, musk and probably birch also contributes to it. The fragrance is really unique. Later the fragrance becomes softer - it becomes more amber, sweet and vanilla. Then you can feel a combination of tobacco with the addition of spices (it reminds me of the smell of smoking pipe) and vanilla. It is not (thank goodness) a sweet pot (I unfortunately do not digest Tom Ford with his weird, feminine and refined tobacco vanilla - but I understand that many people may like it). This fragrance for me is more exquisite, complex and with a greater male component. Besides, it naturally paints pictures in front of my eyes. Its disadvantage is, unfortunately, its durability - 3 to max. 5 hours on my body (5 ... is really very close to the body). In my opinion, it is worth knowing and having. Even though it is not a tiring, sweet, bisexual TOM FORD-tobacco vanille spike massacre (which is a huge advantage for me).

This is a luxury fragrance. A rich and rebellious woman in the Victorian era is packing her pipe with a fresh blond tobacco while wearing her new and supple leather gloves. There is a woody vanilla base that is addictive. These notes would typically be heavy in other fragrances but this fragrance is light and delicate.

It was 2021, I was 22 years old and shopping for a trip to Boston I was taking. I stumbled upon an Aedes Perfumery near Chinatown. I went in there for a tobacco vanilla type of perfume because I had a tobacco vanilla candle that I was obsessed with. The SA didn’t have any perfume but he pointed me to Tabasco Toscano when he asked me if I didn’t mind cologne and I said no.

Tobacco Toscano is a sexy, sheer tobacco-honey fragrance with a rubber twang that recalls Bvlgari Black stripped of its green edges. It also strongly recalls the sweet, bready musk and vanillic paper/cardboard notes of Dzing! but features none of that scent's elephant dung. But most of all, Tobacco Tuscano has a distinctly Tobacco Vanille vibe.

What a beautiful discovery for me: Santa Maria Novella. After the first two tests of Tabacco Toscanao, I always had the feeling that I had smelled this scent before... but what was it... who... when... Now it has come to me. Amber and vanilla blend here just as skillfully as in Confetto. Only lighter, more buoyant, a Cologne indeed.

I bought the perfume in Como on a hot July day. Something about it really spoke to me at the time; the sweetness combined with a hint of wood perfectly matched the vibe of life by Lake Como. Since then, I associate the scent very much with Italy and summer, so it is often brought out in such situations. It is definitely long-lasting for me.

I don’t find this heavy at all? It IS one dimensional; but that’s kind of what Montale does. Although the notes make it look to be an amber tuberose, on me this wears almost beachy. The oud is cool, almost medicinal, and gives a narcissus-type waxy “yellow” background for the tuberose and cloves. It blooms in the heat with a slight shampoo element that I get a lot from frangipane fragrances. Lovely!
Heavy floral based in jasmin and tuberose mostly. Sweet but not much, this is extremely feminine and may smell a little dated. Sillage is heavy and lasting power is over 12 hours easily.

Citta di Kyoto is one of the most recent releases (2004) of a house that claims a continuous production since 1612. Anyone who is familiar with their releases knows that they are quirky, not always easy to wear but always come through as unpretentious, clear and yet sophisticated fragrances. So how is this managing with its recent releases? In one word, perfectly. Citta di Kyoto was released to celebrate the 40 year old affiliation of Florence and Kyoto and what better way to do that than combining notes of florentine iris and japanese lotus. I must admit I am not familiar with how lotus smells but had I read the official note listing I would have been put off: “The perfume opens with vibrant, fruity and fresh top notes of jasmine and ylang-ylang, which are punctuated by the deeper hints of bergamot and orange. These are followed by base notes of Florentine iris and lotus”. No, no, no, no! It starts with a magnificent paint diluent note (admittedly this can be attributed to ylang ylang as it sometimes has a mentholated aspect)that quickly fades into the driest, palest, softest cedar. The most opulent orris butter kicks in to smooth out the rough woody surface. The overall effect is that of velvety, dusty suede. It makes me think of smelling uncooked rice. Much to my astonishment this is listed as a feminine scent which together with the official description are doing a great job at restricting this fragrance’s target group. This is dry, woody, leathery iris at its best and Dzongkha lovers please give this a try. In another perfume world Citta di Kyoto could very well pass as a masculine version of Equistrius. It wears close to the skin, feels like it sinks into the skin and radiates from there but it has an exceptional longevity even though it is an eau de cologne. Notes from my nose: paint diluent, cedar, butter, iris, rice, incense tears

I don’t mind the soft projection or poor longevity of Cittá di Kyoto, but what I can’t forgive is its vagueness. It is mostly iris – that rooty, plaster-of-Paris iris material that Santa Maria Novella uses – over a blob of bitter, musky cedar, but it is dry enough for people to imagine they smell Japanese incense, sweet enough for people to think they smell fruit, and softly hawthorn-ish enough to make people think of Daim Blond. However, nothing ever tilts too firmly in one direction or another, so you get this diaphanous, blown out blur of root and wood and petal refuses to commit to even one of those ideas. It flip flops between one thing and another so quickly that it could get elected to local government at least. Some people find this charming. I find it irritating, just as I do that dreamy, opaque way old Irish people have of answering every question with a half-laughed ‘ah sure, now, you know yourself’ when in fact, no, we don’t know, which is why we asked the question in the first place, you muppet. I suspect that were it not for the evocative name or the inspiration, nobody would peg it as smelling particularly like Japanese incense or the woody air of an onsen in the forest, and so on and so forth. Indeed, in the hands of any other brand, it might even be called – gasp – unfinished. I bought a bottle, and not even blindly, simply because I had successfully mind-swindled myself into hearing the rustle of silk screens and bamboo mats. But repeated wear just erodes the fantasy of Cittá di Kyoto a bit more each time. I can squint my eyes all I like but no amount of mental acrobatics is going to turn that damp, bitter blob of cedar into the airy, silvery-green hinoki of my imagination, nor is that dry iris and hint of smoke ever going to transform into a wisp of coreless Shoyeido incense, which itself smells far more characterfully of cloves, benzoin, and aloeswood that anything suggested by this milquetoast of a perfume. Every spring since 2015, I have dutifully taken the frosted bottle out of the cupboard, dusted it off, and hoped that this would be the moment when it reveals its true beauty to me. And in truth, I don’t hate it. It is not a bad fragrance, objectively. But life is just too short for such low-impact fragrance.

This was one of my blind-buys that sprung from pure curiosity and from the fact that Santa Maria Novella was not available in Japan at the time. The perfume was created to celebrate the relationship between two cities I love, Firenze and Kyoto, featuring a flower that I adore, the iris. I can see why it will never be a popular perfume that you will smell on every corner, à la BR540. Città di Kyoto opens with a strange vibe, a foggy citrus that comes across less floral and more dry powder and glue, the smell of a freshly papered shoji screen in a cold house. She remains cool and aloof throughout, never once sketching a smile or any scrutable expression. She is graceful but not pleasing, she doesn`t want to please or connect. I can sense the lotus floating in the heart notes with a touch of lavender, but there`s no trace of a peach or an iris such as I know the iris to be. What I sense are violets. Astringent violets. As the perfume warms up on my skin, the violets become a little sweeter, so I suppose that must be the peach doing her part. The woody notes start to become more apparent, leading me once again back to the idea of a papered shoji in a cold minka, an old wooden house somewhere in a Kyoto alley on a grey spring day, far back in time when the city had a pulse and wasn`t a corrupted Disneyland for throngs of tourists with no connection to the place or its culture. Città di Kyoto is a kind of mourning for something precious that has been lost and may never be recovered.

Even as a young girl, I was drawn to the simplicity and modesty of Japanese spaces. Back then, I wished I could furnish my future apartment in that style. At 15, one doesn’t think about how rooms are heated with paper walls or where all the stuff can be stored when there are no cabinets. The only thing that remains from those daydreams is my aversion to dust collectors of any kind, and decorations for the apartment are allowed to come in only as single pieces, and only one at a time. I prefer to switch things up every now and then. I’m not quite sure, but I believe my love for the books of Pearl S. Buck played a role in this phase. Today, she is often criticized for having written rather trivial literature - something she shares with Rosamunde Pilcher. But I remember devouring "The Good Earth" or "East Wind - West Wind." I certainly did not envy the main character for the agony she had to endure because of her bound feet. Even today, 13 books by Pearl S. Buck languish in my bookshelf. I think I’ll revisit them. Città di Kyoto, of course, was created much later, as it was made to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the partnership between Florence and Kyoto. Thus, with this fragrance, one understandably does not experience a Mediterranean feeling, but rather, the scent reminds me much more of L'original by A. Putman. It embodies for me the simple beauty of Japanese spaces or ink drawings and makes me feel as if I can truly breathe again. Since our Japanese clients either opted for very light fragrances or loved everything that came from France, I’m not sure if Città di Kyoto would have suited their taste, as the fragrance impresses with clarity, clean floral notes, and indeed a hint of woodiness in the base, but it surprises me with its unexpected longevity, at least on my skin. The Italian perfumers have obviously pulled out all the stops, as the pyramid sounds much more floral-heavy than the scent actually is, yet it accompanies me for many hours with its almost meditative aura. The theme of partnership between East and West is excellently represented here. Italian craftsmanship meets Asian ambiance; Santa Maria Novella showcases all its skill not only with this perfume.

What does Città di Kyoto smell like? Come here to me and sit down. I will describe it to you! Imagine you are in a beautiful garden or park somewhere in Japan. You have just bought a silk dragon and want to let it fly in the park. The wind is gentle, but strong enough. It carries a lot with it. The air is infused with delicate notes of citrus fruits. Its scent is slightly bitter-green. You walk along the endless path through the park, releasing more and more dragon string as you run faster and faster. Scents brush against your nose. You perceive the fragrance of delicate flowers. They are indescribable but beautiful. Fine and delicate is their scent. The silk dragon is now very high in the radiant blue sky, moving in calm and gentle motions. It is shaped like a koi and has been painted accordingly. The painting resembles a precious Japanese ink drawing in the most watery pastel colors. The silk ribbons on the stylized fins of the dragon flutter gently in the airy height as if it were swimming up there. Then you lie back on the moist grass by a large pond and look up at the sky where the silk dragon stands almost meditatively. The lotus has bloomed and mingles with the delicate scent of damp woods and roots. A gentle hint of fresh water hangs in the air. You hear soft giggles behind you and glance around slightly. Three geishas are walking along the path behind you by the pond. They fall silent when they notice you and nod to you kindly and in unison. Their faces are flawless and made up with iridescent rice powder. They seem to float above the ground as they step over the wooden bridge where the irises grow. As you continue lying on your back, watching the silk dragon still meditatively in the crystal-blue sky, you slowly begin to feel more tired. You still hold the dragon string taut in your hand. And then you can hear it! It sounds like a geisha playing a string instrument in the distance. But it is not! It is the wind you can hear through the dragon string in your hand. It is the song of the wind in endless heights. You notice how your hand slowly opens while you gently glide away and fall asleep, releasing the dragon. And then it flies away softly. Like all your worries and sorrows in the wind in that one moment. This is exactly how Città di Kyoto smells. Like a silk dragon in the wind. Carefree, meditative, light, and infinitely free! https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=BTZl9KMjbrU

At the urgent suggestion of a highly esteemed perfume enthusiast, I am following up my comment on 'Acqua di Cuba' with one on 'Citta di Kyoto.' Both fragrances have impressed me immensely, although they couldn't be more different.

We set off in the middle of the night. We didn't notice much of the narrow path leading up the mountain to the ruins of the abbey. In the light of our lamps, we climbed steeply through dark forests and past crumbling fortifications. Higher up, the terrain flattened out, and in the light of the stars, we could make out the dark outlines of the dilapidated buildings.

I stumbled upon this Eau de Cologne by chance last week. We were in Frankfurt for 4 days to once again explore the museums of the Main metropolis, visit the fragrance exhibition in the Palm Garden, meet up with friends, and pay a long-overdue visit to a dear perfumer.;):) Additionally, we of course indulged a little in shopping.

Astonished. Lately I'm realizing that less is more, that I'm attracted (at least when testing/smelling) to perfumes with """poor""" and """common""" notes. Don't want to be heretic, sphemous, absolutely. But hey, I know you get the picture of my thought. I smell of a white, crystalline, bright and green rose. Not a bitter/raw rose (like the Paul Smith rose). Splendid geranium that gives an unusual twist to a rose perfume. Patchouli is also beautiful and it elevates the parfum to a persistent level. I feel like putting it in the clean category. Montale DNA not detected (I belong to the Montale team, even though I don't have a full bottle of it yet) I think that all perfumes should always have the fig element within ^_^ Where there is the green part of the fig, for me, masterpieces can born!

As summer approaches its peak and the heat in the apartment is already fought off in the morning with lowered blinds and shade-giving awnings, I always feel a bit melancholic. The trigger for this is unmistakable signs that the time we longed for during the still bare and damp spring is drawing to a close. Instead of a concert of birds, nature only provides us with the chirping of crickets, instead of mild breezes, sometimes oppressive heat roars, and when gladioli unfold their splendor in gardens, fields, and even in the supermarket, all that remains is the hope for a beautiful Indian summer, a golden October, and the wish that the current heatwave does not bid farewell with frightening storms. And yet - this time, which I can indeed enjoy, is not only melancholic but shows us year after year how powerful nature is, not only in adversity but also in pouring out its cornucopia of treasures over us. A stroll through the city market, a walk along farmer's gardens, the rich harvest of the orchard meadows, which shows us what the abundance of blossoms in spring promised, leaves me in awe every year. And it is exactly this power, this splendor of colors, scents, delicacies, and aromas that the sun makes possible, all of this I find captured in Cala Rossa, this so unusual fragrance. Mediterranean feeling does not only mean thyme, rosemary, basil, and plenty of limoncello, but also the salt of the sea, the aromas of various minerals that the sun-heated rocks of the coasts radiate, which are not interchangeable with the flat sandy beaches typical of so many holiday regions. Those who do not just want to lie on the beach but also venture into the hinterlands of Italy or Croatia will know what I mean. And this very fluidity embodies Cala Rossa for me. So powerful, so aromatic, so full of energy is hardly any other perfume for me. Unconventional, herbaceous, unrestrained, and yet harmonious, the perfumers of Santa Maria Novella have managed to capture summer beyond tourist paths. Already in the top note, neither bergamot nor citrus is employed, but the medley of Mediterranean herbs opens the fragrance energetically, almost masculinely. This remains the case throughout its development and concludes with a green-spicy finish. I marvel at the listed fragrance notes, for in essence, we know each of these individual notes. Nothing is exotic or reminiscent of the chemistry lab of modern niche perfumes, and yet the totality of these ingredients results in a completely unusual and, for me, appealing fragrance that touches me every time I indulge in it. Now I enjoy summer as long as it lasts, and with Cala Rossa, I can bring it back to me all year round. And for those who want to capture this mood with me, I recommend reading the poem "Abseits" by Theodor Storm again. It encapsulates in rhyme what Santa Maria Novella has immortalized in a fragrance.

When in summer the sun leaves the coast and no one lingers there anymore, the scents bloom between the rocks, awakening another world in the cove. Turquoise shimmering veils drift like speech bubbles over sparse herbs, the ethereal lilac lavender attentively breathes wild little clouds into evaporating eucalyptus tufts, barely allowing the small green mint to speak. And while the fennel begins to draw fine threads of a slightly harsher sweetness into the fresh activity, herbaceous cistus candies the wild little clouds a bit softer, accompanying the floral-earthy bass of the straw flowers from rocky meadows. Then thoughts of Werther's incense wander through the brownish humming of the cove, as roasted rosemary from the day smells like the light on the rocks. Eucalyptus-like, the myrtle remembers once more, softly singing lavender songs, the cliffs glow in herb red, four to five hours, then everything sleeps again. (With thanks to Mörderbiene)

Now they are back. Those barefoot days in the shimmering sunlight. Alone, I wander over the dry grounds. I listen to the maquis. It whispers in the wind like myrtles and blooming rockroses, leaving small scratches on tanned skin. Far away from everything. Back to the world, the sun on my face. Memories of warm sand and waves, as silvery as eucalyptus leaves. But here and now, there is only the scent of the heated terracotta stones of the terrace under the shadows of the dragon trees. I already suspected that they are self-sufficient, just like the withered summer meadows, and I brush my hand over the wild herbs in the garden, the rampant verbena. A bouquet of straw flowers still hangs at the door. There is a hint of salt in my hair as the daytime fatigue sinks into the sound of the sea. A little too much sun and a little too much wind. Lavender-blue clouds whisper of the cool-warm promise of a summer night. Of nighttime dog barking. A distant shimmer from the rest of the world. Moths that once danced around the orange lanterns in the trees, the chirping of crickets to soft guitar sounds, and the stars so close above the hammock, as you counted the freckles on my cheeks in their light. The sky within reach. Like in a dream. ** Cala Rossa is something special right from the first second after spraying: The fragrance is marketed by Santa Maria Novella as Eau de Cologne and has the typical radiance of the genre, yet it comes completely without citrus notes. Here, a cooling freshness effect is created in the top note with menthol and camphor-like facets of eucalyptus (leaves, not oil), mint (according to the pyramid), and verbena (according to my nose), which are underpinned by darker, warm herbal notes of myrtle, rockrose, and rosemary that smell very authentic of sun-warmed maquis. At the center blooms a bright blue, almost fruity lavender, and brittle, small whirls of lightly caramelized immortelle occasionally waft into the nose. In this way, a completely unromantic, primal variation of the Mediterranean theme is created, far from the beaten tourist paths. I cannot really detect a pronounced progression or a classic pyramid structure, but I believe that after a while I perceive a kind of base of light sandalwood and oak moss. Fine musky veils weave the notes together very delicately, without overly smoothing the edges and corners, and above this tension field of cool-green and spicy-warm, mineral notes hover like warm stones. Only they make the fragrance shimmer like the air on a hot summer day on a sun-drenched Mediterranean island above the brittle maquis. Cala Rossa is an unconventional summer scent, never loud, but certainly energetic, herbaceous without becoming bitter, stubborn without being scratchy, and despite its dreamy melancholy, it possesses an optimistic earthiness. I can’t imagine a more beautiful fragrance to read Milena Agus, Elena Ferrante, or Judith Hermann on languid sunny days. Dear Annabraucht, I thank you from the bottom of my heart for this heartwarming short vacation!

I can only warmly recommend a visit to the oldest pharmacy in Europe to anyone traveling to Florence, namely the "Farmacia de Santa Maria Novella" at Via della Scala 16, which is located in a beautiful, historic building in the old town of Florence. It is an interesting mix of perfumery, pharmacy, and museum. The well-known perfumes probably make up the most important part and revenue generator. In one of the impressive, venerable rooms, all the fragrances are available for testing, along with friendly advice on the individual perfumes. The largest group here consists of the typically Italian Acqua di Colonia. I tested several there and ultimately bought the "Alba di Seoul," which is a lovely olfactory reminder of Florence for me. However, I want to write about another cologne from this brand that I bought in Berlin, namely "Cala Rossa." Cala Rossa is by far my favorite cologne for summer. An incredibly naturally smelling, very spicy cologne that completely does without citrus notes. The moderate freshness is conveyed in the opening by eucalyptus and mint. The top notes settle quite quickly, revealing a strong spiciness that reminds one of dry herbs and the sun-drenched landscapes of Italy. I particularly enjoy the interplay of myrtle and rosemary here. The naturalness with which this scent presents itself is truly magnificent. If someone were to tell me that only natural essences are used here, I would believe it. Generally, this is not the case with modern perfumes, and it actually doesn't matter if the scent is good, as in this case. The coolness that others have described, I only find in the opening. Once the top notes are gone, it is more of a warm scent for my nose. On very hot days, I might prefer a fresher citrus scent; Cala Rossa might be more suitable for spring or late summer. However, I would have no problem wearing it in autumn or winter as well. With Cala Rossa, you get an unusual, wonderfully spicy, very stylish cologne. And in my opinion, it is also one of the best from the brand. It pairs wonderfully with a linen blazer and loafers (less so with sneakers and a hoodie). The price of 125 euros/100 ml is still acceptable to me. The bottle could perhaps be a bit nicer for that price.. The only downside is the cologne-typical, rather low longevity. However, this should not be a downside for a scent of this kind. There are many colognes with significantly lower longevity, which should also be mentioned.

First "Un Jardin à Cythère | Hermès", then "A'mmare | Carthusia" - now this one. They all convey an image: Mediterranean landscapes with typical herbs, dried or at least very dry meadows, and sometimes with a sea breeze (A'mmare), sometimes with a certain bitterness (Un jardin…), While I found the Hermès fragrance too bitter, the Carthusia fragrance thrilled me immensely. Cala Rossa differs, although it conveys the same image, as eucalyptus is quite present here and somehow allows me to breathe easier. At first, a brief hint of mosquito spray (eucalyptus), then just lovely. More of a summer fragrance. Refreshing and somehow cooling.

Oriental Flowers; Wow, what a powerhouse. A couple of syringes and you smell the whole day and evening. I do not like the brand Montale (often rough and hard) but it is very good composition. I was standing at the checkout in the supermarket and a woman asked me what perfume I had on? I think I had a pretty scent trail. If you want to wear a distinctive fragrance that stands out, this is your fragrance! Beautiful flowers with incredible power.

To my surprise, Montale ORIENTAL FLOWERS lists no patchouli among its notes, although it was the first thing I thought that I smelled upon application. I'm rather baffled by this, to be honest. One hypothesis I came up with is that when my box of samples arrived and a couple of them had come loose from their cards, perhaps I reaffixed them to the wrong cards. I had compared the colors of the strays side-by-side with another set I had received earlier since there were some helpful overlaps. I think that I won't really believe that this is ORIENTAL FLOWERS until I test another vial attached to a different card. For now, let me simply say that peru balsam plus orris appears to impart an earthy quality bearing serious similarities to patchouli. In fact, the huge sillage and potency of ORIENTAL FLOWERS even reminded me a bit of Juliette Has A Gun VENGEANCE EXTREME--and that's saying a lot since I only wear that perfume at home and have also discovered that it is quite effective at covering up any lingering traces of nearly any perfume which I've tested and do not like. My preference in such a situation is to take a long dip in a hot bath, but on occasion that is not feasible, which is fine since I always know that I can count on VENGEANCE EXTREME instead. Back to ORIENTAL FLOWERS: this smells really wonderful. Very rich with an oozing golden balsam quality. The oriental facet definitely outweighs the floral aspect of this composition, so I find it quite unisex although I suppose that the sillage is going to be too overwhelming for a lot of people--guys and gals alike. This is an example of a perfume which wears you, so don't expect to be able to devote your full attention to anything since it is impossible not to notice the tent of scent which ORIENTAL FLOWERS generates. That's a good thing in this case, in my view, because the notes blend together perfectly, but this is a textbook example of a try-before-you-buy perfume! ----- Update: I tested a second sample and still smelled patchouli! Perhaps it's an olfactory illusion, or perhaps there really is patchouli in this perfume!

The flowers of the Orient - these are truly not delicate wallflowers blooming by the wayside - Pierre Montale has once again succeeded in creating a real power flower with this fragrance - of truly oriental, opulent dimensions. One sniff is enough - and whoosh - you land on a racing carpet of scent right in the middle of 1001 Nights. In the chambers of Sheik-al Radj, where the ladies of his harem are currently burning bergamot, guggul resin, and blossoms to pamper their lord and master with all the fragrances of the Orient. A fragrance blend emerges, which initially presents the typical freshness of bergamot, but beneath it, the balsamic warmth of the resins gradually makes its way. An almost medicinal scent impression, paired with an underlying rubber note that somehow made Black by Bvlgari irresistible. Flowers like rose, ylang-ylang, and jasmine unite to give the fragrance a feminine touch and engage in a battle for dominance with the resinous, earthy notes - a confrontation that ends in a draw, leaving both parties reconciled. Sheik-al Radj has now also picked up the scent trail of these extraordinary, even for royal sheikh noses, unfamiliar fragrances; his first journey into the royal garage remained unsuccessful - where and how the search continues is left to the reader's imagination ;-). PS: Any similarities to living persons are purely coincidental and not intended.

This is not something I’d usually go for but I really love it. I also love the history behind Santa Maria Novella. In 1966, Florence suffered heavy rainfall causing the Arno River to flood the city. This resulted in everything being covered in thick mud. Volunteers from across Europe flocked to Florence, risking their lives to help rescue important art, artefacts, and to clean up the city. They were aptly named the “Mud Angels”. Angeli Di Firenze was created in their memory. This is the perfect spring or summer fragrance. The peach and orange notes combined actually give the impression of a juicy cantaloupe or honeydew melon. This is refreshing, light, clean, and crisp. It’s sweet, but not too sweet. I find this really very unique. I’ve never smelt anything like it. This doesn’t smell like a marine scent to me either, and I honestly can’t pick out a single one of the listed notes. I don’t get any woodiness, musk or powder in this fragrance. I’ve had my bottle a year and it hasn’t changed either. All I smell is this gorgeous, light, fresh, sweet melon. While I do find most of their scents very soapy, I don’t get any kind of soap from this. It’s just a great feminine freshie! I’d say ignore the notes because if you like melon scents (but the jolly rancher watermelon in Wavechild was too much for you, like it was for me) this is a brilliant option! It was a successful blind buy for me, and one I’ll definitely continue to repurchase in the future. I absolutely adore this scent!

This scent is incredibly similar to Il Sentiero degli Déi minus the pool float accord. It's a pretty delicate citrus and white flower scent that has some marine notes which, probably due to the acerbic quality of the black currant, turn a bit funky on me. This is why it's so important to try everything on your skin before writing a review or blog post, and most importantly before making a purchase: on paper and in the tester pod at the Santa Maria Novella store, this is absolutely incredible and potent; on my skin, performance leaves a lot to be desired, and the scent evolution does not resemble the perfume on paper at all. If you're lucky to have a different pH than I do, this could be a pretty, delicate, unisex summer cologne.

Angeli di Firenze (Angels of Florence) is a sweet, soapy floral mélange of jasmine and rose that creates a golden aura around the wearer. Angeli di Firenze spikes the buttery, floral heart with a juicy apple shampoo note, giving it a fun, youthful vibe that I quite like. My positive reaction to Angeli, in fairness, is probably due to a nice memory it conjures up for me than the actual smell itself. Specifically, Angeli reminds me strongly of J'Adore by Dior, immediately taking me back to my days of living in Belgrade, when I exclusively wore that scent. My job at the time was to travel around the Balkans, often on local buses, trying to sweet talk donors into giving us more money, a job I was really terrible at. I was only really at the office in Belgrade once or twice a week before heading off on my lonely travels, but I remember that I never felt welcome there, or part of the team. However, the receptionist at the front desk, a beautiful Serb girl with the highest heels I have ever seen on anyone, would always take the time to stop me and say, 'You smell sooooo beautiful'. The day I handed in my notice, I walked up to the receptionist, handed her the rest of my big bottle of J'Adore, kissed her and told her that she had made my life in Belgrade bearable. I remember that her eyes filled up with tears, which embarrassed me because I suddenly understood I could have made her this happy earlier. Why hadn't I just handed over the bottle to her the first time she complimented me on it? I never wore J'Adore again.

Angels of Florence was released in 2006 on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the catastrophic flooding of the city. What happened was that on November 3, 1966, three air currents collided: warm polar air, a Moroccan sirocco, and arctic cold air. The result was a wild high-altitude hurricane that swept from Rome across northern Italy over the Alpine ridge into Austria at 120 kilometers per hour. However, northern Italy was hit the hardest. Millions of livestock were lost in the Po Valley, thousands of houses were partially severely damaged, there was no light, no drinking water, no gas, no telephone. Hundreds of people drowned or were crushed by collapsing walls, and hundreds of thousands had to evacuate their homes. Perhaps the worst thing for the population was that meteorologists had been aware of the potentially threatening development. However, only the prison directors (!) were warned by the authorities, who could transfer the worst offenders to other parts of the country. The general population, on the other hand, was completely taken by surprise by the disaster! The Uffizi was flooded, artworks, paintings, and books were irretrievably destroyed. But even after the disaster, the Italian authorities did not cover themselves in glory, as they argued more about who was responsible for the cleanup than actually getting to work! In the end, it was the people from the community - the very first were hippies, by the way - who joined forces with their usual adversaries, the police, to rescue families trapped by the water! Soon, helpers came from many other regions and countries, and these helpers became known as "angeli del fango" (which is also the reference for the name of the perfume). This November 4, 1966 is deeply ingrained in the collective memory of the Florentines, so it is no surprise that this event should be remembered even after 40 years, and the helpers were honored with a newly created perfume by the Florentine-based Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella. One would expect that the house SMN would have made a special effort in this regard. The fragrance starts with a fresh-citrusy note (orange blossom), which is soon accompanied by floral aspects - I particularly detect jasmine. The heart note also has a slight fruity hint (peach, melon?). What is very nice about the fragrance is that this floral-fruity medley has a green-spicy undertone (whatever that is, I unfortunately cannot identify). In the drydown, a very discreet woody (?) base with a vanilla tone joins in. However, one should not imagine the progression to be very dramatic; the fragrance does not change its character significantly. Overall, I must say that Angels of Florence (in comparison to the windy catastrophe) is rather a mild breeze. But perhaps the fragrance refers to the time afterwards, when everything was in bloom again the following year? Be that as it may, for those who enjoy citrus-floral scents, it is a very nice alternative. A beautiful, solid fragrance, but somehow it lacks excitement in my eyes. The longevity is very good! One can therefore make a dose last a long time. PS: There is also a very good film in which the flood plays a role. It is called "Die besten Jahre" in German and is something like an Italian cult film. Update from 06.08.2011: After multiple applications of this fragrance, I have the impression that it bears a distant resemblance to La vie de Chateau by Nicolai. The latter has a more grassy-green-spicy opening, while Angels comes across as more floral-fruity. However, both are warm and soft, calm, and a bit noble in the base.

You can feel their presence in the sky over Florence: their cheerfulness, their laughter, the scent they playfully spread: Everywhere, in all the alleys, all the parks, whether at the cathedral, by Michelangelo's David, truly everywhere, and despite the tourist lines, one joyfully calls out: “Senti, gli Angeli di Firenze sono qui!” And so it is no wonder that a traditional brand like “Officina Perfumo Santa Maria Novella” followed in the footsteps of these heavenly scent messengers and as a result was able to fill their classic stylish flacons with a sparkling summer composition, namely “Angeli di Firenze.” For all these cheerful celestial beings bring different fragrance notes with them: One carries richly blooming branches of sensual white jasmine, another some tendrils of exotic ylang-ylang with its honey scent, a third has snatched some coarse flower stems from the shy alpine violet and is now joyfully waving them around. The little angels tumble around, laughing and singing, allowing these floral notes to mix summery right from the start. The next group of little rascals carries ripe fruits: The slices of fresh watermelon must be handled by two little fellows; in their exuberance, they throw them like fragrant frisbees to each other - from cloud to cloud - and their high-summer aroma meets the already present floral scents. Velvety peaches and black currants playfully roll through the wide Florentine summer sky: Hopefully, they don't overdo it in their childish English exuberance! For already the proud iris shakes out a generous portion of its fragrant powder from its noble head: Angelini, cosa stai facendo? This softly admonishing call does not disturb the little angels, and so a lively mélange of flowers and fruits continues to develop. Noble woods, vanilla pods, and smoky chunks of white musk become playthings of the English good mood, flying through the sky blue: they cross the flight paths of other fragrance notes, knot and intertwine with them into an extraordinary fragrance pattern - again and again! Thus, through this playful cheerfulness, a vibrant, sparkling summer scent with special charm is created. “Angeli di Firenze” delights me with the graceful lightness with which flowers, fruits, and noble fragrance notes are lovingly assembled, creating this wonderful fragrance experience. Truly not an eyecatcher, not a “crowd-pleaser” in fragrance form, blowing through the old alleys and across the wide piazzas, but a creation full of typical Italian charisma! A summery rich sillage and average longevity tempt one to spray more often than strictly necessary: For every new encounter with “Angeli di Firenze” is a true celebration of the joy of fragrance art. This reminds me of a quote by Jimmy Hendrix, which is also a book title. Doesn't fit, one might assume? On the contrary, it fits perfectly: “Excuse me while I kiss the Sky!” And that is exactly what I will do now: Of course with “Angeli di Firenze!” Stai allegro, amici! ---- Turandot reminded me that this fragrance was created in 2006, 40 years after the Arno flood of 1966, in memory of all the "Angeli di Firenze" who came from all over the world to free the city from the mud again, and a portion of the sales proceeds was donated. So it was dedicated to diligent, selfless helpers; for they bore this name.

Last spring, I sniffed through the offered fragrances at SMN in Florence and spontaneously fell in love with this one. It's true, it doesn't undergo a dramatic transformation and is not an eccentric scent either. Instead, Angels of Florence smells light, fresh, and thankfully not too sweet.

This fragrance from Santa Maria Novella is by far the most beautiful scent. I ordered the sample box with eight different fragrances as well as two free scents because I wanted to test the scent Rosa Gardenia. Among all these fragrances, I liked Angeli Di Firenze the best. This scent is so light and fresh and simply smells clean.

Bravo, Santa Maria Novella for this beautiful iris perfume that emphasizes the iris flower rather than the root. The iris is not alone in this composition: it shares the stage with neroli, jasmine, geranium and champaca, but the iris flower is the show stealer. It smells just like the irises that bloom on the islands of the Japan Inland Sea: only a touch of sweetness, a sprinkle of green, and a papery, woody accord that is really feminine without being too girly. I adore it and want to add it to my iris garden scent collection.

Despite the name, neroli and jasmine end up being the prima donnas- but with iris driving it forward, L'iris becomes a gently cascading floral scent. I'd mentioned a comparison to being a gentler En Passant, and I still think that's the case, in addition to it being a bit like a muskless Fleur de Peau (especially since not taking to musks too well was the starting point for my search for an iris scent/an alternative to FdP): it's cool to the nose, elegant and very soothing. Suitable for year-round wear, when you feel like being cozy. A little off-topic with its composition, but I really do like it. Sillage is low-moderate, whereas longevity can comfortably reach 5 hours.

Iris scents usually highlight the root, ranging from powdery, starchy, cold, or even buttery. L’iris is not about the root. Most iris flowers are odorless, but a few varieties are selected for their fragrance. L’iris reminds me of a springtime garden with irises in full bloom, where I have stopped to admire the scent. If you try this expecting the familiar iris root scent, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re curious about what iris flowers smell like, this is decent.

There is a lovely painting by Gaston Bussiere of a pair of frolicsome nymphs bathing in a pool of purple iris. If you could bottle that scene and its cool, playful atmosphere of ephemeral spring florals, the greenest violet leaf, and some sort of woody-musky-powdery mystical fairy soap flakes, you'd have L'Iris.

Santa Maria Novella has a gift, several of their fragrances transports me into Jane Austen world; it happen with Mughetto, and L’Iris made me immediately think of Elizabeth Bennet, and I LOVE Pride and Prejudice, so, I’m not exaggerating in saying this perfume moves me. It’s floral, it’s powdery, it’s luminous, it’s vaguely soapy, it’s elegant: to my nose this smells like beautiful things, and it’s the clean scent of my dreams. One of the brightest interpretations of Iris. I absolutely adore it.

The scents from Santa Maria Novella have always been something special in my collection. I have experienced them as exceptional, often with a strong recognizability and always with character. Therefore, my eagerness to grab the new fragrance as soon as it was announced can be explained by my curiosity for a new highlight, as I usually hold back on blind purchases.

The first spray was quite promising……fresh, rich, and floral-light green…… But instead of galbanum, neroli quickly takes the lead, followed immediately by the scent of a synthetic blend….. Research revealed: this is Alpha-Isomethyl-Ionone……which creates a woody-floral-powdery scent reminiscent of violet and iris. And here lies the catch for me…….

I was recently invited to a friend's place for a relaxed evening, some music, conversations, nothing earth-shattering. Just before heading out, I spontaneously grabbed Intense Starry Nights, simply because I was curious to see how it performs in real life. Right after spraying, there was that Montale moment we all know. Loud, immediately present, no time for small talk. Bergamot opens up, then comes the rose - unmistakably Montale DNA.
