Think lavender vanilla bean shortbread cookie bath bomb bedtime treat.

This perfume reminds me of two things: my grandfather’s Brut cologne and the Neutrogena Rainbath shower gel I used in the 1990s. All three have that lavender, woody, tonka, anise (even though Gris Clair doesn’t list anise, I can smell it).

Great lavender opening but dries down to a sweet powder. Actually i feel disappointed with Gris Clair... i did expect more from a Lutens. It's more suitable for a woman in my opinion. Sillage, lasting power and projection are weak. Updated January 2014

are untested samples of all kinds. Tested ones go into a separate box, quickly moving on to beloved perfumes that I think they might like or at least want to test. But sometimes there are also tested scents in the cookie jar that I am not yet finished with for various reasons and that touch me (positively or negatively) I ponder things like rating: Top or Flop?

What??? It’s not supposed to be erotic? *Looks dumbfounded* At the risk of being laughed at, I confess - Gris Clair is for me the most erotic lavender scent of all time! Pure sexiness. I didn’t even know that lavender could be sexy at all.

I take the lavender blossom, freshly cut from the bush, by the stem. There stands the wooden box with the watercolors, there is my glass. I dip the lavender brush into the water. And then I mix them, all colors, because that’s how the most beautiful gray is created. The light falls through the window, dust particles in the light.

The note listing for this one is odd. It sounds to me like three different perfumes in the top, heart, and base. But I am always searching for good coffee and orange perfumes, so I got a sample. To my nose, it doesn't smell like orange or coffee. Actually, I'm not sure I smell any of the listed notes. Rather, it's a chemical mishmash with hints of Murphy’s Oil Soap. It wouldn’t bother me to smell this as a public bathroom air freshener, but I don’t want to smell like this myself.

The typical 'sexy' scent is usually something oriental or sugary sweet, so you can imagine my surprise when I discovered that Very Sexy by Victoria's Secret was peppery and fresh. I see this fragrance shown quite often on YouTube in perfume collection videos. From what I can gather, it is one of their best selling fragrances at Victoria's Secret. I have never tried the original Very Sexy, so I have nothing to compare it to. Honestly, I don't find it all that sexy, and neither does my boyfriend. It is certainly appealing, don't get me wrong, but it's not the first fragrance I'd reach for if I wished to spice up my image. My orientals and gourmands do that just fine. What this fragrance does do, is make me feel fresh, spicy and clean. In some ways, the strong pepper note makes this fragrance smell a little fiery and crisp. Very Sexy is versatile and a sure crowd pleaser. The opening has a real bite to it, with zesty clementine and sneeze-worthy pepper. It also has a slightly masculine edge. I was glad that Very Sexy showed signs of complexity early on, cancelling out my fears that this fragrance would become linear and generic. The heart is where the vanilla orchid and jammy blackberries are most prominent, later settling into a slightly powdery and warm drydown. From beginning to end, this fragrance is quite strong, so I suggest applying it with a light hand. I would recommend this fragrance to those on a budget, who want something a little different to suit all seasons and occasions.

Victoria's Secret was running a sale and I bought a set with a lotion and mini perfume in this fragrance. It definitely smells nice and there is a sensual vibe to this fragrance but I would personally call the vibe more flirty than sexy. I think I might not be a fan of mimosa because both this and The University of Tennessee for Her have that and they both have kind of a strange floral note that reminds me of formalin from my dissection labs in undergrad but I have to work pretty hard to detect it. The clementine and blackberry definitely play well together. This is honestly another one of those sweet fruity florals that smells good but isn't anything groundbreaking. This is definitely something you could wear on a date or to bed (for sleep or otherwise), but it honestly could work for a daily fragrance too.

10/10 On every front. This is a winner for all the ages. Simply beautiful and quite remarkable in my opinion. My hubby likes this one too... So many people give me compliments when wearing this beauty. The cactus is GIVING! LAST ALL DAY LONG! Just gets lovelier with time. Smells very similar to the original. I may wear this one to church tomorrow. It will really shine bright in this 40 degree weather we are currently having.

I wore this in high school, circa 2014/15. Loved it at the time, nowadays it just gives me unpleasant flashbacks and a headache. I still have that original bottle and I never wear it, but I can't bring myself to get rid of it! Sometimes I want to have war flashbacks to one of the worst times of my life. For funsies. Definitely very overpowering. If you're sensitive to strong smells, beware!

Like a smokey eye, or your favorite bra, Very Sexy invites a simple but easy way to feel, well, sexy. This scent isn’t totally mature, there is something about it that’s playful and fun. It’s wonderful to layer with! I’ve found many shower gels, lotions, and mists that pair with Very Sexy. The scent is delightful but not distinctive. It is not a long lasting perfume.

I remember stealing the 2007 version from my mom and it made me feel so grown up. Possibly the beginnings of my love for perfume. true to the name, it does smell sexy and evokes a femme fatale sort of image. Smells like how I remember the 2007 version smelling!! Leans more unisex/masculine. Peppery, woody, and floral.

"Sweetheart, do you think too much perfume makes one indifferent?" "I don't care..." This is how I could imagine a dialogue that could very well revolve around this product. Because the bottle is already the sexiest thing about this scent. The deep, warm red and the suggested rhinestones on the dark cap seem promising and elegant to me.

Ah yes, the notes sound so beautiful here and I let myself be tempted by them. And now I am searching for the sexy. Not present. Instead, we have a chaotic mixture of indefinable substances, which ends in a fruity slush. So a fruit salad of the rather unappetizing kind for me. It lingers for a long time. The base then becomes somewhat more bearable and softer.

“Arabie” is the first perfume I've sampled from the renowned house of Serge Lutens. Having read numerous reviews of his fragrances, ranging from the words of high praise, to the comments insisting that while the fragrances are unquestionably unique, they're practically unwearable, down to the utterly negative reviews, I became quite curious about what effect Lutens' creations would have on me. As the name suggests, “Arabie” is supposedly a bottled replica of the aroma exuded by an Arab market (or a Moroccan market, with which Serge Lutens must have some “nose-on” experience). I've never been to an Arab market but should “Arabie” capture its olfactory atmosphere even semi-accurately, visiting a place like this goes straight onto my bucket list. From the very beginning, “Arabie” announces its presence on my wrist intensely, first with spices, the most dominant of which is cumin. The cumin is joined by nutmeg and cloves. Also, in the background, the dried fruits start to emerge and gradually reduce the spiciness and add a dash of sweetness to the composition. The sweetness in the heart and the base is further sustained by the date. My final verdict: “Arabie” is an adorable scent. I especially like the fact that it lives up to its name and proves that even in today's perfume industry there are still individuals bold enough to translate their visions and dreams into fragrances without being too concerned about the criticism they may attract. “Arabie” is a rather challenging perfume as it preserves its dense, spicy-sweet aroma throughout its development. Yet at the same time, I see it as a very promising introduction to the Serge Lutens line and, oh boy, now I can hardly wait to try some more!

This is one amazing whirlwind of a scent. There are so many aromas swirling in this perfume. Sweet stewed fruits, rich resins, warm spices and something that somehow evokes the image of a wild nocturnal animal in a dark forest. I imagine that what I am picking up is reminiscent of the natural animal notes used in classic perfumery – things like ambergris, civet and natural musk. I've always wondered what the term animalic meant, and I really think I get a hint of that quality in this perfume – it somehow smells alive. This scent is dark and exotic and truly one of the most uniquely complex creations I've ever smelled. It also has this intriguing quality in that, when sprayed on my wrist, it smells different in the center (where I imagine the spray hits the heaviest) than on the sides of my wrist where the scent is not just fainter but of a different character. The “edge” of the scent is somehow more ethereal than the dense center - with a powdery sweetness and a hint of something vaguely like calamine lotion or coca cola. Fascinating though it is, I'm not sure it is something I could wear - it seems a bit too masculine for me. I can see this being intoxicating on a man.

Arabie makes me understand the attraction of the dessert or gourmand fragrance, a category that otherwise doesn’t captivate me. Granted, Arabie is spared from the gourmand category by its emphasis on woods, but it is also sweeter than many gourmands, so the distinction seems weak. Yes, Arabie is over the top: too much spice, way too sweet, too many dried fruits macerated in syrup. All true. But isn’t it lovely? Applied with a moderate hand it is my favorite sweet fragrance. I can’t say that there is any particular element that actually balances the sweetness, but the benzoin twists the sweetness a bit and makes it appealing.

This is a fragrance with a personality! I really love how the fragrances of Serge Lutens manage to challenge me constantly. To me that is a sign of a very good fragrance you don't want a fragrance which is too predictable or similar to the same trends time and time again. Instead, here I find a fragrance which challenges my nose and which gets me interested. What I love about Arabie is that Lutens and Sheldrake have thrown away the rule book here. Instead of having a top, middle and base, you get the whole weight of the fragrance in one spray. As soon as you spray you get the spices, the stewed fruit, the amber and resins and myrrh. It's an explosion of colour and spice all at once. To me it smells very festive, like Christmas in fact. This is like rich heavy desserts of spiced fruits and rum and deep, rich flavours. Some people say this smells like cooking. If that is true, then to me this represents more of desserts and dried fruits, or the process of making them. Cloves, cinnamon, plumbs, apricots & raisins. All these I get out of this fragrance. Very Moroccan! All these ingredients are found in Moroccan and Arab North African cuisine. The ironic thing is that this fragrance is named Arabie, which means "Arabia". Now to me, anything "Arabian" (when applied to fragrances) means Oud, or Agarwood. Here, Sheldrake has interpreted all of these "oriental" notes through fruits and spices (and not with Oud). So I find it original and creative, and I really admire this fragrance. Personally, I think to wear this one you have to be confidant in yourself, because people will notice that you smell "different". Basically you will smell like a walking, spicy fruitcake. But in a subtle way, because I want to stress that there is nothing too loud about this fragrance. People will smell you but it's not a beast. Overall, I would advise people to wear this in cooler weather, and especially around Christmas. If anything, to me Arabie is the perfect Christmas fragrance. You could wear it all year round, but you need the confidence and personality for it, as you will be noticed, and in a good way too. Very original and creative effort by Lutens and Sheldrake with this one. Good stuff!

"This smells familiar" was the first phrase out of my mouth upon applying Serge Lutens ARABIE. Then it only remained to determine what, precisely, I was reminded of by this intoxicating—or is it suffocating?—perfume. With the help of many able reviewers at various locales across the world wide web, I have deduced that ARABIE approximates a collision of my grandmother's brandy-soaked dark fruitcake (not the wimpy light kind, but the one that is black as night, filled with raisins and dates and pecans and candied maraschino cherries and citrus rind, and so drenched in brandy that you could actually catch a buzz from eating a slice) and morrocan couscous with a very strong curry piled up on top. Or perhaps my grandmother, her sight failing as she grew older, reached for the cumin instead of the cinnamon as she prepared her cake? What an odd assortment of rich and dark notes! But is it perfume? I think that, in the end, the combination of the dark, boozy fruits and the cumin-rich curry just puts me over the top. Similar to the way I'd feel if I feasted on a huge curry dinner and then my host insisted that I eat a fat slab of fruitcake before permitting me to leave. As the flavors mingle in my aching stomach, I begin to feel like a pot of chutney simmering on the stove, thick gurgling bubbles fighting their way slowly to the surface before popping. My speech begins to slur. My head is spinning, and it seems that I might actually hurl. There is simply too much going on in this kaleidoscopic culinary composition. In a word: No. De trop! If ever there were a "try before you buy", ARABIE would be that. Does cumin mingle well with your skin? Spritz on this powerful potion and observe your friends' behavior. Do they appear to be sitting farther away from you than usual?

I adore this fragrance, although it did take some getting used to. Arabie is one of those deliciously strong and potent spicy orientals that you can't stop admiring. It's also borderline gourmand, having a fascinating syrupy accord that really adds to its appeal. At first, Arabie reminds me of clove cigarettes. A little smokey, aromatic and strong.

I am not a big fan of cumin notes in scents....or rather I am not a fan of BIG cumin notes in scents. Kingdom was just too troublesome & stomach-churning for my tastes. Luckily, Arabie is not a cumin-criminal on my skin...just a pseudo-exotic, candied fruit & spice-bomb with good bone structure & a sweet tooth.

Dried or old fruits? Maybe. Hard to use? Yes. Unique smell? Indeed. Arabie must be worn for several times in order to be understood. I did hate the first times, and now i do recognize a unique and wonderful smell on this. Lots of dried fruits, cloves and nutmeg all over a resin base that makes this fragrance really complex and challenging.

I blind bought his fragrance some years ago & while I normally have a good track record of blind buys, this was not one of them, What made me interested in this fragrance was the notes, Dried fruits, dates, benzoin, tonka etc... I thought this would be a hit but yet it was a miss.

Arabie by Serge Lutens is a captivating and intense fragrance. Its rich blend of spices, dried fruits, and resins creates a truly unique and memorable scent experience. I particularly appreciate how it evokes the exotic and opulent atmosphere of an Arabian market, filled with the aromas of spices and sweets.

How is this so basic and yet so pretty??? With my chemistry, this is just...gorgeous. The cherry is light: crisp and juicy, not candied and overpowering. The peony is fresh, a bit green, like you plucked a flower and dropped it directly into the perfume. The vanilla is subtle, neither overwhelmingly rich and dark nor cloyingly sweet. I can see where some people are getting synthetic, but I consider it forgivable. It's a dewy, flirty floral. Linear? Absolutely. Basic? Totally. Overpriced? I mean...I think all the VS scents are overpriced, so your mileage may vary. Am I in love? BITCH I MIGHT BE. -- This review previously appeared on another site under the name "PrincessPrickleson." That's me! I'm moving my collection to Parfumo.

At 32 degrees Fahrenheit water turns into ice, and at the same temperature Serge Lutens’ - L’eau turns into an emotion. The citrusy, peppery flavor of this perfume tells the brain of summertime and spring, though the heart tells another story. A refined man puts this on during the holiday season. Let me tell you a story - I walked out to fetch the mail on a cold December day. Jack Frost is here, but he is young - and still very joyful. The sound of packed snow crunches under my feet in a delicate, hearty way. The snow falling around me is as loud as an orchestra but simultaneously mute. As I return to the empty garage stall my senses are illuminated. I halt on the concrete floor and ponder, the snow on my boots quickly melting to the floor. A faint metallic glow resounds through my nose, a citrusy glint of summer. I’m seeing pieces and memories of summer scattered around the garage, yet I’m feeling winter. L’Eau keeps her confidence confidential, though she isn’t afraid to be bold. This fragrance is like having the money to buy a new aggressive and all black BMW M5, but opting for the more mature white on white 550i. This fragrance is for the man who surely owns an extensive time piece collection, but has the confidence to wear none at all.

The initial cloud is lipsticky, almost powdery. Not in a sweet way, just has the same weird kind of texture to it. Fluffy. Kind of like winter sheets. Herbal more than it is floral. The kind of scent a flower seller would tell you "oh no, it doesn't smell at all" about, but once you go in for a sniff – yes, it does? It clearly does. Just not in an obvious rosy way. It's a lazy morning in bed. Do you know the movie trope of a flashback to protagonist's dead wife smiling under white sheets? That are super brightly lit inside and out for some reason? Smells like those sheets. Clean. Fresh. Flannel. I don't quite like the larger sillage cloud (a bit too heavy, projects about half an arm's-length wide, lipsticky), but close to the skin – it's gorgeous. A smell of clean aired out laundry without the usual twinge of synthetic fabric softener. Just fresh spring air and good soap. Takes about ~40 minutes to settle close to the skin. Once there, it's very subdued, but never lacking. The kind of smell that, if I felt it on someone else, I probably wouldn't even think they're wearing perfume. Just that that person is clean and smells very good. Faded away in less than ~3 hours. Left a soapy aftertaste in my mouth that, for some reason, I didn't really mind. An interesting little thing as far as "fresh laundry" perfumes go, but eh? I don't know. I just didn't feel particularly drawn to the experience.

I have tested the Serge Lutens fragrances quite extensively; I found some good, many okay, and a few terrible, but they are all certainly well made. Almost all of them are eventually spoiled for me by the incense and/or the abundant spices. That's a matter of taste. In any case, I see here the reason for the relatively poor rating of L'Eau: it is so completely different from its brothers and sisters that for the Lutens lover (no incense! no spices!!) it really is just water (and if one still considers the Lutens fragrances a niche, then these are the ones who have caught wind of Serge's water and then rate it). For me, it is irresistibly beautiful and serves as proof that Serge Lutens is a master of his craft (or Christopher Sheldrake, depending on how the division of labor was) and I, as a philistine, simply cannot appreciate the other Lutens fragrances properly due to my subjective preferences. L'Eau Serge Lutens smells like the evaporated water rising from white, sun-dried, freshly washed shirts. That’s something to achieve; I find such 1:1 scent reproductions fascinating anyway. Whether it is actually detergent or fabric softener or whether the sun in a white shirt in water vapor has a very specific scent of its own, I mean the latter, because air-dried laundry smells different from laundry that hasn't been air-dried. Thus, it smells exactly as Serge promises in the accompanying advertisement video; only the coolness conveyed visually feels different to me, because despite all the purity and freshness, Serge's water is never cool, rather it conveys a feeling of security, a moment of stillness, a sense of being at peace with myself. And the sun seems to shine. I can understand the marketing as an anti-fragrance (the Serge devotees surely can too ^^): Against the downside of olfactory overload (= stink), L'Eau is the upside. If one had a teenager in the acute hormonal transition phase, including the accompanying odors, two sprays of L'Eau would at least erase the olfactory strains. The name fits fantastically in that regard as well. It can be used as a shield against any unpleasant surrounding odors. When one doesn't want to smell too much unpleasantness and still has to be around people. No one should really find it unpleasant; boring (no incense, no Arabian spice souk, no oriental desert wind) is fine, but that’s how it should be. Who knows, maybe the creation took so long because Serge, after tinkering all day with the latest scent bomb, always took a break with L'Eau in the evenings and very early in the morning. And because it was his favorite, he jealously kept it a little for himself and then a little longer. A masterpiece.

The first appearance of today's presentation is Mr. Sage, who briskly enters the stage and quickly and routinely presents his program. Following him, a mandarin glides in with dainty steps. At a certain level of ripeness, it is anyway one of the tamer among citrus fruits. Here, it offers everything in terms of ethereal-anemic slightness that seems conceivable. In the second hour, the door, oh what, the portal swings wide open. Behind it lies - a laboratory! Aldehydes? Ozone? Well, okay. But if that isn’t the one with the extra portion of Hedione… At least that’s how it seems to me. So we welcome: Hedione, Hedione, Hedione! … Uh, yes: Hedione. Hmm. What can I tell you about Hedione to bridge the surely short wait until the next fragrance note appears? I highly recommend Ronin's commentary on Aqua Vitae by MFK as essential reading. He explains it really well. And the commentary by Seelanne right below it is simply incredibly funny. … Well, uh, this metallic-chemical smell is presumably meant to refer to the term ‘ozone’. Taken literally, that would undoubtedly be a joke. Not that ozone doesn’t smell! On the contrary, the term is even derived from the Greek word for ‘to smell’. But wanting to bottle up that nasty stuff? No, the use of the term is simply meant to evoke certain oxygen associations. And just think of all that comes to mind! The chemist might be reminded of the aggressiveness of the element oxygen. The biologist might admire how oxygen plays the turbo for metabolism. Although it must not be overlooked that in virtually every office, there are colleagues whose metabolism clearly prefers to operate based on the more sluggish lactic acid fermentation. The interdisciplinary scientist with a penchant for philosophy might wistfully ponder what price we pay for the afterburner fueling with the help of such a toxic substance. How we bring ourselves closer to death with each breath, almost greedily and unfortunately not merely in random coincidence regarding the time that passes. Similar to how a burning candle does not merely approach its extinguishing due to the passage of time. The newspaper reader thinks of ‘ozone’ in relation to ozone pollution in city centers during summer. Or - almost philosophically - of non-ozone, namely the ozone hole. A former marine colleague recalled a line from the Hessian comedy duo ‘Badesalz’ on this topic: “Oh the ozone hole - ohoh, I haven’t seen any until now…”. With this contribution, we better end the free fall in quality. … Well, Hedione… um… By the way, “Hedione” is not translated to “Hedine” in German. One might think so. After all, Harry Potter's best friend is called Hermione in the original English and Hermine in the German translation. But that’s something else. … You all undoubtedly remember how Schäuble, while waiting for some documents, had publicly humiliated his spokesperson Michael Offer in the most despicable manner? Such nastiness is completely foreign to me, even if someone makes me wait… a little longer. And who should I be mean to anyway? With Lutens, you never really know what’s still to come. … I give up. Ladies and gentlemen, may I ask for one last round of applause for Hedione? The time scheduled for the presentation is only halfway through, and I can’t even promise you a partial refund of the ticket price. But what should I do? Have a nice rest of the day! The further performances are hereby canceled - until late spring. … Good day, esteemed audience! My name is Musk. Huh? Where has everyone gone?

It has been so long … yet the memory is still clear and vivid. A bright early summer day, pure and as sky-blue as it can only be in children's dreams. White laundry flutters on the line, and the shadows of the nimble swallows flit across like fleeting ink drawings.

Abstract. Theoretical. Reduced. L´Eau by Serge Lutens is clean and pure, yes, puristic. The citrus notes are merely hinted at, from the very beginning a fine floral note and a minty freshness prevail. But that's not all. A very subtle spicy note at the start is quite plausible.

First, I want to thank the noble sample dispenser. Otherwise, I probably wouldn’t have tested this fragrance. On the strip, it smells very sharp like disinfectant. On the skin and clothing, we then have the original scent of laundry detergent. It’s like putting your nose in a bag of the same.

Dear Mr. Lutens, I have heard a lot about your fragrances. Unfortunately, until yesterday, I had not had the pleasure of testing your exquisite creations. I would like to preface this by saying that, based on various descriptions, I have already made a sort of pre-selection.

Hooked by the comments here, I wanted to reach for a fragrance again that conveys pure cleanliness, wrapped in a delicate aura that is still palpable. Fresh, dignified, and extremely accommodating is this water from dear Mr. Lutens. I am overwhelmed by beautiful feelings, and the power of life bubbles up within me. Clear water that fills you up.

Comparing this OG formula (same bottle design pictured but with the white heart cap), against the newest release (available now in VS stores as of 2022): OG: - cardamom takes center stage throughout, and mimics somewhat of a subtle saffron or curry edge; makes it feel like something to wear on a chilly fall night - the other notes are blended so perfectly that it's hard to tell what else is in the background other than something soapy, musky, powdery, "cashmeran", and cozy - all notes remain present during wear CURRENT: - no cardamom is present, which is the biggest difference; this takes off the "spicy" edge and leaves the fragrance feeling only clean, soapy, fresh with a subtle, sweet musk in the background - smells like a "sexy soapy" fragrance - suitable for wear anywhere, any time of year, any time of day or night - if you love "lactonic baby wipe" fragrances, you'll love this FINAL VERDICT: - while I do love the OG formula, I actually prefer the current over the OG - OG's spice feels too intimate to me for something casual, and also seems like it wouldn't work as well for spring/summer as it feels very cozy - OG's spice does give it a special, unique, and alluring feel, that would be perfect for special occasions Read all 3 of my breakdowns to see the differences, listed in order from oldest to newest: - Dream Angels Heavenly (this one) - Heavenly (2013) Eau de Parfum - Heavenly (2023) Eau de Parfum

Dream Angels Heavenly is actually quite a beautiful fragrance. I'm not surprised that it won an award at the FIFIs in 2000. I don't think it could be possible to detest this fragrance. There's a lot to like about it. First off, it reminded me of Emporio Armani She, with a touch of L'eau par Kenzo for Women. It's a mixture of floral creaminess and fresh powderiness. Quite difficult to describe, but pretty nonetheless. It could easily pass as a scent from a more upmarket designer brand, as the quality is fairly evident. Although admittedly a tad linear, the overall composition is pleasant and well thought out. The soft, soapy and powdery qualities which Dream Angels Heavenly conveys, are hard to fault. To my nose, this composition is mainly made up of powdery vanilla, earthy iris and a touch of spicy cardamom. Towards the drydown it becomes muskier and more sensual. Both myself and others find Dream Angels Heavenly rather sexy on the skin. I'm certain that it has wooed a number of men and women since its release. This fragrance has that very distinctive, Victoria's Secret, 'clean approach'. You'll either love it or find it boring. I personally love it. Adding to the already lovely scent, Dream Angels Heavenly also lasts for a wonderful eight hours.

The opening has a Soapy Plasticy Begining at first but it dries to a semi sweet Vanilla But it has a bitter base of Quince an innocent sweetness of freesia and intoxicating orchid. and the drydown turnes powdery of Iris Violet and musk. I can also pick up a note of incense in this too it's clean fun flirty & sexy!

A few years ago, I ordered 2 fragrances from Victoria's Secret without ever having tested a scent. Mainly because I am a fan of the fragrances from the competing brand La Perla. I thought that VS would have similarly fragrant offerings. Of course, that is not the case. I was very disappointed with both fragrances. This review will focus on Dream Angels Heavenly. You can tell one thing about the scent: it is of low quality. Even for a drugstore fragrance. Mexx and Bruno Banani can still boast better quality. It just smells cheap. Without peeking at the fragrance pyramid, I couldn't really say what the scent actually smells like. Something floral. Peony? Lotus? Freesia? Or is it the orchid from the base note? There’s something watery in there too. It could be mandarin and quince. Yes, I admit I peeked. It really couldn’t be helped. Let’s agree that it smells sweet and chemical. What exactly belongs to the top, heart, or base note is something I can't determine anyway. It’s all wildly mixed together. However, the scent is not very intense. I have the "Angel Mist" variant here. I assume that should be something like an Eau de Cologne. You can spray it on nicely, it lasts at least 6 hours, but stays close to the body. Because of this, the scent is not really unpleasant. It just doesn’t make much sense for me to wear it since even at the lower end of the price spectrum for perfumes, there are significantly better options that don’t scream "Long live cheap". I can actually find a similarity to She by Emporio Armani. They share some fragrance notes. Somewhere I still have the Armani lying around, haven’t worn it in a long time, but as far as I remember, the two are really quite close. Only Armani smells, of course, a bit more high-end. But I also wonder who is supposed to wear this fragrance. Someone who can afford the expensive lingerie from Victoria's Secret will probably also have the spare change for a higher-quality scent. I could imagine the fragrance on a child or young teenager. It’s not disgusting or stinky... it just has something of a plastic toy that you let the kids play with. Because if it breaks, it’s not really a loss. At 11 or so, I would have surely liked to wear the fragrance, but a child wearing perfumes from a label for luxury lingerie??? That sounds kind of absurd. Maybe one could sell the fragrance to a 14-year-old who dreams of looking as fabulous as the VS models someday. Hmmm... I would still recommend something better to her.

One thing i noticed in the last times about Serge Lutens is how they are becoming more and more obscure at the time to list the ingredients of their fragances. And i would say it is a trend other niche fragances are following too (i am thinking of LÁrtisan, for example) Not much could be found when researching L´Orpheline. Mostly, a mere reference to incense and a lot of lutensian literature (written in that ambiguous Confucius/Chesire Cat way that only rises more questions) about orphans and Orpheus. Which actually prepares one for the mood of the fragance. So i expected a classical incense. Avignon type. Well, nope. I mean, it is a very incense centered fragance, but dont expect warm spirals of smoke. L´orpheline is ghostly, a steel-cold incense, incredibly clean and fresh, with an inorganic vibrant feeling coming from aldehydes and woody aromachemical, also cool spices, i smell hints of clove and pepper. Indeed, i can sniff in L´orpheline elements from other SL fragances, that interact very well. The buzzing-high pitched etheric note in Miel De Bois, like fictional woods. The cool spiciness of Vitriol d´Oeillet and the sparkling aldehydes of Laine de Verre and De Profundis, and also the clean musk of Laine. Miel without the honey, Oeillet without the flowers. If you enjoyed those perfumes, you might like L´orpheline. As the fragrance develops in my skin, i feel it less metallic, gets smokier and the texture of dark wood and humid soil is more obvious. It is refined in a low key way, almost austere and ethereal. I personally find it easier in a man, but of course, as all Serge Lutens are conceived for, it is wearable for women.

This fragrance is far more complicated than the two listed notes - Frankincense (on the website just plain "incense") - and musk. People are saying they're smelling everything from lavender, to a barbershop fougere, to hospital wound dressings, to a dentist's office. Let's look into why! First, a little bit of information. Frankincense is a resin extruded from trees in the genus Boswellia, which grow all up the mid to Northeast coast of Africa, from Somalia to the Arabian peninsula. It has a piney, sometimes lemony, and resinous smell, and has been traded in the Eastern Hemisphere for thousands of years. It perfumes churches and temples to this day. I first looked into if the smell was the adhesive used in bandages, but frankincense resin is not used in medical adhesive. Interestingly, tincture of benzoin (another perfumery ingredient) is. But benzoin comes from a different tree, and has a sweet, vanilla (sometimes also a bit sweaty) smell instead of the piney woody smell of frankincense. So what else could be giving the impression of hospital wound dressings? If it doesn't smell like the adhesive, could it smell like antiseptic? Well - the connection could be found in phenols. Frankincense has tons of polyphenols. In high quantities, phenols have a smell: they're sweet, not in the best way - like tar - and smoky/musty. And - the phenol group cresols is used in industrial Lysol, bandaids as a disinfectant, and dentists' offices as antiseptics and disinfectants. They're also present in Sharpies. I think we might have found the connection. Now, about the other listed note, the musk: It's a clean, white, synthetic musk. Ancient musk perfume was made from the musk pod of male musk deer from Asia, removed, dried, soaked in ethanol and diluted. When undiluted it was poopy, with the essence of decay - when diluted, had a dirty-skin odor that many people found sexy, then and now. Simultaneously with animal musk, there was plant musk - created from compounds from angelica or ambrette - two plants that exude a milky, musklike odor created by a molecule called lactone. Now, there also exists synthetic musks, close to the plant musk in smell, which dupes either the animal musks (ketone) or the "clean" plant musks (lactone). We've gone through many iterations of synth musks - from the cancer-causing yet reliably stinky nitro musks to the (also probably) cancer causing and unbiodegradable polycyclic musks like Galaxolide often found in laundry detergent, to the macrocyclic ketones and lactones that are probably better for us and the environment. I have no idea what the musk in this is, except I know it's not civettone or a natural musk, because it is very clean and not poopy. It's powdery, very tenacious. Sweet. Lightly floral, actually gorgeous. People on Basenotes have said Exaltolide (a natural component extracted from angelica root, transparent and floral), Galaxolide (polycyclic laundry musk, cheap and used in almost everything - clean and functional) - I don't know. Finally, let's get to patchouli: The secret, ignored accord on the Lutens English website - although the ingredients list betrays it. Under the "ingredients" tab, of course the main fragrance formula is hidden under "fragrance." But, you can see that patchouli oil is present in larger quantities than the water in the ingredients list. And it's perceptible, too, despite not being present in the notes list. Something scratchy, almost minty, and earthy. Present in the beginning and at drydown. Reminding me of the patchouli in Coromandel Eau de Parfum - which is powdery and not very earthy. It's there, and it anchors and strengthens the whole composition. Finally, present in smaller quantities, below "aqua," are sunscreen filters, Iso E Super, clove oil, the clove derivative eugenol, limonene, coumarin, menthol and mint. Most of these are fixatives, and we probably won't perceive the smell in such small quantities. But I do think it's fascinating, and good, that the Lutens company would include sunscreen to counteract any photosensitizing effects of their ingredients. I think that's a good protective step, and I wonder if this is an EU requirement. So the picture is far more complicated than what we see in the notes list. Modern perfumery is really an orchestra of technology that constantly has to be rebalanced, as new ingredient restrictions show up, as natural ingredients become more expensive and less available, and the company has to keep the perfume smelling the same. This is a marvel of science that plays on our very complicated memories of sometimes profoundly negative things, like hospitals, church and the dentist - and makes an emotional connection out of them, all while smelling deceptively simple.

Serge Luten’s L’Orpheline is one of those fragrances that it took a really long time to interpret and appreciate. At first sniff, for the longest time, all I really smelled was a ghostly, soapy mist of fleeting, fading florals. I thought this was meant to be frankincense, so confused and underwhelmed, I always sort of checked out and never really paid any further attention to how it unfolded on the several occasions I tried to revisit it. Today, I think I am starting to understand. It is oddly incensey, in a way; if there were an incense of musty, dried bouquets, spectral resins from unearthly realms, and milky, artificial woods, freeze-dried, crumbled and lit over a cold blue phantom flame. This is a fragrance faintly ominous and disquieting, of silence, and dust, and memories, and melancholia. The scent of a locked room that hasn’t been opened in over a century and witness to secrets best left well alone.

Serge in a bottle. This scent is my favourite for november. When it is still fall, but almost winter, cold, rainy and grey. I absolutely adore incense, and this fragrance is a beautiful and simple interpretation. Cold and warm at the same time, soft and also sad a little bit. When you are sad, because something happened in the past, not the "in the present" kind of sadness, when this feeling running through your mind over and over again, but the tame, almost comforting kind of sadness. This is the most beautiful scent for all souls day.

L’Orpheline was my first foray into the house of Serge Lutens. As a large fan of gothic and melancholy fragrances, this had to be my starting point. Upon the first spray, I was surprised that L’Orpheline pays quick homage to the classic barbershop fougere. It’s the spicy, musky shaving foam profile but is very much toned down. About a minute later, something cold creeps in. I literally felt a cold sensation on my nose while smelling it, but didn’t get any menthol type smell. It was so odd. I was intrigued. Then L’Orpheline slunk into a musk forward scent with light incense in the background. The incense and musks took turns taking center stage through the duration of the wear. This fragrance brings to mind a person walking through cold stone streets at night in an old European town in the winter time. Nothing tragic has happened to them recently, but the bitter cold and darkness has them thinking about all they have lost or all that could have been. The only light illuminating the streets is an old Catholic Church in the distance. The front door is open and the faint scent of incense whispers in the frigid breeze.

L'Orpheline is an elegantly minimal, almost austere fragrance. It is intimate in the manner it cloaks your skin. It lacks the journey more complex scents take you on, but it is exactly what I wanted. A strong, dry, smoky incense with a musky dry down. It smells like midnight mass in a remote church.

Cold spicy resin with a powdery soapy dry down. The soapiness lurks from the very beginning, but only after an hour or so it really becomes prominent on my skin. Although this is often described as a sad-cold-unapproachable scent, I feel like want to look at it in a different way. Maybe slightly melancholic, but ultimately a clean fragrance.

L’orpheline-Serge Lutens Imagine walking from a work on a cold january evening,you’re smoking a cigarette and wearing headphones,you don’t want to talk to anyone. Or maybe nobody wants to talk to you. You smell the the cold air as you walk thru a fog,the smell of an aftershave of the passersby.

L’orpheline isnt traditionally ‘sexy’, but i feel oddly alluring in it. It’s so cold and stark that it draws you in and you want to know more. I’ve seen the opener described as barbicide, and i have to agree, but theres a bit more spice to it and incense quickly comes through. Incredibly contemplative kind of fragrance.

L'Orpheline opens with a brief shot of aldehydes, but then the strongest note by far is lavender. I get some musk up top, weaving in and out of the lavender. The lavender continues for me throughout L'Orpheline. And soon, it is joined by a vanillic sweet hay, which tips me off to the distinct presence of coumarin.

If you're like me and not sure what "datura" smells like, this is what it felt like to me: a mix of hibiscus, powder, and a bit of sugary/nectar-y musk. There's definitely a woody/resinous element to this too. Not my favorite overall - the powdery element feels like baby powder that turned a little acidic, and the sugar musk was a little too sharp; so it was a pass for me. (This review is for the 2022 release of the "mini mist exploration set".)

This is just lovely, absolutely love it. So creamy delicious, powdered sugar (but not to sweet) with a woody base. Sure i recognize it being close to Ariana Grande Cloud, but it's still different and I can't decide which one i prefer more. They are perfect to layer together, smells so good. I hope thay never stop producing this one, i am on my second bottle and that says alot because I don't really use bodymists.

For me it’s just not a scent that I would want on me, I like more feminine scents and this one is very masculine. It smells like cologne like it’s made for a man. It is very woodsy. Like almost a bon fire type of smell or if you just blew out a candle and you smell the smoke. It’s Smokey woods mixed with mens axe body spray is the best way I can describe this scent.

I like a lot Nuit de Cellophane. Among the whole range of Serge Lutens, Nuit de Cellophane is a young, naïve spirit that probably feels a bit out of place surrounded by so many adult, mundande, exotic characters. The scent of this fragance transports me to my childhood itself: in our school´s playground there were some ornamental bushes that in spring bloomed with little, waxy, yellow-green flowers. This flowers had a strong sweet-green scent, and dripped a sticky nectar and after a couple weeks, the scent was even more intoxicating as they over-ripen. This shrubs were not chinese osmanthus (i checked) but Nuit de cellophane recalls that plant and its glossy hard leaves. I understand the associations with shampoo, maybe due to a very clean musk? I didn´t think of it immediately, though, but it makes sense. Newness and neatness are qualities that i can associate to this perfume. So,how does Nuit de Cellophane smells if you didn´t go to my school or use that shampoo? To me, like moist apricot pulp, enhanced with heady honeyed flowers and lush green accents , a touch of orange and mandarin too. It is a happy, young, gentle scent. The clean musk/woody base keeps it from being too cloying. and after the juiciness of the opening calms down, it becomes a bit more sophisticated and adult version of itself, more floral and indolic, where lily glows over the apricot/osmanthus botanical sap sweetness. Now and then nuances of bitter almond milk. After such a long, fun sleepless night, it will dry down to a dizzy honeysuckle-like floralcy and musk. Definitely interesting and enjoyable, although not extraordinarily complex.

I had a very interesting testing experience of Serge Lutens NUIT DE CELLOPHANE because one of my two tester vials apparently was not properly sealed, so nearly all of the liquid had evaporated. What remained was a very thick, perfume oil-like elixir. I applied it to my skin in the manner of parfum, and discovered a beautiful osmanthus-jasmine scent with a slightly soapy drydown. Next, I added water to the empty "parfum" vial, covered the top with my finger, shook it up and poured the contents all over me. It smelled really beautiful: a resinous, clear jasmine. Finally, I applied the edp liquid from my properly sealed vial and discovered at last the cellophane aspect of this composition. The jasmine now clearly dominated over the osmanthus and even seemed ever so slightly indolic. I enjoyed this creation in every concentration I tried! If I acquire a bottle, I may siphon some off and let the solvents evaporate to produce a small volume of the "parfum" in my unsealed vial. -------------------- UPDATE: I received a fresh sample of NUIT DE CELLOPHANE with a recent order and discovered that it really is fundamentally a shampoo floral, just as Aromi and others have observed. I am reminded, in particular, very much of Bond no 9 CHELSEA FLOWERS. I'm not saying that Chris & Serge copied anyone but there does seem to be a shampoo floral movement underway. I was considering the possibility of acquiring a bottle of this perfume, but now I am thinking that if the day arrives when I succumb to the temptation to add something from this twenty-first-century fragrance group to my collection, I'll probably opt for one of the big Bond no 9 bottles instead (it was not all that difficult to drain my CHELSEA FLOWERS purse spray)... For now, I'll continue to wash my hair.

Nuit de Cellophane is a fragrance that, while quite simple, manages to be incredibly pleasant. It offers a soft, tender apricot scent, which actually comes from the osmanthus. This note wraps you in a gentle embrace, evoking a sense of warmth and affection. It’s the kind of fragrance you’d associate with a feeling of love, light and comforting, with a delicate, almost dreamy quality. Despite its simplicity, there’s something quite captivating about its subtle sweetness.

Sticky osmanthus candy in a white plastic wrapper. I thought the name was another inside joke generated by Serge Lutens’ delightfully Dadaist naming system, but nobody told the cellophane, so up it rolls to the party and proceeds to hold court. A big ole juicy square of pink Hubba Bubba and a bottle of Garnier Fructis both try to get a word in now and then, but no dice. Listen, I’m usually happy to slum it with the B sides of the Serge Lutens back catalogue – they are usually easier to wear and have a surprising amount to say once removed from the company of their overbearing, talky brethren (Arabie, Chergui, et al) – but even I will go so far as to call this one a waste of space. Serge was always going to do something painfully ignoble to the osmanthus. We were all licking our chops for it, remembering the cheap suntan oil treatment of datura in Datura Noir, or the rub of schweddy ballz against the sunny face of orange blossom in Fleurs d’Oranger, but, but, BUT! Why take such a complex-smelling flower and jump through what must have been a series of hoops to embalm it in such a simple sugar syrup? Jesus, Serge, why do you always have to be so weird?

As an avid perfume collector, having spent thousands on building a decent wardrobe, you would think that my boyfriend would enjoy at least one of them on me. The only scent that drives him wild is the scent of my hair after using TRESemme's Moisture Rich Shampoo, for less than $10 a bottle. For the last six months I've searched high and low for a perfume that smelt similar to my shampoo. I have finally found it in the form of Nuit de Cellophane by Serge Lutens. Whenever I smell this fragrance, I am in the shower, with my long hair lathered in shampoo. It's a crisp fruity smell, with clean osmanthus, jasmine and almond oil to nourish the hair. It reminds me a lot of the Salvatore Ferragamo Incanto line. Nuit de Cellophane doesn't smell niche or unique to me at all. It's not something that I would normally like, however I'm giving it a chance because I know that my boyfriend adores it. Ah, the things we do for love! Unfortunately I'm more of a fan of Serge Lutens' heavier, spicier offerings. As much as I hate to say it, Nuit de Cellophane is a loud, sometimes offensive fruity floral to my nose, with a dominant, slightly watery osmanthus note. The composition is also fairly linear, which shocked me a little. I feel that Nuit de Cellophane is trying too hard to be mainstream. Like most Serge Lutens, Nuit de Cellophane lasts on the skin and has strong projection. I would recommend this fragrance to anyone that enjoys clean, sparkling fruity florals, especially those that love the scent of freshly washed hair. Nuit de Cellophane is best suited to Spring and Summer. Original review written: February 2013.

This fragrance has light sweetness, a little honey/nectar, and shampoo-like fluffy clean scent. It’s weirdly “safe” for a Lutens, but I like it. I need to use a light hand with it, because it can be a bit headache inducing, but I do like a light application. It’s pretty—not super remarkable, but pretty.

I was initially undecided about this the first time I wore it. I thought it was pretty but nothing special. Then the next time I wore it I fell in love with its elegant simplicity and effortless uncomplicated style. This is lightly fruity, and just a smidgeon soapy making it clean and fresh, with beautiful florals, and the delicious, sweet almond note I loved in Datura Noir.

This isn’t the most unique fragrance ever, but it’s a very pretty and inviting white floral. It has that classic thick, heady white floral feel, almost a bit powdery and dewy at the same time. It reminds me of a luxurious bar of soap. It’s a very safe and easy choice for those who love straight-up white floral scents.

This is a cosy fragrance. Very soft and velvety aroma surrounds this fragrance while maintaining a cleanness. It is incredibly well blended, a beautiful composition. I am just not in love with it. It’s performance is not worth the price. It’s airy and non-offensive. I imagine wearing this to coffee dates in spring, to work or during the summer.

I`ve always associated osmanthus with the variety I know and love in Japan, the orange flowers that perfume the sidewalks come October-November, the 金木犀 (kinmokusei). Japanese osmanthus is delicate, like ripened apricots, and has amazing silage that projects meters away from its roots.

Huge burst of delicious, dripping fruits to start - oh so very juicy. Blackberry and pear stick out most to me, and they're utterly mouth-watering. Once this has time to develop on your skin after a white, its 'noir' qualities start shining through - the sweet vanilla, warm amber, dusky plum... I'm not sure where the powder is, however. It stays quite juicy to me until it starts fading away. Which doesn't take very long, sadly. I've had a problem with Victoria's Secret scents having poor longevity in general.

On my skin, this Sexy Little Thing is dark apricots, vanilla, and a touch of spice (the jasmine effect I think.) I'm loving it and wondering why the lasting power & sillage couldn't be a touch stronger. Still... I LOVE it! This is my favorite VS perfume so far. :o)

The first time that I tried Victoria's Secret SEXY LITTLE THINGS NOIR, my reaction was that this fragrance has nothing to do with noir. (was there a translation error at VS, perhaps?) Relative to SEXY LITTLE THING, however, SLT NOIR is much more oriental and a bit darker. The fruity opening is not like a juicy maraschino-cherry-topped fruit cup in heavy syrup--as one might fear upon gazing at the lengthy list of exclusively fruit top notes--but more of a spiced, no-sugar-added compote. But shortly thereafter, the vanilla and the florals assert themselves. The fragrance finishes, as advertised, in an amber muskiness accented by slightly sweet vanilla and tonka bean. SLT NOIR detectably develops through three stages, albeit rapidly, and culminates in a long-lasting layer of oriental vanilla fragrance that is more comforting than sexy to me.

Cédre is deceiving. As others have noticed, there is lack of an obvious take on cedar wood. You wont find it in the opening. Cèdre starts with clove and more, very camphoraceous and medicinal , like a herbal remedy for cough, and this harsh opening might put some off. It is not pretty, but i find it tonic and invigorating. From the menthol-rub rise some white petals. The tuberose is so indolic i hardly recognize it, but it will evolve and bloom into a more distinctive one, but never up to the point you say "this is a tuberose perfume" Cèdre´s floral nuance is dark and deep. Mora a baritone than a tenor. Cèdre is a low key Tubereuse Criminelle. Slightly the cedar appears, in the background, dusty, smoky and a bit sombre, in contrast to the waxy, animal tuberose. And i like it despite i am not in the mood of this moody tree. A sweet cinnamon makes Cèdre kinder. Then a rather dirty musk makes it sexy. Cèdre is shadowy and dense. And raunchy. I understand when Serge Lutens refers himself to Cèdre as a patisserie de bois, because it has a baked quality. Like out of a wood-fired oven... in between the thin dry layers of this croissant´s puffed pastry the butter is made with emulsioned and thickened tuberose petals and cedar sawdust. And under the toasted surface, the core is tender and soft and warm. Is not gourmand like Jeux de Peau, but the butteriness is there. When i am already think "I got you", after a couple hours, i smell other flower. Violet? nah...impossible... and now a familiar plumy fruitiness, where have i smelled this and why i dint´t notice it before? The perfume is changing suddenly, fast, and i am in a dèja vú state... and then, out of the blue, ta-dah, i am wearing Feminité de Bois. Like if an unnoticed perfume pixie had scrubbed Cèdre from my wrist and hand and sprayed it with FdB. I start to believe that many Serge Lutens perfumes are different combinations of the same ingredients. The woody drydown on my skin is exactly the same cedar of Feminité de Bois, but ashier (radiant, overripe, autumnal, flowery) which i love, so i am pleased. But not everybody was pleased that day: my beloved wrinkled his nose and said "whatever you are wearing smells like asscrack sprayed with expensive perfume" So i underlined "animalic" in my notebook.

With the veritable flood of cedar-rich perfumes and colognes on the market--many of which appear to feature iso-E-super--it will likely surprise many to find that Serge Lutens CEDRE is nearly (if not completely...) devoid of that note! I'm sure that many gentlemen were probably expecting Serge's take on the cedar cologne. But no, nothing of the sort is found in CEDRE! Instead, CEDRE appears to be a metaphorically named tribute or ode to cedar. It is sometimes suggested that the most important part of a text is the blank space--what is not said--and that's my best guess of the explanation for the near (or total...) absence of cedar from this composition. I seriously doubt that the perfumer somehow "forgot" to include cedar, so there has to be another explanation. CEDRE is a fairly sweet floriental perfume which is very tame and almost mainstream relative to the typical offerings of this house. The tuberose is not loud enough to warrant calling this a tuberose perfume, it seems to me. There is a gentle florality along with a measured spiciness (nothing like most of Serge's orientals...) all of which is tinged with a likeable sweetness. This perfume seems more feminine than masculine to me. To pay tribute to cedar, which figures in many, many masculine colognes, this creation offers a counterbalancing feminine collection of complementary notes.

Looking over the reviews of Cèdre I realize I’m one of only a handful who actually like it. Yes, the name’s a bit odd, but only a bit. If you’re looking for the airy, crystalline cedar of the Lutens Bois perfumes you won’t find it here. What’s here is the oily, dusty cedar like straight-up cedar essential oil. The oily quality mixes with the syrup of the amber and the booze of the camphorous tuberose. Floriental usually implies the hybrid friendliness of amber fragrances and prettiness of florals. Cèdre subverts the genre, being more melancholic than affable, alluring rather than pretty. Lutens is considered to have reinvented the oriental. Maybe this is his reinvented floriental.

Serge Lutens' Cèdre can easily be described with one word, confusing. If you are a serious Serge Lutens fan, you might know that cedar is Serge's favorite tree. With that in mind, Cèdre should be a clearly focused, intensely woodsy scent. Not so, Cèdre has a twist. The opening of Cèdre is a very soft, like a whisper. The cedar note makes its entrance very quietly and almost unnoticed. There is a floral note that appears but it is muddled at this point. As we wave a quick goodbye to the uneventful opening, the movement towards the heart notes are served with a heaping of dried fruit and lots of sweetness. This fragrance's namesake seems to be taking a back seat to a syrup-laden cinnamon and amber duet. Where is the tuberose you ask? It appears, like a child running in and out of the room completely ignorant of its place in this fragrance. Maybe because the tuberose is being smothered by the overly sweet ambitious duet is the reason why it's hardly noticed. The tuberose is subtle and nothing terribly distinct. The base of Cèdre gives us just a bit more cedar but also another generous helping of even more sweetness. There is also a animalistic note in Cèdre in the form of musk. This may give the fragrance a more substantial base but doesn't really improve its overall linear performance. One of the problems with this fragrance is its simplistic construction of notes. Sometimes a simple assembly can prove to be an interesting fragrance, but Cèdre is muted, vague and extremely linear. Most Serge Lutens fragrances have great longevity and sillage. Usually, that is the desired effect, and Cèdre is no different. If you're looking for a light floral that's syrupy-sweet with a hint of cedar, you might give Cèdre a try. Considering the show-stopping performances of most of the other fragrances in the Serge Lutens collection, Cèdre might leave you disappointed.

The name Cedre can be a little misleading. Surprisingly this is a soapy and elegant tuberose fragrance, with a spicy and woodsy drydown. The cedar note is barely evident in this fragrance's composition, so don't go expecting any masculine woodsiness while testing Cedre. Surprises aside, I really love this fragrance. I would go so far to say that this is one of my favourites from the house of Serge Lutens. The tuberose opening is clean, feminine and smooth, with a subtle hint of spicy cinnamon and clove. The more the fragrance develops, the stronger the spices in turn become. I find it to be a really pleasant balance between spicy and soapy. During the heart and drydown, Serge Lutens' signature amber note reigns supreme. The overall blend, to my nose, smells heavenly. It is lush and warm at the same time. A rather unique and fascinating fragrance to say the least. For the most part, Cedre strikes me as being quite feminine and polite on the skin, however I could picture a man wearing it too. It has a fairly strong presence without being too overbearing. Like most fragrances from this house, Cedre lasts the entire day. It's a complex scent, but also an easy one to wear and enjoy. I'm surprised that I hadn't discovered Cedre earlier. You would think that it would be more popular than it is. Either way, it needs to be more recognised. I highly recommend. Original review written: March 2013.

Cross-border, because sweet wouldn't have more been allowed to be. But I was calmed fast - it is wonderfully coherent. At first one breath menthol, it then will take soft, creamy and the spices on the wood place. But no dominance enters. Dreary winter's days get alive! And for this reason my list of things desired gets longer.

Easy to imagine what this one might be, but on first sniff I smell civet and orange. That can’t be right. Actually, the real notes do simulate that impression at first: amber, clove, cinnamon, musk, tuberose and cedarwood. What I can’t find is the cedar. Overall, for me, this is an intriguing come-hither perfume. An accomplishment.

When you name a fragrance Cèdre, one expects a blast of cedarwood. Not here. Tuberose, cedarwood and spices are the main players but sometimes it’s more about tuberose, sometimes it feels more like a cedar fragrance. One of Lutens' highly unique scents that make the brand so desirable.

Cèdre is a somewhat difficult chapter for me. Having tested it under the assumption that I would find a soft woody scent with spice and warmth, I was very disappointed back then. What I smelled was a powerful, oily, matronly tuberose, underlaid by a bitter aftershave, and over everything hovered a dense cloud of hairspray.
I am not nice. Not fundamentally and certainly not always. Even though I do try (most of the time) to be, I am by no means always just friendly and relaxed.

Vanilla Lace is not an overly-sweet vanilla. I used to think it was "vanilla musk" back when I used it in the early 2000s, but now when I smell my bottle I smell the distinct note of incense instead. It increases the vanilla's warmth and depth, but incense isn't something I personally enjoy anymore so I have other vanillas I prefer to this one. Still a classic, nostalgic vanilla. It's well done, but I'm baffled by how expensive it is now on resale platforms - guess it goes to show that a well done vanilla is actually not easy to find/replace. Edited to add dupes/similar fragrances: - "Somethin Special" (small perfume business - I'm not affiliated) makes a dupe of this that they call "Vanilla and Pearls"; nearly identical to Vanilla Lace - Glitter Hustle is another discontinued VS mist that isn't a dupe, but smells very similar and is cheaper/easier to find than Vanilla Lace

Sandalwood often whispers, and I think the fig here helps to make a fuller statement. I can't pick out the fig on it's own, so I feel like it's there for supplementary, textural reasons—to add roundness and body. Cardamom and bergamot are also there in the opening, but I wouldn't call it spicy at all. You know when you try to fold a plush knit sweater, but they don't stay folded since they're so thick? So they end up half-organized, tumbled together in a pile somewhere in the top of your closet. It reminds me of that — the warmth and familiarity of a knit sweater, but without the seasonal holiday association. I don't think it's a dupe, K-version, or any sort of "take" on Santal 33. It's just another sandalwood fragrance.

The listed notes for this fragrance are not in a traditional pyramidal structure. The listed notes are Patchouli, Cinnamon, Amber, Woodsy Notes, Incense, Clove, Spices, and Ebony Wood. I was gifted a sample of Serge Noire, and I like it. I am surprised there are not more positive reviews of it. This is definitely a warm and spicy scent. I smell cumin, cloves, and incense mostly. There are other spices--I cannot delineate cinnamon from the lot-- but I do not have a highly tutored sense of smell, either. It is not sweet smelling to me. It has very little projection. It is a skin scent on me. Longevity is not very good. I expect it would wear longer on clothing than on skin. I find it enjoyable for myself to wear on the right day/night, but I do not imagine wearing it for others, and I would not say that it is sexy in any way. It is not especially feminine in the way some orientals such as Samsara are "feminine." It is definitely unisex, or more precisely non-sex. I would label it "neuter." Fragrance: 5/10 Projection: 3/10 Sillage: 3/10 Longevity: 3/10

The topnotes of Serge Lutens Serge Noire - smoky, dried fruit incense - draw me in every single Goddamn time, like a mermaid's song. And then I am dashed cruelly against the rocks that are this scent's downfall - the unmistakably oniony sweat of unwashed (male) armpits. Ask me how I know. No, really. I first smelled this when I was visiting Mont San Michel with my family when I was seven. The children had sat down in a grumpy, sun-beaten heap on the doorstop of the nth church, refusing to indulge our parents any further in their unquenchable thirst for the various religious icons and tchotchkes of French medieval churches, which seemed to us to be identical to the ones we had back home, only a little older and grimier. From our vantage point, we got to study the interiors of everyone's nostrils, skirts, and armpits. People passed over us; we were ignored, perhaps not even seen. A middle-aged man stopped under the mantel and leaned against the cool wall for a moment to gather himself, and in that moment, I understood that dried sweat could smell like onions and black pepper and celery - the makings of a mirepoix, practically - when suspended in droplets in the thicket of a man's armpit hair. The onion sweat accord can be parsed out later as clove, cumin, black pepper, and incense. While I love clove in stuff like Eau Lente (Diptyque) and the Eau de Parfum by Commes des Garcons, I admit that it can come off as sweaty and metallic to an almost objectionable degree. But the operational word is almost. There's always something in those fragrances to reign it in  herbaceous oppoponax, a bit of honey, some sandalwood. In Serge Noire, the clove business simply goes too far. It sidles up to the breaking point of human endurance and then waltzes brazenly past it, lurching unchecked into pure onion sweat territory whence it cannot be redeemed. I keep trying it, hoping I am wrong or that my perception will loosen up, allowing me to glimpse the true beauty of this scent as others describe it. But as of May 2020, and upon my 14th attempt, I have to admit defeat

It is absolutely brilliant, master perfumer at work. Spicy smoke, very masculine. Cloves and incense are dominant. Not a huge fan of cloves but here it's perfectly blended in, not in a bothersome way. Give it a go to find out what's been missing in your life:))

I don't think this fragrance is particularly challenging, even among SL scents (La dompteuse encagee is my nemesis :D). It's simply an incense scent with particularly dry woods and spices. I can smell a little bit of cloves and quite a bit of cumin. The other way around would've been much better. I find it rather mild, at least in comparison to other spiced incense scents I know, such as Sorcinelli's Quando Rapita... Serge Noire is not a scent I would see myself reaching for, but I'm glad I tried it.

Lovers of spice, particularly clove should probably put this on their list to sample. There is always something interesting to try from this house, and this one is no exception. Thank you for watching.

After not writing a comment for 100 days and using the holidays more for wine, Vienna, and singing, I guess it’s time to write one on the weekend. Let’s imagine the following tricky situation: A hardened bachelor in his early 30s, in his prime, has to fend off attempts to set him up - far too many people in his gigantic circle of acquaintances mean well for him...

Serge noire, it begins with a cunning play on words, because 'the black Serge' that we intuitively suspect is a man and would be a 'Serge noir' as such. 'La serge', on the other hand, is a textile, more precisely a fabric in twill weave, a material of solid, simple construction.

Every year, Leipzig is invaded by strikingly dressed people for the WGT (Wave Gotik Treffen): Goths, baroque, medieval, and steampunk outfits can be admired all over the city - a celebration of self-presentation characterized by a relaxed and tolerant atmosphere.

What a perfume! Pure madness. Serge and I, we are an absolute love match. My entire body chemistry and his olfactory creatures just fit perfectly together. So much for sympathy. I even forgive the quirky advertising texts. The scent starts off extremely disgusting. Extreme curry blast, cumin, sweat smell - help! This was a blind buy, and at first, I regretted it. But then...

Serge Noire is what remains of my day as the evening smolders in the fireplace, the match crackling in the ashtray. A scent that screams of a cigarette and the only one that, in my opinion, can withstand it when the sillage embraces the smoke. 21 Grams is said to weigh the soul. Duncan MacDougall was convinced of this after his experiments with dying people on the scale.

For Rest opens with an incense-y citrus note,  a sort of shadowy yuzu–not smoky per se, but sort of dim lit and flickering. Hinoki can sometimes strike me as a little harsh, but combined with the nutmeg and peppery musk, I think it lends a bright, spiced sweetness here. This is really beautiful. It’s a scent that’s too earthy and grounding to be called mystical or mysterious, but it’s too interesting for me to think of as cozy or even mundane. Perhaps it’s a perfume that straddles both worlds in the sense that it’s somehow deeply familiar and surprisingly evocative, a scent that lulls you into a comfortable reverie even as it leaves you with a lingering sense of wonder.

This smells like the fruity soft drinks Lilt (pineapple and grapefruit flavoured from the UK and Ireland) and Fresca (grapefruit flavoured from the US and Latin America), despite the fact that neither grapefruit nor pineapple is listed as a note. If you've never smelled either of those, they smell quite synthetic. This is far from the worst thing I've smelled, but I don't like it. It's definitely unique. If you're a fan of unique fruity scents, you might want to sample this.

One of the highly sugared breakfast cereals here in the US is called Froot Loops. I suspect that it can't actually be called "Fruit Loops" because the percentage of actual fruit is so low that it would be misleading. It's a guilty pleasure for me and a purely space-age one. The colors (especially the blue) and scents of these little oat-sugar rings aren't even close to anything found in nature. So it is with VS Love Spell. It is a super-strong synthetic scent that I have no words to describe, other than "FROOT." Not my thing, but I'm sure there's someone who wants to smell like this.

Harry Potter... Even those who are not familiar with the books and movies have at least heard of them. I'm not a hardcore fan, but I really enjoyed this imaginatively described magical world! With the title of this fragrance ("Lovespell"), I think of the unfortunate Merope Gaunt - in my opinion, one of the most tragic figures in the Harry Potter novels, according to Severus Snape. She was the only kind-hearted member of a family of rather malevolent wizards. Her father and brother treated Merope like a maid. She was hopelessly in love with the attractive (non-magical) neighbor boy Tom Riddle, but he didn't spare her a glance. With the help of a love potion, she was able to bind Tom to her for a while and break away from her family. At some point, Merope hoped that Tom would have affection for her without magic - but she was mistaken! Abandoned and completely powerless, she died shortly after giving birth to her son Tom Riddle Jr. - the later Lord Voldemort. No, Merope surely used something other than a potion like "Lovespell"! LS smells fruity-sweet and reminds me of those sugar-coated peach hearts. It's not the scent of fresh peaches but rather this slightly artificial peach aroma. I can't detect any flowers, especially jasmine. LS doesn't smell unpleasant, but I really perceive it only as a sweet little potion. Of course, one might ask: "Why do you even buy fragrances from this brand?" Because Victoria's Secret does indeed offer some nice scents! "Secret Charm" is a successful floral fragrance for me. I also find "Aqua Kiss" (which I only have as a body spray) very pleasant. However, LS was not a hit for me as a blind buy.

I love leather perfumes, but apparently don't understand the leather note. The 'leather' note in perfumery doesn't have any relationship to leather for me. Not in Bandit. Not in Rien. Not in Knize Ten. I have a layperson's understanding of the the components, the aromachemicals used in leather perfumes. I even understand the taxonomy and historical role of leather scents in perfumery. It's just that 'leather' doesn't smell like leather to me. Do you think the 'leather' from the start of the 20th century was the 'aquatic' of the end of the century? Was it just marketing of the aromachemicals that that were coming into play at the time? Given this blind spot in my nose, the perfume that differentiates suede from leather should leave me confused. But I love Daim Blond. It is distinguished and identifiable, but swings through my mind triggering all sorts of associations. A less jammy Robert Piguet Visa (contemporary version.) Sharp and cold like Chanel 19. Powdery-fine like PG Cuir d'Iris. It also fits perfectly into the Lutens line. What Bois de Violette does to its predecessor Feminite du Bois, Daim Blond does to Arabie. Less dense, more crystalline, higher-pitched. So I forget leather and remember the chilled, sweet cardamom dessert broth my boyfriend and I used to love at a favorite restaurant 20 years ago. Daim Blond's cold, precise spiciness keeps the fruitiness on a short leash. It balances sharpness and powdery sweetness through drydown.

Daim Blond is a handsome take on leather (or suede, for the case) If this note can be dusky, conservative and grave, reminiscent of old money, luxury and death, in this Serge Lutens creation is still highly refined but young, gentle and spring-like. The impression of a soft, flexible suede is succesfully achieved with the addition of a creamy orris and powdery musk to the leather accord. This velvety suede is illuminated with the sunny notes listed: sweet, green cardamom and the lush, tad disturbing sweetness of hawthorn flowers. Then the little almond that lies within the apricot pits gives off a very interesting both bitter and fruity nuance to Daim Blond. Apricot kernels remind to bitter almonds indeed. You have this in here, but also a pungent unripe apricot (the fruit) up to a point you imagine the fuzzy skin of the apricot and the elastic suede are so mingled they become the same thing, a bright yellow suede. The almost liquor-y fruitiness can be overpowering when we reach the drydown (as i see others have noticed too!) once the bitter and leathery notes have lost their ability to balance the sweetness of the persistent blackberry-like musk. Luckily this happens after several hours, most of the times I only notice it the day after. Overall Daim Blond triumphs at being carefree whithout loosing its gracious manners and aristocratic nature. A blond, smiling prince.

I'm revisiting Serge Lutens' Daim Blond, a scent I thought I didn't care for. It's objectively "nice", but it just doesn't resonate with me. I smell the things that people love about it: the elusive whiff of soft suede from the inner pocket of an expensive handbag, the cool floral iris, the bowl of apricots basking in a beam of afternoon sunlight. But those things, they're over there. And I am here. And we don't connect. It's the career woman who got married, had kids, holds an executive position somewhere, and does hot yoga and spin class. So very not me. It makes me think of that photo of Maureen Prescott that you see in the first Scream movie. She looks like a put-together lady. But you later find out she had a past, and it was complicated and fraught, and the catalyst for the entire franchise. Today when I smelled a previously undetected bit of pensive cedar, and wistful violet it made me think about Maureen's pain and trauma and tragedy, and I recognized how layered we all are, and how no one's life is ever quite how we imagine it from the outside. That's something to sit with, and so too, I suppose, is Daim Blond.

Every single perfume of this house gives me the impression of Serge Lutens directs his perfumes to be made of his diary. For being amused with dozens of craps in so-called niche perfumes I was awkwardly away to give this genuine leather a go on my skin. Initiates with tender creamy saltiness that promises of a suede softer than silk. A fresh green yet juicy apricot brings lactonic aura to this sweet sour leathery vibe like a thin film of gold over tanned skin. In a way it gives me the same mood of Jeux de Peau in a more common and standard way. The base is ornamented and strengthen by a fluent accent of musk. Impressive feminine scent, bold and distinctive, not an ordinary stuff and sort of sexy skin-loving smell. 4/5

Daim Blond is an oxymoron. Stripped of the usual curlicues it's a spartan oriental, more understated than Arabie or Ambre Sultan, I would say more ground breaking. It's beautiful in it's own way, but it's a hard beauty to find. Daim Blond doesn't work on paper, this bitter-sweet fruit of the desert only ripens on skin, and then not for long.

Daim Blond translates as blond suede. It starts with a dried apricot accord, similar to Kiste by Slumberhouse. That one then takes a turn for tobacco, this one goes to soft leather, or suede. Iris and musk are noticeable among other minor notes but it is mainly apricot leather. Not too sweet, just right as usual with Lutens. Unique, comforting, stupendous.

Daim Blond is a dry, dusty suede lightly decorated with the scent of apricots. Not the juicy, sweet flesh of ripe apricots but the desiccated husk of skin when shriveled up to almost nothing. Iris provides the bitter, gray powder, and osmanthus the delicate tannin of apricots and black tea.

A translucent veil of suede, so thin it's almost weightless, warmed by the first rays of the sun on a winter quite morning.
