There's supposed to be a whole host of other notes, but my untrained nose just can't pick them up. I'm glad to report the Lutens-Sheldrake collaboration led to the creation of a rather unconventional but perfectly delicious and expertly blended gourmand fragrance. What I enjoy most about “Jeux de Peau” is the fact that it makes me appreciate and savour the smell of such basic foodstuffs as bread, dairy products or jam, and thus reminds me of a frequently overlooked fact: that the best things in life are oftentimes the most commonplace ones. Yum!

Is it a new genre? The "woody yummy"? The opening is wonderful - loads of cedarwood and incense , but the heart is too much of a "gourmandise" fragrance for me: burnt almonds and buttered cookies. I don't get any licorice from this scent, neither do I smell apricot or osmanthus (all mentioned in the pyramide). On my skin, the fragrance dries down to a sweet almond dessert - probably much better worn in fall/winter than in the warmer season, provided you like this kind of "foody" style in fragrances. It certainly conveys a cosy atmosphere, but I must confess that I prefer other scents by SL to "Jeaux de Peau", which does not live up to its name. "Jeux" de peau? The plural "jeux" suggests a multi-layered, more complicated fragrance, but I perceive it as monotonous. "Woody yummy by Serge Lutens" is not quite my cup of tea.

Jeux de Peau smells like the air in a food product preparation lab, where the air swirls with all kinds of flavor molecules added to enhance our perception of what we're actually eating. I don't think Jeux de Peau is foody per se (because it is not something that tempts me to eat it), but I do think it relies heavily on food aromachemical notes to produce it overall effect. I smell cylotene, a molecule that tastes of slightly burned maple syrup, bread, and coffee beans and is often added to real maple syrup to enhance the flavor/smell, and pyrazines, synthesized molecules responsible for the very intense smell of coffee, chocolate, woods, and bread brought to burning point under intense heat. Like other pyrazine-rich perfumes, such as Aomassai, Un Bois Vanille, and Eau Noire, the effect in Jeux de Peau is intensely aromatic to the point where it can smell somewhat overcooked, or burned to a crisp, and like those other perfumes, a licorice or anise note has been added to underscore the deep 'black' or burnt nuances. The butyric undertone to the sandalwood is taken to the limits here, so it smells both richly oily and more than a little rancid, like a butter dish left out to fester under a hot lamp. When the toasted bread notes meet the buttery oilslick, the effect is unhealthy in that doughy, yeasty way that always reminds me of when a businessman slips off his loafers on a plane - that steamy odor of slightly-cooked feet pervading a closed-in space, always the same regardless of how spotless his socks, shoes, or feet actually are. The opening of Jeux de Peau forces that same unwanted intimacy on me, and I fight through it, gnashing my teeth until the intensity dissipates somewhat. In the heart, the overly rich, stale butter notes are cut with a dash of salt, which I think is coming from a very herbal licorice or anise note, and the grassy, spicy tones of immortelle. The savory notes are perfectly balanced by a delicious and delicate apricot jam accord (osmanthus flower), as well as the gentler milk tones coming out from the sandalwood. The sandalwood material is just incredible - sweet and salty, richly, brownly aromatic, like an ancient elephant figurine carved from Mysore sandalwood held up to a fire to bring out the aroma hidden deep within its fibers. Burned toast and butter, you say? No, Jeux de Peau smells more complex than toast and butter. It also smells a lot less natural. The combined effect is a blur of intense flavor impressions that attract and repel at the same rate. I think it is high art. It is, however, an occasional wear for me rather than an easy reach.

Whatever’s in this fragrance conspires to smell like a bakery. Looking it up, Serge wants to conjure not just the smell of warm bread, but the feel of it on a cheek. Childhood memories. How he managed to simulate this uniquely French smell I can’t imagine—this is definitely a baguette, not for instance a ciabatta. Check out the many notes. Oh, what’s that technology called? Head space. It may have been that. Must have been. Either that or a great deal of experiment. How else know these unlikely notes would yield the unmistakable smell of a baguette? Is it wearable? Not for me, but it’s quite smellable. Like similar compositions of his, Jeux de Peau is subdued but accomplished. — from June 7, 2015 forum sniff fest.

Jeux de Peau is food in a bottle. Good news is that it’s not an over-sweetened vanilla-packed gourmand. Imagine creamy sandalwood with amber and around it: toasted bread with butter, licorice and sweet apricot. This perfume is so bizarre that it fascinates me. It can be a warm, comforting scent for cold days. I prefer to spray my wrist in the evening and marvel at the abstract art of making French pastry into a beautiful perfume.

It is a musky-woody fougere, that smells to me like a blend of freshly baked savory pastry with a kind of "body odor"-like musk (in a pleasant sense;)), anice, soft spices and wood. Pure cosiness in a bottle.

Where to start with this one? Serge Lutens - Jeux de Peau opens with a beautiful smell of bread yeast which turns into the smell of freshly baked buns straight out of the oven. It's a lovely smell, and it's light! It's not so heavy or "gourmandish" even though it's sweet. In other words, it can be worn anywhere at almost any time.
Jeux de Peau from Serge Lutens, composed by Christopher Sheldrake. Undisputedly my all-time favorite gourmand perfume.

Damn you, Serge Lutens, and your insistence on putting this in the $300 Flacons line. This was love at first sniff. I’ve never smelled anything like this. This has a very lactonic opening with wheat. There’s some milky sweetness but it’s not cloying. I have tried cheap “freshly baked bread” body sprays and I hated them all but this is not like those.

Jeux de Peau is a comforting, cozy fragrance that captures the charm of a bakery stand at an autumn farmers market, and the intimacy of a winter morning spent baking at home, with the scent of fresh bread wafting through the air. It begins with an inviting blend of sweet apricot, creamy milk, and aromas of warm baked goods.

I went online to buy my usual VS perfume, Tease, when I came across Very Sexy Night. This is not sold in stores near me, so I just discovered it this winter. I took a chance on it and ordered a bottle, figuring if I didn't like it, I could run down the road to VS and exchange. I purchased the full size bottle of perfume, lotion and also a roller ball. I'm so glad I took the chance! I was in love with the black and gold bottle and thought "I bet whatever is in that is amazing!" I wasn't wrong! This is a very sexy smelling perfume, but it's light and subtle. It's not overpowering and it's not demanding...but will definitely be noticed by your s/o! It's spicy/woodsy, with a touch of sweetness for those that don't like overly sweet perfumes. I don't care for "sexy" perfumes that take over a room. I don't want others going home smelling like me. The plum and apple notes are the perfect mysterious blend when paired with velvet wood notes. If you want to kick it up just a notch, pair with just a touch of Gucci Guilty!

The opening of this fragrance is slightly salty, but the dominant note throughout is a masculine, woodsy scent with a hint of fruit. It's not unpleasant, but it's also not particularly unique. Longevity is poor.

Since many classics show me their worst side somehow (see Angel, Poison...) with few exceptions, I have somehow landed in the aquatic, often lighter category. These fragrances develop surprisingly well on me. Just like the Victoria's Secret fragrances. While the exact same scents seem to come from very cheap, rundown establishments on two of my colleagues, they smell neither as sticky sweet on me as on my colleagues nor as incredibly cheap and flat. It's astonishing how the same fragrances can develop so differently (Bombshell for example, or Victoria, very sweet loses that sticky sweetness on me). Thus, I tested more and more fragrances, including Night, simply because the bottle is so beautifully designed, and I am currently sniffing through the entire range. But unfortunately, Night, even on me, is very flat. The fragrance doesn't start off very sweet, interesting, but the development can only be guessed at, as the scent has completely vanished before it can even develop.

Notes unseen, I'm presented with the idea of a garden in someone's front yard at 11am. It's bright with the warmth of the sun, but not hot. There's greenery that's not necessarily wild, but not too manicured either. Just pleasantly overgrown and bushy. It's the idea of cutting a handful of herbs and giving them a rinse of cold water at the kitchen sink. It's domestic, uplifting, and optimistic. Looking to the notes, I'm shocked by the simplicity of the notes: citrus, sage, and cedar. Smelling it a little more closely now, it's the lime that takes centerstage. Who know lime had so much depth and complexity? I don't typically care for citrus notes or "freshies", and I wouldn't consider this a freshie either. This is one of those scents that feels more than the sum of it's parts. This is what MM Replica's From the Garden SHOULD have been. (Instead we were given that mandarin orange disaster! Lol)

The French have a way of making love then, without washing, putting on their clothes and walking proudly about. Not all of them. Certainly some I’ve encountered at business meetings. This perfume reminds me of passing by a recently-loved female native of that country—well perfumed, of course, it being France. Thus subtle Jasmine, Lily, Tiaré. Douce Amére has nailed these women. The scent must be beguiling because hubby smelled a sample and promptly bought the Bell Jar for me, unasked. I am wearing the perfume now, at his request. He says it smells womanly. It certainly does. After the initial animalic assault, this well-constructed and only briefly off-putting perfume really does settle into the heady muskiness of unwashed perfumed bodies. Where’s the musk coming from? The Tagetes, I’d say, and a floral I’m not familiar with called Musk Tiarella. This isn’t a loud perfume, though. Douce Amére almost turns into a skin scent, which is just as well since it suggests a woman’s thoroughly and recently kissed skin. In short, it’s a bit dirty. I, a bather and washer of sheets, rarely smell like this. Maybe I should. Maybe that’s why hubby bought me Douce Amêre. Perhaps you need it, too.

Douce Amère is a strange one. I am not sure I like it but I love wearing it. Another one of those scents where what I smell has nothing to do with what most people will tell you it does. It opens with a thick, sweet exotic flower burst (it actually reminds me of datura) but from early on bitter notes are playing hide and seek with the flowers. As it settles on the skin everything becomes, stickier, creamier, less floral. The unforgettable smell of sweetened condensed milk becomes the centre of the attention but right there, in the end of of the sweet milk trail awaits one of the most cryptic, nostalgic, ironic notes I have ever smelt in fragrance: a rubber teat, a pacifier. I am sure I don’t recall this smell from the time I was using one but I remember being disgusted by it when I was watching my younger cousins grow up. The overly sensitive smell of the five-year-old that I was could not believe that they were sticking that thing in a baby’s mouth and expected to eat from this. And I remember my parents telling me that I was a cry-baby and wouldn’t go to sleep without my pacifier and I just couldn’t believe it! So annoying was that smell to me. Now after all these years rediscovering the combination of sweet milk and rubber strikes strange chords. Douce Amère is way too sweet for my tastes but every time I wear it I get this nostalgic feeling of sheltered childhood. Soft clouds of fuzzy cotton wrap around me, I feel the warm sensation of snoozing in a dimly lit room knowing that someone is watching over me. I am not sure where these feelings come from but it almost feels like they are popping out the depths of my subconscious, right from the time I was actually using that bottle full of milk. The word “nostalgia”cannot describe exactly how I feel. The portuguese word “saudade” is the only word that explains this. A strong feeling of missing something that is part of you, is now missing and possibly can never be found again, filling you with a restrained sadness that will always be a part of you.

Douce Amère is not a simple perfume, but it wears like the simplest and sheerest of gauzes. It is a scent that reveals different layers over the course of a day – hazelnuts, smoke, Ouzo, cinnamon, licorice root, green leaves, all ending in a salted lily cream as unctuous as a bowl of ice cream. It is more than a little offbeat. You’ll tie yourself into knots trying to figure out whether it’s a bitter tonic for your liver or a creamy, bready, vanilla-soaked gourmand, but either way, that persistent thread of sharp greenery marks it out as something unique. Douce Amère satisfies because it gives you all of the interesting parts of a full-on oriental and none of the stodge.

At first sniff, I get a pollen-like effect – a lightly sweet, somewhat powdery scent with a bit of a dry herbal quality. This floats atop the aroma of a blooming white flower (I pick up jasmine mostly). The white flower scent is definitely present, yet somehow softened, almost as if it were bleached by the sun. As the perfume dries down, it develops more of a gourmand character. The sunny floral /herbal smell remains, but is now dusted with flakes of creamy chocolate just starting to melt in the warm air. The cinnamon and anise are not easily detectable to me, but do lend a delicate spiciness to the mix. This fragrance is so well blended that none of the notes take over, but rather combine to form something unique and lovely. Sadly discontinued.

This one starts off like a sweet herbal tea: soft, sugary, with a hit of anise that gives it instant personality. The amère part kicks in soon after — aromatic herbs, a little green bite, almost like a light bitter note. Then suddenly it switches lanes: dry vanilla, a powdery vibe, and that “freshly washed skin” feeling. From enchanted potion to French soap in a heartbeat. A mix of sweet, herbal, and clean that keeps shifting as you wear it.
This fragrance opens with an unusual accord of sweet, spicy and floral notes. At first I think I see chocolate, but it is all an illusion created by florals along with the vanilla and cinnamon note.

Douce Amère is one of the most wonderful fragrances there is for me. I stumbled upon this scent many years ago, when it was fortunately still available everywhere. Today, it’s a bit more difficult to find. Back then, I repeatedly read comparisons between Douce Amère and Macadam by Il Profumo, my signature scent.
But it’s not a joke that comes out, rather one of the most underrated perfumes by Serge Lutens/Chris Sheldrake.

Discovered 3 years ago, fell in love, bought it immediately. Still on my list of fragrances that I will love forever. Even though I own so many scents, Douce Amére is regularly taken out of the cabinet. Douce Amère, the bitter sweet, has something magical about it, indescribable, intangible. In a way, it is floating, gently accompanying yet always in the background.

The pyramid lists absinthe as the first note. So I expect a bitter, if not harsh, vermouth note, but I can't detect that. Instead, there's anise at what I find to be an unmistakably high concentration. I don't like anise; it reminds me too much of cough drops, which may soothe bronchitis but is not how I want to smell.

Im upset this was limited edition, it was one of the best scents Victorias Secret put out in a hot minute, plus it is something new, you don’t get a lot of mint chocolate fragrances. Smells exactly like an Andes Mint. The chocolate note is more on the powdery side and the mint is very sweet without being harsh. It is a lighter scent but I enjoy that, it makes it even cozier.

This had a beautiful minty-chocolate opening: powdery, chilly, and sweet. But the notes quickly moved into the middle, where the opening notes disappeared and a toasted marshmallow solinote sat quietly. Dry-down, which came within just a few minutes, was a really burnt marshmallow + firewood. It reminded me of a sweeter, more smokey, and synthetic version of "Replica - By the Fireplace | Maison Margiela" . Very headache-inducing for me. A better alternative for a minty-chocolate mist: Christmas Cocoa & Mint . That one keeps the chocolate and mint notes - and doesn't have anything woody, smokey, burnt, or synthetic.

When I read Sanchez/Turin The Guide I was taken by the idea mentioned in the review of Equipage. It was said to be fashioned after the scent of cold pipe. My mind went to plumbing. The image stuck with me long after I put the review down. Over the course of time, it dawned on me that Turin had meant the kind of pipe you smoke. Not too bright, I know, but it did make me seek out Hermès Equipage, a fragrance I loved from first sniff. But Serge Lutens has redeemed me! He has made a fragrance that smells like condensation on cold metal pipes. L'Eau Froide smells like cold metal, it smells like a stony brook in autumn, it smells like drinking melted water from a metal camping cup in winter. It's made if frankincense, but it smells like snow. We use the expression 'skin scent' as a placeholder for a perfume's later stages of coziness, quiet and low sillage. It’s when the scent has faded to the point that you must jam your nose to your wrist to make it out, at which time you're actually smelling your own skin far more than the perfume applied 12 hours prior. 'Skin scent' coziness can be applied to almost any perfume, but it will never be used to refer to l'Eau Froide. L'Eau Froide points out that the scent of live warmth is the true olfactory association with skin, as if we can smell the blood within the flesh. L'Eau Froide might pass as the scent of a marble bust, but that is as close as it comes to flesh. You'll never mistake it for a skin scent. from centhurdle.com

In a card game, a joker is a playing card that can replace any other. Giving a look at the reviews on the German Parfumo, I get the impression that also L'Eau Froide might act like a joker: everybody seems to see something different in it. I would like to support one statement that described L'Eau Froide as a spicy fir resin note – but with rather a sharp vinegar note in the top notes instead of citruses. To me, L'Eau Froide very much resembles the scent of spruce needle bubble bath of which I used to happily splash about in the bath tub when I was a little boy. And without remorse I would have filched from mama's perfume board if L'Eau Froide would have been available at that time. But being a grown up man, reminding my fellow human beings about that by wearing such a perfume is a different matter. It may not be fair to denounce L'Eau Froide as bubble bath. Indeed, it is just close to it – but it is these pictures that one can come close to those new molecules from obscure laboratories which I suppose being used here. We should not take the released scent notes too literally. Difficult to judge about L'Eau Froide: On one hand it is a great scent experience that surely will attract impulse buyers. On the other hand L'Eau Froide is in a strange way inanimate – just as lifeless as a perfume usually is that consists mainly of one single synthetic molecule. Inanimateness against liveliness, chemical science against artistry – whoever appreciates the scent of coniferous forests in his perfume should take the effort to compare L'Eau Froide with the old classic Acqua di Selva!

The wait is officially over and it was a very long winter anticipating more "cool" to come from Serge Lutens, but well worth the wait. I just went the whole day wearing the new eau de parfum release from Serge Lutens called L'eau Froide. Directly translated, L'eau Froide means "Cold Water". L'eau Froide is the second in Lutens' thematic "water" series, the first being L'eau Serge Lutens. It appears that Lutens wanted L'eau Serge Lutens, released in 2010, to be an "anti-perfume" and as fresh as a laundered shirt. Lutens made the following statement about L'eau Serge Lutens "When I presented L'eau to my team, I felt like Saint-Just informing the nobles they were going to lose their privileges" Prior to laying my hands on this hot new property from the king of spice, I was trying to conjure up an image in my mind of this fragrance's note structure. L'eau Froide was kept well under wraps and very little information was released, except for only a single note discussed, and that note was frankincense. Not surprising for the spice and incense master, but how will this frankincense note translate into a "cool" fragrance? When we hear the word frankincense, we usually associate it with the burnt variety, but Lutens' L'eau Froide is incense in its resinous state with base notes dabbling in the white musk range. This "cool" fragrance is not one of icebergs and glaciers, but the sense of coolness that can be evident in Somalian incense blended with aromatics or mineral note. When we think of "cool" in the abstract form, it might also suggest aldehyde or crisp eucalyptus notes or even mint. The opening is reminiscent of smell of pure cool water that is laced with a light herbal or perhaps mineral quality and a small bit of citrus. This freshness is aquatic and interestingly refreshing. The opening continues to metamorphose with slightly peppery notes and traces of frankincense, which makes L'eau Froide an interesting sensory experience. The heart presents a cool refreshing mint note that appears to have been rescued from a blazing forest fire just before being engulfed in flames. L'eau Froide is by no means a complex fragrance. The base notes tread dangerously close to the soapy arena but the resinous frankincense seems to keep them in check. A fresh aromatic pine or even a green woody note blends softly with the smoky mint, giving a strangely clean sensibility. A few have complained about the longevity of L'eau Froide but my wearings have got me a hefty 8-10 hours of longevity. Few people have been accepting of this new philosophy from someone who build a reputation for deep, dark and spicy scents. This series seems to be the direct opposite of Lutens' previous fragrances, and maybe that's his intention. L'eau Froide is quiet and somewhat reserved and has a subtle cleanness about it. It is easily wearable in an office environment without offending even the most delicate of senses. The consensus is that Serge Lutens created his two "Water" fragrances to appeal to the ever-popular "clean scent" customer, and to cash in on the demand. Perhaps he did, but L'eau Froide carries Serge Lutens' heavy-handed and very unusual signature. Anyone who knows his fragrances well enough would recognize L'eau Froide to be Serge Lutens' creation.

L'eau Froide opens with aldehydes, mint, lemon and ginger. In a few moments, I also got a light whiff of pepper from this fragrance. That's a lot going on up front, but it serves to set a mood. Serge Lutens is signaling that this is his take on a "clean, fresh" fragrance. And then... the frankincense. A cool, fresh incense note, wending its way up, and becoming more prominent as the citrus and spices recede. Cool and fresh incense? Yes, for about three hours on me. And I enjoy those hours very much. And then it fades to that light, "clean" skin scent found in all of those transparent white musk fragrances that were so popular a few years ago. It's that part of the drydown that makes me wonder whether Monsieur Lutens is laughing at everyone who buys a bottle of this stuff. I say reapply every three hours instead, and keep that incense going.

This was a blind buy, and I was sure I was not going to regret it. The fragrance turned out to be exactly how I imagined it to be. The name says it all: cold water. Without anything too artificial or tacky. It smells of mint, of a sunny morning, a fresh linen. It’s very unobtrusive and decent. It stays close to my skin, but remains there for a long time. There is nothing here that could be offensive, nauseating, too heavy. Nothing here is going to give me a headache, nothing here is too much. It’s my favourite choice for travelling because it indeed is like cold water, giving a feeling of freshness without really smelling of anything in particular. And if I don’t feel like wearing any of my other fragrances, I can always come back to this one.

I got a decant of this one, and the seller said that this fragrance saved them during the hot summer days. I was curious but also worried that the mint would overpower everything and give me a headache. It did not. The incense is gorgeous here, and mint is strong at first but does not overstep its boundaries and mellows out quickly.

When I first caught a whiff of L’Eau Froide, I immediately had Chicks on Speed in my ear with their 2001 remix of Malaria's hit "Kaltes Klares Wasser" from 1981. And the corresponding clip in my mind. So, in a way, a merged sensory trio. I don’t even perceive L’Eau Froide as *that* cold.

The water is still cold. Ice cold. Every morning at 4:30 AM I get up. Every morning at 4:30 AM I am tired. And every morning I think: “Damn cold water! If only there was warm water here!” A boiler could be organized. It wouldn’t be that complicated. But no one here cares.

The void is a strange place. For some, it is simply nothingness; for others, a longed-for home. Yves Klein belongs to the latter group. For him, the void is the place where everything begins and where everything can succeed. October 19, 1960, is a dreary autumn day in Paris.

Before testing L’Eau Froide, I expected a soulless, anemic lab cellar ghost like the disappointing L’Eau Serge Lutens (sorry, dear fans…). I was pleasantly surprised. Why is this one better? Although it is also quiet and has a significant synthetic touch. What is that mysterious spark of the gods that makes the difference? We will see.

One spray gives me a thick, cloying, powdery assault of an old-school perfume that does not seem like a Victoria’s Secret scent one would expect. This is a sweet, heavy and intense cloud that will surround you if you over-spray. And over-spraying would be more than one push of the nozzle. Syrupy amber? Yes. Intense florals? Most definitely. Spicy and nutty with an oily feel, Rapture takes me back decades when perfumes were powerhouses and strong-willed. This baby stung my eyes wide open. Drydown reminds me of the unpleasant smell of opening an old musty cedar chest. The one spray that I’ve used has lasted for nine hours so far and I’m washing it off. It’s far too fleshy for me and headache-inducing. There is no middle-ground for perfume-lovers here. It’s a love or hate fragrance. My review is based on a bottle from the early 2000’s.

This underrated early 1990s floriental has warm, amber undertones with an orange flower and honey top. Well-blended. A bit like Givenchy Organza, but less syrupy and moire versatile. I don't know if the formulations have held up but the older one I have I recommend highly.

Or "Oh my God, when will you finally pick me up?" In search of a new vintage scent, I stumbled upon this super cute heart bottle. Oh, is the fragrance still available?... Only 3 times at my preferred online retailer?! Before I quickly buy it blind again, maybe I should take a look at some reviews (this time even with video!). "Super heavy scent" "Heavy, oriental" "So different from any other perfume!" "Unique, but powerful, like the scents from back then" "I have an original heart from 199-something, and also the new rectangular version: Yup, it's the same scent" Okay, I'll give it a try. ... I sense it already, first spray: The experience I’ve had with every vintage scent up to 1995/ Poême Eau de Parfum : Soap. Okay. Bathroom spray-something. Hmm. No transcendence, still on the ground, the JWs need to push the date further back. After half an hour still bathroom citrus. Disappointed. After 45 minutes, musk and vanilla come through. You can actually smell the vanilla distinctly (too much!! for me). After letting every resident of the house sniff it: No flowers!! After an hour, the scent is gone! (ENCHANTED!!!) Spraying again for safety: I smell... LIQUEUR. Then... a bit of musk and vanilla. Maybe rose comes out after 20 minutes? Very faint?? Imagination??? Conclusion: Oriental power?? This is called powdery vanilla. The heart bottle???!!! Ah I hate you corporate!!! Why is fantasy and whimsy banned nowadays??? Sniff. Should I let the scent mature? Nope, Quelques Fleurs L'Original Eau de Parfum has been open for over a year and hasn’t changed a bit.... (Soap) (And the bottle redesign too ... ._.) Yeah, a vintage scent that doesn’t smell like soap nowadays is probably Vanderbilt Eau de Toilette ... Maybe also Maroussia Eau de Toilette ? I haven’t tested that yet... Nothing special.... At least it’s not musty.

Bapteme du Feu is another recent release from the quirky category. The name means "Baptism by fire" and the scent is supposed to represent a village fair. You get a weird combination of the smell of gunfire, gingerbread, candied orange and some spices. Overall feel BdF gives is cold spicy, with metallic notes (gun shooting?) lingering on.

I had a sample of this and tested it completely expecting it to be a " meh" going off the earlier reviews. Boy was I wrong! This starts out on me as a very jammy orange that calms down and gives way to a Moreish gingerbread, but never disappears totally. Woody notes creep into the mix and it switches from harshness to loveliness constantly creating the most addictive aroma. Its silage and longevity are both great and I just find it such a mysterious, intoxicating scent and from so few ingredients! Who knew?!

First of all, I have to mention I HATE gingerbread in the real life and in scents also...but, here I don't sniff gingerbread. ..not a crumb thanks God :). What I feel is a well blended spicy resinous start, then the most adorable makeup scent I ever felt ( not counting the Lipstick rose of course :)). The head notes fade so fast(faster than I would like), after the first 30 minutes the fragrance changes into the make-up scent. The sillage is unbelievable and the longevity also! I have to mention the colour of the liquid...ahhhh....I fell in love that colour at first sight.

This perfume is so strange, my first impression was "WHAT'S THIS?!", but the more I sniff it, the more I like it. Probably I wouldn't wear it to go out but it's fascinating...I can smell the smoky effect / burnt wood, like during winter's evenings when you go out and smell that odor coming from chimneys, I love the smell of burnt. I can feel the gingerbread and especially the tangerine, actually this last reminds me a little bit of that product to wash dishes or to clean public toilets, but it's not disturbing, it's a particular mix. Got myself a 10ml decant!

The smell of an overdose of joy at a Christmas party. Gingerbread biscuits and fireplace. Christmas carols and twinkinling lights. And then, if you focus, pure darkness. It hides something subtly sinister and eerie, just like finding out that this party is held by zombies. It’s cozy with its warm and spicy cinnamon and then it gets metallic, powdery, smoky and animalic at the same time. Nothing smells like this. A true gem in the most recent Serge Lutens’ outcomes.

It's the final moments before the band appears on stage. I'm right at the front and I can feel the tension in the air as the crowd pulsates restlessly behind me. We've all been waiting too long and now it feels like something is about to happen. I taste metal in my mouth. The air crackles with the peppery smell of dry ice.

This may mislead one at first into deeming it a rather bogstandard spice-bomb & "that,'s all folks!". But no! Do have patience with it. A little will do. It unfolds into a really ^very^ rich & solid 'fume - amply pungeant, & with plenty of balsamic-woody-muskiness going on.

Bapteme du Feu should be the official fragrance for the Tim Burton animated movies. The orange and spices say Christmas!, but the evolution is totally Halloween. After the initial warm clove-citrus pomander, something prickly your way comes. Metallic, sinister and dark, the ghosts of Christmas Eve start lurking in the background.

Before we get into my review, let’s see how Serge Lutens describes this fragrance: Imagine a village fair where the smell of gunfire from the shooting range mingles with the sweeter aroma of gingerbread, cinnamon, clove, and candied orange and you have Bapteme du Feu! Right from the start, you know this is going to be an odd fragrance. I mean, just read the description.

Okay, I admit, a rather reddish gray. But please add up all the comments below, and this time I really mean absolutely all of them, Bam, done, the absolute biggest gray area nonsense of all time. Everyone is just stumbling around in the gray. People, this is nonsense.

I love this perfume a lot. I had never bought anything from Victoria's Secret before this — but I went just to test perfumes and this one IMMEDIATELY caught my attention! The name "Seduction" certainly fits this perfume, because it sure seduced me. It smells identical to honeysuckle to me, and I just HAD to buy it! I've worn it every day since I got it. It's a bit pricey, but it's great! It's floral, sweet, a bit creamy and musky, and certainly seductive. My new favorite!

Hello. Me again. Today is my 1st year anniversary in Parfumo so I wanted to write a review. Hope you enjoy friends. (: I have to say Im not fan of Victoria's Secret Bombshell. Because it smells fruity and cheap to me. We dont get well along. Not bad maybe but not my taste. I like fruity scents but not in a cheap way. Luckily I found this. Tuberose in notes and grabbed my attention. Its oriental floral tuberose but in a soft, creamy way. According to notes there are 3 ingredients= tuberose, sage and musk. Dominant one is tuberose. In here, scent style is quite cold floral. Not complex and beast mode. Longevity and sillage are not the best, generally a ''skinscent''. Only people come closer can smell you. Age= doesnt have any strict age criteria but people who dont like florals maybe wont enjoy. Season= Spring, winter, autumn days. Occasion= eveywhere.

This fragrance with the promising name Bombshell Seduction (2018) Eau de Parfum gives me the impression of the pure white, new bed linen in a hotel room furnished with light-colored furniture. The halogen lamps provide soft light after nightfall. Equally gentle is the green-lovely-citrusy opening with sage, which quickly transitions into a creamy-tender tuberose. Nothing about the tuberose here is gummy or overpowering. Just as softly as the musk cradles the creamy-white tuberose, the ultra-soft down comforter of the hotel suite cradles you. Time and again, the sage peeks out cheekily, slowly preparing for the night. On this night, much can happen.

Fierce, sweet & savoury oriental enrobed in veils of smoke. If you are looking for the pervasive perfume of a Nargile lounge you have found it. An almalgum of old-fashioned, rose-scented powder compacts, club smoke machines, pot pourri, old church pews & dust assaults my senses on first blast. My initial view of this scent is far from favourable - but wait, the magic is yet to begin! Within minutes a curl of smoke snakes from my skin - I can almost feel the dry heat from the burning coals. It is intense, realistic & I love it. Can you powder puff charcoal smoke? I believe Christopher Sheldrake has succeeded! FT settles into a more tame, smokey, balsamic scent of sweet tobacco, hay, candlewax with a touch of refined (not animalic) leather & warm skin. The sillage is inoffensive but the lasting power is good. If you don't do somersaults for intense smokey scents - steer clear. I adore the scent of bonfire on my skin, love the smell of smouldering charcoal before the BBQ begins & the sweet, fragrant smoke from a Hookah pipe. This fragrance has my nose a-twitch. In summation: truly a "'fume", an ode to the Nargile. A dense, dry, smokey scent with a touch of brown sugar sweetness & spice. Magic, daggers, smoke & mirrors - hooked.

Fumerie Turque opens with smoke, smoke, and more smoke. The smoke is very dry and thick, almost tangible. I hate cigarettes and cigarette smoke, but this is a lovely smelling smoke. I compare it with the smoke from incense sticks: thick, dry, tangible, almost stifling and choking, but deliciously sweet and fragrant, and I can't get enough of it. Sometimes after I burn incense and I come back into the room, the air still feels dry and smokey: that's what I get in the top of FT. I can also detect a bit of hay. The dry smokey smell lingers, and gradually the sweet notes come forward. There is also something earthy, which is probably the patchouli . This is the good kind of patchouli, maybe a bit similar to the patch in Coromandel, but less fresh and bitter, much softer. Still the smoke remains the most prominent note to me. As I get to the drydown, the scent is still dry and a little smokey, but it is no longer stifling, it has settled to something rather dusty or powdery and with a sweet fragrance, which reminds me a bit of sugar almonds (maybe the tonka bean?), and chamomile tea with honey. In many perfumes honey is animalic and sometimes reminds people of a urine note, but in FT the honey is soft, gentle, sweet, a mere teaspoonful in chamomile tea, nothing dirty or sour. I can also detect a bit of a dusty rose, just enough for me (I'm not a big fan of big roses in perfume). I can't smell the leather note though. The general "feel" of the drydown is the same I get in Keiko Mecheri's Loukhoum: the powdery dry smokey sweetness that is so addictive. I'm not saying FT is similar to Loukhoum, Loukhoum is 100 times sweeter than FT, it's just that feeling I get. Fumerie Turque is a big LOVE for me.

It was not at all the tobacco scent that I had imagined it to be. Some people had compared it to Odori Tabacco, but this is much more dry. And less sweet. It does last an incredibly long time. I believe it lasted over 20 hours on my skin. I have tried the current formulation bell jar on one hand and the rectangular bottle on the other hand, I found that the perfume from the rectangular bottle projected longer and a little better than the perfume from the bell jar. They were also slightly different, although I'd attribute that to a batch difference, rather than reformulation.

Fumerie Turque opens with an almost black currant-like semi-sweet tobacco accord mixed with accents of dirty patchouli and spice. It actually is quite nice, and shows promise for what is to come. The scent adds what I can only describe as a black licorice note just after the opening that may be anise (even though it is not listed in the official notes). Fumerie Turque then turns quite smokey while retaining the tobacco, and then adds a hint of leather into the mix for good measure. Finally the tobacco and leather scent sweetens just a bit further with hints of tonka bean to finish things off. Sillage and longevity are both above average. My final impressions are that I like Fumerie Tuque but don't love it. This is more a preferences issue rather than a fault in the scent's fine composition by Sheldrake. Fans of the category should certainly have Fumerie Turque on their short list when seeking a tobacco and leather combo scent. 3.5 stars out of 5.

Fumerie Turque is the reference tobacco scent. While Chergui is the popular pick, FT is what niche snobs wear. Women and children, stay away! Smokey bar, leather sofas, cigarette ash and sweet animalic honey. Fortunately, it doesn’t come off as sweet as Chergui. Tobacco here is both sweet and sour. FT isn’t for everyone but if you take your tobacco frag game seriously, this is the one to try or even to have in the collection. It is totally unique and no other scent comes close. Whether you love it or not, you won’t stop sniffing your wrist.

Another charming composition from the house of Serge Lutens is Fumerie Turque. A favorite among house fans, although for me, it barely cracks the top 10. That speaks volumes in itself. I never thought of Fumerie Turque as a tobacco perfume, as the accord is displayed softly, although it is more of a tobacco composition than Chergui for sure.

The fragrance is inspired by the Turkish shisha The fragrance contains floral honey (rose and chamomile), resinous (patchouli and styrax), softened with tonka and vanilla without being too sweet, mixed with tobacco and suede, a unique accord that, in cold weather, gives you a unique aura with beautiful complexity and depth. I have the 2018 version and it performs great.

Nowadays, it is no longer in vogue to lounge around in establishments where other people and animals sit and walk, drink and eat, puffing and smoking. After all, one wouldn’t want to disturb anyone with their smoke. The smoke is unhealthy, and everything that comes with it is, by nature, as well. However, there are still places where smokers can be among their own kind.

.. lies the power to calm us internally.. Fumerie turque has been sitting at home for ages, just as a sample, after I received it from a colleague who bought two Serge Lutens fragrances, including this one. I watched him closely and literally devoured the scent with my senses when we went on a business trip together.

Oh man, what a day! Arriving home, I went straight to the mailbox, hoping new fragrance mail had arrived. And to my luck, it had. *YES :) It was there. The long-awaited sample of Fumerie Turque. My thanks to a very nice Parfumo user. The sample had to be tested immediately. So I closed the door behind me, prepared a cloth for spraying, and off I went.

Interestingly, the dry down of this perfume actually smells like a powdery/cottony sweet rose to me. I don't know if it's the combination of juniper + apricot blossom + cotton, but I've been smelling it all night on the tester card - and that's what came to mind before I ever read what the notes were. A friend's mom smelled very similar to this in my childhood. She would love on me like I was her own, and she was such a safe space for me - and this fragrance took me right back to her. Even if you didn't have a nostalgic tie to these notes, the combination smells fresh, clean, cozy and comforting. Like hugging someone trustworthy and supportive, who is wearing clothes that are fresh out of the dryer. Perfect for a bedtime scent, appropriate for office wear, beautiful and classic enough for an evening out.

I would claim that it was truly love at first sniff. When sprayed, it is still fresh and minimally fruity, drying down to a scent that is really hard to describe. It is special. Not extraordinary, but special in a subtle way. It’s not a scent that blows me away, that garners compliments and fills entire rooms. Rather, it cuddles up to you. Like a T-shirt that is freshly washed but has already been worn for a day, pleasantly smelling of a mix of laundry detergent and skin. I love the feeling of security that "Love" gives me and this unspectacular nature. It just fits always and has thus evolved into my everyday signature. A sign that a scent doesn’t have to be special, but it has to feel like it belongs to you.

I received this fragrance as a birthday gift from my sister-in-law in 2016, and while I usually approach gifted perfumes with skepticism, because you know best what you like and what you don't, I fell head over heels for this scent right away. I would even go so far as to say that it has become my signature fragrance. The top note opens with a very intense yet rounded blackcurrant. Zesty, refreshing, fruity, slightly sweet, and very caressing. In the heart note, a light powderiness unfolds through the violet iris, which cleverly blends with the freshness of the blackcurrant. Floral, woody, and slightly earthy in the base note, the iris root reveals itself, giving the fragrance a certain depth. Overall, a very complex and multifaceted scent that I wouldn't want to miss in my collection. Unfortunately, the fragrance was reformulated due to the ban on the ingredient "Butylphenyl Methylpropional," which, in my opinion, has caused it to lose some of the depth that I loved so much. The longevity of the old formulation was enormous (8+ hours). Regrettably, I can only perceive the new version very faintly on myself after just 4 - 5 hours. But it is, nonetheless, still an incredibly wonderful fragrance.

This opens up with the strongest hit of menthol i've ever experienced. It reminds me of early mornings, going downstairs to roll myself a method filtered cigarette. It's spring, and my neighbours floral and unkept garden is sending beautiful fresh, cooled by the morning breeze , wafts of tuberose and jasmine my way. There is the early morning smell of the past presence of animals in the garden, and possibly a small den of hedgehogs or mice nearby. It's chilling, refreshing, and energising. It makes you want to chill out, be easy, but also has a restlessness that lies within it. Very similar to smoking while having a glass of wine with friends. The nicotine and tannin heavy alcohol dance around each other, in a dark sultry way in brightly lit, bone cold room. This is beautiful and yet so unsettling. It makes me want to start smoking again, and grab my old leather jackets, skinny jeans and generally nonchalant yet always sharp sense of style. This is brooding. The wearer needs to have a certain presence and sense of self to pull this off for it to make sense. Only downside is the sillage isn't great, which is odd as the fragrance is so fragrant, one would expect it to travel... but it doesn't. It's not necessarily a bad thing as I could imagine the scent upsetting some more fragile souls, and it could easily become cloying despite it's frostiness. I would highly recommend everyone find the opportunity to experience this fragrance for themselves. It is not a safe blind buy in my view... although i did blind buy it. This is definitely a challenging and polarising scent. A fantastic creation from Sheldrake and Lutens.

Tubéreuse Criminelle is a beautiful creamy white tuberose fragrance with tons of personality, spun by none other than Serge Lutens and perfumer Christopher Sheldrake. This fragrance is an interesting twist on the classic tuberose genre, so be prepared. The opening is a strange, astringent wintergreen and camphor attack with whiffs of fragrant eucalyptus. This opening scent combination might have you checking for a gasoline spill, but don't worry. No fuel spills here. Over a short period of time, the opening metamorphoses as the tuberose fights its may up through the thick intense layers of green aromatics. You'll find a beautiful parade of florals, like jasmine, orange blossom and hyacinth following close behind. From the first time it appears, the tuberose ages and matures into an amazing floral extravaganza. The wintergreen and camphor are now but a whisper, but still standing in the wings just as a reminder. The tuberose is dusted with the scent of leather and just a bit of spice and smoke. The rich base of musk and vanilla give the florals a velvety and luxurious feeling. Tubéreuse Criminelle is not your typical tuberose fragrance, nor is Serge Lutens you typical perfumer. This combination of wintergreen with the polar opposites of waxy intense florals and just a touch of smoke, is a memorable and exotic combination. This a perfect tuberose fragrance for men because of its aromatic green structure combined with the dry-down combination of leather and spice notes. If you looking for something completely different from a tuberose fragrances, Tubéreuse Criminelle might be it?

This is just as others have described, so I won't belabor the crazy roller coaster ride- it must be experienced. BenGay/Menthol burns the nose hairs at first whiff and I almost start to dry heave when I remembered the Obe-Wan voice in my head saying "Use the force...step away from the sample for about 10 minutes then return to it." Sure enough it was opening up on the paper enough so that when I handed the tester to my DH he said "Wow! that smells fantastic!" so then I decided this was the one and only sample I would test on today's smell adventure. Indeed we had the same macabre dance for about 10 minutes on my wrist...I begin to pray to several different deities that by the time we got to the Indian restaurant to meet our friends I wouldn't be wreaking of menthol-liniment and they wouldn't be whispering how I have aged so much in the last year, 'it really is tragic how's she has let herself go...' In the next 30 minutes I had a full bi-polar olfactory experience raging from mania- fear and sheer panic to deep regret to hopeful to curious appreciation settling into profound admiration and joy at the end over the gorgeous full sexy tuberose in peaceful, meditative pond of vanilla and a single drop of warm clove essence. The sillage of one generous spray also took a similarly ragged path on my nerves from deafening to just slightly over the top monster sillage to the perfect after thought and now after 7 hours is a nothing more than the 'careless whisper of a good friend'. I am almost wondering if I need to talk to a professional after this experience. I've been I put this on my list of top ten Tuberose fragrances every Perfumista must try along with Carnal Flower, Fracas, Vamp A NY. Is this something I could wear on a regular basis? There's not enough Prozac in the world!

This made me smile. It's Vicks vapour rub with tuberose and I love it. It smells much much better on skin than on paper so don't judge it on paper alone. Actually don't judge it at all on the opening. The opening is a little testy for those who are not forewarned, like I said it smells like Vicks or menthol(cloves, nutmeg and mint with some sweetness). The tuberose shows up when the opening notes calm down and they all get along very well together! I would never have thought of mixing a narcotic white flower with mint but hats off to Serge Lutens once again for another quirky and lovable twist on a familiar theme. Sillage is about an arm's length on me and the scent stayed with me throughout my day, sending up lovely wafts every now and then as I moved around. My jaded nose really loves wearing this and I'm happy to own a bottle of this interesting minx.

Bombastic wintergreen, menthol, bubblegummy opening, which I personally adore! It was just what I was looking for. It settles into the most beautiful, creamy tuberose with an undercurrent of the wintergreen vibe, GLORIOUS!

Ok, you guys are probably, at this point, rolling your eyes when I make another purchase and write about it. I said I was finished, but I saw this for a steal of a price and just had to have it, as this was on my wish list for many years. With that out the way: This is PHENOMENAL!

Any Tuberose perfume can be quite criminal for me.;) But fortunately here it is a bold, enveloping and creamy whitefloral with gorgeous liqueur tuberose, spices, wax and wood. A bit tropical. The only criminal (yet cool!) things that my nose can randomly detect there, are the nuances of rubber, salt and leather. And yes, I can call it a masterpiece.

Four years ago I developed an immense urge to sample Fracas, the yardstick by which all other Tuberose fragrances seem to be measured. Some internet investigation revealed the existence of a few modern interpretations of this note, this being one of them. No matter how hard I tried, I couldn't even manage to procure a sample of Tubéreuse Criminelle ...

The start is pure Pepto-Bismol. Seriously, mentholated, wintergreeny (must be methyl salicylate), and medicinal, it takes a good 15 minutes before I sniff my wrist voluntarily. Is what follows worth that being sucker punched up front with a whole load of what-the-hell?

This stuff is brutal, especially in the beginning. The start is aggressive, disturbing, unpleasant. Interestingly enough, the heart of the fragrance is not putrid at all, on the contrary. It has rare poetic qualities and is utterly beautiful. Obviously a fascinating structure, made of first rate natural ingredients - and very originial. The strongest tuberose I know.

From Wonderlust, I get a terrific blast of florals in the opening that refuses to quiet down with time. I am a lover of almond fragrances, and sadly, I don't see this as almond forward like others seem to. It is heavy with jasmine and soft with heliotrope, like someone has just given me a delightful bouquet. Or, perhaps, I've been handed the bouquet from my butler while I'm feasting on a delicious almond treat - I am too enchanted with the bouquet and the pleasant scent it gives me to focus at all on the dessert I've long left on the table. I would say that this perfume isn't gourmand. It doesn't ring sweet like other almond scents do to me, it rings beautiful. I could imagine this at a wedding. I could even imagine this at a funeral. It is classy, beautiful, perhaps even mournful in the right context, but gracious and happy in others. I do not dislike it one bit! The longevity is okay. It's not fleeting, but it doesn't stay with me all day like a clingy lover or an anxious dog. It projects well, and amongst knitters and scrapbookers, this has been a big hit! Compliments galore.

Discover a place filled with wonder, where endless adventure awaits. Almond milk dianthus sandalwood from Sri Lanka. Up top with Wonderlust, I get the creamy almond milk, along with a nice citrus spritz. This gives Wonderlust a somewhat tropical feeling, with a bit of jasmine peaking through. However, the citrus moment is pretty short lived and that’s when this scent is at its sweetest. The next phase, is the true introduction of the dianthus, which adds a slight spice to the mix, and the almond is still persisting for the duration. It’s not a floral note that I’m too familiar with, but it stands out for a time, and I enjoy how it works in the composition. For a while, that sweet/spice of dianthus meets a might powdery heliotrope, and the sandalwood emerges from the base. This middle phase is probably my favorite part of the wear, since it’s actually sticking around for more than that opening semi-tropical act. Finally, it moves into being mostly about almond and sandalwood alone. Though, there is some remaining powdery qualities. It’s warm, creamy, and has an attractive coziness to the aroma. That’s what it ends up being for the rest of the wear.

Sprayed some on my arm today because, sniffing it from the bottle, I quite liked it. But...oh no...after a few minutes it was all I don't like in a perfume. Way too much of everything and cloyingly sweet. All I dislike in most modern scents ugh! I kept smelling it while I had to do some more shopping and it really annoyed me and gave me a headache. Once I got home, I couldn't wait to wash it off, which wasn't easy I can assure you. So longevity is impressive, in this case too imressive.. I really can't analyse the notes in this, I didn't get something fresh like mandarine; maybe the almondmilk notes don't match quite well with mandarin, I actually can imagine those two can easily clash. Heliotrope often doesn't perform well on my skin, so this may also be the problem. I also find nothing authentic in this scent, it even briefly reminded me of Maroussia which I detest.

Michael Kors. I don't really know his fragrances at all,… should I? Anyway, I’m currently holding a sample of this brand that has been released in recent years: Wonderlust. Strange name. For a comic fan … um, rather a comic freak like me, the hot Wonder Woman immediately comes to mind, but I’d better not write any more about this superheroine… especially not in combination with the term “lust” and… yes yes, I know, some are probably saying again that I urgently need a girlfriend… *sigh* I know that myself, so don’t say anything!!! :DD (And just to clarify, I’m not really that into Wonder Woman; if anything, I prefer Supergirl or Power Girl or or or… :D). Argh! Let’s get to the scent instead, which contains, among other things, mandarin, almond milk, and jasmine, as the fragrance pyramid reveals, which sounds quite nice to me. Great… by the way, I’ve been thinking for so long about what to write in the introduction that even my tea has gone cold. … I’ll quickly replace it with hot tea and be right back… :D The Scent: Basically, the fragrance starts with all the notes listed in the top notes of the fragrance pyramid. The mandarin and almond milk stand out the most at first, with the pink pepper becoming stronger afterwards. I can also already smell the sweet jasmine. The beginning is nothing special, or rather, nothing new, which isn’t a problem since it smells nice and feminine, maybe a little synthetic, but that’s not too bad either. From the heart note, you can smell more sweet notes as the jasmine truly unfolds. The slightly citrusy notes from the beginning completely disappear and are replaced by floral notes, although you can’t smell the clove among them. There’s also a light marzipan-like scent, which should come from the heliotrope. Additionally, the fragrance is very soft, so gentle, that you feel quite comfortable with it, even if, as mentioned, there might be a slight synthetic aftertaste. In the base, the fragrance continues to smell very sweet and floral. Moreover, the scent remains very soft as described due to the benzoin. A nice fragrance, but it doesn’t have any notable strengths. The Sillage and Longevity: I find the sillage to be above average to just okay. You’ll be able to smell the fragrance well on someone, and it leaves a small scent cloud behind. The longevity is also average, and the fragrance lasts about seven to eight hours on the skin. The Bottle: The bottle is oval with a very thick bottom, and the glass of the bottle seems to have a slight cream-colored tint. The upper part, just like the cap, is chrome-plated. On the front, the name and brand of the fragrance are simply written at the top. It’s nothing special, but it’s okay. Yes, the fragrance itself isn’t bad. Despite the sweetness, it doesn’t smell overwhelmingly suffocating and can therefore be used as a daytime fragrance. But it should also be suitable for going out since it smells quite nice. A rather feminine, floral-sweet fragrance indeed. Nothing special, but just nice. The problem is that you’ve probably smelled a fragrance like this a thousand times everywhere, but there’s nothing wrong with a fragrance smelling like 100 other fragrances, as long as it’s pleasant. It’s just that it’s only recommended for those who don’t already own such a fragrance, but even then, I would honestly recommend something like Alien or other fragrances. Well, it’s of course a matter of taste! Aside from that, this one, as mentioned, has a slight synthetic touch, which isn’t very disturbing, but you do notice it from time to time, just so you know. Aaah, I wonder what Wonder Woman smells like... :DD

I apologize for my completely unpoetic and utterly lacking in expertise comment. Unfortunately, my nose is not yet trained to distinguish different fragrance directions. But I still have an impression, even if I can't articulate it very well :) Although I like sweet scents, even sticky-sweet, this sweetness should have something special attached to it. Wonderlust is sweet. But not special. This fragrance seems to have crossed my path hundreds of times. In the 80s, 90s, and 00s ..... this scent appeared again and again. Many fragrances were very popular for a time and then disappeared into oblivion ..... Wonderlust seems to belong to this category. Not that the scent is bad - I don't want to say that. But it's also not super, not stunning, not special. It’s like a sticky sweet ice cream that you eat and forget. If you like it: Bon appétit.

After sniffing through various Michael Kors fragrances and thinking I was done with them, the Wonderlust bottle caught my eye. Without high expectations, I sprayed it on the inside of my arm and was surprised at how wonderfully soft this scent caressed my nose. Slightly powdery, minimally soapy, fresh but by no means aquatic, and a little breeze of floral notes awaited me.

Thanks to a dear perfumer, I recently had a sample of Wonderlust included in my fragrance package. According to the fragrance pyramid, it sounded quite promising (even if it might have too much jasmine for me), so I applied it. Wonderlust starts fresh and fruity. The first note I detect is bergamot, but it is quickly overtaken by mandarin as the dominant note.

Today at the flea market, my fragrance dealer recommended a Michael Kors scent to me. I haven't had much experience with Kors fragrances so far, as they usually come across as too angular and direct for my taste. Additionally, I'm not a fan of hiking. I prefer leisurely walks in the flat countryside. However, the spritz from the sample card caught my attention.

That I immediately treated myself to a large bottle again :-) Bought in the year of its release and fell in love right away. This scent just won't leave my mind. After the body lotion ran out, no, not the one from 2016!!! I thought to myself, oh dear, you pastel mood booster darling, I needed you back. I already like this apricot-colored bottle.

It is 2018 and we are on our way to the Maya temples in Tulum, Mexico. Quickly grabbed my girlfriend's perfume since I had forgotten mine. This morning I used my AF, my bottle has been empty for years. Flashback to Mexico, fitting for the weather. Here we have a sweet, floral but fresh scent. I smell mandarin, almond milk, and jasmine.

Since this wonderfully light and fresh scent has unfortunately been discontinued, I ordered the body spray from Notino. Unfortunately, it smells sweeter and more overpowering, not as weightless and freshly showered as the Eau de Toilette. I hope that VS will bring it back - lately, I've often seen re-releases of old scents and have even written to them about it. (I was recommended Mandarin & Honeysuckle as an alternative, but I haven't been able to test that yet.)

That's how I would describe the scent in a few words. I have not been a big fan of VS fragrances so far. Nor of the body sprays. The scents have always been too fruity-sweet for me, and I generally don't like body spray. The exception here is the Acqua Colonia body sprays, especially Lime & Nutmeg, which refresh wonderfully. Only Secret Charm piqued my curiosity when I read the comments about it. Unfortunately, our Müller didn't have a tester for it, but since the EdT was reduced to €9.95 this week, I took it home untested. If necessary, it can go to the swap meet, I thought. Still, I was sure I would like the scent. The comments sounded promising, and I also really like honeysuckle and jasmine. Serafina criticizes the low sillage, so it can't be a powerhouse. And indeed, I like the scent. Quite a lot, actually. It is really quite close to the skin, which I prefer not only in spring when everything outside is blooming and fragrant. Still, it is well perceivable for me; 2-3 sprays are more than enough. The scent starts with honeysuckle, and jasmine quickly follows. The two create a lovely duo, and you don't get much more than that. So, if honeysuckle and jasmine are too little for you, you will be disappointed. Overall, the scent is remarkably linear. After the first 5 minutes, nothing more happens. The scent simply becomes weaker over time. This is not a drawback for me; I don't like scents that completely change over time. I spray fragrances according to my mood, sometimes also according to the occasion. Therefore, a strongly changing scent progression is more annoying than pleasant for me. I prefer to use another scent after a few hours when the fragrance has faded, or I just reapply. Secret Charm lasts about 4 hours, which is perfectly sufficient for me. I don't like scents that stubbornly cling to me like glue - 4-5 hours are the ideal longevity for me. Anyone looking for a fresh-floral, light scent for spring and summer who doesn't want to spend too much should definitely give this one a try! Edit: I've just realized which scent it reminds me of. It's "Daisy" by Marc Jacobs. Only that it lasts significantly better than the expensive daisies!

I never thought I would find a fragrance at Victoria's Secret that felt tailor-made for me. I had been very skeptical about the brand's perfumes until now, although I’m not exactly sure where these prejudices came from. But I do know. VS is a successful lingerie label and could sell anything just because that name is on it, which everyone associates with flawless, winged top models. They don’t even have to put effort into the scent composition; it’s just commercialism to extract money from mainstream girls. That’s what I thought, anyway. After Secret Charm, I’m not so sure anymore. When I stood in the VS store in front of the many bottles, I decided to give one of them a chance since I was already there. I chose Secret Charm because it was blue (my absolute favorite color) and the name sounded quite promising. So I sprayed it on and expected all my prejudices to be confirmed. I anticipated a sticky, artificial, kitschy sweetness and already envisioned myself walking out of the store empty-handed. And then I cautiously sniffed my wrist... ...and was blown away. Secret Charm is unpretentious, gentle, and natural. I really didn’t expect that. Restraint and sophistication, unpretentious elegance...from VS?! The scent is very warm, light, and floral on me; honeysuckle and jasmine complement each other perfectly, and neither is synthetic but rather close to nature. It truly suits me and fits into my everyday life. That’s why I ended up buying it. Not so praiseworthy is the longevity; the scent fades rather quickly, but I’m happy to overlook that for this fragrance. I can always reapply it, and I enjoy doing so. By now, I’ve worn it several times and even received a compliment from my best friend. “You smell amazing, what is that?” Me: “Victoria's Secret.” “What?!” she sniffed again, incredulously. “Yeah, I never thought so either...” I smiled.

I acquired some fragrances from Victoria's Secret because I really liked the corresponding body butter. Well, most of them are really just for a light scent after bathing in the evening (when you don't have anything special planned for the night), as they do smell a bit artificial. However, Secret Charm is a wonderfully pleasant surprise! The combination of honeysuckle and jasmine has a floral and slightly sweet scent, but it feels completely natural to me. I only deduct points for the low sillage and longevity (I'm referring to the EDT here, not the body spray, which is used more generously anyway).

Fourreau Noir´s limited edition bottle (that sadly i don´t own) was decorated with a crouching cat watching the moon, and how appropriate is the image of the cat to describe this scent! I cannot be more against the use of furs, as clothes and as names, so i was happy to know the fourreau in question was still on its legitimate owner and that this one is no other than a feline. To be honest, Fourreau Noir didn´t trigger my curiosity from the beginning since it features a very traditional tonka bean-lavender. Of course, being a Lutens it couldn´t be in the expected, conventional, fougere way. Nevertheless, let me tell you, Fourreau Noir is one of this Lutens that are not difficult to wear at all, and many of the Lutens-skepticals will find it pleasant and lovable. So this fawn fluid smell first and foremost to tonka. Picture an elastic body covered of the smoothest hair, moving with a wild elegance. Sweet, warm and balsamic, full of nuances as tonka is. Then the most important modifyer is a truly invisible lavender, just as a subtle herb/camphor fresh overlay that brings vivacity to the tonka. This incognito lavender is a drop of full awaken grey that balances the warmth of the fragance: the crystalline cat eyes, the spark of a fang or a claw breaking the sweet/smoky evenness of the fur. This is not a decorative dead skin, it has well-tempered muscles and nerves of steel underneath. This seamless blend, the way lavender is there but it is not, and the smokiness, is what makes this perfume IMHO remarkable in its category. The evolution is pretty linear. In any case, it starts slightly sweeter and it gets more balsamic, after a while... but its a perfect ratio of sweet, aromatic and smoky, with master touches of spice, resin and seductive animalic musk. Noir? probably not, dark, yes. Dun fur. Fourreau Noir is not an attention seeker, but captivates unintentionally instead; like we admire the cat graciously running with swift feet along the balcony´s railing: defying gravity, totally in control of his furry body, careless of being noticed or not, leaving us in awe.

Fourreau Noir makes me consider the possibilities of copying and repetition. Part of a series, variation on a theme? Uninventive, deliberate, derivative? Sequel, flanker, gender counterpart, homage? However it’s come about, Fourreau Noir smells remarkably similar to Chergui. A little less raspy and a bit cooler and herbal from the lavender. It’s syrupy, sweet and woody. It’s a spin on the coumarin accord of Chergui, a range that Sheldrake and Lutens do very well. Sadly, it holds no surprise here, but then again, I’m not a great fan of Chergui. Worse luck, Fourreau Noir has a large helping of the same masculine contemporary notes linking ‘freshness’ (I can’t quite use that word without qualifier) and wood that Chergui has. This capitulation is what turned Chergui for me, and it does the same to Fourreau Noir. It fact, this is where the similarity of the two is to be found. Sheldrake and Lutens manage to make many distinctive perfumes in what might seem a small range of spicy syrup (see Arabie, Cedre, Cuir Mauresque). But in both Chergui and here in Fourreau Noir, the perfume makers cede the middle ground to convention and, despite Fourreau Noir’s lavender, which could be a logical entree to the world of the contempo-homo (my stage name for the state of current perfumery for men), Fourreau Noir winds up fairly faceless and undistinguished like Chergui. Clearly, I’m not hiding my preferences, but to take a step back, how are we to view Fourreau Noir? Lutens don’t group it with Chergui in their “Sudden Sweetness” series where Chergui is found, but the composition is similar. The generous thing to do would be to paint the two as a Bernard Chant/Estee Lauder gender pairing such as Azuree/Aramis or Aromatics Elixir /Aramis 900. Less generous would be to call Fourreau Noir a retread. from scent hurdle.com

With one stroke, this satisfied my hunger for a lavender based scent as well as a tonka dominant scent, hence knocking Guerlain's Tonka Imperial off my want list and saving me wads of cash. After an almost futile search of finding a lavender perfect for me in a Goldilocks fashion of none too herbal, none too sweet, this is my perfect lavender over L'erbolario (too herbal, too sleep aid but a true lavender) and also from the same house, Gris Clair, which a very very kind member here sent me samples of. This is a smoky, sweet and dark lavender on me and fits its colour very well. I smell everything all at once and yet I would not describe it as a linear scent. All the ingredients just seem to dance around each other in perfect step. Sillage and longevity are very good, but I have not had an issue regarding both when it comes to Lutens, to my great benefit!

This fragrance opens with almond and tonka bean notes. A subtle smokey accent counterbalances the two top notes and heralds the arrival of the principal note: lavender. The highly aromatic herb gradually reveals itself, not to overwhelm the sweeter notes and to change the scent's direction, but to enhance the best features of the composition. I now see a rich, sensual oriental fragrance that is easy to wear and pleasant to smell on others. Compared to Louve and Rahat Loukum, Fourreau Noir is - in my opinion - the superior scent, for its depth and compelling presence put it in a league of its own. The intoxicating tonka-vanilla-lavender blend lasts for several hours until the opening notes slowly start to retreat - the fragrance enters its final stage. What remains is an earthy-smokey lavender note with a pale vanillic halo.

This is one hard to pin down perfume. At first spray, I am bowled over by a darkly glamorous, very film noire-type scent. I picture a femme fatale wearing this, with deep red stained lips and a full-length black mink coat - seductive and mysterious. The lavender is not too pronounced to me. I get more of a smokey, slightly sweet, gourmand aroma with a hint of radiant citrus that somehow reminds me of the bergamot at top of Shalimar. The scent is really stunning. At this point, this confirmed Lutensophile is convinced she has found a new favorite. Ok.... that was the incredible beginning. For me, the middle phase of this perfume is not quite so appealing as I find it quite dirty in an animalistic and musky way. The change in the character of this fragrance is striking. The drydown does lose that animalistic aspect and mellows into something sweeter, but still musky and also with a certain murkiness. I do like this phase of the perfume better than the second, but not as much as the first. As with many Serge Lutens perfumes, Fourreau Noir takes you on a multifaceted journey to many places. I just would have prefered to spend more time at first stop. Still, an incredible creation.

The overall effect, for me, is of a lavender-studded cake dripping with a lurid purple sugar glaze, left to smolder a touch too long in the oven and tasting like smoke from the grill. The deep, almost honeyed tobacco in the dry-down has an intimate, musky skin-like effect that is quite sensual (although not sexy).

I blind bought this because I could not find a sample of it anywhere, and the notes/description were calling to me. It's an interesting one, and hard to describe. Some reviews describe it as similar to Chergui, and I guess I agree a little, but not wholeheartedly.

Every morning, when I commute to work, the MonGuerlain enthusiasts, the Florabonics fans, and the Cloudists get on the bus. I'm always amazed when I get off the bus and a different scent comes from every side. It's still pleasant, as the temperatures are bearable in the morning and my nose is challenged. I love that. But let me tell you, when it gets colder, I will come.

Every year again, winter descends upon us, and we addiction junkies, conditioned by clichés, long for warm, cozy scents, preferably something heavier, like a wool blanket under which we can hide from Father Frost, hoping that the cold won’t spare our sacred sense of smell.

After being thrilled by Rahät Lokoum yesterday, today I gave another hidden, extremely rare Serge Lutens a chance with Fourreau Noir (black casing). And again, it's really a shame that it can't be purchased normally. Perhaps I would have chosen this rare gem from France over the creamier, cozier, fluffier Gris Clair in a direct comparison back then.

Michael Kors is one of those brands that I would never have thought of by myself, but I am a fanatic for white florals. So when I came across this one by accident, I had to put my nose on it. As it turned out, I had a lovely day wearing Gorgeous! The scent starts with a fierce ash-white tuberose and settles down when jasmine joins in. There is a faint fruity-tobacco note that connects this white floral opening with the woody notes in the base. Into the drydown, the scent loses some of its clarity, especially when its standard base formula is revealed. Nevertheless, it remains a fairly fresh floral-woody scent without unnecessary sweetness. Gorgeous! is nothing spectacular or groundbreaking, but as an everyday casual perfume it does a perfectly fine job. Not at all bad.

This perfume is typical in the sense that it’s every woman’s perfume. One could easily gift it and I’m pretty sure it would be worn by most women. The jasmine sambac is married to the tuberose with orange blossom as a child. It’s pleasant. I smell nothing else in it. This is not a perfume that screams romance or lust. It’s perfect for church or work, basically every day use. I enjoy wearing it, though I’ve only a sample, but I’ve also sprayed it on myself when I go to Ulta, and it’s nice. Longevity several hours, sillage an arm’s length. Price, well to me it’s not expensive, but it’s a splurge to many, I believe. Will I buy a full bottle? That’s the big question, one which I can’t yet answer.

soft, sweet and intense at the same time. one spritz is already enough. smells like spring in a bottle. it’s giving a *very very* soft version of j’adore. once it settles down it’s soft and lovely. unfortunately it isn’t very long lasting and will fade away within 2-3 hours. so, it would be nice for a dinner date but if you’re wearing it in the office, you might have to reapply it.

This gives me Replica Beach Walk and Jimmy Choo Rose’ Passion vibes. Beachy, transparent white florals and creamy woods. Milky almost. Lasts forever of clothes, 24hr+. Moderate scent bubble. Glad I only bought a small 5ml bottle to test for a few days, I don’t really like it but could see how some might love it. It’s definitely a type, just not mine.

Signorina Gorgeous is a beauty, timeless, classic, and elegant. She has a youthful aura, that charm, and a delightfully cheeky smile. As a summer child and flower girl, her time begins when the first blossoms open, when the ice cream parlors are open, and when one can leave the house without a hat, scarf, and gloves, without ending up as a frostbite. She is no longer a teenager, as she looks too wise, and the laugh lines under her eyes speak for themselves. On the question of how old she is, opinions differ - and so every guess from 22 to 99 is included.* When Signorina smiles, the world smiles back, and sometimes, fully aware of her effect on others, she rides her retro bicycle with a flower garland around the handlebars through her small town, waving at complete strangers, only to find that they are happy and wave back just as cheerfully. Women who do not know her roll their eyes at the first sight of Signorina Gorgeous as she dances barefoot through the pedestrian zone, as if the world belongs to her and as if life were a pony farm. However, when she comes closer and puts on her radiant, captivating smile, shakes her red curly hair, and lets a pleasant Fa-/DuschDas-orange note fill the air, any aversion dissipates. You simply have to like Signorina Gorgeous. She does not impose herself, she is sweet, pure, and graceful. And she does not smoke! I have to take a little point off her collar here, although it doesn’t bother me that she is a non-smoker, as I search for her in vain - (after a maximum of three hours) in my hair, where she does not hold as well as on the skin. Hold on, Signorina! That wasn’t the agreement! And besides... her guest appearances are of relatively short duration. Such a pity, as I truly enjoy her company!
