La Myrrhe is a sensational myrrh fragrance, and unfortunately hard to find these days unless you live in Europe and can order direct from les Salons du Palais Royal in Paris. It is worth the effort and expense, though, especially, if you prefer the gauzier, more light-filled creations of Serge Lutens over the stickier, fruitcake-and-incense ones, like Arabie, Fumerie Turque et al. With the anisic, rubbery bitterness of the resin perfectly juxtaposed against the sweet, frothy soapiness of aldehydes, La Myrrhe will appeal enormously to lovers of Douce Amère, Chanel No. 5 Eau Première, Chanel No. 22, Guerlain Vega, Rêve d’Ossian by Oriza L. Legrand, and Miriam by Tableau de Parfums (Tauer).

One of the things I love most about perfumery is the art of creating beautiful illusions. If someone were to ask me, “What is perfumery to you?”, as an enthusiast I would probably answer like this. I’ve, let’s say, borrowed a little from what I’ve heard many perfumers say, fascinated by how one can, for instance, create the scent of a rose without ever using a rose.

Uncommented Fragrances No. 19 It's about time for one or two confessions: First of all, I have been a big fan of Serge Lutens for many years. There is nothing wrong with that. However, there is a small catch. If you look at my collection, you will notice that I don't actually own that many fragrances from the brand, currently only two.

When the three wise men from the East make their appearance in Monty Python's classic "Life of Brian," gold and frankincense quickly win over the hospitality of Brian's shall we say "rather stern" mother. However, myrrh meets with similar skepticism as the esteemed visitors did before. Even the explanation that it is a valuable balm does not really convince her.

“Should there not only be gold and incense in your life, but also suffering and bitterness, as myrrh foretells, the world adds pain to you, I feel it like you.” The scent reminds me of these lines from the musical “Bethlehem” by Dieter Falk. Myrrh is a challenge. It is bitter, herbal-green, sharp, resinous. In this fragrance, it takes center stage with high presence.

Finally, I have it. I’ve been so eager for this the whole time. Has this noble brew ever been available in a “proper” spray bottle? Well, I ordered it, and 5 days later it arrived. With trembling hands, I opened the completely black-wrapped package, very stylish overall. I found what felt like 100 Serge samples packed in a small black fragrance pouch.

~ Inspiration ~ "MK" bags and wallets are currently very present. I prefer to focus on fragrances and wanted to test "Sexy Amber" and "Glam Jasmine," now also "Sexy Rio de Janeiro" by designer Michael Kors. ~ Bottle ~ The elongated, rectangular shape with a gold logo plaque has been retained, this time in orange-pink with gold lettering - like a beautiful sunset. The name "Sexy Rio de Janeiro" is meant to bring the sunny Brazilian lifestyle to us as well. ~ Scent ~ It starts with zesty citrus mandarins and fruity-sweet mangos. Sunny jasmine absolute, lily of the valley, and gardenia create a floral heart. With sandalwood, exotic Tahitian vanilla, and musk, it finishes warm and sensual. ~ Longevity ~ On my skin, it lasts about 2-3 hours (on clothing and hair, unfortunately not much longer). 3 sprays are sufficient, the sillage remains close to the body and unobtrusive. ~ Occasion ~ A lovely scent for the warm days and evenings in spring, summer, and late summer. To use it daily as an office scent would be too special (and expensive) for me. ~ Conclusion ~ While I do like the combination of mango-jasmine-vanilla, unfortunately, a synthetic hairspray note develops on me -.-

Michael Kors is currently THE designer in the field of bags and fashion for 20 - 35 year olds. The fragrances have been highly praised by him, which naturally sets high expectations for this scent - in vain. This perfume is fruity, sweet, and slightly floral. The scent is nothing special, but also not totally boring. The mandarin and mango give the perfume a special sweet and pleasant note that immediately rises to your nose after application. However, this fades after a few minutes, and then the floral aspect comes into play, which perfectly reminds one of spring and light summer days. - I can't really pick out the rose, though. The biggest downside: The perfume completely disappears from my skin after 2 hours - and I mean completely! And for this price... What a shame, Michael, I really expected more from you!

This is like fresh rye bread out of the oven and a dried wheat field baking under a hot sun. It starts sweet and spicy then loses some of the sweetness for a clean spicy smell. Its mass appealing because its lacks the "wow" or "unusual" factor that I tend to associate with this brand. Its a safe and unisex fragrance. The projection is fairly weak, it was mostly a skin scent with a tiny scent bubble that I could only catch during the hottest parts of the day. On my skin the fragrance lasted about 4 hours. There is only the 100ml and it goes for $150

An opening of artificially mandarin-like sweetness - cotton candy with wannabe fruit? I read on, irritated, and see that I am by no means the first to have such an association. A slight, rough undertone is not enough to elevate the scent from the ranks of the so-called fruit candy perfumes. It can also do little to counter the impression of stale, yet still enjoyable soda after half an hour. By the end of the opening hour, a kind of vetiver sneaks in through the freshness door. The sweetness recedes, the prickly nature of the so-called fruit is taken over by the vetiver - yet it remains a strange representative of its kind. Any earthy-nutty-primitive component seems to have been stripped away, while it simultaneously fails to fully tap into its green-fresh potential. Instead, diffuse candy, soda, and laboratory-like hesperidic reminiscences dance around the molecules. Frankincense? Grain? Aha. Frankincense is fine, of course rather sparingly dosed, but grain? If I subtract all - really all - the aromas that do not fit this statement, grain might possibly come into play. Unfortunately, this likely applies analogously to pea soup, cow dung, or left-turning compost acids in such a condition. Well, there is something dusty hinted at, which I cannot reconcile with the indecisive, half-Fanta half-green vetiver, a feeling that persists throughout the long dénouement of the scent in the afternoon. To clarify: Nothing here truly smells bad. L’Eau de Paille presents itself simply in line with the other Lutens eaux. Some appreciate their unobtrusive-clean-fresh appearances very much. A matter of taste - I find them all rather unexciting. Alternatively put: I find L’Eau de Paille somehow pille-pa(i)lle. I thank Gerdi, from whom I received not just a sample, but even a miniature.

I always follow L'Eau with great interest, as Serge's series is always highly innovative with a slightly eccentric touch and interesting associations around the theme of water! I love the cool metallic streaks, often embedded in or surrounded by incense. Eau Froide is still for me THE fragrance that best captures and translates the metallic coldness and hardness of a mountain stream. At first, I am always very taken with the scents because they offer something new to my nose, but after 30-40ml, I often experience a kind of fatigue. If I don’t smell them for 5-6 months, they exert a special fascination again; I just love clean scents... L'Eau Serge is the prime example for me. With L'Eau de Paille, it seems to be a bit different this time. The significantly larger marketing effort alone is surprising. Until now, the L'Eau candidates simply stood next to the other Lutens fragrances. Last Saturday, there was a small promo stand at Breuninger (Reutlingen), where small SL bags with 5ml miniatures were handed out. The nice Shiseido lady, after a pleasant conversation, kindly gave me one... that doesn't happen every day! Also yesterday at Albrechts in Frankfurt, there was a large stand... Serge apparently wants to make a statement now;-)! So how does it smell now? Definitely different than expected, at least when considering the pyramid. It starts fruity-sweet, very slightly citrusy with minimal bright incense streaks. In its basic orientation, it is not unlike Laine de Verre. Which fragrance notes are responsible for the sweetness (Vetiver???) I cannot say for the life of me... is it the grain that has been soaked in water for a long time, releasing starch and sugar, like a roll that you chew for a long time and then becomes sweet! The lady from Shiseido said "the sweet smell of warm, dry (????) water"... huh?!?! So... okay... ah... cough... clear throat... laugh... what???? Although... yes, it smells like water... but like aftershave, slightly piercing-sharp, but not unpleasant at all, masculine-spicy, normally the death knell for me with a fragrance, but here nothing feels old school, the notes have been combined with great skill. The fruity sweetness alone would do justice to any designer fragrance top note (not meant positively), but in combination with the masculine note and the very nice bright, soft incense, it becomes a complete, serious fragrance. Tending, of course, to a lighter essence, like all L'Eaus, but it has a bit more "kick" than the 3 predecessors. The longevity is quite decent at 5 hours, the dry musk remnants (like in Laine de Verre and L'Eau Serge) in the base are still perceptible for longer, the sillage is quite strong in the first hour, then just above skin close, which is also known from the series... hence I also immediately got the 100ml version... reapplying is therefore no problem. I like it very much; it fits well into spring and the mild summer... even though I haven't figured out the secret of the straw water.

Those who have had the opportunity to study the works of the French artist Claude Monet in museums, on calendar pages, or postcards likely remember primarily his late work, namely the Water Lilies series painted between 1916 and 1926. Perhaps they also recall the famous piece "Impression, Sunrise," which is not only characteristic of the Impressionist painting era but also gave its name to this style period. Much less known is the series of the presumably eighteen versions of the grain shed discovered during a walk in 1890 (a pile of grain, straw, or hay traditionally stacked in agriculture after the harvest). But more on that later. I first smelled L'Eau de Paille (translated as Straw Water) during a so-called scent reading, a very lovingly conducted sales event by the Japanese cosmetics company Shiseido. With relaxing music, hot tea, and ginger cookies, there are initially insights into the life of Serge Lutens, followed by selected fragrances presented for the evening, accompanied by stories recited from a thick book about perfume, specifically regarding his personal memories, feelings, and ideas that all contributed to the development of each fragrance. Afterwards, the scents are sprayed, and the noses of all participants hover over scent strips and wrists. With the L'EdP released in 2016, SL takes us on both a scent and a time journey into his youth. It is the olfactory representation of his memories from early childhood when he watched the hay harvest in the fields of France on a hot summer day in 1954, with straw poking through the socks into his ankles or being carried in his blonde hair. On the skin, the fragrance initially starts sweet-floral, underlaid with a light citrus note. Gradually, tonka bean dominates for me, minimally underlined by delicate incense. Alternatively, a sweeter vetiver seems possible, which is at least listed in the pyramid. The term hay is also mentioned there, but it has not even remotely revealed itself to my nose. During the first hour, lavender mixes in, but does not push itself to the forefront; instead, it remains very subtle, even more reserved than the incense, adding a spiciness. Gradually, L'EdP also becomes herbaceous, greener, now tending towards a shaving water scent and shifting the balance between masculine/feminine more towards the masculine. I found the "shaving water note" particularly piercing when sprayed on a cloth, while I perceived it as milder on the skin. Perhaps aldehydes have also sneaked into the scent progression... but there is still nothing to smell from the hay. At least not from the hay I know as animal feed from the past. With a lot of goodwill, perhaps the everyday breakfast cereal. Even if hay is defined as biomass from herbs or grasses, the scent simply does not take the final curve, does not seem authentic, until it gently fades away. While the sillage is relatively strong in the first hour, it quickly weakens to a skin-close level. The existing base sweetness and the incense are surprisingly perceptible on the skin for a good 9 - 10 hours, albeit extremely weak. L'EdP belongs to the EAUX COLLECTION, which must be viewed in isolation from the other in-house fragrances. This series, currently consisting of four different creations, impresses more with its overt compositional simplicity without large Eastern ingredients compared to the spice-laden Orientals like Arabie. Rather airy, light, and delicate. All are wearable on particularly hot summer days and also gladly in the office. Even in an open-plan office, they behave quite inconspicuously, just in the style of a little water. The difference between the collections is also visually expressed in the appropriate simplicity of the slender bottle, crafted from double-walled glass. While Lutens' fragrances are usually adorned with elegant beige or brown-anthracite labels on brightly colored alcohol, the L'Eau bottles are labeled with rather uninspired black-and-white labels; the perfume has no coloring. In its original state, a pouring bottle is delivered, but each original packaging comes with a spray nozzle for exchanging to suit personal preferences. Those who like it personalized can choose an additional engraving when purchasing from the SL website. Up to 3 initials are possible, but also the first name. Whether that is worth the additional 77 euros must be decided by each person for themselves at the time of purchase. Monet varied the simple motif of the grain shed solely through the number of sheds or slight changes in their distance. The season was represented through corresponding color schemes, with warm colors like red characterizing summer and cool colors like blue representing winter. The starting point for this entire series is the extraordinarily artistically crafted impression of nature. He was concerned with the mood, the impression, and the representation of the feeling that nature evoked in him, not the motif. Even Kandinsky recognized the shed only by the catalog designation during an exhibition visit, while he liked and was inspired by the painting on its own. Lutens processes his impressions of nature like Monet. If I understand SL correctly, with L'Eau de Paille, he aims for the "realistic" olfactory depiction of a hot summer day during the hay harvest, where the wearer should feel like little Serge in front of the harvest fields, inhaling the scent of hay. However, in my opinion, his implementation does not truly meet the artistic claim and disappoints as a niche product across the board, driven by two core problems. While the fragrance always conveys a kind of "warmth" and may simulate a hot, actually rather warm summer day, it lacks the final perception of hay or straw. Equally surprisingly negative was the prevailing synthetic quality in the style of One Million. Thus, the fragrance not only lacks the shed, but it also does not fascinate in the slightest. If the fragrance had been released under a different name in the mainstream sector, it might have received a slightly better rating, but this triviality from the house of Lutens can, and with all due affection & respect for his earlier fragrances, be safely disregarded.

At the moment, I am exploring the Lutens fragrances. After the beautiful Fille and the also catchy Chergui, "Strohwasser" is already harder to read and describe. I am puzzling over the name Strohwasser - because I cannot recognize straw. In anticipation of a pleasant "stable scent," I am now somewhat confused. I have spent a lot of time in stables, and the scent of straw and grain is well known to me. But I do not find that soft warmth in Paille. The fragrance has a sharp-edged freshness that is not even unpleasant - just different than expected. The vetiver is green and sweetish - mixed with subtle incense. On my skin, it develops intensely and invigoratingly - but also a bit intrusive to loud. I would wear it on particularly self-assured days.

I can't quite grasp this "straw water." The fragrance notes could have been spared, as I don't recognize any of them. LEdP is fruity, peppery, and vegetable-like (I think I detect celery), and after many hours, a warm, unsweet vanilla seems to come into play. The whole thing happens rather chaotically.

The straw water - the name could hardly be more fitting. Just as little is it more mysterious... "L'eau de Paille" is the latest fragrance from Serge Lutens' L'eau line, of which I like the previous perfumes without needing to buy them. This water here made of straw is the warmest, sweetest, most flattering scent in the series & embodies its name perfectly.

It was my 1st Lutens fragrance, Paille, and although I am a long-time true perfume lover, I can't describe the scent or categorize it within fragrance families. I can faintly detect grains and a fresh note. The longevity is excellent for me. It smells fresh, natural, and slightly spicy all day long with just 3 sprays. For me, it’s a perfume that can be worn year-round.

It doesn’t smell bad, somehow soft and sweet. However, the listed notes don’t really match him. They are there, but the sweet scent dominates. A bit more feminine than unisex, I somehow have the image of a "middle-aged artist" in my head when I smell it, as it would fit perfectly. For a sweet fragrance, it also smells very natural.

So I finally tested it myself, "Sheer Love" by Victoria's Secret. The brand name does justice to this fragrance, as the exact composition of the individual scents is always kept a secret. Because what can we read; white cotton and pink lily. One imagines a perfume that smells like freshly washed sheets with a hint of a good lily scent. Therefore, I was also surprised when I read something about "banana" in the comments and wanted to test it myself. And now: it is indeed true, as soon as you spray it for the first time, you smell a huge portion of squashed bananas and nothing else at first. Shortly after, an indefinable fabric softener scent joins in, which I would attribute to the lower price segment; the lily note is probably also included, which I couldn't directly identify. And that’s it. No more comes, base note nonexistent. The bottle looks just as pretty as the packaging of the care line, and all products in the line are relatively inexpensive, but it doesn’t help, just like with made-up people in branded clothes, if the content doesn’t match. I’m sorry, I would have liked to write something more positive, but my expectation of a good cotton scent was unfortunately completely disappointed. You can still use the fragrance, for example, to freshen up bed linens or worn clothes, or simply as a room or toilet spray. Still, here’s the warning again: If you are looking for a good cotton scent, you are in the wrong place; you’d be better off with "Softly" by Jil Sander, "Perfect Cotton" or "Pure" by Avon, or (carefully dosed) "White Linen" by Estee Lauder.

This is how I would describe this VS in a few words. Our Müller has had a lot from VS for some time, but only these body spray series, along with DG, BL, and the EdT. Most of them are too sweet for me, but two of them were allowed to join my collection last summer. In July, we were invited to a milestone birthday. Stuttgart in July can be very uncomfortably stuffy and warm, so I was looking for a suitable fragrance. At home in my collection, I somehow couldn't find anything. I wanted a simple scent that doesn't create a cloud in stuffy rooms and doesn't distract me, as we were responsible for entertaining the guests with our band at this birthday. I can't use an intense fragrance for that.... I had something along the lines of Marc Jacobs in mind - and I found it at VS. Anyone who knows Daisy and the other fragrances from Marc Jacobs can easily imagine Sheer Love. The listed fragrance notes are just part of it; there's definitely more in there. It reminds me a bit of Honey by MJ. It's floral-fresh, pleasantly fresh-fruity, but also very clean. It fits wonderfully in summer, even for very warm days, but even now, on a gloomy October day, it spreads sunshine and good mood. It doesn't cost much, yet it doesn't smell cheap or synthetic. I also tolerate it well; it doesn't give me headaches and doesn't irritate my nose. The longevity is about 4 hours, while the MJ ones barely last 2 hours on me.... 30ml usually costs around €14 - I don't think that's much. Nevertheless, it doesn't need to hide behind expensive current releases and smells more high-quality than what you usually find in this price range at drugstores. If you like the fragrances from Marc Jacobs, you should take a closer look at Sheer Love and Secret Charme.

Bois De Violette from Serge Lutens. Another poetic and complex creation from the house, one that keeps me guessing whenever I wear it. To be more specific, I don't smell much of the violet flower here nor the violet leaf, at least not in a "tangible" way. The perfume is all about the spices, mostly cumin and the woods, with an ever-present purple hue that leaves room for interpretation. I wonder why Monsieur Lutens decided to add no color to this perfume. He loves suggesting what his perfumes are about to unfold by painting them accordingly. I would have had Bois De Violette, a light purple color. Yet he decided Sarrasins should be a deep purple. That, I never understood. For me, Bois De Violette stays true to the Feminite Du Bois structure (the perfume that sprang the entire "Bois" series), taking away the difficult facets and perfecting them. I could never bring myself to like Feminite. As much acclaimed and loved as it is, I never fancied it - always felt too sharp on the spices and the cedar, and too fruity. More suited for women, I feel. Bois De Violette tones down the spices but keeps the cumin, maybe even amplifying it a touch, smooths out the woods in the base by adding a touch of oakmoss and fluffy musks, and tempers the fruity aspects to a mere suggestion. It smells how I wanted Feminite to smell - more melancholic, poetic, rounder and well-behaved, unisex. The opening is spicy but focuses mainly on the cumin note, not overly done but present. Immediately, the purple color starts to permeate the scent profile. At this point, I am left guessing the source of it. Is it plum, or violet, perhaps both? A fresh and crisp breeze blows through it like the chilly air caressing the grass in the forest. And then the cedar in the base feels supported by some additional creamy woods, musks, and bitter-green moss. A spicy and woody take on violet, devoid of trivial sweetness and full of surprises. Whatever creates the omnipresent purple sensation is going to be a perpetual source of intrigue for me. And that is why I feel this perfume is among the most poetic and intelligent from this house. It lets the wearer add his/her hero to the plot while laying down the grounds for the story. IG:@memory.of.scents

The first time I tried Bois de Violette I kicked myself for having bought Feminité du Bois a few months earlier. You know that shitty feeling of having bought the good, and then finding the better? I quickly came to the conclusion, though, that I prefer Feminité for most purposes and would choose it over BdV if I were to have just one. BdV brings into relief a feeling about Feminité that I could never quite get my nose around. Feminité’s boozyish combination of fruit, wood and flower expresses itself with a dried-fruit resinousness that I find nowhere except in the SL Feminité and Bois perfumes. Without using any of the classic perfume resins/oils (benzoin, olibanum, myrrh, spikenard, peru balsam, cistus labdanum) Feminité synthesizes a flower/fruit/wood that has the same stickiness and chewy quality that we associate with botanical resins. Bois de Violette, while gorgeous, removes the stickiness of Feminité in order to focus on the highs of the added violet. The result is that it speaks in a higher, perhaps prettier register, but loses some of the implicit harmony of Feminité’s middle register. The Feminité / BdV dilemma fleshes out an understanding that I’ve been coming to. I’ve always preferred the range of the viola to that of the violin. In the small bit that I’ve experienced of opera, I’m instantly drawn to the mezzo soprano rather than the soprano. The majority are drawn to the most prominent, the one that shines the brightest, the highest in the hierarchy. But just listen to a recording of Marilyn Horne singing Rossini and you’ll understand why I’ve come to prefer Feminité du Bois to Bois de Violette.

Now here's a cedar-violet composition from le Grand Serge for me. When I donned FEMINITE DU BOIS earlier today, I seriously worried that I might be suffering an "anosmic moment". I literally could smell NOTHING for a couple of minutes. BOIS DE VIOLETTE has solved that problem by basically tripling the violets and doubling the cedar to produce a gorgeous creation obviously intended precisely for me, the world's biggest violet 'ho' (big in passion, not in size). There is some real depth to this deceptively simple combination of notes. Ironically, the first Serge Lutens perfume to go into the "must buy" category of my wish list is also the one that costs 50% more than the others. Why? I ask most sincerely. Violets? Cedar? What's the special ingredient which justifies the "special" price? I wonder. Well, let's not get bogged down in ignoble mundanities. This perfume is beautiful--that's the bottom line.

This scent is pretty linear. The Cedar and Violet leaf are dominant throughout with a touch of powder from the violet flower. The sillage is low and the scent is rather short lived. It is very beautiful while it lasts though. This one makes me think of sundresses with little floral patterns. All dainty and girly. This is also a very comforting scent for me, which is why I've considered buying it despite it's short longevity. May 23 2014

The name means wood of violet, I imagine. First sniff is an almost candied violet with a sharp wood note. Our database says blossoms, violet leaf, cedarwood. The initial sweetness and sharpness die down quickly and we’re left with a subdued loveliness of the listed notes. Though beautiful, it’s not for me. Too sedate.

I love woody fragrances, and I love several Lutens fragrances, including Cuir Mauresque, Chergui, and Fille en Aiguilles, so I am sad to say that I am very disappointed in BdV. Unlike many other reviewers, I detect neither candied violets, powder, candied plum, peach, orange blossom, rose, cardamum, cinnamon, clove, musk, vanilla, nor honey in this fragrance.

Violets - delicate little flowers with velvety, bright lilac-blue petals, whose sight can transport me to ecstasy and whose fresh, bright scent brings a delightful mood to my spirit. Anyone who knows one or another fragrance from the house of Lutens will not expect to find an ordinary violet scent here.

Some time ago in Paris, on a damp spring afternoon, in crowded streets, among people, umbrellas, and wet dogs, Cerutti and Armani, there was a hint of violet. I looked up, held my face to the wind, and shortly thereafter caught this scent from a lady in front of me - I followed, trying to keep pace in the crowd, not wanting to lose that violet from my nose... and yet.

Violet always sounds much more playful and cute than the French "Violette," which is also a female first name. Violette, let’s take away the -e and we immediately have the matching color "violet," where I just notice that in everyday language the clumsy "purple" has often crept in incorrectly.

This is a body mist, so I never have high expectations for longevity. But I absolutely love this scent for bed or home days. Soft, sweet, light, and slightly nutty. I will say, when I first bought it, I smelt it only on paper. When trying it on my skin at home, it initially smelt a bit off. However, after a week, the scent profile finally started to make sense. I mainly get the vanilla glaze with a touch of almond. So happy that I didn’t return it!

THIS is what I've wanted out of a pistachio fragrance! So many gourmand pistachios have fallen flat for me lately - like "Yum Pistachio Gelato | 33 | Kayali" (not gourmand + too synthetic), Pistachio Brûlée Eau de Parfum (too powdery for my taste), "Praline & Pistachio | Tru Fragrance / Romane Fragrances" (I got buttered popcorn), etc. To my nose, Pistachio Crème smells like a realistic creamy puff pastry - filled with a sweet, pistachio-flavored custard center. It's rich, ultra gourmand, and delicious - not overly nutty, salty, or "buttery", the way many pistachio notes come across. But sadly, I didn't experience the same magic on my skin as I did on the tester strip. It ended up smelling like expired cereal on me, so I unfortunately had to pass on this one.

I did not try the last pistachio scent from Victorias Secret, mainly because it was a dupe for SDJ 62 and i dont need another lol. So i can’t say how similar the notes are, especially the pistachio note. However, this is SO good! I actually rarely get the pistachio note in this scent, it is mainly the vanilla and almond. The vanilla in here smells exactly like melted vanilla ice cream, the melted is important because the scent of vanilla ice cream does differ when it’s “frozen” and melted lol. It is super warm and creamy, the almond isnt really strong in here, I mainly get it in the background. It does have a slight “sharpness” with it but that fades pretty fast and i only noticed it in the lotion.

The purism that is supposed to reside in this fragrance, the only two ingredients listed above, and the diabolical color were the reasons why I ordered this Lutens for testing. Orange peel and clove (some also mention mandarin and nutmeg) are indeed the dominant notes here, and the color truly matches the content. The orange peel itself is the strong determiner at the beginning. Harvested almost a bit unripe, a robust, slightly bitter, yet refreshingly spicy peel penetrates the nose, while the accompanying clove does not hold back either. Some might think of Christmas, but the complete absence of winter aromas (like vanilla or amber) manages to carry the clove into warmer realms. Recently, when I tasted a red wine aged in a bourbon barrel on my Insta-wine blog, I was reminded once again how much the presence or absence of just one single component can shift the overall structure. The wine slid completely into the winter category, having lost all bright fruitiness due to the sweetness and candy-like quality of the whiskey barrel and donned a winter coat. Here, however, it is the opposite: The dominance of the inherently summer-appropriate orange (peel) allows for entirely different atmospheric associations, although I fear that one or two (as can be read below) are so strongly shaped by clove=Winter in their life experience that the mental imagery inevitably kicks in and conjures up a visit to the Christmas market. Nevertheless - an interestingly crafted fragrance, which becomes a bit too prominent towards the end, particularly in the middle part (when the orange fades), where it swings the clove around a bit too aggressively. But worth testing.

Many Lutens fragrances from the COLLECTION NOIRE are too much for me. I recognize the quality, but I don't like to smell them on myself, as they often feel too loud and overwhelming. So far, I haven't found anything in the lighter scents from the LES EAUX DE POLITESSE line either. The new one didn't appeal to me during the first test. The clove was too annoying. My first association: It smells like a Kretek cigarette. Attracted by the unusual emerald green color of the perfume, I took another sniff last weekend and was surprised. Now the citrusy orange came through nicely and blended with the pleasantly spicy clove into a wonderful, warm, strangely patchouli-like scent. Lutens describes Des clous pour une pelure as a refreshing and cleansing fragrance. I agree. And it looks quite nice next to my Pink After Shave in the bathroom.

Very Sexy Orchid is the big sister of Britney Spears' Midnight Fantasy. Something about the fruit + orchid/iris in both results in a dark, boozy warmth. It's smooth, bold and confident. If Midnight Fantasy is like a teenager sneaking sips of cherry cordial from grandma's liquor cabinet, Very Sexy Orchid is a former stripper/current wine mom. Her lips are always curled into the smile that implies she Knows Things and Has Secrets. She may have had a brief hot mess era, but she's definitely got it together now. She wears expensive lingerie under her clothes to run basic errands. She is...Stacy's Mom. In some ways, Very Sexy Orchid reminds me of an 80's perfume - she is NOT shy, tame or innocent - but the fruit has sweetened and gentled what could have been a rather dated scent bomb. Honestly, I like it! The end result with my chemistry makes me smell a bit like a slutty blueberry cobbler, rather than a sophisticated MILF, but sometimes I want to smell like a slutty blueberry cobbler. I'm sorry to learn VS discontinued it (?), even though I wouldn't reach for it often. It is genuinely beautiful. -- This review previously appeared on another site under the name "PrincessPrickleson." That's me! I'm moving my collection to Parfumo.

For those who are passionate about Victoria's Secret fragrances, this one may not be your cup of tea. Unlike the typical VS scents, which tend to be fruity, youthful, energetic, and sometimes generic, I believe this fragrance breaks away. You won't find the usual burst of fruitiness here. Instead, you'll be welcomed by a warm and cozy embrace of patchouli. If you've ever experienced Kayali Vanilla 28, you'll notice that the opening patchouli notes bear a striking resemblance. also, the blend of black currant and flowers is masterfully executed. While I typically steer clear of floral perfumes, this one strikes a perfect balance between floral and fruity notes atop a robust and velvety patchouli base. I don't know if this scent will be your signature, but it will definitely be a good choice for an occasion like a dinner date. Super sexy and appealing perfume.

This smell has been affecting me since I smelled it for the first time. It was the first time I smelled the scent with my darling.When I first felt the opening of this perfume, good emotions were awakened in my soul.It was raising my libido and there was a feeling of happiness inside of me.Smells great on my darling's skin ???????? I think the main theme of this fragrance is "flowers" and and I like "fruity -floral" fragrances like this. This perfume is the most impressive fragrance in the category of fruity floral fragrances. If you like floral scents, you might like this. This may be the smell of heaven on earth. A fragrance usually suitable for spring and summer. Also suitable for special occasions

Santal de Mysore used to be the most expensive perfume in the SL lineup as the house stocked up with real Mysore sandalwood just before the ban and continued to use it in this fragrance. It is a heavenly blend that opens with food spices. If you like cumin, it doesn’t get much better than this. A touch of tasteful balsamic sweetness, not the overused vanilla or tonka type. SdM is a warm and dark scent. Its drydown will reward all patient niche snobs with subtle but wonderful creamy sandalwood. If you care about sandalwood, this one is highly recommended.

When I first smelled Santal de Mysore, I said to myself, as long as Serge Lutens keeps making this fragrance, I will be happy. If all my other bottles were to be destroyed in a fire, I'd be ok with just this one. Hyperbole? Probably. Just trying to get across how much I love it. What I value most about it is its dichotomy. It is both wet and dry, and intensely so at the same time. At first, the wet elements come to the nose - a big, spicy red butter curry with blisteringly hot black peppercorns crushed to release their oil, and something green, frondy, and aromatic, perhaps dill or fresh fenugreek. There is a tamarind sourness to it but it is also very sweet, as if cubes of salted caramel have been set on top to slowly sweat down into pools of butter. I don't understand when people say a perfume smells like a curry like that's a bad thing? I can think of no better smell than this. My mouth waters at the host of hot spices and aromatics. I slaver like Pavlov's dog every time I go near the stopper. Talking of the stopper, sniffing Santal de Mysore from the bottle gives me a jolt of recognition every time, because it smells like real Mysore sandalwood. But on the skin, this impression disappears, as the big building blocks of flavors and spices jostle each other for position. Drawing your nose back from your arm, you notice these clumps of notes magically coalescing into a true Mysore aroma - deep brown, buttery, arid, resinous. Salted butter dried and made into a red dust. Put your nose back to that spot on your wrist, and the Mysore impression falls apart again. This is a fragrance that plays peek-a-boo with its wearer, and it's mesmerizing. The wet, creamy curry accord hangs around, but it flips on a switch to dry, aromatic sandalwood dust when you're not looking. Look again and it switches back to wet and spicy. When I catch glimpses of the dry, dusty facet, it smells like zukoh, a powdered sweet incense that combines camphor, cloves, and sandalwood. The drydown is pure magic, the curry notes fading away to a caramelized sandalwood incense aroma, with hints of honey and amber rounding out the dry woodiness. Why do I find Santal de Mysore such a gorgeous, satisfying wear? Because it's not a straightforward representation of sandalwood like Tam Dao or Wonderwood. It takes you to a fantasy Mysore sandalwood destination by way of the Silk Road, weaving through curry spices, aromatic oils, and incense sticks as we go. It's also a scent that makes your perceptions of it turn on a dime: wet then arid, savory then sweet, creamy then dusty, spicy then herbal and green. Sandalwood in a House of Mirrors - its basic shape remains the same but what we see each time we look is different.

This is indeed my favorite sandalwood. Is there any real mysore in there? Dunno. Probably not. I’ve tried sooooo many sandalwoods, some expensive aged mysore, some literally vintage mysore, some definitely not even mysore (all synthetic, Australian etc) and even though I love quite a few of them THIS is the one that completes me. Yes, it’s all the fenugreek in the open (I don’t really get any immortelle on me? They can smell a little similar in the maple bits maybe?) which definitely has a slightly sweet toasted curry aspect; but I don’t at all feel too foodie wearing it. It IS definitely gourmand though. It’s a gorgeous spicy, extra creamy sandalwood; like they distilled only the creamy aspects and jettisoned most of the wood. Love it.

Santal de Mysore (SdM) is an excellent sandalwood scent. It opens with a mélange of spices that does, indeed, feel a bit reminiscent of the smell of Indian food. That being said, the opening still manages to be enticing and to me and comes off as a more interesting than off-putting. The scent changes quickly and as the spices mellow and dissipate I can pick them out individually. There is cardamom, clove, cumin, carraway, ginger, cinnamon and the note that briefly tricks the mind into registering curry: immortelle. Suddenly the scent flips to a delicious spiced fig and maple syrup vibe, and then moves from there into a dry down of smooth, buttery sandalwood inflected with bits spice, fig, creamy resins and the occasional whiff of immortelle. It is a bit spare in the dry down though, which makes it feel more like a delicious smell then Perfume with a capital P. While SdM is an intriguing aroma to me, it won't be for everyone. It is not particularly easy to wear. This is not a safe blind buy for anyone.

Serge Lutens is where I started and got my inspiration for perfume. I like the uniqueness of this brand. Today, I received a 5 ml decant of Santal Mysore (blind buy) and sadly, thus far, I have to say that I’m a bit disappointed. Where I live, it was early spring like temperatures today, so it may not have been ideal wearing temps for this fragrance. First whiff: takes me to a beach somewhere, and I’m smelling a peculiar cocktail drink and sunscreen. In the opening, there’s warm sweetness drizzled over the multi-scented spices. Then, strong scent of pencil shavings, caramel, and glazed carrots. The longer it sits on my skin, I’m warming up a bit to the scent—not to say I approve of it! It’s not the Santal Mysore that’s the problem; it’s my nose. For some reason, my nose and Santal aren’t jiving to the same song. So, in my little experience, I know it’s helps to get a second take on the fragrance—probably wait a couple days for the temperatures to reach burrrrr, it’s cold again. So many things can affect your reaction to a scent—so don’t give up the first smelling! Okay, 45 minutes later I’m in first grade again. Spiced cookies, crayons, and pencils. It’s weird, and I think maybe I like it—I don’t for sure. It smells like candied spices. Very woody-spicy on the dry down. For me, the spices and perhaps the sweetness cloud up the sandalwood a bit. However, I’m beginning to like the scent okay now. Not great, but okay. I won’t be purchasing a full bottle of the juice. Many people love this fragrance, and I think that’s great—Serge Lutens is a great brand/product. I definitely like this fragrance better on the dry down. Also in the opening, you get a good dose of curry. That may be my dislike---curry. Curry is not one of my finest spice scents. Once I let my guards down from my dislikes and the dry down begins, Santal Mysore is actually a comforting scent overall. Then there’s ginger, cinnamon, and caraway, and Vanilla, all simmered in butter. Benzoin. Benzoin is just gorgeous. The longer I wear this fragrance, it becomes more sensual and luscious. My first impression of this frag was about 2.5 or 3 stars out of 5. Now, it’s about a 4.5. Now you know why I’m fond of Serge Lutens. It’s brilliant how his fragrances can change over time, and in this case becoming more seductive. That’s how I see it. There’s another one by Serge called Santal Majuscule with sandalwood, rose, cocoa that I would like to try. Serge Lutens, Cedre is phenomenal. I wish it was edible. My favorite SL is Chergui. Diam Blond is great too. Most of SL fragrances are unisex. To sum it up: I like this scent. Obviously, it’s not the best SL fragrance in my opinion, but I like it and will wear it. The 5 ml Santal Mysore purchase will not go to waste, that’s for sure! I’ll discover more interesting things about Santal Mysore the next time I wear it. It’s always an experience wearing SL fragrances. I do recommend getting sample first—that goes for all (or most) fragrances. This is a wonderful fall and winter frag. Good for many occasions.

I have owned a bell jar for some time now, and it has taken me forever (years) to be able to write anything about it because...frankly I can barely detect it! It is so light and ethereal, how does one figure out how it smells when it's there one moment and not the next? I have tons of the highest quality raw materials. You can always smell them.
Which sandalwood?

Santal de Mysore is a dark and angular scent; it does not develop on my skin as balsamically as described below. It is very idiosyncratic, full, warm, and above all, spicy. Unfortunately, I can't describe it well; you have to test it. I can rather say how it does not smell. In my opinion, it has little of the bright and soft fullness of a true Mysore sandalwood essential oil.

I almost wanted to buy this scent in a "blind purchase." I thought I would simply have to like it. Sandalwood always reminds me of my teenage years; I had these tiny perfume oils, and the sandalwood bottle with the Yin and Yang symbol on it was my absolute favorite.

I feel like every time I've tried a rose-based perfume recently, they've been heavily green garden scents rather than the velvety sweetness of summer roses. More woody thorns and rose leaf than blossoms, really. Dried potpourri rose petals at best. (Demeter's Dark Roses I'm looking at you.) Bombshell Passion nails it, though. This is a wet, sweet rose and delicate, airy peony. Soft, bright, cheerfully femme. It's simple, but uplifting: an instant good mood. The cassis rounds out the profile to keep it from being completely immature and bubble gum pink, but it still feels quite young on me -- the kind of young I feel like I've never been, if that makes any sense. Carefree! Optimistic! Utterly unafraid of accruing credit card debt! It's also definitely giving casual daytime shopping trip rather than hitting the club, which would be more what I expect from a VS scent. But I may be biased; I did grow up during the VS Angels' heyday, when VS = the hot party girl. It seems outrageous given the branding, but this would be a perfect fit for both a peppy twenty-something on her own for the first time OR her younger tween sister. Is Bombshell Passion kind of basic? Sure. But though its notes are fewer, I think this particular flanker has more going for it than the original version. I admit it's possible I've just smelled Bombshell too many times out there in the real world, so now it just reads as "bland," and this feels fresher and more pleasant as a result. Final Verdict: It's straightforward, happy and girly. If you're into that? Go for it. -- This review previously appeared on another site under the name "PrincessPrickleson." That's me! I'm moving my collection to Parfumo.

My first impression of this is that of a wine spritzer! It's lifted, but fruity in a marginally adult way - not a *simple* straight-up fruit. It has that exceedingly familiar fresh floral+vanilla+clean musk trio that we find in many, many current market releases. The vanilla is light, but there certainly is some within this despite not being listed (I suspect that is standard for nearly all VS perfumes). This smells like it could be within the Carolina Herrera Good Girl line. If you enjoy some of those, you might like this. The best thing about this is that it never gets very heavy. Despite the deeper bottle color, it's actually fairly fresh. My gut reaction is telling me - 'Summer evening.'

I bought it in a full bottle because the roller-ball was incredibly beautiful. Fruity sweet but not in a too childish way, very feminine! However, the spray didn't convince me as much, as a scratchy note comes through and it then smells too sour for me. I will still continue to try it out.

As with most Bombshell scents, you get exactly what is indicated in the fragrance pyramid. So, if you are someone who enjoys surprises and twists, you will likely be very disappointed here. Personally, I really like the scent, as all the fragrance notes fit together very well and harmonize beautifully. The black currant smells deliciously ripe and not scratchy sour. The delicately fragrant peony soon mingles with the tasty currant scent. The rose is also subtle here and not too strong or soapy. These three components are finely interwoven and perceptible throughout the fragrance. Bombshell Passion is a fruity floral spring and summer scent. Certainly not the surprising "WOW-effect" fragrance, but still lovely. I like to wear it in between when I don't feel like my "blockbusters" or when they would simply be inappropriate. Sillage and longevity are average. I can perceive the scent on myself for about 4 to 5 hours. Since I have also received compliments, it is certainly noticeable to others. The bottle is color-coordinated and looks quite chic. Anyone who does not like black currant or rose should not test this fragrance. For fans of these notes, it is certainly worth a try.

Today I became aware of the Michael Kors fragrances, which I had not known until now - and I immediately got drawn to the elegant golden bottle 24 K Brilliant Gold. The bottle already hints at the exclusive scent, which impressively stands out from the other tested perfumes. The mandarin flashes briefly, but only as an intro, then white floral notes unfold, not sweet, but bright and clear. The spicy woody elements dim the bright sea of flowers - but do not darken it. 24 K has a quirky elegance - not everyday and also not for everyday use. Although it could also gild the everyday. It would certainly match excellently with chic second-hand clothing, along with genuine vintage gold jewelry and an evening at the theater where a controversial play is performed. Because the scent is attractively and interestingly unconventional.. Made for sympathetic free thinkers - without being aggressive or difficult. A well-tempered fragrance that charmingly makes its statement - and stands by it. Nothing for the faint-hearted.

I'm going to be honest but this perfume kind of smells like grapefruit to me when I spray it. Maybe a hint of berries but totally grapefruit! It isn't overpowering but not weak. Anyways, after that it just drifts into more of a rosy citrus. This perfume has a citrusy clean scent to it with a flirty vibe somewhere in there. It great for spring! I however don't really recommend this because it doesn't last as long and after about 2 hours, it's completely gone so I will have to respray after that. Also the scent isn't event hat complex and unique so I don't think it's worth your money and you can get something much better for a little more money.

I didn't expect this to be anywhere near the original perfume that VS offered of the same name; nonetheless, it's a shame they recycled the name. It's a similar situation from the vintage Miss Dior to the current flankers from 2005 and beyond. If I recall correctly, the explanation of the new fragrance was to reflect on what women supposedly like nowadays: the fruity floral gourmand. It is indeed fruity with the berries, and the creme brulee does shine through for a short amount of time...but it's all berries. It's not a complex scent at all, and it really has the quality and longevity of VS's body sprays that you can get 5 for $30 (or something like that). I was appalled that the store was charging $40 for 0.8 oz of the perfume in a plain-looking bottle. For an "upgrade" you pay $68 for the packaging that is a knockoff of a Nina Ricci bottle and some more of the juice. This is another perfume that I hope ends up in the sale bin because it's NOT worth its price at all.

I admit, the bottle is even too girly for me, too light pink, and a perfume called Victoria, I don’t know, I wouldn’t buy it like that. But yes, if you’re wandering around the airport again, and are magically drawn to the black Victoria's Secret letters on rich pink (see Noire Tease), and then there are many, many sale products, why not test it :) Since I like perfume samples and miniatures, testing scents a bit, wearing them a bit longer, and often they can become tiresome, a few milliliters are enough. This one was in a 4-pack, 4 times 10ml, one of them being Victoria. Well, since it’s in a four-pack, good size, available cheaply, why not. I decided on impulse to get it. Fragrance tested on my colleague's skin. Cardboard sweet. Really, although I’m a sweet lover, not nice anymore. The same with Bombshell, which was also included. Likewise with Body by Victoria (that one is also annoyingly sweet for me, not recommended). Even for me, the scent starts off alcoholically sweet, but not in that sticky cardboard sweetness. And then the fragrance even becomes a bit more bitter. Yes, despite berries and roses, it turns bitter for me. Even more extreme with Bombshell (which even drifts into a citrus-aquatic territory), but in both cases in a very pleasant way. I wouldn’t have guessed berries and roses. The scent starts off very alcoholic for me, bright, light, with a lot of imagination leaning towards fruity. It drifts a bit into the bitter, but still bright, and over time a soft, gentle powderiness joins in. Not warm, but beautifully fluffy, like a light padded pillow, cozy, cuddly, but surprisingly not warm (and there’s nothing to smell of caramel, not even with a lot of imagination). The sillage is underground, very close to the body, but apparently these scents have something that appeals to my friend very much, he gets compliments for each one. But only for a short duration, after that it is only perceived very closely by very fine noses. Again, a perfume that I would classify more as a fragrance water, but since I like light fragrance waters, it was a try worth taking (but only at sale prices, I wouldn’t pay CHF 60 for such a light, shallow, but still interesting little fragrance (it was CHF 40 for the perfume, with a miniature (very nicely done), shower gel, and body lotion, can’t complain about that :) ). So folks, give it a try and form an opinion, because somehow the scent is quite unknown. :)

Strangely, I smell zero roses in this perfume. Literally none. However, my husband says he smells them when I wear this perfume. Also very odd is that it comes off as gourmand to me. The bottle is pretty and very tall with a nice glitter. Longevity is a good portion of the work day and sillage with one or two sprays is about three feet. Spray more and it radiates very well. My friend from art class in high school married Michael Kors and is the creative director for the brand. Wish he had been more approachable in high school because I’d love to share perfume insight with him.

I have now been registered/active on Parfumo for two years!:))) Of course, at the beginning, I can't say that it was easy for me here, but fortunately, it has turned out positively!:) I have had the pleasure of discovering many wonderful perfumes here that still accompany me on Parfumo!:) I have also learned a lot of new things about perfume and about myself here!:) In short, I have been able to develop through Parfumo!:))) Many scents/treasures that I currently have/own I probably would never have discovered or even come to LOVE without Parfumo!:))) THANK YOU, THANK YOU PARFUMO!:D Anyway, I wanted to write a comment/text about a fragrance today, but at first, I was unsure which one to write about... The fragrance should also be special in my opinion!;D And I came to the conclusion that I would write about my new treasure in my collection, which, in my opinion, really smells special and different from my other treasures that I have:) And MK Starlight Shimmer edp smells almost too different from my current fragrances!:D It may sound to you like I don't like it, but that's not the case! It smells toooooo good to be true!*.* TOO GOOD!*.* I still remember exactly how excited and surprised I was when I tested it for the first time! I was captivated by this scent from the very beginning!*.* I couldn't stop sniffing my wrist! It was like a drug:D Because the more the scent developed/unfolded, the more beautiful and magical it became!*.* The sad news is that the fragrance has unfortunately been discontinued!:(((( But thankfully, I was still able to get a 50ml bottle for a very fair and great price!:) So I was lucky!:) Now that it is very cold outside, this fragrance is PERFECT! It is a very mysterious, delicious, but also extremely feminine scent!*.* I love to wear Starlight Shimmer on my scarf, especially when I go for a walk or when I go out occasionally:) Sooo, since I don't want to keep anyone in suspense, I will start with the scent development:D... The scent... Starts very, very sensual!*.* The vanilla is wonderfully creamy and balsamic at the same time... The rose is the star of the scent development!*.* Pure eroticism and femininity... But also wonderfully dark at the same time!*.* The rose is laid on a fine bed of vanilla, saffron was sprinkled in small amounts over the rose, and amber gave the whole development a sensual sweet note but also a lot of warmth!*.* Although no vanilla note is listed in the top notes, I can very intensely smell the vanilla in the top note:) I also occasionally detect a lipstick note in the scent development, which I personally find extremely interesting!:) I personally think you can only like this fragrance if you LOVE smoky scents! I also have to say that I have never smelled such a dark fragrance like this one in such a beautiful way!*.* Somehow, I always think of a vampire when I wear this scent!:D A very pretty vampire lady!:D With long pitch-black hair, poison green eyes, blood-red lips, and of course, smoky eyes!;D I don't really know why I think of a vampire lady... Probably because the scent is so beautifully dark:)))) H+S is very good, lasting about 10 hours on both my clothing and my skin!:) I want to thank each and every one of you again for the motivation you have always given me here! But also for sharing our passion together... namely scents/perfume!:)❤

This is neither "pear" nor "glacé" - smells mostly like chamomile, cassis and aloe. The combination honestly smells like a grass shot from Jamba Juice, or like how the South American Maté drink tastes. If you love earthy, green, fresh scents then you might be okay with this - but it's quite bitter and sour. Nothing like the original formula - VS changed this so much, that it might as well be named something entirely different. (This review is for the 2022 release of the "mini mist exploration set".)

A bottle as enchanting as this one, which resembles a delicate flower, (I’m still trying to upload a picture) cannot possibly contain such a strong scent---I thought---I was wrong. At the spray nozzle, I caught a gentle pear-fruit scent, but when sprayed on the skin, Pear Glace emits an artificial pear note that is unbearable for me. This pear is not a burner - rather a nose-piercer. The scent doesn’t exactly hurry to disappear. Instead, it gives the impression that it "bites" into the skin. Washing it off doesn’t help either.

This fragrance is possible to divide audience.It is an idiosyncratic,unique,warm blend which balances betweensweet and bitter.The oppening is strong with a sweet,herbal and less spicy essence with a delicate bitterness and it's dificult to ignore the cyprees and sage vibes.There are also cinnamon but not in the same way as CK Obsession.I recognize also a slightly touch of pennyroyal and myrtle(the memories of this smell is always in my mind as I remember my grandma, when I was child in Samos island ,to boil water in the fireplace mixed with sage,myrtle and other herbs which she was collecting from the forest for our bath with green oil soap in the metall washbowl.Yes, she had no a proper bathtube...)Sorry me for being a little nostalgic. At the drydown there are also woody(cedar) and less powder vibes finishing with a very,very small drop of ''poison'' ( is the tolu balm ? ) inside the sweet and bitter wrapper. The longevity is OK for me (7,5) ,in clothes stay more than a day ,in my scin about 6-7 hours and the sillage is a little bit more than moderate (7 plus). I suppose it's a little bit synthetic, but well done. For me it is suitable for the evening or night out and not for the hot weather. Recommended, but first test it.

This pepper is not savory. It won't make you sneeze or crave a sizzling steak to grind it on. Rather it's the sweet, carbonated scent of a freshly poured,cool Dr. Pepper. Later as the nutmeg kicks up its heels in dry down, it begins to resemble a proper Indian chutney or even a Korean peppery dressing. Interesting, but the silage leaves me craving more. It becomes a skin scent a little too quickly.

At first spray, Poivre Noir is an unapologetic assault of pure pepper, sharp, overwhelming, and almost off-putting. It's a challenging opening, one that might leave you wondering if there's more to discover beneath the surface. But then, slowly, something green and intriguing begins to emerge, softening the initial intensity. This undefined green facet adds depth and balance, transforming the composition into something much more approachable. By the time it settles, Poivre Noir becomes a rather pleasant scent. However, to my nose, it leans distinctly masculine. It's worth exploring for pepper lovers, but personally, I find it more intriguing than wearable.

This one knows how to make a good impression. At the beginning, it seems to be well blended and rather seductive. It’s like a more outgoing, flirtatious brother of Orpheline by the same brand. But when you take a closer look, you can see that there isn’t that much hiding behind the pretty façade. The fragrance does not develop well, its individual components seem to be falling apart leaving something which is still pleasant, but lacking harmony and sophistication. What seemed to smell like black pepper at the beginning deteriorates into something unpleasantly warm, like a pack of nutmeg and ground chilies that stayed opened for too long. Pleasant but disappointing.

First impression: A niche Royal Oud (I consider Creed luxury vs niche). Mainly due to the strong cedar, incense and clove; albeit this has nutmeg. Definitely no oud in this. In fact, you can appreciate the oud in Royal Oud better after comparing them side by side. It’s not a 1:1, but unless you’re into this scent profile i would compare and get one or the other. The Creed is more posh vs Poivre Noir’s outgoingness. I find that after you own a good lot of really good, well established, scent profiles, anything thereafter is just going to be a variation. Bottom line: awesome scent.

The journey to Hogwarts, that boarding school in the north of Scotland where the story of the famous wizard student Harry Potter takes place, is essentially made by train, starting at platform 9 3/4 of London’s King’s Cross station. The final leg, however, is traversed by boats across the lake and - seemingly - driverless carriages. It is only later, in his fifth year, that Harry notices that these carriages are not actually driving themselves, but are pulled by black, emaciated creatures whose form is reminiscent of reptilian horses. These beings are called Thestrals, and they can only be seen by those who have witnessed a person’s death. So far, so unsettling. But Thestrals are also creatures of darkness - initially frightening in their appearance, especially when one sees them for the first time and then understands why - for they are indeed gaunt, silent beings of the night. Their skinny bodies and large bat-like wings are dull and shiny like silk and neither warm nor cool. Their demonic heads resemble those of dragons, their eyes pupil-less and seemingly empty. However, when tamed as mounts, it is said that a Thestral can find any location its rider wishes to reach. And so Harry and his friends also arrive on Thestrals at the Hall of Prophecies in the Ministry of Magic when time is of the essence. A very similar narrative follows - an initial moment of flinching and then only silence and darkness far beyond categories like cold or warm - in Lutens' Poivre Noir, which carries both the biting sharpness and the darkness in its name. The accord of crushed pepper at the outset is bright and piercing and almost disturbing - like the realization of the black winged horses and why one sees them for the first time. However, the duration of this opening is limited, and it fades into a hollow, strangely nameless echo - like dry hay that has been in the shade for far too long, or old, yellowed, and cracked paper (that is the immortelle!) - too cool to be warm, and too warm to appear cool. Conclusion: Pepper fragrances can be polarizing - as is this one, whose opening is sharp and biting and almost provocatively unpleasant. But beyond that, Poivre Noir is a dry scent full of pale darkness and silence - no comfort and no sweetness - just like the gaunt, black winged horses with dragon heads, which can only be recognized by those who have already seen death.

I had the idea to buy a proper, pungent black pepper. Something modern, aromatic, dark, and rough that would curl my toenails. So I typed the term into Google and found a fragrance called Poivre Noir / Serge Lutens. Black pepper from the Great Gravedigger? This must be it! * Modern pepper after 2015? Like a broken window. Until around 2010, pepper was just kitchen pepper.

“Poivre Noir” - from my now highly esteemed favorite Maison Serge Lutens, I find truly - noteworthy. And in my opinion, it is absolutely underestimated. When I first sprayed it in the perfumery I trust, - I was instantly in love with it.

There are days that are brighter - and days that weigh heavier. Today I started sorting through my perfume samples and came across Poivre Noir. Meanwhile, my playlist was playing "Wake Me Up When September Ends" by Green Day - and suddenly it hit me: fears, sadness, all the negativity came rushing back.

It's hands down my favorite bare vanilla variation of all times. It's ridiculously good!! Sadly however it is extremely light. But EXTREMELY! The sillage is pretty poor, the longevity even worse. I used an entire bottle in around 20 days. It is that bad in terms of strength. I wish they made a perfume version of this. I would definitely spend $80-$100 on something like this. Btw some bare vanillas are very similar to the OG one, so they're not entirely worth it. But this one is definitely different enough to actually get one

I grew up with dogs - with female dogs, to be precise. There were three in total. The first one ran into a car one day, the second was very sick. The third and last - and my favorite - female dog simply didn’t come one evening when she was called in. She had never done that before. We searched for her into the night, but found her nowhere - and the next day there was no trace either. Only later did we find her little body curled up at the back under the hedge - where she had retreated to fall asleep alone. Until then, I hadn’t known that dogs do such things. And anyone who has lost a pet knows how that feels. Most scents that address the animalistic - at least all those I know - are inherently self-assured. Unabashed. Present. Animalistic can be lustful like an open lap or primal like a predator's cage. Yet such scents are always challenging, provocative, some are downright vulgar - and we love them for it. With Muscs Koublaï Khän, Mr. Sheldrake and Mr. Lutens show us this side of the animalistic - although this elder among the 'musk stinkers' fades away wonderfully gentle and intimate. Here, they are now addressing a new and unfamiliar side of the animalistic, for Veilleur de Nuit is none of that. Veilleur de Nuit is quiet and very intimate - and infinitely sad. It lacks the primal, it lacks - despite the quite noticeable chocolate note - the softness, the sweetness, the gourmand quality. Nothing here is pressing, nothing is demanding, nothing is loud. There is a certain sweetness - tuberose can’t be anything else - but it takes a back seat to the soft, dark gray of cocoa and vetiver - unusually coldly arranged among the animalistic accords. This may all sound hardly inviting, but Veilleur de Nuit offers a scent experience even to saturated noses - a quiet one, not a pompous, impression-making one. Those with sad memories - who doesn’t have any? - may think of them while wearing it. Like our female dog, who now lies under the winter jasmine next to the shed. Conclusion: a scent full of sadness and farewell, told in a calm, quiet language.

Until a few weeks ago, I would have answered the initial question with a no... I haven't been into this for long, just a few months, and yet I've already tried quite a few fragrances during this time. Many received the rating "Okay, but I don't need it," a few got a "Must have," but I never dreamed of any of the scents. Then I won a niche sample collection on eBay, and this fragrance was included. I will never forget the moment I carefully sprayed the first spritz on my wrist. I have never smelled such a sexy, dark, wicked, soft, and yet gentle chocolate top note.... After a while, the chocolatey aspect faded a bit, but it was still present. The base then turned into a gentle, dark cream, slightly wicked and a bit suggestive. Incredible! Of course, I immediately researched the original bottle and almost fell off my chair.... 650 euros. Yeah, right. The motto was to forget it as quickly as possible. Especially since the scent was only very faintly perceptible after 3 hours. The longevity is really not great... But that was easier said than done. With other gourmands (even though this one isn't really a true gourmand), every time I sprayed them, I thought of that breathtaking top note. Every fragrance that leaned a bit towards chocolate was immediately compared in the back of my mind with this one. Nothing, absolutely nothing came close. I even dreamed of that soft chocolate-musk cloak.... I still couldn't afford it (although I have seen it on sale recently for "only" 470 euros). Well, then I stumbled upon a dupe. I'm not a huge fan of dupes, but I have to admit that I looked at some fragrances as dupes first to save money and only bought original samples and/or decants of those I really liked. I had a bit left in the original sample and could compare them. And what can I say? The top note is absolutely identical for my clumsy nose, the further development only deviates minimally, and the dupe lasts at least 6 hours instead of 3. And yes, the dupe has moved in. The scent has lost a bit of its shine. It's somehow shocking that the fragrance can be quite accurately replicated for 35 instead of 650 euros... Despite everything, I always keep an eye out in the souk. Maybe there will be a leftover bottle or a sharing after all; I would definitely be in on that! And when I finally marry rich/inherit/win the lottery, I will bathe in that scent every morning and every evening.

If you were to ask me what this smells like, my answer would be spice. Specifically, the spice of cloves, or clove spice, or at least a spice that stood or lay very close to cloves, and then adopted the scent of cloves and its spice, and thus smelled quite similar, or even almost exactly like it. Because, if you were to experimentally (and plate-wise) completely remove the clove from this fragrance, there would be no spice left at all, meaning the perfume would smell totally unspicy and who wants that. No, quite the opposite, clove spice manufacturers and clove spice wholesalers know that this is the note that is well received by many clove spice lovers, and that’s why they have generously incorporated this spicy essence into this really lovely clove spice fragrance. Good so. Twin: "Epic" for Man, Amouage.

Oh-something very, very dark and mysterious is coming towards us from the deepest depths. At first, I smell the best Belgian chocolate that tickles my nose and wants to be tasted, with an as yet unclear underlying note - tuberose or civet??? I leave it alone for now - it needs a lot of time (30 minutes) to develop so that I can give an accurate statement. But then... I have the impression it sits tightly on my skin, like glued, but beautifully so. It flashes me directly into another dimension. In my opinion, the scent is only perceivable to those in my immediate vicinity; it is not a "room-filler." It lasts at least 8-10 hours and leaves a wonderful scent trail that is fine and characterized by the most exquisite ingredients. One cannot necessarily smell the individual scent elements clearly, but the whole is like a composition by Mozart; all the notes together create this beautiful scent melody. This perfume is something for absolute lovers of perfumes at the highest quality level. This perfume is neither feminine nor masculine, but simply intended for a person, whatever or whoever "it" represents. Those who can identify with this perfume have found their scent skin and may wear it for a lifetime... so it should be. This perfume reminds me of very old, very valuable, thick, and soft black or dark purple velvet that one touches with reverence. I hope I have expressed well with this last sentence how beautifully this scent has touched me.

When I got to know Veilleur de Nuit, I had just rediscovered Terry Pratchett's Night Watch novels. I love the crazy, ironic Discworld and especially the characters of Commander Vimes and his wife Lady Sybil. Veilleur de Nuit could be Vimes' signature scent, although the good man would probably reject perfume as an unnecessary luxury in his down-to-earth manner. This fragrance combines the earthy essence of Ankh-Morpork's streets, the animalistic and gritty nature of all the different species in the city, alongside Sam Vimes' good-natured, somewhat old-fashioned view of his city and the gentle, loving influence of his wife. Lastly, the noticeable chocolate conveys the comforting feeling of coming home after a long night shift. I find Veilleur de Nuit just as likable as the Night Watch. I appreciate its warmth. Even though the scent is supposed to be unisex, its aura is rather masculine. I find it somehow cozy. And it is just as steadfast as Commander Vimes: it lasts not only for the Night Watch but at least for the day after as well. Veilleur de Nuit is as unusual as the Discworld, dark and magical - yet strangely familiar in many ways. I wouldn’t use it in everyday life; it’s too special for that. But sometimes, the right moment just calls for a night watch.

Dream Angel from Victoria's Secret is a lovely, fluffy, fruity, candy/marshmallow, a little peppery and sweet scent. Reminds med alot of Ariana Grande's Ari and Sweet like Candy, like a mix of the two. A very young and girly perfume, but I don't care I really like it even if I'm getting old. I don't really think that perfumes has a age or season, though i prefer some perfumes in certain seasons and so on.

This is so sweet and tart. Bitter almost. Where’s the floral at? This was a blind buy for me as I expected it to be an aquatic floral on maybe a creamy sandalwood base. Nope. It is slap you in the face litchi on sour candy. Maybe some peony and orchid but it’s coming across as sweet pea to me. This is the first perfume I’ve tried, out of over 100, in the last 10 months that I would describe as cloying. Longevity and sillage are minimal to moderate however I am trying this on a cold snowy day with really dry air.

The name leads me to expect a woody Opium, yet the notes in our database show no florals. Instead, there’s a hint of the fruitiness of Bois & Fruit and the musk of Bois et Musc. Add amber, honey & spice and you have Bois oriental, another warmly appealing sultry scent. It also has cedarwood. I really like what Serge Lutens has done with these. They all give a different take on beautifully musky, seductive skin and in that they remind me of a certain mademoiselle I once knew who I learned was captivated by the same dashing gentleman who’d captivated me. What lovely wars we had, battling each other with our dresses.

As a big lover of Lutens, I think this is one of his solid and timeless creations. Dried fruit, strong cedar wood, a hefty dollop of spices, with just a little bit of honey - it's alluring and delicious. It's got everything what I wish Feminite du Bois had (the modern version). Similar to Bois et Fruits, but spicier and woodier. Warm and beautiful.

I run my finger over his shoulder blade. Tanned skin at the salty beach. My skin smells of him, woody and spicy. It’s a moment that will pass, I already know that. I am still young, but not foolish. He tilts his head to the side, blinks in the sun, smiles at me. Mischievous and without a thought for later. Our kisses are tender and summery. His neck smells of honey and pineapple. At every spot on his body, a new nuance of this scent unfolds, which doesn’t seem to suit him at all. Warm sand plays with my feet. Plop, plop sounds in the distance as a tennis ball hits the rhythm of the waves. The slanted rays of the sun end a long day of doing nothing. “Tomorrow again?” he asks. I nod, smiling, noncommittally, and think, yes, maybe. I want to know what kind of perfume he is wearing. He thinks for a moment and answers disarmingly honestly: Bois Oriental - I took a few drops from my father’s bottle. Ah, that explains a lot. I watch him as he gets smaller on the beach, disappearing into the dunes. His father, an interesting man.

I would like to express my sincere thanks to our dear perfumer "Bellemorte" for allowing me to test this wonderful fragrance. Bois Oriental begins with a beautiful honey note, slightly sweet and resinous, but not sticky. The scent immediately conveys a feeling of grounding, of calmness, I would almost say, but that doesn’t mean this fragrance is quiet in the sillage; that is by no means the case here. 10 minutes later, I perceive a distinct plum note, ripe and ready to be picked, with that beautiful color one associates with ripe plums. I also think I can detect a hint of sour cherries alongside this plum note. With this fragrance, I envision a wonderfully set breakfast table in perfect weather on a terrace, where nothing is missing. Fresh rolls from the oven, plum jam, honey, good butter, and Ellie's coffee are already on the table. This constellation lasts for about 4 hours, then it becomes a bit darker and spicier. I can make out cardamom and coriander, and perhaps a small hint of thyme? The scent is heavy, but at the same time has something lightly balsamic, which I can imagine might be thyme. The wind keeps bringing me this beautiful spiced and fruity honey note, which also develops a somewhat waxy quality after about 5 hours, which can only come from beeswax. My first association was still warm candle wax from white household candles. This is not poorly done at all in Bois Oriental; I believe it allows the other fragrance notes to stand out, and it gives the impression that the scent holds like Pattex. Which is true. Bois Oriental lasted a good 10 hours on my skin before it beautifully faded with musk and cedarwood; I perceive these two notes as the last. However, musk and cedarwood are unfortunately not a well-chosen combination for my skin, which of course is not Mr. Lutens' fault. For the last 2.5 hours, I had a slightly musty, cellar-like note reminiscent of old things, which came across as a bit piercing when I sniffed over the sprayed area. Musk and cedarwood can smell absolutely wonderful when they harmonize well with a skin type, even erotic, but unfortunately not on me. I can also imagine that the projection, meaning how the scent is perceived from a distance, especially regarding musk and cedarwood, has a completely different "scent color"; unfortunately, I could not test this, as I tested this fragrance at home and no one could sniff along. My roommate was out at the time - what a pity. But, as they say, you can't have it all. Bois Oriental has a very nicely conceived sillage; for the first 4 hours, it is quite noticeable, and if it is also slightly windy, the scent will be perceived over several meters. The sillage fades slowly and calmly with the fragrance. Chapeau, Mr. Lutens.
