All in all, there are no major changes in the scent. It's rather linear. A classic no-brainer; when you don't know what to wear, you reach for it. Longevity and sillage could certainly be improved. After about 3-4 hours, I no longer noticed it.

If you blindfolded me and sprayed this on a tester strip - not letting me see or hold the bottle - I would never have guessed this was a Victoria's Secret mist. It comes across as smooth, well-blended, and classy; feels much more expensive than it is! I mostly detect: [60%] sweet, resinous amber [30%] a subtle lift of baby powder [10%] smokey warmth, like incense + a bit of whiskey Smells like getting a big, welcoming hug from my hypothetical sophisticated auntie in her upscale penthouse. She's always well-put together and has jazz music playing softly, a bottle of whiskey ready to pour as you tell her about your day at the office. She's wearing a dark velvet blouse, and a lightly-tinkling charm bracelet moves with her well-manicured hands. She calls you honey, and makes you feel right at home - but also pushes you to be the best version of yourself. That's the type of person who wears Amber Aperitif - and it feels empowering, but somehow also comforting at the same time.

I don’t know what exactly it is that makes it smell like peaches to me. Specifically the marc jacobs daisy love daze perfume scent, this is what it smells like to me. It was very perfumey feeling, which isn’t the worst thing ever but im not a fan of it. It was very syrupy and really sweet, the mist even more than the lotion.

Le perce-vent is a cool breeze through clary sage fields. Surely, there's some lavender in here as well? I seem to feel the mentholated pinch of lavender on my olfactory nerve. Simple, understated, effective. The scent that you can bring with you to work or to an outing with your friends, a laid-back summer vibe that feels neat and clean. I love the minty herbs in the opening, but the dry down of chilled musk is also very pleasant and welcome. An easy scent to wear and love, but I do find myself having to reapply after a couple of hours, as longevity is not the greatest (4-5 hours on skin).

Initial cloud fills the whole room. Powdery. Fresh. Thick fog infused with hazy herbal florality. Unique. Peculiar. Lipsticky sweetness that turns sharp and medicinal once you lean in for a kiss. Minimalistic. Fascinating. A rather ambient composition, but all-engulfing at the same time. Both lulling and unnerving. Calm, peaceful – yet there is constant anxiety tugging at your senses, as if on the very edges of your peripheral vision something is lurking in the pale lilac fog. Projects strongly for the first ~2 hours, gets airier and slowly settles closer to the skin over the next ~2,5. Lasts forever afterwards – was still clearly visible when I fell asleep ~12 hours after spraying it. Gets flatter with time though. Sage and musk separate about ~6 hours in. Musk still envelops your body in a mellow cloud (about half an arm's-length wide). Sage settles on your skin – a herbal bittersweet surprise for anyone who gets too close. Left a lasting impression. I didn't necessarily like the flavor profile, but I loved what it managed to create from it. A great example of when less is more.

Despite the notes listed, I didn't detect any coconut milk, mango, or musk. To me, this is mostly just vanilla with lactonic elements - reminding me a lot of the Bare Vanilla DNA, but without the musk and caramel. Sizzling Vanilla came across like a combination of: - bourbon vanilla, but without the sharpness of bourbon and more just the purity of vanilla extract - condensed milk, but without the tooth-achingly sweet overdose of sugar and more of a "balanced" approach to the creaminess It's in a similar vein of Fresh Cream Eau de Toilette (but without the "baby vomit" feel). Pretty on its own, but simple enough that it would do well in layering. While I enjoy simplicity, I have other vanillas I love more (I prefer Fresh Vanilla Blossoms and Bare Vanilla over this) - so I think it's a pass for me. But if you're looking for a well-done basic lactonic vanilla, give this a try. P.S. The name is odd to me, as the word "sizzling" makes me think of meat that you're cooking on a smoker or grill in the summertime - and that there must be some type of smoke, spice, or "heat" to the vanilla... but there's nothing smokey or spicy about this.

That Serge Lutens sees himself as a fragrance ARTIST is evident in his scents. They do not always strive for "mass appeal," but rather serve as an expression of an "Inner Mission" that is carried outward. From what I have read about him, he seems to be a kind of loner who only places great trust in his "partner" Christopher Sheldrake. At least in the olfactory sense regarding the fragrances. I can also identify something like "periods" or "phases," similar to other artists like painters. With this scent, as with several others, the theme of "Dark Secret" is prominent. The fragrance consists of very few, but high-quality ingredients that represent a (not entirely new) contrast between fragrance notes. Here, we have dark woods (oud, cedar, ebony?) and rose petals. Red and black. Vitality and agony. Mysterious and obvious. Soul-soothing and quietly fear-inducing. Containing deep magic. Applied thickly without showing off. A contradictory character. Lutens has always remained true to this. In the ambiguity of most of his fragrances. Only the themes change. Nothing repeats itself. And yet there is always something like a "Lutensian" essence, reminiscent of Guerlain with its typical "Guerlainade." Just very subtle unique characteristics.

There are moments when I would rather just dissolve into thin air: like when the Floating Peach Blossom takes me shopping for laundry - as if SHE didn’t already have enough options in that regard - and I can’t sneak off to the nearest café because I might get lost in the middle of South Tyrol. So here I am with HER in the middle of a lingerie store, waiting for a fitting room to become available for HER, feeling like a best-ager among numerous young women who could all be my daughters, a bit out of place, like a driven mix of sugar daddy and voyeur. So where to look innocently when the partner has eventually disappeared into a fitting room? God bless it, Victoria's Secret sells perfumes among thongs and bikinis. "Mander, it’s time!" ... if not here, then where? Due to the low price, Victoria's Secret skips the outer box; the bottle has to speak for itself. A nice large cylinder with an appealing gradient from pink to orange, topped with a golden cap. Yes, it’s okay, nice and heavy, I really like that. The sprayer produces a rich mist, which I find noteworthy in this price range. You are immediately enveloped by the entire fruit salad mentioned in the pyramid. The guava has a watery quality, the pineapple adds fresh acidity, mango and passion fruit provide tropical vibes and the indispensable sweetness. It gets a bit sticky, but not too much. Fruit, acidity, and sugar are well balanced. The fruit aromas inevitably remind you of some well-known gummy bears, ice creams, and yogurts; they must have sourced from the same supplier shelf. Admittedly, it smells a bit synthetic, but not too much, and I never find it disturbing or inappropriate. As the fruity intensity diminishes after a while, dry light woods quietly round off the scent, combined with a slightly mineral sea breeze. The fruit cloud noticeably retreats after about an hour, yet I am quite amazed that even after 7-8 hours in summery, sweat-inducing heat, I can still detect a light fruity shimmer on my skin. Since the fruits were not paired with the usual flowers as a counterpoint and it is overall not overly sweet, the scent never comes across as purely feminine. A good summer and vacation fragrance, also quite suitable for men. It’s definitely worth it. For the budget price being asked, absolutely. Why the fragrance ultimately didn’t make it into my collection is quickly explained: I got distracted, was then allowed to assist in selecting new swimwear and some bras, and by the time I left the store, as so often, I already had both hands full.

Un Bois Sépia surprised me greatly, as it is a southern French perfume that develops in a very varied way and has a good sillage. Scents of nature, walks through a cypress grove, a forest, an arboretum park, or an avenue where cypress trees meet moss-covered oaks. It is shortly after the rain and in late summer or early autumn when a distinct smell of damp earth from the rain, earthy patchouli, cypress bark, and green leaves, as well as the dry essence of Gris Clair and a hint of sweet mint can be detected. After a few hours, the last sip of coffee that one enjoys so much while hiking on a wooden bench from a thermos comes through, something I did not expect at all, given the completely contradictory reviews, which are rare; I could not imagine the perfume at all. The more I felt drawn to it. So I blindly reached for the bottle and do not regret it in the slightest. No flimsy goods. Vintage collectors and nature lovers will get their money's worth here. A sensual, elegant, and very pleasant aromatherapy that caresses the senses and the soul. It feels like wrapping oneself in a light, sheer scarf that evokes memories of the summer just passed and the autumn to come.

If someone had held the scent under my nose blindfolded - or even just announced it as a Serge Lutens - my reaction would have been a definite NO! A Lutens? Never! Even though I am sitting here now reading the list of ingredients, I imagine a completely different fragrance. As I wore un Bois Sepia on the back of my hand, a scent association immediately came to mind, *g* I envision a tanned, well-built man diving off a cliff into the blue sea and then basking in the sun with his water-droplet skin. An aquatic-sounding men's fragrance like Cool Water. *shudder* But the ingredients are quite different! Still, it has a typically freshly washed but clearly masculine scent of an aftershave from a blue bottle. I imagined the scent to be more green based on the name and the fragrance notes - not at all - it’s blue. In any case, I don’t perceive any of the beloved vetiver. Patchouli, sandalwood, cypress are all building blocks I greatly appreciate, yet I can’t distinctly identify any of them here. Then there’s opoponax… Shouldn’t that provide the famous Lutensian balsamic richness? It doesn’t. *scratches head* Where on earth does the aquatic come from? I like it neither on myself nor on a man. So I’m not getting anywhere here, sorry. May someone come to my aid.

Smells so delicious Is very fruity, fresh, kinda spicy, and sweet I think is perfect for Summer!! Perfect for night-out (you'll receive compliments!), leisure and evening. I would give it a 10/10 cuz I LOVE fruity perfumes, and ofc this one is really fruity! I love ittt You may find it by $20 normally if there's no special offers!

When I think of neroli, I think of bitter, earthy citrus. There was none of that here, at all! This is BBW's "Midnight Blue Citrus" candle... but in a perfume form + amp up the volume on the scent a bunch, add a giant bag of fruity Haribo gummy bears... and now you have "Very Sexy Sea". It does smell summery, due to how fruity and bright it is - so in that regard, I can see how this would be a "sea"/beach or hot weather fragrance... but the bergamot was too sharp/screechy/synthetic for my taste. I didn't get any cedar/woodsy notes, and this didn't smell at all to me like a refreshing, soapy, or aquatic/ozonic scent like some have said. Definitely test this in store before buying!

I've never been to Bali, although I know many people who have, including my parents who chose to fly there for their honeymoon many years ago. Like all of the Island flankers, Very Bali is also very fresh and aquatic. While these types of fragrances aren't really my cup of tea, I do enjoy smelling Very Bali even though I'd probably never wear it or buy myself a bottle. The jasmine note in this fragrance is very soapy and crisp, further complimented by a strong marine accord. The composition is surprisingly lacking in citrus accords, instead drawing focus to an interesting blend of fresh, airy florals and cooling salt water. Its freshness alludes to a tropical destination, however I also think that Very Bali smells a little bit like sheets fresh from the dryer, particularly towards the drydown. The base notes are an interesting and rather potent mixture of white musk, woods, freesia and sea water. I'm really impressed with this perfume's sillage and longevity. It's a relatively new fragrance that has a lot of devoted fans already. I think I actually prefer Very Bali to the original Island. I quite like Michael Kors' approach to this Island series, and I can't wait to see what he comes up with next.

This is the Lutens I felt in love when I discovered Chêne, Fumerie Turque, Santal de Mysore.. years ago. A drop of it and you are sure to be taken in a journey. L’Innommable is a really well made combo of spices, dried fruits and resins. Cumin is quite prominent and remember me the aura of Chêne and El Attarine, but this latest issue seems to be on steroids ! Drydown is all about rounded and caramelized benzoin.

After last year’s Bourreau des Fleurs, Serge Lutens seems to continue his olfactory exploration of immortelle with this year’s L’Innommable. The fragrance opens with delicious dried stone fruits. Apricots, plums and peaches are carefully dried under the sun, then spiced up by cumin, piquant but not necessarily sweaty. A few drops of honey and caramel drip from the immortelle and benzoin onto the dried fruits, just enough to complement their sweet flavour without thickening the texture. Finally, a pinch of salt rounds everything up, amping up the gourmand sensation without leveling up the sweetness. This kind of spicy dried fruits appearing rather frequently in Lutens’ compositions, it’s now widely regarded as one of his olfactory signatures. As a result, L’Innommable instantly pops a few names into my head: Arabie, El Attarine and the aforementioned Bourreau des Fleurs. I didn’t compare them side by side, but from my memory, I’d say the spices, especially the cumin, play a much stronger role and are overall sharper in Arabie than in L’Innommable, while Bourreau des Fleurs feels more caramel-y. El Attarine has the least fruity elements out of these four, but its emphasis on honeyed caramel-cumin duality of immortelle combined with a certain dense animalic muskiness makes it closer to L’Innommable in the dry down. To be clear, L’Innommable doesn’t have the same muskiness as El Attarine, but it achieves a similar effect via the intermediate of something reminiscent of tuberose and sandalwood. The tuberose is not at all camphorated or diffusively sweet or creamy, but somehow is bent inward and rendered densely nutty by the sandalwood-like nuance. These two emerge from underneath about 1 hour in, lending the dried fruits a surprisingly leathery touch. The combined effect is not dissimilar to the leathery immortelle-tuberose of Histoires de Parfums Tubéreuse 3 Animale. L’Innommable then stays more or less the same until the end, with occasion woody smokes sizzle through the musky tuberose and leathery dried fruits. The sillage is relatively close with an 8-hour longevity on a hot day. Overall, I quite enjoy L’Innommable, especially its leathery and musky tuberose twist on the immortelle and his signature spicy dried fruits. However, the fact that it reminds me of several other fragrances does make me pause. Granted, its price, while high-end, is not the most outrageous in that category. But it doesn’t seem as efficient as other more reasonably priced immortelle or immortelle-tuberose fragrances, either. Personally, I’d be more excited if it was released in the regular range, but if you happen to be exploring immortelle in perfumery, it would be interesting to sample too.

Cumin, fenugreek, and immortelle are likely to be forever condemned to be simplified in Western forums to curry, Indian cooking, and subcontinental grocery stores. I wonder if in corresponding forums in India or Bangladesh, Jicky (1889) et al. are also mentioned in the same breath as Coq au Vin and rosemary potatoes?! L'Innommable - named after a Beckett play (why not) and a clear offshoot of Bourreau des Fleurs (2017) - is one of Lutens’ most pronounced immortelle perfumes. With its cumin, benzoin, clove, and sandalwood notes, it indeed evokes memories of spice blends - specifically the complexity of Japanese 'Indira' curry powder: seemingly familiar at first, yet complex, exotic, and opulent due to numerous ingredients, including unexpected ones like orange zest. L'Innommable works similarly: there is more at play here than indicated. As a fan of Sables (1985), I always perk up when someone mentions 'curry' in relation to perfumes - it could be a hidden immortelle. Those who cannot appreciate this note will quickly seek refuge from L'Innommable. Lutens has already presented fragrances with a spectrally broader integrated immortelle note, such as Arabie (2000), Chêne (2004), or Le Participe Passé (2018); here, it is brought to light in a more reduced manner. Fenugreek-like and cumin, a dark floral note with clove-spicy aspects are at the forefront; beneath the benzoin note lies a slightly sweet and subtly bitter trace of immortelle absolute. Late in the dry down, I also suspect the Ambrarome base recently used by Sheldrake with Rauque (2023). The whole thing slightly reminds me of the early Lutens Santal de Mysore (1997), albeit more balsamic here. Why such a special-interest perfume was chosen as the kickoff for the 'Gratte-Ciel' repackaging - along with the associated price development that almost resembles a retirement plan for Lutens - is peculiar. Nevertheless: L'Innommable is one of the most beautiful newer Lutens.

Moldy smells in hotel closets and stale pub odors that have settled into clothes regularly bring me to the brink of death. Recently, on the train from Strasbourg to Paris, I endured 2 hours of olfactory remnants from onions, Munster cheese, bacon, and smoke, which clearly originated from an Alsatian Flammkuchen stand. And now they were emanating from a denim jacket hanging right behind my head. Since the train was full, I couldn't move and tied a silk scarf sprayed with Chanel 22 around my nose as a makeshift solution. Although facial veiling is prohibited in France. But I would have had good arguments for it. Somehow, after nearly 2 hours, I stumbled out of the train at Gare de l'Est and even found the dusty-sweet smell of the Metro a relief. That says a lot because I actually hate that smell too. Fortunately, my business appointment ended quicker than expected, and I unexpectedly had the afternoon free. So off I went to the Palais Royal, to the garden, past the usual silly selfie tourists, under the arcades - to Lutens. Made it!! I wanted to buy El Attarine, no idea why, probably the subtle dried fruit notes had stuck in my synapses. In the dimly lit Lutens shop, there is always a stunning saleswoman Madonna bustling around with flowing hair, reciting her usual line: "Je peux vous aider?" Yes, of course, El Attarine. But first, I had to try the house's new fragrance, L'innomable, the one that cannot be named, the Madonna raved. Sounded very promising. Until I got a spritz of it on my hand. And I almost threw up: A plate of saffron rice with curry chicken at the Indian restaurant, the smell of which had lingered in a denim jacket. I was done; the train ride's smell was still haunting me, and I had to step outside for a moment, through a delicate automatic iron door, the saleswoman Madonna got a fright, I breathed deeply outside and stared into the garden. I-don't-want-to-smell-like-food!! Damn it. When I came back in, the Madonna informed me that it was probably the "Siam-Benzoe." I smiled politely. It wouldn't have helped to tell her that it was more likely the smell of a Siamese cat steamed in curry. So I grabbed my El Attarine and fled. In the black luxury bag, I also found several samples, including L'innomable. The Madonna seemed determined to convert me. A few days later, and after overcoming the clothing stench, I bravely sprayed it into the air. No, folks. Who wants to smell like an Indian restaurant? Not at all.

This one was a bit of a surprise for me. It's very powdery, and has a more mature and sophisticated vibe than most other Victoria's Secret offerings, which tend to have a fruity, juicy flair for the younger crowd... but this is different. It has a timeless quality, probably due to all that powder. Patchouli is strong here, but not offputting, for those who are hesitant about the note. It dances effortlessly with the plum and white floral notes, just the right blend to create a soothing, dark, sophisticated and seductive scent. Very well done, and a shame it's discontinued. This is similar to Natori, except that Natori has a sparkling, effervescent (aldehydic) quality to it that Basic Instinct lacks. Not that that's a bad thing, they're just a bit different.

The Licorice Equator is one of those invisible lines that winds its way somewhere along the Frankfurt Main line, and, according to the press offices of Katjes and Haribo, separates potential customers into licorice lovers and licorice haters. There are certainly more such equators; the Weißwurst equator runs at similar latitudes but also quickly ends at the border to Austria. When it comes to mushrooms, one often speaks of mycophilic and mycophobic countries, almost continents. The confectionery manufacturers can present concrete sales figures and sometimes point out that south of the Licorice Equator, licorice is derogatorily referred to as bear dung - whether this term originates from the name of the former Nuremberg confectioner Karl Bär and his licorice patents - one of the few licorice cultivation areas north of the Alps - is not discussed in detail. I appreciate some perfumes where a licorice note plays a role with its anise and fennel facets: foremost, Jean-Michel Duriez's charmingly discreet Yohji Homme (1999), Dior's brilliant Eau Noire (2004), Ellena's fluffy lavender Brin de Réglisse (2005), Caron's atypical powerhouse lemon + licorice combination Eau de Reglisse (2006) - also Eau de Gloire (2005) with its Bonapartist licorice powder detail or Annick Menardo's original version of Body Kouros (2000). In La proie pour l'ombre, licorice plays in a broader, deeper, more voluminous register. Similar to the transformation from licorice to licorice, where squeezed roots are boiled down to a thick, molasses-like brew that ultimately has little to do with the bittersweet woody taste of chewing licorice. The opening is dense, impenetrable, monolithic. Not much shines through; a brilliantly sealed surface does not allow for closer inspection. The mentioned leather and vanilla notes remain concealed beneath this cooked licorice note, and leather is not at all classic like in Lutens' spicy Knize-Caron commentary Cuir Mauresque (1996), but rather like the leather of the licorice shoe soles that Charlie Chaplin devoured en masse. La proie pour l'ombre aligns itself more with Le participe passé (2018) and L'Innommable (2018). The sympathetically cacophonous Le participe was more original, and L'Innommable was more reduced, cumin-heavy and harsher, both successful takes on immortelle notes. La proie pour l'ombre also plays a scene where the mentioned Eau Noire could appear with given distance, coffee-like, and in this combination, it vaguely reminds one of Series 7: Sweet - Wood Coffee (2005). Especially in the dry-down, these coordinates become visible in the distance - in this most beautiful section of La proie, which is essentially more about de-intensification than the emergence of components that are not yet recognizable, I discover a structure that hints at a slightly smoky vanilla, licorice with bitter substances (not yet cooked down). The progression is WYSIWYG, surprises are hardly to be found here; the fading intensity curve leaves a fine, lasting trace of La proie pour l'ombre, where everything fits well. I tested against Dutch, unsalted licorice and Calabrian licorice from two sources; despite two listed cooking ingredients, this is not a complete dessert - the sensations during consumption are too different. Has the Licorice Equator already been talked about at Shiseido? Equators do not end at national borders, and if I extend this line on the map, including the curvature of the Earth, it remains questionable where this perfume, named after a relationship drama by Alexandre Astruc, will find friends. Among the partly rather bizarrely good releases that Lutens has been presenting from time to time over the past few years, La proie pour l'ombre is in good company. P.S. A starting point was certainly Bourreau des Fleurs (2017), which was released in the high-priced section d'Or. Both La proie pour l'ombre and L'Innommable are, for me, connected to Bourreau des Fleurs.

I 100% fully agree with the other comments, sadly, the name has nothing to do with the actual scent. It's really not giving neither cocoa nor chocolate. It's rather really fruity and pepperish, like just full on red fruits with a very nice touch of vanilla soap, but very synthetic as well. If you expected or expect a gourmand (creamy chocolate cacao), you're really not buying the right item.

No chocolate, it just smells like a failed attempt at a marshmallow scent. I can see the vision they went for, but it just doesn’t hit the mark. Smells like peppery marshmallow…. Really not what I was expecting. Definitely a PASS for me. Really was hoping for a melted chocolate scent… bottle design is really cute though! Just wish the scent was actually smelled like advertised

i'm not sure if there was a labeling error with this fragrance, since i know that that's happened with some vs scents before, but i don't get hot cocoa vibes from this at all. if anything, i feel like this would layer well with the recently launched glazed warm & cozy. like others have said, this is a clean, sweet scent with some indistinct fruity/floral notes and a nice lactonic base. it's a nice scent, don't get me wrong, but it's nothing like the marketing for the notes.

I ended up being majorly disappointed with this scent. It doesn’t smell bad at all - it’s actually quite pleasant and I enjoy wearing it to bed. However, this smells nothing like the hot chocolate with marshmallow scent that was promised. Instead, it comes off more as a berries and whipped cream scent. Slightly fruity, slightly airy, a smidge creamy. It projects well for a body mist on my skin, and lasts decently (again, for a body mist). Overall, I will continue using it, I just wish it was named differently.

Michael Kors GOLD wafts in undulating waves of Dior J'ADORE, which must have something to do with the big, bad freesia found in both compositions. GOLD also offers blasts of tuberose and magnolia, along with the usual peony, and as the fragrance dries down it starts to seem like something of a floral cacophony, along the lines of EL BEAUTIFUL. I don't find GOLD very appealing, unfortunately. Although I might appreciate these floral notes individually, they are battling here for dominance in a somewhat undignified way. Something like a cat fight between the strong floral components, each attempting to eliminate the other contenders by any means necessary. There's just too much raucous competition for the starring role. The biggest bouquet on the block is by far freesia, but the other flowers, no matter how bruised and battered they become in this battle to the finish, refuse to back down. In the end, no one is willing to leave the island, the underdogs preferring instead to flout the rules to which they agreed before entering into the game.

The opening dances around between notes that are hard to detect - some sort of almond liqueur, and possibly a powdery almond blossom? It almost feels like a less musky/less woodsy version of Velvet Petals in the beginning, and is a bit synthetic right out of the gate. I sprayed it on my arm and let it sit. Then later, I caught a whiff of something very familiar: Bianco Latte . I turned to see if there was someone nearby, but then I realized that I was actually picking up Sugared Petals ! Bianco Latte isn't one of my favorites - the coumarin note drowns out a lot of the rest of the notes for me, and thankfully that isn't the case here. Sugared Petals smelled more to me like "Eclaire / اكلاير | Lattafa / لطافة" (another Bianco Latte "dupe"): mainly creamy vanilla, a hint of something floral, a bit of praline, and synthetic "cashmeran" musk. Since I don't enjoy Eclaire or Bianco Latte, I didn't buy it. But if you love Bianco Latte , "Eclaire / اكلاير | Lattafa / لطافة" , or even Velvet Petals , this one is worth a try.

It is a nice typical sweet floral scent. There is a “sharpness” in the background but it does not stay too long. Really sugary smelling, I think the lotion pulls more of the white florals whereas the mist pulls more of that sugary macaron and wood. Has a creamy feel to it, but it definitely is overpowered by that sugary feel.

I was so excited when I dusted off a nearly full bottle in the bay last spring! In the meantime, I've also gotten rid of it there. Since there's nothing written about Island Bermuda here yet, I thought I'd quickly sing a swan song. Or an obituary... But swan song sounds a bit more dramatic given this misery :D There's hardly anything to be found about the scent on the internet. Considering how trendy Michael Kors bags and fragrances usually are, I'm a bit surprised, although in my opinion, the scent is really not good. It smells to me like stagnant, old flower water. The typical tipping note is missing, so that can't be it. The blackcurrant buds probably belong to the top note. Maybe there are also a few sour blackcurrants in there. I think I can sniff something like that. The floral heart note could actually be harmless, but it smells too musty to me. Is it the hibiscus that doesn't fit in? The impression intensifies over time. The base notes blend into an indefinable must. Cedar? Possibly. I would have never thought of leather.. After about 5 hours, the spell is over. Sillage is stronger on me than I would like.

prominent cool, rooty orris opening. it does compare to iris silver mist here, but only briefly, as a buttery leather note that also reads soapy and slightly powdery / floral emerges. from here the leather becomes the dominant note to me until the base notes come to the fore. at a point in the mid it develops a strange, almost sweaty / acidic tone to the leather which i don't enjoy, i figure a component of the mentioned 'spice' notes, but it doesn't last long thankfully. it definitely reads as 'old world' or 'antique' in its nature - not as in a vintage scent, but suggesting those actual things. i understand the mentions here of it smelling like a museum, or an oil painting. very 'grey' in tone. the performance is subdued, becoming a slightly sweetened, musky skin-scent very quickly after the opening, but it does last quite a while. it's good. i don't regret buying it and will likely use it all, but for the price? it's a lot to ask for what it is and for the performance. saying that, i do kind of wish i had bought sidi bel-abbes instead. that seems to have more going for it and has more presence.

Zurafa is my favourite of le Royaume des Lumières collection. This scent is like the love child of Cuir Mauresque (iris and leather scent) and Boxeuses (fruity leather). The leather is not as dry and harsh as in Cuir Mauresque. The leather in Cuir Mauresque was the deal breaker for me. All the fragrances from that collection are pure perfume collection The price is a bit too steep for me though: 380€ for 100ml. Otherwise I would grabbed a bottle the very day I tried Zurafa for the first time.

I am always on the lookout for the “tropical island” scent. And in some airport duty-free perfumery, I discovered the Michael Kors Island range, including this “Hawaii.” It’s a nice fragrance, a bit fruity at first and then floral. Orange mixed with jasmine. The orange might be a bit “sharp,” but then jasmine, in just the right dosage-not too much, as it would quickly become “sharp” too, and not too little so that it “gets lost.” After a while, the fruity note completely fades, and the remaining jasmine note blends with a woody, balsamic scent. I thought for a long time about what this reminded me of; somehow it felt so familiar. Then, when I was chopping wood for our tiled stove, it hit me: tree resin! The base note of the “Hawaii” perfume smells like fresh resin with a hint of jasmine and sandalwood. In my eyes, it’s a very interesting scent, not everyday and something different. However, I secretly hope that Hawaii doesn’t smell like this. :) Personally, I am a bit disappointed. I actually expected a completely different fragrance: a scent that reminds me of a tropical island, the heavy-sweet scent of exotic flowers and fruits, of beach and sea, and not the smell of the Hawaiian forest.

that is the question here. Actually, I can only agree with the first commentator on Cannibale (from this line), because the pricing policy behind this series can hardly be understood otherwise. I am more than disappointed with all the scents from this line. The saleswoman claims it is only available before Christmas. I think they will be lucky if anything sells before the Christmas after next. This scent is the most disappointing of all that I have tested. I can smell neither rose nor anything else, only an intense, nose-whipping - yes, is it laundry detergent? - I have a memory, I once had a dish soap that smelled like this. I never bought it again. I cannot detect any scent development; I had hoped so much that this penetrating laundry detergent smell would stop, as I was out in the city with no way to wash it off. Fortunately, it doesn't last long; after 2 washes, the rinse comes, which smells similar, only the intensity has decreased. Now it smells more like a plastic bag. Well, what a fine little scent! What was dear Serge thinking? Maybe: let's see if I can get away with this. His recent creations have already made me doubt a bit, but this one takes the cake. Sorry, it's a total flop, but maybe it's due to the shock I received from this.

I hope VS never stops making Bare Rose. It’s beautiful! It’s such a fresh, sweet, jammy floral. I get stopped by people asking me what I am wearing. It gives Delina Exclusif vibes without the PDM price tag! VS is notorious for discontinuing scent. I would be so totally heartbroken if they stoped producing bare rose.

Bare Rose is a transparent dewy floral perfect for spring and summer and anytime you just want to feel pretty. It’s fresh, feminine, flirty, and a crowd-pleasing (if not exactly revolutionary) scent. The rose here is a pink, dewy and petal-soft - not powdery or vintage, nor green and stemmy. It mingles beautifully with a bright and juicy pear. The dry down is a soft creamy sandalwood that this perfume shares with the original Bare . This isn’t groundbreaking but it’s a really nice scent and the entire Bare line is a breath of fresh air amongst the Bombshells and Teases.

Wood and musk. A hynoptic and complex muskiness rises immediately, created by beeswax, coconut and saffon as well as musk. It’s really intoxicating. Almost seductive. And here I thought a person needed Jasmine for that. I’m going to wear this one for a day to see if I fall in love. The same cedarwood seems to have been used in all Serge Luten’s “Bois et —“ perfumes. They’ve managed to instill the distinctiveness of cedar without its sharpness. Well done.

Bombshell has become a very common one. This is more mature. Only thing I don't like about Victoria Secret is it's longevity according to the price. I tried roll on. It projects for maximum 1 hour. And the longevity is maximum three hours. Which disappoint me a lot. On cloths it's stays for whole day but vanishes from pulse point within 5 hours.

I don't see this reflected in the main accords, but I think this is the most powdery scent I own. I'll also say that this might be the scent that got me to begin considering other powdery scents! I think the Victoria's Secret Bombshell line and also Heavenly really make that powder factor more pleasant and mature (because straight baby powder is godawful). This is also my favorite Bombshell flanker, followed by Summer 2017. I don't care for Beach, which smells like a public bathroom. Celebration is warmer and sweeter. I also swear up and down that I hate peony, but then I guess I'm a liar because it's apparently a big star in this fragrance. I think it's appropriate any season, day or night. It does not give "holiday spice" even though it was marketed as a holiday scent. It's more New Year's than Christmas, but I wear it to work all the time. A quick note on sillage: I wore this today and someone in the gas station store smelled amazing. Some dude was wearing Patchouli 24 or SOMETHING good. The woman who rang me up mentioned it and I was like "yes! that guy smelled amazing!" and she said "no yeah he smelled good, but now I can smell you and I really like that scent." Of course I was like "lol THANKS it's a dumb Victoria's Secret Bombshell fragrance," but I really do think it's better than the usual lineup. I think this basically demonstrated that we're not talking Le Labo levels of sillage, but that arms length sillage between me and that woman is where Celebration travels.

This smells like a combination of Bombshell Magic and Heavenly (2013) Eau de Parfum . Bombshell Celebration is a high-end, creamy bar of sandalwood soap: calming, luxurious, and something you'd find in a spa with all-white cold marble floors and fresh robes. Comparing Bombshell Celebration to its (in my opinion) closest flanker, Bombshell Magic-- Both share a similar: - spicy-sexy-sweet patchouli base (while not listed in Bombshell Celebration, it's distinctive to me and so similar to the base in Bombshell Magic) - cool-green woody/earthy element (the blue spruce note in Bombshell Celebration; in Bombshell Magic, I get a strong juniper berry wreath/pine/spruce note) - projection + longevity (both are among the strongest fragrances in my collection) - overall DNA (when you smell both side by side, you can tell they're similar flankers) They differ in: - seasonal wear (Bombshell Celebration feels like it could be worn in the cooler days of Spring, Fall, and Winter; Bombshell Magic only feels like it could be worn in Winter due to its depth and stronger spicy-ness) - dominant notes (Bombshell Celebration is a sandalwood-forward fragrance; Bombshell Magic is more "green wreath blend"-forward) Both flankers feel very different to me from the OG Bombshell Eau de Parfum , or any other Bombshell flankers - which might be why I like both of them so much. I get zero champagne in this, and the peony is more soapy than anything - not particularly sweet or "watery" like peony often is. Bombshell Celebration is feminine, woody, soapy, and signature-scent worthy!

It is getting colder again and the cozy scents are coming back to the forefront. The Chergui Eau de Parfum is, in my opinion, always a candidate when one is looking for a very cozy and sensual fragrance. I have had the regular Eau de Parfum for a while and I enjoy wearing it when I seek that typical warming vibe. Since 2021, there has been this Confit de Parfum. What can one imagine under this? Perfume oil. Whether this is pure perfume oil, I do not know, but in any case, a very thick drop comes out of this spray that is very oily. According to the manufacturer, one spray is enough to project an intense scent impression. 1-2 sprays are definitely sufficient, as a drop the size of a pea comes out, making it very economical. I am not the biggest fan of perfume oil, but I am pleased with this Chergui. You can get this Chergui as perfume oil, referred to here as Confit de Parfum. In addition to this Chergui, you can also get the other bestsellers of the brand Ambre sultan Confit de Parfum & La fille de Berlin Confit de Parfum as Confit. The Chergui immediately appealed to me, but the MSRP of €152 for 25ml was a bit steep for me. By now, you can already get it for half the price, which is fair for oil. The downside-and sometimes also an advantage-of oil is that it does not have a really good sillage due to the oil content. Those who want an intimate and sensual scent can give this a chance. Those who prefer a larger sillage should choose the EdP, or even a combination of both. One should, of course, be careful with this oily consistency on clothing, as it can leave an oily film. It is best to let it dry a bit. The scent comes in a lovely small bottle that is just so pretty. A beautiful purple hue that appears quite dark and mystical. It looks expensive and is made of great glass. The bottle has a long cap including a spray nozzle. As mentioned, the spray nozzle dispenses a good drop that is very economical. There is not much of a difference in scent from the EdP. Due to this oily consistency, this fragrance naturally appears richer, more elegant, and also very sensual-intimate. The wonderful hay note is also present here, providing that cozy warm autumn aura. Of course, the pyramid is not complete here and also not in the Chergui. Notes like honey and soft amber are missing. But this is what makes the scent: this oriental amber note with straw-like hay and sensually warm honey. These beautiful warm spices and the tobacco note also contribute to this wonderful DNA. Overall, a safe purchase if you want the original in oil form. The performance here is not better than that of the EdP. Especially the sillage is significantly reduced due to the high oil content. Some may appreciate this, while others may not. However, a sensual-intimate sillage can certainly have its charm. The longevity is quite decent. It should be around 8-10 hours. Overall, a great scent without many surprises. The fragrance DNA appears richer and more elegant, with some compromises in sillage. For Chergui fans, it is certainly a great gimmick that can be worn well on elegant occasions.

There's not much to really report here, it really is *simply* fresh juicy pomegranates with nondescript florals. It's pretty, uplifiting, body wash-y and light. There's no surprises or twists. It's sweet pomegranate, not tart or bitter at all. This smells reminiscent of Pure Seduction, but cooler in temperature. PS almost has a coziness about it, and feels suitable for autumn, but Pomegranate & Lotus is the sort of fragrance you want to apply at the height of summer. I've heard it said that this smells like Chanel's Eau Tendre, and I disagree. If anything, it's more similar to Versace Bright Crystal, yet juiciest, lighter, and less dimensional overall. Still, all of these are within the same vein.

Seduction? Not at all. With this fragrance, you get a floral, somewhat synthetic freshie. In my opinion, the price-performance ratio is fantastic. The longevity lasts all day for me, but it becomes more skin-close after 3-4 hours. I think it’s the perfect scent for work or just to relax on the sofa. The fragrance is very linear, but the musk is pleasant - not at all hairspray-like, as it is with many musk fragrances. In my opinion, this fragrance is super underrated and a real insider tip. Generally, I’m not a fan of Victoria's Secret fragrances. However, this one is really nice.

PDM Layton is a bold, sensual fragrance with truly incredible staying power. The scent projects beautifully, lingering on my skin post-shower and on my clothes for days. While it's a bit too sweet for summer days, its versatility makes it a winner for clubbing, date nights, and cooler weather. The hype might be overblown, but Layton's performance justifies giving it a try. Forget the negative reviews – sample this on your own skin before deciding. If you love a strong, classy fragrance, Layton's sweetness and longevity won't disappoint.

So here's another attempt to write some words about one of the most known and relevant contemporary fragrances - it's like trying to review a can of Coke, by saying something that hasn't been expressed before. Fairly impossible. Anyway, there you go... Layton, was originally crafted by perfumer Hamid Merati-Kashani and launched in 2016. It's almost 10 years old, but it is still one of the best among the brand's lineup. Not all of their fragrances have been well received (beyond the TikTok sphere), nevertheless PdM is not just a niche clone house hyped by refined marketing, as many think. Among the house's offerings, Layton holds a cherished spot in my personal collection. It is one of my all-time favorites, even if Pegasus (Exclusif) aligns a bit better to my personality. Scent profile wise, the introduction is a blend of crisp apple, lavender, zesty bergamot, and a hint of mandarin orange. If you read these notes while you're smelling it, you will be able to isolate them... a sign of quality blending. This combination offers an immediate freshness that's both invigorating and elegant. As the fragrance unfolds, nuances of light florals emerge: geranium, violet, and jasmine. These smell rather genderless. The foundation is a blend of vanilla, cardamom, sandalwood, pepper, guaiac wood, and patchouli, providing warmth and decent longevity. In fact, Layton's longevity is above average. It lasts throughout the day and into the evening. I'd say 8-10 hours, depending on the usual factors. Its projection is not overpowering, making its presence known without offending. What I like about Layton is that despite its sophistication, it remains versatile. Whether attending a formal event or enjoying a casual outing, this fragrance is always a good option. Absolutely office safe, if not oversprayed. In the vast realm of perfumery, Layton distinguishes itself as a fragrance that joins tradition with modernity - pretty much PdM's declared mission. Its blend of notes created a contemporary staple which, as we all know, has been often replicated in many forms. To me, the original still stands out and I own a full bottle of it... but if you want to save your $$$, you'll have plenty of choice.

I own the two different batches of Layton. 78%vol: Opens up more sharp and the apple is toned down a bit. I think the geranium is stronger in this. More vanillic than the 82% batch. It has more depth to it. 82%vol: Airyer and less sharp than the old batch. The cardamom is more spicy and sweet in this batch. A fresher version. Conclusion: 78% wins without a doubt. It has more depth, longer lasting, better projection. To my nose, there is a big difference between the two batches. I was lucky to get my hands on a sealed 2020 batch 78% batch of Layton. If you are able to get your hands on the older batch, then do it. Sad they reformulated this one

Layton by Parfums de Marly is a Amber Floral fragrance for men. Layton was launched in 2016. The nose behind this fragrance is Hamid Merati-Kashani. THE SCENT ; This is definitely a compliment getter . Lady’s are loving it . Opens with a masculine spicy menthol vibe what makes it quite unique experience in my opinion.

The opening of Layton is a crisp blend of apple and bergamot. It is a very green and tart apple aroma with just that touch of citrus provided by the bergamot. I think that the apple note in here smells pretty darn realistic and not like some artificial Jolly Rancher candy, as it has the right amount of juiciness.

Genuine item from Selfridges. Vanilla bomb for first ten minutes. Skin scent for an hour afterwards then just a faint whiff of vanilla on skin for a further hour. Nothing special. I often wonder if it’s my nose but, I also wonder if these supposedly great scents contain some kind of hypnotic effect causing mass hysteria with positive reviews.

Layton is a perfect fragrance for who is beginning in the Nische world, yes is a nice fragrance a creamy vanilla little bit sweet on a fruity woody base , how can anyone dislike this fragrance ? Is simply a mass appealing fragrance, a head Turner and compliment getter, that's is guarantee.

Layton, another winning horse? Named after one of the most prolific lines of thoroughbred horses in history, Layton continues perfume houses' extravagant and historic fragrance line. The fragrance has a fruity and floral oriental slant, with many profiles enclosed in a spray. The scent of it drives me crazy!

Mmmm this is delicious! I can't stop sniffing myself. This version of Bombshell has to be my favorite of them all. It brings back memories of playing in my grandmother's orchards in the summer with all the citrus fruits growing on the trees, the berry bushes lining the fences, and her beautiful flower gardens that we passed on the way there. All the while the sun beats down on my sugar coated face. It's all of these wrapped up into this perfume. It's fresh and inviting, fun and energetic, beautiful and light. It's definitely a "feel good" perfume. Nothing too complex, but it's definitely one of my favorites for summer.

Scent: going to take a slightly different approach, and do a comparative analysis: -comparing it to Spicebomb Extreme, they certainly have a similar vibe. SE is sweeter and more aggressive (spicier) in the opening, while Herod is also sweet but much smoother (not as spicy). -As the initial blast dissipates, SE definitely reveals itself to be fairly fresh (there's lavender). Herod is a warmer fragrance. -The main accords I get in SE are "cinnamon" (there's no cinnamon, here, but perhaps the mix of tobacco, caraway, and black pepper seems to create the accord), and not long after that the scent calms a bit and becomes a little smoother (thanks to the vanilla). Herod's cinnamon accord is actually cinnamon, and definitely comes off as more than just a representation of it. -The tobacco note is so smooth (as compared to SE and also DG The One, in which the accord is a bit dirtier, harsher, though not off-putting); though smooth, the tobacco it is definitely the most detectable accord. The vanilla provides a smooth sweetness, that seems to calm the black pepper and cinnamon here (those two can come off as extremely spicy, I find it astounding at how smooth the scent is in light of that). The foundation of the sweetness is definitely the cinnamon, which seems to stay a while. There is a tiny, tiny hint of freshness, which probably comes from the vetiver in the base (though the actual scent of vetiver is virtually undetectable, it's just the vibe). -Overall, if comparing Herod to SE, it is clear that Herod is a niche fragrance. The quality of the ingredients and their blend is so well done. It is very difficult to truly distinguish the other notes, like the incense (slight vibe), osmanthus, and labdanum in the heart, or even the woods in the base. The only other presence I can detect outside of the main accords is a bit of muskiness. Performance: lasts 12+ hours on my skin, projects ok for the first 3 or so, seems to get a little stronger during that time, then basically a skin scent after 8 hours, but I didn't have to dig my nose into my arm to smell it. Definitely stays on my skin much longer. I took a shower the next morning (almost 20 hours later), and as my skin started to heat up from the hot water, I started smelling it again.

Parfums de Marly Herod is definitely one of the most accurate interpretations of a smooth, pipe-type (but with a further more sophisticated glorious floral-woodsy articulation) and subtle soapy-floral tobacco's acception out there. This fragrance firstly strikes due to its claim to represent an idea of super silky (almost rubbery in one of its fleeting effects as well as we see in the central Gianfranco Ferrè for men's stage of development) vest/consistency of pipe tobacco-dominant fragrance which in this case projects also the luxurious (almost liquorous) noble facet a quality tobacco tends as well to express (namely a sparkling/intoxicating, super sophisticated, kind of aristocratic and baroquely floral sort of aura). Soapy frankincense, mild-freshly peppery spices, smooth vanilla, cypriol oil, a silky and languid osmanthus and a general widespread muskiness are all key elements revolving around this dominant pipe-soapy tobacco and working sinergically in order to turn it as a musky, well rounded and soapy affair. I have to say anyway that this rounded tobacco (and I suppose a tobacco flower works as well on its side) is really central in this fragrance and is supported by floral patterns, a touch of toasted smoke and fluidy-mild spices (cinnamon and cardamom in particular) in order to switch a sophisticated and prickly kind of velvety floral undertone under our noses. I don't get in particular any vetiver or patchouli but more properly a sort of suedish/pipe/soapy/plummy-figgy/rubbery/musky woodsy aura which is particularly chic as I equally perceive on others glorious spicy tobaccos a la E. Marinella Tabacco Imperiale (or several floral decadent tobaccos). Vanilla and cinnamom in particular provide an almost gourmandish honeyed twist a la Tom Ford Tabacco Vanille (in particular along the central stage of the trip), turning the tobacco in to an almost edible form (but never overwhelming the final dominant pipe tobacco vibe). I have to say anyway that Herod is more subtle, sophisticated and well calibrated than the more yummy/vanillic Tobacco Vanille under my profane nose. Along dry down the floral notes recedes and a drier noble (vintage and "cultured") pipe/cigar tobacco vibe (a la Teatro Olfattivo di Parma Bell'Antonio or Montagne Tobacco Noir) keeps lording alive and kicking. Performances (in particular its projection) are moderate on my skin. An adulthood refined fragrance perfect to be worn in front of a fireplace while reading a book with a glass of whisky and talking confidentially with profound and learned persons.

I received a sample of this niche perfume, and I must say that from the very first notes, Herod turns out to be an intriguing fragrance that is well suited to my tastes in terms of perfumes. A brief introduction before diving into the cologne. One of the most accomplished racehorses of 18th century Europe, Herod was a horse of uncommon achievement descended from a famous line of Turkish warhorses. To honour him, Parfums de Marly has created a genuinely spectacular fragrance. So, they named Herod after a prodigious horse and not after Herod the Great, the client king of Judea or Herodian Kingdom. Tobacco fragrances are fantastic, in particular, if well blended and not sweetened a lot. Herod is a warm fragrance with hints of cinnamon, tobacco, and vanilla that envelop you and give you that warm spicy sensation. It opens with those two spices on display. An explosion with a waxy flavour, especially in the first few minutes, and earthy accords combined with a woody note in the background. The waxy softens and transforms almost as fast as it appears. The spiciness of the pepper is notorious: if I hold my nose too close to the skin, it pinches my nostrils as the tobacco wakes up. Then, after a few more minutes, the fragrance becomes drier and woody. A timid presence of hot and spiced cinnamon appears and lasts until mid-growth, sitting on a smoked vanilla base. Slowly, the tobacco develops, is not very strong, and blends well with the other notes already present in the composition. The tobacco note here is superb, and the perfumer used a slightly different type of tobacco than the other fragrances. Here I don’t feel it too aromatic nor too fragrant. There is no scent of honey or cherry pipe tobacco, at least not at first. Instead, I perceive pure and dry tobacco, almost humid, used to produce Tuscan cigars. And this imposing tobacco plays and contrasts with the sweetest spices and notes. I distinguish a mild smoky church incense, almost powdery scent, with leathery labdanum and peach osmanthus, the latter adding a fruity touch and more delicate nuance. Despite the osmanthus flowers, the perfume never crosses the female territory. Still, the incense is never complicated. The mild smoking of the incense ensures that the spice is not like a punch in the face and simply adds a soothing texture to the aroma. It’s a fabulous combination, but I’m torn about how I feel about it. Just an aside, thinking of Herod as a dominant tobacco fragrance is misleading for me because tobacco is never the most pungent note. It mixes well with other notes and, in fact, loses its power as the fragrance runs out. The fragrance loosens up, and the base pushes it further into the traditionally masculine area, especially when the cypriol takes the stage. Cypriol comes from a plant of the papyrus family and has a smell similar to dried and smoked parchment. It is an earthy, dirty, vegetal, and green smell and a cross between dry cedar, patchouli, and vetiver. It’s an important note that I don’t think is highlighted enough in fragrances. And it’s a real shame because I love particularly bizarre and unusual notes. Oddly enough, a friendly vibe of cherry tobacco mixed with creamy smoked vanilla appears. The smoked cigar turns into sugary pipe tobacco. Tobacco, labdanum and vanilla create a soft, slightly sweet trio that grows in strength as you use it. In the end, it enhances the woodsier and earthier aspects, and I get a bit of woody from the cedar and Iso-e Super, and a hint of earthiness from the vetiver, patchouli, and musk, perhaps the same earthy impression I got in the opening. Herod is unisex with a masculine slant, and seasonally, it is a perfume suitable for cold weather. I wear it on the heavier days of fall and then the colder days of winter, and it fits perfectly, even on cool spring nights. It is not a scent that screams out for attention regarding the performance. If you’re looking for a powerhouse, this is not it. Projection stays around your arms, though it lasts several hours as a skin scent. It’s a type of fragrance that can fit well during the day at the office. It’s not stuffy or pushy, but it also has a level of sensuality that makes it suitable for a night out or date. Herod is very cosy and warm with just the right amount of sweetness which is fine, seeing as I prefer scent with a masculine slant. I base the review on a decant I have owned since November 2021. -Elysium

A masculine fragrance smells so good and modern. A perfect blend of cinnamon, vanilla & tobacco.And vetiver and cedar notes make this fragrance so masculine. Suitable for parties at night.Sillage&Longevity so good.

Herod opens with a sweet, sugary, soft and mellow accord of tobacco, resins, candied notes, sweet spices (cinnamon) and pleasant whiffs of myrrh, vanilla and light vetiver. Few notes and all quite detectable. Halfway some “candied” Lutens (like Arabie) and soft-sweet tobacco scents like Tobacco Vanille or Tabacco Toscano by Santa Maria Novella (to which the tobacco note in Herod resembles quite much; I am pretty sure they used the same aromachemicals here too). The head notes provide a light fresh breeze, I smell something halfway silky bergamot and a greenish-balsamic note (I guess this may all be due to osmanthus, which is in fact a tea-ish sweet-fresh note a bit balsamic and a bit floral). But most of all it’s tobacco and resinous spices. The tobacco note is close to the smell of fresh and humid tobacco right out of the bag, so nothing “dark” or too masculine – on the contrary, slightly humid, quite plushy and sweet. Among the Parfums de Marly range, which for what I’ve tested so far I always considered below mediocre, this is one of the nicest for sure; derivative and quite uncreative, but crisp, rich and pleasant, not (too much) synthetic, with a nice set of nuances which work fine. Good persistence and quite bold projection. Just a bit tacky perhaps, but a nice “Christmas tobacco” scent which I’d (moderately) suggest to all tobacco fans. 6,5-7/10

While some perfumes can make me feel confident and put-together, Herod literally fills me with happiness. It's a cozy and inviting fragrance that still has a masculine character due to some spiciness and a mild tobacco note. You have to like your sweet stuff to enjoy Herod.

Herod really seems like an amalgamation of other scents that I’ve enjoyed. Other than Pure Havane, it has elements of Man in Black, Burberry London, as well as B Men. Man in Black has an especially similar profile, with the spices and tobacco notes playing off of sweet ingredients. Are they exactly the same?

This is heavenly fragrance and has nothing to do with Tobacco Vanille.First of all this one takes you to an infinete meditating love journey, whereas TV keeps you standing still.I can frankly assure you that this is my very best tobbaco fragrance.

One whiff in Nordstrom, and I absolutely HAD to have it. Such a smooth spiciness; creamy and round, and a touch of exquisite tobacco. $300 later, and here we are. I hope it’s olfactory fatigue, because this absolutely VANISHES off of my skin in 3 hours. How is this possible with a PDM? Why did I choose this over Haltane? NOOOOOO!!!

Finally, Herod was arrested under 145$ for 125ML from the official Amazon store, after several attempts, and continuous monitoring, I was tired a lot, but I find it worth it in order to return it again to my perfume collection [1] - WHAT IS SPECIAL ABOUT HEROD ?

You must love "powder" to enjoy - but to me this is absolutely one of the most gorgeous scents VS has ever created, and one of my favorite scents of all time. This is signature scent-worthy, something that a "clean girl" would wear - it's effortless, clean, refreshing, feminine, and timeless. To my nose, it's: - apple blossom mixed with faint white florals - a splash of watery green apple - powdery-fresh "shampoo" notes Some cheap dupes, since it's hard to find/super pricey now with it being discontinued: - Beautiful Day Eau de Toilette (the mist released in 2023 is closer than previous versions - it's just a bit more powdery/floral than Endless Love is in dry down) - Wild Lime & Gardenia (this one is SO close to Endless Love in dry down, just not quite as strong in projection as Endless Love)

Althaïr by Parfums de Marly is a soft, comforting fragrance. Vanilla, of course, is the main star here but the other player is a woods and musk accord that is reminiscent of fresh laundry. Opening with a good amount of citrus in the form of bergamot, Althaïr gives me a bit of Ani Extrait de Parfum vibes when it is first sprayed. Citrus, some spices and florals to round it out, with the vanilla in the background. However, that’s where the similarities end with the Nishane fragrance. While Ani heads deeper into the gourmand space, Althaïr introduces the aforementioned woods and musk accord, listed as guaiac wood, musk, and ambroxan in the note pyramid. I am reminded of Creed Original Santal or Montblanc Individuel Eau de Toilette but without the eponymous sandalwood. Instead the creaminess is provided by vanilla and the floral notes, listed as orange blossom. The vanilla itself is described as "bourbon" vanilla and it does give some boozy or tobacco tones. Although vanilla is the main note, I wouldn't really describe this as a gourmand fragrance per se. For me, the cinnamon and praline are not that prominent, and the scent profile is better described as woody and sweet. It is a powerful fragrance. Projects well over 5-6 hours and lasts all day on the skin. Overall, really happy with my blind buy! It seems I’m enjoying all of Hamid Merati-Kashani’s creations of late. I even got a sample of Pegasus Exclusif with this purchase that is definitely full bottle worthy!

Althair is a great winter scent as it feautures notes as praline, cinnamon and vanilla. It lasts pretty good as i get around 8 hours of scent wearing it. Havent met anyone who doesnt like the scent when its on skin and have recieved a good amount of compliments wearing it. Could recommend this to someone who is looking for a great winter scent!

If you are a man on a date and wear this, you are probably cheating. I can see a woman ready to jump your bones based on this smell alone - a caramel, cinnamon, dessert-like scent that somehow is still decidedly masculine. I think it's the cinnamon that keeps it masculine. For an easy way to think of it, it smells like a gingerbread cookie. I don't like sweet scents, and this is borderline for me. That said, it's one of those I kept smelling on myself over and over it was so good. Not getting it since I just can't pull the trigger on a sweeter scent like this. But it's high-quality, and if I wanted to be devious and was only trying to turn a woman on with no regard for whether I like the scent myself, this would be my top choice. What the The Devil would wear.

For context: There isn't a single fragrance in the top 50 "men's" list on this site that I can even tolerate, let alone enjoy. I dislike them all, except this one. On first spray I get an opening that reminds me of the medicinal herbals of Brecourt's Mauvais Garcon with the same fresh aromatic opening and underlying depth of spice, amber, and vanilla.

Safe to say this year there has not been anything as overhyped as Althaïr and TLDR: the underlying product does not justify as much as an ounce of this hype. The red lights are glaring into your nose as soon as you spray it on. Prominent synthetic tones, the first accords I get are sweet & white floral.

This is my all-time favorite fragrance. It might not be the most unique one quiet simple, but PDM really nailed it. It is a very sweet, gourmet scent but still in a masculine way. It’s incredibly addictive once you smell it, you just can't get enough.

This is a Vanilla scent for those that like to give long hugs or cuddle with someone. It’s addictive and gets better the closer you get to someone who is wearing it. Now at first glance it isn’t anything complicated.

Amazing scent, small collections need this for sure. If your a casual fragrance fan, and want a sweet dark bomb, this is it. No designer smells like this lmfao idk what you all are on about. If you can name 3 scents similar. I bet 2 or them are niche. Case closed.

Oh yes! No one can compare to you gurl! The 1900s and early 2000s...there is no era that can compare. I loved this fragrance SO much and I hate that it was discontinued. So fresh, green, strong, yet pure.... Simplistic and refined. Although I currently own the 2013 release, it's not entirely the same. Not disappointing, just not 100%. However, it does satisfy my longing for this one. This was tha BOMB back in the day!

I've allowed Victoria's Secret Pink to stay on my skin the entire day, despite wanting to wash it off when I first applied it this morning. I'll start by saying that this fragrance certainly lasts. Very few inexpensive fragrances have managed to achieve this, so that's a huge feat in itself. The scent is not really my cup of tea, but putting personal preferences aside, Pink is very fun, crisp and girly. The best seasons in which to wear this fragrance would be during Spring and Summer. In the colder months this fragrance comes across as a little jarring and sharp. On my skin, the opening was very strong and acidic. The citrus accords play a huge part in this fragrance's composition and aren't always pleasant, at least not to my nose. Thankfully, once settled, Pink shows a softer side with the introduction of soapy freesia, lily of the valley, peony and a green, tart-like neroli accord. Although not particularly complex nor outstanding, Pink does grow on you over time. The drydown is actually more than pleasant. A powdery floral blend with a subtle hint of citrus and musk. It is at this stage that I understand how this fragrance could have inspired countless flankers after its release. Pink seems to be very well-received. In terms of citric florals, Pink does have its good points. Its clean and feminine approach would certainly appeal to many women, and even young girls, searching for something inoffensive and easy to wear. Admittedly I am not overly thrilled with Pink, but I am glad to have tried it. Victoria's Secret lingerie and products are not sold in Australia.

Christmas is slowly coming, and I am longing for fragrances fitting to my festal mood. This is exactly, what I get from OAJAN. Pie, honey cake, cinnamon, sugar-coat. OAJAN presents you generously his sweetness and broad smile. Not only you, but everyone who stays in the same airspace with you. Be careful, if you have guests, they will expect cake from you :-) Top is a whirl driving you deep in acceptance of OAJAN. Enormous richness is buried under the coating. Woods, spices, divine davana, almond, resins, a totally gourmand fragrance, which is still more complex than a normal gourmand. Heart is the real miracle here. Base is simplier and easy to understand the overflowing sweetness, vanilla kicks out others from the ropes. I tested it before going to German lessons, and learning and concentrating was a really tough task. Conclusions after testing (and falling in love with) OAJAN: - strong, not feasible for daily wear, and especially not for business issues - unisex - winter fragrance - comparable perfume: NOEL AU BALCON - hopeless fact against acceptable financial status: I want a full bottle.

Yes, Oajan smells very much like Ambre Narguile and its counterparts Helium and Or du Serail (and Haram, though I don't remember it well.) What is different? For one, Oajan has the strongest sillage and longevity of all those mentioned above. It is also quite expensive but you get more for your money than with Ambre Narguile. However, AN has a smoother character and is overall just a little bit better done than Oajan. Oajan is sour and honeyed with some cinnamon (wish it had more cinnamon) and benzoin. There is a strange liqueur-like character to it. I would recommend Oajan for sweet-lovers and lovers of Ambre Narguile-type scents but don't find that AN lasts or projects enough. Do you need both? I do, but I don't think the average person does. If you want an "expensive" smelling prestige creation, go for AN. If you want a sillage monster that lasts all day, do the Oajan.

That’s MY opinion on this one. From the first time I smelled it, I absolutely HAD to have it. The only thing that prevented me from grabbing it right there on the spot the first time was that my wife wasn’t as into it as I was. I finally grabbed. With spice heavy scents, you really have to enjoy the style. Spicebomb, Burberry, etc. If you don’t like the “spice cabinet” vibes they give, you won’t like them. This one EXPONENTIATES that. Such a rich feeling it gives with such high quality notes. The cinnamon is absolutely GORGEOUS. It takes gourmand to a new level. Projection is fantastic, going 3-4ft in radius for an easy 8 hours, and the sillage trail you’ll leave behind will leave people longing to know where it is coming from, and where you went. It checks ALL the boxes in this department. It’s a staple for well dressed special events in colder weather, and you will SHINE when you use it. Try before you buy, but if you like Spicebomb Extreme, and want a comparison, this one would be named “Nuclear Spice Ultimate”.

You know what they say if you want to sell your house you’ve got to bake an apple pie, so the smell makes you feel at home. This fragrance also makes this friendly welcoming gesture. Maybe it’s not exactly apple I’m smelling but it’s definitely got that vibe with its cinnamon and vanilla. Definitely gourmand going on here. I’ll put this in the same category as "Angels' Share | Kilian" . I find these fragrances both smelling incredible and they paint this festive kind of painting when you close your eyes. I read people complaining about longevity but I have no issues with it. In the Christmas holidays I wore it sometimes smelling it all day long. Review based on a sample from the discovery set in 2024.

I've been hearing about Oajan and how it smells like Christmas spirit and spicy apple pie. Now that we're in the week and days leading up to Christmas, I had to try it for myself and see if it was true. Definitely more masculine to me, which is the reason why I won't be getting it, but it's a very nice scent nonetheless. Warm, comforting and all-around lovely to wear for comfort, but also for feeling elegant and put-together. It really does have that Christmas vibe I heard about. Instead of smelling like apple pie though, it smells like spiced apple juice to my nose, even though there's no apples in the notes. Breaking it down, I have the impression cinnamon is why our nose picks up on an apple vibe. Honey is also present, giving a sirupy, almost liquorish aspect to the fragrance. The middle notes are all about warmth and an ambery, resinous accord. The drydown has some powdery vanilla and tonka beans. Davana is a strong note on my skin (always has been when I've encountered the ingredient in fragrances). It reinforces the liquor and adds a touch of exotic spiciness. Patchouli finally adds some woodiness at the end of its drydown. Like I mentioned previously, it leans masculine to my nose due to the spicy aspect and the liquorish facet I'm getting which is why I won't be getting it. I do have to say though, it's a great cold weather choice for a man and I wouldn't mind smelling it on somebody else's skin. Try it out for yourself!

The composition here is actually quite complex, but what you get is primarily a warm and cozy cinnamon, honey and amber with creamy vanilla, sweet fluffy tonka, resinous benzoin, slightly earthy patchouli and musk. There is a bit of a waxy feel with nuances of leather which I can attribute to the labdanum, artemisia and osmanthus. Very nice.

I’ve cherished Oajan since 2018, initially owning just a modest 10ml decant. It wasn’t until 2020 that I finally invested in the 125ml bottle, specifically the older version with the italic font, filled to 80% volume. As many fragrance lovers have said, Oajan truly embodies the essence of Christmas or a snuggy and cosy winter evening.

I do get annoyed when people compare perfumes to others, especially when there’s a massive difference and timeframe between them,nOajan is a unique fragrance in its own right. Composed 7 years before Angels Share, so if you were to try to compare, Angels Share would be a dupe. But I’m not saying that, similar compositions, does not mean similar perfume.

This fragrance was my first experience with a true gourmand, and perhaps the reason why I find myself chasing gourmands more than I'd expected to. My second blind-buy, I was looking to treat myself with a new fragrance last Christmas. I couldn't resist the temptation of the notes and descriptions I'd read, so I bought Oajan .

Oajan perfectly portrays the beauty of winter. A cold Christmas Day by the fireplace and you eat a hot cinnamon apple pie. Overall I believe that oajan is just a perfect winter fragrance for both genders however it does lean more to the masculine side. Price is fair considering the performance and the beauty of the scent.

If diamonds had a smell this is what it would smell like: Sharp scent that's vanilla, metalic, amber and a lil earthy from the almond+green apple fruity sweetness. This reminds me a lot of Bond No.9 Laffayette street. It can be a little too sweet or strong for some but you can wear this anywhere if you like it. Super versatile, daytime anytime fragrance.

Oh boy I’m quite a Pafums de Marley fanboy but this one doesn’t sit well with me at all. We started off pretty good. Cool, it’s got this almond note which I love and look out for in hand soaps etc. So I got this really clean vibe after getting up, having a shower and then a bit of Pegasus. But it doesn’t take long before this dense, cloying, heavy smell of white flowers takes the wheel and literally goes for a joyride for hours! It just doesn’t end! It appears that I am particularly sensitive to white flowers like jasmine. And therefore this is the first PdM I had to scrub off my body because I couldn’t stand it anymore.

PDM Pegasus is an incredibly creamy, powdery and sweet blend. It opens up similar to a cream soda with hints of orange, possibly due to the jasmine and bergamot combination with almond. The drydown continues to go into a similar direction but a bit more linear. Vanilla and sandalwood provide a clean base which is not to sweet unlike most other gourmands. Performance is quite good, can feel it in the air hours after application and stays on clothing for a while.

The aroma of this is very bright, & also very rounded in the sense of there being no sharp corners or vorsprungen (somehow that word seems to fit better than 'prominences'). It' s one of those 'fumes that seem °slender° on first assay, but transpires well hefty in course of actual wearing; & it's a long time ago now that I learned not to be putten-off by that, whereas had I not learnt it I would have boughten ~Layton~ instead. I do think this could plausibly be deemed an °oakmossless chypre°. In its particularities it is a tremendously unique fragrance; and I wonder whether its uniquity proceeds from the use of the bitter-almond (presumably cyanide-free (otherwise the IFRA ^might just^ get involved!)) ; but whatever it is, the synergy of it and the lavender engenders a really quite lovelily astringent quasi-chypre effect. And the muskiness is 7 to 8 on the muskiness-richter scale, and a surpassingly thoroughly polished & spirity muskiness at that!
when i used it i felt Orgasm .. it's really has the charm of men. you all have to try it. that's what I've been looking for .. thank you.

this is an all time best! It is the only Niche fragrance I am willing to shell out a Niche fragrance price! I have how ever found a true clone! so I no longer have to, but with any fine art collector you prize your original pieces!

PDM scents are often enjoyable and interesting. However, Pegasus has only the former characteristic, and not the latter. The scent opens fresh, reminds me a little of shower gel. Yet, unlike other shower gel scents, Pegaus is warm; likely due to the vanilla note. As it develops, the almond note gradually takes the dominance. Pegasus is enjoyable and enjoyed.

Something about this fragrance feels a bit off to my nose, making it my least favorite from Parfums de Marly. it’s not a bad fragrance—just not one I’d purchase a full bottle of. The fragrance opens with a blend of marzipan, delicate florals, and woody nuances. At the top, I mostly pick up heliotrope with a hint of cypress, giving it a softly elegant vibe.

Wouldn't call it gourmand. I'd call it creamy fresh. It has a soft laundry detergent smell that blends with almond and lavander. It's very smooth, safe, and powerful for 3 hours then later relaxes into an almond creamy type scent. Over its very smooth and almost fresh. Uplifting while unique and inviting. The name fits very well.

I had been eyeing the Pegasus for a while now. I always liked Herod from PDM, but recently fell in love with Layton, hence it was hard to make up the decision about Pegasus while I enjoyed sniffing the 2mL sample of this aromatic gem.

I wasn't sure if I would like this all that much since I haven't liked any other Bombshell release, but I'm really liking this. It has a bit of a soapy opening that lasts for like 30 seconds before it smooths out into this sweetened floral scent on my skin. The deep dry down is sugar-sweet and I love it. Would recommend trying this one skin though, because the card did nothing for the scent.
