Athalia. Dark, noble, and mysterious, the bottle exudes an aura of elegance. Cool, distant, and different from her sisters, the fragrance unfolds. Initially, I feared that Athalia would overwhelm me with its olfactory power. That the scent would be cumbersome and unruly to wear.

What have I done? Inspired by the reviews on Parfumo, I took a blind buy plunge. I'm trembling. Yes, because I hold my package with my latest catch in my hands. Was it wise? No idea. That will soon reveal itself to me. At least I took advantage of a special offer. The pain of a bad purchase can thus be slightly mitigated. I hope. I really hope.

Back then, Athalia, together with the wonderful Delina Exclusif, was my entry into the niche world and also into the category of iris fragrances. The black and gold design of the bottle intrigued me and made me reach for it immediately. Once sprayed, I was instantly enchanted. A cool, silky scent welcomed me right away.

I never actually wanted to write a review because I don't feel competent enough as a newcomer. But Athalia inspires me to share my impression with you. Please forgive me if it isn't expressive enough. I learned about Athalia through my best friend. "Smells musty + like an old governess," she said.

…and saw that this is being heralded as a “hidden gem”. I dug a bit deeper, and saw it was compared to Reflection and Le Male, so I pulled the trigger. I’ve given it a few wearings, and I do see why people would compare them, but it’s much closer to Le Male than it is to Reflection. Reflection is like if Le Male were made of Diamonds and Gold. A sheer elegance. Not the same thing, but a very successful, very very distant relative. Now Darley is right in between the two, but closer to the Le Male feeling. Still a much higher tier in quality, but you smell the similarities more. It’s much fuller and richer, and if you smell them side by side it’s obvious. However….. a non-fraghead might not pick up that difference, so be aware of that…. If you’re going to get all mental if someone mistakes your PDM for JPG, it might not be what you want. The scent is gorgeous, but I have that bias. I like these types of scents. Better than JPG, not as good as Amouage. Performance wise? It’s got a moderate projection 1-3ft, with a nice sillage that follows you for 3 hours, then becoming a skin scent for another 3-4 hours. Is that worthy of $300+? Nope, but you can find it at discounters for a more worthy price. I don’t regret it, and I love PDM, but Amouage is my favorite house for a reason. ;-)

I always dismissed the see-through bottles of Parfums de Marly as the cheaper, lesser releases. The pony releases as you will. That is, until I sprayed it on my neck one day visiting the perfumery. First I smelled nothing. Hah there you have it, I thought. But during my trip homeward this creamy, soothing smell started to manifest. Weirdly it gave me childhood flashbacks. It reminds me a bit of vitamin drops we got as a kid. Difficult to categorize this. It isn’t woody. It isn’t floral. Just creamy I guess. Okay so it isn’t the most prominent outspoken smell. It doesn’t radiate like a mad man (I wish it did a little harder). But I still find it rather unique and definitely a winner in my book. Maybe a pony but still an award winning fullblood.

This is definitely one of the most underrated from the house. I really enjoy this scent, it’s minty fresh with some added citrus and spice. It’s a more refined version of JpG le male so if you like that DNA you will Like this as well. Versatile and could be worn year round in my opinion. I don’t think anybody could find this offensive. Good easy reach that smell very pleasant

My last comment for now on a Parfums de Marly fragrance. There may be a few more to follow on occasion. My summary for this beautiful brand: Most fragrances are very safe and will likely appeal to the general public. I have tested Layton, Pegasus, Herod, Godolphin, Oajan, Carlisle, and also this Darley. The others haven't convinced me from the pyramids yet, but those I have tested are very solid and some are worth purchasing. Some, however, are a bit overpriced. Now to Darley: A fragrance with little attention here. 3 comments and 2 statements. Justified or definitely worth a test? In my opinion, a fragrance with little recognizability, where I expect more for the money. A really pleasant scent that doesn't stand out unpleasantly anywhere. It is indicated here as a fragrance twin to Reflection Man. Rightly so? Broadly speaking, perhaps in a similar direction, but upon closer inspection, there are very large differences. Even though this Darley has slight floral notes, they are rather in the background. At the start, it begins with a lot of mint, very pleasantly fresh paired with subtle citrus notes and fresh lavender. From the DNA, I find it more similar to Le Male than Reflection. Here, however, it is significantly lighter due to a lot of fresh mint. A pleasant freshness with a touch of sensuality. Also pleasant due to the beautiful base with soft woody notes, amber, patchouli, and a nice but subtle sweetness from the tonka bean. This is very well balanced and doesn't lean too much in one direction. A very gentle fragrance that should appeal to many. The performance is decent, but the sillage is quite close to the skin. Even freshly sprayed, it is rather subtle and disappointing for this DNA. The longevity is okay with a few hours. Thanks to the rather weak sillage, it is versatile. Unisex is justified, although I find it more masculine. Especially due to the similarities to its fragrance twins. Due to the high price, I cannot recommend purchasing it. The price is 185 euros for 125ml. In many shops, you can get it a bit cheaper, but still significantly overpriced for this DNA. Reflection is not much more expensive than this. As a budget alternative, I consider Rasasi Maa Arwaak for him. A great low-budget fragrance that goes in a similar direction and has a significantly better performance. I give it an 8.0 because it is really very pleasant. However, I wouldn't buy it for this price. Addendum April 2022: I have since purchased this fragrance. About half of the MSRP. Probably more of a slow seller, and for that reason, they are likely sold at a discount more often. Definitely a fair price, as this Darley already has elevated designer quality. Smells like a freshly showered Le Male in an elegant way. A fragrance that can be worn anytime and never causes too much friction. It should definitely only be bought on sale, as I believe it offers too little for the Marley prices.

At Parfums de Marly, they love horses. Once again, the name hints at equestrian sports! Tonka bean, sandalwood, lavender, orange blossom, mint - just by looking at the pyramid, certain similarities become apparent to the perfume enthusiast. Exactly, here the successful scents of Francis Kurkdjian are being interpreted: Le Male and Fleur du Male. This has often been attempted in the budget segment, but rarely in the high-priced category. For good reason, because despite or precisely because of the controversy that Le Male and Fleur du Male provoke, the air here is very thin. Surpassing something unique (and demanding a higher price for it) is a rare challenge. This challenge has been successfully met by Rancé's Francois Charles, which is why it is used as a comparison scent. It leans towards a spicy direction, with the gasoline-like Le Male note being underpinned with a certain breadth and balanced by neroli hints. However, Darley has a slightly darker, rougher character. The gasoline note feels less refined and has this somewhat tar-like undertone. It is thus darker than in Le Male and aligns more with the interpretation in Fleur du Male. On the other hand, it lacks the fully opulent floral quality of Fleur du Male. Orange blossom seems to be a tricky note. It easily becomes too sweet, too opulent, too sticky. It is probably a challenge for a perfumer to tame it. Here, it is done with a lot of mint, more than in Le Male. The mint carries its freshness into the drydown. Without a doubt, Darley is a very good perfume. The quality is right. However, I prefer the overall finer, gentler, and yet more complex Francois Charles. And Darley does not surpass either Le Male or Fleur du Male. The gasoline-tar note corresponds more to Fleur de Male, but Darley shies away from its eccentric floral quality. Tonka and mint bring it closer to Le Male again. Viewed this way, it is neither fish nor fowl. And by no means better than the obvious models.

This is a beautiful masculine scent, more suited for the evening. Rosemary, mint, and lavender showcase the sweetness with their coolness so beautifully that the fragrance constantly plays with the contrast of warm and cool. In the heart, you can already sense tonka bean and spicy notes; there’s a moment when I smell something that reminds me of anise.

Not immediately noticeable after the first spray, but becoming clearer over time: you have smelled this fragrance note before! Except for the very prominent mint, which pushes itself to the forefront in the top note, the similarity to Le Male is undeniable.

Hello everyone, I began my fragrance journey in 1999 with Le Mâle Eau de Toilette and after over 20 (!) empty bottles, I think I can give you a decent opinion on it. I also know Reflection Man very well since 2012, and it was my wedding fragrance - the third comparison follows here.
This is my third test of Parfums de Marly and this time I really like the scent. “Darley Arabian is one of the three founding stallions of the English Thoroughbred.

In my opinion, a very noble, fresh, slightly powdery, and not overpowering clean scent, which is ideal for the office - if the day is nice enough for it. In winter, I probably wouldn't wear it due to its delicacy.

When PDM announced an exclusif version of Valaya was being released, I was super excited mainly because I wasn’t crazy about the harshness of the OG. While I do like citruses, I think the composition of Valaya lacks balance and rhythm. However, I think switching out some of the notes in the OG definitely upgraded the scent profile and wear in this new Valaya Exclusif. To start, that pesky peach note is thankfully gone. I’m sorry to anyone that liked it, but it added an unnecessary cloying-ness to an already flamboyant scent. Instead, a smooth almond is substituted and gives VE a softer, smoother opening. Paired with the powdery notes in the heart, VE is notably more powdery than the OG, which may or may not work for you depending on your preference. As someone not fond of powdery scents, I quite enjoy the powder here cause it helps to soften the sharp citrus and dry woods in the base. It still has that “clean” feel without being as soapy as the original. VE is also much more wearable than the OG, without losing its strength. It’s sweet, pretty, and feminine, just like the OG, but has a little more of a mature vibe. Lastly, I will say that I agree with the commenter that said this one and the OG aren’t synonymous to Delina and it’s Exclusif. If you have the OG, you can probably skip this because the scent profiles are very similar (unlike the Delina’s!). But if you’re like me and couldn’t stand certain aspects of the original, definitely give this one a sample. It’s new in my collection and I’m excited to test her out more when the weather gets warmer.

You can definitely detect the original Valaya DNA but here it's less crisp. It's softer, a little gourmandy, peachy and creamy. It has a more forgiving, musky motherly vibe, while Valaya is the youthfull high energy princess in a blindingly bright white, tight dress. Equally as long lasting (on clothes it lasts through a wash), but a little less loud.

I've always liked the idea of the original Valaya more than the scent itself. I never got that ethereal angelic vibe people talked about; it always came off as screechy and chlorine-like on my skin, which I was so disappointed by, but I am so pleasantly surprised by the exclusif version. It removes that aldehydic peach scent I was bothered by, but introduces these soft and powdery almond notes that balance the fresh citrus and florals. My favorite from the house so far because their other scents are too sweet and feminine for my liking(mainly Oriana, Delina, Cassili). Might grab the 30ml of this, but need to test it out more.

Tested with 2ml and there’s something odd about the nutty almond sweetness and added powdery notes mixed with the sharp Valaya DNA (still very present - the dry down smelled almost exactly the same as the OG with that peppery yet still feminine vibe). The original just makes more cohesive sense to my nose. This is definitely not as different as Delina is to Delina Exclusif…if you already have one Valaya, do not think you need the other unless this is your signature scent.

In a nod to Valaya OG, this opens with a burst of Peach Schnapps on ice with white lemonade, but you only get time for a few sips. It settles quickly into a sweet floral, freshened with the mandarin and a hint of creamy almond. And then… oh…. Is that?? Is that ANANYA!! What the?? … ok… Hello,,, YOU! Yes, stalker vibes here because I’ve been on the hunt for a perfume that smells like Ananya Perfume Oil from The Body Shop for 20 years. This was a beast of a sweet, fruity, fresh yet creamy, floral scent that could’ve knocked out a horse from 20 miles. My mother hated it because it gave her a headache, damn, it even gave me a headache. But that didn’t stop teenage me from dousing myself in it, whilst triple layering my Rimmel coffee shimmer lipstick. But it was so different and it was SO beautiful and I shan’t be told different! Despite a description of notes and aromas that never seemed to match up on the ongoing hunt, this holy grail of the 90s has remained ever elusive. And here I am! I found you! Excited much? Oh yes! So now I can’t properly review Valaya Exclusif. My scent memory has kicked my nostrils right in the emotional feels. My nose enjoys ambroxan but it’s a struggle to describe the dry down because my brain is fixated on Ananya. There’s creamy vanilla, yet fresh slight woodiness from the Akigalawood yet it’s sweet and clean. This doesn’t have the powering strength of Ananya, it’s delicate in comparison and defo more sophisticated with a powdery, milky cashmere edge to it… maybe it’s an Ananya for grown ups?

This perfume grows on me enough to like it. At first, I am ambivalent. The top notes hit, and I don't mind them, but I don't really like them. More than anything, I get a sense of smelling of good soap in a clean bathroom that has decent potpourri. It's pleasant, but I don't necessarily want to be wearing it.

A creamier, less sharp version of the OG, with a touch more almond. Warm and clean at the same time, with lots of underlying powder. Very elegant and sweetly feminine; a scent Cinderella would wear to the ball. Beautifully fresh, and somehow almost angelic. Reminds me a little of lemonade. Projection is quiet, longevity moderate.

I didn’t purchase Valaya Exclusif when it was launched as I didn’t actually like Valaya as much as their other perfumes. I seem to have some kind of pattern as Valaya Exclusif works the same as Delina Exclusif did, it is a beautiful and well balanced perfume without the loud screechiness.

I have experienced some great fragrance loves, but when it comes to sweets, there can only be one for me: Raffaelo. The delicately melting coconut cream, the crunchy almond core - and that wonderfully beautiful advertising scenario. How I would love to be the blonde beauty in the white dress, enjoying Caribbean flair and coconut creations all day long! In my search for the perfect summer scent, I have long been on the lookout for that Raffaelo feeling. Unfortunately, in vain. As lovely as I smelled of coconut, the fragrances only transported me to the local swimming lake - nothing like a luxury vacation by the turquoise sea. But then, on a beautiful summer day, I happened to come across a mini of Very Sexy Now 2014. One spray and I could almost hear the airport announcement: Flight A123 to Aruba, ready for take-off. The surprising thing is: Very Sexy Now doesn’t actually smell like Raffaelo tastes. This coconut ball is more zesty than velvety. Creamy, but not cream. Sweet, but not a candy. I smell delicious coconut milk and fruits, juicy and with a sparkling acidity. And yet, the scent immediately transports me to the Caribbean beach. Stylishly dressed, I lean back on my lounge chair, let a Raffaelo melt on my tongue, and bask in the admiring glances of others. The only thing that keeps me from a permanent Caribbean vacation: My personal coconut dream is unfortunately a limited edition and no longer available anywhere. So I guard the last drops like a treasure - and allow myself to be whisked away to paradise only when I suffer from acute summer withdrawal.

This remains one of my favorite fragrances. It compliments every occasion. First date, second date, fourth date, work, brunch, dinner with the family. It’s so innocent and unassuming but simultaneously elevated. I feel youthful and mature. One thing I love above all? A good dichotomy. it is so divine. I tried this as a decant first, and ultimately purchased a full bottle that I got for a REALLY good price. The juice in my full bottle is a bit more nuanced than the decant I purchased, and it carries so much more *je ne sais quoi* that feels like the embodiment of who I am. It is currently one of my comfort scents. It doesn’t bother you while you’re wearing it. In fact, I was at a friends house last night. I took off my hoodie, and when I was putting it back on, I thought “holy fuck what is that smell” — it was like a warm comforting hug. That’s how good it is to me. I’m actually confused as to why anyone would be extremely disappointed by this perfume. If you smell the scent, and if you understand its energy, then you should recognize that is not a fragrance that is best complemented by a loud sillage. This is the kind of perfume that reaches those within an arms length. So there is some there is some space it claims and occupies, but it does not dominate and that was not an oversight. I’ve been getting into Violet presumes lately. I adore them. This is not Violet on an island, alone and overwhelming. It has that soft powdery touch that places you upon a cloud, and there is a sweetness. Almost like a more mature ‘DIME I love your smell, baby’ gorgeous, sweet, but so subtly you believe without question.

Palatine is lovely fresh but linear violet scent with a bit of fruitiness. The sillage and longevity are moderate and definitely much weaker than in Delina or Valaya. I understand why a lot of people are disappointed with this fragrance since it feels a bit generic and you can probably find similar fragrance cheaper. But as Parfums de Marly is my favourite house, I own most perfumes from their women’s collection. What I like about this house is that from their collection you can find a perfume for every occasion and season. Palatine is very versatile and easy reach, and as it isn’t beast mode, suits many occasions. I think it holds its place in my collection and the purple bottle is very pretty.

My impression from notes and reviews was that PdM was kind of a "bro" line, mostly appropriate for clubbing with fruity sweet and loud perfumes. When considering the entire Parfums de Marly's Arabian Breed collection, Nisean is right on the money. A modern day classic. It really strongly reminds me of Epic Amouage at first, which is definitely a good thing. Also it resembles the resinous Jubilation XXV, for me at least. Rich, opulent scent, dusty a bit. Smells like a mature and refined gentlemanly scent, very masculine. Top shelf stuff !

So far, I have always felt a slight discomfort when it comes to scents that are sour, resinous, smoky, and animalistic. Parfums de Marly has quite a bit to offer in that regard. Sometimes, however, I find myself inexplicably drawn, as if controlled by an external force, to a very specific shelf (Hamburg, Alsterhaus, back right, the last stand before the leather goods). Here, I feel not only spatially but also olfactorily in the "niche." Especially the dark matte bottles from Marly seem to have a special effect on me. "Nisean" It starts citrusy-peppery (pink pepper, lime, grapefruit, exactly as described). Some of the other components are already recognizable or can be sensed. The citrusy-peppery aspect seems to be skillfully layered. The base consists of incense and light, bright wood notes. At this stage, the scent feels somewhat (I’m collecting words now) cool, vibrating, metallic, aloof, and precisely polished. Yet, the whole composition still feels homogeneous (perhaps due to a hint of rose with sandalwood?). I find no comparison to other perfumes. This phase lasts on the test strip for 5 - 6 hours without budging in either direction. On my skin, it becomes a bit softer after about 3 - 4 hours but not "warmer." It’s like a kind of tension arc of citrusy, peppery, resinous that remains ever-present, around which the other ingredients form a sort of cloud or shimmering corona. I sense no trace of sweetness. No oriental opulence. Nisean is very idiosyncratic. And that’s a good thing. And to conclude the scent journey, I’ll take a wide swing. Horse enthusiasts and fools may want to test it themselves. Towards the end, a fine, very subtle scent wafts that I would describe as grainy-dusty (like pouring oats into a feed box) and leathery-animalistic (tack, saddle). That may sound really strange, but that’s how I perceive it. And even better, I find it smells incredibly good. It smells high-quality. Test it yourself and take your time with it. Progression: Lime / Pepper >>> Resins, Incense >>> Woods (hint of grain, hint of leather, hint of animalistic) Nisean is one of those fragrance creations that will polarize. A typical love-it-or-hate-it scent. There’s nothing in between. It doesn’t ingratiate itself. How did I read it recently? Something like this: "In love and in war, the middle way means certain death." (Unfortunately, this can also apply to perfumes sometimes). Yes,.....want to have. Point.

Today is my 5th Parfumo birthday and this is my 80th comment. When I registered here and only owned one perfume, I never thought I would engage with this topic so deeply. It is all the more beautiful to look back on the collected experiences and to have gained some insights. This can be well illustrated using Nisean as an example: 1) Both personal preferences and olfactory perception change over time. It is therefore worthwhile to test certain fragrances again after a longer period. If I hadn’t done that, I wouldn’t own Portrait of a Lady and Nisean now, for example. 2) Even brands that initially seem uninteresting can still launch fragrances that you really like. Parfums de Marly offers many gourmands/sweet scents - a category that I do not like at all. I am equally uninterested in horses. And yet, I have two fragrances from the brand in my collection: Percival and Nisean. 3) It is basically impossible to realistically assess sillage/projection. One's own perception has its limits, and the nose - or rather the brain - quickly adapts to certain fragrance ingredients, so that you often no longer perceive them correctly. Although Nisean lasts quite a long time, I initially categorized it as more intimate, but feedback from others made it clear to me that the performance is significantly better. 4) Sometimes names or background information about perfumes lead you to acquire certain trivia. For instance, I would never have known that 'Nisean' refers to a long-extinct Iranian horse breed that was particularly sought after for its large, robust physique and speed... (The list could certainly go on.) And how does Nisean smell now? - Overall, it is less complex than the listed notes might suggest, yet still interesting and balanced enough. Right after spraying, lime and grapefruit are already noticeable, but rather sour and not typically refreshing, as the woody-resinous side that essentially defines Nisean reveals itself right from the start. As is often the case, the fresh facets on my skin are less intense than on paper. Saffron is very present in the first hours and gives the fragrance a pleasant spiciness without being too demanding. I would never have recognized floral notes in a blind test, as the characteristics that best describe Nisean are woody, dry, and balsamic. Patchouli is one of the dominant notes, but in the form of the fragrance ingredient Akigalawood, it is significantly cleaner and less earthy than usual. Sandalwood also contributes a warm woodiness but does not come across as creamy, as is sometimes the case. Through cistus/labdanum, Nisean acquires a darker, resinous quality, which fortunately is not accompanied by a heavy amber accord. Certain synthetic fragrance ingredients were probably used here to prevent Nisean from becoming too heavy and too dark. Therefore, I am not bothered that the development - aside from the top notes - is quite linear. I find it pleasant that no overpowering spiciness, no flowers, and especially no cloying sweetness ruin the fragrance. Nisean feels calming to me, yet strong and somewhat dark. But who knows...

This is quite a noble little water! I read numerous reviews and watched videos about this scent. It was said to be very resinous and musty and not for everyone. I thought the 113 euros were a waste. But when I sprayed it for the first time, I was more than pleasantly surprised. Yes, this scent is resinous and earthy, but for me in a totally noble way.

This will be my first somewhat "longer" comment and I hope it's not all rubbish what I'm going to write here. :D Very interesting scent! When I first smelled it, I thought, "WHAT IS THAT?! What have you gotten yourself into this time? :(" (yes, it was a blind pick :D) When I dug it out of the last corner of my apartment a few weeks later and sniffed it again...

The Nisean is, in my opinion, a truly beautiful and really good fragrance. Here we get a certain kind of freshness, a distinctly peppery freshness. This is paired with lovely woody undertones and dark spicy-smoky vibes. The Nisean also comes across as oriental and is generally just a very high-quality smelling fragrance that is simply beautiful.

I'll start from the beginning: this is my first comment on one of the first fragrances I managed to snag as a sample here in the Souk. Before that, I only dared to try the big names from PdM, and Layton really hit my taste. When I first smelled Nisean, I thought at first, "smells kind of old," resinous and a bit citrusy in the top notes. But interesting.

Hello everyone, Tonight, I would like to talk about a fragrance that has been forgotten and overlooked... many of us know PDM's usual suspects, like "Layton | Parfums de Marly," "Carlisle | Parfums de Marly," "Herod | Parfums de Marly," "Pegasus | Parfums de Marly," etc., but in almost every (!

This is definitely a fruity floral; the flower note being in the center stage. On me it opens with a mild citrus note and quickly goes into a fresh & clean honeysuckle note. I love this lighthearted phase, as honeysuckle tends to be a little heady on me. However the dry down veers into a more masculine route. It almost smells smoky - the unmistakable trace of vetiver on my skin. It also serves to anchor the honeysuckle very well and gives it a bit more dimension. Overall, I'd say this is just another typical Victoria's Secret fruity floral however, that slightly indolic honeysuckle note really hooked me in so I purchased a full bottle. :)

First of all: I love Victoria's Secret, and whenever I see a store, I can't hold back. So, two years ago, the scene: Copenhagen Airport. I saw the sign, whispered to my husband: "just a quick one, something small" :) and was in a cloud... After what felt like 15 minutes, I returned with Heartbreaker and Heavenly in my bag and... an oversized beach bag that I got as a gift. My husband, of course, didn't know that; he thought I had bought out the whole store, laughed his head off, and said, "that's just typical..." That's why Heartbreaker is a feel-good scent for me, even though it really doesn't last long on me. After two hours, it's time for a reapplication, but I love the bergamot opening the most anyway. (and the bottle is so delightfully kitschy!)

Big juicy vetiver with a hint or slight incense coming through.........i'm guessing because of the cardamom and resin notes. The quality is clear and present, not cheap smelling, at all. Maybe green enough for summer and incense-y enough for cooler temps. Good life and radiates well. Felt good wearing this one.

At first, very different smelling masculine vetiver dominated fragrance. Nicely blended. No surprise there since PDM perfumers are all masters. Definitely for mature male user. Tried it just few times, experience improved gradually. This type of fragrance grows on you over time. Acquired taste is the expression. You get in a habit of wanting to smell it, then you get used to it. Then you like it. However, my collection is jam packed, so I ended up gifting it to my father. He likes it. I received this Byerley as a gift, at least it made my father a happy person. It quickly became his No.

Good evening folks, how are you doing? I think I should be especially polite to the ladies here today because I’m about to say something that might not sit well with them. The fragrance we’re discussing today is Byerley by Parfums de Marley. So, Byerley is the name of a legendary horse from the 17th and 18th centuries, which, along with two other horses (Godolphin Barb and Darley Arabian), is considered one of the founding fathers of today’s Thoroughbred horses. And why should all this annoy the ladies? Well… because I’m about to admit that, personally, I find horses a bit boring and have never really connected with them :D Sure, in medieval movies or fantasy films, I find horses as mounts extremely cool, but as “sport animals” that excite the masses, I personally find them rather dull. I like all animals in general, but I just can’t relate to horses (and no, I don’t just like cats…!). Therefore, I also don’t understand the obsession many women have with these creatures… and no, it’s certainly not because of the “somewhat long thingamajig” of these beings, as many guys would immediately think and start fantasizing about or wishing to have such a long… appendage to, well… then also pass as a “stallion” and show off with it… :DD But as I said, I don’t know why so many women love horses so much… So, before you all behead me, either because I mentioned something dirty or called horses boring (which also includes unicorns… ugh… what’s the deal with unicorns (preferably under a colorful rainbow, right?…)?? :DD), let me at least describe the fragrance here first :D The Fragrance: The fragrance starts off quite citrusy fresh with bitter and woody notes. I can distinctly smell the bergamot, which comes across as a bit riper, somewhat like those barbershop scents, just less old-fashioned. The cardamom adds a nice, spicy sweetness, and as mentioned, there are woods, with cedarwood being the most prominent. Over time, the fragrance becomes a bit more balsamic and softer, although it still retains its citrusy and fresh scent. The woods now also smell with a combination of indeterminate resins, and I would also say that now and then you can catch a whiff of a pine forest from all the woods, which I find nice. Towards the base, it smells a bit more barbershop-like, but still not necessarily very old-fashioned, even though the fragrance gives the impression that it’s not meant for the younger crowd. By the way, the fragrance is no longer particularly fresh at this point but rather warmer and significantly more balsamic soft. In the base, the woods now predominantly smell, but they also leave a softer impression than a crisper cedar, meaning that the woods smell more like guaiac wood and pine. There’s also a bit of vetiver, which adds a green-earthy note to the fragrance. All in all, the fragrance is quite nice. The Sillage and Longevity: The sillage is good, so you’re enveloped in a (somewhat smaller) cloud of fragrance for a while, which smells good for a longer time. The longevity is okay at about six hours. The Bottle: The bottle is rectangular and dark green, but it looks like it could use a bit more color since everything on the bottle is in the same shade. I find the raised and thus tactile horses that are rearing quite nice, which represent the brand's logo and are not there just because the fragrance is named after a horse. All in all, very nice. Conclusion: So, that was the fragrance. I found it quite nice. Not very outstanding in terms of standing out from other fragrances, but still very pleasant. It’s a typical daytime scent for most gentlemen who want to use distinctive fragrances or fragrances with distinctive notes like (initially) bitter woods and barbershop-like notes (so these aftershave-type scents) and is therefore more suitable for adults who are no longer necessarily in their 20s,… and perhaps have long since passed their 30s… like me… *sigh* :D By the way, the fragrance is listed here as unisex, but I find that it doesn’t smell feminine at all and smells like a pure men’s fragrance, even though many believe that fragrances shouldn’t be divided into male and female categories. Well, whatever. In any case, it’s worth a test if you don’t already own this kind of fragrance. As mentioned, this is not a going-out fragrance, but really a daytime scent that you can wear constantly and also at work. And it works as an all-rounder regardless of the season. And with that, I’m done with another fragrance. I hope the ladies forgive me for speaking disparagingly about horses (...and unicorns :D) (hey, being able to ride must be cool… still, I find horses (AND unicorns!! :D) a bit boring as animals… camels are much cooler :DD), he he. Well then, have a lovely evening everyone and see you soon :)

Byerley is one of those for me. In its dark green camouflage suit, I initially imagined a fir-like forest scent. With plenty of coniferous surroundings and a fitting conifer aroma. However, it’s not quite that. Primarily, Byerley impresses with a solid woody-resinous impression, more of the lighter, brighter kind, but with spicy as well as balsamic and almost (shoe) creamy nuances. That’s a bit surprising - and the surprises continue, as from this pleasant scent, very subtle smoky elements develop, which fit well into the overall picture and radiate a certain mystery - and indeed quite elegantly. In this, especially Guaiac and cedar wood act as a continuous supporting pillar for Byerley. The latter becomes somewhat more dominant as the scent progresses and, together with the fresh vetiver, bears a significant resemblance to Terre d'Hermès. It could at least pass as a flanker. All in all, Byerley undergoes an interesting scent development - and does not strictly adhere to the pyramid, as the balsamic notes appear earlier than expected and the cedar wood lingers longer than anticipated. For anyone who is really into TdH and is looking for another variant in the same scheme, this composition could be a revelation. But even I, who have grown a bit weary of TdH, find it appealing.

I have taken a bit of a break from vetiver scents lately. In certain autumn moments, I actually quite enjoy wearing them, as they can create a beautiful mood equivalent to foggy, solitary, mystical natural landscapes, but in the other seasons, they often feel simply too overwhelming to me. "Byerley" now starts - especially in the initial phase - with those somewhat gloomy forest landscapes in autumn and conjures images of creaky, misty wood and fragrant, slightly resinous firs in my mind's eye. In any case, it features a very classic, almost conservative use of vetiver, a bit strict, not exactly the mild beginner's type. However, this harsh phase only lasts a good 10 minutes; through guaiac wood and probably also the aforementioned balsams, the Marly scent becomes a bit milder, softer. "Friendlier" seems a bit exaggerated to me, as the base tone remains quite attached to the slightly serious, distinctive milieu. Nevertheless - the balsamic notes increasingly embrace the creaky-green vetiver and at least soften it at the sharpest edges and corners. Qualitatively, it is a very authentic and naturally appearing vetiver, in contrast to "Encre Noir," which now seems too artificially affected in its aroma to me. Yes, this is something you can work with. I probably will only do so in this small autumn time window from early October to mid-November, but that's fine. Vetiver fans should definitely give it a try.

"Encre Noir" was an important game changer for me, a vetiver masterpiece & milestone. This fragrance genre has likely not been changed & shaped as much since Guerlain's classic. It's no wonder that it has also attracted imitators, admirers & copies. Some worth testing, some trivial, some simply shamelessly stolen.

(In my experiment "Blind Flights," I comment on perfumes that I test blindly, without knowing the name, brand, or fragrance pyramid. This way, I want to convey my unvarnished and unbiased experience with the scent.) The first few minutes are truly unpleasant. A medicinal, biting note pokes around in my nasal mucosa. A bitter green.

The title sounds a bit violent, and it is. When applying the fragrance, I was almost overwhelmed by a citrus spice club and secretly dismissed the scent internally. This is not it, I thought! Too piercing, too many spices, too many impressions pushing me into the farthest corner, threatening to engulf me. Herbal, Byerley settles on my skin, it prickles and stings everywhere.

I like the “She Wood”s from Dsquared and have all 4 (blind buy) .....or rather, I would like and wear “Crystal Creek Wood”, “Velvet Forest Wood” and the original if it weren't for that damn violet and its leaf - this supposedly delicate little flower ruins everything. “Byerley” smells just like I wished the Woods would.

Short and compact: Test on a strip (spontaneous impressions, I really mean it this way) 1. Ramazotti with lemon peel 2. After about 5 minutes traces of stale Sinalco Cola again with lemon peel 3. After 15 minutes subtle hints of MAOAM lime ...but then 4. After 1.5 hours a very nice, rather dark floral-resinous note (really elegant) 5.

Oh noooo. Literally had to scrub this off both times I tried it. I thought maybe I’d been too harsh the first time, so I tried it again, but no. It’s full on sharp screechy 1990s era green and white florals that remind me of a cheap knock off Eternity—a perfume I don’t actually like much in the first place. It also made me sneeze. Major sad face, or more accurately, mad face that even though I scrubbed it twice with strong soap, I can still smell it.

Short and sweet, simply terrible.. It has only happened to me a couple of times that I had to wash off a fragrance after an hour, but I just had to wash off Darcy because I could no longer stand the “scent”.. Piercing and sharp to the heavens.. I see people at the cemetery, all dressed in black with black lips and dog collars as jewelry.. Chills... I usually love bergamot and orange scents, but I only smell some piercing, floral, indefinable notes. I see a black rose, murky and dark, with a piercing orange in the background.. After 20 minutes, my nose almost hurt and I had to surrender to Darcy..

Even though I like some Marly fragrances, Darcy - otherwise very hyped - is a flop for me. No plan, no concept, personality disorder in a bottle, that would be the short version. If I hadn't known that I was smelling a fragrance from the luxury sector, I would never have guessed it blind. For me, it's quite mainstream in the opening and not worth the price. I love bergamot and orange scents, but here I don't smell either, instead, I get piercing, floral, and in the drydown, undefinable notes. Carnival sweets and just at that moment, a man walks by, his aftershave lingers in the air. Generic, interchangeable, and arbitrary. Similar to some Montale fragrances, just shorter-lived and less overwhelming. A bit similar to Panthere by Cartier, which I also didn't like. Some say it smells like Mademoiselle by Chanel, but I only find the first 30 minutes similar. My main problem with this fragrance is that it smells so arbitrary. The sillage is good, the longevity is poor, and I would rather wear this scent in colder seasons. More of an evening fragrance. A very contradictory scent development, as if the fragrance suffers from a personality disorder. Initially very feminine, sweet, and omnipresent, in the end, aftershave vibes. No blind buy and for me, not a buy at all, 10 ml vial has to go too.

Hello everyone, this will be a relatively short review. I know there are different tastes and that is a GOOD thing... The scent is strange, difficult, scratchy, and somehow unpleasant - really. (Although it starts sweet floral, a bit green herbal, and in the drydown slightly sweet and soft. Ultimately, it reads very pleasantly, but the composition is really odd for the house and, in my opinion, not fitting if you know the brand's standard...) I cannot recommend it to you! The H/S is quite good to good, however after testing it once or twice, my wife and I could no longer smell it - she also found it extremely unpleasant and she is a big fan of the house. What PDM has done here is beyond my understanding, it is an absolute mystery to me, really! We are not dealing with a budget brand here, but a high-end niche house and those exact words offend me a bit! Why? I have been a big fan of the house since 2011 / 2012 and MANY scents have been really good, and I am talking about scents for both women and men, but here, phew... The bottles, sprayers, and caps at PDM ultimately hardly differ (by gender), except in color, BUT one must say the house really does a lot right, anything less than a 9 or 10/10 is hard for me to understand (I like those)! And now have a nice day/evening or whenever you read this review, best regards, Benny _______ And now, almost finally, regarding the "lovely price," I will say this: if we say we have a certain desire for luxury products/fragrance products in the niche sector, then I find it difficult or, to be honest, nearly pointless to criticize this as something negative. No one forces us to spend this money. If you ask me now: Benny, is it WORTH it? Then I say, if you want to spend it, test it and then buy it, but I recommend everyone to try it at least once! You just have to experience it - the art of what is possible / can be. Now a brief note on my opinion: I am not sponsored, influenced by anyone, receiving money or anything else. I approach the topic of perfume as I am, honestly, anything else is not my style. My true personal opinion is very VALUABLE to me and I hope maybe ;) that this is noticeable. If I don't like something, such as the packaging, bottle, sprayer, or H/S, then I communicate that too!

I am a big fan of Parfum de Marly, so I didn't hold back and tried more fragrances from the line: Darcy. Expectations were high, but in practice, it was unfortunately a bit lackluster. I expected a lot more, more depth, more character. It is by no means a bad fragrance, but nothing that would "catch" me. The scent smells like many others, simply thrown together, without any standout character - just as one knows from Marly. Longevity is as usual: quite good and long-lasting. It also lingers in the nose for a long time. After some time, a rather delicate version of it remains, which is much more pleasant than the initial part. Nevertheless, it's nothing I would be hyped about or recommend further. Fine for testing, but not for future use.

I tend to like Very Sexy Dare a little more than its predecessor, Very Sexy. It settles much smoother on my skin, with a delicious nutmeg, sandalwood and blood orange blend. It reminds me a little bit of Hugo Boss Deep Red. I draw this comparison from the dominant accord of blood orange, which both these fragrances share. I agree with a majority of reviewers that have pointed out its somewhat masculine approach. It's not ultra-feminine, but I'm yet to suggest it to men. I can't believe that I'm saying this, but Very Sexy Dare is quite unique. While the opening is fresh and fruity, the nutmeg suggests early on that this fragrance may not be what you expect. Once settled, Very Sexy Dare is a soft and powdery woods blend, with aromatic nutmeg and vanillary tonka bean. I don't find the scent particularly sexy nor daring. But I do consider it luxurious, sensual and soothing. Although perhaps not easy to love, I am personally very impressed by Very Sexy Dare. You could wear this fragrance almost anywhere. If applied sparingly, Very Sexy Dare is very inoffensive and soft. It could even make an excellent office-appropriate perfume. While the sillage is weak, the lasting strength is not. From what I've managed to test so far from the Victoria's Secret range, their fragrances are very lasting on the skin. I recommend.

For me, Victoria's Secret is a company that is predestined for crazy naming. Very Sexy "X"? (countless flankers to this name) Dare??? Probably the risk, the jab, the challenge is that a women's perfume smells like a men's perfume, or at least could pass for one. But: I like wearing "unisex" scents, I even advocate for a return to "fragrance without gender assignment." I still think this categorization is due to the advertising and marketing departments... OOOps (got sidetracked), back to DARE. Dare is a "women's" perfume that has some echoes of various aftershave qualities: Nutmeg, blood orange, and sandalwood are the strongest notes. Lily plays another strong role. These 4 notes are always detectable for me - but with varying intensity depending on how long I've been wearing it. The tonka bean is very similar to Joop! Homme here. I find the scent very pleasant to wear on colder days; the spices, sandalwood, and lily are very enjoyable as none of the nuances become overpowering. I don't understand how a lingerie company can have such a different concept of SEXY than I do - but at least it's not one of their usual fruit-syrup cocktails. I think the scent is good, as I didn't pay much for it, I get a lot of blood orange in a woody-spicy fragrance that never becomes intrusive or heavy. But sexy per se - nope. I don't feel that way, and I can't claim from the male side that there have been incredible reactions. No man has fallen over me, swooning after me because of the scent - however, no one has said I smell like a guy either. It's not particularly great, but I definitely don't regret having gotten it from the US.

Victoria's Secret SEXY LITTLE THING is a cool fruity floral with a tad of metallic soapiness. There is no true development to this fragrance, so what you get at the opening persists consistently through to the end. I find the lasting power of the edp to be pretty good, and I did not detect the alcohol that another reviewer found problematic (perhaps she was testing the body spray? that's my best guess, since all of those--no matter the brand--seem to have a strong top note of ethanol!) SEXY LITTLE THING seems misnamed to me. This fragrance, while pleasant, seems more refreshing than sexy to me. In fact SLT reminds me of a label that my sister and I used to apply (back when we were both avid runners...) to certain fragrances which serve the purpose of making one smell and feel clean even when one is not: SHOWER IN A BOTTLE! Perhaps a better name for SLT would be: CLEAN LITTLE THING.

Like a fellow Parfumo wrote earlier: this brand has kind of a "bro line" image. I guess that is due to its huge fanboy base and the numerous reviews on social media that only seem to ventilate a hype rather than giving a nuanced opinion. That also made me reluctant to consider any of their perfumes so far. But their samples kept piling up in my drawer, so today I decided "what the heck, just give them a try". Since the market is so saturated, it is easy to qualify all rose/oud scents as generic. After all, they are all somewhat alike. This one does not really stand out in any way. Being obnoxiously loud is not a unique selling point either in this genre. But, admittedly, I can see there are some nuances to Akaster, which kept today's tryout interesting the least. The note breakdown is relatively straightforward. Rose plus oud obviously, with some freshness to begin with and some warm spice and musk to round it off. The opening is not so much a big bang, but a smooth fade in. Slowly the volume increases to 120%. Little to no development after that. I am no oud specialist in any way, so no comments on the quality or the species. I can only say it is relatively mild compared to some other ouds I have experienced; nothing medicinal or fecal here. The rose is prominent. Instead of those deep-red, so called 'jammy' roses, this rose is on the dry potpourri side. It does give off a very floral feel to the composition, without going typically feminine. There is some mustiness to the scent, which may well be from the combination with musks and cardemom. It is strong and a bit dirty in the first half hour and slowly wears off. This mustiness was actually one of the nicer aspects of the scent. It darkened the mood somehow, without getting itself into overly smoky or greasy territories. Interesting. In conclusion, it is always good to keep an open mind and try something outside of your comfort zone. Akaster did not convince me to try more rose/ouds nor did it excite me to try the rest of the PdM line. But it was also not as bad as anticipated. I expected a generic alpha male mess and I got a somewhat positive feeling out of today's wear instead.

One of the best rose-oud scents out there. Very complex indeed. Cool freshness at the beginning, matures into something deeper quickly. Remains well balanced throughout the longevity of the scent. Very modern oud, a trend started by Armani Privé Oud Royal. A new twist on the oud, scent that dates back to the Ancient Egypt. Exquisite rose scent is used too, PDM used Bulgarian rose and Taif rose. One very common type, the other not so common. Convenient choice anyhow. Premium blend of fine choice ingredients, quite worth it's price.

While there is a lemon top note to Akaster, it is very subtle and just a hint of citrus to what is otherwise a very woody and rose-laden fragrance. There is a crisp forest element and a bit of spice, just to change things up somewhat. However, the two main attractions here are the rose and the oud notes. I’m usually pretty hesitant with rose colognes, because it’s not my favorite note, and it can be absolutely too much. However, I think that Parfums de Marly really did a great job of blending this cologne. The oud isn’t too powerful and the rose isn’t too overbearing, there is a firm balance between the two, and it makes this fragrance better than it otherwise would’ve been. Akaster is a very straightforward, linear, cologne. You are going to get a oud base that is flanked by a fresh and crisp array of other tree notes. Other than the oud, I get a good deal of the cypress. Very green. This is all surrounded by an air of roses growing in a garden and a squeeze of lemon. Simple, but actually quite effective.

I have tested Akaster multiple times now and have really desperately searched for a justifiable reason why Akaster is so expensive and was once exclusively available at Harrods, but I simply found and still find no reason! Scent: The same problem as with Pegasus: It smells floral and spicy and simply does not develop at all on me! I can't smell the lemon, cardamom, guaiac wood, etc. For me, it smells floral (probably the rose(s) and geranium?), and you can just barely detect the pepper, which always made my nose tingle when sniffing, and I thought I would have to sneeze, and this despite the fact that I am healthy! The spiciness I smell could possibly be the oud? I have no idea how oud smells, as I don't really go for unusual scent notes (oud, castoreum, civet, ...). Everything else listed as fragrance notes I cannot smell at any time, and as I said, Akaster does not develop for me in any way; it simply smells consistently floral-spicy from beginning to end. Whether it is due to my nose or skin or whatever else, I cannot say; I just don't know. I also find it a bit strange, as Herod and Layton unfold and develop wonderfully on me and smell heavenly, but with Pegasus and Akaster, it is exactly the opposite; nothing happens at all. Longevity is good; unfortunately, I don't know about the sillage. The bottle looks nice like all Marlys (at least I like the bottles). However, Akaster is suitable for going out or dining out and possibly also for business, as long as one does not overdo it.

It's a shame that I don't hear much about this Akaster - because it is still available for purchase (even though it is written here that it has been discontinued; there are surely still remaining stocks)! And in contrast to many other Parfums de Marly, this one leans more towards the niche direction. For me, Akaster is a floral, woody scent. Yes, even a rose-oud fragrance! The top note is floral, spicy, fruity; but the fruity aspect dominates. The heart note is characterized by broad, spicy, pleasant, non-pungent, almost juicy roses. In the base, we have the woodiness, especially with the clearly apparent oud. A fragrance with many facets, an exciting perfume; with a complex character. I think Akaster is more suited for men. However, assigning this Parfum de Marly a suitable place of use is difficult. In any case, I would use it discreetly - then it is even suitable for the office. Is it an oriental scent? It is definitely balsamic and has something exotic about it. When I am energized and want to experience something, meaning I have a certain sense of adventure, then it is a loyal companion, as it conveys security and curiosity! Therefore: Please, more of such de Marlys!

I am a huge fan of Dream Angels Heavenly - and Dream Angels Divine feels like a close sister to her. While Heavenly feels distinctly warm, Divine feels distinctly cool - but both are a powdery, clean, musky ("sexy soapy" profile) scent. Divine is more of a true, cool-undertone, "bar soap" scent (still feminine but leaning slightly more unisex; fresh/clean, as though you'd lathered up with a Dove bar in the shower). Heavenly feels more "sexy musky" - still soapy, but slightly sweet. Divine is the perfect skin must scent: it's very unoffensive, refreshing, and universal. Nothing about this will demand attention - it's a soft caress, pure class, timeless. If you found Heavenly to be too musky, or if you were put off by the cardamom in the OG formulation, you may like Divine instead. If you want a cheaper but comparable blend: Sea Island Shore (earlier versions - not the 2022!) has similar DNA of "cool", powdery, clean, musky, fresh.

If you're like me, and appreciate that feeling of joy you get from smelling clean and fresh, then you'll most likely enjoy Dream Angels Divine. I would describe this fragrance as sweet, flowery and soapy. It's not too much, having just the right balance to make this fragrance work. While some may find it boring, I consider Dream Angels Divine to be well-composed and delightfully refreshing on the skin. I don't wear clean scents all the time, but whenever I do happen to spritz one on, I am always impressed. Soapy florals are such a universally pleasing genre, especially in the sense that they re-create that 'straight out of the shower' sensation. Dream Angels Divine, although mostly a white floral and musky soap blend, does have an element of smokey vanilla towards the heart and drydown, which intrigues me greatly. Perhaps it is my skin chemistry which encourages this twist in the composition, but I tend to believe that it's there to add some complexity. Either way, it works for me. You could wear this fragrance pretty much anywhere. I also find it great for both the warmer months and even the chilly weather. It's very versatile, that's all I'm saying. If you're a bit of a perfume snob, those that hold on to the assumption that all Victoria's Secret fragrances are cheap, then honestly, you need to get over yourselves. This soapy beauty needs to be more recognised. I highly recommend.

This is a much sweeter sister version of Victoria's Secret Dream Angels Heavenly the opening once again starts off plastic but in this one dries down of the sweet and tangy scent of cyclamen dries into a sharp bittersweet sweet of Hiacynth but amber is the dominating scent here it dominates the other scents easly the Finishing is of sandalwood and Powdery Rose makes it an impression on me.

Parfums de Marly Shagya is an earlier release from this French house of many hits this past decade, though there are still some older offerings in its catalogue that I’ve never tried. Shagya smells like a woody oud with a slightly heady citrus/floral/spicy mix that gives it some attitude, versatility, and freshness. The standout notes are lime, pink pepper, oud, geranium, vetiver, and cedar. The oud and vetiver aren’t particularly dirty, instead of forming the bassier part of the sharpness throughout, achieved on the higher/brighter end by the geranium, especially. It feels constructed like a men’s signature scent, perhaps a bit more for the colder weather than warm. I quite like Shagya as a more year-round-friendly alternative to the also-under-discussed Nisean, a darker mix featuring patchouli and oud, but Shagya falls slightly short of Nisean’s richness/boldness, though this makes sense, given that Shagya is surely the more agreeable of the two. Shagya performs very well, perhaps not as well as the stronger PDMs (Herod, Nisean, etc.). Currently the best price I see for it on the market is $170 for the larger 125ml size on FragranceX, generally about half of the retail pricing of most PDM perfumes. 7 out of 10
Shagya is one of the best marly's fragrance's.. professional mix of citrus & Oud.. Very Very Good Longevity & Silage

A new fragrance note is recognized after experiencing it in three different perfumes. After Papyrus de Ciane by PG and Baudelaire by Byredo, Shagya is my third perfume featuring Papyrus. This note, which truly smells of reeds and wickerwork, is well noticeable in Shagya, framed by beautiful woods. It's already evident in the top notes. The usually overwhelming Oud is here restrained and initially allows others to take the lead. Only after a while does the Oud become a bit forward. Vetiver provides a nice green note and a bit of bite, but is well integrated. And the musk adds a touch of creaminess and volume. Due to the musk, this does not have an overly dark woodiness. The usual citrus top notes are merely an addition. This perfume gets straight to the point with woods. However, there is a development in the unfolding of the medicinal Oud note, which recedes in favor of the vetiver during the drydown. Shagya serves as a subtle alternative to the opulent Oud perfumes from Montale, offering a distinct, elegant, and slightly citrus-fresh base tone. It is not a Montale “light.” Shagya is a very elegant Oud perfume, light and subtle enough to be worn during the day. Highly recommended!

The topic of Oud is endless and offers countless facets that one could discuss. Starting with the question of quality and local differences in the raw material to the subject of "how much hype does a person need?". This all should be less of a focus here; however, Shagyar by Parfums de Marly seems worth a few sentences. My first experiences with Oud were with Montales, all quite intense, strong perfumes with little restraint and, unfortunately, often somewhat artificially perceived undertones. Here on parfumo, comparisons to hairspray are often drawn, which has become a cliché and does not do justice to the fragrances in every case. Personally, I find the more important question is whether everywhere Oud is claimed, there is indeed Oud present. And I am sure that not every little potion that adorns itself with this label can actually deliver what it boldly promises. With such a limited raw material, it is simply impossible. Now to Shagya, which has not received much attention here - unjustly so. It possibly contains real Oud; slightly balsamic-spicy-medical components that break through almost from the start indicate this. To me, it feels quite authentic, almost a bit unspectacular when compared to the common Oud-saffron-rose bombs. I find the opening of Shagya sensational; it reminds me of a cocktail that has just been freshly shaken with ice and strained into a glass in front of you. Setting: Naturally, an open beach bar with a thatched roof, a cool morning breeze, the sea… I have never experienced Oud like this, fruity fresh, with unheard-of lightness and almost a bit cooling. Nothing feels artificial, but the top note does fade very quickly, which is truly a shame. However, even afterwards, thankfully, Shagya is not a typical Oud muff. One completely misses floral components (rose geranium??), which I do not see as a drawback; on the contrary, it emphasizes the woody-spicy component of the Oud. The combination with cedar is wonderfully harmonious, which is sensationally dry and gives the fragrance transparency. Surely this buoyancy is also due to the vetiver, but it lacks any sour or overly earthy-smoky impression that is often associated with sweet grass. And musk almost always works, making the fragrance broader, denser; you can't go wrong there. With Shagya, in a way, no risk was taken. A buoyant, light summer Oud with cologne aspects that still possesses enough complexity and radiance to provide joy over a longer period (and throughout the whole year). It’s strange that it hasn’t found more followers yet. Shagya could easily be from Creed, and then everyone would probably be clamoring for it. The longevity is ideal and just survives a day of urban asphalt heat. More would be too much. The sillage is certainly okay, although that is difficult to assess with simple testing on the wrist. Price: €150 / 125mL is reasonable for the quality offered.

This was my first test of Shagya. After the first spray on my forearm, I waited 10 minutes. My first impression was: "I can hardly smell anything, where has the scent gone?" It may be that I need to get used to this type of fragrance. In my perception, it lies just barely above my threshold of detection. For the first two hours, I couldn't even begin to describe what it smelled like in my own words. Gradually, I had an idea. It smelled extremely subtle like "dentist's office." Normally, that would have been the death knell for any perfume test. "Whatever," I thought, and continued walking through the city to do some shopping. On the way home, I was stuck in traffic for about twenty minutes. When people have to wait in traffic, various behaviors emerge. One person is chatting on their hands-free device, another is drumming on the steering wheel, one is putting on makeup, and many just look blankly. And one person suddenly started smelling their forearm every few moments. Something started to emerge...woody? smoky? Not sweet, not spicy-oriental, but very "different." In the previous comment, the "medical note" is associated with oud. Unfortunately, I can't say anything about that. I lack the experience. I mean, the initial dentist note became woodier and peppery-smoky over time. I found the development increasingly better. When I smelled the spot again eight hours after spraying, it went "Bong." Now it smelled fantastic. Pepper, smoke, wood, resin. The whole thing very quiet and restrained, yes, subtle. This very "quiet" scent has piqued my interest. I am increasingly enjoying immersing myself in these subtle fragrance notes and their nuances. I believe Shagya is worth being discovered gradually. I think there is something very noble slumbering deep down in the scent progression. Scent: (I'll hold back for now) Longevity: > 12 h, but as I said, very subtle Sillage: very low (maybe that's why it's so interesting?) Bottle: it's okay, (I prefer the dark-matte ones). Final verdict appears as a statement.

I must unfortunately admit that I cannot recommend this fragrance from Parfums de Marly. PdM usually produces great scents, but this one is truly a disappointment. The sillage is very weak compared to other fragrances. Quite disappointing, really. I don't want a fragrance that is barely noticeable... even if the scent is okay... What a shame.

There's a lot of dishonesty, jealousy, misrepresentation and such within the fragrance community. And sometimes the cracks begin to show right in front of our very eyes. In the latest unexpected turn for mainstream French niche house Parfums de Marly, the brand has chosen to release 3 Extraits at a €450/100ml price point and the community on both Parfumo as well as competing sides have resoundingly sounded the alarm that these are poor products. So lets have a better look: are the 3 Extraits actually poor products or is there something else to the story? Kicking off my coverage with Eragon , a fragrance which opens with sweet-spicy and slightly boozy touches, instantly followed by masculine aromatic ones. Without looking at the notes, the primary note that I smell is clearly tonka and that's why you'd probably assume this was Tom Ford or a different designer based on the way the scent smells, albeit Marly isn't the only one making designer-adjacent fragrances in niche (see: Penhaligon's). Somewhat surprisingly, I am not reminded of any other products from PDM, despite owning 4 and having sampled more than 30. Once I saw the scent pyramid, allocating my experience to the listed notes became quite a bit more obvious. It appears that the primary profile is driven by the tonka, vanilla & sweetening spices which are then opposed by the patchouli and perhaps the woodier heart notes (davana and cypriol). There was a very light fruity touch in the top, but it is not a core part of the profile. Furthermore, I'd say it smells more-so sweet-spicy and perhaps creamy than it does leathery (to the point where I'm surprised to even see the note listed). On the opposite end, the fact that the scent doesn't list lavender is also surprising as the masculine aromatic (designer) aspects of the profile are very prominent and allocating all of that to the tonka feels inaccurate. The deeper we go, the easier time I have separating the cinnamon which coincides with the tonka and vanilla to balance out the patchouli. This fragrance has no synthetic qualities about it and smells about as easy-going as many others from Marly. I definitely don't like any comparisons to Naxos nor Oajan , but I'll let designer comps like YSL's La Nuit de L'Homme Eau de Toilette slide for now as it's definitely a lot closer to the latter than it is to either of the former. Based on the last 2 paragraphs, it's fairly evident that the product itself isn't the problem. Unsurprisingly, there are dozens (if not hundreds) of fragrances which I've rated a 5 and everyone else loves. I firmly believe that with these 3 Extraits from Parfums de Marly, some people are taking it personally and that lack of integrity is extremely apparent when you look at how the 3 scents are being rated. Just a few years ago, everyone tried to tell me that Althaïr was the real deal as it now sits in the Parfumo top 10 for men's fragrances (that fragrance sucks btw). Now those same audiences are turning the table on Eragon and I'm right there to pour cold water on it yet again. I would estimate that a standardized rating for Eragon would place it somewhere between 7.6 and 8.1 based on the positivity bias visible everywhere else on Parfumo. For a Marly, the sillage is a bit light and while the longevity is solid at an approx. 8-10 hours, the overall package from a value perspective is still subpar due to the general scent profile and the retail pricing. However, I have enough awareness to understand that the scent profile is separate from the rest of the package and I am not denting the scent's rating for underdelivering in other categories. Sometimes I wonder if others on here have caught onto this concept yet or if they're just talking out of their *sses.

Eragon opens spicy, with bright pink pepper, cardamom and cinnamon. Soon it settles into the straightforward fragrance it will smell like till the late drydown: a combination of vanilla, patchouli, and leather. It's a nice signature monolith kind of fragrance where I can see it fulfilling the same role as Babycat (although they don't smell anything similar), a smooth, classy fall/winter staple. It has depth and class, really feels like a private line designer fragrance that doesn't go too far into experimental territory but uses good quality ingredients. I'm not a huge fan of the leather/vanilla genre, so I'm not exactly the target audience for Eragon, but I can easily see this beating out Althaïr for PDM's best vanilla-forward masculine fragrance for a lot of folks. I feel like I have smelled the same vanilla/patchouli combination before but I can't remember where; I'm sure at some point the community will figure it out and it will shoot to the top of the "smells similar" list. I don't find any overlap whatsoever with Angels' Share Eau de Parfum and if this does indeed smell anything like Khamrah all that proves is that Khamrah is a terrible clone. My first of the 3 extraits I'm reviewing in this collection and it seems I (randomly) picked the one that most are hailing as the best in the line. It's not bad, not a game-changer either, and definitely not worth retail price. But I expect it will be plenty discounted in a year or so's time so I'm reserving my judgment on pricing till then: rating it a 5. Would be like a 3 if it doesn't get discounted, and like a 7 if it can be found for $200 or so. Bottle-wise, I'm rating a 7 because I like the bottles in a vacuum, but just confused as to the theming. It looks like a mid-century modern kind of feel which is really out of place with PdM's Louis XV Rococo styling. Would probably be an 8 or 9 if the theming was spot on.

When Parfums de Marly launches a new fragrance - or in this case even fragrances - it is sure to attract the attention of the Parfumo community. As certain as the Amen in church or the Petri Dank to the Petri Heil or the obligatory "Gesundheit" to the currently regular sneezing fits in German offices. This time, PdM presents and offers us its fragrance creation even in a high-concentration and high-priced [...] uh, excuse me dear readers - I mean, of course, in a highly potent Extrait version! So, having discovered the PdM new releases on the well-known and beloved Parfumo homepage, I was absolutely delighted, highly interested, and on the verge of ecstasy - well, that's how I justify it to my brain, which has been completely numbed by generic fragrance profiles. I clicked through all 3 new fragrances and lo and behold, the Eragon, yes! That could be something again, or become something! So I "sneaked" in - or, to put it in old German, “secured myself a place with cleverness and skill” in an ongoing sharing and placed my market order for a whole 2ml - yes, I've really become cautious. In the end, I have to push the remaining milliliters onto my father and pretend I'm doing him a favor *cough* - and I eagerly await updates from the sharing starter. Said and done, waited, it was finally time and the fragrance was shipped. I don't know if it happens to you sometimes, but I often forget which fragrances I have on the way and then look quite astonished into the mailbox, thinking "huh??!!" which fragrance did you order this time? This time was similar, and today, on my way to the basement to check the heating system (it has gotten quite cold in the apartment without a functioning heater), I remembered that the Eragon (by the way: cool fantasy series) is on its way to me. So on my way to the basement, I quickly opened the front door and checked the mailbox, and lo and behold: the fragrance mail has arrived on time. Excited as a bowstring - another deception attempt by my brain - I made my way to the living room and unpacked the fragrance mail. First of all (yes, it's written together, I googled it specifically) I "struggled" through the diabetes-inducing goodies from the nice and attentive Parfumos (I like that) and sprayed a double dose of Eragon from the atomizer onto my wrist. First impression: Cardamom, as far as the nose can reach. But that can't be all. So, renewed concentration and eager sniffing. Indeed (I know, it is currently used as an inflationary filler word) cardamom is at first the most prominent note in Eragon that I perceive. The scent spreads out dominantly and leaves little room for other notes. After the first cardamom near-death experience, I slowly perceive the mandarin listed in the fragrance pyramid. Very lightly/cautiously dosed, it seems to shimmer quite authentically in the background. So, now I have to "go somewhere" for a moment. Do you know the challenges of washing your hands when you're testing a fragrance on your wrist? "Write it in the comments and acti [...]" Over time, the spicy cinnamon shows itself, which comes across soft and a bit boozy in connection with the Davana note. Here, memories of Khamrah Qawa or Boss Bottled Absolu are awakened. The fragrance ends with a mix of bourbon vanilla, slightly earthy patchouli, and the universally popular tonka bean, ultimately fading into generic meaninglessness... And at this point, I would like to conclude my description of the fragrance. To be honest, it is not worth any further words, nor does it require any further words to describe the fragrance accurately. Don't get me wrong, the fragrance is certainly solid and wearable, but in my opinion, it does not do justice to the price or the PdM brand. When comparing Layton, Herod, or Pegasus to Eragon, it quickly becomes clear that this one differs significantly from its famous brothers in style and character. For this price (the market will take care of it and make a price correction), I simply miss the creative craftsmanship and a fragrance character with unique and recognizable features. Unfortunately, this type of new release - in my perception - runs through so many fragrance houses. A good example is also many new Creeds, TF's, and many, many others! When comparing the old releases with the new ones, you get the feeling that only generic mushy fragrances are being developed for the masses to achieve maximum sales. I say Dior and you say: ??!! Conclusion: those who want to test the fragrance should certainly do so, but in my opinion, this release was unnecessary in the fragrance universe of PdM. It's a shame, my brain remains numb, as it often does these days... PS: I no longer have the inspiration or motivation to check my text for spelling errors, and since PdM doesn't pay me a fee (Demi Rawling does, I bet my a* on it!) I fortunately don't have to.

After Valero clearly ruined my start with the "Les Extraits" collection, the Eragon performed better on the other arm. But is that enough to justify 450 bucks? "Oh hell no!" • After spraying: Dominant vanilla pairs with mandarin or orange and cardamom. Something floral and creamy is also immediately present. Speaking of "start": Unlike the Valero, the Eragon is a true "loudmouth." The opening is loud, the whole room knows what's up. I can already sense early on that this one lasts SIGNIFICANTLY longer than its blue counterpart from the Extraits collection. • After 15 minutes: Vanilla and tonka bean in abundance. Plenty of patchouli and cardamom create a rather spicy cinnamon note. Mandarin is still there, but is already fading a bit. Very sweet overall ... it's not really to my taste, especially when it’s so overwhelming this early. • After 55 minutes: (Very) sweet vanilla cream with light, rather fading leather and a developing rum/alcohol spice. I find the first hour, or rather between minute 30 to almost 60, very challenging, unbalanced. I'm used to something completely different, more "mature" from PdM. • After 1.5 hours: The tonka bean has developed further. The creamy vanilla continues to power on. The already subtle leather is now swapped with patchouli. The alcohol spice is becoming more prominent. Interesting, as it acts as a counterpoint to this very challenging vanilla sweetness, which almost gives it a cake-like gourmand quality. • After 2.25 hours: Sweet-creamy, boozy, and tonka bean is its great-grandfather. (Rum-)spice meets gourmand. • After 4 hours: The vanilla has transformed into this vanilla cream reminiscent of the original Magnum ice cream. The bourbon vanilla is dipped in plenty of rum. The entire dry down remains a very, very sweet affair. • After 5.5 hours: The vanilla note now has a rather synthetic impression. Interestingly, this might also be the reason why I suddenly get a hint of mandarin again?! Patchouli, alcohol spice, and a creamy gourmand. • After 7 hours: Spicy alcohol fumes are now taking over more and more. Vanilla and tonka bean are present, but recede into the background. The scent suddenly becomes louder for me again, so the sillage is definitely still there. Drawback: Not balanced. I find the notes in the dry down generally overwhelming and poorly balanced. Rather uncharacteristic for PdM, as it gains quite a bit of edge because of this. • After 10 hours: FINALLY, peace has settled in the vanilla. Alcohol/liquor/rum spice is only very faintly detectable, leaving a vanillic-sweet spray spot with a high "cuddle factor" :P • After 12 hours: Vanilla and a bit of wood remain. "Longevity" is now completely gone for me. But - and I have to give it to him - "stamina" is definitely something Eragon has! ------- Conclusion: Not as bad as the "Valero | Parfums de Marly," but I still see no reason to shell out 450 bucks for this PdM. This strong, vanilla-heavy base reminds me of "Herod | Parfums de Marly," while the cardamom use and the dry down remind me of "Emporio Armani - Stronger With You Absolutely | Giorgio Armani." Here, too, one tends to tread well-worn paths rather than daring to venture something new - especially for this price, including a completely new collection. A shame, but at least I know where 450€ will NOT be going ... What can be said in its favor: Anyone looking for a vanilla-dominant scent for autumn and winter for going out or "after 6 PM" will find it with the Eragon. Strong sillage and good 12-hour longevity are impressive for a PdM. For me, it’s clearly unisex, although I feel such a sweet gourmand leans more towards a feminine touch.

In keeping with the "sandwich" principle, I would like to conclude my three-part review with something positive. Of all 3 extraits, Eragon is probably the one that best captures the current zeitgeist. For 450€, you don't get exceptionally much (and certainly nothing unique!), but it is overall the most enjoyable. The opening is cinnamon-forward and dominated by cardamom. I recognize "La Nuit de L'Homme (Eau de Toilette) | Yves Saint Laurent," I recognize "Noir Extreme (Eau de Parfum) | Tom Ford," and even a bit of "Layton | Parfums de Marly." It also gives me distant vibes of "Ambre Nuit (Eau de Parfum) | Dior," although that is almost an insult to the beautiful Dior scent. The progression is dominated by tonka and vanilla. It remains relatively linear but performs best of the 3: a solid 8 hours with a good sillage.
