Compared to "Carios | Parfums de Marly," it leans more masculine, yet is still more unisex than "Valero | Parfums de Marly." Conclusion: To put it in the words of Falco: "What else can I say to you? Everything has already been said!" You probably already know what follows. Eragon is really nice, and the DNA meets all the requirements of today's gourmand-heavy fragrance world. However, I can't help but express my outrage once again at how outrageously overpriced this thing is. For 450€, you can get an entire fragrance collection from Lattafa & Co. for every conceivable occasion. The also very high-priced London Eau de Parfum costs a full 120€ less and leaves Eragon far behind in direct comparison. No matter how you look at it, the fact remains that the prices of the 3 new extraits de parfum from Parfums de Marly are in no way justified!

Thus, the sample Eragon rose before me like a stately knight from the noble lineage, seeking splendor, as if to deceive the eyes and empty the wallet. The price that the merchants demand struck me and called forth my dismay.

Here they came, my three manufacturer samples to test. Carios deeply disappointed me. But I really like Eragon ! In the opening, there’s a lot of cardamom. You have to like it - I do. Also, there’s something fruity thanks to mandarin and bergamot. I also perceive pink pepper very clearly, and I really like that too.

Eragon is a lightly gourmand yet still fresh fragrance: First, zesty bergamot and mandarin, then a warm cinnamon-vanilla feeling that can come across as quite elegant. It feels fresh enough for everyday wear, but with a sweet depth that stands out.

I keep sniffing my arm after spraying Valero to see if there's anything I missed. Some depth, some meaning, some extra note that might set it apart from a drugstore fragrance. But no, nothing. I recently was talking to @NicheOnly about scent ratings, about how much originality should play a role in how high or low of a rating you give the scent. I usually will dock a scent a point or two for being a bit derivative or clearly being inspired by another specific scent. But Valero...Valero is a special case. I thought from the reviews that people were overreacting and it was going to be something like Sedley or Percival where it puts a bit of a spin on a classic male genre. But it doesn't. It's just...an amberwood. Like an amberwood you find in any department store for $100 (I guess now it's more like $150). A Versace pour Homme Dylan Blue Eau de Toilette , a Luna Rossa Ocean Eau de Toilette , a Myslf . And it's not innovative or interesting in ANY way. Sedley put a fizzy 7-up spin on the blue genre; Percival introduced a sweet mandarin note and better longevity and smoothness to the Fierce Cologne -shower gel genre. But Valero is just an amberwood. And not a particularly good one at that. Let me describe the scent I guess. It's a vaguely aromatic opening with lavender/bergamot (more like aromachemical approximations), some geraniol and hedione thrown in for a floral mid, and a headache-inducing ambroxan base, along with other "amber" aromachemicals. Smooth creamy sandalwood? Elegant earthy patchouli? You wish. It's unbelievable the lack of value for money. I'm not just talking about the markup from the raw materials. You're getting shafted on that even if it was chock full of naturals. But usually what you pay for, ESPECIALLY if you're paying $500+ for a fragrance, is for artistry, originality, R&D, some kind of work by the perfumer. Here it just seemed like they had this formula lying on a shelf for a cheap designer company like Calvin Klein or Coach to come along and just be like, "give me that 'generic male scent #7.'" Then Parfums de Marly goes up to the perfumer for their new extrait series and the perfumer's expecting them to set some complex parameters and vision for what they want, and PdM is like "no, no, no, we can't be speding THAT kind of money on R&D, just give us whatever you got." I bet the perfumer themself was shocked. No one should buy this fragrance under any circumstances. At any price. I mean, unless it somehow gets to $50. There's literally hundreds of aromatic amberwoods to choose from by designers that cost a fraction of this at discounters. And you'll even be getting something less derivative! Just unbelievable, PdM releasing a basic amberwood in 2025. Worst release of 2025. By far. By a mile. It's only the beginning of October but I'm calling it. P.S. They called it "Valero" because it's the kind of fragrance you can buy at a gas station. Ba-dum-tiss

It’s honestly impressive how Parfums de Marly continues to orbit around its own gravitational pull of mediocrity, finding new and interesting ways to produce something that feels expensive yet distinctly unremarkable. Valero, the latest addition to the brand’s increasingly predictable lineup, is a textbook example of how you can polish a product to a high gloss without ever addressing the underlying emptiness of its structure. From the first spray, you’re greeted with a sweet-citrus opening that seems determined to convince you of its brightness but quickly settles into that all-too-familiar Marly syrup. It’s polished, sure, but there’s an almost algorithmic quality to it, as if someone fed “commercially safe niche” into a machine and let it iterate until the output met an internal brief. If I were to be charitable, I’d say Valero does succeed in one regard: it’s cohesive. The citrus-spice opening smoothly transitions into a creamy, slightly ambery base, and there’s a kind of professional neatness to that. The issue is that it never escapes its own design language. The tonka and vanilla combination that Marly keeps recycling is once again the backbone here, leaving the heart notes to flutter weakly around it. There’s some talk of lavender, cedar, maybe a touch of cinnamon, but all of it feels dialled back, as though deliberately engineered to offend no one and impress even fewer. Statistically speaking (and yes, I’ve tracked this across upwards of 50 contemporary releases in this segment) the average consumer associates this exact scent profile with “premium quality.” And perhaps that’s the real trick: Marly has learned to chase perceived luxury rather than deliver it. Performance-wise, Valero behaves as expected. Moderate projection for the first 40 - 60 minutes, tapering down to a soft skin scent that lingers for maybe six hours in total. It’s linear, predictable, and arguably versatile if your idea of versatility is wearing the same scent to work, dinner, and bed without anyone noticing. I could generously say that the blend quality is higher than in some designer equivalents, but that’s a faint compliment when we’re talking about a, what, 500$ bottle? Even if you came into this hobby with capital, some transgressions are too big to go unnoticed; and what makes this even more amusing is the inevitable gathering of Marly loyalists calling it “well-rounded” or even “masterpiece”. Those descriptors are ill-fitting at best, deceitful at worst. The real story, though, isn’t Valero itself. It’s the community’s reaction to it. Watching people rate this fragrance anywhere between 0 and 2 is like watching a group of children collectively echoing their parents’ scathing remarks about last night’s football game. The collective inability to separate presentation from performance, price from profile, and branding from balance has reached pathological levels. The same voices that praised Castley or (especially) Althair as “masculine perfection” are now bending over backwards to slam Valero because the bottle looks silly and the people who got there first expressed their discontent before the ever-present glazers arrived. Objectivity in fragrance reviewing has become the equivalent of a myth - everyone claims to believe in it, but no one’s seen it. So - yes, Valero is about adequately technically competent, about adequately blended, and about adequately wearable. But let’s not kid ourselves: it’s also terminally bland, conceptually lazy, and priced like a product that thinks it’s smarter than you. Maybe it's simply trying to stay in line with the remainder of modern "niche"? Harry Knows.

As if the Eragon review didn't stir the pot enough, here I am again to have another bite at the latest from French niche house Parfums de Marly. And maybe if I send the message enough times, it will actually stick. In the second review of Marly's Les Extraits collection, I am covering Valero . A few weeks back I wrote a review for Widian's London Extrait de Parfum where I lambasted the broader community's lack of having an approach to their ratings. In the current top review from @Omnipotato, he has highlighted his approach and why he believes Valero is an F tier fragrance. Indirectly, those parts of his review revisit the criticisms I have for people who lie somewhere in the middle with this hobby: those who have a history of offering opinions on product while also not having any framework to it. This is relevant, because ratings are only worth so much when the writer doesn't have a defined approach to assigning them. The reader doesn't even need to know your system, just that you have one. Omni has stated his case, but what case is everyone else stating? At the time of writing, Valero is holding a 5.5/10 rating, significantly lower than various other fresh products from Marly and even lower than basement-dwelling cheapie product like Hawas for Him . Is there any truth to the story (i.e. the low rating)? Unlike many others on here, I came into this hobby with capital, so I completely bypassed designer outside of the bottles of Sauvage and Givenchy's Gentleman that are collecting dust somewhere at my parents' house. I am highlighting this, because a lot of the other reviews and comments I've seen so far feature a lot of comparisons to both designer products and cheapies; two genres where I essentially have no experience whatsoever. Luckily, I have experience with niche brands making designer style scents and that also extends to Parfums de Marly through the bottles of Sedley and Percival that I bought back in mid-2022 which remain in my collection to this day. Somewhat ironically, those two Marlies tell a lot of the story about the opening of Valero as well since Valero has some of the lemonade-like touches that feature in the opening of Sedley and those touches are followed by the macho masculine aromatic DNA from Percival with a huge blast of geranium, ambroxan and PDM's signature style lavender. The scent is sweeter in the top and the masculine aromatic parts of the DNA begin to dominate in the eventual dry-down, so within Marly's own catalogue, Percival is clearly the closest comparable Marly product. Shortly on the blending, depth and performance. The leading notes are the geranium, lavender and ambrox; I also get mild citron in the top to offer a touch of Sedley. That citron (or an unlisted citrusy note) doesn't blend as well in the on-skin dry-down alongside that macho masculine DNA. Additionally, there are some musky tones in the base that don't appear to sit well, so those are 2 flaws that I notice. Performance is around average, trending light. So how do we rate it? In the niche world, this genre is led by Clive Christian's VII: Queen Anne - Rock Rose , yet when you compare it to a scent like Percival , there's not exactly a whole lot improvement and that's because the masculine aromatic macho/shower gel DNA doesn't actually have a lot of depth, regardless of whether you're looking in the cheapie, designer, niche or indie market. Percival is one fragrance that I've already re-rated and I have it down as a 3.5/10. Valero features more nuances in the top and worse execution in the base, yet when compared to other poor ambroxan fragrances like Kilian's Blue Moon Ginger Dash , it executes better. For the moment, Valero will land at a 3.0. It's nowhere near the worst fragrance I've smelled in 2025 (and it wouldn't be the worst for 2024, 2023, 2022 etc either), but you can rest assured that the 0/10 value score I've given it is as close to warranted as it gets. Ultimately, Valero is just another reflection of the poor landscape niche perfumery finds itself in as we near the end of 2025, yet from the perspective of the community's rating of it, some of the audience is doing too much.

Sorry Parfums de Marly, but my entry into the "Les Extraits" collection was a flop. The €450 can be saved by anyone, because a mix of Sedley X Le Mâle Eau de Toilette is nice - but not worth the money. • Immediately after spraying: Fresh, spicy, slightly floral. The bergamot and lemon really kick in, accompanied by a bit of juniper and cypress. Pleasant, but unremarkable start. • After 15 minutes: The citrus notes are already fading. What a pity, a short appearance :< The floral-spicy notes are now increasing, but not the H/S. It is indeed, similar to other freshies, not particularly impressive. • After 55 minutes: Longevity and sillage have already diminished. And this for an "Extrait"?! Honestly, I'm not surprised: The spraying area was hardly shiny, so there isn't much oil in it (or at least not enough to justify the MSRP of €450). The Valero becomes sweet-spicy, but also very generic ... • After 1.5 hours: Fresh-soapy, floral (mainly lavender), subtle spice with pink pepper or something? Funny ... somehow I'm getting vibes as if Le Mâle Eau de Toilette and Sedley were mixed together. • After 2.25 hours: Vanilla-floral. The freshness is gone. As is the sillage. • After 4 hours: Vanilla and flowers continue to dominate on a light sandalwood base. Spice? Unfortunately already 70% gone. I still get a bit of patchouli, but nothing that blows me away. • After 5.5 hours: The last hour has struck. Only very weak longevity remains. Vanilla and a bit of tonka bean (at least I get something slightly creamy) on wood - with a lot of imagination. Speaking of imagination: It officially ends for me after about 6.5-7 hours. -------- Conclusion: A nice rounded glass bottle with a horse that looks like it came from an AI mixer, with generic, by no means €450-justifying "juice" inside. Acceptable for half the price, but for me, a miserable start to the new "Les Extraits" collection. What a shame, Parfums de Marly - this is not how €450 should smell.

...that is the question for me as I was able to test this fragrance. What exactly am I paying 450 euros for!? Now one might say for the "name," for the "brand." Alright, a few extra bucks, I can go along with that, but just for that? No! And, the point should also be clearly stated, just because I indulge in a PdM doesn’t mean I have a Porsche parked outside, I mean to say, the brand is certainly not THE flagship of the niche perfume industry. Speaking of niche, PdM does try to appear quite pleasing in many moments, which has made me wonder more than once, is the brand actually worth its money? With a "Sedley | Parfums de Marly," we are also in the race at 220 euros, yet it has a somewhat special freshness, it feels valuable and the mint is finely balanced. But even here we are already at the limit in terms of price-performance ratio, if you ask me. Yes, I own it, yes I like it, and yes, I acquired it at a good price. Back to Valero, what am I paying for then? For a grand fragrance? - Not at all, Valero is mundane, dull, insignificant! For a niche fragrance with edges and corners that comes across differently? - Not at all, Valero is polished, mediocre, well-known! For a bottle that enhances my display? - Not at all, because the bottle radiates what the fragrance ultimately is. A boring, blue-tinted, and by the way, distinctly too sweet fragrance water. I really have no idea what I should spend such a large amount of money on here. Valero is, as already hinted, a trivial collection of some bergamot, a lot of geranium, a bit of lavender, and noticeable ambrox. The freshness fades after just a few moments, a distinctly too sweet note develops and makes the fragrance seem cheaper and less interesting until one comes to the conclusion: Valero is an outrageous sham! Yes, I would like to mention one positive point, namely the first minutes of the top note. They are really great, I had associations with crystalline and shiny freshness, wonderfully emerging juniper, really wonderful. But hardly does the enthusiasm ignite, there is a clear cut and the descent begins. For me, Valero, especially in view of the price-performance ratio, is one of the worst fragrances that have ever come my way. I actually feel some outrage here and cannot understand the thoughts of the company behind it. Pure greed and profit perversion can be the only reasons. This has nothing to do with character, soul, or even the art of fragrance..

First of all - Haltane, Oajan, Carlisle, Althair, and Greenly are among my absolute favorite fragrances. They embody elegance, character, and that unmistakable PDM feeling that has captivated me for years. But I also know that I no longer belong to the target audience of the new les Extraits Collection. Perhaps that’s a good thing.

And once again, curiosity triumphed over my reason, which is why I joined a sharing of the 3 new PdM Extraits ( Valero , Carios , and Eragon ) a few weeks ago. Much speculation had preceded this, and the rumor mill was in full swing. There were talks of AI-generated bottles and completely overpriced fan service.
No idea why "cheap" scents in designer bottles attract me? Maybe I'm crying out for “I am the victim you’ve been waiting for” or maybe I have self-destructive character traits...

I haven't written too many reviews yet, but somehow I felt compelled to say a few words about this scent. First of all, I want to emphasize that I absolutely agree with my predecessors regarding the pricing. I also understand that a perfume must be measured by its price.

I get jasmine, chocolate, and berries here - with the chocolate and berries being the most prominent notes. Picture chocolate-covered berries, drizzled with a creamy jasmine glaze. It's a bit synthetic, but has a fun throwback-feel - similar to the more gourmand offerings from Victoria's Secret in the early-to-mid 2000s, like the Insatiable line ( Chocolate Covered Berries or Chocolate Craving ). The chocolate + berries dissipate quickly, leaving the bulk of the fragrance as a watery jasmine in dry-down. On my skin, the jasmine takes over even more quickly than on paper - and also feels like there's something like cedar in the background. It was significantly more synthetic on my skin unfortunately, or else I would have loved this one.

This smells identical to Victorias Secret limited edition Tease Cocoa Soiree to me. It is a berry, white floral with chocolate scent. However, just like with Cocoa Soiree I only got the white florals and some berries. That chocolate note is nonexistent. My mom who loves Cocoa Soiree also thinks it smells like it, so she’s definitely pairing them together lol. However she did mention the lotion is a bit more berry heavy. If you missed out on it, or want something similar in my opinion, go check out this scent.

Wow this is a strong one. I think you are going to love it or hate it. This starts with like you have a muscle plain and you are using a tiger balsam, but slowly changing to a strong leader, (like you are walking in a fabric full of leather jackets) i have to say in my opinion this one is little similar like TF white suede (only less sweet) it has olso some animalistic scent smels like a horse but very pleasent. Not bad at all. There is a strong longevity and a good silage. I get a lot of compliments with this one olso.

This one is such an underrated gem. And I am glad to have found out about it. This one has nothing to do with the aesthetics of the house, it's original, not mass-appealing, very complex, bold, and unapologetic. I find it to be utterly seductive and alluring but I can see why many find this repulsive. First of all, there are no animalic musks or synthetic oud accords in here. However, there are two phases of this perfume that could be challenging for many. This one is a very complex perfume that changes a lot after application, so, do test it on the skin, and do wait for it to transform. The first part, is a weird combination of very dry woods, a powerful clove punch(very mentholated), gummy resins, and a hint of honey. This first part almost has an antiseptic or shoe-polish vibe from the cloves, and it can be offputting. It's not my favorite part, but I find it to be very intriguing. Soon after this assaulting opening, the leather accord and the incense accord start to creep in and slowly assert themselves as the main players. The cloves dial down, and you start to get this beautiful brown leather, quite rugged, almost baked in the sun, that also has a buttery and salty quality to it. It feels alive and does smell of horses and stables. To that, you add a beautiful incense accord, creating this dirty and smoky leather feel. In the base, the styrax adds a hint of dirtiness, sweetness, and oriental mysticism. As I said, very complex perfume. This one does pay tribute to the two beautiful stallions on the front of the bottle, as it does smell like being around these beautiful and majestic creatures. I would say, if you are a fan of the house, stay away from this. If, however, you like to explore and expand your horizons, and you are into smoky-dirty leathers, orientals, and animalic perfumes, and you find the house laughable, boring, and commercial, then this one is not to be missed. It's quite unique, I can't compare it to anything else, but it is in the same league as Tauer's L'Oudh, Afrika Olifant, Tom ford's London, Dior's Leather Oud (OG). A gorgeous perfume.

I agree with it smelling a bit industrial. When i went to their distribution store in Manhattan and asked for anything with incense and was spritzed with this, I immediately thought it smelled of motor oil. It was only after having taken the sprayed strip home and leaving it on my bureau and periodically walking past it, did I happen to appreciate it. I almost pulled the trigger on the purchase until i was told the price. Fortunately I didn’t because later I found (imo) Gucci Guilty Absolute to bare a heavy semblance to it, albeit not as camphoric and rich. Not to mention: waayyy cheaper. If money weren’t an issue: Hamdani > Guilty Absolute.

Well, Hamdani surely does not hold back. The opening shot is brutal with its cloves of the medicinal, camphorous kind. This miraculously transforms into an animalic type of leather. I get an image of brown, suntanned animal skin with a golden honey glow. The references to 'arabian horses' are quite accurate. Along the way, the resins come forward and smoothen out some of the hairy edges, while the scent keeps getting richer and darker. A Parfums de Marley that slaps you in the face and then turns you in a funky old stinker. No wonder this has low scores. This one caught me by surprise and definitely won me over. Especially the mid-phase with its golden-brown glow is highly enjoyable and worth another wear.

7:20 AM. Sunrise. The clear chill of the past October night still lingers in the air. I sit on the remnants of a once proud oak tree that adorned my grandparents' garden. Unfortunately, over the years, this oak became an increasing danger to the small bungalow that stood under its proud crown. The decision was made. After more than 40 years, the oak's end had come. Everyone helped out. The neighbors, my uncle, family friends, and I, just before my 20th birthday, had to pitch in. It took several days, but in the end, the remains of the oak were scattered throughout the garden. Everyone took what they could use. One of the neighbors built himself a wooden chair from a particularly thick piece. Well, at least from his perspective. Aside from the stump, nothing was left of the oak. And there I sat. Enjoying the morning sun shining on the stump. The tranquility of the waking world and the coffee. The scent of the wood and the disturbed earth. Five years later, the end came for my grandparents' garden. For health reasons, they could no longer make the 2-hour journey from Berlin to Brandenburg to the garden colony. And so the garden, which my grandparents had tended for 50 years and which had been a huge adventure playground for my sister and me for as long as we could remember, was sold. I pondered for a long time whether to write a comment about Hamdani, as I would not wear the fragrance. Nevertheless, it is something very special to me, something very intimate. It is a memory capsule for a long-gone time. When I spray it on a scent strip, I smell the wood again, the disturbed earth mixed with leaves, the smoky remnants from the grill, and the stone slabs. All the beautiful childhood memories (getting caught by grandma while sneaking strawberries) come flooding back. And now please excuse me. I have to return to the garden.

For me, definitely attractive! I see no connection with horses or stables. I tested the perfume in mid-August last year; Finally, I bought it after months of wondering what fascinated me about it so much. It is bulky, rough, salty, spicy, unconventional, and above all smoky! smoky! smoky! (but no incense).

It only smells like horse when you spray it up close and then hold your nose to it. At a distance, it is a wonderfully harmonious and spicy scent. Surely it is exceptional, and I can even understand the associations with a stable, but if you are into fragrances that you don't smell on every corner, then it is worth a try.

A long time ago, it must have been sometime in the early to mid-nineties, I was on Düsseldorf's Königsallee and wanted to quickly stop by the bank. I can't remember if it was Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, or Sparkasse at the time; it doesn't really matter. In any case, it was a massive branch with a lot of pretentiousness and splendor.

I was worried about this at first because it came out on my body and paper smelling like alcohol. But after a few minutes later that alcohol scent disappeared and I was left with a beautiful super sweet pink cotton candy. A yummy gourmand sugary edible realistic cotton candy with a hint of vanilla and strawberry.

It smells the way that bubblegum amoxycillin tastes. its incredibly sweet, lasts a long time, and had a decent village. I found the only notes I ever got were sweet and creamy ones and I liked it as a result. nIt's not a complex scent at all and really is for people who like an almost medicinal type of sweetness imo. I always get compliments on it and ive been rationing the last couple sprays since it's no longer made.

My skin doesn't always like white flowers, but Sedbury works very well! It starts off strong and can be quite piercing if you spray too much. I didn't like it the first 2 times I tried it, then I began to notice how all the powder swirled around me, I was in a cloud of tuberose and jasmine that lingered long on my perfume-eating skin and even more on my clothes. I can imagine that the amber-lavender-sage combination may not work for everyone, definitely test it a few times before buying. I find it develops best in mild temperatures; too cold or too hot brings out metallic or rubbery notes. The white flowers are already a bit creamy, but you really have to like luxurious, white flower-scented body lotions and powders. It's a perfume for confident, perhaps somewhat distant people, clearly feminine. Sedbury is a woman over 40 who even at home wears a perfectly tailored black jacket, pearls, and sunglasses. Maybe in England. It has grown on me and I'm glad I have a bottle. I like the confidence it sometimes gives me on certain days when I've worn too much oud and rose and vintage and don't know which perfume to wear, and I feel protected in its secret powdery cloud.

Hello everyone, Today, at a late hour, I would like to share a few words about "Sedbury | Parfums de Marly." First, the packaging, bottle, cap, and sprayer: Everything receives a very good 10 out of 10, but one thing must be highlighted, and that is the sprayers, which have always been incredibly good and a 10 out of 10. To put it bluntly, they are so good that I would place them on the same level as those from Chanel and Dior (the best on the market)! Now, about the scent: At the end of the day, one can say you are a fruity sweet and floral creamy fragrance that does not "rub people the wrong way," is well-received, pleasant, and nice, and is, by the way, in a truly beautiful bottle - so if that isn't classy. But those are also its advantages, yet indirectly also its disadvantages... What do I mean by that? Sedbury seems as if PDM thought, let’s create a fragrance that is primarily one thing - SAFE. And it is! But apart from the bottle + the price, it has nothing special... - no particular scent direction - no special ingredients - no edges or corners - No impressive performance (S/I) - ... It is safe, it is beautiful, and you can't go wrong with it - as it is, among other things, pleasing, but unfortunately, nothing more! It is simply the elevated average (in a truly beautiful bottle)! And now, have a nice day/evening or whenever you read this review, best regards, Benny _______

Strangely enough, I can't think of much to say about Sedbury.. I find the scent simply boring and more than unspectacular.. Nothing new or interesting. Extremely old-fashioned in a strange way.. Actually, I like scents with lavender but Sedbury does nothing for me.. What saves Sedbury a bit is the note of sage.. Sedbury has no soul for me. I have no image in my mind. Who could wear this scent?? Honestly, I have no idea, maybe a lady 70+... Smells quite nice, no more and no less.. Lavender with a bit of sage and for me a lot of patchouli.. In my opinion, patchouli plays a very big role in Sedbury.. Overwhelming and slightly nauseating.. My husband's response when he held his nose to my arm was very brief: No. Quite terrible.. Somehow, I just can't warm up to most perfumes from Parfums de Marly.. Either too girly: “Delina”, too “mainstream” “Safanad”, too boring “Sedbury” or just plain awful “Darcy”... Sedbury belongs to the category of boring.. I find just one scent from Parfums de Marly absolutely fantastic and that is Athalia.. Meliora is also very nice. All other scents are, as I said, absolutely nothing for me..

If Eragon is private-line designer level, and Valero is slop destined to stay rotting on department store shelves, then Carios is bang in the middle. It's something I'd expect from a designer extrait or the newfangled "elixir" that is pretending to be a concentration. It's the same problem I had with Lucius (and they kind of smell similar too), just isn't a step up from designers for the price, which is about double or even triple the high end department store frags. Carios opens with a fruity burst, which is not really reflected in the notes. I was expecting it to have blackcurrant or pineapple or fig, something sticky-sweet, when I pulled up the notes after applying. There's a tiny bit of the burnt-rubber saffron also lingering, without being too overt or offensive. I'm not getting the comparisons with Oud for Greatness Eau de Parfum or Haltane at all. It smells more like a fruity take on Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum with some spices. Kalan -adjacent but a lot more sweet, and a lot more flat, airy, and "perfume"-y. The drydown is pretty tame, just a run-of-the-mill masculine woody base that you've smelled a million times before. Surprisingly, with these extraits, it seems that PdM has taken a step down, without even considering the price increase. While Eragon can be mentioned in the same breath as Althaïr or Oajan , it's probably middle-of-the-road in terms of PdM releases (again, ignoring the price). Carios is a definite step down. Doesn't smell like a niche product, even a niche version of a well-established genre. If I smelled this in a department store, I wouldn't blink an eye. It would probably be one of the more unique/better designer releases of the year, but still not something I'd consider purchasing at $150-$200. And Valero ? Just straight up trash. Amberwood slop that is completely out of touch and out of fashion. My thoughts are that prices are going up across the board, with inflation spiking, plus tariffs being introduced by the lovely country I happen to be a citizen of. And brands don't want to have their customers riot with pitchforks, so they are not increasing prices too quickly on their existing lines. However, they are introducing new lines (e.g. Amouage with the Essences) that are slowly going to take over their main collections, or just simply charging more for new releases (e.g. Oud Zarian ). Same with designers. They are getting away with charging upwards of $200 for new elixirs/extraits. So I think the new normal is going to be: designer retail prices starting around $200 for EdTs and EdPs, and niche/private line retail prices starting around $500, but it's not going to happen overnight.

The coverage of Parfums de Marly's Les Extraits comes to an end today with Carios and in some ways, I feel like Carios is the best example of the argument I've made in the other reviews: people are slamming the product for non-fragrance-related exogenous factors since the product itself is essentially average. In the top, the first accords I smelled were fruity-sweet, but those accords are instantly followed by the dark woody smell from Initio's hero franchise Oud for Greatness Eau de Parfum . I, for one, find that amusing, because Marly already has a product mimicking Oud for Greatness, that being Haltane . Without looking at the notes, I wrote down that the fruitiness is strawberry and I placed it between products like Oud for Greatness and Xerjoff's Indochine . But the main thing that I noticed is the fact that it objectively smells decent and is nowhere near a 6.1/10 by the standards with which people vote here on Parfumo. As the scent transitions into the heart and I see the notes, I will say I'm a bit surprised there isn't an actual fruity note listed. The saffron from Oud for Greatness Eau de Parfum plays a prominent role in the structure throughout, but the scent does transition in a fresh-spicy direction as the geranium and ambroxan begin to oppose the dark woody and light fruity touches I experienced in the top. That is to say it lacks the quality of Oud for Greatness, a statement that I'm sure some people will find very amusing. I believe either the geranium or the ambroxan is giving Carios a light muskiness on-skin to the point where Carios almost feels like an alternative to Oud for Greatness' flanker, that being Oud for Greatness Neo : Neo also smells fresh-spicy (same realm as Torino22 ), but doesn't build its structure around geranium and ambroxan (instead utilizing fir balsam and lavender, delivering a better product in the process). Those notes are actually the lone issue with Carios since I feel like most of the depth this scent has is featured in the top and a lot of that doesn't carry through into the base where you mostly get fresh-sweet-spicy with a light fruitiness, almost like it's not even in the OFG realm anymore. That is to say the dry-down is very much barebones. I've smelled many takes of this genre and while I haven't revised my Initio ratings yet, I've historically been firm on the idea that Oud for Greatness Eau de Parfum is the market-leading scent in its own genre. However, due to the crowdedness of that realm (meaning the scent's success has led to many imitations), I will be lowering the ceiling of its rating. Various niche takes like Outcast Blue Eau de Parfum , Liwa Extrait de Parfum and even Haltane have not brought any relevant improvements, instead just trying to earn a quick buck off the same DNA. Carios is certainly towards the bottom of this genre, even if we extend our reach to fresher takes like Neo and Torino22. However, the bottom in this genre is still product that fits the criteria of a median fragrance, especially in today's market. The performance is average-to-moderate and the value is still terrible just like the other 2, but those criticisms are, yet again, separate from the underlying product. The core takeaway from Carios and the other Les Extraits is that of a souring sentiment within the niche community: people's bitterness towards the commercialization of niche perfumery has rendered them unable to offer (or attempt to offer) objective coverage. Make no mistake, some of you are overselling the story: Parfums de Marly hasn't been at the forefront of niche perfumery for at least half a decade now and I'm puzzled why people even come to Parfums de Marly in hopes of finding great releases in the first place. Ironically, when Marly has launched new products post-COVID, all of you seem to love it and it feels like I'm among a select few saying the product is average-to-subpar. So I just have to know: where was this criticism when they launched Terre d'Hermès Eau Givrée (Perseus), Club Black Eau de Toilette (Althair), Fleur Narcotique Eau de Parfum (Valaya), Love Don't Be Shy Perfume (Oriana) and several other inspired-by products? There's no space for flipflopping, either put up or shut up.

Umm, really let's not! The nicest thing I can say about this stuff is that the bottle is great. Unfortunately, you can't wear the bottle. This sweet, fruity uneventful, lackluster offering from PDM, makes you ask why? Why didn't PDM know better. Why didn't someone pull this before it was released? Why would they put a price like this on it? If this stuff came with a complimentary bottle of Creed Aventus and MFK Baccarat Rouge 540, it still wouldn't be worth the price on it. Let this be a cautionary tale for those prone to blind buying...DON'T DO IT!!!! PDM, rarely misses but we've arrived at rarely.

After my rant regarding the botched "Valero | Parfums de Marly," I of course made it a point to test the other two newcomers. I found Eragon to be quite alright, but still too expensive. I would say something similar about Carios, but ultimately I want to claim that it is still the best of the three overpriced Marlys. Even if it may seem boring to keep hammering on the price, in the end, one must also be measured by it, and a high monetary value usually stirs a certain level of expectations. Long story short: Carios is also way too expensive! But why do I consider it the best? For me, this fragrance brings a certain depth and a rather interesting contrast, namely that of saffron and rather fresh, citrus notes. I must say, it is exactly this kind of contrast, or interplay, however one wants to see it, that I have come to love since acquiring "DesirToxic L'Intense | M. Micallef." No, the fragrances don't have too much in common in terms of their basic structure, but the charming relationship between saffron and citrus unites them. Probably also due to this personally cherished combination, I rate Carios with the term "the best of the three newcomers." The presentation of the red mandarin works quite well for my nose, with slight tendencies of grapefruit also being noticeable. The rose geranium, fortunately, holds back significantly here. In my opinion, this benefits the fragrance. Thyme, pepper, and vetiver form a fitting cocoon around the top notes, which never completely disappear and are almost delicately enveloped. A slightly woody base note, which fits well, allows the cocoon to rest appropriately. Whether and to what extent Ambrox swings its club here, I cannot reliably tell you, as I do not have a high sensitivity to this fragrance component and probably like it quite well for that reason. For me, it is rather subtle and appropriate. Carios is potent and radiates significantly in the first 3-4 hours, so the dosage here, depending on the "application location," should be chosen carefully. After 4 hours, the projection calms down, but it lingers on the skin for a very long time, for me a good 8 hours. I am at 7.75 points here, but due to the price, I refuse to apply the mathematical rules and round up, but down - Sorry!

After the rather lackluster start with Valero , I turned to the 2nd Extrait de Parfum from Parfums de Marly. Carios is probably the most neutral unisex fragrance of the three, with a slight tendency towards the feminine. What do you get here for 450 euros? Well, unfortunately not much. The opening is very sweet, and alongside saffron and pink pepper, citrus notes are also recognizable. However, these quickly fade away, leaving essentially just a vanilla Ambroxan base. The performance is unfortunately more than meager; at first, I thought something was wrong with my nose because the scent was only very faintly perceptible. A slight sweetness with subtle fruitiness and a hint of synthetic woods - you don't get much more than that here. H/S are below average - max. 4 to 5 hours with an almost non-existent sillage. Conclusion: What I could still justify with Valero is completely missing in Carios : here, not only is the performance poor, but the scent itself is unfortunately as well. A delicate, slightly alcoholic, sweet-fruity note that transitions into a woody-vanilla base. No depth, zero complexity, weak performance. I don't know Oud for Greatness Eau de Parfum , but I've been told that it is supposed to go in roughly the same direction. However, the Initio costs only half as much, and I would bet my entire collection that the French one offers a far better performance and a stronger scent experience.

Here, Parfums de Marly offers a truly beautiful fragrance. In my opinion, it is the best of the 3 new scents presented. It has an incredibly fruity-fresh opening that lasts into the drydown. I primarily smell a blend of rose and mandarin. This fades a bit later, and Ambroxan comes through in the base with a pleasant spiciness from the pepper notes.

I LOVE THIS I’M OBSESSED AND I NEED A PERFUME DUPE FOR IT IMMEDIATELY. it’s the right amount of boozy and sweet. does have a hint of fruitiness to it , but it’s still so luxurious and i hate that this is discontinued. i’m afraid of using it still. i don’t care what anyone else says about this. it’s the perfect night time scent.

Don't believe the notes. This smells nothing like vanilla, nothing like bourbon, and nothing like amber. It's an extremely fruity scent. I have no idea who's idea it was to put vanilla bourbon as the name when it's not that at all. It's a nice scent, don't get me wrong, but it's not vanilla, it's not gourmand, it's not edible, it's not bourbon, it's just another fruity fragrance by VS

Ispazon is quite a special horse from the Parfums de Marly stable. And unfortunately, I can't really warm up to it. While it does feature some rather decent fragrance notes in its structure, the interplay doesn't really harmonize - at least not for my nose. Right from the start, this crumbly, unclean citrus/lime note annoys me, which oddly reminds me of "Boris Becker" from LR, so to speak the bottom of the Parfumo ranking. That's really a terrible beginning. If you give the fragrance a little time to breathe, the cedarwood becomes more prominent, but it remains increasingly dusty and harsh, accompanied by sweaty undertones that one would actually associate with cumin and have a hint of a wet horse blanket. Towards the end, Ispazon becomes even woodier with a warm musk flank, but by then the whole horse has more or less fallen into the well, meaning that nothing can be saved at this stage, although some appealing elements shine through, which must be denied from the listed ingredients of orange, lily of the valley, amber, and vanilla. The horse breed Ispazon, as some previous commentators have noted, is a mix of noble black Friesians (though I somehow have a mare like "Black Beauty" in mind, which certainly belongs to a different breed) and Iberian warmbloods. It sounds substantial, but when sniffing it, I thought more of "Little Uncle," the spotted gray (more specifically, a Knabstrupper) from Pippi Longstocking. I'm sorry for all the PdM fanboys, but apparently, Ispazon was such a lame mare commercially that they ultimately gave this Eau de Parfum the mercy shot and removed it from the program.

"Ispazon" tends to get overshadowed by "Layton," "Godolphin," or other bestsellers from the brand... but it shouldn't! It is a light, sharp-citrusy cedar daydreamer that can still be considered a hidden gem nearly a decade after its launch - is that great or a shame? Well, I discovered it for myself and I'm very glad about it. I always like cedar in fragrances, but I haven't experienced it like this before. Sunny, Mediterranean, warm. Naked and dressed up. Naturalness without limits. No man can go wrong with this, never ever. Unless one has no use for cedar at all and takes offense at the wood's certain "sweatiness." Otherwise, this is top-notch. It has a human touch at a high level. Spicy, laidback, a perfect blend. Can be worn discreetly dosed deep into the height of summer. Chill sweating in the shade of the cedars... what an image! Bottle: heavy, thick glass, almost like small dumbbells. High quality. Sillage: very self-assured but relaxed Longevity: no weakness here either - at least 7 hours. Conclusion: a beautifully relaxed, sunny cedar scent, initially zesty from lime, sharp from bay leaf, and later becoming increasingly pure and relaxed. Never sweet, never generic. Masculine and sexy. Underrated! An absolute must-have in the Parfums de Marly lineup that you should grab before it gets discovered (or worse: discontinued!) someday. Wonderful!

Parfums de Marly, that sounds like a French traditional house, but it probably isn't. It's about Louis XV and his fondness for perfumes. And he is said to have lived in the Château de Marly. The fact that a Frisian horse breed is named after one of these perfumes shows that the preservation of tradition might not be so strong after all - but who cares! Ispazon starts off citrusy-herbaceous and a bit sharp. Orange and thyme in the top notes are quite discernible. However, my perception then diverges from the descriptions. Is this dirty note still bay leaf, or is it already cumin? And where, please, is the lily of the valley? Is that meant to indicate the very light floral aspect? Or the very subtle freshness? And why do I smell hints of cinnamon here? And is the dry spice that unfolds in the heart perhaps coriander or nutmeg? The cedarwood is well integrated, providing a dry element without standing out itself. It only reveals itself in the drydown. The base, with its rather cozy notes, fortunately isn't too opulent. It provides a pleasant, warm backdrop for this perfume, which is overall situated on the herbaceous-spicy, sharp side. Ispazon is more to be classified as a spicy fougère. Not a pure oriental, despite the amber and vanilla. I like Ispazon. It is a well-crafted blend where fresh, citrusy, herbal, spicy, floral, woody, and oriental notes come together in good harmony. So, there’s actually a bit of everything here! For me, a spicy-peppery core character prevails. It’s made very piquant. It gives good vibes like a glass of champagne in the morning and tingles like a pinch of snuff. But don’t worry - you won’t have to sneeze from it. In style, Ispazon reminds me a lot of Le Dandy by d'Orsay and justifies for me the classification as a masculine, bright spice fragrance. Despite the sharpness, it is pleasant to wear and highly recommendable.

I acquired Ispazon as a blind buy during a sharing. Since the fragrance pyramid seemed highly interesting and rich in tension - bay leaf and cedarwood rounded off with lily of the valley, thyme, musk, and vanilla - I had to strike twice and signed up for 20ml. Today I finally got to try the scent at home, at my own table. And what can I say? It is the South in a bottle. This fragrance is a real spice and wood bomb. I've never smelled anything like it before. The further away my nose is, the more citrusy it comes across to me - but when I get really close, it is bitter and so dry that it is (almost) dusty. It smells of the South, of rock and dry, dusty roads lined with bitter spice shrubs. Those who only appreciate sweet fragrances or cannot do without sweetness will be miles off with Ispazon. However, anyone looking for a harsh, dry challenge, something strong with a lot of spice and lemony, acid-free freshness will find a good companion in Ispazon. I would describe the longevity as solid, while the sillage was a bit restrained for me. As a woman, I would only want to wear it in summer. However, I can very well imagine it on a man year-round. Addendum: After being able to test it more extensively for a while, I had to adjust my rating upwards.

Ispazon - The Friesians - The Netherlands So the second horse flank is up, which should actually suit me a bit more, because Friesians are beautiful horses to me. The name Friesian comes from a province in the Netherlands. Their nickname is "Black Pearl," as their flowing long mane in pitch-black color is absolutely impressive. It is the oldest horse breed in Europe, and even Julius Caesar appreciated the original Friesian. It was the horse of the nobility in the Middle Ages and is enjoying increasing popularity today. The opening of Ispazon begins very citrusy-fresh. Lime and lemon set the tone here. After that, the scent becomes a bit spicy, almost bitter and herbal. Herbs also sneak in. The citrus notes remain subtle in the background, and the scent feels very masculine and herbal. I wouldn’t classify the scent as oriental. Overall, this would be a nice men's fragrance for me.

Ispazon is already a somewhat older fragrance from the house of PdM and not very well known or widely represented. I have always wanted to test it, and I have now done so. So what can I say? Admittedly, it’s not quite my DNA. It starts with fresh-citrusy notes, but immediately underlined by a certain spiciness that I personally don’t quite warm up to.

Ispazon is a rather difficult fragrance to evaluate. On one hand, the scent is wonderfully fresh and (spicy), but on the other hand, the individual fragrance components are hard to distinguish, and the scent profile is hardly comparable to anything else. The opening of Ispazon is wonderfully fresh, with a hint of citrus and a light spiciness.

- Who finds Delina EdP too strong and too sticky-sweet? - Me! (I bought it enthusiastically after a test and had to give it up after 2 days, way too much) - Have you tried the Hair Mist? - No. Is there one? With Hair Mists, the sillage is usually too weak. - Give it a try. - Okay, I went on a blind date. (blind sought) - And, how was it? - GREAT! An absolute hit! I immediately "fell in love." p.s. I even wear Delina Hair Mist at home, which I never do with other fragrances. I just want to have the scent around me all the time. I'm really glad to have discovered this wearable version of the beautiful but far too dominant Delina.

The hair perfume from Delina is the perfect companion for your handbag and while traveling! And it is surprisingly long-lasting for a hair perfume. Delina is a Safe Space for me: fresh, bright, light, clear, pleasant, soothing, and so beautifully feminine, it enchants everyday life and brings a touch of sophisticated sparkle with its simply being. The fresh lychee-rhubarb breeze is accompanied by fluffy vanilla and envelops every woman in a light pink cloud without being overly sweet, squeaky, or intrusive. Delina always brings good vibes, no matter where, when, or who else is around (;

I really like the scent, but it doesn't last as long as the original. If you're looking for something to layer to intensify the fragrance of the perfume, you've come to the right place. However, for a hair perfume, I find the scent quite long-lasting. The scent itself doesn't differ; I would only say that it's a bit lighter and not quite as overpowering. However, you don't get a strong sillage solely from the hair perfume here.

Haunting, like seeing a ghost in a white nightgown; you're safe, in your house, but curiosity hits too much. Nose pressed to your window, you keep glancing at the ghost hoping she will not notice you. Delicate but eerie, alluring. I don't find it a clean-shower scent, but mostly something beautiful from the past haunting you. It's beautiful, it just has a very low sillage sadly.

I first bought the discovery set. Before buying the set, I knew I'd like this one because the notes are already similar to the ones I already have. I fell absolutely in love. It smells powdery, musky, woody and floral. It feels like cuddling with someone. It's very comforting that I decided to buy the full bottle. Also, in some powdery scents, usually there's a sharp note, this one does not have that. If you're not a fan of powdery scents, this might not be for you. Otherwise, I suggest to try this one out.

I have always liked Love Spell, but I absolutely love this version. It doesn't really remind me of the original Love Spell much other then the peach note they both share being similar. Love Spell Splash smells exactly like a citrus peach tea or a fruity punch. It's perfect for summer or going to the beach, I love wearing it on sunny days. The only downside like many have stated is it doesnt last very long because it's a body spray.

I love raspberry in bodymists! Not in classic Love Spell, but this flanker made me fall in love with. But I think that limited versions of classic are more interesting, but they have that fruity charm. It exactly smells like Lipton peach tea, fine for pool and summer! Peachy tea with a bit of raspberry mixes good with any peach perfume. For example, Bitter Peach by Tom Ford

o.g. was never really my thing—it felt synthetic and made me feel a little nauseous. But this splash version? It’s like sipping a refreshing tropical drink on a sunny day. The peach is loud (in a good way), and there’s this soft tea vibe in the back that keeps it from being too much. Juicy and vibrant.

One of the best Love Spell flankers! It’s a bit synthetic - but smells like sipping on a chilled glass of Hawaiian Fruit Punch on a bright, sunny day at the pool. Red, juicy-berry-punch blend you knew and loved from childhood - but with a grown-up twist. The peach tea note has a "fruity fresh shampoo" vibe; it's refreshing in the dry-down and adds more dimension to the blend. This is playful, youthful, delicious - named well, as it is truly a “splash” of fruity fun. If you loved the “Escada” summer releases of the 2000s, you’ll probably enjoy this too. Perfect for the hot days of summer and one of my favorite mists. Only downside: the longevity is poor; within 30 minutes, it fades fast on my skin. But it's a mist - and for the low cost, plus the juicy scent profile, I don't mind reapplying. Similar, longer-lasting scent profile: Tropadelic for Girls

I bought the discovery set. Before buying the set, I knew I won't like this one because of the tangerine. All I could pick up was the very realistic tangerine peel, from the first spray until it completely disappeared. I don't like that note and it was just not for me. If you like fresh fruity scents, maybe you'll like this one.

This fragrance is a little different to the classic Very Sexy for him, but the changes are all good. Icy bergamot in the opening blends well with the sexy, musky base from the original Very Sexy for Him. My partner is a huge fan of this one and at the price, it's a solid buy. I definitely recommend it. Doesn't last all day but it's great for a summer night out.

Nishane Ani is an important fragrance. For those of Armenian descent like me, many boycott all Turkish products. They believe that all Turks are to blame for continuing to deny the genocide committed against the Armenian people in 1915. So how much more rare that a perfumer of Armenian descent, Cécile Zarokian, has collaborated with a Turkish brand based in Istanbul, Nishane, to create a perfume? Ani represents unity in a substantial way. Part of Nishane’s “No Boundaries” collection, Ani attempts to mend one of the most contentious borders in the world, the one between Turkey and Armenia. In ancient times, the town of Ani was a hub of culture and religion in the Ararat plains. The “City of 1000 churches” was home to over 100,000 people and was one of the most important cities in the Kingdom of Armenia. Today, it is little more than ruins, and is located well within the borders of Turkey. A few hollow churches with their crosses removed stand as a testament to the invasion of this city by Ottoman forces. Today, Armenians consider Ani as part of our heritage, even though it has not been in our borders for hundreds of years. It is little more than a memory. “Ani” in Turkish also happens to mean “memory,” and this scent was created in memory of one of the founders’ friends who had recently passed away. The memory of cities like Ani and the memory of the Armenian Genocide still scars relations between Turkey and Armenia. This scent, a coming together between Armenians and Turks, gives me hope that scars can be healed, and that forgiveness can begin and denial can end. Well, with all that out of the way, let's talk about the actual fragrance. At its core, Ani is sweet creamy vanilla, and that is apparent from first spray — the other notes are there as modifiers or just decorative. There is a substantial citrus component in the opening, which Ani X takes even further, but here it simply leads into the spicy heart of the fragrance, which features cardamom and ginger. The few hours you get of this spicy accord resting on a bed of creamy woody vanilla makes this fragrance hard to beat as my favorite vanilla scent of all time. Despite the large number of base notes in the pyramid, the drydown is not complex: a cedarwood/sandalwood-vanilla that just lasts and lasts, slowly fading away, like the monument frozen in time that is the city of Ani.

It just so happens that today, 17th of October, marks one year since I've been on Parfumo. And quite conveniently, it just so happens that "Ani" in my language (Romanian) means "Years". Looking back at where I was last year, glorifying Lattafa's crap juice and dreaming about owning JPG or anything influencers glazed without remorse, I must say I never though I'd reach the point where I would be reviewing niche fragrances from Amouage and Nishane. And I only got here thanks to the community here on Parfumo. Otherwise, who knows in what unrecoverable state I would've been, collection full of Armaf and Lattafa; a stranger to true perfumery... Regardless, let's now focus on Ani Extrait de Parfum itself. Being one of the most hyped niche fragrances on social media, portrayed as one of the best vanilla fragrances there is, I did come with a little bit of hope. But as we all know (or should know), when a fragrance starts making waves on the social media scene, it's best to stay away. And as for Ani Extrait de Parfum , it's nice, but not as nice as influencers make it seem. The opening strikes with a squeeze of citric bergamot, followed by a dosage of pink pepper, which is less actually peppery and more sweet-spicy. Some green crispness, reminiscent a bit of galbanum but fresher, take a seat further back. But the real deal here is the blue ginger, which is arguably the best and most unique part of the whole composition. It brings the typical ginger warmth and spice, but it is not overpowering or too sharp, as it is accompanied by a smooth floral sweetness and some clean muskiness. This pairs nicely with the other top notes, but unfortunately, it doesn't last too long, mostly gone 20-30 minutes into the wearing. But until that happens, the heart notes accompany it to its grave, with a sweet and dark fruity blackcurrant, slightly tart and even aromatic. The cardamom keeps the warm spice alive with mild minty undertones, while also sweetening things up. The Turkish rose appears briefly and just as quickly it dissipates, adding a mild creamy-honeyed rose aroma which is not too strong, but undeniably smooth and well-incorporated. But now, this is acclaimed as a top-level vanilla fragrance, so the base really must hit the spot. Well... not at all. Sure, vanilla is the main protagonist once things dry down, but it doesn't strike me as impressive in any way. Frankly, there's a very noticeable lemony undertone present too, which in combination with the vanilla here evoke a clear picture in my mind: Dr. Oetker vanilla/lemon pudding powder. Can't really un-smell it once you make this connection. As for the rest of the notes, the benzoin adds a nice dose of ambery sweetness, while the musk and ambergris strongly convey musky warmth. There's not much woodiness to talk of, at best a creamy sandalwood creeping through. And the patchouli, you can tell it's there, but things are so well-integrated and blended that it's hard to pinpoint things on their own. And that's probably Ani Extrait de Parfum 's highlight - the blending and balance of the notes. It all comes off as very smooth and well-put together, but the scent itself just fails to stir any emotions in me. It's just a nice, sweet fragrance. Performance didn't really impress either. On my skin, about 7 hours was the most I got out of it, with projection being decent. The first hour I got a little over 2 feet of projection, mellowing down slowly afterwards but staying consistent up until around hour 4 where it turned into a skin scent. It's a pretty easy fragrance to wear, overall. Apart from the warmer weather, Ani Extrait de Parfum is quite versatile, and I could see it work from formal events to daily school/office wear (that if you can afford Nishane as a daily). Perfectly unisex too. Now, you can easily find Ani Extrait de Parfum for $170, so it's not even the most expensive of options from Nishane, and it's one of their nicer compositions too. I can see why it gets all the love it gets online, but when it comes to "endgame vanilla fragrance", I don't think Ani Extrait de Parfum should even be considered. It's just a very easy vanilla fragrance to like (like most, really), and apart from that blue ginger at the opening and the Dr. Oetker products resemblance, nothing else really makes it stand out. It's definitely worth a sniff, more so because of its blending quality rather than its scent structure. But I'm convinced there's better vanilla fragrances out there. Overall Rating: 6.5/10

Ani, a name that may refer to a ruined Armenian medieval city in Turkey, but also the word memory. No matter what, on my skin and in the air Ani reveals itself as a blend of spicy, fizzy, and zesty ginger and aromatic bergamot, which here takes on the appearance of lemon, sour, so vivid that it seems to suck a candy Bali’s Best Zesty Lemon Ginger Chews. Supporting these two sour ingredients is a lovely pink pepper, very peppery, which is more noticeable on the paper strip, clearer, and more recognizable, like the aroma it releases when we crumble its pink berries between our fingers. In the backdrop, we find resins, spices, and woods that show the way and this wonder's slightly spicy, chypre, and gourmand character. I wrote gourmand because right away its creamy and vanilla accords remind me of a vanilla cake batter with grated lemon zest, a Lemon Vanilla sponge cake with a soft lemon glaze that is not too sweet, without being too edible, cloying, or unbearable. To be clear, despite there being a hefty dose of vanilla and sweetish resins, Ani never approaches the territory occupied by other gourmands such as Baccarat Rouge 540 Eau de Parfum or Bianco Latte , which have been very popular lately. The opening is so praiseworthy that I would never stop respraying it just to smell this accord. When the undeniable initial freshness calms down, the balsamic and mentholated hints of cardamom expand and, together with the tart blackcurrant, add a new nuance to the citrus and peppery accord. The cardamom is noticeable but balanced by the other heart notes. Maybe I should wear Ani many more times, but so far I can’t get any clear rose in the middle phase. That means don’t expect or think of Ani as a rosy, jammy, or dewy floral essence. Surely, other notes nicely blend with the subdued rose. There is a subtle sweetness here, balanced by the spicy and herbal notes that make it sophisticated yet approachable. The fragrance is warm without being overly sweet. It takes several hours to approach the dry-down, when Ani becomes powdery, creamy, spicy, smooth and comforting. The vanilla is smooth and not too sweet. The benzoin sap has a rich, intensely sweet, balsamic, vanilla-like aroma, with a subtle spicy nuance reminiscent of cinnamon. Although I have read many reviews declaring Ani as the best vanilla-based perfume, on my skin, the benzoin is more discernible. There is a sort of sawdust nuance that gradually emerges from the base, I bet courtesy of the cedarwood or the Iso E Super molecule, that slowly makes its presence felt as the fragrance evolves, catches my attention and makes it more enjoyable for me than a purely vanilla-focused essence. A touch of recognizable dirty patchouli, a little musky moss and some blond woods make the scent slightly masculine, earthy, and exciting. Despite the fresh, tart and sparkling opening, the aftermath is dense and bold, warm and sumptuous. There is a magical fusion in the base that brings you back to the primal instinct. Ani blends elements of citrus, spices, resins and woods into a fragrance that evolves over time. Although there are many aspects to Ani, it is mainly lemon cake and vanilla as the dominant note. So I see Ani as an evening option for events and dinners. But it can be an everyday scent if dosed correctly. It is perfect during the Christmas holidays when it is cold outside. So, any winter month, but in summer, because it could be unpleasant. This fragrance lasts for hours, with the base notes lingering on the skin for a long time without fading and leaves a beautiful and warm trail without being too overwhelming. It may not be for everyone, especially those who prefer strong and sweet vanilla. This is my experience with a bottle I have owned since December 2024. -Elysium

This is such a lovely, sweet and soft fragrance that has the freshness and spice to make it versatile enough for almost any season and occasion. At first spray, it's undeniably fresh with the bergamot, ginger, and green notes. The vanilla is also noticeable from the start and, with the bergamot, has an almost key lime pie-like scent. The vanilla is very smooth and creamy, and not sickeningly sweet. It remains green and sweet for the first few hours with the spices warming it up a bit. The bergamot begins to fade after about three hours when the rose and blackcurrant emerge and the vanilla becomes slightly powdery. At five hours into the wear, it becomes briefly aromatic when the sandalwood comes out. In the next hour, when the musk and patchouli make their appearance, that aromatic quality becomes less pungent and it returns to a silky, slightly herbaceous vanilla. This lasted for well over ten hours on my skin. Overall, this is a beautiful extrait that is quite multi-faceted and wonderfully balanced. The vanilla is definitely present throughout the entirety of the wear, but it refrains from becoming cloying with the help of the bergamot, spices and woods. P.S.: for the Ultimate Vanilla Combo, it layers beautifully with Orchidée Vanille by Van Cleef & Arpels.

From the moment you open the pack box the smell is all over the room. This perfume is a masterpiece and it automatically made me fall in love with NiShane as a brand. The perfume is a full statement without uttering a word. If you wear this perfume without a compliment then the people around you do not deserve a great smell you are oozing out. . For me it’s a total 100 over 100.

This is the first Nishane fragrance that I ever smelled and it is the one that got me interested in this house. As soon as you spray it on, you get blasted with a mouth watering citrus, combined with a fizzy spicy ginger. You can already sense the vanilla hiding under everything.

This is my first Nishane, very happy with the sweet choice. The beautiful sweet creamy vanilla is outstanding and long lasting. With a hint of orange in the background, my partner said it’s like an melted orange creamsicle. I love to wear it all year round. Very unisex, very warm, holiday vibe type. The quality and performance of Nishane is trustworthy.

One of Nishane's more popular releases in the last few years is Ani, created by Cecile Zarokian. Vanilla lovers might have been aware of the hype around this one. Here is my review and as always, thank you for watching and hope you enjoy.

Okay I hardly every leave reviews here BUT omg Ani is so worth the hype. I thought I was crazy since lemon isn’t listed in the notes yet on my skin is smells like the sweetest creamiest lemon pastry with this warm little bit of spice and black currant.. it’s addictive! And apparently others in these reviews get the lemon like note as well so I’m not completely nuts lol.

- The perfumer (Cécile Zarokian) had classified her perfume (Ani) as (daring to wear) surprisingly almost all perfume lovers around the world, as I do, didn’t agree with her classification at all, defiantly this masterpiece is so lovely and easy to wear, as if perfume (Ani) rebelled against (Cécile Zarokian) the perfumer who made it.

While I love a complex perfume with many layers and twists, when the temperature climbs over 33-35C with 80% humidity and the sun mercilessly beats down on you (aka Japanese summer), I don't want or need all that. During summer, give me a fresh green scent that doesn't need constant reapplication, a scent that's cool and comforting and can carry me through the day. Wūlóng Chá Extrait de Parfum checks all those boxes and has been part of my daily summer rotation for a few good years now. It's been accused of being too simple, of lacking development, of smelling like a spa scent. true. I still get a lot of pleasure from wearing it. Imagine a Japanese commuter train at rush hour with everyone smelling rancid in their suits and now loads of funky tattooed tourists cramming you in with their own BO: in that hell of hells, this perfume is my little oasis of freshness and escape. Nothing else performs like it to last and project well enough that at least within my own personal space the stench of others doesn't intrude. The bergamot with oolong is always there. I don't get much fig. Sometimes simplicity is best.

Over the course of my testing process, Wūlóng Chá Extrait de Parfum has steadily grown on me, first striking me as too simple and unassuming. And frankly, it is pretty simple and easy-going, but that only fuels my liking towards it now. The opening is a delightful burst of citruses, with the orange dominating and the mandarin orange adding a slightly sweeter undertone. The Litsea cubeba adds this intensely clean herbaceous edge, with a faint lemon-like aroma and floral lightness. Like a refreshing squeeze of lemon into your cup of tea from grandma. And speaking of tea, that's the star of the show here. As the citruses start diminishing their presence, the oolong tea warms things up with a soothing, complex mix of florals, reminding me of orchids, jasmines, and even a peachy sweetness hidden somewhere. It mimics the scent of tea as a whole remarkably, with the remaining citruses from the start reminding you that tea shouldn't be sweetened with sugar, but enriched with some sourness. Then there's the nutmeg, trying its best to shine through, but ultimately settling with adding just a warm and mild spiciness beneath it all. It's there for sure, but it sticks closer to the bottom of the tea-filled cup. The base of most Nishanes I have tested so far were particularly lacking, both in presence and development. But I'm happy to report that Wūlóng Chá Extrait de Parfum brings my hopes back up. The combination of the fig's distinct sweet (but not too sweet) fruitiness, and the warm, clean, and slightly powdery musk work beautifully in creating a comforting base. They extend the soothing and warm sensation of the oolong tea and nutmeg long after they're gone. Frankly, the tea vibe disappears roughly around the one hour mark, leaving you with the musk/fig combo. Overall, great quality and blending, although quite a simple development throughout the wearing process. Now, how long do you get to enjoy this warm cup of tea before it gets cold? Well, coming as a surprise, I got about 7-8 hours of longevity on my skin, exceeding my expectations by a significant margin. Unfortunately, projection is nowhere near as good, with somewhere about one and a half to two feet of projection for the first 30 minutes, then settling closer to a steady one foot projection for an hour more. After that, it gets more intimate (skin scent). Anyone, anywhere, anytime - that's what I would say about versatility. It's actually one of the most versatile scents that I've encountered. It's fresh and citrusy to fit daily usage, but it's also distinct enough to work at certain events. And if you're one of the more unlucky users that don't get outstanding projection/sillage (like me), then you're safe to add a generous amount of sprays. Although I don't have much experience regarding tea-like fragrances, I believe that Wūlóng Chá Extrait de Parfum is hard to top. It's simple, yet different. It's soothing and calming. And it's one of the most enjoyable scents out there, purely because anyone can enjoy it. Now, does all of that justify its price tag of $200-$300? Hardly. But it's definitely worth giving a try, and I'm betting you'll find it a hard scent to hate. Overall Rating: 6.1/10

This was a blind buy as I couldn't find Nishane perfumes to test and I am usually easily satisfied by tea scents so I said why not. The first few sprays were not pleasant. I sprayed this on myself and on my boyfriend. Two days later I was carrying the laundry basket and got an accidental whiff. It got so much better and became so soft and clean. It has become one of the bottles with the biggest dents in my collection ever since. I love Wulong Cha.

Nishane wulong cha was one of the first scents i tried when learning more about niche perfumes. When i first smelled it i found it quite wierd because i hadnt really smelt tea before in perfumes and it smelled like grass? But i did try it again later and decided to wear it and that was the right choice for sure! In the wear i felt the amazing note of oolong tea change and also the different citrus notes coming through. Wulong cha is now one of my favorite tea scent and im glad i decided to retry it! Longevity is sadly not great as i get around 6-8 hours with it but it is okay as the scent is quite light.

By no means a sophisticated fragrance, however, it is a significant cut above the sea of anemic "blue" fragrances. It's the quintessential summer scent, as you'll stand out from the rest of the crowd. Wearing this indicates taste for the art of perfumery. Ingredients are well blended, and it is of very high quality. This is the fragrance you'd wear when you're looking for something more relaxing, cooling, and uplifting; Wulong Cha is worn for yourself, more so than for others. That said, it remains incredibly easy to wear. It opens with a complex concoction of citruses, which then divulges into a musky, tea accord, with an added pinch of sweetness from the fig note. Performance is exceptional for a fragrance with citruses; expect about 8 hours of longevity, and projection that sits closer to you. This is what you'd go to for the summer/spring months, for any occasion. I have worn this in the colder months of the winter; can see how this may counteract any seasonal disorders by enveloping you in a scent sphere of Zen, a longing for the warmer months to come.

This is a great extrait but not exactly what I was hoping for. At first spray, it's bright, orange citrus and slightly floral. The orange notes paired with the bergamot and litsea cubeba really just make the opening a citrus powerhouse with a vague, yellow floral undertone.

I've been reading so much hype about this fragrance, I just had to see what it was all about. I have to say, from the first blast, I was bracing myself for utter disappointment. At first it was a sharp herbal almost pine smelling parsley mixed with lemon that reminded me of Pinesol or some other strong cleaning product.

This is not a zesty fragrance. It's not zingy. It's not in-your-face (or anybody else's for that matter). It's not a "blast" of anything, and it's not a "bomb". What it IS, though, is a mellow, calming, and sophisticated experience that will stay cool and collected, all day long. The vibes, as the kids might say, are immaculate.

This is the third Nishane fragrance I have tried and even though I loved both Hacivat and Ani, Wulong Cha impressed me the most. This is definitely a summer fragrance, which I enjoy wearing during the daytime when it's really hot and humid. It really makes you feel as if you have turned into a dragon-like creature of sorts, taken straight out of the Chinese mythology.

Gorgeous warm weather fragrance! Very citrusy and incredibly refreshing tea scent. Even though the scent isn’t unique it definitely performs well for a fresh citrusy scent. It reminds me of Chanel Cristalle Eau Verte, maybe because of the bergamot, lemon, and musk notes.

I love this! It was tea leaves in a bottle. Specifically, mint leaves that are still on the stem. At first, it was just the tea leaves, then the wood note will start to appear. It was beautiful. I'm still considering buying the full bottle since I prioritized Midnight. But I might just buy wulong cha instead. Still, this was my 2nd place in their discovery set.

I'm not a fan of the now hyped niche brands and the rise of arabic brands, but Im not against their existence. People that like beast mode scents, have plenty of choices nowadays. I'm more into dynamic French compositions with aromatics, woods and spices. Creed is a brand that i really like due to their great rounded and well blended scents, but their prices are crazy for me. I dont play those prices for a fragrance, no matter how good they are. But that's just my perspective. Nishane is an example of a brand that have powerful blends but with a row finish. Fan your flames is a beast mode coconut with tobacco that i dont care. I sold my bottle cause its very static and pushy. Not my thing. This one, surprised me in a way. There's an obvious resemblance to Aventus but different enough to be a stand alone composition. Aventus is dynamic, super fresh, well blended, with a smoky birch note, a great bergamot, a addictive blackcurrant and a soft aura overall. This is just straight to pineapple juice with a high dose of moss in the background. Yes, it has bergamot too. The grapefruit give that bitter quality and there's patchouli and cedar in the middle, which round things up. But the moss and pineapple are so strong that the other notes have a minor role here. The smell is static and dont change during the lifetime of the fragrance. And talking about longevity, this is beast mode. 5 sprays are enough to smell like pineapple and green moss for 12+ hours. I usually overspray fragrances but this one, with 8-10 sprays, it's super strong and headache inducing. Overall, Aventus is miles better that this in terms of composition, but in longevity and price point, this is much better. The smell is likeable, dont get me wrong. And in fact, is probably the best from the brand, but its a bit synthetic and not rounded enough, specially in the first 2h, where the fragrance hás a strong projection.
